# Patrologia Latina, volume 55 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 55

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, comprehensive, convenient, economical, and universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition produced during the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with numerous manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with doubtful and apocryphal works, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture and in what places of their works they did so.

This is the most accurate edition and one easily preferable to all others, if one considers the neatness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price. Above all, this collection is single, systematic, and chronological: it brings together, for the first time in our library, six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [First Part of Volume Two of Leo the Great]

## [Col. 0009]

# Preface

### 1

The Book of the Sacraments that we present first, without any doubt the oldest of all, was attributed to Leo the Great and printed in 1735 by Father Joseph Blanchinus in the fourth volume of Anastasius the Librarian, with the following title:

> An ancient book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church, composed by Saint Leo the pope, now published for the first time from a manuscript written more than a thousand years ago, which is preserved in the library of the distinguished chapter of Verona.

The codex is not complete but mutilated: many leaves have fallen away at the beginning, namely from January through the middle of April. Consequently, the title by which Saint Leo the pope is presented as the author or compiler of this Sacramentary was not taken from the manuscript but was added on the editor’s judgment.

This opinion has been approved by not a few scholars. Among them we especially mention Cajetanus Cennius, in his dissertation on the Roman See, inserted in volume four of Anastasius the Librarian, sections 11 and 12, p. 152; and the editors of the Paris Missal of 1739. While commending this same Sacramentary with an outstanding encomium, they profess that from it they took many prayers breathing an exceptional piety and reflecting the style and doctrine of Leo the Great, to whom they attribute it as its certain author.

### 2

Others, however, adopted different opinions. Father Joseph Augustine Orsi of the Order of Preachers, celebrated for many reasons, expressed his view in a manuscript letter at the request of the same Blanchinus. There he maintains that this Sacramentary is the true and uncorrupted Gelasian Sacramentary, so that the work published by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius and attributed to Gelasius belongs to an author later than that pontiff.

The same opinion was defended by Father Cajetanus Maria Meratus, a Cleric Regular, in his observations and additions to Bartholomew Gavanti’s *Treasury of Sacred Rites*, vol. I, part I, p. 8.

Father Eusebius Amort, a Regular Canon of Polling, in a manuscript letter to Father Blanchinus, did not believe Gelasius to be the author of this Sacramentary. Yet he did not attribute it entirely to Leo either. He says:

> It is not the work of any one pontiff, but is the Sacramentary of the Roman pontiffs, received in use in the earliest times, though enlarged and interpolated by various pontiffs down to the time of Pope Gelasius. In particular, the hands of Sixtus III, Leo I, and Felix III are recognized in this Sacramentary.

Ludovico Muratori, in his dissertation on the origin of the sacred liturgy prefixed to the work entitled *The Ancient Roman Liturgy*, chapter 3, thinks that this Sacramentary should be assigned to the time of Felix III. Yet he does not believe Felix III himself to have been its author, but rather some other person who gathered into one codex all the prayers and prefaces he found, without the careful selection and arrangement demanded by the importance of the matter.

After these, Count Jacobus Acamius undertook the defense of Blanchinus’s opinion in a more extensive work written in Italian and printed at Rome in 1748, entitled:

> On the antiquity, author, and merits of the Veronese Sacramentary published by the Most Reverend Father Giuseppe Bianchini of the Congregation of the Oratory in volume IV of Anastasius the Librarian: a three-part apologetic dissertation.

Finally, Father Antonius Franciscus Vezosius, a Cleric Regular, in his preface to volume VI of the works of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius—since his sole concern there is to defend the Sacramentary published by that cardinal—refutes only the opinion that assigns to Gelasius the Sacramentary published by Blanchinus. Although he did not think it useful to investigate its author more precisely, he nevertheless declares in note 2 to the same preface that those who assert its authorship for Leo have not entirely satisfied the difficulties.

Thus far we have set forth the various opinions. What, however, seems certain or more probable to us amid so much diversity we shall now explain.

### 3

First, we consider it certain that this Sacramentary is Roman and the oldest of all those that have so far been published. That it is Roman—that is, that it contains the proper Masses of the Roman Church—is proved, among many other things, by the very formulas of the prayers, which assert that the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saints John and Paul were buried in the City itself; by the Masses for the consecration or burial of Roman pontiffs, one of which is expressly for the burial of Saint Sylvester, together with another prayer for the burial of Saint Simplicius;

[Note: [Col. 0009] See the last Mass of October.]

by the announcements of fasts together with Saturday vigils at Blessed Peter’s; and by the mention of cemeteries and places in the city of Rome where sacred rites were celebrated,

[Note: [Col. 0009] See the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, letter 25, chapter 1, in volume XX of the *Patrologia*.]

all of which correspond exactly with those described in the Bucherian Calendar, which everyone agrees is Roman.

That it is the oldest of all is demonstrated by comparison with the Gelasian Sacramentary, which, as it has been published, received several additions from a later period. In our Sacramentary, however, nothing is encountered that goes beyond the fifth century. Consequently, it does not incur any of the objections that heterodox writers have improperly brought against the Gelasian Sacramentary in order to diminish its antiquity.

Whether this work, rather than the one published by Cardinal Thomasius, is the true Sacramentary of Gelasius, we shall discuss later.

### 4

It is likewise certain that this Sacramentary contains many things by different authors. Yet quite a few passages display the style and spirit of Leo the Great so strongly that it is highly probable that they were composed by this holy pontiff.

That there was not one author of all the prayers and prefaces is shown, apart from the evident difference in style—more restrained in some passages and more elevated in others—also by the number of Masses assigned to certain solemnities, as is clear:

[Col. 0011]

for it is not credible that so many Masses and prayers, so different from one another, for one and the same feast were composed by a single writer.

Yet everyone, even though they have adopted various opinions concerning the author of this collection, unanimously acknowledges that very many of its contents bear the mark of Leo’s manner of writing.

Quesnellus perceived that certain Leonine passages survive in the *Pontifical* and *Roman Missal*, passages known to have been derived from our Sacramentary. We insert here the notice prefixed by him to three documents excerpted from it and published after the sermons, since it remarkably establishes the point we have proposed:

> Anyone who reads the *Pontifical* and *Roman Missal* somewhat attentively will readily detect that very many passages inserted in them are thoroughly redolent of Leonine phrasing and diction. Thus I have no doubt that a large part of what is either recited in ecclesiastical offices, especially on the ancient solemnities—Easter and Pentecost, for example—or used in the celebration of the sacred orders, was composed or restored by the most holy pontiff Leo I.
>
> Among these, it seems to me, must be counted the Prefaces placed before the Canon of the Mass, as well as two others found in the *Roman Pontifical*: one at the consecration of a bishop and the other at the ordination of a priest. We have thought it appropriate to insert both of them here, together with a certain address of the archdeacon to the bishop, found in the same *Pontifical*, concerning the reconciliation of penitents.
>
> The style itself cries out that these should be attributed to Leo. For the second Preface we have as an advocate Henry Valesius, celebrated for his exceptional learning. In his notes on Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*, when he cites part of this Preface from an ancient Pontifical of the Church of Sens, he assigns it to our Leo. In fact, Leo is no more like Leo than the style of this Preface resembles the style of the other works of our pontiff.
>
> What he generally asserts about the Prefaces placed before the Canon is too sweeping: we could prove that some cannot be attributed to Leo. But concerning the three documents selected by him, we readily agree. Two of them are read in our Sacramentary; we have no doubt that the third was inserted in the portion that has perished.

After Quesnellus, Cardinal Thomasius, speaking of the Gelasian Sacramentary, into which several passages from ours were transferred, believed Leo to be the author of so many prayers that he did not hesitate to write in his preface:

> That Saint Leo the Great applied his hand to this distinguished work among other holy bishops is plainly shown by his very style, which immediately reveals itself to anyone even slightly acquainted with his writings.

If the cardinal, otherwise most cautious in forming judgments, pronounced this on the basis of certain prayers and addresses that appear to be Leonine and that were received into the Gelasian Sacramentary, what should we think of the far greater number that breathe Leo no less, or even more clearly, and that repeatedly occur in our older Sacramentary?

Although it cannot be asserted with certainty that everything that appears to bear Leo’s diction belongs to Leo, it is nevertheless highly probable that much of it was composed by him. Muratori noted some of these passages in the dissertation mentioned above, while Acamius listed many more at greater length. We shall identify the principal examples in the annotations.

### 5

That Saint Gelasius the pope was not the author of this Sacramentary comes very close to certainty. Acamius’s argument from the decree of that pontiff concerning apocryphal Scriptures appears decisive.

We take it as certain that this decree was issued by Gelasius, as we shall confirm at greater length in volume three. In this decree, however, the heretics are said to hold the opinion that the holy apostles Peter and Paul suffered death at different times:

> He [Paul], he says, was crowned with a glorious death while struggling together with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero, not at different times, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on one and the same day.

Yet our Sacramentary, in the Preface for the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, numbered 26, presents their deaths as assigned to the same day but to different times:

> Thus, gathering the one family of Christ by a different dispensation, although at different times, the one recurring day and the one crown joined them forever.

This opinion, so plainly rejected by Gelasius, excludes our Sacramentary from his authorship. For if he himself had compiled the work before the decree mentioned above, he would not have attributed to the heretics an opinion that he had previously received into his own Sacramentary. If, on the other hand, he had worked on this Sacramentary after issuing the decree, he would not have inserted an opinion that he had condemned with so severe a censure in his decree.

For other arguments, see the aforementioned Acamius and Father Vezosius. This one argument seems sufficiently invincible to us, since the conjectures brought forward by others and adequately refuted by those same authors do not weaken it.

### 6

It is not certain that this Sacramentary was composed by our Leo. Acamius brings forward five substantial reasons for assigning the work to Leo:

1. In many prayers and prefaces, its style and ideas correspond with those of other works certainly written by Leo.

2. The heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches are attacked, and the same pontiff opposed them.

3. The Manichaeans are discussed as having been brought back to sound understanding or driven from Rome, as occurred under Leo.

4. The errors of the Pelagians concerning original sin and the necessity of divine grace are refuted—errors against which the holy pontiff wrote.

5. The incursions of the Huns, the Vandal invasion, the devastation of the City, and other events that occurred during Leo’s pontificate are indicated.

For the moment we omit the fact that some of these matters may be referred to the time of other pontiffs. Even if all these points are thought to fit Leo, they prove only that this pontiff was the author of those prayers and prefaces in which such matters are mentioned.

Whether the same pontiff, apart from composing these pieces, collected and arranged the entire Sacramentary cannot be certainly concluded from these arguments. Another may have been the author or compiler of the Sacramentary, inserting such Leonine prayers and prefaces among the others.

Thus many Leonine passages are also read as inserted in the Gelasian Sacramentary; but Leo cannot for that reason be called its author. It is one thing for Leo to be the author of many prayers that are written in a particular Sacramentary; it is another for him to be the author of the Sacramentary itself, in which prayers of several different pontiffs were collected and arranged.

[Col. 0013]

Moreover, some things are found in our Sacramentary that are later than Leo’s age, such as the prayer for Pope Simplicius, the successor of Leo and of Hilary, and the mention of the dedication of the basilica of Saint Stephen, which we shall discuss in its proper place as having been performed by that same Simplicius.

Add also the Mass for the vigil of Pentecost with a fast. This appears to show that the fast was unknown in Leo’s time. His fourth sermon, on the fast of Pentecost—that is, the Four Ember Days after Pentecost—seems to indicate this. There he teaches that, after the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost have been spent chiefly in the joy of the feast, one must return to the remedies of fasting; by this he plainly signifies that all those fifty days were free from fasting.

Nor should this be understood as some extraordinary fast proclaimed by Leo. Since such a fast would not bind a future period, this Mass would not have been inserted into a Sacramentary compiled for use in a later period. It would rather have to be said that Leo instituted this fast near the end of his pontificate, while the sermons that exclude it belong to earlier years.

Alternatively, it might be said that this Mass, like the prayer for Simplicius and the Mass for the dedication of the basilica of Saint Stephen, is a later addition that was added to Leo’s Sacramentary. But these replies would have some force if the fact that this Sacramentary belonged to Leo had first been established on other grounds. Similar solutions to similar objections have force in the Sacramentaries of Gelasius and Gregory the Great, whom we know from other evidence to have composed books of the Sacraments.

But since we have several ancient testimonies concerning Gelasius and Gregory, while concerning Leo there is not even a hint, this negative argument has some weight. Although such an argument is not usually considered very important when positive and sufficiently probable arguments are available, where arguments of that kind are lacking it has considerable force, at least to exclude the probable certainty now under discussion.

If the sermon on the Maccabees were Leo’s, we would have a certain positive argument by which this Sacramentary could be excluded from the authorship of that pontiff: the feast in question is not found there, although from that sermon it has hitherto been believed to have been celebrated at Rome in Leo’s time. But since we have discovered that this sermon was wrongly attributed to the holy pontiff and have therefore relegated it to the appendix, nothing can be inferred from it.

Two positive arguments, however, which in our judgment are sufficiently compelling, will soon be brought forward. They exclude not so much Leo as any other Roman pontiff from authorship of the Sacramentary itself.

### 7

It seems more probable to us that this Sacramentary was not compiled by any Roman pontiff, at least with public authority for the use of the Roman Church, but was the product of some private individual who collected, in an unsuitable order, whatever prayers and prefaces he found to have been written at different times by Roman pontiffs, especially by Saint Leo, and entered them into a codex that was not intended for public use.

Two considerations move us to this conclusion. The first is the decree of Gelasius mentioned above. If this Sacramentary had been collected by Leo or another pontiff and received in the Roman Church with public authority, how could Gelasius have charged the heretics with holding the opinion that the apostles Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom at different times—a view that he could not have failed to know had been inserted into that very Sacramentary by Leo or by another predecessor closer to him and received in the Roman Church down to his own time?

If, on the other hand, the author was some private person after Leo or during the time of Gelasius, so that this Sacramentary was not in use in the Roman Church, there is no difficulty. Although the Mass inserted in it that contains the opinion in question may once have come from some older pontiff, it could nevertheless have been unknown to Gelasius, just as he was unaware that Prudentius and other Catholic writers had followed that opinion, so that it would not have had to be charged to the heretics.

### 8

The second consideration is clearer still. A great mass of prayers and Masses, extremely disordered and defective in many places, may well belong to a private individual who collected by his own diligence whatever he found. But it is wholly incredible that it should belong to a supreme pontiff who, with public authority, compiled a book of the Sacraments for the use of solemn prayers and offered it for preservation.

Even if the Masses collected in this codex are by many authors and therefore exhibit different styles and different characteristics, nevertheless, if there had been a single compiler—especially if he had been some supreme pontiff who entered various Masses into a codex so that they might serve the public use of prayers on solemn days—he would first have described, month by month, the Masses of the saints who were celebrated with solemn feasts in the Roman Church.

Then in every Mass he would have placed at least three prayers and one Preface. Wherever he placed common Masses, he would have grouped them together rather than interspersing them among different Masses.

For the purpose of such books, when they are issued for public use, is that the proper Masses to be said on each month and feast day should readily be found in their proper place, complete with their prayers and prefaces, while the common Masses should be found together and capable of being repeated from a definite location.

Imagine any compiler, even one of little expertise, who intends to prepare a Sacramentary for public use. He would certainly understand that this order and method had to be observed and followed above all.

Indeed, the Sacramentaries arranged by the holy pontiffs Gelasius and Gregory for the use of the Roman Church display this order and method; the same is true of others that served other Churches.

In our Sacramentary, however, you will look in vain for the Masses of very many saints who were formerly celebrated in the Roman Church on a fixed feast, as is clear from Bucherius’s catalogue. The feasts of some are noted in the titles, but their Masses are omitted, as may be seen in July and December.

In quite a few Masses the most necessary prayers are absent—for example, the Secret or the Postcommunion, and sometimes both, or even the first prayer. In others, two or three prefaces are joined together without the Postcommunion prayers, or even without any prayer at all.

The common Masses of martyrs are scattered across three months: April, July, and August. In April, where several Collects are found, the prayer of Saint Tiburtius—whose feast belongs to August—is placed before the common Masses of several martyrs at number 6. Two Masses of confessors are inserted at numbers 9 and 10; at number 20 there is a Secret prayer for Saint Lawrence and a common Mass for the conversion of sinners; at number 29 there is a common Mass of the apostles; and at number 34 a Mass for the dedication of Saint Peter’s basilica.

What should we say about the other defects, which are wholly incompatible with a public book?

In May, in the Mass of Pentecost, the prayer *Hanc igitur oblationem*—“Therefore this offering”—is improperly placed before the prayer *Communicantes*. Among the Masses for the fast of the fourth month, two Masses for Pentecost Sunday are inserted, although they ought to have been placed earlier. Conversely, in November, two Masses for the feast of the same apostle precede the Mass for the vigil of Saint Andrew; and in December, four Masses for Christmas Day precede the Mass for the vigil of the Nativity of Christ, numbered 5, although they ought to have followed it.

No disorder is more evident than that of August and September.

On the fourth day before the Nones of August, the feast of Saint Stephen in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way is listed. Masses for Saint Stephen the protomartyr follow. Yet the Preface of the seventh Mass itself declares that his natal day was celebrated at Rome not on the fourth day before the Nones of this month but on 26 December, after the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity:

> And therefore, by the festival of his passion, [Stephen] rightly follows before all others the Nativity of your Son.

If the dedication of the basilica of Saint Stephen perhaps fell on the fourth day before the Nones, as is discussed in Mass 9, then the title “Feast of Saint Stephen” was incorrectly written there, since that expression designates the day of his death. It was also incorrect that the Masses for his feast day, which should have been placed in December, were described here in first position. See the annotation appended to the aforementioned title.

There are also two Masses for the vigil of Saint Lawrence. One, numbered 1, is placed before his feast, while the other, numbered 12, follows it. The proper Masses of this month for Saints Felix and Adauctus are followed by other common Masses of several martyrs, and the seventh contains a Preface for the apostles.

In September, on the fourteenth day, a Preface for Saint Euphemia is inserted among the Masses for Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, although two Masses for her are subsequently described in their proper place on the sixteenth.

In the same month, which belongs to the notice of the fast of the seventh month, not only is an Invitation of the people for the fast of the tenth month found at number 8, but several Masses proper to that fast and month are also presented, while others are later placed in their proper location in December.

We are not greatly troubled by the common Masses of the Nativity of bishops assigned to December, among which one Mass is inserted at number 7 with the prayer for the consecration of a bishop performed at Easter time. Likewise, in October, among the common prayers for various needs, a prayer proper to Easter time is read at number 3, and at number 6 a Preface and prayer for the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.

I say that these matters do not greatly trouble us. They should be referred not to the month but to the common Masses under their respective titles. In these, all the Masses and prayers belonging to the same title may properly have a place, even if they are to be recited during Easter time, since some such office may fall within the Easter season.

What troubles us more is that the titles prefixed to the Masses sometimes correspond only to the first prayer and not to the other prayers or Masses that follow, even though they bear the inscription “Likewise another,” as though all belonged to the same title.

See, in July, near the beginning, the title “During the fast”; in September, number 8, the title “To be offered for a bishop”; and in October, the Mass entitled “For dryness.”

Among the Masses for the dead described in October is a Mass of Saint Sylvester whose third prayer is for Pope Simplicius. Here two Masses appear to have been confused into one.

We do not deny that one or another less serious defect may also be found in other ancient Sacramentaries, and that something may be attributed more readily to a copyist’s carelessness than to the author. But who would assign to a Sacramentary that had been compiled by some supreme pontiff and issued with public authority for the daily use of the Roman Church so many and such serious defects, and such manifest disorder throughout the entire Sacramentary, all of which can be attributed to a single compiler?

Indeed, this collection’s imperfection and confusion reveal not only the work of a private individual but also the character of the original hand. Collecting by private decision whatever he found, that hand showed little concern for order and none for public use. Yet even he, if he had wished to publish the work for public use, would undoubtedly have revised it a second time and restored it at least to a more suitable order.

### 9

From this disordered arrangement, especially from the insertion of certain Masses in inappropriate places and from the assignment of common Masses—which are not inherently attached to any month—to one month or another, we draw the important conclusion that it cannot properly be inferred that a relatively obscure feast was celebrated in the month in which its Mass is described.

Thus, from the Mass for the dedication of Saint Peter’s basilica, listed among the common Masses in April, it would be unsafe to infer that some feast of Saint Peter or the dedication of his basilica was celebrated in that month. Likewise, it would be entirely wrong to say that the feast of Saint Stephen was celebrated in August merely because the Masses for that feast are presented in that month.

The same must be said of the Mass for a day of fasting that is noted in July under the feast of some martyr. This is a common Mass, to be used on a day when a fast coincides with the feast of a martyr.

Something similar applies to the Masses or prayers described in April that contain the name of Saint Tiburtius or Saint Gregory the Martyr. These are not Masses proper to that month but common Masses of martyrs collected there in that month.

### 10

This very notable confusion of Masses and prayers plainly reveals the original character of the Roman Sacramentary as represented in our codex.

If some older Sacramentary received into the use of the Roman Church had been before the compiler’s eyes, he would certainly have avoided at least many of these defects by following its order and method.

Thus the disorder that seems to detract somewhat from this collection returns as a considerable recommendation of it, because it demonstrates its antiquity.

It follows that the first Sacramentary proposed for the public use of the Roman Church was the Gelasian Sacramentary, which certainly displays a very proper order. Our Sacramentary, on the other hand, is indeed earlier, but is a private collection that was not intended for public use.

And if the name of Pope Simplicius did not enter the previously mentioned Mass in place of Sylvester through the error of a later copyist, this collection was compiled after Pope Simplicius, under Felix III or at the beginning of the pontificate of Gelasius. For the later addition that some have suspected in this Mass is the sort of addition normally received only by public Sacramentaries when they are subsequently copied for the use of the Churches.

### 11

Nor should this codex be valued less because it was arranged by a private individual without an elaborate order and was not used in the Roman Church; nor can it for that reason not be called the Sacramentary of that Church.

It is the Sacramentary of the Roman Church because it gathers into one body the liturgical documents of that Church which were used at different times before Gelasius. It is all the more valuable than others because it has preserved for us a greater number of older monuments useful for learning about the ancient discipline and confirming the Catholic faith—monuments that one would seek in vain in other Sacramentaries.

This has had to be set forth at length in advance in order to establish the author and date of our Sacramentary. From it we have also sufficiently recognized its excellence.

### 12.

Now, in order to shed some light on the more ancient Roman liturgy, we believe that certain things can be gathered from our codex. If this was the first private collection of the Roman Sacramentary, as we saw earlier, it becomes clear that no public Sacramentary existed in the fifth century—one, that is, which presented the Masses of the Roman Church for the whole year and for all its feasts, arranged and collected in a definite order. Certainly no one will prove the contrary, nor has anyone thus far found anything earlier than the Gelasian Sacramentary that was clearly published for public use.

From several very ancient Fathers we have learned only that the Canon, along with certain more solemn prayers, particular formulas of prayer, and a certain order of prayers—namely, at the beginning of the Mass, before the Canon, and after Communion—had been introduced and received even in the earliest times. But who could prove that these or those prayers and Prefaces were assigned to each feast, as they are read in Gelasius?

It is indeed clear from our codex that, before Gelasius, certain proper Masses for particular feasts celebrated with greater solemnity in the Roman Church had already been composed. But that these very Masses had not been collected and arranged in a single book is clearly shown, for example, by the Mass of Saint Stephen. For if these Masses had previously been entered into a codex for the public use of the liturgy, the same compiler would certainly have copied them from that public and more accessible codex under the month of December, in which Saint Stephen’s feast was celebrated.

Our compiler therefore found them loose and separate; and consequently it is not surprising that, amid such confusion among numerous Masses, he was not always able to preserve a strict order in his initial efforts. Perhaps he also took them from various archives and attempted to bring together in one codex not only complete Masses but also whatever parts he found, thus striving to assemble the first exemplar of the Sacramentary.

This explains why he supplied several incomplete Masses—that is, either Prefaces alone without prayers, or prayers without a Preface, or only a single prayer, and so forth. Complete Masses were not always newly composed; sometimes only Prefaces or prayers were composed. Although there is no doubt that, when the Mass was celebrated, other necessary parts were added from the common prayers or from prayers already in use, the separate manuscript copy of these items was nevertheless found apart from the others.

This also explains why some prayers or Prefaces are repeated in our codex: when a new prayer or Preface was occasionally added to complete a whole Mass, the remaining portions were taken from the common or previously used material, and our careful scribe consequently found and repeated them.

### 13.

Since we find no proper Masses in this Sacramentary for the Sundays after Easter, after Pentecost, or during Advent, it is quite probable that the order of Sunday Masses found in later Sacramentaries had not yet been established.

In this regard we have observed especially that, in the time of our Sacramentary, the prayers and petitions used on the Sundays after Pentecost were taken from the common prayers for the sacrifice of the Mass, or from prayers for various causes and needs, according as each person preferred. Some of these Collects appear in the third book of the Gelasian Sacramentary under the title “For Sundays,” so that the Masses of Sundays lacking a proper Mass were to be taken from them.

Finally, in the Gregorian Sacramentary each Sunday is read as having its own proper Mass assigned to it. We are nevertheless somewhat uncertain whether this should be attributed to Gregory or whether it was added to his Sacramentary later. For if Saint Gregory had been the author of this institution and method, the same prayers and Prefaces would be found in all his codices for every Sunday after Pentecost. Yet the prayers of several Sundays differ in the different manuscripts of Muratori and Menard, as they also do in the Roman Missal.

We have indicated several examples in the annotations to our Sacramentary. Compare especially Mass XXXIII among the common Masses for the month of July. Its first prayer is read in Book III, no. 9, of the Gelasian Sacramentary “For Sundays”; but in Muratori’s Gregorian books it occurs for the Fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost, in Menard for the Fifteenth Sunday, and in the Roman Missal for the Thirteenth Sunday. From other examples as well we have recognized that this difference in numbering is consistent.

As for Masses of the saints, the proper Masses of only a few martyrs are read in our codex. For the others, common Masses were used. Hence several common Masses for martyrs occur in our Sacramentary in which two or three otherwise common prayers bear the proper name of a martyr—for example, Agapitus, Gregory, and so forth.

Among the very many Masses for martyrs, very few are read for ordinary confessors, since martyrs were more numerous and better known during the time of persecution. There are no proper Masses for the apostles except those of Saints Peter and Paul, Saint Andrew, and Saint John the Evangelist.

Since, however, a Mass for all the apostles is found within the octave of Saints Peter and Paul, whether the particular feasts of the other apostles were not celebrated at Rome at this period, but a common commemoration of them was made on that day, or whether the Mass for each one’s feast was taken from the common Masses, is left to the judgment of others.

### 14.

From our Sacramentary we also learn how ancient is the origin of most of the prayers, and of several Prefaces, which are contained not only in the Gelasian and Gregorian codices but also in the Roman Missal. We shall indicate these in the annotations.

When the individual texts are compared, it will become apparent how far certain prayers underwent minor changes of wording, and how, sometimes, several Prefaces in one Sacramentary were combined into certain Prefaces of the Missal by extracting and joining together sentences and words from one place and another.

We offer here one example concerning the Prefaces. The Preface of the Ascension of the Lord, which is the same in the Roman Missal and the Gregorian Sacramentary, was assembled from fragments of two Prefaces in our Sacramentary. The words, “Who, after his resurrection, appeared openly to all his disciples, and, while they watched, was raised into heaven,” are found in the first Preface of our codex; but the words, “that he might grant us to be partakers of his divinity,” are read in the second.

We give another example concerning prayers and the slightest changes of wording. That prayer of the Roman Missal for the Saturday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent, which begins “Your protection over us,” occurs in our Sacramentary in September among the common prayers, § 39, no. 12. There the words “may make us peaceful through the completion of his works,” or, as in the Gregorian codices, “pleasing,” were changed in the said Missal to: “May they make us pleasing to you through the completion of his work.” We leave other similar examples to be compared elsewhere.

### 15.

Moreover, many things occur in this most excellent and most ancient Sacramentary that are useful for confirming Catholic dogmas against recent errors and for understanding the discipline of earlier times. Since these cannot be referred to later additions foreign to this codex, recent heretics will not be able to evade them by the argument with which they attempt to diminish the authority of other Sacramentaries.

If the testimonies of the ancient Fathers are highly esteemed, how highly ought we to esteem the testimony of this Sacramentary, which displays the doctrine and discipline—not of one or another holy Father, but of the chief and most ancient pontiffs and of the principal Church—set forth and expressed in public services?

On nearly every line testimonies will meet the eye concerning the divinity of Jesus Christ; some concerning his real presence in the Eucharist; many concerning the worship and invocation of the saints; concerning their glory, both of martyrs and confessors; concerning the worship of sacred relics; concerning the necessity and efficacy of grace; concerning original sin; concerning the usefulness of fasts; concerning the excellence of the vow of continence; concerning the blessing of marriages; concerning suffrages for the dead; concerning the great number of martyrs; concerning the eminence of bishops; concerning the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs; and concerning other doctrines of various kinds.

The antiquity of fasting together with a vigil before the feasts of the apostles may be gathered from the third Mass on the feast of Saint Andrew. Anyone can discover the rite of veiling the spouses in the blessing of marriage, the ancient use of milk and honey in baptism, the dedication of churches, the celebration of the sacrifice in the cemeteries of martyrs, and other features of more ancient discipline.

If the first gatherings of leaves of the codex, which contained the more solemn Masses of Epiphany, Lent, and Easter from January through the beginning of April, had not perished through the injuries of time, many more things could be found.

### 16.

It remains to say certain particular things about the manuscript itself. Two series of numbers are noted in it. Some numbers are written in the margin, while others are inserted into the text.

The numbers written in the margin continue in uninterrupted succession from the beginning of the Sacramentary to its end; they indicate the division of the entire work and the distinction of its principal chapters or titles. Because several leaves are missing, the first number is IX, at the beginning of May. Before it come several Masses inserted under April, which are known to belong to number VIII. The last number, which ends at the close of December, is XLIII.

Muratori omitted these numbers; we shall report them in the margin in their proper place, where they occur in the codex.

The other numbers, inserted into the text, generally indicate the number and division of the Masses under each title. The compiler was not always very exact, however, and sometimes forgot to distinguish two Masses, placing them under a single number.

Furthermore, variant readings are inserted into the text in many places, usually without any distinction; usually, I say, although sometimes the sign “variant otherwise” is prefixed. These various readings seem to have come from different copies of the same Mass that had fallen into the compiler’s hands. For they are often of such a kind that they cannot be attributed to the carelessness or discretion of copyists, but are recognized as deriving from those who, intending to repeat the same prayer or Preface in the sacred ministry, wished to alter something.

Finally, certain passages are very corrupt. Father Blanchini often proposed suitable conjectural emendations in his notes. Muratori frequently accepted these and inserted them into the text without indicating the reading of the codex. Indeed, he also accepted some of the emendations that Blanchini himself later revised in the leaves prefixed to the Sacramentary—leaves that escaped Muratori’s attention.

We shall always present the manuscript reading either in the text or in the annotations, except in a few places where an obvious scribal error is detected.

---

## THE MOST ANCIENT BOOK OF SACRAMENTS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, ATTRIBUTED IN THE VULGATE EDITIONS TO POPE SAINT LEO (C, S)

### 1. IN THE MONTH OF APRIL

[Col. 0021A]

[**Lacuna**] so that they may be pleasing to you for the festival of the holy martyrs, and may bring us the help of your favor. Through, etc.

### 2.

It is truly right. For a festive solemnity is celebrated for you; for you the consecrated day is observed, which the blood of your blessed [variant: holy] martyr Tiburtius, poured out in testimony to your truth, marked with the magnificent honor of your name. And therefore, with the angels, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0021B–C] This Preface is not proper to Saint Tiburtius, but is taken from the common Masses of the holy martyrs, among which it is read below at no. 38. It is copied again on the Ides of August for the feast-day of Saint Hippolytus, no. 1. In both places the plural number has been changed to the singular by inserting the martyr’s name. The birthday feast of Saints Tiburtius and Valerian is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May in the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory. Here it concerns Tiburtius alone, as likewise in the same Gregorian Sacramentary and in the Gelasian Sacramentary on the third day before the Ides of August. Hence Tiburtius, who is named here by our compiler alone, is different from the one venerated with Valerian in April; and his Preface was not inserted in this month because his feast belonged to April, but because several common Masses for martyrs were collected in this month, among which one Preface has Tiburtius’s name inserted. Similarly, a little later, at no. 20, another common Mass for several martyrs, likewise inserted in April, contains a prayer bearing the name of Saint Lawrence, whose feast nevertheless falls in the same month of August and for whom this Sacramentary itself provides several proper Masses. The words *beati*, “blessed,” and *sancti*, “holy,” one of which is superfluous, and other similar words frequently inserted into the text, seem to be variant readings which the compiler found in different copies of the same Mass, or transferred from the margin of one copy into the text.]

**It is truly right.**  
[Note: [Col. 0021C] Acamius thinks from this passage and from the following Masses that the feast of all martyrs was celebrated in April for several days and with an octave in the fifth century; and consequently he calls into question the testimony of Anastasius, as he is called, the Librarian, since Anastasius attributes the dedication of the ancient Pantheon as the church of Saint Mary ad Martyres—by which this feast is said to have been instituted—to Boniface IV.

But, apart from the fact that Paul the Deacon agrees with Anastasius in Book IV, chapter 37, and Book V, chapter 11, of his History of the Lombards, this dedication feast is assigned not to April but to May in all the liturgical books that preserve its memory. It is absent from the Gelasian Sacramentary, as it is also absent from some of the more reliable manuscripts of the Gregorian Sacramentary, because its institution was later. If it is present in other Gregorian manuscripts, it must be attributed to a later addition.

Moreover, since the Masses for martyrs in April in our codex are common Masses inserted at the compiler’s discretion, nothing in them suggests the institution of the feast of all the saints. These days are indeed said to have been celebrated as feasts on which confessors and martyrs obtained their palms; but the very commemoration of Saint Tiburtius, included in the preceding Preface, indicates that this formula is not proper to the feast of all the saints but common, and for that reason it is read again in numbers 7 and 38.

Other formulas also belong to common Masses for several martyrs—formulas that Acamius brings in—so that no special feast of all the saints extending over several days should be inferred from them. Perhaps some of these Masses were once said in cemeteries in memory of the martyrs buried there, when it was impossible to mention each one individually.]

For whenever the feasts of these days are celebrated in your Church, we marvel at your powers, Lord, and at your victories: these days, which the palms of your illustrious confessors and martyrs have consecrated for the perpetual memory and solemn joy of the faithful peoples. Through, etc.

You satisfy with heavenly gifts, Lord; defend us with your protection, so that, freed from every harmful thing, we may run with our whole heart after your saving [**lacuna**]. Through, etc.

[**Lacuna**] grant to your suppliants the abundance of your [grace], we ask, Lord, so that, following your commandments with you at work within us, they may receive consolation in the present life and attain the joys of the future. Through, etc.

### VII. Another.

Grant us, Lord, your mercy, implored through the intercession of your saints; and make those whom you have given us as our intercessors continually entreat your majesty and obtain salvation for us. Through, etc.

God, who, seeing that we are not fit to entreat your magnificence as we ought, have granted us the protection of those who have pleased you: grant that we may be helped by the prayers of those whose assistance you, in your mercy, have provided for us. Through, etc.

Hear, Lord, your people supplicating you with the patronage of your saints, and grant that we may rejoice in the peace of temporal life and find the help of eternal life.  
[Note: [Col. 0022C] This prayer appears in the Roman Missal on January 19, in the feast of Saints Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abachum.]

Be present, our God, to your servants, and, having been appeased by the intercession of your saints, look favorably upon our offerings, so that what our confidence does not merit may be made acceptable by pious supplication. Through, etc.

[Col. 0023A]

Grant us, Lord, the effect of your goodness, and, with your saints commending us, look favorably also upon our gifts. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For it is the work of your power and your goodness that the innumerable multitude of your saints has been granted not only to believe in your Son, our Lord, but also to be able to suffer for him; so that those whom faith justified, the end might glorify. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For your powers, Lord, etc., as above.  
[Note: [Col. 0023D] In the manuscript this Preface is repeated in full, as it is read in the preceding Mass. Only the words “of confessors … and” are omitted here.]

### VIII. Another.

Be favorable, Lord, to our supplications, and graciously hear our prayers, with the merits of your saints lending them support. Through, etc.

Receive our prayers favorably, Lord, we ask, and guard us through the intercession of your saints, so that we may serve worthily at your altars. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For you are glorious in your saints, to whom you have granted strength in confession and victory in suffering. Therefore, with the angels, etc.

Filled with the sacramental offering of the sacred Body and precious Blood, we ask, our God, that what we perform with pious devotion we may receive with certain redemption. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0023D] This prayer is found in Muratori’s edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary, from the Vatican and Ottobonian manuscripts, in the Mass for the Birth of Many Confessors; and in the Roman Missal in the Mass of Saints Processus and Martinian, as well as in the Mass of Saint Peter in Chains.]

### IX. Another.

Watch over your people, Lord, and, ever helped by saving protections, raise them up continually through benefits of mind and body. Through, etc.

Almighty and eternal God, who guard us through the intercession of your saints: grant that, nourished by whose merits, we may advance by the examples of pious confession. Through, etc.

May our supplication to you, Lord, and our offering likewise be pleasing; for, when it is presented in commemoration of your saints, may it obtain indulgence for us through their intercession. Through, etc.

It is truly right. You are marvelous not only in the virtue of your martyrs but also in that of your confessors. For although those who endured bitter punishments under manifest tortures are renowned for their suffering, these too, afflicted and tormented by the deliberate discipline of hidden chastisement, followed their footsteps through the disciplines of spiritual observance. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0023D] These words are also read in the Gothic Missal edited by the venerable Cardinal Tommasi, p. 328 of the latest Roman edition of Father Vezzosi, and on p. 644 of volume II of Muratori’s Liturgy. This Preface and the following one also prove the ancient worship of the saints whom we now call confessors. The particular formulas of this Preface, which present a certain account of that worship, seem to belong to the first institution of these Masses.

In Book II of the Gelasian Sacramentary, where the common Masses are not for one but for several saints and martyrs, as in our codex, one occurs as number 74, whose second prayer celebrates the memory both of martyrs and confessors: “God, who surround and protect us with the solemnities of the holy martyrs and the glory of confessors,” etc.]

### X. Another.

Hearken to the offerings of your people, Lord; and may they feel that those which they devoutly celebrate in honor of your saints advance toward their healing. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0024D] Nearly the same is the second prayer in the Roman Missal among the common and various prayers, number 7: “For prelates and the congregations entrusted to them.”]

It is truly right. While even now you glorify your confessors with so great a solemnity, you teach at the same time that no holy purpose before you is without reward, and, apart from the harder struggles, you invite even the weak to the gift of your recompense. Through, etc.

Receiving the pledge of the heavenly mystery, and placed on earth yet already satisfied with heavenly bread, we beseech you, Lord, through the prayers of your saints, that what is mystically accomplished in us may be truly fulfilled. Through, etc.

May the just prayer of the saints obtain help for your faithful, we ask, Lord; and may those devoted to the celebration in whose honor they are gathered become participants in their perpetual lot. Through, etc.

### XI. Another.

May the intercessions of your saints, granted to us, profit us, Lord, we ask; so that what we cannot obtain by our own prayers, we may attain through the prayers of those who please you. Through, etc.

Grant that we may be cherished by the supplications of your holy martyrs, Lord; so that we who yearly attend with reverence upon their venerable [supply: day] may be commended both by their intercessions and by their merits. Through, etc.

### XII. Another.

God, who see that the capacity of our conscience is insufficient to entreat you, make all your martyrs pray for us, whom you can worthily hear. Through, etc.

We offer you, Lord, the solemn gifts of your faithful, trusting in the intervention of the holy martyrs; so that what we perform in an inadequate service may rather be made acceptable through their merits. Through, etc.

It is truly right. You so destroyed the devices of the ancient enemy that he rendered even his saints, armed with the Spirit of truth, stronger than the devil whom he had overthrown by his power, so that they would neither fear the cruelty of their persecutors nor doubt the eternity of the promised blessedness. Recalling their glory in today’s solemnity, we offer you sacrifices of praise, with the angels, etc.

Having received the grace of the sacred gift, we humbly beseech you, Lord, that, with your holy martyrs imploring you for us, we may spiritually perceive the effect of divine power that we have received bodily. Through, etc.

Protect your people, Lord, as they supplicate you with the patronage of your saints and trust in your goodness; purify them inwardly and outwardly, so that through what they have tasted in the divine sacrifice they may deserve both the salvation of their minds and that of their bodies. Through, etc.

### XIII. Another.

Extend your mercy to us, Lord; and grant that your saints, through whose patronage you have made us to be helped, may continually entreat your majesty for us. Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, the sacrifice of appeasement and praise, which, through the intervention of the saints, may lead us to forgiveness and establish us in perpetual thanksgiving. Through, etc.

Filled with the substance of restoration and life, we ask, Lord our God, that through these heavenly gifts which you deign to provide for us, you may grant that we cling to heavenly things. Through, etc.

God, protector of those who hope in you, save your people; watch over them and order them, so that, freed from sins and secure from the enemy, they may always persevere in your grace. Through, etc.

### XIV. Another.

Be favorable to your people, Lord, and make help from the holy place come swiftly to us. Through, etc.

Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us the gifts of your salvation. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] In the Roman Missal this is the Secret prayer of the Mass for a non-pontifical confessor.]

It is truly right. We humbly entreat your majesty not to allow those for whom you have provided such great remedies to perish; and may the protections granted not result in an accumulation of condemnation for the guilty, but rather lead to the effect of salvation. Through, etc.

May the venerable reception of the sacrament, after cleansing us, we ask, Lord, from every old condition, transform us into a new creature. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0025D] In the same Missal this is the Postcommunion prayer for the Wednesday after Easter, where “may transfer” is better than “may bring.”]

May our inadequate supplication in service not prejudice your faithful, Lord; but, going before our merits, sanctify, govern, save, and accompany your Church; and confirm it, devoted to you without ceasing, by perpetual redemption. Through, etc.

### XV. Another.

Hear our prayers, Lord, and guard us by the protections of the holy martyrs. Through, etc.

Look upon the gifts that we present in commemoration of your saints, Lord; so that those gifts which are pleasing in their honor may, through their perpetual intercession, become beneficial to us. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0025D] This is the Secret prayer in the Roman Missal on September 22, in the Mass of Saints Maurice and his companions.]

It is truly right. For all your saints praise and bless you, and to them you have granted strength in confession and victory in suffering. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord our God, that the sacraments of those whose feast we celebrate with votive devotion may be made salutary to us through their intercession. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0025D] The same prayer is the Postcommunion of the Mass of Saint Martin, bishop, on November 11 in the Roman Missal.]

Watch over your suppliants, Lord; sustain the weak; cleanse those who are earthly; and, as we walk amid the mortal darkness [variant: of mortals], enliven us always with your light. Kindly rescued from every evil, grant that we may reach the highest goods. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0026D] “Of mortals” is a variant reading.]

### XVI. Another.

Grant, we ask, Lord, that we may continually celebrate the merit of your martyrs, whose constant assistance we experience. Through, etc.

We offer you a sacrifice, Lord, for the birthdays of the holy martyrs, so that, rejoicing in whose protections, we may frequent their glory. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For we recognize that we are protected by the prayers of the holy martyrs; and we implore your majesty more abundantly, so that you may command us to be supported temporally by these protections and helped spiritually. Through, etc.

Grant us, we ask, Lord, that with the solemnity of the holy martyrs we may rejoice in perpetual protection. Through, etc.

May the Christian people exult in the glorification of the great members of your Son; and, the more eminent they are than others, the more may those below rejoice with them in their exaltation. Through, etc.

Be favorable, Lord, we ask, to your people; and, with your saints lending aid, grant us forgiveness of sins. Being appeased, grant peace, so that in your favor you may generously grant assistance. Through, etc.

Through, etc.

It is truly right. For all your saints bless and praise you, and to them you have granted strength in confession and glory in suffering. Through, etc.

Through the prayers of the saints, Lord, we ask, may salvation be granted both to our minds and to our bodies; so that your gift may become for us both abundant blessing and generous protection. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0026D] The codex incorrectly reads “for those receiving.”]

Give help, Lord, we ask, to those subject to your majesty and power, so that whatever they do not dare to claim by their own merits, they may obtain through the prayers of your saints. Through, etc.

Hear us, Lord our God, as we supplicate you with the patronage of your saints; so that we who celebrate their triumphs may be able to maintain steadfastness. Through, etc.

Extend your mercy to us, Lord, and grant that your saints, through whose patronage you have given us help, may continually entreat your majesty for us. Through, etc.

Help our weakness, Lord, so that through the intercession of your saints we may not be judged unworthy of the merits of those whom you deign to appoint to such great offices. Through, etc.

Grant that we may serve your gifts with a free mind, so that, through the intervention of your saints, the gifts we present may work for us both healing and glory. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0027C] A similar Preface occurs above in Mass VIII.]

[Note: [Col. 0027D] This Preface is also read above, with a few changes, in Mass VII.]

Through the offering of the renewed sacred Body and precious Blood, we ask your mercy, Lord, so that what we perform with frequent devotion we may receive with certain redemption. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0027D] A prayer related to this occurs in Mass VIII.]

### XX. Another.

May we be helped by the prayers of your saints, Lord; and may what our ability cannot obtain be granted to us through their petition. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0027D] This prayer is read in Menard’s Gregorian Sacramentary and in the Roman Missal on the feast of Saint Matthew, where “that” is more correctly written.]

It is truly right. For, like the lights of heaven, you instruct us through the examples of your saints amid the darkness of the world, and you accompany us through their intercession. Through, etc.

Among the countless helps of your goodness, we are confident that you do not abandon our weakness, because such great patronage of those who please you has been provided for us. Through, etc.

God, you show the light of truth to those who wander so that they may be able to return to the way; grant to all who are reckoned among those professing Christianity both to reject what is hostile to this name and to follow what is fitting for it. Through, etc.  
[Note: [Col. 0027D] This should be read, together with the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries and the Roman Missal, which present this prayer on the Second Sunday after the octave of Easter: “who wander, so that they may be able to return to the way.” This is a Mass distinct from the preceding one, for the conversion of sinners; through the compiler’s carelessness its separate number was omitted.]

Almighty and eternal God, who command those participating in your table to abstain from the devil’s banquet, grant, we ask, to your people that, having cast away the taste of deadly profanation, they may approach the feasts of eternal salvation with pure minds. Through, etc.

It is truly right. Whose Church is now governed amid a mingling of true and false confessors, yet so that the changeability of human frailty must always be guarded against and no one’s conversion despaired of; therefore we beseech you more earnestly, that since steadfast devotion cannot endure without you, you may grant perseverance to the strong and repentance to the weak. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0027D] The false confessors who are here said to be mingled with the true within the Church are not—as someone has thought—the false confessors of whom Cyprian speaks in his book *On the Unity of the Church*; for Cyprian places those outside the Church. Rather, they are sinners, those who go astray, who are reckoned among Christians but nevertheless do not reject what is hostile to that name; hence prayers are poured out here for their conversion. In the Gelasian Sacramentary, on Friday of Holy Week, an oration is read which, we believe, would also be found in our Sacramentary if the portion belonging to Lent had survived; it was transferred into the Roman rite and is still recited on the same day in these words: “Let us pray also for all bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, lectors, doorkeepers, CONFESSORS, virgins, widows, and for all the holy people of God.” Here the confessors, listed after all the clerical orders and before virgins, widows who have professed chastity, and all the other laity, were men who, even if they were not in the clergy, nevertheless professed a continent and ascetic life; like virgins and widows who had professed continence, they occupied a kind of intermediate position between clergy and laity. See more about them in the dissertation on ascetics by the distinguished Nicolaus Antonellus, included in the newest edition of the sermons of Saint James of Nisibis, pp. 132 ff. Among these confessors there were both true and false ones, whose mention occurs in the preface of this Sacramentary.]

Grant, we ask, Lord, that your people may abstain from the devil’s snares, which they have renounced, and prostrate themselves before you with their whole heart. Through [him], etc.

[Col. 0028C] XXI. Another.

May the blessed supplication of the martyrs reconcile us to your majesty, Lord, so that we, who continually offend through our actions, may be cleansed by the unceasing prayers of the righteous. Through [him], etc.

May our gifts be pleasing to you, Lord, gifts established by your commands, and may the glorious solemnity of the saints commend them. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. We praise you in the confessions of your saints; while their solemn festivals are celebrated, richer examples of faith are set before us; while their victories are more frequently recalled, more abundant aids are supplied to us; while their merit and glory are proclaimed more abundantly in many ways, the hope of eternal blessedness is more earnestly impressed upon us. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0028D] “In many ways” is a variant reading.]

Filled, Lord, with the heavenly mystery, and supported by the blessings of those who intercede, we give thanks to your name: you accompany us with a saving gift and, in your kindness, raise us up through the patronage of the saints. Through [him], etc.

XXII. Another.

May the festivals of your martyrs always gladden us, Lord; and may we experience the help of those whose merit we celebrate. Through [him], etc.

We magnify your name, Lord, almighty and merciful God, who, coming to the aid of our frailty, not only bestow divine mysteries upon us, but also grant that through their prayers we may be made worthy of them. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For we celebrate the precious birthdays of your righteous ones; while they shine every day throughout the whole [world], they are always both begun as things already fulfilled and fulfilled as things continually beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0029A] Supply “throughout the world.”]

Satisfied by frequent reception of the sacraments—or, according to the variant reading, enriched—we ask, Lord, that those whose honor is thereby doubled may benefit us through saving prayer. Through [him], etc.

May your mercy be present to your people, Lord; appeased by the intercession of the saints, may it always cleanse them from sin, defend them from the enemy, advance them with temporal aids, and lead them to the everlasting joys of the saints. Through [him], etc.

XXIII. Another.

Multiply for us, we ask, Lord, the gifts of this sacred festival, as we recall the hopes of our salvation and are aided by the patronage of those who have pleased you. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Read: “so that, when we recall the hopes of our salvation, we may be aided by the patronage of those who have pleased you.”]

Practicing the glorious exchange, Lord, we offer what you have given, so that we may deserve to receive you yourself. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For although all the things bestowed at the beginning upon human substance are immense—namely, that you created it from nothing; that you granted it the power of possessing knowledge of you; that you set it above all living creatures by its participation in supreme reason; and that you enriched it with possession of the whole world—far more wondrous, nevertheless, are your works: you not only give life again to earthly and mortal matter after it has been extinguished, but also make it divine. Through [him], etc.

XXIV. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] This Mass and the following two are not about saints.]

We gladly offer earthly gifts upon your altars, Lord, so that we may attain heavenly things; we give temporal things so that we may receive eternal ones. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For who could, or would dare, cease from praising you, considering the effects of your wondrous arrangement—that from the substance of sinful humanity an immaculate victim should be born, by whose offering you might be appeased on behalf of the guilt of that same nature?

[Note: [Col. 0029D] Correct to “arrangement.”]

Through [him], etc.

[Col. 0030A] XXV. Another.

Grant us, we ask, Lord, to frequent these mysteries; for whenever the remembrance of the victim pleasing to you is celebrated, the work of our redemption is enacted. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0030D] Read “to frequent.” It is uncertain whether “of the pleasing victim” should be read below. This same prayer, with its beginning changed, is read in the Roman Missal on the ninth Sunday after Pentecost.]

It is truly right. For when the whole world experiences and sees the fallen beginnings of the human race raised up, things grown old renewed, and things brought low restored to the summit, just as the ancient saints recognized that what they believed ought to be done would be fulfilled, so it confidently awaits what is now promised.

[Note: [Col. 0030D] This does not seem unlike the style of Leo.]

Through [him], etc.

XXVI. Another.

We celebrate, Lord, a sacrifice which ought to be perpetual for us, just as we continually desire to be made eternal through its operation. Through [him], etc.

PASCHALI SC F SP.

[Col. 0030B] It is truly right. He offered himself to you on our behalf to be sacrificed, and in the same person presented himself as both Priest and sacred Lamb. Through [him], etc.

Grant us your mercy, Lord, by which we may both be absolved from our offenses and be fittingly prepared for these mysteries. Through [him], etc.

XXVII. Another.

Almighty and everlasting God, who adorns the sacred body of your Church with the confessions of the holy martyrs, grant us, we ask, both to follow what pleases you in their teachings and to imitate them in pious example. Through [him], etc.

Hear the prayers of those who beseech you, Lord, and let the commendation of your saints make acceptable those whom our merits abandon. Through [him], etc.

Receive, Lord, the votive gifts of your peoples; and may they be pleasing to you through the prayers of those for whose solemnity they are offered. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. You grant us to celebrate continually the glorious victories of the holy martyrs. For they are confessors of that name in which, eternal Father, you have placed the one protection of our salvation. And so that we may approach knowledge of it, in your kindness you both instruct the faith of our little minds through their testimonies and raise us up through their intercessions. Through [him], etc.

Trusting in the prayers of the saints, Lord, we ask that through what we have received we may obtain eternal remedies. Through [him], etc.

Guard your suppliant people, Lord, with your protection; and let them not with difficulty obtain what they piously and justly ask, since the merits of your saints support them. Through [him], etc.

XXVIII. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0030D] This occurs in the Gregorian Sacramentary on the feast of Saint Fabian, thirteen days before the Kalends of February, and elsewhere; also in the Roman Missal, in the secret prayer for the common of one martyr who is a bishop.]

Kindly receive, Lord, the offerings dedicated to you by the merits of your saints, and grant that they may come to us as an everlasting aid. Through [him], etc.

[Col. 0031A] Grant us, Lord, we ask, to escape together all sins and dangers of body and mind, since you surround us with the pious confession of countless martyrs. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031C] In the Roman Missal this is the secret prayer of the Mass of Saint Hermes on 28 August.]

We offer you, Lord, a sacrifice of praise in the commemoration of the venerable saints. Grant, we ask, that what bestowed glory upon them may profit us for salvation. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. You grant us, while we venerate the palms of the blessed martyrs on the days they marked with their blood, to exult in your power and always rejoice, Lord, in your honor. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031C] Read “to exult.”]

[Note: [Col. 0031D] This is the Postcommunion prayer of the Mass of Saints John and Paul on 26 June in the Roman Missal.]

Having received the heavenly sacraments while celebrating the solemnity of your saints, we ask, Lord, that through their intercession you grant us to attain in eternal joys what we carry out temporally. Through [him], etc.

[Col. 0031B] XXIX. Another.

May apostolic prayer always protect us, Lord, so that the Church may be guided by the same advocates in whom she glories as her leaders. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Something is missing; perhaps “through their intercession.”]

Be, Lord, a singular refuge for your wretched people through your saints, by whose honor and merit you are pleased on our behalf. Through [him], etc.

As we approach the festivals of your martyrs, Lord, we come before you with gifts dedicated to your name, so that by offering them reverence we may obtain forgiveness for ourselves. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For you are glorified in your saints, to whom you granted endurance in persecution and bestowed victory in suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] “You granted” and “you bestowed” are variant readings.]

Remember, Lord, we ask, the condition of humanity, so that your saints may always entreat your clemency for us and be heard without ceasing. Through [him], etc.

XXX. Another.

Protect us, Lord, by the prayer of your righteous—[or, according to the variant reading, “saints”]—so that, surrounded by their intercession, we may be cherished by their aid. Through [him], etc.

Grant us, we ask, Lord, always to offer you these vows, by which, while celebrating the birthdays of your saints, we may proclaim your glory. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For we repeat the solemnities of your saints, whose venerable confession both fulfilled the wonders of your power, sought heavenly reward for them, and prepared patronage for us. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] This formula, which we repeat for the Mass of the octave, is used in Mass XIV of Saint Lawrence, as its final prayer. It appears that when an octave of a martyr was to be celebrated, this common Mass was used.]

[Col. 0032A] May the frequent solemn celebrations of your righteous ones profit us, Lord; for the more fragile we are, the more we need protections pleasing to you. Through [him], etc.

XXXI. Another.

With the multitude of our sins prevailing, Lord, we recall the annual festivals of your saints, Lord, beseeching your mercy through them as a singular help—those whose patronage you wished to aid us. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] The second “Lord” is superfluous. Immediately below, “by your mercy” is more correct than “your mercy.”]

Do not regard the offenses of those offering gifts to you, Lord, we ask; but look favorably upon the merits of the intercessors. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. We glorify you in the confession of your saints, who, by the wondrous dispensation of your wisdom, prepared both everlasting blessedness for them and aids suited to our frailty; so that, having foreseen those whom you judged worthy to appease you, you might, being reconciled by the worthy prayers of those who have pleased you, look with favor upon us. Therefore we suppliantly implore you: just as eternal happiness awaits them, so may their continued prayer for us never be absent. Through [him], etc.

We have sinned against you, almighty and merciful God. We have no remedy unless you have mercy on us through the prayers of your saints. Through [him], etc.

XXXII. Another.

Grant us, almighty and merciful God, that, while celebrating the birthdays of your saints and proclaiming their triumphs, we may truly imitate their faith. Through [him], etc.

We offer, Lord, gifts pleasing to you on the solemnities of your saints, beseeching your clemency that what serves their glory may profit us for forgiveness. Through [him], etc.

It is truly right. For the venerable blood of the blessed martyrs, poured out in confession of your name, manifests your wonders—you who perfect strength in weakness—and likewise gives progress to our efforts and provides aid to our frailties. Through [him], etc.

XXXIII. Another.

With the saints interceding, Lord, may our service be pleasing to you, and may the offerings of our gifts become protections for the faithful. Through [him], etc.

Look upon us, Lord, entreated by the prayers of the venerable martyr Gregory, granting in your mercy that, just as his passion has brought us together today in your power—or, according to the inserted variant, “joy”—so may his merit also support us. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Blanchinius and Muratorius think “of Gregory” should be read, since his feast falls on 23 April. They arrived at this by assuming that this Mass belongs to April. But we have observed in note 1 (Col. 21, n. a) that the compiler placed common Masses of the saints here arbitrarily and inserted also prayers of Saints Tiburtius and Lawrence, which do not belong to April. The birthdays of the martyrs Gregory and Chrysogonus, however, are noted in this same Sacramentary on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. In the ancient Roman monastic Missal of the Lateran, recently published by the distinguished prelate Nicolaus Antonellus and included in volume I of Father Azevedo’s *Liturgical Collection*, p. 764, there is a Mass of Saint George the martyr, which is found in no other older Roman books; but it is assigned to the ninth day before the Kalends of January. From this date the learned annotator concludes that this must be Saint Gregory the martyr of Sipontum, whose memory is marked on the same day in other ecclesiastical documents. He thinks that this Mass was introduced into this Roman Missal by monks because the feast was celebrated among them—whom he believes were summoned from Spoleto to Rome, as he states on p. 31—at some monastery erected in Gregory’s honor. A little farther on, the word “joy” is inserted in the text as a variant reading.]

May the sacrificial victim, Lord, we ask, be made acceptable by the celebration of the precious martyrdom, and may it both purify our hearts and reconcile to you the vows of your people. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] In the first draft the copyist had written “sins”; in the second he substituted “hearts.”]

It is truly right. We earnestly beseech you that, just as you, foreseeing our weakness, have bestowed abundant aids through the righteous, so you may grant that we be refreshed through their intercession. Through [him], etc.

Hear us, Lord, as we cry out to you, and raise up with necessary protections those whom you do not abandon in the sacraments. Through [him], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] The words “At the dedication” appear to have been written in the margin by another antiquary; P. Blanchinius first noted them. But in corrections prefixed later he honestly confessed that the words were by that same antiquary, as Bartholomaeus Campagnola informed him after carefully consulting the codex at Blanchinius’s request.
