We complain about these things with such pitiable presumption when neither the quality of our produce nor any prosperity comes to us according to our desires, as though we ourselves were eager to fulfill your commands, and not rather, having contemptuously disregarded those same commands, deserved not only to be struck by scanty provisions but to be deprived of every means of support. Yet your mercy does not abandon us for this reason: so that we may be concerned by the chastisement of our poverty and devoted because your compassion has not been withdrawn. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] You will find this in Menardus’s Gregorian codex on the Thursday after Passion Sunday.] May the sacred libation of your table always invigorate and renew us, Lord; may it govern and protect our frailty amid the storms of the world and lead us into the harbor of perpetual salvation. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] The manuscripts of Muratori’s Gregorian codices agree in the Mass on the Saturday after Passion Sunday.] May your right hand protect your praying people, Lord. May it purify, sustain, and instruct them, so that, comforted in the present, they may advance toward future goods. Through, etc.

During the fast.

**VIII. Another [prayer].**—Almighty and eternal God, who bring us to the annual feasts of this observance, [Col. 0109B] graciously grant that the effect of pious devotion may provide us with substance both for our minds and for our bodies. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] Marginal note in the codex: Before food.] O God, who cause bodily sufficiency to arise for the fruitfulness of our souls, lest we deserve to lack outward supports, grant, we beseech you, that we may be made fruitful in inward gifts. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] It is read in Muratori’s Gregorian codices and in the Roman Missal on the Thursday after Passion Sunday.] Lord our God, who have ordained that, among these creatures which you created as a support for our frailty, gifts should also be set apart for dedication to your name, grant, we beseech you, that they may become for us both a help in the present life and a sacrament of eternity. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For your holy fasts nourish us, [Note: [Col. 0109D] The codex has *et esuriens*. But Blanchinius noted that *esuriens* was written for *esuries*, just as elsewhere *thesauris* is preferred to *thesauris*, *obtunsis* to *obtusis*, and *quotiens* to *quoties*. Hence the emendation adopted by Muratorius, *esurientes sacrata libatio nos reficit*, is unnecessary.] and sacred hunger refreshes us, if through salutary restraint the thorns and brambles of our conscience fade away and pure grain takes their place; if the barrenness of vices comes to an end, as we desire, and a joyful abundance of virtues is present. For lack of faults provides an abundance of prosperity. Hence, by restricting our resources and not refusing what is moderate, you so order us by your moderation that, as we strive toward heavenly things, we are not altogether abandoned with respect to temporal nourishment, and are so guided by passing supports that, chastened by their scantiness, we advance toward eternal things. Through, etc.

Continually accompany with your favor, Lord, those whom you refresh with the divine mystery, and accompany with saving consolations those whom you have instructed in heavenly ordinances. Through, etc.

May your protection, Lord, be present with the humble and continually guard those who trust in your mercy, so that, suitably aided by the necessities required by human nature, they may attain the gifts of immortality. Through, etc.

[Col. 0109D] **Invitation of the people during the fast of the tenth month.**

This week we must observe the fasts of the tenth month. Therefore we exhort your loving faithfulness to carry them out with the customary processions on Wednesday and Friday, and on Saturday to complete the same observance with solemn vigils, so that, with the merits of the apostles interceding, our perseverance in the service owed to God may obtain the favor of our God. Through, etc.

**IX. Other petitions.**—Almighty and eternal God, who console us both with annual supports and with solemnities, grant, we beseech you, that what is withdrawn from these things in accordance with the character of our way of life may be supplied by the abundance of your omnipotence. Through, etc.

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that we may be relieved by correction of conduct, because when you have bestowed these gifts, you will not deny us anything beneficial. Through, etc.

**Over the offerings.**—[Note: [Col. 0110D] This is found in the Roman Missal among the common prayers for a time of famine.] O God, who nourish and renew the twofold substance of the human race through the food and sacrament of the present gifts, grant, we beseech you, that they may provide support both for our bodies and for our minds. Through, etc.

[Col. 0110B] It is truly right. You do not cease to govern what you have created by eternal counsel. It is clear that we sin when, ignorant of heavenly ordering, we complain about the administration of your secrets; and we are recognized as thinking rightly only when, trusting not in our own but in your providence, we continually judge your mercy and justice worthy of prayer—confident that if you do not abandon the unjust and wicked, you will much less fail to govern with kindness those whom you have granted to be yours. Through, etc.

**After Communion.**—[Note: [Col. 0110D] It is read in the same common section there.] Govern, we beseech you, Lord, with temporal aids those whom you deign to instruct through eternal mysteries. Through, etc.

**Over the people.**—Rule your people, Lord, and, we beseech you, multiply within them the gifts of your grace, so that they may be free from every offense, not deprived of temporal aids, and may rejoice in eternal ordinances. Through, etc.

**X. Another [prayer].**—Almighty and eternal God, who created the human being in such a way that, suitably equipped with temporal benefits, you might advance him to heavenly gifts, grant, we beseech you, that, just as through illicit desires we fell from the region of the blessedness granted to us, so through nourishment distributed by your gift humanity may be sustained in its transitory condition and eternity, once lost, may be recovered. Through, etc.

It is truly right. We glorify the Creator both for things past and, by entreaty, for future fruits, so that, when we are not found ungrateful for what we have received, we may not be judged unworthy of what we are to receive; but rather, having presented the solemn devotion of the fast, may we advance in soul together with bodily supports. Through, etc.

We have received the glorious mysteries, Lord, through which, although placed on earth, you already make us participants in heavenly things. In these things among which we live, govern us, Lord, we beseech you, so that you may lead us to those things. [Note: [Col. 0110D] The codex has *quae sine per*. Blanchinius preferred *quo*. We have preferred Muratorius’s emendation.] Through, etc.

[Col. 0111A] Be present, Lord, with your suppliants, and graciously protect those who place their hope in your mercy, so that, cleansed from the stain of sins, they may remain in a holy manner of life and, obtaining sufficient temporal provision, may become heirs of your promise. Through, etc.

**XI. Another [prayer].**—Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that we may bend our hearts to your prayers, and, trusting that all things are possible for you, may we not hope for what will benefit us from the effects of the elements, but humbly implore it from your power. Through, etc.

O God of the heavenly powers, who grant more than we ask or deserve, grant, we beseech you, that your mercy may bestow upon us that for which confidence in our merits has no claim. Through, etc.

[Col. 0111B] [Note: [Col. 0111D] In the margin of the codex: Before food.] O God, who anticipate the requests of those who ask, grant, we beseech you, that we may not lack bodily nourishment and may be freed from fear of enemies. Through, etc.

Lord God, who alone foresee and provide what is appropriate for our frailty, grant that we may be supported by present aids and instructed by eternal ones. Through, etc.

Order us by your mercy, Lord, we beseech you, because we shall lack no assistance if we are governed by the clemency of your providence. Through, etc.

Direct your Church, Lord, by heavenly ordering, so that, having always been prepared in your presence before the foundation of the world, it may reach, under your guidance, the fullness and glory promised. Through, etc.

Receive us, we beseech you, Lord, with favor in proportion to the special offerings you have imposed for dedication to your name, [Col. 0111C] so that whatever is not fulfilled by the duty of our service may be reckoned through the graciousness of your indulgence. [Note: [Col. 0111D] *Indixisti* would be preferable.] Through, etc.

It is truly right. You do not cease to cherish and restore by divine means the image of your reason, established in the regions of the world and among human beings. For it was fitting that, after the fruits of the earth had passed away, a heavenly seed should arise, and that, once the nourishment of mortal life had been completed, the shoot of immortality should appear. And, once carnal foods had been set aside, food for souls should wondrously be born; and, when the season of wheat, wine, and oil had soon passed, there should ineffably be consumed that which, for the children of God progressing in the likeness of angels, would bring down from heaven not only its substance and name, but would provide eternal bread. Through, etc.

[Col. 0111D] May participation in the divine sacrament always increase your grace within us, Lord, and, cleansing us by its power, make us capable of so great a gift. Through, etc.

Absolve the offenses of your peoples, Lord, we beseech you, [Col. 0112A] and purify what mortality contracts [Note: [Col. 0111D] The codex erroneously has *mortalitatis*, unless it should be read in the plural, *contrahunt*, as likewise in what follows.] through frailty, so that, with you driving away every danger of mind and body, we may endure by your consolation, and the inheritance of the redemption promised by your grace may be completed. [Note: [Col. 0111D] So the codex. Muratorius: *haeres*, “heir.”] Through, etc.

**XII. Another [prayer].**—We beseech you, almighty God, both to correct our minds by heavenly ordinances and not to cease granting your benefits to those who have been corrected. Through, etc.

To overcome our enemies, Lord, grant, we beseech you, that we may obtain your help through fasts pleasing to you and good works. Through, etc.

We approach your venerable altars, Lord, with sacrifices of praise. Grant, we beseech you, that they may both reconcile your pardon and obtain your favor for us. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] This is the preface for the Wednesday of the seventh month in the Gregorian codices. The Leonine wording appears to be preferred in this and the other prefaces under this heading.] It is truly right. You wished us, after gathering the fruits of the earth, to give thanks to you through abstinence, so that through this very kind of devotion we might recognize that we received these things not for bodily abundance but for the sufficiency of our frailty; and that what we consumed more sparingly might benefit as nourishment for the needy, so that salutary chastisement might moderate the insolence of mortality and piety might make us imitators of your kindness. Thus we would use temporal gifts in such a way as to learn to yearn for eternal ones. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] In Menardus’s Gregorian Sacramentary on the Friday of the tenth month.] May the mysteries we have received benefit us, Lord, we beseech you, and may they at once strip us of sins and raise us up through the protections of your favor. Through, etc.

Look upon the prayers of your family, Lord, and grant help to those who humbly implore it, so that they may persevere in confessing your name with suitable supports. Through, etc.

[Col. 0112C] **XIII. Another [prayer].**—Compose our conduct, Lord, we beseech you, by your mercy, so that no adversities may dominate us and no saving benefits may be lacking. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0112D] In Muratori’s Gregorian codices it occurs among the evening and morning prayers; in Menardus, among the daily prayers.] Foster us, Lord, with every aid, and graciously make us suited to your disciplines. Through, etc.

We bring forward a sacrifice from the gifts you have bestowed, Lord, so that we may receive more securely and abundantly what is to be received. Through, etc.

**110** It is truly right. And at the same time to proclaim your generosity both for the general gift by which we live and for each individual support, [Note: [Col. 0112D] The codex has *ne non latis*, erroneously. Muratorius emended it to *ut non latis*. We have adopted Blanchinius’s correction from his second studies prefixed to the Sacramentary, since it is preferable; it is repeated below in this same prayer, §29, Mass XI, where shortly afterward we have written *segnius* for *signius*, as the codex erroneously presents it. In the same Mass XI, *mentibus* occurs for *sensibus*.] lest, ungrateful for benefits conferred, we be proved unworthy of benefits to be conferred; and deservedly may we be aided by the consolations of passing things if we pursue abiding goods no less eagerly, our senses purified by the sacred fast. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that we may not be deprived of temporal aids, though you nourish us with eternal food. Through, etc.

[Col. 0113A] [Note: [Col. 0113D] In the Gregorian codices it is listed among prayers for sins. At the end Muratorius has *et futuris*, “and future.” We have followed the reading of the codex, which the Gregorian codices also retain.] Help your suppliant people, Lord, we beseech you, and graciously grant your aid to the sick, so that, devoted to you with a sincere mind, they may rejoice both in the remedies of the present life and in those of the future. Through, etc.

**XIV. Another [prayer].**—Turn our hearts toward you, eternal Father, because those whom you have made subject to your worship will lack none of the necessities. Through, etc.

O God, who chastise your people when they sin in such a way that you do not abandon them with kindly consolation, grant, we beseech you, that the anger due to the guilty may be transferred to pardon when they pray. Through, etc.

Look favorably upon our prayers, Lord, we beseech you, so that those who serve at the sacred altars may be grounded in the truth of faith and conspicuous in purity of mind. Through, etc.

[Col. 0113B] It is truly right. You restore us through the blessed passion of your Christ; preserve in us the work of your mercy, so that in the celebration of this mystery we may live in perpetual devotion. Through, etc.

**XXVIII. Consecration of bishops.**

[Note: [Col. 0113D] This prayer is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book I, no. 99, and in the Rheims codex cited by Menardus, note 765.] Hear the prayers of your suppliants, Lord, so that what must be carried out through our ministry may rather be strengthened by your power (Alternatively: accomplished). Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] It is found in Gelasius in the same place and in the Roman Pontifical, under the consecration of bishops.] Receive, Lord, we beseech you, the offerings of your servant N., and graciously preserve your gifts in him. Through, etc.

Therefore, Lord, graciously receive this offering which we offer to you for that servant of yours whom you have deigned to advance to pontifical glory, [Col. 0113C] so that what he has obtained by divine gift he may carry out through divine effects. Through, etc.

**111** Be present, merciful God, so that what has been performed through the duty of our service may be strengthened by your blessing. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] It is read in the same place in Gelasius and in the Roman Pontifical.] Be favorable to our supplications, Lord, and, bending over these servants of yours the horn of priestly grace, pour upon them the power of your blessing. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] This prayer, which is found in the same Gelasian and Pontifical books, as well as in Menardus’s Gregorian book, Quesnellus appended to the sermons of the holy pontiff as Leonine.] O God of all honors, God of all dignities that serve in consecrated orders for your glory; O God, who, speaking to your servant Moses in the intimacy of a secret conversation, among the other instructions of heavenly worship, also instructed him concerning the form of priestly clothing, and commanded that the chosen Aaron be clothed in mystical vesture amid the sacred rites, [Col. 0113D] so that the following generation might derive understanding from the examples of those who came before, and so that no age might lack the instruction of your teaching; since among the ancients the very appearance of the signs commanded reverence, while among us the realities themselves provide clearer evidence than the riddles of figures.

For the clothing of that earlier priesthood is the adornment of our mind, and pontifical glory is no longer commended to us by the honor of garments but by the splendor of souls; because even those things which then delighted bodily eyes demanded rather that what was contained within them should be understood.

Therefore, Lord, grant this grace, we beseech you, to these servants of yours whom you have appointed to the ministry of the highest priesthood, so that whatever those coverings signified in the gleam of gold, the brilliance of gems, and the variety of workmanship of many kinds may shine forth in their conduct and actions. Complete in your priests the fullness of your mystery, and sanctify those equipped with the ornaments of complete glorification through the outpouring of heavenly anointing. May this flow abundantly upon their head; may it run down upon the lower parts of their faces; may it descend to the extremities of their entire body, so that the power of your Spirit may fill their inner parts and surround their outward parts. May steadfastness of faith, purity of love, and sincerity of peace abound in them.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] In the Gelasian codex several periods are added at this point, [Col. 0114D] which were also received in the manuscripts of Ratoldus and Rheims, as well as in the Roman Pontifical and the commonly circulated Order. But they are absent from some of the Orders in Martène, from Menardus’s Gregorian book, and from the codex of Rodradus cited by the same Menardus, note 777. Our most ancient Sacramentary demonstrates that these periods are additions.] Grant them an episcopal chair for governing your Church and your entire people. Be their authority; be their power; be their strength. Multiply your blessing and grace upon them, so that, made fit by your gift always to entreat your mercy, they may be devoted through your grace. Through, etc.

**112 Blessing over deacons.**

[Note: [Col. 0114D] It is read in Gelasius, book I, no. 22.] Lord God, mercifully hear our prayers, [Col. 0114C] so that what must be carried out through our service you may graciously accompany with your help, and those whom, according to our understanding, we believe should be offered for the execution of sacred ministries, you may rather justify by your own choice. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0114D] See Gelasius in the same place, the Roman Pontifical, and Menardus’s Gregorian Sacramentary.] Let us pray, beloved, to God the almighty Father, that he may mercifully pour upon these servants of his, whom he deigns to call to the office of the diaconate, the blessing of his grace, and graciously preserve the gifts of the consecration granted to them. Through, etc.

O God, magnificent consoler of sacred dignities, we beseech you to grant these servants of yours, whom you deign to call to the office of Levites, sufficient ability to fulfill the ministry of the holy altar; and, overflowing with every gift of grace, make them acquire confidence in your majesty and offer others an example of perfect devotion. [Col. 0114D] Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0114D] It exists in the three books cited.] Be present, we beseech you, almighty God, [Note: [Col. 0114D] Thus the codex, as also in Menardus, whose note 746 should be read; there the reading *bonorum*, adopted by Muratorius, is removed. Shortly afterward the codex has *disponis* [Col. 0115D] together with the Gelasian Sacramentary. But we have retained the more suitable emendation *disponens*, which Menardus’s exemplar confirms.] giver of honors, distributor of orders, and arranger of offices. You who, remaining in yourself, renew all things, and, ordering everything through your Word, Power, and Wisdom, Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, prepare all things by eternal providence and distribute what is suited to each time.

You grant that his body, your Church, distinguished by the variety of heavenly graces and joined together by the distinction of its members, united by the marvelous structure of the whole through law, may grow and expand for the increase of your temple; establishing the service of the sacred office to serve your name in three grades of ministers, choosing from the beginning the sons of Levi, who, remaining in faithful watchfulness over the mystical works of your house, might possess by perpetual lot the inheritance of eternal blessing.

Look favorably also, Lord, upon these servants of yours, whom we humbly dedicate to the office of the diaconate, [Col. 0115B] to serve in your sacred treasuries. [Note: [Col. 0115D] In his first studies Blanchinius proposed either *sacris aris*, “sacred altars,” or, what he preferred, *sacris altaribus*, as in the Roman Pontifical. Since Gelasius’s codex has *sacris* and the Gregorian codex *sacrariis*, Blanchinius noted in his second studies that no correction was necessary.]

And we, as human beings ignorant of divine understanding and supreme reason, judge the life of these men as far as we can. But, Lord, things unknown to us do not escape you, nor do hidden things deceive you. You are the knower of sins; you are the examiner of souls. You can truly exercise heavenly judgment upon them and grant even to the unworthy what we ask.

Send forth upon them, Lord, we beseech you, the Holy Spirit, by whom they may be strengthened with the sevenfold gift of your grace for faithfully carrying out the work of the ministry. May every form of virtue abound in them: modest authority, steadfast modesty, purity of innocence, and observance of spiritual discipline. In their conduct may your commands shine forth, so that, by the example of their chastity, they may gain the imitation of the holy people; and, bearing forward a good testimony of conscience, may they remain firm and steadfast in Christ and, through your grace, deserve by worthy advancement to receive greater things from the lower rank. Through, etc.

**Consecration of a presbyter.**

Let us pray, beloved, to God the almighty Father, that he may multiply heavenly gifts upon these servants of his whom he has chosen for the office of the presbyterate, so that, with his help, they may carry out what they receive through his gracious favor. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] It is in the same books.] Hear us, God our salvation, and pour upon these servants of yours the blessing of the Holy Spirit and the power of priestly grace, so that those whom we offer for consecration before your loving-kindness may be accompanied by the perpetual abundance of your gift. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] It is found in the same books. Henricus Valesius recognized this prayer as Leonine, and Quesnellus reprinted it after Leo’s sermons.]

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, distributor of all honors and of all dignities that serve you, through whom all things advance, [Col. 0116A] through whom all things are established, as the increases of rational nature are always enlarged for the better in an order arranged by fitting reason. Hence the ranks of priests and the offices of the Levites grew, instituted through mystical sacraments, so that, when you had appointed the supreme pontiffs to govern the peoples, you might choose men of the next order and of secondary dignity to assist their fellowship and work. [Note: [Col. 0116D] Our manuscript and the Gelasian book erroneously read *elegeris* (“you have chosen”). Shortly afterward both manuscripts read *Moyse* (“Moses”).] Thus, in the wilderness, you spread Moses’ spirit through the minds of seventy prudent men, and, using these assistants among the people, he easily governed innumerable multitudes. Thus, in Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, you transferred the abundance of their father’s fullness, so that the merit of the priests might suffice for the saving sacrifices and the sacraments of their more frequent ministry.

By this providence, Lord, you added to the apostles of your Son teachers and companions in the faith, through whom they filled the whole world with subsequent preachers. Therefore, Lord, we ask you to grant these aids also to our weakness, for the more fragile we are, the more we need them. Grant, Father, we ask, the dignity of the presbyterate to these your servants. Renew within them the spirit of holiness. May they receive from 114 you, O God, the gift of a secondary rank of merit, and may they commend the discipline of conduct by the example of their way of life. May they be worthy fellow workers in our order. May the full pattern of justice shine forth in them, so that, when they must render a good account of the stewardship entrusted to them, they may obtain the rewards of eternal blessedness. Through [Christ], etc.

### XXIX. For the anniversary of bishops

[Col. 0116C] I. — O God, author and guardian of your work, graciously receive the thanksgiving that, as the year returns, we offer in recollection of the beginnings of our dignity, which we have taken up as a solemn observance, so that what was instituted by your beginnings may, once increased, be governed by your protection. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0116D] The Gelasian book I, no. 101, made two prayers out of this one.] Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we may show your faithful people an ordered devotion, and graciously pour into us also the spirit of loving them, so that, in sincere faith, hope, and charity, a sacrifice pleasing to you may be offered by both people and bishop. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. And to entreat you more earnestly that, in me, whom you have advanced to the priestly ministry without any support of holiness, but solely through the gracious favor of your grace, by continuing your gifts you may bring them to perfection; and that, as time advances, you may grant me rather the progress of good works. For this will be the true celebration of pontifical glory, this the certain joy: if, through a rational rule of presiding, your people’s increase in number [Note: [Col. 0116D] A corrupt passage, which we leave for others to emend.] and the care of those who govern, as well as the growth and well-being of the flock, become the joy and crown of shepherds. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0115D] [ [Col. 0115D] This note appears at the foot of column 115, but the callout letter (b) has not been printed in the text.] It is found in Gelasius, book I, no. 20, in Gregor Menardus, and in the Roman Pontifical.]

[Col. 0117A] Therefore, this offering, which I, your servant and priest, offer to you because you have granted me—trusting in no justice whatsoever, but through the abundance of your ineffable mercy—to undertake priestly service, we ask you graciously to accept and, in your goodness, to strengthen what you have worked in us; and in your most merciful governance to order my days. Through [Christ], etc.

By this offering, together with the whole Church rejoicing with me, you, O God, in all things …

Almighty and merciful God, who have brought us to the celebration of this day, grant, we ask, that through receiving your sacrament both the security we desire (or: that will benefit us) and integrity of religion may come to us. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, Lord, we ask, that your household may have peace with its rulers, so that those who rejoice in their honor may rejoice in their holy way of life; and may your grace grant both moderation to those who govern and obedience to those subject to them. Through [Christ], etc.

115

### II. Another

God, who most powerfully accomplish great things and wonders from small beginnings, graciously carry out in me the gifts of your mercy, so that, where no merits of my conscience are worthy of you, may the grace of your piety alone always shine forth. Through [Christ], etc.

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who deign to raise up the lowly and do not despise the rejected, lift up those whom you raise and govern those whom you exalt. Grant me, your servant, sufficiency for the governance entrusted to me. Grant peace to your Church, over which you have willed me to preside, so that, in one and the same spirit, both the devotion of the people and that of their bishop may be pleasing to you. [Col. 0117C] Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] It is found in Gelasius, book I, no. 100, in Menardus’s manuscript, vol. III, col. 227, and also in the Roman Missal among the common prayers, no. 20, with a few changes.] God, creator and ruler of the world, graciously attend to the prayers of my humility, and make me, your servant, whom you have appointed to serve the heavenly mysteries not through any merits supporting me but through the immense abundance of your clemency, a worthy minister at the sacred altars, so that what is proclaimed by my voice to be celebrated may rather be confirmed by your sanctification. Through [Christ], etc.

Almighty and everlasting God, shatter, we ask, the weapons of our enemies, so that with undisturbed minds we may perform your holy rites. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant us, almighty God, that, withdrawing from wicked desires, we may follow the rectitude of your commandments; and you, who grant even the wayward what they desire, grant better things to those who have been corrected. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0117D] May every human perversity depart from us when you, Lord, have cleansed us, so that with pure senses and minds we may celebrate your mysteries. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. To beseech your majesty with every faculty, lest, occupied with our own pleasures, we either neglect the household entrusted to us or strive to harass those subject to us; but, as the rule of the Gospel shows, administering food to fellow servants at the proper time, may we be found ready at the Lord’s coming; and while striving to correct your servants with love and to love them with necessary discipline, [Col. 0118A] and while rationally carrying out the whole service entrusted to us, may we not incur guilt for neglecting the Lord’s increase, but may the multiplication of the divine talents be granted to us as a reward for our stewardship. Through [Christ], etc.

God, who do not cease to nourish us with your sacraments, grant, we ask, that the refreshment bestowed through them may confer eternal life upon us. Through [Christ], etc.

Look graciously upon your household, Lord, and grant everlasting mercy to those who implore you, so that, since without it no one can accomplish anything truly worthy by himself, through it they may deserve to fulfill your saving 116 commandments. [Al. “the things you command.”] Through [Christ], etc.

### III. Another

God, who have taught your Church to keep all the heavenly commandments through love of your Divinity and of one’s neighbor, grant us the spirit of peace and [Col. 0118B] grace, so that your whole household may be devoted to you with all its heart and agree with itself in pure intention. Through [Christ], etc.

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, grant that we may be increased by the favor of your grace, and, [Note: [Col. 0117D] The manuscript reads *mortalis* here. The emendation is supplied by this same prayer repeated below, no. 5.] trembling with awareness of our mortality, strengthen us through the instruction of your piety, so that, with you working all things in all, the progress of your flock may be the form of its shepherd. Through [Christ], etc.

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, continue in us the gifts of your grace, and mercifully bestow by your Spirit what human frailty cannot achieve by its own capacity, so that those who serve at the sacred altars may be established in integrity of faith and conspicuous in clarity of mind. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0118D] It appears, with a few changes, in Gelasius, book I, no. 102.] God, who by the power of your majesty apportion the number of our days and the measures of time, [Col. 0118C] graciously look upon the service of our humility, so that the abundance of your peace may fill our times. Through [Christ], etc.

God, who promised that you would not be absent from your Church until the consummation of the age, nor that the gates of hell would prevail against the apostolic confession, graciously perfect your power also in our weakness, and show the fulfillment of the divine promise by deigning to be present even in your weak servants. For we undoubtedly feel your presence when you fittingly apportion what should be desired in each period and guard us with continual protection from every assault of adversity. Through [Christ], etc.

Remember, Lord, what you have worked in us, and consider not what we deserve but the grace of your bestowed gift, so that, just as your gracious favor has commanded me to serve at the sacred altars in the pontifical office, it may likewise make me worthy in merit. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, we ask, Lord our God, that we may turn aside harmful appetites and reject desires that bring guilt upon us, because then we shall be able to overcome external enemies if we conquer those within. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant us, almighty God, we ask, that, presenting ourselves through your grace as is worthy of you, we may offer your faithful people an example of upright conduct. And may the eternal salvation of your people become the priest’s reward. Through [Christ], etc.

117 [Note: [Col. 0119D] The manuscripts of Gregory, Muratorius, and the Roman Missal assign this prayer to the Thursday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent.] Purify us, merciful God, so that the prayers of your Church, which are pleasing to you, may become more pleasing when we offer sacred [Al. “devout”] gifts with cleansed minds. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. To glorify you for your gifts. For who would be worthy of this office unless, anticipated by the grace of your compassion, he were made fit for it? Since, therefore, it is your gift and not our merit, it will nevertheless belong to your governance that it should not become everlasting punishment for the negligent, but rather, when competently carried out, should become the cause of eternal reward. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] In the Gelasian manuscript, book III, no. 37, this prayer is assigned to the anniversary of a presbyter.] Rejoicing in the abundance of your gifts, Lord, we humbly beseech you: grant sufficient grace for ministering to those to whom you have granted the capacity for this ministry. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] This appears among the daily prayers of Gregory’s manuscripts in Muratorius.] May the people, Lord, always rejoice, trusting in your blessing, and advance through frequent participation in heavenly things, so that they may be helped by temporal benefits and instructed in eternal ones. Through [Christ], etc.

### IV. Another

Grant us, Lord, we ask, the governance of holy discipline, so that through your grace both moderation may come to those who govern and obedience to those subject to them. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Gelasius, book II, no. 60, transferred this prayer to the Saturday of the seventh month. At the end, the manuscript erroneously reads *cunctis transeat*. We have emended it from Gelasius.] Grant, we ask, Lord, that your faithful may be fittingly prepared by the Paschal fasts, and that the bodily discipline solemnly undertaken may pass over to the fruit of all souls. Through [Christ], etc.

Take away our iniquities from us, Lord, we ask, [Col. 0119C] so that we may deserve to enter the holy of holies with pure senses. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. You who fittingly apportion what is to be observed in each period. For it is more suitable and more appropriate in these days [Note: [Col. 0119D] Here the ordination of a bishop is indicated. It falls during the Lenten fast, designated by the word “observance” and expressed in the second prayer, around the time of Easter. Some think that this was adapted for Felix III, who was ordained on 6 March 483. But since Zosimus was consecrated on 18 March, as all scholars now agree, we do not wish to conjecture to which of them this Mass more properly belongs.] that we celebrate the beginnings of the episcopal office undertaken, in which the devoted observance of the whole Church joins, and the anniversary of the sacrament itself is honored—that of the one to whom the priestly ministry has been assigned. And while, living more strictly and more chastely, we are transferred into the members of the supreme pontiff as we advance, we hope that this honor, acquired temporarily, may rather become eternal. Through [Christ], etc.

118 [Note: [Col. 0120D] It is read in Gelasius, book I, no. 97, for the anniversary of the consecration of a deacon.] Grant, Lord, we ask, that we may rejoice both in the increase of our advancement and in the fitting observance of the Paschal sacrament. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0119D] Graciously multiply your blessing, Lord, upon the people who implore you, [Col. 0120A] so that they may always rejoice in the good conduct of their bishop and take delight in the celebration of the sacred feast. Through [Christ], etc.

### V. Another

Lord God, Father of glory, source of blessings, although you do not cease to enrich your Church, spread throughout the whole world, with the abundance of your gifts, yet you regard the see of your blessed apostle Peter all the more attentively [Note: [Col. 0120D] The words *intueris, quanto sublimius*, which are absent from the manuscript at this point, have been supplied from this same prayer repeated shortly afterward; from it we also add the words *hujus* below.] the more exalted you have willed it to be. Grant me, your servant, to perform fittingly the office assigned by the arrangements of your providence, confident that you will bestow upon all the Churches whatever you grant to that one, insofar as [Note: [Col. 0120D] *Cunctae* seems to be the reading required.] they all look to it. Through [Christ], etc.

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, grant that we may be increased by the favor of your grace, etc. [Note: [Col. 0120D] This is the same as the second prayer of Mass III.]

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, [Col. 0120B] who have appointed me, though endowed with no confidence in my merits, to preside over your household through the gift of your ineffable grace, lift up those whom you raise and govern those whom you exalt, so that, since you are the author of their good works, you yourself may be their perfecter. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] It differs little from the third prayer of the same Mass III.] God, whose entire way is always mercy and truth, continue the gifts of your work, and bestow through your benefits what human frailty cannot achieve by its own capacity, so that those who serve the heavenly mysteries may be established in integrity of faith and shine conspicuous in purity of mind. Through [Christ], etc.

Lord God, Father of glory, source of blessings, etc. [Note: [Col. 0120D] The repetition of this prayer in the same Mass should be attributed to the carelessness of the collector or copyist.]

Almighty and merciful God, who always work kindly so that we may fulfill what you command, be present to the shepherd of the sheep beloved by you, because it is your gift and your power that those to be governed may be obedient and the rulers may be approved. Through [Christ], etc.

Merciful God, eternal King, grant a prosperous course to our service. And, so that we may please you through the devotion of your people, preside over your holy flock and direct all their wills toward observance of your 119 commandments. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] It is found in Gelasius, book I, no. 98, and book III, no. 37.] God, at whose command the order of all ages runs its course, graciously look upon the time of our generation, and, so that our service may please you, preserve your gifts in us. Through [Christ], etc.

God, powerful and kind governor of our days and times, graciously regard the gifts bestowed upon me through your grace, and direct the heart of people and bishop toward this purpose, so that neither the flock may lack obedience to its shepherd nor the flock’s shepherd care for the flock. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0120D] VI. Another. — God, who, for arranging the governance of your Church, have so exalted its leaders that you do not abandon even the least, grant, we ask, that we may follow, however distantly, the traces of apostolic faith and teaching, imitating what we accompany, although with a feeble office. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] It is found in the Gelasian manuscript, book I, no. 100, and in Gregor Menardus, vol. III, p. 227.] To the glory of your name, Lord, as we repeat the annual feast of the beginning of priesthood, we offer you a sacrifice of praise, humbly entreating that, although unworthy, we serve you in the place of that ministry, we may be made acceptable through its intercessions. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. Trembling with exultation and rejoicing with fear. For just as we rejoice in your gift, so we fear because of our frailty. And as much as we dread the excesses of human condition, so much do we trust in your grace, which perfects power in weakness, [Col. 0121B] earnestly imploring you: do not allow the one whom you have adorned with the honor of so great a see to be unworthy in conduct; and grant that he whom you have appointed as successor in the likeness and name of another may, by whatever effort of good conduct, become a follower of the exemplar whose successor in name you have made him. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, Lord, we ask, that with the passage of time there may be an increase of upright governance, so that what we bear foremost in dignity we may carry out in just actions. Through [Christ], etc.

Multiply, Lord, we ask, in your Church the spirit that you have given, so that through the worthy institution of its bishop the holy devotion of your faithful may grow. Through [Christ], etc.

### VII. Another

Almighty and everlasting God, source and perfection of all virtues, grant us, [Col. 0121C] we ask, both to practice what is right and to proclaim what is true, so that we may provide instruction in your grace to your faithful both by our actions and by our 120 teaching. Through [Christ], etc.

Receive, Lord, we ask, the offerings and prayers that we humbly present both out of reverence for Easter and for the solemn commemoration [Note: [Col. 0121D] The annual solemnity and commemoration of the day on which someone was raised to the pontificate are indicated. This prayer is known to have been used on a day coinciding with the Paschal season. To which bishop it applies we leave for others to judge. Perhaps, when the annual anniversary of Zosimus or Felix III fell during Lent, as noted above (note 74 [Col. 0119, no. e]), and when at this time bishops, occupied with many duties, could not hurry to Rome for the synod customarily held on the bishop’s anniversary, as stated in the admonition to the first sermon of St. Leo, no. 3, the solemnity was transferred to after Easter.] of the beginning of priesthood, so that through the intercession of those whom you appoint for us as teachers and patrons of this office, our circumstances may be prosperous. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. To implore you more abundantly that what is now a pious burden for us may be an honor that lasts forever. May the privilege of rank delight us less than the appropriate exercise of dignity, [Note: [Col. 0122D] The manuscript erroneously reads *ut quae*.] and, in accordance with blessed Paul the apostle, who teaches, “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work,” may the truth of the sacred name be displayed in us by the results of holy conduct. And although we preside over the rest by position, may we be subject to all with rational affection. May the harmful exaltation of power not raise us up, but rather may the legitimate administration of charity make us humble. Through [Christ], etc.

God, who kindly both begin and perfect every good thing, grant us to rejoice in perfection just as we glory in the beginnings of your grace. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] It is found in Gelasius, book I, no. 100, and in Menardus, vol. III, p. 228 of the works of St. Gregory.] May the hearts of your faithful, Lord, we ask, be filled with your consolations, and may they report votive joys both concerning the progress of the Church’s bishops and concerning their own progress; and, encouraged by temporal comforts, may they desire eternal things more eagerly. Through [Christ], etc.

### VIII. Another

God, who, although you order the whole human race by heavenly law, nevertheless govern your Church by a special dispensation, graciously grant that we may offer you ministry worthy of you and, through your grace, offer worthy ministers. [Col. 0122B] Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, almighty God, we ask, that what we supply through fragile service may rather be perfected by your action. Through [Christ], etc.

Graciously regard the offerings of all of us, Lord, we ask, so that both what has been performed through the service assigned to us and the prayers of the faithful peoples may be confirmed rather by your gracious favor. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. Humbly imploring you to perfect both our service and that of those whom, through the abundance of your gift, we appoint as bishops over the sacred household, so that it may be well pleasing to you. Through [Christ], etc.

121

### To be offered for a bishop

Therefore, this offering, which we offer to you on behalf of your servants (N. and N.), to whom you have bestowed the supreme priesthood, we ask you kindly to make effective and to continue your gifts in them. Through [Christ], etc.

Graciously enlighten your Church, Lord, so that the progress of your flock may everywhere advance and, under your governance, its shepherds may become pleasing to your name. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, Lord, we ask, that your faithful may love their bishops and be loved by them in return; and grant, we ask, that they may persevere forever, so that neither justice nor compassion may be lacking to either. [Note: [Col. 0122D] The manuscript erroneously reads *utrumque* (“both” in the singular form).] Through [Christ], etc.

### IX. Another

[Note: [Col. 0122D] In Gelasius this is Mass IV, for Sundays; in Muratorius’s manuscripts, the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost; in Menardus, the Tenth Sunday; in the Roman Missal, the Eighth Sunday. In our manuscript the common Masses begin here.] Grant us, Lord, we ask, the spirit of thinking and acting promptly on what is good, so that, since we cannot exist without you, we may be able to live according to you. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant us, Lord, we ask, that, truly trusting in your grace, we may ask for what is worthy of you and continually receive what we ask. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant that we may obtain the effect of the offering dedicated to you, Lord, so that, cleansed from the conduct of earthly antiquity, we may be renewed by the advances of heavenly life. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. So that we, who were created with you as our author, may be saved with you as our restorer; and we, who readily depart from your righteousness, may be recalled to it by your mercy. May we not be abandoned to our excesses, but may we be mercifully and unceasingly subjected to your will. Through [Christ], etc.

Perfect kindly in us, Lord, we ask, what we profess in the sacred mysteries, so that we may carry it out in devout actions. Through [Christ], etc.

Restore your people, Lord, inwardly and outwardly, so that, since you do not wish them to be hindered by bodily pleasures, you may make them flourish in spiritual purpose; and so support them with passing things that you may instead grant them to cling to what is eternal. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0123B] X. Another. — Almighty and everlasting God, who defend us, though undeserving, from our enemies, grant, we ask, that uprightness of conduct and faith may be present in us, 122 through which we may deserve the increases of your piety. Through [Christ], etc.

We ask, Lord our God, that the security of your favor bestowed upon us may not make us negligent, but rather render us acceptable to the worship of your name. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] This prayer is found in Gregory’s manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on the Tuesday after the Third Sunday of Lent.] Cleansed, Lord, by the sacred mysteries, may we obtain both forgiveness and grace. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. To ask your clemency with all our heart, so that you, who protect us from bodily adversities, may also free us from enemies of the mind; and those whom you allow to rejoice in outward tranquility, may you make peaceful inwardly. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0123C] [Note: [Col. 0123D] It is found in Gregory’s Sacramentary of Menardus and in the Roman Missal on the Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord.] Filled with sacred gifts, Lord, grant, we ask, that we may always remain in thanksgiving. Through [Christ], etc.

Govern your Church, Lord, graciously, so that, directed by powerful moderation, it may receive increases in freedom and persist in religious integrity. Through [Christ], etc.

### XI. Another

Turn our hearts to you, eternal Father, because those whom you have made subject to your worship will lack nothing necessary. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] This prayer and the following one are found above in Mass XIII, §17, for the fast of the tenth month. Therefore, in the following prayer we have more securely emended *securi* here to *securius*, which the manuscript gives erroneously at this point.] Graciously nourish us with every aid, Lord, and make us fit for your disciplines. Through [Christ], etc.

We offer a sacrifice from the reception of your benefits, Lord, so that we may receive more securely and abundantly the benefits yet to be received. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0123D] It is truly right. To proclaim your generosity both for the universal gift by which we live and for each individual support; lest, having received gifts, etc. [Note: [Col. 0123D] What follows is as in the preface of the Mass mentioned above.]

Grant, Lord, we ask, that through temporal things, etc. [Note: [Col. 0123D] A similar prayer is found in the same place.]

Come to the aid, Lord, we ask, of the people who implore you, etc. [Note: [Col. 0123D] A similar prayer occurs in the same Mass XIII, so that, apart from the first prayer, the remaining prayers agree with that Mass.]

### XII. Another

Almighty and merciful God, multiply the gifts of your favor; and, when all enemies have been subdued by heavenly power, grant us an increase of religion and peace. Through [Christ], etc.

God of the heavenly powers, carry out the gift of your promise, so that the hearts of those who rebel against evangelical truth may be subjected. Through [Christ], etc.

Insert, we ask, Lord, the grace of your reconciliation into our gifts, so that you may both protect the remedies 123 bestowed upon us and perfect those that are to be bestowed. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0124B] It is truly right. We beseech you, so that, graciously reconciled, you may make us follow you with devoted heart. [Note: [Col. 0123D] The manuscript reads *tibi*, which did not agree with the verb *sectari*. Muratorius changed this word to *famulari*. We have more easily emended it to *te*, retaining *sectari*, since it properly corresponds to the following verb *sequi*.] For just as the cause of every adversity is disobedience to your commandments, so the result of every prosperity is fittingly to follow the author of all good things. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] It is related to a prayer in the Roman Missal on the Saturday after the Fourth Sunday of Lent. In Gregory’s manuscripts, on the same day, it is identical except for *pacatos* (“pacified”), where they read *placitos* (“pleasing”). It is also found in Gelasius, book I, no. 54.] May your holy things purify us, Lord, we ask, and may their effects make us at peace. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] It is found in Gregory’s manuscripts among the prayers for sins.] May the devotion of the people subject to you move your compassion, Lord, we ask, and may faithful supplication obtain your mercy, so that what it does not presume upon the basis of merits it may receive through the abundance of your forgiveness. Through [Christ], etc.

### XIII. Another

[Note: [Col. 0124D] In Muratorius’s manuscripts it is found among the morning or evening prayers; in Menardus, among the daily prayers.] In your mercy, Lord, absolve our sins, and compassionately turn away whatever we deserve for our sins. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] Both of Muratorius’s manuscripts place this among the daily prayers.] Grant, we ask, almighty God, that, running along your way with devoted mind, [Col. 0124C] we may escape the snares of sins that steal upon us. Through [Christ], etc.

May the heavenly fulfillment of the sacrament purify us, Lord, and always renew us through its divine effects so that we may receive your magnificence. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. So that we, who subsist with you as our author, may be directed by you as our dispenser. May we not be left to our own senses, but, always brought back to the path of your truth, may we strive to practice what you command, so that we may receive the gifts you promise. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0124D] In Gregory’s manuscripts and in the Roman Missal it is found on the Friday after Passion Sunday.] May the perpetual protection of the sacrifice we have received not abandon us, Lord, and may it always drive every harmful thing away from us. Through [Christ], etc.

Be present to your faithful, Lord, and increase the effect of devotion in those who celebrate your holy things, so that they may always offer you the service that is owed and continually advance toward eternal remedies. Through [Christ], etc.

### XIV. Another

Look upon us, God, creator and ruler of all things, and grant that, so that we may feel the effect of your favor, we may serve you with all our heart. Through [Christ], etc.

For confidently 124 seeking your benefits, Lord, we ask that you graciously grant us both the will and the ability to do what is pleasing to you. Through [Christ], etc.

God, author of sincere devotion and peace, grant, we ask, that through this gift we may fittingly venerate your majesty and, through participation in the sacred mystery, be united in faithful understanding. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. You who kindly willed us to exist as your image, so that we might imitate equally the pattern of supreme justice and piety; this we can accomplish in short order if, through your grace, it is granted to us both to strive to love you as our creator and truly and freely to love ourselves, whom you have made. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] This prayer is found in the Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on the Friday before the First Sunday of Lent. It is found again in the same Missal and in the same manuscripts on Easter Day, where the words *uno coelesti pane* (“with one heavenly bread”) have therefore been changed to *sacramentis paschalibus* (“with the Paschal sacraments”).] Pour into us, Lord, the spirit of your charity, so that those whom you have satisfied with one heavenly bread you may make united in one devotion. Through [Christ], etc.

Strengthen, Lord, we ask, the hearts of your children and fortify them by the power of your grace, so that they may be devoted to you in supplication and sincere in mutual love. Through [Christ], etc.

### XV. Another

We ask, almighty God, that you not consider the multitude of our perversity, but draw the fragile away from sins and direct the wills of your people toward what is right. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0125C] Do not repay us, Lord, we ask, with what we deserve for our evil works; rather, protect those whom you rightly correct as having departed from the truth, once they have been corrected through your mercy. Through [Christ], etc.

May the mysteries we have frequently received benefit us, freeing us from earthly desires and teaching us to love heavenly things. Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. So that, continually following divine grace, we may appease through better conduct your justice, which we ceaselessly offend by our sins. And to those who, in their perversity, deserve punishment, may forgiveness be granted when they cease from iniquity. Through [Christ], etc.

May the sacraments we have received cleanse us from every error, Lord, and pour the sweetness of your goodness into our minds. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0125D] [Note: [Col. 0125D] It is found in Muratorius’s Gregorian manuscripts among the daily prayers.] Grant your people, Lord, we ask, the spirit of truth and peace, so that they may know you with their whole mind and, following with all their heart what is pleasing to you, may always possess the benefit of your good gifts. Through [Christ], etc.

125

### XVI. Another

God, protector of those who hope in you, grant, we ask, that we may praise your majesty without ceasing; and, so that we may continually serve you, grant us salvation of mind and body. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] It is found in Gregory’s manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on the Wednesday fast of the seventh month.] May our frailty endure through the remedies of your mercy, Lord, we ask, so that what has failed by its own condition may be restored by your revitalizing power. Through [Christ], etc.

We ask, Lord our God, that these mysteries, which you willed to provide your servants as support in both respects, may confer health upon us inwardly and outwardly. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] A marginal note in the manuscript: “After illness.”] It is truly right. You who scourge your servants bodily for this reason, so that they may advance in mind, powerfully showing how glorious is the salvation of your compassion, when you grant that illness itself may also work medicine for us. Through [Christ], etc.

God, who chastise by loving and refresh us by chastising, [Col. 0126B] grant that we may always be able to give you thanks for both. Through [Christ], etc.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] It is found on the Friday before the First Sunday of Lent both in Gregory’s manuscripts and in the Roman Missal.] Protect your people, Lord, and mercifully cleanse them from all sins, because no adversity will harm them if no iniquity rules over them. Through [Christ], etc.

### XVII. Another

Deliver us, Lord, we ask, from those things that are contrary to the divine will. And since everything by which we live is your work, grant that we, your servants, may be able to please you. Through [Christ], etc.

We ask, Lord, that you not allow us to become such that adversities may rightly hold dominion over us. Rather, grant that we may become the kind of people who are not continually judged unworthy of your benefits. Through [Christ], etc.

May the effect of the sacrifice offered, Lord, we ask, make us suitably fit for the same. Through [Christ], etc.

[Col. 0126C] It is truly right. Imploring your majesty with devoted minds, so that, just as from you we have received the fact that we are what we are, so through your grace we may receive both the willing and the ability to do the good that we desire. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, almighty God, that through the power of the holy mysteries our life may be strengthened. Through [Christ], etc.

May your people, purified by heavenly sacraments, understand what they receive; may they grasp in their conduct what they taste and partake of; and may they receive through your mercy what they seek in 126 just prayers. Through [Christ], etc.

### XVIII. Another

We magnify your clemency, Lord, who grant both forgiveness to sinners and help to the wretched. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant glory to your name, eternal God, since you do not fail to do good even to those who are undeserving. [Col. 0126D] Through [Christ], etc.

It is truly right. Giving thanks and praying that, by making us pleasing to you, you may graciously accept us, though unworthy, whom you assist. Through [Christ], etc.

However much we are able to proclaim you, Lord, [Note: [Col. 0126D] The manuscript erroneously reads *qui perire meritis*. Blanchinius’s emendation is supported by the text of the following prayer.] you who likewise grant joy from sorrow to those who are undeserving. Through [Christ], etc.

Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that your people may turn to you with their whole heart; for those whom you defend even when they transgress, you protect with greater compassion when they are sincerely devoted to you. Through, etc.

### XIX. Another prayer

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that amid the countless errors of the present life we may always be guided by your direction. Through, etc.

Make us, we beseech you, Lord, always pursue what is right and cherish both integrity of conscience and good reputation. Through, etc.

We trust that by the saving effects of your sacrifice, Lord, we are both cleansed and enabled to merit your remedies. [Note: The manuscript has, incorrectly, *servimus effectibus*. We have adopted Muratorius’s emendation.] Through, etc.

It is truly right. Since you are the supreme Reason, and have made us rational beings, it is certain that we depart from participation in you to the extent that we stray from the path of justice, and that we remain in your likeness to the extent that we are not torn away from the order of truth. [Col. 0127B] Through, etc. [Note: The manuscript reads *permaneamus*, incorrectly.]

May your holy things, Lord, both renew us by giving us life and give us life by renewing us. Through, etc.

May the desired blessing confirm your faithful, Lord; may it never allow them to depart from your will, and may it always grant them joy in your benefits. [Note: This is read on the Saturday after the First Sunday of Lent in the Roman Missal.] Through, etc.

### XX. Another prayer

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that we may not heed the insults of corrupt minds, but, having trampled down their perversity, may rationally carry out what is fitting for your household. [Note: The first part of this prayer is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 67, and in the Gregorian codices of Muratorius and Pamelius among the prayers against slanderers.] Through, etc.

God of the heavenly powers, we beseech you, that, despising the falsehoods of the ungodly, we may pursue what will benefit our conscience and reputation. Through, etc.

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that the effect of this offering may enable us both to reject what is displeasing to you and to love what is right. Through, etc.

It is truly right. May you mercifully free us from workers of iniquity, and not permit us either to become guilty through our own excess or to give consent to the impieties of others. But shape our conduct by moderation, so that we may preserve what is just both in ourselves and in others. Through, etc.

Cleanse us, Lord, from our hidden faults, and in your kindness release us from the perversities of others, so that we may receive your holy things with a pure mind. Through, etc.

Look with favor upon your household, Lord, in your reconciled majesty, so that it may be neither infected by its own vices nor bound by external sins, but, freed from both, may always serve you purified. Through, etc.

### XXI. Another prayer

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may serve you with our whole heart, for no hostility will prevail against us if we truly trust in you, Lord. Through, etc.

[Col. 0128A] Come to our aid, Lord, we beseech you, through the reconciliation effected by this sacrifice, whose remedies you graciously use to absolve sinners. Through, etc.

It is truly right. For, while you bestow your benefits upon the undeserving, you admonish us with great compassion that we shall receive far greater gifts if we advance both through instruction in your commandments and through our deeds. Through, etc.

We humbly beseech your majesty, Lord, that you never cease both to cleanse us by heavenly mysteries and to foster us with perpetual protection. Through, etc.

Look favorably upon your household, Lord, we beseech you, and make it more devotedly subject to you, since you do not abandon it in your kindly protection, so that it may receive more abundantly your grace, which it takes up though it has no claim to it. Through, etc.

### XXII. Another prayer

God, who love righteousness and condemn what is unjust, grant us, we beseech you, both to love what is right and to avoid what is perverse. Through, etc.

God, author of truth and mercy, who willed us both not to be sluggish in diligence and not to harm anyone, grant, we beseech you, that we may desire to inflict injury on no one and may beware of the attacks of those who strive to harass us. Through, etc.

May your holy things, Lord, cleanse us from our hidden faults and defend us by perpetual strength from external errors. Through, etc.

It is truly right. We beseech your mercy, Lord, that you grant us to devote ourselves sincerely to divine matters, and do not permit us, under the appearance of religion, to attack sacred realities. For in every way those who strive to oppose your will are enemies of themselves, working rather the destruction of their own salvation than intending, with a hostile mind, to harm your ordinances. [Note: Since *potius* is absent from the manuscript, Blanchinius in his first revisions, and following him Muratorius, more freely substituted this reading: “Who, working the ruin of their own salvation, strive with a hostile mind against your ordinances.” But the emendation noted by Blanchinius in his second revisions, which repairs the text by adding only the adverb *potius* (“rather”), seemed more probable.] Through, etc.

May the reception of the divine gift, Lord, we beseech you, always remove our sins from us and drive away external evils. Through, etc.

Take possession of your people, Lord, through heavenly teachings, so that, avoiding everything evil and pursuing every good thing, they may obtain not your indignation but your constant mercy. Through, etc.

### XXIII. Another prayer

Grant, almighty God, that we may attain the fullness of joy and be more devoted to your majesty. Through, etc.

[Note: This is found in the Gregorian codices and in the Roman Missal among the common prayers for driving away storms.] Lord, we offer praises and gifts, giving thanks for benefits already granted and humbly asking for those still to be granted. Through, etc.

It is truly right. You alone perform great wonders, and not only do you refrain from repaying us according to what we deserve for our sins, but you also bestow the gifts of your consolation upon the undeserving. Granting us, in your loving generosity, a greater impulse toward the worship of your name rather than compelling us by deserved chastisement, you mercifully allow servile fear to pass into the affection of children. Through, etc.

Prostrate before you, Lord, with our whole heart, we humbly implore your goodness: do not cease to support us with temporal aids, and do not fail to instruct us in eternal things. Through, etc.

May your people rejoice, Lord, we beseech you, raised up by your right hand and recovering breath from tribulation; may they be protected by continual assistance, advance in religious conduct, and rejoice both in present and future blessings. Through, etc.

[Note: The manuscript has in the margin: “During a fast.”] We beseech you, almighty God: in your mercy remove all perversities from us and kindly drive away every wickedness. Through, etc.

### XXX. For consecrated virgins

[Col. 0129B]

[Note: This prayer and the following one are found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book I, no. 103, in Gregorian codices, in the blessing of a virgin to be pronounced by the bishop; in the Roman Order apud Hittorpium; and in the Roman Pontifical. These prayers exhibit Leo’s eloquence and formulations.] Look favorably, Lord, upon these your maidservants, so that the purpose of holy virginity, which they undertake at your inspiration, they may preserve under your guidance. Through, etc.

God, gracious inhabitant of chaste bodies and God who love incorrupt souls; God, who restore in your Word, through whom all things were made, the human substance corrupted in the first human beings by the devil’s deceit, so that you not only restore it to the innocence of its first origin but also lead it to the experience of certain blessings to be possessed in the new age, and already raise those still bound by mortal condition to the likeness of angels: look, Lord, upon these your maidservants, who place the purpose of their continence in your hand and offer their devotion to him from whom they received the vows themselves.

For when would a mind enclosed in mortal flesh overcome the law of nature, the freedom of license, the force of habit, and the impulses of age, unless you mercifully kindled this flame, kindly nourished this desire, and supplied this strength? For your grace, poured out upon all nations, adopted heirs of the New Testament from every nation under heaven into an innumerable multitude like the stars. Among the other virtues that you implanted in your children—begotten not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, but from your Spirit—this gift also flowed from the fountain of your generosity into certain minds: although no prohibition had diminished the honor of marriage and the original blessing remained upon holy wedlock, there nevertheless arose souls of higher aspiration who disdained union in the coupling of man and woman, desired its sacrament, and did not imitate what is enacted in marriage but loved what marriage prefigures.

Blessed virginity recognized its author, and, emulating angelic purity, devoted itself to the bridal chamber and the bedroom of him who is the bridegroom of perpetual virginity just as he is the son of perpetual virginity.

Therefore, since they implore your help, Lord, and desire to be strengthened by the consecration of your blessing, grant them the protection and guidance of your defense, lest the ancient enemy, who assails higher aspirations with more subtle snares, creep in through some negligence of the mind to obscure the palm of perfect knowledge and snatch from the purpose of the virgins what ought also, in conduct, to be found in married women. [Note: In the Gregorian codices of Muratorius, the consecration of virgins is set out in these formulas through the end. They also preserve many variant readings.]

May prudent modesty, wise kindness, grave gentleness, and chaste freedom be in them through the gift of your Spirit. Let them burn with love and love nothing outside you; let them live commendably and not desire to be praised. May they glorify you in holiness of body and in purity of mind. May they fear you with love and serve you with love. May you be their honor, their joy, and their will. In sorrow, be their consolation; in uncertainty, their counsel; in injury, their defense; in tribulation, their patience; in poverty, their abundance; in fasting, their food; in sickness, their medicine. May they have everything in you, whom they have chosen above all. Through, etc.

### XXXI

[Note: In the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 52, where this entire Mass is found except for the prayer *Suscipe*, and in the Remesian codices of Menardus and the Gellonensis apud Martene, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 9, section 5, it is entitled: “Here begins the nuptial rite.” In fact, *actio* was used not of the prayers but of the Canon of the Mass, as may be seen more fully in Ducange, s.v. *Actio*, who therefore criticized Menardus when, at no. 1134, he explained *actio nuptialis* as the solemn celebration of Masses in which marriages are blessed. Menardus derived this from the title of his codex, where *actio nuptialis* is called the Mass celebrated for blessing marriages. But that an error entered this heading, which seems to have been transferred from the Gelasian Sacramentary into other sacramentaries, is revealed by our manuscript. This Mass is called the nuptial veiling because a veil was placed upon the couple when the bride and groom were blessed. Saint Ambrose mentions this rite in Letter 19 to Vigilius, no. 17, writing: “Marriage itself ought to be sanctified by priestly veiling and blessing.” Siricius likewise testifies that the same rite existed in the Roman Church, Letter 7 in the edition of P. Coustant, no. 3: “We do not indeed reject the vows of marriage, which we attend with the veil.” The following statement of Nicholas I, *To the Questions of the Bulgarians*, chapter 3, also seems relevant: “Both are led to the nuptial covenant, and first they are placed in the church of the Lord with the offerings which they ought to offer to God through the hand of the priest; then and only then do they receive the blessing and heavenly veil.” Saint Isidore of Seville, book II *On Offices*, chapter 19, and Gratian, cause 30, question 5, canon 7, also touch upon this rite. The following four prayers are also found in the Roman Missal for the Mass for bridegroom and bride; from the fifth, however, only certain sentences were excerpted.] Here begins the nuptial veiling.

Hear us, almighty and merciful God, so that what is administered through our ministry may rather be accomplished by your blessing. Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, we beseech you, the offering presented for the sacred law of marriage, and, as creator of this work, be its director. Through, etc.

Look favorably, Lord, we beseech you, upon this offering of your maidservant (name), which we offer to you for your maidservant (name). For her we humbly implore your majesty: just as you have granted her to reach an age suitable for marriage, so, joined by your gift to marital companionship, bring her to rejoice in the offspring she desires, and kindly lead her, together with her husband, to the desired succession of years. Through, etc.

We beseech you, almighty God, accompany the institutions of your providence with loving favor, and preserve in lasting peace those whom you join in lawful society. Through, etc.

Be present, Lord, to our supplications, and kindly assist your institutions by which you ordained the propagation of the human race, so that what is joined with you as its author may be preserved with you as its helper. Through, etc.

Father, creator of the world, begetter of those who are born, founder of the multiplication of offspring: with your hands you added to Adam a companion, whose bones, growing from his bones, displayed a corresponding form through wondrous diversity. From this, for the increase of the entire multitude, the commanded partnership of the marriage bed bound together the bonds of the human race, so that they might join the whole world together.

For this necessarily pleased you: since what you had made like the human being was far weaker than what you had made like you, God, the weaker sex was added to the stronger, so that two might become one and offspring, mixed from both, might flow forth as an equal pledge. Thus descendants would proceed in ordered succession, and those who came later would follow their predecessors, nor would perishable posterity set itself any limit within so brief a span.

Therefore, Father, sanctify these beginnings of your handmaid for the things to come [the transmitted wording is corrupt], so that, joined in a good and prosperous partnership, she may keep the rights of the eternal law. [Note: In the other cited codices the reading is: “The institutions of the law have been given (read: are given; alternatively, laws) for the future (alternatively, future things). Therefore, [sanctify] the beginnings of this your handmaid,” etc. Whether something has fallen out here in our copyist’s text, or whether later writers added something to explain this obscure passage, we do not know. Blanchinius would prefer to delete the preposition *ad* and the word *venturae*, reading: “Therefore sanctify these beginnings of this your handmaid, Father,” etc.] May she remember, Lord, that she has been entrusted not merely to marital freedom but to the observance of God and the keeping of holy pledges. [Note: The other sacramentaries read *fidei* (“of faith”); shortly afterward, for *delegatam* the other codices have *diligatam*, perhaps *obligatam* (“bound”).] [Note: This prayer is exceedingly corrupt in all the manuscript sacramentaries. *Venturi* seems to be the correct reading. Soon afterward, the other codices have *proponerent* instead of *posteritas*.]

May she marry faithfully and chastely in Christ, and remain an imitator of holy women. May she be lovable to her husband like Rachel, wise like Rebecca, long-lived and faithful like Sarah. May that deceitful author of transgression seize nothing from her; may she remain steadfast, relying upon faith and the commandments. [Note: Two codices have *subdolus* (“deceitful”); the Gelasian has *susceptivus*. The other manuscripts have *nexa* rather than *nixa*.]

May she strengthen her weakness with the force of discipline. Joined to one marriage bed, may she avoid illicit contacts in life. [Note: Our manuscript and the other codices read this way. In the Roman Missal only the word *vitae* (“of life”) is omitted. We therefore cannot approve the emendation indicated by Blanchinius in his first revisions and inserted into the text by Muratorius: “May she avoid illicit contacts.” Blanchinius himself stated in his second revisions that this passage required no correction.] May she be grave in modesty, venerable in chastity, and instructed in heavenly teachings. May she be fruitful in offspring; may she be approved and innocent; and may she reach the rest of the blessed and the heavenly kingdoms. [Note: Some codices have *usque ad coelestia* (“even to the heavenly things”).] Through, etc.

### XXXII. In October: concerning the dryness of the season
