[Note: This is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 44, in Gregorian manuscripts, and in the Roman Missal, as a prayer asking for rain.] God, in whom we live and move and have our being, grant us suitable rain, so that, sufficiently aided by present resources, we may seek eternal things with greater confidence. Through, etc.

Dwell favorably in your household, Lord, we beseech you, and purify the hearts of those subject to you, so that, by clinging to what is pleasing, they may deserve to receive everything that is good. Through, etc.

[Note: This is read in the Gregorian codices of Muratorius in the series of evening or morning prayers.] Hear us, Lord our God, and govern your Church, tossed amid the storms of the world, with merciful direction, so that on a tranquil course it may find the harbor of perpetual security. Through, etc.

[Note: In the Roman Missal it is the Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost; in the Gregorian codices apud Muratorius, the Twelfth; in Menardus, the Thirteenth.] Look favorably, we beseech you, Lord, upon our service, so that what we offer may be an acceptable gift to you and an aid to our weakness. Through, etc.

It is truly right. To whose immeasurable glory it belongs that you not only come to the aid of mortals through your Godhead, but also provide us a remedy from our very mortality, and save the lost from the very source from which (or, according to another reading, by which) they had perished. Through, etc.

[Note: In the same codices and in the Missal, this is read on the Saturday after the Third Sunday of Lent.] We beseech you, almighty God, that we may be numbered among the members of him whose body and blood we share. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the Gregorian manuscripts of Muratorius among the daily prayers and again among the Paschal prayers.] May your right hand perpetually surround your household, Lord, with assistance; and may it, defended from every perversity, accompany it with heavenly gifts and lead it, through the generosity of your grace, to the rewards of good things. Through, etc.

### II. Another prayer

Almighty and eternal God, look favorably upon our senses, so that, abstaining from earthly pleasures, we may meditate more earnestly upon heavenly things. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that through these things which are to be accomplished in these offerings we may be saved. Through, etc.

It is truly right. We implore your mercy with poured-out prayers: looking upon the capacity of human condition, grant that those for whom you have provided such great remedies may be made capable of them. Through, etc.

May the working of your power, Lord, be poured into our minds and bodies, so that what we have received by participation we may obtain in full redemption. Through, etc.

May your faithful people advance, Lord, moved by your compassion and devoted with saving contrition; may they gratefully carry out what you command, so that they may receive what you promise. Through, etc.

### III. Another prayer

[Note: The manuscript has in the margin: “Near Easter.”] Grant us forgiveness of sins, Lord, so that we may carry out the Paschal observances with dispositions pleasing to you. Through, etc.

[Note: The codices of Muratorius and the Roman Missal present this prayer on Septuagesima Sunday and elsewhere.] Having received our gifts and prayers, Lord, cleanse us through heavenly mysteries and mercifully hear us. Through, etc.

It is truly right. We humbly ask that you grant us both security in our circumstances and an increase of religious devotion, so that we may celebrate with peaceful and devout minds the great mystery of your mercy and of peace. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the same codices and in the Missal in the Mass for the Saturday after Passion Sunday.] Satisfied by the generosity of the divine gift, we beseech you, Lord our God, that we may always live in participation in it. Through, etc.

[Note: In the Gregorian manuscripts of Muratorius it is read among the daily prayers.] Preserve your household, Lord, we beseech you, and mercifully purify it by the abundance of your blessings, so that it may be increased both by your teachings and by your gifts. Through, etc.

### IV. Another prayer

Show favor, Lord, to the peoples who trust in you, and extend the right hand of your protection to guard the Roman name, so that the kingdom devoted to your majesty may always be defended by your power. [Note: In the preceding Mass, and in another shortly afterward, no. 6, there is mention of the Paschal festivals. Perhaps this and the following intermediate Masses, in which divine aid is sought against the Roman enemies, were composed on the occasion of Attila, whom some reasonably suppose to have invaded Italy around Easter.] Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, we beseech you, the offerings of minds devoted to your name, through which you have granted us both to be cleansed from earthly contamination and to draw near to heavenly fellowship. Through, etc.

[Note: It corresponds to the Gelasian preface, book I, no. 65, for the Sunday after the Ascension.] It is truly right. By whose ineffable grace this singular mystery is at work among us: that, once lost and cast down, we may now return to that glory in which, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we may be called a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a people for possession, and a holy nation. Through, etc.

[Note: With a few changes at the beginning, the same text is repeated above in section 27, no. 3. See note 26 there (Col. 107, no. b).] May this sacrament of yours, Lord, we beseech you, be for us the abolition of sins, the strength of human weakness, and a bulwark against the dangers of the world. May this communion cleanse us from guilt and grant us to share in heavenly joy. Through, etc.

### V. Another prayer

[Col. 0134A] Almighty and eternal God, perform the ancient miracles of your arm in protecting the faithful peoples, so that, after our enemies have been subdued by your power, Roman devotion may serve you in safety. Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, we beseech you, the offerings which we present to you for the salvation of your people, and grant that, serving through heavenly sacraments, we may be free from every fault. Through, etc.

It is truly right. You who, through the ineffable power of your Word, are both the creator of the human race and its most merciful restorer. Through, etc.

### VI. Another prayer

God, who have established the remedies of human salvation in the solemnity of the present mystery, grant us that, just as we have learned of them through the preaching of your apostles, so we may obtain them through their intercession. Through, etc.

Mercifully receive the gifts of your people, Lord, we beseech you, so that what they profess with the devotion of faith they may grasp through heavenly sacraments. [Note: The plural number is frequently used when the collective noun *plebs* (“people”) governs the verb. Thus the emendation to the singular *profiteatur* (“let it profess”) and *apprehendat* (“let it grasp”) is unnecessary.] Through, etc.

It is truly right. In whose wondrous resurrection death killed the redeemed, and life arose for believers. And therefore, with the angels, etc.

### XXXIII. For the dead

#### I

Almighty and eternal God, who have granted your faithful the remedies of life after death, mercifully and graciously grant, we beseech you, that the soul of your servant (name), cleansed from every sin, may rest in the portion of your redemption. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 100, and in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratorius in the Mass for several deceased persons.] We humbly present offerings to you, Lord, that through these offices of devoted reconciliation the soul of your servant (name) may obtain perpetual mercy. Through, etc.

[Note: This is also read in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 104. We have retained the manuscript’s reading, so that there is no need to delete the words “(name) your servant” and write *offerimus* (“we offer”). The manuscript alone has the erroneous *offeret* (“will offer”) instead of *offert* (“offers”).] Therefore look favorably, Lord, upon this offering of your servant (name), which he or she offers to you for the soul of your servant (name), and in the abundance of your mercies grant that whatever was contracted through earthly life may be cleansed by these sacrifices and, released from the bonds of death, may deserve passage to life. Through, etc.

#### II

[Note: It is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 98, and in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratorius, in the Mass for the dead who were unable to obtain the desired penance.] Almighty and merciful God, in whose power every human condition rests, release the soul of your servant (name), we beseech you, from all sins, so that it may not lose the fruit of penance which its will desired because death came first. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the Gelasian and Vatican manuscripts mentioned in the preceding note.] May the offering of the present sacrifice satisfy you, Lord, we beseech you, on behalf of the soul of your servant (name), and may it find the forgiveness of sins which it sought; and what it could not complete through the ministry of speech, may it receive through compensation for the penance it desired. [Note: In the manuscript, and consequently in the printed editions, *Per* (“Through”) is wrongly inserted and the text begins anew with “And what through the office of speech.” Yet the present prayer continues, as is clear from the Gelasian and Vatican codices. In the margin of the manuscript is added: “Therefore, this offering,” indicating that the same prayer described in the preceding Mass is to be repeated here as well; indeed, it is repeated in the cited codices.] Through, etc.

This offering, therefore, etc. (as above).

#### III

Almighty and merciful God, before whom the human will is regarded as deeds, grant, we beseech you, that for the soul of your servant (name) it may suffice, for obtaining complete remedy, to have desired penance with longing. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, remission of sins to the soul of your servant through these sacraments of eternal redemption, so that the devotion of penance which his or her heart bore may obtain the effect of perpetual salvation. Through, etc.

[Note: It is read in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 98, and in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratorius, no. 107.] God, from whom every good thing is inspired in human hearts: just as you granted the soul of your servant the desire for penance, so in your compassion grant the forgiveness it desired. Through, etc.

[Note: In the Gelasian Sacramentary, no. 100, and in the Roman Missal, for several deceased persons.] God, to whom alone it belongs to provide healing after death, grant, we beseech you, that the soul of your servant (name), stripped of earthly contamination, may be counted among those who share in your redemption. Through, etc.

By these sacrifices, Lord, we beseech you, through which you grant purification both to the living and to the dead, mercifully release the soul of your servant, so that it may await the day of resurrection with the sure hope of rejoicing. Through, etc.

[Col. 0135C] [Note: In the Gelasian Sacramentary, in the same place.] Grant, Lord, we beseech you, everlasting mercy to the soul of your servant (name)—or, according to another reading, immeasurable mercy—so that, freed from mortal bonds, eternal light may possess it. Through, etc.

[Note: It agrees with the prayer for several deceased persons found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 95, the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratorius, no. 110, and the Roman Missal.] God, creator and redeemer of the souls of the faithful, grant your servant remission of all sins, so that he or she may obtain the forgiveness always desired. Through, etc.

#### IV

[Note: In the Gelasian Sacramentary this prayer and the first prayer of the following Mass are found in book III, no. 95. But the name of Laurence is omitted, and the common formula has been substituted, indicating that the ancients celebrated both the feast of the saints, or of a particular saint, and offered intercession for a bishop who had died on the same day, in one and the same Mass. From our Sacramentary it can be inferred that the death of a Roman pontiff occurred on a feast day or within the octave of Saint Laurence. From the fourth to the fifth century, this can fit no other Roman bishop except Sixtus III. Since he is said in the Pontifical to have been buried near the body of Saint Laurence, it seems to us highly probable that he died within the octave of this martyr. For Leo, his successor, was consecrated on 29 September 440, as we shall show in note 1 (Col. 193, no. a) of Quesnell’s first dissertation for that same year. After the death of Sixtus III, the Roman Church remained without a bishop for forty and more days, awaiting the arrival of the deacon Leo with remarkable peace and patience, as Prosper says in his Chronicle under the year 440. Two points should be observed here. First, it does not say merely forty days but “forty and more,” which may signify approximately three or four days beyond forty. Second, these intervening days refer not to Leo’s ordination but to his arrival in the city. Even if he was ordained on Sunday, 29 September, as was customary, he could nevertheless have returned to Rome several days earlier, so that the Sunday of his ordination still had to be awaited. With these points established, if from Leo’s arrival several days before the Sunday that then fell on 29 September one counts backward forty and more days, one arrives conveniently at a day within the octave of Saint Laurence, on which Sixtus III can be understood to have died. And if Sixtus was ordained on Sunday, 24 July 432, then, counting the eight years and nineteen days assigned by Prosper to his pontificate, one finds that he died on 11 August, the second day within the octave of Saint Laurence. Perhaps Leo, his successor, composed some of these prayers, which were used on the anniversary of Sixtus’s death.] Through the intercession of your blessed martyr Laurence, Lord, we beseech you, protect us, and join the soul of your servant (name), the bishop, to the company of your saints. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 97.] Look favorably, Lord, we beseech you, upon our offerings, which we present both in honor of your holy martyr Laurence, to the name of your majesty, and which we humbly offer for the repose of your servant (name), the bishop. Through, etc.

[Col. 0136B] It is truly right. You both refresh us by the commemoration of your saints and defend us by their prayer. Through, etc.

This offering, therefore, etc.; and grant that he may be counted among the priests pleasing to you. Through, etc.

#### V

[Note: The same is found in the same place, no. 95.] Help us, Lord our God, entreated by the prayers of your blessed martyr Laurence, and place the soul of your servant (name), the bishop, in the light of eternal blessedness. Through, etc.

Remember, Lord, we beseech you, the soul of your servant (name), the bishop, and, since you willed him, while established in the body, to hold the helm of the apostolic see, place him among the number of your chosen priests. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the same Gelasian Sacramentary, in the same place, no. 93, in the Gregorian manuscript of Menardus, and in the Roman Missal in the Mass for a deceased priest.] Receive, Lord, we beseech you, offerings for the soul of your servant (name), the bishop, so that, to him to whom you granted pontifical merit, you may also grant the reward. Through, etc.

[Col. 0136C] This offering, therefore, etc., so that he who followed the see of the blessed apostle Peter in the vicarious office may also, through the generosity of your grace, receive a perpetual share in apostolic dignity. Through, etc.

[Note: It is found in the same codices and in the Missal, as well as in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript of Muratorius among the prayers for ordaining a bishop, p. 272. Shortly afterward Muratorius has *in coelesti sede* (“in the heavenly seat”), as in the Missal. But all the Gelasian and Gregorian codices likewise delete the preposition *in* (“in”).] Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that the soul of your servant (name), the bishop, whom you adorned with sacred gifts while he dwelt in this world, may always rejoice in glory in the heavenly seat. Through, etc.

[Note: See the Gelasian Sacramentary, book III, no. 92; the Gregorian codex apud Menardus; and the Roman Missal for a deceased bishop.] God, who made your servant (name) a flourishing bishop among the apostolic priests, grant, we beseech you, that he may also possess their eternal seat. Through, etc.

### XXXIV. Saint Sylvester

[Note: This Mass does not pertain to the feast of Saint Sylvester, which falls on the final day of December. Rather, it was once composed for his burial and, having been found by the compiler, was placed by him among the Masses for the dead.] God, portion of the dead who confess you, mercifully receive our prayers, which we offer at the burial of your servant Sylvester, the bishop, so that he who faithfully discharged ministry in your name may rejoice in the perpetual fellowship of your saints. Through, etc.

Look favorably, Lord, we beseech you, upon this offering, which we humbly sacrifice in commemoration of your holy confessor and bishop Sylvester, so that the devotion of this act of piety may benefit us and everlasting blessedness glorify him. Through, etc.

We humbly implore your majesty, Lord, that the soul of your servant [Note: Some think that, through a copyist’s carelessness, the name Simplicius was written instead of Sylvester, who is named in the two preceding prayers, so that this would be the postcommunion prayer of the Mass of Saint Sylvester. But since it is not foreign to our compiler to insert among the common Masses certain prayers bearing the name of a particular saint—as we have seen with Saint Tiburtius, Saint Gregory, and Saint Laurence—so here he placed after the common prayers for the dead prayers displaying the names Sylvester and Simplicius. These prayers seem to have been taken from the common prayers for a deceased bishop and recited at their burials.] Simplicius, the bishop, stripped of everything he acquired through human life, may be counted among the company of the holy shepherds. Through, etc.

### XXXV. In November: on the feast of the four Crowned Saints
[Col. 0137C] I.— [Note: [Col. 0138C] This is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book II, no. 62, where, after a few intervening words, our manuscript likewise reads *recurrimus*, so that there is no need to emend it to *recolimus*.] We return annually to the vows of your martyrs, Lord, earnestly beseeching your majesty that, together with temporal increases, we may receive an increase of eternal prosperity. Through, etc.

For the anniversaries of the martyrs, Lord, we heap your altars with gifts. Grant, we beseech you, that holy joys may grow for us, by which the devotion of our dedication may advance. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0138C] See a similar preface in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratori, p. 340, and in another manuscript of Menard, p. 139. Moreover, the word “patrons” shows that the church was dedicated in antiquity under the name of the four holy Crowned Martyrs.] It is truly worthy. As we celebrate the anniversaries of the holy patron saints, because, while the glory of your name is continually proclaimed through them, the help of our frailty increases. Through, etc.

II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] It is found in Gelasian, book II, no. 62, and in the Roman Missal on 29 July, at the commemoration of Saints Felix, Simplicius, and their companions.] We bring you offerings, Lord, in commemoration of your martyrs, beseeching that they may bestow upon us alike pardon and salvation. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For you are magnified in the praise of your saints. Whatever pertains to their precious passion is the wondrous work of your power: you mercifully grant the ardor of this faith; you inspire [139] steadfastness in endurance; you bestow victory in the contest. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Gelasius, in the same place.] May the festivals of your saints, Lord, always gladden us and commend us to your majesty through perpetual appeasement. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] It is read in the Roman Missal on 29 July, at the anniversary of Saints Felix and his companions. At the end, the manuscript has *celebrant* and *comprehendant* in the plural, because the word *populus* is often understood as a plural collective noun, as we have observed elsewhere.] Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that just as the Christian people rejoices together in the temporal solemnity of your martyrs, so it may enjoy the eternal one, and may attain in reality what it celebrates in its vows. Through, etc.

XXXVI. On the anniversary of Saint Cecilia.

I.—Lord, we beseech you, let us experience your propitiation through the present celebration, so that, when our offerings have been received through the intercession of that holy woman, [Note: [Col. 0138D] The manuscript has *interveniente*, perhaps for *interventione*, as shortly afterward in another prayer it has *interventionibus*. Muratori, together with Blanchini, emended this to *intercessione*, repeated from the same prayer in the Mass of Saints Clement and Felicity. This is a common prayer, as is recognized from its very formula; for that reason it was also adapted to the feast of Saints Clement and Felicity.] you may grant us pardon and bestow saving gifts. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. On this day of the present festival, on which Saint Cecilia became a martyr through confession of your name. Although devoted to a human marriage, she scorned a temporal bridal chamber and, in anticipation of the reward of chastity, took as her bridegroom him who would be eternal; [Col. 0138C] she preferred eternal life to giving origin to a worldly lineage. To her glory this too was added: she joined Valerian, to whom she was to be united by the law of marriage, to herself forever as a chaste martyr-companion, and led him with her to the crown. Through, etc.

We rejoice together both in receiving the bread of righteousness and in the festival of your saints, Lord, because we trust that what we have received through the intercessions of those pleasing to you will benefit us for eternal life. (Another reading: “will advance us.”) Through, etc.

[Col. 0139A] Faithful hearts, subject to your name, ask for your help, Lord, so that, since without you they can accomplish nothing that is just, by the mercy you bestow they may both grasp what is right and receive everything that will benefit them. Through, etc.

II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] It is found in the Gelasian Sacramentary, book II, no. 64. The beginning of this prayer agrees with the opening of a prayer read in Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on the anniversary of Saint Agnes, and elsewhere. Its ending, however, is different.] Almighty and eternal God, who choose the weak things of the world in order to confound all that is strong, grant us to rejoice with fitting devotion on the festival of Saint Cecilia the martyr, so that we may both praise your power in her passion [140] and receive the help prepared for us. Through, etc.

God, author and giver of every good thing, who, in order to summon the human race to confession of your name, perfected martyrdom even in a frail condition, grant, we beseech you, that your Church, admonished by this example, may neither fear to suffer for you nor fail to desire the glory of the heavenly reward. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] It is found in Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on 3 May, at the anniversary of Saints Alexander and his companions, and elsewhere.] Upon these offerings, Lord, we beseech you, let abundant blessing descend, which may mercifully work sanctification in us and gladden us through the solemnity of the martyrs. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] This preface is supplied by the Gothic Missal apud Cardinal Thomasius in the Mass of Saint Cecilia.] It is truly worthy. You perfect strength in weakness. Thus blessed and glorious Cecilia, scorning worldly marriage and striving toward the heavenly fellowship, was hindered neither by unstable age, nor recalled by the allurements of the flesh, nor deterred by the frailty of her sex. Rather, amid girlhood, amid the blandishments of the world, amid the tortures of her persecutors, the chaste virgin and martyr completed a manifold victory and brought with her into the heavenly kingdoms, to a more excellent triumph, the man to whom she had been married. Through, etc.

[Col. 0139C] III. Another.

Let the gifts of the supplicant Church, Lord, be pleasing in your sight; and, that they may benefit our salvation, let the blessed intercession of the saints be present. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. In order that a greater triumphal procession might be led over the enemy of the human race, you destroyed the devil’s tyranny not only through Christ our Lord; and not only, for the overthrow of the first parent, do you return reciprocal, deserved vengeance to the deceiver through the manly sex of the blessed martyrs, but also, through the female condition, you rightly turn retribution against the enemy of our mother Eve. Thus he who had wickedly cast down both sexes, trusting in their paradise-felicity, might now be trampled by both through your grace. Saint Cecilia, bearing witness to this in her confession today (another reading: “accomplishing this”), nevertheless, so that she might not depart from the faith promised in marriage, made the man whom she was to have as her husband (another reading: “whom she was to receive in marriage”) a companion of her passion. Through, etc.

IV. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] On the anniversary of Saint Prisca, 18 January, this prayer is found in Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal.] Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we may both rejoice in the annual solemnity of Saint Cecilia the martyr [141] and advance through the example of such great faith. Through, etc.

As we recall the festivals of Saint Cecilia, we offer prayers and sacrifice offerings. Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that they may provide us with both temporal protection and increases of life [Note: [Col. 0139D] The manuscript erroneously has *perpetua*, “perpetual.”]. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For just as the devil rightly struck down the human race in both sexes through a perverse confession, so through a magnificent confession in both sexes he is conquered by your grace. [Note: [Col. 0140D] Muratori, following a marginal note by Blanchini, thought *utriusque* should be restored; but he did not notice Blanchini’s later retraction. The manuscript reading agrees quite well with the verb *triumphatur*, “is triumphed over.”] The victory is more illustrious when that exalted substance, which vaunted itself to be like the Most High and rejoiced that in the fall of man it had overthrown God’s work, is overcome through the female condition. Blessed Cecilia the martyr illumines the day of this glory for us: assigned to earthly marriage, she married in heaven; dedicated to worldly wedlock, [Col. 0140B] she attained divine fellowship; and she made the temporal husband to whom she was to be joined according to mortal custom eternal to herself, a chaste virgin through the bond of martyrdom. Through, etc.

V. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] It is found in Gelasian, book II, no. 64, and in the Ambrosian Missal apud Pamelius.] We beseech you, God of the heavenly powers, that the sacrifices offered for the solemnity of Saint Cecilia may teach us to scorn temporal desires and cause us to seek the gifts of heavenly joys. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For a wondrous reversal has been granted to us today: our enemy, who overthrew man, conspicuous for the happiness of paradise and ignorant of every death, when, trusting in his own integrity, he did not seek divine protection, through serpentine cunning is now cast down amid the miseries of this world and the exile of the condemned human condition by mortal frailty, trusting in you. And whereas the first woman is reported to have led her husband to the fall, now a maiden’s confession, going before her husband, leads him to the reward. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] In Gelasian, in the same place, and in the Roman Missal among the common prayers of virgins.] Hear us, God our Savior, so that, just as we rejoice in the festival of Saint Cecilia, we may likewise be instructed in the devotion of a pious commitment. Through, etc.

Look upon your people, Lord, we beseech you, rejoicing in the glorification of Saint Cecilia the martyr, and grant that the service of minds consecrated to you may become pleasing, so that those who do not cease to honor you in your saints may obtain the perpetual abundance of your gifts [142] and may grasp invisibly what they perform visibly. Through, etc.

XXXVII. 9 Kalends of December. The anniversary of Saints Clement and Felicity.

[Col. 0140D]

I.— [Note: [Col. 0140D] It is reported in Menard’s Gregorian manuscript and apud Pamelius, vol. II, p. 354.] Almighty and eternal God, who are wondrous in the virtue of all your saints, grant us to rejoice in the annual solemnity of blessed Clement, who, as the martyr and bishop of your Son, confirmed by his witness what he carried out in his ministry and strengthened by his example what he preached with his mouth. Through, etc.

Your propitiation, Lord, etc. [Note: [Col. 0141D] Here the first prayer is repeated, the one read above in the first Mass on the anniversary of Saint Cecilia.]

[Note: [Col. 0141D] It is found in Cardinal Thomasius’s Gothic Missal on the anniversary of Saint Clement. Moreover, this preface and the third and fourth prefaces are taken from the books of the *Recognitions* attributed to Saint Clement, which Rufinus translated into Latin and which Gelasius later listed among the apocryphal writings.] It is truly worthy. As we celebrate the anniversary of your martyr Saint Clement, who left family and homeland and, traversing lands and seas for the fragrance of your name, denying himself, took up the cross of pilgrimage in order to follow you in the footsteps of your apostles. To him, Lord, according to the promise of your Son, you repaid a hundredfold reward both in the present age and in the future. For, after he had soon been handed over to the instruction of the most blessed Peter, you restore to him in a foreign region the parents whom he had lost in his native land [Note: [Col. 0141D] In our manuscript, as also erroneously in the Gothic Missal, *restitues*, “you will restore,” is found. After a little more, only our manuscript has *constitues*, while the Gothic Missal correctly has *constituis*, “you establish.”]; you return to him as participants in the divine nature those whom he had lost through earthly generation. Then, by appointing in succession the vicar of his teacher [Note: [Col. 0141D] Here *vicarius* is understood as “successor,” as it frequently is in other authors; the context itself shows this. A little later, in place of *proque*, the manuscript through scribal carelessness has *pro quae*; the Gothic Missal has *pro quo*.], you establish him as ruler of the Roman City, whose dignity he had despised for your sake, and instead of transient splendor you make him renowned with heavenly honor. Finally, exalted by the glory of martyrdom, you raise him from temporal achievements to an eternal crown. Through, etc.

II. Another.

May our prayers rise to you, Lord, and may the vows of your faithful reconcile the offerings humbly presented, so that, even if we do not deserve this through our own works, we may, we beseech you, deserve it through the intercession of the saints. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For rightly, Lord, we glory in the triumphs of your martyrs, because in their victories we confess your wonders, rejoicing today in the festival of your priest [143] and martyr Saint Clement; him whom heavenly dwelling received, instructed by the teachings of the blessed apostle Peter, raised to the pontificate of the apostolic see, and crowned with glory at the end of his renowned martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0142D] The manuscript incorrectly has *finis*, “end.”]. Through, etc.

III. Another.

May your devoted Church, Lord, reverently receive the anniversary of your blessed priest and martyr Clement, and may it become more devoted through love of his great glorification. Through, etc.

May the intercession of Saint Clement, your priest and martyr, reconcile our gifts with your mercy, Lord, so that what our merits do not supply may be balanced by the supplication of your saints. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For through the generosity of the Holy Spirit that blessed Clement consecrated the feeling of our rejoicing today in the contest of his magnificent passion [Col. 0141D]; noble in the world, nobler through love of Christ, conspicuous for his devoted labor, and wondrous both in the seeking and recovery of his parents, he shone forth as an excellent priest and distinguished martyr, received as the most faithful pupil of apostolic preaching. Through, etc.

IV. Another.

Receive, we beseech you, Lord, the offerings granted to us through your favor, since they proceed from you as their creator, and since you established the causes of human salvation and glory through which they are pleasing to you. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For today the praises of Clement, blessed for us, must be proclaimed again. Inflamed by divine inspiration, he left his homeland, following your preachers [Note: [Col. 0142D] Something is missing here.], and found his lost parents in foreign lands. Humble in foreign regions, he followed the glory of Christ and received the highest dignity of his own city. He placed the present life after Christ and deserved the triumph of eternal blessedness. Through, etc.

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that for the honor [Col. 0142B] of your name we may also be strengthened by continual prayers, whose distinguished deeds we celebrate. Through, etc.

On the anniversary of Saint Felicity.

I.—Merciful and almighty God, who make us, as we run from virtue to virtue in due veneration (another reading: “service”), rejoice through the prayers of your saints [144], grant that those whose solemnities console us may be aided by prayers. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] It is found in the Roman Missal on 7 March, at the anniversary of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, and among the common prayers of many virgins and martyrs, and elsewhere.] Regard, Lord, we beseech you, the gifts placed upon your altars in commemoration of Saint Felicity, your martyr, so that, just as through these blessed mysteries you conferred glory upon her, you may bestow pardon upon us. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. In the rejoicing of today’s festival, on which the blessed mother perfected through your grace the sacred flock begotten in the flesh by death. Behold the one in whom, as it is written, Wisdom built herself a house, furnished with seven columns. Behold the woman who fulfilled in deeds what she had anticipated in name; and not only was Felicity glorious through the prosperity of her fertility, but she remained the same even amid adversity, which death could not take away from her, but rather made eternal. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] In Gelasian, book II, no. 92, at the anniversary of Saint Cecilia.] As we pour out the blessed mysteries of your table, Lord, we beseech you that through the intervention of the holy martyrs they may grant us both present (another reading: “temporal”) mercy and eternal mercy. Through, etc.

Protect your people, Lord, and grant through the prayers of the just that the people whom you make devoted through the continual festival of your martyrs may always become pleasing to you. [Col. 0142D] Through, etc.

II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] This prayer is reported by the Roman Missal in the places indicated in the notes, 22 (above, no. g).] Grant us, Lord our God, to venerate the palms of the holy martyrs with unceasing devotion, so that those whom we cannot celebrate with a worthy mind we may at least honor through humble services. Through, etc.

Receive the gifts of your faithful, Lord, for the solemnity of the holy martyrs; and grant, through the generosity of your grace, that our services may be pleasing to you. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For great are your works, Lord, and immense your marvels, through which the joy of today’s festival has come to us. Truly, the sons of Felicity—and true is the Felicity of her sons—were begotten by the fertile mother, first through the chaste fruitfulness of a holy marriage, and again, conceived in the womb of sacred confession, were more happily borne by the blessed martyr through faith as martyrs to the crown. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] It is found in Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on the Monday after the Third Sunday of Lent, and on the feast of Saint Theodore.] Grant, Lord, we beseech you, through the intercession of your saints, that what we have touched with our mouth we may receive with a pure mind. [Col. 0143B] Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] It is found in Muratori’s Gregorian manuscripts among the series of daily prayers.] Deliver, Lord, we beseech you, the people who pray to you from sins and enemies, so that, living in holy conduct, they may be afflicted by no adversities. Through, etc.

[145] III. Another.

May the holy martyrs, Lord, we beseech you, aid us both by their names and by their prayers, so that your Clement may ask us to follow wise clemency, and Felicity, consecrated to you, may ask us truly to be happy. Through, etc.

As we proclaim you wondrous, Lord, in the precious passions of your saints, we bring votive gifts. Grant, we beseech you, that just as their merits are pleasing to you, so the services of our devotion may be made acceptable. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For today, by your gift, the magnificent mother and martyr is celebrated. A glorious offspring through a similar passion. A glorious Church in such members. And rightly blessed in all things is Felicity. Through, etc.

We have been filled, Lord, with the sacraments and joys that in the celebrations of your saints we both frequently attend and receive. Through, etc.

Lord, we beseech you, always cause your people to rejoice in the patronage of the holy martyrs, so that it may continually receive through the support of your just ones those benefits which it is not sufficient to obtain by its own supplications. Through, etc.

XXXVIII. 8 Kalends of December. The anniversary of Saints Chrysogonus and Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The Mass of Saint Chrysogonus, whose name was formerly inserted in the Canon, is read on 8 Kalends of December in the Gregorian Sacramentary. But nowhere have we found mention of Saint Gregory by Saint Gregory on this day. Yet, just as one does not easily find elsewhere information about several holy martyrs who are mentioned in this Sacramentary in December, so it is not surprising that this Saint Gregory is not mentioned in other records. Concerning him, see also above, in April, Mass XXXIII, and note 40 there (Col. 31, no. i).]

[Col. 0143D]

We rejoice, Lord, in the multiplied festival of the saints, because we do not doubt that we shall receive your gifts, for the obtaining of which you have granted us such great patrons. Through, etc.

Perfect, Lord, the votive mysteries, and may the suffrages that proclaim you in the veneration of the martyrs become for us the means of perpetual redemption. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For that heavenly fire so inflames the hearts of the blessed martyrs that everything pleasant in the light of this world is rejected for love of your name, and whatever is bitter in temporal terms is endured, so that they may receive the rewards of your promise. Through, etc.

May the precious endurance of the just, Lord, we beseech you, increase in us the feeling of love and always exercise in our hearts the steadfastness of sacred faith. Through, etc.

[Col. 0144B] God, who gave your saints strength for a devout confession amid torments [146], grant faithful peoples constancy in the truth amid the temptations of this world, so that, just as the Holy Spirit strengthened those saints and led them onward to everlasting glory, so may your grace continually guide these people and bring them to eternal mercy. Through, etc.

XXXIX. The day before the Kalends of December. The anniversary of Saint Andrew the apostle.

I.— [Note: [Col. 0144D] In the Gregorian Sacramentary this is assigned to Vespers of the same holy apostle.] Grant us, we beseech you, Lord our God, to be lifted up through the intercessions of your blessed apostle Andrew, so that through those by whom you granted the Church the beginnings of heavenly grace, you may bestow the aids of perpetual salvation. Through, etc.

[Col. 0144C] [Note: [Col. 0144D] The first part of this prayer is adapted to the feast of Saint Apollinaris on 23 July in the Roman Missal.] Regard, we beseech you, Lord, the gifts that we bring for the commemoration of your blessed apostle Andrew, earnestly imploring that we may be helped through his intercessions, for whose merits they are sacrificed. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] It is found in the Gelasian manuscript, book II, no. 69, and in the Vatican Gregorian manuscript apud Muratori in the Mass of the vigil, and in another Mass of the feast of the same apostle; in Menard’s Gregorian Sacramentary, at the anniversary of Saint Thomas the apostle.] It is truly worthy. For you granted your Church to stand upon apostolic foundations. As we celebrate the solemnity of blessed Andrew from their fellowship, we do not remain silent about your praises, Lord. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] This prayer is supplied by Gregorian manuscripts and by the Roman Missal at the anniversary of Saint Andrew.] We have received the divine mysteries, Lord, rejoicing in the festival of your blessed apostle Andrew; perfect them, we beseech you, so that, just as they benefit your saints for glory, they may benefit us for pardon. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, to your household that it may celebrate in security and always pursue with its whole mind the joy of heart that it has received from the veneration of your blessed apostle Andrew. Through, etc.

II. Another.

We humbly ask you, God, to grant us to celebrate this day with fitting joys, on which the sacred anniversary of your blessed apostle Andrew has dawned, magnificent through confession of your majesty [145]; and likewise grant us more abundant times and progress in this devotion. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] It is found in the same Gregorian manuscripts and in the Missal in the Mass of the vigil of the same apostle.] We offer you, Lord, a sacred gift, by which, as we recall the solemnity of blessed Andrew, we also implore purification for our minds. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. In this present festival, on which the venerable blood of your apostle Andrew was poured out. He is kin to your glorious apostle [147] Peter in the lot of his birth, in fellowship of faith [Note: [Col. 0145D] See Pamelius, vol. I, p. 436.], in the fellowship of apostolic dignity, and in the glory of martyrdom, so that those whom your grace had bound with so many bonds of devotion in the course of this life might be joined by a similar crown in the heavenly kingdom. Through, etc.

[Col. 0145B] May the saving reception of your sacrament benefit us, we beseech you, Lord, in the commemoration of your saints, so that it may both free us from the vices of mortality and make us companions of perpetual mercy. Through, etc.

Be propitiated, Lord, and be the protector and ruler of your people; at the prayers of your saints, grant them remission of sins; grant the effect of a better life; in your kindness provide temporal consolations; and lavish upon them the promised gifts of eternity. Through, etc.

III. Another.

God, giver of all virtues and good things, grant, we beseech you, that the solemnities of your blessed apostle Andrew may always be present to us for veneration, and his desired protections for our aid. Through, etc.

As the faithful people rejoices in the gifts offered, Lord, because it trusts that both the joys of the apostolic passion [Note: [Col. 0145D] This prayer appears corrupt, and something is missing in it.] and the proclamation of you as wondrous in them contribute to the increase of its salvation. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. You wondrously work remedies for us through the worship of your name and the veneration of the saints. By this very fast, which, as we anticipate the festivals of your blessed apostle Andrew, we offer before the eyes of your majesty, may we likewise receive salutary abstinence of mind and body, advance through an observance that will benefit us, and, with the senses of the body quieted, be prepared in greater purity for so great an anniversary. Through, etc.

May we be instructed and helped, Lord, we beseech you, by these celebrations, through which the martyrdoms of your blessed apostle Andrew, having gone before, grant us heavenly joy. Through, etc.

May the Christian people report the effects of holy rejoicing concerning those whom it has embraced with devout dedication, so that it may become both joyful through the veneration of your blessed apostle Andrew and secure through his intercession. Through, etc.

[Col. 0146A] IV. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] It is found in Gelasian, book II, no. 69, in all Gregorian manuscripts, and in the Roman Missal.] We earnestly beseech your majesty [148], Lord, that just as the holy apostle Andrew was a preacher and ruler of your Church, so he may be its perpetual advocate. Through, etc.

We recount the solemnity of your blessed apostle Andrew, Lord, so that we may receive your benefits through his aid, for whom we offer you sacrifices of praise. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Compare this preface with the fuller version in the Ottobonian Gregorian manuscript apud Muratori, on 3 Kalends of December.] It is truly worthy. For there is present the day of the magnificent votive martyrdom on which the venerable Andrew showed himself kin to the blessed apostle Peter both in the preaching of your Christ and in confession, and in a shared passion and glory completed and filled out the number of apostolic dignity [Note: [Col. 0145D] Something appears to be missing here. See Pamelius, vol. I, p. 436, and the cited Ottobonian manuscript, vol. II of Muratori, p. 343.], so that, since they had one cause of struggle, they might have one reward and one recompense. Through, etc.

We beseech you, almighty God, not to allow us to be wounded by worldly assaults, since those whom you have established under your providence are not abandoned by apostolic protections. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we beseech you, that your Church may rejoice under such great princes and understand what it follows in devotion, so that, governed by your dispositions, it may deserve through perpetual participation to reach those whom it now venerates in service. Through, etc.

XL. In December. 8 Kalends of January. The anniversary of the Lord and of the martyrs Pastor, Basileus, Jovianus, Victorinus, Eugenia, Felicity, and Anastasia.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] We have found the first four holy martyrs of this day, 8 Kalends of January, in no calendars or martyrologies. [Col. 0146D] Likewise Muratori, vol. II of the *Anecdota Latina*, p. 191, published from a papyrus document a list of holy oils containing the names of several holy martyrs otherwise unknown.]

[Note: [Col. 0146D] It is read in the Gelasian manuscript, book I, no. 5, and in all Gregorian manuscripts among the prayers for the Nativity of the Lord. In the Roman Missal, with a few additions, it is prescribed in the order of the Mass to be said while the priest blesses the water to be mixed in the chalice.] God, who wondrously created the dignity of human substance and reformed it even more wondrously, grant, we beseech you, that we may be participants in the divinity of Jesus Christ, your Son [Note: [Col. 0146D] The words “of Jesus Christ, your Son” are a variant reading. Muratori omitted *ejus*, “of him.”], who deigned to become a participant in our humanity. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0146D] It is found in the Gelasian manuscript, book I, no. 3. Shortly afterward, the words *et sempiterne Pater*, “and eternal Father,” appear to be an excess arising from a variant reading.] Grant us, we beseech you, almighty and merciful God and eternal Father, that the solemnities of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, which we anticipate through the present rites, may be new to us and remain continually renewed, and may persevere perpetually, so that, because of their wonder, they may always remain new. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For whatever is celebrated in the devotion of the Christian confession takes its beginning from [149] this solemnity and is contained in the mystery of this gift. This was declared in the very parents of the human race, when the Apostle testified, speaking about the first human beings: “This mystery is great. But I speak of Christ and the Church.” [Col. 0147A] The patriarchs signified this through various actions and words. That observance of the Law, which was figurative, affirmed it. The proclamations of all the prophets foretold it. In it is the fullness of the ancient ceremonies. In it is the present ministry of heavenly graces. In it is the promise of future goods. Since in it what had been foretold is most clearly proved to be fulfilled, we reasonably believe and wisely trust that what is promised will come to pass. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Gregorian manuscripts and the Roman Missal offer this prayer in the Mass of the day of the Nativity of the Lord.] Grant us, we beseech you, Lord our God, that we who rejoice to celebrate the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ may deserve through worthy conduct to belong to his fellowship. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] It is found in the same place and in Gelasian, book I, no. 5.] Grant, we beseech you, Lord, an increase of faith, hope, and charity to your servants, so that those who glory in the Nativity of our Lord, your Son, may, with you as their guide, experience no adversities of the world and may receive without end what they desire to celebrate temporally. Through, etc.

II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] It is read in Gelasian, book I, no. 3, and in Gregorian manuscripts on the same feast. Shortly afterward, *sacrae* is a variant reading, or it should be supplied, as in Gelasius: “the sacred birth of blessed Mary the Virgin.”] God, who caused the birth of the blessed Virgin—begotten without human desire and coming into the members of your Son—not to be held under paternal pre-judgments, grant, we beseech you, that, having received the newness of this creation, we may be stripped of the contagions of ancient corruption. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. For behold, as he spoke through the mouth of the prophets, a Virgin conceived in the womb and bore a Son, and his name was called Emmanuel, and “God is with us”; because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Behold, a child is born today; a little one is given to us, and sovereignty has been made his, whose power is upon his shoulders; [Col. 0147C] and he shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace, upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it from now and forever. In all these things we clearly recognize God and man, who, by assuming what is ours, deigned to grant us what is his. Therefore, with overflowing joys, etc.

[150] III. Another.

Graciously regard, Lord, the offering of your people, in which neither alien fire is brought to your altars nor the blood of irrational animals poured out; rather, through the working power of the Holy Spirit, our sacrifice is already the body and blood of the priest himself. Through, etc.

It is truly worthy. Especially on this day, when you revealed the very mystery of our salvation as a light to the nations and promised it through the ineffable bringing forth from the secret of the virginal womb: “Raising up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David your servant, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins, through the tender mercies of our God, in which the Dawn from on high has visited us.” Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; who, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, is God the Lord and has shone upon us, so that he might make us, who were in darkness and the shadow of death, a kingdom of perpetual (another reading: “eternal”) light. Therefore, with overflowing joys, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Gregorian manuscripts offer this prayer on the same feast.] Almighty and eternal God, who in the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ your Son granted the beginning and perfection of the whole of religion to stand together, grant us, we beseech you, to be counted among his portion, in whom the sum of all human salvation consists. Through, etc.

IV. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] It is found in Cardinal Thomasius’s Gothic Missal, in the Mass of the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0148D], and apud Pamelius, vol. II, p. 188.] May the offering of today’s festival be pleasing to you, Lord, we beseech you, so that, through your grace bestowing it, by these sacred exchanges we may be found in the form of him in whom our substance is with you. Through, etc.

[Col. 0148B] [Note: [Col. 0148D] Compare Gelasian, book I, no. 4, and Pamelius, vol. II, p. 550.] It is truly worthy. Always offering the sacrifice of your praise, whose figure righteous Abel instituted, the legal lamb also displayed, Abraham celebrated, and Melchizedek the priest presented; but the true Lamb and eternal High Priest, Christ, born today, fulfilled it. Therefore, with overflowing joys, etc.

Grant, we beseech you, Lord our God, that he who was born today for the destruction of the devil and the forgiveness of sins may both cleanse us from the stealth of faults and defend us from the assault of enemies. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] It is described in Gregorian manuscripts among the prayers for the Nativity of the Lord.] Grant, we beseech you, Lord, inviolable firmness of faith to your people, so that those who confess your Only-Begotten, eternal with you in your everlasting glory, born in the reality of our body from a Virgin Mother, may be freed from present adversities and admitted to enduring joys. [Col. 0148C] Through, etc.

[151] V. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] This is the Mass of the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. This prayer is found in Gelasius, book I, no. 1, in the Gregorian Sacramentary, and in the Roman Missal.] Grant us, almighty God, that just as we anticipate the adorable anniversary of your Son, so, rejoicing, we may receive his eternal gifts. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] In Gelasian, in the same place.] We beseech you, Lord, grant us to anticipate these solemnities with a service all the more ready, insofar as in them you show the beginning of our redemption to stand firm. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. For the solemnity of heavenly peace enters, Lord. We ask that, through the grace by which the world was reconciled to you through the remission of all sins, we too, cleansed from every offense, may be fitted for the remedies of your mercy, and that we may attain, by recalling the principal gift, the mystery that came into the world for its salvation. Through, etc.

O God, who touch us through participation in your sacrament, work the effect of its power in our hearts, so that, by receiving your gift, we may be made fit for that very gift. Through, etc.

[Col. 0149A] May your blessing, Lord, descend abundantly upon the people who entreat you, so that those whom you created as their maker and restored as their author may be saved by your continual action. Through, etc.

### VI. Another.

O God, who work the restoration of the human condition even more wonderfully than you created its substance, grant, we ask, that in us there may be brought to completion both what the divine generation of your Word created and what the glorious Nativity of that Word made man restored. Through, etc.

With so many meanings, Lord, we celebrate today’s sacrifice, by which the beginnings of that very sacrifice were born for us. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. For the magnificent exchange of our restoration shone forth when the new man was healed from the old man; when mortality was healed from mortality; when the human condition is healed by the remedy accomplished from that same human condition; and when, from a generation subject to sin, offspring wholly ignorant of sin arises. Not only is our frailty, assumed by your Word, made worthy of perpetual honor, but by a wondrous sharing you also make us eternal. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] The codex reads: “Having existed, healed; mortality from mortality.” The wording has been emended and supplemented from the context; nor was it proper to correct *mortalitas* (“mortality”) to *immortalitas* (“immortality”), since *mortality* must be referred to the verb “is healed.”]

### 152 VII. Another.

Rejoicing, Lord, we come with gifts to the venerable altars, because today both the fulfillment of all our prayers and the cause of our redemption have arisen. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. For truly great, singular beyond example, marvelous beyond human reasoning, is the sacrament produced by your mercy. And therefore, just as it was precious to the first believers in believing it, so now it leaves no conscience excusable that does not follow the truth of the saving mystery, even though the whole world bears witness to it. For just as at the beginning it might have seemed difficult when the human race was said to be destined to come to this mystery, so it is impious to deny the work of immeasurable majesty when it is seen conspicuously everywhere. Therefore, with poured-out offerings, etc.

[Note: These words appear to have been written against the Eutychians, who denied the truth of the Word’s incarnation. Against them Catholics—as is handed down in the final prayer of Mass IV—confess that the only-begotten Son of God the Father was born of the Virgin Mother in the truth of our body. The style is not unlike Leo’s.]

Grant us, Lord, we ask, to receive your holy gifts with a heart pleasing to you, and may whatever is defective in our mind be healed by the remedy of that gift itself. Through, etc.

### VIII. Another.

O God, who have deigned to save the human race, lethally wounded by its own prince, through the birth of your Christ, grant, we ask, that we may not remain attached to the author of destruction, but may be transferred into the fellowship of our Redeemer. Through, etc.

May the offering of today’s feast be acceptable to you, Lord; through it the perfect appeasement of our reconciliation has proceeded, the fullness of divine worship has been bestowed upon us, and the way of truth and the life of the heavenly kingdom have appeared. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] See Pamelius, vol. II, p. 550.]

Truly worthy. For today the true light of our Savior has come forth, which has made all things clear to us, both in understanding and in sight. Through its splendor it would not only direct our present life, but also lead us to behold the very glory of immeasurable majesty. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] This prayer is found in Gregorian codices and in the Roman Missal [Col. 0150D] at the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.]

Grant us, Lord, we ask, to be strengthened by the newly commemorated birth of him whose heavenly mystery nourishes and gives drink to us. Through, etc.

### 153 IX. Another.

Grant, Lord, we ask, that we may deserve to belong to the beginning of today’s saving birth, aided by apostolic prayers. Through, etc.

May your universal Church rejoice in the present sacrifice, Lord, through which the first fruits of its weakness were assumed, so that it itself might become a sharer in divine power. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. On the day of today’s solemnity, when an ineffable yet entirely fitting mystery is brought forth: the Virgin Mother could produce no offspring except a divine one, and God, having deigned to be born as man, could fittingly be generated only from a Virgin Mother. Therefore, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] In Gelasius, book I, no. 4, and in Gregorian codices. In the cited Missal it is placed last among the prayers for this feast.]

Grant, merciful God, that the Savior of the world, born today, may be for us, just as he is the author of divine generation, also the giver of immortality. Through, etc.

O God, who did not permit the creation of the human condition to perish through the devil’s wickedness, carry out the remedies of your propitiation, so that hostile deceit may not prevail in it, but that the redemption of your compassion [Another reading: “mercy”] may triumph. Through, etc.

## XLI. [Note: The Masses of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, which were to follow the Masses of the Nativity of the Lord, are printed at the beginning of August and are therefore to be repeated from there.] The Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist.

### I.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] This occurs here in Gregorian codices; in the Roman Missal, however, on the feast of Saint Bartholomew.]

Almighty and eternal God, who have granted the venerable and holy joy of this day through the feast of your blessed apostle John the Evangelist, grant your Church, we ask, both to love what it has believed and to proclaim what he taught. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] It is read in Gelasius, book I, no. 7, and in Gregorian manuscripts at Vespers of this feast.]

O God, who through the mouth of your blessed apostle John the Evangelist opened to us the mysteries of your Word, grant, we ask, that we may grasp with fitting understanding what he impressively poured into our ears. Through, etc.

[Col. 0150D] May the offering of your people, Lord, be acceptable through apostolic intercession, so that your Church may always be aided by the intercessions of those by whose teachings it is continually instructed. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] This preface, with a few changes, is reported in the Gregorian codex of Ottoboni and in Muratori, Menardus, vol. III, col. 10, and Pamelius, vol. II, p. 551.]

Truly worthy. We venerate the Nativity of your blessed apostle John the Evangelist, who, having accepted the call of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, rejected his earthly father so that he might find a heavenly one; cast away the nets of the world in which he was entangled, so that with a free mind he might pursue the gifts of eternity; abandoned the ship tossed by the waves, so that he might stand firm in the tranquility of ecclesiastical governance; ceased catching fish, so that he might draw out with the reed of saving doctrine the souls submerged in worldly abysses; and withdrew from the deep sea, becoming an investigator of divine secrets. He advanced so far that, at the sacred banquet of the mystical supper, he reclined upon the breast of the Savior himself; that the Lord, set upon the cross, appointed him as his substitute and gave him as a son to the Virgin Mother; and that he was the first to proclaim the Word, which was God with God, before all others. Through, etc.

[Col. 0151B] Grant us, Lord, we ask, to be aided by apostolic teachings and prayers, so that what we celebrate through the present rites we may attain in the joys of eternal salvation [Another reading: “redemption”]. Through, etc.

Accompany your people, Lord, so that, supported by temporal consolation, it may always celebrate the blessed Nativity of the holy apostles, and, redeemed by eternal mercy, recognize it. Through, etc.

### II. Another.

Lord, we ask that we may receive the gifts of the Nativity of Saint John the apostle, so that through his glorious prayers the blessed Evangelist may continually ask both that we believe what he taught and that we follow it. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] See Gelasius, book I, no. 7, and Pamelius, vol. I, p. 308, and vol. II, p. 190.]

Through the apostolic supplications of the blessed John the Evangelist, Lord, we ask that the offering of your Church, which is instructed by his magnificent preaching, may be commended to you. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. We recount the glory of the blessed apostle John, who was so familiarly loved by your Only-begotten Son and inspired by revelations of immeasurable grace that, transcending every creature, he perceived with exalted mind and declared with evangelical voice that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God,” [Note: [Col. 0151D] “And” seems to be preferable to “who.” Muratori reads “and,” as does the clause beginning “because.”] who “was in the beginning with God.” For by saying “was,” he demonstrated eternity without beginning. By adding “and the Word was God” and “he was in the beginning with God,” he both expressed personal distinction and revealed that you possess one Godhead with your Son. By the radiance of eternal majesty thus brought forth, the Gentiles, when called, would yield to the supreme Divinity, and, once the cunning of heretics had been refuted, would neither assert a confusion of union nor diminish the truth of co-eternity. Through, etc.

Merciful and compassionate Lord, who do not abandon us amid the continual mysteries of the heavenly martyrs, grant, we ask, that we may receive with grateful obedience what we diligently celebrate with devotion. Through, etc.

[Col. 0152A] 155 [Note: [Col. 0151D] It is nearly the same in Gregorian codices and in the Roman Missal.]

Kindly enlighten your Church, Lord, so that, illuminated by the apostolic teachings of the blessed John the Evangelist, it may attain the gifts that you promised to the faithful as their reward. Through, etc.

## XLII. The Nativity of the Innocents.

### I.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Compare Gelasius, book I, no. 8.]

O God, who, through your good gifts, anticipate even the hearts of infants who do not yet know your sacrament, grant, we ask, that abundant indulgence may always precede us, who have no confidence in our own conscience. Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, we ask, the offerings of your devoted servants, and purify those who serve your divine mysteries through your merciful goodness, by which you also justify the ignorant. Through, etc.

[Col. 0152B] [Note: [Col. 0151D] This is found in all Gregorian codices.]

Truly worthy. For through the precious deaths of the little ones whom wicked Herod killed with bestial cruelty because of the infancy of your Son, our Lord and Savior, we recognize the immeasurable gifts of your clemency. For grace alone shines more brightly than will, and confession is clear before speech; suffering preceded the existence of limbs capable of suffering; they were witnesses of Christ who had not yet become aware of him. O boundless goodness! When they were slaughtered for his name, he did not permit the merit of glory to perish, even though they did not know it; rather, when bathed in their own blood, they both fulfilled the salvation of regeneration and received the crown of martyrdom as their account. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The word “name” has been supplied from the cited Sacramentaries, which repeat this preface.]

Lord, we have received the effect of today’s solemnity: great joy from little ones. We humbly beseech you to preserve this abundance also in our salvation. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] The same source, ibid., p. 308.]

May your Church always rejoice, Lord, in the celebration of your saints, and continually experience the effect of your mercy, whereby human frailty may endure and divine redemption may not be denied to the suppliant. Through, etc.

### II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] This is found in the Gregorian codices of Menardus and Muratori and in Pamelius.]

O God, who, although you are great in great things, nevertheless work wonders more gloriously in small things, grant us, we ask, to rejoice in the celebration of those who bore witness to your Son, our Lord, even without speaking. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] It is read in Gelasius, book I, no. 8, and in Menardus, vol. III, p. 12.]

Be present, Lord, with the gifts to be consecrated on the feast of the Innocents, and grant, we ask, that we may imitate their sincerity, whose infancy, dedicated to you, we venerate. Through, etc.

[Col. 0152D] Truly worthy. For we have heard the prophet say that Rachel, weeping for her children, refused to be consoled because they are not. She mourned, therefore, because those who were crowned with so great a gift did not come from her offspring. They were born, in fact, from the stock of Leah; divine grace anticipated their understanding, suffering their comprehension, and the wondrous palm of martyrdom their age, so that even the venerable infancy of our Savior might be glorified by the testimony of those of his own age. Through, etc.

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that just as you made those whose Nativity we celebrate pleasing to you by the outcome of their age through your grace, so salutary humility may make us acceptable to your mercy. Through, etc.

Grant, Lord, we ask, that your faithful, as the Apostle says, may not become children in understanding, but may be found innocent of malice like little ones, and may follow in the simplicity of mind the martyrs of today’s feast, whom they cannot equal in merits.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] “And” was written instead of “so that,” as Paul’s sentence requires.]

## XLIII. During the Fast of the Tenth Month.

### I.

O God, who with eternal foresight see what is fittingly adapted to each season, grant us, we ask, that, along with the changing course of worldly things, we may also grow toward eternal goods through the advance of devoted dedication. Through, etc.

Look favorably upon our days, Lord, and make those whom you multiply through the present course secure by righteous works. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] In Gelasius, book II, no. 85, on the Wednesday of the fast of the tenth month, and in Pamelius, vol. II, p. 362.]

Mercifully receive, Lord, the offerings of your Church, which you both graciously granted to be offered and powerfully cause to pass into the mystery of our salvation. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. For through the things that are seen we are instructed in the ways by which we ought to strive toward things unseen. Finally, the succession of the year reminds us to pass from past things to future things and from oldness to newness of life, so that, freed from earthly supports, we may receive more eagerly the abundance of the heavenly gift, and through that food which is granted in alternating benefits may arrive at nourishment that will endure without end. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] In the margin of the codex: “After the foods.” It occurs in Gelasius at the cited place, in Gregorian codices, and in the Roman Missal on Thursday after the First Sunday of Lent.]

Raise us up, Lord, through the abundance of your gifts with temporal supports, and renew us with eternal ones. Through, etc.

Your people, Lord, governed by various forms of assistance, may receive both the present and future remedies of your mercy, so that it may be comforted by the necessary consolation of passing things and strive more confidently toward eternal realities. Through, etc.

### II. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] In the same margin: “Before the foods.”]

We recognize, Lord, the generosity of your clemency toward us. Therefore we ask more confidently that those whom you never cease to feed though they are undeserving, you may both make capable of serving you worthily and accompany with more abundant gifts.

[Col. 0154A] [Note: [Col. 0153D] This is found in all Gregorian codices and in the Roman Missal on the Saturday after the Second Sunday of Lent.]

Grant, we ask, Lord, a saving effect to our fasts, so that the chastisement undertaken by the flesh may pass over into the strengthening of our souls. Through, etc.

Receive, Lord, the sacrifice by whose offering you graciously wished to be appeased, and grant, we ask, that, cleansed by its working, we may offer you an affection of mind pleasing to you. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. You instruct us like little children through nourishment [Note: [Col. 0153D] Muratori preferred the correction “as a nourisher instructing little ones,” but it is unnecessary; nor is it necessary shortly afterward to write *incrementa* (“increases”) instead of *crementa* (“growth”), although the latter noun is less usual, as Blanchinus noted in his second thoughts.] by distributing food for mind and body; through the growth of human prosperity you foster us, until, each according to his measure, we attain immortal satisfaction when mortality has ended. Through, etc.

[Col. 0154B] Having reverently received your mysteries, Lord, we ask that we may be armed against the error of our condition and against the devil’s snares. Through, etc.

May participation in the divine sacrament be continual protection for your people, Lord, so that they may not be held liable to bodily vices, may be free through spiritual delight, may be subject to your majesty with complete devotion, and may continually desire and abundantly receive the salvation of mind and body. Through, etc.

### III. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] In the margin of the codex: “After the foods.”]

We humbly ask you, Lord, that, sufficiently aided by the benefits of earthly fruits, we may advance toward you, the author of all things. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] This prayer occurs in Gregorian manuscripts and in the Roman Missal on Monday after the Third Sunday of Lent.]

Pour kindly into our hearts, Lord, we ask, that just as we abstain from bodily food, so we may also withdraw our senses from harmful excess. Through, etc.

[Col. 0154C] [Note: [Col. 0154D] In Gelasius, book II, no. 85, on Friday of the fast of the tenth month.]

Grant us, Lord, we ask, the proper measure of this restraint, so that what we take away from the license of the flesh may obtain for us the saving fruit of the mind. Through, etc.

Subject our wills to you, Lord, we ask, so that we may always follow both in faith what you command and in action. Through, etc.

We pray, almighty God, that from transitory resources [Note: [Col. 0154D] Muratori reads “works.” We have retained the codex’s reading “resources,” since the verb “we may perform” is here understood of the distribution of alms, as the aforementioned Blanchinus noted in his second thoughts.] we may perform rather those deeds by which both hope and ability may be available to us for attaining eternal joys. Through, etc.

Grant us peace of mind and body, Lord, so that visible enemies may be subjected to our frailty and invisible ones excluded. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0154D] In Gelasius at the cited place and in Pamelius, vol. II, p. 362.]

Grant, Lord, we ask, that we may offer an affection of devotion appropriate to the gift that has been dedicated. Through, etc.

[Col. 0155A] Truly worthy. For by the healthy begging of the fast we attend to what is necessary for healing, and through the observance of fitting discipline we become more grateful for the gifts received and those to be received, so that we may rejoice not only in earthly fertility but may receive with purified minds the birth of the eternal bread, worthy of honor. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] It appears in the Roman Missal and in Gregorian codices on January 28, the second feast of Saint Agnes.]

We have received the votive mysteries of the annual celebration, Lord. Grant, we ask, that they may provide us with remedies both for temporal life and for eternal life. Through, etc.

Protect your people, Lord, and accompany them as they recall the sacred solemnities with the abundance of heavenly grace, so that, aided by visible consolations, they may be more readily stirred toward invisible goods. Through, etc.

### IV. Another.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] It occurs in Gelasius at the cited place, from which *proficere* (“to advance”) was emended for the erroneous *profiteri* (“to profess”) found in the codex.]

Look favorably, Lord, upon your people, and release from all sins those whom you grant to advance through the divine sacraments. Through, etc.

Come to the aid of your people, Lord, we ask, and do not permit anyone who wishes to become a companion of your truth to follow error. Through, etc.

We ask, almighty God, that you administer the seasons of your Church with merciful governance, so that, with the multiplication of holy solemnities, it may both receive understanding of heavenly things and make progress. Through, etc.

Grant, we ask, Lord, that we may be filled with spiritual joys, so that we may pursue inwardly what we perform outwardly. Through, etc.

We offer you gifts, Lord, asking that we may carry out with full devotion what we celebrate in submissive [Another reading: “pious”] services. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. You are shown to be not only ineffable in the heights but also immeasurable in the smallest things. For when your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, said that the whole world would yield to his name, who would not have thought it absurd? Who, when he sees it happening, would deny that it is divine? And when he sees the promises being fulfilled, who would not rightly refrain from doubting that what was likewise foretold is to come? Just as those who believed in things not yet visible are more blessed, so we are more inexcusable if we do not confess what we have experienced; yet we are more grateful if we trust that what is not manifest will come. Through, etc.

[Col. 0156A] [Note: [Col. 0155D] It is read in Gelasius, book II, no. 85, on Friday during the fast of the tenth month, and in Gregorian codices and the Roman Missal on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper. From these sources the word *exsequimur* (“we carry out”) has been supplied, since it was absent from the damaged codex.]

Refreshed with life-giving nourishment, Lord, we ask that what we carry out during the time of our mortality we may attain through the gift of your immortality. Through, etc.

May abundant blessing descend upon your people, Lord, we ask; may forgiveness come, consolation be granted, holy faith increase, and eternal redemption be made firm. Through, etc.

### V. Another.

Be favorable, Lord, to your people, and do not abandon them in temporal consolation, though they strive toward eternal things. Through, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] It is found in the Gregorian manuscripts of Muratori and in the Roman Missal in the Mass on the Saturday after the Third Sunday of Advent.]

Look favorably, Lord, we ask, upon the present sacrifices, so that they may contribute both to our devotion and to our salvation. Through, etc.

Truly worthy. You not only forgive sins but also justify sinners themselves; and you release the guilty not only from punishment but also grant them rewards. Through, etc.
