[Note: [Col. 0156D] This prayer, directed against the error of the Eutychians, does not differ from the thought and style of Leo.]

Grant, we ask, Lord our God, that this sacrament may be understood without distinction in your Churches, so that one Christ, in the truth of God and man, may be worshiped, neither divided from our nature nor distinguished from your essence. Through Christ our Lord.

May our mouths praise you, Lord; may the soul praise you, and life also. And since it is your gift that we are, may everything we live be yours. Through Christ our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] These three crosses, which are written in the codex after the preceding prayer, seem to indicate the end of the Sacramentary, so that what follows must be attributed to an extraneous addition.]

+ + +

Receive, venerable martyrs—although [we are] unworthy worshippers, we offer [lacuna] the vows of the whole people for [lacuna]—and attend; so that, secure in the reward of your merits, you may be concerned for the remission of our crimes.

Here begins the blessing of the font.

We pour out a prayer to you, Lord of all things, eternal Father, almighty God, whose Spirit was borne over the waters, whose exalted eyes looked upon the river Jordan while John was baptizing those who confessed their sins in repentance. Therefore we ask your holy glory that your hidden hand may be over this water, so that you may cleanse and purify the worse man who will be baptized from it, and that, delivered from deadly offenses, he may be reborn and revived as a new man, reborn in Christ Jesus, with whom you live and reign in the unity of the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

## [ADDRESS FOR THE RECONCILIATION OF PENITENTS]

[Col. 0155]

### NOTICE

Of the three prefaces of the Roman Pontifical that Quesnellus, because they bear Leo’s style, appended to his Sermons, two have been published in the Sacramentary presented above. The third, which we have no doubt would also be found in the same work if the section concerning the reconciliation of penitents during Lent were not missing, we append here. The preface *Exsultet* at the blessing of the paschal candle would likewise have to be added if we considered it probable that this was Leo’s work, as some have thought, cited by Mabillon in his note on the Gothic Missal. But since its style is utterly unlike Leo’s and, so far as we know, no codices support this opinion, we append here only the preface—or rather, the archdeacon’s address for the reconciliation of penitents—which breathes the spirit of Leo, following the older Gelasian codex, where it is more complete and fuller, since our Sacramentary does not assist us.

[Col. 0157]

[Note: [Col. 0157B] Quesnellus published this from Part III of the Roman Pontifical: “On the reconciliation of penitents, which takes place on the fifth day, the Lord’s Supper,” and from Hittorp’s Roman Order. In the Gelasian Sacramentary it is read in book I, no. 38.]

### ADDRESS OF THE ARCHDEACON TO THE BISHOP FOR THE RECONCILIATION OF PENITENTS

[Note: [Col. 0157B] In the Gelasian codex this address is attributed to the deacon.]

[Col. 0157A] Behold, venerable bishop, the acceptable time is here, the day of divine propitiation and human salvation, in which death received its destruction and life received its eternal beginning. It is the time when, in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, a planting of new shoots is to be made so that the accursedness of old things may be purged. [Note: The Gelasian codex reads “and healing”; we judge the reading of the Roman Order and Pontifical preferable, as also below “more abundant,” for which Gelasius erroneously reads “and more bountiful.”] [Note: [Col. 0157B] The Pontifical adds “of branches,” and shortly afterward reads *sarcienda* (“to be repaired”) instead of *facienda* (“to be made”). We follow the Gelasian codex, with which Hittorp’s Roman Order agrees.]

For although no time is empty of the riches of God’s goodness and mercy, now forgiveness of sins is more generous through indulgence, and the reception of those reborn is more abundant through grace. We are increased by those regenerated; we grow by those who return. The waters wash; the tears wash. From one side comes joy at the reception of those called; from the other, gladness at the absolution of penitents. [Note: [Col. 0158B] We preferred the reading of the same Roman Order and Pontifical. The Gelasian codex reads “gladness.”]

Hence it is that your suppliant, after falling into various forms of crime through neglect of the heavenly commandments and transgression of disreputable conduct [Note: [Col. 0158B] Read: “disreputable conduct.” Another reading: “approved conduct.”], cries out to God with the prophetic voice, humbled and prostrate, saying: “I have sinned, I have acted impiously, I have committed iniquity; have mercy on me, Lord.” Receiving the evangelical saying with an ear that does not frustrate it—“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted”—he ate, as it is written, the bread of sorrow; he watered his bed [Note: [Col. 0158B] The Pontifical adds “his own.”] with tears; afflicted his heart with grief and his body with fasts, so that he might recover for his soul the health it had lost. Thus there is one aid of repentance, which benefits individuals and comes to the assistance of all together.

[Note: [Col. 0158B] Up to this point Quesnellus follows the Roman Pontifical. What follows is in the Gelasian codex and the Roman Order.]

Therefore, while he is stirred to the practice of repentance by such examples [Note: [Col. 0158B] Another reading: “aroused.”], before the sight of the grieving Church, the venerable bishop, he protests and says: “I acknowledge my iniquities, and my sin is always before me. Turn your face from my sins, Lord, and blot out all my iniquities. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit.”

While he thus entreats and asks God’s mercy with an afflicted heart, restore in him, apostolic bishop, whatever has been corrupted when the devil tore it apart; and, with the merits of your prayers providing their protection, make the man close to God through the grace of divine reconciliation, so that he who previously displeased the Lord through his perversions may then rejoice that he pleases the Lord in the land of the living, when the author of his death has been overcome. Through the Lord.

## [ON THE VOCATION OF ALL NATIONS]

### NOTICE ON THE BOOKS ON THE VOCATION OF ALL NATIONS

1. Quesnellus published these books under Leo’s name. Why, however, we thought they should be taken away from that pontiff and relegated to an appendix will become clear from the observations appended to Quesnellus’s second dissertation, in which we shall reduce his arguments to calculation. These same books were first circulated among the works of Saint Ambrose from a codex that bore Ambrose’s name. It not only abounded in many errors but also lacked the lengthy testimony that Pope Saint Gelasius had quoted from this work.

In his Louvain edition of 1565, Joannes Sotellus inserted these books among the works of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, on the authority of three manuscript exemplars: those of Saint Martin of Louvain, Camberon, and Bonefay, which prefix Prosper’s name to them. But he corrected nothing in the text and supplied nothing. In the Douai edition of the works of Saint Prosper of 1576, Joannes Olivarius did supply, from the same Camberon codex, the significant passage that was missing; but, while adding variant readings in the margin, he for the most part left the text untouched. In addition to these variants, Quesnellus used another codex, the Thuaneus, which, as we believe from other evidence, was inscribed with Prosper’s name; with the assistance of these two exemplars he corrected several errors in the text. The most recent Parisian editor of Saint Prosper, in 1711, used a third codex, the Jolien, of better quality, which likewise bears Prosper’s name, and restored from it quite a few passages.

2. We compared chiefly three Vatican manuscript books. The first is codex Vat. Reginae 293, a parchment quarto manuscript of approximately the eleventh century, in which the books are attributed to Prosper under this title: “Here begins Prosper’s first book, On the Vocation of All Nations.” This codex bears at its front the inscription: “Book of Saint Peter and Saint Rodobert of Cella,” indicating the library to which the codex once belonged.

The second is Vat. 268, likewise a parchment folio manuscript of approximately the same century, which assigns the work to Ambrose. The third is Vat. 262, a quarto manuscript of the fifteenth century, which displays Prosper’s name at the front. Although this codex is more recent, it generally supplied sounder readings; moreover, from this one manuscript we restored the passage that had been sought in vain in the others.

So that we may not be too lengthy in citing these codices, we shall designate the first manuscript by the Arabic numeral 1, the second by 2, and the third by 3, as follows: Vat. 1, 2, or 3. Besides these there are three other codices: Vat. Palatinus 236, of the ninth or tenth century; Vat. 558, of the eleventh century; and 559, of the fifteenth century, all of which likewise bear Prosper’s name; and one, Vat. 281, of the fourteenth century, which prefixes Ambrose’s name.

3. The examination of these codices suggests two observations that may perhaps be useful for conjecturing the author. First, it is false that the Vatican codices preferring Ambrose are older than those inscribed with Prosper’s name. For Vat. 268 is not nine hundred years old but is recognized as having been written around the eleventh century, whereas Palat. 236 is earlier by one or even two centuries, as is also the manuscript that Hincmar possessed when he cited this work in several places under Prosper’s name.

The codices Vat. Reg. 293 and Vat. 558, however, are of the same century as the one prefixed to Ambrose. Second, of the codices so far used, only three prefer Ambrose—namely, Vat. 268 and 281, as well as the one from which these books first appeared under Ambrose’s name. All of them are equally corrupted by many errors, and all likewise lack the lengthy testimony restored in chapter 7 of Book I from manuscripts that prefix Prosper’s name. Thus they are known to derive from one and the same corrupted and abridged exemplar.

Eight codices, however, are prefixed with Prosper’s name: Camberon, Thuane, Jolien, Palat. 236, Vat. Reg. 293, Vat. 262, 558, and 559. All are much more correct, and none omits that notable testimony.

### 4.

From these two observations, it may be permissible to draw and propose a certain conjecture useful for determining the author. Since all the manuscripts that bear Ambrose’s name are equally mutilated and corrupt and derive from a single defective exemplar, it could have happened through the carelessness or decision of that first copyist either that the name of Prosper, which stood in the older manuscripts, was changed to Ambrose, or—which is more probable and happens more frequently in other works—that the books were placed among Ambrose’s works without an author’s name; from this later copyists may have taken the opportunity to attribute them to Ambrose. Yet they certainly cannot be ascribed to him, as Quesnellus clearly demonstrates in Dissertation 2, nor do we know that they were attributed to him in earlier times or manuscripts.

Conversely, since all the manuscripts bearing Prosper’s name are more correct and not so abridged, and some are also older, it is plain that they derive from a very ancient and more faithful original, on which Prosper’s name was likewise written. May we not therefore conjecture that some Prosper was truly the author of these books, although we do not know which Prosper he was? In this way everything is satisfactorily reconciled.

For the difficulties raised by Quesnellus in Dissertation 2 against the opinions that introduce Prosper as the author establish only that the author of these books was not Prosper of Aquitaine. But if it is said that the author was some other Prosper, otherwise unknown, who lived in the age of Leo and before Gelasius, those objections have no force; and in this way the authority of the older, more numerous, and more accurate copies remains intact.

The authority of Cassiodorus can likewise be reconciled in a similar manner; he attributes the books *On the Promises and Predictions of God* to Prosper. This would have occurred through error if Prosper of Aquitaine had necessarily been intended, for the author of those books is evidently an African. But Cassiodorus consistently calls him Prosper in two books, while he does not identify his homeland. Since Cassiodorus himself lived almost at the same time as this author, it is not easy to say that he was mistaken about his name, when another Prosper may be understood. Rather, those should be thought to have been misled by no slight prejudice who, presuming that the Prosper named by Cassiodorus was Prosper of Aquitaine, thought that this twofold testimony had to be rejected and marked as erroneous. Why, then, could the same thing not have happened in our case?

### 5.

The text of Pope Gelasius offers no contradiction, since he could have called him “Teacher of the Church” as a mark of honor, whoever at that time may have been called Prosper in the manuscripts. For we are not thereby compelled to say that these books were published without an author’s name—although some have thought that this should be inferred from Gelasius’s citation alone, in which the name is omitted.

### 6.

Nor should it be an objection that some add that the manuscripts could have erred in attributing these books to Prosper just as they erred in claiming for him the books *On the Contemplative Life*, whose author is Julianus Pomerius. For other manuscripts have been found, and are cited by the most recent editor of Prosper, which attribute these books to Julianus Pomerius. Among them are one Vatican Regina manuscript, no. 291, of the eleventh century, and another Ambrosian manuscript of a thousand years’ antiquity, identified by Muratori in volume III of the *Italian Antiquities*, p. 847. In it, while excerpts from ancient writers are being copied, one passage from chapter 21 of book II of *On the Contemplative Life* is cited as follows:

> “Here begins the third book” (the second should be read, unless another division had been adopted) “of Pomerius to Julian.”

On the other hand, no manuscripts have so far been found that attribute the books *On the Calling of All Nations* to anyone other than Prosper or Ambrose. Consequently, since they cannot be Ambrose’s, one Prosper remains. Since we are not compelled to understand Prosper of Aquitaine—no manuscript calls him Aquitanian—we may believe that another Prosper was the author, even if it is not clear who he was.

We submit this conjecture, whatever its worth, to the judgment of readers, especially those who may be able to inspect and compare other manuscripts.

[Col. 0159]

As for the elucidations with which the Ballerini edition supplements the work, we reproduce them here in full. Quesnellus assigned this little work to Saint Leo; other authors, however, more correctly wished it to be attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine.
