[Col. 0161]

> **[Note: [Col. 0161B]]** No manuscript has so far been available against which this letter could be collated. All the editions were transcribed from the first one; consequently, nothing could be corrected. We found four Vatican manuscript copies, numbered 262, 268, 281, and 284. We chiefly collated the first two and shall correct several passages from them.

## LETTER TO THE SACRED VIRGIN DEMETRIAS, OR A TREATISE ON HUMILITY,

which Quesnellus attributed to Leo the Great.

> **[Note: [Col. 0161C]]** See Quesnellus’s Dissertation 4 and our observations on it.

(C, G, S)

### ARGUMENT.

He commends true humility with great praise and depicts the pride opposed to it in its own colors. Then he exhorts the virgin devoted to Christ to avoid arrogance and to fortify herself with the protection of genuine humility.

[Col. 0161A] **259 CHAPTER I. How great were Demetrias’s nobility and virtue.**

> **[Note: [Col. 0161C]]** In the old editions of Ambrose, this heading is prefixed: “Ambrose, bishop, to the sacred virgin Demetrias.” In the Louvain edition of 1365, however, it reads: “Prosper, bishop, to the sacred virgin Demetrias.” From this inscription some have concluded that Prosper of Aquitaine was a bishop. But this inscription arose solely from the judgment of the Louvain editor. Since he possessed no manuscript of this letter and had transcribed it from an edition of Ambrose, he attributed it to Prosper on the basis of the supposition that Ambrose could not be its author. In copying it from the commonly circulated editions of Ambrose, he altered the name Ambrose in the inscription to Prosper by his own decision, while retaining the rest, including the word “bishop.” In the four Vatican manuscripts mentioned above, however, no such inscription is found. In Vatican manuscripts 268 and 281 this letter follows the books *On the Calling of All Nations* attributed to Ambrose; but it is copied without any author’s name, under the title: “Here begins [the work] on true humility, to the sacred virgin Demetrias.” In Vatican 262, after the same books *On the Calling of All Nations*, attributed to Prosper, it is found without any title, with several blank pages intervening. Only Vatican manuscript 284 bears this inscription: “Of Ambrose, to the virgin Demetrias.” See more in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 4.

Since you piously and wisely understand that the lofty purpose of your most splendid holiness rests upon the foundations of humility, you stoop so far, O sacred Virgin Demetrias, to the condescension of your dignity that you even require your progress to be assisted by my pen. I would refuse this in every way, considering the weakness of my ability, and I would not presume to apply my little exhortations to so mature and learned a mind, unless I had gained confidence that I could accomplish what you command from the one who commands it, and unless I trusted that, through your merits and prayers, it would be granted that water should spring up in the desert (Psalm 106:33), and that rivers should flow in dry land (Psalm 104:41; Isaiah 43:19).

Therefore you and I must work together, so that he who gives wisdom to the little ones and makes the tongues of the mute eloquent (Wisdom 10:21) may command to flow from the aridity of my heart something that your thirst may worthily draw up. What subject, then, will be supplied to my pen, and from where shall an occasion for speaking with you be taken? If I undertake to write your praises and unfold the succession of your ancestors, which is greatly illuminated through you, I fear that I may appear burdensome and shameless, either by flattering you into a temptation toward human glory or by presuming that my talent can equal the praises of you and your family.

If, however, I discuss the commendation of the good of virginity, the introduction of that subject will now be superfluous, since from the first flowering of your age you chose it without human exhortations. And concerning this, many who at that time held high rank in the Church rightly did not remain silent.

> **[Note: [Col. 0162B]]** We learn from the same teacher’s Letter 143, now 188, to Juliana that Demetrias, at Augustine’s urging, rejected the marriage arranged for her and adopted the purpose of virginity. The Author had not read this letter when he incorporated its words into the text.

For it was a very remarkable thing, and one to be counted among the chief examples of divine grace, that you, the virgin Anicia, elevated above the highest summit of *trabeated nobility*—that is, nobility marked by the *trabea*, the ceremonial robe of consuls, augurs, and kings—from whose fertility descendants were expected in response to the wishes of ancestors, family, and country, suddenly turning your mind away, rejected mortal marriage out of desire for a heavenly wedding; and, so that you might consecrate your entire lineage with the distinction of this virtue, you pledged yourself as the first perpetual virgin of your family to the Son of the Virgin.

> **[Note: [Col. 0162B]]** The printed editions, together with Vatican manuscript 262, read: “the first perpetual virgin of your stock.” The correction was supplied by the other, older manuscript, Vatican 268.

> **[Note: [Col. 0162C]]** “See Augustine, Letter 143, now 188, to Juliana, Demetrias’s mother, and 179, now 150, to Proba and Juliana. Also Jerome’s Letter 8 and Pope Innocent I’s Letter 14. See also the letter that the heresiarch Pelagius wrote to this same virgin, to which the Author seems to have offered this work as an antidote.” **QUESN.**

> **[Note: [Col. 0162C]]** Two of our Vatican manuscripts, which we collated, erroneously read *trahens beatae nobilitatis* (“drawing along the blessed nobility”), as the editions also read before Quesnellus’s correction, which was accepted by the last editor of Saint Prosper. Quesnellus added the following note: “The *trabea* was the insignia of consuls, augurs, and kings. On this, see Bayfius, *On the Art of Dress*, chapter 11, where you will also find earlier authorities.”

The most learned men rightly stirred that age and those beginnings of yours with their exhortations. Although the supreme farmer provided powerful growth for your advancement, the cooperators of God’s grace nevertheless applied their pious cultivation at the proper time, so that the tender shoot might receive the strength of firmness and the tree of your purpose might bear fruits worthy of its nobility.

What place, however, will there be for our pages? After the highly ornamented writings of excellent teachers, what benefit will you find in the speech you have deigned to request, unless perhaps, because habit advances toward higher stages of virtue through both their teachings and your own efforts, I may warn you to beware of arrogance and commend to you, through faithful counsel, the sincerity of humility, so that in all the actions in which your conscience tells you that you are acting well, you may never dare to be secure.

> **[Note: [Col. 0163D]]** Thus more correctly according to the same Vatican manuscript. The common editions, together with another Vatican manuscript, read: “to be avoided.”

### CHAPTER II. True virtues must be distinguished from false ones.

Let us therefore discuss this most fitting for you and most salutary good which the Lord has bestowed, so that not only its visible aspects but also its hidden realities may be disclosed to our examination.

> **[Note: [Col. 0163D]]** We added “for you” from the manuscripts and from the editions of Prosper.

For the quality of this virtue is manifold. Although it is beautiful in outward matters as well, it is much more splendid and much brighter in its innermost parts, where there is nothing obscure, nothing troubled, nothing restless, because “there is great peace for those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Psalm 118:165).

As we approach the contemplation of blessed humility, let us repel all that abasement which weighs down sluggish and fickle minds. Nor should the general name exclude us so completely from the judgment of discernment that we consider all who are humble in any way worthy of praise. Necessity often imitates the will, and the appearance of sluggishness differs little from the image of modesty. But one thing burdens, another exercises; nor do the unremitting labor of misery and the sought-after strength of endurance reach the same end.

There is one name for poverty, but the mind of the poor is not one and the same, because it is not the same thing to rejoice in wealth well spent, to lament wealth not acquired, or to grieve over wealth that has been lost.

Nor is there any distinction in the name of the fear by which God is feared; but it is one thing to fear because you have sinned and another to fear lest you sin. In the former there is dread of punishment; in the latter, concern for reward. For this reason it is said of that servile fear, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), but of this free and filial fear: “The holy fear of the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 18:10).

> **[Note: [Col. 0163D]]** We added the word “holy,” which also occurs in the Psalm, from both Vatican manuscripts. In the more recent manuscript Vatican 262, *permanens* (“remaining”) is read instead of *manens* (“remaining”).

Having therefore removed that appearance of humility which is entirely fruitless, let us weigh only voluntary dispositions. Even if they are unequal when found at different levels of merit, they are nevertheless not opposed to virtue itself.

[Col. 0163D] ### CHAPTER III. The first good of humility is to preserve love and harmony among human beings.

The first principle of humility, then, concerns the duties of common life, through which both divine clemency is won and human society is bound together. It contributes greatly to strengthening love when, in accordance with apostolic teaching, people anticipate one another in showing honor (Romans 12:10), and when, considering one another superior to themselves, they gladly love to serve as subjects and do not know how to swell with pride as superiors.

This occurs when the poor do not hesitate to place the rich before themselves, and the rich rejoice to make the poor their equals; when the eminent do not grow proud of the glory of their ancestry, and the poor are not exalted by their sharing in human nature; when, finally, greater value is not assigned to great wealth than to good character, nor is the decorated power of the wicked considered greater than the unadorned justice of the righteous.

From this equitable and modest law of harmony—where there is no contest over the higher rank,

> **[Note: [Col. 0164D]]** We supplied the word *est* (“is”) from the same manuscripts.

and where one’s own prosperity does not inflate a person or another’s prosperity burn him—many advance beautifully and wonderfully toward that strength of humility which places itself outside every dignity and prefers to be suited for receiving injuries rather than capable of repelling them, so that what the Lord says may be fulfilled:

> “If anyone wishes to go to law with you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well; and whoever forces you to go one mile, go with him two more” (Matthew 5:40).

> **[Note: [Col. 0164D]]** The editions read *illud* without the enclitic conjunction *-que*. Our manuscripts supplied this conjunction, which is especially necessary here.

And likewise what the Apostle teaches when he says:

> “Why not rather accept the wrong? Why not rather suffer fraud?” (1 Corinthians 6:7).

Such people come very close to imitating our Lord and Savior himself, who, although he was rich, became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9); and when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, and he did not threaten the one who struck him (1 Peter 2:23). Since he had said, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44), he himself prayed for those by whom he was being crucified, in order to confirm such benevolence by his example.

### CHAPTER IV. The truly humble disdain the glory and wealth of the world.

Those who faithfully and intelligently understand by what work they have been saved and at what price they have been redeemed do not wish to belong among the wise of this world, nor do they wish to belong among the strong. For, as the Apostle says:

> “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; and God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; and God chose what is lowly and despised in the world, things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

That is, no one should think that he pleases God through the wisdom of the world, which is entirely carnal and, with all its vanity, is destroyed by true wisdom. For “the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” (Psalm 93:11).

When the disciples of truth therefore flee human glory and withdraw from love of temporal things, so that they may set their minds on the things of God and not on the things of human beings, they advance in understanding rather than decline. They do not lose the vigor of their hearts but receive the light of the highest intelligence. They live in this world, indeed, but leave behind all the noise of the world, “redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16).

At what price, however, is the peace of this present age more suitably purchased than by pouring back into the world itself all wealth, all dignities, and the material of every desire, and by buying Christian freedom through a holy and blessed exchange, so that the children of God become rich through poverty, strong through patience, and exalted through humility?

It is not, as lovers of this age think, the mark of a wicked heart or a sluggish mind to despise earthly riches, to disdain passing honors, and not to seek glory where “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts unjustly is blessed” (Psalm 9:23).

Therefore, if it is truly understood toward what and what sort of things this contempt for present affairs tends and yearns, nothing more upright, nothing more elevated, will be found in such minds. Through sacred desires they transcend everything and aspire not toward any creature, however powerful and marvelous, but toward the Creator himself of all things visible and invisible. To draw near to him is to become radiant; to fear him is to rejoice; to serve him is to reign.

> **[Note: [Col. 0165C]]** “P. Nannius wishes *abeunt* [‘they depart’] to be read.” **QUESN.**

> **[Note: [Col. 0165C]]** This reading of our manuscripts is better than the common *electius* (“more choice”).

### CHAPTER V. Not only the poor, but also the rich can be adorned with Christian humility.

This virtue, then, which is indifferent to temporal abundance and power and strives toward eternal life by a narrow and difficult way, ought not to admit voluntary paupers into the fellowship of Christian humility while excluding from participation in this good those who possess broad estates, magnificent patrimonies, and many resources in this age.

For there have always been many among God’s people who used wealth well, and it is in no way permissible either to say or to think that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—whose God the Lord declares himself to be (Exodus 3:6)—lacked true humility because they were not poor.

Nor that the most sacred man Melchizedek, who prefigured our Lord and Savior (Hebrews 7:3), was not perfectly humble because he excelled both in priesthood and in kingship.

Nor that this virtue was lacking in blessed Job, concerning whom God declares:

> “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a man without blame and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job 2:3).

Was this virtue lacking because, as it is written, he possessed seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred she-asses, and a very large household, and that man was greater than all the people of the East (Job 1:3)?

If he became a participant in this grace when, after losing all his possessions, his entire household, and his children, and after being struck with a most grievous wound from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, he scraped the discharge with a potsherd while sitting on a dung heap (Job 2:7), then later he was recalled to the likeness of arrogance and temptation when his bodily health was restored, when he again became the father of seven sons and three daughters, and when his entire substance was doubled (Job 42:10, 13).

> **[Note: [Col. 0166D]]** The editions read *quasi tunc* (“as though then”); and after some intervening words Quesnellus added *aut* (“or”) before *ad imaginem elationis* (“to the likeness of arrogance”), though that word was absent from the editions. In either form the reading is corrupt, about which the latest editor of Prosper conjectured somewhat; but, lacking manuscript evidence, he followed Quesnellus’s reading. Our manuscripts supplied the true reading.

> **[Note: [Col. 0166D]]** Because of the corrupt reading *quasi*, Quesnellus added *aut*, as we noted in the preceding annotation. Once the true reading had been established with the support of our manuscripts, this addition was unnecessary. Shortly afterward we added *tentationisque* (“and of temptation”) from the same manuscripts.

Far be it from the minds of the faithful to entertain so irreligious a belief that anyone among the saints, to whom God granted both riches and honors, should be thought to have been hindered by wealth or dignity from obtaining the merit of true humility, since both served to advance them in this virtue.

Although the whole life of a human being is a time of testing on earth (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint), and both abundance and poverty commonly become material for sin—when the rich are lifted up into pride or the poor leap into complaint—there have nevertheless always been, and in our own age there are still, good poor people as well as good rich people.

Nor does blessed Paul the Apostle warn Timothy without reason:

> “Command the rich in this present age not to be proud, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly gives us everything for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

There is no doubt that this occurs throughout the universal Church, which is spread across the whole world. The poor of Christ are not supported only by the resources of those who, in order to follow the Lord more freely, stripped themselves at once of all their possessions. The possessions of those who preside over their estates no differently than over the property of the poor and serve the needs of the Church under a kind of stewardship also contribute to the same work.

Each of them labors according to the measure of his strength so that what is necessary for the food and clothing of God’s household may be supplied, while at the same time seeing to it that in their own houses kindness may cherish everyone and discipline may restrain everyone under a just and holy order.

The Apostle says:

> “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for the members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8).

> **[Note: [Col. 0166D]]** Quesnellus read *et opulentia* (“and wealth”). We corrected this from the published editions of Prosper and from our manuscripts.

> **[Note: [Col. 0165C]]** The editions had *patientiae* (“of patience”). Quesnellus, guided by his own judgment, restored *sapientiae* (“of wisdom”), because the sense seemed to resist the word *patientiae*, as he stated in a short annotation. The latest editor of Prosper adopted this reading. Our manuscripts supplied the true reading, *potentiae* (“of power”), which agrees especially well with what precedes.

> **[Note: [Col. 0165D]]** It was formerly read in this way: “It is sent to eternal life by a narrow and difficult way.” Before us, someone attempted to substitute another word in place of the final word. Petrus Nannius of Alkmaar, in his scholia on Saint Ambrose, first published at Basel in 1551, thought that the passage could be corrected as follows: “It sends by a narrow and difficult way”—which would be excellent if he had written *enititur* (“strives”) instead of *mittit* (“sends”). A similar expression occurs in *Sermon 2 on Pentecost Fast*, chapter 1: “For because they avoid the narrow and difficult ways,” etc. This refers to Matthew 7:14: “How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life is.” Leo our author always renders it in this form: “The narrow and difficult way that leads to life,” as in *Sermon 5 on the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 1, and *Sermon 7 on Lent*, chapter 1, and elsewhere. This also provides some evidence by which this letter itself may be vindicated as belonging to Saint Leo. **QUESNELLUS.** He therefore published: “It strives toward eternal life by a narrow and difficult way.” But we preferred the reading of our Vatican manuscripts, which we have inserted into the text, to this arbitrary emendation.

[Col. 0167A] **266 CHAPTER VI. All the holy children of the Church, though unlike in other respects, are made equal by humility alone.**

Since the Church of God, which is the body of Christ, is woven together in such manifold variety that even things which are not equal converge into a single beauty, and since from every kind of human being, every rank of service, every measure of works, and every quality of virtues there arises an inseparable connection and impartial beauty of the whole edifice—so that nothing is lacking to the solidity of the whole that is not lacking to a part, and such peace and harmony exist there that what belongs to all must also belong to each—it is indisputably evident that there is a certain virtue which joins together and harmonizes the manifold unity and beautiful diversity of the saints.

This virtue is true humility, which can never be different from itself among any levels of merit. For there is much difference both in the succession of offices, in the gentleness of meekness, and in the choice of voluntary poverty; one person is greater or lesser than another in devotion to his purpose. But in true humility nothing is divided and nothing is unsolid; therefore it makes all its participants one, because it admits no inequality.

### CHAPTER VII. True humility consists in a perfect and complete confession of grace.

The distinctive character of this good consists in the confession of God’s grace, which is entirely rejected unless it is entirely received. For just as one who dissents in any respect from Catholic truth is outside the number of the faithful and the lot of the saints, so the person who denies anything of the fullness of grace is placed outside grace, as though a human being needed God’s help in some part of his actions but did not need it in another, and as though there were any time or moment when it could not be harmful for the Holy Spirit to be absent from him.

According to the essence of true divinity, the Holy Spirit is wholly everywhere and comprehends all things. Yet he is understood in a certain manner to withdraw from those whom he ceases to govern. The cessation of his help is taken as absence, and the person who rejoices that he himself, rather than God, has acted in the things he has done rightly considers this absence madly advantageous to himself.

God’s grace must therefore be confessed fully and truthfully. Its first gift is that his help is perceived. Hence the Apostle says:

> “We have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12).

> **[Note: [Col. 0167D]]** Thus our manuscripts and the common editions read: *sint* (“are”).

If there is anyone who thinks that he possesses certain good qualities whose giver is not God but of which he himself is the author, it is clear that he does not possess the Spirit of God but the spirit of the world, and that he swells with the teaching of secular wisdom, concerning which the Lord says:

> “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the intelligent I will reject. Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Corinthians 1:19).

According to this wisdom, as the Apostle says, some, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools (Romans 1:21).

Do you see what retribution is owed to the proud and with what reward they are filled—those who, if they have in some way approached knowledge of the truth, attribute this to their own wisdom and glory in their natural intelligence, as though they had known God not through God’s gift but through the power of their own understanding?

All the elements of the world and the entire nature of created things themselves demand, by their very appearance, that the invisible things of God should be perceived through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20). In the beauty of heaven and earth there are, as it were, pages always open to everyone’s eyes and never silent about their author; their testimony resembles the teaching of teachers and the words of Scripture.

> **[Note: [Col. 0167D]]** One Vatican manuscript reads *sint* (“are”).

But whatever it may be that strikes the exterior senses of the body, in the field of the heart where this cultivation is undertaken it can neither put down a root nor send forth a shoot unless that supreme and true farmer applies the power of his work and brings what has been planted to living growth.

Whether the contemplation of created things, the sequence of sacred volumes, or the knowledge of learned interpreters proclaims the truth with sincere and constant testimony, “neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

### CHAPTER VIII. The ruin of the proud is the gravest of all.

Among all human falls and all the sins committed, none is more serious than the ruin of the proud, especially when arrogance aims at injury to God. For some are puffed up by a desire for singular exaltation, seeking to be preferred to everyone else; others swell up because, rejecting God’s help, they strive to accomplish by their own power what cannot be done without his work. They take their hope away from the Lord and transfer it to themselves, so that what is written may be fulfilled in them:

> “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17:5).

This pride took its beginning from the devil. Because he took pleasure in the power and dignity that he had received from the Creator, and compared himself with the glory of his author, he was cast down from heavenly humility together with the angels whom he had drawn into agreement with his impiety.

> **[Note: [Col. 0167D]]** Perhaps “from sublimity.”

He was therefore able to harm the first human beings because, through poisonous lies, he persuaded them in their evil credulity that they would become better if they sprang into the freedom of their own choice than if they remained in the guardianship of the law that had been given.

> **[Note: [Col. 0168D]]** Quesnellus, together with the Paris edition of Saint Ambrose from 1569 and the latest edition of Prosper, reads *sicut* (“just as”). Some copies, and likewise our manuscripts, read *in libertate* (“in freedom”). 

### CHAPTER IX. Pride, by which a person wishes to be the author of his own good, is the beginning of every sin.

Whether, then, in the fall of the devil or in the transgression of the human being, pride is the beginning of sin. It is appropriately also called avarice, because both names signify a desire that longs to exceed its own measure and is unwilling to be rich except through what belongs to itself—as though it had this similarity to God: that it itself should be the source and it itself the abundance of its own goods.

This arrogance arises from the perverse use of God’s gifts. For if the Creator of natures had bestowed nothing beautiful or exalted upon rational natures, they would have nothing from which to exalt themselves.

> **[Note: [Col. 0169D]]** The common text corruptly reads *non enim* (“for not”). Our manuscripts supplied the correction.

No one takes pride in what he has not received, nor can anyone become inflated by something that is foreign to participation in him. The drunkard never boasts of sobriety, the envious person of benevolence, the savage of gentleness, or the shameless person of chastity. Vices themselves separate themselves from virtues. When people act in sins, they love what has been conceived not by nature but by evil will, as their own, because, as it is written, “the liar speaks from his own” (John 8:44).

But when a praiseworthy life is led in good and upright actions, what is done belongs to God, and what is loved belongs to God. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

Therefore, since boasting is either absent or rare among vices, and the person who boasts of disgrace is easily despised, the evil of pride must be guarded against above all in the virtues, because it lies in wait most opportunely for those to whom rightful praise is owed.

> **[Note: [Col. 0169D]]** The Prosper edition reads *sit* (“be”).

269 **CHAPTER X. Pride and the Pelagian heresy arose from good works; and likewise the remnants of the Pelagians.**

When, therefore, through the ineffable mercy of God, freedom is restored to captives, salvation to the lost, and life to the dead; when, in the sacrament of Christ’s cross and resurrection, oldness returns to newness and impiety is regenerated into innocence, the ancient enemy rages more malignantly and burns more fiercely. While he strives by countless arts of harming to overthrow the human race—sowing discord, arousing anger, sharpening desires, advising shameful things, devising falsehoods, and multiplying the snares of error through ingenious opinions—he is consumed more by the virtue of those who stand firm than he rejoices in the weakness of those who fall.

For many who serve God and meditate day and night on his law have crucified their flesh with its desires and passions, and have subdued the incentives of every allure­ment. They were not conquered by losses, broken by persecutions, or corrupted by prosperity; they neither loved this world when it obeyed them nor feared it when it threatened them. With what assault, then, could the devil attack such great firmness and so lofty a purpose, unless he should inject a desire for praise into those whom he had been unable to persuade to love vices? [Note: [Col. 0169D] So read our manuscripts and Prosper’s printed editions. Quesnellus reads: “so that from there.”] And was the final temptation to be devised from the very source from which the first deception had caused harm?

Accordingly, glory in the eyes of men did not creep in among the sluggish and lukewarm, nor among the inactive and uncultivated, but rather among certain diligent souls, radiant with the excellence of good deeds. Those whom he had not moved by assault, he cast down by exaltation. For the more distinguished they were in merits, the more suitable he found them for his snares. He incited those established in the paradise of the Church and abounding in the delights of virtue to confidence in their free choice, so that they should place their progress in themselves and stretch out the hand of presumption toward the tree of their own will.

Indeed, innumerable hearts of the saints resisted this impiety [Note: [Col. 0169D] The ancient edition of Prosper reads “countless.” Quesnellus’s correction is supported by our manuscripts.], and not only the learned bishops, but also the universal peoples of the Church, following the example of the apostolic see, recoiled from the madness of the new doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0169D] Quesnellus criticizes this passage in dissertation 4, ch. 6, no. 5, as though the author, wishing to exalt the glory of the Roman see, attributed to it what Prosper asserts of the Africans. But from Prosper himself we shall show in the observations on the cited dissertation, no. 8 and following, in what sense and how truly the author wrote.] [Col. 0170B] But certain men found [Note: [Col. 0170D] Thus our manuscripts agree with Quesnellus. In the latest edition of Prosper, the reading is “certain persons.”] viperous counsels by which to pour the venom of their teaching into others and to arm their tongues through the deceitful arguments of false reasoning. Hence came that fraudulent praise of human nature and that defense of the original dignity allegedly left unharmed in all human beings. Hence it was asserted that Adam’s sin had harmed his descendants by example, not by transmission; and that, just as it had been possible for him not to violate the commandment, so it was free for each person to avoid sin. Hence came the nullification of the baptism of infants, who, they said, were granted adoption alone and absolved from no guilt. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Thus the same manuscript books. The printed editions read “nevertheless.”] Finally, there was a feigned and insincere confession of divine grace: that grace was given according to merits, rather than that merits arose from it.

Some retained this portion of the proud proclamation while rejecting the rest. [Note: [Col. 0170D] Quesnellus attached this note: “The remnants of the Pelagians, the Semi-Pelagians,” as though what follows concerned the Semi-Pelagians. But we shall show in detail in the notes on dissertation 2, no. 4, that these matters concern certain concealed Pelagians.] Yet there is no doubt that they did this either with excessive ignorance or with great wickedness, in order to raise the universal ruin of humanity by the privilege of merits. Although among our own people they acknowledged the wounds of original sin, they nevertheless showed that among their own they held this position: that the transgression of the first human beings had harmed only those who imitated them; that natural capacity had lost nothing of its own through another’s sin; and that, by voluntary devotion, it was both possible and free for a person to earn the abundance of grace.

### CHAPTER XI. All are born in sin and alienated from salvation unless they are reborn in Christ.

But Catholic minds readily understand and rightly detest this portion of the condemned doctrine. For when the Lord Jesus says, “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke 5:31), these men are convicted of crying out in their pride even without speaking: “We are healthy; we have no need of a physician. What assistance from the help of grace should we await, when we possess strength from the soundness of nature?”

John does not testify in vain when he says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Nor is it written in vain: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint); and: “Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (ibid., according to the Vulgate).

For this reason, just as the Savior’s ordinance remains in the Church today—“Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5)—so the law had most sacredly provided that, if a male child were not circumcised on the eighth day, his soul would be cut off from his people (Genesis 17:14), having no share in Israel’s inheritance. The Holy Spirit would not have inserted all these testimonies, and many more, into the sacred writings with such care if the nature of Adam’s descendants had been as it was originally established in Adam himself.

271 But because the Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) and to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), it is clear that all are subject to condemnation in Adam by birth, unless they are liberated in Christ by rebirth.

We must therefore carefully consider what takes place in the gift of regeneration itself. Although all the elements of the same mystery converge toward one end, what is visibly performed is one thing, and what is invisibly celebrated is another. Nor is the form in the sacrament identical with its power: the form is supplied through the service of a human minister, whereas the power is provided through the effect of the divine work. [Note: [Col. 0171D] The printed editions, together with one of our Vatican manuscripts, add “with”; we deleted it on the authority of another manuscript.] To this power, certainly, we must refer the fact that, while the outward person is washed, the inward person is changed; the old creature becomes a new creature; vessels of wrath are transferred into vessels of mercy; sinful flesh is changed into the body of Christ; the impious become righteous; captives become free; and children of human beings become children of God—those who were born “not of bloods, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:13).

Since we have received this without doubt, what the Apostle teaches is most true when he says: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Romans 8:14). Let those, therefore, consider whose children they wish to be regarded who have defined all human beings as governed by their own will, when the same Apostle declares: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

### CHAPTER XII. Glory is to be given to God alone, from whom come every virtue, glory, and wisdom.

Having therefore refuted the impious vanity of the proud, by which even those things that appear praiseworthy in them are turned into sin, let us choose that humility whose virtue and glory is God [Note: [Col. 0171D] Thus Quesnellus and the latest editor of Prosper. Earlier editions of the Vulgate, together with a more recent Vatican manuscript, read: “whose virtue is the glory of God.” Another Vatican manuscript reads: “whose virtue and glory is God.”], knowing that the prophet David sang of the saints:

“Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they shall rejoice all the day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted; for you are the glory of their virtue” (Psalm 88:17).

In another place also he devoutly confesses that the Lord is to be praised in his saints, saying: “God is wondrous in his saints; the God of Israel himself shall give strength and power to his people” (Psalm 67:36). [Note: [Col. 0171D] Printed editions read “Hence also.” The reading of our manuscripts is better.]

Jeremiah agrees with him and says: “Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jeremiah 9:23–24).

The Proverbs of Solomon disclose from whom understanding and knowledge come, saying: “For the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 11:6). [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Vulgate reads “Hence in the book of Ecclesiastes,” or “in Ecclesiastes.” We preferred the reading of our Vatican manuscript.]

In the book of Ecclesiastes we read that both the hearts and the works of the righteous are in the hand of God, and that they advance in their pursuits only as far as he has advanced them. “However much,” he says, “a man may labor to seek, he will not find. And whatever the wise man may say in order to know, he cannot discover, because my heart has seen all this: that the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 8:17; 9:1). [Note: [Col. 0172D] The same manuscripts read “whatever he may have loved.”]

Such is what the Apostle proclaims when he says that every good word and every holy work is a gift of the Holy Spirit, without whom nothing is rightly done. “Therefore,” he says, “I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus,’ and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit; varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; varieties of works, but the same God who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; [Note: [Col. 0172D] Thus the same Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read “to another.”] to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of utterances. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:3–11).

### CHAPTER XIII. Without Christ working in us, we can do no good; yet free choice is not removed but assisted.

There are also countless other testimonies which, in a kind of united proclamation, confirm from the pages of both the New and the Old Testament that this is the supremely excellent dignity of true humility: that everything which makes a person Christian is to be referred to the gift of divine grace. It would have been excessive, however, to gather such a multitude of passages into one place, especially since I was speaking to Your Holiness, to whom, from the pattern of the things we have recalled, they would all present themselves either in memory or upon reading. Some of them, moreover, though extremely brief, possess such fullness and power that no ingenuity opposed to them can twist them into another meaning. [Col. 0173A]

For what contradiction can be admitted in what Truth itself is reported to have said to his disciples through John’s Gospel?

“As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5).

Is not the branch convicted of being proud when it is emptied of all fruitfulness if it is not nourished by the abundance of the vine? For who can produce the fruit of righteousness without the help of grace? Or who dares say that he is not separated from Christ while he denies that Christ works in him?

Or should we perhaps fear that we seem to remove free choice when we say that everything by which God is made favorable is to be referred to him? That this does not follow is clearly shown by the light of truth [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Vulgate had “is shown by the truth,” without the word “light.” Quesnellus suspected a defect and noted: “The word ‘voice,’ or something similar, seems to be missing here.” One of our manuscripts supplied “light”; another supplied the phrase differently: “truth shows.”]: while the Spirit of God works, choice is assisted, not removed. Grace accomplishes this: that the will, corrupted by sin, drunk with vanities, surrounded by seductions, and obstructed by difficulties, does not remain in its sicknesses, but, healed by the aid of the merciful physician, grows strong again and rejoices that, without asking, it has been taught, and without seeking, has been sought.

For daily what the prophet Isaiah foretold is fulfilled: “Those to whom he was not announced shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isaiah 52:15).

John teaches how this happens when he says: “We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of evil; and we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son” (John 5:19–20). The Lord also continually accomplishes this now by the same power, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). [Note: [Col. 0174D] The word “now” was also added from an older Vatican manuscript.]

### CHAPTER XIV. In no respect is the operation of grace preceded by human willing.

Therefore, it is the mercy of God that we seek the mercy of God, for he says: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy” (Romans 9:15). Through Jeremiah the same Lord wonderfully makes clear that no one precedes God’s grace by his own merit, but that, because of the love with which God loves even those who have turned away, they are drawn to mercy.

“With everlasting love,” he says, “I have loved you; therefore I have drawn you to compassion, because I shall build you, and you shall be built, O virgin of Israel” (Jeremiah 31:3).

The apostle John also agrees with this statement when he says: “Not as though we loved God, but because he himself loved us”; and shortly afterward: “Therefore let us love, because God first loved us” (1 John 4:10, 19).

The apostle Paul expresses the same conviction when he says in the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Share in the labor of the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us before eternal times” (2 Timothy 2:8–9). [Note: [Col. 0174D] In the same manuscript, a later hand adds the word “his” before “holy.”]

Writing also to Titus, he teaches that God’s grace is preceded by no human merit:

“For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, he saved us—not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the washing of regeneration of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:3–7).

Every devout movement of enlightened minds, then, cannot indeed be separated from a person’s own will, since no one will do anything rightly except what he does willingly. Yet for the mind’s intention to move toward what is just and useful, it is conceived from the inspiration of that eternal and unchangeable will.

Just as the physician’s art enables clouded eyes to see what they do not see—and yet the sight bestowed by medicine is still truly theirs—so in hearts that are slow and dull, the film covering their vision is wiped away by the Holy Spirit, and from the true light they receive light, though their lamps had already become dark and failing. Nevertheless, whatever brightness they have received will still belong to them.

Therefore the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). He likewise commands that our lamps should always be burning, so that the mind, kindled by heavenly fire, may not grow lukewarm but may strive always to burn; and if some adversity disturbs its vigor, it should ask to be rekindled from the source from which it first began to flame.

### CHAPTER XV. The commandment is given so that the help of the one who commands may be sought, and a person may cooperate with it by obeying.

Therefore, since prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic teaching most clearly wishes us neither to be proud nor idle, we must be diligent cooperators with the grace of God, following watchfully and soberly the grace that arouses, assists, enriches, and daily advances us. We must never cease giving thanks, because amid the prosperity and adversity of this life, by which we are continually struck with a twofold temptation, we are nourished by it when we progress, sustained by it when we stand, and restored by it when we fall back.

For the Spirit says through the prophet David: “The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall take pleasure in his way. When he falls, he shall not be shattered, because the Lord supports him with his hand.” It is not therefore in vain that we are commanded to be good when it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:23–24, 27).

Nor does the Lord say through Jeremiah in vain: “I will put my fear into their heart, and I will visit them in order to make them good” (Jeremiah 32:40–41).

Nor was the apostle Paul’s command to the Romans superfluous: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Romans 12:21), when he says to the Corinthians: “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7).

For in all God’s admonitions and commandments there is one and the same principle of divine grace and human obedience. A commandment is never given for any other reason than that the help of the one who commands may be sought. The voices of teachers and the letters of the pages, which serve God for the instruction of those who hear or read, are not without the power of the one whom they serve. And when what is commanded is fulfilled obediently, the effect of the divine work is revealed. [Note: [Col. 0175D] On the authority of an older Vatican manuscript, we preferred “obediently” to “by the obedient one.”]

### CHAPTER XVI. How greatly pride in good works must be avoided, since it corrupts everything.

The snares of the tempter remain vigilant, so that where devotion advances, pride may creep in, and so that a person may glory in a good work in himself rather than in the Lord. The Apostle’s warning against this danger urges us when he says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to act according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Therefore, the more excellently people progress in God’s commandments, the greater are their reasons for fear and trembling: lest the mind, conscious of its own increase in goodness and eager for praise, be carried away into the excess of pride, and become impure through vanity while it appears to itself radiant with virtue.

Let us hear what blessed Peter proclaims against this danger in his First Epistle: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him minister as from the strength that God supplies, so that God may be honored in all things through Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and dominion forever” (1 Peter 4:11). [Note: [Col. 0175D] Quesnellus reads “Likewise in the Epistle.” The latest edition of Prosper reads “Likewise he himself in the Epistle.” Vatican manuscript 262 reads “He himself in the Epistle.” We adopted the reading of the older manuscripts.]

In the same man’s Second Epistle: “May grace be multiplied for you in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, who by his divine power has granted us everything pertaining to life and godliness through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue. Through these he has granted us very great and precious promises, so that through them you may become participants in the divine nature, having escaped the corruption of desire that is in the world” (2 Peter 1:2–4).

If, then, God has granted us by his divine power everything pertaining to life and godliness, nothing must be fled from more than the appetite of this desire, which denies the power of the divine work out of love for its own dignity. While other desires diminish only those goods opposed to them, this desire, by drawing everything to itself, corrupts everything at once.

Although the general name of all pride is hateful—whether it swells with honor, nobility, or excessive wealth [Note: [Col. 0175D] We inserted the particle “of” from the manuscripts and from Prosper’s latest edition.]—this form of it is found to be more harmful than all temptations because it appears to befriend the very virtues that it wishes to destroy. Yet because whatever is more exalted falls more grievously, the prince of pride rejoices when those whom he has been able to overthrow by his assault have grown to greater heights.

### CHAPTER XVII. Through humility a person is truly subjected and united to God.

The firmest good of humility confronts this evil. We called it true humility because it is the unconquerable strength of all the virtues and, in a certain sense, the life of its own members. We distinguish it from those practices that it can share even with the wise men of the world, and we define its distinctive character by this: it is subject to God in all things.

Nor can it lose anything of its merits, because it places the causes and progress of those merits not in itself but in its author. It is fitting that the image of God should shine with God’s splendor and be adorned from him, saying: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7). Otherwise it is adulterous and alienated from the divine marriage if it displays in the mirror of its heart the beauty of anyone else, or consents to be adorned with any jewels except those which it has received from the bridegroom’s treasures as the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER XVIII. Demetrias has greater need of humility, both because of the purity of her virginity and because of the splendor of her family.

If every Christian soul must be fortified by the solidity of this continence, since all have received the sacrament of marriage in whatever order of their calling, how much more must the dignity of your person be armed with the protection of this virtue, since so many occasions for boasting present themselves to you from the exceedingly rich gifts of God’s grace.

Although your virginity is shared with the purity of many virgins, there is not easily found one who can be compared with you in the magnificence of your household and the splendor of your most ancient family. You must not grow proud of these things, nor ascribe to yourself the fact that you have placed Christ above them. [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Vulgate reads “itself.” We preferred the reading of Vatican manuscript 268, which seems very appropriate and also agrees better with what follows.] He himself is true humility, true charity, and true virginity.

The mind is free from every contamination when, whether in itself or in another, it loves nothing except what it does not doubt is from God. For to love something that is not from the work and Spirit of God is not chaste love. It is enough for the tempter to have violated lofty and distinguished souls by this deception: those whom he did not drive toward illicit things, he cast down into self-exaltation through the desire to please themselves. [Note: [Col. 0176D] Earlier editions read “by pleasing themselves into exaltation.” Quesnellus emended this to “from exaltation.” Both our manuscripts read “of pleasing themselves”; one adds “to exaltation,” the other “to flattery,” which appears to be a scribal error for “to exaltation.” We preferred the former.]

### CHAPTER XIX. Without charity, which does not seek its own interests, nothing is beneficial.

The Apostle was certainly speaking of this charity, and was refining its distinctive character through the most subtle distinctions, when he said:

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

We would labor at the obscurity of these definitions if what follows did not show what kind of charity this is—the only charity through which so many labors of works and so many merits of virtues do not perish. Let it be granted that a manifold skill in speaking, extending not only to every art of human eloquence but also to the capacity of angelic speech, is comparable to the useless sound of bronze and the clanging of cymbals if it lacks charity. Let it be granted that one who possesses prophecy and knowledge, and faith commanding demons, is nothing because he is empty of charity. Yet that even one who has distributed his possessions to feed the poor, or who has handed over his body to be burned in confession of Christ, could be without this charity would seem incredible, unless blessed Paul had said it.

Nevertheless, when he described the members of this same charity and taught what this virtue is, without which no virtues can be beneficial, he said: “Charity is patient, charity is kind; charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5), and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0177D] The editions of Douai and Cologne’s Prosper read “did not precede.”]

### CHAPTER XX. The vain glory of one’s own merit is more harmful than every sin.

Pride, ambition, and the proud defense of one’s own goods can destroy almsgiving and empty martyrdoms—if someone pours out great wealth for love of human praise, or endures savage tortures not with the strength God has granted but with the strength he has presumed upon in himself.

For this is to be puffed up by confidence in oneself; this is to pursue empty glory at whatever cost; finally, this is to refuse to possess what belongs to God and to establish one’s merit where divine assistance has ceased. This pride is more harmful than every sin and more deranged than every kind of exaltation. [Note: [Col. 0177D] Perhaps “more incurable.” Quesnellus. Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript reads “the help of his restorer”; another, “the help of his restorer” in a different grammatical form.]

A person rises easily from any fall into sin when, struck down, he seeks help from his restorer. But nothing assists this ruin, because the proud person either recognizes his sin only with difficulty or, even if he understands it, does not run to the physician but promises himself a remedy from himself. Healing never advances where the disease itself is the medicine.

### CHAPTER XXI. The poison of pride is excluded only by humility and charity, which embrace one another.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Quesnellus reads “But hence,” and then, with the other printed editions, “its breath.” Our manuscripts supplied the better reading.] The spirit of true humility and true charity excludes this most corrupt condition of the disease. These virtues are never separated from each other, and their connection is so inseparable that whoever is built up in one possesses both at once. For just as humility is a part of charity, so charity is a part of humility.

If we recall those things that the Apostle declared fruitless without the good of charity, we shall find that, if true humility is absent, they possess the same kind of quality. [Note: [Col. 0177D] While the printed editions had “charity,” Quesnellus substituted “vanity” and added this note: “In all printed manuscripts one reads ‘charity,’ but everyone sees how foreign this is to the author’s mind. Someone wrote ‘truth’ in the margin of this passage in volume 3 of the works on Grace, published at Louvain in 1648. Although that can produce some meaning, I nevertheless judge it more convenient and suitable to substitute ‘vanity,’ or ‘uselessness,’ or another word of equal force, as anyone will understand from the sequence of the context.” Thus he. Our manuscripts, however, remove the entire difficulty by consistently presenting “quality.”]

What fruit will knowledge have with arrogance, faith with human glory, generosity with boasting, or martyrdom with exaltation? Since both humility and charity aim at the destruction of pride, let whatever has been discussed concerning one be understood concerning both. [Note: [Col. 0178D] The printed editions had “in strictness.” Quesnellus thought it should be emended to “toward strictness.” Our Vatican manuscripts give the better reading, “toward the destruction.”]

### CHAPTER XXII. We have no good of ourselves, since even right prayer is not from ourselves.

It remains now, most sacred virgin of God, that with the sober and chaste judgment of your holy heart you examine its hidden chambers [Note: [Col. 0178D] The printed editions read “ark,” wrongly; corrected from the Vatican manuscripts.] and, having crushed the goad of every kind of exaltation, investigate and count within yourself what gifts your bridegroom has bestowed upon you and of what kind they are. I ought not to enumerate them, lest I either weave together too many or pass over too few. Even true praise would burden your modesty, and I would act against my own argument if, after urging someone to restrain herself from human glory, I should urge you toward it by my praises.

Enter, then, the court of your mind; in the chamber of your purest conscience look around at the ornaments stored there. Whatever you find splendid, beautiful, and precious, do not doubt that it is the work and gift of God. In all the wealth of your good qualities, acknowledge both the grace of the giver and the right of ownership. For you have received what you possess, and whatever has increased through the diligence of your labor has been increased for you by him through whom it had begun.

Therefore you must use what God has bestowed [Note: [Col. 0178D] Thus the same manuscripts. Others read “them.”], and you must always ask from the same one that you may use his gifts faithfully and wisely. For what good can we have without him, when even the ability to pray rightly comes from him? The Apostle says:

“For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should; but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God” (Romans 8:26–27).

And lest there be any doubt about which spirit he was speaking of, he had already said above:

“For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:15–17). [Note: [Col. 0179C] The conjunction “also” has been added from our manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER XXIII. Every right affection, thought, and word of ours comes from God.

The Holy Spirit fills his own instrument, and the finger of God touches the hearts of the saints like the strings of a harp. Therefore, when on the day of Pentecost he flowed upon the apostles and the people of believers, as he had been promised by the Lord, he appeared in the form of fiery tongues and caused those upon whom he rested to speak in the languages of all nations. Thus it would be unmistakable that, through his inspiration, a useful affection and rational speech were supplied to the minds of the faithful, just as the Lord himself intimated to his disciples when he said:

“When they hand you over, do not think about how or what you will speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19).

Let us not believe that this happens only in times of great tribulation and is not granted in peace. Let us hear the Apostle defining that even our thoughts cannot be right unless they have been implanted in us by God. “We have such confidence through Christ toward God,” he says, “not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:4–5).

 [Note: [Col. 0179C] Thus according to Vatican manuscript 268. Another Vatican manuscript, 262, reads “so that it may not be in solitude.” From the same Vatican manuscript 268 we have written “but not” in place of the printed editions’ “but also.” At the end of the chapter Quesnellus had “so, as though from us.” We deleted “so” on the authority of our manuscripts and Prosper’s editions.]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Whatever virtue and charity the saints possess in this life, they possess from God; for whatever they will possess in heaven will also come from him: their portion comes from the one from whom their fullness will come.

Therefore, since from God there is in the souls of the saints a useful meditation, a just petition, and an effective action, from God also come firmness in faith, patience in tribulation, and victory in persecution, great is the happiness found in true humility, for which God is love, God is wisdom, God is counsel, and God is strength. Nor is there any doubt that this submission is already established in large part through participation in that future blessedness where God will be “all in all” [Col. 0180A] (1 Cor. 15:28); 281 yet this cannot be fully attained in the present life because our mortal nature has not yet put on immortality, nor has corruption passed into incorruption. The flesh still desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; nor is such harmony found in any human being that the law of the mind is not opposed by the law implanted in the members.

For this reason, what the apostle John says is understood as spoken on behalf of all the saints: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Yet the same apostle also says: “Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God” (1 John 3:9). Both statements, therefore, are true: no one is without sin, since no one is without the law of sin; and the one who is born of God [Note: [Col. 0180C] The word *est* was deleted by Quesnel; we restored it from our manuscripts and Prosper’s printed editions.] does not commit sin, because through the law of the mind—that is, through charity, which is the seed of God—he does not commit sin.

“For charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8); [Note: [Col. 0180C] The printed editions read *sine qua* (“without which”), and later *per hanc* (“through this”); since this was senseless, Quesnel, retaining *sine qua*, corrected it to *per hanc*. But our superior Vatican manuscript taught that *per quam* (“through which”) should instead be retained and *sine ea* (“without it”) corrected.] and without it no good is of any benefit, since through it every sin is destroyed. Therefore, while “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wis. 9:15), it is not yet attained [Note: [Col. 0180C] The common editions mistakenly read *anima* (“soul”). All our manuscripts confirm Quesnel’s correction, *omnia* (“all things”).] that God should be all in all, because no one is without the spur of temptation and the uncertainty of changeability. But because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17), without doubt the portion of every virtue is possessed from the one from whom its fullness will come; and each person is happier and more closely joined to God in proportion as divine grace, rather than human action, is greater in him.

Bless the Lord, therefore, at all times, and let his praise always be in your mouth (Ps. 33:1); but let your soul consent to be praised only in the Lord. The proud will indeed resist this, but the meek [Note: [Col. 0180D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “will hear and rejoice.”] will hear it and rejoice (ibid., 3).

[Note: [Col. 0179C] “In all other editions of this letter, *ut illis* was read instead of *utilis*; this alteration, slight in itself but combined with faulty punctuation, completely overturned the meaning of so excellent a sentence. Although we restored it by conjecture alone, we are nevertheless no less confident of the correction. Yet lest anyone complain that an old reading has been taken from him [Col. 0179D], we reproduce it here: [Col. 0180C] ‘Therefore, since from God there is in the souls of the saints that there be for them a just meditation, an effective petition, and an action from God, firmness in faith, etc.’ QUESNELL.]

# [A BRIEF TREATISE AGAINST THE ARIANS]

[Col. 0179]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BRIEF TREATISE

### 1

The following short work, inscribed to our Leo with the words, “Disputation of the most holy Pope Leo against heretics,” was discovered when, at our request, his works were being sought in the Ambrosian Library. It was found in a manuscript marked I, no. 119; since it was believed to be unpublished, a careful transcript of it was sent to us. Louis Muratori likewise mentions this same work, preserved in the same library under the same title, in volume II of *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation 44, p. 928. Yet, by indicating a codex marked P, no. 154, he seems to refer to a different copy, unless perhaps these shelf-marks were later changed. He too believed the work to be unprinted, but left its attribution to Leo uncertain.

We found the same work, likewise bearing Leo’s name, in an old manuscript of the Fathers of the Hermits of Saints Philip and James at Padua, appended to several works of St. Cyprian; with the assistance of Father Master Antonio Manentio, we were also able to collate it. There the inscription reads: “A Brief Treatise of Pope Leo against Heretics or Schismatics.”

### 2

With the same title, *A Brief Treatise*, but without the author’s name, Father Jacques Sirmond had formerly found this same treatise, together with Leo’s works, in two codices, one Corbie and one Pithou; they prefixed to it the title “A Brief Treatise against the Arians,” or “A Brief Treatise against Heretics.” It was published by Sirmond himself and appears in volume I of *Various Works*, p. 224, and thereafter in volume VII of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 8.

Sirmond prefixed the following title:

“An Brief Treatise of the Faith against the Arian Heretics, in which the equality of the three divine persons is clearly demonstrated by numerous passages and arguments from Holy Scripture, by an uncertain but very ancient author.”

Although he presented the author as uncertain because neither of the two manuscripts mentioned names an author, he says in his preface that, since this *Brief Treatise* is embedded in both codices among Leo’s works and seems comparable to them in age, it occurred to him that it might reasonably be believed to be the *Brief Treatise of the Faith* which Pope Leo states in Letter 60 (now 113) that Julian of Coa had sent him but which had not yet reached him. He further thought that, whoever its author was, both Eugenius of Carthage, in the *Statement of Faith* which he presented in his own name and that of his colleagues to King Huneric, and Idatius, in his book against the Arian Varimadus, appeared to have borrowed from it.

### 3

Quesnel, in note 2 on the cited Letter 113, opposes this conjecture and Sirmond’s opinion, and rightly so, as will be clear from that same note. Although it is correctly established there that the *Brief Treatise of the Faith* sent by Julian of Coa to Pope Leo was nothing other than the definition of faith promulgated at the Council of Chalcedon—which elsewhere is repeatedly called the *Treatise of the Faith*—it is recognized as entirely different from this work.

Nor does this work appear to have been written in the East for the Eastern Church, but in the West for those regions of the West in which the Arians were dominant and repeated baptism; this practice is condemned in the final chapter of the work. So far as we know, it does not fit the Arians of the East, but rather the Africans or Spaniards who are reported to have repeated baptism under the Vandals or Goths.

As for the Africans, this accords especially well with Leo’s period. For the author of the book *On Promises and Predictions*, who was an African and wrote while Valentinian III was still alive, before the year 455, says of these heretics: “The Arian attacks by blowing upon and rebaptizing the members of the lamb which Christ had already consecrated with his own blood.”

### 4

We shall add an observation of no little importance. In our *Brief Treatise*, section 24, we read:

“Just as, if someone puts bread that has already been baked once back into water and wishes to mix and bake it again, it loses its former dignity and is changed into blackness and earth, so anyone who permits baptism to be repeated in himself becomes such.”

Since this same comparison, with the same purpose and argument, was used against the Arian Genseric by Sebastian the Count, a Catholic man, in Victor of Vita, book I of *The Vandal Persecution*, some have wondered whether Sebastian learned this comparison from our *Brief Treatise*, which was already circulating in Africa.

But Victor of Vita openly presents that same Count as the author of the comparison and argument. “To him [Genseric],” he says, “Sebastian, finding the matter remarkable and necessary for many, gave an apt reply suited to the occasion” (see Tillemont, *Life of Eugenius*, article 12, volume XVI). We shall quote the complete text in its proper place, note 55 (below, column 00, note a).

It therefore seems more probable that the author of our *Brief Treatise* took this argument from the reply of Count Sebastian, which was famous among the Africans, since neither Genseric nor the other Arians could refute it. Sebastian’s action occurred around the year 449; consequently, on the hypothesis just mentioned, the *Brief Treatise* should be said to have been written shortly afterward by an African against the Arians occupying Africa. This could have coincided with Leo’s pontificate and the later years of his pontificate.

### 5

Chifflet, in his preface to Ferrandus the deacon, writes that he found this *Brief Treatise of the Faith* attributed to the deacon Alcuin in a manuscript of the Charterhouse of Portes. Yet the work cannot be assigned to this author, who is certainly known to have written three books on the Trinity: first, because it is utterly unlike his style; and second, because the rebaptism practiced by the Arians does not belong to Alcuin’s period. Nor does the old interpretation of several passages of Holy Scripture used in this work fit his period.

### 6

Moreover, since the work is inscribed to our Leo in two or three manuscripts, and in two others found by Sirmond it was inserted among the works of that same pontiff, although the manifest difference in writing seems to make attribution to the pontiff impossible, it may nevertheless perhaps have had some connection with him that has not come down to our knowledge. For this reason we have thought it not without justification that it should not be omitted from this appendix.

[Col. 0181]

# A BRIEF TREATISE AGAINST THE ARIANS

We have already published this *Brief Treatise* in volume XIII of our edition, column 653; see it there. **EDITOR**

# [THE LIFE AND SHORT WORKS OF ST. HILARY]

[Col. 0181]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING WORKS

Quesnel prefixed the following short preface to the *Life and Short Works of St. Hilary of Arles*, which he believed should not be separated from Leo’s works:

“So close is the bond between Leo and Hilary in age, talent, eloquence, dignity, and the events of their lives that it was almost necessary to append Hilary’s *Life* and short works to Leo’s writings. The necessity was increased, at least with regard to Hilary’s *Life*, both by the almost infinite number of errors with which it abounds and by the scarcity of copies.

“As for this *Life*, in the manuscript of Arles which the most distinguished man, Lord Saxius, canon of the Church of Arles, courteously shared with us, its author is called Reverentius, Hilary’s successor. Yet there is no successor of Hilary by this name. The one who immediately succeeded him was Ravennius, and the *Life* itself makes clear that Ravennius was not its author.

“Furthermore, there can scarcely be doubt that this is the very *Life* which Gennadius, in the final chapter of his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, testifies was written by Honoratus, bishop of Marseilles and Hilary’s pupil. The *Life* itself also suggests this, since it states that its author attended Hilary’s funeral. ‘He himself,’ says Gennadius, ‘composes for the edification of posterity the Lives of the holy Fathers for reading, especially that of his teacher’—Barralis appears to have read *benefactor*—‘the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles.’

“Philippus Labbe believed this *Life* had perished, in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, because he distinguished it from the Life of Hilary which Barralis inserted into the Lérins Chronicle and which appears in Surius. But Barralis’s Life of Hilary is none other than the one written by Honoratus, as Barralis himself most accurately conjectured; he published it from, as he says, a very ancient parchment manuscript of the monastery of Lérins.

“I believe that the Reverentius to whom the Arles manuscript attributes the writing of the *Life* is none other than Honoratus, who may have wished to conceal himself under the name Reverentius while preserving the meaning of his own name: *honor* and *reverence* signify the same thing. This conjecture is supported by the example of several writers of the same age who issued various treatises either without their own names or even under another person’s name.

“Hilary, as Gennadius records, published some other small works, evidence of an educated mind and faithful tongue. Among them, his principal and most useful work for many was the composition of the *Life of St. Honoratus*, his predecessor. We publish it here [Col. 0183] according to the Arles manuscript and the Bollandist edition, having collated the text anew. We add the *Meter on Genesis*, dedicated to Pope Leo, and a very brief letter written to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon.

“The account of the miracles of St. Genesius, which is read under Hilary’s name in Surius, is foreign to his eloquence and rather resembles the style of Honoratus of Marseilles, whom Gennadius also testifies to have written several works concerning the Lives of the holy Fathers.

“Trithemius says that Hilary delivered almost innumerable homilies, many of which perhaps lie hidden among the works attributed to Eusebius or Eucherius. But we have neither the time nor the ability to distinguish them. The author of his *Life* lists several others in chapter 11:

“‘His grace,’ he says, ‘can without hesitation be recognized from those works which he conceived, brought forth, adorned, and produced with the same force of expression: namely, the Life of the bishop Honoratus; homilies prepared for the festivals of the entire year; an exposition of the Creed requiring careful attention; a very large number of letters; and also verses on the burning spring.’
