“Some writings of secular learning are also indicated by these words from chapter 1: ‘The monuments of his eloquence handed down splendidly to posterity bear witness to an inexhaustible fountain of eloquence and to the true inner teaching of philosophical doctrines.’

“We are both astonished and grieved that, from so many and so distinguished works of this holy and eloquent bishop, only these few have survived to us. At least make use, reader, of these works—which are far more accurately corrected than before—and farewell.”

Thus far Quesnel.

What we think about these matters, and what new material has been added by us to this edition, everyone will learn from the two notices which we shall place before the *Life of St. Hilary* and his short works respectively.

[Col. 0183]

# THE LIFE AND SHORT WORKS OF ST. HILARY, BISHOP OF ARLES

We have transferred these short works to their proper place in volume L of our edition; see them there. **EDITOR**

[Col. 0183]

# DISSERTATIONS OF PASCHASIUS QUESNEL ON THE WORKS OF ST. LEO THE GREAT, WITH THE BALLERINI BROTHERS’ NOTES AND CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS ON THEM

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO QUESNEL’S FIRST DISSERTATION

We would have preferred to omit the following dissertation on the life and deeds of St. Leo, and it would have been easier to compose a new and exact life of that pontiff. Quesnel omitted some matters that seem especially worthy of notice; others he presented insufficiently accurately according to chronological order, thereby producing confusion. He raised certain matters on conjectures that were not sufficiently firm, and, indulging some of his own prejudices, distorted others.

Moreover, several readings and chronological notes have been corrected; several letters previously unpublished, as well as several documents published after Quesnel, have brought new light. From these, not a few matters must either be corrected or added. All these difficulties could easily have been avoided by composing a new *Life*.

But since, according to the plan of our work, everything Quesnel inserted into his edition must be reprinted by us, we have been compelled to publish his first dissertation. In order not to repeat the same *Life* twice, we have decided entirely to refrain from composing a new one. While indicating Quesnel’s deficiencies in the notes, we shall provide such remedy as may be possible; and we hope that fair-minded readers will pardon the necessity that binds us, if in this work—certainly more burdensome for us—they do not find the life of the holy pontiff arranged as conveniently as we would have thought appropriate to present it according to our own judgment.

## FIRST DISSERTATION

### On the Life and Deeds of St. Leo the Great, Bishop of the Roman Church, in which, with the order of the years preserved, both his distinguished deeds and each of his writings are reviewed

[Col. 0183]

### [Col. 0183A] 399

#### I

St. Leo, the first Roman pontiff of that name, is said to have been born in Tuscany by the author of the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs*, followed by most of the other writers of the *History of the Pontiffs of the City*. [Note: [Col. 0183A] The Volterrans among the Tuscans claim this pontiff as their fellow citizen, but prove it by no document. See the Bollandists, 11 April, p. 16, §2.]

Yet I am led to believe that he was Roman by the testimony of an older and better-authorized writer. Prosper, Leo’s contemporary and friend, narrating his election, says:

“Accordingly Leo, summoned from an official mission and presented to his rejoicing fatherland, was ordained the forty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church.”

Rome, therefore, was Leo’s fatherland, according to Prosper.

But why seek testimony from others when we have Leo himself clearly making this claim about himself? In Letter 27 (now 31), chapter 4, excusing himself for not appearing at the Second Council of Ephesus, which the emperor Theodosius had wished, he gives this reason:

“Because the extremely uncertain condition of present affairs would not allow me to be absent from the peoples of so great a city, and the minds of those in turmoil would be driven into a kind of despair if, on the pretext of an ecclesiastical matter, I appeared willing to abandon my fatherland and the apostolic see.”

The words are clear and need no interpreter. Nor does the testimony of Anastasius, or of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, decisively oppose this. Although the common manuscripts assert that Leo was Tuscan by nation, two manuscript codices, the Royal and the Mazarin, from which variant readings were extracted and published at the end of the Royal edition, describe Leo as Roman by nation. I also remember reading the same in more recent writers.

Finally, our fourth argument may be taken from what we shall say below: namely, that Leo was brought up in the bosom of the Roman Church and baptized there; that from childhood he attached himself to the presbyter Sixtus; and that he discharged lower ministries in the Roman Church. It is therefore probable that Leo’s father, Quintianus, was born in Tuscany, but that Leo himself was born at Rome, after his father transferred his home and household to the city of Rome.

### II

I have found nothing written in the ancient records of the Church concerning the year of his birth. Nor can anything certain be conjectured from what survives concerning his life, or from the age at which he died, since the length of his life is likewise uncertain—although it is certain that he enjoyed not only a glorious life but also a long one.

For when he was raised to the pontificate, he must already have been mature in age and experienced in many affairs and responsibilities, since at that time he was in Gaul attempting to restore the dissident commanders of the Roman army to harmony. Indeed, long before this he had already been serving Pope Celestine in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs. To this must be added the fact that he held the pontificate for many years.

A reference to Leo’s baptism occurs in Vigilius of Thapsus, bishop, at the beginning of the fourth book against Eutyches, or in his defense of St. Leo’s letter to Flavian of Constantinople. When replying to the Eutychianist who criticized Leo because, while reporting the words of the Creed, he had said that the faithful believed in God the Father but had not said “in one God the Father,” in accordance with the decree of the Council of Nicaea, Vigilius responds:

“But at Rome, even before the Nicene Synod convened, from the time of the apostles until now, and under Celestine of blessed memory, to whom this man rendered testimony concerning the true faith, the Creed is handed down to the faithful in this form.”

I would not hesitate to assert that this passage of Vigilius refers to the handing over of the Creed that was customarily performed before baptism—or with Leo himself as witness. “That which,” he says in Letter 24 (now 28), chapter 1, “is proclaimed throughout the whole world by the voice of all who are to be regenerated”; and in Letter 97 (now 124), chapter 8: “Forgetting the saving Creed and the confession by which, when you pronounced it before many witnesses, you received the sacrament of baptism.”

Yet this raises a difficulty, because Vigilius seems to assert that Leo was baptized by Pope Celestine. This cannot be true, since Leo was already an acolyte under Pope Zosimus, as we shall conjecture below, and—what is entirely certain—was serving as archdeacon around the year 430, during the pontificate of the same Celestine. It would scarcely seem plausible to anyone that he had risen to that rank only seven years after baptism.

Either Vigilius was mistaken, or we must say that Vigilius intended only this: Leo was not baptized by Celestine when he was already pope, but that Leo handed over the Creed to Celestine when Celestine was still a presbyter under Pope Innocent, or that Leo was baptized by Celestine while the latter was still a presbyter.

For from Innocent’s letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, chapter 3, it is clear that at Rome presbyters were permitted to baptize even when the bishop was present; and from canon 78 of the Council in Trullo and canon 45 of Laodicea it appears that the Creed could be handed over by a presbyter.

These are the words found on page 237 of an ancient Roman codex:

“Those who are to be baptized must also receive the Creed of the faith and hand it over on the Thursday of the final week either to the bishop or to a presbyter.”

If this was permitted anywhere, it was certainly permitted at Rome rather than in any other Church, both because of the greater number of those being baptized and because of the innumerable affairs that occupied the pontiff and compelled him to transfer the burden of receiving the candidates’ profession of faith to the presbyters.

I conjecture that this was practiced by our pontiff from the fact that, although all his sermons have been carefully collected—sermons which, in accordance with his office and supreme facility of speech, he delivered to the people not only on the principal solemnities but also on the occasions of announcing fasts and whenever opportunity arose—we nevertheless possess none of his sermons on Baptism to catechumens or on the Creed and its handing over, although many such sermons by other bishops are in circulation.

Furthermore, that Celestine could have served as a presbyter under the pontificate of Innocent is demonstrated by the same letter to Decentius, chapter 8, where mention is made of Celestine the deacon, already participating in ecclesiastical administration; he could easily have advanced in due course to the presbyterate.

Leo’s baptism at Rome also confirms our opinion, stated above, that he was born and raised at Rome.

The things he did as a young man up to the time of his diaconate are obscure. Pennottus writes that he was first enrolled among the clergy of the Lateran basilica. Although this is a conjecture, I would not wish to reject it. For in that golden age young men were prepared for the clergy in the very bosom of the priests; they began their priestly training in the sacristy and discharged the lower ministries by degrees.

Whether, however, the Lateran basilica, where they say Leo served as a cleric, was at that time the principal basilica of the City, or whether it was St. Peter’s Basilica, is rightly doubted.

In any case, it is certain that the young man possessed such virtue and such talent that he was both an example and an object of admiration to the others.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Augustine, Letter 29, no. 10, testifies that St. Peter’s Basilica was a place remote from the bishop’s daily company. The election of Boniface I as having taken place at the Lateran is indicated by the letter of the Roman presbyters to Honorius on behalf of that same Boniface; and Damasus was also consecrated in the same basilica, as is evident from the pamphlet of Marcellinus and Faustinus to the emperor.]

---

## YEAR OF CHRIST 418; SECOND YEAR OF POPE ZOSIMUS; TWENTY-FOURTH YEAR OF HONORIUS, ELEVENTH OF THEODOSIUS, EMPERORS; HONORIUS XII AND THEODOSIUS VIII, CONSULS

What opinion the Roman clergy held of Leo as a young man and acolyte is shown by the affairs entrusted to him in this year 418 of Jesus Christ.

At that time the Pelagian heresy was raging, and the evil was growing through the schemes of Pelagius and Caelestius, who had introduced this plague into the world. For some time the wicked men had concealed themselves by disguising their error and had mocked Zosimus, the Roman pontiff; at last, when the heresy was exposed, he condemned it by a public and solemn anathema.

The judgment of the pontiff had long been awaited in Africa. Leo the acolyte was sent there to carry the letters of condemnation to Aurelius of Carthage, Augustine of Hippo, and the other bishops of the African Church.

This mission of Leo is not recorded in the ecclesiastical annals, but Augustine testifies to it in a letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, who later succeeded Celestine in the pontificate. In that letter he writes that Sixtus had sent a short but forceful letter to Aurelius of Carthage against the Pelagians, and that it had been brought together with letters from Zosimus, by which he reminded the African Fathers of the judgment he had pronounced against Pelagius and Caelestius:

“Together with the letters,” he says (Letter 105), “of the apostolic see sent to Africa concerning their [the Pelagians’] condemnation, your letter also reached the venerable old man Aurelius. Although it was brief, it nevertheless sufficiently indicated your vigor against their error.”

That letter is certainly none other than the one about which Augustine speaks in Letter 104, addressed to the same Sixtus, where he again mentions the shorter letter which Sixtus had sent to Aurelius of Carthage and says that it was brought by the acolyte Leo:

“For we have copied your very brief letter, which you sent concerning this very matter to the most blessed old man Aurelius through Leo the acolyte” (Letter 104).

The chronology agrees with Leo the Great, then an acolyte. These events occurred in the year 418 of Christ, the second year of Zosimus’s pontificate. It is further suggested by Leo’s constant attachment to Sixtus, whose letter he was carrying.

Finally, this is demonstrated by what Leo did against the Pelagians, both under the pontiffs Celestine and Sixtus, whom he greatly assisted by his work and counsel, and later, when he himself succeeded them and governed the Roman Church.

During that journey, having admired the great bishops—the lights of the African Church, and Augustine above all—I think he resolved to imitate them and was inflamed by their hatred of the Pelagians. We shall describe this below.

---

## YEARS OF CHRIST 430, 431, 432; YEARS 8, 9, AND 10 OF POPE CELESTINE; YEARS 24, 25, AND 26 OF THEODOSIUS; YEARS 7, 8, AND 9 OF VALENTINIAN, EMPERORS; CONSULS, THE SAME AUGUSTI, BASSUS AND ANTIOCHUS, AETIUS AND VALERIUS

### I

How long Leo remained an acolyte, and by whom he was ordained deacon, is uncertain. This is certain: he served in the office of deacon, or even archdeacon, under Pope Celestine. Celestine used his counsel and assistance in handling ecclesiastical affairs, as we shall relate below from Leo himself and other records.

Who, moreover, could believe that Celestine would summon a man who had not yet risen to the rank of deacon to share in the pontiff’s responsibility? Furthermore, Cassian’s work *On the Incarnation against Nestorius* was dedicated to Leo the deacon. It is clear, however, that the book was written before the Council of Ephesus under Celestine, because Cassian makes no mention of the synodal condemnation of Nestorius and attacks Nestorius as though he had not yet been deposed from the episcopate but were still exercising his office in the Church of Constantinople—although it is certain that he did not return there after the Council of Ephesus.

Finally, Cassian exhorts the citizens of Constantinople to detest Nestorius’s error and avoid his company; this would have been pointless unless the heretic still resided in Constantinople at that time.

[Note: [Col. 0187D] Cassian’s work was dedicated to Leo because it was written at Leo’s request, as is clear from Cassian’s dedicatory letter itself. Leo could have come to know Cassian when Cassian spent some time at Rome under Innocent. It seemed especially useful to Leo that, through Cassian—formerly a deacon of the Church of Constantinople and a disciple of St. John Chrysostom—the Church of Constantinople should be warned to avoid Nestorius.]

### II

I pass over the fables related at length by a certain admirer of Cassian, who, while attributing many inventions to Cassian, also fabricates much about Leo.

Where did he obtain the claim that Leo was already a deacon under Pope Innocent; that Cassian, under that same Innocent, lived at Rome with Leo and discussed the disputes of the East and the affairs of John Chrysostom; that Leo joined himself to Cassian as his companion in order to lead a solitary life with him, but was prevented by Innocent? This is no more true than the further claim which he confidently asserts: that the Church of Cassian at Marseilles was consecrated by Leo the archdeacon as legate of the apostolic see.

These statements, brought forward without reliable witnesses, and utterly foreign both to Leo’s age and to the discipline of the Church, deserve neither credence nor response. The bull of Benedict, which that author produces, is entirely spurious and offers nothing except vague rumors and uncertain human traditions.

Here are the words of the Benedictine bull:

“We judged that the monastery of the aforesaid martyr Victor, founded near the city of Marseilles in the time of the emperor Antoninus, ought to be fortified with this care. It was afterward established by the blessed abbot Cassian and, at his request—as is said by our elders—consecrated by the most blessed Leo, bishop of the Roman see, and exalted by his apostolic blessing and authority. In it they founded a larger church in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and all the apostles, and another in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of St. John the Baptist, dedicating them with relics bestowed by many saints.”

This bull contains many statements based on uncertain reports from our ancestors and far removed from the truth. For an archdeacon could not dedicate a church contrary to ecclesiastical rule and custom, as Guesnaeus imagined; nor could Leo, already pontiff, himself consecrate a church at Marseilles, since during his pontificate he never came to Gaul, and he did not attain the pontificate while Cassian was alive.

### 405 [Col. 0188B]

And what are we to make of the statements concerning the monastery’s foundation under the rule of Antoninus, at a time when monasteries had not yet been founded anywhere in the world, much less in Gaul?

But I pass from these fables to the more certain deeds of Leo the deacon.

### III

How great was Pope Celestine’s confidence in the work and counsel of our Leo in administering ecclesiastical affairs, and how widely this was known throughout the Church, is shown by Leo’s own letter to Maximus of Antioch. From reading it we learn that Leo assisted Celestine as his principal administrator and that the more laborious affairs, about which the pontiff needed to be informed, were first referred to him.

When, at the First Council of Ephesus, Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, was seeking primacy over the province of Palestine, Cyril thought that the apostolic see ought to be warned about Juvenal’s audacious attempt, lest he obtain the consent of the Roman bishop through improper methods and the production of forged documents.

For this reason Cyril wrote to our Leo, so that through him Celestine might be informed of Juvenal’s ambitious attempts and carefully guard against his deception.

Leo’s words are these (Letter 92, now 119, chapter 4):

“At the Synod of Ephesus, which struck down the impious Nestorius together with his doctrine, Bishop Juvenal believed that he could succeed in obtaining primacy over the province of Palestine and sought to strengthen his audacious attempts by fabricated writings. The bishop Cyril of Alexandria, of holy memory, rightly horrified by this, informed me in his letters what the aforesaid man’s ambition had dared to undertake and earnestly requested that no assent be given to unlawful efforts.”

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Compare note 24 (previous volume, column 1043, note h) on Letter 119.]

### IV

This relationship between Celestine and Leo supports our conjecture that, around this same period, Celestine used Leo’s literary services to compile those chapters on grace and free will which are usually appended to this pontiff’s letter to the Gauls and which, until the present time, have been believed to belong either to Celestine or to Prosper.

At that time Prosper of Aquitaine had hurried to Rome to seek the assistance of the apostolic see against the remnants of the Pelagians and the opponents of Augustine’s teaching, who were then growing numerous in Gaul. Their chief was Cassian, whose errors Prosper disclosed to the Roman bishop; and it is reasonable to believe that Prosper conferred with Leo.

He made especially clear that the men hostile to them were most opposed to Augustine’s teaching, which they thought they were particularly undermining through the decrees of the pontiffs and of the apostolic see.

This gave Celestine the occasion to order the archives of the Roman Church to be investigated more carefully and to entrust this task to Leo. We shall prove in Dissertation 3 that Leo collected these chapters.

As Prosper was about to return to Gaul, he received a commission from the apostolic see to defend Augustine’s teaching on its authority, as he testifies that he did in the preface to his *Responses to the Vincentian Objections*. In order to have a precise understanding of the teaching of that see, he received from the pontiff himself—perhaps from Celestine—a letter to several bishops of Gaul together with chapters or statements of the bishops of the Roman see. This later led to the circulation of these chapters appended to that same letter.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] This commission is not as certain as is commonly believed; see the observation in Dissertation 3, no. 7.]

## V. Return to the Province

After returning to the province, Prosper [Note: [Col. 0189D] We shall show with sufficient probability in the observations on Dissertation 3, no. 7, that Prosper’s response to the Vincentian objections was written by him before he went to Rome, and before Celestine’s letter to the Gauls.] wrote against the Vincentian objections and against the *Collator*; and in these little works he seems to me to have used [Col. 0189B] the sentences he had brought from Rome, since he argues with precisely the same testimonies that are found in them.

After Prosper’s departure from the city, I believe that our Leo wrote the splendid [Note: [Col. 0190D] We shall deny these to Leo in the observations on Dissertation 2; from this the whole narrative that Quesnellus has woven here collapses.] treatises *On the Calling of All Nations*, in which he refutes the errors of the Semipelagians, having been accurately instructed about them, evidently, by Prosper. I believe that Leo wrote these chiefly with the intention of bringing Cassian back from his error.

For he was bound to Cassian by the bond of friendship, and he grieved that so great a man had been swept into opinions alien to the faith—opinions which unwary souls imbibed all the more easily and dangerously because they were mingled with writings highly esteemed both for their elegance of expression and for their remarkable teaching about spiritual matters. Certainly, these writings contained very much that pertained to good morals, piety, and the formation of a holier life; nevertheless, certain things had been introduced that opposed the grace of Christ.

Cassian indeed condemned in writing and speech the wicked opinions of Pelagius and Coelestius concerning grace; but he likewise recoiled from Augustine’s position. He had persuaded himself, namely, that Augustine had thought impiously about the grace of Christ and had gone beyond due measure in correcting Pelagius and overstepped certain limits, carried away by a kind of ardor in debate. While he falsely entertained these thoughts about Augustine—whom the Catholic Church had adopted as its teacher and champion of grace—Cassian himself fell into error.

For when he wrote certain discussions about grace with excessive subtlety, he introduced Pelagianism, if not altogether, at least to some extent. Those who later defended these views were therefore called Semipelagians, and Cassian is regarded as either their author or their standard-bearer. Leo, meanwhile, was deeply distressed that such things were being published by his friend.

Yet, lest he seem to neglect either the cause of the Church and the grace of Christ or his friendship, he devised the following course. He wrote a book entitled *On the Calling of All Nations*, and silently omitted the names of Augustine and Cassian, so that he would appear to have undertaken the cause of the Church, not of individuals, and to wish rather to correct his friend than to expose him. Indeed, he concealed his own name as well and fought as though his face were covered by a veil, lest, while attacking the enemy, he should recognize the friend who might moderate the force and heat of the contest.

I am well aware that the author of this work has been disputed, different writers assigning it to different persons. Some attribute it to Ambrose, some to Prosper, and others to Hilary of Syracuse, Prosper’s associate. It is certain that it is not the work of the first, since it mentions the Pelagians, who arose only after Ambrose’s time. Nor is it Prosper’s, as we shall discuss at length elsewhere; rather, we shall reclaim it for Leo alone. This is demonstrated by the style and character of the writing, by the time at which it was written, and by the subject itself. But more on this elsewhere.

## VI.

We also restore to Leo, as its author, that distinguished letter to Demetrias which until now has been read among the works either of St. Ambrose or of St. Prosper. [Note: [Col. 0190D] We shall likewise remove the letter to Demetrias from Leo in the observations on Dissertation 4.]

I shall briefly review the reasons for which it was written. Demetrias, a virgin born into the Anician family, illustrious no less for virtue than for birth, fled from Rome to Africa after Rome had been captured by the Goths. While she was staying at Carthage, she happened to hear St. Augustine speaking about virginity, and she was so inflamed with the desire to preserve that virtue that she immediately professed herself consecrated to God and broke off the marriage she had been contemplating.

The Fathers vied with one another in praising the resolve of the most distinguished virgin. St. Jerome and Pope Innocent sent elegant letters on this matter to Demetrias. Pelagius himself—whose more austere life had won him reputation and esteem, while the ulcer he nourished in his veins had not yet burst—also sent her a letter. Whether he was prompted by the requests of Juliana, Demetrias’s mother, or moved to write of his own accord is uncertain; but it is clear that the letter was infected with Pelagian poison.

Augustine sensed the hidden virus and took care to expose it, lest others should be contaminated by this writing as by some contagion. Several years later St. Leo also wrote to Demetrias. It is not easy to say when or where he wrote; but, as far as I can infer from conjecture, it happened before he was raised to the pontificate. Certainly, in the letter, written a long time after the earliest period of her consecration, he implies that he was writing at that time.

“If I were to speak,” he says, “of commending the excellence of virginity, it would now be superfluous to commend that purpose which you chose from the first flower of your age without human exhortations, and about which, at its very beginnings, many who then held a prominent place in the Church rightly did not remain silent” (*Letter to Demetrias*, chap. 1).

These words sufficiently indicate both that she was no longer in the first flower of her age and that those who had previously praised her in their writings had died. I therefore believe that Demetrias was about forty, or perhaps forty-five, years old, and that she had by then returned to Rome.

For the Vandals had laid waste to Africa with a hostile army, and, in my opinion, Demetrias—who had left her homeland out of fear of the Goths—did not remain in a foreign land while Genseric was ravaging Africa. The affair certainly prospered so greatly for the Vandal that he seemed to have come to Africa only to see and conquer: he captured Hippo and Cirta, which had resisted for some time, and stormed Carthage itself in the year 439.

Ecclesiastical annals, and Leo himself, record that in those most wretched times a great multitude of people fled into Italy. Nor do I hesitate to assert that this was the same Demetrias who, after Genseric had sacked Rome, devoted herself to restoring basilicas and built, on the Latin Way at the third milestone from the city, a basilica in memory of St. Stephen.

She had evidently brought from Africa relics of this holy protomartyr, whose body had been miraculously discovered several years earlier. From that time his relics were honored throughout the world, but especially in Africa the name of Stephen was venerated, since the historian Orosius had brought some of his bones into that province.

Thus Demetrias, distinguished by blood and nobility, and still more distinguished by her virtues, easily became known to Leo. He formed a friendship with her, and the holy virgin shared with him Pelagius’s letter at the time when the wound had broken out again. Therefore Leo began to correct the heretic’s errors in a second letter to her.

And the more Pelagius had exalted the powers of the human will while neglecting the grace of Christ, the more earnestly Leo strove to expose the stain inflicted upon the human will by sin and to show how the powers of free choice toward the good had been overthrown—powers for whose restoration the grace of Christ, purchased at the price of his blood, alone suffices. Thus he taught the virgin to think humbly and modestly of herself, and not to esteem lightly the merits of Christ, acquired at so great a price and bestowed upon us at so great a price.

Around the year 430 or 431, perhaps after the Council of Ephesus had already been convoked, while Nestorius was spreading his doctrine in the East—sometimes by whispers, sometimes by letters, sometimes by public addresses to the people—Pope Celestine omitted nothing in the West that could contribute to the speedy suppression of the wicked heresy.

Leo assisted Celestine’s concern with all the effort and industry he could command. Understanding that not only the authority of emperors or pontiffs had to be opposed to the malice of heretics, but that their writings also had to be destroyed by suitable writings, he urged John Cassian to write in defense of the Incarnation against Nestorius.

Many considerations moved Leo to call upon Cassian’s hand and industry above all. Cassian was either a Scythian, as many writers say, or a Gaul, as Holstenius (*Preface to the Rule of the Monks*, chap. 3) and Norisius (*History of Pelagianism*, book II, chap. 1) establish by many arguments. Yet he had been educated in the East, where this heresy had gained strength; he had been the disciple and deacon of St. Chrysostom, whom piety joined to singular learning, together with the fresh memory of the life he had recently completed in exile, had made famous—not only Chrysostom himself, but also those who had absorbed his discipline and teachings.

Moreover, John Cassian possessed outstanding gifts of mind and talent, uncommon knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, and a reputation for piety and holiness celebrated throughout both East and West. He was also known in the deserts of Egypt and Syria; and if the virulence of Nestorianism had perhaps reached some of the monks’ caves, he was capable of driving the disease away.

Add to this that his life at Massilia, the monasteries he founded, the discipline of the ascetic life, and the gathering of pious and learned men who, attracted by the desire for a stricter life, had fled to him, had made him famous throughout the West.

What shall I say of his useful writings, which had earned Cassian no ordinary praise and won him the friendship of great men, especially Leo the archdeacon, who believed that he would render a service useful to the Church if Cassian, by the teaching of Scripture and the tradition of the holy Fathers, would utterly strangle the already growing heresy?

Finally, as we have said, Cassian was a deacon of the Church of Constantinople and a disciple of St. John Chrysostom. His teaching, therefore, as though drawn from his own Chrysostom, was bound to be most welcome to the citizens and clergy of Constantinople. [410] Leo also knew that the Nestorians placed great hope of support in the remnants of Pelagius’s followers. To deprive them of this hope, he wished to set Cassian against them [Note: [Col. 0191D] This conjecture is entirely gratuitous. We know that the Romans were not acquainted with the Semipelagians until St. Prosper came to Rome in 431 to defend St. Augustine’s teaching against them. Yet Cassian’s books *Against Nestorius on the Incarnation* were published in that same year. Therefore, when Leo requested this work from him somewhat earlier—namely, at least in 430—there is no evidence that he had discovered Cassian’s Semipelagianism; far from that, it cannot be asserted that he entrusted this work to him for the purpose alleged by Quesnellus.]—Cassian, the standard-bearer of the Semipelagians, who would attack both the Nestorians and the Pelagians who favored Nestorianism, while also distancing himself from their fellowship and teaching.

When I consider these matters more carefully, I am easily persuaded that Cassian, overcome by the writings either of Prosper or of Leo, had already returned at that time to a sounder mind, or at least had suppressed his opinions in silence for a while. For it is not permissible to believe that Leo would set him against heretics unless Cassian was Catholic in every respect and had laid aside every suspicion against Augustine. In fact, in his book *On the Incarnation*, he praises Augustine enthusiastically and ranks him among the great teachers of the Church.

Cassian therefore wrote seven books *On the Incarnation* and dedicated them to Leo, as the letter prefixed to his work testifies. In it he calls Leo the recipient of his affection, as well as the glory of the Roman Church and of the divine ministry. He closes the letter with these words:

“Therefore this matter is yours, this task is yours, this is the work of your honor: pray and entreat that your choice not be endangered by my ignorance, and that, although I obey well through the grace of obedience, you may nevertheless appear to have commanded badly through lack of careful judgment, if we fail to correspond to so great an opinion of us” (Cassian, *Letter to Leo*).

These words sufficiently testify to the esteem in which Leo was held at Rome. Cassian, laden with years and glory, speaks of him in such honorific language that his prayers and exhortations carried the force of a command.

## Year of Christ 433; 2nd year of Pope Sixtus III; 26th of Theodosius; 9th of Valentinian, the emperors; Theodosius XIV and Anicius Maximus being consuls

Pope Celestine, dying in the year 432, had left the Roman See to Sixtus III. After one or perhaps two years of his pontificate, a certain Anicius Bassus, an ex-consul who measured his hatred by his wealth and power, summoned Sixtus on the charge of violating a consecrated virgin and, by a shameful accusation, separated Valentinian and the empress from his communion. He also stirred up a large part of the powerful, the clergy, and the people against the pontiff by every lawful and unlawful means.

Leo the deacon, as certain of the falsehood of the charge as he was confident of the pontiff’s innocence, not only refused to abandon Sixtus, but supported him and publicly pleaded his innocence. Then, as the Acts report, Leo said: “If my offenses are brought against me, why is no proof produced?” The proposal seemed fair. Valentinian immediately assembled the senate and the people, and Sixtus assembled the clergy. Everyone was present in the Helenian Basilica.

Then the pontiff, turning to Valentinian, said: “Let those who separated the Son from the Mother enter and prove all the coverings of their hearts.” The emperor Valentinian remained silent. The deacon Leo answered and said: “The request is just; let it not be concealed” (*Acts of the Roman Council for the Purification of Pope Sixtus*, chaps. 4 and 5).

The matter turned out well and favorably for Sixtus, with Leo supporting him. He was vindicated from the accusations, while the accusers were convicted of slander and prohibited from sacred functions. These events are drawn from the very corrupt Acts of the Roman synod [Note: [Col. 0192D] These Acts have been demonstrated by Father Constantius (*The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, appendix, p. 111) to be not only highly corrupt but entirely spurious;] to which one would scarcely wish to grant any credence.

## Year of Christ 439; 8th year of Pope Sixtus; 32nd of Theodosius, 15th of Valentinian, the emperors; Theodosius XVII and Festus being consuls

### I.

The ecclesiastical annals do not report what our Leo did throughout the seven years from the beginning of Sixtus’s pontificate, except for the defense of the pontiff that we have just related. Yet the events recorded under the year 439 in Prosper’s *Chronicle* do not permit us to doubt that he accomplished great things, highly beneficial to the Church, being prepared—as the Fathers of Chalcedon say—for the Church’s victory.

An event occurred in this year that shows with what hatred our Leo pursued other heretics and especially the Pelagians. “At this time,” Prosper says in his *Chronicle*, “Julian of Eclanum, the most boastful defender of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for his long-lost episcopate was driving on, attempted by various arts of deception, while presenting the appearance of correction, to creep back into communion with the Church.

“But Pope Sixtus, alertly countering these ambushes at the urging of the deacon Leo, allowed no access to be open to his poisonous efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the rejection of the deceptive beast, as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time beheaded the most arrogant heresy.”

The prudence and sagacity of Leo were confirmed by the outcome. For the deceitful heretic again attempted to disturb the Church and to attack by his pen the grace of Christ the Savior, so that it became clear that he was nourishing one thing in his heart and professing another with his lips.

### II.

Meanwhile military disturbances weighed upon the empire. Aetius and Albinus, commanders of the Roman army in Gaul, were at odds, and their hatred was on the verge of erupting into civil war if it were encouraged. The collapse of the empire was almost at hand, while Barbarians roared on every side and entered the provinces with hostile standards.

A remedy for the impending evil was sought. The archdeacon Leo came forward, for he could reconcile the commanders’ minds. He was a man of exceptional prudence and tested experience in affairs, capable of bringing matters to completion, hated by neither of the contending parties, and agreeable to both. Either through the force of his speech, in which he was powerful, he could persuade them to peace, or through the authority of his name he could break the anger of their minds.

He was indeed retained at Rome by ecclesiastical affairs; but, as he himself says, the necessity of a long journey made him absent. He approached the army, negotiated with the commanders about erasing their injuries, and warned them not to stir up civil wars while the enemy was roaring at the gates. He had such influence that he was able by his wisdom to calm their minds and reconcile friendship between the commanders.

This was the last work of the deacon Leo.

## Year of Christ 440; 1st of Pope Leo; 33rd of Theodosius, 16th of Valentinian, the emperors; Valentinian V and Anatolius being consuls

### I.

Meanwhile Sixtus died [Note: [Col. 0193D] Prosper does not report that Sixtus III died on the Kalends of April, as Quesnellus himself clearly saw and noted in § 12, under the year 461, no. 1. Nor does the author of the *Pontifical Book* assign that same day in the more reliable manuscripts. We, however, have more probably inferred from our most ancient Sacramentary that Sixtus III died on 11 August, in annotation 23 (Col. 135, no. g) under § 33. Since, moreover, the Roman Church waited more than forty days after the death of Sixtus III for Leo’s arrival, as Prosper testifies, we believe that his ordination should be assigned to 29 September [Col. 0194D], which in the year 440 was a Sunday. On this day each year, under St. Leo, a gathering of bishops was held, according to Letter 16, at the end. We learn from Sermon 2, chap. 2, and from other testimonies indicated in the preliminary notice to Sermon 1, that an episcopal gathering was customarily held on the anniversary of the ordination of the Roman pontiffs. Compare the cited annotation on the Sacramentary, from which this date for Leo’s ordination receives considerable confirmation.] on the Kalends of April, as the chronicler Prosper writes.

At that time the Christian commonwealth needed a supreme pontiff who could settle the disputes of Christians by authority and wisdom, especially when the affairs of the Church [413] were in the greatest turmoil—whether because of the fury of heretics, because conflicts more than civil were tearing the Church apart, because corruption and vice were spreading, or because Barbarians were rending the empire.

In this confusion of affairs, when so many evils, as though drawn up in battle formation, were bearing down upon the empire and the Church, and when the death of Pope Sixtus added to the burden, Rome, deprived of its pontiff, lay in mourning. Yet God provided that the Church should suffer no harm by appointing Leo in Sixtus’s place. Leo combined with the highest piety a knowledge of doctrine and many years of tested administration of ecclesiastical affairs, so that the Romans seemed not to have lost a bishop.

When he was elected, it benefited Leo—something that rarely happens—that he was then absent from Rome. For he was sought with more ardent prayers precisely because he was absent, and it was clear that he had attained the pontificate by merit, not ambition. Hence Leo himself says: “In our lowliness the Lord remembered us, and blessed us, he who alone has done great wonders for me” (*Sermon 1 on His Anniversary*).

St. Prosper writes that Sixtus died on the Kalends of April. “After he had died,” he says, “the Roman Church was without a bishop for more than forty days, awaiting with marvelous peace and patience the arrival of the deacon Leo, whom Gaul was then detaining between Aetius and Albinus for the purpose of restoring friendship.” Nor was the delay in his return without praise, as though, in the words of St. Prosper, he had been kept away longer “so that the merit of the one elected and the judgment of those who elected him might be tested” [Al. “so that his arrival might be delayed longer”].

### II.

Immediately an honorable delegation was sent to him so that he might learn the support of the entire clergy, the will of the Roman people, and the prayers of all good men; and in the name of all he was asked to hasten his return and comfort the Church by his presence.

Although Leo was far removed from a desire for honors, he nevertheless obeyed. To reject a duty he had not sought would not have been obedience to God; to flee the pontificate under the appearance of virtue would have been to betray the Church and, as it were, to hand over the See to plunder. Such were at that time the ambitions of certain men and the schemes of heretics, who feared a bishop with eyes open and ever vigilant.

He therefore came to Rome and, received with the acclamation of the people and the joy of the entire clergy, was finally ordained bishop of the Roman Church. Thus Prosper continues: “The deacon Leo, summoned by a public embassy and presented to his rejoicing homeland, was ordained the forty-seventh bishop of the Roman Church.”

### III.

It is worthwhile to learn briefly what pious thoughts and holy impulses he conceived when he was raised to the highest summit of the Church. He was indeed affected by joy—not, as usually happens, because he had obtained a more powerful chair and towered over the Christian world, but because he would serve and minister to more people, as though others had brought him the honor while he himself undertook the labor.

He himself testifies to this: “We rejoice not so much in presiding as in serving” (*Sermon 4, now 5, on His Assumption*, chap. 5).

Another reason for joy was that he understood that many things had been forgiven him, and that he, though unworthy, had been heaped with many blessings, so that he might love God more fervently:

“I have true cause for rejoicing to the glory of God, who forgave me much so that I might love him greatly; and, in order to make his grace wonderful, bestowed his gifts upon one in whom he found no merits to commend him” (*Sermon 1, now 2, on His Assumption*).

Yet that joy was restrained by fear of sinning amid the multitude of affairs and the magnitude of the office, which he knew was exposed to innumerable dangers. “The very greatness of the work,” he says, “is a frequent occasion of offense” (*Sermon 4, now 5, on His Assumption*, chap. 2).

Nor was this fear that of an inert and timid spirit, as though he dreaded the labor; rather, it was the fear of a prudent and provident helmsman who, contemplating the vast seas and weighing the dangers in his mind, indeed shrinks from command because he considers himself unequal to the circumstances, yet does not remove his hand from the helm. Trusting not so much in his own skill as in the favorable influence of the stars, he safely guides the ship through shoals and shallows.

“Lord,” he says, “I have heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I trembled. For what is so unusual, so fearful, as labor imposed upon the fragile, exaltation upon the humble, dignity upon one who does not deserve it? Yet we neither despair nor fail, because we rely not upon ourselves but upon him who works in us” (*Sermon 2, now 3, on His Assumption*, chap. 1).

Thus he trembled at the danger that stood near, but, trusting in God’s help, undertook to govern God’s people:

“For although it is necessary to tremble regarding merit, it is nevertheless religious to rejoice regarding the gift; for he who is the author of my burden [Al. “honor”] will himself become the helper of my administration. And lest the weak man collapse beneath the greatness of grace, he who conferred the dignity will give strength” (*Sermon 1 on His Assumption*).

### IV.

Attributing nothing to himself, therefore, but referring all good things back to God their author, and advancing the Christian cause with the power and name of Christ—whom he knew to be not merely the guardian of the sheep but the Shepherd of shepherds—he judged that Christ would not fail him, since he had promised to be with us until the end of the age.

“In this matter of trembling,” he says, “what confidence in the service we must discharge would we have unless he who guards Israel neither slumbered nor slept; unless he deigned to be not only the guardian of the sheep but also the Shepherd of the shepherds themselves . . . since we piously and truthfully confess that, in all the right things we do, Christ carries out the work of our ministry; and that we glory not in ourselves, who can do nothing without him, but in him, who is our ability” (*Sermon 4, now 5, on His Assumption*, chap. 2).

These are proofs of modesty, humility, and distrust of himself. Behold an example of a grateful spirit toward God. Frequently turning over in his mind the divine benefits bestowed upon him, he openly and publicly proclaimed these things. Whenever he preached about his elevation to the pontificate, he stirred the minds and mouths of his hearers to express the gratitude of his own heart, considering himself unequal to such benefits:

“Let my mouth speak the praise of the Lord, and let my soul, spirit, flesh, and tongue bless his holy name; for to keep silent about divine benefits is a sign not of modesty but of ingratitude. It is altogether fitting that the consecrated priest should begin his service with sacrifices of the Lord’s praise: for in my lowliness the Lord remembered us and blessed us, because he alone has done great wonders for me, so that your affection for holiness might see me present, whom the necessity of a long journey had made absent.”

And again:

“Magnify the Lord with me, beloved, and let us exalt his name together, so that the whole meaning of today’s solemnity may be referred to the praise of its author” (*Sermon 1 on His Assumption*).

This gratitude and remembrance of divine generosity inflamed the holy bishop intensely with love of God and with readiness to undertake whatever he judged beneficial to the Christian cause. No labors or dangers ever deterred him from that holy purpose.

But to recount individually all the virtues with which his pontificate shone like so many stars would be too long. To trace in writing how vigilantly he exercised the pontificate, how diligently and steadfastly he administered the Church, how prudently he acted, how many wars against heretics he successfully concluded, how many labors he endured for the Christian and public cause, and how, when affairs were almost ruined and desperate, he did not yield—this would be a laborious task, belonging not merely to this place but to the whole of this work.

Before I undertake to deal with these matters in any fashion, I shall briefly begin by saying how troubled the times were when Leo assumed the pontificate—a great support, certainly, for the battered condition of the Church and the empire.

### V.

After the elder Theodosius died, the Barbarians, despising either the age or the negligence of the later emperors, invaded the Roman Empire like a torrent after its barriers had broken. The prefects, charged with protecting the emperors and caring for the state, began to contend with one another in mutual hatred and, through rivalry for power, to make room for foreign aggression.

The Goths, under the leadership of Alaric, captured Rome. From then on, whether because the fate of the empire was pressing onward or because God was avenging the vices of mortals, affairs went from bad to worse. Hordes of Barbarians rushed into the provinces and, according as each was stronger in weapons or forces, devastated regions. They expelled or subdued the inhabitants, settled in the places they had invaded, and established new kingdoms out of the mangled parts of the state.

Although during this period the Persians, Saracens, Zani, Isaurians, and Huns threatened the East, this hideous storm bore chiefly upon the West. Britain was harassed by incursions of the Picts and Scots; the Franks crossed the Rhine and established settlements in Gaul; the Burgundians occupied the Saône and Rhône; the Goths seized the Nine Peoples and that part of Spain lying nearer the Pyrenees. These things occurred under the rule of Honorius.

Nor was Valentinian’s fortune more favorable than that of his uncle, nor was his spirit more ready to repair the losses of the state. Although, through the valor of the commander Aetius, the empire of the West seemed to lift its shoulders, rivalry, envy, and the internal hatreds of commanders were almost more harmful to the state than the Barbarian enemy, numerous and manifold as he was. Add to this the recent disaster of Litorius, a vigorous commander who nearly equaled Aetius in valor and military reputation. Such was the condition of the Western Empire.

### VI.

Nor was the condition of the Church any more peaceful. The Barbarian was no less hostile to the Catholic faith than to the Roman state. The Burgundian, Goth, and Vandal, imbued with Arianism, weakened the faith by force and arms together with the empire.

Nor did the enemy attack only from without. At home the audacity of heretics was growing stronger, and while affairs were disturbed this corruption, like a cancer, infected the sound parts. The Nestorians troubled the East, and many things were rising again from the head that had been struck off. The impiety of the Manichaeans, not yet extinguished by the many blows it had received, recovered its strength and harassed the West.

Why should I mention the monstrous doctrines of Priscillian, which again terrified Spain? Add the perversity of the Pelagians, which for a long time had been troubling the Church under the new leadership of Julian. By new methods and with the force of eloquence, talent, and industry, he renewed a harsh war; and their unhappy offspring were the Semipelagians, whose doctrine was all the more harmful because their life and discipline were more holy and austere—the incurable evil that injures the mind while it tickles it.

Such was the condition of the Church and the empire when Leo obtained the pontificate. But another evil, far more serious, was looming: the audacity of Eutyches. It was chiefly to restrain this that Leo was raised by divine providence to this height of the Church, so that he might stand there like a watchtower and a bulwark against the approaching heretic.

For at that time God acted as he had formerly provided and arranged for the Church whenever a more violent storm threatened religion. Thus Athanasius was a pillar of Catholic doctrine while the fury of the Arians raged. Thus, more recently, Cyril of Alexandria stood forth while Nestorius was disturbing the Church. Thus Augustine stood invincible for the faith against the Pelagians and Manichaeans.

We shall describe Leo’s struggles and victories below, and we shall marvel that he so bravely defended Christ’s empire against so many enemies, without being unequal to them.

### VII.

Leo’s first concern as bishop was to associate with himself men distinguished for learning and doctrine, renowned for knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs and integrity of morals. By their counsel he could conduct affairs and keep them ready and attentive, lest he be deceived by the wicked arts of those who assess the Church’s affairs according to their own advantage and, as commonly happens, regard sacred and secular things alike as sources of profit.

Among those whom he took as companions in his labors, Prosper of Aquitaine held first place. Scaliger calls him the most learned man of those times. He was already known throughout the Christian world, for as a defender of the grace of Christ and heir to Augustine’s doctrine and studies, he was attacking the remnants of Pelagianism with his pen.

Prosper had long been dear to Leo, from the time when Prosper came to Rome under Celestine in order to stir up the Roman pontiff against Augustine’s enemies. Leo and Prosper possessed all the bonds that ordinarily constitute friendship: a remarkable harmony of minds and talents, the same interests in promoting the affairs of the Church, and in both of them the highest piety and singular learning.

Leo was in Gaul when he was elected bishop, as has been said. I can readily persuade myself that he brought Prosper back with him, so that Prosper might be to him, as Jerome once was to Damasus, his adviser and correspondent.

Certainly Prosper assisted Leo greatly by word and deed, especially against the heretics who had determined to attack the Catholic faith secretly and through underground passages.

### VIII.

Leo also gave a remarkable sign of pastoral concern in that, as soon as he had been placed upon the papal watchtower, he undertook to stir up the people entrusted to him not only by the example of his life but also by the duty of his own lips.

Indeed, he was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to undertake this office, if Sozomen is to be believed, when he writes [Note: [Col. 0195D] “Neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches in the church here.” Sozomen, book VII, chap. 1.]:

“In that same city—Rome—neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches the people in the church.”

But [Note: [Col. 0197C] Sozomen shows himself poorly acquainted with Roman discipline when, in book VII, chap. 16, he reports that throughout the West, and especially in the Roman Church, a presbyter was appointed to receive the confessions of penitents, as Henry Valesius proves in his notes. Yet he was manifestly mistaken when, in book V, chap. 39, he wrote that at Rome neither the bishop nor anyone else taught the people, if this is to be understood generally. The testimonies cited by Quesnellus establish the error; Prudentius may be added to them. In hymn 2 *On the Crowns*, while describing the Roman basilica of St. Hippolytus, he testifies that the supreme pontiff customarily addressed the people:

> Opposite the façade, a lofty tribunal  
> Is raised on steps; from it the bishop proclaims God.

The same point is confirmed by our most ancient Sacramentary of the Roman Church, which we published at the beginning of this volume. In July, § 17, Mass IX, the final prayer reads:

> They are your people, Lord, who await the ministry of our voice.

If the people awaited this, Roman pontiffs certainly used to preach. And in September, § 29, *On the Anniversary of Bishops*, Mass VII:

> Grant us, we ask, both to practice what is right and to proclaim what is true, so that we may offer the instruction of your grace both by acting for your faithful and by teaching.

But if Sozomen’s statement is believed to be restricted to Easter Day alone, as Quesnellus judged in a later discussion (see below, no. 12, near the middle), no published monument known to us so far exists by which this too can be proved false.

Some may perhaps doubt whether this interpretation of Quesnellus is obvious and consistent with the context. Here we shall add that nothing should be inferred from Cassiodorus, an expert in Roman affairs, to whom the *Tripartite History* is attributed and in which this testimony of Sozomen is found transcribed.

For Cassiodorus’s purpose in publishing the *Tripartite History* was to present in Latin an ecclesiastical history compiled from three Greek writers translated into Latin by Epiphanius the Scholastic. He corrected nothing in Epiphanius’s translation but used the translation exactly as it stood. Hence the passages quoted from Sozomen in the *Tripartite History* acquire no authority from Cassiodorus; the entire credibility rests with Sozomen, whose interpretation, rendered by Epiphanius, Cassiodorus left untouched.

See what Quesnellus observes on this matter in Dissertation 6, no. 16, where he exposes the error concerning Saturday fasting in the Roman Church found in Socrates, although it is nevertheless included in the *Tripartite History* in Latin words rendered from Socrates.]

In this matter, we can scarcely, if at all, agree with Sozomen.

First, what kind of bishops are those who renounce the duty of teaching, which is the most important of all? “Whoever approaches the priesthood,” says Pope Gregory I, “undertakes the office of a herald” (St. Gregory the Great, *Register*, Book I, Letter 14). And, as Julianus Pomerius, a contemporary or near-contemporary of Leo, writes, “Whoever else perishes, if no obligation to teach rests upon him, alone will pay the penalties for his crime; but he to whom the stewardship of the word has been entrusted, even if he lives holily, nevertheless perishes together with all those who perish while he is silent, if he either blushes or fears to rebuke those who live ruinously” (*On the Contemplative Life*, Book I, chapter 20).

### IX. 2.

That this was customary among the Roman Pontiffs even before Leo is suggested by Leo’s Sermon 82, delivered on the Feast of the Seven Maccabean Brothers.

[Note: We have rejected this sermon as Leo’s and relegated it, restored to Augustine, to the appendix; consequently, testimony extracted from it proves nothing for establishing the sermons of the Roman pontiff.] There, as he continues the praises of his predecessor Sixtus III, he uses expressions which indicate that the people had been publicly instructed by Sixtus, the Roman Pontiff:

> “A magnificent builder of walls, but a more magnificent BUILDER OF SOULS, extending the works of piety beyond the limits of his age, so that his devoted posterity might enjoy the benefits of HIS INSTRUCTIONS even in the present age, both by inhabiting what he founded and by doing what he TAUGHT.”

It is clear that these words—“builder of souls,” “the benefit of his instructions,” and “he taught”—are to be understood of public and solemn sermons delivered to the people. For he would not publicly exhort the people to recall the teachings handed down to them by their shepherd if he had poured them forth only to a few and within the secrecy of a private home. “Therefore,” he says, “dearest brothers, take all that you see with your eyes and remember in your minds as contributing to your edification.”

### X. 3.

Leo repeatedly says that it is his duty to deliver a sermon to the people, and he fears that it may be imputed to him as guilt if he neglects this part of his ministry.

*Sermon 3 on the Epiphany*: “Nevertheless, so that nothing may be lacking in our duty, I shall dare to speak of this same feast insofar as the Lord grants it.”

*Sermon 7 on the Passion*, chapter 1: “The greatness of the divine work,” he says, “must not be considered by me in such a way that I despair OF THE SERVICE THAT I OWE, since the mystery of human salvation may not be left unspoken, even if it cannot be explained.”

*Sermon 11*: “IT IS NOT PERMITTED for a priest, in so great a sacrament of divine mercy, to withhold the ministry of preaching from the ears of the faithful people.”

*Sermon 2 on the Resurrection*, chapter 1: “The DUTY OF OUR SERMON must also be added, so that, just as I perceive you to DEMAND IN DEVOUT EXPECTATION THE DEBT OF CUSTOM, so the exhortation of the priest may be joined to the most sacred solemnity of the reading.”

The Pontiff would certainly not have spoken in this way unless he had found the practice of preaching firmly established in the Roman Church through long usage and custom.

### XI. 4.

Writing to Maximus of Antioch and to Theodoret, Saint Leo explicitly asserts:

> “It must not be permitted that anyone established outside the priestly order should assume for himself the rank of preacher. Since all things in the Church of God ought to be ordered, so that in the one body of Christ the more excellent members may fulfill their own office, and the inferior members may not resist those above them.”

Since he wished this decree to be made known by the bishop of Antioch to all the metropolitans and bishops of his diocese, this indicates that it had always been observed by all bishops throughout the Church that they themselves should strive to feed Christ’s flock with the word of God. Otherwise, he would not have thought that a bishop’s duty was fulfilled unless he discharged the ministry of preaching, provided he was not legitimately impeded (Council of Trent, Session 5, *On Reform*, chapter 2, and Session 23, chapter 1).

### XII. 5.

Sozomen is refuted as a liar by a sermon of Pope Liberius, which Blessed Ambrose transcribed in full in Book III *On the Veiling of Virgins*, and which he says was delivered in the Basilica of Saint Peter on the Lord’s Nativity to Ambrose’s sister Marcellina, who at that time was professing virginity together with several others.

Some object that this was not a sermon to the people but merely an exhortation to Marcellina, a private address contrary to the custom of the Roman Church. Who does not see that this is said gratuitously and blown away by mere denial? What, after all, is required for this sermon to be called solemn? It was delivered in the Basilica of Saint Peter, in which the Roman bishops performed all the duties of their pontificate. It was delivered on the greatest solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity. It was delivered before a vast and numerous crowd, whom the twofold solemnity of the Lord’s feast and the consecration of virgins had summoned to the basilica. The bishop of Bologna was also present. What more is required?

Moreover, whoever says that Liberius acted contrary to the custom of his Church in so great a solemnity, amid so great a gathering of the people and in the splendor of so august a basilica, scarcely, I think, shows sufficient regard for Liberius’s honor. It is more plausible that the Pontiff acted according to the custom of his Church and, on the occasion of consecrating the virgins, added only a few words to the virgins after the greater part of the sermon, which concerned the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity.

For it is clear that this sermon is not preserved in full in Ambrose, who inserted into his writings only what suited the subject then under consideration and was appropriate to his sister.

### 6.

I adduce an even earlier witness than Pope Zephyrinus: Tertullian. From him we at least know with certainty that, when penitents were reconciled, the Roman Pontiffs delivered a sermon to the people. In his book *On Modesty*, which he composed after he had already separated from the Catholic Church, he introduces Pope Zephyrinus moving the faithful to mercy and to restore penitents to favor. Thus he writes in chapter 13:

> “And you, indeed, bringing the adulterer’s repentance into the Church to implore the brotherhood … with how many enticements of mercy you can, as a good shepherd and blessed pope, preach concerning that man’s restoration, and seek your goats in the parable of the sheep, and so forth.”

It is therefore false to say that no sermon older than Leo’s can be found which was delivered by a Roman bishop.

Even if that were true, Sozomen’s opinion would not thereby acquire much strength. We possess no sermon of any bishop of Milan, Arles, Ravenna, or Hippo delivered by the predecessors of Ambrose, Hilary, Peter Chrysologus, or Augustine. Who, on that account, would say that no bishops of those Churches older than the men I have named ever delivered a sermon to their own people?

It is therefore better to admit that Sozomen was mistaken and deceived by false rumors; or else to say, with Saint Gregory the Great: “The Apostolic See refuses to accept Sozomen’s history, because he tells many lies” (Gregory, *Register*, Book VI, indiction 15, Letter 31 to Eulogius of Alexandria).

When I was working on the first edition, no other way of escaping this difficulty occurred to me. Four years later, the most learned Joannes Garetius, a member of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur, devised another solution in his preface to a new edition of the great Cassiodorus. He conjectures, namely, that a corruption entered the place in his Cassiodorus which had been excerpted from Sozomen, and he strengthens his conjecture by the authority of the Santheodorian manuscript, where, instead of *docet* (“he teaches”), *dicit* (“he says”) is read.

“This reading,” he says, “produces an entirely different and most truthful meaning.” Cassiodorus there speaks of the hymn *Alleluia* in the following manner:

> “Among the Romans they sing Alleluia once each year, on the first day of Easter, so that the Romans regard it as an oath to be worthy to hear this hymn.”

Cassiodorus immediately adds in the *Tripartite History*:

> “In that Church neither the bishop nor any other speaker says anything before the people”—supply: “that first Easter Alleluia.”

I would gladly subscribe to this conjecture if truth did not stand in the way. For who, in fact, says that hymn if neither the bishop nor anyone else says it before the people? Why would the Romans gather to hear it if they had no one saying it? Yet the conjecture is supported by only one manuscript, nearly six hundred years old, of the *Tripartite History*.

But among so many codices of so many editions and editors—some printed, some manuscript—of both the *Tripartite History* and Sozomen, what is safer than to consult the fountainhead rather than pursue a stream’s shadow? Who would dare assert that the text of the Greek author was corrupted after being subjected to the labors of so many learned critics, in none of whose works did it ever suffer even the slightest suspicion of blemish?

Indeed, just as a careless scribe could easily have shifted from the genuine word *docet* in the Latin translator to the similar *dicit*, so a slip from one to the other of the corresponding Greek words would be far more difficult.

What, then? Do we prefer this learned man’s conjecture to our suspicion that Sozomen was mistaken? Not at all. But, setting both aside, we propose a new interpretation, one which, if I am not mistaken, is more persuasive.

I am certain that Sozomen is writing here about a public sermon, but a specifically Easter sermon. His words should be explained as follows: among the Romans Alleluia was sung once each year, on the first day of Easter; and the rite of this sacred hymn was so solemn for them that everyone flocked to the church to hear and sing it, while many even regarded it as an oath and vow to be worthy to hear and sing this hymn.

For on that sacred day of Easter this one, very brief hymn took the place of the entire sermon, since in that city neither the bishop nor anyone else delivered a sermon on that day to the people gathered in the church.

That this is Sozomen’s meaning is proved by an examination of the subject he is treating. Throughout the entire preceding chapter, which is chapter 18, he speaks only of the Easter festival. In the present chapter, chapter 19, he says a great deal about Easter and discusses nothing except in connection with Easter, reporting various customs of the Churches for the sole purpose of excusing Churches that formerly differed over the day of this feast—some observing different traditions of Saints Peter and Paul, others those of Saint John.

“For they considered it foolish,” he says, and rightly so, “that those who agreed on the principal points of religion should separate from one another because of customs.” After this he sets out the various practices of the Churches, including the Roman practice of singing Alleluia once at Easter, and then adds others not connected with that feast. Yet, as he says when closing the chapter, “it was because of this that I have entered into this discourse concerning these matters.”

Once Sozomen is understood in this way, he can no longer be said to have written something false about the Roman Church, as I formerly believed. Nor need we ask, as the learned Garetius does, how Cassiodorus, when excerpting Sozomen, could have omitted what precedes and follows and copied only what he knew with complete certainty to be false.

For what he excerpted is true, and it is not true that the remaining material was not excerpted by him—namely, the discussion of the custom that arose on account of Arius, according to which at Alexandria only the bishop preached. What else can these words of the preceding chapter, chapter 38, mean?

> “At Alexandria a presbyter does not deliver a sermon, and this practice began from the time when Arius disturbed the Church.”

Senator therefore did not omit this material but transferred it to the preceding chapter.

Furthermore, that it is just as true that the Roman Pontiffs were not accustomed in those times to deliver a sermon to the people on Easter Day as it is false that they did not teach publicly at other times—when Sozomen, understood in this way, asserts the former—cannot be called into doubt by any plausible argument, especially since no Easter sermons of our Leo, or of any Roman Pontiff before the sixth century, appear to have survived.

As for the two sermons attributed to Leo as belonging to this solemnity in earlier editions, we proved in their proper place, from the context of both sermons, that this was an error of the editors. We also adduced the testimony of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, and of Florus of Lyon, and demonstrated that they were delivered not at the Easter festival but on Holy Saturday. See the notice prefixed to each sermon. Observe also that I deliberately do not extend this custom of the Roman Church beyond the beginning of the sixth century, because the homilies delivered by Gregory the Great to the people on the same solemnity clearly show that matters subsequently stood otherwise.

### XIII.

What our Leo did for the affairs of the Church during the first three years of his pontificate, the writers are silent about, and we do not learn it with certainty from any of his letters.

[Note: At the outset we placed two other letters, one to the bishop of Aquileia and the other to Septimus of Altinum, which we showed in the notice to have been written about 442. Conversely, of two letters which Quesnel believed to have been issued at the beginning of Leo’s pontificate, the first, to the African bishops, is Letter 12 in this edition, because we believe it was written after 445; the second, to Rusticus, is Letter 167, since we consider it to have been delivered after 24 October 458. The notices prefixed to each should be consulted.]

We have assigned two letters to this otherwise vacant interval. Several considerations persuade me that they were written during that period, as I explain more fully in the notes.

Africa had been devastated in the preceding years, and Carthage itself had been captured by the Vandals in 439. A very large number of people crossed over to the lands beyond the sea, either being placed on ships whose vessels were broken, as Victor of Vita relates (*On the Persecution of the Vandals*), or voluntarily withdrawing from the savagery of the Vandals.

At that time Mauretania Caesariensis still obeyed the Romans. From there many people traveling to Rome informed Leo about ordinations unlawfully carried out in that province and contrary to the provisions of the canons.

At that time Bishop Potentius, apparently an African, was staying in Rome. As he was departing from the city, Leo entrusted him with this responsibility: to investigate, concerning the bishops whose election was said to be blameworthy, what the truth was (Letter 1, now 12, to the African bishops, chapter 1).

Potentius also received from Leo a letter to be delivered to the Africans, but that letter was lost through the misfortunes of the times. After returning to the province, Potentius reported in a careful written account, as he had been asked, what evils afflicted the Church of Mauretania Caesariensis.

This gave the holy Pontiff an opportunity to write again to the African bishops of that province.

There survives [Note: We have published this letter in a double form, and have clearly vindicated the part which Quesnel rejected as spurious. See the notice, in which we also assigned, at no. 14, the reason for the double edition or form. It will there become clear that not only Potentius, but after him also David, an African bishop, and other Africans migrated to Rome, and that Leo, in response to the new information which arrived, added to the first composition material constituting the complete letter. From this document we learn how much authority the Africans attributed to the Roman See and with what zeal the holy pontiff provided for the correction of abuses which had crept in and for the restoration of discipline. The appeal of African bishops may also be understood from the case of Bishop Lupicinus.] that distinguished letter in which he condemns bishops improperly created, especially those who lacked knowledge and good morals. He warns that hands should not be laid upon bishops hastily, and that no one should be raised to this summit except by degrees and after long experience of merit. He orders that those who had taken a second wife, or a widow, or another woman after dismissing their first wife, be barred from the priesthood. Neither the opportunity to win the favor of the Africans, nor the necessities of the times, nor the extreme scarcity of ecclesiastical ministers could induce Leo to grant dispensation to such men.

### XIV.

He judged that those who had been promoted directly from the laity to the episcopate should be treated more leniently. Yet he held that this was an indulgence, not a law or a custom, and that it did not prejudice the contrary statutes or decrees of the Apostolic See.

His words against bishops who lay hands too hastily and recklessly should not be omitted:

> “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22).

“What is it to lay hands quickly except to confer priestly honor upon men who have not been tested—before the maturity of age, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, before experience of discipline? And what is it to share in the sins of others except to make oneself an ordainer of the kind of man who is himself unworthy to be ordained?” (Letter 1, now 12, chapter 2).

Although Saint Leo could have written this from his knowledge of Scripture and tradition alone, we know from another source that he had been taught how great the discernment of those to be ordained ought to be.

The author of the little work called *The Spiritual Meadow* relates that Saint Leo was warned from heaven to pay particular attention to those whom he selected for the Church’s sacred ministry, since God would demand an account from him concerning them.

> “When Abba Amos was going down to Jerusalem and had been ordained patriarch, all the abbots of the monasteries of the desert came to venerate him. Among them I too was present with my abbot. The patriarch began to say to the fathers: ‘Pray for me, fathers, for a great and intolerable burden has been imposed upon me, and the dignity of the priesthood terrifies me exceedingly. To govern rational souls belongs to men like Peter and Paul; but I am wretched and a sinner. I fear the burden of ordination more than anything else, for I found it written that the most blessed Leo, equal to the angels, the pope who presided over the Roman Church, remained for forty days at the tomb of the Apostle Peter, persisting in vigils and prayers and asking the Apostle to intercede for him with God, so that his sins might be forgiven him. When the forty days had been completed, the Apostle Peter appeared to him and said: “I have prayed for you, and all your sins have been forgiven, except for the laying on of hands. For this alone you will be required to give an account.”’”

This is found in that book, whose authority was approved by the Fathers of the Seventh Council when they cited parts of it in its fourth session.

### XV.

The same African disaster that gave occasion for Leo’s letter to the bishops of Mauretania compelled many people from the African regions to cross over to the shores of Gaul. Some of them did not know from which sectarian group they had received the sacrament of baptism. [Note: Having shown that our Letter 167 to Rusticus of Narbonne was written after 24 October 458, further reasons for doubt arose which place it later than the African disaster, as each reader will understand from the notice.] Hence a question arose among the Churches of Gaul as to what should be done.

Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, judged that the Roman bishop should be consulted both on this matter and on many other points of ecclesiastical discipline. Leo replied in a longer letter (Letter 2, now 147), which we have placed second, for the reasons given there; they may be seen in the notes.

In this letter the prudence, knowledge of the canons, and apostolic charity of our Leo shine forth wonderfully. First, he raises and consoles Rusticus, who was becoming discouraged in spirit because of the scandals that had arisen and was considering withdrawal; he urges him not to withdraw from the episcopal burden, enticed by the desire for a more peaceful life.
