He then gives highly learned answers concerning the sacraments of baptism, ordination, penance, and marriage; the continence of clergy; the consecration of virgins; and other matters of this kind relating to the morals and governance of the Church.

## The Year of Christ 443; the Fourth of Pope Leo; the Thirty-Sixth of Theodosius, the Nineteenth of Valentinian, Emperors; the Consulship of Maximus and Paterius

### I.

Leo’s first confrontation was against the Manichaeans.

Several matters preceded this confrontation. First, two letters, now lost, concerning the uncertainty over Easter in the year 444: one to Saint Cyril of Alexandria, the other to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum. Only Paschasinus’s reply survived. A fragment of Saint Cyril’s reply is included in this edition.

Both letters were written later, in the year 443. That the date of Easter used to be announced in the preceding year is inferred from Letters 131 and 138, written in 454. These letters concern Easter in 455. In Letter 131, chapter 2, dated 9 March 454, the day of the announcement is said to be approaching—the day entered on the formal notices. From Letter 138, by which the same Easter was announced to the Gauls, it is clear that this announcement was made on 28 July of that same year, 454.

Before the announcement, however, whenever uncertainty arose, the opinions of the Easterners had to be reconciled. Hence these letters to Cyril and Paschasinus concerning the uncertain Easter date of 444 had to be sent sufficiently early for their replies to arrive in time. They must therefore be believed to have been delivered at the beginning of 443, or even in 442; and perhaps the letter to Cyril in particular was written in 441.

Certainly, in order to resolve the uncertainty about Easter in 455, Leo began writing in 451, as is clear from Letter 88, chapter 4.

The second matter preceding the confrontation with the Manichaeans was Letter 4 to the Campanians, delivered on 10 October 443. We have sufficiently shown in the notice to Letter 1, number 23, that the Manichaeans were discovered only toward the end of that year.

Several members of that impious sect had come to Rome after their affairs in Africa had been ruined and the province had been devastated by the Vandals. This filth of heretics remained hidden for a long time beneath the mask of devout people, who concealed their impiety by their appearance, manner of walking, simple dress, and stricter way of life.

Outwardly they professed sincere faith, but secretly they held a shameful and depraved doctrine, eager to instill their poison in others. This evil was concealed with such skill that it seemed impossible to detect the authors of the crime.

For almost two full years, whether they sheltered themselves by their own devices or whether Leo’s vigilance made them fearful, this wickedness remained hidden from the Pontiff. At last, however, it was exposed at the beginning of the third year of his pontificate.

When Leo learned of it, he publicly warned Christians not to allow themselves to be deceived by a counterfeit appearance of virtue or by the deceptive shadow of piety, since a corrupt life, depraved conduct, and vices are often concealed beneath such disguises.

“Therefore,” he says (*Sermon 4 on the Epiphany*, chapter 5), “let nothing be shared by any Christian with such people; let there be no association or partnership with them. Let it benefit the universal Church that many of them have been discovered by the Lord’s mercy, and that the sacrileges in which they lived have been revealed by their own confession.”

He further explained the method and means of recognizing those who had given their names to this criminal sect: they held sacred the first and second days of the week in honor of the moon and sun, and passed both days in fasting.

One crime involved multiple sacrileges: they worshiped the heavenly bodies as gods, and they violated the Lord’s Day and the discipline of the Church.

“Let none of you,” he says (*Sermon 4 on Lent*, chapter 5), “be touched by the impiety of this contagion. These people are polluted above all by their very abstinence, serving the creature rather than the Creator and devoting a foolish abstinence to the lights of heaven. No one can doubt that those who are discovered fasting in honor of the sun and moon on the Lord’s Day and the second day of the week are Manichaeans. For by one perverse act they are impious and profane twice over: they establish their fast both for the worship of the stars and for contempt of Christ’s resurrection.”

He then adds more certain indications.

The faithful Christians of those times customarily received Communion under both forms, the body and blood of Christ, as they put it. The Manichaeans, in order not to reveal their impiety openly, did not abstain from the sacred mysteries; they received the body under one form, but they considered it a religious duty to avoid drinking Christ’s blood under the other, because they regarded wine as the work of the demon and an invention of the evil principle.

Leo warned the Christians about this pernicious doctrine:

> “When, in order to conceal their unbelief, they dare to participate in our mysteries, they so restrain themselves in the communion of the sacraments that they sometimes lie hidden more safely. With an unworthy mouth they receive the body of Christ, but they altogether avoid drinking the blood of our redemption. We have wished your holiness to know this so that such people may be exposed by these indications and, once their sacrilegious pretense has been detected, may be marked and exposed and expelled from the fellowship of the holy by priestly authority.”

Finally, he strongly exhorts everyone not to withhold their assistance in searching out those heretics.

“For great piety,” he says, “is it to expose the hiding places of the impious and to defeat the devil himself whom they serve.”

Then, so that this heresy might be hateful to everyone, he lists its principal doctrines and sketches them as if on a brief tablet: how the Manichaeans reject the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets in word and deed; how, in their impiety, they assert that Christ was born only in appearance; how they regard his Passion, death, and resurrection as pure dreams and spectacles apparent to the eyes; how they diminish the power of baptism and corrupt the morals and discipline of the Church; and how, finally, they overthrow the whole Christian religion.

“Among them,” says Saint Leo, “nothing is holy, nothing sound, nothing true. They must be guarded against, lest they harm anyone; they must be exposed, lest they establish themselves in any part of the city.”

### III.

He further complains about the simplicity of certain people who imitate their depraved practices.

The Manichaeans accustomed to go with the Christians to the Basilica of Saint Peter. When they reached the entrance, they immediately turned toward the rising sun and saluted the rising sun with a bow of the body and a movement of the eyes.

This was indeed an ancient religious practice and an old discipline of Christians, but it had been defiled by a wicked usage—partly, as Saint Leo says, through the fault of ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism.

It was equally harmful to the faithful and to those recently initiated, because the former seemed to approve the sacrileges of the Manichaeans by doing the same things as they did. It became an occasion for sinning twice over: while they were not forbidden to salute the sun, they continued to worship it.

Leo resolved to abolish the practice in order to remove the stumbling block of error. It has always been within the proper authority of priests, according to the suitability of times and places, to establish and abolish the rites of the Church and the laws of discipline. The principle of faith and its one unchanged integrity nevertheless remain constant and are subject neither to human discretion nor to changes of time.

### IV.

After Leo had drawn the minds of the faithful away from that sect through frequent sermons, he searched the city for those infected by this disease. He corrected many whom he found, restored them to health, and learned from the perpetrators themselves about their clandestine and hidden sacrileges. He burned their innumerable books.

And, so that the sect might be exposed and the wickedness of the Manichaeans might be known to all, he summoned a large assembly.

[Note: On this gathering and the proceedings held in it, through which the Manichaeans were exposed, see what we said in the dissertation on lost letters, no. 4. The gathering was indeed held toward the end of 443; but Quesnel wrongly relates that the sermons in which the sect is discussed as already exposed preceded this gathering. Although the five sermons on the Fast of the Tenth Month and the four on the Lord’s Nativity were delivered in the same year, the four sermons on the Epiphany and the four on Lent must be assigned to the following year, 444.]

Leo calls it both a judgment and a gathering (Letter 15 to Turibius and Homily 5 on the Fast of the Tenth Month); Valentinian Augustus calls it a gathering (*Novel* concerning the Manichaeans); Baronius calls it a council (*Annals*, year 445).

But a council was not necessary—for Saint Prosper does not in fact mention one—since the matter concerned neither the proscription of a new heresy nor the affirmation of the faith, but the imposition of punishment according to the canon of the Church. Nor is it a council when part of the senate and part of the people are present together with the priests.

Whatever the proper designation, the chosen men and women of the Manichaeans were present in a large assembly, as leaders of their impious superstition. When questioned, they disclosed the sect’s detestable doctrines, much about its horrible ceremonies and institutions, and shameful crimes and obscene rites were publicly revealed by their confession.

It is shameful to relate. A ten-year-old girl was present, having been violated. The girl’s corrupter was also present, together with two women who were privy to the crime, as well as the bishop himself, who had arranged the unspeakable offense.

Everything was set out in order: what the rites were; who the bishops and priests of the sacrilegious religion were; in what places they held their forbidden gatherings; and into which provinces this contagion had spread.

At Saint Leo’s urging, many returned to a good way of life. Having abjured the heresy publicly and condemned it in word and writing, they were subjected to the laws of penance. Others, for whom the shamefulness of the religion had greater power, were driven into exile and deported to places where the flock of Christ could not be contaminated by the contagion.

The madness was also restrained by imperial edicts. One or two years later, Valentinian, in a constitution addressed to Albinus, the prefect of the praetorian guard, declared that they were subject to public prosecution; prohibited them from military service; excluded them from ordinary human society; deprived them of the power to make wills; and likewise excluded them from every succession to an inheritance. He denied them the assistance of advocates and judges and finally enacted that the laws issued against them at various times should remain in force.

### V.

There is also a letter of Leo to the bishops of Italy against the Manichaeans (Letter 8, now 7), written in 444 after their treachery had been discovered and condemned at Rome. It was sent through the provinces to all the bishops. [Note: In the table of Collection 5 it is called the General Letter on the Manichaeans; and the manuscripts of Collections 2 and 5 give this heading: “To all bishops established in the various provinces.” From this we learn that this constitution was an encyclical sent alike to bishops of different provinces. Accordingly, in a manuscript seen by Quesnel it is said to have been sent “by that acolyte”; this formula, substituted for the proper name of the acolyte named in the letters themselves, indicates that several acolytes carried different copies into different provinces.]

Idatius, a bishop and a writer contemporary with those events, mentions it. Leo’s vigilance deserves praise, but so does its example. An investigation into this heresy was conducted throughout both the West and the East. The bishops vied with one another in driving these monsters from their hiding places and freeing the provinces from this destructive contagion.

Theodoret especially praises Leo’s faithfulness for this reason.

“Many other indications of this,” he says, “can also be found; but your zeal against the wicked and accursed Manichaeans, which your holiness recently displayed, is sufficient, showing your devotion to God” (Letter now 52 to Saint Leo).

Baronius assigns this to the year 444; we have assigned it to a year earlier. For Prosper, who may have been present at the gathering, records that the proceedings occurred during the consulship of Maximus and Paterius, that is, in the year 443.

Leo’s letter to the bishops of Italy was indeed given the following year, but toward the end of January. From this I infer that the event itself took place in the preceding year. For investigating the Manichaeans, exposing their meetings and assemblies, extracting a confession from them, holding a gathering concerning the matter, exhorting them to repentance, and punishing those who resisted with exile was not the work of a few days. Nor was the letter to the bishops written until after the event had occurred, as Leo himself states.

Moreover, there is a homily of Saint Leo on the Fast of the Tenth Month in which he speaks about this matter as having just taken place—indeed, as not yet completed. This fits the month of December 443 better than the year 444.

The Pontiff attacks the same people in *Sermon 4 on Lent*, chapter 5, where he says that, so that they might not remain completely hidden, “they receive the body of Christ with an unworthy mouth, but altogether avoid drinking the blood of our redemption,” and he warns that they can be detected by these indications.

From this it seems not unreasonable to infer that Communion under both forms had not previously been imposed as a command, and that afterward it was either commanded or at least strongly commended.

VI. After these highly successful actions undertaken for the faith against the Manichaeans, St. Leo set about restoring the discipline that had been allowed to decline, whether through the fault of the times or of individuals. Concerning this matter he wrote a letter to the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscany (Epistle 3, now 4), which chronologically precedes the letter that, as we have said, was written about the Manichaeans.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] A second action of Leo must be recorded here, on the authority of a contemporary author of the book *On the Promises*, part IV, chapter 6: “While we too were established in Italy near Campania, the venerable pope Leo, who must be named with apostolic honor, was overthrowing the Manichaeans, crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian; while a certain Florus was seeking access, etc.” From this we learn that, at the time when Leo overthrew the Manichaeans, he also crushed the Pelagians and Julian. More on this is given in the preliminary note to Epistle 1, no. 23, where we also mentioned the pamphlets against those same Pelagians that Prosper presented at Rome.]

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Epistle 4, addressed to the Campanians, was dated 10 October 443. It not only precedes Epistle 7 to the bishops of Italy in chronological order, but also precedes the assembly at which the Manichaeans were discovered. Otherwise, in this letter he would have warned the bishops of Campania about avoiding Manichaeans who had already been discovered in the same way that he warned the bishops of Italy in Epistle 7, which was issued at the beginning of the following year.]

In it he forbids slaves to be made priests, and forbids others to be promoted unless they possess both nobility of birth and nobility of character, lest this bring disgrace upon the Church and defraud their masters. “For,” he says (ibid., chapter 1), “the man who is to be enrolled in divine service must be free from all other obligations, so that he may not be drawn away from the Lord’s camp, in which his name is entered, by any bonds of necessity.”

Likewise he forbids the ordination of husbands of widows, or of men who have married twice, since this is contrary to the canon of the Church and the authority of St. Paul the apostle. Those who are such he removes both from office and from the priesthood. Finally, he orders stern action against any cleric who practices usury, denying that this is lawful for laymen, much less for clerics.

# THE YEAR OF CHRIST 444;—THE FIFTH YEAR OF POPE LEO;—THE 37TH YEAR OF THEODOSIUS AND THE 20TH OF VALENTINIAN, EMPERORS;—THE 18TH CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS AND THE CONSULSHIP OF ALBINUS

## I.

There was a major dispute this year concerning the date of Easter.

[Note: [Col. 0206C] The dispute—or rather investigation—concerning the date of Easter in 444 did not take place in that year, but in the preceding years. See annotation I (Col. 202, note c) under the preceding year. The basis of this question is explained more precisely in the notes to the Fragment of St. Cyril’s letter to Leo, which we placed before Paschasinus’s third letter.]

Formerly there had been various controversies in the Church concerning this feast. They were eventually settled at the Council of Nicaea, where it was decreed that, after the equinox, the feast should be celebrated on the Sunday immediately following the fourteenth day of the moon. Since the art of observing and calculating the course of the heavenly bodies flourished at Alexandria, the responsibility was assigned to the bishop of Alexandria of announcing the date each year to the Christian world. Several paschal letters of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, are still extant.

After more carefully investigating the revolutions of the moon and sun, he published a cycle that was in use and highly regarded in the time of Leo the Great.

[Note: [Col. 0206D] It was not Theophilus’s cycle, or period, of 418 years, which began in the year 475, but his hundred-year table, which began in the year 380—or rather the Alexandrian computation derived from that table—that caused the controversy about the date of Easter in 444. In the sixty-fifth year of that table, corresponding to the year of Christ 444, Easter was marked as falling on 23 April, whereas the Latins, following their eighty-four-year cycle, which Prosper had corrected, maintained that Easter in that year should be transferred to 26 March. Compare the notes mentioned above on Cyril’s Fragment.]

Accordingly, according to the computation of this bishop, Easter in the year of Christ 444 was postponed until 23 April. In the West it was commonly believed that there was an error in the cycle and that the paschal date should not be deferred so far. In connection with this controversy Leo first consulted Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, and then Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, whose distinguished memory is preserved in the Council of Chalcedon. Both confirmed Theophilus’s cycle. Paschasinus also approved it on the basis of the computation of the Hebrews and of a miracle that occurred during the pontificate of Zosimus.

[Col. 0206C] Paschasinus’s letter was published, in which he defended Theophilus’s cycle and the date of Easter in that year—23 April—from attack. Baronius thought that the controversy concerned 25 April, but this is a hallucination, from which another error in the annals arose: he assigns this controversy about Easter to the year 455, an eleven-year chronological error, and confuses two controversies concerning the same matter. It is not the place here to discuss these questions in greater detail. In any case, there is no doubt that Leo agreed with Cyril and Paschasinus.

Prosper, who was living at Rome and was close to Leo, and who otherwise did not favor the Alexandrian computation, writes the following in his *Chronicle*: “This year Easter of the Lord was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, and there was no error, because the ninth day before the Kalends of May was the day of the Passion; out of reverence for it, the birthday of the city of Rome passed without circus games.”

## II.

Toward the end of that same year Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, sent the presbyter Nicholas to Leo with a letter (Epistle 4, now 6), asking him, according to the custom of his predecessors, to exercise Leo’s authority in Illyricum.

[Note: [Col. 0207C] It was not toward the end but at the beginning of this year—specifically, on the day before the Ides of January—that Leo replied to Anastasius and to the metropolitans throughout Illyricum. Accordingly, Anastasius’s letter to Leo and the transmission by the presbyter Nicholas belong to the year 443. Before this action, another letter of Leo to the same Anastasius should be placed, in which he had instructed him, as he says in Epistle 5 to the metropolitans of Illyricum, chapter 5, “to keep informing us from time to time by his report about the condition of your churches.” In obedience to this instruction Anastasius sent the aforesaid letter to Leo through the presbyter Nicholas. Compare the dissertation on the lost letters, nos. 5 and 6.]

Leo replied graciously, and, granting his request, indicated that just as Siricius had once entrusted authority over the churches of Illyricum to Anysius, his predecessor, who had deserved well of the Apostolic See, so he was entrusting his own authority to Anastasius.

He then instructed him to follow the examples of those whose privileges he was using; to ensure that priests attained the priesthood through their life and character, not through favor, canvassing, or purchased votes; and likewise he excluded men who had married twice from the priesthood. He defines as a “man married twice” one who married a wife before baptism and, after her death, having already received baptism, married another.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] Several points omitted by Quesnell must be supplied here. St. Leo forbids the bishops of Illyricum to be ordained by the metropolitans without the knowledge of the bishop of Thessalonica. He orders the metropolitans themselves to be ordained by the bishop of Thessalonica. He commands every bishop who is summoned to a synod to attend without delay. He reserves major cases and appeals to the judgment of the Apostolic See, in accordance with the tradition of the ancient practice.]

Finally, he declares that priests, like bishops, are to be consecrated only on Sunday.

[Col. 0207B] In other letters he warns the metropolitans that he has entrusted his authority to the bishop of Thessalonica, yet that the rights of the churches are not thereby diminished; rather, discipline and the laws of the Church are preserved by this arrangement (Epistle 5, to the bishops of Illyricum).

There is also a letter of Leo to the same metropolitans (Epistle 12, now 13, to the bishops throughout Achaea), dated to the year 446, from which it is clear that Leo received the letters they had sent with a calm mind.

## III.

To approximately the same period I assign the events reported in the work *On the Promises of God*, which is commonly, but falsely, attributed to Prosper. There Leo is said to have taken up arms against the Pelagians and their leader Julian.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] Here Quesnellus distorts the facts and chronology and transfers them elsewhere. Two actions of Leo against the Pelagians must be distinguished. The first was directed against those in the province of Aquileia who had been received without the required guarantees, as Septimius of Altinum had warned. The second was directed against the Pelagians who had begun to disturb Rome itself and who vanished when Prosper brought forward written accusations against them, as must be inferred from the order of these proceedings given by Photius.

[Col. 0208C] The testimony of the author of the book *On the Promises* seems to refer to these latter Pelagians, not to the former. Since he connects this Pelagian event with the actions against the Manichaeans, both must be assigned to the end of the year 443, while the first action against the Pelagians of the province of Aquileia belongs to the earlier part of 442. See more on these matters in the preliminary note to Epistle 1, nos. 23 and following.

It should also be added here that Pope Gelasius, in Epistle 5 to Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia, referring to these actions of Leo, lists him among his predecessors who fought vigorously against the Pelagian heresy: “Or perhaps you do not know that this heresy was long ago overthrown by the Apostolic See through the blessed Innocent of honored memory, and afterward through Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo, by continuous and ineffable judgments?”]

“There in Italy,” says that author, “while we were established near Campania, the venerable pope Leo, who must be named with apostolic honor, was overthrowing the Manichaeans, crushing the Pelagians and especially Julian, etc.” (*On the Division of the Times of the Promises and Predestination of God*, chapter 6).

From these words it is clear that Leo conducted a campaign against the Pelagians in Campania. The author seems to have mentioned Campania precisely for this reason—“while we were established in Campania”—and because Julian was bishop of Eclanum, a town in Campania.

Nor, in my opinion, was he trying to suppress Pelagianism only in Campania, but also in the other provinces of Italy, especially Aquileia. I gather this from two letters of Leo, one addressed to the bishop of Aquileia and the other to Septimius, bishop of Altinum.

Photius mentions this matter when he says that the Pelagians, renewing their errors, again attacked the grace of Christ, but that Leo, having been warned by Septimius, struck down the enemies with the greatest force.

Here are the words of Photius, which he appears to have taken from authentic copies of the proceedings:

**COPY OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE WESTERN BISHOPS AGAINST THE NESTORIAN DOCTRINES**

The following is found there:

“When, as time went on, the members of this sect had been restored to the Church after renouncing their heresy, the evil again took its beginning from them. Thus, when the same plague was being reborn in the time of Bishop Septimius, it had to be suppressed before it spread farther. Letters were sent to Leo, who at that time occupied the Apostolic See at Rome, and Leo fought against the impious with ardent zeal” (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, book 1, codex 54).

[Here Photius says “Nestorian doctrines” instead of “Pelagian,” because of the affinity between the teachings.]

Leo replied to Septimius and also to the metropolitan bishop of the province, whom corrupt manuscripts call Nicetas. Letters to those bishops are still read today. He stirred both of them against the Pelagians, but he rebuked the metropolitan especially because he did not suppress the resurgent heresy and because he admitted Caelestians to communion without first requiring a condemnation of their errors.

[Col. 0208B] He instructed him to convene a provincial synod immediately, lest the evil spread farther, and lest anyone conceal the stain through a fraudulent pretense of correction. No one from among the Pelagians or Caelestians was to be admitted to the Church unless, after a public detestation of the heresy, he had approved by hand and signature whatever the universal Church and the Apostolic See had established by synodal decrees for cutting off this hydra.

[Note: [Col. 0208D] See what we observed in Quesnell’s notes 2 and 3 on Epistle 6, now 1.]

## IV.

Here it is necessary to correct the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, whether their highly learned author was misled by the errors of others or by a conjecture of his own. He writes that the author of the work *On the Promises of God* was Prosper, and in this way leads him on long journeys through Italy and Africa; he also attributes new wars against the Pelagians to him. All of this proceeds from the same source.

For that work is not Prosper’s, but belongs to an unknown and anonymous African author. Anyone who impartially assesses the facts can easily judge how far his style and manner of expression differ from Prosper’s.

[Col. 0208C] The former’s discourse is humble, meager, and simple; Prosper’s manner of speaking is abundant and rich, vigorous in strength and sinew, and full of substantial ideas. It is useless to say that this work was written by Prosper as a young man, since it was written by a man advanced in age, as the author himself attests concerning himself and as is evident from many passages.

Gennadius, certainly a contemporary of these events, when compiling his catalogue of Prosper’s books, does not mention the book *On the Promises of God*.

Nor do the things that anonymous author records about himself fit Prosper well. The writer spent the years of his youth in Africa, as he himself testifies when speaking about Caelestius’s church in Carthage, Africa:

“When the holy solemn feast of Easter was being celebrated, a multitude of priests gathered there from every direction, driven by every sort of curiosity and also arriving from elsewhere. The father and bishop Aurelius, worthy to be named with honor, already a citizen of the heavenly homeland, both held the chair there in the place of Caelestius and sat in it. I myself was then present with companions and friends; and as the impatience of youthful age carried us about in every direction, while in our curiosity we examined each detail according to its importance, etc.”

This happened during the episcopate of Aurelius of Carthage, around the year 420. We also read in the same author that he was still in Africa during the consulship of Aspar, that is, in the year 434. There can therefore be no doubt that Africa was his homeland, where he spent his life, and from which at some point, on account of the Vandal persecution, he crossed to Campania in Italy.

Prosper, however, was born and educated in Gaul, and he himself suggests in his letter to St. Augustine that he had never lived in Africa, since he tells Augustine that he was unknown to him by face.

With these points established, we depart from Baronius, who, on the authority of Photius, reports that Prosper fought against the Pelagians in Campania. Photius, in fact, says rather that he fought against them at Rome than in Campania. His words are:

“Not long afterward, when the Caelestian heresy once more began shamelessly to arise and spring up, as it were from an evil root, certain men at Rome also spoke openly in favor of the heresy. Prosper, a truly godly man, easily scattered and extinguished them by publishing pamphlets against them for the public, while Leo, whom we have mentioned, was still governing the Roman See” (*Bibliotheca*, book 1, codex 54).

It is sufficiently clear that this took place at Rome, and probably toward the end of Leo’s pontificate.

## V.

Nor did Baronius write more accurately when he said that Leo published certain writings against the Pelagians, whose existence is mentioned by Photius but which have not survived to us.

“Saint Leo, the Roman bishop,” says Photius, “also wrote about the Pelagians who had been converted, explaining in writing how they ought to be received when they convert, and condemning their own opinion in writing.”

Here the reference is certainly to the letters to the bishops of Aquileia and Altinum, which we have just said were written against the Caelestians. Baronius, whether prudently or imprudently, passed over them in his *Annals*.

# THE YEAR OF CHRIST 445;—THE SIXTH YEAR OF POPE LEO;—THE 38TH YEAR OF THEODOSIUS AND THE 21ST OF VALENTINIAN, EMPERORS;—THE SIXTH CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN AND THE CONSULSHIP OF NOMUS

## I.

In this year a dispute arose between St. Leo and Hilary of Arles—whether something human happened to these most holy men, or whether the affair resulted from circumstances and the fault of causes that must have arisen in the preceding year.

This was the occasion of the litigation. Celidonius, a bishop of the province of Vienne, as I suppose, was accused in a synod presided over by Hilary and attended by St. Germanus of Auxerre on the grounds that before becoming a bishop he had been the husband of a widow, and that earlier, while exercising a secular administration, he had sat as judge and condemned an accused man to death; nevertheless, he had been ordained bishop.

This was judged contrary to the laws of the Church, and for that reason he was removed from office and deprived of his bishopric. Unable to endure the judgment, Celidonius came to Rome and complained of the injustice to the pope, making many accusations against Hilary and asserting that he was being oppressed by the calumny of his accusers. He also brought witnesses with him who could clear him of the charge, whether true or fabricated.

Leo restored Celidonius to his see. Hilary, who had also gone to Rome, was displeased that the judgment reached in the council had been revoked.

[Note: [Col. 0209D] Two false assumptions are made here: first, that Hilary left Rome after Leo had issued his judgment, a claim based on the spurious letter to the bishops of Vienne that we relegated to the appendix; second, that he exercised the same metropolitan authority throughout his life that Leo had taken away from him. See the observations on Quesnell’s fifth dissertation, part III, chapter 2, where we shall demonstrate that both of these hypotheses of Quesnell are false. It will also become clear from this that Hilary left Rome before Leo issued his judgment in Epistle 10.]

Since he did not approve the pope’s judgment, he left the city and returned to Gaul. Angered by this unexpected departure, Leo sent a letter full of anger to the bishops of the province of Vienne (Epistle 10, formerly 89), and acted through the emperor Valentinian so that, the province having been entrusted to Aetius, Roman jurisdiction would have its proper authority.

[Note: [Col. 0209D] Aetius was not Praetorian Prefect, but patrician and master of both military forces, as is established even by Valentinian’s own novella, which we have in Epistle 11.]

He deprived Hilary of the rights and privileges of his Church.

Nor should it be held against St. Leo if he was deceived.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] Whether Leo suffered deception cannot be determined with such certainty; this will become clear from what we shall say in our observations on the same fifth dissertation, part I, chapter 3, and part III, chapter 3, no. 2.]

For who is so sharp-sighted that he cannot be blinded by the treachery of witnesses or the changeable ingenuity of human beings?

I have treated the matter briefly here; elsewhere I shall discuss it more fully.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] He cites in the margin the fifth apologetic dissertation in defense of St. Hilary of Arles. Our notes and observations must not be separated from that work, so that a fair judgment may be formed concerning the whole matter.]

## II.

While these events were taking place in the West, that great man Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, died in the East. Dioscorus succeeded him, a man of shadowy virtue, who by the appearance of respectability and the display of holiness crept into the Church’s highest honors.

[Col. 0210B] As soon as he had been elected, he sent Leo a letter through the presbyter Possidonius from that region concerning his ordination. I believe this was the same man whom Cyril had once sent to Rome against Nestorius.

After remaining in Rome for some time, he saw and admired the flourishing condition of the Church. As he was preparing to leave, Leo gave him a letter (Epistle 11, now 9), in which he tried to persuade Dioscorus to correct certain practices in which the Church of Alexandria appeared to have departed from the institutions of the Roman Church, recalling St. Peter the apostle, who had first governed the Alexandrian Church.

First, he warned him not to ordain presbyters and deacons on any day other than Sunday, the beginning of which is reckoned from the evening of Saturday. Nor should the sacrifice be offered only once in the basilicas on feast days, lest, because of the multitude of the faithful, part of the people be deprived of the offering of the sacrifice:

“But as often as the presence of a new congregation has filled the basilica in which the service is being held, so often let the following sacrifice be offered.”

The same letter provides an example both of authority and of modesty. The Alexandrian bishop is admonished concerning his office by the Roman pontiff, but more from paternal and fraternal affection and charity than from command.

[Col. 0210C] “Therefore,” he says, “a paternal and fraternal conference ought to be most welcome to Your Holiness, and you ought to receive it in such a way as to understand that it proceeds from us.”

Then he adds:

“Therefore, what we know to have been preserved with especially careful attention on our part, we wish to be guarded by you also. For this reason you will have acted piously and laudably in conforming to the apostolic institutions if you observe this form for the ordination of priests, etc.”

Finally:

“Therefore we earnestly and familiarly admonish Your Love not to neglect, through your own care, what has become established in our custom through the pattern of paternal tradition.”

## III.

There is also a letter of the same Leo to Anastasius of Thessalonica (Epistle 12, now 14). I have not discovered when it was written, but I readily assign it to this year, as is explained more fully in the notes.

[Note: [Col. 0210D] It will become clear from the following annotation that this letter belongs not to this year but to the next. To this year, 445, must be assigned two letters—the letter of the Illyrian bishops and that of Anastasius of Thessalonica to Leo—which have been lost. These will be discussed in the following annotation.]

The occasion for writing it was that Anastasius was abusing metropolitan or exarchal authority and was exercising Leo’s authority more through force of temper than through prudence. Leo therefore rebuked him in very serious terms and urged him to conduct himself with moderation and restraint, and, if anything needed correction in the priests, to do so through counsel and charity rather than through anger and power.

Here are golden words expressing a moderate spirit:

“Toward those who need correction, benevolence should accomplish more than severity; exhortation more than agitation; charity more than power. But those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, easily depart from this rule. And while it pleases them to dominate their subjects rather than to advise them, honor inflates pride, and what was provided for harmony turns toward harm.”

# THE YEAR OF CHRIST 446;—THE SEVENTH YEAR OF POPE LEO;—THE 39TH YEAR OF THEODOSIUS AND THE 22ND OF VALENTINIAN, EMPERORS;—THE CONSULSHIP OF AETIUS AND SYMMACHUS

In the present year, during the consulship of Aetius and Symmachus, Leo wrote to the metropolitans of Achaea a letter (Epistle 13, from Holstenius), which we have transferred here from Holstenius’s posthumous work entitled *The Roman Collection*. It was written in connection with the vicariate of Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Note: [Col. 0211B] The manuscript from which this letter was published gives Achaea; but we have shown in annotation 2 (previous volume, Col. 663, note h) to Epistle 13 itself that Illyricum must certainly be restored. In this letter, chapter 1, mention is made of a letter from the Illyrian bishops to Leo, and in chapter 3 there is mention of a report from Anastasius to the same pontiff. Since this letter was dated 6 January 446, that letter of the Illyrian bishops and Anastasius’s report belong to the year 445.

Leo had subjected all the churches of Illyricum to the bishop of Thessalonica by an apostolic delegation, and had informed all the metropolitans of Illyricum of this by Epistle 5, written on the day before the Ides of January 444, ordering them to reply. It is credible that they did not delay very long in answering. Hence we think that other letters of theirs are missing, preceding those by which he replied on 6 January in Epistle 13.

From this letter we learn that six metropolitans were enrolled there, not all of them obeying the Thessalonian vicar and Leo’s commands. Thus the holy pontiff threatens to correct the disobedience of some of them.

Moreover, from Anastasius’s report the same pontiff learned that the metropolitan of Achaea had performed unlawful ordinations. Among these he specifically mentions the ordination of the bishop of Thespiae, who had been appointed over the unwilling and protesting inhabitants without their knowledge.

At the same time that Leo replied to the bishops of Illyricum, he also replied to Anastasius’s report, which chiefly concerned the action of the metropolitan of Achaea. Some other matters were inserted there, which the same Anastasius was to bring to the attention of the bishops of Illyricum from chapter 4 of Epistle 13.

Quesnellus believed that this response of Leo was Epistle 14 to Anastasius. But the affair of Atticus shows both that another letter of Leo, now lost, was sent to Anastasius at this time and that Epistle 14 was later sent in response to other letters from Anastasius.

It is inferred from Epistle 14, chapter 1, that Anastasius sent Leo two letters concerning the case of Atticus. In the first he had indicated only that Atticus, having been summoned to the synod, was delaying his attendance and pleading illness. St. Leo replied to this in a letter that has been lost; we believe it was dated on the same day, 6 January, on which he wrote Epistle 13 to the Illyrian bishops.

Then, in Epistle 14, Leo complained to Anastasius that, without waiting for his reply and fearing that Leo might order Atticus to be treated more leniently than Anastasius wished, he had acted with the Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum so that Atticus might be brought by force to Thessalonica during the winter.

This occurred in the winter at the end of 445 or the beginning of 446, before Leo’s reply reached Thessalonica. After Anastasius had obtained this, he sent another letter to Leo through deacons. In it he concealed the violent manner in which he had compelled Atticus and reported only that Brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had signified his agreement by a written declaration.

Shortly after these letters had been carried to Rome by the deacons, Atticus himself arrived with several bishops of his province and complained before Anastasius’s own deacons about the harsh manner in which Anastasius had treated him. They did not dare to offer any reply.

You see the metropolitan of eastern Illyricum fleeing to Rome with several of his fellow provincials and appealing to the Apostolic See.

Leo replied to this second letter of Anastasius in Epistle 14. In it he rebuked his violent manner of acting and set forth other admirable decrees concerning ecclesiastical discipline.

From this it is understood that Epistle 14 was written somewhat after the sixth day before the Ides of January in the year 446.

To this period belongs Leo’s Epistle 12 to the bishops of Mauretania, written after 445, which Quesnellus discussed under the year 440, no. 13.]

He considers that major cases should be referred to Anastasius. He rebukes the metropolitan of the province of Achaea [Col. 0211B] because he had consecrated a bishop against the wishes of the inhabitants of Thespiae, and he establishes that no bishop may claim another bishop’s cleric for himself without the authority of the bishop to whom that cleric belongs.

[Col. 0211B] 439–440

# THE YEAR OF CHRIST 447;—THE EIGHTH YEAR OF POPE LEO;—THE 40TH YEAR OF THEODOSIUS AND THE 23RD OF VALENTINIAN, EMPERORS;—THE CONSULSHIP OF CALEPIUS AND ARDABUR

## I.

On the day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Ardabur and Calepius, St. Leo wrote to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia (Epistle 14, now 18), against the heretics, ordering that they not be admitted to Catholic communion unless they had publicly professed their detestation of the heresy.

[Note: [Col. 0212C] We showed in annotation 15 (previous volume, Col. 708, note q) that the letter to Januarius was written on the third day before the Kalends of January. From annotations 5 and 6 (ibid., Col. 707, notes c and e) you will infer that the subject there is the Pelagians, not the Donatists or Novatians.

As for the occasion of this letter, we conjectured in the preliminary note to Epistle 1, no. 26, that the Pelagian heresy had entered the province of Aquileia as early as the time of Zosimus. Under that pope, a pamphlet distinct from the two that Julian and the other Pelagian bishops presented to Zosimus was delivered to Augustine, bishop of Aquileia, by certain persons in that province who had been infected by Pelagian errors.

Just as those who returned from this group to the Catholic faith gave occasion for Epistles 1 and 2, so the remnants of the group supplied the reason for writing this letter to Januarius.]

Presbyters, deacons, and clerics of every rank are to count it a benefit and favor that, if they return from heresy to the Church, they remain in the order in which they are found and are not to hope for further promotion.

If the Pelagians are meant here—the same men whom we have already said were disturbing the Church under the leadership of Julian—I would suppose that this letter was written on that account. After Julian had been deposed from the episcopate and expelled from Italy, he wandered in exile and had no fixed dwelling anywhere.

First he fled to Constantinople. But after being expelled from there following the Council of Ephesus, where both the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies were condemned, he migrated to Gaul as to an asylum, knowing that there were men there who opposed Augustine’s teaching on grace.

Hilary, who had been made bishop of Arles after being a monk of Lérins, certainly did not especially favor Augustine’s doctrine of predestination, although, as Prosper writes in his letter to St. Augustine, he professed himself Augustine’s admirer and follower in all other matters.

At that time Faustus was serving as abbot on the island of Lérins. Julian arrived there as an ill-starred guest, for he infected the abbot’s mind with the stain with which Faustus’s writings were afterward contaminated.

The very learned man Jerome Vignier, a priest of the Oratory of Jesus, had promised that he would uncover these and other matters of the same kind, which are hidden from many, and establish them with certain proofs drawn both from Fulgentius and from others. He discussed Julian at the beginning of volume II of the supplement to the works of Blessed Augustine. But, overtaken by premature death, he was unable to fulfill his promise.

[Note: [Col. 0212D] “Until these proofs are brought forward, we may meanwhile suspend our assent,” says Cardinal Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 13.]

Julian then returned from that island to Italy and stirred up new disturbances, wishing to vindicate himself from error, whether by pretense or by fraud. His supporters, attempting the same thing, wished to return to the Church.

Hence, I believe, came Leo’s letter to Januarius—if, as some think, the subject here is the Pelagians. For my part, I rather think that the discussion concerns either the Donatists or the Novatians. We shall present our conjectures on this matter more conveniently in our dissertations.

## II.

But behold, new wars in Spain against the Priscillianists. While Suevian, Vandal, and Gothic forces were ravaging cities and provinces, they began to renew their errors. While each person was fighting for his household against the barbarian, they themselves were sowing deadly wars in men’s minds and inflicting wounds far more serious upon the unwary than the external enemy.

Turibius, bishop of Astorga, since the disease was growing worse, discussed the matter with the bishops of the province. He sent Leo, through Pervincus [reading uncertain], a deacon of his Church, a letter and a booklet in which the monstrous doctrines of the sect were contained and refuted.

[Note: [Col. 0213C] The *Commonitorium* must also be added. The booklet was composed by Turibius before his episcopate; all that survives of it is the dedicatory letter to Idatius and Ceponius, which we included in the appendix to the Letters. Compare the preliminary note to this letter and the dissertation on the lost letters, no. 16.]

Leo replied, and his letter survives (Epistle 15, to Turibius). In it he proves that the heresy had been formed from the dregs of other heresies, and he crushes each of its doctrines separately. He then briefly explains what must be done to eradicate the monster.

In other letters he summoned Turibius and the bishops of Gallaecia and Lusitania to a council.

[Note: [Col. 0213C] Four letters of Leo must be distinguished in this affair. One, which survives, is the reply to Turibius. In it he ordered that a general synod be assembled from the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica; or, if some obstacle made this impossible, that at least the bishops of Gallaecia, among whom the error was spreading, should meet without fail so that a remedy might be applied to the growing evil.

The second letter was addressed to the bishops of the four provinces mentioned above, whom he urged to convene the same council. When he learned that these bishops, but not the Galicians, were to assemble at the Council of Toledo, he sent a third letter to them, ordering that the statement of faith they were about to issue—or had issued—be sent to Balconius, metropolitan of Braga in Gallaecia.

Finally, he sent a fourth letter to the special synod of Gallaecia and to Balconius the metropolitan. See what we have discussed about these letters in the dissertation on the lost letters, nos. 17, 18, 19, and 20.]

These letters have been lost. But if a general synod could not be convened amid the clash of arms, he at least ordered several bishops to meet, so that together they might determine what should be done for the Christian cause against the spreading heresy.

[Col. 0213C] 441
### III

In October Leo sent a very weighty letter to the bishops of Sicily, rebuking them because they solemnly celebrated baptism on the day of Epiphany (Letter 16 to the bishops of Sicily). The reason was that it was commonly believed that Christ had received the baptism of Saint John on that day. [Col. 0214A]

Leo confirms the custom of the Church, according to which the practice of publicly administering baptism on the days of Easter and Pentecost was an ancient custom derived from the apostles. He then supports it with many arguments: baptism is an image of the resurrection; through this mystery the Christian person comes back to life; the three-day burial is signified by the threefold immersion; and the person is raised from the waters as from a tomb. “Therefore,” he says, “the very nature of the action teaches that the legitimate day for the universal celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose.”

He adds that Pentecost too was consecrated to this celebration, as a kind of supplement to Easter: on that day the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the apostles, and on that day three thousand people were baptized by Peter. [p. 442] With these and similar arguments he exhorts the Sicilians to retain the ancient custom. [Col. 0214B]

Toward the end of the letter he gives the Churches this salutary advice: three bishops should be sent to Rome twice each year, and should deliberate together for the common good of the Church, in order to preserve the decrees of the holy Fathers and eliminate errors from the Church:

> Since it must always be deliberated in common in the presence of the blessed apostle Peter, so that all his constitutions and the decrees of the canons may remain inviolate among all the priests of the Lord.

(Letter cited above.)

Gerardus Vossius, that Catholic theologian, published another letter of Leo to the same bishops (Letter 17, to the bishops of Sicily), in which Leo prohibits the alienation of Church property unless it is for its increase and benefit, and even then not without the consent and approval of the clergy.

[Note: In this letter I have defended Letter 17 in the admonition and annotations.] [Col. 0213D]

But in this letter I miss the style of Saint Leo, nor can I easily persuade myself that two letters were written to the same persons within so short a time—one on the twelfth, the other on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur. [Col. 0214C] Nevertheless, whatever its character, I have not removed it from the letters of the holy pontiff. More about its possible forgery will be found in the observations.

### IV

Nor will I pass over the memory of Leo’s letter, although the letter itself has perished; it is mentioned in the Council of Chalcedon. [p. 443] [Col. 0213D] The occasion of the letter was as follows.

[Note: Tillemont thinks that these events, which are assigned here to the year 447, should be assigned to the year 448, note 10 on Leo. [Col. 0214C] This depends on the different ways of reckoning the four years between this event and the Council of Chalcedon: some think that they should be reckoned as complete years, with several additional months, whereas others count them as years already begun and short by several months.

Moreover, how many fabrications Quesnellus subtly inserts in this matter, in order to diminish pontifical authority and subject the judgments of the Apostolic See to a general council! The complete and straightforward sequence of events, which is not found in his work, will expose the fraud and the error.

Bassianus, a presbyter of the Church of Ephesus, having incurred the hostility of Memnon, its bishop, had been unwillingly ordained by him bishop of Evazus, so that he might be removed from Ephesus. Since Bassianus could not be induced to go and govern that Church, Basilius, Memnon’s successor, taking pity on the forced ordination, granted him, while he remained at Ephesus, the name and honor of a bishop, and consecrated another bishop for the Church of Evazus.

After the death of Basilius, the same Bassianus was installed as bishop of the Church of Ephesus by only one bishop, Olympius of Theodosiopolis, who had been brought there by force. The violence and manner of this installation plainly show that it was carried out contrary to the canons. [Col. 0214D]

Nevertheless, through the agency of the emperor Theodosius, Bassianus was received by Proclus of Constantinople. Synodical letters were issued to the entire clergy and people of Ephesus and also to all the bishops of Asia, and for four years he peacefully possessed that same Church, ordaining not only clerics but also bishops.

Later, however, disputes among certain clerics stirred up a popular tumult; Bassianus was driven from the Church and shut in prison. When this matter was reported to the emperor Theodosius, he sent Eustathius the Silentiary to Ephesus to investigate the affair and report back. Nothing definite could be brought against Bassianus except his unlawful installation.

The emperor is said to have written about this to the bishop of Alexandria, and probably also sent letters to the Roman pontiff and to the other bishops of the principal sees, since all of them replied that Bassianus ought to be removed. [Col. 0215B]

Tillemont observes here, volume XV, page 464, that no other reply could have been given, since only the beginnings of his episcopate, which were contrary to the canons, had been reported; nothing had been added about his four-year peaceful possession, introduced and confirmed by the synodical letters of Proclus of Constantinople and accepted by all the bishops of Asia and by the entire clergy and people. [Col. 0215C] For this, Cyprian’s testimony from Letter 35 could have been cited.

Meanwhile the emperor, who is said to have deposed Bassianus, ordered that another bishop be given to the Ephesians. A council of forty bishops ordained Stephanus, while Bassianus lived unhappily at Constantinople. At the time of the Council of Chalcedon, however, he asked the emperor Marcian, Theodosius’s successor, that his case be examined in the council. There both Bassianus and Stephanus were removed.

This is the true history of the events, which can be gathered solely from Action 11 of the Council of Chalcedon. There is no judgment here of an Asian council by which Bassianus was deposed. The council of forty bishops performed only the ordination of Stephanus.

That there was no conciliar judgment concerning the deposition of Bassianus is clear from the fact that Meliphtongus, bishop of Juliopolis, stated, together with those sitting beside him, that Bassianus had been cast out without accusation and without judgment (volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1615d; ibid., p. 1620b). Hence, at the Council of Chalcedon itself, the bishops of Asia wanted him restored; they would not have done so if they had thought that he ought to be deposed after a judgment had been rendered.

Quesnellus therefore invented the claim that Bassianus’s deposition had first been carried out by the bishops of the province. He erred much more conspicuously in this when he reported that the letters of the Roman pontiff and of the other sees had been issued after that council, although they preceded the entire council.

He is also mistaken when he asserts that Stephanus wrote to Leo after his ordination. Before his ordination, the emperor had written so that he might learn from the bishops of the principal sees what should be decreed concerning Bassianus.

Leo’s letters, by which, as it seems, he replied to the emperor, stated that Bassianus ought not to be a bishop because of the unlawful beginnings of his episcopate. Although they seem to present a judgment of the Apostolic See, since this judgment was issued without investigation and without any formal record, in a matter and circumstance susceptible to misrepresentation they do not bar access to a new and explicit examination, especially if circumstances arose that had not been disclosed to the pontiff. [Col. 0216B]

How many new judgments of the Roman See are established in this way, lest the authority of the Apostolic See thereby suffer prejudice? Thus Bassianus’s peaceful possession for four years, begun by the authority of Proclus and strengthened with the approval of all the bishops of Asia, appeared to have cleansed his unlawful beginnings and to deserve a new investigation. [Col. 0216C]

Had Bassianus requested this from Leo himself, he would not have been rejected. When the Council of Chalcedon was being held, while he requested this new investigation from the council, he requested it also from Leo, who presided over the council through his legates—as is seen from the fact that those four petitions of the Alexandrians were first addressed to Leo and were presented to the Council of Chalcedon. He therefore did not think that Leo’s judgment had to be subjected to the authority of the council; rather, with new grounds brought forward, he thought that a new judgment could be established in the council and by the authority of that same Leo.

For this reason the legates of the Apostolic See did not resist this new investigation, and Julianus of Cos could hold that neither man ought to be cast out. [Col. 0216D] Nevertheless, just as Leo’s judgment had been especially brought forward, so Bassianus’s deposition was also confirmed by Leo’s judgment.

If Bassianus, who had not accepted the replies of Leo and of the other principal sees, obeyed the judgment of the council, this was because he himself was heard in the council and the entire case was investigated; nothing remained that could mark the judgment as the result of misrepresentation (Acts 3, pp. 1267, 1274, 1282, 1290).]

After the death of Basilius, bishop of Ephesus, Bassianus was ordained in his place contrary to the canons. After several years Stephanus, having forcibly expelled Bassianus, occupied his place; this disturbed the Church of Ephesus. [Col. 0215A]

Stephanus complained about Bassianus’s violent ordination both to Leo and to the bishop of Alexandria and to others, and he had received letters from Leo in which Leo had decreed that Bassianus ought to be deposed. Yet the disturbance did not cease until the Fathers gathered at Chalcedon against Eutyches.

Bassianus brought a charge of violence against Stephanus, and the case of both men was reconsidered before the Fathers, along with the question of their ordinations. Then mention was made of the letter of Saint Leo, in which he had declared that Bassianus ought to be removed from office.

But after the matter had been examined, the council’s judgment removed both men from the episcopate, since it had been discovered that the ordination of each was defective.

This letter is mentioned in Action 11 of the Council of Chalcedon.

It should be noted that Bassianus’s deposition was first carried out by the bishops of the province. It was then confirmed by the judgment not only of the Roman bishop but of all the principal sees. Thus it is stated in the Council of Chalcedon (Action 11):

> Bassianus was expelled by the holy Fathers, and by the most holy Leo of royal Rome, and by Flavianus of Constantinople, of blessed memory, and by the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch; by these he was expelled by imperial judgment.

And again:

> The Roman bishop deposed him, and the Alexandrian bishop condemned him.

Note that for “condemned,” the Greek has καθεῖλε, “deposed,” so that in this matter nothing is attributed to one that is not also accorded to the other. [p. 444] [Col. 0215B] [Col. 0215C] [Col. 0215D]

### V

Although both Leo’s letter and the judgments of the principal sees were brought forward, the case nevertheless proceeded to a retrial, with none of the legates of the Apostolic See objecting. [Col. 0216A]

When opinions were requested, some judged that both men ought to be deposed, while others thought that one or the other should be retained. Among the latter was Julianus, bishop of Cos and himself a legate of the Apostolic See. Setting aside, as they say, Leo’s judgment, he thought that Bassianus might retain his see:

> Julianus, most reverend bishop of the city of Cos, himself also the representative of the Roman Apostolic See, said: “Both ought not to be cast out.”

(Council of Chalcedon, part II, Action 12.)

Finally the judges pronounced sentence of deposition against both men, first praising the vote of Anatolius of Constantinople and then that of the legate Paschasinus:

[Note: Anatolius was praised first, not because he possessed authority superior to that of the pontiff’s legates—for what Catholic would not attribute primacy of authority to the Apostolic See? Hence, at the beginning of Action 11, the first place is assigned to the legates—but because Anatolius had been the first in this matter to give his opinion.] [Col. 1216D]

> The most illustrious judges said: “Since the opinion of the God-loving archbishop of royal Constantinople, Anatolius, and of the most reverend bishop Paschasinus, occupying the place of Leo, the God-loving archbishop and senior of Rome, has pleased everyone,” and so forth.

(Ibid.)

Then Bassianus, who had not stood by the judgment either of the principal sees or of Leo himself, submitted to the judgment of the synod, because the authority of an ecumenical synod is supreme and its judgment final. [Col. 0216B]

From this it becomes clear how vainly the author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Baronio, for the year 447, and a recent writer who published an unfortunate volume intended to diminish episcopal dignity concerning the canonical deposition and judgment of bishops, have taken comfort from this example.

(The work, written in French, is by a certain David: *On the Canonical Judgment of Bishops*.)

They think that Leo asserted for himself the right to judge even Eastern [p. 445] metropolitans and exercised that power against Bassianus. Yet Stephanus does not say that Leo wrote this; he merely says that Bassianus “ought not to be a bishop”:

> ὅτι τοῦτον μὴ δεῖν εἶναι ἐπίσκοπον  
> “that this man ought not to be a bishop.”

[Note: If Stephanus expressed Leo’s sentence in this passage with the words “that this man ought not to be a bishop,” elsewhere he reported it with these words: “The Roman bishop deposed him,” which suggest that Leo claimed the power of deposition. This comes from Stephanus’s report alone. If Leo’s own letters existed, we would know more precisely what Leo wrote.

But if other bishops of the principal sees are also reported to have used the same or similar words, then, since a peculiar right over all Eastern bishops cannot be denied to the Roman pontiff by reason of primacy, the right to judge even Eastern metropolitans cannot be denied to him either—unless by one who either denies primacy or attributes to him, with the heterodox, a primacy merely of order. More on this right may be found in the observations on Dissertation 5.] [Col. 0216D] [Col. 0217D]

Nor did the legates hold this view, since they either judged as though the matter were still open or moderated Leo’s sentence. For the Roman pontiff [p. 446] had said that Bassianus ought not to be a bishop; Julianus, the pontiff’s legate, said that he could be a bishop. In speaking about the two men who were disputing the episcopate, he declared that both ought not to be cast out, thereby indicating that one or the other should be appointed to the see of Ephesus:

> Κατὰ μὲν κανόνας οὐδὲ εἷς ὤφειλεν εἶναι, κατὰ δὲ φιλανθρωπίαν ἡ σύνοδος ἢ Ἀσιανὴ ἐπιλέξεται τίς ὀφείλει εἶναι  
> “According to the canons, neither ought to be [bishop]; but according to mercy, the synod—or the Asian synod—will choose which one ought to be.”

(Council of Chalcedon, Action 12.) [Col. 0217A]

## Year of Christ 448; 9th of Pope Leo; 41st of Theodosius and 24th of Valentinian, emperors; in the consulship of Posthumianus and Zeno

### I

On the Ides of March of this year Saint Leo wrote to Dorus, bishop of Beneventum (Letter 18, now 20). Dorus had promoted a recently ordained presbyter to a higher rank and position, passing over other presbyters who surpassed him in age and merit. Moreover, some others, through servile flattery, had voluntarily surrendered their legal right and position. [Col. 0217B]

Leo accused Dorus of betrayal, the young man of arrogance, and the presbyters of abject flattery. He therefore ordered that each person preserve, according to the canons, the precedence of his ordination. He excepted those who, by voluntary renunciation, had made themselves unworthy of this honor; even these he wished to remain inferior, by their own judgment, to the man whom they had preferred to themselves.

“And so,” he says, “in order that they may pronounce the sentence of their own judgment, they too will be inferior to the man whom by their own decision they preferred to themselves”; while all the presbyters remained in their own order, which the time of each one’s ordination had assigned to him.

[Note: Here the mention should not have been omitted of the two works written in this case: namely, the petition of complaint presented to Leo by the presbyter Paulus, and another letter of Leo, now lost, to the bishop Julius, to whom he entrusted the execution of this decree. See the dissertation on Lost Letters, numbers 22 and 23.] [Col. 1218D]

### II

Leo also accomplished so much for the Church that he seemed to have surpassed his predecessors up to that time, whether by slaughtering Priscillian’s corrupted flock, destroying the clandestine movements of the Manichaeans, celebrating his triumph over the defeated Pelagianism, or sternly defending the discipline of the Church. What would have been the height of another man’s achievement became for Leo merely a path to greater things.

He accomplished these things courageously and successfully, but against enemies who were wounded and already weakened by many blows. [Col. 0217C] Behold a new enemy, recent and uninjured, attacking the incarnation of Christ and shaking the foundations of the Christian religion. Certainly he was to be feared: bold in conceiving his crime and ready to carry it out; an admirable intellect, if he had turned it toward better things.

His profession of piety and his reputation were equally harmful, because he used them against the faith. What need is there to recount the gratitude, favor, and friendships of princes and magnates, which he had secured by lawful and unlawful means in order to advance his designs? Yet all this served to make Leo’s victory more glorious.

This was Eutyches, an archimandrite of Constantinople, who, driven on by an evil demon, sowed new errors in the Church, mixing the two natures in Christ and asserting that they had coalesced into one. The consequence was either that the divine nature was subject to sufferings and human passions, or that what happened to Christ as man—his labors and death, through which he brought us salvation—was mere mockery. [Col. 0217D]

At first he communicated these views secretly with the monks who shared his table, and then privately with friends and with those whom he knew to be eager for novelty. Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum in Phrygia, who was a friend of Eutyches, initially tried in a friendly manner to correct his perverse doctrine. When he understood that the monk could not be corrected by counsel, he considered the matter of religion more important than friendship and began to denounce the crime, so that it might be suppressed before it acquired strength. [Col. 0218A]

### III

At that time a synod was being held at Constantinople by Flavianus, bishop of Constantinople and successor of Proclus. Thirty bishops had assembled to settle a dispute brought by Florentius, bishop of Sardis and metropolitan of Lydia, against the bishops of his province, John [p. 447] and Cassianus. [Col. 0218B]

At the urging of Flavianus, to whom he had reported Eutyches’s audacity, Eusebius brought the matter before the council. The Fathers immediately detested the man’s depravity and asked Eusebius, in accordance with the rights of friendship, to approach Eutyches and persuade him to adopt better views.

Eusebius then refused, saying that he had already tried every possible means, but without success; the wound was not to be treated with a gentle hand but cut away with the knife before it seized the healthier parts. Eutyches was already openly preparing weapons against the Church, going around the monasteries of the city, offering a document for the monks to sign, and asking them to swear allegiance to his doctrine and his name.

After hearing this, the Fathers sent a presbyter and a deacon to investigate each point. The presbyter went directly to Martin, the archimandrite, and asked him many questions about Eutyches. Martin admitted that Eutyches had sent the deacon Constantine with a written statement to which he was asked to subscribe. He said that the statement contained no other faith than that sworn at the Council of Nicaea and handed down and received from Cyril; but he had rejected it with this reply:

> Μὴ εἶναι ἐμὸν ὑπογράφειν, ἐπισκόπων δὲ μόνων  
> “It is not mine to subscribe; it belongs to the bishops alone.”

A grave answer, and one that should be remembered by posterity.

When this had been reported to the synod, the Fathers decided that Eutyches should be summoned to the council. Summoned once and again, he scorned to come, saying that it was not lawful for him to leave the monastery. He evaded a third summons as well by feigning illness. At last, after several days, the monk came to the synod in military attire. With him came Florentius Patricius, a turbulent phalanx of monks, and a troop of court attendants and praetorian soldiers. [Col. 0218C]

The eunuch Chrysaphius had provided him with this support. Chrysaphius abused the favor and authority of the emperor according to his own pleasure. He was as dear to Eutyches as he was hostile to Flavianus, because [p. 448] when Flavianus had assumed the episcopate, he had refused to win Chrysaphius’s favor.

The Fathers, however, were not frightened and questioned him about the faith. They asked Eutyches what he believed concerning Christ. In their presence he did not hesitate but confessed that there were two natures in Christ before the Word was united with the flesh, but that they had coalesced into one after the Divinity had been joined with human nature in one hypostasis:

> Ὁμολογῶ ἐκ δύο φύσεων γεγενῆσθαι τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν πρὸ τῆς ἑνώσεως, μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἕνωσιν μίαν φύσιν ὁμολογῶ  
> “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union; but after the union I confess one nature.”

The Fathers taught that this doctrine was alien to the faith, and earnestly urged him to retract his errors, condemn them, and receive the Nicene confession. But he refused to listen and persisted resolutely in his position. Therefore, by the judgment of the Fathers, he was removed from the priesthood, deprived of the office of archimandrite, and excluded from ecclesiastical communion. [Col. 0218D]

### IV

When Eutyches, with the authority of Chrysaphius and the protection of the emperor, saw that neither he nor his doctrine was safe and secure, he fled to the Roman pontiff, thinking that his condemnation would be invalid if he could entangle so great a pontiff on his side.

This was easy for him to imagine, because it is simple to deceive someone who is absent. [Col. 0219A] He knew also that rivalries over the episcopal see had long produced something like hostility between the Roman and Constantinopolitan bishops.

[Note: No disputes or hostilities between the Roman and Constantinopolitan sees are reported to have arisen until after the Council of Chalcedon subjected three dioceses—Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—to the see of Constantinople. Nor did Leo resist this out of rivalry over the episcopal chair, as though it thereby created some prejudice against the Roman bishop; rather, he resisted because this canon injured the privileges of the sees of Alexandria and Antioch, as well as the rights of the metropolitans of those dioceses, which the Council of Nicaea had ordered to be preserved intact.

Why did Quesnellus not offer the more equitable and true reason for Eutyches’s appeal to the Roman bishop? Clearly, Eutyches knew the prerogative of the Roman See, by which it could exercise jurisdiction, when necessary, even over Eastern bishops?] [Col. 0219B]

Finally, Eutyches hoped for Leo’s friendship, having tested his disposition several months earlier. Indeed, after first devising his crime, lest Leo oppose him when it emerged, he had sent Leo a letter in which he cast suspicion of Nestorianism upon certain Catholic men (Letter 19, now 20). Leo, suspecting nothing of the kind, had praised his vigilance and concern.

[Note: Quesnellus mentions one letter of Eutyches to Leo, which he says was written after Eutyches’s condemnation, and he thinks that Leo replied to it in Letter 20. But in the note that he appended in the second edition to Letter 20, he discovered that this reply belonged to another letter that Eutyches had sent to the same pontiff before his condemnation. [Col. 0219C]

Two letters of Eutyches must therefore be distinguished. In the year 447 great disturbances arose against several Eastern bishops who were being accused of suspicion of Nestorianism. Theodoret noted in Letter 3 that these disturbances originated at Constantinople. Eutyches, the Constantinopolitan archimandrite, was their principal author; while attacking those men, he passed over into the opposite error. He branded as Nestorians those who opposed his own error.

Facundus states in Book XII, the final chapter, that Domnus, bishop of Antioch, was the first to resist Eutyches’s impiety after it had been exposed, when he sent a synodical letter to the emperor. See this entire synodical letter inserted in Dissertation 7. It should therefore be said to have been written in the year 448 rather than in 449, as Cardinal Baronius preferred, although Tillemont adduces several arguments for Baronius’s view in note 10 on Theodoret.

Certainly, in the year 448 Eutyches sent his first letter to Leo, complaining that Nestorianism was springing up again. Leo replied to this lost letter in Letter 20, on the Kalends of June in the year 448. Since he did not know by what spirit Eutyches had been led to bring forward that accusation of Nestorianism—for this is what Saint Leo’s remarks in Letter 34 concern—he praised Eutyches’s zeal and concern.

Meanwhile Eutyches was accused by Eusebius of Dorylaeum and condemned by Saint Flavianus in the Constantinopolitan synod on 22 November of that same year, 448. After his condemnation, some mention was made in that synod of his appeal. He lied, however, when he claimed that he had presented a petition of appeal to the Roman pontiff and that it had not been received.

He then sent a second letter to Saint Leo, attaching four documents: Eusebius of Dorylaeum’s petition of accusation; his own petition of appeal, which he claimed had been presented but not received; his profession of faith, together with a protest addressed to the people of Constantinople; and several testimonies, for the most part forged. See the dissertation on Lost Letters, number 26.

We published this second letter of Eutyches among Leo’s letters as Letter 21. At the same time he wrote to Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna. These two letters appear to have been sent to Italy together with the emperor Theodosius’s letter to Leo. The emperor, deceived by Chrysaphius, had undertaken the protection of the heretic.

When the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod were later reread, some stated that Eutyches had also appealed privately to the councils of the bishops of Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica. Perhaps he sent letters to the bishops of those sees.

At about the same time Flavianus reported to Leo, the pontiff, the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, as will be explained more fully in the following annotation.] [Col. 0219D]

The letter of the heresiarch has perished, but we understand what he wrote from Leo’s letters to Theodosius and [p. 449] Flavianus. Eutyches complained that although he held no belief different from the faith, he had nevertheless been accused unjustly; that Eusebius had charged him with heresy but had shown nothing explicitly and clearly for which he could be accused; that when summoned to judgment he had not refused to appear; that although he assented to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, [p. 450] he had been deprived of communion; and that the petition of appeal which he had presented had not been received. [Col. 0220B]

We learn from the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod, which are included in the acts of Chalcedon, how falsely Eutyches wrote these and other things. We shall explain them more fully in the dissertation on his case. [Col. 0220A]

## Year of Christ 449; 10th of Pope Leo; 42nd of Theodosius and 25th of Valentinian, emperors; in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes
## I.
