Saint Leo, informed by Flavian of none of the events taking place at Constantinople, wrote to Theodosius and Flavian lest he either condemn an innocent man or acquit the guilty (Epistle 20, now 23, and 21, now 24):

[Note: We have shown in the Admonition to Epistle 22 that Flavian wrote to Leo shortly after the council at which he condemned Eutyches, toward the end of the year 448, or later, at the beginning of the year 449. Quesnellus, following his own prejudices, inverted the order of Flavian’s letters, so that he presented the second as the first and the first as the second. There we restored each to its proper date and clearly defended the view of Cardinal Baronius, which he had attacked.

To make the history of the events in the case of Eutyches clearer—for Quesnellus has not arranged it with sufficient accuracy—we thought it worthwhile to append here, in this first note, a Brief Chronological-Historical Account of the documents of this year, from which it will easily be possible to assign the proper date to each.

Since Eutyches’ letter, together with the imperial letters favoring him, had been sent with urgency, it reached Rome sooner than Flavian’s letters. Consequently the holy pontiff replied to Theodosius on 18 February of this year, 449, before he had received Flavian’s letter. It was therefore also the case that in Epistle 23 he complained to Flavian that he had reported nothing concerning so important a matter, and that, being cautious rather than deceived, he requested the documents necessary for reaching a judgment. Meanwhile, however, he postponed his reply to Eutyches.

But this heretic, without waiting for the pontiff’s reply, presented the emperor with a petition in which he requested a general council. Through Chrysaphius, his patron, he arranged for Dioscorus of Alexandria also to write to Theodosius that a general synod ought to be convened. This was in fact announced by imperial letters signed on 30 March of this year, 449, to be held at Ephesus on the Kalends of August.

While there was murmuring about the convocation of this council, the two aforementioned letters of Leo arrived at Constantinople: Epistle 23 to Flavian and 24 to Theodosius. On this same occasion Epistle 25 of Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches also arrived, as we inferred in the admonition to that letter.

That this occurred before the synod was formally announced may be gathered from another letter of Flavian. For when he learned from Leo’s letters that Eutyches had written to the pontiff, but that his own earlier letter had not yet been delivered to him, he soon sent another letter, 26, to the same pontiff. In it he attributed so much authority to the Apostolic See that he held it by itself sufficient to put an end to this controversy, so that the council of which there was rumor would no longer be necessary. Such a letter would not have been written after the formal announcement of the council. Hence, with Quesnellus, we believe that this letter of Flavian was composed before 30 March. See his text, no. 9.

To prepare an easy defense for himself at the council already announced, Eutyches obtained a review of the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod, as though they had been abridged and corrupted. But, apart from a few minor matters which did not appear worthy of inclusion in the acts, his defenders could prove nothing to have been falsified. This review, in which mention is made of Leo’s letter received shortly before, took place at a Constantinopolitan assembly on 8 and 13 April.

Meanwhile Leo indicated in Epistle 27, dated 21 May, that he had already received Flavian’s first letter, number 22. He replied briefly to that letter of Flavian, promising to send a fuller response as soon as possible. When he hinted at disturbances stirred up against that same bishop—of which there is no indication in Flavian’s Letter 22—he had evidently detected them sufficiently from other people’s letters.

From the word “we reply” (*rescribimus*)—unless it should be read “we shall reply” (*rescribemus*)—which Leo uses in Epistle 27, it may be inferred that he was at that time occupied in composing the fuller letter which he promised. The gravity of the matter required more prompt application. At the time he wrote this, he had not yet begun to think of sending legates, or he did not expect that they could be prepared so quickly. Hence he promised to send the fuller letter through the man who had brought Flavian’s letters.

But when, because of the difficulty of the circumstances and the imminence of the Ephesian council’s convocation, he judged that legates ought to be sent more urgently, he entrusted them with the fuller letter, 28, to Flavian. Since that letter had been written earlier, the legates are mentioned only at the end, apparently in a later addition, in which no mention of a synod is made.

Together with this celebrated Epistle 28, other letters—to Theodosius, Pulcheria, the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, the Ephesian synod, and Julian of Cos—were dated on the Ides of June and entrusted to the same legates. After they had departed, Flavian’s second letter, number 26, reached Leo. The pontiff replied in Epistle 36 on 20 June, and on the same day sent another letter, Epistle 37, to the emperor. We indicated the reason for that letter in Note I to it (previous volume, col. 811, n. c).

We believe that Saint Flavian sent a third letter to Leo, before the Ephesian Robbery, through the deacon Basil, although it has not reached us. We established this in Note 2 to Epistle 38, in which Saint Leo replied to him on 23 July. Compare below, Note 6 (col. 224, n. e). He sent Flavian new letters on 11 August, expressing his concern to learn what was taking place. See Epistle 39.

On the 8th of that month the Ephesian council, or rather robbery, began. Quesnellus treats it sufficiently in this year, nos. 11 and following. We showed in the admonition to Epistle 54, no. 1, that Saint Flavian died not long after this robbery, while he was being led into exile, namely toward the end of August.

Nor can the Greek Menologia, which assign his feast to 18 February, be set against the authorities we cited there. For, besides being of more recent origin, Flavian’s death certainly cannot be extended to February of the year 450, since Anatolius had been substituted for him before the end of this year, 449. Moreover, his first translation to the City cannot be assigned to February 450, since it occurred after July of that same year. It is therefore necessary that the same Menaea indicate a later translation or feast in the month of February.

This death was concealed for some time, either to allow greater caution in choosing a successor or to prevent a tumult which might have been feared from the clergy and people, who were exceedingly devoted to Flavian. Hence the acclamations of the Constantinopolitan populace on behalf of Flavian, as though he were still alive, against the Ephesian Robbery were entered in the public records around the beginning of October 449. They were transmitted together with letters from the clergy and people of Constantinople to Leo, at approximately the same time when the holy pontiff, likewise unaware of his death, wrote Epistles 50 and 51 to them on the Ides of October. Compare Note 4 (previous volume, col. 866, n. l) to Epistle 59.

At the same time the archimandrites Martin and Faustus also sent letters to him, declaring their steadfastness on behalf of Flavian and the true faith. On this same occasion the Empress Pulcheria probably wrote as well. Thus, having received these three letters together, Saint Leo replied to them on the same day through Epistles 59, 60, and 61, in March of the following year.

The reason Leo wrote Epistles 50 and 51 on the Ides of October was that news of the unhappy outcome of the Ephesian Robbery had been brought to him by the deacon Hilary, who had escaped astonishingly from that same assembly immediately after Saint Flavian’s condemnation.

Hilary reached Rome at the time when a council of bishops was being held on 29 September for Leo’s annual anniversary-day. After hearing what had been wrongly done, the Roman synod appears to have been prolonged until the third day before the Ides of October, so that remedies might be applied. During those days several letters were sent in Leo’s name, or in the name of the synod. See Epistles 44 through 51, one of which is Hilary the deacon’s letter to the Empress Pulcheria.

In Epistle 44, written to the emperor Theodosius, and in Epistle 45 to the same Pulcheria, Leo condemned the Ephesian Robbery and requested that a council be held in Italy. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, who had been deposed in that same robbery, lodged an appeal with the same pontiff in Epistle 52.

When Flavian’s death was subsequently made public and someone had to be substituted for him, the emperor instructed the clergy of the Constantinopolitan Church to propose to him certain men more suitable for governing, from among whom he himself would choose the better candidate.

When they disagreed among themselves—perhaps because some wanted a man attached to Flavian while others wanted such a man excluded—the same emperor ordered that a bishop be chosen from among the clergy of other Churches who were staying in Constantinople on other business.

Thus, apparently by the vote of all, Anatolius, a presbyter of the Alexandrian Church who was conducting the affairs of his Church in the imperial city, was elected and ordained in a synod by Dioscorus of Alexandria himself.

Anatolius immediately wrote to Saint Leo concerning his ordination; we have given a notable fragment of it in Epistle 53. His ordainers, the emperor Theodosius and the Empress Pulcheria, also wrote to the same pontiff concerning this ordination.

We proved in the admonition to Epistle 53 that these events occurred toward the end of this year, 449. Meanwhile Saint Leo sent new letters to the emperor on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, again insisting that a council be convened in Italy. These letters, published with a corrupted chronological notation, created several difficulties. But once the month had been corrected from our excellent Regensburg manuscript, no difficulty remained. See Epistle 54.

Although no imperial letters received by Leo are mentioned here, we nevertheless have no doubt that Leo’s letter was a reply to Theodosius’ letter which, as we showed in the dissertation On Lost Letters, no. 38, Theodosius had sent to him after the Ephesian Robbery.]

It is not difficult to say why Flavian did not write—whether he believed that Eutyches would submit to the judgment, or that the case had been conducted according to the Church’s canon in the council and that the monk of his own diocese had been lawfully condemned and was not to be heard elsewhere.

Baronius believes that Flavian’s letters were either intercepted or delayed by Eutyches. But it is certain from Flavian’s very letter, whose beginning is “Piety,” etc., that Flavian had written nothing at all:

“He was accused,” he says, “that is, Eutyches, by the most reverend Eusebius; and when he appeared before the holy council and exposed his own sect by his own voice, and was found alien from the right faith, we condemned him, as all the proceedings concerning him will show—proceedings which we have sent with this letter of ours” (Epistle now 26).

You see that Leo had received from Flavian no letter or acts of the synod before this letter. A little later he says:

“But after these events had taken place, a letter from Your Holiness was delivered to us by Count Pansophius, through which we learned that the same Eutyches had sent you petitions full of every kind of deceit and cunning” (ibid.).

[Note: Since the preceding note makes clear that Flavian had reported to Leo this matter concerning the faith before being prompted by the pontiff’s letters, it is manifestly false that the statements placed here below are correct.]

From these words it is equally clear that Flavian had not previously thought of writing to Leo about the matter, but did so only after learning that the pontiff, deceived by Eutyches’ wicked stratagems, had formed a false opinion concerning the Constantinopolitan judgment.

Indeed, so long as this contamination remained confined within the boundaries of the Constantinopolitan Church, there was no need for Flavian to seek the assistance of his colleagues. For the bishop knew that the whole of Catholic truth had been entrusted in its entirety by Christ the Lord to all bishops, and that each was bound to defend it according to his ability and to suppress errors rising against it as the ordinary judge within that portion of the Church which he had received.

But when, informed by Leo, he learned that the arch-heretic had spread his letters throughout the West, was scattering his poison, and that the powers of the world were preparing snares against Catholic doctrine, then he thought it his duty to approach the Roman pontiff. In this way the pontiff could be informed about the whole matter, as was owed to the head of the Church, and could diligently use the favor he enjoyed with the emperor to prevent the schemes of the heretics from spreading widely and to prevent the Church from being disturbed by the convocation of a council, in which there was rightly reason to fear that wicked men would possess great influence.

In any case, Leo, not yet informed of what had been done concerning Eutyches, wrote to the emperor concerning the judgments of heretics and laid down the following rule:

No judgment should be pronounced unless the matter has been carefully examined. “It is necessary,” he says (Epistle 21, now 24), “that there no longer be room for underhanded proceedings; but first we must be informed concerning the matters on which he is thought to be accused, so that judgment may be fittingly rendered on the basis of matters thoroughly known.”

[Note: Leo’s words refer to the accusation presented by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, in which the holy pontiff desired the meaning of the heresy he had detected in Eutyches to be set out more clearly, so that he himself could judge the matter. Leo therefore does not here establish—this is the sense governed by the word which Quesnellus prefixed to the passage—that a presbyter must not be branded with the mark of heresy unless the sense in which he had erred had been clearly explained.]

“A presbyter must not be branded with the mark of heresy unless the sense in which he has erred has been clearly explained. But although he was bringing against the presbyter the charge of heresy, he did not expressly state what meaning he had accused him of holding” (ibid.).

[Note: Leo’s complete words concern Eutyches’ petition, in which Eutyches asserted that, while observing the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, he had been unjustly accused of differing in faith. These are not Leo’s words establishing that a man whose mind had departed from the faith was not rightly reproved if he openly professed what had been decreed at Nicaea. Leo merely thought that judgment should be deferred concerning Eutyches’ protestation, since he had nothing certain before him and, on the contrary, had read a similar profession in the petition of Eutyches’ accuser. He therefore suspended judgment until more certain documents could be transmitted. When he received those documents, he did not hesitate to condemn Eutyches for heresy, even though Eutyches repeatedly professed that he held and followed the decrees of Nicaea.]

“It is not right to accuse as having a mind alienated from the faith a man who openly professes what has been decreed in the Nicene statutes”—namely, “asserting that, while observing the constitutions of the Council of Nicaea, he had been unjustly accused of differing in faith” (ibid.).

The former statement was addressed to Theodosius, the latter to Flavian.

Judgments must not be carried out hastily but slowly, especially when the matter concerns the severing of communion. One must labor not so much to strike down the error as to correct the person in error; nor should the mind be so indulged under the appearance of defending the truth that there is no room left for charity. For, he says (Epistle 20, now 23), “in such cases it is especially fitting to ensure that, without the clamor of disputes, charity is preserved and truth defended.”

## III.

Flavian replied to Leo and sent him, together with his letter, the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod concerning the case of Eutyches. But the letter reached Leo only after a delay.

When Flavian heard nothing concerning the letter, he sent another in which he mentioned the earlier letter and the acts which he had sent at the same time.

[Note: In Epistle 22, which we have shown to be the first, no mention is made of an earlier letter. Quesnellus, who insists that this letter itself was the second, had an interest in discovering in it a reference to a previous letter. For this purpose he used the words of the ancient version, as they appeared in the Leonine editions: “Whatever we have done previously, we have sent to Your Beatitude letters in which we explained,” and so forth.

But since these words do not agree with the Greek original, the Roman editors of the Councils corrected the passage here according to the Greek text as follows: “Concerning what we did regarding him some time ago, we have sent letters to Your Beatitude in which we explained,” and so forth. In this reading *dudum* (“some time ago”) was substituted for *olim* (“formerly”). The particle refers not to a letter written previously but to the earlier proceedings against Eutyches.

The Greek word ἀπεστείλαμεν, rendered in Latin as *misimus* (“we have sent”), has here been shown to refer not to earlier matters but to the very letters which Flavian was writing. See Note 17 (previous volume, col. 727, n. b) to Epistle 22, where we gave other examples of this meaning.]

Baronius, deceived by the disorderly sequence of the manuscripts, believed that the letter written second had been written first; in fact, it occupied the first place in the published manuscripts up to the present time.

But the contrary is proved by the sequence of the letter itself, which mentions an earlier letter sent together with the acts of the Constantinopolitan council. It is further proved by Epistle 34, now 38, written to Flavian on 23 July, where Leo testifies that he had not received that other letter until his legates had already departed for the East.

The legates had not yet left the city on 17 June, as Epistles 32 and 34, now 36 and 38, to Flavian demonstrate. When these letters are compared, it clearly appears that between the writing of the one and the other the legates sent to the synod had set out on their journey.

## IV.

From both letters we recognize Flavian’s piety and the vigilance of a pastor who carefully looks after his Church.

He writes how properly and according to the canon he had taken action against Eutyches, who had not been condemned without the case having been brought; then he recalls Eutyches’ errors.

Flavian did not write this because he was placing his own authority in opposition to Eutyches, but to inform the Roman pontiff of what had occurred, so that the pontiff and the bishops under him might take care that heresy did not flourish in those regions, and so that Leo might inform Theodosius what errors and disturbances the wickedness of a single monk was introducing into the world.

“But lest by saying too much,” Flavian says, “I make the letter long, formerly we sent to Your Beatitude letters concerning whatever we had done. In these letters we explained that he had been stripped of the presbyterate, because he had been caught in this manner; and we ordered that he have no dealings with the monasteries, and we excluded him from our communion. Therefore, when Your Holiness has learned what was done concerning him, may you deign to make his impiety known to all the bishops living under Your Beatitude, lest some, being unaware of what he believes, should speak with him as though he were orthodox, either by letter or by some form of association” (Epistle 22, now 27, of Flavian to Saint Leo, chap. 4).

## V.

At this point Cardinal Baronius admonishes the reader (Annals, year 449, no. 5) to observe that, according to ancient custom, Flavian and Eutyches, disputing with one another, unquestionably confessed the Roman pontiff to be the lawful and principal judge of ecclesiastical controversies, to whom both plaintiff and defendant voluntarily hastened to prosecute their rights.

I bow to the dignity of the pontiff with greater reverence than anyone else; but since Leo himself acknowledges that all the bishops of the Church share a common dignity with the Roman pontiff—

[Note: Leo admitted a common dignity of episcopal honor among bishops and the Roman pontiff. At the same time, however, he taught that the general hierarchical order is not uniform, since authorities are distinguished according to the diversity of hierarchical rank. The Roman pontiff presides over all bishops by a primacy which is not merely one of honor but of principal jurisdiction, as all Catholics profess. See what we observed on this point in Epistle 14, Note 52 (previous volume, col. 675, n. e).

Moreover, we shall prove in the observations on Dissertation 6 that Eutyches referred this case to the Roman pontiff as the principal judge of controversies by a petition of appeal, and that, when Flavian learned of this, he too requested the same judgment in his second letter. From those observations it will become clear how empty are the arguments here advanced against Baronius.]

—far be it from me to wish that what I venerate in one should be trampled upon in the others.

We willingly acknowledge the Roman pontiff as a legitimate judge and, when compared with individual bishops, as the principal judge of ecclesiastical controversies. But who could therefore tolerate Flavian—whom the prerogative of his see, his singular holiness, and his steadfastness in the faith, persevering even to martyrdom, ought to have commended so greatly—being made equal and joined in judgment with a rebellious, ignorant, obscure, and worthless monk; a deposed presbyter being compared with the bishop of his own and so eminent a see; the judge with the defendant; and both of them being brought before Leo as though they were quarreling over a common inheritance and fighting over an uncertain outcome?

Far be such an injury from the most sacred assembly of bishops.

Flavian was not the plaintiff, most illustrious cardinal, but the judge. He did not bring Eutyches forward to be condemned, but presented him as already condemned by himself. Nor did he request a new judgment from Leo. Rather, he asked that the sentence he had pronounced be made known, through the care of the Roman pontiff, to his colleagues in the West, so that all might labor on behalf of the common cause of the faith with common care, common effort, and common concern.

## VI.

After receiving Flavian’s letters, Leo promised his assistance and support against Eutyches. Through the distinguished man Rhodanus he sent a letter, which we now publish for the first time from Cardinal Grimani’s manuscript. This was followed by another letter to Theodosius (Epistle 23, now 54), in which he professes adherence to the Nicene faith, condemns the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches, and requests that a synod be convened within Italy.

In that letter he promises a fuller letter through Flavian’s messenger. That famous letter to Flavian was indeed written (Epistle 24, now 28), the divine work of the Great Leo, praised by Chalcedon, approved by the Fathers, and preserved by the Church as the standard for explaining the faith concerning Christ’s incarnation, so that by it, as by a touchstone, genuine and adulterated faith might be tested.

Pope Gelasius strikes with anathema anyone who removes even a single point from it:

“We approve the letter of the blessed Pope Leo, addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone should contest it even to a single iota [variant: should dispute it], and should not receive it in its entirety with reverence, let him be anathema” (Roman Council on Apocryphal Books).

Among writers both of that period and of later times its memory is illustrious.

The *Viridarium*, or, as it is commonly called, the *Spiritual Meadow*—whether it is the work of John Moschus or of Sophronius of Jerusalem makes no difference; in any case it is an ancient work, received by the Seventh Synod, Act 4, by Photius, and by others—relates that Leo’s letter was divinely approved.

The abbot Mennas, father of that same monastery, also told us that he had heard the same abbot, Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, say:

“When I had gone to Constantinople, I enjoyed the companionship of the lord Gregory, Roman archdeacon and an extraordinary man. He told me about the most holy and blessed Leo, Roman pontiff, saying that it was written in the Roman Church that, when he had written a letter to Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against the impious Eutyches and Nestorius, he placed it upon the tomb of the chief of the apostles, Peter. He devoted himself to prayers, vigils, and fasts, and prayed to that supreme apostle, saying: ‘If, as a human being, I have written anything incorrectly or with insufficient caution, you, to whom this see and Church have been entrusted by our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, correct it.’

“After four days [or: after forty days] the apostle appeared to him and said: ‘I have read it and corrected it.’ Then, taking the letter from the tomb of blessed Peter, he opened it and found it corrected by the apostolic hand” (*Spiritual Meadow*, chap. 147; this chapter survives only in Latin).

But, as the most eminent Cardinal Baronius wisely writes, it is better to hear Peter’s judgment than Peter’s vision:

“We have a more certain prophetic word than any vision.”

For that letter derives a stronger defense of the faith from the divine Scriptures, the traditions of the holy Church, the common agreement of the holy Fathers, and the public declaration and proclamation of the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon than from the vision just recounted.

[Note: We demonstrated the fame of this letter at greater length in the admonition to Epistle 28. Even before it was published, Flavian believed that, by the authority of the Apostolic See, it would by itself suffice to bring the entire controversy to an end, so that a general council would no longer be necessary. Saint Peter Chrysologus likewise urged Eutyches in Epistle 25 to be satisfied with it, because he held it certain that Peter lives and teaches in his successors to those who seek the truth.

After it had been published, even before the Council of Chalcedon was convened, the whole Church received it. All the Catholic bishops subscribed to it—not in order to add force or authority to it, but to prove themselves Catholic and to avoid being regarded as heretics if they refused. See more on this in the same admonition.

For the comparisons and confirmations of the doctrine defined by Leo below, compare what will be said in Note 22 (below, col. 263, n. a) concerning the year 451.]

The Council approved this letter in its fifth session:

“Since it agrees with the confession of that great Peter, and exists as a kind of common pillar against those who think perversely.”

Formerly this entire letter was read publicly in the Roman Church during Advent, as Baronius notes from a Roman manuscript. From a manuscript of the Royal Library we learned that the same practice was once followed in the Churches of Gaul.

459

Meanwhile, while Leo and Flavian were jointly working for the good of the Church, Eutyches stirred up new disturbances.

[Note: These new disturbances were raised by Eutyches in April, before the holy pontiff wrote the dogmatic Epistle 28. More concerning these disturbances is found in Note I above, col. 220, n. c.]

A desire to overturn the decrees of the Constantinopolitan synod arose (Baronius, Annals, year 449, no. 39). For this reason he presented supplications to the emperor, alleging that the acts of the synod had been abridged and falsified.

Theodosius, deceived by the speeches of the eunuch Chrysaphius, ordered the acts to be reviewed and everything to be examined with exactness, to determine whether anything omitted, mutilated, or corrupted could be found.

For this reason he ordered the same bishops who had held the synod in the preceding year to assemble again. He placed Bishop Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia over them, removing Flavian of Constantinople, who was deprived of his right and prerogative of sitting.

Cardinal Baronius calls it the Second Constantinopolitan Council, although it scarcely deserves that name. I would call it an appendix to the synod held at Constantinople in the preceding year, or a prelude to the ecumenical council which we read had been announced for the Kalends of August.

Thus, at the beginning of April, the assembly was held. The acts were brought forward for examination; nothing corrupted or altered was found; and everyone approved that everything had been written down just as it had occurred.

Then the representatives of Eutyches, deceived by a vain hope—

[Note: Namely, the appeal which Eutyches claimed to have lodged at the earlier synod.]

—brought forward an appeal to the Apostolic See.

The reverend deacon Constantine said:

“While the sentence was being read, Eutyches appealed to the holy council of the most holy Roman, Alexandrian, Jerusalemite, and Thessalonian bishops; and they complained that these things were not contained in the acts.”

Patritius Florentius confirmed this. He said that, while the council was being dissolved, amid the noise of those rising, he had heard Eutyches speak to him about an appeal to the Roman council, and that this had been reported to Flavian as he was leaving.

Hence Bishop Basil said:

“These matters too were not inserted in the acts.”

The magnificent Patritius said:

“When a disturbance had occurred and the assembly had been dissolved, he spoke to me quietly, appealing to the Roman, Egyptian, and Jerusalem council. And I, judging it improper that this should remain hidden from that most holy and reverend archbishop Flavian, went away and told him:

“‘The most reverend Bishop Basil said: “I say this truthfully: while the assembly itself was still sitting and the holy synod was proposing that this man should say that there are two inseparable and unconfused natures in the one Lord, and this after the union, I know that the religious archimandrite Eutyches said: ‘If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I shall say this very thing.’ But he did not say it as an appellant; he said: ‘I have not dared to say it because of the Fathers.’”’”

When the Fathers were asked about the appeal, they all replied that they had heard nothing.

[Note: We established Eutyches’ appeal to the Roman pontiff, which Quesnellus attempted to undermine on two grounds in Dissertation 6, in our observations on that same dissertation. There we also discussed the refuge taken by a man conducting a desperate case in appealing to various bishops and different synods, so as to spin out longer delays and, if possible, arrange somewhere for Flavian’s sentence to be rescinded.]

Eutyches appealed to the Roman, Alexandrian, and Jerusalem councils, believing—as circumstances then stood—that the authority of bishops of the principal sees, or a more numerous synod, could invalidate the sentence of another.

There is silence concerning Antioch, because the bishops of that diocese were suspected of Nestorianism.

## VIII.

When Eutyches understood that by this route every avenue had been closed to him, he turned elsewhere—namely, to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. Dioscorus’s bold and fierce temperament, his private hatred of Flavian, his rivalry and jealousy concerning the sees, and the power of Chrysaphius easily drove him into Eutyches’ camp. They conspired together for the destruction of Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum.

Accordingly, Dioscorus first wrote to the emperor and requested another synod. The emperor approved the petition and summoned it to Ephesus for the Kalends of August; everything had been arranged according to plan through the agency of Chrysaphius. By imperial letter Dioscorus was ordered to preside over the council.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] This refers to another letter of the emperor Theodosius, issued at the very time of the council to Dioscorus of Alexandria. In it, primacy in this affair appears to have been granted to Dioscorus because the emperor, deceived by the schemes of Eutyches and having taken up his defense, believed that the man whom he had recognized as Eutyches’ defender should preside over the council—or, more accurately, over the Ephesian robbery. He also added as Dioscorus’s companions Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, and Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, because he knew that they would agree with Dioscorus. Dioscorus’s usurped primacy is censured by Saint Prosper in the complete Chronicle, by Rusticus the deacon in his note on this imperial letter, and by Victor of Tunnuna in his Chronicle. Liberatus likewise reports in his *Breviary* that the legates of the pontiff resisted this primacy of Dioscorus; but what could they do against force? Saint Leo, plainly disapproving of it in Letter 89 to Marcian, wished his own legate to preside at Chalcedon. See note 9 (previous volume, col. 931, n. c) on that same letter, where we also saw that Lucentius charged Dioscorus himself with this usurpation of primacy at Chalcedon.]

He was instructed to select for the synod ten metropolitans from his own diocese and ten other bishops from elsewhere, men distinguished above all for holiness and learning. Theodoret was expressly rejected, because he had written against the anathemas of Saint Cyril of Alexandria—or rather because he was hostile to Dioscorus and openly opposed to Eutychian doctrine.

I think that the synod had been contemplated earlier, even before the Constantinopolitan assembly. For when the question was being considered whether Eutyches’ representatives should be admitted—Eutyches, who was accused of a crime and whose own presence the bishops therefore wished to secure—Bishop Meliphtongus, while giving his opinion on the matter, wanted the accused to be present, though he held that he could nevertheless be heard through representatives if that was the emperor’s wish. The matter, he said, ought to be submitted to examination again, since the emperor had ordered a universal synod to be held at which the more important cases were to be decided:

> Εἰ καὶ μάλιστα οἰκουμένικη ἐκελεύσθη, γενέσται σύνοδος, καὶ περύλανται τὰ καιριώτερα τὴν ὧν πραγμάτων ἐν ἐκείνη τῇ σύνοδῳ

that is:

> “Especially because he ordered a universal synod to be held, and [the more important matters concerning these affairs] must be reserved for that council.”

[Note: [Col. 0228D] Bishop Meliphtongus said this in order to remove from the Constantinopolitan assembly the case which, by the emperor’s command, had been referred to a universal synod—not in order to claim that major cases could be decided nowhere except in a general council.]

## IX.

Meliphtongus was speaking of the synod already summoned on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Indeed, Flavian, writing to Saint Leo immediately after receiving his first letters, testifies that rumors of the calling of a council had already been spread.

Moreover, Flavian’s letter appears to have been sent before the Constantinopolitan assembly of April: first, because Bishop Seleucus stated at that assembly that Leo’s letters had arrived before it and that Flavian had immediately replied to them; second, because Flavian speaks to Leo only of the earlier assembly and would certainly not have been silent about the second if it had already been convened; third, because Leo replied to Flavian’s letter on 21 May, not immediately upon receiving it, but after waiting for an opportunity:

> “We indicate that your Belovedness’s letters reached us as soon as we found the opportunity presented by the arrival of our son Rodanus.”

From this one may readily conclude that Flavian’s letter had been written scarcely before the Kalends of April.

It is therefore clear that no error—of the kind Baronio thinks occurred—crept into the date on which Theodosius’s letters to Dioscorus were issued, namely the third day before the Kalends of April. On the contrary, Leo had received Theodosius’s letters concerning the convocation of the synod on the third day before the Ides of May, and they must have been sent a full month earlier, as Leo testifies in writing to Pulcheria Augusta (Letter 27, now 31, chap. 4).

There is no doubt, however, that what had initially been arranged by the emperor was later altered. For the acts of the Ephesian pseudo-synod clearly show that at first only a few bishops were summoned and that later, after a change of plan, more were called: more than one hundred are said to have been present. Permission was therefore granted not only to the Egyptians but also to the Easterners to come to the council.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Quesnellus wrote this because he supposed that the imperial letter summoning the council to be held at Ephesus on 30 March had been addressed to Dioscorus alone, as its published address indicates. Yet on the same day a letter of like tenor was sent to other bishops as well, as is noted after the recital of these same letters in Act 1 of the Ephesian acts inserted into those of Chalcedon (Venice edition, vol. IV of the *Councils*, col. 874): “Letters of the same tenor were also written to the other most reverend bishops, that they should assemble at the synod.” Julius, Leo’s legate, also disclosed that letters of similar—not identical—tenor had been sent to Leo; their slight verbal differences indicate the particular reverence due to the Roman see, as we explained in note 29 (previous volume, col. 793, n. j) on Letter 31. Thus Quesnellus’s subsequent remarks about a change in the emperor’s intention rest on a false hypothesis, since all the bishops were summoned to the council on the same day. Dioscorus’s name appears in the published letter because, controlling everything at the Ephesian robbery at his own discretion, he inserted into the acts the letter addressed to himself.]

The archimandrites and monks of Constantinople were not admitted, because they had rejected Eutyches. One man, Barsumas, an archimandrite from Syria, attended in the name of all; he was notorious for crime and treachery and was a fierce champion of Eutychian impiety.

Later Pope Leo himself was summoned, as is evident from his letters (Letter 27, now 31, chap. 4, and Letter 33, now 37). He too was asked to attend the synod and replied that it was not customary for the bishop of Rome to attend councils outside Rome; nor were these times, with the Hun enemy pressing upon them, such that he could abandon the city; nor was a synod necessary for the defense of the faith, since the faith was so evident. Nevertheless, if a council had to be considered, it would be more expedient for it to be convened in the regions of Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] These remarks about convening a synod in Italy are not found in the letters cited in the margin at 31 and 37, but in Letter 54. Because of an erroneous chronological notation, that letter was thought to belong to the Ephesian synod, whereas according to our correction it belongs later, after the Ephesian robbery. In order to seek a remedy for that robbery, Leo asked Theodosius that a free synod be convened in Italy.]

Leo could not obtain this. Nevertheless, lest he appear to be failing the faith, he would send men to act in his place, who would be sufficient for so manifest a case. Thus Leo sent as legates Julius, bishop of Puteoli; Renatus, priest of the title of Saint Clement; Hilarus, deacon; and Dulcitius, notary.

Had P. Christianus Lupus not disdained to read these matters, he would easily have extricated himself from the difficulties which he could not otherwise resolve except by the words “I do not know.” In his notes on chapter 44 of the *Ephesian Monuments*, while preparing whose edition he died, p. 262, while discussing the sacred command of Theodosius for the convocation of the Second Ephesian Synod, he writes:

> “It was issued in the consulship of Posthumianus and Zeno, in the same year in which Saint Leo wrote his letters in reply to Eutyches and in which Saint Flavian held his synod against that same man. And indeed, on the third day before the Kalends of April. But this letter was issued on the Kalends of June, whereas that synod began on the sixth day before the Ides of November. Moreover, the Ephesian council was summoned to reopen the judgment of that synod concerning Eutyches. Hence the question arises how its summons could have preceded its celebration by half a year. Furthermore, the Ephesian robbery is said to have taken place in the same year, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, three months before Saint Flavian’s synod. The same question arises concerning the rescript of the Great Leo. I answer that there is an error. I know no other answer.”

But he could have learned something else. First, Leo’s letter to Eutyches, issued on the Kalends of June in the year 448, cannot in any way belong to Flavian’s judgment, whether the first or the second, since it preceded the first by almost seven months. It belongs rather to Domnus’s synod. After the Antiochene Domnus had warned Theodosius about the renewed Apollinarian heresy propagated by Eutyches, Eutyches in turn thought that Leo should be warned by letter about what he falsely alleged to be the re-emerging error of Nestorius among Domnus and the other Easterners, although he expressly named neither Domnus nor anyone else.

I had already pointed this out both in the present place and in my note on Leo’s letter to Eutyches.

Second, since Father Lupus chose to assign the Ephesian pseudo-synod—which certainly took place on the sixth day before the Ides of August in the year 449—to the year 448, when Posthumianus and Zeno held the consulship, when Leo wrote to Eutyches on the Kalends of June, and when Flavian pronounced judgment on the same man, it is not surprising that he finds the Ephesian synod three months earlier than Flavian’s Constantinopolitan synod, when in fact it was nine months later.

Third, he asserts that Theodosius’s decree for convening the Ephesian synod was issued during the consulship of Posthumianus and Zeno, following the error of the Latin edition, although it was written after their consulship, as the Greek sources themselves and the sequence of events indicate.

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Add also the ancient Latin manuscripts, in which, as Baluzius observes (vol. IV of the *Councils*, col. 873, note a), one reads *P. C. Zenonis et Posthumiani*. The sigla *P. C.*—*post consulatum*—indicate that the document was issued after the consulship.]

## X.

Saint Leo sent several letters at the same time through his legates to the East, and in them he mentions the legates. They were issued on the same day, namely the Ides of June.

Among them was that highly celebrated letter to Flavian (Letter 24, now 28); others were addressed to the emperor Theodosius (Letter 26, now 29), to Pulcheria Augusta, to Julian, bishop of Cos (Letter 27, now 31, and Letter 30), to Faustus and Martin, archimandrites of Constantinople (Letters 25 and 31, now 35 and 34), and to the bishops of the Ephesian synod (Letter 28, now 32). In the latter he indicates that he had written more fully to Flavian (Letter 29, now 33) concerning his own judgment.

There are also two other letters to Julian of Cos and Pulcheria, issued on the same day as the preceding ones. Why two letters were sent simultaneously on the same day to the same persons, I cannot state with certainty: perhaps because of a messenger who had preceded the legates, or perhaps because Leo feared that the legates might be prevented from approaching the Augusta—which in fact happened, as is sufficiently clear from Letter 41, now 45.

For the other letter to Pulcheria briefly summarizes what had been written through the legates. We also learn from the shorter letter to Flavian (Letter 32, now 36), which Leo sent again on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, that the legates had been detained in Rome for some time:

> “You are to be more fully informed through what they will themselves bring in writing.”

And again:

> “I indicate that those whom it pleased us to appoint for this matter will follow.”

[Note: [Col. 0230D] We have seen from the corrected reading of the shorter Letter 36 to Flavian, sent on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, that the legates had not been detained but had already departed for the East when Leo wrote it.]

## XI.

The day appointed for the council was now approaching when the emperor wrote to Elpidius. He ordered him to attend the council with armed soldiers for the peace and security of the synod, and commanded that disturbers of concord be thrown into chains.

These measures appeared honorable in form, but in reality they were designed to overthrow the faith and crush the defenders of Catholic doctrine. The bishops who had previously condemned Eutyches were forbidden to give their judgment; indeed, they were ordered to await a judgment concerning their own judgment against Eutyches.

The emperor also sent letters to the proconsul of the province, to the magistrates, and to the army commanders, so that they might enforce the decrees of the council. Finally, he wrote to the synod itself, addressing Flavian as a turbulent man who was attempting innovations in religion, but addressing Eutyches honorably as a good man steadfast in Catholic truth.

With matters arranged in this way, a synod was held by approximately one hundred and thirty bishops. Among them were especially prominent Domnus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Flavian of Constantinople, and Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Flavian was given a place after the bishop of Jerusalem. Eusebius of Dorylaeum was admitted not as a judge but as an accused party.

Dioscorus presided. The legates of Saint Leo excused his absence on the grounds and for the reasons he had given. When they prepared to have his letters read, especially the letter to Flavian, Dioscorus deceived them. Time was consumed in reading other matters, and the question of the faith was not taken up immediately.

Eutyches was brought in and at once began to wash away the stain of heresy and to present a confession of faith. It was read publicly, full of falsehood and pretense and confused by an elaborate ambiguity of words. His condemnation was then reconsidered.

The legates intervened in vain and vainly implored that Leo’s letters be read. Several writings of Saint Cyril were read. While the reading was taking place, Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, said in a voice loud enough for everyone to hear that it was not the teaching of Saint Cyril and Saint Athanasius that two natures should be confessed in Christ.

> Ού δου, τοιγαρονύ νοεῖν φύσους, αλλὰ μίαν φύσιν τοῦ λόγον σεκσακωμὲνην.

“That is why,” he said, “one must not understand two natures, but one nature of the Word made flesh.”

He failed to understand the intention of those Fathers, who sometimes used *physis*—φύσις, “nature”—indiscriminately for hypostasis and person.

The remaining bishops, either terrified by threats or corrupted by promises, did not so much as open their mouths, much less betray the faith of the Church by a nod, by silence, or by their voices. Thus Eutyches, appearing to triumph, was accepted by all: he was declared innocent and released from the bond of excommunication.

## XII.

Nor did Dioscorus’s madness stop there. It is shameful to relate: not only was Eutyches proclaimed innocent, but Flavian, that defender of the faith and pillar of religion, was condemned together with Eusebius of Dorylaeum. Both were removed from their office and see as torches of sedition and corrupters of the faith of Nicaea.

Thus, as our Leo says (Letter 43, now 47, chap. 1):

> “Ancient rivalries and private hatreds rage against Flavian.”

Rivalries arose because of the increasing splendor of the see of Constantinople; private hatreds were those which Chrysaphius exercised against the holy bishop.

When the bishop of Iconium approached Dioscorus’s feet in Flavian’s favor and attempted to break his anger, he not only met with rejection, but Dioscorus, now raging, summoned the soldiers who were at the doors. Immediately many of them, in great numbers and with even greater tumult, filled the place: their faces were threatening, and they brandished chains with savage intent.

Then all the bishops began to tremble and were struck with terror and fear, and they subscribed to Flavian’s condemnation. Many bishops were proscribed and condemned with him, among them Ibas, bishop of Edessa; Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus; and, last of all, Domnus of Antioch. Anyone who refused to swear allegiance to the words of the heretic was punished by deposition.

As Liberatus writes concerning the acts of this synod, the bishops, out of fear, subscribed to Eutyches’ absolution and to the deposition of the orthodox bishops who did not accept the heresy. and how they opposed all its proceedings—or, as I think the text should be read, [the deposition] of those who in whatever way opposed all its proceedings.

## XIII.

When Flavian heard the judgment, he lodged an appeal. In Liberatus’s *Breviary*, a written appeal is said to have been immediately delivered by Flavian to the legates of the apostolic see; there will be another occasion to discuss it.

Then the heretics began to rage and became inflamed beyond measure. They struck Flavian and treated the great pontiff in an unworthy manner, to such an extent that he breathed out his soul under the violence of their blows and wounds and thus met death as a martyr for the faith.

There are, however, various reports concerning his death. Prosper says that Saint Flavian, while in the hands of those who were leading him into exile, passed to Christ in a glorious end. Nicephorus reports that he died three days later.

In Marcellinus Comes and in the Greek *Menologion* I find that he was banished to Epypa in Lydia and there, overcome by weariness, grief, and tortures, died. The *Short Account of the History of the Eutychianists* gives a similar account:

> “Flavian is led into exile and died at Epypa, which is a city of Lydia, whether death overtook him or was inflicted upon him.”

The *Synodical Book*, chapter 85, says that he was killed by kicks. The acts of the Council of Chalcedon accuse the monk Barsumas of being the author of the slaughter. Evagrius, in Book XI, chapter 11 of his *History*, on the testimony of Eusebius of Dorylaeum, attributes his death to Dioscorus; he is said to have been attacked by Dioscorus with kicks, expelled from the Church, and killed.

No one doubts that he was brutally mistreated at Dioscorus’s instigation. At the Council of Chalcedon many called Dioscorus the striker and murderer of Flavian and another Cain.

In such desperate circumstances, however, the legates of the apostolic see did not lose courage. They firmly resisted the heretics’ efforts against Flavian’s condemnation and publicly protested everything that had been done.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] We know that the legate Hilarus escaped. What happened to Julius of Puteoli and Dulcitius, the notary of the apostolic see, is unknown. Renatus the priest, however, was overtaken by death on the island of Delos before the synod itself, as is clear from the *Short Account of the History of the Eutychianists* (vol. V of the *Councils*, col. 173).]

Therefore, after the public faith had been violated, they were placed in custody. Hilarus alone escaped by flight and, after various wanderings and vicissitudes, eventually sailed to Rome. Thus the Ephesian pseudo-synod was completed as an outright robbery.

## XIV.

Meanwhile Leo was deeply troubled by concern for the synod. He anxiously awaited news and letters from Flavian and pondered what the factious monk and the eunuch, powerful through favor and influence, might do.

In addition, he wrote to Flavian (Letter 35, now 39) and complained of his silence. But when he learned from the deacon Hilarus how matters stood, he did not surrender so completely to grief that he neglected a remedy. He therefore immediately convened a council.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Both Leo and the Fathers thought that this should be done in order to provide a remedy for the Ephesian robbery amid the extremely difficult circumstances of the time. To move Theodosius’s mind more easily, the holy pontiff represented the petition and tears of all the bishops.]

The Fathers decided that Leo should write to Theodosius and place before his eyes the miserable condition of the Church: the wounds religion had received from the Ephesian robbery; the danger in which the Catholic faith stood if Dioscorus and Eutyches were allowed to do and decree everything according to their own will.

If he wished to provide a remedy for this evil, a general synod had to be convened. This was the desire of all the bishops of those regions, and no other remedy could be sought after everything had been handled by force at Ephesus, after the protest of the legates, and after Flavian’s appeal, in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. At that time, the canons of Sardica were cited in this connection.

Leo himself explains the appeal as an appeal to the synod of the bishops of those regions, or of the West, over which the Roman pontiff himself presides.

> “All the priests of the churches of our party, all of them, with sighs and tears, entreat your Mildness that, since our own men have faithfully protested and since Bishop Flavian has submitted a written appeal to them, you order a general synod to be held within Italy. Let it either remove or mitigate every offense, so that nothing further may remain doubtful in the faith or divided in charity, with the bishops of the Eastern provinces certainly attending . . .”

And below:

> “That this must necessarily be requested after an appeal has been lodged is demonstrated by the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world.”

(Letters 39 and 49, now 43 and 44.)

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Here Quesnellus added a note referring readers to Dissertation 8 on Flavian’s appeal. There he works at length to evade the appeal which Flavian lodged to the Roman pontiff and to show that it was lodged instead with a synod of Western bishops. Our observations appended to that dissertation, however, will, as we trust, scatter all his efforts. There also the matters added here from the Council of Sardica and the letter of Galla Placidia will be explained.]

Leo’s reasoning—that he derives from the canons of Sardica the necessity of a synod—would be wholly futile unless he had been convinced that the synod intended that whoever wished should understand, under the Roman pontiff, a synod of the Westerners, without of course excluding the Easterners from it.

Galla Placidia, writing to Theodosius about this matter, explains Flavian’s appeal in the same way:

> Διά τὸ λίβελλον στεῖλαι πρὸς τὸν ἀποστολικὸν θρόνον, καὶ πρὸς πάντας τοὺς ἐπισκόπους τῶν μερῶν τούτων

that is:

> “Because he sent a written appeal to the apostolic see and to all the bishops of these regions.”

At that time, and on the same day, Leo sent many letters to the East: to Pulcheria (Letter 41, now 45), in the name of the Roman council, a letter together with a copy of the one he had sent to Theodosius. He also sent one to Flavian of Constantinople (Letter 42, now 49), to Julian of Cos (Letter 44, now 48), and to Anastasius of Thessalonica (Letter 43, now 48), whom he greatly congratulated for having been absent from the Ephesian council.

Three other letters are also found, which Leo likewise wrote in the words of the synod. One was to the archimandrites (Letter 47, now 51), and two to the clergy and people of Constantinople (Letters 45 and 46, now 5 and 59). They contain splendid teaching concerning the incarnation of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Only Letter 50 was given to us as belonging to this year, 449. The other, Letter 59, was written around the middle of March in the following year, as we proved in note 48 (previous volume, col. 871, n. m) on that same letter.]

How Leo could have held a council in so short a time can scarcely be said. Yet councils were frequently held at that time. As we stated above, according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea and Saint Leo’s letter to the Sicilian bishops, three bishops from that province were sent to Rome each year to celebrate a council on the third day before the Kalends of October, which was the time of the deacon Hilarus’s return.

Whether the synod was convened in this way; whether Leo was uncertain about the Ephesian synod; or whether, warned by rumor and report, he had already summoned bishops from the Western regions to Rome, it is certain from his letters to Theodosius, Pulcheria, and the clergy, people, and archimandrites of Constantinople (Letters 40, 41, 45, and 47, now 44, 45, 50, and 51) that a synod was convened at Rome against the Ephesian council and that, by its authority, the decrees issued at Ephesus were condemned and rejected.

We have a witness to the same fact in the deacon Hilarus, who wrote to Pulcheria Augusta:

> “Therefore let your venerable Clemency know that the aforesaid pope, together with the entire Western council, rejects everything that was done at Ephesus against the canons, amid tumult and secular hatreds, by Dioscorus the bishop. These actions cannot in any way be accepted in these regions, since they were committed through the power of the aforesaid man, not without injury to the faith and prejudice against that most holy and innocent man.”

But this pseudo-synod was not merely null and void and without authority because of Leo’s declaration and that of the Roman synod; it was also so by its own fault and because the whole Church protested against it. Baronius explains this admirably, although elsewhere he says that the synod was not rejected until Leo had so decreed.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] Although the Ephesian robbery was in itself null, you will find in the observations on Dissertation 8, no. 14, an explanation of why Leo’s declaration was nevertheless necessary.]

Thus he writes about that synod:

> “In it nothing was attempted or extorted except by force and fear; in it swords and clubs took the place of the sacred books; in it the freedom of voting was bound in chains; in it the threats of soldiers were heard instead of praises to God; in it a perfidious heresiarch was patron; in it heresy was established; in it no order of judgment preserved by the holy Fathers was observed, and no censure of the canons and decrees prevailed; in it the bishops were silent; in it impiety triumphed over the Catholic faith, and the devil erected trophies from the spoils of fallen bishops; and finally, the proud tyrant Dioscorus triumphed over the slaughter of the martyr.”

Leo acted prudently when writing to the East in the name of the Roman council: he avoided the term “pseudo-synod,” lest he offend Theodosius, who had already been embittered by the speeches and accusations directed against the synod. He had been no less cautious in deciding to ask the emperor to permit a council in the regions of the West.

## XVI.

During this period Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, learned that he had been condemned in absentia at Ephesus and deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] On Theodoret’s appeal, compare what Quesnellus discussed in Dissertation 10 with what we noted in our observations on that dissertation. From these it will become certain that he appealed to apostolic authority.]

He too lodged an appeal to the synod of the West, as he wrote to Renatus, a Roman priest and one of the legates.

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

> Διά τοι τοῦτο τὴν ὑμετέραν ἁγιωσύνην παρακαλῶ πεῖσαι τὸν ἁγιώτατον καὶ ὁσιώτατον ἀρχιεπίσκοπον τῇ ἀποστολικῇ χρήσασθαι ἐξουσία, καὶ εἰς τὸ ὑμέτερον ἀναδραμεῖν κελεῦσαι συνέδριον

(Theodoret, Letter 116, to Renatus.)]

> “For this reason I beg your Holiness to persuade the most holy and most devout archbishop to use apostolic authority and to order me to hasten to your council.”

And again, in his letter to Anatolius the Patrician:

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

> Ἀντιβολῶ τὴν ὑμετέραν μεγαλοπρέπειαν ταύτην αἰτῆσαι τὴν χάριν τὸν καλλινικὸν κορυφὴν (sic), ὥστε με τὴν ἑσπέραν καταλαβεῖν, καὶ παρὰ τοῖς ἐν ἐκείνῃ θεοφιλεστάτοις ἐπισκόποις δικάσασθαι

(Theodoret, Letter 119, to Anatolius the Patrician.)]

> “I beg your Magnificence to obtain this favor from the victorious emperor: that I may go to the West and be judged by those most beloved of God and most holy bishops.”

Theodoret did not come to Rome, yet, as the acts of the Council of Chalcedon relate, he was restored to his see. Whether this occurred through an explicit judgment of the Roman council, through the rescinding and rejection of the Ephesian pseudo-synod, or through the granting and receiving of communion, I will not assert. The second explanation, however, is more probable.

But the whole case of Theodoret will be discussed more fully elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0234C] We shall touch briefly on what Quesnellus omitted for this year, 449, concerning the ordination of Ravennius of Arles.

After the death of Saint Hilary, the bishops of the province consecrated Ravennius, a priest of the Church of Arles known and approved by Leo, as his successor while Ravennius had been in Rome on Hilary’s business. Ravennius and the ordaining bishops then wrote to Leo, and he replied to them in Letters 40 and 41, dated on the twenty-second—or, according to Sirmond’s reading, the twenty-sixth—of August in this year, 449.

When the holy pontiff learned from the clerics sent by Ravennius to Rome that a certain Petronianus, a wandering man, was boasting throughout Gaul that he was a deacon of the Roman Church and was visiting various churches under that name, he sent another letter, Letter 42, to the same Ravennius on the twenty-sixth of that month. In it he ordered that all bishops be warned to expel Petronianus from communion with every Church, so that he might no longer usurp this title.]

---

**THE YEAR OF CHRIST 450; THE ELEVENTH OF POPE LEO; THE FORTY-THIRD OF THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS; THE TWENTY-SIXTH OF THE EMPEROR VALENTINIAN; IN THE CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN XIV AND AVIENUS.**
## I.

In the present year, in the month of March, two letters are recorded as having been sent by Leo: one to Pulcheria Augusta (Epistle 48, now 60), the other to the presbyters Faustus and Martin (Epistle 49, now 61). In both, pastoral vigor and steadfast concern for the faith shine forth. I judge that the letters of the emperor Valentinian (Epistle 50), and those of the Augustae to the emperor Theodosius, as well as the Roman synod which they mention, also belong to this same year. The following considerations persuade me that this was a different synod from the one in whose name Leo wrote several letters immediately after the crimes of Dioscorus became known, in October of the preceding year.

[Note: Quesnell omitted not only the two letters—Epistle 60 to Pulcheria and Epistle 61 to Martin and Faustus—written in this year 450, but also Epistle 59, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, which had been assigned to the year 449 because it bore the mark of an interpolated chronicle.]

1. This synod was convened on the feast of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, as Valentinian expressly says:

“After the venerable night of the apostle’s day, I was asked to write to your gentleness by the Roman bishop and by the others gathered with him from various provinces concerning the faith.”

[Note: Here the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter is indicated, not the feast in June, as we proved in the admonition prefixed to the imperial letters in Epistle 55. To remove all confusion, and also to supply several omissions by Quesnell, we append a Chronological-Historical Summary of the events of this year.

Leo hoped that the scandals of the Ephesian Robbery could be remedied if a free council were convened in Italy. He had already requested this from Theodosius in Epistles 43, 44, and 54. He had received no answer, however, when the emperor Valentinian and the Augustae Placidia and Eudoxia came to Rome on February 21. On the twenty-second, when they had assembled in the basilica of this apostle to celebrate the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, the holy pontiff, together with many bishops who had come from various provinces, obtained from those same Augustae that they write letters to Theodosius—Epistles 55, 56, and 57—in which, after rejecting the proceedings at Ephesus, they urgently demanded that a general council be held, especially necessary in these circumstances. Placidia Augusta also sent another letter, Epistle 58, to Pulcheria for the same purpose. From all these letters everyone will see how much authority was attributed to the Roman pontiff.

After these letters had been sent toward the end of February, letters from the clergy and people of Constantinople, from Pulcheria Augusta, and from the archimandrites Martin and Faustus finally reached Rome in March; we have seen that they were written around October of the previous year. Leo was filled with joy when he discovered that the cause of the faith had been defended in the imperial city itself by so many champions. He strengthened them in their constancy in the true faith in Epistles 59 and 61, sent on March 17; on that same day, in Epistle 60, he further and further encouraged Pulcheria to press more vigorously, by her authority, for measures of remedy.

Up to this point Leo had learned nothing of his letters written in the preceding year, nor of Flavian’s death. After March 17, and perhaps in April, he received letters concerning the ordination of Anatolius, through which he learned of Flavian’s death. Many things troubled Leo in this matter, especially the fact that the letters sent on this occasion by the emperor, Anatolius, and his ordainers indicated nothing to us—“apart from what concerned the ordination of the new bishop,” he says—“about the errors that had been suppressed or renounced.” In this obscurity of affairs, he thought that he should meanwhile write nothing rashly in either direction: he did not deny affection to Anatolius, but awaited a manifestation of Catholic truth. Compare Epistle 70, now 91.

Since, however, he suspected Anatolius’s faith less because of the new bishop’s concealment of an explicit profession of faith than because of the wickedness of Dioscorus, his ordainer, and other extremely difficult circumstances—and since he feared the greatest danger to the faith from the emperor’s patronage—he undertook a more deliberate consideration of the matter before replying.

The presbyter Petronius and the deacon Regulus had arrived in Rome shortly before, with a petition from the bishops attached to the Church of Arles, a matter which Quesnell discusses under the following year. Leo kept them there for a long time, because the interests of the faith required them to participate in the aforementioned deliberation and to learn everything that could be reported through them to Ravennius and through Ravennius communicated to all their fellow priests, as is related briefly in Epistle 67, written to Ravennius on May 5 of this year.

The holy pontiff chiefly desired two things from the Gallican bishops, matters which could be suggested orally but were not to be entrusted to writing. First, that they subscribe to his dogmatic Epistle 28 to Flavian. For this reason he sent them a copy, together with Cyril’s letter to Nestorius, Flavian’s earlier letters to Leo, and other documents concerning Eutyches; on these see Note 5 to Epistle 67. There we also pointed out that Leo’s and Cyril’s letters are joined and commended to the Easterners with equal concern in Epistles 69 and 70, written in the affair of Anatolius, just as in this Epistle 67, addressed to the Gallicans, they are joined and commended. From this we recognize that Petronius and Regulus were detained in Rome for a long time because of the deliberation held concerning Anatolius, and that they were instructed about the whole matter.

Second, he considered it extremely useful if those same Gallicans, after subscribing their names to their letter to Flavian, would write to the emperor Theodosius and add their own prayers for a remedy to the Ephesian Robbery. This is sufficiently clear from Epistle 99, in which the Gallicans, replying belatedly to Leo, commended his dogmatic letter with the fullest possible subscriptions and indicate in chapter 4 that they had refrained from writing to Theodosius because, having received news of his death and seeing affairs changed under the new emperor, they had judged such action entirely unnecessary.

Somewhat later, whether in the same month of May or in June, Theodosius’s replies to Valentinian and the Augustae were conveyed in Epistles 62, 63, and 64. From these Leo learned that Theodosius’s mind was opposed to every remedy. Amid these evasions he sent the four legates—Bishops Abundius and Asterius, and the presbyters Basil and Senator—to the East. Delaying his reply to Anatolius, he wrote only to Theodosius and Pulcheria in Epistles 69 and 70, adding Epistle 71 to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites. All these letters are dated July 16.

The legates, who were sent after that date, received instructions together with testimonies from the Fathers confirming the Catholic doctrine defined in Leo’s letter against the Eutychian heresy. It is therefore clear why Leo delayed so long his reply to the letters concerning Anatolius’s ordination, although he had received them much earlier, at least in April. The difficulty of the circumstances, the need for prolonged consultation and deliberation, the expectation of Theodosius’s replies to the letters of the emperor and the Augustae, and the selection and instruction of the legates together with the testimonies of the Fathers required a considerable delay.

When the legates reached Constantinople is unknown. When Saint Leo wrote Epistle 75 on November 8, he was confident that they had already arrived. Yet although Marcian’s Letter 73 had been brought by Count Maximinus, from which he learned of Marcian’s accession to the empire, he had received no news of the legates’ arrival. Only in Marcian’s Epistle 76, dated November 22, is it mentioned that the legates had been received with honor.

After Theodosius died on July 28 and Marcian came to the throne, the appearance of affairs changed. The new emperor, with the powerful assistance of his wife Pulcheria, directed his first thoughts and concerns toward repairing the scandals against the faith. In his letter to Leo concerning his accession, Epistle 73, written at the end of August or the beginning of September, he declared his eagerness for a council to be convened as soon as possible. He ordered Saint Flavian’s body to be transferred to Constantinople and Eutyches to leave that city.

As soon as Leo’s legates arrived, a synod ἐνδημοῦσα—“a resident synod”—was convened. There Leo’s dogmatic Epistle 28 to Flavian was read, together with the testimonies of the Fathers that had been sent through the legates. Anatolius and all the bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, and deacons subscribed to the same letter and pronounced anathema upon Nestorius and Eutyches and upon their errors.

These proceedings, praised in Epistle 80 to Leo, were sent to him by Carterius, Patricius, and Asclepiades, Constantinopolitan clerics, together with the legates’ report, as we learn from Epistle 79. Three letters were also sent to the pontiff: one was Pulcheria’s Epistle 77; the other two, from Anatolius and Julian of Cos, are lost. On this same occasion Marcian’s other letter to Leo, Epistle 76, dated November 22, also appears to have been sent. Since Saint Leo replied to all these letters on April 13 of the following year, in Epistles 78, 79, 80, and 81, which he handed to the clerics returning to the imperial city, it seems that all were transmitted and received together through those same clerics. Compare the Dissertation on the Lost Letters, no. 45, where we show that another letter of Marcian, which is said to have been lost and sent on this occasion, should not be asserted.

From the same Constantinopolitan synod was sent a letter of the venerable archbishop Leo to all the metropolitans everywhere. It was subscribed, as is reported in the Council of Chalcedon, Act 4, concerning Photius of Tyre, in the fourth book of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1435.

Theodoret, who in the previous year had extolled this same letter of Leo to Flavian with the highest praises, later wrote to Abundius, Leo’s legate, after the Constantinopolitan synod of this year. He sent him a copy with his own subscription and testifies that Ibas of Edessa and Aquilinus had done the same.

With these events the year 450 concludes.]

This synod, therefore, was held in June of the year 450, not in October of the preceding year.

2. In replying to Valentinian and the Augustae, Theodosius says that he had already written to Leo at greater length, more fully, more clearly, most fully, and often about the matters Leo had mentioned. But Leo wrote to Theodosius immediately after the disturbances at Ephesus, from the October synod. If Valentinian’s letters concerning this same affair were sent from that synod to the same emperor, how can we believe that Leo had previously received Theodosius’s frequent replies before Valentinian had received them?

3. That Theodosius sent letters to Leo very late, and that Leo seems to have received them scarcely before June of this year, is evident from Epistles 52 and 53, now 59 and 71. In these Leo first gives thanks to Theodosius for the letters received and admonishes the Constantinopolitan presbyters.

Certainly, we possess no letters from Leo to the emperor between October 15 of the year 449, when he first demanded that a synod be held within Italy, and July 16 of the year 450.

[Note: In the intervening period we have Epistle 54, which, according to a certain correction, was written on December 23, 449; see Note 8, column 225, section b, under the preceding year.]

Moreover, from Epistle 49, now 61, to the presbyters Martin and Faustus, it is clear that on March 17 the pontiff had still heard nothing about the receipt of those first synodal letters, written five months earlier. Leo’s mind was extraordinarily anxious because of this silence. For Theodosius had received his request for a synod within Italy with deaf ears. Therefore, as soon as the opportunity arose to address the emperor and the Augustae, Leo attempted through their letters and insistence to obtain what he had been unable to obtain personally.

4. The fact that a synod was then convened at Rome, with the affairs of the Church in such disorder, is made credible by the ancient custom of bishops, who were accustomed to assemble from everywhere, even from more distant regions, at the memorials of the saints, in order to celebrate together their natal feast. Thus it was customary for bishops to gather at Rome at the apostles’ tomb and at Tours for Saint Martin.

5. It is also clear that there were different synods from the fact that Saint Leo expressly writes in Epistle 52, now 69, that the synod which had requested in its own letter that a council be held in Italy had met at Rome for this reason, and indeed before October 15.

The synod, or assembly, of bishops by whose multitude Leo was surrounded when he approached Valentinian and the Augustae and urged them to write, had been gathered on the occasion of the apostolic solemnity and, as the Augustae put it, “for the primacy of their own see,” or for its dignity.

## II.

As for the solemn feast of the apostle mentioned in the imperial letters, Cardinal Baronius prefers to interpret it as the day of the dedication of Saint Peter’s basilica, so that the assembly of bishops noted by Valentinian is to be understood as the same autumnal synod of 449 from which, as we have said, Leo sent several letters to the East. Thus far no one has refused to agree with the cardinal.

Nevertheless, I cannot adopt that view. First, who would not immediately think of the apostle’s natal day when it is called “THE DAY OF THE APOSTLE,” as it is in that letter? Second, who would suppose that bishops who, according to the ancient canon and Roman custom, were accustomed to assemble at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, continued to assemble in November to celebrate the dedication of the basilica? And who would give credence to Baronius when he admits that the same synod was gathered on the third day before the Kalends, yet writes that it lasted until November 18, the day on which the dedication of Saint Peter’s basilica occurred—and thus makes the bishops hold a synod for fifty days? Who, I ask, could persuade himself of this, especially when the synod appears already to have concluded on October 15, with letters having been sent from it to the Eastern regions?

The matter therefore, if I am not mistaken, stood as follows. Leo had written to Theodosius from the autumnal synod of 449 and had demanded that a synod be convened in the regions of Italy. Theodosius, surrounded by the Eutychians, did not grant his request and replied only that a synod was unnecessary, since the Council of Nicaea was sufficient and its faith and decrees had to be maintained.

This reply is suggested by Epistle 52, now 69, to Theodosius:

“Amid those anxieties which we endure for the faith, all the letters of your piety have provided us with the greatest hope of security, by commending the Council of Nicaea, so that, as you often write, you do not permit the priests of the Lord to deviate from it.”

When Leo saw this and perceived that the cause of the faith was in danger in the East, he went to meet Valentinian, who was coming to Rome with the Augustae Placidia and Eudoxia for the feast of Saint Peter. He was accompanied by a gathering of bishops who had assembled for that same feast. Together they implored the emperor and the Augustae to act through letters with Theodosius on behalf of the faith and to obtain the convocation of a synod in Italy.

[Note: Since this Roman synod was held in February, as we indicated in Note 2, column 235, section b, and since we demonstrated in the Chronological-Historical Summary there that Leo’s legation of Abundius and his companions was sent after the assembly held at Rome, in May, this point should be understood accordingly.]

I think that the legation of Abundius, Asterius, Basil, and Senator was decreed by that Roman synod; it is mentioned in Epistle 52, now 69, and in the following letters, which are recorded as having been sent on July 16 and 20. I do not know whether anyone would ever remember such a numerous legation being decreed outside a synod in that age.

Nevertheless, I do not wish to conceal what seems contrary to our view: Galla Placidia, in her letter to Theodosius concerning Flavian, speaks as though he were still alive:

Ἐν τῇ στάσει τῆς ἱερωσύνης ἀβλαβοῦς μένοντος ἐν πᾶσι Φλαυιανοῦ,

that is:

“With Flavian remaining entirely unharmed in the state of the priesthood.”
