But what if Placidia Augusta merely means that no deposition from the priesthood should be considered to have occurred? What if the Augusta still did not know of Flavian’s death at that time, and perhaps the pontiff himself did not know?

[Note: In February, when we showed in Note 2, column 235, section b, that the letters of Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia were written, both Placidia and the pontiff were ignorant of Flavian’s death. Certainly they knew of this death by May 5, when Leo deliberated concerning the ordination of Anatolius, his successor. It is therefore false that Leo learned of Flavian’s death and Anatolius’s election only a few days before July 16. It is true that on this date the pontiff first replied to the letters announcing that Anatolius had been ordained; but we have seen in Note 2, cited above, that he delayed his reply for several months. This must be recalled if all these matters are to be understood.]

John Garnerius, who adopted the contrary opinion, was moved especially by the consideration that it is incredible that, after almost eleven months, nothing should have been learned in the West about the death of a bishop of so important a see. Why he mentions eleven months, I do not know. From February 18, to which he assigns Flavian’s death, to the end of June, when the apostle’s feast occurred, there are no more than four months and approximately ten days.

It should not seem surprising that Flavian’s death remained unknown at Rome for those four months. We observed above that Leo remained ignorant for five full months whether the synodal letters written to Theodosius, Pulcheria, the clergy and people of Constantinople, and several others had been received. Nor does he seem to have learned anything about them before July.

He could certainly have learned of Flavian’s death even later, and with greater reason. Flavian had died in exile at Hypaepa, and perhaps news could not immediately be sent to Constantinople. When the bishop’s death became known in that city, the first thought that came to Theodosius or anyone else was not of anything other than choosing and ordaining a bishop for the imperial city. If I am not mistaken, the emperor and Dioscorus arranged this so that Leo would not learn of Flavian’s death before the ordination of his successor, lest the election of Anatolius—a man suspected because of his friendship with Dioscorus and his choice by him—be disrupted.

Indeed, Leo appears to have learned both facts from the same messengers and only a few days before July 16, since on that day he first replied concerning Anatolius’s ordination. Why should we not press an argument of this kind as readily as Garnerius? He says:

“If Flavian’s death had occurred before February, what reason could there be for Saint Leo not to have said a single word about it, or at least not to have written about Anatolius to Theodosius, Pulcheria, or others before the month of July? Why did Theodosius not ask, before Lent or even before Easter, that Anatolius be received into communion by Saint Leo?”

By the same reasoning with which he argues from Flavian’s death, I can argue, with much greater right, from the report of his death; Leo’s and Theodosius’s silence is equally applicable to both.

For the rest, I readily accept the learned man’s opinion concerning the day of that bishop’s death—not because it lends some support to my view that the synod occurred in June, but because it is supported by the authority of the Brief History of the Eutychianists, the Greek Menologion, another work by Maximus of Cythera, and a third from the library of Cardinal Sirletus. They testify with equal agreement that Flavian ended his life in exile after many afflictions and hardships. This indicates that he died only after several months.

[Note: The election of Anatolius, his successor, which occurred at the end of 449, demonstrates that Flavian’s death cannot be assigned to January 18 of this year 450. See what we said concerning the time of this death in Note 1, column 220, section c, under the preceding year.]

Whatever may be the truth concerning this point, it certainly appears beyond doubt that Placidia’s letter was not written in October or November of 449, nor from the autumnal synod. For when Theodosius replied to this letter, he referred the Augusta to letters which he had often written on this matter—that is, concerning the convocation of a council in Italy—“more fully and more clearly”:

ἐντελέστερόν καὶ σαφέστερον πολλάκις

“more completely and more clearly, often.”

This could undoubtedly not have happened until several months after October, when Leo first wrote to Theodosius about a synod after receiving news of the Ephesian Robbery. If we have written anything contrary to this in connection with those letters, I wish it to be corrected in light of what has been said.

## III.

Valentinian therefore came to Rome with his mother Placidia and his wife Eudoxia, to the apostles’ tomb in the basilica of Saint Peter. Leo approached the emperor with a great number of bishops and spoke at length about the pitiable condition of the Church: about the evils which the monk and eunuch had inflicted upon it; about the injuries suffered by the defenders of the faith; about everything that had been done by force at Ephesus; about the subscriptions extorted and the proscriptions imposed upon bishops; and about religion profaned by the impious hands of the attendants.

In addition, he invoked the faith of Saint Peter and earnestly begged Valentinian and Placidia to aid the tottering Church. He lamented and wept so greatly that tears arose in everyone out of compassion.

Moved by the speeches of the holy pontiff, the emperor, and likewise Placidia and Eudoxia, wrote letters to Theodosius, while Placidia wrote privately to Pulcheria. They begged the emperor not to allow himself to be deceived by the wickedness of Eutyches and to beware lest the heresy gain strength under his authority. They earnestly requested that, by common agreement, a universal synod be held in Italy, where the new and perverse doctrine could be subjected to examination.

Theodosius, deceived by hatred of Flavian and by the whispers of heretics, replied as though he were defending not error but the faith. He claimed to be most observant of his ancestral religion and to guard the faith of the Church and the traditions of his forefathers as a sacred deposit. For this reason, he said, the council had been held at Ephesus, where votes had been free and everything had been judged impartially and according to equity and goodness.

He testified that the same things had been stated more fully in the letter written to Leo:

“It has been indicated to that same Leo more broadly and more fully, as we believe.”

Thus Theodosius was turned against the Church, not so much by his own judgment as by that of others; for he favored the heretics more than the heresy.

Dioscorus, meanwhile, confident of the emperor’s favor and emboldened by the success of events, contemplated greater deeds. He was angry to hear that the Ephesian council was being called a robbery and that its acts had been rescinded at Rome. In uncontrollable anger and thirst for vengeance, he undertook an unheard-of crime after discussing the matter with ten bishops whom he had taken as his companions: he cut off Saint Leo from communion with the Church. This greatly disturbed the minds of good men and divided the Churches of the East into factions and schisms for almost two years.

For, as the deacon Liberatus reports, “the Egyptian, Thracian, and Palestinian bishops followed Dioscorus; the Eastern, Pontic, and Asian bishops supported Flavian of holy memory.” This schism continued until the death of the emperor Theodosius (Brief History, chapter 12).

## IV.

Not yet had two years elapsed when Chrysaphius, the author of the Eutychian treachery, at last paid the penalty for his crimes.

[Note: Chrysaphius was not punished by Theodosius, but after his death. The lector Theodorus and Marcellinus attribute his death to Pulcheria. Victor of Tunnuna and Prosper say that it preceded Marcian’s election. In the Alexandrian Chronicle he is said to have been killed at the gate of the imperial city leading toward Melantiades. The accounts given here from the later Greek writers Nicephorus and Cedrenus should therefore not be preferred.]

The emperor finally recognized that the eunuch was abusing his favor and authority to the destruction of the Church and the state, and stripped him of his possessions and honors and banished him to an island. Nicephorus records this (Book XIV, chapter 49) and also relates that he was swallowed by the waves during the voyage.

Cedrenus records in his account (page 334 of the Regius edition) that he was killed on that island by Jordan, whose father had suffered an unjust death at the eunuch’s command. Jordan, however, had been handed over by Pulcheria. This is why Count Marcellinus says that he was killed “at the prompting of Theodosius’s sister, together with his greed.”

Theodosius did not long survive. Some write that he died of illness, others that he died after a fall while hunting, from a dislocated vertebra. All good men, however, believed that his death had been hastened by divine providence, so that rulers might learn that heresy must not be protected and that, in matters of religion, those should be heard who possess authority and the right to administer the Church.

Nicephorus and Cedrenus write that before his death he was afflicted by sorrow over his error and turned his vengeance against its author, seeking punishment for Chrysaphius’s audacity. For this reason, they say, he became hostile toward his wife Eudoxia, because out of hatred for Flavian she had inflicted many losses upon the Church. Yet, so that she might suffer nothing harsher, he allowed her to go to Jerusalem under the pretext of fulfilling a vow. Whether she went immediately or somewhat later is uncertain; it is certain, however, that she went there and remained until her death.

## V.

I believe that what is said about Eudoxia’s sending her daughter—who was Valentinian’s wife—a chain as a special gift, the chain with which the prince of the apostles had once been bound by Herod, should be referred to this second pilgrimage, if the story is to be believed; no well-qualified witness is produced for it.

[Note: If credence is to be given to the verses once read in the Church of Saint Peter ad Vincula and published by Floravante Martinello in *Roma Ethnico-sacra*, page 284, they seem to belong to a later Eudoxia, who flourished during the time of Pope Pelagius. The verses are:

“This temple of the Lord had previously been dedicated to Peter;

The third bishop, Sixtus, once consecrated it.

Afterward it was destroyed in civil war;

Eudoxia entirely renewed it there.

Again the blessed Pope Pelagius consecrated it,

Storing the bodies of the holy Maccabees.

He added Peter’s precious iron bonds,

Which the illustrious woman brought from Jerusalem,

And with which Peter was bound in Nero’s time,” and so forth.

As far as we know, no civil war occurred under the Eudoxia who ruled at this time by which this temple, after Sixtus, was destroyed. Just as Pelagius consecrated the renovated temple, so Eudoxia, who is said to have rebuilt it, is known to have lived during the pontificate of that same pope. The transfer of the holy chains from Jerusalem must therefore be assigned to this woman and this period.]

Baronius says that this occurred during her first journey to Jerusalem. Yet although many authors mention that journey—Socrates, Evagrius, Nicephorus, the Chronicle of Marcellinus, the Acts of Saint Melania, and others—it is remarkable that not one of them has even a word about the sending of Peter’s chain. The authority of inscriptions is worthless, since their date is uncertain.

But even if someone prefers to refer it to her first journey, it nevertheless falls within the time of our Leo. Since she set out from Constantinople for Jerusalem toward the end of 438 and built many monastic settlements (*lauras*), monasteries, churches, and even the city walls, and performed many other deeds there to glorify God the Savior, as Evagrius testifies, she did not return to Constantinople before the end of the following year, 439. She could scarcely have sent that gift to Rome before Leo’s pontificate, which he began almost at the start of the next year.

Whatever the case may be, on the occasion of these relics of Saint Peter we must not omit what the unimpeachable witness Gregory the Great reports about our Leo in Book III, Letter 30, to Constantina Augusta:

“Let your most tranquil Ladyship know that it is not the Roman custom, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body. Instead, only a *brandeum* is placed in a small box and laid beside the most sacred bodies of the saints. When it is taken up, it is reverently deposited in the church being dedicated; and through it such great miracles occur there as if their bodies themselves had been specially brought to that place.

“Thus it happened in the time of Pope Leo of blessed memory, as our ancestors relate: when certain Greeks doubted such relics, the aforesaid pontiff cut the *brandeum* itself with scissors that had been brought, and blood flowed from the incision.”

## VI.

An anonymous author, a minister of the Calvinist sect in Rouen, rejects this account of Gregory the Great as fabulous and adduces it as an example of senseless credulity. To counter it, he proposes six rules, as though they were so many oracles, by which he wishes all historical accounts to be tested as by a Lydian stone.

“The fourth rule,” he says, “is this: when equal or nearly contemporary witnesses are lacking, one should not immediately place faith in some later writer who declares that a notable event, which he is the first to report, was known throughout the world. An example is the story told by Damascenus that the emperor Trajan was freed from hell through the prayers of Pope Gregory I, which he asserts was commonly known throughout the West.”

And shortly afterward:

“I wish learned men had used this rule to refute the famous story told by Gregory,” and so forth.

After quoting Gregory’s words reproduced above, he says:

“Gregory alone relates this as though it were known to the whole world; and yet, in my opinion, no one sees anything who does not see that the whole account of Gregory must be counted among fables.”

In my opinion, no one sees anything who does not see that the whole discourse of the dissertation’s author must be counted among ravings. The comparison of those two events is as unjust as a comparison between darkness and light. The application of that senseless rule—even to the story of Trajan’s liberation from hell—is so absurd that nothing could be more absurd.

For even if a thousand witnesses were produced, not merely later witnesses but contemporaries of Gregory, faith would still have to be denied to an account of this kind. First, it is futile to parade a cloud of witnesses to prove something that surpasses all the testimony and diligence of witnesses—namely, everything that is done by almighty God, especially concerning souls separated from the body. Second, against the Catholic doctrine of faith, by which we are taught and profess that there is no redemption in hell, no witness could ever have been qualified.

This rule above all should have been established by that author: it is more certain than all the others and is repeatedly useful for refuting little stories invented through pious fraud.

## VII.

As for Gregory’s account of what happened to Leo, it is first of all false that Gregory narrated it as something known to the whole world; not even a syllable indicates this. Gregory discusses the custom of the Romans and confirms it by the act of his predecessor. He adduces as witnesses to this custom his own ancestors, who were not far removed from the age of Leo. Gregory could have heard it from people who had themselves seen Leo.

Moreover, to whom should greater credence be given when he speaks about a Roman pontiff than to another pontiff of the same see, whose Church’s affairs and traditions are ordinarily better known to him? Thus, just as credence is rightly denied to John Damascene, a Greek speaking about ancient Western matters of which he had previously heard nothing, so it is easily granted to Gregory: a Roman speaking about events at Rome, not very ancient, and about practices that in his own time were still occurring before everyone’s eyes.

If what Gregory relates about Leo is to be rejected among fables, including what concerns relics of this kind and the miraculous event granted by God on their account, what are we to make of the other events which Gregory himself testifies occurred in his own age? No one was more Gregory’s contemporary than Gregory himself. Yet this man of the greatest sincerity and candor indicates that it was the Roman custom to place a *brandeum* in a small box, set it beside the most sacred bodies of the saints, deposit it reverently in the church being dedicated, and that through it such great miracles occurred as if the bodies themselves had been specially brought there.

Finally, let this fourth rule of the heterodox author prevail against Gregory’s account of Leo, if ancient writers who carefully and fully treated Leo’s deeds survive and omitted only this event; if it is still certain that all who wrote about these matters have survived to our own time; and if anything contrary is found written somewhere in the ancient sources.

But if none of these conditions is true, then the dissertation writer’s entire effort against Saint Gregory’s account, and against the veneration of the sacred relics which his impatience and hatred moved him to consign to the realm of fables, plainly falls fruitlessly to the ground.

## VIII.

With Eudoxia absent and Chrysaphius expelled, Pulcheria’s authority returned, even before her brother’s death. After he was removed from the world, she married Marcian, a very good and courageous man, but on the condition that she would share with him the throne rather than the marriage bed. Thus the woman retained the empire and preserved even in marriage the virginity she had vowed to God.

Both possessed an equal disposition toward religion, which under their rule began to revive.

### 481

Theodosius had written to Leo toward the end of his life concerning Anatolius, who had been substituted in Flavian’s place, asking that Leo admit him to communion. Anatolius had been ordained by Dioscorus and had formerly served as his *apocrisiarius* at Theodosius’s court. Leo replied on the sixteenth or seventeenth day before the Kalends of August that he did not refuse to love him as a brother, but that he was awaiting his judgment concerning the faith, provided that he believed what accorded with the teaching of the Fathers who had shone forth in both Churches, and that concerning the Incarnation he held what Cyril had formerly held and what the Council of Ephesus had defined against Nestorius. Anatolius was to attest his faith by his signature before clergy and people and accept the points consonant with Catholic truth that Leo had fully set out in his letter.

Leo also indicates that he was sending the bishops Abundius and Asterius, together with the presbyters Basil and Senator, “through whom,” he says, “you may graciously recognize what the form of our faith is”; they were also to be witnesses to the faith professed by Anatolius and not hesitate to admit him to peace if he agreed with him in faith. On the same subject he wrote on the sixteenth or seventeenth day of July to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites (Epistle 53, now 71). In that letter he complains of Anatolius’s silence and informs them about the legates sent concerning the faith. Not long afterward he wrote another letter [Note: This letter to Pulcheria, Epistle 70, was assigned to the same day, 16 July, as the two preceding letters because of the correction of the chronological notice] to the empress Pulcheria (Epistle 54, now 70), and letters to the presbyters Martin and Faustus (Epistles 55, now 74, and 56, now 75), all breathing the same zeal for the Catholic faith. In the penultimate of these he expresses confidence that his legates had by then arrived in Constantinople.

### IX

Theodosius had already died when the legates arrived in Constantinople, and Marcian had already been hailed as emperor. They delivered Leo’s letters to him. Anatolius, whose faith under Theodosius had been doubtful, judged that under a religious prince there was no longer anything to hesitate about and condemned Eutyches together with his errors. Formerly closely allied with Dioscorus and ordained by him, Anatolius had consecrated the bishop of the Church of Antioch contrary to canonical rule. He approached Marcian and Pulcheria as a suppliant and asked them to secure for him Leo’s friendship and communion.

The Roman pontiff, concerned for the peace of the Church, readily consented, so that, as he himself wrote the following year (Epistle 78, now 104), “what he is known to have obtained through your favor” might not be disturbed “by the perversity of any desire.” “For, keeping in view the intervention of your faith, and although the beginnings of his consecration were wavering because of those who had ordained him, we wished to be more lenient toward him than strict.” He wrote nearly the same thing to Pulcheria in the following letter.

After the arrival of the legates, Anatolius convened a council, or assembly, of the bishops who were in the imperial city, so that it might approve his faith. [Note: This does not concern the assembly at which Anatolius signed Leo’s letter, but an earlier assembly held shortly after Anatolius’s ordination. In that assembly, with Theodosius’s support and to the prejudice of the bishop of Tyre, the province of Phoenicia had been divided in two. This question was debated at Chalcedon, as will be clear from the reading of the fourth session. See vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1435D ff. Tryphon of Chios cited examples of other similar assemblies called synods in order to prove that the earlier assembly had been a synod. These two assemblies—one said to have been held then, the other now—must be carefully distinguished; otherwise further errors of Quesnellus will be exposed.]

This assembly is mentioned in the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon, where the question was debated whether it deserved the name of a council:

> “If the assembly of those staying in the imperial city is to be called a synod” (*Εἰ σύνοδον χρὴ καλεῖν τῶν ἐπιδημούντων τῇ βασιλίδι πόλει τὴν συνέλευσιν*),

the bishop Tryphon of Chios replied:

> “It is called a synod, they assemble, and those suffering oppression obtain their rights” (*σύνοδος καλεῖται καὶ συνάγονται, καὶ οἱ καταπονούμενοι τῶν δικαίων ἀπολαύουσιν*).

Anatolius added that ecclesiastical cases were also dealt with there and that he had attempted nothing connected with novelty, but only what had been granted to the bishop of Constantinople by ancient custom. What was done in that assembly, or synod, may be learned from fragments of the *Commentaries* of Abundius, who was one of the legates.

He reports, then, that Leo’s holy letter was read and that testimonies of the holy Fathers, who had written both in Latin and in Greek, were brought forward. When compared with one another, they were found to cohere and to converge upon one faith. This took place in the synod before the bishops. Leo’s letter to Flavian was also produced there, and all confirmed it by their signatures: Anatolius, the bishops, the archimandrites, the presbyters, and all the deacons who were present. All pronounced an anathema against Nestorius and Eutyches and against their teaching. Thus the Eutychian heresy was proscribed at Constantinople, and there was one faith among all.

Leo’s letter was subsequently sent by the synod to the other metropolitans. They approved it orally and by signature together with the bishops of their provinces. Theodoret likewise returned it, bearing his signature, to the legate Abundius. We know that all these things took place as described above partly from the Acts of Abundius and partly from the session concerning Photius held after the fourth session of Chalcedon. Leo himself wrote to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, in a previously unpublished letter, which we now publish from the manuscript codex of Cardinal Grimani (Epistle 68, now 88). He says that at Constantinople the testimonies of the holy Fathers had been cited by his representatives, and that the entire Church of Constantinople, together with all its monasteries and many bishops, had given its assent and by their signatures anathematized Nestorius and Eutyches together with their dogmas:

> “You should also know that very recently I received a letter from the bishop of Constantinople reporting that, when the bishops throughout the provinces received the *tractoria* sent through their provinces by the bishop of Antioch, all the bishops had given their assent to my letter and had condemned Nestorius and Eutyches by an equal signature.”

Before we finish speaking about the synod, I shall add—not in a contentious spirit but for the sake of historical truth—that this council was not summoned by the legates, as it appears in the *Annals*, but convened by Anatolius. This is stated in the very fragments of the Acts of Abundius that Baronius reported (*Annals*, under the year 449, no. 28), and it is also suggested by the fourth session of Chalcedon concerning Photius. [Note: In this session the first assembly held under Anatolius is mentioned; nothing is said of the second, from which its convocation might be attributed to Anatolius. Since Saint Leo, when he sent the legates to the East, had neither foreseen nor expected the change brought about by Theodosius’s death, he did not plan the convocation of a Constantinopolitan assembly at which everyone would sign his letter. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that, after circumstances had changed, the legates acted so that, once an assembly had been convened, the praised letter would be signed by all, and that it would also be sent from the same assembly to all the metropolitans of the East, so that all the bishops likewise might sign it.]

No canons or privileges of that see permitted anyone other than Anatolius to convene a synod at Constantinople. Nor were the legates sent for the purpose of holding a council, but, as they themselves state, to make the Catholic faith known to everyone, and, as Leo himself wrote to Theodosius:

> “Through them you may graciously recognize, by the instruction contained in what we have sent, what the form of our faith is.”

He explains this more fully in Epistle 54 (now 70) to Pulcheria. Finally, in Epistle 55 (now 74) to the presbyter Martin, he writes that the legates had been sent to strengthen the courage of holy minds.

Nor is it true that bishops were summoned from the provinces to the synod. Rather, those who happened to be in the imperial city were gathered together with presbyters and archimandrites, as was noted above and confirmed by the session concerning Photius within the fourth session of Chalcedon. There it is said that only a few assembled, and that no others were present except those who happened to be found in the city:

> “Just as now, when a few had assembled at Constantinople, the letter of the blessed archbishop Leo was sent to the metropolitans who were everywhere and was signed, so then what had seemed appropriate was brought forward before the most holy bishops who were present and was signed.”

Finally, in this synod the bishops who had defected from the faith were not reconciled or granted communion with the Catholic Church; they were ordered to remain content with communion in their own Churches. [Note: Compare note 19 in the preceding volume, col. 914, note r, on Epistle 80. From the reading of that letter corrected by us, it will be clear that the legates’ decision was approved and that this matter had not been reserved for other legates to whom it would later be entrusted. In Epistle 85, dated 9 July—not 7 July—451, no authority in this matter is said to have been granted to new legates; only the earlier decision in chapter 2 is confirmed.]

Nor were the names of Dioscorus and Juvenal removed by decree of that synod. For in Epistle 60 (now 80) to Anatolius, Leo writes not as though describing an accomplished act, but as though the matter still had to be settled by the legates together with Anatolius:

> “Whatever our representatives stationed there shall have said ought to be done.”

Indeed, it is clear from letters written on 7 June of the following year that this matter had been reserved for the other legates, Lucentius and Basil.

Although, therefore, in what we wrote above concerning the signature of the Constantinopolitans with Anatolius, of all the bishops of the Eastern diocese, and of all the metropolitans throughout the world, we may have followed others in attributing all these matters to the same time and year, together with the embassy of Abundius, I do not wish to assert that everything occurred at the same time, in the same year, or in the presence of Abundius himself.

Abundius had departed from Rome around 17 July 450. On 8 November Leo had still not received confirmation of his arrival, as appears from Epistle 56 (now 75), written on that day. [Note: We proved in note 4 on Epistle 83, in the preceding volume, col. 919, note e, that Abundius and his companions returned to Rome shortly before 9 June 451. On 13 April Leo was indeed awaiting them, but he had received an account of their actions not orally but by letter. See note 5, ibid., col. 913, note c, on Epistle 80.]

Letters dated 13 April of that year persuade us that they had returned to Rome before Easter. In those letters the pontiff commends other legates who had then been sent, gives thanks for the earlier legates aided by the empress, and mentions that he had reviewed an account of the actions and report of these men:

> “From the report of our brothers whom we had sent to Constantinople, we have learned” (Epistle 60, now 80).

To this embassy, therefore, belongs only the signature of Anatolius, the Constantinopolitan clergy and archimandrites, and the bishops who customarily attended the resident synod (*ἐνδημούση*). The Acts of Abundius, Pulcheria’s letter to Leo, to which Leo replied on 13 April of that year, and Leo himself in letters written at the same time mention nothing more.

As for Maximus of Antioch and the bishops of his Eastern diocese, Leo wrote to Paschasinus on 27 June and had only just then been informed by Anatolius of what was being reported there concerning the bishop of Antioch. It is therefore clear that this took place only after Easter and after the legates’ departure from Constantinople. In the same Epistle 68 (now 88) to Paschasinus, the events concerning Anatolius and the Constantinopolitans are separated from those concerning Maximus and the Eastern diocese: the former are described as having already been completed, while the latter are described as recent. Leo wrote about the same Easterners to Anatolius in Epistle 70 (now 91) on 26 June:

> “Since you yourself have graciously indicated that all the Eastern priests signed in accepting the Catholic faith and condemning Eutyches and Nestorius.”

He had learned this only then; concerning Anatolius himself, he had learned it two months earlier.

[Note: Here Quesnellus denies that Leo’s letter was sent for signature from the Constantinopolitan synod, at which Anatolius and the others dwelling in the imperial city signed it, through the efforts of Abundius and the other legates of the Roman Church. He maintains that a different, later assembly was held on this matter. Yet Theodoret, who was absent and on this occasion signed the same letter, seems to have sent his signed copy to the legate Abundius for no other more probable reason than that it had been sent into the East on Abundius’s authority; hence, at the beginning of the same letter, he attributes to it the Easterners’ adherence to the right faith. Another assembly should not be posited without more certain authority. Quesnellus’s further arguments are exceedingly weak. Leo’s silence proves nothing, since letters do not always state every circumstance. The word *now* in the session concerning Photius of Tyre denotes the later and more recent assembly and contrasts with *then*, denoting the earlier and more remote assembly; thus there is no need to posit another assembly held before the Council of Chalcedon. If few bishops are there said to have been present, whereas Leo, writing of the Constantinopolitan assembly in Epistle 88, calls them many, thirty or forty bishops could, from different viewpoints and in different accounts, be called either few or many. To Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, they were called few in comparison with the number of bishops who had confirmed, in the earlier assembly, letters favorable to him. Since Leo did not have that comparison in mind, he appropriately called them many for his purpose. Theodoret, Ibas, and Aquilinus signed Leo’s letter privately because they were deposed and exiled and could not attend Eastern synods.]

Finally, it seems clear to me that Anatolius had not yet sent Leo’s letter from his resident synod (*ἐνδημούση*) to all the metropolitans of his provinces for signature, as is reported in the Chalcedonian session concerning Photius. This appears both from Leo’s silence—he would not have omitted the matter when writing to Paschasinus on 24 June about two other closely related points—and from that same session concerning Photius, in which the word *now* indicates that the act had taken place not long before October, when that session was held.

Moreover, Saint Leo says that many bishops attended the Constantinopolitan assembly at which Anatolius signed together with the clergy and monks, whereas the session testifies that only a few assembled at another gathering, from which the letter was sent to the metropolitans of their provinces for signature. Nothing prevents the entire matter from having been carried out in the presence of the Roman legates Lucentius and Basil. Saint Leo repeatedly writes in chapter 3 that this was one of the matters entrusted to the legates, and he exhorts Anatolius in Epistle 65:

> “Therefore, dearest brother, strive faithfully and effectively to carry out with these brothers, whom we have chosen as suitable agents for so great a responsibility, whatever accords with the Churches of God.”

Nor is the letter of Theodoret to the legate Abundius contrary to this, whether that letter is spurious or genuine. The signatures of Theodoret, Ibas, and Aquilinus, which it mentions, were private and arose from their own decision; they were not common signatures given at the command of the primate. Those three signed their own copy of the letter. The others, compelled to sign by *tractoriae* circulated through the provinces on the authority of the primate and under the supervision of the metropolitans, satisfied the requirement in the common original document intended to receive everyone’s signatures.

### Chronological Summary for the Year 451

To avoid confusion, a brief historical and chronological summary of this year, 451, should also be prefixed.

The Constantinopolitan clergy, who after the synod held at Constantinople toward the end of the preceding year had sent to Rome the acts of that synod together with the report of the legates and the letters of Marcian, Pulcheria, and Anatolius, seem to have arrived not long after the beginning of the present year, 451. Leo was satisfied by what Anatolius had done and written and consequently did not hesitate to grant him communion.

Provision also had to be made for the other bishops who had yielded to impiety and, having returned to repentance, were asking for communion. Since the legates had not been instructed about this unforeseen matter and did not possess suitable authority, they could not grant these men apostolic communion. They had determined two things: first, that those who repented should meanwhile remain content with communion in their own Churches; second, that the names of Dioscorus of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Eustathius of Berytus, who had been the leaders of the Ephesian Robber Synod, should not be recited at the altar.

For these reasons the pontiff judged that other legates should be sent with appropriate instructions and authority and joined to the returning Constantinopolitan clergy. He decided to await Abundius and his companions, whom he had learned would return as soon as possible, so that from their own spoken account he might understand more fully whatever was necessary.

For this reason he detained the Constantinopolitan clergy longer. In Epistles 78, 79, 80, and 81, dated on the Ides of April and sent through those same clergy to the East, he indicates that new legates had been sent or were to be sent. These letters had been prepared before Easter, when he was planning to send the new legates at the same time. But when the return of Abundius and his companions was excessively delayed, he postponed the dispatch of the new legates and decided to send only the Constantinopolitan clergy on the Ides of April with the letters mentioned above. He retained the date in the text, even though that text indicates that new legates had been sent. Compare note 7 on Epistle 78 in the preceding volume, col. 909, note d, and note 5 on Epistle 81, ibid., col. 916, note o.

After the Constantinopolitan clergy had departed, Tatianus, prefect of Constantinople, delivered Marcian’s letter to Leo. In it the emperor insisted that a general council be convened. Leo replied on 23 April. He mentioned that legates were to be sent immediately and stated that they would explain his view of the council more fully. Since circumstances had changed, he no longer considered a synod necessary.

Meanwhile Abundius and his companions returned to Rome with other letters from Marcian and Anatolius. Having received from them fuller information about those who were requesting communion, Leo finally sent new legates on 9 June: the bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basil. He also added Anatolius of Constantinople as a companion of the delegation, so that they might grant apostolic communion to fallen bishops who, by an unambiguous profession, anathematized Eutyches together with his doctrine.

As for the leaders of the impiety, if they should perhaps repent and appear to offer suitable guarantees, Leo reserved the question whether they ought to be received for the more mature deliberation of the Apostolic See. Four letters were given to these legates on this matter: Epistle 83 to Marcian, 84 to Pulcheria, 85 to Anatolius, and 86 to Julian of Cos. In these letters Leo states that he was sending the legates solely to reconcile the fallen and indicates that the appropriate time for convening a synod had not arrived.

On 19 June he wrote Epistle 87 to Anatolius. From it we learn that the presbyters Basil and John had fled to Rome to dispel suspicion of Eutychian or Nestorian heresy. After clearing themselves before the Apostolic See by issuing a profession of faith, Leo sent them back in peace and commended them to Anatolius.

Not long after the legates’ departure, Marcian’s letters arrived in Rome. They had announced that a council was to be convened at Nicaea on the Kalends of September; the announcement had been issued on 17 or 23 May. This unexpected summons surprised the pontiff. Nevertheless, so as not to resist the emperor’s desire, Leo immediately appointed Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, as legate to the council by letters that are now lost. Then, on 24 June, he sent another legate, the presbyter Boniface, so that together with the aforementioned Paschasinus and the two legates previously sent, Lucentius and Basil, he might preside over the council.

On that same day Leo gave Boniface several letters bearing instructions: a new Epistle 88 to Paschasinus, Epistle 89 to Marcian, and another lost letter to Lucentius and Basil, which explained this delegation. Four further letters followed two days later: Epistle 90 to Marcian, 91 to Anatolius, 92 to Julian—who had long been residing in Constantinople and was thoroughly informed about everything, and whom Leo added to the four legates already mentioned—and 93 to the synod.

Leo seems to have received two letters from Marcian and Pulcheria through Theoctistus the *Magistrianus*. Through him he sent two letters back to them on 20 July: Epistle 94 to the emperor and Epistle 95 to the empress.

After receiving Leo’s letters sent through the Constantinopolitan clergy on 13 April, and the others transmitted through Tatianus on 23 April, the two Augusti understood that the pontiff was opposed to a synod then being convened and that he was sending legates solely to receive the fallen. Since the synod had nevertheless been summoned—on 17 May according to the Greek account, but on 23 May according to the ancient Latin versions—they pressed the matter with greater urgency.

Pulcheria seems to have raised a difficulty concerning Leo’s instruction that the names of the leaders of the Ephesian Robber Synod should not be recited from the diptychs. Some, like Anatolius earlier, thought that this should be deferred until those men had been deposed, unless they repented. Leo replied by recalling his concern and indulgence toward the fallen, in order to bring them back to a sound mind and receive them. He indicated that he had forbidden their names to be recited at the altar for no other reason than that those who had not yet suffered the punishment for their crime and still lay in impiety might at least be roused by this stimulus to seek peace. If they offered satisfaction, he signified that peace should be granted them.

If in Epistle 95 to Pulcheria, chapter 3, he mentions that nearly all the fallen had been reconciled—a reconciliation that was to be accomplished by the legates Lucentius and Basil—one should not therefore believe that he had already received news of this reconciliation. The approximately forty days that had elapsed since the legates departed from Rome was too short a period for the journey to Constantinople to be completed, reconciliation to be granted to nearly everyone, and letters about the matter to be brought back to Leo.

It is therefore more probable that Leo wrote this because, when he composed the letter or when it reached Constantinople, he assumed that his legates had granted reconciliation to nearly all those whom he already knew had requested it.

Abundius and Senator, returning to their province of Milan after the Constantinopolitan embassy, delivered Leo’s letter to the metropolitan Eusebius. The pontiff had instructed him to convene the most numerous possible synod of his province, at which everyone would sign Leo’s letter to Flavian. This was done in the synodical letter that is Epistle 97 among Leo’s letters.

Leo received it after the legates had already departed for the Eastern synod. Perhaps he had wished to deliver it to them if it had arrived sooner, just as he would have done with the synodical letter of the Gauls had it been returned earlier, as he wrote back to the Gauls in Epistle 102. What follows concerns the synod, which will be discussed in the summary of that synod.

### The Year of Christ 451; the Twelfth of Pope Leo; the Twenty-Seventh of Valentinian, and the First and Second of Emperors Marcian; the Consulship of Marcian Augustus and Adelphius

### I

Having obtained the imperial power in the preceding year, Marcian sent Pope Leo a letter announcing his election. The pontiff seems to have replied no earlier than the Ides of April of this year. [Note: Leo replied to Marcian’s Epistle 73, written concerning his accession to the empire at the end of August or beginning of September 450, by a letter now lost, dated around 8 November, as we saw in note 2 on Epistle 78 in the preceding volume, col. 908, note i. To Marcian’s other letter, Epistle 76, written on 22 November, he replied with Epistle 78 on the Ides of April.]

Four letters are recorded as having been sent in response: to Marcian (Epistle 58, now 78), to Pulcheria (Epistle 59, now 79), to Anatolius of Constantinople (Epistle 60, now 80), and to Julian of Cos (Epistle 61, now 81). Leo had received letters from all of them as well, apparently through the clergy of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and sent his own letters back through them for delivery.

When Anatolius had made his faith known in the Constantinopolitan synod, and the legates approved it as entirely consonant with the teaching of the holy Fathers and with Saint Leo’s letter, Anatolius sent three legates to Rome at the beginning of this year: the presbyter Casterius and the deacons Patricius and Asclepiades. [Note: This dispatch of the Constantinopolitan clergy more probably occurred toward the end of 450, as may be seen in the dissertation on the lost Epistle, no. 45.] They were to bring Leo letters attesting to his faith, affirm it orally in his presence, and, moreover, communicate to him many matters that had been discussed in the synod. Anatolius’s legates attached their report concerning the same matters to their letters. The principal matter was this.

Many bishops, whose steadfastness rather than whose faith had wavered, were earnestly asking to return to communion with Leo. At the synod the pontiff’s legates had advised them to remain content with communion in their own Churches until Saint Leo should decide otherwise.

Leo ordered that they be received (Epistle 60, now 80), provided that before the legates and Anatolius they gave evidence of their faith and condemned both the madness of Eutyches and themselves for having, whether through fickleness or fear, approved the acts of the Ephesian Robber Synod.

Concerning the recitation in the diptychs of the names of Dioscorus of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Eustathius of Berytus, Leo instructs Anatolius to follow what the legates had advised. [Note: Saint Leo confirmed what the legates previously sent had already decided in the assembly of the preceding year. Compare note 13 on Epistle 80 above, col. 245, note a, in the preceding year.] Above all, he was to take care that nothing offend the memory of Flavian and that the names of those who had defended impiety not be used indiscriminately together with the names of the saints.

Leo also commends to Anatolius Julian of Cos, the defender of Flavian, and asks him to care for the Church of Eusebius of Dorylaeum and not to let this work turn to Eusebius’s harm—which Heaven forbid—for Eusebius had endured many hardships for the cause of the faith and shared Leo’s communion.

Eusebius, the accuser of Eutyches, had been stripped of his episcopate through the Ephesian pseudo-synod and had fled to Rome as to an asylum, where he issued a confession of faith to remove the stain with which malicious heretics had besmirched him and by which, as commonly happens, they charged him with heresy because he opposed them. In his confession he professed the decrees of the earlier synods—the doctrine of Nicaea, Constantinople, and especially Ephesus—in order to remove suspicion of Nestorianism. He publicly testified to this himself at the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: Quesnellus interprets these words of Eusebius of Dorylaeum as referring to the profession of faith that Eusebius issued at Rome, since at this time no question other than the question of faith was being discussed. In the context of the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon, however, they refer to the canon established in the Constantinopolitan council under the elder Theodosius in honor of the see of Constantinople. Since Leo had most strongly opposed this canon when it was renewed at Chalcedon, it seems incredible that Eusebius would have read it and accepted it. Hence Rusticus appended this note to Eusebius’s testimony: “Either Eusebius is lying, or he deceived Saint Leo at that moment.” See vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1754, note 6.

Leo seems to have anticipated something concerning this canon, or concerning the efforts on behalf of the see of Constantinople, when he instructed Boniface, the legate sent to the council, as follows: “If any, trusting in the splendor of their cities, should attempt to usurp something for themselves, strike this down with the firmness it deserves.” Thus in the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon.]

Eusebius says:

> “I reread this rule to the most holy pope in the city of Rome in the presence of the Constantinopolitan clergy, and he accepted it.”

These words indicate the date of Leo’s letter, which he wanted Anatolius to make public to everyone.

### II

In his letter to Marcian, Leo briefly congratulates him on his diligent care for religious affairs and on undertaking their defense (Epistle 58, now 78). Marcian’s piety was certainly exceptional, and his love for religion ardent.

After being hailed as emperor, Marcian, as we have said, sent Leo a letter announcing his election (Marcian’s Epistle preceding Epistle 68, now 73), asking to be aided by holy prayers before God and indicating how earnestly he desired the settlement of the Church through a general council, which Saint Leo had requested. Later, in another letter in which he spoke honorably of the arrival of the legates, he invited Leo to the East for a universal synod (Marcian’s Epistle following Epistle 61, now 76). If Leo could not come, Marcian said that he would await his reply and then summon bishops from Illyricum, Thrace, and the East to the synod by letter.

Pulcheria also wrote gratefully to Leo (Pulcheria’s Epistle following Epistle 58, now 77). She reported that Anatolius’s doctrine was whole and sound and that Leo’s letter to Flavian was held to have been ratified by Anatolius’s signature; that the emperor intended a synod at which matters relating to the faith and the bishops who had fallen at Ephesus would be decided; that Flavian’s body, brought to Constantinople at the emperor’s command, had been honorably buried in the Basilica of the Holy Apostles; and that the exiled and banished bishops had been recalled, so that at the universal synod they might be restored with honor to their sees and priesthood.

Saint Leo replied (Epistle 59, now 79) that he considered it most welcome that she defended the cause of the Church and earnestly and successfully devoted herself to condemning Nestorius and Eutyches.

But in addition to and before all the letters that Leo wrote to the East during this year concerning the Eutychian heresy, there is a letter dated on the eighth day before the Ides of November of the preceding year, which we publish here for the first time. It was addressed to the presbyters Faustus and Martin (Epistle 56, now 75). Leo wishes it to be circulated as an encyclical among all Catholics, so that each person might fight courageously for the faith against the spreading heresy.

### III.

While Leo was diligently laboring to destroy the Eutychian depravity, the bishops of the province of Vienne had written to him in the preceding year (the *Letter of the Gallic Bishops to Leo*, before Letter 50, now 65). Saint Hilary of Arles had died in 449, and Ravennius had been appointed in his place. We have explained above the causes of the anger arising from Celidonius, who had been deposed by Hilary and restored by Leo. [Col. 0251A] Hilary had not obeyed the judgment of the Roman pontiff [Note: We shall prove in the observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 5, Part III, chapter 2, that Hilary obeyed Leo’s judgment. Before the sentence, he alone resisted the appeal and introduced other proceedings, on account of which he was deprived of metropolitan jurisdiction, as we shall explain at greater length in those same observations.]. For that reason Saint Leo had stripped the Church of Arles of its privileges and transferred the rights of a metropolitan see to the Church of Vienne.

The bishops of the province of Vienne, believing that the supreme pontiff’s anger toward Hilary had died with him, sent him, on Ravennius’s behalf, a letter or petition, asking that their metropolitan’s rights and the rights of his Church be restored. I know that some have suspected this letter of being spurious. Baronius was the first to incorporate it into his *Annals*, using a manuscript from Arles. I found the same manuscript, or certainly a similar one, in the library of D. Thou, together with the same letter and Leo’s reply, in which he prudently settled the dispute. He assigned four Churches to the metropolitan see of Vienne—Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Gratianopolis—and placed the rest under the Church of Arles. In this way its rights were restored to Arles to some extent, while the Church of Vienne was not deprived of all honor.

The presbyter Petronius and the deacon Regulus were delegated to Rome to deliver the petition of the province of Arles to Leo. [Col. 0251B] They were detained at Rome for a long time, so that they themselves might observe where the Eutychian machinations would finally lead. When they were sent back, they brought the reply of the holy pontiff and his judgment concerning the case of the province of Vienne. They also brought Leo’s letter to Ravennius (Letter 51, now 66), to which he attached his letter to Flavianus (Letter 52, now 67), instructing him to share it with the bishops of Gaul; and he urged them to commend their faith in this matter.

He entrusted the delegates with other instructions as well, but by word and oral communication rather than in writing. [Note: What Leo entrusted to Petronius and Regulus, and why he explained it orally rather than in writing, we have explained in the *Breviary of the History of the Preceding Year*, observation 2 (above, col. 235, note b). He entrusted it, I say: for he did not ask Ravennius—as Quesnel puts it—but commanded him, as is clear from those words in Letter 67: “If you carry out these things as we believe, and as we have COMMANDED,” etc.; these words indicate that the secret commands were to be effectively executed. Quesnel repeatedly avoids terms of command; it is enough to have noted this once.] I could readily persuade myself that Ravennius was asked to have the bishops of Gaul receive Leo’s letter to Flavianus at the synod 492 and formally subscribe to it; this would show the Easterners, if necessary, that the Westerners were of one mind and one faith, and that Leo’s doctrine was the doctrine of all the bishops of his part of the world. The conscientious man did not convey this in writing, lest he be said to have sought the bishops’ suffrages too eagerly, or to have anticipated the date of a synod not yet publicly announced.

The matter was drawn out for a long time. From the return of Ravennius’s delegates to Gaul until the date when the Roman pontiff’s delegates departed for the council in the East, more than a year passed; yet Leo had still not received the response of the Gauls when the delegates for the council left Rome. After the synod had concluded, he wrote to them as follows:

> We would indeed have wished to receive the letter of your Fraternity at the time you had promised, so that, when our brothers were setting out for the East—those whom we sent in our place to the holy synod for the defense of the Catholic faith—the profession of your judgment might also be joined to theirs (Letter 77, now 102, chapter 1).

At last he writes that the letters had been delivered to him belatedly by the bishop of Embrun, together with the subscription of forty-three bishops (Letter before 78, now 99, and Letter 77, now 102). He congratulates them on their doctrine as holy and undefiled, and as heavenly doctrine taught by the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, which Eutyches had tried in vain to overthrow. He also informs them of the happy outcome of the Council of Chalcedon and asks them to make it known to the bishops of Spain, just as the letter to Flavianus had previously been sent through them together with other material. Idatius, a writer of that period, did not omit this in his *Chronicle*, under Olympiad 130:

> From Gaul, letters are brought concerning the letter of Bishop Flavianus, sent to Leo the bishop, together with the writings of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Nestorius of Constantinople concerning Eutyches, the heretical Ebionite; and Leo the bishop’s reply to him. These are sent to the Churches together with the deeds and writings of the other bishops.

Thus in former times the faith and teaching of the Fathers were customarily transmitted from Gaul to Spain.

### IV.

About the same time, Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus, bishops of Gaul, after reading Leo’s letter to Flavianus, wrote to Leo (Letter now 68). They congratulated him on the holy and sound faith of that letter and testified to the care he had undertaken to remove heresy from Gaul. They declared the esteem and authority in which the letter was held among them, and sent him a copy so that, if anything had gone wrong through the fault of the copyists, or anything had been corrupted, or if he himself wished to remove or add anything, he could do so; the letter could then be returned complete and sound, so that bishops and laypeople 493 who eagerly desired to read it might do so without danger of error or suspicion of forgery.

I think Leo granted their reasonable request, and I have no hesitation in saying that the corrected letter was sent by those same bishops to Eusebius, bishop of Milan. For Eusebius wrote to Leo in a synodical letter bearing the subscriptions of all his fellow-provincial bishops that it had been delivered to him by Ceretius. “That letter,” he says, “reached us from your holy admonition through our brother and fellow bishop Ceretius” (Letter now 97). The printed editions incorrectly read *Cyriacus* in place of *Ceretius*; Baronius’s *Annals* and the manuscripts have *Ceretius*.

[Note: Eusebius received no other letter from Leo than the one sent through Abundius and Senator; and as soon as it was possible, he obeyed Leo’s command. Consequently, the explanation that the response was delayed because it was something new to compel bishops to subscribe to a letter without the authority of an ecumenical synod is fictitious. Just as the Gauls did, so too did the bishops of the province of Milan add their subscriptions before the ecumenical council, solely on the authority and command of the pontiff; the same had also been done at Constantinople and in the East. Similarly, long before any ecumenical synod, all the bishops, Eastern and Western alike, subscribed to Zosimus’s *Tractoria* against the Pelagians, as Marius Mercator teaches in the Baluze edition, p. 138:

> The letter of Zosimus, of blessed memory, called the *Tractoria*, by which Coelestius and Pelagius were condemned, was confirmed both at Constantinople and throughout the whole world by the subscriptions of the holy Fathers. Julian and his other accomplices refused to subscribe, and were unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same Fathers; consequently they were deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees, and were expelled from all Italy.]

A synod was not immediately summoned and convened by Eusebius—either because it was something new to compel bishops to subscribe to a letter without the authority of an ecumenical synod, or because of Leo’s command concerning the matter, or because Abundius, one of Saint Leo’s legates and a member of this province, was awaited. When he had returned from Constantinople to Rome, he received from Leo a letter to Eusebius of Milan. In it Leo urged him, after holding a synod of the province, to have all the bishops approve the encyclical letter by their subscriptions.

Eusebius’s reply follows; from it we learn that Leo was satisfied and that the letter had been praised in the council [Note: The word *ut* does not appear in the letter of the Milanese bishops; Quesnel inserted it here in italics, as though they had subscribed to Leo’s letter because they had recognized it as “full of the simplicity of faith,” and so forth. Those same Fathers did indeed testify that the letter shone with the full simplicity of faith; nevertheless, we have no doubt that they subscribed to it on the authority of the Apostolic See itself. For, as we believe, the statement of Saint Peter Chrysologus was common to all of them. In Letter 25, admonishing Eutyches to heed Leo’s letter obediently, he added this reason, deriving its binding force from the special prerogative of the Apostolic See:

> Since blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, provides the truth of faith to those who seek it.

Guided by the same conviction, the Gallic bishops Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus wrote in Letter 68 to Leo, concerning that same doctrinal letter to Flavianus:

> The primacy of the Apostolic See was rightly established there, from which the oracles of the apostolic Spirit are still uttered; where the oracles of the apostolic Spirit point to Peter teaching in his own see and in his successors.

This apostolic definition was received by all the Gallic bishops as so certain an oracle of faith that, as they wrote in Letter 99 to the same pontiff, when they compared its teaching with their own and found their own teaching conformed to it, they rightly rejoiced that they had always held it through their paternal tradition, “as your apostleship explains.” They then rejoiced in this agreement of doctrine because it gave them the opportunity to speak freely and confidently, with the authority of the Apostolic See also supporting them, and for each person to assert what he believed.

They did not think any examination necessary by which they should decide concerning the doctrine of those letters before accepting them. Rather, from the letters themselves—which they had received as an oracle—they were confirmed in the knowledge that the doctrine they held was Catholic and sound. Nor should we therefore deny that what Leo had defined was subjected to examination, since Vigilius testifies in the *Constitutum*, chapter 15, that this was done at the Council of Chalcedon. But we have explained at greater length, from Leo himself, how free that examination was while the authority of the Apostolic See nevertheless remained intact: see observation 14, volume preceding, column [Col. 0254D] 1048, note l, on Letter 120. Compare also what we shall add at greater length in observation 1, ibid., column 1400, note d, concerning Quesnel’s notes on Letter 97.]

The letter was judged to be “full of the simplicity of faith,” firmly established on the authority of the prophets, evangelists, and apostles, consonant with the writings of blessed Ambrose, and harmonious with the tradition of the Fathers and the faith of the Church; whereas those whom the Apostolic See had declared alien to the faith were rejected and condemned.

I will not linger over Baronius, who believed that Leo’s letter had been sent twice to Eusebius of Milan, something that cannot be inferred from Eusebius’s reply. There is indeed mention of two letters: one concerning the convening of a synod at Milan, which Abundius had brought; and the other, the letter to Flavianus, delivered through Ceretius, which Eusebius says agreed with the faith of the ancestors. It is obvious that these letters differed in substance and subject.

Some of these matters have been stated by us in retrospect and others in anticipation, because of the affinity between the events. But let us return to the East and consider the Church’s preparations for calming the disturbances provoked by the Eutychian heresy.

### V.

Marcian and Leo were equally resolved that a council should be held 495 [Note: While the emperor Theodosius was alive and protecting the Eutychians, Saint Leo believed that a council in Italy was necessary in order to provide a remedy for the scandals. But after Theodosius’s death, circumstances changed, and Leo did not acknowledge the same necessity, as we have shown near the end of observation 7, volume preceding, column 909, note d, on Letter 78. Nevertheless, he did not wish to resist the desire of Marcian, the new Augustus, as is clear from Letters 89, 90, and 91.]; but they differed over the place and time. Leo preferred that the synod be convened and held in Italy. An external enemy was abroad. The Hun, under Attila, terrified the West; in the East, the faction of the heretics threatened danger. Many followed the party of Dioscorus and Eutyches, and the recent memory of the Ephesian robbery aggravated the situation. Leo himself, the pontiff, ardently desired to attend the council, but he could not leave Italy. The emperor had decided that it should be convened in the East. The heresy should be cut down where it had revealed itself—just as the ancestors had once extinguished the heresies of Arius, Macedonius, and Nestorius where they had arisen. Leo also judged that his presence would greatly contribute to victory and that the council’s date should not be postponed any longer, lest the heretics grow bolder and the courage of Catholics weaken through waiting too long for the council.

At that time, after the return of the four legates about whom we have spoken, Leo sent other legates to Constantinople, as he had previously promised Marcian by letter: Lucentius, bishop of Asculum, and Basil, a presbyter. He sent them to receive the confession of those who had fallen at Ephesus and admit them to the communion of the supreme pontiff. He also entrusted them with other business and gave them two letters to Marcian (Letters 62 and 63, now 82 and 83), and letters to Pulcheria, Anatolius (Letter 65, now 85), and Julianus of Cos (Letter 66, now 86).

He praises Marcian’s faith because he cares no less for the welfare of the Church than for the commonwealth; he gives thanks that Marcian had received his legates well and commends the new ones. Near the end of the letter he speaks of postponing the synod, so that those whom fear of war was holding back might attend the council.

He discusses Pulcheria’s piety at greater length. Concerning those who had fallen, he advises that those who promise amendment and penance should be treated more leniently. He then asks the Augusta to remove Eutyches far from the city, since he was too near it; to deprive him of the company of those whose minds he had infected; and to arrange for a new abbot to be placed in his position, one who would cleanse the minds corrupted by the Eutychian stain.

He admonishes Anatolius that he is sending Lucentius and Basil so that, after consultation, they may do whatever appears useful and advantageous to the Church. Those who wished to return to Catholic communion were to be admitted, but only with a definite profession of faith and repudiation of the Eutychian doctrine. If any were found to have committed more serious offenses, they were to be referred to the Apostolic See, so that it might determine what should be done. He forbids the names of those who had betrayed the faith to be recited at the altar. [Note: Leo does not speak of all who had acted treacherously, but of those who had sinned more seriously in this affair and had therefore claimed a higher position for themselves in that same unhappy synod, the Ephesian synod. He orders that, if they repent, their names not be recited at the altar until the Apostolic See, after considering all the circumstances, has pronounced judgment concerning them. See Letter 85, chapter 2.]

Regarding the memorandum that the clerics had presented to him, he adds that he had instructed the legates to give their reply orally and verbally. Finally, he explains the hopes that the Church entertains under a prince whose disposition is not only Christian but also priestly.

A fourth letter, which we now publish for the first time, urges Julianus of Cos to assist the legates in fact and in action in the Church’s business, where counsel and prudence were needed, and to labor vigorously to break the waves raised by the Ephesian storm.

From these letters we understand what had been entrusted to the legates. They had not been sent to a universal synod, although Baronius thinks otherwise. Marcian and Leo had written to each other about a synod, but it had not yet been convened; indeed, as we have said, they were still debating its place and time. An edited manuscript misled Baronius.

There is an error in the date on which the letter formerly numbered 43, now 73, is commonly said to have been written—in this edition, Letter 90. In place of “the fifth day before the Kalends of June,” the date should be restored as “the sixth day before the Kalends of July,” as the manuscript of Cardinal Grimani has it. Since Baronius believed that Boniface had been sent from Rome to Constantinople on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, he also thought that Lucentius and Basil had been sent at the same time to the synod. Yet they departed from Rome on the sixth day before the Ides of June, and subsequently completed their legation at the Council of Chalcedon.

While these events were taking place, the presbyters Basil and John, falsely suspected of heresy, came of their own accord from the East to Rome, in order to remove suspicion of Eutychian or Nestorian depravity. After professing the faith before the holy pontiff, they were sent back with honor and with letters of recommendation to Anatolius (Letter 67, now 87).

### VI.

Although the Roman pontiff wished the synod to be postponed and to be held in Italy, Marcian, compelled by circumstances and encouraged by the wishes of the Easterners, nevertheless began to plan for the convocation of a synod. Leo anticipated the emperor’s intention, whether through rumor or by his own judgment, and also from Marcian’s own letter, to which the pontiff replied in Letter 63, now 83. So that the Church might not appear to have been neglected, since he could not attend the synod himself, Leo selected Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to act in his place.

Paschasinus certainly deserved Leo’s judgment. Perhaps several men surpassed him in rank and the prerogative of their sees; few equaled him in learning, holiness, and reputation. He possessed uncommon steadfastness, tested by harsh and prolonged captivity among the barbarians, as he himself relates to Leo. His learning was exceptional and known to Leo, who had consulted him about the calculation of Easter and had followed his answers. He was so observant of ancient discipline that Leo entrusted him with the task of reforming the conduct of the Sicilian Church, as is clear from Letter 16. Nor were other qualifications lacking: mature experience and prudence joined to a corresponding seriousness of character.

Leo immediately wrote him a letter (Letter 68, now 88) 497 as though preparing him for the legation, although he omitted mentioning either the legation or the approaching synod. [Note: When Leo gave Letter 88 to Paschasinus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, he had already received the notice summoning the synod, as is clear from Letter 89, written to the emperor on the same day, as we have corrected it; that letter names the legates appointed to the synod. Therefore Letter 88 did not prepare Paschasinus for the legation but furnished him with new instructions. Leo had already appointed him his legate in an earlier letter, now lost. See observation 4, volume preceding, column 930, note q, on Letter 89.]

He discusses Eutychianism at length and sets forth the Catholic doctrine of Christ’s incarnation. He sends Paschasinus the letter he had written to Flavianus and recalls how it had been received and confirmed at Constantinople in the assembly of bishops presided over by Anatolius. He explains what the bishop of Antioch had done in his own diocese, sending *Tractoriae* throughout the provinces so that the same doctrine might be strengthened by the subscriptions of the Eastern bishops. Finally, he introduces the question of the paschal cycle, about which there will be discussion elsewhere.

This letter is found in a manuscript of Cardinal Grimani and is dated the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

Leo had scarcely written this to Paschasinus when, behold, the emperor’s letter arrived announcing that a synod had been summoned at Nicaea in Bithynia for the Kalends of September. In my opinion, Leo had not yet received the letter of convocation when he wrote to Paschasinus, although Marcian’s letter of convocation had been written a full month earlier, since letters to other bishops are recorded as having been sent on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. Certainly the journey from Constantinople to Rome takes a month.

### VII.

After receiving the emperor’s letter, Leo was displeased that the synod was neither postponed nor held in Italy, as he had indicated through his legates, and that the wishes of Anatolius and the Easterners had prevailed over his own. Nevertheless, it was not the intention of the supreme pontiff to abandon plans for peace by delay.

He immediately considered sending legates and dispatched the presbyter Boniface to the East. He arranged for Bishop Paschasinus to sail there from Sicily and instructed them that those who had previously undertaken the legation should exercise Leo’s authority at the synod together with the men named above. He also added Julianus of Cos to their number:

> Since we know, says Saint Leo (Letter 71, now 92), that you have greater knowledge than our men of all that is being done there,

he sent three letters on this subject: to Marcian (Letter 69, now 89), Anatolius (Letter 70, now 91), and Julianus (Letter 71, now 92), dated the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

To Marcian he modestly complained of the shortness of time, the difficulties of the provinces, and the unsuitability of the season for summoning bishops; nevertheless, these matters were to be overlooked for the sake of peace. He wished Paschasinus to preside over the synod. [Note: Saint Leo indicated that the prerogative of presiding belonged to his legates in Letter 93, addressed to the synod initially summoned at Nicaea. There he says:

> In these brothers, the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius and the presbyters Boniface and Basil, who have been sent by the Apostolic See, let your Fraternity consider me presiding over your synod.

As for the text of Letter 89 supplied by Quesnel, compare what we observed in observation 9, volume preceding, column 931, note c, on that same Letter 89.]

He did not assert that his legates were entitled by right to the first place and the prerogative of presiding, but attributed this to the defection or inconsistency of the Easterners:

> Since some of the brothers were unable to hold the Catholic judgment against the storms of falsehood, it is fitting that the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Paschasinus preside over the synod in my place.

Calvin is plainly delirious when he tries to use this passage to deprive the Roman pontiffs of the right to preside over ecumenical councils.

In his letter to Anatolius he makes the same complaint: the times were unfavorable because of the disturbances of war and the shortness of time; many bishops from more remote provinces would not be present. Then, after mentioning the legates, he expresses good hopes for the synod, having received reports from it that Nestorius and Eutyches had been condemned by all the Eastern bishops.

In the third letter he wishes Julianus of Cos to carry out his responsibilities at the synod. We now publish these latter two letters for the first time from our manuscript. There are also two other letters dated the following day. [Note: Letter 73, now 90, and Letter 72, now 93, which are attached to the text, were not dated on the following day but on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, like our Letters 91 and 92.]

One was addressed to Marcian (Letter 73, now 90), and was to be delivered at the synod. It was dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, not, as in the printed manuscripts, the sixth day before the Kalends of June. The other was addressed to the synod (Letter 72, now 93). Its commonly transmitted superscription is false. [Note: We have corrected the superscription from our manuscript of Regensburg.]

The matter is clear in itself and is still confirmed by the testimony of Evagrius. For in Book II, chapter 11, he writes:

> First, the bishops who had been summoned came to Nicaea. When Bishop Leo of Rome sent them a letter through Paschasinus, Lucentius, and the others whom he had sent there to represent him, he addressed it as follows: “To the bishops assembled at Nicaea.”

In his letter to the emperor Marcian, Leo first earnestly implores him not to permit the faith to be reconsidered as though it were doubtful—the faith that the Fathers proclaimed had been handed down from the apostles. Nor should he permit matters condemned by the decrees of the ancestors to be brought into dispute. Leo suspected from the emperor’s letter that Marcian had some such intention.

He wrote nearly the same to the Fathers of the synod:

> Therefore, dearest brothers, let the vain unbelief of those who err be utterly silenced, with all audacity of disputation against the faith divinely inspired rejected; and let no one be permitted to defend what he is not permitted to believe.

### VIII.

With matters thus arranged for the synod, Lucentius and Basil arrived at Constantinople. 499 As Leo had instructed them, [Note: Quesnel states that the legates discussed postponing the synod and disputed with Anatolius concerning the lapsed because he thinks that, for this reason, Marcian and Pulcheria wrote to Leo the letters to which the pontiff replies in Letters 94 and 95. We have shown in the *Breviary* that those letters were sent to Leo before the legates’ arrival and for another reason. It is therefore entirely false that Anatolius resisted the legates more obstinately and thought that the reconciliation of the lapsed belonged to his own discretion.]

they discussed postponement at length and dealt with Anatolius concerning the reception of the lapsed. They requested that the authors of the disturbances not be admitted immediately but reserved to the Apostolic See, and they forbade their names to be recited at the altar.

Whether the legates pressed the matter too vigorously, or Anatolius resisted too stubbornly and insisted that these matters belonged to his own discretion, the affair seemed likely to erupt into internal hatred unless Marcian and Pulcheria immediately intervened. They ordered letters to be carried to Leo in Rome by forced marches.

The holy pontiff replied kindly to both (Letter 74, now 94). To Marcian he said that he willingly accepted the synod and had not demanded that it be held within Italy except so that more bishops from the most distant places might attend. The legates had already set out for the synod and would arrive at the appointed time, although the shortness of the time pressed hard upon them. Concord could easily be restored to the Church if the faith of the Fathers were retained and the doctrine of the ancestors proclaimed.

He wrote at length to Pulcheria as well (Letter 75, now 95), especially concerning those returning to the Church. He had determined that peace should not be denied to those who requested it.
