Although the heresy was worthy of hatred and detestation, those who washed away its stain through penance were not to be excluded from mercy:

> Rather, he says, “we groan with those who groan, we weep with those who weep; and we employ the justice of correction in such a way that we do not neglect the remedies of charity” (ibid., chapter 3).

He then adds that he had taught this not only by words but also by deeds. Many had obtained pardon who had rescinded what they themselves had decreed and condemned what they themselves had written. He had done everything according to judgment so that he might extinguish the heresy without harming anyone.

Indeed, even concerning the authors of the disturbances, so that they might be stirred more quickly to penance, he had relaxed something of the customary discipline. They were not, among Catholic brethren, to have the same standing and esteem they had possessed before the impious crime committed at Ephesus; nevertheless, they were to retain both their sees and the honor of the episcopate.

Thus Saint Leo sought by counsel and prudence to suppress the seeds of hatred at their very origin. These matters are drawn from the letters sent to Marcian and Pulcheria on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

When the emperor’s letters had been delivered throughout the provinces to the metropolitans, and the bishops had been summoned through them, many immediately set out for the synod at Nicaea, where they waited for the emperor, who had also promised that he himself would attend the synod.

The Kalends of September had already passed—the day appointed for the synod—yet Marcian had not arrived. [Note: We insert here certain material omitted by Quesnel. Since the emperor, hindered by the disturbances of war, could not immediately reach Nicaea as he wished, he sent a letter to the Fathers of the synod, asking them to wait for a short time. Since Marcian had perhaps gone elsewhere because of public necessity, Pulcheria sent letters to Strategus, the consular governor of Bithynia, ordering him to expel from Nicaea the clerics, monks, and laypeople whom she had learned had entered the city and were stirring up disturbances.

Not long afterward the bishops, impatient with this delay, wrote to the emperor that some of the Fathers were suffering from illness and other difficulties. Marcian replied that public necessity still prevented him from coming and, in addition, that Leo’s legates did not wish to enter the synod unless they could do so with him. He advised the bishops to move to the nearer city of Chalcedon, so that he could more easily travel there.

The Fathers did not immediately agree to this transfer because they feared that in Chalcedon, which was close to Constantinople, the supporters of Eutyches could easily provoke riots. This was conveyed to Marcian by the deacon Atticus, as the older manuscripts read, not by an archdeacon, as the commonly transmitted Greek exemplar has it; according to that reading, the name should be Aetius.

Then the emperor delivered a letter to the Fathers at Heraclea on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, ordering them, without fearing any disturbance, to hurry to Chalcedon without delay.]

The bishops then wrote to him asking that the synod be held according to the custom of the ancestors, since many were failing to attend either because of the hardships of the journey 500 or because of poor health. The emperor replied that it had seemed good to the legates of the Apostolic See that the synod should not be held unless he were present; that he had thus far been detained by affairs of state; yet that he would fail the empire rather than the Church. If the bishops wished to come to Chalcedon, he would set out there immediately, although concern for the commonwealth was drawing his attention elsewhere.

At that time, the Huns, under Attila, having first ravaged the provinces of the East, had burst into the West with hostile standards. But after Attila was defeated by Aetius in a drawn-up battle on the Catalaunian Plains, he fled, more like a plunderer than a conquered man, and began to make his way toward the East, attempting to seize Illyricum; he was prevented by the emperor’s forces.

This affair kept Marcian at Constantinople. So that he might not be far away, he suggested to the Fathers that Chalcedon be chosen in place of Nicaea. The Fathers were displeased that the synod was being transferred elsewhere. They therefore replied through Atticus, the Constantinopolitan deacon, that they feared that, if the synod were held at Chalcedon, Eutyches—who possessed influence through his faction—might exploit the location, create disturbances, and frustrate the Fathers’ expectation.

Marcian replied that he would ensure that Eutyches attempted nothing against the synod. He therefore urged them to come to Chalcedon, lest delay prove more harmful than fear and alarm.

**501 SYNOPSIS OF THE ACTS OF THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON.**
The Fathers, having received the emperor’s letter, came of their own accord to Chalcedon. The council was assembled in the basilica of Saint Euphemia the Martyr [Col. 0258A] outside the city on the eighth day before the Ides of October, and concluded on the Kalends of November. At that time there were [Note: [Col. 0257D] The number of sessions of this council cannot be determined with certainty. Seven sessions, concerning general matters of faith and discipline, were preserved both in Greek and in Latin manuscripts. Indeed, Pelagius II testifies in his letter to Elias and the bishops of Istria, no. 19, *Conciliorum* vol. VI, Venetian edition, col. 275, that most of the older Greek manuscripts contain the council only in six sessions, followed by the canons, and omit altogether the other matters raised through private initiative.

The particular cases are not transmitted uniformly in the surviving manuscript books. Some sessions survive in Greek copies but are missing from the Latin ones, such as the sessions concerning Photius of Tyre and Carosus and Dorotheus. Others survive in Latin but are absent from the Greek, such as the session concerning Domnus of Antioch, which the manuscripts of Rusticus place first. Still others occur in certain Greek manuscripts but are found neither in other Greek copies nor in Latin ones, such as the session in which Leo’s letter to the council was read. We found this only in the Greek manuscripts of Saint Mark’s Library at Venice and inserted it into the appendix to Saint Leo’s letters.

The Greek manuscript used by Evagrius likewise lacked the sessions concerning Photius of Tyre and Carosus and Dorotheus. They were also absent from the Alexandrian manuscript which Liberatus received in Latin translation; for each of them, in recounting the history of the sessions of Chalcedon, omits these two sessions. A single Latin Vatican manuscript presents another session concerning Domnus, published by Baluze and to be reprinted by us in the notes to Dissertation 9; it is useless to seek it in any other Greek or Latin book.

Since each manuscript suffers from some omission, we do not know whether, even from all the copies discovered so far, we possess every session, or whether some still lie hidden or have perished. If, however, two sessions are added to the nineteen previously published—one concerning Domnus, published by Baluze, and the other concerning the aforesaid letter of Leo, which we published—the sessions of Chalcedon that have appeared up to the present number twenty-one. Quesnell counted only eighteen previously published, because he considered the published session concerning Domnus spurious; this will be discussed below in note 27 ([Col. 0267], no. a).

[Col. 0258D] Manuscripts differ not only in the number of sessions but also in their order. All agree on the first session. In others, however, the second session is the deposition of Dioscorus, which is placed third in the printed editions; and they move the printed second session into third place. Such are the Greek manuscripts of Saint Mark’s Library at Venice, nos. 164 and 555, as well as the Greek copy from which Evagrius presents this order.

The same order evidently prevailed in the Greek copy used by the Fathers of the Fifth Council. This can be inferred from Collation 6, in which they quoted Leo’s letter from the third session of what was done at Chalcedon, although it belongs to the printed second session. The ancient Latin version contained in the Paris manuscript cited by Baluze likewise presents a similar order. Facundus also testifies that he saw similar copies, book V, chapter 3.

Rusticus too, although he followed the printed order in his edition, cites manuscripts having the same order. For example, in his annotation on chapter 7, before the acts, where he speaks of Leo’s letter to Flavian, he says: “It is not placed with these letters because in the acts of the holy and universal council of Chalcedon it is inserted into the THIRD session.” Today it is in the second.

The printed order seems to have been followed among the Greek manuscripts used by the Roman editors. In the Greek Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark, no. 555, although the first hand called the session concerning Dioscorus “second” (*δευτέρα*), and called the session in which Leo’s letter was read “third” (*τρίτη*), the second hand erased *δευτέρα* in the first place and wrote *τρίτη* over it, while in the second place it deleted *τρίτη* and wrote *δευτέρα* over it.

In the margin of the session concerning Dioscorus, whose title was corrected first, this note appears:

> “Let the reader know that, by mistake, the third session has been placed before the second; the one written after this must be read first, where the sign o-o appears.”

This Greek annotator seems to have obtained some older manuscript from which he derived this order and this correction. Rusticus and Liberatus likewise followed the same order.

The dates marked both in the Greek and in the Latin manuscripts certainly prove that the session in which Leo’s letter was read came earlier, while the session concerning Dioscorus came later. The former is dated the sixth day before the Ides, the latter the third day before the Ides of October. Only in the Paris manuscript of the ancient translation do we read “on the Ides” instead of “on the sixth day before the Ides,” where the numeral VI was accidentally omitted; otherwise it should have been written “on the day of the Ides,” or “on the Ides.”

This notation of the dates, preserved in the very manuscripts that present a different order, is so clear to us that, unless other manuscripts offer a different chronological indication, there should be no doubt on this point. Facundus, however, thinks that this order was altered in the manuscripts against the authority of the originals, and that the session in which Dioscorus was deposed was joined to the first. He gives as the reason that in the first session the same Dioscorus had been judged deserving of deprivation of episcopal honor, so that his condemnation would naturally follow immediately.

He adds: “Moreover, not only the preliminary notation of the dates, but also the substance of the sessions themselves—that is, the second and third—when they are read, shows that in the manuscripts the third session, concerning Dioscorus, was placed before the second; and perhaps for this reason Facundus, Rusticus, and the others restored the original order.”

See Tillemont, note 45 on Saint Leo, where he lucidly confirms this printed order from the context of the sessions.

Another difference of order concerns the session containing the twenty-seven canons. In the printed editions, and likewise in Liberatus and Rusticus, this is session XV. The Greek manuscripts used by the Roman editors agree. The Greek manuscripts of Saint Mark’s Library at Venice, however, present the canons in session 7. The same was found in the Latin Acumitan manuscript cited by Rusticus in his annotation on session 15:

> “The Acumitan manuscript: Ecclesiastical regulations promulgated by the holy, great, and universal council assembled at Chalcedon.”

The same manuscript:

> “Session VII.”

In the most ancient manuscript of the Veronese chapter, no. 55, which contains an unpublished translation of these canons from the Greek, the following title is placed before them:

> “Acts of the seventh session of the council of Chalcedon.”

Two manuscripts of the ancient version, the Paris manuscript and that of Queen Christina of Sweden, cited by Baluze, place the canons after the sixth session. Evagrius agrees with this, writing in book II, chapter 18, that the canons were established when the emperor exhorted the council during the sixth session.

Pelagius II, in his letter to Elias and the bishops of Istria, no. 17, testifies that in many manuscripts the canons are assigned to the seventh session. He says:

> “In its sixth session the profession of the holy faith is completed; immediately afterward, in the seventh, the rule of the canons is established for the instruction of the faithful. In the later sessions nothing concerning the cause of the faith is addressed, but only private affairs are handled. Since your representatives were uncertain whether this was so, we took care to demonstrate it by examining many manuscripts.”

Anatolius’s letter 101 to Leo, which we have published, seems plainly to confirm this view. For in chapter 4, after recounting the proceedings at Chalcedon concerning the faith, which were concluded in session 6, he adds:

> “Since it was also necessary for us to consider other matters, so that so great a council might be seen to address everything without omitting anything requiring correction or approval, whether in canonical or ecclesiastical matters, etc.”

By placing the canons before the ecclesiastical matters, he indicates that the session concerning the canons preceded the other sessions concerning ecclesiastical affairs.

It is strange that in this session of the canons neither the day nor the persons who were seated are recorded, although this is preserved in all the other sessions. For this reason Pelagius, in the passage cited, no. 18, thought, not implausibly, that the canons did not properly belong to a session distinct from the preceding sixth. We might more correctly say that they did not belong to a distinct day. For although the subjects of faith and of the canons were different, they could have been assigned to different sessions even if established on the same day.

Indeed, when the emperor was present at the sixth session, after the definition of the faith and the subscriptions of the Fathers, and before dismissing them, he proposed to those same Fathers that four canons be enacted; these are found among the twenty-seven. They seem to have satisfied the most deserving Augustus immediately, so that the customary opening was unnecessary.

The dates marked in the following sessions confirm the printed order. It should only be noted that the sessions concerning Photius of Tyre and Carosus and Dorotheus, which have emerged solely from Greek manuscripts, although dated the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, and therefore placed before the fifth session in the printed editions, are nevertheless written in the Greek Venetian manuscripts of Saint Mark after the final session. The same was found in the manuscript of Balsamon, who, in his scholion on canon 29 of Chalcedon, says that the session concerning Photius was written at the end of the Fourth Council. Cardinal Casanata found the same thing in two Greek Vatican manuscripts, nos. 831 and 1138, as Baluze testifies.

This occurred because these two sessions were absent from all, or nearly all, manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection at the beginning, and were later discovered and added at the end of those manuscripts. Baluze and Hardouin, together with Father Lupus, suspect an error in the date of the session concerning Photius of Tyre, because the affairs of the bishops are reported as having been treated after the definition of the faith. But those who transmitted this account were writers whose manuscripts lacked these sessions. Eustathius of Berytus’s statement in the same session concerning Photius shows that the case was heard before the definition of the faith.] eighteen sessions. Liberatus, in his *Breviary*, counts fifteen. Sixteen are found in the Acts, with several placed under the same number.

## 503. Session I

In the first session, Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum and legate of the Apostolic See, requested that Dioscorus withdraw from the council. This was Leo’s mandate: Dioscorus was to be admitted not as a judge but as an accused party; otherwise Paschasinus would withdraw with his colleagues.

The matter was prolonged for some time by dispute. It seemed harsh to expel the chief primate of the East from the council. The judges ordered that he sit in the middle, so that he would appear more like an accused man than a judge.

[Col. 0260A] Then Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, requested permission to accuse Dioscorus, saying that he had been treated by him in an unworthy manner, that the faith of the Church had been corrupted, and that Flavian had been struck down by him.

The written accusation was then read. Eusebius had first presented it to Marcian, but it had been reserved for the council. Dioscorus replied that Flavian’s condemnation had been lawfully pronounced in a council assembled by the emperor’s authority. He therefore requested that the Acts be read, so that his own innocence might be established. He thought that the Fathers had neither so much leisure as to spend their time reading the Acts nor the ability to repel the accusation by alleging that the Acts were false.

But when Eusebius also demanded this, and many were preparing to expose the falsity of the proceedings, Dioscorus changed his position and requested that the matter of the faith be addressed first. The judges, on the contrary, ordered that the Acts of the pseudo-council of Ephesus be reread.

When the decree of Theodosius concerning the council was being read, the reading reached Theodoret, whom the emperor had ordered to remain away from the council. The judges requested that Theodoret be brought into the council, since he had been summoned by Marcian and restored to his seat by Leo after being admitted to communion.

The Illyrian, Palestinian, and especially Egyptian bishops objected and demanded with loud cries that he not be admitted. Nevertheless, a place was given to him in the middle, so that he might sit as an accuser. The judges adopted this middle course for calming tempers, partly because Theodoret had presented the emperor with a petition in which he rejected the charge of heresy, and partly because, although he had been received by Leo, his case was not considered concluded.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] More accurately: He had not yet actually been restored to his own see. Although Leo, by letters bearing his signature to Flavian, received him into communion and thereby restored his episcopate to him in some sense, actual restoration was left by Leo to his legates at the council, as will be explained more fully in the notes to Dissertation 10.]

Certainly it was known that he and the other bishops deposed at Ephesus had been deposed contrary to the canons, where everything had been conducted as in a brigandage. Thus the Eastern bishops said:

> “The soldiers deposed them more than we did, because in everything we did we were compelled by fear,”

as the Acts record.

But were they therefore free from guilt? Let others decide. The Egyptians spoke better:

[Note: [Col. 0261D] “A Christian fears no one; an orthodox Christian fears no one. Let fire be brought, and we shall learn. If they feared human beings, they would not be martyrs.” *Acts of Chalcedon*, session I.]

> “A Christian fears no one; a catholic fears no one. Let fire be brought, and we shall learn. If they feared human beings, they would not become martyrs.”

Afterward, driven by the goads of conscience, all the bishops cried out:

[Note: [Col. 0261D] “We have all sinned; we all ask forgiveness.” In the same session below.]

> “We have all sinned; we all ask forgiveness.”

The reading of the pseudo-Ephesine council then continued, and Dioscorus was accused of having forbidden the reading of Saint Leo’s letter. The Acts of the Constantinopolitan council held under Flavian were also read, including the condemnation pronounced against Eutyches. The proceedings of the Constantinopolitan assembly were reported, together with several writings of Saint Cyril and certain passages from the great Council of Ephesus.

Then everyone’s support for Flavian became evident. Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum were cleared of the stain of heresy, and it was declared that they had been removed from the priesthood and deprived of communion contrary to justice and right.

Dioscorus of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eusebius of Ancyra, Eustathius of Berytus, and Basil of Seleucia—the authors of the Ephesian brigandage—were declared subject to the same punishment which they had unjustly inflicted on Flavian and the others, on the following condition:

> “If it should please our most divine and pious Lord,”

as the Acts state, to whom the Fathers judged that the whole session should be referred.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] It was not the Fathers but the imperial judges who made this judgment at the end of session I.]

“And all the matters that have subsequently been conducted,” they added, “are to be referred to the sacred imperial presence.”

I would not have this omitted, so that earlier editions of the councils may be corrected, for they also led Baronius into error. It is clear from this that Marcian was not yet present at the council. He is not found to have arrived before the sixth session, nor was it necessary to refer to him matters handled in his presence.

## 506. Session II

In the second session, held on the sixth day before the Ides of October, the matter of the faith was addressed; indeed, as the judges said, it was chiefly for this reason that the council had been assembled.

All immediately agreed that no other rule of faith should be received than that which had formerly been approved by the 318 Fathers at Nicaea and the 150 at Constantinople. Against Eutyches, the exposition of the faith expressed by the most holy bishop Leo in his letter was sufficient. All had subscribed to it; all professed this faith; it had been received by everyone.

The Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds were then read, along with two synodical letters of Cyril—one to Nestorius and the other to John of Antioch—and Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] The testimonies of the Fathers do not belong to the Acts of Chalcedon. Consequently they are found neither in the Greek nor in the Latin manuscripts, nor even in the ancient editions of the councils in this session. They were merely appended to the Greek version of Leo’s letter to Flavian, which had been copied before the Acts and was improperly transferred here by the Roman editors. See our admonition in letter 28, no. 8.]

The testimonies of the Fathers, which are reported in the Acts, were also brought forward. Then the Fathers unanimously burst into these acclamations:

> “This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the apostles. We all believe this; the orthodox believe this. Anathema to him who does not believe this. Peter has spoken thus through Leo. The apostles taught thus. Leo taught piously and truly. Cyril taught thus. Eternal memory to Cyril. Leo and Cyril taught alike. Leo and Cyril taught thus; anathema to him who does not believe thus.”

When the Syrian and Palestinian bishops anxiously inquired about certain passages in the letter, these were confirmed by similar testimonies of Cyril. Then every opportunity for doubt was removed: Leo’s letter was declared to be the faith of the Church.

The most magnificent judges and the most illustrious senate said:

> “After all this, who still doubts?”

The most reverend bishops replied:

> “No one doubts.”

The session concluded with the acclamations of the Eastern bishops, who demanded that Dioscorus be sent into exile, while the Illyrian bishops objected that, since all had sinned, all should be spared.

## Session III

The third session took place on the third day before the Ides of October. Dioscorus was accused, and Eusebius of Dorylaeum acted as prosecutor. When a charge concerning heresy and impiety was brought, it was decided that Dioscorus should be summoned to judgment.

He was summoned a second and a third time but refused to come, at one time pleading illness and at another alleging that the judges were absent. The reply was that, when canonical judgments were under examination, according to the rule of the Church, neither judges nor laymen had a place.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] “For when canonical matters are being examined, neither rulers nor any other laymen ought to be present,” etc. *Acts of Chalcedon*, session 3.]

Meanwhile petitions were read against Dioscorus from Ischyrion, a deacon of Alexandria; Athanasius, a presbyter and formerly the nephew of Cyril; and Sophronius. In these petitions Dioscorus was charged with numerous crimes.

But when Dioscorus contemptuously refused to come even after being summoned a second and third time, the legates of Saint Leo—with the exception of Julian, who delivered his judgment according to his own order—pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him.

Since he had been found guilty of heresy, he was deprived of episcopal dignity and priestly ministry. He was also condemned because he had received Eutyches into communion after Eutyches had been canonically excommunicated; because he had forbidden Saint Leo’s letter to be read at the Council of Ephesus; because he had dared to cut Saint Leo off from communion; and because, after being summoned three times to the council to answer the charges, he had refused to come.

The Fathers were then asked to give their judgments as well. They pronounced according to the judgment of the legates and approved the condemnation by their subscriptions.

The council’s judgment was announced to Dioscorus. A written report of the matter was sent to the Alexandrians, to the emperor, and to the empress. Since Dioscorus was boasting that he would be restored to his see, the council gave a formal notification to the Constantinopolitans and the Chalcedonians, making it clear that, with all hope of his see removed, Dioscorus had been deposed from the episcopate.

## Session IV

The fourth session began briefly on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November. After the matters previously conducted had been reread, the judges asked what the Fathers thought of Saint Leo’s letter.

The Fathers said in order that it agreed with the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople. Each word had been carefully examined. It contained no doctrine other than that proclaimed in the ecumenical councils. It was the doctrine which Cyril had expounded in his exposition of the faith at Ephesus and in his letters, and for this reason they subscribed to it.

Some bishops indicated that certain passages seemed perplexing and doubtful to them. But when they were reminded that their doubts arose from particular words and expressions, they freely subscribed, each in his own terms.

Some said:

> “Certain words in the letter itself hindered us, as though they indicated division and separation. We wished to understand these matters in that way, and from the beginning, before your Clemency, we were uncertain about them. Then, ordered by your Magnificence to withdraw, we heard from the holy Fathers—bishops and presbyters who occupied the place of the most holy, God-loving, and eminent archbishop Leo—that they say there is no division in our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, but that he is one and the same Lord, the Son of God. For this reason we agreed and subscribed to the Tome.”

These statements concerned Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, in the presence of the legates. None of them was disturbed or complained that the letter of so great a pontiff—sent from the Roman council and subscribed by many bishops of both East and West, a letter never more authoritatively approved, more maturely decreed, or published with greater splendor—was again subjected to examination.

[Note: [Col. 0263B] In the second session, when the imperial judges requested an exposition of the faith, the Fathers declared that Leo’s letter, which all had subscribed as a standard, was sufficient against the errors of Eutyches. Thus Cecropius, bishop of Sebastopolis, said: “Matters concerning Eutyches have arisen, and a standard has been given concerning them by the most holy archbishop of the city of Rome; we follow him, and we have all subscribed to the letter.” The most reverend bishops cried out: “We all say this; what has been expounded is sufficient; another exposition may not be made.”

To satisfy the judges in some measure, since they desired universal agreement, Leo’s letter against the Eutychian heresy was read after the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds and Cyril’s letters against Nestorius, and it was immediately approved without any special examination. After the letter had been read, the most reverend bishops cried out: “This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the apostles. We all believe thus; the orthodox believe thus. Anathema to him who does not believe thus. Peter has spoken thus through Leo,” and so forth.

When the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops, because of the difference of language, expressed doubts about certain passages of the letter, five days were granted so that, after discussion with Anatolius, those who doubted might be instructed.

The examination was instituted solely to bring those who doubted to the correct meaning; it was not because the Fathers believed that anyone could safely doubt the letter, which they had already universally received as the standard of the faith. Thus Anatolius openly declared the necessity of meeting in council together with the pontiff’s definition in these words, letter 101:

> “It was necessary … that everyone’s understanding should converge upon the meaning of your correct faith.”

When those who had been uncertain had been instructed at the meeting held with Anatolius, the votes of all the bishops were sought in session IV so that the agreement of all might be publicly manifested. The letter itself was not read again, nor was it subjected to a new examination. The votes of those who had doubted also showed that the examination had been useful, since the difficulties obstructing their understanding had been resolved. Thus, by the one spirit and agreement of all, the Catholic faith shone forth ever more clearly and error was condemned.

In this sense and with this purpose the Fathers’ examination of the same letter was free, while the authority of the Apostolic See remained intact. Leo taught this in letter 120, chapter 1. An examination of a dogmatic letter in which it is weighed as uncertain, with freedom to dissent, is hostile to apostolic authority. But an examination seeking universal agreement, the instruction of those who doubt, and their assent—or one in which a judgment distinct from that of the pontiff but harmonious with it is given in council by those who judge matters of faith—does no injury to that authority. It more easily draws the others toward unity and obedience.

Thus the holy pontiff, who in letters 90, chapter 2, and 94 refused to allow discussion in council of the faith established in his letters, as though what had been defined in those letters were still doubtful, did not reject an examination of the same letter when its purpose was to instruct those in error and lead them to accept the truth already defined. The outcome itself showed that this examination had been useful and necessary. Compare what we said in note 14 (previous volume, col. 1048, no. l) on letter 120.

In this same sense, when Vigilius wrote in the *Constitutum*, chapter 15, concerning this letter that he required it to be approved “by comparisons,” he did not mean any other necessity, although some improperly press this interpretation upon the passage. Vigilius’s purpose was to show that the letter to Maris the Persian, which he maintained was not written by Ibas, had not been approved by the Council of Chalcedon. To prove this, he contrasted it with Leo’s letter, which had been approved at that council.

When the Palestinians, the Illyrians, and the supporters of Eutyches objected that Leo’s letter seemed discordant with the Nicene Creed and with the doctrine of Saint Cyril confirmed at the Council of Ephesus, it was necessary, in order either to instruct or refute them, that the agreement of that letter with the Creed and with the Ephesian council—or with Cyril’s doctrine confirmed at that council—be impressed upon the Fathers of Chalcedon through their approvals. In this sense, therefore, Vigilius required it to be approved “by comparisons.” Since this was not done with the letter to Maris the Persian—which, as Vigilius adds, expressly rejected the First Council of Ephesus and defined the dogmas expounded by blessed Cyril to be heretical—he concludes that it cannot be said to have been approved by those same Fathers.]

Then the judges announced to the Fathers, in the emperor’s name, that they were free to decide concerning the supporters of Dioscorus: namely, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea, Eusebius of Ancyra, Basil of Seleucia, and Eustathius of Berytus.

These men were summoned to the council. After approving the council’s faith, pronouncing an anathema against Eutyches, and confirming the Fathers’ decrees by their subscriptions, they were admitted.

A greater dispute arose with the Egyptian bishops. Their subscriptions were demanded. They did not hesitate to curse Eutyches, but they refused to subscribe. Their pretext—or reason—was that it was the custom of the Egyptians and that it was not lawful to subscribe unless the Alexandrian bishop led the way. If someone were given to subscribe and to carry the torch before them, they would not refuse their subscriptions.

The matter was conducted amid great disputes, and the bishops were on the point of being condemned when the judges obtained that, since the Egyptians did not doubt the faith, their subscriptions should be postponed until after the ordination of the Alexandrian bishop. After giving sureties, they were dismissed. Thus the threatening storm was calmed by the prudence and judgment of the judges.

Then the archimandrites and monks were brought in, whose fortunes differed according to the difference of their condition. Some presented petitions on behalf of Eutyches. The council’s common judgment was that they should be sent outside. Their petitions were nevertheless read, and they could not be compelled to condemn Eutyches.

The entry of the others was more welcome. They cursed Eutyches and proclaimed the faith of the council. Then the case of Carosus and Dorotheus, the archimandrites, was taken up first. They were adherents of the Eutychian sect.

## 510. Session V

The session concerning these men followed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. It is placed after the fourth session, although it is not called the fifth. The case of the archimandrites who favored Eutyches was continued.

Three days were granted to Barsumas and the others so that during this interval they might consult among themselves and return to better judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0265C] This concerns the earlier session concerning Carosus and Dorotheus, held on 17 October. In the session held on 20 October, Alexander reported on the petition of these same monks to the emperor and on the emperor’s mind, and they were granted a thirty-day delay.

Tillemont raises several considerable difficulties concerning this session, which we possess only from Greek manuscripts, in note 47 on Leo; nevertheless he does not dare to expunge it as spurious. This session, like the following one concerning Photius of Tyre, was held on 20 October and should properly be session 5. But since these sessions are absent from some Greek manuscripts and from all the Latin ones, while in the other Greek manuscripts discovered up to now they were added at the end, the Roman editors, preserving the old numbering of the sessions, inserted them after the fourth session in accordance with the chronology.]

The monks arrogantly rejected the council’s condition.

The controversy between Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, followed. The dispute concerned the province. Eustathius had claimed jurisdiction over Phoenicia Prima on the basis of letters called *pragmaticae*. The council settled the matter by judgment: the metropolitan right was restored to Photius, from which Eustathius had been deprived, and it was provided that the *pragmaticae* should have no further force.

Since the *pragmaticae* were contrary to the canons:

[Note: [Col. 0265D] “All the *pragmaticae* shall cease; let the canons prevail. For thus the faith is preserved, and each Church will have a secure condition.”]

> “All the *pragmaticae* shall cease; let the canons prevail. For thus the faith is preserved, and each Church will have a secure status.”

## Session V

[Col. 0265B]

On the ninth day before the Kalends of November, the constitution, or creed, of the council was read. The legates of the Apostolic See protested that many things were lacking for overthrowing the Eutychian heresy and that many matters had not been expressed in clear terms.

The matter was referred to the emperor. He decided that six bishops should be selected from the Eastern diocese and three from each of the other dioceses, who, together with Anatolius and the legates, would determine the wording of the definition; alternatively, all the bishops could give their judgment through the metropolitan of each province. He threatened that, if they refused, they would go to the West to a council.

The first condition was accepted. The constitution was completed and received. It contained the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds together with the synodical letters of Saint Cyril. Against the Eutychian perversity, Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian was proclaimed, and it was added that the letter was to be received wholly and entirely:

> “Since it agrees with the confession of that great Peter and serves as a common pillar against those who think perversely, it has been suitably adapted for the confirmation of correct doctrines.”

## Session VI

On the eighth day before the Kalends of November, Marcian, together with Pulcheria and the leading officials of the court, attended the council and addressed it. The definition of the faith was read, approved by the subscriptions of all, and confirmed by various acclamations for the preservation of the Church’s concord.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] We established Pulcheria’s presence in note 12 (previous volume, col. 979, no. c) on letter 101. From this previously unpublished letter of Anatolius we learned several circumstances useful for illuminating this session. Among them, the following is especially important here: the definition of the faith was first placed upon the altar and afterward handed over to Marcian and Pulcheria.]

Deposition for clergy, dismissal from service for soldiers, and exile for the populace were decreed if they presumed to disturb the Church.

Then certain chapters were enacted before the emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] In this session the emperor proposed four chapters for the Fathers to enact. These were established together with the other canons in the session numbered 15 in the printed editions, but in reality session 7, as we proved in note 18 above, col. 257, no. b.]

Monks were forbidden to undertake the founding of monasteries without the bishop’s permission. Clerics were forbidden to lease estates or undertake administration. They were likewise forbidden to transfer from their own Church to another.

## 512. Session VII

The seventh session, held on the seventh day before the Kalends of the same month, settled the case of Juvenal of Jerusalem and Maximus of Antioch, both by the judgment of the council and by the mutual agreement of the parties.

The dispute concerned the provinces: the two Phoenicias were assigned to the Church of Antioch, and the three Palestines to that of Jerusalem.

## Sessions VIII, IX, and X

In the following session, which was the eighth, the proceedings concerning Theodoret were conducted. First he was ordered to pronounce an anathema against Nestorius and Eutyches. Then Leo’s judgment concerning his restoration was approved and confirmed.

The ninth and tenth sessions concerned the case of Ibas, bishop of Edessa. The proceedings conducted concerning him at Antioch, Tyre, and Berytus were reviewed. He had been deposed by the Eutychians and had presented a petition to the emperor. But when the matter was referred to the council, he was found to have lived well and to possess an unimpaired faith, and so he was restored to the priesthood and to his see.

Concerning Nonnus, who had taken his place, the synod decreed that Maximus of Antioch should determine the matter: it pleased the synod that he should not be deprived of the honor of the episcopate until the matter could otherwise be judged together with the bishops of his diocese. It was further decreed [Col. 0266C] that the memory of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus should be abolished and that it should be struck from the number of synods; and that the emperor should be asked to forbid by edict that it be called a synod or that its acts be received. The holy synod had already approved the ordination of Maximus as valid:

> [Note: [Col. 0266C] This was the sole reason by which the synod of Chalcedon, in act 10, approved the ordination of Maximus, as Anatolius reports: namely, that when St. Leo received him into communion, he judged him to preside over the Church of the Antiochenes; following this precedent, Anatolius himself approved it, as did the entire holy council then present. Consider how much deference was paid to apostolic authority! The other bishops likewise confirmed the same point. Only Stephen of Ephesus, who likewise stated this as the sole reason, incidentally said that Maximus had been made bishop canonically; yet Leo contradicts him, testifying that he had accepted Maximus’s ordination—celebrated contrary to the provisions of the canons and without any precedent—out of love for restoring the faith and from a desire for peace (epistle 104, ch. 5, and epistle 106, ch. 2). Quesnellus himself, in note 2 on epistle 81, now 106, could not deny that an ordination of this kind had been carried out contrary to the rules of the canons, since Maximus had been ordained by Anatolius of Constantinople, to whom the see of Antioch did not belong; it must also be added that this occurred while Domnus was still alive, though he had been invalidly deposed in the Ephesian Robber Synod. In Dissertation 10, no. 31, however, he nevertheless deduces the canonical character of Maximus’s ordination from his supposition that it had been celebrated at Antioch. But he advances this without any witness. Anatolius was consecrated bishop of Constantinople toward the end of the year 449; the ordination of Maximus was performed by Anatolius some time before the death of Theodosius, which occurred toward the end of July 450. After Maximus’s ordination, while Theodosius was still alive, a gathering was held at Constantinople in which, on behalf of Eustathius of Berytus, a decree was issued against Photius of Tyre. Although Maximus, despite being present at Constantinople, had not taken part in that decree, he later subscribed to it. Which is more credible: that within a span of a few months Anatolius immediately after his own ordination left Constantinople, hastened to Antioch to ordain Maximus, and then returned to Constantinople and held a gathering concerning Photius of Tyre; or that Maximus, who was staying at Constantinople when this gathering was held, was ordained there as bishop of Antioch—there, where the metropolitans of other provinces subject to the bishop of Constantinople were also accustomed to be consecrated [Col. 0267C], as is clear from act 16 of the Council of Chalcedon—and that Leo censured this action as having been carried out especially contrary to the rules of the canons and without any precedent?]

because [Col. 0267A] he had been legitimately consecrated by the bishops of the province and admitted into communion by the most holy patriarch Leo. For this reason the objection mentioned by a few was superfluous, since the legates of the apostolic see also declared that it should not be counted among the acts of Ephesus. The action concerning Domnus, which follows,

> [Note: [Col. 0267C] This action, held on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, is inserted in the Corbie manuscript of Rusticus’s edition after the action concerning the case of Maximus of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem, and before the action concerning Theodoret, held on the seventh day before the Kalends of the same month. In the other manuscripts of Rusticus—the Veronese, the Vatican manuscripts, and both Divion manuscripts—it is placed before both of these actions. In the printed editions, however, it was more correctly placed, according to the notation of the day, after those same actions, and also after the two actions concerning Ibas, which were held on the sixth and fifth days before the Kalends according to the Greek, or perhaps more correctly on the seventh and sixth days before the Kalends according to the Latin. We shall prove this action concerning Domnus to be genuine in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 9, where we shall reprint another action held in the same case of Domnus and Juvenal on the day of, or the day before, the Kalends of November.]

is fictitious, as we prove elsewhere.

## Actions XI and XII

XII. The controversy between Bassianus and Stephen then occupied actions 11 and 12. The former had been deposed from the see of Ephesus, as we have said, and the latter had been substituted in his place. The judgment was that neither should occupy the see; a third should be ordained; and that the Church should provide the expenses of both.

> [Note: [Col. 0267C] Action 11 was held on the fourth day before the Kalends, and action 12 on the third day before the Kalends of November.]

This was on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

## Actions XIII and XIV

XIII. In the thirteenth action, which took place on the following day, the dispute between Eunomius of Nicomedia and Anastasius of Nicaea was heard. Eunomius complained that, by the edict of Valentinian, the bishop of Nicaea was claiming for himself the rights of a metropolitan. It was judged that Nicaea was subject to Nicomedia; that the edict of Valentinian had conferred honor, not jurisdiction; and that, according to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, there was to be only one metropolitan see in a single province.

The fourteenth action concerned the dispute over the episcopate of the Perrhaeans. Athanasius, the bishop, had been accused by his own people and, when summoned for the third time [Col. 0268A] to appear in court, had neglected to attend. He was therefore deposed. Sabinianus, ordained in his place, was driven from the see by Dioscorus. After the matter had been examined in the synod, the case was referred to Maximus of Antioch, so that he himself might decide concerning Athanasius and settle the dispute by his own judgment within eight months. If Athanasius were found guilty, he was to be deprived of his see; but if innocent, restored. Sabinianus was to retain the honor of a bishop, but not the jurisdiction.

> [Note: [Col. 0267D] On that same day, the day before the Kalends of November, another action was held, in which Leo’s letter to the synod was read. We have published this action, previously unknown, from Greek Venetian manuscripts in the appendix to the preceding volume of St. Leo’s letters.]

## Action XV

XIV. When matters had thus been settled, the clerics of the Church of Constantinople requested that, after the decision concerning the faith and the treatment of the more important affairs, certain matters of lesser importance should, as was customary, be submitted to the synod; they asked that the Fathers establish certain provisions concerning the see of Constantinople. Then the legates, having perceived what was at issue, refused, saying that this was not included in their instructions. The judges declared that the matter belonged to the synod, so that they would not be obliged, if asked, to pronounce a judgment; they immediately withdrew from the synod, followed by the legates. For this is how the matter is reported in the following action [Col. 0268B]. Nevertheless, several of the Fathers drew up canons.

> [Note: [Col. 0267D] The 27 canons attributed to action 15 in the Greek and Latin manuscripts were composed in action 7, as we stated in note 18. Concerning the three other canons that are added in the common editions of the Councils and in the Greek collections of canons later than John the Scholasticus, see the admonition concerning the action of the Council of Chalcedon, which we published from Venetian manuscripts in the aforementioned appendix to the letters of St. Leo. The action concerning the prerogative of the see of Constantinople bears the date of the fifth day before the Kalends of November. But an error has crept in. For in action 13, held on the third day before the Kalends of November, the judges said: “Whatever belongs by right to the most holy Church of Constantinople concerning the ordinations of the province will be examined in due order before the holy council”; by these words the canon concerning the see of Constantinople is indicated as not yet established but still to be enacted. Moreover, when in that same action the ordination of the bishop of Basilinopolis had been assigned to the metropolitan of Nicomedia, Aetius, archdeacon of the Church of Constantinople, protested that no prejudice should be brought against the bishop of the royal city, and added this reason: “For the most holy see of Constantinople either itself performs the ordination at Basilinopolis together with the others, or permits it to be performed.” This right of ordaining all bishops, even those who were not metropolitans, was taken away from the bishop of Constantinople by the Chalcedonian canon, by which only the ordination of metropolitans was reserved to him. Since Aetius therefore wished to prevent this prejudice in that action, the canon concerning the prerogative of the bishop of Constantinople had not yet been established; otherwise he would not have protested when the ordination of the bishop of Basilinopolis was assigned to the bishop of Nicomedia. The canon concerning the see of Constantinople was therefore more correctly dated in the Divion manuscript, in the first hand, to the Kalends of November. In all the manuscripts, both Greek and Latin, it is described in the last place, and Evagrius and Liberatus likewise record it after the action held on the day before the Kalends of November.]

The Greek manuscripts have 30 canons and the Latin 28, of which the twenty-eighth concerns the see of Constantinople. It was renewed and confirmed that, since the Roman Church enjoyed privileges which the Fathers had granted because of the imperial city, the hundred and fifty Fathers assembled at Constantinople under Nectarius had likewise granted corresponding privileges to the see of Constantinople, because New Rome had been adorned with empire and senate just like the old Rome: namely, that it should enjoy the first honor after Rome and should have jurisdiction and authority over the dioceses of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia, and should ordain their metropolitans and the bishops of the barbarians.

> [Note: [Col. 0268C] The privileges of the Roman Church were not granted to it by the Fathers because of the empire, but were established by God through Peter, the prince of the apostles. Having fixed his see at Rome, Peter transmitted to the Roman pontiffs, his successors, the same primacy of divine institution and pre-eminent jurisdiction. The patriarchate by which the Roman pontiff presides over the Western Church under that particular title derives not from Rome as the imperial capital, but from Peter, who established his see in that city and from there propagated the religion throughout the West. The rank of the see of Constantinople, however, which was established by the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople solely because of the imperial prerogative, does not approach the Roman pontificate either in divine institution or in jurisdiction. Therefore it cannot be said that equal privileges were conferred upon it. For this reason the legates of St. Leo immediately opposed the Chalcedonian canon, which uses similar language, because it appeared injurious to the Roman see; St. Leo himself rejected it, and the Fathers of Chalcedon and Anatolius sufficiently acknowledged in epistles 98 and 101 that the canon required his confirmation. Nor did the Latin Church ever approve it after St. Leo. Indeed, the more ancient Greeks themselves did not receive it into their collections of canons before Photius, as is clear not only from Dionysius Exiguus and three other ancient interpreters, who translated the Chalcedonian canons from Greek collections into Latin but did not translate this one, but also from Theodore the Reader and John the Scholasticus, Greek authors of the sixth century, who mention only 27 Chalcedonian canons. Furthermore, the Greek text of the Constantinopolitan canon on which this Chalcedonian canon was constructed uses the words τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς μετὰ τὸν Ῥώμης ἐπίσκοπον (“the prerogatives of honor after the bishop of Rome”), which signify not a primacy or any special jurisdiction, but merely pre-eminence of honor after the bishop of Rome. Since the same word, πρεσβεῖα, is used in the Chalcedonian canon, it must be understood in the same sense, so that by this formula only a pre-eminence of honor after the Roman pontiff was assigned to Constantinople; consequently, it was granted second place after Rome and before the other patriarchs. There was therefore no comparison or discussion of the jurisdictional primacy of the Roman pontiff, which all Catholics have always professed to flow from St. Peter and from divine institution, but only of honorary privileges. Even in these, the bishop of Constantinople was not considered to have an equal or identical rank with the Roman bishop, but a second rank.

> After the Chalcedonian canon had been read, after the legates of the pontiff had been heard—legates who, reciting the Nicene canon according to the customary Latin interpretation, had opposed to it the primacy of the Roman Church expressed by the term τὰ πρωτεῖα—and after the Constantinopolitan canon had been read, which claimed for the bishop of Constantinople pre-eminences of mere honor after the Roman bishop, the judges drew from all these points the conclusion that primacy and pre-eminent honor were to be preserved for the Roman bishop, while the bishop of Constantinople was worthy of the same pre-eminences of honor:

> “Before all else, the primacy [τὰ πρωτεῖα] and the exceptional honor, according to the canons, must be preserved for the God-beloved archbishop of old Rome; but the bishop of the city of New Rome must enjoy the same honorary privileges.”

> By these words they understood that the strictly so-called primacy, τὰ πρωτεῖα, was to be attributed solely to the Roman bishop; but they judged that honorary pre-eminences could be shared with the bishop of Constantinople, while the pre-eminent honor and place nevertheless always remained with the Roman see. Thus Anatolius, in epistle 101 to Leo, reported that it had been established that the bishop of Constantinople should have honor and the first place after the most holy Roman see, because Constantinople too was New Rome. Similar statements occur in epistle 98 of the Council of Chalcedon itself.

> While the particular right of the Roman see over the whole Church remained untouched, as did its patriarchal right over the West, and while the second rank and honor granted to the see of Constantinople by the Council of Constantinople was not to be deprived of every right, the Council of Chalcedon assigned to it jurisdiction over the three dioceses of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace. It assigned this jurisdiction in such a way that, since Leo’s approval was repeatedly sought by letter, this very right was acknowledged to depend upon the Roman pontiff. See, among other passages, epistle 132, ch. 4. Consequently, nothing by this canon was taken away from the right of the Roman see.

> If, then, the privileges of this see were derived from the prerogatives of the empire and of the city of Rome, this was not done in the sense that the Fathers of Chalcedon failed to acknowledge the pre-eminences and rights of the Roman chair as derived from Peter—for elsewhere they professed and revered Peter himself and Peter’s authority in Leo, as is clear from acts 1 and 2 and from the reports addressed to Leo and to the emperor—but because, in approving the canon concerning the see of Constantinople, no other reason could support it except one drawn from similar imperial prerogatives. In this sense, the privileges assigned to both sees were called equal because of equal imperial prerogatives: insofar as Constantinople was granted second place after Rome, both sees stood equally before all the others in honorary pre-eminence.]

## Action XVI

XV. On the following day, when the synod had assembled, Paschasinus, the legate of the apostolic see, made a serious complaint before the judges: after his judgment and departure, certain things had been done contrary to the canons, and he wished them to be read again in his presence. The judges agreed. Beronicianus, secretary of the divine consistory, read a document presented to him by Aetius the archdeacon, in which the privileges of New Rome were set out. When it had been read, Lucentius, the legate of the apostolic see, exclaimed that the bishops had been deceived and compelled [Col. 0269B] to subscribe: the decrees of the Council of Nicaea and of the 318 Fathers had been set aside, and constitutions had been proposed by the distinguished Fathers, though no mention of them existed in the synodical canons. If these privileges were in use, what need was there to confirm them again? If they had never been in use, why ask the synod for a judgment concerning something contrary to the canons and never practiced?

Aetius then asked the legates to produce whatever Leo had instructed them concerning this matter. Boniface, a presbyter and legate of the apostolic see, read this mandate of the most blessed Leo from a written document:

> “You must not permit the constitution of the holy Fathers that has been brought forward to be violated or diminished by any presumption; in every respect preserve the dignity of our person among you, whom we have sent in our place. If anyone, relying on the splendor of his own cities, should attempt to usurp such things for himself, repel him with all the firmness that the matter deserves.”

The canons by which each side defended its case were then read. The judges, however, dared to establish nothing. Lucentius asked that the proceedings of the previous day, which had taken place in the absence of the legates, be expunged; or, alternatively, that the legates’ protest be entered into the record so that they could bring it before the Roman bishop, enabling him to pronounce judgment concerning either the injury done to his see or the overturning of the canons.

Thus the Council of Chalcedon was completed. St. Gregory attributed to it, as to the other three ecumenical councils, only those matters that pertained to the faith.

> [Note: [Col. 0270D] St. Gregory approves only those matters that concern the faith: book II, epistle 10; book IV, epistle 3; and elsewhere.]

He was accustomed to say that he embraced those four councils just as he embraced the four Gospels.

XVI. The outcome of the synod, however, was varied. The defenders of the faith rejoiced; those who had wavered became firm; those whom the Ephesian Robber Synod had led into error came to their senses. The heretics, by contrast, raged, devised new schemes, rushed headlong to destruction, and by their collapse and ruin overwhelmed many, whether knowingly or unwittingly.

Before the Fathers departed, they addressed the Augustus respectfully, either orally or in writing. The Acts preserve that speech, προσφωνητικός (“an address”). The Fathers declare that they give thanks to God above all because they had obtained an emperor whose faith was unshaken and Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, equipped with doctrine, piety, and courage as with weapons for victory. They then explain that what happened in this synod had also happened formerly in other councils, where new falsehoods had been refuted by new definitions, and a new stain healed by a salutary novelty; amid all this, the faith had remained whole and unharmed. They then develop at greater length the sacred οἰκονομία (“dispensation”) and union of the two natures in Christ. They defend the letter of the most holy Father Leo not only from the charge of novelty, but also approve it as consistent with Holy Scripture, the writings of the Fathers, and the decrees of the Council of Nicaea against the doctrines of Eutyches.

XVII. There is also a letter, or report, which the Fathers send to Leo concerning the proceedings of the synod. They extol his letter to Flavian with extraordinary praises; they say that they had been invited by his letter to the synod as to a banquet; and they call him the guardian of Christ’s vineyard. They explain the condemnation of Dioscorus and the proscription of his doctrine. Above all, however, they mention what they had decreed concerning the see of Constantinople and ask that he not withhold his approval of it. The legates had indeed opposed it, but they ask Leo himself to be the author of its confirmation, just as he was of the faith and of sound order.

> [Note: [Col. 0271C] From epistle 101 of Anatolius, which we recovered from a Vatican manuscript and which was sent to Leo together with Marcian’s epistle 100, written on 18 December, it is clear that the legates had already sent the report and acts of the council beforehand; more probably, after the Council of Chalcedon in the month of November, as we observed in note 4 on the same epistle 101 [Col. 0271D] (preceding volume, col. 975, n. c).]

It is uncertain when this letter was written. For I think that the Fathers did not depart immediately, both so that the acts might be transcribed and so that their authority might remain attached to the decrees. It is also established that the legates had not yet returned to Rome two months after the synod: for Leo,

> [Note: [Col. 0271D] We have corrected the date to the sixth day before the Kalends of February from the Ratisbon manuscript. See epistle 102, note 31 [preceding volume, col. 987, n. k).]

writing to the bishops of Gaul at the Kalends of February about the synod, expresses his wish for the safe return of his legates.

Around the beginning of that same month, Marcian restrained by edict the audacity of certain people who were stirring up disturbances from street to street to discuss the faith. In March, by another edict, he confirmed the decrees of the Fathers and ordered them to be observed. In Holstenius’s Roman collection I read a letter of Marcian dated the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the following January and sent to Rome,

> [Note: [Col. 0271D] Through this same Lucian, Anatolius’s epistle 101 was also sent; we published it from a Vatican manuscript. Several matters in these letters deserve attention: first, the necessity of agreeing with the definition of the faith that Leo had issued, ch. 3; second, the necessity of referring to that same pontiff whatever had been done in the synod, chs. 1 and 2; third, the defense of the canon concerning the see of Constantinople, whose approval and confirmation are requested from the pontiff as though necessary, just as Anatolius repeats in epistle 132, ch. 4, saying: “Since the entire force and confirmation of the proceedings has likewise been reserved to the authority of Your Blessedness.” Since the legates had opposed this canon, and the action had been dissolved because of their opposition, everyone understood that the express confirmation of the canon was all the more necessary for it to have force. Therefore the synod in its report, Marcian in his letters, and Anatolius all insisted particularly on obtaining it.]

through Lucian the bishop and Basil the deacon. The Augustus congratulates Leo on the happy outcome of the synod and then asks him to approve as valid the decrees made in favor of the see of Constantinople, which, as is evident from Leo’s replies, had also been written by the empress.

# The Year of Christ 452; the Thirteenth of Pope Leo; the Thirty-Eighth of Valentinian; the Third of the Emperors Marcian; the Consuls Herculanus and Sporatius

I. After hearing what had been done at Chalcedon, St. Leo was uncertain and hesitant. He was affected at once by joy and grief: at one moment considering in his mind the victories of the faith, at another anxiously reflecting on the recent wound inflicted on ecclesiastical discipline by Anatolius, whose treatment was by no means straightforward. Although he wished to address this evil immediately, he nevertheless decided to await the return of the legates, so that he could arrange everything according to judgment and prudence. Meanwhile he informs the bishops of Gaul about the successful proceedings at Chalcedon and the defeat of Dioscorus (epistle 77, now 102), and recommends that they report the same to the bishops of Spain. Again, after the legates’ return, he sends them an encyclical letter concerning the same matter. This is clear from his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne (epistle 82, now 103), Ravennius of Arles, and the other bishops of Gaul, in which he indicates that he is then sending, or had previously sent, copies of the sentence issued against Dioscorus.

After the legates of the Roman apostolic see had returned, St. Leo became certain that Anatolius was disturbing the Church through a new act of ambition. He therefore sends legates with letters to Marcian (epistle 78, now 104), Pulcheria (epistle 79, now 105), Anatolius (epistle 80, now 106), and Julian of Cos (epistle 81, now 107). They were dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. In them he praises the triumphs of the Church as highly as he rebukes Anatolius’s audacity. But I think it worthwhile to investigate briefly, from the beginning, the genuine or doubtful rights of the see of Constantinople, so that everyone may perceive how just Leo’s cause was.

II. The emperor Constantine, setting Rome aside, transferred the seat of the empire to Byzantium. To prevent the impression that he had changed the empire along with its seat, he brought to the new city the same magistrates, the same fasces, and the same insignia, and ordered it to be a new, or younger, Rome. Later, adorned by the glory and splendor of other rulers, the city began to rival the size and power of ancient Rome. As the city increased, the bishop of Byzantium also grew in honor, and gradually a desire to enlarge his power came upon him. Since it was considered improper to impose upon another Church boundaries different from those it had possessed from the beginning, he gradually, as though by stages, began to make his way toward the summit of ecclesiastical power: first claiming for himself the rights of a metropolitan; then seeking the prerogatives of the principal sees; and finally usurping a power equal to, or even greater than, theirs. How he achieved this I shall briefly explain.

At the beginning of the Christian era, the Churches were founded by the apostles from gatherings of the faithful. As the number of believers increased and the faith was disseminated throughout the provinces, a certain Christian πολιτεία (“constitution,” or quasi-commonwealth) began to be established, organized almost according to the pattern of the Roman Empire. Each city had a bishop, and each parish had its own defined boundaries. Several Churches, or cities, of one and the same province were then, as in the empire, subject to a single metropolitan see. I maintain that this arrangement already existed from the apostolic age; nor will anyone who has diligently studied Christian affairs from their very origin deny it.

> [Note: [Col. 0272D] If one excepts the Roman, Alexandrian, Antiochene, and a few other principal sees of the East, which displayed a certain appearance of metropolitan jurisdiction in the age of the apostles, the establishment of the other ecclesiastical metropolises cannot be defended on any basis as contemporary with the apostles. This hierarchical form was certainly established earlier in the East, where the apostles founded several Churches; in the West, it arose later. Something will be said about this in the observations on part II, chapter 5 of Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, where we shall also see that the form of the civil provinces was not preserved in every respect.]

The Council of Nicaea further says that the rights and privileges of the principal sees—the Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian Churches—had arisen from ancient custom. The prerogative of a primate consists of two things: one is honor, the other power and jurisdiction. The latter again has two aspects: first, the ordination of metropolitans; second, the right and ability to summon a synod. It is the constant opinion that the Church of Byzantium then possessed no authority or jurisdiction outside its own parish. Indeed, like the other Churches of Thrace, it was subject to Heraclea of Thrace.

But after the imperial seat was transferred to Asia, the bishop of the new city, as we have said, began to increase first in honor rather than in power. He therefore first sought the prerogative of place, or πρωτοκαθεδρία (“first seat”), and this was granted in the Constantinopolitan synod under Nectarius around the year 381: that he should have the first honor after the Roman bishop. This is found in canon 3, which contains these words: “The bishop of the city of Constantinople is to have the privileges of honor, πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς, after the Roman bishop, because it is New Rome.”

III. Nor was this arrangement considered new in the Church. For previously the privilege of honor, or prerogative of place, had been assigned in canon 7 of the Council of Nicaea to the bishop of Jerusalem. I know that the distinction is this: honor was granted to the bishop of Jerusalem after the three principal sees, and to the bishop of Constantinople after the Roman bishop. Many believe that power and jurisdiction began at the same time as the prerogative of honor. But they should attend to canon 2 of that same council, where the ancient immunity and privileges of the dioceses of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—over which the bishop of Constantinople might otherwise have been able to claim patriarchal jurisdiction—are preserved. It is decreed that the diocese of Asia is governed by the bishops of Asia, the Pontic diocese by the bishops of Pontus, and the Thracian diocese by the bishops of Thrace; and it is provided that the bishops of Alexandria and of the East should not exercise jurisdiction outside the boundaries of their own dioceses. Those three dioceses, therefore—Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—were decreed to be governed by their bishops, that is, by the synods of their own bishops. The bishop of Constantinople consequently had no power over them. Indeed, by this same canon 2, he, like other bishops, was forbidden to hear any case outside his diocese.

IV. Conversely, if jurisdiction of the see of Constantinople had been established in this synod, as they suppose, the decrees of the Council of Nicaea would certainly have been weakened rather than confirmed, and Leo later complains that they were violated by canon 28 of Chalcedon. At that time, then, no power or jurisdiction was granted; only honor and the prerogative of seating were first attributed to the bishop of Constantinople.

Although that canon was rejected and disapproved by the Roman bishop, it was nevertheless put into practice. The evidence is what we read in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, where the acts of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, presided over by Dioscorus, were read. Dioscorus had ordered Flavian of Constantinople to sit after Juvenal of Jerusalem and Domnus of Antioch. When this was read, the Eastern bishops exclaimed:

> “Why did Flavian not sit in his proper place? Why did they place the bishop of Constantinople fifth?”

> Paschasinus, the most reverend bishop, said: “Behold, by God’s will we have the lord Anatolius in the first place, whereas they placed the blessed Flavian fifth.”

> Diogenes, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Cyzicus, said: “Because you know the rules.”

> [Note: [Col. 0273D] Act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon: “Why was Flavian not seated in his proper place? Why did they place the bishop of Constantinople fifth? Paschasinus, the most reverend bishop, said: ‘Behold, by God’s will we have the lord Anatolius in the first place, whereas they placed the blessed Flavian fifth.’”]

Here the honor of place was conspicuously vindicated for the bishop of Constantinople by the very legates of the apostolic see, who accused Dioscorus of the audacity of ordering Flavian to sit fifth. The Council of Chalcedon is praised for granting Anatolius second place, and for doing so on the basis of rules and canons. From this it is clear that only first honor was attributed to the bishop of Constantinople, in honor of the royal city that the emperors had ordered to be New Rome.

V. Thereafter the bishops of Constantinople also began to seize jurisdiction. The opportunity presented itself in this way. Several bishops, as commonly happens, went to the imperial court, sometimes certainly compelled by the needs of their Churches, but more often, as Hosius once complained about the Fathers assembled at Sardica, in order to seek honors and offices for themselves. Consequently there was a great gathering of bishops at Constantinople, and as many as sixty bishops, for the most part, were seen in the royal city. They often went in procession to the Augustus. Many disputes concerning ecclesiastical affairs were then brought before the emperor, and were settled by the counsel and judgment of the bishop of Constantinople. If there were matters of greater importance, they were handled by an assembly of the bishops who were in the city, presided over by the bishop of Constantinople. The Greeks called this kind of council σύνοδος ἐνδημοῦσα (“a resident synod”), because it consisted of bishops who were ἐνδημοῦντες (“resident”).

Although such a gathering did not deserve the name of a council, and although such judgments had force and authority only by the consent of the litigants, the authority of these synods grew through custom. At first, the discussion concerned the governance of the Church; afterward, however, it concerned disputes among metropolitans and questions of faith. Thus Eutyches was condemned under Flavian of Constantinople, and the case of Florentius, bishop and metropolitan of Sardes in Lydia, was heard together with two bishops of his province, as recorded in act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon.

It is difficult to say when these gatherings began. If conjecture has any place, perhaps they began in the time of St. Chrysostom. Driven from his see by the hostility of malicious men, he was later restored after a council had been convened from among the bishops then residing at Constantinople, and the sentence of the previous synod had been rescinded. Thus the bishop of Constantinople acquired the right to convene a synod.

### VI

[Col. 0274C] The procedure for appointing metropolitans was established as follows. The bishop of Constantinople was held in esteem and honor because he resided in the imperial city, where he had the opportunity, through personal intervention and practical assistance, to help others and, by the influence he enjoyed at court, advance their affairs and business. Accordingly, whenever ambitions arose—as commonly happened, and usually produced disturbances—concerning the acquisition of bishoprics and priestly offices, he was summoned. He would immediately appear, suppress the ambitions through the authority of the powerful, and gradually claim for himself a right in the elections.

Moreover, the canons both of the synod of Constantinople and of other synods permitted invited bishops to attend the ordinations of other provinces, and most bishops considered it an honor to have the bishop of the imperial city as a participant in their ordinations. This custom had already become established in the time of St. Chrysostom. Thus he deposed the metropolitan of Ephesus and other bishops found guilty of simony, and appointed others in their place. Even if St. Chrysostom undertook this not out of a desire to extend his jurisdiction, but by the authority of a council, the practice nevertheless became customary, so that afterward he did not hesitate to preside over the ordinations of metropolitans and of the bishops of the other Churches of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace.

Finally, what had been established by usage and long custom was easily transformed into law and right. This is what Anatolius accomplished at the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0275A], when the Fathers promulgated Canon 28. By it he was granted not only the privilege of precedence in seating, but also the right to convene a synod and to ordain metropolitans and other bishops; power and jurisdiction over the three provinces of Asia, Thrace, and Pontus were likewise assigned to him. Those provinces, moreover, belonged to no diocese or patriarchal district; rather, they were then governed by their own synods, in which elections rarely occurred without disturbances, because the bishop of Constantinople advanced their affairs and plans.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] The synod of Constantinople, under Theodosius the Elder, had assigned the bishop of the imperial city second place after the Roman pontiff purely as a matter of honor, without any jurisdiction. The rights which the bishop of Constantinople afterward claimed could therefore be described as usurped rights. Some complaint about this is indeed recorded before the Council of Chalcedon, directed against St. John Chrysostom and against St. Proclus. At Chalcedon, however, Anatolius was attacked three times: first, in the proceedings concerning Photius of Tyre, when the question was raised whether the gathering of bishops who were in Constantinople, convened by him, ought to be considered a synod and whether he possessed the right of a synod. Second, at the end of Action 11, when the bishops of Asia requested that the bishop of Ephesus be ordained not at Constantinople but by them in the province; the bishops, agreeing with them, loudly declared that this was required by the rules of the canons. Third, at the end of Action 13, when the council declared that the ordination of the bishop of Basilinopolis belonged by the canons to the bishop of Nicomedia, not to the bishop of Constantinople.
