For this reason Anatolius, fearing that he might someday be deprived of the right his see had claimed for itself, judged that he must not let this synod’s opportunity pass. And, so that the same right might be confirmed more easily, he yielded the ordination of bishops while insisting that the consecration of metropolitans alone should be entrusted to him. This was easy to obtain because the emperor and the senate favored it, and the bishops of the East showed them great deference. Those whose interests were involved in preventing the elevation of the see of Constantinople were either absent or did not dare to oppose it. Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, had been deposed, and his successor had not yet been ordained; no Egyptians are mentioned among those who signed the proceedings. Maximus of Antioch, ordained by Anatolius, owed him a great deal. Juvenal of Jerusalem, having obtained jurisdiction over the three Palestines contrary to the canons of Nicaea, could not resist what was being granted to the bishop of Constantinople in a similar manner. The chief bishop of Heraclea in Thrace did not attend; in his place Lucian of Byzia signed, and he was so devoted to Anatolius that in this very matter Anatolius sent him as legate to Rome. After Bassianus and Stephen had been deposed, there was no chief bishop of Ephesus in Asia. Only Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia was present; but, having been admitted among the bishops through the highest favor, he did not sign, and in the very proceedings he used words whose meaning is uncertain. No circumstances more favorable could have arisen for Anatolius to accomplish his purpose at the council.]

### VII

As we have said, the legates of the supreme pontiff, observing that these things were being done to the detriment of ecclesiastical discipline and to the injury of the Roman see, publicly opposed the Chalcedonian canon by a formal protest. Leo himself could not be persuaded to confirm this decree—not by the emperor, not by the empress, not by Julian of Cos, his own legate, nor by the earnest petitions of the Fathers of Chalcedon. On the contrary, he resolved to resist in every possible way and to invalidate the decree by the strongest arguments.

First, he maintained that the synod had been summoned to defend the faith [Col. 0275B] and destroy the Eutychian perfidy, not to serve Anatolius’s ambition:

> “By unheard-of and never-before-attempted excesses you have so anticipated events that you have turned the holy synod, which was convened solely for the destruction of heresy and the confirmation of the Catholic faith through the zeal of the most Christian prince, into an opportunity for ambition, and have driven it to grant you its connivance” (Epistle 80, now 106, to Anatolius, ch. 2).

He then charged the bishops with having been either enticed by promises or terrified by threats:

> “This proud elevation tends toward the disturbance of the entire Church. It wished to abuse the synodal council in such a way that it could corrupt and lead to agreement with itself, or compel by fear, brothers who had been assembled only for the business of the faith and who had completed the definition of the matter that had to be settled” (ibid., ch. 3).

Third, he argued that Anatolius’s plans tended toward disturbance and scandal in the Church:

> “Understand wisely what judgment of God you will have to face, since you do not fear bringing scandal upon so many Churches and so many priests” (ibid., ch. 5).

And later:

> “If you seek what is not permitted, you yourself, by your own work and judgment, will deprive yourself of the peace of the universal Church” (ibid., ch. 6).

Fourth, he repeatedly emphasized that the canons of Nicaea had been violated and despised:

> “I grieve that your Love has advanced so far in this matter that you have attempted to infringe the most sacred constitutions of the Nicene canons—as though this time had conveniently presented itself to you, in which the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of the third dignity, so that, with these sees subjected to your authority, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor.… These acts, therefore, are exceedingly wicked and exceedingly perverse, since they are found to contradict the most sacred canons” (ibid., ch. 2).

It is evident that Anatolius violated many decrees of the Council of Nicaea. For Nicene Canon 6 commands that certain provinces belong to their own jurisdiction and be governed by their own synods; this is clear wherever the rights of the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch are asserted. Thus the canon says:

> ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὴν Ἀντιοχείαν καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἄλλαις ἐπαρχίαις τὰ πρεσβεῖα σώζεσθαι ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις.

“Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges be preserved for the Churches.”

Canon 2 of the Constantinopolitan synod explains that those provinces were Pontus, Asia, and Thrace [Col. 0276A], whose jurisdiction Anatolius had invaded.

Furthermore, the bishop of Constantinople had arrogated to himself second place after the bishop of Rome, and had thrust the bishop of Alexandria down to third place and the bishop of Antioch to fourth. This too was contrary to the Council of Nicaea, where it had formerly been established that each Church should retain its own honor.

The rights of exarchs and metropolitans were likewise abolished. The metropolitan, or exarch, of Heraclea in Thrace was stripped of his jurisdiction by the bishop of Constantinople. At first Constantinople itself was subject to him; then, when the order of affairs was changed, he became subject to the bishop of Constantinople by usurpation. Under the pretext of the honor of being first after the bishop of Rome, the bishop of Constantinople gradually deprived the bishop of Heraclea both of the right to preside over the synods of his province and of the right of ordination. St. Leo rebuked this:

> “Let not the rights of the provincial primates be overturned” (same epistle, ch. 5).

He is speaking of the exarchs of Thrace, Asia, and Pontus, to whom the metropolitans of their respective dioceses were subject. [Col. 0276B] St. Leo adds:

> “Nor let metropolitan bishops be deprived of the privileges established from ancient times.”

This concerns the metropolitans subject to those three exarchs. Our pontiff continues:

> “Let nothing be lost from the dignity of the see of Alexandria, which it merited through the holy evangelist Mark, the disciple of blessed Peter; and, although Dioscorus has fallen through the obstinacy of his impiety, let the splendor of so great a Church not be darkened by the shadows of another’s wrongdoing. Let the Church of Antioch also, in which the Christian name first arose when blessed Peter the apostle preached, remain in the order of its paternal constitution, so that, placed in the third rank, it may never become inferior.”

### VIII

Anatolius and the other Fathers who had established Canon 28 at Chalcedon defended the Chalcedonian decree by appealing to Canon 3 promulgated at Constantinople under Nectarius. Leo, however, attempted by many arguments to destroy its force, asserting that it had not come to the knowledge of the Roman pontiff and that nothing could have any validity which was vain and void from its very origin:

> “In no respect does the written decision of certain bishops made, as you claim, sixty years ago support your persuasion—never having been transmitted by your predecessors to the knowledge of the apostolic see. From the beginning, you wished to bring forward late and useless supports for something already fallen and long collapsed, extracting from the brothers the appearance of a consent which their wearied modesty would offer you to the injury of their own dignity” (same epistle, ch. 2).

St. Leo complains that the Constantinopolitan canon was not indeed spurious, but unknown and not reported to the apostolic see. From the Acts of Chalcedon it is clear that it was unknown to Lucentius and the other legates, for Lucentius denied that it was found among the synodal acts.

[Note: [Col. 0276D] “It appears to have been added to the decrees of the three hundred and eighteen and to those one hundred and fifty subsequently mentioned, although these are not included among the synodal canons, which they say were established.” Acts 16 of Chalcedon.]

Leo adds:

> “It is an additional circumstance that, with the constitutions of the 318 set aside, the 150 are known to have been mentioned only by way of reference, although they are not found in the synodal canons.”

But after the Constantinopolitan canon had been read from the acts, they did not dare to say anything further against it. I know that some writers say that the decree of Constantinople was rejected by Damasus. But how can this be reconciled with what is stated by St. Leo, who says that it was unknown to the apostolic see and says nothing whatever about a protest by Damasus—something which he certainly ought not to have omitted?

### IX

St. Leo next argues that the Chalcedonian canon is outweighed by the excellence and superiority of the Nicene synod of the 318 Fathers, whose authority can be shaken by no force and by no decree. St. Leo says:

> “As though what a multitude may have unlawfully desired could not be refuted, and as though that ordinance of the Nicene canons, established through the truly Holy Spirit, could be dissolved in any respect. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the multiplication of their assemblies, and let no number of priests, however much larger, dare either to compare itself with those 318 bishops or to place itself above them. The Council of Nicaea was consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more persons, whatever differs from the constitution of those Fathers is entirely devoid of authority” (same epistle, ch. 2).

He repeats this frequently in his letters, and in the same letter also writes:

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius together with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would endure to the end of the world live among us and throughout the whole world in their constitutions. And if anything is ever presumed contrary to what they established, it is annulled without hesitation” (same epistle, ch. 4).

From this it is clear that the Nicene canons were held in the highest veneration, both because of the authority and holiness of those who established them and because of the faith which they had courageously professed even at the risk of life and blood, thereby confirming ecclesiastical laws drawn from apostolic men.

Hence Leo’s magnificent judgment concerning that council: he proclaims himself its executor and guardian and declares that nothing could induce him, for Anatolius’s sake, to contradict its decrees. He says:

> “Even if Anatolius had been lawfully and solemnly ordained on the basis of the greatest merits and the soundest judgment, nevertheless, against the reverence due to the canons of the Fathers, against the statutes of the Holy Spirit, and against the examples of antiquity, he could be aided by no support” (Epistle 78, now 104).

And again:

> “The privileges of the Churches established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable synod can be overturned by no wickedness and violated by no innovation. In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, I must necessarily persevere in service, because a stewardship has been entrusted to me, and it will become my responsibility if, with my connivance—which God forbid—the rules of the paternal decrees established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of God’s Spirit are violated” (ibid.).

Petrus de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse, comments that St. Leo rejected the Chalcedonian canons because they had been written against the Nicene canons. “Therefore,” says that celebrated author, “Leo does not reject the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon under that designation”—as though they would have had no force unless Leo had first been willing to approve them—but he declares that the nullity of the canon was derived from its contradiction of the Nicene canons. This was indeed a magnificent and illustrious privilege of his primacy, or principate, but one that ought not to be extended and carried into an authority exercised over the body and determinations of a council.

[Note: [Col. 0277C] Leo did not use this argument because, since he insisted upon observing the Nicene canons, he had no need of it. The Fathers of Chalcedon confidently assumed that the canon issued for the see of Constantinople, although contrary to the Nicene canons, would be ratified if Leo were willing; therefore they urgently requested his confirmation as entirely necessary.

[Col. 0277D] See Epistles 98, 101, and 132, ch. 4.

Moreover, it was certain to the holy pontiff that, without danger to the soul, the Nicene canons—venerated by the whole Church—could not rashly be diminished, nor could prejudice be inflicted upon the privileges of the apostolic Churches and ancient metropolitans, privileges confirmed by so great a council, merely to favor the new ambitions and aspirations of the bishop of Constantinople.

When the good of peace and concern for the faith demanded it, he did not hesitate, by a certain pastoral accommodation, to depart from the strictness of those same canons, as when he received Maximus of Antioch into communion, although he had been ordained contrary to the Nicene canons. Through this single act of Leo’s accommodation, Maximus was received at the Council of Chalcedon itself as the true bishop of Antioch, as we saw in note 26 above [Col. 0266, n. e], concerning the preceding year.

But to abolish a Nicene canon, some important cause relating to the public good or to the necessity of the Church is required. Since Leo did not see such a cause in the case of the Constantinopolitan canon, he believed that he must not depart from the Nicene rules, giving this reason: “Because a stewardship has been entrusted to me,” and so forth.

[Col. 0278C] The power of the pontiff is certainly supreme; but since it was conferred for edification, not destruction, he ought to promote observance of the canonical laws in force in the Church, not abolish them without just cause and reason. Therefore, even if Leo could, by absolute authority, have confirmed the Chalcedonian canon and derogated from the Nicene canons, as the Fathers of Chalcedon requested, he nevertheless ought not to do so rashly or without an especially just cause—which did not appear to him as just as it was represented by those who requested it. Thus he wrote with complete truth:

[Col. 0278D] “It will become my responsibility if the rules of the paternal decrees … are violated with my connivance.”]

If, however, the Council of Chalcedon had made a decision concerning some question not yet settled by the Nicene rules, far from Leo having opposed that constitution by alleging the defect of nullity, he would rather have adhered officially to the council’s judgment by approving its synodal acts.

Pope Leo elegantly suggests this in his letter to Maximus of Antioch (Epistle 92, now 119, ch. 5), speaking of the matter:

> “Whatever is brought before episcopal judgment apart from the particular causes of synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication, if nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever is at variance with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.”

Such is the comment of the learned archbishop.

### X

Anatolius also defended the rights attributed to him by appealing to the dignity and greatness of the imperial city [Col. 0278B]. St. Leo entirely rejects this argument, because patriarchal authority arose not merely from an imperial city but also from an apostolic see:

> “Let him not despise the imperial city, which he cannot make an apostolic see” (Epistle 78, now 104, to Marcian, ch. 3).

Although ecclesiastical polity took account of the primacy of the great cities, patriarchal authority was asserted for the cities of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch not so much because they were primary and most noble cities as because it was derived from apostolic institution and from ancient and long-standing custom, as the Council of Nicaea states. This in no way applies to the see of Constantinople, whose rights were first decreed at the Council of Constantinople approximately sixty years earlier [Col. 0278C]. St. Leo rebukes this:

> “It is exceedingly presumptuous, in order to dissolve the decrees of the venerable Fathers, to bring forward the agreement of certain bishops, when the succession of so many years has denied it effect” (Epistle 79, now 105, to Pulcheria, ch. 2).

For nearly sixty years, he says, this connivance is alleged to have existed, by which the aforementioned bishop thinks he is supported.

Leo adds that it achieved no effect—not because the bishop of Constantinople did not enjoy in the East the honor of precedence in seating, but because that right was not recognized in the West.

Since the legates of Leo had approved the second place of honor granted to the bishop of Constantinople from the beginning of the Council of Chalcedon and had complained that it was denied to him in the pseudo-synod by Dioscorus, this is why St. Leo declares that, whatever may have been permitted or admitted by his legates, was entirely rescinded:

> “If anything is said to have been done by these brothers whom I sent in my place to the holy synod beyond what concerned the cause of the faith, it will have absolutely no validity, because they were sent from the apostolic see for this sole purpose: that, errors having been cut away, they should be defenders of the Catholic faith” (Epistle 92, now 119, to Maximus of Antioch, ch. 5).

Finally, he accuses Anatolius’s plans of invading the rights of others by taking advantage of a time when both primates of the East appeared unworthy of their prerogative and rank, one having departed from the faith and the other having abandoned the defense of the faith:

> “As though this time had conveniently presented itself to you, in which the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of the third dignity, so that, with these sees subjected to your authority, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor” (Epistle 80, now 106, to Anatolius, ch. 2).

He then adds:

> “The sees are one thing; those who preside over them are another.… Although Dioscorus has fallen through the obstinacy of his impiety, let the splendor of so great a Church not be darkened by the shadows of another’s wrongdoing” (ibid.).

He further proves that it is unlawful to scatter the rights of many and strip numerous metropolitans of their authority so that Anatolius’s dignity may increase and the ambition of one man may be served while ancient custom is neglected:

> “It will become my responsibility … if the will of one brother is more important to me than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord” (Epistle 78, now 104, ch. 3).

And again:

> “It is exceedingly proud and immoderate to extend oneself beyond one’s proper boundaries, to trample upon antiquity and seek to seize another’s right, and, in order that the dignity of one man may increase, to attack the primacies of so many metropolitans” (Epistle 79, now 105, ch. 2).

These and similar things were said by St. Leo against Anatolius. What followed from them we shall discuss below in its proper order.

### XI

In the same year in which Leo was dealing with these matters with the Easterners, he received a letter from Theodore, bishop of Forojulium in Gaul, who consulted him about the discipline of penance. Leo replied (Epistle 83, now 108) that God’s forgiveness cannot be obtained except through the supplications of priests; sinners must wash away their offenses through the practice of penance and afterward be admitted to communion.

Those, however, whom imminent danger or the force of illness presses should not be denied reconciliation if they request it, or if the testimony of the faithful standing around them proves that they had previously requested it.

Nor should I omit to mention that St. Leo rebuked this bishop because he had approached him without first consulting his metropolitan:

> “In matters that concern the general observance of all the priests of the Lord, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates.”

So deeply was Leo’s mind imbued with love of justice that he wished nothing to be taken away from the rights of his fellow bishops, nor did he wish his own dignity to grow through the diminution of another’s.

### XII

In the same year in which these events occurred, Attila, after his defeat on the Catalaunian Plains, came through Pannonia into Italy and captured and plundered the imperial cities of Aquileia, Ticinum, and Milan. Then, elated by his success, he hastened toward Rome.

The whole city was now in panic. Since Valentinian could not repel the enemy by force of arms, he began to avert the danger by counsel. He sent St. Leo and assigned highly distinguished men as his companions.

Behold, the great pontiff came to Attila, soothed his savage spirit with words, broke his anger by eloquence, persuaded him to accept peace, and compelled him to withdraw from Italy. The event is described at greater length in Prosper’s Chronicle, published from the manuscript codices of Sirmond and Chifflet by André Duchesne:

> “In the consulship of Herculanus and Sporatius, Attila, having restored the strength he had lost in Gaul, intended to enter Italy through Pannonia, while our commander Aetius made no preparations according to his conduct in the earlier war, so that he did not even employ the Alpine passes by which the enemies could have been stopped. He believed that the only hope remaining for his people was to withdraw from all Italy with the emperor.

> “But when this appeared full of disgrace and danger, shame restrained fear, and it was believed that the ferocity and greed of the enemy had to be satisfied by the broadest devastation of so many noble provinces. Among all the counsels of the emperor, the senate, and the Roman people, nothing appeared more salutary than to seek peace through legates from the most savage king.

> “The most blessed Pope Leo undertook this task with Avienus, a former consul, and Trigetius, a former prefect, relying upon the help of God, whom he knew never to have been absent from the labors of the faithful. The result was no different from what faith had anticipated. For, having received the entire embassy graciously, the king rejoiced so greatly at the presence of the supreme priest that he ordered the war to cease and withdrew beyond the Danube after promising peace.”

Among St. Leo’s companions Cassiodorus counts Carpilion, his father (Var. book I, epistle 4), and, being excessively fond of his father’s glory, names him the leader of the embassy and the author of the peace.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Carpilion was not the father of Cassiodorus, but the son of Aetius, master of the soldiers. He served as an envoy to Attila together with Cassiodorus’s father, the tribune and notary, as appears from Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book I, epistle 4. Since, moreover, Avienus and Trigetius were Leo’s companions according to Prosper’s complete Chronicle, it may be inferred that the embassy of Carpilion and Cassiodorus’s father was different and earlier.]

But all writers, including Cassiodorus himself in his Chronicle, attribute the achievement to the supreme pontiff:

> “When Pope Leo was sent to Attila by Emperor Valentinian, he made peace.”

Some add that, when Attila was asked why he had yielded so easily, he replied that he had been frightened by a prodigy. For, while Leo was speaking, he had seen an old man of venerable appearance and priestly dress threatening him with a sword unless he obeyed Leo. Struck with terror, he had collapsed as though his strength had been exhausted.

But I do not find this account in the ancient writers in whom it is reported by later authors—not in Jordanes, Theophanes, Suidas, Marcellinus Comes, Cassiodorus, Anastasius, Hermannus Contractus, Marianus Scotus, or Martin of Poland; not in Prosper, who was living at Rome, was close to Leo, and described the entire event carefully.

They do not write that Attila was overcome by a vision, but that he was softened by Leo’s eloquence and presence. For Prosper says, in the passage cited above:

> “Having received the entire embassy graciously, the king rejoiced so greatly at the presence of the supreme priest that he ordered the war to cease.”

Jordanes writes:

> “A peaceful embassy came to him from Rome. For Pope Leo himself approached him in the territory of the Veneti, at Ambuleius, where the river Mincio is crossed by the frequent passage of travelers. He immediately laid aside the anger that had been aroused in him and, returning by the way he had come, withdrew beyond the Danube after promising peace” (*On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths*, ch. 42).

The *Miscellaneous History* says nearly the same, and no more:

> “Leo the Great, sent by the emperor Valentinian, approached him and rendered him so mild that, having immediately promised the firmest peace, he departed beyond the Danube, never to return.”

Cassiodorus describes the barbarian as conquered by the power of eloquence, not terrified by a vision; but, as we have said, he presented his own father as the author of the achievement, not Leo:

> “He found a proud king but left him pacified; and he destroyed his slanderous disputes with such power that he made the man seek favor whose interest it was not to have peace with a most wealthy kingdom.… He brought back a peace that had been considered hopeless. What his embassy accomplished may be understood from the fact that it was received with as much gratitude as it had evidently been desired.”

### XIII

[Note: The matters related in Sermon 81 (now 84) concern not Attila’s invasion but the incursion of the Vandals, as Quesnel himself demonstrated in his annotation on that sermon, which we included in the prefatory notice to it.]

Leo himself, in Sermon 81 (now 84), on the Octave of the Apostles, says that the hearts of the raging barbarians were softened, not terrified.

From where, then, did the story of the terrifying vision arise, and how did it enter the readings of the Roman Breviary? It is reported by Sigebert of Gembloux. Cardinal Baronius also cites Paul the Deacon in his *History of Roman Affairs* in support of the story; he appended it to Eutropius.

But both writers are certainly too recent—the one having lived in the eighth century and the other in the twelfth—to deserve credence without the support of any more ancient authority.

It is also surprising that Paul the Deacon should have been made the patron of this story by the most eminent compiler of the *Annals* under the year 452, no. 58. For the appendix to Eutropius which Baronius cites and attributes to Paul the Deacon is itself the *Miscellaneous History*, which the same author, under that year, no. 54, denies to Paul the Deacon; and Philippus Labbeus proves in his historical dissertation on ecclesiastical writers that it does not in fact belong to him.

Whatever author may claim this work, most of its earlier editions do not contain that vision—whether those published from the manuscripts of Bongarsius, Amerbachius, and the Pithou brothers, or those issued through the efforts of others.

Only Janus Gruter, who collected the lesser Latin historians of the Augustan period into one corpus, presents the *Miscellaneous History* in a much fuller form than it had previously appeared, drawing it from Palatine parchment manuscripts which, as that most learned man writes, are of an utterly select quality and were written in Saxon letters at least seven hundred years ago.

I am reluctant to depart from the judgment of so great a man. Nevertheless, additions of this sort do not seem worthy of such esteem on the authority of a single manuscript against the testimony of so many others, especially since they contain much that reveals the ignorance of the writer.

Among these errors is the claim that Aquileia was besieged by Attila for three whole years; that the embassy of St. Germanus to Britain occurred after Aquileia had been captured; and that St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, after Italy had been devastated by the Vandals—a devastation which occurred in the years 455 and 456—spent himself on the redemption of captives, although the holy bishop had already died more than twenty years earlier. Learned men of the present time rightly regard this story about him as false.

We leave the remaining matters for others to examine. For the present, we hold as certain that these additions to the *Miscellaneous History* appear to have been inserted by another hand, partly taken from Jordanes, partly from uncertain writers, and partly even from false rumors.

This must be believed above all concerning the interpolated account we are discussing, which begins and proceeds as follows:

> “They say, therefore, that after the pontiff’s departure, Attila was asked by his men why he had shown the Roman pope such extraordinary reverence, since he had obeyed nearly everything the pope had commanded. Then the king replied that he had not revered the person of the man who had come to him, but that he had seen another man standing beside him in priestly dress, of more august appearance and venerable with age. That man had drawn his sword and terribly threatened him with death unless he fulfilled everything the pope requested.”

Attila plainly did not need such terrors to turn him away from his plan to attack the city. He was already wavering greatly, having been deterred by his own people and having little confidence in the success of the expedition. He considered it sufficient glory that the Roman pontiff and the Roman nobles stood before him as suppliants and subjects.

Jordanes, who flourished in the time of the emperor Justinian, vividly describes this hesitation of the barbarian and confirms it by the authority of the historian Priscus:

> “When his mind had been intent on approaching Rome, his own men, as the historian Priscus relates, dissuaded him—not out of concern for the city, to which they were hostile, but by setting before him the example of Alaric, formerly king of the Visigoths. They feared for the fortune of their king, because Alaric did not survive long after Rome had been broken, but soon departed from human affairs.”

Jordanes continues:

> “Therefore, while his mind wavered between going and not going in this doubtful matter, and he delayed while deliberating with himself, a peaceful embassy came to him from Rome. For Pope Leo …”

The same account appears in the addition to the Palatine manuscript, undoubtedly taken from Jordanes, since nearly the same words are used.

Finally, I will add that Janus Gruter, although inclined to insert such patches, nevertheless felt scruples about incorporating them into the actual text of the *Miscellaneous History* and instead relegated them to his notes on the work. This provides some indication that he was uncertain in his judgment concerning the addition.

### XIV

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that Rome experienced the honor brought by Leo’s embassy, the city’s deliverance by divine intervention, and the present assistance of the blessed apostles. As I have said, St. Leo himself reported this while preaching to the people. On that occasion he removed the people from the spectacles and instead exhorted them to venerate the blessed martyrs.

He says:

> “The religious devotion, dearest brothers, by which the entire body of the faithful used to gather to give thanks to God on account of the day of our chastisement and deliverance, has been neglected by almost everyone, as the very small number of those who attended demonstrates. This has brought great sadness to my heart and caused me the greatest fear. For it is a great danger to be ungrateful to God and, through forgetfulness of his benefits, neither to grieve over correction nor rejoice over forgiveness” (Sermon 81, now 84, on the Octave of the Apostles).

And again:

> “It is shameful to say, but necessary not to remain silent: more is spent on demons than on the apostles, and insane spectacles attract a larger crowd than the blessed martyrdoms. Who restored this city to safety? Who rescued it from captivity? Who defended it from slaughter? The circus games, or care for the saints? Certainly it was through their prayers that the sentence of divine judgment was bent, so that we, who deserved anger, might be preserved for pardon.”

Thus he concludes:

> “Return to the Lord, understanding the wonders he has deigned to work among us, and attributing our deliverance not, as the impious suppose, to the influences of the stars, but to the ineffable mercy of almighty God, who deigned to soften the hearts of the raging barbarians.”

The fame of so great an event spread throughout the whole world, and its memory endured in the eastern regions even into a late age. Thus, when the Easterners later wrote to Pope Symmachus and sought his aid and communion, they thought that his charity could be kindled by no example more effectively than that of our Leo going to meet Attila and making him weep. For, they say (Letter of the Easterners, after Epistle 8 of Pope Symmachus):

> If Leo the archbishop, who preceded Your Blessedness and has been numbered among the saints, did not think it beneath him to hasten personally to Attila, then an erring barbarian, in order to correct his bodily captivity—not only of Christians, but also, as is believable, of Jews and pagans—how much more does it belong to Your Holiness to hasten, not for the correction and conversion of bodily captivity, which is brought about by war, but of souls that have been taken captive or are daily being taken captive?

[Note: After Epistle 108, addressed to Theodore of Forum Julii and dated 11 June, no epistle was listed for that year. From a manuscript at Regensburg we have brought forth Epistle 109, addressed to Julian of Cos and dated 25 November; consequently, it is sufficiently probable that Leo’s embassy to Attila occurred during the intervening period, for which we possess none of his letters. Those who assign this embassy to around Easter of the year 452 rely on no foundation. Indeed, since Leo, shortly after the return of his legates from the council—whose return he mentions in Epistle 103, written to the Gauls at the end of February or the beginning of March of this year 452—received Lucian and Basil, the Constantinopolitan legates, who discussed with the same pontiff at length the prerogative of the see of Constantinople; and since these legates were sent back to Constantinople with four letters, Epistles 104, 105, 106, and 107, written on 22 May (see note 1 in the preceding volume, col. 987, n. m, on Epistle 103), there is no indication or probability that Leo had departed from Rome before that time to meet Attila and negotiate peace with him. Moreover, Julian of Cos wrote to Leo at the beginning of the year 453, expressing such sympathy with the pontiff over the evils inflicted on Italy by Attila that it is clear that those evils had already passed and, consequently, that Leo’s embassy too had ended, as may be gathered from Leo’s reply, Epistle 113, dated 11 March 453. Therefore Leo’s embassy may suitably be assigned to approximately the middle of the year 452, and certainly before 25 November.

Furthermore, from the aforementioned Epistle 109 to Julian we learned that Julian had informed Leo of the disturbances of the Palestinian monks, aroused both by letters written against the Council of Chalcedon and against Leo’s own definition of faith, and by violent acts even against Catholics and against Bishop Juvenal. Until then it had been believed that news of these disturbances had reached the pontiff only later. Leo requested that their instigators be restrained by the emperor and separated from the others by exile, hoping that the rest would more easily come to their senses if they were freed from the incitements of their insolent teachers. He sent them Saint Athanasius’s letter to Epictetus as an answer.]

# The Year of Christ 453; the Fourteenth of Pope Leo; the Twenty-Ninth of Valentinian and the Fourth of Marcian, Emperors; Opilio and Vincomalus, Consuls

[Col. 0283A]

## I

Leo the Great could not break Anatolius’s pride as easily as he had broken Attila’s ferocity. For Anatolius, embittered by the rebuff and by the letters of the supreme pontiff, turned his mind toward hatred and the disturbance of the Church. He began to favor heretics and to embrace those who had defended Eutyches and Dioscorus; meanwhile he persecuted the friends of Flavian and opposed those whom he knew to be defenders of the faith.

At that time Aetius was serving at Constantinople as archdeacon and was distinguished for his faith. Anatolius decided to remove him from office, because the man who held that position could either impede or advance his designs. For the holder of this dignity had great power in the Church. He presided over the college of deacons; it was his responsibility to care for the Church’s property and resources, distribute to each cleric his portion from the Church’s goods, exercise jurisdiction over rural presbyters, and settle quarrels and disputes among the clergy of the city. There were also other duties of this kind that made the office highly influential.

Anatolius therefore, thinking that it was in his own interest to appoint an archdeacon according to his wishes, removed Aetius from the office. But because Aetius was renowned both for his faith and for his integrity, Anatolius did not wish to appear to punish him undeservedly. Under the pretext of honoring him, he ordained him a presbyter, although Aetius resisted; by this means he excluded him from the archdeaconate, since it was customary that only a deacon should preside over deacons. He added exile as well, under the pretext of entrusting Aetius with the administration of a cemetery to which he assigned him. In his place he appointed Andrew, who had previously been deposed on account of heresy because he had adhered to the party of Eutyches and Dioscorus.

Julian of Cos immediately informed Leo of these events. Like a man stationed on watch, Julian kept vigilant guard over the affairs of the faith in the East. Leo promptly sent letters on the matter to Marcian, Pulcheria, and Julian of Cos. He complained of Aetius’s deceptive removal, since his faith was known and his conduct upright, and of Anatolius’s fraud, by which he had deposed Aetius under the guise of promotion:

> Since he found nothing in his faith to accuse or in his conduct to disapprove, he accomplished the downfall of an innocent man under the appearance of advancement; and he added this further injury to the sentence, that by assigning him to a cemetery he condemned him, in a manner, to exile.  
> (Epistle 84, now 111, chapter 2.)

He also criticized the fact that Aetius’s ordination had not taken place on the lawful day, since it had occurred on Friday rather than, according to custom, on Sunday or after the beginning of Saturday night:

> He was so disturbed by excessive agitation that, in bestowing an ordination as an injury, he inflicted it on Friday, either ignorant of or forgetful of the apostolic tradition—as though the defect in that ordination belonged more to a bishop than to a presbyter.  
> (Ibid.)

This custom appears at that time to have infected the Eastern Churches generally in opposition to apostolic tradition; for our Leo rebuked it as already established in the Church of Alexandria in his letter to Dioscorus. Perhaps Anatolius also deliberately arranged for this defect to occur in Aetius’s ordination, so that it might later furnish grounds for his deposition: he had ordained him a presbyter not with the intention of promoting him, but rather of bringing him down.

The final words of Leo support this suspicion, since they indicate that the defect was to be imputed to Anatolius, not to Aetius:

> As though the defect in that ordination belonged more to a bishop than to a presbyter.

## II

Since Anatolius, in order to remove from himself the blame for Aetius’s deposition, was investigating Aetius’s life, Leo wrote that, even if something blameworthy were found, it would be safer to overlook it on account of the faith than to place a heretic in his office:

> For even if, in the judgment of a Catholic bishop, there appeared to be something in the archdeacon deserving anger for whatever reason, it ought to have been passed over out of reverence for the faith rather than that a most wicked heretic should occupy the place of a Catholic.  
> (Epistle 86, now 113, to Julian, chapter 2.)

Aetius nevertheless cleared himself of the accusations. Hence Saint Leo later wrote:

> We rejoice that the presbyter Aetius, whom you say was examined, was found, after the inquiry, to have been cleared of everything.  
> (Epistle 100, now 127, to Julian, chapter 3.)

But the more warmly Leo embraced Aetius’s cause, the more vehemently he attacked Andrew, whom he called an Eutychianist:

> What reason or occasion arose, he asks, for degrading under the appearance of honor Aetius, the archdeacon, a man of the Catholic faith and consistently opposed both to the Nestorian and Eutychian heretics, and for suddenly transferring the entire administration of the Church’s affairs and responsibilities to Andrew the Eutychianist?  
> (Epistle 84, now 111, to Marcian, chapter 2.)

Andrew, he says, had already taken the heretics’ side and had revealed himself among the Romans as a defender of the Eutychian heresy:

> He had taken up the cause of the heretics even in his own sphere; he had declared himself among us a defender of the Eutychian heresy.  
> (Epistle 85, now 112, to Pulcheria, chapter 1.)

Finally, Andrew had been deposed by Anatolius himself because of that crime:

> Andrew, who had been cast out because of his association with heretics, is taken up; yet Anatolius himself had acknowledged that he had rejected him.  
> (Epistle 86, now 113, to Julian, chapter 1.)

And, as it stands in the recently published letter:

> He who had been judged deserving of rejection.  
> (Letter to Pulcheria cited above.)

## III

I shall discuss below what outcome this affair had. For the moment I shall assert one point from Leo’s replies to Julian of Cos: Aetius, harassed by injuries, complained to Leo about Anatolius. But, in my opinion, Leo stopped at complaints; I infer this from the letter that we are publishing for the first time:

> There is no doubt that this change concerns an injury to the Catholics. For the present, however, these things must be endured patiently, lest we seem to exceed the usual measure of making things right.  
> (Epistle 88, now 117, to Julian.)

[Note: We have corrected the reading to *moderationis* from the excellent manuscript at Regensburg. Leo believed that he should not depart in this case from the moderation he habitually displayed even toward heretics, so that he might provide for the public good by the gentler course; he did so because he considered it more useful, not because he could not act more strictly against Anatolius. Anatolius had injured the Christian cause by removing Aetius from the archdeaconate and promoting to that rank Andrew, the defender of the Eutychian heresy, whom he himself had previously cast out.

Why are the Nicene canons brought forward here? Was not the promotion of a man who had at some time defended heresy, and who had been deposed for that reason, sufficiently blameworthy to deserve just correction? Aetius, now a presbyter, could not be restored to the archdeaconate. But Saint Leo wished Andrew removed from that rank, and the matter with Anatolius was settled in no other way.

You therefore see that Leo’s moderation did not exclude the exercise of pontifical authority, but led it to the point at which he could more easily and swiftly safeguard the faith and bring Anatolius to an appropriate satisfaction.]

Leo indeed indicates that the Christian cause had been injured by Aetius’s deposition; nevertheless, he would do nothing more severe, lest he appear to take up another’s case against the Nicene canons. For when bishops administer their Churches according to the sacred rules of the canons and attempt nothing contrary to ecclesiastical custom, they have, as Saint Cyprian says together with the African synod, “free discretion in the administration of the Church,” and will render an account of their conduct to the Lord.

Gregory the Great did not hesitate to profess the same. “When guilt does not demand it,” he says, “we are all equal according to the principle of humility.”  
(*Register*, Book VII, Epistle 65.)

[Note: Gregory calls the Roman pontiff equal to the other bishops according to the principle of humility, but not in jurisdiction, by which he presides over all by divine right. For this reason Gregory had prefaced the same letter—now Epistle 59 of Book IX—with these words: “If some fault is found in bishops, I do not know which bishop is not subject to it.” Even when no crime is involved, the supreme pontiff can prescribe many things for the proper governance of the Churches by virtue of that same jurisdiction, which all Catholics acknowledge to have been established by Christ.]

In the matter we are treating, nothing contrary to the rules of the Church appeared. Everything was outwardly plausible. For it is not contrary to canon law to make a presbyter from an archdeacon and substitute another in his place. Although the faith of the latter had not been entirely approved, it was not then publicly known to be doubtful. Although Aetius’s authority was greatly diminished, in keeping with the circumstances of that time, he nevertheless gained far more in dignity from the presbyteral rank.

Finally, there was scarcely any basis on which an accusation against Anatolius could be brought, since he possessed the discretion and supreme authority to make decisions concerning the offices and ministers of his own Church according to the canons. Leo therefore went no further than complaints in his letters to Marcian and Pulcheria, lest he seem to exceed the usual measure of making things right. With both of them he acted only through prayers and exhortations, earnestly entreating them to protect Aetius against Anatolius’s plots. He also reminded Julian that, for the time being, it might be enough for Aetius that he was protected by the favor of the most merciful emperors:

> To whom, he says, I have recently commended him in my letters in such a way that I have no doubt his favor with those most religious minds should be increased.  
> (Epistle 88, now 117.)

## IV

Leo sent another letter to Julian, bishop of Cos (Epistle 86, now 113), containing many matters. After first giving thanks because Julian had shared in his pious grief over the many and savage sufferings experienced through Attila’s devastation, Leo adds something concerning Aetius and Andrew.

He then entrusts Julian with his own representation at the imperial court. This was a new practice, not previously adopted by the pontiffs of the Roman Church. Its model was the bishop of Alexandria, whose representative Anatolius had been at Constantinople before he was raised to the see of Constantinople.

For, says the brief treatise of the Eutychianists, discussing the Alexandrian bishop on the occasion of Anatolius:

> It is the custom of the aforesaid bishop that clerics be sent to the imperial court as representatives, lest some matter or necessity should arise.

[Note: When Leo entrusted Julian with his representation at the imperial court, he did not do so with the intention of following the example of the bishop of Alexandria or of other distinguished Eastern sees. For at that time Rome was not subject to the Eastern emperor in the same way as the Eastern cities, where a minister was needed to transact various causes and affairs with him.

This practice was first established under Justinian, who ruled not only the East but also Italy. To this development must be referred the institution of the Roman Church’s *responsales* and *apocrisiarii*, which introduced the service of a cleric at the court of his own prince, a service necessary for many matters.

Leo wished Julian to exercise his representation at the imperial court for this particular reason alone: that, watching over the integrity of the faith with apostolic zeal, he might take care that the Catholic faith suffered no harm from the Nestorians or Eutychians, and that, whenever necessary, he might seek the emperor’s protection and aid in this matter.

The holy pontiff was moved especially by the fact that he had found in Anatolius, the bishop of Constantinople, none of the Catholic vigor that circumstances required.]

What Leo then established in response to the needs of the times was later taken as a model and gave occasion for the *apocrisiarii*, or representatives, of the pontiffs. In the earlier period this office had been entrusted to clerics or presbyters; and for that reason it had originally been established and confirmed by imperial edicts that bishops should not come to the imperial court, as is clear from Justinian’s Novel 6, chapter 11.

The situation is different now, when bishops are torn away from the embrace of their Churches and sent to the most distant regions, and are ordered not to depart from the imperial court. Indeed, they are often honored with episcopal dignity for no other purpose than to perform the office of representatives and *apocrisiarii*.

## V

As for Julian’s vicariate, Leo explains the reasons and duties of this institution. He entrusted Julian with his own representation so that Julian might ensure that heresy did not spread, not so that he might assume the government of the Churches:

> Setting aside the handling of those cases that ought to be settled in each Church by the judgment of its own bishop, assume this special care in my place, so that neither the Nestorian nor the Eutychian heresy may revive in any quarter.  
> (Ibid.)

He then adds that he confers this office on Julian because Anatolius is handling the matter of the faith carelessly:

> Because there is no Catholic vigor in the bishop of Constantinople, and he is not greatly concerned either for the sacrament of human salvation or for his own reputation.  
> (Ibid.)

He therefore exhorts Julian to take care that the faith suffer no harm. If any danger should arise, Julian is to approach the Augustus, whose faith was renowned, and to warn him by letter:

> Supported by divine aid, do not cease to watch over the situation of the city of Constantinople, lest the impious storm of the doctrines mentioned above arise anywhere. And because the faith of the glorious emperors is so great that you can confidently lay before them what must be brought to their attention, make use of their piety for the benefit of the universal Church.  
> (Ibid.)

Leo commends Julian to the emperor at length and writes that he has entrusted Julian with his own representation for the preservation of ecclesiastical peace:

> For, trusting in the sincerity of his faith, I have delegated to him my own representation against the heretics of our time, and, for the preservation of the Churches and of peace, I required that he should not be absent from your court.  
> (Epistle 84, now 111, chapter 3.)

Leo also mentions this in his letter to Pulcheria.

In the same letter to Julian (Epistle 86, now 113, chapter 3), Leo asks him about certain documents that the presbyter Aetius had reported as having been sent earlier. He says that he has not yet received the summary of the faith that Julian had sent, and asks whether Julian had received the letter to Flavian that Leo had sent through the deacon Basil.

[Note: Leo’s words refer to Epistle 35 to Julian himself, not to Flavian, as Quesnellus correctly noted in a marginal postscript at this passage.]

Concerning the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, Leo specifically orders Julian to have everything gathered into a single codex and translated into Latin in a fully complete rendering, because, owing to the difference of language, the material was insufficiently clear to Westerners.

He asks about the disturbance of the monasteries of Palestine. Since these matters require explanation, we shall dwell on them briefly. The previously unpublished letters that we are now making public will contribute considerably to illuminating this history.

## VI

Once Dioscorus’s cause had been ruined and the Eutychian heresy proscribed at Chalcedon, many monks, thinking that their own cause was at stake because the archimandrite had been condemned—the man to whom they were bound both by his profession of life and by fellowship in doctrine—began to grow intensely angry. At first they secretly detested the Fathers’ decrees; then they resolved to do so openly, defend Eutyches, and, having taken courage, plot everything anew in order to assert Eutychianism.

A certain Theodosius, a monk of Palestine who had come to Chalcedon to advance the interests of the Eutychian faction and who wielded great influence among the monks, was especially violent. But when he saw that the heretic whom he supported had been defeated, he fled like a madman to Palestine, to the monks gathered around Jerusalem. He spread hostile reports about the Council of Chalcedon, declaring that the faith had been overthrown at the council—for so he called the heresy—and that Juvenal of Jerusalem, who had previously sworn allegiance to Eutyches at Ephesus, had defected from the faith.

By whispering these and similar claims sometimes secretly and sometimes shouting them openly, he stirred up the already turbulent minds of the monks. Juvenal of Jerusalem, having left the council, returned to Jerusalem.

At his arrival the mad faction of these men rose up against Juvenal as a traitor to the faith. Everyone became tumultuous and threatened him with death unless he revoked the decrees sworn to at Chalcedon. Unable to withstand so many enemies, he fled to Constantinople while the disturbances subsided with time and delay.

According to Evagrius, the monks acted in Juvenal’s absence; according to the explicit account of Nicephorus, they acted while he was present. Marcian’s letter to the Alexandrian monks, preserved in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, gives the same account. They made the monk Theodosius bishop after deposing Juvenal. Likewise, in the sees of those bishops who had not yet returned from Chalcedon, but who had confirmed the Chalcedonian faith by their presence and votes, they installed other men from their faction as bishops.

Afterward Theodosius left nothing undone to propagate the heresy. By force or persuasion he compelled everyone to execrate the Council of Chalcedon. He filled the region with slaughter and blood. He was restrained neither by the authority of presbyters nor by that of bishops; rather, like a savage beast, he ravaged all who refused to pronounce an anathema against the faith.

At that time Eudoxia, the wife of that younger Theodosius, was living at Jerusalem. Having first been steeped in the poison of Eutyches, whom she had once supported against Flavian, she brought considerable weight and authority to the faction. Was this because of private hatred toward Pulcheria, or because she remembered Theodosius, under whose rule the faith had been destroyed at Ephesus? Whatever the reason, this woman inflicted a grievous wound on the Church.

## VII

At Rome, the first report of the Palestinian disturbance was a vague rumor that serious anger had broken out between the bishop and the monks; but the cause was unknown.

[Note: Already in the preceding year Saint Leo had been sufficiently informed from Julian’s letters about the disturbances of the Palestinian monks against Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, and about their evil design, as we noted from Epistle 109, now published for the first time, in note 7 above, col. 281, n. a, under the preceding year. It must be said that another matter, previously unknown to us, subsequently arose, causing Leo to entertain some doubt about the design of those monks, so that in this year he requested fuller information from Julian. See note 17 in the preceding volume, col. 1026, n. k, on Epistle 113.

Quesnellus presents the chronology of the events concerning these monks less accurately. In the year 452 the emperor ordered Dorotheus to strengthen Jerusalem with a garrison in order to suppress the Palestinian disturbances. The monks then sent a petition to the Augusta Pulcheria, complaining about the soldiers and revealing their evil disposition. To this petition not only Pulcheria but also the emperor Marcian replied. At the end of the year 452 or the beginning of 453, he sent letters to the same monks, seeking first through gentleness, instruction, and persuasion to restore them to a sound mind.

But when he accomplished nothing by this milder course, he ordered Theodosius, the leader of the sedition, to be arrested and thrown into prison. When Theodosius anticipated this, he escaped from Palestine. Once he had been removed and Juvenal restored, the disturbances were settled toward the end of that same year, 453.]

Leo was uncertain whether the monks were contending for the cause of the faith, and he asked Julian of Cos to write to him about the matter:

> Concerning the Palestinian monks, who are said to have been in the turmoil of dissension for some time, I do not know with what state of mind they are now acting. No one’s account has made clear to me what causes they appear to be putting forward for the aforesaid dispute. Whether, that is, they are serving the Eutychian perversity with such fury, or whether they are implacably grieved that their own bishop could have been handed over to this impiety—he who had departed from the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, against the testimony of those very holy places by which the whole world is instructed—and whether they think that what it pleased God to heal in others through indulgence is not pardonable in him. For this reason I desire to be more fully informed about these matters.

While Leo was writing this, a letter arrived from Julian of Cos giving him a fuller account of the entire tragedy.

It consoled the holy pontiff that Marcian’s spirit, in defending religion, was not merely Christian but also priestly. When he heard that the monks, under the leadership of Theodosius, were disturbing the Church, he ordered Dorotheus, the governor of Palestine, to omit nothing in restraining the rebellious monks. He ordered Theodosius, the firebrand of the sedition, to be put in chains.

He then issued a rescript in which authority was joined with clemency and religious devotion with majesty. At one moment he tried to calm the rebellion through gentleness; at another he attempted to suppress it by command.

Meanwhile the monks attacked Pulcheria and sent her petitions. But they did not so easily enchant her mind as they did her eyes. Pulcheria replied in agreement with the faith and in opposition to heresy.

Informed of these events by Julian, Leo praised the Augustus and Augusta in his reply:

> I signify that I rejoice greatly over the edict of the most Christian emperor, by which he showed what the ignorant madness of certain monks deserved, and over the most pious reply of the Augusta, by which she rebuked the heads of the monasteries. I do not doubt that this fervor of faith has been conferred upon them by divine inspiration, so that it may appear that their excellence belongs not only to the royal throne but also to priestly holiness.  
> (Epistle 88, now 117, chapter 2.)

## VIII

Julian had sent a copy of the edict. In it one may admire the wisdom and moderation of the emperor, who wished peace to exist in the Church but was not preparing either to compel the wills of those who dissented or to inflict violence upon their minds:

> Our clemency has imposed no necessity whatsoever upon anyone, so that he might subscribe or consent against his will. For we do not wish to draw anyone to the way of truth by terror or violence. The remedy for defects and errors of the mind must be applied not by force but by prudence; such an evil becomes worse if one treats it more harshly and severely.

Leo sent grateful replies to Marcian (Epistle 89, now 115) and Pulcheria (Epistle 90, now 116). He called this policy of wisely caring for the Church a distinguished work and congratulated the Church that it had obtained such rulers, in whom royal power was joined with priestly teaching:

> For we recognize that the rulers of our time possess not only royal power but also priestly learning.

## IX

We understand how great Marcian’s desire was to reconcile peace in the Church from the fact that he himself urged Leo to write to Eudocia and persuade her to adopt better convictions.

Leo accepted the wise advice. As I think, it was conveyed not in writing but by the living voice of a messenger. He immediately wrote to Eudocia and acted with Valentinian, Eudocia’s son-in-law, so that he too might exhort her by letter to undertake the defense of the faith.

We learn of these events, long hidden, from Leo’s letter to Julian, hitherto unpublished:

> Because the most merciful emperor deigned to instruct me more privately through our son Paul that our most merciful daughter Eudocia should be admonished, I did what he wished, so that she might recognize through my letter how fruitful it would be for her if she favored the Catholic faith. I also obtained that she should be admonished on this matter by a letter from her son, the most merciful emperor. I have no doubt that she too would labor with pious zeal so that the authors of the sedition might recognize the purpose of their profession, and that, if they do not understand the preaching of those who teach, they might at least fear the power of those who punish.  
> (Epistle 88, now 117, to Julian, chapter 3.)

[Note: *Eudociam* should be read here and in the passages that follow, as will become clear from note 6 in the preceding volume, col. 1067, n. h, on Epistle 117.]

## X

Leo’s letters to Eudocia have not survived. But there are two other letters, one to the monks of Palestine (Epistle 97, now 124) and the other to Eudocia (Epistle 96, now 123).

To the monks Leo explains at length and with great clarity the sacred incarnation of Christ and exhorts them to the unity of the faith and the peace of the Church. To Eudocia he requests that she not support the monks’ heretical perversity by her authority. Rather, he urges her to labor diligently so that they may eventually come to their senses, change their opinion, condemn Eutyches, and profess the same faith as the Catholic Church.

From this letter we understand that Eudocia had not replied to Leo’s earlier letters, since there is no mention there of any response. Nor, I think, did she gain anything from Leo’s admonitions. For it is clear that Eudocia did not return to the Church until a year or more after Juvenal had been restored to his see. Leo testifies that this restoration was owed to Marcian and Pulcheria, without mentioning Eudocia; he would not have omitted her if she had been involved.

Indeed, I think that she did not acknowledge her fault until after the two disasters suffered by her family—Valentinian’s murder and Eudocia’s capture by Genseric—and that, instructed by the sermons of Saint Euthymius, she professed the Catholic faith.

Nevertheless, Leo’s admonitions may have had this effect: when Juvenal returned, Eudocia did not obstruct him, and by refraining from assisting the monks she made them more peaceable.

## XI

While these events were occurring at Jerusalem, Anatolius, certain through the legates Bishop Lucian and the deacon Basil that what had been defined at Chalcedon concerning the see of Constantinople was not approved at Rome, became angry at the rebuff and began to slander Leo. He secretly spread the claim that the Council of Chalcedon had been rejected by the Apostolic See, as though the supreme pontiff denied the faith because he had checked Anatolius’s pride. By these devices he concealed his deceit in order to lead more people into error.

Heretics readily believed what they desired; Catholics believed what they feared.

Marcian himself was almost deceived by Anatolius’s words. To learn the facts from Leo himself, he wrote that the heresy had indeed been struck down at Chalcedon but had not yet been completely defeated; it could be utterly overthrown if Leo testified to all the Churches that he accepted the Council of Chalcedon:

> Your Clemency judges that this can more easily be accomplished if it is made known throughout all the Churches that the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon were pleasing to the Apostolic See.  
> (Epistle 89, now 115, chapter 1.)

[Note: We possess Marcian’s Epistle 10, written on 10 February 453, which Quesnellus received after writing this account and added to the second edition. From it it is clear that it was not Anatolius but the Eutychians who spread rumors against the definition of faith established at Chalcedon, as though the Apostolic See had rejected it.

Although Leo had sufficiently confirmed the Chalcedonian definition in Epistle 106 to Anatolius, he had at the same time rejected the canon concerning the prerogative of the see of Constantinople. Because that letter was not published, a rumor spread among the people that the same pontiff had written against the Council of Chalcedon. The Eutychians seized the opportunity to slander the very definition of the faith, as though it had been rejected by the pontiff. See note 4 in the preceding volume, col. 1019, n. b, on Epistle 110.

For this reason the emperor sought from Leo an explicit confirmation of the Chalcedonian faith, while also praising Leo’s firmness, by which he refused to allow the privileges of the Churches established by the Nicene canons to be violated and resolutely opposed the canon issued at Chalcedon concerning the see of Constantinople. See note 3 above, col. 285, n. a.

Paul brought the emperor’s letters to Rome and at the same time delivered Julian’s letter together with Marcian’s and Pulcheria’s letters to the Palestinian monks. Through the same Paul Saint Leo sent Epistle 114 to the Council of Chalcedon, 115 to Marcian, 116 to Pulcheria, and 117 to Julian. All these were written on 21 March 453.]

Leo replied that there was no need to approve by letter the faith decreed at Chalcedon, since he had already sufficiently attested it in the letter to which all had subscribed and had confirmed it by letters to the emperor himself, as well as in his letter to Anatolius. Anatolius had preferred to conceal this rather than expose his own ambition.

Nevertheless, Leo would comply with Marcian’s wish by adding his own support and judgment to the synodal decrees. In this way he subscribed to the Catholic faith and condemned heresy:

> There was no reason for doubt, since the consensus of all who subscribed had joined itself to that faith which I issued according to the form of apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers. Through my brother Bishop Lucian I also sent to Your Glory and to the bishop of Constantinople such letters as clearly showed that I approved what had been defined concerning the Catholic faith in the aforesaid synod.

> But because in those same letters I had criticized what had been improperly attempted on the occasion of the synod, the aforesaid bishop preferred to keep silent about my congratulation rather than reveal his own ambition. . . .

> Since, however, the most religious will of Your Piety must be obeyed in every way, I have willingly added my own judgment to the synodal constitutions that pleased me concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith and the condemnation of the heretics.

Thus, as he says in his letter to Pulcheria:

> Lest the deceptive pretense of anyone should wish my judgment to be considered uncertain.  
> (Epistle 90, now 116, chapter 2.)

And, as he writes in his letter to Julian, which we publish from our manuscript codex:

> On account, namely, of those who, as an excuse for concealing their perfidy, wish the council’s decrees to appear weak or doubtful, as though they had not been strengthened by the judgment of my consent.  
> (Epistle 88, now 117, chapter 1.)

## XII.

Leo therefore, to thwart all Anatolius’s devices, writes an encyclical letter to the bishops who had attended the Council of Chalcedon (Epistle 87, now 114), and sent Julian two copies (Epistle 88, now 117). To one of these he appended a copy of his letter to Anatolius; to the other he appended nothing, leaving it to Julian’s preference which he should return to the emperor.

“I prepared two letters of equal form for the synod: one to which I had a copy of my letter to Bishop Anatolius appended; the other without an appended copy. I leave it to your judgment to deliver whichever you think should be given to the most clement prince, retaining the other with you.”

To the bishops he indicates that he accepts the synod’s decrees wholeheartedly: “with my whole heart,” he says, he had embraced them. He explains that he is writing this, not because it was necessary, but because it pleased Marcian, so as to remove any suspicion that he was refusing to approve the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon:

“So that, through malicious interpreters, it may not appear doubtful whether I approve what your unanimity established concerning the faith at the Council of Chalcedon.”

He then testifies that he had already given his assent to the synodal acts through his legates, but that he is making it public so that everyone may know of his agreement. Such, evidently, was the reverence and obedience of the supreme pontiffs toward the decrees of sacred councils [Col. 0290D]:

> Leo’s reverence and obedience toward the definition of faith at Chalcedon is true in this sense: the definition agreed with his doctrinal letter to Flavian and had already been sufficiently and clearly approved by that same pontiff in Epistle 104 to Marcian, and especially in Epistle 106 to Anatolius, dated 22 May 452. Otherwise, just as he resisted the canon in Anatolius’s case, so too would he have resisted the definition of faith if he had detected in it anything contrary to his doctrinal letter. For this reason he rejected the Ephesian Robber Council, although it bore the appearance of a general council.

[Col. 0290C] Leo wishes every suspicion, however slight, of disagreement to be removed with the utmost care:

> So that both the universal brotherhood and the hearts of all the faithful may know that I have united my judgment with yours, not only through the brethren who acted in my place, but also through my own approval of the synodal acts—solely, that is, in the matter of faith, as must often be said—for the sake of which it pleased us that a general council should be convened, both at the command of the Christian princes and with the consent of the Apostolic See.

## XIII.

Anatolius, unmoved by these things, moves every stone to bring the councils he had begun to completion. He either sends to Illyricum or goes there himself, communicates with the bishops of that province, and asks them to subscribe to what had been decreed at Chalcedon in honor of his see. But Euxitheus, Bishop of Thessalonica, prevents this [Col. 0291A]. He had recently been appointed in place of Anastasius and had sent a bishop to Rome to announce his ordination and at the same time to disclose Anatolius’s plans. We learn all this from the letters already cited to Julian of Cos.

“We also want you to know that after our admonition Bishop Anatolius persists so rashly in the recklessness of his presumption that he summoned the Illyrian bishops in order that they might subscribe to him; this was reported to us by the bishop sent from Thessalonica as the messenger of his ordination” (Epistle 88, now 117, ch. 5).

Since Anatolius made no progress through admonitions, Leo, who thoroughly understood the character of arrogant minds, undertook to change his proud spirit through silence and contempt. The outcome confirmed this policy, as we shall see in its proper place. Anatolius bore this more heavily than threats and therefore complained to Julian of Cos about the pontiff’s silence. Julian invited Leo to write back. Leo replied:

“For this reason we did not wish to write to him, although you yourself requested that it should be done, because we perceived that he did not wish to be corrected” (ibid.).

[Col. 0291B]

## XIV.

Egypt was not tranquil at that time. After Dioscorus had been deposed at Chalcedon, the Egyptian bishops returned to Alexandria after the council and, having summoned the clergy together with the city’s nobles, undertook to appoint another bishop in his place. But the people, forming a coalition, disrupted the election—whether because many favored Dioscorus, or because they did not want a bishop to be ordained while another was still alive. Liberatus bears witness to this in his *Breviary*:

> “They were unwilling to ordain anyone at all, lest they should appear adulterers, since Dioscorus was still alive.”

Nevertheless, once Proterius had been proposed, they all gave their assent, because he was dear to Dioscorus, who, when absent, had entrusted the Alexandrian Church to him. But after Proterius had been raised to the pontificate, the populace renewed the revolt and split into factions. One party demanded Dioscorus and opposed Proterius; another favored Proterius—to such an extent that he required a military guard to restrain the violence and assault of the people.

Leo, before receiving the Alexandrian reports, foresaw what was happening, turning over in his mind how powerful the Dioscorian faction was. He therefore sent a letter to the Alexandrian bishop [Col. 0291C], or to his ordainers or clergy, and copies to Julian of Cos, so that Julian might report to the emperor what Leo had written. The letters have perished, but those written to Julian that year mention them. In these Leo also inquires about the Egyptian monks: whether they were steadfast in the Catholic faith, whether they loved peace, and how matters stood at Alexandria:

> “I desire to know how peaceful the Egyptian monks are, or what their faith is, and what reliable reports reach you concerning the peace of the Alexandrian Church; and I wanted you to know what sort of letters I sent to its bishop, or to his ordainers or clergy, by sending you copies” (Epistle 86 to Julian, now 113).

[Col. 0291D]

> This is false. Leo had received three letters concerning Proterius’s ordination: one from Proterius himself, another from those who had ordained him, and a third from the Alexandrian clergy. The holy pontiff replied with an equal number of letters, which are missing, as we noted in the dissertation on lost letters, no. 61. It is so certain that Proterius wrote to Leo concerning his ordination that the same pontiff asked him for a fuller exposition of the faith. See Epistle 127 to Julian, ch. 1.

## XV.

At nearly the same time he sent letters to Maximus, Bishop of Antioch, and to Theodoret of Cyrrhus (Epistles 92, now 119, and 93, now 120). Maximus had sent the presbyter Marcian and the deacon Olympius to Rome to congratulate the supreme pontiff on the victory of the faith and the defeat of the heretics at Chalcedon. Through them he had warned that the heresy had not yet been so thoroughly crushed that it could not still flex its muscles; there were still many who rejected the faith professed at Chalcedon.

Through the same messengers Leo sends his reply. He praises the faith Maximus had professed in his letters and urges him to defend it against the efforts of the heretics, whether they were followers of Nestorius or of Eutyches. Both, he says, must equally be condemned:

> “For it makes no difference by what sacrilege they disagree with the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, so long as what they most perversely believe is accepted neither by the authority of the Gospel nor by the meaning of the sacrament” (Epistle 92, now 119, to Maximus, ch. 1).

He then advises Maximus to retain the privileges of the third see and not allow them to be diminished by anyone’s ambition, but to defend firmly the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. No effort or authority could persuade him to derogate from them. At the same time he sends him his letters to Anatolius and wishes them to be made known to the bishops of Maximus’s province, so that all may learn with what spirit he had undertaken to restrain Anatolius’s efforts.

Near the end of the letter he adds:

> “You should also take care, my beloved brother, to guard against this: apart from those who are the Lord’s priests, no one should dare claim for himself the right to teach and preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning. For although it is desirable that all the sons of the Church should understand what is right and sound, it must not be permitted that anyone outside the priestly order assume for himself the office of a preacher, since everything in the Church of God ought to be orderly; and in the one body of Christ, the more excellent members should fulfill their office, while the inferior members should not resist the superior” (ibid., ch. 5).

[Col. 0292B]

## XVI.

He also wrote a very weighty letter to Theodoret (Epistle 93, now 120, ch. 1). He proclaims the decrees issued at Chalcedon as proceeding from God and established by an irrevocable decision, because they had first been formulated by the Apostolic See but were then confirmed by the irretractable authority, as Leo puts it, of all the bishops:

> “Therefore we glory in the Lord, singing with the prophet: ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth’; for he did not permit us to suffer any loss among our brethren, but confirmed with the irrevocable assent of the whole brotherhood what he had previously defined through our ministry. Thus he showed that what had first been formed by the first of all sees truly proceeded from him, since the judgment of the whole Christian world received it, so that in this also the members might agree with the head.”

“In this,” he continues, “our cause for rejoicing increases still further, since the enemy has been struck all the more severely in proportion as he rose up more fiercely against Christ’s ministers.”

[Col. 0292D]

> We examined a similar marginal note by Quesnel in Annotation 2 (previous volume, col. 1046, no. 1) on Epistle 120. It must be recalled here so that Leo’s genuine meaning may be understood as distinct from Quesnel’s interpretation.

Because of the labors and injuries he had endured from Dioscorus, Leo praises Theodoret further and encourages him to eradicate completely the remnants of Nestorianism and Eutychianism. He advises him to follow the middle path of Catholic doctrine, deviating neither to the right nor to the left from the straight road, since error lies on both sides:
