> “On this occasion we believe that this must especially be urged, dearest brother: whenever, with divine grace assisting, we either overwhelm or cleanse those who are outside from the fountain of doctrine, let us weigh our words with every precaution, departing in no respect from those rules of faith which the divinity of the Holy Spirit set forth at the Council of Chalcedon.”

He then asks Theodoret to write back if the Lord’s teaching is making progress in those regions (ibid., ch. 4).

Regarding Anatolius’s plans and regarding monks and laymen, he says the same things as he had said to Maximus: they must not intrude upon the ministry of preaching and teaching through rash presumption, because, as was defined in the councils, this is the principal duty of bishops (Council of Carthage IV, ch. 20; Council of Trent, session 8, ch. 2, and session 24, ch. 4).

[Col. 0292D]

## XVII.

In the printed editions there follow other letters, about which we have either already spoken or shall speak later. There is also another letter addressed to Bishop Julian, dated 7 Kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio (Epistle 98, now 125). In it Leo briefly explains his concern for the faith, asks Julian for frequent letters concerning ecclesiastical affairs, and requests that what he had previously writ— to the emperor and to Julian be put into execution.

# Year of Christ 454; 15th year of Pope Leo; 30th year of Valentinian, 5th of Marcian, emperors; in the consulship of Aetius and Studius

[Col. 0293A]

## I.

As I believe, Leo had inquired about the affairs of Palestine in his preceding letter to Julian. From the following letter to the same man we learn that peace had been restored to that province by this time.

There is also a letter to Marcian (Epistle 99, now 124), which we found in our manuscript. It was written on the fifth day before the Ides of January, and in it Leo indicates that he had received Marcian’s good letter. We gather from the letter to Julian what the emperor’s letter contained. In his earlier letter Marcian had described what he had done on behalf of the faith and for the restoration of peace to the Church. In his second letter he was trying to restore Anatolius to Leo’s friendship and asked Leo not to deny Anatolius his communion, promising that Anatolius would obey Leo in all matters pertaining to the faith.

[Col. 0293C]

> Not communion, from which Anatolius had not been excluded by Leo, but the pontiff’s favor—for Leo uses this term in Epistles 127, 128, and 130—which the emperor sought to obtain for him.

Nevertheless, from the letter to Julian written at the beginning of this year (Epistle 100, now 127, ch. 3), we learn that Anatolius had held a council at Constantinople in the preceding year, composed of bishops who were then in the city. We have just spoken of such councils. At that synod the letter which Leo had written, at the emperor’s request, to the bishops recently assembled at Chalcedon was read. But since everything at that synod was done at Anatolius’s direction, only what Leo had said about the faith was read, not what he had discussed at length concerning Anatolius’s plans. The case of Aetius was also debated there. He had been burdened with various accusations, but once again he easily dispelled the calumnies.

## II.

In the same year, as we read in other letters of Leo to Marcian and Julian, dated the fifth day before the Ides of January, Leo also received letters from Proterius, the Alexandrian patriarch, brought by Bishop Nestorius, probably of Pharagonea. From Liberatus I gather that Nestorius had attended both Proterius’s consecration and the recent Council of Chalcedon.

Nestorius did not come directly to Rome, but traveled through Constantinople and brought Leo letters from the emperor, who spoke magnificently of Proterius, the new Alexandrian bishop. At first Proterius’s faith was suspect to Leo [Col. 0293C], because Proterius had formerly been dear to Dioscorus, who had entrusted him with the care and protection of the Alexandrian Church when Dioscorus departed for the council.

[Col. 0293C]

> Proterius’s faith was not suspect to Leo simply because he had once been dear to Dioscorus. Leo indicates nothing of that kind. Only because he did not find in Proterius’s letter concerning his ordination as full an exposition of the faith as the circumstances of the place and time seemed to require did Leo ask him to explain the matter more fully and explicitly in another letter. Proterius most readily complied.

Leo welcomed Proterius’s letters because, as Marcian had previously testified, they declared his orthodox faith. Leo replied to them splendidly (Epistle 103, now 129). The letter had long remained hidden; with the help of our manuscript we have brought it out of darkness. Fragments of it are also found in St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 11, article 2, reply to objection 2, and in Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, ch. 42. Concerning these fragments and Bede’s corresponding error, consult our annotations to this letter.

Leo first expresses his joy to Proterius:

> “The letter of your affection, which our brother and fellow bishop Nestorius brought in the service of piety, has made me glad” (Epistle 103, same chapter, ch. 1). “For it was fitting that such a letter should be sent from the bishop of the Alexandrian Church to the Apostolic See: a letter showing that the Egyptians had learned from the teaching of the blessed Apostle Peter, through his blessed disciple Mark, from the beginning, what the Romans are known to have believed.”

He then vigorously defends his letter to Flavian against the accusations of the heretics. He wishes it to be read in a frequent public assembly, so that the Alexandrians may be assured that his teaching is the same as that of the Alexandrian bishops. He further asks Proterius to compare publicly the testimonies of the Fathers which he had supplied with his own letter, so that it might be evident that he detested Nestorius and Eutyches alike.

[Col. 0294A]

## 550

The same letter shows that Leo had also sent Proterius copies of the letters he had sent to the bishops of the council, to Marcian, and to Anatolius. In them he confirms as valid what had been defined concerning the faith and declares invalid what had been done at Chalcedon to the prejudice of the Alexandrian see.

The Eutychians, offended by the decree of the Council of Chalcedon and by Leo’s faith, openly accused his letter, twisting it into perverse meanings. They watched every individual letter and syllable with malicious care:

> “The enemies of the cross of Christ,” he says, “lie in wait for all our words and syllables” (Epistle 103, now 129).

Since they could not corrupt its integrity, they falsified it through a perverse interpretation. To counter these attacks, Leo asked Marcian (Epistle 104, now 130) to have the letter translated into Greek—either by Julian of Cos or by some other person skilled in both languages—and to send it, sealed with his own seal, to the Alexandrian judges. They were to read it publicly to the people together with the passages from the holy Fathers which Leo had appended, so that the people would not be deceived by the calumnies of the heretics and all would know that Leo condemned both Nestorius and Eutyches.

“What,” he asks, “has the crafty wickedness of certain heretics not done to disturb the simplicity of others? They are said to have falsified my letter, which I sent to Flavian of blessed memory, so that, by changing certain letters or syllables, they might assert that I was a recipient of the Nestorian error. I beg your venerable clemency to order that this same letter of mine be translated fully and carefully into Greek by my brother Julian, or by those whom your piety chooses as suitable for this work, and that it be delivered by a qualified messenger under the impression of your seal to the Alexandrian judges. Let them have it read to the clergy and people of that city together with the preaching of the bishops mentioned above, whose teaching agrees with my writings, so that they may recognize that they must no longer be deceived by the fraud of deceitful men, and so that the sincerity of the Apostolic See may be proved. Neither Eutyches nor Nestorius has any place there, because, just as the universal Church condemned the other heretics, so it condemned these two” [Col. 0295A].

[Col. 0293D]

> At first Leo believed that the Alexandrians could not accuse his letter of Nestorianism except because certain passages had been falsified and corrupted in a defective Greek translation. Later, when he wrote Epistle 152, he seems to have recognized that the objections raised against the same letter did not arise from a Greek translation corrupted by the heretics, but from the frivolity of the accusers, who, refusing to submit to the truth, quibbled over the words and syllables of the Greek version and twisted them toward a Nestorian meaning. He therefore asked the emperor to restrain them.
>
> Indeed, those who attacked Leo’s letter, since they also opposed and rejected the Council of Chalcedon, were not accusing any Greek interpretation of the letter other than the one incorporated into the Council of Chalcedon and disseminated throughout the East. Yet no Catholic would assert that this translation was falsified and nevertheless approved by the council. Nor, as far as we know, did any other Greek version exist, and the one that survives has not so far been found corrupted in any copy.
>
> Only under Pope Anastasius II did the opinion that the translation had been corrupted gain currency, though for a different reason. The corruption which Leo was thought to attribute to the Eutychians—as though they had corrupted the translation of his letter in order to accuse it of Nestorian taint—was later attributed to the Nestorians, who wished to persuade people that the holy pontiff agreed with Nestorius.
>
> In a libellus presented to the legates whom that same pontiff had sent to Constantinople to restore unity with the Orientals, the Alexandrian apocrisiarii reported that the interpreters of Leo’s letter—mistakenly called by them the letter sent to the Council of Chalcedon—were those who at that time had been followers of the Nestorian heresy together with Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus. They said this so that they could more freely assert that Nestorius had not held perverse opinions.
>
> Then, to show that certain passages in this version had been twisted toward a Nestorian meaning, they added that Photinus, a deacon of the Thessalonian Church, had stated that, when he was discussing the same translation at Rome before Anastasius, the pontiff himself had acknowledged that the translation of the letter contained errors, while the Latin letter itself had been issued according to the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. They further declared that the pontiff’s own legates had confirmed this to them:
>
> “Your Holiness,” they said, “has deigned to teach us not once but repeatedly that the errors inserted in the interpretation of the letter were not conceived in the Latin text.”
>
> Yet even concerning this matter we have serious doubts. The apocrisiarii who reported these things were heretics, enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, and manifest defenders of Dioscorus, Timothy the Cat, and Peter the Hoarse. When they sought communion with the Apostolic See, they attributed the Nestorian taint to the Greek interpretation in order to give some explanation for the rejection of Leo’s letter. Their predecessors, believing the same fault to be present in the Latin text, had separated themselves from communion with the Roman Church.
>
> The apocrisiarii claimed to have discovered from the testimony of Photinus and the legates that this was false. Yet they still rejected in practice the letter translated into Greek and approved by the Council of Chalcedon. They hoped to be accepted on the grounds that, by assigning the errors solely to the translation, they displayed a mind not at all alien to the Latin text of the praised letter. By this fraud they tried to steal Roman communion.
>
> They certainly erred when they said that this letter had been sent to the Council of Chalcedon, for it had not been written to that council but to Bishop Flavian. This error arose because they actually knew and attacked no other Greek interpretation of the letter except the one incorporated into the Council of Chalcedon. They were equally mistaken—or rather, they wished to deceive—when they invented the story that the letter had been translated into Greek by Nestorians and sprinkled with Nestorian taint.
>
> Leo’s own testimony confirms this invention: although he at times suspected the Eutychians of being corruptors, he never suspected the Nestorians. Nevertheless, it was easy for Photinus and the other Eutychians to impose and recommend this fiction to Pope Anastasius and other Romans who did not know Greek, or who did not compare the Greek version of the letter with the Latin original. They placed their trust in the Eutychians when the latter, producing and explaining the alleged errors of the translation according to their own interpretation, deceived them about the fact of the translation.
>
> But although the Eutychians deceived them concerning the history of the translation, they did not deceive them about the substance of the doctrine. No one was admitted to unity and communion with the Apostolic See unless he accepted, in carefully examined professions of faith, both the Council of Chalcedon and the letter of Leo accepted by that council.
>
> These matters required fuller explanation because the opinion that Leo’s letter had been falsified is widely held, and because Leo’s testimony is thought to be confirmed by this document of the Eutychianists, as though the two accounts agreed, when in fact they make entirely different assertions.

## III.

There is also a previously unpublished letter to Julian of Cos on the same subject (Epistle 102, now 131). Leo asks Julian to translate his letter to Flavian from Greek into Latin. So that nothing might be hidden from him, he sends Julian copies of the letters to Marcian and Proterius [Col. 0295B].

Nevertheless, as we have already said, the heretics continue to corrupt Leo’s letter, insert spurious meanings, circulate a distorted version among the people, and deceive many through their wicked perversity.

## 552

The evil continued even after Leo’s death. In the year 497, during the pontificate of Anastasius, the apocrisiarii of the Alexandrian Church presented supplicatory libelli to legates sent from Rome. From these I learn that many had been deceived by the false translation. Ignorant of the corruption, they accused the letter of Nestorianism, and the Roman legates, no less than Proterius, labored to defend it against the heresy.

I think that Marcian and Julian of Cos accomplished what Leo had requested. For when the emperor heard that Egypt was being disturbed on account of religion, he issued an edict preventing riots and imposing fines, exile, and capital punishment upon those infected by the poison of Eutyches who refused communion with Proterius, and upon those who, under the appearance and pretext of religion, organized private meetings and assemblies.

[Col. 0296C]

> Two actions of the emperor Marcian must be distinguished: the letter to the Alexandrian monks, by which he tried, through exhortations and the authority of the Alexandrian bishops, to recall them to sound doctrine and reconcile them to their bishop, St. Proterius; and the edict to Palladius, by which he restrained the disobedient and factious with penalties.
>
> Since that letter states that John the Decurion was sent by the emperor to Egypt, and Leo understood that John had been sent there when he wrote Epistle 141, dated 11 March 455, it is known that the imperial letter was issued either toward the end of 454 or at the beginning of 455.
>
> As for the edict to Palladius, although in the Justinianic Code it bears the consulship of Constantius and Rufus, in the year 457, on the Ides of August—perhaps because the same edict was renewed under Leo Augustus—it was in fact issued on the Kalends of August, not in the consulship of Studius and Aetius, that is, in 454, as Baronius and Quesnel believed, but in the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius, namely in 455, as the same law is dated in the manuscripts of Quesnel’s, the Spanish, and the Isidorian collections.
>
> Nor is this contradicted by Epistle 107, our Epistle 136, to Marcian, dated 29 May 454. For the words which Quesnel quotes from it do not signify something already carried out by the emperor, but something which Leo hoped would shortly be done.

Baronius believes that the edict was published in this year (Baronius, year 454, no. 6), and that it was not issued under Constantius and Rufus, as is commonly written, since they entered the consulship during Leo’s reign, but under the consuls Studius and Aetius, while Marcian was still reigning. I accept this correction, and it is supported by a letter of Leo dated the fourth day before the Kalends of May [read: June], published by Holstenius and reprinted by us.

## 553

Thus Leo writes in that letter together with the emperor:

> “Since, with God assisting you in all things, we believe that the remaining traces of every perverse doctrine will soon be extinguished throughout Egypt, you are kindly caring for those from whom you remove the freedom to practice execrable error” (Epistle 107, now 136).

## IV.

Meanwhile Eutyches, struck by an anathema and burning with anger, prepared to spread poison far and wide. He strove to attack the Chalcedonian Fathers and did not cease to disparage the sacred economy of Christ.

Warned by Julian through letters, Leo immediately wrote to Marcian (Epistle 105, now 134, ch. 2) that the heretic should be sent far into exile, since proximity to the city allowed him to misuse his position for vice and corruption. The archimandrite appointed in place of Eutyches was to be strengthened through frequent conversations with Julian, so that the monks suffering from the disease of their superior might return to health.

[Col. 0296D]

> These statements about Eutyches or Anatolius being hostile to Julian are entirely gratuitous. The testimony of Leo, quoted shortly afterward from Epistle 134, ch. 3, more probably refers not to Julian but to the Constantinopolitan clergy, whom Leo feared Anatolius might oppress; for he had not yet received the latter’s letter, in which Anatolius sought to satisfy him and return to his favor.

For Eutyches was keeping Julian away from the friendship and companionship of the new archimandrite; or, as I conjecture, Anatolius himself was hostile to Leo and therefore ill-disposed toward Julian, Leo’s legate. This is easily persuaded by Leo’s letters to the emperor. Leo commends his friends to the emperor, asking that Anatolius not harm them:

> “I ask that you especially protect against every attack those whom you know to be pleasing both to me and to your gentleness because of their love of the faith, so that the Bishop of Constantinople may have no power to injure them” (ibid., ch. 3).

## V.

Thus Anatolius, indulging his greed and anger, neglected to defend the affairs and rights of the Church. Here one may admire the vigilance of St. Leo, who considered nothing belonging to the Church foreign to his concern.

At that time there was a corrupt practice in the Church of Constantinople: the Church’s steward submitted accounts of its property and offerings to the public judges, rather than, as custom required, to the bishop and clergy of the Church.

The first stain of this evil was the greed of the clergy. While they turned God’s business into a source of profit and measured the Church’s property according to their own advantage, they brought lawsuits and disagreements against one another. They were not competent to settle these disputes because the priests themselves were involved, and they too were judges; thus there was conflict among the judges. The cases were brought before public magistrates, and gradually this corrupt example became customary—indeed, in our own times, almost a necessity—so long as those concerned cared more for their own affairs than for the Church’s.

Gennadius, Anatolius’s successor, labored to cut out this plague of greed. For we read that Marcian ordered his steward to ensure that each basilica enjoyed the offerings belonging to it, which the principal church had previously retained (Theodore the Reader, *Collection*, book I; Nicephorus, book XV, ch. 22).

Leo therefore, wishing to remedy this evil, wrote to the emperor concerning the judgments of clergy, and reported that he had already written earlier about this matter. We have published this letter from our manuscript.

> “I have reasonably thought that this too should be joined to this letter, concerning what I previously asked your piety in my earlier letters: that you not allow the stewards of the Church of Constantinople, contrary to established custom and especially during the times of your piety, to be heard by public judges, and that you remove this injury also from the sacred orders; but that you order the Church’s accounts to be examined according to the traditional practice through priestly judgment” (Epistle 108, now 137, ch. 2).

## VI.

But to return to Anatolius: in this year he wished to return to friendship with St. Leo, whether sincerely or deceptively. The question is whether he was moved by repentance for what he had done, by grief over his unsuccessful efforts, or—more truly—whether he was overcome by Leo’s steadfastness and by Marcian’s will, since the emperor’s mind was inclined toward peace.

This is how matters stood. First Marcian wrote to Leo about restoring Anatolius to his favor, promising better conduct from him. We learn this from St. Leo’s letter to Julian of Cos, which is dated the fifth day before the Ides of January of this year (Epistle 100, now 127, ch. 3).

Leo replied to Marcian in a letter devoted entirely to the correction of Anatolius (Epistle 107, now 136). In it he reproves Anatolius as the author of dissensions and praises Marcian as a lover of peace, since he wished to calm the storms Anatolius had raised. Leo promises friendship on the condition that Anatolius first testify in writing that he had abandoned his culpable ambition:

> “Let him satisfy the canons and write back that he will preserve the favor of all the priests; let him indicate that he has abandoned his culpable ambition.”

Anatolius had said that he would do everything according to Leo’s wishes. To this the supreme pontiff replied:

> “Let him accomplish in his heart what he promises only in words.”

If Anatolius refused, Leo threatened that he would act freely and firmly:

> “But if he chooses with stubborn purpose what displeases God and your piety, then, with all due respect for your gentleness, I shall use greater freedom and firmness against the arrogant man, with all and on behalf of all, while you too lend your support. As I must often say, I would rather embrace him in brotherly charity for the sake of holy deeds.”

“With all and on behalf of all,” he says, because the matter concerned not only Leo but also the others: if he restrained Anatolius’s pride and ambition, he would be defending the force and authority of the canons and vindicating the privileges of the Churches against injury. He added, “while you lend your support,” because it is also the duty of rulers to protect the decrees of the Church.

## VII.

In the Holstenian collection there is a letter of Anatolius (after Leo’s Epistle 105, now Epistle 132). From it we learn that he had returned to a sounder frame of mind. He expresses his distress at Leo’s contempt and silence and indicates that he had carried out what Leo had requested:

> “I immediately fulfilled what was contained in those letters, as you wished; both the common advantage of peace and what was fitting urged me to do so.”

He then adds that Aetius had been restored to his position, while Andrew had been deposed and removed from the Church [Col. 0298A], together with Eutyches and all the Eutychians, even though they had outwardly detested the heresy and had subscribed to Leo’s letter to Flavian.

He says that the decree made in honor of the see of Constantinople had been sought not by him but by the clergy of his Church, who had reserved everything for Leo’s confirmation.

[Col. 0297]

> Whether Andrew was truly cast out of the Church, see Annotation 7 (previous volume, col. 1085, no. f) on Epistle 138.

Leo received this letter of Anatolius together with Marcian’s letters and replied on the same day (Epistle 106, now 135).

To Anatolius he wrote that it was Anatolius’s fault if he had been deprived of Leo’s letters, because Anatolius had not satisfied him and had acted contrary to the canons. Nevertheless, Leo rejoiced that Anatolius had received Aetius into friendship, removed Andrew from the archdeaconate, and deposed Euphrates, Flavian’s accuser. They could nevertheless be ordained priests if they removed suspicion of Nestorianism and Eutychianism [Col. 0298B]. Another person whose faith was beyond suspicion was to be appointed in Andrew’s place. Those spoke with little sincerity who blamed not themselves but the clergy’s ambition; they had dared nothing except with Anatolius’s support.

### IX.

He does not say that Aetius the archdeacon should be restored, because, as we have said, ordinarily only a deacon held the office of archdeacon, and it was only after many years that the custom was established whereby an archdeacon became a presbyter. To make him a presbyter, therefore, was to bar him from that office. And perhaps for this reason Leo indicates that Andrew and Euphrates could be ordained priests, provided that they were sound in the faith, in order to prevent them from gaining any further access to that office and thereby acquiring excessive influence in the Church of Constantinople.

The holy Leo had requested that Aetius, restored to his own Church, should be reconciled with Anatolius; and he rejoices that this had been accomplished. “Therefore,” he says, “because you indicate that certain matters concerning the offices of the clergy in the Constantinopolitan Church have been corrected, so that you have restored your presbyter Aetius to your favor and affection, and have removed Andrew from the exercise of the archdeaconate, I write back that this has pleased us” (Epistle 106, now 135).

Baronius writes (under the year 453, no. 8) that Aetius was restored. “Leo,” says the author of the *Annals*, “reproached Anatolius himself so severely that, unless he wished to remain entirely deprived of Catholic communion, he would restore Aetius to his former position.” But Baronius’s opinion is not only foreign to the custom of those times; it is also contrary to the words of Saint Leo.

These words indeed occur in Anatolius’s letter to Leo: “The most reverend presbyter Aetius of our holy Church has been restored to us to his former position and ecclesiastical honor” (Epistle, now 132, chapter 2). I do not believe that he was restored to the office of archdeacon, but to his own Church, since previously he had been assigned to the cemetery. For how else are Leo’s words to be explained, when he says that another man of approved faith must be selected?

“First, let a man be chosen and approved who can fulfill the office of archdeacon—that is, one whom no report of any of the aforementioned impieties has ever stained” (Epistle 106, now 135, chapter 2).

In the same letter he shows that Aetius had merely been reconciled with Anatolius:

“So that you have recalled Aetius,” says the same holy Leo, “your presbyter, to your favor and affection.”

That restoration, therefore, of “position and honor”—if the translation is genuine and faithful and agrees with the Greek text of Anatolius—is to be understood as referring to Anatolius’s favor and the honor of the Church, not to the office of archdeacon.

### X.

In the Holstenian collection there is a letter of Saint Leo written at this same time to the emperor Marcian (Epistle 107, now 136). We publish it again, in a corrected form, from our manuscript. Leo speaks magnificently of Marcian, praising at length his zeal for preserving peace and reconciling harmony among the bishops. He also urges him to eradicate the heresy completely in the East, just as in Palestine, so that there might likewise be good hope for Egypt.

He further asks him to restrain the audacity of the monk Carosus, who, paying no attention either to the council’s definition or to the emperor’s authority, was corrupting the faith of many.

Baronius refers to this passage a fragment of an imperial constitution, which he claims was issued to defend the rights of the principal sees against Anatolius’s efforts. But anyone who reads it carefully will admit that it does not concern patriarchal jurisdiction, but certain rights granted to particular Churches—for example, the right to granaries for feeding the poor, and perhaps jurisdiction over civil cases assigned to bishops.

“We decree,” it says, “that the privileges which earlier emperors, by general constitutions, granted to all the holy Churches of orthodox religion shall be preserved perpetually, firm and unimpaired. We order, moreover, that all pragmatic sanctions obtained against the ecclesiastical canons through favor or ambition shall be deprived of their force and validity.”

There is nothing about this sanction in Saint Leo; and the words, stated generally, apply to Anatolius alone. Who, moreover, would claim that the rights of the principal sees had been granted to them by imperial constitutions, as that fragment asserts? Nevertheless, it is certain that Anatolius yielded to Saint Leo.

### XI.

At about this time news arrived from Palestine that the province had been pacified through the care and diligence of Juvenal, who, having been restored to his see, convened a council. After the council had been dissolved, he sent legates to Leo—Andrew the presbyter and Peter the deacon—both to report that everything had been settled at Jerusalem and to return thanks for the excellent service Leo had rendered before the emperor, as well as for the authority he had exercised against the monks’ revolt.

He also sent him, together with gifts of blessing, a fragment of the Lord’s cross—unless this portion has been interpolated in Leo’s letter, which reports it (Epistle 110, now 139).

The holy Leo therefore replied. He does not conceal that Juvenal himself had been the cause of the disturbances, because he had attacked Flavian and defended Eutyches. Nor, he says, would the province have been troubled if Juvenal had stood steadfastly for the faith. Then, taking occasion from the Church over which Juvenal presided, he recalls Christ’s life at Jerusalem and the signs and miracles performed through the power of the cross, all of which proclaim most wondrously his incarnation.

### XII.

But now, behold, the long-desired news from Egypt. Julian of Cos writes to Leo that Dioscorus had died, although he would have preferred that the heretic be healed rather than die. Nevertheless, he openly expressed his joy, hoping that the heresy would soon perish once its author had been removed.

This is clear from the letter of our manuscript codex to Julian of Cos. “With the mercy of God assisting,” says Saint Leo (Epistle 111, now 140), “the correction of those who have gone astray is more easily to be hoped for; and the preaching of the Gospel will be more effective when the defender of falsehood has been destroyed.”

Here the *Oriental Chronicle*, recently translated from Arabic into Latin by Abraham Ecchellensis, must be corrected. It errs twice: first, when it says that Dioscorus was sent to an island situated in the West; and second, when it says that he remained there for seven years. He was in fact deported to Gangra, a city of Asia Minor, where he died this year—that is, in the fourth year after the sentence pronounced against him.

The death of Dioscorus occurred for the good of the Church, and among the Egyptians there was hope of recovering peace, since no longer were two bishops simultaneously in place, nor was rebellion being fostered by the concealed ways of the heretic or by his clandestine counsels.

“While we are established in this anxiety,” he says in the same place, “the divine safeguards are never absent. They allow nothing to the pretenses of hypocrites and confound their hidden wickedness by manifest destruction. For although all the devices of the heretics have long since been shattered, and the right hand of truth has taken away all their strength, nevertheless now, as you have written, with Dioscorus perishing, they have fallen into deeper ruin. Once the instigator of their perfidy has been removed, certain unstable and foolish souls have something they may obey, but nothing they may follow.”

Saint Leo’s religious expectation was pious, but, because of the evil disposition of the Egyptians, it proved vain and empty. For the Alexandrians did not cease to honor the memory of Dioscorus. The superstition lasted into the age of our fathers, when Gabriel, patriarch of Alexandria, sent a delegation to Pope Clement VIII in 1593 with a confession of faith in which an anathema against Dioscorus is hurled.

## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 455; THE SIXTEENTH OF POPE LEO; THE THIRTIETH OF VALENTINIAN, THE SIXTH OF MARCIAN, EMPERORS; THE EIGHTH CONSULSHIP OF VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS AND ANTHEMIUS AS CONSULS

### I.

This year contains no letters of Leo in the earlier editions, and we would have nothing to say about our pontiff unless several letters had emerged from the Grimanic manuscript codex and the difficulty concerning the date of Easter had been reserved for this year—a matter about which he had sent several letters in the immediately preceding years.

The question was precisely on which day Easter, in this year numbered 455 from Christ’s birth, fell. The reason for the uncertainty was as follows. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria and highly skilled in ecclesiastical computation, had published a hundred-year cycle whose beginning was reckoned from the first consulship of Theodosius the Elder. According to his calculation, in the year 453—the seventy-fourth year of this cycle—Easter had been celebrated on the day before the Ides of April. In the following year, 454, the seventy-fifth year of the cycle, Easter had fallen on the day before the Nones of April. But in this year of Christ 455, the seventy-sixth year of the same cycle, Easter was postponed to the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Leo asserted that there was an error in the cycle and that the limits of Easter had been extended too far. They ought to have been bounded by the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and the twelfth day before the Kalends of May. He therefore assigned Easter for this year to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Leo himself speaks of this controversy in his letter to Marcian (Epistle 94, now 121, chapter 1):

“Although the feast of Easter, in which the mystery of human salvation is chiefly contained, must always be celebrated in the first month, it is nevertheless made variable by the conditions of the lunar course, so that the choice of the most sacred day is often uncertain. From this it frequently happens—which ought not to happen—that the whole Church does not observe together what ought to be one single observance.

“The holy Fathers therefore sought to remove the occasion of this error by entrusting the entire responsibility to the Alexandrian bishop, since among the Egyptians the expertise in this calculation had apparently been handed down from ancient times. Through it, the day on which the aforesaid solemnity would fall each year was to be communicated to the apostolic see, whose written announcement would circulate as a general notification to the more distant Churches.

“But Theophilus, of holy memory, bishop of the city of Alexandria, after compiling one hundred years of this observance, determined that the Easter feast of the seventy-sixth year should be kept very differently from what the others had decreed. Beginning with the first consulship of Theodosius the Elder, of august memory, he set down the successive order of the sacred observance, so that the reckoning of a longer period might be preserved in his writings. The seventy-fourth year of this cycle is the year 453, in which we celebrated holy Easter on the day before the Ides of April. In the following year, 454, by God’s favor, the same feast was to be observed on the day before the Nones of April, as the regular order of the centenary notation declares.

“But in the year that would be the seventy-sixth, 455, a date for Easter is found entered which the authority of no precedent and no regulation since the Lord’s Passion permits us to accept. For we know that the eighth day before the Kalends of May was assigned by him, and that it exceeds the limit of the ancient regulation excessively, whereas others assigned the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to this feast, since the legitimate interval has been fixed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.”

[Note: The notation of one hundred years was not a cycle in which, after one hundred years, the Easter dates returned to the same starting point. Rather, it was a table consisting of five cycles of nineteen years and five additional years, in which Theophilus had recorded the Easter feast over a period of one hundred years. See note 8 (previous volume, column 1056, note j) on Epistle 121. Concerning the whole controversy regarding Easter in the year 455, compare the preliminary admonition to Epistle 88.]

### II.

From Leo’s words we have learned the cause of the entire controversy. Leo consulted all the experts, especially Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily. We now bring to light a previously unknown letter from the frequently praised manuscript codex. After instructing Paschasinus concerning the brief mission he was soon to undertake at the Council of Chalcedon, Leo lays out the state of the whole controversy, discusses at length the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, and entrusts him with the task of carefully investigating the Easter calculation. He asks him to discuss the matter with learned men, so that no room for further uncertainty or error about the date of Easter would remain.

“So that every form of uncertainty may be removed,” he says, “you should deal with this matter most carefully with all who are skilled in it, so that we may guard against an error of this kind in the future.”

Paschasinus’s reply has not been found. There is indeed an extant letter of his to Leo concerning the date of Easter, but, as we have noted, it belongs to another question. It is therefore clear that the *Ecclesiastical Annals* contain an error, where Paschasinus’s letter is referred to this controversy.

It is nevertheless certain that there were two disputes under Leo concerning the date of Easter. The first occurred in the sixty-fourth or sixty-third year of the Roman calculation, that is, in 444, as the better manuscripts and the more accurate calculation indicate. That cycle began with the consulship of Antoninus and Syagrius, as Paschasinus’s letter states. The second occurred in the seventy-sixth year of the Theophilian cycle, in 455, as is certain from Leo’s letter to Marcian. That calculation began with the first consulship of Theodosius the Elder and therefore preceded the Roman cycle by two years.

The two periods in which the controversy over Easter was debated must therefore be distinguished. Paschasinus’s letter belongs to the earlier dispute; the letters we are publishing for the first time—Leo’s letters to Paschasinus and Marcian—belong to the later one (Epistle 68, now 88, and Epistle 108, now 137).

Although Leo had already raised the controversy several years earlier, he had refrained from a more exact investigation because he was occupied with the affairs of the council. Once the synod had been dissolved and Proterius had been appointed to the see of Alexandria, he reopened the matter. As we have said, he wrote to Marcian (Epistles 112, now 142, and 94, now 121) and to Julian of Cos (Epistle 95, now 122).

This last letter is commonly read as having been written to Eudoxia, but the inscription is corrupt. Both the context of the letter itself and our more accurate manuscript codex prove that it was written to Julian. Leo asks him to summon experts in computation to investigate and determine the true and legitimate date of Easter.

“I earnestly requested,” he says, “that the emperor order those who seem to possess complete knowledge of this calculation to assemble together.”

Accordingly, as Leo had requested (Epistle 105, now 134), Julian sent a messenger to Alexandria and inquired of the Alexandrians about the true date of Easter. We understand this from Epistle 68 and the others.

### III.

Meanwhile, the time for announcing Easter and sending the customary circular letters to the bishops was approaching. Leo wrote to Julian as follows:

“Be concerned about the coming Easter, as I have often written already, and communicate the matter at the proper time in my name to my most merciful emperor, so that he may inform me what reply has been made to him; for the days are approaching when we must know what date we ought to enter in the circular letters, and so that every suspicion on this matter may more clearly be removed” (Epistle 102, now 131).

The letter was dated the sixth day before the Ides of March in the previous year. At almost the same time, however, Leo received a letter from Marcian stating that Theophilus had correctly assigned the date to the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Although Roman custom favored celebrating Easter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, Leo nevertheless accepted the decision, lest, if he dissented, he appear not to have chosen the better course but rather to have divided unity. Thus he wrote to Marcian:

“Since another method pleased the Egyptians, I gave my consent, so that no disagreement might arise throughout the provinces concerning the observance of so venerable a feast” (Epistle 108, now 137, chapter 1).

Proterius had written Leo the same things that Marcian had written to Leo. This is undoubtedly the letter that Petavius published at the end of his work *On the Doctrine of Time*, and which, following others, we placed in its proper position among Leo’s letters.

Leo also sent Proterius the same reply that he sent Marcian, as is clear from the same letter to Marcian:

“I inform you that I have received the letter of my brother and fellow bishop Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, to which I replied to Your Piety concerning my consent—not because clear reasoning had demonstrated this, but because concern for the unity that we guard above all had persuaded me” (ibid.).

The author of *On the Reckoning of Time*, whether the work is Bede’s or another’s, writes that Leo consulted Proterius about Easter and that Leo answered his Easter letter with that celebrated epistle beginning, “Your letters have brought me joy,” and so forth. Yet in that letter, a fragment of which appears in this work, there is a remarkable silence about this matter. There is a lengthy discussion of Proterius’s ordination and of the faith, but not a single word about the Easter question.

I do not see how Bede was deceived, unless he inferred this from the fragment and had not read the entire letter. We now publish the letter in full from the manuscript.

### IV.

In accordance with Marcian’s letter and the decision of the Egyptians, although it differed from his own opinion, Leo sent circular letters to all the bishops. The letters he sent to the bishops of Gaul and Spain are preserved (Epistle 109, now 138).

At that time letters were again brought from the emperor concerning the same controversy. Saint Leo replied (Epistle 112, now 142) that he had already thanked him by letter and that he had followed the judgment of the Alexandrians, which he had communicated to the bishops of the western regions.

“On the same occasion,” he says, “on which I reverently received the communications of Your Piety, I offer the words of greeting that are owed, and inadequately give thanks because Your Piety, with priestly concern, reminded me about the most sacred day of Easter. Although I had long ago professed my acceptance of this rule of observance and had announced to all the priests of the western regions the same day declared by the instruction of the Alexandrian bishops—that is, that Easter should be celebrated in the present year on the eighth day before the Kalends of May—I have set aside every scruple for the sake of unity and peace.”

Prosper records that Leo wrote two kinds of letters to Marcian concerning this Easter controversy: some in which “the reason for the truth being investigated was clearly set forth”; and others through which the Catholic Church could be instructed that this decision had been tolerated for the sake of unity and peace rather than approved.

The former are Epistles 94 and 105, now 121 and 134, published long ago. The latter are Epistles 108 and 112, now 137 and 142, both now published for the first time and, even on the testimony of Prosper alone, to be counted among the genuine letters. Thus this controversy over Easter came to rest.

On this occasion there first arose among the Latins in the West a competitive effort to investigate the date of Easter and to calculate more carefully the movements of the sun and moon. They no longer tolerated the imposition upon them by the Alexandrians of a fixed rule for announcing the date of Easter.

Prosper of Aquitaine, who was then living at Rome in attendance on the pontiff, therefore composed his own cycle. Gennadius and Isidore attest to it (Gennadius, *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, chapter 88; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17), unless he had already published it around the year 444, when a similar difficulty had arisen.

Whatever the case may be, there is no doubt that Leo prompted him to write it. Certainly, since Prosper writes somewhat more angrily about the Easter of this year 455, with which he closes his *Chronicle*, it appears that he himself argued for his own position.

“In the same year,” he says, “the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May through the obstinate determination of the Alexandrian bishop, whom all the Easterners thought they ought to follow, although holy Pope Leo protested that the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May ought rather to be observed. (In that case there would have been no error either in the calculation of the full moon or in the limit of the first month.)

“There exist letters of the same pope addressed to the most merciful emperor Marcian, in which the reason for the truth being investigated is clearly set forth. From them the Catholic Church may learn that this decision was tolerated for the sake of unity and peace rather than approved, and that it must never thereafter be imitated—so that what brought a fatal offense may forever lose all authority.”

Victorius of Aquitaine also composed a paschal canon at the request of Hilary, archdeacon of the Roman Church, to whom this responsibility belonged both by his office and by Leo’s command. Victorius dedicated the canon to him in the year 457, during the consulship of Constantius and Rufus, as he himself testifies in the preface addressed to Hilary.

Victor of Capua later criticized this canon, in the year 545, publishing another one. But these matters do not belong to our present undertaking, except insofar as the whole enterprise appears to me to have proceeded from the mind, counsel, or command of our Leo, as Bucherius once also believed.

[Note: Even before the year 414, Prosper had corrected the Latin eighty-four-year cycle, in which the lunar leap was inserted every twelfth year, so that the same leap was admitted only every fourteenth year. See note 4 on the fragment of Saint Cyril’s letter to Leo, volume I, column 602 (previous volume, column 602, note d), and note 14 (ibid., column 1056, note q) on Epistle 121, where we show that this correction of the lunar leap had taken effect in the year 454.]

### V.

This year contains a letter of Leo written to Anatolius on the third day before the Ides of March (Epistle 104, now 143). Leo says that Anatolius’s letter had been welcome and urges him to maintain vigilance and firmness of spirit against the men of corrupt doctrine who were still propagating heresy at Constantinople. He identifies the archimandrites Carosus and Dorotheus.

At the Council of Chalcedon, the monks of the Eutychian party had regarded Carosus as the leader of their faction. They had been heard and rejected at the council. Once the heresy had been condemned, they appeared to assent to the council through fear of excommunication, to which they would be subject unless they accepted the council’s decrees within thirty days. Nevertheless, they did not become any better and continued to corrupt the faith of the monks.

Leo had written to Marcian about them, as appears in the letter concerning Anatolius’s correction. We also understand this from Leo’s letter to Marcian (Epistle 112, now 142, chapter 2), which we have copied from our manuscript.

The emperor had ordered that the seditious monks be transferred elsewhere, where they would have little opportunity to do harm.

“Concerning Carosus and Dorotheus,” he says, “who defended errors condemned for the destruction of many because of their heretical depravity, I rejoice that Your Piety, as my venerable brother Julian the bishop has informed me, most beneficially ordered that, after being removed from their monasteries, they should be commanded to live among people whom they could not harm. I hope that this will prove a remedy for many whom you have freed from perverse teachers, while in every respect the merits of Your Glory increase.”

[Note: Two men named Carosus have been improperly confused as one and must be distinguished: one is mentioned in Epistle 141, while the other is the subject of Epistle 142. This distinction is established by the correction suggested by our Regensburg manuscript in the chronological note to Epistle 142. From that correction it is evident that both letters were given at approximately the same time. Thus Carosus, who is said in Epistle 142 to have been driven into exile together with Dorotheus on account of heresy, must be different from the man who, in Epistle 141, is said to have been corrected in his confession of faith.]

Carosus, overcome either by punishment or by conscience, had issued a confession of faith consistent with the council’s decrees. Yet Anatolius did not admit him to communion. It is uncertain whether this was because of private enmity or because his correction was regarded as doubtful.

Regarding this matter Leo wrote to Julian in a letter dated the fifth day before the Ides of March, which is now being published for the first time, extracted from the highly valuable Grimanic manuscript codex:

“You indicate that Carosus has been corrected in his confession of faith, but that he nevertheless remains in some sort of hostility toward our brother Anatolius, so that, because of this disagreement, he still refrains from communion” (Epistle 113, now 141, chapter 1).

I have found nothing further about these monks.

### VI.

The same letter shows that the emperor Marcian sent the honorable man John to Palestine this year—not in 452, as Baronius thought—to the monks, in order to confirm their faith, which had been ensnared by the schemes of the wicked Theodosius.

That bold monk had intruded into the see of Jerusalem after expelling Juvenal, the legitimate pontiff, as we have written. After Juvenal’s restoration, Theodosius escaped imprisonment and withdrew as an exile to Mount Sinai. Moving from one monastery to another and repeatedly changing his lodging, he evaded punishment. The monks received and protected him as though he were innocent.

For this reason the emperor sent the decurion John, so that he might inform them of what had taken place at Chalcedon in his presence and of what had occurred in Egypt.

“You indicate,” Leo writes, “that the honorable John, a man praiseworthy for the sincerity of his faith, was sent to Egypt for the sake of the faith. When he returns, let me know how much he has contributed to peace and correction. I do not doubt that you will do this even without my reminder” (ibid.).

[Note: John the Decurion was sent by the emperor not to Palestine but to Egypt. This is clearly indicated not only by Leo’s words in Epistle 141, quoted below, but also by the imperial letters sent to and presented to the Alexandrians, published in volume II of the Councils, column 1794. See note 4 above, column 296, note a, on the preceding year.]

The same letter mentions Maximus in these words:

“But concerning the condition of the bishop of Antioch,” he says, “I am distressed with great sorrow, if—which God forbid—the accusations brought against him are true. Yet, beyond the priestly diligence whose concern for the common good I do not doubt, I place the greatest confidence in the justice and benevolence of the most glorious emperor. I am certain that he will provide, insofar as possible, that deception can prevail in no direction” (Epistle 113, now 141, chapter 2).

The matter seemed obscure to me when I was working on the first edition. For the passage in Nicephorus’s *Chronicle* had not yet come to my attention, and it clarifies the whole affair. He writes explicitly that Maximus, who had attended the Council of Chalcedon and had been appointed in the place of Domnus, was expelled from his see on account of a lapse, after having occupied the see of Antioch for four years:

“Maximus, who was at the fourth council at Chalcedon, was expelled because of a lapse, in the fourth year.”

It is therefore certain that Maximus was deposed as guilty of a carnal sin, not because of a public crime, as I had previously conjectured in error, indulging too freely in speculation.

Basil appears to have taken Maximus’s place in this very year, if Nicephorus is to be trusted, since he limits Maximus’s episcopate to four years. Basil had already been elected to replace Domnus before the Council of Chalcedon and had been confirmed by its authority in 451. His ordination cannot have been delayed beyond the year 456. Saint Leo writes that he learned of it from a letter of the emperor Marcian, who died in January 457. Thus he writes in Epistle 118, now 149, which we have brought out of darkness:

“Your Beloved’s ordination ought, according to ecclesiastical custom, to have become known to us through your own communication or through that of our provincial brother bishops. But since there were causes that could impede this diligence, and since Marcian, of holy memory, made your consecration known to us in his own letter, and so forth.”

[Note: “On the deposition of Maximus, consult Nicephorus’s *Chronology*.” —Quesnell. See also our dissertation *On the Lost Letters*, no. 79.]

### VII.

After Valentinian was killed, Maximus seized the Western Empire and took as his wife Eudoxia, who was unaware of the murder. This woman, resolute and courageous, later discovered that Valentinian had been killed through Maximus’s agency and resolved to avenge her husband’s death. Giving excessive rein to her anger, she also prepared vengeance through the destruction of Rome.

She summoned Genseric, king of the Vandals, from Africa. He immediately transported a huge army into Italy and attacked and entered Rome by surprise.

Then the Senate and Roman people presented a shameful spectacle: Rome was exposed to Arian soldiers.

The holy Leo, who had once softened Attila, fierce in arms, foresaw the disaster with prudent judgment. He had preached a sermon about the impending danger because the citizens’ morals had not changed once the immediate crisis had passed.

“It is a great danger,” he said, “to be ungrateful toward God and, through forgetfulness of his benefits, neither to be moved by correction nor to rejoice in forgiveness” (Sermon 81, now 84, on the Octave of the Apostles).

“Therefore, beloved, I fear that the prophetic voice may seem to have rebuked people of this kind when it says: ‘I struck them, and they did not grieve; I chastised them, and they refused to accept discipline.’”

Although he had foreseen the cause of the evils, he did not withhold his aid from the endangered city. He went to meet the Vandal as he entered Rome and addressed the king at length. The barbarian king was preparing to destroy the city by sword and fire; Saint Leo obtained that he should be satisfied with plunder and refrain from fire and slaughter.

Genseric therefore carried away Rome’s wealth and led many thousands of captives to Africa, transporting Eudoxia and her daughters there as well.

Thus the *Miscellaneous History* says (book I): “Genseric immediately seized the city, emptied of its defenses, and, softened by the meeting with Pope Leo, preserved Rome from fire, slaughter, and torture, although he carried away all its wealth and transported many thousands of captives from there to Carthage, together with the empress Eudoxia and her daughters.”

[Note: We wish to add the testimony of Prosper, a contemporary writer, from the complete *Chronicle*, which had not been published when Quesnell wrote. Under the year 455 he says: “After the death of Maximus, the Roman captivity, deserving of many tears, immediately followed. Genseric gained possession of the city, empty of every defense, when Bishop Saint Leo met him outside the gates. Through God’s agency, Leo’s supplication so softened him that, although the city had been handed over to him and everything lay within his power, he nevertheless refrained from fire, slaughter, and torture. After fourteen days, Rome was emptied of all its wealth through a secure and unrestricted search, and many thousands of captives—chosen according to their age or skill—were taken to Carthage with the empress and her daughters.”]

Saint Leo also defended the three principal basilicas—the Constantinian basilica, Saint Peter’s, and Saint Paul’s—from plunder. When, after the disaster, Leo turned his attention to repairing the damage, he ordered the large and weighty silver vessels once given by Constantine to the three Constantinian basilicas—Saint Peter’s and Saint Paul’s as well—to be melted down and distributed among the city’s titular churches, as the *Book of the Pontiffs* records:

“He renewed, after the Vandal disaster, all the sacred silver furnishings throughout the titular churches, from six melted-down vessels: two for the Constantinian basilica, two for the basilica of blessed Peter the Apostle, and two for that of blessed Paul the Apostle. Constantine Augustus had presented them, and each weighed one hundred pounds.”

Platina adds that Saint Leo founded new churches and that the basilica of Saint Stephen on the Latin Way was constructed at the expense of the virgin Demetrias and under Leo’s direction.

“That author says that Leo, after turning his attention to restoring the city and its churches, moved Demetrias, the handmaid of God, to build a basilica to blessed Stephen on the Latin Way, three miles from the city, on her estate.”

Paul the Deacon says the same:

“In the time of this holy Leo, Demetrias, the handmaid of Christ, built the church of Saint Stephen at Rome.”

Leo’s care was not directed toward the churches alone. He undertook to restore the city itself while its magistrates were still stunned, to set everything in order and to fail no one. And although ecclesiastical jurisdiction had its limits, his charity had none.

## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 456; THE SEVENTEENTH OF POPE LEO; THE SEVENTH OF THE EMPERORS MARCIAN AND AVITUS; THE CONSULSHIP OF JOHN AND VARANES

[Column 0306A]

After the Vandal had devastated Rome and transported the booty to Africa, he sent a large crowd of captives to the king of the desert people Capropictus, as Victor of Vita reports.

[Note: Victor of Vita reports that only four captive brothers were sent to the king of the desert people Capropictus. From his account it is not clear whether these were the same people captured at Rome, and still less whether what he adds about envoys sent to Rome belongs to Leo’s pontificate or to a later period. The latter seems more probable.]

That nation was devoted to the empty superstition of idols. The Romans suffered less from the pain of exile than from the profane worship. While they still possessed, even in chains, the vigorous freedom of a Christian spirit, they recalled to the freedom of Christ people subjected to the slavery of demons and proclaimed the holy Gospel to them.

Then many of the barbarians, having shaken off the yoke of demons, submitted their heads to Christ and embraced the captives as liberators.

But because there was a shortage of presbyters and bishops, they sent envoys to Rome to Saint Leo, either because the neighboring province of Caesarean Mauretania—as we shall soon say—needed suitable ministers, or because the rest of Africa was oppressed by the rule of the Arian Vandals. In any case, they went to Rome, where doctrine was purer and ministers more plentiful.

[Column 0306B]

The envoys reached Rome by byways and hidden paths. They reported to the supreme pontiff how Christ’s dominion had been extended through the work of the captives, but that presbyters and bishops were needed. Leo received the envoys kindly and, with joy, granted their requests.

## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 457; THE EIGHTEENTH OF POPE LEO; THE FIRST OF THE EMPERORS LEO AND MAJORIAN; THE CONSULSHIP OF CONSTANTINE AND RUFUS
## I

While these things were taking place, the emperor Marcian died on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, to the great grief of all. His own merits had raised him from an obscure corner to the highest position; indeed, God himself, as though leading him by the hand through various circumstances, had elevated him to the summit of imperial power, so that in those most wretched times he might be the empire’s protection and the Church’s support. Good citizens mourned a great ruler; the orthodox mourned a Christian: one whose virtue matched his fortune, whose piety was singular, whose faith was unshaken, and whose justice was steadfast; in short, one to whom the commonwealth owed much, and the Church much.

Marcian departed this life while preparing an expedition into Africa, intending to avenge the destruction of the City [Col. 0306C] and the injury inflicted upon Eudoxia and her daughters. Leo succeeded him, heir not only to the empire but also to the virtues of his predecessor. Saint Leo immediately congratulated him on the imperial office by letter, and speaks of him with high praise in many places. He says that his election, to which the votes of all had assented, was as welcome to religion as to the empire; the testimony of the ancient writers agrees with this. Thus he writes to Anatolius:

> Thanks be to God, who, after the passing of Marcian, of holy and venerable memory, provided by the choice of all such a ruler that, in his virtues, both the Roman commonwealth and the Christian religion might rejoice.  
> (Epistle 106, now 146, ch. 2.)

## II

[Note: [Col. 0306D] Two disturbances of the Eutychians occurred after Marcian’s death, one at Constantinople and the other at Alexandria. Quesnellus deals sufficiently with the second. We learned of the first from Epistle 144 to Julian of Cos, which we recovered from a manuscript at Regensburg and which was written on 1 June. The Eutychians had begun plotting various measures concerning the new emperor Leo in order to win him to act as their patron. But all their efforts were destroyed through the activity of Julian and other Catholics. Leo learned these things from Julian’s letters; at the same time, certain reports about the Alexandrian disturbances reached Rome, though they were not accurately known until Anatolius’s letter, about which Quesnellus speaks below.]

In Egypt, when the heretics heard of Marcian’s death [Col. 0307A], they again began to stir up disturbances, thinking that, once the defender of orthodox faith had been removed, an empire already long troubled by the rivalry of competing claimants would be thrown into confusion, and that the faith could be overthrown amid disorder. They therefore used the opportunity to kindle a rebellion long conceived in secret.

The leader of the revolt was Timothy Aelurus, an Alexandrian presbyter formerly a monk. He ran about the city, surrounded by monks as though by bodyguards, and gathered the populace, eager for novelty and disturbances. He then summoned two bishops who had been deposed from the priesthood because of heresy, seized the place of Proterius, and ordered them to lay hands upon him, after the legitimate bishop had been removed. Proterius, learning that the faction was prevailing and fearing violence—for it was the season of Holy Week— withdrew into the baptistery.

The supporters of Aelurus rushed there in tumult. Neither the dignity of the episcopal office nor the sacredness of the place restrained them: they killed Proterius, dragged him with a hook through the streets, and mocked his corpse. They tore it to pieces, committed the pieces to the flames, and scattered the ashes. It is also reported that their madness went so far that some of them tore Proterius’s limbs apart with their teeth and swallowed them.

After the crime had been committed [Col. 0307B], the heretics undertook to overthrow the faith. They condemned the synod held at Chalcedon, struck Leo’s letter to Flavian with an anathema, and demanded a new synod. When these demands were brought to Constantinople, the emperor, abhorring the sacrilege and parricide, condemned by word and deed the audacity of the frenzied heresy and took away its hope of a synod.

In this disturbance of affairs, Anatolius wrote to Saint Leo, uncertain what he should do. He described what had happened at Alexandria and sought remedies for so many and such great evils. Saint Leo replied with a letter hitherto unpublished, which we now present and from which we have drawn this account. Leo says:

> The faith of this emperor is so praiseworthy, and his devotion so ready, that he has spontaneously supplied, without anyone’s intervention, what was suitable for the peace of the Church, as you yourself indicate, repelling every ambush of the heretics, who thought they had found an opportunity when the decrees of the holy Synod of Chalcedon might cease to be effective.  
> (Epistle 106, now 146, ch. 1.)

## III

[Note: [Col. 0307D] Saint Leo had written the previous month to the emperor a letter—Epistle 145, to Leo Augustus—corrected from our better manuscripts with its chronological notation, on the same month and day on which Epistle 146 to Anatolius was written.]

The previous month Saint Leo had written a letter to the emperor [Col. 0307C] (Epistle 115, now 145). He praised his zeal in securing peace, congratulated him on having deprived the heretics of hope for a synod, and asked that a bishop be elected by the Alexandrians whose faith was beyond doubt and whose holiness of life was well known.

He sent similar letters to Julian (Epistle 117, now 147) and to Aetius, in the letter which we have published from a manuscript. To frustrate the heretics’ plots, he sent encyclical letters concerning the faith of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0307D] The three letters mentioned above—145 to Augustus, 146 to Anatolius, and 147 to Julian—were written immediately after Anatolius’s report concerning the Alexandrian disturbances, on the fifth day before the Ides of July. The five following letters—148 to Leo Augustus, 149 to Basil of Antioch, 150 to Euxitheus of Thessalonica and the other metropolitans of Illyricum, 151 to Juvenal of Jerusalem, 152 to Julian, and 153 to Aetius—were sent on the Kalends of September on another occasion concerning the same matter. We have published a sixth letter of that same day, Epistle 154 to Anatolius, from the Regensburg manuscript. From it one may also infer Leo’s prudence and caution in the case of Atticus. When the first report reached him that Atticus, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, was openly fostering heresy, the holy pontiff, not entirely trusting the report, entrusted Anatolius with investigating the matter privately. If he discovered in Atticus’s heart any admixture of heretical poison, Anatolius was either to correct him and make him Catholic or, with the necessary severity, drive him from the Church.]

He sent letters to Basil of Antioch (Epistle 118, now 149), to Euxitheus of Thessalonica, vicar of Illyricum, and to Juvenal of Jerusalem (Epistle 119, now 150), whom he here counts among the metropolitans. He directed his letters to Julian of Cos and to the presbyter Aetius so that they might deliver them to those to whom they were addressed. He also attached copies of the letters he had written to the emperor, to the patrician Aspar, and to others, so that those acting in his place might know about his affairs.

In his letter to Julian (Epistle 120, now 152), written on the Kalends of September, he says that he is astonished that there are some who slander his letter to Flavian by alleging that it contains obscurities or ambiguities either of meaning or of language, although there is nothing in it that was not derived from evangelical and apostolic teaching:

> I am truly astonished that, through the vanity of those who slander, anything in my letter—which pleased the whole world—should still appear obscure, so that they think it ought to be more suitably explained. Its proclamation is so full and solid that it admits no novelty either in meaning or in expression. For whatever was then written by us is demonstrably taken from apostolic and evangelical teaching.

He likewise sent Aetius copies of the letters written to him by the bishops of Gaul and Italy (Epistle 121, now 153, ch. 2), to show that there was one faith in the West and that the teaching of all the bishops in those regions was his own:

> We have likewise sent copies of the letters which the bishops of Gaul and Italy sent to us in harmonious agreement, so that it may be clear that their faith also is one with ours.

Taking the opportunity, Leo wrote to the emperor for the third time. He commended the affairs of the Church to him and praised his faith [Col. 0308B], because he had shown himself an enemy of the heretics and a defender of the faith of Chalcedon:

> You resisted the shamelessness of the heretics so firmly that you declared yourself, for the peace of the whole world, the guardian of the Synod of Chalcedon.

## IV

After the Alexandrian bishop had been murdered and Timothy had intruded himself into his see, the orthodox bishops, for whom nothing was safe in Egypt after the slaughter of Proterius, decided to save themselves by flight and concealment. Those whom age permitted went to Constantinople [Col. 0308C], and there they humbly appealed to the emperor’s authority against the raging heresy. They presented petitions, recounted the evils that the Catholics had suffered, and explained at length the faith they professed.

The heretics likewise sent envoys to Constantinople and presented their letters to the emperor. They explained their faith in the same way: they professed to accept the Synods of Nicaea and Ephesus; they proclaimed the Robber Council of Dioscorus, or the false Synod of Ephesus; they rejected the synod held at Constantinople under Flavian as well as the Council of Chalcedon; they demanded that Augustus confirm Timothy in the Alexandrian see; and they asked him for letters to Timothy.

Several bishops had subscribed the petitions of the orthodox. There were no signatures to the letters of the heretics, as though they were ashamed both of their name and of their small number. Our Saint Leo says:

> Petitions were presented to Your Piety, copies of which you appended to your letters. But in those belonging to the Catholics there is the subscription of men lamenting their condition; and since their cause is credible, the names of each individual, or the dignity of his office, is confidently disclosed. In those petitions which heretical deceit did not fear to present to an orthodox ruler, however, the definite name is withheld beneath an uncertain designation of the whole body, so that not only the smallness of their number but also their worthlessness might remain hidden. They consider it useful to conceal the number of those whose character has been judged; and, not without reason, they fear to disclose from what place they come, since they have deserved condemnation.  
> (Epistle 125, now 156, ch. 4.)

The petitions of both sides are found among the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, part three.

The emperor Leo referred the matter [Note: [Col. 0308D] This matter was referred by the emperor not only to Anatolius but also to all the metropolitans, and especially to the Roman pontiff. This is made clear by the Encyclical Codex, which was not sufficiently known to Quesnellus. The compiler of this codex gathered documents prepared in this matter at the insistence of the emperor Leo. Since most of the documents were Greek, the Greek compiler also published the codex in Greek. But the Greek text is lost [Col. 0309C]. Only the Latin version remains, which Epiphanius Scholasticus composed. The order of this codex, as it is preserved in the manuscripts, is published in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 33 and following.

The matter proceeded as follows. After the Eutychians had intruded Timothy Aelurus into the Alexandrian see and Saint Proterius had been murdered, and after a great disturbance had arisen on this account between them and the Catholic Egyptians, both parties fled to the new emperor Leo with petitions. Since the Eutychians were attacking the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, the emperor thought that they might be recalled from their error if, instead of the new council they requested, the judgment of all the bishops were communicated by letter [Col. 0309D]. He therefore sent both petitions, together with his own letter, to all the metropolitans and especially to the Roman pontiff, asking that each one convene a synod in his own province and state his opinion in writing.

The imperial encyclical to Anatolius is copied in the celebrated codex at chapter 6. Then, in chapter 11, the names of the other bishops to whom the same letter was sent separately are appended; among them it is said to have been given first to Leo, the most reverend pontiff of the city of Rome. This encyclical was sent with great speed to all the metropolitans around October of this year, 457, through the Magistrians. It was delivered so carefully to the Roman pontiff that he was the first of all to reply to the emperor, in Epistle 156, on the Kalends of December. Accordingly, in the Encyclical Codex, immediately after the bishops’ names have been given, his letter is copied first, at chapter 12 [Col. 0310C].

The emperor gave Anatolius no other responsibility than that he too should convene a synod and communicate in writing his own judgment and that of his synod. If Anatolius sent an encyclical to the Roman pontiff and to all the metropolitans on the same occasion on which the emperor wrote, he did not do so by the emperor’s command, as though the emperor had especially entrusted this matter to him. Rather, he did so to satisfy the Catholic Egyptian bishops, who, in another petition delivered to him and copied in the celebrated codex at chapter 8, had asked him to make known their groans and the necessity of their faith to Leo, the most holy pontiff of the Roman Church, and to the other metropolitans.

To Anatolius’s letter to Leo, which was written on this matter and is now lost, the pontiff replied on the Kalends of December in Epistle 157. On the same day he also issued another letter, Epistle 158, to the Catholic Egyptians living at Constantinople. Epistle 155 to Anatolius, although it speaks of these bishops, was written in reply to earlier letters of Anatolius; and we showed in note 1 to that same letter that the title *On the Report against Timothy of Alexandria*, which Quesnellus incorrectly prefixed to it, is erroneous (previous volume, column 1125, note c).]

to Anatolius [Col. 0309A], so that in a synod *ἐνδημοῦσα*—that is, composed of bishops who were present in the city—judgment might be given concerning Timothy and the matters decreed at Chalcedon. It is evident from his letters to Augustus that Timothy was condemned and that the doctrine professed at Chalcedon was vindicated.

I therefore think that Anatolius received the report submitted by the Egyptian and orthodox bishops, namely the report later added to the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. They asked Anatolius to inform the bishops of Antioch, Jerusalem, Thessalonica, and especially Rome about the Alexandrian heretics, and to report what they had insolently done against the defenders of orthodox faith.

Anatolius wrote to Saint Leo (Epistle 124, now 155), and Saint Leo replied on the fifth or sixth day before the Ides of October. In our manuscript the letter bears this title: *On the Report against Timothy of Alexandria*. In the same hand he writes to the Egyptian bishops who had fled to Constantinople (Epistle 123, now 154). The title of that letter is: *To the Catholic Bishops from Egypt Residing at Constantinople* [Col. 0309B].

He consoles them because they are suffering so many evils for the cause of the faith. This is, he says, an occasion for joy rather than grief, since they have earned the praise and name of confessors. He urges them to defend courageously the faith upheld at Chalcedon. We were the first to make this letter public.

Nor did Anatolius write only to those whom we have mentioned; he also wrote to all the metropolitans of the East, both out of love for the faith and from a desire to advance his authority. The emperor Leo likewise wrote to all those to whom Anatolius sent letters. He first asked Saint Leo to come to Constantinople for the sake of pacifying the Church (Epistle 125, now 156, ch. 1). At the same time he sent them the reports of both the Catholic and heretical parties, so that they might give an impartial judgment.

The metropolitans, after receiving the letters of the emperor and Anatolius, convened provincial synods and read the reports publicly. They abhorred the evils perpetrated by the heretics in Egypt and judged that Timothy ought to be deposed. They approved the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon and denied [Col. 0309C] that what had been sanctioned there ought to be reconsidered.

Only Amphilochius, bishop of Side, although he condemned Timothy, rejected the Council of Chalcedon—perhaps because he was ignorant of the facts.

## VI

Before proceeding further, I have thought it necessary to insert here certain matters for the clarification of the history. The illustrious founder of the *Annals of the Church* writes that the reports we have discussed were sent from Egypt. But from what we have related [Col. 0310A] it appears that they were presented by the Egyptian bishops themselves, who were then refugees living at Constantinople.
