The learned cardinal adds that the reports were not delivered to the emperor until letters had been sent to all the metropolitans [Col. 0310A], from whom the emperor requested a profession of faith. But this does not agree with the emperor’s letters or with the bishops’ replies, which expressly discuss the reports that had been composed. The same is established by the letter of the monk Varadatus and by the testimony of Liberatus the deacon himself, who says that the emperor’s letters were sent only after the reports had been received.

## VII

Among the bishops’ letters there is a letter from Julian, bishop of Cos, to the emperor Leo. From it one may infer his return to his own Church [Note: [Col. 0310D] We have shown in the introduction to the letter of Julian inserted in the appendix, no. 2, that Julian remained at Constantinople for a longer period, at least until approximately the year 459. See volume I, column 1477 (of the previous volume of this edition, column 1241).], from which he had been absent for several years while conducting the business of the universal Church.

When he departed, he left the administration of affairs to Aetius, with whom Saint Leo was also accustomed to communicate by letter. Nor do I think that Julian remained any longer in the City after Marcian died. For I do not find that he informed Saint Leo about the Alexandrian revolt, nor do I think that he notified Leo of his departure. Leo addresses his letters to Aetius as well as to Julian, uncertain whether Julian was still staying in the City.

Moreover, Saint Leo himself complains of Julian’s silence in the letters common to Julian and Aetius. He says:

> Although I received a letter from Your Dilection some time ago, I am nevertheless surprised that you allowed the opportunity for replying to pass in silence, an opportunity which our brother Anatolius necessarily used, since, given the circumstances of the time and the matters involved, conversations ought to be more frequent.  
> (Epistle 117, now 147, ch. 1.)

And on the Kalends of September, when he had received no letters from Julian, he wrote to him as follows:

> Since an opportunity has arisen, it was fitting to send a letter to Your Dilection, by which we encourage your zeal in ecclesiastical matters and in those pertaining to the faith.

But because Leo inferred Julian’s absence from his silence, he also wrote to Aetius on the same occasion. After this, Julian of Cos is not mentioned again in Saint Leo’s letters.

## VIII

After receiving the letters of the emperor and Anatolius, Saint Leo was disturbed by the reports of the Alexandrians, because he saw that doubt was being raised about Timothy’s case and that the authority of the Council of Chalcedon was being endangered, with the emperor consulting the bishops as though the matter were uncertain.

He wrote to Augustus (Epistle 125, now 156) and indicated that his journey to Constantinople would be useless, because his presence would be harmful both to the decrees of the synod, which had been duly sanctioned through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and to the peace of the Churches [Col. 0311A], as though the faith of the synod were wavering—although otherwise he would defend it in every possible way.

After setting the reports of the orthodox and heretics against one another, he moderately yet wisely criticized the emperor’s uncertain judgment concerning Timothy:

> Is it not obvious whom Your Piety ought to assist and whom it ought to oppose, lest the Alexandrian Church, which has always been a house of prayer, should now become a den of robbers?  
> (Ibid., ch. 5.)

In the same letter he restrains the audacity of the heretics, who dared to demand what could not be requested even for the innocent, much less for sacrilegious parricides:

> With Your Piety’s permission, I say that they darken the brightness of your serenity with a kind of contagion, since sacrilegious parricides dare to request what even the innocent are not permitted to obtain.  
> (Ibid., ch. 3.)

At the end of the letter he promises several things that might take the place of a longer conversation. This gave rise to Epistle 134, now 165, in which many testimonies from the holy Fathers are brought forward to affirm the holy incarnation of the Word.

He also sent another letter to Anatolius [Col. 0311B], praising the emperor’s faith, which almost surpassed the vigilance of the priests (Epistle 126, now 167, ch. 1). He says that he has great hopes of Anatolius and trusts that, through his care and vigilance, the Alexandrian Church will be rescued from the hands of the heretics and that the enemies of the faith will be driven from the see to which they had made their way through murders and sacrilege.

He also does not conceal his joy that only four bishops adhered to Timothy’s heresy and criminal usurpation. He earnestly urges Anatolius to receive with every kindness the bishops who had fled Egypt, and to remove from the heretics their hope of convening a new synod.

Finally, he strongly reproves him for having allowed the presbyter Atticus publicly to argue at Constantinople against the faith professed at Chalcedon. He threatens that he will act by his own authority if Anatolius refuses to cut off from communion Atticus and Andrew, his partner in impiety.

This letter is preserved in our manuscript without a date or consuls. We publish it for the first time from that manuscript [Col. 0311C]; nevertheless, it was certainly written at this period.

## IX

Anatolius took it badly [Note: [Col. 0311D] Leo’s Epistle 163, ch. 1, indicates that Anatolius was displeased with the pontiff’s zeal, by which he warned him to beware of those said to oppose the common faith. The reference is to Atticus, a Constantinopolitan presbyter who was reported to have disputed publicly against the faith of Chalcedon.

Anatolius did not take this badly because he thought Leo was attending to his own affairs or to matters belonging to others; rather, he saw himself being accused of negligence or connivance by the several letters of the holy pontiff written on this subject.

First, Leo sent him Epistle 151 on the Kalends of September of this year, 457. Yet, in order not to injure Anatolius’s dignity, he entrusted the entire matter to him for investigation. He returned to the matter in Epistle 155, which he sent to him on another occasion, 11 October. He touched upon it again in Epistle 157, on the Kalends of December. On that day, while writing to the emperor about another matter, he commended this very important business to Augustus.

When he received no reply from Anatolius about it, he inserted further remarks on the same matter in Epistle 161, to the Constantinopolitan clergy, on 21 March of the following year, 458.

Soon he finally received Anatolius’s reply, which indicated that Leo’s zeal and concern had displeased him. The holy pontiff immediately replied in Epistle 163, dated—as we have corrected from our manuscripts—28 March.

Since the first mention there is made of a profession of faith sent by Atticus, it is sufficiently credible that Atticus sent it with Anatolius’s letter and through Anatolius himself. But there is no document to prove that Atticus was impelled to write this profession by the emperor rather than by Anatolius, as Quesnellus and others later suggest.

Since the profession of Atticus did not fully satisfy him, Leo demanded another, more explicit one. We indicated in note 3 to Epistle 163 that its formula has been preserved in ancient collections (previous volume of this edition, column 1147, note g).]

as though Leo were attending to his own affairs and to business belonging to others, and he indicated this to him in a letter sent the following year through the deacon Patricius.

Leo received Anatolius’s complaints with moderation and replied that he had not written these things with the intention of injuring him, since he had left him full authority to investigate everything:

> Nor have I in any respect injured your honor, since I entrusted to you for investigation the matters that had been reported to me.  
> (Epistle 28, now 163, ch. 1.)

What especially troubled Anatolius were Leo’s letters to Augustus, in which he was reproved for not expelling from his Church clergy whose faith was ambiguous, and indeed for tolerating carelessly the fact that some held and expressed perverse opinions about the faith:

> For this evil, which pestilently obscures the purity of the Church of Constantinople, ought to stir the priestly and apostolic spirit of Your Piety toward the justice of punishment. Certain clerics are found there who agree with the thinking of the heretics and who, by their assertions, assist the heretics within the very entrails of the Catholics. If my brother Anatolius is found sluggish in driving them out because he spares them with excessive kindness, deign, in accordance with your faith, to provide this medicine also for the Church: let such men be expelled not only from the clerical order but also from residence in the city, lest the holy people of God be further polluted by the contagion of perverse men.  
> (Epistle 125, now 156, ch. 5.)

Stimulated by Leo’s words, the emperor compelled Atticus to write to the Roman pontiff concerning his faith and, by a considered profession, to remove every suspicion concerning his doctrine. Atticus fulfilled outwardly what Augustus had ordered: he composed and sent to Rome a confession of faith, but it was obscure and entangled in verbal circumlocution.

He seemed to hate Eutyches, but not to reject Eutyches’s errors. He openly declared himself Eutyches’s enemy, but this could be understood as a matter of private hostility. His failure openly to condemn Eutyches’s heresy made his faith suspect.

Saint Leo described Atticus’s letter in the following year:

> By sending writings of doubtful faith and uncertain profession, he confirmed rather than dispelled everything that report had brought to us about him. For if he had wished to prove his conscience sincere, he ought to have confessed not merely that Eutyches was hateful to him, but that he rejected and condemned his perfidy. For human hostilities, even among Catholics, are one thing; the devil’s errors, which the Catholic faith condemns, are another.  
> (Epistle 128, now 163, ch. 1.)

Leo therefore demanded from him not a disguised but an explicit condemnation of Eutychianism, a clear and sincere confession agreeing with the faith of Chalcedon. If Atticus continued to refuse, Leo declared him liable to the penalties that the synod had imposed against heretics.

One may admire the vigilance as well as the prudence of the supreme pontiff. Although he carefully guarded the rights of the Churches, as we explained above, he nevertheless pressed the matter of negligent bishops whenever he judged that it served the interests of the Church and necessity required it.

Meanwhile, although the heretics were hated by everyone, especially by the emperor, they nevertheless tried by covert means to attack sound faith. They sought to delay the Church’s affairs by postponement and circumvention and to advance their own interests [Col. 0312C].

At this time Basiliscus was powerful at court and secretly favored the heretics; he was the man who later usurped the empire. Through his influence and favor the heretics were abusing their position to the destruction of the Church. I would readily be persuaded that, through Basiliscus’s efforts, hope was given for a new synod and that Timothy was handed the letter of Leo, the Roman pontiff, to the emperor—a letter condemning the ordination of the sacrilegious man, as Evagrius records in book II, chapter 1 [576].

Timothy issued a reply in which he did not hesitate to criticize either Leo’s letter or the Council of Chalcedon.

In the meantime, the Egyptian bishops who were living at Constantinople as exiles for the sake of the faith were tormented by the heretics’ delays and evasions. They therefore fled to Leo and requested help.

We have fortunately recovered the reply which he gave on the Kalends of December (Epistle 127, now 158). In it he begins by consoling their tears with tears [Col. 0313A]. He testifies to his own grief and replies that he had already anticipated their request in the letters he had written to the emperor. He urges them to promise themselves much from the goodness of God and the emperor’s faith, and finally to hope for a favorable outcome to their affairs.

He then encourages them to endure persecutions by the example of the apostles and not to consider their labors fruitless, since an immeasurable reward is joined to them.

# The Year of Christ 458; the 19th year of Pope Leo; the 2nd year of the emperors Leo and Majorian; the same Augusti as consuls

## I

The emperor’s policy increased the Catholics’ hope. As we said in the preceding year, the heretics had requested a synod at which the decrees issued at Chalcedon might be reconsidered. Augustus, concerned for the peace of the Church and the empire, had been hesitant about convening a synod, thinking that the disturbances of the Church might be calmed if a synod were held.

Later, persuaded by Leo’s letters, he removed the heretics’ hope of convening a council. Yet the fury of the heretics did not cease. Once their hope of a synod had been cut off, they requested a public conference with those whom Pope Leo might choose.

The request seemed reasonable, and in fact many were deceived by these tactics. Rumors were spread that they sincerely wished to be instructed in the truth of the faith and were not so attached to their opinions that they would refuse correction if their falsehood were demonstrated.

This was what they said openly, but in reality they requested a conference with the intention of procrastinating. They were considering better times for themselves, since affairs are subject to many changes. Moreover, the danger to orthodox faith occupied their minds: it might again be put at risk, and matters defined by the authoritative judgment of the Fathers might be reopened.

Add to this that, if they fought in this conflict with uncertain prospects, they might request a new synod while their own position had not yet been defeated in the conference.

Having arranged matters in this way, they approached the emperor under the appearance of peace, through courtiers favorable to them, and persuaded him to agree to a conference. Surrounded by counsels that seemed useful, he wrote to Saint Leo about the matter (Epistle 132, now 162, ch. 2). He confessed that a synod was being requested in vain after the Council of Chalcedon had ended the controversy:

> Perfection does not admit increase, and fullness does not admit addition.

Saint Leo himself praised these splendid words of the emperor in his own letters and transmitted them to posterity.

## II

The emperor further asked the holy pontiff to send bishops from the West, since Leo could not properly travel to Constantinople, in order to clarify certain questions. The perceptive pontiff recognized the heretics’ cunning and replied in these words:

> You clearly recognize what is being attempted through the great plots of the heretics: that a more searching discussion should be held, as though nothing had previously been defined, between the disciples of Eutyches and Dioscorus and the one whom the Apostolic See has sent. What all the Catholic priests of the world approved and rejoice to see established in the holy Council of Chalcedon would thus be made weak, even to the injury of the most sacred Council of Nicaea.  
> (Ibid., ch. 1.)

Nevertheless, he promised to send bishops—not to renew the struggle against the enemies of the faith. For it was not to be tolerated that matters once established at Nicaea and Chalcedon should be recast:

> Let Your Piety therefore know in advance, venerable emperor, that those whom I promise to send will not depart from the Apostolic See to fight with the enemies of the faith or to contend against them. For we dare not enter into any discussion concerning matters defined, as God willed, at Nicaea and at Chalcedon, as though the things established with such authority through the Holy Spirit were doubtful or insecure.  
> (Ibid., ch. 3.)

At the end of the letter he commends the collapsing Alexandrian Church to the emperor and urgently asks him [Col. 0314A] to expel the parricides from the city and finally restore the Church to freedom.

## III

To this letter he added another (Epistle 130, now 160) to the bishops and clergy who, driven from their homeland by the faction of the heretics, were staying at Constantinople [577]. The letter deserves to be brought to light; we have rescued it from darkness for the first time.

Its address names fifteen bishops. He consoles them in their exile and warns them not to be disturbed by the arrival of the Western bishops whom, at the emperor’s request, he is sending to Constantinople to explain questions of faith that were troubling certain minds.

He then urges them to continue fighting steadfastly for the faith and to take care lest their disagreement dissolve their cause and they again join battle with the heretics, deceived either by the appearance of a conference or by that of a disputation.

He added a third letter to the Constantinopolitan clergy (Epistle 131, now 161). He congratulates them on the sincerity of their faith, urges them to steadfastness, and asks them not to allow the proscribed heresy to rage within their own entrails. They are to remove from their company those whom they know to be infected with this evil.

He refers to Atticus and Andrew, whom we said were suspected of heresy, and orders them removed from office unless they condemn in word and writing the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches and openly swear allegiance to the faith of Chalcedon.

He further adds the names of those whose faith was doubtful and which he had already reported to Anatolius. From this I infer that the letter to that same bishop mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0313D] He means Epistle 163 to Anatolius. We showed in note 12 to that same Epistle 163 that it was written after Epistle 161 to the Constantinopolitan clergy, with its chronological notation corrected (previous volume, column 1148, note j).

If, in Epistle 161, Leo writes that he had indicated the names of those whose faith was doubtful in letters previously sent to Anatolius, he does not mean Epistle 163, which was sent later, but Epistles 151, 155, and 157, which had previously been written to him.]

was not sent at that time but had been sent earlier, as we explained above.

### IV.

Five months had already elapsed before Saint Leo sent the bishops whom he had promised—whether suitable men for so important a matter were lacking at Rome, or whether something else delayed their departure, which, as we learn from a previously unpublished letter, took place toward the end of August. Baronius rightly judged that there had been another letter besides Letter 78, now numbered 132 (but currently 162), in which, according to custom, the appointed legates, their names, and their commendation were discussed. We have found this letter and now make it publicly available. It is indeed an outstanding letter, celebrated in antiquity, known to Facundus and excerpted by him—as we learn from his writings—and cited by the supreme pontiffs Vigilius and Pelagius as evidence in the controversy over the Three Chapters. It was also copied almost in its entirety by Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, as we discuss more fully in the notes.

At once, he briefly excuses the delay in the departure of the bishops Geminianus and Domitian. It is not easy to say who these bishops were. Some identify Domitian as the bishop of Mutina; Geminianus, however, they believe was summoned from Gaul, from Châlons, since it is difficult to find another person of that name in that period. The matter is obscure and of little importance.

In this letter he earnestly begs and adjures Augustus not to permit an opportunity for the dispute to be renewed: the question of faith must not again be reopened, nor the definitions reached at Chalcedon brought back for examination. He should assist the Church of Alexandria and, without delay or pity, remove from the episcopate Timothy, who had occupied the see for two full years, as though he were a parricide. “Therefore,” he says,

> What the impious parricide committed in invading the holy Church and in the most savage murder of its bishop cannot be expiated by human remissions, unless he is entreated who alone can punish such crimes and alone can release them through his ineffable mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0314D] Evagrius is referring not to Letter 164 but to Letter 156, as we proved in the prefatory notice to that letter.]

This, I think, is the very letter praised by Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 10:

> Therefore, first Leo, bishop of elder Rome, wrote in defense of the council of Chalcedon. He also rejected Timothy’s ordination, since it had been performed unlawfully and without due deliberation. The emperor Leo sent this letter of Leo to Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, through Diomedes the *silentiarius*, who carried out the imperial commands. Timothy replied to him, criticizing both the council of Chalcedon and Leo’s letter.

That is: First, Leo, bishop of elder Rome, wrote in defense of the Council of Chalcedon and rejected Timothy’s ordination as having been performed unlawfully. The emperor Leo sent Leo’s letter to Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, through Diomedes the *silentiarius*, the bearer of the imperial commands. Timothy replied to him, criticizing the Council of Chalcedon and Leo’s letter.

I do not think that this passage is to be understood of any letter other than Letter 133, now numbered 164, which is being published for the first time here. For I cannot interpret it as referring to the very lengthy Letter 134, now numbered 165, supported by testimonies from the holy Fathers, because that letter contains not a word about Timothy’s rejected ordination, although Evagrius says that Leo wrote about that matter in it.

### V.

Besides these letters, three days later he sent another to the same Augustus (Letter 134 to Leo Augustus, now 165), although he had promised it long before, namely on the first day of November—December, rather—as is clear from Letter 125, now 156, chapter 6. There is no doubt that it was written on the occasion of the same embassy, as both the timing and the character of the letter indicate. It contains a longer and more careful treatment of the mystery of the Incarnation, together with many extensive testimonies of the holy Fathers, by which it is shown that the error of Eutyches had long since been proscribed in the Church. Finally, at the end of the letter, the pontiff most earnestly asks Augustus to provide for the peace of the Churches of the Lord by his decree and to defend God’s gifts among all who are subject to him.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] We have shown in the prefatory notice to Letter 165, note 2, that it was delivered not three days later but on the same day as Letter 164.]

### VI.

In this same year Leo, no less concerned for the observance of ecclesiastical discipline than for the integrity of the Catholic faith, wrote two letters of the kind called decretals: one to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, and the other to Neon, bishop of Ravenna. Both arose from the devastation inflicted upon the regions of Italy by Attila two years earlier (Letter 129, now 159).

Aquileia, a city powerful in the wealth of Italy and renowned for the size of its population, was once regarded as almost another Rome. But, exposed to barbarian invasions, it experienced a changeable fate. Attila, having traversed the empire with his army and devastated its most distinguished towns, captured and plundered this city. After destroying it, the barbarian led away a great number of people into captivity.

Then many women, widowed by the loss of their husbands—some killed, others presumed unable to return in the future—and unable to endure widowhood sufficiently, sought other marriages and did not hesitate to marry other men. When circumstances were restored and their former husbands returned from captivity, they reclaimed the marriage bed. The men who had married the abandoned women planned to keep them.

While the marriage beds were being contested and it was uncertain which husband had the stronger claim, Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman Church whom our Leo had perhaps sent to Aquileia to investigate the condition of that Church, returned to Rome. He reported several points of controversy and stated that Nicetas had asked what the apostolic see thought about them; for he had brought no written document containing the consultation.

Saint Leo replied concerning the first point, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, “What God has joined, let no human being separate”: the bonds of lawful marriage must be restored, and each person must recover what belongs to him or her.

Against those who, compelled either by fear or by necessity, had eaten sacrificial foods, he writes that they must be cleansed through penitential satisfaction, which should be measured not so much by the length of time as by the contrition of the heart. He likewise adds, concerning those who had been baptized a second time, whether led to it by fear or by error, that their fault must be washed away through penance and that, by the judgment of the bishop, they should be received back into the unity of communion. Those, however, who had received baptism from heretics were to be confirmed solely through invocation of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands (the same Letter, chapters 1–7).

### VII.

The Letter to Neon of Ravenna was formerly assigned to the year 451 (Letter 135, now 166), because it was read as bearing the consulship of Marcian. We have substituted Majorian for Marcian and restored the letter to the present year; the reasons for this correction are given in the notes.

Leo decrees two things. The first concerns children carried away into captivity. If nothing certain can be learned about their baptism, he says:

> Let such a person approach without fear to receive grace, knowing that there is no trace of it in himself; nor should we fear to open to him the door of salvation, which he is taught never to have entered . . . . For an act whose having been performed is wholly unknown cannot incur the charge of repetition.

Regarding those baptized by heretics—the second point—he establishes the same rule that he had defined in the preceding letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] To these two letters, to Nicetas and Neon, must be added Letter 167 to Rusticus of Narbonne, which we have shown in its prefatory notice to have been written around this time, and which Quesnell discussed under the year 440, note 15.]

### VIII.

A constitution of the emperor Majorian issued this year is also read. It forbids parents to compel virgins to make a profession of virginity and forbids them to accept from their parents the veil before the fortieth year of age. Widows are likewise condemned if they refuse a second marriage not out of love for continence but from a desire for a freer life.

The *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* reports that Leo established the same rule concerning virgins:

> Here too he established that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-covering unless she had been proven to have remained a virgin for forty years.

(Letter 125, now 156, chapter 3.)

The letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, also contains certain matters belonging to the same subject. This readily persuades me that the edict of Majorian was promulgated through Leo’s efforts and advice. We therefore understand that it did not seem unusual to bishops for rulers to establish laws concerning monastic profession and discipline. Indeed, the pontiffs themselves were often the advisers of kings when such laws were enacted. They considered it part of royal authority to provide both for the interests of the commonwealth and for the good of the Church.

Saint Leo wrote this very thing to the emperor Leo:

> You must recognize without hesitation that royal power has been conferred not only for the governance of the world but especially for the protection of the Church.

## YEAR OF CHRIST 459; 20TH OF POPE LEO; 3RD OF THE EMPERORS LEO AND MAJORIAN; CONSULS RICIMER AND PATRICIUS

In this year our Leo wrote, on the day before the Nones of March, a single letter to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum (Letter 136, now 168). He reproved them because they baptized on the feast days of martyrs, omitting the sanctification associated with exorcisms and fasts and abandoning other rites of this kind. He decreed that baptism should not be administered on any days other than Easter and Pentecost.

In the same letter he forbids the publication, in a written booklet, of a confession concerning the particular kind of each person’s sins, since the guilt of consciences is sufficiently disclosed to priests alone through private confession. He does not, however, disapprove if someone, of his own accord, out of the fullness of faith and fear of God, is not afraid to feel such shame before others that he wishes to make his own conscience public.

## YEAR OF CHRIST 460; 20TH OF POPE LEO; OF THE EMPERORS LEO AND MAJORIAN; CONSULS MAGNUS AND APOLLONIUS

### I.

To return now to the sequence of events in the East: we have said that in the year 458 Leo sent the bishops Domitian and Geminian to Constantinople, where they were to conduct the pontiff’s case concerning the faith. What success they had in carrying out their embassy is obscure. For neither Leo’s letters nor ecclesiastical historians report what they did at Constantinople.

The only certain fact is that Anatolius died in the preceding year, before the arrival of the legates.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Anatolius died not in the preceding year, 459, but in the year 458. Since Nicephorus’s *Chronicle* assigns eight years and as many months to his episcopate, while Theophanes reckoned nine years, and since he obtained the episcopate toward the end of 449, he died in 458, in August or on 3 July, the date on which the Greeks celebrate his feast.]

It is thought that his death delayed their plans, while time was consumed in choosing a successor. It is also certain from Leo’s letter to Gennadius (Letter 138, now 170) that they did not return to Rome before this year, 460, around the month of June.

But what happened during this interval? If one may arrive at a conjecture, a council was held at Constantinople at which the letters that the metropolitans had sent to Augustus, each with the subscriptions of the bishops of his own province, were read aloud. The letter of Saint Leo, Letter 134, now 165, to Leo Augustus, together with the appended testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the Incarnation of the Word of God, was also read.

After these documents had been read, as though a general council had been held, with the common agreement of those present and absent and with the emperor’s authority added, Timothy was condemned and ordered to leave the episcopate which he had seized by force.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] This conjecture appears to have been taken from Cardinal Baronius. He believes that, at the synod held by Gennadius against the simoniacs, the matters concerning the Eutychians indicated by Quesnell were likewise conducted in the presence of Domitian and Geminian, legates of the apostolic see; see under the year 459, notes 1 and following. Baronius wrote this because he had seen the synodical document of that council against the simoniacs without the subscriptions of the Fathers. Since, however, all the subscriptions, carefully published in volume V of the Councils, column 49, lack the names of the bishops Domitian and Geminian, Baronius’s conjecture—that certain matters concerning the Eutychians were conducted at that same synod in the presence of the legates—is recognized as weak. Nor is there any documentary support for imagining another Constantinopolitan synod. For when Leo writes to Gennadius concerning Timothy, “constrained by the judgments of all the priests of the Lord,” he is referring not to some general or nearly general council at Constantinople, of which no memory survives, but to the judgments pronounced against Timothy by all the bishops throughout the world in letters sent to the emperor.]

Leo refers to this sentence against Timothy in his letter to Gennadius, who had succeeded Anatolius: “constrained,” he says, “by the judgments of all the priests of the Lord.” Letter 137 to Leo Augustus likewise records that the emperor added his authority to that of the bishops, so that the impious Timothy was compelled to leave the episcopal see:

> Let Your Clemency know that all the Churches of God rejoice and exult together with praise for you, because the wicked parricide has been driven from the yoke of the Church of Alexandria, and the people of God, upon whom the criminal plunderer had imposed himself, have been restored to the ancient freedom of the faith. They can now be recalled to the way of salvation through the preaching of faithful priests, since they see that the whole seedbed of poisons has been cast down together with its author.

### II.

Once driven from his see, Timothy, being of an adaptable disposition, resorted to stratagems. He yielded to circumstances because he could not resist the judgment of all the bishops and could no longer condemn the Council of Chalcedon. He therefore pretended to accept the bishops’ judgment and obey the decrees of the council, thinking that prompt obedience would remove suspicion of obstinacy or heresy and that, through the favor and influence of his friends, his see might thus be restored to him.

When matters had been arranged in this way, he hastened to Constantinople with the emperor’s permission and communicated with the Catholics as though he were innocent. Warned by Gennadius’s letters and by two bishops, Leo complained at length about this matter to the emperor and to Gennadius himself (Letter 138, now 170). He demonstrated in many ways that Timothy was unworthy of the episcopate not only because of heresy but also because of the parricide and sacrileges he had committed: he had forcibly occupied the see while Proterius was still alive, kindled the fires of sedition in the Church of Alexandria, and inflicted death upon its bishop.

Above all, Leo commended to Gennadius that he exclude the sacrilegious parricide not only from the Church’s public assembly but also from the private fellowship of the faithful:

> Therefore your Dilection must strive and labor with the earnest concern for which you are distinguished, lest any conversation, private or public, take place with so wicked a man; and lest, under the guise of correction, an opportunity be offered for some gathering with him, so that he may obtain complete freedom to return—although the most Christian prince has already judged him by his edicts.

He begs Augustus (Letter 137, now 169) to order that another bishop be appointed to the see of Alexandria, one whose faith was no less approved than his character was upright, and that he be ordained according to the ancient custom, as we read in the letter to Gennadius. These words were deliberately inserted into the letter: Leo silently criticizes the custom introduced by Anatolius, who had claimed for himself and his see, contrary to ancient practice, the authority to ordain bishops, especially those of the principal sees. For this reason he admonishes Gennadius not to preserve the innovation introduced by his predecessors, but to observe the ancient law prescribed by the canons.

### III.

Scarcely two months had passed when, behold, legates from the Church of Alexandria arrived: Daniel, a presbyter, and Timothy, a deacon, bearing letters from the new bishop of Alexandria, duly consecrated. They brought joyful news: Timothy had been expelled from Alexandria by imperial decree and sent far away; and, by the common consent of clergy and people and by the votes of all, Timothy surnamed Salophaciolus had been duly and solemnly elected and ordained.

Leo immediately sent three congratulatory letters, written on the same day; they are recorded as having been dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September. He wrote the first to Salophaciolus himself (Letter 139, now 171): he congratulates him on his election and urges him, as he had declared in his letters, to restore heretics who had been driven astray to the straight path of the faith.

The second was written to the Alexandrian clergy (Letter 140, now 172); the third to the bishops who had ordained Salophaciolus (Letter 141, now 173). He shares his joy with them because a man had been ordained to whom neither ambition, nor the reckless violence of a disorderly crowd, nor sedition, nor intrigue had contributed anything.

These were Leo’s last letters, and the last work, so far as I know, of the great bishop.

## YEAR OF CHRIST 461; 22ND OF POPE LEO; 5TH OF LEO AND 2ND OF SEVERUS, EMPERORS; CONSULS SEVERINUS AND DAGALAIPHUS

### I.

At last Leo, the supreme pontiff, after enduring many labors for Christ and waging fierce battles against the enemies of the faith, and after subduing heresies by his writings and words, died. From what we have related, it is easy either to know or to grasp inwardly with what wisdom he governed the helm of the Church, with what steadfastness he held the rudder without yielding to any storms, and with what vigilance he provided for difficult circumstances.

After completing so many works with success, he departed to Christ, so that he who had served as Christ’s representative might enter into a share of his eternal inheritance. Truly blessed was the pontiff who, while life remained, always stood unshaken amid the disturbances of divided Churches, amid the conflicting aims of bishops and the schemes of heretics, terrified by neither the harshness of times nor that of circumstances. He did not yield to the majesty of kings; he was not overcome by the imposing authority of a false council; nor was he deceived by the strategies of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople.

Greater than every danger, he turned his victories to the advancement of the faith. He calmed the quarrels of the Churches, checked reckless men who dared too much, corrected or punished the crimes of wicked people, and, roaming everywhere with watchful eyes, neglected nothing that could contribute to the welfare of the Church and of the Christian empire.

It was his magnificent and glorious achievement that he obtained the pontificate when almost the whole of the East was troubled by shameful heresies and the pillars of the Church had either been overthrown or were tottering. He died when peace had been secured everywhere and the principal sees were occupied by bishops who showed as much care in preserving peace as others had shown eagerness to kindle war or cowardice in extinguishing it. Gennadius had been substituted for the most vain Anatolius; Timothy Salophaciolus for the most impious Timothy the Cat; and Anastasius for Juvenal of Jerusalem, who had fallen in courage in the cause of the faith.

To this must be added that, just as after being raised to the Roman see he settled private disputes even among military commanders, so throughout the entire course of his pontificate he devoted himself to calming the disturbances of the Church. At last, a man born for the happiness of the empire and the Church, he brought peace to both.

### II.

In addition to all that we have related, the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* records that, through his piety and care, several basilicas were built at Rome. In particular, it says that he restored the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul:

> Here he renewed the basilica of the apostle Peter and made a vaulted chamber there, which he also adorned; and he renewed the basilica of Saint Paul after the divine fire. He likewise made a vaulted chamber in that basilica and in the Constantinian basilica.

Pope Adrian, in his letter to Charlemagne, gives a fuller account of the decoration of this basilica:

> Likewise the outstanding and wondrous preacher of the sacred Fourth Council, Saint Leo the pope, also built churches, which he adorned by painting in mosaic various histories or images. Especially in the basilica of the holy apostle Paul, he made the great arch there and painted in mosaic our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, and adorned with verses the twenty-four elders, named individually; and from that time until now they have been faithfully venerated by us.

The most illustrious author of the *Annals* writes that this image of the Savior remained intact until his own time, but that the twenty-four elders had been disfigured by age and decay. An inscription by Gruter, composed in four verses and copied from the larger arch of this basilica, shows that the work was carried out through the generosity and expense of the empress Galla Placidia and through the zeal and care of Saint Leo:

> THEODOSIUS began; HONORIUS completed the hall  
> Of the Teacher of the world, consecrated by the body of PAUL.  
> PLACIDIA, pious in mind, rejoices that all the glory of her father’s work  
> Shines through the zeal and splendor of the pontiff LEO.

Baronius, under the year 461, note 12, reports the inscription in another form and says that it was carved at the basilica of Saint Laurence, restored through Placidia’s generosity and Leo’s zeal:

> PLACIDIA, pious in mind, rejoices in the zeal and splendor of the pontiff LEO.  
> The Lord removed the darkness, so that, once the light had been created,  
> A radiance now shines in these former hiding places.  
> The body once had narrow, passable approaches,  
> Where now a more spacious hall receives the people.  
> The excavated level lay open, cut away beneath the hill,  
> And the ruin, once dangerously oppressive, has been removed.

He also built, as the *Book of the Pontiffs* records, a basilica for Saint Cornelius, bishop and martyr, beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way . . .

> Here he established a monastery near the blessed apostle Peter . . .  
> Here he established that during the action of the sacrifice it should be said: “THE HOLY SACRIFICE, THE UNSTAINED OFFERING,” etc.  
> Here too he established and appointed, over the tombs of the apostles, guardians from the Roman clergy, who are called chamberlains; “whom,” says Baronius, “we now call chaplains,” for among the ancients a chamber was the same as what we now call a chapel.

Radulphus, dean of Tongeren, *On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 23, says:

> In certain Chronicles it is read that Leo I established that, after the offertory had ended, incense should be placed over the offering in memory of Christ’s death.

And shortly afterward:

> The priest, standing, urges the people to pray, saying: “PRAY FOR ME,” which is attributed to Pope Leo.

Then, after inserting much material:

> The beginning of the prayer is: “THIS, THEREFORE,” etc., which they attribute to Saint Leo the Great.

Finally, toward the end:

> It follows, he says, “LET US BLESS THE LORD,” or “GO, THE MASS IS ENDED”; to which all respond: “THANKS BE TO GOD.”  
> And Pope Leo established that these words should be said.

We noted above that, through his care, the virgin Demetrias built a basilica in honor of Saint Stephen; it is mentioned by Paul the Deacon, Hermannus Contractus, Platina, and Cuspinian. The *Book of the Pontiffs* adds the following:

> Here he held four ordinations in the month of December in the city of Rome: eighty-one presbyters and one hundred eighty-five bishops in various places. He was also buried near the blessed apostle Peter on the third day before the Ides of April. The episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

The Roman Breviary says nothing about his ordinations, although it does not omit the ordinations of other Roman pontiffs. In the Thuanean manuscript, whose title is *The Order of the Bishops of the City of Rome from Peter to Hadrian under Charlemagne*, Saint Leo is numbered as the forty-seventh pope, and these words are found there:

> Here he held seven ordinations: seventy-seven presbyters, thirty deacons, and one hundred seventy-five bishops.

### III.

It is easy to say on what day the holy pontiff closed his final day if we follow the common opinion; it is not so easy if the matter is subjected to more careful examination. The records of the present Church state that he departed this life on the third day before the Ides of April, that is, on the eleventh day of the month. The consensus of more recent writers supports this date, placing it under the consulship of Severinus and Dagalaiphus, or in the year of Christ 461, after he had administered the Roman Church for twenty-one years less thirty days.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] The catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, together with the *Pontifical Book*, assign Leo twenty-one years, one month, and twenty-six days—or, better, thirteen days. We believe that this question concerning the day of Saint Leo’s death, which Quesnell discusses at length, can be settled more briefly from older books and more reliable evidence. From the three dates associated with Leo in ecclesiastical books, three opinions concerning the day of his death have arisen. Some prefer 11 April, others 28 June, and others 10 November. Quesnell, defending 30 October on the basis of the single Corbie manuscript of Dacherius, introduced a fourth opinion. Finally, Antonio and Francesco Pagi added a fifth, assigning Leo’s death to 4 November. The view that Saint Leo died on the fourth day before the Ides of November is by far the most probable and has generally been accepted by scholars.

Among all the books that mark the day of Leo’s death, the oldest is the so-called Hieronymian Martyrology. All copies of this Martyrology have, on the fourth day before the Ides of November: “The deposition of Saint Leo the pope.” That this refers to our Leo is clear from the fact that the Martyrology predates the period of the other pontiffs of this name.

Not only the other ancient Martyrologies abridged from the Hieronymian, together with Rabanus and the Beauvais Lectionary cited by Quesnell, agree with this date, but also the length of the pontificate assigned to Leo. We proved that he was ordained on 29 September 440 in note 1 to the year 440. His catalogued pontificate is twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. Although some catalogues, differing in the number of days, give twenty-six days and some twenty-eight, the more authoritative and more numerous ones give thirteen days, as is evident from the Corbie manuscript ending with Vigilius; another Corbie manuscript published by Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume III; another very ancient manuscript among the Bollandists, volume I of April; and others cited by Pagi under the year 461, note 3. To these must be added two more: one perhaps the oldest of all, ending with Hormisdas, which we found in the Vatican manuscript Regina 1997; and another published from a very ancient Veronese manuscript by Father Joseph Bianchini, volume IV of Anastasius, in the prolegomena, page 6.

The paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul also agree, as does an inscription from a Verdun manuscript printed in Mabillon’s *Analecta* and reproduced below by Quesnell, note 11; all give the same number of days. If one counts twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days from 29 September, Leo’s death falls on the fourth day before the Ides of November.

In the inscription cited above, Leo is said to have been deposited on the third day before the Ides . . . . Since the name of the month is missing, some have thought that April should be supplied, so that his death would be assigned to the third day before the Ides of April, the date on which several writers, together with the *Pontifical Book*, say that he was buried.

But these documents are later than the Hieronymian Martyrology and should not be preferred to it, especially since the length of Leo’s pontificate recorded in all the catalogues, beginning with his ordination on 29 September, in no way agrees with death in April. Add that this cannot be reconciled with the ordination of Hilary, which Quesnell, note 4, correctly places in November.

He is wrong only in assigning Hilary’s ordination to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, because he thought that the year 461 had the Dominical Letter F. Since the Dominical Letter of that year was A, Hilary must be said to have been ordained on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, that is, on 19 November 461.

If Saint Leo had died on 11 April, the Roman see would have to be regarded as vacant for seven months and more, something inconsistent with the customs of that period. The same catalogues that, together with the published Anastasius, report that Leo was buried on the third day before the Ides of April immediately add that his episcopate ceased for seven days.

This agrees perfectly with our view: if Leo died on 10 November, Hilary could have been elected seven days later, with his ordination postponed by two days so that it might be conducted on a Sunday.

On these grounds Quesnell’s opinion collapses, according to which Leo died on the third day before the Kalends of November, that is, on 30 October. A single Corbie calendar, which is not free from other errors, cannot have enough authority to be preferred to so many documents and arguments set forth above. The opinion of both Pagis fails even more decisively, since no document supports it concerning Leo’s death. They prefer only Marianus Scotus, who assigns Hilary’s ordination to the second day before the Ides of November.

Since other documents indicate that the Roman see was vacant for seven days, they inferred that Leo’s death should be placed on 4 November. But the older documents by which we assigned Leo’s death to 10 November—if indeed the Roman see was vacant for seven days—show that Marianus Scotus wrongly advanced Hilary’s ordination to the second day before the Ides of that same month.

The opinion assigning his death to the fourth day before the Kalends of July, that is, to 28 June, is also mistaken. The Roman Church’s *Capitulary of the Gospels* testifies that on this date not Leo’s death but the translation of Saint Leo was celebrated.

John Fronto was the first to publish this under the name of a calendar. But from the editions of the venerable Cardinal Tommasi, Domenico Georgi, and others, it is clear that the *Capitulary of the Gospels* itself is extremely ancient. In it, according to all editions and manuscripts, we read under 28 June: “The translation of the body of Saint Leo.” An inscription mentioned by Mabillon records that this translation took place on that same day under Sergius in 688, in these words:

> He was deposited on the third day before the Ides . . . . . . and was again translated here by Blessed Pope Sergius on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the first indiction.

Whether on 11 April we should admit another, earlier translation or elevation appears sufficiently probable from Bede’s genuine Martyrology. Shortly after Sergius, in addition to 28 June, it assigns 11 April to Leo’s feast.

Since, according to the established facts, neither Leo’s death nor his ordination can be assigned to this date, some translation or elevation of him, earlier than Sergius, must be posited for that day. Perhaps for this reason the cited inscription says that Leo was translated under Sergius “again,” that is, a second time.]

This, I say, is the common opinion, which I believe was first drawn from Anastasius or from some other author of the *Pontifical Book*. Yet no scholar denies how weak and deplorable the reliability of this little work is. Accordingly, when it states that the apostolic see was vacant for seven days after Leo’s death, it is rightly rejected by the illustrious Cardinal Baronius, both on the testimony of Marianus Scotus and especially on the date when Pope Hilary was substituted for the deceased pontiff.

### IV.

The first point, therefore, that may be established with certainty in this question is that Hilary was substituted for Leo as his successor in November of the year 461, in which Leo departed this life. We have as a witness Marianus Scotus, the distinguished chronicler:

> Pope Hilary, the forty-sixth after Peter, was ordained on the second day before the Ides of November.

But Hilary himself provides an older and more substantial testimony. For he testifies in his letter to Ascanianus, chapter 2, that the Roman council held in the year of Christ 465, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December according to the commonly published Acts—or on the thirteenth day, as in the appendix to the Dionysian manuscript and in the Mainz manuscript, or on the sixteenth day, as those same manuscripts note in the margin—was held by brothers, his fellow bishops, assembled for the anniversary of his accession:

> The celebration of my natal day had gathered them together.

Since the pontiff ought to have been consecrated on a Sunday, we may reasonably assign Hilary’s ordination to the preceding Sunday, which was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, if indeed the letter F designated Sunday in that year.

Alfonso Chacón, in his *Life of Leo*, writes—without doubt on the basis of ancient records of the Roman Church—that the apostolic see was vacant for eighteen days. [Note: [Col. 0322D] Many catalogues, together with the published Anastasius, give only seven vacant days. No ancient document known to us gives eighteen days.] If eighteen days are counted backward from that Sunday, or from 16 November, one arrives at the eighteenth day, that is, at the death of Saint Leo on the third day before the Kalends of November.

Yet—something you may perhaps find surprising—we read that Saint Leo’s death was marked on that very day in an old calendar which the distinguished man Lucas Dacherius, renowned for piety and learning, included from a Corbie manuscript in volume X of his *Spicilegium*. Dacherius, guided by serious conjectures, believed that the calendar had been compiled in the year 826. Thus we read in the calendar:

> 3 Kalends of November: The deposition of Saint Leo the pope.

We read of no other Leo who died at that time. Nor is it permissible to interpret as referring to anyone other than the first Leo whatever is said without qualification about a pontiff named Leo in ecclesiastical calendars.

The lectionary book that most nearly agrees with the Corbie codex is the one which Baluzius published from the manuscript codex of the Church of Beauvais at the end of volume II of the *Capitularies*. For in the month of November it reads as follows: “On the fourth day before the Ides of November, at Rome, the deposition of Saint Leo the bishop and of Saint Mena.” November 10 is not far removed from October 30; and it is not certain whether in this codex—which its editor admits to be corrupt and interpolated, and which in fact has much material disordered in several places—the deposition of Leo was formerly entered on the third day before the Kalends of November, or whether it was transferred from October 30 to November 10 in the Church of Amiens, for whose use the book was written, on the occasion of some feast proper to that day and of the feast and octave of All Saints immediately following. In this book the feasts of the saints are absent from October 26 through November 8.

### V

This date is confirmed by the fact that, since we cannot doubt that a successor was given to Leo in the month of November, and since it is improbable that during those most peaceful times of the Roman Church the election of a successor was long delayed after the pontiff’s death—for when writing to Anastasius of Thessalonica Leo wished it to be burdened by no delays (*Epistle* 14, now 12, chapter 6)—it appears almost certain that the death of Saint Leo must be confined within the month of October.

The common chronology conflicts with our position. But apart from the fact that this chronology has prevailed with the sole support of the authority of the *Liber Pontificalis*—an authority that should not be highly valued—it is also opposed by several other chroniclers. For example, Marianus Scotus writes of our Leo: “Pope Leo the Great died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.” Martinus Polonus says that this same Leo sat for 21 years, 9 months, and 27 days; Hermannus Contractus says that he sat for 22 years. These and similar statements approach more closely the position assigning Leo’s death to October than the common position, which assigns it to the third day before the Ides of April.

### VI

It is worthwhile to examine Marianus Scotus more carefully, since his account is singular and explicit. It sheds considerable light on the distinction between the feasts of Leo I and Leo II, which for a long period were celebrated confusedly. Since in the present age June 28 is observed almost everywhere in the Churches as a sacred day for Pope Leo II, it is nevertheless clear that this happened through error, both from the passage of Marianus Scotus cited above and from what will be said below, by which we learn that Leo II was substituted in the place of Leo I. For in the Roman Martyrology we read under the fourth day before the Kalends of July: “At Rome, Saint Leo, Pope II.” And in the Roman Breviary on the same day there is an office for this same Leo II, who is there said to have been buried in the basilica of Saint Peter on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

Recent writers maintain that Leo II did not die on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. They prove this from Anastasius, or the *Liber Pontificalis*, where it is said that he celebrated his ordination on June 27 but was buried at the blessed Apostle Peter on the fifth day before the Nones of July. Marianus Scotus supports them by writing that Leo II died on the fifth day before the Nones of July.

### VII

I would not wish to deny that Leo II died on June 28; for the evidence adduced on the other side favors this opinion rather than opposing it, with the exception of Marianus, who was deceived by misunderstanding the words of Anastasius. As for Anastasius himself, he does not write that Leo died on the fifth day before the Nones of July, but only that he was buried then. It is very easy to understand that someone who died on the fifth day before the Kalends of July was buried four days later. Since the author of the lessons of the Roman Breviary and Marianus do not distinguish these matters, each fell into a different error: the latter wrote that Leo died on the fifth day before the Nones of July, while the former said that he was buried on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

Nor does the mention of the ordination celebrated on June 27 cause difficulty. Who would count it among impossibilities that someone who had performed priestly consecrations before dawn on June 27 or 28 should be struck by a sudden illness and die on the following day or on that very day? Indeed, it is quite easy to suppose that this happened to an elderly pontiff, exhausted by the vigils and labor of the preceding night. Add that the passage of Anastasius concerning the date of the ordination seems to many to be corrupt. That it ought to have been celebrated either on June 4 or June 11 is learnedly proved this year by the most distinguished Carolus le Cointe, a priest of the French Oratory, in his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, year 686, no. 33, although he does not think that Leo died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. Nevertheless, it is difficult to devise any other explanation for why the feast of this pontiff was attached especially to this day, even after Leo I’s feast had been removed from it, except that it was known that Leo II had died on that day in the Roman Church.

> **Note:** Since the feast of Leo II was attached to this date—the fourth day before the Kalends of July—only very considerably later, while all the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs report that he was buried on the fifth day before the Nones of July, that assignment of the feast does not seem to have had the cause Quesnellus conjectures. In the *Breviary of the Camera* according to Roman usage, printed at Venice on June 20, 1494, by the art and at the expense of Andrea de Torresanis of Asola, the feast of this Leo II is presented on June 28 with three proper lessons; but in them there is nothing about the date of his burial, as is now read in the Roman Breviary.

### VIII

Although Leo II had died on this day, the same day was not sacred to him in the ancient monuments of the Church, but to Leo I. Numerous proofs of this assertion can readily be produced from ancient historians, Martyrologies, Lectionaries, Breviaries, Missals, and calendars.

Let Saint Gregory the Great, Pope I, come forward first; he was earlier than Leo I. In his Sacramentary he records the feast day (*natale*) of Saint Leo the pope under the fourth day before the Kalends of July. Learned men rightly suspect that this was added to the Sacramentary on the evidence of the Reims codex praised by the most learned Hugo Menardus; nor would I deny it. Nevertheless, two facts prove that the addition is extremely ancient. First, so few manuscript codices have been found that lack it that Menardus praises the Reims codex as the only one, although he also testifies that in that same Reims codex the feast day of Saint Leo the pope is entered under the third day before the Ides of April; in the other codices, however—

> **Note:** The oldest Gregorian Sacramentary codices that have so far come to our attention are one Vatican codex and another Ottobonian codex, published by Muratorius in volume II of his *Roman Liturgy*. Since these likewise present a Mass for Saint Leo on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, we believe that this Mass was added to the Gregorian Sacramentary immediately after Leo’s translation, which took place on the same day under Sergius. For this reason, in the oldest Gospel capitularies, in which that translation is recorded on the same day, and in the Roman calendar prefixed to the Responsorial and Antiphonary of the Roman Church, which the venerable Cardinal Thomasius published from a codex of the Vatican Basilica in volume IV, p. 9 of the latest edition, and finally in the ancient Lateran Missal recently printed in volume I of the *Liturgical Collection*, p. 228, the feast of Saint Leo is indicated only on that day. We do not deny, however, that three other Gregorian Sacramentaries—the Reims Sacramentary praised by P. Menardus, note 354, and the Theodorician and Gemetician Sacramentaries cited in the notes to Menardus—record the memory of Leo not on June 28 but on April 11. In the *Ordinarium* of Saint Peter above the Dives, P. Martene found a commemoration of Saint Leo without an office on April 11; in six other books of the same kind, which he cites, the feast of the same saint is recorded on June 28.

The second fact is that the Sacramentary contains the feasts of very few saints who were not martyrs, and of even fewer Roman pontiffs. It would scarcely have occurred to anyone to omit Leo I while not omitting Leo II. Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims, undoubtedly took from the same Gregorian Sacramentary the secret prayer of the Mass of Saint Leo, which he reports in his lengthy work *On Predestination*, on the final page, and which he indicates was customarily recited in the Roman Church, in these words:

> “This sacrifice, we beseech you, Lord, may cleanse our sins; sacrificed upon the altar of the cross, it bore away the offense of the whole world.
>
> “And likewise: Grant us, Lord, that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo; by offering it, you granted that the sins of the whole world might be forgiven.
>
> “And: Look, almighty and merciful God, upon this family of yours, for whom our Lord Jesus Christ did not hesitate to be handed over into the hands of the wicked and to undergo the torment of the cross.”

Here one may observe in the secret prayer for Saint Leo the more scrupulous diligence of a later age. In place of the words, “that this offering may benefit the soul of your servant Leo,” these other words were substituted: “that this offering may benefit us through the intercession of blessed Leo.” No religious scruple prevented the former wording from being recited in the time of Hincmarus, Gregory, and perhaps earlier pontiffs. This form of prayer also seems to me to reveal the antiquity of the office; perhaps it arose because a day in honor of this pontiff was celebrated immediately after Leo’s death, when the faithful, according to the custom and devotion of the Church, prayed during the solemn celebration of Mass that one so recently deceased might receive the joys of eternal happiness. An explanation of that alteration in the secret prayer of the Mass of Saint Leo may be found in Pope Innocent III’s rescript to a former archbishop of Lyon named J., which is cited under *Cum Marthae*, *On the Celebration of Masses*.

In an ancient Martyrology said to be by the Venerable Bede, we read under the same day, June 28: “Leo the pope, who after the Apostle Peter sat in the city of Rome for 21 years and 12 days,” followed by other details that clearly designate Leo I. The author apparently refrained, on the advice of others, from mentioning the day of his death or burial.

In an old Roman calendar—or rather, a lectionary book—which the most learned Joannes Fronto, regular canon of Saint Augustine and chancellor of the University of Paris, recently published from a manuscript codex of his monastery of Saint Genevieve, written in letters of gold and, as he believes, more than nine hundred years old, there is nothing about Saint Leo in April. In June, however, it reads as follows: “On the 28th: Translation of Blessed Leo.” This must undoubtedly be understood of Leo I, as it also seemed to the learned Fronto. For the Lectionary records the memory of only four confessors; it is not likely that Leo II was admitted among them while Leo I was denied a place. Moreover, we read of no ancient translation of any Saint Leo except that of Leo I, whom Pope Sergius I transferred to a place in the basilica of Saint Peter for the sake of honoring him, as Anastasius testifies, as will be explained more fully below.

Usuardus, who flourished at the beginning of the ninth century, mentions Saint Leo the Great in his Martyrology under the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in these words: “The feast of blessed Leo, pope and doctor.” Who among the pontiffs named Leo was ever adorned with the title “doctor,” apart from Leo I? Joannes Molanus acted improperly when, after interpreting this word “doctor” as referring to Leo I in the first edition of Usuardus, he later changed his opinion and relegated it to the margin in the second edition of this Martyrology, which he prepared at Antwerp in 1583. He substituted the name “confessor” for that word and added other material of his own that fits Leo II. This is contrary to all the manuscript codices.

> **Note:** The ancient and distinctive cult of Saint Leo in the Roman Church is established by the Church’s old litanies, which Cardinal Thomasius accurately reprinted from a codex of the Vatican Basilica in volume V of *The Ancient Book of Masses*, p. 299; we have also found them in other manuscripts. In these, Saint Leo is listed among the holy confessors who were pontiffs as follows: “Saint Sylvester, Saint Leo, Saint Hilary, Saint Martin, Saint Gregory,” and so forth. In other, shorter litanies of the same Church, from the codex of Ratoldus cited by Menardus in the Gregorian Sacramentary, note 741, we find: “Saint Sylvester, Saint Leo, Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine.” In the shortest litanies, inserted into Roman Orders 13 and 14, in volume II of Mabillon’s *Italian Museum*, pp. 227 and 254, only these two pontiff-confessors are invoked: “Saint Leo, Saint Gregory.” For the title “doctor,” see what we said in the dedicatory epistle of volume I above. As for Ado, in the three ancient codices of his Martyrology used by the distinguished Dominicus Georgius in the Roman edition, June 28 is recorded on p. 303: “On that day, the feast of Saint Leo the pope, who on account of his outstanding intelligence is rightly called Leo the Great among the Romans.” These same codices also record the feast of the same Leo on April 11.

Around Usuardus’s time, Leo was numbered among the doctors of the Church, as is testified by the litanies found in the prayer book of the Emperor Charles the Bald, copied from a Colbertine manuscript by Baluzius in his notes to the *Capitularies*, p. 1486, where Saint Leo is invoked after the four doctors of the Latin Church. The new Breviary of the Church of Paris, printed in 1680 and corrected with great care through the assistance and labor of learned men—especially the distinguished Jacobus de Sancta Bova, doctor, Sorbonist fellow and professor, and my teacher—restored this title to our pontiff.

Ado of Vienne, who wrote his Martyrology in the same ninth century, lists Leo only under the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in this form: “On that day, the feast of Saint Leo the pope.” Leo is indeed also mentioned under the third day before the Ides of April in the commonly circulated codices; but Joannes Mosander and Heribertus Rosweydus, who published Ado with great care, reject this entry on the authority of numerous manuscript codices.

The manuscript *Book of Sacraments* of Ratholdus, written in the tenth century; the manuscript calendar of Saint Michael of Conflent in Catalonia; the calendar of the Christian Church published at Helmstedt in 1585 at the end of David Chytraeus’s *Chronology*; the manuscript calendar of Saint Thierry near Reims; and many other monuments of uncertain age and provenance do not record the memory of Leo except on June 28. Who, then, would believe that Leo II, with Leo I set aside, as we have already said, was honored with a celebrated and solemn cult, especially in the Roman Church?

The ancient Martyrology that Rosweydus marketed as the old Roman Martyrology is nothing other than an epitome of Ado. It contains nothing about Saint Leo under the third day before the Ides of April; under the fourth day before the Kalends of July it has: “At Rome, Leo the pope.”

Wandelbertus, who rendered Usuardus’s Martyrology in verse, has the same material about Leo as Usuardus, both under the second day before the Ides of April and under the fourth day before the Kalends of July. That metrical Martyrology of Wandelbertus is found in Molanus’s Martyrology and in volume I of the works of the Venerable Bede the priest; this is the opinion of learned men. Under the third day before the Ides of April, Usuardus, published at Leuven in 1568, has:

> “At Rome, the feast of Blessed Leo the pope, in whose time the holy Council of Chalcedon arose,”

and in the margin: “The first Leo, whose feast is on June 28.” In the same place Wandelbertus has this couplet:

> “The third [day before the Ides] shines, with the supreme pontiff Leo shedding light,
>
> Who fed Christ’s flock by word and deed.”

Under the fourth day before the Kalends of July it has: “The feast of blessed Leo the pope and doctor”; and in the margin: “Concerning Leo, *Pontifical Book*, chapter 47, and Canisius before the Works.” Wandelbertus, however, writes:

> “The fourth [day before the Kalends] rejoices in Leo, bishop and teacher of the Word.”

From this the erroneous correction attempted by Molanus in Usuardus’s later editions is demonstrated: it was contrary to the author’s intention and to the testimony of the manuscript codices. The laws of verse forbid adding that correction to Wandelbertus.

Marianus Scotus, in his *Chronicle*, completed around the year 1083, writes that Pope Leo the Great died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July. In my judgment, he was guided chiefly by the fact that the memory of Leo the Great was celebrated on that day.

The Abbot of Ursperg, who died in 1240, says under the year 461 of his *Chronicle*: “Pope Leo departed this life on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.”

Martinus Polonus explains Marianus and the Abbot of Ursperg and confirms our assertion by his own testimony. “Here also,” he says, “he was buried near the basilica of the holy Apostle Peter, whose feast is celebrated on the vigil of the Apostles.” Therefore, even in the year 1277, to which Martinus brought his *Chronicle*, the feast of Leo II was not being celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, but that of Leo I in the Roman Church. Martinus could not have been unaware of its custom and rite, since he served in that Church as penitentiary under Pope Nicholas III.

Saint Antoninus, who flourished in 1450, writes the following about our Leo in part II of his *Chronicle*: “The feast of this saint is celebrated on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul.”

Wernerus Rolewinck of Laer in Westphalia, a Carthusian, who composed a calendar and Martyrology as well as the *Fasciculus Temporum*, which he brought down to the year 1480, likewise assigns the feast of our Leo to the same day. “His feast,” he says, “is celebrated on the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul; some say April 11.”

Finally, Joannes Trithemius, reported to have died in 1516, writes of Leo I as follows: “At last, after many labors for the benefit of the Church, he died under the Emperor Leo in the year of the Lord 461, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.”

Most of the Breviaries and Missals printed before the beginning of this century record the memory of Saint Leo only on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, that is, June 28:

The Roman Missal, or Missal according to the custom of the Roman Curia, printed at Venice in the year of the Lord 1481; the Missal published for the Basilica in the year of the Lord 1487; the Missal printed at Lyon in the year of the Lord 1501; the Orléans Breviary of the year 1504; the Breviary of the Order of the Most Holy Trinity of 1514; the Breviary of the Church of Tours of 1519; the Carthusian Breviary of 1521; the Breviary of the Regular Canons of 1523; the Roman Breviary, Paris, 1524; the adapted Curial Breviary, or Breviary according to the custom of the Roman Curia, of the year of the Lord 1525; the Paris Breviary of 1545; the Roman Missal printed at Venice in 1549; the Breviary according to the use of the great monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims, published in the same year; the *Portiforium*, or Breviary according to the use of the Church of Salisbury, published at London in the year of the Lord 1555; the Roman Breviary, Paris, 1556; the Orléans Breviary of 1573; the very ancient Breviary of Fontenay; the ancient Breviary of Noyon; the manuscript Breviary of Saint Victor at Paris; the Breviary of the Regular Canons of the year of the Lord 1609; and the Breviary of Saint Martin of Tours of 1635.

In all these works, and undoubtedly in many others, the memory of Saint Leo occurs on June 28, not April 11. I say “memory,” not a complete office, because the vigil of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul occurred then and was exceedingly famous. Otherwise, if Leo’s feast fell on a Sunday, the vigil being transferred to the preceding Saturday, an office for Saint Leo was held on the Sunday itself, if I correctly understand the sense of this rubric appended to most of the Breviaries listed:

> **Note:** A similar rubric is found in the Responsorial and Antiphonary of the Roman Church, volume IV of Cardinal Thomasius’s works, p. 120: “If the vigil of Blessed Peter falls on a Sunday, we anticipate it on Saturday and celebrate all the offices of the vigil; but on Sunday we perform everything for Saint Leo the pope.” In Roman Order 15, however, in Mabillon’s *Italian Museum*, volume II, p. 517, we find: “Likewise, on the vigil of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul we perform the office of Saint Leo; the Mass is said for the vigil, with a commemoration of Saint Leo.”

“If the feast of Saint Leo falls on a Sunday, the feast is celebrated with a commemoration of Saint John the Baptist; but on whatever other day it falls, a commemoration of him is made in the Mass of the vigil.”

Traces of this commemoration still survive in the collect which is read both in the Gregorian Sacramentary and in the Breviaries listed above for the memory of Saint Leo. A few years ago it was transferred to Leo II and assigned to his office without even the slightest change. Here is the collect:

> “O God, who have made blessed Leo the equal of your saints in merit, grant, we beseech you, that we who devoutly celebrate the feasts of his commemoration may also imitate the examples of his life.”

When it says, “you have made him equal in merit to your saints,” I suspect that “the Apostles,” or “Peter and Paul,” should be understood: their solemn day was occurring, and the collect proclaims Leo equal to them in merit. Unless one imagines that he wished to compare Leo with some particularly distinguished member of the heavenly host, the praise is less well composed when a saint is simply said to resemble saints. In any case, our Leo is more than once compared with the Apostles by ancient writers:

> “Leo, pope of Rome, equal to the Apostles” (*isapostolos*, ἰσαπόστολος),

that is, “Leo, pope at Rome, to be ranked with the Apostles,” as the synodal booklet says (chapter 94). The Fathers of Chalcedon likewise called Saint Leo, in their *prosphonetic* address to the Emperor Marcian, “an apostolic man” (*ton apostolikon andra*, τὸν ἀποστολικὸν ἄνδρα). All these considerations will readily persuade anyone who is not obstinate or contentious that the memory of Leo I was formerly entered on June 28.

Nevertheless, I do not deny that ancient codices are also found which assign Leo’s feast to April 11. But there is no necessity compelling us to interpret them as referring to the day of his death, since they may be understood either of some translation or of his ordination. Such is the genuine Martyrology of Bede the priest, recently brought to public light by Godefridus Henschenius: under the third day before the Ides of April it mentions Leo the pope and confessor, and under the fourth day before the Kalends of July, Saint Leo the pope. The same is true of the manuscript Breviary of Monte Cassino, approximately six hundred years old, preserved in the house of the institution of the Oratory of the Lord Jesus near the walls of Paris. From what was said above, it is clear that Usuardus commemorates the feast day of Leo I in both places.

On the same day the old calendar published in volume X of Acherius’s *Spicilegium* from a manuscript codex eight hundred years old reads: “On the third day before the Ides of April, the feast of Saint Leo the pope.” The same appears in the calendar prefixed to the manuscript *Book of the Sacraments of Saint Gregory* in the Paris Oratory codex. Add to these the Paris Missals of 1517 and 1541; the Breviaries of 1545 and 1584; and the Roman Breviary printed at Venice in 1570. The Amiens Breviary of 1607 has nothing about Saint Leo on June 28, but only on April 11; the same is true of the Laon Breviary of 1584. In these books it is not a complete office but only a commemoration of Saint Leo that is made on April 11, with nothing in June.
