It should be observed that in most Breviaries and Missals which have an office for Saint Leo only on June 28, the office is taken from the common of pontiff-confessors and contains nothing by which it can be determined whether it is celebrated for Leo I or for Leo II.

### X

From the foregoing I readily persuade myself that in former times three days altogether were consecrated to the memory of Saint Leo the pope, Leo I, and that one of them was celebrated in some Churches, another in others, and two of them with annual observance in certain places.

The third day before the Kalends of November, that is, October 30, was sacred to the deposition of this holy pontiff; it is assigned to him in the Acherian calendar, eight hundred years old, although perhaps no office was celebrated for him on that day. For in the early periods of the Church I would scarcely believe that the deposition or death of that saint was honored with a solemn office, unless he had completed his martyrdom by shedding his blood for Christ. Hence the day of Leo’s death is recorded in so few monuments that so far only one codex has been seen in which it is entered on October 30.

### XI

June 28 was regarded as a day made famous by the translation of the body of Saint Leo. On that day it is recorded in the very ancient Martyrology or Lectionary of Joannes Fronto, which he believed to be more than nine hundred years old; under the fourth day before the Kalends of July it reads: “The translation of the body of blessed Leo.” A calendar formerly intended for the use of the Roman Church, copied from a very ancient Vatican Library codex likewise more than nine hundred years old, agrees with it. Leo Allatius inserted it in full in his dissertation *On the Sundays and Weeks of the Greeks*, at the end of his work *On the Perpetual Agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches*. On p. 1490 we read:

> “The fourth day before the Kalends of July: the translation of the body of Blessed Leo, pontiff and confessor.”

In that calendar no memory of Leo is recorded on any other day. Which Leo could it be except the first, whose only translation is recorded by Anastasius the Librarian—or by whatever other author of the *Liber Pontificalis*—in the account of Pope Sergius?

> “He,” it says, “placed the body of blessed Leo, that most excellent father and pontiff, which had been set in a hidden part of the lower sacristy of the aforesaid basilica [of Saint Peter], in a carefully constructed tomb in a public place in the aforementioned basilica, as had been revealed to him, and adorned the place itself.”

The same account, with a few changes, is found in the manuscript codex of Oriel College in the University of Oxford—namely, the codex from which the Roman book of canons was produced and which also contains a great deal of Leonine material. Among these is a twofold narrative of the deeds of Saint Leo, Pope I: one, on folio 91, agrees almost entirely with the narrative of Anastasius, although it is shorter; the other, on folio 214, is as follows:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 440, Leo the pope the Great, forty-fourth after Peter, sat for twenty-one years and two months. He died on the third day before the Ides of April.
>
> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 688, Sergius the pope, eighty-fourth, sat for fourteen years and eight months. In the account of his deeds we read:
>
> “‘He placed the body of Leo I, that most blessed father and pontiff, which had been set in a hidden part of the lower sacristy of the basilica of blessed Peter, in a carefully constructed tomb in a public place in the aforementioned basilica, as had been revealed to him, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and adorned the place itself.’”

The codex then contains an inscription consisting of twenty verses, which is printed here. I would call attention to one point observed in the excerpt from the deeds of Sergius: the chronological notation, to which the Mabillonian codex soon to be mentioned agrees. For both codices, together with the Martyrology of Fronto and the calendar of Allatius praised above, are four witnesses whose authority seems to establish with certainty that June 28 was consecrated to the translation of Saint Leo I.

From the same excerpt from the deeds of Sergius we learn that our Leo was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, an honor granted to none of his predecessors. For, says the author of *Subterranean Rome*, he was the first to be numbered among the holy pontiffs who were not martyrs—not, however, beside Saint Peter, but in the vestibule of his basilica, before the sacristy, that is, at the far end of the same vestibule, on the left as one enters. This is indicated by verses 6, 7, and 8 of the epitaph soon to be described.

Many pontiffs were later buried there, so that the tomb of Saint Leo lay hidden beneath the tombs of others. Pope Sergius I, who sat in Rome toward the end of the seventh century, was warned by a prior revelation; he brought Leo’s body out of its more obscure place and transferred it higher up and nearer the altar, either into the oratory on the right of the main apse near the altar of Saint Peter, as the same author of *Subterranean Rome* writes. Sergius also constructed a magnificent tomb for Leo with the following epitaph, which appears in Janus Gruterus. We have corrected it against a copy of the Oxford manuscript codex recently sent to us by the most distinguished E. Bernard. The same epitaph was found by the learned Mabillon in a Verdun codex of the monastery of Saint Vannes, among other epitaphs said to have been found in the Church of Saint Peter and reported by Mabillon in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 431:

> The body of this apostolic man was the first to be buried here [Oxford manuscript: *magni*, “of this great [apostolic man],” instead of *primum*, “first”],
>
> And he was worthy of a tomb in Peter’s citadel.
>
> Hence [printed editions: *hunc*, “this man,” instead of *hinc*, “hence”] the company of seers and noble men whom you see present
>
> Have their limbs covered beneath this splendid house.
>
> But long ago, as the great shepherd Leo,
>
> Guarding the enclosures and flock of Christ’s people, was doorkeeper of the citadel,
>
> He warns from the tomb of what he accomplished while he lived,
>
> Lest the lurking wolf ravage God’s sheepfold.
>
> The books sent forth for the true doctrine bear witness,
>
> Books which pious hearts honor and the wicked crowd fears.
>
> He roared, and the hearts of the beasts were struck with terror;
>
> And the sheep follow the commands of their shepherd.
>
> Yet here he lay beneath the temple’s final marble,
>
> Now covered [Vulgate: “hidden”; Oxford manuscript: “beautiful”] by many tombs of pontiffs.
>
> Sergius the bishop, moved by divine love,
>
> Transferred him from there to the front of the sacred house,
>
> Adorning the gleaming tomb with costly marble [Vulgate: “the gleaming tomb”],
>
> In which those who ask behold heavenly wonders.
>
> And because once he excelled in wondrous virtues,
>
> The pontiff’s final glory will be greater.

At the end of this epitaph the Mabillonian codex contains the following chronological addition:

> “He sat in the episcopate for 21 years, 1 month, and 13 days. He was deposited on the third day before the Ides … and was again transferred here by blessed Sergius on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the first indiction.”

This is what can be said about the first translation of the body of Saint Leo and about his tomb, which was famous for miracles and, as the following verse shows, was a present help to many:

> “In which those who ask behold heavenly wonders.”

### XII

We stated above that it is also certain from ancient codices that April 11 was sacred to the memory of the same pontiff. But we have no completely established knowledge of the manner or occasion on which this came about. The opinion today, recorded in the current calendars and Breviaries of the Church, is that his death was commemorated on this day. Yet the testimonies of Marianus Scotus, Martinus Polonus, and the others cited above do not permit us to follow it: some assign the feast, others the death, of Saint Leo to a day other than April 11.

> **Note:** See note 1 above.

I would readily believe that this day was consecrated to the anniversary of his elevation to the pontificate.

First, because the general opinion agrees that his ordination occurred around this time. I know that our conjecture cannot be reconciled with the common chronology, which teaches that the death of Sixtus III occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, since from Prosper we have it as certain that the Roman Church was without a pontiff for forty days and more. But on whose authority is the death of Pope Sixtus assigned to that date? Certainly not Prosper’s, as it seemed to Ciaconius, who was misled by the words of Baronius. Nowhere is it recorded by that chronicler, nor by any writer older than Anastasius. Anastasius’s diligence is so suspect and his lapses so frequent that every assertion resting solely upon his authority is exceedingly weak and unstable.

Second, the old calendar mentioned above, published in volume X of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, records the deposition of Saint Leo the pope on the third day before the Kalends of November, but under the third day before the Ides of April, or April 11, it records the feast day (*natale*) of the same man. Here *natale* cannot mean the day of death, since that is assigned to October. What day, then, can it signify except the day of consecration? This term was used for their ordination by other pontiffs as well. Sixtus III, Leo’s predecessor, called his ordination by this name in *Epistle* 1 to Cyril of Alexandria:

> “The synod,” he says, “which my feast day (*natale*) had assembled”;

and in *Epistle* 2 to John of Antioch:

> “The whole brotherhood heard what had gathered for my feast day.”

Hilary, Leo’s immediate successor, writes in *Epistle* 2 to Ascan the other bishops of the province of Tarragona, chapter 2:

> “When your letters had been read at the assembly of the brethren whom the celebration of my feast day had gathered.”

Saint Paulinus likewise says in *Epistle* 16 to Delphinus that he had been invited by Pope Anastasius to his feast day. Saint Ambrose, in book VIII, *Epistle* 1 to Felix, bishop of Como, commemorates his feast day—that is, his ordination. I pass over Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 32 *On the Words of the Lord*, and homilies 24 and 25 among the fifty.

Third, it is clear that in this Martyrology or calendar *natale* does not always signify the day of death, but any kind of feast. This is evident from the feast of Saint Benedict the abbot, which is entered twice: once in March, when he departed this life, and again on July 13, when his translation is commemorated. Yet the calendar’s author calls the latter a *natale*. It should therefore not seem strange that the same term was used for the day of Saint Leo’s ordination, just as the Greeks used it for the ordination of Saint Ambrose in their *Menologion*, where they record it under the designation *natale* on December 7, following the example of the Latin Church.

A fragment of an ancient parchment was inserted by Aegidius Bucherius into his work *On the Doctrine of Time*, taken from the papers of Heribertus Rosweydus. It resembles a calendar or Martyrology. Under February we read:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of March: the feast of Peter of the Chair,”

a feast by which the apostle’s ordination or pontificate is, as it were, celebrated.

4. What solemnity was customarily observed for an ordination is demonstrated by the feasts that have been or still are sacredly celebrated for the ordinations of Saints Paulinus, Ambrose, Augustine, Pope Hilary, and Martin of Tours, in the Roman, Gallican, Italian, and African dioceses. Add to these the ordination of several other pontiffs, still celebrated in the Church’s present-day calendars, as can be seen in the Roman Martyrology, which reports the ordinations of Saints Basil of Caesarea, Ambrose of Milan, Gregory of Rome, and [Col. 0331C] Zeno of Verona, each honored with annual solemnity on his respective day. Indeed, it is quite plausible that, when in the earliest centuries of the Church only the memory of Christ’s martyrs was celebrated with solemn rite, the first festivities of the holy pontiffs were added to the solemnities of the martyrs, and for this purpose the day of each one’s ordination was selected; so that the day kept as a feast each year while the pontiff was alive would be commemorated in the same way after his death. This is all the more believable of our Leo, since his election took place amid the most fervent wishes and with the greatest consensus of all, and his ordination had customarily been commemorated throughout the twenty-one years [602] of Leo’s lifetime. Add also that, because of the magnitude of his illustrious achievements, the singular reputation of his holiness, and the fact that Rome was twice saved from slaughter through his aid—by which he deserved twice to be called father of his country—the memory of so great a pontiff would have been especially cherished at Rome. It therefore seems wholly absurd to believe that the memory [Col. 0331D] of Leo the Great, a pontiff so dear to the Roman Church for so many reasons, was buried in oblivion for so many centuries.

The most learned Papebrochius, in his chronological-historical essay on the catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs, assigns Leo’s ordination to 8 September and therefore thinks that what was celebrated on 11 April was his second burial at the Vatican, which Anastasius, following older catalogues, called a burial.

But Pope Leo I now has a fixed and certain feast on 11 April, whose office is celebrated with double rite, especially in the Roman Church. I would not, however, pass over without comment a distinctive privilege [Col. 0332A] of this office: at the first nocturn, it has the same readings from the First Epistle of Saint Peter that are found in both solemn celebrations of the Chair of Saint Peter; at the third nocturn and at Mass, it has the same Gospel reading as the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter and as his own feast (Sermon 2, now 3). It was taken from chapter 16 of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew, doubtless for the reason that Leo so devoutly, courageously, and learnedly explained and defended against Eutyches the faith in the Incarnation and Peter’s confession—which, inspired by God the Father in the apostle’s heart, rises above the uncertainty of all human opinions and received the firmness of a rock (Epistle 98). Hence his epistle was approved by the ecumenical synod as consonant with Peter’s confession, and he himself was called by those same Chalcedonian Fathers:

> appointed interpreter of the blessed Peter’s voice to all.

XIII. Besides [Note: [Col. 0331D] We suspected that another earlier elevation by Sergius took place on 11 April; see note 1. After Sergius, however, the *Liber Pontificalis*, in Leo IV’s Life, attributes either the translation or the elevation of Leo I to Leo IV. Paschal II likewise did something similar, as Peter Manlius, a canon, testifies in his description of the old Vatican basilica, vol. VII of the *Acta Sanctorum*, June, p. 39.] that translation of Saint Leo’s body which we have just discussed as having been carried out by Pope Sergius, we read that his sacred relics were also carried to various parts of the Christian world. Martin of Troppau must be understood as referring to some portion of the body when, in his *Chronicle*, he says that under Pope Sergius I the following took place:

> With God’s revelation, he transferred the body of Pope Leo I to Würzburg in East Franconia;

unless, however, this author is presenting as a translation from one place to another the transfer from a lower to an upper location in the Basilica of Saint Peter. In any event, while the body was being moved, it would have been easy for someone from the Church of Würzburg, who was then residing at Rome, to obtain some portion of it and carry the sacred relic home—[603] a relic which popular error later sold as the entire body.

It will also not be unwelcome to report what we read in a book entitled *On the State of the Church of Périgueux from Its Foundation in the Faith*, by John of Puteo, a recollected member of the strict observance of Saint Francis. Under the year 1476, he writes that, through the efforts of Elias Burdellius, a bull was obtained from Pope Sixtus IV, under Bishop Radelphinus of Périgueux, granting a ten-year jubilee of indulgences to those who annually visited the churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Front on the day sacred to their respective commemorations. Concerning the church of Saint Stephen, the bull adds:

> In it rest certain relics of that same saint, together with the bodies of Pope Leo, called Leo the Great, and of the blessed Patroclus and Saint Sabina the martyr.

The same author, under the year 1551, relates from the official report of the mayor and consuls of Périgueux that all the sacred furnishings and holy relics kept in the treasury of the Périgueux chapter were plundered by heretics in the dead of night. Among them he counts the head of Pope Saint Leo, and says that these relics were later found in a certain garden and buried beneath the high altar. From the same source, I believe, the most illustrious Bishop of Toul, André Saussay, drew what he writes in the supplement to the *Gallican Martyrology* under 11 April:

> The body of the most holy pontiff Leo I, an instrument of so many divine miracles, was in the course of time transferred from Rome to Aquitaine and honorably placed in the principal church of Périgueux, under the title of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Pope Sixtus IV testifies in his bulls that it rests there together with the sacred bones of Saint Patroclus and Saint Sabina the virgin. [Col. 0332D]

XIII. I consider more reliable what Clarius, a monk and author of the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living at Sens*, relates in volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. He says:

> Ansegisus asked Pope John (VIII) to give him relics of the pontiffs and doctors Gregory and Leo, and he obtained what he requested; for he very often celebrated the sacred solemnities of Mass at the Apostolic See. Pope John gave him the head of the blessed Pope Gregory the Universal, son of Gordianus, enclosed in lead, and the arm of Saint Leo, pope and doctor. [Col. 0333A] Having received this gift, Ansegisus carried it to Sens, to the Basilica of Saint Peter, where it has been preserved with great honor down to the present day.

Ausegisus flourished after the middle of the ninth century, while Clarius continued his work down to the year 1124. Odorannus gives the same account in his *Chronicle*, as does Robert of Auxerre in the chronology of Saint Mariani, and Martin of Troppau in his account of John VIII. Since Martin consulted ten chronicles in composing his own, yet does not mention the three accounts reported above, he must be believed to have taken from other sources what he recounts about the relics given to Ansegisus. Geoffrey of Cologne, a member of the monastery of Saint Peter the Living, likewise endorses these accounts in a manuscript chronicle.

Concerning this same arm of Saint Leo, the *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living* adds, under the year 999, when Seuvinus, archbishop of Sens, died—the man who had rebuilt this monastery. It says:

> Then, obtaining with much entreaty from Abbot Raynard and the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter the arm of Pope Saint Leo together with the fingers of Saint Ebbo (the abbot himself was the nephew of that archbishop, as the same author writes above), he adorned it with gold and gems and presented it to that house of God—that is, the church of Saint Stephen. In return, and for the remedy of his soul, from the altar of Saint Savinian, which is thirty paces from the monastery crypt; from the altar of Saint Peter, which is in the village called Alson; and from the altar of Saint Lupus, which is in the village called Naudus, he granted perpetual privileges to Saint Peter and his monks, with the consent and approval of the Roman pope and his fellow bishops.

The domestic records of the monastery of Saint Peter assert that Saint Leo’s arm was later restored to the monastery. Among these records they produce a list of the relics kept there, drawn up in 1552. They say that it was stolen around the year 1628 by a certain chaplain of the church of Saint Stephen who, under the pretext of devotion and piety, was attempting to wipe and clean the sacred reliquaries and stole several of the relics from them; among these, he gave Saint Leo’s arm to the Carmelite nuns of Sens. We ourselves recorded this account in the monastery of Saint Peter from a manuscript chronicle which the devout ascetics of that monastery most courteously shared with us. The truth of the narrative rests with them.

The Parisian abbey of Saint Magloire once preserved sacred relics of this holy pontiff. I read this attested in a very ancient Sammaglorian cartulary, which contains a catalogue of the monastery’s relics, drawn up in 1321 when a public inventory was made of all the relics kept there. According to the codex, Peter de Latilly, bishop of Châlons, was present; by order of the king he had then been assigned as guardian of the monastery.

XIV. If these reports are true, it is difficult to explain how the body of Saint Leo I was found completely [Note: [Col. 0333D] Untouched—that is, with none of the principal portions of the bones missing or moved, except for the head, which had been reduced to several fragments of bone, as James Grimaldi, appointed to compose the Acts, relates; these were inserted into the more recent Acts concerning the translation of the four Saint Leos, printed at Rome in 1715.] untouched in the year 1607, when it was moved in order to be transferred to the new basilica. I think the writer means only that whatever was found at that time was intact and untouched by worms. I give the entire account from book II, chapter 8, of *Subterranean Rome*, reproducing the author’s own words:

> Besides the first Leo, “three other most holy Leos, supreme pontiffs—namely, the second, third, and fourth of that name—were also buried in the same oratory (to the right, namely, of the principal apse, near the altar of Saint Peter in his basilica), and were happily discovered there on 20 May in the year of the Lord 1607, during the reign—more properly, the pontificate—of Paul V, when, by order of that pontiff, the four blessed bodies were all to be carried into the new basilica at the same time. For when the altar of the oratory itself had been dismantled, the sacred bodies of the other three appeared to the eyes of those present in a chest assembled from marble slabs. One of them, however, had been placed in a small wooden chest enclosed within it, and everyone undoubtedly believed that it was the body of the blessed pontiff Leo IV; for it was more intact and less damaged than the others. Beneath this urn, separated from it by a stone pavement, another wooden chest was found, raised above the ground on certain iron rods. In it the body of Saint Leo I was enclosed, entirely intact and adorned with pontifical ornaments. The most blessed pontiff wore a mitre on his head, as was customary; he was covered with a sufficiently ample chasuble, as the ancients used to wear, beneath which his hands, likewise folded, could be seen. Above this he was encircled by a pallium, which displays the fullness of pontifical power. Even then it was possible to see relics of that sacred pallium, especially two very small red crosses that projected from it, and also a golden needle attached to the same vestment, which had served to fasten the pallium. The body measured seven palms and three-quarters of a palm in length. After the reverence due had been paid to these most sacred pledges, they were all transferred in the same year, on 27 May, as something whose value could be equaled by nothing, to the new basilica. They were devoutly deposited in a most noble sarcophagus, skillfully fashioned from marble and carved with sacred histories, in the uppermost chapel facing south. The body of Saint Leo I was placed in the same wooden chest, which was enclosed within another, leaden chest; the other three were placed in a cypress chest, set upon iron rods, so that their bones might be kept entirely separate and distinct from the body of Saint Leo I. On the sarcophagus itself, a memorial of the following kind was affixed on a sheet of lead:

> [606] THE BODIES OF THE HOLY LEOS, THE FIRST, SECOND, THIRD, AND FOURTH, SUPREME PONTIFFS, BURIED IN THE RIGHT-HAND PART OF THE BASILICA, BESIDE THE HIGH ALTAR OF THE PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES, BENEATH THE ALTAR OF THE OLD ORATORY, WHICH WAS COVERED BY A PAVEMENT BUILT OVER IT.
>
> REMOVED FROM THERE BY ORDER OF PAUL V, SUPREME PONTIFF, EVANGELISTA PALLOTTA, CARDINAL OF THE TITLE OF SAINT LAWRENCE IN LUCINA, OF THE CUSENTINE LINE, ARCHPRIEST OF THIS BASILICA, CARRIED THEM IN SOLEMN PROCESSION INTO THE NEW CHURCH AND PLACED THEM BENEATH THIS ALTAR IN THE SAME SOUTHERN PART ON 27 MAY, THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE ASCENSION, 1607.
>
> IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE PONTIFICATE OF OUR MOST HOLY LORD.”

XV. Paul Aringhus, a priest of the Oratory, gives this account of the second translation of Saint Leo’s body, celebrated in 1607, in his *Subterranean Rome*. While this work was at press in 1651, a third translation [Note: [Col. 0334D] Innocent X built an altar for Leo I. His translation was carried out under Clement XI, and Benedict XIV describes it most accurately in book IV, part II, chapter 23, of *On the Beatification and Canonization of the Servants of God*, nos. 7–14. Specifically, on 20 May 1713, Benedict—then canon archivist of the Basilica of Saint Peter—producing documents concerning the earlier translation under Paul V, the sacred body of Leo the Great was found in a separate chest beneath the altar of Saint Mary of the Column and was identified. Then, on 20 March 1714, it was transferred from that altar to the chapel of Saint Nicholas of Bari. On 2 April of the same year a new identification was carried out; afterward, on the 11th of that month, the day dedicated to Saint Leo, the body was identified for a third time in the presence of Pope Clement XI and several cardinals, and was precisely described by an expert. His drawing may be seen in Francis Blanchinus, vol. III of Anastasius, p. 161. Finally, on the feast of the same saint in the following year, 1715, the sacred body was carried out in solemn procession and placed beneath its own altar of Saint Leo, which Innocent X had built. See further in the same Benedict XIV, at the place cited.] was being planned by Pope Innocent X, as the same author reports in the same place, a little later. He says:

> Finally, we add that, by order of Innocent X, supreme pontiff, a chapel is presently being prepared in the Vatican basilica in his honor, to preserve the memory of this apostolic man. There, on a marble panel by the hand of the Bolognese knight Alessandro Algardi, foremost among sculptors in the statuary arts, the same pontiff is presented carved before the eyes of those who look upon him, as he encounters Attila in order to free the city; and the sacred altar beneath which his body is afterward to be placed is splendidly adorned, like a most noble painting.

XVI. Such, then, are the services lavishly bestowed upon the relics of the holy body. But no less precious are the surviving writings of Saint Leo, like venerable relics of a soul filled with God, through which health has often been restored to minds corrupted either by vice or by error. Here are always ready the weapons of the Church, with which to slaughter heresies, defeat the devil, and pierce the monsters of vice. It has often been demonstrated by miracles and extraordinary signs that those illustrious monuments of the great pontiff were divinely transmitted [Col. 0335B]. Indeed, after his death he was once seen to be present in order to return thanks to those who had defended his epistle to Flavian—if faith may be placed in the author of the *Spiritual Meadow*, who records this story in the following words:

> Theodore, he says (chapter 148), the most holy bishop of Dorna (or Derna), in Libya, told us, saying: When I was chamberlain to the holy Pope Eulogius, I saw in a dream a man of venerable appearance and tall stature who said to me: “Announce my arrival to Pope Eulogius.” I replied: “Who are you, that you order me to announce you?” He answered me: “I am Leo, the Roman pontiff.”
>
> I therefore entered and announced, saying: “The most holy and blessed Pope Leo, bishop of the Roman See, wishes to meet with you.” When Pope Eulogius heard this, he rose quickly to meet him. After greeting one another and praying, they sat down. Then the lord and distinguished Leo said to Saint Eulogius: “Do you know why I have come here to you?” He replied: “No.” He said to him: “I have come to thank you, because you properly and magnificently answered on behalf of my epistle, which I sent written to my brother Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople, setting forth my understanding and judgment and closing the mouths of the heretics. Know, brother, that by your divine labor and zeal you have benefited not only me, but also the supreme head of the apostles, Peter, and above all the Truth itself that is preached by us, who is Christ our God.”
>
> Seeing this not once only but two and three times, and being confirmed by the threefold apparition, I related it to the holy Pope Eulogius. When he heard it, he wept; extending his hands toward heaven, he gave thanks to God, saying: “I give you thanks, Ruler of the world, Christ our God, who, although I am unworthy, have deigned to make me a herald of your truth and, through the prayers of your servants Peter and Leo, to receive our small and modest zeal, like the widow’s two small coins, with your supreme and ineffable kindness.” [608]

XVII. In his *Annals*, the most learned Cardinal Baronius presents, from the archive of Laelius Pasqualinus, a bronze coin struck in memory of Pope Saint Leo, bearing on one side the image and name of Saint Peter and on the other the name of Saint Leo himself; he also investigates the mysteries of this coin (under the year 461, no. 12). But Nicolaus Alemannus, in his dissertation *On the Lateran Walls*, and after him Andreas Victorellus, in his additions to Ciaconius, [Note: [Col. 0335C] This silver coin, rather than a bronze one, belongs to Leo VIII, as may be seen from the work *The Earlier Denarii of the Roman Pontiffs*, formerly published by Giovanni Vignoli and enlarged again through the study and care of Benedetto Floravanti, Rome, 1734, pp. 3 and 78. See also Muratori, vol. II of *Italian Antiquities*, dissertation 27, coin 45, col. 558. On the abbreviated mark DN., Vignoli observes on p. 78: Baronius and Alemannus wrongly interpreted this abbreviation as *Domino nostro*, since the letters are not divided by a point, but have a line above them, showing that they form a single word. For at that time the title *Domni* was customarily written in abbreviated form. The more recent coins of Queen Joanna of Naples and King Ladislaus, in the same Muratori, col. 640, coin 8, and col. 639, coin 7, seem to be referable to Leo I: on their reverse is read “Saint Leo, pope,” whereas on other coins of the same age and reign “Saint Peter, pope” occurs in Saint Leo’s place.] reasonably think that this coin should be referred to Leo III, for the following reason: the title “Lord” contained in the letters of the coin, D. N. LEONI PAPAE, does not suit Leo I but Leo III, to whom Charles the Great, king and emperor of the Franks, had restored and confirmed dominion over the city, as Alemannus says—or rather, as he ought to have said [Note: [Col. 0336C] This is disproved by what the most reverend John Augustine Orsi, master of the Sacred Palace, argues at length in his dissertation entitled *On the Origin of the Dominion and Sovereignty of the Roman Pontiffs over Their Temporally Subject States*, Rome, 1742, chapter 8. There he demonstrates that the Roman pontiffs had possessed supreme dominion in the City long before. As for the provinces of that same territory, insofar as the title of restoration accompanied the title of donation, he shows at length in chapter 6 that Charles the Great returned them to Saint Peter.] had first bestowed it.

Whatever may be the case with this bronze monument, our Leo certainly erected for himself a monument more enduring than any bronze: his never-dying writings, the holiness of his life, to be remembered by Christians as long as the Church endures, and the greatness of his illustrious deeds and labors undertaken for the Church and the empire. All these together present, in one Leo, Ambrose’s steadfastness, Chrysostom’s eloquence, Augustine’s learning, and Peter’s own faith in a single view.

## APPENDIX

To the foregoing dissertation on the life and achievements of Saint Leo—which concludes with the latest notices concerning his cult—one final document must be added. In it the supreme pontiff BENEDICT XIV ordered that this same Leo the Great be honored throughout the universal Church with the title and cult of DOCTOR. We were particularly eager to include it, as will be clear from the dedicatory epistle to the same supreme pontiff attached to the first volume. The special apostolic constitution by which this cult was decreed for Saint Leo seems all the more deserving of transcription here because anyone who reads it will find both selected encomia of him and the reasons proposed for decreeing his cult, and will also come to know the learning of its most wise author and his notable devotion toward our Saint.

[Col. 0337A] 609

**BENEDICT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.**

God, author and ruler of the Church militant, built her upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets and willed her to rest upon Christ Jesus, the supreme cornerstone. In his provident plan he also took care that outstanding and holy doctors should keep watch over her custody and protection until the end of the ages. By the example of their lofty virtue they would not only shape the conduct of the faithful toward holiness and justice, but also, through the power and excellence of their teaching, preserve them in the sincerity of faith and the truth of saving knowledge. The common Lord and Master showed how highly he valued their labor by calling them the salt of the earth and the light of the world. For they were destined not merely, like the other pastors of holy peoples, to consult for the salvation of the populations then present through the ministry of the living voice, but, enriched by the special light of wisdom through the gift of the Holy Spirit, to instruct the universal Church through learned books and to educate the posterity of all ages in religion.

Hence the Church herself, imbued with the spirit of her Bridegroom and striving to preserve his institutions, has been accustomed to honor those glorious men, filled by God with an abundant gift of teaching, with this special distinction: at the solemn sacred celebrations held on the recurrence of their feasts, both in the sacrifice of the Mass and in the ecclesiastical offices, she orders that prayers, readings, and praises of such a kind be used as both confer upon them the title of holy doctor and proclaim their wisdom and teaching in a special manner.

[Col. 0337C] Among those whose feast days we have always considered rightly adorned with this special rite and privilege, we must surely number our predecessor, Saint Leo I, Roman pontiff, who—as we may use the words of the most learned Cardinal Baronius—because of his outstanding virtue and learning and his most vigilant zeal in pastoral care, deservedly received from our ancestors the surname “the Great.” The excellence of his teaching shines forth with singular gravity and abundance of priestly eloquence, whether in explaining the higher mysteries of our faith and defending them against rising errors, or in handing down rules of discipline and precepts of conduct. It is recognized as so brilliant, and has been so richly celebrated by the praises of so many people and by the study and agreement of councils, Fathers, and ecclesiastical writers, that this most wise pontiff seems scarcely to be placed behind any of the holy doctors who have flourished in the Church, either in fame or in esteem.

Indeed, the holy universal synod assembled at Chalcedon not only called him the interpreter of the blessed Peter’s voice, but, reverently receiving his doctrine concerning the Incarnation of the Lord, did not hesitate to exclaim:

> Peter has spoken through the mouth of Leo.

The same holy pontiff was called by the council held at Constantinople under Menas “the illuminator and pillar of the Church”; by the Sixth Synod he is proclaimed “the support of orthodox faith”; and in a very ancient Book of Synods he is called “the defender of the apostolic doctrines” and “to be ranked with the apostles.” What, moreover, did the most illustrious leaders and Fathers of our religion say? Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, affirmed that Leo was the most holy luminary of the Roman Church, indeed of all that is beneath the heavens. To pass over countless other testimonies, Pope Saint Nicholas I, writing to the emperor Michael, freely asserted that unless God had raised up Leo’s virtue and teaching against the Ephesian Robber Council, the Christian religion would have utterly collapsed.

Although the Church has not yet included the holy pontiff Leo by a special decree among those whom she distinguishes with the title and designation of doctors, she has nevertheless shown that she holds his teaching in such great honor that she has ordered his writings to have frequent place in the divine offices, just as those of the men whom she has long venerated as her principal teachers and doctors of religion. Especially in those solemn celebrations throughout the year at which the greater mysteries of our faith are commemorated, she has wished the entire clergy and people to draw solid instruction and spiritual nourishment from readings taken from his sermons.

In addition to what we all believe and have long considered in our minds concerning Saint Leo’s merits and glory, there is a particular reason, shared by us with few others, which once greatly kindled and increased our devotion and veneration toward him. When we held a minor canonical dignity in the Basilica of Blessed Peter at the Vatican, his sacred body—having long rested beneath the altar called Saint Mary of the Column—was to be transferred with solemn rite and ceremony to another altar erected and dedicated in the same basilica in the name of that holy pontiff. We were present at the elevation and examination of his venerable bones, and considered it the height of happiness to behold them with our own eyes and honor them with the worship due to them. We mentioned this matter elsewhere, namely in book IV, part II, chapter 23, of our work *On the Canonization of Saints*.

What we have therefore always judged, for the reasons given above, to be just and right, and what our singular devotion toward the holy pontiff urges us to do, we have now resolved actually to perform by the authority of the Apostolic See, in which we have succeeded him—although the interval of time is great, and the interval of merits still greater. Therefore, following the examples of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, who, besides the supreme doctors of the Church, decreed that other most holy men who had flourished in the Church with outstanding renown for learning and enriched it by their writings should be honored with the title and cult of doctors, by our own initiative, with certain knowledge, and from the fullness of apostolic power, we will, prescribe, [Col. 0339A] and command that in the Breviary of the divine office, on the feast of Saint Leo, pope and confessor, the antiphon at the Magnificat in both Vespers be the one beginning, “O most excellent doctor”; and that at Mass the Introit be said: “In the midst of the Church”; [613] and after the Collect there follow the reading from the Book of Wisdom, “The just man will give his heart,” with the Gradual, as in the Common of Doctors; and after the Gospel the Creed be said. The rest is to be as in the customary proper Mass of Saint Leo.

We establish and decree that this be observed perpetually in all the Churches, and respectively by all and each of those bound to recite the divine office, notwithstanding any contrary rubrics, usages, or customs, even those expressly approved and confirmed by the Apostolic See, and anything else whatsoever to the contrary.

[Col. 0339B] Therefore, no one among mankind may violate this page of our precept, command, statute, decree, and will, or rashly dare to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1754, on the Ides of October, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate.

J. Cardinal, Pro-Datary. D. Cardinal Passioneus.

**SEEN**

From the Curia: J. C. Boschi.

In place of the + lead seal.

L. Eugenius.

Registered in the Secretariat of Briefs in the year of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1754, in the second indiction, on the ninth day of November, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of the most holy father in Christ and our lord, Lord Benedict, by divine providence Pope XIV. The aforesaid constitution was affixed and published at the doors of the Innocentian Curia, in the Field of Flora, and in the other customary and usual places of the City, by me, Dominicus Contini, apostolic courier.

Antonius Befani, master courier.

# SECOND DISSERTATION

**On the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, commonly attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine: in which they are withdrawn from Prosper and vindicated for Leo the Great**

[Col. 0339]

[Col. 0339B] 615

I. It is long since learned men brought forward and debated at length the question of the author of the two little books *On the Calling of All Nations*. Hardly any writer has published commentaries, in this or the preceding century, either on the divine aids of grace or on ecclesiastical writers, who has not eagerly offered his judgment concerning the genuine parent of this little work. Nor is this without good reason. It is of considerable importance for ecclesiastical doctrine that so learned a theologian and so rich a witness to ancient teaching should not remain unknown. A celebrated writer, H. Bullingerus (*Commentary on the Second Epistle to Timothy*, chapter 1), does not hesitate to grant him this praise: all who stand aloof from controversies and are unwilling to attribute either sin to God or spiritual good to man ought to learn from this author the genuine judgment of antiquity and follow it as the safest path between Scylla and Charybdis.

Great praise—but true praise, even though it came from the mouth of a heterodox writer. Whatever his intention in offering it, we embrace it because no one has more successfully grasped the Augustinian and therefore Catholic doctrine concerning the predestination of the saints and the grace of God, and no one has explained it more learnedly and eloquently. Vossius calls him a man of exceptionally disciplined and refined judgment (*History of the Pelagian Controversy*, book VII). Hugo Grotius shows himself extraordinarily attracted by the same author’s manner of writing and ideas, indicating that he read the work with the greatest care. He repeatedly calls him a great and excellent writer, especially hostile to Pelagius, and pious, writing piously and wisely. Nor did Desiderius Erasmus, a man not excessively lavish in praising others, restrain himself from commending this author. “The work itself speaks,” he says (*On the Calling of the Nations*): “the man was evidently thoroughly practiced in the sacred writings, with a sound and acute intellect. The very phrasing is so rhythmically musical, adorned with those Isocratean figures, that—although this is especially difficult in a subtle subject—you nowhere miss clarity of style, nowhere are you offended by the tiresomeness of studied elegance, and nowhere does the affectation of pointed observations grow cold; rather, what he had learned as a boy in the schools of the rhetoricians, he successfully adapts to the serious treatment of Scripture.” Nor is eloquence lacking, and that without inducing weariness.

II. Various persons therefore vindicate this excellent little work for different authors. It was first assigned to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Francis Cumel (*On the First Part of Saint Thomas*) considered it certain from the words of this author that the Pelagian heresy flourished in the time of Ambrose; I believe he reached that conclusion for no other reason than that he had read this work among Ambrose’s writings, among which it still retains its place today. Yet it is most certain that it belongs to someone else. “Even if there were no other argument for this,” says Erasmus (at the place cited), “the dissimilarity of the entire style is nevertheless so great that the reader detects at the first taste that someone other than Ambrose is speaking.” Would that the man who inserted this work had inserted many such little books among Ambrose’s writings. We could easily tolerate such forgeries when they substitute gold for gold.

To the dissimilarity of style must be added the mention of the Pelagians, who plainly arose only after Ambrose had already been received among the saints. The work mentions not only the Pelagians but also the Semi-Pelagians, whom it attacks throughout, especially; yet these were not heard of in the Church until [Note: [Col. 0339D] Perhaps through a scribal error “twenty” was written instead of “thirty.” Ambrose died in 397, whereas the error of the Semi-Pelagians began to be heard of in the Church in 427, as is clear from Augustine’s Epistle 217, written to Vitalis in that year.] twenty years after Ambrose’s death.

### III.

Erasmus seems to suspect that this work is by Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, when he observes that its style is not wholly unlike Eucherius’s phrasing. The suspicion may be strengthened by the fact that Eucherius seems first to have arrived at the island of Lérins [Col. 0340D], when he was seeking the solitude of the desert, and later lived on Lero, which lies close to Lérins; he was also familiar with the monks of this island. Since discussions about grace were then especially heated among them, it could easily have happened that Eucherius became involved in them. He was also very close to John Cassian and Hilary of Arles—by “them,” I mean the most distinguished opponents of Augustine’s doctrine of grace—so that, as we said concerning Leo, he might have wished by this writing to turn his friends away from erroneous opinions. For Norisius infers from the writings of Eucherius and his son Salonius that Eucherius himself adhered to Augustinian doctrine [Col. 0341A] (*History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 13).

But these conjectures are drawn from too far afield; nor does the similarity of the two styles seem to me sufficient to establish that they had the same author. That tuneful and ringing phrasing which Erasmus recognizes in the books *On the Calling of the Nations* is not found in Eucherius: nor is there the same weight of thought, choice of words, or majesty of the entire discourse that we admire in this little work.

### IV.

There are those who think that the work should be attributed to Hilary; John Latius inclines in this direction in his book *On Pelagianism and Semi-Pelagianism*. But which Hilary? For we read of three men of this name in that period: Hilary of Syracuse, whose letter to Augustine and Augustine’s reply on several points concerning grace are preserved among the holy Doctor’s letters (Letters 88 and 89); another, who wrote from Gaul to the same Augustine and joined himself to Prosper as his companion in defending Augustine’s teaching; and finally the bishop of Arles.

Some appear to have conflated the three into one; Hincmar of Rheims discusses such people in his book *On Predestination*. [Col. 0341B] Hincmar himself (*On Predestination*, chapters 13 and 18) does distinguish the Syracusan from the bishop of Arles, but confuses the bishop of Arles with the companion of Prosper. This is also the opinion of Cardinal Baronius and Gerardus Vossius. I, however, distinguish the Syracusan from the bishop of Arles, and the bishop of Arles from Prosper’s companion, in agreement with learned authorities; as for Prosper’s companion, I readily persuade myself that he was the same person as the monk Hilary of Syracuse.

### V.

That the monk Hilary of Syracuse was someone other than Hilary of Arles can readily be established from the chronology. The Syracusan wrote to Augustine around the year 413 or 414. The letter of Saint Augustine who replied cannot be dated before 412, since it mentions the judgment held against Caelestius at Carthage. But since Orosius, who had come there in the spring, carried the letter to Palestine, and it was read at a meeting of presbyters held in July 415, it is clear that the letter of this monk Hilary cannot be assigned later than 414. [Col. 0341C] In that year, however, Hilary who later became bishop of Arles was not yet beyond his thirteenth year of age: for he died in 449 at the age of forty-eight, according to Honoratus of Marseille, the author of his life.

### VI.

The following conjectures lead me, moreover, to think that Hilary of Syracuse was the same person as Prosper’s companion—that is, Prosper’s associate in defending Saint Augustine. Both of them, if they were two persons, were disciples of Saint Augustine and adhered to him for some time in Africa. Both opposed Pelagian errors. Both were laymen and, I think, monks. Both possessed only modest learning concerning the doctrines of the Church, about which the one who was uncertain questions Augustine in a similar manner, as their letters show. Finally, the style of both letters is not dissimilar.

I call him Hilary of Syracuse not because I think that he originated at Syracuse. If he was the same person as Prosper’s companion, he must be regarded as a Gaul. For this man, writing from Massilia, as I think, or from some other city of Gaul, greets Augustine in the name of his parents; and near the end of his letter he adds the following:

> Let Your Holiness know that my brother, for whose sake above all we departed from here, has, together with his wife, by mutual consent vowed perfect continence to God.  
> —Hilary’s letter to Saint Augustine

From this it is clear that Hilary’s paternal family was in Gaul. Certainly, when Hilary left his father’s house on the occasion of some disagreement with his brother, he could have crossed over to Africa and offered himself to Augustine for instruction at Hippo. After several years, a desire to revisit his homeland came upon him. As he was returning there, he wished—as was the custom of monks in that age—to visit the more celebrated monasteries. He therefore arrived at Syracuse, accompanied, I believe, by several citizens or clerics from Hippo. When these men were returning from Syracuse to Hippo, he entrusted to them, as he himself writes, a brief letter for Augustine, warning him about the Pelagian doctrine that was spreading at Syracuse [Col. 0342A].

Finally, after returning to his homeland, when he discovered that his teacher’s teaching was detested by many in Gaul, he thought that Augustine ought to be warned—perhaps remembering that, while he was previously at Syracuse, Augustine had asked this of him in the following words:

> You will confer a great benefit if you do not allow me to remain ignorant of what the holy brothers there are arguing against the empty talk of these men.  
> —Saint Augustine, Letter 89 to Hilary, at the end

### VII.

That Hilary, Prosper’s companion, is wrongly taken for the bishop of Arles was demonstrated with the greatest clarity by the most celebrated and invincible defender of the teaching of the holy Fathers in a French work published twenty years ago (*Apology of the Holy Fathers on Grace*, part I); and the recent historian of Pelagianism, Henry Norisius, likewise proves it (*History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 2).

The matter can be settled by this one argument. Hilary of Arles was already a bishop when the other Hilary wrote to Augustine together with Prosper; yet this Hilary was merely a layman at the time when he wrote his letter. He reveals this himself in the following words of his letter [Col. 0342B], in which he identifies the principal adversaries of Saint Augustine, especially Hilary of Arles:

> Some of these persons are such that ecclesiastical custom requires us to show the highest reverence to laymen. With God’s help, we have been careful to observe this, so that, when necessary, we did not tear them apart.

Prosper’s letter to Augustine agrees with this. “We can,” he says, “be steadfast in believing; but we are not equal in authority to those who hold such opinions, because they surpass us greatly both in the merits of their lives and because some of them, having recently attained the highest honor of the priesthood, stand above us” [Col. 0342C].

Moreover, this Hilary was still a layman when, after Augustine’s death and therefore not before the year 430, Pope Celestine wrote to the bishops of Gaul. He calls Prosper and Hilary “sons,” not “brothers,” as he should have called fellow bishops; nor does Saint Augustine himself address them otherwise at the beginning of his book *On the Predestination of the Saints* than as sons.

But Hilary of Arles had already been established in the see of Arles at the beginning of 429 [Col. 0342C], after the death of Honoratus. Honoratus had been appointed in place of Patroclus after Patroclus was killed in 426, and, according to Honoratus of Marseille, he held the episcopate for only two years (*Life of Saint Hilary*). This is further confirmed by the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*. When Germanus returned from his British mission and went to Arles in 429, according to Baronius—or in 430, according to others—Constantius says that “at that time the city was being illumined by Hilary the priest, precious for his manifold virtue.”

Finally, Saint Prosper expressly mentions Hilary’s episcopate at Arles in his letter:

> Let Your Beatitude know that one of them, a man of the highest authority and spiritual zeal, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles, is in all other matters an admirer and follower of your teaching, and that concerning the matter for which he brings a complaint he has long wished to communicate his opinion to Your Holiness by letter.

Cardinal Baronius considers the words “bishop of Arles” to have intruded into the text and thinks that they should be deleted; Vossius largely agrees with him. “It is much more satisfactory,” he says, “if *Hilary* is replaced by *Honoratus*,” as the most learned Espencaeus reports that it was written in his commentaries on the Letter to Timothy, book I, chapter 9. “Whether he did this,” Vossius himself says (*History of Pelagianism*, book VI), “on the authority of manuscripts or by conjecture, his opinion is in our judgment highly plausible.”

I hope, however, that no one will approve this emendation, since the testimony of the manuscripts, chronological considerations, and Prosper’s very words altogether oppose it: “We can indeed be steadfast in believing,” and so forth. This is the first basis for distinguishing the two Hilarys, derived from the episcopate of one of them, an office with which the other was never invested.

### VIII. 2.

The disposition of the two Hilarys toward Saint Augustine’s teaching was also very different. Although Hilary of Arles professed himself, in all other matters, an admirer and follower of Augustine, he nevertheless brought Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination under accusation; he was one of those whom the darkness of this opinion—an opinion opposed to the Augustinian position—obscured.

Hilary, on the other hand, Prosper’s companion, was entirely devoted in every respect to the teaching of Saint Augustine, as he himself testifies in these words:

> I do not wish Your Holiness to think that I am writing these things as though I had any doubt about what you have now published.… I am so far removed from this suspicion that I rather regard as noteworthy my own weakness, in that I bear such men with too little patience.

There is no doubt that among those whose conduct distressed him was the bishop of Arles himself, since, although Hilary does not state his name, he portrays him in the same colors as Prosper does. “But I must not,” he says, “keep silent about the fact that they say they admire Your Holiness in all deeds and words except this one matter.”

Here, then, is the prelate of the Church of Arles whom Prosper above described as an admirer and follower of Augustine’s teaching in all matters except the question that he brought under accusation.

### IX. 3.

Prosper’s companion was the one who urged Prosper to write to Saint Augustine, and he sent his letter to Africa together with his own, as he himself relates at the end of his letter. There he also mentions other letters that he had previously written to the same Augustine, with whom he seems to have maintained close and frequent contact.

Saint Prosper, by contrast, writes at the same time that it had occurred to Hilary of Arles some time earlier to approach the bishop of Hippo by letter, in order to compare his own opinion with Augustine’s teaching; he nevertheless says that he does not know whether Hilary would actually do so. This is entirely sufficient to demonstrate that one was different from the other. The former was familiar with Augustine; the latter was not.

### 4.

Hilary, Prosper’s fellow soldier, had once adhered closely to Augustine and had for some time been nourished in Africa on the milk of his teaching; he indicates this himself:

> Let my punishment be enough for me: exiled from the delights of your presence, where I was nourished at your health-giving breasts, I am tormented not only by your absence but also by the obstinacy of certain people.

Hilary of Arles, however, never traveled to Africa [Col. 0343C]. From his life and from that of Honoratus we learn that, through Honoratus’s zeal and efforts, Hilary was led away from the delights of the world to the discipline of monastic life and steadfastly remained at Lérins until, after Honoratus’s death, he was appointed in his place—not yet thirty years old.

### X.

Once these distinctions between the two Hilarys have been clarified, the assertion of Vossius and others disappears. They thought that the work *On the Calling of All Nations* should be attributed either to Hilary of Arles or to Prosper’s companion only because they had conflated two persons into one.

I add one argument concerning each separately. As for Hilary of Arles: nothing occurs in the work *On the Calling of All Nations* that even faintly suggests the Semi-Pelagian taint with which Hilary of Arles is known certainly to have been deeply infected. On the contrary, all the errors of the Semi-Pelagians are overthrown by this writing.

As for Prosper’s companion—whether he was the same as the Syracusan or a different man—he is not the author of so distinguished a little work. Neither of them had such a name in the Church that Gelasius would have judged him worthy to be numbered among the Church’s teachers and doctors, as he numbered the author whom we are examining. Neither was renowned for such holiness or learning that the virgin Demetrias would have wished him to write for her a treatise on the commitment to virginity. For, as we shall show below [Col. 0343D], the same person was undoubtedly the author of both writings; the affinity of their styles alone demonstrates this.

By contrast, the phrasing of both Hilarys is far removed from the style of the books *On the Calling of the Nations*: their style is meager, lowly, and halting; that of the other is adorned, elevated, and exuberant almost to extravagance. Finally, neither of their letters displays any characteristic that would lead one to expect something resembling such elegant and learned writing.

The letter of the Syracusan, in fact, is too brief and compressed for what should have been written by an educated man about such questions. The other Hilary openly acknowledges the weakness of his powers; he also seems not to have sufficiently grasped how harmful the doctrine of the opponents of Catholic teaching was, since he doubts whether they could be tolerated. He excuses himself to Augustine for having written differently about their opinion in his earlier letter from the way he is now writing.

Finally, conscious of his own weakness and afraid that he might once again report the opinion of the Semi-Pelagians with insufficient dignity and understanding, he informs Augustine that he has entrusted to Prosper the task of explaining it more adequately. He thus appears to have possessed a more ardent zeal for the grace of Christ than the knowledge required of its defender.

### XI.

This same consideration prevents me from agreeing with another conjecture of Vossius [Col. 0344B], who thinks it scarcely doubtful that we owe this work on grace to the zeal and labor of Prosper, bishop of Orléans.

For how much eloquence in speech and writing can we suppose that he possessed when he was forced to borrow the style of Apollinaris Sidonius (book VIII, letter 15) so that the deeds, character, merits, and virtues of Saint Anianus, likewise bishop of Orléans, might be commended to memory? Sidonius reports that this happened. Surely Prosper would not have declined this task; following the example of other bishops, he would himself have written the life of his predecessor if he had possessed as much eloquence as learned men admire in the little books *On the Calling of the Nations*. Besides, I scarcely believe that the controversy in question had penetrated as far as the places where that Prosper lived.

To attribute this work by conjecture to the other Prosper, who signed the councils of Carpentras and Vaison, as some prefer, requires no refutation [Col. 0344C]. Pope Gelasius could not have praised a man who was already dead, since he died in 496—that is, more than thirty years before either of those synods. The first was held in 527, the second in 529.

I add that the book was written around the beginning of the controversy that arose against Augustine, whereas that controversy preceded this Prosper’s lifetime by a full hundred years. Here one must fault the carelessness of Vossius, otherwise a very diligent man, because he does not distinguish between Prosper of Orléans and this later Prosper.

### XII.

At last we come [Note: [Col. 0343D] Compare the observations appended to this dissertation, § 1.] to Prosper of Aquitaine, Leo’s secretary, or whether he later became a bishop, as is commonly held [Note: [Col. 0343D] This opinion, by which some believe that Saint Prosper of Aquitaine was at some time honored with the episcopate, rests chiefly on the commonly circulated superscription of the letter to Demetrias. We have nevertheless shown that this superscription is arbitrary and false in note 2 on that same letter.], or whether he never rose to that rank, as is now generally maintained among learned scholars.

It may seem all the more difficult to deny him possession of this little work, since it is said to have been secured by eight hundred years of prescription, by the testimony of all the surviving manuscript codices, and by the support of the entire Gallican Church; since the votes of almost all writers also converge in his favor; and since, in nearly all editions of his works, this writing has long been regarded as his genuine offspring [Col. 0344D].

There is indeed agreement between Prosper and this author concerning the doctrine of Christ’s grace. Both echo Saint Augustine. Yet they appear to differ in words and modes of expression, and this author descends to a way of explaining the matter, and to such apparent softening qualifications, to which Prosper is never recorded to have resorted. This led Gerardus Vossius to assert that, in his judgment, the author’s position does not correspond exactly to Prosper’s doctrine, but rather follows a middle course between Augustine’s position and that of the Semi-Pelagians. Whether this is true will have to be investigated below.

#### 2.

The difference in style also argues for distinguishing the authors; this was first noticed by John Latius in book II, chapter 3, of his work on the Semi-Pelagians. Cassander and Coster attributed the work to Prosper on the authority of ancient codices; but its style diverges from Prosper’s style, and its treatment of the subject is different.

This, I think, was likewise the reason why several very learned men declared that this golden little work—as learned men often call it—was not Prosper’s. Among them, besides Latius, are Gerardus Vossius, Hugo Grotius, Antonius Arnauld, Henry Norisius, now a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and several others.

Certainly, the style of the author of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* is much more polished and harmonious than Prosper’s; the diction is more elegant; the periods are more carefully proportioned; contrasts between ideas and clashes between words occur more frequently; figures of speech are used more often; and the whole discourse is much more rhythmically modulated by the deliberate recurrence of metrical patterns.

This last point deserves particular attention, since it can arise only from deliberate design and effort. Such patterns do not appear only when the discourse seems to run toward them spontaneously—as one may occasionally find in Prosper—but also in other places where they could have been employed only intentionally.

#### 3.

The method of writing familiar to the anonymous author differs greatly from Prosper’s manner. Prosper openly and publicly presents himself as the defender and champion of Saint Augustine; everywhere he vigorously and energetically defends every detail of Augustine’s teaching; he carefully follows all his footsteps; and everywhere he breathes the spirit, doctrine, and entire thought of the holy Doctor.

Nothing of this sort appears in the two little books. There is not even the slightest mention of Saint Augustine, so that the author might seem either not to know him—which no one would believe—or to have suppressed his name deliberately and for definite reasons.

When Prosper writes, he everywhere proclaims and disseminates the authority of the Roman Church, since he enters the arena in its name and under its commission. The other author draws his style from his own ingenuity, with a desire not so much to fight as to exercise himself; he resembles an inquirer more than one defending certain doctrines already established and sanctioned.

Prosper openly attacks the Semi-Pelagians and pursues them as adversaries of Catholic doctrine. This author, however, attacks them less deliberately than incidentally, as though occupied with something else; nor does he do so with the force and zeal displayed by that holy disciple and defender of Augustinian doctrine.

### XIII. 4.

Although it is certain that the little work was written some time before the age of Pope Gelasius, it is nevertheless difficult to assign a particular period that suits Prosper. If one wishes to place its composition at the very beginning of the disputes, or shortly after they arose, the author himself contradicts this in the opening of his book, where he expressly asserts that controversy over these questions had already existed for a long time.

> A great and difficult question has long been debated between the defenders of free will and the preachers of God’s grace.  
> —Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 1

If one readily concedes what cannot be denied—that this controversy had long been raging between the Augustinians and the Semi-Pelagians—then, when the author applied himself to writing, he must already have been someone other than Prosper.

For as soon as the remnants of the Pelagian poison began to be disseminated through the Genoese extracts, the chapters of the Gauls, or the *Conferences* of John Cassian, Prosper quickly seized and sharpened his pen, and attacked the novelty of those expressions with all his strength. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Nations*, by contrast, suggests that this is his first work on the subject, composed long after the questions had been raised:

> A great and difficult question has long been debated.… I shall endeavor, insofar as the Lord assists me, to inquire with what measure and moderation one ought to think about this conflict of opinions, exercising and testing the limited capacity of my powers in matters that, as far as I judge, have soberly taken root in my heart.

Here are the words of someone writing after a long dispute among these opinions, undertaking his first effort and first attempt in this work; a man more inquisitive and self-exercising, examining the matter by his own effort and according to the measure of his ability, than confidently asserting and defending it from the teaching of the Fathers under commission from the apostolic see.

Indeed, he writes very timidly and hesitantly. Although he was presenting propositions entirely consistent with Augustinian doctrine and with the doctrine received in the Church, he was nevertheless introducing new modes of expression. He knew that novelties of language are rightly regarded with suspicion in the Church even when the ancient doctrine is preserved. Accordingly, after the words quoted above, he adds:

> So that, if the style should proceed according to rules containing nothing offensive and nothing corrupt, it may be useful not only to us but also to others that we have reached some boundary which we ought not to cross.

Finally, those who have argued that the work should not be denied to Prosper have said that the distinction might arise from the fact—as some have maintained—that Prosper wrote it at a time when he had not yet fully imbibed the streams of Augustinian doctrine, especially the teaching found in the later books he wrote toward the end of his life. But this is easily disproved by the firmly established date of this writing given above.

### XIV.

Moved by these and similar considerations, learned men undertook a fresh examination of the author of the little work, setting aside all the prejudices noted above. After more careful investigation and assessment of the considerations and arguments thus far advanced, they determined that the following three points should be regarded as certain.

First, none of those whom we examined before Prosper is the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*.

Second, although stronger arguments may favor Prosper of Aquitaine, the arguments brought against him are stronger still. Nor are the arguments in his favor more compelling for attributing this work to Prosper than similar arguments by which the work *On the Contemplative Life* was attributed to him down to our own age.

For that work too has been praised under Prosper’s name for eight hundred years in the synods of the Gallican Church; Prosper’s name likewise appears in manuscript codices of the same period; it has likewise long been included in printed editions of his works; and it was finally believed without opposition by all writers of later ages.

Nevertheless, it is now agreed among learned scholars that Prosper’s work *On the Contemplative Life* is not his. Nor was it thought improper to withdraw belief from such ancient and suitable witnesses, even on the sole basis of a difference in style. Everyone agrees that the work belongs to Julianus Pomerius, partly on the testimony of Isidore, bishop of Seville, and partly on the evidence of manuscript codices.

One copy was long ago praised by learned men; it had first belonged to the viscount of Saint-Salvator and later to Charles de Monchal, the most illustrious and learned archbishop of Toulouse. We have recently found the other in the library of the Abbey of Notre-Dame de la Trappe. From a little obscure monastery, where regular discipline had been completely blotted out, it suddenly became a very large and holy religious house through the zeal and piety of its most devout abbot—thus, in our own age, giving the Gallican Church its Bernard and returning to Bernard his Clairvaux.

Third and finally, the conclusion reached by learned writers after laborious investigation is this: the author of these books is entirely unknown. They have therefore denied them to everyone to whom they had previously been attributed and assigned them to no one.

### XV.

I cannot express sufficient wonder that, while every learned scholar devoted to ecclesiastical affairs hunts for the author of this distinguished little work, no one has suspected anything concerning our Leo, nor has that splendid light of the Roman Church entered anyone’s eyes.

Indeed, it surely did enter them; but while some thought only of the pontiff and others saw in the work a manner of writing unlike that of a pontiff, they feared to attribute our little books to him. They failed to notice what we regard as certain: just as our Leo had long before his pontificate fought against the Pelagians with fervent zeal, so it may readily be thought that he fought with his style and writings, since he possessed both a knowledge of the sacred Scriptures and an exceptional ability in speaking and writing [Col. 0347A].

I am therefore entirely convinced that Pope Leo wrote the books *On the Calling of All Nations* before he was elevated to the summit of the pontificate. It was not difficult for me to become persuaded of this, since, as I have repeatedly reread the writings of Saint Leo out of the requirements of my calling, Leo’s phrasing and his entire manner of expression have become thoroughly familiar to me.

Whether I shall find it equally easy to persuade others of this, I dare not promise. I do promise this one thing: there is nothing by which our opinion can be shaken. On the contrary, whatever has been observed by the various writers who have cultivated this field as distinctive of this author, and many other features besides, agree wholly with Leo and point to him almost with a finger.

I mean his period, homeland, character of writing, familiar use of Scripture, particular citation of certain passages, frequent recurrence to others, especially the similarity of his doctrine concerning the grace of Christ [Col. 0347B], his distinctive manner of explanation, similar opinions, deliberate repetition of certain words, identical construction of periods, the same arrangement of discourse, frequent clashes and antitheses of words, variety, elegance, dignity, abundance, and fiery vigor of diction. In short, the entire face, so to speak, of the style proclaims that the author is exactly the same—apart from the fact that both men also had the same occasions that could have moved them to write this work.

### XVI.

First, as regards the date of composition [Note: [Col. 0347D] See the observations to be appended, no. 10.], it is most evident that the work falls within the lifetime of our Leo. The author began to write when the disputes against Augustinian doctrine had already long been raging; these had arisen while Augustine was still alive. Thus he was composing the work around the year 432 or 433, not far removed from 440, the year in which Leo was elected pope.

Moreover, the author wrote only after reading the works of others against the Semi-Pelagians—that is, after the writings of Saint Prosper, who at that time refuted the *Conferences* of John Cassian, who was still alive [Col. 0347C].

It should also be added that Pope Gelasius praised this little work as having been written several years earlier by some teacher of the Church. Pope Gelasius, however, left the pontificate and this life in 496.

Finally, it is now certain among learned scholars that the author of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* and the author of the letter to the virgin Demetrias are the same person. That letter is counted among and attributed to Prosper’s works, but the affinity of style demonstrates its common authorship.

The letter too seems to have been written around the period we have assigned. Demetrias had embraced the commitment to virginity in 413, at the first flowering of youth, as the author of the letter says—perhaps at the age of twenty or eighteen. Yet the author praises her mature and learned mind from the very beginning of the letter, which could scarcely have been written before approximately 433, when Demetrias had reached her thirty-eighth or fortieth year.

Certainly, the following words indicate that the letter was written after Augustine’s death. In them the author praises, as though already dead, those who had encouraged the most devout virgin with their exhortations at the very beginning of her consecration:

> Concerning this matter, many who at that time held a preeminent place in the Church did not remain silent even at the very beginning; among them, no one will doubt that Augustine was numbered.

### XVII. 2.

It is highly probable that this author was born in Italy, or at least lived there [Note: [Col. 0348D] Compare observation no. 11.]. He must certainly be claimed either for our Gauls, for the African Church, or for the Roman Church; outside these regions, one could not have found during that period either such eloquence or such learning as the little books contain.

It seems to me that he was not an African, as may be proved by his profound silence concerning Saint Augustine. This indicates a less ardent devotion than an African should have displayed toward a fellow countryman. He would not have been unaware that Augustine was the glory of the African synods, and he would have loved to say of so great a man, with Prosper, that he was

> …among all those who, from the holy flock,  
> Drove away the mad beasts, greater in diligence,  
> And filled the whole world with a work greater and more excellent.

He would have praised him, I say, or defended him from the insults and malicious accusations of his opponents. Nothing of the sort appears, so that it seems that no contact or relationship existed between the two men.

Furthermore, we should have some memory of so great a man in the African Church: Augustine would have enlisted him as a companion in the struggle against heretics, and he would have undertaken here to harass them after the holy Doctor’s death.

Finally, the clarity and harmony of this author’s style have nothing in common with the inflated, or even barbarous, diction of the Africans of that period [Col. 0348B]. As the barbarians invaded a large part of Africa, they also introduced barbarism into literature, so that Augustine—who had once sought the reputation of eloquence among other distinctions—has nothing in this respect that can be compared with our author.
