If you say that he was a Gaul, it is difficult to imagine why Gennadius, otherwise such a careful cataloguer of Gallic writers, either failed to know him or passed him over. Why also would he not have joined himself to Prosper as a fellow soldier against the detractors of Augustinian doctrine, since he possessed such an abundance of eloquence and learning, and since there was such a shortage of defenders of grace in Gaul that scarcely anyone could be found to confront its attackers?

“Indeed,” says Saint Prosper (*Letter to Saint Augustine*), “apart from a few fearless lovers of perfect grace, no one has dared to oppose the extensive arguments of our predecessors.”

At a time of such necessity, I say, would this author have hidden away in Gaul like an unarmed or trembling champion, while Prosper alone fought, with one companion—or rather instigator of the battle—in the monk Hilary, who, as appears, was not sufficiently fit for the struggle?

### XVIII

It remains to declare that this author was Italian; and this too we can make probable by several considerations. The elegance and polish of his style point to a man educated within or near the Roman civic sphere, where the Latin language was better defending itself against the encroaching barbarism. One will scarcely, and perhaps not at all, find a contemporary of Leo whom the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations* does not surpass in refinement of composition.

Moreover, the author has the following in Book II, chapter 33:

> “Other barbarians, while assisting the Romans, learned in our regions what they could not have known in their own lands, and returned to their homes with the instruction of the Christian religion.”

It is uncertain what expedition is meant here; but I do not know whether it can more suitably be referred to any other event than the war against the tyrant Eugenius, brought to an end by the great Theodosius. Its memory was then still recent. The victory won in that battle was decisive for the interests of the empire. A vast multitude of barbarians followed the emperor as he proceeded from the eastern regions to war, as far as the Alps, where the tyrant was defeated and a large part of them was killed by the enemy. It was easy, however, for their children to be instructed there in the rudiments of the Christian religion and to be baptized, Theodosius arranging this favor for them, perhaps out of gratitude, since on the same occasion we learn that he willingly extended this concern even to the children of his enemies.

“Those children of his enemies,” says Saint Augustine, “whom not his command but the violence of war had carried away, and who, although not yet Christians, were fleeing for refuge to the Church, he wished on this occasion to become Christians, and he loved them with Christian charity” (*City of God*, Book V, chapter 26).

But the more obvious sense of the words “in our regions” requires, unless I am mistaken, that they be understood of Roman territory, since they are joined with the words “while assisting the Romans.” Erasmus, however, to whom this thought also occurred, considers the argument less conclusive, because wherever the Roman empire extended itself, that territory could be called Roman. Let the reader decide.

Perhaps a stronger conjecture is drawn from Book II, chapter 16, where he praises in magnificent words the primacy of the Roman Church and describes its jurisdiction as propagated far and wide under the title of the faith disseminated everywhere. For although all Catholics throughout the world acknowledge the primacy of the Roman see and profess the singular prerogative owed to Peter’s successor, the head of the Church, our author nevertheless seems to take delight in these modes of expression, which reveal a man either Roman by birth or closely associated with the Roman clergy.

Finally, this little work is nowhere found cited by the African Church; in the Gallican Church, not until after the year 800. But in the Roman Church it is praised before the year 496, namely by Pope Gelasius I, who, although he leaves the author’s name unmentioned, indicates that it was composed by some wise teacher and doctor of the Church:

> “Just as a certain teacher of the Church wisely instructed us, saying: ‘The material of conflicts has been preserved for the great benefit of the faithful, so that holiness may not grow proud while weakness is being assailed.’”

Who else, then, was there in those times—a wise doctor and teacher of the Church—to whom this work could be attributed, since we have already judged that it must be denied to Prosper and to the other more eminent men who then held first place in knowledge and eloquence within the Church?

### XIX

Since the author’s age and homeland agree with Leo, we must now inquire whether his style and manner of expression also correspond. There are certainly many features common to both.

The first is that both use the new translation of Saint Jerome. [Note: Col. 0349D. See Observation no. 12.] This similarity deserves all the more consideration because very few writers are found who used that version before the middle of the fifth century, the period in which this work is known to have been written.

A notable passage occurs in Job 14:4 [Note: Col. 0349D. See the observations in Dissertation 4, no. 5.], cited in this form by Saint Leo, *Sermon* 8 on the Nativity of the Lord, and in Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 8:

> “Who can make the clean from an unclean seed? Is it not you alone?”

According to the old translation, the passage reads:

> “No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but a single day.”

The same verse is used according to both translations in the letter to Demetrias, chapter 11. From this one may reasonably suspect that the author of the three works is the same. Certainly, this mixed use of both versions further inclines me to believe that he was not African but Roman. For I think that Jerome’s version was adopted later in Africa, where it had to endure opposition from Augustine, than at the Roman see, where Jerome’s authority was considerable; and Gregory himself testifies in the letter prefixed to his exposition of Job that both versions were in use there before the pontificate of Gregory I.

Both read the following verse of chapter 4 of the First Epistle of John:

> “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God.”

Although these words occur in the writings of some other Fathers, they are not found in many. They are certainly absent from all Greek manuscripts and from the versions published by heretics. Socrates writes (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 32):

> “All who sought to separate Christ’s divinity from his humanity did not hesitate to erase and remove this statement from ancient copies.”

He says that this was likewise attested by the ancient interpreters. The passages are Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 23, and the famous Letter 24, now 28, to Flavian, chapter 5.

Both render verse 33 of Jeremiah 31 in this form:

> “I will give my laws in their understanding, and I will write them upon their hearts.”

The author does so in Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapters 8 and 9; Leo does so in *Sermon* 95, *On the Steps of Ascent to Blessedness*, chapter 1. From these words both observe, in the same place, that the severity of the law was changed into mercy through the infusion of grace.

Both read and frequently use the Apostle’s text in this form:

> “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus.’”

The saying from Job is familiar to both:

> “The life of man upon earth is a temptation.”

And when they describe the condition of the nations living without God and without the light of faith before the Lord’s incarnation, they very often cite these words from chapter 14 of Acts:

> “He allowed the nations to go their own ways.”

Both use this passage from chapter 28 of the Gospel according to Matthew to prove that Christ the Lord never ceases to work through the ministers of his word and sacraments:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

Saint Leo, Letter 83, now 108, to Theodore of Fréjus, chapter 2:

> “In this work”—namely, the reconciliation of sinners through the ministry of priests—“the Savior himself continually intervenes, and he is never absent from the things he has entrusted to his ministers to perform, saying: ‘Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.’”

And Letter 2, now 167, to Rusticus of Narbonne:

> “Strengthening the preachers of the Gospel and the ministers of the sacraments: ‘Behold, I am with you,’ and so forth.”

The author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 2:

> “And lest the ministries of preachers appear to be carried out merely through human effort: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I am with you,’ and so forth.”

Both also—and this is especially noteworthy—cite verses 31 and 32 of chapter 22 of Saint Luke in the same distinctive form. Thus they read [Note: Col. 0350D. Compare the observations appended to this dissertation, no. 13.]:

> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked to see you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have finally turned back, strengthen your brothers; and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

Within these very few words there are three or four expressions in which they agree with each other and differ quite markedly from others, as is clear from the reading of the Vulgate edition, which is as follows:

> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have returned, strengthen your brothers.”

Saint Prosper has a nearly similar reading to that of our author, but it is not altogether the same. In the first passage, namely in the letter to Rufinus, he does not have *cerneret* (“might see”) instead of *cribraret* (“might sift”), although the rest agrees. In the book *Against the Collator*, chapter 35, where he uses the same text again, he omits the final words, “and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

Saint Leo, however, in *Sermon* 3, now 4, on the anniversary of his assumption, chapter 3—the only place where he cites these words—agrees in every respect with the author of *On the Calling of All Nations*.

Someone will doubtless object that *cerneret* is not found there instead of *cribraret*. I admit that it is not read thus in printed books; but we have proved from manuscripts of the highest quality that this passage was corrupted. Since the expression was familiar to everyone, and since *cribraret* is read everywhere in all manuscripts, some learned scribe did not hesitate to correct what he considered an error to conform it to the Vulgate reading, restoring *cribraret* in place of *cerneret*. But that the latter is the reading to be retained is shown by three manuscripts: one Victorine, another Cistercian, and a third belonging to Saint-Marien at Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian order, formerly belonging to the Cistercian abbey of Régniac, not far from that city. Hincmar, bishop of Reims, reads it in the same way in his work on the fifty-five chapters, chapter 16, where he transcribes this passage of Leo.

### XX. 2

[Note: Col. 0351D. See Observation no. 14.]

The doctrine of this work concerning the grace of Christ is entirely the same as Saint Leo’s doctrine. Since it contains certain ways of explaining and expressing this subject which at first sight seem to depart from Augustine’s position, those same formulations are also repeatedly found in Leo.

Among them especially is the author’s frequent discussion of a certain universal grace bestowed upon every age and every human being. He places this grace in the harmonious discord of the elements, in the structure, order, and, as it were, speech of earth, heaven, and all creatures, which proclaim the omnipotence and goodness and wisdom of the Creator in an ineffable manner.

Thus Saint Leo, *Sermon* 7 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 2:

> “Through the very elements of the world, as through public pages, we receive an indication of the divine will; nor does divine instruction ever cease, since even through those things which serve us we are instructed.”

*Sermon* 8 on the same subject, chapter 2:

> “We understand that nothing is empty of the divine commands, and that all the elements serve the instruction of the Word of God, while through the pivots of the world, as through the four Gospels, we continually learn what we must preach and do. For when the prophet says, ‘The heavens declare the glory of God,’ and so forth, what is there through which the truth does not speak to us? His voices are heard by day, his voices by night; and the beauty of things created by the workmanship of the one God does not cease to impress upon the ears of the heart the reason that is their teacher, so that the invisible things of God may be perceived through the things that have been made, and that service may be rendered not to creatures but to the Creator of all.”

*Sermon* 6 on the fast of the seventh month:

> “There is nothing by which divine providence does not assist the devotion of the faithful. For in training minds and bodies toward holiness, even the elements of the world serve us, while the distinct and varied cycle of days and months opens certain pages of instruction to us, so that what the sacred institutions admonish, the seasons too may in a certain manner speak.”

*Sermon* 6 in Lent, chapter 1:

> “Beloved, the earth is always full of the Lord’s mercy, and nature itself is instruction for every believer in the worship of God, since heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them proclaim the goodness and omnipotence of their Author; and the wondrous beauty of the elements that serve him demands from the rational creature a fitting act of thanksgiving.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 4:

> “Heaven and earth and every creature that can be seen and understood were chiefly arranged for the benefit of the human race, so that rational nature might be instructed in the worship and love of its Author. For although salvation is far from sinners, nothing is devoid of the presence and power of that salvation … What testimony, then, always serves the Lord and never ceases to speak of his goodness and power, except the ineffable beauty of the whole world and the rich and ordered abundance of his ineffable benefits? Through these, certain tablets of the eternal law were offered to human hearts, so that in the pages of the elements and the volumes of the seasons the common and public teaching of divine instruction might be read. Heaven, therefore, and all heavenly things, the sea and the earth, and all that is in them, in harmonious agreement with their beauty and order, proclaimed the glory of God and, in perpetual proclamation, spoke the majesty of their Author.”

And chapter 5:

> “Although Scripture declares these and many similar truths, we nevertheless believe and devoutly confess that the care of divine providence has never been absent from the whole human race. Although it directed the people it had chosen toward piety through special institutions, it nevertheless withheld the gifts of its goodness from no nation of human beings, so that they might be shown to have received the prophetic utterances and legal commandments through the service and testimony of the elements. Hence they were made inexcusable, because they made gods for themselves out of God’s gifts; and they worshiped as objects of devotion what had been created for their use.”

Both authors discuss this kind of universal grace—understood in the broader sense of the term, and including the law and everything useful for the knowledge of God—at length, for the most part in the same words. This is proved not only by the passages quoted above from Saint Leo and from the other work, but also by additional passages.

Saint Leo, *Sermon* 80, now 82, on Saints Peter and Paul, chapter 2:

> “The good, just, and almighty God has never denied his mercy to the human race, and he has always instructed all mortals alike in the knowledge of himself through his most abundant benefits.”

*Sermon* 5 on the Epiphany:

> “God’s kindness remains over all, and he denies his mercy to no one, since he bestows many blessings indiscriminately upon all.”

*Sermon* 8 on the same feast:

> “God, urging all toward knowledge of himself through universal gifts, rains upon the just and the unjust, and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 10:

> “The experience of all ages has taught that God’s mercy is just and his justice merciful, and that it has never been absent either from nourishing human bodies or from teaching and assisting their minds. For he has always rained upon the good and the evil; he has always made his sun rise upon the just and the unjust.”

Book I, chapter 5:

> “According to Scripture we believe, and we devoutly confess, that the care of divine providence has never been absent from the whole human race. Although it directed the people it had chosen toward piety through special institutions, it nevertheless withheld the gifts of its goodness from no nation of human beings.”

Chapter 21:

> “Although we see that the assistance of grace has been completely withdrawn from no human beings.”

Book II, chapter 17:

> “That general measure of assistance, which has always been provided from above to all human beings, is nevertheless not denied to them”—that is, to the pagans.

Chapter 25:

> “That God wills, and has always willed, that all human beings be saved is demonstrated in no other way than by those benefits and by that providence of God which he extends commonly and impartially to all generations … Upon those gifts, which throughout all ages proclaim their Author, special grace has been poured.”

Book II, chapter 4:

> “As the prophet says, ‘The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord’: mercy which has never been absent from any age or generation. The providence by which he governs and sustains the whole order of things he has always extended to the governing and nourishing of created natures.”

See also chapter 9 of the same book.

Both speak in the same way of the law and the mysteries of the law, which they generally call the testimony of the law, the signs of the Old Testament, the oracles of the prophets, and the decrees of the Old Testament.

Both likewise press hard against the champions of the will. Leo, Letter 6, now 1, to the bishop of Aquileia, chapter 3, writes that they strive with all their might to make it appear that the grace of God is given according to the merits of those who receive it; and therefore, he says, they assert that grace is preceded by natural effort, so that what is already made illustrious by personal exertion before grace may seem not to have been wounded by original sin.

The same point is expressed in other words in Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 22, and in the letter to Demetrias, chapter 10.

### XXI. 3

Not only do the same thoughts and concepts occur in the matter of grace, and the same manner of expression; they also appear in many other subjects—for example, when the authors speak of the foundation, extent, and dignity of the apostolic see in the city of Rome.

Saint Leo, *Sermon* 1 on Saints Peter and Paul, chapter 1:

> “So that the holy nation, the chosen people, the priestly and royal city, having been made the head of the world through the sacred see of blessed Peter, might preside more widely through divine religion than through earthly dominion. For although you have increased through many victories and extended the right of your empire by land and sea, what military effort has subjected to you is less than what Christian peace has subjected … In order that the effect of this ineffable grace might be spread throughout the whole world, divine providence prepared the Roman empire, whose growth it brought to those boundaries at which the whole neighboring and contiguous multitude of nations might be found. For the work divinely ordained was especially suited to this: that many kingdoms should be joined together under one empire, and that general preaching should quickly find accessible peoples whom the government of a single city held together.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 16:

> “For the accomplishment of this work we believe that the extent of the Roman empire was prepared by God’s providence, so that the nations called to unity in the body of Christ might first be joined together under the law of a single empire. Although Christian grace is not content to have the same boundaries as Rome, and has already subjected to the scepter of Christ’s cross many peoples whom Rome did not subdue by her arms, she has nevertheless been made greater through the primacy of the apostolic priesthood, by the stronghold of religion rather than by the throne of power.”

When both describe the Apostle Peter rising again after his threefold denial, they use nearly the same terms, although these are not so commonly employed. They refer the whole event to the secret gaze of Christ the Lord, and from it they infer that, for no one living this life, however just and pious, is the danger and fear of falling absent.

Saint Leo, *Sermon* 3 on the Passion:

> “The Lord looked upon Peter. Amid the accusations of the priests, the falsehoods of the witnesses, and the insults of those who struck and spat upon him, he addressed the troubled disciple with those eyes by which he had foreseen that he would be troubled.”

*Sermon* 9 on the same Passion:

> “Peter, terrified by weakness, encountered the danger of denial. For this reason, as appears, he was permitted to hesitate, so that in the chief of the Church a remedy of repentance might be established, and no one might dare to trust in his own strength, when even blessed Peter could not escape the danger of changeability. But the Lord Jesus, who was held bodily within the priestly council, saw with divine insight the disciple’s trembling outside; and as soon as he looked upon him, he raised the spirit of the terrified man and moved him to tears of repentance.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 28:

> “If the faith of so great an apostle was destined to fail unless Christ prayed for him, then undoubtedly there was in him that changeability by which he could waver in temptation … For such great disturbance shook him even after these events that, frightened by the questioning of a single maidservant in the house of Caiaphas, he was brought to a threefold denial of Christ, with his steadfastness failing. He, therefore, who then addressed the troubled heart of the Apostle not with human but with divine eyes, and by his powerful gaze moved him to abundant tears of repentance, could confer this firmness of spirit upon his distinguished disciple … In the uncertainty of the present contest, where the whole of life is a temptation and even victory itself is not safe from lurking pride, no one is free from the danger of changeability.”

Speaking of the name of the same chief of the apostles, Saint Leo says:

> “Blessed Peter … drew the solidity both of his virtue and of his name from the principal Rock.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 28:

> “Who would doubt the strongest rock, which received from that principal Rock both its fellowship and its virtue and its name?”

Concerning the conversion of sinners, Saint Leo writes:

> “While we live in this body, the restoration of no one must be despaired of; rather, the correction of all must be desired, with the Lord’s help, who raises those who are crushed, releases the bound, and enlightens the blind.”

In *Sermon* 4 on the Epiphany, chapter 5, section 4, and in the *Collection*, chapter 2:

> “Restoration is not denied to those who have been crushed.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, final chapter:

> “If someone should perhaps fall, overcome by some temptation, let him not be swallowed up by sadness or distrust the mercy of him who raises all who fall and lifts up all who are crushed. For while we live in this body, the correction of no one is to be neglected, and the restoration of no one is to be despaired of.”

In *Sermon* 3 on the Passion, chapter 3, Judas is called an “unconvertible man.” Letter 125, now 156, chapter 2:

> “The Antichrist, or the devil, persevering in his wickedness, is unconvertible.”

The same word is used in another sense in Letter 93, now 120, chapter 3, concerning the “unconvertible nature of God.” *On the Calling of All Nations*, Book I, chapter 25:

> “Could that power of grace, which subjected to itself those whom it willed, not convert those who remained unconvertible?”

Speaking of the final day and the last judgment, Saint Leo says in *Sermon* 5 on collections and almsgiving, chapter 3:

> “When all the nations have been gathered … in what will those who stand at God’s right hand be praised, except in works of kindness and duties of charity? What, however, will be charged against those on the left, except neglect of love—as though those on the right had no other virtues, or those on the left no other offenses?”

*Sermon* 7 on Lent, chapter 4:

> “When those on the left have been thrust into the fire of Gehenna because of their inhumanity, the eternal blessedness of the heavenly kingdom will receive those on the right, praised for their merciful almsgiving.”

*Sermon* 4 on collections and almsgiving, chapter 2:

> “The peoples of all nations will be gathered before the throne of his power … and when the sons of piety have received the kingdom prepared for them after the works of mercy have been recounted, the unjust will be reproached for the hardness of their sterility. And having nothing in common with those on the right, those on the left will go into the fire,” and so forth.

And *Sermon* 16:

> “Therefore those on the left did not do only this, nor because …”

*Sermon* 96, now Appendix 14, on the Chair of Saint Peter, chapter 4:

> “To escape the number of the left-hand goats who live in wantonness.”

*On the Calling of All Nations*, Book II, chapter 8:

> “In the gathering of all nations, some are led to be placed on the right, others on the left. The right are praised for works of charity; the left are charged with nothing other than neglect of mercy and kindness.”

### XXII. 4

[Note: Col. 0353D. See Observation no. 15.]

Nothing is so similar and so harmonious with another thing as the style of this little work is with the style of Saint Leo; I am therefore greatly surprised that no one has noticed this until now. For it is—as the apologist of the holy Fathers, whom no praise can adequately honor, describes it—a style elegant and elevated, speech polished and open, marked by a not unpleasant variety of figures, filled with frequent clashes of opposed words; full of weighty reasoning, with concepts containing nothing low or mean; everywhere filled with Catholic and wholly heavenly doctrine; breathing throughout the teaching of sacred Scripture; and completely suffused with that fiery vigor of piety which is usually present in the writings of the saints.

Moreover, it takes delight in different members of periods that fall and end in similar ways. Finally, the entire composition is neatly distributed into nearly equal and proportionate parts, presenting graceful and highly polished discourse. What could be said that would agree more closely with Saint Leo’s style or express his manner of speaking more clearly? Or what could be said of one that could not equally be pronounced of the other?

The frequent clash of antitheses and the affectation of measured, ringing prose did indeed lead the writer whom we have praised several times to suspect that this author was African. But, if I may say so without offending so great a man, this manner of speaking is no more characteristic of Africans than of Italians, and I can easily believe that it passed from Italy at various times into other regions.

For it is clear from the writings of Saint Leo as well as from those of other writers older than he, who were either Italians or educated in Italy, that this affectation of writing prevailed especially in those regions. Since this was the grace and elegance of an already aging language, I believe that it first arose in Italy, as though in the language’s cradle, rather than in the other provinces of the Roman empire.

If such antitheses and rhythms occur somewhat less frequently in this work than in other works of Saint Leo that were formerly regarded as genuine, this must be attributed entirely to the difference in period, subject matter, and the author’s age. No one is unaware of how much the oratorical style differs from the epistolary, and how many things are tolerated in letters that are entirely excluded from dogmatic works. If no one has wondered that such figures are fewer in letters than in sermons, why should it be surprising if they are rarer still in this work, which is wholly devoted to explaining doctrine?

### XXIII. 5

If we examine individually the words that are more familiar and common to this author and to Saint Leo, although they are not so frequently used by others, and if we inspect their construction, such equality and similarity will immediately appear everywhere, and such harmony, that no one could rightly think it came about by chance or through an attempt at imitation.

Besides those expressions already noted by the apologist of the holy Fathers as common to the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations* and the writer of the following letter, we set before the eyes of readers more than one hundred and twenty others:

- *Discipulus veritatis*: disciple of truth.
- *Paginae elementorum*: pages of the elements.
- *Paginae veteris Testamenti*: pages of the Old Testament.
- *Urere et uri invidia*: to burn with envy and to be burned by envy.
- *Parcitas et largitas gratiae*: the sparingness and generosity of grace.
- *Consortium*: fellowship, participation.
- *Evincere*: to prove conclusively, establish.
- *Communio naturae, aetatis, nominis, peccati, dignitatis*: fellowship of nature, age, name, sin, dignity.
- *Laquei deceptionum, erroris, captionum, mortalitatis*: snares of deceptions, error, captivity, mortality.
- *Dextri, sinistri*: those on the right, those on the left.
- *Parilis, parilitas*: equal, equality.
- *Variare, varietas dispensationum*: to vary, the variety of dispensations.
- *Refutare*: to reject.
- *Abdicare*: to repel.
- *Dispensationes*: dispensations.
- *Dispositiones*: arrangements, dispositions.
- *Materia dimicandi, certaminis, formidinis, querelarum, confusionis, ruinae, virtutum, gaudiorum, gratulationis, cupiditatum, peccati, caecitatis, gloriandi*: material or occasion for struggle, contest, fear, complaints, confusion, ruin, virtues, joys, rejoicing, desires, sin, blindness, boasting.
- *Moestitudo*: sorrow.
- *Poenitudo*: repentance.
- *Convenire oculis, litteris, monitis*: to address or meet with one’s eyes, by letters, or by admonitions.
- *Colluvio*: filth, foul mixture.
- *Contagium*: contagion.
- *Colluctationes*: struggles, wrestlings.
- *Census*: wealth, resources.
- *Vitiare, vitiatus*: to corrupt, corrupted.
- *Indicere*: to impose, proclaim.
- *Universitas, numerositas, plenitudo, omnis numerus, summa*: the whole, multitude, fullness, the entire number, the sum total, used for “all.”
- *Portio*: portion, opposed to fullness.
- *Protestari et pronuntiare*: to attest and declare, when citing sacred or ecclesiastical authorities.
- *Primordia*: beginnings.
- *Exordia*: origins, beginnings.
- *Incitare*: to impel, incite.
- *Virus invidiae*: the poison of envy.
- *Vincula peccati, transgressionis, consuetudinis, culpae, captivitatis, originalia*: bonds of sin, transgression, habit, guilt, captivity, and original sin.
- *Incitamenta doctrinae*: incentives to instruction.
- *Redire, transire, transferri de uno ad alterum*: to return, pass over, be transferred from one to another.
- *Necessarie*: necessarily, continually.
- *Doctrina prophetica, evangelica, apostolica*: prophetic, evangelical, apostolic doctrine.
- *Veritatis Evangelium, sententia, judicium, vox, filii, schola, magister, doctrina, discipuli*: the Gospel, opinion, judgment, voice, children, school, teacher, doctrine, and disciples of truth.
- *Vigor fidei, mentium, pietatis, cordis, animi, auctoritatis*: vigor of faith, minds, piety, heart, spirit, authority.
- *Constitutio legis, constitutio divina, constitutiones impiae*: establishment of the law, divine ordinance, impious ordinances.
- *Testificatio legis*: testimony of the law.
- *Denuntiationes propheticae*: prophetic declarations.
- *Oracula prophetarum*: oracles of the prophets.
- *Temperare, temperamentum*: to regulate, regulation or balance.
- *Temerare*: to violate, profane.
- *Disputatio et disputator*: discussion and discussant, used for treatise and author.
- *Inspicere, inspector, inspectio*: to inspect, inspector, inspection.
- *Sublimare, sublimis, sublimitas*: to exalt, exalted, exaltation.
- *Significationes*: signs, used for the figures of the Old Testament.
- *Insinuare, insinuatio*: to insinuate, insinuation.
- *Praejudicium peccati, vetustatis, originis*: the presumption or prejudice of sin, antiquity, origin.
- *Sordescere*: to become filthy.
- *Famulari, obsequium elementorum, famulatus*: to serve, the service of the elements, service.
- *Moderari*: to govern, regulate.
- *Incommutabilis*: unchangeable.
- *Compugnantia, compugnantes*: conflict, those in conflict.
- *Experimenta virtutum*: experiences or proofs of virtues.
- *Sacramentum occultius*: the more hidden sacrament.
- *Instituta disciplinarum*: institutions of disciplines.
- *Evacuare*: to empty, nullify.
- *Distringere, districtus, districtio*: to constrain, constrained, constraint.
- *Forma*: form, used for manner or image.
- *Formam praeferre*: to present a form, bear an image.
- *Cooperatores gratiae*: fellow workers with grace.
- *Virtute nitescere, nitor virtutis, pudicitiae, mentium, luminis, vitae*: to shine with virtue; the splendor of virtue, chastity, minds, light, and life.
- *Obloqui*: to speak against.
- *Rectus, pravus*: upright, crooked.
- *Germina virtutum*: shoots or seedlings of virtues.
- *Summus, supernus aut coelestis agricola*: the highest, heavenly, or celestial farmer, used for God.
- *Ager cordis*: the field of the heart.
- *Novi Testamenti vel gratiae decreta*: decrees of the New Testament or of grace.
- *Devotio bonorum operum, voluntatis, propositi, arbitrii*: devotion of good works, will, purpose, or choice.
- *Cultura spiritualis*: spiritual cultivation.
- *Occiduus, succiduus, prociduus*: declining, cut down, falling.
- *Qualitates operum*: qualities of works.
- *Corde concidere*: to fall in heart.
- *Incidere periculum, tentationem, laborem, laqueos*: to encounter danger, temptation, labor, snares—very frequently without the preposition *in*.
- *Mutabilitas*: changeability.
- *Periculum erroris, deceptionis, mutabilitatis, negationis*: danger of error, deception, changeability, denial.
- *Tentatio formidinis*: temptation of fear.
- *Tentationis stimulus, concretio*: stimulus, accumulation or concentration, of temptation.
- *Discretio, discretus*: discernment, discerning.
- *Pigrum otium*: sluggish leisure.
- *Iners desidia*: inactive idleness.
- *Indesinenter*: unceasingly.
- *Plantationibus suis Deus incrementa praebet*: God grants growth to his plantings.
- *Deceptiones*: deceptions.
- *Inclinare, inclinatio*: to incline, inclination.
- *Cernere*: to see, used for “sift.”
- *Extraneus, alienus*: foreign, alien, used for “reprobate.”
- *Adoptivus et vocatus*: adopted and called, used for “elect.”
- *Erudire, eruditio divina, Spiritus sancti eruditor*: to instruct; divine instruction; the instructor who is the Holy Spirit.
- *Obscurum*: darkness, used for “darkness.”
- *Imbuere*: to teach, instruct.
- *Dispoliare*: to strip, despoil.
- *Obumbratio, fragilitas, firmitas*: overshadowing, fragility, firmness.
- *Solidare, soliditas*: to make solid, solidity.
- *Extraneus, exsors*: foreign, without a share.
- *Religiosus*: religious, devout.
- *Sacratus, sacratissimus*: sacred, most sacred.
- *Incertum interpretationis*: uncertainty of interpretation, used for “uncertain interpretation.”
- *Incertum agonis, mutabilitatis, vitae*: uncertainty of struggle, changeability, and life.
- *Divini operis esse et muneris*: to be the work and gift of God.
- *Recidere, tumescere*: to fall back, swell.
- *Elatio, elatus*: elation, elated.
- *Praesumere, praesumptio*: to presume, presumption.
- *Impar*: unequal.
- *Possibilitas*: capacity, used for power.
- *Mensura possibilitatis, intelligentiae, juris, legum, ultionis, munerum*: measure of capacity, understanding, right, laws, vengeance, and gifts.
- *Meritorum suffragia*: the support or claims of merits.
- *Provehere, provectus, provectio*: to advance, advanced, advancement.
- *Inflammare*: to inflame.
- *Praesidia*: defenses, aids.
- *Languere*: to grow weak, languish.
- *Augmentum*: increase.
- *Impendere, impensus*: to bestow, bestowed.
- *Praecipuus magister, discipulus*: distinguished teacher, disciple.
- *Speculum*: mirror.
- *Privilegium meritorum, humilitatis, honoris, perfidiae*: privilege of merits, humility, honor, faithlessness.
- *Coaptare*: to fit together.

And very many others of the same kind.

### XXIV

Some of these require closer consideration, since they display the author’s distinctive character more clearly. For example, those who are drawn to Christ by the inner voice of grace are called “the called.”

Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 8:

> “He inserts his will into the hearts of the called.”

And chapter 9:

> “He distinguished one class of believers and unbelievers under the designation ‘the called.’”

Saint Leo, *Sermon* 6 on the Nativity, chapter 2:

> “Let earthly wisdom bring no darkness here into the hearts of the called.”

*Sermon* 6 on the Epiphany, chapter 1:

> “We perceive this becoming clearer in the illumination of all the called.”

He likewise calls the will, heart, and choice of sinners “dark.”

Book II of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 3:

> “Although truth, which is to be revealed, still withholds its rays from dark hearts.”

And chapter 15:

> “From such dark minds he made for himself a faithful people.”

Saint Leo, *Sermon* 6 on the Epiphany, chapter 1:

> “Whatever of the new light appears in dark hearts.”

*Sermon* 5, chapter 4:

> “Let the lamps of your minds always be burning, and let nothing dark remain in your hearts.”

*Sermon* 4 on the Nativity, chapter 4:

> “In that path of the detestable doctrine there is nothing that is not dark, nothing that is not slippery.”

*Sermon* 1 on Pentecost, chapter 5:

> “The Spirit of truth makes the house of his glory shine with the splendor of his light, and in his temple he wishes nothing to be dark or lukewarm.”

Letter 8, chapter 1:

> “Lest heresy be sown among you with dark roots.”

*Sermon* on Saint Lawrence, chapter 1:

> “This is the nature of true virtues: that they lead many away from dark error, since their light is bright.”

*Sermon* 10 on Lent, chapter 4:

> “Dark prisons.”

Letter to Demetrias, chapter 14:

> “From the true light the dark and already failing lamps receive light, yet whatever brightness they have received will belong to them only insofar as it comes from themselves.”

Letter 79, now 105, chapter 1:

> “That dark enemy, namely the devil.”

Both call those who follow Catholic doctrine or piety “disciples of truth.”

Book II of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 24:

> “All disciples of truth understand that this was proclaimed in a detestable manner.”

Letter to Demetrias, chapters 4 and 13:

> “Truth itself is said to have spoken to its disciples.”

> “When, therefore, the disciples of truth flee human glory …”

From a comparison of these two passages, among other things, the apologist of the holy Fathers infers a similarity of style and a single author for the two writings. How much more properly, then, should this be asserted of our Leo, with whom this designation occurs far more frequently?

*Sermon* 3 on collections:

> “Those most blessed disciples of truth,” he says of the apostles.

*Sermon* 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 3:

> “Nothing commends faithful and devout disciples of truth more.”

*Sermon* 8 on Lent, chapter 2:

> “The Christian mind, fleeing falsehood, is a disciple of truth.”

*Sermon* 10 on the same Lent, chapter 2:

> “Servants of God and disciples of truth.”

See also *Sermon* 80, now 82, on Saints Peter and Paul, chapter 1, and Letters in this edition 24, now 28, chapter 1; 59, now 79, chapter 1; 62, now 82, chapter 1; 93, now 120, chapter 2; and 97, now 124, chapter 1; as well as Letter 140, now 172, in the middle, where the same expression occurs.

*Book I of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 7: “Thus what was by nature good was made evil in **QUALITY**; and that movement of the soul **WHICH CAN NEVER EXIST WITHOUT SOME KIND OF LOVE**, that is, without some act of will, did not lose its appetite but changed its affection.”

Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on the fast of the seventh month, chapter 3: “There are two loves, from which all acts of will proceed, differing in their **QUALITIES** as they are divided according to their sources; for the rational soul, **WHICH CANNOT EXIST WITHOUT LOVE**, is either a lover of God or of the world.”

Both call the work of grace and virtue participation in God. *Book I of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 8: “With God, what nature lost did not perish; for wisdom is eternal, truth is eternal, goodness is eternal, justice is eternal; indeed, the light of all virtues is eternal, and everything that is virtue is God. If he does not work in us, we can participate in no virtue. For without this goodness there is nothing good; without this light nothing is luminous; without this wisdom nothing is sound; without this justice nothing is right.” And in book I, chapter 4, of the same work: “The animal will, without participation in the highest love, moves among earthly and perishable things.” Chapter 3 of *On Grace and Free Will*: “No one is good of himself, unless he who alone is good grants him participation in himself.”

Saint Leo, Sermon 9 on the fast of the seventh month, chapter 2: “Whatever reaches me reaches me through participation in me”; and Letter 15 to Turribius, chapter 5: “No human being is truth, no human being is wisdom, no human being is justice; but many participate in truth, wisdom, and justice. God alone has need of no participation.”

Both are thoroughly familiar with the terms *regere* (“to govern”), *rector* (“governor”), and *regens* (“one who governs”), when speaking of God and the soul, the soul and the body, or the bishop and the Church. Leo commonly calls those whom others ordinarily call bishops “governors.” There are hundreds of passages of this kind. See, if convenient, Letter 1, chapter 1; Letter 12, chapter 3; Letter 14, toward the end; Letters 115, 128, 138, 139, and 140 (now Letters 12, chapter 1; 14, chapter 3; 18, toward the end; 145, 163, 170, 171, and 172), and so forth.

Likewise Sermon 2 (now 3), chapters 1 and 3; Sermon 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 2: “Let the faithful soul receive from its author and **GOVERNOR** unfading love.” Sermon 8 on the Epiphany, chapter 4: “Let him have no doubt that God is both his **GOVERNOR** and his inhabitant.” Sermon 3 (now 4) on the anniversary of the Assumption, chapter 1: “For what is so kingly as that the mind should be the **GOVERNOR** of its own body while subject to God?” Sermon 1 on Lent, chapter 1: “But if the **MIND IS SUBJECT TO ITS GOVERNOR**, etc.” Sermon 4, chapter 2: “The mind, established under God’s direction, ought to be the **GOVERNOR** of its own body.” Sermon 7, chapter 4: “The body should be used in such a way that the inferior nature offers its necessary service to its **GOVERNOR**.” Sermon 7 on the Passion, chapter 3: “Judas, unwilling to have Christ as his **GOVERNOR**.” Sermon 2 on the fast of the seventh month, chapter 1: “Let the lower, outward human being acknowledge that he is the **GOVERNOR** of his exterior self.” Sermon 5 on the fast of the seventh month: “What deviation into sin can there be where there is one passion belonging both to the **GOVERNOR AND THE SUBJECT**, that is, to the soul and the body?” Just as he expresses their one passion in these words, so he depicts in the same way one action of God and man. “When,” he says in book I of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 6, “through communion between the one who illuminates and the one illuminated, the one who justifies and the one justified, the **GOVERNOR AND THE SUBJECT**, every action is referred to one, and what is referred to one belongs to both.” And in book II, chapter 10, he says: “The Spirit of God was the **GOVERNOR** of all the saints.”

Leo speaks of the infusion of grace in this way, Sermon 3 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1: “This field of the heart, **WATERED FROM ABOVE BY THE DEW OF GOD’S GRACE**, is sown with almsgiving, made fruitful by prayers, etc.” And Sermon 7 on the Passion, chapter 1: “We believe that the grace of God will be present, sprinkling the barrenness of our heart with **THE DEW OF ITS INSPIRATION**.” *Book II of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 1: “This abundance of grace . . . does not nullify that grace **WHICH RAINED AS DEW UPON ONE ISRAEL UNDER THE LAW**.”

Leo, Sermon 5 on the Nativity of the Lord, chapter 1: “The way that leads to life is not found only in the work of virtues or only in observance of the commandments, but also in the **PATH** of faith, a narrow and difficult road.” *Book II of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 20: “In this narrow but nevertheless straight path of understanding, there is no small difficulty, etc.”

*Book II of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 21: “It is never nearer to being able to live than to being able to fail.” Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on Lent, chapter 2: “It is exceedingly near and contiguous, so that even great souls are shaken by these things, etc.”

*Book I of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 1: “Concerning this conflict of opinions, etc.” And book II, chapter 28: “Peter endured this conflict [between willing and not willing], etc.” And chapter 33: “All the conflicts of variations.” Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on the Passion, chapter 2: “the conflict of diverse affections.” Sermon 10 on the Nativity, chapter 1: “Conflicting judgments.” Letter 67 (now 87): “Conflicting doctrines.”

*Book II of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 15: “They would conceive a flame by which the blessed Apostle Paul, **SET ABLAZE**, etc.” Letter to Demetrias, chapter 14: “From the point at which he began to be inflamed, let him seek to be **SET ABLAZE**.” Saint Leo, Sermon 1 on the Ascension, chapter 2: “Enlightened hearts conceive the flame of faith.” Sermon 3 on Pentecost: “That the Father might be reconciled, the Son might reconcile, and the Holy Spirit might **SET ABLAZE**.” Sermon 1 on Pentecost: “The utterance was conceived as fiery.” Sermon 96 (now Appendix 14), on the Chair of Saint Peter, chapter 1: “Joined to the fiery gatherings of the blessed spirits.” Sermon 4 on the Collects, chapter 1: “When the field of the heart has been occupied by the roots of greed.” Sermon 3 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1, twice speaks of the field of the heart.

Sermon 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 3: “Let what the earth did not give arise **FROM THE FIELD OF THE HEART**.” Sermon 1 on Lent, chapter 5: “The seeds of virtue are then well nourished in us when every foreign shoot is uprooted **FROM THE FIELD OF OUR HEART**.” Sermon 2 on the Ascension, chapter 5: “Greed, from whose root the shoot of every evil emerges; unless it is killed in its own sources, it is inevitable that in **THE FIELD OF THAT HEART** in which the plant of this evil has grown strong, the thorns and thistles of vices, rather than any seed of true virtue, will arise.” Sermon 6 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1: “From the soil of our heart, too, may the shoot of justice and the fruit of charity arise.”

*Book II of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 11: “The seeds of spiritual gifts and the plants of virtues do not grow **IN EVERY FIELD OF THE HUMAN HEART** in such a way that all that they are destined to become is produced equally.” From this comparison of the heart with a field arose other expressions that he often uses: he calls God the heavenly farmer; grace and inspirations, dew, watering, and showers of dew; virtues, God’s plantings; and other expressions of this kind, which will occur to any reader.

Both attribute judgment to the will. *Book I of* On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 8: “By the devil, **THE JUDGMENT OF THE WILL** was corrupted, not removed.” And chapter 7: “It did not lose its appetite but changed its affection, receiving through desire what it ought to have rejected by **JUDGMENT**.” Saint Leo, Sermon 9 on the Passion, chapter 4: “The fountain of charity washed away the words of fear; nor was the remedy of abolition delayed where there was no **JUDGMENT OF THE WILL**.” What is said in Sermon 11, chapter 4, should likewise be understood of the will: “The wicked man [Judas] rose up against himself, not through **THE JUDGMENT OF ONE WHO REPENTS**, but through the fury of one who perishes.” Letter 37 (now 41): “By the **JUDGMENT OF THE WILL** he fulfills the rule of the command.”

*On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book I, chapter 9: “So that they may receive knowledge of God not through the work of human teaching but through **THE INSTRUCTION** of the highest teacher.” And book II, chapter 33: “They presided over the **INSTRUCTION** of faith.” Sermon 2 (now 3) on his Assumption, chapter 3: “Every tongue . . . is imbued with **THE INSTRUCTION** of this utterance.” Sermon 2 on Lent, chapter 4: “Taught by **THE INSTRUCTION** of our Redeemer.” Sermon 14 (now 12) on the Passion, chapter 5: “Many things have been enlarged by evangelical instruction.” Letter 140 (now 172): “Let that unity in all things be sought through the instruction of the Holy Spirit.”

*On the Calling of the Gentiles*, book I, chapter on Paul: “He transformed the entire method of exposition into astonishment.” Leo, Sermon 18 on the Passion, chapter 4, concerning Christ: “He transformed the whole punishment into triumph.” Sermon 5 on the Nativity: “If the remedies themselves are transferred into discipline.” Sermon 3 on the Epiphany: “Wrath has been transformed into pardon.” Sermon 9 on Lent, chapter 3: “If you transfer every offense to forgiveness.” Sermon 4 on the fast of the seventh month: “So that what you withdraw from your own needs you may transfer to the nourishment of the poor.” Sermon on the Steps of Ascent: “So that he might transfer external cures to internal remedies,” etc.

I pass over the rest, which anyone will readily observe while reading. I will only urge that closer attention be paid to the use of these same figures of speech, to the identical number and order of the clauses, and to the identical construction of the words. A piling up of opposites occurs frequently, with the verb on which the meaning depends postponed to the end; the number is usually no more than three, although it often extends to four. We offer below, as an appetizer, several examples from the letters and sermons of Leo and from the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles*.

Saint Leo, Letter 1 (now 12) to the African bishops, chapter 4: “So that the inexperienced may be preferred to teachers, the new to the old, the untrained to those who have completed their service.” Letter 12 (now 13) to Anastasius of Thessalonica: “Permit nothing to personal favor, nothing to ambition, nothing to purchased votes.” Sermon 9 on the fast of the seventh month, chapter 2: “If there is any love of empty glory, if there is any root of greed, if there is any poison of envy present.” Sermon 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 2: “From enemies he makes reconciled persons, from strangers adopted children, from the impious righteous.” Saint Leo contains hundreds of examples of this kind. There are also very many in the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, although the subject matter of the books does not permit quite so many. Book I, chapter 8: “Who will be the one who, by his own judgment alone, can break off so many struggles of opinion, so many bonds of custom, so many prejudices of antiquity?” Book II, chapter 4: “So that rational nature, from contemplating so many forms, from experiencing so many good things, and from receiving so many gifts, might be imbued with the worship and love of its author.” And chapter 7: “But whence these members are fitted, whence useful, whence beautiful, the same teacher explains, etc.” Chapter 20: “Where the same misery, similar weakness, and a common cause exist, etc.” Chapter 36: “So that through the labor of works, through the persistence of supplications, and through the exercises of virtues, there may be increases of merits.”

Finally, just as it often happens with human faces that something emerges from them and strikes the eyes of those looking, so that you declare them similar to others even though you cannot express in words precisely what it is—this same thing happens to a reader with both this little work and the writings of Saint Leo. For something—I do not know what—sounds in the ears of those listening and conveys such similarity and equality of style that it scarcely permits doubt that the same person speaks in this work as in the letters and sermons of Saint Leo, although perhaps the matter cannot adequately be expressed in words.

### XXV

To remove every ground for doubt, someone might wish for the authority of at least one manuscript codex bearing the name of Saint Leo. Deprived of such evidence, we may seem to have labored in vain up to this point. But, to say nothing of how often the reliability of manuscript copies is uncertain [Note: [Col. 0359D] Concerning manuscript codices, see the admonition prefixed to these books.], as is clear from the manuscript codices of the books *On the Contemplative Life* and of this work *On the Calling of the Gentiles*—codices that, for nearly eight hundred years, marked with Prosper’s name, misled everyone (for today the more learned reject both little works as Prosper’s)—I add that I am convinced that no such codex will be found attributing this work to Saint Leo; nor, indeed, was its genuine author ever known.

Those who in this age attributed it to Prosper and inserted it among his works did so on the evidence of several manuscript codices. The manuscript codices attached Prosper’s name on the authority of ninth-century writers, who frequently cited it under the name of this holy man. Consequently, these writers came to believe that Saint Prosper had composed these books because they did not know their genuine author. Because of the subject matter of the book, its agreement in doctrine with Prosper’s writings, the period in which its author wrote, and its references to the heretics whom he attacks, they thought it should be attributed, with greater right than to anyone else, to the man who, after Augustine, had been the most vigorous defender of the grace of Christ against the Pelagians and their remnants.

But since this suspicion, although strengthened by the agreement of so many years, must be rejected when the considerations brought forward above are weighed, it must also be admitted that even in the ninth century the name of this author was unknown. Indeed, I think that it had already been erased from human memory in Leo’s own century, the fifth. Otherwise Pope Gelasius, when adducing his testimony in the work he published against the Pelagians, would certainly not have refrained from naming him—a man so distinguished that Gelasius did not hesitate to number him among the teachers of the Church. Nor would he have been content to designate this writer in the manner ordinarily used for wholly unknown authors. For it appears that he honors him with the title of teacher for no other reason than that the author had proved by his writing that he deserved this distinction.

### XXVI

If, then, this work is finally accepted as the genuine offspring of Saint Leo [Note: [Col. 0360D] See Observation no. 10.], I do not think it very difficult to determine the period in which its author published it. For it seems certain that he composed it before he was himself appointed Roman pontiff. During that period the most watchful shepherd would not have had so much leisure as would have been necessary to devote to a composition of this kind. Nor does anything occur throughout the work that reveals pontifical authority; indeed, as we have said, he everywhere acts as a private individual.

It is therefore more likely that he wrote it when he was still a deacon of Pope Sixtus III and was keeping watch against the Pelagian heretics, at the time when Pope Sixtus, on the advice and urging of his deacon, repelled Julian, who was attempting to enter the communion of the Church by a feigned profession of faith, as Prosper testifies in his *Chronicle*. Or rather, since in this work he attacks the Semipelagians more than the Pelagians, I think it was written at the time when he was occupied with recalling his necessary friend Cassian from error. The work, having been sent to Gaul for Cassian to read and later found among his papers after his death without the author’s name, was thought to have been written by no one more likely than Prosper, whom Cassian had had as his principal opponent in this controversy.

Certainly this writing everywhere breathes a friendly spirit, and one of the kind that our Leo always displayed toward Cassian. I can readily persuade myself that, just as Saint Prosper had attacked Cassian openly, Leo sought to assail him by a more hidden strategy. For Leo had already induced him to take up his pen against Nestorius, not only with the intention of cutting down the spreading heresy but also in order to inflame him more vehemently against the Pelagians, whom he knew to be the forerunners of Nestorius. By this strategy he would make the Semipelagians—sprouts, as it were, growing from those earlier heretics—more detestable and sever every connection that might exist between them.

So in the present work, while attacking Cassian’s error, he rises up more vehemently against the Pelagians, whom alone he names. He seems to attack the Semipelagians only indirectly, as though gradually and imperceptibly guided along by the thread of his discourse. Yet no attentive reader can fail to see that the greater part of the writing is spent in tearing down the principles of the Massilians. He treats the same questions that Saint Prosper treats in his book *Against the Collator*. He does not so much address those who wholly denied the necessity of grace as those who maintained that their free will was sufficient for the beginning of a good work, or at least of a good intention, and who withdrew something from the operation of grace.

He declares this immediately at the beginning of his work, where he says: “They deny grace when they do not wish it to be the guide of the human will but its companion.”

From the same intention of indulgence toward Cassian, whom he was striving to lead back to the Catholic understanding, arises the humanity he displays toward the Semipelagians. He calls them merely defenders of free will and patrons of human volitions. He also handles these questions with great calm, in the manner of a theological exercise—not so much refuting an alien position as explaining his own. Finally, by refraining from adducing the name and authority of Saint Augustine, he wished to create no prejudice in this dispute, knowing that Augustine did not carry as much weight with Cassian in this matter. He also wished to show his friend that he judged not doctrine by its teachers but teachers by their doctrine, and that he embraced Augustine’s view of grace not so much because it was Augustine’s as because it flowed from the purest sources of sacred Scripture and ecclesiastical tradition.

### XXVII

There are those who think that the conjectures we have set forth thus far can be strengthened by the fact that certain treatises on grace seem to have been written by Saint Leo, though they are now missing. They are led to this conclusion by the words both of Saint Prosper—or rather, of the anonymous author of *On the Promises of God*, in *On the Promises of God [of ‘a half-time’]*, chapter 6, preserved among Prosper’s works—and of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, who says in his *Bibliotheca*: “Saint Leo, Roman bishop, also wrote concerning converted Pelagians, explaining how they ought to be received when they convert, when they convert, condemning their opinion in writing.””

Yet although it is certain that our Leo always fought vigorously against the Pelagians, and although it is very likely that he also wrote other books as circumstances required—for who, so powerful both in doctrine and eloquence, and whom we have so often seen engaging the Manichaeans, Eutychians, and other heretics, could reasonably be believed to have watched the Pelagians spread through the Church with impunity?—we must nevertheless admit that the testimonies just cited do not at all prove what the aforementioned authors claim.

The earlier writer merely says that Saint Leo overthrew the Manichaeans and crushed the Pelagians, especially Julian. We have no need to interpret this as referring to writings, since, on the contrary, it is more naturally understood of the priestly care, burning zeal, and apostolic authority by which he vigorously suppressed the repeated efforts of Pelagians emerging within the Church.

As for Photius’s testimony, it means nothing beyond what is contained in Saint Leo’s letters to Septimius of Altinum and to the bishop of Aquileia. Those who, following Baronius, cited these words of Photius and asserted that the writings he mentions had perished failed to notice that everything the patriarch reports is found in the cited letters: namely, the order by which bishops were warned by the Roman pontiff not to receive any Pelagian who requested restoration to ecclesiastical communion unless he had condemned his former errors in writing, sealing that condemnation with his own hand.

### XVIII

Gerardus Joannes Vossius, the learned historian of the Pelagian controversy, in book I, chapter 20 of his *Pelagian History*, where he discusses the author of the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, considers that it must be denied to Prosper for the reason that the opinion of this writer does not correspond exactly with Prosper’s doctrine. Henry de Noris agrees with Vossius in book II, chapter 14 of his *Pelagian History*. To strengthen his opinion, he adduces several passages from both authors, which it is our purpose to subject to examination.

Although we readily agree with both historians of Pelagian affairs that the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are not Prosper’s, we cannot in any way accept their arguments; nor will we allow Leo, to whom we attribute this little work, to be accused of having abandoned the doctrine of Augustine and Prosper. The most learned man, therefore, will not take it amiss that we undertake this examination, not from a desire to contradict but for the sake of clarifying the truth.

#### Noris’s first argument

“I see,” he says, “that the writer of those books followed a path different from Prosper’s. For in book II he expends a great deal of effort to make the grace of God common to all.”

This accusation strikes Leo, not only because he was the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, but also because many passages in his other incontestable works, that is, in his sermons, agree with the doctrine of those books, so that we rightly drew an argument from this affinity of doctrine in support of attributing these books to our Leo.

We collected several such passages above, and they may be read there. But it is easy to clear both these passages and those others before an impartial reader of the accusations of Noris and others, and to prove two things beyond dispute.

First, when our Leo makes the grace of God common to all, both in the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* and in his sermons, he uses the word “grace” in a far different and broader sense than Prosper does. Second, when Leo uses the same word “grace” in the same sense as Prosper, he also proclaims the same doctrine concerning grace that Augustine teaches with Prosper.

Thus, in those passages where he asserts that the grace of God has been given to all, he understands by it the external and natural gifts of God, which are offered indiscriminately to everyone. Sometimes he means the precepts of the Mosaic law, and at other times the preaching of the holy Gospel, which is denied to no human condition.

He explains this threefold class of grace in other passages as well, especially in book II, chapter 9: “Let us return,” he says, “to the point from which the discussion digressed, namely, to consideration of the differences by which the works and gifts of divine **GRACE** have been varied. For the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, whose judgments are unsearchable and whose ways are inscrutable, has always so tempered his mercy and justice that, by the most secret will of his eternal plan, he did not wish the measures of his gifts to be equal in all periods, among all generations, or among all human beings.

“For he **HELPED** in one way those whom it was fitting to summon to knowledge of him by **THE TESTIMONIES OF HEAVEN AND EARTH**; in another way those for whom he provided assistance not only through the **SERVICE OF THE ELEMENTS**, but also through **THE TEACHING OF THE LAW, THE ORACLES OF THE PROPHETS, THE SIGNS OF MIRACLES, AND THE COOPERATION OF ANGELS**; and in a much greater way he declared his mercy to all human beings **WHEN THE SON OF GOD BECAME THE SON OF MAN**, so that he might be found by those who were not seeking him and appear to those who were not asking about him.”

He teaches that the Incarnation was declared to all human beings because the Lord Christ commanded the apostles, as they went, to teach all nations and, as they went throughout the whole world, to preach the Gospel to every creature, as is recorded in Matthew 28 and Mark 16.

“Was any distinction made among nations or human beings in this command?” asks the author in book II, chapter 2. “He excluded no one on the basis of merit, separated no one by birth, distinguished no one by condition. The Gospel of the cross of Christ was sent to absolutely all human beings.”

Hence the Gospel was not destined for one particular people but for all nations; in this it differs from the law, which was given only to the Jews. It is therefore easy to recognize what universality he attributes to this kind of grace and in what sense he bestows the name “grace” upon it.

It remains, then, that here this author properly calls only the first kind of grace common to all periods, all peoples, and all human beings individually: the testimonies of heaven and earth, the service and ministry of the elements, and, finally, the beauty and adornment of the entire world. To call these things “grace” is characteristic of a writer contemplating the original state of the whole human being, not the present condition of fallen humanity. But to grant sufficiency for salvation to external grace of this kind is characteristic only of someone infected with the Pelagian disease.

This explanation sheds light on all the passages from which the most learned men Noris and Vossius took occasion to establish a distinction between Prosper’s Augustinian doctrine and the doctrine transmitted by the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*. If all these passages were examined a little more carefully, they would be found to contain nothing else concerning general grace than what we have just explained.

A particularly notable passage occurs in book II, chapter 4: “Yet even in past ages this same grace, which after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ has been spread everywhere, and of which it is written, ‘Your flashes have illumined the world,’ **WAS NOT ABSENT FROM THE WORLD**.

“For although it is established that the people of Israel were chosen by God’s special care and indulgence, while all the other nations entered upon their own ways—that is, were permitted to live according to their own will—nevertheless the eternal goodness of the Creator did not turn so completely away from any human beings that it failed to admonish them by signs of any kind to know and fear him.

“For heaven, earth, and sea, and every creature that can be seen and understood, have been arranged principally for the benefit of the human race, so that rational nature, through contemplation of so many forms, experience of so many good things, and reception of so many gifts, might be imbued with the worship and love of its author; while the Spirit of God fills all things, in whom we live and move and have our being.”

It is evident that this author’s sole purpose in these words is to establish a comparison among those three means—or, as he calls them, kinds of grace—through which the supreme and most excellent God imparted knowledge of his name to human beings throughout the various ages.

He establishes the first, consisting in the contemplation of heaven, earth, and all creatures, as common to all human beings. The second he makes particular to the Jews, to whom, in addition to the pages of the elements, as he often calls them, God added the teaching of the law. Finally, he places the third, which shone forth after Christ’s resurrection, in the preaching of the Gospel. This grace, added to the consideration of creation and to the teaching of the law, declared the mercy of God to all human beings in a much greater way.

The grace, therefore, that he makes common to all human beings is the contemplation of creation: natural, I say, and external grace. As he writes in chapter 10 of the same book, it was never absent in teaching and helping the minds of human beings. For it always rained upon the good and the evil; it always caused its sun to rise upon the just and the unjust; it always supplied life-giving breezes; it always provided the alternation of day and night; and it always bestowed abundance upon the fields, multiplication upon seeds, and fertility upon those being born.

In the chapter just cited, chapter 4, he says that this grace is that testimony of which Paul says in Acts 14 that God did not leave himself without a testimony. “What,” he asks, “is this testimony, which has always served the Lord and has never been silent concerning his goodness and power, except the very **INEXPRESSIBLE BEAUTY OF THE WHOLE WORLD** and the rich and ordered abundance of his innumerable benefits? Through these, certain tablets of the eternal law were offered to human hearts, so that in **THE PAGES OF THE ELEMENTS AND THE VOLUMES OF THE AGES** the common and public teaching of divine instruction might be read.”

No one would say that this grace is the same one that Saint Prosper denies to be common to all, unless he were to place the true grace of Christ, with the Pelagians, in the teaching of the law and the preaching of the Gospel. For the author says that the whole force and efficacy of that grace consists in admonishing by signs, in imbuing people with the worship and love of God—that is, in teaching—and in displaying the eternal law as though on tablets, offering it to be read as a common and public teaching of divine instruction on certain pages.

He also calls this the law which has become for many “an odor of death unto death” and “the letter that kills.” For he continues and concludes that fourth chapter of book II in this way:

“Heaven, therefore, and all heavenly things, the sea and the earth, and all that is in them, with the harmonious concert of their appearance and order, proclaimed the glory of God and, through perpetual proclamation, spoke of the majesty of their author. Yet the greatest number of human beings, because they were permitted to walk in the ways of their own will, neither understood nor followed this law; and the odor of life, which breathed toward life, became for them an odor of death unto death, so that even in those visible testimonies it might be learned that the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

How it happens that this grace becomes for the greatest number of human beings a killing letter and an odor of death unto death is readily understood by anyone who is not ignorant of what the Apostle Paul teaches concerning the Mosaic law. The function and office of both are the same: to instruct and admonish a human being.

But external admonition and knowledge puff up and overthrow the person whom the inward spirit of charity and faith does not build up and transform. “This faith,” he says, “before that seed came of which it was said to Abraham, ‘In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,’ was confined within the people of a single stock, while the hope of our redemption remained alive among true Israelites.

“For although there were some foreigners whom the Truth graciously illuminated in the times of the law, nevertheless **THEY WERE SO FEW THAT IT CAN SCARCELY BE KNOWN WHETHER THERE WERE ANY**” (*On the Calling of All the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 14).

Without that inward light of the grace of Christ, what the light and teaching of this external grace can accomplish in human hearts is shown by the same author in book II, chapter 17:

“Yet for those nations that have not heard of Christ, that general measure of assistance which has always been provided from above to all human beings is not denied. Although human nature has been wounded by so grievous an injury that spontaneous contemplation is fully able to instruct no one in the knowledge of God—such is the general assistance of which he speaks—unless the true light has dispelled the darkness of the heart, God, just and good, has not poured it out in past ages in the same way as in the last days, according to his inscrutable judgment.”

Finally, to understand how entirely foreign to this author’s mind is the interpretation of the general grace he asserts and makes common to all as the true grace of God through Christ the Savior, one must read what he says in chapter 31. There he himself discloses what his purpose and position had been in the preceding discussion, lest his words be twisted into an alien meaning by a perverse interpretation:

“I have labored, insofar as the Lord has assisted, to prove that not only in the last days but also throughout all former ages the grace of God was present to all, with an equal providence and a general goodness, but through manifold operations and in varying measure.

“For whether secretly or openly—that is, whether through hidden and inward grace or through manifest and outward grace—he himself is, as the Apostle says, the Savior of all human beings, **ESPECIALLY OF BELIEVERS**.”

If this statement, of the utmost subtle brevity and greatest force, is considered with a calm gaze, it settles the entire controversy under discussion. By saying, **WHO IS THE SAVIOR OF ALL HUMAN BEINGS**, he confirmed that God’s goodness is general toward all human beings. By adding, **ESPECIALLY OF BELIEVERS**, he showed that there is a part of the human race which, by virtue of divinely inspired faith, is advanced through special benefits to supreme and eternal salvation.

This is accomplished without any injustice on the part of the most just and merciful God, whose judgment in these dispensations is not to be examined with arrogance but praised with trembling. It would be superfluous to copy here passages from Saint Leo’s sermons that are similar to these, since those set out above may be consulted. What we have just explained is sufficient to illuminate them.

Noris adds that this author is plainly in conflict with Prosper in this matter. “For he,” Noris says, “entirely rejected this common grace for the reason that the Gospel was not immediately announced to all nations, whereas the other makes grace common because the apostles were sent to all to preach the Gospel.”

With your permission, most learned sir, these authors are not in conflict with one another; at most, there is a slight conflict of words, not of meanings. It is certain that the true grace of Christ is not common to all human beings, while the general natural grace that, as we have shown, this author establishes in the contemplation of creation is common to all. These propositions are plainly not contradictory or contrary.

It is no less certain that Prosper is speaking of the grace of Christ (*Poem Against the Ungrateful*):

> Tell me, then, how you prove that the grace of Christ  
> Passes over no human being at all, among all who are born,  
> To whom it does not grant the kingdom and blessed life . . .

He wishes to impart [something]. It is clear, however, that the other author is speaking of external and natural grace, which, fulfilling the function of the law, admonishes us to fear and love the Creator, but does not itself impart fear and love, as we have amply demonstrated. Moreover, he indicates in hundreds of passages, so to speak, of the same little work that he does not regard the true grace of Christ as common to all. [Note: See the sense of these passages in Observation no. 18.] Thus, in Book I, chapter 13, he says:

> “That the grace which saves some passes others by, and that the Church’s prayer has not been received on their behalf, must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice; and we must acknowledge that, in this life, the depth of this secret cannot lie open to us.”

He repeats this in several other passages. Thus, in chapter 25:

> “Such were those who were drawn as are those who were left in their hardness. To the former grace, in its wonderfulness, gave what it willed; to the latter truth, in its justice, gave what was due; so that God’s judgment is more inscrutable in the election of grace than in the recompense of justice.”

And in Book II, chapter 19:

> “Let those who have been deprived of grace be reproved for their wickedness; and let those who have shone forth in its light glory not in their own merit but in the Lord.”

Yet so far is he from making the true grace of Christ the Savior common to all, that precisely because it is not common to all he proposes, in chapter 25—the last chapter of the first book—the difficulty to be examined in the following book: namely, how that proposition can be reconciled with that article of faith which professes God’s universal will for the salvation of human beings. Nevertheless, he says after the words just quoted:

> “But lest that article of faith by which we piously believe that God wills all human beings to be saved through the recognition of the truth appear, on account of what is clearly demonstrated concerning the effects of grace, to have been weakened, we must strive, with Christ’s help, to see the stability of this definition.”

## 651. Norisius’s Second Argument
