XXIX. “The author of the books *On the Calling of the Nations*,” he says, “in Book II, chapter 20, considers that objection drawn from infants by which Augustine and his followers sang their triumph over the Pelagians. In chapter 23 he responds as follows:

> ‘I think it may be believed without irreligion, and understood without incongruity, that these human beings of only a few days belong to that portion of grace which has always been bestowed upon all nations universally; and that, if their parents had made good use of it, they too would certainly have been helped through them.’

“To this, he says, Prosper writes the opposite in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 31:

> ‘And yet from these the merciful grace chooses some,  
> and again, once born anew through baptism, transfers them  
> into the eternal kingdom, while leaving many in death,  
> whose cause was similar, from the same wound.  
>   
> Nor can you attribute this to the merits of their parents,  
> as though the pious care of the good had benefited those  
> destined for redemption,  
> while another’s negligence had taken life from others;  
>   
> when you see many born of holy parents  
> unable to be saved by any effort of their own parents.’”

Our author in no way departs from Prosper’s teaching; indeed, he subscribes to it with both hands. For in Book I, chapter 16, after beginning in the preceding chapters to prove why grace is given to one rather than another, that this is a secret withdrawn from human knowledge and must be referred to the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, he confirms the same point in this chapter by the example of infants. He says:

> “Consider also the universal multitude of infants, in whom—apart from that offense by which the human race is known to have been brought under condemnation—neither past merits nor future merits can be taken into account. For all of those of whom we are now speaking, before any use of understanding, before freedom of the will, pass over either into eternal blessedness, regenerated, or into perpetual misery, not regenerated . . . Human justice finds nothing by which to distinguish them; but God’s ineffable grace has something by which to choose,”

and so forth.

He says nothing at all about the merits of the parents, just as Prosper does. If he had introduced them, human justice would already have something by which to distinguish them, and God’s judgment would not be wholly inscrutable. In chapter 22, however, he attacks more vigorously those who are ashamed not to know something and who refer every distinction by which God chooses some and does not choose others to the merits of the human will:

> “This definition, even while we leave aside the truth of grace for the moment, seems to display some sort of plausible reasoning concerning those who use free will. But concerning infants, for whom, without any merit of good will, there is a common cause with the rest of mortals in the original wound, NO EXPLANATION CAN BE OFFERED THAT WOULD SHOW WHY THESE ARE SAVED AFTER BEING REBORN, WHILE THOSE PERISH WITHOUT BEING REBORN, under the providence and omnipotence of him in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh.”

And below:

> “In vain do those who establish the cause of election in the merits of those who are chosen attempt to open the depth of inscrutable grace through free will. After advancing many foolish and false claims about the will and judgment of the wicked, THEY NEVERTHELESS FAIL WHEN IT COMES TO THE DISTINCTION AMONG INFANTS,”

and so forth.

You see that this author sings himself a triumph over the Pelagians on account of the election of infants no less than Augustine, Prosper, and the other disciples of Augustine. You see that he excludes every personal merit from infants, yet does not have recourse to the merits of their parents. If he admitted those merits, he would falsely assert that no explanation could be offered showing why some are saved after being reborn while others perish without being reborn; nor would the Pelagians fail any more in the matter of distinguishing among infants if, according to the author’s intention, they could attribute the premature death and eternal condemnation of children to the evil merits of their parents than Catholics and the author himself fail in chapter 22 when they refer the cause of infants’ premature death and condemnation to Adam’s original offense.

This is what the author says in the first book, where he treats the question at greater length. In chapters 20, 21, 22, and 23 of the second book, where he again considers the case of infants, he does not in any way alter his earlier position, but rather confirms it with several arguments. Throughout this book he had proved:

1. That God wills all human beings to be saved;

2. That this will of God is made manifest through the general gifts bestowed upon all, and through nothing else;

3. That those general gifts, being external and natural, are nevertheless insufficient for knowing God without the special gift of the true grace of Christ the Savior. [Note: That the author also admitted a general internal grace bestowed on all and distinct from special grace will be proved in Observation no. 17.] For, he says, human nature has been wounded by so grievous an injury that “spontaneous contemplation is able to instruct NO ONE in the knowledge of God,” unless “the TRUE LIGHT has dispelled the darkness of the heart”;

4. That this special gift, by God’s inscrutable judgment, has not been granted to all.

“Whether, therefore, we contemplate the latest ages,” he writes in Book II, chapter 25, “or the first or the middle ages, IT IS RATIONALLY AND PIOUSLY BELIEVED that God wills, and has always willed, all human beings to be saved; AND THIS IS DEMONSTRATED FROM NO OTHER SOURCE than from those benefits which God’s providence bestows commonly and indiscriminately upon all generations . . . . . . . But God was pleased both to bestow this special grace upon many and to remove that general grace from no one, so that from both it might appear that what has been granted to a portion has not been denied to the whole; but that in some GRACE has prevailed, while in others NATURE has recoiled.”

With these points established, the consideration of infants, as he says in chapter 20, presents considerable difficulty. Infants use no judgment of reason by which, perceiving the benefits of their author, they might be able to approach recognition of the truth . . . . . Hence, since God wills all human beings to be saved, “what is the reason that so great a multitude of infants is alienated from everlasting salvation?”

If the author had thought this should be attributed to the fault of the parents, the answer would have been easy, and there would have been no need to resort to God’s inscrutable judgments and unsearchable ways. Yet this is where he takes refuge. “Our heart,” he says in chapter 21, “will not be disturbed by this height of God’s discrimination if, with firm and steadfast faith, we believe every judgment of God to be just, and do not desire to know what he willed to remain secret: so that, where it cannot be investigated why he judges in this way, it is enough to know who it is that judges.”

He then teaches that there is no other cause of this matter than the sentence which the human race received through the transgression of Adam, its first parent, and the heavy yoke that lies upon Adam’s children from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all. Nor is there any reason to complain about the early onset of death, since, once mortality entered our nature through sin, it made every day of our life subject to itself. Hence he concludes that, by a most just judgment, all infants who depart this life before being washed in the saving bath perish, while by gratuitous mercy all those are delivered who, contrary to the common law of mortality, do not die immediately after being born:

> “So that, with the general necessity varied, the Lord might reserve for himself the causes of mercy and correction; and there might be, in the one common debt of all, something that the merciful could remit and the just could exact.”

It follows from this teaching, as he immediately adds in chapter 23, that the cause of the gifts which grace grants to certain infants is more inscrutable than the cause of the miseries which nature has merited and justice repays to countless others. “In this work of grace,” he says in chapter 24, “who but the most arrogant and vain person would complain of divine justice, because it does not provide a similar providence for all infants, and either remove by its power or forestall by its mercy all the dangers that can prevent the regeneration of those who are dying? This would certainly be done for all if it ought altogether to be done in this way.”

The author is therefore very far from attributing, in that chapter 23 from which the objection is drawn, the salvation or condemnation of infants to the good or evil merits of their parents. At the very beginning of the chapter he asserts that the cause of the gifts which grace grants is more inscrutable than the cause of the miseries which nature has merited—namely, those arising from Adam’s offense, which, as he had said above, is the true cause of the condemnation of infants. Yet, according to Norisius’s opinion, he ought to have attributed this to the merits of the parents in order to oppose Prosper’s position.

The author of this work therefore raises no question concerning this chapter. He is concerned with only one matter: how, with respect to infants who perish, the saying of the Apostle Paul—that God wills all human beings to be saved—can be true. For this, he says in chapter 25, “is demonstrated from NO OTHER SOURCE than from those benefits which God’s providence bestows commonly and indiscriminately upon all generations.” Infants, however, he says in chapter 20, use no judgment of reason by which, perceiving the benefits of their author, they might be able to approach recognition of the truth. Nor does God grant them the period of life in which they might become capable of receiving grace through voluntary faith.

He replies that those infants belong to that portion of grace—or to those general benefits of the Creator—which have always been bestowed upon all nations universally. Although they could not receive them by themselves, they nevertheless received them in their parents, of whom they are considered a part until they have passed beyond the beginnings of non-rational infancy. Through this general grace, or munificence of the Creator, if their parents made good use of it, the infants themselves would certainly be helped through them.

Several points in this response deserve notice.

1. He does not assert that proposition as his own and personal view, but merely presents it as a position to be held by those who do not wish to declare that infants of this sort, dying without baptism, are wholly deprived of every kind of grace.

2. He puts forward this explanation timidly and hesitantly, not as resting upon Scripture or the tradition of the holy Fathers, but as something that may be held without religious offense. “I think,” he says, “it may be believed without irreligion, and understood without incongruity, that these human beings of only a few days belong to that portion of grace which has always been bestowed upon all nations universally.”

3. He says not a word about the merits of the parents, from which it might be believed that he was defending a position contrary to Prosper’s teaching.

4. There is a broad distinction between the question whether condemnation comes upon unbaptized infants from the evil merits of their parents, and the other question whether the parents are to be blamed because the infants do not become participants in the Creator’s general gifts. The author denies the former, with Augustine and Prosper; the latter he cautiously suggests on his own, and in the manner of someone asking a question. In this respect he may seem to differ from Prosper in his manner of speaking, but in reality he agrees with him.

For suppose that general grace is not lacking to the parents, and through them to the infants—the grace which we have explained in Prosper’s words. Since this grace is insufficient for salvation either to the parents or to the infants unless they are aided by the special, or true, grace of Christ, through a more excellent work, a more generous gift, and a more powerful efficacy, the question arises again: if the former is given to all, why is the latter denied to so many? Why, when the children of the just often die without baptism, although their parents have omitted nothing to have them washed in the saving water, do the children of the wicked, abandoned by their own parents, come to baptismal grace through the kindness of strangers? At this point also he takes refuge, with Prosper, in the inscrutable judgments of God and the unsearchable decree of predestination.

5. From these points, therefore, it should be noted that the author’s judgment concerning infants dying without baptism is no different from his judgment concerning adults who use only the benefit of that general grace. Just as he does not weigh the personal merits of the latter in their election, so he does not consult the merits of the parents in the case of the former in order to investigate the cause of election.

These are the author’s words in the very chapter that is brought forward as an objection:

> “Just as, among adults, besides that general grace which touches the hearts of all human beings more sparingly and secretly, a special calling is exercised through a more excellent work, a more generous gift, and a more powerful efficacy, so also the same election is manifested among countless infants. This election was not lacking even to those who were not reborn, in their parents; but it was present to those who were reborn in preference to their parents, so that often, when the piety of their own parents abandoned many, the care of strangers served them, and they came to regeneration through outsiders, although what had to be provided for them was not provided through their relatives.”

## Norisius’s Third Argument

[Col. 0368C] XXX. “Moreover,” he says, “the same writer speaks quite hesitantly about predestination in the final chapter; indeed, he seems more than once to posit foreknowledge as preceding it. When he sets against himself the objection that ‘our prayers and labors are useless if election rests upon the unchangeable purpose of his Christian grace,’ he responds there as follows:

> ‘They do not understand that the knowledge of God, which embraces past, present, and future things, is not held within time.’

“And after explaining this briefly, he concludes:

> ‘This eternal and always tranquil knowledge imposes upon us no necessity to sin,’ etc.

“In the same place he asserts election to grace without merits, but makes election to glory depend upon merits:

> ‘Therefore God gives those whom he elects, without merits, the means by which they may be adorned and acquire merits. And it is vain to say that the elect have no reason for acting, since they act even for the purpose of being elect.’”

I am astonished that a learned man should be so moved by these passages as to think the author alien from Prosper’s teaching on that account. He knows that Augustine and Prosper commonly use the terms “knowledge” and “foreknowledge” when explaining the eternal decree of predestination; it is therefore not surprising that this author uses them in the same way.

Saint Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14, says:

> “This predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge, that is, the preparation, of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered.”

And again:

> “That obedience, therefore, is itself God’s gift, which God, as every Christian confesses, foreknew that he would give to those whom he calls. This, then, is the predestination which we faithfully and humbly proclaim.”

In chapter 17 he says that God prepared his gifts in foreknowledge, and that to arrange his future works in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, is nothing other than predestining.

Prosper, in his eighth response to the *Extracts of the Genoese*, says:

> “Let us therefore wisely acknowledge and piously confess that God immutably foreknew to whom he would give the gift of believing, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them. And if he foreknew these things, he also foreknew the benefits by which he deigns to free us; and this is the predestination of the saints, namely, the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s grace, by which they are most certainly delivered.”

If Norisius thought that, by the foreknowledge through which our author defines predestination, he meant either the knowledge of simple understanding—that is, of possible things—which both precedes and directs God’s free decree; or conditional foreknowledge, that is, middle knowledge of things that will never occur, namely, what a person would do if such grace or condition were supplied, whereby God would know which combination and order of graces would bring salvation if they were bestowed—if, I say, Norisius thought this concerning our author, he rightly declared that the author held a view different from Prosper’s.

But let us not attribute this meaning to him. Let us rather be convinced that in this passage he teaches no other foreknowledge than the knowledge of vision, that is, of future things which God himself will bring about. He repeatedly calls this foreknowledge, with Augustine, “foreknowledge,” “election,” “predestination,” and “promise.”

Discussing this knowledge in Book II, chapter 33, he says that it embraces all times and temporal things together in an eternal and stable vision, and that it has already repaid all things to all, because “WHATSOEVER THINGS ARE FUTURE, HE HAS ALREADY MADE.”

This is the meaning of the blessed Apostle Paul when he writes to the Ephesians:

> “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy,”

and so forth, connecting there the rest of his proclamation in the same sense. He teaches that the gift and work of grace have always remained in God’s eternal counsel, and that all the children of adoption were chosen not only at the time when, already existing, they were called, but also before the world was founded.

No human being who was not foreknown in Christ can be joined to this election by any reasoning. For all who are to come into THE KINGDOM OF GOD, from the calling of whatever age, have been MARKED OUT in this adoption which preceded all the ages. And just as no unbeliever is counted in this lot, so no godly person is excluded from this blessing. For from the fullness of the members of Christ’s body, THE FOREKNOWLEDGE OF GOD, WHICH CANNOT BE DECEIVED, LOSES NOTHING; nor can THE FULLNESS FOREKNOWN, and PRESELECTED in Christ before the eternal ages, be diminished by any loss.

Here it is clear that he is speaking not only of election to grace but also of election to glory, and of that foreknowledge which at once decrees for the elect both the kingdom of God and all the means by which they can most certainly attain it.

He confirms the same teaching in many other passages. “Although,” he says in Book II, chapter 29, “many who love their darkness do not receive the brightness of truth, and many who had been enlightened become darkened, the word of God nevertheless remains forever, and nothing falls away from the truth of the promise. Every day the multitude of the nations, FOREKNOWN AND PROMISED, enters, and every nation, tribe, and tongue is blessed in Abraham’s offspring. For what the Father gave the Son, the Son does not lose; nor can anyone snatch from his hand what he has received. God’s firm foundation stands, and the building of the temple that will remain forever does not totter, with the truth and mercy of God set before all. What is denied to no one—and, as he explains above, to no nation, tribe, or tongue—and what is owed to no one, is accomplished by God in THOSE WHOM HE PROMISED.”

And below:

> “He always foreknew how great a number of the godly would belong to eternal blessedness through the help of grace and the service of obedience, SO THAT, WITH NONE FALLING AWAY FROM THE FULLNESS OF THOSE PROMISED, he might glorify those whom he chose from among all.”

From these passages it is evident that our author agrees entirely with Prosper and Augustine in the doctrine of predestination. He insists that predestination depends upon foreknowledge and promise in such a way that God accomplishes in those alone whom he promised what is denied to no nation or tribe. He plainly understands that promise in the sense in which Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10:

> “He promised not on the basis of the power of our will, but on the basis of his own predestination.”

For he promised what he himself was going to accomplish, not what human beings were going to accomplish.

As for the author’s final passage, where Norisius thinks that he makes election to glory depend upon merits, it must certainly be admitted that this passage presented a serious difficulty until now. But now that we have restored the passage to its integrity with the aid of a manuscript codex of the Thuane Library, not only does the difficulty disappear, but it also provides a most powerful argument for upholding, on the authority of this work, the Augustinian doctrine of predestination:

> “Therefore God gives those whom he elects, without merits, the means by which they may be adorned and acquire merits. And it is vain to say that the elect have no reason for acting, since they have been elected precisely in order that they may act.”

The reading is not, as it was formerly printed:

> “Since they also act in order that they may be elect.”

He therefore makes neither glory nor the works that merit glory depend upon merits; rather, he makes both depend most clearly upon God’s election. Although this could already be inferred from the sequence of the doctrine, it is now demonstrated still more decisively by the author’s very words, corrected on the authority of the manuscript codex. Such is the value of carefully collating the writings of the ancient Fathers with manuscript codices and restoring them to their original purity.

Finally, Norisius adds one further point to establish a distinction between Prosper and this author: namely, that Prosper praises Saint Augustine everywhere, whereas this author does not mention him even once in the books *On the Calling of the Nations*. This is entirely true, but at the same time it confirms our judgment concerning Leo, whose characteristic is everywhere apparent in the writings composed against the Pelagians or the remnants of Pelagianism. In none of them does he either praise or name Augustine: not in the letters to the bishops of Aquileia and Altinum, which have always been attributed to him; not in the letter to Demetrias; not in that selection of authorities of the Apostolic See—even though an opportunity to name him would have presented itself spontaneously in both of these works.

Leo consistently observed this practice, lest he appear to defend Augustine’s position from a preconceived opinion about Augustine, but so that he might defend the doctrine itself, with all prejudices in favor of its defenders set aside, from Scripture and tradition.

XXXI. There are also certain passages in Saint Leo from which he may seem to have held something alien to the teaching of Augustine and his disciples, and not to agree entirely with the books *On the Calling of All Nations*. But since whatever I could contribute toward demonstrating the harmony of the two pontiffs has already been undertaken by the highly learned Church of Lyon—which, in the ninth century, wrote against John Scotus Eriugena in the style of its bishop Remigius—I shall not repeat what has already been done or appear to envy another’s praise. I reproduce in full chapter 19 from his work *On Three Letters*.

## Chapter 19 of the Book of Saint Remigius, Archbishop of Lyon, *On Three Letters*

[Col. 0370D]

> [Note: See Observations nos. 25 and 27 concerning this lengthy text of Saint Remigius.]
>
> “Blessed Leo places certain words in some of his sermons to the people from which some persons, either paying insufficient attention or understanding insufficiently, may perhaps think that he taught and believed that our Lord also suffered for the ungodly who persist in their ungodliness, and that he may be called their Redeemer. Such is the passage in which he says:
>
> > ‘Look at last, Jew; look, and, laying aside your unbelief, turn also to your Redeemer. Do not be terrified by the enormity of your crime. Christ calls not the just but sinners; nor does he reject your ungodliness, for when he was crucified he prayed for you.’
> >
> > (Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on the Epiphany, chapter 11.)
>
> “But to those who understand these words correctly it is clear that, according to the customary usage of human speech, he addresses the whole Jewish people under the person of a single Jew. Therefore, as though speaking in the person of all, he cries out to one and says: ‘Turn also to your Redeemer, laying aside your unbelief.’ This does not mean that there is no unbelieving Jew whose Redeemer the Lord is; rather, it means that the Lord deigns to be the Redeemer not only of the other nations but also of that Jewish people whose crime and ungodliness crucified him, if that people turns to him. Therefore he says: ‘For when he was crucified he prayed for you.’
>
> “This does not mean that no unbelieving Jew exists for whom the Lord did not pray on the cross when he said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ For the Lord himself plainly says: ‘I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me from the world.’ Rather, it means that even within that unbelieving people there are and have been many for whom the Lord mercifully prayed, so that they might turn from their error and be saved; and what he prayed for, he effectively obtained and accomplished.
>
> “The blessed teacher therefore rightly says, as though speaking to that entire unbelieving people under the person of one man: ‘For when he was crucified he prayed for you,’ because plainly there were, are, and will be people from and within that people for whom he prayed.

“These words of blessed Leo are to be understood in precisely this way. He himself explains them so clearly elsewhere in the same sermons to the people that no one should have any doubt about them. Thus, in one passage he says:

> ‘Our Lord so provided for the human race by his death that he did not deny the sacrament of salvation even to his persecutors. For he who had come to forgive all sins to all believers did not wish to exclude the Jewish crime from the general pardon.’
>
> > (Saint Leo, Sermon 19 on the Passion, chapter 2.)

“Likewise, speaking elsewhere of the same Lord:

> ‘Such was his great devotion even toward his executioners that, pleading with the Father from the cross, he asked not that he himself be avenged but that they be forgiven, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” It was through the power of this prayer that the preaching of the Apostle Peter converted to repentance the hearts of many of those who had said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children”; and on a single day nearly three thousand Jews were baptized. Thus there came to be one soul and one heart among all who were prepared to die for the one whom they had demanded should be crucified.’
>
> > (Sermon 11 on the Passion, chapter 2.)

“We have drawn these remarks on the interpretation of the preceding words from blessed Leo’s own words. Immediately afterward he adds:

> ‘The traitor Judas could not attain this pardon, because the son of perdition, with the devil standing at his right hand, passed into despair before Christ fulfilled the sacrament of the general redemption. For after the Lord had died for all the ungodly, even he perhaps could have obtained a remedy if he had not hastened to the noose.’
>
> > (Ibid., chapter 4.)

“Someone who considers and understands these words insufficiently could interpret them in such a way that the expressions ‘the sacrament of the general redemption’ and ‘after the Lord had died for all the ungodly’ might be taken as requiring belief that both that general redemption and that death of the Lord were accomplished for all the ungodly, including those who do not believe and perish in their ungodliness.

“But for which ungodly people he says that the Lord died, and what he wishes ‘general redemption’ to mean, we think he himself carefully explains in the words quoted above:

> ‘For he who had come to forgive all sins to all believers did not wish to exclude the Jewish crime from the general pardon.’
>
> > (Sermon 19 on the Passion, chapter 2.)

“Thus the Lord’s death was truly offered for all those ungodly people to whom he forgives all sins as believers. And he is understood to have used the expression ‘general redemption,’ or ‘general pardon,’ because neither the Jewish people nor any race of human beings is found to have been excluded from that redemption and pardon.

“But in the words whose meaning we have explained by repeating these passages, he clearly shows that the traitor Judas in no way belongs to Christ’s redemption and could not obtain a remedy, because he hastened to the noose. Christ’s Passion therefore benefited him nothing, because he passed into the condemnation of those who, already being punished in the underworld, could not become participants in the Lord’s redemption.

“Yet elsewhere, as though rebuking that unhappy and ruined man himself, he speaks to him as follows:

> ‘You sold your Redeemer, so that he might not spare you’ [Alternatively: ‘so that you might not spare him’].
>
> > (Sermon 16 on the Passion, chapter 4.)

“This does not mean that he redeemed Judas, whom the same teacher had already shown unable to attain redemption; nor is he who remained and perished in his ungodliness to be understood as having Christ for his Redeemer. Rather, it means that, within the general redemption of Christ’s Passion, Judas too might perhaps have obtained a remedy if he had not hastened to the noose.

“Therefore Leo says to him: ‘You sold your Redeemer,’ because Christ truly would have become his Redeemer too if, even after so great a crime, Judas had piously and faithfully sought pardon from him.

“It would be altogether too lengthy, and entirely unnecessary for those trained in the reasoning of the faith, to explain with such care every one of this blessed teacher’s statements wherever an opportunity for such an interpretation might arise, as has been done in these very few examples.

“Only this point appears especially worthy of emphasis: whenever he mentions a general bond, a general agreement, or a general security, the general condemnation of the entire human race introduced through Adam is to be understood. Whenever he speaks of general redemption or general pardon, the expression is to be understood as referring to the whole human race or to all nations. And whenever he teaches that the Lord underwent death for all the ungodly, this is to be understood as meaning all those who turn from ungodliness and believe in him, as his own words themselves make clear in many places.”

These are the words of Remigius, Archbishop of Lyon, together with his Church. In the same work he also explains several other passages of Saint Leo concerning predestination, grace, and the death of Christ—for example, in chapters 9, 16, 27, and so forth. The same is true in his *Resolution of the Question* and in *On Maintaining the Truth of Scripture*, chapters 8, 13, 15, and so forth.

# Observations of the Ballerini on Quesnel’s Second Dissertation Concerning the Author of the Books *On the Calling of All Nations*

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371D] 661

1. In the question of who was the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, since they are found in manuscript codices sometimes under the name of Ambrose and sometimes under that of Prosper, some have thought that they should be attributed to Saint Ambrose, others to Saint Prosper of Aquitaine. But since extremely strong arguments stand against Ambrose, and not insignificant ones against Prosper of Aquitaine, it was necessary to resort to conjectures.

Hence these same books were attributed by some to Hilary—either Hilary of Arles or Hilary of Syracuse, or to that friend of Prosper whom they thought different from the Syracusan. Others assigned them to Saint Eucherius of Lyon. Nor were there lacking those who, setting aside Prosper of Aquitaine, substituted Prosper of Orleans or the Prosper who attended the synods of Carpentras and Vaison. No one had thought of Saint Leo the Great.

Quesnel was the first of all to attempt, in the dissertation mentioned above, to assert this work for Leo by means of several conjectures. But Joseph Antelmius, a canon of Fréjus, deliberately opposed him in a work entitled *Critical Dissertations on the True Works of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great and Prosper of Aquitaine*. There he attempted to overturn Quesnel’s arguments and labored vigorously to establish Saint Prosper of Aquitaine as the author of these books.

Quesnel soon replied to him in a letter written in French, almost the whole of which was inserted in the work entitled *Journal of the Learned* [*Le Journal des Savants*], 8 and 15 August 1689. Antelmius was not satisfied and produced two further letters in the same year, which are appended to the dissertations just mentioned in the Paris edition of 1689. Quesnel nevertheless persisted in his position, as is clear from the second edition of 1700, in which he inserted the preceding dissertation unchanged.

2. For a distinct judgment to be made concerning this dissertation itself, its three parts must be distinguished: the first, in which he refutes those who thought that Ambrose, Eucherius, Hilary, or some Prosper was the author of these books; the second, in which he piles up conjectures in support of Leo; and the third, in which he responds to objections.

## § I. Quesnel’s Position That These Books Are to Be Withheld from Prosper of Aquitaine Is Confirmed. A Reply to Antelmius. Photius’s Passage Explained.

[Col. 0373B]

3. As for the first part, which refutes the opinions of others concerning Ambrose, Eucherius, Hilary, and also Prosper of Aurelianum and that Prosper who flourished in the years 527 and 529, there is no need to add anything, since Quesnellus has brought forward sufficiently effective arguments in each case. Only something must be said, for Antelmius’s sake, about St. Prosper of Aquitaine, whom Quesnellus does not mention even once in the dissertation prefaced above. If, in order to judge correctly between the two, Quesnellus’s arguments for excluding Prosper are compared with Antelmius’s arguments for establishing that the same Prosper was the author of the books, everyone will see that the decision must be awarded to Quesnellus. Of the four arguments that the latter produced, the fourth is almost self-evident. When the author of the books writes at the beginning that the question had long been debated between the contending parties, he clearly indicates that he is not writing at the [Col. 0373C] beginning of the controversy, 663 but much later. When he adds, “I shall undertake to investigate, exercising and testing the measure of my ability in these matters,” he plainly suggests that he is undertaking this question for the first time and therefore had written nothing about it previously. This does not at all fit Prosper of Aquitaine, who had composed and published several works immediately at the beginning of this controversy and therefore could not present himself as a newcomer in the matter. This argument seems so effective to us that, even if the others were lacking, it would suffice to overturn all Antelmius’s reasons.

4. Concerning Quesnellus’s first argument, however, about the doctrine of grace—which, although he admits that it is in reality the same in the books *On Vocation* and in Prosper’s works, he contends nevertheless to differ considerably in wording and in its gentler manner of exposition—allow me to add, by way of confirmation, one argument that should not be disregarded. In the books *On Vocation*, the name “grace” is sometimes applied to God’s natural gifts, even external ones, to the institution of the law, to the preaching of the Gospel, and so forth. But that this term was used by Prosper in this sense cannot be proved by any testimony, as the most recent editor of Prosper himself states in his admonition. For in the passage—indeed the only one—Antelmius produced from the book *Against the Collator*, chapter 7, formerly chapter 14, where the power of God’s grace is mentioned, the new edition has deleted the word “grace” on the authority of the manuscripts. Apart from this, Prosper teaches there nothing other than that God works in human minds and hearts—clearly through interior grace—when, with external aids employed, people are converted to God.

5. Antelmius’s arguments by which he endeavors to claim the books for Prosper are reduced to four: first, the authority of the manuscripts; second, the testimony of Hincmar; third, the similarity of doctrine and style; fourth, a certain testimony of Photius. Quesnellus has adequately answered the first three. Antelmius himself weakens them still further. For since he thinks that the work was published without the author’s name and moreover maintains that the author deliberately sought to conceal himself, and consequently remained unknown for a long time, at least until the time of Gelasius, everyone can see how much this consideration undermines the credibility of the manuscripts. From where, then, could those who first inserted Prosper’s name into manuscripts after Gelasius have obtained it, if until that time he had been unknown and his name had been written in no manuscript? Could they not have been equally mistaken in placing Prosper’s name before these books as those were mistaken who prefixed Ambrose’s name to the same books, or who placed Prosper’s name before the books *On the Contemplative Life*, *On the Promises*, and *On the Predictions of God*?

The testimony of Hincmar therefore also falls, since he was deceived by manuscripts that had been incorrectly inscribed, just as others older than Hincmar were likewise deceived for the same reason when they claimed for Prosper other books that are not his. Antelmius also attenuates the similarity of doctrine and style. As for style, the parallel tables themselves, which he presents over many pages, diminish its force. In them scarcely any uniformity is detected beyond certain words, many more of which Quesnellus found in Leo and which may likewise be found in other writers treating the same subject. The same applies to similarity of doctrine, since it is very easy—and almost inevitable—for several Catholic writers treating the same dogma to agree in many propositions. Moreover, Antelmius reports that Prosper concealed himself and deliberately altered his style somewhat, explaining the doctrine by another, gentler and milder route so that he might remain hidden more easily. By this he himself concedes a certain difference of style and doctrine appropriate to a different author.

6. There remains the testimony of Photius, to which we find that Quesnellus responded nowhere. In codex 54 of the *Bibliotheca*, after reporting the proceedings of the bishops of the West against the Pelagians and, following the aforementioned letter of Leo to Septimus, in which the holy pontiff fought against their heresy, Photius adds:

“Not long afterward, when it had again begun shamelessly to appear and spring up as though from a bitter root, certain persons in Rome also spoke openly in favor of the heresy; but the truly godly man Prosper easily scattered and extinguished them by publishing against them little books for public circulation, while the aforementioned Leo was still governing the Roman see.”

Antelmius contends that these little books published under Pope Leo were none other than the books *On Vocation*. For it is certain, he says, that Prosper composed and published other books before Leo’s pontificate. He further asserts that great weight must be given to this testimony, since Photius relates the whole matter on the authority of the acts given by the bishops of the West against Nestorian doctrines. He observes that Quesnellus quoted this passage of Photius on another occasion, in Dissertation 1, under the year 444, no. 4, and also conceded that these events took place at Rome, probably near the end of Leo’s pontificate; but he complains that Quesnellus investigated nothing further concerning the little books themselves.

7. Antelmius ought to have observed that the very name “little books” (*libelli*), which is also found in the Greek, is scarcely suitable for the two rather extensive books *On Vocation*. Moreover, it cannot be applied to books that attack the error of the Semipelagians in a gentler style, since they could hardly have so easily scattered the Pelagians of whom Photius speaks. For just as the Pelagians properly so called were those whom Leo reported that he had defeated in Letter 2 to Septimus, so those whom Photius immediately goes on to describe as having later revived at Rome and been scattered by Prosper must also be called Pelagians.

What, then, does the word *libellos* mean? The word Λίβελλος (*libellos*), which Photius uses, is of Latin rather than Greek origin, though adopted by the Greeks. It signifies not books or treatises—works that the Greeks, and Photius in particular, ordinarily designate by various other proper names—but, in the forensic language of the Romans, little documents of citation, accusation, memorials, and the like. This is clear, among other evidence, not only from the ancient Greek version of Leo’s Letter 23 to Flavian, where the word is used three times in the same sense in both Latin and Greek, but also from the Greek acts of the Council of Chalcedon, sessions 1 and 3, where the same word, Λίβελλος, denotes the petitions presented to the council itself by Eutyches, Theodore, Ischyrion, Athanasius, and others. See also the Greek version of Flavian’s Letter 26 to Pope Leo.

Thus Photius’s text signifies only that, as soon as St. Prosper discovered the Pelagians at Rome, he presented to Pope Leo—or even to the emperor’s officials—little documents briefly exposing their error and identifying the persons involved. Since the matter had already been condemned and was also forbidden and restrained by imperial laws and penalties, this was sufficient to cause them immediately to flee the City and disappear. The less precise Latin translation, by which the *libelli* were incorrectly understood as books published for public circulation, misled Antelmius, p. 291.

The Greek text will make the matter clear; we shall append it translated literally into Latin:

> “Not long afterward, when the shameless bitter root again seemed to be sprouting, certain persons in Rome spoke openly in favor of the heresy. But a certain Prosper, a man truly of God, by presenting petitions against them caused them to disappear, while the aforementioned Leo was still governing the Roman see.”

That is:

> “Not long afterward, when the shameless bitter root again seemed to be sprouting, certain persons in Rome spoke openly in favor of the heresy. But a certain Prosper, a truly godly man, caused them to disappear by presenting documents against them, while the aforementioned Leo was still governing the Roman see.”

8. Finally, Antelmius’s hypothesis must not be passed over: he repeatedly insists that St. Prosper wished to conceal himself in the books *On Vocation*. From this, he says, it resulted that Prosper published the work without his name, pretended to have a different style, adopted a gentler and milder approach than in his other works, suppressed the name of his teacher Augustine, and indicated at the beginning of the work that he had written nothing previously on the subject. Thus he uses this single hypothesis as a general principle by which to overturn all objections.

He affirms in Dissertation 3, p. 166, that Prosper concealed himself because, in the final book *Against the Collator*, chapter 22, he had promised that he would write no further. But if it were permissible to construct hypotheses out of such conjectures, and thereby weaken objections of the greatest weight, then anyone could introduce several hypotheses of this kind on equally conjectural grounds, and nothing among the critics would be so solid that it could not be overturned in the same way.

If Antelmius had proved from other evidence that Prosper of Aquitaine was the author of these books, this conjecture could plausibly have been offered to resolve or reconcile the objections. But since he has produced no effective evidence elsewhere for establishing St. Prosper of Aquitaine as their author, this conjecture—which introduces one hypothesis and then several others that are highly difficult—will rightly persuade no one.

It will appear still less probable if one considers the steadfastness of spirit with which St. Prosper fought vigorously and openly against the adversaries of grace. Even if it were granted that, in the book *Against the Collator*, he indicated that he would write no further, could he have failed in his duty, or feared some reproach, if a new occasion or necessity required a new work? If he had wished to conceal himself, was it necessary not merely to alter his style but to pretend to be an inexperienced writer? Does not someone who deliberately tries to disguise his style usually turn it for the worse, rather than for the better? Here, however, the opposite would have occurred, since the style of the books *On Vocation* is acknowledged to be more polished, elegant, and elevated than Prosper’s style.

Finally, the words of chapter 22 of *Against the Collator* do not at all convey the public and open promise of abstaining from writing that is presupposed. They imply only that, so long as the adversaries have not been separated from fraternal fellowship, they must be tolerated. Therefore, until the matter is settled by the leaders of the Church, “our task,” he says, “will be to repay hatred with calm and modest patience, to avoid disputes with foolish persons, not to abandon the truth, and not to contend with falsehood.” By these words he seems to indicate that he would avoid not all discussions, but only foolish disputes.

## II. Quesnellus’s conjectures by which he endeavored to establish St. Leo as the author of these books are refuted. The date of the work is conjectured with probability. The use of different interpretations of Sacred Scripture. How weak an argument is derived from similarity of style.

9. Let us now proceed to the second part of Quesnellus’s dissertation, in which the unprecedented opinion—unheard of before Quesnellus—is advanced that the books *On Vocation* should be attributed to St. Leo before he entered the pontificate. Each point must be examined. He endeavors to prove that everything fits Leo: his age, country, distinctive interpretation of certain scriptural passages, and similarity of doctrine and style.

10. As for the date, it is certain that these books were composed long after the controversy of the Semipelagians arose, which began in the year 427, and were published before the pontificate of Gelasius, who mentions them in a work against the Pelagians as having been written by a certain teacher of the Church; consequently, they appeared before the year 496.

Quesnellus assumes as virtually certain that the author of the books *On Vocation* was the same as the author of the letter to Demetrias, since the latter work fits especially well with Leo’s age before his pontificate. But this is not as certain as is believed. The manuscripts would provide considerable support for assigning both works to the same author if these two compositions were always found joined together in manuscript copies. But that is not what occurs. For Olivarius, Prosper’s editor, who used the Cambéron manuscript for the books *On Vocation*, did not find the letter to Demetrias in it. The same happened to Quesnellus in the Thuaneus manuscript, and to the most recent editor of the works of St. Prosper in the Jolius manuscript, which were useful for establishing the text of the books *On Vocation* alone.

We likewise found only these books, and not the letter to Demetrias, in the Vatican manuscripts Palatine 236 of the ninth century, Vatican 558 of the eleventh century, and another Vatican manuscript, 559, of the fifteenth century, as well as Vatican Regina 293, approximately of the eleventh century. If we found the letter together with the aforementioned books in three Vatican manuscripts, 262, 268, and 281, in the latter two, which are older, the letter is indeed placed after the books *On Vocation*, which are attributed to Ambrose, but without any mention of an author, under these words: “Here begins *On True Humility to the Holy Virgin Demetrias.” In the former manuscript, which is much more recent, the aforementioned books are first copied under Prosper’s name; then, after several blank pages, the letter itself begins without any title. It may therefore be thought to have been appended by chance and accidentally rather than with the intention of assigning it to the same author. Accordingly, in another Vatican manuscript, 284, the letter alone is read without the books *On Vocation* and is inscribed to Ambrose.

Similarity of style alone could prove something in establishing the same author for both works. Yet how weak this argument is may readily be gathered from what will be said below, where style will be discussed. Some may perhaps judge that the disputes of the Semipelagians subsided for a time after Prosper’s books had been published, even during Leo’s pontificate. Just as Leo, while still merely a deacon, urged Sixtus III against the Pelagians, and as pontiff exercised his zeal against the same group, so he would likewise have fought against the Semipelagians if, during or shortly before his pontificate, they had attacked the doctrine of divine grace.

For during this period there is no indication of such a dispute from any other source. It is clear only that the controversy revived after Leo’s death under Bishop Faustus, and that, in the case of Lucidus, who was accused of the Predestinarian heresy, certain persons employed in a Semipelagian sense the Pauline text, “God wills all human beings to be saved,” which had given occasion to the books *On Vocation*. Hence these books may appear to have been composed during this period.

11. But leaving this aside, even if Leo was a contemporary of the books *On Vocation*, or even if he was the author of both those books and the letter to Demetrias, Quesnellus has nevertheless not proved that Leo’s homeland suits him. The arguments he has brought forward to deny that the author was African—namely, that he never praised Augustine, that he is in no way commended in the records of the African Church, and that he does not display the inflated or barbarous diction that Quesnellus considers common among Africans of that period—are so weak in several respects that they cannot establish anything highly probable.

The arguments he introduced to deny that the author was Gallic prove even less, especially his appeal to Gennadius’s silence. Gennadius did not list all the writers of his own time living in Gaul; thus he omitted Edesius, Eusebius, Domnulus, and Sylvius, who are celebrated in the *Life of St. Hilary of Arles*. Quesnellus did not hesitate to pronounce the author Italian and Roman, or Roman by education, on the basis of the polish and elegance of his style, as though no one outside the City could have acquired an equally good style.

He emphasized the passage in Book II, chapter 33, where the author writes:

> “Other barbarians, while assisting the Romans, learned in our regions what they could not have known in their own lands, and returned to their homes with the instruction of the Christian religion.”

The words “learned in our regions,” joined with “while assisting the Romans,” seem to indicate that the author and the barbarians shared the same region—the place where the barbarians, while serving as Roman auxiliaries, learned the Christian religion.

Now, if this passage is to be understood as referring to the war waged by Theodosius against the tyrant Eugenius in the year 394, as Quesnellus conjectured, and if the barbarians serving as auxiliaries to Theodosius advanced as far as the Julian Alps, where a notable victory was won, then the author of the books must be said to have shared a region far removed from Roman soil.

There were several other expeditions closer to the author in which other barbarians assisted the Romans during the fifth century. Most of them, however, took place far from the City and in Gaul. The most famous was the campaign under Aetius in the year 451, in which Franks, Sarmatians, Armoricans, Lycians, Burgundians, Saxons, Riparii, Ibriones, and Alans aided the Romans.

Nothing, therefore, can be concluded from this testimony in support of a Roman writer. Quesnellus himself perceived this, admitting that Erasmus had found the argument less convincing. Nor can the author’s praise of the primacy of the Roman Church prove any more that he was Italian or Roman than it can prove Prosper of Aquitaine to have been so, since a very similar testimony is found in Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful*, lines 40 and following.

The words of Gelasius, by which the author of these books is called “a teacher of the Church,” establish nothing in favor of Leo, since anyone else could have received this title because of the excellence of the work itself. Indeed, this passage weighs significantly against Leo. If St. Leo had been the author of these books, Gelasius, who knew either the pontiff himself or his associates, would scarcely have been unaware of it. Nor would he have called such a distinguished predecessor of his “a certain teacher of the Church,” especially since the word “certain” is particularly noteworthy. In accordance with the custom of the Roman pontiffs, he would have called him either by his proper name or at least “his predecessor.”

13. Quesnellus thinks that he has stronger support in the manner of quoting certain testimonies from Sacred Scripture. Two seem especially important: the first and the last. For the other four or five that he adduces can just as easily be found in other writers and therefore cannot establish anything distinctive in favor of Leo.

The first testimony is Job 14:4. It is quoted both in Book I of *On Vocation*, chapter 8, and by St. Leo in Sermon 8 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, from Jerome’s version, which Quesnellus describes as peculiar to the Romans in that period. He then adds that the same text is also cited according to the ancient version both by Leo and in the letter to Demetrias, which he assumes to have been composed by the same author as the books *On Vocation*.

It is surprising that such force should be placed in this text. If the fact that this passage occurs both in the books *On Vocation* and in Leo according to St. Jerome’s version proved that the books should be assigned to Leo, it would prove still more strongly that they should be assigned to St. Prosper of Aquitaine. Prosper cites from Job, and from the same version, not one but two other passages in *Against the Collator*, chapter 15, formerly chapter 34; each is quoted in exactly the same words in Book I of *On Vocation*, chapters 14 and 22.

One passage is Job 12:10:

> “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh.”

The other, in the same place, no. 13, is:

> “With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding.”

Prosper also transcribes other verses from Job according to the same Hieronymian version in the chapter cited above. Consequently, this version is known to have been used in the fifth century by others who were not Romans. This occurred especially in the book of Job, since, according to Jerome’s testimony, its ancient version was riddled with errors and lacked nearly seven or eight hundred verses.

The indiscriminate use of both versions, which Quesnellus presses with respect to Jerome’s version, is evident in the quotations from Job. With respect to the ancient version, it is apparent in the other texts from the sacred books, which are generally quoted from this version both by Leo and in the books *On Vocation*. The same is also true of Prosper, as will be clear to anyone who compares several testimonies.

As for what Quesnellus particularly emphasizes concerning the use of both versions in the aforementioned verse of Job 14, both by Leo and in the letter to Demetrias, this will be examined fully in the observations on the fourth dissertation, which concerns the author of that letter. How empty this argument is will become evident from two other non-Roman writers contemporary with Leo who quote the same verse in the same way.

13. Quesnellus takes his second and most noteworthy testimony from Luke 22:31–32:

> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked that he might sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers; and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”

Leo quotes this text in Sermon 3, now Sermon 4, *On the Anniversary of His Assumption*, chapter 3; the author of the books *On Vocation* quotes it in Book I, chapter 24, and Book II, chapter 28, in the same distinctive manner.

Quesnellus does not conceal that Prosper also produces this testimony in two places, but he says that it is not altogether the same reading. In the letter to Rufinus, he says, the word “sift” (*cerneret*) is absent and “winnow” (*cribraret*) is found instead. In *Against the Collator*, chapter 35, now chapter 15, the final words are omitted: “And pray that you may not enter into temptation.” Yet in that passage the words “And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” are also omitted, and this omission could not be attributed to a variant reading.

We find a much greater diversity of reading between the books *On Vocation* and Leo than between Prosper and those books, so that it is especially surprising that Quesnellus asserts the readings to be virtually identical. We pass over the fact that some manuscripts have *cribraret* rather than *cerneret* in the cited sermon. On the authority of all the manuscripts we have seen, *cribraret* is also found in another sermon of the same pontiff, Sermon 83, *On the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul*, which Quesnellus incorrectly relegated to the appendix.

Here it is enough to note that the word *cribraret* is likewise read in the most ancient manuscript Gospel book of the Church of Vercelli, recently published, which presents the old version. Therefore Quesnellus should not have described this reading as adulterated or corrected toward the Vulgate reading. Why, after indicating this one variant, did he silently pass over other, more certain ones?

First, even in Leo, in Quesnellus’s edition, *expostulavit* is read instead of *postulavit*; then *aliquando* appears instead of *tandem*. Finally—and this is the principal point—“and pray,” or “and pray ye,” is omitted, as we have corrected the books *On Vocation* on the basis of the manuscripts.

Thus Prosper’s reading agrees more closely with the reading of the books *On Vocation* than Leo’s reading does. By what right, then, is such great similarity derived from this passage, in a way that establishes Leo rather than Prosper as the author of these books?

It should rather be observed here that different authors quote this Gospel passage with a certain addition at the end, one that is found neither in the Vulgate nor in the Greek, but is found in four of the oldest manuscript Gospel books of the ancient edition, as we observed in annotation 22 (previous volume, col. 600, note a) on Sermon 4 of St. Leo.

From this one may recognize how entirely weak and feeble is the argument drawn from the similar interpretation of certain scriptural testimonies in order to determine one rather than another person as the author of an anonymous little work. Since several writers might have used those or other similar Gospel books, the same reading and version may be found in several authors.

14. The similarity of doctrine concerning divine grace, specifically general aids, which Quesnellus proposes in no. 20 between Leo and the books *On Vocation*, can establish only that the books are not incompatible with Leo; it does not prove that they are Leo’s. Quesnellus himself admits that Prosper teaches a similar doctrine when he responds to the objections, yet he does not for that reason judge Prosper to be the author.

Only certain distinctive expressions occurring in the aforementioned books may appear to correspond to Leonine formulas. Quesnellus therefore dwells chiefly on these (Dissertation 3) and marks similar words in capital letters. But apart from the fact that Antelmius himself noted many similar words and expressions in Prosper, this belongs to the general character of the style, which we shall examine more fully shortly.

One point, however, should be added here. As we observed in no. 5, the books *On Vocation* sometimes apply the word “grace” to God’s general aids, including external aids. You will never find this in Leo, as can be seen from the very passages Quesnellus quotes.

What can the remaining similarities in certain propositions concerning the prerogatives of St. Peter prove, when all Catholics shared the same doctrine? The manner of expressing this doctrine, which is found to be similar in some places in Leo and in the books *On Vocation*, likewise belongs to diction and style. From these Quesnellus could indeed adduce something capable of influencing some readers. For this reason he devoted more space to the argument and arranged numerous parallels and several observations into a series of numbered sections.

15. For this argument to be examined more precisely, two things must be distinguished in style: vocabulary, and syntax—that is, the entire character of expression. The parallel testimonies presented by Quesnellus consist almost entirely of several similar words; Antelmius likewise exhibited many such words in Prosper in several tables. It would be difficult to find two authors discussing the same subject who at some point did not agree not only in their propositions but also in several words relating to the same matter, or who did not use the same formulas of expression.

If anyone were to read other Fathers treating similar subjects with the same diligence as Quesnellus, we have no doubt that he would find many more parallels of the same kind, as well as many corresponding words and formulas. Yet this labor will be fruitless, since style is not marked and distinguished by individual words alone, even when they express the same meaning. The whole structure and character of the discourse must be considered above all.

Quesnellus declares in no. 15 that it was not difficult for him to reach this judgment, since, having reread the writings of St. Leo again and again for the purposes of his edition, he had become thoroughly familiar with the Leonine phraseology and the entire character of his expression. But since he attributed the sermon *On the Chair of St. Peter* to Leo because of certain similar words—a sermon that we showed in the admonition to be utterly foreign to Leo when considered as a whole, and even foreign to him in certain individual words—we fear that he may, through a similar prejudice, have judged less correctly concerning the style of the books *On Vocation* and assigned them to Leo with the same facility.

Indeed, we shall not deny that several passages in these books closely accord with Leonine syntax and rhythm. But a few passages excerpted here and there are wholly insufficient to prove the same style when other passages occur that display diction and style, or an entire character, altogether dissimilar and different.

Leo’s style is always consistent with itself: equally rhythmical and equally lucid in all his works. But in the books *On Vocation* certain passages that depart too far from that syntax and rhythm, ending weakly or rather harshly, immediately strike ears accustomed to the Leonine manner; they do not sound like Leo. The clarity that is the foremost and most constant characteristic of our pontiff is also plainly lacking in several passages of these books.

Some longer periods, entangled with several particles and ideas, deserve consideration—especially the period that constitutes the whole of chapter 19 of Book II. Anyone familiar with Leo’s works will easily understand whether it is credible that Leo wrote in such a manner.

Add also certain allegories extended through a longer meaning, which depart from Leo’s practice. Among others there is the passage in Book II, chapter 11:

> “But those who do not know the sweetness of these waters and still drink from the torrents of this world, or who, even if they have tasted something of the fountain of life with their first lips, nevertheless delight, intoxicated, in Babylon’s golden cup…”

There is also the passage in chapter 23 of the letter to Demetrias—to touch briefly on that work as well:

> “The Holy Spirit therefore fills his own instrument, and, like God’s finger touching the strings of a lyre, touches the hearts of the saints.”

Finally, the style of these books is fuller and sometimes more inflated, and more frequently employs epithets and elaborate clauses, than is found in Leo.

If all this does not demonstrate altogether clearly that the style is foreign to this pontiff, it nevertheless introduces sufficient doubt to prevent us from confidently believing that Leo’s style is present in these books. Since it could very easily have happened that several persons at that time, both at Rome and elsewhere, 675 possessed a manner of writing that agreed to no small degree, no certainty can be extracted from mere similarity of style—whatever may be claimed concerning the resemblance between Leo’s style and that of the books *On Vocation*—so as to assign them to the same pontiff.

The remaining conjectures of Quesnellus, built upon the sufficiently weak foundation of style, may rightly be called, with Cave, under the year 440, rather a procession of conjectures than a series of arguments. They require no distinct response. As for the observations that we prefixed to the books themselves in the admonition, based on several and more important manuscripts, each prudent reader will judge how much weight they should carry in determining the author.

## III. Several passages of Quesnellus are examined. The author of the books *On Vocation* admits general grace for all nations, not only external but also internal, and teaches that it can be resisted and that many do resist it. To what extent he establishes sufficient grace. Leo’s doctrine concerning Christ’s death for all. St. Remigius’s opinion explained.

16. Having completed what pertains to the principal point of the controversy concerning the author of these books, Quesnellus responds to several objections by which Cardinal Norisius had argued that the doctrine of these books differed from the doctrine of St. Prosper.

It was very important to Quesnellus to establish agreement between the doctrines, lest Leo—whom he put forward as the author of the books—be thought to have taught differently in the matter of grace from Prosper, who adhered most firmly to Augustinian doctrine. But we, who have rejected these books as the work of neither St. Prosper nor St. Leo, do not require this discussion to the same extent for our purpose. Nevertheless, since Quesnellus has inserted in his responses certain statements that entirely diverge from the author’s mind, whoever he may be, and that can sometimes even be twisted into the meaning of condemned propositions, we have thought it appropriate to append several observations.

17. In his response to the first objection, Quesnellus asserts that, in passages where the author of the books *On Vocation* maintains that God’s grace has been given to all, he understands by it God’s external and natural gifts, which are offered indiscriminately to everyone; sometimes the teachings of the Mosaic law, and at other times the preaching of the Holy Gospel, which is denied to no human condition. Thus he represents the author as asserting only external grace, common to all human beings, and not internal grace.

Yet there are eminent theologians, including Thomists, to whom this seemed false. Accordingly, in proving that all adult human beings, at least at some time, receive some sufficient internal grace, they draw their stronger testimonies from these books.

In certain passages this author did indeed signify only external aids by the name “grace.” But he did not assert that these alone were common to all. In some places he also taught that internal grace is common to all. Among other clear passages is Book II, chapter 23:

> “Just as, in the case of adults, in addition to that GENERAL GRACE THAT TOUCHES THE HEARTS OF ALL HUMAN BEINGS MORE SPARINGLY AND MORE SECRETLY, a special calling is exercised through a more excellent work, a more generous gift, and a more powerful efficacy…”

This grace, which secretly touches hearts, is plainly interior. Quesnellus himself admits as much when, in the same response to the first objection, he explains another testimony of the author and interprets the words “secretly” or “in secret” as follows: “That is, through hidden and interior grace.”

Nevertheless, this same author taught that such general internal grace touches the hearts of all human beings. The same theologians think that he likewise indicated this grace when he wrote in chapter 15:

> “For a certain measure of heavenly instruction was always provided for all human beings; and although it was a grace more sparing and more hidden, it nevertheless sufficed, as the Lord judged, for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony.”

The words “a more sparing and more hidden grace” plainly correspond to those previously cited from chapter 23, namely, the grace that touches hearts “more sparingly and more secretly,” which the author professed to be both general and internal.

Therefore, in this second testimony the author does not understand by the name “grace” a merely external instruction common to all, including the Gentiles, but an instruction joined with a somewhat more sparing yet more hidden and internal grace, which not only enlightens the minds of all human beings but also touches their hearts.

It is therefore not surprising that he taught that this grace was sufficient for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony, without attributing sufficiency only to external aids—which would have been Pelagian and entirely foreign to the principles of the author himself.

18. Nor are these statements opposed by those passages which Quesnellus adduces from the same books toward the end of his cited response. The principal text is that of Book I, chapter 13:

> “That saving grace has passed over some—as we see happen—and that the Church’s prayer has not been accepted on their behalf must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice.”

Here “saving grace” plainly signifies grace that in reality and effectively saves, as is evident from what precedes. For these words refer to the prayer of the Church concerning which, in the preceding chapter, the author had said:

> “But what does he ask for these people—pagans, Jews, heretics, and schismatics—unless that, having abandoned their errors, they may be converted to God?” etc.

He adds that thanks should be given to God for those who have been saved:

> “Let us also hope that those who have not yet been enlightened will, by the same work of divine grace, be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life.”

Immediately afterward the disputed passage follows:

> “But if saving grace has passed over some, as we see happen,” etc.,

where he indicates grace that actually rescues people from the power of darkness and transfers them into the kingdom. The other testimonies adduced are of the same kind, as will be clear to anyone who considers them. Thus, in Book I, chapter 25, the author speaks of those who have been drawn; and in Book II, chapter 19, when he mentions those who have been deprived of grace, he understands special grace, which he had mentioned earlier and often declares not to be common to all.

If, in Book II, chapter 3, he admits unknowable delays of illumination—among which many certainly perish in unbelief—the subject there is not, as Quesnellus interpreted the words in a marginal annotation, a suspension and denial to many Gentiles of all interior grace, although elsewhere he affirms that it was given to all. Rather, the subject is grace consisting in the preaching and calling of the Gospel, delayed for a time, as will be evident from the context.

19. On this occasion, since we have mentioned the interior grace granted to all, which the author states was sufficient for some as a remedy, we may consider another passage of the same writer in Book II, chapter 13, where we read:

> “When God was speaking such words to Cain, is it doubtful that he willed, and acted in such a way as was sufficient for the method of healing, that Cain should recover from that fury of impiety?”

The words especially deserving notice are: “as was sufficient for the method of healing.” Here Quesnellus, following Prosper’s previously published editions, inserted the word *illum*, so that the text reads: “for that method of healing.” After noting, “The word *illum* is not found in the manuscript of Thuanus, nor in any of the editions of the works of Saint Ambrose in which the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are included,” he appended the following lengthy commentary—or rather, fabrication—in the same annotation:

> “Yet what difference in meaning this variation of the reading produces, I confess I cannot grasp. One thing, however, I see with complete certainty: this sufficiency of which the passage speaks cannot in any way refer to that sufficiency of the interior grace of Christ the Savior, concerning which modern theologians contend with such intense struggle and fervor. Indeed, it will be clear to anyone who reads through the sequence of this chapter with an impartial mind that our author added this clause for no other reason than to prevent unwary readers from directing their attention to the sufficient operation of interior grace, and rather to warn them that this sufficiency is not to be understood of any other method of healing than the one treated throughout the chapter. In doing so, he deliberately refrained from the terms grace, assistance, aid, help, and mercy, using only the words instruction, goodness, patience, and counsel. In truth, he showed that the sole method of healing was that which is effected through exhortations, counsels, and corrections, by which the Lord deigned paternally to calm Cain, who envied the merits of his holy brother and was contemplating his murder with a fratricidal heart (Saint Gregory, *Moral Works*, Book II, chapter 9). But Cain could be admonished by the divine voice and yet could not be changed, because, as his guilt required, God had already abandoned his heart inwardly, while outwardly he spoke words to him for the sake of testimony. For the Holy Spirit must work inwardly if the medicine applied outwardly is to have any effect. Otherwise, even if God himself, using a creature subject to him in some human form, should address human senses in a manner suitable to them, and should not govern and move the mind by interior grace, all preaching of truth would profit a person nothing (Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 9). And indeed, when God had spoken to Cain in the manner in which he had spoken to the first human beings—through a subject creature, or as their companion, in a fitting form—what benefit resulted? Did he not carry out the crime he had conceived, the murder of his brother, even after the divine admonition? Although this benefit brought no remedy or correction to the hardened man, it nevertheless proves that his aversion was not the result of a divine decree but of his own will (*On the Calling of the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 13), just as our author speaks in the same words about the descendants of that fratricide at the end of this chapter.”

In so lengthy a circuit of argument, Quesnellus insinuates, to put it briefly, that the clause “as was sufficient for the method of healing” does not refer to interior grace, by which Cain was deprived by God as punishment for his wickedness—a conclusion he proves from the testimony of Saint Gregory—but only to the outward aids of exhortations, counsels, and corrections. He confirms by Augustine’s authority that these cannot heal without interior grace. Thus, in the author’s judgment, he thinks that Cain received no interior grace from God, but only exterior grace.

20. If the author, mentioning only external correction, had refrained from the formula that presents a sufficient method of healing, it could perhaps be questioned whether he believed that interior grace had been withdrawn from Cain as punishment for his sin, as certain other Fathers taught. But once those words asserting sufficiency are added, this entire withdrawal of interior grace could neither be indicated nor understood by a Catholic teacher, nor by the author of these books, whom Gelasius called a teacher of the Church (*Treatise Against the Pelagians*, vol. V of the Venetian Council edition, p. 374).

To grant sufficiency for salvation through exterior grace is characteristic only of a person infected with the Pelagian plague, as Quesnellus himself stated in his response to the first objection. The author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, whom Quesnellus likewise shows to be remote from the Pelagian position, taught from Augustine’s doctrine, in Book I, chapter 8, and elsewhere, that interior grace is necessary if what is preached outwardly is to be effective; and in Book II, chapter 26, he confessed that this same inward grace operates in every kind of healing.

Therefore, when he wrote that God, in correcting Cain, willed and acted “in such a way as was sufficient for the method of healing … that he should recover,” he could not have written “was sufficient” in any other sense than that he believed some interior grace had been granted to Cain together with God’s external correction. This grace was sufficient for the method of healing, had Cain not stubbornly resisted. Hence, immediately afterward, assigning the cause to his obstinacy, he added:
