> “But his persistent wickedness became all the more inexcusable because of the very thing by which he ought to have been corrected.”

This passage, moreover, harmonizes wonderfully with another text explained earlier, in which the author affirmed, in Book II, chapter 15, that God’s external aids, granted to all, were joined with some interior grace that touched the hearts of all people more sparingly and more secretly; and that this grace was sufficient for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony.

For those who followed the impulse of grace, it was sufficient as a remedy; for all the others who resisted, it will serve as a testimony to their obstinacy and wickedness. That this is indeed the genuine interpretation of the passage is clear from what precedes. At the end of chapter 14 the author had stated:

> “Nor for this reason are the nations excusable, who, alienated from the fellowship of Israel, [lacuna] perished, because that abundance of grace which now waters the whole world did not previously flow with equal generosity.”

He immediately gives the reason for this proposition at the beginning of chapter 15:

> “For a certain measure of heavenly instruction has always been supplied to all people; and although it was a more sparing and more secret grace, it was nevertheless sufficient, as God judged, for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony.”

And for this reason those who perished are inexcusable.

These remarks have been made to explain the author’s true meaning. Whether, however, this doctrine of his concerning a general grace—also interior, supplied to all, however perverse and unbelieving—differs from the teaching of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine need not here be investigated or determined. If it is thought to differ, this will provide still stronger confirmation that these books cannot be attributed to Saint Prosper.

[Col. 0383C] 21. We should not proceed further without first considering in another way the words of Quesnellus’s previously quoted annotation on Book II, chapter 13:

> “One thing I see with complete certainty: this sufficiency of which the passage speaks cannot in any way refer to that sufficiency of the interior grace of Christ the Savior, concerning which modern theologians contend with such intense struggle and fervor,” etc.

Quesnellus here seems less concerned with denying Cain internal grace than with removing this author from the theologians who defend sufficient interior grace, that is, grace that can be resisted. He therefore continues by warning that the sufficiency admitted by the author is located not in the interior aids of grace but in external ones.

Some may perhaps also wonder whether, with this same purpose, in the marginal annotations attached to this work he not only praised the power and efficacy of grace, writing at the beginning of Book II, chapter 26, “The office and efficacy of grace,” and likewise in chapter 7 of the letter to Demetrias, “The powerful operation of God’s grace”—expressions that indicate efficacious grace alone—but also noted, on Book II, chapter 15:

> “God gives grace that cannot be overcome,”

and again, on chapter 33 of the same book:

> “Nothing can resist the grace of God.”

These propositions, explained without any qualification, can readily be turned into the Jansenist proposition condemned by the Church: “Interior grace is never resisted”; and also into Quesnellus’s tenth proposition, proscribed in the constitution *Unigenitus*:

> “Grace is the operation of the hand of almighty God, which nothing can hinder or retard”;

and into proposition 13:

> “When God wills to save a soul and touches it with the hand of his interior grace, no human will resists him.”

22. Several testimonies of the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, none of which we find annotated by Quesnellus, show how far he abhorred this condemned position. In one place he did note the insufficiency of external aids, and he also, in a certain way, noted the power of dissenting under efficacious grace in Book II, chapter 28, in these words:

> “How does the power of dissenting remain under efficacious grace?”

But nowhere did he clearly indicate dissent from or resistance to interior grace, even though certain passages explicitly mention it.

His testimony in Book II, chapter 26, where Quesnellus annotated “The office and efficacy of grace,” is perfectly clear. After the author had affirmed that the more abundant grace is so benign—or, according to the reading he followed, so powerful—that we should in no way think it violent, and after describing various ways in which that grace also provides interior assistance, he adds:

> “This assistance is supplied to all in countless ways, whether hidden or manifest; that it is rejected by many is due to their own wickedness, while that it is received by many is due both to divine grace and to human will.”

The words “the assistance of grace, supplied in countless ways, is rejected by many” plainly declare resistance to grace, including interior grace, since the ways are not only manifest and external but also hidden—that is, interior. The following words at the end of chapter 28 of the same book agree with this:

> “God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth by diverse and countless means; but those who come are directed by God’s help, while those who do not come resist through their own obstinacy.”

The countless means by which many obstinately resist are not so much the manifest and external means as the hidden and interior ones discussed in the preceding text.

23. To prevent anyone from quibbling that, in these two passages, the words “is rejected” and “resist” refer only to the manifest or external means of grace, which the author placed under the disjunctive particle, recall and compare the two passages described shortly beforehand. You will clearly perceive that, according to the author’s meaning, those words must also be understood of the hidden and interior means of grace.

The first passage is from Book II, chapter 23, where general grace is said to touch the hearts of all people more sparingly and secretly; it plainly designates interior grace, as Quesnellus himself evidently interprets it. The other passage is from chapter 15, where the more sparing and secret grace—that is, interior grace—which was sufficient for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony, distinguishes those who assented to or resisted that same grace.

For it is said of the same grace touching the hearts of all people, or interior grace, that it was sufficient for some, not for all, as a remedy; this concerns those who assented and obeyed. But it is taught to benefit all—even those who did not use it as a remedy—as a testimony, which pertains above all to those who resisted and who resist through their own obstinacy.

Finally, in the passage concerning Cain, which occasioned this discussion, we seem to have shown that, in the author’s view, the divine correction resisted by Cain was not devoid of all interior grace that was sufficient for the method of healing. Thus, everything converges to establish the existence of truly interior grace, which many resist and which theologians commonly call sufficient grace.

The two passages in Book II, chapters 15 and 33, where Quesnellus noted that divine grace cannot be overcome or that nothing can resist it, are in no way contradictory. In neither passage does the author discuss that intrinsic power by which someone can resist interior grace bestowed on him—a resistance he acknowledged in some people. Rather, he discusses an external force, which has no bearing on the present issue, and declares that when this force is brought to bear externally against the interior grace inspired by God, it cannot resist that grace.

In the first passage, speaking of the martyrs, the author says:

> “That fire of love which the Holy Spirit had kindled in the hearts of the faithful could in no way be extinguished by their oppressors, since those who were tortured burned ever more intensely,” etc.

In the second passage, discussing the disturbances of war through which certain barbarians serving as Roman auxiliaries came to the faith, he noted that the work of divine grace could not be hindered by these external disturbances, in these words:

> “Thus nothing can resist divine grace, preventing it from accomplishing what it wills, since even conflicts draw people toward unity and wounds are turned into remedies, so that from the very source from which the Church feared danger, it receives increase.”

24. In various passages the same author commends the power and efficacy of grace, by which God effectively obtains whatever he wills. Nowhere, however, did he write the general and indefinite proposition, “We will what God wills us to will,” which Quesnellus placed in the margin beside the author’s words in Book II, chapter 27:

> “Those who come [to the faith] are led by love; for they have been loved, and they have loved; they have been sought, and they have sought; and what God willed them to will, they willed.”

He is speaking of those who, having actually come to the faith, willed what God willed them to will. He is speaking of those who reached the faith through God’s efficacious will, in whose hearts God brought about belief through more abundant and efficacious gifts and effected their willing, as he had said shortly before.

He is not speaking of everyone whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. As the same author shows throughout the work, God also wills all to come to the faith and supplies assistance to all through countless means of grace, partly manifest, partly hidden and interior, as we have seen from the testimonies quoted. But not all therefore will this, because they resist and dissent from God’s will and from the assistance of grace, including interior grace. Of such people the author therefore states in the same passage:

> “Those who dissent do not approach”—

namely, they do not approach God, who wills and assists them—

> “but withdraw.”

25. The fifth objection in Quesnellus’s preceding dissertation likewise concerns the proposition “God wills all people to be saved,” into which the Catholic doctrine that Christ died for all leads. The objection arises from his manner of explaining the question of Christ’s death.

Certain testimonies of Saint Leo are there cited. Quesnellus attempts to explain the sense in which they should be interpreted, as though they might express something foreign to Augustine’s teaching and inconsistent with the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*. And, so that no one might think he was presenting merely his own opinion, he makes use of a lengthy passage from Saint Remigius, archbishop of Lyon.

This objection and response greatly astonished us. The testimonies of Leo—which Quesnellus thought needed explanation lest they be misunderstood, namely, those concerning Christ’s prayer and death for all, including even those who are not saved—by the obvious sense of their words present no doctrine other than one harmonious with Saint Augustine and approved and taught by the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 3:

> “Although he [Christ] died for all, nevertheless not all receive the benefit of his death, but only those to whom the merit of his passion is communicated.”

The words and arguments of Remigius, by which Quesnellus thought Leo should be explained, are so involved and ambiguous that they can be twisted into a perverse sense opposed to the cited teaching of Trent and favoring the fifth Jansenist proposition. For this reason the Jansenists, in defense of their error, especially parade these and other similar passages of Remigius. Catholic theologians, in order to wrest them from the Jansenists, seek to interpret them, in light of the purpose of Remigius’s entire work and of his other passages, in a sense that in reality returns to Leo’s obvious meaning and can be reconciled with the Tridentine dogma.

Thus Remigius may appear to depart from the same meaning as the disputed passages only because he uses words spoken with a different intention.

It is therefore surprising that Quesnellus feared that Leo’s testimonies, which plainly present a sound and Catholic meaning, might be wrongly understood unless they were clarified by some interpretation. But we were much more surprised that, without any fear of danger, he thought they should be explained by Remigius’s lengthy words, which, unless carefully received and explained, can be diverted into a perverse and condemned doctrine—yet he supplied no indication of either danger or interpretation.

Did he thereby wish to prepare the way for propositions 30 and 32, akin to the Jansenist thesis and condemned in the constitution *Unigenitus*, by which Christ is implied to have died only for the elect who are actually saved?

26. Saint Leo plainly teaches in Sermon 1 on the Nativity, chapter 1, that no one held by any sin, and consequently no one even among the reprobate, was excluded from the intention of Christ the Redeemer:

> “Just as he found no one free from guilt, so he came to free all.”

The very testimonies of Leo that Remigius cites testify that Christ is the Redeemer of all, including Judas and the Jews who crucified him, with no one excepted, and affirm that he prayed for them as well—even though this redemption and prayer did not benefit everyone, because not all wished to be converted to God and repent.

Augustine likewise, so that Leo may not appear to have departed from his teaching, presented Christ as Savior even of those crucifiers who were condemned, in *Tractates on John*, tractate 4, number 1:

> “They crucified their Savior and made him their condemner.”

And concerning Judas, in Psalm 68, Sermon 2, number 11:

> “He threw away the price of silver for which the Lord had been sold by him, and did not recognize the price by which he himself had been redeemed by the Lord.”

And concerning Christ’s universal prayer, in Sermon 382, attributed to Augustine, number 2:

> “When he prayed hanging on the cross, he saw and foresaw all his enemies; but he foresaw that many of them would become friends. Therefore he asked forgiveness for all”—not, he says, “for many.”

27. When Saint Remigius explains Saint Leo’s testimonies as referring only to the elect who were actually redeemed, he plainly speaks of Christ’s redemption and prayer with respect to efficacy arising from an absolute and efficacious will, but not with respect to the sufficiency of redemption prepared and offered to all by an antecedent will. That he acknowledges the latter is indicated by his words concerning Judas:

> “He would truly also have become his Redeemer, if, even after so great a crime, he had piously and faithfully sought pardon from him.”

These words demonstrate that the name “Redeemer” is attributed to Christ in the sense of an actual effect with regard to efficacy; they also sufficiently imply that the same name is not denied him with regard to sufficiency, since it is granted that Christ’s redemption could have benefited Judas had he repented.

That redemption is therefore shown to be useless to him, not because of any insufficiency or defect in Christ’s redemption or will—for in chapter 12 Remigius professed that Christ does not will the sinner’s death, but that he should turn and live. Theologians call this an antecedent and general will, which nevertheless is not efficacious for all—but because of Judas’s own defect. As Remigius admits with Leo, Judas could have obtained the remedy had he not hastened to the noose.

It is therefore evident that Remigius admitted, from an antecedent will, a general redemption sufficient for all, and restricted only redemption that is actually efficacious to those to whom the merit of Christ’s passion is actually communicated.

Hence, in chapter 20, he affirms that he does not reject the opinion of those Fathers who may say that the Lord was crucified even for the impious who would remain in their impiety:

> “If it is pleasing—as it is also very pleasing to us—that the opinion of these men, arising from piety, should not be rejected, for the sake of peace and of the venerable piety of honorable Fathers…”

He believed that the other interpretation, by which redemption is restricted to the elect, should alone be preferred because, understood in the sense already indicated—as referring to its efficacious effect—it is most true and rests upon numerous testimonies of the Fathers and Scripture.

From the other opinion, however, he feared that redemption might be believed to have been bestowed upon all through an equal will and benefit of Christ, and that, in a Pelagian or Semipelagian sense, it might be derived from the merits or natural beginnings of human will rather than from divine election and God’s special aids.

Accordingly, speaking in chapter 13 of this opinion or interpretation, which he had described earlier as the fourth, he gives the following reason for postponing it:

> “In the fourth manner, however, this must undoubtedly be avoided: it provides an occasion for Pelagian depravity, since it asserts that God awaits human wills in order to save people.”

You see, therefore, that Saint Remigius did not reject this opinion but rather approved it cautiously, provided it was not understood in an evil sense. He merely warned against its abuse and avoided the danger of error. Had he foreseen the abuse and error which the Jansenists derive, by an opposite effort, from the interpretation he himself defended, he would not have preferred that interpretation to the fourth; or rather, he would have approved both when rightly explained, as Catholics now do, and would have warned against the errors threatening from either side.

In substance, therefore, Remigius agrees with Saint Leo and with Catholic dogma, although in his wording he may appear to differ.

28. Finally, nothing need be added concerning the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, whom Quesnellus invokes in the objection mentioned above. His entire purpose is to prove that God wills all people without exception to be saved. In the same general sense, in Book II, chapter 13, he teaches that Christ died for all, including the impious and sinners; and if anyone is found free from their number, Christ did not die for all.

In chapter 31, interpreting Paul’s words in 2 Timothy 4:10 concerning Christ—“who is the Savior of all people, especially of believers”—he plainly includes even all the reprobate among “all people,” as helped by general aids and general goodness. He distinguishes from them the elect, who are brought to salvation by special gifts and whom he says are especially signified by the words “of believers”:

> “By saying, ‘WHO IS THE SAVIOR OF ALL PEOPLE,’ he confirmed that God’s goodness is general toward all humanity; but by adding, ‘ESPECIALLY OF BELIEVERS,’ he showed that there is a part of the human race which, by the merit of divinely inspired faith, is advanced through special benefits to the highest and eternal salvation.”

# THIRD DISSERTATION, IN TWO PARTS

In which the CAPITULA, or AUTHORITIES OF THE FORMER BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE CONCERNING THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE CHOICE OF THE WILL, are ascribed to SAINT LEO THE GREAT, although they are commonly attributed to Pope CELESTINE; and the celebrated exception concerning the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise is reconsidered.

[Col. 0387]

## FIRST PART

[Col. 0387B]

We place among the works of Saint Leo the *Capitula* concerning the grace of God and free choice of the will, which were long ago attributed to Pope Celestine and appended to his letter to the Gauls. [Note: The contrary will be established in the observations below, no. 6.] Many will perhaps accuse us of excessive boldness for daring to do this without the authority of any manuscript—which we admit—and without the example of any earlier edition or the conjectural support of any author, whether more recent or more ancient.

Nevertheless, we venture to do so, and we are confident that our proposal will not be condemned by those who undertake to compare and weigh these *Capitula* with the genuine and unquestioned writings of Saint Leo—a task we have performed with no little diligence—and who strive to read our conjectures without a prejudiced mind.

I. These *Capitula* are given various names by the author himself and by others. Sometimes they are called *Authorities*, as in the preface, as well as in the title and at the end of the little work; sometimes *Sentences*, as in the same preface and in the final chapter; occasionally *Rules of the Apostolic See*, as in that final chapter; and finally they are called a concise *Index* in the short preface.

Others cite them under the name *Decrees*, or as “the Letter of Pope Celestine to the Gauls”; others call them *Capitula*, using the more general term.

Under this last name they are cited not long after the beginning of the sixth century. I willingly endorse the conjecture of a most learned man, who thinks that these *Capitula* were mentioned by the Roman pontiff Hormisdas in a letter to Possessor written around the year 520. His words are:

> “Concerning free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves can sufficiently be recognized from the various books of blessed Augustine, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. Nevertheless, explicit *Capitula* are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives. If you lack them and consider them necessary, we shall send them to you” (*Letter 70 of Pope Hormisdas to Possessor*, at the end).

Of what other *Capitula* could these words be understood? Or by what clearer words could those *Capitula* be designated than those used by this pontiff?

The correspondence is evident with what we are asserting concerning their attribution to Leo. First, they concern free choice and grace, since both the title and the conclusion express precisely this:

> “Here begin—or here end—the Authorities of the former bishops of the Apostolic See concerning the grace of God and free choice of the will.”

Second, they are called explicit *Capitula*, that is, excerpts from the writings of the Roman pontiffs or decrees approved by them. Third, from them it is possible to learn with certainty what the Roman and Catholic Church follows and preserves concerning the grace of God and free choice. Fourth, they are not attributed by name to any of the Roman pontiffs. Fifth, they are said to be contained in the ecclesiastical archives. Before Dionysius Exiguus inserted them into his own codex, no codex is known to have contained them; they were kept only in the archives of the Roman Church, from which the abbot Dionysius copied them.

But, beyond controversy, they are found cited around the same time by Peter the Deacon and others who had been sent from the East to Rome in the cause of the faith, in the final chapter of *On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, addressed to Fulgentius.

They are subsequently attributed to the same pontiff by Cresconius, an African bishop, at the end of his collection of canons, issued around the year 690. Finally, in later centuries they are cited by Florus, a master of the Church of Lyon, writing against John Scotus Eriugena in the name of the Church of Lyon:

> “From this comes that ecclesiastical and most faithful definition which blessed Pope Celestine sets forth in his decrees, saying: ‘Thus God works in the hearts of human beings and in free choice itself,’ etc.”

They are also cited by Hincmar of Reims in *On Predestination*, chapter 22, pp. 128 and 130; chapter 22, p. 133; and the epilogue, chapter 5, p. 379.

Likewise, blessed Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, vindicates this little work for Celestine in his *Collections*, question 2. Its commendation is strengthened by the fact that, for this reason, he numbers Celestine among the great teachers:

> “Pope Celestine, too, must be numbered among the great teachers. As befitted so great a pontiff, he instructed everyone concerning free choice. These words are from his decrees: ‘In Adam’s transgression all human beings lost possibility and innocence,’” etc.

He then cites more passages from *Capitula* 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Remigius, bishop of Lyon, does likewise with his Church in *On Three Letters*, chapter 23, and in his little book *On the Absolution of the Question*, etc.

I pass over Ivo and many other authors who attributed the *Capitula* to Celestine. Before all of them came Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, who, when compiling or arranging the codex of the decrees of the Roman Church around the year 500, inserted these *Capitula* among Celestine’s decrees and thereby gave later writers occasion for error, since they cited them under Celestine’s name.

II. Although so many witnesses contradict this attribution, many considerations persuade us not to believe that they were written by Celestine. For this reason, more discerning scholars long ago suspected that the author of these sentences was someone else.

Thus, some 150 years ago, John Wendelstinus already perceived the matter. He published at Mainz, in 1525, a code of canons and pontifical decrees not very different from that of Dionysius. On the margin he wrote without hesitation:

> “The following eleven chapters are not by Pope Celestine, but have been inserted by someone else.”

Those who arranged the collections of councils for publication after Merlin transcribed this judgment in somewhat moderated form: Crabbe in 1538, Surius in 1551, and Nicolinus in 1581:

> “The following eleven *Capitula* seem rather to have been inserted by someone else than to be by Pope Celestine himself.”

The most eminent and learned cardinals, Antonio Carafa and Caesar Baronius, likewise remove them from Celestine’s authorship. Baronius does so under the year 431; Carafa in the collection of decretal letters edited by him, published at Rome after his death in 1591 and dedicated to Pope Innocent IX.

Add to these Francis Suárez, *Prolegomena* 6 *On Grace*, chapter 1, number 11; Jacques Sirmond, in his notes on volume I of the *Gallican Councils*; and Gerard Vossius, Book I of *Pelagian History*, chapter 30. The last, however, thinks that the *Capitula* are partly by Celestine and partly by the Gallic disciples of Saint Augustine, because they were collected and presented to Celestine by those men and later published under his name and authority.

2. If they were Celestine’s and had been appended by him to his letter to the Gauls, he would certainly have mentioned them somewhere. Yet not even a syllable of the letter refers to them. Nor would he have added this closing formula:

> “May God keep you safe, dearest brothers,”

which demonstrates the end of Celestine’s letter.

3. When Saint Prosper attacks his opponent and heaps up against him all the testimony both of councils and of the Roman pontiffs, pressing him with the authority not only of Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface but also of Celestine, it is unthinkable to suppose that he would have omitted anything from the decrees promulgated by the Apostolic See against the adversaries of grace.

Prosper mentions only one letter of Celestine, namely, the letter to the Gauls. Although it greatly exalts Augustine’s authority and teaching concerning the grace of Christ, it is completely silent concerning the particular articles and proofs of his doctrine.

I would almost call so great a man guilty of prevarication if he had kept silent about so outstanding a collection of authorities emanating from the Apostolic See—one that could not have escaped the notice of so vigorous a defender of grace, who was championing it under the auspices of the Roman Church.

4. Vincent of Lérins, a presbyter and monk, praises this same letter of Celestine at great length in the final chapter of his *Commonitorium* against the heresies; and Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, much later, when reviewing it in his *Bibliotheca*, says in these words: “He also wrote to the bishops of Gaul concerning the faith of Saint Augustine.” Both of them, with equal silence, pass over the Capitula in question. This is evidence that neither writer had knowledge of those Capitula, at least as a work of Pope Celestine.

5. Nor does the author of this compilation employ a manner of speaking or an authority that would present him as the supreme pontiff. For although he repeatedly cites the bishops of the Roman Church—Innocent and Zosimus, for example—he nowhere calls them his predecessors, as is especially customary both among the other Roman pontiffs and in Celestine himself in that letter to the Gauls. Moreover, he speaks throughout in such a way as to reveal himself as a disciple of the Roman pontiffs and of other writers as well, rather than as a Roman pontiff. For example: “Our most pious fathers have taught us”; “The writings of the apostolic see have taught us”; “They contradict our teachers.” Elsewhere he shows himself to be someone other than the Roman bishop [Col. 0390A], when he says of the bishops of this see: “The most sacred see of the blessed apostle, through the ministry of its bishops, etc.”; “the rulers of the Roman Church”; “the apostolic prelates.”

6. If these Capitula had then been regarded as part of, or an appendix to, the letters of Pope Celestine, would Vincent of Lérins have cast aside all shame and made such a great trumpet sound in his own behalf and that of his associates—that Celestine had written for them in those letters 693—as he did in his *Commonitorium*? For he who dared to throw back upon the disciples of the holy Doctor the charge of novelty that Celestine had imprinted upon Augustine’s adversaries would have feared that he might be refuted and convicted of shameless falsehood by the Capitula’s open definitions, in which the errors of his Massilian and Lérinian associates were repeatedly condemned.

7. As I have already said, Dionysius Exiguus gave everyone the occasion for this error when he attached the Capitula under discussion to Celestine’s letter. From him, indeed, Cresconius, the deacon Peter, and all the ninth-century writers [Col. 0390B] who contended for the grace of Christ derived their testimony. But if Dionysius’s codex is examined more carefully, nothing will be found from which it can be established that these Capitula formed part of Saint Celestine’s letter. On the contrary, the sequence of the codex itself and the deliberately inserted marks of distinction that appear in it loudly proclaim that Dionysius’s intention was to distinguish one from the other.

Whenever he wishes to separate the writings of one pontiff from those of another, he always places this title at the beginning of the first decree or letter:

**HERE BEGIN THE DECREES OF N., POPE**

He does not repeat it at the beginning of the subsequent decrees or letters of the same pontiff. This mark of distinction, moreover, can be read at the head of the *Authorities on Grace*:

**HERE BEGIN THE AUTHORITIES ON THE GRACE OF GOD OF THE FORMER BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE**

Second, at the beginning of each letter of the same pontiff, the author’s name is never omitted. But Celestine’s name does not appear at the head of the statements on grace. From this I infer either that Dionysius did not know the author’s name [Col. 0390C] or that he omitted it deliberately.

Third, he placed an even stronger mark of distinction on this writing than on the letters of the other pontiffs of different periods. For at the end of the Capitula we read this clause:

**HERE END THE AUTHORITIES ON THE GRACE OF GOD AND FREE CHOICE OF THE FORMER BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE**

Celestine’s name is everywhere omitted. Nor is this clause, or anything similar, found at the end of the entire codex. It therefore appears that Dionysius wished, with such diligence, to block every path to error concerning those statements; and that he attached this *Commonitorium* to Celestine’s letter for no other reason than that he knew it had been composed on the occasion of that letter and handed over at the same time to Prosper.

8. It is also useful to draw an eighth argument from our ancient Roman codex. Although its author collected and brought together in the codex all the letters of the bishops of the City, whether doctrinal or decretal—including, among others, those of Pope Celestine—he nevertheless omitted the letter to the Gauls concerning Prosper and Hilary. Why, unless because it contained nothing concerning doctrine or discipline? It would have contained a great deal of doctrine [Col. 0390D] if the Capitula had been part of the letter. 694 For there is scarcely any letter in the entire codex that contains more numerous, more precise, or in every respect better statements concerning one particular article of Catholic doctrine.

The work therefore was not recognized as a decree of Celestine in the time of Leo, from whom, I infer, the decrees of his predecessors were inserted into the codex elsewhere. Dionysius, however, who supplied in his own collection the letters of Saint Leo omitted from the ancient codex, also supplied the Capitula on grace, placing before them the letter written in favor of Saint Augustine and his disciples.

III. [Note: [Col. 0389] That these Capitula should rather be attributed to Prosper, and on what occasion they were written, you will read in observations nos. 7 and 8.] From the affinity between the questions debated by Prosper and by the author of the Capitula, and also from the very manner of treatment, there arose the conjecture—or rather the conviction—of others who attributed this little work [Col. 0391A] to Prosper. Thus we read in the edition of the collection of decretal letters prepared at Rome by the most learned Cardinal Antonio Carafa, and in the Binian collection of the councils:

“There seems to be no doubt that what follows is by Prosper, so closely do both its subject matter and its style resemble his writings. Certainly, in the book against the *Collator*, he touches upon certain points not unlike those found here.”

Hincmarus also seemed to the learned author to have had no other writings in mind than those contained in these Capitula, when, in his book *On the Deity Not Threefold* (p. 42 of vol. I in Sirmond’s edition), he cites the decrees of Pope Celestine, “by whose delegation blessed Prosper overcame and suppressed in Gaul, through the authority of Scripture and the teaching of blessed Augustine, the heresy that had arisen.”

From this the author of this suspicion devised a very broad distinction between the works that Prosper undertook privately, out of personal Catholic zeal for defending doctrine, and what he considers to have been composed by Prosper as a kind of formula of faith, acting as the deputy and delegate of the same Roman pontiff. In the former works, he supposedly indulged a freer intellect and pen, examining at length every obscure question concerning grace and predestination; in the latter, he supposedly touched only on very few matters, and those almost universally known, lest he depart too far from the brevity especially appropriate to a profession of faith.

Yet the reason I do not accept this conjecture is, first, that what is inferred concerning Prosper’s delegation from Hincmar’s words and applied to these Capitula rests on an insufficiently firm foundation. [Note: [Col. 0391] On this supposed delegation of Prosper, see Observation no. 7.]

Although it is undisputed that Prosper was delegated by the apostolic see to defend the Catholic Church’s doctrine of the grace of Christ, that delegation is construed far too narrowly if it is restricted to these few and very brief Capitula. For from Prosper himself, in the preface to his *Response to the Vincentian Objections*, we learn that he composed far more against the enemies of grace by order of the apostolic see—and therefore that these very works in which he is said to have discussed deeper questions were included. Thus it is almost 695 certain that whatever writings Saint Prosper published on grace, at least after the Roman protection, were all issued by him at the direction of the Roman pontiffs; and that he asserted, as though they were part of the faith, the propositions that he defended in his books against the Semipelagians.

For he writes:

“Having set out sixteen Capitula one by one, under each of them: our understanding and the FAITH WHICH WE DEFEND AGAINST THE PELAGIANS BY THE AUTHORITY OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE.”

(*Preface to the Response to the Vincentian Objections*)

From this, that distinction disappears by which Prosper is made to fight sometimes privately and sometimes publicly; sometimes by his own ingenuity and sometimes by the authority of the apostolic see; here examining every difficult question and there abstaining from obscure matters. For everywhere and in all his other writings he fights and conquers, equipped with the same method, the same weapons, and the same authority of the Church. He involves himself in every question that concerns grace, including matters requiring more difficult and subtle investigation—not merely those with which a theologian might exercise himself, but also those to which a Christian must adhere if he wishes to think with the Church, as the passages cited make clear.

Furthermore, as regards Hincmar, even in the passage cited he does not refer Prosper’s delegation to the writing or promulgation of these Capitula, but rather to all those things that Prosper either wrote or discussed after returning to Gaul. For Hincmar speaks only of those works in which Prosper “overcame and suppressed among the Gauls the heresy through the authority of Scripture and the teaching of blessed Augustine.” But the author of the Capitula fights with no argument drawn from Scripture and none drawn from Augustine’s teaching. He argues solely from the authority of the Roman Church: partly from the decrees of the pontiffs, partly from the African decrees that the Roman Church had made its own by approving them, and finally from what is contained in its solemn prayers and ceremonies. [Col. 0392A]

By contrast, in several other passages Hincmar speaks of Prosper’s delegation in such a way that he never introduces him without the person of a delegate, nor ever depicts him writing without the right and authority of his legation. Thus, in chapter 1 of his work *On Predestination*, and in the book *On the Deity Not Threefold* in the same sense (p. 15 of Sirmond’s edition), he says that the heretics were reproved and convicted by “Prosper’s urgent intervention, acting by delegation from the holy universal Church.” Hence, from the preface to the *Vincentian Objections*, he says that, by delegation from the apostolic see, Prosper brought into order what was disordered in the regions of Gaul. Hence, in chapter 3 of the same work, he calls Prosper simply “the legate of the Roman Church and its faithful interpreter.” And near the end of the same book, he indicates that whoever wishes to think differently concerning the predestination of God from what “blessed Prosper defined by delegation from the apostolic see at the command of Saint Celestine” plainly does not think correctly. This cannot in any way be applied to the Capitula, which expressly say nothing about predestination.

Finally, neither in this passage nor anywhere else does Hincmar attribute the Capitula to Prosper. [Col. 0392B] He counts and praises them in six hundred places among Celestine’s decrees, and under that name commends them.

696 IV. 2. It seems most unlikely that such a writing was published under the name and authority either of Celestine or of any Roman pontiff. Rather, it was composed by a private person, or by one assuming the role of a private person—not as a public and authoritative rule of faith, but as the private *Commonitorium* of a Catholic teacher: one who investigates, elucidates, and presents the faith of the Church, but does not promulgate it with apostolic authority.

For everywhere the author acts as a peaceful conciliator and as the compiler of “a concise summary,” as he himself puts it, not as the public herald of an ecclesiastical edict. He reports the “authorities of the former bishops of the Roman see,” rather than circulating the authority of the bishop then occupying the see; and he seems more intent on instructing an erring friend than on teaching the universal Church.

This is not Prosper’s familiar manner of treatment. Prosper never writes except as an appointed Patron of the Church, bringing the whole authority of the Church to bear in defending its truth. Nothing of the kind is found in this author, who says:

“It was necessary,” he says, “to investigate, etc., so that those who are uncertain about any point might be more fully instructed, and so that we might present the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a concise summary.”

And later:

“If anyone is not excessively contentious, let him acknowledge, etc.”

3. The author of the Capitula indicates clearly enough that he had not publicly and expressly fought against heretics, since, when speaking of those who treated more extensively the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions under discussion and resisted the heretics, he points to Augustine and Prosper almost with his finger, and distinguishes himself from them in this respect. Elsewhere he says: “They contradict our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary.” That this is wholly inconsistent with Prosper is clearer than daylight.

V. Whom, then, shall we call the author of this writing? I certainly would consider him no other than the one who composed the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, which in the preceding dissertation we vindicated for our most holy pontiff. I mean Leo. I am entirely convinced that this concise summary was compiled by Leo—not after he had assumed the pontificate, but during the period when, serving only as a deacon, he was assisting Pope Celestine as minister of ecclesiastical affairs. At that time, we believe, he was also striving to bring Cassian back to the mind of the Church and wrote the two little books *On the Calling of All Nations*.

Apart from the fact that scarcely anyone of that age remains to whom this little work can be attributed once Prosper is excluded, except our Leo, or the author of the book *On the Calling of All Nations*, I seem to find in the two works so identical an intellect and purpose, and such a close correspondence between them, that nothing more similar occurs to my mind.

[Col. 0393A] First, the aim of both writings is this: to establish precisely what a Catholic must believe concerning the mystery of predestination and divine grace, setting aside the more obscure questions; 697 to determine what in this matter is hidden and what is manifest; and to identify the limits that may be reached in discussion and must not be crossed. The intention of the author of both works aims solely at this, as will become clear to anyone reading both what we present here and the many other things we omit.

Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 1:

“No limit to conflicting arguments can be found so long as one does not distinguish what is manifest from what is hidden. Concerning this conflict of opinions, therefore, I shall endeavor, insofar as the Lord assists, to investigate with what measure and moderation one ought to think . . . so that it may be useful not only to us but also to others that we have reached some boundary which we ought not to exceed.”

Similar statements occur in chapter 14 of the same book and in Book II, chapters 1, 9, 10, 22, and elsewhere.

The author of the summary reveals the same purpose in his preface [Col. 0393B], where he indicates that he wrote on this occasion because certain people who boast of the Catholic name nevertheless, as he says, “contradict our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary.” Later he writes:

“If anyone is not excessively contentious, let him acknowledge that the entire connection of the arguments depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, and that no basis for contradiction remains for him if he believes and speaks together with Catholics.”

And at the end:

“As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions under discussion, which those who resisted the heretics treated more extensively, just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not consider it necessary to establish them. For confessing the grace of God—which must in no way be deprived of anything belonging to its work and gracious favor—we believe that whatever the writings of the apostolic see, according to the rules stated above, have taught us is sufficient, so that we should not at all regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the propositions set forth.”

For this reason, I would believe that this index of statements was written at nearly the same time and with the same purpose as the little work *On the Calling of All Nations*. The aim of both is one and the same, although they pursue it by different paths. In the little work *On the Calling of All Nations*, he makes principal use of the divine testimonies of Sacred Scripture and tests every question against them as against a Lydian stone—that is, a touchstone. In this summary, however, he settles the whole matter solely by the ecclesiastical authority of councils and Roman pontiffs and, as an added confirmation, by the rites and priestly prayers. For this reason, I am easily persuaded to believe that one of these little works supplements the other.

In the earlier work, the adversaries, defeated from Scripture, withdrew as into a fortress into the authority of the apostolic see; from that fortress they are cast down with the aid of this later work. Thus, just as we conjectured that the two little books were published by Saint Leo, then a deacon, to assist his friend Cassian and Cassian’s followers, who were suffering in some measure from the Pelagian disease, so we also believe that this index of Authorities was composed by the same author: so that those who were still fighting from the doctrine of the Roman pontiffs, which they claimed as their own, might be refuted by the authority of those pontiffs. With these facts in view, I readily believe that Cassian imposed silence upon himself and changed his mind—both because Leo would not otherwise have urged him to defend the Church’s teaching concerning the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius unless Cassian had by then given hope of abandoning his error, and because Cassian was always exceptionally devoted to the Roman see.

VI. 2. In both works the Semipelagians rather than the Pelagians are attacked, but with equal restraint and equal moderation. Both refrain from harsher language; neither applies the name “heretic” to those whom he instructs. Instead, in their respective prefaces, both call them merely “defenders of free choice” and “patrons of the will.” Both suppress the name and authority of Saint Augustine deliberately, because the Semipelagians were disparaging Augustine as one who, in discussing grace, had exceeded what was necessary; they were far from being prepared to submit to his authority.

Therefore, setting aside for a time the advocate of the cause, he undertook to defend the cause itself on the authority of councils and Roman pontiffs, entering upon a path different from that followed by Prosper. Since the Semipelagians were hostile to Augustine, he had discovered that this path was more suitable for overthrowing them than for converting them.

Both points are confirmed by what is read in the preface to the Capitula, as follows:

“So that those who are uncertain about any point may be more fully instructed, let us present the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a concise summary.”

He calls this instruction “more complete” in vain unless he is referring to another instruction to which it was to be added—one that evidently required the authority of councils and Roman pontiffs. This series of statements is concise and brief, as the author himself calls it, rather than full or fuller, unless he intended it as part or an appendix of some more extensive work. No other work now remains except the two little books *On the Calling of All Nations*. For Prosper’s labors contain the same matters found in the summary, explained in more expansive language.

VII. 3. The argument drawn from ecclesiastical prayers in chapter or statement 8, in support of the necessity of grace, is precisely the same argument introduced in Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 12—not, perhaps, in exactly the same words, but with the same intellectual character and the same structure of discourse.

[Note: [Col. 0393] The following two paragraphs are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 12.

“Concerning this rule, then, of apostolic doctrine, with which the universal Church is imbued, let us inquire what the universal Church itself thinks, lest we wander into a divergent understanding according to our own judgment, etc. 699 The Apostle therefore commanded that supplications be made . . . The whole devotion of all priests and all the faithful observes this law of supplication in such harmony that there is no part of the world in which such prayers are not celebrated by Christian peoples.

“Everywhere, therefore, the Church of God supplicates not only for the saints and those already reborn in Christ, but also for all unbelievers and enemies of the cross of Christ, for all worshipers of idols, for all who persecute Christ in his members, for the Jews, whose blindness prevents the light of the Gospel from shining upon them, and for the heretics and schismatics who are alienated from the unity of faith and charity. What does it ask for them except that, abandoning their errors, they may be converted to God, receive faith, receive charity, and, freed from the darkness of ignorance, come to knowledge of the truth?

“Since they cannot grant these things to themselves, being weighed down by the burden of evil habit and bound by the chains of the devil, nor are they able to overcome their own deceptions, the merciful and just Lord wills that supplication be made for all. Thus, when we see innumerable people rescued from such profound evils, we should not doubt that God granted what he was entreated to grant; and, giving thanks for those who have been saved, we should hope that those who have not yet been enlightened will likewise, by the work of divine grace, be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life.”

Chapter 8.

[Col. 0394B]

“Let us also consider the sacramental rites of priestly supplications, which, handed down by the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the whole world and in every Catholic Church: so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing. For when the bishops of holy communities, acting as ambassadors by a mandate entrusted to them, conduct the cause of the human race before the divine clemency, the whole Church groans with them and asks and prays that faith may be granted to unbelievers, that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety, that, once the veil has been removed from the hearts of the Jews, the light of truth may appear to them, that heretics may recover through receiving the Catholic faith, that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity [Col. 0394D], that the remedy of repentance may be granted to the fallen, and finally that, once catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of rebirth, the heavenly court of mercy may be opened to them.

“That these petitions are not made to the Lord superficially or in vain is shown by the effects of the matters themselves. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of the Son of his love, and making them vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath [Col. 0395A]. The whole of this is so clearly recognized as the work of God that thanksgiving and the confession of praise are continually offered to God, who brings about these things, for the illumination or correction of such persons.”

[Col. 0395B] In these words, a multiple similarity both of subject matter and of vocabulary is readily detected. First, both acknowledge this public law of prayer as handed down by the apostles. Second, both assert that it is observed harmoniously throughout the universal Church. Third, both observe everywhere a similar and uniform rite of prayer. Fourth, neither excludes anyone from supplication; indeed, prayers are poured out for all, including unbelievers, idolaters, Jews, and others. Fifth, both say that the whole Church groans together with the priests in this supplication and that the people are not separated from the bishops. Sixth, both infer the necessity of divine grace from the Church’s supplications. Seventh, both establish the same conclusion from the act of thanksgiving. Eighth, both teach that anyone whom we see being freed from the snares of sin is rescued wholly by the work of God and by the operation of divine grace. Ninth, in chapter 8 we read “the law of praying”; in chapter 12 of the book *On the Calling of the Nations*, “the law of supplication.” Tenth, in the former work we read of celebrating prayers [Col. 0395C], and in the latter of celebrating the sacramental rites of supplications. Eleventh, the first says, “whom he may rescue from the power of darkness and transfer into the kingdom of the Son of his love”; the other says that they are “to be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God.” Twelfth, both distinguish and enumerate in the same order the unbelievers, idolaters, Jews, heretics, and schismatics for whom prayer is offered, and both say that the gifts of conversion, faith, and charity are requested for them. Thirteenth, both express the grace of conversion through the language of illumination and enlightening, which is also familiar to Saint Leo.

VIII. 4. In both works, a twofold class is established among those who remained in the opinions of the heretics: some clung to them through ignorance, others through perversity. Thus, in chapter 1 and in chapter 10 of the letter to Demetrias. It is beyond doubt that the Semipelagians did this either with excessive ignorance or with great wickedness.

5. The style of both writings is exceedingly similar. The same turns of phrase and the same words are familiar to both authors, such as: “most sacred,” “contradiction,” “perversity,” “upright” and “perverse,” “teachers” for doctors, “disputant,” “rulers,” “assistance of grace,” “authorities,” “the opinions of heretics,” “beginnings,” “growth,” “plausible efforts,” “to be the work of God,” “idle,” “rule,” “fellow workers with grace,” “those who encounter,” “uniformly,” “gaze,” “inviolable decrees,” “rescued from the power of darkness,” “natural possibility,” “depth,” and so forth.

Whenever passages from Scripture or the holy Fathers are to be cited by either author, both generally employ nearly the same formulas: “with him proclaiming and saying”; “he bears witness, saying,” and so on; “he instructs us, saying,” and so on.

Chapter 9 reads:

“For he acts in us so that we both will and do what he wills; nor does he permit those gifts within us to be IDLE which he has given to be EXERCISED, not neglected, so that we may also be FELLOW WORKERS WITH THE GRACE OF GOD.”

Similar statements are found in Book II of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 35:

“It is said in vain that those who are elect have not been given the means of action, since they have been elected precisely so that they may act. For the GIFTS OF THE VIRTUES cannot be IDLE.”

And chapter 26:

“For this purpose the will has been aroused by the aforementioned aids, so that it may COOPERATE WITH THE DIVINE WORK within itself and begin TO EXERCISE for merit what it conceived from the heavenly seed for aspiration.”

*On the Fast of the Seventh Month*, sermon 1, chapter 2:

“Let iniquity cease, but let justice not be IDLE . . . We are under the eyes of the just Judge; he knows how much ability to do good he has given to each person. He does not wish HIS GIFTS TO BE IDLE.”

Sermon 5 on the Epiphany, chapter 3:

“Considering the INEFFABLE ABUNDANCE OF DIVINE GIFTS toward us, let us be FELLOW WORKERS WITH THE GRACE OF GOD THAT WORKS IN US.”

Sermon 6 on the Nativity, chapter 4:

“He himself who gave the will will also grant the ability, so that we may be FELLOW WORKERS IN HIS WORKS.”

Sermon 9 on the Passion, chapter 3: “FELLOW WORKERS IN BOLDNESS.”

Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 23:

“This whole work, whether THROUGH FELLOW WORKERS WITH GRACE or through the ministry of the Spirit, is begun by him and increased by him, etc.”

Letter to Demetrias, chapter 1:

“FELLOW WORKERS WITH GOD have appropriately applied a devout cultivation.”

And chapter 15:

“He does not wish us to be proud or sluggish; WE MUST BE FELLOW WORKERS WITH THE GRACE OF GOD.”

Chapter 9:

“By this help and gift of God free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes luminous, what was perverse upright, what was weak healthy, and what was imprudent prudent.”

We have already noted in the preceding dissertation how familiar to our Leo this construction is, in which several antitheses are accumulated and the verb that completes the sense is deferred to the end. Of the many examples, you have a few under no. 24; here are some more.

Sermon 4 on the Anniversary of the Assumption, chapter 5:

“Sorrows are turned into joy, labors into rest, discord into peace.”

Sermon 7 on the Nativity of the Lord, chapter 2:

“From impious they begin to become just, from avaricious generous, from continent chaste, from earthly heavenly.”

Sermon 6 on Lent, chapter 2:

“We know that very many have passed from the worst habits into the best: from drunkards to sober people, from cruel people to merciful, from rapacious people to generous, from incontinent people to chaste, from fierce people to tranquil.”

Nor, in the words of chapter 9 quoted above, is only the structure to be observed as familiar to Leo. Scarcely a letter of the alphabet fails to recall Leo’s style; there is hardly a little word that our pontiff did not make almost his own, especially as regards the epithets by which he describes human choice, whether corrupted by sin or healed by the grace of Christ.

How frequently he uses the word “dark” can be recognized from the passages cited in the preceding dissertation; add these two as well.

Letter to Demetrias, chapter 14:

“From the true light, darkened and already failing lamps receive light.”

Sermon on Saint Laurence, chapter 1:

“Dark error.”

When he also speaks of a “luminous” choice after justification, he agrees with Leo, who commonly uses the language of light to describe the effects of grace: hence “enlightened minds,” “enlightening,” “enlightened,” and so on. Thus, defining grace through participation in God, Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 8:

“Without this good,” he says, “there is no good; without this light, nothing is LUMINOUS; without this wisdom, nothing is HEALTHY; without this justice, nothing is UPRIGHT.”

[Col. 0396D] Here you also see two other epithets for choice, “healthy” and “upright”; and there is nothing more frequent in Leo than the latter, to which “perverse” is opposed. Finally, the word “prudent” occurs very frequently in Leo: “to admonish prudently,” sermon 4 on Lent, chapter 5; “to preside prudently,” *On the Fast of the Seventh Month*, sermon 5, chapter 1; “prudent authority,” sermon 6 on the Passion, chapter 2; “a prudent ruler,” in letter 103 to Proterius, chapter 3.

702 In both works the Pelagians and Semipelagians are called “defenders of free choice.” Book I of *On the Calling of All Nations*, chapter 1, begins with these words:

“For a long time there has been a great and difficult dispute between the defenders of free choice and the preachers of the grace of God.”

And chapter 1:

“What they have judged concerning the most harmful defenders of free choice . . .”

Chapter 5:

“Because no one pleases him for any reason other than what he himself has bestowed.”

Book I of *On the Calling of the Nations*, chapter 24:

“That all the good things by which one pleases God are gifts of God.”

Chapter 6 reads:

“Because through him we can do some good, without whom we can do nothing.”

Saint Leo, letter 2 (now 167) to Rusticus, in the preface:

“Without whom we can do nothing; through him we can do all things.”

Sermon 11 on Lent, chapter 4:

“So that through him we may be able to accomplish all things, without whom we can do nothing.”

Leo frequently uses the words “idle” and “gaze,” which occur in chapter 9 arranged in the order favored by the holy Doctor. Here are several examples; more will readily come to mind.

“Let us contemplate with no idle gaze”; chapter 9.

“Not to pass by in an idle course”; sermon 1 on the Ascension.

“Let us not receive with idle hearing”; sermon 12 (now 13) on the Passion, chapter 1.

“Let him reach with spiritual insight”; sermon 6 on the Nativity.

“They are not seen with bodily sight”; sermon 2 on the Ascension, chapter 1.

“If you direct the gaze of your mind toward them”; Book I of *On the Calling*, chapter 17.

“Let the gaze of a sober heart be applied”; Book II of *On the Calling*, chapter 21.

“Let it be considered with a tranquil gaze”; Book II of *On the Calling*, chapter 31.

“He requires a purer gaze of the mind”; sermon 5 on the Passion, chapter 1.

It should also be observed from the preceding dissertation that what is found in chapter 1 agrees with many passages of Leo: “No one is good by himself unless the one who alone is good grants him a participation in himself.” See no. 24.

IX. These points suffice to restore to Leo this splendid selection of testimonies, which was attributed to Celestine because Dionysius Exiguus’s single codex was examined far too hastily in this matter. Although I say that this little work was wrongly attributed to Celestine on the basis of Dionysius, one may nevertheless argue from the same source, to some extent rightly, that it belonged to the Roman Church and arose within it.

For why was it listed and inserted among the decrees of the pontiffs? Why was it attached to Celestine’s letter, although distinguished from it and not inscribed with Celestine’s name [Col. 0397C], unless it was known to have been composed in Celestine’s time and at his command, and to have been arranged by the person to whom, at that time, because of the office of archdeacon, the principal care of ecclesiastical affairs and custody of the apostolic see’s archives had been entrusted, and to whom, because of his exceptional learning, everything of this kind that was to be written in the Roman Church was referred?

Everyone can see how greatly these considerations support our opinion, since Cassian establishes that Leo was serving as archdeacon in the Roman Church at that time.

Therefore, the affinity between these Capitula and chapter 10 of the book against the *Collator*, where the same testimonies of the pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus and of the Africans are cited, did not arise because both works were arranged by the same Prosper, as the learned Noris conjectured. Rather, it arose because the summary, handed over to Prosper when he was returning from Rome, lay before his eyes while he was writing against the *Collator* in Gaul. [Col. 0397D] It had been given to him for this purpose, so that it might serve him as a *Commonitorium*, from which he could take his response to the Massilians who opposed the authority of the apostolic see—and that is what he did.

Indeed, if this writing had been regarded as an authentic decree of the apostolic see, or had been composed with the intention of being made public, it would have been issued in the name of the Roman Church. Would Prosper have neglected and omitted it? Would he not rather have brought it forward with praise, either in the place where he introduces the same testimonies or elsewhere, when he attacks the Semipelagians?

## X

Now, then, we conjecture when and on what occasion these Chapters were composed, how they came to be attributed to Celestine, and how they were attached to his letter.

After the death of Saint Augustine, which occurred in August of the year of Christ 430, when some of the Gallican presbyters—and indeed even some bishops—had risen up more vehemently against that most holy teacher of grace, as though they had regained strength from the death of that most valiant champion of the Church, Prosper and Hilary, followers of Augustine’s teaching, went to Rome to seek the aid and authority of the apostolic see against the rivals of their master and of Catholic doctrine. The Roman Church was then governed by Celestine, for whom the archdeacon Leo rendered distinguished service in administering ecclesiastical affairs.

After Prosper had explained the reason for his journey, he received from Celestine a letter to be delivered to the Gallican bishops. In it the memory and teaching of Saint Augustine are commended in a remarkable manner and defended against the insults of his opponents. Among the Gallic presbyters who were defaming Augustine’s doctrine, Cassian stood out both for his reputation for piety and for his facility in writing. Prosper identified him to the pope as the chief of the others and as the author of the booklet *On the Protection of God*. Prosper also accepted from the apostolic see the task of directing his pen against Cassian’s writings, as can be gathered from the preface to his *Response to the Vincentian Objections*.

Catholic doctrine had already been asserted many times against these remnants of Pelagianism and confirmed by the authority of the Holy Scriptures. But at that time they defended their cause and attacked Saint Augustine’s teaching especially on the ground that it opposed the salutary doctrine of the Roman see and its decrees: “What that most sacred see of the blessed Apostle Peter decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops.” They professed that they followed and approved only this doctrine (*Preface to the Chapters*). By this device they sought both to diminish the authority of Saint Augustine’s writings and to draw the bishop of the apostolic see into the defense of their own cause.

I believe that this new way of conducting the struggle was the reason for Prosper’s journey to Rome. That clear-sighted man understood that, before answering those who raised such objections, the matter had to be discussed with the pope himself and with the other leaders of the Roman Church, so that he might refute his opponents with greater confidence, fortified, naturally, by the authority of the apostolic see itself, whose cause was then especially at stake. He also examined its archives, from which he could draw the decrees of the Roman pontiffs to direct against the rivals of Augustine’s doctrine.

The letters of the pope himself indicate that this was the chief reason why Prosper had gone to him. Celestine’s sole purpose in them is to teach the Gallican bishops that there was nothing in Augustine’s writings inconsistent with the doctrine of the apostolic see; that Augustine had always remained in communion with it during his life and had never been brought under even the slightest suspicion of error; and, finally, that he had been so outstanding a teacher that the bishops of the Roman see had always counted him among the Church’s best teachers.

“Augustine,” he says, “a man of holy memory, we have always held in our communion on account of his life and merits, nor has even a rumor of unfavorable suspicion ever touched him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that he was always regarded, even by my predecessors, among the best teachers” (*Letter of Pope Celestine to the Gallican Bishops*).

Celestine also ordered that the archives of the apostolic see be carefully investigated, so that whatever might serve to repel the insolence of those presbyters could be brought out and delivered to Prosper, who had come to Rome for this purpose. That this task fell to Leo would be demonstrated by his office alone, even if we had not already established it from the character of his style and from other considerations. For the care and administration of the Church’s archives belonged to the archdeacon: one of his duties was to deposit the apostolic decrees there and to retrieve them from there whenever the needs of current affairs required recourse to the authority of the archives.

From these materials, therefore, Leo compiled a brief memorandum, which he handed over to Prosper along with other writings of the same kind, so that it might assist him in refuting the objections of the Massilians. Indeed, in his book *Against the Collator*, which he composed after Celestine’s death, he cites almost the same authorities as the author of the Chapters: the same excerpts, namely, from the letters of the pontiffs Innocent and Zosimus, as well as from the Council of Carthage and the rescripts of the Africans. Thus he appears to have had the memorandum before his eyes.

Moreover, when he summarizes at the end of his work all Cassian’s propositions and errors drawn from his writings, he notes precisely the same propositions, and nearly the same number, as the author inserted into his Chapters: for example, those concerning original sin; the necessity of grace for overcoming temptations and for every act of piety, from the very dawn of faith to the final goal of perseverance; while omitting many other propositions that were disputed among Catholics, Pelagians, and Semipelagians.

What we have said presupposes that the memorandum was compiled before Saint Prosper wrote that work against the *Collator*. This seems certain to me, first because otherwise its author would have labored in vain, and it would not have been necessary—as he says it was—to inquire carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged and thought ought to be held concerning the Pelagian heresy, since Prosper would already have supplied this abundantly. It is certain also because the booklet against the *Collator* was published after Celestine’s death, while Sixtus governed the Roman Church. The fact that the memorandum, or reminder, was written shortly before Celestine’s death is shown both by the state of affairs concerning the Pelagians and by its being found among Celestine’s decrees in the most ancient manuscript of Dionysius. It should therefore be assigned to Celestine’s time, and this appears to have been the opinion in the age of that abbot.

Those who have thought, on the basis of the same collection, that it was a work of Celestine and a portion of the preceding letter did not sufficiently observe that Dionysius—or whoever else was responsible—placed it after that letter in such a way that it was more clearly distinguished from it than other letters are from one another. It bears the heading, “Here begin the [authorities] of what preceded,” and at the end another notation, “Here end the authorities,” neither of which is found as a distinction between letters.

## The Second Part of the Dissertation

### XI

Having completed the first part of the dissertation, which vindicates this booklet for Leo, we proceed to its concluding section. Although many commentators have already treated it, we do not dare to pass over it untouched.

There are consequently not a few recent writers who wish the “deeper and more difficult questions” mentioned at the end of the Chapters, where the subject is grace, to be understood as all those matters that are not expressly contained in this memorandum. [Note: [Col. 0399D] On this, see observation no. 10.] Accordingly, they would consign to the class of disputed doctrines all those points concerning the doctrine of Christ’s grace that Saint Augustine treated at greater length against the Pelagians and the Massilians—points that we neither dare to disregard nor need to affirm, if they are not found asserted in these Chapters.

Thus, whatever the teacher of grace may have consistently advanced beyond these matters, whatever he may have solidly proved from Scripture and tradition, whatever he may have safely proposed as a dogma of the Catholic faith, and whatever the Church later confirmed with the supreme consensus of all ages, these theologians consider it unnecessary to affirm if they have either not read those things or have thought they did not read them in this concise memorandum of Catholic propositions.

With this one response, like a battering ram, they overthrow the Catholic doctrines concerning the predestination of the elect—not on the basis of foreseen merits, but from God’s gratuitous mercy—concerning concupiscence, the punishments of sin, the distinction between Christ’s grace and Adam’s grace, and other points of Catholic doctrine derived from these as from fountains. They reject these doctrines, or everywhere proclaim that they are *ἀδιάφορα*—“indifferent matters”—left to each person’s free assent or dissent.

It is not difficult to demonstrate how far from Celestine’s mind are those who attempt by such reasoning to shake Augustine’s doctrine. First, however, we must recall that in Saint Augustine’s writings there are four orders of questions and propositions.

The first consists of those that concern the faith and that he asserted and defended against heretics as unshakable dogmas of faith. Such are his teachings concerning the nature and effects of the divine grace of Christ the Savior, and concerning the omnipotent power that God possesses to incline human hearts wherever he wills.

The second consists of those dogmas that are recognized as flowing naturally from the former. For example, from the nature of that grace, by which God invincibly accomplishes in human will whatever he wills, it follows, even by the natural light of reason, that whoever is governed by such grace to the end of life is led and brought to the sure and unalterable goal of predestination, and that this grace is assigned to such persons, but not to others, from God’s gratuitous goodness.

The third order consists of those matters that Saint Augustine pronounced inaccessible to the human mind, because they have neither been revealed by God nor can be penetrated by the natural light of reason—for example: Why does he draw this person and not that one? Why is one person so persuaded that he is convinced, but not another?

Finally, the fourth order consists of those points in whose investigation Augustine labored exceedingly, yet never dared to affirm that he had attained certainty. At one time he inclined more toward one opinion, at another toward another, because the matter seemed obscure to him and beset with difficulties. We shall present several examples of such opinions below.

### XII

The author of the Chapters certainly did not judge that the first and second classes of opinions were open to a Catholic to reject or embrace. At the very time when this memorandum was being composed—or rather, at a time contemporary with its composition—Celestine was writing his letter to the Gauls. In it he attacks the Semipelagians especially because they claimed that Saint Augustine had taught things that it was unlawful to teach. He affirms that Augustine had never been touched even by a rumor of unfavorable suspicion, but had always been regarded by his predecessors among the best teachers; and he declares that those who attacked the memory of so great a man had to be resisted.

But if any of the things that Augustine proposed and asserted as certain and indubitable concerning the predestination of the saints, Christ’s liberating grace, and similar matters against the Pelagians and the remnants of Pelagianism were open to abandonment, then the Pelagians and Massilians would have been accused unjustly for abandoning them, for regarding Augustine with suspicion in certain matters, and for refusing to accept his opinion concerning predestination and grace. For the most learned Cardinal Bellarmine correctly observes (*On Grace and Free Will*, book II, chapter 11) that Prosper and Hilary brought to the apostolic see a complaint that certain presbyters in Gaul were criticizing Saint Augustine’s doctrine of predestination, and that this doctrine was then strengthened by the public approval of the Church.

### XIII. 2

In the very preface to these testimonies the Semipelagians are restrained because they said that Augustine had exceeded what was necessary in his writing. For this reason they are charged with ignorance, depravity, or presumption; and although they boasted of the Catholic name, they are said nevertheless to cling to the condemned opinions of heretics.

Therefore, according to the judgment of the author of the Chapters himself, Augustine did not exceed the proper measure in what he wrote against the Pelagians and consistently asserted. Nor did he put forward and defend as certain and indubitable any dogma that, according to the same author’s view, a theologian ought not to regard as certain and indubitable. Otherwise Augustine would have greatly exceeded the proper measure if he had asserted and taught as something to be held on the authority of the Church what in fact was not Church doctrine, what did not need to be affirmed, and what could freely be rejected or embraced.

### XIV. 3

The author of the memorandum, or Chapters, was moved, as he himself states, to inquire carefully what the Roman bishops had judged and considered ought to be held concerning Christ’s grace against the defenders of free will. These men were accusing Saint Augustine as though he had exceeded the proper measure in his writings on grace. Consequently, the author had no other purpose in mind than to repel this calumny against Augustine’s doctrine by means of the very testimonies of the Roman pontiffs, whom the adversaries claimed taught a doctrine contrary to Augustine’s and conforming to their own.

Unless, therefore, he is said to have forgotten his purpose, it must be established from the testimonies he cites and explains that Augustine exceeded the proper measure in nothing, but that everything he taught in his writings agreed perfectly with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the African synods. If, nevertheless, you say that we are not obliged to affirm some of these things, you must likewise say that we are not obliged to affirm the decrees of the pontiffs and synods with which Augustine’s teaching agreed. For who, in the judgment of the same author, would wish to reject one of two things that agree with each other while admitting the other?

### XV. 4

If by those “deeper questions,” neither to be disregarded nor necessarily to be asserted, we mean what Saint Augustine consistently wrote and taught concerning the predestination of the elect, calling according to purpose, and other matters of this kind, then Saint Prosper labored almost in vain even in the things he defended on the authority of the apostolic see. He did virtually nothing for Augustine’s doctrine against the Massilian presbyters and their followers.

For these were the principal points of Augustine’s doctrine that they attacked—or at least everything the adversaries disputed against Augustine or Prosper depended upon them.
