These are the matters for which this disciple and defender of Augustine fought most fiercely; these constitute the subject matter of all his booklets. Anyone who denies this will be very easily refuted by examining those works themselves.

What, after all, did the Gauls object to in those fifteen Chapters to which Prosper responds, except matters that were either Augustine’s very doctrine of predestination and calling according to purpose, or consequences that, through a mistaken understanding of it, seemed to follow contrary to the Catholic faith? The fifteen objections of the Gauls themselves proclaim this, as do Prosper’s responses and the equal number of statements appended to them. In these, as is clear from the preface, he professes that he departs in no respect from the path of the definitions contained in the disputations of the holy man Augustine, but that in every respect he follows the doctrine that Bishop Augustine of holy memory asserted apostolically for many years in writing against the Pelagians, the enemies of Christ’s grace and despoilers of free will.

The sixteen objections of Vincent likewise arose from the same doctrine concerning predestination and God’s gratuitous calling. In answering them, Saint Prosper both explains Saint Augustine’s doctrine and professes that he is defending the faith against the Pelagians on the authority of the apostolic see.

As for the questions of the Genoese, just as they are excerpted from one of Augustine’s works on the predestination of the saints, so they contain nothing else apart from the holy doctor’s opinion concerning predestination.

Finally, in the booklet against the *Collator*, although Prosper chiefly and specifically attacks the error that Cassian had inserted into his thirteenth Conference—namely, that grace is given according to merit and that some beginning of good will comes from man rather than from God—he nevertheless declares with complete confidence in that work, which he composed on the authority of the apostolic see, that all Saint Augustine’s writings had been approved by the apostolic see, so that absolutely nothing in them had been rejected and nothing had even been touched by a rumor of unfavorable suspicion.

This would plainly be false, at least concerning those matters for which the Gallic presbyters were being blamed, or which were being marked as novelties precisely because they were placed outside the memorandum of Catholic doctrine and relegated to the class of useless disputes.

### XVI. 5

If the words in question from the Chapters attacked Augustine and his asserted doctrine of predestination and grace, the Semipelagians would never have passed them over. Rather, they would have constructed from them an impregnable fortress against Augustine’s writings.

For if Vincent of Lérins did not hesitate to use even Celestine’s clearest words in favor of Augustine, from his letter to the Gauls, against the defenders of the holy doctor—as though the pope had uttered them against Augustine—when, by writing “Let novelty cease to assail antiquity,” he accused Augustine as an inventor of novelty; and if the Semipelagians dared, on the basis of the same pontiff’s silence concerning the titles of Augustine’s books, to spread among the people the claim that the teacher of grace’s later works had been rejected by the apostolic see, how much more would they have celebrated their triumph if they had known that such things had been written concerning Augustine’s doctrine of the gratuitous predestination of the saints and calling according to purpose—if not by the Roman pontiff, then at least by his archdeacon and secretary, whom Cassian himself calls “the ornament of the Roman Church and of the divine ministry” in the preface to his books *On the Incarnation of the Lord*?

“Against this trumpet of the clearest praise”—by which Prosper means Celestine’s letter—“against this dignity of the most sacred testimony, does anyone dare to utter a murmur of malicious interpretation and cast a cloud of oblique ambiguity over a plain and utterly sincere statement, so as, because the title of the books at issue was not stated in the pope’s letter, to make it appear that they were not approved and that this praise of Saint Augustine was bestowed for the merits of his earlier writings?”

Those who turn the praises conferred upon Augustine against Augustine himself—would they have neglected the writings in which the doctrine was more broadly explained by him and most openly asserted in numerous works? Could this have escaped Vincent? Could the Genoese and Massilian presbyters have omitted it? Could this finally have escaped Faustus? I say nothing of those writers who, around the ninth century of Christ, rose up with renewed efforts against Augustine’s doctrine.

### XVII. 6

It is evident from what we presented at the beginning of this dissertation that these Chapters were known to the ancients, whether councils, pontiffs, or ecclesiastical writers. They not only knew them but believed that they had proceeded from the apostolic see, since they are found praised under the name of Pope Celestine.

It is equally certain that they took account of the objection concerning the deeper questions. Nevertheless, they suspected nothing unfavorable from that objection against Saint Augustine’s doctrine, nor did they refrain, because of those words, from praising all of this doctor’s writings. Indeed, they especially praise and commend that very part of his writings which the Semipelagians attacked and which contains and defends the doctrine that recent writers have relegated to the category of such deeper questions.

Thus Pope Hormisdas—to pass over the others—in his letter to Possessor, an African bishop who had consulted him about what opinion should be held concerning the writings of Faustus, writes words that absolve Augustine from every unfavorable implication of those statements. Although we have already quoted them above, it is useful to place them once more before the eyes of readers.

After declaring that Faustus’s books were not received by the Church, he says toward the end of the letter:

“As for free will and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves may sufficiently be recognized from the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially from those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. Nevertheless, the ecclesiastical archives also contain Chapters set forth in explicit form. If they are lacking there and you consider them necessary, we shall send them.”

### XVIII

From these words we draw several conclusions relevant to the present matter.

First, Faustus’s books—which chiefly attacked that part of Augustine’s doctrine that they now relegate to the deeper questions—were rejected by the Church; consequently, the contrary doctrine concerning predestination and God’s grace was approved by the same Church.

Second, the pontiff refers Possessor, and everyone who wished to inquire what the Roman, that is, Catholic, Church held concerning God’s grace and free will, to Augustine alone, asserting that the judgment of the Catholic Church could be abundantly recognized from his writings.

Third, so far was he from excluding certain books of Augustine that the Semipelagians claimed had been disregarded by the apostolic see that he commends them above all others: “Especially,” he says, “those addressed to Prosper and Hilary.” That is, the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, which Augustine composed in his extreme old age and near death, and in which his entire doctrine concerning predestination and the grace of Christ is explicitly and extensively asserted.

Hormisdas attributes this doctrine to his own see. He says that from these books “especially” it can be abundantly recognized what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves. And should the remnants of Semipelagianism dare to separate these books from the general praise and approval bestowed by the pontiffs upon Augustine and his writings, and reduce them to superfluous questions and opinions, which anyone may freely embrace or reject?

Fourth, when Hormisdas wrote these words, he had not forgotten the Chapters concerning God’s grace that we are discussing. Indeed, they were before his eyes. He therefore regarded it as entirely certain that those deeper questions either did not concern Augustine or consisted only of opinions about which he had written by inquiry and experimentation rather than by assertion—not of those dogmas that he had defended with all his heart, all his strength, and without fear as the doctrine of the Church.

Fifth, the agreement of Augustine’s doctrine concerning predestination and grace with the judgment of the Roman and Catholic Church, and with the Chapters themselves, is evident from Hormisdas’s assertion that one could be known indifferently from the other. He left it open to anyone wishing to inquire into the doctrine of the Catholic Church to turn either to the records of the Roman Church, to Augustine’s books, or to the Chapters preserved in the ecclesiastical archives.

Sixth, he nevertheless presents Possessor with an option in which Augustine comes first. For Hormisdas’s first thought was to refer the bishop, who had consulted him about the Church’s doctrine concerning human free will and God’s grace, to Augustine’s books as though they were the Church’s authentic archives. Then he indicates a shorter route by suggesting the Chapters, though he did not consider them necessary for someone who wished to consult Augustine himself: “If they are lacking there and you consider them necessary, we shall send them.”

### XIX

These final words of Hormisdas suggest another response to the last chapter of this memorandum: its authority should not be judged as great as most people have hitherto considered it.

The name of Celestine, the pontiff of the apostolic see, or of Prosper—who was writing at his direction and was deeply devoted to Augustine’s doctrine—gave the work its greatest authority. But now that almost everyone considers it certain that the work belongs neither to Celestine nor to Prosper, much of its weight is removed.

Leo the pontiff certainly possesses no lesser authority—indeed, among everyone, far greater authority. But the same cannot be said of Leo the deacon, who was still a young man. Let us grant that he received from Celestine the order to strengthen this memorandum with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Yet whatever he added from his own resources after compiling the memorandum, beyond excerpts from apostolic decrees, must be attributed not to the apostolic see but to the ingenuity of the deacon himself.

Since he cared about bringing his friend Cassian back from error, Leo was especially concerned not to appear too devoted to Augustine. He therefore moderated his discourse in such a way that, while taking nothing away from the most holy doctor, he might seem in some respect indulgent toward Augustine’s adversaries, and thus more easily restore their estranged minds to Catholic understanding.

Hormisdas’s words confirm this response. He attributes these Chapters neither to Celestine, nor to the apostolic see, nor to Prosper, but presents them as a booklet by an uncertain author. Although he reports that they were preserved in the ecclesiastical archives, he does not thereby confer upon them the authority of his see. Indeed, he rather lukewarmly promises to send the Chapters as though they were not especially necessary: “If you consider them necessary.”

This manner of speaking is plainly very different from the manner Roman pontiffs customarily use when they speak of the decrees of their predecessors or of matters issued by the authority of the apostolic see. Hormisdas speaks in such a way that, if Augustine’s writings differed from the Chapters, or if the Chapters contained anything hostile to them, he would prefer Augustine to the Chapters. He proposes the Chapters for no other reason than that they represent, in a concise memorandum, the Catholic doctrine that Augustine explained more fully.

We consider this the appropriate response to those who have obstinately maintained that the final part of the Chapters was intended as a disparagement of Saint Augustine’s writings. Nevertheless, we think—and I believe that all fair-minded judges of these matters will think with us—that greater weight should be given to the preceding and following responses.

### XX. 7

Who would count the doctrine of the predestination of the saints among the “incidental questions” in the subject of grace, among those difficulties that spring up unexpectedly, as it were, when one is dealing with the mysteries of assisting grace? On the contrary, it is the principal point of all and the foundation and basis of everything.

For the measure of the gifts of grace by which man is advanced toward that blessed end depends upon God’s eternal plan concerning human salvation. What else, then, is predestination according to Saint Augustine than the preparation of the means by which all who are saved are most certainly liberated?

“For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

Therefore, if someone wishes to investigate why one person is called and another is not, why one receives the gift of perseverance and another does not, the explanation readily follows from predestination: namely, that by God’s inscrutable decree the former, and not the latter, was predestined to eternal life.

But why one person was predestined and another was not must be referred to the incomprehensible judgments of God and his unsearchable ways. It is therefore evident that the question of predestination is not treated merely because of an incidental occasion, or as something extraneous to the subject, when a discussion is undertaken concerning the aids of divine grace.

### XXI. 8

Saint Augustine’s doctrine of predestination is not included among those more difficult and incidental questions that we are not obliged to affirm in order to confess God’s grace fully. On the contrary, it is contained in the Chapters described earlier, as though in their principles or connected dogmas.

For there we are taught that all human beings lost in Adam their natural capacity and innocence; that no one rises from that condition unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up and grants him participation in the one who alone is good; that no one uses free will rightly except through Christ; that no one is pleasing to God for any reason other than what God himself has granted; that we must be overcome when the one by whose help we conquer ceases to help us; that no holy thought, pious resolve, or movement of good will exists unless God works it in human hearts and in free will itself; that all desires, works, merits, victory over every temptation, and all virtues by which one moves toward God from the beginning of faith are gifts of God, who works in us so that we may both will and do what he wills; that nothing at all is to be taken away from the work and gracious favor of grace; and, finally, that God will bestow eternal rewards only for those things that he has himself granted.

When we read these statements there, I say, we unquestionably understand that God’s gratuitous election and predestination are presupposed: by this election and predestination he prepared for those alone whom he decided to liberate the benefits by which they would most certainly be liberated. The merits of perseverance are denied to others for no other reason than that he did not decree that eternal rewards should be given to them.

### XXII

“But why,” you will say, “was what is contained implicitly in this concise memorandum through the connection of its dogmas not explained in explicit words and by an open definition?”

The reason is readily apparent and is expressed with complete clarity in the preface to the Chapters. The compiler’s purpose was not to present a full and perfect profession of faith on this subject. Rather, he was concerned solely to overthrow the adversaries of Saint Augustine from the one stronghold to which they had been driven to flee by a fuller discussion—namely, their claim that they followed and approved only what “that most sacred see of the blessed Apostle decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops.”

To remove this veil of error, the author confined his memorandum within these limits: he would inquire what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their time, and what they had considered should be held concerning God’s grace against the most harmful defenders of free will.

He was so determined in this inquiry not to go beyond the limits of the Roman Church that, when he cited the African decrees—whose omission in this matter would have been impious—he expressly stated that he listed them solely because the apostolic bishops had made them their own by approving them, and because he himself embraced them as virtually the proper decrees of the apostolic see.

Nothing concerning predestination had been defined against Pelagius and Celestius either by the Roman pontiffs or by the Africans, because the heretics, who acknowledged no stain of original sin transmitted from Adam to his descendants, had not explicitly raised a controversy about it. Consequently, there was no need to labor against them in order to establish the eternal election and predestination of human beings rescued from the mass of perdition.

Nevertheless, the author understood that these Chapters did not openly contain everything that a complete confession would require. The words quoted from the preface testify that his sole purpose was to inquire into what precisely concerns the confession of God’s grace: “What is to be held concerning the grace of God.” He repeats this in the conclusion of the memorandum: “For the confession of God’s grace, from whose work and gracious favor nothing at all is to be subtracted.”

By “the work of grace” he designates the effective operation of God’s grace in human hearts and in the working of free will itself. By “gracious favor” he expresses the gratuitous bestowal of grace, undeserved by human merits.

In the preface he writes that the connection of all the disputes depends upon these two points, and that no basis for contradiction remains concerning the other questions connected with them for anyone who assents to the concise memorandum of the authorities cited below:

“So that those who are in doubt about any matter may be instructed more fully, let us set forth in a concise memorandum the constitutions of the holy Fathers. Thus, if anyone is not excessively contentious, he may recognize that the connection of all the disputes depends upon the brevity of the authorities set forth below, and that no basis for contradiction remains for him if he believes and says with the Catholics,” and so forth.

Therefore, not all the points belonging to this subject are explicitly expressed in the memorandum, but they are presented concisely. Therefore, other disputes are connected with these and depend upon them; and, once someone has assented to the propositions set forth in the memorandum, he has no grounds for contradicting Augustine concerning them—unless he is excessively contentious.

What, then, are these questions, if not questions concerning predestination, which depend upon this definition? That nothing whatsoever is to be subtracted from the grace of God’s **work and gracious favor**; that no one can **make good use of free choice** except through Christ; that the **beginnings of good will**, the growth of praiseworthy endeavors, and perseverance in them unto the end are to be referred to the grace of Christ; that God must be acknowledged as the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and virtues by which one strives toward God **from the beginning of faith**; and that it must not be doubted that all human merits are **preceded by his grace**, through whom it comes about that we both **begin to will** and to do something good; finally, that **our merits are God’s gifts**, since he is to bestow eternal rewards for those things which he has granted.

The Semi-Pelagians plainly relied upon this one foundation: that they suspended the eternal election and predestination of human beings upon their merits. For they posited certain human merits as the beginning of good will and faith—merits that were not the work of God’s grace, but rather meritorious of grace for attaining righteousness and bringing a good work to completion. For this is their definition and profession:

> The propitiation for all human beings, which is in the sacrament of Christ’s blood, is offered without exception, so that whoever **wishes** to approach faith and baptism may be saved. But God foreknew, before the foundation of the world, those who were going to believe and those who were going to remain in the faith which was afterward to be **assisted by God’s grace**; and he predestined them for his kingdom—those whom, having been called freely, he foresaw **would become worthy of election** and would depart this life with a good end.

And below:

> As far as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared **for all**; but as far as freedom of choice is concerned, it is grasped by those who have believed in God **of their own accord** and have received the help of grace **as a reward for their belief**.

Those whose contradiction distresses us, although previously holding better opinions, turned especially to this preaching of grace for the following reason: if they professed that all good merits are preceded by grace and are granted by grace so that they may exist, they would necessarily have to concede that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment and manifest work, creates one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, since no one is justified except by grace and no one is born except in transgression. But they shrink from confessing this and fear to ascribe the merits of the saints to the divine work. Nor do they accept that the number of the elect has been predestined and can neither be increased nor diminished, and so forth. (Prosper, *Letter to Saint Augustine*.)

From these words it becomes clear what connection exists between Augustine’s doctrine of predestination and the propositions asserted in the *Indiculum*. Since the Semi-Pelagians maintained that predestination depended upon merits preceding grace, while conversely they refused to profess that all good merits are preceded by God’s grace, lest they be compelled to acknowledge gratuitous predestination, it is plainly evident that predestination dependent upon merit is overthrown, while gratuitous predestination is affirmed precisely by the fact that all good merits, and faith itself in its beginning, are preceded by gratuitous grace, with nothing preceding grace itself. This is demonstrated as certain and indubitable on the authority of the Fathers.

[Col. 0406C] In truth, we learn from the letters of Leo and from the works *On the Calling of the Nations* and *To Demetrias* that the whole controversy with the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians ultimately came down to this question: whether grace was given according to merits and whether no grace preceded merits. Thus, in Letter 6 to the bishop of Aquileia, chapter 3, Leo says:

> Although they pretend to condemn and set aside all their definitions, as though this made it easier to creep in, by all their art of deception they reserve this one point, unless it is understood: that God’s grace is thought to be given according to the merits of those who receive it . . . and to be preceded by natural diligence.

A large part of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* is devoted to confirming this assertion: that grace is not given according to the merits of those who receive it. In particular, in Book I, chapter 22, the following is said of the Semi-Pelagians:

> But these people, who are ashamed not to know something and who, under cover of obscurity, stretch out snares of deception, refer every distinction by which God chooses some and does not choose others to the merits of the human will. They teach, namely, that no one is saved freely but by recompense, because it is naturally implanted in everyone that, if they wish, they can become participants in the truth, and that grace flows to those by whom it has been sought.

In the *Letter to Demetrias*, chapter 10:

> Hence, finally, there arose a simulated and insincere confession of divine grace—grace which would be given according to merits, not grace from which merits would arise. Some, while rejecting the rest, retained this part of their proud preaching.

From the preservation of this portion of the Pelagian doctrine, the author demonstrates in those three passages that nature has not been wounded by any injury of original sin, since by its own effort it is naturally bright before all grace. This parallel in the argument deserves notice as confirmation of our assertion concerning the author of these works.

XXIII. The doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning predestination and concerning the other points connected with the necessity of God’s grace for each individual act—such as what he expressly taught against Julian concerning the works of unbelievers—having, I say, been vindicated from the objection raised by that final chapter, we scarcely need to show what the author understood by the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions under discussion. For it is enough to have proved that none of the things Saint Augustine consistently taught concerning grace and predestination can be relegated to those parts as though they were not certain dogmas of the Church. Nevertheless, we shall offer our conjectures concerning them.

When the Pelagian heresy first arose and was condemned by the African bishops and by Pope Innocent, it was practically confined to two principal points: namely, the denial of original sin and the denial of the necessity of God’s grace for each individual act. In the course of time, this twofold branch, which had grown from the root of the doctrine that Adam was created mortal, put forth further branches, whose pruning was undertaken by the teachers of the Catholic Church.

Some of these questions have such an evident and altogether necessary connection with both of those doctrines that one cannot possibly be understood without the other. Others have a very close connection with them, but not one so evident or so necessary that it immediately presents itself to the mind without laborious inquiry, or that one can easily determine what the Church’s judgment concerning them is.

The question of the predestination of the saints belongs to the first class. To the second belong several questions treated more extensively by Augustine, such as: whether a human being can be without sin in this life; what punishment is inflicted upon infants who die without baptism; whether diseases arise from guilt or from nature; how infants who die before baptism are to be judged by Christ; how original sin is transmitted to descendants; whence so many evils have been introduced into marriage, which is good and instituted by God; what sin is, what concupiscence is, what its nature is, and what its effects are—a subject embracing almost infinitely many related difficulties; whether and how Christ benefited the ancients under the Old Testament; whether anyone was ever saved without faith in Christ; and finally, that celebrated and thorny question concerning the origin of souls: whether they arise through propagation or through creation. This question troubled Augustine for a very long time and gave occasion for more extensive disputations.

I believe that these and similar questions are the ones he calls deeper, more difficult, and more extensively treated—questions which Catholics did not dare to despise, but which they nevertheless did not need to assert. Yet these words must be understood more strictly than they commonly are. He does not say that it is unnecessary to assert those questions under discussion, but rather that it is unnecessary to assert their deeper and more difficult parts. Nor does he say that the aforesaid rules or propositions are sufficient for confessing the grace of God; he says, rather, “whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the aforesaid rules.” This manner of speaking seems to embrace the connection of all the disputes, which depends upon the brevity of the authorities set out below, as he expressly says.

Among the other questions listed, I think that the author of the *Indiculum* had especially in mind two deeper and more difficult ones: first, how original sin is transmitted from parents to children; second, the origin of the soul. Augustine himself judged the latter to be deep, difficult, and unnecessary. Indeed, the holy Doctor calls this same question one under discussion, unnecessary, artificial, and introduced by the Pelagians, in Book IV *To Boniface*, chapter 2:

> To this praise of the creature they add the claim that the Lord Christ was entirely unstained by any blemish of sin, insofar as his infancy is concerned, because they assert that his flesh was completely pure from every contagion of sin, not on account of his own excellence and singular grace, but through the participation of nature which is present in all infants. To this belongs also the question they introduce concerning the origin of the soul, thereby attempting to make all the souls of infants equal to Christ’s soul, since they want them likewise to be unstained by any blemish of sin.

This praise of the creature and the related question concerning the origin of the soul were among the devices by which the Pelagians, when pressed by defenders of Catholic doctrine, attempted to divert and mock them by turning them elsewhere:

> When, therefore, the Pelagians are pressed by these and similar testimonies and declarations of the truth . . . they introduce clouds of other questions, in which their impiety may lie hidden from simpler or slower people, or from those less instructed in the sacred writings. These are the clouds concerning the praise of the creature, the praise of marriage, the praise of the law, the praise of free choice, the praise of the saints, and so forth. (Chapter 8.)

And in chapter 9:

> In these five matters which I have proposed, in which they seek hiding places and from which they construct accusations.

Finally, in chapter 10:

> The Pelagians certainly add to the clouds of their hiding places an **unnecessary question** concerning the origin of the soul, so that, by confusing manifest matters with the obscurity of other matters, they may contrive a place in which to hide. For they say that we associate the transmission of souls with the transmission of sin.

Finally, I believe that this last chapter is explained by that outstanding synodal letter of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia, which is thought to have been written in the style of Saint Fulgentius. It seems to me that the author of the letter, whoever he was, had seen the *Capitula* we are discussing. For Possessor appears to have received them from Pope Hormisdas, unless they had already circulated among the Africans; and I do not hesitate to assert this on the basis of the passage from Hormisdas’s letter to Possessor quoted in that synodal letter.

In this letter of the exiled bishops (*Councils*, Labbé, vol. IV, col. 1591), the principal doctrines concerning grace are asserted as belonging to the faith of the Church. At their head stands Augustine’s doctrine of the gratuitous predestination of the saints:

> To oppose this predestination, he says, or to entertain any struggle against it, is the height of obstinacy . . . and whoever denies that Christ and his saints were predestined perversely attacks the apostolic faith. (No. 21.)

This predestination is said to be through gratuitous mercy (No. 7), through gratuitous goodness (No. 8), and through the gratuitous benefit of his mercy:

> In this mercy he chose him not according to the merits of any future good work, but because he foresaw that he would bestow upon him himself, faith, and good works. (No. 9.)

The most learned confessors transmit this doctrine while following the gift of the same grace, which grace itself deigned to pour into the hearts and tongues of the holy Fathers (No. 6).

Finally, after setting forth the doctrines of the faith concerning the predestination of the saints, the grace of God, and human free choice, the letter adds an exception somewhat similar to the one contained in the final chapter, but more fully explained, in these words:

> As for the question concerning souls, we ought either to leave it unspoken or to discuss it without contention. For whether they come through propagation or are newly made for each individual body—a matter which the authority of the sacred Scriptures does not expressly pronounce—we must investigate it with caution, especially since the faithful may remain ignorant of it without detriment to the faith. (No. 24.)

The same Saint Fulgentius, writing under his own name in Book III, chapter 18, of *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, discusses this same question as an appendix to the controversy concerning predestination and grace. He expresses Augustine’s view and his own in these words:

> The blessed Augustine, recognizing the depth of this question concerning the soul as inscrutable to him, wished to offer no definite judgment on the matter. He considered it wholly inappropriate to wish to affirm without hesitation something that another person could overturn with an opposing answer . . . He withheld assent from either definition, lest he undertake the labor of so great a disputation in vain, since a rash definition of either opinion would render that labor useless, and so forth.

Would you not say that Fulgentius had those *Capitula* attributed to Celestine before his eyes and was following in the footsteps of that writer? This should suffice for explaining the passage, which several writers have diverted into an alien meaning and from which some, excessively hostile to the gratuitous predestination of the saints, have prematurely sung themselves a triumph.

After these writings had been completed and were on the point of being sent to the press, I came upon the *Augustinian Vindications* of the most learned Henry de Neris. From its eighth chapter much could aptly and honestly have been transferred here. But since the work is pressing, it will suffice to indicate the place; no reader will regret consulting it. Whoever has leisure should consult the French book entitled *The Tradition of the Roman Church concerning the Predestination of the Saints and Efficacious Grace*, vol. I, part III, pp. 336–363, where the author explains this portion of the *Capitula* and its conclusion at greater length and by another route.

# Observations of the Ballerini on Quesnel’s Third Dissertation, in which he attributed to Saint Leo the Great the *Capitula*, or *Authorities concerning the Grace of God*, appended to Saint Celestine’s Letter to the Gauls

[Col. 0409]

[Col. 0409A] 719

1. To reach a fair judgment concerning the first part of the foregoing dissertation, in which a conclusion is drawn concerning the author of the *Capitula* appended to Celestine’s letter, it must first of all be observed that the first mention of these *Capitula* is found in three writers at the beginning of the sixth century.

Dionysius Exiguus appears to have preceded all the others, when he inserted them into his collection of canons compiled at Rome and appended them to Pope Celestine’s first letter to the Gauls. Since he published the latter part of his collection, containing the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, at the request of Julian, a presbyter of the Roman Church who had been a disciple of Gelasius and had attended the Roman synod under Symmachus in the year 499, it is highly probable that he published that part not long afterward. He undoubtedly found these *Capitula* together with Celestine’s letter. Hence he attached them to that letter in such a way that he believed they belonged to the same pontiff.

Indeed, when he divided all of Celestine’s decrees into twenty-two titles, he distributed the letter to the Gauls and the appended authorities of the Roman pontiffs among the first thirteen titles, or decrees, of that pope, so that the letter constituted the first two decrees and the authorities the eleven that followed. The difference in the inscription prefixed to the *Capitula*—“Here begin the authorities concerning grace of the bishops of the apostolic see who came before”—and also the difference in the closing formula—“Here end the authorities,” and so forth—indicate a distinction between these authorities and the letter itself, but not a distinction of authorship, or of the collector. If Dionysius had believed the author to be someone other than Celestine, he would certainly not have listed these authorities among the decrees of that pontiff.

2. The second testimony is that of Peter the Deacon and his associates, in the letter which they wrote from Rome around the year 520 to the African bishops exiled in Sardinia. These men, who were Scythians just as Dionysius Exiguus was, could have obtained their knowledge of the same authorities from his already published collection. Hence they too attributed them to Celestine. For, when reciting *Capitula* 11 and 12, they praised them under the explicit name of the most blessed Celestine, in his letter to the Gauls. Moreover, when transcribing the final words of the *Capitula*, they affirmed that the same letter ended with those words.

3. The third witness is Hormisdas. In the very year 520, after these monks had departed from Rome, he wrote to Possessor in Letter 70:

> As for free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and maintains, or elsewhere, asserts, may indeed be learned from the various books of blessed Augustine, especially those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. Nevertheless, the ecclesiastical archives contain explicit *Capitula*. If you lack them and believe them necessary, we shall send them to you.

The learned agree that no other *Capitula* are indicated here than these, which certainly concern grace and free choice and bear that title. It must be noted, however, that this pontiff does not attribute the *Capitula* themselves to Pope Celestine. He merely asserts that they are contained in the ecclesiastical archives—that is, those of the apostolic see—and that from them it can be learned what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and maintains, or asserts, concerning the grace of God and free choice. By these words the apostolic approval of the *Capitula* is expressed clearly enough.

4. From these facts we draw two conclusions.

First, these *Capitula* came to light from Rome and were kept in the Roman archives. For this reason the aforementioned Hormisdas wrote concerning them: “If you lack them . . . we shall send them,” meaning that they were to be retrieved from the Roman archives.

Second, since Dionysius, who prepared his work from documents collected at Rome, published them together with Celestine’s letter to the Gallic bishops, they appear to have been kept and discovered in the apostolic archives together with that letter. 721

5. Among the arguments brought forward by Quesnel in number 2, three in particular clearly show that these *Capitula* cannot be attributed to Celestine.

First, if they had been sent by the same pontiff to Gaul together with the letter to the Gauls, some mention of the material to be appended would certainly have been made in the letter itself, as regularly happens in the letters of other Roman bishops when they append something to them.

Second, Saint Prosper, who very carefully opposed all the authorities of the apostolic see to the adversaries of Augustinian doctrine, would certainly not have omitted these *Capitula*, which attacked the opinion of his adversaries more openly and explicitly. If Celestine, by sending these *Capitula* to Gaul most recently, had settled the controversy with the Gallic adversaries in more explicit terms, why, in his book *Against the Collator*, chapter 10, would Prosper have been content to produce only the earlier decrees of Innocent and Zosimus? Why, in chapter 21, where he praises Celestine’s letter for having undertaken the defense of Augustine, would he have cited nothing from the *Capitula*, in which the opinions of the adversaries are especially overthrown, if these had been promulgated by the same pontiff together with that letter?

Third, Augustine’s critics, when they continued to resent his doctrine even after receiving Celestine’s letter, replied—so as to withdraw themselves from the authority of that letter—that although Augustine’s earlier books had been approved in the letter, his later books had not, in which the same Doctor had taught more explicitly a doctrine contrary to theirs concerning the attribution of the beginning of faith to grace, and so forth. Those who made this claim had undoubtedly received Celestine’s letter alone, without the *Capitula*, in which the doctrine explicitly taught in Augustine’s later books is chiefly confirmed.

6. Quesnel’s opinion, which attributes these *Capitula* to Saint Leo the Great, rests upon the hypothesis that he was the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*. Since we have shown in our observations on the second dissertation that this hypothesis is entirely false, once the foundation of his opinion has been removed there would be no need to add anything further.

Nevertheless, we shall not omit one point. If Saint Leo had collected the authorities of the apostolic see at the time Quesnel supposes—when he was serving merely as a deacon and assisting Pope Celestine as minister of ecclesiastical affairs—Saint Prosper, whose benefit Quesnel thinks the collection was intended to serve, would have made particular use of them when he wrote his book *Against the Collator*. For a very strong argument would have been added from a document which so important a minister of Pope Celestine had handed over to Prosper for refuting the errors.

But since no indication of this document and no use of it is found in Prosper, it follows plainly enough that this work cannot be attributed to Leo. If the arguments which Quesnel introduces from the agreement of the style and doctrine of this little work with the books *On the Calling of All Nations* prove anything, they prove that the *Capitula* should be attributed to the author of those books, whom we have shown to be someone other than Leo.

7. If these *Capitula* are thought to be attributable to someone on account of the agreement of their style and doctrine, we think they should more readily be attributed to Saint Prosper of Aquitaine. For when writing against the Semi-Pelagians, he not only attacked the same errors that are censured in these *Capitula*, but was also accustomed to defend Catholic doctrine from the authority of the apostolic see, as is done in these *Capitula*. We do not find this practice to be equally characteristic of the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*.

Antelmius, in Dissertation 1, *On the Genuine Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, part II, whom Pagi followed for the year 431, number 49, not only believed that these *Capitula* should be attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, but also thought that Prosper referred to them in the preface to his work *Against the Vincentian Objections*, where he says:

> After setting out sixteen *Capitula* one by one, under each of them we shall place the meaning of our position and of the faith which we defend against the Pelagians on the authority of the apostolic see.

Antelmius thinks that these words indicate not a response written at that time against the Vincentian objections, but another little work previously composed on the authority of the apostolic see. He takes the words “on the authority of the apostolic see” to mean by apostolic mandate, on the basis of which Hincmar attributes an apostolic delegation to Prosper in his books *On Predestination* and *On the Non-Trinal Deity*.

But no other little work written by Prosper by apostolic mandate or delegation can be identified unless these *Capitula* are attributed to him, since in them he collected the authorities of the apostolic see against the Pelagians. So argues Antelmius.

Yet none of this proves the point. Prosper’s book *Against the Vincentian Objections* appears to have been written before he traveled to Rome and obtained Celestine’s letter to the Gallic bishops. Otherwise, if he had written it afterward, he would have made use in that book especially of the authority of this letter. Consequently, by the testimony which he inserted in the preface, he could not have been referring to these *Capitula*, which, as Antelmius himself concedes, were written after the letter to the Gauls. Certainly, at a time when Prosper had not yet reached Rome, it is incredible that he received from the pontiff a commission to write these *Capitula*.

Hence the delegation, or mandate, of the apostolic see which Hincmarus appears to have inferred from this same testimony rests upon no foundation. The words in which Prosper says that he defended the faith “on the authority of the apostolic see,” since they do not signify a pontifical mandate, express nothing other than Prosper’s customary practice. In his earlier letter to Rufinus and in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, he likewise employed the authority of the apostolic see against the Pelagians. Nothing, therefore, can be deduced from these words in support of identifying the author of the *Capitula*.

What rather moves us to believe that these *Capitula* belong especially to Prosper is that, in addition to his practice of setting the authority of the apostolic see against the Pelagians, he inserted in his book *Against the Collator* nearly the same testimonies of Innocent, Zosimus, and the African Fathers that are collected in the *Capitula* cited above. Thus he appears to have summarized in that little work what he had discussed at greater length concerning the grace of Christ in the book.

8. Father Coustantius conjectures the occasion of this work as follows in his note to Celestine’s first letter, number 8:

> While Celestine was still alive, Prosper, accompanied by his associate Hilary, went to Rome and obtained a letter to the Gauls (Letter 21, no. 2). In that letter the praised pontiff sharply rebuked Augustine’s critics and testified that this Doctor had never been touched even by a rumor of sinister suspicion, but had everywhere been held in both love and honor by all. He therefore seemed to have left his rivals nothing that they could bring against him.
>
> Yet, says Prosper (*Against the Collator*, chapter 21, no. 59), against this trumpet of the most distinguished praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, someone dares to utter the murmur of a malicious interpretation and to cast a cloud of oblique ambiguity over a clear and most sincere statement—namely, by arguing that because the title of the books under discussion is not expressed in the Pope’s letter, it follows that the books which were being criticized were not approved, and that this praise of Augustine was bestowed on account of the merits of his earlier writings.
>
> Not content to demonstrate from the complete agreement of Augustine’s later books with his earlier ones how unjust and foolish this sinister interpretation was, Prosper, so that no avenue of escape might remain for his adversaries, decided that he must also have Augustine’s doctrine approved by Pope Sixtus. Hence he adds:
>
> > Lest this be secured by the snares of hypocrites—so that Augustine’s latest books may be thought not to have been approved by the apostolic see—we trust, with the Lord’s protection, that what he accomplished through Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, he will accomplish also through Sixtus; and that, in the keeping of the Lord’s flock, this portion of glory may have been reserved for this pontiff: just as those earlier pontiffs drove away manifest wolves, so may he drive away hidden ones.
>
> At that time, therefore, so that he might more easily induce Sixtus to accomplish this, Prosper may reasonably be thought to have composed the *Indiculum*, in which he demonstrated that the doctrine which the adversaries criticized in Augustine’s latest books was consistent with the definitions of the earlier bishops of the apostolic see.

Thus far Father Coustantius. Yet we cannot agree with him when he adds that this *Indiculum* was confirmed by Sixtus in such a way that what is taught in its explicit *Capitula* concerning grace and free choice subsequently became the proper doctrine of the Roman Church, and that Prosper thereby successfully attained what he had hoped for from that pontiff.

We cannot agree, I say, because there is no indication anywhere that Sixtus III decreed anything concerning this matter. And if he had established something by which these *Capitula* were confirmed, there would be no reason why they should be attributed to Celestine rather than to Sixtus. Moreover, if these *Capitula* had been expressly and publicly approved by Sixtus, it cannot be understood why, after such apostolic confirmation, Faustus of Riez and other Gauls, who continued to write against the doctrine of the *Capitula*, were not regarded as heretics.

9. It seems more probable to us that the *Capitula*, although composed by Prosper for the purpose conjectured by Coustantius, were presented to Pope Sixtus before being published. Why Sixtus did nothing new in the matter is unknown. Perhaps Augustine’s critics, after Prosper’s book *Against the Collator*, in which the same authorities of the apostolic see had been inserted, became quiet under Sixtus and thereafter until Faustus, so that it was judged that nothing further was necessary.

The *Capitula*, having been received by that pontiff and approved as highly satisfactory, were deposited in the apostolic archives and attached to Celestine’s letter because that letter commended Prosper’s concern and dealt with the same subject. They seem to have remained there until they were brought out of those archives and published, together with Celestine’s letters, through the work of Dionysius Exiguus.

When Hormisdas mentions these *Capitula*, he makes no mention of either Sixtus or Celestine, because they had been confirmed by no decree of the former and did not truly belong to the letter of the latter. It was enough for him to mention only the apostolic archives, in which documents approved by the apostolic see were customarily stored and preserved.

The first public approval of these *Capitula*, therefore, must be referred to the aforementioned letter of Hormisdas to Possessor, in which he declared that they were preserved in the ecclesiastical archives and conformed to Roman and Catholic doctrine. It is therefore not surprising that before this kind of approval Faustus and other Gauls could defend the contrary position without incurring the charge of heresy.

Indeed, this could also have happened for some time afterward, since many people in Gaul may have been unaware of Hormisdas’s letter to Possessor, which was sent to Constantinople. Moreover, although that pontiff approved the *Capitula* in the letter, he did not publish them, and neither their contents nor the doctrine approved in them could be sufficiently inferred from the letter.

The edition of these *Capitula* which appeared through the agency of Dionysius, spreading gradually, did not immediately reach everyone’s hands or awareness. This concludes what concerns the first part of Quesnel’s argument.

10. Concerning the second part, we think that one point should be observed. Although Augustine’s doctrine of predestination was not included in these *Capitula*—as both Quesnel and Cardinal Noris maintain—among the deeper and more difficult parts of the questions under discussion, concerning which the author said, “Just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not need to assert them,” it does not follow that the doctrine must therefore be regarded as one of the defined dogmas of the faith, so that anyone who thinks otherwise must be considered a heretic or guilty of violating the faith.

For although this doctrine is confirmed by many of the clearest testimonies of Augustine and other Fathers and follows very closely from defined principles, it cannot yet be said to have been defined by the Church. On this matter it will be useful to hear Father Louis Thomassin. Although he vigorously defends the gratuitous predestination declared by the Fathers, he nevertheless thought the following warning necessary in volume I of the *Dogmatic Theology*, Book IX, chapter 19, number 8:

> One point remains on which readers must be warned: namely, when we have so consistently denied that the decree concerning gratuitous predestination was left undecided by the holy Fathers . . . , it was not our intention to affirm that this decree had been received as a dogma of the faith. It is one thing for the doctrine of gratuitous predestination to have been asserted by Augustine and by nearly all the Fathers of both Churches, and another for it to have been adapted by the Catholic Church as a rule of faith . . . .

This was why we repeatedly said that Augustine’s view concerning the election of grace is connected with the dogma of the faith. It was not left undecided or superfluous, as though suspended between alternatives, but rather as something coherent with or consequent upon the faith—not, however, as something incorporated into or implicit in the substance of the faith.

# FOURTH DISSERTATION

## Concerning the author of the little work, or letter to the virgin Demetrias, hitherto attributed to PROSPER: in which it is argued from conjectures that it is neither PROSPER’S nor anyone else’s work, but that of Saint Leo, Pope I

[Col. 0413]

[Col. 0413B] 727

I. The style of the letter to Demetrias agrees so closely with the style of the books *On the Calling of the Nations* [Note: [Col. 0413D] Compare the observations to be appended, no. 4.] that the two works have rightly been attributed to the same author, whether they were assigned to Ambrose or to Prosper. For this reason, since in the second dissertation we vindicated one of them for Saint Leo with many arguments which, as we trust, are neither weak nor frivolous, we would consider it superfluous to undertake a separate treatment to attribute the other to him as well, were it not necessary in a matter of such importance to accumulate proofs upon proofs and to spare no diligence.

Accordingly, referring the reader back to the earlier dissertation so that he may be instructed concerning the date when this letter was written and may also read there much concerning the similarity of style, doctrine, and formulation of ideas between Saint Leo and the author of the books *On the Calling of the Nations*—similarities that can likewise be transferred to the author of the letter—we shall dispose briefly of the remaining points peculiar to this work.

[Col. 0413C] First, then, I observe that this letter has the following feature in common with the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles* and with certain works of Saint Leo: [Note: [Col. 0413D] See the same observations, no. 5. In the following sections, the points indicated below will be examined.] it cites Holy Scripture from Saint Jerome’s translation. It has this further affinity with Saint Leo: it uses both versions, namely the Vulgate and the Hieronymian version. This occurs in the same verse, Job XIV.4, where, according to the Vulgate, we read in Saint Leo, Sermon 8 on the Nativity, and in the middle of the letter to Demetrias:

> Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?

And according to the Septuagint translators, in Saint Leo’s Sermon 1 on the Nativity and in the cited passage of the letter:

> No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day.

This is, I think, a strong argument for what we wish to establish, since no one will readily persuade himself that it happened by chance that, in the same age, two different writers adopted the same verse of the same book from Saint Jerome’s translation, which had not yet come into general use and is scarcely found to have been employed by any other author of that period.

[Col. 0413D] 2. To prove that Christ the Lord is always present with and cooperates with the ministers of the sacraments and of the Gospel, he adduces a passage from Matthew XXVIII, which we said was employed by Saint Leo and by the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* for the same purpose. “Certainly,” he says, “the Lord now continually works with the same power, who says: ‘Behold, I am with you,’ etc.” See above, [Col. 0414B] Dissertation 2, no. 19, where the passages from Saint Leo and from the work *On the Calling of the Gentiles* are set out.

## II. 3.

When this letter describes the various snares of Satan and his more violent attacks by which he assails those whom he sees being snatched away from him through the consecration of baptism and the profession of a better life, and when, conversely, it warns with what zeal and vigilance one must fight against him, it uses almost the same words as our Leo. Take the example from chapter 10:

> When, through the sacrament of Christ’s cross and resurrection, the old condition returns to newness and ungodliness is regenerated into innocence, the ancient enemy rages more maliciously and burns more fiercely; and when he strives by countless arts of doing harm to turn the human race aside, sowing dissensions, stirring up anger, sharpening desires, suggesting shameful things, fabricating falsehoods, and multiplying the snares of error through the inventions of opinions, he is more tormented by the virtue of those who stand than he rejoices in the frailty of those who fall.

Saint Leo, Sermon 6 on the Epiphany, chapter 3:

> Those dangers must be guarded against vigilantly which arise from the very leisure of peace. For the adversary, who was ineffective in open persecutions, rages through a concealed art of harming, so that those whom he did not strike down by the assault of affliction he may overthrow by the fall of pleasure . . . . Those whom he did not break by losses, he corrupts through desire. He inflames with lusts those whom he cannot harass with torments. He sows dissensions, kindles anger, incites tongues; and, lest more cautious hearts withdraw from unlawful deceits, he thrusts before them opportunities for completing crimes.

And Sermon 2 on Lent, chapter 2:

> Now greater caution and more watchful prudence must be assumed by you, when this same enemy rages with a sharper envy . . . . As the birth of the new creation approaches, spiritual wickedness is expelled from those whom it possessed. Therefore the impious fury of the stripped enemy rages; and he seeks a new gain because he has lost his ancient right. He therefore inflames anger, nourishes hatred, sharpens desires, mocks self-restraint, and incites gluttony.

Sermon 3 on Lent:

> From the moment when we renounced him in baptism, and by divine regeneration passed from that origin over which he ruled into a new creation, he persecutes us with more violent hatred and fiercer envy . . . . The ancient enemy does not cease to spread the snares of sin everywhere against us.

In these passages, besides the similarity and harmony of meaning, construction, and vocabulary—which indicate one and the same author—many expressions in the letter are also words that Saint Leo uses repeatedly, such as: “the inventions of opinions”; “the sacrament of Christ’s cross and resurrection”; “iniquity returns to innocence, and the old condition to newness”; “to be tormented by the virtue of those who stand”; “the frailty of those who fall,” and so forth.

## III.

The author of the letter writes:

> The evil of pride must be guarded against above all among the virtues, because it lies in wait for none more opportunely than for those to whom rightful praise is owed.

And in chapter 10:

> Those whom he could not persuade to love vices, he instills with a desire for praise . . . . Through glory he entered the human heart; and those whom he did not move by assault, he cast down by elation.

In chapter 16 he speaks to the same effect:

> The tempter’s snares are vigilant, so that where devotion advances, elation may creep in, and so that a person may glory in a good work in himself rather than in the Lord. But the Apostle’s solicitude warns us against this danger, saying: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.” Therefore, the more excellently each person advances in the commandments of God, the greater are his reasons for fear and trembling, lest the mind, conscious of those very increases in goodness and eager for praise, be swept away into the excess of pride, and become defiled by vanity while it seems to itself radiant with virtue.

Saint Leo has very similar words in Sermon 4 on Lent, chapter 3:

> Do not doubt, he says, that the devil arms the force of his wickedness for this purpose: that he may set snares for piety from piety itself, and that those whom he could not overthrow through distrust he may attempt to overcome through glory. For the evil of pride is near to righteous actions, and elation always lies in wait for virtues close at hand. It is difficult for human praise not to captivate one who lives laudably.

And Sermon 8 on the Epiphany, chapter 2:

> “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling,” the Apostle says; “for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.” And this is a reason for the saints to tremble and fear: lest, elated by the very works of piety, they be abandoned by the help of grace and remain in the weakness of nature.

Discussing Melchizedek, the letter says:

> The most sacred man Melchizedek, prefiguring the form of the Lord and our Savior.

Saint Leo, Sermon 4 (now 5) on his Nativity:

> He himself is the one, Christ, whose form Melchizedek the high priest prefigured.

The Letter and Saint Leo speak in the same way about law and grace. The letter says:

> A command is never given for any other reason than that the help of the one who commands may be sought.

Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on Lent:

> Let the one who commands be approached again—he who gives the command for the purpose of arousing desire and providing help.

And more explicitly, Sermon 11 on the same subject:

> For this reason the command is given, so that the help of the one who commands may be sought.

On poverty and riches, the letter says:

> Both abundance and want are ordinarily occasions of sin, since the rich are either lifted up into pride or the poor leap into complaint.

Saint Leo, Sermon 11 on Lent, chapter 1:

> It is no less dangerous to lack what one desires than to abound in what has been granted. There are snares in the breadth of riches and snares in the narrowness of poverty. The former lift one into pride; the latter incite one to complaint.

Saint Leo, Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne, chapter 1:

> Christ placed the apostolic office principally in Peter.

The author of the letter:

> Nature was principally established in Adam.

Here both writers use the same word in a sense that includes both an original establishment and primacy. The word is rarely used in this way.

These three writings also have this in common: they frequently employ the passage in Acts XIV, “He allowed the nations to enter upon their own ways,” and likewise often use the passage from the Book of Job, “Human life upon earth is a trial.”

## IV.

Concerning the condition of the present life, Saint Leo writes in Sermon 7 on the Passion, chapter 3:

> They were saddened, not by the guilt of conscience, but by the uncertainty of human mutability.

And in Sermon 14 on the Passion, chapter 3:

> Although it belongs not to this life but to the eternal one that God should be all in all; nevertheless, etc.

The letter to Demetrias, chapter 24:

> It is not yet the case that God is all in all, because no one is without the spur of temptation and without the uncertainty of mutability, etc.

And above:

> In the fellowship of future blessedness, God will be all in all. This cannot be fully attained in the present life because this mortal condition has not yet, etc.

In both works God is introduced under the image of a farmer cultivating the human soul and making it fruitful with the good fruits of righteousness. For this reason God the supreme and true farmer is named; his devoted care for human beings is called cultivation; the soul, the field of the heart; virtues, seeds; and good works, shoots of righteousness.

The author of the letter, chapter 1:

> Although the supreme farmer provided his plantation with vigorous growth for your advancement, the co-workers of God’s grace nevertheless applied devoted cultivation at the proper time, so that the tender shoot might receive the strength of courage and the tree of your purpose might bear fruits worthy of its nobility.

And chapter 7:

> But whatever it is by which the external things of the bodily senses are struck, in the field of the heart, to which this cultivation is devoted, it can neither take root nor put forth a shoot unless that supreme and true farmer applies the power of his work and brings what has been planted to fruitful life.

Book II of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 6:

> This good will is the first planting of the heavenly farmer . . . . Good will is the first shoot of all the virtues.

Saint Leo, the final sermon on the fast of the tenth month:

> For God, the true and supreme farmer, is the author not only of bodily fruits but also of spiritual ones; and he knows how to cultivate both kinds of seeds and both kinds of plants by a twofold cultivation, giving the fields the growth of shoots and giving souls the increase of virtues.

Likewise, Sermon 3 on the same fast of the tenth month:

> In the Lord’s field, whose laborers we are, we ought prudently and vigilantly to practice spiritual cultivation . . . . If these good works are neglected through idle leisure and inert sloth, our soil will produce no noble shoot, etc.

Sermon 6:

> From the soil of our heart let the shoot of righteousness and the fruit of charity arise.

Sermon 1 on Lent:

> The seeds of the virtues are then well nourished in us when every foreign shoot is torn out of the field of our heart.

Sermon 4 on the Pentecost fast, chapter 3:

> For unless the soil of our flesh is subdued by continual cultivation, it quickly, etc. We must therefore guard the nobility of all the shoots and seeds that we have conceived from the planting of the supreme farmer, etc.

Similar passages occur in Sermon 2 on the Resurrection and likewise in Sermon 2 on the Ascension.

Let the reader also consult what we reported in the second dissertation, both from Saint Leo and from the author of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, concerning that silent testimony of creatures to their creator which is always open to everyone. The author of the letter depicts it in chapter 7 with equivalent, and indeed identical, words:

> All the elements of the world and all the natures of created things themselves demand this by their appearance: that the invisible things of God may be perceived and seen through the things that have been made. In the beauty of heaven and earth there are certain pages always open to the eyes of all and never silent concerning their author; their testimony imitates the teaching of teachers and the utterances of the Scriptures.

Saint Leo, Sermon 11 on Lent, chapter 6:

> Whoever gives some portion of his substance should understand that he is a minister of divine mercy, which has placed the poor person’s portion in the hand of the giver.

And Sermon 5 on Collections, chapter 1:

> Earthly and bodily resources proceed from his generosity, so that he will rightly demand an account of those things which he entrusted not so much to be possessed as to be administered.

The letter to Demetrias, chapter 5:

> Those who preside over their possessions no otherwise than over the affairs of the poor, so that they may serve the usefulness of the Church under a kind of stewardship, each laboring according to the measure of his strength so that what is necessary for the nourishment and clothing of the household of God may be supplied, etc.

Letter to Demetrias, chapter 10:

> Hence the emptying of the baptism of infants, who, they would say, are granted adoption alone but are not absolved from any guilt.

Book II of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 24:

> Nor would it have been impiously said by someone concerning the baptism of infants: “Grace has what it may adopt; the water has nothing that it may wash away.”

The author of the six books of the *Hypognosticon*, book V, chapter 8, records this opinion of a Pelagian from the writings of the Pelagian whom he refutes. [Col. 0417A] John Garnerius conjectures that this Pelagian was Julian, and that the other was Pope Sixtus III (*Dissertation 6 on Marius Mercator*, chapter 6). If this conjecture were true, it would support our position. Since our Leo adhered to Sixtus, he could have received from him Pelagian writings that may have been familiar to Sixtus when he favored Caelestius.

The letter, chapter 5:

> To strive toward eternal life through narrow and difficult paths, etc.,

unquestionably refers to verse 14 of chapter VII of the Gospel according to Matthew, which Saint Leo always cites in this form:

> Narrow and difficult is the way that leads to life.

See the examples in Dissertation 2, no. 24.

Saint Leo, Sermon 8 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1:

> So that the soul . . . . . may be free to attend to divine wisdom in the court of the mind.

The letter to Demetrias, chapter 22:

> Enter, then, into the court of your mind itself and into the inner chamber of your purest conscience, etc.

Saint Leo, Sermon 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1:

> God gives the means by which we may do what he himself works in us, kindling, that is, the lamps of our minds and setting us aflame with the fire of his charity.

The letter to Demetrias, chapter 14:

> From the true light, already darkened and failing lamps receive light . . . . . Let the mind kindled by heavenly fire not grow lukewarm . . . . . From the source where it began to be inflamed, let it ask to be set on fire.

In Dissertation 2, no. 24, we observed that Saint Leo was familiar with this last expression.

The letter, chapter 24:

> Without doubt, the portion of all the virtues is obtained from the source from which their fullness will be obtained.

Saint Leo, Sermon 2 on the Passion, chapter 2:

> What the impious portion of your race lost, let the faithful fullness of the nations attain.

Sermon 15 (now 14), chapter 4:

> He who was the first of human beings to rise again is a portion of that fullness which he preceded.

The letter, chapter 17:

> It is fitting that the image of God should shine for God and should be beautiful and adorned from that source, saying: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us.” Otherwise she is adulterous and estranged from the divine marriage if she displays in the mirror of her heart the beauty of anyone else.

Book I of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 8:

> Let the Lord seek his image, and, after the accumulation of all the filth that has fallen upon it has been wiped away, let him clear the mirror of the human heart.

Sermon 95 on the Degrees of Blessedness, chapter 7:

> Let the Creator appear in the creature, and in the mirror of the human heart let the image of God, expressed through the lines of imitation, shine forth.

Sermon 5 on Lent, chapter 3:

> Let us wipe the mirrors of our hearts with more diligent care . . . . . For the brightness of minds created in the image of God is not so removed from the smoke of all vanity that it cannot be darkened by any stain.

Sermon 1 on the fast of the tenth month, chapter 1:

> We shall find that human beings were created in the image of God so that they might imitate their author; and that this is the natural dignity of our race: that the form of divine goodness may shine in us, as in a kind of mirror.

Sermon 4 on the Nativity, chapter 2:

> So that human beings, living according to the image and likeness of their author, might preserve the form of God’s goodness and righteousness in the brilliance of imitation, as in the brightness of a mirror.

[Col. 0417D] The letter, chapter 7:

> God’s grace is wholly rejected unless it is wholly received . . . . . Whoever denies anything of its fullness is placed outside grace . . . . . God’s grace must be confessed fully and truly, since its first gift is that its help is perceived.

Chapter 10, *On Grace and Free Will*:

> In confessing the grace of God, nothing whatever must be subtracted from his work and gracious favor.

The letter, chapter 8:

> No ruin is more grievous than that of the proud, especially when that very elation tends toward an injury to God.

Saint Leo, Letter 80 (now 106) to Anatolius:

> This proud elation tends toward the disturbance of the whole Church.

This is a very common manner of expression in Saint Leo.

The letter, chapter 10:

> So that they might raise up the general ruin of all human beings by the privilege of their merits.

Saint Leo, Sermon 7 on the Epiphany, chapter 4:

> God made our exceedingly bad cause good through the privilege of humility.

The letter, chapter 18:

> The mind is free from every contamination when it loves nothing, either in itself or in its neighbor, except what it knows to be from God. For to love something that is not from the work and Spirit of God is not chaste love.

Book I of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 6:

> They love themselves well who love God’s works in themselves. For God also loves in us what he himself has made, and he hates what he himself has not made. If, then, we love God’s work in us, we rightly love good will, which would not be worthy of love if it were not God’s work.

There is a frequent construction and accumulation of words, together with the use of figures, which we observed in Dissertation 2 to be characteristic of Saint Leo.

The letter, chapter 6:

> From every kind of human being, from every rank of duties, from every measure of works, from every quality of virtues, let there be formed an inseparable cohesion and impartial beauty of the whole edifice; and let nothing be lacking to its solidity that was not lacking to its portion.

Apart from the construction of the words, scarcely anything here is not characteristic and familiar to Leo.

Chapter 10:

> When freedom is restored to captives, salvation to the lost, and life to the dead; when the old condition returns to newness and ungodliness is regenerated into innocence.

Chapter 4:

> Let the children of God become rich from poverty, strong from patience, and exalted from humility.

You will find hundreds of similar passages in Saint Leo’s other works. See Dissertation 3.

## VI. 4.

If now we wish to examine in detail the affinity of style and the words more familiar to both writers, we shall easily discover that these are precisely the same, and that the structure of the diction as a whole is also the same. They use the following words either with unusual frequency or, even when not frequently, in a manner beyond common usage:

“Voluntary devotion”; “the generosity of grace”; “to incite”; “to be set on fire”; “a disciple of truth”; “prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic doctrine”; “to return, pass over, or be transferred into innocence, and to proclaim newness”; “to impose”; “murmurs of complaints”; “without hesitation”; “to inspect, inspector”; “sublimity”; “to transcend”; “to increase”; “to serve, service”; “to insinuate, insinuation”; “guidance”; “unchangeable will”; “to grow lukewarm”; “sluggish and lukewarm”; “to empty”; “the madness of a new doctrine”; “a portion of doctrine”; “serpentine”; “to bear the form”; “co-workers of grace”; “to devote”; “loss”; “to advance, advancement”; “to take one’s beginning”; “agreement” used for “consent”; “the measure of the gifts of grace”; “unequal”; “to swell, to become swollen”; “elation”; “to presume, form”; “the whole” used for “all”; “to fall back”; “frailty”; “to belong to a divine work and gift”; “solidity”; “sacred, most sacred”; “to be joined in alliance”; “religious”; “burdensome”; “obscure” used for “obscurity”; “to instruct, instruction”; “discerning, discernment”; “a portion,” opposed to “fullness” and “solidity”; “the sacrament of the Passion and Resurrection”; “to burn, to be consumed by envy”; “the poison of envy”; “inventions”; “the evangelical pages of the Old and New Testaments”; “deceptions”; “snares”; “right-hand, or left-hand”; “communion of nature,” etc.; “knowingly”; “matter”; “shoot, seed, field of the heart”; “participation”; “God provides growth for his plantings”; “to vary, variation”; “unceasingly”; “the spur of temptation”; “the danger of mutability”; “the uncertainty of mutability”; “to conceive in the heart”; “cultivation”; “darkened minds”; “to incline”; “western”; “to reject” used for “to cast away,” and so forth. “Teachers,” used for the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church; “the institution of the Savior,” etc.

### 5.

Here we strengthen the preceding conjectures. The polish and elegance of this letter’s style do not belong to an African, but rather to someone nourished at the very cradle of the Latin language. Certainly, if he had been an African, he would not have been unaware that Demetrias had formed her resolve to preserve virginity chiefly from Saint Augustine’s exhortations. Nor would he have written that she had chosen this very purpose without human exhortations, since from Augustine’s Letter 143 to Julian, Demetrias’ mother, we learn that this devout virgin embraced the resolve of chastity through his ministry.

> Through our ministry, when you received the word of the hearing of God, as the Apostle says, you received it not as the word of human beings, but, as it truly is, the Word of God. By the help of the grace and mercy of the Savior, such fruit has arisen from this ministry of ours in your household that, although holy Demetrias’ human marriage had already been arranged, she preferred the spiritual embrace of that Bridegroom who is beautiful beyond the sons of men, etc.

It is not surprising that an Italian living far from Africa and perhaps at that time still a young man, as Saint Leo was, should not have known this circumstance.

Moreover, the author of this letter clearly reveals himself [Note: See observations, no. 8.] to be a fosterling of the Roman Church when, everywhere emulating its glory, he asserts that the apostolic see had been an example to everyone, both priests and peoples, so that they might abhor the madness of Pelagian doctrine. Yet this distinction belongs to the African bishops, who were the very first to raise the standard against Pelagius, as Prosper sings:

> You, Africa, pursue the cause of our faith
