> With fiercer zeal; and when the seat  
> Of apostolic authority joins its strength with yours,  
> You crush the savage entrails of war  
> And strike down the defeated along a broad path.  
> Your holy bishops came together from every city,  
> And in a celebrated assembly of elders  
> You decreed what Rome would approve  
> And what kingdoms would follow.

## VII. 6.

Our assertion is further supported to no small degree by the singular relationship and holy intimacy that existed between the virgin Demetrias and Saint Leo. From this relationship Saint Leo even derived the confidence to urge her to build a basilica to be consecrated under the invocation of Saint Stephen, as various writers attest.

Platina writes:

> Leo, having turned his attention to restoring the City and its churches, urged Demetrias, a handmaid of God, to build in her own estate a basilica to blessed Stephen on the Latin Way, three miles from the City.

This is also reported in the Roman Breviary.

I do not see why this should be understood, or could be understood, of another virgin named Demetrias, since neither the writers of that age mention another woman of this name who was at all distinguished, nor do they distinguish the Demetrias of whom we are speaking by any qualification when they mention her.

There is only one circumstance that might move anyone: namely, that Demetrias, already fleeing the barbarian savagery of those who had captured Rome in the year 410, crossed into Africa together with her mother Juliana and her grandmother Proba, and established a home at Carthage.

But if one recalls [Note: See the same observations, no. 11.] that the Vandals invaded Africa in the year of our Lord 427, with an almost innumerable army that savagely devastated that region; that after Hippo was conquered in 431 all the provinces of that territory were subjected to the arms of the barbarians, except only two cities, Cirta and Carthage; and that this last city finally fell into their hands in 439, I do not think anyone can be persuaded that Demetrias remained in that province, where she would certainly have encountered, unless she saved herself by flight, the fury of heretical barbarians, among whom the Catholic faith and virginal chastity—qualities in which Demetrias shone—were regarded as equally grave crimes.

Indeed, no one can fail to believe that, just as the devout virgin fled to Carthage when Rome was captured by the Goths, because it was then the safest refuge from the barbarians, so, when the Vandals invaded Africa, she left Carthage for much stronger reasons and returned to Rome. There she had her homeland, relatives, friends, and—as is indicated more than once in this very letter—the extensive possessions left to her by her parents.

It is also highly probable that she did not remain in Africa until the Vandal invasion: either she brought Juliana, still surviving after the Goths’ departure from Italy, that dearest pledge, back with her to the City; or, after Juliana’s death, Demetrias herself voluntarily sought her homeland again, since she could scarcely have remained at Carthage without the help and consolation of her relatives and fellow countrymen.

On returning, therefore, to the City, she found Leo easily holding the first place in doctrine and piety among all who were then distinguished there. Since, as archdeacon of the Church, he had the more important responsibility for the care of virgins dedicated to God, Saint Leo undertook, as part of his official duty, to guide Demetrias toward the perfection of a life holier than the one she had professed. In turn, the holy virgin, as was her right, asked Saint Leo that she herself might be increasingly enkindled in the observance of her sublime purpose.

Saint Leo did not refuse the burden imposed upon him, but wrote this outstanding letter to her. He judged that its subject ought to be Christian humility, which he rightly feared was endangered in this holy virgin, commended as she was by the splendor of her birth, the lavish distribution of immense wealth among the poor, and her singular piety. He feared that elation might snatch away in a single moment the palms won through so many labors and the continual practice of good works. His other writings testify in many places how readily he otherwise praised this virtue.

## VIII.

Let this distinguished letter, then, belong to Saint Leo, not to Prosper, whose name it bore after it was printed among his works under the title: “Prosper, bishop, to the holy virgin Demetrias.” That title is demonstrably an addition for two reasons. First, roughly a hundred years earlier, when this work was counted among the works of Saint Ambrose, it had always appeared without this title. Second, it is certain among learned men that Prosper, the disciple and champion of Augustine, was never distinguished by priestly rank, nor perhaps by any ecclesiastical ministry at all. Gennadius himself, a Gaul and the most diligent of the Gallic writers, praises him merely as a man of the Aquitanian region.

Gelasius, too, when he reviewed at the Roman council the writings of orthodox Fathers, whom he distinguished by the most exact designation according to each one’s rank, added the title “bishop” to the names of those whose writings he enumerated who had held episcopal dignity. After listing their works, he speaks of Saint Jerome in this way:

> Likewise, the little works of blessed Jerome the presbyter.

Finally, when he comes to Prosper, he concludes:

> Likewise, the little works of Prosper, a most religious man.

This sufficiently suggests that, although entirely worthy of the episcopal dignity, Prosper was never adorned with it.

The same point is established from the chronicle of Victor of Aquitaine to Hilary, the Roman pontiff; from Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*; from Bede’s *Martyrology*, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July; and elsewhere. See further in Sirmond’s notes on Book VIII, Letter 15 of Apollinaris Sidonius.

But leaving aside that pseudepigraphical title, the difference of style and its affinity with the style of the author of the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* prove that this letter is not Prosper’s. Although Prosper’s prose, as they say, sometimes sounds throughout with certain rhythms—which is not unusual among all writers of that age—those rhythms are less frequent in Prosper, who also appears to have made a point of avoiding them on many occasions, as will be clear to the reader.

Nor is he as concerned as the author of the two books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* with arranging and precisely constructing his prose or with cutting his periods into balanced members. Just as Prosper surpasses the other writer in the weight and skill of his reasoning and is more vigorous in his assertions, as Gennadius says of him, so he is far inferior in purity of diction, brilliance of expression, and elegance of composition.

This is further demonstrated by the difference we noted above between them. One says that the Roman Church preceded all the bishops in overthrowing the Pelagian heresy; the other asserts that the African Church anticipated even the apostolic see in this struggle. This proves that they had different authors.

Finally, Prosper’s profound silence concerning Saint Augustine deprives him of any claim to this work. Prosper never lets an opportunity pass to mention Augustine’s name with praise. What more suitable and more obvious opportunity could he have had to celebrate that unconquered teacher of grace than in a letter wholly concerned with the grace of Christ and with humility, the guardian of grace; a letter in which he attacks Pelagian doctrine and Pelagius’ letter to Demetrias; which mentions the bishops who opposed that arch-heretic, among whom Augustine was a principal figure, “the chief portion,” as Prosper himself calls him, of the Lord’s priests (*Letter to Augustine*); and in which he addresses a virgin whom he had begotten for Christ through the ministry of the word—or rather, whom, emulating God’s zeal, he had betrothed so that she might present a chaste virgin to the one man, Christ?

Prosper, the most inquisitive investigator of everything connected with Augustine, could not have been ignorant of this, nor could he have kept silent about it, since he would not have doubted that it would be most agreeable to the holy virgin.

Finally, when he says that Demetrias’ resolve to preserve chastity had been rightly mentioned, from the very beginning, by many who then held leading positions in the Church, and that she had reasonably stirred the most learned men by her exhortations, no one can believe that Prosper could have forced himself to restrain and suppress a speech that would spontaneously have flowed into Augustine’s name and praise.

If the reader considers all these points with a mind free from every prejudice, I do not doubt that he will readily subscribe to our conjectures and judge that this little work should be restored to Saint Leo, its genuine parent.

## VIII.

I shall do nothing foreign to my purpose if I here bring again under examination what a recent author reports about the devout virgin—or, better, what he reports against the devout virgin, whose honorable memory he unjustly disfigures with disgraceful accusations.

He charges Demetrias with three or four crimes. First, that, being eager for human glory, she contaminated whatever good she did with this stain. Second, that she willingly received the Pelagian poison administered by Julian, her kinsman. Third, that she gladly supported people of this sort. Fourth, that, as an admirer of talent—a new crime—she showed excessive favor to ambitious and proud men who pretended to piety.

I reproduce the author’s own words:

> Julian had breathed his poison upon a family connected with him by marriage, and Demetrias, being more enamored of a little glory, received it more readily. Though contemptuous of wealth and the world, she was an admirer of talent and favored men of this sort, who so preferred the appearance of a stricter discipline that they nevertheless wished to seem to hold preeminence both in eloquence and in evangelical perfection.

—Joannes Garnerius, Dissertation 6 on Marius Mercator.

But from where, learned man, do you claim that the devout virgin drew Pelagius’ poison? If you have no suitable witness for this assertion, are you not afraid to be accused before God of having defamed the memory of a girl consecrated to God?

If, moreover, you regard it as a major argument for her adoption of the heresy that the holy girl was born from the Anician line, that Aemilia was connected with the Anician family, and that Aemilia had in turn given birth to Julian’s wife, then not Demetrias alone but all who were connected with both families by blood or affinity must be said to have been infected with the Pelagian stain. Indeed, scarcely any Roman nobleman will be free, so to speak, from this original plague.

“On the contrary,” he says, “that poison was not transmitted to all Julian’s relations, but Demetrias, being more enamored of a little glory, received it more readily.”

And how do you know this? Where, I ask, do you find that Demetrias was more enamored of a little glory? Was it because she was nourished and educated in Christian discipline and humility, as Augustine testifies (*Letter 188*, formerly 143, to Juliana)? Or because, although first in the Roman world by nobility and wealth, she despised all these things and considered herself not noble, not preeminent in riches, but simply a human being?

Was it because she surpassed the years of girlhood through the ardor of faith and began where others had ceased, at the perfection and consummation of virtue, as Saint Jerome says in his letter to Demetrias?

Perhaps she is called more enamored of a little glory for this reason: because she piously and wisely understood that so sublime a purpose must rest upon the foundations of humility? Because the Anician virgin, raised above every height of senatorial nobility, suddenly turning her mind away, rejected mortal marriage out of desire for a heavenly union . . . and advanced through her pursuits toward the higher degrees of virtue, as the letter to Demetrias, chapter 1, says?

If these are indications of an elevated spirit and a hunger for glory, I confess that no one was more enamored of a little glory than Demetrias. But if, on the contrary, they are evidence and merit—or rather, to speak with Saint Jerome, a miracle—of the deepest humility, then even Garnerius himself will admit that the desire for human glory has been most unjustly attributed to this devout virgin.

[Col. 0422A] **IX.** Demetrias was, moreover, repeatedly warned to avoid the remnants of Pelagius and to flee pride. Granted; but if being warned to avoid a fault or to flee an error is taken as an admission of it, and no one can act as an admonisher without simultaneously acting as an accuser, I do not know who, absolved from every charge, would dare to trust himself to be so. All the Romans would have been guilty of the impiety of Manichaeus and of all the heresies of Arius, Nestorius, and Eutyches, since Leo so often warned them to flee these things. All the apostles—indeed, all Christians—would have been infected with the Pharisees’ leaven, which is hypocrisy, since the Lord Jesus so often urged them to beware of it. Timothy, too, would have to be called immoral and devoted to profane novelties of language, since the Apostle writes to him that he should keep himself chaste and avoid profane novelties of language (1 Timothy V.25; VI.20).

Indeed, who would be surprised that Leo chose to speak of humility rather than of the other virtues when addressing Demetrias, who had been raised to that summit of virtue at which the evil of pride—so close to every virtue—is especially to be feared, as Leo writes (To Demetrias, ch. 16), and which seems to be friendly to those virtues that it desires to destroy? “Hence,” he says, “nothing must be fled more than the appetite for this desire, which denies virtue through love of its own excellence rather than through love of the divine work.” Pelagius had breathed this love into the pious virgin with all the power of his eloquence in his letter; against it our Leo fights with all the eloquence at his command.

But if Demetrias must be thought to have accepted Pelagian doctrine for the reason that she had received a letter from Pelagius, let her rather be believed to have accepted and preserved Catholic teaching, because letters were sent to her by the holy priest Jerome, the bishop Augustine, the Roman pontiff Innocent, Leo—then archdeacon and later also bishop—and other most distinguished teachers, as he calls them, who at that time held precedence in the Church. These letters were addressed either to Demetrias herself or to her mother Juliana, and by them she was kindled no less to love Catholic doctrine than to love virginity.

Certainly it is much more consistent with Christian charity to form about a virgin so well fortified by such protections the opinion that Augustine himself formed, even though he was thinking of nothing concerning them. “We,” he says (Epistle 143), “regarding the Christian discipline and humility of the holy virgin, in which she was nurtured and brought up, think that when she read those words—if indeed she read them—she groaned, beat her breast humbly, and perhaps even wept; and that she confidently prayed to the Lord, to whom she has been dedicated and by whom she has been sanctified, that, just as those words are not hers but another’s, so her faith might not be such as to make her believe that she possessed something for which she might glory in herself rather than in the Lord.” And below: “Far be it altogether that such a thing should have been produced in the mind, not to say of you or of your holy virgin daughter, but of any servant or maidservant of yours of the least merit, by this book.”

**X.** Now, since Saint Augustine wrote not to Demetrias but to her mother Juliana, I do not know whether the praised author derives from this fact any great support for his position. The holy girl Demetrias spent especially the beginnings of her consecration in silence, and drew no letters from others to herself; this was appropriate neither to the modesty of virginity nor to humility. Juliana, however, anxious about her daughter’s progress, earnestly sought the assistance and exhortations of the saints, so that Demetrias might become more ardent in observing and persevering in her holy purpose. The letters written to Innocent, Jerome, and Pelagius—then still distinguished for piety and learning—testify to this.

The same explanation applies to Saint Augustine. When he received a letter from Juliana, not from Demetrias, he wrote back not to Demetrias but to Juliana, certain that the mother would receive nothing that she could not share with her daughter. Let us hear Augustine. “We would not have known,” he says (Epistle 133), “how that exhortation of ours had then been received by the faithful and noble virgin, unless, after a short while, when she had professed virgin sanctity, we had learned of this immense gift of God through the joyful announcement and truthful testimony of your letter.”

The reason why Augustine, in writing back to Juliana, warned her against the snares of Pelagius is obvious. It is common to all the teachers of the Church that, when they have undertaken the task of fighting against an error recently born within the Church, they then neglect no opportunity to rise against it, and carefully dissuade from such a heresy all those to whom they speak or write. Anyone who has even glanced at the writings of Augustine or Leo knows this.

There is a clear example in the present matter. Jerome’s chief concern was with the adherents of Origenist doctrine; hence, when addressing Demetrias, he strongly urged her cautiously to defend herself against that doctrine. Augustine had begun to engage the Pelagians in combat at the same period; therefore he deterred Demetrias from the greatest Pelagian error.

[Col. 0423B] Augustine himself supplies a further, particular reason. “How,” he says (Epistle 143), “could we conceal from you—whom we owe so great an affection and whom we must warn to avoid other things—after we had read the book written to holy Demetrias? Who wrote it, or whether it reached you, we prefer to learn from your reply.” Augustine would therefore almost have shown himself guilty of treachery had he not applied the medicine of Catholic doctrine against the poison administered to the holy virgin through a heretic’s letter. The letter of the holy teacher contains no other hidden meaning.

Moreover, that Juliana, together with her entire household, had always been far from the error of the Pelagians is testified by Juliana herself in the explicit words reported by Augustine. In an earlier letter Augustine had warned her to avoid this heresy, and Juliana had given abundant thanks for the pious warning, adding the following (ibid.): “But let your priesthood know that I and my little household are far removed from persons of this kind; and that our entire household follows the Catholic faith so faithfully that it has never strayed into any heresy, nor ever fallen—not merely into those sects which are scarcely expiated, but not even into those which seem to contain only small errors.”

Augustine well understood that Juliana counted the Pelagian sect among those that seemed to contain small errors. For, since the deadly nature of the poison of Pelagius and Coelestius was not yet fully known, especially to the less educated sex, their sect and doctrines seemed more tolerable when compared with those sects and doctrines that are scarcely expiated. Augustine teaches Juliana that this error was not a small one, in order to make the sect still more hateful to her—a sect into which she clearly professes that neither she nor her household had ever fallen and from whose adherents she declares herself to be far removed. Yet it never occurred to Augustine, so far as we know, either to accuse this profession of faith of obscurity or to suspect it of insufficient sincerity; nor should this sinister suspicion enter the mind of any honorable and Christian person.

**XI.** Finally, the author wonders that Demetrias, who once professed virginity amid such rejoicing throughout the whole world, later remained hidden in obscurity and was praised by no one at all, except perhaps by a certain Prosper. I should call him excessively eager for praise who says that Demetrias was praised too sparingly. What could one praise better in a virgin than her profession of virginity? What could one praise in a virgin who was foremost in nobility and wealth throughout the Roman world more than that she despised all these things, so that she might consecrate herself as a living, pleasing sacrifice to God and, without any stain, to eternal chastity (Jerome, Epistle 8 to Demetrias)?

This is what Jerome praised; this is what Innocent praised; this is what Augustine praised; this is what all the most distinguished teachers who then held precedence in the Church praised. This is what the whole world celebrated. If anyone thinks this insufficient, I do not know what would satisfy him.

But remaining hidden in obscurity after professing virginity is itself no insignificant praise for a virgin consecrated to God and hiding from the sight of God in obscurity. Her ardent endeavor and the merit of her entire virtue are precisely this: to love not to be known. Yet the progress of the pious virgin did not remain obscure. After nearly thirty years, an exceptional letter—not by some Prosper, but by Leo the Great—made it known to the whole Church.

From Leo it is evident how great Demetrias’s merit was. He draws from it a great argument for her humility: “To what extent,” he says, “O holy virgin Demetrias, do you incline the dignity of your dignity, that you even require your progress to be assisted by my pen? Considering the weakness of my ability, I would refuse this in every way and would not presume to offer my little exhortations to so mature and learned a mind, unless I derived from the one issuing the command the confidence to accomplish what is commanded, and trusted that it must be accomplished through your merits and prayers,” and so forth.

Finally, Demetrias did not remain obscure in her later years, for several ecclesiastical writers praise her because, at Leo’s urging, she built on her estate beside the Via Latina a basilica in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. Her memory is not so obscure that it is not rather on the lips and in the hands of all who perform the daily task of ecclesiastical worship; every year it is recalled everywhere in the churches on the anniversary feast of Saint Leo. Thus I might almost say that in the virgin Demetrias was fulfilled what the Lord Jesus foretold concerning Mary Magdalene: “Wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her” (Matthew XXVI.13).

# Observations of the Ballerini on Quesnell’s Fourth Dissertation, concerning the author of the little book, or letter, to the virgin Demetrias

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423D] **1.** This letter was first published among the works of Ambrose, at the end of his letters, as Epistle 84, and was inscribed in his name, as we learned from the Basel edition of 1492. Since the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, added in later editions, do not appear in that edition, this is a clear indication that the first editor found the letter without those books, either at the end of a manuscript of the Letters of the holy doctor or in some manuscript of a similar type—such as Vatican manuscript 284—in which this very letter is read without the books *On the Calling*, with the inscription: “Ambrose’s letter to the virgin Demetrias.”

When it was noticed, however, that this letter could not be attributed to Saint Ambrose, both because of the mention of the Pelagians occurring in it and because of Demetrias’s age, it was omitted from the Roman edition of 1581, while the books *On the Calling*, which had previously been added to Ambrose’s works, were retained.

[Col. 0424D] **2.** Joannes Sotellus, who in 1565 had added the books *On the Calling* to his edition of Prosper at Louvain, on the basis of three manuscripts in which those books were attributed to Prosper, although he had found no copy that likewise ascribed this letter to Prosper, nevertheless thought that, especially because of its similarity of style to the praised books, it should be assigned to the same author and inserted among his works.

Although several manuscripts were subsequently found by us with the aforesaid books inscribed to Prosper, we were unable to find any that supported Sotellus’s opinion. Most manuscripts that attribute the books *On the Calling* to Prosper lack this letter. Of the three Vatican copies numbered 262, 268, and 281, in which the letter is written after the two books *On the Calling*, the last two, 268 and 281, attribute the books *On the Calling* to Ambrose; but they append the letter without the author’s name, under the title: “Here begins *On True Humility*, addressed to the holy virgin Demetrias.”

The first and more recent manuscript, 262, attributes the books *On the Calling* to Prosper both in its inscription and in its final clause. But it begins the letter, as though it were a little work not belonging to the same author, after several blank pages and without any inscription, starting immediately with the first sentence. Thus it may appear to have been accidentally placed after the books attributed to Prosper.

**3.** Nevertheless, since the opinion had gained currency—on the basis of similarity of style as well as similar statements concerning grace—that the books *On the Calling* and the letter to Demetrias were by the same author, and since those books had been attributed to Prosper in several manuscript copies, it became generally accepted that this letter too should be assigned to him, although no manuscript supported the attribution.

Paschasius Quesnellus was the first to raise the banner against this view. He argued that, together with the books *On the Calling*, this letter too should be claimed for Saint Leo. Joseph Antelmius wrote at length against him in Dissertation 2, *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, in order to maintain, in accordance with the common opinion, that the same letter belonged to Saint Prosper; each subsequently replied to the other in shorter writings.

In judging fairly between these conflicting opinions, since nothing could be drawn from the manuscripts in favor of Prosper, and much less in favor of Leo, we must first examine the conjectures proposed by Quesnellus to exclude Prosper and claim the letter for Leo. Then a few points will be added concerning Antelmius’s opinion, by which Saint Prosper is asserted to be the author.

**4.** First, the hypothesis that Quesnellus establishes at the outset—that the author of those books and of the letter is the same—is not as certain as is assumed. Two reasons are offered for this hypothesis: both that the style in the two works appears identical and that the same errors of the Semi-Pelagians are attacked in both.

But it seems clear to us that the errors noted in the letter to Demetrias are not those of the Semi-Pelagians but of the Pelagians. Quesnellus referred to the Semi-Pelagians the following passage from chapter 10: “Some, while rejecting the rest, retained that part of the superfluous preaching”—that is, the various errors spread by the Pelagians—“so that they might raise up the general ruin of all human beings by the privilege of merits; and, while admitting among us the wounds of original sin, nevertheless showed among their own people that they held the view that the transgression of the first human beings had harmed only their imitators.”

But these words do not at all fit the Massilian Semi-Pelagians or their other supporters. They sincerely admitted original sin and were not joined with the Pelagians in this error. The passage instead indicates certain covert Pelagians who, while afraid to reveal themselves openly, admitted original sin among Catholics but denied it among their own people. They seem to have been of the same kind as those hidden Pelagians mentioned by Saint Leo in Epistle 1, who used general and ambiguous professions to conceal themselves and whom the same pontiff ordered to be compelled to condemn each error openly and explicitly.

The style of the letter, moreover, appears to differ from that of the books *On the Calling* in several respects that sharper and more exact minds will not overlook. Even if a broader similarity is asserted, since this broad kind of stylistic resemblance repeatedly occurs among different writers of the same age and training, such general similarity alone cannot certainly prove that two works have the same author.

Nothing, therefore, certain is available for asserting a common author. Indeed, the profound silence concerning Semi-Pelagian errors in the letter, where a suitable occasion arises, may seem incredible to some if its author were the same as the writer of the books *On the Calling*, who is recognized in those books as inflamed against them.

In the present matter, however, if we at least posit the doubt whether the author of the letter differs from that of the books, then, since it cannot be denied that the style of the letter agrees more closely with the style of the books *On the Calling* than with the style of Saint Leo or Prosper, and since this greater similarity contributes nothing toward establishing whether the letter should be attributed to the author of the books *On the Calling*, it will be much more uncertain—indeed, more difficult to believe—that it belongs to Leo or Prosper, from whose style it differs more markedly.

**5.** But setting this aside for the moment, and also assuming the hypothesis that the two works have the same author, since nothing can be drawn from it to establish Leo rather than Prosper as the author, let us continue our examination of Quesnell’s dissertation.

In favor of Leo, Quesnellus first adduces the author’s indiscriminate and distinctive use of the old version and Jerome’s version of the same verse—Job XIV.4—which is read according to both interpretations both in Leo’s Sermons and in the letter to Demetrias. He celebrates this as a strong argument, since no one would readily persuade himself that it happened by chance that, in the same age, two different writers adopted the same verse from the same book from Saint Jerome’s version, which had not yet come into use and is scarcely found employed by any other author of that period.

How weak this argument is, although he considered it strong, is clear from a contemporary author of the work *On the Promises and Predictions of God*. He quotes the same verse of Job from both interpretations in Part I, chapter 4, and in the same context joins the two versions in precisely the way they are joined in the letter to Demetrias, but not in Leo’s Sermons.

Add that the same verse is also quoted simultaneously from both versions by the author of the *Hypognosticon*, Book V, chapter 4, who flourished in this same century. He quotes it in such a way that this double interpretation of the verse of Job appears to have been especially a standard argument against the Pelagians, rather than something attributable to the individual practice of either author.

After reproducing the verse from the ancient version, he adds: “We have set this down according to the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which was translated from Greek into Latin speech. Hear it more clearly, for your reproach, how the same thing was translated from the Hebrew word into Latin: ‘Who can…,’” and shortly afterward: “Whether, therefore, the Seventy, from Hebrew into Greek, or another likewise, from Hebrew into Latin speech, have declared one and the same thing in unaltered words, though not in truth: that little children are guilty through the filth of sin…”

[Col. 0426B] **6.** The similar statements that Quesnellus proposes in second place, since they can be found—and are found very frequently—not only in Leo but also in other writers who undertake to discuss the same subject, prove nothing.

**7.** The third argument, based on style—even if the style of the letter is assumed to be similar, indeed identical, to that of the books *On the Calling*—proves nothing in favor of Leo, just as we have seen in the observations on Dissertation 2 that the style of the books *On the Calling* proves nothing in favor of Leo.

Indeed, since in that work, after examining the style of those books more precisely, we showed that it differs considerably from Leo’s style because of certain very dissimilar features of expression that the letter to Demetrias shares, this aspect of the style rather establishes that the author of this letter too was someone other than Leo.

**8.** After presenting long parallels of words and statements with Leo’s words and statements, to which Antelmius found and set alongside other similar passages in Prosper, Quesnellus advances another argument in section 6, no. 5. It is based on the fact that the author presents himself as a pupil of the Roman Church:

“While everywhere emulating its glory, he asserts that the apostolic see had been an example to all priests and peoples, so that they might abhor the madness of Pelagian doctrine; yet this distinction belongs to the African bishops, who were the first of all to raise the standard against the Pelagians.”

But Prosper too, although neither Italian nor Roman, is recognized as having conveyed this very point when two passages are compared with one another. First, in the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, verse 39, where he writes:

> “The Roman See of Peter was the first to cut down  
> the plague that was creeping in; it was made  
> the head of pastoral honor for the world, and whatever  
> it does not possess by arms, it holds by religion.  
> From there, the no less vigilant care of the Eastern  
> rulers shone forth and, having captured the author  
> of the wicked doctrine, constrained him by a kindly law  
> to condemn his own invention,” and so forth.

He then indicates in the following verses, which Quesnellus quoted, the later African councils that were approved by the authority of the Roman see under Zosimus.

Second, in the *Book Against the Collator*, chapter 21, elsewhere numbered 41, where, reviewing in chronological order the judgments issued against the Pelagians, he gives first place to Innocent I in these words:

“Then the machinery of these men was shattered. Then they fell together with the associates and leaders of their pride, when Innocent, of blessed memory, struck the heads of the wicked error with the apostolic sword; when the synod of the Palestinian bishops compelled Pelagius to pronounce judgment against himself and his followers; when Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, added the force of his judgment to the decrees of the African councils,” and so forth.

**9.** Those who assert that the Africans were the very first to declare war on the Pelagians rely on the assumption that Innocent did nothing against them until, warned by the Africans, he issued his famous letters in the year 417.

But from the two testimonies of Prosper just quoted it is clear that the pontiff had taken some action against the Pelagians before the Palestinian council of 415. In the first passage, the particle “from there” indicates that this Eastern council was held after some judgment of the Roman see, which had been the first to cut down the creeping plague. In the second testimony likewise, Innocent is said to have struck the heads of the wicked error before the judgment of the Palestinians.

We must therefore say that this same pontiff did something against the Pelagian heresy before the famous letters of his that survive from the year 417, although we do not know what it was. Hence it can be understood how accurately Photius wrote in the *Bibliotheca*, based on manuscript 54, copied later, toward the beginning of the sixth century: that the Pelagians and Coelestians were expelled from the Church as heretics in the time of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome.

Some reject this testimony because they think that the Pelagians were first condemned at the Council of Carthage in the year 412, as they suppose, after the death of Theophilus, which occurred at the beginning of that year. Others, unwilling entirely to reject this testimony, excerpted by Photius from such an ancient manuscript dealing with the acts of the Pelagians, think that “Theodore of Antioch” should be corrected to “Theophilus of Alexandria.”

But on the basis of Prosper’s words just cited, this passage of Photius should neither be rejected nor corrected. Everything fits perfectly if we say that, while Theophilus was still alive, Innocent did something against the Pelagians, when perhaps their leader Pelagius began to spread his heresy. That this happened before the conference held at Carthage on the first of June 411 may be gathered from Augustine’s *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 22, where he says of Pelagius: “Report began to bring us word that he was arguing against the grace of God.” He then relates that Pelagius was received on the shore of Hippo during his absence, and finally adds: “Afterward, as I recall, I saw his face once or twice, when I was extremely occupied with the business of the conference that we were to hold with the Donatist heretics.”

Thus, at least around the year 410, the Pelagian heresy began to be heard. It can be inferred from the same Augustine that it was heard especially at Rome, where Pelagius lived for a very long time (*On Original Sin*, chapter 21). This may also be deduced from the same teacher’s book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, in which he relates that Pelagius disputed with an African bishop at Rome concerning grace, prompted by a statement of Augustine’s that had been included in the book of the *Confessions*.

Since Pelagius left Rome before the conference, while Augustine was preparing for it and saw him in Africa, and then proceeded to Palestine, where he was still living in the time of Zosimus, this dispute appears to have taken place at Rome around the year 410.

This same dispute, and other similar disputes famous at Rome, together with the detestable doctrines spread there, also seem to be indicated in the book *On Original Sin*, no. 24:

“Other statements of his [Pelagius], brought to light in the city of Rome, where he had lived for a very long time and where he had previously been involved in such discussions and contentions, were made public through the diligence of faithful brothers. Pope Zosimus attached them in his letters as detestable, as you can read.”

It therefore seems plausible that a man spreading detestable doctrines at Rome against divine grace and disputing freely with Catholics was rebuked by Innocent and expelled from the Church. Perhaps compelled by this to leave the city, he came to Africa and from there eventually withdrew to Palestine.

Thus the Roman see fought against the Pelagian heresy before the Carthaginian synod held after the conference in 412—or, as we believe, toward the end of 411 (Noris, *Works*, vol. IV, *History of the Donatists*, Part II, chapter 12, p. 577). Consequently, it preceded the others by its example, as is related in chapter 10 of the letter to Demetrias.

But whatever the truth of this may be, since it is established that the author of this letter wrote the same thing as Saint Prosper, who was not Roman, however the matter may ultimately be explained, this statement contributes nothing toward establishing that the author was Roman or a pupil of the Roman Church.

**10.** This is the position under the commonly accepted hypothesis, namely, that the author of the letter is speaking of the first judgment of the Roman see in condemning the Pelagians. But we fear that his words should not be understood in this sense. For in the cited chapter 10 he says:

“Indeed, the upright hearts of countless saints resisted this impiety; and not only the learned pontiffs, but also the peoples of the universal Church, following the example of the apostolic see, abhorred the madness of the new doctrine.”

The words “following the example of the apostolic see,” which the peoples of the universal Church followed—not merely the learned pontiffs—fit only the *tractoria* of Zosimus sent throughout the world. For not only did all the learned pontiffs, that is, those of sound doctrine, confirm it by their subscriptions, but all the peoples of the entire Church, having been warned about this heresy, also abhorred the madness of the new doctrine.

In nearly the same sense Saint Prosper wrote concerning this same Zosimus in *Against the Collator*, no. 57:

“He armed the right hands of all with Peter’s sword for the beheading of the impious, so that all the Catholic bishops, subscribing to his *tractoria*, also incited all their peoples to condemn the same heresy.”

**11.** Quesnellus then proceeds through several conjectures in order to establish the occasion and time at which this letter was written by Leo in chapter 7. But since he has not yet sufficiently proved that this pontiff was its author, all such conjectures, resting on a weak foundation, collapse.

As for the date of the letter, it is said to have been written after Demetrias had returned from Africa to Rome. Quesnellus thinks that this occurred after the Vandal invasion of that province in 427. Although he does not deny that she could have returned before that time, he nevertheless adheres to the former view as the more probable, upon which he willingly builds his other conjectures.

But it is clear from a letter of Pelagius to the same virgin, written in the year 414, that Demetrias had already returned to Rome by then. It contains these words: “Provide for yourself also, in the City, a solitude” (Augustine, Appendix, vol. II, Epistle 17, chapter 23). The words “in the City” properly signify Rome. Hence Pelagius, living in the East, indicates in chapter 1 that he is replying by letters from overseas, which he had received from Juliana, Demetrias’s mother, when her daughter had evidently returned to the City.

Saint Jerome likewise, in Epistle 130, elsewhere numbered 8, written to the same woman in that year, urges her to follow the faith of Innocent, without mentioning either Aurelius, who had veiled her at Carthage, or Augustine, who had urged her to vow virginity. This indicates that she was then at Rome. The same conclusion is also drawn from Augustine’s Epistle 188 to Juliana, as the Benedictine Fathers prove at greater length in *The Life of Augustine*, Book VII, chapter 6, no. 6.

Nevertheless, several considerations suggest that our letter was composed later. Not only does chapter 10 imply that the Pelagian heresy had already been condemned throughout the world, after the *tractoria* of Zosimus, which was issued in 418, but the words of chapter 1 also indicate a long interval since the purpose of virginity that Demetrias adopted in the flower of her early age:

“If, however, I were to speak in praise of the good of virginity, it would be superfluous now to introduce that purpose of yours, which you chose from the flower of your earliest age without human exhortations, and about which, at its very beginnings, many who then held precedence in the Church rightly did not remain silent.”

These words plainly show both that Demetrias had already passed beyond the flower of youth and that those who had praised her purpose in writing had already died. Augustine, her principal praiser, died in 430; therefore this letter was written after that year.

Moreover, since chapter 10 mentions certain more concealed Pelagians, professing one thing among their own people and another among Catholics—of whom there were especially many under Pope Leo—if the letter is thought to have been composed at that time, it will be even clearer that it cannot be attributed to Leo, who then held supreme authority in the Church.

Some passages in the letter are so humble and submissive that Antelmius did not think them suitable even to Leo as archdeacon of the Roman Church (Dissertation 2, no. 20, p. 108). He especially quotes the passage in chapter 1, where Demetrias’s “condescension to her dignity” is exalted in commissioning, as though commanding, the writing of this letter, and the author’s greatest respect for her is expressed.

These words are certainly appropriate to a monk or any private person, but they are not at all suitable to an archdeacon of the Roman Church who, as Quesnellus thought, would be writing this by virtue of his office and responsibility for virgins. Let it therefore stand that there is nothing requiring us to attribute this letter to Leo; indeed, there are certain considerations that make us think it should be withdrawn from him.

**12.** The letter can be claimed for Prosper even less, since its style differs much more openly from Prosper’s than from Leo’s, as may be gathered from the observations on Dissertation 2. Even the omission of Augustine’s name, although a suitable occasion for mentioning him had arisen, separates the little work from Prosper, as Quesnellus rightly observed. For the explanation that Antelmius proposed for concealing Prosper’s name in the books *On the Calling* cannot be alleged here.

There is also the error inserted at the beginning of the letter, where Demetrias is said to have adopted her purpose of virginity without human exhortations. Prosper, who was thoroughly acquainted with the works of Saint Augustine, does not seem likely to have been unaware that this holy teacher had urged the same virgin in a celebrated letter to undertake that purpose.

The other considerations that exclude Prosper may be found in Quesnellus. Having therefore excluded Leo and Prosper, we have judged that this letter should be assigned to an unknown author.

# FIFTH DISSERTATION, OR APOLOGY FOR SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF ARLES, AND FOR THE ANCIENT RIGHTS OF THE HOLY CHURCH OF ARLES, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS

On Letter 10, elsewhere numbered 89, of Saint Leo, pope, to the bishops of the province of Vienne.

[Col. 0429]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0429C]

[753] We are undertaking a difficult task, one that no ecclesiastical writer up to the present time has attempted in every respect: namely, to vindicate Saint Hilary of Arles, an eminent glory of the Gallican Church, from the slanders and reproaches by which his most holy memory has until now been savagely assailed on account of Saint Leo’s letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne.

They commonly portray him as a man of stubborn defiance, unrestrained rashness, and insolence; as one who utterly disregarded all episcopal and metropolitan rights, who, caring nothing for ecclesiastical canons, did everything according to the inclination of his will (Marca, letter to H. Valesius); as one who turned his pontificate—or, as they say, the vicariate granted to him by the pontiff—into a tyranny; as one who, like Diotrephes, refused to receive the pontiff himself (Morinus, *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, Book I, Exercise 23); and finally as one who, through that apostolic delegation and primacy, broke out into such arrogance and haughtiness that he was already designating for himself the supreme pontificate, or, so to speak, the papacy, in Gaul (Filesac, Dissertation *On the Sacred Authority of Bishops*, chapter 9, section 12).

They assert that Hilary suffered the most just penalties for these and many other crimes, and that he was eventually restored to Leo’s favor and enrolled among the vindicated saints in no other way than by completing serious and steadfast penance for so many and such great offenses.

No one who has hitherto attempted to clear all this away and assert the innocence of so great a pontiff has come to our notice, except one author—and he a Spaniard—namely Francis Bivarius, Cistercian abbot. He published and adorned with commentaries the fictitious Chronicle of Dexter, continued by Marcus Maximus, bishop of Zaragoza, to the year 754. For the year of Christ 449, where Pseudo-Dexter relates that Hilary of Arles ended a life full of merit and holiness by a glorious death, Bivarius openly and plainly proclaims this man’s holiness and exceptional modesty. Everything that either Leo or others brought forward against him he counts among the calumnies fabricated by his adversaries. “For the rest,” he says, “to express my own opinion: having perceived the man’s extraordinary holiness, I can by no means be brought to Baronio’s view, so as to believe that Hilary committed at that time anything deserving penitence. Rather, I incline to the position that nothing less can be understood than that a dispute arose between Hilary and Leo in which both sides had a just case—like that once between Paul and Peter, when Paul reproved Peter; between Chrysostom and Epiphanius; or between Athanasius and Lucifer; and, to reach further back, between Gabriel and the guardian-prince of the Persians. For the great Leo, surrounded by many whispers and accusations, could justly have become angry with Hilary, trusting, to be sure, everything that ill-disposed persons alleged against him; and Hilary himself could nevertheless have remained free from every charge.”

We plainly do not know what deterred our writers from defending their Hilary, unless either they had not sufficiently understood the matter, hastening each according to his own purpose toward other subjects; or they feared that they would be branded as guilty of rashness and of violating the pontifical majesty if they called into question, or acquitted him of, so many crimes brought forward by Leo against Hilary—him against whose condemnation both powers had at one time armed themselves with terrifying decrees.

But in that matter they trembled with fear where there was no fear. As though Hilary could not be defended without offending Leo, when we rather think that the two apologies are so closely joined to one another that Leo’s own reputation cannot be safeguarded except by clearing Hilary in the manner we have undertaken. For the holiness of the bishop of Arles, and his contempt for worldly affairs, have been celebrated by the most distinguished ecclesiastical writers—quite apart from what we should say about the particular author of his life—to such an extent that Leo cannot be excused by any other means for having written against a man—ah, what sort of man, and how great!—things equal to which, if we believe Bivarius, could scarcely be alleged against the most criminal person, except by frankly admitting first, and subsequently demonstrating fully, that Leo had been deceived by evil arts.

Why, indeed, should we not be permitted to address our Leo in the same words with which Bernard addressed Pope Eugenius?

“They came to you in sheep’s clothing, indeed in shepherds’ clothing, in holy garb: their appearance deceived you. What wonder? You too are a human being.”

Nor would Leo himself have found it difficult to be persuaded of this about himself. As soon as he had attained the pontificate, he groaned under the weight of so great a dignity and repeatedly complained, both privately and before his people, of the almost inescapable necessity of erring in many matters. “If this condition,” he says, “holds all priests generally, how much more does it burden and bind us, for whom the very greatness of the task undertaken is a most frequent occasion of offense” (Sermon 4 on His Own Assumption, chapter 2). The fear he feared came upon him, and what he dreaded happened. In this dispute with Hilary, he allowed himself to be surrounded by the false rumors and stratagems of Hilary’s adversaries, so that, while persecuting an entirely innocent man—indeed, a wholly apostolic priest—he believed himself to be attacking in Hilary a disturber of all the churches, an enemy of the whole discipline, and guilty of almost every crime.

Yet these words are not so much mine as those of the most eminent Baronius, who speaks as follows concerning the similar case of Hilary and Mamertus:

“Do not wonder, reader, that the Roman pontiff rises so vehemently against Mamertus, a man whom the outcome proved to be distinguished for holiness. In matters belonging to contentious litigation, anyone can very easily be deceived. Something very similar happened also to holy Leo, who for virtually the same reason attacked holy Hilary with the utmost severity. Who does not know that the ears of pontiffs are often filled with false accusations and underhanded representations, and that, when they think they are doing what appears just, they harass an innocent man?” (Baronius, under the year 464, no. 8).

Binius, following his usual practice, borrowed this from Baronius and transferred it to the end of Hilary’s eleventh letter, adding to it this further testimony from Baronius:

“What happened to the most holy pontiff Saint Leo in the case of Hilary of Arles, whom he most fiercely attacked as an innocent man in Letter 89, could likewise have happened to the pontiff Hilary in the case of Mamertus through an underhanded representation.”

This great writer of the Annals, then, pronounces Hilary innocent. He should therefore rightly be considered to have wished to retract what he had said under the year 445, where he discussed the whole case in rather harsh words and without sufficiently weighing the facts. We shall follow his later reflections, as the wiser ones, and, imitating him, correct his earlier statements in this dissertation that we are beginning.

So that the discussion may proceed in a more orderly and lucid fashion, it will be divided into three parts. In them we shall examine everything that Leo brought forward against Hilary in that celebrated letter. The first part, therefore, will concern the case of Celidonius, which set this whole turmoil in motion; there we shall discuss the right of the bishop of Arles over the province of Vienne. The second will concern the bishop’s superordination in the place of Projectus; there we shall discuss the right of that same bishop of Arles over the Narbonnese provinces and the other provinces that Hilary claimed for himself. Finally, in the third part, setting aside all prejudices, we shall bring the remaining charges contained in Leo’s letter back under examination.

## PART ONE. THE CASE OF CELIDONIUS

### CHAPTER I. The origin and position of the entire controversy

When blessed Hilary had been raised from the monastery of Lérins, to which he had formerly devoted himself, to the see of Arles in place of the deceased Honoratus, around the year 429 of Christ, he regarded nothing as more sacred than to feed by his word the flock of Christ entrusted to him and to govern it with pastoral care.

Just as his care, insofar as he was a bishop, concerned only the Church of Arles, so it extended to all the churches and bishops of the province of Vienne by virtue of metropolitan jurisdiction, which the bishop of Arles had long possessed.

In carrying out these pastoral journeys, he usually had as his companion that great Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, whom both the fame of his holiness and his apostolic prudence extraordinarily commended. I believe that Hilary summoned him to share this responsibility not only for that reason, but also because at that time there were several cities of the province of Vienne that did not belong to Roman rule but obeyed the Burgundians.

[Note: During the period in which Hilary lived, only the part of Savoy granted by Aetius was in the possession of the Burgundians, who still honored the Romans as their masters. Several cities of the province of Vienne came under their power only after Valentinian’s death and the collapse of the Western Empire. During Hilary’s lifetime, however, they obeyed the Romans, together with Maxima Sequanorum and the city of Auxerre itself, as is clear from the Life of Saint Germanus. See Pagius, under the year 445, no. 12.]

After the Burgundians had been conquered by Aetius, Savoy had been left to them, to be divided thereafter with the native inhabitants in such a way that, as their boundaries were subsequently extended by force of arms into neighboring regions, they established themselves in Lugdunensis Prima, Maxima Sequanorum, Vienne, and other provinces. Hilary could therefore have sought Germanus’s help for this reason: among peoples under another jurisdiction, Germanus was highly esteemed as one of their own countrymen, and episcopal authority and ordination would consequently have carried greater weight.

Whatever the truth about this explanation, Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, relates in the Life of our Hilary that when Hilary and Germanus, while touring the province, arrived at a certain city, their arrival was not known before a multitude of people streamed together from every direction in eager competition. Most of them were not from the lowest common people but from the more distinguished and honorable classes. They had one voice and one accusation against Celidonius: namely, that he had formerly taken as his consort a woman who had previously been married, which was entirely contrary to the canons; and that, having served in a secular prefecture before receiving ordination, he had condemned certain people to the ultimate punishment.

After hearing this, Germanus and Hilary, men firmly devoted to ecclesiastical discipline, immediately convened a synod of the most reputable bishops. They prepared the case and declared that Celidonius, having been convicted, ought to be removed from his see. But it is better to hear Honoratus himself recount in his own words both what we have just related and what followed Celidonius’s deposition.

“In their journeys,” he says, “who could adequately explain how much benefit his presence brought to the Gallic cities, when he repeatedly sought out Saint Germanus, with whom he discussed the life of priests and ministers, as well as their progress and failings? When his arrival became known, the zeal of nobles and commoners alike, inflamed, flocked to both men, asserting that Celidonius had taken as his consort a woman who had previously been married, which the authority of the Apostolic See and the provisions of the canons prohibit. At the same time they alleged that, after serving in a secular administration, he had condemned some people to capital punishment.

“Moved by the novelty of so serious a charge, they ordered witnesses to be prepared. The most reputable priests from other places assembled; the matter was examined with every degree of reason and prudence, and the accusation was confirmed by testimony. A true and straightforward decision was applied: the man whom the rules of Scripture excluded ought, by his own will, to remove himself.

“He believed that he ought to appeal to Rome, and there he maintained that he had been condemned with unjust severity. When the blessed man learned this, he set out on foot and entered Rome in haste, without a horse or pack animal. After paying his respects at the shrines of the Apostles and martyrs, he immediately presented himself to blessed Pope Leo, offering dutiful service with reverence and humbly requesting that he regulate the condition of the churches in the customary manner. He maintained that certain men in Gaul had deservedly received a public sentence, while in Rome they were attending the sacred altars.

“He asked and insisted that, if the pope had willingly received his representation, he should order its correction in private. He had come for official duties, not for litigation; to report what had been done in the manner of a protest, not an accusation; and, if the pope wished otherwise, he would not become troublesome.”

Hilary did not immediately leave Rome. He awaited a council of bishops—namely, those who happened by chance to be staying in Rome at that time. The Easterners called such a synod an *endemousa* (ἐνδημοῦσαν), that is, a synod of bishops residing in the place. In that synod many things were brought forward on both sides. Saint Leo sent its Acts together with his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne.

“Thus,” he says, “the order of events demonstrates in written documents what was done and completed among us in the case of Celidonius the bishop, and what Hilary said when he was heard in the presence of that same bishop” (Letter 10).

The author of Hilary’s Life undoubtedly had those Acts in his possession, but refrained from reviewing them, lest he seem to renew the disagreement that had already been settled in heavenly peace between the two most blessed pontiffs. “Because,” he says, “I do not dare, even in a narrative, to subject the judgments of such great men—especially men already called to heavenly grace—to debate, it is enough to say briefly: that he alone withstood so many; that he was in no way frightened by their threats; that he instructed those conducting the inquiry; that he defeated those disputing with him; that he did not yield to the powerful; and that, when his life was in danger, he absolutely refused to enter into communion with the man whom he had condemned along with such great men.”

Here we certainly encounter something at once astonishing and grievous about the weakness or ignorance of the human condition. Behold how differently Leo and Honoratus depict Hilary—each a bishop, each conspicuous for holiness, and each devoted to the truth.

Saint Leo writes (Letter 10, chapter 3) that Hilary had nothing reasonable to answer in the council of holy priests. Honoratus praises him for having alone withstood so many, instructed those conducting the inquiry, and defeated those disputing with him.

Leo complains that Hilary had resorted to such hidden matters of his heart that no layman could state them and no priest could hear them. Honoratus says nothing of the kind. Rather, he marvels that Hilary was not at all frightened by threats, did not yield to the powerful, and, when his life was in danger, absolutely refused to enter into communion with the man whom he had condemned along with such great men.

Leo censures the swelling of Hilary’s mind, inflated by a spirit of pride, and his excessively impious presumption. He says that Hilary was such a man that he refused to be subject to blessed Apostle Peter and repeatedly sought a sentence of condemnation through rash and insolent words.

Honoratus, on the contrary, testifies that Hilary immediately presented himself to blessed Leo, offered him dutiful service with reverence, and humbly asked him to regulate the condition of the churches in the customary manner.

Auxiliaris, the prefect who was then in Rome and appears to have been an eyewitness, supports Honoratus. Among other things, he writes to Hilary as follows:

“But since you are steadfast in your purpose and always the same, and are never carried away by the gall of agitation, just as you are not lifted up by any alluring pleasures of joy, I do not remember even the least action of Your Beatitude being darkened by the taint of arrogance. But people are impatient when we speak in this way, as we know ourselves to be. Moreover, the ears of the Romans are drawn by a certain tenderness,” and so forth.

Finally, Leo bitterly complains that Hilary, conscious of his own merit, believed he should withdraw by a shameful flight when he was summoned to answer the case. But that other author attributes it to Hilary’s wisdom and courage that, when guards had been placed over him and the harshness of winter was raging, he believed the guards—whom he had not been able to persuade by reason—should be left behind.

From the first moment of his arrival in Rome, Hilary had already warned Leo that he had come for official duties, not for litigation; to report what had been done in the manner of a protest, not an accusation; and that, if Leo wanted something else, Hilary would not become troublesome.

All this is reported by Honoratus, who wrote after both men had died. He should therefore be considered free and exempt from any desire either to flatter or to deceive.

The bishop of Arles, foreseeing that Leo had decided to reopen Celidonius’s case completely before himself and to place greater trust in the witnesses produced by that bishop than in all those who had testified against Celidonius before the synod of the Gallic bishops, thought it better to depart from Rome. He feared that, while contending for his own prerogatives and those of the Gallic churches, he might inadvertently or too combatively say something that would inflame the anger of the Roman pontiff rather than advance his own cause. He also feared that, by awaiting a judgment which Saint Leo was prepared to issue to the detriment of the earlier one, he might create a prejudice against the authority of councils and bishops—one that later ages might draw upon as an example.

The letter that the Roman pontiff later wrote to the bishops of the province, and the imperial constitution that he caused Valentinian Augustus to direct against Hilary, testify to how bitterly Leo bore Hilary’s departure from the city.

Such writings did not, however, immediately follow Hilary’s departure. After he had left, Celidonius was acquitted as bishop, Saint Leo says, and the judgment was removed which had been expressed in this form: that, as the husband of a widow, he could not hold the priesthood.

Then Leo wrote a brief letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne to make them better informed about the entire matter and to indicate that, after Hilary had been deprived of metropolitan authority over the province of Vienne, that authority had been transferred to the bishop of Vienne according to ancient right.

Leo sent this letter not only to the province of Vienne but also, as its title indicates, to the other bishops throughout Gaul—that is, to those established throughout the seven provinces.

This letter, if indeed it is genuine, seems to have served as a prelude to that longer treatise which we are discussing. Since the matter was of the greatest importance, it had to be worked out in a more elaborate style. Indeed, the pontiff did not decide to send it to Gaul until he had turned the entire matter over in his mind for a long time and with great care.

Accordingly, an interval of five months is found between the two letters. The latter was issued on the eighth day before the Ides of June, at the same time, namely, as Valentinian’s constitution; the earlier on the eighth or third day before the Ides of January. This fits very well with the time of Hilary’s return to Gaul, which occurred while the severity of winter was raging, as we related above from his Life.

Meanwhile the bishop of Arles returned to his own church. And, so as to omit nothing that might, in keeping with priestly gentleness and charity, appease the angered Leo, he “turned his whole self,” Honoratus says, “with inclined humility toward calming his mind,” first sending Saint Ravennius, then a priest and later his own successor. He then sent Saint Nectarius and Saint Constantius, eminent priests.

Although Hilary employed this conciliatory measure to preserve, insofar as it depended on him, the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, do not suppose that he therefore surrendered his right, as the most eminent Cardinal Baronius believed (under the year 445, no. 18). Baronius also adds that Hilary offered no small example of Christian modesty: although so harassed by both pontiff and emperor, he nevertheless remained entirely quiet and did not defend his cause by publishing counter-apologies, even though he possessed both the force of eloquence necessary for doing so and the support of rights claimed by his predecessors.

On the contrary, Hilary actually did what he could do. Always steadfast in his purpose and always consistent, he maintained the rights of his church to the very end of his life and vigorously defended them with the eloquence at his command. This is demonstrated both by the fragment of the prefect Auxiliaris’s letter preserved in his Life and by the author of the Life himself, who writes: “How much he dictated in this case, I cannot in any way connect with this work,” and so forth. We shall discuss this more fully below.

There is no doubt, however, that, yielding to the requests of the prefect Auxiliaris, Hilary occasionally adapted himself to what he called the excessive “tenderness” of the Romans. Whatever could be conceded with a completely intact right of his church, he granted with the greatest willingness.

“The ears of the Romans,” that clear-minded prefect says, “are drawn by a certain tenderness. If Your Holiness occasionally accommodates yourself to it, you gain a great deal while losing nothing. Grant me this, and calm the small clouds by the brightness of a slight change.”

This is sufficient for the present. We must now examine more carefully the charges brought against Hilary on the occasion of this controversy. Nearly all writers attack him as an invader of another’s jurisdiction, because he dared to depose Celidonius, a bishop who was not only innocent but in no way subject to him. Before everything else, however, we must inquire in which province Celidonius served as bishop.

## CHAPTER II. In which province did Celidonius hold the episcopate? Was it in Maxima Sequanorum? An examination of the passage in the Life of Saint Romanus the Abbot

Several questions arise here that must be discussed. Once clarified, they will shed much light on the entire controversy.

For it is asked: Of what city—or at least of what province of Gaul—was Celidonius bishop? Was he within the seven provinces, or in one of the remaining Gallic provinces that formed a separate body? Again, was he merely a bishop, or had he also been endowed with metropolitan authority?

It is very important not to overlook these questions, since the whole crux of the dispute depends upon them. The matter concerning Hilary must be judged very differently if he deposed a bishop from his own province, differently if he deposed a metropolitan. Again, the state of the question is entirely different if he did this within the province of Vienne; different if he did it in one of the other seven provinces; and different again if he did it outside this particular body of provinces—for example, in Lugdunensis, Maxima Sequanorum, or another province. These possibilities must therefore be separated as carefully as possible, so that it may be discovered where Hilary either erred or appeared to err.

Cardinal Baronius believed Celidonius to have been bishop of the province of Vienne, although he does not appear to have investigated the matter. This opinion took root in everyone’s mind until John Francis Chiffletius produced, in his History of the City and Church of Vesontio, or Besançon, a certain fragment of the Life of Saint Romanus the Abbot. It had been taken from a manuscript of the monastery of Jura and transmitted to Chiffletius by Peter Francis Chiffletius, S.J.

[Note: We shall defend the authenticity of this fragment in the observations, part I, chapter 1, nos. 4 and following, and throughout chapter 2, where we shall also confirm, by other documents, that Celidonius was bishop of Vesontio.]

For this fragment expressly calls Celidonius bishop of Vesontio. “Hilary,” it says, “with the support of patrician and prefectural favor, had removed the venerable Celidonius, patriarch of the aforesaid metropolis of Vesontio, from his episcopal see without any valid reason, claiming for himself an unjust monarchy over Gaul.”

It is remarkable how eagerly and favorably this was received by all students of ecclesiastical history. They understood, of course, how much light it would cast upon Hilary’s case, how clearly it would reveal the fairness of the sentence of Pope Leo, and how greatly it would illuminate this most distinguished branch of ecclesiastical discipline.

The entire chorus of scholars therefore joined Chiffletius’s opinion and henceforth believed Celidonius to have been bishop of the Church of Besançon. Among them were J. Sirmondus, *Councils of Gaul*, volume I; the illustrious Peter de Marca, *Dissertation on the Primacy of Lyon*, no. 77, and *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, book V; the continuator of that work, Étienne Baluze; Francis Hallier, *On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*; and many others throughout their writings.

I scarcely allow myself to be separated from this learned company; nevertheless, I do allow it, because many considerations move and persuade me that this Celidonius, the subject of the controversy, was never bishop of Vesontio. This fragment of the Life of Saint Romanus rightly arouses my suspicion that it was inserted into that Life by interpolation—not to say openly through fraud or error.

The Life of Romanus was recently published in its entirety by Bollandus under February 28. There I saw that fragment inserted in its proper place. I also read the whole Life of Romanus carefully, together with the history of his brother Lupicinus and of Eugendus, who succeeded him, which the same author appended. I did this in order to detect the character of the writer and to investigate whether anything bore upon the matter we are treating.

That author declares himself to have been a disciple of Eugendus and relates many things about him which he testifies that he learned with his own eyes. Thus, if we grant without argument that Romanus and Lupicinus were contemporaries of Hilary, the author—who professes himself a disciple of Eugendus, their disciple—must be believed to have flourished either toward the end of the fifth century or at the beginning of the sixth—that is, around the year 515 or 520.

Yet many features of these narratives seem entirely foreign to that period and strongly suggest a much later age. We must therefore say either that the author is lying when he makes himself a disciple of Eugendus, or that, if he wrote at the time alleged, these works were corrupted and interpolated by some frivolous writer of a later age.

Once either of these alternatives has been established, no complete confidence can be placed in the entire composition. Distinguishing what is true from what is false, and what is genuine from what has been added, would then require lengthy investigation and laborious effort. No one is unaware how often and how shamelessly both practices have been carried out by certain people.

A burning desire for ancestral nobility sometimes drives people into delirium, as Baronius says in a similar case. Nothing is more common among monuments of this kind than writings either wholly spurious or at least mutilated, supplemented, and interpolated in part, and sprinkled with countless little tales, revelations, and miracles fabricated for fraud or as a mockery of piety. Bollandus himself therefore rightly thought that, at the beginning of his work, he should warn the reader not to place light and careless trust in such histories. He even pointed out several works whose sincere author had been subjected to the hands of tale-sellers and whose writings had been filled with rubbish and ravings.

In my judgment, the Lives of Saints Romanus, Lupicinus, and Eugendus have come down to us in this condition. They contain the following words, which I find it difficult to believe were in use at the end of the fifth or beginning of the sixth century:

*Repausare* (“to rest again”); *super formulam conquiescere* (“to repose upon the bier”); *religio* and *religiosus*, used for the monastic order and a monk; *Father Romanus* and *Father Lupicinus*, in the sense now current among monks; and “the wooden soles which, he says, Gallic monasteries commonly call *socci*.” These and several other expressions plainly bear the stamp of a more recent Gallic usage.

The author uses the unqualified noun “priest,” which in earlier centuries meant a bishop, for a presbyter; “patriarchs” for metropolitan bishops; “basilicas” for a monastery’s chapel; *epistola regularis* (“regular letter”) for a decretal; and “archimandrite” for an abbot—a title scarcely known to Western monks at that time. All these features point to a later age of the writer.

The same is true of the expression “to break the bonds of profession.” Since the author appears to understand this as referring to monastic vows of the kind made today, it cannot belong to the sixth century.

He speaks of Saint Romanus’s dalmatic, which Lupicinus is said to have received from him and, at his own death, handed on to his disciple Eugendus—the garment which Lupicinus himself had used while alive. It is not easy to determine whether the author means a sacred festive garment or an ordinary one. We know of no ordinary garment for common and unrestricted use that was adorned with such a name. Nor was the dalmatic, which is now the distinctive garment of deacons serving at the altar, readily granted for use to just any clerics or monks.

At the end of the sixth century, Aregius, bishop of Gap in Gaul, both personally while he was staying in Rome and later through his deacon, earnestly requested Pope Gregory the Great that he and his archdeacon be permitted to use dalmatics. The pontiff replied that, since consideration of reason did not allow him rashly and suddenly to grant this “new” privilege, the fulfillment of the request had been delayed. “But now,” he says, “calling back to mind the goodness of your charity, by this letter of our authority we grant what you have asked, and we have granted that you and your archdeacon should be adorned with the use of dalmatics. We have sent those dalmatics, carried by our most beloved son Cyriacus the abbot” (Gregory the Great, book VII, Letter 3, indiction 2).

If a dalmatic was scarcely granted even to a bishop, who would believe that Romanus the presbyter used one, together with Lupicinus and Eugendus, who perhaps had not been initiated into the sacred orders? It is therefore scarcely conceivable either that Lupicinus assigned a sacred vestment to Eugendus for ordinary use, as these words perhaps suggest—“Know that this dalmatic, approved for you among the benefits received, is to be assigned to you”—or that so magnificent a mention would be made of an ordinary garment, or finally that it was then lawful for these men to put on a sacred dalmatic for sacred ministries, when its use was scarcely granted to a bishop a hundred years later.

In the Life of Saint Eugendus, the author writes that Eugendus reintroduced in the monastery the pious reading that is customarily practiced at table. What decline in piety and discipline must have entered there if a custom that was practiced everywhere in monasteries had already disappeared? Who, however, would believe that this happened immediately after the death of the celebrated founder of that ascetic establishment, while his immediate successor was still alive?

He includes a story about two monks traveling as pilgrims to Rome, whom he brings back from there laden with relics of the holy Apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew. Anyone who has read even one letter of Gregory the Great knows how much this conflicts with the customs of that age—namely, Letter 30 of book IV, addressed to the Empress Constantina, whom he addresses in these words:
