“Greater sorrow took hold of me because of that rash act which I can neither do nor dare to do … For in Rome, or throughout the regions of the West, it is altogether intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should perhaps wish to touch the bodies of the saints. If anyone should presume to do so, it is certain that such rashness will in no way remain unpunished … Therefore, most serene lady, who could now be so rash as knowingly to dare not merely to touch their bodies, but even to inspect them in any way?”

Moreover, at that time a filing or scraping from the chains in which the Apostles had been bound was regarded as a great gift. Thus those monks must either have been impostors, or the author of the Life is more recent than he wishes to appear, or this little work was interpolated.

He discusses the founders of the coenobitic life in such a way that Basil appears as the first of all, followed by the Fathers of Lérins, then Pachomius, and finally Cassian as though he were the last of all. Who could believe that this was written by an author of the fifth century, one not far removed from Cassian’s own time? Who would think that such a disturbance of chronology belonged to an ancient writer?

Furthermore, when he compares the constitutions and manner of life of all these men with the laws of Jura, he says that the latter accord more closely with the customs of the Gauls than do the constitutions of those Easterners—plainly counting the monks of Lérins and Marseille among the Easterners.

To exalt Eugendus’s supreme piety and religious devotion, he writes that Eugendus was afflicted by continual illnesses, yet in such a way that he never failed in the canonical course until the end. Here he appears to be speaking of the task of the canonical hours, as we call it. No one, however, will deny that this was certainly not then called “canonical,” nor imposed by ecclesiastical law.

He says that Saint Lupicinus abstained from tasting water itself for approximately eight years before his death. This is of doubtful credibility, as is also the story of a certain Agrippinus, a count of Gaul falsely accused before the emperor and divinely preserved.

He mentions a certain Sabinus, an abbot of Interamnis in Lyon, whom he says was a companion of Romanus. Yet the most ancient monuments of this monastery are entirely silent about him, while they record other abbots who lived during that period.

If the reader attends to all these matters, he will easily decide that the Life of Saint Romanus is of such a character that nothing certain at all can be established from the reports of its author. For the demonstrated spuriousness of some parts completely removes credibility from the rest.

Yet even if the credibility of the other portions did not waver, I would still regard as certainly spurious—and I do regard as such—the section dealing with Celidonius’s deposition, which deceived so many learned men. It appears to be a marginal annotation by some scholarly person. When he encountered the mention of Hilary, bishop of Arles, ordaining the monk Romanus near Vesontio, a city lying at such a great distance from Arles, he was reminded of that letter of Saint Leo in which Leo attacks Hilary as claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul. He therefore did not hesitate, in the same period and during the same journey, to suppose both that Romanus had been ordained and that Celidonius had been deposed by Hilary.

This conjecture was also remarkably strengthened by the popular tradition of the people of Besançon concerning Celidonius, the bishop of their city. A monk of Jura had easily absorbed this tradition together with the rest from the Breviary of Vesontio, from which Chiffletius likewise drew it. If Chiffletius had been less devoted to the stories of his homeland and more devoted to truth, he would not have sold childish tales as certain and indisputable histories.

That scholarly person therefore judged that his conjecture ought to be written in the margin. From there, through the ignorance or carelessness of scribes, it later slipped into the text.

So that everyone may judge our conjectures more accurately, we place before their eyes the whole passage of the Life of Saint Romanus that we are discussing. What we believe was not written by the author of the Life but was added and inserted by another, more recent writer is printed there in italic type.

[Col. 0438D] “Having heard,” says the author of the *Life*, “of the fame of those mentioned, Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, having sent clerics on this business, caused the most blessed Roman to meet him not far from the city of Vesontio. Extolling his zeal and way of life in a most worthy eulogy, he honorably permitted him to return to the monastery after conferring upon him the dignity of the presbyterate.”

“For the aforesaid Hilary, supported by the favor of Patricius and the Prefect, had driven the aforementioned Celedonius, a venerable patriarch of the said metropolis, from his episcopal see without any legitimate reason, claiming for himself an unlawful monarchy over the churches throughout Gaul. Consequently, after being found to have acted improperly at Rome in the hearing of the most blessed Pope Leo, and after Celedonius had likewise been restored to the episcopate, he was regularly rebuked by apostolic authority for his illicit usurpation.

“Finally, there exists from that time a canonical letter of the aforesaid venerable pope to the bishops of Gaul, containing an examination of the proceedings and inserted into the canons; in it, by trampling down Hilary’s excess, he restored the ancient privilege of the metropolitans throughout Gaul. Thus the most blessed Roman, having received the priesthood, returned to the monastery, as we have already said above, 766 and so forth.”

Thus far from the *Life of Saint Romanus*.

That these words were not written by the author of the *Life*, but were added by another person, can easily be understood, first, from the continuity of the discourse, with which they appear in no way to agree or cohere. [Col. 0439A] Rather, this is a patch having nothing whatever to do with the *Life of Saint Romanus*, and reflecting the meditation of an idle reader.

After the author had narrated Saint Romanus’s ordination and had, as it were, accompanied him as he returned to his monastery, the mention of Hilary is taken up again, although it ought already to have been concluded, since Romanus had returned to his own affairs. Then the story of Celedonius’s deposition, which had no relevance whatever to the subject, is expounded in an untimely narrative, so that the writer is compelled once again to speak of Saint Romanus’s ordination and return, lest the discourse, interrupted by this extraneous narrative, be left completely disjointed. “Thus,” he says, “the most blessed Roman, having received the priesthood, returned to the monastery, as we have already said above,” and so forth.

2. When the genuine author of the *Life* first narrated Saint Romanus’s ordination, he mentioned Hilary in terms of the highest honor and bestowed upon him the title of holiness: “Saint Hilary,” he says, “bishop of Arles.” But immediately afterward, when the author of that patch takes up his pen, he represents Hilary as though casting him down from a heavenly seat. He not only ceases to call him holy, saying instead “the aforesaid Hilary,” but also portrays him as afflicted by unrestrained ambition, driven to do everything by force, claim for himself the rights of others, expel bishops from their own churches, and, “without any legitimate reason,” finally ravage all the churches of Gaul by tyrannical power. No one will say that this is the style of one and the same writer, or that it proceeds from the same spring, which “from the same opening pours forth sweet and bitter water” (James 3:11). Rather, it is the offspring of two writers: one had a good understanding of Saint Hilary’s merits; the other knew Hilary from no source except Leo’s letter.

3. He calls Celedonius the patriarch of the metropolis of Vesontio; but at the beginning of the sixth century this was not customary among Westerners as a designation for metropolitans.

4. When the author of the *Life*, Germanus, describes Saint Romanus’s ordination, he uses the expression “the dignity of the priesthood was conferred”; this word was ordinarily used in that period to designate priests. But the other writer, who stitched on the patch, uses the word *sacerdotium*, which, when standing alone, was understood only of bishops, and never of priests except with the addition “of the second order,” or some similar expression.

5. It is said that Leo’s letter against Hilary of Arles was inserted into the canons—that is, into a book of canons, as the phrase may be interpreted. Yet only three books of canons occur to us that would have been in use during the sixth century, whether in the Roman or the Gallican Church.

In the Roman Church there was the most ancient book of all, which we are now publishing for the first time and which remained in use until approximately the time of Pope Symmachus. Around the beginning of the sixth century, 767 a new collection—or rather translation—of the canons, produced by Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, succeeded it. To this was appended another collection of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, from Siricius to Anastasius.

In the Gallican Church, no other collection was received until the time of Charlemagne—about whom we shall discuss expressly below, in Dissertation 16—except the ancient collection compiled from Eastern sources, which one might most appropriately call the book of the canons of the universal Church. For these Eastern canons were, as it were, the common law of all the Eastern and Western churches, at least after the Council of Chalcedon. By adding the canons of their own councils to these canons, the several churches—for example, the Gallican, Spanish, and British churches—constructed books of canons proper to themselves.

It is this kind of book that you must understand when the patch says that Leo’s letter was inserted into the canons. For the Gallican book did not contain the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Although the bishops of Gaul esteemed those decrees highly and used them in their councils whenever occasion arose, they did not incorporate them into the Gallican book unless the bishops assembled in synod had expressly decreed that they should be regarded as law by inserting them into their own canons. This was done, for example, with the letter of Pope Innocent I to Exuperius by the Council of Agde, canon 9.

As for the Dionysian collection, or any collection earlier than Dionysius’s, we find in neither of them Leo’s letter against Hilary. Neither was in use in the Gallican churches before the time of Charlemagne. Therefore the author of this annotation was not living in the sixth century, since at that time no officially authorized collections existed in which the celebrated letter of Leo had been inserted.

This letter is contained in the printed collection circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, although I have not found it in the manuscript copies of that work. But this collection was not published before the time of Charlemagne; indeed, it seems to have begun to appear toward the end of the eighth century, as Father Pithoeus notes in his *Glossary of the Capitularies*. The bishops of Gaul made extensive use of this Isidorian collection in synods held during and after the time of Charlemagne, as did the synods of other churches. Following their example, the compilers of later periods—Burchard, Yvo, Gratian, and others—embraced the same Isidorian collection, without distinguishing among the letters that that impostor had forged or fraudulently presented as having been forged by someone else.

6. Finally, Gregory of Tours makes the history of Romanus much more recent than does the author of this *Life*, whom, as a writer of uncertain name and one interpolated in many places, we judge must be placed after Gregory. We have examined this portion of the *Life of Saint Romanus* with particular care, 768 because those who have made Celedonius bishop of Vesontio have hitherto been guided by no other basis than this author’s testimony. How little confidence that testimony deserves I leave to the reader to judge.

Although, in accusing this passage of being spurious, we have distinguished it from the rest of the written *Life*, it is not my intention to accept the remaining material as certain and indisputable either—not even the report that Romanus was ordained by Hilary not far from Vesontio.

If this was done by the bishop of Arles, he would have sinned against the canons all the more seriously, since he could claim no right by which he was permitted to ordain priests in another’s parish. Since, then, neither the author of Hilary’s *Life* reported this event, nor Leo nor Celedonius—who could not have been unaware of it—charged Hilary with it, one must conclude that the author of this *Life* drew the story from false rumors or popular opinion and carelessly committed it to writing.

If Hilary nevertheless did perform this act, I say that it was permitted to him through Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. It is well known how close a relationship existed between the two men. Because of that relationship, just as Hilary permitted Eucherius to attend and sign the First Council of Orange together with the bishops of Vienne and the neighboring provinces, so Eucherius allowed Hilary to consecrate as a priest in his diocese of Lyon a man distinguished for his piety. The monastery of the Jura, whose territory is still subject to the jurisdiction of Lyon, was also under that diocese. Since neither Geneva, which belongs to the province of Vienne, nor Lyon nor Vesontio is very far from it, it is not difficult to believe that Hilary, while visiting the churches of his own province, met with Germanus of Auxerre and Eucherius of Lyon.

Let us now proceed to other proofs by which we shall show that Celedonius was not bishop of Vesontio, indeed not bishop of any metropolitan city.

## CHAPTER III. It is proved by other arguments that Celedonius was neither bishop of Vesontio nor bishop of any metropolitan see.

Once the testimony drawn from the *Life of Saint Romanus* has been discredited, no other evidence remains by which metropolitan dignity at Vesontio can be claimed for Celedonius. [Note: [Col. 0439D] This chapter is refuted in Observations, Part I, chapters 2 and 3; however, in chapter 3, no. 8, we show more probably that Celedonius was not a metropolitan but a mere bishop who presided over the chief city of the Sequani. [Col. 0440D]] Nor is there any reason that even slightly supports assigning another metropolis to him. On the contrary, there is no single consideration that does not make it plain that he was not a metropolitan.

[Col. 0441A] First, in the account that Leo gives of this affair in his letter to the bishops of Vienne, and in that very part of the letter where he gathers together everything that, in Leo’s judgment, Hilary had arrogated to himself contrary to the canons and the rules of discipline, not even a word can be read from which the faintest suspicion could arise that Celedonius possessed metropolitan dignity. Let every syllable and every letter of chapter three be examined, especially the section dealing with Celedonius: nothing of the kind will be found.

There Leo imputes only this offense to Hilary: that he had deposed a bishop who deserved no such treatment, since he had not been convicted of the crime for which the penalty of deposition was imposed. Leo also reproves him for having uttered many things contrary to the reverence due to the apostle Peter and to priestly gentleness.

But with respect to that matter, Leo does not charge him with lacking jurisdiction over Celedonius, with diminishing the rights of any metropolitan bishop, or with violating the boundaries of another province. He would certainly not have omitted these points; rather, he would have pressed them with the greatest force, since they would have made the authority and sacred character of the Nicene canons appear even more seriously violated. Thus, when he discusses the case of Projectus, he immediately sets against Hilary the established boundaries of the provinces, which it is unlawful for metropolitans to cross: “What is Hilary seeking in another province?” and so forth.

He presses nothing of this kind on behalf of Celedonius. Instead, he makes only this point against Hilary’s unjust deposition of him: that the falsity of the charge brought against Celedonius had been exposed by the manifest response of the witnesses.

2. Let an affirmative argument follow this argument—which, although merely negative, nevertheless appears decisive. That Saint Leo did not recognize metropolitan dignity in Celedonius, but rather openly acknowledged that Celedonius was subject to Hilary’s metropolitan authority, is proved by Leo’s words declaring that Hilary’s sentence against Celedonius ought to have been carried into effect if the accusation of having taken a widow as his wife had been established by lawful and trustworthy witnesses.

“For the sentence pronounced against him would have stood,” he says, “if the truth of the charges had been established.” What is this, in very truth, except an endorsement of Hilary’s metropolitan rights and an acknowledgment of his jurisdiction over Celedonius? Leo would certainly not have done so if Celedonius possessed the same rights in some province—especially if he was in Maxima Sequanorum, a province whose subjection to his own authority Hilary had never even dreamed of contemplating.

Hilary would then genuinely have possessed a right over another province, although he was so bitterly accused of having sought that right improperly.

3. We derive another proof from other words of the same letter, in chapter 2:

“Let your fraternity therefore acknowledge with us that, out of reverence for the apostolic see, it has been consulted by the priests of your province through countless reports, and that judgments have been either reconsidered or confirmed through appeals in various cases, as ancient custom required,” and so forth.

If the matter concerned a metropolitan or a bishop from a province other than Vienne, together with his appeal, why would Leo call upon the bishops of the province of Vienne to recall the reports and consultations sent by their own priests, and the appeals formerly lodged with the apostolic see according to the ancient custom of that province? Why does he not instead mention appeals brought from the province over which Celedonius presided by metropolitan right, if that is what his opponents maintain?

Leo did not do this. Rather, he drew examples of appeals from the province of Vienne, because the question truly concerned the appeal of a bishop situated within that province.

4. If Celedonius had not belonged to that province but to Maxima Sequanorum, why did Saint Leo appeal to the bishops of the former province rather than those of the latter against Hilary? Why did he send letters to the bishops of Vienne rather than to the Sequani, whom it would certainly have been easier to stir up against Hilary, since they were bound to him by no relationship, whereas the bishops of Vienne held Hilary in the highest esteem because of his outstanding reputation for holiness and learning, as well as his skill in conducting affairs?

“But,” you will say, “Saint Leo did in fact write to the bishops of Maxima Sequanorum.” We have the learned Sirmondus as witness to this. In listing at the end of the first volume of the *Councils of Gaul* the additions to be included in his notes, he says that in an old document the letter in question is addressed not only to the bishops of the province of Vienne but also to those of Maxima Sequanorum, in this form:

“To all the most beloved bishops established throughout the provinces of Maxima Sequanorum and Vienne, Leo.”

I strongly suspect that this old document is not very old, but rather comes from the same workshop as that spurious patch attached to the *Life of Saint Romanus*. Who, then, would prefer a sheet of uncertain age and reliability to all the copies, both printed and handwritten, that have hitherto presented this letter to us without any mention of the bishops of Maxima Sequanorum?

Second, if the letter had likewise been intended for the bishops of this province, why would nothing in its sequence indicate that the pontiff was addressing them? Yet throughout the entire letter, wherever it is extant, there is not even the slightest trace of this. On the contrary, it everywhere indicates that he is addressing the bishops of the single province of Vienne, as when he says in the preface: “Let your fraternity acknowledge that the apostolic see has been consulted by the priests of your province,” and so forth.

Third, the very form of the title exposes the impostor. Who has ever read of a “province of the Viennenses”? We do read of the city of the Viennenses, inhabited by the Viennensian people, just as we read of the city of the Lugdunenses, inhabited by the Lugdunensian people. But just as one does not say “the First Province of the Lugdunenses,” “the Second Province of the Lugdunenses,” and so forth, so the province of the Viennenses was never so called. The people called Viennenses did not occupy the entire province to which they gave their name, but only a small part of a province divided among twelve other peoples.

Against this opinion of ours concerning Celedonius’s episcopate, 771 someone may object to these words of Saint Leo, in which Hilary is accused of claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul and of transferring to his own authority the dignity due to metropolitan priests. These words are commonly thought to confirm the view that Celedonius was judged and deposed as a bishop outside the province of Vienne.

I reply that, in this letter, we must distinguish certain matters that concern Celedonius’s case, others that concern Projectus’s case, and still others that are common to both. The material contained in the preface belongs to the latter category. There Leo addresses all of Hilary’s alleged excesses in general: some concern Projectus, some Celedonius, and some both.

Leo had Projectus’s case before his eyes when he accused Hilary of claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul. On that occasion he burst out with the words: “What is Hilary seeking in another province?” and so forth.

That this cannot be understood of Celedonius’s case is clear from the fact that his case did not concern an ordination but the deposition of a bishop. Hilary had not yet appointed anyone in Celedonius’s place, as is evident from Saint Leo’s silence: Leo issued a decree concerning the person who had been appointed over the sick Projectus, but he made no such ruling concerning Celedonius.

In Projectus’s case, by contrast, the dispute concerned not a deposition but an ordination, or appointment over another. Accordingly, everything that Saint Leo says here about illicit ordinations must be referred to Projectus. To clarify this passage further, some points still need to be said; but they will more suitably be deferred to the second part of this dissertation. There we shall try to explain in what sense the word “ordination” must be understood here, and within what boundaries Gaul must be confined when all its churches are mentioned in this passage.

5. If one considers the condition of Gaul at that time, one will understand how little it accords with the belief that Celedonius was then bishop of Vesontio. [Col. 0443A] For, unless I am mistaken, everyone agrees that Maxima Sequanorum and the neighboring regions were at that time subject not to the Romans but partly to Gallic rulers and partly to the princes of the Burgundians.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] This argument and the following one rest upon a false hypothesis: for at this time these regions were subject to the Roman Empire, as we noted in annotation 1 above, col. 431, note a, in chapter 1.]

But who would believe that Hilary, a bishop under Roman rule, dared to claim metropolitan authority in territory belonging to another jurisdiction, act as visitor in a foreign province hostile to the Romans, convene a synod, and depose a bishop of the first order? The Burgundians certainly would never have tolerated this. Nor would the clear-sighted Hilary ever have attempted it. The *Life* of Romanus testifies that Hilary consecrated Romanus as a priest and summoned him from the Jura for no other reason than that he was not permitted to enter the Jura—territory under Burgundian rule—to perform priestly functions there.

6. From this last argument another follows: namely, that the emperor Valentinian would not have taken so badly the deposition of Celedonius by Hilary, nor undertaken so ardently to defend Celedonius’s case against Hilary’s sentence, if Celedonius had been a bishop outside the boundaries of Valentinian’s dominion. Indeed, Valentinian would have found it most agreeable that a bishop under Roman rule had claimed rights and authority over churches that had been torn away from that rule. For this would have helped prepare the way for the Romans to bring those regions once again under their yoke.

From what has been said it is clear that Celedonius belonged to no province other than Vienne. Saint Leo also indicates this in both of his letters to the bishops of Vienne, in which he states that Hilary was rightly deprived of authority over the province of Vienne because he had wrongfully usurped it or had misused it—not certainly in the case of Projectus, who belonged to another province, but therefore in the case of Celedonius:

“Let him know,” he says, “that he has been deprived not only of another’s right, but also of authority over the province of Vienne, which he had wrongfully usurped.”

This authority, then, properly belonged to Hilary, since it is expressly distinguished from “another’s right,” from which he is said above to have been expelled, as something legitimate, although not legitimately usurped.

## CHAPTER IV. Saint Hilary of Arles was Celedonius’s legitimate judge, because metropolitan authority over the province of Vienne belonged to the bishop of Arles. Traces of this authority from the time of Saint Trophimus to the Council of Turin.

We have abundantly proved in the preceding discussion that Celedonius was a bishop seated in the province of Vienne. It follows that the whole controversy must now be reduced to this question: whether Hilary judged the case improperly for one of three reasons—either because he unlawfully claimed metropolitan authority over the province of Vienne for himself, or because he removed from episcopal dignity a bishop who had neither confessed nor been convicted by lawful testimony and who deserved no such treatment, or finally because he refused to hear Celedonius when he appealed to the apostolic see and would not permit his own judgment to be reconsidered and corrected by the primatial see.

These three points must be examined in their proper order. First, we must discuss and prove the metropolitan right of the bishops of Arles, namely, that it had always belonged to them, 773 and had not belonged to the bishops of Vienne.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] No one will believe that metropolitan right had always belonged to the bishop of Arles from the time of Saint Trophimus and the third century, if he reads what will be said in Part II, Observation, chapter 5, no. 2, concerning the late establishment of ecclesiastical metropolises in Gaul.]

Indeed, throughout all the centuries from the preaching of the Gospel in Gaul to the time of Hilary—for this is sufficient for our purposes, and we undertake no broader inquiry—the privileges and prerogatives of the Church of Arles shine forth everywhere. There is scarcely any monument of Gallican antiquity in which some distinctive indication does not appear of the metropolitan dignity held by the bishops of Arles.

After Trophimus—who was sent by the apostolic see and was the first to establish and govern the Church of Arles, although his date has been left to the scholarly debate of learned men—we know of no bishop of this see earlier than Martianus, whose memory is preserved by Saint Cyprian in Letter 66 to Pope Stephen.

Faustinus of Lyon wrote to Saint Cyprian of Carthage concerning the removal of that Martianus, a supporter of the Novatian party, from the communion of his colleagues and from the episcopate. He had also written, together with other Gallican bishops, to Stephen, bishop of Rome; and Cyprian himself sent to Stephen the letter we have mentioned.

From this letter we derive what seems to me a powerful argument in favor of the Church of Arles. If the bishop of that see had not held primacy in the Roman province, there would have been no reason for the Gallican bishops to have recourse to bishops beyond the Alps and beyond the sea in order to deal with Martianus’s deposition.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] Since metropolitans had not yet been established at this time, it is not surprising that the Africans and Gauls wrote concerning Martianus to the Roman pontiff, since at that time he alone presided with higher authority over all bishops, especially those of Gaul. [Col. 0444D]]

The authority of a metropolitan would have been available—whether, as some maintain, that of Vienne, or that of some other see. For even if the form of the ecclesiastical hierarchy had not yet been so constituted and consolidated there as it was afterward, there is nevertheless no doubt that one bishop held precedence among them, charged with governing the others and, when necessary, convening them in synod. He might have held that position by virtue of the dignity of his see, the antiquity of his priesthood, or the common vote and choice of the priests.

This, then, was the person whom Faustinus and the other Gallican bishops would have urged to press for Martianus’s deposition. If he had evaded the matter, the negligence of this leading bishop would surely have been noted either by Faustinus when writing to Cyprian or by Cyprian when writing to Stephen.

2. Thus Cyprian addresses Pope Stephen:

“Therefore you ought to send the fullest possible letter to our fellow bishops established in Gaul, so that they may no longer tolerate Martianus,” and so forth.

And below:

“Let letters from you be directed to the province and to the people residing at Arles,” and so forth.

If someone other than the bishop of Arles had governed that province by metropolitan right, would Cyprian not rather have said: “To our fellow bishop, the metropolitan or primate of the province”—using the African term—as the Roman pontiffs did on other occasions when they heard that something contrary to the provisions of the canons was being perpetrated with impunity in the regions of Gaul?

3. There would have been no reason for Catholic clergy or laity from other regions to direct themselves to the bishop of Arles rather than to another Gallican bishop, or to have formal letters addressed to him, unless he had stood above the others by the privilege of his see and by metropolitan or similar dignity. For this was the privilege of the great metropolitans and even of exarchs.

Cyprian writes as follows:

“Clearly inform us who has been appointed at Arles in place of Martianus, so that we may know to whom we ought to direct our brothers and to whom we should write.”

This was the state of affairs around the year 255 after Christ. From that time until the First Council of Arles, no ancient monument of the Gallican Church is known to occur.

Nearly sixty years later, by order of the emperor Constantine, the famous council was assembled in the city of Arles. [Col. 0444D] The fact that the council was held in that city itself supports the dignity of its church and its bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0444D] This council contributes nothing to establishing metropolitan right for either the bishop of Arles or the bishop of Vienne, since, as we have said, there were then no metropolitans in Gaul. As for why Marinus is first in the heading of the council’s letter, although he was not a metropolitan, see Observation, Part II, chapter 5, no. 4.]

I do not press this point, nor do I press the order of the subscriptions, in which the bishop of Arles precedes the bishop of Vienne. For I do not believe that the names of the bishops who attended this synod were subscribed in the same order in the original and authentic copy of the synod as they are now set out in the published acts of the council; we shall discuss this matter somewhat more fully below.

Nevertheless, we can at least establish this much: at the time when this scribe, whoever he was, wrote the document, the bishop of Arles was considered worthy to be placed before the bishop of Vienne.

More important and weighty is the fact that Marinus, bishop of Arles, is named first at the head of the synodical letter and alone in the *Breviary* prefixed to its canons. To me this is a certain indication of metropolitan dignity in his person.

He could not have held the chief place in the synod or acted in all matters in the name of the synod unless he had been the leading bishop of the province—either of Vienne, if it had already been separated from Narbonensis, or of the entire Roman province, if Narbonensis still remained undivided.

For the following custom always prevailed: the metropolitan of each province presided over a synod convened within the boundaries of his province, even when the city in which it met had its own bishop.

For the moment, let the Council of Diospolis suffice as an example. It was presided over by Eulogius, bishop of Caesarea, in the year 415, although Diospolis lay under the bishop of Jerusalem.

If, therefore, the city of Vienne had at that time been honored with metropolitan dignity, Verus, bishop of Vienne, who was present at the council, would not have allowed his right to be taken from him. He would have subscribed first of all and would himself have composed the synodical letter in the name of everyone, reporting to the Roman pontiff concerning the entire synod.

The Fathers of the Second Council of Arles understood that this example greatly favored the privilege of Arles when, in canon 18, they cited it to confirm the right of a synod to be convened at the discretion of the bishop of Arles.

The continuator of the illustrious Petrus de Marca, Baluzius, asserts in Book V, chapter 30, no. 4, of the *Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire* that Marinus of Arles did not claim metropolitan right for his see in the synodical letter. On the contrary, he says, an old catalogue of the bishops who assembled at the Council of Arles calls him bishop of the province of Vienne.

But where, learned man, do you find that Marinus did not claim this right for himself? If the reason is that he is called bishop of the province of Vienne in that old catalogue, then for the same reason primacy must also be taken away from Verus, bishop of Vienne, to whom, as I believe, you assign it. For the bishop of Vienne does not subscribe otherwise; nor do the bishops of Marseille, Orange, or Vaison.

The one distinction that appears in favor of Arles is that its subscription is placed before the names of the others, except that of the bishop of Marseille, who does not appear in the ancient editions but only in Sirmondus’s edition of the Gallican councils.

At the Council of Cologne against Euphratas, over which Maximinus of Trier presided by metropolitan right, Valentinus of Arles is listed immediately after him and gave his vote before everyone else. Although this does not openly assert metropolitan right, it does to some extent indicate the dignity of his see.

The Council of Arles followed the Council of Cologne seven years later. Saturninus, bishop of that same city, presided over it. He was indeed attached to the Arian faction; but since neither Hilary nor Sulpicius Severus marked him as guilty of having improperly arrogated the presidency, the proof derived from this fact remains intact for us in support of the right of the Church of Arles.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] What is collected here and in the following sections from the acts of Saturninus of Arles is shown to be worthless in Observation, Part II, chapter 6, no. 5. Consequently, no firm evidence has so far been produced for an earlier metropolitan right of the bishop of Arles. [Col. 0446D]]

At the Council of Béziers, too, the same Saturninus held the primacy, as can easily be gathered from Hilary, Sulpicius Severus, and Jerome. They do not deny him either the right to convene the council or the right to hold first place in it, despite his being a very crafty man. Nor did the Fathers of the Council of Paris deny it when they declared him excommunicated for no other reason than that he had impiously opposed salutary decrees.

## CHAPTER V. What the Council of Turin contributed to the primacy or metropolitan authority of the bishop of Arles.

Up to this point, the bishop of Arles appears to have possessed primacy everywhere in the province of Narbonensis, with no one contradicting or resisting him. We see him taking precedence over everyone in all affairs of importance. As for the bishop of Vienne, there is everywhere profound silence.

But contention over primacy began to arise between the two around the time of the Council of Turin, which is commonly believed to have been held in the year 397, though it is more accurately assigned to the beginning of the following century. For several letters of Pope Zosimus show that Briccius, the successor of Saint Martin, was then bishop of Tours; the more learned chronologists, following Severus Sulpicius, report that he died on 11 November in the year 400 or even later. Whoever accepts this calculation must necessarily say that the council, whose preface indicates that it was convened in September, was not held before the year 402 or the year following.

What occasion, then, do we suppose gave rise to this controversy?

[Note: [Col. 0446D] We shall reveal the true occasion of the controversy in Observation, Part II, chapter 5, no. 9 and the following number; there the fabrications of Quesnellus, which are here heaped together in remarkable fashion, will be exposed.]

I believe it arose partly from the new division of Gaul and partly from the immense disturbances that shook that region of Gaul at the end of the fourth century.

For Maximus seized the tyranny in Britain in the year 382 and established his imperial residence at Trier. In 383 he killed the emperor Gratian at Lyon after Gratian had been abandoned by his own men, through the agency of the commander Andragathius. Eugenius likewise, relying on the support of the count Arbogast, aspired to and forcibly usurped the empire in the year 391. Finally, in the following year, that same Arbogast killed the emperor Valentinian at Vienne.

Amid these storms, it is highly probable that the bishop of Vienne raised his head in pursuit of primacy. The recent division of the province of Narbonensis into several parts provided an opportunity for this ambition; the province of Vienne had been given its name from the city, and that same province of Vienne had been split between two distinct and hostile rulers. Some cities obeyed the tyrant under Vienne, while others remained under Roman rule together with Arles.

It was easy for the bishop of Vienne—whose city had once been a metropolitan capital in the imperial administrative register and whose antiquity gave it prominence—to persuade the tyrant that ecclesiastical primacy should be established where he had his imperial seat, or at least where his power had begun.

With these titles as the basis of his primacy and with whatever supports he could find to defend it, he brought forward no other general foundation for the metropolitan dignity he sought than the antiquity of the city and its former possession of the same dignity in civil affairs.

The controversy had reached this point in the early years of the fifth century, when, for the purpose of resolving it or at least bringing it somehow to an end, the Council of Turin was convened at the request of the Gallic bishops [Col. 0447A]. Its second canon runs as follows:

> Then, concerning the dispute between the bishops of the cities of Arles and Vienne—observe that Arles is named first—who were contending among us for the honor of primacy, the holy synod has decreed that whichever of them proves that his city is a metropolitan city shall possess the honor of primacy over the whole province and, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons, shall himself have authority over ordinations. Certainly, in order to preserve the bond of peace, this more useful arrangement has been decreed: if it pleases the bishops of the aforementioned cities, each of them shall claim for himself the cities within the province that are nearer to him and shall visit those churches which are shown to be closer to his own towns, so that, mindful of unanimity and concord, neither may trouble the other by usurping for himself what is nearer to the other.

From these words of the synod it is clear, first, that for a long time extremely troublesome dissensions had been raging among the bishops of Gaul concerning the primacy of the province of Vienne, and indeed of other provinces as well [Col. 0447B]. For the rights of those bishops and the boundaries of those provinces had become obscure and obstructed by difficulties as a result of the disturbances arising within the Gallic provinces from the tyranny of Maximus; so much so that, since this controversy could scarcely be settled by Gallic bishops acting as judges—for most of them were occupied either by their own interests or by those of their friends—the bishops of those regions proposed to refer the case to neighboring co-bishops, as though by a submission to arbitration. Bishops of the Italian diocese, being contiguous to the province of Vienne and to the other provinces, were selected for this purpose, all the more willingly because, I suppose, the Gallic prelates had long earnestly desired that the primate of that diocese, Saint Ambrose, should judge their disputes. For this reason they repeatedly urged him by embassy to attend their synod.

It is easy to understand that Ambrose himself was referring to this matter when, speaking at Valentinian’s funeral, he testified that he had been summoned to Gaul by a rescript of Valentinian himself, so that Ambrose might be his guarantor of faith before Count Arbogast, and had been informed, in order to hasten his journey [Col. 0447C], that he had been summoned not to a synod of Gaul but to the baptism of Valentinian Augustus. “He added,” Ambrose says, “that I should hasten more quickly and should not suppose that the purpose of my journey was a synod of Gallic bishops, on account of whose frequent dissensions I had often excused myself, but that he himself was to be baptized immediately upon his departure.”

Ambrose said this in the year 392, in which Valentinian was killed. Hence we infer that, after the death of Maximus the tyrant—who had altered the condition of Gaul and the arrangement of its provinces [Note: No change in the provinces under Maximus can be established. Quesnel makes not a few gratuitous assertions.]—the bishops of Gaul had begun, four years before, to contend over the rights of their churches, especially the bishops of Arles and Vienne, between whom the dispute concerned the primacy. But the province from whose disturbances Ambrose, being uninvolved in the dissensions, withdrew, was later undertaken by his successor Simplicianus, overcome by the pleas of the Gauls, or by Venerius, who succeeded Simplicianus. It is reasonable to believe that one of these two presided over the Council of Turin. Its celebration was delayed by the storms that followed Valentinian’s death and by the disturbed condition of Gallic affairs resulting from the subsequent tyranny of Eugenius [Col. 0447D].

A second point is also made clear by the words of the synod: the whole controversy had come down to the question of which of those cities was the metropolis. It was evidently certain in the judgment of the judges that the honor of ecclesiastical primacy should be assigned to the city that held the same position in the civil administration. The Fathers of Turin themselves sufficiently indicate in this definition which side they favored. For although, in their own judgment, they seemed to assign the primacy to neither city, in reality they awarded it to Arles [Col. 0448A], which at that time was acknowledged to be the metropolis [Note: At this time it was not Arles but Vienne that was the civil metropolis; this will be established clearly in Part II of the *Observations*, chapter 4, nos. 5 and following, and no. 2. We shall examine Quesnel’s arguments in favor of Arles. Furthermore, in the same place, chapter 5, no. 9, we shall prove that the judgment of the Fathers of Turin must be understood not of the civil but of the ecclesiastical metropolis.].

Accordingly, that definition seems to me to have been drafted with considerable skill. It does not decree that metropolitan dignity should be attributed to the one who proved that his city had formerly and from ancient times been a metropolis—which would have left the matter uncertain and opened the way to laborious investigation—but rather to the one who proved that it was a metropolis at that particular time. This amounted to pronouncing in favor of Arles.

For the Emperor Honorius Augustus, in an edict addressed to Agricola, prefect of Gaul, in the year 418 (scarcely fifteen years later than the Council of Turin), expressly calls Arles a “metropolitan city” (apud J. Sirmond, notes on Sidonius, p. 245). This demonstrates that it had long been distinguished by that honor and title. Accordingly, when he orders that an assembly of the seven provinces be held there, he indicates that this was not being instituted anew, since it had already been ordered by the prefect Petronius and had been observed pursuant to a plainly reasonable and approved policy, but rather restored, because, as Honorius Augustus complains in the same edict, it had been interrupted either through the negligence of the times or through the indolence of tyrants [Col. 0448B].

Among these tyrants, understand especially Constantine, who conquered Arles, withdrew into it as into the principal city of the whole province, and, after being besieged there by Honorius in the year 411, was compelled to surrender. Once it had been conquered, says Sozomen, “that province again returned to the rule of Honorius and obeyed the commanders appointed by him.”

Nor does the elevation of the city of Arles into a metropolis seem attributable to Petronius. It surpassed the prefectural authority, and it preceded the age of Petronius (the Gallic bishops’ petition to Saint Leo). For the Gallic bishops assert in the memorial that they submitted to Pope Leo on behalf of the bishop of Arles that this city had been enlarged by the Emperor Valentinian through special privileges—such as the seat of the prefecture and others—and had even been called a metropolis. For what does it mean for a city to be the mother of all Gaul except that it is the metropolis of all the cities? Yet the bishops of such integrity and prudence would never have dared to assert in a public memorial that this had been conferred upon the city of Arles by either the first or the second Valentinian—unless they regarded it as certain—especially since the memorial had to be scrutinized by the eyes of the opponents, the Roman pontiff, and the entire City, and since nothing would have been easier than to charge as false whatever falsehood had been inserted into the petition [Col. 0448C].

But many years before either Valentinian, Arles is found to have been so ennobled by Constantius Augustus, the son of the Emperor Constantine, that there is scarcely room for doubt that he regarded it as a metropolis. For whenever he was in Gaul, he was accustomed to stay there; there he presented theatrical performances, there he held circus games, and there he also entered upon his seventh consulship, which he made famous by the presentation of circus games. “While Constantius was spending the winter at Arles,” says Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, “after theatrical performances and circus games had been presented with lavish magnificence, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, which brought to an end the thirtieth year of his reign,” and so forth [Col. 0448D]. And below: “Constantius, after entering upon his seventh consulship and his second as Caesar, departed from Arles and proceeded to Valence,” and so forth.

The Gallic bishops testified in the aforementioned memorial that these same things had also been done at Arles by other Augusti and consuls. From their account, as also from the edict of Honorius just cited, we learn that the name Constantina was given to the city of Arles by Constantine the Great. Just as he built a new Rome in the eastern regions after the model of ancient Rome and adorned it with his own name, so in Gaul he wished Arles to be such a city that the splendor and adornment of both cities might be communicated to it. For this reason it was called Constantina by the emperor himself and “Little Rome of Gaul” (*Gallula Roma*) by Ausonius [Col. 0449A].

Such was Arles in civil matters, from Constantine, the first of the Christian emperors, down to Valentinian III, who was contemporary with Leo and Hilary. But what it had been under the pagans we learn from a single witness, our own Leo; thus it would be superfluous and idle to search through more ancient records. For, after considering the allegations of both parties’ present clerics, he readily admits that the cities of Vienne and Arles had once possessed a common right, and that this had been handed down from the pagans (*Epistle* 50, chapter 1, in reply to the memorial of the bishops of the province of Vienne).

## CHAPTER VI

The decrees of Pope Zosimus asserting metropolitan authority for the bishop of Arles are examined and cleared of suspicion of forgery.

The Council of Turin was followed by exceedingly turbulent times, during which several tyrants occupied Gaul, and Goths, Burgundians, and other barbarians also invaded it. As a result, the entire ecclesiastical order in those regions was utterly ruined [Col. 0449B]. “Nowhere,” says Salvianus, an eyewitness of the churches of those times and places, “was pleasure more depraved, life nowhere more defiled, discipline nowhere more corrupt.” Consequently, it must be thought that during that period neither the arrangements of that council nor the earlier statutes had any practical force.

When the affairs of Gaul had been brought to some degree of peace, the leaders of the Church and of the empire seriously considered restoring both ecclesiastical discipline and civil government. Above all, they undertook to restore the sacred and civil privileges of the Church and city of Arles. Honorius’s constitution, cited above, is evidence concerning the civil privileges; it was issued in the year 418 and may be consulted in J. Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius (p. 245). Concerning the ecclesiastical privileges, we possess an exceptionally rich record in the letters of Pope Zosimus. Since these precede the edict of Honorius by one year, it is evident from this alone that the ecclesiastical splendor of the city of Arles did not arise merely from imitation of secular arrangements [Col. 0449C], but was founded upon the native rights and primordial prerogatives of that Church.

781 Of Zosimus’s letters, those concerning other rights of the bishop of Arles we reserve for another place; for now, let us attend to those that establish metropolitan authority. Thus, in *Epistle* 5, addressed to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces, he says:

> We have ordered that the metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles, as he has ALWAYS held it, retain the principal authority in the ordination of priests;

and below:

> The OLD PRIVILEGE of the metropolitan city of Arles must in no way be diminished. To it Trophimus, the supreme pontiff, was first sent from this see, from whose fountain all Gaul received the streams of the faith.

I pass over other passages that amount to the same thing or will be discussed more appropriately elsewhere.

It is also worthy of notice that Zosimus does not say that he is creating a new right or confirming an institution established only yesterday; rather, he declares it to be an OLD PRIVILEGE, which the bishop of Arles had ALWAYS possessed. He asserts that it was founded upon the supreme pontificate of Trophimus, who was evidently the first to imbue those provinces with the faith of Christ and to govern them by episcopal authority. It would therefore have been a sacrilege to violate the rights that had passed, by lawful succession, to the heirs of his see [Col. 0449D].

[Note: Although Zosimus’s letters are genuine, being drawn from manuscripts of the Arles collection, which bears no sign of anything spurious, it will nevertheless become clear from Part II, chapter 2, of the *Observations* that, through Patroclus’s subreption, they falsely assert an ancient metropolitan right for the bishop of Arles.]

The testimony of this pontiff is so open and decisive that the advocates of the opposing view leave nothing undone to weaken and invalidate it. Some accuse Zosimus of excessive credulity, which he also displayed in other matters—for example, when he allowed himself to be so deceived by the heresiarchs Pelagius and Coelestius that both they and their petitions were judged Catholic by him, while the African bishops, those invincible defenders of grace, were accused by that pontiff of levity and ill-considered zeal because they had condemned both men—even though Zosimus thought that both held Catholic opinions—on the basis of the writings of frivolous informers.

Others spare Zosimus himself but accuse the writings published under his name of forgery, claiming that they regard this as certain for many reasons and on many grounds. Since it is very important not to diminish their credibility lightly, the arguments of learned men must be examined after all prejudices have been set aside.

First, then, they say that the forgery of Zosimus’s letters is made evident by this one fact: they assert that the bishop of Arles had always been metropolitan. Zosimus could never have written this, they say, since it contradicts all the ancient descriptions of the provinces, in which the city of Arles is recorded as subject to Vienne as to its metropolis.

But, I ask, which deserves greater confidence: such descriptions, whose date and authority are uncertain, or the letters of Zosimus? Indeed, since those descriptions were unknown to antiquity and have been brought to light only within the last few years, their credibility is highly unstable [Col. 0450B]. Nevertheless, because several copies of them are produced that closely resemble one another, and because they are not found in only a few manuscript codices, I do not wish to deprive them of all authority. But since they can have no force against the rights of Arles unless it is established that they were composed before Zosimus, the proof drawn from them will be wholly futile once we have demonstrated that such descriptions began to be written not only after Zosimus but even after Saint Leo. We shall establish this below.

Once that has been done, the weapon may be turned back against the opponents. For if the authority of Zosimus’s letters is preserved, then the proof derived from them in favor of the metropolitan status of Arles will be invincible. Other arguments that the opponents derive from the same primacy will also be more conveniently disposed of in what follows.

Second, it is wrongly objected that the decretal letters are attributed to Zosimus, although they are contained neither in the code of the Roman Church compiled by Dionysius Exiguus nor in the collection of Isidore [Col. 0450C].

Yet this objection scarcely requires a response. How many letters of other pontiffs, and of Zosimus himself and our own Leo—letters that are unquestionably famous and of undoubted authenticity, and whose preservation for posterity was of the greatest importance to the Roman See—how many, I say, of this kind are found inserted in neither collection? And, not to stray beyond the limits of the present controversy, the lengthy letter to the bishops of Vienne on which we are now engaged escaped the diligence of both those collectors. Likewise, another letter of Leo that settled the entire dispute between the bishops of Arles and Vienne was praised by Symmachus, but was first published by Cardinal Baronius in his *Annals* and was unknown to all collectors of papal decrees. Countless others, which come to mind to anyone reading this, even without my saying so, are found in none of the codices of the decretals. Yet it would be extremely troublesome for all students of ecclesiastical antiquity to have their authenticity challenged on the basis of the silence of Isidore and Dionysius [Col. 0450D].

The third objection—that the Roman pontiffs Symmachus and Leo were silent about these letters—is partly true and partly false.

Symmachus was indeed silent, but why is that surprising? It would rather be surprising if he had repeated the decree of his predecessor, which he wished to abolish. For Symmachus in no way took account of Zosimus’s arrangement concerning the present matter (*Epistle* 9, to the bishops of Gaul), but only of Leo’s, whose decision he resolved should remain unshaken. Nor did he issue a new edict; rather, he brought into the light, as he himself says, what had been promulgated by Leo through his own pronouncements.

[Col. 0451A] As for Leo, he did not expressly mention Zosimus’s name, but in this letter—*Epistle* 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne—he made such an explicit reference to his decree that it could not have been clearer. For what else do these words signify?

> What is Hilary seeking in another province, and why is he usurping what none of his predecessors possessed before Patroclus? For even what appeared to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment.

Everyone sees that Leo could not have been referring to a decree of any Roman pontiff issued in Patroclus’s favor unless he meant the decree of Zosimus, by which Patroclus obtained confirmation of his jurisdiction over the province of Vienne and the others. Thus, by the very argument through which the credibility of Zosimus’s letters was thought to be utterly overthrown, it is instead more firmly strengthened. No other argument need be sought to establish the authenticity of those letters after Leo’s testimony, so authoritative and so explicit.

“But at least,” you say, “in this letter or elsewhere Saint Leo says nothing about the two Narbonnese provinces.” What follows from that? It is evident that Ravennius voluntarily relinquished his claim to both Narbonnese provinces, which his predecessors had defended, and asserted for himself only the metropolitan authority of the province of Vienne. The Roman pontiff who confirmed this authority to Patroclus could have been cited by our Leo as no one other than Zosimus.

This answer would be sufficient for us. I maintain, however, that the words “What is Hilary seeking in another province?” and so forth, refer to one of the Narbonnese provinces. For Leo is not speaking here of Vienne, which he never considered foreign to Hilary and which no Roman pontiff before Leo had taken away from him. But these matters will be treated more fully in Part II of the dissertation, on the Affair of Projectus, where we shall examine Leo’s testimony.

Fourth, they object that the style used by the author of that decree is too elevated to suit Zosimus. It begins:

> It has pleased the apostolic see, etc.

Those who think that these words display too commanding an attitude should read our own Leo in many of his letters—for example, those addressed to the Africans, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, and even this very letter to the bishops of Vienne. Let them also read Zosimus’s letter to the African bishops concerning the case of Coelestius. They will find nothing more imperious; and yet they will not judge that these letters should be denied to Zosimus as alien to his style.

### 5. The omission by Leo and Symmachus of any mention that the bishop of Arles was to issue the *formatae* is thought to cast considerable suspicion of forgery upon the letters wherever the *formatae* are mentioned.

I reply that there was no need to mention the *formatae*, since the right to issue such letters was necessarily included among metropolitan duties. Zosimus was moved to mention them, and compelled by necessity to do so, because, on account of the disturbances that had shaken Gaul in preceding years and the disputes that had arisen among the bishops concerning the primacy [Col. 0451D], the use of the *formatae* had been interrupted or had been unlawfully usurped by others. Zosimus restored it for this reason:

> Because, as he himself says, many persons, pretending to be bishops, priests, or ecclesiastics, since no document of the *formatae* exists by which they can be refuted, intrude under the name of veneration and obtain undeserved respect.

(Zosimus, *Epistle* 5, to the bishops of Gaul.)

That this privilege had long before been granted to the bishop of Arles is clear from the letter of Saint Cyprian that he wrote to Pope Stephen concerning the deposition of Marcianus of Arles, discussed above.

[Note: The privilege of the *formatae* granted to the bishop of Arles by Zosimus extends not merely to his own ecclesiastical province, or to the whole Narbonnese province assigned to him by that pontiff, but to every part of Gaul, as *Epistle* 1, chapter 1, shows. This right cannot be proved ancient, since it was accepted in both East and West that clerics received *formatae* from bishops, while bishops received them from metropolitans, as P. Coustant teaches in his preface to that same letter of Zosimus. There he also expresses surprise that Quesnel adduces testimony from Cyprian’s letters to Pope Stephen, in which no mention of *formatae* occurs.]

### 6. The learned author presses this clause of the fifth letter:

> If any matter of business should arise there, we have decided that it should be reported to his attention, unless the gravity of the case should also require our own examination.

“These words,” he says, “are taken from letters of later pontiffs, who entrusted their authority to the bishops of Arles, and they are not appropriate to the time of Zosimus.”

We satisfy this objection in more than one way. First, I cite the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, who testifies that in the Arles manuscript from which he had Zosimus’s letters copied, the same clause was read at the end of the letter addressed to the bishops of Gaul, Africa, and Spain as in the preceding letter—the one under discussion—addressed to all the bishops throughout Gaul and the seven provinces. It ran from the words:

> We have ordered that the principal authority, etc.,

up to:

> unless the gravity of the case should also require our own examination.

(Baronius, under the year 417, no. 48.)

Hence it may be conjectured that these final words, which Zosimus omitted in the letter to the bishops of Africa and Spain, were likewise omitted in the letter concerned solely with Gaul and were added later by someone [Note: The following words are also found in both letters; and Baronius’s text suggests that they were not omitted from the letter to the Africans either.].

But, yielding to this conjecture, I reply that Pope Zosimus undertook to defend the rights of the bishops of Arles while nevertheless ensuring that he did not entirely forget his own interests. Accordingly, he sought to subject the province of Vienne and the others to Patroclus in such a way that Patroclus himself would remain subject to Zosimus in the exercise of this authority. He accomplished this by decreeing to Patroclus, as though by privilege, the right to issue *formatae*, while reserving to himself the examination and judgment of certain cases [Col. 0452B].

Thus Zosimus followed the example of his predecessor Innocent, who, writing to Victricius of Rouen, says in chapter 3:

> But if more important cases should arise, they are to be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod has decreed, after episcopal judgment.

Saint Leo imitated both of them and added the same exception to the letters by which he delegated the office of his vicar to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica. Therefore no one should be surprised that one who intended to establish an apostolic vicariate in the metropolitan see of Arles, modeled on the delegation in Illyricum, reproduced in this matter the pattern of that earlier arrangement.

[Note: When Zosimus ordered that ecclesiastical matters be reported and reserved more important cases for apostolic examination and judgment, he was not pursuing a matter outside his competence but exercising his own right. This right proceeded openly not so much from the primacy of divine institution over the whole Church as from his special jurisdiction over the churches of the West, which the apostolic see had always exercised, as we could prove by many more ancient examples if there were time. Here too Quesnel displays his hostile attitude toward apostolic authority.]

### 7. But if the letters attributed to Zosimus were genuine, who could believe that such contrary letters could have been written by his successors Boniface and Coelestine, and that they wished to overturn the decrees of their predecessor? For Boniface, in his third letter to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, accuses Patroclus of the unlawful ordination of the bishop of Lodève in the province of Narbonne.

I do not clearly see what can be inferred against Zosimus’s letters from Coelestine’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne. But let us grant that both Coelestine and Boniface—what Boniface in fact did—wrote something contrary to the decrees of their predecessors. It is proved by so many examples that this was not unusual that a threefold instance occurs in the very case we are discussing [Col. 0453A].

Saint Leo asserts that what had appeared to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was later removed by a better judgment (*Epistle* 10). This must be understood of Boniface, who is said to have issued decrees contrary to those of Zosimus. We have Pope Symmachus speaking on this matter in his first letter to Eonius of Arles, saying that Anastasius II abrogated Saint Leo’s constitution, that is, the arrangement of his predecessors, transgressing it—improperly—under whatever necessity. But Symmachus himself also rescinded the arrangement of Anastasius, adhering to Leo’s constitution concerning the division of the province of Vienne and strengthening it.

### 8. The memorial presented to Leo by the Gallic bishops in favor of Ravennius does not mention Zosimus’s name—which is made an objection—but these words of the memorial cannot be understood of anyone else:

> Hence it came about that the priest of the Church of Arles, not only by recalling to his constant care and concern the arrangement of the province of Vienne but also that of three provinces, in consideration of Saint Trophimus, just as the authority of your holy predecessors has disclosed to him, etc.

The memorial not only reports Zosimus’s judgment but also uses his words, as is readily apparent to the reader. Moreover, the bishops were addressing Leo, who was not ignorant of the decrees of the apostolic see. To name the pontiffs from whom those decrees had proceeded would have been superfluous and, to some extent, unbecoming, since they might have seemed to wish to set pontiffs against pontiffs.

I think the reader has noticed that, while satisfying the objections of the opponents, we have at the same time brought forward numerous positive proofs establishing the authenticity of Zosimus’s letters. As a final confirmation, we add the testimony of the Council of Frankfurt, held in the year 794 in the presence of Charlemagne. Its eighth canon runs as follows:

> Concerning the dispute between Ursio, bishop of Vienne, and Eliphantus, bishop of Arles, the letters of the blessed Gregory, Zosimus, Leo, and Symmachus were read. The letters of Leo and Symmachus determined that the Church of Vienne ought to have four suffragan sees, over which that fifth see should preside, etc.

What letters of Zosimus, I ask, are referred to in these words, unless they are the very letters now before us? Nor should the testimony of Gregory himself the Great be disregarded in this matter (*Book* IV, *Epistle* 50, indiction 13). When he wrote to Virgilius of Arles, intending to entrust his authority to him, he sufficiently indicates that Zosimus’s letters were then before his eyes. For from them he repeated what he reports there concerning the antiquity of the privilege of Arles, the ancient custom of the apostolic see, and the certainty—“which is clear to everyone,” as he puts it—of the place from which the holy faith had proceeded in the regions of Gaul.

From what has been said it is evident how deservedly Morinus laughs at Scaliger (*Ecclesiastical Exercises* 24; Scaliger, *Epistle* 348), because Scaliger dared to declare the letters written by Zosimus concerning the controversy of Arles to be spurious and ridiculous, fabricated by men who had retained more leisure than faith [Col. 0453D]. But whether Morinus remained of the same opinion, I doubt. For in the margin of Binio’s edition of these letters, in the manuscript used by that most learned man, I read notes written in his own hand. They set out reasons drawn from the harsher style, the silence of writers, the contrary decrees of successors, and the descriptions of the provinces. On these grounds he writes that the letters are of suspect authenticity and were fabricated during the period of Arles’s rule, so that Arles might be elevated above Vienne, formerly the seat of the Burgundian kingdom. But how many years earlier than the kingdom of Arles were the authors who support the authenticity of Zosimus’s letters by their testimony? This is perfectly clear from their chronological order [Col. 0454A].

As for those who do not deny credibility to Zosimus’s letters but diminish the authority of Zosimus himself [Note: You will recognize Zosimus’s deception in Part II, chapter 2, of our *Observations*], because he was excessively credulous toward Pelagius and Coelestius and allowed himself to be ensnared by their cunning, I reply that the circumstances of the two matters were entirely different. In theological questions, especially those concerning the more obscure issues of the grace of Christ, it is exceedingly difficult even for the most subtle minds not to be deceived, since the most cunning heresiarchs commonly conceal the poison of highly destructive doctrine beneath a covering of Catholic language.

Such were Pelagius and Coelestius. The former, scarcely inferior to anyone in eloquence and skill in argument, could easily deceive Zosimus, a Greek, through the verbal ambiguity of expressions he shared with Catholics. He had previously deceived by his tricks that wretched synod of Diospolis, as Jerome calls it. But in the examination of metropolitan rights [Col. 0454B] there was nothing whatever comparable to the investigation of hidden mysteries. If Zosimus had happened to be mistaken in that discussion, he would have been warned of his error by the letters of the bishop of Vienne and the others. Nor would he have written so many letters concerning the same matter—letters that, as we observe, displeased no one except Proculus, bishop of Marseille.

## CHAPTER VII

Honorius Augustus; the Roman pontiffs Boniface, Coelestine, and Leo himself; and likewise Valentinian III Augustus regarded Hilary as metropolitan.

I shall not repeat what we cited above from the constitution of Honorius Augustus in favor of the city of Arles, which expressly calls it metropolitan. It will suffice to have pointed this out for the purpose of observing the chronological sequence.

I now come to Boniface, who assumed the pontificate toward the end of that same year. No one would suspect that he was especially favorable to the Church of Arles if he had merely read the letter he wrote to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, in which he accuses the bishop of Arles of the unlawful ordination of the bishop of Lodève. Yet in both letters concerning Gallic affairs he most clearly confers metropolitan authority in the province of Vienne upon the predecessors of our Hilary [Col. 0454C].

For, writing to the bishops of Gaul concerning Maximus, bishop of Valence, who had been accused of various crimes, he names Patroclus first among all those to whom the letter is addressed. The fourteen bishops who are listed, as I believe [Note: He makes this supposition gratuitously, as is his custom. Since this letter is said to have been written not only to the bishops of the province of Vienne but also to the others established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces, it is conjecture to suppose that the fourteen named in the inscription were bishops of the province of Vienne alone—especially since the description of Gaul lists only thirteen cities in that province.], constituted the province of Vienne.

Although the names of subscribing bishops are not arranged according to the dignity and prerogative of their churches, the first place is nevertheless always reserved for the metropolitan, whether in letters written to the bishops of an entire province or in those written by provincial bishops.

In the other letter, which he wrote to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, Patroclus is indeed accused of having ordained someone in another province—namely, the First Narbonnese—after setting aside its metropolitan and contrary to the rules of the Fathers [Col. 0454D]. This proves that Patroclus possessed a province of his own and is blamed for overstepping its boundaries and violating the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which prescribes that each metropolitan must have authority in his own province and that no one should have two provinces subject to him. This constitution would scarcely be cited here if Patroclus were not numbered among the metropolitans.

Three years later, this letter was followed by Valentinian’s constitution concerning various ecclesiastical matters, sent to Gaul in the year of the Lord 425. In chapter 2 it orders that the various bishops who followed the nefarious error of the Pelagian and Coelestian doctrine be summoned “by Patroclus, the prelate of the most holy law,” and, unless they corrected their errors, be expelled from the regions of Gaul and replaced by faithful priests. All of this speaks of a metropolitan bishop.

Pope Coelestine, the successor of Boniface, was undoubtedly referring to Boniface’s letter when, in his letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, he decreed in chapter 4 that, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, each province should be content with its own metropolitan:

> As the statutes contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne state . . . each person should be content with the boundaries granted to him; no one should presume anything in another’s province.

Accordingly, these words likewise confirm the metropolitan authority of the bishop of Arles, since Coelestine assumes that the bishop of Arles had a province subject to him. [Col. 0455B]

In the third chapter, moreover, when speaking of Daniel, who had been ordained bishop despite being guilty of many crimes, Coelestine sufficiently indicates that the bishop of Arles was a metropolitan:

> A letter was sent to the bishop of Arles through Fortunatus the subdeacon, so that Daniel might be brought before an episcopal tribunal.

Why would he have written to him rather than to someone else to arrange for Daniel to be brought before an episcopal tribunal, unless the bishop of Arles at least enjoyed metropolitan rights in the province of Vienne?

These events come close to the time and episcopate of Hilary himself, whose case we are discussing. We find that he signed first among the subscribers to the two distinguished synods, that of Riez and the First Council of Orange. Without doubt, we would likewise find him first among the subscribers to the First Council of Vaison and the Second Council of Arles, had their subscription lists not perished. Nevertheless, we shall not dwell on these matters—even though they were conducted without anyone’s opposition—because, as an invader of another’s jurisdiction, he is for this very reason ill-regarded by most people; although it is clearer than daylight that nothing was extorted by force from the bishops and that nothing was carried out except with the assent of everyone’s votes. [Col. 0455C]

But setting aside the testimony of the Gallican bishops, let us also inquire what Leo himself, our Hilary’s accuser, thought about his metropolitan authority, even in the letter that he wrote against him. We have already proved at length above that metropolitan dignity had not been taken away from the Church of Arles by our pope, when we maintained that Celidonius had belonged to the province of Vienne, and that nothing had been charged against Hilary concerning an authority arrogated to himself against the law. This is certainly evident in both letters addressed to the Viennese. For Leo accuses him, not of having improperly assumed the right to judge Celidonius, who was subject to another’s authority, but of refusing to accept Celidonius’s appeal when he had appealed legitimately; likewise, not of having arrogated to himself the office of ordination, but of claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul and transferring to his own dignity what belonged to the other metropolitan bishops; and finally, not of wishing the bishops of the province of Vienne to be subject to him by metropolitan right, but of desiring to subject them to his authority in such a way that he would not allow himself to be subject to blessed Peter the Apostle.

## 2.

What does Saint Leo mean when he writes as follows in chapter 3 of the same letter?

> “For would the sentence pronounced against him have stood, if the truth of the charges had been established, unless Celidonius had been accused and judged by lawful authority, with canonical order observed, and unless nothing were lacking to the sentence pronounced against him except the truth of the charges—so that authority was not lacking to Hilary as metropolitan of the province?”

[Note: After we had more fully proved in the observations, part 1, chapter 2, that Bishop Celidonius belonged to a province outside Hilary’s jurisdiction, we explained this testimony of Leo—which Quesnellus brings forward here and elsewhere—in such a way that it neither supports the assertion of Hilary’s jurisdiction nor requires recourse to the vicariate authority granted to Arles. [Col. 0456D]]

Explained according to our view, these words of Leo cause no difficulty but yield a wholly coherent meaning. The authors of the opposing opinion, however, twist them in a remarkable fashion.
