To prevent the dignity of the metropolitan see of Besançon from being overthrown by these words, they are forced to take refuge in the vicariate authority delegated by Bishop Zosimus to the bishops of Arles, authority which, they claim, granted them some right to convene synods throughout Gaul, at which episcopal cases referred to them would be settled by the sentence of the vicar of the apostolic see.

But if I am not mistaken, the authors mentioned above, by this reply—which they intend to satisfy others—do not satisfy themselves. How alien, indeed, were the customs of that age and region from a vicariate authority of this kind, one that would have enabled a person to invade metropolitan rights and would have granted powers never attempted in later centuries, when observance of the canons had receded still farther? Just as the right of ordination belonged solely to the proper metropolitan, so too did the right of deposing one who had been ordained. Nor did vicariate authority ever extend so far that someone would convene a synod in another province for the sole purpose of ejecting from his own see the bishop of that province, who was not subject to him. Yet they think that Hilary attempted precisely this in the present case.

Furthermore, these same authors speak inconsistently. If Hilary possessed, in the name of his vicariate, the authority to convene synodal councils in Gaul and to establish judicial proceedings there concerning bishops, why do these same authors insist that no bishop had any authority in the province of the Sequani, just as in the other provinces, except the priests of that province itself?

> “Let each province,” says our Leo, as reported by Marca (*Dissertation on Primacies*, no. 78), “be content with its own councils, and let Hilary no longer dare to announce synodal assemblies”—he is referring, they say, to the assembly held against Celidonius—“and by intruding himself disturb the judgments of the priests of the Lord. Let him know not only that he has been excluded from another’s jurisdiction, but also deprived of the authority of the province of Vienne, which he had wrongly usurped.”

Thus far Leo.

Now, if Hilary’s sentence against Celidonius was to remain in force because, by using the pope’s authority as his vicar, he had possessed the right to convene a synod, then he must have been permitted to exercise some authority in the province of the Sequani, as in the other provinces; and, by announcing synodal assemblies, he would not have been intruding upon and disturbing the judgments of the priests, but exercising an authority granted to him. Since these propositions are mutually incompatible, the explanation of this passage must be sought—as we maintain—in the metropolitan dignity of the Church of Arles.

## 3.

This is therefore confirmed by the words of Leo quoted above:

> “Let him know not only that he has been excluded from another’s jurisdiction, but also deprived of the authority of the province of Vienne, which he had wrongly usurped.”

For Leo plainly distinguishes two authorities in Hilary: one belonging to another, which he designates by the expression “another’s jurisdiction”—namely, the authority that Zosimus had granted over both provinces of Narbonne—and another proper authority over the province of Vienne. For what belongs to another is opposed to what is one’s own; and he would call the first authority foreign and unlawful quite pointlessly unless he acknowledged the other, which he contrasts with it, as legitimate and proper.

The wording does present some difficulty, since Leo speaks of authority over Vienne “which he had wrongly usurped.” But in the notes to this letter we shall show either that *usurpare* is used here in the sense of “to exercise,” in which sense it is not taken negatively unless accompanied by some adverb of malicious character, such as *male* (“wrongly”) here; or else that an error has entered the text and that, instead of *usurpaverat*, we should read *usus fuerat* (“had exercised”). For in ancient manuscript books it is easy for one form to slip into another.

## 4.

In the shorter letter to the Viennese—if, that is, it is genuine—Leo explicitly acknowledges the privilege of the Church and city of Arles:

> “Removed from the privilege of his own city, let him learn in a humble position what he refused to retain in the great gift freely granted by our predecessors. Let the privilege and ancient right of the Viennese bishop be restored, which apostolic benevolence transferred in part to the city of Arles.”

Here Leo affirms that metropolitan authority had formerly been conferred upon Vienne; nevertheless—and this is sufficient for Hilary—he admits that at that time the same authority belonged to the bishop of Arles, and indeed had been granted through the favor and gift of the apostolic see.

# CHAPTER VIII

## The metropolitan dignity of the Church of Arles is confirmed by what was done after Hilary’s return to Gaul until his death, and in the ordination of Ravennius.

Although it has already been proved abundantly that the Church of Arles was then adorned with metropolitan dignity, when Hilary deposed Bishop Celidonius, who had been established in that same province, the matter will become still clearer if we examine what was done after Saint Leo’s decree, whether by Leo himself in writing or by the Gallican bishops.

[Col. 0457B] [Note: When Quesnellus cited this shorter letter in the preceding chapters, he added approximately these words: “if, however, it is genuine.” He now assumes it wholly genuine, in order to maintain that apostolic authority was disregarded by Hilary and by the Gallican bishops. We demonstrated in the prefatory admonition to that same letter and in the appendix that it is spurious. Therefore Quesnellus’s entire following argument, hostile to apostolic authority and injurious to the Gallican bishops themselves, who were most observant of that authority, entirely collapses because it rests on so false a hypothesis. [Col. 0458D]]

When Leo’s judgment had been heard in Gaul, and his first and shorter letter—said to have been written on 8 January—had been received, it is not entirely clear what opinion the Gallican bishops held among themselves concerning Hilary’s condemnation. Nevertheless, it is extremely probable that they always retained the same attitude toward Hilary and conceded him no less authority over their churches than they had done before. I am readily persuaded to believe that the Church of Arles did not allow any of its rights to be taken away.

This was the reason why, five months after his first letter, Saint Leo wrote another, much longer letter to the same bishops, composed with prolonged reflection and care. In it he tries to soothe the anger of the Gallican prelates provoked by the Roman judgment, sometimes with conciliatory words and sometimes by frightening them with harsher ones. At one moment he removes from their minds the suspicion they had formed—that Leo was considering transferring to himself the ordinations of the Gallican churches; at another he threatens those who voluntarily transferred all authority to Hilary in provinces distinct from Vienne; finally, he adjures, implores, and appeals under God’s name that they remove every cause of dissension from their provinces by repudiating Hilary.

But because he foresaw that the Gallican bishops, determined to preserve their policy and their rights, would be no more moved by his later letters than by his earlier ones, he resolved to call imperial authority to the aid of the pontifical authority. He therefore obtained from the Emperor Valentinian a constitution addressed to Aetius, master of the soldiers in Gaul, ordering that the sentence pronounced against Hilary by the holy Pope Leo should receive full effect. By an everlasting sanction it decreed that neither the Gallican bishops nor those of other provinces should be permitted to attempt anything contrary to ancient custom without the authority of the venerable pope of the Eternal City; rather, it was to be law for them and for everyone that whatever the authority of the apostolic see had decreed or would decree should be observed, and so forth.

Strengthened by such defenses, Leo’s letter was sent to Gaul. We do not learn from historical writers what success it had. The author of the *Life of Saint Hilary* [Note: We have shown in the observations, part III, chapter 2, nos. 1 and 2, that these events occurred not after but before Leo’s judgment. We shall also prove that after that judgment Hilary attempted nothing but obeyed.] relates that Hilary then turned his whole attention to calming Saint Leo’s mind, with humbled submission. The author thus suggests that Hilary lowered himself, not as one guilty of obstinacy and yielding the submission that was due, but through voluntary and freely offered humility, as one indebted to Christian charity and reverence.

With this purpose he sent Ravennius, a priest of his own church and later his successor, to Rome. He then sent the most holy bishops Nectarius and Constantius, through whose agency he sought to demonstrate to Leo the rights of his dignity and the justice of the judgment decreed against Celidonius. He also wrote much in this case which, if it had been transmitted to us by Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, in whose keeping it remained—as is clear from the *Life of Hilary* that he wrote—would have placed us under the greatest obligation to him.

But when the prefect Auxiliaris of the City saw that all these disputes and struggles were irritating Leo’s mind more than calming it—which was what Hilary desired—he advised Hilary, out of their common relationship, to accommodate himself for a while to the tenderness of the Romans and to calm the small clouds with the brightness of a minor change, so that by this course he might gain much while losing nothing.

> “Since you are steadfast in your purpose and always consistent, and are not carried away by the gall of agitation, just as you are not lifted up by the allurements of joy, I do not remember that even the least action of Your Beatitude has been darkened by the stain of arrogance. But people bear it impatiently if we speak as we know ourselves to be speaking; moreover, the ears of the Romans are drawn by a certain tenderness. If Your Holiness occasionally lowers yourself to this, you will gain very much while losing nothing. Grant me this, and calm the small clouds with the brightness of a minor change.”

The following words of Honoratus almost certainly establish that Hilary granted the small change which Auxiliaris so amicably requested:

> “Perceiving such things,” he says after reporting Auxiliaris’s advice, “he devoted himself entirely to prayer, preaching, and activity, as though beginning anew.”

And later:

> “By abstaining from food, applying himself to work, and completing journeys on foot, he so weakened, wearied, and exhausted himself that he scarcely completed the circle of his forty-eighth year.”

From these facts it is clear that neither Saint Leo changed his sentence nor Hilary surrendered his rights; rather, Hilary, by ceasing from such disputes, no longer troubled Leo. He devoted himself entirely to assisting and cultivating the souls entrusted to him through prayer, preaching, and pastoral care.

Applying himself diligently to these duties, he brought his life to an end—a man more concerned for ecclesiastical peace than for his own dignity. It is certain that his death occurred in the year of Christ 449, on 5 May. For before Saint Leo’s response to the bishops who ordained Ravennius—which was issued on 22 August of the year 449—there must have occurred the solemn funeral of Hilary, the convocation of a council from several provinces perhaps, the council itself, the consecration of Ravennius, the drafting of the consecrators’ letter to Leo, and the journey to Rome of the legates sent by the ordainers. These and other events that may have taken place earlier could not have been completed in less than three or four months.

It also follows that Blessed Hilary survived the imperial constitution of Valentinian and the constitution of Pope Leo, received in Gaul, by scarcely more than three or four years; and that he lived scarcely two or three years after, moved by the prayers of the prefect Auxiliaris and by his love of peace, he agreed to abstain from every dispute and devoted the rest of his life entirely to the duties of a bishop.

The situation was therefore unsettled between the Roman and Gallican bishops when Hilary departed this life. During that period of two years no occasion had arisen—and Hilary had not sought one—in which it would have been necessary either to oppose Leo’s decree or to surrender the customary duties and privileges. The first such occasion, as is clear, was the ordination of the bishop of Vaison, which stirred up the dormant, not extinguished, dispute between the bishops of Arles and Vienne.

[Note: Leo’s constitution did not hinder Ravennius’s ordination. Since it had penalized Hilary’s person alone, after his death his fellow-provincials were permitted to ordain a successor, to whom all the rights of the see of Arles would pass, with Leo himself not dissenting. See what we shall discuss on this matter in the observations, part III, nos. 5 and 6. [Col. 0459C]]

But how far the prelates of those provinces were from carrying Leo’s constitution into effect became clear in the very ordination of Ravennius. For, setting aside the Viennese priest, twelve bishops—or fourteen, if the bishops of Vienne and Arles are added to those twelve—or even bishops from other provinces, assembled in synod and unanimously consecrated Ravennius according to the wishes of the clergy, the leading citizens, and the people.

[Note: Bishops came to Ravennius’s ordination not only from the province of Vienne but also from the province of Narbonne II and from the Maritime Alps. Asclepius, bishop of Apt, belonged to Narbonne II, while Nectarius of Digne belonged to the Maritime Alps. [Col. 0459D]]

Saint Leo not only did not condemn this ordination—*Epistle* 36, now 40—but rather strengthened it by his judgment as a good work of priestly brotherhood, granted by God’s favor and accomplished through divine inspiration:

> “For we believe that the peaceful and harmonious election, to which neither moral merits nor the zeal of the citizens was lacking, was indeed a human petition, but was inspired by divine inspiration.”

Moreover, it is clear that the bishop of Vienne did not participate in it, as is evident to anyone who reviews the names of the bishops who sent Leo the letters attesting to the ordination. Among them, Constantine holds first place as the leader of the ordination. That he was not bishop of Vienne is made certain by another letter (*Epistle* 65), which the same ordainers, together with seven others, wrote to Leo on behalf of the see of Arles.

[Note: Five of the bishops who ordained Ravennius did not write this second letter; consequently, their names are not listed in Leo’s response. [Col. 0459D]]

In Leo’s response (*Epistle* 66), where he lists all of them in order, the same Constantine is likewise recorded in first place. No one would say that he would have written on behalf of the rights of the Church of Arles if he had been bishop of Vienne.

Saint Leo did not send a letter of congratulation only to the ordainers, but also to Ravennius himself after his ordination. He urges him, having turned aside pride—which is close to falling—to love humility, which is always destined to increase; and he urges him to confine all the rights of his authority within the rules and limits of the ecclesiastical laws.

By these words Leo unquestionably both censures Hilary and warns Ravennius against invading another’s jurisdiction. Yet he neither suggests nor criticizes any neglect of the Viennese metropolitan in Ravennius’s ordination. It is therefore reasonable to conclude that Leo did not wish by his judgment to strip the Church of Arles of its metropolitan right, but only to punish Hilary; once Hilary was dead, Leo judged it equitable that everything should return to its former condition.

Nor did Leo wish Ravennius to be adorned only with metropolitan authority, but also with that prerogative by which, in view of Saint Trophimus, the see of Arles stood out among the other metropolitans of Gaul—that is, with the privilege of the first metropolitan.

[Note: The Gallican bishops acknowledge in *Epistle* 65, chapter 3, that this prerogative derived neither from the right of the see of Arles itself nor from its earlier and ancient establishment, but from a concession of the apostolic see. They say that the bishop of Arles had also been granted this honor and dignity: not only was he to govern these provinces—those belonging to metropolitan jurisdiction—by his own authority, but also to keep all Gaul, entrusted to him in the place of the apostolic see, within the bounds of ecclesiastical order.

The words “in the stead of the apostolic see” clearly indicate an apostolic concession. This is expressly shown by Zosimus, who in *Epistle* 7, according to P. Constantius, describes the bishop of Arles as endowed with apostolic authority; and in *Epistle* 10 he mentions an apostolic delegation.

Hence, when the bishops mentioned above ask that the rights which the Church of Arles had either received from antiquity or later claimed by the authority of the apostolic see be confirmed, they indicate by the former words a metropolitan right derived, as it were, from Saint Trophimus, while by the latter they imply a right in another province that was later granted by the apostolic see.

This latter right chiefly concerns two matters: the issuance of *formatae* and the convocation of synods from all the Gallican provinces. Zosimus granted him the right to issue *formatae* to all clerics who traveled abroad. We have also conjectured with considerable probability in the observations, part II, chapter 6, no. 8, that the right to convene synods from other Gallican provinces—over which the bishop of Arles did not preside by his own right—should likewise be attributed to that pontiff. [Col. 0460C]]

This right gave him authority to convene synodal assemblies in other provinces, to issue letters of passage to traveling clerics, and to promote and maintain everything pertaining to the common faith or discipline of the Church throughout Gaul. Saint Leo freely conferred these powers upon Ravennius—not by a new decree but in accordance with an earlier and ancient institution. This is attested both by the general synod of those provinces, which Ravennius undertook to convene on the occasion of Leo’s letter to Flavian, as we shall later say, and by Leo’s letter addressed to Ravennius concerning a certain wandering man named Petronianus, who falsely claimed to be a deacon of the Roman Church throughout Gaul.

To oppose that man’s audacity, Leo wrote that Ravennius should expose him in his falsehood, after warning the bishops of the entire province as well, and expel him from communion with all the churches so that he might not continue this usurpation.

Here the word “province” must be understood in a broader sense as referring to all seven provinces, since Leo mentions both Gaul as a whole and all the churches. Leo would not have made adequate provision against the audacity of that wandering impostor if he had ordered such an inquiry to be conducted only within the boundaries of the province of Vienne.

# CHAPTER IX

## The same conclusion is established by the ordination of the bishop of Vaison, the division of the province that followed it, and Leo’s letter sent concerning the matter.

The affairs of the Church of Arles stood in this condition, and there was hope that, once the disputes arising from Hilary had been buried in eternal oblivion, it would enjoy its former splendor and authority in the future. For even if Saint Leo had greatly desired to diminish some part of that supreme authority over the Gallican churches—

[Note: This entire paragraph is a pure fabrication. No document can prove either that Leo had any great desire to diminish the authority of the see of Arles, which it possessed by right, or that the Gallicans attempted anything against the pope’s own constitution by which he punished Hilary, so that Leo, fearing their conspiracy, thought it necessary amid the extremely difficult circumstances of the time to dissemble and to confirm the privileges of Arles in Ravennius.

On the contrary, the holy pontiff was always so unwilling to diminish these privileges that, when he issued his decree against Hilary, he deprived only Hilary himself of them and wished them to be preserved for his successors. Compare note 3 above, col. 459, note a, in the preceding chapter. [Col. 0460D]]

—nevertheless, the complete unanimity of the Gauls, who were united in support of the greatness of the see of Arles, stood in the way of his hope that this might someday occur. Their unity had shone out both in Hilary’s case and especially in the ordination of Ravennius. Therefore Leo had judged it preferable to ignore these actions, although they were attempted to the prejudice of his constitution, rather than to have the Gallican Church resisting and hostile.

He was made especially mild and inclined to dissemble, however, by the Eastern disturbances that had recently arisen on account of the new Eutychian heresy, and by the unfortunate outcome of the false synod of Ephesus. In that synod the affairs of the Church were overthrown, the reverence due to the apostolic see was diminished, Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, was killed, and Domnus of Antioch, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Theodoret of Cyrus, and other bishops devoted to the Roman see were deposed. Dioscorus of Alexandria was using force to accomplish everything and was advancing rapidly toward domination over the entire Church, with the support of the emperor Theodosius and Eutyches. Leo’s letters were rejected, the Roman legates suffered indignities, and they were forced to seek safety in flight.

Leo therefore had good reason to fear that, if he made the Gallican bishops more hostile by depressing the see of Arles, he would find them opposed to the struggle he was preparing against the East. He was also certain that the bishops of the neighboring regions would be difficult to separate from the Gallican bishops—namely, the Britons, the Spaniards, and those from the Italian diocese who were nearer to Gaul. In my judgment, this was why Saint Leo allowed himself to be appeased and became more favorably disposed toward Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul.

Meanwhile, an occasion arose that brought about some change in the situation. When Auspicius, bishop of Vaison in the province of Vienne, had departed this life for a better one, Ravennius undertook, by virtue of his metropolitan right, to ordain another in the deceased bishop’s place, a man named Fonteius, and in fact ordained him.

The bishop of Vienne bore this with the greatest difficulty. He claimed the ordination of the province as something due to him both by ancient right and by the recent constitution of Leo. He therefore sent a delegation to the Roman pontiff and wrote a letter complaining that the bishop of Arles had usurped the ordination of the bishop of Vaison.

When the Gallican bishops learned of this, they thought it in their interest to send legates to the pontiff in their own name as well, and to compose a letter in the form of a petition. In it they would set before Leo the foundations and reasons for the dignity of the Church of Arles, lest the legates of the bishop of Vienne deceive him and extort a judgment contrary to the rights of Arles.

Nineteen bishops from different provinces assembled to prepare this petition—for that is the number to whom Leo later sent his reply—and it is clear from the language of the petition that it was sent on the occasion of the Viennese delegation. It criticizes the city of Vienne, which, it says, was now shamelessly and conspicuously demanding unlawful primacy for itself.

Whether the Gallican prelates served their own interests well by this delegation is for others to judge. Certainly they seemed to detract somewhat from their own right when they voluntarily requested that a matter already beyond dispute be brought under examination again, relying merely on the consent Leo had given to Ravennius’s ordination, which had taken place without the authority of the bishop of Vienne; and when they themselves sent legates to Leo to plead their case, together with a petition and other documents of litigation.

[Note: A refutation of this prejudice and of the entire paragraph may be found in the observations, part I, chapter 7, no. 7. [Col. 0461]]

Hilary had shown himself much more cautious. When he entered Rome, he openly declared to Leo that he was bringing a report, not a petition; that he had come to perform duties, not to plead a case; that he was presenting what had been done in the order of a protest, not an accusation; and finally, that he was asking nothing else than that he should regulate the condition of the churches according to customary practice.

These same points could have been put forward with equal justice. But those bishops thought they had to proceed differently, either because they foresaw that Leo would summon them and hear the legates of both sides dispute before him concerning the primacy of the province of Vienne—a necessity imposed upon them by the imperial constitution issued by Valentinian against Hilary:

> “If any bishop, summoned to the judgment of the Roman prelate, neglects to come, he shall be compelled by the governor of the same province to appear”—

or because they trusted so confidently in the justice of their case that they feared none of the decrees subsequently issued by Leo. For Leo himself appeared to have settled the matter by his consent to Ravennius’s ordination. For this reason they prominently recalled that consent at the beginning of their petition, to suggest that he had no room to retract it.

Whatever the case, the delegation was undertaken by the priest Petronius and the deacon Regulus. No one who knows how painfully Saint Leo had borne Hilary’s avoidance of the judgment of the apostolic see with such firmness can doubt that this delegation was most welcome to him.

He therefore gladly received the unexpected delegation and the judgment concerning Gallican primacy that had been voluntarily submitted to him by both parties in dispute. No such favorable opportunity had yet arisen, since the faith had been established and ecclesiastical discipline founded in Gaul, for the authority of the Roman see to be secured in Gaul with the assent and invitation of the Gallican bishops themselves.

He settled the dispute in the manner explained by his letter to the nineteen bishops of Gaul. He assigned to the bishop of Vienne four cities over which he was to preside: Valentia, Tarantasia, Geneva, and Gratianopolis (*Epistle* 66 of Saint Leo, to the Gallican bishops). Together with Vienne itself, these made five cities whose ecclesiastical care belonged to the bishop of Vienne. The remaining cities of the same province were placed under the authority and ordination of the bishop of Arles.

Thus that great province of Vienne, which had been the cause of such a long dispute between the two bishops, was divided by the decree of our Leo, as though by a new Solomon, into two parts (*1 Kings* 3), half being given to one and half to the other.

Although Leo’s judgment appears to have greatly diminished the right of the bishop of Arles, a closer examination of the matter shows that in the same letter Leo acknowledged and confirmed his ancient privilege and right.

First, there is nothing in which he does not at least make the bishop of Arles equal to the bishop of Vienne, nor anything in which he places the bishop of Vienne above the bishop of Arles. For he asserts that they had possessed a common right among the nations with respect to civil precedence.

Then, regarding ecclesiastical precedence, he says that, by turns and according to the circumstances of various cases, one or the other had excelled in ecclesiastical privileges. This, he says, was clear from consideration of the arguments of both parties’ clergy who were present (*Epistle* 66 of Saint Leo).

But how much more he was persuaded of the right of Arles is evident from what follows.

## 2.

Saint Leo testifies that Ravennius’s predecessor had lost this authority because of excessive presumption. Hilary therefore was not deprived of it because it was foreign to him and had been seized unlawfully.

## 3.

The same pontiff suggests that he was led to this administrative division of the province in order to preserve the goodwill of all the Gallican prelates and to foster peace within the province of Vienne.

## 4.

He acted for the honor of the apostolic see. Since that see had conferred upon Vienne, together with the metropolitan authority taken away from Hilary, the metropolitan authority, it might have appeared compelled to rescind its own judgment if Vienne ceased altogether to be a metropolitan see.

> “We cannot permit Vienne to be wholly dishonored, especially since, in receiving its privilege, it is already using the authority of our disposition; we have judged that the authority taken away from Hilary should be assigned to the bishop of Vienne” (*the cited Epistle*).

## 5.

He also acted in some measure for the honor of the bishop of Vienne, who, having been metropolitan of the whole province that he had claimed for himself by Leo’s decree, would otherwise immediately have been cast down into the lower order of bishops.

> “So that he may not suddenly appear to have been made inferior to himself, he shall preside over the four neighboring towns,” and so forth (*the same Epistle*).

## 6.

Leo sufficiently acknowledges that these towns ought not to have been withdrawn from the jurisdiction of Arles if the matter were treated according to the strict points of law. For he excuses himself to Ravennius in some measure and appeals to him, in the interest of charity, peace, and moderation, to endure patiently what appeared to have been done contrary to right because of ecclesiastical necessity.

> “Because of his moderation, we believe that he will be so devoted to charity and peace that he will by no means consider taken away from himself what he sees granted to his brother” (*Epistle* 66, to the nineteen bishops, chapter 22).

## 7.

Nothing shows more clearly that the whole province belonged to the bishop of Arles, and that Leo was persuaded of this, than the fact that, of the twelve cities constituting the province of Vienne—if the notices published by Sirmond and others are to be trusted—he assigned only four to the bishop of Vienne, leaving the remaining eight under the authority of the bishop of Arles.

[Note: Thirteen cities are counted as belonging to the province of Vienne in the *Notices of Gaul*, including Vienne itself and Arles. Leo assigned only three of these thirteen to the bishop of Vienne, for the fourth, Tarantasia, belongs according to the same notices not to the province of Vienne but to the Graian Alps. [Col. 0463D]]

[Col. 0463B] 8. Finally, this argument, as well as those advanced above, is confirmed by Pope Symmachus. Writing to the bishops of Gaul concerning the same controversy, which had flared up again in his time, he decreed that the definition of his predecessor Leo must be upheld. He writes as follows:

“IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE INDULGENCE”—a point that deserves careful notice—“of the aforesaid pontiff, let the bishop of Vienne claim as belonging to his own right the towns of Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble. Let him not presume to claim anything beyond what was once granted to him by the Apostolic See. But let the bishop of Arles, with the passage of time, defend all the other parishes or dioceses by his own PRIVILEGE AND HONOR” (Symmachus, Epistle 9, to the bishops of Gaul).

[Note: [Col. 0463D] If Symmachus used the word “indulgence” here, he nevertheless declares the right of the bishop of Vienne shortly afterward in the same letter, writing: “Let him claim his own right.” The Fathers of the Synod of Turin recognized that this right of Vienne did not yield to the right of Arles. Yet, perceiving that the controversy could not be judged in one direction because weighty considerations existed on both sides, they proposed that the province be divided. Saint Leo himself also sufficiently acknowledged this right of Vienne. After hearing the arguments advanced by both parties, although he was more favorably disposed toward Ravennius and saw that Arles was more distinguished in his own age and had been preferred by the bishops of its own province, he nevertheless could not assign the entire province to the bishop of Arles. Compelled by the force of the reasons and rights belonging to both sees, he had to exercise justice with such moderation that he divided the province in accordance with the judgment of the Fathers of Turin.]

Thus, if we believe Symmachus, Saint Leo made use of indulgence toward the bishop of Vienne when he wished part of the province to be subject to Vienne’s administration. Out of love for peace, however, the bishop of Arles allowed something to be taken from his own right when he permitted those four towns to be transferred to the authority of Vienne [Col. 0463C]—Leo having prevailed not so much by decree as by entreaties. Everything in Symmachus’s words deserves attention. Just as he mentions the indulgence and the concession of the Apostolic See when writing about the parishes assigned to Vienne, so he mentions the privilege and honor of Arles when speaking of the cities subject to its right. He indicates no right asserted for Vienne except by concession of Saint Leo; whereas he represents the right of Arles as resting upon a privilege and honor established from ancient times.

I said that the bishop of Arles was overcome more by entreaties than by Leo’s decree. For in the letter that Leo wrote to Ravennius on the same day on which he wrote to the nineteen bishops, he says not a word about the assignment of those four towns to the bishop of Vienne. It therefore cannot be doubted that, through his legates Petronius and Regulus, Leo addressed Ravennius orally and earnestly begged him, for the sake of peace and in order to settle the ancient controversy, to yield the administration of certain cities to Vienne. These, I think, are in part the matters which, as Saint Leo writes in the same [Col. 0464A] letter, he did not think should be committed to writing. [Note: [Col. 0464D] We exposed the erroneous interpretation of this testimony, upon which this entire paragraph rests, in Annotation 7 (previous volume, col. 887, note b), in the letter itself, Epistle 67, where we gave its true explanation.]

“But what,” he says, “was not to be committed to writing, once you have learned it through the communication of our aforesaid sons, you will, trusting in the Lord’s help, carry out effectively and laudably” (Epistle 67).

It was not to be committed to writing because it scarcely accorded with the dignity of the Apostolic See for it to humble itself in public letters to the point of prayers and supplications, so that its decree concerning the administration of the Churches might be received by the Gallican bishops and brought into effect. The circumstances of the time and the dignity of the first metropolitan of Gaul greatly contributed to persuading Ravennius of this. Saint Leo hoped thereby to strengthen him. An opportunity to exercise that authority presented itself at the same time: namely, that Ravennius should share with all the bishops of Gaul Leo’s letter written to Flavian; or even—something he plausibly received as a confidential instruction—that he should convene a synodal gathering from all the provinces, at which the same letter would be approved by everyone [Col. 0464B] and the consent of all, committed to writing, would be sent to Saint Leo.

## CHAPTER X. The objection drawn from the catalogue of the provinces and cities of Gaul against the antiquity of metropolitan dignity in the Church of Arles is resolved; and the date of that catalogue is now established for the first time.

Having traced through every period, from the establishment of the faith in Gaul, the dignity of the Church of Arles, I believe it stands out so greatly among the others that scarcely anything remains doubtful which could incline our judgment even slightly toward Vienne. Everywhere Arles holds the primacy; Vienne nowhere.

Nevertheless, some regard as serious an objection advanced in favor of Vienne against Arles from the catalogues of the provinces and cities of Gaul that circulate widely. J. Sirmond prefixed one of these to the first volume of the Councils of Gaul. He conjectures that it was compiled in the time of the Emperor Honorius, when it was customary to distinguish Gaul into seven provinces. Andreas Du Chesne collected several others, not greatly different, [Col. 0464C] from manuscript codices in the first volume of his Collection of the Writers of Gallic History. In all of them, moreover, the city of Vienne is called the metropolis of the Viennenses; Arles is made subject to it and even occupies the lower position in the same province. Hence, they say, it is clear that the right of the bishop of Arles is not ancient, and that the bishop of Vienne possessed it not only in early times but also in the time of the Emperor Honorius, precisely when Arles began to be enhanced by greater privileges and honored by the assembly of the provinces.

But the entire structure of this argument must collapse if it is proved that such catalogues of the provinces [Note: [Col. 0464D] See what we say about the catalogue of Gaul published by Sirmond in Observations, part II, chapter 4, where this entire chapter of Quesnell is examined and refuted.] were compiled not in the time of Honorius but much later, and that they are later than the age of Hilary and Leo.

I establish this first from a constitution of the Emperor Honorius himself, issued in the year 418, in which he simply calls Arles the metropolis. “In the metropolitan city,” he says, “that is, in the city of Arles.” Either, therefore, the catalogue that makes Arles subject to Vienne is false, [Col. 0464D] or it was written at a time other than that of Honorius, whose constitution deserves more credence than I know not what catalogues of uncertain date.

### 2.

Who could believe that in public acts or records Arles was not merely counted among the cities subject to Vienne but placed second from last among all of them, at the very time when it was being honored with the highest distinctions by the emperors and their prefects and was being raised above the other cities of Gaul? Yet the same edict makes clear that, several years earlier, the assembly of the seven provinces had been established by the prefect Petronius at Arles; that the seat of the prefecture had been placed there; and that the city had been ennobled by every kind of prerogative. Everything that contradicts its splendor must therefore be relegated to other times.

### 3.

If this catalogue had been drawn up before the time of Saint Leo, we would read among the cities of the Maritime Alps the fortress or city of Nice. Since it is clear from a letter of Pope Hilary to certain bishops of Gaul [Col. 0465B] that the fortress of Nice, until the final years of Leo, had its own bishop, distinct from the bishop of Cemenelum, it follows that it ought to have had a place in the catalogue. Since it is omitted from it, we must believe that the catalogue was drawn up at a time when this fortress had been reduced to such straits and poverty that it ought not even to have been counted among the fortresses; for many such places are added to the cities in the catalogue.

This certainly had not yet happened during the earlier years of our Leo. At that time Nice was still honored with an episcopal see. Indeed, even in the time of Pope Hilary, the people of Nice scarcely endured being deprived of that dignity: they took care to have a bishop ordained for themselves, but by Pope Hilary’s decree he was removed on account of Leo’s constitution. Thereafter both places were reduced to the governance of a single bishop.

### 4.

I scarcely believe that the provinces of Lugdunensis Secunda and Belgica Secunda were in the condition displayed by the catalogue during the time of the Emperor Honorius. For there we read that Rouen held the primacy in a very extensive province, although in the time of Honorius the bishop Paulinus of Nola marvels at it as having emerged, so to speak, from darkness.

“Finally,” he says, “now we hear that Rouen, previously renowned only by a modest name in the neighboring regions, is also respectfully named in distant provinces and counted among the cities made illustrious by sacred places,” and so forth.

As for the city of the Morini, which the catalogue lists as adorned with an episcopal see, the entire stretch of the Nervian coast had scarcely received, as the same Paulinus says, the breath of the faith of truth before Victricius preached there:

“Before Victricius preached there, in whom it first shone forth, grew brighter, and appeared more ardently and more closely,” and so forth.

“Like the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee; and those who sat in the region and shadow of death saw a great light; so now also in the land of the Morini, situated at the edge of the world, which the Ocean, roaring with barbarian waves, beats against, . . . their hardened hearts, rejoicing in the light obtained for them from the Lord through your holiness, were laid down for Christ as he entered,” and so forth.

I do not know whether all this can be reconciled with catalogues of the provinces [Col. 0465D] which—as is especially worth noting—appear to have been drawn up for ecclesiastical use. Evidence of this is that all those catalogues, both those published by J. Sirmond and those edited by Andreas Du Chesne, which are commonly found in the manuscript codices of the Thuane Library, occur only in manuscripts containing exclusively ecclesiastical records.

### 5.

If that catalogue had been made in the time of Honorius by public authority or on the basis of universally certain knowledge, the Fathers of the Council of Turin—which was held during the reign of that same emperor—would not have remained hesitant and uncertain about which of the two bishops, the bishop of Arles or the bishop of Vienne, should be granted metropolitan dignity in ecclesiastical affairs. Nor would they have been forced into the decision that whichever of them proved his city to be a metropolis should obtain the primatial honor of the entire province. This shows that the state of affairs at that time was less clearly defined and that the rights were less certain than the catalogue represents.

### 6.

Sidonius Apollinaris, in Book VII, Letter 7, testifies that the city of Marseille first began, during his own lifetime, to be counted among the last cities of the province. This befell it as a punishment because, concerned more with private advantage than with public interests, its people had entered into an alliance with the Gothic kings that was neither useful nor honorable.

“By doing this often and for a long time,” he says, “you have now begun not to be the first of your fellow provincials, but the last.”

By these words he sufficiently indicates that until that time—that is, at least until the year 470—Marseille had held the first place among the cities of the province of Vienne after the metropolis. That place was rightly accorded to a city whose ancient nobility made it surpass the others, so much so that it had even been adorned for a time with metropolitan dignity by decree of the Council of Turin.

But in Sirmond’s catalogue [Col. 0466B] and in the others, Marseille is written as the very last of all, immediately preceded by Arles. It is therefore clearer than daylight that the catalogue under discussion is much later in date than the time of Honorius and must be assigned to the age of Sidonius.

Indeed, it is highly probable that it was compiled around the time when Euric, king of the Visigoths, invaded Gaul and seized Arles and Marseille, or perhaps several years earlier. Since the Burgundians held most of the province of Vienne, almost only Arles and Marseille remained under Roman control; and around the year 470 they fell into the hands of Euric, the Arian king of the Visigoths.

As Sidonius Apollinaris reports in Book VII, Letter 6, to Basil, Euric either put to death most of the bishops of those provinces or forced them into exile, without subsequently appointing bishops to replace the deceased. Thus a sorrowful despair over the interruption of the faith weighed upon peoples deprived of their bishops; no care was given to the deserted dioceses and parishes; and it seemed not so much that priests had died as that the priesthood itself had perished [Col. 0466C].

These are approximately Sidonius’s words. From them we can understand how favorable an opportunity then presented itself to the bishop of Vienne to recover the rights he claimed had been unjustly seized from him by the bishop of Arles. He possessed many cities of the province subject to himself and the Burgundians. Seeing that all communication with Arles was prohibited because Arles lay under Roman or Gothic rule, those cities easily submitted voluntarily to Vienne—evidently with the support of the Burgundian ruler—and no one on the side of Arles resisted, since at that time the bishop of Arles was not even permitted to speak or protest.

It is therefore most probable that Sirmond’s catalogue and the others were compiled during this period, when the bishop of Vienne took care that Arles and Marseille should be listed among the cities that he claimed had formerly belonged to his jurisdiction.

Although we do not possess an author who expressly reports these events, they are sufficiently suggested both by comparing the catalogue itself with the condition of the city and Church of Arles that we have described and by considering what occurred during the time of Pope Symmachus. It is evident that Symmachus issued a constitution in favor of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, because the bishop of Vienne had exceeded the boundaries established by Pope Leo and had attempted to claim the whole province for his own authority through secular patronage or under cover of some other pretext. [Col. 0466D] For this reason the pontiff again confirmed the decree of his predecessor and declared that Caesarius’s rights were to remain intact.

## CHAPTER XI. Other objections are dispelled by which metropolitan dignity is apparently claimed for the bishop of Vienne.

An objection may also be advanced in favor of the bishop of Vienne against the bishop of Arles from the First Council of Valence, held in the province of Vienne in the year 374. Florentius, bishop of Vienne, appears to have presided over it, while Concordius—said at that time to have been bishop of Arles—subscribed among the bishops of the province.

[Note: [Col. 0465] We shall explain what should be inferred from the Council of Valence in Observations, part II, chapter 5, no. 2.]

But this argument is entirely weak. First, the subscriptions of the bishops that are now read at the end of the canons are absent from the older editions and were first published by Sirmond in volume I of the Councils of Gaul.

Second, although Sirmond praises the four manuscript codices that he used in revising this council, the subscriptions in question were found in only one of them, the Reims manuscript. It is therefore permissible to suspect that they were arranged by some idle reader, with the names taken from the beginning of the letter.

Third, it is contrary to more usual practice for the names of those writing, once listed at the beginning of a letter, to be written out again at the end. This can be seen in the letter of the First Council of Arles to Pope Sylvester, and also in the letter of that same Council of Valence to the clergy and people of the Church of Fréjus.

Fourth, at the beginning of both letters twenty-one bishops are listed. The third is Florentius, supposedly bishop of Vienne; Concordius of Arles is twelfth in the first letter and fourteenth in the second. But in the appended subscriptions, Florentius is placed before everyone else after the omission of the first two.

Fifth, only Florentius’s see is recorded.

Sixth, he alone subscribes in a manner different from the others: “I, Florentius, bishop of the Church of Vienne, have subscribed.” All the others are written beneath in this form: “I, N., wish you, brothers, good health in the Lord.” The latter form, beyond doubt, is more suitable for a letter than the other method of subscribing.

Seventh, before the beginning of the sixth century it was not customary for bishops to subscribe in the form “bishop of the Church of N.” They subscribed either simply “bishop,” or “bishop of the city,” for example, “of Vienne,” or “bishop of the Viennenses.” This practice seems first to have been changed at the First Council of Orléans.

Florentius’s subscription, then, was forged, I think, undoubtedly for the purpose of making it appear that the bishop of Vienne had presided over this synod by metropolitan right, and that the bishop of Arles had been subject to him. For that reason Concordius is found relegated to the last place of all. These considerations certainly give rise to a considerable suspicion of fraud.

### 2.

No other record testifies that Florentius was bishop of Vienne at that time. Indeed, the people of Cahors claim him for themselves, and in all editions of the works of Saint Paulinus the letter that is number thirty-two in the Rosweyd edition is addressed to Florentius, bishop of Cahors. Fronton du Duc and Rosweyd, very diligent writers, report this in their notes.

Although these matters are not free from difficulty, they leave the question unresolved and provide nothing that can be extracted in favor of Vienne. On the contrary, this synod argues entirely against Vienne, since Foegadius is said to have presided over it, and no one makes him bishop of Vienne.

See the succession and acts of the Church of Cahors, which claim this Florentius for that Church, as well as the Chronicle of Ado, which places Nicetas, bishop of Vienne, around this period; he may perhaps be the same person as Nicetius, whose name appears in the synodical letter of the Council of Valence.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] The succession of the bishops of Vienne inserted in Ado’s Chronicle appears to derive from the diptychs, so that the series should not be rejected merely because the events and dates assigned to those bishops do not stand. Indeed, if other reliable documents are compared with this series and the proper period is restored to those bishops on that basis, everything will be found to fit together well. Thus Verus, who is wrongly advanced in that Chronicle to the apostolic age, will be recognized from the First Council of Arles as having lived at the beginning of the fourth century; and Florentius, since he fits the Council of Valence perfectly, should be preferred—not Nicetas, who was the immediate predecessor of Mamertus and flourished around the middle of the fifth century. Compare what we observed concerning a similar catalogue of the bishops of Ravenna in the admonition to Epistle 156, nos. 3 and 4. See also what Tillemont discusses concerning this catalogue of the bishops of Vienne in volume III, under Irenaeus, note 3.]

But someone may object that the very name of the province speaks for Vienne.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] We establish this argument more fully in Observations, part II, chapter 4, no. 5, where we also discuss the testimony of Eusebius.]

Why, they ask, was it called Viennensis unless the city of Vienne was the metropolis of the entire province?

This argument is no more substantial. What occurred among the pagans in the various divisions of the provinces cannot in any way legitimately be transferred to ecclesiastical affairs. And although ecclesiastical organization generally followed the civil distribution of the provinces, it was sometimes necessary to depart from that arrangement, as is clear from Innocent’s letter to Alexander of Antioch and from Leo’s own ordinance concerning the province of Vienne.

By the same method of reasoning one would conclude that the Churches of the provinces of Lugdunensis Secunda, Tertia, and Quarta once had the same ecclesiastical metropolitan—the bishop of Lugdunum—because they were called Lugdunenses. Or one would have to subject the Churches of Narbonensis Secunda to the bishop of Narbonne for the same reason, since the entire Roman province once took its name from Narbo.

Nothing, therefore, can be established in this matter from the names. This can again be proved by an example drawn from the province of Vienne. Since the province of Narbonensis Secunda was cut off from Vienne, it ought to have been called Viennensis if the matter were judged by the force of names. Yet the opposite occurred: it was called Narbonensis, not Viennensis.

What, then, should we say about the ancient authors who call Vienne a metropolis? I answer that the meaning of the word differs according to the various divisions involved. If one looks to the first division, that of Augustus, it is already certain that Vienne was not the metropolis of the whole of Narbonensis, within whose boundaries it was contained. For the ancient authors assign primacy to Narbo, from which the province was named. Strabo, in Book IV, and Pliny, Book III, chapter 4, say:

“Narbo, a colony of the Romans, is the capital of the entire region reduced by Quintus Fabius into a province. In the division made by Augustus Caesar, it is the metropolis, or principal city, of the fourth part of all Gaul.”

Strabo indeed calls Vienne a metropolis in the passage cited [Col. 0468C], but he calls it the metropolis of the Allobroges. The meaning of this author is therefore that the Allobroges, who were one of the peoples of the province of Narbonensis, had Vienne as their principal city—or rather, the only substantial city he names. In reality, according to the same Strabo, the territory of the Allobroges was bounded by the rivers Rhône and Isère and lay between their banks, almost like an island.

Moreover, the word “metropolis” did not then have precisely the same meaning that it acquired in later centuries. I do not recall whether, after the subdivision had been made, Vienne was called a metropolis; hence the serious controversy that arose at the time of the Council of Turin.

Eusebius does indeed mention Lugdunum and Vienne as though they were the two metropolises of Gaul. But first, he speaks as if he were not entirely certain of the matter and were reporting what he had learned from others: βεβούνται, “they are said.” Second, he must be understood in the sense of the ancient geographers: Vienne was the metropolis of the Allobroges, and that only in the civil order. For there was never an ecclesiastical province of the Allobroges.

Finally, the city of Vienne had once been illustrious among the pagans, and Eusebius speaks from the standpoint of that reputation. Yet, as I remember reading, Lugdunum had eclipsed Vienne. Since this passage of Eusebius is especially relevant to our subject, however, I shall take the opportunity afforded by this objection to investigate more fully, in the following chapter, the condition of the province and thereby to determine the rights of the Church of Vienne over it.

## CHAPTER XII. The condition of the Church of Vienne in the time of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, when the martyrs of Lugdunum completed their contest.

The advocates of the Church of Vienne appear to derive great support from Eusebius in order to vindicate its rights and primacy. Eusebius, they say, expressly calls Vienne a metropolis and places it after Lugdunum, so that it should be regarded as either the first or at least the second city of Gaul.

For Eusebius writes in Book V, chapter 1:

“In Gaul a stadium was established for the contests described above. Its cities are easily the leading μετροπόλεις, ‘metropolises,’ and are said to excel all the others in common report: Lugdunum and Vienne, and so forth.”

The letter that the martyrs wrote to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia begins in this manner:

“The servants of Jesus Christ who dwell in Vienne and Lugdunum, to the brothers in Asia and Phrygia,” and so forth.

No one will call into question the ancient splendor of the city of Vienne among the pagans [Col. 0469B]. But those who attempt to assert the rights and distinctions of its Church—and especially its primacy—from such a splendid civic condition appear to me to act with little prudence.

Although in later periods of the Church, when the foundations of ecclesiastical discipline had been laid and the order of the hierarchy established, ecclesiastical ranks were arranged according to the pattern of civil government, the dignity of episcopal sees was stabilized, and the power of metropolitans erected, it is nevertheless the action of a man who, in my judgment, confuses ancient and modern matters to seek that same form of discipline in the century immediately following the apostolic age, especially in Transalpine Gaul, which accepted the faith only late.

[Note: [Col. 0469D] See Observations, part II, chapter 5, no. 12.]

Everyone can see that Eusebius is speaking of the civil dignity of the city of Vienne, which the circumstances of the time do not allow us to transfer to ecclesiastical affairs. At that time, moreover, Vienne had already fallen far from the primitive splendor that the pagans had bestowed upon it.

### 2.

Since Eusebius is using information received from geographers [Col. 0469C], rather than his own knowledge, there is no doubt that he must be understood in the same sense as the Greek author Strabo. From Strabo we learned above that Vienne was the metropolis only of the Allobroges, who occupied only that region which, as Strabo himself testifies, was enclosed by the banks of the Rhône and Isère, almost in the form of an island.

This is also suggested by Eusebius’s manner of speaking when he writes:

“The distinguished and superior metropolises of Gaul are said to be Lugdunum and Vienne.”

### 3.

Even authors who hold the contrary position admit that the beginnings of the Church of Lugdunum are owed to Bishop Pothinus, who was sent to that region by Polycarp of Smyrna in Asia, a bishop and disciple of the blessed Apostle John. This is confirmed by Gregory of Tours in Book I of his History of the Franks, chapter 24, and by Sulpicius Severus, who writes in Book II of his Sacred History that the fifth persecution was carried out under Aurelius, the son of Antoninus, and that at that time martyrdoms were first seen within Gaul, the worship of God having been received later beyond the Alps.

Indeed, those who suffered at Lugdunum at that time are called προτομάρτυρες, “first martyrs,” in the letter of the Churches of Lugdunum and Vienne. Nor is it credible that the faith was first received by the Viennese, who were so close to the people of Lugdunum that they would gladly have poured out the same gift upon them; had the Viennese already been imbued with the faith, there would have been no need to await it from Asia.

Who, moreover, could suppose that at the very beginnings of the faith there was already a plan to establish two ecclesiastical metropolitans in two Churches so close to one another, so recently founded, and composed of so small a number of Christians, when neither the name nor the power of ecclesiastical metropolitans had yet emerged?

If, therefore, Vienne had its own bishop at that time, it is certain that he was not adorned with metropolitan authority.

### 4.

There are weighty conjectures that move me to believe that the Viennese at that time had no bishop placed over them other than the one who governed the people of Lugdunum.

[Note: [Col. 0469D] On this very difficult controversy, consult what Tillemont observes on both sides in note 3 under Irenaeus, volume III, and what Father Jean-Antoine Blancus argues against Quesnell’s position in Book II of *Della esterior Polizia della Chiesa*, chapter 1, § 9, no. 9. We could make further observations in this and the following chapter; but since they are not necessary to our purpose of vindicating Leo and would draw us too far afield, we think they should be omitted.]

First, this may be inferred with considerable probability from the proximity of the two places, as well as from the shortage of episcopal personnel that one may reasonably suppose existed in that still-nascent Church. Just as this shortage of bishops prevented each city from having its own bishop, so the small number of believers meant that one bishop was sufficient, and more than sufficient, for several cities. Bishops could therefore be sent to more distant cities to preach the faith and administer those sacraments that cannot be conferred by anyone other than a bishop. In the meantime, presbyters were appointed in the nearer towns to govern the Churches living there under the bishop’s authority.

What the Council of Sardica and many other councils later said about a small city for which one presbyter is sufficient—that a bishop ought not to be established there—must certainly also have been practiced in the case of large cities for which presbyters alone were sufficient. This was especially so when the faithful were few and the metropolis was nearby, making it easy to summon a bishop either for the laying on of hands or for other episcopal functions.

This arrangement ought to have been maintained by Lugdunum toward the Church of Vienne with even greater right, and could have been maintained more easily because, as we infer from the condition of those neighboring cities, the gift of the faith had been transmitted to Vienne from Lugdunum, which had first received the faith from Asia.

### 2.

We see the Christians of both cities writing together and jointly about their martyrs, and sending a single legate, taken from the Church of Lugdunum—namely, Irenaeus—to the Roman pontiff, partly to inform him about the condition of their Churches and partly to submit to him the judgment of the Gallican Church [Col. 0470C] concerning the controversy that had arisen in Phrygia over the false prophets Montanus, Alcibiades, and Theodotus.

### 3.

In this celebrated account of the martyrdom, there would surely be some mention—indeed, frequent mention—of the bishop of Vienne if that city had had its own bishop, especially in the passage where we read:

“The most distinguished men from both Churches, and all those through whose greatest labor and diligence the affairs here had been established, were SIMULTANEOUSLY ALL held captive.”

But just as the account does not remain silent about the bishop of Lugdunum, whose courageous contest it commemorates, so it says not even a word about the bishop of Vienne. The letter ought to have distinguished him from the rest of the martyr band—as it distinguishes the deacon—if he had been arrested and suffered with the others.

If, on the other hand, he escaped the attention of the pagans and evaded their hands—which is nevertheless not credible either of a bishop of those times or of such diligent investigators—Eusebius would at least have presented him to us as concerned for Christ’s flock and assisting the suffering Church, especially after Pothinus had completed his contest. His death made the care and solicitude of a bishop of Vienne necessary for both Churches. The bishop of Vienne himself would have written to others, and especially to the bishop of Rome, about the martyrs’ contest, the false prophets, and Irenaeus, if anyone had in fact been established there.

### 4.

Since one of these Churches borrowed ministers from the other—from Vienne, the Church of Lugdunum—there is some indication that both were administered by one and the same bishop. We read this concerning a deacon of the Church of Lugdunum named Sanctus: he was born at Vienne, ἀπὸ Βιέννης, “from Vienne,” and yet belonged to the clergy of Lugdunum and served there in the ministry of deacon, as the very learned interpreter of Eusebius, Valesius, rightly judged.

### 5.

When the Churches of Gaul sent a letter to Pope Victor concerning the controversy over Easter then being debated, the sole bishop Irenaeus wrote in the name of all the brothers [Col. 0471A]. Nowhere does the bishop of Vienne appear, although he should not have been omitted in a matter of such importance, which was troubling all the bishops of the entire Church and had already compelled them to assemble frequently in synods.

Certainly, given the close relationship between those two cities and Churches, the letter would have been subscribed by both bishops, and the bishop of Vienne would not have failed to contribute his vote. From this I seem justified in concluding that at that time no bishop had been established there other than the one who had his see at Lugdunum, from which he governed the Christians scattered throughout Vienne and the other towns through priests of secondary rank.

The very learned Henri Valerius objects that this opinion is refuted by the letter itself. For, he says, it states that Pothinus was bishop at Lugdunum, not at Vienne; it also expressly distinguishes between the Church of Lugdunum and the Church of Vienne. Nor, he adds, was it customary among ancient writers to apply the name “Church” to anything except the mother Church, which we call the cathedral.

To the first point we readily answer that it has never been customary, either formerly or now, for a bishop who has several cities or towns subject to his jurisdiction to be called the bishop of several places. He is called the bishop only of the place that is principal and contains the bishop’s see. This also occurred with places that had once been adorned with episcopal dignity.

Thus, when the city of Cemenelum and the fortress of Nice were united under one bishop, the former alone gave its name to the bishop. When the see of Antibes was transferred to the city of Grasse, and that of Malleacum was established at La Rochelle, the bishop of the former was not called both bishop of Grasse and of Antibes, nor the bishop of the latter both bishop of La Rochelle and of Malleacum.

Much less was this done when other cities or towns that had never been honored with such dignity were subject to the bishop of a distinguished city. Who today, for example, would call someone the bishop of Langres and Dijon, or of Sens and Meaux, or of Arras and Douai, or of Tournai and Lille—and so with six hundred other examples?

As to the second part of the objection, I say that a distinction must be made between the Churches of Lyons and Vienne, even if no distinction is made between the bishop of Lyons and the bishop of Vienne. The meaning of the word “Church” is well known: among the apostle Paul and the apostolic writers it is ordinarily used for any gathering of the faithful. This usage was current in the time of Pothinus, a disciple of apostolic men, and it remained in use in succeeding centuries.

St. Athanasius, in his *Apology 2 against the Arians*, says the following, which confirms our position concerning the Churches of Lyons and Vienne living under one bishop [Col. 0471D], and concerning the name “Church” being bestowed even upon cities that were not episcopal sees:

> “Mareotis,” he says, “is a region of Alexandria, and there was never any bishop there, not even a chorepiscopus; but all the Churches of that region are subject to the bishop of Alexandria. The individual presbyters, however, have their own villages, and very large ones—sometimes ten or more.”

We also read the following in Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 19 of his *History*:

> “Although there are many cities throughout Scythia, all of them have only one bishop.”

Canon 15 of Sardica says:

> “If there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, let him go there, so that he may not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without a Church.”

Here one sees that even long after the time of Irenaeus the people of a city were administered not by a bishop but only by a presbyter, and yet were honored with the name “Church.”

The same word was used in this sense in the Roman Church, as Pope Innocent I testifies in his letter to Decentius, chapter 5:

> “As for the fermentum which we send on the Lord’s Day to the titular churches, you wished to consult us needlessly, since all our Churches within the city are established.”

Athanasius, in the same *Apology 2* cited above, also says that the Roman synod, by which he had been received into communion, was celebrated in the Church where the presbyter Biton gathered the people.

In the Gallican diocese under discussion, the Council of Riez in the year 439 granted that, after Armentarius had been expelled from the see of Embrun, any one of the bishops might surrender one of his parishes, in which Armentarius could be supported either under the name of chorepiscopus, as in the same canon of Nicaea 8, or, as they say, by an alien communion. In this canon the word “Church” is used five times in this sense; it is also used twice in the fourth canon and as many times in the fifth. And, lest we leave untouched any of the more illustrious Churches, the same is clear to us concerning the African Church from canons 33, 98, 99, and others of the African code, where other churches are distinguished from the mother church while nevertheless enjoying the same title. See the canons cited by Dionysius Exiguus; for the sake of brevity we shall refrain from transcribing them.

[Col. 0472B] **6.** From the ancient tradition of the Churches of Valence and Arles, from Usuard’s *Martyrology* on 23 April, and from the *Acts of the Martyrs* preserved in Surius, we learn that very many peoples neighboring Lyons were converted to the faith of Christ, either by Irenaeus’s preaching or through his sending missionaries, and that he laid the foundations of Christian worship throughout those regions.

For the *Acts of the martyrdom of Saints Felix the presbyter, and Fortunatus and Achilleus the deacons* say:

> “Therefore the most blessed Irenaeus, bishop of the city of Lyons and subsequently a martyr, at a time when, by divine providence, the foundations of the faith to be established stood fixed with marvelous firmness, appointed Felix—alike in conduct and in name—Fortunatus, whose very name already promised the riches of the future consummation, and the deacon Achilleus to the city of Valence, as the seedbed for the preaching to be imparted.”

Here the author asserts generally that, by divine providence, the foundations of the faith to be established there had been laid in Irenaeus; and, more particularly, he records that heralds of the faith were sent by him to Valence [Col. 0472C].

We find the same event recounted in the Arelatan Breviary on 23 April, the day on which the solemnity of these same holy martyrs is celebrated. Both records also mention others sent by him to Besançon, namely the saints Ferreolus and Ferrutio. The *Acts* preserved by Surius say that “the aforementioned most blessed bishop [Irenaeus] had sent them to Besançon, so that the foundation of the Church of that city might be laid by establishing its groundwork.”

From these facts it is evident that even after Pothinus’s death the Christian faith was exceedingly rare in those regions. And what we chiefly wish to establish is that the Church of Vienne did not have a bishop different from the bishop of Lyons. For if it had had its own bishop, it would have been his responsibility to imbue nearby Valence with the Christian faith, not that of the bishop of Lyons, who was much farther away and had Vienne lying between himself and Valence, both cities being situated on the Rhône.

**7.** In the petition of the provincial bishops of the metropolitan see of Arles, presented to Pope Leo [Col. 0472D], it is confidently asserted that Arles was the first city in Gaul worthy to have as its priest the holy Trophimus, sent by the blessed Apostle Peter; and that from him the gift of faith and religion was gradually poured into the other regions of Gaul:

> “It is manifest that other places deserved to receive a priest from this stream of faith, whose waters of apostolic teaching flowed to us, before the city of Vienne, which now shamelessly and conspicuously demands for itself unlawful primatial rights” (*Epistle* 65).

The bishops do not say, as it seems to me, that Vienne received a bishop from that stream of faith—that is, from Trophimus. Even if they had said so, I do not know whether anyone could prove them false. Rather, they say that other places received bishops from that stream of faith before the city of Vienne had its own priest. They assert that this was evident, and so evident that they call it a conspicuous act of shamelessness for Vienne to demand primatial rights contrary to such clear justice.

If this is so, and if, according to Gregory of Tours, the arrival of Trophimus occurred many years after the time of Pothinus and Irenaeus [Col. 0473A], it is clear that Vienne did not have its own bishop in their time.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] These Gallican bishops, favoring the see of Arles, derived this statement from the letters of Zosimus; Zosimus, in turn, derived it from the report of Patroclus of Arles, who, through underhanded practices and deceptions, is shown to have brought forward several falsehoods [Col. 0474D] in *Observations*, Part II, chapter 2.]

You may say that this was asserted without evidence by the Gallican bishops, either because they were supporting their cause by a lie or because they were less well informed than they ought to have been. But who would wish to think so poorly of the wisest and most learned bishops of the Gallican Church that they would so confidently assert before the Roman pontiff something that was either not certain to everyone or that they themselves knew very well to be false? This is especially unlikely since at that time the ancient condition of the Gallican Churches was not so obscure as it is today, and since a lie once exposed could only make Leo more hostile and more opposed to the rights of the Church of Arles.

Finally, the pontiff raised no such objection. After considering the allegations and the clergy present from both parties, he appeared to assent to both sides, asserting the metropolitan right of each and assigning particular cities to each.

# Chapter XIII. That it is probable that there was only one bishop in Gaul at the time when Irenaeus presided over the Church of Lyons

[Col. 0473B]

**8.** So far am I from believing that a bishop of Vienne had then been appointed over that city that I am almost convinced that there was an episcopal see only at Lyons. This suspicion is strengthened not only by the arguments advanced above but also by several passages of Eusebius more carefully considered.

For in Book V, chapter 24, he seems to assert that Irenaeus at that time presided over all the Christians who were in Gaul, when he admonished Victor by letter not to cut off the Churches of Asia from his communion. He says:

> “Among these [bishops], Irenaeus also, writing a letter on behalf of the brethren dwelling in Gaul, over whom he presided,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] Ἐν οἷς (ἐπισκόποις), καὶ ὁ Εἰρηναῖος ἐκ προσώπου ὧν ἡγεῖτο κατὰ τὴν Γαλλίαν ἀδελφῶν ἐπιστείλας — “Among these [bishops], Irenaeus also, writing on behalf of the brethren over whom he presided in Gaul” (P. de Marca, *Dissertation on the Primacy of Lyons*, no. 112).]

If Irenaeus presided over the Christians of Gaul, he undoubtedly presided over them by priestly authority. As for what the most illustrious scholar says—that by the word *brethren* (ἀδελφῶν) the other bishops of Gaul are to be understood, over whom Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, presided either by metropolitan or exarchal authority [Col. 0473C]—I am astonished that such an idea occurred to a learned man.

For who could believe that in the second century of the Church, when the foundations of the Christian faith had scarcely been laid beyond the Alps; when the newborn Church in these regions was scarcely permitted even to murmur; and when the principal city of Gaul scarcely had a second bishop besides Pothinus, a form of hierarchy had already been introduced into the Churches that subjected bishops to metropolitans and metropolitans to exarchs? It is exceedingly difficult to find such an arrangement even before the Council of Nicaea, including in those regions that had been founded by the apostles and had received the first fruits of the Spirit of faith and discipline.

Anyone who considers the usage of those times, Eusebius’s familiar manner of speaking, and finally the very letter of the martyrs of Lyons, will have no doubt that by “brethren” the Christian people are meant. That letter calls Eleutherus, the Roman bishop, “Father,” and designates Christians by the name “brethren” at least eight times. This custom had been introduced into the Church of God chiefly because they acknowledged one Father, God—“as Tertullian, almost σύγχρονος, a contemporary, of Irenaeus, says in his *Apology*—drank of one Spirit of holiness, and had sprung forth from the womb of the same ignorance into the one light of truth.”

[Col. 0473D]

From another passage of Eusebius, chapter 22 of the same book, considerable light is shed upon this matter. While listing various synods—the Roman, Palestinian, Pontic, Osrhoenian, and Corinthian, or Achaean synods, which had assembled against those in Asia who Judaized concerning the date of Easter—he adds to these a Gallican synod formed from the parishes or Churches administered by Bishop Irenaeus:

> καὶ τῶν κατὰ Γαλλίαν δὲ παροικιῶν ἃς Εἰρηναῖος ἐπισκόπει

That is:

> “And the Churches or parishes of Gaul over which Irenaeus was bishop, or which he administered as bishop.”

Several points must be observed here.

First, this says of Irenaeus in another way the same thing that we previously reported as being said of the brethren dwelling in Gaul, over whom Irenaeus presided. To preside over the brethren and to govern the Churches or parishes as bishop mean the same thing.

Second, it is clear from this that Irenaeus was placed over several Churches, so that it is not absurd to suppose that he administered both Lyons and Vienne.

Third, no bishop other than Irenaeus appears here any more than in the letters subsequently written in the same controversy, or in those written by the martyrs.

Finally, Eusebius’s manner of speaking deserves the greatest attention. When he discusses the decrees of other provinces, he expressly calls them synods of bishops, and names the bishops themselves, from whose mouths the decrees had proceeded. But when he speaks of Gaul, he no longer mentions a decree of bishops’ synods; rather, he records a decree of the Churches [Col. 0474B], one that had proceeded from the Churches of Gaul, which Irenaeus governed with episcopal authority.

This is what I think the word ἐπισκόπει signifies; consequently, it cannot signify that Irenaeus exercised authority over other bishops.
