I certainly profess that I would believe this: if there had then been several bishops in Gaul, one man would not have entered the arena on behalf of all of them, especially since this controversy concerning Easter seemed to require a decision from a smaller or larger number of bishops.

We are not unaware that Rufinus, in translating Eusebius, used the word “bishops” in place of “brethren.” But learned men are also aware that Rufinus scarcely deserves the name of translator, since he generally does not attend closely to either the words or the meaning of the author whose work he has undertaken to translate. He usually renders everything according to his own inclination and will, assuming the role of a paraphrast more than that of a translator.

To return to Eusebius: he seems to have introduced the discussion of the Easter controversy on the occasion of the various synods, from which he sought to place before his readers the most distinguished bishops who flourished in the provinces at that time. Therefore, if any others besides Irenaeus had flourished in Gaul, he would certainly have listed them.

That this is how Nicephorus Callistus understood Eusebius is clear from Book IV, chapter 26 of his *History*, where he closely follows him:

> “Letters of the synods celebrated at that time are still in circulation. They identify the bishops of the various Churches in different places: Victor of Rome, Narcissus of Jerusalem, Theophilus of Caesarea in Palestine, Cassius of Tyre, and Clarus of Ptolemais. The same letters indicate that the most ancient Palma then presided over the Churches of Pontus, and that Irenaeus presided over the Churches of Gaul and also of Osrhoene.”

Here he identifies Irenaeus as the sole bishop of Gaul. Since he agrees with Eusebius on this point, he should not be rejected, although he must be rejected where he disagrees with him concerning Osrhoene, which he likewise subjects to Irenaeus and which an old translator of Nicephorus interpreted as a region of Gaul situated beyond the Rhine. Hence one may suspect that there is an error in the Greek text of this author.

**9.** Our opinion is supported by the author of the *Life of Saint Saturninus, Bishop and Martyr of Toulouse*. Its antiquity is confirmed by Gregory of Tours, who copied several passages from it in Book I, chapter 2 of his *History*. He says:

> “In the time of this emperor [Decius], seven men who had been ordained bishops were sent to Gaul to preach, as the history of the passion of the holy martyr Saturninus relates.”

For that history says:

> “Under the consulship of Decius and Gratus, as faithful memory preserves it, the city of Toulouse first began to have the holy Saturninus as its priest.”

[Col. 0475A]

The same words are likewise read in the *Life of Saint Saturninus* preserved by Surius on 29 November. I would suppose that Gregory excerpted only this passage from that author in order to establish a definite date for Saturninus’s episcopate. Since he knew from another source that Trophimus and five others had arrived in Gaul with Saturninus, he inferred the dates of the others from that of one of them.

For the rest, he did not borrow the names of the six remaining bishops from that *Life*. Otherwise he would have reproduced the author’s very words, which do not now appear in Surius’s *Life of Saturninus*. If anyone should insist that Gregory did take them from the *Life of Saturninus*, I shall not dispute it. I shall only point out that nothing is thereby taken away from the authority of the *Life* preserved by Surius.

For it is certain that the Lives of saints of this kind were generally copied from ancient lectionaries. When such Lives were inserted into those books for recitation among the public prayers of the Church, they were usually shortened, with whatever was understood not to belong specifically to the feast removed, so that the services would not be prolonged beyond what was proper.

I add one further point, lest the prologue prefixed to the beginning of the *Life* deceive anyone and bring contempt upon the work. It is as clear as daylight that this is not the author’s prologue but a reading taken from some Breviary, badly transferred here and attached in the place of a prologue [Col. 0475B].

Once the antiquity and authority of this narrative have been established, it makes the condition of the Gallican Church extraordinarily clear, both in the time of the emperors Lucius Verus and of Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, and also in the age of the consuls Decius and Gratus and of the bishop of Arles, Saint Trophimus.

For this author agrees with the testimony of Sulpicius Severus, who asserts that the religion of God was embraced later beyond the Alps, and he makes it clear that there were few Christians at that time and consequently very few bishops.

Thus, at the very beginning, concerning the time of Decius and Saturninus, he says:

> “At that time when, after the bodily coming of the Lord and Savior, the Sun of justice itself, rising in the darkness, had begun to illuminate the western region with the splendor of faith—for gradually and step by step the sound of the Gospel went out into all the earth, and the preaching of the apostles shone forth in our regions by a slow advance—”

(The author includes under the name “apostles” also apostolic men and the successors of the apostles. He continues:)

> “While rare Churches were arising in certain cities through the devotion of a few Christians, and while, through the frequent and miserable error of the pagans, temples smoked in every place with foul odors, many years earlier—that is, under the consulship of Decius and Gratus, as faithful memory preserves it …”

And again, after the middle of the narrative:

> “There being at that time only a few Christians.”

I plainly do not understand how these statements can be reconciled with the multitude of bishops asserted by others.

Certainly Theodoret speaks of Saint Irenaeus in his first dialogue, entitled *The Immutable*, in such a way as to signify that he was the apostle of Gaul:

> Εἰρηναίον, inquit, ὃς τοῦ Πολυκάρπου διδασκαλίας ἀπήλαυσεν, ἐγεγονει δὲ φαστὴρ Γαλλατῶν τῶν ἑσπερίων

That is:

> “Irenaeus, who enjoyed the teaching of Polycarp and became the light of the Western Gauls.”

And in the dedicatory letter of the *Summary of Heretical Fables* to Sporatius he says:

> Εἰρηναῖου, inquit, τοῦ τὰ Κελτικὰ καὶ γεωργήσαντος καὶ φωτίσαντος ἔθνη

That is:

> “Irenaeus, who cultivated and enlightened the Celtic peoples.”

**10.** It is worthy of notice, and an argument of no little force in support of our opinion, that Eusebius never mentions any of the Gallican bishops of those times, except Pothinus and Irenaeus—whether when he speaks of the foundation of the Churches, of the persecution of the pagans, of the trials held against heretics, or finally of the Easter controversy, the assemblies held concerning it, and the letters written to the Churches.

Everywhere one bishop of Lyons is mentioned; nowhere is the bishop of Vienne mentioned, nor the bishops of any other cities. This is clear in that remarkable letter of the martyrs and throughout Eusebius’s entire account of them, in Book I, chapter 1.

It is clear also in chapter 3, where a dispute arose concerning Montanus, Alcibiades, and Theodotus, the false prophets:

> “The brethren who were in Gaul,” he says, “attached their private judgment concerning these matters to the same letter.”

[Col. 0476A]

It is clear in chapter 23 concerning the Easter question. There Eusebius mentions the councils and synodical letters of the bishops of Palestine, Pontus, Rome itself, and other places; then he adds concerning Gaul:

> Καὶ τῶν κατὰ Γαλλίαν δὲ παροικιῶν ἃς Εἰρηναῖος ἐπισκόπει.

“And also the Churches of Gaul over which Irenaeus was bishop.”

There is also extant a letter of the Churches of Gaul over which Irenaeus presided. And in chapter 24:

> Ἐν οἶς καὶ ὁ Εἰρηναῖος ἐκ προσώπον ὧν ἡγεῖτο κατὰ τὴν Γαλλίαν ἀδελφῶν ἐπισέλας.

“Among whom Irenaeus also, writing on behalf of the brethren over whom he presided in Gaul…”

It was on behalf of these brethren that Irenaeus wrote the letter.

**11.** There are still many considerations that persuade us that the preaching of the Gospel had not spread very widely throughout Gaul, and consequently that few bishops had been established in many places during the time of Pothinus and Irenaeus.

First, there were very few preachers of the Gospel around Lyons, where the faith of Christ was first announced, and that almost by way of opportunity. They could scarcely have sufficed to imbue two very large cities with Christian teaching, and even then they did so secretly and covertly because of the governors’ diligent investigations.

Next, long after Pothinus’s martyrdom, we read that Besançon and Valence had not yet heard the faith of Christ. Irenaeus sent men to both cities to preach there, as we reported above, but the testimony does not say that those men had yet been appointed bishops. Yet Besançon is not a long journey from Lyons, and Valence is much nearer still.

Finally, ancient records testify how completely the subsequent persecutions tore up the seeds of faith planted throughout that region and devastated the Churches as they were coming into being. The persecution that took Pothinus, under the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, raged so fiercely:

> ᾢστε συλλεγῆνας ἐκ τὸν δύο ἐκκλησίων πάντας τοῦ ἀπουδαίοις, καὶ δι` ὦν μάλιστα συνειστήκει τὰ ἐνθάδε

“That all the most distinguished persons from the two Churches, and those through whose labor and industry the work here had chiefly been established, were seized together” (*Letter of the Church of Lyons* in Eusebius, Book I, chapter 1).

The *Acts of Saint Epipodius*, who was crowned with martyrdom in the same persecution, add that nearly the entire name of Christ was then believed by the pagans to have been extinguished [Col. 0476C].

In another persecution under Severus, which sent Irenaeus, the successor of Pothinus, to heaven, Usuard and other writers of Martyrologies show us the devastation inflicted upon the Churches when they relate that Irenaeus was crowned with glorious martyrdom together with almost the entire population of his city.

Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 27, supports this account—if indeed that chapter is his. It is missing from some manuscript copies and contains several features that render it suspect, such as his statement that the martyrdom of Vettius Epagathus and the other forty-eight martyrs followed the martyrdom of Irenaeus.

For this reason, I think that what Gregory says about those later martyrs should be joined to what he wrote at the beginning of the chapter concerning Pothinus, with the interpolated material that appears to have been added being removed, as follows:

> “Among them the first bishop of the Church of Lyons was Pothinus. Full of days, he suffered various punishments and suffered for the name of Christ. After him forty-eight martyrs suffered; among them, we read, the first was Vettius Epagathus.”

If anyone nevertheless prefers the account concerning Irenaeus—which may otherwise be true and may have been copied from reliable records—I have this to say: so great a multitude of Christians was slaughtered with Irenaeus for confessing the Lord’s name that, as a result, rivers of Christian blood ran through the streets. We have not been able to gather either their number or their names.

These persecutions therefore devastated the Churches, which were scarcely beginning to grow, almost extinguishing them. Thus it is not surprising that the author of the *Life of Saint Saturninus* says that there were rare Churches of a few Christians in Gaul when Saturninus was sent to them together with Trophimus and five other fellow bishops.

**12.** Since the policy of the Roman emperors and governors was to destroy the Christian religion completely in Gaul, where it had first appeared to rise under Lucius Verus, there is no doubt that they investigated Christians most diligently throughout all Gaul.

Yet nowhere is there any record of a persecution directed against another Church, apart from the one that afflicted the faithful of Lyons and Vienne. Who, then, could believe that no report of such a persecution, if it had occurred, would have reached Eusebius, or that the martyrs of Lyons would have made no mention of it? They would certainly have cherished with their affection and concern those Churches whose foundations they themselves had laid and which they knew to be no less dear and precious to the Asians and Romans.

We must now meet an objection that will easily occur to anyone against our opinion that there was only one bishop in Gaul.

“If this is so,” you say, “from whom did Irenaeus receive the honor of the priesthood after Pothinus’s death, through the imposition of hands—which no one will deny to have been necessary?”

I answer that Irenaeus obtained this dignity and consecration from the Roman pontiff. I think that this occurred during the journey he undertook at the delegation of the martyrs, as Eusebius testifies. A considerable difficulty, however, arises concerning that journey.

I see the most distinguished authorities divided into three different opinions: Cardinal Baronius, Franciscus Feuardentius, and Henricus Valesius (H. Valesius, notes on Book V, chapter 4 of Eusebius).

Valesius thinks that this embassy was arranged by the Church of Lyons, with the support of the martyrs, both to Asia and to the Roman pontiff. Irenaeus, he believes, was selected by the clergy to undertake it and recommended by the martyrs; but when Pothinus died, the embassy was transferred to someone else, while Irenaeus was retained at Lyons, lest the Church, soon to be deprived of its shepherd, should in such difficult circumstances be deprived of its chief light and support.

Franciscus Feuardentius, in the *Life of Saint Irenaeus* prefixed to his works, thinks that Irenaeus carried out both embassies while Pothinus was still alive. He writes that Irenaeus was sent by Pothinus and the other martyrs, who were imprisoned, to Pope Eleutherus and to the brethren in Asia [Col. 0477C].

Finally, Baronius, under the year of Christ 179, thinks that Irenaeus was sent by the martyrs to Pope Eleutherus—saying nothing about the journey to Asia—and that he actually fulfilled this embassy.

We embrace this last opinion, which is that of Baronius and Petavius, with only a few exceptions.

First, it is more consistent with Eusebius’s narrative. That author reports from the martyrs’ letter that Irenaeus was sent by them to Rome; he nowhere asserts that Irenaeus failed to fulfill his embassy [820], something Eusebius would certainly have noticed, since it was very important that this should not remain unknown.

Second, we have Jerome as a supporter. Jerome lived for a very long time in Rome and had access to the apostolic archives; he could have learned this partly from the tradition of the city and partly from records that still survived at that time. We should be torn away from both authors only with great difficulty, and only if compelled by the most serious evidence and arguments—none of which arise in the present matter.

For the most learned commentator on Eusebius, Valesius, writes:

> “It is not credible that after the death of Bishop Pothinus, the Church of Lyons, deprived of its shepherd, would have sent Irenaeus the presbyter so far away, and that in the very heat of the persecution. Irenaeus was the chief light and glory of the Church of Lyons, as we learn from the letter of the martyrs; and the entire Church of that place was chiefly sustained by him alone.”

This argument, I say, has force only against those who think that Irenaeus went to the brethren in Asia and Phrygia. Against those who, with Jerome—or rather with Eusebius—think that he went only to Rome to visit Eleutherus, it has no force at all.

It is not absurd to believe that Irenaeus went to Rome immediately after Pothinus’s death on important business; nor would it have been absurd for him to have been sent there by Pothinus and the other martyrs while they were still detained in prison. Was the Church of Lyons then less deprived of its shepherd? Was the heat of the persecution less intense? Was Irenaeus less necessary to the Church in its struggle, as the light and support of the afflicted flock?

Indeed, he was more necessary then. After Pothinus and the other children and ministers of the Church had been removed by martyrdom, the fury of the pagans subsided for a time and the heat of the persecution abated.

Moreover, the journey to Rome was not so long for a man stationed at Lyons—it could easily be completed within forty days—that any kind of difficulty could have deterred Irenaeus from undertaking it.

There are also several passages in Irenaeus’s works that imply that he went to Rome, including what he writes about the Roman Church and the Roman pontiffs, and what he writes against the schismatics living in Rome.

Finally, the honor and reverence of Christians toward the martyrs was too great for them to disregard or render void the counsels and wishes they had formed amid the very squalor of their prisons. The martyrs of Lyons deserved still greater consideration because Pothinus, who was the head and shepherd of that entire Church, had also been the leader and chief of the martyrs in Gaul.

But what if Irenaeus went to Eleutherus before the death of Pothinus and the martyrs? In that case Valesius’s objection disappears entirely, even by his own admission, and in any event it does no harm to our position.

In fact, the sequence of Eusebius’s narrative suggests that Irenaeus went to Rome while Pothinus was still alive. Eusebius first mentions Irenaeus’s embassy and then relates Pothinus’s death and Irenaeus’s appointment in his place. (The earlier statement about the death of that bishop resulted from the necessity of not interrupting the letter of the martyrs; it should not be attributed to Eusebius as part of his own narrative.)

Jerome also suggests this. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he says the following about Irenaeus:

> “Irenaeus, presbyter of Pothinus the bishop who governed the Church of Lyons in Gaul, was sent by the martyrs of that place as an envoy to Rome concerning certain matters of the Church. He carried to Bishop Eleutherus letters commending him and honoring his name. Afterwards, when Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus was appointed in his place.”

Here Jerome distinguishes the sequence of events with complete clarity. Irenaeus first fulfilled his embassy—not sent by the Church of Lyons but by the martyrs—and afterwards was consecrated in the place of the deceased Pothinus.

In this Jerome either interprets Eusebius as not distinguishing the times of the events so carefully, or he reports this account from other authors as well. Jerome had evidently consulted other authorities on the matter, as several differences between his account and Eusebius’s suggest.

Eusebius expressly says that Pothinus was more than ninety years old; Jerome says that he was nearly ninety. Jerome calls Irenaeus the presbyter of Pothinus; Eusebius calls him the presbyter of the Church of Lyons. Jerome says first that Irenaeus carried letters honoring his name; nothing of this kind appears in the fragment of the letter preserved by Eusebius, although that fragment seems to have contained praise of Irenaeus corresponding to his name.

Indeed, as Eusebius writes in Book V, chapter 24:

> “Truly corresponding to his name, and peaceful not only in name but also in the conduct and purpose of his life, he admonished and pleaded these things for the peace of the Churches.”

Jerome had seen similar statements concerning Irenaeus in the complete letter of the martyrs, which may have been preserved in Hegesippus. Jerome often praises Hegesippus as a careful investigator and writer of ecclesiastical affairs.

For Hegesippus, according to Jerome in the same book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*,

> “wove together histories of all ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord to his own time, and says that he came to Rome under Anicetus and continued there until Eleutherus, the bishop of that city.”

Since Irenaeus visited Eleutherus at the beginning of his pontificate, Hegesippus could have seen Irenaeus in Rome. But whether he saw him or not, he certainly lived into the period when these events were taking place in Gaul. Who could believe that he omitted them from his history?

Therefore greater credit should be given to Jerome, to whom this author was familiar, than to anyone else.

[Col. 0479A]

Now, to turn Valesius’s argument into support for our opinion, I shall never persuade myself—or anyone else who considers the matter carefully—that those confessors and martyrs of Christ, Pothinus himself the pontiff, and that entire Church, took the decision to send Irenaeus, the chief light and glory of Lyons, indeed of the whole Gallican Church, upon whom alone rested the weight of this new building, so far away in the very heat of the persecution.

At that time the bishop was imprisoned and about to receive the final sentence of death; many in that Church were denying Christ; all, as Eusebius says, were struck by the gravest fear and were hesitating because the outcome of their confession was uncertain; and the most distinguished persons from both Churches, those through whose labor and industry the work there had chiefly been established, had been seized and were all being held together in prison.

I say that it is scarcely, if at all, believable that Irenaeus, so necessary to the trembling Church, would at that time have been sent to Rome merely to deliver a letter to Eleutherus and the judgment of the Gallican brethren concerning the recent prophecies of Montanus and men of the same kind.

There must therefore have been another reason for this journey, one of far greater importance, which concerned that very Church more closely and involved unavoidable necessity. In my judgment there was no other reason than that the Roman pontiff might assist the Church, which was about to be deprived of its shepherd, by consecrating another.

Since at that time there was no other bishop, at least in that part of Gaul, who could impose hands, it was necessary to have recourse to the Roman bishop, both because of his proximity and because of his more powerful “primacy,” as Irenaeus himself calls it. This was not so that another bishop might be placed over Pothinus while Pothinus was still alive, but so that Irenaeus might either be established in another Church or be appointed to the Church of Lyons—as in fact happened when news of Pothinus’s completed martyrdom was brought to Rome.

This, as far as I understand, was the intention of the martyrs and their plan when they sent Irenaeus to Rome with letters of recommendation. Their outpouring of praise was directed toward having Irenaeus sent back to Lyons adorned with priestly honor.

For they would not otherwise have extolled his merits, called him a zealous preacher of the Gospel of Christ, and commended the rank of presbyter with which he was adorned than in order to advance their wishes for him to receive the episcopal office before they were consumed by martyrdom. Almost the entire clergy was in prison with its bishop.

They say:

> “We persuaded our brother and companion Irenaeus to bring these letters to you; and we urge you to prefer him to the others (ἔχειν σε αὐτὸν ἐν παραθέσει), as one endowed with extraordinary zeal for the Testament of Christ. If we thought that justice could be conferred upon someone on account of a particular place or dignity, we would have recommended him to you above all as the presbyter of the Church—for that is the rank he holds.”

By these words, ἐν παραθέσει, they show that they desired Irenaeus to be preferred to the others, as Christophorsonus previously observed in his translation of Eusebius. It seems to me that they wrote this to Pope Eleutherus with a view to the episcopal dignity which they ardently desired to have conferred upon him.

In order finally to meet the difficulty drawn from the end of chapter 3—where the martyrs’ letter concerning the pseudo-prophets of Montanus seems not to have been delivered before Pothinus’s death, since Eusebius is said to have appended it to that very extensive letter of the Church of Lyons concerning the martyrs—I say that two things must be distinguished in Eusebius’s account, which are commonly not distinguished. For a twofold embassy is indicated there: one to Asia and [Col. 0480A] Phrygia, which was not assigned to Irenaeus; the other to Eleutherus, and Irenaeus was asked by the martyrs to undertake this one alone. Those who were to carry out the Asian mission did not depart immediately, since a ship did not at once present itself that was sailing to Asia and Phrygia and could transport the envoys there; no such opportunity arose before the martyrs’ struggle had ended. But because an opportunity for undertaking the journey to Rome was always available, and because the matter that was pressing Irenaeus to go to Rome was more urgent, there was nothing to keep him longer at Lyons; consequently, as soon as he had been chosen for this task, he set out on his journey.

I conclude the whole matter in a single word: since the conjecture of those who deny that Irenaeus undertook the Roman embassy seems rash, it makes no difference to me whether Irenaeus began his journey before Pothinus’s death or after Pothinus had died. But if he departed after Pothinus’s death, as most people prefer, and therefore before Pothinus’s successor had been ordained, our position becomes decidedly more probable. For it is an argument that at that time the ordination of a bishop [Col. 0480B] could not have been celebrated without the assistance of neighboring bishops. Otherwise that Church would have thought of nothing before appointing a bishop in Pothinus’s place, a matter absolutely necessary amid such great difficulties; nor would it have waited for the return of its Irenaeus from so distant a journey. Nor would the clergy of Lyons ever have permitted his departure.

After these matters have been examined and clarified, it is evident, unless I am mistaken, that nothing can be extracted from this passage of Eusebius—which we have scrutinized with no little care—that could shake or overthrow the rights of the Church of Arles.

## CHAPTER XIV. What should be thought about Celidonius’s appeal to the Apostolic See? And whether Hilary, by opposing it, disturbed the order preserved by his predecessors; first, concerning the case of Marcian, bishop of Arles

We must now hasten to other matters that our Leo presses against Hilary in his letter. In the first place, we must examine Celidonius’s appeal to the Apostolic See, which Hilary had found extremely objectionable and against which he vigorously maintained that his judgment ought not to have been retracted by Leo. This was the origin of the most serious hostility between the two men.

Accordingly, in that letter Saint Leo addresses the bishops of the province of Vienne, defending his right on the basis of the ancient custom received in Gaul:

> “Let your fraternity acknowledge with us” (Letter 10) “that, out of reverence for it, the Apostolic See was consulted by the priests even of your province through innumerable communications, and that, through appeals concerning various cases, as ancient custom required, judgments were either reconsidered or confirmed. Thus, while the unity of the Spirit was preserved in the bond of peace, and letters traveled back and forth, what was being done in holiness advanced perpetual charity. For our solicitude, seeking not its own interests but the things of Christ, did not remove the dignity divinely bestowed either from the Churches or from the priests of the Churches. But Hilary, intending to disturb the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the priests by new presumptions, abandoned this course, which had always been well established and salutarily preserved among our predecessors. He wished to subject you to his own authority in such a way that he would not allow himself to be subject to the blessed Apostle Peter,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] What is brought forward in this and the following chapters is cut back to the quick in the *Observations*, Part I, chapters 4 through 7. It will become clear from that work that this controversy must be reduced to a question not merely of fact but of law; that Leo judged Celidonius’s appeal lawfully; that neither custom nor the canons, and still less divine law, supports Quesnel’s position; and that Hilary’s defense has been badly constructed by him.]

The hinge of the controversy is whether the canons then received in Gaul, together with the practices and customs of the Gallican Church, required Hilary to allow a sentence duly and canonically pronounced in a Gallican synod to be brought before the Roman bishop for review, and, by force of an appeal, either confirmed or rescinded.

It is not my purpose here to inquire what was done or ought to have been done in later centuries, what was done in our own age or that of our predecessors under what they call a new law, or what practice may have been introduced during those times in other provinces: none of this bears upon Hilary’s case. For the most holy memory of Hilary will be fully vindicated from every mark of improper ambition or suspicion of violating papal jurisdiction if we show that he presumed nothing inconsistent with the custom of the Gallican Church, and that from the very beginnings of the faith until the time of Hilary of Arles no appeal from the Gallican regions was ever brought before the tribunal of the Roman bishop.

Our entire work, therefore, and all our labor will consist in examining the facts, not in discussing the law, which lies outside our purpose. For the matter to be investigated properly and according to the laws of the law itself, it must not be examined from Leo’s letter and other writings; no one is a suitable witness in his own case. Rather, it must be examined from the surviving public records of the Church, which sincerely display what was done in the cases of bishops as they arose.

Furthermore, from the earliest beginnings of the Gospel’s being planted in our regions, this conviction took root in the minds of the Gallican bishops—a conviction that the Africans had held throughout these four hundred and fifty years and more: namely, that the episcopate is one and undivided, with each bishop holding a share of it in full; and consequently, if anyone from that portion of Christ’s flock assigned to him, which each shepherd rules and governs, should happen to fall into some crime, he ought to be compelled to plead his case before the bishop concerned, while retaining the right to appeal to the provincial synod or even to a greater synod.

If anyone acted otherwise and wished to flee by an appeal to foreign judges, he was rightly considered to be breaking the concord that bound the bishops together and to be tearing apart their unity. The authority that each bishop possessed over his own priests and the other members of his flock was likewise conferred upon metropolitans, together with the council of the province, over the bishops of their province, by a kind of natural right and a custom accepted by all—a custom that the sacred authority of councils later confirmed.

We have this form of discipline attested by a distinguished example, the one surviving example in Gallican records from the events preceding the Council of Nicaea: namely, the case of Marcian, bishop of Arles, who supported the Novatian party in Gaul and had long infected many members of his Catholic flock with that poison.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Compare *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, numbers 6 and following.]

I am not unaware that Saint Cyprian’s letter to Stephen, the Roman bishop, which unfolds the history of Marcian for us, has been considered by some to be of doubtful authenticity, and has even been charged with manifest νοθέια—spuriousness—by the most learned investigator of antiquity, Jean Launoy. Yet the procurators of all the editions of Cyprian regard it as genuine, especially the distinguished scholar Rigault, as well as the learned Lombeert, who, both in private letters written to us on this matter out of our common friendship and in the public notes with which he recently adorned his elegant edition of Cyprian, has most learnedly defended the letter as Cyprian’s.

The same letter is also found in very ancient manuscript codices. Among these, the Verona manuscript deserves praise as being of the finest quality; it is mentioned in the published Cyprian codex of the Thuane Library, in whose margin various readings extracted from different Italian libraries have been recorded. Finally, there is nothing in it that is alien to Cyprian’s diction or foreign to his mind, so that Cyprian should rightly be believed its genuine author.

Marcian, then, bishop of Arles, infected with the Novatian stain, was laying waste to Gaul, relying upon the greatness of his see. Since the other Gallican bishops dared do nothing against a man so powerful in his own province, and the circumstances of the times did not permit it; and since, moreover, the people of Arles, deceived by Marcian’s frauds, supported and defended their bishop, as may be inferred from Cyprian’s letter, they sought assistance from the other bishops of the foreign provinces, especially from the Roman and Carthaginian bishops, whose authority in the Church was very great, though far from equal.

Faustinus, bishop of Lyons, and the bishops of the entire Roman—that is, Narbonensian—province therefore sent letters to both. Above all, they urgently appealed to the Roman bishop as the head and summit of the episcopal body, asking him, relying on the authority of his see, to assist the Church suffering under the yoke of a schismatic bishop. They acted for this reason: Marcian had no immediately superior bishop in that province, and the Church of Arles had not long before received Trophimus, sent from the Apostolic See; consequently, they had the right to bring before the Roman bishop their complaint about Marcian, Trophimus’s unworthy successor.

When Stephen delayed and provided no assistance, the Gauls wrote again to Cyprian, asking him to press the Roman bishop more urgently to secure Marcian’s deposition. Cyprian did what they asked. He wrote a letter to the bishop, setting forth the complaints and pleas of the Gallican Church, in which one may observe the mind and discipline of both Churches.

While Cyprian was approaching Stephen by his letters, and the bishops of Gaul were approaching him through Cyprian, what, I ask you, did they wish and request Stephen to do? Did they ask him to summon Marcian and bring him before his tribunal? Certainly not. Did they ask him to send someone from his side into the province to judge the rebellious bishop with delegated authority? No more than that.

Perhaps they wanted him to issue a sentence from his see and entrust its execution to the Gallican bishops as executors; or to order those bishops to formulate a judgment against Marcian, which, once sent to him, he would examine and, as he deemed appropriate, either confirm or overturn? Cyprian dreamed of nothing of the sort.

If Cyprian had authorized the Roman bishop to do anything like this, he would surely have feared that he might appear—as the heirs of Cyprian’s vigor and episcopate later wrote to Pope Coelestine in the case of Apiarius—to introduce into the Church of Christ “the smoky arrogance of the world,” into a Church that offers the light of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see God.

What, then, did they ask of Stephen? Only this: that he warn the Gallican bishops and the people of Arles not to communicate any longer with Marcian, but, after avoiding him, to elect another in his place.

I am aware that certain authors of great reputation have strangely brandished this letter in support of the Roman bishop’s supreme power to depose bishops. A recent writer, imitating or even surpassing them, piles up much material more suited to a man devoted to conducting forensic cases than to one versed in theology.

First, he says that Cyprian’s letter concerns the deposition of Marcian, bishop of Arles. Second, from the fact that Cyprian did not ask that Marcian be sent back to a provincial synod, he concludes that the power of provincial synods to depose bishops is thereby undermined. Third, he asserts that in this letter Cyprian recognized in the Roman bishop supreme power to judge bishops and to issue the initial sentence of deposition against them. Fourth, he says that the cause and foundation of this power in the Roman pontiff is that the Roman See is the fountain and source of the priesthood of Jesus Christ. For he interprets Cyprian’s words, “From where the unity of the priesthood arose,” as meaning: “What is the origin of the priesthood of Jesus Christ?”

As to the first point, it is entirely untrue that the letter concerns a deposition. The word does not even appear in the letter. Rather, it concerns abstention, and anyone who does not understand the difference between abstention and deposition approaches the treatment of canonical judgments, as the saying goes, with unwashed hands and feet.

Cyprian assumes that Marcian ought to be subjected, without any synodal sentence or other judgment, to the sentence already pronounced against Novatian. What would a synod have done? Would it have condemned his error? But that error had long before been condemned in Novatian by a council of many priests, as Cyprian says, and he testifies that he himself had been a member of that council.

Would it therefore have organized a judgment against Marcian so that he might be proved to belong to the number of schismatics? But all the bishops and the entire province had before them a defendant openly confessing his guilt, who did not need to be convicted of defending an error. As Cyprian testifies, Marcian openly insulted the college of bishops; he had long boasted and proclaimed that, favoring Novatian and following his obstinacy, he had separated himself from ecclesiastical communion; he mocked the bishops and presumed to judge the majesty and dignity of the Church; by joining himself to Novatian, he stood forth as an enemy of mercy and piety; and he himself had already been judged by all the priests (Letter 67, Pamel’s edition).

Or would a synod finally have assembled so that a sentence of deposition might be pronounced against Marcian? But he himself had already pronounced it, as we have just seen, by separating himself from the communion of the Church, from the truth of the Catholic Church, and, as Cyprian says, from “the fellowship of our body and priesthood,” while holding fast to “the exceedingly hardened depravity of heretical presumption.”

Thus, when Cyprian says of Marcian, “Let him not pronounce the sentence, but receive it,” he is not writing of a new sentence to be issued either by a synod or by the Roman pontiff, as that author supposes. Cyprian explains himself sufficiently when he immediately adds, by way of interpretation: “Since he himself has been judged by all the priests”—namely, by Lucius and Cornelius, the Roman pontiffs, who judged that peace should be granted to the fallen and signified in their letters that, after penance had been performed, the fruit of communion and peace should not be denied them. “This,” Saint Cyprian adds, “we all everywhere have judged.”

Once a sentence had been pronounced against the author of a heresy or schism, it was considered to have been pronounced against all his followers as well. Otherwise it would either have been excessively burdensome for the bishops to meet in synod every time one of the bishops or priests made himself a supporter of a condemned error, especially in those times; or the safety of the Church would not have been adequately protected if, once only the author of a heresy or schism had been condemned, his disciples were allowed to range through the Church with impunity.

Hence Cyprian’s words:

> “How vain it is, dearest brother, that, although Novatian has recently been beaten back and refuted and has been avoided by the priests of God throughout the whole world, we should now tolerate his flatterers mocking us and judging the majesty and dignity of the Church.”

Certainly, if the sentence of Pope Felix—“Once a synod has been held against any rejected error, it consequently involves all its followers”—was ever to be put into practice, the necessity of obeying it was greatest at that time, when the fury of tyrants was ravaging the Churches everywhere and bishops were unable to come out into the light of synods.

Marcian was not the inventor of a new or private error—as Pope Gelasius said in the case of Acacius, in Letter 4 to Faustus—so that new decrees might be issued against him. Rather, he had joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. Therefore, as the same pope says before the words already cited, “not only the Apostolic Bishop may do this, but any bishop may separate anyone or everyone from Catholic communion according to the rule of the heresy itself, which has previously been condemned.”

By the authority of this sentence, Marcian should long before have been avoided by the Gallican bishops and the people of Arles. Cyprian censures their delay, excusing it only on the ground that they did not dare to avoid a man whom they saw had not yet been avoided by the bishops of the great sees:

> “Since he does not yet appear to have been avoided by us, although he has long boasted,” etc.

For, as may be inferred from the end of the letter, the brothers were still sending messages to Marcian and writing him letters of communion, not yet having fully recognized his obstinacy.

Cyprian therefore asks that the bishop of Arles be avoided by the Gallican bishops and by the still newly established Church of the Roman province. Rebuking Stephen’s delay, he demands, as a matter of the common right of the Churches, that Stephen indicate in his letters that Marcian had been avoided by him:

> “Therefore you ought to write the fullest possible letters to our fellow bishops established in Gaul, so that they may no longer allow Marcian—an obstinate and proud man, an enemy of divine piety and fraternal salvation—to insult our college, since he does not yet appear to have been avoided by us.”

By the word “us,” he makes it sufficiently clear that the Gauls were not attending only to the sentence of the Roman pontiff but also to that of the bishop of Carthage. The words themselves do not permit us to doubt that Cyprian had written to Gaul on his own part as well, especially since he had said above: “It is our duty to take counsel and provide assistance in this matter, dearest brother,” and later states that the Gallican brothers had requested his help:

> “They ask for the consolation of our assistance.”

No one, however, unless ill-disposed toward the Apostolic See, will deny that the letters of the Roman pontiff possessed correspondingly greater weight and authority than Cyprian’s, insofar as Rome surpasses Carthage, and the Apostle Peter—and Stephen, heir of the Apostolic See—surpasses the other apostles and bishops.

As for what that author asserts in second place—that Cyprian made no mention of a synod—and his intemperate attack upon the most learned bishop Peter de Marca, as though he had fruitlessly sought in this letter something favorable to the authority of synods, the claim is written with extraordinary foolishness.

First, it is clear from what has been said that there was no need to convoke a synod. Marcian had long before incurred the sentence of condemnation passed against Novatian, and it was sufficient for the Roman Church—which was the chief of all the Churches and also the mother of the Church of Arles through the sending of Trophimus—together with the Church of Carthage, to indicate that Marcian had been avoided by them and that the clergy of that Church and all the bishops of the province should likewise avoid him.

Moreover, at that time the assembly of councils was scarcely possible in that part of Gaul, since the hatred of the unbelievers against the newly established Church was raging. If the bishops had come out of hiding into the light of synods, they would certainly have exposed themselves to the danger of death.

If someone nevertheless wishes to argue against that author that the entire matter of Marcian was debated and settled in a Gallican synod, he will not make the claim without reason or foundation; rather, he will easily prove it from Cyprian’s letter itself. For it is certain that another bishop could not have been appointed and consecrated in Arles in place of Marcian without several bishops gathering together to celebrate the laying on of hands. Who would consider such a gathering unworthy of the name “synod”?

Moreover, Cyprian’s words indicate that Marcian’s abstention had first been declared in that same synod, since he connects the two matters:

> “Let letters from you be sent into the province”—that is, to the fellow bishops established in Gaul, as he had said earlier—“and to the people residing at Arles, so that, after Marcian has been avoided, another may be substituted in his place, and the flock of Christ, which to this day has been scattered and wounded and despised by him, may be gathered together” (the same Letter 67 of Saint Cyprian).

All these matters belonged to the business of a synod. It is therefore more reasonable to believe that a synod was assembled, if the circumstances of the times permitted it. Whether “abstention” is understood in its proper sense or improperly as meaning deposition, as it appears to be understood by Jean David, there is nothing in Cyprian’s letter that does not confirm the authority of synods, much less anything that overthrows it.

It is not the place here to inquire what Cyprian thought about the Roman pontiff’s power concerning the deposition of bishops; he expresses his mind clearly enough elsewhere. For the present case, it is sufficient to have shown that the Gauls asked Pope Stephen for nothing in Marcian’s case that they had not likewise asked of Cyprian; that Cyprian wished the Roman pontiff to write to Gaul nothing that he himself had not written; and that the entire case was ultimately left to the authority of the Gallican synod.

The doctrine opposed by David—not the prophet, of course—is as novel as it is injurious to the sacred order of bishops. It ought not to have been established except by a proposition that theological ears cannot endure, since it is discordant with antiquity and insulting to the priesthood of Christ.

Who could tolerate the origin of the Christian priesthood being referred to anyone other than the Mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, by whom it was immediately instituted, and who, as the one fountain and source of episcopal power and holiness, diffuses both throughout all bishops?

“For by God and through God,” as Cyprian says (Letter 69, to Florentius), “his priests are established in the Church.”

I would not hesitate to prove this at greater length if I were dealing with a theologian. Although we spare him for that reason, who could nevertheless patiently endure someone’s attempting to draw support for a heretical doctrine from Cyprian by means of a corrupt translation, when he renders Cyprian’s words, “From where the unity of the priesthood arose,” as: “What is the origin of the priesthood of Jesus Christ”? It is as though “the priesthood” and “the unity of the priesthood” were identical.

[Note: [Col. 0485C] Here Quesnel introduces only the meaning alleged by the heterodox, so as to exclude from Peter’s chair the primacy of preeminent jurisdiction. Since the Gallican Church recognizes in Peter’s See the center of unity, does it not intend, by the force of these words, to signify something more than a mere representation and image of unity? Certainly, the origin of unity, which Cyprian consistently inculcates in many places, expresses a certain power for binding unity together. And since Saint Cyprian likewise teaches in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, “Unity is preserved in its origin,” he must have recognized in Peter’s chair a certain preeminent power, not so much for forming as for preserving unity—not merely its representation or figure. Thus, in this preeminent power, some special right of Peter must be understood, by which all the priests of the entire Catholic Church, together with their respective Churches, ought to adhere to Peter’s chair, lest, if they separate from it, they be outside the Church. In this way it is properly understood how the unity of the priesthood arose from Peter, or from his chair, as in Letter 55; and how Christ established the unity of the Church itself and the origin of its unity from Peter, as in Letter 73.]

The reader will understand in what sense Cyprian refers this to Peter and Peter’s chair from these words of his book *On the Unity of the Church*:

> “Although after his resurrection he granted equal power to all the apostles . . . nevertheless, in order to manifest unity, by his authority he established the origin of that same unity as beginning from one person.”

The other apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with an equal share of honor and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church might be shown to be one.

## CHAPTER XV. The case of Marcian of Arles, settled in a synod, illustrated from the discipline of the same period

We have examined Marcian’s case at somewhat greater length in order to establish, by this single example—the only one that survives for us from that earliest Gallican antiquity—that no other judgment anticipated a Gallican judgment and none was reconsidered. For both in Gaul and in other regions, all power over bishops of the same province resided in synodal assemblies.

A second example is supplied by another letter of the blessed Cyprian, Letter 68, concerning Martial and Basilides, bishops of Spain.

[Note: [Col. 0486C] See the *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, number 6.]

A sentence of deposition had been pronounced against them in a provincial synod after they had been convicted of idolatry. After Basilides, following the exposure of his crimes and the laying bare of his conscience through his own confession, went to Rome and deceived Pope Stephen, who was far away and ignorant of what had occurred and of the concealed truth, seeking to have himself restored unjustly to the episcopate from which he had been justly deposed (Saint Cyprian, Letter 68, Pamel’s edition), Cyprian nevertheless replied, when consulted by the Spanish bishops, that the earlier sentence had to stand. Stephen’s judgment was set aside, since it could not lawfully rescind the ordination of another bishop, which had been validly performed in Basilides’ place.

By his appeal, Basilides accomplished nothing except to increase his offenses and add to his previous sins the crime of deceit and circumvention.

The Council of Nicaea reveals that the cause and origin of this discipline were grounded in the nature and sacred privileges of episcopal dignity. It sanctioned and confirmed that unwritten right by written canons consecrated, as Leo says, by the reverence of the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The Nicene and Constantinopolitan canons cited here, when establishing rules concerning episcopal judgments, do not affirm appeals to the Roman pontiff, but neither do they exclude them. For the canons by which this right is established, see the *Observations*, Part I, chapter 6.]

Canon 5 reads as follows:

> “Concerning those who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, let the regular sentence of the bishops in each province remain in force, so that those who are rejected may not be received by others.”

And later:

> “It has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, when all the bishops have been gathered together in common, such questions may be examined.”

Although that canon does not explicitly identify the deposition of bishops among these questions, anyone who is willing to hear the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople interpreting Nicaea in its second canon will easily persuade himself that this is the genuine sense of the canon.

> “Bishops who have not been invited,” they say, “must not go beyond their diocese for the ordination of anyone or for the settlement of any ecclesiastical matters, while the rule already written concerning each diocese is preserved. For it is manifest that the provincial synod must administer and govern everything in each province, according to what was defined at Nicaea.”

The most illustrious Peter de Marca, in Book VII, chapters 2 and 5, of his *Concordia of Sacred and Imperial Law*, shows that judgments against bishops are included in the word “administration” just as other ecclesiastical matters are. We also have the Fathers of the African Council as supporters of this interpretation.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The position of the Africans is explained in the same chapter, number 20 and following.]

In their letter to Pope Coelestine they address him as follows:

> “The decrees of Nicaea most clearly entrusted both clergy of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans. For they wisely and justly recognized that all matters should be settled in the places where they arose, and that no province would lack the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which equity might be both prudently discerned and most firmly maintained by Christ’s priests. This is especially so because each person has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who heard the case, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council.”

Pope Innocent also supports the same position in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] On Innocent, see the *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, number 20.]

So too does canon 15 of the Council of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Concerning the Antiochene canon, which alone seems to remove appeals, see the same work, chapter 6, number 3.]

That canon provides that a sentence issued by all the bishops of a province may neither be reconsidered nor overturned by other bishops.

It is customary to bring forward the Council of Sardica in this matter and to draw from it, as from a decisive argument, the proof that the right of appeal from synods to the Apostolic See had already been established by canonical authority at that time.

Although Saint Leo, when dealing with appeals in this letter to the bishops of Vienne, makes no mention of that council and refers only to ancient custom—“as ancient custom required”—the origin of those appeals is nevertheless attributed to that council. Leo himself later cited its canons under the name of the Nicene canons in the case of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

From Sardica, I say, the Roman pontiffs derived a rationale for the practice of appeals, although the Fathers of Sardica in fact issued no decree concerning appeals. They merely granted the Roman bishop the power to order the reconsideration or review of a case, as the most illustrious Peter de Marca demonstrates in Book VII, chapter 3, of *On Councils*, and as is evident from the very reading of the Sardican canons.

Although this power to order a reconsideration in the province itself is far inferior to the right of appeal, Hosius proposed it with extreme hesitation and uncertainty. He pleaded for a new measure, entirely inconsistent with the Nicene canons and contrary to established custom, invoking almost submissively the honor due to the memory of Saint Peter:

> “If you are willing,” he said, “let us honor the memory of the holy Apostle Peter.”

But the Council of Sardica did not possess such authority among either Eastern or Western bishops that they thought its definition had to be adopted immediately. The Eastern bishops always cast off this yoke of reconsideration from their shoulders. Perhaps for this reason they did not include the canons of that council in their collections, just as the Gallicans did not.

Nor did the Africans ever admit that prerogative of appeal or reconsideration. This is clear from the synodical letter to Pope Coelestine, which testifies that it was an ancient custom and discipline that the cases of bishops and priests should not be allowed to wander outside their provinces, but that matters should be settled where they arose, by the authority of the metropolitans.

It is therefore clear that the Africans had not even heard of the Sardican canons, but used the canons of the one Council of Nicaea, together with their own, as their rule.

As for the Gallican Church, it is worth noting that Saint Leo makes no mention of the Sardican canons in this complaint against Hilary, which arose over an appeal. The pontiff appeals only to custom against Hilary’s ambitious efforts, as he considered them.

This is a strong indication that Leo had learned, either through Saint Prosper—a Gaul whom he kept as his secretary—or from his own experience while he was in Gaul, that the Gallican Church did not receive these canons, so that it would have been superfluous to bring them forward. For if they had been inserted into the Gallican codex of canons, Leo would have acted perversely in his own case by omitting to mention canons that gave very considerable authority to the Roman See and by which Hilary could have been judged a violator of canons received even in Gaul.

Unless one says that Leo refrained from mentioning them because he knew of the rebuff Pope Coelestine had suffered from the Africans on account of attributing these canons to the Nicene Fathers; or because, with his customary intelligence, he saw that the Sardican canons established nothing concerning appeals or the reconsideration of a sentence in Rome, but granted the Roman pontiff no more than the power to order a new judgment to be held in the same province—a measure that Leo had not carried out in Celidonius’s case.

Fearing, therefore, that his letter would have little force among the Gauls, since no canons supported it and ancient custom, strengthened by the canons, rather exposed its novelty, he arranged for it to be reinforced by an imperial constitution. In that constitution Valentinian, to strengthen the greatness of the Apostolic See, mentions Peter’s merit, the dignity of the Roman Church, and the authority of the sacred synod. Yet he preserves a remarkable silence concerning the Council of Sardica when asserting the right of appeal.

This is evidence that the discipline introduced by the Sardican decrees was unknown to the Gauls, and that the Romans did not dare to oppose it to them.

## CHAPTER XVI. Other episcopal cases arising in Gaul before Hilary, after the Councils of Nicaea and Sardica, examined

[Col. 0488A]

The first of the Gallic cases treated after the Nicene Council is the case that occupied the Council of Agrippina in the year 346. At that council Euphratas, bishop of Cologne, was condemned and deprived of office because he denied that Christ was God. He did not even consider bringing the synod’s sentence by appeal before the Roman See.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] For these cases, in which no appeal intervened, see what will be said in the *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, number 4.]

It does not appear that an appeal was made from the Council of Arles, which unjustly deposed Paulinus, the Catholic bishop of Trier, in 353; from that of Béziers in 356, through the agency of Saturninus of Arles, which drove Saint Hilary into exile; or from the Council of Paris of 362, which condemned Saturninus himself—although Paulinus’s and Hilary’s unjust condemnation would each have granted them a special right to seek refuge with the Roman pontiff.

From the Council of Bordeaux in 385, Priscillian appealed to the emperor [Col. 0488B]. “This was permitted,” says Sulpicius Severus (*Sacred History*, Book II), “by the inconsistency of our people, who ought either to have pronounced sentence against the man resisting them, or, if they themselves were regarded as suspect, to have reserved the hearing for other bishops.” Instantius, however, who was the first ordered to state his case, was declared unworthy of the episcopate after he had insufficiently cleared himself. ^835 There is no mention of either of them having appealed to the Roman bishop. Indeed, when earlier Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian, condemned in their absence by the Council of Zaragoza [Note: [Col. 0487D] See there, no. 10.], had gone to Rome to clear themselves before Damasus, then bishop of the City, they were not even admitted into his presence. For the synodal sentence issued against them had added that, if anyone received the condemned into communion, he should know that the same sentence would be pronounced against him (*ibid.*).

But more significant is the case of Proculus, bishop of Marseille, whose [Note: [Col. 0487D] Zosimus did not draw the hearing of this case to himself; rather, Patroclus, the Gallic bishop, brought it before Zosimus. On the right of the apostolic see to hear such cases in the first instance, see *Observations*, Part I, chapter 7, nos. 6 and 7; from these it will be clear how improperly Quesnell writes that Zosimus labored to enlarge the authority of his see. What the dispute between Zosimus and the Africans was, and whether it can be inferred from it that Zosimus wished to extend his authority, will become clear from chapter 6 of our *Observations* in Part I, no. 20 and following.] first hearing Zosimus is also said to have taken up, at the insistence of Patroclus of Arles, through whose efforts he was deposed. The illustrious Pierre de Marca says that this was done at Rome after the promulgation of Gratian’s law, which had entrusted metropolitans to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, and which the Gallicans, rightly and with good reason, did not generally observe, since it was contrary to ecclesiastical custom and accepted regulations.

Whatever may be said of this law, which could not weaken the authority of the canons, there is no reason why this attempt of Zosimus should greatly trouble us. First, no right can arise for anyone from a mere fact, especially when the patrons of the opposing party resist and protest against it. Second, Zosimus’s action has nothing whatever to do with the right of appeal, nor can it derive any support from the Sardican canons: for these say nothing either about a first hearing or about an appeal, but only about arranging for a reconsideration of a case in the province itself. Third, even if we do not wish to detract from the credibility of Zosimus’s letters, the whole course of this affair nevertheless remains insufficiently known, since it is disclosed only by those letters. Since he is shown by the African records, which we have already mentioned above, to have labored very earnestly to enlarge the authority of his see [Col. 0488D], we may reasonably conjecture that Zosimus suffered the same rebuff in Gaul as in Africa. And although other writings that might inform us about these matters are lacking, Zosimus’s own letters are sufficient to establish our earlier conclusion: that the canons of the Council of Sardica had not been accepted among the Gauls, and that the authority of the Roman bishop over the deposition of bishops in that region was at that time by no means recognized there.

[Col. 0489A] For it is clear from reading them that, when ordered by Zosimus, ^836 Proculus did not obey and did not go to Rome, where he was summoned to be judged [Note: [Col. 0489D] We have inferred from another consideration why Proculus initially did not obey, in *Observations*, Part II, chapter 6, no. 3, so that he should not be thought not to have acknowledged the apostolic right in such cases. Whether, after his deposition, he conducted himself as a bishop, we have shown there to be less certain than Quesnell maintains.]. Yet he seemed to be summoned not so much to judgment as to a fraternal meeting, at which his rights and those of Patroclus might be amicably examined. “He refused,” I say, “to go there.” Hence this complaint of Zosimus:

> Proculus was discovered to have usurped many things contrary to ancient custom by improperly celebrating the ordinations of certain persons, which we recently examined in a lengthy hearing; although, kept waiting for a long time and impatiently bearing the delays granted him, he avoids appearing in court.  
> (*Zosimus, Letter 7 to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne II*)

Although Zosimus attributes this to a certain man’s disdainful arrogance, we consider it impious to think this of a man whom Jerome celebrates for his sanctity—especially since Proculus was known to Zosimus only through the testimony of Patroclus, who was exceedingly hostile to Proculus and, as an invader of another see and a man accused of many crimes, was hardly a suitable witness for giving such testimony [Col. 0489B]. I would rather believe that Proculus avoided the Roman judgment because the Gallic bishops were not accustomed to submitting themselves to judgments from beyond the Alps, nor could they be induced to do so down to that time. For this reason they bore with extreme displeasure the fact that Proculus’s case had been brought to Rome by Patroclus; they willingly undertook his defense and did not allow Zosimus’s decree concerning Proculus’s deposition to have any force in Gaul, since it was contrary to the ecclesiastical custom of the Gauls.

These are the men whom the same pontiff rebukes for this reason in Letter 12 to the people of Marseille:

> He adds to himself and joins with himself men of restless mind, and those who alone can show favor to a condemned man; through them, relying on this alliance, he may accomplish what he devises as a lover of disturbances.  
> (*Zosimus, Letter 12 to the people of Marseille*)

For if the few men of restless mind whom he says favored the condemned Proculus were not prominent bishops of Gaul, Patroclus would not so readily have yielded to them. Yet from Zosimus’s letters we know that Patroclus did not dare to pursue Proculus any further, nor to use the power which the pontiff had granted him against the bishop of Marseille. For in Letter 11 Zosimus complains that Proculus had been released by Patroclus from his unlawful ventures:

> Although you have learned the matter in person, and although you yourself have been warned by our frequent letters to use the authority of the metropolitan which we have confirmed to you by the pronouncement of the apostolic see against those ventures and efforts of Proculus, by which he still thinks that he can cause some disturbance . . . I wonder what Proculus may be permitted to do after this, so that he may be free to commit the things he was accustomed to commit—or worse.  
> (*Zosimus, Letter 11 to Patroclus, bishop of Arles*)

It is clear from these words that Proculus did not regard himself as deposed, nor was he so regarded by the Gallic bishops. Rather, with the knowledge and approval of the Church of Gaul, he acted as a bishop, with no less confidence and authority than before. The same letter establishes that Proculus ordained bishops by virtue of a privilege which the Council of Turin had granted not to his see but to his person. Zosimus says:

> After this delegation, behold, a report reached us that Proculus, as though playing his customary games and following his usual practices, had joined himself to certain men fit for causing disturbances and, after the things that we forbade him, had ordained others.  
> (*Zosimus, Letter 12 to Patroclus*)

Finally, it is probable from Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne [Col. 0490A], chapter 4, that Proculus persisted in his episcopate and outlived Patroclus. There Celestine speaks of a priest of the Church of Marseille who, “which it is impious to say,” had rejoiced so greatly at the death of his father that he went to meet the man who had arrived stained with his father’s blood, intending to share his portion with him. I would judge this very Proculus to have been the man who suffered such a calumny before Celestine on the occasion of Patroclus’s death. Patroclus was killed around this time by a barbarian tribune, at the secret command, as Prosper writes, of Felix, the master of the soldiers. From all this it is clear that the decrees of the Fathers remained unshaken in Gaul: by them the judgments of the bishops of each province were held valid without any confirmation from another judgment, and the bishops of that region in that age did not bow to the Sardican canons or to the novelty of appeals.

From the letters of the same Pope Zosimus we learn that several other bishops in Gaul were subjected to sentence, among them Lazarus, bishop of Aix, and Ursus, whose see is unknown. Yet we read of no appeal by any of them [Col. 0490B]. So far was the Roman bishop from attempting to pronounce the first sentence against them that the fact that this was first attempted in Proculus’s case must be attributed to the wickedness and audacity of Patroclus [Note: [Col. 0489D] Compare *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, no. 17. There we proved, in no. 18 and 20, the more ancient practice of appeals within Gaul itself. Patroclus may rightly be criticized, not for bringing this case to Zosimus, but for deceiving him by subreption. See *Observations*, Part II, chapter 2. On Zosimus’s unjust rebuke, compare note 3 (below, col. 613, n. a).]. For, fearing that the Gallic bishops might annul his ordination as contrary to the sacred canons, he won the goodwill and favor of the Roman pontiff by various devices and held out the prospect of greatly advancing his authority in Gaul. Zosimus eagerly seized this opportunity, so that Gaul—until then impervious to such a custom and to such practices regarding the judgments of bishops and the administration of other matters—might at last be made accessible to them; yet the outcome he desired did not follow. ^838

Under the pontificate of Boniface, who immediately succeeded Zosimus, we encounter only the case of Maximus, bishop of Valence. Although the clergy of the city of Valence had brought him before him [Note: [Col. 0490D] Boniface could have taken up Maximus’s case, but he preferred to refer it to the judgment of the bishops of the province, so that it would not thereby follow that Boniface lacked the right. When cases can be heard by two judges, if one is approached, it cannot therefore be inferred that the other is deprived of that right. We have established the right of the Roman see in *Observations*.], he did not draw the hearing of the case to himself, but declared that a judgment should be prepared by the bishops of the province [Col. 0490C]:

> We have decreed, addressing the bishops of Gaul, that the judgment ought to take place within your province, and that a synod should be assembled before the first day of November, so that, if he wishes to be present, he may answer the charges if he has confidence; but if he neglects to appear, he should not gain a postponement of the sentence by his absence.  
> (*Pope Boniface, Letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul*)

Pope Celestine, who occupied the see after Boniface, appears to have summoned a certain Daniel to his tribunal. But Daniel was a vagrant who, after committing many crimes among the Eastern peoples, was accused before the Roman pontiff and, as it were, handed over to him; he was sought throughout Gaul for a long time in order to be brought to trial. This case, however, is exceptional, and Celestine should not be thought to have claimed any similar right over the Gallic bishops. At the end of the same letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, he leaves the case of the bishop of Marseille to be heard, according to custom and law, by the college of his own province.

Of Sixtus III, who succeeded Celestine, we read of no priest summoned before the tribunal of the Roman see [Col. 0490D]. On the contrary, we see that Armentarius, who had been placed over the see of Embrun, was deposed by the Council of Riez, without protesting either by a petition of appeal or by invoking the Sardican or any other canons in his defense.

[Col. 0491A] Such was the condition of the Gallican Church until the time of Saint Leo. Therefore, when he said [Note: [Col. 0491D] See *Observations*, Part I, chapter 5, no. 18 and following.] that, through the appeal of various cases, judgments had been either reconsidered or confirmed—as ancient custom required—he must either have suffered a lapse of memory, or have been deceived by Celidonius, who flattered and imposed upon him, or finally have possessed other records concerning events in Gaul that have not come down to us.

As for what he adds concerning consultations and reports, by which he says the Gallic bishops were accustomed to approach the Roman see, this in no way diminishes the authority of synods. It is proper that the decisions of synods should be referred to the apostolic see, which is the head of all the Churches, either when the pontiff wishes to be better informed about them or when they have been issued against bishops of greater sees. This was so that the chief bishop of the Church might not be unaware to whom he ought to grant his communion, from whom he ought to abstain, and to whom he could send letters of communion or *formatae*. ^839

But if Hilary did not report to Leo the synodal sentence issued against Celidonius, this happened either because Celidonius departed suddenly: Hilary preferred to pursue him all the way to Rome and report to the pontiff in person rather than send written information about his case; or because Celidonius was not a bishop of a greater see, as we have proved. Nevertheless, I can scarcely persuade myself that the pontiff was not informed of the sentence by the synod, since Leo did not make this charge against Hilary. Nor would Hilary himself have rightly complained that Leo allowed Celidonius to participate in the sacred rites at Rome—although Celidonius had rightly received a public sentence in Gaul—unless the pontiff had first been informed of that sentence by letter.

Anyone who has carefully and without prejudice examined all that we have discussed up to this point, I have no doubt, will easily lay aside his preconceived opinion that Hilary was obstinate, covetous, and ambitious. He will instead persuade himself that Hilary followed in the footsteps of his predecessors when he defended with such constancy [Col. 0491C] and courage the sentence issued in the synod by the most holy bishops. But, on the other hand, he will wonder that [Note: [Col. 0491D] See *Observations*, Part I, chapter 7, no. 12.] Saint Leo departed from a custom and discipline maintained in such an unbroken succession, showing excessive concern for the grandeur of his see—a weakness even holy men possess.

Yet Saint Leo seems to have paid still less attention to the canons in the present conflict with Hilary in another respect. Here too [Note: [Col. 0491D] Recall note 6 above (col. 486, n. g), in the preceding chapter.] he departed from the Sardican canons, whose authority he was chiefly relying upon, by undertaking to examine Celidonius’s case outside the province and reconsidering it in his own judgment without the participation of the original judges. His predecessors had never before attempted this; at least, they had not exceeded the limits of the Sardican canons.

These canons restore to the Roman bishop the power to reconsider the judgment of provincial synods, but in such a way that he is to appoint new judges from a neighboring province, who are to participate in the renewed examination together with the judges whose sentence is being appealed. This was required by the Sardican decrees: the original judges were to take part in the later examination, as the illustrious de Marca observed. “If he judges,” says canon 3 of Sardica, “that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges.” Only two options are given: either he may decree that judges should be sent who, being present with the bishops, will judge together with them, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were appointed; ^840 or, if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he may do what he judges in his wisdom to be best.

Saint Leo did neither. He reserved the entire case for himself, to be subjected to his own examination and concluded by his judgment [Col. 0492A]—and yet, to use the words of the African council addressed to Pope Celestine, with the greatest prudence and justice [Note: [Col. 0491D] On the mind of the Africans and Cyprian, see our *Observations*, Part I, chapter 6, no. 20 and following.]. The Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, or even of Sardica, provided that all cases should be concluded in the places where they arose, and that no province would lack the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which equity might be both wisely discerned and steadfastly maintained by holy priests—especially since each person has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who examined his case, to appeal to the councils of his own province or even to a universal council of the region.

“Unless perhaps there is someone who believes that God can inspire justice in an examination in one person and deny it to innumerable priests assembled in council. Or how will that overseas or transalpine judgment be valid to which the necessary witnesses could not be brought, either because of their sex, or because of the weakness of old age, or because of many other impediments?”

The most blessed Fathers had drawn these rules of discipline from their vigorous predecessor Cyprian, among whom Augustine was a principal figure [Col. 0492B]. For blessed Cyprian weighs almost the same considerations in Letter 55 to Pope Cornelius:

> Since it has been established as both right and just that each person’s case should be heard there where the crime was committed, and since a portion of the flock has been assigned to each shepherd, which each is to govern and direct, rendering an account of his conduct to the Lord, it is certainly necessary that those over whom we preside should not run about from place to place, nor by their deceitful and treacherous recklessness shatter the harmony binding the bishops together; rather, they should conduct their case there where they can have both their accusers and witnesses to their crime.

Who could fail to believe that these most holy prelates of the African Church were pleading the case of our Hilary? Who would not yield to so many considerations, against which I plainly see nothing that can be brought forward, unless Saint Leo believed that, for the good of the Church and to diminish Hilary’s power—which was giving courage to the adversaries of the grace of God as they gained strength in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0492D] Whether Leo acquired a new right for himself will become clear from *Observations*, Parts I, chapters 5, 6, and 7.], he ought to acquire a new right for himself, secured by imperial authority, whose disposition he could bend at will [Col. 0492C].
