Third, Leo seems to have departed from the canons contained in the Gallican collection when [Note: [Col. 0492D] See *Observations*, Part I, chapter 8, no. 1.] he admitted Celidonius to communion with him and allowed him to participate in the sacred rites before a new examination of his case had been undertaken. This was unquestionably contrary to the canonical provision which, for the sake of the undivided unity of the Church and the priesthood, laid down that those who had received a sentence of condemnation from individual bishops should be considered condemned by all the priests established throughout the Church. Accordingly, following canon 5 of the Council of Nicaea, canon 53 of Elvira, and canon 16 of the First Council of Arles, the later Gallican synods and the Roman pontiffs decreed under grave threat that no one should receive an outcast into communion. The same was decreed by the Council of Turin at the beginning of the fifth century, canon 7; the First Council of Orange, canon 11; the Second Council of Arles, canon 8; and Pope Innocent I, Letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 7.

How much more wisely, then, Saint Leo would have imitated the leaders of the Roman Church. In former times Marcion, the heresiarch, had been expelled from the Church by his own father, a bishop. He approached those leaders to be restored to ecclesiastical communion, but could never obtain this from them, as Saint Epiphanius testifies in *Against Heresies* 42, which concerns the Marcionites. Instead, they rejected him with this reply:

> “We cannot do this at the command of your venerable father. For there is one faith and one harmony of minds; nor can we undertake anything against your father, our highly respected colleague.”

Thus the elders of the Roman clergy, instructed, as Epiphanius says, by disciples of the apostles, considered it impious to violate the apostolic tradition.

[Col. 0493A] Finally, fourth, he seems not to have been entirely mindful of ecclesiastical custom when [Note: [Col. 0493D] On this matter, see the same chapter 8, no. 4.] he was the first to attempt to weaken the custom of the Gallican Church by an imperial enactment and elicited this edict from Valentinian III:

> Let nothing be permitted to the Gallican bishops, any more than to those of the other provinces, without the authority of the venerable bishop of the eternal City; but let whatever the authority of the apostolic see has decreed or shall decree be law for them all.

Who cannot see that our Leo, by acting in this way, ordered the condition of the Gallican—and indeed of all—Churches differently from their accustomed practice, as Hilary complained? He freely granted his communion to a bishop canonically deposed, without reopening the case; he weakened the sentence of a synodal judgment pronounced against a bishop who had been duly accused and convicted; he subjected the case to a renewed examination outside the province; and finally he stirred up the secular powers against Hilary and the entire Gallican Church.

By contrast, it is clear that Saint Hilary, when he opposed the pontiff’s advice; when, without awaiting his sentence, he departed as a good shepherd hastening to visit his flock again [Col. 0493B]; and when he utterly refused to join the communion of Celidonius, whom he had condemned together with such distinguished men—even at the risk of his life, as the author of his *Life* writes—did not disturb the condition of the Churches or the harmony of the priests through new presumption. Rather, he preserved them religiously. He did not abandon the path that had always been well established and beneficially maintained among his predecessors, as Saint Leo charges [Col. 0493C]; instead, with apostolic vigor, he vindicated that path after others had abandoned it.

## PART TWO. ON THE CASE OF PROJECTUS, THE BISHOP

### CHAPTER I. The Question Is Set Forth, and the Province of Which Projectus Was Bishop Is Investigated

After the case of Celidonius has been fully treated, the case of Projectus, likewise a bishop, must be examined. Since he is mentioned nowhere except by Saint Leo, we have fewer things to say about him than about Celidonius.

At the outset, however, we must observe that this case does not seem to me to have been dealt with in Hilary’s presence, since the author of his *Life*, who gives a careful account of his journey to Rome, does not mention Projectus even once. From this it may be conjectured that Projectus’s letters and the complaints of his fellow citizens were not brought to Rome until after Hilary’s return. When they heard that Leo was hostile to Hilary and that everything had gone according to Celidonius’s wishes before the apostolic see, they decided that their own case should be brought to Rome. This occurred within the space of at least those six months that elapsed between Hilary’s return and the writing of this letter.

Accordingly, letters from Projectus, the bishop, described by Leo himself as tearful and grievous (*Letter* 10), were sent to Leo concerning a bishop superimposed upon him. A letter was also submitted by his fellow citizens, confirmed by the numerous signatures of individuals, and filled with extremely hostile complaints against Hilary: that Projectus, their bishop, had not been free to suffer illness; that his priesthood had been transferred to another without his knowledge; and that Hilary, as though invading an empty possession, had introduced an heir while the possessor was still alive.

Later they add:

> What does Hilary seek in another province, and why does he usurp what none of his predecessors before Patroclus possessed?

And shortly afterward:

> Certainly the wishes of the citizens, the testimony of the peoples, the judgment of the honored men, and the election of the clergy ought to have been awaited—things which, in the ordinations of priests, those who know the rules of the Fathers customarily preserve, and so forth. But he came upon us unexpectedly, while we knew nothing, and departed unannounced, covering many journeys with rapid travel [Col. 0494A] and rushing through distant provinces ^843 with such immaturity that he seems to have sought glory from clownish speed rather than priestly moderation. These are the words of the citizens’ letter sent to us: “He departed before we knew that he had come. This is not returning but fleeing,” and so forth.

After recounting these matters, Leo finally pronounces this sentence:

> Nevertheless, believing that what we are about to do will be pleasing to you under God’s judgment, and consulting all the brethren together, we have decreed both that the man improperly ordained should be removed and that Bishop Projectus ought to remain in his priesthood.

From Leo’s words it is clear that Hilary was accused of several things in this case:

1. That he had appointed a successor over a bishop who was ill;
2. That he had done so in another province;
3. That he had acted without awaiting the wishes of the citizens, the testimony of the peoples, the judgment of the honored men, and the election of the clergy;
4. That he had arrived unexpectedly, without their knowledge, and had departed unannounced, as though with clownish speed.

These charges contain two kinds of accusation [Col. 0494B]. One might have been shared by Hilary with Honoratus and his other predecessors: namely, the complaint that an ordination had been attempted in another province. The other is peculiar to Hilary and comprises the three remaining points, numbers 1, 3, and 4.

It is fair to suspend one’s judgment and opinion concerning these matters, since we know them only from Hilary’s adversaries [Note: [Col. 0493D] Unless Quesnell wished to portray Saint Leo as a judge acting as Hilary’s adversary, he certainly regarded Projectus, the bishop, and all the citizens who brought their complaints to the same pontiff as Hilary’s enemies. Whether suspicion might arise from these witnesses’ public account of events that all had conspired to slander him, let every prudent person judge. On the fact itself, compare *Observations*, Part II, chapter 1.].

I am certainly not one who wishes to assert that Hilary was free from every error and fault. Nor am I unaware how easily anyone can be led astray by his own temperament, even when he is pious or holy—especially when he believes himself to be defending not so much his own rights as those of the Church. Nevertheless, the charges brought against Hilary here are so alien to the character attributed to him by Saint Eucherius, Julianus Pomerius, Constantius the priest in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, Auxiliaris the prefect, Prosper, Hilary, and finally Honoratus of Marseille in his *Life*; indeed, they are so unworthy of a bishop devoted to the discipline of the sacred canons and ecclesiastical order, such as Hilary is presented by so many Gallican synods held through his agency and under his presidency [Col. 0494C], that they ought rightly to be numbered among the slanders of his hostile and envious adversaries.

We shall therefore refrain from laboring at greater length to clear him of these accusations, since the *Life* of this holy bishop, which we shall have printed at the end of this volume, will serve in place of an apologetic treatise. In this second part of the dissertation, then, we undertake to examine only this point: one which concerns the rights of the Church of Arles and which, once clarified, seems likely to contribute no little to knowledge of ecclesiastical history.

Above all, we must investigate, as far as conjecture allows, in which province of Gaul Projectus had been established as bishop. By calling that province “another” province, Saint Leo sufficiently indicates that it must be sought outside Vienne, which Hilary himself does not deny in his letter to have been his own province. Accordingly, the eminent author of the *Annals* must be corrected at the year 445, no. 13, where he says that Projectus belonged to the ordination of the bishop of Vienne, in whose province he was a bishop.

These are Leo’s words:

> What does Hilary seek in another province, and why does he usurp what none of his predecessors or Patroclus had possessed? For even that which seemed to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment.

This is how all earlier editions of the letter read, except the edition prepared by J. Sirmond in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*. Two manuscript codices, the Thuaneus and the Corbeiensis, support Sirmond, and read as follows:

> What does Hilary seek in another province, and why does he usurp what none of his predecessors before Patroclus had possessed? [Col. 0495A]

These two readings give rise to two different conjectures. Whoever prefers the first must believe that Projectus came from a province which not even Patroclus had subjected to himself. This excludes both Vienne and the two provinces of Narbonne, which had been ordered by Zosimus’s decree to be subject to Patroclus. Only two provinces therefore remain among those that once constituted Narbonne as a whole, outside which Hilary claimed no jurisdiction for himself: the Graian and Pennine Alps, and the Maritime Alps. Projectus could not have come from the province of the Graian Alps for two reasons.

First, with respect to the metropolitan province of Vienne, that province could not be called foreign before the division made by Saint Leo, since of the two cities listed in the administrative record, the more important—Tarentaise—belonged to the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Vienne.

Second, that province had at that time been removed from the number of the five provinces [Note: [Col. 0495D] We shall see in *Observations*, Part II, chapter 3, no. 7 and following, that the Graian and Pennine Alps were excluded not only from the number of seven provinces but also from that of five. There too we shall prove that the body of seven provinces had been constituted several years before the prefecture of Petronius [Col. 0496D].] by the prefect Petronius, when he formed the body of the seven provinces from the remaining four together with the other three—both Aquitanias and Novempopulania [Col. 0495B].

It remains, therefore, that the province of the Maritime Alps was the one in which Projectus had been established as bishop. This conjecture is confirmed by the fact that no metropolitan is recorded as having intervened in Projectus’s case to complain about Hilary’s usurpation. This suggests that the metropolitan of the province called “foreign” here voluntarily yielded his right in favor of Saint Hilary and that for this reason Saint Leo tacitly censures him in this letter as a deserter of his own dignity.

> Let each person be content with his own boundaries and limits, and let him know that he is not permitted to transfer to another the privilege owed to himself. If anyone, neglecting the apostolic sanctions and showing greater favor to a person, wishes to become a deserter of his own honor, believing that he can transfer his privilege to another, then not the one to whom he has yielded it, but the one who within the province is senior to the others by the antiquity of his episcopate, should claim for himself the power of ordaining priests.  
> (*Letter 10 to the bishops of Vienne*, chapter 7)

This rebuke seems to fall upon Ingenuus, metropolitan of the Maritime Alps. For Pope Hilary testifies that he had once been censured by his predecessor Leo for an unlawful surrender of his metropolitan right. Writing to Leontius, Victurus, and Veranus, bishops of those regions, in order to settle the controversy that had arisen between Ingenuus and Auxanius over the governance of the Churches of Cimiez and Nice, he speaks as follows:

> Let our brother and fellow bishop Ingenuus therefore retain the pontifical authority of his province, concerning whose former unlawful surrender he was censured by the apostolic see, and let all those things be observed which, as we have said, the authority of my predecessor of holy memory defined concerning the Churches of the city of Cimiez and the castle of Nice.

These words cannot seem to refer to anyone other than our Leo, who is in fact said to have been angered by such an unlawful surrender and whose handling of this case is attributed by Hilary. This, in my opinion, is how we should reason concerning Projectus’s see, according to the first reading of this passage.

Those, however, who prefer the other reading, “before Patroclus”—and it does indeed seem more worthy of approval because of the authority of the manuscripts and of the sequence of the discourse itself—must assign Projectus to another province. For from these words:

> What does he usurp that none of his predecessors before Patroclus possessed, when even that which seemed to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment?

we establish that the province under investigation was one of those which Zosimus claimed for Patroclus. It must therefore have been either Vienne or one of the two provinces of Narbonne. It cannot refer to Vienne, since that was not foreign to the bishop of Arles. It must therefore refer to one of the Narbonese provinces [Col. 0496A].

But in order for me to think that it was the first of these provinces [Note: [Col. 0496D] We shall confirm this in the same *Observations*, Part II, chapter 1.], the words of Saint Leo are decisive. He indicates that the province whose jurisdiction Hilary claimed in Projectus’s case was the one that had been taken away from Patroclus by a better decree of the apostolic see:

> For even that which seemed to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment.

Here he undoubtedly alludes to the decree—or letter—of Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, by which he asserted the jurisdiction of Narbonne I to him and reproved the bishop of Arles for having presumed to celebrate the ordination of the bishop of Luteva in that same province. Celestine likewise confirmed this judgment in his letter to the bishops of the provinces of Narbonne and Vienne.

The third opinion concerning Projectus’s episcopate is found in the *Gallia Christiana* of the most distinguished Sammarthani brothers, who, on the authority of Polycarpus de la Rivière, a Carthusian, in his *Annals of the Church and City of Avignon*, and of Joannes Columbus of Manosque, S.J., in his book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Die*, number Projectus among the bishops of Die under the year of Christ 440. If this is so, Projectus must be placed in the province of Vienne, which conflicts with Leo, as we have already noted, since he did not consider the province of Vienne to have been alien to Hilary. Moreover, Projectus belonged to that province which Leo says had been taken away from Patroclus by a better judgment; here he undoubtedly refers to the letter of Pope Boniface to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, which Celestine confirmed.

Yet so far is it from being the case that either of these pontiffs took the province of Vienne away from Hilary, that rather it is clear from both letters that Hilary was regarded by both as metropolitan—and of no province other than Vienne. For Boniface declares the ordination of the bishop of Luteva invalid for this one reason: it had indeed been performed by Hilary as metropolitan, but Hilary was not metropolitan of Narbonensis, where Luteva lay. “In another province,” he says. To prove that this was contrary to the canons, he was compelled to expand Canon 4 of Nicaea by paraphrase, so as to derive from it the statement: “Two provinces ought not to be subject to any one metropolitan.” This argument against Hilary would have been empty and entirely without force unless he had possessed some province subject to him.

The same point is drawn from Celestine’s letter. In the same case he relies upon this single proof: each province ought to be content with its own metropolitan, and no opportunity for usurpation should be granted to any priest through injury to another; each person ought to remain content within the limits assigned to him, and no one may presume to do anything in another’s province. All this presupposes that the bishop of Arles lawfully possessed and exercised metropolitan authority over some province—clearly Vienne—and consequently that Projectus’s see must be sought outside that province.

We therefore adhere to one or the other of the two earlier opinions, and ought to be satisfied with these conjectures until greater light shines forth from ecclesiastical records that perhaps lie concealed somewhere. Whether, however, Saint Hilary rightly and justly claimed for himself the ordination of both those provinces—Narbonensis and the Alpine province, I mean—must be investigated in the following sections.

## CHAPTER II

**That the bishop of Arles was once the metropolitan of the whole unified province of Narbonensis and justly claimed its principal parts for himself after the division; here that division is examined, and inquiry is made into the subscriptions of the First Synod of Arles.**

As I considered by what fate it had come about that, of all the ecclesiastical provinces of Gaul, Vienne alone had once been shaken by so many conflicts, so that controversies which in various ages had arisen among the metropolitans and other bishops of that region were scarcely brought to an end even by the authority of synods and supreme pontiffs, it immediately occurred to me that the cause and origin of such disagreements must be sought in the various divisions of those provinces.

For since the Church exists within the empire, and since it once seemed consonant with equity to the first founders of the Church that ecclesiastical provinces should likewise be arranged according to the administration of the civil provinces,

> **[Note: [Col. 0497D] Why we should not believe this to be true will become clear from the observations, part II, chapter 5, number 12.]**

whenever it happened by imperial decree that one of these was divided into several, the bishop of that city which had been made the metropolis of the new province in civil affairs immediately assumed metropolitan authority over it, and the former metropolitan’s yoke was shaken off, the new city becoming the head of its own province. Since no provinces anywhere underwent as many changes of division as did those ancient parts of Narbonensis, this was the source of such great disagreements.

On the other hand, the minds of the ancient metropolitans had been deeply impressed, even before the time of Innocent, by what that pontiff later wrote on the basis of the tradition of his see and the judgment of the ancient Fathers: namely, that metropolitan bishops ought to be appointed according to the ancient custom of the provinces; that when provinces are divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolises come into being, two metropolitans ought not to be appointed (*Innocent*, Letter 20); and, finally, that it is not fitting for the dignity of the Church that God’s Church should be altered according to the shifting demands of worldly affairs, or undergo the honors or divisions which the emperor might decide to establish for his own purposes.

The bishops of Arles undoubtedly relied upon this foundation when they claimed for their jurisdiction all the provinces which they had once held subject to themselves, when those provinces had formerly been joined into one unified Narbonensis.

> **[Note: [Col. 0497D] It is here assumed that the bishop of Arles was metropolitan of the whole unified Narbonensis before the division into five, and subsequently seven, provinces. This, however, will be shown to be false both by the earlier division of Narbonensis, which we shall establish in the observations, part II, chapter 3, and by the late establishment of metropolises in Gaul, which will be treated in the same work, chapter 5, numbers 1 and following.]**

Just as this was more consistent with the origin of the Churches, so it was also proved by later ecclesiastical sanctions to be entirely consonant with reason. For this purpose the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon enacted Canon 12, so that, when a civil province was split in two by imperial sanction, it would not likewise be divided between two metropolitans. Hence, as Pope Gelasius I asserts in Letter 13 to the bishops of Dardania against Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, that royal city is not only not counted among the sees, but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights. “For,” he says, “one is the power of secular kingship, another the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities.”

If, therefore, it is once proved that during that period the bishop of Arles held primacy in Gaul and was adorned with metropolitan dignity, while the ancient province of Narbonensis was still intact, and that after the division he retained metropolitan rights over its parts, then there will be no reason to brand Hilary with the mark of ambition or to defame him as an invader of another’s rights. Before attempting to establish this, however, the manifold division of Gaul must be recalled, by which its condition became subject to frequent changes and disturbances.

Caesar Augustus first divided the whole body of Gaul into four members: Narbonensis, Aquitania, Lugdunensis, and Belgica. In the course of time each of these was subsequently subdivided into other parts for various reasons and according to various policies. It is not our purpose to investigate the three latter divisions; we are concerned only with Narbonensis.

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D] We shall explain the various divisions of unified Narbonensis more precisely in the same work, chapter 3, and from that discussion some things incorrectly asserted here by Quesnel will have to be corrected.]**

It was therefore divided again into four provinces: Narbonensis, Vienne, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps. Third, Vienne was split into two—Vienne, that is, and Narbonensis Secunda—and together with three other provinces these formed the body of the Five Provinces. Finally, when the Graian Alps had been removed, Petronius formed from the remaining four, together with both Aquitanias and Novempopulania, the body of the Seven Provinces; he ordered its assembly to be held at Arles, later confirmed by a constitution of Honorius in the year 418.

Which of these four divisions prevailed when the foundations of religion and discipline were first laid in these regions is not easy to determine. It is certain that the third and fourth were much later than the beginnings of the faith; the entire difficulty concerns the first and second. Indeed, those who think that the faith of Christ was preached in these provinces from apostolic times cannot doubt that the first division of Gaul made by Augustus was still intact when Ptolemy, who flourished under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus after the year 130, followed that division in his description of Gaul.

But since the opinion of others is much more probable—those who, guided by the authority of Sulpicius Severus and Gregory of Tours, assign the establishment of the Churches in the Roman province (for the region of Lugdunensis must be considered differently) to the time of Decius, around the year of Christ 250—it remains to inquire whether at that time the first division of Augustus still prevailed, leaving Narbonensis undivided, or whether a second division had succeeded it, one which had distributed it into four parts.

The date of this division is highly uncertain because of the silence of the ancient writers. Some assign it to Hadrian, others to Constantine or Theodosius. It can scarcely be attributed to Hadrian, since Ptolemy, who flourished under Hadrian and Antoninus, follows the division of Augustus in his description of Gaul. Peter de Marca, discussing the division of the entire body of Gaul in his dissertation *On Primacies* (no. 113), declares it to be far older than Constantine.

Let this be true of certain Gallic provinces, which do not concern our subject—for he himself admits that the division was not introduced into all the provinces at one and the same time. But concerning Narbonensis there is no ancient testimony from which it may even be suspected that it was divided before Constantine. For the evidence produced by the most distinguished prelate from the subscriptions of the First Council of Arles, where the province of Vienne is mentioned, in order to prove that already at that time—that is, in the year 314—Vienne had been separated from Narbonensis, is, in my opinion, entirely without weight.

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D] We shall discuss these subscriptions—or rather, the catalogue of the bishops of the First Synod of Arles—at length in the observations, part II, chapter 3, number 14; there all Quesnel’s quibbles will be demolished. It will also become clear there that at this time the province of Vienne had been separated from Narbonensis.]**

For I strongly suspect that those subscriptions were not made by the bishops themselves in the manner and order in which they are now presented, but were arranged some years later according to the number of provinces from which the bishops had assembled: first those from the Roman diocese, then those from Italy, next those from Gaul, and so on with the others. In arranging this catalogue, the compiler used both other records that were then still extant and the synodal letter containing the names of those same bishops.

### 850

Our conjecture rests upon the following arguments.

1. It was not the custom of synods for bishops to subscribe according to the order of the provinces. Although the practice was not always the same everywhere, it was generally observed that the order of consecration was followed. At times all the metropolitans subscribed first; among them, too, the prominence and dignity of their sees were sometimes taken into account, so that they were placed before the others.

2. The placement and arrangement of these subscriptions vary greatly in manuscripts and printed editions. In some they precede the canons; in others they follow them; in some they are attached to the First Council of Arles, in others to the Second, as in the Merlinian, Crabbean, and Nicolinian editions. In those same editions and several others, as well as in the manuscripts of Reims and elsewhere, the designation of the provinces and cities precedes the names of the bishops; in others, such as the Corbie manuscript followed by Sirmond, it follows them.

All this suggests that the catalogue was a fragment distinct from the acts of the synod and was compiled by a private person, who, having circulated it in various places, had not yet found it a fixed home.

3. The names of the bishops lie in such disorder that the arrangement can in no way be called synodal. Why, for example, is Marinus of Arles, who is listed first at the head of the synodal letter containing the authentic acts, not likewise listed first among the signatures at the end of that brief record? Why do the presbyters sent by Sylvester subscribe in fifth place? Is it because they ought to have subscribed after the bishops of the Urban Diocese? Yet Theodorus, bishop of Aquileia, who precedes them, belonged to the Italian diocese.

Why, after all the others, are two bishops and two presbyters of the Roman province found subscribing separately from the other bishops of that same diocese? Finally, why is there such a discrepancy between the names in the letter and the subscriptions, and even between the lists of provinces? Where the ancient editions have “from the city of Carpentoracum,” others read “from the harbor of Nice.” The former display a single Aquitania; the latter distinguish the First and Second Aquitanias. In some there is mention of the province of Narbonensis and the city of Béziers; others are silent about these. Some mention the Roman province, others do not. Some include the city and bishop of Massilia, of whom nothing is read in the others.

These things clearly indicate that the index was drawn up solely to display the diversity of the provinces from which the synod had been assembled. Its author compiled it according to his own understanding, and those who came after him corrected it according to their own views and the period in which they wrote, insofar as the division of the provinces then in use seemed to require.

4. If the names of the Fathers of Arles had to be added anywhere, surely their signatures ought to be found at the end of the genuine acts. But the only genuine acts of that synod are those found in the synodal letter. The other document in which the bishops are subscribed contains only the *Breviarium*,

> **[Col. 0499D] We shall remove this suspicion of interpolation in the same number 14.**

which I would not wish to declare free from every suspicion of interpolation. For these words of Canon 1—“And according to custom, direct letters to all,” namely concerning the day of Easter—are not found in the letter itself to Sylvester, where they ought especially to occur if they had truly been written by the synod. Moreover, such Easter letters do not appear to have been in use before the time of the Council of Nicaea.

Since the names of the bishops are not found at the end of the acts, or of the synodal letter, this is evidence that the index attached to the *Breviarium* was compiled from the letter itself and perhaps from other copies of the acts.

5. The title of the subscriptions itself shows that this catalogue was transcribed not by the bishops who were present, but by some learned person who wished to discover how many bishops had assembled at the council and from which provinces they had come. The author wished to investigate this for the purpose of proving that the council had truly been called universal and a council of the whole Church by Augustine (*On Baptism*, Book II, chapter 9, and Letter 162).

Or rather—and this amounts to the same thing while also explaining why the catalogue is found prefixed to the Second Council of Arles in ancient manuscript and printed books—it was intended to establish the truth of Canon 18 of the Second Council of Arles. According to that canon, “from all parts of the world, especially from the Gallic regions, we read that a council and assembly was held in the time of Saint Marinus.”

One can scarcely imagine any other reason why this catalogue was attached to that council than the elucidation of this canon. For merely by the mention of Pope Sylvester in these subscriptions, of Saint Marinus in the canon, and of the Bonosians in the preceding canon, any reader would be sufficiently warned that fitting one to the other would be no easier than fitting a horse’s neck onto a human head.

I have noted these matters in order to show that there is nothing in the ancient records from which it can be inferred that the division of unified Narbonensis into four parts took place before the middle of the fourth century.

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D] See the observations, part II, chapter 3.]**

That it originated around this time becomes probable, first, because the earliest writers who mention it—namely Rufus Festus (*Breviary*) and Ammianus Marcellinus (Book XV)—flourished in that period; Rufus Festus dedicated his *Breviary* to the emperor Valens or Valentinian in the year 365.

Second, this may also be inferred from the fact that before that time no disagreements are reported to have arisen in Gaul among bishops concerning the boundaries of the provinces. The first complaints concerning them were brought to the Council of Turin. For how could the holy Proculus, bishop of Massilia, have claimed the right to preside as metropolitan over the Churches that appeared to be situated in the Second Province of Narbonensis, and to perform himself the ordinations of the chief priests in that province, if he alleged that those Churches were either his parishes or that he had ordained bishops in those same Churches?

By what right, I ask, would Proculus have claimed these things—something none of his predecessors had presumed—unless the new division of the provinces had furnished a pretext?

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D] The disagreements concerning metropolitan authority did not arise from the division of the provinces, which we shall show had taken place long before, but because ecclesiastical metropolises began to be introduced before the end of the fourth century, as will be evident from the observations, part II, chapter 5, number 8.]**

Nor does he himself appeal to the possession of his ancestors; and the bishops of this Second Province of Narbonensis raise no other objection than the diversity of the province. Had this diversity not arisen from a recent division, they would undoubtedly have brought forward the contrary custom of the ancient bishops of the city of Massilia.

Third, in addition to these arguments, partly negative and partly resting only on conjecture, we have from Jerome an affirmative proof of considerable force, if attention is paid to the authority of a writer who not only traveled through Gaul with care but also lived there for some time. Thus, in Letter 11 to Ageruchia, *On Monogamy*, while describing the invasion of the barbarians into Gaul, after listing the principal cities of Belgica which the fiercest nations had laid waste, he adds three other parts of Gaul according to the division of Augustus:

> “Aquitania, and the Nine Peoples, Lugdunensis, and the province of Narbonensis—all have been devastated.”

You see that Jerome lists a single Narbonensis, and that the fourfold division of Gaul either still endured when this learned doctor wrote, or—what I consider more likely—the division of Narbonensis into four provinces was still so recent that writers not yet accustomed to the new division continued to use the ancient manner of speaking.

> **[Note: [Col. 0500D] Whoever names the Aquitanias in the plural together with the Nine Peoples undoubtedly presupposes the division of the provinces already in effect, by which the two Aquitanias had been separated. Saint Jerome did not wish to indicate the division of the provinces here, but merely listed those provinces that had been devastated by the barbarians in his own age. When he calls Narbonensis “the province” in the singular, he means not unified Narbonensis but Narbonensis Prima; hence in what follows he mentions Toulouse, which belongs to Narbonensis Prima.]**

4. It is very likely that the division of the province of Narbonensis was recent when the Synod of Turin was assembled, and that the synod was assembled because of this division. For at that council it was disputed who ought to preside over the Second Province of Narbonensis by metropolitan right, so that no one yet appears to have possessed such authority over that province. This will become clearer from what we shall say in the following section.

If, then, the unity of Narbonensis remained undivided until the times we have noted, there can be no doubt that according to the canons it was likewise subject to a single metropolitan. I believe that we have shown with sufficient clarity that this metropolitan was the bishop of Arles in the first part of this dissertation, where we set out in order all the records of Gallic antiquity.

Although we have said that the new division does not appear before the middle of the fourth century, this will not suffice for anyone who rejects our opinion merely to produce a testimony by which it might be shown to have occurred before that period, unless he proves that it was introduced before the year 250. Since nearly all the more learned writers, with few exceptions, assign the beginnings of religion and discipline in Gaul to that period, if there was then one province and one metropolitan, the rule of Pope Innocent I will apply:

> “Metropolitan bishops ought to be appointed according to the ancient custom of the provinces, and God’s Church ought not to be changed according to the shifting demands of worldly affairs.”

Accordingly, Hilary did not disturb the Church when he undertook to vindicate the ancient rights of his Church, following his predecessors Honoratus, Patroclus, and the others more ancient than either of them.

## CHAPTER III

**That both Narbonian provinces were once subject to the bishop of Arles is proved from the letters of Pope Zosimus.**

We are not informed solely by the date of the division that the bishop of Arles had unified Narbonensis subject to his pontificate. It is also clear from what followed the division that the said bishop retained the same authority over those provinces which had previously been parts of Narbonensis—namely, Vienne, both Narbonian provinces, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps—even though he appears voluntarily to have relinquished some of his rights in certain of them.

### 854

We dealt at length with the province of Vienne in the earlier part of the dissertation. We must now treat the remaining provinces, insofar as the scarcity of records from that age and region permits.

With regard to both Narbonian provinces, there is a clear decree of Pope Zosimus. By it he commands that not only the province of Vienne should be subject to the bishop of Arles, but both those provinces as well. He confirms in him the authority both to ordain bishops and to perform the other metropolitan duties, and declares that anything attempted contrary to this shall be unlawful and void.

> “We have ordered that the metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles retain the special authority which he has always possessed in the ordination of priests. Let him recall the provinces of Vienne, Narbonensis Prima, and Narbonensis Secunda to his pontificate. Whoever hereafter presumes to ordain anyone in the aforesaid provinces contrary to the statutes of the apostolic see and the commands of the ancestors, omitting the metropolitan bishop, or whoever permits himself to be illicitly ordained there, let each of them know that he is deprived of the priesthood.”

Here the pontiff declares that he is not establishing a new right but restoring an ancient one, which the commands of the ancestors had vindicated for the bishops of Arles and which they had in fact always possessed—except perhaps for an interval of a few years during which, because of the new division and the disturbances that had shaken Gaul, those provinces had been wrongly diverted from them.

> **[Note: [Col. 0501D] By the words “commands of the ancestors,” Zosimus does not indicate any decree of the ancestors by which unified Narbonensis had been assigned to the bishop of Arles—for no such decree could certainly be produced—but understands the sixth Nicene canon, which provides that no one is to be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.]** Hence Zosimus orders that they be recalled to the pontificate of the bishop of Arles, not newly attached to it, and rebukes and restrains the bishops of Vienne and Massilia, who were troubling the bishop of Arles in this matter, as invaders of others’ territories.

The same pontiff gives the same decision in his letter to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne. He is exceedingly angry with him because, having disregarded the truth, Hilary had surreptitiously obtained from the apostolic see an unwarranted privilege, contrary to ancient custom and the old institution.

“But that ancient custom which Zosimus praises was not very ancient,” says the continuator of de Marca. “Indeed”—may I say this with the learned man’s pardon—it was most ancient. Hilary himself of Narbonne did not dare deny it. While wishing to secure the interests of his own claims and desires, he disregarded the truth and ‘colored his report merely under the appearance of honesty,’ asserting that priests ought not to be ordained in another province by someone else, whereas he certainly ought to have reported not what seemed right to him, but what ancient custom had established” (*Sacred and Imperial Concord*, vol. II, book V, chapter 30, no. 5).

It is therefore better to trust Zosimus (Letter 8, to Hilary of Narbonne), who, after hearing and examining the allegations of both parties, and with the opponent himself offering no contradiction but putting forward only the appearance of honesty on the occasion of the new division, asserts that the custom was ancient—rather than trust anyone who, after so many centuries, denies the same thing without proof.

Certainly Zosimus was not attending to the Council of Turin, as Baluze thinks; indeed, he could not have been.

First, that synod had not pronounced upon this controversy; nor had the bishops of Vienne and Arles contended before it except concerning the province of Vienne alone, while Proculus claimed the Second Province of Narbonensis for himself.

Second, Zosimus’s foundation would have been weak if, relying solely upon the Synod of Turin, he had asserted the antiquity of the rights of the bishops of Arles. For the synod had offered not so much a definitive judgment as friendly advice concerning a common division, assigning no city to anyone, but merely deferring to the person of Proculus until either party should prove his city to be the metropolis.

Third, Zosimus was far from asserting that any right had been created by the Synod of Turin. He regarded it as a serious misfortune that the dispute over metropolitan authority had been brought before that synod by Proculus and Simplicius, and that it had given its judgment, as he testifies in his letter to the bishops of the First and Second Provinces of Narbonensis and in another to Patroclus, bishop of Arles.

Fourth, who could believe that Zosimus spoke so foolishly as to call “ancient custom” and “the old institution” something whose beginnings were owed to the Synod of Turin? Since it is certain that the synod was assembled several years after the death of Saint Martin, Zosimus’s letter to the bishops of Africa, Gaul, and Spain could not have preceded his letter to Hilary of Narbonne by fifteen years. Hence, in the year 439, the Council of Riez in Gaul, praising the definition of the Council of Turin, calls it recent in Canon 1.

Zosimus therefore had before his eyes more ancient records: namely, the very origin and institution of the episcopal see through Trophimus, sent by the apostolic see to Gaul at a time when unified Narbonensis had not yet been divided into parts and was subject to a single metropolitan.

> “It has been sufficiently established that by ancient institution it was granted to the priest of the Church of Arles that he should ordain bishops not only in the province of Vienne but also throughout both Narbonian provinces. For Trophimus, the priest of holy memory, once sent from the apostolic see to the city of Arles, first brought to those regions the reverence due to so great a name, and not unjustly transmitted to others [alternatively: to other regions] the authority which he had received.”

He also had before his eyes the ancient decrees of the apostolic see, which he mentions and which have now disappeared. He had the judgment of his predecessor Innocent, founded upon the very dignity of the Church, which—as we reported above—forbade that it be changed according to the shifting demands of worldly affairs. Finally, he had the decrees of Nicaea itself.

> “What of the fact that, with Patroclus, the metropolitan bishop of the city of Arles, passed over, and without whose authority, according to the canons of the ancestors, no ordination at all could have been celebrated, priesthoods are being tumultuously and disorderly thrust upon unqualified men?”

At last he concludes his letter to Hilary of Narbonne by gathering together four titles and foundations by which this authority was asserted for the bishop of Arles:

> “When you see this, you see that it is conferred upon the bishop of the city of Arles by the apostolic see, by the reverence due to Saint Trophimus, by ancient custom, and by our recent and most evident definition.”

We do not deny that the bishop of Narbonne possessed metropolitan authority over the First Province of Narbonensis for several years. But just as this had been obtained surreptitiously on the occasion of the new division,

> **[Note: [Col. 0503D] It was not on the occasion of the new division, but because ecclesiastical metropolises began to be instituted around this time, that the bishop of Narbonne obtained an apostolic privilege. We shall show that it was entirely free from subreption in the observations, part II, chapter 2, numbers 2 and following.]**

so it was corrected as soon as possible by the apostolic see. That institution of the metropolitan bishop of Narbonne was so recent in the time of Zosimus that the pontiff himself asserts that the earlier custom—by which the bishop of Arles held those three provinces subject to him—had continued until almost his own time.

> “This custom of ordaining and the pontificate of that place, which the first and rightful possessor, Trophimus, had obtained, were preserved until almost our own time, as is proved by the records kept among us and by the testimony of many fellow priests” (Letter 8).

The same pontiff says nearly the same thing in Letter 1 to the bishops of the province of Vienne and the Second Province of Narbonensis. There he attacks Proculus especially as the architect of that entire ambitious scheme. Proculus, endeavoring to draw the ordinations of the Second Province of Narbonensis to himself, had induced Simplicius of Vienne to demand that he too be permitted to decide on the creation of priests in the province of Vienne. Zosimus counts this as shamelessness and declares that it must be cut away by that golden sentence:

> “An indecent attempt, to be cut away at the very vestibule: to extort from bishops assembled in council for definite reasons what, contrary to the statutes of the Fathers and to the reverence due to Saint Trophimus, who was sent from this see as the first metropolitan of the city of Arles, not even the authority of this see could grant or alter. For among us antiquity lives with roots that cannot be shaken; the decrees of the Fathers have established reverence for it” (Zosimus, Letter 7).

The seven letters of Zosimus written on this matter ought to be transcribed in full. The reader will find them separately edited by others in volume I of the *Ancient Councils of Gaul*, under the care of Jacques Sirmond. But just as no one doubts Zosimus’s judgment, so most maintain that these letters were written by him with insufficient prudence, and, agreeing with our Leo, contend that this privilege—which appeared to have been granted temporarily—was later removed by a better judgment.

We have already resolved, in the earlier part of the dissertation, the objection concerning the supposed nature of these letters of Zosimus and his excessive credulity. It remains only to compare Boniface’s judgment, which Leo and others call the better one, with Zosimus’s decree and letters, and to determine which of them allowed himself to be deceived and imposed upon.

## CHAPTER IV

**Boniface’s decree is examined, compared with Zosimus’s letters, and the latter are defended against the charge of subreption.**

After receiving Zosimus’s letter, Hilary appears to have withdrawn from all metropolitan functions and to have caused Patroclus no further trouble. Patroclus likewise took over the administration of the province of Narbonensis and, when the bishop of Luteva in that province died, consecrated another in his place.

Hilary of Narbonne did not even murmur at this, nor did he complain that his rightful authority had been taken from him by Patroclus. Indeed, the pontiff reproached him for his silence and apparent sluggishness.

The citizens and clergy of Luteva, however, did not endure with equal patience the ordination performed by Patroclus. For Boniface, writing to Hilary, says:

> “Behold, as your Charity recognizes from what has been reported, the order of the clergy or the petitions and tears of the people of the Church of Luteva have, as we understand, been sent to us with great sorrow. They say that our co-bishop Patroclus, without their petition, has ordained some unknown person in another province, in place of the deceased bishop, passing over the metropolitan and acting contrary to the regulations of the Fathers. We can in no way bear this patiently, since it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of our fathers.”

Thus Boniface wrote against Patroclus, whom the people of Luteva had represented as an invader of another province and a violator of the sacred canons. To restrain him from such attempts, he adds:

> “No one, surely, is unaware of the constitution of the Synod of Nicaea, which commands—in its very words, so that we may set them down precisely—that in each province the metropolitan rights ought to belong to a single metropolitan, and that no one should have two provinces subject to him . . . . . Therefore, dearest brother, if matters are as they are reported, and the boundary of your province encloses the aforesaid Church, then, admonished by our authority—something you ought indeed to do of your own accord—and having regard to the desires and wishes of those who petition, etc., let such presumptuous conduct cease under the pressure of our authority, namely that of those who extend the limits of their dignity beyond what is lawful, etc.”

There is much that persuades anyone who compares this with the decrees of Zosimus that Boniface’s decision concerning the same controversy should more rightly be thought to have been issued hastily and obtained by subreption.

> **[Note: [Col. 0504D] We shall show in the cited place that Zosimus’s rescripts were obtained from him by Patroclus through subreption; there, in number 7, Pope Boniface’s decree will be defended.]**
858 For, first, this is a very well-known rule of canon law: such rescripts are to be regarded as null and considered subreptitious when they establish something new that is contrary to earlier decrees of councils and pontiffs, yet make no mention whatsoever of those decrees. For this is the clearest possible indication either that the matter was handled with extreme carelessness or that fraud was practiced upon the pontiff, or that some human error befell him. Such is Boniface’s decision, which is entirely silent about the rescripts of Zosimus. Zosimus’s decrees are of a different kind: they mention the rescripts of his predecessors and, although they decide nothing contrary to them, decree what is wholly consonant with them.

[Col. 0504D] 2. Boniface’s decision was issued in favor of the bishop of Narbonne without the opposing party having been heard or given an opportunity to defend its rights. When, however, Zosimus wished by his letters to confirm the privileges of the bishop of Arles, he weighed the allegations of both parties and sent a letter to the bishop of Narbonne, in which he also rebuked him for having, while neglecting the truth, disguised his report under the mere appearance of propriety.

3. It is clear from Boniface’s letter that he examined the matter with insufficient care and that he lacked knowledge of facts which ought to have been preliminary to resolving the dispute. He did not perceive the actual state of the controversy [Col. 0505A], which did not concern whether the metropolitans of provinces that had long been distinct ought likewise to be distinct, or whether one metropolitan might invade the rights of another—for that is what the Nicene decree forbids—but rather this question: whether, when provinces are divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolitan sees are created, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be appointed (Letter of Pope Innocent to Alexander of Antioch). This was what Alexander of Antioch had asked Innocent, Boniface’s predecessor. The controversy ought to have been decided according to Innocent’s decree, in which, by interpreting the Nicene canon, he ruled that the Church of God ought not to be altered according to the changing necessities of worldly affairs.

Moreover, Boniface was so poorly informed about the condition of the Gallican Churches that he speaks with extreme hesitation: “If matters are so,” and he did not even appear to know where the city of Luteva was situated. Finally, it is clear that the matter was not weighed with sufficient deliberation, since as soon as he received the complaint of the people of Luteva [Col. 0505B], he issued a definitive judgment and brought the entire controversy to an end in a single letter.

Zosimus acted in a very different manner. He omitted nothing that was necessary for investigating the truth of the matter and determining the rights of the parties. He did not settle the affair in a single letter and, as it were, in a single moment, but wrote seven letters concerning it and examined the matter over the course of an entire year—not superficially or precipitately, but, as he himself says, with great diligence. He did not investigate it alone, but discussed it with a numerous body of advisers or in an assembly; not according to human preferences, but under the judgment of God; not from conjecture or any sort of prejudice, but after carefully examining the facts themselves, ancient custom, and the decrees of synods and pontiffs. Everything was determined by him neither without the knowledge of the parties nor without hearing them, but only after both had been heard and admonished. It is therefore astonishing that some writers should assert that Zosimus was deceived in this matter by a subreptitious petition.

4. Who would call a judgment equitable when it was rendered solely from an examination of the testimony of the adversaries [Col. 0505C], and when the accused was given no opportunity to defend himself? This is what Boniface did. Zosimus acted otherwise: he awaited the report of Hilary of Narbonne and even invited Proculus of Marseilles to come to Rome and plead his own case.

5. Even if everything had been done by the pontiff according to the rules of law and equity, the judgment would still have possessed no force in itself, since it was hypothetical and depended upon the supposition that Hilary of Arles had attempted something contrary to the Nicene canons. Hence room was still left for investigation. Once that investigation had been completed, it ought to have been accepted as certain—as we have often shown—that the bishop of Arles had not violated the Nicene canons but had rather obeyed them according to the interpretation issued by Innocent I, when he claimed for himself a province that had anciently been subject to his see, setting aside the more recent division established by temporal authorities.

6. Finally, it is far more equitable to attend to the judgment of the metropolitan bishop himself, whose rights are said to have been violated [Col. 0505D], than to the complaints and murmurs of clerics and citizens. Yet Hilary of Narbonne brought no complaints before the Apostolic See and acquiesced in the ordination conducted by Patroclus in the Church of Luteva. He ought therefore rightly to be believed to have assented silently to the privileges of the bishop of Arles. For the words of Pope Boniface sufficiently indicate that Hilary had not even considered consecrating a bishop for Luteva, since he had to be stirred by the pontiff’s admonitions to approach the place where such an ordination was said to have been celebrated, fortified by the right of a metropolitan and relying upon the pontiff’s commands. “This,” Boniface says, “you ought indeed to have done of your own accord”—and Hilary appears not to have done it even after being admonished.

Those clerics, however, while Hilary remained silent, approached the Roman pontiff by their letters [Col. 0506A]. They were not so much distressed that the bishop of Narbonne had been omitted from the ordination as that their own petition and consent had been disregarded—something that was in fact contrary to the authority of the canons and the decrees of the Fathers. They nevertheless introduced the claim that metropolitan jurisdiction had been violated, in order to stir up more intense hostility against Patroclus and to win greater credibility for themselves, appearing to be moved not so much by private and personal rights as by zeal for public and common discipline. Moreover, it seems to me that Hilary not only disapproved their plan by his silence but openly refused to draw the consecration of the bishop of Luteva to himself. For when Boniface urges him to prepare for the ordination, which he ought indeed to have undertaken of his own accord, while taking into account the petitions and wishes of the supplicants, he plainly implies that their petitions had been disregarded by him and that their wishes had not previously been taken into account. This is very far from the view of Marca, who thought that Hilary himself had appealed to Boniface; [Col. 0506B] indeed, the pontiff issued his judgment without being appealed to by any bishop, and the decision is therefore not particularly commendable on that account or under that title.

As for what Saint Leo asserts in this letter to the bishops of Vienne—that the very thing which had temporarily appeared to have been granted to Patroclus by the Apostolic See was later removed by a better judgment [Note: [Col. 0505D] How rightly Leo wrote this, and how rashly Quesnellus here attempts to tear passages from the judgment of so great a pontiff, will become evident from chapter 2 of our observations, part II, [Col. 0506D] below.]—it was spoken somewhat angrily against the bishop of Arles and was not proved. It is therefore not entirely consistent with the truth, if I may say so without offense to so great a teacher. Nor do we insult the pontiff, for it is no more in his interest that Boniface’s decree be upheld than that of Zosimus.

For who could regard as the better judgment one that was issued both in a momentary proceeding and in the manner we have described, and that was contrary to ancient custom? Either Leo, occupied with more important matters, had not examined this question carefully; or he had suffered a lapse of memory; or, while pursuing Hilary with somewhat excessive vehemence, he judged that to be truer which accorded more closely with his preconceived opinion. He did not notice that, although immediately before Patroclus those provinces did not obey the bishop of Arles [Col. 0506C] [Note: [Col. 0506D] This proposition rests upon the single testimony of Zosimus, whom we shall prove in that place to have been deceived by Patroclus.], this had nevertheless not been so from the beginning.

Certainly, greater credence ought to be given to Zosimus, who asserts that the custom of ordaining bishops and the pontifical authority of that place, first possessed by the rightful Trophimus, had been preserved until a very recent time—“as is proved,” he says, “by the proceedings held among us and by the testimony of many of our fellow priests”—than to Leo, who denies this without evidence. Since Leo lived farther removed from those times and had not examined the matter specifically, he could easily have been led into error by Chelidonius and the other advocates of that cause.

Indeed, he touched upon this argument only very briefly and hastily, distrustful of its strength, although great weight ought to have been placed upon it if it were true that before Patroclus none of the bishops of Arles had possessed jurisdiction over both provinces of Narbonne. For once this had been proved, it would have been easy to accuse Zosimus both of rashly introducing a novelty and of trampling upon antiquity. The sacred canons, which commanded that the rights of all metropolitans remain unimpaired, were certainly not to be violated for anyone’s benefit—still less for the benefit of Patroclus, an unscrupulous man who had mounted the see of Arles through the unjust and violent expulsion of his predecessor.

Indeed, Leo himself could scarcely be absolved from the charge of prevarication if he had allowed a privilege that had been obtained by so cunning a man against ancient law and the sacred canons to be usurped in equal measure by Patroclus’s successors, even before the complaints of Chelidonius and Projectus arose. For Leo knew very well what was being done in Gaul: before the beginning of his pontificate he had spent some time there, and he was also fully acquainted with the affairs that had been brought to Rome under the pontiffs Celestine and Sixtus III [Col. 0507A], in whose administration of ecclesiastical affairs he had continually labored.

From all this it is evident that nothing was established by Zosimus except after mature deliberation, while Boniface established nothing contrary that either touched upon the actual state of the controversy or had been accepted by the Gallican bishops.

## CHAPTER V. Whether Boniface’s Constitution Took Effect in Gaul, and What Happened after Him Concerning This Affair in the Two Provinces of Narbonne

Boniface’s decree sent to the Gallican bishops [Note: [Col. 0507D] These points are refuted in the observations, part II, chapter 2, numbers 8 and 9.] was not esteemed by them so highly that they thought it ought to be preferred to ancient custom and even to the earlier decrees of the Roman pontiffs. For Patroclus continued to exercise the same authority over the provinces and transmitted it to his successors, Honoratus and Hilary.

We learn this from Leo himself. Although he writes that none of Hilary’s predecessors before Patroclus had claimed rights over those provinces, he must be understood to admit, by this exception, that all Patroclus’s successors asserted such a privilege for their own see. Otherwise he would not have said “no one before Patroclus,” but “no one except Patroclus.”

Furthermore, it is clear that Honoratus, who governed the Church between Patroclus and Hilary of Arles, did not allow any of his predecessor’s rights to be taken from him, but had those three provinces subject to him. For this is why Pope Celestine, Boniface’s successor, writing in July 428 to the bishops of the province of Vienne and of Narbonne, while Honoratus was still alive, complains that the rights of certain metropolitans had been diminished and the boundaries of their provinces violated contrary to the decree of his predecessor, which he orders to remain intact and firm.

“According to the decrees of the canons,” he says, “let each province be content with its own metropolitan, as the decrees sent by our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne contain; and let no priest be given an opportunity for usurpation to the injury of another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province; and let foreign and alien clerics, and those previously unknown, not be placed over clerics who have served honorably in their own Churches and are commended by the testimony of their fellow citizens, lest some new sort of institution, from which bishops are made, appear to be established as a collegium.”

These words point to Honoratus, who had been elevated to the see of Arles from the monastery of Lérins. Since several men in that period had been transferred from there to episcopal sees, it appeared to be a new sort of institution from which bishops were being produced. Through the ordination of this foreign and alien man, Honoratus, clerics who had served honorably in their own Churches and had deserved well of their fellow citizens appeared to have been passed over. The opening words of the decree also imply not only that Honoratus administered those three provinces but that the metropolitans themselves had voluntarily yielded, since Celestine forbids any priest to be given an opportunity for usurpation to another’s injury.

Whoever wishes to assert that this was wrongly conceded either by the Gallican bishops or accepted and maintained by Honoratus and Hilary would inflict the gravest injustice upon so many holy men, entirely free from ambition. No one flourished in that period who surpassed Hilary and Honoratus in holiness, or who ought to be preferred to the holy Germanus of Auxerre and Lupus of Troyes. Without their counsel, assistance, and support, Hilary never undertook anything of importance; the same must likewise be believed of Honoratus.

Whatever the truth may be, the bishops of Gaul did not sin against the Apostolic See when, adhering to its earlier and ancient sanctions, which Zosimus recalls, they refused to assent to its later decrees. For those later decrees had been issued without consulting them and without sufficient consideration of the matter, not at the request of any bishop but solely in response to the complaint of certain clerics of no standing. Those bishops knew what Symmachus later wrote in the same case (Letter 2 to Eonius of Arles): that it belongs to the very sacred Catholic religion that there should be no disparity between the decisions of the Church’s earlier and later bishops, whose entire authority is undermined unless everything once established by the priests of the Lord remains perpetual.

“For just as the power of the Trinity is one and indivisible, so the priesthood is one through the various bishops. How, then, is it fitting that the statutes of the earlier bishops be violated by those who follow them?”

Relying upon these arguments, as soon as Hilary of Arles was appointed in place of the deceased Honoratus, he undertook to administer those three provinces under metropolitan jurisdiction, with all the Gallican bishops giving their support by unanimous consent. This is certain from Leo alone, who for that reason censures his audacity, because, as Leo thought, he had presumed to exercise pontifical office in another’s province.

Yet even by the single title of possession he ought to have asserted both provinces of Narbonne, apart from Vienne, for his see, since both the sanctity of his predecessor and the consensus of the bishops themselves forbade that other bishops of Arles should be accused of attempting to exercise rights belonging to another.

Apart from what we have so far discussed concerning the two provinces of Narbonne in relation to the constitution of Zosimus, there are other considerations that specifically assert that Narbonne II was subject to the bishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 0507D] See the same observations, part II, chapter 6, number 2 and following, where we shall examine each of the points that follow in detail.].

First, it is clear from canon 1 of the Council of Turin that the bishop of Aix—who alone afterward arrogated metropolitan dignity to himself within Narbonne II after the death of Proculus—did not at that time claim such a right. If he, or anyone else from that province, had been metropolitan, he would not have claimed that Proculus of Marseilles possessed the Churches of that province as his own parishes, or that he had ordained bishops in those same Churches. A metropolitan would either have accused him of falsehood or complained that the rights of his metropolitan dignity had been usurped. Nothing of this kind was brought against Proculus; no one asserted metropolitan authority. The bishops of that region contended only that a priest from another province ought not to preside over them.

“But,” you will say, “this argument likewise excludes the bishop of Arles from authority over both provinces of Narbonne, and especially over the second, which is under discussion here. Since he is not recorded as having opposed Proculus at this Council of Turin, the argument is that he did not act as the metropolitan of that province.”

To resolve this difficulty, we must observe that the Gallican provinces, and especially the undivided province of Narbonne, were thrown into the greatest disorder by the tyranny of Maximus, Arbogastes, Eugenius, and others, who occupied those regions toward the end of the fourth century. In a constitution concerning various ecclesiastical matters sent in the year 425 to Armatius, prefect of the Gauls, the emperor Valentinian III complains that through their agency the Churches and clergy of Gaul had been stripped of their privileges. In a constitution of the year 418 addressed to Agricola, prefect of the Gauls, Honorius Augustus indicates that through the negligence of those same men everything had been turned upside down [Col. 0508D] in the province of Vienne, when he censures the fact that, through their negligence, the assembly of those provinces had not been held at the city of Arles.

The circumstances themselves cry out that ecclesiastical discipline could scarcely have found any place amid the disturbances of the civil wars. Therefore, since it was extremely difficult for the bishop of Arles, with the armies of both sides scattered throughout all the provinces, to attend to the needs of the Churches and travel to distant cities in order to ordain successors to deceased bishops according to his right, he was compelled by the necessities of the times to permit the bishops of certain more prominent cities to consecrate, when necessary, the bishops of neighboring Churches.

Since Proculus, a man whom Saint Jerome judged to be most holy and learned (Letter to Rusticus), surpassed the other bishops not only in the antiquity of his priesthood and the nobility of his city but also in the prerogative of his Church—which was then the first among the Churches of the province of Vienne, as may be gathered from Sidonius (Letter 7, Book VII)—it was easy for the honor and authority of consecrating bishops during that period to be voluntarily entrusted to him both by neighboring bishops and by the bishop of Arles.

When, however, the affairs of the Empire were later restored to peace and a new division of those provinces was introduced by imperial sanction, a dispute arose among the bishops. Some, opposing the bishop of Arles, denied that two provinces ought to be subject to one metropolitan; others maintained that a metropolitan ought not to be taken from another province, contrary to Proculus, who claimed Narbonne II for himself. At the same time, Proculus asserted that he rightly possessed jurisdiction over the Churches of that province because they had either been his parishes or had received their bishops from him, so that he might assist them with the honor of primacy as a father assists his sons (Council of Turin, canon 1). This appeared to be entirely consonant with the rules of equity.

It should be noted here that the bishop of Marseilles advanced no other claim than the ordination that established the most recent basis for his right; nor, on the other side, was this kind of ordination accused of having been improperly attempted. This makes it clearer that the entire arrangement had been brought about solely by the necessities of the times and by the indulgence of the metropolitan.

What, meanwhile, was the bishop of Arles to do? He saw all the rights of his see being attacked and overthrown on every side. The bishop of Vienne was disputing with him over the primacy of Vienne. The bishop of Marseilles, a man highly esteemed by the Gallican bishops, was seeking Narbonne II and was asserting the title of possession and consecration, and perhaps also the consent of the bishop of Arles.

He therefore judged it more advantageous to his interests to yield to Proculus, so that Proculus might possess the province of Narbonne II during his lifetime, on the condition that after his death the ordination of that province would return to its ancient metropolitan. The council appears to have understood this condition when it expressed no other. In this way he secured the goodwill of Proculus and of the other Gallican bishops, which he needed in order to preserve intact the rights of his primacy against the bishop of Vienne.

In fact, after the death of Proculus, the bishop of Arles again undertook the administration of Narbonne II [Col. 0509C]; indeed, Zosimus had vindicated it for the bishop of Arles even before then, as is known from his letters.

Although some of these considerations rest only upon conjecture, they are nevertheless so probable that it is scarcely possible to conceive that events occurred otherwise. For Proculus, a most holy man who had not previously been adorned with metropolitan dignity, could not have arrogated to himself the ordination of those Churches except under pressing necessity and with the consent of the bishops. Since those Churches could not be without a metropolitan, they likewise could not previously have had any other than the metropolitan of the whole province of Narbonne, whom we have proved to have been the bishop of Arles.

Therefore, by yielding temporarily to Proculus, the bishop of Arles sufficiently safeguarded his right over Narbonne II, provided that he vigorously defended his primacy against the bishop of Vienne. It is therefore clear that no prejudice is created against the bishop of Arles by his silence at the Council of Turin concerning Narbonne II.

Nor is it clear in whose favor the bishops of Narbonne II lodged their protest. From the zeal that they later displayed on behalf of the bishop of Arles, it may reasonably be judged that they favored him even then. It may also be added that only the canons of this council are presented to us, not its Acts, in which we would doubtless find the complete statements of all those bishops, had the Acts not perished.

Perhaps we do not possess all the canons, since the matters that Pope Zosimus reports as having been treated at that council in the case of Bricius, bishop of Tours, and Lazarus, his accuser, are missing (Letter to the bishops of Africa, Gaul, and Spain). In another letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne and Narbonne II [Col. 0510A], he likewise testifies that much more was done at the Council of Turin than the question of metropolitan jurisdiction and the distinction of provinces.

2. In addition to the argument that we have developed at length from that council, we derive another from the same letter of Zosimus just cited. Proculus is accused of having promoted Lazarus to episcopal dignity, although Lazarus had been condemned at that council as a false accuser.

Since Lazarus was the bishop of Aix and had not been ordained by the bishop of Narbonne II but by Proculus of Marseilles, it is clear that there was no metropolitan in that province except the bishop of Arles, who had temporarily yielded his right in favor of the bishop of Marseilles.

3. It is evident that the bishop of Aix, and consequently the whole of Narbonne II, was once subject to the bishop of Arles from the fact that the latter retained for a very long time the right to summon him to himself either for a synodal council or for the purpose of ordination. From this it may be concluded [Col. 0510B] that the bishop of that see became a fully established metropolitan only at a very late date.

This is clear from the sequence of the petition presented to Pope Symmachus in the year of our Lord 514 and from that pope’s rescript to Caesarius of Arles. For, apart from the fact that the petition asserts that this authority still belonged to the bishop of Arles at that time, that it had been established by the authority of the ancients through many generations, and that the venerable Roman See had once commanded by an enduring sanction that it remain undisturbed, Symmachus himself writes in his letter that it was founded upon the venerable statutes of the Fathers and strengthened by antiquity.

“Therefore,” he says, “it is reasonable that the holy Church of Arles should enjoy its own privileges, and that what antiquity has granted and the authority of the Fathers has strengthened should not be violated by a new presumption . . . . Therefore, throughout the individual Churches, let the benefits that have long been preserved remain in force. Even if the bishop of the Church of Aix, or any other person summoned according to the definition of the canons to the metropolitan bishop, should refuse to obey, let him know that he will be subjected—which we do not wish—to ecclesiastical discipline.”

From where, then, did so singular a privilege and so ancient a prerogative flow to the Church of Arles, that its bishop could summon to himself the metropolitan of another province? Was it from the small number of fellow-provincial bishops in the province of Vienne, which supposedly compelled its metropolitan to seek the assistance and support of neighboring bishops? Certainly not. Vienne was the largest and most populous of the five provinces; all the others contained fewer cities. Yet the metropolitans of those provinces did not claim the same right over other metropolitans.

Did the bishop of Arles possess this right through the vicariate of the Roman pontiff, which some wish to have been entrusted to him? Even if we grant that he had been invested with such a vicariate, Aix would not have been subject to him alone on that account; rather, all the metropolitan bishops of those provinces would have been subject to him.

This custom therefore derived from no other source than the fact that, in ancient times, the metropolitan rights over the cities of Narbonne II belonged to the bishop of Arles [Col. 0510D]. Although he later renounced those rights on the occasion of the new division, he did not consent to be stripped of them except while retaining for himself the power of summoning the bishop of that province. This power would thus remain a lasting memorial of the ancient right and of the privilege once granted.
