Hence the bishop of Aix acquired all metropolitan rights only at a very late date, so that some uncertainty concerning the matter remained until the time of the Council of Frankfurt, by which the Apostolic See was granted the power to exempt that see. His status also appears still to have been uncertain at the time of Charlemagne’s death, since the city of Aix is not listed among the metropolises in his will.

4. A distinguished argument and example of this assumed authority remains for us in the Council of Riez, assembled in the year 439 in the province of Narbonne II, within which the city of Riez was situated. When Armentarius had been ordained contrary to the canons, a synod was assembled at Riez so that, after he had been expelled, another might be chosen in his place.

The principal element of metropolitan jurisdiction is the convocation and summoning of a provincial synod, something that no one has ever dared to attempt outside his own province. Nevertheless, Hilary of Arles performed this very act, with the support of numerous bishops of Gaul, thirteen of whom signed after him [Col. 0511A], with no one objecting and with the approval of the Apostolic See, which could not have been unaware of so celebrated a case—and not even with the objection of Armentarius himself, whose interest it especially was to invalidate and reject the synod as having been held contrary to the canons.

There is therefore no lawful basis for doubting that this assembly was both legitimate and provincial. For the order prescribed by the canonical statutes was that a bishop who had acted contrary to the canons should be judged by his fellow-provincial bishops, not by bishops of another province.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Right of the Bishop of Arles over the Province of the Maritime Alps

Having examined the rights of the bishop of Arles over both provinces of Narbonne, we now come to the Maritime Alps [Note: [Col. 0511D] See the observations, part II, chapter 6, number 10.], which he once claimed under the same metropolitan right [Col. 0511B].

That the holy Hilary of Arles acted as metropolitan of this province is demonstrated by this same example of the Council of Riez in the year 439, which he summoned in the case of Armentarius of Embrun, ordained contrary to the canons. When the clergy and citizens of Embrun—whose city had become a civil metropolis after the division of Narbonne I—desired that the see of their Church should likewise be adorned with the same rank in ecclesiastical matters, they attempted, after their bishop had died, to substitute another in his place without consulting the bishop of Arles. Yet I believe that by this attempt the privilege of the bishop of Arles was not diminished but made still more evident.

First, it is manifest from this that the bishops of Embrun had never previously attempted anything of the kind, or at least had never peacefully enjoyed such a right, since not a word of this appears or is brought forward against Hilary.

2. How unanimous the Gallican Church’s support was for the bishop of Arles is evident from the ordination of Armentarius itself. For not even three bishops could be found to complete the canonical number, and Armentarius could scarcely enlist two who would conspire in that ordination. Those men must have been either entirely ignorant of ecclesiastical sanctions or contemptuous of them, since they undertook so unfortunate a consecration against the manifest statutes of the Council of Nicaea and of other councils.

In fact, canon 1 determines that they should nevertheless be treated with some leniency, because those who had fallen into such perversity had, from the very day of their fall, sought forgiveness everywhere, repented of their fault, and attributed it either to ignorance or to deception.

3. The defects of Armentarius’s ordination [Col. 0511D] were noted not only because it had taken place without the presence of three bishops and without letters from the fellow-provincial bishops, but also because he had been consecrated without the metropolitan’s authority and with his will disregarded.

Everyone agrees that the metropolitan bishop whose neglected presence or consent rendered the ordination invalid was none other than the bishop of Arles. But did Hilary claim that this right belonged to him as the ordinary metropolitan of that province, or as the first metropolitan of the Gauls?

Stephanus Baluzius thinks the latter, in chapter 31 of Book V of *The Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, which he supplemented. He believes that Hilary, following the letters of Pope Zosimus and imitating the vicariate of Thessalonica, assumed for himself the dignity of first metropolitan and wished serious cases arising throughout the provinces to be referred to him. Since the case of Armentarius was rightly counted among such cases, Baluzius holds that Hilary for this reason summoned the Council of Riez.

I do not deny that the word may sometimes have various meanings, so that at times those great primates, the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, were also called metropolitans by our own Leo. Yet nowhere do we read that, in the period under discussion, this term designated the new kind of metropolitan that Baluzius introduces and adorns with the prerogative of primacy after the model of the vicariate of Thessalonica. I do not think the Fathers of the Council of Riez had even dreamed of such an arrangement.

Furthermore, since both the preface of the council and its second canon enumerate three conditions without which, they say, nothing at all exists that makes a bishop, namely, the presence of three bishops, letters from the fellow-provincial bishops, and the will of the metropolitan, it is certain that the term “metropolitan” is being used in the same sense throughout the canon: for the proper and particular metropolitan of each province. The omission of his consent is there said to render the election invalid.

Those canons are none other than the Nicene canons, whose fourth canon expressly includes the same three conditions:

“Three bishops shall in every case meet for this purpose, provided that those who are absent give their consent and approve the ordination by letter. Confirmation of what is done in each province shall be entrusted to the metropolitan.”

By the agreement of all the Churches and synods that dealt with this matter, this has always been understood to mean the ordinary metropolitan of each province.

Moreover, if this council had been intended to refer to some first metropolitan, its definition would have been extremely ambiguous and would have provided material for new disputes every day, since some would have interpreted it as referring to the first metropolitan of the Gauls and others to the metropolitan proper to the province.

Finally, no one attributed this meaning to the canon of Riez before Baluzius [Col. 0512B]—and even he departs from the intention of his own source. The most illustrious Petrus de Marca understood the word according to its common meaning in his *Dissertation on Primates*, number 73, adding, however, that Hilary’s action could not be made into a precedent, since Leo rebuked him for transferring to himself the dignity belonging to metropolitan bishops.

[Col. 0512C] Hilary’s claim to authority over that province is further suggested to us by the First Council of Orange, at which Ingenuus, bishop of Embrun, who had been substituted in place of the deposed Armentarius, signed among the fellow-provincial bishops.

If he had been the metropolitan of a distinct province, as Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, was, his signature would be found in the same form as Eucherius’s, to signify metropolitan authority:

“I, Eucherius the bishop,” he says, “have signed, awaiting the consent of my holy fellow-provincial priests concerning these matters.”

Eucherius happened to be in those regions at the time when the bishops of the province were assembling in synod. Invited to attend as a mark of honor, he did not dare to sign among the bishops of another province except with the expectation that the fellow-provincial bishops would give their consent to the matters decreed at the synod.

Nor can anyone say that this was not a provincial synod convoked under metropolitan jurisdiction, but one summoned by an authority greater than that which Hilary assumed over those provinces, whether by right of the vicariate of the Roman pontiff, as some maintain, or as the first metropolitan of the Gauls, as others have devised.

For canon 29 makes clear that this was the kind of synod which the statutes of the Fathers had ordered to be celebrated twice each year—namely, the fifth of the Nicene canons, which mentions no synods other than provincial ones:

“Each year, in every province, let synods be held twice,” and so forth.

Moreover, the Council of Orange belonged to the class of synods which the bishops there determine ought not to be dissolved without notice of another assembly; and they in fact announced that a similar synod was to be convened in the following year. This applies only to provincial synods, not to general councils or to those assembled from several provinces [Col. 0513A]. Such councils were accustomed to be summoned not annually and at fixed times, but more rarely and as the circumstances of the times and affairs required.

We derive a third proof from Pope Hilary’s letter to the bishops Leontius, Veranus, and Victurus, where he says that Ingenuus of Embrun had formerly been censured by the Apostolic See for the unlawful cession of the episcopal office of his province. From this it is clear that Hilary of Arles, with the consent even of the bishop of Embrun, held the province of the Maritime Alps subject to his metropolitan jurisdiction. This is precisely the matter about which Saint Leo protests so vehemently in his letter to the bishops of Vienne:

“Let each person,” he says, “be content with his own limits and boundaries, 870 and let him recognize that he is not permitted to transfer to another the privilege due to himself. But if anyone, neglecting the apostolic decrees and showing greater favor to a person, wishes to become the deserter of his own dignity, believing that he may transfer his privilege to another, then not the one to whom he has yielded it, but the one who within the province precedes the others by the antiquity of his episcopate, shall claim for himself the power of ordaining priests.”

But when Hilary says in the same letter that Ingenuus had always been supported by the honor of metropolitan of the province of the Maritime Alps, he says this at the suggestion of Ingenuus himself, after the appearance of those provinces had changed. Once the rights of metropolitan power, assumed from the new division and formerly neglected, began to be pursued and claimed by him, he spoke as though Hilary had obtained authority over that province solely through Ingenuus’s voluntary cession. Moreover, he does not say that the Church or city of Embrun, but that Ingenuus, bishop of Embrun, had always possessed this authority: these are separated from one another by a considerable distance, and this could prove rather that the recent privilege was first claimed by him than that this metropolitan see was ancient. I add that only the honor is mentioned, not power and jurisdiction. For there were some metropolitans who enjoyed almost nothing more than the title of honor and were nevertheless subject to another metropolitan, either with respect to the synodal assembly or with respect to ordination. Such was Aix at that time within Gaul, as we said in the preceding chapter. Such also among the Easterners was the patriarch of Jerusalem, who received a certain honorary privilege of this kind from the Council of Nicaea, as you will find explained in the most learned dissertation of the illustrious Peter de Marca, *On the Establishment of the Patriarchate of Constantinople*. Finally, in matters of fact, it is not enough merely to assert a matter unless the assertion itself is supported by suitable proofs, especially when, as here, the contrary is demonstrated both by long possession and by arguments that cannot be disregarded.

**4.** Since from the foregoing, and especially from the Council of Riez, it is clear that the Gallic bishops held so constant an opinion that the province of the Maritime Alps was subject by metropolitan right to the bishop of Arles, it is not plausible that Hilary was the first to subject that province to himself. Rather, his predecessor Honoratus and Honoratus’s predecessor Patroclus had likewise possessed it. For who would not have risen up against Hilary if he had attempted to subject to his jurisdiction a province that none of his predecessors had possessed, when our Leo treated him so harshly as an invader of another’s jurisdiction on account of both Narbonnese provinces, although he freely admitted that these had been administered before him by both Honoratus and Patroclus? Who, moreover, would persuade himself that the addition of this province to the others subject to Arles was due to the industry of Honoratus, when Honoratus governed that see for scarcely, or not even, two years? As for Patroclus, since that man, who was exceedingly eager for his own advancement, contended with no one over that province, which his successors claimed for themselves, this is evidence that he administered it without anyone’s opposition—unless it was considered part of the ecclesiastical province of Vienne. In that case Simplicius of Vienne was seeking it in a single stroke, and Patroclus defended it with the same industry with which he retained for himself the metropolitan primacy of the province of Vienne.

And indeed those provinces seem even in the fourth century to have been included under the name of Vienne. For in the subscriptions of the First Council of Arles, if they are genuine, no other province besides Vienne is named, although certain delegates from Nicaea, which belonged to the Maritime Alps, and from Apt, which belonged to the Second Narbonnese, attended the council. Since the province to which those places belonged is not recorded, they seem to have belonged to the province mentioned above. For why would the name of the province of Vienne alone be read there unless it embraced all those provinces that later acquired another name when the province was divided into parts—or at least included the Maritime Alps, whose metropolitan was for so long subject to the authority of the bishop of Arles, as metropolitan of the province of Vienne, and the Second Narbonnese, which was severed from Vienne?

We offer another conjecture drawn from the Council of Aquileia. For from the synodal letter written by the Fathers to the bishops of the province of Vienne and of the First and Second Narbonnese after the council had been completed, it appears that no Gallic delegates attended it from any other provinces than these three. Yet Theodorus of Octodurum and Amantius of Nicaea are recorded in it as having expressed their judgment. The latter was from the Maritime Alps, the former from the Graian Alps. You may therefore reasonably assert that the two Alpine provinces were included under the name of the province of Vienne, at least in the ecclesiastical understanding of that time.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Province of the Graian Alps. What Jurisdiction the Bishop of Arles Exercised over It

[Note: At Col. 0513D, see *Observations*, part II, ch. 6, no. 11.]

Although the memory of the province of the Graian and Pennine Alps is quite obscure in ecclesiastical records before the time of Pope Hilary, it is nevertheless clear that the bishop of Arles possessed considerable jurisdiction over it, even in Leo’s time. For since, according to the catalogue of Gaul published by Sirmond, it consisted of only two cities, the first and principal of them—Tarentaise, namely—was assigned to the bishop of Vienne as a part of the undivided province of Vienne in that division by which our Leo distributed the province between the bishops of Vienne and Arles for the sake of peace. From this it may be inferred that the province had once been part of Vienne, at least ecclesiastically.

**1.** First, the fact that Leo, so vigorous an assertor of metropolitan rights, assigns Tarentaise to the bishop of Vienne as a part of the province of Vienne is a decisive argument that it was not part of another province. From such a province—and one so small—he would never have detached the larger city, leaving only the single and modest city of Octodurum, which would then have been subject to Tarentaise with respect to ordination. Even if he wished to favor Vienne, he would never have attempted this to the injury of a third metropolitan, especially since he could have detached one of the cities that he was leaving under the authority of the bishop of Arles and given it to Vienne in place of Tarentaise.

**2.** That province seems to have possessed no metropolitan jurisdiction either ecclesiastically or civilly; rather, it possessed only the status of a city. This is evident from Sirmond’s catalogue of Gaul, which assigns no metropolitan see to this province, although it assigns one to all the others. Yet the custom of that age did not permit a province that had no metropolitan in the civil order to have one in the ecclesiastical order.

**3.** There is no trace in the ancient writers from which one could even suspect that the bishop of Tarentaise had ever discharged metropolitan functions or claimed any such jurisdiction at that time before the period of Pope Hilary. From that period there remains a single letter in which the bishops of the Pennine Alps are distinguished from the bishops of other provinces. I fear, however, that there is an error in the title of the letter, so that in place of “the Pennine Alps” one should read “the Alpine province” or “the Maritime Alps.” There is more than one reason for this correction.

First, when the same Pope Hilary wrote another letter to the bishops of those same provinces to whom he had written the first—namely, the provinces of Vienne, Lyons, the First and Second Narbonnese, and the Alpine province—the sole difference between the two letters is that in the first he mentions the Pennine Alpine province, while in the second he simply mentions the Alpine province. Hence Hilary appears to have recognized a single Alpine province distinct from the others. It is much more reasonable to suppose that this was the Maritime Alps, which consisted of eight cities, than the Pennine Alps, which consisted of only two.

Next, who would believe that Hilary, when writing to almost all the provinces of Gaul, omitted the very extensive province of the Maritime Alps and mentioned only a small province that was not even provided with a metropolitan see? Finally, when the same pontiff wrote about the same case of Mamertus, which he mentions in the later letter, to twenty bishops by name, he lists Ingenuus among them, and Ingenuus was metropolitan of the Maritime Alps. It is therefore clear that the Alpine province mentioned by Hilary in the title of the later letter must be understood more probably as the Maritime than as the Pennine Alps; and from this the title of the first letter should likewise be corrected, where the Pennine Alps are mentioned.

**4.** When Petronius, prefect of the Gauls under Honorius, organized the body of the seven provinces and established that their council should assemble annually at Arles, there can scarcely be any doubt that he included the Graian and Pennine Alps among them. For if, in order to enlarge this body, he was compelled to attach the two Aquitanias and Novempopulania to parts of the ancient Narbonnese province, would he have diminished it by removing the Pennine and Graian Alps? This is certainly not plausible. It is more reasonable to believe that the Alps were attached to Vienne as part of that same body of the seven provinces.

And certainly our Leo would never have counted Tarentaise indiscriminately among the other cities of the province of Vienne and assigned the ordination of its bishop to Vienne if it had belonged neither to the province of Vienne nor to any part of that body of seven provinces, since it cannot be proved by any example from antiquity that such a thing was ever done. As for the fact that this province is so often counted separately from the others in the frequently cited catalogue of Gaul, I think that this occurred either through an error or, more probably, because of the change introduced into those provinces by the incursion of the Visigoths, who occupied part of them around the later period that we assigned above to the date of this catalogue. Accordingly, even from this difference it is proved that this catalogue is later both than the Emperor Honorius and than Pope Leo I. Moreover, the illustrious Peter de Marca was not correct in deleting the province of the Graian Alps from the body of those provinces (*Dissertation on Primacies*, § 67), since it is clear from Leo that it was counted with Vienne when he assigned Tarentaise to the bishop of Vienne.

**5.** When Ravennius was ordained bishop of Arles in place of the deceased Saint Hilary, the ordainers informed Leo of his ordination by letter. In his reply Leo counted twelve ordainers; hence there is no doubt that the same number of twelve took part in that ordination. Since that ordination belonged solely to the province of Vienne, you would search for that number in vain within the province unless the bishop of Tarentaise were counted among them. For, excluding the bishops of Vienne and Arles, only eleven remain in that province according to Sirmond’s catalogue if the bishop of Tarentaise is not included.

That the bishop of Vienne did not attend this ordination is beyond doubt: first, because he would never have yielded to another the honor of consecration, although it appears probable from his inscription—which occupies the first place in Saint Leo’s reply—that this honor had been offered to Bishop Constantine as the senior bishop of the province; and second, because when all the ordainers signed the petition of the Gallic bishops presented to Pope Leo on behalf of the bishop of Arles, with the sole exceptions of Auspicius of Vaison, who had died, and four others who survived—Nicetas, Florus, Chrysaphius, and Rusticus—the bishop of Vienne certainly cannot be numbered among the subscribers. Otherwise he would have been a traitor to the rights of his own Church. None of the four just named was bishop of Vienne; had the bishop of Vienne been present, he would have wished to be listed first of all, whereas Rusticus appears only in third place, Nicetas in fifth, Florus in seventh, and Chrysaphius in twelfth.

Now, if the bishop of Tarentaise took part in Ravennius’s ordination, this is evidence that Tarentaise belonged to the province of Vienne, since ecclesiastical custom did not permit bishops from a foreign province to attend as witnesses of an ordination in the synodal assembly held for that purpose. This was not even allowed to the bishop of Embrun within the province over which the bishop of Arles presided, although Embrun belonged to the same synod.

**6.** Finally, the jurisdiction of the bishop of Arles over this province shines forth remarkably from the life of Saint James, the first bishop of Tarentaise. Bollandus inserted this life, drawn from an old manuscript through the work of the Jesuit Peter Francis Chifflet, in volume II of the *Acts of the Saints* under 16 January.

For from that life, if it is genuine and was written, as it appears, by an ancient author, it is evident that James first entrusted himself to Honoratus, abbot of the monastery of Lérins, for instruction in the monastic life. Then, after Honoratus had been raised to the see of Arles, James was sent to the town of Centron and the valley of Tarentaise to convert to the faith of Christ the people living there under pagan practices . . .

“Accordingly,” the author adds, “Honoratus summoned the other bishops, ordained James bishop, and sent him to the aforesaid town and valley of Tarentaise to preach the word of the Lord.” Having undertaken this office, James brought the whole people to the faith of Christ, built a basilica, established sacred ministers, and organized the hierarchy. He also obtained from the duke of the Burgundians, who at that time occupied those regions, the surrounding fields and attached them to the Church of Tarentaise.

The illustrious Andreas Saussaius, now bishop of Toul, writes very similar things in the supplement to his *Gallican Martyrology*. From this it is clear that the Church of Tarentaise, which was the principal church of that province, owed its beginnings to the bishop of Arles, who had both given it the faith through the mouth of his disciple and consecrated its first bishop. He therefore rightly claimed it for himself by right, and consequently claimed the other churches of the same province as well.

As for Octodurum, which in the catalogue enjoys the right of a city, there might be some difficulty, since it is mentioned in the Council of Aquileia long before the episcopate of Honoratus, and nowhere is it said to have been subject to Vienne, Arles, or any other metropolitan of Gaul. But this catalogue need no longer cause us anxiety, since we have shown above that it must be assigned to a later period.

As for the Council of Aquileia, setting aside Peter Chifflet’s conjectures about the fabrication of its acts—conjectures to which I regret having given some credence in my first edition—I reply that the council favors my view more than it harms it. For since the acts mention the bishop of Octodurum, yet do not mention any other Gallic provinces that sent delegates to the council besides Vienne and the First and Second Narbonnese, Octodurum must have belonged to one of those two provinces. I am therefore free to assert that it was then counted among the rights of Vienne.

## PART THREE

Once both parts of the dissertation that we have placed before this had been completed, there was scarcely any need to add a third. For whoever has once accepted the conviction that Hilary attempted nothing in the entire affair of Celidonius and Projectus beyond the legitimate rights of his see will easily dissolve the remaining charges of the accusation.

If Celidonius exercised the episcopal office in no province other than Vienne, which we have proved to have been subject to Hilary by metropolitan right, Hilary summoned him to his tribunal and deposed him after conviction not by another’s authority but by his own. There was no place for an appeal, since nothing had been done in this affair except in accordance with the sequence prescribed by the canons, as we asserted in the first part of the dissertation.

Likewise, if all those provinces that had formerly been parts of the ancient Narbonnese continued even after the division to recognize the metropolitan of Arles, there is no reason why Projectus’s ordination [Read: “the ordination of the bishop,” in place of “of Projectus”], attempted in one of those provinces, should be charged against Hilary on the ground that he had exceeded his proper boundaries. But whether certain circumstances intervened in either affair that made him guilty of rashness, pride, or some other crime—this is what we must examine in this third part, as we review the remaining charges in Saint Leo’s letter, one by one and without prejudice.

## CHAPTER I. Whether, and in What Sense, Hilary of Arles Claimed or Could Have Claimed for Himself the Ordinations of All the Churches throughout Gaul

This is the chief and summary of all the accusations that Hilary’s adversaries constructed against him: namely, that he exceeded his authority in an attempt to disturb the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the priests by new acts of presumption, desiring so to subject the bishops of the province of Vienne to his authority that he would not allow himself to be subject to the blessed Apostle Peter; that he claimed for himself the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul and transferred to his own dignity what was due to metropolitan bishops.

[Note: Quesnellus inserted the words “the bishops of the province of Vienne” from his own interpretation, because he believed that Hilary’s judgment concerning Celidonius, to which Leo refers, belonged to the province of Vienne subject to the bishop of Arles. We have shown this opinion to be false. You will find a refutation of this chapter in *Observations*, part III, chapter 1.]

To answer these points one by one, I reply that it is sufficiently clear from what we said above that Hilary did not disturb the condition of the Churches at all. On the contrary, this was the one thing he repeatedly asked Leo to do: to regulate the condition of the Churches according to the customary practice. Nor did he exalt himself through new presumptions; rather, he adhered to the ancient privileges of his Church. As we have proved, he had received these privileges successively from his predecessors, and if he had voluntarily abandoned them, he would have incurred the charge of treachery.

So far was the bishop of Arles from disturbing the harmony of the priests that almost all the bishops of Gaul united and conspired together to defend his rights. This is evident from the fact that, with their approval, he continued to exercise the same authority throughout his life, even though Leo opposed and the Emperor threatened him.

[Note: We shall prove in the same place, chapter 2, that Hilary did not usurp metropolitan jurisdiction after Leo’s decree, nor did the Gallic bishops conspire against that decree or take any action against it.] After his death, they unanimously consecrated Ravennius in his place, as Leo himself says, and the greater part of the Gallic bishops approached Leo by a petition, with one accord, so as to compel him amicably to revoke that harsh decree promulgated against the bishop of Arles.

He desired to subject the bishops of the province of Vienne to his authority only insofar as the sacred canons required provincial bishops to obey metropolitans, to depend upon their word and command, and to venerate them as the source of their dignity and consecration. Yet he did not assume the ordination of the province as his right in such a way as to deny the submission due to the See of Peter. Rather, as a member to its head and as a metropolitan to the primate, he freely rendered that submission.

But what Magnus Gregory later asserted from apostolic tradition was not unknown to Hilary, who stood closer to the source of that tradition: namely, that the prerogative of primates over lesser bishops is inactive and ineffectual when nothing is being demanded from the latter except what is in accordance with the canons. “If some fault,” he says (*Book VII, Letter 65, indiction 21), “is found in bishops, I do not know what bishop is not subject to him; but when fault does not require it, we are all equal according to the rule of humility.”

We have already said and fully proved in the preceding part of this dissertation that Hilary did nothing against the canons. Indeed, Hilary’s actions were undertaken only for the protection of the canons: either against Celidonius, by a decree issued in synod, or at Rome, before the pontiff. Therefore, when he firmly opposed Leo’s desire to rescind a sentence full of equity, this was not evidence of obstinacy in him, but of an unconquered spirit and the most steadfast adherence to discipline.

As for the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul that Hilary is said to have claimed for himself, it is useful to make several observations. Once these have been considered, whatever ambition seems to emerge from those words will easily disappear. Almost every expression here requires interpretation, or must be brought back from a more general to a narrower meaning.

Everyone has been mistaken—unless I myself am mistaken—who has thought that the word “ordinations” here means the consecration of priests or bishops, as though Saint Leo had accused Hilary of arrogating to himself the consecration of all the bishops throughout those parts of Gaul of which he speaks, setting the metropolitans aside. To me it is entirely certain that this is far from Leo’s intention. Rather, “ordination” here is used for the administration or oversight that belongs to a metropolitan, ordinary, or primate over a province or some district of provinces.

This is first clear from the fact that Saint Leo did not say “the ordinations of priests,” but “the ordinations of Churches,” between which no one can fail to see a great distinction. To ordain bishops or priests expresses the single function of consecration; but to ordain Churches denotes any other act or exercise of jurisdiction over Churches.

**2.** When Leo wrote these words, the affair of Celidonius was before his eyes, the matter over which there had been contention between the pontiff and Hilary. Yet on that occasion no one had been consecrated by Hilary; rather, Celidonius had been deposed in a synod assembled at Hilary’s command. This is included under the designation “the ordinations of Churches.”

Finally, it is entirely familiar for writers of that age to use the word “ordination” in this sense. Anyone who reads them will encounter many such examples throughout, as in Leo himself, in his sermon on the Apostles: “While the Apostle Paul was occupied with the ordinations of other Churches.” But in this very case, and in the very letter under discussion, Leo distinguishes and employs two meanings of the word.

When he deals with the affair of Projectus in chapters 4 and 5, and later speaks of the consecration of bishops, he uses the precise expression “the ordination of priests.” But when he discusses the general administration of provinces, he calls it “the ordination of provinces.” Thus, in my judgment, the words of chapter 3 must be understood:

“Let each metropolitan, as we have already said, defend the ordination of his own province, together with those who by the antiquity of their priesthood precede the others, now that the right has been restored to them by us.”

Although we do not deny that “the ordination of a province” or “of provinces” is sometimes used by ecclesiastical writers for the consecration of the priests of a province, it does not seem to me to be used in that sense here. Rather, it means administration. For when bishops were consecrated, not only those who preceded the others in the antiquity of their priesthood used to meet with the metropolitan; the entire province gathered and acted together. But for the administration of a province and the consideration of its affairs—which often arose within each province—it was not necessary that all the bishops of the province should repeatedly be ordered to meet in synod. It was enough for those matters to be handled by the metropolitan with the advice of several senior fellow priests, in accordance with Leo’s present ruling.

Moreover, in the same passage Leo speaks generally of not invading another’s jurisdiction and commands that each person remain within his own boundaries. He thereby indicates that he is speaking also of the general ordination, or administration, of provinces.

Likewise, in the final chapter of the same letter he says:

“For we are not defending for ourselves the ordinations of your provinces—a claim that Hilary may perhaps, in his customary manner, falsely make in order to corrupt the minds of your Holiness—but we claim them for you through our solicitude.”

Here too, I think, “ordination” means administration. For who at that time would ever have dreamed that the Roman bishop was considering the ordination or consecration of the bishops of the Gallic provinces? But it would not have been the act of a dreamer to suspect that he wished to take upon himself the care of those provinces, convene their synodal assemblies, arrange their trials, and draw to himself other matters of this kind that until then had belonged to the bishop of Arles.

Leo nevertheless removes this suspicion far from himself. He asks that this care be entrusted to Leontius, bishop of Fréjus, “for the sake of honoring antiquity,” as he says; that is, the very care that he had previously said he did not wish to defend for himself.

[Note: Leontius, whom Leo mentions, is different from the bishop of Fréjus. The latter had already died around the year 432, as Tillemont proves in volume XV, note 3, on the Life of Saint Maximus of Riez, and Pagius under the year 433, no. 20.]

Nor does he grant Leontius the power to consecrate bishops. On the contrary, he expressly forbids it by immediately adding this exception: “With the dignity of the metropolitans’ privilege preserved.” In several places of the letter Leo himself also asserts that the right of consecration belongs to the metropolitans.

Valentinian Augustus himself, when in his constitution he sharply rebuked Hilary at Leo’s prompting, said that “a definite sentence had been issued against him for the things he had wrongly ordered.” Here he is not speaking specifically of consecration, but generally of everything that he considered to have been wrongly done by Hilary in the Churches.

Finally, not to be too lengthy, Hilary himself, according to the author of his Life, addressed Leo in these words, asking him to “ORDER the condition of the Churches according to customary practice.”

However we interpret the word “ordination,” Hilary’s defense requires us to restore the following words to their genuine sense. For if they were understood of all the Gallic provinces wherever they extended, Hilary would plainly have to be judged guilty of intolerable audacity.

First, it is certain that the Gallic provinces at that time were not subject to the rule of a single prince. Some obeyed the Roman emperor, some the Goths, and some the dukes or kings of the Franks. Hilary could therefore in no way have claimed for himself the ordination of all the Churches throughout the whole of Gaul. Princes never tolerated the bishop of a foreign people or dominion administering Churches situated in their kingdom, removing bishops from them, or assembling synods.

We have an example in the First Council of Orange. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, happened by chance to be present there with our Hilary, who presided over the council and was very close to him. Yet Eucherius did not dare to subscribe absolutely to the acts of the synod, but only on condition that he obtain the consent of his fellow provincials.

“I, Eucherius, bishop,” he says, “have subscribed, while awaiting the assent of my holy fellow priests of my province concerning these matters.”

From this synod, which preceded Celidonius’s deposition by only three years, it is evident that Hilary claimed no jurisdiction over the bishops of Lyons, and consequently over the more distant provinces of Gaul. He did not compel Eucherius to subscribe absolutely because he knew that Eucherius did not belong to his synod.

[Note: Since Celidonius was a bishop of Besançon and subject to the metropolitan of Lyons, as we shall show in the observations on this dissertation, when Hilary deposed him he exercised judgment in the province of the metropolitan of Lyons. For this reason Leo asserted that Hilary had claimed for himself the ordinations, or administration, of all the Churches throughout Gaul. It is therefore entirely false that the name “Gaul” here should be understood as meaning the whole of Narbonnese Gaul. Quesnellus himself indicates the weakness of the remaining points he advances near the end of the chapter.]

It is therefore not permissible to understand “the other Gauls” here except as those that formerly constituted the undivided Narbonnese province. This was first called the province of Gaul and later simply “the Province.” Since it was distinguished from the other provinces in civil administration, it necessarily followed that it was likewise separate in ecclesiastical administration.

I suspect that this distinction between the two groups was also sometimes expressed in the following way: those provinces that had formerly formed the Narbonnese province were called simply Gaul or the province of Gaul, while the others were called the Gallic provinces.

For at the Council of Paris in the year 362, the bishops who formed the synod are everywhere called Gallic bishops, and Saturninus is said to have been excommunicated by all the Gallic bishops. The synod seems to have been assembled so that the evil actions committed by Saturninus, the Arian bishop of Arles, at the councils of Arles and Béziers could be rescinded.

But because there was a danger that Saturninus might either convene a new synod against the Council of Paris or at least use his authority to urge those bishops whom he had previously armed in defense of his error to trample the decree of Paris again, the synod decreed that anyone who thought it necessary to resist what it had established “WITHIN GAUL” should be excluded from communion and deprived of his priestly see. By “Gaul,” in my opinion, it meant those regions in which Saturninus was present and possessed authority, and whose bishops had become suspect because of their previous actions.

Likewise, in the First Council of Vaison in the year 442:

“It was resolved,” says canon 1, “after deliberation, that bishops coming FROM THE GALLIC PROVINCES should not be investigated WITHIN GAUL; it should be enough that no one has forbidden any of them communion. For among those living nearby and almost known to one another, the upright do not need so much testimony as the corrupt need exposure and denunciation.”

Here a distinction seems plainly to be made between Gaul—or the five or seven provinces whose bishops were present at the synod—and the Gallic provinces, whose bishops were being considered for investigation.

That Leo himself understood “Gaul” in the same sense, as referring to the parts of the undivided Narbonnese province, appears from Letter 38 to Ravennius, bishop of Arles. “We have learned,” he says, “that a certain wandering Petronianus . . . boasted THROUGHOUT GAUL that he was our deacon, and under the pretext of this honor went around the various Churches of that province.”

Likewise, he addresses the letter to the bishops of the synod of the five or seven provinces, which formed a body distinct from the others, in this way: “Leo to Ravennius, Rusticus, and the other bishops established THROUGHOUT GAUL.”

These are the conjectures that we submit for examination by more learned men. We do not rely on them so heavily that we wish our opinion to depend upon them—namely, that Hilary did not wish to subject all the provinces of Gaul to himself, but only those that had become, through the division of the undivided Narbonnese province, separate provinces with respect to civil administration. How legitimately the bishop of Arles claimed these for himself has been sufficiently and abundantly stated above.

## CHAPTER II. Whether in This Conduct, Which the Pontiff Rebuked in Hilary, There Appeared Anything of Pride, Presumption, or Arrogance

[Col. 0521A]

Our Leo is entirely occupied with attacking the pride of the bishop of Arles, and scarcely a line can be found in this whole letter, extensive as it is, that does not breathe this accusation in sharper and very frequent language.

He repeatedly denounces him as a man subject to no law, who believes himself bound by none of the rules of the Lord’s institution; as one who, with excessively impious presumption, wishes to violate the most sacred firmness of the Rock constructed by God’s building; as one who attempts to weaken its power by indulging his desires, presuming upon what is unlawful, and diminishing the reverence due to the most blessed Peter through his overbearing words.

It has been shown at length that Hilary arrogated nothing to himself beyond the rights of his own Church. But whether he defended the privileges of his see—or rather the authority of the entire episcopal order—in such a way as to violate the reverence due to the Apostolic See is not entirely clear. Saint Leo does indeed assert this, but Leo, as the most learned Baronius writes, was easily deceived in matters belonging to contentious litigation, was ensnared by Celidonius’s schemes, and, because of the accusations of his adversaries, lent his ears too readily…

Who, moreover, would say that the testimony of an accuser is sufficient to convict the accused, especially in his own case, in which everyone ought to be suspect to himself? Certainly, when I read in this letter of Leo:

> “After Hilary had no reasonable answer to give before the council of holy bishops, they turned to those hidden matters of his heart which no layman could utter and no priest could hear”—

when, I say, I read this, I am reminded of the statement of Auxiliaris the prefect, which Honoratus of Marseilles reports from a letter written by him to Hilary himself concerning this matter:

> “Men impatiently endure it if we speak as we know ourselves to be. Moreover, the ears of the Romans are drawn on by a certain tenderness.”

For my part, I believe that this prefect, a friend of Leo and Hilary, ought to be heard more readily than either Hilary himself or Leo—although the minds of both, whether through rivalry over their own privileges or through love of victory, may have been clouded somewhat. You understand, sincere reader, how far Auxiliaris the prefect—an observer of the entire affair and its proceedings—was from accusing Hilary of obstinacy, since he rather attributes all Leo’s complaints to that affection from which scarcely anyone is free when someone opposes his own opinion and himself somewhat too freely, and to that tenderness of hearing which he declares to be innate in the Romans.

He also reveals his mind much more clearly in the same letter, where he asserts that, as one fully informed about and a witness of the whole dispute, he had found absolutely nothing in Hilary that suggested a haughty or insolent spirit:

> “Since you are steadfast in your purpose and always even-tempered, and are never carried away by the gall of agitation, just as you are not lifted up by any allurements of joy, I do not remember even the least of your actions having been darkened by the contagion of arrogance.”

This was the conviction not only of the prefect Auxiliaris but also of all the bishops of Gaul. They appear to have received from Leo the records of what had been done in the Roman synod, containing everything brought forward by Hilary, as I infer from these words:

> “The order of events, entered into the written records, demonstrates what was done and concluded among us in the case of Bishop Celidonius, and what Hilary said while he was being heard in the presence of the aforesaid bishop.”

Yet although they had all been made participants in everything Hilary had done and said, [Note: That this is asserted gratuitously and falsely will be evident from the same *Observationes*, part III, chapter 2.] they did not therefore abandon him. Setting aside the judgment of the transalpine assembly, they consistently upheld the decision of the Gallican synod pronounced against Celidonius; they continued to show Hilary the same honor; and they did not permit his place to be invaded by Leontius or anyone else—although that was Leo’s wish and advice when he wrote to them.

Even if the support of these bishops and of the prefect Auxiliaris had been lacking in Hilary’s favor, such accusations ought nevertheless not easily to have been admitted, since Hilary had always been especially commended, both before this affair was undertaken and after it was concluded, for his profound humility and his contempt for every form of pride.

Thus, when recounting the Life of his kinsman and predecessor Honoratus, he passed over the nobility of his lineage in silence, lest the praises customarily bestowed upon his family redound upon himself:

> “He himself, in praising his venerable kinsman, preferred to ennoble his lofty lineage by rejecting it, to commend it by passing it over, and to magnify it by disdaining it.”

Nor is it surprising that he maintained a humble disposition, since he had been placed in a dignity to which he had ascended only through humility. For, as the same writer of his Life says:

> “Just as he was highest in the rank of priesthood, so by descending into humility he attained the summit of exalted greatness.”

The same bishop of Marseilles, after demonstrating Hilary’s humility by many examples, continues:

> “It is therefore evident that he acquired the heights of humility by his own self-contempt, and in like measure merited the lofty summit of the virtues. He was stern toward the proud; he was terrible to those swollen with the wickedness of the world and to those swollen with the vanity of hospitality (*xenodochiae*, as printed). But before the holy congregation and perfected men he most readily prostrated not only his heart and mind but also his body.”

He practiced this no less frequently at Rome than in Gaul. As soon as he entered the City, after completing his visits to the apostles and martyrs, he immediately presented himself to the blessed Pope Leo, rendering reverent service and humbly requesting that he regulate the condition of the Churches in the customary manner.

Finally, so that we may not perhaps be satisfied with the testimony of only one writer of a Life, whom some might suspect, let us produce the support of Auxiliaris, whom the same writer calls an author of Roman eloquence—a brief testimony, indeed, but beyond all exception. He addresses Hilary himself in a letter, a fragment of which is preserved in his Life:

> “Since you hold first place in the other works of modesty and good conduct, forgive me for saying less than I should about you with such care, because virtue always blushes when it praises itself.”

Now, after Hilary returned from Rome to Arles, we learn from Baronius himself, the narrator, how many signs of genuine humility he gave. He says:

> “Certainly he displayed no ordinary example of Christian modesty, although he had been so harassed by both the pontiff and the emperor: ‘For as is Leo’s roar, so too is the king’s anger.’ Nevertheless, he became completely quiet and did not defend his case by publishing counter-apologies, although he possessed both the power of eloquence to do so and the support of the rights claimed by his predecessors.”

[Note: Quesnellus is rather mistaken when he asserts that Hilary wrote apologies after Leo’s decree was sent into Gaul. See Observationes, part III, chapter 2, section 1.]

The cardinal is nevertheless mistaken when he asserts that Hilary afterward became entirely quiet and published no apologies by which he defended his case. Here we dissent from the eminent man, because the author of Hilary’s Life expressly states the contrary:

> “Alone he endured such great things; he was not at all terrified by threats; he instructed those who investigated; he overcame those who disputed; he did not yield to the powerful; and, placed in danger of his life, he in no way consented to be joined in communion with the man whom he had condemned together with such great men.”

After returning to his own Church, he sent frequent legates to Leo and published so many apologies that the same writer of his Life was compelled to omit listing them all. He says:

> “And because I cannot in any way incorporate into this work how much he dictated in this case, I have thought that the opinion of Auxiliaris, then prefect, should be inserted,”

and so forth.

Thus, while we depart from Baronius’s opinion when he denies that such apologies were written, we agree with him in affirming Hilary’s modesty. For it is truly characteristic of an episcopal man both to defend vigorously the rights of his dignity and nevertheless not to depart at all from Christian humility and priestly modesty.

Both the entire course of Hilary’s Life and the writer so frequently praised persuade us that Hilary showed himself to be such a man in this affair:

> “On withdrawing from the city, he turned his whole self, in lowly humility, toward appeasing the mind of Saint Leo, first sending Saint Ravennius, who was then a presbyter and later his own successor; and then Saint Nectarius and Saint Constantius, distinguished priests.”

And because I cannot in any way incorporate into this work how much he dictated in this case, and so forth.

Let us therefore not retain in our minds so unfavorable an opinion of so holy a bishop, an opinion generated both by the calumnies of his opponents and by the letter of Saint Leo, who had become somewhat agitated. Although it is difficult in this disagreement to acquit one of two men distinguished by exceptional holiness without implicating the other, it nevertheless seems less insulting to the spirit of grace if we say that Leo did not at that time have sufficient knowledge of Hilary’s holiness, and that the Roman pontiff did not understand Hilary’s words in the sense in which they were spoken by the bishop of Arles, rather than suppose Hilary guilty of such brazenness, arrogance, and pride when he was so highly commended for singular modesty and voluntary self-abasement.

## CHAPTER III. What is to be made of the statement in the letter that Hilary had no reasonable answer to give before the council of holy bishops? What of the witnesses produced by Celidonius?

The laws removed from everyone the ability to give testimony in his own case, as the emperors Valens, Gratian, and Valentinian formerly decreed when writing to Gracchus, prefect of the City (*Codex Theodosianus*, book II, title 2). This greatly weakens the force of the earlier complaints of Saint Leo and also answers those now before us.

For this was Leo’s chief grievance: Hilary was vigorously resisting his attempt to draw the affairs of Gaul to himself. [Note: See *Observationes*, part III, chapter 3, section 1, concerning the witnesses.] It is therefore not surprising if he found nothing reasonable among the things produced by the bishop of Arles; no one willingly subscribes to the arguments of his opponents, and it is implanted in every litigant by corrupt nature that he believes all the force of law and weight of evidence to serve his own side.

Moreover, if we consult Honoratus of Marseilles, who wrote after Hilary’s death and therefore must be believed to have been free from every form of flattery, Hilary spoke in his own case in such a way that he instructed those who investigated and overcame those who disputed.

Although I think he spoke very sparingly, since he did not gird himself for litigation but always rested upon this principle as upon an immovable stone: that he had come for official duties, not for a lawsuit; and that he was presenting what had been done in the order of a protest, not of an accusation. The canons then received in Gaul and the customary ordering of the Churches did not permit these matters to be reopened and examined in a new trial.

[Note: Which canons received in Gaul did not permit Celidonius’s case to be examined in a new trial at Rome? You will recognize the falsity of this from *Observationes*, part I, chapter 6, section 17. On the custom, see also chapter 5 of the same part. Hence the statement made shortly afterward with such audacity is false: “By Leo’s action the customary form of judicial proceedings was altered, and in this way a new yoke was prepared for the Churches of Gaul.”]

This was the one point Hilary maintained; this our pontiff did not consider reasonable: he thought that the authority and dignity of his see required that whatever judgments were held throughout the Churches of the world should always be recalled anew to Roman examination.

Therefore, the fact that Hilary appeared to abandon his case in the Roman synod, and, as Leo says, had nothing to answer, did not arise from lack of legal grounds, deficiency of evidence, or inability to speak. It arose because Leo’s action altered the customary form of Gallican judicial proceedings and in this way prepared a new yoke for the Churches and priests of Gaul—a yoke which neither they nor their fathers had ever been able to bear.

If Hilary, the summit of the Gallican Churches, had allowed this yoke to be placed upon them, his fellow bishops would have accused him as both a deserter of his own dignity and a betrayer of Gallican liberty. Hilary’s silence, therefore, was prudence, not weakness; reverence, not obstinacy; defense, not abandonment. He pleaded his case more eloquently by remaining silent than he would have done by delivering a speech.

As for the witnesses—whose manifest response, Leo says, had shown that Celidonius had been unjustly deprived of the priesthood—I think there is some doubt whether the reference is to witnesses heard in Gaul by the Gallican synod, or to witnesses whom the deposed bishop summoned from the province to Rome and produced before the Roman council.

If the latter is meant, everyone can see how suspect witnesses generally are who are dragged across long stretches of road. They are very often bought with money to travel to distant places, and are led more by hope of profit than by a zeal for truth. Moreover, they are absent from places where they are known and may perhaps be guilty of crimes and unfit to give testimony.

Finally, the necessary persons of opposing testimony, as the African bishops say, cannot be brought forward either because of their sex, the weakness of old age, or many other impediments.

For this reason it was established, and rightly so, as Saint Cyprian testifies in Letter 55 to Pope Cornelius, that each person’s case should be heard there “where the crime was committed . . . where they can have both their accusers and witnesses to their crime.” Civil law accordingly exercises great caution concerning witnesses summoned over long journeys because of the danger of fraud that commonly attends such proceedings.

But if Saint Leo is speaking of witnesses produced by Celidonius in Provence, Hilary’s position is far stronger. The pontiff appears to be speaking of these witnesses, first, from the form of expression he uses: he does not say “he showed” but “he had shown,” by which I believe a Gallican and more remote synod is indicated; and second, because he does not mention the witnesses’ presence at the Roman synod but only their response, which, as one may infer, was submitted in writing.

Yet when he immediately speaks of Hilary, he says:

> “So that Hilary, sitting with us, had nothing that he could bring forward.”

If this is so, and the discussion concerns witnesses produced by the accused bishop in the Gallican synod, who would wish to compare Celidonius’s account—where he appealed at Rome to the response of certain witnesses given in Gaul—with the testimony of those who accused Celidonius himself, convicted him, and condemned him?

They were not a few witnesses hired for money, such as Celidonius could easily have procured for himself, or driven by fear or favor. Rather, the zeal of noble and ordinary people alike flared up and gathered, asserting that Celidonius had taken a woman previously married into his marriage-bed and at the same time alleging that, after administering secular office, he had condemned certain persons by a capital sentence (*Life of Saint Hilary of Arles* by Honoratus).

Not content with these witnesses, Saints Hilary and Germanus also ordered that others be prepared. Through their efforts and zeal, highly reputable priests came together from other places. By them the matter was examined with every kind of reason and prudence; the accusation was confirmed by testimony; and finally a true and simple judgment was pronounced, so that the man whom the rules of Scripture removed should remove himself by his own will.

Moreover, if at that time Celidonius had brought forward any witnesses—or any competent witnesses—as he reported at Rome, who could believe that Hilary and Germanus, men of such holiness, and the other highly reputable priests whom Honoratus mentions, were so blinded or had so completely forgotten justice that they would prefer to condemn a fellow priest as guilty rather than acquit an innocent man?

If the innocence of this man had for a time been obscured by the power or schemes of his enemies, it would eventually have become visible to the eyes of the Gallican Church. It would afterward have become known to Hilary himself, and also to Germanus, a man of such great grace. Nor would the most holy bishop of Arles have clung so firmly to his former judgment as to wish to die in it, contrary either to his own knowledge or to the public knowledge of his brother’s innocence.

[Note: He repeats the same refrain, which we refuted in the place cited immediately above, chapter 2.]

Yet Hilary never recanted. He was himself called by Leo “of holy memory after death,” and, as the writer of his Life, so often praised, testifies, even when placed in danger of his life, he in no way consented to be joined in communion with the man whom he had condemned together with such great men.

## CHAPTER IV. The remaining points of the accusations are examined, especially those by which Hilary is accused of being harsh and inhuman.

We could have refrained from examining these matters, since they appear to have been omitted by Honoratus—either because by that time Hilary’s memory had been cleansed of all such charges, or because the holy man really did suffer some human weakness in certain respects while occupied with the various affairs of the Churches, carrying out some matters somewhat too hastily as he hurried on to others, inflamed by zeal for discipline.

Nevertheless, Leo himself does not hesitate to acknowledge that the very magnitude of the work he had undertaken frequently provides an occasion for offense, even to pontiffs free from every ambition or desire. Something of this kind may have occurred in the affair of Projectus, concerning whom Saint Leo complains that another man was placed over him while he was still alive—and, as Leo himself insists, in another’s province. We have discussed the truth of this in the second part of the dissertation.

But while Projectus perhaps pursued his rights with excessive ardor, and while the citizens of the city whose Church he governed supported the complaints of their bishop with excessive zeal and thought themselves neglected in the election, since the election was completed without awaiting their votes and testimony, they attacked Hilary with extremely hostile written letters.

I would find it difficult to believe that Hilary, a man commended for his zeal for discipline, had done all this solely on his own initiative. I would rather think that this affair occurred during one of those journeys which he undertook with Germanus of Auxerre as his companion and confidant.

Nor is it reasonable to believe that he ordained a bishop alone, since both in the Council of Riez and in the First Council of Orange, which he presided over and subscribed to and whose decrees he composed, he attacked in the strongest words and with threats those who either allowed themselves to be ordained by only two bishops or ordained another without summoning a third to join them.

At Riez he pronounced a sentence of deposition against Armentarius, bishop of Embrun, because he had been ordained by only two men; and he removed the ordainers themselves from every ordination and council, decreeing that they must abstain from them. At the synod of Orange, likewise, he decreed in canon 21 that those who dared to do such a thing were to be condemned as presumptuous violators of the ancient statute.

Nor did Leo himself or the citizens of Projectus accuse Hilary of attempting that ordination alone. Since he acted with several others, scarcely anyone can be persuaded that it was done without counsel or without some reason.

Saint Leo continues in these words:

[Note: Perhaps this criticism arose because Hilary was said to have claimed an unwarranted monarchy throughout Gaul, supported by the favor of a patrician and a prefect, as we learn from the *Life of Saint Romanus*.]

> “A military force, as we have learned, follows the priest through the provinces, and, armed and supported by the presumptuous confidence of protection, serves to invade the Churches amid tumult” (*Letter 10, chapter 6*).

There is nothing that cannot be turned into an accusation when a matter is presented apart from its circumstances. Thus it was easy for Hilary’s opponents to report this affair in an odious light, although Hilary had permitted it either because necessity compelled him or because his friends acted of their own accord.

It is easy to believe that many who hung upon Hilary’s words and revered his holiness voluntarily offered themselves as companions to their bishop when he set out to visit the provinces subject to him—both because those regions were frequently shaken by military disturbances and because his ardent zeal for discipline and hatred of sin had created enemies for him among the ungodly.

Whatever the truth may be, we know this with certainty: Hilary was far removed from all worldly pride and splendor. Those who wrote about his deeds report this:

> “For he had risen from the most exalted seat of worldly power,” says Eucherius (*On Contempt of the World*), “into the name of religion, having courageously gone forth from his own country and from his kindred, and, having long before distributed all his wealth to Christ’s poor, had become rich in Christ.”

They say that he was therefore accustomed to be called “the father of the poor” (*The Praise of the Desert*), because, although himself poor and a lover of poverty, he supported the poor with attentive care.

What is more, his life was sustained with such great frugality that he rarely invited any of the secular people to his table. Devoted to reading, dedicated to vigils, and continually given over to prayer and fasting, he weakened his body through the harshness of the hair shirt. Not even in the severity of winter, when rushing rivers are usually bound by icy cold, did he cover his feet with additional clothing, nor did he ever cover his breast with woolen fabric (*Life of Saint Hilary*). Truly, as his epitaph says:

> **Bishop of the Lord, who, preferring love of poverty to gold,  
> seized the heavenly kingdom.**
>
> **Even undertaking rustic tasks for Christ,  
> he did not disdain to perform servile service.**
>
> **In office he lived as the least, but in rank as the highest.**

Finally, during the very journey to Rome which he undertook on account of Celidonius, he did not fear to complete the journey on foot:

> “Undaunted, he entered the city of Rome swiftly, without a horse, without a pack animal or traveling cloak, overcoming every difficulty.”

Who could believe that such a man traveled through the provinces of Gaul accompanied by a military force? If he did perhaps allow armed men to accompany him on his journey, this must have happened for an entirely different reason than the one suggested by our Leo on the basis of Hilary’s opponents’ misrepresentation.

The calumny is plainly inconsistent with itself when it says both that Hilary was surrounded by a military force and that he was supported by the presumptuous confidence of armed protection in order to invade the Churches amid tumult.

For if these things are so, how could he have come unexpectedly upon the citizens, who knew nothing of it in the affair of Projectus, and departed without warning? And how should someone be thought to have invaded the Churches amid tumult who, as they claim, entered the city so secretly and stealthily that he departed before the citizens even learned that he had come?

On the other hand, how can he be thought to have come secretly and stealthily when it is certain that he celebrated the episcopal ordination only after summoning several fellow bishops of the province?

Now, the way in which Leo portrays Hilary as harsh and inhuman is in no respect consistent with what is narrated in his Life. The pontiff says:

> “It is apparent how gentle Hilary is in heart, since he thought that the delay of a brother’s death was harmful to his presumption. For, insofar as it lay within his power, he deprived Projectus of light and took away his life; he inflicted this grief by substituting another in his place, so that Projectus would have no means of returning to health.”

He also rebukes this inhumanity below, where he attacks Hilary on the ground that he readily denied communion, at the command of an angry man, for offenses and light words, even to those who had in no way participated in the crime.

“But what wonder,” he says, “that he behaves in this way toward laymen, when he is accustomed to rejoice at the condemnation of priests?”

Let us hear, however, how differently the trustworthy witness Honoratus portrays Hilary, and with what feeling of compassion his heart was moved toward sinners, pouring forth a rain of tears.

> “Whenever he imposed penance . . . after completing his admonition, he began his petitions with tears, so that by praying he might strengthen the fruit of repentance which he had bestowed by admonishing.”

A little later he adds other words that wonderfully express the same compassionate disposition in the bishop of Arles:

> “He displayed the insignia of his compassion in those whom he sent ahead to the kingdom of heaven with such intimate affection that no one could imitate him. At the passing of even the least reader, his spirit was so wounded inwardly that he was shaken by sobs and poured out abundant tears, just as though he had been deprived of the consolation of an only child. He regarded the misfortunes and illnesses of his people as his own wounds.”

The author confirms this by the example of a certain deacon named Cyril, whose foot was crushed when a mass of marble fell upon it from above:

> “For the groaning and pain of this man, the blessed bishop received no less a wound in his heart than the crushed man suffered in his body.”

Finally, believing that in the recovery of his neighbor there should be a loss of his own limbs, he fulfilled the divine command—indeed, he surpassed it happily—when the Lord said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Here this blessed man is found to have loved his neighbor more than himself: insofar as his mind’s judgment allowed, he offered his own limbs to be amputated in order to heal another’s.

Let us therefore return Leo’s own words to him: it is apparent how gentle Hilary was in heart, how far he was from inflicting grief upon his brothers, taking away their light, or depriving them of life. On the contrary, he made another’s grief his own; he followed the deaths of his people with so many groans; and he did not hesitate to place a brother’s life before his own.

## CHAPTER V. Hilary’s compassion for the poor is examined, and several testimonies concerning him from illustrious men are reported.

We have read in the preceding chapter how ardently Hilary received sinners who were performing their confession, and with what compassionate feeling he shared the grief of his brothers. Indeed, we perceived it with our own eyes, so that in this respect Hilary’s kindness and gentleness are secure against the calumnies of his opponents.

Yet his character will shine forth even more splendidly if we report what he was like toward the poor and needy, both from his Life and from the writings of others who discussed the virtues of so great a bishop.

Thus Honoratus says:

> “His heart was shaken by mercy and compassion as though he alone were being urged by the pages of heaven to redeem [the captives]. He deliberated with himself, considered the matter, and brought it about that sacred vessels should provide captives with consolation rather than Churches with ornament. Whatever silver all the basilicas possessed he immediately assigned to the redemption of captives. When he learned that everything had been spent, he rejoiced and gave thanks, because through his administration he saw the faithful’s vows sent ahead to heaven’s dwelling.”

Can the compassion that dwelt in his heart be measured—he who believed that everything ought to be sold until one came even to the patens or glass chalices?

> “Inclined toward pity and most ready to give, he was not content merely to provide what was forbidden unless he added streams of tears to the streams of consolation.”

Julianus Pomerius praises the compassion of this bishop of Arles toward the poor in *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, as we shall immediately report. Peter of Equilinum asserts that he nourished the poor with great and attentive care. Trithemius commends him in the same terms in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “He was so compassionate toward the poor that, after cheerfully distributing all his possessions for their use, he was thereafter called and was indeed ‘the father of the poor.’”

Gennadius, who was nearly contemporary with Hilary or at least his contemporary, praises his charity toward the afflicted with great enthusiasm in these words:

> “Hilary, bishop of Arles, a man learned in the holy Scriptures, a lover of poverty, and zealous for the provision of the needy, distinguished himself not only by the compassion of his mind but also by the labor of his body. For, in order to feed the poor, he practiced farming beyond his strength, although he was a man of noble birth and had been raised in a very different manner. Nor was he neglectful in spiritual matters.”

Ado of Vienne transcribed Gennadius in his *Chronicle*.

What Honoratus reported above about Saint Hilary—that compassion dwelt so deeply in him that he believed everything ought to be sold until one came even to patens or glass chalices—clearly shows that he spent not only sacred vessels for the use of the poor. It is evident that he did not spare the estates and possessions of his Church either, before coming to the glass chalices.

We learn from another source that this also happened: in Letter 8 of Pope Hilary, chapter 4, he testifies that a petition had been presented to him in the name of Leontius, bishop of Arles. It stated that certain parishes of his Church had been transferred by his predecessor Hilary to others, contrary to law, and requested that they be restored to their former right by Hilary’s authority.

On the occasion of this complaint, the pontiff issued a decree providing that estates which were neither abandoned nor burdensome and which belonged to the Church—estates from which assistance was customarily provided to the needs of many—should not be transferred by any legal process to another person unless the reason for the alienation had first been demonstrated before a council, so that what ought to be done might be considered by the common deliberation of all.

The pontiff wisely and properly protected the patrimony of the poor by this constitution. He did not wish anything of this sort to be attempted without the assent and knowledge of a council, lest wicked men someday squander the possessions of the Churches under the pretext of charity.

Yet circumstances often reach a point at which councils cannot be assembled because of military disturbances, while the poverty of the poor and the miserable condition of captives allow no delay. When the barbarians withdraw and return to their own lands with their spoils, captives can be rescued from their hands only by immediate payment.

A similar circumstance may have compelled Hilary—if this is indeed what happened—to order the Church’s property to be sold for the use of the poor without the assent of a council.

It is certain that during the period in which Hilary governed the Church of Arles, Gaul was shaken by frequent military movements and barbarian incursions—by the Huns, Burgundians, Goths, and others—against whom, as Prosper writes, Aetius maintained the Roman state as best he could.

It is equally certain that, although Hilary believed that everything should be sold until one came even to patens or glass chalices in order to relieve the poverty of the poor, he was nevertheless so far from diminishing the revenues and possessions of his Church that he left them to his successors much more abundant than before.

We have as a witness Julianus Pomerius, nearly σύγχρονος—contemporary—with Hilary himself. He exercised an episcopate in Gaul.

[Note: Quesnellus overlooked this: Julianus Pomerius was only a presbyter.]

He says the following about our bishop of Arles in book II, chapter 9 of *On the Contemplative Life* (in our volume LI):

> “What of Saint Hilary? Did he not likewise leave all his possessions to his relatives, or sell them and distribute the proceeds to the poor? Yet when, by the merit of his perfection, he became bishop of the Church of Arles, he not only possessed what that Church then had but also increased it by receiving numerous inheritances from the faithful.”

These words fully answer the complaints by which Leontius attacked the memory of his predecessor Hilary. If he had alienated some estates of his Church for the sake of the poor, his charity had produced for it possessions far greater than the wealth it had removed.

The testimonies of so many and such great men therefore establish that whatever was reported to the Roman pontiff against Hilary’s other virtues, and especially against his gentleness, must be dismissed as the calumny of his opponents.

This happens to every bishop who, breathing apostolic vigor, rises against the scandals of impious and obstinate Christians and cuts them off from the grace of communion with a spiritual sword.

For how easy it is for wicked men to accuse their judges of cruelty, so that the sentence turned against them may be attributed not to their own crimes but to the harshness of the bishop who strikes them! By this device Pelagius deceived Zosimus. By a similar lie Eutyches temporarily imposed upon our Leo, when, in a petition sent to the pontiff, he complained that he had been unjustly deprived of communion, even though he adhered to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, and nearly persuaded Leo of this.

Without doubt, the same deception was suggested to Leo’s ears by certain people: that Hilary readily denied communion, even for light words and offenses, and made those who had in no way participated in the crime share the same punishment.

To regard these and all the other matters we have examined thus far as inventions concerning a bishop praised by everyone’s voice and writings would be the mark of a man lacking both judgment and religious seriousness.

Anyone who wishes to learn accurately the illustrious and holy deeds of this bishop should consult the complete Life written by Honoratus, bishop of Marseilles, which we have arranged to append to the Works of Leo for this purpose.

## CHAPTER VI. Whether Saint Leo was moved against Hilary because he was tainted by Semipelagianism, and whether Hilary persevered in it until death; ancient testimonies are reported in Hilary’s favor.

If anything can be inferred by conjecture concerning this obscure matter [Note: This conjecture is wholly arbitrary and supported by no indication, however remote.], I strongly suspect that it was not merely the complaints of Chelidonius and Projectus, nor the charge of having usurped in Gaul another’s jurisdiction, that caused our Hilary to be received so harshly by Leo.
