If I am not mistaken, both Leo and Prosper—who at that time served Leo in his secretarial and ecclesiastical affairs—retained deeply in mind that Hilary either still was, or had until quite recently been, a leader among those in Gaul who opposed St. Augustine’s teaching on grace. Accordingly, both believed that it would greatly benefit the peace of the Gallican churches and Catholic doctrine if, taking advantage of these complaints, which they believed to be well founded, Hilary were removed from the authority that his learning, piety, and the splendor of his see had won for him. For by the authority of his dignity and reputation he was drawing very many over to his opinion, and scarcely anyone was so uninfluenced by reverence for, or esteem of, so great a man as not to be moved away from the Catholic understanding.

Thus Prosper, writing to Augustine, says:

> We may indeed be steadfast in believing, but we are not equal to the authority of those who hold such opinions; for they greatly surpass us both in the merits of their lives, and some of them, having recently attained the highest priestly dignity, surpass us in rank as well. Nor has anyone, except a few fearless lovers of perfect grace, easily dared to oppose the disputations of such superiors. Hence danger has increased not only for those who listen to them but also for those who are listened to, since reverence for them either restrains many in an unprofitable silence or leads them to assent without concern; and what is scarcely censured by anyone’s contradiction seems to them most salutary.

That these words of Prosper were written about Hilary, bishop of Arles, is clearer than daylight, and is decisively proved by what Prosper adds near the end of the same letter. There, among those whom the obscurity of this Semipelagian opinion concealed despite their merits and honors, he names one man of outstanding authority and spiritual zeal: St. Hilary, bishop of Arles. Augustine supports this in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21, where he clearly identifies the same Hilary as infected by the error of the Semipelagians. It is therefore surprising that several more recent writers have denied this concerning Hilary—Bruno Neusser in *Prodromus Velitaris*, p. 50, and Anthelmius in Dissertation 9, *On the Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*. Their opinion is excellently refuted by the most eminent Norisius in Dissertation 4 appended to the Roman edition of the author of the *Scruples*, p. 251.

Since matters stood thus, who would not believe that Leo and Prosper, whose minds and purpose were one, lent a readier ear to Hilary’s accusers, and considered it advantageous to the Gallican churches that something be taken away from the authority of Hilary, which they believed harmful to Catholic doctrine? No one who has read the letters that both Prosper and the layman Hilary wrote to Augustine will deny that this was once the desire of both men.

> “They are persons,” says Hilary the layman, “to whom, by ecclesiastical custom, laymen must necessarily show the highest reverence.”

Here he means Hilary, bishop of Arles, as is clear from the words that follow shortly afterward:

> “It is certainly your prudence to discern what must be done so that the intention of such and so great men may either be overcome or moderated. I already consider it of little benefit for you to render an account, unless authority is also added—authority that contentious hearts cannot tirelessly transgress.”

Prosper writes in agreement with this, both in the words quoted above and in what he says near the end of the letter concerning Hilary of Arles:

> “Add instruction for the humble; add rebuke for the proud.”

Some learned men consider it highly probable that, when this disagreement arose between Leo and Hilary, Hilary had departed from his earlier position and had either embraced Augustine’s doctrine or at least had ceased to attack it. The most learned Gilbert Mauguin persuades himself that this was so in his *Refutation of the Predestinarian Fable*, part II, chapter 2. He argues first that this was what one should hope concerning a man who had always conducted himself with the greatest moderation in those controversies, and whom Prosper testifies to have followed Augustine’s doctrine in every other respect; Prosper also says that Hilary had long wished to confer with the most holy teacher concerning his position on the matter for which he was being criticized. Mauguin further argues that it is probable that, shortly afterward, having examined the beneficial books of that most holy and gentle teacher, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—in which all the difficulties by which Hilary was held fast, as by little hooks, in the filthy mire of the Pelagian remnants would have been completely resolved, and the truth of the absolute predestination of the elect, together with the truly gratuitous, ever-victorious grace of Christ, firmly and irresistibly established—Hilary humbly and sincerely embraced that most salutary doctrine.

A substantial argument for this conversion, he adds, is that Hilary is not listed among those censured by the papal judgment in Pope Celestine’s decretal to the bishops of Gaul. Otherwise, as metropolitan, he would have been named first, before Venerius, Marius, and the other bishops of his province.

With all due respect to this distinguished man, however, I would say that those named at the beginning of the letter are not the men who preached a doctrine opposed to Augustine’s. Rather, they are those who, although endowed with episcopal dignity, permitted certain presbyters—as Celestine says—to bring undisciplined questions into public discussion and to preach obstinately what was contrary to the truth. By these he undoubtedly means the presbyters and monks of Marseille and Lérins, with whom Prosper was contending on behalf of Augustine’s doctrine.

This is why he names especially Venerius, bishop of Marseille, and Leontius of Fréjus: the former had John Cassian and the other Massilian presbyters in his diocese, while the latter had Faustus, Vincentius, and the other men of Lérins—both groups being prominent among St. Augustine’s adversaries. He names not only these men but also four others for a similar reason, and then adds the remaining bishops of Gaul. I would not therefore suppose that Celestine considered all of them infected with the Pelagian contagion. He accuses them, as the entire letter loudly proclaims, of silence and of having permitted innovators the freedom to preach:

> “For what are you doing in the churches if they are to retain the chief authority to preach? Unless perhaps this stands in the way: that it is not yet established by authority or supported by reason that some of the number of the brethren, recently admitted from the company of laymen into our college, may not know what they ought to claim for themselves.”

How inappropriate it would have been for him to name Hilary of Arles, whom he had learned from the reports of Prosper and the other Hilary to be especially favorable to those presbyters and to lead the attack on Augustine’s doctrine! I therefore infer from the omission of his name that Hilary had not at that time changed his position. Otherwise Celestine’s letter ought to have been directed to him, so that, both as evidence of his conversion, he might restrain the novel doctrine and, by the exceptional authority he possessed among the Gallican churches, impose silence on those presbyters and encourage the other bishops to suppress the rashness of the innovators.

That Hilary later abandoned Semipelagianism may perhaps be proved more strongly from the fact that, although our Leo gathers in his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne every accusation he can against Hilary, even collecting from all directions several charges unrelated to the cases of Chelidonius and Projectus, he says not a word about Hilary’s errors concerning the grace of Christ. This could certainly not have been omitted, since Hilary never misused his authority more perniciously than when, through carelessness, he supported the adversaries of Augustine and of Catholic doctrine and emboldened them to sow the doctrines of their error.

Still more certainly, however, Hilary of Arles seems to have renounced the doctrine of the Semipelagians from his final words, spoken when he was already near death. He exhorted the congregation of his clergy who stood around him and appeared to fortify them against the Pelagian poison. Thus, in the *Life of Hilary*, chapter 20, volume I of this work (in our volume L), he says:

> “We have fought against the rulers of this world, with whom the Apostle describes an unceasing war as being waged. No one will be without this struggle who wishes to attain blessedness, with heavenly grace going before and effort following.”

[Note: In Hilary’s sermon on the *Life of St. Honoratus*, delivered in the year 430, three other testimonies occur, at nos. 3, 23, and 37, which either declare him to have preached the necessity and power of divine grace or show that even at that time he was free from Semipelagianism.]

Whatever the truth may finally be—whether Hilary had by then recovered from his evil opinions or not—it was both just and merciful on God’s part that Leo should have regarded him as an adversary and publicly rebuked him throughout the churches of Gaul, indeed throughout the entire Christian world, as a man utterly unable to govern himself, an invader of another’s jurisdiction, impatient of subjection, disturber of priestly concord, oppressor of his fellow bishops, despiser of the canons, and architect of lies and evil devices. Against him Leo rose not only with the full force of his own authority but also stirred the imperial authority, by which Hilary was nearly crushed and only through the favor of the Gallican bishops [Note: We have refuted these points at wearisome length in the *Observations*, part III, chapter 2.] retained the rights of his church. It was, I say, a great proof of mercy and justice that the bishop of Arles should not seem to have lent his mind and assent, even temporarily, with impunity to a doctrine alien from Augustine’s and therefore from Catholic teaching; and that this servant of Christ, of such virtue and religion, to whom the Gallican churches owed the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline, should not depart from this life before enduring these troubles and thereby washing away the guilt of the fault he had committed.

Before I bring Hilary’s defense to an end, I shall report whatever remains that was written in his praise by ancient authors whom we have not mentioned above. A certain poet named Livius, a contemporary of Hilary, crowned him with this encomium, as Honoratus reports:

> “If Augustine had come after Hilary, he would have been judged inferior.”

This is indeed hyperbolic praise, very like a poetical fiction, proceeding from one to whom Hilary was better known than Augustine and who, apparently, preferred the teaching of Marseille to that of Hippo. Nevertheless, it splendidly demonstrates how highly Hilary was esteemed in Gaul.

The praise of Eucherius is all the more worthy of Hilary because Eucherius himself, in holiness, learning, and dignity, had risen above praise and every suspicion of flattery. His own Hilary continually appears before him as an object of praise. In his paraenetic letter to Valerian on contempt of the world, he writes:

> “Hilary recently, and Petronius, now a bishop in Italy, both rose from that seat of worldly power which, as they say, is completely full—one into the name of religion, the other into the priesthood.”

In the preface to the first book of the *Instructions*, or *Questions on the Old Testament*, addressed to his son Salonius, he says:

> “Scarcely ten years old, you entered the desert and, among those holy hands, were not merely instructed but also nourished by Honoratus—that father, I mean, who was first the teacher of the islands and afterward also of the churches. There the teaching of the most blessed Hilary, then a novice of the island but now the supreme pontiff, formed you in every discipline of spiritual matters.”

He also dedicated to Hilary himself his book *On the Praise of the Desert*, with this title:

> “To the holy lord, most blessed in merits, and most glorious in Christ, Hilary: Eucherius.”

At once, at the beginning of the work, he addresses him as follows:

> “With great courage you once departed from your home and your kindred and penetrated to the remote retreats of the desert beyond the great sea. Yet you sought the desert again with greater virtue than you had sought it at first. For when you first entered it as a visitor, you had as your guide and, as it were, the forerunner of your journey one whom you afterward followed as the teacher of the heavenly warfare; and, leaving your parents, you nevertheless followed a father. But now, when you thought that you had to accompany that same man, summoned to the summit of the pontificate, love brought you back to the familiar solitude of the desert. Thus you are now nobler and greater as an example. Formerly, when you sought the wilderness, you seemed to be accompanying a brother; now, when you have returned to the wilderness, you have even left a father behind.”

And later:

> “Although long ago you poured out your entire wealth, rich in Christ, upon Christ’s poor; although you are younger in years but older in character, and distinguished in understanding and eloquence, nevertheless I have admired and loved nothing in you more than the fact that you so eagerly desired the dwelling-place of solitude. Therefore, since you often ask me to answer your most extensive and eloquent letters at greater length, you must bear for a little while—since you yourself are wise—with my foolishness, and so forth.”

How great the esteem for Hilary still was is shown both by Eucherius himself and by Apollinaris Sidonius, who relate that his return to the monastery of Lérins was the greatest source of joy for the whole island. Sidonius writes in his *Eucharisticus* to Faustus:

> “And also celebrating in those praises  
> the journey of EUCHERIUS as he came, and of HILARY as he returned.”

Eucherius, in his book *On the Praise of the Desert*, nearly concludes with these words:

> “You, my dearest Hilary, restored to and incorporated into their fellowship, have contributed greatly to yourself and greatly also to them, who now rejoice with lively exultation at your return.”

Prosper himself, who attacked Hilary’s teaching on grace in his letter to St. Augustine, nevertheless calls him in that same letter “a man of outstanding authority and spiritual pursuits,” one by whom he was greatly surpassed in the merits of his life. When the same Prosper records Hilary’s death in the *Chronicle* edited by the care of P. Pithoeus, he says:

> “Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, and Hilary, bishop of Arles, brought their distinguished lives to completion in death.”

St. Leo also bears witness to the holiness of our Hilary. In Letter 36 to the bishops who ordained Ravennius, he indicates that Hilary had been approved by him and further calls him “a man of holy memory.” He says:

> “Since, in the city of Arles, after the death of Hilary of holy memory, you consecrated Ravennius, a brother who was also approved by us …”  
> *(Letter 36, now 40.)*

[Note: Although St. Leo indicates no change in Hilary, Quesnel has by no means proved that he did not depart from his purpose. Compare our observations in Part III, chapter 2, where we show that he obeyed Leo’s judgment; and for this reason the same holy pontiff adorned him with the title “of holy memory,” because he had learned that, having complied with the pontifical judgment, Hilary spent the remainder of his life more fervently in pastoral cares and in pursuing his own perfection.]

This exceptional praise does not imply any change in Hilary. We have seen above that he never departed from his position. Rather, it proves that St. Leo, after the cloud of calumnies that had obscured his mind and prevented him from seeing Hilary’s holiness and innocence had finally been dispelled, afterward cast aside all unfavorable suspicions concerning so great a bishop and wished, by this brief eulogy, to wipe away the stain heedlessly placed upon Hilary’s reputation from him, now changed into another man.

This selection of testimonies, and the entire defense of Hilary, will be closed by Constantius the presbyter, his contemporary, who, while describing the life of St. Germanus and his arrival in the city of Arles, writes:

> “This city was illumined by Hilary the priest, precious through manifold virtue. For he was a fiery torrent of faith, an indefatigable worker of heavenly speech and divine instruction.”

# OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI ON QUESNEL’S FIFTH DISSERTATION, WHICH PREFERS A DEFENSE OF ST. HILARY OF ARLES AND OF THE ANCIENT RIGHTS OF THE CHURCH OF ARLES

[Col. 0533]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0533B]

### 1

Although before Quesnel there were not lacking even Roman writers who, judging that an error of fact had insinuated itself into St. Leo’s case against St. Hilary through false witnesses, offered some defense of Hilary, nevertheless all writers, including the Gauls, maintained that Hilary had suffered something human in the entire handling of his case and had rightly been reproved and restrained by Leo. Quesnel was the first to undertake to vindicate him in every respect.

Yet, lest his defense be thought injurious to Leo—which would have been highly prejudicial to the *Apology*—Quesnel warned at the outset that the two defenses were so interconnected that, as he says, “we believe that Leo’s reputation itself can be safeguarded only after Hilary has been cleared in the manner I have undertaken.” In the same preface he promises to demonstrate in Leo only an error of fact and the insinuation produced by evil practices—something that can occur even in holy men and in the supreme pontiffs themselves.

[Col. 0533C]

### 2

If he had kept within these limits in the dissertation itself and had established his position by fair arguments, we would have had nothing to oppose. But he not only failed to prove his proposed error of fact with sufficient fairness; under the appearance of a question of fact he also entangled a question of law. The discussion gradually proceeded to the point that Hilary’s defense turned into an accusation of Leo and, most seriously, violently attacked the prerogatives of the pontificate itself, presenting them as rights that Hilary had justly challenged.

For Quesnel does not merely attempt to show that Leo wrote and decreed certain severe measures against Hilary through a simple error of fact. He also contends that Leo proceeded to matters exceeding his authority—against the custom of his predecessors, against the rights and privileges of the churches of Gaul, and against the discipline of the canons. He praises Hilary not only for resisting Leo with firmness before the sentence but also for having paid no attention to the sentence, as though it possessed no force; and he invents from his own imagination that Hilary continued to exercise the same authority throughout his life, even in defiance of Leo.

[Col. 0533D]

### 3

Let the impartial reader judge whether this is to join a defense of Leo to Hilary’s defense—or rather to accuse Leo, indeed to impose upon Hilary himself the grave crime of disobedience and contempt. Hence observations on the fifth dissertation will be judged especially necessary. We shall divide them into three parts, so that, after an appropriate response has been attached to each part of the dissertation, everyone may understand what ought to be held both concerning the facts and concerning the law.

Wherever possible, we shall not omit a fairer method of defending St. Hilary. We do not shrink from defending so great a man; indeed, we desire it most earnestly, provided that the defense be pursued without injury to Leo and without offense to pontifical authority.

## 901. FIRST PART: ON THE CASE OF CHELIDONIUS

In which the law governing episcopal appeals to the Apostolic See is discussed at greater length.

### CHAPTER I. The Documents Available in This Case, and the Authority to Be Assigned to Them

There are five ancient writers who have transmitted something concerning this case. Three present the accusation of Hilary: St. Leo’s Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne; the emperor Valentinian in the *Novella* that we gave as Letter 11; and the Jurensian monk, author of the *Life of St. Romanus*. Two seem to favor Hilary: the author of his *Life* and the prefect Auxiliaris in a letter addressed to Hilary, which is read as inserted into the aforementioned *Life*.

The matter must be explained and decided solely from these documents. Whatever is thrust forward from personal invention without any foundation in them must be regarded as empty.

### 2

To diminish the authority of the records opposed to Hilary, Quesnel casts suspicion on Leo on various grounds and likewise represents Valentinian as having been prejudiced and forestalled by Leo. He accuses the *Life of St. Romanus* of being a forgery, or at least rejects the passage in which this case is discussed as though it were a scrap wrongly inserted into the work. He elevates the authors who favor Hilary and, wherever the author of Hilary’s *Life* appears to introduce material contrary to Leo, insists that greater trust should be placed in him than in Leo. Quesnel takes it as certain that this author was St. Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, and presents him as writing after the deaths of both men, free and exempt from every desire either to flatter or to deceive.

### 3

Whether it is so certain, as Quesnel preferred to maintain, that the author of this *Life* was St. Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, will be evident from the notice prefixed to the *Life* itself, inserted before the works of St. Hilary in this volume (volume I of this edition). Whoever the author may have been, he belonged to the community that Hilary himself governed in his own house.

For that reason he favored Hilary so zealously that, in order to vindicate him from the Roman judgment, he produced only the honorable letter of the prefect Auxiliaris to Hilary, while passing over in silence all the letters of the emperor Valentinian and of Leo that were opposed to him. He likewise passed over the entire case of Projectus, in which no one could completely excuse Hilary, as will be shown in Part II. Finally, in chapter 21 he carefully inserted these words, said to have been heard from the people of Arles after Hilary’s death:

> “This day has forever cut away the complaints of unjust accusation.”

Since all these things reveal an author devoted to vindicating St. Hilary, anyone who understands what partisan zeal can accomplish will easily see with how much reserve he must be read when he discusses events that took place at Rome.

As for Leo, whether so great and holy a pontiff, seized by some emotion or prejudice, acted or wrote with undue severity in defense of an unlawful right will become clear from what follows. When St. Leo and the author of the *Life* appear to relate contradictory accounts of matters belonging simply to the facts, everyone can see which of the two deserves greater belief.

Setting this consideration aside for the moment, another substantial indication for judging the matter may be drawn from the more recent Gallican writer of great reputation, Antonio Pagius. After recounting the differences between Leo’s narrative and that of the *Life*, and citing Quesnel’s judgment that prefers the author of the *Life*, he adds under the year 445, no. 14:

> “But Papebrochius much more rightly establishes that, in the narration of this case, the authority of St. Leo is preferable to that of the author of St. Hilary’s *Life*: for Leo was so holy that he would not wish to lie, and so ancient that no one closer to the matter can be considered a witness to it than he who took part in it and himself acted as its judge. Moreover, little injury would be done to the author of St. Hilary’s *Life* if it were said that, in recounting what had happened at Rome in the year 445, he wrote from hearsay and from the report of the clergy of Arles twenty or thirty years later and therefore narrated some things less accurately. But great injury would be done to St. Leo if it were doubted that he had written the truth in his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne. For good faith in reporting what he had heard could excuse the former; Leo could not avoid condemnation for the most shameless calumny if he had written what was false. Who, I ask, if he understands how holy a man Leo was, would hesitate to believe him and detract from the other, however holy, when he writes contrary things?”

This is what Papebrochius says.

Indeed, anyone who pays attention to what happened to several holy men when they reported matters at which they themselves had not been present will not hesitate to conclude that St. Honoratus was poorly informed about what had taken place at Rome in the case of Chelidonius before St. Leo. Pagius offers the example of St. Avitus, who wrote concerning the case of Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople and his contemporary, and concludes:

> “The same thing happened to Honoratus, bishop of Marseille, as happened to Avitus, metropolitan of Vienne. Just as the latter had an insufficiently accurate report concerning the case of Macedonius, so the former had an insufficiently sincere report concerning the case of Leo—or, rather, of Chelidonius.”

### 4

Leo testifies to facts that occurred at Rome in his presence and that of many others. He does so not in a private writing, which no one could refute, but in public letters sent to the bishops of the province of Vienne themselves, among whom Hilary was living. Hilary could have exposed an error or calumny if anything false had been inserted in those letters.

The author of the *Life*, however, wrote not only after the deaths of both men but many years later. Nor did he derive what he inserted about the Roman events, as Quesnel claims, from the official acts themselves, which he nowhere indicates that he had read. Even if he had read them, they could not be considered contrary to his letter, since Leo himself had likewise sent those acts to Gaul. Rather, the author derived his account from the report of the people of Arles. These people, being well disposed toward their bishop but not accurately informed about what had occurred at Rome, may reasonably be believed to have been ignorant of some things, to have wrongly received others through false rumor, and, as commonly happens in popular tradition, to have added, removed, or altered still other details over the passage of time.

Who, then, would think that a writer composing many years later from popular report should be preferred to a holy pontiff, who, while Hilary was still alive, publicly testified to what had taken place in his own presence?

### 5

As for the charge of forgery brought against the *Life of St. Romanus*, as well as against the *Lives of Saints Lupicinus and Eugendus*, which Quesnel attributes to the same author, no one who has examined the objections will agree with Quesnel. Hence not only Pagius defends these *Lives*, but also Tillemontius. Although Tillemontius strongly favors Quesnel in this very controversy concerning Hilary, he declares concerning the *Life of St. Romanus*, article 1:

> “Thus we have few histories that can be said to be more authentic than this one.”

In his first note he responds to Quesnel’s principal objections, omitting those unsupported by any proof. Mabillonius also, whom no one can fail to recognize as highly skilled in criticism, regards it as genuine both in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict* and in the *Annals*.

### 6

Since the anonymous author of the *Life*, a Jurensian monk and disciple of St. Eugendus, wrote after the beginning of the sixth century, Quesnel improperly claims that the terms found in the *Lives* he composed were too foreign to the usage of his age: namely, *repau­sare* and *repedare*; *religio* and *religiosus* for the monastic order and a monk; *Father Romanus* and *Father Lupicinus*, in the sense in which monks now use those expressions; *priest* without qualification, meaning a presbyter of the second order; and *patriarch*, meaning a metropolitan, or rather a bishop—for the bishop of Besançon was merely a bishop.

Quesnel also claims that the handing over in Rome of relics of Saints Peter, Paul, and Andrew to monks, and the use of a dalmatic, were contrary to the customs of that age. Finally, to pass over his other and lighter objections, he represents the expression “canonical course” as referring to canonical hours, although he asserts that at that time these hours were neither called canonical nor prescribed by any canon.

### 7

Pagius excellently refutes each of these points by adducing several testimonies from approximately the same period in which similar words are found in the same sense. He omits only the word *patriarch*. To this, however, one may respond with the testimony of Athalaric, king of the Goths, in Cassiodorus, book IX, letter 15, and with two other examples from Vandal speech in Victor of Vita, book II, nos. 5 and 18. When the author of the *Life* wrote, he was living among the Burgundians, then masters of the region of the Seine; perhaps they used the same word just as the Goths and Vandals did.

Concerning the objection about the relics, one may make the following observation. The customary response is that when St. Gregory the Great says that it was permitted neither at Rome nor throughout the West to touch or move relics, he is reporting the discipline of approximately his own time, not of a considerably earlier age. Mabillonius lists many cases of the elevation or translation of relics, not only in the East but also in the West, in the preface to the second age, no. 43.

St. Gaudentius also mentions distinguished gifts of relics in Sermon 17, as does St. Paulinus of Nola in the *Natale* II of St. Felix. Another Paulinus mentions them in the *Life of St. Ambrose*, in addition to the event that Pagius reports as having occurred at Rome itself under Hormisdas, from the *Life of St. Eleutherius of Tournai*.

We shall offer another, perhaps more probable, response. In the petition of the legates to Hormisdas, described in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 645, we observe that the Roman custom is indeed emphasized: fragments of the bodies of saints were not given as gifts. In their place, however, *sanctuaria* were customarily sent—that is, linens, oils, cloths, or coverings kept in reliquaries, which had touched the bodies or tombs of the saints.

These *sanctuaria* were also called relics. Hence the aforementioned petition says that Justinian would consider his request sufficiently granted if, from the same source from which *sanctuaria* of the apostles had been given throughout the world, he too might be permitted to receive relics. From the context it is clear that the apostles’ relics there mean *sanctuaria*, which alone the legates asked Hormisdas to send him:

> “Command that the *sanctuaria* of the holy apostles Peter and Paul be generously given to him, according to custom.”

Similarly, in the same letter 30 to the empress Constantina, which Quesnel cites, Gregory says:

> “It is not the Roman custom, when they give the RELICS of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body; rather, only a *brandeum* is sent in a small box and placed upon the most sacred bodies of the saints.”

Here he plainly calls the *brandea*, or *sanctuaria*, relics.

The same pontiff frequently uses *sanctuaria* and *relics* interchangeably, as may be seen in Letter 54 of Book I, Letter 15 of Book IX, and elsewhere when he recalls that relics were to be used in the dedication of churches. Following Roman custom, he undoubtedly means these same *sanctuaria*. Likewise, in *Dialogues* II, chapter 38, he plainly takes relics to mean *sanctuaria*, in which no fragment of the bodies themselves was contained.

Hence Muratorius rightly concluded in volume II of the *Latin Anecdotes*, *Disquisition on the Index of Holy Martyrs*, p. 196:

> “From this we learn that the name ‘relics’ was applied not only to ashes but also to the very objects that had touched holy men or their tombs.”

Thus both bones and *sanctuaria* were called relics. Indeed, during this period, under the Roman discipline of the age, while the bodies of the saints remained untouched, the name relics referred only to *sanctuaria*.

Accordingly, those relics of the apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew are more probably to be understood as these *sanctuaria*, those tokens of the saints’ patronage, or those small reliquaries enclosed beneath the altar, of which the *Life of St. Eugendus*, chapter 9, speaks. Nothing, therefore, can be inferred from this either against Roman custom or contrary to the speech of that age.

As for “canonical course,” Fortunatus, a writer of the same century, uses the expression in a similar manner in the *Life of St. Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, when he says that the entire course had been completed from the canon.

Quesnel objects that St. Gregory of Tours makes St. Romanus more recent than the author of this *Life*. But he offers nothing to prove this, and Tillemontius declares that nothing can be offered except the ambiguity between the two Chilperics. In those narratives in which one appears to differ somewhat from the other, no one will prefer the Gregory of Tours of a later age, whom one will not find entirely exact in every matter.

Quesnel’s remaining objections are so slight that they require no answer.

### 8

So far is it from being the case that anything foreign to that age is found in the text touching the case of Chelidonius—whether in its words or its subject matter—that, on the contrary, the expressions “supported by patrician and prefectural favor,” inserted into the text, agree most closely with the language and history of the event and show that the author was exceptionally well informed about what had happened.

For both Leo’s letter and Valentinian’s *Novella* testify that Hilary used armed force. The adjective “patrician” indicates Aetius, the patrician and master of both military commands; “prefectural” suggests the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul who favored Hilary. This precise double mention of dignities, explained neither by Leo nor by the emperor, displays not a later annotator but a man close to the events and well informed from other particular records or witnesses.

For this anonymous author of the *Life* was a disciple of St. Eugendus, who had been educated by St. Romanus, a contemporary of the event, and could have heard the facts concerning Chelidonius from him and transmitted them to his anonymous disciple. Hence his authority in this very account of Chelidonius must be regarded as of the highest importance.

9. Before bringing this chapter to a close, I should like to note another objection, rather slight in itself and very easy to refute, but clothed in many false prejudices which ought not to have been left unexposed, lest they deceive anyone. Quesnellus, no. 5, presented as deserving censure—and falsely—the claim that Leo’s letter against Hilary is said by the author of the *Life* to have been inserted into the canons, that is, into a canonical collection, as the expression may be interpreted. He merely mentions three canonical codices, or collections, in which that letter is not found. But, first of all, that letter could have been found in the particular collection of some church in the province of Vienne [Col. 0537D], or in some codex belonging to the Church of Besançon itself, to which the letter belonged no less than did the Jurensian monk who wrote the *Life*; for it is clear from the celebrated Arles codex that several churches had their own particular collections. In that codex alone are contained several decretal letters issued for the Church of Arles.

What, then? Quesnellus’s error rests upon the hypothesis that he supposes no collections to have existed in the sixth century except authoritative ones—that is, collections published by public authority and accepted as law. This is what those words imply: “Since at that time no authoritative collections existed in which the aforesaid letter of Leo had been inserted.” He declares that he knows only three collections of this kind: the one edited by himself and attributed to Leo, the Dionysian collection, and the Gallican collection, in none of which the present letter is read. As for the Gallican codex of canons, he asserts that it contained neither this letter nor any other decretal letters.

First, it is false that in the sixth century there were no collections except authoritative ones [Col. 0538A], since several were produced during that same century through the work of private individuals. The collection of Dionysius Exiguus itself was privately circulated at the beginning of that century and obtained authority only much later. Elsewhere we shall demonstrate that the collection edited by Quesnellus is not a codex of the Roman Church, but the work of a private Gallican. Nor does he explain at all what he means by the name “Gallican collection.” Several collections of this period are known to us, which we shall soon indicate; but all lack public approval.

If, under the name “Gallican codex,” he understood these private Gallican collections, it is false—indeed, utterly false—that they contain no decrees of the Roman pontiffs. For not only are several decretal letters of the pontiffs transcribed in the ancient Gallican collection edited by Quesnellus, but also the most ancient Corbie codex, which Quesnellus likewise used and which was written in the age of Vigilius, most certainly exhibits the Gallican collection, as Quesnellus himself admits in dissertation 16, nos. 4 and 12. The Morbach codex, praised by many, and another similar to it, Vatican-Palatinus 574, in which a purely Gallican collection is preserved, as well as the very ancient Veronese codex 59, which contains an abridgment of the Gallican collection, reproduce not a few decretal letters [Col. 0538B]. The same is true of the celebrated Colbertine-Fossatensis codex, which is likewise Gallican.

Quesnellus admits that the bishops of Gaul valued these decrees of the Roman pontiffs highly and used them in their councils whenever occasion arose. Unless—which is unbelievable—they all retained them only in memory, they must certainly have consulted them in codices whenever occasion required. The author of the *Life* indicates that Saint Hilary himself used letters of the supreme pontiffs in the case of Celidonius, when, in chapter 16, he states that Celidonius was barred from the clergy for having married a widow, since “the authority of the apostolic see and the decrees of the canons forbid it.”

But why pursue the matter further, when Quesnellus himself, perhaps better instructed by the time he wrote dissertation 16, explicitly proves in nos. 4 and 12 that canonical codices had formerly existed among the Gauls even before Dionysius, and that they contained decretal letters inserted into the canons by the supreme pontiffs [Col. 0538C]? Perhaps, when in the aforementioned dissertation he denied the existence of such a codex, he meant a codex made authoritative and approved by the public authority of the Gallican bishops—a matter, however, about which the author of the *Life of Saint Romanus* says nothing—and nevertheless did not mean to deny that such letters were present in other private canonical codices.

Since, in fact, several private codices of this kind existed, it cannot be denied that Leo’s decretal letter concerning the case of Celidonius was inserted in one of them. Indeed, in the aforementioned dissertation 16 Quesnellus does not deny this; rather, from the Third Council of Orléans, held in 538, where, in canon 3, Leo’s own words from chapter 5 of this letter are found transcribed, he concludes that the letter had been inserted into the codex then used throughout Gaul. Indeed, it was inserted into these codices to such an extent that it has reached us only through Gallican manuscript collections. It is found only in the copies of the most ancient Corbie collection, and in collections 12 and 24, which are Gallican, as we have shown elsewhere. Thus Quesnellus’s entire argument [Col. 0538D] for refuting the testimony just cited is useless.

Having therefore vindicated the authenticity and authority of the account relevant to our subject, which is read in the *Life of Saint Romanus*, let us state more explicitly the episcopal see of Celidonius as it can be established from this *Life*.

## CHAPTER II. Celidonius Is Established as Bishop of Besançon

### 1.

How important it is to know of which church Celidonius was bishop is sufficiently shown by Quesnellus’s lengthy discussion of the matter. Since he presumes that Hilary could scarcely be excused if he judged and deposed a bishop who was not subject to him, he endeavors to prove by many arguments that Celidonius presided not over the Church of Besançon—which lay outside Hilary’s jurisdiction, as everyone had agreed after the publication of the testimony from the *Life of Saint Romanus*—but over some see in the province of Vienne.

Accordingly, he first attempts to show that the celebrated *Life of Saint Romanus*, which expressly assigns the bishopric of Besançon to Celidonius, is either spurious or at least interpolated, and to exclude the bishopric of Besançon from him [Col. 0539A]. He then seeks, in several chapters, to establish that this same bishop was subject to Hilary and to vindicate the metropolitan rights of the bishop of Arles for this purpose.

But since in the preceding chapter we demonstrated that the *Life of Saint Romanus*, once cleared of Quesnellus’s objections, is entirely genuine, it follows clearly enough that Celidonius’s bishopric was situated at Besançon, in Maxima Sequanorum, and was removed from all jurisdiction of Hilary. The same point can be confirmed more fully by other documents.

### 2.

Although Leo does not expressly assert that Celidonius was bishop of a foreign province not subject to Hilary, the emperor Valentinian, who issued his *Novella* on the basis of Leo’s report, indicates this plainly enough when he complains of Hilary: “He removed others incompetently.” This refers to Celidonius’s deposition by Hilary, and the adverb “incompetently” identifies a judge who exercised incompetent judgment over someone not subject to him.

Let everyone judge whom it is more reasonable to believe: the emperor, who denies that Celidonius was subject to Hilary—and denies it in a public law, which Quesnellus could not even call into question—or Quesnellus, who attempts in several chapters to prove that Celidonius was subject to Hilary, yet produces no ancient testimony contrary to the *Novella* and labors only over conjectures to which he too readily gives free rein, on the hypothesis that Celidonius was not bishop of Besançon and that the *Life of Saint Romanus* is apocryphal or falsified.

It is not, therefore, the *Life* alone that removes Celidonius’s bishopric from Hilary’s jurisdiction; the emperor’s *Novella* itself does so, and Quesnellus has offered it no answer. Since, then, by the force of this *Novella*, Celidonius’s bishopric must be sought outside the province of Vienne, in what city shall we believe it to have been situated, unless at Besançon, where the *Life of Saint Romanus* places it and where we have shown the *Life* to be genuine? Thus Quesnellus’s opinion, which assigns Celidonius a bishopric in the province of Vienne, is openly refuted by the same *Novella*, while the fact that his bishopric was wholly outside Hilary’s jurisdiction is strongly confirmed.

### 3.

Let us add two other testimonies that confirm the same point. First, the author of the *Life of Saint Hilary* relates the following in chapter 16:

> “But who could adequately explain, during his journeys, how much benefit his presence brought to the cities of Gaul, when he repeatedly sought out Saint Germanus, with whom he discussed the life, progress, and failings of priests and ministers? When his arrival became known, groups of both noble and ordinary persons hastened eagerly to the two men, asserting that Celidonius had taken a widow as his wife, and so forth.”

Quesnellus interprets this in chapter 1 as though Saint Hilary, while visiting the churches subject to him in his province of Vienne, had Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, as his companion; and as though, when the two of them arrived together at some city in that province, Celidonius’s accusers had come there from a neighboring city in the same province.

By this interpretation he suggests that Celidonius’s bishopric was situated in that same province. But the very words of the text—“when he repeatedly sought out Saint Germanus”—plainly indicate that Hilary repeatedly met Germanus at Auxerre. Tillemont likewise understood them in this sense in article 14 of the *Life of Saint Hilary*, volume XV, page 71, writing:

> “Saint Hilary therefore went to see Saint Germanus of Auxerre, as he did fairly often; as soon as it was known that he had arrived there, various distinguished persons and others of lesser rank came to make serious complaints about Quélidoine to the two saints.”

This passage therefore indicates that Celidonius’s episcopal city was near Auxerre, since the groups not only of nobles but also of ordinary people hastened to Auxerre when they heard that Saint Hilary was there. They would not all have found it convenient to undertake a more distant journey. If Celidonius had held the bishopric of another city in the province of Vienne, his accusers would more easily have gone to Arles than to Auxerre, which lay in the Fourth Lyonnaise, or Senonia. Moreover, Besançon is not far from Auxerre.

This also explains why Hilary’s judgment is reported in the same *Life* [Col. 0540A] as a consequence of the journeys which that saint undertook outside his own diocese, and why it is counted among the benefits that came to the cities of Gaul.

### 4.

Another testimony may be drawn from the superscription of Saint Leo’s letter, which Jacques Sirmond found in an old codex. Its wording is as follows:

> “In an old document—the marginal note in the edition of the Councils cites *VV. CC.*, that is, *veteres codices*, ‘old codices,’ or at least an old codex—the following letter is inscribed as having been sent not only to the bishops of the province of Vienne but also to those of Maxima Sequanorum, in this form: ‘Leo to all the most beloved bishops established throughout the provinces of Maxima Sequanorum and Vienne.’”

This decretal was sent to Maxima Sequanorum, whose chief city was Besançon, because it concerned Celidonius, bishop of Besançon, so that the decretal particularly belonged to that province. Tillemont therefore acknowledges this superscription as a strong argument for Celidonius’s bishopric at Besançon in note 5 to the *Life of Hilary*, page 845.

Quesnellus, however, following his usual practice, piles up several flimsy conjectures in chapter 3 in order to undermine confidence in this superscription. He appeals to all copies, both printed and handwritten, that lack it. But all the printed copies derive from Merlin. Furthermore, no one used the codices except Sirmondus and Quesnellus. All the codices of this Leonine letter that he praises so extravagantly are reduced to the three mentioned by him in his notes on the same letter. Of these, he admits that two—the Corbie and the Thuane codices—are similar and belong to collection 2; the third is the Victorine codex, which we know from elsewhere to belong to collection 24.

We have seen several copies of the two later collections, 12 and 24, but all are of one origin, as is clear from their nearly identical variants. All these manuscript books, which lack the words “of Maxima Sequanorum” in the superscription, derive from the archetype in which this decretal had been sent only to the bishops of the province of Vienne. Sirmondus’s particular codex, however, which preserves a different superscription mentioning Maxima Sequanorum [Col. 0540C], demonstrates another and most ancient origin.

We learn that several copies of this same letter were sent by Leo himself, with different superscriptions, to the bishops of different provinces. Although Saint Leo, writing in chapter 2 to “the priests of your province,” mentions only one province, because he is addressing the bishops of whichever province the particular copy and title were intended for, nevertheless he mentions several provinces together and addresses their bishops in chapter 6:

> “Remove every cause of dissension from your provinces.”

And in chapter 9:

> “For we do not defend the ordinations of your provinces.”

To prevent anyone from thinking that these statements concern several territorial or civil provinces rather than several ecclesiastical provinces subject to different metropolitans, consider the following passage from chapter 6:

> “Let each metropolitan, together with those who surpass the other priests in the antiquity of their priesthood, defend by our authority the ordination of his own province.”

Since, then, the subject is the restoration of the right of metropolitans over several provinces, and the address is directed to the bishops of several provinces, it is plainly impossible that this letter was sent only to the bishops of the province of Vienne. Rather, it must be understood as having been delivered, in copies bearing different superscriptions—as was customary—appropriate to each province, to all those concerned. Consequently, there is no reason to reject as spurious the superscription of Sirmondus’s codex, which represents Maxima Sequanorum, merely because the commonly transmitted superscription mentions only the province of Vienne.

If it cannot be denied, on account of Projectus—whom, together with Quesnellus, we shall probably regard as bishop of Narbonensis Prima—that the decretal was sent to the bishops of that province, even though no codex has transmitted that superscription to us; and if, on account of Leontius, who was appointed president over councils of various provinces, it likewise cannot be denied that the letter was delivered to all the bishops of those provinces, then it will be even less possible to deny that it was directed to the bishops of Maxima [Col. 0541A] Sequanorum, whose superscription the Sirmondian codex has preserved.

This occurred because of Celidonius, who is discussed in the decretal. Accordingly, it is known that he belonged to that province and was bishop of Besançon. For this reason the records of the Church of Besançon reasonably report that Celidonius was bishop at this time, that Importunus was appointed in his place at the same time, and that Importunus was later expelled as a pseudo-bishop when Celidonius was restored—something found in no documents of any other church.

All the evidence, therefore—the *Life of Saint Romanus*, the emperor’s *Novella*, the *Life of Saint Hilary* itself, and the superscription of Leo’s letter—confirms Celidonius’s bishopric at Besançon. Who would listen to Quesnellus when he denies this without a single document?

### 5.

Nor should the following words of Leo from chapter 3 of the letter, which Quesnellus cites in chapter 3, no. 2, move us against so great an authority:

> “For the sentence pronounced against him [Celidonius] would have remained in force if the truth of the charges had been established.”

Here Leo seems to acknowledge Hilary’s jurisdiction over Celidonius, and consequently Celidonius is believed to have been bishop not outside Hilary’s province, in Maxima Sequanorum, but in Vienne.

But this is mistaken. Since all the ancient documents so far considered establish that Celidonius was bishop of Besançon and outside Hilary’s jurisdiction, the sentence would have remained in force against Celidonius not by the authority of Hilary, whom the emperor himself, on the basis of Leo’s report, exposed in the *Novella* as an incompetent judge, but either by the authority of the other bishops of Celidonius’s province who had been summoned to the council—for the author of the *Life of Hilary* states that highly esteemed priests had assembled—or, rather, as a matter of fact: if the truth of the charges had been established, Leo would not have absolved Celidonius, but would have ratified by his own decision his deposition, otherwise invalid for lack of jurisdiction, yet supported by the canons and thus confirmed in accordance with them.

Shortly before, he had testified concerning the judgment pronounced against Celidonius—that he could not retain the priesthood as the husband of a widow—in these words:

> “For our part, observing the legal statutes, we have wished this to be guarded with particular care, not only among priests but also among clerics of lesser rank.”

### 6.

Still less should one be influenced by what Quesnellus introduces in the same chapter, no. 5, concerning Maxima Sequanorum’s alleged subjection to the Burgundians. He claims that, since the Burgundians were hostile to the Romans, they would never have permitted the judgment of Hilary, the Roman metropolitan. But we have shown that in Hilary’s time the Burgundians were neither enemies of the Romans nor masters of Maxima Sequanorum, first in note 1 [Col. 431, no. a] to chapter 1, and more clearly still through the proofs of Antonius Pagius and Tillemont.

### 7.

Once, on the basis of what has been said, Celidonius’s bishopric at Besançon has been established, and the arguments brought by Quesnellus in chapters 2 and 3 to exclude it have been refuted, there is no need to examine or refute what he adds at greater length from chapter 4 through chapter 13 to establish Hilary’s jurisdiction over the entire province of Vienne. These matters have no bearing on the present controversy concerning Celidonius, except on the hypothesis that his bishopric at Besançon has been properly eliminated.

Nevertheless, concerning the matters we are now passing over, discussion will return in part II, chapter 3, where the case of Projectus will call for a timely reconsideration of them.

### 8.

Meanwhile, the first charge in the controversy concerning Celidonius against Hilary is that he usurped judgment over a bishop removed from his province, although that judgment did not belong to him. Hence Quesnellus himself wrote near the end of chapter 1:

> “He is assailed by nearly all writers as an invader of another’s jurisdiction, because he dared to depose Celidonius, a bishop who was not only innocent but in no way subject to him.”

This accusation would be much more serious if Celidonius had been not an ordinary bishop but a metropolitan, as some infer especially from these words in the *Life of Saint Romanus* [page 915]:

> “Celidonius, patriarch of the aforementioned metropolis [Besançon].”

But the words do not compel that conclusion. For the word *patriarch*, as is well known from the testimonies of Cassiodorus and Victor of Vita cited in chapter 1, was used among the Goths and Vandals for the ordinary bishop of a particular city. It could likewise have been used in the same sense by the Burgundians, who, when the author was writing the *Life*, ruled Maxima Sequanorum. From the usage adopted among them, the author could call Celidonius the patriarch—that is, the chief bishop—of his region, even though Celidonius enjoyed no metropolitan jurisdiction.

In the later synods of the sixth century, the bishops of Besançon are indeed found subscribed not among the metropolitans but among ordinary bishops. See, among others, the Synod of Mâcon of 583. The author of the *Life* called Besançon a metropolis because it was the principal city of Sequania, since it was the metropolis in the civil organization of that province, as is evident from the *Notitia Galliarum*.

### 9.

But whether Celidonius was a bishop or a metropolitan, Quesnellus’s defense is always a poor one, since he attempted to remove him from the bishopric of Besançon. A fairer defense of Hilary in this matter would have been the one Quesnellus used near the end of chapter 2 to clear him of usurping another’s jurisdiction when he ordained Saint Romanus a priest not far from Besançon. Quesnellus says that Hilary was permitted to do this by the presumed consent of Eucherius of Lyon, his very close friend, in whose territory the Jura monastery was believed to have been situated, as it is today.

Since, according to the *Life of Hilary*, priests from other places had assembled at Besançon for the judgment, and Saint Germanus of Auxerre also appears to have gone there—for he and Hilary had instructed Celidonius’s accusers to prepare their witnesses—Hilary may be understood to have deposed Celidonius with the consent of his fellow provincials and even with their judgment. Perhaps he did so also with the assent of Eucherius as metropolitan, if Besançon was not yet an ecclesiastical metropolis subject to the bishop of Lyon. For Saint Leo complains in chapter 6 that certain metropolitans, granting greater weight to personal privilege, had transferred to Hilary a privilege that properly belonged to themselves.

## CHAPTER III. Hilary’s Deposition of Celidonius and Leo’s Restoration of Him Are Examined

### 1.

These two judgments must first be examined with regard to their substance and natural justice. The author of the *Life of Hilary* describes Hilary’s judgment in chapter 16 in such a way that nothing could appear fairer. It is reported that the accusers brought two impediments against Celidonius, asserting that he had taken a widow as his wife and also alleging that, while administering a secular office, he had condemned certain people to death.

The account then adds concerning the judgment:

> “Highly esteemed priests assembled from various places”—

which gives the appearance of a council—

> “The matter was examined in every way, with prudence and care. The accusation was confirmed by testimony. A true and simple decision was given: the man whom the rule of Scripture excluded should, by his own will, remove himself.”

Whether Celidonius was present at this judgment, or, if he was present, whether he made no response to the witnesses brought against him, is nowhere stated. Indeed, his appeal that followed shortly afterward, and even more clearly the contrary witnesses produced at the Roman trial, sufficiently show that he had something to answer. We therefore do not know on what grounds Quesnellus affirmed in chapter 1 that Celidonius had been convicted.

His appeal to the pontiff is expressed in these words:

> “He [Celidonius] believed that Rome must be sought, and there accused himself of having been condemned with unjust severity.”

These words are highly ambiguous. Celidonius may not have denied the alleged impediments altogether, but may only have complained of the excessive and unjust severity of the sentence. Before the pontiff he plainly lodged complaints about the falsity of the accusations and the injustice of the judgment.

Hilary likewise proceeded to Rome and submitted the sequence of events. Leo’s judgment, moreover, is clear from letter 10, chapter 3. A holy council of priests was held; witnesses were brought forward in Hilary’s presence, and they answered on Celidonius’s behalf so effectively that Hilary, sitting with the bishops, had nothing to bring against them. When questioned in the same assembly, he had no reasonable response to make; rather, he entangled himself in his own answers. Finally, as is related in chapter 7, when he was summoned to answer the case [Col. 0543A], he thought he should withdraw by a shameful flight.

Thus his judgment was set aside, and Celidonius was restored to his church. We omit for the moment Leo’s complaints against Hilary, whom Leo reports in the same chapter 3 to have said things that no layman could say and no priest could hear, and whom he asserts in chapter 2 to have diminished, with arrogant words, even the reverence due to the most blessed Peter. Nor do we now examine the sense in which Hilary’s defenders explain these statements. They have no bearing on the justice of the judgment concerning Celidonius, which alone is under discussion here, and they will be considered shortly in a more suitable place.

But from the simple account we have presented, who cannot see the fairness of Leo’s judgment? Valentinian confirms it in the *Novella*, where he clearly censures Celidonius’s deposition by Hilary. The anonymous Jurensian author of the *Life of Saint Romanus* bears more explicit witness to it, affirming of Hilary:

> “He had cast the aforesaid Celidonius down from the episcopal see without any valid reason.”

If Celidonius is believed to have been numbered among the saints, as Chiffletius indicates from the records of the Church of Besançon [Col. 0543B], this would provide another substantial confirmation. For it is incredible that a holy man would have wished not only to deceive Leo by means of false witnesses and procure an unjust sentence, but also, against his conscience, to retain until death a bishopric from which every law excluded him.

### 2.

Nor does the author of the *Life of Saint Hilary* appear to offer an objection. Although in chapter 16 he called the decision—that is, the judgment against Celidonius—“true and simple,” nevertheless in chapter 17, indicating that Leo’s judgment was contrary to Hilary’s, he declares that he does not dare to submit the judgments of such great men to examination. Whoever does not dare to do this plainly does not disapprove Leo’s judgment; if he does not approve it over Hilary’s judgment, at least he does not condemn it.

He then adds several statements that seem to contradict Leo’s account and to attribute truth and reason to Hilary, but preoccupation and deception to Leo. He says:

> “It is enough briefly to have touched upon the fact that he alone endured so much [lacuna] that he instructed those making inquiry, that he defeated those who disputed [lacuna], and that he believed those whom he had not persuaded by reason should be left behind.”

If these words refer to Hilary’s action in the case of Celidonius, while the case was being conducted at Rome in Hilary’s presence, they are utterly false according to Leo’s testimony. Hilary did not instruct those making inquiry, nor did he defeat the disputants in this case. Indeed, he had nothing that he could oppose to Celidonius and the witnesses, nor anything reasonable that he could answer in the holy council of priests. Consequently, he did not leave behind those whom he had failed to persuade by reason; rather, when summoned to answer the case, he withdrew from those whom he could not persuade by reason, since he had no reasonable response or counterargument to offer.

In chapter 1 we showed, however, that on this hypothesis Leo’s testimony must be preferred to that of the author of the *Life*, where the two accounts are thought to conflict. This is confirmed all the more by the fact that Leo is not the only one to testify to the justice of his judgment: the emperor Valentinian and the anonymous Jurensian author of the *Life of the saint* do so as well.

### 3.

In the letters just mentioned, Saint Leo reports concerning Saint Hilary matters that had not only been publicly conducted but also appear to have been entered into the public records. At the beginning of chapter 3 he first stated:

> “The sequence of events recorded in the documents demonstrates what was done and concluded among us in the case of Celidonius the bishop, and what Hilary said when he was heard in the presence of the aforementioned bishop.”

Immediately afterward he gives what is virtually a summary of the records, containing the matters we related above.

When Leo writes these things about Hilary—things that appear to have been committed to the records of a public judgment—and writes to the Gallican bishops while Hilary was still alive, Hilary could have refuted the claim by producing the fathers and records of the Roman council if anything false had been stated in the letter. Leo must therefore unquestionably be presumed to have written the truth, rather than the author of the *Life*, who wrote after both Hilary and Leo had died, concerning an event in which he himself had not participated, and who wrote not from the public records but from the report of those who favored Hilary. His obscure account envelops the matter rather than explaining it.

### 4.

I said “envelops” it. For anyone who carefully considers the entire context will find that the author not only withdraws from passing judgment on the decisions of Leo and Hilary in the case of Celidonius, but also indicates that Hilary withdrew from conducting the same case. It will therefore be uncertain to what the words refer and what particular point they suggest.

For it will not easily be understood how, without contradiction and empty boasting, one could write that Saint Hilary instructed and defeated by reason those whom he is nevertheless said not even to have persuaded by reason—if both statements are referred to the same question concerning Celidonius and to the same persons.

The author of the *Life* had previously stated that Hilary said to Leo at the outset that he had come for official duties, not for the trial; to protest according to proper procedure, not to accuse; and to submit the record of what had been done. Quesnellus seizes upon this and argues that Hilary declined every action and dispute in the case of Celidonius before the pontiff because, in his view, the custom of the Gallican churches forbade a case decided in Gaul to be reopened and examined by a new judgment at Rome.

See the third part of Quesnellus’s dissertation, chapter 3. There he does not deny, in this matter and in this sense, the truth of what Saint Leo affirmed: that Hilary had nothing to answer. As Quesnellus explains it, this was not because of lack of legal grounds, lack of evidence, or difficulty in speaking, but because Leo’s action altered the customary form of Gallican trials, and Hilary did not wish to prejudice that form.

What should be thought of this interpretation and of the entire system by which the right of the apostolic see is attacked will be discussed shortly. For now, it is enough that the adversaries themselves confess that Hilary in fact did not answer, nor did he oppose the witnesses produced on Celidonius’s behalf with anything by which he could convict them of falsehood.

That is sufficient for Leo’s judgment to be recognized as entirely just in substance. Whatever the reason Saint Hilary may have had for not opposing himself, since the justice of judgments is inferred from the allegations and proofs, Saint Leo acted most justly in restoring Celidonius after carefully examining the witnesses, who were not refuted by the man capable of refuting them.

The question here is not whether Leo could or ought to have delivered judgment against Hilary’s resistance; we shall discuss that shortly. The question for the moment is the intrinsic fairness of Leo’s judgment. Given the circumstances in which Hilary was found to have made no response, but rather to have avoided the matter by flight, no other judgment could or ought to have been rendered.

### 5.

The entire question, then, can be reduced to the issue of jurisdiction: namely, whether Saint Leo, despite Saint Hilary’s opposition, reopened and judged at Rome, by a new trial, the case of Celidonius, which had already been judged in Gaul. Quesnellus labors over this entire issue from chapter 14 to the end of his discussion, reproaching Leo as though he had acted contrary to the canons and the custom of the Gallican churches, while not only defending Hilary but also lavishly praising him for bravely resisting Leo and fighting in defense of those same canons and customs.

Thus the discussion turns from the facts to the celebrated legal question of appeals brought by bishops before the Roman see. Since this is the principal and most important issue in the present controversy—one concerning not merely Saint Leo but the distinguished prerogative of the Roman see—it must be examined with greater precision.

## CHAPTER IV. Leo’s Right in the Case of Celidonius, Judged in Gaul by Hilary of Arles; or, On the Right of Appeals to the Apostolic See

Some principles are set forth in advance by which the whole matter must be resolved. The omissions in Quesnellus’s discussion. How poorly Quesnellus has constructed Hilary’s defense. In a question of fact, which he had proposed to treat exclusively, he entangles a question of law and audaciously represents Hilary as refusing to recognize the apostolic right over episcopal appeals and as resisting it justly.

### 1.

So that we do not labor fruitlessly or wander into uncertainty, certain principles must first be established, without which the matter could not be understood and judged fairly. The entire confusion of Quesnellus’s discussion and all Quesnellus’s error arise from his failure to grasp the principles that ought to have been set forth first [Col. 0545A], or at least presumed—indeed, from his entirely passing over the principle on which the judgment in this question chiefly depends.

### 2.

Ecclesiastical jurisdiction can be established on three grounds: custom, canon law, and divine law.

Ecclesiastical jurisdiction is proved by long-standing custom, not because custom in itself grants a right, but because custom either presumes some title belonging to ecclesiastical or divine law, by which the jurisdiction was conferred long ago, or, where no title existed at the beginning, jurisdiction is shown over time to have been acquired either by the consent of those concerned or by the operation of the law itself, as occurs in cases of prescription.

Thus the ancient custom alleged at the Council of Nicaea, canon 6, in favor of the bishop of Alexandria’s jurisdiction over Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis proved his jurisdiction, which was confirmed at that same council. In the same sense, the privileges and rights of the bishop of Antioch and of the other metropolitans, which rested on custom, were likewise confirmed.

Jurisdiction is established by canon law when it is shown to have been granted to someone through canons or decretal letters, unless that jurisdiction has been abolished by some more powerful right, or prescription against it has arisen through disuse—or rather through the contrary custom of others.

Finally, jurisdiction is established by divine law when it is shown to have been conferred on someone by God himself. Such jurisdiction, however, cannot be prescribed away by any opposing custom or abolished by any human law, just as the divine law by which it was conferred is subject to no human prescription or abrogation.

Only if no limit at all was assigned to that jurisdiction by divine law may its exercise be confined by custom or ecclesiastical law within definite boundaries and procedures, for the sake of the common good and suitable order.

### 3.

This, however, can arise for two reasons. First, from the will of one who possesses unlimited divine-law jurisdiction, if, for the sake of the common good, he consents to its being restricted in some definite manner. In this way the pontiffs have consented that their own and unlimited right under divine law be circumscribed by their own decrees or those of their predecessors, by which they were plainly not bound by coercive force—for no one has authority over himself, and no equal has authority over an equal—and similarly they have consented that this right be confined within certain boundaries, or exercised in certain ways, by the decrees of particular councils. Since these councils are also subject to the pontiffs—even according to the Gallicans—the pontiffs could not be bound by their canons except by their own consent.

For the present we omit the limits established by general councils, merely indicating this one point: their decrees likewise possess the force of a general synod only by the consent of the Roman pontiffs. This is clear from the Council of Chalcedon itself, whose decree in favor of the see of Constantinople did not have the force of a general council so long as the consent of Leo and the Roman pontiffs was lacking. Nor could anyone reproach Leo or his successors for opposing that decree, since it did not bind without their consent.

If the decrees of a general synod had no binding force without the consent of the pontiffs when they prejudiced the rights of the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch—rights which were not supported by divine law but were merely ecclesiastical and had been confirmed at Nicaea—who could suppose that those decrees possessed the force of a general synod without the consent of the Roman pontiff if they were issued to restrict a pontifical right whose origin derived not from ecclesiastical but from divine institution? [Col. 0545C–D]

Second, unlimited jurisdiction under divine law can be confined within certain modes and boundaries by the authority of a superior who, possessing by divine law a greater jurisdiction, establishes for the public good a definite mode and definite limits for inferiors who preside, even by divine right. Thus no one doubts that general councils could restrict episcopal jurisdiction under divine law. The Gallican theologians and canonists themselves likewise acknowledge that episcopal jurisdiction, as regards its limitation and exercise, is subject to the jurisdiction of the pontiffs, as can be seen in Gerson and others.

### 4.

Anyone who undertakes to establish that a jurisdiction belongs to someone need only prove that it belongs to him under one of the three aforementioned headings: either by a custom that has not been abrogated, by canon law that remains in force, or by divine law, provided that it has not been limited by someone who, by divine law, possesses jurisdiction of a higher order.

But whoever undertakes to deny someone’s jurisdiction has not done enough if he proves that it is lacking under one or another heading; he must prove that it is lacking under all of them. Otherwise, the jurisdiction may belong to that person under one heading that remains untouched. The matter is self-evident and therefore requires no further explanation or confirmation. [Col. 0546A]

### 5.

Since it can happen that, in ecclesiastical courts no less than in secular ones, several persons enjoy the same judicial power or right, whether under the same or different titles, no one can complain of a violation of the right belonging to someone if another exercises jurisdiction, unless it has been established that this right, which belongs to the former, belongs to the latter under no title whatsoever.

Thus, under the discipline established among the Africans at the Council of Carthage in 416, recorded by Dionysius as canon 125, the right to hear appeals from presbyters and other clergy of inferior rank belonged both to the African councils and to the primates of the provinces. The right of the councils could not be said to have been violated if the primates judged the cases, nor the right of the primates if judgment had been referred to the councils. [Col. 0546B] 923

It also follows that one cannot properly deny someone’s right in a particular place merely because he did not himself exercise jurisdiction there, but someone else did, unless it can be proved that he did not exercise that right because it truly belonged to him under no title. Thus the right of the plenary councils of Africa to hear appeals could not be denied if, perhaps, no appeals from some African province had been brought before such councils, but all had been settled by the judgment of the primate.

Here one must apply the excellent distinction of Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, century IV, dissertation 20, proposition 2:

> It is one thing always not to use a right; it is another not to possess that right.

In this matter otherwise learned men have been deceived because they do not distinguish the substance of a right from its perpetual and uninterrupted use.

### 6.

Finally, someone may resist another in court, on behalf of his right or custom, in two ways, so that the other does not assume jurisdiction.

1. By denying that he has the right. If he denies it justly, because that right belongs to the other under no title, then he resists justly and is not obliged to obey one who lacks the right. The situation is otherwise, however, if some title supports the other’s claim. To resist one who possesses a right, and thus to resist him as though he exercised no right at all, displays manifest injustice; and if someone refuses to obey and submit to that right, this is not steadfastness but obstinacy. [Col. 0546C]

2. By insisting and urging that no one use the right belonging to him, because it is not expedient to alter established customs, or because dangers and frauds are feared. If this is done moderately, and only dangers, whatever their force, are brought forward—provided that the right itself is not denied and that the common good alone is sought—it cannot be reproved. In the same way, Aurelius, Augustine, and the other African bishops are not reproved, although they resisted overseas appeals with equal moderation in their letters to Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine.

Fault arises, however, if, out of zeal for the common good, someone oversteps the bounds of moderation in the manner of resisting; and still more if he resists so obstinately that he appears not merely to be pursuing the common good but to be denying the right of one who enjoys an indisputable right. [Col. 0546D]

### 7.

With these points established, if Quesnel wished to vindicate Saint Hilary fairly when he resisted Leo, so that judgment might not be held at Rome in the case of Chelidonius, contrary—as he thinks—to the custom of the Gallican Church, he ought to have proved:

1. That it was the custom of the Gallican Church that appellate judgments were either never received or were held only in Gaul;

2. That this Gallican custom excluded every pontifical right belonging to the Apostolic See, a right belonging to it not so much by custom as by ecclesiastical law and, above all, by divine law, by which its primacy over the Gauls was established;

3. Or at least, if he acknowledged that the Roman pontiffs possessed some right to hear appeals—especially in episcopal cases—that Hilary resisted Leo not by denying the right belonging to him, nor by resisting him as though he possessed no right, but by insisting upon custom and warning of dangers and frauds, doing so with appropriate zeal while preserving moderation, so that he neither appeared to deny the right nor violated the reverence due to the Apostolic See. [Col. 0547A]

### 8.

Quesnel does none of this. First, he establishes no custom of the Gallican Church—although it would have had to be proved by numerous appellate judgments—with even a single witness or fact. Much less does he show that it excluded every pontifical right.
