Although he devotes all his efforts to weakening certain recorded acts of appeal to the Roman See, and thus thinks that the custom has been taken away from that see, and although he also touches somewhat upon ecclesiastical law in order to remove that as well, he passes over divine law, from which the prerogatives of the Roman See chiefly derive.

Moreover, how poorly proved, and how entangled in how many fallacies, are the very matters that he either elaborates at length concerning custom or merely touches upon concerning ecclesiastical law! [Col. 0547B]

Indeed, after the beginning of chapter 14, he expressly testified that he would not discuss the law but only the bare fact of custom; he even declared that this legal question was foreign to his undertaking:

> Our entire work, our entire effort, will therefore consist in examining the fact, not in discussing the law, which is foreign to our purpose.

But what can this accomplish toward vindicating Saint Hilary when he resisted Saint Leo, if, even granting the presumed Gallican custom, Leo possessed elsewhere—especially in the very cases of appeal—a right stronger than custom, above all a divine right, against which Hilary resisted with all his strength and without due moderation?

Unless, therefore, the question of law is first discussed, and unless it is proved that Leo had no right to judge the case of Chelidonius, Quesnel’s entire discussion of the mere Gallican custom in appellate cases—which, even if proved, leaves the pontifical right in those cases untouched—would contribute nothing to a fair defense of Hilary, unless it were developed in such a way as to portray Hilary as laboring vigorously for the custom of his churches, but with due moderation, neither denying nor attacking pontifical right. [Col. 0547C]

### 9.

But is Quesnel’s discussion constructed in this way? On the contrary, anyone who reads it attentively will find a number of passages inserted in which, while he seeks to show that Leo lacked every customarily established right of appeal in Gaul, he also insinuates, not obscurely, that the pontiff possessed no other right.

Before examining the facts from which the custom is inferred, he establishes a principle indicating that, from the nature of the episcopate—which Christ instituted as one and indivisible, and of which each bishop holds a portion in full and undivided possession—it follows almost from the Lord’s own institution that appeals should be brought before the provincial or even the greater synod. Thus, he suggests, if anyone acted otherwise and sought to flee by a written appeal to foreign judges, he would rightly be considered to be striking against the harmonious concord of the bishops and rending their unity.

Here he appears to include the Roman pontiff among any foreign bishops or judges who enjoy no right of appeal. He then adds that the right to hear appeals from bishops was conferred upon metropolitans together with the provincial synod by a kind of natural right and by a custom accepted by all, which the authority of the sacred councils subsequently confirmed—as though anyone who transferred or received appellate cases elsewhere were resisting this natural right, this universally accepted custom, and the authority of the councils.

Hence, in chapter 16, he praises Hilary for steadfastness and courage when resisting Leo, and reproaches Leo as though, in receiving Chelidonius’s appeal, he had been excessively concerned with the grandeur of his see. He asserts that Leo relied chiefly upon the authority of the Sardican canons, as though no divine right supported him and only the ecclesiastical right of those canons could be invoked—although Quesnel also attempts to remove that right.

He likewise declares that the same pontiff attempted, by the authority of the emperor, to acquire a new right for himself, as though previously no such right had belonged to him under any title. [Col. 0547D–548A]

In part III, chapter 3, he portrays as Leo’s prejudice the belief that appeals ought to be brought to his see because this was owed to its authority and splendor. He asserts that Leo thereby prepared a new yoke for the Gallican churches and priests, a yoke that neither they nor their fathers had ever been able to bear; and that, if Hilary had allowed this yoke to be imposed upon the Gallican churches, his fellow bishops ought to have convicted him as both a deserter of his own dignity and a traitor to Gallican liberty.

Finally, he asserts that Hilary resisted Leo not only before the sentence but also afterward. For this reason, near the end of part I, chapter 1, he writes:

> He maintained the rights of his church to his final breath and vigorously defended them with the eloquence at his command.

And in part III, chapter 1:

> The bishop clung to the ancient privileges of his church; with the assent of the Gallican bishops, he continued throughout his life to exercise the same power, even while Leo opposed him and the emperor threatened him.

He proves this by arguing that it posed no obstacle to the reverence due to the Roman See, because it was not unknown that the prerogative of the chief bishops over inferior bishops was inactive and ineffective when nothing was claimed from the latter except in accordance with the rule of the canons. [Col. 0548B]

### 10.

These assertions cannot be considered true unless Leo is assumed to have been deprived of every right of appeal. Consequently, Quesnel’s discussion—which announced from the beginning that only the question of fact and custom was to be examined—in reality tends toward denying the law, concerning which he had professed that he did not wish to raise a question. Yet that law had not only to be investigated but also established before he inserted into his discussion the matters we have extracted from it.

What he failed to do, we shall do, so that a correct judgment may be formed concerning everything. After we have demonstrated the pontifical right with complete certainty, it will become clear whether Quesnel’s apology—which portrays Hilary as obstinately resisting Leo’s right—is an adequate defense of him or, more truly, a most serious accusation.

Indeed, since Quesnel arbitrarily attributes to Hilary disobedience after Leo’s decree itself, although he neither proved nor could have proved it, we shall understand that he has burdened Hilary far more heavily than the facts warrant. For the present, let us proceed to examine each title of jurisdiction; near the end we shall explain what a fairer defense of Hilary might be. [Col. 0548C]

## Chapter V

The title of custom asserted by Leo concerning appeals of bishops to the Roman See is vindicated, and Quesnel’s attempts to take it away from him are refuted.

### 1.

No one can be persuaded that it was the custom among the Gauls that no appeals from the judgments of provincial councils were received in Gaul, whether by other judges in Gaul or outside Gaul. Some have interpreted Quesnel’s position in this sense on the basis of what he indicated in part I, chapter 15.

That would amount to saying that the protection of appeal—introduced by the law of all nations for the sake of the innocent who had been wrongly condemned at the initial hearing, whether through error or malice—was denied to even innocent Gallican bishops if they had been unjustly condemned by the judgment of provincial councils, although this protection was not denied to clergy of inferior rank when they felt burdened by the sentence of their bishop. It would therefore mean that the condition of bishops was worse than that of clerics, which is plainly most absurd. [Col. 0548D]

If, then, Gallican bishops were permitted to appeal, there is no doubt that the custom prevailed among them that they at least sometimes appealed to the Roman pontiff, since the Sardican canons, which approve such appeals, were received by the Gauls, as will be shown in the following chapter. The points that follow will make this clearer.

### 2.

The custom of appeals, which arises from a series of cases, is proved by witnesses who either indicate particular appeals from which similar ones can be inferred, or expressly testify to the custom of appeals itself.

As regards particular appeals, given the great scarcity of ancient records, it is not necessary to demand records for every individual church. If several ancient appeals survive from different churches of the West and East, it should be enough to infer from them the custom of those churches from which, because of the ravages of time, no such documents survive—especially if those churches were subject to the Roman See by a special right and, being nearer to it, had an easier opportunity to appeal. [Col. 0549A]

### 3.

To evade this proof drawn from particular records, Quesnel first carefully examines each recorded case of Gallican judgments whose memory or indication he has found. Almost all of these, however, are cases involving bishops in which there was no appeal—as though it followed from cases in which there was no appeal that no appeal ever existed in other cases.

Thus the case of Marcian of Arles, which Quesnel discusses at length in chapter 14, is an inept basis for excluding Gallican appeals, since it contains not even the shadow of an appeal. Equally irrelevant are the cases of Euphratas of Agrippina, Paulinus of Trier, Hilary of Poitiers, Saturninus of Arles, Lazarus of Aix, and Armentarius of Embrun, none of whom even thought of appealing, as Quesnel himself reports in chapter 16. The same is true of the cases of Priscillian and Instantius, who did not appeal to the Roman pontiff from the sentence of the Council of Bordeaux.

Nor should anyone be moved by the unjust condemnation of Hilary and Paulinus, which, as Quesnel observes, would have granted both of them a special right to appeal to the Roman pontiff if the custom of appealing had then been in force. For, oppressed by the Arians, to whom would they have appealed—Liberius, the pontiff, being himself likewise oppressed by those same Arians and driven into exile for the same reason, so that he could not assist them? [Col. 0549B]

### 4.

Among these cases, in which there was no appeal, Quesnel inserts, in chronological order, the cases of Proculus of Marseille under Zosimus, Maximus of Valencia under Boniface, and Daniel, a wandering and disgraceful man, accused by the Orientals before Celestine and long sought by the Gauls for Roman judgment. These are all cases of an initial hearing, not seized by the pontiffs but brought before the Roman See either by those same Gauls—Patroclus of Arles and the clergy of the Church of Valencia—or by the Orientals. [Col. 0549C] 929

Although these cases do not involve appeals, they sufficiently show that the authority of the Apostolic See was recognized even by the Gauls in cases of initial hearing; they therefore demonstrate even more strongly that the same authority was observed in appeals. If Quesnel had proved anything against such facts, he would have proved it against cases of initial hearing, about which we shall say something in chapter 7. But for eliminating the appeals now under discussion, he would have proved nothing.

### 5.

It may be noted in passing that Quesnel displays an obvious inconsistency. In part I, chapter 6, and part II, chapters 3 and 4, he devotes all his efforts to showing that all the decrees of Zosimus establishing the rights of the Church of Arles over Second Narbonensis against Proculus of Marseille—who is said to have usurped ordinations there—were just and valid and accepted by the Gallican bishops.

Yet in chapter 16 he contends that those same decrees were void and unaccepted when they ruled against Proculus, who did not at all desist from his unauthorized ordinations even after Zosimus’s prohibition. Thus the same decrees are presented as valid and accepted whenever it suits him, but as void and rejected whenever it does not. [Col. 0549D]

### 6.

Of all the cases involving appeals, Quesnel presents and examines only two Spanish cases that bear some appearance of an appeal to the Roman See. One is the case of Basilides, a Spanish bishop who, having been deposed in the province along with Bishop Martial on the charge of idolatry, fled to Rome to Stephen and appears to have been restored by him to the episcopate together with Martial.

Quesnel had declared in chapter 16:

> It is not my intention here to inquire what was introduced by custom in other provinces, since it has no bearing on the case of Hilary.

It is evidently true that the customs of other provinces were sometimes different. Just as a custom prevailing in one place need not be thought to have prevailed elsewhere, so a custom that was not in force in one province does not thereby fail to have existed in another.

But in the matter of appeals, it is easy to understand how important it is to know the custom of Spain and of the other provinces in order to judge the case of Gaul. Although the custom may sometimes differ among provinces, if a practice is found in all the others—especially if it derives its origin in some way from divine law—the same practice must likewise be held to have existed in Gaul unless positive documents demonstrate otherwise.

Quesnel, however, could not show by positive arguments or examples—which were lacking—that appeals were excluded from Gaul. Perhaps for this reason he thought he should introduce two appeals from Spanish judgments, which he believed he could weaken, so that the same judgment might be formed about Gaul from these two Spanish examples. [Col. 0550A–B]

### 7.

How poorly he weakened the appeal of Basilides and Martial will become clear from the fact that this appeal above all proves that the custom was most ancient among the Romans. Quesnel could produce nothing that would cast doubt upon either the appeal itself or the Roman judgment in it, from which the existence and antiquity of the custom are sufficiently established.

After merely indicating the appeal and the Roman judgment, he appended certain words of Cyprian which, if they proved anything, would prove it not against the facts and custom now under discussion but against the law, which Quesnel did not wish to debate. For the passage of the holy martyr, presented as it is apart from its context, suggests that the judgment of Saint Stephen the pope in this case must be regarded as empty, since it COULD NOT rescind the valid ordination of another bishop who had been substituted in Basilides’s place. These words appear to attack not the fact but the right. [Col. 0550C]

### 8.

To make clear how improperly Quesnel has here departed from the proper course and cited Cyprian’s words contrary to Cyprian’s meaning, the facts themselves must be presented more exactly.

After Basilides, bishop of León and Astorga, and Martial, bishop of Mérida, had been deposed and restored by Stephen through an appellate judgment, Sabinus and Felix, who had been substituted for them in the episcopate, found themselves excluded as a result of their restoration, which had been decreed by the Roman judgment and, as appears, carried into execution. They therefore sent to Saint Cyprian in Africa with letters from Felix the presbyter and from the peoples of León and Astorga, as well as from Laelius the deacon and the people of Mérida; finally, they sent a letter from Felix, bishop of Zaragoza, who was interceding on their behalf.

Soon a synod was assembled at Carthage under the presidency of Cyprian. He, together with the entire synod, wrote back to the aforementioned Felix the presbyter, Laelius the deacon, and the peoples, on behalf of Sabinus and Felix and against Martial and Basilides—not because he believed Stephen lacked the right of appeal, but because he thought Stephen had been deceived by Basilides. The complete text must be quoted:

> Nor can he rescind an ordination lawfully completed, since Basilides, after his crimes had been exposed and his conscience laid bare even by his own confession, went to Rome and deceived our colleague Stephen, who was far away and ignorant of what had been done and of the concealed truth, in order to seek his unjust restoration to the episcopate from which he had been justly deposed.

This is intended to show not so much that Basilides’s offenses had been erased as that they had been multiplied, so that the crime of deception and circumvention was added to his earlier sins.

You see that one act of deception and circumvention is offered as the reason for the judgment: “Nor can he rescind an ordination lawfully completed.” Cyprian therefore wrote that the earlier judgment, by which Basilides and Martial had been deposed, must stand—not because of any defect in pontifical right, but because of the deception and fraud to which the Apostolic See does not wish its judgments to lend support. He invoked the authority of Saint Cornelius, bishop of Rome, who had decreed that such men could indeed be admitted to perform penance but were to be barred from ordination to the clergy and from priestly honor. [Col. 0550D–0551A]

The pontiffs themselves, although they certainly defended their own right, have at times declared that judgments obtained through deception could not favor deceivers. None of this, therefore, bears upon weakening the right, nor does it invalidate the practice of appeals.

### 9.

What actually happened is unclear, since only Cyprian’s letter survives. From it, however, it seems that Basilides and Martial were restored to their sees by Stephen’s judgment, so that Felix and Sabinus, having been expelled because of this, sought the protection of Cyprian and the Africans.

Thus, although Cyprian wrote against Basilides and Martial, lacking the authority by which he could exclude them or order their exclusion, he merely warned the peoples not to communicate with them as though they were actually presiding over an episcopal see. He made no mention of communion with Felix or Sabinus, who had been expelled.

Several bishops, apparently Spanish, are also indicated as communicating with Basilides and Martial; Cyprian urges that the peoples not follow their example. Since only the letters of the bishop of Zaragoza, who was more distant, were brought against them, a significant indication arises that all the neighboring bishops—not to mention nearly all the others—had at least after Stephen’s judgment adhered to them.

Perhaps the greater part of the clergy of each church had also received them or communicated with them. For out of the entire clergy of León and Astorga only one presbyter, and out of the entire clergy of Mérida only one deacon, promoted complaints against them; Cyprian’s letter is addressed solely to these men.

This division among the Spanish bishops and among the clergy, together with the communication maintained with Basilides and Martial by several bishops and clerics—while one presbyter, one deacon, and one bishop of Zaragoza are shown to have stood apart—casts some doubt upon the merits of the case itself.

Cyprian represents Stephen as having been deceived by Basilides. Someone might perhaps suspect that Cyprian himself had been deceived by Felix and Sabinus, who had been driven from their sees, so that, being far away and ignorant of what had happened and of the concealed truth, he experienced what he himself believed had happened to Stephen.

The same may most easily be supposed of Felix of Zaragoza, who was situated in a more remote part of Spain. Thus the presumption should rather favor the neighboring bishops, who appear to have communicated with Basilides and Martial.

The letters of a single presbyter or deacon, together with the people or a portion of the people, written on behalf of expelled bishops, may be attributed to special favor or faction—especially if the greater part of the clergy is thought to have communicated with Basilides and Martial together with another portion of the people.

In any event, whatever the truth may be, let us return to the question of appeals. It is worth hearing Stephen Baluze, who certainly cannot be accused of having been excessively indulgent toward the prerogatives of the Roman See. He says:

> Baronius rightly inferred from this that the most ancient practice in the Church was for bishops who believed that they had suffered injustice at the hands of their colleagues, even from the most distant regions of the world, to appeal to the Roman pontiff as the chief bishop of the universal Church.

After praising the annotation of Pamelio, who had reached the same conclusion, he adds:

> What Goulart wrote here against Pamelio is worthless.

[Col. 0551B–D] 933

### 10.

Another example of an episcopal case mentioned by Quesnel is that of Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian, who, having been condemned in their absence by the Council of Zaragoza, went to Rome to Damasus, wishing to clear themselves, as Sulpicius relates, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 48. They were not even admitted into his presence.

The Council of Zaragoza likewise belongs to Spain. It is therefore clear that an appeal of some kind was lodged, although it was not received by the pontiff, because their crimes were known and an appeal introduced in favor of the innocent ought not to become patronage for manifest heretics.

How many other appeals are read as having been rejected for the same reason by those who were acting under the most certain right?

Quesnel, however, wrongly attributes their exclusion from the pontiff’s presence to the following matter, as though this were Sulpicius’s explanation:

> For the synodal sentence against them had added that anyone who received the condemned men into communion should know that the same sentence would be pronounced against him.

Anyone who thinks that these words refer to the supreme pontiff himself must necessarily believe that the Council of Zaragoza—that is, not so much a general as a provincial synod—was superior to the Roman pontiffs.

But it was Quesnel, not Sulpicius, who alleged this as the reason for their rejection. For, in explaining the decree of Zaragoza, Quesnel had reported these words in chapter 47 before saying anything about their rejection at Rome. [Col. 0552A]

### 11.

Quesnel reports no other example of an appeal. Thus, throughout his entire discussion of the custom of appeals, in order to eliminate the custom of appealing to the Roman pontiff, he thrusts forward eight cases in which no appeal was lodged, and three in which the issue concerns an initial hearing rather than an appeal. Consequently, nothing can be drawn from them for excluding judgments of second instance; rather, something can be drawn in support of them.

He examines only two episcopal cases brought before the Roman See. Since he could not deny them, he tried to weaken not the credibility of the facts but the pontifical right, which pertains to the question in which law is at issue, not to this question, which concerns fact and custom. [Col. 0552B]

### 12.

Nor should it be thought that these are the only appeals mentioned by writers that are older than Leo. Other examples of appeals from Africa survive, which Quesnel perhaps intended to indicate and at the same time refute when he praised the Africans for resisting appeals.

We do not deny that they resisted them, although moderately, in order to prevent them with respect to the lower order—as will be established in the following chapter—not because they failed to recognize pontifical right, but because this opportunity for appeal, given the great distances between the regions, repeatedly became a refuge and scandal for wicked men. The difficulty of sending witnesses from Africa also produced dangers of deception and fraud. [Col. 0552C]

At the same time, however, they readily acknowledged several examples of episcopal appeals, which demonstrate the custom. This is clear from Augustine’s letter 209 to Pope Celestine—otherwise letter 1 among Celestine’s letters in P. Coustant, number 8:

> There exist examples in which the Apostolic See itself judged, or confirmed the judgments of others, certain persons who, because of particular offenses, were neither stripped of episcopal honor nor left altogether unpunished.

After indicating both ancient and recent examples of this kind, he adds:

> Rather than seek examples most remote from our own times, I shall mention recent ones.

He then offers three examples, all from the single province of Caesarea, and only in a particular type of judgment corresponding to Augustine’s case, in which a person was neither stripped of episcopal honor nor left altogether unpunished. From these examples everyone will infer several more from other provinces and other kinds of judgments.

P. Coustant adds this note concerning the passage:

> The power of the Apostolic See in the judgments of the Africans—and, we may add, the custom—is openly proclaimed here.

The case of Antonius, bishop of Fussala, about which Augustine speaks in the same letter, was an appeal, first to Pope Boniface, to whom the primate of Numidia himself gave his assent by providing him with letters of recommendation addressed to Boniface; and then to Celestine, to whom Augustine is shown to have sent the records, not resisting but obeying his judgment.

To omit other examples from the Africans, it will be enough to mention the appeal of Lupicinus, an African bishop, which Leo himself records in letter 12 to the bishops of Mauretania, chapter 12. Compare what we shall discuss more fully concerning these African appeals in the following chapter, no. 25. [Col. 0552D]

### 12.

The appeals of Eutyches, Theodoret, Flavian, and others from the churches of the East are famous; they will be discussed against Quesnel in the notes to the following dissertations. [935]

Also famous are the still earlier Eastern examples of Athanasius, Marcellus, and other bishops of Thrace, Coelesyria, and Palestine, who went to Rome and complained that they had been treated unjustly, as Julius I testifies in his letter to the Eusebians, no. 18. [Col. 0553A]

Nor should anyone be troubled if he denies that Athanasius’s action was properly an appeal. What difference does it make if Athanasius did not formally lodge an appeal, when, after the Eusebians—Athanasius’s enemies—had brought his condemnation before the Roman See in order to forestall the Roman pontiff, Athanasius likewise sent his own legates to the pontiff, came to Rome when summoned, and obtained judgment there? That judgment was not a judgment of first instance but of second instance, a reconsideration of the earlier judgment, and it was approved by the whole Church.

What displeases Quesnel and what he attacks with all his force is not the appeal itself but a judgment of second instance to which a judgment of first instance is subjected. If, therefore, a judgment of second instance took place in the case of Athanasius, it is entirely proper to infer from it the custom of those judgments that are usually rendered because an appeal has been lodged, and which come into question whenever appeals are debated. For this reason the ancients also rightly cited the example of Athanasius in support of appeals.

Why should we recount the cases of appeals from Illyricum, where the Roman pontiffs, especially in ancient times, exercised such a particular authority that they appointed the bishop of Thessalonica their vicar throughout Illyricum? See what Leo indicates concerning Illyrian appeals in letter 5, chapter 6, and letter 6, chapter 5, where he declares that this was done not so much as a transmission of an ancient institution as according to ecclesiastical custom. [Col. 0553B]

14. If from these examples a custom is discerned of submitting and receiving appeals to the Roman pontiff from the provinces not only of the West but also of the East, who would not infer an equal custom in Gallican cases, since the Gallican Church was subject to the Roman bishop by the same, or even some superior, right, and, being nearer to him, afforded easier submission and consideration of appeals? [Col. 0553C] Quesnellus himself admits, chapter 14, that the Gallican Church, and especially the Church of Arles, owed its origin to the Roman see. The very letter of St. Cyprian concerning Marcian of Arles, which he wrote to Pope Stephen after receiving the letter of the Gauls, demonstrates this special authority of Stephen in Gaul. Cyprian was so far from doubting—here we quote the words of P. Coustant, who is by no means suspect—that Stephen would send letters to the province and people of Arles at his own advice and urging, ordering both that Marcian be excluded and that another bishop be substituted in his place, that he also asked that the name of the person substituted be communicated to him. . . . In this affair Cyprian, by unambiguous testimony, acknowledged the authority of the Roman pontiff both to remove the bishop of Arles from his see and to substitute another in his place.

15. Paschasius Quesnellus, however, was egregiously mistaken when, in chapter 14, near the end, he wrote that the Gauls had asked Pope Stephen for nothing in Marcian’s case that they had not likewise asked of Cyprian. An Anglican heretic sang a similar tune, which Coustant also censured:

> For one should not listen to the recent writer of the Cyprianic annals, whose opinion is that Cyprian asked Stephen for nothing—which would have been to authorize him to send letters to the province—that he himself was not prepared to do, unless one understands this to mean that he would have done so had he been in the same see and place, namely, in the See of Peter.

Baluzius likewise agrees with Coustant; he too cannot be regarded as suspect. See his note 11 on Cyprian’s letter 67. Indeed, what authority over Gallican bishops had ever been granted to the bishop of Carthage, when everyone asserts that such authority belonged to the Roman bishop? Moreover, if Cyprian himself could have done this, what would he have asked from Stephen, who was reputed to be slow in such matters, through the longer circuit of correspondence in the present emergency and danger? But neither did Cyprian himself recognize in his own person the authority that he acknowledged in Stephen; nor should the Gauls be thought to have asked anything else of him except that he spur Stephen with his own letters, since they had obtained nothing from Stephen. For, as Coustant rightly observed in the same place:

> Those who preside over great affairs, when they are compelled to delay some matters either by excessive occupation or out of prudence, are often blamed as sluggish; but when they apply diligence, they can scarcely avoid the suspicion of acting precipitately.

937 16. What Quesnellus adds in the same chapter 14 is empty: that Marcian ought not to have been deposed by the authority or counsel of the Roman bishop, because, having separated himself from the Catholics in open schism, he had already long before been condemned among the authors of the schism. How many other schismatics and heretics have been deposed, even though they had openly displayed their heresy or schism, or had separated themselves from the Catholics? Were not many Catholics still in communion with Marcian because they saw that he had not yet been deposed by legitimate authority? Was it not for this reason that Faustinus of Lyons and the other bishops of that province first wrote to Stephen, asking him to exercise his authority, and then wrote to Cyprian, asking him to urge Stephen? Nor does what Cyprian adds concerning compelling bishops to elect a successor—which Quesnellus presents as though it were a synod—alter the matter. Cyprian insisted that, according to the discipline of his time, bishops were to be compelled by Stephen’s command to carry out the election and ordination alone, not the deposition. Stephen’s authority had to be interposed so that, by declaring Marcian excluded from communion by him and therefore condemned and deposed, he might compel the Gauls also to abstain from him, and order that another be elected and ordained according to custom to the vacant see.

Although these matters are not necessary to our present purpose, they have not seemed superfluous for refuting Quesnellus’s most audacious opinion. Meanwhile, the person who, as Cyprian testifies, could remove Marcian in Gaul and order the election of a successor—and could do so not so much at Cyprian’s request as at the insistence of the Gauls themselves, who had previously written to Stephen and were pressing their demand through Cyprian—could certainly, in accordance with the actual discipline of the Gauls in that period, pronounce a sentence of first instance against Marcian himself or against other bishops, much more so than merely decide a case of appeal. The fact that a first hearing in the cases of Proculus of Marseilles and Maximus of Valencia was brought by those same Gauls—by Patroclus to Zosimus and by the clergy of the church of Valencia to Boniface—confirms still more strongly that this same discipline persisted among the Gauls. Thus those who did not resist even the first hearing are plainly known to have resisted appeals still less.

17. For the present, then, it should suffice for us to believe that a custom of appeals existed in Gaul, just as we have already seen it prevailing in the other provinces of both West and East. If all, or at least more, of the acts of the pontiffs who preceded Leo had been committed to the memory of posterity, we do not doubt that appeals of several Gallican bishops would be found to have been brought to Rome and judged before that of Celidonius, with no one objecting. [Col. 0554D]

An indication of this appears faintly in the case of St. Bricius, bishop of Tours. When he had been accused of the most shameful crime, expelled from the episcopate, and Justinian had been ordained in his place—which could not have been done by the ordaining bishops without at least an implicit deposition of Bricius—he fled to Rome; Justinian also immediately hastened there, at the insistence of the people of Tours, to conduct his own case. This bears the appearance of an appeal resembling that of Celidonius. Justinian, however, died at Vercelli on the journey, and Bishop Armentius was immediately substituted for him. Perhaps frightened by Justinian’s example, Armentius refused to travel to Rome.

What was done when Bricius explained to the pontiff the circumstances that had arisen is not recorded. We know only that he was received there to celebrate the sacred mysteries. Although the Roman see’s judgment recognized his deposition as invalid and unjust, he nevertheless did not immediately seek to reclaim his see, for another reason that commends his holiness. Instead, he is said to have been restored and received by the authority of the pope after seven years; by that authority Armentius would have had to be expelled, had he not died when St. Bricius returned to Tours. Read Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 1, and book X, chapter 31.

If other documents were available, the same point would be clearer from other examples. The only thing lacking is specific Gallican documentation recording such appeals—not merely because of the notable scarcity of records in that period, a deficiency shared even by more important subjects, but also because writers passed over cases of this kind, whether exceptional or ordinary, unless they displayed something distinctive or famous. Since, therefore, the custom of Gallican appeals cannot be inferred from particular cases of Gallican bishops mentioned by writers, it must be inferred from the custom and appeals of the other Churches that we have indicated. For in the general custom of all the provinces of the West and East, to exclude the Gauls alone, without any contrary proof [Col. 0555B] or document, is plainly utterly baseless.

18. What if, in the absence of particular examples of Gallican appeals, there are suitable witnesses who most explicitly attest this older custom? The testimony of St. Leo is perfectly clear in letter 10, written to the bishops of Vienne, chapter 2:

> Let your fraternity acknowledge with us that, out of reverence for it, the apostolic see has been consulted by the priests even of your province—he is speaking of the Gauls themselves and of the Viennese—in countless reports, and that, as the OLD CUSTOM required, judgments have been either reviewed or confirmed through appeals in various cases; so that, while the unity of the spirit was preserved in the bond of peace, and letters passed back and forth, what was done in holiness might advance perpetual charity.

Quesnellus excludes this clear testimony in chapter 14 on the ground that no one is a suitable witness in his own case. Nothing could be more audacious, not to say rash. On this reasoning, councils could not be believed when they testify about their own affairs. Caesar and other historians of nations are believed when they write about their own deeds. But Leo, testifying about the custom of appeals to the apostolic see—not about a hidden matter but a public one, not in a private writing but in a public letter delivered to those same Gauls, and citing letters sent and received in both directions—is not to be believed? A witness may be called into doubt when another witness of at least equal authority is produced against him. But where there is nothing contradictory, who could introduce a reasonable doubt? Quesnellus produced no witness against Leo’s testimony; moreover, we neither can nor ought to doubt anything false concerning a pontiff so holy and so remote from any suspicion of lying or ambition.

19. Perhaps Quesnellus will bring forward the statement concerning Hilary, who is said to have asked Leo to organize the condition of the Churches according to the customary practice—as though the customary practice implied another custom of the Gallican Church, one that knew nothing of appeals brought to Rome. Does he therefore consider Hilary a suitable witness in his own case, although he did not regard Leo as suitable in his? Nor should one reply that Honoratus, or whoever the author of the *Life* may have been, ought to be trusted. For since in this passage he reports not his own words but those of Hilary, Hilary is always the witness being cited.

Besides, since the author of the *Life* wrote long after Hilary’s death, it may be questioned whether these were Hilary’s exact words. Words that pass from mouth to mouth commonly undergo some alteration through the passage of time and ordinary transmission; hence it is not certain that Hilary’s own testimony has been preserved in its authentic form. Add that the words are quite obscure and should not be set against Leo’s well-established testimony as though they clearly expressed the contrary. They are generally thought to refer to the custom of appeals, although no explicit mention of it appears in the text. But what if someone maintains that they refer only to what follows immediately afterward, asserting that certain persons in Gaul had deservedly received a public sentence and were taking part in the sacred altars in the City? For the subject proposed was not the customary practice of Gaul but that of the Churches. Against the customary practice of the Churches, however, it might seem improper for someone who had received a public sentence to take part in the sacred rites at Rome; it would not imply that appeals were received in the City, appeals that we have seen brought to Rome from all the Churches of both West and East.

If someone wishes to interpret these words as referring to the custom of appeals itself, the customary practice may be understood to concern the more frequent occurrence of such proceedings: namely, that cases were more frequently concluded in Gaul and that appeals were not very frequent. This would in no way contradict Leo’s testimony. For just as, to establish the custom of appeals to Rome in the other provinces, it is enough that some cases were repeatedly brought to the apostolic see, so it is enough in Gaul. Thus there is no reason why the custom of Gallican appeals, most explicitly asserted by Leo, should be called into doubt on the basis of Hilary’s very obscure and uncertain testimony.

Perhaps Quesnellus himself was ashamed of his proposition in chapter 14, by which he attempted to undermine Leo’s testimony on the ground that Leo was a witness in his own case. Hence in chapter 16 he wrote on another basis:

> When Leo said that, through appeals in various cases, as the ancient custom required, judgments had either been reviewed or confirmed, he was either suffering from a lapse of memory, or had been deceived by Celidonius’s flattery and imposition, or finally possessed other records among his own materials of events in Gaul that have not reached us.

The first explanation, the lapse of memory, and the second, the invented fraud of Celidonius, are unsupported by any indication. The third, however, strongly favors us, and seems to have been indicated by Leo himself when, in the passage quoted above, he cited letters that had been sent and received but are now missing. Coelestine sufficiently suggests that more acts of Gallican bishops had taken place than have reached us when, writing to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne in letter 4, no. 5, he says that many of them had spent a considerable period of time at Rome. Similarly, other testimonies from different periods record that Gallican bishops had been in that same City. The reason for the scarcity of documents remains hidden. But when the frequent visits of Gallican bishops to the Roman see make it easy to perceive how much respect they showed for the dignity and authority of that see, then, in view of such observance of its dignity and authority, there can be no doubt that several cases of appeal were brought there—cases that Leo, who was not lacking in records, sufficiently attests.

20. So that no suspicion may still remain concerning Leo’s reliability, we shall produce another, earlier witness, who was not at all implicated in Hilary’s case and was exceptionally free from partisan zeal. He is St. Innocent, who, after legislating in his letter to Victricius of Rouen, a Gaul, concerning lesser matters—that is, cases involving clergy—adds the following concerning major cases, no. 6:

> If major cases should come forward, let them be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod has established and as BLESSED CUSTOM requires, after episcopal judgment.

No one doubts that judgments concerning bishops are to be counted among major cases. When, therefore, Innocent orders that these be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, he is not referring only to reports, as some have wished to interpret him, but also to appeals, whenever such appeals seemed necessary. For he does not prescribe an empty report, but one by which the episcopal judgment is submitted to the Roman judgment, so that, wherever there is a place for an appeal, the matter is entrusted to the authority and discretion of the Roman bishop: according to his pleasure, he may appoint judges in the province, send a legate from his side, or judge the matter himself in the City, as the Council of Sardica prescribed.

This is surely why Innocent immediately mentioned that synod, when he said, “as the synod has established.” Nothing similar is recorded as having been established at Nicaea. Apart from the Nicene canons, however, only the Sardican canons were cited by the Romans of this period under the name of the Nicene canons. The Sardican council explicitly established provisions concerning appeals of bishops to the Roman see in canons 3, 4, and 7.

Coustant, note c, argues that these words should be referred not to those canons but to the letter of the same synod to Julius, in which it declares that it is fitting, and most fitting indeed, that priests should report the Lord’s affairs from each and every province to the see of the Apostle Peter. But of these words, which do not take the form of a statute, one could scarcely say, “the synod has established,” as one can most properly say of the canons cited. Moreover, anyone who considers the individual citations of the ancient decretal letters will see that the Roman pontiffs, when citing statutes, invoked only the Nicene and Sardican canons that were attached to the Nicene canons and inscribed under the name of Nicaea; this will perhaps be demonstrated more fully elsewhere. Accordingly, Hincmarus, the Gallican bishop, in volume II, p. 774, interpreted this text of Innocent most correctly as referring to appeals.

Furthermore, the words “blessed custom”—or, as other older manuscripts read, “ancient custom”—which confirm Leo’s testimony, are indeed absent from the manuscripts of Dionysius and the others followed by Sirmondus, Labbeus, and Quesnellus. But they are found in the manuscripts of three very ancient Italian collections: Vatican Regina 1997, Barberini 2888, and Lucensis 88; also in manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, in the Oxford manuscript of the Quesnellian collection, in the very ancient Colbert manuscript 784, and in another Colbert manuscript, 3368, cited by P. Coustant and in Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 45, chapter 12. The Roman editions and the older editions of the councils follow these readings. Coustant therefore retained the words and strengthened them with other testimonies of the same Innocent.

21. But now it is time to pass from custom to ecclesiastical law. For custom alone does not establish the right of the apostolic see in appeals. Rather, since custom, as we saw in chapter 4, does not in itself confer a right but presupposes one from elsewhere, whether from ecclesiastical or divine law, everyone will recognize much more clearly that the custom of appeals that we have thus far established for the Roman pontiff is legitimate and introduced by law, once we have explained first ecclesiastical law [Col. 0557C] 943 and then divine law. It will be evident that Quesnellus accomplished nothing in this entire discussion: relying solely on custom, he wrongly attempted to weaken it, while he either touched only lightly and captiously upon the other, principal titles of ecclesiastical and divine law, or passed them over.

## CHAPTER VI. On Appeals to the Roman See by Ecclesiastical Law

The fourth Antiochene canon, which appears to exclude every appeal, is examined. The Sardican canons are explained. Quesnellus’s fabrications concerning them are dispersed. How widely they were received even in Gaul. What is to be said about the African canons. Papal constitutions concerning appeals. An observation on the canon of the First Council of Constantinople.

1. We inquire into the ecclesiastical law of appeals not because we believe that the right of appeal belongs to the Roman see by ecclesiastical law—for it flows from the higher law of God, which is implicitly presupposed in the ecclesiastical law establishing appeals to the Roman see—but for this reason: to expose Quesnellus’s fabrications, which he inserted into this part of his dissertation as well. [Col. 0557D]

2. He first brings forward, in chapter 15, the fifth Nicene canon, where cases of appeal are remitted for discussion to provincial synods. But apart from the fact that this canon speaks only of cases involving laymen and clergy, not bishops, it designates as judges of appeals those whose consideration was more readily accessible in each place, so that the pontiff nevertheless cannot be said to have been excluded.

Indeed, it is clear from the following that by this decree the Nicene synod did not reject appeals to the apostolic see: at the Council of Sardica, which was composed of many of the Nicene Fathers and was regarded as a kind of appendix to the Council of Nicaea, such appeals are expressly approved. For one should not believe that the same Fathers contradicted themselves, or that they erased from this matter the synod for whose protection they had labored so strenuously. By the same reasoning, it is understood that the second canon of the Council of Constantinople, which Quesnellus adds because it prescribes the same Nicene rule in the very cases of bishops, poses no obstacle.

3. What is brought forward from canon 15 of the Council of Antioch may appear stronger. It is expressed in these words:

> If a bishop accused of specific crimes is condemned by all the bishops of the same province, and all unanimously issue the same form of decree against him, he is in no way to be judged by others, but the sentence of the bishops of the province, who have agreed together, is to remain firm.

Those who wish the judgments of provincial synods to be unappealable even in cases involving bishops rely on this canon. Quesnellus magnified it in part I, chapter 15, as though a sentence issued by all the bishops of one province neither ought nor could be reviewed by other bishops.

Some will reply here that the Antiochene canons were issued by the Arian Eusebians, and that for this reason they were rejected by Innocent I in letter 7, chapter 3. But setting this aside—for we shall reveal the true authors of these same canons in volume III, in the treatise on the ancient collections of canons, where the Greek collection will be discussed—we observe first of all that canon 15 does not abolish every appeal or review. It merely denies, when all the bishops of one province agree, the new hearing by bishops of a neighboring province that had been granted in the preceding canon.

As for the right of appeal or review before a fuller synod or another higher tribunal, it says not a word. Moreover, canon 15 excludes a new hearing only in a case in which the crime is so manifest that all the bishops agree in the condemnation, with not even one bishop dissenting. This does not ordinarily happen in legitimate trials, instituted without haste or prejudice, except when the accused has either confessed or at least been convicted. In such a case some civil laws, both ancient and more recent, also forbid an appeal.

The Antiochene Fathers could therefore reasonably have judged it equitable in their provinces not to reject an appeal when someone considered himself unjustly burdened. They had adequately provided for a new hearing before a fuller synod in canon 12:

> If a bishop should perhaps be condemned by a synod . . . he ought to appeal to a greater council of bishops, present to the larger number of bishops what he believes to be just, and await their examination and judgments.

But if, even in circumstances in which a bishop had been condemned by the sentence of all the bishops of his province, he should feel himself burdened for some reason, and if every appeal or renewal of judgment is to be regarded as removed by canon 15, then this canon was certainly never received in that sense either by the Greek or by the Latin Church. Consequently, in both East and West, cases of appeal always remained in force, and the authority of the later Sardican canons prevailed. By sanctioning access to appeals, those canons corrected the Antiochene canon and at the same time safeguarded the right of the apostolic see in appeals.

[Col. 0558D] 4. The Sardican canons, then, which clearly assert appeals to the Roman bishop, must be treated more fully. Before discussing them, it is worth observing what Quesnellus himself noted in letter 6 to Anastasius of Thessalonica. When St. Leo, in chapter 5 of this letter, reserved the appeals of Illyricum to himself, he says, the reason for the exception is, as Quesnellus states in note 6, that the Illyrian provinces, as a portion of the Western regions, belonged to the Roman pontiff by a SPECIAL RIGHT.

Here he admits that the Roman pontiff possessed a special right in cases of appeal throughout the whole West, even over the Greek Illyrians, who were so far distant and had the bishop of Thessalonica as vicar of the apostolic see; consequently, all the more over the Gauls, who were Westerners and nearer to Rome. Yet in this dissertation he attempts to deny this right.

He continues in that note as follows:

> What St. Leo writes here concerning appeals, he asserts from the Sardican canons, as the mention of the ancient institution and reverence for the apostolic see demonstrates.

Thus he traces this right to the Sardican canons, although in chapter 15 of part I of the dissertation cited above he strives to distort those canons in a remarkable way. Behold the man’s extraordinary consistency. And how many errors he has woven into a few short periods in this effort! So that the whole matter may be known clearly and with certainty, we shall first quote the canons themselves and then offer a more accurate explanation.

5. The relevant canons are found in Dionysius Exiguus as canons 3, 4, and 7; the last is more correctly numbered canon 5 in the Greek. It is sufficient to transcribe this final part of canon 3, which alone concerns the present matter and is for that reason set out under a separate number in the manuscripts of other ancient Latin collections:

> If one of the bishops has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good case, so that the council may be renewed again—thus Dionysius; the other Latin collections, together with the Greek, read “judgment”—if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the Apostle Peter, so that those who examined the case may write to Julius, the Roman bishop—other Latin collections add: “or the bishops who reside in the neighboring province.” If he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that the acts already performed should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall be confirmed. Does this please everyone? The synod replied: It pleases us.

Canon four:

> Bishop Gaudentius said: If it pleases you, let this be added to the sentence which you have delivered, full of holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places, and he has proclaimed that his case must be conducted in the City of Rome, let another bishop absolutely not be ordained to his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

Canon seven, elsewhere five:

> Bishop Hosius said: It was also decided that if a bishop has been accused, and the assembled bishops of his region have judged and cast him down from his rank, and if the one who has been cast down appeals and flees to the bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, if the Roman bishop thinks it just that the judgment or examination of the case be renewed, let him deign to write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they may carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth. But if the one who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his side, it shall be in the power of the bishop to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. And if he decides that those who are present should be sent to judge together with the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, it shall be within his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most prudent counsel.

6. These canons appear to have been enacted against the Eusebians. Just as, against those who had earlier unjustly condemned St. Athanasius and, by denying him every hope of restoration, had elected a successor in the Antiochene pseudo-synod, the Sardican Fathers wrote synodical letters declaring the Alexandrian bishop innocent and restoring him to his see, so they appear to have enacted these canons to silence the unjust complaints of the Eusebians against Pope Julius, as though he had violated the rights of the Eastern synods when he undertook to judge the cases of Athanasius and other Eastern bishops who had fled to the Roman see after their deposition.

They preferred the following principle—as is clear from Julius’s letter to them and from their own pseudo-synodical letter at Sardica: just as the Eastern bishops did not subject to their judgment cases decided by Western bishops, but accepted their judgments as valid, so neither should the Western bishops, nor the Roman pontiff himself, interfere in the affairs of the East or review the judgments of Eastern synods, as though nothing were subject to the primacy of the Roman see.

7. To discern the genuine meaning of these canons, it must be observed that the words of the third canon, “If one of the bishops has been judged in some case,” indicate the condemnation or deposition of a bishop, as is gathered from canon 4, where a deposed bishop is discussed. The words “If it pleases you, let this be added to the sentence,” and so forth, clearly indicate that this fourth canon refers to the same case as the preceding canon.

For this reason Dionysius also placed a reference to a condemned bishop in the title of chapter 3: “If a condemned man appeals to the Roman pontiff.” Dionysius, as well as the author of the Quesnellian collection in its title and Ferrandus in his *Breviary*, assumed that this canon concerned an appeal to the Roman pontiff. They appear to have inferred this from the fact that the entire matter is submitted for decision to the supreme pontiff.

But if a bishop’s own appeal to the apostolic see had been inserted here by a deposed bishop, Hosius would have expressed it clearly in the canon itself, as he did in canon 7, elsewhere 5; nor would the same decree have had to be repeated at the beginning of canon 7. Certainly the words of the third canon indicate nothing more than that the subject is a bishop condemned in the first hearing who, as was customary, seeks a new hearing of his case from the bishops of his province:

> He thinks that he has a good case, so that the council may be renewed again.

This second-hearing judgment was sought, according to the easier and more frequent practice, where no express appeal to the apostolic see had intervened, by summoning neighboring bishops into a synod. It is decreed, however, that in honor of the memory of St. Peter the judges of the first sentence themselves write to Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges that a new hearing should be held, he is to appoint judges from the neighboring bishops; hence, after this second judgment by bishops who reside in neighboring places, something is added in canon 4.

8. It should further be observed that only in this third canon did the Fathers employ the formula, “Let us honor the memory of the Apostle Peter.” Where no express appeal to the Roman see intervened, the new judgment that was sought was ordinarily obtained from neighboring bishops, as is clear from canon 14 of Antioch and from other testimonies; apostolic authority was not necessary for this.

Since, therefore, the Sardican Fathers ordered this procedure to be observed not by a right that compelled them, but out of reverence for the apostolic see, so that by this means they might promote the authority and honor of that see, which the Eusebians had attempted to diminish, they appear to have used this formula. In doing so, they had regard to the papal primacy.

For those same Fathers did not show this honor to the Roman see because they thought that no right in appeals belonged to it—a point they sufficiently declared in the following canons—but because, even in the case where judges were to be appointed from neighboring provinces, they believed that such judges would be appointed more quickly by the see which, by reason of its primacy, had jurisdiction over all the provinces of the Church than by a metropolitan bishop, who in himself possesses no jurisdiction over the bishops of a neighboring province.

They refrained from this formula in the following canons, where the discussion concerns an appeal properly so called to the supreme pontiff, because here they recognized not merely an honor that was otherwise unnecessary, but the proper right of that same see. The words of the cited canon, “If it pleases you,” are not the words of people trembling and hesitating, as Quesnellus wrongly interpreted them. They were a common formula, as is clear from other canons of the same council, which, although they established definite and most just laws, admitted no hesitation or fear.

9. The distinction between canon 3 and canon 7, elsewhere 5, is thus readily understood. The former concerns a mere request for a new judgment without an appeal to the Roman pontiff; the latter concerns an appeal properly so called to the Roman bishop, to whom the deposed bishop is said to flee and before whom he advances the judgment of the appeal. For this reason canon 7, elsewhere 5, but not canon 3, was inserted by Zosimus into the *Commonitorium* that he gave to the legates sent to the Africans in 418, when he wished to prove an appeal properly so called confirmed by the Sardican council.

In this case of appeal, Hosius proposed two methods of judgment, if the Roman bishop should think it just that the examination be renewed. The first was that he should deign to write to the bishops who were in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they might carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth. This was a form of delegation, and the more obvious and easier one.

The second was that he should send from his side a presbyter—or, according to the Greek, presbyters—who would judge in person together with the bishops of the neighboring province, possessing the authority of the one by whom they had been sent. This was the more explicit form of delegation, and it was rarer and more difficult; for that reason it required the particular petition of the appellant.

10. It remains to explain the fourth canon. This is an appendix to canon 3, as is indicated by the words, “Let this be added, if it pleases you, to the sentence which you have delivered, full of holiness.” The following words appear to indicate that this addition concerned the hypothesis in which the deposition of a bishop, decreed by the bishops of his own province in the first judgment, had also been confirmed in the second judgment by the neighboring bishops whom the Roman pontiff had appointed as judges:

> When a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places—

that is, by the second judgment, which could concern only the neighboring bishops.

If, therefore, the person who had been deposed, refusing to acquiesce even in this judgment, should proclaim that his case must be conducted in the City of Rome, it is decreed that another bishop should absolutely not be ordained to his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

Although two uniform judgments of deposition had preceded—one in the council of the bishops of the same province, the other by the bishops of neighboring provinces—a third judgment was granted by virtue of an appeal to the apostolic see, an appeal that the deposed bishop, as the third canon presents the matter, had not previously interposed in the proper sense. This third judgment was to take place in the City, so that the case might be concluded in the judgment of the Roman bishop. From this, perhaps, the ecclesiastical practice of granting three judgments arose.

### 11.

We have followed the Latin reading, which in this canon especially is the same not only in all of Dionysius’s manuscripts, but also in six codices [Col. 0561C] of other collections. Although these collections agree at the root of the Sardican canons with Dionysius’s edition, they do not derive from Dionysius—namely, the Veronese 58, the Vatican Regina 1997, the Barberinian 2888, the Lucan, the Quesnellian, and the Hispanic collections. This most strongly confirms what Dionysius expressly asserts:

[Note: [Col. 0561D] In his letter to Stephen of Salona he says: “The decrees also of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which have been published in Latin, etc.” Therefore, just as the African canons were certainly published in Latin, so too were the Sardican canons.]

Dionysius Exiguus expressly asserts that the original of these canons was Latin. For translations of different origin from the Greek could not have preserved so great a similarity. The reading of these canons also agrees with the reading of the two canons that were brought out from the Roman archive by Zosimus in the case of Apiarius and inserted into the memorandum of the legate Faustinus, and which were recited at the Council of Carthage in 419.

But if one insists that the Greek text was the original, it will have to be said that there were two original versions written at Sardica: one Latin for the Latins, who were more numerous there, and another Greek for the Greeks, whose case in particular the council was handling. Certainly the Latin text is fuller and more complete. For although two canons are read in Greek containing matters peculiar to the Greeks [Col. 0561D], which could have been omitted in the Latin text, nevertheless several matters not peculiar to the Latins have so far emerged only from the Latin; and several passages of the Latin text also present a clearer and more suitable meaning than the Greek.

Perhaps we shall discuss this double original of these canons more fully in volume III, in the treatise on the Collections of Canons.

### 12.

Although the Greek reading of the fourth canon does not offer so explicit a mention of an appeal and of a trial to be held in Rome as the Latin reading does, nevertheless the same thing is in fact sufficiently indicated by the words translated from the Greek. These words require the Roman bishop’s investigation, without mentioning any new delegation of other judges, in order that the case may be brought to an end:

> If any bishop has been deposed by the judgment of the bishops who are in the vicinity, and says that he ought again to have an opportunity for defense, no other person shall be substituted in his see before the Roman bishop, having investigated the matter, has brought it to an end.

Certainly, it cannot be denied that one who can investigate a case through delegated judges or through a legate can, by the same right, also decide it personally. The very formula of Hosius, in which, while proposing the delegation of neighboring bishops or the dispatch of a legate, he says, “may he deign to write,” does not impose a law upon the pontiffs, but refers to easier and more expeditious methods of hearing appeals within the province, chosen by those same pontiffs. Nevertheless, it does not prohibit them, whenever this seems expedient, from hearing cases outside the province, just as Julius did at Rome with the approval of the Sardican Fathers, and as the same Fathers of Sardica afterward judged the case of Athanasius of Alexandria in Dacia.

Thus the Greeks themselves understood the Sardican canons before they slipped into the Photian schism: namely, that the Roman pontiffs could hear and judge cases of appeal either through delegates or personally. Let the elder Theodore Prodromus be heard, who, before the schism, was the first of all to interpret the sacred canons in his celebrated work *On the Interpretation of the Canons* (*περὶ ἑρμηνείας κανόνων*). Here are his words on the Sardican canons, published from a manuscript of the same work by Nicolaus Comnenus Papadopoulos in the *Mystagogical Preliminary Instructions*, p. 367:

> πάντοτε, καὶ ἐν πάσῃ τῇ κρίσει τοῖς κατακριθεῖσιν ἔξεστι τὸν Ῥώμης τῆς πρεσβύτερος ἐπικαλέσαι κἀκείνου ὀρίζοντος, κριθῆναι πάλιν, παράτε αὐτοῦ, ἢ τῶν ἀποστόλων αὐτοῦ.

That is:

> Always, and in every judgment, those who have been condemned may appeal to the Roman bishop, and, at his command, be judged again, either by him himself or by his legates.

### 13.

Quesnellus’s errors can now easily be detected. First, it is false that he says the origin of these appeals is owed to this council. For in the two canons, 4 and 7, which speak of an appeal to the Roman pontiff, one finds nothing that establishes, or even slightly indicates, the creation of a new right. The faculty of lodging or receiving such appeals is not granted; it is presupposed as established. Only in canon 7 is a different procedure designated, dependent upon the pontiff’s pleasure. Canon 4, meanwhile, restrains the audacity of those who, while an appeal to the apostolic see is pending, attempt to appoint a successor to a bishop as though he had been absolutely deposed. This seems to have been enacted, in some measure, against the Eusebians, who, after Athanasius’s case had been brought to Rome, had consecrated Gregory bishop of Alexandria in the pseudo-synod at Antioch.

Moreover, canon 7, when it declares that apostolic delegates, if the pontiff judges that they should be sent, possess the authority of the one by whom they were appointed, clearly shows that the right in such cases was not granted by the council but belonged to the pontiff himself. This right, in appeals—not so much in those of the West as of the East—can be referred solely to the primacy, by which the Roman bishop presides over all bishops of both East and West, not merely in rank but also in jurisdiction.

That the right of appeal has its root in the primacy will become clear in the following chapter. When the emperor Valentinian III, in the letter inserted into the collection of Chalcedon and counted among Leo’s letters as Letter 55, asserted that Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, had appealed from the judgment of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus to the Roman see “according to solemnity”—or, according to the Greek, “according to the solemn custom of councils,” which had especially become established after the Sardican canon—he attributed the origin of this matter not to the Council of Sardica but to the primacy.

For, after mentioning that primacy, by which the Roman bishop possesses the position and authority to judge concerning faith and priests, he added:

> For by this grace [that is, the primacy], according to the solemn custom of councils, the bishop of Constantinople also appealed to him [the Roman bishop] by written petitions.

### 14.

[Col. 0563A] Secondly, it is false that the Sardican Fathers decreed nothing concerning appeals, but merely granted the Roman bishop the power to order the reconsideration or revision of a case, as the most illustrious Peter de Marca demonstrates in *On Concord*, book VII, chapter 3, and as is evident from the very reading of the Sardican canons.

If this proposition is joined to the preceding one, an obvious contradiction immediately appears. In the first, the origin of appeals is attributed to Sardica; here, it is said that Sardica decreed nothing concerning them. Even if canon 3 does not expressly mention an appeal in the proper sense, the reading of canon 7—or canon 5—makes it manifest. And no one will deny that a judgment of revision or reconsideration, when it is instituted by a superior authority of the Roman see through judges appointed for that purpose, as happens here, is in reality equivalent to a judgment of appeal—unless someone wishes pointlessly to play with synonymous expressions and deceive the inexperienced.

Quesnellus’s error arose from the fact that, following de Marca, he supposed that the Roman bishop was required, by virtue of these canons, to entrust the case to the original judges, adding other bishops from the neighboring regions, or even a legate. But when the original judges must also give their votes in a new judgment, he calls it not a true appeal but a mere revision by the same judges.

How false this hypothesis is, everyone will understand from the explanation of the canons given above. Canon 7, or canon 5, plainly states that neighboring bishops are to be designated; and the words of canon 3, “let him appoint judges,” must be understood in the same sense. But concerning the admission of the original judges, there is not a word.

We also demonstrated shortly before, from canon 4, the falsity of Quesnellus’s assumption that Sardica approved only a reconsideration to be decided within the province itself. This is confirmed by the practice immediately following, which is the most secure interpreter of canons and laws. For several cases of appeal mentioned in the preceding chapter are recorded as having been decided at Rome, so that neither the case of Chelidonius was the first example of this kind, nor did Saint Leo depart in this judgment from the Sardican discipline.

### 15.

From the preceding chapter it is also clear that Quesnellus’s further assertion is false [Col. 0563C]: namely, that this synod was not immediately received by the bishops of the East, or even by those of the West. For the examples that we indicated there, although few because of the scarcity of documents, nevertheless sufficiently prove that the Sardican discipline was received both in the East and in the West.

It must especially be observed in this matter that the Sardican canons do not command appeals to the Roman bishop in every case, as though they prohibited other means of obtaining a new judgment that prevailed in the provinces. Rather, they affirm that appeals, when lodged, are legally lodged and are to be resolved by the pontiff, either through delegated judges or personally.

Therefore, to show that this discipline was received, it is not necessary to produce many examples of such appeals immediately afterward. It is enough to indicate a few whose memory has survived. Anyone who dares to assert that the discipline was not received must produce examples of cases in which Eastern and Western bishops resisted an appeal.

Something could be brought forward in this matter from the Africans alone, but we shall explain shortly why it does not constitute an obstacle. From the other Westerners or from the Easterners, however, there is nothing—unless, perhaps, one introduces the schemes of those wicked men who perversely resisted the Roman judgment concerning Saint Athanasius even after the Sardican synod.

### 16.

Quesnellus further adds that, perhaps for this reason, the Easterners did not include the canons of this council in their collections, nor did the Gauls. As regards the Eastern collection, or the Eastern code of canons, we do not understand how he can prove this in the first place.

The Greek code used by John the Scholastic, later patriarch of Constantinople and an author of the sixth century, contained these canons. Nor should one believe Christopher Justellus, who published a Greek code of canons without the Sardican canons. For this Justellian collection was not discovered by him in any Greek manuscript; it was fabricated from his own ingenuity.

The title placed at its head—*Code of the Canons of the Universal Church* [Col. 0564A]—is so utterly false, as Coustantius proved, that it sufficiently reveals the fiction. Justellus cites no manuscript witness except the royal codices of canons with the commentaries of Zonaras and Balsamon, which he used to correct the Greek text of Tilius’s edition. Hence the code published by Justellus is in reality identical with the codices of Tilius, Zonaras, and Balsamon, in which the Sardican canons are read; they were omitted arbitrarily, solely because of Justellus’s prejudice.

A Palatine codex of Stephen of Ephesus is cited as entirely corresponding to the supposed code of the Universal Church. But it is evident that this is asserted without basis, since Justellus himself confessed in the preface, p. 16, of volume I of the *Bibliotheca of Ancient Canon Law* that he had been unable to obtain it.

The Greek code that Dionysius Exiguus translated into Latin seems to have lacked the Sardican canons, as may be gathered from his letter to Stephen of Salona. But whether other Greek codes of canons likewise lacked them cannot be asserted, since the aforementioned John of Antioch, who flourished shortly after Dionysius in the same century, had obtained an older exemplar that contained the Sardican canons along with other canons.

This certainly suggests that canons written in Greek existed among the Greeks from the time of the synod itself. The evidence is not so much the different order of these canons from the Latin as certain canons that were omitted by the Latins and therefore could not have been taken from the Latin code.

For this reason we have also found, in the most ancient Veronese manuscript 55, a Latin translation of these same canons written more than a thousand years ago. It was taken from a Greek code apparently similar to the one possessed by Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and the Fathers of Chalcedon themselves, as will be demonstrated more fully in volume III. It is therefore clear that these canons existed in at least other Greek codices also in the time of Chalcedon.

Furthermore, the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople, in their letter to Damasus and the Westerners, no. 5, cited one of the Sardican canons—not obscurely, although they cited it under the name of Nicaea. From this it is known that these canons were in use among the Greeks at so early a date.

More will be discussed on all these matters in the aforementioned volume III, in the treatise on the ancient Collections, part I, chapters 1 and especially 6.

### 17.

As for the Gallican collection, or the Gallican codices of canons, Quesnellus’s assertion is utterly false. For the Sardican canons are found in all the ancient collections of the Gauls, such as the Quesnellian, the Colbertine 1868, cited by Coustantius in the preface to volume I of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 77; the Fossatensian and the Morbacensian, which resembles the ancient Palatine codex 574.

This last collection presents an older and purer codex of the Gallican Church. Apart from the Nicene and Sardican canons, which were placed under the Nicene canons according to Roman usage, it contains no canons other than Gallican ones. Thus it is known that in ancient times the Gallican Church, like the Roman Church, received not the Antiochene but the Sardican canons.

Here one must especially observe how far Quesnellus departs from the truth and from the reliability of the ancient Gallican codices. In part III, chapter 1, he says that Saint Hilary resisted Leo in Rome in this case in defense of the canons certainly received in Gaul, because the canons received there did not permit the case of Chelidonius to be reopened and examined in a new judgment, as he explains in chapter 3.

He could have meant the Antiochene canons, by which alone he thought appeals were excluded; yet those canons had not been received in Gaul. Conversely, he represents the Sardican canons—which approve appeals—as not received in Gaul, although they are found received in every Gallican codex with the same honor as the Nicene canons.

Is this not to represent the true as false and the false as true?

### 18.

Nor should it be answered that, when Quesnellus denied that the Sardican canons were inserted into the code of canons, he meant a public code approved by the Gallican Church in some synod, of which none of those mentioned was such a code.

For this hypothesis of a public code in those ancient times of which we are now speaking is utterly groundless. No such code then existed.
