On this reasoning, not only the Sardican but also the Nicene canons—which are copied in the aforementioned codices in the same manner and cannot be shown in any other code approved by the public authority of the Gallican Church—would have to be said not to have been received by the Gauls. That would plainly be absurd.

Who, moreover, could deny that the Sardican canons were received in some manner by the Gauls even in a synod, if he considers that several bishops of Gaul took part in the Council of Sardica, where those same canons were established and confirmed by the subscriptions of the bishops?

### 19.

Nor does Quesnellus’s conjecture help to exclude the Sardican canons from the Gallican codices merely because they are not mentioned in Leo’s letter to the people of Vienne—Letter 11, now 9—in which he complains of the violation, as Quesnellus thinks, of the right of appeal against Hilary.

For can such a negative conjecture, which may waver for many reasons, be preferred to the certain and ancient codices of the Gauls that contain the Sardican canons?

Saint Leo passed over these canons in the aforementioned letter for the reason that he thought it necessary to insist not so much on custom as on the higher right of the primacy. Moreover, Valentinian, who in the same case of Hilary issued a famous novel constitution on the basis of Leo’s report and judgment, sufficiently indicated these canons when, at the beginning, he mentioned the authority of the sacred synod.

### 20.

It remains for us to make some observations concerning the Africans, whom Quesnellus presents in three chapters—14, 15, and 16—as opponents of the Sardican discipline.

First, however, it is pointless to bring forward African resistance when the question concerns not African but Gallican discipline, especially since the Gauls received the Sardican canons by inserting them into their codices, whereas the Africans, when they resisted, plainly did not know them.

The case in which the Africans opposed appeals after the Council of Sardica was the case of Apiarius. That they resisted in this case because they were ignorant of the Sardican decrees is clearly demonstrated by the fact that, when those decrees were presented to them by the Romans as Nicene, they not only wrote in their letter to Coelestine that these canons were not found even in the authentic Nicene canons, but also, indicating that they had examined other synods as well, added: “In no synod of the Fathers have we found this established.”

From this it is evident that, despite the diligence then employed, they nowhere found the acts of Sardica, in which those canons would have been found.

[Note: [Col. 0565] See note 5, preceding volume, col. 1515, note b, in Quesnellus’s observations on Letter 13.]

For at that time the Africans knew no other Council of Sardica except the one that the Arians held at Philippopolis after departing from Sardica, whose encyclical letters they fraudulently headed with the name of Sardica. Hence Augustine wrote in book III of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 34:

> Learn, then, what you do not know: the Council of Sardica was Arian, as has long been known.

But those who resisted the canons of the true Council of Sardica for the reason that they had not found them in any synod of the Catholic Fathers did not properly reject the canons of that synod. Rather, they showed that they would have received them had they known the true Council of Sardica and found the canons in it.

Coustantius himself admits this candidly (*The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 1062, note e), although he is otherwise by no means favorable to such appeals. In his note on these words of the Africans he writes:

> If, therefore, they had learned that this had been established at the Council of Sardica, in which Gratus, bishop of Carthage, took part, they would apparently have accepted it without difficulty.

And again, in note d on Zosimus’s Letter 15, he confirms the point in this way (ibid., p. 982):

> It was enough for him [Zosimus] to propose the authority of the Sardican synod to the Africans, who in canon 10 of the Second Council of Carthage profess, and in chapter 13 of the Code of the Canons of the African Church repeat: “The ancient statutes must be observed by us.” Nor did he have to fear that they would reject decrees which they would have learned had been approved by their own primate [and, add, from Athanasius, by thirty-five other African bishops], either by their presence or by their subscription.

The Africans write in Letter 2 to Coelestine, no. 4, that they could not concede the decrees which Zosimus had called Nicene, only for this reason:

> Because, they say, we have found no such thing written in any synod of the Fathers.

Who would doubt that, if they had found it established in so grave a synod, they would immediately have obeyed Zosimus’s will? Tillemont likewise admits the same point in article 324 of his *Life of Augustine*, volume XIII, p. 864.

Since the Gallican bishops had examined these canons and had also received them in their own codices, they could not, according to the very reasoning of the Africans, have resisted them. Consequently, African resistance proves nothing concerning an equivalent resistance by the Gauls.

It is especially strange and absurd that those very people who know that the Sardican canons were issued by a most grave and ancient synod, and who admit that they had already been received in all the Latin and Greek codices of canons, should so frequently bring forward African resistance against the right of appeal to the Roman pontiff asserted in those same canons.

Nicolaus Comnenus Papadopoulos refutes the Photian Greeks excellently on this point in the *Mystagogical Preliminary Instructions*, response 6, section 2, no. 15, p. 366:

> If Zosimus’s assertion did not convince the Africans, who were ignorant of the Council of Sardica, would it not convince the Photian Greeks, who know the Council of Sardica, receive it, and receive it as having the force of ecclesiastical discipline?  
>   
> The Africans said: “We recognize none of its canons, nor is any of them held among us.” Can you yourselves make the same assertion, when Harmenopulus repeatedly brings the canons of the Council of Sardica before you, and Photius, Balsamon, Aristenus, Margunius, and finally all who have given even a brief explanation of the canons expound them fully?

Therefore, the judgment of the African Fathers is of no use to you with respect to the matter under discussion. If it is valid even against schismatic Greeks, it ought much more strongly to prevail against those Latins who are utterly removed from schism and cannot deny that the Sardican canons were received especially by the Latin Church.

### 21.

Secondly, it is false that, when the Africans resisted the canons recorded in Zosimus’s memorandum because they were ignorant of the true Council of Sardica, they in reality resisted them with the intention of excluding episcopal appeals, which are the subject here.

Certain words in the Africans’ letter to Pope Boniface may give rise to a considerable suspicion that, when they resisted Sardican canon 5, otherwise canon 7, which concerns episcopal appeals, they also resisted in order to reject such appeals. But in order to remove every such suspicion, we must explain more precisely than has yet been done what the dispute at that time concerned, and to what extent the canon on episcopal appeals entered into the controversy.

The appeal to the Roman pontiff that occasioned the great dispute between the Africans and the Romans was not the appeal of a bishop but the appeal of the presbyter Apiarius. The African bishops considered it entirely novel and contrary to African discipline, and they were so displeased by it that, for the first time, they immediately prohibited it in an express canon at the synod of 418, canon 125 according to Dionysius: presbyters and clergy of other lower orders were not to appeal to transmarine tribunals [Col. 0566D], by which term only the Roman bishop could be understood as the superior of the Africans.

This decree particularly troubled Pope Zosimus, to whom Apiarius had fled. Since he anticipated that the Africans would become more difficult after such a decree, he judged that the appeal should be settled in Africa so that the matter might be concluded more easily. For that reason he sent not one but three legates—as is customary in matters of the greatest importance: Faustinus, bishop of Potentia, and Philip and Asellus, presbyters of the Roman Church. Together with the neighboring bishops, they were to investigate and judge the case.

The fact that the appeals of presbyters were to be judged by neighboring bishops could not have displeased the Africans, for at the Council of 418 itself the method for hearing such appeals had been established in canon 125 according to Dionysius:

> It is resolved that, in cases which presbyters, deacons, or other clergy of lower order may have, if they complain of the judgments of their own bishops, the neighboring bishops should hear them, etc.

The one thing that could have disturbed the Africans in this matter was the apostolic delegation by which the aforementioned pontiff had decided that the appeal should be handled.

Since this delegation was new to the Africans, Zosimus inserted into his memorandum the Sardican canon 5, otherwise canon 7, which established such a delegation, together with two other Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons, as they were inscribed in the codices of the Roman Church. He followed the order in which they were read in those codices.

For this reason, canon 5, otherwise canon 7, concerning episcopal appeals to the priest of the Roman Church, occupied the first place in the memorandum. The second was canon 8, concerning bishops’ rash journeys to the imperial court; and the third was canon 17, concerning the hearing of cases involving presbyters and deacons by neighboring bishops when they had been unjustly excommunicated by their own bishops.

### 22. The Canons Were Simply Inserted into the Memorandum

The canons were inserted into the memorandum without explanation. Their use in the question then under discussion was indicated by the legates not in writing but orally. For Faustinus says at the synod of 419:

> Some things have been entrusted to us by the apostolic see in writing, and some also in instructions—as we recalled in the earlier proceedings.

Would that the acts of that earlier synod had survived! At that time, after the aforementioned legates had entered Africa, the Fathers whom they were able to assemble more quickly in 418 met before the plenary synod of 419 was convened. While carrying out their legation concerning Apiarius’s appeal, they produced the canons recorded in the memorandum and explained orally how they applied to the matter in question.

From those acts it would become clear in what sense the canon concerning episcopal appeals had been applied especially to the case of an appeal by a presbyter.

A major and prolonged dispute, contained in extensive volumes of proceedings, is reported in the Africans’ letter to Boniface, nos. 1 and 3. At the synod of 419, Faustinus indicates only that the earlier proceedings had dealt chiefly with the Nicene canons, so that both their decrees and their custom might be preserved:

> Some matters are governed by order and canon; others are confirmed by custom.

What relevance could this distinction between canon and custom have to Apiarius’s appeal? As we believe, it indicates that the canon concerning episcopal appeals to the Roman pontiff was introduced into the case of the presbyter so that apostolic delegation in appeals might be recognized as approved by that canon. The mention of custom was perhaps added because the same delegation, approved in episcopal appeals, was also customary in appeals by presbyters and other clergy.

Thus the African bishops would not have objected if what had been decreed concerning the first kind of appeals had to be received in the appeal of the presbyter Apiarius—especially since the legates of the apostolic see, sent to Africa for this purpose, were not to judge alone but together with the neighboring bishops, according to the African discipline itself, as the other Sardican canon inserted in the memorandum established.

In this way it can reasonably be understood in what fair sense both canon 7 and canon 17 were introduced in this case; otherwise both would have been irrelevant. For Sardican canon 17 alone, since it decrees an appeal by presbyters to neighboring bishops but not to the Roman pontiff, would have had no relevance to the appeal lodged by Apiarius, which was the matter in dispute. Sardican canon 5, otherwise canon 7, would have contributed even less unless it had been applied to the presbyter’s appeal in the sense we have explained.

Therefore, so that these two canons may not be said to have been cited beside the point—namely, beside the question that most concerned the Africans, concerning appeals by lower clergy—and so that it may not be believed that the apostolic delegation and the dispute with the Africans were occasioned by another question, namely episcopal appeals, for which there is no indication in these circumstances, the proposed use and explanation will be judged sufficiently probable.

### 23.

Throughout this entire dispute, the Africans seem to have recognized that neither Sardican canon 5, otherwise canon 7, concerning an appeal to the Roman see, nor the custom alleged by the legates supported Apiarius’s case.

That canon speaks of appeals by bishops, not of appeals by presbyters or other clergy of lower order. As for the custom by which it was said that the same result was obtained in appeals by such persons, even if it perhaps prevailed elsewhere—that is, in Italy—it did not prevail in Africa. There, the only decrees known to all and observed were those of the Council of Nicaea, in which nothing of this kind was found.

This, we think, is suggested by the words of the Africans in their letter to Pope Boniface. In no. 4 they ask him:

> Just as the Fathers at Nicaea dealt with or established these matters, so make them be observed by us; and make those things which the legates brought in their memorandum be practiced among you.

And below, in no. 5, they ask not to be compelled to submit to these canons if they were not truly Nicene, even if they were observed in that order or among the Romans in Italy.

Hence also, in the letter to Coelestine, no. 3, they say:

> By no decree of the Fathers, they say, has anything of this kind been taken away from the African Church.

For the canon concerning episcopal appeals, even if it were genuine, did not apply to cases involving presbyters; nor had any African custom extended it to appeals by such persons.

### 24.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that, on the occasion of this canon, which legislates concerning bishops, the dispute and controversy could have turned toward episcopal appeals themselves, insofar as they are proposed in that canon.

Although African discipline did not prohibit bishops from appealing to Rome and having their cases heard there, as we shall soon demonstrate, and although custom also provided evidence for several such appeals, this method of apostolic delegation was entirely new.

The bishops may have feared that, if it were once accepted, it would prejudice African discipline in some way—either because such appeals would become more frequent by this route, or because, following the example of Faustinus, who had favored Apiarius, they feared the delegates, or for some other reason. They may therefore have opposed the canon that proposed this procedure, not in order to exclude all episcopal appeals, but to prevent this new method of delegation.

In this sense, when they promised in their letter to Boniface that they would observe the canon themselves while a more careful investigation was being made into the Nicene canons, they sufficiently indicated that they did not wish to be compelled to accept this procedure if it had not been established by a Nicene canon. Although it may have been received in Italy, it was unknown to the Africans.

Thus there was no dispute concerning episcopal appeals except with regard to the procedure.

### 25

That such appeals were accepted in Africa by another method is demonstrated [Col. 0568D] by several documents concerning episcopal appeals. In the appeal of Antonius, bishop of Fussala, the Africans were so far from resisting that they did not wish to produce anything against it—lest they create prejudice against the Africans, as S. Hilary is believed to have done—but rather the primate of Numidia himself commended him to Boniface, and afterwards reported the whole matter to Celestine; and Augustine, when transmitting the proceedings, added arguments by which he might advance the fairest judgment of the pontiff.

What, moreover, should be said about the three other cases which Augustine praises as more recent? Even if the case of Laurentius [963] could have occurred after the council of May 419, to which he is believed to have subscribed, the other two could not likewise have done so. For it is incredible that three cases of the same kind, from one province of Caesarea, were suddenly brought to Rome within a short interval and decided with similar moderation, if none had ever previously been brought there.

Therefore it cannot be asserted that the cases of Priscus and Victor, which Augustine reports before the case of Laurentius, occurred after 418, unless one adopts the hypothesis that episcopal appeals had previously been rejected. That may indeed be presumed, but it cannot be proved. As for the conjecture by which the Laurentius named by Augustine at the end [Col. 0569A] is believed to be Laurentius of Icosium, who subscribed to the council of 419 as legate of the province of Caesarea, the Priscus named first by Baluze (*Tom. III Concil.*, p. 211) is believed to be Priscus of Cudia, who subscribed to the conference of 411, no. 243; his bishopric is likewise known to have belonged to the province of Caesarea from the *Notice of the Provinces and Cities of the African Church*.

If anyone should suppose that the cases of Priscus and Victor of Mauretania occurred, or became known to Augustine, before the case of Apiarius—since Augustine himself and other bishops, [Note: See Augustine, Letters 190 and 191, chap. 1, and Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 14, in vol. V of the Councils, p. 267.] compelled by the ecclesiastical necessity imposed by Zosimus, had been drawn into Mauretania and had long been detained there, now in one place and now in another—we do not see how this can be refuted.

Furthermore, in the same Letter 209 Augustine indicates other examples of appeals and judgments of the Roman see that were much more remote from his own times, which, content with the more recent examples, he thought should be passed over. What, then, are these very remote examples that Augustine signifies here? To understand by them suburban cases of first instance [Col. 0569B] is sheer fantasy. For if the common Italian discipline and the practice of Sardica were unknown to the Africans, as we saw shortly before, suburban cases must have been still more unknown to them; and it would not have been easy for an African writer to investigate and learn about them. These very remote examples, therefore, just like the recent ones which Augustine added, concern Africa. Otherwise he would have said, “I shall not inquire into more remote and foreign examples; I shall mention recent examples belonging to us.”

These very remote African examples, like the recent ones, when brought before the apostolic see, concern judgments of second instance, not of first instance: unless someone should perhaps think that the Roman pontiff was at some time granted first-instance jurisdiction over African cases as well.

There therefore existed several African cases of older appeals in which the apostolic see either judged at second instance, applying a moderation that had not been applied in the first instance, or, if it had been applied in the first instance, confirmed the judgments of others.

Nor should you say from this testimony of Augustine [Col. 0569C]—who refrained from investigating older examples—it cannot be inferred that some such judgments had in fact preceded these. For although it cannot be stated with certainty whether, when Augustine sought more remote examples, he would have found any of that kind favorable to his case, it nevertheless follows with certainty that he thought some might be found. This presupposes as something established and entirely certain for him that cases of bishops, from Africa, had been brought before the apostolic see for second-instance judgment in older times no less than in recent times—cases which certainly cannot be referred to the period of the alleged permission.

Certainly earlier is Augustine’s Letter 43, in which the following is written about Caecilian of Carthage and his fellow African bishops, no. 7:

> For the matter concerned not presbyters or deacons or clerics of a lower order, but fellow bishops, who could reserve their case intact for the judgment of other fellow bishops, especially of the apostolic Churches.

The matter was indeed an episcopal case, in which there was a major division among the Catholics and the African Donatists concerning bishops and judgments. Yet Augustine does not refer the reason for transferring judgment [Col. 0569D] to the apostolic Churches—to which, as the context and other testimonies make clear, Rome is intended—to these particular circumstances. Rather, he refers it to the fact that those whose case was at issue were not presbyters or deacons and so forth, but bishops. Here it is openly signified that, by the very discipline of the Africans, it was lawful to refer their case to the apostolic see when it was an episcopal case, not a case of presbyters or deacons and the like, for whom alone the African discipline generally did not permit recourse overseas.

### 26

Certainly no decree is found against episcopal appeals, just as the first canon against appeals of clerics of the lower orders is recorded [Col. 0570A] as having been inserted in the synod of 418. This was first prohibited to those clerics at that time, on the occasion of the appeal of Apiarius, because for them to appeal to judgments overseas was contrary to discipline [965] and custom; but it was not so for bishops, since it had always been accepted by numerous examples, especially because the canons of Sardica approving episcopal appeals had been signed by Gratus, primate of all Africa, and by other African bishops.

At the synod of Hippo in 393 and at the Carthaginian synod in 397, permission was granted to all, both bishops and clerics, to appeal from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority. If clerics complained of the judgment of their bishop, they could appeal to neighboring bishops, and from these again take refuge in the plenary synods of Africa or before the primates of their provinces. Thus, if they had perhaps been burdened by an unjust judgment, the assistance of an appeal was available to them within Africa itself, so that they would not have to flee to overseas tribunals.

But since the cases of bishops were to be brought for first-instance judgment before the primate [Col. 0570B] or the universal African council, as was established after the Council of Hippo by canon 19 of the Carthaginian synod of 397, it cannot be believed that a second judgment was denied to these alone; consequently, an appeal to the Roman pontiff could not have been prohibited.

### 27

Nor should you reply that this prohibition is indicated in the Carthaginian council of 419, canon 28 in Dionysius, where, after the same or nearly the same words of the earlier council of 418—canon 125 in the same Dionysius—by which presbyters and the remaining clerics are forbidden to seek overseas tribunals, there is added: “as has also often been established concerning bishops.”

There are distinguished authors, including Frenchmen, who believe that this addition—“as has also often been established concerning bishops”—was improperly inserted, since it is absent from the similar canon of the earlier council of 418, from which this entire canon was taken. Nor does it seem likely that the Fathers added this clause at the council of 419, at which the same writers, in their letter to the pontiff Boniface, declared that they would [Col. 0570C] meanwhile observe that discipline concerning appeals until more certain answers could be brought from copies of the Council of Nicaea.

They further say that it seems incredible that, if something had often been established concerning episcopal appeals, no such canon should be found among the many canons surviving from so many African councils that establish rules about episcopal judgments, whereas several canons are found repeated concerning the prohibited appeals of presbyters and other clerics of the lower orders.

Yet we do not think the addition should be suspected in these words, which are read not only in the collection of Dionysius but also in three other ancient collections that, through a different division of the canons of the same Carthaginian synod of 419, display a different origin. These are the collections of the Vatican Regina 1997, Barberini 2888, and Lucensis, similar to Colbertinus 784.

Indeed, something must be supplied from these collections that is not read in this canon in Dionysius, nor in the Greek text [Col. 0570D] of the so-called manuscript of the African Church, which in reality is nothing other than a Greek translation of the Africans’ canons from Dionysius. For there this canon is presented as follows, no. 33:

> It was likewise decided that presbyters, deacons, or other clerics of the lower orders, in cases which they have, if they have complained about the judgments of their bishops, should be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and that whatever matter there may be among them should be decided by bishops summoned in by that bishop. But if they should think that an appeal ought also to be made from these, they should not appeal to overseas tribunals, but to the primates of their provinces or to the universal council, as has also often been established concerning bishops. But whoever should think of appealing overseas is to be received into communion by no one within the same province.

The words “or to the universal council” are absent from Dionysius. Yet that they ought not to be omitted is clear from the words of the Africans’ letter to Celestine, which will shortly be quoted, and from the canon of the earlier synod of 418, which is repeated here [Col. 0571A] and likewise appears, in similar form, in Dionysius, canon 125, where it reads:

> But if they should think that an appeal ought also to be made from these, they should appeal only to the African councils or to the primates of their provinces. But to overseas tribunals, and so forth.

It should further be observed here that some alteration was introduced when this canon was repeated. For where in 418 it was written, “they should appeal only to the African councils,” and so forth, in 419 it was expressed as follows: “they should not appeal to overseas tribunals, but to the primates,” and so forth.

If the earlier reading had been retained, the addition “as has also often been established concerning bishops” would indicate that it had often been established that bishops too should appeal only to the primates, and so forth, or to the universal council. That would [967] amount to declaring that overseas tribunals had likewise been prohibited to them.

But the alteration of the wording appears to have been introduced for a particular purpose, contrary to the usual practice: namely, so that this addition would not be referred to the prohibition of overseas tribunals [Col. 0571B], but only to the other part, by which the judgment of the primates and councils of Africa is granted to clerics, just as it had often been established for bishops.

Before this time, that is, after the judgment of their bishop, presbyters had recourse only to six neighboring bishops, who decided their case. Hence Augustine wrote in Letter 65 of 402, no. 2:

> It has been established by council that the case of a presbyter be terminated by six bishops.

This was established, namely, at Hippo in 393 and at Carthage in 397, where the *Breviary of the Canons of Hippo* was read and confirmed.

But when, on account of the appeal of Apiarius in 418, an appeal to overseas tribunals had been prohibited to all clerics, a third instance was also granted to them under a new rule, so that they would not complain about this judgment being taken from them. The same judges were appointed for clerics who had often been appointed for bishops. Therefore, in their letter to Celestine written on this matter, the Africans, on account of this new decree issued in favor of the clerics [Col. 0571C], demonstrate that an appeal overseas was unnecessary, adducing this principal reason, no. 3:

> Especially because it has been granted to everyone—for they are speaking of clerics of the lower orders—if he has been offended by the judgment of those who have heard the case, to appeal to the councils of his province, meaning the primates, or to the universal council.

That this addition must be understood in this sense is evident from the fact itself. Since several African canons are found that prohibit clerics from appealing overseas, but not even one that prohibits the same thing to bishops, it is plainly incredible that such a prohibition had often been established.

### 28

Nor should you say that not all the canons of the earlier African synods have come down to us. For although not all the African councils survive with their canons, nevertheless, on the one hand, many such documents were carefully inserted into ancient collections of canons; and, on the other, it was customary among the Africans to repeat and confirm the canons of earlier synods in subsequent councils. Thus at least some trace of the ancient canons remains [Col. 0571D] in the synods that we possess, whose canons are for the most part not new but consist of material taken from ancient sources.

This is so certain that Dionysius Exiguus, when reporting the synod of 419, listed all the earlier synods held under Aurelius from 393 onward, yet omitted the canons of several of them because they had already been set out by him in an earlier synod or were to be set out in a later one.

We found in the most ancient manuscript of the chapter of Verona an unpublished Carthaginian synod of 421, to be inserted in volume III. In it not a single canon is new; rather, all are found here and there in councils already published, received and repeated.

Moreover, even if Dionysius, who was reluctant to repeat the same canons, allowed some rare canons to escape him, nevertheless, since the controversy over appeals was debated at the synod of 419 [Col. 0572A], which he deliberately included in his collection, he was extremely careful in reporting all the African canons pertaining to appeals. Indeed, because of a difference in wording or because of the addition mentioned shortly before, he reported twice the canon that prohibits clerics from appealing overseas, as canons 28 and 125.

He who was so attentive to appeals that he took account even of a few words would certainly not have omitted a canon prohibiting the same appeals to bishops, had he found one anywhere—especially since there would have been no reason for him to repeat it. He therefore reported no such canon because he found none among the many African councils incorporated into the synod of 419.

But if no such prohibition existed among the canons issued by Aurelius in so many synods and also received by the elders, in which the entire discipline of the African Church is contained, who could still suspect that this prohibition had often been established?

Since, then, no canon prohibits episcopal appeals overseas, and the examples of certain bishops mentioned shortly before demonstrate more clearly that such appeals were accepted rather than forbidden, the addition cannot refer to the clause “they should not appeal to overseas tribunals.” [Col. 0572B]

Since, moreover, judges were often established for bishops—either the primates or the universal council of Africa—as may be read in the synod of Hippo in 393, the Carthaginian synod of 397, and other synods, the addition, which is attached in these very words, must be understood to refer to this: that they should appeal only to the primates of their [969] provinces or to the universal council.

### 29

Someone might perhaps wonder whether what was not prohibited to bishops until the synod of 419 was forbidden in the subsequent council of approximately 425, when Apiarius, having relapsed into new crimes and the legate Faustinus having again been sent to Africa, was judged.

For from the twentieth council under Aurelius—which is the same as that synod of approximately 425—this decree, or rather an abridgment or title of a decree, was received in the synod held by Boniface of Carthage in 525:

> Let no one dare to appeal overseas.

Yet three considerations persuade us that this decree did not include bishops. First, even after this synod of Aurelius [Col. 0572C], certain African bishops appealed to the Roman pontiff without anyone objecting, as is clear from the appeal of Lupicinus, which we shall discuss below.

Second, by the time of Boniface the canons of Sardica approving episcopal appeals were already known in Africa. Hence, around that same time, they were incorporated under the explicit name of Sardica by Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, into his *Breviary of the Canons*.

If they were known then, there can be no doubt that they had also been received by the Africans, since they had been confirmed at the Council of Sardica by Gratus of Carthage. Moreover, the Fathers of the councils of 418 and 419 indicated that they too would receive that Sardican canon which displeased them most if they found it in any Catholic synod, as we observed above.

Once these canons had been received, Boniface could not list among the canons to be observed one that prohibited the episcopal appeals approved by Sardica. We therefore believe [Col. 0572D] that the canon concerned not episcopal appeals but those of clerics, which Sardica had passed over.

Nor should the general and indefinite word “no one” trouble anyone. For a similarly general expression is used in the same synod of Boniface for another decree, or rather an abridgment of a decree, from the sixteenth council under Aurelius, in these words:

> Whoever should think of appealing overseas is to be received into communion by no one within Africa.

This sixteenth council is the one held in 418, whose canon 125 is found in Dionysius. From the complete form of that canon it is known that only clerical appeals were prohibited. The same, therefore, must be believed concerning the canon of the twentieth synod, although a general formula was used in Boniface’s summary.

We derive what seems to be a third, decisive argument from the very letter of the African Fathers to Pope Celestine, which was written at that same twentieth synod. In it, episcopal and clerical appeals are discussed, but in different ways. [Col. 0573A]

When they speak of clerical appeals, they ask that these be admitted in no way. They say, no. 3:

> May your holiness, as is fitting, reject the wicked evasions of presbyters and subsequent clerics, since by no definition of the Fathers has anything been taken away from the African Church.

This is equivalent to saying that the canons brought forward by Faustinus do not pertain to such appeals.

When, however, they speak of episcopal appeals, no. 2, they do not demand that they be rejected absolutely, but that they not be received too readily:

> We beseech you that henceforth you do not too readily admit those coming from here to your ears, nor wish any longer to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated.

That the subject here is bishops is shown by what follows. After citing the decree of the Council of Nicaea, they add this reason:

> For although it seems that provision is made there concerning clerics of the lower orders or laymen, how much more did he wish this to be observed concerning BISHOPS, lest those suspended from communion in their own province appear [Col. 0573B] to be restored to communion by your holiness too hastily or improperly?

Then they pass to clerical appeals:

> Presbyters also, and so forth.

Here the particle “also” confirms that the preceding remarks concerned not clerics but bishops.

What else can this different manner of speaking about bishops and clerics mean except that appeal was prohibited to the latter but not to the former? By this petition alone—that episcopal appeals not be received too readily—they wished both to guard against excessive frequency and abuses and to indicate that, although they desired such appeals to be rarer, they did not prohibit them as permitted by African discipline.

If the same letter, no. 3, supplies reasons that apply equally to episcopal appeals and to appeals by clerics of the lower orders, it is one thing to insert, incidentally, reasons common to all; it is another to reject and prohibit all appeals equally and absolutely. The latter is found only with respect to [971] clerical appeals.

For this reason they perhaps inserted these arguments in the paragraph where they discuss clerics [Col. 0573C], but not in the paragraph concerning bishops, whose appeals they thought it sufficient to have received less readily, since African discipline did not prohibit them.

This letter therefore yields a new argument by which the acceptance of episcopal appeals by the Africans is confirmed.

### 30

We consider the reason for which these bishops resisted clerical appeals worthy of attention. Whether one reads the acts of the synod of 419 or the letters written to Boniface and Celestine in the case of Apiarius, not a word will be found by which the right of the apostolic see in these cases is called into question.

All the arguments concern difficulties arising from the distance of places, the dangers of delay and fraud, and the abuses of wicked persons; examples of these were demonstrated in the very appeal of Apiarius. Although he had been justly deposed for crimes known with certainty to the Africans, he nevertheless protected himself by this evasion and so circumvented the legate Faustinus that Faustinus seemed rather his patron than his judge. Relying on his patronage, Apiarius was compelled to confess his crimes [Col. 0573D] only after three days of disputation.

Stirred to zeal by this disastrous example and abuse, the African Fathers wrote that such appeals—or rather, the refuges of wicked clerics—were prohibited by African discipline and ought to be entirely rejected by the apostolic see.

Although they had prohibited this as early as 418, nevertheless they not only did not reject Faustinus and the two other legates sent by the apostolic see, but, acquiescing in their sentence, restored Apiarius to communion.

So greatly did they venerate apostolic authority even in these appeals by clerics that, although Apiarius, after his first restoration in 419, relapsed into new crimes and consequently was deposed and again fled to the Roman pontiff; and although a new delegation of Faustinus had been sent at a time when the Africans already knew that the canon produced in support of it was not found among the Nicene canons, and therefore were no longer bound by the condition under which they had obligated themselves—namely, only until a more diligent investigation of the Nicene canons had been completed [Col. 0574A]—nevertheless, out of respect for the apostolic see, they received the same legate Faustinus as judge.

They complained to Celestine only that he had undertaken Apiarius’s patronage rather than his judgment and had acted more as a defender than as a judge. For this reason, moved by zeal for justice and presenting only considerations concerning frauds and dangers, they asked the pontiff no longer to receive such appeals, which through the abuse of wicked persons turn to destruction, and not to employ delegations of this kind, which they had found established in no synod and which they had learned from these first examples had turned out badly.

Thus everywhere the right itself was left untouched; only dangers and scandals were put forward, on account of which they resisted with modesty and humility and thought that such appeals ought to be prohibited.

Let those who boast in this matter of the African masters and leaders observe with what moderation they must be understood. Let them also recognize how improperly they transfer this resistance of the Africans, which concerned only the appeals of clerics [Col. 0574B], to episcopal appeals, which we have shown were never prohibited by the Africans and were always accepted.

But this is incidental. For the present, let it stand that the African bishops did resist the appeals of clerics of the lower orders, but modestly and without touching the right itself; that on this occasion they rejected the Sardican canons concerning episcopal appeals solely through ignorance, and only with respect to the method of apostolic delegation; and that, in reality, by admitting the appeals of bishops, they accepted those same canons in substance, although at that time they were ignorant of them, especially because they were presented under the name of the Nicene canons, even though those canons had formerly been confirmed and received by their ancestors.

### 31

From these points the falsity is demonstrated of that lengthy annotation in which Quesnel declares chapter 12 of Leo’s Letter 12 to the Mauretanians spurious under that particular pretext: namely, that it presents the appeal of Lupicinus, an African bishop, to the Roman pontiff, while, on the basis of the documents published in the case of Apiarius [Col. 0574C], he portrays the Africans as certainly abhorring such appeals.

But since we have proved elsewhere that this chapter is entirely genuine, we should instead recognize from it that the Africans by no means rejected the discipline of episcopal appeals, especially since no controversy on this matter is recorded as having arisen and the Africans’ profound respect for Leo, the Roman pontiff, shines through the entire context of the letter.

In any event, if not at this time, certainly not long afterwards the Sardican canons themselves appear to have been received by the Africans. Perhaps in the course of time they learned [973] either through more careful investigation or through instruction from the Romans that these canons were distinct from the Nicene canons, had been approved under the name of Sardica by Gratus of Carthage and their other ancestors, and had been praised by that same Gratus in the Carthaginian synod.

Whatever anyone may think about the Africans with respect to the Sardican canons, nothing is proved by it concerning the Gauls or others who inserted the Sardican canons into their own codices, as we showed above.

### 32

The letter of the Roman synod written under Damasus to the emperor Gratian, together with Gratian’s law, must be placed after the Sardican canons. [Col. 0574D] These documents establish the discipline of episcopal appeals and set forth the principal basis and defense of the appeal of Chelidonius.

The Roman council asked Gratian for a law by which the order of ecclesiastical judgments might be strengthened against recalcitrant persons, protected by the secular, as they call it, arm. A law plainly answering this request was issued. Since it is more correct and more consistent with the meaning, the reading of the Roman synodical letter found by Sirmond in a single and less accurate codex must be corrected from it.

Thus, in the synodical letter of the Roman council, the Fathers first ask the emperor, no. 9:

> May your piety order that whoever has been condemned either by his judgment—that is, the judgment of the pontiff Damasus, as is clear from the context and from Gratian’s own law—or by ours, who are Catholics, and who wishes unjustly to retain the Church, or, when summoned to priestly judgment—or, as it should be read from Gratian’s law, “to priestly judgment”—refuses through contumacy to appear [Col. 0575A], whether summoned by the illustrious prefects of the praetorium of your Italy or by the vicar, come to the city of Rome.

Since there was one prefect of the praetorium of Italy, while there were several vicars subordinate to the prefect of the praetorium of Italy, there is an obvious error in the words “the prefects of the praetorium of your Italy” and “the vicar.” Moreover, in what follows, a clause corresponding to the preceding words appears to be missing.

The text is better and more complete in the law [Col. 0575A], from which this passage of the synodical letter must likewise be corrected—or rather supplemented:

> Or he shall be referred to episcopal judgment by the illustrious prefects of the praetorium of Gaul and Italy, or by proconsuls or vicars acting with authority—a clause referring back to the preceding words “when summoned to priestly judgment,” and missing from the synodical letter—or shall arrive at the city of Rome under escort.

These provisions concern first-instance judgments for places near Rome. The same synodical letter immediately adds provisions concerning such judgments for places more distant from the Roman city, in almost the same words as the law:

> Or, if such a question should arise in more remote regions, he shall be brought to the metropolitan’s examination through the judgments of the places [Col. 0575B]; or, if he himself is the metropolitan, he shall without delay be ordered to proceed necessarily to Rome, or to those whom the Roman bishop has appointed as judges.

Since this command is addressed not only to the prefect of the praetorium of Italy but also to the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, as well as to the proconsuls—namely, of Spain and Africa—and to the vicars of the prefects, a general discipline is clearly being set forth by this law, one that concerned the whole of the West, and specifically the Gallican Churches.

In places not very distant from the city of Rome, the first-instance judgment of any bishop is asserted either for the provincial synod or for the Roman bishop. In more remote places, as regards bishops, it is granted to the metropolitan, with his provincial synod understood; as regards metropolitans, it is granted to the Roman pontiff or to those whom that pontiff has delegated as judges. It is also ordered that if anyone summoned to judgment refuses to appear, he is to be compelled by the secular arm.

Then, concerning an appeal from the judges of first instance, it is added: [Col. 0575C]

> Certainly, if the favor or injustice of a metropolitan or of any other priest should be suspect, he may appeal either to the Roman pontiff or, at least, to a council of fifteen neighboring bishops.

Two grounds for appealing are indicated, or two ways of making an appeal. The first is freely granted to anyone before the Roman pontiff if the judges of first instance come under suspicion.

Hilary could have been suspect to Chelidonius, since Hilary was not his metropolitan and had usurped an incompetent jurisdiction. The other bishops of Gaul could also have been judged less suitable for his case, since it is suggested not only in the *Life of S. Romanus* but also in the letter of S. Leo himself that Hilary exercised the greatest authority over them. Consequently, for this reason also, Chelidonius was especially permitted to appeal more quickly to the Roman pontiff than to the neighboring Gallican bishops.

Nor does it matter whether he appealed before or after Hilary’s judgment. For, apart from the fact that it is unknown whether he was present at Hilary’s judgment, certainly anyone who is permitted to appeal before judgment because of some suspicion [975] [Col. 0575D] is permitted to do so much more after judgment if he discovers that what he had previously suspected as a grievance has in fact befallen him through the judgment. For this reason, appeals are granted by every right even from judges concerning whom there had previously been no suspicion.

### 33

The decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs must be numbered among the rules of ecclesiastical law. Quesnel himself admits, in dissertation 16, to be published in volume III, § 12, that the Gauls venerated these letters, inserted them into their collections of canons before Dionysius, and treated them as having the force of statutes. He admits this as though the contrary view would require one to believe that for five hundred years they had so despised the authority of the apostolic see that, before Dionysius, they had never thought of collecting those decrees.

He adds:

> But we hold better and more religious opinions about the Gallican Churches and the other Churches in their relation to their head and primate.

Accordingly, for the present matter, the letter of Innocent to Victricius of Rouen must not be omitted. The same codices praised by him certainly contain it [Col. 0576A], as do the Morbacensis, Palatinus 574, and Fossatensis codices, which contain purely Gallican collections.

That Victricius came to Rome to clear himself in a Roman judgment of some crime falsely imposed upon him can be gathered from S. Paulinus’s Letter 37, written to him.

This decretal of Innocent, delivered to the Gallican bishop who was requesting a norm and authority from the Roman Church, primarily concerns the Churches of Gaul. In chapter 3 it is established that major cases—among which judgments concerning bishops are certainly considered the most important—are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the synod has established and blessed custom requires.

This decree establishes the right of appeal when someone considers himself unjustly condemned—a right which we have shown was both established by the Council of Sardica and confirmed by custom.

Shortly before, the same letter had commanded that cases even of the higher order—that is, cases concerning bishops—be settled in a council of the same province. No one was permitted to flee from the judgment of the provincial bishops [Col. 0576B] to other provinces, but without prejudice to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in every case. This preserves intact the right of appeals to that Church.

### 34.

I shall conclude this chapter with the example of the bishop of Constantinople in ecclesiastical law. At the First Synod of Constantinople in 381, the bishop of Constantinople had been decreed the primacy of honor after the Roman bishop, on the ground that the city itself was younger than Rome. Subsequently, the bishops of that city—Nectarius, Saint John Chrysostom, Atticus, Sisinnius, and Saint Proclus—repeatedly adjudicated cases and appeals concerning bishops that had been brought before them from various provinces of the East. This was later confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon, canons 9 and 17.

[Col. 0576C] Since this could not in itself be attributed to the bishop of Constantinople by any right—for he had not even been a metropolitan, but was a suffragan of Heraclea—it began to be supported and defended by reference to the aforementioned canon of the First Council of Constantinople, as though the primacy of honor granted to this see, because it was the New Rome, implied not merely a degree of honor but participation in the same privileges. This may be inferred from act 16 of the Council of Chalcedon, as well as from its communication to Saint Leo. Thus, just as the Roman pontiff exercised judgment in cases involving episcopal appeals, it was judged, on the basis of the decree of the Constantinopolitan synod, that the bishop of Constantinople likewise could judge such cases.

Accordingly, this right, which belonged to the Roman see even in these times before Leo and which was exercised frequently, especially in cases involving Western bishops, ought to have been universally recognized, so that the bishop of Constantinople might suppose that he too should exercise a similar right over Eastern bishops by virtue of the honor shared with the New Rome. The Roman see strongly resisted this prerogative. It did so not only because it had formerly known nothing of the canons of the Constantinopolitan synod and had never accepted them, but also because in reality that synod had conferred upon the Constantinopolitans merely a rank of honor after the Roman bishop, and no jurisdiction whatsoever.

[Col. 0576D] Yet what seems most extraordinary to us is that no one censures the bishops of Constantinople for having usurped the right of hearing Eastern appeals without any canon granting it to them, relying solely upon the pretext of a canon that claimed a merely honorary prerogative; while some accuse the Roman pontiffs of usurping a right when they exercised one that was wholly certain to the ancient Eastern and Constantinopolitan Churches, and that is asserted far more openly—not merely by custom, but in the Council of Sardica and other ecclesiastical documents. What if cases of appeal belong to the Roman see not only by this ecclesiastical right but also by divine right? This will be established with complete certainty in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER VII. Appeals to the Roman See by Divine Right, and the Extent to Which the Right of Appeal Has Its Root in the Primacy

### 1.

[Col. 0577A] This is the principal foundation of pontifical jurisdiction, upon which both custom and ecclesiastical law itself concerning appeals rest. Hence Valentinian III, in his letter to the emperor Theodosius, which is numbered 55 among Leo’s letters, asserted to the same see, on behalf of the primacy, the same right of appeal as having been granted to the apostolic see both by custom and by councils, in the case of Flavian, which was a case of appeal, as we saw in the preceding chapter.

For this reason Leo too complained, in chapter 2 of letter 12, that the rights of the primacy had been violated by Hilary when he appeared to resist Celidonius’s appeal. Quesnellus, part I, chapter 15, while attempting to prove that the custom of appeals had been rejected, states that the cause and origin of this discipline were founded upon the nature of episcopal dignity and its sacred and inviolable privileges—that is, upon divine right, which he calls unwritten law.

On this hypothesis, whenever, under either ancient or more recent discipline, judgments concerning bishops were brought by appeal to the apostolic see, the divine right of episcopal dignity would have been violated. Who could ever admit such an absurdity? [Col. 0577B] It is therefore of no small importance to explain and establish that pontifical right concerning appeals derives from the primacy by divine right, so that no one may consequently believe that episcopal judgments have thereby suffered any injustice.

Quesnellus himself occasionally perceived this point. For in dissertation 16, which we shall include in volume III, section 14, no. 4, he openly declares that the Gallicans, when they accepted appeals, had regard to the dignity of the pontifical primacy and to “the more powerful principality,” as Irenaeus calls it.

The Church of Africa has incorporated the following common rule into its canons, canon 15 in Dionysius: from any ecclesiastical judges it is permitted to appeal to other ecclesiastical judges “where there is greater authority.” Hence the right of appeal to the Roman pontiff cannot be denied throughout the Church except by someone who dares, together with heretics and schismatics, to deny that the supreme pontiff possesses greater authority over all the Churches of the whole world. This greater authority must be referred to the primacy, or “the more powerful principality.”

[Col. 0577C] But in order that we may understand more easily and correctly the extent to which this right of appeal proceeds from the pontifical primacy and therefore from divine right, we must turn our attention for a little while to the original origin of ecclesiastical jurisdiction; first we must examine what Christ instituted concerning the right of the Roman pontiffs over bishops. Rights cannot be known better than from their very institution and origin.

### 2.

It is agreed among Catholics that all the apostles were equal among themselves by divine constitution, except for Peter, who, through Christ’s concession, obtained over all the others a primacy not merely of rank but of a special jurisdiction. Consequently, none of the other apostles possessed jurisdiction over the others by divine right; Peter alone possessed it by that same divine right.

Since bishops succeeded the apostles by the same right, yet, by Christ’s institution, did not receive greater jurisdiction than the apostles had, while the Roman pontiff succeeded Peter and succeeded him with the same jurisdiction of primacy, it follows that no bishop except the Roman pontiff alone received jurisdiction by divine right over the other bishops.

[Col. 0577D] To this jurisdiction over bishops belongs the authority to hear and judge the cases of bishops; for that is jurisdiction which belongs only to a superior. Therefore, by Christ’s institution and by divine right, no individual bishop can hear and judge the cases of other bishops; the Roman pontiff can. Hence Valentinian, in the aforementioned letter 55 to Theodosius, counted among the rights of the pontifical primacy the general power “to judge concerning the faith and concerning priests,” that is, bishops.

### 3.

Accordingly, no patriarchs or metropolitans were instituted by divine right to whom this jurisdiction was likewise granted by divine right. Rather, they derive both their origin and their authority from ecclesiastical institution.

[Col. 0578A] Since Peter and his successors, the Roman pontiffs, could neither be present everywhere nor conveniently attend everywhere, as their right required, to all the cases of all bishops, ecclesiastical institution provided that in each province certain individuals, and again others in larger dioceses, should possess greater authority than belongs to the episcopate. By virtue of this authority, among other things, they would hear cases concerning bishops according to a definite procedure and manner—cases which by divine right only Peter and his successors could hear in the first instance.

In this way, which is certainly the true explanation, the special jurisdiction of Peter and his successors, originating in divine institution, was in a certain sense communicated to others by ecclesiastical delegation. These are the persons who were later called patriarchs or metropolitans.

In this ecclesiastical institution, by which Peter’s own right and that of his successors was communicated to other bishops, Saint Peter himself, or at least his successors, must undoubtedly be considered to have consented, interpretatively speaking. No one else, being in himself without that jurisdiction, could have transferred it to anyone without the knowledge or consent of the one who alone possessed it, not by human but by divine right. For that legal principle is universally known: “No one can transfer to another more right than he is recognized as possessing.”

[Col. 0578B] If, moreover, the apostles, by virtue of the extraordinary apostolic authority over the universal Church—which did not pass to their episcopal successors—were able to communicate to certain bishops a jurisdiction that they themselves possessed over bishops, and if they are presumed actually to have communicated it to some bishops of the greater sees, then, since they communicated a jurisdiction that by ordinary and divine right belonged solely to Peter and his successors, they must be said to have communicated it with at least the interpretative consent of those successors, or at least without prejudice to them, so that the jurisdiction belonging to them by ordinary and divine right should suffer no diminution.

### 4.

The canons of councils subsequently approved this jurisdiction of patriarchs and metropolitans, or restricted it within definite limits as necessity or usefulness required. At the beginning, however, in many places a particular procedure prevailed merely by immemorial custom, and definite boundaries were prescribed that were regarded as law; these boundaries are found confirmed in the canons.

[Col. 0578C] Whatever the canons or custom attributed to patriarchs or metropolitans concerning this jurisdiction, since it belonged purely to ecclesiastical law and institution, could not prejudice the original and divine right of Peter and the Roman pontiffs. For whatever belongs to ecclesiastical—even apostolic—law cannot take away the slightest part of divine right.

Therefore, whatever jurisdiction over episcopal cases was established for patriarchs or metropolitans by ecclesiastical or even apostolic authority must always be understood to preserve the divine-right authority of the Roman pontiffs. Just as, before that ecclesiastical institution, they could by divine right hear episcopal cases in the first instance, so after that institution they can equally do so by their own right.

[Col. 0578D] Thus neither the canons nor custom, any more than the apostles themselves, could bring it about that the Roman pontiffs—who alone are the immediate superiors of bishops by divine right—should not enjoy the same immediate jurisdiction over bishops that descends from divine right, or that the first hearing of episcopal cases should not belong to them by that same right, if they judged it expedient to recall to themselves a jurisdiction that, although communicated to others by ecclesiastical institution, still belonged to them by the same right.

If they did this, they would not be seizing another’s right, nor unjustly usurping or violating the jurisdiction of patriarchs or metropolitans. They would instead be reclaiming and exercising their own right, which belonged to them by divine institution.

Accordingly, Patroclus of Arles cannot be accused of injuring the privileges of the Gallican bishops when he brought the case of Proculus of Marseille, or that of Hilary of Narbonne, to the apostolic see for a first hearing. Nor can the decrees of Zosimus, issued against Proculus in defense of the rights of Arles, be branded as an usurpation of jurisdiction. Quesnellus himself, in part II, chapter 4, endeavors to vindicate them as entirely just.

Similarly, the clergy of the Church of Valence cannot be criticized when they brought the case of Bishop Maximus directly to Pope Boniface for adjudication.

### 5.

[Col. 0579A] It could indeed be argued under certain circumstances that recalling this original right would not be expedient if an established judicial procedure in the provinces were abolished, because several disadvantages or scandals might follow—things that must be prevented by natural and divine law, and for whose prevention ecclesiastical institution had provided.

Thus, although this institution is ecclesiastical, to alter and abolish it in order to reclaim the original, albeit divine, right might, under the hypothesis in question, open the way to many disadvantages and scandals. It could amount to wishing to exercise the power of divine right to the destruction of the Church, although that power had been conferred solely for its edification.

But it is one thing to ask whether something is expedient or permissible; it is another to deny the power and the right itself, which is certain by divine institution, and to accuse someone of usurping another’s right.

[Col. 0579B] Whoever disputes only the first question—provided that he is guided not by passion or prejudice but by zeal and truth, acts solely with a view to the public good, presses and promotes by every possible means the considerations appropriate to preventing scandals, always observing the respect and moderation due, and advises that an ecclesiastical institution strengthened by custom should be preserved intact and that innovation should be avoided—yet advances nothing that strikes at the pontifical and certainly divine institution, has not merely done nothing wrong but will act holily and commendably.

Thus everyone greatly praises Saint Bernard when he criticized exemptions of monasteries from episcopal jurisdiction that had been sought solely out of ambition and granted without regard for the common good, either because of the magnitude of the offices involved or merely at the pontiff’s discretion; and when he attempted to deter Eugene III from granting such exemptions in the future. He did not do so because the grant exceeded pontifical authority or invaded and unjustly violated the rights of bishops, but because it was opposed to reason and justice in their broadest sense, which forbids the fostering of ambition and vice and commands that access be closed to the scandals flowing from them.

[Col. 0579C] “By acting in this way,” he says to Pope Eugene (*On Consideration*, book III, chapter 4, no. 4), “you prove that you possess the fullness of power, but perhaps not so much of justice. You do this because you can; but whether you ought to do it is the question.” He develops this point at greater length.

Here one can see the distinction between power or right—which is not called into question but rather plainly asserted—and an unlawful exercise of it, because such exercise is not expedient. Bernard insists only upon demonstrating the latter, without violating the right or power itself.

The same doctor acted similarly in book III of *On Consideration* addressed to the same Eugene, chapter 2, and in letter 178 to Innocent II, when he opposed appeals to the apostolic see. He focused on the abuses and scandals that arose from them, or on what was expedient, while always leaving untouched the right that he acknowledged as flowing from the primacy:

“Appeal is made to you from the whole world. This indeed bears witness to your singular primacy. But you, if you are wise, will rejoice not in the primacy but in its fruit,” and so forth.

### 6.

[Col. 0579D] If all who argue for preserving the customs or institutions of ancient canons in their own regions used this same method and moderation, there would be nothing to censure. But if they move from the question whether something is expedient and ought to be done—the only question that can properly arise in matters of this kind—to denying or calling into doubt pontifical jurisdiction, which is utterly certain by divine right, would that not be an obvious perversion and an injurious and unjust argument?

Thus, if the question concerned reserving to the apostolic see the first hearing of episcopal cases, anyone who, by this perverse and false reasoning, thought that the jurisdiction of other judges should be defended where a different discipline prevailed, and who therefore branded the pontiffs as usurpers of another’s right, would, in defending those judges’ ecclesiastical right, attack and violate the more certain and higher right of the pontiffs, which proceeds from divine institution.

[Col. 0580A] And while adducing and defending the canons and customs of the Churches, which belong to ecclesiastical institution, he would oppose the divine institution upon which pontifical jurisdiction rests. Indeed, he would also be fighting against the canons themselves, which very frequently confirmed this supreme jurisdiction of divine institution and intended it always to be understood as preserved in every ecclesiastical enactment.

He would likewise have to accuse the Council of Trent of injustice, since it asserted to the Roman pontiff the first hearing of more serious cases involving bishops, in session 13, chapter 8, and session 24, chapter 5. The reasons why this reservation should be considered expedient need not be investigated here; our sole concern is pontifical right.

### 7.

At this point Quesnellus’s audacity cannot be passed over. In part I, chapter 9, he angrily reproaches the Gallican bishops who supported the bishop of Arles because, together with the bishop of Vienne, they submitted to Saint Leo’s judgment the controversy over metropolitan jurisdiction that had revived under Ravennius.

[Col. 0580B] For the same reason he criticizes Patroclus of Arles in chapter 16, because he approached Zosimus over a similar controversy. This writer is exceedingly displeased that Gallican cases should be referred to the apostolic see for adjudication. Indeed, if Saint Trophimus himself, the first bishop of Arles, sent into Gaul by that same apostolic see, had referred to the Roman pontiff certain disputes that arose among bishops, one might wonder whether Quesnellus would have scattered even some reproaches and complaints against Saint Trophimus, as though by this example he had created a prejudice against the Churches of Gaul.

He does not complain that the case had previously been submitted at the Council of Turin to the judgment of the Italian bishops, before Leo and Zosimus, even though those Italian bishops had no inherent right of jurisdiction over the Gallicans. He recoils only from the judgment of the Roman bishop, who possesses jurisdiction over the whole Church and especially over the Gallican Churches, whose jurisdiction proceeds immediately from Rome; and he portrays the Gallicans who approach this tribunal as the authors of the gravest prejudice.

[Col. 0580C] He presents Hilary as an example that everyone should imitate. When Hilary went to Leo, he openly declared that he had come to perform his duties, not to litigate a case; to present what had been done in a spirit of protest concerning procedure, not of accusation. Quesnellus therefore considers this example of Hilary, interpreted in his own manner, preferable to all others.

He invokes custom and the canons, as though custom and the canons did not support Roman jurisdiction, or as though the divine right of the apostolic see could have been weakened or abolished by any canons or customs.

Quesnellus’s complaint is still more astonishing because the controversy between Vienne and Arles was of such a kind that it could be neither defined nor settled by the Gallican bishops or by the fathers of the Italian Council of Turin. Was it to continue boiling perpetually and dividing the bishops into factions merely to prevent its being brought before the Roman tribunal?

Zosimus, at Patroclus’s initiative, adjudicated the matter in favor of Arles. But since Zosimus’s judgment had been obtained by misrepresentation—as we shall prove in part II, chapter 2—it could at least have been regarded as corrected by Boniface with respect to the metropolitan jurisdiction of Narbonne and as weakened with respect to the rights of Vienne.

[Col. 0580D] When the same controversy therefore revived under Leo, to whom could one have had recourse except to the see that had previously heard and decided the same case?

Nor, when Saint Leo approved the ordination of Ravennius, did he wish to decide anything in that controversy in favor of Arles. By the fact itself he approved only that the bishop of Arles was a metropolitan distinct from the bishop of Vienne. He established nothing concerning the particular and, so to speak, individual right of Vienne or Arles.

Moreover, since on that occasion the bishops also dealt with confirming the particular prerogatives granted by Rome to the see of Arles—among them the right concerning *formatae* (formal ecclesiastical letters) and to convene synods from all Gaul—if any doubt had arisen especially on this point, was it not just to approach the very source of the privileges, so that every doubt might be removed by a certain confirmation?

[Col. 0581A] What prejudice does Quesnellus imagine in these matters? Can it be a prejudice, when controversies and ambiguities concerning ecclesiastical jurisdiction arise among the Gallicans, to seek a judgment from the see from which all the jurisdiction of the Gallican Churches originates?

Nor should anyone bring forward the honor once sought for Saint Trophimus. Is the honor of Saint Trophimus—who was sent into Gaul by the Roman see and received all his jurisdiction from it—to consist in this, that his successors should in no way acknowledge the jurisdiction of that same see and should take the greatest possible care to avoid it as a danger to their own rights?

Could anyone even suspect such a thing except a person who, because of hostility toward the Roman pontiffs, judges less than correctly? But let us return to the path.

### 8.

Although the present matter does not concern the first hearing of episcopal cases, to which we have briefly referred, everyone nevertheless sees that if these arguments have great force in the question of the first hearing of such cases, they have much greater force in the question of appeals.

[Col. 0581B] If the Roman pontiff, by reason of the primacy and by divine right, can immediately judge episcopal cases in the first instance, he can much more do so in cases of appeal, which after the judgment of patriarchs or metropolitans in provincial synods are by right referred to a superior—no Catholic doubts that the Roman bishop is superior to patriarchs, metropolitans, and the provincial synods themselves.

If in certain regions, especially those distant from the Roman see, ancient custom established that such cases should also be heard and decided by neighboring bishops or by a fuller synod, this too was introduced by ecclesiastical institution, not by any special right that by divine institution belonged either to neighboring bishops or to a fuller council. It was introduced to facilitate and expedite the matter, and to prevent the greater delays that might arise from the distance of journeys and the difficult transport of witnesses—delays by which scandals might continue longer and false or fraudulent reports might more easily infiltrate.

[Col. 0581C] Accordingly, in this matter too, if circumstances require it, one may argue that introducing an innovation is not expedient. For, as Augustine observed in letter 118, even a change of custom that is beneficial in its usefulness causes disturbance by its novelty. One may not, however, argue that the pontiffs lack jurisdiction.

Indeed, if this jurisdiction in such cases were called into doubt under the pretext of custom or the canons, custom and the canons would, through the grossest abuse, be preferred to the divine and certain right of the Roman pontiffs, to which every human right must yield.

### 9.

The same should be said of the Sardican canons, which imply that cases of episcopal appeal are to be heard by judges delegated by the Roman pontiff in the province, or by a legate sent there by him. This likewise concerns what was believed to be more expedient, not any belief that pontifical jurisdiction was restricted by this limit.

Hence canon 4 of that same synod mentions episcopal cases as to be brought before the city of Rome and determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

[Col. 0581D] Similarly, when the African bishops pressed in their letter to Celestine that judgments concerning appeals should be rendered in Africa, they were laboring to preserve the discipline of their Churches, which they considered more useful. They therefore set out the difficulties of such judgments if instituted outside Africa: the wicked retreats of the guilty, their deceit, and the fraudulent reports that could easily creep in. These matters concern what is expedient; they did not in any way attack pontifical jurisdiction. This is sufficiently clear from section 30 of the preceding chapter.

### 10.

Near the end of chapter 16 Quesnellus introduces those words of the same Africans—or of Cyprian—and other similar statements, according to which it is called just and reasonable that every matter should be concluded in the place where it arose and that cases should be heard there where the crime was committed.

[Col. 0582A] The emperors Valentinian and Valens likewise established this in laws 10 and 13 of the *Theodosian Code*, under “Accusations and Indictments.” But this concerns only what is expedient. Just as the emperors did not by those laws deprive themselves of the right they possessed to hear such cases personally wherever they occurred, so the Fathers, in the words quoted, did not deny to the pontiff the jurisdiction that they certainly knew belonged to him.

If in some places they appear to have touched upon that jurisdiction to some extent, this is not unusual. In the heat of argument, words sometimes slip out that go somewhat too far and prove more than they ought, or more than those who use them would themselves wish.

### 11.

Shortly after the beginning of chapter 14, Quesnellus brings forward the words of the Africans—or of Cyprian—in the book *On the Unity of the Church*: “The episcopate is one and undivided, and each holds a part of it in full.” He then turns to the form of judgments and appeals in the provinces and adds:

“If anyone acted otherwise and wished to flee by a written appeal to foreign judges, he was rightly considered to be breaking the harmonious concord of the bishops and splitting the unity.”

He also refers to other words of Cyprian from letter 55.

[Col. 0582B] It is indeed true that Cyprian wrote in the first passage that the episcopate is one, a part of which each holds in full. But when that part is held by the Roman pontiff to the exclusion of the others—and the primacy consists not in rank but in pre-eminent jurisdiction—and when Cyprian himself does not deny this, since he affirms that same primacy on several occasions, it cannot be denied that, because of the primacy, he possesses jurisdiction by divine right over all bishops, who are otherwise equal.

Consequently, it cannot be denied that by the same right he can judge them, whether in the first or the second instance. An appeal to him cannot be called an appeal to a foreign judge who lacks jurisdiction.

Moreover, if the words about “breaking the harmonious concord of the bishops” are taken from Cyprian’s complete text, they will be recognized as entirely unrelated to any assault upon pontifical jurisdiction. He is speaking of schismatics who, after being condemned, had fled to Rome to seek support for their schism. He says:

[Col. 0582C] “Those over whom we preside must not run about, nor by their deceitful and treacherous rashness break the harmonious concord of the bishops.”

The context clearly shows that these words were produced not as a censure of pontifical jurisdiction but in condemnation of the rashness of treacherous men who were maliciously attempting, through deceit and falsehood, to separate Pope Cornelius from Cyprian, with whom he was united.

Leaving aside, then, these and similar testimonies that are wrongly represented as attacks upon pontifical jurisdiction, we must follow the authority of those most learned and holy pontiffs who asserted that right as grounded upon firm principles.
