Or, at most, where circumstances seem to require it, we must follow the example of Saint Bernard, who, while upholding pontifical jurisdiction, fought solely for the public good and the rights of bishops against the disadvantages that might otherwise arise, with the moderation and respect due to the apostolic see.

This is the fairest rule for discussing controversies of this kind. Whoever does not observe it properly and, in the name of customs or canons received in the provinces, argues against pontifical jurisdiction concerning appeals, improperly attacks the jurisdiction of divine institution—and does so with great scandal as well, since that scandal cannot be separated from an attack upon the right of the primacy.

### 12.

[Col. 0582D] What has been set forth thus far concerning the right of appeal is sufficient for the matters presently before us. Our purpose was not to rework this controversy in its entirety, as many have done, nor to examine every single issue arising within it, but only to select and present from it those points that may serve as principles, so that we may determine what ought to be thought concerning Celidonius’s appeal.

To summarize this entire discussion briefly: when Quesnellus began treating the case of Celidonius’s appeal in chapter 14, he presented it verbally as a mere question of fact and announced that he would examine what had prevailed in Gaul during that period.

[Col. 0583A] But since this fact involved the custom and canons received in Gaul, and since he presumed that Leo’s right to hear appeals could have rested solely upon them, he in reality complicated a question of law with a question of fact. By denying that custom and the canons supported Celidonius’s appeal, he sought to show that Leo had heard the case without any right and that by this hearing he had attempted to acquire a new right for himself in Gaul, as was demonstrated in chapter 4 by his words quoted there.

We, however, have shown in the two preceding chapters that both custom and the canons grant the apostolic see the right of appeal in episcopal cases. In this chapter we believe we have sufficiently explained and established the extent to which that right is founded upon the prerogative of the primacy and descends from divine law.

Therefore, when Saint Leo judged Celidonius’s case, even though Saint Hilary of Arles resisted, Hilary was not fighting on behalf of custom or the canons received in Gaul, nor was Leo acting against custom and the canons, as Quesnellus claims. Rather, if Hilary resisted this judgment as incompetent, he would have opposed the received custom and canons; indeed, he might even have appeared to Leo to be attacking the divine right of the primacy.

But Leo, in judging that case, did what he could rightly do, both by custom and by the rules of the canons, and especially by virtue of the prerogative of the primacy.

[Col. 0583B] Since we cannot believe that Hilary was ignorant of, and still less contemptuous of, this custom, these canons, and this divine right without doing him the greatest injustice, we in no way think that he opposed the Roman judgment in Celidonius’s case because he did not recognize in Leo the right of appeal.

### 13.

We believe instead that he resisted for another reason: namely, because he did not think it expedient that this case should be heard and judged at Rome.

For that reason, if circumstances seemed to require it, he could indeed have opposed the proceedings modestly and offered reasons in such a way as to leave pontifical jurisdiction untouched. Whether he used such moderation, however, is a very obscure question of fact, since reliable documents indicating all the circumstances of the dispute are by no means available.

[Col. 0583C] The author of Hilary’s *Life* portrays moderation and respect throughout his narrative. Nor is there any word in Hilary’s address to Leo, which he describes in chapter 17, that suggests a dispute concerning pontifical jurisdiction. On the contrary, he sufficiently indicates Hilary’s deference to pontifical jurisdiction in the words by which he writes that Hilary declared that, if Leo wished something else—namely, if he wished to decide the case—Hilary would not be troublesome. These words present him as obedient and as not denying the right.

The author attributes to Hilary’s virtue and steadfastness the fact that, while defending his judgment concerning Celidonius at Rome, he alone endured such opposition; that he was not at all frightened by threats; that he instructed those who questioned him; that he defeated those who argued with him; that he did not yield to the powerful; that he in no way consented to be reunited in his communion with the man whom he had condemned together with such eminent men; and that he believed those whom he had not bent by reason should be left behind.

But these statements are too general to establish whether Hilary observed moderation in arguing only about what was expedient, or whether, in acting more fervently on this point, he let slip certain words that might appear to strike at the right itself.

[Col. 0583D] On the other hand, Leo does not obscurely indicate in letter 10, chapters 2 and 3, that Hilary used insolent and arrogant words by which he seemed in some way to diminish the reverence due to blessed Peter and to attack his authority. This need not necessarily be referred to a legal dispute concerning appeals, since a more heated argument about what was expedient could itself have produced words that seemed to attack the authority of the apostolic see. Compare what will be said in the observations on part III, chapter 1.

The deputy prefect, in the letter to Hilary inserted into this *Life* in chapter 17, although he removes from Hilary any intention of arrogance, nevertheless indicates that Hilary let certain harsher expressions escape him, expressions that offended Roman ears.

The author of the *Life*, however, who presents Hilary as fighting bravely at Rome, shows that he was not obstinate. He reports that, after returning to Arles, Hilary turned toward appeasing Saint Leo with a humbled and submissive attitude. Although the statements he is remembered as having dictated in this affair may be thought to belong to his defenses, it nevertheless seems beyond doubt that he defended himself moderately in them, so as not to irritate Leo still further while attempting to appease him.

### 14.

[Col. 0584A] In such great obscurity concerning the events, so long as the pontiff’s right is not denied, we do not wish to censure those who strive to defend Saint Hilary with moderation. We think it better to reserve the judgment to God than rashly to determine something. The author of Hilary’s *Life* proposed the same course when he wrote:

“Of such great men, Leo and especially Hilary, who have now been called to heavenly grace, I do not dare to debate their judgments even in my narrative.”

Quesnellus, however, must be wholly refuted. When he undertook to defend Saint Hilary, he thought that Hilary should be defended in such a way that he not only accused Leo but even presented the pontifical right itself as having been rightly attacked by Hilary.

## CHAPTER VIII. Two Charges Brought Against Leo in the Affair of Celidonius Are Refuted

### 1.

We shall not conclude our observations on the first part until we have first dispelled two very serious accusations with which Quesnellus dared to mark Leo at the end of the final chapter of part I.

[Col. 0584B] First, he accuses Leo of allowing Celidonius, after admitting him to his communion, to take part in the sacred rites at the altars before a new examination of his case had been instituted—something that, he says, is forbidden by several canons.

He believes that the passage in chapter 17 of Hilary’s *Life* should be interpreted as referring to Celidonius. In that passage Hilary complained before Leo that certain people in Gaul had rightly received a public sentence, while in Rome they were permitted to take part in the sacred rites at the altars.

In the first place, however, the canons are speaking of a legitimate sentence issued by a legitimate judge. We have seen that Hilary’s sentence against Celidonius was issued by an incompetent judge. Valentinian therefore described Celidonius as having been deposed incompetently. But which canons that prescribed observance of such a sentence—plainly null and void—could he have meant?

2. Furthermore, the canons that are cited, when they forbid receiving excommunicated persons from others, abstract from the circumstances of a legitimate appeal, and give no indication whether the same rule is to be observed also in the case of an appeal having been lodged. [Col. 0584C] That a legitimately lodged appeal, unless some specific exception is made, suspends the effect of a sentence is a general and very well-known rule, which Quesnellus himself professes in Dissertation 8, no. 1. Indeed, when the Sardican Council was discussing the case of an appeal to the Roman pontiff lodged by one who had been deposed, it decreed in canon 4 that, while the appeal was pending, no one should be ordained in his place. This plainly presupposes that the effect of the deposition was suspended by the appeal itself, for the legitimate deposition of one bishop entailed the ordination of another. But if the effect of the deposition was to be suspended with respect to the ordination of another, it followed that the deposition itself seemed to be suspended, so that the man was still to be regarded as bishop until his case had been determined by a new judgment. Hence, in the same canon, such a bishop is perhaps not called absolutely “deposed,” but one who “seems to have been deposed,” as though, through the appeal’s suspensive effect, he continued in the rank of bishop and could be received in episcopal communion, or in the rank of bishop, especially by the one to whom he had appealed.

[Col. 0584D] 991 3. That this discipline prevailed in the Roman Church—namely, that anyone who had been deposed from his rank and deprived of the communion belonging to that rank, but had appealed to the apostolic see, was restored to communion in his own rank until the case had been determined—is plainly shown by the case of the presbyter Apiarius. The African bishops wrote in their letter to Pope Celestine that “your Holiness, believing that he had appealed, although he could not prove it, had restored him to communion.” Here the reason for restoring Apiarius to communion is referred not to a new trial, which had not yet taken place, but to the appeal itself. The Africans do not condemn this except insofar as no appeal had in fact been lodged and could not be proved.

Leo says that the same practice of the Roman Church was followed in the case of the African bishop Lupicinus, whom, although deposed, “we restored to communion before the judgment of the second hearing on this ground” (Epistle 12, chapter 12 [Col. 0585A]; we have convincingly defended this chapter against the charge of being spurious), “because, since he had appealed to our judgment, we saw that he had been unjustly suspended from communion while the matter was pending.” You plainly see that a suspensive effect is attributed to the appeal, so that communion was restored to Lupicinus as though he were still a bishop. Leo therefore followed this Roman discipline in the same way when he restored Celidonius to communion, permitting him—after he had appealed, having been deposed on account of the imputed impediment of bigamy—to attend the sacred rites in his own rank before the Roman judgment concerning him had been rendered.

4. Quesnellus’s second accusation against Leo is that he presents him as having somewhat forgotten ecclesiastical custom when, by means of an imperial sanction, he was the first to attempt to undermine the custom of the Gallican Church and induced Valentinian III to issue the following edict: “Let nothing be permitted to the Gallican bishops, any more than to those of other provinces, to attempt without the authority of the venerable bishop of the Eternal City; but let whatever the authority of the apostolic see has decreed or shall decree be law for all of them.” [Col. 0585B] Shortly afterward he complains of Leo: “While he stirred up the secular powers against Hilary and the whole Gallican Church.”

Valentinian III’s law, found among Leo’s letters as Letter 11, was issued so that Leo’s letter to the bishops of Vienne might be effectively carried out. That letter restrained Hilary from usurping the rights of other metropolitans, exercising incompetent judgments, resisting appeals, and governing the whole Gallican Church at his own pleasure. Whoever complains that imperial power was employed in this matter presupposes that Leo’s actions were contrary to law, or were an oppression of another’s rights. But who could criticize the invocation of secular power in defense of law and to compel the disobedient? Numerous and more ancient examples of the holiest bishops and pontiffs, which no one will condemn, sufficiently vindicate this practice.

[Col. 0585C] Quesnellus has attempted to show that Hilary was in the right. But how fruitless his effort has been, we have already seen in the case of Celidonius and shall see in the following part in the case of Projectus. Quesnellus’s accusation therefore rests solely upon a false presumption. Imperial authority was needed all the more against Hilary because, according to Leo and Valentinian, he was said to have abused military force and armed protection in advancing his plans against another’s rights. Is it not permissible to criticize Hilary for employing secular power against the law, while Leo is criticized for invoking that same power on behalf of law and observance of the canons, so that Hilary might be restrained—the man who was abusing the support of a patrician and a prefect?

“Is it not by royal power that those who disturb the Church are to be restrained,” as Quesnellus himself noted in the marginal annotation to chapter 1 of Letter 118? Not only heretics and schismatics, but also those driven by excessive zeal and overbearing power can disturb the Church and provoke scandals to such an extent that they may rightly be restrained when royal power is called in to assist.

If Quesnellus complains that the power of the Roman see in judgments and appeals was approved by that law, the basis in law for this approval has already been demonstrated. [Col. 0585D] In matters of appeals, the Roman synod did not hesitate to seek imperial legislation from Gratian long before the imperial law in question. See the synod’s letter and Gratian’s law itself in Coustant, volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, among the letters of Damasus, nos. 6 and 7. If what chiefly displeases him is that obedience to pontifical laws was prescribed by an imperial sanction, has not the Catholic Church, including the Gallican Church, always professed that all owe obedience by divine right to the apostolic see on account of its primacy? It was therefore not Leo who, in obtaining the imperial law, forgot ecclesiastical custom—or rather, law—but Quesnellus, when he wrote this criticism.

993 **INTO THE SECOND PART: ON THE CASE OF PROJECTUS; concerning the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolitan sees of Gaul.**

**CHAPTER I. It is shown that Quesnellus wrongly set forth two counts of accusation against Saint Hilary of Arles in the case of Projectus.**

[Col. 0586A]

1. Quesnellus reduces to two categories the charges brought against Hilary in the affair of Projectus. The first is that he appointed a successor over the sick Projectus, and did so without awaiting the citizens’ votes, the testimony of the people, the judgment of the leading men, or the election of the clergy. The second is that he carried out this ordination in another province.

Since he could not prove the first charge, Quesnellus tried to cast suspicion upon it on the ground that we have it attested only by Hilary’s adversaries. But since he admits that the matter is mentioned nowhere except by Leo, who describes what happened on the basis of letters from Projectus himself and from the citizens of that same city, Quesnellus must be understood to regard as Hilary’s adversaries, if not Leo the judge, at least Projectus the bishop and the citizens of his city. Thus the words he adds must also be understood of them: namely, that these charges were so unworthy of a bishop devoted to the discipline of the sacred canons, such as Hilary is presented by so many Gallican councils [Col. 0586B] celebrated under his direction and presidency, that they ought rightly to be numbered among the slanders of envious adversaries.

It is especially incredible that Projectus and his fellow citizens falsely burdened Hilary, and that Leo readily believed these slanders and inserted the matter into a public letter—a letter whose falsehood could easily have been exposed. Moreover, was Leo alone in reporting the matter? The emperor Valentinian also clearly indicated this action in a public law. To this belong the words of Letter 11: “He indecorously ordained others—bishops—against the will and opposition of the citizens.” Quesnellus may assert that the emperor imbibed this slander from Leo. But since he cites no ancient witness who even suggests the contrary, he will find no one to believe him.

The very silence of the author of Hilary’s *Life*, who is wholly devoted to his praises and vindication, suggests that Leo did not report anything slanderous in this affair. Since Leo’s letters, which particularly censured this act, were certainly not unknown, had the charge been calumnious, the author would not have failed to expose it.

[Col. 0586C] 2. Quesnellus saw that this defense of Hilary was sufficiently weak, and so, in Part III, chapter 4, he adopted another method of vindicating him. Although he considers it quite credible—as we too do—that so holy a man was led to carry out this ordination not by some presumption, but by zeal arising from circumstances unknown to us, nevertheless, since he cannot deny that the action was contrary to the canons, he thinks that the holy man should nonetheless be pardoned. While occupied with various matters arising in the Churches, he may have carried out certain actions somewhat too precipitately, hastening on to other matters after being inflamed with zeal for discipline.

We willingly accept this excuse, since, while clearing Saint Hilary of malice, it does not accuse Leo. It is enough to vindicate Leo’s censure of Hilary if, by Quesnellus’s own admission, Hilary must be said to have acted contrary to discipline. Indeed, this example of Hilary’s precipitancy in so important a matter makes it plausible that he acted with similar precipitancy in the case of Celidonius as well; it is therefore unsurprising if he was deceived in that judgment. Enough has been said about the first part of the accusation.

[Col. 0586D] 3. More must be said about the second part, on which Quesnellus argues at greater length, since he sees that the charge—that Hilary usurped the right of ordination in another province 995—cannot easily be excused if true.

A few words would in fact suffice here as well, since Leo, who attests that the province was another’s, ought to be believed more readily than Quesnellus, who denies it on the basis of weak conjectures alone. No one has reported to which Church Projectus belonged. Quesnellus, however, conjectures that he was bishop of the province of Narbonensis Prima, which he maintains was subject to the see of Arles.

But since Leo says that Projectus was bishop of another province, Leo’s testimony required one of two conclusions: either Projectus was not bishop in Narbonensis Prima, if that province belonged to Arles; or, if he was bishop in that province of Narbonensis, then it did not belong to Arles.

[Col. 0587A] 4. We consider it most probable that Projectus was bishop in Narbonensis Prima. For this reason we have preferred the reading of Leo’s text found in the manuscripts:

“What does Hilary seek in another province, and what is he usurping that none of his predecessors possessed before Patroclus, when even that which seemed to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment?” (*Epistle* 10, chapter 4).

These words indicate a bishopric belonging to another province—one which Patroclus had obtained with Zosimus’s permission, but which he later lost when Zosimus’s grant was revoked, so that in Leo’s time it was another’s. This is true only of Narbonensis Prima, since Zosimus first granted only that province, which had been taken away from the metropolitan bishop of Narbonensis, to Patroclus; and afterward Boniface explicitly restored it to the bishop of Narbonensis after removing it from Patroclus.

Projectus was therefore bishop in this province. When Hilary appointed a successor over him, he sought to carry out an ordination in another province. This ordination [Col. 0587B] seems to have taken place after the judgment held at Besançon in the case of Celidonius, so that Hilary, traveling from Besançon to Narbonensis Prima, quickly ordained a bishop and then proceeded to Rome against Celidonius.

In this way the words of Leo’s Letter 10, chapter 5, are readily understood: “Making many journeys with swift travel, as we have learned, and rushing through distant provinces . . .,” and so forth. A considerable distance between provinces lies between Besançon, in Maxima Sequanorum, and Narbonensis Prima; this would not be the case if Hilary had passed from Arles into the province of Narbonensis. Hence, too, Projectus’s complaint is said to have been brought to Leo after the Roman judgment concerning Celidonius had been completed, when Hilary had already left Rome.

5. This ordination, carried out in another province, could in some way have been defended against the charge of usurping another’s right if it were said to have been performed with the metropolitan’s consent. Leo’s words in chapter 6 seem to suggest this, where, speaking of ordinations belonging to the metropolitans of the individual provinces, he says:

“Let no one dare to claim another’s right for himself. Let each be content with his own limits and boundaries; and let him know that he is not permitted to transfer to another the privilege due to himself. But if anyone, neglecting the apostolic sanctions and attributing greater weight to personal favor” (these words seem to refer to Hilary), “wishes to become a deserter of his own honor, believing that he can transfer his privilege to another, then not the one to whom he has yielded it, but the one who, by the antiquity of his episcopate, precedes the other priests within the province, shall claim for himself the power of ordaining.”

Such careful declarations and regulations would not have been made in Hilary’s case unless those metropolitans, including the bishop of Narbonensis, had surrendered their privilege to Hilary as a result of personal favor.

6. Quesnellus was not satisfied with this mode of defense, which is condemned by the apostolic decrees. With considerable effort he advanced another defense of Hilary: that Hilary had acted in defense of his own right, and that this ordination had been carried out not in another province, as Leo reported, but in his own province of Arles. This will be examined in the following chapter.

997 **CHAPTER II. It is demonstrated that Hilary carried out an ordination in another province. Narbonensis Prima, always subject to the metropolitan of Narbonensis, is removed from the metropolitan jurisdiction of Arles. Patroclus obtained Zosimus’s decision by deception concerning the mission of Saint Trophimus.**

[Col. 0587D]

1. To support his opinion, Quesnellus gathers much concerning the rights of the see of Arles in several chapters; what bears upon the present matter may be summarized as follows.

First, he maintains that from the beginning the bishop of Arles presided with metropolitan jurisdiction over the whole of the undivided province of Narbonensis and therefore had Narbonensis Prima as a subject province—the province in which Hilary ordained Projectus’s successor. He further maintains that the bishops of Narbonensis later asserted this province for themselves by mere deception, but that this was annulled by Zosimus’s decree when the rights of Arles were restored.

Since he could not deny that the successors of Zosimus, Boniface I and Celestine, had issued decrees in favor of the metropolitan right of the bishop of Narbonensis over the same province—decrees that revoked what Zosimus had established in this matter—he argues secondly that, because of the ancient right of the Church of Arles, these decrees did not take effect in Gaul. Consequently, when Hilary appointed a successor over Projectus, he ordained a bishop in his own province, not in another’s.

[Col. 0588A] 2. To resolve these two points of controversy as briefly as possible: as regards the first, which concerns the period before Zosimus, Hilary of Narbonensis had sent Zosimus the reliable evidence of apostolic letters supporting the metropolitan right of the bishop of Narbonensis over Narbonensis Prima. No earlier document opposed to this in favor of Arles is cited.

Zosimus alone, in Letter 6 to Hilary of Narbonensis, declared this apostolic privilege of the see of Narbonensis to have been obtained by deception: “The matter having been voided, since you are shown to have obtained it from the apostolic see by deception.” And in Letter 1 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 2, he expressly stated that the see of Arles had always possessed the right of ordination in both Narbonian provinces. [Col. 0588B]

Quesnellus’s entire authority rests on these and similar testimonies of Zosimus alone. Leo, however, testifies against Zosimus that none of the bishops of Arles before Patroclus had claimed for himself the right of ordination in the province where Projectus was bishop: “What is he usurping that none of his predecessors possessed before Patroclus?” (*Epistle* 10, chapter 4).

The whole dispute, therefore, resting on these two conflicting witnesses, depends on which one is more deserving of belief: Zosimus, who affirms an ancient right of the bishop of Arles over Narbonensis Prima, or Leo, who denies it. There is, however, considerable presumption that Zosimus was deceived.

3. That this pontiff placed excessive trust in Patroclus of Arles and was deceived and misled by him, while Patroclus was present and employing evil methods, is absolutely certain from the case of Heros.

Patroclus was evidently well received by Zosimus because he enjoyed the friendship and patronage of Constantius, the consul and master of the soldiers, “whose favor,” Prosper says, “was sought through him” (*Chronicle*, under the year 4122). When he had invaded the see of Heros, it was in Patroclus’s interest that Heros should be condemned by Zosimus, thereby securing Patroclus in the see of Arles.

Just as Zosimus, excessively credulous, swallowed and committed to writing the accusations that Patroclus brought against Heros for this purpose, so he readily accepted and incorporated what Patroclus advertised as the right of the see of Arles over Narbonensis Prima. These claims therefore deserve no greater confidence than those which Patroclus advanced against Heros.

Nor do the proceedings and the testimony of many fellow priests, which Zosimus cites in Letter 6, chapter 1, to Hilary of Narbonensis in support of the prerogative of the see of Arles, offer stronger proof. It would have been easy for Patroclus, a fraudulent and violent man, to win over to his favor and opinion those bishops to whom, as Prosper Tiro testifies in his *Chronicle* under the twentieth year of the Emperor Theodosius, he sold priestly offices through an infamous commercial transaction.

Others, perhaps, were compelled not so much by deception as by fear, lest they make an enemy of the man who, relying on Constantius’s favor, was persecuting Heros.

[Col. 0588D] Moreover, these witnesses and the proceedings, judging from their testimony, were concerned with tracing the establishment of the metropolitan right of Arles back to Saint Trophimus, from whom the right of ordination over Narbonensis Prima was said to have been transmitted to his successors at Arles and preserved down to recent times. This is said to have been confirmed by the proceedings held before us and by the testimony of many fellow priests. 999 Thus Zosimus writes in the same Letter 6, chapter 1.

But the facts reported by this pontiff concerning the mission of Trophimus—supposedly on the authority of those same proceedings and witnesses—display several indications of falsehood, which themselves cast the proceedings and witnesses into considerable suspicion.

4. First, Zosimus asserts that Trophimus’s mission was the first of all missions to Gaul, so that he says all Gaul received its streams from that source, in Letter 1 to the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

And in Letter 6 to Hilary of Narbonensis, speaking of the ordinations of the bishops of the province of Vienne and of the two Narbonian provinces, he says: “To those regions he first displayed the reverence of so great a name”—that is, of the episcopate—“and not undeservedly transferred to others” (or rather, to other regions) “the authority he had received.”

[Col. 0589A] For these statements to be true, Saint Trophimus’s mission would have to be placed in apostolic times, before Saints Pothinus and Irenaeus, under whom the Churches of Lyon and Vienne flourished at the beginning of the second century.

The bishops favoring the metropolitan of Arles do assign this apostolic age to Trophimus’s mission in their petition to Pope Leo, Letter 65 among the Leonine letters. They state that Saint Trophimus was sent to Arles by Saint Peter and the apostles, and that from there the gift of faith and religion was gradually infused into the other regions of Gaul.

These claims, asserted as familiar knowledge to all Gauls and supported by apostolic documents, depend upon Zosimus’s letters, which had already been circulated in Gaul. The entire authority for this antiquity therefore returns to Zosimus, or rather to Patroclus and the fellow priests whom Zosimus cited.

[Col. 0589B] It was necessary for Patroclus to introduce an apostolic origin in order to persuade people that his see of Arles was older than, and the mother of, Vienne, with which he was chiefly in conflict.

This antiquity belonging to the apostolic age is plainly refuted by the older Gallic writer Sulpicius Severus. Guided by no partisan interest and well versed in ancient affairs, especially those of Gaul, he sincerely professed that the Christian religion had been brought to Gaul only later. He writes in Book II, chapter 32 of *Sacred History*: “Later, the worship of God was received beyond the Alps.”

The diptychs of the Church of Arles, published by Mabillon in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 432, likewise exclude this apostolic antiquity. For they list only four bishops down to Marinus, who took part in the First Council of Arles in the year 314.

Hence, at the Council of Turin, where the case between Arles and Vienne was debated with the greatest contention before Zosimus, and where the bishops’ allegations are reported to have been heard, the bishop of Arles either did not produce this apostolic mission of Trophimus because he had not received it from his predecessors, or, if he did produce it, could not prove it with any suitable document. Otherwise, the case would most certainly have been awarded to that bishop, who by means of so ancient a mission would have demonstrated fully and decisively that his Church was the mother of Vienne.

These older documents are clear indications of Patroclus’s imposture, so much so that Quesnellus himself does not hesitate not merely to abandon, but rather to mark as false, the apostolic origin of Saint Trophimus’s mission. See his notes on Letter 65, where, concerning Saint Trophimus’s mission by Blessed Peter the Apostle, he says: “And I consider this utterly false.”

Gregory of Tours assigned this mission to the time of Decius, that is, to the middle of the third century. Some writers have departed from Gregory’s view only through prejudice and confidence in the testimony of Zosimus—or, more truly, of Patroclus and the Gauls who followed Zosimus or Patroclus.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Tillemont also intimates this somewhat differently in volume X, p. 681: “As regards the Churches of Arles and Vienne, whether the bishop of Arles used his argument from Saint Trophimus, or whether it had not yet been invented, it is clear that the Council of Turin paid no attention to it.”]

[Col. 0589D] 5. A further and more evident imposture shines forth in the claims that Saint Trophimus is presented as the first metropolitan of the city of Arles, sent forth from that see (Letter 5), and that the same metropolitan right was always preserved by his successors from that time onward (Letter 6). This is as false as anything could possibly be.

For during those ancient times when Saint Trophimus was sent to Gaul and persecutions were raging, no one in Gaul possessed metropolitan dignity. Quesnellus himself readily concedes this in Part I, chapter 13, no. 8. Speaking of that form of hierarchy in which bishops are subject to metropolitans, he says: “It is very difficult to find this before the time of the Council of Nicaea.”

And in chapter 12 he says that to seek this hierarchical structure in that period, especially in Transalpine Gaul, which accepted the faith late, “is the act of a man mixing ancient and modern things.” Compare what will be said about the late beginnings of the Gallican metropolitan sees in chapter 3, section 2.

[Col. 0590A] If, as Quesnellus agrees with Gregory of Tours in Part I, chapter 13, no. 9, and in the notes cited on Letter 65, six other bishops were sent into Gaul together with Trophimus to spread the faith there and establish Churches, there is no greater reason why the same metropolitan right—understood as the right of ordination—should be attributed to Trophimus rather than to the other six bishops. Among them, that same right would have been transmitted to his companion Paul, who first presided over the city of Narbonensis, which at that time was the metropolis of the entire province and for that reason was called Narbonensis.

These indications of falsehood are recognized as attached to the deceptions of Zosimus, Patroclus, and his supporters. Accordingly, Tillemont rightly did not hesitate to write in note 1 on the *Life of Saint Dionysius of Paris*, volume IV, p. 707:

“The mission of Saint Trophimus by the apostles and by Saint Peter rests only upon authors who advance it solely to support a claim that may be pronounced untenable. In that claim M. de Marca admits that Patroclus had taken Zosimus in by his lies (*obreptum Zosimo per falsam Patrocli suggestionem*). There is therefore scarcely any reason to dwell upon it.”

And in note 2 on the *Life of Zosimus*, volume X, p. 838, he says:

“All this rests upon Patroclus’s good faith; one may attribute every kind of lie to him without injuring his reputation.”

Similarly, Faidit—or the Gallic author of the work entitled *Eclaircissements sur la doctrine et sur l’histoire ecclésiastique des deux premiers siècles*, published at Maastricht in 1695, p. 157—offers the following in the very title or synopsis:

“That the tradition which has Saint Trophimus sent by Saint Peter into Gaul to convert the Gauls to the faith is a fable invented by Patroclus of Arles to support his metropolitan claims over Vienne. Conjectures that Saint Trophimus did not come to Arles until about the year 255, where he succeeded Marcianus. Proofs that others had preached the faith in France before him and had founded Churches there in the first and second centuries.”

[Col. 0590C] 6. Once these arguments for imposture and deception have been established, who would believe that Zosimus’s testimony affirming the ancient right of the bishop of Arles over Narbonensis Prima should be preferred to Leo’s testimony, which affirms that no one before Patroclus possessed this right? Can similar arguments of deception and fraud be identified in Leo?

Zosimus settled this matter on the basis solely of the suggestions of Patroclus and his supporters, who had traveled to Rome, while Hilary of Narbonensis was absent and unaware of what they had put forward. When Zosimus requested by letter that Hilary send documents concerning his right, Hilary considered the apostolic letters sufficiently suitable—those letters that confirmed the prerogative and possession of his see—and, being absent, he could not answer the evidence by which Patroclus had deceived Zosimus.

Saint Leo, however, was adequately informed about Zosimus’s deception by the later decrees of Boniface and Celestine, through which Zosimus’s decrees were revoked. These pontiffs would not so quickly have abrogated the decrees of their predecessor Zosimus in favor of the see of Narbonensis unless they had discovered that he had been deceived by Patroclus and that the account of Saint Trophimus had been fabricated.

[Col. 0590D] Moreover, after the ordination of Ravennius, when Saint Leo received the petitions of the Gallic bishops who supported the see of Arles, in which the same decrees of Zosimus and the same account of Saint Trophimus were advanced so that this see might be preferred to Vienne, he carefully examined the allegations of both parties as presented by the clerics who were present. Yet, with respect to Trophimus’s mission, he found nothing that would justify awarding the case to Arles.

He found only that both cities, Arles and Vienne, had always been distinguished, so that by an alternating distribution of certain privileges, sometimes one and sometimes the other had precedence in ecclesiastical matters. He therefore established the division of the province recommended by the Council of Turin. [Col. 0591A] He left the bishop of Narbonensis in possession of his right over Narbonensis Prima; and just as that bishop had once obtained this right confirmed by apostolic privilege, so he continued to possess it after Leo’s decree.

7. From this the third point of Quesnellus is also overturned: he exalted the right of Arles over this province to such an extent that he claimed that Boniface’s decree had been obtained by deception and had not been received in Gaul.

As for the alleged deception, once we have shown that the decrees of Zosimus—which, through the influence of the violent and cunning Patroclus, subjected Narbonensis Prima to the see of Arles contrary to ancient practice and apostolic privilege—were deceptive, how can Boniface’s decree be branded as deceptive, when it cut away the deception imposed upon Zosimus?

Boniface does not mention Zosimus’s rescripts. [Col. 0591B] But since those rescripts were so solemn and had been issued in the presence of Boniface, then a presbyter of the Roman Church, they could not have escaped him. This is sufficient to prevent his silence from being interpreted as evidence of deception or ignorance.

Nor was it necessary to hear either Patroclus of Arles, who was known to have deceived Zosimus through fraud, or Hilary of Narbonensis, for whom the letters he had sent to Zosimus together with the apostolic privilege of his see spoke sufficiently—letters which Boniface, then present at Rome, knew about.

How, then, can the decree of this pontiff be called deceptive when none of Boniface’s successors revoked it, and when Celestine confirmed it as wholly valid and just? Leo, in Letter 10, affirmed that “even that which seemed to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward removed by a better judgment,” and it was removed in such a way that the bishop of Narbonensis always continued to enjoy the same right.

“Seemed to have been granted,” Saint Leo says, because he regarded Zosimus’s decree as invalid on account of its fraud and manifest deception. Yet, in defending this decree, Quesnellus does not hesitate to charge not so much Boniface as Celestine and Leo with having been deceived.

[Col. 0591C] 8. The conjectures that Quesnellus advances in chapter 5 to show that Boniface’s decree was neither received in practice in Gaul nor put into effect are so incongruous, weak, and far-fetched that they accomplish nothing by themselves.

Whether a decree has taken effect in practice is established by actions. The sole action of the Church of Luteva that has so far been reported concerns the province of Narbonensis Prima; moreover, it occurred no later than Boniface’s constitution.

In this very action, Patroclus alone, attempting to put Zosimus’s decree into practice, insisted on giving a bishop to the people of Luteva. But when the clergy and people of that Church knew that Zosimus’s decree had been obtained by deception, they sent legates to Boniface, who complained about Patroclus, among other things, on the ground that he had ordained in another province, bypassing the metropolitan and acting contrary to the regulations of the Fathers.

This pontiff paid no attention to Zosimus’s rescripts, which he knew well, and considered them so invalid that he wrote to Hilary of Narbonensis in Letter 12:

“Having been reminded by our authority—which indeed you ought to have done of your own accord—and having regard for the wishes and will of the petitioners, proceed to the same place where such an ordination is said to have been celebrated, equipped with the right of the metropolitan and relying upon our commands. Understand that, according to the regulations of the Fathers, whatever must be done has been entrusted to your judgment by us, so that, when everything has been completed, whatever you decide may be made known to the apostolic see through your report, since it is clear that the ordination of the entire province has been entrusted to you.”

He does not say that he is entrusting this to him by virtue of the decree, but that it is clear that it had been entrusted to him—namely, by the ancient right of his see, which, as he seems to have believed, had not in reality been diminished by Zosimus’s deceptive constitutions. Thus he declared that Hilary could already have done the same of his own accord and had no need of apostolic authority to rescind Zosimus’s enactments.

So that no doubt might remain, by this letter he declared and confirmed Hilary as metropolitan of that province, lest anyone should perhaps think that Zosimus’s decrees constituted an obstacle.

After this rescript of Boniface, no other action concerning the province of Narbonensis Prima is committed to memory [Col. 0592A] before Saint Hilary, who appointed a successor over Projectus. We therefore marvel at Quesnellus’s boldness in declaring, without any supporting action, that this decree had not taken effect in favor of Arles before Saint Hilary, or had not been received in practice. This is especially surprising since the same decree was confirmed by Celestine, and since Leo himself, while affirming that Zosimus’s decrees had temporarily granted Patroclus a right over that province, censures Hilary of Arles for usurping the same right after Boniface’s annulment of them. Leo thereby assumes that no one after Patroclus and after Boniface’s decree had presumed to claim that right for himself.

9. Yet, he says in chapter 5, since Saint Leo writes that no predecessor of Hilary claimed metropolitan jurisdiction over that province before Patroclus, it follows that Patroclus’s successors exercised the same jurisdiction thereafter, disregarding Boniface’s decree. This, however, is mere caviling of the emptiest kind. Since Saint Leo in that passage wished only to vindicate the ancient possession of Arles that was alleged to predate Patroclus, and to make clear the justice of the decree of his predecessor Boniface—for he immediately adds that by it the decree of Zosimus had been corrected—only Patroclus’s predecessors needed to be mentioned. A stronger-looking argument may be drawn from Celestine’s letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne. In it, while confirming Boniface’s decree, he rules that no one may go beyond the boundaries of his own province or presume anything to the injury of another bishop. Quesnellus thinks that this refers to Saint Honoratus of Arles, as though, neglecting Boniface’s decree, he had governed all the provinces granted by Zosimus, including Narbonensis I. But the letter’s heading mentions, together with the province of Vienne, only one Narbonensis. How, then, can one conclude that it speaks rather of Narbonensis I than of Narbonensis II? In the latter province, indeed, the bishop of Aix was to exercise metropolitan jurisdiction by Boniface’s decree, as we shall explain in chapter 6, section 5. Yet because that decree was not expressed with respect to Narbonensis II as explicitly as it had been with respect to Narbonensis I, Honoratus may perhaps have thought that jurisdiction over it still belonged to him. The words of Celestine could refer to this; hence that testimony should not be transferred to Narbonensis I. Since Narbonensis I had expressly been excluded by Boniface from the metropolitan jurisdiction of the bishop of Arles, it is rash and injurious to the memory of this holy man to assert, without any certain witness, that Honoratus despised the decree.

Moreover, Celestine’s aforementioned letter is divided, as it were, into two parts. The first, contained in three chapters, plainly rebukes the abuses that had been reported to the pontiff; and in it nothing is found that suggests an usurpation of another’s jurisdiction. The second part appends certain general rules of discipline, and no particular complaint is indicated as having occasioned their insertion. Indeed, at the end of chapter 3 the only reason given is that, although the statutes of the Apostolic See were known to most people, each person might hasten, by this repetition, to be recalled to the standard of discipline. Just as it cannot be inferred that certain prohibitions in these rules were violated by Honoratus, so neither can it be inferred that he violated the first statute, concerning the nonviolation of metropolitan rights. That statute, being more recent, having been issued by Boniface, and relating to the same provinces, was evidently thought worthy of being repeated first among the others.

Thus all Quesnellus’s efforts are finally dissolved. In attempting to excuse Hilary of Arles, he maintains, against Leo’s explicit testimony, that Narbonensis I had been subject to the metropolitan of Arles. At the same time it becomes clear how justly that same pontiff reproved Hilary on this further ground: because he consecrated a successor to Projectus in another bishop’s province.

# CHAPTER III

## On the civil arrangement of the provinces of Gaul, especially concerning Narbonensis as a whole

The five provinces were not cut out from Narbonensis alone, but included Aquitania and Novempopulana. Another division of six provinces under Theodosius I. The division into seven provinces made in the fourth century demonstrated. The division of all Gaul into two dioceses, subordinate to two vicars under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. On the *Notitia provinciarum* edited from the Veronese manuscript, shown to be older than the *Book of Provinces* and the *Notitia Dignitatum* of both Empires. The catalogue of the bishops of the First Council of Arles defended; and another internal division of Narbonensis as a whole proposed.

[Col. 0593A]

### 1.

Until now we have made no observation concerning the civil and ecclesiastical division of the provinces in Gaul, a subject on which Quesnellus discusses at length in both the first and the second parts of his preceding dissertation, because that highly intricate dispute was not necessary for defending Leo. Now, however, since Leo has been sufficiently defended on other grounds, we do not hesitate to offer several observations on this subject, by which Quesnellus’s errors will be exposed. First, we must speak of the civil division, to which the ancient division of the ecclesiastical provinces is thought to have been adapted.

### 2.

It is universally agreed that Augustus divided Gaul into four parts, or rather into three Gauls—Celtica or Lugdunensis, Belgica, and Aquitanica—and into Narbonensis. The last, because it had been left to the Roman people as a possession of ancient right, was honored with the distinctive name of the Province. This province, which is chiefly at issue in the case of Saint Hilary, embraced the entire region that in a later division was divided into the province of Vienne, the two Narbonenses, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps.

This division of Augustus continued for a long time. An ancient author of the *Book on the Deaths of the Persecutors* testifies in chapter 7 that under Diocletian a new and notable division of the provinces was made:

> The provinces were also cut into fragments, many governors and numerous offices came to bear upon the individual regions and almost upon the individual cities; there were likewise many financial administrators, commanders, and vicars of prefects.

Everyone agrees that Constantine introduced something new into the division of the provinces. What exactly Diocletian or Constantine established, however, is not so certain that anything definite can be affirmed. Constantine’s division is ordinarily explained from the *Notitia Dignitatum* and other notices of the provinces. But these notices were compiled at the end of the fourth century or in the fifth, when other divisions and alterations of the provinces had already taken place. They are therefore less suitable for establishing Constantine’s distribution with certainty; hence numerous errors have arisen from this source.

P. Giovanni Antonio Bianco should be consulted, *On the Power and Politics of the Church*, vol. IV, book II, chapter 1. We must therefore use other evidence and employ the aforementioned notices cautiously, in those passages where they can contribute to illuminating the earlier arrangement.

### 3.

We must now examine whether, in Diocletian’s or Constantine’s division, anything was altered in Narbonensis as Augustus had constituted it, and what new arrangement was introduced. Quesnellus adopts the view, in part II, chapter 2, that nothing was altered before the middle of the fourth century, at which time he supposes it was divided into four parts. For he says:

> There is nothing in the ancient monuments from which it can be conjectured that the province of Narbonensis as a whole was divided into four parts before the middle of the fourth century.

Moreover, in chapter 5, speaking of Narbonensis II, he indicates a new division into five parts toward the end of the fourth century, after the tyrants who had torn Gaul apart had been suppressed:

> When afterward the affairs of the Empire had been restored to peace, and a new division of those provinces had been introduced by imperial sanction, etc.

Here he clearly points to a new division into five parts. He supposes that in the first division Narbonensis as a whole was divided into Narbonensis, Vienne, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps. For Sextus Rufus, who flourished around the middle of the century and dedicated his *Breviary* to the emperors Valentinian I and Valens around the year 369, mentions only one Narbonensis. Since two Narbonenses are mentioned after Sextus Rufus, he seems to understand this division of one Narbonensis as reducing four provinces to five, so that the five provinces mentioned by several witnesses were cut from Narbonensis as a whole—namely, the two Narbonenses, the province of Vienne, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps.

### 4.

This opinion of Quesnellus is shared by most people, if not by everyone. For, excepting Pagius and one or two others with him, all agree that the five provinces were formed from Narbonensis as a whole and did not extend into other parts of Gaul. This widespread prejudice among so many scholars rests chiefly on the fact that they saw the five provinces distinguished from Gaul. Thus, at the Council of Valence in 374, “Gaul and the five provinces” are mentioned; similarly in the letter of the tyrant Maximus to Pope Siricius in 375, and at the Council of Turin around the year 401.

Since only Narbonensis as a whole had been separated from the three Gauls—Celtica, Belgica, and Aquitanica—they concluded that the five provinces had been taken from Narbonensis alone. For this reason they did not agree with Pagius, who counted Aquitania I among the five provinces while excluding the Graian Alps, which are separated from them in the notice presenting seven provinces of Gaul.

### 5.

But we have discovered that this argument, which appeared conclusive, is false. Although during the first three centuries Narbonensis as a whole was customarily distinguished from Gaul, following the example of Julius Caesar, in the fourth century, when a new division of the provinces was made, we find Aquitania rather than Narbonensis distinguished from Gaul. Four witnesses from the fourth century are sufficient.

Sextus Rufus says in his *Breviary*:

> There are eighteen provinces in Gaul, together with Aquitania and the Britains.

Philastrius, speaking of the Priscillianists in heresy 84, says:

> They are found in Gaul, Spain, and Aquitania, as abstainers.

Ausonius writes of Arles:

> Gaul, which they enjoy, and Aquitania with its fertile bosom.

Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 41:

> But this seemed disgraceful to our Gauls—that is, to the Aquitanians—and to the Britains.

Let us add the testimony of Paulinus of Nola in *Natale* XI, on Saint Felix, verse 154, written in the year 404:

> Gaul took Martin, Aquitania took Delphinus.

This distinction of Aquitania from Gaul, which we do not find before the division into five provinces, provides sufficient evidence that Aquitania—which under Augustus’s arrangement had been joined to the Gauls, Celtica and Belgica—was separated from those same Gauls in the new division into five provinces and was included among the five provinces customarily distinguished from Gaul. In the same way, everyone later counted Aquitania among the seven provinces, although these too were distinguished from Gaul, as in Zosimus in 417 and in the first letter addressed to the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

Nor do we deny that Aquitania could still be called Gaul. For Narbonensis as a whole is also sometimes found included among the Gauls; hence the designation “Gaul of Narbonensis.”

### 6.

That Aquitania and Novempopulana, which is part of Aquitania, were counted among the five provinces is made plain by Philastrius. In heresy 51, designating the Priscillianists under the name of the Manichaeans, he reports that they lurked in Spain and the five provinces; then, in heresy 84, he testifies that the same people, called abstainers, were found in Gaul, Spain, and Aquitania. Here he calls “Aquitania” what in the earlier passage he calls “the five provinces.” For only Aquitania—which Sulpicius Severus of Aquitania clearly shows in book II, chapter 48 of his *History* to have been the region in which the Priscillianists spread their errors—can be referred to the five provinces mentioned above.

Philastrius’s testimony is so clear to us that, if Aquitania, which according to Sulpicius’s testimony they certainly infected, is thought to be excluded from the five provinces, no other place can be assigned and demonstrated as the location in which the Priscillianists, entering the five provinces, lay concealed. Indeed, if he had not known that Aquitania was included among the five provinces, Philastrius would have mentioned Aquitania, which was especially infected by the Priscillianists, earlier in the first passage rather than the five provinces.

### 7.

Furthermore, by the name Aquitania Philastrius signifies not so much Aquitania properly so called as Novempopulana, which is part of Aquitania. This is evident from the testimony of Sulpicius, who, while teaching that Aquitania was infected by the Priscillianists, reports among other things that Elusa was corrupted by them; Elusa was situated in Novempopulana:

> Their route—Priscillian’s and that of his companions—passed through inner Aquitania. There, after being received with great honor by the inexperienced, they scattered the seeds of their falsehood and especially corrupted the people of Elusa by a few sermons.

Aquitania and Novempopulana, therefore, were included among the five provinces. Sextus Rufus openly confirms the same thing when he says in his *Breviary*:

> There are eighteen provinces in Gaul, together with Aquitania and the Britains: the Maritime Alps, the province of Vienne, Narbonensis, Novempopulana, the two Aquitanias, the Graian Alps, Maxima Sequanorum, the two Germanias, and the two Belgicas. In the Britains: Maxima Caesariensis, Flavia Caesariensis, Britannia I, and Britannia II.

Several points in this passage deserve attention. By distinguishing Aquitania and the Britains from “Gaul” in the strict sense in his opening words, he indicates three bodies of provinces, consisting of eighteen provinces. He explicitly declares which provinces belonged to the Britains in the words: “In the Britains: Maxima Caesariensis,” and so forth. The remaining, earlier provinces must be divided between Gaul and Aquitania.

Although he does not designate with equal explicitness which provinces belonged to Gaul and which to Aquitania, the matter is easily understood if one observes that he describes the Maritime Alps, together with the remaining provinces through the two Aquitanias, in continuous geographical succession, as the maps show. The Graian Alps, however, since they are extremely far from the Aquitanias immediately preceding them, are named in continuous succession with Maxima Sequanorum and the provinces that follow. It is therefore clear that the author distinguishes two series of provinces, one of which he assigns to Gaul and the other to Aquitania.

That the series beginning with the Graian Alps must be referred to Gaul in the strict sense is evident from the provinces that follow—Maxima Sequanorum, the two Germanias, and so forth—which always belonged to Gaul strictly understood. The other series, therefore, beginning with the Maritime Alps, pertains to Aquitania.

Since this series includes the Maritime Alps, the province of Vienne, and Narbonensis—provinces that no one doubts belonged to the five provinces—it cannot be doubted that all Aquitania was also counted among the five provinces. If Sextus Rufus, in this series, lists two Aquitanias and therefore enumerates not five but six provinces, we believe this occurred because, by the time he was writing, the five provinces had become six through the new division of one Aquitania into two.

He wrote under Valentinian I, around the year 369. Yet before that time, as Pagius observed under the year 374, section 9, there was only one Aquitania under the same emperor. This is clear from an inscription in Gruter, no. CCCCXLV, 8:

> To Saturninius Secundus, vir clarissimus, governor of the province of Aquitanica and master of the records . . . . . On account of his outstanding services to the state, our lords Valentinian and Valens, ever-victorious and triumphant Augusti, ordered that a statue be erected and placed under a gilded canopy.

You see that Saturninius is called governor of the province of Aquitanica, not governor of the province of Aquitania I or II, as would have had to be written if Aquitania had then been divided into two.

This is proved much more clearly by Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, a city that later belonged to Aquitania II. Writing before Sextus Rufus, Hilary composed his book *On the Synods* toward the end of the year 358. In the heading prefixed to it he distinguishes two Germanias, two Belgicas, and two Lugdunenses, but designates only one province of Aquitania, just as he designates one Novempopulana and one Narbonensis:

> To the most beloved and blessed brothers and fellow bishops of the province of Germania I and Germania II, of Belgica I and Belgica II, of Lugdunensis I and Lugdunensis II, and of the province of Aquitania and the province of Novempopulana; and to the people of Narbonensis and the clerics of Toulouse, and to the bishops of the provinces of the Britains: Hilary.

If, therefore, one places a single Aquitania in Sextus Rufus’s series, as existed in Hilary’s time, it will become clear what the five provinces were before Rufus. They were the Maritime Alps, the province of Vienne, Narbonensis, Novempopulana, and Aquitania.

The five provinces, therefore, did not arise from Narbonensis alone, but from Narbonensis together with Aquitania. Nor did they include Narbonensis as a whole in the same way that they included all Aquitania. For the Graian Alps, cut from Narbonensis as a whole, were transferred into Gaul properly so called, as we learn from the same Rufus.

### 8.

This division into five provinces, earlier than Sextus Rufus, may perhaps have originated with Constantine. Since, in this division, Aquitania—formerly counted among the Gauls—was joined with Narbonensis to form the five provinces and began to be distinguished from Gaul, Constantine appears to have divided all Gaul into two parts. He distributed the provinces of Aquitania and Narbonensis among the five provinces, while retaining the name “Gaul” for the other provinces, which included ancient Belgica and Lugdunensis; and he seems to have included among them the Graian Alps, which lie nearer to those regions.

Thus he established two dioceses in Gaul, designated in the notice published by the Marquis Maffei from the most ancient manuscript of the Veronese chapter: namely, the diocese of Vienne, which contained five provinces and was governed by the vicar of the five provinces mentioned in law 15, *On Pagans*, of the year 399, addressed to Proclianus, vicar of the five provinces; and the diocese of Gaul, designated in the same Veronese notice, which contained the remaining provinces. There can be no doubt that it too was governed by another vicar under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, just as under the prefect of the praetorium of Italy there were two vicars for the two dioceses, one for the City and the other for Italy.

When Sextus Rufus, at the beginning of the text cited above, mentions three bodies of provinces—Gaul together with Aquitania and the Britains—he seems to indicate three dioceses under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, governed by three vicars. Sulpicius Severus conceives the same division into three dioceses, similarly distinguishing Aquitanians, Gauls, and Britons. There the name “Aquitanians,” like that used by Rufus, refers to the provinces that included Aquitania and ancient Narbonensis and were otherwise called the five provinces.

The distinction of these three dioceses is indicated still more clearly in the *Notitia Dignitatum* of both Empires, where the financial administrators of the treasuries and the financial administrators of the private estate are mentioned for the five provinces, Gaul, and the Britains.

### 9.

Against this vicar of Gaul, whose existence we have asserted, one might object on the basis of the *Notitia Dignitatum*. While it mentions the provinces under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, distributed at that time among four dioceses—namely, Spain, the seven provinces, Gaul, and the Britains—it lists only three vicars: those of Spain, the seven provinces, and the Britains. When it names the vicar of the seven provinces, it describes not merely seven but seventeen provinces, that is, all those of both the seven provinces and Gaul, as though they were all subject to the vicar of the seven provinces. For this reason, some suspected an error in the heading “under the authority of the vicar of the seven provinces” and thought it should be corrected to read “under the authority of the vicar of the seventeen provinces.”

But law 15, *On Pagans*, names the vicar of the five provinces—which were later called seven—without assigning any of the provinces of Gaul to him. Nor does the notice published by the Marquis Maffei allow us to doubt the existence of a vicar of Gaul. In that monument three dioceses are distinctly named: the diocese of Gaul, the diocese of the Britains, and the diocese of Vienne, the last of which was otherwise called the diocese of the seven provinces, as there were then seven.

All these dioceses were under the authority of the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. Every diocese, unless it was governed by a proconsul—who, presiding in the emperor’s place, was in no way dependent upon the prefects of the praetorium, as P. Giovanni Antonio Bianco demonstrates, *On External Politics*, book II, chapter 2, section 7, no. 1—had a vicar subject to the prefect, as everyone knows.

The diocese of Gaul, therefore, which depended upon the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, was not without a vicar. In the *Notitia Dignitatum*, then, where the vicars of the Britains and of the seven provinces are noted, only the vicar of Gaul is omitted through error; and under the authority of the vicar of the seven provinces, as he is called, seventeen provinces are wrongly listed, although ten belonged to the authority of the vicar of Gaul.

### 10.

In this *Notitia Dignitatum*, which was composed after the provinces of Spain had been placed under the prefect of Gaul, four dioceses are not obscurely indicated. Under the authority of the illustrious *comes sacrarum largitionum* are named four financial administrators of the treasuries: of Spain, the five provinces, Gaul, and the Britains. Under the authority of the count of the private estate are placed an equal number of financial administrators of the private estate: for Spain, Gaul, the five provinces, and the Britains.

These are not provinces but four dioceses, each of which contained several provinces. Accordingly, four vicars must likewise be assigned under the authority of the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul: those of Spain, the five or seven provinces, Gaul, and the Britains.

The omission of the vicar of Gaul in the *Notitia Dignitatum* must be attributed to the author’s ignorance or negligence. We could demonstrate several other places in which he fell into error. It is clear that he wrote in the East, from the extreme precision of his account of the regions of Constantinople and the provinces of the East.

When describing the regions of Constantinople, the author mentions, among other things, the house of Placidia Augusta in regions 1 and 10; this house existed at Constantinople in the years 423 and 424. In region 10 he names the house of Eudocia Augusta, who was called Augusta by Theodosius the Younger in that same year, 423. The notice may therefore be said to have been written no earlier than that year.

Since the author accurately described matters relating to the East, while the matters concerning the West were taken from records that he found, he mixed together not a few new and ancient things and reported some matters not as they then existed but as he had encountered them in earlier documents. Thus in the Britains he recorded dignities and Roman military commands that did not exist in his own time, since the Britains had already been withdrawn from the Roman Empire from approximately the year 409 onward. He placed Trier among the cities of Gaul, although that city had long since been destroyed, and he noted other similar matters that it is unnecessary to append here.

In this less exact description of Western affairs, therefore, the fact that we do not find a vicar of Gaul should not prevent us from believing that the bipartite division of Gaul which we have established—under two vicars, that of the five provinces, later called seven, and that of Gaul—should be attributed to Constantine.

### 11.

This is sufficient concerning the division into five provinces, which remained in force until Valentinian I. Under him Aquitania was divided into two provinces, so that, as we have learned from Sextus Rufus, the five provinces became six.

Since Ammianus Marcellinus, who wrote under Theodosius I, calls two Narbonenses—and since the Council of Aquileia in 381 likewise calls them two, in its letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne and of Narbonensis I and II—we acknowledge that a third division was introduced not long after the second, by which the same provinces became seven. These are the seven provinces listed in the notices.

In the notice of the provinces edited from the Veronese manuscript by the Marquis Maffei, we read:

> The diocese of Vienne [read: Viennensis] has seven provinces: Vienne [read: Viennensis], Narbonensis I, Narbonensis II, Novempopuli, Aquitania I, Aquitania II, and the Maritime Alps.

In the *Notitia Dignitatum* these are placed under the authority of the *vir spectabilis*, the vicar of the seven provinces.

This division into seven provinces is therefore older than is commonly believed. These seven arose from the five without any addition; nor did those five comprise Narbonensis as a whole alone, as scholars have hitherto maintained—namely, that the five later became seven through the addition of the two Aquitanias and Novempopulana.

### 12.

A difficulty may be raised by the designation “five provinces,” which is found in documents written toward the end of the fourth century and the beginning of the fifth, such as the Council of Turin held around the year 401. This is chiefly why the division into seven provinces has been thought to have occurred after the beginning of the fifth century: namely, because the five provinces commonly believed to have been formed from Narbonensis as a whole supposedly became seven through the addition of the two Aquitanias and Novempopulana.

But since we have shown from Philastrius that Aquitania and Novempopulana belonged to the five provinces, the mere designation “five provinces” cannot prove that the five became six through the division of Aquitania under Valentinian I, which Sextus Rufus distinctly records. Nor can it prevent the six from having become seven through a new division of Narbonensis II, proved by two documents of the fourth century.

The designation “five provinces” could have continued after such a division not only because the double subdivision of Aquitania and Narbonensis into two provinces had been made within those same five provinces, without receiving any new addition from elsewhere, and because people accustomed to the ancient expression therefore did not abandon it; but also because, although the seven provinces had been divided, they had not yet been united by public authority into a single body called “the seven provinces.”

That union occurred under Honorius, around the year 407, when Petronius, prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, ordered that a general assembly of the seven provinces be convened annually at Arles. From that public sanction onward, the name “seven provinces” began to be substituted for the designation “five provinces.”

### 13.

Furthermore, this earlier division into seven provinces should have been recognized from the *Book of the Roman Provinces*. Andreas Schottus and Surita first published it after the *Itinerary of Antoninus*; Petrus Bertius reprinted it in volume II of the *Geographical Treasury*, p. 35; and Schelestratius published a more corrected text from the Vatican Regina manuscript in volume II of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, appendix, p. 549.

Cardinal Norisius shows in *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, dissertation 4, chapter 1, that this book was composed under Theodosius I. Nevertheless, it already lists the seven provinces as divided, before the ten provinces that belong to Gaul properly so called.

[Col. 0598D]

But lest anyone perhaps argue from the enumeration itself of the seven provinces that this book is later, the same point is confirmed more clearly by the Veronese notice printed by the distinguished Maffei, which we can demonstrate was composed under Theodosius the Great. Although extracted from a single manuscript—however ancient, yet careless—and therefore not free from several errors and omissions, it nevertheless bears many indications of antiquity.

First, in its description of the provinces of Gaul it presents only two Lugdunenses, as do Sextus Rufus and Ammianus Marcellinus. From this it is recognized as older than the *Book of the Provinces* mentioned above, in which four Lugdunenses are listed. It is therefore clear that the Veronese notice was composed when the two Lugdunenses had not yet been divided into four, indeed before they had been divided into three. We believe that this previously unknown division can be inferred from a remarkable inscription inserted by the Marquis Maffei in *Antiquities of Gaul*.

[Note: In *Antiquities of Gaul*, letter 20, no. 3, an inscription is produced in which Geminus of Agrippina is said, after holding the office of governor, to have been administrator of the accounts of nine provinces. Some think that Novempopuli, or Novempopulana, is meant. But Novempopulana was one province, not nine. Moreover, no mention of nine Western provinces occurs in the notices or in the authors. Sextus Rufus and the Veronese notice describe only eight provinces in Gaul; in later notices these are counted as ten, because the two Lugdunenses mentioned by Sextus Rufus and the Veronese notice were divided into four. Perhaps, however, before they became four they were divided into three; thus for some time there were nine provinces of Gaul, and during this period Geminus, who came from Agrippina and was himself in Gaul, was administrator of the accounts of these nine provinces. No more equitable explanation of this inscription seems possible.]

Next, in the diocese of the East, which includes Egypt, Arcadia is omitted; and in the Pontic diocese, Honorias does not appear. These two provinces, described in the *Book of the Provinces*, are thought to have been named by Theodosius after the names of his sons.

Furthermore, only five provinces of Egypt are read, as in Ammianus Marcellinus, not six; and in the Britains only four, as in Sextus Rufus, not five—although those six and those five already existed before the end of the fourth century.

What seems still clearer to us is that three contiguous dioceses are described: those of the Britains, Gaul, and Vienne of the seven provinces, which we have shown were placed under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. From these three, with the Italian diocese interposed, the diocese of Spain is separated; and the diocese of Africa is immediately placed after it. This is because at that time Spain was not yet under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, but, like Africa, was governed *vice sacra*—that is, in the emperor’s place—by a proconsul, not in the place of the prefect of the praetorium.

This notice, therefore, was written at a time when the governors of Spain were proconsuls and before Spain received a vicar dependent upon the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. From Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, chapter 49, it may be inferred that Spain ceased to be governed by proconsuls and received a vicar in the final years of Gratian and the first years of Theodosius the Elder.

Nor does the division of the two dioceses of Illyricum present an obstacle. In the Veronese notice they are called the diocese of Moesia and the diocese of Pannonia. Since these are far removed from the Italian diocese, they do not represent the division into Eastern and Western Illyricum that was introduced after Theodosius and that placed Western Illyricum under the prefect of the praetorium of Italy. Rather, they exhibit the older division, when all Illyricum, subject to its own prefect, belonged to the Western Empire until that same Theodosius I, as P. Giovanni Antonio Bianco establishes in book II of *On the External Politics of the Church*, chapter 1, section 8.

This notice contains a remarkable and ancient arrangement of the dioceses. First it describes the dioceses subject to the prefect of the praetorium of the East; then those subject to the prefect of the praetorium of Illyricum; next those subject to the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul; afterward the diocese of the prefect of the praetorium of Italy; and finally the two subject to proconsuls, Spain and Africa.

If, therefore, this notice, composed in the early years of Theodosius I, already describes the seven provinces mentioned above, nothing remains that could cast doubt upon the division of this period.

14. Thus far, three divisions of the provinces have been made in the fourth century. We may now submit for the learned reader’s consideration another, earlier division of Narbonensis as a whole. The catalogue of the bishops of the first Council of Arles, held in the year 314, provides evidence for it. Quesnellus vainly attempts to diminish the authority of this catalogue, part II, chapter 2. To dispel all his objections, it must first be observed that he incorrectly calls this catalogue the “subscriptions of that council.” [Col. 0599D] For, as he himself likewise admits in section 3, it is a list of the bishops and clergy who assembled at that council from different provinces, recorded according to their respective provinces; consequently, one must not seek in it the order of the subscriptions.

Moreover, we do not contend that this catalogue was made at the council itself. We say only that it was arranged from records of that period, at an age when the division into five provinces had not yet been established. [Col. 0600A] Manuscripts must, however, be distinguished from one another. There are two sources from which this catalogue emerged. The editions published before Sirmondus depend on manuscripts of the Isidorian and Hispanic collections. Sirmondus published the catalogue from a manuscript of the most ancient Corbie collection; another equally ancient manuscript of a different collection, which Coustantius found in the Colbert manuscript 3368 and from which he published it in volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, p. 343, agrees with it completely in this catalogue.

These two extremely ancient manuscripts, containing two distinct Gallican collections older than the Hispanic collection from which the Isidorian collection derives, preserve a more authentic form of the catalogue; and the uniformity of its presentation in them lends it the greatest authority. In the later Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, certain things were altered in the names of the provinces that do not fit the time of the Council of Arles—for example, Aquitania Prima and Aquitania Secunda, a division that we have shown to be later than the first Council of Arles. Since this error and arbitrary alteration are not found in those two [Col. 0600B] older manuscripts, in which nothing is inconsistent with the age of Arles, we understand from this alone that the catalogue in these manuscripts was written around the time of Arles, and that the arrangement of the provinces preserved in them was the arrangement expressed in the original at that same time.

For if anything had been altered in these manuscripts from a later period, as happened in the Hispanic manuscripts and consequently in the Isidorian ones, some correction of the same kind would have been made according to the arrangement of the provinces of that later age.
