Nor, in order to weaken the credibility of this catalogue, can one, with Quesnellus, cast suspicion upon that letter of the first Council of Arles to Silvester, under which the catalogue itself is found appended in the manuscripts—as though only the other letter of that council to the aforesaid pontiff had been published from a single Arles manuscript, whereas this one were a *Breviarium* later compiled and interpolated in places by some learned man who had likewise compiled the catalogue of bishops.

But the very form of this letter, as it is presented in all the manuscripts, demonstrates that it too is the letter of that council, not a *Breviarium*. And if there is no reason to doubt the other letter, even though it is supported by only one Arles manuscript, there is much less reason to suspect this one, which is supported by so many ancient manuscripts of different origins and by that same Arles manuscript—especially since it contains nothing that does not agree most closely with the other. The interpolation that Quesnellus suspected in those words of the first canon concerning Easter—“And according to custom, you shall send letters to all”—is entirely groundless. Since the two letters of the same council must be accepted, can it be called an interpolation if the Fathers, in the second letter, in which they sometimes repeated the same canons more briefly, thought it appropriate to omit words that they had expressed sufficiently in the earlier letter?

Certainly, in order that the same day of Easter might be observed by all according to the decree of those Fathers, provision had to be made for the one who presided over all to announce that same day by paschal letters. The Council of Nicaea did not institute the practice of sending paschal letters; it decreed only—according to Cyril’s testimony in the *Paschal Prologue*—that the Alexandrian bishop, because of his expertise in calculating Easter, should announce the day of Easter to the Roman pontiff, by whose authority all would learn and observe the same Easter day. From this testimony we recognize an older custom of paschal letters.

Once this letter has therefore been vindicated, nothing remains in Quesnellus from which one could doubt the antiquity and authenticity of the catalogue. The reason he gives for thinking that the same catalogue was arranged later—namely, that it was composed to establish the truth of canon 18 of the second Council of Arles, in which the first Council of Arles is said to have been gathered from all parts of the world, and hence that the catalogue is found prefixed to the second Council of Arles in the manuscripts—is, I say, so arbitrary and weak that it rests upon two false hypotheses.

The first is that the second Council of Arles was truly a council, whereas it is in fact merely a collection of canons compiled at the beginning of the sixth century, as will be demonstrated in volume III. If the catalogue had been written at that time for the purpose Quesnellus supposes, the provinces of that age ought to have been specified.

The second is that the catalogue is prefixed in the manuscripts to the second Council of Arles, as though it referred to that council. This may indeed be inferred from certain older editions, in which the catalogue is separated from the first Council of Arles and placed before the second. But this happened through the carelessness of the editor. When he found the catalogue copied, in the Isidorian manuscripts or editions that he used, between the first and second Councils of Arles, which followed one another there continuously, he separated the councils and concluded that the catalogue referred to the second Council of Arles. He failed to observe more carefully the entire heading prefixed to the catalogue, which most clearly refers it to the preceding first Council of Arles.

Do such empty conjectures not confirm the catalogue’s authenticity and antiquity rather than weaken them? Hence Tillemontius rightly wrote concerning Quesnellus’s attempt: “For those who have wished to say that this was added later have no proof of it” (*Tom.* XV, under Hilary, article 8, p. 52).

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from believing that this catalogue was composed at the time of the first Council of Arles from its own acts. Quesnellus himself was forced to admit this on another ground when, in section 4, he wrote that the list attached to the *Breviarium* was compiled from the letter itself and perhaps from other copies of the acts.

15. From this catalogue, as it is described in the more authentic and older Corbie and Colbert collections, we learn that the Maritime Alps had not yet, in the time of the first Council of Arles, become a province distinct from Viennensis. For the deacon Portus of Nicaea is described as belonging to the Maritime Alps under the heading “From the province of Viennensis,” not “From the province of the Maritime Alps,” as would have been necessary if, at the time of the first Council of Arles, the Maritime Alps had constituted a province distinct from Viennensis. [Col. 0601C]

The same seems to be true of the Graian Alps. Although no one from their cities is reported at that council, so that the matter cannot be confirmed from that source, the later notices of the provinces of Gaul sufficiently indicate that the Graian Alps, like the Maritime Alps, were once parts of the province of Viennensis, since they call the Graian Alps Viennensis III and the Maritime Alps Viennensis II.

This designation seems to have no other origin than that both provinces were included within Viennensis before the division—just as, in the same notices, Lugdunensis II, III, and IV are given these names because they had previously been assigned to Lugdunensis as a whole. Since the province of Viennensis was cut off from Narbonensis as a whole, it is now clear that this was the first division of Narbonensis as a whole: namely, into two parts. One, on this side of the Rhône, was called the province of Viennensis and included the Graian and Maritime Alps; the other, beyond the Rhône, where Narbo lies, retained the name of the province of Narbonensis.

While this first division remained in force—perhaps with Diocletian as its author—the first Council of Arles was held. A second division then followed, apparently under Constantine, when the Maritime and Graian Alps were cut off from Viennensis in the establishment of the five provinces, as we explained above. In the third division, by which six provinces were made from five, nothing was cut off from the ancient Narbonensis or Viennensis; only Aquitania was divided into two.

But in the fourth division, under Theodosius I, by which seven provinces were established, Narbonensis II was cut off either from Narbonensis or, as others more probably judge, from Viennensis, to which it was adjacent, with the Rhône and the entire province of Viennensis lying between it and Narbonensis I. It therefore could not have been part of Narbonensis I from which it was separated.

In the catalogue mentioned above of the first Council of Arles, the presbyter of Apt in Narbonensis II is listed under the heading “from the province of Viennensis,” because at that time the city belonged to it. The name Narbonensis II could nevertheless have been retained even if it had been cut off from Viennensis, insofar as before the division of Viennensis from Narbonensis it had formerly been contained within Narbonensis as a whole.

This concludes what must be said about the various civil arrangements of the provinces in Gaul, especially in Narbonensis.

## CHAPTER IV. The prerogatives of Arles and Vienne in the civil arrangement. The beginnings of both metropolises established. The *Notitia Galliarum* presents a civil, not an ecclesiastical, arrangement. Its antiquity defended against Quesnellus’s censures.

### 1

After establishing the civil arrangement of the provinces of Gaul, and especially of Narbonensis as a whole, we must state more precisely certain matters concerning its principal metropolises, Vienne and Arles, which are especially relevant to our subject. For, in order to assign primacy to Arles, Quesnellus greatly exaggerated its civil prerogatives. As for Vienne’s privileges and dignity, if he did not entirely pass them over, he certainly tried to diminish and suppress them.

The Gallic bishops devoted to the city of Arles attempted, in their letter 65 to Saint Leo, chapter 4, to exalt it above Vienne on account of its civil privileges. Among these, the chief was that the praetorian prefect and the other authorities always resided there—something equivalent to declaring it the metropolis of all Gaul.

Saint Leo, by contrast, who had weighed the claims of both sides, testifies in his response to those same bishops, letter 66, chapter 2, that Vienne and Arles had once possessed a common right from the nations—that is, with respect to civil prerogatives.

To understand how true this statement was, we must explain the origins and dignity of both metropolises, which are especially relevant in the civil arrangement. Let us begin with Arles.

### 2

Arles, situated in the province of Viennensis, although formerly famous under several names, did not attain the honor of a metropolis until around the year 405 or 407, when, because of the barbarian invasions, the praetorian prefect Petronius transferred the seat of the prefecture of Gaul from Trier to Arles and ordered the assembly of the council of the seven provinces to be held there every year.

At that time the city, because it was the seat of the prefect himself, began to be not merely the capital of the seven provinces but the metropolis of all Gaul. For this reason it is called a metropolitan city in a law of Honorius dated 418. [p. 1023] This is the first testimony to that honor that has been found. Certainly Quesnellus could produce none earlier.

He nevertheless labors hard, part I, chapter 5, to show that this dignity was older. But nothing compels such a conclusion. For what he opposes from the same law of Honorius—where the annual assembly of the seven provinces, from which Arles’s metropolitan right is inferred, is said to have been interrupted by the negligence of the times and the indolence of tyrants—refers to the intervening period, during which Constantine, Constans, and other tyrants occupied and disturbed Gaul and Arles after the assembly had been instituted by Petronius.

That assembly, having Petronius as its author, cannot be said to have been instituted before he transferred the seat to Arles. Consequently, Arles cannot be proved to have been a metropolis from the assembly prescribed there before the year 405 or 407, to which the transfer of the seat and the summoning of the assembly are assigned, as may be seen in Pagius under the year 401, section 36, and Tillemontius, under Zosimus, article 1, volume X, p. 682, and under Honorius, note 2.

### 3

Perhaps more serious will seem the testimony that Quesnellus likewise adduces from letter 65 of the bishops attached to Arles, addressed to Pope Leo, where they say that this city was called not only by Honorius but also by Valentinian I or II “the mother of all Gaul.”

They say:

> The most faithful princes Valentinian and Honorius, of most clement memory, adorned it with special privileges and, to use their own words, by calling it the mother of all Gaul.

But we observe that these bishops, in their zeal to magnify Arles’s dignity, spoke with excessive rhetorical liberty. This is evident from the surviving constitution of Honorius. For whereas the emperor calls the city merely metropolitan, the bishops testify that it was called “the mother of all Gaul” in the emperor’s own words: “to use their own words,” they say.

Nor do we therefore think that they used an appellation that did not belong to Arles in their own age or in that of Honorius. Arles truly was the mother of all Gaul from the time when it became the seat of the praetorian prefect, insofar as, by virtue of that seat, he presided over all the cities and provinces of Gaul.

Nor should this be thought to have been said by Valentinian I or II. Under those emperors the seat of the praetorian prefect—from which alone that title could have arisen—was not at Arles but at Trier. At that time only the city of Trier was, and could be called, the metropolis of Gaul. It is clearly in this sense that Athanasius, who spent some time at Trier, calls it the metropolis of Gaul (*Apology for His Flight*, section 4, volume I, p. 322).

It is unbelievable that Valentinian should, contrary to the facts, have granted Arles the title that at that time belonged exclusively to Trier. The bishops therefore seem to have used, in their favor of Arles, a freer formula in citing the testimony of Honorius; and, in joining Valentinian and Honorius together, they appear to have employed that figurative expression by which, in the plural number, two or more persons are credited with things that ought to be distinguished between them individually.

Who does not know—as Quesnellus himself admits in the notes to this very testimony of the bishops, section 7—that this figure is frequently used, in which the plural stands for the singular, especially when several persons have been mentioned immediately before?

Hence Pagius, under the year 401, section 45, reasonably judges that the bishops’ words, although expressed in the plural and joined by conjunction, should be understood disjunctively: the privileges mentioned first belong to Valentinian, whereas the title “mother of all Gaul” must be referred to Honorius alone.

### 4

Still less do the matters that Quesnellus adduces concerning Constantius’s taking up the consulship and giving games at Arles, or concerning the names Constantina and Gallula Roma, contribute to establishing Arles as a metropolis before the fifth century.

These are indeed indications of a distinguished city, but not of a metropolis; and we read that similar things happened to other cities that were not metropolises. Thus Arles could be called Constantina, just as Cirta in Numidia was so called, and two other cities, certainly not metropolises, in Phoenicia and Arabia were given the same name.

Ausonius, however, attributes the title “Little Rome of Gaul” to Arles because of the city’s size, population, and commerce, by which it in some sense rivaled Rome. Thus no testimony has been able to establish the civil beginnings of the metropolitan status of Arles earlier than approximately the year 407.

### 5

Vienne’s metropolitan origin was earlier. The ancient name of the province itself is the first indication. The ancient designation “province of Viennensis,” which is confirmed by several documents from the fourth century as well, could have arisen for no other reason than that, from the very division of the provinces under Diocletian or Constantine, Vienne—not Arles—was the civil metropolis of the province of Viennensis.

Quesnellus’s objection to this most evident argument, concerning the provinces of Lugdunensis II, III, and IV, whose metropolis was not Lugdunum despite their Lugdunensian name, is entirely worthless. Although these three provinces, once cut off from Lugdunensis as a whole, each had its own metropolis distinct from Lugdunum, before they were divided into parts they all acknowledged the same city of Lugdunum as their metropolis. They therefore retained the name Lugdunensis because, before the division, Lugdunum had been their metropolis.

In the same way, the three provinces of Viennensis are called “Viennenses” in certain notices of a later age. Although after the division they had their own proper metropolises, they appear previously to have acknowledged Vienne as their common civil metropolis. Narbonensis II likewise received that name because it had formerly had Narbo as its metropolis, and Narbo had given its name to Narbonensis as a whole.

No provinces are found to have received their name from a city unless that city had at some time been the metropolis of the province itself. This designation of the province of Viennensis therefore leaves no room for doubt about Vienne’s metropolitan prerogative.

### 6

The testimonies of Eusebius of Caesarea and of the *Notitia Galliarum* provide further support. In the age of Constantine, when the province of Viennensis took its name from Vienne, Eusebius explicitly calls that city a metropolis in book V, chapter 1 of his *History*. Likewise, the *Notitia Galliarum* published by Sirmondus, whose very ancient exemplar is found in the manuscript of the chapter of Verona, calls Vienne a metropolis in its description of the province of Viennensis.

Quesnellus does not oppose Eusebius’s testimony. “No one,” he says, part I, chapter 12, “fails to see that Eusebius is speaking of the civil dignity of the city of Vienne.” He thinks it should be understood only of a geographical, not a civil, metropolis; and in chapter 11 he cites Strabo, who called Vienne the metropolis of the Allobroges—as though Eusebius, in the age of Constantine, when a different division of the provinces was in force, had spoken in the same sense. Anyone can see how weak this argument is.

He devotes an entire chapter to attempting to diminish and undermine the authority of the *Notitia Galliarum*, in which Vienne is most plainly presented as a civil metropolis. He maintains that it is an ecclesiastical, not a civil, notice, composed later for the benefit of the bishop of Vienne, when the Burgundians occupied the district of Vienne around the year 480.

### 7

But many things make it clear that the notice is civil, not ecclesiastical. If it were an ecclesiastical notice describing ecclesiastical provinces with their metropolises, not only Vienne but also Arles would have had to be counted among the ecclesiastical metropolises.

Moreover, Narbonensis II, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps would not have been listed as separate provinces whose cities were subject to the metropolitan of Arles or Vienne. Add that in Maxima Sequanorum three forts and one harbor are named, although these have no relevance whatsoever to an ecclesiastical arrangement.

Finally, to pass over other points, after the ten provinces of Gaul have been described, this heading is added:

> Also, in the seven provinces.

This distinction between seven provinces and ten provinces undoubtedly points to that division which is not ecclesiastical but civil—namely, the division by which all Gaul was divided into two dioceses, as we saw in the preceding chapter.

This notice is preserved in the very ancient manuscript 50 of the chapter of Verona, after the *Bordeaux Itinerary*, under the following heading:

> Here begins the annotation of the provinces and cities of Gaul, together with their privileges.

These privileges refer to the civil metropolises designated there.

### 8

The age of this notice is sufficiently indicated by its complete agreement with the division of the provinces of Gaul presented in the *Notitia Dignitatum*. Just as the latter was written shortly after the year 423, so it seems that the same should be judged of the former.

This is demonstrated still more clearly by the title “the seven provinces,” which we cited from the *Notitia Galliarum*. For it is found in documents written shortly after the beginning of the fifth century—namely, in the letters of Zosimus and Boniface I, in the law of Honorius dated 418, and in the aforementioned *Notitia Dignitatum*—but nowhere in later monuments.

We reserve for section 11 the task of establishing, by no slight argument, an earlier date than this for the notice.

### 9

Quesnellus’s opinion therefore collapses completely. Since this is a civil, not an ecclesiastical, notice, it cannot be said to have been composed for the benefit of the bishop of Vienne, who would have required a description of the ecclesiastical arrangement.

Since it was composed near the beginning of the fifth century, Quesnellus also vainly imagines that it was written under the Burgundians. Especially if it were believed to have been written at that time, it would not present the civil arrangement that existed under the Romans, but a different arrangement produced under the barbarians, who were splitting the Roman provinces into parts. Instead, it presents the Roman arrangement that prevailed under Roman rule at the beginning of the fifth century.

Quesnellus interprets the testimony of Sidonius, which he cites in support of his view, in an excessively forced manner. When Sidonius wrote to the bishop Graecus of Marseille around the year 475, in book II, letter 7:

> You have now ceased to be first among your fellow provincials and have become last,

he was not speaking of the people of Marseille, whose city is designated last in the *Notitia Galliarum*. Rather, he was speaking of Leontius of Arles, Faustus of Riez, Basilius of Aix, and Graecus of Marseille. These men, living under Roman rule and seeking to protect themselves and their cities from the barbarians, were endeavoring to surrender the city of the Arverni, over which Sidonius presided, to those same barbarians and thus make peace.

Sidonius reproves them and foretells that, by this surrender of cities, they would no longer be first in the civil arrangement, as they had formerly been because of Arles, which was the seat of the praetorian prefect of Gaul, but would become last. For, by this method of handing over cities, so few cities would remain to the Romans that Roman territory in Gaul would already be minimal, and those men could no longer be called great, since, as he immediately adds, they were beginning to have no lesser men beneath them.

This is Sidonius’s genuine meaning. Quesnellus therefore invents an interpretation of the passage alien to the author’s meaning and intention. All his conjectures, by which he attempts on the basis of that interpretation to explain how the notice could have been composed under the barbarians, are shown to be arbitrary and empty.

### 10

The observations that he makes about the notice itself, in order to persuade us that it belongs to a later age, are no less weak. First he objects that Arles, which is declared a metropolis by the law of Honorius dated 418 and which at that time presided over all Gaul because it was the seat of the prefecture, is listed in the notice not merely without any metropolitan title but among the last cities of the province of Viennensis.

But it must be observed that, although the notice was composed in the time of Honorius, it records the metropolis of each province. The metropolis of the province of Viennensis was Vienne, both from the time when the province of Viennensis was divided from Narbonensis as a whole and under Honorius, since Vienne retained that same prerogative.

When Arles became a metropolis because the seat of the prefecture had been transferred there, it became the metropolis of the seven provinces, but not of the province of Viennensis, over which Vienne still presided by virtue of its older privilege.

Although a city that presided over several provinces with metropolitan honor would generally enjoy the same honor in its own particular province, this did not happen in the case of Arles, since Vienne’s older possession was not displaced. Nor was the ancient name of the province of Viennensis altered; yet that would have happened if the metropolitan right of the province itself had been transferred from Vienne to Arles.

What wonder, then, if in a notice that, according to the ancient custom, marks only the metropolis of each province, Vienne alone, and not Arles, is called a metropolis?

### 11

Thus far we have spoken on the assumption that this notice was written shortly after the beginning of the fifth century. If we may now state what we believe more probable, we think the notice is earlier than the fifth century.

Until now it has not been considered older, because it mentions the seven provinces, whose division was universally thought to have been made after the beginning of the fifth century. But since we have shown in the preceding chapter that these seven provinces were established under Theodosius I, nothing follows from this that prevents the notice from being judged earlier than the fifth century.

Likewise, the division into four Lugdunensian provinces presents no obstacle, since we find it in a little book of the provinces that Cardinal Norisius has shown to have been composed before the fifth century (*Epoch. Sur. Maced.*, dissertation 4, chapter 1).

The reason for believing the *Notitia Galliarum* to be older is that, in the description of the province of Viennensis, Arles is listed without the title of metropolis. Arles was raised to metropolitan honor around the year 407, when it became the seat of the praetorian prefect and the capital of all Gaul, as we saw shortly before.

A city endowed with such honor would not have been listed without any indication of that honor in a notice written after that time. Quesnellus therefore believed the notice to be much later on the basis of this observation, although Arles, even in a later age, did not lose that degree of honor within the Roman arrangement presented in the notice.

The notice should therefore, with much greater probability, be regarded as earlier—written at the time when Arles had not yet been raised to metropolitan dignity. There is consequently nothing surprising in its being listed among the fellow cities of the province of Viennensis without any metropolitan title.

Its being listed among the last cities has this explanation: the author of the notice followed the order presented by geographical location. First, after the metropolitan city of Vienne, he recorded the nearer inland cities; then those facing toward the sea, among which Arles and Marseille occupy the final place.

### 12

Quesnellus’s remaining observations on the *Notitia Galliarum* are less substantial. He assumes that the omission of the fort of Nicaea from the notice—although it enjoyed episcopal status before the time of Leo—indicates that the notice is ecclesiastical, whereas we have already shown it to be civil.

Since the same civil notice mentions three other forts of the Sequani and two of Lugdunensis I, the omission of Nicaea must be attributed either to the author’s negligence or, more probably, to the fact that at that time it was so small and confined that it did not seem worthy of being counted among the forts. Hence Pope Hilary calls it not a fort but, diminutively, a little fortress.

The points he next adduces from Paulinus of Nola are entirely foreign to the author’s meaning. In letter 28, addressed to Victricius of Rouen, Paulinus speaks of the renown by which Rouen, on account of the distinguished achievements of that bishop, stood out among the sacred cities. This has no relevance whatever to the civil arrangement with which we are now concerned.

Although that city had already been a civil metropolis before that time, it had not before Victricius been so celebrated among the sacred cities. The same is true of the city of the Morini, which Paulinus mentions in the same place with reference to religion, not to the civil arrangement, which alone the notice describes.

Finally, the argument from the Council of Turin has no relevance here, since at that council the doubt concerned not a civil but an ecclesiastical metropolis, as we shall show in the following chapter.

Nothing, therefore, invalidates the authority of the notice. It consequently supplies solid evidence for saying that Vienne was a civil metropolis, and indeed older than Arles—namely, from the very establishment of the province of Viennensis, which received its name from the metropolitan city of Vienne.

Indeed, before Arles was raised to the metropolitan dignity not only of the seven provinces but also of all Gaul because the seat of the prefecture had been transferred there, it appears that Vienne was the seat of the vicar of the praetorian prefect while the prefect remained at Trier, and therefore that it was the metropolis not only of its own province but also of the five provinces that were later called seven. This may be inferred from the very ancient Veronese notice, in which the diocese of Vienne is called the Seven Provinces, over which the vicar presided.

For this diocese could have received the name of Vienne for no other reason than that the vicar had his seat there.

From all these points it becomes still clearer how rightly Saint Leo wrote that “Vienne and Arles once had a common right from the nations” (*Epistle* 66, chapter 2). “Once,” he says, because at different times one surpassed the other: Vienne in the earlier age, when it was the metropolis of its own province and, more probably, also the seat of the vicar; Arles in the later age, when around the year 407 it became the seat of the prefecture.

We now turn to the arrangement of the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises.

## CHAPTER V. The ancient establishment and arrangement of the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises in Gaul, especially in the provinces divided from Narbonensis as a whole. Their beginnings were late; and it is shown that they did not exactly follow the civil arrangement.

### 1

Two matters must be established concerning the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises in Gaul, in order to judge the statements that Quesnellus has scattered in many places. First, when this structure was introduced; and second, whether it followed the structure of the civil provinces and metropolises.

If the ecclesiastical provinces of Gaul had been established during any of the first three centuries and had been modeled exactly on the civil provinces, as Quesnellus assumes in more than one place, then, since at that time Narbonensis as a whole had not yet been divided, and since Narbo was always at that time the metropolis of the entire province—as Quesnellus himself admits in part I, near the end of chapter 11—it would be beyond doubt that the bishop of Narbonensis had been established as the metropolitan of that province, not the bishop of Arles or anyone else.

But from Quesnellus himself we have learned that it is entirely futile to seek in Gaul, during those three centuries and before Nicaea, a structure of ecclesiastical hierarchy. We cited his testimonies in chapter 2, section 5.

Since he stated this with sufficient clarity, it is difficult to understand how he could write without contradiction, part II, chapter 2:

> Since all the more learned writers, with few exceptions, refer the beginnings of religion and discipline in Gaul to that period—I had previously noted the year 250—if at that time there was one province, namely Narbonensis, and one metropolitan, the rule of Pope Innocent I will apply: “According to the ancient custom of the provinces, metropolitan bishops ought to be appointed; nor ought the Church of God to be changed according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs.”

On this view, one bishop of Narbonensis would have been established as metropolitan of the whole of Narbonensis according to the civil arrangement, and such a constitution could not, according to Innocent’s intention, have been altered.

Quesnellus, however, intended here to indicate that the bishop of Arles had been placed over all Narbonensis, as he supposes, from the middle of the third century onward because of the mission of Saint Trophimus—a mission that we showed in chapter 2 to be entirely inadequate for proving this.

If Saint Trophimus came to Gaul around the middle of the third century, as Quesnellus judged from Gregory of Tours, then Gregory likewise reports that Paul was sent together with Saint Trophimus, and that Paul established his seat at Narbo, just as Trophimus did at Arles. Consequently, from this mission the city of Narbo would have benefited no less than Arles; indeed, much more, since at that time Narbo was the metropolis of the entire province.

Quesnellus can be cleared of contradiction only on the ground that he does not absolutely affirm the establishment of an ecclesiastical metropolis in Gaul around the middle of the third century, but states it conditionally: if at that time there was one province and one metropolitan.

Accordingly, we accept from him as the more probable view what he taught more explicitly—namely, that the structure of ecclesiastical metropolises was introduced and established in Gaul after the Council of Nicaea.

2. We, however, consider it still more probable that the Gallican bishops began to think about establishing this hierarchical arrangement later, and that even after the time of the Council of Nicaea they retained the ancient method that had prevailed during the preceding three centuries: namely, that when metropolitan bishops had not yet been established, the synod of bishops would be presided over either by the oldest bishop or by the bishop of the city in which the synod was convened. Thus, when Foebadius presided over the Council of Valence in 374—or, as others write with Sulpicius Severus (*Hist.* II, 44) and in the published acts of the councils, Foegadius, bishop of the Church of Agen, which never had a metropolitan—the other bishops of the more distinguished sees, Arelate, Vienne, Trier, and Lyons, being listed after him, the only possible reason for his precedence was his greater age, since the institution of metropolitans was not yet firmly established. Indeed, after their institution it was no longer customary for metropolitans—whoever might be present—to yield place to an ordinary bishop, however much older.

And if, as Quesnellus boasts on the basis of Zosimus—or, more accurately, of the insinuations of Patroclus and his supporters—the bishop of Arelate had always held that rank and primacy in Gaul from the mission of St. Trophimus onward, Concordius, bishop of that same Church, would have held the same rank at this council of his province. Nor, if he had received from his predecessors the same tradition and custom that Patroclus introduced in the following, fifth century, would he ever have allowed an ordinary bishop to prejudice this most ancient and distinguished privilege of his see. Patroclus’s imposture can also be confirmed by this evidence.

3. Nor do the difficulties that Quesnellus opposed to this argument in Part I, chapter 11, on the basis of the subscriptions of the Council of Valence, present any obstacle. For the name of Foegadius does not appear first in the subscriptions, but in the headings of two letters of that same council. Quesnellus considered these headings so authoritative that, against the subscriptions themselves, he preferred the order of the headings, from which, as he says, Foegadius is read to have presided over the same council.

4. If Marinus of Arelate is named first in the heading of a letter of the Council of Arelate of 314, this should be attributed not to metropolitan jurisdiction but either to his seniority, or rather to the fact that, as the bishop of the place, he had been specially appointed by the Emperor Constantine in the case then under consideration. Where there were no metropolitans, precedence was given either to the oldest bishop or to the bishop of the place. In a letter to Pope Miltiades, preserved by Eusebius, the same emperor names the judges whom he had selected for that case in this order: Reticius of Autun, Maternus of Cologne, and Marinus of Arelate. The same order is preserved in the acts of the Roman synod, at which those same judges had gathered before the Council of Arelate for the same matter, as may be seen in Optatus, Book I.

Moreover, Reticius of Autun was certainly not a metropolitan. Marinus, therefore, who is placed after an ordinary bishop, was not a metropolitan; and if he is listed before Reticius at the Council of Arelate, although Reticius had been given precedence over him at Rome, the only possible explanation is the fact that Marinus was the bishop of the place.

3. Nor is the evidence reported concerning Saturninus of Arelate an obstacle, namely, that at the pseudo-council of Arelate in 353 and at that of Béziers in 356 he arranged for St. Hilary of Poitiers to be condemned. For it cannot be inferred from such acts that he presided over those pseudo-councils by metropolitan right over the provinces of Vienne or Narbonne. Nor can one infer that the bishops Valens and Ursacius, who certainly were not metropolitans, exercised metropolitan jurisdiction when, at various pseudo-councils, they obtained many measures against the Catholics according to their own arbitrary will.

Just as these powerful leaders of the heretics and principal heads of their faction are named by writers as the authors of their acts, so Saturninus of Arelate is named as well—not, however, so that metropolitan jurisdiction should thereby be attributed to him, any more than to them. We confirm this comparison from Sulpicius Severus, who writes in Book II of his *History*, chapter 40:

> Valens and Ursacius, and the others whose names we have given, infected Italy, Illyricum, and the East; in our Gauls, Saturninus, bishop of Arelate, an insolent and factious man, was exerting pressure.

6. Let no one regard as strange or incredible what we have considered concerning so late an institution of metropolitans in Gaul. For in Italy itself and in Spain, at approximately this same period—that is, after the middle of the fourth century—ecclesiastical metropolises also began to be established. We have set this forth at greater length concerning the Italian ones—Rome must always be excepted—in a dissertation already prepared, *On the Origin of the More Ancient Churches and Metropolises of Italy*. The same point could also be demonstrated concerning Spain. Thus, at the Council of Saragossa, held shortly after the Council of Valence, the aforementioned Foegadius of Agen, since at that time there were no metropolitans, occupied the first place on account of his age, as at Valence, above all the other bishops, even those of the more distinguished Spanish sees.

A somewhat earlier indication of Spanish metropolitans occurs in Siricius’s first letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 8, written in 385. If, however, at the much earlier Council of Elvira the bishop of the first see is mentioned in canon 58, Cajetanus Cennius very clearly shows that this designation should be understood, in the African manner, not of a metropolitan—there was none at that time—but of the oldest bishop; see volume I of his *On the Antiquities of the Spanish Church*, chapter 4, no. 8.

Here one should compare what we shall discuss concerning the Sardican canons in volume III, where this late institution of ecclesiastical metropolises among the Latins will be confirmed to no small degree by two canons expressed differently in the original Latin and in the Greek.

7. Nor should anyone suppose that, before this period, the bishops of the principal Gallican cities exercised some metropolitan jurisdiction, if not in councils, at least in the ordination of bishops. Those who possess the right of ordination are the true metropolitans, and, as such, they were always given the chief place before the bishops in councils. Therefore, if the first place was not assigned to the bishops of the more distinguished cities at the Council of Valence, it appears evident that at that time none of them possessed any right in episcopal ordinations.

When canon 21 of the First Council of Arelate, held in 314, mentions ordinations in these words:

> Concerning those who usurp for themselves what ought to belong to them alone, namely, the right to ordain, it has been decided that no one should presume to do this unless he has taken seven other bishops with him; if they cannot obtain seven, they must not dare to ordain without three brethren;

the word “usurp” sufficiently indicates that no one possessed such a right. Certainly those who usurped it are not called metropolitans, as they are called in the Eastern councils of Nicaea, Laodicea, and Antioch; for at this period no established metropolitans endowed with the right of ordination yet existed in the Gallican provinces, as they did in the East.

8. That this right of ordination did not yet exist in Gaul at the very time of the Council of Valence, and that it only began to be introduced and established toward the end of that century, can be proved even more clearly from the questions brought before the Council of Turin. These questions will increasingly confirm the late institution of ecclesiastical metropolises. Three questions debated there deserve particular consideration.

The first was a complaint against Proculus of Marseille, because he had ordained bishops in Narbonne II. This complaint was not brought against him by the bishops of Arelate or Vienne, who elsewhere contended with one another at the same council over the vindication of metropolitan jurisdiction; only the bishops of Narbonne II complained in this matter. They did not do so in order to preserve this right for the bishop of Vienne or the bishop of Arelate, as though either one of them were their ancient metropolitan, but because they maintained that the priest of another province ought not to preside over them. This reasoning excludes Proculus of Marseille as much as it excludes the bishops of Arelate and Vienne. Since all three belonged to the same province of Vienne, they all equally belonged to another province.

It clearly follows from this that the beginnings of ecclesiastical metropolises were so late that, at this time, neither the bishop of Arelate nor the bishop of Vienne had exercised or obtained metropolitan jurisdiction in the ordination of the bishops of Narbonne II. Thus, the same men who were disputing among themselves over metropolitan jurisdiction in the province of Vienne took no action regarding Narbonne II against Proculus of Marseille, who had first sought to claim that same right there as his own through episcopal ordinations and consequently asserted that he ought to preside over it as its metropolitan.

The bishops of that province, resenting the preference given to a bishop of another province, sufficiently indicated that, in accordance with the Nicene canons, they would not refuse a bishop of their own province as metropolitan. These circumstances likewise suggest that they had not yet received an established metropolitan.

9. The second question put to the Council of Turin arose between the bishop of Arelate and the bishop of Vienne. Each claimed the right of ordination and primacy in the province of Vienne. The Fathers seem to have been uncertain about this matter because, after hearing the allegations of both sides that had been submitted to them, it still remained unclear which city was the metropolis. The synod therefore decreed that whichever of them could prove that his city was the metropolis should possess the honor of primacy over the whole province.

There is considerable disagreement among scholars as to whether the Fathers understood “metropolis” in a civil or an ecclesiastical sense. Most interpret it civilly. Pagius, however, in the year 401, no. 37 and following, refutes this opinion. There could have been no doubt which city was the civil metropolis. We have shown in chapter 4 that, at the time of the Council of Turin, only Vienne was the civil metropolis. Yet if both cities had then been metropolises under different designations—and the Fathers of that council could not have been unaware of this—they would not have issued a decision that presupposed only one city to be the metropolis.

Since, therefore, they were speaking not of a civil but of an ecclesiastical metropolis, the difficulty could not have arisen because the bishop of Vienne had only recently arrogated metropolitan jurisdiction to himself against the bishop of Arelate, as though the latter alone had previously exercised it. In that case, it should have been certain that Arelate alone was the true metropolis, and the recent usurpation of the bishop of Vienne would have created no prejudice against it.

The uncertainty, therefore, could have arisen because, when ecclesiastical metropolises were recently being established, both the bishop of Vienne and the bishop of Arelate preferred that this right belonged to them. Each claimed that his own see was the mother, or metropolis, of the other churches of the same province: the bishop of Arelate on account of the mission of St. Trophimus, and the bishop of Vienne on account of the more ancient origin of his Church, which surpassed the age of St. Trophimus.

To this ecclesiastical argument, so to speak, each perhaps added reasons drawn from the civil prerogatives of the individual cities. These too, under Leo, are known to have been brought forward on both sides, at length and in abundance, in the allegations presented to him, as may be learned from Letter 66. They were so weighty on both sides that they produced equal uncertainty in the mind of the pontiff himself. As a result, he judged that the province should be divided between the bishops of Arelate and Vienne, in accordance with the advice given by the Fathers of Turin.

This question appears to have been raised for the first time at Turin because, not long before that council, these two bishops had begun to exercise the ordination of the bishops of the province of Vienne as though it were their own right, at the time when metropolises were being introduced. Otherwise, the controversy would have arisen much earlier. This, then, is how the Council of Turin shows that ordinations based on metropolitan jurisdiction began shortly before that time.

10. Quesnellus may perhaps have perceived the force of this argument when, in Part I, chapter 5, he attempted to propose another occasion for the controversy. He presupposes that he had already proved in the preceding chapter that Arelate had always possessed primacy in Narbonne I, without anyone objecting, although in the preceding chapter he produced nothing by which that primacy could be established, as will be evident from the annotations appended to it.

The argument that we advanced shortly before confirms this generally as well. For if the possession of Arelate had been certain and ancient, while the effort of the bishop of Vienne was recent, as Quesnellus boasts, how could the Fathers of Turin have remained uncertain and failed to adjudicate the case in favor of Arelate?

But what Quesnellus gathers in chapter 5 to identify the occasion and cause of the bishop of Vienne’s recent effort is false and fabricated. It is false that the division of Narbonne I, from which the bishop of Vienne supposedly took the occasion for his claim, had occurred only recently, or not long before the Council of Turin. The province of Vienne had already been divided under Diocletian or Constantine, as we established in chapter 3.

It is also false that the disturbances raised under the tyrant Eugenius divided the province of Vienne into factions, and that on this occasion the bishop of Vienne persuaded Eugenius to order an ecclesiastical primacy to be established wherever he had the seat—or at least the beginnings—of his empire: some cities obeying the tyrant together with Vienne, while others remained under Roman rule with Arelate. After the murder of Valentinian II, the tyrant Eugenius occupied all Gaul, let alone the whole province of Vienne; nor was there any division of that province into factions that could have provided an occasion for introducing the primacy of Vienne.

It is also false that the Gallican bishops had long been seeking Ambrose’s intervention so that he might investigate and judge the disagreements among the bishops that had allegedly arisen for this reason at a Gallican synod. For the testimony of Ambrose himself, which Quesnellus cites from his sermon at the funeral of the Emperor Valentinian, does not concern the disagreements invented by Quesnellus, but those indicated by Sulpicius Severus (*Hist.* II, at the end, and *Life of St. Martin*, Dialogue 3, no. 13). The Gallicans, divided into factions on account of the Ithacians, had produced a kind of schism, which is also mentioned in canon 6 of the Council of Turin.

Once these inventions of Quesnellus have been rejected, no more equitable explanation remains for the disagreement over metropolitan jurisdiction between Arelate and Vienne than that, during the recent establishment of ecclesiastical metropolises, shortly before that council each contended for primacy on the basis of his own prerogatives.

11. This recent institution becomes still more evident from the third question decided by the same Council of Turin in canon 3. Four bishops—Octavius, Ursus, Remigius, and Triferius—were summoned in an accusation intended to bring them into disrepute over a certain usurpation concerning the ordination of priests. They were plainly ordinary bishops, not metropolitans. They proved that they should not be condemned on this account by saying that they had not previously been summoned to trial.

The council accepted this excuse for their past acts and imposed no penalty upon them. Therefore, episcopal ordinations, which before the prohibition of this synod had incurred no penalty, were not previously bound by any law or custom to the right of any particular see. Otherwise, they would have been sufficiently summoned on the charge of usurpation.

There were therefore no established metropolitans before this council; they only gradually began to be introduced. The same bishops were forbidden to arrogate anything similar to themselves thereafter, because the institution of metropolitans, which had begun shortly before, was confirmed by that council.

If all these observations concerning the first three chapters of the Council of Turin are taken together, and joined with what we observed from the Council of Valence, nothing will be lacking to establish the late institution of metropolitans in Gaul.

12. Having settled this first question, another remains: whether the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises were adapted to the arrangement of the civil provinces and metropolises.

Here we are not asking what occurred in the course of time. It is certain that, in a later age, the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises in Gaul are generally found to have been made to conform to the civil arrangement. But this occurred only after the Roman Empire had been extinguished in Gaul and the old structure of the Roman provinces, though the names alone remained, had become completely confused and had been abolished.

We are asking about the beginnings, when ecclesiastical provinces and metropolises were introduced while the civil arrangement was still in force. Quesnellus was convinced that they had been adapted to the civil arrangement. For in Part I, chapter 12, he writes:

> When the foundations of ecclesiastical discipline had been laid and the hierarchical order established, the ecclesiastical ranks were arranged according to the form of the civil administration; the dignity of the episcopal sees was fixed, and the power of the metropolitans was erected.

Nothing could be more evidently false. For if this civil arrangement had been observed, then, once Narbonne I had been divided—as we saw in chapter 3—into Vienne, the two Narbonnes, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps, the latter being assigned to Gaul properly so called, an equal number of ecclesiastical provinces and an equal number of metropolitans would have been established in the metropolis of each province.

That did not happen. Certainly Narbonne II, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps remained for a long time without their own metropolitan and were subject to the metropolitan of Arelate or Vienne.

Moreover, since there had never been any controversy with the bishop of Narbonne before Patroclus of Arelate, he appears to have peacefully possessed his right in the province of Narbonne I, and that right was also confirmed by an apostolic privilege. Only Patroclus, under Zosimus, brought a suit against him, although no one before Patroclus had claimed anything for himself in that province, as we learned from Leo.

Thus, in this province the ecclesiastical arrangement was adapted to the civil arrangement. But this was not so in the province of Vienne. For at the time when metropolitans began to be established, Vienne alone was the metropolis of the civil province, as is clear from the discussion in the preceding chapter. If the ecclesiastical arrangement had been derived from the civil one, primacy should have been granted to the bishop of Vienne alone.

Nevertheless, it is certain that after the Council of Valence, as we have seen, both the bishop of Vienne and the bishop of Arelate exercised episcopal ordinations in that same province of Vienne, and each believed that he did so by his own right—not on the basis of the civil arrangement, which at that time recognized Vienne alone as the metropolis, but on the basis of the ecclesiastical prerogatives of each. These they chiefly alleged at Turin.

When the nature of those prerogatives was examined there, and it remained uncertain which Church held precedence over the other and was the mother, or metropolis, of the other Churches, the Fathers of that synod advised that the province should be divided between those bishops on the basis of this uncertain right.

What was later decreed by Zosimus in favor of the bishop of Arelate proves nothing, since, as we have seen, it was extorted from him by Patroclus through surreptitious means. Rather, the testimony of St. Leo in Letter 66, chapter 2, based on his consideration of the allegations of both parties and of the clergy then present, proves the opposite:

> The distinguished cities of both your provinces, that of Vienne and that of Arelate, have always been so prominent that, by an alternating distribution of causes, now one, now the other, has excelled in ecclesiastical privileges.

Since these words demonstrated the ancient exercise and almost possession of the right by both cities—so that primacy could neither be granted to nor taken away from either—Leo divided the province between them in accordance with the judgment of the Fathers of Turin. This arrangement was observed thereafter.

Thus, even in the province of Vienne itself, the civil division of the provinces did not serve as the model for the ecclesiastical provinces.

13. From these considerations two corollaries can be drawn against Quesnellus.

First, since ecclesiastical metropolitans had not yet been established in Gaul at the time of the Council of Valence, and since the bishop of Arelate consequently did not occupy the first place in that council, which Quesnellus claims was convened in his province of Vienne, it is recognized as false what Patroclus and his supporters insinuated to Zosimus: that the bishop of Arelate had always held primacy out of reverence for St. Trophimus. Even if this had been asserted concerning the right of ordination, primacy in councils would also have arisen from such primacy in the right of ordination and for the same reason.

Furthermore, from the very late institution of metropolises in Gaul it follows that the ecclesiastical metropolis of Arelate began to be established after the middle of the fourth century, since Quesnellus does not dare deny that the bishop of Narbonne also exercised metropolitan jurisdiction in Narbonne I, on the occasion, as he thinks, of the new division. He says in Part II, chapter 3:

> We do not deny that the bishop of Narbonne possessed metropolitan jurisdiction for several years over the first province of Narbonne … on the occasion of the new division, which he affirmed in chapter 2 to have been made before the middle of the fourth century.

But if, at approximately the same period, the bishops of Arelate and Narbonne were exercising metropolitan jurisdiction, then Quesnellus improperly boasts that the bishop of Narbonne usurped for himself in Narbonne I a right belonging to Arelate, as though Arelate had obtained that metropolitan right before Narbonne.

It is also clear from this that the ancient custom and primitive institution attributed by Zosimus to Arelate, in order to convict Narbonne of a more recent usurpation, rested on nothing but the imposture of Patroclus. Both metropolises had the same late beginnings.

If Hilary of Narbonne was unable, from Zosimus’s Letter 6, to suggest what support ancient custom had to offer, it was because he was more honest and did not wish, for the benefit of his own see, to introduce those ancient fictions that Patroclus fabricated in favor of Arelate in Hilary’s absence and without his knowledge.

14. Since the ecclesiastical arrangement was not adapted to the civil division of the provinces, it is shown to be false that Quesnellus attempted to promote the claim that the bishop of Narbonne usurped metropolitan jurisdiction in Narbonne I on the occasion of a new civil division—namely, when Narbonne I was separated from Vienne.

For the division of those provinces did not take place in the middle of the fourth century, as he supposes, but, as we saw in chapter 3, at the beginning of that century. The institution of their ecclesiastical metropolises was much later. Since that institution did not derive its origin or occasion from the civil division, it was introduced on another basis by the bishops of Narbonne, Arelate, and Vienne: namely, because their Churches were more ancient and more distinguished in their respective provinces and were adorned with many prerogatives.

Among these, only the bishop of Narbonne possessed an ancient apostolic privilege, which could be recognized as having been obtained surreptitiously through the frauds of Patroclus before Zosimus. But after his deceptions had been exposed by Boniface I, Celestine, and Leo, the successors of Zosimus, that privilege was maintained intact.

## CHAPTER VI. On metropolitan jurisdiction in the Churches of the provinces of Narbonne II, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps

1. Quesnellus contends that all the provinces divided from the unified province of Narbonne belonged, from the very institution of metropolises in Gaul onward, to the jurisdiction of the bishop of Arelate.

We showed in the preceding chapter that metropolises began to be introduced and established in Gaul toward the end of the fourth century. We also demonstrated in chapter 2 that, at approximately the same time, Narbonne I had its own metropolitan and was transferred into the jurisdiction of Arelate only through the surreptitious action of Patroclus of Arelate before Zosimus; this was revoked immediately after Zosimus by Boniface.

It remains now to discuss the three other provinces divided from unified Narbonne, concerning which Quesnellus attempts, in the final three chapters of Part II, to establish the rights of Arelate. A few observations concerning each will expose the fabrications of Quesnellus.

2. Let us first discuss Narbonne II. We showed in chapter 5, section 8, from the Council of Turin, that before the end of the fourth century, when the metropolis of Arelate began, Proculus of Marseille ordained bishops and exercised metropolitan jurisdiction in that same province.

Although Proculus was contradicted at this council, the contradiction did not come from the bishop of Arelate but from the bishops of the same province. They did not oppose him because they wished to be subject to Arelate, but because, excluding every metropolitan of another province, they wanted to have the metropolitan of Narbonne II itself, as we observed there.

The Fathers regarded Proculus’s possession, which had begun earlier, as so certain that they did not think the same right should be taken from him. They would certainly have attributed the right to Arelate if the bishop of Arelate, being present, had been able to demonstrate an older and longer possession of it, by which Proculus’s ordinations could have been excluded as usurpations.

But while only the bishops of Narbonne II were speaking, the bishop of Arelate remained silent, because he could produce no acts and no right over that province; nor was he considering subjecting it to his own jurisdiction.

3. The emptiness of Quesnellus’s conjecture is therefore evident. In order to establish the jurisdiction of Arelate over this province, he imagines that Arelate yielded to Proculus of Marseille because of the difficulties of that time, as though Arelate had always previously possessed a certain right and a certain possession—neither of which can be proved by any suitable document.

Certainly, he has not proved that the metropolis of Arelate was established before the Council of Valence; nor, we believe, could he have proved it against the evidence we have produced. What he adduced from the letters of Zosimus has likewise been shown in chapter 2 to be fabricated and attributable to the surreptitious action of Patroclus.

Proculus, therefore, who was fortified by the authority of the Council of Turin—

[Note: It is false, among other things, that the account given in Letter 5 of Zosimus to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne II reports that something entirely different was done at that synod. For the very preface makes clear that it was convened on account of several episcopal matters, the first of which concerned Narbonne II, which Proculus had claimed for himself.]

—clearly knew the falsehoods insinuated by Patroclus. Believing that he was not bound by those letters, since they had been obtained surreptitiously, he did not obey them at first. Whether he was equally disobedient when Zosimus pressed him with new letters and treated him as deposed is unknown.

Zosimus, indeed, indicates in Letter 11 to the people of Marseille that Proculus had been deposed and was nevertheless consecrating bishops, writing: “Although he is no longer a bishop, he makes bishops.”

P. Coustantius understands this as referring to a condemnation mentioned in the earlier letters, especially Letter 7. But all those letters understand “condemnation” in a broader sense: they express merely an interdict by which Proculus was forbidden to ordain bishops in Narbonne II. They contain no indication of deposition, as will be evident to anyone who reads them.

We think it probable that some deposition is indicated only in Letter 11. Whether Proculus continued to conduct himself as a bishop or not cannot be determined because of the lack of documentary evidence. It is especially surprising that Quesnellus, without any reliable witness, should have asserted that these letters were disregarded not so much by Proculus as by the Gallican bishops, and should have attributed this to the claim that judgments issued by the Roman pontiffs against Gallican bishops were held in Gaul to be worthless.

He preferred to introduce this explanation from his own prejudices against the Roman See rather than admit the surreptitious character of Zosimus’s letters and assign to Proculus, who knew of that surreptitious action, a more equitable excuse.

[Note: Quesnellus relies on Celestine’s Letter 4 to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne when he praises, without naming him, the bishop of Marseille. That letter more probably concerns Venerius, not Proculus. See Tillemont, under Zosimus, article 9. If Tillemont adds testimony from the *Life of St. Honoratus*, although that testimony does concern Proculus, it does not refer to the period when he had been deposed. The context indicates a much earlier period, as Tillemont himself admits in his account of the *Life of St. Honoratus*.]

4. It seems beyond doubt that, after the letters of Zosimus ordering him to appoint another in Proculus’s place, Patroclus of Arelate returned to Gaul, relying on the authority of those letters, and, supported by the patronage of Constantius, consecrated a new bishop for Marseille. Unless perhaps Proculus—whom we believe no longer resisted—so appeased the minds of Patroclus and Zosimus by this obedience that he was left in his own see.

Only at this time, therefore, did Narbonne II first pass under the jurisdiction of Arelate.

5. This limited jurisdiction acquired by Patroclus through the letters of Zosimus lasted only a short time. For when Boniface erased Zosimus’s decree with a better judgment, as Leo says, restoring authority to the bishop of Narbonne in Narbonne I, he added the general rule that extends to all the other ecclesiastical provinces:

> No one, he says, can be unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands—as we shall reproduce the precise words—that each metropolitan should have jurisdiction in a single province, and that no one should have two provinces subject to him.

This agreed with the judgment of the bishops of Narbonne II, who had argued at the Council of Turin that their province ought not to be subject to a bishop of another province. Therefore, since Proculus had now died, and this province had been assigned to him only for as long as he lived, it plainly followed from Boniface’s decree and from the Nicene canon cited by him that Narbonne II ought to enjoy its own metropolitan and ought not to be subject to the bishop of Arelate, lest one bishop preside over two provinces.

Consequently, metropolitan jurisdiction over Narbonne II seems, by that same canon and decree, to have been assigned to the bishop of Aquae—the more important city.

6. No earlier pontiff ever indicated or recognized this Nicene canon in the form in which Boniface recites it. Otherwise, since everyone showed the greatest deference to the Nicene canons, they would not have permitted the opposite discipline in the provinces of Italy and the Suburbicarian provinces: namely, that most of them should lack their own metropolitan, and that one metropolitan should preside not merely over two but over several provinces.

In Italy, although there were seven civil provinces, there were only two metropolitans, those of Milan and Aquileia. Pope Boniface introduced no change in this arrangement; the see of Ravenna was raised to metropolitan jurisdiction only under Celestine or Sixtus III.

For a still longer period, in the ten Suburbicarian provinces, the bishop of Rome alone acted as metropolitan. When Zosimus ordered Patroclus of Arelate to preside over the province of Vienne and the two Narbonnes, he was so unfamiliar with the discipline prescribed by the Nicene Fathers that he claimed instead to be acting according to the rules of those Fathers in Letter 5.

In fact, no such canon is found among the Nicene canons—not in the Greek text, not in any ancient Latin version, and not in Rufinus’s abridgment. Nor is it found among the Sardican canons, which Roman pontiffs were accustomed to cite under the name of the Nicene canons.

Since the bishops of Narbonne II had already argued at the Council of Turin that a priest of another province ought not to preside over them; since Hilary of Narbonne had asserted in Letter 6 of Zosimus that priests ought not to be ordained in another’s province by someone else; and since the people of Lectoure in Narbonne I had complained to Boniface that Patroclus had ordained in another province against the rules of the Fathers, Coustantius’s conjecture seems sufficiently probable to us.

Boniface did not intend to reproduce the actual words of the Council of Nicaea. Rather, he repeated words that may have been expressed summarily in the petition of the people of Lectoure from the Nicene canons—perhaps from the final words of canon 4, where metropolitans are mentioned in each province—and declared them as though they were his own.

This decree of Boniface was expressly confirmed by Celestine in Letter 4 to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, no. 6:

> First, he says, let each province be content with its own metropolitan, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, as the provisions sent by our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish; and let no priest be permitted, through usurpation, to inflict injury upon another. Let everyone be content with the limits granted to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province.

### 7

From these apostolic decrees, which assigned metropolitan jurisdiction to the bishop of Aix—so that he was in fact the metropolitan of the province of Narbonensis Secunda—St. Leo seems to have proceeded when he wrote in Letter 10, chapter 6:

> “Let each metropolitan defend for himself the ordination [lacuna] of his own province, by the right restored to him by us. Let no one dare claim another’s jurisdiction. Let each be content with his own boundaries and limits; [Col. 0615D] and let him know that he is not permitted to transfer to another the privilege owed to him. But if anyone, neglecting the apostolic sanctions and showing greater favor to a person than to his own honor, wishes to become a deserter from that honor, believing that he can transfer his privilege to another, let not the one to whom it was yielded, but the priest who within the province surpasses the other bishops in episcopal seniority, claim for himself the power of ordaining.”

He is speaking of metropolitans who, showing greater favor to a person, had believed that they could transfer their privilege to others. This cannot be understood except of metropolitans who, out of regard for someone, were unwilling to pursue and exercise the jurisdiction belonging to them. Perhaps the bishop of Aix, out of deference to the bishops of Arles, abstained from the jurisdiction that belonged to him by virtue of the apostolic decrees cited above, and left them the entire exercise of it in his province, just as we shall likewise see in the case of Ingenuus of Embrun, who was therefore censured by the same Leo for the unlawful cession of his province. For the bishop of Embrun had no other origin for his metropolitan jurisdiction in the province of the Maritime Alps than the bishop of Aix had in Narbonensis Secunda. [Col. 0616A]

Only the letters of Boniface and Celestine, which cite the Nicene canon, can be alleged in support of the rights of both bishops; and perhaps Leo included these letters under the designation “apostolic sanctions.” From this, moreover, it is clear that the bishops of Arles, even after Boniface’s decree, remained in possession of Narbonensis Secunda and, as its metropolitans, ordained bishops there. Accordingly, the bishops adhering to Arles—including Asclepius, bishop of Apt in Narbonensis Secunda—write to Leo in Letter 65, chapter 2:

> “It is established that both our predecessors and we ourselves were consecrated to the supreme priesthood by the priest of this Church [that is, the Church of Arles], through the gift of God.”

Since Bishop Auxanius—apparently the bishop of Aix—obtained from Pope Hilary, while serving as legate at Rome either from a Gallican synod or from Leontius of Arles, a privilege permitting the ordination of the bishop of Nice in the province of the Maritime Alps [Col. 0616B], it is highly credible that he worked all the more energetically for the ordinations of the bishops of his own province, Narbonensis Secunda, and sought to have his metropolitan jurisdiction restored to him.

### 8

Quesnellus nevertheless thinks that even after Pope Hilary the bishop of Aix, and consequently the whole of Narbonensis Secunda, was subject to the bishop of Arles. He infers this from the sequence of the petition presented to Pope Symmachus in the year 514 and from that pope’s rescript to Caesarius of Arles; for from these it is evident that the bishop of Aix could be summoned by the bishop of Arles to a synod.

This argument, however, is not altogether conclusive. For it is clear from several sources, and from Leo himself, that the bishop of Arles possessed the right to convene a synod from several provinces and to summon the metropolitans themselves. Indeed, in Letter 10, where St. Hilary of Arles is censured, two of his rights are distinguished: metropolitan jurisdiction over the single province of Vienne, and the right to convene a synod from other provinces. [Col. 0616C] The first right is taken from Hilary and transferred absolutely and independently to the bishop of Vienne; but regarding the right to summon councils from several provinces, Leo decrees that the consent of Leontius, the senior bishop, must be sought:

> “And because antiquity must always be honored, we wish our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, a priest worthy of approval, to be honored with this dignity, if it pleases you, so that, apart from his consent, no council of another province may be summoned by your holiness … while the dignity of the metropolitan privilege is preserved.”

Is it not thereby acknowledged that there was a right to summon the metropolitans themselves to the synod? If this right had not belonged to Hilary, there would have been no reason to make provision for supplementing this faculty through the senior bishop.

This decree was temporary, for as long as Hilary lived. Therefore, after his death, St. Leo likewise instructed Ravennius, his successor, to convene a synod from several provinces, at which all the bishops subscribed the letter he sent to Flavianus. This right seems to have been assigned to the bishop of Arles by Zosimus, under whom Patroclus possessed very extensive authority. He is said to have been supported by the authority of the Apostolic See in Letter 7 of that pontiff [Col. 0616D], and apostolic delegation is mentioned in Letter 10. Referring to this, the Gallican bishops affirm in Letter 65 to Leo, chapter 3, that the authority of the Apostolic See had been entrusted to the bishop of Arles.

Perhaps in one of Zosimus’s letters to Patroclus, now lost, this power to summon such synods was expressly contained. Hence Pope Hilary assigned a kind of primacy over Narbonensis Prima to Leontius of Arles, who succeeded Ravennius, in Letter 7; and in Letter 8, chapter 2, he confirms more explicitly this right to summon the metropolitans themselves to the synod:

> “Accordingly, every year an episcopal council is to be held from the provinces from which it can be assembled, so that, at suitable places and times and according to the arrangement of our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, to whom we have entrusted the responsibility of gathering the brethren, it may be celebrated after the metropolitans have been notified by his letters.”

And in Letter 10:

> “Let synodal councils be held each year, the principal responsibility for which we have decreed should rest with our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, priest of the Church of Arles.” [Col. 0617A]

And shortly afterward:

> “When the annual assemblies have been arranged by our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, after the metropolitans have been notified—as must often be said—be so good as to hold them in places where no traveler will encounter difficulty in assembling.”

Therefore the bishop of Aix, even if he had been a metropolitan, could be summoned by the bishop of Arles to the synod. He should not for that reason be called his suffragan, just as several other definite metropolitans who assembled at other Gallican synods presided over by the bishop of Arles cannot be called suffragans of the See of Arles.

### 9

One point in Symmachus’s Letter 10 appears stronger, since it identifies the bishop of Arles as the metropolitan of Aix and of the other bishops in these words:

> “Although even the bishop of the Church of Aix, or any other [bishop], [with respect] to the metropolitan bishop, etc.”

The matter is stated still more clearly in the petition to which Symmachus replied:

> “Command also that the bishop of the city of Aix be admonished by your holiness, in accordance with the established regulations, so that when he has been summoned by the metropolitan bishop of the Church of Arles to a synodal council, or when divine religion should require his presence for some matter of ordination [Col. 0617B], he may not fail to come without good reason.” (Tom. V of the Councils, col. 439.)

Here he is called a metropolitan not merely because of the right to summon him to a synod, but in connection with ordinations, to which only bishops of the same province were summoned—unless some unusual case occurred similar to that when, because his comprovincial bishops were unavailable, Sidonius summoned other metropolitans to an ordination in his letter to Agroecius of Sens.

Indeed, at the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549, and the Second Council of Auvergne in the same year, the bishop of Aix is recorded among the subscribing bishops not as a metropolitan but as an ordinary bishop (Tom. V of the Councils, col. 119). This sufficiently shows that during these periods also he lacked all metropolitan jurisdiction and was therefore subject, together with the whole of Narbonensis Secunda, to the bishop of Arles.

### 10

Let us turn to the Maritime Alps. Although Zosimus greatly magnified the rights of the See of Arles, since he assigned to it only three provinces—namely Vienne and the two provinces of Narbonensis [Col. 0617C]—it may appear that the Maritime Alps were not subject to the jurisdiction of Arles at the time when they, like the Graian Alps, had already long been constituted as provinces.

Perhaps Zosimus named only those three provinces either because, according to the old formula, both the Maritime and Graian Alps were included under the province of Vienne, or, more probably, because he thought it necessary to mention only those provinces that he wished to withdraw from the metropolitans they possessed and assign to the jurisdiction of Arles. Narbonensis Prima, however, recognized Hilary of Narbonne as its metropolitan; Narbonensis Secunda recognized Proculus of Marseille; and Vienne, at least in part, recognized Simplicius, bishop of Vienne.

In any event, Ingenuus of Embrun is reported by Pope Hilary in Letter 4 to have been supported by the perpetual honor of metropolitan dignity in the province of the Maritime Alps and to have been censured for the unlawful cession of his province, formerly made to the Apostolic See—that is, to Leo. This concerns the constitution of Boniface mentioned shortly before, by which he had established, on the basis of the Nicene canon, that each province should have its own metropolitan. [Col. 0617D]

The unlawful cession refers to those acts by which we know that he had been numbered among the suffragans of Arles and had subjected himself and his province to the jurisdiction of Arles. Nevertheless, he could be called “supported by the honor of metropolitan dignity” not because of what he had done, but by right, insofar as his cession could not prejudice the privilege of his see, which had been confirmed by apostolic letters.

For this reason, we think that Leo censured him together with the bishop of Aix in Letter 10, where he accuses not one but several deserters from their privilege. It may be questioned, however, whether Leo’s censure of Ingenuus for the unlawful cession attributed to him by Hilary long before indicates the general reproach inserted in Letter 10, or whether it indicates a separate and particular censure of Ingenuus, perhaps arising when Leo decreed in a now-lost letter that the Churches of Nice and Cimiez should be governed by one bishop. (See the dissertation *On the Lost Letters*, no. 97.)

Hilary’s words seem in fact to indicate a particular censure of Ingenuus. Certainly Ingenuus, perhaps after this last reprimand from Leo [Col. 0618A], tried, strengthened by Leo’s authority, to assert his rights.
