He therefore brought complaints before Pope Hilary concerning the rescript that had been granted to Auxanius—apparently the bishop of Aix—to his own prejudice, regarding the aforementioned Churches of Nice and Cimiez, which were situated in the province of the Maritime Alps.

He could not have called this “his prejudice” if he had thought that the Churches of this province belonged not to him but to the metropolitan of Arles. Not long afterward, however, the bishop of Embrun returned to his former subjection to Arles. For in several councils of Gaul his subscriptions show him occupying the place not of a metropolitan but of an ordinary bishop. See the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585.

### 11

A few words about the Graian Alps. We have found nothing certain concerning them, unless account is taken of the *Life of St. James, Bishop of Tarentaise*, which states that he was ordained by St. Honoratus of Arles and sent into this region.

One thing is certain: this episcopal see [Col. 0618B] was assigned by St. Leo to the metropolitan of Vienne. This indicates that it had previously belonged either to the bishop of Arles or to the bishop of Vienne. Since Octodurum, another city of these same Alps, is listed in the *Notitia Galliarum* and is not assigned to Vienne, while it lies beyond Tarentaise near Maxima Sequanorum and farther from Arles, it cannot be said to have been among the cities left to the bishop of Arles. For it would more readily have been granted, together with the nearer Tarentaise, to the bishop of Vienne. Consequently, it is highly credible that the bishop of Octodurum was subject to another metropolitan, for example the bishop of Lyon.

Nor does the conjecture made by Quesnellus from the Council of Aquileia stand in the way. For it is false that the acts of that council mention no other provinces that sent legates to the council except Vienne and the two provinces of Narbonensis, so that Theodorus of Octodurum would necessarily have belonged to one of them. The heading of one letter from that same council does mention the province of Vienne and the two provinces of Narbonensis, together with their legates [Col. 0618C], because the letter was sent to the bishops of those provinces.

But since Justus of Lyon also attended that council and is called in the acts the legate of the Gauls, Sirmondus rightly considered it most probable that another letter had existed, delivered to Justus on his return, addressed to those provinces of Gaul whose representative he had been at the same council. From these acts, therefore, it cannot be inferred whether Theodorus of Octodurum came to the council from the former provinces or, with Justus, from the latter ones.

If the explanation we have proposed seems more persuasive—namely, that Octodurum was subject neither to the bishop of Vienne nor to the bishop of Arles—it will become evident that the whole of the Graian Alps did not belong to the ecclesiastical province of Vienne or of Arles.

## INTO THE THIRD PART

### Chapter I  
### Quesnellus’s Improper Dissolution of Leo’s Two Censures against St. Hilary; A More Equitable Defense of St. Hilary Is Proposed

#### 1

Since in the observations already made [Col. 0618D] we seem to have refuted equally the first and second parts of Quesnellus’s dissertation, most of what is brought forward in the third part, resting as it does upon those earlier parts, will be easily dismantled. Here Quesnellus attempts to clear St. Hilary of certain censures of St. Leo, which seem to brand him with temerity and pride.

The censures are reduced to two principal charges. First, that Hilary, claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul, went too far in intending to disturb the order of the churches and the concord of the priests by new acts of presumption. Second, that he diminished the reverence due to St. Peter by excessively arrogant words.

The first accusation concerns Hilary’s improper deposition of Celidonius and the ordination of another bishop in the place of Projectus. On account of these acts, the pontiff declares there that Hilary had transferred to himself the dignity due to metropolitan bishops. From the context it is beyond doubt that, with the name “all Gaul” understood in the broader sense, the foreign provinces and churches were indicated as having been disturbed by these acts. [Col. 0619A]

It is evident from what was said earlier how poorly Quesnellus has weakened this first accusation by arguing that Hilary deposed Celidonius in his own province, not in another, and appointed another bishop over Projectus. We have pointed out a more equitable way of defending Hilary: namely, if we say that he did these things not out of any presumption or impulse of pride, but from a certain ecclesiastical concern and zeal for discipline, and not without at least the tacit consent and permission of the metropolitans themselves. Whether because of friendship or because of the reputation for holiness that he enjoyed, they deferred greatly to him, to such an extent that, showing greater favor to a person, they believed they could transfer to him the privilege owed to themselves. Since this was forbidden by the decrees of the Fathers, and since in both of the cases mentioned it had in fact led to a bad outcome, Leo rightly censured it.

#### 2

More difficult is the defense against the second accusation, according to which the pontiff states that Hilary diminished reverence for St. Peter by more arrogant words. The words are identified as words [Col. 0619B] that no layman could utter and no priest could hear.

These words escaped Hilary when, on coming to the Roman council, where Celidonius’s case was being summoned for examination, he refused judgment. Hilary could have resisted this Roman judgment for two reasons: either because he thought that the pontiff had no jurisdiction in the case, or because, considering the circumstances, he did not believe that a case of this sort ought to be heard and judged again at Rome rather than in Gaul.

Quesnellus attributes the first reason to Hilary. Since that position conflicts with the pontifical jurisdiction that we established in Part I, Quesnellus, while attempting to defend Hilary, instead presents him as guilty of a grave injury. We believe that another reason moved him—one that does not infringe pontifical jurisdiction, as we explained in Part I, chapter 7, numbers 12 and 13. Only in this matter does he seem to have gone too far by using words less cautiously than he should have.

For if anyone maintains that he said nothing more serious, he must necessarily accuse Leo, who testifies to the contrary, of calumny. The testimony of the prefect Auxiliaris is set against Leo’s account. But Auxiliaris was not present at the actual dispute; he merely affirms [Col. 0619C] that he does not remember any action of Hilary’s being even slightly darkened by the contagion of arrogance. He says that he knows how impatiently people bear such accusations, “if we speak in this way,” as we ourselves are conscious of doing. His testimony does not therefore seem weighty enough to be preferred to Leo’s testimony concerning a matter recent and public—especially since, if Leo’s account had been false, it could have been refuted from the very acts that Leo himself transmitted.

Auxiliaris speaks of Hilary’s earlier conduct and words as known to him, from the time when he was prefect in Gaul and at Arles and enjoyed Hilary’s familiarity. These circumstances have no bearing upon the acts and words performed and approved before the entire council, about which St. Leo alone bears witness.

Hilary’s earlier conduct, together with his humility and holiness, certainly creates a strong presumption in his favor. But it is not a presumption capable of convicting Leo, a most holy and gentle pontiff—whose moderation even toward heretics is universally known—of deliberate calumny. Who does not know that even holy men sometimes let fall things that are not entirely right when they are carried away by the heat of dispute?

Nor am I unaware, Quesnellus himself admits in Part II, chapter 1 [Col. 0619D], how easily anyone may be led astray by his own disposition, even when he is pious and holy, particularly if he thinks that he is defending a most just cause not for his own sake but for the public good.

Hilary considered Celidonius’s deposition most just, to such an extent that he believed, given the circumstances, that it ought not to be reopened by a new judgment at Rome, without prejudice to the right of the Apostolic See. Thus he protested that he had come for official duties, not for the case itself (*Life of Hilary*, chapter 17).

It could therefore have happened that, while he thought the measures he proposed for preventing the Roman judgment were entirely appropriate and effective, he discovered that he was persuading no one. For we think that this is the meaning of Leo’s words: “Hilary had no reasonable answer that he could give in the council of holy priests.” It could, I say, have happened that, while arguing or even complaining about this matter with excessive fervor, certain less cautious words escaped him—not from a bad intention but through thoughtlessness, which is very easy in such circumstances—and that these words appeared arrogant and contrary to the reverence due to St. Peter. [Col. 0620A]

It could even have happened, as Quesnellus suspects in chapter 2, that Leo did not at that time possess sufficient knowledge of Hilary’s holiness, and that, amid the heat of the dispute, the Roman pontiff did not understand Hilary’s words in the sense in which the bishop of Arles uttered them.

Whatever may be brought forward in Hilary’s excuse, so long as we believe that he left pontifical jurisdiction untouched, we shall gladly accept it.

#### 3

Innovators seek in vain to derive support from this dispute between the holy bishop and the supreme pontiff, unless, with Quesnellus, they improperly refer it to a denial of pontifical jurisdiction. Catholics, on the contrary, admire in such an event the providence of God, which sometimes permits certain lapses even in holy men so that, having thereby been made more humble, they may advance to greater things.

This is what happened to Hilary. After returning to his homeland from such a dispute, he not only immediately—as the author of his *Life* relates—turned entirely, in humbled submission, to appeasing Leo’s spirit; he also humbly bore the sentence pronounced against him by the pontiff and applied himself with greater fervor to the pastoral duties of his office and to the pursuit of perfection. [Col. 0620B]

> “The author of the *Life*, chapter 17, says: ‘He devoted himself entirely to prayer, preaching, and works, as though beginning anew; strict in discipline, constant in compassion, and most ready in generosity,’ etc.”

And shortly afterward:

> “By abstaining from food, applying himself to work, and making his journeys on foot, he so weakened, wearied, and exhausted himself that he scarcely completed the course of his forty-eighth year.”

Quesnellus attempts to pervert this marvelous arrangement of divine providence, by which the lapses of the saints themselves are turned to good, when in chapter 1 he imagines that St. Hilary, even after St. Leo’s decree, persisted in his position and continued throughout his life to usurp metropolitan authority, despite Leo’s opposition and the emperor’s threats.

In chapter 2, moreover, so as not to leave Hilary alone, he draws the Gallican bishops also into the same contempt for the Roman judgment. He declares that, setting aside the judgment of the Transalpine assembly, they consistently upheld the sentence pronounced by the Gallican synod against Celidonius, and that in electing a successor [Col. 0620C] they disregarded and treated as invalid the decree of Leo against Hilary.

Thus this man, hostile to apostolic authority, under the pretext of vindicating the memory of St. Hilary, defames him and seeks to represent Hilary himself as the champion of his own disobedience and stubbornness—qualities proper not to holy men but to rebellious ones. The following chapter will demonstrate how fictitious these claims are and how foreign they were not only to Hilary but also to the Gallican bishops.

## Chapter II  
## It Is Demonstrated against Quesnellus That Neither Hilary nor the Gallican Bishops Resisted Leo’s Decree

#### 1

Quesnellus prefers to present Hilary as resisting Leo’s sentence. Accordingly, in chapter 2 [Col. 0620D] he asserts that even after the sentence Hilary wrote defenses in support of his right and sent legates to Rome.

To this he refers the account given by the author of the *Life*:

> “And because I can in no way connect with this work what he dictated in this case, I thought that the opinion of the prefect Auxiliaris should be inserted.”

Quesnellus assigns these words to the period after the Roman judgment, although they concern writings composed by Hilary and sent to Rome through legates before the judgment, when there was still an opportunity for defense. Hilary’s purpose was not so much to demonstrate that his judgment concerning Celidonius was, as he thought, just, as to appease Leo by adopting more humble language, lest Leo strip him and the See of Arles of their privileges.

This is sufficiently clear from the context of the *Life*. The author relates that Hilary, who had left Rome before the sentence, returned to Arles and immediately devoted himself entirely, with humbled submission, to appeasing Leo’s spirit. For this purpose he sent legates to the City: first the presbyter Ravennius, and then the bishops Nectarius and Constantius.

He next mentions the written statements or defenses known to have been sent to Rome through these same legates, and finally appends the letter of the prefect Auxiliaris to Hilary himself. According to that letter, once Hilary had received it, he made no further effort to defend his right but remained at peace for the rest of his life.

Hilary left Rome in the severe winter weather, evidently at the end of January or the beginning of February. Leo’s sentence, however, was issued on 8 July. [Col. 0621A] These events therefore took place in the intervening period, and consequently the defenses were composed and published before the sentence. If these defenses were sent immediately after Hilary’s return in order to appease Leo’s spirit, they cannot have been postponed until after 8 July—especially since defenses written after the sentence, if directed against Leo, would have served not to appease but to embitter his spirit.

In Part I, chapter 8, Quesnellus portrays Hilary as resisting after the Roman judgment on the hypothesis that Leo’s sentence was issued on 6 January, the date attached to a shorter letter of Leo to the bishops of Vienne. Since Hilary did not accept that sentence, Quesnellus supposes that St. Leo therefore wrote another, much longer letter to the same bishops five months after the first, one prepared through prolonged reflection and care.

But this hypothesis is false. In that eighth chapter Quesnellus assumes the shorter letter to be genuine [Col. 0621B]—although elsewhere he had expressed doubts about its authenticity—in order to represent Hilary as resisting Leo’s judgment. Yet it must be counted among the spurious letters, as will become clear from our note.

#### 2

After the genuine letter written around 8 July, which presents Leo’s sentence against Hilary, Quesnellus could indeed assert that Hilary continued to pursue his right and throughout his life continued to usurp the metropolitan authority of which he had been deprived; but he could not prove it. No action, no testimony, will be produced.

The words of the author of the *Life*, in which he presents Hilary as remaining steadfast in his purpose, are quoted by Quesnellus near the end of chapter 3:

> “Placed in danger of his life, he absolutely refused to be joined in communion with one whom he had condemned together with such distinguished men.”

Quesnellus quotes these words in such a way that they appear to refer to the whole period of Hilary’s life. Yet the author wrote them about the time when Hilary, while at Rome together with Celidonius, refused to participate in the sacred rites with him.

The same author, after reproducing the letter of the prefect Auxiliaris [Col. 0621C], in which he had urged Hilary in unmistakable terms to humble himself and submit, immediately adds:

> “Having received such words, he devoted himself entirely to prayer, preaching, and works, as though beginning anew,”

along with the rest of the passage that we quoted near the end of the preceding chapter.

All these things are duties of the episcopal ministry that remained to Hilary and the obligations of a holy life. They cannot be reduced to the functions of metropolitan jurisdiction. Indeed, this manner of writing presents a holy man who, following the advice of Auxiliaris and offering no further resistance, devoted himself entirely to episcopal care and the cultivation of his own soul.

Quesnellus himself rightly maintained in Part I, chapter 8 [Col. 0621D], that from the words of the *Life* just cited it could be inferred that Hilary, having ceased such disputes, no longer troubled Leo. He would have troubled him if, after such a solemn judgment had been issued, he had still wished to exercise metropolitan jurisdiction. Instead, he devoted himself entirely to aiding and nurturing the souls entrusted to him through prayer, preaching, and pastoral care, and while diligently attending to these duties he came to the end of his life.

Indeed, shortly afterward Quesnellus states that throughout the entire period of Hilary’s remaining life no occasion arose—and Hilary himself had not sought one—in which it would have been necessary to oppose Leo’s decree. The first such occasion, as is clear, was the ordination of the bishop of Vaison, which was carried out after Hilary’s death by his successor Ravennius.

But when no occasion to exercise metropolitan jurisdiction arose, it cannot be said that Hilary conducted himself as a metropolitan or continued throughout his life to usurp metropolitan authority.

What is more, those who maintain that he persisted in usurping metropolitan power introduce an incredible claim. For once the emperor’s law had been added to Leo’s decree, and the execution of that decree had been ordered in Gaul itself, if Hilary had attempted anything contrary to it, the imperial officials—who were bound by the imperial mandate—would not have permitted it.

Hence Quesnellus himself, speaking of this law in Part I, chapter 9, says: [Col. 0622A]

> “The imperial constitution issued by Valentinian against Hilary had made obedience necessary.”

This completely refutes what the same author, contradicting himself, wrote in Part III, chapter 1:

> “Hilary continued throughout his life to usurp the same authority, even … while the emperor was threatening him.”

Contradictions readily arise in one who defends a falsehood.

#### 3

Regarding the Gallican bishops, Quesnellus boldly asserts in Part III, chapter 2, that they, setting aside the judgment of the Transalpine assembly, consistently upheld the sentence pronounced by the Gallican synod against Celidonius.

How easy it is to sell falsehoods without evidence! We know rather that Hilary’s judgment against Celidonius was regarded as invalid after the Roman synod and after Leo’s judgment. This is clear from the fact that the Church of Besançon records the said Celidonius—restored by Leo, dead, and buried in his own see—as having been restored to his see, while Importunus, whom Hilary had installed in his place, was expelled when Celidonius reclaimed his see after the Roman judgment. See Chiffletius, *Besançon*, vol. II, pp. 115 and 136.

Valentinian’s law itself leaves no room for doubt that the restoration of Celidonius decreed by Leo was certainly carried out. [Col. 0622B]

#### 4

But how far the bishops of those Gallican provinces were from putting Leo’s constitution into effect became clear in the very ordination of Ravennius, Quesnellus says in Part I, chapter 8—as though this ordination, by which Ravennius was elected as metropolitan of Arles, conflicted with Leo’s decree, which had granted metropolitan jurisdiction to the bishop of Vienne.

To make clear how empty this argument is, one must observe that the bishops adhering to the See of Arles accepted Leo’s decree so completely that, recognizing Hilary as deprived of all metropolitan jurisdiction, they requested that this jurisdiction be restored to Ravennius, his successor, by a new decree.

Thus they write in Letter 65, chapter 1:

> “We do not desire that anything new be instituted through you, but that the ancient and former arrangements be restored. For it is not just that the honor of him whom, as we have shown, you greatly love should be diminished by the matter in which another [Hilary] offended your piety. And certainly it is evident that the Church of Arles enjoys the favor of divine grace, since it has been granted such a priest, through whom the privileges of its ancient dignity—which it grieved to see diminished for a time [Col. 0622C]—might rejoice in being restored forever by the more recent authorities of the Apostolic See.”

If they had regarded Leo’s judgment—by which Hilary had been stripped of the privileges of the See of Arles—as invalid, those privileges could never have been called “diminished for a time.”

The Gauls spoke in this way because they knew that those privileges had truly been taken away from Hilary. Accordingly, Leo expressed their petition in his reply, Letter 66, chapter 1, so that “what his predecessor had lost through the merit of his presumption might be restored.”

They added the phrase “for a time” because, according to Leo’s understanding, those same privileges, taken away as punishment for Hilary alone, were reserved for the See of Arles after Hilary’s death. Leo, who did not permit anything to be shaken or removed from the privileges of the churches—as he likewise states in Letter 66, chapter 1—intended to punish Hilary alone, not to strip the see of its prerogatives.

Thus, if the whole of Letter 10 is read attentively, only Hilary’s person will be found to have been punished: [Col. 0622D]

> “Nor should Hilary henceforth dare to convene synodal assemblies. Let him therefore take part in no ordination; let him not ordain. Let him know that he has been removed not only from another’s jurisdiction, but also deprived of authority over the province of Vienne, which he had wrongly usurped.”

Everything concerns Hilary alone; there is not even a word about the see or his successors. Perhaps this punishment of the person alone, which would not pass to his successors, was expressed more clearly in another lost letter, in which the jurisdiction taken from Hilary was transferred, by a temporary arrangement, to the bishop of Vienne.

Leo himself says in Letter 66, chapter 2:

> “The authority that we took away from the bishop Hilary—not from the See of Arles—we believed should be assigned to the bishop of Vienne.”

Perhaps, then, it was from this lost letter that the Gallican bishops learned the pontiff’s intention more clearly and therefore stated in their aforementioned letter to Leo that the dignity of the bishop of Arles had been diminished for a time.

### 5

This was certainly the ancient discipline of the Church: if any metropolitans, because of some fault of theirs, were deprived not of their episcopal see but only of metropolitan jurisdiction, this penalty affected their one person and lifetime, but did not pass to their successors; meanwhile, as long as they lived, metropolitan jurisdiction belonged to the senior bishop.

This is made clear by the eighth letter of Pope Hilary, who immediately succeeded Leo. When Hermes had been promoted from the episcopate of Béziers—which he had been unworthily expelled from—to the see of Narbonne, Hilary, recognizing that this had been done contrary to the canons, left him the see of Narbonne but transferred the metropolitan authority of ordaining bishops to the senior prelate of that same province:

> We have removed from him who is now permitted to preside over the Church of Narbonne the authority of ordaining bishops, because of these things that were wrongly done. We have judged that this authority should belong to our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, bishop of the Church of Uzès, since he is said to be first in dignity by age; so that, if he should die while Bishop Hermes survives, this responsibility may fall to whoever the episcopal order finds to be first. But when Bishop Hermes is dead, the custom of appointing prelates shall promptly be restored to the Church of Narbonne, which lost it not because of the city but because of the cause of presumption.

Likewise, when Saint Leo, in the same letter 10, where he deals with Saint Hilary, chapter 6, wished to remove another possible abuse of the metropolitans, he enacted a general decree: if any metropolitan did not obey the commands, the right of ordaining should belong to the one who, within the province, preceded the other priests in episcopal antiquity. He plainly wished to punish only the person of the offender, so that, once that person had died, the same prerogative would return to his successor—the prerogative which the city had lost, not because of the city itself but because of the cause of presumption.

If that same pontiff, when he deprived Hilary of metropolitan jurisdiction, had regard only to his lifetime for the same reason, and in the same letter 10, chapter 9, granted to Leontius, the senior bishop, the right to convene synods of different provinces, while transferring the other metropolitan prerogatives in another letter, now lost, to the bishop of Vienne, we must suppose that he did this for the special reason that the bishop of Vienne claimed jurisdiction, in rivalry with Arles, over at least some of the Churches of the same province.

This nevertheless does not prevent the decree transferring either jurisdiction—whether to Leontius, the senior prelate, or to the bishop of Vienne—from affecting only Hilary’s lifetime, so that, after Hilary’s death, both jurisdictions returned to his successor Ravennius. Hence, from Ravennius’s election, it cannot be concluded, with Quesnel, that the bishops of the province disobeyed Leo’s decree by electing the metropolitan of Arles.

For when Hilary died, the force of Leo’s decree ceased. Since the pontiff had punished Hilary’s person alone and left the rights of the see of Arles intact, the bishops of the province rightly assembled after his death to elect a metropolitan without the bishop of Vienne; and Leo approved this in letters 40 and 41.

Quesnel himself was forced to admit this in part I, chapter 8, of the dissertation cited above, writing:

> Nothing in Ravennius’s ordination suggests or censures any neglect of the metropolitan bishop of Vienne. Hence it is easy to conclude that Leo did not wish to strip the Church of Arles of its metropolitan jurisdiction by his decision, but only to punish Hilary; and, when he had died, he judged it right that everything should return to its former state.

He is mistaken only in supposing that this arrangement was introduced for reasons of expediency after Ravennius’s election, and in failing to understand that the same force had belonged to the decree from the beginning, by the discipline of that period.

### 6

“But why,” you will ask, “did the bishops of the province request that the ancient jurisdiction taken from Hilary be restored to Ravennius, if, after Hilary’s death, it had already returned to him according to Leo’s intention and according to the discipline itself?”

This arose from the longstanding controversy with the bishop of Vienne. Since, by Leo’s decree, while Hilary was alive, he had obtained jurisdiction over the Church of Arles, even after Hilary’s death he continued to assert his right over several Churches, especially the Church of Vaison, to which Ravennius had appointed a bishop when the ancient jurisdiction revived.

Therefore Ravennius and the bishops of the province asked Leo for a new decree—not so that, after the death of a bishop deprived of metropolitan jurisdiction, the ancient right might return to his successor, but so that, in the disputed jurisdiction between the bishops of Arles and Vienne over Vaison and other Churches—a jurisdiction that had been transferred to Vienne while Hilary lived—the privileges of Arles might remain wholly intact, lest what had been temporarily taken away as a punishment imposed on Hilary alone should become a permanent disadvantage to his successors and to the see.

### 7

The ordination of the bishop of Vaison, therefore, which after Hilary’s death returned to Ravennius, his successor, in accordance with the ancient discipline, proves nothing in support of Hilary’s right. It proves even less that Hilary possessed the same right which the Gallicans expressly said had been taken from him, with the assent of the Gallic bishops, and that he continued to usurp this authority throughout his lifetime, even in defiance of Leo.

When Quesnel asserted this, instead of providing Hilary with a fair defense, he burdened him with a grave accusation of disobedience and contempt. Nor does the reasoning he adds in chapter 1 vindicate him: namely, that it was not unknown that the prerogative of the chief bishops over inferior bishops was inert and inactive whenever the latter claimed nothing for themselves according to the rule of the canons.

This assumes that Hilary had done everything according to the canons and had claimed nothing for himself outside his own province. Yet Quesnel tried unsuccessfully to prove precisely this, as was shown earlier. Moreover, when he actually attributes to Hilary disobedience and obstinacy—qualities most alien to him and proved by no canons—his sanctity especially abhors such a defense, which protects crimes under the appearance of law and in the name of the canons.

## CHAPTER III  
### Leo’s statements that Hilary had produced nothing reasonable are defended. On the witnesses produced by Celidonius. Saint Leo’s judgment defended. What should be thought concerning certain accusations against Hilary inserted in Leo’s letter.

#### 1

Quesnel interprets Leo’s statement about Hilary in letter 10, chapter 3—“He had no reasonable answer to make in the holy council of priests,” the meaning of which we have explained elsewhere (see chapter 1, no. 2)—as referring to the right of appeal. He does so to such an extent that he makes Leo’s sole grievance that Hilary opposed Celidonius’s appeal.

This likewise assumes that Leo lacked the right of appeal, which we have established with the greatest clarity. Quesnel further calls the same words suspicious on the ground that the laws removed from everyone the opportunity to give testimony in his own case.

If those words referred to a legal right, and Hilary had resisted on this point, then, since we have produced the clearest testimony from custom, the canons, and divine law in support of the right of appeal (part I, chapters 5–7), could anything Hilary might have brought forward against it have been considered reasonable?

But if the words refer to the facts, how can something be considered reasonable when the judge testifies that it was not reasonable? (See the observations in part I, chapter 2.) Whether a judge who accepts a case within his jurisdiction, condemns one deficient in answers and proofs and withdrawing from judgment, and declares that he has produced nothing reasonable, can thereby be treated as a witness in his own cause, we leave to others to determine from the laws themselves.

#### 2

Quesnel’s further discussion in the same chapter of the witnesses produced by Celidonius at the Roman synod seems to prejudice Leo’s judgment but favor Hilary’s: judgments concerning facts are more easily and cautiously made in the place where the events occurred, where witnesses are less able to deceive, than in a very distant place—especially if only witnesses brought by the accused have arrived there.

Thus, the judgment held by Hilary at Besançon, where Celidonius was bishop and where several witnesses were found, might seem less liable to deception than Leo’s judgment held at Rome, where only witnesses produced by Celidonius were present.

This would indeed be significant if the matter concerned something that had occurred at Besançon. But that is not established; indeed, the opposite is much more probable.

The impediment alleged against Celidonius was his marriage to a widow whom he was said to have married before becoming a bishop (Life of Hilary, chapter 16). Another impediment was also alleged, as it is called, of leniency (*lenitas*): namely, that, after having administered a secular office, he had condemned certain persons to death.

But where he exercised this secular administration, or the office of judge, is not stated. Such administrations and offices were carried out in various places. It could therefore have happened that, while exercising secular administration somewhere other than Besançon, he married a woman from that place; and consequently that the matter concerned an event that had taken place not at Besançon but elsewhere.

Who knows in what city and province this happened? Indeed, if the matter had occurred at Besançon and had been known there, as is assumed, it would have come to light before his election. While the customary consent of the clergy and people was being sought, at least someone would have brought this impediment forward and prevented his ordination.

Therefore, from the very fact that his election and ordination were peaceful, it may be inferred that the marriage later alleged belonged to some other distant place. Thus foreign witnesses would have had to be brought to Besançon no less than to Rome, and no greater credibility or authority can be drawn from the witnesses for the Besançon judgment than for the Roman judgment.

In the judgment at Besançon, the use of unreliable witnesses may be indicated by the fact that the impediment of leniency, which the witnesses at Besançon also confirmed in their accusation, was not established. Consequently, no further question concerning it was raised at the Roman trial, and there is no indication that Leo considered it.

Thus both accusers and witnesses may have been false in the matter of bigamy, just as they appear to have been in the matter of leniency. Some people hostile to Celidonius may have spread false accusations and perhaps produced false witnesses based only on hearsay; these may have deceived Hilary, who was carried away by zeal for discipline, and the other judges assembled at Besançon.

But Celidonius may have brought to Rome more impartial and better-informed witnesses who knew him in his official administrations, and to whom Hilary, although he had brought with him the records of what had occurred, was unable to respond.

This is the stronger presumption, which, from the witnesses themselves, gives greater credibility to the Roman judgment than to the judgment at Besançon.

Certainly the monk of Jura, who lived near Besançon and was nearly Hilary’s contemporary, wrote the Life of Saint Romanus. On the basis of the reputation and tradition of that same Church, he accused Hilary’s sentence of having been issued without any valid reason.

Here, then, from Besançon itself—the place where Hilary had deposed Celidonius—we have a judgment in favor of Leo’s decision. This testimony is greater than the mere testimony of the author of the Life of Saint Hilary, who wrote from the reputation of Arles alone and not from that of Besançon. But more will be said about this in the observations on part I, chapter 3.

We do not deny that the witnesses produced by Celidonius could have deceived Leo. But since they were questioned in Hilary’s presence, and since Hilary, although thoroughly informed about the witnesses and the proceedings at Besançon, had no response to make, a strong presumption arises in their favor. Accordingly, Leo’s judgment should be regarded as entirely just, as such cases generally require.

#### 3

Nor can we conceal Quesnel’s great audacity in representing Leo as having acted in this case out of a preconceived hostility toward Hilary.

Father Jacques Longueval, *History of the Gallican Church*, book IV, volume II, p. 35, dismisses so serious an accusation in a few words:

> Father Quesnel, who seems to have undertaken to comment on the works of Saint Leo only in order to prosecute that great pope, accuses him of acting with prejudice against Saint Hilary. But Saint Leo had witnessed Hilary’s conduct at Rome; he had examined the documents of the trial over which he was judge. Can anyone, without rashness, judge that so great a man and so holy a pope acted out of passion against another saint?

Indeed, if the discussion concerns the judgment held in Celidonius’s case, by which Hilary’s sentence was overturned, what, I ask, should Leo have done when Celidonius appealed, persisted in his claim, and produced witnesses, while Hilary offered no response and withdrew from judgment? What else could he have done but follow the solemn principle of all laws and tribunals: “When the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant is acquitted”?

No one can be angry with Leo in this matter unless he considers him deprived of the power of judging such appeals and therefore an incompetent judge.

That is the only point Quesnel brought forward in defense of Hilary. By attaching this utterly false opinion to the holy man, he referred all Hilary’s statements, all his silence, and even his flight from the Roman judgment to it.

Thus he reduced the entire case to a legal question, although at the outset he had accepted it as concerning a purely factual matter. Yet since this pontifical right has been established with the greatest clarity, as it seems to us, from custom, the canons, and divine law, Saint Leo, who was well acquainted with this right, could not have judged otherwise. No one can justly criticize his judgment except one who, with Quesnel, denies the pontifical right.

But while Quesnel, in order to conceal both himself and his prejudice, attributes to Saint Hilary this opinion, which is utterly opposed to every legal principle, he portrays Hilary as resisting apostolic authority and, under the name of an apology, brings upon him a grave accusation and disgrace.

We, venerating the outstanding sanctity of so great a man—a sanctity that Leo himself testified to after his death when he called him “of holy memory” in letter 40—have sought to vindicate him by another and more equitable approach. If this approach is not satisfactory, any other better and more probable explanation will gladly be accepted and approved, provided that it does not injure the pontifical right, which is supported by all antiquity and authority.

#### 4

If the discussion concerns the various accusations against Hilary inserted in Leo’s letter and arising incidentally in, or apart from, Celidonius’s case, since they concern facts that do not touch the right of the apostolic see, we do not deny that Leo could have been mistaken and deceived in these matters no less than Hilary.

We would certainly wish that these accusations could be cleared in such a way that, while Hilary was defended, Leo would not be accused. If only we had been permitted to imitate the author of Hilary’s Life, who thought it better to refrain from relating certain matters, giving this reason (chapter 17):

> “Because I do not dare to examine the judgments of such great men, especially those who have already been called to heavenly grace.”

But since Quesnel, under the pretext of clearing Hilary, attacked Leo, it was our duty to produce those arguments that seemed most useful for vindicating him. If, as a result, some censure falls back upon Hilary, this must be attributed not to us but to the surviving records.

Leo’s letter is of great importance in this matter, since it testifies to the dispute held at Rome; the account of that dispute was incorporated in the official proceedings sent to Gaul together with the letter. We cannot suspect that the most holy prelate falsely slandered Hilary.

Moreover, Leo wrote these letters not immediately after the heat of the dispute, but about five months later, when all agitation, if there had been any, had entirely subsided. He also wrote after receiving and hearing Hilary’s legates, who had been sent to appease the pontiff and to excuse or clear Hilary. We learn from letters 40 and 41 that Ravennius was approved by the pontiff.

Having therefore been better informed after so long an interval, if Leo had previously formed any impression contrary to the evidence of the proceedings and to the truth of the matter, he would undoubtedly have corrected it.

Although this letter indicates that Hilary may have said something rather harsh, by which apostolic authority appeared to be injured, it does not state what that was. If the records in which the entire dispute was described had reached us, Hilary’s words might perhaps be explained with a fairer and more certain interpretation.

In this obscurity, however, we consider the interpretation we have proposed sufficiently fair and probable: we should not believe that Hilary said or thought anything against the apostolic right concerning appeals, against ancient custom, or against the Sardican canons themselves, whose acceptance in Gaul we have demonstrated.

As for the other censures of Hilary, which concern facts occurring far from Rome, we cannot determine, in the absence of other documents, whether Leo was deceived anywhere.

# SIXTH DISSERTATION  
## On the observance of the Saturday fast in the Roman Church in the time of Pope Saint Leo I

The meaning of these words from his letter 11, now numbered 9, to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, chapter 1—“With the Saturday fast continued”—and of this clause from the sermons on the fasts of the seventh and tenth months and of Pentecost—“Let us fast, therefore, on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us likewise keep vigil beside the blessed Apostle Peter”—is demonstrated. These words should be rejected from sermon 4 on Lent, where they have until now been incorrectly inserted, and the origin of the interpolation is explained.

## I

That the Churches once had various and differing customs concerning the Saturday fast is expressly stated by Saint Augustine in several places and is established with certainty from many other authors. But, if we wish to investigate more precisely what the Roman Church chiefly observed in the age of our Leo, we are invited to do so by the memory of this Roman pontiff, whose writings we have reviewed, and by several passages in his letters and sermons in which either the Saturday fast is mentioned or its observance appears to have been omitted by design.

Several kinds of Saturdays must be distinguished in this dissertation. The question may concern the Saturdays occurring during the weeks of Lent; those following Wednesday and Friday of the Ember seasons; or any Saturday occurring throughout the year outside both those periods. To these may also be added the Saturday vigil of Pentecost. We shall discuss these separately, leaving aside the fast of Holy Saturday, about which no similar controversy has arisen.

## II

First, the evidence is so clear that the fast was observed in the Roman Church on the Saturday of every week outside Lent and the Ember seasons, and also outside the paschal fifty days before Pentecost, that anyone who denies it must be thought to love controversy more than to seek the truth.

Nicholas I, the Roman pontiff, writing to the Gallican bishops, relates that the Saturday fast had been instituted from the time of Silvester, or even earlier:

> Concerning the Saturday fast, he says, the matter was sufficiently discussed and debated in the time of Saint Silvester, confessor of Christ; and it was definitively ordained that it should be celebrated everywhere. After this, no one presumed, with reckless boldness, to act or even to murmur against that ordinance.

**[Note: [Col. 0627D] Nicholas I took this from the Acts of Saint Silvester, which many Romans were still reading in the time of Gelasius, as Gelasius himself testifies in his decree on apocryphal books. But since these Acts are proved by Baronius, under the year 315, no. 17, to have been disfigured by numerous falsehoods, and since, after other learned men, Papebroch and Janning have demonstrated that a considerable part of them is false, they deserve no credibility in this matter concerning the Saturday fast, which must be counted among their inventions.]**

If Nicholas wrote this truthfully, I think he derived it from apocryphal fictions or from popular Roman tradition. For where could he have learned about Silvester what was unknown to Ambrose, Augustine, Cassian, and even Innocent I?

If the Saturday fast had been discussed, enacted, and definitively established under Silvester, it could not have been unknown to Innocent, who was closer in time to Silvester. Nor would Innocent have omitted it when writing to Eugubinus, since he gathered together everything that could support the Roman custom.

I would suppose either that Nicholas had suffered a lapse of memory and substituted Silvester for Innocent, or that the scribes had fallen into error. I support this by a twofold conjecture.

First, Nicholas would have added the authority and decree of Innocent to Silvester’s authority, and would have referred Photius, who was calumniating the Roman Church, to Innocent’s reasoning. This would certainly have had greater force than recalling some debate held before Silvester and unknown to everyone.

Second, if Nicholas had said that, after Silvester’s definition, no one had dared to act or even murmur against that ordinance, Photius would immediately have produced from the Roman archives Innocent’s letter to Decentius. That letter makes it clear that, not long after Silvester’s time, the Saturday fast had been both murmured against and debated even in the suburbicarian diocese.

I know from Saint Peter Damian’s *Opusculum* 55 and from the Life of Saint Romuald written by him that, at that time, a writing under the name of Pope Silvester concerning the Saturday fast was being circulated, and that a fragment of it is quoted in the work just mentioned. But writings of doubtful antiquity and authenticity, attributed to so ancient a pontiff without the support of ancient authorities, do not gain much patronage from an eleventh-century author.

## III

The observance of the Saturday fast in the Roman Church must therefore be established from monuments of better quality.

It is certain that around the year 387 the custom was in force which we know from letters 86 and 118 of Saint Augustine. When Saint Monica, finding that the Church of Milan did not fast on Saturday, was uncertain what she should do, Ambrose, questioned by Augustine while he was still a catechumen, replied:

> When I am here, I do not fast on Saturday; when I am in Rome, I fast on Saturday. In whatever Church you come, observe its custom, if you do not wish either to suffer scandal or to cause it.  
> —Saint Augustine, letter 118 to Januarius, chapter 2

The celebrated letter 86 shows that this custom continued in the same Church around the year 392. Augustine wrote it after becoming a priest in order to rebuke the insolence of a certain Roman who abusively attacked almost all the Churches that differed from the Roman Church in this observance.

That it was maintained after the year 395 is confirmed by Augustine’s letter 118, which he sent to Januarius when he was already a bishop. When he says there, “Some fast on Saturday,” the Romans must be understood, as is sufficiently indicated by Ambrose’s reply, which Augustine immediately reports.

In letter 19 to Jerome, concerning the same fast, Augustine writes:

> I would like your kindness to tell me whether any holy Easterner, when he comes to Rome, fasts on Saturday deliberately, except on the day of the Easter vigil.

Jerome himself, writing to Lucinius the Spaniard in letter 28, also mentions that the Saturday fast was observed at Rome.

In the year 416, when Pope Innocent was writing to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, so far from anything having been relaxed concerning this custom of the Saturday fast, he insisted that it must be observed in full:

> We do not deny that one must fast on Friday; but we also say that this must be done on Saturday . . . . . We must not pass over Saturday.

He proves this both by various arguments and by different traditions, whether ecclesiastical or apostolic. From one of these he sufficiently indicates at the beginning of the letter that the Saturday fast was celebrated in the Roman Church, when he suggests that what he says about ecclesiastical institutions and apostolic traditions applies to each section of the letter.

John Cassian, who stayed at Rome while Innocent was bishop and lived until the year 435, makes the same custom of the Roman Church known to us in *The Institutes of the Coenobia*, book III, chapter 10; we shall quote his words shortly.

Socrates, a contemporary of Innocent, who continued his history to the seventeenth consulship of Theodosius—that is, to the year 439—writes explicitly:

> At Rome they fast every Saturday.  
> —Book V, chapter 22

## IV

The following year, approximately twenty-four years after Innocent’s death, Leo was made pontiff. Since he was a man especially faithful to the custom of his predecessors, it cannot reasonably be believed that, during his pontificate, the Roman Church’s devotion to fasting on Saturday cooled.

Indeed, we have an explicit testimony to this observance in Leo, a testimony that I am surprised has been neglected by those who have treated this subject.

It occurs in his letter to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria (letter 11, elsewhere numbered 81), whom, at the beginning of his episcopate, he urges to conform the discipline and institutions of his Church to Roman customs. The first chapter reads as follows:

> What, then, we know to have been observed by our fathers with particular care, we wish you to preserve: priestly or levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but the beginning of the night following Saturday, which dawns on the first day of the week, should be chosen. On that night, those who are to be consecrated should be fasting, and the sacred blessing should be conferred by those who are fasting.  
>   
> The same observance will be maintained if the ceremony is celebrated early on the Lord’s Day itself, with the Saturday fast continued. The beginning of the preceding night does not cease to belong to that day, which, as is also made clear at the Lord’s Pascha, undoubtedly pertains to the day of Resurrection.

You see that it was customary among the Romans to fast on Saturday, since Leo wished the Saturday fast to be continued by those who either ordained or were ordained on Sunday morning. For who would say that something which had not been observed could be continued?

I know what may be objected: that Leo is not speaking here of every Saturday, but of Holy Saturday, which everyone was accustomed and bound by religious practice to spend fasting.

This is inferred both from the mention of Pascha introduced here and from the fact that the Sunday is called the day of Resurrection. Those who in earlier editions either supplied or approved the following title by preserving it were persuaded of this:

> On the ordination of a priest or deacon, so that it may be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, on Sunday.

But it is obvious how ignorant the hand was that composed such a title, since there are almost as many serious errors as words. It supposed that by “priests” only presbyters were meant, and that “priestly ordination” meant the ordination of presbyters, whereas these expressions signify bishops and the ordination of bishops.

Furthermore, it confuses Sunday with Saturday. Finally, it restricts what is said generally about Saturday to Holy Saturday. It is enough merely to point out the first two errors; I do not know whether anyone would wish to defend the third.

## V

Certainly, it is easy to prove that Leo is speaking here of every Saturday and every Sunday.

1. The consecration of bishops was never attached either to Easter Day itself or to the fixed Sundays of the Ember seasons. It had to be celebrated either on any Sunday, as in ancient times, or also on the feasts of the apostles, as today.

2. All the considerations weighed by Leo apply as much to all other Sundays as to Easter Sunday: the beginning of the world, the sending of the apostles with the power to baptize, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and so forth. These things were not fulfilled on Easter Day but on Sunday as such.

3. The authority of Scripture and the example of the apostles, which are drawn from the Book of Acts, do not apply only to Easter Sunday but to Sundays generally. The apostles did not lay hands on Paul and Barnabas and send them to preach to the Gentiles on the solemnity of Easter.

4. Leo speaks generally of Saturday:

> After the day of Saturday, the beginning of that night which dawns on the first day of the week should be chosen.

The fact that he calls the immediately following Sunday the day of Resurrection should not trouble anyone. It was very familiar among ancient writers to call any Sunday the day of Resurrection, while they called Easter Day itself Holy Pascha or the paschal feast.

Leo himself, in his letter to Turibius, chapter 4, says that the Priscillianists fasted on Sunday, “which is the day of Christ’s Resurrection.”

5. So far from the mention of Pascha persuading us that Easter Sunday is meant, it rather demonstrates the contrary. To show that the night immediately following Saturday belongs to Sunday, Leo gives Easter itself as an example:

> As is also made clear at the Lord’s Pascha.

On that occasion, the night following Holy Saturday was assigned, in the Church’s practice, to the paschal feast. In our time the celebration is held very early on Saturday morning; in those days it was held only after the beginning of the following night. In that celebration the words are frequently repeated:

> This is the night in which, after the bonds of death had been destroyed, Christ rose victorious from the underworld. O truly blessed night, which alone deserved to know the time and hour when Christ rose from the dead! . . . . . For these are the paschal feasts, and so forth.

6. Even if the records of ecclesiastical history did not show that very many bishops and presbyters were consecrated outside Easter Day itself, reason alone would suggest this. Who could persuade himself that Churches were left for many months at a time without pastors—something the sacred canons forbid with grave threats—although this must often have happened if ordinations were confined to Easter?

Indeed, ordination blessings were never celebrated at Easter, because the entire solemnity was devoted to the regeneration of catechumens. Rather, the month of December was assigned to the ordination of priests. Hence, at the end of the histories of the pontiffs, this clause is so often added:

> He held ordinations in the month of December, and so forth.

It is therefore certain that when our Leo writes:

> So that blessing may never be given to those who are to be consecrated except on the Lord’s day of Resurrection, and so forth,

this must be understood not of Easter Day but of any Sunday, which is sacred to the Resurrection. Consequently, the Saturday preceding it, whose fast is commanded to be continued, is not Holy Saturday but any Saturday occurring during the year.

## VI

There is no agreement among all authorities concerning the occasion and reason for which this custom of the Saturday fast was introduced into the Roman Church.

Saint Augustine writes in letter 86:

> There is indeed another opinion held by many, although most Romans declare it false: that the Apostle Peter, about to contend with Simon Magus on Sunday, fasted on the preceding day with the Church of that city because of the great danger of temptation involved; and that, after achieving so successful and glorious a victory, he maintained the same custom, which some Churches of the West imitated.

Cassian likewise reports that, in his time, this reason was advanced not only by the Romans but also by certain other Churches in the western regions. In book III of *The Institutes of the Coenobia*, chapter 10, he writes:

> Some people in certain western cities, ignorant of the reason for this discipline, and especially at Rome, think that the relaxation of the Saturday fast should on no account be presumed, because they assert that the Apostle Peter fasted on that same day before contending with Simon.

Since this reason was rejected by most Romans in Augustine’s time, was ridiculed by Cassian, and was not mentioned at all by Pope Innocent, who treated the matter expressly in his letter to Decentius, it plainly appears to be an invention.

Augustine therefore reports another reason:

> Others, like the Roman Church and certain Churches of the West, chose to fast because of the humiliation of the Lord’s death.

In the passage cited above, Innocent strongly presses this reason, holding that it is an equally religious practice to honor the memory of Christ’s death by the Saturday fast, to commemorate his Passion by the Friday fast, and to celebrate the joy of his Resurrection through the gladness of Sunday.

> If they think, he says, that one must fast only once, on one Saturday, then Sunday and Friday must likewise be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the representation of Sunday and Friday is to be renewed every week, it is foolish to observe the custom of two days while omitting Saturday, since it has the same reason as Friday, on which the Lord suffered and went to the underworld, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two days of sorrow.

Both authors suggest a third reason, although it easily reduces to the preceding one. They derive it from the example of the apostles.

Augustine writes in letter 86:

> Because the disciples mourned the Lord’s death as human beings would . . .

Innocent adds, in his letter to Decentius of Gubbio:

> For it is certainly established that during those two days the apostles were both in sorrow and concealed themselves because of fear of the Jews.

It is beyond doubt that they fasted during those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments were not celebrated at all during that period.

[Col. 0631B] Some add a fourth reason, namely, that they might withdraw farther from Jewish customs. For those perfidious people not only do not fast on the Sabbath, but rather feast luxuriously and sumptuously, and treat it as a festive day with solemn observance. Cassianus hints at this reason in the passage cited above, when, defending the Eastern custom against its opposite and answering, as it were, a Roman objection, he writes:

> This suspension of the fast is not to be regarded as participation in a Jewish festival, especially by those who are shown to be alien from every Jewish superstition; rather, it pertains to the refreshment of the weary body, as we have said. For when it fasts continually for five days throughout all the weeks of the year, unless it is restored by at least two intervening days, it easily becomes slack and fails.

From that same hatred of superstitions arose the fact that the Church especially abhorred fasting on those days which she observed the Manichaeans consecrating by their fasts. “To fast on the Lord’s Day,” says Augustine (Epistle 86), “is a great scandal, especially after the detestable heresy of the Manichaeans had become known—a heresy very much opposed to the Catholic faith and to the divine Scriptures—which established this day for its hearers as though it were a legitimate day for fasting. As a result, fasting on the Lord’s Day came to be regarded as more horrible.”

## VII

Having explained these matters concerning the first class of Sabbaths, we proceed to the second, namely, those Sabbaths which follow the Wednesday and Friday of the Four Seasons. That familiar clause of Leo’s gave occasion for doubt, which he is accustomed to append at the end of all his sermons on this fast:

> Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us hold vigils at Saint Peter’s.

For by these words he seems to indicate that there was one observance for those weekdays and another for the Sabbath, assigning only vigils to the latter while imposing the obligation of fasting upon the former. But this is not Leo’s intention. Rather, he means that vigils were to be added to the fast on Saturday. For just as it was necessary for the fast of the other days to be announced to the Christian people, so it would have been entirely superfluous to mention the Saturday fast, since the Romans were already bound to that fast by a particular law and custom.

Moreover, to whom could it have occurred that the Romans observed the Saturday fast with such religious devotion throughout the remaining weeks of the year that they considered themselves bound to it by apostolic tradition, by the example of the apostles, and by the necessity of commemorating the mysteries—and that Innocentius would call it madness to observe a two-day custom while omitting Saturday—yet that at this time, and during those very weeks consecrated by the more solemn fast of the Four Seasons according to apostolic institution, they omitted Saturday, as though the law of custom from which they had adopted the Saturday fast were then less binding?

“But,” you will say, “the vigils immediately following Saturday prevented this. The faithful, exhausted by the fast of that same day, would not have been equal to bearing the vigils. Cassianus says that this was the reason why Saturday was free from fasting among the Easterners.”

> From apostolic times, he says (*On the Institutes of the Coenobites*, book III, chapter 10), the solemnity of vigils assigned to this night, which precedes the light of Saturday, has likewise been observed throughout the whole East down to the present day. Therefore, it is not without reason presumed that the cessation of the fast after the labor of the vigil was established by those same apostolic men throughout all the Churches of the East.

This is entirely correct as far as the Easterners are concerned. But what has it to do with the Western Churches? Among them, those that observed the Saturday fast plainly paid no attention whatever to the fatigue caused by the vigils; the same Cassianus bears witness to this in the same passage:

> Some, ignorant of the reason for this moderation in certain Western cities, and especially in the City, therefore think that the cessation of the Saturday fast should by no means be presumed.

### 3

From the decree of Leo concerning the ordination of priests, which we reported above, it is clear that an ordination could fall on any Sunday, including a Sunday of the Four Seasons; and for its celebration it was necessary that the Saturday fast should continue. Since Leo makes no exception, it must be understood that those Sabbaths were no more exempt from the law of fasting than the others.

### 4

Augustine writes in Epistle 86 as follows, and his words seem relevant to our subject:

> Not only the Pharisee, who fasted twice on the Sabbath, but also the Christian who is accustomed to fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday itself—which the Roman populace frequently does—will be surpassed in the labor of fasting.

After many remarks in which he attacks that Urbicus, or Roman, who had boastfully extolled the Saturday fast as familiar to the Romans, to the insult of the other Churches, he writes again:

> Let him therefore see how great an insult he inflicts upon the Roman Church itself, where even during those weeks in which fasting is observed on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, people nevertheless eat for three successive days—namely, on Sunday and then on Monday and Tuesday.

Who, on reading these words, does not recognize that Augustine is designating the fasts of the Four Seasons? For what other weeks are there in which fasting is observed on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday except those weeks customarily celebrated by fasting during the four seasons of the year? This was not done according to anyone’s individual vow or devotion, but by custom; not by a few people, but by the whole Roman Church—“the Roman populace”; not once or twice, but frequently, that is, four times a year, or at least three times if Lent is set aside.

Certainly, if any other fixed fasts had been regularly observed in Rome throughout the year by ecclesiastical custom, some evidence of them would appear in the writings of the ancients, especially in those of our Leo, who so carefully recorded all such customs of his Church, so zealously practiced them, and so religiously ensured their observance by his exhortations to the people.

One of Calvin’s followers dreamed that these words of Augustine were to be understood not of the fast of the Four Seasons but of Lent, so that he would not be forced to acknowledge that the observance of the Four Seasons had already been religiously maintained among the Romans from the fourth century of the Church. Dallaeus was ashamed of his colleague’s such abject ignorance in interpreting Augustine’s statement as referring to Lent. Yet Dallaeus was unwilling to refer it to the fasts of the Four Seasons, since he writes that these were not yet in use when Augustine wrote his epistle to Casulanus, although he is immediately compelled to admit that, perhaps while Augustine himself was still alive, these fasts of the Four Seasons—at least in the form in which Leo describes them—were adopted.

Indeed, on page 754 he admits that in Leo’s time Rome fasted four times a year, once in each season, whether Leo himself or others had instituted the practice—which seems more likely—already before him. How much better and more effectively Dallaeus would have argued if, from the fact that in Leo’s time, indeed even before him and perhaps while Augustine himself was alive, this custom of fasting during the four seasons had been received in the Roman Church, he had concluded that it had likewise already been established and received when Augustine wrote to Casulanus! For between Augustine’s lifetime and Augustine’s writing, unless I am mistaken, there are not long intervals of time.

[Col. 0633A] ## VIII

We must now discuss the Lenten Sabbaths. On this point, however, I understand that scarcely anyone raises an objection against us. For Joannes Dallaeus, who, as a writer of greater reputation among the Calvinists, seems to have received from his associates the task of attacking ecclesiastical fasting, freely admits that among the Romans the Sabbath of every week, including during Lent, was consecrated to fasting:

> This is so clear from a single epistle of Augustine to Casulanus that it cannot be denied except with the greatest shamelessness.

And certainly anyone who considers the zeal with which Saint Innocentius defends the Saturday fast, and how religiously he regards its observance, will not easily be persuaded that among those for whom it was a sacrilege to omit it on any Saturday, it was relaxed during Lent.

The accusation directed against the Roman Church in canon 55 of the Council in Trullo will be equivalent to all proofs. “Since we have learned,” say the Greeks, “that in the cities of the Romans, during the holy Lenten fasts, people fast on its Saturdays, contrary to the ecclesiastical tradition, the holy synod has deemed it necessary that in the Roman Church also the canon which says, ‘If any cleric is found fasting on the holy Lord’s Day or on Saturday, except on one Sabbath alone, let him be deposed; but if he is a layman, let him be excluded,’ should be firmly enforced.”

In commenting on this Trullan canon, Balsamon and Zonaras make the Romans’ persistence—or, as they call it, obstinacy—in this Lenten Saturday fast a matter of record. “The synod,” says Zonaras, “tried to correct this sin of the Latins; but in their arrogance they have remained in their obstinacy down to the present, and they remain so today.”

## IX

There are nevertheless some whom the authority of Socrates the Historian, of our Leo, of Cassiodorus, and of the venerable Bede moves. Among them, Henricus Valesius, a man of singular learning, persuaded himself in his notes on book V, chapter 22 of Socrates, that in the time of Socrates and Leo the Romans did not fast on the Sabbath during Lent, but that Leo designated only three days in each week for fasting, while Socrates designated five.

As for Bede, whose little book *On Offices* Valesius praises, those *Collectanea* of Bede that were given the title *On Offices* scarcely deserve the name. Nor, I think, is the constitution of Telesphorus reported in that book of more certain authority in Valesius’s eyes. Be that as it may, it nowhere appears there that during Lent most people did not fast on Thursday and Saturday, at least among the Romans.

For Bede relates that, according to the constitution of Telesphorus, the Lenten fast began fifty days before Easter. Of those fifty days, counted from Quinquagesima to the holy Resurrection:

> If you subtract the eight Sundays on which fasting may not be observed, forty-two days remain. These two additional days, Thursday and Saturday, which exceed the number forty, are counted by some as fasting days, while by others they are regarded as days of refreshment on account of the Lord’s Supper and the holy Sabbath.

Anyone can see that this is not said of every Thursday or of every Sabbath of Lent, but only of those two days that belong to Holy Week.

A little later he adds these other words:

> Quinquagesima is therefore said to be celebrated by the faithful so that they may both render the tenth part of the days to God and nevertheless be able to relax from fasting on Thursday and Saturday.

But Bede says this without a witness from the earlier age, and with considerable hesitation—*it is said*—and he seems to have paid attention to some custom of his own time and region rather than either to the rite of the Roman Church or to the period of which we are now speaking.

Let us therefore proceed to the other authors, who are far more weighty on this subject and who also present a greater difficulty.

## X

The passage of Socrates reads as follows:

> Those who are in Rome fast for three continuous weeks before Easter, EXCEPTING SATURDAY AND THE LORD’S DAY.

Various writers go to extraordinary lengths to untie the double knot found in these words: one concerning the number of weeks in the Lenten fast, the other concerning the exception of Saturday in the Roman Church.

I do not now have time to investigate the first matter more carefully. I say only this: the authority of Joannes Cassianus is greater than that of Socrates. Cassianus lived at nearly the same time, spent some time in Rome, was familiar with our Leo, and finally lived for a long time near Massilia, which belonged to the Roman province of Gaul and maintained frequent intercourse with the Romans.

In *Conference* 21, chapters 24 and following, he bears witness that in the Roman Church people fasted for six full weeks, excepting Sundays. “What is the reason,” asks Germanus (*Conference* 21, chapter 24), “that Lent is celebrated for six weeks, although in certain provinces a more zealous concern for religion seems perhaps to have added a seventh week, when neither number reaches the total of forty days once Sunday and Saturday are subtracted? For only thirty-six days are contained in those weeks themselves.”

Just as there can scarcely be any doubt that Abbot Germanus—later a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople—is speaking of the custom of that Church when he mentions the observance of seven weeks, so it is certain that what he says about six weeks must be understood of the Roman rite, as is made clear by these words in chapter 27:

> These people have prescribed for themselves the observance of six weeks, because they think that one must fast on Saturday also. Thus they complete six fasts in each week, and by going through six weeks they complete those same thirty-six days.

Anyone who remembers that Cassianus wrote in book III, chapter 10 of *On the Institutes of the Coenobites* that the Saturday fast was observed especially in the City will not deny that the Romans are being designated here by the same author. Thus Dallaeus unjustly attacks Bellarmine for saying that Cassianus was speaking of the Latins.

## XI

To examine the other part of the Socratic text, which concerns the fasting of the Lenten Sabbaths, nearly everyone agrees that the passage is corrupt; but they do not agree on how it can or should be corrected.

Dionysius Petavius, in his notes on Saint Epiphanius, page 360, and Hugo Maenardus, in his notes on the Gregorian Sacramentary, page 53, believe that Socrates was speaking not of old Rome but of the new Rome—that is, Constantinople—and that the word *νέᾳ* (“new”) was omitted through the carelessness of scribes. They therefore think that the text should be restored so that, instead of *ἐν Ῥώμῃ* (“in Rome”), one reads *ἐν νέᾳ Ῥώμῃ* (“in New Rome”).

They support their conjecture from Socrates himself, who shortly afterward asserts that the Romans fasted every Saturday:

> Ἐν Ῥώμῃ πᾶν σάββατον νηστένουσιν  
> In Rome they fast every Saturday.

They cannot persuade themselves that a sensible man would have written statements so contradictory.

The conjecture is ingenious, but for several reasons it cannot be accepted.

1. All those who have hitherto devoted themselves to editing Socrates—Musculus, Grynaeus, Christophorsonus, Suffridus Petrus, Robertus Stephanus, Joannes Curterius, and H. Valesius—found nothing of the sort in the oldest manuscript codices they used, which they obtained from the library of the Most Christian King, from the Vatican, Florentine, Allatian, and other collections.

2. Who could easily believe that the books of Socrates were already corrupt when Cassiodorus was composing his *Tripartite History*, indeed when before him Epiphanius Scholasticus was translating Socrates into Latin, a translation used by Cassiodorus? Both authors reproduce the same reading that we now have in Socrates.

I say nothing of Nicephorus, who transcribed the same material from Socrates (*Book XII*, chapter 34). Nor is it reasonable to believe either that no corrected copy of Socrates then survived or that Nicephorus did not possess one, since he relies upon Socrates to a very large extent.

3. What Socrates writes cannot be referred to the custom of the Church of Constantinople, namely, that only three continuous weeks before Easter were spent fasting. For Theophanes and others after him testify that in the time of the emperor Justinian the Lenten fast among the people of Constantinople consisted of eight weeks. Indeed, Sozomenus, who lived at the same time as Socrates, expressly states that when he was writing it was already customary at Constantinople to fast for seven weeks during Lent.

> Others count seven weeks, as at Constantinople and throughout all the surrounding provinces as far as Phoenicia.

By these words he explains what Socrates himself had expressed more obscurely:

> But those who live in Illyricum and throughout Greece, and those who dwell in Alexandria, fast for six weeks before Easter, and so forth.

## XII

Some therefore take another route. Jacobus Capellus believed that the parenthetical phrase *πλὴν σαββάτου καὶ Κυριακῆς*—“excepting Saturday and Sunday”—had been moved from its proper place and should be transferred approximately two lines later. He thus understands it not of the Romans but of certain other Churches of the Eastern regions, which are known to have kept Saturday free from every fast throughout the year, except Holy Saturday.

He thinks the passage should be read in this manner:

> For those who are in Rome fast for three successive weeks before Easter; but those who live in Illyricum and throughout Greece, and those who dwell in Alexandria, fast for six weeks before Easter, EXCEPTING SATURDAY AND SUNDAY.

This conjecture would not lack probability if it were supported by the authority of some manuscript and if the first two arguments—which overturn the suspicion of Petavius and Maenardus—did not also oppose it.

Christianus Lupus likewise contributed his own proposal in the scholia on canon 55 of the Council in Trullo. “Socrates,” he says, “is inconsistent with himself when he says in the same chapter of the same book: ‘IN ROME THEY FAST EVERY SATURDAY.’ Perhaps he means that Rome, which in his own time was fasting in this way, formerly did not fast on Saturday. This would be entirely consistent both with the truth and with his purpose there.”

In my judgment, this is an unsuccessful conjecture. First, it is not at all evident that it is consistent with the truth that the early faithful of the Roman Church formerly abstained from fasting on Saturday. For Jerome indicates that this custom was introduced into the Roman Church by the command of the ancestors, a command that must be regarded as descending from apostolic law:

> Let each province abound in its own judgment and regard the precepts of its ancestors as apostolic laws.  
> (*Epistle 28, to Lucinius Baeticus*)

In Augustine’s time also it was the opinion of many that the Romans had adopted the Saturday fast in imitation of the apostle Peter and from his time onward. Augustine himself says that the apostolic tradition of the Romans could be opposed by an equally apostolic tradition among the Easterners. Cassianus bears the same testimony. Innocentius I also sufficiently indicates that this custom of his Church was then regarded among his people as having been received from the apostles.

It is therefore highly uncertain when Lupus writes that Rome formerly did not fast on Saturday. The only passage that seems to favor him is this statement of Tertullian in *On Fasting*, chapter 14:

> Although you also sometimes prolong the Sabbath, you never fast except at Easter, according to the explanation given elsewhere.

Yet Tertullian has nothing whatever to do with Roman custom. He is writing not against the Romans but against all Catholics, and, in order to argue from their practice, he considers rather what was customary among the African, Eastern, and most Western Churches—such as the remission of the Saturday fast—than what the few Western Churches, together with Rome, were accustomed to do.

What Lupus adds, namely, that his conjecture is consistent with Socrates’ purpose, is entirely removed from the truth of the matter. Socrates’ purpose was to set forth the various rites of various Churches, which in the period when he was writing were practiced both in the East and in the West. His manner of expression also indicates this: he always uses present-tense forms, as though discussing a matter presently existing.

“First,” he says, “you will find that the fasts observed before Easter are practiced differently by different peoples. Those who are in Rome fast …,” and so forth.

This is no different from the words read in the same chapter:

> Those who are in Rome fast every Saturday.
