By contrast, when he narrates customs or controversies belonging to an earlier age, he ordinarily casts his speech in past-tense forms.

## XIII

What, then, shall we say about Socrates? I will say this plainly:

1. Socrates is here speaking of old Rome, not of any period other than his own; he wrote no differently from the text as we now read it; and his words should not be thrown down from their place into the sentence below.

2. Socrates was egregiously mistaken. He was a Greek living nearly six hundred leagues from the city of Rome, ignorant of Roman discipline and deceived by uncertain rumors, and he gave others occasion to err.

Who does not know how frequently and easily those who undertake to narrate events separated from them by vast distances of place or intervals of time fall into error? The possibility of error is even greater when the material to be narrated is drawn solely from rumor—as Socrates himself admits happened to him at the beginning of book II—than when it is taken from the histories of ancient writers.

Certainly not even Valesius himself can deny this concerning his Socrates, whom he repeatedly accuses of error in his notes. There is scarcely a page in them on which he does not affix a black theta to their author.

Sozomenus seems to have corrected Socrates’ error when he omitted the statement. For if, as Valesius considers probable, Sozomenus was younger than Socrates, although living at the same time; if he wrote later and had Socrates’ history before his eyes; and if he added certain things and corrected others, then we must plainly conclude that he detected Socrates in error. For in book VIII, chapter 19, while explaining the same variety of Lenten fasting, he thought it necessary to say nothing at all about the fasting of the Roman Church for those three weeks or about the relaxation of the fast there on Saturday.

3. It is exceedingly probable that Socrates, if he was not infected with the Novatian stain, was at least attached to the Novatians—as H. Valesius freely admits—whether because he was connected with them by association and familiarity, or because he approved their discipline and abstinence.

Among other things, the Novatians professed that whatever the Church had decreed in synods concerning observance during the Paschal festival ought neither to be undertaken nor imposed under compulsion; each Church was free to follow its own custom, and the whole matter was indifferent. For this reason they liked to be called *ἀδιάφοροι*, “the indifferent ones.”

From this arose Socrates’ purpose of ranging through the various rites of the Churches and describing their diversity more carefully, especially the fast that precedes Easter. Hence also he willingly represented the Roman Church as differing most sharply from the others, restricting the Lent of that Church to only three weeks and making Saturday, no less than Sunday, exempt from fasting. He did this partly to make the Novatian indifference appear approved by the example of the Catholics, especially the Romans, and partly also, by displaying the more lenient discipline of that Church, to commend the stricter practices of those whom he was striving to favor.

## XIV

To some, what we have said—that Socrates may have imposed something upon the Roman Church either through carelessness or from a desire to favor the Novatians—seems beyond belief.

“Certainly,” says Dallaeus, speaking of the first part of the Socratic text, “the matter concerns not some hidden article of faith but a fact, as they say, obvious to anyone and exposed to everyone’s senses. Is it likely that Socrates wanted to lie about such a matter? Its prompt and straightforward proof was daily before the eyes of all. Surely he must have been not a heretic but a madman, a man out of his mind, if he knowingly and deliberately slandered the Church on this subject.”

It is indeed difficult to persuade anyone that such an insane and reckless plan could have entered the mind of a man of good character. Yet examples of this kind are not so rare that one does not immediately think of them.

Who, for example, after a thousand years, when reading Dallaeus’ book *On Fasting and Lent*, will dare to question what he wrote and published before everyone’s eyes about the Catholic, and especially Gallican, discipline of fasting in his own age? Who will not accept as true what he asserts in book I, chapter 11: that in the year of the Lord 1654, when he was writing, the public laws of the Catholics required nothing else of the faithful than abstinence from meat at appointed and fixed times; that they freely allowed them to eat lunch and dinner luxuriously and sumptuously, provided that they did so without meat; and that they maintained that such people could not be reproved?

Who will not believe that we regarded bare and simple abstinence from meat as true fasting, in what he calls an outrageous and utterly childish error? Who will not suppose it sacrilegious to disbelieve what he says about the discipline of the Catholic Church in his day—namely, that it commanded fasting on Friday and Saturday every week throughout the year?

For Dallaeus asserts this without hesitation in chapter 14 of the same book. Again, in book IV, chapter 5, he says that among his opponents—that is, the Catholics—the fast of Friday is not voluntary but obligatory, and that it is known to be observed by all and by individuals alike, not according to each person’s choice and spontaneous devotion, but by a public and necessary law, so that if anyone does not fast on that day—as they themselves put it—those people judge him guilty of a very grave crime and indeed worthy of eternal death.

After many years have passed, I say, many may perhaps hesitate to reject Dallaeus’ testimony: a Frenchman writing seriously about the customs of his own time in Gaul, and asserting that in his age the fast of Advent was strictly observed throughout Gaul.

“Nor,” he says, “is the adversary”—Bellarminus—“more troublesome to us concerning the fast of Advent, since he likewise maintains that it is observed by many not so much by precept as by counsel or vow. Yet among us—that is, in Gaul—I see this fast both ENJOINED AND OBSERVED by our opponents no less carefully or religiously than any other.”

How plainly false, how slanderously invented, and how shamelessly written these and many other statements of Dallaeus are, no Frenchman can fail to understand unless he is insane or out of his mind. Yet after several centuries, who will not at some point make the same argument on Dallaeus’ behalf that Dallaeus now makes on behalf of Socrates?

“Is it likely,” someone will say, “that Dallaeus wanted to lie about such a matter, whose prompt and straightforward proof was daily before everyone’s eyes? Surely he must have been not a heretic but a madman, a man out of his mind, if he knowingly and deliberately slandered the Church on this subject.”

I have pursued this point at somewhat greater length so that the example of our own age might make clear how deservedly suspect the testimony of writers may be when they are presumed to be inclined toward heretics. One should no more assent to the Greek Socrates writing about the fasting of the Romans at Constantinople than to the Frenchman Joannes Dallaeus, living and writing in the metropolis of Gaul, when he tells such ridiculous tales and slanders the fasting of the Gauls with such brazen effrontery.

## XV

Finally, Socrates presumed to judge the entire discipline of the Roman Church from the relaxation practiced in certain Churches near Rome, or even from the practice of some Romans who departed from the common law—whether they were Manichaeans who long concealed themselves in Rome under the Catholic name; Jews who observed the Sabbath as a feast day; or Catholics who trampled upon the laws of the Church, as many do today.

For Petrus Chrysologus, a contemporary of Leo and Socrates, laments that considerable diversity had been introduced into the Lenten fast at the neighboring Church of Ravenna through the intemperance of many people:

> If, therefore, the simple, pure, uniform fast of forty days, handed down to us by the Lord through so many witnesses, under the mystery of so great a number, is fully taught, whence this diversity? Whence this novelty? Whence these weeks, now relaxed, now strict; now excessively indulgent, now severe? Whence this practice of intemperate fasting, which either afflicts without pardon or relaxes into gluttony? … Let the fast be uniform, and let it be observed as it was handed down to us, for the discipline of body and soul. Certainly, whoever cannot fast should not presume to introduce novelty; rather, let him acknowledge that what he relaxes proceeds from his own weakness, and let him redeem by almsgiving what he cannot make up by fasting.

Much light shines upon our subject from this excellent testimony of Chrysologus.

1. It appears that at that time many people had begun to introduce diversity into the Church of Ravenna—and why not into other Churches as well?

2. The bishop condemns this diversity as a novelty.

3. The principal feature of this diversity and novelty was that people did not fast for forty days, and thus violated the fast handed down by the Lord under so great a number of mysteries.

4. Their forty-day fast was not uniform, but sometimes strict and sometimes more lenient.

5. Some of their Lenten weeks were relaxed and others strict. The relaxed weeks seem to have been those in which certain days were released from fasting; as a result, the mystery of the sacred number forty was broken, as he had previously noted.

There can scarcely be any doubt that Saturday was among those relaxed days, since examples from so many neighboring regions also favored such a relaxation, as did the symbolism of representing either the Lord’s Day or heavenly rest. 

6. It can be inferred that those who could not fast were not content merely to relax the fast on account of their weakness. They wanted to introduce some novelty into the observance of Lent, so that, with everyone conspiring in the same practice, they themselves would neither complete the forty-day fast nor be marked with the stigma of singularity by differing from others.

This is why he says:

> Whoever cannot fast should not presume to introduce novelty; rather, let him acknowledge that what he relaxes proceeds from his own weakness.

From innovations of this kind, therefore, there could have arisen the false opinion that Socrates formed concerning Roman Lent. For since the Easterners were somewhat too hostile toward the Romans, they readily lent their ears to slanderers and claimed as the custom of all Romans what was actually either the indulgence of a few or the departure of neighboring peoples from the common law.

## XVI

After examining the text of Socrates, we come to the authority of Cassiodorus. It seems more weighty and stronger because Cassiodorus himself, having been senator, consul, and praetorian prefect in the city of Rome, could not have been ignorant of the custom of the Roman Church in observing the Lenten fast.

In the *Tripartite History* he inserted the passage of Socrates that we have just examined, in these words:

> For the Romans fast continuously for three weeks before Easter, excepting Saturday and Sunday.

“Who, then, could believe,” they ask, “that he would have placed these words of Socrates in his History if he knew that the matter had been otherwise? Certainly, if Cassiodorus had known this to be false, he would deliberately have omitted Socrates’ words, so as not to lead his reader into error. Since he did not do so, it is evident that what Socrates said about the fasting of the Romans is true.”

So says a most learned man.

Yet this does not persuade me. For who does not know that those who devote themselves to writing abridgments or stitching together centos from the labors of several authors commonly copy errors no less carefully than statements consistent with the truth? They are concerned to represent not their own judgment but that of others; they do not undertake to correct what they find, but merely to report it.

Let the passage of Sozomenus serve as an example. Cassiodorus likewise transferred it into his own *Tripartite History*. Sozomenus writes in book VII, chapter 19:

> In the city of Rome neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches the people in the Church.

It is probable that this was false, as we assert elsewhere (see *Dissertation 1 on the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo*, for the year A.D. 440, no. 8 and following), or at least false for the period to which the end of Sozomenus’ History belongs. But if he composed it during Leo’s pontificate, as is exceedingly likely, there can be no doubt about its falsity.

Now I argue as follows: Cassiodorus either knew this or did not know it. If he did not know it, he is an unsuitable witness concerning Roman discipline, and he should no more be listened to when he speaks of fasting than when he speaks of the silence of the Roman pontiffs. He would therefore be wholly incompetent to correct either Socrates or Sozomenus.

But if he did know that the contrary custom prevailed at Rome both in Sozomenus’ time and in his own, and yet neither corrected Sozomenus nor even warned his reader of the contrary custom introduced by Pope Leo, then we have certain proof that Cassiodorus’ intention was to leave untouched what he read in Sozomenus or Socrates, and to perform only the office of an excerptor, not of a corrector.

Another example is readily available from Sozomenus. In chapter 16 of book VII, while discussing the presbyter appointed over penitents, who secretly heard the confessions of those confessing in the place of the bishop, and who was eventually removed from this office in the Church of Constantinople, that author adds:

> Among the other sects, however, this custom still continues. And in the Western Churches, especially in the Roman Church, it is carefully observed.

H. Valesius consistently asserts in his notes, and proves at length, that Sozomenus is mistaken both when he speaks of all the Western Churches and especially when he speaks of the Roman Church; he attempts to demonstrate this from Sozomenus himself.

Cassiodorus nevertheless neither omitted nor corrected the statement. What he found narrated by his author he faithfully transcribed into his own cento in book IX, chapter 35. Thus it is clear and certain that he had no other intention than to gather, as he himself says in the Preface, extracts from the individual historians and arrange them in sequence under the name of their author.

### XVII

At last we come to Leo, chiefly on whose account the thought arose of discussing fasting. Here, they say, in Sermon 4 on Lent, he appends the following clause, familiar to him in proclaiming fasts:

> “Let us therefore fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter, who, never ceasing to care for the flock entrusted to him, will obtain protection for us through his prayers.”

This passage has greatly perplexed all who have hitherto dealt with the subject of the Lenten fast; and how unsuccessfully they have labored to elucidate it, anyone will easily understand from what follows.

Cardinal Bellarmine thought that Leo was speaking of the four days added before the first Sunday of Lent, so that the number forty might be completed (*Tom.* III, *Controv.* 3, book II, chapter 15), although they were not the same days as in former times. Hugo Menard, commenting on the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*, rightly rejects Bellarmine’s explanation and shows that those four days were not in use even in Gregory’s own time, much less in Leo’s. He himself adopts the view that, in reality, no more days were then devoted to fasting at Rome than those designated by Saint Leo in that sermon.

Dallaeus agrees with Menard and attacks the most learned Bellarmine in more insolent language; nevertheless, he thinks that Saturday must be added to those three days according to the customary Roman practice throughout the year. Henry Valesius does not even think that Saturday fasting was then observed at Rome during Lent, and adduces no proof beyond this passage of Leo. Thus, between orthodox and heterodox writers, each draws our Leo this way and that into his own opinion, yet no one understands or explains the passage. The true solution of this knot is this: the words objected to are not Leo’s, but were added to his sermon—not with fraudulent intent, but for a certain occasion and purpose, which we shall disclose, if we first establish beyond doubt that what we have mentioned is an interpolation.

### XVIII

Nor is that the only material to be removed from Leo. There is also an entire, fairly lengthy piece attached to it in the following manner. After these genuine words of the pontiff, placed at the end of the sermon—

> “Only then do we offer to God the sacrifice of true abstinence and true devotion, when we restrain ourselves from every form of wickedness”—

the manuscripts hitherto published add the following:

> “But let us not be joined by any agreement with the enemies of the cross of Christ, lest the holiness of the faithful be polluted by association with the impious. Let light be separated from darkness, and let the sons of truth flee the sons of the devil. For nothing contaminated ought to be brought into the temple of the Lord, which is the Church of Christ, and nothing profane ought to be admitted, so that, with every impurity excluded from the inner chambers of the heart, our fast may be sanctified, and we may become the eternal dwelling of the Holy Spirit, who may always deign to cleanse us from the filth of sins, possess us, and rule us. Let us therefore fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter, who, never ceasing to care for the flock entrusted to him, will obtain protection for us through his prayers.”

First, the concluding words of this piece do not fit very well with the clause that follows, which genuinely belongs to Leo:

> “With almighty God assisting us in all things, etc.”

When Leo uses this clause, he inserts and joins it to the other words with remarkable skill. The interpolated passage, on the contrary, connects perfectly with what preceded it in this form:

> “When we restrain ourselves from every form of wickedness, with almighty God assisting us in all things, etc.”

2. What previously preceded this piece, but in our edition brings the sermon to a close, clearly constitutes the true ending of the sermon:

> “Only then do we offer [to God] the sacrifice, etc.”

If Leo had added anything else after these words, he would seem to have begun the completed sermon all over again.

3. The words—

> “But let us not be joined by any agreement with the enemies of the cross of Christ”

seem to refer more particularly to the Jews than to the Manichaeans, although Leo had undertaken in this sermon to attack the Manichaeans alone.

4. The sermon treats the two groups differently from the interpolated piece. In the sermon Leo discusses hidden heretics, or Manichaeans. He marks them out for the faithful by definite signs, commands that their error be avoided, and orders that, once recognized, they be exposed so that priestly authority might expel them from the fellowship of the saints. The interpolated piece, however, does not deal with people who were hidden—whether heretics or Jews—but with those who were openly known to everyone; and it does not advise exposing them, but avoiding them.

5. The style of our Leo seems to be absent from this addition. What, for example, is the character of the expression, “he will obtain protection for us through his prayers”? It is far removed from the brilliance of Leo’s diction.

6. Although we possess twelve sermons of Saint Leo on the observance of the Lenten fast, there is none—apart from this one—that has ever contained, or now contains, such a notice of the weekdays, whether Monday, Wednesday, and Friday or any others. Moreover, if either the weekdays named here, or certain other selected days, had been consecrated to fasting, who could believe that Leo would not have proclaimed them as often as he addressed a sermon to his people? He observed this practice so conscientiously when speaking of the fast of the Four Seasons. But if, in the other eleven sermons, he refrained from such a proclamation, we should not believe that he used it in the sermon under discussion. Rather, it must be removed from it as an interpolation foreign to his mind.

### XIX

7. If Pope Leo had assigned only three days to the Lenten fast, as this addition suggests, how unlike and contradictory to himself he would have been! For in his sermons he so often speaks of a forty-day fast.

* Sermon 3, chapter 2: “So that the Christian people might prepare for the paschal feast by FORTY DAYS OF SELF-DISCIPLINE.”
* Sermon 5, chapter 3: “Let us prepare ourselves most beneficially by a FORTY-DAY FAST.”
* Sermon 6, chapter 2: “Let the apostolic institution be fulfilled by FORTY DAYS OF FASTING.”
* Sermon 7, chapter 1: “THE FORTY-DAY FAST that precedes the paschal feast.”
* Sermon 8, chapter 4: “During these FORTY DAYS OF FASTING, etc.”
* Sermon 10, chapter 1: “It is fitting that we be prepared by a FORTY-DAY FAST, etc.”
* Sermon 12, chapter 1: “May the FORTY-DAY FAST exercise us, etc.”

But in this very Sermon 4, which we are examining, he speaks in chapter 1 as follows:

> “By the great saving power of the divine institution it has been provided that FORTY DAYS OF DISCIPLINE should heal us, IN WHICH the sins of other times might be redeemed by pious works, and PURE FASTS might be brought to maturity.”

He continues:

> “Therefore, dearly beloved, as we are about to enter upon the mystical days consecrated to the remedies of fasting, etc.”

Thus, in the Roman Church, forty days were counted from the beginning of Lent until Easter and were consecrated to fasting, except for Sundays. It would have been superfluous to mention the exception of Sundays, since it was known to everyone and was religiously observed by all throughout the Church. Leo himself had sufficiently declared this when he censured the impious custom of the Manichaeans, who polluted the Lord’s Day with their fasts. Since he did not except any other day, he did not exempt any other day from fasting.

Since, therefore, the clause has been weakened by so many arguments and contradicts the clearest testimonies of this pope, it ought rightly to be eliminated rather than Leo—whom Dallaeus depicts as especially devoted to clarity and, though not prolific, eloquent and prudent (*On Fasting and Lent*, pp. 535 and 546)—be judged to speak against himself.

8. But why do we delay? Let the opponents finally be confronted with the oldest and most trustworthy manuscripts, which possess the authority, right, and standard for deciding doubtful cases concerning the offspring or interpolations of ancient writers.

[Note: We have received the edition of the Sermons of Saint Leo published at Rome by Father Peter Thomas Cacciarius in the preceding year, 1753. In his note on Sermon 4 on Lent, p. 112, he attempts to vindicate, against Quesnell, the lines expunged from five Vatican manuscripts, numbers 541, 544, 545, 546, and 547. But all of these, which we likewise examined, are manuscripts of the three more recent collections—the third, fourth, and fifth. We have unquestionably considered the exemplars of the two older collections, the first and second, preferable to them, especially the two Lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter, which are Roman, and four others that we mentioned in note 36 on the same sermon, volume I, column 162 (*previous volume*, column 281, note a). Father Cacciarius himself saw another Lectionary in Vatican manuscript 1268, likewise lacking the lines in question. We explained at length in the preface prefixed to the Sermons how highly those Lectionaries—certainly Roman for the most part—should be valued in comparison with the collections, especially the later ones. The cited Father Cacciarius mentions Vatican Palatine manuscript 432, in which the expunged lines are present except for the final words, “Let us therefore fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, etc.,” which create the greatest difficulty in this piece. But this single German Lectionary should not be preferred to most of the others, which are more authoritative, nor to the Roman ones, which omit the entire piece.]

Five manuscripts, therefore, support us, all of them extremely old and highly trustworthy. The first is from the royal library of our Augustus, number 341. The second is from the library of the most illustrious Monsieur de Thou, number 46. The third, also belonging to de Thou, is number 108; it once belonged to Saint Peter of Fossatensis and was written in the year of our Lord 1057. The fourth comes from the Navarre College Library in Paris. The fifth, finally, was brought to Paris from the celebrated and ancient library of the monastery of Corbie; it is preserved in the famous abbey of Saint-Germain in Paris, and at the end is written:

> “In the year in which King Philip, son of King Louis, was anointed.”

In all these manuscripts the entire piece that we described above is absent. It must therefore rightly be judged an interpolation and removed from this sermon, as we have in fact removed it.

### XX

Since we promised to disclose on what occasion these words were inserted and adapted, it is worthwhile to investigate the matter.

Everyone knows that it was customary, among monks and among clerics devoted to reciting or singing the ecclesiastical office, to adapt and accommodate the homilies and sermons of the holy Fathers to their own uses according to the variety of the offices that occurred. They also frequently added to such sermons passages that either suited a particular solemnity or responded to the needs of the present time. Hundreds of examples could be brought forward if the matter required proof.

Something similar happened with this Sermon 4 on Lent. It was transferred from the Lenten fast to another fast that was observed in some places by clerics or monks. Then, so that, according to Leo’s custom and also the practice of the locality, a solemn proclamation could be made during the offices of the weekdays assigned to these fasts, a clause of the following kind was composed:

> “Let us therefore fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, etc.”

Those who first undertook to collect the sermons of Saint Leo into a single body and publish them copied it in good faith from the Lectionary books.

Anyone who recalls canon 9 of the First Council of Mâcon will readily admit that this is so. The Fathers of that council were assembled from nearly twelve provinces of Gaul in the year of our Lord 581, according to Jacques Sirmond, or rather in 583, as the most learned Charles Le Cointe more correctly judged in volume I of his *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, under that year. They express their ninth decree as follows:

> “From the weekday of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, let there be fasting on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and let the sacrifices be celebrated according to the Lenten order. On those days we decree by special determination that the canons are to be read, so that no one may claim to have sinned through ignorance.”

Who does not see that the words which have so long been vainly labored over in explanation were taken from this decree? Moreover, since bishops and many metropolitans were present from so many provinces, and it is probable that they carried this rite into their own provinces for observance by the clergy, this explains why many manuscripts have been found in which this sermon of Saint Leo is read with the clause added.

I believe that the Fathers of Mâcon borrowed this law of a three-day fast, extending from the feast of Saint Martin to the Nativity, from the Church of Tours. Gregory of Tours is witness to this in book X, chapter 31. He relates that the perpetual bishop of that city, who was Leo’s contemporary or near-contemporary, instituted three weekly fasts from the deposition of Saint Martin until the Nativity.

### XXI

A question remains concerning the rest of the words in this piece:

> “But let us not be joined by any agreement with the enemies of the cross of Christ, etc.”

For what reason were these words sewn onto it? Why should Leo’s sermon have grown by this addition? The reason need not be sought far away. Canons 13, 14, 15, and 16 of the same Council of Mâcon, which were enacted against the Jews, persuade us altogether that these words were appended against them.

Canon 15 says:

> “Let no Christian presume to participate in Jewish banquets. But if anyone—whether a cleric or a layman—should presume to do what it is sacrilegious to name, let him know that he must be restrained from the fellowship of all Christians, whoever has been polluted by their impieties.”

The reader may consult the other canons if he wishes.

The Jews were evidently numerous throughout the Gallic provinces at that time, so that the bishops of Gaul, frequently assembling in synod, repeatedly warned the Christian people to abstain from their contagion and fellowship. Their number also increased around the year 616, when Sisebut, king of the Spaniards, drove far from the Gothic territories all Jews who refused to profess the name of Christ; many of them, according to Ado of Vienne, withdrew into Gaul. Fredegarius relates that they were expelled from the kingdom under King Dagobert.

While the king labored to carry out this matter through his edicts, the bishops through their canons and exhortations, and the clerics and monks through more frequent fasts proclaimed at the bishops’ command, the rest of the faithful undoubtedly acted through their vows and prayers so that the sworn enemies of the cross of Christ might be removed from the fellowship of the faithful.

### XXII

Having explained these matters, I believe that no doubt remains concerning the passage of Leo. From this one passage alone it is clear how important it is, both for the honor of the holy Fathers and for ecclesiastical truth, that the monuments of ecclesiastical writers be accurately corrected from ancient manuscript codices.

Behold how many men have been exercised by a single corrupt passage, and how it has frustrated all their efforts! Writers, some Catholic and some heretical, brought forward everything that might occur to a sensible person’s mind if the interpolation of the passage went unnoticed. Yet neither group reached the mark; nevertheless, they should not for that reason be mocked.

Accordingly, when one of the heterodox, John Dallaeus, attacks the most learned Cardinal Bellarmine with such insolence and, as though exulting and triumphing, lashes him with insults and abuse, what else does he expose to everyone’s view than his own pitiable and ridiculous condition? He not only failed to solve this knot more successfully than the others, but also miserably abused the corrupt passage in defense of his desperate cause, plainly showing that he had sung his triumph before winning the victory. This is characteristic of heretics. For when passages of the holy Fathers have generally been corrupted—if they themselves have not corrupted them—they are accustomed to abuse them against Catholic doctrine. But when the truth at last shines forth, the Church draws those same passages into the defense of her doctrine.

Now that it is certain that among the Lenten sermons of Saint Leo there is none in which he prescribed particular days to be properly observed as fasts during each week of Lent, it follows that absolutely all the days of the Lenten weeks, except Sunday, were consecrated to fasting in the Roman Church. Otherwise our Leo—especially devoted to clarity and, though not prolific, eloquent and prudent—would not have omitted this point in the greatest and most sacred fast, when he observed it so carefully in many sermons on the fast of the Four Seasons. This is especially true since his frequent mention of a forty-day fast could at least have given the uneducated grounds for suspicion and doubt.

Certainly, if Saint Leo and his predecessors, who occupied the Roman see after the rise of the Manichaean heresy, had been free to select at will only certain days for completing the Lenten fast, they would never have selected Monday. They would thereby have seemed to descend to the detestable practice of those heretics, who consecrated Monday to the honor of the moon by fasting on it. Leo our own explains this at length in the same sermon. Since he had expressly commended fasting on this weekday to the Christian people, there would have been a danger that the less instructed might think that Leo either condemned in the Manichaeans what he himself prescribed for his people with evil intent, or wickedly commended to his own people what he condemned in the Manichaeans.

### XXIII

To complete this discussion of Saturday fasting, a question remains concerning the Saturday vigil of Pentecost: was a fast proclaimed for the faithful on that day in the Roman Church, at least in the time of our Leo?

Some affirm this, having the newer discipline more immediately before their eyes than the ancient one. But anyone who has even approached this matter will not doubt that Saturday was free and exempt from fasting for as long as it was considered unlawful in the Church to violate apostolic traditions.

Tertullian says in *On the Crown*, chapter 3:

> “On the Lord’s Day we consider it unlawful either to fast or to adore while kneeling. We rejoice in the same exemption from Easter until Pentecost.”

Saint Ambrose, as quoted in *Distinction* 76, chapter 8, says:

> “Throughout these FIFTY DAYS we have a continuous and uninterrupted festival, so that DURING THIS ENTIRE PERIOD we neither introduce fasts to be observed nor bend our knees in supplication to God.”

And below:

> “Accordingly, the entire span of FIFTY DAYS is celebrated in the likeness of the Lord’s Day, and all these days are reckoned as Sundays; for it is the Lord’s Resurrection.”

Jerome, in his letter to Lucinius of Baetica and elsewhere; Augustine, in his letters to Casulanus and to Jerome, Letter 82 (alternatively 19), §14, and elsewhere; Epiphanius; Isidore; and countless others say the same. But let us be content with our Leo and his exact contemporaries.

In his sermons on the fast of Pentecost, Leo sufficiently indicates that the Roman Church had not fasted at all before this festival. Thus he says:

> “Therefore, after the days of holy joy which we spent in honor of the Lord rising from the dead and then ascending into heaven, and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, the practice of fasting was instituted as something salutary and necessary”—that is, immediately afterward.

And in Sermon 2:

> “It is most plainly evident that, among the other gifts of God, the grace of fasting was also given at that time, and that it IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWS today’s festival.”

And in Sermon 4 on the fast of Pentecost:

> “Therefore, dearly beloved, the present time invites us to this salutary purpose: after fifty days have elapsed from the Lord’s Resurrection until the coming of the Holy Spirit—days that we spent in the joy of the chief festival—let us return to the remedies of fasting.”

He says the same in his sermons on Pentecost itself. From these passages it is clearer than midday that the vigil of Pentecost was not then counted among the days of fasting.

John Cassian may be added to Leo; he was a careful investigator of ecclesiastical customs. In *Conference* 21, chapters 11 and 19, he introduces Germanus asking why fasting was prohibited throughout the days of Pentecost, when Christ had remained with his disciples for only forty days after the Resurrection.

After much intervening discussion, Theonas replies:

> “These ten days also are to be celebrated with the same solemnity and joy as the preceding forty. The tradition of this festival, transmitted to us by apostolic men, is to be observed, he says, with the same consistency. For this reason the knees are not bent in prayer during these days, since the bending of the knees is a sign of penitence and mourning. Hence we also maintain throughout them the same solemnity as on the Lord’s Day, on which our ancestors, out of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection, handed down that neither fasting should be practiced nor the knee bent.”

This was not observed only in the Roman Church, but throughout the universal Church, until the fasts of the Rogation days instituted by Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, were adopted by many provinces far and wide, and by the Roman Church itself under Leo III.

I do indeed find Cassian reporting in chapter 11 that the remission of fasting during Pentecost was not then observed with equal care in the monasteries of Syria. But the discipline either of the Roman Church or of the universal Church must not be determined from the practices of certain monasteries, whose inhabitants lived far from the crowds of the people and were granted considerable latitude out of reverence for penitence. Isidore testifies to this in book 2 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 42:

> “From Easter until Pentecost, although the tradition of the Churches has relaxed the rigor of abstinence by means of meals, nevertheless, if any monks or clerics wish to fast, they are not to be prohibited. For Antony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are read as having abstained even on these days in the desert, and as having interrupted their abstinence only on the Lord’s Day.”

Jerome writes to nearly the same effect in his letter to Lucinius of Boetica:

> “Would that we could fast at all times! For in the Acts of the Apostles we read that, during the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day, the Apostle Paul and the believers with him did so, etc.”

Even if we occasionally find the paschal period of fifty days interwoven with certain fasts, I do not know whether the vigil of Pentecost was observed as a fast before the eleventh century.

[Note: The fast of the vigil of Pentecost has a much more ancient origin in the Roman Church. This is made certain by the *Sacramentary* published at the beginning of this volume, which we showed in the preface, number 10, to have been compiled under Felix III or, at the latest, at the beginning of the pontificate of Gelasius. There a Mass is found for the day before Pentecost, in which explicit mention is made of that day’s fast. A similar mention also occurs in the Gelasian *Sacramentary*, book I, number 77, in the first prayer.]

The Council of Seligenstadt, celebrated in 1022, decrees in chapter 2 that if the June fast of the Four Seasons falls on the vigil of Pentecost, it is not to be celebrated on that day, but during the solemn week of Pentecost itself.

Therefore, as for what some object from the sermon of Saint Ambrose quoted in *Distinction* 76, chapter 11:

> “We celebrate the day of Pentecost with no less joy than that with which we observed holy Easter. For then, just as we have done now, we fasted on Saturday, etc.”

this cannot be Ambrose’s statement. First, the council just cited testifies that the practice was otherwise; and second, the contrary is found in Ambrose himself. As we saw above, he excludes all fasting altogether from those fifty days, writes that the festival is continuous and uninterrupted throughout those fifty days, and finally reckons all those days as Sundays and as equivalent to Sunday.

It must therefore remain certain that, in the Roman Church in the time of our most holy Leo and around his time, this Saturday was completely free from fasting. Let this suffice for the moment concerning the fasting of all Saturdays among the Romans.

---

# SEVENTH DISSERTATION

## On the Case of Eutyches, Archimandrite of Constantinople, Condemned by Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, in Synod

Concerning Letter 20 of Saint Leo the Pope—now Letter 23—to Flavian himself, and Letter 21—now Letter 24—to the Emperor Theodosius Augustus.

[Col. 0645]

### I

There are many points that some people commonly extract from these letters in order to persuade us that the right of appeal to the Roman see from every region of the Christian world, and especially from the East, was voluntarily granted by the bishops of those regions even in the earliest centuries of the Church.

Far be it from me to begrudge this prerogative to the first and chief of all apostolic sees. Rather, I would wish with all my heart to uphold and defend its authority and eminence, established by the most sacred canons. But just as the true foundations on which the structure of the apostolic primacy rests remain immovable and unshaken, so those weak and counterfeit arguments by which certain people’s misguided zeal commonly props it up must collapse of themselves. Whoever attempts to expose their emptiness will certainly have earned no small gratitude from the apostolic see.

For us, however, who by the burden we have undertaken are forbidden to leave untouched anything in our Leo that requires clarification, it was necessary to make certain observations concerning the fabricated appeal of Eutyches, though, in our concern for brevity, omitting what others have already covered.

I therefore maintain that neither of these two letters of Leo contains anything by which it can validly be proved that Eutyches appealed to the Roman pontiff separately and apart from the other patriarchs and bishops of the greater dioceses. This seems certain to me from the acts of that gathering of thirty bishops at Constantinople, which was convened by order of the emperor to reread and review the acts of the Council of Constantinople, at which Eutyches had been condemned under the presidency and action of Flavian.

Indeed, the matter is clear from the very words of the monk Constantine, whom that heretic had appointed to answer in his name at the gathering. There Constantine expressly stated that Eutyches had appealed not only to the Apostolic See, but also to the synods of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica.

Eutyches had not done this openly and publicly, but secretly and in private had whispered it into the ear of the patrician Florentius, after the sentence had been pronounced and the synod dissolved. From this the truth of Flavian’s words becomes clear. When Leo complained to him that Eutyches had neglected to appeal to the apostolic see, Flavian replied:

> “Eutyches sent you petitions full of every kind of deceit and cunning, saying that at the time of the judgment he had submitted petitions of appeal both to us and to the holy council assembled here, and that he had appealed to Your Holiness. This was in no way done by him; indeed, in this matter also he lied, thinking that by the deceit of a falsehood he might steal his way into your holy ears.”

(*Letter of Flavian*, chapter 3, volume I, p. 473.)

These are the words of the monk Constantine speaking at that gathering; its acts are reproduced in action 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, near the end, when the acts of the Constantinopolitan council were reread:

> “The deacon Constantine said: When the condemnation was being read, Eutyches appealed to the holy synod of the most holy bishop of Rome, and to the synod of Alexandria, and of Jerusalem, and of Thessalonica; and these things have not been inserted in the Acts.”

[Note: The Greek reads: “The most devout deacon Constantine said: As the deposition was being read, Eutyches appealed to the holy synod of the most holy bishop of Rome, and to the synod of Alexandria, and of Jerusalem, and of Thessalonica; and these things are not contained in the records.”]

In the face of so clear and evident a testimony, I would never have guessed what could be said in reply. But now a recent writer, who directed his bitterest pen against the illustrious Peter de Marca—indeed, against the most sacred rights of bishops—opportunely shows us how easily this testimony can be blown away. He says:

> “The testimony of the monk Constantine, a heretic, is weak and burdened with many difficulties; Florentius the patrician himself contradicts it; indeed, it was rejected even by the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople. It ought not to be valued above the clearest assertion of the most holy Pope Leo and of the vigorous martyr of Christ, Flavian, who affirm in such clear and explicit words that Eutyches appealed to Leo alone.”

### II

This response must be weighed carefully and fairly in its several parts.

First, the writer seeks to diminish the credibility of the monk Constantine on the ground of heresy. I ask whether he should be considered a greater heretic than Eutyches, the arch-heretic, whose testimony David nevertheless accepts without hesitation.

Next, if credibility is to be denied to a heretic on this point, it must also be denied on the other point. Justice does not permit Constantine’s truthfulness to be rejected when he speaks of the sees of Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica, while being applauded when he speaks of Rome—unless the truth of this final part and the falsity of the earlier part can be established by some other means. We shall show below that this cannot in any way be done.

I add that, even if Constantine acted as the representative of his archimandrite, he should not for that reason be branded with the stigma of heresy. This could have occurred at that early stage partly through ignorance of the heretical teaching and partly through human affection, which he may later have set aside in order to obey the sentence of the bishops. That this is not improbable is shown by the fact that, although we see the monks Carosus and Dorotheus, followers of Eutyches, condemned together with their master at the Council of Chalcedon, we read nothing of the kind concerning the monk Constantine. This suggests that Constantine did not adhere to Eutyches except while his cunning had not yet been sufficiently perceived and he could still be regarded as Catholic by inexperienced and simple monks.

2. Whatever may be the case regarding this monk’s faith, let us examine the matter itself.

We must first note that Constantine did not attend Flavian’s council, convened in the case of Eutyches, except briefly—namely, in action 4, when he accompanied the archimandrite Abraham, who had been delegated by Eutyches to represent him at the synod, together with two other deacons of Eutyches’ monastery, Eleusinus and Constantius. These men were again present on behalf of Eutyches at the gathering held at Constantinople the following year by approximately thirty bishops for the review of the acts of this council.

After that action, which was occupied with questioning and hearing the statements of the delegates, Constantine appears nowhere. He is not mentioned at this synod except in the following action, action 5, where the archimandrite Martin is reported to have said that, when the presbyter Peter had been sent to his monastery, a note had been delivered to him on the preceding Friday by a certain deacon Constantine, who had unsuccessfully urged him to sign it.

Since Constantine was therefore not present at the synod or at the condemnation of Eutyches, whatever he said at the later gathering under discussion was not spoken from his own knowledge. He recited it by reading from the acts of the synod that Eutyches had handed over to him.

For this purpose the bishops were summoned to the house of Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: the purpose was to verify the truth and integrity of the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod. Eutyches complained that certain statements contrary to what had actually taken place had been inserted into them, as is shown by his petitions submitted to the Emperor Theodosius and by the course of this action.

When the deacons and notaries of the Church of Constantinople produced their records, in which the acts of the council had been written down, the patrician Florentius said:

> “As each section is reread, let the party of the reverend monk state what it considers objectionable; and, once the writings held by the aforesaid reverend monk’s party have been produced, let them be compared with the reading of the authentic Acts.”

And when both parties had presented their records, etc.

(*First action of the Council of Chalcedon, after the acts of the Constantinopolitan council under Flavian.*)

It is therefore not so much the credibility of Constantine the reciter that is at issue here as that of Eutyches himself, from whom Constantine had received the synodical records and against whose reliability the acts of the council were being examined.

Moreover, if Eutyches lied when he said that he had appealed to the council of the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica, he must likewise be thought to have lied when he wrote to Saint Leo that he had given Flavian a petition of appeal by which he appealed to the Roman pontiff himself.

[Note: Although Eutyches lied when he stated that he had submitted a petition of appeal in court and that Flavian had not received it, we shall show in the observations, number 3 and following, that he truly sent Leo a petition of the fabricated appeal.]

Flavian himself asserts that Eutyches lied, both in his letters to Saint Leo and at this very gathering. The patrician Florentius asserted the same; so did Julian, Seleucus, and all the other bishops who were present at this proceeding.

I therefore reduce the entire matter to a single dilemma: either Eutyches lied when he claimed that he had appealed, or he did not lie.

If he did not lie, then all thirty bishops of this Constantinopolitan gathering lied; Flavian above all lied, as did Florentius. It would also have to be admitted that the acts of the Constantinopolitan council had been falsified, since they make no mention of the appeal that Eutyches said he had lodged.

But if he lied, he appealed to no one, and consequently no more to the Roman bishop than to the Alexandrian, Jerusalem, or Thessalonian bishop. For no distinction is made among them in the Acts, whether by Florentius, Flavian, the notaries, or anyone else.

Indeed, I believe that Eutyches was guilty of falsehood in both instances: when he spoke before Leo of an appeal made to Leo, and when he spoke before the Eastern bishops of an appeal to their council. He did so, in Flavian’s words, “thinking that by the deceit of a falsehood he might steal his way into your holy ears” (*First Letter of Flavian to Saint Leo*, chapter 3).

### III

I am astonished, however, that the author whose work we are examining should have so entirely forgotten his own case that he brought forward in his defense the words of the bishops who, while the trial was being conducted, testified that they had heard no word of an appeal from Eutyches—thus cutting his own throat with his own sword. “While the council was in session and the interrogation was taking place,” said Bishop Seleucus, “we heard nothing of this kind said by the archimandrite Eutyches concerning an appeal.” The most reverend bishops said: “We too confess the same thing” (*Acts of Constantinople*, after the deposition of Eutyches). Certainly, if an appeal had been made to even one Roman bishop in the hearing of the bishops, they would have known that it had been said—something they deny having heard; nor would the complaint of the monk Constantine, who protested that mention of the appeal had been omitted from the synodal Acts, have been rejected altogether. Indeed, Julian, bishop of Coë, who had been present both at the synod and at the later assembly, would have supported his complaint.

Julian was an extremely devout worshiper of the apostolic see in which he had been brought up, as Leo himself testifies (*Ep.* 86, now 113, ch. 2). Later, that see entrusted to him, by maternal right, the Catholic cause against the Nestorian and Eutychian heretics. Throughout that entire crisis he acted in the eastern regions as the representative of the Roman pontiff, and immediately after the Council of Constantinople he wrote to him concerning Eutyches, who had been condemned. If Eutyches had therefore appealed to the Roman see, Julian would undoubtedly have contended for the rights of that see. When Patricius simply requested that the bishops say whether they had known the religious monk to be appealing, Julian would have replied that he had heard Eutyches appealing to the Roman bishop. Yet Julian was so far from saying this that, first of all and more emphatically than anyone, he steadfastly asserted that he had heard nothing of the kind: “Before God I say: I heard nothing of this sort from the monk Eutyches in the assembly.” Since the Acts preserve the words of only two bishops who answered this question, I do not think it accidental that, by a special act of providence, Julian’s testimony in particular was rescued from oblivion, so that through the voice and judgment of a sincere disciple of the apostolic see we might possess certain knowledge of what had taken place there.

Although it is false that Eutyches appealed when his condemnation was being read, we nevertheless extract something true from his lie. When he put into the mouth of the monk Constantine words that were supposed to contain the formula of his appeal, we should believe that this exceptionally shrewd man suggested no other words than those ordinarily used in framing an appeal. For a lie that is not shaded with the appearance of truth is excessively vulgar. We therefore learn that, up to that time, it was not the custom of the Easterners to appeal to only one of the bishops, but to all those who had not participated in the judgment from which the appeal was made—not merely to the council of the Roman pontiff, which represented the whole West, but also to the synod of other patriarchs who were not suspected in the case.

[Note: These points will be refuted in observations no. 5 and following, and especially no. 9.]

And in fact, at the very time when Eutyches was writing to Saint Leo that he had appealed to him, he also wrote to Dioscorus of Alexandria, asking that an ecumenical council be convened at which Flavian’s judgment might be examined. Liberatus teaches us this in chapter 12, although he must be corrected when he says that Eutyches did not think about such a council until after the Constantinopolitan assembly had ended, at which the Acts of Flavian’s synod were reread. For below, from the Acts of this assembly, we shall show that the Council of Ephesus had already been summoned at that time. It is therefore clear that, when Eutyches appealed to the apostolic see, he either did not thereby summon the tribunal of that see alone, but that of the entire ecumenical synod, in which the pope would at least be present through his legates; or else he feared incurring the displeasure of all the Easterners if he subjected his case, contrary to customary practice, to the judgment of the Roman pontiff alone.

Another point is also true: Eutyches uttered the words of an appeal not publicly before the Fathers of the council—neither while the case was being investigated nor while the sentence of condemnation was being pronounced—but silently, as Florentius says, after the assembly had already been dissolved. This cannot be declared false, since Flavian freely admits that he had not heard it from Eutyches himself, but from the most magnificent Patricius: “As I was going up,” says Flavian, “to the upper part of the house after the synod had been dissolved.”

Finally, it is true that Eutyches did make some mention of the Roman and Alexandrian bishops while the Fathers were engaged in examining the case—not, however, in order to appeal to them, but in order to adopt the manner of speaking that they prescribed. For when Bishop Basil heard the names of the bishops whom Constantine and Patricius were listing, he began to remember what had slipped from his memory:

“Now, truly,” he said, “I say that, while the assembly was still sitting and this holy synod was proposing that he should say that there are two inseparable and unconfused natures in one Lord, and this after the union, I know what the religious archimandrite Eutyches said: ‘If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I say this very thing.’”

He did not say this as one appealing, but rather said: “I did not dare to say it because of the Fathers.”

From these words—some of which he had uttered to some people and others to others, partly on one occasion and partly on another, sometimes publicly and sometimes silently, at one time as if appealing and at another merely explaining his own position—Eutyches took the boldness to impose upon Saint Leo by letter and upon the Eastern Fathers at the Constantinopolitan assembly through Constantine. Hence he fabricated the appeal. He hoped easily to persuade them of something whose memory, six months after the council had been dissolved, had been so effaced that only uncertain and doubtful traces remained in the minds of some.

By the same deception he called a certain document, which he had presented to the Fathers of the synod and which the synod had refused to accept, an appeal-document when he wrote to Saint Leo; but in the Constantinopolitan assembly, as the bishops there complained, he called this document a profession of faith, delivered through the deacon Eleusinius.

Thus it is clear how the very arguments that John David assembled in his own defense against the illustrious Peter de Marca actually work against him. There is, nevertheless, one brief statement of his that I cannot wholly rescue from the criticism of this recent author: namely, where he says that Eutyches omitted Domnus, bishop of Antioch, in mentioning the appeal because Domnus had subscribed to Flavian’s sentence.

For when Eutyches whispered this fiction of an appeal into the ear of Florentius, Domnus of Antioch could not yet have known what had been done concerning him in the synod. Yet that writer has no reason to applaud himself so greatly. In place of Peter de Marca’s argument we shall substitute other arguments—many of them, and genuine ones. If he tests their force, he will be a great Apollo in my eyes.

First, it must be observed that Domnus’s omission was not accidental but deliberate. This is evident from the fact that his name nowhere occurs in Eutyches’ words—whether they are reported by Constantine the Monk, by Patricius Florentius, or by Bishop Basil when he recounts the other words spoken in the assembly itself: “If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me,” and so forth.

Although different witnesses omitted different bishops—Basil names only the two patriarchs, Roman and Alexandrian; Patricius adds the patriarch of Jerusalem; Constantine also adds the bishop of Thessalonica—all agree in leaving out Domnus of Antioch. No one would say that this happened without reason.

Facundus, bishop of Hermiana, and the deacon Liberatus, indeed the Acts of the Council of Ephesus as well, make the reason clear to us. No one who has even touched the history of the Nestorian heresy with his fingertips can be unaware of the bitter hostility that once flared up between John, bishop of Antioch, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, on account of Nestorius of Constantinople. Cyril attacked Nestorius as an impious corrupter of Catholic doctrine; John, on the contrary, defended him as a champion of the faith.

Their hostility proceeded so far that John condemned Cyril and Cyril condemned John with anathemas in their respective councils. Although their friendship was later restored, the old hostility revived after repeated disputes between them concerning Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia. This is the first reason why Domnus was hostile to Eutyches: Eutyches had always favored the party of the Alexandrian bishop and had declared war both on Nestorius and on all whom he considered infected with the Nestorian taint.

Domnus, the nephew of John of Antioch, who had undertaken the defense of Diodore and Theodore—and even of Nestorius—through his sister, was allied both in sympathies and in party with Theodoret of Cyrus and with Proclus and Flavian, the bishops of Constantinople. Against these Dioscorus of Alexandria and Eutyches had already conspired. Hence Domnus repeatedly fabricated accusations against Theodoret, attempting to invade the rights of the Church of Antioch and to diminish the see of Constantinople. Eutyches, for his part, denounced them in his letters to the apostolic see for Nestorian heresy. There is no doubt that he is referring to them in the letter of Eutyches that was followed by Leo’s reply, which still survives.

### 2

The reason why Eutyches, being hostile to Domnus, did not include his council along with the others in his appeal is that Domnus had once written against Cyril’s chapters. For this reason, later, at the Ephesian Robber Council, although he had obeyed Dioscorus’s perfidy in every respect, he was nevertheless deposed by Dioscorus himself.

“When his letters,” says Liberatus (*Breviary*, ch. 12), “which Domnus of Antioch had written against Cyril’s twelve chapters because they were obscure, and so forth, were brought forward in the midst of the proceedings—”

### 3

The occasion of the dispute was the case of Ibas, bishop of Edessa. At least initially, Ibas had adhered to the party of Nestorius; he had also written against Cyril of Alexandria and was a devoted partisan of his patriarch Domnus. When he had been accused before Domnus, his accusers were condemned, while Ibas himself departed without condemnation, since his innocence had evidently been proved.

This moved the Alexandrian bishop and his supporters—among whom was Eutyches—violently against Domnus. It persuaded Eutyches sufficiently that he could expect no protection from Domnus against Flavian if he appealed from Flavian’s sentence to Domnus, especially since the slanderers of Ibas had been brought to this accusation by the advice and instigation of Eutyches. Ibas himself testifies to this in the ninth action of the Council of Chalcedon:

“Uranius, bishop of Himerum, doing everything for the sake of Eutyches, arranged for certain clerics to accuse me,” and so forth.

And in the tenth action:

“Eutyches fabricated certain false charges against me concerning the faith, and did not allow me to enter the synod,” and so forth.

### 4

Eutyches well knew how deeply Dioscorus resented the conspiracy once formed by Domnus with Proclus to preserve the third canon of Constantinople and to defend the privileges of that royal see, privileges which Dioscorus had long coveted.

[Note: Domnus’s alleged conspiracy to preserve the third canon of Constantinople, and his supposed dispute with Dioscorus on this account, are gratuitously asserted.]

Accordingly, he would have handled his own affairs very badly if, when appealing to Dioscorus, whose tribunal he was invoking, he had also appealed to Domnus, who regarded Dioscorus as his bitterest enemy. This would have diminished Dioscorus’s power in the council, on which Eutyches placed his greatest hope and confidence.

### 5

Since the bishop of Antioch had always favored the prerogative of the see of Constantinople and the common rights of the churches, Eutyches had good reason to fear that his case would fail before one who, having learned that he had been properly accused, convicted, and condemned in a synod, would also have learned that he had appealed from the sentence of his own bishop without any justification.

### 6

But what harmed Eutyches most of all, and what the recent author ought not to have overlooked, is what we learn from the account of Facundus, bishop of Hermiana: namely, that Domnus of Antioch was the first of all to oppose the infamous heresy that Eutyches was already beginning to produce.

“Venerable Domnus of Antioch,” says Facundus (*Book XII*, final chapter), “holding to the judgment of his predecessor John and of his other predecessors, was the first to resist Eutyches, who was attempting to revive the impiety of Apollinaris, the arch-heresiarch, and who was presuming to anathematize Diodore and Theodore for that reason. Domnus wrote to the emperor Theodosius.”

Domnus wrote not in his own name alone, but also in the name of the entire Eastern synod, which had therefore preceded Flavian’s judgment and the Council of Constantinople. Facundus reproduced this synodical letter, either in full or for the most part, in Book VIII, chapter 5. We have thought it worthwhile to transcribe it here as well, since it is found only in Facundus, whose copies are now rare, and since it was also omitted from the latest edition of the Councils, where nothing is said about the Antiochene synod from which the synodical letter was sent.

It also greatly illuminates the history of the Eutychian heresy, whose condemnation by Flavian in the Constantinopolitan synod, and later by the ecumenical council, it preceded. Finally, it will shed considerable light on the case of Domnus himself, which we shall discuss in the ninth dissertation.

### VI

[Note: On this synodical letter see annotation 3 (col. 219, note b) to Quesnellus’s first dissertation, under the year 448.]

“Now therefore,” says Facundus (*Book VIII*, chapter 5), “let us also recall the synodical letter of Domnus of Antioch, who, like his predecessor John, wrote to the emperor Theodosius:

‘We are compelled to inform Your Piety that the presbyter Eutyches is attempting to revive the impiety of Apollinaris, the arch-heresiarch, and to undermine the apostolic teachings by corrupting the doctrine of the mystery of the Incarnation; calling the divinity and humanity of the Only-Begotten one nature; asserting that a commingling and confusion have taken place; attaching the saving Passion to the undefiled Godhead itself; and presuming to anathematize Diodore and Theodore, who were pillars of the truth and defenders of piety, and who clearly displayed courage against every heresy. In this he resembles the folly of Apollinaris.

For Apollinaris moved his tongue against the great Diodore because Diodore rebuked him for acting impiously. This too is a clear sign of kinship between their doctrines: whoever attacks the great champion of piety, Diodore, with blasphemous words, thereby shows, by contrast, that he himself embraces the likeness of that man’s folly.

But this great Diodore has as a witness to his piety the great Basil, whose famous struggles are well known. For Diodore flourished at the time when those who supported the impiety of Arius were entangling the souls of the emperors and stirring their power against the truth. He pursued his course of struggle at Antioch, contending rigorously against the harshness of the heretics.

The holy man of God, Meletius, from whom the guardians of the apostolic doctrines among us derive their name—for the followers of Arius call us Meletians—appointed the most sacred Diodore governor of all Cilicia and entrusted Tarsus to his administration. In the imperial city, together with Gregory and the others who shared his convictions, Diodore ordained the thrice-blessed Archbishop Nectarius.

He was the teacher of the great John, who adorned the see of the imperial city and filled the whole world with his teaching. He nourished the widely celebrated Theodore in those doctrines, instructing him clearly and courageously in his labors and sending him into the ranks of the heretics.

The most sacred Diodore flourished together with the great Athanasius, Peter, and Timothy; Theodore, on the other hand, flourished with Theophilus and with men who, like heavenly lights, illumined the world and adorned the see of Alexandria. These men were their praisers throughout their lives; no one anywhere dared openly accuse them.’”

Thus far Domnus’s synodical letter.

### VII

I think no one can now be in doubt why the name of Domnus was omitted by Eutyches from the fictitious document of appeal. Why, however, the bishop of Thessalonica—who seemed more likely to be omitted—was inserted is another difficulty, though not one important enough to require a lengthy dissertation.

Although the diocese of Eastern Illyricum, whose chief city was Thessalonica, depended upon the Western patriarch, it had nevertheless been cut off from the Western Empire during that period. It was therefore appropriate that special mention should be made of its bishop, since the bishops of that region were not accustomed to appear at the council of the Western patriarch, and could not do so without an edict of the Eastern emperor.

[Note: Atticus of Nicopolis, metropolitan of Old Epirus, who certainly belonged among the bishops of Eastern Illyricum, came to Rome under our Leo, according to the pope’s own Epistle 14, ch. 1. Much later, under Pope Boniface II, Theodosius, bishop of Echinus, came to the Roman synod in 531 in the name of his metropolitan Stephen of Larissa and of three other bishops of Thessaly, in order to proceed against the bishop of Constantinople; and Abundantius, bishop of the city of Demetrias, who likewise belonged to Eastern Illyricum, was also present at that synod. Yet no edict of the Eastern emperor was needed. See vol. VI of the Venetian edition of the Councils, cols. 835, 839, and 842.]

Moreover, this diocese was so extensive and adorned with so many privileges that it ought not to have been confused indiscriminately with the others. I shall omit the privileges it possessed before the division of Illyricum. At that time, however, it was governed by its own special praetorian prefect and enjoyed precedence in councils above the others, as is clear from the Council of Ephesus, where it held its place after the bishops of Jerusalem and Ephesus, and from the Council of Chalcedon, where it held its place after the patriarchs.

I add that the vote of the Illyrian bishops was so important at the Council of Chalcedon that, when they expressed doubts about one or another passage of Saint Leo’s letter and asked the Fathers for time to compare it with the writings of Cyril and the other Fathers with calm and undisturbed minds, they obtained their request. The entire council, which was preparing to subscribe to Leo’s letter, was kept in suspense by postponing the subscription to another time.

“Let the hearing be deferred,” said the judges, “for five days, so that during this interval Your Holiness may meet with the most holy Archbishop Anatolius and discuss the faith together, so that those who are in doubt may be instructed” (*Part II*, action 2).

They nevertheless did not subscribe until seven days later, in action 4, held on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November. On that occasion they did not proceed in the ordinary manner followed by the others, but in a manner peculiar to themselves: they dictated from a document the longer formula of their agreement, which they had composed among themselves, indicating that they had been satisfied concerning those passages which, because of their ignorance of the language, they had not been able fully to understand.

When this had been completed, all the Illyrian bishops said: “We have all given the same voice from Illyricum, and we all agree with it.”

You see, John David, that although the Illyrian bishops were subject to the jurisdiction of the Roman see, they nevertheless exercised their own rights at that time.

[Note: When, at the Council of Chalcedon, the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops expressed doubts about certain passages of Leo’s letter, both groups were given time for the purpose, as the Fathers of the council say, “so that those who are in doubt may be instructed … because it is fitting to persuade all who are in doubt.” Who, however, would infer from this with Quesnellus that the Illyrian bishops were exercising their rights when they requested time to be instructed? Could there be a right to doubt an authoritative decision of the apostolic see, which the whole Church had already received as the rule of faith through the subscriptions of the bishops? See note 22 in Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the year 451, where we discussed this matter more fully.]

Finally, since all the bishops of the Eastern regions were at that time divided into two parties—some adhering to the Alexandrian bishop and being intensely hostile to Nestorius or to those suspected of sharing his opinion, while others adhered to the bishop of Antioch and, on the contrary, regarded the others as more inclined toward the heresy of Apollinaris—Eutyches perhaps knew that many of the Illyrians would be more indulgent toward him, as indeed they were.

For they willingly lent their hands to the abominable decrees of Dioscorus, acquitting Eutyches by their vote and condemning Flavian and the other defenders of Catholic doctrine. Therefore, at the Council of Chalcedon, the Illyrians above all, together with the most reverend bishops who stood with them, cried out: “We have all sinned; have mercy on all of us.” They repeated this a second and a third time, both in that action and in others, separating themselves from the flock of the other provinces.

Thus no one should be surprised that the bishop of Thessalonica was named together with the patriarchs and the bishops of the greater sees, on account of the exceptional prerogative of that very great see and of those provinces.

### VIII

[Note: The arguments which Quesnellus here and in what follows heaps up in order to represent Saint Flavian as not at all favoring the right of the apostolic see in Eutyches’ case will be sufficiently dismantled in observations no. 6 and following.]

As for the words of Saint Flavian, which are set against the words of Constantine, and in which no one besides Leo is named as the person to whom Eutyches appealed, the answer is not difficult.

This was done for no other reason than that Flavian was addressing Leo alone at that time, and the arch-heresiarch had named Leo alone when he wrote to him: “Thinking that by the deceit of a lie he was insinuating himself into the holy ears of Leo,” as Flavian himself writes to Saint Leo. Leo also stood unquestionably above the patriarchs and metropolitans to whose council Eutyches was said to have appealed, and he stood above them by a twofold right: he held primacy in the Church and was the head of the entire synod to which the appeal was made.

Although the same pontiff may seem to have drawn the whole case to himself, since he asks to be informed about every detail and complains about Flavian’s silence—“Although he ought first to have disclosed everything to us”—that is not in fact the case. Any other bishop, if an appeal had been made to his judgment, would likewise have asked to be informed about the affair and would likewise have complained of silence.

Leo therefore rightly, and with stronger claim, wished the account and knowledge of the entire affair to be brought before him—indeed, brought before him first, as primate, since he was to decide the matter with and above the others if an appeal were admissible.

[Note: Whoever held that Leo, as primate, was only to decide Eutyches’ appeal together with the others and before the others would be asserting a primacy of mere order, not of principal jurisdiction. We have seen, in the observations on Dissertation 5, Part I, ch. 7, that the right of appeals belongs to the apostolic see, or Roman pontiff, by virtue of the primacy of jurisdiction. How far Saint Leo exercised this right in Eutyches’ appeal will be shown in the observations on this seventh dissertation, no. 8.]

For the pontiff himself says to Flavian (*Ep.* 20, now 23, ch. 1):

“We, who desire that the judgments of the Lord’s priests should be mature, can decide nothing, with facts unknown, to the prejudice of either party, before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.”

These are not the words of a man arrogating to himself alone the entire right of delivering judgment, but of a prudent, watchful, and perfectly impartial judge who does not wish, without knowing the case, rashly to cast his vote.

But why should we waste time answering arguments of this kind drawn from Leo himself? In the present case we are not asking whether Leo claimed that prerogative, but whether Eutyches actually appealed, and whether he appealed to the Roman pontiff alone.

If he had done so—as Saint Leo believed he had, on the basis of his crafty and lying document—it would not be surprising that Eutyches, appealing to the Roman see, was willingly received by the Roman pontiff, especially since the faith of Nicaea appeared to be at stake. Both Eutyches himself and his accuser professed themselves firmly attached to it.

For the chief duties of the Roman bishop, as the head of the episcopal crown, are these: from the first chair, as from a watchtower, to guard the preservation of the canons and to act as guardian of the Catholic faith.

### IX

Let us not, however, put our faith in Eutyches, that most cunning impostor; nor let us lend our ear even to Leo himself, holy though he was, when he was pursuing the splendor and rights of his own see.

[Note: See observations 6 and 10.]

Let us listen to Flavian, bishop of New Rome and most courageous martyr of Christ, whom the Easterners’ attitude and custom concerning appeals—and Eutyches’ entire course of action—could not have escaped.

Did Flavian think that the judgment of his council concerning Eutyches had to be sent to Leo so that it would stand if Leo approved it and disappear if he rejected it? Nothing of the kind appears in either of his letters. Nothing is recorded as having been done by him that lends even the slightest support to this opinion.

He did indeed write to Leo concerning the condemned and contumacious heretic, informing him that Eutyches had been deprived of the presbyterate; he also sent him the series of Acts from the Council of Constantinople. But for what purpose and with what intention? Was it to discharge the obligation of making a necessary report? This does not emerge from his words.

Even if bishops were accustomed to do this in major cases, such as that of a heresiarch spreading a new error throughout the churches, it was nevertheless not necessary when the case concerned a layman or cleric who was not the author of a new heresy but a defender of an ancient and already proscribed one—such as Eutyches was then considered, and as Leo himself later called him.

Perhaps Flavian wrote to Leo and sent him the Acts against Eutyches so that they might receive the strength of confirmation from him? Yet not even a hint of this can be seen.

Let us therefore hear Flavian himself explain his purpose:

“We have sent to Your Blessedness,” he says, “the proceedings that were formerly completed concerning him [Eutyches], in which he was convicted of such things and was expelled from the presbyterate, from the administration of the monastery, and from our communion, so that Your Holiness, learning what was done concerning him, may deign to make his impiety known to all the bishops living under Your Blessedness. Otherwise, some who do not know what he believed and of what he was convicted might be found communicating with him, as with a partner in the faith, either by letters or by some other means” (*Ep.* now 26, ch. 4).

The matter is plain and needs no interpreter. Flavian knew that the sentence of the Council of Constantinople, over which he had presided, was definitive, and that no laborious investigation was needed.
