It was only necessary to declare that this wretched man, who was reviving the impious doctrines of Apollinaris and Valentinus, already condemned long ago by an ecumenical synod, had been separated from the communion and ministry of the Church.

In his other letter he gives yet another reason—indeed, several reasons. Eutyches, made more angry and stubborn by episcopal censure, was disturbing the Church of Constantinople. Flavian foresaw that this slippery man would soon carry lying complaints to other sees, especially to Rome, and occupy the ears of the pontiffs—as he actually did—unless Eutyches’ schemes and deceptions were forestalled in good time by a genuine and authoritative account of what had taken place.

In addition, this impious monk had already had notorious pamphlets posted throughout the streets and crossroads of the imperial city. Flavian says that he publicly displayed accusations filled with insults and curses, by which he attacked the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople and denounced their sentence as unjust. He knew for certain that these complaints would soon spread not only through the Eastern provinces but also through the Western ones.

Third, Eutyches had approached the imperial majesty and presented petitions full of arrogance and insolence. Through the efforts and advancement of Chrysaphius, the result would be—as events themselves demonstrated—that Theodosius would undertake Eutyches’ defense.

Since Flavian considered that Leo possessed great influence with the emperor, both on account of his rank and because of his virtue, he thought that Leo should be approached on behalf of the common cause of faith and discipline, so that he might use all his strength to uphold the emperor’s faith and draw him away from defending Eutyches.

Finally, when rumors were spreading that the emperor was considering the convocation of a universal synod at which Eutyches’ case would be reconsidered, it was fitting that Flavian should inform the primary see of this plan and at the same time provide a fuller account of the occasion of the synod and of the entire controversy to be examined there, by presenting the actual proceedings. Through the care of the Roman pontiff, these would also become known to the other bishops of the Western regions.

### X

It is worth considering what Flavian replied after being admonished by Leo, especially in the final part of his letter. From Leo’s words he understood that, having learned of Eutyches’ appeal, Leo was preparing himself for a new examination and judgment. Recognizing that this was entirely superfluous, Flavian strives to persuade the Roman pontiff of precisely that.

[Note: How far Flavian considered Saint Leo’s judgment superfluous in Eutyches’ case may be learned from observation no. 6.]

First, therefore, he warns him not to allow himself to be ensnared by the devices and frauds of this extremely cunning man. Then he suggests that the Roman pontiff must labor no less zealously to ensure that the sentence of the Eastern bishops achieve its full effect than if he himself had pronounced it.

For he understood well that, since the Church is one, the episcopate too is one, and that one episcopate watches everywhere over the one faith. Each bishop ought to make the judgments of all the churches spread far and wide his own, provided that nothing had been done contrary to ecclesiastical rule and the accepted canons.

“Act confidently,” he says (*Ep.* now 26, ch. 3), “as befits the priesthood, making the particular cause a common cause and making it your own the discipline of the holy churches.”

Third, he asks Leo to make Eutyches’ condemnation known to all the priests of his own region.

Fourth, since the condemnation had been carried out regularly and canonically, there was no place for its retraction or renewed examination. The case required not a new discussion and new judgment, but only the pontiff’s intervention and exhortation before the emperor, lest the peace of the churches be disturbed or the emperor rashly create some prejudice against the faith by undertaking Eutyches’ defense at the instigation of certain courtiers.

So that we may not falsely attribute anything to Flavian, his words are these:

“At the same time, deign to declare that the condemnation against him was regularly carried out and to make it known through your own writings; strengthen, moreover, the faith of our most pious and Christ-loving emperor. For the case needs only your support and defense, by which you ought, through your own agreement, to bring everything to tranquility and peace. For thus, with God cooperating, the heresy that has arisen and the disturbances caused by him will most easily be destroyed through your most sacred letters.”

Flavian therefore requests from Leo not judgment but support; not a sentence but letters; defense, not confirmation; personal writings, not synodal decrees. For once the episcopal judgment had pronounced an anathema against Eutyches, the case was finished—unless a universal council wished to draw the examination to itself or it were voluntarily referred to the West.

[Note: Flavian did indeed say that a general council should be prevented if Leo confirmed the Constantinopolitan judgment by his own right. See observation no. 6. But if Eutyches’ case was referred to the Roman pontiff while the Council of Ephesus was nevertheless convened, this was brought about by the efforts of the heretic’s patrons; who could use that fact to diminish the right of the Roman see?]

Flavian quite rightly thought that the latter course should be avoided in this circumstance:

“Lest,” he says, “the most holy churches everywhere be disturbed on account of the error and malice of one restless and seditious monk.”

Concerning the [Note: [Col. 0655D] In the calling of the general synod, the emperor himself required Leo’s consent, as is clear from Letter 33. Compare Annotation 8 (preceding volume, col. 789, note b) on Letter 30.] synod of this kind, however, people were already thinking of assembling it. From this it is most certainly demonstrated that at that time the Easterners did not depend upon the word of the Westerners. For either this plan was undertaken before Leo had been consulted and informed about Eutyches’ condemnation—and thus it is evident that Flavian’s judgment was not referred back to Leo’s decision, since, with Leo’s tribunal passed over, another higher one was being prepared—or, after letters had been sent to him and his consent had been received, the plan of a universal synod was conceived. This shows even more clearly that, even after Leo’s consent, a synod was considered necessary so that the judgment of the earlier proceedings might be reviewed and, if necessary, reformed. Or finally, the pretext for decreeing a synod was sought merely from Eutyches’ petition of appeal, whether genuine or forged. This proves that among the Easterners it was established that Eutyches’ appeal had not been referred to the one bishop of Rome alone, but also to the other patriarchs and their synods, to be convened in a universal council.

But lest anyone seize upon the consent required from Leo as an opportunity for quibbling, there is no one who does not know that, even from the supreme pontiff, the consent of other bishops was customarily required in similar cases; just as Leo himself did after the Ephesian Robbery, when he sent letters on that account to almost the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0656D] The very reasoning that Quesnellus adduces proves this to be false. For after the Ephesian Robbery Leo did not seek the bishops’ consent; rather, by letters sent to many, he declared that Robbery null and void.] Finally, I wish to warn the reader that the translation of Flavian’s preceding letter to Saint Leo appears insufficiently accurate. If it had been possible to correct it against the Greek [Col. 0656C] [Note: [Col. 0656D] The Greek text was subsequently brought to light, and Quesnellus himself added it to the second edition. How much it supports our position we shall see in the observations.] text, which has perished through the injuries of time, perhaps we would have found something clearer in support of our opinion. Nevertheless, from this translation, although it may perhaps have been made by a Western and Roman man, enough and more than enough light shines for the sincere reader who does not look for a knot in a bulrush.

### XI.

As for what is suggested by a man of outstanding learning—namely, that after reading the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, Saint Leo approved and confirmed everything in such a way that both Saint Flavian and Saint Leo judged that the general synod ought not to be called—I say, with due respect to this excellent man, that this is exceedingly far from the truth. [Note: [Col. 0656D] Flavian said that the general council should be removed if Leo, by his own right, confirmed the Constantinopolitan judgment concerning Eutyches. See Observation 6. What follows, then, can easily be refuted by anyone attempting to weaken the right of the Apostolic See.]

Flavian did indeed think that the council whose assembly was being announced should be removed, as he writes to Leo; but for what reason? Was it because, as the aforementioned scholar thinks, the case had been concluded once the Roman pontiff’s confirmation had been received? Yet Flavian was so far from then possessing Saint Leo as an approving or confirming authority that, rather, he found him almost angry, because he had struck Eutyches with what he regarded as too severe a judgment, whereas Eutyches appeared to cling to the statutes of the Council of Nicaea. For when the bishop of Constantinople wrote these things about the council, Saint Leo had not yet received copies of the proceedings against Eutyches—or at least he had not yet written back that they had been received and approved or rejected by him. Only Eutyches’ letters had been delivered to him. After reading them, Leo complained both to the emperor Theodosius and to Flavian himself that the petition of Eusebius, the accusing bishop, contained nothing establishing the evident character of the charge; and although it pressed the charge of heresy against a presbyter, it did not clearly state what sense or meaning it was accusing him of holding. He adds that he still did not understand by what justice Eutyches had been separated from communion with the Church; and he expressed displeasure that, even then, Flavian was keeping silent about the things done in so serious a case. Finally, he urged him to hasten to report everything to him as fully and clearly as possible, which he ought to have done earlier (Letter 20, now 23; and 21, now 24).

Accordingly, when Flavian was speaking to Leo about removing the council that was being prepared, he was not even dreaming of confirmation of the proceedings held by him against Eutyches. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Indeed, we shall prove in the same Observation 6 that Flavian asked Leo to confirm the proceedings against Eutyches, and that after such confirmation he did not consider a general synod necessary.] Out of priestly concern, he feared only that, once bishops had been summoned to an ecumenical synod, the most holy Churches everywhere might be disturbed. These are his very words in the first of the letters he wrote to Leo.

He considered that synod entirely unnecessary because whatever impious doctrine Eutyches had spewed forth had long before been condemned and proscribed in the case of the ancient heretics Apollinaris, Valentinus, and others, by the judgments of earlier councils or bishops. Eutyches had also advanced propositions contrary to the teaching of the holy and universal Council of Ephesus, assembled only a few years earlier, and had thereby made himself liable to its anathema and judgment. Flavian says that Eutyches, treating these things as nothing, believed that he would not suffer the penalty prescribed by that holy and universal council. What need, then, was there to move the bishops of the entire Christian world from their sees so that they might assemble in synod to declare that penalty? “Once a synod has been held,” says Pope Felix, “it consequently involves all the followers of every error that has been rejected” (Letter 12 to the Emperor Zeno, before the middle of the collection). And according to Gelasius, Letter 4 to Faustus, this is permitted not only to the apostolic prelate but to any bishop: they may separate anyone or everyone from Catholic communion according to the rule of the heresy already condemned. For Acacius—understand the same thing of Eutyches—was not the inventor of a new or personal error, so that new decrees should be issued against him; rather, he joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. Indeed, Eutyches did more: he made a condemned error his own not merely by communion, but by assertion and defense.

### XII.

This was the genuine reason that deterred Flavian’s mind from calling a synod. Saint Leo plainly agreed with him when, after receiving Flavian’s letters and the proceedings, he understood what the matter was about. He immediately wrote back to the bishop of Constantinople in these words:

“I have received the letter of Your Charity, together with the proceedings concerning the matter of the faith that were completed among you. And because the most merciful emperor, concerned for the peace of the Church, wished a synod to be assembled, although it is clearly evident that THE MATTER AT ISSUE ABSOLUTELY DOES NOT REQUIRE SYNODAL DISCUSSION, nevertheless, dearest brother, I signify that those whom it has pleased him to appoint for this matter will follow” (Letter 32, now 36).

And in the following letter, addressed to Theodosius, he says:

“Since the case is so evident, it would have been more reasonable to refrain from calling a synod … because this is not the kind of question that can or ought to be doubted” (Letter 33, now 37).

Thus, when the pontiff had gained a clear view of the entire sequence of events, he judged that the synod should not be held. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Leo inserted the words quoted above into his letters after examining the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod and after confirming that synod’s judgment; consequently, he considered a general council superfluous after the confirmation of the Apostolic See.] As is perfectly clear, he argued that the synod was superfluous not because of approval or confirmation by the Apostolic See, but because it was useless: the case to be examined was certain, and the question itself was so evident that he considered it impious to call it into doubt.

This conviction was later strengthened by circumstances of place and time prescribed by the emperor Theodosius for the synod’s assembly. Leo learned that it was to be called outside Italy and was to be convened within such narrow time limits that he saw that most bishops from the Western regions would be prevented from traveling to the council. This was Leo’s view after he learned that the synod had been called.

But before all these matters were known to the pontiff, and after Flavian had instructed him concerning the whole sequence of events, Leo not only considered a synodal gathering beneficial to the interests of the Catholic cause but also sent an earnest letter to the emperor to obtain one. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Because of a chronological error that had crept into Letter 54, Quesnellus transferred these words to a time earlier than the pseudo-synod of Ephesus. Once that error is corrected with the help of the manuscript of Regensburg, it becomes clear that Saint Leo asked the emperor for a general synod in Italy in order to remedy the scandals of the Ephesian Robbery. We shall explain this more fully in the observations on Dissertation 8.]

“If Your Piety,” he says, “deigns to assent to our suggestion and supplication, so that you order an episcopal council to be held within Italy, then, with God’s help, all the scandals that have been stirred up to the disturbance of the whole Church can quickly be cut away. Thus, with the integrity of the Catholic faith preserved throughout your entire realm, we may rejoice both that Christian peace remains and that your glory before God increases” (Letter 23, now 54).

From these words and from those of several subsequent letters, it is clear that Leo then believed that a synod would bring the greatest benefit, and this for several reasons.

First, for the manifestation of the truth itself: because an ecumenical gathering of the Church would have much greater weight with the heresiarch than the authority either of any single bishop or of a particular synod. [Note: [Col. 0658D] It could only be Quesnellus’ perverse commentary, wholly remote from the mind of that pontiff—not Leo’s own words—that introduced these following reasons as less compatible with the authority of the Apostolic See. The true reason Saint Leo assented to the council called by the emperor was that it could not be prevented; and, not foreseeing the machinations of the Eutychians, he hoped it would prove useful.]

“Your Piety,” he says, “which most religiously loves the Catholic truth in honor of God, established a synodal judgment at Ephesus, so that THE TRUTH MIGHT BECOME KNOWN to the ignorant old man concerning the matter in which he is deeply blind” (Letter 26, now 38).

Second, so that, if the heretic wished to return to a sounder mind, he might be restored through episcopal clemency to the rank from which he had fallen by the greater synod.

“And if he who had gone astray,” he says, “should repent and plead for pardon, priestly benevolence would assist him; and if, by a written petition of satisfaction, he condemned his own error, communion in his proper order would not be denied him” (ibid. and following letters). [Note: [Col. 0658D] Why is the Antiochene canon thrust in here as though it directed Leo’s counsel, when it is certain that those canons had not yet been received by the Roman Church? The extent to which this canon detracts nothing from the authority of the Apostolic See is not the subject of discussion here.]

For it had been provided by Canon 12 of the Council of Antioch and by others that if someone—whether a presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, or a bishop perhaps condemned by a synod—became troublesome to the emperor, he ought to turn to a greater council of bishops, present to many bishops whatever he believed to be just, and await their investigations and judgments. All these provisions, which applied especially well to Eutyches, had again been enacted in the Constantinopolitan ecumenical council.

Third, so that through diligent investigation—greater diligence being applied in ecumenical councils than in any other judgments—the mouth of the heretic might be closed. Otherwise he would always complain that he had been circumvented and deceived by his opponents, unless his case were subjected to the general examination of the bishops.

“The most merciful emperor,” Leo says, “out of the benevolence and piety of his mind, wished that the condition of this man, who previously appeared honorable, should be judged MORE CAREFULLY; and for this reason he considered that an episcopal council should be called” (Letter 31, now 34, chapter 12).

Fourth, so that the entire matter might be ended by a full, final, and irrevocable judgment. Writing to the synod itself, which had been summoned to Ephesus, he says:

“The most Christian emperor wished an episcopal council to be held piously and religiously, so that BY A FULLER JUDGMENT every error might be abolished” (Letter 29, now 33, chapter 2). [Note: [Col. 0659D] How complete and irrevocable Leo considered his judgment concerning the entire Eutychian case, so that it could not even be called into doubt by a general council, will become clear from what is said in the observations on Dissertation 8.]

Therefore, since Saint Leo was deeply concerned about the matter of the faith and wished to learn through Flavian’s letters what outcome it would finally have in the synod, he earnestly requested that Flavian make him better informed about the resolution of the entire case. He evidently judged that the case could not otherwise be resolved decisively and irreformably, so to speak, than by the fuller and definitive judgment of an ecumenical synod.

Fifth, because the convocation of a council brought the matter to a conclusion, even though it was more laborious to bring six hundred bishops together into a single tribunal than to establish the judgment of one bishop or a provincial synod. [Note: [Col. 0659D] We do not know how he can establish this as a matter of experience. Some abandoned heresy without general synods, obeying especially the authority of the Apostolic See; others, on the contrary, remained stubborn in error and yielded to no authority, as is clear in the cases of the Arians, Nestorians, and Eutychians. Concerning Leo’s testimony from Letter 54, compare Annotation 19 (above, col. 657, note c).]

For experience teaches that heretics, even those wavering in the faith, have scarcely accepted the decree of anyone other than a universal council. Accordingly, Leo says that all the scandals stirred up to the disturbance of the whole Church could then be cut away if the emperor’s piety deigned to assent to his suggestion and request and ordered an episcopal council to be held. By this means, throughout the entire empire under Roman rule, the integrity of the Catholic faith was to be preserved, Christian peace guarded, and the emperor’s glory before almighty God increased. These points are plainly contained in Letter 23, now 54, to the Emperor Theodosius Augustus, whose words we quoted above (above, no. 12).

### XIII.

But while Saint Leo, placed in this uncertainty, was considering these matters—at one moment more inclined to assemble a synod, at another to remove it—Augustus Theodosius ordered that it be convened at Ephesus, [Note: [Col. 0659D] The argument drawn from the erroneous chronological notation of Letter 54, which gave the date as May 25, is eliminated by the correction of the day and month. Compare Annotation 19 [Col. 0660D] (in the place cited above). We proved in Annotation 8 (preceding volume, col. 789, note b) on Letter 30 that, in calling the synod at Ephesus, the emperor sought Leo’s consent.] without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff.

This is clearly established both by Saint Flavian’s first letter, in which he wished the council that was already being announced to be removed, and by several letters of Saint Leo the pope and by the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. The letters are accessible to anyone; from the Acts I establish the point as follows.

Leo sent a letter to Theodosius Augustus in which he earnestly begged him to order an episcopal council to be assembled. This letter is found dated on the eighth or ninth day before the Kalends of June, that is, May 25. But before it could be delivered to the emperor—indeed, before it had even been written—the Ephesian synod had already been called by Augustus, namely before the fifth day before the Ides of April, that is, April 9.

For at the gathering of thirty bishops held in Constantinople after Eutyches’ deposition, under the consulship of Protogenes, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, to review the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod, Bishop Meliphtongus spoke in these words:

“We request that this be referred to his [Theodosius’] Clemency … especially because he ordered a universal synod to be held, and it is necessary to reserve the more important cases for that council; and many have been summoned. It is right that what has been commanded by the most devout prince should be carried into effect.”

The same point is also confirmed by the words of Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum:

“I adjure you,” he says, “by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to reserve this matter for the future universal council, in accordance with the decree of the Christ-loving emperors.”

### XIV.

From what we have said and established thus far, I shall briefly gather a synopsis. First, it was not the custom of the Easterners for synodal proceedings—whether drawn up in a provincial council by the metropolitan or in a diocesan synod, as we now call it, by the bishop—to be sent to the West for examination. They were transmitted there only when either a particular controversy or accusation had developed into a public matter of the faith; or when someone condemned in a synod appealed to the other bishops; or when heretics, abusing the emperor’s favor, made it necessary to approach the bishop of the principal see, who could act with the prince, and to stir up his concern against the evil schemes of obstinate heretics.

Thus Flavian was doing nothing contrary to ancient canon and custom (Christian Lupus, volume I, Scholies and Notes on the Canons of the Councils, under the discussion of the Ephesian Robbery), although Christian Lupus accuses him on the ground that he did not report the proceedings of his synod to Rome. [Note: [Col. 0660D] It is evident from Letter 22 that Flavian immediately sent the proceedings of his synod against Eutyches to Leo. We showed in the preface that this letter was written immediately afterward, while refuting Quesnellus, who maintains that it was not Flavian’s first letter but a second one. His opinion rests on this false hypothesis: that the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod were sent to Rome not from the beginning, but only after the disturbances raised by Eutyches.]

For, to cite examples solely from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, who would believe that the Acts of the synods of Antioch and Berytus, held not long before the Constantinopolitan synod in the case of Ibas, were sent to Rome? Who would say the same of another Antiochene synod in the case of Athanasius of Pherae? Who would say that the proceedings of six hundred other synods had been sent to the Western regions up to that time?

Rather, Flavian would have acted contrary to custom if he had thought of sending them before Eutyches’ obstinacy, the publication of the written protests, the letters sent to Leo, fear of imperial power, the rumor or announcement of the council to be convened by Theodosius, and other circumstances of this kind had imposed upon him the necessity of informing the principal see about a case that had already become a common concern.

Second, I conclude that, if Eutyches appealed to Leo the pontiff, he was persuaded of one of two things: either that his appeal would not take effect, since at the same time that he wrote to Leo he also wrote to Dioscorus and requested a synod in the East; or that it had to be reduced and understood in the sense expressed by the words of the monk Constantine, so that it included the other metropolitans and exarchs rather than excluding them. [Note: [Col. 0660D] To prevent these points concerning Eutyches’ appeal from deceiving anyone, see Observations 3, 4, 5, and 9.]

Third, when the emperor himself ordered a synod to be assembled, either he took account of Eutyches’ appeal brought before Leo—for he could not have been unaware of it—or he gave it no consideration at all. If the former, then he understood it in the same way in which we have shown that Eutyches himself understood it: as admitting the other greater metropolitans and sees. If the latter, then he did not think Eutyches’ appeal should be granted; or at least he thought that Eutyches’ case should immediately be brought before the Church’s supreme tribunal, lest the matter be prolonged indefinitely. [Note: [Col. 0660D] Since Eutyches was doing everything possible to obtain protection for himself, and his supporters had induced the emperor to call a synod, who could rightly infer from this act the conclusions that Quesnellus thrusts upon us?]

Fourth, I observe that, when Augustus conceived the plan of assembling a synod, he had no thought whatsoever of consulting the Westerners, but later invited Leo by letter to attend the synod. [Note: [Col. 0661B] See above, Annotation 13 (col. 655, note c).] Leo raised no complaint about this matter with the emperor.

We leave the remaining arguments that that forensic theologian advanced on this subject for others to examine, since my purpose is not so much to refute alien positions expressly as to shed light, whenever necessary, on the writings of our Leo.

### XV.

Nevertheless, since they draw a powerful argument from the mention of the petition submitted by Eutyches, I shall add several points that may illuminate the letters of Saint Leo under discussion and the entire Eutychian case.

I think, namely, that four distinct kinds of petitions must be distinguished—petitions that Eutyches, condemned by his bishop, either submitted or falsely claimed to have submitted.

The first was the petition of appeal, which we have discussed.

The second was the written protest, which Saint Leo mentions in Letter 20, now 23, to Flavian, chapter 1. After an appeal has been lodged, letters must be given by the person from whose judgment the appeal was made to the person who is to hear the appeal; these letters are called letters of dismissal, or apostoli. “But if he does not accept this, let him protest.” Thus it is stated in the Digest, book XLIX, title 6, On Letters of Dismissal.

Accordingly, because Eutyches wished to persuade people that he had appealed, he publicly claimed that the petition of appeal had been presented by him but not accepted. He posted petitions throughout the streets of Constantinople and, as Liberatus writes, “he put up edicts in Constantinople and protested to the people that he had suffered injustice” (Part II of the Acts of the Ephesian Synod, act 3).

The third petition was one of complaint:

“For he sent to the Apostolic See, by a petition of grief, a complaint about his suffering,” says our Leo in Letter 21, now 24, to Theodosius Augustus.

A petition of complaint or grievance is properly and correctly said to be submitted by a presbyter against a bishop, or by a son against his father. “It is just and customary,” the jurists say, “for a son who complains of injuries inflicted by his father to be heard; scarcely anyone would tolerate that same son accusing him.” Thus the ancients moderated the matter, so that they adopted neither a milder form of appeal than the gravity of the judgment warranted nor a harsher one than filial piety itself required.

The fourth petition, namely a supplication, Eutyches submitted against Flavian’s judgment—or rather, several petitions, as may be seen in Act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon.

These four kinds of petition must first of all be distinguished, lest the force and significance of one be attributed to another, thereby obscuring the whole matter. Thus there was:

1. A petition of appeal to the council [Note: [Col. 0662B] Read Observation 3.];

2. A written protest to the people of Constantinople;

3. A petition of complaint or grievance to Saint Leo;

4. A supplication to the emperor.

The first was fictitious and was not actually submitted; the other three were genuinely submitted. Saint Flavian mentions all these petitions in his first letter to Saint Leo.

## LETTER OF EUTYCHES THE HERETIC

In which, writing to Leo, pope of the city of Rome, he denies two natures in Christ—that is, divinity and humanity.

“Confiding in my hope in the Lord and God of all, Christ,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0662B] We gave this letter in full, together with the fragments attached to it, from the Cassinese manuscript from which it was published, among the Leonine works, volume I, Letter 21.]

## APPENDIX TO DISSERTATION VII: ON EUTYCHES’ PETITION OF APPEAL, PUBLISHED FROM THE CASSINESE MANUSCRIPT BY CHRISTIAN LUPUS: WHETHER IT REALLY IS A PETITION OF APPEAL

[Col. 0661]

It is astonishing with what confidence Christian Lupus asserts, and cries out as though triumphant, [Note: [Col. 0661D] On this matter see Observation 4.] that the document which he transcribed from the Cassinese manuscript into his work on appeals is the very petition of appeal said to have been sent by the heretic Eutyches to Pope Leo I, by which he requested that the judgment be reconsidered by the Apostolic See.

First of all, Lupus is pleased to bestow upon this document the name “petition,” even though the document’s own heading resists this, and, more importantly, even though the writer himself resists and contradicts it. Eutyches himself clearly distinguishes between petitions and this letter of his. “I have appended to this letter of mine both petitions,” he says, “the one submitted to the synod by my accuser, and the one that was indeed brought forward by me but not accepted.” Here he calls each document by its proper name: he calls his own petition and that of Eusebius a “petition,” while designating his own letter by no other name than “letter.”

Saint Leo did use the name “petition,” because it is judicial terminology. Yet he did not call it a petition of appeal; rather, he called it a petition of grief or complaint. When he mentions the petition of appeal, he means not the document that Eutyches had sent to him, but the one that Eutyches claimed to have submitted during the trial, as the formalities of appeals required, as Saint Leo says—or, as Flavian writes in reply, he was lying, “through petitions full of every kind of deceit and cunning.”

If Eutyches wrote this to Leo, it was certainly not in the present letter, which contains nothing of a canonical appeal, nor in the passages that Lupus cites for this purpose.

The first passage is at the very beginning of the letter. Eutyches says:

“Confiding in my hope in the Lord and God of all, Christ, before all else—with God the Word as witness, recognizing in such thoughts the proof of truth—I also invoke your holiness as a witness [Note: [Col. 0661D] I correct this to “as a witness,” instead of “in testimony,” since both the sense and the construction require it, since the preposition *in* equally governs the word *rationes* that follows. QUESN.] of my heart and of the reasons underlying my thoughts and words.”

What else could the heresiarch mean by these words except to secure confidence in the account he was about to give, calling upon God the Word, who knows all things, as witness to the sincerity of his mind, and then addressing the very reader to whom he is speaking, so that the reader might judge what error was contained in this sincere profession of his faith? Perhaps he alludes to the Apostle’s words in 2 Corinthians 1:23: “I call God as witness upon my soul.”

That he invokes Christ and Christ’s vicar here in the same sense is demonstrated by the connection of the words—“before all else, as witness,” and “I also invoke”—and indeed by consideration of the entire passage, especially if it is punctuated only with the commas we have supplied. Thus the crude and poorly arranged translation of that Greek letter ought to have precisely this meaning:

“I, secure concerning my own faith and hope and concerning my mind, first call upon the very Son of God, who knows well the sincerity of my profession, as a witness to my heart; then I also call upon Your Holiness as a witness concerning the reasons underlying my thoughts and words—that is, so that you yourself may judge my words and thoughts and weigh their reasons with your fairness.”

Eutyches used a similar preface before handing over his confession of faith to be read aloud at the pseudo-synod of Ephesus:

“I commended myself,” he says, “to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, and to the word of truth of your justice, and I have you as witnesses to my faith.”

He uses the same idea more briefly in the confession of faith itself: “With both God and Your Holiness bearing witness for me.”

Whoever therefore insists that these words have the sound of a legal appeal shows that he has not read the heresiarch’s words with sufficient attention.

Nor do these other words contain an appeal any more clearly:

“I was asking that these things be made known to Your Holiness, and that I would follow in every respect whatever you judged appropriate.”

These are the words of someone making a request, not of someone appealing and demanding judgment as a matter of legal right. For just as no one to whom an appeal has been properly made may reject a petition of appeal, so the appellant expresses his desire not in submissive words but in words that require a judgment to be followed as a matter of necessity. If an appellant promises that he will obey the sentence of that judgment, as Eutyches does here, he plainly offers himself up to everyone’s ridicule. It would be as though the necessity of obeying the judgment of superiors did not exist.

Unless, perhaps, Lupus should say—which I would scarcely believe—that by these words Eutyches deprived himself of the ability to appeal from the pontiff to an ecumenical synod if the pontiff’s judgment were contrary to him. Finally, it is useful to compare the words in question with others spoken at Flavian’s second gathering in Constantinople.

When Eutyches’ supporters claimed that he had appealed at the first gathering, the bishops denied it, including Basil:

“I speak truly,” he says. “While that gathering was still sitting and the holy synod was proposing that this man should say that there are two natures after the union, I know that the religious archimandrite Eutyches said: ‘If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I will say this very thing.’ But he did not say this as one making an appeal; he said, ‘I have not dared to say it because of the Fathers.’”

This is precisely what Eutyches wished to indicate when he addressed Leo in these words—something that Lupus vainly attempts to turn into an appeal.

A third passage of the letter remains:

“To you, therefore, defenders of religion and those who execrate such factions, I flee … and I beg that, without any prejudice being created against me on account of the things done against me by treachery, you pronounce whatever judgment concerning the faith seems right to you.”

You see, my dear Lupus, what you do not wish to see: Eutyches flees to the defenders of religion, not to appeal to judges; he begs that no prejudice be created against him on the basis of Flavian’s judgment, rather than proclaiming that the judgment is null by virtue of an appeal; and finally, he asks that a judgment be pronounced concerning the faith, rather than concerning his deposition and excommunication, although, if he had appealed, the latter should have been dealt with first.

These points are more than sufficient to refute Christian Lupus. Nevertheless, by an abundance of legal argument, I add that if this entire document, whose parts we have already examined, was sent to Pope Saint Leo, [Note: [Col. 0663D] Compare the same Observation 9.] it was not sent to him alone, nor was it composed for him alone. Rather, it was an encyclical letter to all the bishops of the principal sees, whose authority Eutyches wished to mobilize against Flavian’s judgment and turn to his own advantage.

For even when those acting on behalf of the heresiarch at Ephesus falsely claimed that he had appealed, they did not name the Roman pontiff alone.

“When the condemnation was read,” says the monk Constantine, “Eutyches appealed to the holy council of the most holy bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica; and this was not inserted in the proceedings.”

The Most Illustrious Patricius said:

“When the crowd had gathered and the meeting had been dissolved, he quietly said to me, appealing to the Roman, Egyptian, and Jerusalem councils …”

The most reverend Bishop Basil said:

“He said: ‘If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I will say this very thing.’ But he did not say this as one making an appeal.”

Thus Eutyches directed this encyclical letter—which Saint Leo calls a petition of complaint—to all those bishops to whom he had either appealed or wished people to believe that he had appealed. One copy of it reached Leo the pontiff, to whom it was chiefly owed. [Col. 0664C] Hence the author of the heading correctly and without falsehood noted that it had been written to Pope Leo, although Christian Lupus calls him its compiler or copyist and its promulgator.

The letter itself loudly proclaims, in its entirety, that it is an encyclical. It contains not even a syllable about the Apostolic See or the Roman pontiff, whose prerogatives and splendor a man so intent at that time on winning the favor of everyone whose support he needed would certainly not have failed to praise. He therefore used only words appropriate to all the bishops of the principal sees.

To which of them do these words not apply?

“I invoke your holiness … so that these things might be made known to Your Holiness … To you, therefore, defenders of religion and those who execrate such factions, I flee.” [Note: [Col. 0663D] From these expressions in the Latin translation, which can be used out of courtesy in letters delivered to a single person, a thoroughly weak argument is drawn for inferring that this letter of Eutyches was an encyclical sent to several persons. See Letter 68, where Ceretius and two other Gallican bishops, writing to Leo in the plural, address him with “you have been forewarned,” etc. The same occurs in Theodoret’s Letter 52 to the same Leo. Many further examples could easily be adduced.]

Certainly these latter words alone—“to you, defenders of religion,” and so forth—make it clearer than the midday sun that this document was sent not to one person but to several.

## OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI ON QUESNELLUS’ DISSERTATION VII, “ON THE CASE OF EUTYCHES”

[Col. 0663D] 1123

1. Why Quesnel undertook to discuss this case of Eutyches in a separate dissertation is sufficiently apparent from its very opening, where he proposes to rebuke those who strive to persuade people that the right of appeal to the Roman See had been voluntarily extended from every region of the Christian world—and especially from the Eastern regions by the bishops of those parts—even in the earliest centuries of the Church. This right of appeal, which he found objectionable in the case of Celidonius, a Gallican bishop, displeased him much more in the cases of Easterners; and therefore he attempted to eliminate Eutyches’s appeal to Pope Leo on two grounds: first, he says, Eutyches did not truly appeal; second, his alleged appeal was not particular to Leo, or to the Apostolic See, but common to the Roman, Alexandrian, Jerusalemite, and Thessalonian synods, so that no special right was recognized in the Roman pontiff.

2. In the observations on Quesnel’s fifth dissertation, we clearly established the pontifical right to receive appeals from the entire Christian world, and we seem to have demonstrated quite plainly the extent to which this right belongs to him by virtue of the primacy itself. In the present controversy, however, insofar as it concerns Eutyches’s actual conduct, it must readily be admitted that he lodged no appeal to the Roman pontiff during the Constantinopolitan trial itself. From the acts of that same synod of Constantinople, at which Eutyches was condemned, and still more clearly from the rereading of those acts at another Constantinopolitan assembly held on 13 April 449—materials that were inserted into the first session of the Council of Chalcedon—it is clear that he offered before the sentence a single document of confession of faith, not a libellus of appeal.

Only if the testimony of the deacon Constantine is to be trusted did Eutyches, while his condemnation was being read or reread, appeal to the holy council of the most holy Roman, Alexandrian, Jerusalemite, and Thessalonian bishops. But according to Florentius Patricius, after the assembly had been dissolved, he said to me quietly, appealing to the Roman, Egyptian, and Jerusalemite council.

Later, writing to St. Leo, he said (Epistle 21):

> And indeed I immediately offered written documents, adding my signature to them, showing my confession concerning the holy faith. But when the holy archbishop Flavian neither received the libellus nor ordered it to be read, although he heard me and replied to me in these very words concerning the faith set forth at Nicaea and sought by the holy synod: that I should confess two natures, etc.

Here he distinguishes the libelli, or libellus, from the writings appended concerning the faith; and likewise, at the end of the same letter, he mentions two things distinctly: namely, “the libellus which,” he says, “was thrust forward by me, but was not received,” and “the exposition of my faith.” If he had said that the document of confession of faith had been offered to and not received by Flavian—who ordered Eutyches himself to read it aloud—he would have said something true. But when he asserted that a libellus had been offered and not received, distinguishing it from the document of confession of faith, he plainly meant a libellus of appeal and lied shamefully, as is brought out by the acts mentioned shortly before and as St. Flavian noted in Epistle 26 to St. Leo. See note 5 (vol. preceding, col. 715, no. c) on Epistle 21.

3. Leo testifies in Epistle 23 that this libellus, distinct from the confession of faith, which has not been preserved for us but had been attached to Eutyches’s letter to Leo, was a libellus of appeal. He could learn this not so much from Eutyches’s own Epistle 21 as from reading the same libellus attached to that letter.

In this matter it is especially astonishing that, in the appendix to the dissertation just mentioned, Quesnel should take such pains to show that Eutyches’s Epistle 21 to Leo was not a libellus of appeal but a libellus of complaint—as though, even if Eutyches pretended to have lodged an appeal to the pontiff during the trial, he nevertheless sent him after the trial only a libellus of complaint. Hence, at the end of the dissertation, where he distinguishes four libelli of Eutyches, he states that a libellus of appeal was given to the council, whereas a libellus of complaint, or grievance, was given to St. Leo.

This is all the more astonishing because, in his notes on St. Peter Chrysologus’s Epistle 25 to Eutyches, he writes unequivocally in no. 4: “It is evident that Eutyches could not have requested the judgment of the bishop of Ravenna except through a libellus of appeal, whether genuine or fabricated.” Why does he concede that what he declares necessary in Eutyches’s writings to the bishop of Ravenna—who had no right in appeals from the East—was done, yet deny that the same occurred with Leo, to whom that right belonged, and from whom we learn by the pontiff’s own testimony that an appeal, even if fabricated, was lodged at the time of the Constantinopolitan trial and later transmitted to Leo?

Quesnel’s entire error depends on his having considered only the letters of Eutyches to the same pontiff that have been preserved for us, in which an appeal is not expressly declared. He gave no thought to the libellus attached to those letters and distinct from the document of confession of faith. Since Eutyches falsely wrote in the same letter that this libellus had been offered in court but not received, Quesnel ought to have acknowledged that it was a libellus of appeal, however fabricated. For what Eutyches invented belonged to an appeal, as becomes clear from the rereading of the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod, and as Quesnel himself admits in the dissertation.

The heretic therefore sent Leo not only a letter—which may reasonably be called a libellus of complaint—but also, among the other documents attached to it, a libellus of appeal, which he most falsely represented as having been presented by him in court and not received.

4. In any case, Quesnel did not need to exert himself greatly in the appendix against Father Lupus, who thought he saw an appeal in Eutyches’s letter itself. This most crafty heretic, having pretended that an appeal had been lodged during the trial itself, did not wish to prejudice his fabricated appeal by making a new appeal after the trial, as though he regarded the former as worthless. Hence in the letter he refrained from words about lodging an appeal a second time, and was satisfied to send Leo, together with the letter, the libellus of the fabricated appeal that had supposedly been lodged before the sentence. In requesting Leo’s judgment and sentence concerning the faith, he simultaneously asked for what followed from that request: namely, that everything done against him should be annulled if the Constantinopolitan judgment concerning the faith appeared deserving of rejection.

Let us carefully consider these words of Eutyches:

> I beseech you, let no prejudice be done to me from what has been done against me through snares; pronounce such judgment concerning the faith as may seem right to you; permit no further calumny against me from factious men to proceed; and let me not be shaken out and removed from the number of the orthodox (Epistle 21).

Does he not, in these words, although he does not use the word “appeal,” plainly address Leo as a judge, asking him to pronounce judgment on the Constantinopolitan trial? When, besides a judgment concerning the faith, he also asks that provision be made for him, does he not demand judgment concerning his own person by an equivalent form of appeal?

Why does Quesnel attempt, through violent interpretations, to distort these words so that they may not appear to contain anything of an appeal? What does it matter that the explicit name of an appeal is not found in a letter translated from Greek into Latin, which may have fallen to a less competent translator, if Leo is in reality asked for what would have been sought through an appeal? It is not the word “appeal” that must be considered, but its force and legal effect.

The force of an appeal consists in seeking from a superior a judgment concerning the judgment of an inferior, and seeking it in such a way that the superior pronounces sentence on the matter and, if he recognizes the judgment as unjust, rescinds it, so that thereafter no prejudice arises from it for the condemned person. Since, therefore, Eutyches, in the words quoted and throughout Epistle 21, asks Leo to pronounce judgment on Flavian’s Constantinopolitan judgment concerning the faith, and, at the same time, hoping that this judgment will be rejected, asks that no harm or danger come to him from that judgment and that he not be removed from the number of the orthodox, has he not in reality expressed sufficiently the force and substance of an appeal and vindicated the right of appeal to Leo?

5. We have noticed two other, much more important features in this appeal, which Eutyches falsely claimed to have lodged during the trial itself. They will contribute considerably to understanding the Eastern attitude toward the pontifical right in appeals.

First, although this appeal was not lodged during the Constantinopolitan trial itself, and Eutyches therefore lied, nevertheless the man who not only invented this appeal but also sent the libellus of his fabricated appeal to Leo together with his letters of complaint, and requested Leo’s judgment, unquestionably assumed that the right of appeal to the Roman See was recognized and established among Easterners as well. He assumed it to be such that, if the appeal had genuinely been lodged during the trial itself, it would have suspended the proceedings or rendered invalid whatever was subsequently done in contempt of the appeal.

For if Eutyches had known that, among Easterners, the right of appeal to the Roman pontiff was regarded as worthless, would he have been so foolish as to invent something that, according to the Eastern understanding, could do him no good?

6. Second, if the testimony of Eutyches, a deceitful and criminal man, is to count for very little, should not the testimony and conduct of St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, count for very much? In Epistle 22—which, as we established in the note, was written immediately after Eutyches’s condemnation and was his first letter—Flavian, knowing nothing about the libellus of appeal sent to Leo, sent the same pontiff a simple account of Eutyches’s error and condemnation together with the acts of the council, asking him to make the matter known to the Westerners, lest the cunning man deceive someone who was insufficiently informed.

Thus several hypotheses constructed by Quesnel fall, including the claim that Flavian’s Epistle 22 to Leo was not his first but a later letter. After receiving from the pontiff a letter from which he learned of the appeal asserted by Eutyches, Flavian replied in another letter, Epistle 26. There he exposed Eutyches as a liar, while at the same time acknowledging the Apostolic right to review the judgments of the Easterners themselves, even when an appeal is brought after the trial. He therefore sent not only the Acts against Eutyches, but also submitted them to Leo’s judgment, asking him to make the common cause and discipline of the holy Churches his own and at the same time to **DECIDE** concerning the condemnation regularly pronounced against him and to deign to do so through his own writings:

> The case requires **ONLY** your support [Col. 0667C] and defense, by which, with your own agreement, you ought to bring everything to tranquility and peace. For thus, with God cooperating, the heresy that has arisen and the disturbances that have already occurred because of it will most easily be destroyed through your most sacred letters. The council also, which is being announced as about to take place, will be removed, so that the most holy Churches may not everywhere be disturbed.

Quesnel comments:

> Flavian therefore requests, he says, not Leo’s judgment but his support; not a sentence but a letter; defense, not confirmation; his own writings, not synodal decrees.

What a bad interpreter! Does “to decide concerning a condemnation regularly pronounced” not signify judgment and confirmation? The force of the Greek word used by Flavian, συμψηφίσασθαι, indicates a legal sentence that adds its vote to, or confirms, another judgment. For the verb ψηφίζεσθαι, from which it derives, is, in the common forensic formula, equivalent to “to pronounce sentence”; hence a sentence is also called ψήφισμα.

Furthermore, when Flavian added that the case required only Leo’s letters and assistance, did he not not only request confirmation of the judgment he had issued, but also show that such confirmation was necessary? And did he not show it to be necessary in such a way that no similar confirmation need be sought from any other see?

What is more, he added that the result of this confirmation would be that everything would be restored to tranquility and peace, that the heresy which had arisen and the disturbances stirred up by it would easily be destroyed, and that the very general council said to be about to be convened would be prevented. Could such numerous and important effects have been expected from letters that were neither judgment, sentence, nor confirmation? Is it not evident that Flavian sought something solemn, issued with the special authority of the Apostolic See? Were not the letters believed to possess authority for ending the case—after which the general council would be set aside as unnecessary—an authority equivalent to that of a general council, which under another hypothesis might still have been judged necessary?

Let every fair-minded reader therefore see how wrongly Quesnel interpreted Flavian’s intention and letters, lest it be thought that Flavian attributed nothing to the authority of the Apostolic See in the judgments of the Eastern bishops.

7. If we weigh Flavian’s words more precisely, it was not Flavian alone who attributed so much to this authority; he also assumed that the Easterners shared and acknowledged the same view, when he declared that everything in the East was to be settled and the heresy that had arisen was to be dispersed through Leo’s letters. Unless Flavian knew that all Easterners showed a comparable obedience to the Roman See, he certainly could not have made these assertions.

Indeed, if that celebrated Epistle 28 to the same Flavian—by which St. Leo, having examined the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod and pronouncing judgment on the entire matter, confirmed the condemnation of the Eutychian heresy—if, I say, that letter had not been maliciously concealed and suppressed at the general synod, which was convened at Ephesus not from any necessity but at the instigation and command of the emperor Theodosius, who favored Eutyches, those scandals would not have arisen through which that synod became a pseudo-synod and disturbed the entire East. Instead, all who did not support the heresy would have acquiesced in the apostolic letters, as we saw happen at Chalcedon.

8. In Leo’s letter there is another point especially relevant to the present matter. The holy pontiff did not merely pronounce judgment on Eutyches’s heresy, which had been proscribed at the Constantinopolitan synod, and confirm his just condemnation. He also subjected the judgment of that synod itself to examination and pointed out two matters requiring attention. Since they imply some correction of the synod’s own proceedings, they admirably establish the Apostolic right to reconsider and, where necessary, even correct the judgments of the Eastern bishops.

First, in chapter 6 he censured Flavian’s Constantinopolitan judgment because it had passed without any censure over Eutyches’s statement:

> I confess that our Lord was from two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature.

Concerning this, the holy pontiff says:

> I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession of his was not rebuked by any reprimand from the judges, and that a speech so foolish and so blasphemous was omitted as though nothing offensive had been heard (Epistle 28, chapter 6).

Is this not a correction of the Constantinopolitan judgment itself?

Second, although Eutyches had been condemned absolutely in that judgment, with no hope of restoration held out to him should he repent, St. Leo decided in the same chapter that this decree ought to be softened by showing mercy toward him if he condemned his error.

Lest anyone perhaps suspect that Leo had usurped an authority not due to him in these matters in order to advance his own rights, the Council of Chalcedon and the whole Catholic Church—which received this dogmatic letter and all its parts with such great praise, recognizing it not as a private letter but as a solemn judgment proper to apostolic authority—plainly refute this notion.

It was therefore not Eutyches alone, nor merely Flavian or Leo, but also the general synod of the Church and the universal Church herself that legitimately affirmed this Apostolic right. Only Quesnel and those hostile to the prerogatives of the Roman See can portray it as an usurped and incompetent right.

9. We now turn to the second point, in which he contends that Eutyches appealed not only to the Roman pontiff but also to the Alexandrian, Jerusalemite, and Thessalonian councils. Thus, if the right of appeal is to be inferred from this, nothing should be attributed to the Roman bishop over and above the Alexandrian, Jerusalemite, and Thessalonian bishops; or, if those bishops and their councils had no right above Flavian’s Constantinopolitan judgment on the basis of Eutyches’s appeal, then no such right can likewise be inferred for the Roman pontiff.

First, we observe that Eutyches did indeed spread his appeal among all those from whom he hoped to receive protection. But, so far as we know, he sent the libellus of appeal only to Leo; and it is clear that judgment was instituted by Leo alone and that the sentence was issued in Epistle 28.

We do not bring Eutyches’s conduct in this matter forward to establish the true right of appeal. It is well known that criminal and obstinate men, when condemned by a just sentence, also seek illegitimate support and strive by every means available to stir up disturbances and deceive the uninformed.

He also wrote to St. Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, because he had heard that Peter was a man of great renown and possessed considerable influence with Valentinian, although he had no right whatsoever over the bishop and synod of Constantinople. Hence he received from Peter the response found in Epistle 25, chapter 2: that he could not investigate and judge such matters without the agreement of the bishop of the Roman city.

It is astonishing that, in his notes on this letter, no. 2, Quesnel should present Eutyches’s action in such a way that, although he conceded that Peter Chrysologus had no right in this matter and did not deny that the Roman pontiff had such a right, he nevertheless contended in no. 4 that Eutyches had lodged an appeal with that same bishop of Ravenna, and consequently inferred that he had also lodged it with the other metropolitans of the West as well as with the Roman pontiff.

All this is asserted gratuitously, without any documentary evidence. But let us grant that Eutyches presented an appeal to others besides the Roman pontiff, although they had no right of appeal in this case. When he actually sent a libellus of appeal to the Roman pontiff, did he send it to one who did not possess that right?

10. To judge this right safely, one must consider not merely Eutyches’s conduct, but above all what Flavian and the Council of Chalcedon did on the occasion of that conduct, whether promoting or accepting Leo’s judgment.

We would like Quesnel to remember what he wrote in no. 9: “Let us not trust the most crafty impostor Eutyches . . . . Let us listen to Flavian, bishop of the New Rome and the bravest martyr of Christ.”

Certainly, although Eutyches spread his appeal among many, indeed even to the universal synod, Flavian nevertheless confessed—as we have seen—that the case required Leo’s judgment alone. He did not believe that the same judgment should be demanded from other metropolitans or patriarchs, whereas he requested it from Leo alone in such a way that he considered the judgment of neither any metropolitan or patriarch nor even the general council itself to be necessary.

And since, according to Quesnel’s own testimony in no. 9, “the mind and practice of the Easterners concerning appeals could not have been unknown to Flavian, bishop of the New Rome,” we must acknowledge that this was the mind and practice of the Easterners concerning appeals: they believed that the judgment of the Roman pontiff alone was sufficient and that neither the sentence of other sees nor that of a general council was required. Flavian himself declared that, after the judgment of the Apostolic See, the general council should be set aside as unnecessary.

The Council of Chalcedon likewise confirmed this pontifical authority when it accepted the judgment issued by Leo in this case in Epistle 28, by which a decree was made not only concerning Eutyches’s heresy but also concerning Flavian’s Constantinopolitan council.

What more? Quesnel himself could not deny this pontifical right in his notes on the aforementioned letter of Chrysologus. His only means of diminishing it to some extent was to present the appeal brought to Peter as one brought to him as head of the Western Church, as though what was referred to the Roman bishop should be regarded not as referred to the Roman See in itself but to the Western council.

“The Western synod,” he says in no. 1, “and its primate were concerned with those cases of appeal.” And in II.3:

> Moreover, when an appeal was made to the Western bishops, the agreement of the Roman bishop, unquestionably the chief of all the others, had to be ascertained; he was both, in a special sense, the head of the Western synod and, especially in matters of faith, the representative of the universal Church and the principal executor of the canons that had formerly been enacted in ecumenical councils against heretics.

Observe how many qualifications he uses to circumscribe this pontifical right, which he is forced to confess.

The extent to which this right belongs to the Roman bishop in his own person, even apart from cases of faith, was shown in the observations on the fifth dissertation. In Eutyches’s case of appeal, however, Epistle 28 was issued in Leo’s name alone because this right belonged to him by reason of the primacy. There was no necessity of convening a Western synod. The letter was issued with the authority of the Apostolic See, requested by St. Flavian, received by the Council of Chalcedon and by the entire Catholic Church, and recognized as possessing the highest force.

The testimony relevant here is therefore not that of Eutyches alone, but that of Flavian, who requested this judgment from Leo; and that of the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon and the whole Church, which received the same judgment issued by Leo with such great veneration.

You see, therefore, how this allegedly fabricated appeal of Eutyches contributes greatly, precisely in the case of appeals from the East, to establishing the right of the Apostolic See. Quesnel’s remaining conjectures—or rather quibbles—collapse sufficiently under what has been said and reveal his hostility toward the Roman See; they require no further response.

# EIGHTH DISSERTATION

## On the Case of Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, Condemned and Deposed in the Ephesian Pseudo-Synod

On St. Leo’s Letters to the Emperor Theodosius, 39 and 40 (now 43 and 44)

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669D] 1133

I. Of the appeals said to have been brought to the Apostolic See in the earliest centuries of the Church, the most celebrated of all is the one submitted by Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, after a sentence had been issued against him by Dioscorus. For, they say, the appeal was made not from a provincial or diocesan synod, but from one that enjoyed the title of an ecumenical synod, being composed, that is, of bishops collected from everywhere, and attended by the three principal primates and patriarchs of the Church: the Western one through legates, and the Eastern ones in person.

The decision to undertake at least a brief discussion of this appeal—which constitutes almost the entire and principal subject matter of Letters 39 and 40 (now 43 and 44)—requires such a treatment, although the subject does not demand a more extensive discussion, having long since been thoroughly debated by more learned men.

It should first be noted that St. Leo never wrote that his own See had been appealed to by Flavian. Rather, he speaks generally of an appeal having been lodged, as he says in chapter 3 of this letter; he also says that his legates faithfully protested, and that Bishop Flavian gave those same legates a libellus of appeal.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] We shall prove in Observation no. 4 and following that this was a libellus of appeal to the Apostolic See.]

The Greek Acts of the Ephesian synod, reread at the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, agree with Leo. They report nothing else as having been said by Flavian except this:

[Note: [Col. 0670D] On this formula, see Observation no. 2, where the following quibbles will also be refuted.]

> I reject you, παραιτοῦμαί σε,

and, according to Hilary, Leo’s legate:

> It is contradicted, κοντραδίκιτουρ.

Whether Flavian understood a genuine appeal, as the recent writer laboriously contends against Marca, or a rejection, as others assert and David himself finally admits, makes no difference. I assert only this: Flavian did not mention Leo, whether he was appealing or rejecting.

Although I should say a word about Flavian’s rejection, as asserted by Peter de Marca, I am astonished that David should defend so obstinately in this passage the customary formulas of canonical trials. Everything was undertaken by Dioscorus contrary to law and right, and the ordinary practices and formulas of trials could in no way be adapted to the Ephesian robbery.

Let us grant that, according to the order of law, there is no place for rejection except before sentence has been pronounced, and no place for appeal except after judgment has been delivered. That is entirely proper when either a legitimate judge has reasonably become suspect or judgment is being arranged by an incompetent judge. But you will find nothing of the kind in the Ephesian robbery.

At the beginning, the synod had been lawfully convened by command of the emperor and with the assent of the pontiff, who was also present through his legates; it therefore could not in any way have been rejected or repudiated. It remains, then, that Dioscorus and his synod could first have been rejected when Dioscorus, claiming everything for himself through violence and crime and overturning every judicial form, appeared to change from a bishop into a robber and murderer, and to transform a previously legitimate synod into a criminal assembly.

At that point there was room not so much for an appeal—which presupposes a legitimate and competent judge—as for rejection and protest against an assembly which, as St. Leo says, no principle permits to be called a synod.

Indeed, rejection and appeal differ widely in several respects. One is that rejection nullifies a sentence as having been delivered by an incompetent judge; appeal, however, merely suspends the effect of the sentence, as having proceeded unjustly from a judge who was nevertheless qualified, until it is recalled for examination by a superior.

Leo repeatedly and emphatically declares that the Ephesian judgment was unworthy of the name of synod, even before a renewed examination. He thereby sufficiently indicates that rejection had more relevance than appeal. For how could that assembly be called a synod where everything was conducted like a raid? Where, as Leo complains, those gathered pronounced concerning the faith and those in error not according to custom? Where the leaders of the synod spared neither those who resisted them nor those who consented? Where we learn that not all who had assembled were present? Where some were rejected and others admitted, men who, at the sole discretion of Dioscorus, gave their captive hands to impious subscriptions? Where violence was inflicted upon all the Churches? Where the writings of the Apostolic See were not permitted to be published to the ears of the bishops? Where the pontiff’s legates were not granted their proper place? Where, as the Fathers of Chalcedon complain, violence was used, force accompanied by blows, condemnation was threatened, threats of exile were made, and soldiers pressed forward with clubs and swords? Where there were swords and clubs—what kind of synod is that? (Epistle 39, now 43, chapter 1; Epistle 75, now 95, chapter 2; Epistle 39, now 43, chapter 1; Epistle 40, now 44, chapter 1; Council of Chalcedon, part II, session 1.)

[Col. 0671D] Hence you see how rightly and legally Flavian cried out:

> Παραιτοῦμαί σε—I reject you.

Nevertheless, because the agreement and subscription of almost all the bishops gave the impious assembly some appearance of a synod, and because the authority of the emperor and the civil powers intervened, Flavian, when he later handed a libellus of appeal to the legates of the Apostolic See, thought it appropriate to use the language of appeal, so that, by virtue of the right of appeal, an opportunity might be provided for a new synod.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] In the Observations we shall show two things: (1) that Flavian appealed to the Apostolic See and to the Roman synod, which Roman pontiffs customarily convened in such cases; (2) that the authority of these synods lay chiefly in the supreme pontiff, whose power was principally involved in appeals. See no. 5 and following, through no. 12.]

II. In appealing, however, Flavian did not mention Leo’s name, as I have said. Here Leo himself also supports us. Although he frequently discusses this appeal and the repetition of the council in letters written after the Ephesian assembly, he never says that his own See had been appealed to. A pontiff so devoted to the rights of his See would never have omitted that point if it had been so. Instead, he simply asserts that an appeal was lodged.

He says (Epistles 39 and 40, now 43 and 44, chapter 3):

> Concerning the confession of Christ’s true divinity and true humanity, which is now impiously opposed by a few heedless men, all the Churches of our regions and all the priests of our side entreat Your Clemency with groans and tears: since our representatives faithfully protested and Bishop Flavian gave those same men a libellus of appeal, command that a general synod be celebrated within Italy. Let it either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further remains doubtful in the faith or divided in charity. Let the bishops of the Eastern provinces assemble, so that any of them who, overcome by threats and insults, have strayed from the path of truth may be restored wholly through salutary remedies; and let those whose case is more difficult, if they accept better counsel, not fall away from the unity of the Church.

That this should necessarily be requested after an appeal had been lodged is testified by the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, established by the priests of the whole world and appended below.

Here I read that the legates protested; I read that an appeal was lodged; I also read that a libellus of appeal was given to the legates. But I do not read at all to whom the appeal was made.

On the contrary, John David says that from these very words it is evident that the Roman pontiff was appealed to. Every appeal, he says, necessarily has to be brought before some judge. Since Flavian gave the libellus of appeal to the legates, he did so because he recognized in them jurisdiction that enabled them to receive an appeal. Such a right could not belong to private individuals; therefore he must have handed over the libellus as to papal legates, because he recognized the pontiff as a suitable judge for examining the appeal.

I am astonished that a man devoted to handling lawsuits and conducting legal proceedings should be so ignorant of the norm and practice of jurisdiction as not to know what no one who has even crossed the threshold of a court is unaware of. Who ever imagined that a libellus of appeal should be handed to the person to whom one appeals, or to his deputies?

On the contrary, according to the form of Roman law, it is handed to the person from whom the appeal is made, who grants the litigant apostoli—that is, letters of dismissal—which say: “Let it be known to you that R. has appealed from my sentence, and therefore I dismiss him from my judgment and direct him to yours,” as in the Digest, *On Letters of Dismissal*, book 1.

Thus the Apostle Paul, when he appealed to Caesar from the governor Festus (Acts 25:10), directed the words of appeal to none other than that same governor. Nor was the appeal received by anyone else, or the appellant dismissed to Caesar by anyone else:

> Then Festus, after conferring with the council, replied: “You have appealed to Caesar? To Caesar you shall go” (ibid., 12).

And later:

> Since he had appealed to Augustus, I decided to send him (ibid., 25).

Now, when Flavian appealed from Dioscorus and his disastrous synod to another council, to whom could he have handed his libellus except to the Roman legates, who alone, or almost alone, had not consented to Dioscorus’s wicked machinations?

First, because Dioscorus, acting entirely through violence and arbitrary power, would not permit any legal form to be observed; second, because almost all the prelates of the synod had given their captive hands to Dioscorus; third, because Flavian was appealing especially to the Western bishops, as was Theodoret, and therefore it was necessary that Flavian’s appeal be made known to their patriarch and to the chief of them all.

Finally, when one appeals to the universal council of the whole Church, whom should one approach with the libellus of appeal rather than the one who is both the supreme summit of the entire Church and, in a matter of faith, its universal guardian, who bears the principal responsibility and care for convening an ecumenical synod, and who, finally, possesses the right to the first vote and the first place in councils?

These are the true reasons that moved Flavian to place the libellus of appeal or rejection in the hands of the legates. For this purpose it was not necessary that they possess jurisdiction in their own right or in the pontiff’s name; it was sufficient that they were part of the council and suitable witnesses to the appeal that had been lodged.

### III

As for what that writer decides—namely, that every appeal must invoke some judge—it is so, if this is David’s meaning: whenever an appeal is made, it is made to someone. But two points must be noted, lest these words deceive anyone. First, he wrongly confuses two persons: the one who receives the appeal document and the one whose task it is to judge the appeal. We have shown that these are separated by a considerable interval, since the person who received the document was rather the one from whose judgment the appeal had been made. Second, it must be noted that, although an appeal is always made to someone, it is not necessarily required that his name be specified either orally or in writing. The formal requirements of an appeal demand nothing more than that, immediately after judgment has been pronounced, while the judge is still sitting on the bench, the litigant say aloud: “I APPEAL.” When an appeal is made after an interval by means of an appeal document, it is sufficient to state who is appealing, from whom, and from what judgment, even if the name or office of the judge to whom the appeal is made is not expressed.

The deception that David attempted to insinuate from the words of Saint Leo therefore disappears. Not only do Leo’s words, which he tried to twist by an alien interpretation, fail to support his position; the very silence of Leo concerning the pontiff’s see altogether contradicts the meaning David strove to attribute to them. Even if we grant that a negative argument does not always possess great force, here it has the greatest force, since it is certain that the pontiff was not so forgetful of his own case that he would suppress in silence the appeal which the bishop of Constantinople had expressly brought before the Roman see, and would appear voluntarily to reject the prerogative thus offered to him.

### IV

Moreover, from the words quoted from Letter 40 (now 44), we have another extremely powerful argument [Note: This argument will be examined in Observation no. 13, and Leo’s meaning explained in no. 14 and following], by which it is established that the appeal was made to a synod and then to Leo as the head of the synod. Since, on the basis of that bishop’s appeal, Leo invokes the necessity of convening an ecumenical synod, it is clearer than daylight that the appeal was made to a synod, and that the appeal document did not challenge the authority of someone else so that he might judge the sentence of the Ephesian Robber Synod.

“But what,” he says, “is necessarily demanded after an appeal has been lodged, the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify.” For if an appeal had been made to one Western bishop together with a provincial or diocesan synod, why should he not alone, together with his comprovincial bishops, prepare the judgment? Why are the priests of all the Churches removed from their sees if the case can be concluded by the judgment of one man?
