Why is an ecumenical synod necessarily demanded when the appeal was not made to an ecumenical synod? If the primary see has been approached by an appeal document, let the pontiff summon the litigants before his own see, investigate the matter, seek the opinion of his fellow bishops, and pronounce judgment—and the case is concluded.

But Leo judged that a general synod had necessarily to be demanded after the appeal was lodged because he understood from Flavian’s own appeal document and from ecclesiastical custom that Flavian had demanded one. He did not consider it to have been left to his own prudence and judgment whether the calling of a synod should be abandoned or pursued. Rather, he held that, from necessity and from the obligation of his office, he had to seek it, even—as he himself says—with groans and tears, and, as Liberatus writes (*Breviarium*, chapter 12), to plead prostrate on his knees.

Thus Pope Innocent I, after the deposition of Saint John Chrysostom, sought to convene an ecumenical synod, as Sozomen says in Book VIII, chapter 26. Writing to the clergy of Constantinople, he says:

> But what remedy shall we presently bring to these circumstances? A synodal investigation will be necessary; indeed, we have already said long ago that it must be convened. For it alone can blunt the assault of storms such as these. Until we obtain it, it is expedient to entrust the cure of this calamity to the will of the great God and of his Christ, our Lord.

And later:

> We are giving much thought to how an ecumenical synod may be convened, through which, by the will of God, these turbulent disturbances may be brought to rest.

As we have said, Saint Leo understood that this burden rested upon him. The other bishops of the Western regions understood it as well. When they heard the news of the appeal, they embraced this cause as common to all of them and proper to each, and through Leo’s letters they approached the emperor as suppliants, asking him to order the convocation of a general synod. There, after Eutyches’ doctrine had again been examined and the cases of Flavian and Dioscorus had been investigated, they could pronounce a judgment that would bring this affair to an end.

“All the priests,” Leo says (*Epistle* 40, now 44, chapter 3), “of the Churches of our regions—all of them—beseech your Clemency with groans and tears: since our representatives faithfully protested, and Bishop Flavianus gave them his appeal document, order that a general synod be held within Italy, with the bishops of the Eastern provinces assembling there.”

All the Western bishops had not yet been able to communicate their wish to Leo. But the pontiff, as the head and voice of all, explains to Theodosius the mind of all and pursues and presses before him the right of all, with no hesitation that all wished the appeal brought before him to be examined in a synod once it had been convened. Nor did he arrogate to himself the right to demand a synod in his own name alone, lest he appear to make common right his own and reserve it exclusively to himself.

It must also be carefully noted from these words of our Leo that all the Western bishops and Churches did not petition for a synod merely because the matter of the faith, being common to all, was in danger, or for some other reason, but chiefly because the representatives of the apostolic see had protested and Flavian had given them the appeal document. According to Leo’s testimony, all the Western bishops derive their right from this fact, and here they put forward no other reason.

### V

From this, two conclusions of the greatest importance seem necessarily to follow. The first, which we discussed above, is that Flavian’s appeal devolved not upon some single pontiff, but at least upon all the bishops of the West. The second [Note: These matters and what follows will be examined in Observation no. 25 and following] is that the representatives of the apostolic see participated in the Second Ephesian Synod not merely in the name of the Roman pontiff, nor were they otherwise accustomed to participate in the ecumenical councils convened in the East, but also in the place of all the bishops of the entire West, whose procurators they were when those bishops could not be present in person.

It was customary for the Roman bishop, as soon as a universal synod had been announced, to notify all the bishops of his patriarchate concerning it and himself to convene a synod at Rome, to which the Western bishops who had been invited would gather. There they would discuss the matter collectively and choose representatives to fulfill the role of those who were absent.

Those who were sent as representatives from that Roman synod were therefore not representatives of the pontiff alone, nor were they said to have been sent by him alone. They had been sent by the entire synod and acted in its place, although they always retained the title “representatives of the apostolic see,” because the pontiff was the leader of all the Western bishops. This becomes perfectly clear from the Third Ecumenical Synod at Ephesus. There Cyril, summarizing the judgment of the representatives of the apostolic see, speaks as follows:

> For they deposed him, supplying the place of the apostolic see and of the entire synod of the most holy and most beloved-of-God Western bishops.

(*Acts of the Council of Ephesus*, Part II, Action 3.)

And in the report sent to the emperor:

> The most pious archbishop of your great Rome, and the entire Western synod, through the most holy bishops whom it itself sent to us, etc.

The same is evident from the acts of the Sixth Council, where the bishops of Portus, Paternus, and Rhegium are said to have occupied the place of the council of ancient Rome, at which one hundred and twenty bishops had assembled. Hence, very often, when our pontiff sends representatives from a synod, he writes not only in his own name but also in the name of the council, in this form: “Leo and the holy synod which assembled at Rome,” and so forth.

If wars, public calamities, or the shortness of time prevented the pontiff from convening a synod from all his dioceses, then each diocese convened its own council. From it representatives were sent to the Roman synod, carrying the judgment of the bishops of that diocese. That judgment was then entrusted to the common representatives of the entire patriarchate who were to proceed to the ecumenical synod. These representatives, sent by the apostolic see—the foremost of the others—where the council had assembled, and to whose bishop all the Western bishops had gathered through representatives or letters as to the *κορυφαῖος* (“leader”), as Basil calls him, received the title “representatives of the apostolic see.”

Thus, when our Leo announced the Council of Chalcedon, he sent to Gaul so that the assent of the Gallican diocese, sent from its synod to Rome, might be conveyed to the ecumenical synod by the representatives of the apostolic see. We have Leo himself as witness in the letter that he wrote in reply to the Gallican bishops after receiving their letters. “Indeed,” he says (*Epistle* 77, now 102, to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 1), “we would have wished to receive the letters of your Brotherhood at the time you had promised, so that, when our brothers were departing for the East—those whom we sent to the holy synod in our place for the defense of the Catholic faith—the profession of your judgment might also be joined to theirs.”

Finally, when the time fixed for convening the ecumenical synod was so short that it permitted neither the votes of other dioceses to be awaited nor even letters to be sent to them, a council was convened either from the diocese of the City or from those bishops who were then staying in the City. Representatives were sent from it who received and exercised from the patriarch and from his diocesan or provincial synod the procuratorship of the entire Western patriarchate, and who represented all the Western bishops at the ecumenical synod.

This is what Leo did after he received from the East the news that the Second Ephesian Synod had been announced. For, as the pontiff relates (*Epistle* 27, now 31, to Pulcheria, chapter 4), the emperor, wishing to settle the disturbances as quickly as possible, fixed an excessively short and narrow period for the episcopal council that he wished to be held at Ephesus, setting the day of the Kalends of August for the assembly, although most of the remaining time had to be consumed in arranging the departure of the priests who were capable of dealing with the matter.

With affairs arranged in this way, nothing remained except for the pontiff, confident in the faith of his Western bishops, to send to the East those who would represent the cause of all, and unquestionably to write concerning everyone what he later said he had written concerning the Gallican bishops for the Council of Chalcedon. “With good reason,” he says (*Epistle* 77, chapter 2), “we acknowledge that we informed our brothers and fellow bishops in the East that, according to the evangelical and apostolic tradition, there was one and undivided confession among all of us concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

From this it is clear how badly John David served his own case when, from the fact that the appeal document was said to have been handed to the representatives, he asserted that Flavian had appealed to Leo alone. For it is evident from what has been said that the representatives did not act in the person of the pontiff alone, but in the person of all the Western bishops; consequently, the appeal was brought before all those in whose name they participated in the synod. Accordingly, all the bishops of the Western regions rightly and properly demanded a synod, as Saint Leo testifies, and argued for its necessity on the basis of the representatives’ protest and of the appeal document that Flavian had handed to those same representatives.

### VI

“But,” that writer says, “Saint Leo adduces the authority of the Nicene canons—that is, in this context, the Sardican canons—in order to assert the fairness of his demand on the basis of Flavian’s appeal. Yet the Sardican canons mention no appeal except one that concerns the Roman bishop alone. Therefore,” he says, “either Saint Leo improperly and irrelevantly abuses the decrees of the synod, or he understood that Flavian’s appeal had devolved upon himself.”

I would say that a man who supports his case with such weak props and such mutually contradictory arguments is acting perversely. For those decrees enacted at Nicaea, which Saint Leo cites, are so obscure to most people that nothing could be more obscure. Nothing of the kind is found among the Nicene canons, and David is forced to take refuge in the Sardican canons, which he conjectures Leo cited under the name of the Nicene canons, as many had conjectured before him.

We readily grant this much [Note: See Observations no. 20 and following, in which Quesnellus’s entire subsequent line of reasoning is subjected to critical examination]: Leo did bring forward the Sardican canons, dressed here in another name, in order to argue for the necessity of an ecumenical council. But I insist that what David wishes to infer from this is utterly absurd—namely, that it was then known to no one that Flavian’s appeal had challenged the tribunal of the apostolic see alone, since the Sardican canons decree only concerning appeals of that kind. There is no one who would not consider such a method of argument unworthy of Leo.

If the Sardican canons established anything only concerning appeals to the Roman pontiff, then an ecumenical synod must be convened to judge Flavian’s appeal.

But the Sardican canons establish matters only concerning appeals to the Roman pontiff.

Therefore, an ecumenical synod must be convened to judge Flavian’s appeal.

You see, my David, how absurd that major premise is, although your argument must necessarily rely upon it. Leo would have seemed to draw the opposite conclusion more correctly in favor of his own see:

The Sardican canons concern only appeals to the apostolic see. Therefore, by the authority of the Sardican canons, the apostolic see alone ought to judge Flavian’s appeal.

But Saint Leo does not draw this conclusion. Rather, from the decree of the Sardican canons he concludes that a council must be convened in which the appeal would be examined.

For Leo’s argument to proceed correctly, one point must be assumed—something very far removed from David’s understanding, yet of the greatest importance: namely, that the pontiff was convinced that when the Sardican synod granted bishops the power to appeal to the apostolic see, or to the Roman bishop, it intended the appeal to be brought not to the bishop considered in isolation, but to him surrounded by the bishops of his dioceses. Nor did it consider the appeal capable of being judged otherwise than by all the Western bishops assembled under their patriarch, with the bishops of the Eastern provinces assembling as well, precisely as Leo expresses it here.

On that understanding the pontiff’s reasoning is not defective, as David eagerly insists; rather, it fully accords with the rules of dialectic. To demonstrate this, Leo’s enthymeme must be resolved into a syllogism. From that, no one could fail to see more clearly than in the midday sun what Leo had in mind and what must necessarily be supplied.

The pontiff’s enthymeme, then, from Letters 39 and 40 (now 43 and 44), is as follows:

The tribunal to which the Sardican synod judged that an appeal should be made must necessarily be sought after Flavian’s appeal has been lodged.

Therefore, after Flavian’s appeal has been lodged, the tribunal of an ecumenical council—or of a Western council assembled under its patriarch, with bishops from the East and from the whole world assembling—must necessarily be sought.

The minor premise of this enthymeme must be supplied for it to become a complete syllogism. We give it here:

The tribunal to which the Sardican synod judged that an appeal should be made must necessarily be sought after Flavian’s appeal has been lodged.

But the Sardican synod judged that an appeal should be made to the tribunal of an ecumenical council—or of a Western council assembled under its patriarch, with bishops from the East and from the whole world assembling.

Therefore, after Flavian’s appeal has been lodged, the tribunal of an ecumenical council—or of a Western council assembled under its patriarch, with bishops indeed from the East and from the whole world assembling—must necessarily be sought.

### VII

Moreover, from Leo’s mind and reasoning we obtain not only what we presently wished to establish—namely, that Flavian did not give his appeal document to the pontiff alone, nor did Leo himself assume that he should judge alone after the appeal—but also an excellent and singular interpretation of the Sardican canons, handed down by the Roman pontiff himself. No one more learned, nor anyone more devoted to the rights of his own see, ever governed the Roman Church than this pontiff.

From Leo himself, I say, we learn what should be done by the Roman bishop when an appeal was made to him, and in what sense those canons permitted appeals to him. “For they are the canons,” says Pope Gelasius (*Epistle* 4 to Faustus the Magister), “which wished the appeals of the entire Church to be brought before the judgment of this see.”

To make the matter more readily understood, the Sardican canons must be placed before the reader’s eyes.

#### Canon 3

If anyone has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good cause, so that the council may be renewed, then, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of Saint Peter, so that those who examined the case may write to Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, then what he decrees shall be confirmed. Does this please everyone?

The synod replied: It pleases us.

#### Canon 4

Bishop Gaudentius said: If it pleases you, let this be added to the sentence that you have pronounced with complete holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of the bishops who reside in neighboring places, and he has declared that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop shall be appointed to his see after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

#### Canon 7

Bishop Hosius said: It has also pleased us that, if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops assembled from his region have judged him and removed him from his rank, then, if the one who has been removed appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, and if the Roman bishop judges that the judgment ought to be renewed—or, alternatively, that the examination ought to be renewed—he should deign to write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may diligently investigate everything and determine the matter according to the faith of truth.

If the man who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his entreaty to send a presbyter from his side, the bishop shall have the power to decide what he wishes and considers appropriate. If he decrees that representatives should be sent to judge together with the bishops present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were appointed, the matter shall remain within his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he shall do what he judges in his most prudent counsel.

It should also be noted that this council was convened for the sake of Saint Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, and the other bishops whom the Arians had long been harassing with false accusations. This is evident from the fact that letters were decreed to Julius, then bishop of Rome, for no other reason than that he might understand, by the force of these canons, that Athanasius’s case belonged to him.

1. The first purpose of the orthodox bishops who had assembled there was to bring the case of Saint Athanasius and his companions into the West. This was because most of the Easterners, who held supreme power, and the emperor himself hated Athanasius worse than a serpent and were working with all their might for his destruction. It was also because the majority of the Sardican fathers belonged to Western Churches, and especially because their leader, Hosius of Corduba, was the mind and voice of the entire synod.

3. Those canons were enacted for Athanasius’s benefit and in accordance with his own understanding, as though they had been established on the basis of the precedent created when he himself went to Rome. For approximately seven years before the Council of Sardica, Athanasius had gone there after the Eusebians had sent representatives to Pope Julius to invoke his authority and the tribunal of a Western council against Athanasius. In fact, a Western council was announced as to be convened at Rome in June of the year 341, as though by agreement between both parties, and it was subsequently held.

With these points in view, the Sardican Fathers, in the first of those three canons, presuppose that a bishop has received a sentence from the council of his own province, but that, considering himself wronged, he requests that the council be renewed. Hosius—whom long experience in ecclesiastical affairs and the persistent evasions of the Arians had taught that bishops were very often removed from their sees without any justification and through the cunning of heretics, so that they might be summoned to a council—judged it best that a council should grant someone the power to determine whether and when there ought to be an opportunity for appeal. Otherwise ecclesiastical judgments would be exposed more to the devices and insolence of certain scoundrels than secular judgments are.

For you have, in Book VII of the Code, Title 65: “Whose Appeals Are Not Received.” As the glossator says, an appeal is sometimes suspended because it is unnecessary, and sometimes because the appellant does not deserve to be heard; the entire matter is explained in that cited title. Whom could the synod have honored with this office more suitably than the Roman pontiff, the common father of all, in whom the memory of the apostle Saint Peter was to be honored?

A provincial synod was suspect to the condemned party, while it was not in the interest of ecclesiastical affairs to assemble the bishops of neighboring provinces for this purpose. This burden was therefore assigned to the Roman bishop, who did not need laborious investigation or a careful examination of the entire case for this task, but only a summary acquaintance with it, perhaps from the letters of the previous judges—just as it is easy for a secular judge immediately to determine which appeals the laws of civil law permit or forbid receiving.

If he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, the provincial sentence retains its full force. If he judges that the judgment should be renewed, he orders its renewal and writes to the bishops in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they themselves may investigate everything diligently and determine the matter according to the faith of truth. If he wishes, he also sends a presbyter from his own side, who joins his assistance to that of the bishops who are to judge, with the authority and in the name of the one who sent him.

This is what Canon 7 contains. It makes little difference whether the statements expressed in the other two canons are understood as concerning a simple review or reconsideration of the prior judgment, or a genuine appeal, since the whole matter is established by the authority of the council in such a way that it remains within the litigant’s power to approach that tribunal.

Certainly, in those two canons the word “appeal” does not occur except once: “if he appeals and takes refuge with the Roman bishop.” In its place, however, in the African synod, where Canon 7 is reported, and in the Greek version, we read: “if he appears to have appealed.” From this it seems that the fathers did not honor this procedure with the proper name of an appeal, but more often express it in other words: “to renew the examination,” “to renew the judgment,” “to reopen what has been done,” “to take refuge with the Roman bishop,” and “to have the case heard again.” Therefore, when the canon says, “If he appeals,” it does not add “to the Roman bishop,” but rather intends “another judgment” to be understood. It immediately adds: “and takes refuge with the Roman bishop,” namely, in order to obtain another judgment in accordance with the synod’s decree.

Whether, for this later judgment, newly appointed judges were required to sit together with the previous judges, according to the meaning of the canon, Marca affirms and David denies. From the words of the canon itself, the matter seems obscure and uncertain to me. Yet it would appear altogether unusual for one province to be given authority over another, and for the judgment of the latter to be recalled for examination while that province itself was disregarded.

A course more consistent with ecclesiastical discipline and custom had been adopted a few years earlier by the Fathers of Antioch. Although they were hostile both to Catholic doctrine and to Saint Athanasius, they decreed in Canon 14 that, when a judgment concerning a bishop was to be held and the bishops of his own province were divided, bishops from a neighboring province should be summoned, so that, through them together with the comprovincial bishops, whatever seemed just might be approved.

### VIII

As for the order of those three Sardican canons, Peter Marca, praised by John David, conjectures that the order now found in all printed and manuscript codices is not original. He argues that Canon 7 should be joined to Canons 3 and 4; indeed, David alone insists that it should precede Canon 4.

This conjecture is utterly overturned even by the codices of the Roman Church alone, whether the Dionysian codex or our own, which is older than the Dionysian. Who could believe that, in the time of Pope Innocent I—that is, fifty-five years after the Sardican synod—so great a disorder was introduced into the order of the canons, or that uncorrected copies were sent to Rome or brought from Hosius into the West? Who could suppose that the error entered all the codices in such a way that every copy from every part of the world that has so far come to light suffered from the same inversion of order, with none reproducing the genuine sequence of the canons?

No one, therefore, can fail to pronounce this conjecture audacious: no necessity demands it, no suitable argument makes it probable, and no codex fails to reject it. The fact that the subject matter of those three canons is the same, and especially that Canons 3 and 7 define one and the same matter, suggests rather that they were issued after an interval than that they were composed in a single sequence and by a single act. For if [the material contained in both had been established at the same time and on the same occasion, it would have been incorporated into one and the same canon].

> **Editorial note:** Several points must be noted here that will not have a suitable place in the observations. The Sardican canons were not established at one and the same time, but at different times and in something like distinct sessions: this is a mere fiction, which cannot be supported by any indication from either Greek or Latin codices or editions. All these canons are presented in one continuous context, through different speakers, which is characteristic of one and the same session. The same occurs in other canons of African synods presented in a similar way, which no one doubts were enacted in one session.
>
> Since there were two original exemplars of the Sardican canons, one Latin for the Latins and the other Greek for the Greeks, as will become clear from what will be said in Volume III, in the treatise on Collections, Part I, chapter 5, the canon numbered seventh among the Latins is fifth in Greek copies, immediately following Gaudentius’s Canon 4. That order, which more clearly presents a continuous series of canons dealing with the same subject, seems more reasonable. If anyone prefers, with the Latin codices, to separate Canon 7 from Canon 4, he will have to say that Hosius added it in the same session, with two other canons interposed, not that it was enacted in a later session.
>
> Nor is what Quesnellus asserts here true: that Canons 3 and 7 define one and the same matter, so that, if whatever is contained in both had been established at the same time or in the same session, it would have been put into one and the same canon. Canon 7 deals with an appeal properly so called to the Roman pontiff, whereas Canon 3 says nothing about this, as we have shown at greater length in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, chapter 6, numbers 7, 8, and 9. Gaudentius had dealt with this proper appeal to the apostolic see after a second judgment in Canon 4. Hosius, however, in Canon 7, elsewhere numbered 5, deals with the same appeal after the first judgment, as we saw there, number 10. From this it is clear how greatly Canon 7 differs from Canon 4, and how wrongly it is claimed that one moderates the other.
>
> It cannot indeed be denied that, in appeals to the Roman bishop, Hosius proposed methods of investigating such cases in the provinces that are more expeditious and easier. But he did not decree anything by which Canon 4 was revoked, or by which Roman pontiffs were denied the power to investigate cases outside the province whenever this seemed expedient. On this matter, see the observation cited above, number 12.

Two canons were therefore made because, after some other matters had been debated in the synod, it occurred to one of the bishops, while reviewing the earlier decrees, that the words of Canon 3 concerning the Roman bishop—“and let him appoint judges”—were too brief and did not adequately disclose the form of the judgment in question. He therefore requested that the canon be explained and that the conditions for arranging a new judgment be expressed more distinctly. He obtained this, and Canon 7 was enacted for that purpose.

David, however, argues from these words of Canon 4: “Let this be added, if it pleases you, to the sentence that you have pronounced with complete holiness, so that when a bishop has been deposed, etc.” From these words, he says, it clearly follows that the canon preceding Canon 4 had established something concerning the deposition of a bishop. Yet Canon 3 says absolutely nothing about this; only Canon 7 expressly touches upon it. Therefore Canon 7 ought to precede Canon 4.

Nonsense, nonsense! None of the three canons decrees anything concerning deposition; all of them presuppose it. Canon 3 has this advantage over the others: it encompasses every case involving bishops in which someone who had lost his case might wish to consider appealing for another judgment. Among those cases, there is no doubt that the first place belongs to one in which the penalty of deposition had been imposed upon a bishop.

Gaudentius understood this correctly as being signified by the opening words of the canon: “If anyone has been judged in any case as a bishop”—that is, in any case whatsoever. Therefore he requested that this be decreed in the case of deposition, which was one of those cases and indeed the more serious one. This provision had no place in other cases: while a deposed bishop pursued his appeal before the apostolic see, no other bishop was to be appointed over him until the Roman pontiff, by mandate of the synod, decided whether an appeal should be admitted or the prior judgment upheld, and until the entire matter was finally determined by a new judgment.

### IX

Once the ancient and genuine order of these canons has been confirmed—a matter that John David assumed for no other purpose than somehow to support his novel and twisted interpretation of them—this entire structure collapses of its own accord, since its foundation has been removed.

Two conclusions clearly follow from this. First, the interpretation is not genuine, since it cannot be defended except by reversing the order of the canons, contrary to the testimony of all printed and manuscript codices; contrary to the judgment of all Latin and Greek writers who either published these canons or elucidated them through their interpretations and commentaries; and contrary to the most ancient testimony of the Roman Church, whose interests are chiefly at stake here, a testimony that emerges from both codices.

The second consequence following from this is that the mind of the Council of Sardica must be investigated not so much from the more contracted and obscure wording of canons 3 and 4 as from the fuller and clearer definition of canon 7.

[Note: Since, as was shown in the preceding annotation, canons 3, 4, and 7—elsewhere numbered 5—refer to different circumstances, and since canon 7 was not proposed to moderate the other two, there is no reason why canons 3 and 4 should be explained from canon 7.]

For later considerations derogate from earlier ones, and the interpretation of earlier decrees must be derived from later decrees—unless one wishes to dismiss the common rules of law and common sense alike. If, therefore, as David maintains, less is granted to the Roman pontiff in canon 3 than in canon 7, and less in canon 7 than in canon 4, then, since canon 7 was enacted last, the meaning of the earlier canons must unquestionably be sought from it, and the meaning of the others must be reduced to the sense of this seventh canon.

After considering these matters, no one would rashly suppose that the Eastern bishops who were present at the synod, observing that the words of canon 3—“let him appoint judges”—created an extremely broad right for the pontiff, prescribing nothing concerning the place or form of judgment, and foreseeing that the cases of the East might at some time, by force of this decree, be dragged into the West and settled according to the will of a single pontiff, became alarmed and requested that definite limits be placed upon the privilege granted, so that they would not be judged outside their own provinces.

[Note: Quesnellus conjectures that the Eastern bishops were disturbed and protested by canons 3 and 4, and that they supplied the reason for the enactment of canon 7. This conjecture, supported by no foundation whatever, must be counted among dreams.]

The suspicion of the Easterners was increased by the fact that Gaudentius—whose name and manner of speaking indicate that he was one of the Westerners—while discussing in canon 4 what was to be added to the preceding provision, interpreted the canon’s words in such a way that, in place of these words, “If he thinks that he has a good cause, so that the council may be renewed,” he substituted: “If he declares that his case must be conducted in the city of Rome”; and in place of “Let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges,” he put: “Let the case be determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.” By this interpretation the earlier decree was astonishingly enlarged.

[Note: This Gaudentius was bishop of Naissus in Dacia, as we shall show in volume III, in the treatise on the Collections, part I, chapter 7. It is no objection that here he used the words “if it pleases,” nor that the synod is not recorded as having replied “It pleases.” Other canons of the same synod likewise lack the words *placet* and *placuit*, yet are regarded as legitimate canons. Moreover, in the Greek text after canon 3 the synod’s approval, which is found in the Latin, is absent; but after canon 5, which is attached to canon 4, Gaudentius is followed by a general approval of the preceding provisions in these words: **Ἀπεκρίναντο οἱ ἐπίσκοποι· Τὰ λεχθέντα ἤρεσεν**—“The bishops replied: What was said was approved.” These words seem to include canons 3 and 4.]

For this reason, I think that the protesting bishops were satisfied by the provision of canon 7, by which canon 3 was both explained and moderated, and the suspicion that had arisen in the minds of the Easterners from Gaudentius’s affected interpretation was erased.

This is confirmed by the manner in which these three canons were framed. Canon 3 and canon 7 plainly have the form both of a canon and of a decree. This is indicated by the conclusion of canon 3: “If this pleases everyone?” The synod replied: “It pleases.” Likewise, the beginning of canon 7 presents the authority of the synod decreeing through the mouth of its president, Hosius: “Hosius the bishop said: It has been decided.”

Canon 4, however, contains only the proposal of a single bishop—Gaudentius, that is, who was not presiding over the synod—and he cautiously proposes, from his own initiative, a matter to be examined by the synod: “Let this be added, if it pleases, to this judgment.” The synod did not reply: “It pleases.”

Moreover, he proposed nothing directly concerning the renewal of the judgment or the form of judgment, but only that a bishop not be placed over the seat of the appellant. This is understood from the title inserted in both codices. In our old codex it reads: “That a bishop not be placed over the appellant”; and in Dionysius Exiguus: “That no one usurp the seat of the accused bishop.”

From this it is clear that the ancient leaders of the Roman Church, who were the authors of the codex, did not claim for themselves from this fourth canon the right to receive appeals, but claimed it solely from the third and seventh canons. The title of the former in our codex is: “On an Appeal to the Roman Bishop”; that of the latter: “On Reconsidering the Case of an Appellant in a Provincial Synod.” Finally, it becomes certain that we must adhere to the seventh canon alone, which appears to have been enacted for the explanation of the third and fourth, since both were brought back for examination after several speeches had intervened, at the insistence of the bishops.

I would therefore suppose that our Leo had this canon in mind, and that, consequently, he requested a synod in the West to which the Easterners also would hasten.

[Note: We have seen that Leo referred not to the seventh canon—elsewhere numbered the fifth—but to the fourth canon, in volume I, in the preliminary admonition to epistle 43, where we showed from manuscripts that this fourth canon was appended to that epistle.]

For since the canon grants the Roman bishop the power to decree a synod from a neighboring and nearby province in which the case of a bishop appealing from the judgment of his own province may be reconsidered, if an appeal were made from a universal synod of the Eastern provinces, it follows that the Roman pontiff could request another universal synod in the West, to which the Easterners also might come. Leo in fact requested such a synod, as is clear from what has been said above.

### X

If, moreover, you contend that the Roman pontiffs asserted their right also from the fourth canon, and that Leo likewise had that canon before his eyes, I would not wish to oppose the claim too contentiously. But if you want the appeal mentioned there to refer only to the pontiff, as David appears to maintain, we regard this as contrary to the mind both of the Sardician bishops and of Saint Leo.

The Sardicians say only this: “If a deposed bishop declares that his case must be conducted in the city of Rome, his case is to be determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.” What “the judgment of the Roman bishop” means is evident from the very canons under discussion, in which the renewal of the judgment and the renewal of the council are understood as one and the same thing. Indeed, if “judgment” were taken to mean the sentence itself, it would not have been said “in the judgment,” but simply “by the judgment.” It is therefore established that a council of the Roman bishop is meant here. But what kind of council it was must now be investigated.

The Roman pontiff has several kinds of council corresponding to the several levels of ecclesiastical administration united in his one person. He is simultaneously bishop of the City, metropolitan of the Roman province, primate of the suburban dioceses, patriarch of the Western region, and finally head and summit of the whole Church.

As bishop, he has a parochial—or, as we now say, diocesan—synod; as metropolitan, a provincial synod; as primate, a synod of several dioceses; as patriarch, a patriarchal synod of the whole West; and as head and primate of the Church, an ecumenical synod.

When an appeal is made to him within his own parish or diocese from the sentence of an inferior judge, the appeal is made to his parochial synod, or to him surrounded by the counsel of his clergy; when the appeal comes from the province, it is made to a provincial synod; when from the suburban dioceses, to a diocesan synod; when from the Western region, to a Western synod; and when from other parts of the Church, to an ecumenical and universal synod—unless the free choice and petition of the appellants indicates something else.

[Note: Quesnellus wishes all appeals brought to the Roman bishop to be understood as brought to him on account of his own jurisdiction, but always to a synod—whether parochial, provincial, diocesan, Western, or ecumenical—unless the free choice of the appellants indicates otherwise. To pass over other matters concerning the Roman pontiff as bishop of the City, metropolitan, and so forth, his jurisdiction by reason of the primacy, which must chiefly be considered in the present case, affects his person in the same way that the primacy itself is personal. Consequently, appeals brought to him by reason of that primacy concern his personal jurisdiction. See the observations in dissertation 5, part I, chapter 7, and the following observations, no. 10.]

The meaning of the Sardician canon must, I believe, be elicited according to this norm; and the same principle must be applied to the appeal of Flavian.

Indeed, whoever consults the laws of equity and the character of the human mind, setting aside all prejudices, will never be persuaded to believe that a bishop already condemned by the judgment of his entire province would then, in another synod of a neighboring province, as David wishes, submit to that same sentence, and by the authority of the Roman pontiff—who had sent a legate from his side, was present, and subscribed—wish to entrust his case to that same pontiff alone.

How much more reasonable, then, is it to suppose that this contending bishop, after testing the tribunal of his own province and having tested the pontiff’s help, had begun to think of appealing to a greater synod, such as a Western or an ecumenical synod; and that the Sardician synod granted bishops the right to appeal to such a synod. It named the Roman pontiff as its head and primate, to whom, naturally, the petition of appeal had to be delivered as to the synod’s representative, both by reason of his primacy and by necessity, since the synod to which it was to be delivered had not yet been assembled.

### XI

But why should we rely on conjectures, when we have the pontiff himself, Leo, as the interpreter of the Sardician canon and of Flavian’s appeal?

For since, in the Sardician canon appended to his letter, he indicates that a general synod from the whole world was necessarily to be requested and celebrated within Italy—that is, a Western synod to which the bishops of the Eastern provinces would come—after Flavian’s appeal;

[Note: Compare observation no. 23.]

and since, in that canon, we have no other provision concerning the matter than that the case of a bishop who declares that his case must be conducted in the city of Rome is to be determined in the judgment—that is, in the council—of the Roman bishop;

it follows beyond doubt that this judgment, or council, of the Roman bishop is, as Leo himself testifies, nothing other than an ecumenical council from the whole world, or a general synod within Italy, to which the bishops of the Eastern provinces would certainly come.

In this way the memory of the holy apostle Peter was honored: after an Eastern synod in which the Roman pontiff had not participated, another judgment was permitted to be prepared in the West, over which he himself would preside, which would subject the sentence of the earlier synod to renewed examination through him, and whose judgment would proceed from the mouth of the pontiff. After this, what Leo wrote in his letter to Theodoret could be applied:

“The radiance of the Sun of justice, obstructed by thick clouds throughout the East, shone forth pure from the West, where he established his summit principally among the apostles and teachers” (Epistle 93, now 120, chapter 2).

The letters of Valentinian and of the Augustae clearly support our opinion.

[Note: See observations nos. 4, 5, and 23.]

I have no doubt that these letters were dictated at the suggestion of Saint Leo and written in accordance with his mind and counsel. After he had stated that, according to the solemn custom of councils—he means the Council of Sardica—the bishop of Constantinople had appealed to the Roman bishop by petitions, so that it might be understood that Flavian had not appealed to the Roman bishop considered in isolation, but rather to all the bishops of the West assembled under their patriarch, with the bishops of the Eastern provinces certainly attending, as we explained above, he consequently requests, in accordance with the mind of the Sardician council and Leo’s interpretation, that “the aforesaid priest” (Leo), after assembling within Italy the remaining priests from the whole world, with every prejudice removed, should investigate from the beginning the entire case under dispute with careful examination and deliver the sentence demanded by faith and reason concerning the true Divinity.

Licinia Augusta requests the same thing: that the case of faith and of the Christian religion which had arisen should be thoroughly investigated by a council assembled in the regions of Italy.

Finally, in the same sense, the council which Valentinian wishes to be held within Italy, with the remaining priests assembled from the whole world, and which Leo calls a general synod from the whole world, Placidia Augusta calls “the council of the apostolic see.” She requests that the judgment be transmitted to it, mentioning the Council of Nicaea—or of Sardica—in order to show from its authority that the synod must necessarily be convened; and she likewise mentions Flavian’s appeal, to whom, by the decree of that same synod, the adjudication for which he had appealed was due to him.

She states most distinctly that Flavian’s petition of appeal had been sent to the apostolic see and to all the bishops of these regions—that is, of the Western regions.

From this it becomes entirely certain that the council of all the bishops of the West is the council of the apostolic see; when the bishops of the Eastern regions attend, it becomes ecumenical and general. It is also the same council to which Flavian had appealed when he appealed to the apostolic see.

David would certainly seem not to depart far from what we have said when he writes that, in one and the same petition, an appeal was made both to the pontiff and to the council: for the pontiff is present in the council, and the council in turn is present in the pontiff; no one appeals to one without also appealing to the other; and no one has ever believed that the Roman pontiff could judge alone and without his synod appeals lodged with his see.

### XII

But that writer plainly plays and deceives when he immediately reveals the trick contained in these words in the lines that follow. There he declares that, among all the Western and Eastern bishops assembled in the synod over which the pontiff presides, only the pontiff himself is necessary as judge of the case. The others, he says, attend the synod as persons concerned for a common cause and as those who, through their intervention, are to assist the litigants before the judge—not as judges whose vote and sentence are to settle the dispute.

[Note: “It is not difficult,” says Joannes David, “to discern to whom Flavian sent his act of appeal as the necessary judge of this case, and as having the right to receive the appeal; and to whom he addressed it as persons concerned in this common cause and as those who were to act as his mediators.” David, p. 298.]

Everyone who has even slight acquaintance with ecclesiastical affairs sees how injurious this is to the most sacred order of bishops and how insulting to the holy assemblies of ecumenical councils; no one devoted to the sacred hierarchy can read it without indignation.

It is also contrary to Leo in this very passage. Leo asserts that a general synod ought to be requested not merely for the sake of usefulness but out of necessity; not by way of indulgence but by right itself; not by dispensation and the will of the pontiff but by the authority of the holy Fathers and the regulations of the councils; and not finally for display and magnificence, but so that assistance might be brought to the endangered faith and to its oppressed defenders.

“As to the fact,” he says, “that after an appeal has been lodged this must necessarily be requested, the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify,” and so forth.

It is altogether absurd also that the author cited above writes, on page 294, that the great Council of Chalcedon was convened for no other reason than to hear Flavian’s appeal.

[Note: We shall explain why Saint Leo considered a general council necessary in observation no. 14 and those following.]

For if the other bishops present at the synod are not necessary judges, and only the Roman pontiff is necessary to hear the case, Saint Leo will be guilty of extreme imprudence—to say nothing more—for he earnestly begs, with tears and groans, that priests be summoned from the whole world, leaving the churches with no small damage to the Christian cause, although one pontiff could settle by his own authority the very case for which the council alone was convened.

Finally, who could grasp David’s meaning? Or who would not rather be astonished at a man writing things contrary to himself? In several places he considers it necessary for bishops to assemble in synod so that an appeal brought to the Roman see may be examined and the matter settled, and he denies that a judgment rendered outside a synod concerning an appealing bishop is canonical. Yet elsewhere—indeed, throughout almost the entire book—he strives to assert that the whole of such a matter depends on the nod and will of the pontiff, while the other bishops act as spectators of the synod, promoting a cause common to all merely by their services and prayers.

# BALLERINI OBSERVATIONS ON QUESNELLUS’S DISSERTATION VIII, *On the Case of Saint Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople*

[Col. 0685]

### 1

How many conjectures and sophisms Quesnellus has collected and entangled in the preceding dissertation, in order to withdraw from the apostolic see the appeal of Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople—an appeal of the greatest renown, which confirms the authority of that see over the Eastern Churches and even over their greater bishops—and transfer it to a general council!

So that we do not detain readers too long over individual points, which would demand a more extended and not altogether necessary disputation, we shall reduce the entire matter to definite headings and demonstrate his principal fallacies and futile efforts.

### 2

First, there is no need to labor over the question whether the words pronounced by Flavian in the Ephesian Robbery, after the unjust sentence had been pronounced, constituted a refusal, as the force of the Greek expression **παραιτοῦμαί σε**—“I refuse you”—indicates, or an appeal, as the ancient Latin translator rendered it, “I appeal from you.”

An appeal was indeed more appropriately made after the sentence than a refusal, which, according to the provisions even of ancient laws and according to judicial practice itself, must be made before the sentence is pronounced, when the judge is incompetent, or is perverting the order of judgment, or is afflicted by some preconceived bias and thereby ceases to be legitimate.

But Dioscorus, already acting as a tyrant before the sentence, failed to respect the legates of the apostolic see as he ought to have done; he refused to have Leo’s letters read, although they ought to have been read before everything else; and before Flavian’s sentence he acquitted Eutyches. He could therefore rightly be challenged.

But one who had not challenged so unjust a judge before the sentence, if the customary forms of judicial procedure were to be observed, ought after the sentence not to have refused him but to have appealed from him.

In that robber judgment, however, where everything was disturbed and confused, just as legal forms should not be insisted upon, so neither should one insist upon the words “refusal” or “appeal.” Although a refusal after the sentence in itself implies an appeal to another judge, no judge was named in the very brief formula Flavian used. Therefore nothing concerning the apostolic see can be elicited from that formula alone, whatever it may have been. The matter must consequently be investigated elsewhere.

### 3

The evidence from which Flavian’s appeal to the Roman see is established is the petition which he presented to the legates of that same see after the sentence. Quesnellus himself does not deny that an appeal was expressed in it.

But in section 2 he argues that Leo’s name was not inserted in this petition, and infers this from the letters of the holy pontiff himself, in which he never states that his see had been appealed to. A pontiff so devoted to the rights of his see would never have omitted this if it had been the case.

Relying only slightly on this negative argument, he added a positive one: namely, that the same pontiff and the other priests of the Roman synod actually requested from Theodosius a general council, which Leo himself said was necessarily demanded after Flavian’s appeal.

“Why,” asks Quesnellus in section 4, “was an ecumenical synod necessarily requested, when the synod requested was not ecumenical?”

To make the entire matter clear and remove every doubt, three points must be established:

1. Saint Flavian, having been deposed in the Ephesian Robbery and having delivered a petition of appeal to the legates, really appealed to the Roman pontiff and to the Roman synod, but not to an ecumenical council.

2. Saint Leo, having received this petition, immediately convened a Roman synod and, by the authority of the apostolic see, instituted a judgment by which he decreed that all the acts of the same Robbery were void and that the deposition of Saint Flavian was wholly empty and null.

3. He requested a general council for another reason than that Flavian had appealed to such a council.

### 4

Unmistakable witnesses testify that Flavian appealed to the Roman pontiff.

Why, while bringing forward a merely negative argument from Leo’s silence, did Quesnellus not cite Liberatus? Liberatus, who derived his account of this case from documents he himself had examined, states in chapter 12 of his *Breviary* that Flavian’s appeal was brought to the apostolic see: “Flavian, after the sentence pronounced against him, appealed to the apostolic see by a petition through its legates.”

Why did he pass over at this point the letter of the emperor Valentinian, numbered 55 among Leo’s letters? Since, as Quesnellus himself states in section 11, it was written from Leo’s report and counsel to Theodosius, it permits us to recognize in it the testimony not only of Valentinian but also of Leo himself.

There it is expressly written: “The bishop of Constantinople appealed to him [the Roman bishop] by petitions.”

Quesnellus did not entirely conceal this testimony. Shortly before the end of the dissertation, in section 11, he did report it, but in order to weaken its force he says that in the same letter Valentinian requested a council in which the Eastern bishops would assemble together with the Western bishops—that is, a general council—as though he had understood Flavian’s appeal to have been directed to a general council.

Although that Augustus, on Leo’s advice, requested an ecumenical synod, as we shall explain later, he nevertheless stated so explicitly that Flavian had appealed not to such a synod but to the supreme pontiff that Peter de Marca, whom Quesnellus cannot regard as suspect, wrote in book VII of *On Concord*, chapter 7, section 2:

“It is manifestly proved from Valentinian’s letter that Flavian appealed to Pope Leo, having delivered a petition to his legates.”

And shortly afterward:

“He delivered the petition of appeal to the legates of the supreme pontiff, but in such a way that he appealed to the Roman pontiff ALONE.”

### 5

The empress Placidia also gives the same testimony in letter 56. She states that Flavian’s appeal was directed not only to the one supreme pontiff designated by the name of the apostolic see, but also to all the bishops of these regions.

Quesnellus, in section 11, interprets “the bishops of these regions” as the Western bishops.

He likewise argues in dissertation 10, section 3, that the testimony of Theodoret—in which Theodoret, in his letter to Renatus, appealed to the Roman council after his deposition in the Ephesian Robbery—must be understood of a council of the entire West. In section 2 he gives the following reason, openly preferring an appeal to the council of the West alone while excluding the convocation of the Easterners:

“What else remained for Theodoret to do, when almost all the Easterners were either raging, oppressed, or unable even to speak, except to turn to the Westerners and appeal to their faith and religious devotion?”

If Placidia’s testimony were explained in the same way, with Quesnellus himself interpreting “these regions” as the West, then Flavian would have appealed at most not to an ecumenical synod but to a Western synod. Quesnellus therefore cannot, unless he is insufficiently consistent with himself, extract from those words an ecumenical council to which Flavian appealed.

### 6

But it is false that the bishops of “these regions” in Placidia’s letter signify the bishops of the whole West.

For a proper understanding of these words, which were certainly written in accordance with Leo’s mind, compare what the same pontiff inserted in letter 44 to the emperor Theodosius:

“All the Churches of our regions, all the priests, supplicate your Clemency with groans and tears.”

The holy pontiff wrote this in the name of the Roman synod, as is evident from the very heading of the letter: “Leo the bishop and the holy synod which assembled in the city of Rome.”

This synod, which he held after hearing the news of the Ephesian Robbery and in whose name he wrote these words, was certainly not a synod of the whole West. To assemble such a synod would have required a longer time, and the delay would have been longer than the circumstances allowed.

It was a synod of bishops who had come to Rome from various regions for various reasons, or who could quickly be summoned even from neighboring cities, as used to happen in many other urgent matters. General synods from the whole West are scarcely ever found to have been called.

More probably, it was a synod of those bishops who had gathered in especially large numbers for the celebration of the anniversary of Saint Leo’s ordination on the Kalends of October, as we noted in the observations on dissertation 1 of Quesnellus, note 1 (above, col. 220, n. c), under the year 449.

Therefore, when the holy pontiff expressed the request of his synod under the name of “the Churches and priests of our regions,” the words “our regions” can unquestionably refer only to those bishops who, being present in the Roman synod, were, together with Leo, supplicating Theodosius in their own name and in the name of their Churches.

Likewise, in Placidia’s letter, the words “to all the bishops of these regions” seem to refer to those bishops who customarily assembled in the Roman synod according to the practice of the Roman Church. They should not be extended to all the bishops of the West scattered throughout distant and remote provinces.

If anyone judges otherwise without producing any evidence, he will be shown to interpret the words arbitrarily, contrary to customary usage and meaning.

Moreover, it is hardly probable that Flavian, who by this appeal was seeking a prompt remedy for his calamity, sought something that would require longer delays—namely, the summoning of bishops from the whole West.

If it is believed that Flavian appealed not only to the apostolic see but also to the bishops of the Roman synod, he must be judged to have done so for no other reason than that he knew the Roman pontiffs customarily convened such synods in the most serious cases, so that the matter might be judged more promptly and carefully.

It is credible that for this reason Saint Leo, in the letters sent concerning this matter, inscribed not only his own name, as in his other letters, but also the name of the synod, lest he seem to have disposed of the matter precipitately, without suitable examination.

### 7

Most noteworthy are the words by which Saint Leo, in letter 61, chapter 1, distinguishes his own sentence from that of the synod:

“These writings of ours,” he says, “have been sent not only with the authority of the apostolic see but also with the unanimity of the holy synod, which had assembled in large numbers with us.”

Quesnellus added this marginal note: “Observe the distinction and gradation,” as though there were a progression from the apostolic see to the holy synod, as from a lesser authority to a greater one.

But that is not the case. When the holy pontiff attributes authority to the apostolic see and unanimity to his synod, he plainly indicates that the whole, or the greater part, of the authority in such synods is to be attributed to the apostolic see. He also indicates that the synod assembled with him is not named, nor does it possess force except on account of its unanimity: several persons had been summoned to hear and judge the case, and all adopted the same judgment as their head and as the apostolic see.

Although the unanimity of the synod usually contributes greatly to demonstrating the maturity of the judgment and establishing its credibility, it does not prejudice the authority of the apostolic see. This is so, first, because the see can exercise its right, derived from the primacy, by itself and independently of the synod—and repeatedly does so; and second, because, if the entire force of the synod depends upon unanimity, the effectiveness of that authority rests especially upon the authority and judgment of the apostolic see.

For this reason, most letters of the Roman pontiffs, although written in such synods, were nevertheless issued in accordance with the most ancient custom of the Roman Church not in the name of the synod but in the name and authority of the pontiff alone, as is clear from the letter of the Roman synod to the Eastern clergy and monks in the year 485.

### 8

This authority is much more evident in the case of Flavian, whose appeal concerns an Eastern bishop.

I ask Quesnellus whether he attributes to a particular Roman synod, if separated from the supreme pontiff, the right to hear cases of appeal brought from the East.

The judge of an appeal certainly cannot be anyone other than one who is superior to the judge from whose sentence the appeal was made. The Roman pontiff is superior, by reason of the primacy, to the Eastern judges who had condemned Flavian. Since this personal prerogative belongs to the primacy, his authority in no way depends upon the synod. Flavian could therefore appeal even to him alone, separated from the synod.

But the other bishops of the West or of the Roman synod, separated from the supreme pontiff, do not possess an equal primacy and right; they cannot be called superior to the Eastern bishops. Consequently Flavian could not appeal to them considered separately.

If he did appeal to them also, but only after making his appeal to the apostolic see, or to the supreme pontiff, as Placidia’s testimony indicates, then, since this right flowed to them in some manner not from their own prerogative but from the primacy of the Roman pontiff, whose judgment they unanimously pronounced, Flavian must be regarded as having had regard to the sole or principal right of the Roman bishop.

Nevertheless, following the judicial custom of the apostolic see, he may also have directed his appeal to the bishops of the Roman synod, whom the pontiff customarily summoned in more serious cases of this kind.

### 9

For this reason the aforementioned Valentinian referred the entire basis of the appeal to the primacy of the apostolic see, which belongs solely and personally to the Roman pontiff, in these words of letter 55:

“We must preserve inviolate, even in our own times, the dignity of veneration proper to the blessed apostle Peter, so that the most blessed bishop of the Roman city, to whom antiquity has granted the PRINCIPALITY of the priesthood over all, may have the place and power to judge concerning the faith and concerning PRIESTS. For this reason, according to the solemn custom, or practice, of councils, the bishop of Constantinople appealed to HIM by petitions.”

Do you see that the basis of the appeal is placed in this: that the supreme pontiff, because of his principality, or primacy, possesses the power to judge priests and consequently even the bishop of Constantinople?

### 10

In this principality, or primacy, of the apostolic see—that is, of the Roman pontiff—two essential prerogatives must especially be distinguished.

The first is that the primacy is personal. It is so attached to the person of the supreme pontiff that it is common to no other person. Those who divided this primacy or made it common to Saints Peter and Paul, establishing two heads of the Church and two equal primates, were rejected by the Church.

Quesnellus himself will not call this into question. In his work entitled *The Discipline of the Church*, volume I, page 96, explaining Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 12:11, “I was in no respect inferior to those who are exceedingly apostles,” he says:

“Throughout this, the equality concerns precisely the apostolate, not the primacy of the apostolate.”

Since he admits that the primacy of Peter was not common to any of the other apostles, he necessarily recognizes that this primacy was and is personal to Peter himself and consequently to his successors, and that it depends upon no one.

The second prerogative is that this primacy is not merely a primacy of order and honor but of principal jurisdiction, as even the Gallican writers profess together with the Catholic Church.

This primacy, or principality, therefore, is a special right over bishops, and because it is personal, it cannot be called common to the council of the apostolic see and to the bishops assembled in it. It belongs properly to the supreme pontiff alone.

Likewise, the right involved in Flavian’s appeal to the apostolic see, which was brought there by reason of this primacy, as Valentinian and Placidia testify, cannot be called common to that council and those bishops in such a way that it is denied to the supreme pontiff by himself.

Indeed, if the right belongs to the pontiff by reason of the primacy, then, insofar as it belongs to him as primate, it is his proper right and is not equally common to other bishops who lack that primacy. Nor does the pontiff require the convocation of a synod and bishops in order to acquire or exercise this right, which is his own and depends upon no one, just as the primacy itself does not depend upon anyone, since that right derives from it.

We have established this more fully in the observations on part I, chapter 7, of Quesnellus’s dissertation 5.

Perhaps for this reason Valentinian reported that Flavian’s appeal had been made to the Roman bishop alone and did not think it necessary to mention the bishops of these regions, or of the Roman synod, even if they had been named in the petition of appeal, as may be gathered from Placidia’s testimony.

In the meantime, from what we have discussed thus far, we believe it has been demonstrated by unmistakable witnesses that Saint Flavian appealed to Saint Leo, not to a council of the whole West, still less to an ecumenical council, as Quesnellus maintains.

### 11

Leo’s own action makes the same point still clearer. For after receiving the written appeal brought by Hilary, he either immediately convened a synod of bishops who could readily be summoned from neighboring cities, together with those who for various reasons happened to be in Rome from different parts of the whole West (which explains why Hilary could call it a Western council); or, as we consider more probable, he prolonged for some time the council that he had already convened from nearly these same bishops for the anniversary of his ordination, for the sake of so important a matter [Col. 0689D]. At that council he annulled all the proceedings of the Ephesian Robber Synod, especially those directed against Flavian.

We learn this from Hilary the deacon’s letter 46 to Pulcheria, where we read:

“Therefore let your revered Clemency know that the aforesaid pope, together with the entire Western council, rejects everything that was done at Ephesus against the canons, amid tumults and worldly hatreds, by Bishop Dioscorus against the bishops; and that nothing of these proceedings can in any way be accepted in these regions, since they were carried out through the power of the aforesaid man, not without injury to the faith and prejudice against the most holy and innocent man” (Flavian).

These words plainly signify that Leo issued a definitive decree on Flavian at the Roman synod. The same is confirmed by Leo’s letters 44, 45, 50, and 51, sent from that synod to the East. In them he affirms that Flavian remains in his communion and therefore in the see of Constantinople, and that nothing done at Ephesus can be regarded as valid. He also intimates that everything ought to remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment was passed. [Col. 0690A] Since these letters were written in the name of the synod, Leo wrote not as a private individual but as pope, and therefore with the authority of the Apostolic See, to which Flavian had appealed; the votes of the bishops of the Roman synod were added as well, for Galla Placidia reported that Flavian had lodged his appeal to them too.

For this reason also, at the Council of Chalcedon, session 10, when a reading of the acts of Ephesus was requested, the legates of the Apostolic See opposed it, giving this reason: “because everything done there was regarded as null by the most blessed and apostolic bishop of the city of Rome.” If Flavian had appealed to an ecumenical council, and Leo had not possessed the right to decide Flavian’s appeal without such a council, he could indeed have privately judged the Ephesian acts invalid, but he could not have defined and declared this in a synod, nor written from the synod in a manner that manifests public and apostolic authority and judgment.

It likewise appears from letter 80, chapter 2, that in that same synod all who had assented to the Ephesian proceedings were separated from Leo’s communion. This certainly confirms that apostolic authority had intervened [Col. 0690B].

### 12

Quesnellus, in Dissertation 10, argues that the judgment of the Apostolic See mentioned by Leo in letter 120, chapter 5—the judgment by which Theodoret, deposed in that same Ephesian Robbery, was vindicated—was contained, as he says in section 4, in a letter which he conjectures Leo sent in reply to Theodoret’s letter 52. In it, Leo supposedly wrote that Theodoret need not abide by the sentence pronounced against him or await another judgment, but might govern his Church in the customary manner, “since what was done at Ephesus through the shamelessness” (read: “impotence”) “of one man cannot be allowed to stand by any consideration of the Catholic faith.” And shortly afterward he adds: “Such, in my judgment, is the judgment of the Apostolic See.”

He denies that this was a sentence pronounced after hearing the parties; yet he could not deny that it was a judgment and decree of apostolic authority. If this is true in Theodoret’s case—although what Leo actually wrote is unknown—it must be acknowledged much more emphatically in Flavian’s appeal, on account of which a synod was convened at Rome [Col. 0690C], the Ephesian proceedings were annulled, and letters were issued from the synod decreeing that Flavian had been unjustly deposed and must be regarded as the true bishop of Constantinople.

Who could deny that this was a judgment of the Apostolic See? You therefore possess, in support of Flavian’s appeal to the supreme pontiff, contemporary testimonies of unimpeachable authority; you possess Leo’s own judgment, which we have demonstrated not so much from his letters as from Quesnellus himself, whether interpreting or confessing it. Who, after this, would not recognize as utterly futile Quesnellus’s effort to transfer this appeal from the supreme pontiff to a general synod?

### 13

“But,” you will object, “if Flavian’s appeal did not require a general council, why did Leo, in letter 44, ask Theodosius to order that a general synod be held within Italy, since ‘our legates faithfully protested, and Bishop Flavian gave them his written appeal’? And why did he shortly afterward affirm that this was necessarily demanded after the appeal had been lodged?”

[Col. 0690D] This is Quesnellus’s entire—or at least his principal—argument. Yet for it to prove anything, it would first have to be established that Leo asked for and declared a general synod necessary after Flavian’s appeal for no other reason than that Flavian’s appeal had been directed not to Leo himself or to the Roman synod, but to a general council.

But this argument, which Quesnellus presents as singular and certain, is false. We have seen from contemporary witnesses—whose interpretation Quesnellus himself supplied—that Flavian did not appeal to an ecumenical council. We have also seen that, in the crisis in which Flavian sought an immediate remedy, he ought not to have asked for a general synod. We may add that, on Quesnellus’s own principles, Leo could not have regarded such a synod as necessary.

This is clear from what Leo wrote in letter 26 concerning Eutyches’ fraudulent appeal to him. “The case,” he says, “needs only your consolation and defense, by which you ought, with your own consent, to bring everything to tranquility [Col. 0691A] and peace. For in this way the heresy that has arisen, and the disturbances caused by it, will be destroyed most easily. The council also, which is being reported as about to take place, will be removed, so that the most holy Churches may not be disturbed everywhere” [1163].

If, in the appeal fabricated by Eutyches, Leo attributed such importance to the authority of the Roman See that he affirmed its sole judgment was both required and sufficient, and that the general council being publicly announced would thereby be dismissed as no longer necessary—indeed, because he feared it would provoke still greater disturbances—how could he have judged otherwise in his own appeal after the Ephesian Pseudosynod, where experience itself had taught him that factions and tumults had prevailed?

All this was known to Leo from Flavian’s own written appeal and letters. He therefore could not have declared a general synod necessary on the ground that Flavian had requested such a judgment. Another reason for its necessity must consequently be sought.

### 14

If anyone reads Leo’s letters attentively and considers more carefully the circumstances of that period [Col. 0691B], he will readily understand why, and in what sense, Leo believed a general council necessary.

You will find no indication in any letter of Leo that a general council was necessary in order to annul the Ephesian proceedings lawfully and restore Flavian, who had been wrongly deposed by those proceedings. Since those predatory and unjust acts were openly and evidently null and invalid—as Quesnellus himself proves in Dissertation 10, section 4—no superior ecclesiastical authority could have been necessary either to annul them or to restore Flavian to his own see, from which he could not have been deposed by invalid proceedings.

Only because those proceedings were being treated as valid by their authors and supporters, and had been confirmed by imperial authority, could some superior authority be considered necessary to remove the error widely spread among many people by declaring the nullity, as it is called, of those proceedings. Flavian lodged his appeal for this purpose to the Apostolic See, whose authority he knew other Easterners had invoked [Col. 0691C]. Saint Leo, using the authority of that same See, declared at his synod that the proceedings were null and invalid. Quesnellus himself proves this in Dissertation 10, section 4. He therefore ought to have understood that in this matter Leo could not have judged a general council necessary by any necessity of law, since Leo satisfied that necessity in his own synod when he publicly declared those proceedings null.

### 15

The entire necessity that the holy pontiff could have had in mind therefore concerned fact, not law.

Let it be granted that the Ephesian proceedings and Flavian’s deposition were in themselves null and invalid by the force of law; let it be granted that this nullity had been declared by papal and synodal letters. Nevertheless, because of the power and overwhelming influence of the Eutychians, whom the emperor Theodosius supported, Flavian—deposed and expelled by the gravest crime—could not return to his see. What did it matter that he did not require restoration in law if he was deprived of his see and compelled to endure exile?

Add the other scandals produced by the Ephesian Robbery [Col. 0691D], which awaited a remedy. In law, the authority and declaration of the pope and the Roman synod alone could have been, and ought to have been, sufficient. But the most prudent pontiff foresaw that, amid the unrestrained violence and prejudices prevailing in the East after that Robbery, this authority and declaration alone would not suffice to produce the results he desired.

What could he hope to accomplish merely through his own letters, even those written in the name of the Roman synod, with men who, protected by imperial favor, had suppressed his earlier letters at Ephesus and had paid no attention when the apostolic legates protested? What could he hope for in the East, where such violence prevailed under Theodosius’s protection? Who would expect the ordinary remedies of law to be effective where force, not law, was dominant?

Leo recognized that the emperor had to be withdrawn from this support, lest he continue to protect the violent faction. He also saw that this would not easily be achieved unless the Eastern bishops—by whose number and authority he had been surrounded and deceived—were brought back to sound judgment; otherwise, whatever he wrote with his synod would be powerless while they resisted in person.

To restore at least most of the Easterners to sound [Col. 0692A] judgment, he realized that no more suitable remedy could be found than a general council at which they could meet with the Westerners. There, many learned and Catholic bishops, engaging freely in discussion with those who had been deceived, could more easily instruct, persuade, and bring them back to sound counsel, just as later happened successfully at the Council of Chalcedon with the Illyrians and Palestinians.

He further saw that this council had to be convened outside the East, where, under different Augusti, with every danger of violence removed, the factious would be powerless; thus everything could be settled more easily [1165].

For this reason, therefore—a necessity not of law but of fact—he believed that a general council should be requested in Italy after Flavian’s appeal, as necessary for securing his restoration and cutting away those scandals which, in the circumstances just described, could not be dealt with by any other legal remedy.

[Col. 0692B] Since he foresaw that Theodosius would be difficult to compel to convene this council, he believed that the authority of the three Augusti—Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia—should be brought to bear upon him, and he succeeded in obtaining letters from them to the emperor that would be highly effective.

### 16

[Col. 0692B] Leo himself clearly explained this plan in his letters to Theodosius: the ecumenical synod was requested not for a juridical declaration but as a remedy for the scandals.

Thus, in letter 44, chapter 3:
