“You should order a general synod to be held within Italy, which may either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further may remain doubtful in the faith or divided in charity. Let the bishops of the Eastern provinces assemble; if any of them have been overcome by threats and injuries and have departed from the path of truth, let them be restored through salutary remedies; and let those whose case is more difficult, if they submit to better counsels, not fall away from the unity of the Church.”

Likewise, in letter 69, chapter 2:

“May your Clemency grant that a universal council be held within Italy . . . so that, with all those who have fallen through ignorance or fear assembled together, provision may be made through remedies of correction” [Col. 0692C].

The same agrees with what letter 54 conveys to the same emperor:

“If your Piety deigns to assent to our suggestion and petition, and orders an episcopal council to be held within Italy, then, with God’s help, all the scandals stirred up amid the disturbances of the whole Church can quickly be cut away.”

See also letter 70 to Pulcheria, at the end.

Do you see the purpose of convening the council? When Leo therefore requested a general council as necessary after Flavian’s appeal, he was not looking solely to Flavian’s deposition, but to all the scandals of the Ephesian Robbery—not because he considered the judgment of a general council intrinsically necessary for annulling or declaring invalid the Ephesian proceedings, but so that an effective remedy might be brought to so many evils.

### 17

[Col. 0692D] Quesnellus himself recognized and acknowledged this in Theodoret’s case. Discussing it in Dissertation 10, section 4, he says: “The pontiff immediately understood after the Ephesian Robbery that a council, and a general one, was necessary; this is clear from his letters on the matter to the emperor.”

After quoting the testimony from letter 44 reproduced above, in which no mention is made of Theodoret or of the others deposed at Ephesus, and in which an ecumenical council is requested as a remedy for the scandals, he adds:

“Yet he did not consider either a provincial or a general synod necessary for restoring Theodoret”—that is, necessary in law—“because he was not to be regarded as deposed: it was not a council but a robbery, and not a bishop but a wicked brigand, that had attempted to pronounce a sentence of deposition against him.”

But if a general synod was not intrinsically necessary for restoring Theodoret, how does Quesnellus reconcile this with his assertion that Leo considered it necessary for restoring Flavian, whose faith and innocence he had expressly recognized and concerning whom he had issued a decree at his synod? In letter 50—where Quesnellus himself makes this observation—Leo warned the Constantinopolitans not to let any threats or fear separate them from their own priest, who had suffered a sentence of deposition similar to Theodoret’s [Col. 0693A]:

“Whoever, while your bishop Flavian is safe and alive, dares to invade his priesthood”—this is plainly a decree—“will never be held in our communion, nor will he be able to be counted among the bishops.”

By this definitive judgment of Leo, the necessity of law had been fully addressed. The necessity for convening a council must therefore be referred entirely to the facts, or to the exceedingly difficult circumstances of the situation, so that the scandals might more easily be cut away.

In the same sense, and solely as a remedy for scandals, Pope Innocent I also requested a general synod from the emperor in the case of the unjust deposition of Saint John Chrysostom. This is shown by the pope’s own words in his letter to the clergy and people of Constantinople, quoted by Quesnellus in section 4:

“But what remedy,” he says, “shall we presently bring to these circumstances? A synodal inquiry will be necessary; indeed, we stated long ago that it ought to be convened. For it alone can blunt the force of storms of this kind. Until we obtain it, however, it is fitting to entrust the healing of this calamity to the will of the great God and of Christ his Lord our God.”

And afterward:

“We are giving much thought to how an ecumenical synod might be convened, through which, by the will of God, these turbulent disturbances might be quieted” [1167].

The same force dominated and had thrown the entire East into confusion in both Chrysostom’s and Flavian’s cases. The necessity of a general council was likewise in both cases not a necessity of law but of fact, so that the result plainly demanded by law, but obstructed by force alone, might more easily be obtained [Col. 0693B].

### 18

Valentinian had already indicated that, at this very general council, Leo would possess the principal authority by reason of his primacy, as well as because Flavian’s appeal had been brought before him. In letter 55 he explained the request for a general synod as follows:

“Let the aforesaid priest [Leo], with the other priests assembled from the whole world within Italy, with every prejudice removed, investigate from the beginning the entire case at issue through careful examination and pronounce sentence” [Col. 0693C].

This suggests that the greater, indeed nearly the entire, force of the sentence at the general council would proceed from the pontiff himself.

This should not be understood as though the pope alone, and not the other bishops as well, were judges in councils. Rather, because this case had been brought especially to the supreme pontiff by Flavian’s written appeal, and because it belonged to him in his own right, the sentence seemed particularly attributable to him on the same grounds on which it would be pronounced at a general council by the other bishops unanimously, with him presiding and directing.

Placidia likewise, in letter 56, after mentioning Flavian’s appeal to the Apostolic See and to all the bishops of those regions, asks that, “according to the form and definition of the Apostolic See, which we too similarly venerate as preeminent,” Flavian be preserved unharmed in his priestly office in every respect—because Leo had already sufficiently decreed concerning him at his synod—and that the case be referred to the council of the Apostolic See, “in which the first man worthy to receive the heavenly keys established the primacy of the episcopate” [Col. 0693D].

The general council requested is called a council of the Apostolic See for no other reason than that, in it, the supreme pontiff would settle and determine the whole case with the greater authority that he possessed by virtue of the primacy of his see.

The same empress wrote in the same sense in letter 58 to Pulcheria:

“Let the case of the episcopate” (or, alternatively, “of the bishops”) “be referred to the Apostolic See, in which the blessed Peter, the first of the apostles, who also received the keys of the heavenly kingdoms, held the primacy.”

This is because the matter belongs by right to him who possesses the primacy of the episcopate—not merely a primacy of rank, but a primacy of preeminent jurisdiction.

Do you see whether the ancients attributed to the supreme pontiff merely the first place and the first sentence in a general synod, as Quesnellus did not hesitate to assert in the dissertation mentioned above? He failed to understand sufficiently that on this view papal authority would be reduced to a primacy of mere rank and honor, something utterly alien to Catholic principles [Col. 0694A]. But the nature of this treatise does not permit us to say more on that subject.

### 19

Meanwhile, from what has been argued thus far, it can be gathered in what sense Leo wrote—one by no means contrary to papal jurisdiction—that a general synod was necessarily to be requested after Flavian had lodged his appeal.

The entire necessity in question arose neither from any deficiency of authority in the pontiff, who had already pronounced judgment sufficiently when he declared the Ephesian proceedings invalid, nor from an absolute necessity for a general council in Flavian’s appeal, since Flavian directed his appeal not to a general synod but to Leo himself. Rather, it arose from the difficult circumstances of that period, in which the malice and violence of the wicked left no other effective means of remedy.

That Saint Leo derived the entire necessity from these circumstances is evident from what happened when the circumstances changed after the death of the emperor Theodosius. The new emperor [Col. 0694B] Marcian had recalled the Catholic bishops already driven into exile; under his protection of the Catholic faith, many who had fallen were daily turning to remedies of satisfaction and were subscribing everywhere to the doctrinal letter addressed to Flavian.

Although Leo could not altogether refuse the general council which the distinguished Marcian indicated that he would convene in compliance with Leo’s earlier request, in letters 73 and 76 (now 77 and 82), Leo nevertheless argued that it could be postponed as no longer equally necessary as it had been under Theodosius. He gave instructions to his legates by which, in the meantime, a remedy might be provided for the scandals without convening a general synod. See letters 82 and 83.

In the same way, Innocent I, who in Chrysostom’s case had requested a general council as necessary, after the death of the emperor who favored the opposing party and had stirred up the disturbances, thought no further about convening one once the circumstances had changed. Using his own authority—which the new emperor greatly respected—he settled everything [Col. 0694C].

But when Marcian, out of a desire to establish peace more quickly, had already summoned an ecumenical synod, Saint Leo did not assent because he believed that some necessity still remained [Note: At Col. 0694, see annotation 13 (preceding volume, col. 918, nn.) on letter 82.], nor in order that judgment might be rendered concerning Flavian’s appeal or the Ephesian Robbery, as though those matters had not already been fully settled by his judgment. Rather, he assented to the summons lest he appear to oppose the emperor’s devout will, and so that “whatever had come into complaint and disturbance might, with all dissension suppressed, be restored to the unity of peace and faith” (letter 89). This is precisely what successfully occurred at the Council of Chalcedon.

Here again we see the same purpose of the council: remedying scandals, as Leo expressed it in his other letters to Theodosius. Do you see how everything coheres so well that Quesnellus’s proposed interpretation cannot be extracted—namely, that Leo requested a general synod because Flavian had appealed not to Leo personally but to a general council?

### 20

We must now address another effort of Quesnellus. He twists the Sardican canons cited by Leo in order to establish the necessity of a general synod, as though the intention of those canons required a general council to be convened in Flavian’s case [Col. 0694D].

He derives this interpretation from Leo himself, who writes in letter 44:

“That this [a general council in Italy] is necessarily demanded after the appeal has been lodged is attested by the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea.”

As we have seen elsewhere, by the name of the Nicene canons Leo means the Sardican canons.

Quesnellus argues as follows. If the holy pontiff had thought that the Sardican canons concerned an appeal to the Apostolic See alone, he would have inferred not that a general council had necessarily to be convened, but that Flavian’s appeal had to be brought before his own tribunal alone. Since, however, Leo inferred not this but the necessity of a general synod, then, for Leo’s reasoning to be valid, we must undoubtedly say that he was convinced that the Sardican canons, when they grant bishops the power to appeal to the Apostolic See, or to the Roman bishop, grant it in the sense that the Roman bishop would examine the appeal not in isolation but together with his Western synod, to which, as Leo requested, the Easterners too would come [Col. 0695A].

### 21

Quesnellus’s entire argument rests on the hypothesis that Saint Leo inferred from the Sardican canons the necessity of a general synod in order that judgment might be rendered on Flavian’s appeal, and that he cited those canons for this purpose.

But we have shown from several of Leo’s own testimonies, both numerous and perfectly clear, how false this hypothesis is. They make it evident that Leo had already pronounced judgment in his Roman synod concerning Flavian’s unjust condemnation. He therefore did not request a general council in order to render judgment on Flavian’s appeal, but to secure the effect of restoration and to seek remedies for those scandals which, in the circumstances we have described, could be healed only in a universal synod.

Indeed, in all the letters in which the holy pontiff discusses this synod, you will not find a single word reserving judgment on Flavian’s appeal to such a council [Col. 0695B].

### 22

If the disputed testimony from Leo’s letter 44 is compared without prejudice with the meaning of the Sardican canons, Leo’s intention and plan will appear still more clearly to be remote from Quesnellus’s interpretation.

The Sardican canons certainly do not extend to a general synod the right of appeal which they expressly assert for the Roman pontiff, whatever efforts Quesnellus may make in interpreting them—or rather, distorting them in another direction.

We have set out at length, in our observations on Dissertation 5, chapter 6, the genuine and obvious meaning of the three Sardican canons, which completely destroys Quesnellus’s argument.

The occasion for enacting these canons was the case of Saint Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, and other Eastern bishops whom the Eusebian heretics had deposed while insisting that there could be no new judgment or appeal, even though [Col. 0695C] these bishops had fled for refuge to the Roman See. Their claim was that, just as Easterners ought to arrogate no legal authority to themselves in the judgments of Westerners, so Westerners had none in the judgments of Easterners.

On this reasoning, Catholic and most holy bishops who had been deposed in the East by an unjust judgment would have been deprived forever of every lawful assistance and remedy, and would have had to remain permanently without their sees.

The orthodox bishops at the Council of Sardica therefore thought that some remedy had to be set against this heretical scheme, so that cases of this kind could be settled once an appeal had been lodged. The matter at issue, then, was appeals to the Apostolic See. In the canons cited, the Sardican Fathers assigned this right of appeal to the Roman pontiff in such a way that, as Quesnellus himself admits in section 7, the letter addressed to Julius, then bishop of Rome, was decreed for no other reason than that the synod should understand that Athanasius’s case belonged to Julius by force of these canons.

And shortly afterward Quesnellus writes:

“The principal aim of the orthodox bishops who had assembled there was to bring the case of Saint Athanasius and his companions to the West.”

He should rather have said: their aim was to vindicate the appellate judgments of the Apostolic See, which the Eusebian heretics alone had obstructed, and thereby to provide a legitimate tribunal for the future examination of cases of this kind.

He was compelled to acknowledge this because the prerogative of the Apostolic See in such cases is plainly expressed in the canons themselves. They contain no indication—indeed, not even an obscure mention—of any necessity for convening a general synod [Col. 0695D].

### 23

Observe, however, the long and difficult circuit by which Quesnellus attempts to derive this necessity from the canons and to weaken the right that those very canons assert for the Roman See.

Unable to deny that the same canons assert some special right for the supreme pontiff, he claims that they grant him only this authority: in an appeal, he does not examine the judgment from which the appeal was taken or pronounce sentence upon it, but decides merely whether the appeal ought to be admitted in that [Col. 0696A] case.

Up to this point, papal authority concerning episcopal appeals is placed in the establishment of a purely juridical order—a position that would make the primacy one of mere rank rather than of preeminent jurisdiction.

Then, if the Roman pontiff judges that the appeal should be admitted, Quesnellus believes that, by force of the same canons, he must summon a council. But this council is not always general. It may consist of bishops from the neighboring province, together with any others whom the pontiff judges should be admitted. Or, if the appeal seeks the judgment of the Roman bishop, as in the fourth canon, Quesnellus thinks that the council to be convened must vary according to the standing of the judges from whom the appeal was taken.

Thus, if the appeal was taken from the judges of a province within the diocese over which the pontiff presides as primate, a council of the entire diocese must be convened. If the appeal came from the Western region, a council of the entire West must be ordered. But if an appeal was lodged from the East—as in Flavian’s case—then an ecumenical council was necessary.

On this view, in every appeal by Eastern bishops to the Apostolic See, even when the appeal was entirely just—as was the appeal, or flight for refuge, of Athanasius and the other Catholic bishops—the Roman pontiff could accomplish nothing; indeed, neither could the entire West, unless a synod of the whole world were convened [Col. 0696B].

It would be madness to believe that such an idea ever entered the minds of the Sardican Fathers. What remedy for appeals would there then have been? Could this have been the prudent and efficient provision that those distinguished Fathers thought should be established for innocent men oppressed by unjust condemnation?

Since appeals of this kind could occur repeatedly, a general council would likewise have to be convened repeatedly, and bishops would often have to be summoned from their sees. Who could accept an idea—or rather, a fiction—so incredible?

That Saint Leo certainly did not believe this is evident from the judgment he pronounced immediately.

### 24.

To reveal what his intention was when, in Letter 44 to Theodosius, he invoked these canons as requiring a synod, it should be observed that this citation of the same canons is found only in the letter to that emperor who was supporting the Ephesian pseudo-synod. With so powerful a patron of that assembly, who would have been especially reluctant to endure a new judgment, it was necessary to act more gently and pleasantly; and, in order to bend him more easily, even venerable authority had to be brought forward. The supporters of Eutyches, moreover, treated the Nicene canons with the greatest respect; and since the Sardican canons were regarded as Nicene, Leo cited one of them for the present purpose and even appended it to his letter.

The canon appended to the letter, as we saw in the preliminary notice to Letter 43, was the fourth Sardican canon, which is expressed in these words:

> Bishop Gaudentius said: “If it pleases you, this should be added to the sentence you have pronounced, which is full of holiness: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who reside in neighboring places, and he has declared that his case should be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop should be ordained in his place after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.”

It is clear that the subject is an appeal to the judgment of the Roman pontiff. Two things are decreed by this canon. First, after an appeal, no one is to be ordained in the place of the one who appears to have been deposed until the case of the appeal has been determined. Second, judgment is to be given by the Roman bishop himself.

Leo requested these two things from Theodosius. The first was requested when, in the second chapter of the aforementioned letter, he asked that “you order everything to remain in the condition in which it was before any judgment [of the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod], until a greater number of bishops from throughout the world has been assembled.” The second was requested when, in the third chapter, he asked that a general council be convened in Italy, in which Leo himself could more conveniently take part and give judgment on the entire matter.

Although the holy pontiff did not expressly explain this plan in his letters to Theodosius, it was sufficiently set forth by Valentinian in Letter 55, which, at Leo’s urging and certainly in accordance with Leo’s own opinion, Valentinian sent to the same Theodosius. Although we quoted Valentinian’s words shortly before, we repeat them here:

> “Therefore, when he [Leo] made this request, I did not refuse to agree, insofar as I might press my petition upon your clemency: that the aforesaid priest, once the remaining priests from throughout the world had also been assembled within Italy, with every prejudice removed, should carefully investigate from the beginning the whole case at issue and pronounce judgment.”

Do you see? He did not say, “that, once the remaining priests from throughout the world had also been assembled, they all should pronounce judgment,” but “that the aforesaid priest”—that is, the supreme pontiff—should pronounce judgment. To him, as Valentinian had stated shortly before, it belonged by reason of his primacy to judge concerning the faith and concerning priests.

Nor did Valentinian therefore wish to deny that this power also belonged to a general council, or to other bishops assembled in a general council. Far from it. But since he had spoken of Flavian’s appeal, which Flavian had directed to Leo, Valentinian believed that judgment should consistently be assigned to Leo, since by the force of the appeal it belonged to him.

Thus, since Saint Leo, looking not only to Flavian’s case but also to the other scandals of the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod, requested from Theodosius a general council as necessary in view of the difficult circumstances, Valentinian explained Leo’s mind: Leo was asking for the judgment of the Roman pontiff, sought by Flavian’s appeal, and required after the appeal so that the case might be determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop, as the Sardican canon prescribes.

The holy pontiff therefore did not cite this canon to prove the necessity of a general council. A general council was not required in any way by the force of Flavian’s appeal itself, nor by the force of this canon. Rather, when, because of Flavian’s appeal, Leo requested a general synod within Italy in which the supreme pontiff might pronounce judgment, he cited the canon to prove that he was requesting the judgment which, in the case of an appeal to the Roman bishop, had to be requested by virtue of that canon.

For this reason the empress Placidia, too, in her letter to the same Theodosius—Letter 56—when she requested a general council in Italy, expressed herself in these terms: “with Flavian, who had appealed, remaining untouched in every respect in his priestly status, let the case be referred to a council for judgment by the apostolic see.” These words correspond most closely to the fourth Sardican canon.

Now repeat Leo’s words from Letter 44, and you will understand their meaning:

> “That after Flavian’s appeal this should necessarily be required”—namely, the judgment of the Roman bishop, which, in view of the difficult circumstances, it was useful to obtain—“the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify.”

Those decrees speak of the judgment of the Roman bishop alone, invoked through the appeal.

The same point is expressed in Letter 43:

> “So that it is necessary also to preserve those things which the Nicene canon and the decree of the bishops of the whole world prescribe.”

As though he were saying: “I request a general council as necessary, but at the same time it is also necessary to preserve the Nicene—or Sardican—canon, which, in an appeal brought before the apostolic see, demands the judgment of the Roman pontiff.”

Thus everything is properly understood and reconciled, without any need to accept those violent and distorted interpretations which Quesnellus endeavored to introduce and to attach to Leo’s words against Leo’s true intention, which is otherwise known concerning the right of the apostolic see in appeals.

### 25.

But why should we detain our readers any longer in refuting the interpretations contrived by a man hostile to pontifical authority, in order to show that Flavian’s appeal had been brought before an ecumenical synod? Since the whole question turns on determining to whom Flavian truly appealed, why labor to understand either the Sardican canons or Leo’s words, if the testimony not only of Liberatus but also of Valentinian and Placidia—who had themselves examined the libellus of appeal—makes it clear that Flavian appealed to the apostolic see, and more broadly to the bishops of these regions, that is, to the Roman synod, which Roman pontiffs customarily convened in more serious cases, and not to a general council?

The general council was requested not in Flavian’s libellus—from which we have shown that this idea was completely alien—but at Leo’s initiative. He considered it necessary not in order to pronounce judgment on the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod, since he had already done so in the Roman synod immediately after receiving the libellus of appeal, but because of the difficulty of the circumstances, which scarcely allowed the more obvious legal remedies to be used.

And since this very remedy of a general council would not easily have been obtained from the emperor, the patron of the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod, Leo thought that, to incline the emperor’s mind more readily, he should invoke the authority of the Nicene canons. Since those canons clearly establish not the judgment of a general synod but that of the Roman bishop, Leo could cite them as establishing the necessity of the general synod only in a sense that led back to the judgment of the Roman bishop, as we explained shortly above.

Who, then, could transfer to Flavian’s appeal what the holy pontiff wrote for the convocation of an ecumenical synod for another purpose, when it is established by unmistakable and most reliable witnesses that Flavian’s appeal was directed not to such a synod but to the Roman bishop and to the bishops of the Roman synod alone?

Who could approve the interpretation of the Sardican canons introduced by Quesnellus and transferred to a general council—an interpretation that is not only as far removed as possible from the meaning of the canons themselves, but also from Flavian’s appeal? Who, I say, could approve it?

### Quesnellus’s opinion is examined: he contends that the legates of the apostolic see represented all the bishops of the West at the general synods of the East.

### 26.

Having concluded the case of Flavian’s appeal, we must not omit the argument by which Quesnellus attempts to establish, in section 5, that the legates of the apostolic see attended the Second Ephesian Synod not merely in the name of the Roman pontiff, nor did they customarily attend ecumenical councils assembled in the East only in that capacity, but also in the capacity of all the bishops of the entire West, whose representatives they were, since those bishops themselves could not attend.

This is a matter of fact, and it ought to have been established by documents. His general proposition is that the legates “did not otherwise customarily attend ecumenical councils.” But observe how he extricates himself. According to his system, the legates of the apostolic see are said to have borne the representation and embassy of all the bishops of the West.

Since an express mandate or procuration from the one who delegates is required for an embassy, if it is true that the legates of the apostolic see acted as representatives of all the Western bishops, an express mandate from all of them ought to have been demonstrated.

Quesnellus asserts that this mandate was given by those bishops in two ways. Sometimes, he says, it was given in a Roman synod summoned from the whole West for the purpose of having all the bishops choose legates who would take the place of those absent. At other times, he says, it was given in the synods of the individual provinces of the West, from which legates were sent to the Roman synod with authority to choose legates who would attend the ecumenical council in the common name of all.

He also implies that it made no difference whether this mandate was given through legates or through letters from the individual provincial synods. It is easy enough to assert that these things happened in this way; it is very difficult to establish them by documents.

### 27.

“It was customary,” he says in the same section 5, “for the Roman bishop, as soon as a universal synod had been announced, to notify all the bishops of his patriarchate of the matter and himself to convene a synod at Rome, to which the Westerners who had been invited would assemble.”

If this was customary, it should be capable of proof by several examples. But not a single example will be found in all antiquity. Roman pontiffs did customarily convene a synod of the bishops who were found at Rome, or even of those from neighboring regions, in the most serious cases; but it will be found that they never once summoned a general council from the whole West.

If you review each of the ancient general councils, Quesnellus’s gratuitous and false proposition will become still more evident. The acts of the First Nicene Synod are lacking, and therefore it cannot be asserted or proved that Saint Sylvester convened a Western council on its account. The same is true of the Sardican Synod, which is regarded as an appendix to Nicaea.

It is certain only that legates of the apostolic see attended both councils. Since they are said to have represented the apostolic see alone, it is highly arbitrary to attribute to them, without any testimony, an embassy from the whole West—especially since others who attended other synods in their own and another’s name were accustomed to express in the subscriptions not so much their own name as that of the person whom they represented.

There is no need to say anything about the First Constantinopolitan Synod, since it remained unknown to the Romans for a long time. For this reason the Roman Church, until Leo’s time, accepted only the Nicene canons and those of Sardica under the name of the Nicene canons. Only when Roman pontiffs later approved that synod did it become, from an Eastern synod, a general one.

There remain two ecumenical councils: the First Ephesian and the Chalcedonian. No one will prove that, on account of either one, a synod of all the Westerners was convened by the Roman pontiff. Indeed, there was not even time to convene one.

### 28.

Before the Council of Ephesus, Saint Cyril had been appointed legate of the apostolic see in the Nestorian affair by Pope Celestine. If a synod of the entire West had had to be convened for this delegation, it would have been necessary to wait far too long.

Indeed, Cyril himself testifies—certainly on the report of Possidonius, who brought that letter from Rome—that the synod in which, after many discussions, Celestine wrote the letter containing Cyril’s delegation consisted only of those bishops who were found in the great city of Rome.

Up to that point, although much had been done concerning Nestorius, nothing had yet been done about convening the Ephesian Synod. Theodosius suddenly announced it at Nestorius’s request on 19 November of the year 430. The date fixed for the synod was 7 May of the following year.

News of this proclamation reached Celestine so late that he was unable to send legates until 8 May, when the Commonitorium was delivered to them. Hence, in the Commonitorium itself, there was fear that the synod had already taken place.

In these circumstances it would have been foolish to think of convening a council from the whole West in order to choose legates. In the first Ephesian action, Cyril alone served as the apostolic legate; and we have shown that this embassy was not entrusted to him by a synod of the entire West.

### 29.

On account of the Council of Chalcedon, it was not only impossible to summon bishops from the whole West to a Roman synod; it was not even possible to await letters from the neighboring regions, as we shall see shortly.

Indeed, since the announcement of this council became known at Rome only after 9 June of the year 451, as we have shown in note 3 [Earlier volume, column 930, note p] in Letter 89, Leo scarcely had time to choose and instruct the legates whom he sent rapidly to the council on the 24th of the same month. For this reason he complains in Letter 91:

> “The very shortness of the intervening days does not permit us to summon the necessary priests.”

You see, then, what became of Quesnellus’s claim that it was customary to convene a synod of the whole West—a synod that was never convened.

### 30.

No less gratuitous is his other claim concerning the synods of the individual provinces of the West, which supposedly sent either legates or letters to the Roman synod with authority to choose legates for the general council.

Review the individual general councils again, and you will find nothing of the kind. The one example Quesnellus was able to produce, concerning the Gallican bishops and the Council of Chalcedon alone, actually proves the opposite.

Saint Leo wrote to them in Letter 102:

> “We certainly would have wished to receive the letters of your fraternity at the time when you had promised them, so that, for our brothers departing for the East, whom we sent to the holy synod in our place for the defense of the Catholic faith, a profession of your opinion might also be joined.”

Thus the letters of the Gallicans were lacking as well. How, then, can the custom asserted by Quesnellus be inferred from this isolated example, in which the letters themselves arrived late?

Furthermore, the true reason why Leo had requested these letters from the Gallicans was not that, once a general synod had been announced, it was customary to choose legates in the name of all the Westerners. Rather, because of the difficulty of the circumstances under Theodosius, which we explained earlier, the holy pontiff thought it expedient to oppose the errors of the Eutychians with the opinion of the Gallicans and other Westerners.

For a similar reason he also requested letters from the Milanese. Yet these men, too, although closer, replied only later. When Leo requested these letters, he did not think of choosing legates in the name and with the mandate of all.

If, therefore, neither a Western synod was convened at Rome, nor were legates or letters sent from the synods of the Western provinces to Rome by which legates would be dispatched to the general council in the name of all, how could legates sent by the Roman pontiff have represented all the Westerners?

### 31.

To evade this answer, Quesnellus entered upon a third path when he wrote:

> “When the date of the ecumenical synod had been fixed so near that it did not allow the votes of other dioceses to be awaited, or even letters to be sent to them, then, once a council had been assembled either from the diocese of the City or from those bishops who were then residing in the City, legates were sent. They received and exercised from the patriarch and from his diocesan or provincial synod the representation of the entire Western patriarchate, and they represented all the Westerners at the ecumenical council.”

Since, as we have seen, this was the customary form of a synod, the two forms proposed above—which are supported by no ancient example—should not have been proclaimed customary.

He adds the example of the Second Ephesian Synod, in which the urgency of the moment did not permit longer delays, and says:

> “With affairs arranged in this way, nothing else remained except for the pontiff, secure concerning the faith of his Westerners, to send them to the East to plead the cause of all.”

Thus the entire delegation rests upon an assumption.

This assumption did indeed have considerable force, so that one could affirm that all the Westerners held the same view concerning the faith as the pontiff had defined in his Roman synod—especially since, in such synods, several bishops from different provinces who were then residing at Rome often took part, and could guarantee the teaching of the bishops of their fellow provincials and provinces.

Leo speaks of this agreement in doctrine in his letter to the Gallicans. But when the matter concerns legates, for whose appointment an express mandate is necessary, an assumed consensus of the absent is insufficient.

If legates possess only the authority of the one by whom they were sent, as is stated in canon 7 of the Sardican council, how could legates sent solely by the apostolic see—or at most by the Roman synod—be said to have borne the authority and embassy of those other Westerners by whom they had not been sent?

Only Quesnellus and those who were rashly swept away by his sophistries could have asserted this.

### 32.

When Saint Cyril, summarizing the judgment of the legates at the Council of Ephesus, said:

> “For they [the legates] deposed [Nestorius], taking the place of the apostolic see and of the entire synod of the most holy and most beloved Western bishops,”

and when the Council of Ephesus itself said in its report to the emperor:

> “The most pious archbishop of your great Rome and the entire Western synod, through the most holy bishops whom it itself sent to us,”

they could have meant by “the Western bishops” and “the Western synod” only the bishops of the Roman synod and that synod alone—those bishops who, as we heard from Cyril himself, were found in the great city of Rome. This was certainly not a synod of the entire West.

Moreover, both Cyril in the same address and the council in the same report called the embassy that of the apostolic see and of Pope Celestine alone, because the letters, inscribed in Celestine’s name alone, presented the delegation and procuration of Celestine alone.

Nor should one dwell too subtly on the general expressions “the entire Western synod,” “the whole synod of the Western bishops,” and similar phrases. For the same Ephesian Fathers, in another report to the same emperor, not only said that the Ephesian Synod had the whole West in agreement with it, but also all Africa.

Yet only the deacon Besula had attended from Africa. He had neither been delegated nor could he have been delegated by a synod of all Africa, as Capreolus himself, bishop of Carthage, admits in the letter brought by that same deacon and read in Action 1.

The same wording is also found in the report praised by Quesnellus, whose complete text is as follows:

> “Celestine, the most holy and most pious archbishop of your great Rome, and the entire Western synod, through the most holy bishops whom it itself sent to us, and all Africa, are present at the Ephesian assembly.”

You see, then, how improperly Quesnellus introduced such formulas in order to transform the embassy of the apostolic see into an embassy of the whole West.

### 33.

What he further brings forward as an obvious argument from the acts of the Sixth Council—where the bishops of Portus, Paternus, and Regia are said to represent the ancient Roman council at which 120 bishops assembled—is exceedingly strange.

For if those acts are carefully examined and nothing is omitted, this document not only does no harm but rather supports our position.

It is true that in the individual actions and in the subscriptions three bishops—John of Portus, Abundantius of Paternus, and John of Regia—are called “representing the venerable ancient synod of Rome of 125 bishops beloved by God.”

At the same time, however, it is also true that three others—namely, the two Roman Church priests Theodore and George, together with the deacon John—are called in the same actions and subscriptions “representing the most holy and most blessed Pope Agatho.”

It is further true that these latter men, although adorned only with the rank of priest or deacon, consistently occupied the first place before all the Fathers, even those of the patriarchal sees, because they represented the person of the Roman pontiff, the primate of the whole Church.

The others, although bishops and sent by a full Western synod, were separated from those first representatives and occupied a place after the Fathers of the principal sees.

Does not this distinction in appellation and rank clearly establish a distinction between the legates—namely, that the legates of Pope Agatho were not legates of the entire Western synod, and that the legates of this synod were not regarded as the pope’s legates? Otherwise all of them would have been found mentioned and subscribed together, and the bishops would have preceded the priests and the deacon.

Why, then, did Quesnellus introduce a single mention of the legates of the Western synod and produce this testimony at precisely the point where he had undertaken to prove that the pope’s legates were the same as the legates of the Western synod?

### 34.

If you ask why this distinction between the pope’s legates and those of the synod occurs in this one Sixth Council, it can easily be understood from the same acts.

In letters to Donus, Agatho’s predecessor, the emperor had expressly requested this double embassy: one in the mandate and name of the pontiff himself, and the other in the mandate and name of the Roman council convened from the West.

The same emperor openly indicates this double mandate in another letter to George, archbishop of Constantinople, in these words:

> “Agatho, the holy pope recently ordained in the apostolic see of that ancient Rome, having received these pious letters of ours after Donus’s death, sent Theodore and George, priests beloved by God, clothed in his own person, together with John, a deacon beloved by God; but in the person of his entire council, John, Abundantius, and John, venerable bishops … presenting to us two petitions: one in the name of Pope Agatho himself, and the other in the name of his council.”

Here, then, are two kinds of legates, and an express mandate and procuration of each kind. Hence, too, two letters are recited in the same acts: one inscribed in the name of the pontiff alone, the other in the name of the entire synod.

From this, two points of the greatest importance for the present matter follow.

First, those legates who attended the council solely in the place and name of the pontiff were not regarded as legates of the entire Roman and Western synod. Otherwise there would have been no need to request and send a distinct embassy.

Second, a distinct mandate and procuration from all the bishops of that synod was required for an embassy of the entire synod, as well as an explicit mention of the synod’s embassy. This is indeed consistently recorded in the acts of the Sixth Council.

Since, however, in the other general councils no explicit mandate of the Westerners or of the Roman synod is read, while the legates are called representatives of the pontiff alone or of the apostolic see alone, it is a fiction to advertise them as legates of the whole West or of the Roman synod.

## NINTH DISSERTATION

### On the case of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, and his condemnation; and on the ordination of Maximus, his successor; in which the letters of Saint Leo and the acts of the Council of Chalcedon are elucidated, and the action concerning Domnus inserted into those acts is shown to be fictitious

Concerning Letters 60, 78, and 80 of Saint Leo; now Letters 80, 104, and 106.

[Col. 0701]

### I.

Many people are surprised that Maximus, bishop of Antioch, who was substituted in place of Domnus by the leaders of the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod, was confirmed by the ecumenical council, and they attempt to investigate the matter more carefully.

Almost all Catholic writers who have treated this question offer roughly the same explanation: Maximus, although elected by suspicious men, consecrated by the bishop of Constantinople contrary to canonical rule, and installed over Domnus while Domnus was still alive, was nevertheless received by the council because he had been confirmed in the episcopate by Saint Leo.

Why, however, among the many bishops who had been expelled from their sees by the Ephesian pseudo-synod through the greatest crime, was Domnus alone not restored, while all the others were reinstated? This presents no lesser difficulty.

For all the acts of the Ephesian Robbers’ Synod had been declared null by the Western bishops even before the Council of Chalcedon, and Pope Leo had repeatedly urged the emperor—Letter 40, now Letter 44, chapter 2—to order that everything remain in the condition in which it had been before the ill-fated synod, until everything could be reformed by an ecumenical council.

It followed that the deposition of Domnus and the ordination of Maximus should have been null, and that Domnus should have recovered his own place.

Yet they say that Leo prevented this because, as Baronius says:

> “After examining the case, he understood that Domnus had been justly condemned.”  
> *(Baronius, On the Year 451, no. 128.)*

The eminent cardinal does not explain his meaning more clearly, nor does he reveal in what respect Domnus’s deposition was more just than that of the others.

At the Ephesian Synod, Domnus had indeed allowed himself to be carried away into the sacrilegious designs of Dioscorus; he had subscribed to the condemnation of Flavian and Eusebius, to the restoration of Eutyches, and to the impious decrees, surrendering his hands as captives to them.

But since this fault was shared by many, indulgence ought also to have been shared with the others, as it was in the Council of Chalcedon.

Perhaps he was more blameworthy than the others because recent guilt was added to old suspicions. Since he had been the nephew and successor of John of Antioch, he had been accused of the Nestorian stain no less than John had been.

Moreover, he did not possess the knowledge and firmness of spirit that were necessary for a bishop of so great a city in those exceedingly difficult times.

Finally, perhaps someone might not unreasonably say that Domnus himself had voluntarily lent his hand to his own deposition, attracted by the delights of the solitary life in which he had once been nurtured under the abbot Euthymius.

When he was planning to leave those delights, despite the opposition of the holy Father, in order to assist his uncle John, who was turning away from the Catholic faith, he heard these words from Euthymius, prophetic of what would come:

> “If, neglecting these things and despising the thoughts of endurance, you attempt to leave the laura, you will indeed obtain the administration which your uncle possesses, but evil and more deceitful men will again take it away from you, after you have first been led astray by them through ignorance.”

Cyril the monk reports this while discussing the deeds of Saint Euthymius. He adds that Domnus went to Antioch:

> “And when he had been there,” he says, “everything that had been foretold to him came to pass. Afterwards, deeply repentant because he had not obeyed, he returned to him, tormented by severe pain in his entrails and bitterly lamenting.”

From these words it seems possible to conclude that, after his administration had been taken away—as had been foretold to him—Domnus, moved by repentance, visited Euthymius again and spent the remainder of his life in retirement, voluntarily leaving Maximus in possession of the episcopate of the Church of Antioch, which Maximus had obtained through the favor of the Eutychians.

This, finally, would be the true reason why he did not return to his see.

### II.

Those who think that Leo’s authority brought about the retention of Maximus in the see of Antioch, although he had been placed there under such evil auspices, and that Domnus was compelled to yield his place, say that this is clearly evident from the acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

For in the action entitled *Concerning Domnus of Antioch*, it is expressly stated that Maximus was confirmed by Leo’s authority.

Since I intend to examine this action in order to investigate the truth of ecclesiastical history, it is worthwhile to reproduce it here in full. It is not lengthy, and when it is placed before the reader’s eyes, the reader will more easily form his own judgment.

## ACTION CONCERNING DOMNUS OF ANTIOCH

Part II of the Council of Chalcedon, after Action 10.

In the consulship of our lord Marcian, perpetual Augustus, and of the one who was announced, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, at Chalcedon, in accordance with the command of our most divine and most merciful lord the emperor, the participants assembled in the holy church of Saint Euphemia the holy martyr: the most magnificent and most glorious master of the soldiers and former ordinary consul, the patrician Anatolius; the most magnificent and most glorious master of the sacred offices, Vincomalus; and also Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, most reverend priest, representatives of Leo, the most holy archbishop of Old Rome; Anatolius, most reverend archbishop of Constantinople, the city of the greatest name; Maximus, most reverend archbishop of Antioch in Syria; Juvenal, most reverend bishop of Jerusalem; and the rest of the holy synod, which had assembled in the city of Chalcedon by the decree of our most divine and most merciful lord Marcian, whose names are written below.

When all were seated before the railings of the holy altar, Maximus, most reverend bishop of Antioch, said:

> “I beseech your most magnificent and most glorious judges, and this holy and universal synod, to deign to show humanity toward Domnus, who was bishop of Antioch, and to establish for him fixed support from the revenues of the Church that is under me.”

Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface the priest, representatives of the apostolic see, spoke through Paschasinus, most reverend bishop:

> “The holy and most blessed pope, who confirmed the episcopate of the holy and venerable Maximus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, appears by a sufficiently just judgment to have approved his merit. Indeed, the aforementioned most reverend bishop Maximus, of his own accord, wished to provide for Domnus, so that, out of compassion, he might grant him support from his Church, as he should judge appropriate, so that Domnus, content with his maintenance, might rest in the future.”

This confession was translated into Greek by Beronicianus, a devout man and secretary of the sacred consistory.  
[Alternative: “was handed over.”]

Anatolius, most reverend bishop of Constantinople, said:

> “I too praise the compassion [Alternative: sympathy] of the most blessed Maximus, bishop of Antioch, since of his own free will he offered such petitions that support might be provided for Domnus, who had been bishop of the holy Church under him, while the aforesaid man requested nothing beyond this.”

Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, said:

> “I too embrace the proposal of Maximus, the holy bishop of Antioch.”

The entire synod shouted [Alternative: “exclaimed”]:

> “The archbishop’s benevolence is deservedly praiseworthy. We all praise his intention. This humane thought of the pontiff befits his reputation.”

The most magnificent judges said:

> “Since the holy synod embraces the decision of Maximus, the religious bishop of the Antiochians, which he has approved concerning Domnus, we too agree with it, leaving to his decision what concerns Domnus’s honorable support.”

And in another hand:

> “Let them be issued.”

Thus far the action concerning Domnus.

### III.

I would most earnestly wish this action not to be fictitious but genuine.

For if it were genuine, we would already have before us a most illustrious and ancient testimony to the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff both over synods and over Eastern bishops—over, I mean, the bishops of the greater and principal sees.

For what power it would display if the consecration, or at least the confirmation, of the bishop of Antioch, and consequently of the bishop of Alexandria and of other bishops, had belonged to the Roman bishop, as Cardinal Bellarmine and his apologist Jacobus Gretserus argue from this passage!  
*(Bellarmine, volume I, Controversy III, On the Roman Pontiff, book II, chapter 12; Gretserus, Defense of Bellarmine, volume II, at this passage.)*

What a prerogative it would be if, when many bishops had been deposed by force and crime by the ill-fated synod, their condemnation and deposition were ordered to stand because the Roman bishop judged that they ought to stand; and if the substitution of another bishop in the place of one of them were valid only because that same Roman bishop had confirmed it!

Finally, how clearly this would reveal his supreme power over synods: their acts would have force in that part to which he had added force, while the part that he wished to be null would be void and invalid.

Yet just as it is the mark of a learned and wise theologian to defend the true and genuine privileges of the principal see with all his heart and by solid and authentic proofs, so it is a sign of an insufficiently sincere and generous mind either to extend those privileges beyond their prescribed limits or to support them with uncertain, perishable, and false aids and props.

For truth does not need falsehood. Rather, through association with falsehood, even the most firmly established truth is accustomed to be called into suspicion of falsity.

Such, in my opinion, is everything that ecclesiastical writers have asserted about Domnus on the basis of that session—writers who, hastening toward other matters, had no time to investigate its truth more carefully.[^c0082-1] But after examining the matter more closely, I am certain[^c0082-2] that Domnus of Antioch had already died by the time Maximus became bishop of the Church of Antioch; consequently, that session bearing Domnus’s name is false and fabricated, and is falsely attributed, through a rotten lie, to the holy Council of Chalcedon. In it, namely, Maximus is introduced as distributing to Domnus, who supposedly survived his deposition, provisions from the revenues of his Church, by indulgence of the council. In asserting this confidently, I believe that I have arguments neither slight nor weak.

[^c0082-1]: We shall defend the truth and authenticity of this session in the observations to be added, and there refute all Quesnel’s efforts.

[^c0082-2]: This will be proved false in the same place, no. 2.

### IV

First, this is the only session among all the other sessions of the Council of Chalcedon that is found published solely in Latin,[^c0082-3] and nowhere has it appeared in Greek. This is certainly a significant indication that it was fabricated by some Latin impostor. For if it had really been composed at the council, it would certainly have existed in Greek and would have been read, together with the other sessions, among the Greek acts of this synod. There is no evident reason why this one session should have been separated from the body of the other Greek sessions.

[^c0082-3]: Although this session has appeared nowhere in Greek, we shall demonstrate in the observations that it was translated from Greek into Latin. The fact that the Greek manuscripts which have come down to us are defective proves nothing in particular cases, as will be clear from note 18 (vol. 257, note b) in Dissertation 1 on the year 451. There we made it clear that particular sessions of this kind were generally omitted in many Greek manuscripts, while in not a few others—which do contain particular sessions—the session concerning Photius of Tyre was omitted. What, then, is surprising if this session concerning Domnus was passed over?

### V. 2

This session is transmitted to us by a single manuscript, which was recommended by no authority or antiquity; it was merely on paper and is said to have been obtained from two unknown German scholars. Such is the epigraph with which it is found marked in the Crabbian, Surian, and other editions of the Councils:

> Session concerning Domnus of Antioch, found in the parchment codex of the Fathers of Julia, transcribed from an ancient paper codex, and said to have belonged to Proculus and Albinus, German scholastics.

In the latest edition of the Councils, however, Philippe Labbe praises a certain codex of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, collated, annotated, and punctuated by Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, with Greek manuscripts. In this codex, said to belong to D. Bohier of Dijon, the session concerning Domnus follows the sixth session under this title:

> The sixth session ends. The seventh, concerning Domnus, once patriarch of Antioch, translated from Greek into Latin, begins.[^c0082-4]

[^c0082-4]: We have found another codex, very ancient and of different provenance, whose excellence we shall discuss in Observation no. 3 and following. Quesnel’s error concerning the codex he names here depends on his belief that the heading prefixed to this session in the printed editions was supplied by the editors, as though they had used a recent copy transcribed from another of two German manuscripts when printing it. But this heading—which we shall reproduce in the observations according to the evidence of the manuscript books—has Rusticus as its author, and consequently the manuscripts mentioned in it are also very ancient. See Observation nos. 11 and 12.

Yet Rusticus’s reliability in this matter is suspect. For when this schismatic deacon, subjected to an anathema by Pope Vigilius, saw that his opponents, who demanded the condemnation of the Three Chapters, habitually produced the example of Domnus as one condemned after death, he could have adopted this defense of his cause by means of a lie: he might have fabricated a session concerning Domnus as though Domnus were still alive, in order to assert that he had not been condemned after death, and at least persuade Westerners of this.

Whatever may be said about Rusticus’s reliability and sincerity, it appears certain to me that he reviewed only the first session of the Council of Chalcedon. He appended his name only to that session, in the following manner:

**From the Bohier manuscript codex**

> The first inquiry of the Council of Chalcedon ends. We finished correcting and collating the manuscripts on the day before the Kalends of December [the reading is materially uncertain], Wednesday, in the thirteenth indiction, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. Rusticus, by the grace of God deacon of the holy Roman Church, collated, annotated, and punctuated them. Thanks be to God.

**From the edition of Peter Crabbe, Friar Minor**

> The end of the first inquiry of the Council of Chalcedon, which was completed, corrected, and collated in the year of our Lord 417 [Labbeus says that this is emended in the margin either to 454 or 457, though all the readings are extremely corrupt], on Wednesday, in the thirteenth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. Rusticus, by the grace of God deacon of the holy Roman Church, collated, annotated, and punctuated it. Thanks be to God.

There is nearly the same statement in the Roman edition, with a few variations. From these passages it appears that nothing certain can be established from such annotations, which are mutually inconsistent. Moreover, that notice in the Bohier codex is not the work of Rusticus alone but of several different annotators. Rusticus reread the Council of Chalcedon against a codex which earlier correctors had already corrected and collated; he added his own testimony, just as they had added theirs. They reviewed the remaining sessions, whereas Rusticus does not appear to have proceeded beyond the first.[^c0082-5]

[^c0082-5]: We shall show this to be false in the observation on Quesnel’s note 2 concerning Epistle 113. Quesnel could not have possessed a distinct knowledge of what Rusticus had produced when he wrote this, for Baluze’s emendations to Rusticus’s text had not yet appeared. Anyone who reads them will recognize that the subsequent remarks of Rusticus are worthless.

I add that the years designated by the earlier annotation cannot belong to the lifetime of Rusticus, and that the earlier annotation is rendered suspect by the expression “manuscript.” Before God, the supreme and best, had granted humanity the art of printing books, there would have been no point whatsoever in suggesting a distinction between manuscripts and printed books, as that expression does.

Moreover, even if we grant that all the sessions of Chalcedon were reread and corrected by Rusticus, it is clear that he did not find the session under discussion. The Bohier codex alone testifies to this. In it, the title of the session concerning Domnus is entirely singular; no mention is made of rereading or correcting it. The reference to its translation from Greek is evidence that it was not taken from the Greek codex which Rusticus had in hand while collating.

Finally, Peter Crabbe, Laurence Surius, and others who used codices reread and corrected by Rusticus in publishing the Council of Chalcedon make no mention of Rusticus when they reach the session concerning Domnus. They openly state that they extracted it from the single parchment codex of Julia and brought it to public light. Hence it is evident by how uncertain a route it has reached us, and that its entire credibility rests with two German scholastics.

But I am weary of these trivialities. Let us proceed to other arguments for its fabrication.

### VI. 3

Its position is uncertain, from the time when it was inserted among the sessions of Chalcedon. Since it had been assigned no number, it received whatever place anyone chose to assign it. In the Crabbian and Surian editions, and in the Latin Binian edition of A.D. 1606, it is found placed after the seventh session. The Roman Greek-Latin edition and later editions fix its position after the tenth session. The editors of none of these editions establish or alter the order with any reasoning or authority derived from a manuscript. Thus it is clear that, among the other sessions of the synod,[^c0082-6] it was never numbered, but was added and inserted long after the acts had been collected—hence it is seen tossed about among such uncertain positions.

[^c0082-6]: The same thing occurred with the session concerning Photius of Tyre, although no one would deny that it is genuine. See Observation no. 13 and note 18 (vol. 257, note b) in Dissertation 1 on the year 451.

### VII. 4

It is established that this session was unknown to the Emperor Justinian, since in the lengthy work entitled *Justinian the Emperor’s Confession of the Right Faith against the Three Chapters, directed to the entire body of the Catholic and Apostolic Church*, addressed to the entire body of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, we read the following:

> The holy Council of Chalcedon condemned Domnus, who had become bishop of Antioch, after his death, because he alone dared to write that Cyril’s Twelve Chapters ought to be silenced.

How could Domnus have been condemned after death if, by the council’s decision, Maximus distributed to him provisions from the revenues of the Church of Antioch? Are the emperor and his ministers, whose services he employed in this affair, to be thought ignorant of anything contained in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon—of that council, I mean, for whose sake alone they were disturbing the whole Church?

[^c0082-7]: We shall answer this negative argument in Observation no. 14. There is nothing surprising in Justinian, the Fathers of the Fifth Council, and Facundus being unaware of this session, since it was absent from their codices just as the session concerning Photius of Tyre was lacking from most copies. Nor should it matter that Justinian and the Fathers of the synod cited above state in the passages quoted that the Council of Chalcedon condemned Domnus after his death. Apart from the fact that certain other errors of theirs in historical matters are evident, this assertion is proved false by our session, which was unknown to them. Certainly, there is nothing in the remaining acts from which that condemnation and death could have been inferred. The only statement found there is that Maximus was received by the council as a bishop because Saint Leo had admitted him to communion. See Session 10.

### VIII. 5

Not only the emperor and his advisers, but also the entire Fifth Ecumenical Council held the same view, as is written near the end of the sixth conference:

> The Council of Chalcedon condemned Domnus, bishop of Antioch, because he wrote that the Twelve Chapters of Cyril, of holy memory, ought to be silenced; and it condemned him after his death, having confirmed his condemnation and accepted the ordination of Maximus.

If, then, Domnus was condemned after death by the Council of Chalcedon—for anyone who asserts that the Fathers spoke rashly and without investigating the matter would plainly be acting insultingly toward the holy synod and would himself be guilty of even greater rashness—it follows that Domnus was not alive when the synod was held. Anyone who fabricated and inserted this session is thus convicted of the greatest ignorance and impudence.

But, you will say, there is no more reason to believe the council when it affirms that Domnus was condemned after death than when it asserts that he was exempted from a sentence of condemnation by the Council of Chalcedon. Yet this condemnation is nowhere found among the acts of that council.

The Fathers themselves meet the objection when they show that the condemnation is contained in the fact that they confirmed his condemnation. They confirmed it by not rescinding, insofar as this matter was concerned, the acts of the Synod of Ephesus. And they did not rescind those acts in this matter because they did not order the ordination of Maximus—who had been substituted in Domnus’s place because of Domnus’s condemnation—to be invalid, but rather approved it, without raising even the smallest complaint against that ordination.

From this it is clearer than daylight that, in the time of the Emperor Justinian and the Fifth Ecumenical Council, that session was not read among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Otherwise, what could have been easier than to convict them of falsehood by producing the acts of the Fourth Council?

### IX. 6

When Facundus, bishop of Hermiana in Africa, was composing his little work in defense of the Three Chapters, he examined the Emperor Justinian’s confession of faith with the greatest care and attempted to answer all the arguments of the opponents that had been brought forward in support of condemning those same chapters.

But concerning the condemnation of Domnus after death, not even a single word is found in his work. Yet that most perceptive man, who was wholly intent on defending the cause he had undertaken, would certainly not have omitted it if he had learned either from the acts of Chalcedon or from elsewhere that Domnus had survived until the Council of Chalcedon.

This argument is all the stronger because at that time nothing was more frequently in everyone’s hands than the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, whose authority was chiefly at issue; and because all the defenders—whether of the council or of the Three Chapters—were thoroughly informed about those acts, among whom Facundus stood out.

Finally, Facundus was writing at Constantinople, where there certainly existed the most accurate and unimpaired copies of the acts of Chalcedon; and where the monastery of the Acoemetae was located, against whose codex the deacon Rusticus is said to have reviewed the acts of the synod. Rusticus, in his own cause, would have acted no less perversely than Facundus if he had not used this session to refute the argument of his opponents.

### X. 7

In Book II, chapter 1, Facundus likewise numbers Domnus among the holy Fathers and venerable teachers of the Church of Christ—John, I mean, Chrysostom, and Gregory of Nazianzus. He intended to prepare a defense and patronage for Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, on the basis of their approval and testimony; and he considered it a most dreadful thing if anyone should presume to strike either Theodore or his writings with an anathema.

In Book VIII, chapters 5 and 7, he also feared condemning Theodore lest he wrong Domnus, together with the other holy Fathers whom he considered preferable to Cyril. In the same chapter 5, after recounting Domnus’s letter with praise and numbering Domnus himself among the other luminaries of the Church, he writes:

> I think, most merciful emperor, that it would be a great crime and a great profanation for the judges of these luminaries of the world to trample upon the judgment concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and pass over into the darkness of Eutychian blindness.

Finally, to pass over many other passages for the sake of brevity, on almost the last page of his work he calls Domnus “venerable” and praises him as the foremost defender of the faith against Eutyches.

With what face, then, could Facundus—who liked to be commended for his exceptional reverence toward the Council of Chalcedon—have adorned Domnus with such distinguished praises, made him equal to the Church’s and the world’s greatest luminaries, considered it a great crime and a great profanation to trample upon his judgment, and himself valued Domnus’s testimony for Theodore so highly, wishing the opponents to value it equally, if Domnus had received a sentence of condemnation from the Council of Chalcedon and had been reduced to such a condition that he was forced to seek an allowance from his successor?

### XI. 8

From this arises my eighth argument. Even if Domnus had been deposed by the sentence of the impious Dioscorus and forced, by the judgment of the Fathers of Chalcedon, to yield his place to Maximus, yet, having survived the loss of his former dignity, I cannot believe that he could ever have been cast into such a depth of misfortune that, unless his successor’s discretion provided for him, he would have been entirely without provisions.[^c0082-8]

He was the prelate of so great a see. Having succeeded his uncle, he could not have failed to possess many resources, numerous friends, and considerable influence. It is therefore plainly ridiculous to present him before the synod as though he were a beggar, anxious about his subsistence and asking for nothing beyond it.

He would surely rather have chosen to return to his excellent father Euthymius, who, once inspired by the Holy Spirit, had foretold that Domnus would both succeed to his uncle’s position and at some time be driven from that see through the crime and power of the impious.

[^c0082-8]: There is nothing surprising if Domnus, so that he would not be burdensome to those among whom, according to Cyril’s *Life of Saint Euthymius*, Domnus had withdrawn into the desert after relinquishing the episcopate, received the provisions assigned to other deposed bishops at the same synod, in accordance with an already established custom, as Quesnel himself admits in no. 12.

### XII. 9

There are several features in this session that expose the fraud of its impostor. Although he imitated the style of the other sessions as far as he could, in some places he nevertheless betrayed his carelessness and ignorance.

After listing the principal leaders of the synod, he adds the following for the sake of brevity:

> And the rest of the holy synod, which was assembled in the city of Chalcedon by the decree of our most divine and merciful lord Marcian the emperor, whose names are set down below.

The incompetence of the author of this session is attested by several expressions. For *cetera* (“the rest”) is scarcely ever used in the singular number. Then why is *quorum* (“whose”) made to refer back to it, when no word of the same number or gender precedes it? Finally, where do the names appear below, which he assumes are about to be listed?

I omit the barbarisms with which the whole session teems, such as these: *humanitatem exercere* (“to exercise humanity”); *suo arbitrio* (“by his own judgment”) for *spontanea voluntate* (“voluntary willingness”), as he says below; *confessio* (“confession”); *condolentiam* (“compassion”); *precatorias* (“supplications”); *cogitatum* (“thought”); *honorificentia* (“honorificence”); *benevolentiae laudabiles* (“praiseworthy benevolences”); and so forth.

He also violates the order of the synod and the proper reverence due to the holy Fathers when he represents Maximus directing his petitions to lay judges, while passing over the bishops, the leaders of the synod. At that time, bishops could not even tolerate, as stewards of the Churches, giving an account before lay judges of the administration of ecclesiastical property, as is clear from Letter 108 of our Leo.[^c0082-9] Who, then, would believe that they were the first persons whom the bishop of Antioch would address in the synod, when the question concerned granting a portion of ecclesiastical revenues to a deposed bishop?

[^c0082-9]: We have shown in the preface to the letters of Saint Leo, no. 51, how great were formerly the difficulty and incompetence of Latin translators. The deficiencies censured here by Quesnel will likewise be found in other ancient translations. Some may also have resulted from the carelessness of copyists. The names of the bishops indicated below, but missing from the text, may have been omitted through the tedium of writing, as though they were unnecessary, just as certain speeches were omitted by this same translator in the session concerning Juvenal. Similar omissions occur in the Greek manuscripts themselves; more careful ancient translations or other Greek manuscripts reveal them. Nothing, therefore, can be extracted from this as proof of fabrication.

> I beseech the most magnificent and glorious judges, etc.

Then, forgetting himself, he introduces the legates of the apostolic see as responding, although the matter was usually conducted in the opposite order. In the other sessions, petitions and humble requests are addressed to the entire synod; then the judges seek the opinion of the principal bishops of the synod.

It is also ridiculous that the Fathers should have held a separate and solemn consultation to determine Domnus’s provisions—as though the wealth of the Churches were not the patrimony of the poor, and as though a bishop who had presided over his Church for many years with the highest distinction were not foremost among the poor and worthy of special privilege. It would thus have been necessary for Maximus to obtain permission from the synod to be humane and merciful toward his predecessor.

There are two examples in the same synod of allowances granted to deposed bishops, but the matter was not handled with such elaborate ceremony and display, although it required much greater deliberation. Bassianus and Stephen, having been intruded into the Church of Ephesus contrary to the canons, were removed from the episcopate and, by the vote of one and the other, ordered to be supported by the Church of Ephesus, although it might seem unjust to burden that Church with maintaining such men.

Likewise, Sabinianus—who had been ordained bishop by a provincial council after the deposition of Athanasius of the Church of Perrha, and who, after Athanasius’s deposition had been examined, was to yield the episcopate of Perrha while retaining his episcopal dignity—the synod wished him to receive provisions and settled the matter with a single word: “Let him be supported.” It did not seek the individual vote of the members on the matter, but followed an established custom. Nor was this so much a granting of permission for mercy as an attempt to ensure that those who replaced deposed bishops would not fail to show mercy.

[^c0082-10]: The particular cases of Bassianus and Stephen of Ephesus, and of Athanasius, bishop of Perrha, were discussed in the council. Afterward, a stipend was immediately assigned to them, so that no separate session was needed merely to establish it. Since there was no other particular case to be handled concerning Domnus—who had already yielded the episcopate to Maximus—except this matter relating to his stipend, the issue was treated separately.

### XIII. 10

When Leo, with the agreement of all the Westerners, annulled the acts of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, he never considered making an exception for Domnus’s deposition. He invalidated absolutely everything perpetrated there by Dioscorus, declaring that acts carried out through the impudence of one man, contrary to justice and canonical discipline, could not be regarded as valid for any reason connected with the Catholic faith (Epistle 47, now 51).

He also asked the Emperor Augustus Theodosius to order everything to remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment, until a greater number of priests from the whole world could be assembled (Epistle 40, now 44, chapter 2).

Why, then, should the sentence pronounced against Domnus be thought to have taken effect? Certainly for no other reason than that Domnus had died before Maximus was either chosen or ordained bishop.[^c0082-11]

[^c0082-11]: We shall assign another reason in Observation no. 2.

### XIV. 11

The entire body of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon contains nothing that in the slightest compromises the memory of Domnus of Antioch. Whenever it happens to mention him—which occurred frequently, even with the complete acts of the councils he had held being reported—not a word is said about a condemnation imposed or confirmed against him.

In Session 14, the judges asked Athanasius of Perrha why, when summoned for the third time by the holy Council of Antioch, he had not appeared.

> Because, he replied, he himself who was judging was my enemy—the bishop of Antioch.

You see how he speaks of Domnus as though he were already dead, and how it never entered the judges’ minds, while this case was being examined, to summon Domnus and require him to give an account of the judgment he had rendered and the sentence he had pronounced against Athanasius. That would certainly have been a shorter course than referring the entire matter to the Council of Antioch for an eight-month investigation.

[^c0082-12]: Athanasius’s words, quoted above, do not indicate that Domnus was already dead. The judges did not question Domnus because he was not present at the council.

### XV. 12

If Domnus had survived the predatory synod for any length of time, he would never have been so forgetful of his own case and honor that he would neither follow the example of others by seeking pardon for his fault nor lodge complaints about Dioscorus’s treachery before Saint Leo or before Leo’s legates, who had been sent to Constantinople to repair the disaster of Ephesus.[^c0082-13]

If he had failed to do this and had not sought communion with the Catholic priests, he would rightly have been charged with negligence.
