Indeed, he would have gone to the Council of Chalcedon to complain before the sacred synod about Dioscorus’s violence and treachery—as others did who were in a far worse situation.

Cardinal Baronius indeed asserts that Domnus was present at that time as a private individual. I suppose he was moved by no other argument than that he thought he could extract this from the present session, where Domnus is introduced as asking for provisions.

But even if this session expressly asserted that Domnus had been present, nothing would have been established, since the reliability of such a document is itself at issue. In any case, I do not think Baronius learned of Domnus’s presence at the council from another source, since the silence about it is everywhere so profound that, in the absence of any prejudice, I think that this silence rather proves decisively that Domnus the bishop was neither present nor alive at that time.

[^c0082-13]: After his deposition, Domnus, moved to repentance and contemplating withdrawal into the desert, was not concerned about the episcopate. Consequently, neither he nor his friends did anything—whether before Leo or at the council—to restore him to or vindicate his place.

### XVI. 13

Who could persuade himself that Domnus, who had ruled the Church of Antioch—and consequently the entire diocese of the East—for so many years; who had all the friends of his uncle and predecessor John bound to him; who himself had begotten many sons through consecration; and whom both love of piety and zeal for the faith had greatly commended—who, I say, could believe that this man was so completely deprived of every support, so despised and abandoned by everyone, that no one came forward to defend him, no one appealed to the ecumenical synod, no Antiochene cried out for his bishop to be restored, and no one rejected Maximus as having been set over a living bishop?

This was especially so since Maximus had been consecrated by the bishop of Constantinople contrary to ecclesiastical law and custom, while Domnus had been deposed by the impious Dioscorus in utter violation of every right.

Certainly, the bishops of the Eastern diocese so detested the monstrous crime by which Dioscorus polluted himself at Ephesus that it became the seed and origin of a greater division among the dioceses of those regions. Immediately after the pseudo-synod at Ephesus was dissolved and the bishops had returned to their sees, Liberatus writes, chapter 12:

> A schism arose among them such as had never occurred before. The Egyptian, Thracian, and Palestinian bishops followed Dioscorus; the Eastern, Pontic, and Asian bishops followed Flavian, of holy memory.

When all this is considered, who could think that none of them would have undertaken Domnus’s defense, if he had survived—especially since it is plausible that such a great division arose in part on his account?

They knew, surely, that the ancient rivalry between those two sees, Alexandria and Antioch, had moved Dioscorus to crush his rival by force, even though, through fear of the threatened death, he had miserably allowed himself to be swept into the condemnation of Flavian and the restoration of Eutyches. Nor is it plausible that they had then stripped themselves of all the zeal for their patriarch which they had always possessed so vehemently among the Easterners.

For what disturbances and what seditions were stirred up in the following year on behalf of Dioscorus alone—a wicked man notorious for his crimes! Although he had been publicly condemned and deposed in the Ecumenical Council by the unanimous judgment of more than six hundred bishops, the Alexandrians could scarcely be persuaded to choose another in his place, even though imperial decrees ordered this as well.

For concerning this matter, Liberatus writes, chapter 13:

> Much hesitation arose, since they wished to ordain no one at all, lest they appear to be adulterers, Dioscorus still being alive.

### XVII. 14

Many episcopal cases and depositions were examined with the greatest care at the Council of Chalcedon, including matters that did not belong to the council’s proper subject, and including bishops whose cases had already been debated in councils and whose standing and merit were not equal to those of the bishop of Antioch.

If Domnus had therefore been alive and unharmed at that time, there is no doubt that his case would have been brought back to the anvil for reconsideration, since special consideration was given above all to those who had fallen at the assembly of Ephesus, and there was no other tribunal to which the bishop of Antioch could be brought.

We certainly possess a letter of Leo, Epistle 110, now 139, to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, stating that Christ destroyed that detestable judgment of the Ephesian synod through the authority of the holy Council of Chalcedon in such a way that it excluded **no one** from the remedy of correction.

If it excluded no one, then certainly it did not exclude Domnus; consequently, the entire document must be fictitious if, in contradiction of Leo, it testifies that the bishop of Antioch was shut out from the remedy of correction.

[^c0082-14]: None of those who sought restoration after correction was rejected by Chalcedon. Domnus cannot be said to have been rejected, because, intending to withdraw into the desert, he neither sought nor wished to be restored.

### XVIII. 15

There is no reason why Domnus should have been treated more harshly and less mercifully than the others who had been compelled by their signatures to condemn Flavian. Indeed, he was more innocent than the others and worthy of receiving mercy before them all (Facundus, Book XII, final chapter).

Not only had he formerly been the first of all to strike down the rising heresy of Eutyches and had himself inspired Flavian to take up the struggle by his example; but after, shaken by fear of the soldiers surrounding him, he had consented by his own signature to Flavian’s condemnation, he was the first of all, moved by repentance, to recover his senses. He led those whom he had followed when they were falling by the example of rising again.

Indeed, he suffered the loss of his dignity for this very reason: he freely retracted the consent that had been extorted from him.

We have Nicephorus as a witness to this. It is reasonable to believe that he took this part of the history from much earlier historians, and he had no advantage in inventing it. He writes as follows (Book IV, chapter 47):

> With these men, Domnus also, the successor of John in the Church of Antioch, confirmed the matter at that time by his annotation. But when he had been restored to his authority, he retracted what he had yielded, resisting Dioscorus and the leading men from the imperial court, crying out against the decrees as having been made contrary to ecclesiastical sanctions, calling the synod impious, and finally demanding that his signature be returned to him. But for this reason the synod also deprived this priest of his sacerdotal dignity.

Liberatus appears to give another reason for the deposition, when he writes in chapter 12 of the *Breviary*:

> After all the others, he also deposed Domnus of Antioch, who had remained after the deposition of the orthodox, because he had become Dioscorus’s accomplice in the deposition of the orthodox and the acquittal of Eutyches. He was deposed through Dioscorus’s trickery in this way: after Domnus had consented to everything with Dioscorus, and after the letters which Domnus of Antioch had written to Dioscorus against Cyril’s Twelve Chapters, on the ground that they were obscure, had been produced in the midst of the proceedings, Dioscorus condemned him, sick and absent on that day.

These two authors can easily be reconciled if one says that the first gives the true reason why Dioscorus considered deposing Domnus, whereas the second explains the pretext he offered for his worst treachery. No one will believe that Dioscorus was moved by zeal for the faith to perpetrate it.

Indeed, I think that Nicephorus and Liberatus disagree so little that both supplied the same reason, which the carelessness of scribes or inattentive printers obscured in Liberatus—unless my conjecture deceives me. The text we have just quoted can scarcely, if at all, produce a coherent meaning. For what does it mean that Dioscorus deposed Domnus of Antioch, “who had remained after the deposition of the orthodox,” because he had become Dioscorus’s accomplice in the deposition of the orthodox and the acquittal of Eutyches?

You see that these words contain mere tautology, and that it is scarcely possible to understand what is meant by “who had remained after the deposition of the orthodox.” If, instead, you posit the following wording:

> He deposed Domnus of Antioch, who recoiled from—or rather, returned from—the deposition of the orthodox,

the sense becomes excellent and expresses the same judgment as Nicephorus.[^c0082-15] For *remeantem* (“returning”) differs from *remanentem* (“remaining”) by the transposition of only one letter, and the word is found with this meaning in Saint Augustine, also an African, in Book II of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*:

> We desire that they return to the peace and unity of the holy Church.

And in Epistle 172, to Crispinus:

> Unless they had returned to your communion.

The meaning now becomes clear, and the same judgment as Nicephorus’s is expressed: this unquestionably greatly diminishes Domnus’s guilt, which was washed away by so vigorous and prompt a retraction, and it plainly exposes that session as fabricated.

[^c0082-15]: This emendation—and the reading which Quesnel attributes to Liberatus here as conforming to Nicephorus—is refuted by Liberatus’s own subsequent argument and context.

After this, if Domnus had survived, he would have been received by the synod with precisely the same—and indeed far greater—kindness than the other bishops who had fallen. There would have been no consideration of granting him a portion of the ecclesiastical revenues, since he would have been restored, along with the others, to his former dignity.

### XIX. 16

A reason akin to the preceding one is drawn from the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon. There the judges raise the question whether Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eusebius of Ancyra, Eustathius of Berytus, and Basil of Seleucia in Isauria—all of whom had possessed authority and had been leaders of the cabal, and had condemned Flavian—should, according to the canons, be deprived of episcopal dignity and receive a similar sentence of condemnation with Dioscorus. The matter is referred to the emperor; he sends it back to the Fathers of the council, who unanimously shouted that mercy should be shown to the bishops.

Why, then, did the judges not raise a similar question concerning Domnus? [Note: See note 14 above, column 711, note a.] Why was he not received with equal indulgence? Why was he not admitted to the synod, when he was far more innocent than those men? For he had neither been among the leaders of the synod nor conspired with Dioscorus; rather, he had been driven by fear to subscribe to a sentence already pronounced and immediately came to his senses.

“But,” you will say, “the earlier writings issued against Cyril’s chapters, and indeed against the Catholic faith itself, added weight to his later fault and made him unworthy of pardon.” If this argument is valid, there was no reason to spare Theodoret or restore his see. He too had been the leader of that entire controversy, had fought fiercely against Cyril’s anathemas, and for this reason had been driven from his see by Dioscorus. Others also, as Facundus argued on Theodoret’s behalf in book II, chapter 1, whose testimony we cite, wrote against the same blessed Cyril; nevertheless, they were not named in the anathema. There was therefore no reason why Domnus’s condition should have been worse, since his case was the same as Theodoret’s, or why, after Juvenal and the other fallen bishops had been received back into favor, he alone—if he had still been alive—should have remained subject to the sentence of his impious deposition.

### XX. 17

If Domnus had survived until the ecumenical synod and had been condemned together with the heretics, then, when Anatolius wrote to Saint Leo and asked whether the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius should be recited at the sacred altar, he would likewise have asked about Domnus’s name; and Leo would have given the same answer concerning him as concerning the others. [Note: Leo had written only concerning the leaders of the Ephesian Robber Synod who still held the episcopate. See Epistle 95, chapter 4. Domnus, however, was not among the leaders of the Robber Synod; moreover, intending to withdraw into the desert, he had relinquished the episcopate to Maximus.] The profound silence in both places regarding Domnus proves not only that he had died, but also that he had departed in ecclesiastical peace and in communion with the apostolic sees.

### XXI. 18

The constitution of the emperor Theodosius, in which he confirmed the acts of the false synod, states after relating that by his decree Flavian and Eusebius had been excluded from the episcopate: “But also Domnus, who was bishop of Antioch, and Theodoret, and others, etc.” [Note: “Therefore,” says Theodosius, “he who was bishop of Antioch,” because he did not regard Domnus, once deposed, as a bishop. Likewise, in the third session of Chalcedon, when Dioscorus was deposed, he is called “formerly bishop of Alexandria.” As for Theodoret and the other bishops, although they had been deposed at Ephesus just as Domnus had been, the reason Theodosius did not use the same formula concerning them is that in the cited passage he did not name their episcopates.]

By this manner of speaking—“who was,” a designation which he did not use in the case of the living Theodoret and Eusebius, although they had been expelled from their sees—Theodosius seems to indicate that Domnus had by then died.

This is confirmed by the constitution of the emperor Marcian, by which he invalidated the aforementioned edict of Theodosius and ordered that nothing should prejudice “Theodoret and Eusebius, religious bishops.” [Note: Marcian mentioned Theodoret and Eusebius because they had been restored by the synod to the episcopate. He did not mention Domnus because Domnus had already yielded the episcopate to Maximus.] Domnus should likewise have been mentioned, either so that he might enjoy the same favor or so that he might be excluded from it. But such a mention would have been entirely pointless. Since he was not to be equated with Flavian, who had suffered martyrdom for the faith, Marcian refrained from praising him; and since Domnus had already departed to the better life, there was no need to concern himself with restoring one whose case had ended with his death. This is the only explanation that can be offered. Whoever finds another will do me a great favor by sharing it with learned men.

### XXII. 19

When Pope Gelasius I wrote to the bishops of Dardania concerning the condemnation of Acacius, he gathered every example he could to raise the authority of the apostolic see above that of synods. He listed several bishops whom the apostolic see had absolved after their condemnation by a synod, as well as others condemned by the apostolic see whom a synod had absolved. He also added that the apostolic see had granted pardon to countless people who had acted treacherously in the false synod of Ephesus, when it annulled that synod.

Here surely was an appropriate occasion for mentioning Domnus and his successor Maximus. Gelasius would undoubtedly have observed from the Ephesian acts that this one matter alone had remained intact while the others were annulled: the deposition of Domnus and the election of Maximus, since the pope had confirmed both by his own decision. [Note: Since Gelasius collected examples of those whom the apostolic see either absolved after synodal condemnation or condemned after synodal absolution, the example of Domnus was not suitable for him: although Domnus had been condemned by the false synod of Ephesus, the apostolic see had not absolved him. Nor was Maximus an appropriate example, since, although he had been received by the apostolic see, he had not been deposed by a synod.]

Nothing of this sort occurred to Gelasius, since he knew that Domnus had died before Maximus was appointed as his successor.

### XXIII. 20

Evagrius, book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10, speaking of the bishops deposed by the false synod of Ephesus, writes:

“Bishop Theodoret of Cyrus was also deposed along with others, and likewise Domnus, the bishop of the Church of Antioch; but what afterward happened to him is not known.” [Note: These words prove only that Evagrius was unaware of our session concerning Domnus, as the following words likewise show that Liberatus was unaware of it, evidently because it was not read in their copies. That this contributes nothing to establishing its interpolation will be clear from observation 14. It will not seem incredible that Evagrius, a man of Antioch, did not know what had happened to Domnus, bishop of Antioch, if one considers that Domnus withdrew into the desert of Palestine, which is very far from the Church of Antioch, and there spent a solitary life.]

But if that session concerning Domnus had not been fabricated, and if in Evagrius’s time it had been read among the other acts of the council, Evagrius would have known what had happened to Domnus after his condemnation: namely, that he had not been absolved from the sentence of condemnation; that Maximus had been substituted in his place and his appointment confirmed by the Roman pontiff; that Domnus had asked the council for maintenance and obtained it through Maximus’s efforts; and that, content with this, he had thereafter lived a private life. Once Evagrius knew these facts, what more could he have wished to know about Domnus?

### XXIV. 21

Liberatus, a deacon of the Church of Carthage and a most diligent investigator of matters relating to the Council of Chalcedon, states in his *Brief Account of the Cause of Nestorius and Eutyches* that he received in Alexandria a translation from Greek into Latin of the material he recounts concerning the false synod of Ephesus and the Council of Chalcedon. Yet he makes no mention of the session concerning Domnus held at Chalcedon, although he carefully reviews all the sessions and proceedings and, in accordance with the purpose of his work, arranges his brief account of them in order in chapter 13.

The following chapter, chapter 14, begins as follows:

“Therefore, when the great and venerable Council of Chalcedon had been completed in twelve secretariats and sixteen sessions…”

Thus, by his silence, Liberatus rejects the session of which we are speaking. If it were to be regarded as genuine, the sessions would no longer number sixteen but seventeen.

It is therefore clear that not only the Constantinopolitan copies of the Council of Chalcedon, which the emperor Justinian and the Fathers of the Fifth Council used, lacked that session, but also the African, Alexandrian, Roman, and other copies in the hands of Pope Gelasius, Facundus, Liberatus, Evagrius, and Nicephorus. Consequently, the whole account is a pure fabrication devised by an impostor through malicious craft.

### XXV. 22

I shall argue still further by means of a dilemma. In several places Leo wishes peace and communion to be granted to the bishops who fell at Ephesus, provided that they correct themselves and condemn by their own subscription the things wrongly done; but he wishes the obstinate to be restrained with due severity.

Domnus therefore belonged either to those who corrected themselves or to the obstinate. If he belonged to the former, indulgence was undoubtedly granted to him, as to the others. If he belonged to the obstinate and hardened, he was not even worthy of that portion of ecclesiastical revenue which they wish the synod to have assigned to him at the successor’s request, on the authority of this session. [Note: This difficulty is easily resolved in another way, if we recall what we said above: although Domnus had corrected himself, he was not restored to his see because, moved by repentance, he did not wish to be restored but withdrew into the desert.]

This difficulty cannot otherwise be resolved unless one says that Domnus had by then been taken to the better life and had thought neither about recovering the see of Antioch nor about the necessities required to sustain mortal life.

“But how,” you will ask, “if he had died, could he have returned to Abbot Euthymius—as we said at the beginning of the dissertation—after everything foretold to him had come to pass, especially the prediction of his deposition?”

I reply that the time when Domnus returned to Euthymius is not recorded by the author of his life. It probably occurred as soon as, having come to himself, he reflected on the advice of the holy abbot that he had rejected and was moved to repentance. Moreover, since nearly two years elapsed between his deposition and the Council of Chalcedon, and at least [Note: Domnus was deposed in the Ephesian Robber Council in August 449. We proved in note 26 (column 266, note e) of Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the year 451 that Maximus was ordained some time before the death of Theodosius, who died in July 450. Therefore, not even one year had elapsed between Domnus’s deposition and Maximus’s ordination, which we shall show in observations no. 2 to have been carried out while Domnus was still alive.] one year before the ordination of Maximus, there is nothing to prevent Domnus, repentant of his treachery, distressed by his deposition, and turning over in his mind the prediction of his spiritual father, while ignorant of what ought to be done amid such great disturbances, from fleeing to Euthymius in order to lay down the burden of his anxieties before him and lighten the bitterness of his grief, refreshed by the counsels and admonitions of that most holy man. After this, his final day could have overtaken him before the Council of Chalcedon and before the ordination of Maximus.

### XXVI. 23

An argument could be drawn from the words of the session: “The holy and most blessed pope confirmed the episcopate of the holy and venerable Bishop Maximus, of the Church of Antioch,” and so forth.

First, it was not the usage of that age for the Roman bishop to be designated by the single word “pope” without an additional qualification. Nor, unless I am mistaken, is there any place in the acts of Chalcedon—where he is so often named—in which “pope” is not accompanied by “of the city of Rome,” “of the apostolic see,” or something similar. [Note: Baluzius cites several examples from this period, including two from the Council of Chalcedon itself, sessions 1 and 2, in the preface to the ancient version of that council, no. 48. These plainly refute Quesnellus’s proposition.]

Furthermore, the expression “confirmation of Maximus by Leo” has the style of a later period. [Note: Since, at their ordination, even the Eastern bishops of the principal sees sought letters of communion from the Roman pontiff, those letters contained a certain kind of confirmation, insofar as by them they showed themselves to be Catholic and legitimate bishops. This derives from the primacy proper to the Roman see. For that see is the centre of Catholic communion and unity, with which, on account of its more powerful preeminence or primacy, as Irenaeus says, all the faithful everywhere, and especially bishops, must agree, so as to demonstrate that they are Catholic and bishops in Catholic communion. Although a new bishop also sought these letters of communion from other episcopal sees, no see’s letters possessed so great a force of communion and, as it were, confirmation as those of that principal chair, from which, as Saint Cyprian says in Epistle 55, priestly unity arose, and from which, as the Synod of Aquileia of 381 stated in its letter to the emperors (in P. Constantius, among the letters of Damasus, Epistle 12, no. 4), the rights of venerable communion flow forth to all. Thus, by a most ancient discipline, Catholic bishops especially sought the letters of this see. That discipline was certainly in force in Leo’s time, as is clear from Epistles 149 and 171, where not only its customary character but even its necessity is sufficiently expressed; see note 1 (preceding volume, column 1119, note b) on Epistle 149, and note 6 (ibid., column 1216, note g) on Epistle 171. It will therefore not be surprising if Anatolius, concerned about this matter, sent clerics to Rome to ensure that Saint Leo would more promptly deliver to him letters of communion, which had for some time been withheld, and so confirm his ordination. Nor did Maximus need a mere letter of communion. Since his ordination laboured under several defects, Saint Leo received it by a dispensation for the good of peace and judged him fit to preside over the Church of Antioch, as Anatolius testifies in session 10 of the Council of Chalcedon; see further note 26 (above, column 266, note e) in Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the year 451.] At that time the practice had not yet spread throughout the West whereby confirmation of ordinations carried out in the provinces was sought from the Roman pontiff, and it was even less known among the Easterners.

If you say that Leo confirmed Maximus because he made him a participant in his communion, then Maximus must also be said to have been confirmed in the same sense by the other bishops who did not exclude him from their communion, or even from the beginning of his episcopate.

I do not deny, however, that the communion of the Roman pontiff always possessed greater weight, since he governed the apostolic see, the foremost and most splendid of sees, stood above all others in a more powerful primacy, as Irenaeus says, and held larger dioceses, as the Fathers of the First Council of Arles write. The bishops of those dioceses were generally joined in communion with him to whom the Roman bishop had extended his own communion.

### XXVII

Let us now examine somewhat more carefully the ordination of Maximus and the events that preceded it, for I see that some have proceeded with excessive confidence from preconceived opinions.

1. It is certain that Domnus was deposed by the false synod of Ephesus. Liberatus, Evagrius, Nicephorus, and others cited above are witnesses to this.

2. It is certain that he was deposed last of all, as Liberatus expressly asserts and as the treatise or brief account of the history of the Eutychianists prefixed to the letters of Saint Leo in the Roman edition states:

“After the third day of the synod, on which Flavian of blessed memory was expelled, Domnus of Antioch was also expelled. Dioscorus suddenly departed, and the assembly was dissolved.”

Dioscorus deliberately separated Domnus’s case from those of Flavian and Eusebius so that Domnus would subscribe to the condemnation of both before he himself was condemned. By this artifice and deceit—which is what Liberatus’s expression indicates—he achieved two things that closed every avenue by which Domnus might recover his see: on the one hand, Domnus had against him all those who stood with Dioscorus and had conspired in Domnus’s deposition; on the other, he would encounter the hostility of all the Catholics, who regarded with horror the sentence pronounced by Dioscorus against Flavian and Eusebius.

3. It is certain that Domnus was condemned while absent from the synod, indeed while ill, so that no opportunity was given him to defend himself. Liberatus asserts this explicitly in chapter 12.

4. It is certain that Domnus was unjustly condemned—not only because every judicial procedure was overturned by Dioscorus when he presided as judge and everything was conducted through force and fury, but also because no other crime was charged against him than that he had said, in a letter written to Dioscorus, that Cyril’s chapters, as being rather obscure, should be passed over in silence.

Whatever fault Domnus may have committed had already long since been abolished and consigned to oblivion by the peace restored between the bishops. [Note: If the celebrated peace meant here is that which was established between Saint Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch, by which everything done on both sides was abolished, it could not help Domnus, since his letter to Dioscorus was written long after that time. We do not know what other peace, previously established between Domnus and Dioscorus, could be proposed.]

5. From what we have said above, it is most probable, or rather certain, that Domnus did not long survive his deposition and did not live until the Council of Chalcedon—that is, until the year of the Lord 451. I would readily believe that he did not recover from the illness with which he lay afflicted, as Liberatus testifies, when the sentence of condemnation was inflicted upon him, and that he died exhausted by grief. For, cast down at so unexpected a moment from the second see of the Eastern regions, he saw no one from whom he could hope for any help: Dioscorus’s followers were hostile to him because of his former condemnation of Eutyches, while the Catholics were offended because he had approved Flavian’s deposition. His death soon followed.

[Note: After his deposition, Domnus was driven into exile and was not recalled until the reign of the emperor Marcian, as will become clear from observation no. 2. Since he not only intended to return to the desert but actually did so, as the testimony of Cyril of Scythopolis in the *Life of Saint Euthymius* records, he must be said to have died there—not from the illness from which he was suffering when the sentence of condemnation was imposed upon him.]

6. If Nicephorus is to be trusted, and if our conjectures concerning Liberatus’s obscure passage possess some probability (above, no. 15), Domnus’s condemnation was the fruit of his repentance. He was subjected to it because, repentant of his subscription, he urgently demanded that his signed document be returned to him and did not fear to attack openly and publicly the authors of so great a crime. Hence the plan he had formed, perhaps, of spending his life in private retirement until death was cut short by death itself.

### XXVIII. 7

Finally, nowhere do we read that his condemnation was brought back for examination either by Leo or by the ecumenical council. Only in session 10, where the case of Ibas of Edessa was debated, after the judges had proposed rereading what had been done at Ephesus concerning Bishop Ibas, and after Leo’s legates, Anatolius, and the other three had stated their opinions, did Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, say:

“I too judge that the things done contrary to the canons in the metropolitan church of Ephesus should be annulled, except for what was done against Domnus, bishop of the city of Antioch, because the canonical ordination of the most God-loving Bishop Maximus in his place in the metropolitan church of Antioch was accepted by the most holy Archbishop Leo and by this holy and universal council now present.”

I do not know whether this testimony should be given great weight, since it is the only one and came from a man whom we read in the following session to have been deposed because of the crimes by which he had secured his advancement to the see of Ephesus. [Note: It is not the sole testimony, since two other similar testimonies precede it in the same session, namely those of the legates and of Anatolius. Although they do not expressly mention Domnus, when they except the Ephesian acts insofar as they concern Maximus, whose ordination they affirm was approved by Leo, they can mean only the pseudo-Ephesian acts against Domnus; for nothing concerning Maximus was done at Ephesus. Hence the arguments which Quesnellus subsequently adds in order to weaken and render suspect Stephen’s testimony are seen to be empty.] It is therefore probable that Stephen wished, out of hatred and malevolence, to have Domnus’s condemnation upheld. Just as no one had preceded him in this opinion, no one supported him in it.

Whatever the case, Stephen asserted this on his own authority. He did not say that the acts performed at Ephesus against Domnus were excepted by Saint Leo, when Leo rescinded all the other acts of that ill-fated synod together with the other Westerners. Nor was anything inserted into the definition of the Council of Chalcedon that would confirm Domnus’s condemnation in Stephen’s sense. He alone held this opinion, which strongly supports Domnus’s absolution.

Finally, there is nothing in Stephen’s sentence from which one can assert that Domnus was still alive at that time. Rather, it indicates that he had already died, since Stephen denies that the acts should be rescinded for the sole reason that Maximus’s ordination had been confirmed, “having been carried out canonically.” [Note: Stephen could have understood “canonically carried out” only in the sense that it took place after Domnus’s cession and relinquishment. That is, after his deposition, Domnus, moved by repentance and considering withdrawal into the desert, voluntarily acquiesced in the judgment of the bishops concerning him; this was judged to have made room for a canonical ordination. Leo, however, reported that the same ordination had been carried out contrary to the provisions of the canons; see note 36 below, column 720, note b.]

For it would not have been canonical if Maximus had been superimposed upon Domnus while Domnus was still alive and had not been canonically deposed.

The Fifth Council relied upon this sole testimony of Stephen when it searched everywhere for examples of bishops condemned after death, in order to strengthen the condemnation of the Three Chapters. Lacking such examples, it eagerly seized upon Stephen’s words as though they had been approved by the synod. Since it did not read that Domnus had been absolved by the ecumenical synod, but rather that Maximus had been confirmed, it confidently asserted that Domnus had been condemned after death. Yet it immediately explained both itself and Stephen of Ephesus when it indicated that the entire claim had been made solely on the basis of Maximus’s confirmation.

Nevertheless, as must not be denied, some stain remained upon Domnus’s memory because Catholic bishops had been condemned. This was why the Fathers of the council were slower in purifying his memory.

### XXIX

It is now worthwhile to investigate what happened when a successor was chosen and ordained in his place. First to be noted is the judgment of the four legates of the apostolic see in session 10 of the Council of Chalcedon. They expressly assert that the ordination of Maximus, bishop of Antioch, substituted in Domnus’s place, should not be counted among the acts of the false synod of Ephesus. They also assert that this was Saint Leo’s intention: on the one hand, he judged everything done there invalid; on the other, he received Maximus into his communion.

The words of the legates at the synod were spoken on the occasion of Ibas’s deposition by the false synod of Ephesus, whose acts the judges wished to reread:

“Paschasinus and Lucentius and Julian, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, most reverend presbyter, representatives of the apostolic see, through Paschasinus, said:

‘The synod in which those wicked crimes were reread cannot be brought forward, and for this reason the things done there appear superfluous for reading. Therefore, if everything done there was regarded as worthless by the most blessed and apostolic bishop of the city of Rome—it is clear that the most holy bishop of the Church of Antioch is also outside these matters, whom the most blessed bishop afterward received into his own communion—it is necessary that we again approach that most tranquil and Christian emperor, so that he may command that council not even to be named under his sacred and sovereign law.’”

It must be admitted that these words are seriously corrupt both in the Greek and in the Latin version. In the Latin version, first, the words “whom the most blessed bishop afterward received into his own communion” are superfluous and absent from the original text. We therefore conjecture that, as a marginal gloss derived from the words of Anatolius that follow, they subsequently entered the text. [Note: In the commonly printed Greek text, which Quesnellus calls the original, not only are the words “whom the most blessed bishop afterward received into his own communion” absent, but also the words “for it is necessary,” which are necessary to the context and cannot be treated as a gloss. Certain other passages in the commonly printed Greek of this council are likewise defective and must be supplied from the Latin version. Quesnellus’s assertion here that the sense is complete without Paschasinus’s words is so absurd and false that, rather, without them the sense is incomplete. For after saying that the pseudo-Ephesian proceedings had been held invalid by Leo, Paschasinus adds that Maximus’s ordination is plainly not included in those general words because Leo afterward received Maximus himself into his own communion. The sense would certainly not be complete if Paschasinus had not supplied this reason. Moreover, what follows would have no connection without the words “for it is necessary,” which, though found even in the commonly printed Greek, Quesnellus nevertheless considers to be deleted. Therefore the emendation is unnecessary by which he later, adding some things, removing others, and changing still others at will, labours remarkably to derive a good sense without these words. What he further alleges concerning the word *eumdem* is due to the translator, who rendered the Greek *τοῦ αὐτοῦ* as *eumdem* (“the same one”), whereas here it ought better to have been rendered *ipsum* (“him”). To complete Quesnellus’s refutation, we considered it necessary to compare two Greek manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon, nos. 164 and 555 in the Library of St Mark, Venice. We had already observed that certain other deficiencies in the commonly printed Greek text could be supplied from them, in the prefatory admonition to the previously unpublished session of Chalcedon, volume I, column 1489, no. 1 (preceding volume, column 1249). Nor did our hope deceive us. We found that both manuscripts contain the Greek words corresponding to the ancient Latin version and absent from the commonly printed Greek. Thus the passage there reads: Δῆλόν ἐστιν, ὡς καὶ ὁ ἁγιώτατος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Ἀντιοχέων Ἐκκλησίας ἔξω τούτων ἐστὶν * ὅν τινα μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ μακαριώτατος ἐπίσκοπος ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ κοινωνίᾳ ὑπεδέξατο· καὶ γὰρ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν * ἵνα ἐτὶ (thus, better manuscript 164 than the other manuscript and the commonly printed ἵνα ἐπί) τοῦ αὐτοῦ, etc. The words enclosed by asterisks have been supplied from the Venetian manuscripts. It follows that the defect in the Greek manuscript used by the Roman editors arose from an easy scribal leap, by which the copyist passed in transcription from the second occurrence of ἐστίν to the third. Thus the whole of Quesnellus’s argument is entirely overthrown.]

Second, the little word *enim* (“for”) seems superfluous. We have therefore printed it in a different type from the surrounding text. It may have been substituted for *etiam* (“also”) by a scribe misled by an ambiguous abbreviation; for the oldest edition of Crabbe has *em*, which can signify *etiam* no less than *enim*.

Third, there is no antecedent to which the word *eumdem* (“the same one”) can refer, since no mention of the emperor occurs above.

Fourth, unless the parenthesis that we have supplied is retained and the word *enim* removed, so that one continuous sentence emerges from what precedes and follows the parenthesis, scarcely any connection or coherence can be found in the legates’ judgment. Nor is it apparent why, at this point—where the question of Maximus had not been raised—they appear directly and expressly to prove that Maximus’s ordination did not belong to the Ephesian synod or, as others prefer, that it should be excepted from the rejection of that synod’s acts. With our punctuation and emendation accepted, everything coheres perfectly, unless I am mistaken.

I shall also attempt to emend this passage in the Greek text by another method. It will become clear if the particle *ὡς* (*hōs*, “as” or “so that”), which occurs after *δῆλόν ἐστι* (“it is evident”), is placed before those two words and the other particle *ἵνα* (“so that”) is rejected as superfluous. I would therefore propose reading it as follows:

> Εἰ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ μακαριωτάτου καὶ ἀποστολικοῦ ἐπισκόπου τῆς πόλεως Ῥώμης πάντα τὰ ἐκεῖ πεπραγμένα μάταια ἔστι· ὡς δηλόν ἐστι, καὶ ὁ ἁγιώτατος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Ἀντιοχέων Ἐκκλησίας ἔξω τούτων ἔστιν· ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ τοῦ γαληνοτάτου καὶ Χριστιανικωτάτου βασιλέως ἐπιτύχωμεν· ὥστε ἐκείνην τὴν σύνοδον ἱερῷ ἰδίῳ νόμῳ μήτε ὀνομάζεσθαι προστάττειν.

I translate it as follows:

> “If, then, everything done there has been declared worthless by the most blessed and apostolic bishop of the city of Rome, as is evident, and the most holy bishop of the Church of Antioch is outside these matters, let us approach that most tranquil and Christian emperor, so that he may command that council not even to be named under his sacred and sovereign law.”

The words inserted into the Latin edition but absent from the Greek should likewise be omitted. Peter de Marca, however, believes that the old translator retained them in accordance with the testimony of the ancient manuscripts. He attempts to support this from Anatolius’s subsequent speech, in which Anatolius wishes Maximus’s case to be excepted from the rescission of the Ephesian acts because Leo had admitted Maximus to communion.

But the legates’ own words are sufficient to make their meaning clear. Whether their judgment differs from Anatolius’s opinion or agrees with it, it does not prove that the legates said what the surviving copies of the original acts indicate they did not say. Nor is it necessary that Anatolius and the Roman legates express the same view, since they sometimes do not agree among themselves, as can be seen in the following session of Chalcedon, session 11, in the case of Bassianus and Stephen, bishops of Ephesus. Julian of Coeus judged that one or the other should be retained in that see, while the others argued that both should be removed.

### XXX

It will nevertheless not be entirely useless to examine Anatolius’s speech more closely, for it seems to me to have been composed entirely by a crafty man who was insecure about his own ordination. It follows the words of the legates:

Anatolius, most reverend archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, said: [Note: Greek *αὐτόθεν*, “from that time.”]

“From that moment the destruction of the things recently done at Ephesus took place, since afterward they were most properly and in a manner pleasing to God corrected. Therefore we decree that none of the things enacted in that so-called synod is valid, except what concerns the most holy Maximus, bishop of the great city of Antioch; for the most holy Leo, archbishop of Rome, receiving him into communion, judged him worthy to preside over the Church of Antioch. Following this principle, I too approved it, as did this entire holy council now present.”

Two points in the legates’ opinion troubled Anatolius: first, that they had said that all the proceedings of the Ephesian conventicle of 1209 were null, criminal, and not even to be named; second, that they maintained that the case of Maximus of Antioch had to be considered separately from those proceedings. [Col. 0721B] The shrewd man saw that by either position the foundations of his own ordination were shaken. For if all the proceedings of that synod were to be annulled without exception, Anatolius’s own dignity was endangered, since its authors had been the leaders of that ill-fated synod. But if the ordination of Maximus were separated from the proceedings of that same council, he perceived that, through the legates’ words, the one example by which he could defend his own ordination, even though it had been designated by robbers, was being taken from him; and he feared that they had spoken with the intention of preparing the way for the later revocation of his ordination, just as had been done with the ordinations of others. The extremely shrewd man detected this and attempted subtly to avoid it.

[Note: [Col. 0721C] All this is mere fantasy of Quesnel’s. Since Leo had approved Anatolius’s ordination, there was nothing for which Anatolius, fearing on his own account, would have employed the artifice and cunning attributed to him. It is evident that Quesnel devised this whole fiction in order partly to deprive, partly to divert elsewhere, and partly to cast suspicion upon this bishop of Constantinople’s testimony concerning Leo’s authority in annulling the proceedings of the pseudo-Ephesian synod and confirming Maximus’s ordination.

He interprets Anatolius as attributing the annulment of all the acts of the Ephesian Robbery not to Leo but to the Council of Chalcedon, although his words say nothing of Chalcedon, and although not all the Ephesian proceedings were read and corrected in the first session, but only those concerning Saint Flavian and Eutyches; whereas Saint Leo, by contrast, declared all of them void.

Further, Quesnel imagines that Anatolius invoked Leo’s authority in excepting Maximus’s ordination in order to conciliate the legates and advance his own business, as though Anatolius himself had not yet been approved by the holy pontiff and were in the same situation as Maximus. Yet Maximus was ordained while Domnus was alive, and more probably even at Constantinople; Anatolius himself, however, was ordained in his own see after Flavian’s death. [Col. 0722C]

Finally, Quesnel says that the consent of an ecumenical council was added to Leo’s confirmation of Maximus’s ordination, so that the matter could no longer be reconsidered. But such a design cannot be inferred from Anatolius’s words. Indeed, since the whole synod is reported to have followed the form of the pontiff’s judgment without holding any inquiry into this matter, the only inference is how highly Leo’s apostolic authority was valued by the ecumenical synod. For the whole synod, from the outset, admitted Maximus among the bishops without anyone’s difficulty because Leo had received him. [Col. 0722D]]

First, therefore, since the legates did not wish those proceedings to be reread or examined, as criminal and in every respect rejected by Saint Leo, he begins his speech by saying that those proceedings had become invalid only from the time when they had been properly discussed and corrected—namely, in the first [Col. 0721C] session of the Council of Chalcedon. He thereby wished it to follow that the annulment of the Ephesian proceedings was to be sought properly not from Leo’s decree but from the council’s; and consequently that, if anything from those proceedings had not yet been examined and corrected by the council—such as his own ordination—it should not be considered invalid.

Then, as though issuing a definition, he declares that none of the acts carried out at Ephesus had validity. Yet he cautiously excepts the case of Maximus, so that he might likewise except his own:

> “Except for the case of Maximus, the most holy bishop of great Antioch” (*Πλὴν τοῦ κατὰ τὴν μεγίστην Ἀντιοχείαν ἁγιωτάτου ἐπισκόπου Μαξίμου*).

“Except for the most holy bishop Maximus, who presides over great Antioch.”

But so as not to provoke the legates, whom he was contradicting, he derives and confirms this exception from the judgment of the apostolic see, whose bishop, by receiving Maximus into his communion, had honored him with his approval. In this way he was also advancing his own case, since he too had been received into communion by Leo. He further indicates that the ecumenical council had added its assent, in order to remove from the legates every hope of reopening the case.

But admire, if you will, the man’s cunning. Although he had taken the lead in ordaining Maximus and claimed that ordination for himself against the canons, he dares to boast that he had followed Leo’s example and had not approved Maximus until after learning of Leo’s approval of him through communion. Such is the man’s sincerity and candor of spirit.

**XXXI.** The position of Saint Leo’s legates therefore remains firm and certain: they asserted that the ordination of Maximus was not to be counted among the Ephesian proceedings. And in fact, although that synod may have decreed, after the deposition of Domnus, that another should be elected, Maximus was not ordained until long after the dissolution of the synod.

First, Anatolius himself, by whom Maximus was ordained, was not consecrated bishop at Constantinople until after Flavian’s death. This is learned from the brief history of the Eutychianists prefixed to Saint Leo’s letters in the Roman edition, and from a fragment of Anatolius’s letter to Pope Leo, recently brought to light among the ancient monuments of the Greek Church by the most learned Joannes Cotelerius, p. 66. For, after the account of Flavian’s death, we read:

> “At that time a certain presbyter named Anatolius was residing at Constantinople, having come from Alexandria, etc. He therefore became bishop at Constantinople.”

He thus succeeded the deceased, rather than being imposed upon a living predecessor—something Leo would never have failed to reproach him for, had it happened. Indeed, Leo would never have received him, just as he wrote to the Constantinopolitans:

> “Whoever, while your bishop Flavian is safe and still alive, dares to invade his priesthood will never be counted in our communion, nor will he be able to be numbered among the bishops” (*Epistle* 45, now 50, ch. 1).

Finally, when Leo wrote to the emperor Theodosius Augustus on 10 [Col. 0722C] July of the following year concerning the ordination of the man who had begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople (*Epistle* 52, now 69, ch. 1), he sufficiently shows that Anatolius had been ordained recently—that is, approximately in the tenth month after the dissolution of the Ephesian synod.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] We proved in the admonition to *Epistle* 53, vol. I, that Anatolius was ordained after the death of Saint Flavian, toward the end of the year 449.]

Now some time had to be allowed for establishing the beginnings of his episcopate before he could proceed to Antioch, where, according to the canons, the election and consecration had to take place. That it was in fact done canonically at Antioch is taught by Stephen of Ephesus in the tenth session of Chalcedon.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Maximus was ordained neither at Antioch nor after Theodosius’s death; see note 26 above, col. 266, n. e, in Quesnel’s first dissertation on the year 451.]

There Maximus, who was serving as deacon and archimandrite, was canonically elected and ordained in the city of Antioch, if Stephen is to be believed.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Maximus, a deacon and archimandrite of Antioch and an adversary of Nestorius, is mentioned at the time of the Ephesian synod. But whether he is the same man as the Maximus consecrated bishop of Antioch in 450 cannot be proved with certainty from the similarity of the name alone.] But if Leo is to be trusted (*Epistle* 80, now 106, ch. 2), Anatolius presumed to celebrate such an ordination against canonical rule and against the ordinances of the canons, without any precedent:

> “This,” says Leo (*Epistle* 78, now 104, ch. 5), “we refrained from reopening out of love for the restoration of the faith and from zeal for peace.”

Leo identified this as the one fault in Maximus’s ordination; doubtless he would have noted others if anything else had weakened its validity.

As for what Facundus writes (*Book* V, ch. 3)—that Maximus of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem had previously been tainted either by the doctrine or by communion of the Eutychians—in Maximus’s case this was either a calumny, namely that he was simply one of the Nestorians, as Facundus there seems to insinuate, or merely Facundus’s own suspicion, arising from his supposition that Maximus had been ordained by Eutychians and consequently infected, at least, by their communion. But, as Leo testifies, Maximus was ordained by Anatolius. The Roman pontiff never regarded Anatolius as an Eutychian, although he required from him a profession of faith, which was made necessary by Anatolius’s earlier close relationship with Dioscorus, whose representative he had been.

**XXXII.** From what has been said, we now have several points useful for understanding ecclesiastical history and discipline. [Note: [Col. 0723D] All the points of this recapitulation collapse under the preceding notes.]

1. The session concerning Domnus, ascribed to the acts of Chalcedon, must be removed from them, since it is spurious and entirely fictitious.

2. The fact that Domnus was not restored to his see after the Ephesian Robbery must not be referred to Saint Leo’s judgment, but to Domnus’s own death, which preceded his restoration.

3. The ordination of Maximus is not, according to the understanding of the legates of the apostolic see, to be counted among the Ephesian proceedings.

4. The only fault that could be reproached in it was that Anatolius, exceeding his proper limits, claimed that ordination for himself.

5. Leo concealed this out of love for peace, although it is probable that the Easterners did not intend to revoke the ordination for that reason. [Col. 0723C]

[Note: [Col. 0723D] It is certain from the testimonies inserted in the tenth session that the entire Council of Chalcedon received Maximus among the Fathers without any examination and without anyone’s protest, because Saint Leo had accepted his ordination. Quesnel tried in vain to distort these testimonies. But whether, if the holy pontiff had not received Maximus into communion, his ordination would have caused no difficulty for any Eastern bishop before he was admitted among the council’s Fathers, so that it might consequently have appeared subject to revocation, is not so certain as Quesnel assumes.

Quesnel indeed attempts to defend it by proving that it was carried out neither without precedent nor without some authority in the canons. In doing so he plainly contradicts Leo, who writes in *Epistle* 104 that Anatolius had presumed to ordain Maximus “without any precedent and against the ordinances of the canons.” Leo must be believed rather than Quesnel.

The examples Quesnel adduces concern bishops of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia, whose ordinations were later assigned to the bishop of Constantinople. He could not produce a single example of an Antiochene bishop—the bishop at issue here—ordained by the bishop of Constantinople, or of any bishop of the Antiochene diocese in whose ordinations a bishop of Constantinople had ever intervened.

Moreover, the canons that make an exception for bishops invited by the bishops of a province do not help excuse Anatolius unless it is proved that he was invited by the bishops of the province of Antioch to ordain Maximus. Indeed, since Leo testifies that he ordained Maximus against the ordinances of the canons, it is credible that the provincial bishops had not invited him under the circumstances contemplated by the canons.

And if it is judged more probable that this ordination took place at Constantinople rather than at Antioch, as we conjectured in note 26 above, col. 266, n. e, in Quesnel’s first dissertation on the year 451, no canon can be found that in any way excuses this form of ordination.]

Although Anatolius had plainly acted against the canons if he had arrogated to himself the ordination of bishops belonging to certain Eastern dioceses—all of whom, as the synod of Nicaea had declared, were subject to the bishop of Antioch—nevertheless, since it had prescribed nothing specific concerning the ordination of the Antiochene primate himself, it did not seem to be against the canons if, with all the provincial bishops admitted, the honor of consecration were conferred upon the bishop of Constantinople by their unanimous consent: that is, upon the man who, by decree of the second ecumenical synod, had obtained precedence over all the Eastern sees.

I do not deny, however, that Anatolius undertook this ambitiously and contrary to custom; but he did so not without precedent or without the authority of the canons, which he could invoke in support of his ambition. For Anatolius’s predecessors had brought the dioceses of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia under themselves in no other way than by interfering in metropolitan ordinations—not, indeed, apparently on their own initiative, but after being invited by the provincial bishops and requested, as it were, to restrain ambitious rivalries and avert disturbances, which frequently arose.

Nor did they dare to do this without the support of a local canon. For the Council of Constantinople, in its second canon, after establishing the boundaries of the dioceses, prohibited every bishop from overstepping them, yet did not wish those who, after being invited by provincial bishops, had intervened in the ordinations of other Churches to be regarded as violators of the canons.

> “Bishops who have not been invited,” it says, “must not go beyond their diocese to ordain anyone or to settle any ecclesiastical matters whatsoever.”

When the Fathers of this synod enacted this decree, they undoubtedly had before their eyes Apostolic Canons 13 and 33, as well as the definition of Nicaea. We have as witnesses the bishops of the council themselves, whose synodical letter—whether of this council or of a subsequent gathering—to Damasus and the other bishops of the West Theodoret reproduced in Book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 9. These are his words:

> “Regarding the private administration of the Churches, an ancient custom has prevailed, as you know, together with the definition of the holy Fathers at Nicaea: in each province, the bishops of the province—and, if they themselves wish, neighboring bishops—are to conduct ordinations according to what is expedient. Know that by this arrangement both the other Churches among us are administered and the clergy of the most illustrious Churches have been appointed.”

The Antiochene canons 13 and 22 support this practice, since they permit bishops, when invited by colleagues from another province, to participate in that province’s ordinations.

By these stages they advanced toward the primacy of the bishop of Constantinople. First, by a favorable interpretation of the canons, they arranged to be invited to metropolitan ordinations. Then what had seemed to be granted merely as a favor passed into an acknowledged right. Finally, when the opportunity of a general synod arose, it was sanctioned by ecclesiastical canon.

Anatolius advanced by the same steps toward greater claims. After subduing the metropolitans of the lesser dioceses, ambition drove him to intervene in the ordination of the bishops of the greater sees. First, under the pretext of suppressing the disturbances then to be feared, he inserted himself into the ordination of the bishop of Antioch—either after being invited, as the canons allowed, or sent by the emperor—hoping that what had been granted to meet the difficulties of the time would easily come to be accepted as an inviolable custom, to which an ecclesiastical canon would eventually be added, confirming and permanently establishing the accepted practice.

Since these things are so, the ordination of Maximus could not be annulled on that account: [1214] because, when the bishops of the Eastern province or diocese themselves wished it and invited Anatolius in accordance with the indulgence of the canons, no injury had been done. (See observation 1 on *Epistle* 80, now 106.)

And in fact, although Leo, attacking Anatolius for attempting to diminish the greater sees, reproached him with having usurped the ordination of Maximus, he does not seem to have wished to press the matter against either of them—not only out of love for peace, but also because of the canonical exception concerning invited bishops.

Our Leo, unless I am mistaken, also perceived that Anatolius had done nothing in this matter against the canons of Nicaea, but only against ecclesiastical custom or regulation. For he drew a broad distinction between Anatolius’s two usurpations: one, by which he had presumed to ordain the bishop of Antioch; the other, by which he had attempted to invade the position of second rank. He loudly proclaimed the latter to be against the canons of Nicaea, but the former to be against canonical regulation:

> “After the consecration of the bishop of Antioch, which you claimed for yourself **against canonical regulation**, I grieve that your devotion also fell into this error, attempting to violate the **most sacred constitutions of the canons of Nicaea**, as though this were an opportune time for you, when the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second rank and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third rank,” etc. (*Epistle* 80, now 106, ch. 2).

The rhetorical amplification in the account of the second usurpation should be noted.

For this reason Leo easily concealed the former, but declared that he would never tolerate the latter, as unprecedented and unendurable: for the latter violated and overturned the canons of Nicaea, consecrated by the veneration of the whole world and made more sacred than all others by a unique privilege.

It follows from what has been said that the ordination of Maximus required no dispensation or confirmation any more than it was formerly required when John Chrysostom undertook and carried out so many ordinations and depositions, even of bishops, in the Churches of Asia. This is reported in the twelfth session of the Council of Chalcedon and confirmed by all who have narrated Chrysostom’s actions.

## OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI ON QUESNEL’S NINTH DISSERTATION, ON THE CASE OF DOMNUS OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0725]

### 1.

It is not necessary to investigate for what purpose Quesnel tried, in such a lengthy discussion, to cast doubt upon the Chalcedonian session concerning Domnus, discovered and published by Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, whose authenticity cannot rightly be doubted.

At the beginning of section 3 he says that he would greatly desire this session to be not fictitious but genuine. For, if that were so, we would possess at hand a most distinguished and ancient testimony to the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff both over synods and over Eastern bishops—indeed, over the bishops of the greater and principal sees.

If, while attempting to prove this document apocryphal and fabricated, he had brought forward serious and sufficiently solid arguments, he should be forgiven. But the arguments he presented are so meager and weak that not only Baluzius, who undertook to refute and oppose Quesnel on many points, but also Tillemont, who favors him on several matters, were compelled to acknowledge and demonstrate their weakness.

### 2.

The Chalcedonian session published by Rusticus presupposes that Domnus was still alive. Quesnel, on the other hand, maintains that Domnus had died before the ordination of Maximus.

But that Maximus was ordained while Domnus was still alive is inferred not only from this disputed session, but also from the indisputable testimony of the tenth session, in which an exception was made for Maximus of Antioch after all the proceedings of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus had been annulled.

For to annul all the pseudo-Ephesian proceedings was at the same time to invalidate and declare void all the depositions of bishops sanctioned by those proceedings, to restore those same bishops to their sees, and to remove those who had been substituted for them.

After the proceedings had been annulled, however, not only Maximus, who had been substituted after Domnus’s deposition, but also Anatolius, who had succeeded Flavian after his deposition, remained in their sees according to the mind of the Council of Chalcedon.

Why, then, did the synod make an exception for Maximus alone and not for Anatolius? The reason given there for the exception of Maximus was that Pope Leo had accepted and confirmed his ordination by receiving him into communion.

But before the council that same pontiff had also accepted Anatolius’s ordination; nevertheless, this reason was neither brought forward nor apparently capable of being brought forward concerning Anatolius. The special exception made for Maximus therefore presupposes in him something particular that did not apply to Anatolius.

Since Flavian had long been dead, Anatolius could not fear that, once the pseudo-Ephesian proceedings had been annulled, Flavian would return to his see. But while Domnus was still alive, Maximus could fear that, following the annulment of those same proceedings, Domnus might at some point wish to reclaim his see; and for that reason a special exception for Maximus was necessary.

Why, then, if Domnus was alive, was he not restored to his see at the Council of Chalcedon, as Ibas of Edessa was restored to his, even though Nonnus, who had been substituted for him, was still alive? It seems to have happened for this reason: Domnus, having fallen with the others in the pseudo-synod, was moved to repentance after his deposition, withdrew into the desert, and voluntarily relinquished his episcopate to Maximus. Out of compassion for him, Maximus secured for Domnus at Chalcedon a pension with which he was content, so that he would not be a burden to the monks.

Whatever the reason for this event may have been, the event itself—which is otherwise certain—must not therefore be rejected or denied unless a manifest reason, not yet apparent, proves the contrary.

The testimony of this most certain Chalcedonian session is so destructive of Quesnel’s hypothesis that everything he adduces is powerless against it. It may be useful to add another, perhaps clearer, argument, from which it will become even more evident that Maximus was ordained bishop while Domnus was still alive.

It is certain from Cyril of Scythopolis’s *Life of Saint Euthymius* that Domnus, after his deposition, came to his senses and, moved by repentance because he had not obeyed Saint Euthymius, returned to him and withdrew into the desert.

Quesnel thinks that Domnus went there immediately after his deposition. But since all the bishops deposed in the Ephesian Robbery in the name of heresy were, according to the custom of those times, driven into exile, there can be no doubt that Domnus was subjected to the same punishment.

Exiled bishops were not recalled until after Theodosius’s death, when the new emperor Marcian ordered them to return (Leo, *Epistle* 77). Therefore, while Theodosius was alive, Domnus was not recalled from exile and consequently could not have departed into the desert.

We proved that Maximus was ordained before Theodosius’s death in note 26 above, col. 266, n. e, in Quesnel’s first dissertation on the year 451. Thus this ordination took place while Domnus was still alive, before Domnus was recalled from exile and withdrew into solitude.

This argument seems so clear to us that there is no need to labor over refuting each of Quesnel’s individual conjectures, especially since we have adequately answered them in the notes attached to the dissertation itself at their respective places.

Anyone who wishes to read more should consult Baluzius’s preface to the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon, section 92 and following, and Tillemont’s note 54 on Leo.

Quesnel himself seems to have recognized his own weakness. For when, after Baluzius, he prepared a second edition and attempted to defend nearly everything Baluzius had attacked, in this matter—which Baluzius had treated and assailed at greatest length—although Quesnel inserted something new from Labbe and Cotelerius, he nevertheless offered no reply to Baluzius’s arguments.

It is credible that this happened for no other reason than that he found nothing probable to answer.

### 3.

We shall now add from the most ancient Vatican codex 1322 three sessions of the Council of Chalcedon concerning Maximus. Two of them also concern the case of Domnus, while one is entirely unknown. They provide the strongest confirmation of the authenticity of the disputed session.

Although Baluzius published these from Cardinal Casanata, since he received them from Casanata only at the end of his edition and was unable conveniently to examine and work through what they contained, their contents were not sufficiently noticed. Nor have we found that anyone had previously discovered the one of the three sessions that had not been published.

### 4.

We must first speak about the codex that we were permitted to examine at Rome. It is more than a thousand years old. Since it belonged to the Church of Verona—as is clear not only from the three Veronese documents transcribed at the end, but also from the note in the oldest script, **VERONA**, in the upper margin of page 25—this codex was certainly either one of those acquired at the beginning of the ninth century by Pacificus, archdeacon of the Church of Verona, or among those that belonged to our Church before Pacificus.

It contains the Council of Chalcedon according to Rusticus’s edition, but incompletely, since it begins with the second session. At the end it also contains the report of the council to Saint Leo in an ancient version, with the subscriptions of very many bishops, which are found in no other manuscript.

At the beginning—where the codex is known to be mutilated—there precede twenty-four pages written in a different script from that of the rest of the codex, smaller but ancient. Several documents pertaining to the Council of Chalcedon are found in them. Since these are especially relevant to our subject, they must be examined carefully.

We first give the index, preserving even the defective readings of the codex.

### 5.

On the second page, then—for the first is missing—the following appears:

> “Copies [read: copy] of the second sacred letter that [read: which] were sent to the holy synod that [read: which] assembled at Nicaea, concerning the transfer to Chalcedon. Victor [read: Victors], Valentinian and Marcian, Augusti. As we were hastening to reach the holy synod, public affairs . . . . . . sufficiently hindered [read: prevented] us because of necessary business. But from what your Holiness writes, we have learned that several, etc.”

This is a different reading from the common version in vol. IV of the Council, Venetian edition, col. 843. Our version appears to be the original Latin itself, whereas the common version bears indications of a translation from Greek. For, as we have said elsewhere, such imperial sacred letters were issued in both Latin and Greek.

The mention of a second sacred letter seems to suggest that the missing first page contained the first sacred letter of the same emperors, by which the synod had been summoned to Nicaea and whose Latin original is presented in Quesnel’s collection, chapter 25.

On the reverse of the same page:

> “The emperors Caesar Valentinian and Marcian, victorious Augusti, to the holy synod assembled at Nicaea by divine providence and by our decree. By our sacred letters we have already made it certain to your Holiness that the decisions established by our holy Fathers concerning the venerable and orthodox faith are to be confirmed, so that the orthodox people may no longer appear to be deceived by various errors, etc.”

This is the third sacred letter sent to the Fathers who were still staying at Nicaea. It has a different reading from the common version in vol. IV, col. 846, and appears to be taken from the Latin original.

Then, on page 3:

> “Order of the proceedings held at Chalcedon in the presence of Marcian and Pulcheria, Augusti [read: Augustis], with Paschasinus of Lilybaeum [note: read: Lilybetanus] of the province of Sicily, and Lucentius—or Lucensius—of Asculum, and Boniface, presbyter of the city of Rome, vicars of the most religious and blessed Pope Leo of the Roman Holy Church, and the other bishops who also subscribed. When the most pious and faithful emperor Marcian had arrived, etc.”

[Note: [Col. 0727D] Read *Lilybetano* … and *Lucentio*, or *Lucensi*, of Asculum. Other excellent Latin codices have *Lucensis*, as do the manuscripts of Sirmond cited in the copy of the sentence sent to the Gauls, indicated in note 7 above, col. 990, n. c, in *Epistle* 103; the outstanding Regensburg codex cited in note 11, ibid., col. 919, n. l, in *Epistle* 83; and the Vienna codex of collection 5, note 9, ibid., col. 937, n. f, in *Epistle* 93.

Hence there is substantial reason to suspect that the legate’s true name was *Lucensis*, which, when rendered in Greek in the acts of the synod as Λουκήνσιος, the Latin translator translated as *Lucentius*, or, as in other codices consulted by Baluzius, *Lucensius*. The old version likewise has *Lucullensis*.]

This is almost the whole of the sixth session of Chalcedon: namely, after a shorter introduction—which is also found in Quesnel’s collection, chapter 25—Marcian’s address to the synod, taken from the Latin original and included in the same collection, the acclamations of the Fathers, and the definition of faith, into which two distinct creeds have been inserted.

Only the preceding catalogue of the bishops and other persons present, the subscriptions, and the final section concerning the enactment of the canons are omitted. These acclamations and this definition are presented in an interpretation that has hitherto been unpublished and is inelegant.

After this, on the reverse of page 8, the same definition of faith is repeated from another version, under this title:

> “Here begins what was enacted in the Council of Chalcedon in the presence of these bishops.”

> “The venerable assembly of the whole world, which by the grace of our God, etc.”

Here are found the materials that Baluzius published from this codex and that were most recently reprinted in vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Council, cols. 2063–2065.

Two points should be observed there:

1. Of the two creeds, one is presented as the Constantinopolitan Creed, or as one Nicaean Creed enlarged at Constantinople; at the end there is added the Nicaean anathema against the Arians.

2. To this anathema is appended the confession of Catholic faith attached to Damasus’s letter to Paulinus, which begins:

> “After this Council of Nicaea, which was held in the city of Rome, etc.”

We find this confession appended without distinction to the Nicaean Creed and its anathema in two ancient Vatican manuscripts, 1337 and 1338. Baluzius likewise found it in other Colbertine codices cited by P. Coustant in vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 510, note 2.

Since the Constantinopolitan Council was formerly unknown to the Romans, and since at that council certain additions had been made to the Nicaean Creed to establish the divinity of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonians, those same Romans appear to have placed this confession of faith after the celebrated Nicaean Creed in place of that addition. Through it, among them, the error of the Macedonians had already been condemned before the Constantinopolitan synod itself.

Since this confession held authority in the West and was known to everyone, it seemed appropriate to insert it after the Nicaean-Constantinopolitan Creed in the version of the Chalcedonian definition that we believe was made first.

I say “made first” because Saint Leo implies in *Epistle* 114, chapter 1, that he had examined and approved the definition of faith immediately after it had been rendered into Latin, although he had not yet read the rest of the council’s proceedings in Latin, including the sixth session. He testifies in *Epistle* 113, chapter 3, that he had not yet received the summary of that session transmitted by Julian.

He could have learned and judged certain other proceedings mentioned in those letters from the legates’ report and from a confused view of the Greek acts. But he could not have approved the definition of faith—which requires the most careful examination—as a man ignorant of Greek or insufficiently skilled in the language, without a Latin translation.

After this first translation of the definition, a nearly complete translation of the sixth session appears to have been made. That version consequently contains the same definition of faith in another translation, one more substantially consistent with the Greek exemplar, although very inelegant and, in several details, seriously faulty.

All these materials were translated into Latin during Leo’s lifetime, before the complete interpretation of all the proceedings was later laboriously prepared by a more skilled interpreter of both Greek and Latin.

[Col. 0729A] The summary of the third and sixth sessions follows. These are the two principal sessions of the council, from which the events of the other preceding sessions can be sufficiently understood.

The summary of the third session, in which Dioscorus was condemned, begins as follows:

> “Here begins the proceeding of the Council of Chalcedon, which assembled on the third day before the Ides of October. When the bishops listed above were seated, it was read, etc.”

See vol. IV of the Council, col. 2065.

The summary of the sixth session, in which the definition of faith was issued, begins with this title:

> “The proceedings held at Chalcedon on the eighth day before the Kalends of November contain the following. The emperor is seated with the bishops, etc.”

See the cited vol. IV, cols. 2066–2067.

Then, on page 13, there is added a version of three sessions concerning Maximus of Antioch. The first concerned the settlement reached between Maximus himself and Juvenal of Jerusalem and was held on the seventh day before the Kalends of November. The second was held on the sixth day before the Kalends of the same month and concerns the case of Domnus. The third, although it is not preceded in the codex by any distinguishing title, is nevertheless recognized as different from the other two by its different date, the day before the Kalends of November—or perhaps the day preceding that.

This third session, which concerns Juvenal as well as Domnus, is supplied by this codex alone and refutes Quesnel’s opinion much more clearly. More will have to be said about this matter later, after we have presented the three sessions.

On page 16 Marcian’s address to the synod is again presented under the following title:

> “The address of the emperor Marcian. When they had assembled in the holy Council of Chalcedon, in the presence of the Augusta Pulcheria, he said: ‘At the very beginning,’ etc.”

Page 17:

> “Here begins the constitution addressed to the Council of Chalcedon. The emperor Marcian: ‘At last, etc.’”

As in Quesnel’s collection, chapter 26.

On the same page:

> “Here begins another constitution of the divine memory of Marcian for [read: concerning] the Council of Chalcedon. The emperor Marcian Augustus to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium: ‘The venerable matter of the Catholic orthodox faith, etc.’”

This is recited in the aforementioned collection of Quesnel, chapter 27.
