On page 18: Pope Leo’s letter to the same synod, which in our edition is *Epistle* 114.

Page 19: another letter of his to Anatolius, which in our edition is *Epistle* 87.

Page 20: another to the emperor Marcian, which in our edition is *Epistle* 89.

On the same page: another to the Council of Chalcedon, which is *Epistle* 93.

Page 21: another to Marcian, which in this edition is *Epistle* 94.

Finally, on page 22:

> “The emperor Marcian Augustus to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium: ‘Although also by a most sacred constitution, etc.’”

As in Quesnel’s collection, chapter 28.

### 6

To enable everyone to appreciate the excellence of this exceedingly rare collection, it should be noted that, among the documents indicated, it contains those drawn from the Acts of Chalcedon that were first translated into Latin while Leo was still alive. Of this kind is the nearly complete translation of Action VI, together with another translation of the Definition of the Faith. Hence the author of the Quesnellian collection—which, being earlier than the complete translation of all the Acts of Chalcedon, received only the earliest translations—derived chapter twenty-five from these versions, as we pointed out above.

The very awkwardness and crudity of the translation sufficiently reveal the first effort of a translator, or translators, insufficiently skilled in the Greek language. We shall show with considerable probability in the observations on note 2 of Quesnellus’s letter 113 [preceding volume, col. 1433, n. a] that the summary of the two Actions, the third and the sixth, is the same summary as that which Julian of Cos sent to Leo.

The Action concerning the settlement between Maximus and Juvenal presents a version different not only from Rusticus’s translation, which is printed in volume IV of the Councils, col. 1515, but also from the ancient version printed there at col. 2035. It is recognized as older and, as we shall shortly prove, derived from the original Acts, and indeed from better originals than those available to Rusticus and to the ancient translator of all the Acts.

By the same author, two other Actions were translated into Latin from the same more authentic Greek Acts; we shall return to them. The fact that the original Latin text of the address of the Emperor Marcian—inserted in this version—was unavailable to the ancient translator of all the Acts, and also to the author of the still older version received in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections (for these translators were compelled to render it from Greek), demonstrates that the original and primary Acts of the Council were available to our translator. In those Acts the address had been delivered in both Latin and Greek and recorded in both languages, as we learn from Rusticus.

Finally, the six laws, all original and Latin, together with Leo’s letters, which are exceedingly rare and all authentic, confirm that the collector drew from an excellent source. When all these matters are weighed carefully, no one can fail to see how much credibility they lend to this collection and to the Action itself concerning Domnus, which Quesnellus attempts to expunge.

### 7

We shall now publish the three Actions concerning Maximus of Antioch, two of which concern Domnus, as they appear in the aforementioned manuscript, under this title:

**Copy of the Acts translated from Greek into Latin (sic).**

In the consulship of our lord, the perpetual Augustus, for the seventh time, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, at Chalcedon, in accordance with the command of the most divine and most merciful lord Marcian, the perpetual Augustus, when there had assembled in the holy church of the holy martyr Euphemia [Note: Read: “the most distinguished men, Anatolius, master of soldiers, ordinary ex-consul and patrician,” etc., as is clear from Action 1 and others, in which this same Anatolius is named. It should also be noted that these and the following words through “most reverend bishops” are absent from Rusticus’s manuscripts; in this respect too our translation is more exact.] the most distinguished men Anatolius, master of soldiers, ordinary ex-consul and patrician; Palladius, a most distinguished and illustrious prefect; and Vincomalus, a most distinguished and illustrious master of offices; and when Paschasinus and Lucentius [Note: Read “Paschasinus and Lucensis, or Lucentius.” A little later, read *vicars* for *vicar*.], most reverend bishops, had also assembled, together with Boniface, a religious presbyter and vicar of Leo, archbishop of Elder Rome, Anatolius, the venerable and renowned archbishop of Constantinople, Maximus, the venerable bishop of Antioch in Syria, Juvenal, the venerable bishop of Jerusalem, and the rest of the holy and universal synod assembled that day in the city of Chalcedon according to the holy imperial enactments of the most divine and merciful Lord, while all were seated before the rails of the holy altar, the most magnificent and illustrious judges said:

Our divine and most merciful lord, having been petitioned by Maximus and Juvenal, holy bishops, commanded us to hear from them concerning the matters at issue between them. The aforesaid venerable men, having come together, established certain things between themselves, without any written document intervening, which were made clear to us [Note: Read *constiterunt*, “were established”; after this word the manuscript contains signs of a brief lacuna. The words enclosed in brackets have been supplied from other versions. Shortly afterward, *sanctae synodi*, “of the holy synod,” should be read.] and appear to have been justly established by common consent. We therefore judged it necessary to set each matter forth before the holy synod, so that whatever may be approved both by your decision and by our judgment may be confirmed.

Maximus, the most reverend bishop of Antioch in Syria, said:

It has pleased me and the most reverend bishop Juvenal—after much dispute—to grant to the see of the city of Antioch, which is the see of Saint Peter, the two Phoenices and Arabia, while the see of Jerusalem shall have the three Palestines, provided that this pleases our venerable father, Leo, archbishop of Greater Rome, who desires the inviolable canons of the holy Fathers to remain in force [Note: Thus the manuscript. The common text has *uti*, “as”; but the context shows that the reading should everywhere be emended in this way.] And we ask that this be confirmed in writing by the judgment of your magnificence and of the holy synod.

Juvenal, the venerable bishop of Jerusalem, said:

I too approve the same arrangement: that the holy Anastasis of Christ should have the three Palestines, while the see of Antioch should have the two Phoenices and Arabia. I too ask that this be confirmed by the judgment of your magnificence and of the holy synod.

Paschasinus and Lucentius, venerable bishops, and Boniface, presbyter and vicar of the Apostolic See, through Paschasinus, the venerable bishop, said:

Let those agreements known to have pleased our brothers Maximus, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Antioch, and the holy and venerable Juvenal of Jerusalem, for the sake of peace—namely, that the Church of Antioch should have the two Phoenices and Arabia, while the Church of Jerusalem should have the three Palestines—also be confirmed by our humble intervention, so that no controversy concerning this matter may thereafter remain between the aforesaid Churches.

When this intervention had been translated into Greek by Veronicianus, a devout official and secretary of the Sacred Consistory, Anatolius, the venerable archbishop of the most glorious city of Constantinople, said:

Those matters agreed upon between the most blessed bishop Maximus of Antioch and the venerable bishop Juvenal of Jerusalem will also remain firm through my intervention. Let the holy Church of the city of Antioch have the two Phoenices and Arabia, while the holy Church of the Jerusalemites shall have the three Palestines, so that henceforth neither Church may have any ground for a quarrel or complaint against the other on this account.

All the venerable bishops cried out, whose names are written below:

“We too say these same things and agree with what was said by the Fathers.”

The most magnificent and glorious judges said:

This too has been accomplished by the holy Trinity and by the proposal of our divine and most merciful emperor, so that the matters over which they might have disputed [Note: Read, perhaps: “and this was done by the holy Trinity,” etc.; then *propositi* or *propositionis* for *praepositionis*. The passage is very corrupt. Perhaps it should read: “so that those who could have been disputing might settle the matter by a single decision and in harmony of will,” or something similar.] might be settled by a single decision of will tending to concord.

Therefore, the agreement made between Maximus, the holy bishop of the Antiochenes, and Juvenal, the holy bishop of Jerusalem, just as the exposition of each party stands confirmed by our judgment, shall remain permanently in force by decree of the holy synod. That is, Maximus, the holy bishop, or the holy city of the Antiochenes, shall possess under its authority the two Phoenices and Arabia; while Juvenal, the holy bishop of Jerusalem, or the holy Church subject to him, shall possess under its authority the three Palestines. All pragmatica and other claims of the parties having been set aside in accordance with the command of our divine and most merciful Lord, the corrupt remainder reads: “by divine letters, and many things written in them, for this . . . cause, secular matters” [Note: Perhaps read: “by letters from the parties, divine letters, with many matters written in them, for this very reason.” Another hand adds, etc.]. And in another hand: “Let them be issued.”

**Copy from Greek into Latin.**

In the consulship of the lord Marcian, the perpetual Augustus, and of the consul who shall have been announced, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, at Chalcedon, according to the command of our divine and most merciful lord Marcian, the perpetual Augustus, when there had assembled in the holy church of the holy martyr Euphemia the most magnificent and glorious master of the soldiers, former consul and patrician Anatolius, and the most magnificent and glorious prefect of the Sacred [Praetorian] Consistory Palladius, and the most magnificent and glorious master of the sacred offices Vincomalus, together with Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, a most reverend presbyter and vicar of Leo, the holy archbishop of Elder Rome [Note: Read *vicariis*, “vicars,” as appears from Rusticus and from the context.], and Anatolius, a most reverend archbishop of most eminent renown in Constantinople [Note: Rusticus’s manuscripts likewise have *magnissimi*, “most eminent,” instead of *maximi*, “greatest.”], and Maximus, a most reverend bishop of Antioch in Syria, and Juvenal, a most reverend bishop of Jerusalem, together with the rest of the holy synod, which had assembled in the city of Chalcedon by the decree of our divine and most merciful lord, and whose names are written above, while all were seated before the rails of the holy altar, Maximus, the most reverend bishop of Antioch, said:

I beseech the most magnificent and glorious judges and this holy universal synod to exercise humanity toward Domnus [Read: *Domnum*], who was bishop of the Church subject to me, and to assign him a fixed allowance from that Church.

Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, presbyter and vicars of the Apostolic See, through Paschasinus, the most reverend bishop, said:

The holy and most blessed pope, who confirmed the episcopate of the holy and venerable Maximus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, appears to have approved his merit by a sufficiently just judgment. For the aforesaid most reverend bishop Maximus, exercising his own discretion, wished provision to be made for Domnus, so that, out of compassion, he might grant him from his own Church such support as he judged appropriate, allowing him to remain content with his maintenance in the future.

When this confession had been translated into Greek by Veronicianus, a devout secretary of the Sacred Consistory, Anatolius, the most reverend bishop of Constantinople, said:

I too praise the compassion of the most blessed bishop Maximus of Antioch, in that of his own free will he offered such petitions that support might be provided for Domnus, who had been bishop of the holy Church subject to him, with nothing further being requested by the aforesaid man.

Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, said:

I too embrace the counsel of Maximus, the holy bishop of Antioch.

The entire holy synod cried out [Note: Rusticus’s manuscripts lack three cries, *quorum nomina his*, which convey no meaning. Shortly afterward, with Rusticus, one should read: “Here the humane thought of the pontiff is fitting to his judgment.”]:

“*Decibiles* [unintelligible]: deservedly, the archbishop’s benevolence. We all praise his thought. This is fitting to his judgment—the humane thought of the pontiff.”

The most magnificent judges said:

Since the holy synod embraces the decision of Maximus, the religious bishop of the Antiochenes, which he approved concerning Domnus, we too agree, leaving to his discretion whatever concerns the honor of Domnus [Note: Rusticus has a better syntax: “Leaving to his discretion matters concerning the honor of Domnus.”] And in another hand: “Let them be issued.”

In the consulship of the most pious and Christ-loving Flavius Marcian, the perpetual Augustus, and in the year which shall have been announced, on the Kalends of November, at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, the holy great and universal synod, assembled by the grace of God and by the decree of the most pious emperors, religious men, established the matters concerning him.

Something, at the insistence of the most blessed bishops, brought it about that favor should be shown to Maximus of the great city of Antioch and Juvenal of Jerusalem; for it is just that the remembrance [Note: Here and below, wherever dots are marked, the manuscript has been damaged. Perhaps *placitorum*, “of the agreements,” should be supplied, followed by “and in the presence of this holy great synod and of the most magnificent,” etc.] . . . . [lacuna] peace should prevail. After many things had been said by both parties . . . . [lacuna] in the presence of the holy great synod and of the most magnificent and glorious judges, in the presence of both parties [Note: Perhaps *utrisque*, “by both parties”; afterward, “the eastern provinces”], it was agreed that the two Phoenices and Arabia, in addition to the other eastern provinces, should be administered under the see of the Church of Antioch and should suffice for their administration [Note: Read *earum*, “of them”], and that nothing more should ever be sought; while the three Palestines should belong to the see of the Church of Jerusalem and should suffice for its administration, with nothing more to be sought in the future.

It was also agreed that all matters enacted here, all official proceedings, and everything else that had been done either by the bishops, the emperors, or the judges, should be entirely void as regards both parties [Note: Perhaps *utrisque*, “as regards both parties”]. These most blessed bishops embraced the foregoing not as the result of a judicial decree, but by common agreement, and they consented to accept [Note: Supply “the matters which”].

Therefore, we have received the most blessed bishop Maximus, who asked for humane treatment for Domnus, who had been bishop of Antioch, so that only communion might be granted to him as a layman, and that support might be provided for him from the same holy Church subject to Maximus, while he remained in the condition in which he now is and requested nothing more [Note: The phrase *ut abundat* is superfluous, or *et ei* should be written; similarly, shortly afterward: *et sumptus* should replace *ut sumptus*. The words requiring particular attention here are *ei ut communicationem ut plebeo praestari tantummodo*, “that communion be granted to him only as to a layman.” From this it may be inferred that Domnus, having been dismissed, was content not so much with the episcopate as with the honor of the episcopate, and with lay communion, and that he conducted himself as a layman. This entirely agrees with what Cyril of Scythopolis relates in the Life of Saint Euthymius, in Cotelerius, volume II of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 247, where he indicates that Domnus withdrew into the desert and lived the monastic life with Saint Euthymius.].

We likewise decree and confirm by common decree the foregoing matters, and we sanction them as unalterable and firm.

Paschasinus, Lucentius, and Julian, holy bishops, and Boniface, presbyter and vicars of the most blessed pope Leo, said:

The most blessed pope Leo, distinguished by the honor of apostolic dignity as head of the universal Church, decreed that the privileges of the Church of Antioch should be restored according to the statutes of the ancient Fathers. Therefore, with the consent of the holy synod, we too have decreed that the First and Second Phoenices, together with Arabia, which it had recently lost, should be restored to their former jurisdiction. For, since this arrangement pleased both bishops through the peace-making efforts of the most illustrious and exalted judges [Note: Read *studio*, “through the efforts”], the division of the provinces might calm the matter peacefully [Note: We suspect that this corrupt reading can be corrected as follows: “so that the division of the provinces might bring tranquility,” or something similar.].

Accordingly, let the aforesaid bishop of Jerusalem possess without disturbance the three Palestines, which he formerly held; and let the Antiochene, as justice requires [Note: Read *recipiat*, “receive”], recover the provinces mentioned, so that, dissension having been removed, priestly concord may be preserved inviolate.

For we praise the wish of Maximus, the most reverend bishop of the city of Antioch, which he graciously displayed of his own free will toward Domnus, formerly bishop of that same city, so that he might receive the consolations of humaneness from the Church. We confirm this by our intervention, in such a way that he shall receive 250 solidi annually and shall dare to request nothing more, but shall enjoy only communion and rest in his present condition.

Paschasinus, bishop, agreed and subscribed.

Lucentius, bishop, agreed and subscribed.

The other bishops whose names are written below likewise subscribed, as set forth above.

### 8

It should be observed that these three Actions are inserted in the aforementioned manuscript among the Chalcedonian documents of that most ancient version which is read in the very old Quesnellian collection and which existed before the complete translation of that Council—what is commonly called the ancient version. We have no doubt that it was prepared during Leo’s lifetime, immediately after the Council.

Before that complete version of the Acts of Chalcedon was made—the version called ancient—certain important Chalcedonian documents were immediately translated into Latin. For that reason they are found transferred into the older Latin collections. See what we shall say on this subject in the observations on note 3 of Quesnellus’s letter 113 [preceding volume, col. 1435, n. a]. The version of these three Actions therefore appears to belong to the same period. Hence, as we shall see shortly, their version is considerably earlier than the translations of Rusticus and the ancient translator.

### 9

Since the principal sections and documents of the Acts of Chalcedon that were immediately rendered into Latin were general and of the greatest importance, as will be clear from the observation just mentioned, if anyone asks why, among all the particular cases, with every other one omitted, only the three Actions concerning Maximus of Antioch were rendered into Latin while Leo was still alive, we shall say that we suspect Maximus sent their Greek copy to Leo when he dispatched letters and messengers to him concerning his own interests, and that they were translated into Latin on that occasion.

For it may be sufficiently inferred from Leo’s letter 119 to the same Maximus that Maximus had complained to the pontiff about the privileges of the see of Antioch having been violated. Leo undoubtedly refers to this when he writes there:

“Therefore, if your affection believes that something should be done on behalf of the privileges of the Church of Antioch, let it take care to explain this in its own letters.”

That he is referring to the settlement by which Maximus had ceded the three Palestines to Juvenal, to the prejudice of the see of Antioch, is sufficiently indicated by what follows, where the holy pontiff Leo condemns Juvenal’s presumption and declares the assent of the legates invalid against the canons of Nicaea. For the pontifical legates had given their assent only to the cession of the Palestines, which was contrary to the Nicene decrees.

Maximus, however, had consented to that settlement at the Council of Chalcedon not absolutely but, as our manuscript reads, under this condition:

“Provided that this pleases our venerable father Leo, archbishop of Greater Rome.”

The legates’ assent and the judgment promulgated in the final Action had persuaded him that the settlement was pleasing. Hence Maximus then acquiesced, and the settlement was approved.

But when he subsequently learned, in the case of Anatolius, that Leo did not wish anything opposed to the statutes of the Council of Nicaea to have force, he was encouraged to hope that the same pontiff might refuse to approve the settlement with Juvenal, which manifestly contradicted the Nicene canon. He therefore wished to ascertain Leo’s mind by letter, and appears to have sent the presbyter Marianus and the deacon Olympius for this very purpose, together with the aforementioned Actions of the Council of Chalcedon that concerned the matter. In those Actions his consent is expressed as having been given conditionally, so that, if the pontiff considered the judgment of the legates invalid, an opportunity would remain for restoring the privileges of his Church.

Hence, in the letter cited, Saint Leo, both before and after rejecting Juvenal’s authority over the three Palestines, declares empty and invalid whatever has been attempted against the Nicene canons, even if the legates sent by him consented to it.

Nor should one say that the holy pontiff presents himself in the letter as insufficiently informed about Maximus’s case and asks Maximus for fuller letters—which would not seem possible if he had received the Actions themselves. Even if he had not received these Actions, he would have been sufficiently informed about the case by Maximus’s two legates, so that new letters from Maximus on this matter would not have been necessary.

Moreover, since two matters in that case had operated to the prejudice of the see of Antioch—first, that the settlement with Juvenal had been made at the Council with Maximus himself consenting; and second, that, although the settlement was contrary to the Nicene canon, Leo’s legates had not merely failed to oppose it, as they had opposed the canon issued in favor of the see of Constantinople, but had also approved it—the holy pontiff openly shows that he knew both matters well.

He indicates the first when he wrote in chapter 4 that agreements and pacts of any kind contrary to the Nicene canons could easily be dissolved. He indicates the second when, in chapter 5, he declared that anything approved by his legates against those same canons would likewise be invalid.

But, one may ask, what did Leo request from Maximus? When Maximus sounded out the pontiff’s mind, he appears at the same time to have indicated that the time for action in this matter was then inopportune: all Palestine was disturbed by heretical tumults, and Juvenal himself, who had injured the see of Antioch, had been expelled from his see and did not enjoy by decree the right that was his.

Hence Saint Leo, waiting in these circumstances for Maximus to indicate a suitable time, wrote at the end of chapter 3: “Therefore, when your affection believes that something should be done on behalf of the privileges of the Church of Antioch, let it endeavor to explain this in its own letters, so that we may respond to your consultation absolutely and appropriately.” The adverbs “absolutely” and “appropriately” should be noted.

Meanwhile, he immediately added the general rule of his judgment, suited to Maximus’s circumstances, in conditional rather than absolute terms: “For the present, however, it is enough to pronounce generally on all points: if anything has been attempted by anyone in any synod against the statutes of the Nicene canons, or seems for a time to have been extorted, it can bring no prejudice upon the inviolable decrees; and it will be easier for the agreements of whatever consents to be dissolved than for the rules of the aforesaid canons to be impaired in any respect.”

And similarly in chapter 5: “If, indeed, anything is reported to have been done by these brothers whom I sent in my place to the holy synod beyond what concerned the cause of the faith, it shall possess no validity whatsoever, etc. For whatever differs from the rules of those Fathers [the Nicene Fathers] can never obtain the assent of the Apostolic See.”

Since this last statement concerning the assent of the legates refers solely to Maximus’s case, we recognize that Leo was well informed about it.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from believing that Maximus sent the very Acts of the Council through his legates in order to inform Leo, and that for this reason they had probably already been translated separately into Latin from the beginning.

For this purpose it would have been sufficient for Maximus to send only the two Actions concerning Juvenal. But since the case of Juvenal and that of Domnus are joined together in the last of the three Actions, Maximus thought that the Action concerning Domnus should likewise be transmitted.

Thus all these Actions, written in Greek so that Leo might understand them, were perhaps translated into Latin through the efforts of Maximus’s own messengers. Consequently, this version, made from the Greek copy that Maximus himself sent as accurately and authentically as possible, is found to be superior, as will soon be clear.

### 10

The Action concerning Juvenal, which is available from this version and from our manuscript, agrees entirely in substance with the published Greek and Latin texts. It is nevertheless very important to note certain differences.

In our manuscript, the paragraph beginning “When this intervention had been translated into Greek,” etc., is placed after Paschasinus’s Latin intervention. Since Paschasinus was speaking Latin, his intervention was subsequently translated into Greek.

This arrangement is better in our manuscript than in the Greek text, where that paragraph, together with the words indicating that the intervention had been translated into Greek, is incorrectly appended to Juvenal’s intervention, although Juvenal was using Greek and therefore had no need of a Greek translation.

It is also better than the ancient Latin version, where the same paragraph is placed not only after Juvenal’s intervention but where that intervention is also said to have been translated into Latin, as though the interventions of Greeks at a Greek synod were rendered into Latin.

Rusticus, in his version of this Action, as Baluzius notes, omitted the paragraph, either because it was absent from the Greek manuscript from which he translated it or because, finding it out of place, he rejected it as corrupt and spurious.

Our manuscript and our version therefore preserve a better origin. They also confirm a more accurate source by the words at the end of the same Action:

“And in another hand: Let them be issued.”

These words occur in our manuscript and version but are absent from the commonly published Greek text and from the ancient and Rustician Latin versions. Yet they were likewise added at the end of the Action concerning Domnus, which Rusticus also published.

These two marks of a better and more accurate origin, found in our manuscript, ought to lend credibility to the condition under which Maximus ceded the three Palestines to Juvenal:

“Provided that this pleases our venerable father Leo, archbishop of Greater Rome, who desires the inviolable canons of the holy Fathers to remain in force.”

The expression “of Greater Rome” certainly derives from the Greek source. We explained the reason for the condition above.

If this condition is read neither in the published Greek text nor in the two other Latin versions, while we possess the evidence of the best manuscript and of its better origin, no difficulty should arise for anyone who considers that some things were omitted by different persons—whether notaries at the Council itself or later copyists—not only in the Latin versions but also in the original Greek.

The Greek text and Rusticus’s version of this very Action concerning Juvenal omit several names of bishops that are found only in the ancient version. Has anyone therefore thought that such names should be rejected?

We have seen that Rusticus omitted the paragraph beginning “When this intervention had been translated into Greek.” Similar cases may be observed in other versions, though there is no room to list them here.

There were several notaries at the Councils, and some matters may have been written more accurately by certain notaries that others neglected. Later copyists, too, may have omitted certain things either carelessly or deliberately.

Accordingly, such deficiencies in some manuscripts, whether fewer or more, cannot serve as grounds for branding those manuscripts as interpolated by additions, when they are distinguished by the best marks of authenticity and contain matters omitted in other manuscripts but sufficiently consistent with the context.

If this version derives from the Greek copy that Maximus sent to Leo, there can be no doubt that Maximus’s own notary was more accurate in receiving and transcribing this section.

On the other hand, our manuscript lacks eight interventions that occur after Anatolius’s intervention in the Greek text and in the other Latin versions. Since these were unnecessary, they may have been omitted either by the ancient translator or, more probably, by the copyist and compiler of this collection, whom we have seen to have favored brevity.

### 11

The Action concerning Domnus agrees completely with the one that Rusticus published from the manuscript copy of Julia the patrician. Only in our manuscript is the true order found: this Action follows the Action concerning Juvenal held on the preceding day, whereas in the manuscript of Julia the patrician it was incorrectly placed first, as we learn from Rusticus’s note.

In order to undermine confidence in this manuscript of Rusticus, Quesnellus, at no. 5, insinuates that it was unique, recent, and of the lowest reliability, and that Rusticus received it from two unknown German scholars.

He based this claim on the manuscript’s poor title. Baluzius, using Rusticus’s manuscripts, presented a more accurate form:

“Action concerning Domnus of Antioch, which I found newly copied on parchment in the manuscript of the patrician Julia from an ancient paper manuscript, which he said had belonged to Proculus and Albinus, German scholars—that is, brothers who were advocates.”

Although this manuscript of Julia was new in Rusticus’s time—Rusticus wrote in the middle of the sixth century—it cannot now be called recent; still less can that manuscript of Proculus and Albinus, which was already considered very old at that time, be so called.

Even if these two manuscripts may be regarded as one, since one derives from the other, everyone can see how reliable a manuscript must be if it was already old in the middle of the sixth century and had been written shortly after Chalcedon.

Now another Vatican manuscript has appeared, likewise exceedingly old, which preserves the same Action translated from a Greek copy. Thus another of Quesnellus’s objections is refuted: he suspects that Rusticus fabricated this Action. For the Vatican manuscript in this Chalcedonian collection does not derive from Rusticus.

As for the third objection he raises—that Rusticus devoted his care and labor only to the first Chalcedonian Action—we shall reject it more fully in the observations on Quesnellus’s note 3 on letter 113 [preceding volume, col. 1435, n. a].

### 12

Furthermore, if the manuscript of Julia the patrician had been Greek, and if Rusticus had translated this Action from it into Latin, then, just as the copy from which the three Actions were transcribed was Greek, we would possess not only two Latin manuscripts but also two Greek manuscripts of different origin confirming the genuineness of this Action.

But since the version of this Action published by Rusticus appears similar to the translation in our manuscript, which we have recognized as exceedingly ancient, there can be no doubt that the manuscript of Julia the patrician, and the manuscript of Proculus and Albinus, were Latin.

Rusticus himself indicates in several places that he used Latin rather than Greek manuscripts. He therefore did not translate this Action from Greek, as has hitherto been believed, but transcribed it from an older Latin version.

Thus the manuscripts of Julia, Proculus, and Albinus contained the translation found in our manuscript. That translation is recognized as the oldest from this very fact, and it was derived from the Greek copy which Maximus, for the sake of his own case, sent to Saint Leo. Had Maximus not sent that copy, we would lack this Action concerning Domnus.

For the case of Domnus, in which the question concerns the establishment of an allowance, appeared so insignificant that the Greek compilers of the Acts of Chalcedon neglected it, just as they omitted other matters. Consequently, the Latin version of those Acts does not contain this Action.

It was therefore unknown even to the Greek writers Justinian, Evagrius, and others, and to Liberatus among the Latins. Their silence proves nothing except that they used only those manuscripts of the Acts of Chalcedon in which this Action is absent, and that they did not happen upon any copy resembling ours, or resembling the manuscript of Julia, or those of Albinus and Proculus, from which Rusticus and we have received the same text.

13. The proceeding concerning Domnus is rendered much more authentic by another proceeding, which has emerged from the Vatican manuscript alone. For the pension which the earlier proceeding had left to Maximus’s discretion, so that no further dispute might arise—perhaps at Maximus’s own request—Leo’s legates fixed the amount. The day, opening, and subscriptions show that this was a distinct proceeding. Nor is it surprising that a new Chalcedonian proceeding should appear: proceedings concerning particular matters were omitted by some and transcribed by others, as they saw fit. Thus the earlier proceeding concerning Domnus was found by Rusticus only in the codex of Julia the patrician. The Greek manuscripts contain two proceedings concerning Carosus and Dorotheus, and concerning Photius of Tyre and Eustathius of Berytus, which were lacking in the exemplars used by the ancient translator Rusticus, Liberatus, and Evagrius. Compare note 18 (previous volume, col. 257, n. b) in Quesnel’s first dissertation on the year 451. The assessment of the pension for Domnus is not unlike that which had been decreed two days earlier, in proceeding 11, for Bassianus and Stephanus, bishops of Ephesus. Nor should the title “Head of the Universal Church” given to the pontiff in this proceeding cause concern: for the very same legates who bestowed this title on him used a similar formula in proceeding 1, shortly after its beginning. Concerning Leo they say: “Who is the head of all the Churches”; and, likewise, in proceeding 6, in the subscriptions to the definition of faith: “Of the most blessed and apostolic man, Leo, pope of the universal Church of the city of Rome.” Julian is counted among the three papal legates in the sentence, as at the beginning of proceeding 9 and in proceeding 10, where they forbade the reading of the acts of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus. In this sentence, however, when the same legates had first stated that Leo had established that the privileges of the Church of Antioch should be reformed according to the statutes of the ancient Fathers, they wished it to appear that they had decreed this in accordance with the pontiff’s mind and command, and in conformity with the ancient canons. These points had to be added to defend and clarify this new proceeding, which sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirms another proceeding concerning Domnus attacked by Quesnel. Since, moreover, all suspicion is removed from the praised proceeding concerning Domnus by these outstanding documents of the Vatican codex, which until now had not been sufficiently known or noticed, we now possess in our hands—as we may conclude in Quesnel’s words—a most illustrious and ancient testimony to the supreme authority of the Roman pontiff, both in synods and over the Eastern bishops, that is, over the bishops of the greater and principal sees.

# TENTH DISSERTATION

## On the case of Theodore, bishop of Cyrrhus, deposed by the sentence of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, restored by St. Pope Leo, and cleared at the Synod of Chalcedon

On the letter of Saint Leo written to the same Theodore, Letter 93 (now 120).

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739A] 1237 I. “Blessed,” says St. Leo, “is our God, whose invincible truth has shown you to be cleansed from every stain of heresy, according to the judgment of the Apostolic See. You will repay him with fitting gratitude for so many labors if, for the defense of the universal Church, you preserve yourself such as we have proved you to be” (Epistle 93, now 120).

What that judgment of the Apostolic See was has until now been asked by many, and various opinions have been advanced. Some maintain that St. Leo issued some decree, either in a synod or outside a synod, concerning Theodore’s restoration, after Theodore had brought his case before him by a written appeal. But since not even the slightest trace of such a decree appears, whether in the Acts of Chalcedon or in other records of events at that time, this claim is refuted as easily as it is made.

Others say that Theodore was restored by the same synodal and judicial sentence by which the pseudo-synod of Ephesus had been annulled: namely, at that gathering of bishops in whose midst the Roman pontiff is said, in the letters written on this matter to the emperor Theodosius concerning the rescinding of the acts of that cabal, to have come forth from St. Peter’s to meet the emperor Valentinian and the empresses, surrounded by a procession. In my view, however, it is certain that no sentence intervened in Theodore’s case, whether one issued by Leo alone or one issued by a synod. Rather, Leo recalls only that judgment which was contained in the letters of communion. For when the pontiff freely undertook Theodore’s complaints and granted him his communion, it necessarily followed that he had judged him cleansed from every stain of heresy; and that, among the adversaries’ calumnies, he had set aside whatever they had brought forward in order to exclude him from the synod as suspect in the faith, or even to depose him in the synod as though he had been convicted of heresy. To make this more persuasive to the reader, we shall place the entire matter briefly before his eyes.

[Col. 0739C] **Note:** What this judgment of the Apostolic See was will be explained in the observations, nos. 4 and following, where Quesnel’s evasions will be demolished.

II. Theodore, bishop of Cyrrhus, under the patriarch of Antioch, had for a long time had Dioscorus of Alexandria as an especially hostile adversary, both on account of his exceptional learning and holiness of life—which Dioscorus, a man exceedingly desirous of praise, believed eclipsed him—and because Theodore had formerly opposed the anathemas of St. Cyril, Dioscorus’s predecessor. For this reason the Alexandrian had already begun to brand Theodore as a heretic, pursue him with calumnies, and harass him in every way. Later the Alexandrian prevailed upon Emperor Theodosius to forbid Theodore from attending the synod being prepared at Ephesus: as the keenest patron of the heresiarch Eutyches, he feared Theodore, who had always shown himself a most vigorous opponent of heretics. Nor was he satisfied with this. Since he had arrogated everything to himself in that pseudo-synod by violence and impiety, he expelled Theodore from the episcopal order, directing against him a sentence of deposition [Col. 0740A] just as he had directed it against the other bishops who defended the Catholic faith.

When Theodore learned this, he grieved over his own situation. As he considered privately what counsel he should adopt amid such great confusion and looked around at all the bishops of the Eastern Church, and even at the powers of the world, he found no one whom he could approach or to whom he could bring his complaints. Chrysaphius, by whose counsel the emperor acted, had openly and publicly taken up the cause of Eutyches. The emperor himself, deceived by the skill of the heretics, was defending the sentence of the pseudo-synod by his authority. Dioscorus was the author and principal contriver of that entire storm. Domnus had received a similar sentence of deposition. The bishop of Constantinople, through the crime and brutality of the Eutychians, had not yet died—but, at least, had been nearly killed and was being carried off into exile at Hypaepa. What remained for Theodore to do, with almost all the Eastern bishops either raging, crushed, or not daring even to speak, [Col. 0740B] except to turn to the Westerners and seek their faith and religious support? He therefore sent letters to Leo as patriarch of the Westerners, head of all the bishops, and common Father of the entire Church, imploring his assistance and that of all the bishops of the West alike.

For Liberatus says nothing about an appeal. In chapter 12 he writes only this: “Theodore, bishop, informed the pope how many evils he had suffered through Dioscorus’s machinations, asking that such a case might more quickly be aided through another gathering of bishops.”

[Col. 0739D] **Note:** He attempts to exclude an appeal to Leo and strives to persuade us that all the Westerners were included together with Leo. We shall refute both claims in Observation no. 1 and those that follow.

III. But let us hear Theodore himself addressing our Leo in these words. “I,” he says, “await the decision of your Apostolic See, and I beseech and implore your holiness to aid me as I invoke your just and righteous tribunal, and to command me to come to you and to display my teaching as following the apostolic footsteps.” [Col. 0740C]

Theodore, Epistle to Leo, chapter 5.

By these words Theodore seems to me to be asking Leo for two things. First, he wishes to be instructed by the judgment and counsel of St. Leo, as the most prudent and devout prelate, whether, for the sake of the peace of the Church, it would be better for him to abide by Dioscorus’s judgment than to appeal to the tribunal of other synods, which might perhaps become an occasion for new disturbances. This is the sense of the opening words: “I await the decision of your Apostolic See.” The following words confirm that this interpretation arose not from us but from Theodore’s own understanding. “Above all,” he says, “I beg to learn from you whether I ought to accept this unjust deposition or not; for I await your decision. And if you command me to remain with those who condemned me, I shall remain, and I shall trouble no human being any longer; instead, I shall await the unbending tribunal of God and our Savior.”

[Col. 0740D] **Note:** “But above all I beg you to let me learn from you whether I must accept this unjust deposition or not; for I await your decision. And if you command me to remain with those who voted against me, I shall remain, and henceforth I shall trouble no human being, but shall await the unbending tribunal of our God and Savior.” Theodore, Epistle 113, chapter 6.

From this it can be discerned how sincerely—or how learnedly—the writer who recently discussed the judgments of bishops in France, on page 318, interpreted those words of Theodore.

The second thing Theodore asks is this: if St. Leo should judge that Dioscorus’s sentence ought not to be obeyed, he asks that another council be held in the West by apostolic authority, to which he might hasten to be absolved from the unjust sentence. This is the sense clearly drawn from the words quoted above: “I beseech your holiness to aid me as I invoke your just and righteous tribunal and to command me to come to you.” We derive this meaning clearly from Theodore’s letter, written at the same time and concerning the same matter to Renatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church who had been sent to Ephesus as Leo’s representative. “For this reason,” he says, “I beseech your holiness to persuade the most holy and devout archbishop to use his apostolic authority and command me to hasten to your council.”

[Col. 0741D] Theodore, Epistle 116, to the presbyter Renatus.

**Note:** We shall explain there, in Observation no. 2, why Theodore, appealing to Leo, mentions a council, and you will also find there which council he had in mind.

And again, in a letter sent to the patrician Anatolius at Constantinople: “I beg your magnificence to obtain this favor from the victorious emperor, so that I may reach the West and be judged by those most beloved of God and most holy bishops: and if I myself should be found to have transgressed even in the slightest against the rule of faith, may I be cast into the very depths of the sea.”

[Col. 0741D] Theodore, Epistle 119, to the patrician Anatolius.

Whether, then, Theodore wished this council which he desired to attend to be composed only of the bishops of the Italian region—which I do not think—or of all the prelates of the Western parts, which is more probable, makes no difference to me. For even if I conceded that a council had been requested only of those bishops who customarily gathered from the neighboring provinces to the Roman pontiff, so that, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, a gathering of bishops might be held twice, or at least once, each year in each region, as we learn from St. Leo’s Epistle 16, chapter 7, this would not conflict with our position. For it is clear that Theodore requested such a council [Col. 0741D] not from legal necessity but at the discretion of the litigant himself. According to the custom of the Church of Africa and the decree of the Council of Carthage, he was free to choose for himself a judgment before a synod of Western bishops, on the condition that he would submit irrevocably to whatever sentence the judges chosen of their own accord might issue.

Thus the Carthaginian Fathers made provision in favor of a condemned bishop in the year of Christ 407, as is read in chapter 96 of the code of the African Church; and there was nothing to prevent this from being put into practice in other Churches. “If an appeal has been made,” says the canon, “let the appellant choose the judges, together with the person against whom he has appealed, so that thereafter neither party may appeal from them.”

[Col. 0741C] 1241 Theodore, then, must be said to have convened a synod by voluntary choice, not because the Roman pontiff was legally obliged to do so, if he appealed only to that synod. For if he were legally bound to do this, why did he fear that his petitions might not be admitted by the pontiff and that his recourse might fail to achieve its effect? This is precisely what he repeatedly begs in his letter to St. Leo: “I beg you, do not reject my supplication, nor disregard my wretched gray hairs, after they have been insulted through so many labors.”

[Col. 0742D] **Note:** “I beg you, do not spurn my supplication, nor overlook my wretched old age, which has been subjected to insult after so many labors.” Theodore to Leo, chapter 5.

Why does he court the favor of the presbyter Renatus, so that through Renatus’s action and persuasion he might be permitted to hasten to a council in the West? Why does he urge the archdeacon of the Roman Church to kindle St. Leo’s zeal? “Deign,” he says, “most beloved of God, to kindle the zeal of the archbishop, most holy in all things and most devout, so that the Churches of the East may also enjoy your protection.”

[Col. 0742D] **Note:** “Therefore, most beloved of God, deign to kindle the zeal of the archbishop, most holy in all things and most devout, so that the Churches of the East may also enjoy your care.” Epistle 118, to the archdeacon of Rome.

Finally, why does he promise that he will assent to and abide by the pontiff’s judgment, whatever it might be? Anyone would laugh at such a promise if the judge were one whom he was obliged to approach and obey. For then, whether the appellant wished it or not, he could neither decline the judgment nor refuse obedience to the sentence. Such a promise, however, is not inappropriate when judgment is requested from judges chosen at the litigant’s own discretion, lest they remove from themselves the burden of judging.

Although we say these things about a Roman synod, [Col. 0742B] we nevertheless consider it more probable that Theodore was thinking of a more universal council of the West, since he expressly desires to go to the West and be judged by the bishops of the West.

Our conjecture is extraordinarily confirmed by Theodore’s Epistle 117, which is read as addressed to the bishop of Florence but plainly seems [Col. 0742D] to have been directed to the bishops of the Roman or Western synod.

For, as far as I understand, the title must be corrected. This is the opinion of the distinguished Garnerius, founded upon the gravest indications. “First,” he says, “Theodore writes to several persons: for he always uses the plural number, whereas he was accustomed to address all individuals, even the supreme pontiff and the empress Pulcheria, by a singular title. Moreover, what the translator rendered ‘your holiness’ does not agree with the Greek, *hymeteran hagiosynen* [ὑμετέραν ἁγιωσύνην], nor does what he rendered ‘most holy man’ agree with the Greek, which reads *hagiotatoi* [ἁγιώτατοι]. Second, that the persons to whom he writes were from the Western regions is shown by his contrasting them with the Easterners. Third, that those several persons were also bishops of the West is shown not only by the title but also by the expression ‘your holiness,’ used for a third time. Fourth, that these bishops had not departed from the faith, while the Churches of the East had suffered a common calamity: ‘By God’s grace, he has left us your holiness as a remnant, lest we become like Sodom,’ and so forth. Fifth, that they possessed such authority that they could drive away the calamity of the Churches of the East, condemn the heresy which had arisen, openly rebuke those who had dared to corrupt the doctrine of the Incarnation, undertake the patronage and defense of those harassed for the sake of piety, not despise those unjustly expelled but suppress the injustice with just assistance, and teach those who insolently attacked the truth. Sixth, that legates were being sent to them—namely, the very men who at that time were being sent to Pope Leo.” (See the notes and dissertations of Garnerius in volume 48 of our *Patrologia*.)

[Col. 0743A] If this learned man’s conjecture is not groundless—but rather because it can scarcely be called into doubt—he himself openly settles in his second dissertation, on Theodore’s Epistle 117, the controversy which, given the circumstances, he had considered invidious in Dissertation 1, chapter 9, and had not dared to resolve. For after this, who could deny that Theodore had addressed the entire council of the West, when witnesses to such an appeal are found in Theodore’s own letters to the Western council and in the legates sent to that same council to conduct his case? The other letters to Renatus and Anatolius, as well as the testimony of the deacon Liberatus, support this conclusion.

[Col. 0743D] **Note:** This is refuted in Observation no. 2.

The same Garnerius adds to this authority an argument which it is incumbent upon him to establish. “For,” he says (Dissertation 1, chapter 10), “one of the major cases was being handled: and at that time no such case was debated even by the supreme pontiffs themselves except in an assembly of bishops. That this case was among the major ones is especially clear from the fact that the question concerned the faith of a most renowned bishop, deposed by a synod in which all the patriarchs of the entire world were present, with the exception of the Roman patriarch.”

[Col. 0743B] IV. After receiving the letters of Theodore and the others and hearing Hilary’s report, we do not know what Saint Leo wrote back to Theodore; we inquire what he did. Immediately after the Ephesian Robbery, the pontiff understood that a council was necessary, and a general council at that, as is clear from his letters on this matter to the emperor.

[Col. 0743D] **Note:** In what sense and under what circumstances St. Leo wrote that a general council was necessary was explained at length in our preceding observations on Dissertation 8, no. 14 and following.

“Order,” he says, “that a general synod be celebrated within Italy, which may either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further remains doubtful in the faith or divided in charity; with the bishops of the Eastern provinces, of course, assembling. If any of them, overcome by threats and injuries, have strayed from the path of truth, let them be restored by healing remedies” (Epistle 40, now 44, chapter 10).

For restoring Theodore, however, he considered neither a provincial nor a general synod necessary, since Theodore ought not to be regarded as deposed: the one that had attempted to pronounce a sentence of deposition against him was not a council but a robbery, and not a bishop but an evil brigand. It had attempted this, moreover, against a man whom it had neither summoned to court, nor judged while present, nor questioned about his belief concerning the humanity assumed by our God and Savior (Epistle 52, Theodore to St. Leo).

This was so certain to everyone that whatever had been done in that pitiable gathering at Ephesus was universally regarded by all Catholics as null and void. “Since,” says St. Leo, “what was recently done at Ephesus against justice or canonical discipline through the shamelessness of one man cannot be allowed to stand by any principle of the Catholic faith” (Epistle 47, now 51). Hence he also warns the Constantinopolitans not to let any threats or fear separate them from their own priest, who had received a similar sentence of deposition together with Theodore. “For whoever,” he says, “while your bishop Flavian was alive and unharmed, dared to invade his priesthood shall never be held in our communion, nor be able to be counted among the bishops” (Epistle 45, now 50, chapter 1).

This was precisely what our Leo requested from the emperor Theodosius when he asked him to order that everything remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world could assemble (Epistle 40, now 44). Marcian agreed to this request on Theodosius’s behalf when he succeeded him after his death: he truly convened a larger synod of bishops from the entire world and ordered Theodore to attend it.

[Col. 0743D] **Note:** Indeed, we shall demonstrate in the observations that follow, from no. 4 through no. 8, that Leo had a particular judgment concerning Theodore.

From what has been said, it is clear that our Leo had no judgment for hearing Theodore’s case [Col. 0744A], but remained united with him through uninterrupted communion and replied to his letters that he need neither abide by the judgments nor await another judgment in order to govern his Church in the customary manner, since no principle of the Catholic faith allowed what had been done at Ephesus through the shamelessness of one man to stand (Epistle 47, now 51).

He regarded the sentence issued against Theodore as void all the more readily because new testimony from the East concerning the integrity of Theodore’s faith had been brought to him. For from a letter of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, ordained after Flavian’s death, he learned that Theodore had voluntarily subscribed to the encyclical letter to that same Flavian, and that he had not merely condemned the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches but had also anathematized Nestorius and Eutyches themselves.

We learn from a letter of our Leo to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, which we now publish for the first time, that this had been done by all the bishops subject to the bishop of Antioch, among whom Theodore was one. “You should know,” he says, “that very recently I received a letter from the bishop of Constantinople, which reports that the bishop of Antioch, having sent circular letters throughout his provinces, obtained from all the bishops both their agreement with my letter and their condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches by a common subscription” (Epistle 68, now 88, chapter 3).

From this subscription—or even from the letter which Theodore had written to Leo—the Roman pontiff understood and judged that Theodore was free from every stain of heresy, and that nothing on this account prevented him from granting Theodore his communion in the customary manner, so that he might retain his Church in ecclesiastical peace.

This, in my judgment, is the judgment of the Apostolic See mentioned in the letter we are commenting on. It does not demonstrate that Theodore’s see had been restored by a judicial sentence of the pontiff; it demonstrates only that a certain suspicion of error had been removed—a suspicion which perhaps had clung to him either because of the repeated and frequent calumnies of his adversaries or because of his earlier disputes with Cyril.

[Col. 0744D] **Note:** Compare note 25 (col. 715, n. d) in the preceding dissertation, where the special and more powerful force of communion granted by the Apostolic See is explained.

V. Indeed, if you maintain that Theodore was restored by the Apostolic See for this reason—that the See embraced him within the bosom of its communion—why not declare him restored by the other bishops as well? For Maximus of Antioch, his primate, and Anatolius of Constantinople, together with many other prelates of the Eastern regions, either never severed the bond of communion with him or soon reestablished it.

Who, however, would wish to deny that the Roman pontiff’s desire and the support of his communion were held above those of the others, since he was the bishop of the primary see of all, and moreover a man most holy and learned, and especially in this case a vigorous defender of the Catholic faith?

Yet we cannot assert that the entire matter was brought to an end by Leo’s action, since it is known to everyone who reads the Acts of this synod that the Fathers of Chalcedon brought it back to the anvil for renewed examination.

[Col. 0744D] **Note:** To what extent Theodore’s case was again debated at the Synod of Chalcedon without prejudice to the judgment pronounced concerning him by St. Leo, we shall explain in Observations nos. 9 and 10; the points that follow will be clarified by them.

This was done in accordance with the mind of St. Leo himself. For after the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, St. Leo had requested only that all Dioscorus’s decrees be held in abeyance and that everything remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world had assembled (Epistle 40, now 44). The pontiff’s plan undoubtedly was that, as soon as this larger number of bishops had gathered, all matters should be subjected anew to their judgment and examination, as though no judgment had yet been rendered.

[Col. 0745A] Nor is there reason to think that Theodore’s case should be exempted from this rule, since more than any other it demanded examination by the synod. Most of the other bishops whom the pseudo-synod of Ephesus had expelled from their sees had not come under suspicion of error before the Robbery; and therefore, once the acts of the pseudo-synod had been rescinded, their position remained wholly intact. Theodore, however, had been marked as suspect in the faith long before the Ephesian gathering by defenders of the Catholic position. He had seemed to favor Nestorius, and the emperor had seized upon the suspicion of error as a reason for removing him from the synod.

Therefore, even if he had been received into communion by Leo and summoned to Chalcedon by imperial edict, this alone did not dispel the old suspicions. Rather, the way was being prepared for a future judgment, in which his faith would be examined and the accusations of his adversaries investigated.

For this reason, when the lay judges requested that he be brought into the synod in accordance with the emperor’s edict, not a few bishops, as some think, but by far the greater number—the Egyptians, namely, [Col. 0745B] Palestinians, and Illyrians—shouted: “Have mercy; the faith is perishing!” “The canons exclude this man!” “Send him outside!” “Send out Nestorius’s teacher!” “The Orthodox Synod does not receive Theodore!” “This man anathematized Cyril!”

[Col. 0745C] **Note:** All these men were entangled in the prejudices of Dioscorus and Eutyches in the first proceeding; therefore it is not surprising that they opposed Theodore, whom Dioscorus had condemned as a Nestorian.

Among these bishops the Illyrians had as their leader the bishop of Thessalonica, who, since he was acting as the representative of the Roman bishop in Illyricum, depended upon his direction.

[Col. 0745C] **Note:** Anastasius of Thessalonica was absent and participated only through a legate.

Nevertheless, he did not think that the judgment of the Apostolic See—which had pronounced Theodore cleansed from every stain of heresy—prevented Theodore from being excluded from the synod as a man long suspected in the faith. Again, when the judges insisted that he be received, these bishops finally gave way, as though by indulgence and dispensation—but not before Theodore had been shown, by the testimony of his primate Maximus of Antioch, to be infected by no disease of heretical thought, and before the judges had further promised that his presence would create no prejudice and that the case would be reserved intact for future examination. Only after these conditions had been imposed was Theodore finally admitted.

[Col. 0745D] **Note:** Even after the testimony of Maximus and after the judges’ promise, they continued to protest against him. Only when the judges pressed them a second and third time, in that same first proceeding, was it necessary for them to yield.

VI. When they came to the eighth proceeding of the council, Theodore’s case was summoned for examination. And when the bishops shouted that he should anathematize Nestorius, he resisted for some time—not because he favored that impious heresiarch. For, as we saw from St. Leo’s Epistle 68 (now 88) to Paschasinus, he had already anathematized him together with the other bishops of the Eastern diocese, among whom he was one; and in the first proceeding of Chalcedon, when Nestorius was being discussed, those same bishops testified to this.

“We,” they said, “subscribed on a blank sheet”—not because he was seeking evasive devices by which he could refrain from anathematizing Nestorius; for it is unworthy to invent such things about so great a man—but partly because he was displeased that a different rule should be imposed on him than on the others, when in the fourth proceeding he had professed the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creed together with the others, had embraced Leo’s letter to Flavian, which pronounced anathema against Nestorius, and had confirmed his faith by a solemn subscription; and partly, indeed chiefly, because, when he had protested after being condemned by Dioscorus’s synod, he wished everything to be reviewed and recognized in due order and according to the custom of councils, lest he appear to have sought a secret and seemingly furtive acquittal out of consciousness of guilt.

This is why he first demanded that both his petitions to the emperor and the libelli he had presented to the legates be reread: “If it seems good to you,” he said, “let them be read before you, so that, as I understand it, you may learn the truth.”

Nor did he allow that brief profession, “Anathema to Nestorius,” and so forth, which was demanded amid so many disorderly shouts, to be extracted from him until he had defended his faith, which had so often been attacked by calumnies, with a more extended declaration. After this had been publicly pronounced, he said: “Anathema to Nestorius,” and so forth.

For that holy bishop was more concerned to prove the integrity of his faith—than which nothing ought to be more important to a Catholic priest—than to ensure either that he attend the synod or that he be restored to his Church and dignity. “Truly,” he said, “I will not speak unless I first persuade you [or: satisfy you] how I have learned to please God; for I care nothing about the city, I have no need of honor, and I did not come for this reason, but because I have suffered calumny, I came to prove that I am orthodox” (Chalcedon, proceeding 8).

When these matters had been completed, and every concern—not, as the judges said, merely every scruple but every doubt—had finally been removed, the synod’s sentence followed. Approving and confirming the judgment of St. Leo, who had granted Theodore his communion, it restored him to his see, giving this principal reason for its judgment:

[Col. 0746B] “Since he has anathematized both Nestorius and Eutyches not only in writing but also orally, in the presence of the entire assembly.”

[Col. 0745D] **Note:** Since Theodore’s case was dealt with in the tenth proceeding in order to satisfy those who doubted his faith, and since his public protestation had convinced them, this was chiefly the reason that had to be inserted into the sentence pronounced by the legates for their benefit. Nevertheless, they had prefaced it with Leo’s judgment, just as the universal synod had also commended that judgment in its acclamations. Compare Observation no. 4.

VII. From these statements, learned reader, understand how miserably, in the very noonday sun, those are blind who diminish and deride the sacred authority of bishops assembled in an ecumenical synod—and much more so outside a synod—and maintain that the mere execution of pontifical commands belongs to them by virtue of their office, both in this case under discussion and in all others.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] No Catholic can deny that bishops, especially in ecumenical councils, together with the supreme pontiff, who presides over them as head over members, either personally or through legates [Col. 0746C] (these are the formulas of the Council of Chalcedon itself in its report to Leo, our Epistle 98, chapter 1), are true judges and legislators, and that, acting as such, they define controversies, issue judgments, enact laws, and impose obligations for their execution. Once the decrees of a council have been published, the same bishops subsequently become executors when they put them into practice, as they are obliged to do. In this sense the Roman pontiffs themselves have professed to be executors, lest they nevertheless be denied the power, in matters pertaining to discipline, of dispensing from or altering something whenever that seems expedient. In Theodoret’s case, although the judgment of the Apostolic See, which preceded the council, restored him by restoring his right, his actual restoration was nevertheless reserved to the council, as we shall explain in Observation 10. There too, in Observation 9, we shall show to what extent the synod could, without prejudice to the Apostolic See, examine the matter again after Leo’s judgment, so that those who were doubtful might be satisfied and it might be clear, from Theodoret’s own confession and anathema against Nestorius, that nothing had been deceptively withheld from Leo.]

Yet it is rather one of the Apostolic See’s not least important distinctions that it is the executor of ecumenical synods. For Pope Gelasius gloried in this prerogative and did not hesitate to assert it for his see, in accordance, naturally, with its primacy, in Epistle 13:

> “We are confident,” he says, “that no one who is truly a Christian is now ignorant that, of the constitutions of each synod which the assent of the universal Church has approved, no other see ought to execute them more than this one, which both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it by continuous oversight, in accordance with its primacy,” and so forth.

And below:

> “Let us suppose, nevertheless,” he says, “that no synod had preceded, of which the Apostolic See would rightly become the executor,” and so forth.

Indeed, as regards Theodoret, it is clear that the Council of Chalcedon handled his case [Note: [Col. 0747D] See Observations 9 and 10.] as though it had not already been referred to another tribunal. For although he had been admitted to communion with the Roman bishop; although, as they wish to maintain, he had been restored by that bishop’s judgment; although he had been supported by the suffrage of his patriarch, who was present at the synod; although, even by imperial edict, he had not only been made a participant in the synod but had also been restored to his own Church—for this is chiefly what Saint Leo’s words to Pulcheria must be understood to mean: “You have restored,” he says (Epistle 59, now 79, chapter 2), “Catholic priests who had been unjustly expelled from their Churches”; although, finally, he had subscribed once and again to Saint Leo’s letter—nevertheless, he was proclaimed a heretic by the greater part of the synod and was almost expelled from it (while the Roman legates remained silent and did not intervene either on behalf of Leo’s judgment or on behalf of the sentence which, they maintain, had preceded the synod). At last he was scarcely cleared and restored to his Church, after his faith had been examined anew by the synod itself and he had personally anathematized the heretics in the presence of the entire assembly.

Moreover, the sentence of the synod, which the Roman pontiff had anticipated by his own judgment, subsequently received his assent as well, both in other letters and especially in the one he sent to Theodoret somewhat after the synod had ended. In it he expresses the greatest joy that Theodoret had been shown to be free from every stain of heresy by invincible truth; that the judgment of the Apostolic See concerning him had been confirmed; and, finally, that nothing else was to be desired except that he should preserve himself for the defense of the universal Church as the man whom Leo had previously approved and was then approving as well.

“Blessed,” he says [Col. 0747C] (Epistle 93, now 120, chapter 5), “is our God, whose invincible truth has shown you, according to the judgment of the Apostolic See, to be cleansed from every stain of heresy. You will render him worthy thanks for all your labors if you preserve yourself for the defense of the universal Church as the man whom we have approved and do approve.”

VIII. As I reread these things, I cannot sufficiently marvel that men have recently been found to write that Theodoret’s case—examined, cleared, and restored at the Council of Chalcedon—was not confirmed by Saint Leo, any more than were his other judgments concerning the private cases of bishops. To inquire into the others is not the concern of this place. As for Theodoret, although the words just quoted abundantly demonstrate that Leo confirmed the synodal judgment by which Theodoret had been acquitted, it is nevertheless worthwhile to add other passages from the same letter which follows, making it clear that not only Theodoret’s person was defended in the synod against the plots of the impious, but also his faith against the slanders of his adversaries.

“For when God,” he says (Epistle 93, now 120, chapter 5), “dissolves the deceptions of all slanderers, we recognize the greatest care of the most blessed Peter on behalf of us all. After he had established the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith, he did not permit ANYTHING REPROBATE TO APPEAR CONCERNING THE PERSON OF ANY ONE OF YOU who labor with us for the Catholic faith, because, with the Holy Spirit judging, none of those whose faith had already conquered could emerge from the contest except as a victor.”

From these words of Leo it is evident that his meaning is this: the sentence by which the synod acquitted Theodoret had been issued while the Holy Spirit was judging through the assembled bishops; the accusations by which the bishop’s faith had been attacked were nothing other than the deceptions of slanderers; in the eighth session he had finally emerged victorious over them because his faith had conquered in the fourth; nothing reprobate had thereafter been seen in his case; everything done by the synod in Theodoret’s affair had been approved and confirmed by the Apostolic See; and, finally—which follows from what preceded—apart from the definition of the faith, some of the other things decreed at Chalcedon had also been received and vindicated by Saint Leo, since the most blessed Peter had shown such great care on behalf of the bishops condemned by Dioscorus that, after establishing the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith, he would not permit anything reprobate to appear concerning the person of any one of them.

IX. These matters are so clear that whatever is brought forward against them must necessarily be weak and without force. Nevertheless, the adversaries build a massive argument against these words of Leo from other words of his. “Again and again,” they say, “the pontiff affirms that the holy synod was convened only to extinguish heresy and to confirm the Catholic faith” (Epistle 80, now 106, chapter 2).

“In it,” he says, “I have joined my own judgment with yours, not only through the brothers who acted in my place, but also through the approval of the synodal proceedings, IN THE MATTER OF THE FAITH ALONE, for it must often be said that this was the reason why it pleased the general council to be convened” (Epistle 87, now 114, chapter 1).

From this he draws the following conclusion:

> “If anything is alleged to have been done by these brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place, beyond what pertains to the matter of the faith, it will have absolutely no validity, because they were sent from the Apostolic See solely for this purpose: that, after heresies had been cut away, they should be defenders of the Catholic faith. For whatever is brought before the episcopal tribunal apart from the particular matters of synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication” (Epistle 92, now 119, chapter 5).

From these and similar words of Leo, Pope Pelagius II infers in his letter to the bishops of Istria, and so forth, that Leo, by rejecting the many proceedings concerning particular cases, restricted the authority of the synod to the definition of the faith alone. Later he says:

> “Whatever, therefore, is done apart from the faith, Leo’s teaching shows may be recalled for judgment, since, as he says again, after blessed Leo’s writing grants the right of reconsidering and judging, even if there could have been any authority in private matters belonging to those who were present, it is nullified. Finally, he not only did not in the least confirm the private cases handled there after the definition of the faith, but also permitted them to be reconsidered and judged.”

The same pontiff attempts to prove that the definition of the faith was concluded in the sixth session and that the matter of the faith was thereby finished: first, from the general subscription of all the bishops, which is appended to this session and not to the others; second, from the testimony of the older Greek codices, which confine the whole synod to six sessions, with the canons appended to the sixth and the others omitted, although they are now found in the Latin texts; and finally, from the fact that, once the sixth session had ended, the bishops petitioned the emperor to dismiss them.

These points can easily be dismantled, in my judgment, provided that prejudices are removed. There is, I think, one matter to which the whole difficulty comes down: a single expression, on whose interpretation the entire dispute seems to me to depend—namely, “the matter of the faith.” Because the defenders of the opposing view have narrowed it to a stricter meaning than was proper, they have been forced far from the mind of blessed Leo; indeed, they have set Leo against Leo. Once we have understood what he meant by “the matter of the faith,” light will shine upon this controversy; Leo will be reconciled with Leo; and the path to agreement, which until now has seemed closed to many, will lie open.

The “matter of the faith,” then, for the discussion of which alone Saint Leo writes that the Council of Chalcedon was convened, is not confined to the definition of the faith alone, nor does Saint Leo say that it is confined to that alone. It also includes the examination of the cases and scandals which had arisen on the occasion of the faith and of the Eutychian error that attacked the faith, together with the reconsideration of everything that had been perpetrated at Ephesus through the devices and fury of Dioscorus.

This is the complete matter of the faith. The cases of the persons involved—those, I mean, whose faith had been suspected, accused, condemned, or slanderously defamed—were so closely connected and interwoven with it that, if you remove from the matter of the faith the perfidy and rebellion of Eutyches; the wicked machinations of Dioscorus and the deposition that followed; the condemnation and restoration of Flavian, Eusebius, Theodoret, and the other orthodox bishops, it will already be truncated and mutilated in a large part of itself.

The simple definition of the faith is therefore one thing; the matter of the faith is another, at least in this case. The former consists in the assertion of Catholic truth alone; the latter additionally embraces the condemnation of the heretics who rejected the faith and the acquittal and restoration of Catholics who had been accused, condemned, and deposed by heretics, together with the complete examination of both groups.
