For just as the renunciation of error is not complete if, along with impious doctrines, it does not also condemn their manifest, confessed, or convicted authors, so this defense of the faith is not complete if it does not receive all who think Catholicly; it is not a full assertion if it does not vindicate Catholic bishops who, through the slanders of wicked men, have been brought under suspicion of heresy; and it is not a complete victory if, as our Leo writes concerning Theodoret, anyone were to emerge as no victor from among those whose faith had already conquered (Epistle 93, now 120, chapter 5).

X. This explanation of the matter of the faith, although sufficiently clear in itself, will be shown to be genuine and confirmed still more strongly by Leo’s own letters, some of which he wrote before the synod and others for its reception and confirmation.

When he urgently requested a general synod from the emperor Theodosius, what did he hope it would accomplish? First of all this:

> “That it either repel or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further may remain either doubtful in the faith or divided in charity.”

In addition:

> “That the bishops who, overcome by threats and injuries, had strayed from the path of truth should be recalled to wholeness by salutary remedies.”

Finally:

> “That, with all complaints and prejudices of both parties suspended, everything that had generated offense should be reconsidered more carefully, and that those priests who had been compelled by weakness to subscribe might return to the peace of Christ without injury to the faith and without insult to religion, and that errors alone might be removed” (Epistle 40, now 44, chapter 3).

Who does not see that all these matters concern persons more than the definition of the faith itself? So far from Leo having wished the synod to deal exclusively with the latter, as the adversaries contend, he had instead labored above all, with earnest prayers, to obtain from the emperor that the question of the faith should be left entirely untouched and should not be brought forward again for examination as though it were doubtful.

“Therefore,” he says, “by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the author and ruler of your kingdom, I beseech and implore Your Clemency not to permit the faith which our fathers proclaimed as handed down to them from the apostles to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful” (Epistle 73, now 90, chapter 2).

“Once the audacity of disputing against the divinely inspired faith has been utterly rejected, let the empty unbelief of those who err fall silent” (Epistle 72, [Col. 0749D] now 93, chapter 2).

But the words that follow make it still clearer that the synod was convened more on account of the case of the bishops, with which the faith was intertwined, than on account of the definition of the faith itself, whose integrity could neither be diminished nor augmented. Thus Saint Leo writes in his letter to the Council of Chalcedon itself:

> “Since we are not unaware that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that very many bishops who did not receive heresy have been driven from their sees and deported into exile, while others have been substituted in the place of those who survived, let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds. Let no one be deprived of his own in such a way that another enjoys what belongs to someone else. For if, as we desire, all abandon error, no one ought indeed to lose his own honor; rather, the proper right of those who labored for the faith ought to be restored to them with every privilege” (ibid., chapter 3).

Now, learned reader, you understand that “the matter of the faith” means the case of the bishops who labored for the faith; who, because they did not receive heresy, were driven from their sees and deported into exile; and whom their opponents had stripped of the privilege of honor in order to undermine the Catholic faith and strengthen execrable heresy (Epistle 75, now 95, chapter 2).

No one will deny that Theodoret was one of these, if he remembers that Saint Leo himself adorns him with this same praise (Epistle 93, now 120) and numbers him among those who had labored for the Catholic faith and who emerged victorious while the Holy Spirit was judging, because their faith had already conquered.

You see, moreover, how, after ordering silence concerning the faith, the pontiff wants the sacred synod to apply the medicine of justice first to the wounds of the bishops who had been crushed by the devices and malice of Dioscorus; how he wishes the holy Fathers above all to heal the situation so that no one’s honor might be lost; and how, finally, with the faith left untouched, he desires everything that had generated offense to be reconsidered.

Finally, to add this as the crowning point: when Saint Leo supplicatingly requested from the emperor that an ecumenical synod be convened, he derived its necessity chiefly from the appeal submitted by Flavian. He held, on the basis of the Sardican canons cited under the name of the Nicene canons, that the appeal could neither be annulled nor examined anywhere except in a synod.

All these things show that such episcopal cases belonged to that synod at least no less than the examination of the faith. Who, indeed, would deny that these cases properly belonged to the synod according to the pontiff’s judgment, since he asserted that the synod had to be convened chiefly and FIRST on their account, as is clear from what has been said above? Who would consider that province foreign to the synod, without which the bishops would not be summoned at all, and which, by pressing for action, likewise pressed the necessity of convening the synod?

Saint Leo himself willingly acknowledged that this necessity arose from Flavian’s appeal, in these words:

> “But that this should necessarily be demanded after an appeal has been lodged, the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify, canons established by the priests of the whole world” (Epistle 40, now 44, chapter 3).

From the appeals of the others, and especially of Theodoret, an equal necessity necessarily arose, since he too had been accused, condemned, and deposed; he himself had appealed to the synod; and the canons praised by Leo operated no less in his favor than in Flavian’s. Theodoret shared with Flavian the same cause of the faith, the same labors, and the same sentence of deposition; and Theodoret’s case, because he had survived, was the more urgent.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Compare notes 2 and 3 above (column 739, note b, and column 741, note b).]

Pope Gelasius understood Saint Leo in the same way that Leo understood himself. When he speaks of the matters defined at Chalcedon that are to be received, he never separates what concerns Catholic communion from the definition of the faith. Thus, in Epistle 1 to Euphemius, he says:

> “Therefore, if you truly and certainly follow those things which were defined at the Council of Chalcedon, by apostolic authority, for the faith and Catholic communion,” and so forth.

To prevent anyone from saying that Gelasius wrote this carelessly and without deliberation, the frequent repetition of the same words forbids such a claim, both in the same letter and in others.

In Epistle 13, to the bishops of Dardania, he says:

> “As for the blessed Pope Leo himself, bishop of the Apostolic See, whose authority established the Council of Chalcedon: whatever, beyond what had been delegated by him as something to be done there for the faith and Catholic and apostolic communion, appeared to have been attempted on the occasion of that assembly through a new action contrary to the Nicene canons, he nullified by an appropriate refutation.”

Here Leo rejects only Anatolius’s maneuvering on behalf of his own see, supposedly confirmed by Canon 28, as Gelasius, his successor, testifies—he who lived in the same age. In the treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*, likewise, immediately at the beginning, when he answers the objection of the adversaries of the Council of Chalcedon—“If the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything must be accepted”—he replies that the council is undoubtedly accepted by the whole Church, with the sole exceptions of those things which were brought forward, or rather debated, there through incompetent presumption; things which the Apostolic See had in no way delegated to be carried out, as is made clear by the fact that they were immediately opposed by the vicars of the Apostolic See; things which the Apostolic See did not approve even when the emperor Marcian requested it; things which Anatolius, then bishop of the Church of Constantinople, did not claim to have presumed, and which he did not deny lay within the power of the bishop of the Apostolic See. For this reason, as has been said, the Apostolic See does not receive them, because it in no way tolerates things proved to be contrary to the privileges of the universal Church.

There is nothing here that does not concern Anatolius’s dispute with Leo, or Canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon, the one canon he rejects among all the things decreed in that synod. As for the episcopal cases that were sanctioned, he is far from rejecting them; rather, he approves them as matters defined for the faith and Catholic communion by apostolic authority.

XI. Alongside what we have said, the following words written later by our Leo should be weighed as though on a balance. Speaking of the acts of the synod which he had received, he says that, both through his brothers who acted in his place and through his approval of the synodal proceedings, he had joined his own judgment with that of the Fathers of Chalcedon IN THE MATTER OF THE FAITH ALONE, for which reason it had pleased the general council to be convened.

If, then, the synod was convened for the matter of the faith alone, and if afterward only those things defined in the matter of the faith were received, it follows with complete certainty that everything we said above concerning the bishops to be examined in the synod—and especially Theodoret’s case—was contained within the matter of the faith. For Leo wished these matters to be dealt with FIRST by the Fathers, and it is clear that in Theodoret’s case above all he joined his own judgment with that of the synod. In that case, God’s invincible truth showed Theodoret, according to the judgment of the Apostolic See, to be cleansed from every stain of heresy (Epistle 93, now 120, chapter 5), after the judgment of the Apostolic See had been established in the definition of the faith; nor was anything reprobate permitted to appear concerning him, who was laboring for the Catholic faith.

The case of Theodoret and of the other bishops was therefore among the particular cases of the synodal council, and for that reason the sentence of the entire synod, after the case had duly been brought before its examination, was concluded while the Holy Spirit was judging (ibid., chapter 5). Thus, in the victory of truth, only the authors of violated faith perished, while the integrity of the Church was restored.

> “So that, with Christ triumphant, there might also be one victory for all the priests, and, with the light of truth shining forth, only the darkness of error and its advocates might be driven away” (Epistle 78, now 104, chapter 1).

If, therefore, anything that the synod had done and defined was rescinded and rejected by Leo, it was certainly not what concerned either the condemnation of heretics or the restoration of orthodox bishops. That was inseparably joined to the faith. It was only what Anatolius was said to have attempted in order to enlarge the Constantinopolitan see: that privilege, whose furtive definition Leo’s legates had opposed and which undermined the ancient privileges of the other greater sees.

Let all the letters Leo wrote on this matter after the synod had ended be read.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] Leo, writing in Epistle 119 to Maximus, who had complained that the three Palestinian provinces had been taken away to the prejudice of his see, says in chapter 5: “If anything is alleged to have been done by those brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place beyond what pertains to the matter of the faith, it will have absolutely no validity.” In writing this, he indicates that he did not approve some action which, as the context shows, the legates were alleged to have undertaken and approved contrary to the Nicene canons. The legates openly opposed the canon enacted for the see of Constantinople. They assented only to the settlement between Maximus and Juvenal, and Saint Leo appears in that same place to criticize this settlement as contrary to the Nicene canons. See more on this matter in Observation 9. Therefore, Leo rejected nothing whatever besides Canon 28.]

Nothing else will be found to have been rejected or condemned by him apart from that twenty-eighth canon, by which new privileges were established for the imperial city. That canon was wholly foreign to the matter of the faith; it had been enacted furtively; and it had been condemned by the judgment of the Apostolic See even before it was enacted. For when legates were sent from that see to the synod, they were expressly instructed not to permit such a question to be debated in the council at all.

“If any men,” says the pontiff, “trusting in the splendor of their cities, should attempt to usurp something for themselves, repel this with the firmness it deserves” (Act 16 of the Council of Chalcedon), as the presbyter Boniface, one of the legates, read from the document in the sixteenth session of the council.

It therefore happened that Saint Leo always resisted the authors and supporters of this canon with the greatest firmness, and could never be induced by the petitions either of the emperor or of his own legates [Note: [Col. 0752D] The legates sent by Leo opposed it. Only Julian, who had been added to the legates, interceded with the pontiff on behalf of the privilege of the Constantinopolitan see; for that reason he is criticized in Epistle 107.] to approve what he believed had been done contrary to the constitutions of the holy Fathers.

XII. As for the claim that the synod ended in the sixth session, and that this is clear from the Greek codices, I reply that the testimony of those Greek codices is Greek: for all the editions of this council, both Greek and Latin, which are now in everyone’s hands, whether printed or written by hand, represent the whole and complete synod as consisting of sixteen sessions.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Compare note 18 (column 257, note b) in Quesnellus’s first dissertation, under the year 451.]

We are also persuaded that there were not fewer sessions in antiquity, in the time of the emperor Justinian and Pope Vigilius, from the ancient codices of the monastery of the Acoemetae. At that time Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church—made famous by the controversy over the Three Chapters—carefully revised the acts of the council for those codices. If matters had been otherwise, many of the adversaries would not have failed to accuse him as an impostor.

Among ancient codices of this kind, a notable one is that of Jean Boherius, senator of Dijon, which Pierre-François Chifflet praised at the end of Vigilius of Thapsus, and whose variant readings his editors, Philippe Labbe and Gabriel Cossart, presented in the latest edition of the Councils.

But we also have a strong argument from the Roman Church itself, by which the same number of sessions may be asserted for that synod. Dionysius Exiguus, in the book of canons which the Roman Church adopted toward the end of the fifth century, inserted the twenty-seven canons of the Council of Chalcedon. Yet it is established that these were promulgated only in the final session of all; and he omitted the twenty-eighth because it alone had been enacted without the knowledge and consent of the Apostolic See and had been rejected by Leo as wholly contrary to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] We have shown this to be false in the aforementioned note 18 (column 257, note b) to the first dissertation.]

Our older codex agrees with that of Dionysius.

The remaining objections ordinarily brought against our position need not detain us longer here, since they have almost no force or importance. I shall add one point that supports Theodoret’s case: when the Three Chapters are under discussion, one must not speak of Theodoret in the same way as of the others. His condition appears to me far better than theirs, for they earned and received no such praise and commendation from the ecumenical synod, the Roman pontiff, or the emperor as Theodoret earned and received.

The emperor expressly declared that Theodoret had been acquitted and praised by the ecumenical synod in the edict he issued after the council in favor of Flavian. Leo himself also sent him an outstanding letter, almost every part of which commends his faith and the labors he had undertaken for the faith and the Church, and asserts that he had been rendered free from every suspicion concerning the faith by invincible truth and by the Holy Spirit. Nothing of this kind was ever written by either authority concerning the others.

Leo’s letter is readily found among the others. The edict of the emperor Valentinian, by which he annulled and rendered void the constitution of Theodosius and approved the decree of the synod in favor of the bishops Flavian, Eusebius, and Theodoret, reads as follows:

> “Let that constitution be abolished which is known to have been enacted, through the deceit of wicked men, against Flavian of holy memory after his death; and let everything cease which took its origin from injustice. Let no unjust sentence harm either Eusebius or Theodoret, the most religious bishops, whom that enactment includes, because bishops whom a synodal decree has honored for the preservation of the faith cannot be condemned by an imperial constitution.”

We preferred to transcribe this constitution from the version of Johannes Leunclavius, which he inserted in his notes on the Novels first published at that time at the end of the book *ΒΑΣΙΛΙΚΩΝ JURIS ROMANI* [*Basilica of Roman Law*], Basel, A.D. 1575, because it corresponds more closely to the Greek text than the version found among the acts of Chalcedon, part III. There the words *ἐπὶ τῇ φυλακῇ τῇ τῆς πίστεως* (“for the preservation of the faith”) are not rendered sufficiently explicitly, whether through the scribes’ negligence or by design, I do not know.

This I do know: Theodoret’s case is greatly strengthened by the fact that the emperor indissolubly joins it to the cases of Flavian, the martyr of Christ, and Eusebius, the leaders of those who fought against the Eutychian heresy, in the preservation of the faith.

From this it also follows that Theodoret was restored not merely because he had been deposed by Dioscorus through the predatory violence of a false synod, but also because his faith had shone forth splendidly; because on account of it he had deserved to be adorned with praises by the ecumenical synod; and because in its preservation he had always remained steadfast and unshaken.

These words in defense of so great a prelate are sufficient.

**OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI ON QUESNELLUS’S TENTH DISSERTATION, ON THE CASE OF THEODORET, BISHOP OF CYRUS**

[Col. 0753]

1257 1. After the principles established in the observations on the preceding dissertations, it will be easy to resolve the matters relating to Theodoret’s case and appeal. It cannot be denied that he appealed to the pontiff Leo after being deposed at the Ephesian Robber Synod, except by someone who, hostile to appeals to the Roman See, attempts to twist the clear evidence concerning Theodoret’s appeal in another direction.

Among other things, his own words in Epistle 92 to Leo, chapter 5, are unmistakable:

> “I beg and beseech Your Holiness that your upright and just tribunal may lend aid to me who am ἐπικαλούμενῳ (*epikaloumenō*, appealing), and that it may order me to come to you and demonstrate my teaching, which adheres to the apostolic footsteps.”

Unjustly deposed at the Ephesian false synod under the charge of heresy, he appeals to Leo and desires to appear before his tribunal, so that judgment may be rendered concerning his teaching.

2. In order to suppress this appeal, Quesnellus abuses the common Latin translation, in which *invocanti* (“to one calling upon”) was rendered for *appellanti* (“to one appealing”). He explains the passage as though Theodoret, in these words, had not lodged a genuine appeal before Leo, but had merely requested Leo’s judgment as to whether there was a place for an appeal.

We have shown by other examples that the Greek verb ἐπικαλέομαι (*epikaleomai*) is frequently used in the sense of appealing to a superior judge; see Note 6 on the same letter, column 947 (vol. I, column 851, note a).

Theodoret does indeed state that he is awaiting Leo’s decision as to whether he would accept the appeal. But he begs and beseeches him to accept it, and presents himself as ready, if the appeal is accepted, to submit to judgment and prove his faith.

The assistance he implores from Leo consists in this: that, after accepting the appeal, Leo should order him to come to Rome, where judgment concerning his teaching would be instituted.

He wrote in the same sense to Renatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, in Epistle 116:

> “For this reason I beg Your Holiness to persuade the most holy and most blessed archbishop to exercise his apostolic authority and order me to hasten to your council, in which judgment may be rendered concerning my case.”

Here he understands “council” not as the council of the whole West but as the Roman council, which was customarily convened in such more serious cases, as we observed in the observations on Dissertation 8, concerning Flavian’s case, section 6. Even so, in those synods—and especially in the appeals of Eastern bishops—the right and greater authority belonged to the Roman bishop by reason of the primacy, as we proved there in sections 7 and following.

This is made clear by the letter to Renatus just cited. Immediately after the words “to hasten to your council,” he adds the following reason, which points to what is proper to the Roman See alone, namely, the pontifical primacy and its prerogative:

> “For that most holy see holds primacy over the Churches throughout the whole world in many respects; and, before all these, because it has remained free from heretical contamination, no one who thought otherwise has sat there, and it has preserved apostolic grace intact.”

Then Theodoret adds:

> “Whatever you judge, we shall accept it, whatever it may be, trusting in the equity of your judgment; and we ask that you establish the judgment from the written evidence.”

These words, omitted by Quesnellus, overturn all his quibbling. For they make clear that Theodoret did not merely implore Leo’s protection, but sought through an appeal a genuine judgment.

Since the right and rationale of this judgment are referred to the primacy—that is, to the pontifical primacy—and to other prerogatives proper to the Roman See and to the pontiff himself, not shared with other bishops of the Roman synod, it now becomes evident that Theodoret’s appeal was directed in itself to the Roman pontiff. The Roman council was mentioned only for the reason that we explained in the case of Flavian.

### 3.

Furthermore, there is nothing surprising if that same Theodoret sent a circular letter to Bishop Florentius, or even to the other bishops of the Roman synod, as P. Garnerius conjectured in Dissertation 2 on Letter 117. Nor should it cause any difficulty that, in Letter 119, sent to Anatolius the patrician at Constantinople, he asked him to intercede with the emperor so that he might be permitted to come to the West and be judged by those “most beloved of God and most holy bishops.” He means the bishops of the Roman synod. Yet these bishops had no jurisdiction in the appeal of an Eastern bishop except together with the Roman pontiff. The pontiff himself, however, even without the other bishops, could not be denied such jurisdiction on account of his primacy. See the observations in Dissertation 5, Part I, chapter 7, and in Dissertation 8, no. 10.

Moreover, since according to the custom of those times this jurisdiction was not ordinarily exercised by the pontiffs except in a Roman synod—at which the other bishops of the suburban diocese, as well as those who happened to be present at Rome from elsewhere, assembled—this explains why Theodoret mentions such a council and its bishops, and why letters were addressed to them also. Those references, nevertheless, neither restrict nor exclude the pontiff’s personal jurisdiction. Since these facts establish Theodoret’s appeal to Leo, they likewise establish that the pontifical right of hearing appeals is especially confirmed by the example of this Eastern and most learned bishop.

### 4.

What the holy pontiff did after receiving these letters from Theodoret must now be explained. Leo recalls the judgment of the Apostolic See in Letter 120, chapter 5:

> “Blessed is our God, whose unconquerable truth has shown you, cleansed from every stain of heresy, according to the judgment of the Apostolic See.”

The judges at the Council of Chalcedon, in Act 1, attributed his restoration to this judgment:

> “Let the most reverend Bishop Theodoret enter, so that he may take part in the synod, because the most holy Archbishop Leo has restored his episcopate to him.”

When the same matter was treated in Act 8, where some had raised doubts about his faith, Theodoret, in order to prove his faith, pronounced an anathema against Nestorius. The judges then asked the Fathers to give sentence in favor of Theodoret, so that he might recover his Church, “just as the most holy Archbishop Leo also judged.” The Fathers, agreeing with them, said:

> “Theodoret is worthy of his see … After God, Leo judged.”

There can therefore be no doubt about Leo’s judgment. The fact that the judges and Fathers at the Council of Chalcedon attributed this judgment to Leo also confirms the appeal directed to him.

### 5.

Quesnellus, attempting to diminish this judgment of Leo—which concerns not merely procedure but the substance of the case—argues in no. 4 that the holy pontiff conducted no examination and issued no sentence concerning Theodoret’s case. Since the proceedings of the pseudo-Ephesine council, by which Theodoret had been deposed, were already invalid in themselves, Leo merely remained united with him, as the actual bishop of Cyrus, in uninterrupted communion. Leo replied to Theodoret’s letters that he need not abide by the judgment already given, nor await another judgment, in order to govern his Church in the customary manner. Quesnellus believes that the expression “the judgment of the Apostolic See,” used in these letters of apostolic communion, must be understood in this broad sense.

### 6.

Tillemont himself, however—otherwise an admirer and in many respects even a follower of Quesnellus—thought this opinion should be refuted in note 12 on the Life of Theodoret. He considers it probable that, after receiving Theodoret’s letters and messengers—if indeed they were able to reach Rome—or some other document bearing his signature, in which Theodoret expressly anathematized Nestorius and had subscribed the pontiff’s dogmatic letter to Flavian, Saint Leo found his case sufficiently clear to judge him and declare him innocent without convening a Roman synod.

Leo’s single prior ruling against the proceedings of the Ephesian robber council does not seem sufficient in view of what has been handed down concerning this matter. For the word “judgment,” which Leo and the Council of Chalcedon use in the passages quoted, and the restoration of the episcopate attributed to Leo’s authority, signify something particular concerning Theodoret. A general ruling that the proceedings of the pseudo-Ephesine council were invalid establishes nothing especially in Theodoret’s favor, any more than in favor of Sabinianus and Ibas, who had likewise been deposed by those proceedings. Nevertheless, when the same Council of Chalcedon later dealt with the restoration of those two bishops, neither the judges, nor the Fathers, nor the legates of the pontiff said that Leo had restored them on the strength of that prior ruling, or that Leo had judged their cases.

Since, therefore, this was pronounced only concerning Theodoret, account was not taken merely of Leo’s judgment by which he had declared the aforementioned proceedings invalid. It must instead be said that there had been a particular and express judgment of the pontiff concerning Theodoret. Thus far we have argued from Tillemont.

### 7.

Whether the holy pontiff convened a synod for this purpose—a synod that could easily have been assembled at least from the bishops then present at Rome—cannot be affirmed or denied. The evident proofs of Theodoret’s faith required no lengthy examination; nor was a synod needed for a true and legitimate judgment concerning his appeal, whose force, as we have already shown, depended upon apostolic authority and primacy.

Nevertheless, it seems that knowledge of this appeal, together with suitable documents concerning Theodoret’s faith, reached Rome only later—namely, after Paschasinus and Boniface, the legates, had already departed for the synod that had been summoned. Hence Leo’s judgment concerning Theodoret was issued after their departure. The holy pontiff wrote to those same legates that Theodoret had therefore been received into communion. He would not have needed to inform them of this by letter if he had made the judgment while they were still at Rome and had not yet departed.

Thus those legates said in Act 8:

> “The most holy and blessed Leo, bishop of the city of Rome and bishop of the universal Church, received the most holy and venerable Bishop Theodoret into communion long ago”—in Greek, πάλαι (*palai*), which appears to refer even to a relatively recent time, as is evident also from Letter 22 of Saint Flavian—“as the letters sent by him to our humility testify.”

### 8.

The great caution with which the holy pontiff received into communion those who labored under some suspicion of heresy is made clear by the conditions he required before granting communion to Anatolius of Constantinople. It was well known that Theodoret had once favored Nestorius and had attacked the anathemas of Saint Cyril. For this reason he had been deposed at the Council of Ephesus. His deposition could therefore appear just so long as Theodoret’s faith had not been examined through reliable documents and a legitimate judgment.

Saint Leo could not, lest he appear more severe toward those suspected of Eutychian heresy and more lenient and accommodating toward those accused of Nestorianism, grant communion to Theodoret without subjecting his faith and teaching to examination and establishing from examined documents that he was no less opposed to Nestorian heresy than to Eutychian heresy.

But when these documents were delivered to Leo after the legates’ departure and made Theodoret’s orthodoxy sufficiently clear in itself, while the time for the already summoned general synod was pressing and Theodoret was also required by imperial decree to attend it, the holy pontiff did not think that he should summon Theodoret to Rome, as Theodoret had requested. Rather, judging him innocent and unjustly deposed, and recognizing him as the true bishop of Cyrus, he granted him apostolic communion. Writing to his legates about this, he ordered that Theodoret should likewise be received by them and by the council.

For this reason Theodoret was received immediately in the first session, because “the most holy Archbishop Leo had restored his episcopate to him.” This could have become known either from the letters mentioned above to the legates or from other letters previously communicated privately to Theodoret himself.

### 9.

If, nevertheless, the council dealt with Theodoret in Act 8, this seems to have happened for two reasons.

First, it was necessary to satisfy those who doubted his faith and accused him of Nestorianism. Was not Leo’s own dogmatic Letter 28 to Flavian likewise discussed in that synod, in Acts 2 and 4, so that those who doubted might be instructed and brought to sound doctrine? If that examination was permitted for this beneficial purpose without prejudice to apostolic authority—as Leo himself declared in the same Letter 120 to Theodoret, chapter 1, on which see note 14 (previous volume, column 1048, line 1)—then an examination of Theodoret’s faith could likewise have been permitted without prejudice to apostolic authority, since its sole purpose was to satisfy those who doubted it and perhaps thought that something had been foisted upon Leo.

Just as, in the case of Leo’s dogmatic letter, the result of the examination contributed to the greater glory of God when its correct meaning was explained to those who misunderstood it because they lacked proficiency in Latin—for, as the holy pontiff says in the cited passage, the faith previously taught through Leo was subsequently confirmed by this examination—so the renewed examination of Theodoret produced a favorable result. For in the synod he openly anathematized both Nestorius and Eutyches, and “unconquerable truth showed him, cleansed from every stain of heresy, according to the judgment of the Apostolic See.” Consequently, he was restored to his see according to Leo’s judgment, from whom everyone knew that nothing had been concealed or foisted upon him:

> “Theodoret is worthy of his see … After God, Leo judged.”

Who could condemn the council’s examination, which sought the unanimity of the Fathers’ judgment with the pontifical judgment, so that the members might remain united to the head? Who would regard it as an insult to the head rather than as the most obedient response to it? Who, with Quesnellus, would therefore dream that the Council of Chalcedon treated Theodoret’s case as though it had not already been brought before another tribunal?

Does it not rather follow from what has been said that the pontifical judgment was so fully taken into account at that synod that Theodoret was immediately received on account of Leo’s judgment, and that, when the council later brought him forward in a session merely to refute his adversaries, that same judgment served as the basis and rule of the synodal sentence?

### 10.

The second reason, however, which we have undertaken to present, will overturn the Quesnellian fiction still more decisively. This general synod had been summoned by the emperor especially so that the bishops deposed and exiled by the Ephesian robber council might recover their episcopates and their own Churches through the approval and sentence of the synod and of all the assembled bishops. The Empress Pulcheria wrote this to Leo himself in Letter 77.

The holy pontiff, agreeing with the plan of the most meritorious emperors, had already sent legates to the synod and had addressed a letter to that same synod, in which he ordered that those bishops be restored. See Letter 93, chapter 3.

Under these circumstances, after receiving the documents concerning Theodoret, Leo judged the case that had been brought before the Apostolic See by appeal and received Theodoret into communion. As we have seen, he thereby restored him to his see by restoring his legal status. Nevertheless, the actual restoration still remained to be completed. Since this could appear to have been entrusted to the synod, it was decreed there in accordance with the apostolic judgment by Leo’s legates themselves and by the whole council. See Act 8.

Thus, in this action concerning Theodoret, the Council of Chalcedon followed Leo’s judgment and decreed, in a certain sense, the actual restoration that had been entrusted to it. If, therefore, Theodoret’s case was settled by that synod solely on the basis of Leo’s judgment, Quesnellus acted improperly in daring to claim that the council took no account of that judgment.

## ELEVENTH DISSERTATION

### On the spuriousness of the letter forged in the name of Pope Leo I to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi, or presbyters; this letter is number 88 in earlier editions

[Col. 0757]

### I.

Some may think that demonstrating and laboriously establishing the spuriousness of Letter 88 of Saint Leo, as it appears in all the editions published until now, is the work of an idle man, since most scholars already deny this product to Leo. Nevertheless, I considered it my duty to call the matter once more before the tribunal of examination and to discuss it, both lest I seem rashly to have removed that letter from the number of genuine works, and because there are in fact several writers—even men of the highest reputation in this age—who have not thought that the letter should be counted among the forged documents.

Among these are Franciscus Hallerius and Ludovicus Cellotius, each in his work on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy; Petrus Aurelius, writing against Sirmondus; Dionysius Petavius, in his notes on Saint Epiphanius; Petrus de Marca, On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire, Book II, chapter 13; and several others. On the other hand, it is rejected as spurious not only by the heterodox David Blondellus, in his *Pseudo-Isidore under the Lash*, but also by Joannes Morinus, a priest of the Oratory, and Jacobus Sirmondus, S.J., both of them conspicuous throughout the scholarly world for their learning.

The first criterion (*κριτήριον*, “test”) of its spuriousness is that this letter does not appear in any of the oldest manuscript codices, but only in certain more recent manuscripts copied after the period of the Isidorian collection. This is evidence that it was taken from that collection; otherwise it would scarcely, if at all, be possible for so famous a letter of so great a pontiff, concerning a matter of such importance, written to all the Churches of Gaul and Germany, to have lain buried under the unanimous silence of the ancient codices—especially since several copies would doubtless have been made by bishops of both those regions.

### 2.

There is no ancient writer who even mentions the smallest portion of this letter. Although this would not be surprising in the case of what are called familiar letters, it is entirely unusual in the case of letters called Decretals, which contain many matters of ecclesiastical discipline affecting the whole state and governance of the Church.

No collector of canons or pontifical decrees inserted it into his collections. I mean those who flourished before Isidore Mercator, that is, before the ninth century.

[Note: In the pure manuscripts of Isidore, such as Vatican Codex 630, this letter is not found; it therefore cannot be attributed to Isidore. Apart from the Leonine collections 11, 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24, it is found only in the Additions to the Isidorian collection preserved in the manuscripts of Collection 12, to which Vatican Codex 1340 belongs. Merlin published this Collection 12. Quesnellus, however, who by the name “Isidorian edition” means Merlin’s edition, did not distinguish the Additions from Isidore, and, attributing this letter to Isidore, ascribed it to him.]

Isidore included the letter among the letters of Leo, either because he himself was deceived or because he intended to deceive others. Yet it is not found in his collection in the form in which it was later published. He presents it with an enlargement consisting of a huge patch, which was inserted into the commonly printed edition of Leo’s Letter 87—now Letter 12—to the bishops of Africa in Caesarean Mauretania.

[Note: This patch, which contains the final part of chapter 9 and the three remaining chapters of the genuine Letter 12 of Leo to the bishops of Mauretania, is attached to the spurious letter concerning chorepiscopi only in the manuscripts of Collection 12, among the Isidorian Additions, which should not be attributed to Isidore.]

From these pieces, sewn together as though a horse’s neck had been attached to a human head, there emerges a monstrous, shapeless, and ridiculous sort of letter.

### 3.

Its style is utterly unlike Leo’s and has nothing even remotely akin to his polish. The narrowness of the letter itself also betrays the writer’s childishness. On a matter of such importance, our Leo would have sent a more extended work, complete in every respect, for his eloquence never deserted him in such affairs.

### 4.

The title itself exposes the forgery of this patch. It says:

> “Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and of the Apostolic See, sends greetings to all the bishops of Germany and Gaul.”

Yet Leo never called himself “bishop of the Roman Church,” but rather “of Rome,” “of the city of Rome,” or “of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome,” even though interpolated editions present the matter differently. Nor did he ever describe himself as “bishop of the Apostolic See” in any edition.

Finally, he never wrote either to the bishops of Germany or to the bishops of Germany and Gaul together. That combination reflects the age of Charlemagne or a later period. The practice of joining these two nations together never became established before the second dynasty of our kings; it began only then, when the empire was administered by the kings of the Franks.

### 5.

The opening words reveal the forger’s ignorance and the novelty of the document. In describing a synod held at Rome, he calls it a synod “assembled from bishops, or the other fellow priests, and the faithful of Christ.”

First, who would believe that the lay populace was admitted at that time to a council convened to regulate and decide ecclesiastical affairs? Moreover, since by “the other fellow priests” he plainly means presbyters distinguished from bishops, the writer was unaware that the title “priest” was not ordinarily applied to presbyters except by authors later than Leo; during the first centuries of the Church it had been reserved for bishops. If it was sometimes granted to presbyters, it was never without an added qualification: “of the second order,” “of the second place,” “of the second rank,” and so forth.

Finally, who cannot see that the ugly solecism “an assembled synod” could never have been committed by a writer whose native language was Latin? The fault cannot be attributed to the carelessness of printers, for all the ancient copies—whether manuscripts or printed editions of Canisius, Merlin, Sicardus, Crabbus, the Louvain edition, and even the Roman edition, Volume I of the Letters of the Pontiffs—have the same reading. This reading is common to all of them.

### 6.

We never read that Roman pontiffs, whether contemporary with Leo or earlier, cited any canons other than the Nicene or those of Sardica, which were treated as Nicene. Innocent I explicitly says that no others should be received, as we have noted elsewhere. Nor, before the Council of Chalcedon, were the decrees of particular synods—although some of those synods had already been incorporated into the Roman codex—received as authoritative in most of the Churches of the Western regions.

The authority of the canons of Neocaesarea, presented as though they had already been received by almost the whole Church, therefore shows that the writer was later than Leo. For Saint Leo never happened to cite any canons other than the Nicene ones.

[Note: He means the book of canons, which we shall publish in Volume III, and we shall prove that it is not the Roman collection. Similarly, in the following number 7, when he mentions the ancient version of the Neocaesarean canon, he indicates the version of that same codex and collection. Since he believes this to be the Roman collection, he declares that it was then in use at Rome.]

### 7.

The thirteenth Neocaesarean canon cited in this letter was not taken from the ancient version then in use at Rome, but from the translation of Dionysius, which everyone knows to be much later than Leo. For the words found in it—“chorepiscopi were instituted as an example and model of the seventy”—are Dionysius’s words; his translation can also be detected in other passages.

### 8.

It is evident from the book that Rabanus Maurus wrote on chorepiscopi to Drogo, Bishop of Metz, that the letter written in Leo’s name against chorepiscopi was not yet known in his time. He would never have undertaken to defend the cause of chorepiscopi if he had read their condemnation as proceeding from the Apostolic See and had possessed a letter of so great a pontiff. Such a letter certainly could not have escaped a man so learned and one who was living in Germany, where the letter is said to have been sent.

Or, if he could not conceal it, he would at least have attempted to draw it toward a favorable meaning and explain away an authority of such importance, just as he took care to explain the decree of Pope Gelasius I and the canons of the Councils of Ancyra and Antioch, lest they should appear to harm the cause he was defending.

Finally, if the letter had then been in everyone’s hands, with what confidence could he have written these words?

> “I therefore wonder,” he says, “how those who stir up this controversy despise the order of chorepiscopi so greatly that they attribute to them scarcely anything more in dignity than to presbyters, although this agrees neither with the new nor with the ancient teaching, nor even with the doctrines and customs of the apostles themselves, but differs from them both in meaning and in doctrine.”

How easily Rabanus could have been convicted of falsehood from Saint Leo’s letter, if that letter had then existed, and could have been shown that Leo, the most ancient bishop of the City, attributed to chorepiscopi not merely scarcely anything more in dignity than to presbyters, but nothing at all beyond what was given to presbyters. The alleged author of the letter, speaking in Leo’s name, asserts from the Neocaesarean canons and the decrees of other Fathers that both groups bore the same form and that chorepiscopi and presbyters were the same.

### 9.

That letter is nothing other than the seventh canon of the Second Council of Seville, transferred word for word, as Blondellus and Morinus have already observed. To make the canon appear in the form of a letter, the forger prefixed an utterly foolish and crude introduction, unworthy not only of Leo, so eloquent a pontiff, but of any sensible man.

And, so that no embellishment of his story might be lacking, that compiler added at the end a certain patch.

[Note: Compare note 2 above, column 758, line b.]

This patch is still read attached to the fragment in Merlin’s Isidorian collection. Through an even worse error, however, the editors of the more recent editions of Saint Leo’s works transferred it into his letter to the African bishops, formerly Letter 87.

Yet fraud is usually insufficient by itself unless assisted by another fraud. The forger therefore sought the appearance of authenticity in a corruption of the canon. The Fathers of Seville had spoken only of presbyters, but the words “or chorepiscopi” were added three times to the canon. This is contrary both to the ancient and genuine copies from which Garsias Loaysa published this council of Seville and to the meaning of the canon itself.

[Note: This canon of the Second Council of Seville was published in two forms. First Merlin published it from a manuscript of Collection 12, which accepted not a few arbitrary corrections and several additions to the documents. Later Loaysa published it from the pure codices of the Spanish collection, which know nothing of those corrections and additions. The readings that Quesnellus attached to the margin of the canon in the earlier edition are rightly to be regarded as additions or corrections foreign to the authentic canon. Several sentences from this same Seville canon were also inserted into the pseudo-letter of Damasus to the bishops of Numidia concerning chorepiscopi, which is found in Isidore; Quesnellus cites them in the margin alongside the canon.]

The synod’s Fathers were not even thinking of chorepiscopi; they were deciding only concerning presbyters, against Agapius, formerly Bishop of Córdoba, who had been brought before the synod because he frequently delegated presbyters to perform episcopal functions—namely ordinations, confirmation, and the consecration of basilicas. It was obvious that all these functions belonged exclusively to bishops.

On this occasion the synod renewed the ancient canonical statutes forbidding presbyters to dare to usurp any ministry belonging to episcopal jurisdiction. Since no dispute had arisen about chorepiscopi, however, not even a syllable concerning them appears in the synod’s decree.

Finally, these final words of the canon contain another point of interpolation:

> “All these things are known to have been forbidden to them by the Apostolic See.”

The Loaysan edition reveals that these words are spurious. They were added either from a learned person’s marginal annotation comparing the forged fragment of the letter with the canon, or with the purpose of obtaining support for the letter from the authority of the interpolated canon.

We present both the letter and the canon to the reader’s eyes at the end of the volume in the appendix, so that, comparing one with the other, the reader may judge without another person’s preconceived opinion.

An egg is not more like an egg than this letter is like the Seville canon, if Agapius is replaced with the bishops of Germany and Gaul and the introduction is excepted. That introduction was taken either from Letter 4 or 9—whether genuine or fictitious—of Pope Agapetus II to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, or, rather, the author of both documents copied part of it from Saint Leo’s letter to the African bishops and added part from his own invention.

### 10.

The following will also establish the letter’s spuriousness: it not only twists the words of the synod against chorepiscopi, although the synod was restraining presbyters alone, but also imputes to numerous bishops of Germany and Gaul what the council’s Fathers had written about one man, Agapius of Córdoba—namely, that they were men ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline and had been transferred immediately from secular military service to priestly ministry.

Would anyone readily believe this of so many bishops merely because it may have happened to one or two? Nor would such a claim be consistent with the condition of the Churches of Gaul, which in Leo’s time observed an even stricter discipline than the Roman Church.

### 11.

If this letter is genuinely Leo’s work, how did it happen that, in the many synods celebrated by the bishops of Gaul and Germany against chorepiscopi, the authority of so great a pontiff was never brought forward?

Why do pontiffs remain silent about it in their decrees, and emperors in their capitularies, where chorepiscopi are frequently mentioned—for example, in the Sixth Council of Paris and the Council of Meaux, in the capitularies of the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, and in the letter of Pope Nicholas I to Rodulfus, Archbishop of Bourges?

The unanimous silence of all these witnesses loudly proclaims that the letter is forged. It could not have escaped them, and no one would believe that they failed to recognize how much force their definitions would have gained from the authority of so great and so ancient a pontiff.

### 12.

There are several things in this letter that cannot be reconciled with the custom of the Roman Church. When it decrees that presbyters may not, while the bishop is present, teach the people, bless or greet them, or even exhort the congregation, it assumes that all these things were permitted to presbyters at least in the bishop’s absence.

Yet it is certain that throughout the fifth century no one in the Roman Church other than the Roman bishop performed the office of teacher and preacher. In the Western regions this function was reserved to episcopal dignity, including in our Gallican Churches, until the twenty-ninth year of the following century, when the Council of Vaison—whether the Second or the Third—began to permit it to presbyters for the good of the Church.

What “blessing the people” means in this passage can scarcely be explained.

But what, above all, is meant by these words?

> “Nor is it permitted to presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of the bishop, or, when the bishop is present, to immerse or sign the child.”

As for the opening words, were presbyters not rather required to enter the baptistery with the bishop and, as part of their office, to attend the bishop as he baptized? Some think that *coram* (“in the presence of”) is used here for *ante* (“before”), so that the words of the letter should be reduced to the meaning of canon 53 in Martin of Braga:

> “A presbyter may not enter the baptistery before the bishop, but only with the bishop—unless perhaps the bishop is absent or ill.”

This is a good interpretation, and light is properly drawn upon it both from that canon and from the custom of the Spanish Church, as well as from another canon of that same Church.

But nothing of the kind is ever read concerning the Roman Church. Still less can I believe that the highly eloquent pontiff Leo, writing at Rome and thoroughly familiar with the Roman language, could have used the word *coram* so barbarously as to force it into a meaning entirely foreign to it and never employed by any author.

That Spaniards used the word in this way around the year 619, when the Second Council of Seville is thought to have been held, will surprise no one, since their language had then been infected by many faults through association and intercourse with barbarians. But such usage is unbelievable of Romans.

For this reason, the person who forged another letter to Pope Damasus on the same subject of chorepiscopi changed the word *coram* in the Seville canon into *ante*, so that nothing foreign to Roman usage or ritual would appear to be attributed to a Roman pontiff.

As for the letter’s author writing that:

> “Presbyters may not, when the bishop is present, immerse or sign the child,”

I confess that I do not know how this can be understood.

Whatever is forbidden in the bishop’s presence is implicitly permitted in his absence or with his consent. But it was especially foreign to the practice of the Roman Church that presbyters should have the power to sign those who had been baptized. This is clear from even one passage of Pope Innocent.

He says:

> “Whether they baptize outside the presence of the bishop or in the bishop’s presence, presbyters may anoint the baptized with chrism, but with chrism consecrated by the bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that oil, since this belongs to bishops alone, when they confer the Holy Spirit.”  
> (*Letter 1 to Decentius, chapter 3*)

Indeed, the earlier part of the letter itself forbids this to presbyters:

> “Nor are they permitted … to sign the foreheads of the baptized with chrism.”

[Note: On this matter see more, if desired, in P. Coustant’s note c on Letter 25 of Innocent I to Decentius, Volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, column 808.]

Nevertheless, since the same words that we have noted in this letter also occur in the Seville council, even in the more carefully corrected codices, they must be explained as genuine. To reconcile them with what was said above, I think they should be understood as referring to the public and solemn administration of baptism and the Holy Spirit, which was celebrated every year at Easter and Pentecost. The canon forbids presbyters to presume to perform this rite, or to have it entrusted to them by the bishop for celebration in his presence.

Petrus de Marca objects:

> “The final clause testifies that the synod defined these matters by apostolic authority, by referring to Leo’s rescript.”

But the canon does not read that way. Rather—and this reading is even more favorable to Marca—it reads:

> “All these things are known to have been forbidden to them by the Apostolic See.”

Whichever reading is adopted, the words are not more likely to refer to Leo than to another pontiff. Moreover, we have already shown above, from the genuine edition of Garsias Loaysa, that these words are spurious and were added to the canon itself in order to procure authority for the pseudo-letter.

Finally, Leo’s name would certainly not have been omitted if the matter under dispute had actually been defined by him in so explicit and solemn a decree.

Perhaps a greater difficulty arises from the authority of Leo III, the Gallican synods, and the capitularies, which appear either to have cited or indicated Leo’s letter when they dealt with the cause of chorepiscopi.

Leo III’s reply to the bishops of Gaul is found in the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, Book VII, chapter 187. There the pontiff is said to have replied that chorepiscopi had very often been forbidden and condemned by his predecessors, by many holy bishops, and by synodal decrees; consequently, there was no need to reopen the matter, but only to preserve what had been defined.

He restrains them in chapters 328 and 329 of the same book and in Book VI, chapter 119. Yet when Leo III recalled the decrees of his predecessors and of Leo I, he certainly did not have the letter we are examining before his eyes. For Leo III invalidates all ordinations or consecrations attempted by chorepiscopi on the ground that nothing they presumed to do in the episcopal ministry had been accomplished. It asserts that whatever they had illicitly presumed to do must all be properly performed and brought into better order by bishops canonically ordained:

> “For one who did not possess something could not give it.”

They were not bishops, because they were neither assigned to any episcopal see of a city nor canonically ordained by three bishops.

Leo III confirms this twofold proposition by the twofold authority of our Leo, drawing upon his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, which is included in the Dionysian codex.

He establishes the first proposition—that chorepiscopi are not bishops because they were not canonically ordained—from these words in chapter 1:

> “Since a question often arises concerning honor wrongly received, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred must in no way be attributed?”

He establishes the second proposition—that everything must be properly performed by canonically ordained bishops, which follows from the first—from chapter 15, numbered 14 in our edition, where we read:

> “Since reason does not permit what is not shown to have been done to be regarded as having been repeated.”

These are the matters that Leo III had before his eyes.

The Council of Paris VI, neither that of Meaux nor that of Metz, contains anything that gives even the slightest indication that this letter was known. The Council of Paris cites none of the pontiffs, although the passage is transcribed in the Capitularies, book V, chapter 168. The Council of Meaux cites Innocent as asserting that only bishops possess the power to give the Holy Spirit. The Council of Metz has the following in chapter 5:

“And that basilicas consecrated by chorepiscopi should be consecrated by bishops was confirmed, because, according to the decrees [Col. 0763A] of Pope Damasus, Innocent, and Leo, whatever the chorepiscopi have done in the ministry of the high priesthood is empty and void. And that these men are the same as presbyters is sufficiently established.”

If this passage is considered more attentively, it will be understood that the decrees of those three pontiffs are invoked for the sole purpose of declaring invalid anything belonging to episcopal ministry that had been attempted by men not canonically consecrated as bishops. This is confirmed by the authority of Leo, just as in the Capitularies, book VII, chapter 328; by that of Innocent, who says absolutely nothing about chorepiscopi; and by that of Damasus, whose letter learned men judge to be spurious.

From this it is evident that everything found in the cited passages concerning chorepiscopi adds no weight whatsoever to the letter attributed to Leo. Yet even if it had really been cited by some synods of the eighth or ninth century as having been written by Leo, it would not be surprising if the holiest Fathers, intent on restoring discipline rather than distinguishing spurious productions from genuine ones, had been led into error by a false attribution. The same thing happened at the Council of Aachen [Col. 0763B] and in several other places, when books on the contemplative life were attributed to Prosper, although it is now certain that they were written by Julianus Pomerius. Indeed, we find apocryphal writings cited even by sacred synods of bishops, although it would be improper to count them among genuine works.

Before withdrawing from this inquiry, I shall point out that a middle position may be adopted between these two opinions: namely, that the letter belongs neither to Leo I nor to an impostor, [Note: [Col. 0763C] We cannot be persuaded of this, since it is contrary to the practice of the Roman pontiffs to copy words slavishly from other documents and patch letters together in such a way that they lack a suitable conclusion. For if Leo III had wished to issue a decree concerning chorepiscopi, would he have needed the words of the Hispalian canon in such a way as to adapt to chorepiscopi what is there decreed concerning presbyters, merely prefacing it with a brief introduction, and then issuing the decree without any concluding clause of a letter? [Col. 0764C]] but rather to Leo III.

For during his time the most serious complaints against chorepiscopi arose in Gaul and Germany, and their limits of authority were vigorously debated. Accordingly, while opinions were wavering in various directions, the bishops decided to refer the matter to Leo III, then Roman pontiff. We have already reported the substance of his response from the Capitularies, but the letters that he himself wrote on this matter have not come down to us. Nevertheless, there is [Col. 0763C] no reason to doubt that they were numerous, since the matter was of the greatest importance and had long set the Churches of Gaul and Germany against one another.

It would therefore not be unreasonable for someone to suppose that this letter—or a fragment of a letter—is by Leo III. The close connection between the Churches of Gaul and Germany during that crisis seems to support the conjecture; so do the decrees that envoys from both regions should be sent to Leo, the assemblies of both regions held on this matter at Regensburg and elsewhere, where Leo’s decree was promulgated and then strengthened by synodal sanction; and finally the emperors’ concern and attention to these matters—not once, twice, or three times, but very often, as the Capitularies, book VII, chapter 187, says.

Finally, since before the time of this Leo III [Col. 0764A] the letter is unknown to all ecclesiastical writers and collectors of Canons and Decretals, this is an argument either that it belongs to him or, rather, that it was attached to him than to Leo I.

If someone should raise a slight difficulty from Gratian’s Decree, where the name of Leo I appears prefixed to a decree excerpted from this letter, distinction 68, chapter “Although concerning chorepiscopi,” everyone knows how poor Gratian’s judgment was—quite properly—in distinguishing the legitimate writings of authors from spurious ones. Nevertheless, the mention of Leo I in the decretal should not be charged to Gratian, but to later correctors, who, along with countless other errors, drew it from interpolated editions of the pontifical letters.

For the older editions of the Decree—the Paris edition of 1531, the Lyon edition of Hugo à Porta from 1548, and several others—contain only this:

“Concerning these matters Leo the bishop writes thus to all the bishops.”

The distinguished Baluzius also observed in his notes on Gratian, at distinction 64, chapter 3, “On rejection,” that this letter was not attributed to Leo [Col. 0764B] I in the ancient editions of the Decree. He says:

“In the Royal manuscript, the title of this chapter in Gratian is: ‘Concerning these matters Leo writes thus to all the bishops.’ The Saint-Germain manuscript adds, ‘and to the presbyters.’ The older Victorine manuscript has: ‘Concerning these matters Leo the bishop writes thus to all the bishops.’ A later one has: ‘Concerning these matters blessed Leo the bishop writes thus to all the bishops and presbyters.’ The old Mainz edition has: ‘Concerning these matters Leo the bishop writes thus to all the bishops and presbyters.’ The words ‘and to the presbyters’ are absent from the old Venetian edition and from the editions of Democharis and Contius. The rest are similar. The Roman edition, however, reads: ‘Concerning these matters Leo I writes to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, letter 86, elsewhere 88.’ These are the words of the correctors, not of Gratian, although they have been placed in the text.”

In the oldest manuscript of the Royal Library, containing the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, this letter of Leo is placed before the collection with the following inscription:

“Letter of Pope Leo concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi [Col. 0764C] or presbyters, to all the bishops of the Churches of Germany, Europe, and Gaul.”

Thus far Stephen Baluzius. I add that the Paris edition of 1531 and the Lyon edition of Hugo à Porta from 1548 contain the same wording as that old Mainz edition.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from attributing this work, whatever it may be, to Leo III. If this conjecture seems less attractive because of the great similarity between the letter and the Hispalian canon, making it appear more the work of a plagiarist than of a Roman pontiff, then, adhering to the earlier arguments, we assert this much—which is sufficient for our present purpose: the letter is neither by our Leo nor could it have been fabricated except in a thoroughly clumsy manner.

**END OF THE FIRST PART.**

**[THE SECOND PART OF THE SECOND VOLUME OF LEO THE GREAT.]**

**[Col. 0769]**

**To Our Most Holy Lord Benedict XIV, Supreme Pontiff, Best and Greatest, Brother Peter Thomas Cacciari, Carmelite, Offers Greetings**

Although things offered to supreme princes in the name of duty and obedience ought to be regarded as so properly due and appropriate to them by a special title that no reasons or explanations need be sought for why such gifts are offered to them above all others, nevertheless, most blessed Father, the reasons are so eminent, true, and just that I must inscribe and dedicate this volume of my *Exercitations on the Works of Saint Leo the Great* to your illustrious name; indeed, I should consider myself unable to do otherwise without incurring serious reproach.

For, apart from the fact that this work embraces great and weighty ecclesiastical matters and the deeds of your holy predecessor, and therefore ought to belong to you as heir of his power and successor in apostolic government, it is also especially your own and appropriate to you for this reason: in the same degree of dignity in which divine providence has placed you, you maintain such a manner and rule of action that you seem above all to follow the footsteps of this holy pontiff, to emulate his zeal with the greatest possible devotion, and to approach as closely as possible his apostolic fervor and vigilance.

Indeed, throughout the very long course of his pontificate, Saint Leo did nothing, pursued nothing, and labored at nothing more earnestly than to repel and refute, by his efforts, writings, and indefatigable cares, the enemies of the Church and of the Catholic faith who were then rising up with the greatest force. He established those most salutary laws and holy institutions that provided the other Roman pontiffs with a great model for defending the Catholic religion and vindicating the rights of the apostolic see.

Everyone recognizes that these examples have been wonderfully expressed in you, most blessed Father. For whether we consider the splendid course of your earlier life, it is clear to all that you labored and devoted yourself to nothing more earnestly than to acquire a thorough knowledge of the laws and institutions of the Church, chiefly through the cultivation of sacred and ecclesiastical studies, so that you might employ them, in the many and most serious offices that you administered with such distinction, for the glory of religion, the dignity of the Roman see, and the preservation of the integrity of the laws.

Or whether we contemplate you now established in the supreme pontificate of the Church, what does not recall that ancient image of Saint Peter and of his earliest successors? Even amid the most serious concerns of your principate, you devote yourself so diligently to the pastoral office—which is the chief part of your supreme dignity—and so carefully watch over the salvation, faith, moral integrity, and ecclesiastical discipline of the world entrusted to you, that no matter pertaining to these things has escaped your care: everything has not only been provided for, but also confirmed by regulations, illuminated by writings, and sanctioned and strengthened by the most salutary decrees.

In this matter, the more closely you conform to the rule of your holy predecessors of old, the more you preserve, despite occupying the highest degree of dignity, that same laborious manner of acting as though you were in a private and humble condition. You undertake constant and indefatigable cares so that what belongs to the duties of others may be made known to them without effort.

Hence, most blessed Father, I confidently trust that you will gladly receive and read with pleasure what is reported and explained in this volume concerning the ancient heresies of the Manichaeans, Priscillianists, Pelagians, and Eutychians, which raged so violently against the Church in the time of the holy pontiff Leo. In these accounts you will recognize his strength of mind, zeal, and apostolic authority, as well as the various and most attentive cares that he undertook both in rebuking and convicting the guilty, and in receiving, admonishing, instructing, and releasing penitents who had fallen from the bonds of punishment. You will likewise recognize the Church’s distinctive administration in such matters, and the marvelous providence of the Lord God in governing it.

By this providence, just as God has ensured that, at the time when the Church most needed stronger defenses, he raised up vigorous supreme pastors, adding to them not only the necessary strength and power to defend the Catholic faith and pronounce those supreme judgments drawn from divine and apostolic institutions, but also granting them long lives so that they might complete all things successfully, so we may confidently hope that God, who has divinely appointed you, will long preserve you—something that all Christ’s faithful ought to desire—in safety for his Church.

[Col. 0771]

Through your admonitions, salutary teachings, commands, and constitutions, disseminated throughout the entire Catholic world for the instruction of all bishops and ecclesiastics, you have removed those abuses that oppose either the dignity of sacred rites, ecclesiastical laws, or Christian morals. May you therefore complete the course of your fruitful works.

Among your illustrious and glorious works, most blessed Father, we must count as no small one your promotion of scholarship for the benefit both of the Christian commonwealth and of the republic of letters through your favor, encouragement, and example. These works add great stimulus and enthusiasm to others, encouraging them to dedicate their books to your pontifical name and to expect certain patronage from you. They have given me an even greater stimulus to offer and consecrate these Leonine monuments to your holiness, and for many important reasons.

First, I have more than once experienced your pontifical clemency and kindness in receiving my humble writings, especially when, eleven years ago, I published the books of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, dedicated to your name. Encouraged by that benevolence, I strove to complete what I had then proposed to myself, namely, to prepare this second work.

Further, in pursuing this undertaking and bringing to light the resources by which I might illuminate the teaching and deeds of the holy pontiff Leo, I have made use especially of the Vatican Library and of other monuments made accessible to me through the generosity of the apostolic see. For that reason I have persuaded myself that you would receive this work with an especially kindly spirit, since it is the fruit of those benefactions that have hitherto been granted to me.

Meanwhile, while I continue to desire that your pontifical clemency may be ever more favorable to me and to these labors of mine, I ask and promise myself only this: that through it I may be permitted to rest with a peaceful mind in my religious studies, so that I may continue to devote all my cares and thoughts to the service and reverence of the apostolic see and to the duty I owe to your holiness.

**[Col. 0771]**

## PREFACE

I had scarcely brought to completion the labor of editing the *Eusebian History*, translated by Rufinus, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, together with the books that he himself had composed either from ancient records or from events that had occurred within his own memory, when, intending to undertake something greater, I resolved to return to the interrupted study of correcting the works of Leo the Great, supreme pontiff of the entire Catholic Church.

For several years earlier I had conceived the plan of publicly testifying, in some way, to my devotion toward the apostolic see. I thought that I could do this more splendidly in no other way than by applying myself to polishing and arranging the writings of so great a man with renewed diligence and care. I shall set aside for the moment his eloquence, the dignity and majesty of his style, and the power of the apostolic spirit that everywhere manifests itself in him. No one among the ancient teachers, plainly, either asserted the rights of the supreme see more openly, vindicated them more fully, or made more serious trouble for those who attacked them.

Nor was I unaware that, from the year 1485 down to the present time, Leo’s writings had repeatedly appeared in print through the efforts of distinguished men—especially in Paris and Lyon through the labor and scholarship of Paschasius Quesnellus, and finally at Venice, just as we were arranging for this new edition to be printed.

Yet these latest editions, which might perhaps have dissuaded someone else from the undertaking, supplied me with sharper incentives to complete the work I had begun. For when I examined them more carefully, I encountered much that diverged from the genuine text, especially in Quesnellus; much that was less compatible with ecclesiastical order and practice; and not a little—which is more serious—that was wholly alien to Catholic doctrine. In the end, it became clear that this editor of Leo had not so much applied a remedy to the pontifical writings as inflicted more serious wounds upon them.

Moreover, he not only failed to collect all the monuments, but deliberately omitted some and rejected or mutilated others because they opposed the purpose he had perhaps set for himself, treating them as wholly spurious or at least as filled with interpolations. Thus, since he seemed to me scarcely to have preserved the truth—or not to have preserved it at all—I judged that nothing would be more in conformity with the public good of the Church, the dignity of the Roman Church, or Christian charity than to set aside insults and avoid all verbal ostentation, and to restore Leo to the incorruptible sources of truth. In this way, after the weapons had been taken from the hands of his enemies, the faith that alone ought to be pursued might shine forth more and more.

By this course of action, the enemies of the Church themselves, at last disarmed and terrified by serious fear, and beginning to feel remorse in their hearts, might no longer refuse to return to a better mind.

While I silently reflected on these matters, I first began to read through Leo’s writings in Quesnellus and the other editors. Then I compared what had been published in print with manuscript archetypes. But [Col. 0773] when I encountered such a large number of copies in the Vatican Library alone, I immediately sensed the magnitude of the labor that threatened me and genuinely distrusted my ability to bring the plan to a successful conclusion.

The seriousness of the undertaking was further increased by the exercises in polemical theology to which I had become accustomed to devote myself as part of my office. These teach how to avoid and refute the monsters of every heresy and schism; demonstrate the stronger and more solid foundations of the Catholic faith; and finally disclose the ancient and modern rules of Christian discipline, in which the most ancient monuments of ecclesiastical affairs are both reviewed and reconciled.

The time spent on this burden, which had been entrusted to me in accordance with the extraordinary generosity of the apostolic see, together with the weakness of my own intellect—of which I was well aware—persuaded me that all other labors ought rightly to be set aside. If I attempted to embrace several undertakings at once, I had good reason to fear that I would become less prepared to bring each one to the desired conclusion.

As I turned these matters over in my mind, I had scarcely remained resolved upon the plan for this new edition when I began to reflect that it was an arduous task to undertake at present, especially for someone who wished, after Paschasius Quesnellus, to adorn the writings of the holy pontiff with new printing and with the addition of new monuments.

For Quesnellus did not follow the examples and method of the ancient and modern writers with which the kingdom of Gaul had always been, and still was, richly supplied—a fact we deeply regret. In preparing his edition, he continually indulged in novelties and in his own theories, exercising himself more in controversies than in the search for truth.

Who could fail to know that he had been furnished not merely with necessary but even with excellent resources? In addition to what he could borrow from the examples of the most distinguished men who flourished in Gaul at that time, as we have said, and who had labored on editions of many holy Fathers, he obtained from the flourishing libraries of that kingdom many manuscript codices of the finest quality.

He took from the celebrated Grimanus manuscript twenty-eight letters that had not yet appeared in print; he transferred others from the Roman collection of Luca Holstenius, and still others from the works of Jacques Sirmond. These made his edition richer than the others. If only it had appeared more carefully corrected in every other respect!

But although the man possessed an extraordinarily sharp intellect, he was highly disposed to provoke controversies and quarrels and entirely ready to construct equivocations and fallacies.
