He set himself a different goal from the one pursued by all Catholics, and especially by his fellow countrymen, in preparing and correcting the volumes of the ancient Fathers.

At times he defiled clearer passages of the holy pontiff with obscure, equivocal, and false annotations; he twisted others toward thoroughly violent interpretations; he concealed and suppressed the truth beneath fallacies; and, under the perpetual pretext of investigating and illuminating antiquity, he gradually and everywhere labored to establish systems favorable to the parties of heretics and destructive of the government of the sacred ecclesiastical hierarchy. In doing so, he at times almost abolished, or at least diminished, the true and legitimate jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs over all the other Churches, including those of the East.

Meanwhile, he pretended to be someone else. For when writing his own works and preparing his edition of Leo’s writings, he employed great artifice, affecting reverence, piety, and devotion toward the Roman pontiffs and the apostolic see in order to deceive the unwary. Acting very often in the role of a hidden enemy, after a splendid display of words he poured forth propositions sprinkled with poison, which he imagined could give some false appearance of truth to his erroneous and wholly fictitious systems.

From this it is clear that the labor required of any editor of Leo’s works must now be all the more serious in proportion to Quesnellus’s zeal in perverting the testimonies of our holy pontiff and interpreting his meaning differently.

The task cannot consist merely in restoring, as far as possible, the Leonine text to its original purity and integrity. That work is indeed serious, because the printed copies are full of false and corrupt readings, and because Quesnellus sometimes deliberately removed the ancient summaries of both sermons and letters in order to introduce new and stylistically more elegant ones without the authority of manuscript copies, especially those that he believed favored his own position.

Nevertheless, with the help of the archetypal copies in which the Vatican Library is especially rich, we had long ago achieved this much. We could therefore have published the works of the holy pontiff in a new edition, together with the addition of certain monuments that had not yet appeared in print.

The labor, however, had to proceed further. It was not enough to deal only with the genuine writings of the holy pontiff. It was also necessary to reexamine the grounds on which other monuments had been attributed by our predecessors to other holy Fathers, following the authority of manuscript copies. Such works include the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, the little work entitled *Authorities of the Apostolic See concerning Grace and Free Choice of the Will*, and finally the letter or book addressed to the virgin Demetrias.

We encountered these works attributed to others, and Quesnellus himself admitted that they could not be assigned to Leo without incurring the charge of rashness. He says:

“Although not a single manuscript, whether printed or in manuscript, cries out in support, indeed although the testimony of councils and of many writings extending over more than eight hundred years cries out against it, nevertheless he wished to attribute such works to our Leo.”

Nor could Quesnellus himself avoid this charge of rashness by means of the plea that he appended, writing:

“This alone I ask at present: that those who hold this opinion suspend judgment for a little while from every prejudice, until they have read dissertations 2, 3, and 4, which contain the reasons for our position. Meanwhile, I beg that the charge of rashness not be brought against me, following the example of highly learned men who have not hesitated to claim certain little works for famous writers, and publish them under their names, on the sole testimony of style.”

Learned men did not conceal those three dissertations. Among them was Joseph Antelmius. Since he could not be brought by any reasoning to subscribe to Quesnellus’s opinion, and since he carefully examined the arguments contained in those dissertations, he judged that one ought to depart so far from Quesnellus’s position that, unable to restrain his pen, he composed a celebrated work in which he vigorously rejected each of the arguments individually and proved with the utmost clarity and completeness [Col. 0775] that the authors of these little works were others than our Saint Leo.

Learned men everywhere have sufficiently recognized how deceptive are the conjectures drawn from the similarity of certain phrases, the agreement of style, and the rhythm of speech. It is therefore unnecessary at present to explain how vainly Quesnellus labored to attribute those three little works to our Leo the Great.

Besides what Joseph Antelmius wrote in his dissertation on the works of Saint Leo, there is also the testimony of the distinguished John Salinas, a canon regular of the Lateran, of Stephen Baluzius, and of others. John Salinas, wishing to illuminate the works of Prosper of Aquitaine with notes and observations after Antelmius, examined the Vatican manuscripts and found at least five different copies of excellent quality. Yet he found none that bore the name of Leo.

For that reason he ultimately judged that the works should not be included among Leo’s writings, since it could very easily have happened that there were many men at that time, in Rome and elsewhere, whose manner of writing resembled and echoed Leo’s style.

Besides these cited testimonies, we could report many others drawn from the scholars of Louvain, Baronius, Norisius, Labbe, Sirmond, Stephen Baluzius, and many others. They observed that, in manuscript archetypes, those three little works were attributed now to one author, now to another, without anyone ever suspecting that anything in their phrases and sentences, or in their method and manner of handling subjects, revealed Saint Leo as their author.

I shall not deny that the holy pontiff attacked Pelagians and Semipelagians in various sermons delivered to the people and also in some letters, denouncing those poisonous offspring and speaking magnificently about the gifts of divine grace in accordance with the statutes of the apostolic see.

But what follows from this, when he everywhere employs such expressions and interpretations of Sacred Scripture as are nowhere to be found in the books of those other authors? We could prove this with six hundred examples, if the nature of our present undertaking permitted us to compose a lengthy dissertation explaining why those works ought not to be attributed to Leo.

I do not think anyone is unaware of the aim Quesnellus had set for himself in attributing to Saint Leo those little works that, on the authority of manuscripts and the judgment of learned men, had been attributed either to Ambrose, or to Hilary and Celestine.

He intended to open for himself an immense field in which he could roam about with his system concerning divine grace, scattering here and there, with the help and support of many annotations, a great number of propositions, or preparing the way for others that were later condemned by an anathema of the apostolic see.

Among the others who noticed this depraved and deceitful method of Quesnellus was the aforementioned Father John Salinas, in his *Life of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine*, published at Rome. When he encountered several brief commentaries appended to the second dissertation under numbers 28 and 29, he condemned them as clumsy and erroneous propositions by which the annotator intended to establish and defend his system concerning divine grace.

No one is unaware that this had already been done by many highly distinguished and learned men. Thus Quesnellus, seeking support for his conjectures in every direction, found no one willing to support him.

Unless, perhaps, we wish to suppose that Augustine Savioli, a Venetian printer, judged differently, since, after removing the depraved and violent little commentaries with which Quesnellus had defiled and corrupted the three works, he preferred to attribute them to Leo rather than to Ambrose, Prosper of Aquitaine, and Pope Celestine.

He also transferred those three dissertations of Quesnellus into his Venetian edition, without mentioning their author. When I considered this method of proceeding, I was especially astonished at the man’s ingenuity: how, that is, he could so easily settle a question that had remained under judgment for so long, and which those who had weighed the arguments of Antelmius, Quesnellus, and other most distinguished men on both sides had scarcely dared to decide, without indicating any considerations that had led him to interpose such a firm judgment.

I preferred, however, to remain suspended in doubt and to trust those who had written long ago that no conjecture could be offered sufficient to attribute those three little works to Leo.

Still less could I agree with Quesnellus—or with anyone else, if there are any others—in thinking that that collection of canons ought to be attributed to the Roman Church from which the Parisian writer began the second volume of his edition of Leo’s works.

To this collection he appended sixteen carefully prepared dissertations under the pretext of investigating and illuminating the ancient doctrine and practice of the Churches: their conduct in overthrowing heresies and defining Catholic dogmas; in convening synods and receiving appeals from bishops and others; and, in general, everything pertaining to that sacred ecclesiastical government established by Christ the Lord on earth and transmitted to us through the apostles and their successors.

As for the collection of canons in question, I scarcely think there remains any occasion for me to say much about it, lest I seem to be thrusting my hand into another’s harvest. Two years ago I learned that two very distinguished men had conceived the excellent plan of preparing this collection anew, so that it might become possible not only to identify the author who assembled those canons and monuments, but also to investigate or determine for the use of which Churches they were intended.

To accomplish this more easily and successfully, one of them came to Rome and visited the more important libraries of the city. After examining the ancient manuscript copies containing the collection, he gathered whatever could contribute to the aim of his study.

Since I have heard this from several trustworthy persons [Col. 0777], I have judged it entirely necessary to abstain for the present from this labor and to pass over in silence the most serious reasons that have hitherto moved me to oppose Quesnellus’s opinion completely.

Although I may indicate some of these reasons only lightly in the course of this work, I have kept silent about others that are more serious and compelling, lest I seem to wander beyond the limits I had set for myself. For the present, I am content to await the sound judgment of others.

Let us therefore proceed to those dissertations written by Paschasius Quesnellus under the deceptive appearance of illuminating ecclesiastical tradition and Leonine doctrine. The foremost among them is entitled *On the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo the Great, Pontiff*.

I could scarcely have understood how full this entire dissertation and the others that follow it are of frauds, trifles, and inventions, had I not continually referred, while reading them, to the actual Leonine text in order to inspect the truth of the matters discussed.

Since Quesnellus habitually employs such great artifice that he can gradually draw even honest and upright readers into his perverse opinions and fill them with many prejudices, the present work will show how much labor was required of me.

I can scarcely describe the zeal he displayed in exaggerating his devotion and piety toward Saint Leo and the apostolic see—devotion that he pretends to attest by means of an elaborate style: now by digressing into praise of the saint, now by comparing Leo’s deeds and statutes with the teaching, piety, and religion of other bishops distinguished for their works, and now by introducing the regulations of certain local synods that had prevailed somewhere before Leo’s time, which he asserts that the holy pontiff ought to have followed and obeyed.

What is one to say? At times he constructed such an extensive display of learning to entertain his readers that, while gradually turning ancient ecclesiastical affairs upside down, disturbing and confusing them, he almost concealed the devices he had used to insinuate and establish his perverse systems. He perhaps flattered himself with the belief that, in matters sacred and ecclesiastical, human minds could be persuaded more by ingenuity, rhetorical skill, and philosophical conjectures than by the truth of things and the weight of arguments.

No one will easily understand the diligence and attentiveness of mind I had to employ in reading this and the other dissertations of Quesnellus, except perhaps those who preceded me in composing highly learned commentaries on ecclesiastical affairs.

This was most recently done, as those who have evaluated the six volumes of the distinguished John Anthony Bianchi on the power of the Church know. In conversations between us, he more than once testified that he had never read another writer who employed so many disguises and artifices as Quesnellus.

For whenever Quesnellus perceives that he is about to be easily exposed and defeated, he immediately slips away like a snake. Proceeding from one question to another, or to several others, he mixes the true with the uncertain and equivocal; then again he inserts and entangles false and erroneous propositions with doubtful and probable ones, until he reaches the goal he has set for himself.

It was therefore not enough, for eliminating all the inventions, fallacies, and trifles from Leo’s works and asserting the legitimate rights of the apostolic see, merely to present the naked and sincere text, everywhere cleansed of every fault, equivocation, and false interpretation. It was also necessary to compose, according to an ordered method, certain exercises by which we might bring considerable light to Leo’s deeds, the rights of the apostolic see, and the form and order of ecclesiastical government.

In this respect we chose to imitate the distinguished man Marquis Giovanni Poleni, professor of mathematics and natural philosophy in the celebrated University of Padua. After undertaking to illuminate the books of Vitruvius—a task to which we too supplied those resources that, in his kindness, he acknowledges—he judged that he could not reach his appointed goal unless he exerted every strength of industry and devoted himself to composing certain *Vitruvian Exercises*.

He testifies in his prefaces that he was led to this plan by the most serious reasons. Those who are willing to excuse our mediocrity will judge that we too were moved by similar considerations; they will at least approve, or not disapprove, our sound plan more readily than the labors we have expended.

In composing these exercises, we found our principal occasion in the four chief heresies that, from the time when St. Leo was elevated to the supreme pontificate until the end of his life, assailed the Catholic religion and troubled both the West and the East. Therefore, in order to fulfill the duties of his office and safeguard the Christian faith, he had to devote every effort and exertion to calming the fiercest storms which, while the devil raged furiously, were advancing the destruction of the faith and harassing the dominion of Christ and the Roman Church. From all these struggles the supreme pontiff himself won the victories which the Lord Christ had promised in Scripture to the blessed Peter and his successors.

The first of these heresies was that of the Manichaeans. It was older than the others and, perhaps, had become more obstinate. Although it had suffered many defeats in Africa, it was spreading more violently in Italy and especially in the City itself. His speeches to the people and his letters written to the bishops of Italy reveal that our pontiff employed a distinctive method of judgment in exposing the wickedness of the Manichaeans, who concealed themselves under the name of Catholics. Whenever he spoke about this heresy, he clearly indicated its origin, date, authors, disciples, doctrines, impious mysteries, and many other matters connected with its growth and propagation. At the same time, the holy pontiff himself issued many most salutary decrees for detecting the wickedness of these men, abolishing their rites, and investigating and exposing the hiding places in which they tried to conceal themselves.

For this reason, I considered it not inappropriate that my earlier exercises should, and ought to, deal with these and similar matters, since there is much to be said from St. Leo himself that discloses the ecclesiastical discipline of those times and the manner in which the Roman pontiffs acted. [Col. 0779] Yet, when I had brought my earlier exercises on the Leonine Works almost to completion and was discussing them with the distinguished Thomas Mamachi, then professor at the Urban College of Propaganda Fide and now theologian of the Casanatense, he informed me, out of his friendship toward me, that Isaac Beausobre, a non-Catholic writer, had composed and printed at Amsterdam a history of Manes and the Manichaeans in the French language, divided into two volumes.

My excellent friend therefore urged me to examine it before publishing my exercises. Since I immediately followed his advice, I judged it absolutely necessary to adopt an entirely different method in composing this work: not merely to weigh the arguments that the non-Catholic writer had fabricated against the doctrines of our Catholic faith and against the dignity and excellence of the sacred rites, but also to refute them. In his work he repeatedly twists the text of the Holy Scriptures into perverse and malicious interpretations; overturns apostolic tradition; rages against the ecclesiastical administration of the Roman pontiffs; treats the decrees of councils as worthless; attacks the ancient Fathers of the Church, or brings them upon the stage as though they were guilty of lies, superstition, and imposture. Finally, he has tried to overthrow all the most solid principles of Christian philosophy and theology, assailing with calumnies and curses those ancient writers whose doctrine he could not corrupt or weaken by perverse interpretations.

Since I could in no way conceal the license of this recent writer, I decided to compose two books on the history of the Manichaeans. My purpose was to gather into something like a single body the many details concerning this heresy that are found here and there in the writings of other ancient authors, and to expose the extent and gravity of the danger to which Catholic piety is subjected when it gives credence to the commentaries that Beausobre composed about Manes and the institutions of the Manichaeans.

These first two books are followed by another, the third, concerning the history of the heresy of the Priscillianists. In St. Leo’s time this impious sect had corrupted many parts of the West, to the greatest disgrace of the ecclesiastical community. Very many sacred prelates and men enrolled in the clerical army were infected by this pestilential stain in Spain, Gallaecia, and Lusitania. They adhered so fervently to the institutions of Priscillian that, after the bloody execution inflicted by the tyrant Maximus upon Priscillian and his associates, they did not hesitate to venerate him as a saint and martyr.

They retained the writings of these men and their apocryphal scriptures not only in private houses, but also read them publicly in churches during the sacred mysteries in certain places. They openly professed the most wicked doctrines of this sect, to the greatest detriment of the Catholic name and of souls. In that third book we explain, from the most certain records, what the holy pontiff Leo did, and what he prescribed should be done by the authority of the Apostolic See, for the destruction of this heresy and the complete eradication of its remains. We also address all the questions that some writers raised long ago, whether concerning the synods convened in various places at St. Leo’s command, the rules to be observed in receiving penitents into those synods, or finally the writings of these people, which the same holy pontiff strictly prohibited persons of every rank and condition from either reading or keeping at home, under penalty of anathema. These and other matters of the same kind, while observing as far as possible the order of the times, we have either touched upon in this third book or described at greater length whenever it was necessary to remove or refute the contrary arguments and conjectures of others.

Yet we could not maintain in the following fourth book the method adopted in composing the preceding three. This book concerns the Pelagians, whose heresy was spreading in St. Leo’s time. For many reasons, when about to speak of this heresy, we had to restrain our pen and say nothing about its origin, authors, perverse doctrines, or growth, nor about the African and Eastern synods that were convened at various times for its complete extinction. The most eminent Cardinal Norisius, with the supreme learning in which he excelled, adorned this history with exceptionally erudite commentaries. I therefore do not consider it appropriate to retrace what he wrote long ago, to the great benefit of the entire ecclesiastical and literary world.

I am not unaware, however, that this man, although extremely learned, is censured by others on many points. But what of it? Cicero affirmed that matters that are by no means doubtful, once brought into discussion, can sometimes be made doubtful by the contentious arguments of others—especially when the disputes are initiated by people who are pleased only with the surface of things, or who, wishing to cling too tightly to prejudiced opinions, depart from the rules of true wisdom.

Accordingly, in this fourth book I undertook to explain only those matters that concern the Pelagian history unfolding in the time of St. Leo. At that time the heresy had begun to spread more widely through Campania and other regions of Italy, under the support and instruction of Julian, bishop of Eclanum. For who does not know that, while still a deacon of the Roman Church, St. Leo made many efforts to extinguish that pestilential offspring, the enemy of the divine gifts? Since he persevered in this purpose, his zeal for abolishing it increased from day to day. Especially after he was chosen to govern the universal Church, he began to attack its adherents more vigorously by word, writing, action, and remarkable and varied means, until some came as penitents to seek the peace and reconciliation of the Church, while others, more obstinate, were bound by ecclesiastical censures, deprived of clerical ministries, or subjected to the punishment of exile.

This victory over the enemies of divine grace was all the more glorious for Leo because it was so enduring: during the remaining twelve years of his pontificate, at least openly, the Pelagian doctrine had no further followers or defenders within the boundaries of our Italy.

Yet a harder struggle and a greater victory were being prepared for him because of the new Eutychian heresy, which arose at Constantinople in the year 448. [Col. 0781] In the two final books of these Exercises, according to the limited ability of my intellect, I have drawn from the Leonine writings its origin, progress, crimes, overthrow of churches, scandals, principal supporters, defenders, avengers, and the other evils that occurred to the hatred and contempt of the religion of Christ.

In composing these books, our chief task was to discuss the form and order of the Church’s canonical judgments, which the heretics and lovers of novelty attempted by every means to overthrow, so that they might either completely destroy or at least diminish the universal authority and majesty of the Apostolic See. Their method of proceeding had always been to turn everything upside down in their assemblies, resort to sophistries and equivocations, and confuse questions of law and fact, in order to establish a new form and order of ecclesiastical government, different from that which the Lord Christ established on earth and which the apostles and their successors preserved.

I therefore considered that, in refuting and overthrowing the novel and foreign systems of others, nothing could be more effective than to follow step by step, and with greater care, the acts of the Eastern bishops and of the blessed Leo, so as to draw out the truth of these matters more securely and abundantly.

In view, then, of the purpose I set myself in composing these two books, I think no one can be angry with me for having reexamined very many of the questions that other writers raised long ago. Certain little scholars of our age, who scarcely read more than the summaries of those arguments, find these questions altogether distasteful either because they have clung too firmly to the prejudiced and false opinions of our adversaries, or because they recognize that weapons are being wrested from them for devising innovations against the Apostolic See and new kinds of judicial proceedings.

Nor could I pass over questions of this kind, or, in treating them, avoid or at least withdraw from those disputes that arose because certain men violently and falsely interpreted the Leonine text and acts. Such are the questions concerning the authority of provincial or general synods; those that clearly demonstrate appeals made to the Apostolic See; those concerning the confirmation, preservation, and dispensations of the sacred canons; those that review canonical penalties and their relaxations or reservations; and finally those that disclose and explain the supreme divine and ecclesiastical rights of the Apostolic See, so greatly revered in general synods and proclaimed with the unanimous agreement of the holy Fathers that sane men cannot call them into doubt.

Certainly, I judge the acts of Leo, arising from the affairs of the Eastern Churches on the occasion of the Eutychian heresy, to surpass the others to the same degree that his successors, in administering ecclesiastical affairs, always regarded him as their standard-bearer and strove to imitate him. From him, in particular, they drew examples of courage, wisdom, and prudence by which they might break the obstinacy of heretics and seek and summon the powers of the world to the protection of the Church, so that, once all dangers and adversities had been removed, they might judge more freely concerning the affairs of the faith and of the Churches.

These, then, are the matters about which I had to speak in the preface to these six books, in order to admonish our reader. But when I reflect upon what I have gathered in these six books, I am convinced that there will certainly be some who, following too closely the highly fashionable critical method of our age, and especially those who cling only to the outward appearance of things, will judge this labor of ours, whatever its worth, unfavorably.

They may object that not all the acts of the holy pontiff are explained in this volume, since much remains to be desired concerning the affairs of the Churches of Mauretania, Gaul—particularly Narbonne and Arles—as well as Sicily and Italy. By his decrees he tried to restore and strengthen the discipline of these Churches after its collapse, proscribing those corrupt customs that opposed the canonical rules and that resulted altogether in disgrace to the Christian name, contempt for the sacred rites, and insult to the clerical order and its service.

But the title of the volume itself sufficiently shows that this omission is not my fault for that reason alone; the examples of the most distinguished men make the same point clear. I believed that these matters should be reserved for another period of leisure, lest I wander beyond the boundaries of the four heresies proposed here.

Perhaps I will likewise be unable to escape the criticism of those who take offense at certain phrases and modes of expression, which, as men equipped with more delicate ears, they will condemn as less suitable for these Exercises of mine. Or they may attribute to me certain errors of typography that have occasionally crept into them.

We wish such readers to know that we have not followed the method and art of rhetoricians, but the kind of writing that has become customary in familiar disputations. From last winter until the present I have also suffered from a certain inflammation of the eyes. For this reason we had to make use of the work and assistance of others, both in transcribing what has been collected in this volume and in reviewing and correcting it in type.

Nevertheless, for all those respects in which I have so far been unable to satisfy the minds of readers, I ask and beseech their indulgence. I hope that, when a more suitable period of leisure arrives, I may immediately apply my hand to printing all the writings of the holy pontiff and the remaining records relating to him, which I collected long ago and compared most carefully with various manuscript and printed copies.

For the present I shall prudently conceal what those new records are, and of what kind, and from what sources they were drawn. With God’s help, I shall speak of them in the preface to another volume.

I promise only this: I shall take every possible care that the works still remaining to be committed to print in Greek and Latin may, in due time and through my labor, come to light without any fault. By such diligence, at least, I hope to dispel the censorious mark that I may perhaps incur harshly among certain people on account of these Exercises.

[CONCERNING THE HERESY AND HISTORY OF THE MANICHAEANS.]

[Col. 0783]

TWO BOOKS ON THE HERESY AND HISTORY OF THE MANICHAEANS.

BOOK ONE.

PREFACE.

[Col. 0783A]

1. When the labor of past years had been completed and our inclination urged us to undertake something more worthy, many notable subjects in sacred history presented themselves in which our work could be excellently employed. Our friends’ advice and encouragement moved us to direct our attention especially to the history of the Manichaeans.

Since many distinguished men of outstanding learning have written, for the benefit of the ecclesiastical and Christian commonwealth, histories of various heretics—sometimes of one, sometimes of another—from which the authority, strength of mind, and excellence of office of the sacred pastors shine forth more clearly than light itself in their attacks upon and refutations of those heretics, I was led to believe that I would do something pleasing to readers and to students of sound criticism if I turned my purpose and labor toward undertaking this task.

Nor was it unknown to me that many details concerning this heresy are scattered here and there throughout the writings of other authors and await discovery. If these details were at some point weighed and brought to the strictest standard of truth, then gathered and arranged into something like a single body, readers’ minds would easily be freed from the many great annoyances they are now compelled to endure: both the labor of turning through the volumes of numerous writers and the difficulties caused by varied, undigested materials entangled in the many complications that commonly arise in this kind of discussion and writing. Such difficulties especially torment capable minds and habitually draw them very easily into error.

I likewise knew that the non-Catholic writer J. Beausobre had composed, in French, a history of the Manichaeans more consonant with his own party than with the truth, which he later published in 1734 at Amsterdam from the press of Frideric Bernard, enriched with numerous notes. Yet scarcely anyone, if anyone at all, could explain what and how much this author dared to invent to the hatred and destruction of the Catholic faith. He directed his censorious pen exclusively against the ancient holy Fathers, the pontiffs of the Roman See, and the sacred synods convened on the occasion of this heresy, so as to attack their manner of writing and speaking and their conduct of affairs with false annotations, overthrowing them completely or at least twisting them into a perverse meaning.

For this reason, even in the preface to this work I had to remark that my mind would become entangled in sufficiently troublesome and laborious controversies if I decided to reject these books of Beausobre and purge away their errors. I was able to obtain them only late, and only after I had written seventeen chapters of this history.

But while reading through the books of this non-Catholic writer, I encountered countless things that contradicted both the truth and my own observations. I therefore tried to reduce what I had already written to another method and manner of discussion, lest I appear to have treated Manichaean matters in a barren and meager fashion. Thus, whenever time remained to me after my daily scholarly exercises and the other duties to which I must devote myself, whether within or outside the cloister, I did not resolve to squander my valuable leisure through carelessness and idleness.

[Col. 0783D]

Rather, I reflected upon what could be contributed to the common good, to the literary world, and to the composition of ecclesiastical history. I therefore decided to discuss the entire history of the Manichaeans as truthfully as possible.

In composing these little books, I declare that I shall adhere to no partisan interests, from which a writer’s mind ought to be wholly alien. In these and the subsequent controversies I have resolved, to the best of my ability, to pursue and defend the truth alone.

[Col. 0784A]

CHAPTER ONE. On the principal authors of the Manichaean sect.

The Manichaean heresy, named chiefly after one man of that name, had three principal authors. The very first, however, to lay the foundations of that wicked sect and establish its principal errors was a certain Saracen called Scythianus. He was raised among the Arab people on the borders of Palestine and, having devoted himself to Greek letters, mastered them very well.

1. He first practiced commerce and traveled to India. Within a short time he acquired such an abundance of wealth that, after arriving in Alexandria, he devoted himself entirely to the study of philosophy and to Egyptian learning. Having abandoned commerce, he wished to imitate the Aristotelian life.

Thus, possessing abundant leisure and riches and at the same time endowed with a sharp intellect, he considered introducing new but paradoxical doctrines into the world. They say that, because of this desire and following the opinion of Empedocles, he devised two coeternal principles of reality: one good and the other evil. He called the former God and light, and the latter matter and darkness. This error was one of the principal doctrines of the Valentinians and Marcionites, who in the second century of the Church troubled the Catholic religion of Christ.

He also turned over in his mind and scattered among the people other inventions derived from the principles of Pythagoras, and committed them to writing. Having composed four volumes filled with mere fables and lies, he produced the eggs of wickedness and impiety from which, when Manes later brooded over them, so many and such great diabolical offspring emerged.

He gave each of the volumes a title. The first he called the Gospel, the second the Chapters, the third the Mysteries, and the fourth the Treasures.

With these resources to support him, he set out for Judaea to dispute with the elders of the Mosaic Law. But after being defeated by them with the assistance of the divine Scriptures, he attempted to erase the mark of shame and disgrace through magical incantations and tried to deceive the Jews of Jerusalem with sorcery.

Using the magical arts that he had once learned in Egypt and India, he climbed onto the roof of a certain house. From there, either struck down by God or deprived of his senses, as St. Cyril of Jerusalem writes, he threw himself headlong and died, leaving his possessions and his celebrated books to Terebinthus, his servant, whom he had appointed his heir.

Both ancient and more recent writers have transmitted these details concerning Scythianus’s homeland, character, life, institutions, and books. None of them, however, has precisely determined the period in which he lived. Although Epiphanius (*Heresy* 66) seems to indicate that he went to Jerusalem around the time of the apostles, Guillelmus Caveus contends that his words should be understood in a broader sense [Note: Guillelmus Caveus, *In the Novatian Age*, p. 90], namely, as follows:

3. “In the century immediately following the apostolic age,”

so that Scythianus may be considered to have died as the second century was drawing to its close.

Epiphanius and Caveus, however, were opposed by Beausobre. Speaking about the origin of Scythianus’s and the Manichaean doctrine, he agrees with us that Scythianus was born among the Arabs, not the Scythians. But relying on various and uncertain conjectures, he extends the date of his birth into the third century and invents the claim that he was a contemporary of Manes, allowing only this distinction: that Scythianus was advanced in age, whereas Manes was younger. He further asserts that correspondence passed between them.

Whether this method of reasoning really establishes with certainty the period in which the founder of this heresy flourished, and whether the alleged correspondence was genuine or fabricated, the reader must judge. For our part, we maintain that Beausobre’s celebrated conjectures are entirely unsound. We merely point out that ancient writers, when identifying Christian men who flourished during the decline of the second century of the Church, employed expressions not unlike those used by Epiphanius. Epiphanius therefore cannot be accused for asserting that Scythianus went to Jerusalem around the time of the apostles.

For, as that century was drawing to a close, many hearers of the apostles were still surviving in Jerusalem. Among them was the celebrated Hegesippus; in Asia there were Quadratus and Polycarp. We know that they were called either apostles or apostolic men because they did not dare to depart even slightly from the institutions of the apostles.

[Note: Consult Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapters 15 and 22; book V, chapter 8.]

Eusebius affirmed this in almost countless places. Speaking also of St. Irenaeus, he records that Irenaeus had memorized the discourses of an apostolic man.

It is therefore not surprising that Epiphanius thought Scythianus had gone to Jerusalem around the time of the apostles, since we find that, by divine providence, certain apostolic men—hearers of Christ’s apostles—remained alive until the beginning of the third century.

Photius, certainly a man of keen judgment, whom Beausobre himself praises very frequently and who examined Epiphanius’s writings more than once, was afraid to attack him.

[Note: Photius, book I of the *History of the Manichaeans*, chapter 11: “But if anyone wishes from the beginning to examine their impiety—that is, the Manichaeans—and to see where the first seeds were sown, Cyril, who governed the holy City, will guide him in the history; and likewise the great Epiphanius through his miracles.”]

Indeed, in writing against the Manichaeans, Photius appeals without the slightest suspicion of falsity both to the books written by Cyril of Jerusalem and to those written by Epiphanius against this heresy, and he calls Epiphanius himself “great in miracles.”

Having explained Epiphanius’s manner of expression, we must remove another invention of Beausobre (*Book I, chapter 11*): namely, that Scythianus was a contemporary of Manes.

To persuade his readers of this gradually, Beausobre first reports the prejudiced opinion of the Greeks and Latins, who customarily condemn the character, worship, and philosophy of the Arabs and call them barbarians because they inhabit desert regions. He nevertheless tries to prove that the Arabs were devoted to the study and cultivation of the sciences and liberal arts by the example of the Queen of Sheba, who traveled to Solomon at Jerusalem. He then appeals to the manner in which Pythagoras pursued learning: after acquiring knowledge of the sciences in Egypt, Pythagoras also went to the Arab peoples so that he might subsequently receive fuller instruction from their king.

What more is needed? Beausobre transferred into his own history various praises of the Arabian people that are set out in the *Life of Muhammad* (*ibid.*, p. 20), so that he might infer from them that their native language was smooth and pleasant in every respect, adorned with great eloquence and poetic art; that their people surpassed all others in intelligence and ease of thought; and that the formation of their way of life, transmitted with great simplicity by heads of households to their sons, was known to possess strength.

Nor did the historian of the Manichaeans dwell only on these matters, which contribute little or nothing to our subject. Speaking of the religion of the Arabs, he judged that a purer religion had flourished among them for a longer time than among the Jews, especially since the Israelites, because of various Egyptian superstitions, had very often dared to depart from the true worship of God by undermining the Mosaic Law with false rites.

Proceeding still further, he first proposes a comparison between Scythianus and Muhammad, both architects of heresies and corrupt doctrines and both likewise originating from Arabia. And lest readers persuade themselves that evil demons and spirits of falsehood ruled the inhabitants of that land, he places before them Moses, who was appointed to the service of the Most High God when he had withdrawn into the solitude of the Midianites in Arabia—at the very time, he says, when he had been sent to Egypt to perform a divine mission for the destruction of idolatry.

After Beausobre had prefaced these and similar matters, more suited to displaying frivolity than true learning, he immediately appeals to the tables of the geographers and divides Arabia into its regions. He adds that he could easily have supposed Scythianus to have originated in mountainous Arabia.

The testimonies of Archelaus and Epiphanius seem to support this opinion. They indicate, at least obscurely, that Scythianus had an Egyptian wife and that she originated in the part of Arabia called the Desert. Led by these conjectures, Beausobre believed that Manes had been ordained to the priesthood and had exercised that office in the province of Ahuaz, where he taught while scattering his corrupt doctrines here and there.

[Note: We shall discuss Manes’s priestly office in chapter 4 of this work.]

From such an abundance of material, Beausobre himself thinks that he can conclude, rejecting the testimonies of others, that correspondence passed between Scythianus and Manichaeus, which may prove that Scythianus flourished later and was a contemporary of Manes.

He cites two fragments of letters in support of this conjecture: one from the letter that Scythianus had sent to the Saracen Condatus, and the other from a letter that Manes addressed to Scythianus, preserved for us by Photius, as may be seen in Fabricius’s *Greek Library*, book V, p. 284.

These, then, are the supposedly weighty considerations that could move Beausobre to invent such an exchange of letters, after rejecting the testimonies of Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem,

[Note: Cyril, *Catechesis* 6; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66; Titus, book I; Heraclianus, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 85],

as well as those of Epiphanius, Titus, bishop of Bostra, Heraclianus, and others.

But who has ever asserted that the Scythianus to whom Manes sent a letter—if indeed the letter is genuine—was the Saracen whom we are now discussing? Photius certainly says nothing of the kind. Following the histories of the earlier Fathers, he gave no indication that these accounts smelled of falsehood. Yet he would have indicated it if he had encountered anything alien to the truth in them.

Indeed, Tillemont asserts that there was another man who was commonly called Scythianus and to whom Manes wrote the celebrated letter.

[Note: Tillemont, also praised by Beausobre.]

Tillemont could not persuade himself that the first father of the Manichaean sect, Scythianus, could still have been alive during the third century of the Church, so that Manes could have sent him such a letter. This is especially unlikely because the man under discussion had already withdrawn from the borders of Arabia before he perished by an evil death and had retired to Judaea, where he engaged in various disputes with the elders of the Mosaic Law and tried to deceive the Jews of Jerusalem by magical incantations and sorcery.

Therefore, the aforementioned Tillemont rightly had to distinguish two men of the same name, lest he bring the holy Fathers who wrote about Scythianus’s deeds into disrepute. For this reason Beausobre wrongly reproaches Tillemont with envy, on account of this distinction (*Book I*, p. 26).

Joannes Christophorus Wolfius, in his notes on chapter 12 of book I of the work against the Manichaeans written by Photius, states:

[Note: “You may rightly wonder that this Scythianus is referred by Archelaus, book I, to the time of the apostles, since his account implies that only one person, Terebinthus, stood between Scythianus and Manes, as the former’s first disciple. If Terebinthus was perhaps advanced in age, he might have seen Manes; the fragment of the letter written by Manes to Scythianus might persuade us of this, provided that he is the same man as ours. The fragment may be found in the distinguished Fabricius, *Greek Library*, book X, p. 284.”]

Wolfius not only commented on those two fragments of letters, but also, when discussing Scythianus’s age, accused neither Archelaus nor St. Epiphanius of error. He explicitly called into question whether the Scythianus to whom Manes could have sent letters was the same man, since Terebinthus must be placed between them.

He therefore rightly suspected that Manes’s letter had been addressed to another Scythianus. Indeed, he asserted that Manes himself was sometimes called Scythianus, as Beausobre also admits—a point we shall discuss in chapter 4 of this work.

Wolfius, then, who adorned the two books on Manichaean history written by Photius with learned notes and published them, did not dare to confuse the Scythianus under discussion with the other, perhaps later, Scythianus. He did not infer such a confusion from Photius, and Photius himself supports Epiphanius. Rather, hesitating and suspending judgment, lest he bring the Fathers into disrepute or himself be carried into error, Wolfius at least left the matter without enclosing it within any definite arguments; or he judged that his own mind ought rather to support our opinion.

2. Let us now proceed to Terebinthus, the successor of Scythianus. We shall say much against Beausobre about him in chapter 3 of this work.

When Scythianus died, his heresy did not perish. Rather, through the ministry of Terebinthus, whom some called his disciple and others his servant, it became, as it were, more vigorous. It has been established by the common agreement of the ancient Fathers that Terebinthus was Scythianus’s constant companion and a participant in all his secrets.

After his teacher’s death, Terebinthus remained for some time in Palestine. Then, taking with him the wealth and writings that Scythianus had left to him by will, he fled to Persia, where he was received as a guest by a certain widow and called himself Budda, so that he might remain concealed more safely.

At first he disputed with the priests of Mithras. But after being disgracefully convicted and defeated by them, he turned, following the example of his teacher, to sorcery and magical arts, striving by these means to ensure that no one thereafter would dare contradict him.

Therefore, when he climbed to the upper part of the house, he was struck by a demon and hurled into the air, and died most miserably. The widow with whom he had lodged became the heir to his books and wealth.

As for the inheritance of the books, Socrates asserts that Terebinthus composed them in Persia, and Tollius later followed him in this claim. But since the ancient writers attribute those books to Scythianus, I shall not now linger over this question, which is of little importance.

3. Therefore, as we have learned, the widow of Terebinthus, or heir of Budda, kept these books in her possession until her death. When, some years before she died, she saw that she was without children, she purchased as a slave a certain Cubricus, a Persian by birth, seven years old. After subsequently granting him his freedom, she first arranged for him to be instructed in the disciplines of the Persians. Then, not long afterward, she died, leaving Cubricus by her will all her possessions, together with the books deposited with her by Terebinthus.

Placed, therefore, in so great and elevated a position of prosperous fortune, he was horrified by the former condition of his servitude and, fearing in turn that it might redound to his disgrace, rejected the name Cubricus and assumed for himself that other name, Manes. But what this word most particularly signifies among the Greeks was briefly described by Eusebius of Caesarea, who says (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 27):

> At that time a certain Manes, insane in accordance with his name and driven by demonic inspiration, taught a heresy hated and abominated by all.

Accordingly, because of the madness implied by the name Manes, the Greeks interpreted it in this way in order to seize from it an occasion for ridicule, as Cyril of Jerusalem subsequently also testified (*Catechesis* 6), and Saint Augustine afterward supported them. Wishing to avoid this mark of disgrace, the disciples of Manes extended the name and called him *Manichaeus*, with the letter *n* doubled.

“His disciples,” says Augustine (*On Heresies*, chapter 46), “preferred to call him *Manichaeus*, avoiding the name of madness. Hence some of them, as though more learned and for that very reason more deceitful, call him *Manichaeus* with the letter *n* doubled, as if he were pouring forth *manna*.”

But Caveus has shown from the same Cyril and Epiphanius that among the Persians, Chaldaeans, and Syrians this word indicated something honorable rather than insulting. For the Persians took it to mean “discourse,” since that impostor displayed an exceptional command of dialectic; the Chaldaeans and Syrians interpreted it as “vessel,” as though the sacrilegious and deranged man had wished to signify that, after the manner of Saint Paul, he was a vessel chosen by God.

I think, therefore, that it has been sufficiently explained that this diabolical sect derived its origin from these three sacrilegious impostors: Scythianus, Terebinthus, and Manes. But what Beausobre wrote at length concerning these various names of Manes and their etymologies, and concerning his homeland, practices, and offices, we shall need to subject to examination in chapters 3 and 4 of this work, so that we may strip away as many as possible of this writer’s frivolous arguments and conjectures and defend, to the best of our ability, the tradition of the ancient Latin and Greek Fathers, the ancient discipline of the Church, and the conviction of Catholic writers. We shall then reveal more clearly how far Beausobre indulged his own studies and the interests of the non-Catholic religion.

## CHAPTER II  
### The period when Manes chiefly began to spread his doctrines throughout the world. The testimony of Saint Leo the Great is elucidated, and Paschasius Quesnellus is convicted of excessive negligence.

[Col. 0788C]

1. From a man barbarous in life and character, though possessed of a keen intellect and enjoying the greatest intimacy with demons, who also deceived his hearers in his speeches through the abuse of dialectic, nothing but the evil shoots of wickedness could arise. These burst forth upon the Christian world when Saint Felix was already holding the helm of the Roman See. Among others, Eusebius wrote this at the place cited above (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 27).

In this matter, however, we judge the chronology of Guillelmus Caveus insufficiently precise, since he asserts that the beginnings of this heresy must be dated from the year 277. Felix was indeed proclaimed pope in the year 270, reigned for only five years, and died while Aurelian was emperor, as both Dionysius Petavius and the most distinguished man Franciscus Blanchinus have precisely established from the tables and catalogues of the Roman pontiffs.

But that this heresy broke out much later is by no means indicated by a celebrated testimony of Saint Leo the Great, in which he affirmed during a sermon:

> It became known that Manes was to be condemned at the time when the two hundred and sixtieth year after the Lord’s Resurrection had been completed, in the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already subsiding.

When Paschasius Quesnellus considered this testimony (*Volume I*, notes on *Sermon 2 on Pentecost*, notes 1, 2, and 3), he marked down three principal points, evidently in order to create considerable difficulty.

First, he suspected that there was an error in the passage, as Dionysius Petavius had suggested in his annotations on Epiphanius, page 227; and he held that, with the numeral one transposed, *CCXL* should be read instead of *CCLX*. His reason is that the consulship of Probus and Paulinus fell approximately in the year 277 of the Christian era according to the Dionysian reckoning. From this number, he says, thirty-one years being subtracted, 246 years remain from the Ascension of the Lord.

Thus Quesnellus reasons from Petavius, relying on the authority of the Oxford manuscript, which presents the following Roman numeral: *CCL*. The cause of this error—whether it is to be attributed to printers or copyists—is already made perfectly clear by the many Vatican manuscripts that we shall note in the margin. For the seven codices that we used in correcting the works of Saint Leo do not write the cited total of years in alphabetic letters, but indicate it with numerical signs, which the Romans always used in their calculations and reckonings.

Indeed, if that number of years were allowed to stand as it appears in the printed editions of Saint Leo’s sermons, the entire chronology of Christian and civil affairs would plainly collapse. For Manes would not have become known as deserving condemnation until the end of the third century, namely in the 291st year after Christ’s birth, when the consuls were no longer Probus and Paulinus but Gaius Junius Tiberianus and Cassius Dio. Yet who could fail to know that Manes had already been put to death by decree of the king of the Persians?

2. The second point Quesnellus noted is obvious to anyone, even the blind and the barbers. For there is no learned person who does not know that Probus and Paulinus attained the honor and office of the consulship only after the assassination of the emperor Aurelian, and that this must be assigned to the year 277 of Christ, as Petavius’s tables demonstrate and as Beausobre himself admits in the first part of his *History of the Manichaeans*. We shall see this when, in the fourth chapter that follows, we engage him in debate.

I do not know, however, on what grounds Quesnellus added that the Consular Fasti of Cassiodorus, or the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, ought to be corrected, since they place the consulship of Probus in the year 277 of Christ together with the seventh year of the emperor Aurelian.

For Aurelian, as both sacred and secular records attest, after spending only five years in power, was killed in the year 275 of Christ—through the treachery of Mnestheus, a secretary’s notary, at Caenophrurium, between Byzantium and Heraclea. After Aurelian had been removed, and an interregnum of approximately seven months had followed, Tacitus Caesar was proclaimed by the Senate. Two hundred days later he died at Tarsus from a fever.

When his brother Florianus had been substituted for him, Probus was proclaimed emperor by the greater part of the army. Florianus, bearing this most indignantly and driven to despair, voluntarily opened his veins and died after an interval of sixty days, in the year 276 of Christ.

The *Ecclesiastical Annals*, therefore, could not have combined the consulship of Probus with the seventh year of the emperor Aurelian, since Aurelian governed the Roman Empire for only five years. I think, however, that the cause of the error was this: Probus was also called Aurelius. Since, therefore, in the lists of Roman consuls the following name is found under the year 277—*Aurelius Probus*—some may perhaps have suspected that Aurelian’s reign had to be extended by two years, so that Probus could have obtained the consulship while Aurelian was still alive.

But no one should flatter himself that these considerations can make Caveus’s view concerning the beginnings of the Manichaeans any stronger. For Saint Leo the Great, in the testimony cited, was not at all discussing the origins of this sect, but the time when it had become known as deserving condemnation. He seems to have wished to indicate there that the errors of the Manichaeans had already long before emerged into the world and had been disseminated here and there throughout the various regions of the East, chiefly through the ministry and preaching of the disciples of Manes, so that such diabolical falsehoods and obscene superstitions, already publicized in many places, had become known to the bishops of the Churches themselves.

Who could suppose that this could have happened instantaneously? Especially since such a great distance separates Persia from Rome that, once the heresy had arisen, it could not immediately have been disclosed to the Roman See.

Finally, it should be added that already in the year 277, when Aurelius Probus and Paulinus were consuls, Archelaus, bishop of Caschara in Mesopotamia, distinguished for holiness and learning, had vigorously and steadfastly opposed the fury of Manes, as Epiphanius reports (*Heresy* 66), as does Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* 6).

3. The third point Quesnellus brings forward must be referred to Leo’s words, “when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already raging.” The annotator therefore observes:

> If Leo is speaking there of Aurelian’s persecution, as he plainly seems to be, this was not the eighth but the ninth, as Augustine numbers it in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 61.

But from where does Quesnellus imagine that Leo followed Augustine in numbering the Church’s tyrants and persecutions as eight? Does he persuade himself that ancient and modern writers entirely agree in counting the persecutions of the Church, and that Aurelian must necessarily be included among the tyrants of the Christians? The inference is false.

The Fathers adopted different methods of writing and set themselves different purposes in describing the same persecutions. For Eusebius, speaking of Aurelian, asserts that during the first years of his reign he was never hostile to the Christians. Indeed, when the case of Paul of Samosata was being considered, Eusebius shows that Aurelian presented himself as a defender of ecclesiastical rights to such an extent that, by public authority, he himself ordered Paul to be expelled from the Church.

If afterward, as time passed, the gentleness of his disposition was corrupted by the evil counsels of others, so that he even intended to launch a persecution against the Churches of God [Note: Eusebius of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 22], nevertheless this wicked intention achieved no result. It is said that, after the letters had already been dictated and written, when only the signature remained, God struck the signature from Aurelian’s impious right hand. He was condemned by a sudden death—the man who had been passing judgment on the death of the pious.

I shall therefore have difficulty, on the authority of Eusebius, placing Aurelian among the tyrants of the Church in this enumeration, since he died before the impious edicts had been signed. Lactantius likewise agrees with Eusebius, writing in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> Aurelian was not permitted to accomplish what he had planned, but was immediately destroyed at the very beginning of his fury.

Who, then, will deny that the holy pontiff followed this same method of writing? In reviewing the persecutions of tyrants, he intended to enumerate only those in which countless thousands of martyrs proved, by their very victories, that the Holy Spirit had been given to them.

But where are the martyrs under Aurelian? By which writers are they recorded? How many thousands are enumerated? Let our opponents produce the consular records in which the kinds of punishment or death and the confessions of the martyrs were described. Let Quesnellus himself indicate the names of the consuls and prefects who, obeying Aurelian’s imperial decrees, sought out Christians in order to punish them with death.

No records of this kind, certainly, have been brought forward by Eusebius, Lactantius, or anyone else, so that we can truly affirm that countless thousands of martyrs proved, by their very victories, the fulfillment of what the Lord had promised when he said:

> “But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak. For what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” [Note: Matthew 10:19–20.]

4. To make perfectly clear the purpose of the holy pontiff’s words—a purpose Quesnellus entirely failed to grasp—and what he wished to prove by this mode of argument and impress upon the people in his sermon, let us carefully consider the matter.

Saint Leo the Great proposes there to overthrow the principal doctrine of Manes: that blasphemous and sacrilegious architect of falsehoods claimed to be the Paraclete promised by the Lord, who had not come before the rise of that wretched deceiver. According to this claim, the Holy Spirit had so dwelt in him that Manes himself was nothing other than the divine Spirit. [Note: Beausobre wrongly attempts to clear Manes of this blasphemy. See chapter 4 of this work. Saint Leo, in the sermon cited above.]

To overturn a fiction of such impiety, upon which the entire structure of the Manichaean sect had been built, Leo first appeals to those testimonies of the New Testament by which it is customarily shown that the Holy Spirit had already been promised and given to the apostles while they were still in the flesh, and likewise to the other disciples and believers.

As he enumerates some of the causes of that Spirit’s mission and coming, and some of the effects of his admirable power, he first asserts that novelty of doctrine and the preaching of profane things are wholly alien to that Holy Spirit. For no other truth was to be proposed, and no other doctrine preached, than the one taught by Christ, the Son of God.

“But it was necessary,” he says, “that the capacity of those who were being taught should be enlarged, and that the steadfastness of that charity which casts out all fear and does not fear the fury of persecutors should be increased.”

Saint Leo undertakes to prove from the records of the Church that tyrants, the world, and the demons themselves had always observed these wonderful effects of the Holy Spirit in the apostles and disciples of Christ. When the latter, now trembling under no adversity, trampled beneath their feet the waves of the world and its worldly exaltations through a faith that rose above them, and, despising death, carried the Gospel of truth to all nations, the Spirit’s power was manifest.

To accomplish this more successfully, Leo appeals to those persecutions of tyrants which, like fires or touchstones, tested both the steadfastness of the martyrs and the truth of evangelical preaching. Therefore, in listing those persecutions, he ought to have enumerated only those that occurred from the Resurrection of Christ up to the consulship of Probus and Paulinus—namely, those in which countless thousands of martyrs demonstrated by their very crowns that Christ’s predictions in Matthew 10:19 had been fulfilled.

Since the persecution merely contemplated by Aurelian had not at all been carried out, it was not of this kind, and Leo had no reason to appeal to it. Quesnellus, therefore, is entirely mistaken when he imagines that the holy pontiff was speaking of Aurelian’s persecution. He could not have been speaking of it, since no Christian suffered martyrdom under Aurelian’s decree.

Hence Leo rightly wrote, “when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already subsiding,” without subsequently taking into account Aurelian’s letters and decrees for seeking out Christians to be put to death, since divine vengeance against the emperors had rendered that wicked intention ineffectual.

I am therefore now compelled to wonder that Quesnellus alone—who examined Leo’s writings only negligently—wished to bring this holy pontiff under suspicion of negligence and, with excessive shamelessness, to place upon him the stigma of error. This displays, certainly, an excessive shamelessness in the annotator’s mind: to attribute the mark of error to a man whose virtue and supreme wisdom had always been evident to the whole world, and to whom the affairs of his own Church could not have remained unknown.

If Leo did not agree perfectly with Augustine and other writers in their enumeration of the Church’s persecutions, this ought to be attributed not to fault but to wisdom. For if he had appealed to the ninth persecution, which they call Aurelian’s, he would not have achieved the purpose he had set against Manes, nor would his arguments have retained their full force.

Meanwhile, let no one be angry with me as though I wished to depart from the opinion of Augustine and others. I do not intend either to bring these men into disrepute or to charge them with error; I intend only to disclose Leo’s true and genuine meaning.

For the rest, both Augustine and other writers rightly included Aurelian among the persecutors of the Church, because of his dreadful and savage disposition toward the Christians, whom he would indeed have harassed with every kind of punishment, as he had decided, unless, by the providence of the vengeance of almighty God, he had been killed at the beginning of his fury.

Whether what we have written thus far adequately demonstrates Quesnellus’s negligence, the reader himself will judge. We have had only this one desire: to vindicate the testimony of Saint Leo from every charge of error and at the same time to show that it remains firmly established that, in the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, the errors of Manes had become known as deserving condemnation, when the eighth persecution against the Christians was raging.

5. But what if someone objected that the eighth persecution, attributed to Valerian, had ceased to rage many years before the consulship of Probus and Paulinus? What if that persecution were extended beyond its proper limits, with no consideration whatsoever for Gallienus, Valerian’s son, who survived him in the empire; or for Claudius, who overthrew the tyrant Aureolus; or for Quintillus; or for Aurelian; or for Tacitus, who, after Valerian’s death, held the reins of the Roman Empire?

Could Leo’s words, “when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already subsiding,” refer to the time of Valerian, who departed this life in the year 259? From his death until the aforementioned consulship of Probus and Paulinus, eighteen years had elapsed.

As I reflected upon these matters and, driven by the pursuit of truth—which I have always followed in every kind of writing—set myself the difficult task of resolving this knot, it became necessary to investigate more carefully what was meant by the word *desaeviret* (“was raging”) and in what sense Saint Leo had used it.

Since the ancient Latin writers do not agree, and since they used the verb *desaevio* in different senses, I decided to select and present here the meaning more consonant with Leo’s context. The word *desaevio* was not always used by the ancients to signify the fury of cruelty that someone customarily exercises against others. Rather, with greater propriety, they also transferred it to indicate one who gradually desists from cruelty and, with all anger removed, makes peace with his enemies.

But that Leo really spoke in this latter sense is made clear by the records of the Church. Gallienus, who shared the imperial power with his father Valerian, had indeed joined him in provoking that eighth persecution against the Christians through their decrees. Nevertheless, after Valerian’s death, Gallienus, surviving in the empire and moved by piety toward the Christians, restrained every impulse to cruelty and, revoking the earlier decrees, began to act more gently and moderately toward our people.

If matters stood as Eusebius relates when he discusses the peace restored to the Churches under Gallienus (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 16), who does not see that the difficult knot has now been entirely untied and that the whole interval of time that had been brought forward as an objection has virtually been removed?

Moreover, both the records of the Church and the tables of the Roman emperors show that Gallienus’s reign must be extended to the year 269. Therefore, if, while Gallienus alone ruled, the treatment of Christians throughout the Roman world was gentler and more moderate; if, moreover, Aurelian’s decrees for seeking out Christians to be put to death were never carried out; and if, finally, there were no martyrs under Aurelian himself, who could ever suspect either that Leo spoke there inappropriately or that his words, “when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already subsiding,” contained some error?

But it is now time, leaving aside Quesnellus’s quibbles, to proceed to those matters that expose Beausobre’s absurdities and arguments, set forth against the preceding chapters. [Note: See *Rationarium Temporum*, volume III, page 184 of the Venetian edition.]

## CHAPTER III  
### The false arguments of Isaac Beausobre, opposed to the preceding two chapters, are refuted. The rites and doctrines of the Catholic Church are defended against the criticisms of the same author.

I seem thus far to have accomplished nothing, or at least very little, for those who have either examined with their own eyes Beausobre’s history of the Manichaeans or heard it discussed by trustworthy men—whether in describing the affairs of the principal founders of the Manichaean sect or in determining from the writings of Saint Leo the Great the true time when this heresy became known throughout the world as deserving condemnation.

In that work, as we have already said, the author not only attempts to overturn the tradition of the ancient Fathers of the Church but also, when he encounters in their writings something that appears contrary to his own cause and to his non-Catholic religion, tears the holiest men apart as though with a rabid tooth, accusing them either of error or of ignorance. Such are the passages found in chapters 4, 5, and 6 of the first part of his *History*, as well as those he undertook to write in the second part, when, subjecting Saint Leo’s treatment of the Manichaeans to examination, he attacks, bites, and harasses our most holy pontiff, and rages against him with a kind of envious and blind spite.

1. In the chapters of the first part just mentioned, he therefore deals with those three principal founders of the Manichaean sect. Proposing to rely upon the testimonies of the Greek and Latin Fathers, and following Saint Epiphanius, he agrees with us first of all that Scythianus derived his origin from the race of the Saracens.

Later, desiring to acquire for himself the institutions and sciences of the Greeks, he chose to live in the vicinity of Palestine. But eventually, transferring himself to India in the East and making use of ships, he devoted himself to commerce. In this occupation he always enjoyed prosperous fortune and soon acquired immense wealth, since the advantages of the sea, the fertility of the regions, and the excellence of his intellect smiled upon him everywhere and at all times.

“These two qualities,” says Beausobre—“namely, an abundance of wealth and a keen intellect, together with a complete and multifaceted knowledge of the sciences, specifically medicine, philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy—are rarely found in one and the same man.” He asserts that Scythianus made his name eternal because of the heresies he invented or stirred up.

“But what,” the author adds, “if Scythianus had merely fallen into heresy?” We would not need to hate him, he says, but rather ought altogether to pity him, since heresy must be attributed to weakness of mind and entirely involuntary, distorted thoughts, by which a man’s intellect, withdrawing from the source of truth, allows itself to be deceived and drawn into error.

Thus, wishing always to deal more mildly with Scythianus, Beausobre calls into question another testimony of Epiphanius, cited above, in which we saw that this man had applied his mind to magical deceptions and demonic incantations, the practices to which the Egyptians were accustomed to devote themselves.

“Only Epiphanius,” he says, “a very credulous writer and excessively violent in his assertions, placed faith in this opinion; for, on the other hand, neither Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, nor Cyril of Jerusalem made any mention of Scythianus’s magical art and deceptions.”

I believe that no Catholic is unaware of the sort or quality of absurdities displayed by this Beausobrian manner of arguing. For if heresy is chiefly to be attributed to depraved and wholly involuntary movements of the mind, and consists only in them, why is it treated as a crime? Why has it been established by common agreement that obstinacy of the will constitutes the error of heresy, without which no one can be called a heretic?

Certainly, if the mind involuntarily clung to errors opposed to the dogmas of the faith, it would scarcely fall under accusation, since no act can properly be considered a serious offense if it is not performed voluntarily.

Furthermore, what bearing can his claims about Scythianus’s magical arts have? Does he think that Epiphanius’s testimony can be weakened by the silence of those two Fathers? He is indeed talking nonsense.

Archelaus in particular, whom he invokes as older than Epiphanius, is almost entirely occupied with recounting the affairs of Manes and condemning them, so that he scarcely had the opportunity to discuss Scythianus’s life and deeds at greater length.

Likewise, Cyril of Jerusalem’s purpose in that catechesis was not to describe every crime of the three founders of the Manichaean sect, but merely to consider in passing how three utterly wicked men collected every form of evil and compounded a single heresy filled with blasphemies and crimes.

For this reason, speaking of Scythianus almost in haste, he briefly recalls his origin, homeland, Aristotelian life—which he imitated—the four books he composed, and his death in Judaea; then he immediately proceeds to Terebinthus, heir to his gold, books, and heresy, in order to describe that man’s crimes.

But even if we grant that such an argument drawn from the silence of Archelaus and Cyril proved anything, would not Beausobre’s preceding method of arguing immediately collapse and perish? Where do those writers older than Epiphanius—namely Archelaus and Cyril—mention Scythianus’s commerce, or his study of philosophy, mathematics, medicine, and astronomy?

They truly maintained profound silence concerning all these matters. It would therefore be permissible to infer that Beausobre fabricated all of them and used equally excessive and violent exaggeration in composing his histories, never keeping before his eyes the truth, which he repeatedly asserts in innumerable places to have been his sole objective.

But what if Cyril had not maintained such profound silence concerning Scythianus’s magical art in every respect? For he attributes it to Terebinthus, Scythianus’s successor and heir, as something drawn from Scythianus’s books, writing:

> When he was finally about to be arrested, he fled to a certain widow. Then, ascending to the roof and summoning the brazen demons whom the Manichaeans to this very day customarily invoke in their detestable rites, he was struck by God and, thrown down from the house, died. [Note: Photius supports Cyril, *History against the Manichaeans*, Book I, chapter 12. See Christopher Wolfius’s notes on chapter 12 of the Photian *History*.]

Cyril therefore asserts two things there. First, that Terebinthus devoted himself to magical art and to deceptions aided by demons, practices to which, according to Beausobre, the Egyptians and the peoples of India were accustomed to devote themselves. Second, that the Manichaeans were accustomed to invoke demons in their detestable rites.

Let him say, then, I ask, from what sources they derived this art and these rites, if they did not learn them from Scythianus’s books. Did the members of this sect withdraw to the eastern region of India in order to devote themselves to these abominable studies? For nowhere do we read that Terebinthus visited India.

Unless it may be conjectured that he accompanied Scythianus when Scythianus arranged to be transported there. We may therefore reasonably affirm that both were instructed in the same disciplines; or that Terebinthus and the other Manichaeans—already, according to Cyril, practitioners of magical arts—acquired this discipline by reading the books that Scythianus had written.

Thus, if it is permissible to reason in this way without hesitation, Epiphanius’s testimony will stand all the more firmly, since he affirmed that Scythianus had applied himself to magical deceptions and demonic incantations.

2. But let us set these matters aside and identify another fiction that Beausobre attempts to attribute to the aforementioned Epiphanius, on the occasion of the marital union contracted by Scythianus with a woman from the Upper Thebaid.

Archelaus relates that she was a captive [Note: Archelaus, in the disputation held with Manes], and Socrates supports him. Beausobre himself, supported by the testimony of certain others, asserts that Eastern peoples were not averse even to captive wives.

But he seizes upon this as an opportunity to turn his style against Epiphanius, alleging that Epiphanius wished to transform a beautiful young captive into a depraved and infamous prostitute—as though Scythianus, a man ruined in character and religion, ought to have been ashamed to marry a prostitute.
