Since Beausobre did not know from what source such an anecdote, disgraceful to Scythianus’s reputation, could have been drawn, given that Epiphanius passes over it in silence, he grows angry with Epiphanius and does not hesitate to call him malicious. He consequently supposes that Epiphanius was swept along by nothing but vehement zeal and violence of mind when he described the deeds and character of heretics. [Note: Beausobre censures and attacks Dionysius Petavius because he translated Epiphanius’s text as: “whom from the trade of prostitution and slavery”; he argues that a disjunctive particle, rather than a conjunctive one, ought to have been used.]

13. We shall easily strip away this and similar ways of thinking and writing, which resemble the fabrications of the Pyrrhonists, if we reflect with due attention upon the depraved morals of the Manichaeans.

No sect, even among the pagans, could be found more criminal in its sexual immorality; no other school of men was ever more depraved in incestuous acts of unrestrained lust than the Manichaean. For, casting aside every sense of shame and modesty proper to human nature, they considered it unlawful to restrain the carnal impulses of desire, and they recoiled from marriage in order to prevent the procreation of children; instead, they continually practiced mutual and abominable sexual unions.

What shame, then, what regard for public and private decency, could there have been in a man who taught his followers that marriage was to be execrated and that all of them were permitted to defile themselves with incestuous and most shameful acts of lust?

That the Manichaeans were accused of these crimes, and had already been convicted of them repeatedly by public and authentic records and testimonies, is clearly demonstrated by the acts of the Roman inquisition written down under Saint Leo the Great [Note: See Book II of this work, in which we describe and examine the Roman sacred inquisition against the Manichaeans under Saint Leo the Great], as well as by the records of the proceedings held in the Churches of Africa. We shall discuss these more suitably in their proper place, preserving the chronological order.

But let us return to Beausobre. He concedes, then, that Scythianus’s wife was a captive. From what source, however, does he infer that, just as Scythianus was not ashamed to marry a captive, he would have considered it a religious scruple not to take her as a wife after she had earned her living by prostitution?

Beausobre asserts without authority that she was beautiful and young; and he thinks this can be established by the fact that Scythianus loved her more than the others. Thus, because of this great love, he could have made her a partner in marriage, even though she had long since displayed herself as publicly available throughout the Thebaid.

Nor does it help to say that Epiphanius passed over in silence the sources or older writers from whom this fact was drawn. For no one among the ancients called it into question or reported anything contrary to it. Perhaps all who examined Epiphanius’s writings were led by the conviction that the holy bishop had committed to writing the deeds and character of Scythianus on the basis of the traditions of his predecessors.

If his contemporaries, or at least men of later centuries, tainted by the Manichaean corruption, had opposed his statements and branded him with the mark of falsehood, they would have done so to defend their principal founder from this disgrace, had they known that the matter was otherwise.

Their silence, therefore, joined to Epiphanius’s firm assertions, more fully reveals how little Beausobre’s poorly digested criticism is worth—especially since, without the support of any new records, after so many centuries, Beausobre alone, living at the greatest distance from the age of Scythianus and Epiphanius—for he completed his life in the present century, namely in the year 1739—attempted to overturn and abolish the tradition of the ancient Fathers of the Church by nothing but invented fables.

### 3.

Our critic nevertheless seems to have dealt more mildly with Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, whom he asserts did not fall into error but wished to employ excessive exaggeration. Accordingly, in describing Scythianus’s deeds, Cyril assumed the role of an orator, who strives rather to magnify the arguments placed before him through declamations and hyperbole than to disclose their truth. Indeed, when Cyril was about to speak of Scythianus’s religion, he said that Scythianus had nothing in common either with Judaism or with Christianity. Beausobre claims that he read this in the Greek text of Cyril [Note: The Cologne version in Maternus Cholinus, 1564, has: “There was a certain Scythianus in Egypt, a Saracen by race, having nothing in common with Christianity.”], although the old Cologne version deletes the earlier words “with Judaism.” But even if it be granted that the Greek manuscripts contain both readings, as we read them in Photius [14] [Note: Photius, *Book I Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 12: “Scythianus … neither associating with Christians nor embracing the teaching of the Jews.”], what does Cyril ever say that conflicts with the truth, or that—even if it is not an open error—at least displays excessive exaggeration and hyperbole?

Christophorus Wolfius [Note: Wolfius, notes on Photius, *Book I Against the Manichaeans*, p. 38.] indeed wrote of Scythianus, in preparing the Photian books for publication, which he arranged to have printed in Hamburg with new type: “He was the first among Christians to become the author of the foolish opinion concerning two principles.” But it is already sufficiently clear to everyone that this foolish opinion was one among the many and great blasphemies that the Manichaeans devised concerning the birth, death, and resurrection of Christ’s flesh, and that it utterly overturns the principal and most substantial foundations of the Christian faith; we ourselves shall explain this more fully below. What, then, could that religion have had in common with the faith of Christians which attacks and abolishes their fundamental mysteries?

Certainly, if Beausobre’s conjectures stood, even a pagan who denied the existence of one God and the distinction of three persons, who bestowed divine honors upon created and visible things—namely, the sun, light, and stars—and who blasphemed that the Mother of God and the divine Word of the Father had become human, while professing countless other errors of this kind, could have something in common with us, solely because he dared wrongfully to claim Christ’s name for himself. But what would he ever affirm in accordance with the truth? For the pagan of whom we are speaking, apart from the Christian name that he would sacrilegiously usurp, would have absolutely nothing of the Christians’ faith, morals, rites, or institutions. Indeed, he would strive either to corrupt or to abolish all of them.

I believe that Cyril reasoned in this way with himself when he wrote that Scythianus had absolutely nothing in common with Christianity. And if Beausobre should then imagine that he is contradicting Cyril on the basis of Archelaus’s testimony—who called Scythianus a heretic and apostate, and said that he had failed in his violent ambition to obtain the episcopate, as is known regarding other founders of heresies—our explanation would not waver in the least. For what prevents these things from being true of a pagan pretending to the Christian faith? Especially since, according to Beausobre himself, Scythianus never wished to have a settled dwelling anywhere, but, wandering here and there, inhabited sometimes the regions of the Saracens, sometimes the territories of Palestine, the Thebaid, Judaea, Egypt, and India.

It could therefore have happened that, at some time dwelling among Christians and employing the greatest dissimulation, he also outwardly affected the Christian religion, intending by such deceit to mislead the peoples; hoping, namely, that the honor and dignity of the episcopate might be conferred upon him. By these means he would doubtless have more easily presented to others for belief and profession the perverse doctrines that he had absorbed and was turning over in his mind.

Finally, since in examining the affairs and doctrines of the Manichaeans I have so far found not even one of the articles of the Christian faith—those which they call fundamental—that they preserved intact and in its purity, I can scarcely be persuaded that their principal founder could have had anything in common with Christianity in his institutions. Therefore, as I proceed to other matters, I close this present discussion by reasoning as follows: just as no law could restrain the wickedness of this most depraved man from attempting to shake or overthrow all the doctrines of the Christian faith, so too he fondly flattered himself that, through wicked arts, he would obtain the honor of the episcopate. These two facts show that the statements of Cyril and Archelaus can be reconciled without violent interpretation.

### 4.

Now, if we were to follow Beausobre’s method of writing, as we have determined, only step by step, it would be necessary to discuss Scythianus’s four books. But since we shall speak of these writings elsewhere in this part of the history, we presently omit that discussion, [15] returning once more to Epiphanius in our account.

Beausobre therefore brought him onto the stage again, scourged with insults and abuse, on the occasion of Scythianus’s evil death. He compares Epiphanius’s testimony concerning Scythianus’s death with the statements of other ancient writers; and, observing that they do not correspond in precisely the same words, he became convinced that the heretical man in question had ended his life after being overtaken by a natural illness.

“Archelaus,” he says, “wrote nothing about Scythianus’s death from which it could be argued that he died otherwise than according to nature.” Cyril [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6, § 13.] of Jerusalem, he adds, “who flourished before Epiphanius and was thoroughly acquainted with events that had taken place long before in that city, describes the heretic’s arrival in Judaea, in very concise language, as though he were infecting that region with pestilential contagion; and immediately, without inserting any statement indicating disputes with the teachers of the Mosaic Law, he adds: ‘When that man had been destroyed by disease, the Lord brought the pestilence to an end.’”

Finally, Photius [Note: Photius, in the books *Against the Manichaeans* printed by Christophorus Wolfius, chapter 12, p. 37.], using briefer language, wrote that Scythianus perished by an agonizing death. Beausobre congratulates himself on this variation in the writers’ language and, like one looking for a knot in a reed, rendered Epiphanius’s Greek text into French [Note: Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66.] with many interpolations of notes and observations. He maintains that Epiphanius’s narrative completely collapses, with no one else supporting it, and indeed with the histories of the Jews openly contradicting it. Those histories reveal that both the destruction of the Jewish people and the overthrow of the Temple of Jerusalem were accomplished by the arms and soldiers of Titus and Vespasian. It would therefore have been utterly impossible for Scythianus to engage in disputes with the Jewish priests and afterward to climb the temple of that city by means of illusions and magical incantations.

Thus, once the city had been depopulated and the temple razed to the ground, Scythianus could not have performed all the crimes that Epiphanius relates—especially since he did not come there in the age of the apostles, as we ourselves freely conceded in the first chapter of this work when arguing against Epiphanius’s account, explaining that his words must be taken in a broader sense [Note: See what we said in the preceding chapter to explain Epiphanius’s testimony.].

Who would consider all this to bear the appearance of truth if he had not examined the histories of the Jewish people after the reign of Titus? Those acquainted with Jewish affairs will judge otherwise, for they know that Jerusalem, although not yet completely destroyed by Titus and Vespasian—with various buildings and towers still surviving—was later rebuilt by Hadrian, the emperor of that name, and inhabited not only by foreigners but also by many thousands of Jews.

This occurred when, after its ancient name had been changed to Aelia, Rufus, governor of Judaea, using the armed force assigned to him by the emperor Hadrian, suppressed the Jews who were in revolt under Barcocheba, an energetic and cruel man who had incited the uprising, killing many thousands of men, women, and children. We ourselves noted this second destruction of the Jewish nation under the Roman emperors [Note: Eusebius of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 6. See our Rufinian edition, note e.] in our annotations on the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius of Caesarea. Beausobre therefore cited it entirely wrongly in support of his conjectures.

If the city was afterward permitted to be inhabited by foreign peoples coming from various regions of the earth because it had passed under Roman authority and had changed its religion and name, nevertheless the surviving Jews in that city did not change their legal ceremonies. The succession of priests, Levites, and other ministers was preserved, and, as during the captivities of the Assyrians and Babylonians, they insisted that the Mosaic Law be observed more strictly in synagogues, houses of prayer, and other assemblies. The Pharisees, teachers of the Law, and leaders of the tribes made every effort to prevent the crowds either from embracing Christ’s name or from serving idols after the example of the Romans [Note: Roman enactments merely stipulated that the Jews were not to practice the religious worship of the Mosaic Law freely. But in private houses they devoted themselves to circumcision and the other rites, apart from the legally prescribed sacrifices. Consult our edition of Eusebius, vol. 1, pp. 179 ff.].

How, then, could it not have happened that, as the second century was passing, Scythianus, arriving at Jerusalem—that is, Aelia—attacked the priests of the Jewish people, intending through his disputes to prove that the Old Testament and the Mosaic Law had originated from an evil creator-god? And, after being defeated by his adversaries, why could he not have attempted, in order to erase the mark of disgrace, using the arts of magicians and with the aid of demons, to climb the roof of some house built beside the ruins of the Temple, or one of the ancient towers that had survived the destruction by Titus and Vespasian? I do not see that these things are mutually contradictory.

This is especially so since everyone knows that the third book Scythianus composed, which he called *On Mysteries*, contained refutations of the Law and the Prophets, and abounded in slanders against the sacred writers of the Old Testament. To spread such fabrications and refutations among the people, and to persuade the populace by inventing the claim that the Mosaic Law had been delivered by an evil spirit, he first had to travel to Judaea, in order to infect that region with pestilential contagion [Note: Cyril, *Catechesis* 6.]. For he could not have poured out the poison of his wickedness unless he had held assemblies, addresses, and disputes before the Jews themselves.

But that this man of such blasphemies and sacrileges was struck down by God and suddenly removed from the living is indicated not only by Cyril’s manner of speaking in the words “when that man had been destroyed by disease, the Lord brought the pestilence to an end,” but also by what follows. There Cyril relates that Terebinthus, the disciple of Scythianus’s wickedness and heir to his master’s heresies, was well known in Judaea and Palestine and was expelled from those regions, being consequently compelled to cross into Persia.

The disciple had aroused such hatred and horror among the people on account of his master’s death and crimes that he was no longer permitted to remain there. Photius too affirms that Scythianus’s death was agonizing [Note: Photius: “And when his master had perished by an agonizing death in Judaea, to which he had migrated.” *Book I Against the Manichaeans*, p. 40, in Christophorus Wolfius.].

For a death caused by a natural bodily illness, which separates the soul from corruptible flesh through the dissolution of the limbs, is not ordinarily called agonizing. Rather, we use that term for the death that the guilty undergo violently under God’s vengeance, or that judges and executioners inflict—or order to be inflicted—upon criminals exhausted by the severity of punishments.

Cyril’s manner of speaking suggests that God was the author of Scythianus’s death; and it is probable that Photius indicated by the words “agonizing death” that it was cruel and violent. Finally, the hatred of the Jews toward Terebinthus, and the popular tumult and anger that forced him to leave the borders of Palestine and Judaea as an exile, are plainly revealed by his flight into Persia. We must therefore believe that the disciple at least tried to conceal and erase the mark of disgrace and shame by taking flight, assuming the condition of a servant, and abandoning his former name.

### 5.

Beausobre can in no way be brought to concede this final assertion: namely, that Terebinthus changed his former name to erase the mark of disgrace and assumed the name Budda. To draw his readers more easily into his opinion, he constructed a rich display of learned resources and a magnificent apparatus of words, so that, little by little, he might impugn the good faith of the ancient Fathers of the Church and cause those who were not ashamed to read his work, written in French, to depart from the path of truth.

In the fifth chapter of the book mentioned above, he first brought forward various etymologies and explanations of the name Terebinthus. He thought that, from the readings before him, one interpretation might appeal to him that would either completely dissolve the frauds and deceits of the crafty man or at least greatly diminish them.

He then praises the *Acts of Archelaus, bishop of Caschara*. From these he argues that Budda’s name was by no means assumed by Terebinthus to evade the hatred and vengeance of the peoples; rather, he maintains that it derives from the Chaldean idiom and signifies among the Persians what the Greek word *Terebinthus* signifies.

He adds that the two names correspond precisely to each other, just as do the following pairs found in sacred Scripture: Christ and Messiah; Peter and Cephas; Dorcas and Tabitha. Beausobre would have sold this to his readers as a mystery explained by himself. But when he read Fabricius’s work, he discovered that he had long since been anticipated in his understanding of so profound and hidden a matter. After dwelling at length on these observations, he therefore asserted without hesitation that Terebinthus and Budda conveyed exactly the same meaning.

As exceedingly weighty witnesses for this claim he finally invokes the distinguished Simon Assemani, an expert in the Oriental languages and prefect of the Vatican Library, and Bochart, a learned student of Sacred Geography. He says that, in explaining these Syriac words—namely *Bethma*, *Boutema*, and *Butema*—they believed that, although the words possessed some difference in their letters, they had nevertheless been used by the ancients for one and the same thing, Terebinthus or Budda.

Whether these matters, which Beausobre has exaggerated in the cited chapter, are true or rather fabulous, let the students of Oriental languages and vocabulary judge. For the present, however, we do not dare to place complete confidence in all of them. Our mind, suspended and weighing the matter lest it pass judgment on unknown things, perceives that Beausobre’s preceding accumulation of arguments is not free from contradiction.

Either we believe that Terebinthus was the man’s birth name—he being the servant or disciple of Scythianus and another teacher of the Manichaean school—and that he ought to have retained this name among every nation, including the Chaldeans, although the peoples of that nation might pronounce it with a different sound and flexibility of speech because of the diversity of their languages and their use of different letters. Or else it must be said that Terebinthus had been compelled by some serious reason to change it.

If Beausobre adopts the first position, as he ought to do, why, without preserving the ending of the Chaldean word—whether in *a* or *m*—did they reject the form *Terebinthus* in order to use *Butam* or *Budam*? [Note: Let the reader not mock us on encountering the name *Budda*, spelled in these Exercises with a doubled *d*: we have followed Cyril of Jerusalem and other ancient writers, although Beausobre and other modern authors retain *Buda* for *Budda*.] For who does not see that these forms have no affinity with the heretic’s birth name and do not preserve the radical elements of its letters?

I am therefore not easily moved to agree with Beausobre’s statements, by which he attempts to persuade us that the Assyrians could and customarily did change the proper birth names of persons. The argument he adduces from Bochart completely fails, since the author does not affirm in his *Sacred Geography* that the two words *Terebinthus* and *Butam*, or *Budam*, correspond in meaning among the Assyrians and Greeks. Rather, he says that they denote and correspond to the Persian word *Buddas*, and are used for Terebinthus, the impious teacher of Mani.

### 6.

Even if Bochart were to support Beausobre’s conjectures, this would not trouble us in the least or compel us to cast the opinions of the ancient Fathers into a corner as false. For Cyril plainly wrote: “So that he might not be recognized by his proper name in Persia, he called himself Budda.” In this way he disclosed Terebinthus’s deceitful and fraudulent scheme, by which he sought to conceal his own crimes and those of his master.

Photius confirmed this very point both from Cyril’s statements [Note: Cyril, *Catechesis* 6, cited above.] and from those of Epiphanius [Note: Photius, chapter 12, in Wolfius, p. 41, relates that, after Scythianus had died an evil death, Terebinthus became an object of universal disgrace. While living in Palestine and Judaea, and unable to endure the disgrace to which he had been condemned by the judgment of all the pious, he departed for Persia, having assumed the name Budda.], saying that Terebinthus went into Persia after assuming the name Budda.

His reputation had already spread, and had brought hatred upon the impious man, before he entered into anyone’s company. What more is there to say? Peter of Sicily, who carefully learned the history of the Manichaeans both from the writings of others and from the consistent report and tradition of many people, has supported what has been said thus far.

Yet it seems strange to us that, in turning over the writings of the ancients, Beausobre did not find even one person who asserted that the Greeks adopted the word *Terebinthus* to signify a tree, and that the Assyrians afterward interpreted it as *Budda* or *Butha*. What reason, as he himself says, would there have been for the Persians to impose this latter name upon Terebinthus—as though learned men preferred to call this man in their native idiom rather than in Greek? Strange, I say, that not one person should have testified to this.

Accordingly, the three examples boldly taken from sacred Scripture do not at all apply to the present question. In those examples, two words had to be repeated, in view of the diversity of languages, to designate one and the same person. The sacred writers themselves indicated the reason for the repetition, in order to prevent any ambiguity.

And lest anyone suppose that we now wish to depart from the examples cited, we appeal to those passages of the New Testament in which Christ and Messiah, Peter and Cephas, and Tabitha and Dorcas are mentioned. In all these cases the sacred writers and their interpreters used explanatory formulas to indicate the diversity of languages and interpretations, so that no one, being led into error, might think that two persons were being designated.

John, speaking of Christ and Messiah, wrote [Note: John 4:25; John 1:41–42.]: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ.” More clearly, in another passage, the same John, reporting the words of Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, writes: “We have found the Messiah, which is translated Christ.”

Again, the same John, speaking of Peter and Cephas, says: “You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas, which is translated Peter.”

Finally, Saint Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles [Note: Acts 9:36, 40.], to remove every ambiguity of speech, says concerning Tabitha: “Now in Joppa there was a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas.”

We encounter countless other examples of this kind in Scripture and among the holy Fathers, but we consider it superfluous to pursue them here, lest we proceed at excessive length in rejecting the devices that Beausobre habitually adduces to create deception.

Therefore, bringing this argument to an end, we conclude as follows: since among so many and such varied ancient writers not one has said that the Greek word *Terebinthus* is translated in Syriac as *Buddas*, we are entirely at a loss to understand with what license Beausobre wished to appeal to the preceding examples borrowed from Scripture, in order to lead the ancient holy Fathers and writers who discuss Manichaean affairs into disrepute and to attack them as guilty of imposture and falsehood.

Nevertheless, what Beausobre has written about Terebinthus up to this point might be judged tolerable [Note: Beausobre, chapter 5, Book I of the *History of the Manichaeans*, p. 62.] if he had not afterward opened an even broader path for overthrowing other and more important matters handed down about the Manichaeans by the ancient writers; or if he had not exerted all the zeal of his mind to attempt to abolish those doctrines of the Christian religion that are expressly mentioned in sacred Scripture.

### 7.

The former category includes what he wrote in the same place about the disputations that Budda, or Terebinthus, held at Babylon with the priests of the Sun, which Cyril, Epiphanius, Photius, and the others mention. For this most wicked man, wishing to acquire both reputation and honor for himself, impudently boasted that he had been born from a virgin woman, as can also be gathered from the *Acts of Archelaus*.

The latter category includes what he writes concerning the illusions and demonic art of Terebinthus, in which we have already learned from the testimonies of the ancients that this sacrilegious man was especially well instructed. Beausobre maintains that there is no way he can be brought to believe that evil angels, or demons, can exercise any force or power over the elements, human beings, and other created things. Insisting on this position, he condemns as ridiculous that rite of the Roman Church in which, after divine assistance has been invoked, exorcisms and exsufflations are applied and pronounced over living bodies, the elements, and other things without sensation, in order to drive out demons.

As for the matters of the first category, the aforementioned critic stubbornly denies that Terebinthus, or the Manichaean Budda, could have fabricated and proclaimed that he had been conceived and born from the womb or side of a virgin.

For, he says, one of the principal doctrines of the Manichaeans was to deny the mystery of the Incarnation of the divine Word and the union of two natures in one person. They were led to this position by the reasoning that a virgin woman could never conceive and give birth to a human son without carnal intercourse and the seed of a man.

He adds that the ancient writers assert that such a fabrication must be attributed to another man of this name, who was the founder of the sect of the Gymnosophists. [Note: Some of them also attributed it to Simon Magus.] Finally, Saint Jerome, in his book *Against Jovinianus*, explicitly makes the Indian Budda the author of this imposture, writing:

“Among the Gymnosophists of India, the authority of this opinion is handed down, as it were, from hand to hand: that a virgin bore Budda, their chief, from her own side.” [Note: Saint Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinianus*, p. 345.]

I admit that Cyril, Epiphanius, Photius, and the others who committed the deeds of the Manichaeans to writing do not affirm this concerning the Manichaean Budda; nevertheless, that fabulous birth from a virginal womb is recorded in the *Acts of Archelaus*. But what follows from this? Was such a narrative contained in the autograph *Acts* and in the oldest copies of that disputation? Has anyone anywhere ever asserted this?

Those *Acts*, even with the support of the most learned men, were repeatedly and seriously interpolated and damaged, sometimes through the zeal of translators and sometimes through the carelessness and negligence of copyists, so that at present we can scarcely—or rather, scarcely at all—judge their integrity.

I therefore readily persuade myself that, if we must admit another Indian Budda besides the Manichaean Budda, the founder of the Gymnosophist sect, inexperienced copyists, deceived at some time by the similarity of the name, inserted that fabulous birth into the *Acts of Archelaus* as though it had been proclaimed by the Manichaean Budda.

The silence of the other writers and Beausobre’s own testimony support our conjecture. For in almost countless passages he maintains that Cyril, Epiphanius, Photius, Peter of Sicily, and the other writers, in recounting Manichaean affairs, relied upon the *Acts of Archelaus*—which he calls apocryphal—and transferred everything contained in them, either in summary or at greater length, into their own writings.

Since, then, according to Beausobre himself, no writer later than Archelaus has said a single word about this fabulous birth as something proclaimed by the Manichaean Budda, it will be necessary to judge either that it was not contained in the autograph writings of Archelaus or in their oldest copies, or, if it was contained there, that it was rejected as a spurious addition.

Although this Budda of whom we are speaking perhaps did not fabricate that story [20] of his own birth and spread it among the people, nevertheless we cannot deny, without being accused of audacity, that this second founder of the Manichaeans wished to engage in disputations with the priests of the Sun and the learned men of Persia.

For Cyril, after describing his flight from the borders of Palestine, his change of name, and his passage into Persia, immediately added [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, cited above. Photius, cited above.]: “But there he had as opponents the priests of the Sun, and, after many speeches and disputes had been stirred up, he was refuted. Finally, when he was about to be arrested, he fled to a certain widow.”

Photius likewise, after saying that this deceitful man gained no advantage from changing his name, and that he became known through both his deeds and his teaching to those who had previously been unaware of him, says that he was refuted and expelled by learned men in Persia who did not indeed hold pious opinions, but nevertheless defended a better judgment than his concerning all things.

### 8.

I do not think that I should judge the matters concerning which Budda held questions and disputations with the priests of Persia, lest I incur the charge of rashness. Beausobre, however, tried to investigate the matter more carefully; and, noticing some difference between Archelaus’s manner of writing and Epiphanius’s manner of speaking, he could easily have reconciled their testimonies without any mark of contradiction, but he neglected to do so.

Following the earlier method of his criticism, he maintains that the praised Fathers entirely failed to understand the systems of Zoroaster and the Persians concerning two principles—or only one—and concerning the transmigration of souls from one body into another. He says that he has reserved this matter for himself in another part of his *History*, where he intends to prove it.

Finally, on the basis of Archelaus’s testimony, he concludes that Archelaus did not say that the dispute between Budda and the priests or sages of Persia concerned the existence of two principles, but rather referred to the war waged against God by hostile powers.

But if we carefully weigh these matters, shall we not be compelled to affirm that Beausobre delights only in nonsense? For if, according to Archelaus, the dispute concerned the war that hostile princes or powers had waged against God before the external formation of things, then Budda was already defending, with still greater audacity, two eternal principles opposed to one another, as Epiphanius affirmed [Note: Epiphanius, *Heresy* 66.].

How, then, shall we say that there is any difference in the manner of expression of the two authors [Col. 0803A], when both speeches plainly reach the same goal, with only this difference in wording: Archelaus described the dispute at greater length, whereas Epiphanius described it more briefly and concisely? [Note: Archelaus, in the *Acts of the Disputation*, p. 97.]

Finally, Photius merely asserts [Note: Photius, cited above, in Christophorus Wolfius, pp. 42 ff.] that Budda and the priests of the Sun disputed, and that the priests thought more correctly than that Manichaean.

It is already evident from Archelaus’s narrative that Budda acquired no disciple at all through his disputations, except for that widow—deceived by his tricks and wicked arts—who received him as a guest. Archelaus then added:

“Early in the morning he climbed a certain lofty roof, where he began to invoke certain names, which Turbo told us that only the seven elect had learned.”

What Budda did after climbing onto the roof, and what happened to him when God’s vengeance intervened, Archelaus immediately added:

“When he had climbed up, for the sake of some rite or artifice—I do not know what—and had climbed up alone, so that no one might convict him therefrom … while he was considering these things, the most just God commanded him, through a spirit, to be thrust beneath the earth.”

Beausobre asserts that this account falters for many reasons. For when Archelaus said that Budda invoked certain names, Cyril, departing from him, substituted aerial demons and identified them with those whom the Manichaeans, as Christophorus Wolfius interprets it, customarily invoked in their sacrifices or assemblies [Note: Christophorus Wolfius, in his notes on Book I of Photius against the Manichaeans.].

After this Beausobre observes that the Greek writers do not agree in describing the rites employed by Budda: Archelaus said only that he ascended to the roof in order to invoke certain names, whereas Epiphanius maintained that these rites were magical, performed to produce some supernatural sign and silence the mouths of his adversaries. Archelaus finally concludes that a spirit was commanded by God to hurl Budda from the roof to the ground; Epiphanius called this spirit an angel; and Cedrenus, as though he had presided over this tragic scene, describes an angel attacking the wicked Terebinthus so as suddenly to cast him headlong. [Col. 0803C] Beausobre therefore confidently persuades himself that all these details are suspect, since they could not have become known to anyone without revelation.

To remove these ancient prejudices against heretics, Beausobre next directs his efforts toward this end and, as it were, flatters himself that he can employ more judicious observations for discovering the truth, adhering only to the account of Archelaus, which he calls simple, natural, and innocent. His first observation of this kind is that Budda ascended to the roof of the house early in the morning in order to pray to God. “He ascended alone,” he says, “in order to obey the divine commands, according to which we are told to withdraw from the sight and company of men when we pray.”

His second observation concerns the Manichaean manner of prayer, derived from the institutions of the Zoroastrians. According to this practice, the sect’s followers were commanded to pray with their faces turned toward the East, imagining that the fire seen in the sun signified both a throne and the divine presence [Note: St. Leo the Great, Sermon 7 on the Nativity, chapter 4: “From such institutions also arose that impiety by which, at the beginning of the day’s light, the rising sun is worshiped by certain foolish people from elevated places.” See also Letter 15 to Turibius of Astorga, chapter 11.].

Third, he observes that the peoples of the East were accustomed to climb onto the roofs of their houses for the sake of prayer, as may be inferred from Peter praying at Joppa [Note: Acts of the Apostles 10:32.] and from Esther ascending to the upper parts of the house when she was considering doing something in secret.

Ingenious indeed, Beausobre! Yet I do not understand by what method or license he attempts to proclaim these three things as conforming to the statements of Scripture and consonant with the rites employed in their prayers by the ancient Catholics and holy men. Certainly one ought to pray in secret, both to avoid vain glory and to secure for oneself that concentration of mind which is especially necessary to restrain the movements and thoughts of the heart from wandering away from God. But who will believe that Budda then had prayer as his objective? Or who will ever pretend that he wished, at least in this matter, to obey the divine commands?

The priests of the Sun were already present. Budda had summoned them to the assembly as his adversaries—for he had been defeated by them in their disputations—so that they might be witnesses of his tricks. Moreover, it was a principal doctrine of the Manichaeans that light, and the sun itself, were to be regarded not as the seat and throne of the supreme God, but as the true God and worshiped as such. Among the other holy Fathers, Pope Leo the First attested this in various passages, speaking expressly of the Manichaeans discovered at Rome who worshiped the rising sun, turning toward it and bowing their necks in honor of the brilliant orb.

He judged that this was done partly through ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism, and, grieving over it, added: “For although some perhaps intended to venerate the Creator rather than the beautiful light itself, which is a creature,” he nevertheless demonstrates in a few words that such a manner of worship differs in no respect from the superstitious worship of the pagans, adding: “Therefore let the condemned perversity be cast away from the custom of the faithful, and let the honor due to the one God not be mingled with the rites of those who serve creatures.”

The full text of that sermon makes clear that Leo said and wrote these things in order to remove from such a manner of prayer certain Christians of the Roman Church who had been deceived by the perverse institutions of the Manichaeans. But that the Manichaeans, like the pagans, rendered worship to the sun and stars—although guided by a different principle—will be established by countless arguments.

We next read that St. Peter ascended at Joppa around the sixth hour, not at sunrise, to the upper rooms. Yet nowhere is it stated that he climbed onto the roof of the house. And when Scripture speaks of the prayer of Queen Esther, it merely testifies that she stood in ashes and dung, humbled her body with fasts, filled all the places in which she had previously rejoiced with the tearing of her hair, and [Col. 0804C] continually, turned toward the Lord, said: “Help me, who am alone, and who have no other helper besides you” [Note: Book of Esther 14:1 and following.].

Where, then, did Pricaeus, whom Beausobre praises, find that Queen Esther was accustomed to withdraw to the flat roof of her palace in order perhaps to perform the more secret practices of the Jewish religion? We gather something of this, as though obscurely, from the history of Daniel—a fact Beausobre perhaps concealed lest it press upon his own throat. Concerning the prophet of the Lord, however, the sacred text relates that, at the three appointed hours of the day, he entered his house and, with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, bent his knees and worshiped [Note: Daniel 6:10.]. This manner of acting indicates that Daniel wished to pray with reference rather to the temple constructed at Jerusalem than to the East.

Beausobre therefore cannot prevent us from believing that St. Peter, staying at Joppa with Simon, ascended to the upper part of the house at the sixth hour of the day in order to pray to God with his face turned toward the temple of Jerusalem.

## 9

Let us nevertheless pass over these matters. Although they display a certain poison by which heretics gradually endeavor to corrupt the piety of Catholics and create difficulties for us concerning the most holy rites and ceremonies of Christ—rites which the heterodox themselves attempt either to overthrow or at least to pretend were derived not from the institutions of the apostles and the divine commands, but from human will and judgment, and depended rather upon the practices of different regions and the customs of their peoples—still, they are not so important that they can overthrow the dogmas of the true religion or bring them into open contempt, especially if they do not offend against the authority of the sacred pastors in prescribing ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies [Note: The diversity of rites not derived from the institutions of the apostles was proscribed by the authority of the Roman Pontiffs and councils. This is most recently evident both from the constitutions of Benedict XIV, the supreme pontiff, and from his works published in print. He discusses this diversity of rites in three books on the Sacrifice of the Mass and in other works on synods, which the reader desirous of great learning may consult.].

We therefore had greater reason to grieve that Beausobre’s versatile and tortuous ingenuity should be exercised even upon matters expressly transmitted in the sacred writings, and that he should seek to insinuate his manifest infidelity, surrounded by many slanders, into the minds of others, prefacing it with his customary display of vain and deceptive learning. In this way he sometimes beguiles the unwary reader who takes greater pleasure in novelties than in piety, binding him fast after ensnaring him with enticements and traps.

All the remaining matters that he adds at the end of that chapter, as he brings the history of Terebinthus, or the Manichaean Budda, to its conclusion from the Greek [Note: Beausobre, Book I of the History of the Manichaeans, chapter 5.] and Latin Fathers, should certainly be regarded as belonging to this category.

Investigating the deeds of this heretic more subtly, he asserts and presents as probable that Terebinthus was imbued with the superstitions of magicians for the following reason: he was descended from the Babylonian people, whose philosophers were accustomed to venerate angels not as gods but as ministers of the Divinity. They were led to this belief by the conviction that the angels, in an ordered arrangement, presided over the days and months of the year, as well as over the elements and all the things that ordinarily befall human beings in this life.

And, as though the Catholic Church could have drawn from this Babylonian and Persian superstition the sacred rite and order both of festival days and of divine offices, he boldly asserts that those peoples were accustomed to invoke their angels as intermediaries and mediators, just as more recent Catholics mention some saint in their daily offices and liturgies on each day of the year. He claims that the Muslims call such prayers sorceries and magical incantations.

After this great collection of nonsense and falsehoods, however, Beausobre says that he remains perplexed: whether, because of some secret discipline, the names of the angels, or the intelligences of the heavens, were revealed only to the Manichaean elect, who greatly exceeded the number seven, as Turbo confessed when he appeared before Archelaus, bishop of Caschara. For Augustine, who had once merely been a hearer of this sect, mentions a certain amatory song in which aeons were written down.

It therefore seems to me that Beausobre is inconsistent with himself. He now disregards, or fails to notice, what he had just written about the superstitious institutions of Terebinthus and Budda—that is, of the Babylonians and Persians—and insists that the Manichaeans did not invoke angels, although they rendered them honor and praise. He censures Cyril for confusing angels with demons, charging the Manichaeans with invoking aerial demons enclosed in the space between the earth and the moon.

He asserts that these demons were not invoked but utterly abominated, relying upon the confession of Turbo [Note: “He commanded his elect, when they ceased eating, to pray and to pour oil over their heads after it had been exorcised, invoking many names for the confirmation of this faith. He did not reveal the names to me; for only those seven use these names.” Acts of the Disputation of Archelaus, published at Rome by the distinguished man Zaccagni.]. Turbo said that Manes had commanded his followers, after taking food and drink, to anoint their heads with exorcised oil, invoking, or uttering, certain names signifying the mysteries of that false religion. Knowledge of these names he had reserved for only seven—that is, seventy—elect persons.

Tillemont then wished this exorcised oil to be called “bewitched” according to the Greek and Latin version. Therefore Beausobre, insisting upon these two words, adds: “If ‘exorcised’ must be understood as ‘bewitched,’ what are we to say of so many and such great rites and ceremonies of the Roman Church?” He thus concludes: “If, therefore, the Manichaeans pronounced exorcisms over oil before using it, it now becomes evident that the Manichaeans had been preoccupied by that ridiculous opinion according to which demons could afflict the elements and bodies—a belief that, since it has prevailed so greatly in the Church, has led it to employ supplications and exorcisms to drive them out.”

## 10

We must finally insist carefully upon all these matters in order to rescue the Catholic Church from the deceptions, false accusations, and mockeries with which the impostor Beausobre has dared to attack it. First of all, he confuses the aeons of the heretics with angels and demons. The architects of these aeons were Simon Magus, the prince of heretics; Montanus; the followers of Menander, Saturninus, Cerinthus, Carpocrates, and Valentinus; and others derived from Marcus the Egyptian. Trained in the playfulness of ancient poets and pagans, they fabricated, in the manner of fables, the existence and army of aeons, later bestowing upon them various names according to their own pleasure, because they dreamed that these beings performed different functions.

But the teaching of the ancient pagans was very different. Although they lacked the illumination of faith, Hesiod, first of all [Note: Hesiod, Book I. “These demons were made by the counsel of great Zeus: good, earthly beings, guardians of mortal men, who observe just and unjust deeds. Clothed in air, they go everywhere over the earth, givers of wealth, and they received this royal privilege.”], recognized that between God, who holds the highest place, and human beings, who are placed at the lowest, there existed certain intermediate, immortal spirits endowed with reason and a kind of intelligence. He called them demons or genii; we call them angels.

Plato also spoke most clearly of demons, especially in the Timaeus. He regarded them as bound to the celestial spheres, indeed as the spheres and stars themselves, almost as subordinate gods. Following these demons, he describes others propagated by generation and placed at the lowest level. Although by their nature they are dissoluble and mortal, they will nevertheless, by the supreme will of God—which is stronger than nature—be immortal and eternal.

He asserts that animals were generated by these beings, and even the bodies into which he himself infused human souls. Plato is supported by his interpreter Alcinous, by the magician Hostanes [Col. 0806C], Orpheus, Thales, Pythagoras, and others, who truly and without any doubt affirmed that demons, or angels, exist, although they reasoned differently concerning their nature and properties.

As for the other system, concerning the existence of aeons, it has hitherto appeared to all writers to be an intricate and fabulous invention. Nor has it yet been established by any certain reasoning that these beings had anything in common with the substances whom we call angels or demons, even among the architects of that system.

Therefore, when Augustine mentions that amatory Manichaean song in which aeons were described, he did not believe that angels or demons were meant. Rather, he knew perfectly well the frauds of those heretics, who fabricated those false intelligences fixed in the stars and spheres. Led by superstitious belief, they claimed that the whole of human life depended upon the influences of the stars, elements, or aeons, and they falsely asserted that these influences could be made favorable to them—or at least changed—if prayers were offered to the same beings, namely, when through their wandering movements or fixed continuance they harmed people by certain malignant aspects.

Our Leo the Great attacks in various places both the Manichaeans and the Priscillianists, defenders of these falsehoods, reproaching them in these words: “What, then, is the sun, or what is the moon, except visible creatures and elements of bodily light? One possesses greater brightness, the other a lesser light” [Note: St. Leo the Great, Sermon 26, which is Sermon 7 on the Nativity. See also Sermon 82, on the octave of the Apostles, and Letter 15, chapters 12–14.].

Then, distinguishing the times of day from those of night, he suggests that different qualities, not degrees of life, belong to them, since before the lights and stars were made, three days had passed without the course of the sun and nights without the service of the moon and stars. He therefore indicates in the following words why the Creator of all things made them on the fourth day: namely, that they might exist for human usefulness, “so that the rational creature might not be deceived either in the division of the months, the recurrence of the years, or the counting of times; for through the unequal lengths of unequal hours, the manifest signs of different risings, the sun completes the years and the moon renews the months.”

## 11

If I were now permitted to linger longer over the superstitions of the ancient Babylonian and Persian philosophers, who maintained that various conjunctions of aeons were fixed in each hour, day, and month of the year, and falsely claimed that human destinies depended upon them, afterward begging those beings to assist and favor them, I could more easily demonstrate that these beliefs bear no resemblance or affinity whatsoever to our rites.

For who can persuade himself that Belial agrees with God, or that an idol has any affinity or likeness to the truth? [Note: St. Jerome, volume IV of the Roman edition prepared by the distinguished Pamelio, commentary on Isaiah, Book XII, chapter 42.] An idol is a pure and simple fabrication, invented from falsehood in order to deceive rational substances.

Therefore, if, as Leo teaches—the most learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures—the divine omnipotence arranged that the stars and the other signs of the heavenly host, lacking sense and life, should distinguish the succession of times according to the order of days, months, and years, an order especially expressed in the sacred writings of the Old Testament, then we ought to praise only the divine power and providence, which wished to create such signs for our knowledge, instruction, and benefit.

But when the influences of the heavens, changes of the air, and the risings, settings, courses, degrees, retrogradations, and appearances and disappearances of the stars or aeons are necessarily produced altogether by dead nature and derived from it, what praise, honor, or worship can reasonably be offered to them?

Nothing, therefore, is more superstitious or more contrary to the truth than that vain and deceptive philosophy of both the pagans and the ancient heretics by which, when they observed marvelous events occurring in the world, they attributed them to the influences of the aeons. Accordingly, having invented various names with which to invoke them, they foolishly supposed that they could also make them favorable to themselves in sacred mysteries.

Augustine wrote similarly of Montanus and the Cataphrygians, the founders of heresies [Note: Augustine, Book on Heresies, and volume VI, Book against the Letter of the Fundamental, chapter 3. See also the Synodical Booklet in the collections of the councils, volume I, page 615.]. Instead of the sacred cleansing and regeneration of baptism, they washed their adherents in an unclean bath, reciting as many names of aeons as they dreamed were contained in the complete cycle of the year.

From the Synodical Booklet we learn that Montanus himself devised eight hundred and seventy aeons, each of which he called by its own name.

What affinity or likeness, then, can the institution of Catholic rites and festivals have with these fabulous inventions? Does not the Catholic Church, in arranging the order of festivals and reciting offices and liturgies, honor God almighty with praises, taking account of the diversity of times and the dignity of the mysteries that ought to be celebrated with solemn worship because of their divine institution?

Catholics render the worship of service to God alone in offices, liturgies, and all supplications, both public and private, and direct their prayers, voices, and hearts to him. Where, then, does Beausobre derive the claim that the daily religious rites of Catholics can in any respect be compared with the superstitious ceremonies of the Babylonians, Persians, and magicians?

Perhaps he will think that the likeness or affinity consists in the fact that the Roman Church has consecrated certain annual festivals to particular days of the year and afterward commanded that they be observed with holier rites and ceremonies. Or perhaps because, on each day of the year, when the birth anniversary of some man distinguished by holiness, learning, martyrdom, or virginity returns, it is accustomed to recall to the minds of the faithful the more outstanding and proven deeds of his virtues, both to render praise to God and to arouse in them the desire for imitation.

It is therefore absolutely certain that nothing in these practices corresponds to the superstitious solemnities of the Persians, Babylonians, and magicians, or to the fabulous rites by which they worshiped aeons and stars.

If, then, I were presently dealing with someone other than Beausobre—namely, a pagan by profession, an atheist, or an Epicurean who did not rely upon the sacred Scriptures or divine commands—I would appeal only to arguments drawn from the light of nature in order to explain the sanctity, dignity, and excellence of the rites of the Roman Church.

But since this matter concerns a Christian, though an acatholic, who must accept not only the authority of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which clear mention is made of various established annual solemnities and institutions, but also the commands of the Gospel of the New Testament, and who must likewise profess all those mysteries relating to the conception, birth, circumcision, miracles, passion, death, resurrection, and other such events of Jesus Christ, I understand that Beausobre wished to play the part of a most foolish person in cataloguing these matters. He plays lavishly with the fables of the Persians and Babylonians and, with all the power of his zeal, attempts to mock and deceive readers who are ignorant, excessively credulous, and disposed to think neither piously nor wisely about the Roman Church.

## 12

And—to return to the remaining matters—does the same Beausobre not remember that demons are also called angels in the sacred sayings of the Gospel? Christ calls those spirits angels in Matthew who, having fallen from divine grace through pride together with the devil, were condemned to the torments of eternal fire. The Scriptures themselves, in other passages, designate evil angels by the name of demons.

It is therefore not surprising if Cyril asserts that Terebinthus, or Budda, called upon aerial demons for his protection. His testimony, moreover, agrees with the confession of Turbo, who, while condemning the rites of the Manichaeans, said that after receiving food and drink they were accustomed to anoint their heads with exorcised oil.

By “exorcised” oil one must understand oil magically bewitched, such as necromancers customarily use when calling upon evil spirits for protection—spirits from whom they obtain assistance when, through their tricks, they attempt to accomplish something contrary to the order of nature [Note: See the Council of Elvira with the notes of Ferdinandus Mendoza, volume I of the Councils, page 1237, canon 34.].

Tillemont, therefore, a learned man, could not rightly be accused for wishing to interpret “exorcised” as “bewitched.” The historian of the Church knew that ancient magicians were accustomed to employ bewitched wax candles, lamps, water, oil, and other objects—not to drive spirits away but to summon them, so that they might obtain protection and help from them and acquire knowledge of future events [Note: Concerning these magical practices, see Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 37; Lactantius, Divine Institutes, Book II, chapter 1; Pliny, Book XXX, chapter 2; Cicero, Speech against Vatinius; Horace, Book I, Satire 8, on the sorceries of Canidia and Sagana; Philostratus, Life of Apollonius; St. Augustine, Answers to the Three Questions of Simplicianus, Book II.].

According to Pliny, Osthanes spoke of a similar magical art. Describing its various forms, he said that its practitioners drew divinations from water, spheres, bronze, stars, lamps, basins, axes, and many other things. It is therefore sufficiently probable that the Manichaeans, who were highly skilled in this art, wished to use oil profaned by incantations to summon evil spirits.

Finally, we believe that the word “exorcised” found in Turbo’s confession is in no way opposed to Tillemont’s interpretation. Turbo must have employed the formula of speech used by Manes, whose deeds he recounts. Manes may have called sacred and natural things profaned by wicked rites “exorcisms,” as we shall see more clearly in its proper place.

Once these matters have been disclosed and explained, everyone will judge it unnecessary to labor over them at greater length, since more important points remain to be rescued—points in which Beausobre either asserts that exorcisms deserve to be mocked with ridicule [Note: Beausobre, History of the Manichaeans, volume I, Book I, chapter 5, pages 62 and following.] or says that he can never persuade himself that evil spirits, or demons, possess the power to afflict the elements and bodies.

Why so? How can Beausobre, a Christian by profession, though an acatholic, learned in the Gospel Scriptures and thoroughly instructed in the deeds performed by Christ the Lord and described by the apostles, dare to deny both the power and efficacy of exorcisms in driving out demons and the power and fury of demons themselves in exercising violence upon living creatures and inanimate things?

What else is this than to believe that Matthew, Mark, and Luke invented fables, either when they said that Jesus drove demons from bodies by a word, or when they described the two Gerasene men who met Christ, came out from the tombs, and had demons, and who were so savage that no one could pass along that road [Note: The Evangelists repeatedly testify that people were afflicted by unclean spirits, as is clear from Matthew 8:16, 31; Mark 1:24 and following; and Luke 8:28 and following.].

Furthermore, people could not be afflicted by unclean spirits if the Evangelists, without any ambiguity of language, did not relate that a blind and mute man was brought to Christ: “And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke.”

If, after recalling these and other similar deeds of Christ in Beausobre’s mind, he should still remain suspended and refuse to believe, I would bring forward the passage that St. Luke recorded concerning the father who brought his son to Christ. The boy had a mute spirit, and wherever it seized him, it threw him down; he foamed, gnashed his teeth, and became rigid.

Did not that evil spirit, at the presence and command of Christ the Lord, throw the boy to the ground, rolling about and foaming? Since the son had been tormented in this way from the earliest days of his childhood, the spirit often cast him into fire and water in order to destroy him.

If Beausobre will not yield to these and other certain arguments that we can set before him, and will not allow himself to be persuaded that Terebinthus, or Budda, was thrown to the ground and tormented by a demon and died, what business have we with a raging man devoid of reason, who reasons about religion only according to the impulse of his mind?

But if he should finally attribute these and similar effects, which we still occasionally observe, to diseases of rage or madness, what could be more absurd? The Evangelists’ statement would be wholly nonsensical, when Christ, by the authority of his voice, said: “Deaf and mute spirit, I command you, come out of him, and do not enter him again.”

No less inapplicable would be the cry of the unclean spirits tormenting the men in the synagogue: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?”

Or consider this other petition made by those same spirits to Christ: “If you cast us out from here, send us into the herd of swine.” Then, immediately after they heard the Lord’s voice, “Go,” they went out into the swine; and behold, the entire herd rushed headlong into the sea and perished in the waters.

Experience teaches us that such expressions can have no relation whatsoever to rage, madness, or any other diseases. Diseases are cured; they are not expelled in such a way that they can migrate from one living body into another through a vital progression. We have never heard diseases themselves cry out, emit voices, or make requests. Rather, it is the sick themselves, who are seized by illnesses and feel the force and pain of their afflictions, who break out into cries and howls of grief, asking us to provide them with treatment and relief.

The Jewish people admired this power and authority of Christ the Lord in expelling evil spirits from human bodies. Although there were certainly wicked slanderers who claimed that he used sorcery and tricks to drive out demons, they could not deny that the elements and bodies were sometimes afflicted by evil spirits.

He restrained that accusation—“He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” [Note: Matthew 8:32; Luke 9:10 and following, and 11:15 and following; Mark 9:16.]—along with its authors, adding: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.”

By this manner of speaking it was indicated that the power to exorcise possessed persons had also been given to certain other sons of the synagogue, who could publicly testify that they had driven out demons not by magic but by the name of Christ and by the power and finger of almighty God.

And, most remarkably relevant to our subject, consider what Mark narrated concerning John addressing Christ: “Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, one who does not follow us, and we forbade him.”

But lest John and the other apostles and disciples persuade themselves that the power to exorcise and the force of exorcisms depended upon human ability, Christ immediately commanded them not to forbid him and added: “For there is no one who performs a mighty deed in my name and can soon speak evil of me.”

Let Beausobre the mocker now come forward and consider for himself where the power of exorcisms comes from, what exorcisms contain, to whom the power of exorcising was ultimately given, and then let him mock, if he can, that sacred rite which the Catholic Roman Church has always retained as received from the Son of God.

That the power and efficacy of exorcisms derive from the name of Jesus has been established sufficiently and abundantly from the sacred Scriptures. For there is no other name under heaven given to us by which we must be saved. Above all, at the invocation of that name every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

It is therefore not surprising that, when that name is invoked in exorcisms, the sacred ministers of the Church obtain such protection and authority that, after the evil spirits of demons have been driven far away from the bodies of possessed persons, those who had previously been grievously tormented may afterward, like Magdalene, from whom Jesus had driven seven demons [Note: Mark 9:37; Luke 9:49; Luke 8:2.], suffer no disturbance or diabolical fury at all.

When we turn our attention to the nature or purpose of exorcisms, we immediately understand what they are and what they contain. They cannot be of such a kind that they appear to share anything with magical incantations, since they were instituted by God himself rather to overthrow enchantments.

Beausobre therefore reasons with excessive cunning and malice when he equates these sacred and divine rites with superstitious incantations.

That prayer joined with fasting can also drive out spirits more wicked than the others, Christ himself declared. When certain people asked why his disciples had not freed the demoniac who had been brought to them, he answered: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.”

Let Beausobre therefore see, and finally understand, what ought to be said about this power granted to the ministers of the Church. That the priests and evangelists of Jesus Christ, the sacred ministers of the law, received authority and power over demons is most clearly attested by the Evangelists Luke, Matthew, and Mark.

They said first that, when Christ was sending the apostles to preach the Gospel, he gave them power and authority over all demons [Note: Matthew 10:1; Mark 3:16; Luke 6:13 and 9:1; Luke 7:22.].

Again, concerning the other seventy-two disciples whom he had sent two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come, we read that when they returned from their ministry they said, without any dissimulation of mind or ambiguity of speech: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

If Beausobre, driven only by the desire to quarrel and curse, should attempt to pervert ecclesiastical and divine law and maintain that the power and authority under discussion accompanied only the apostles and disciples of Christ for the destruction of pagan religion and the overcoming of Jewish faithlessness and unbelief, we could in no way accept his assertions.

For it is more broadly established that this power to drive away demons will endure perpetually in the Church, and that it can be exercised equally by good and bad ministers. Luke provides a splendid testimony to this. When Christ was to judge the wicked ministers of the Church, he would by no means grant them the crown of merit and glory, although they would say: “Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name?”

For those who use the power and authority of their ministry but do not seek to conform themselves to Jesus Christ in good morals cannot thereby become worthy of the Savior of humanity, Jesus.

Once anyone understands that enough has been said concerning the power of exorcisms in driving out demons, it will be not at all difficult to persuade the benevolent Catholic reader that Budda, or Terebinthus, a most wicked magician, agitated and struck by demons, suffered a cruel death and was suddenly deprived of the enjoyment of the light of the present life.

At last, Beausobre openly denies that he suffered such an evil death [Note: Beausobre, vol. I, p. 1; chap. 5, p. 63], and, employing the language of a mountebank, has dared with all the effort of his mind to confuse this Budda with another man bearing that name, the pseudo-apostle and disciple Manes. He therefore becomes more generous toward him, granting him a longer life and extending his days to the time when Manes, more renowned for his impieties, had sent here and there twelve proclaimers of his false doctrines to overthrow the evangelical teaching of Christ the Lord. If we judged this painstaking fiction to possess merely the appearance of truth, the present work of our labor would already be useless; it would not merely falter but collapse altogether. And Beausobre’s flatterers, who have hitherto applauded the history of the Manichaeans written by an un-Catholic author, would now have more reason to laugh than to lament, since we would have wished in vain to overturn and remove so many heretical and foolish fables with which that celebrated history is filled.

Meanwhile, let no one be angry with me if, in removing Beausobre’s preceding absurdities, I have not employed the testimonies of the ancient holy Fathers, so that from them readers might more clearly recognize that the text of Sacred Scripture cannot undergo any other interpretation, nor be violently distorted, in order to signify certain kinds of illnesses consisting in the struggle and conflict of humors, spirits, and nerves—conditions which the ancient experts in medicine called “demoniacs” only by analogy with disease. For if we wished even now to examine this type of argument, we would have to expend a great deal of work and would seem to wander, as it were, outside the order of our disputation. For Beausobre neither did nor could set against us, in support of his own studies and party, only one ancient writer of the Catholic Church. He understood very well that the Greek and Latin Fathers of the Church had agreed among themselves in explaining the Scriptural passages just mentioned; they likewise asserted the force and power of the order of exorcists for driving out demons and adorned it with the highest praises.

It was therefore unnecessary to appeal to Tradition, the interpreter of Sacred Scripture. Nevertheless, lest we seem to neglect the authority of the holy Fathers, I shall not hesitate for the present to add one or two testimonies of Saint Leo the Great, especially since we intend to direct our study toward illustrating the writings of this holy pontiff, doctor of the Catholic and apostolic See. In explaining, then, the preceding words of Saints Matthew, Luke, and Mark, he interprets them concerning the spirits of demons with absolutely no ambiguity of language or verbal obscurity, considering the savagery with which the bodies of the possessed are accustomed to be tortured and at the same time indicating the command by which they are accustomed to be driven away, especially when the prayers of exorcists are joined with fasting [Note: Matthew 17:20; Mark 9:28]. Accordingly, when he proclaims a fast in the seventh month, he urges that it be observed by the faithful with greater devotion. For, he says:

> In every contest of Christian struggle, the benefit of self-restraint is of the greatest value, so that some of the most savage spirits of demons, which are driven from the bodies of the possessed by no commands of exorcists, are expelled solely by the power of fasting and prayers, the Lord saying: “This kind of demon is not driven out except by fasting and prayer.” The prayer of one who fasts is pleasing to God and terrifying to the devil.

[Note: Saint Leo the Great, letter to the bishops established throughout Sicily, chap. 6, and Sermon 81.]

Besides this power granted to the ministers of the Church for expelling the spirits of demons from the bodies of the possessed, he also mentions another kind of exorcism, which priests and other sacred ministers customarily employ for the sanctification of catechumens before they are cleansed by the purification of baptism, so that their souls may be rescued from diabolical power. Thus, in his letter to the bishops of Sicily, he writes:

> Therefore, dearest brothers, since there exist so many and such great proofs by which, once every ambiguity has been removed, you clearly recognize that, in the case of the chosen who are to be baptized and who, according to the apostolic rule, must be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching, only two seasons are to be observed: Easter and Pentecost.

Let Beausobre take note, I beg, that the rite of exorcisms derives from no other source than Scripture and the rule of the apostles, as our most holy pontiff wished to indicate here, and as Pope Saint Siricius had affirmed before him in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona. Then let him criticize and attack, if he can, the custom of the Roman Church and the authority of sacred ministers in performing exorcisms and freeing men’s bodies and souls from demonic power. But let us now institute a new contest with Beausobre in the following chapter [Note: See Augustine, book II, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chap. 29, and the chapter *Sedis apostolicae*, attributed to Celestine, chap. 9]. In the meantime, we leave aside many other absurdities and futile conjectures of the same author, which in no way can belong to the ecclesiastical history we intend to write.

## CHAPTER IV  
### On Manes and His Principal Doctrines. Further Fictions of Beausobre Are Exposed and Overthrown

How Beausobre wished to trifle when describing the affairs and morals of Scythianus and Terebinthus, and how audaciously he turned his pen against the Fathers of both the Greek and Latin Churches, even distorting Sacred Scripture toward a perverse or violent interpretation, I believe was sufficiently explained in the preceding chapter. In that chapter I had also intended to report matters that appear to concern the person, homeland, parents, teaching, and errors of Manes. But when I learned that the substance of that chapter had grown too large because of Beausobre’s various arguments—most of which scarcely, or not even scarcely, related to the author’s purpose and to the aim of writing the history, and which might at times have caused our readers difficulty in examining them—I therefore judged it fairer and more prudent, lest our present method of disputation produce confusion, to speak separately here about Manes alone.

We were indeed confirmed in this decision when, while reading through two chapters of Beausobre—namely, the sixth and the seventh—we encountered so many matters of such a kind that, if we wished to answer each of them individually, we would extend our method of writing and disputing almost without limit. Therefore, following the plan of our undertaking, we have proposed to discuss and refute only those points that either undermine the tradition of the holy Fathers or injure and overthrow the sacred rites and doctrines of the Catholic Church, with great harm to souls.

Now, as we begin our discussion with that sixth chapter [Note: Beausobre, in the place cited above, pp. 65 ff.], to which Beausobre gives the following title, *Examination of the History of Manes before His Heresy*, he presents the testimonies of both Greeks and Latins—not in order to rely upon them, but, as he had already done in the preceding chapters concerning Scythianus and Terebinthus, to attack and harass the authors, and to maintain that their testimonies ought to be refuted by his own foolish commentaries.

### 1.

Beginning, then, to discuss the birth year and true name of Manes the Persian heretic, he subscribes to the opinion of our most learned friend Simon Assemani (vol. I, p. 393), who, following the Edessene Chronicle, has the following in his *Oriental Library*:

> Manes was born in the five hundred and fifty-first year; that year corresponds, according to the Greek era, to the two hundred and fortieth year of Christ.

Beausobre had long believed that the testimony of this Edessene Chronicle could be confirmed by another statement of Eutychius, in which one reads:

> Manes appeared in the world under the rule of Gordian.

Gordian, moreover, he says, was proclaimed emperor in the year of Christ 238 and remained in that office until the year 244. But a careful writer, such as Beausobre boasts himself to be, ought to have distinguished among the Gordians. For the elder Gordians usurped the empire in Africa while Maximinus was waging war with the Germans. They were subsequently killed not long afterward, and Balbinus and Pupienus held the empire together with the younger Gordian for one year. The former were slaughtered by the soldiers in the year 238. In that year, however, the son or grandson of that Gordian who was killed in Africa obtained the reins of empire; after winning several victories against the Persians, he was overthrown by order of Philip in the sixth year thereafter. [Note: Eutychius of Alexandria, in his *Chronicle*.]

When Beausobre subjected the history of Eutychius of Alexandria to a more careful examination, he discovered that it did not speak of the year of Manes’s birth, but of the heresy he had already published, on account of which he had been punished. On this occasion he thought it necessary to observe that Eutychius had fallen into a shameful anachronism by wishing to place the reign of Varanes I, king of the Persians and son of Hormisdas, in the third year of Gordian’s reign—a narrative that displays evident falsehood. [Note: Abulpharagius, *Dynasties*, p. 83.]

For Abulpharagius, a Syrian writer, says that Varanes I began to reign when the emperor Probus was proclaimed, namely in the year 276. But Beausobre ought to have noticed that Abulpharagius was mistaken, since, according to the most accurate chronological tables published by the distinguished Dionysius Petavius [Note: Petavius, *Rationarium Temporum*, vol. III, p. 146 of the Venetian edition], Varanes I obtained the kingdom after the death of Hormisdas, namely in the year 273, whereas the one who began to rule the Persians when Probus was proclaimed emperor was called Varanes II, and occupied that kingdom from the year 273 to the year 293. Since these matters are nevertheless of very minor importance, we consider it superfluous to dwell upon them. It is useful, however, to note that the Syrian writers to whom Beausobre continually intends to appeal are not entitled to unquestioned credibility.

### 2.
