Assemani reports that all the ancient writers said that Manes was Persian by origin. Whether, however, he was born in the province of Babylon or of the Chaldaeans does not appear equally certain. Saint Ephraem made him a Babylonian; and Archelaus, bishop in Mesopotamia, in the disputation he held with him, indicated clearly enough that he was Chaldaean by race. But Beausobre noted that Suidas and Cedrenus opposed these writers. Not adhering to the common belief, they wished to assign him another origin, namely that of the Brahmans. That region, extending toward the Ocean, acquired this name from a certain king so called; it was inhabited by people especially devoted to the study of religion and philosophy, as Cellarius mentioned in his commentaries on Ptolemy. More recently, certain devotees of novelty, driven by an appetite for reasoning, have tried by fabulous inventions to persuade people that the Brahmans were ultimately descended from Abraham. Furthermore, in explaining the etymology of that name, they wished to interpret the word *Brachma* as meaning a person thoroughly versed in knowledge of all things.

Those who are accustomed to dispute about the truth of matters only on the basis of sounder arguments now know fully that such forms of argument are frivolous. But who would think them unsuitable for a man whose intellect is always ready to invent? Especially since Beausobre himself devotes his study and industry to appealing to authors who are always in disagreement with one another, so that he may gradually reach the goal he has set for himself: namely, to persuade people with every effort that no credence at all should be given to historical matters handed down and recorded by the ancients.

But since these things may be known to everyone, let us proceed with our subject—namely, to those matters about which Beausobre appears to indulge in fable when he proposes to discuss the heretic’s paternal and birth name. “The Latin writers,” he says, “called him Corbicius, the Greeks Cubricus; but Augustine, in his book *On Heresies*, departing from both of them through the carelessness of his copyist, called him Urbicus.” Beausobre then reasons without an authority that these three names, as though corrupted from the word *Carcubius*, perhaps the homeland of Manes, situated in the Babylonian or Chaldaean region, may be derived from it. He chiefly maintains that this can be inferred because we understand the earlier forms, *Corbicus* and *Cubricus*, to have neither the ending nor the sound of Oriental words.

He offers various conjectures in support of this opinion. One, he thinks, is supplied by the city of Carcoub, or Carcub, which Assemani mentions in writing about Oriental affairs [Note: Assemani, *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, vol. III, part II, p. 744]. From this native place, he persuades himself, the words *Corbicius* and *Cubricus* derived their origin, since all their radical elements are preserved. He draws another conjecture from the supposedly presbyteral rank with which he believes Manes was honored among Christians. When Manes held this office, he says, in Ahvaz, or Ehvaz—the chief place of a small province formerly ruled by the Chaldaeans—and since at that time priests and bishops were not appointed except from cities or at least territories in which they were to exercise their sacred ministries, so that both the institutions of the families from which they originated and their character might be known to those whom they were to govern, he therefore concludes that Manes was born in the province in question. From this conjecture he draws the following inference: Since that province of Ahvaz has within its district a city called Carcoub, or Carcub, it may be concluded that the heretic was called *Carcubius* from his homeland.

### 3.

The arguments Beausobre invented to overthrow the ancient tradition and introduce a new form of ecclesiastical discipline do not merely totter but collapse entirely if we attend to his method of reasoning. First, then, the name *Carcubius*, which was unknown to the ancients, since it is derived from the place or city in which Manes was born, can now be common to all the inhabitants of that place and city. How, therefore, could it have been proper to Manes? How could the ancients have used it to designate this particular heretical man?

Perhaps this could have happened because Manes’s grandfather or great-grandfather built that city of Carcub; or because they acquired such great renown in honor of their homeland through their notable deeds that they received a surname from their native soil, as we understand happened with Antenor, Romulus, Constantine, Aelius Hadrian, Antinous, and other men. But this way of reasoning is prohibited by the consideration of the effort made by the heretic: namely, after the widow who had adopted him as her son and heir had died, he took care to reject his birth name and assume another, more honorable, for himself.

Indeed, all the writers agree that the name *Cubricus* signified something disgraceful or implied a servile condition. Christopher Wolfius, Gataker, Menage, and the other more recent writers support this view. They say that, so as not to bring a mark of reproach upon his domestic condition, he changed it to *Manes*. If, therefore, the name *Cubricus* had referred to his homeland rather than to servitude, he would never have changed it, as Wolfius appears to reason in his notes on Photius’s *History against the Manichaeans*.

“I pass over,” he says, “that a servile name can bring disgrace upon a free man, but cannot impose servitude. Meanwhile,” he adds, “one may wonder that a man exchanged a servile name for another no less servile one. For *Manes*, at least among the Greeks, was a name of servitude”—a fact that Gataker, book I, and Menage, in his notes to Diogenes Laertius, p. 215, have made so evident from passages of the ancients that doubt would be impious.

Among the Greeks, therefore, the name *Manes* indicated disgrace and servitude just as much as that of *Cubricus*, although in the Persian language *Manes* signified an eloquent man and one vigorous in disputation, as the ancient writers handed down. The Greeks, on the other hand, adopted that name merely to suggest a madman, as is taught by Cyril of Jerusalem [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6; Epiphanius, heresy 66; Titus of Bostra, in his books written against the Manichaeans], Epiphanius, Titus of Bostra, and others who discussed the name.

Beausobre attacks and derides these writers as authors of absurdities and frivolous observations. He then inveighs especially against Epiphanius because Epiphanius wrote that divine Providence had arranged for the heretic to assume a name signifying madness, so that the Greeks, who detested that name, might preserve themselves from the errors Manes had taught.

“But,” he adds, “a Manichaean could reply that Epiphanius thought or reasoned wrongly about the arrangements of Providence, since the multitude of Greeks who were ensnared by the allurements of this heresy had already rendered ineffective the plan and arrangements that Epiphanius boasts of.”

Who, without serious agitation of mind, could consider this perverse and impious Beausobrian criticism? Do the counsel and arrangements of divine Providence impose a necessity upon human minds, so that their wickedness does not attempt to withdraw from them and is not very often able to frustrate them?

For our first parents were given the forbidden tree as a defense of original innocence and a protection against death—death, which they themselves ought to have dreaded as the most terrible of all things. But what happened? Deceived by the allurements of appetite and the serpent’s suggestions, having cast off their horror of death, they seized the forbidden fruit with reckless daring and ate from it.

Moreover, to omit other examples drawn from the divine writings, was it not arranged by divine Providence that prisons, chains, crosses, torturers, and names and characteristics full of horror should exist for the preservation of the rights of justice, the protection of the commonwealth, and the maintenance of tranquility? The purpose was that, restrained by fear of punishments, human beings might avoid crimes lest they be forced to undergo those evils.

If, then, no one—unless sacrilegious—could answer that God had arranged less wisely in His providence by threatening our first parents with death, which their nature most greatly dreaded, in order to turn them away from eating and desiring the forbidden food; if only foolish people would assert that so many and such great kinds of punishments had been wrongly devised for the vengeance of criminals and established by the holiest laws, I do not see with what face Beausobre could censure and ridicule Epiphanius because he wrote that divine Providence had arranged for Manes to assume a name full of horror, so that his heresy would be detested by the Greeks.

That name could indeed arouse a certain horror in Greek minds, just as do death, prisons, chains, scourges, crosses, massacres, and torturers. But the Greeks themselves, who had elsewhere been imbued with the depraved principles of Manichaean philosophy and took the greatest pleasure in sensual allurements and immoralities, easily shook off every horror that might have preserved them from such defilements and chose to profess the practices of that wicked sect.

For the present we consider it superfluous to report the other etymologies of this name described by Beausobre [Note: Beausobre discusses other etymologies of this name in part I, chap. 6, pp. 70 ff.]; nevertheless, let the reader consult § 5 of this chapter.

### 4.

As for the priesthood of Manes, we do not deny that Gregory Abulpharagius asserts it without any authority. But I do not see how much credibility we can give him, especially since he describes Manes at the outset as though he were one of the Doctors of the Catholic Church: a man who taught and interpreted the sacred books of Scripture, who was accustomed to dispute with Jews, Magi, and pagans, and who finally departed from the faith and called himself the Messiah.

Now, if we examine this testimony of Abulpharagius [Note: Abulpharagius, *Dynasties*] and reduce it to the true rules of criticism, several features appear to bear signs of falsehood. First, I pass over the fact that none of the Fathers and writers of the third and fourth centuries spoke of such Manichaean actions or of his priesthood, lest I be accused of employing negative arguments to weaken the positive assertion of a Syrian writer—although Beausobre himself reasons almost always by means of similar indications.

Yet I cannot conceal the conduct especially of Cyril of Jerusalem. In his *Catechesis*, while describing the more serious crimes of Manes, he gave no indication, even slight, of this matter—something he certainly would not have omitted if the heretic, initially enrolled in the clerical ranks and priesthood, had fallen into that dreadful and monstrous sacrilege. For he would have set it before those whom he was enlightening as something supremely detestable.

Unless we wished to suppose that Cyril was unaware of the man’s priesthood, or at least wished to conceal it lest the other sacred priests and their order be brought into hatred and contempt among certain pagans and Jews then residing at Jerusalem. But let us imagine that Cyril wished to employ this policy in order to protect the honor of the priesthood. Must the same then be asserted concerning the other writers who described Manichaean affairs? Away with such a fiction.

For all those who spoke of Xenaia [Note: See the acts of the Council of Constantinople under Agapetus, Roman pontiff, and Menna, patriarch, vol. V of the *General Councils*], Severus of Sozopolis, Peter of Apamea, Zoara, and Isaac the Persian did not at all conceal their priesthood or clerical rank. They judged that no harm or disgrace could thereby come upon the priesthood of Christ if they declared that men polluted by the gravest crimes and the stain of heresy were to be held in the utmost hatred—men who, most shamefully departing both from the holiness of the priesthood and from the institutions of the sacred ministries, undermined themselves and the divine mysteries by their wicked crimes.

Who, moreover, is unaware that the sect of the Manichaeans, hiding under the name of the Acephali in the sixth century of the Church, strove to secure the support of the Caesars and emperors of the East, so that ecclesiastical men might more easily and gradually turn women away from nuptials and marriage and corrupt and debauch them through unspeakable and sacrilegious acts of impurity?

The acts of the Constantinopolitan synod under Agapetus, Roman pontiff, and Menna, patriarch of Constantinople; the letters of Pope Hormisdas; and many other documents that will be encountered for reading there clearly reveal that, under the name of the Acephali, during the sixth century of the Church, the Manichaeans occupied the principal sees of the East and spread the perverse doctrines and practices of this sect in various places, as we ourselves shall demonstrate more appropriately, with due attention to the sequence of events.

If, then, the Fathers of the councils and the ancient writers neither sought to conceal nor concealed the priesthood or other clerical orders with which certain members of the Manichaean sect had been honored; if, moreover, those who assembled at the Council of Gangra [Note: See vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 423] did not pass over in silence the priestly order and monastic profession of Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, who in the fourth century of the Church, shortly before the Council of Nicaea was convened, devoted every effort to propagating the Manichaean sect and its practices; then I plainly do not see why, among so many and such great writers who discussed Manes, only Gregory Abulpharagius should assert that he had been initiated into the priesthood.

We therefore judge it more probable that Manes pretended to be a presbyter, and did not shrink from exercising the functions of presbyters in a sacrilegious and reckless imitation. We believe that we may reason in this way on the basis of the following conjecture: without the necessary mission of the Spirit of the Lord, he did not fear to fabricate himself as an apostle and Paraclete of Jesus Christ. By means of those false names and offices, he sought to acquire authority among simpler men and women, so that, more easily deceived, they might render him complete faith and obedience. They would certainly not have granted these to him if they had not known him to perform the offices and ministries of religion.

Finally, everyone can see how weak and false is the conjecture on which Beausobre insists in order to support the homeland and presbyterate of Manes. Indeed, those who are well versed in reading sacred ecclesiastical history will be fully persuaded that he is selling words and fictions. They know especially that, in the first centuries of the Church, when the Catholic religion had to be propagated, priests and bishops were scarcely ever chosen from the places or regions in which they had been born. Rather, the apostles and their successors invested them with sacred orders and sent them to foreign nations; their character and the practices of their proven discipline were sufficiently and abundantly known. We ourselves have demonstrated this amply, in almost innumerable passages, together with Eusebius of Caesarea, in another work we have prepared.

### 5.

Let us now proceed to the other meanings that Beausobre claims are applicable to the name *Manes*, considering the Persian and Syrian idioms and the differing manner of expression used by the Fathers. We shall briefly explain whatever he has reported from the opinions of others.

He asserts, on the authority of Epiphanius, Archelaus, and Ephraem the Syrian, that the word signifies “vessel,” “instrument,” and “garment.” But who does not understand that these celebrated Fathers wished rather to allude to the characteristics of Manichaean conduct than to the genuine meaning of that word? More reasonably, Archelaus calls him “a vessel of wickedness” and “an instrument of Antichrist,” following the phrases of Scripture and especially the manner of expression used by Saint Paul, who declares the subverters of the Gospel and of the Catholic law to be both vessels and instruments of wickedness and Antichrists. It is clear that these names apply to them only when considered in relation to their conduct.

In the same way, Saint Ephraem, cited by Assemani, explains that Manes was clothed in the form and garment of the devil, writing:

> The devil clothed Manes as though in his own garment, so that he might abuse him as his instrument and bring forth his oracles through him.

[Note: He relies upon the metaphorical formulas used by the Fathers when speaking of Manes, and from them seeks to infer the genuine meaning of that name. In my judgment, Beausobre wished to trifle by reasoning in this way, since the Fathers intended by those terms rather to indicate the conduct, false doctrines, and perverse practices adopted by the heretic.]

Since such characteristics apply to all heretics who subvert the Gospel of Christ, I entirely fail to see why they maintain that these characteristics derive from the name of Manes alone. Otherwise, the authors of every false sect would have to be called *Manetes*, since they are vessels and instruments of the devil, and the devil clothes them in his own garment so that he may bring forth his oracles through them.

After this, he attacks Cyril of Jerusalem, who judged that the Persians used the word *Manes* to signify speech. Manes himself, however, affirms in his letter to Marcellus that the eloquence of such speech was not suitable to him. He then rejects as foolish and playful Pearson’s observation that, following the interpretation of the rabbis, he thinks *Manes* is derived from *min*, which signifies a heretical person.

But who can invent a name to which a mark of disgrace and shame was attached and which was common to all the authors of false sects, especially when we find that this name was imposed upon him by no one other than himself? It is therefore not credible that he deliberately abandoned the word *Cubricus*, signifying servitude, in order to adopt another which, if it did not display greater, at least displayed equal, disgrace and infamy—such as *Manes* would be according to Pearson’s opinion. Nevertheless, Pearson maintains that *ὁ Μάνης* (*To Manes*) was originally a title rather than a name, derived from the Hebrew *min*, which signifies “heretic” [Note: Alb. Fabritius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. V, p. 281].

Thomas Hyde, however, states that the name *mani* was interpreted differently by the Persians, proving that it denoted a painter [Note: Hyde: “Manes the Persian is called *Manis* in their books, ‘painter,’ for such was his profession”]. Beausobre says that Wolfius followed the same opinion, writing that Thomas Hyde’s etymology, which he presents in chap. 21, p. 280, of *The Religion of the Ancient Persians*, derives from the substance of the Persian language. For, rejecting Epiphanius’s etymology, Hyde testifies that Manes was properly called *MANI*, because among the Persians the word has the meaning “painter.”

### 6.

Yet who will regard what we have hastily noted thus far concerning the etymologies and meanings of that name as bringing disgrace and dishonor upon this man, unless it is immediately compared with the other matters he adds concerning the word *Manes*?

Beausobre therefore brings forward the opinion of Ussher of Armagh, who, relying upon a certain testimony of Sulpicius Severus [Note: Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book I, 49; Ussher, *Annals*, vol. I, year 3035, p. 82; 2 Kings 15:14, 16], asserts that a certain king of the Israelites was called *Manes*. Yet in the Second Book of Kings he is read as having been called *Manahem*, and by the Seventy interpreters *Manaem*. Beausobre persuades himself that these names correspond to the two other names, “Paraclete” and “Comforter.”

Beausobre asserts that this is a simple and natural origin of the word *Manes*; and because he believed it more honorable than the others, he judged that it ought not merely to be preferred to all the rest but also presented himself as ready to resolve all the knots and difficulties he encountered in it, so as gradually to persuade his readers of it as well.

Undertaking, therefore, to resolve and remove these alleged knots and difficulties, he first thinks it more probable that *Manes* could be formed from *Manaem*, especially in view of the manner of speech and usage of the Orientals. Since it is customary for the Greeks to omit the final letter *m* of these words, they consequently turned them into *Manes*, just as it is established that they did with *Budda*, making *Buddas*.

He falsely claims that Augustine supports this first conjecture when, in his book *On Heresies*, he calls the heretic in question *Manin*, not *Manes*, following the usage of the Latins, who wish the Greek *e* to be changed into *i*. He proves that Augustine was also accustomed to observe this rule by the example of *Adimantus*. For Augustine judged that it should not be written *Adamantus*, but *Adimantus* in Latin.

In the same way, Theodoret wished to write *Manens*, not *Manes*. Suidas appears to support him, saying that the genitive case is *Manentis*. This ought to be an argument that the nominative should be read *Manens*.

Now Beausobre seems to flatter and indulge himself in the belief that he has discovered and explained the genuine origin of the word *Manes*. Therefore he hastens to advance to the other word, *Manichaeus*, by which not only his disciples customarily called the father of their heresy, but also an almost innumerable multitude of writers used that same term.

He asserts that this latter word too must be assigned the same derivation of origin, from the Chaldaean word *Manahem*. Nor does he admit any other distinction between the two names except that which ordinarily arises from different modes of pronunciation and from the flexibility and alterations of human speech. He claims that this can be proved from Pagninus, Junius, and Tremellius. For, using different letter-forms, they write and pronounce *Menaehem* and *Manachem* in different ways, while the Greeks themselves, wishing to add new letters to the words just mentioned, formed *Manichaeus*.

### 7.

Whether these conjectures are sound or mistaken, those learned in Greek and the Oriental languages will be able to judge more carefully. For our part, we cannot at all subscribe to Beausobre’s manner of fabricating explanations. Since names are, in a certain sense, the designations of all things, expressing their origins and properties, these properties are now entirely obliterated—or at least altered—by the addition of letters and by their subtraction according to the arbitrary discretion of individuals. Hence it seems to me that Cicero wished to rescue, or at least snatch away, such abuse from the excessive and vehement human appetite for philosophizing, when he wrote:

“Since you think that Neptune was named from swimming, there will be no name whose origin you cannot explain by changing a single letter.”

[Note: Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, 72.]

What, then, are we presently to judge concerning all the many alterations and additions of letters that we find in those names which Beausobre has collected in order to establish the origin and properties of the word *Manes*? But even if we grant outright that his method of argument ought not to be called frivolous or fanciful, what follows from it? Will *Manes* now be a name of honor because, in the Scriptures of the Old Testament, one of the kings of the Israelites was called by that name? Was not the name Judah likewise honorable and especially praiseworthy in that same Testament? Yet if we consult the New Testament, we shall find that one man—who had been a disciple of Christ and was called Judas—was impious, a traitor, sacrilegious, and the source of many evils. Did he therefore also possess a royal origin, and was the scepter of the Israelites owed to him? Away with such fiction!

But since it might be considered a fault to dwell too long on these matters, we shall pass over almost innumerable examples that would more forcefully expose Beausobre’s errors and overthrow his foolish conjectures. What, then, should be said about the name *Paraclete*, which Manes rashly assumed for himself? We shall now explain this from Leo the Great and others, in order to refute Beausobre’s remaining false conjectures more fully.

### 8. On the doctrines of Manes

As we now begin to discuss Manes’s doctrines, we must first report that which furnished the foundation for all the rest, and upon which that entire structure of sacrilege and fables had been built by that most impious architect.

First of all, we are confronted by that monstrous blasphemy into which Manes broke as soon as he began to spread his wicked heresy among the people. Thus, with sacrilegious boasting, he gloried in a divine power supposedly given to him, both to display the power and authority of the supreme God and to win for himself the faith and veneration of the peoples. At one moment he tried to present himself as assuming the form of Christ; at another he proclaimed that he himself was the Paraclete.

Beausobre calls this latter claim into question. Although compelled by the testimony of others, he does not dare to deny that Manes was called the Paraclete and the Comforter [Note: Beausobre first denies this in the general preface, vol. I, p. 11, and again in book I, chapter 6.], yet he maintains that Manes obtained this designation rather from the widow who had adopted him as her son and heir. After first granting him his freedom, she supposedly wished to have him as the comfort of her widowhood and old age. He says that he cannot imagine that the world and its people were so foolish as to put faith in such a crude contrivance and allow themselves to be deceived by it.

It therefore seems more consistent with reason, he argues, that after his condition as a slave had been changed through the kindness of his benefactress, Manes wished to add some syllable to his name, and, as though made a new man by his freedom, thereafter called himself *Manahem*. He attempts to prove, on the testimony of the learned Assemani [Note: Assemani, vol. I of the *Oriental Library*, p. 204; vol. II, p. 388.], that this name was highly honorable, since Assemani writes that the name *Maanus* was familiar both to Syrian and Arab kings.

Yet Beausobre either entirely concealed or refused to notice that Eusebius of Caesarea opposed these fanciful conjectures (vol. I, book I, chapter 6). Eusebius, who could not have taken his account of Manes’s deeds from Cyril of Jerusalem or Epiphanius, since he was earlier than those writers, but drew it from more ancient records preserved in the archives of the churches—as he testifies in his preface while composing his history of the Church—says that in the time of Pope Felix:

“A certain Manes, insane in accordance with his name and driven on by the prompting of a demon, teaches a heresy hateful and detestable to all.”

[Note: Eusebius of Caesarea, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 26. Saint Augustine agrees with this in book II of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*.]

Here, then, Eusebius gives the heretic’s genuine name and explains its etymology and meaning; at the same time, he indicates the demonic assistance by which Manes spread his errors in every direction. He again mentions there that Manes acquired this madness—or frenzy—through demonic art, and he appeals to the outcome of Manes’s deeds in order to persuade his readers of the point. Accordingly, immediately after this, in order to prove what he had said, he adds the passage we cited shortly before:

“At one moment he tried to assume the form of Christ; at another he proclaimed that he himself was the Paraclete.”

[Note: See what we wrote in chapter II of this book.]

Eusebius therefore intended to establish three things: first, that the heretic was called *Manes*, not *Manahem*, by the Persians; second, that frenzy, audacity, and madness had been brought to completion in him through the power of the demon; and third, that he falsely imitated the form and likeness of Christ the Lord, and proclaimed himself to be the Paraclete sent for the consolation and instruction of the world and the Church.

Who cannot see that these three points utterly overthrow Beausobre’s fanciful conjectures? For if Manes was already attempting to persuade his disciples of all his sacrilegious inventions, he would first have devised the claim that he was an apostle of Christ and the comforter of humankind, pretending that he had been sent by Christ.

And lest I seem to attack and censure Beausobre unjustly as a fabulist, allow me to appeal to Leo the Great, pontiff of the Roman Church. When he undertook a general investigation of the Manichaeans hiding in Rome, he carefully sought to discover what they believed and what they dared to teach as Manes’s disciples. He expressly explained, in the following words, that the Manichaean disciples had believed—or at least proclaimed—this blasphemy:

“His disciples, wishing to appear to follow a great and sublime author, believed that the Holy Spirit had appeared in their master Manes, and that the Paraclete promised by the Lord had not come before this wretched deceiver arose. In him the Spirit of God had so dwelt that Manes himself was none other than the Spirit, who through the ministry of bodily voice and tongue would lead his disciples into all truth.”

[Note: This sermon on Pentecost, in earlier editions, was mutilated and disordered in various places; with the assistance of ancient manuscripts we have restored it to its integrity. In some later printed editions the first two words, “His disciples,” are missing. The reader may observe more concerning this sacrilegious blasphemy of Manes on pp. 19, 24, and 99 of the disputation held with Archelaus, which the learned Laurentius Alexander Zacagnius, prefect of the Vatican Library, committed to print with scholarly notes.]

The truth of the facts must therefore prevail and remove every contrary conjecture of Beausobre. Indeed, we may confidently persuade ourselves that by this principal and most blasphemous lie Manes opened the way to all the many sacrilegious doctrines that either corrupt or utterly overthrow the more sacred mysteries of the Catholic faith. But let us return to the order of the history.

### 9.

For this reason, then, the heretic attempted to acquire books of Sacred Scripture with money; and, in order to draw Christian men to himself by enticements, he mixed certain truths with lies and fables. By this device, while striving to make his sect appear more credible, he gradually instilled his errors into the minds of others. He further reinforced all this with magical arts and illusions, which he certainly used to deceive people, while he did not shrink from attempting things that were at times entirely impossible by human and demonic powers. Such was the case when he unsuccessfully attempted to cure the son of the king of Persia, who was deprived of the assistance of physicians and suffering from a severe illness.

[Note: See what we shall say against Beausobre in the following sixth chapter.]

Having thus laid these sacrilegious and superstitious foundations, he disseminated other doctrines—Eusebius says—borrowed from various heretics who had already been extinguished, and with Persian poisons weakened and utterly corrupted the Catholic religion.

Among the other fictions borrowed from Marcion, Valentinus, Capocrates, and other leaders of the Gnostic sect, the following are customarily numbered. He taught that there were two principles of all things, namely God and the devil; that all good things were produced by the former and all evil things by the latter; that the former was the source of all virtue and perfection, from whom he derived the New Testament, while the latter was the author of sin and of the Old Testament. He taught that the substance of human beings had been produced by both gods, but in such a way that the good God created souls alone, whereas material bodies, as imperfect and always subject to corruption and change, derived their origin only from the other, evil god.

He entirely removed free will from human beings, introducing fate and necessity into human affairs. He further denied the true incarnation of Christ, maintaining that Christ had assumed only a phantom body.

[Note: Manes intended to defend this error in the disputation he held with Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, and said: “Far be it from me to confess that the Lord Jesus Christ descended through the natural sexual organs of a woman.” Then, bringing forward passages from the four Evangelists, which he interpreted violently, he added: “There are also countless other testimonies of this kind, which indicate that he came and was not born.” See the *Collection of Ancient Monuments of the Greek and Latin Church* by Laurentius Zacagnius, p. 85.]

He taught the peoples other doctrines of the same kind which, as we have said, had been taken partly from the most polluted pools of the ancient heresiarchs, partly from the absurd opinions of pagan philosophers, and partly from the perversely explained principles of the Christian religion itself. All these senseless fables and fabricated dreams were described much more clearly by Saint Epiphanius.

By these and other sacrilegious doctrines, Manes attempted to make himself greater and more renowned than the founders of the other heresies. Meanwhile, that most cunning impostor, wishing to display great authority among human beings and to lead especially the common people—who look only at the surface of things—to his own opinions, contrived to imitate Christ the Lord, Savior of the human race, both in the selection of disciples and in matters belonging to the apostolic mission.

This will become clearer in the following chapter, when we begin to discuss the number of his disciples.

## CHAPTER V  
### The number of Manes’s pseudo-apostles established from the Holy Fathers. The opinion of Father Natalis Alexander reported and rejected.

Eusebius of Caesarea first briefly described Manes’s method of spreading the errors of his heresy, saying (book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 27):

“Exalted in madness,” he says, “he chose twelve disciples, after the likeness of Christ, and sent them out to preach.”

All the ancient writers agree with Eusebius, if we except one. The more recent writers likewise support him, among whom is Beausobre, as we shall observe in its proper place. I therefore consider Father Natalis Alexander, otherwise a most learned man, not to be heard on this point. In discussing the number of Manes’s disciples, he was led, I do not know by what hallucination, to increase that number to twenty-two on the authority of Augustine.

In the meantime, he writes (*Ecclesiastical History*, century 3, article 9):

“Drawing many disciples into his error, he selected TWENTY-TWO preachers of his wicked doctrines and impious fables, among whom he wished three to be especially distinguished: THOMAS, HERMAS, and ADDA.”

I say that he is not to be heard. For how would Manes have attempted to imitate Christ the Lord in establishing his disciples if he had chosen others besides the twelve pseudo-apostles? Moreover, it is false that Father Natalis’s opinion has Augustine as its supporter. Augustine, agreeing remarkably with Eusebius, defined Manes’s number of disciples as twelve alone. Indeed, the other ancient writers also followed this opinion, with the sole exception of Epiphanius.

40

Augustine could not have spoken more clearly or explicitly on this matter. He writes (*On Heresies*, chapter 46):

“Hence, in his writings, he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ, because Jesus Christ had promised that he would send, and in him sent, the Holy Spirit. For this reason Manichaeus himself also had twelve disciples, after the pattern of the apostolic office; and the Manichaeans still preserve this number.”

Theodoret likewise used no different expressions when discussing the fables of the heretics. In these few words he described the election of Manes’s disciples and his imitation of the pseudo-Christ (*Book I of the Compendium of Heretical Fables*, chapter 16):

“After designating twelve disciples in imitation of the Lord, he went forth into Mesopotamia.”

What more is needed? The consistent tradition of the following six centuries proved the truth of the matter under discussion. Photius briefly indicated the number of Manes’s disciples and their mission, saying:

“Then he gathered twelve disciples, whom he also sent out as heralds of his error.”

[Note: Photius, in the passage cited above, together with Wolf’s annotations.]

Peter of Sicily, who flourished somewhat later, was exceptionally well informed about Manichaean affairs and institutions. A man distinguished by learning and nobility, he had served on various embassies for the emperor Basil, especially among the Armenians. He committed to writing a history of the origin, progress, and decline of the Manichaeans. In it he not only listed individually the names of those twelve disciples, but also set out their deeds, offices, missions, writings, interpretations, and commentaries in his short Greek-Latin work addressed to the archbishop of Bulgaria.

This writer therefore says the following about Manes’s disciples:

“Moreover, the disciples of Manes the Antichrist were twelve in number.”

He then enumerates them. First he lists the man who succeeded Manes after Manes had been killed by order of the king of Persia, saying:

“Siginus, who succeeded Manes.”

He is followed by another whose name was Thomas, who composed the Gospel of the Manichaeans. Speaking of this Gospel, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem warned Catholics not to read it:

“Let no one read the Gospel according to Thomas.”

[Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6.]

“For he is not one of the twelve apostles, but one of the three disciples of Manes.”

This adulterous work was forbidden to all Catholics by the decrees of the Apostolic See, under penalty of anathema, whether to read it or to keep it in their possession, as we shall see in its proper place.

To these two he added Buddas and Herma, as well as Adantus and Adamantus. He had sent the last of these, as more wicked and audacious than the others, as his herald into various parts of the world and dispatched him as a faithful forerunner. He then appointed three others—namely, Hierax, Heraclides, and Apathonius—as interpreters and expounders of his doctrine and preaching. Finally, he added three more: Agapinus, who composed the *Heptalogue*, Zarvas, and Gabriarius.

Thus Peter of Sicily listed the first hierarchy of the Manichaeans, equally wicked and superstitious.

[Note: Peter of Sicily’s history of the Manichaeans was printed by the compilers of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XVI.]

Although he flourished long after the time of Manes, he nevertheless composed that work on the basis both of the ancient and consistent tradition of the Greeks and Armenians and of the most reliable records, as we shall see in its proper place.

Since this matter is supported by so many and such weighty testimonies, I do not think that Epiphanius was so seriously mistaken when, relying on I know not what foundation or testimony, he expressly stated concerning Manichaeus (*Heresy* 66, no. 3):

“For already the mountebank had gathered his band, whom he called disciples—twenty-two in number.”

But I think that the error should be attributed to the copyists or translators rather than to Epiphanius himself. Or perhaps he intended to allude not to the first hierarchy of the Manichaean sect, nor to its form and number, but to a later hierarchy, which had become larger and about which Augustine spoke elsewhere.

The hallucination of Father Natalis Alexander must be judged more shameful still. In discussing the errors of the Manichaeans, although he had examined Augustine’s works, he entirely failed to notice that the opinion concerning Manes’s twenty-two disciples was highly unstable and in grave danger of error. Or, at the very least, in order to clear himself of this charge, he ought to have set forth the arguments for both positions, so that the reader might choose the firmer and more probable one. Perhaps, however, the learned man, distinguished by his abundance of information and arguments, devoted himself to the opinion that first occurred to him, persuaded that Epiphanius, the most authoritative writer on the Manichaean sect, could not have been mistaken. We have had to note these points in order to forestall the charge of negligence.

Meanwhile, it is especially remarkable that Beausobre—accustomed always to search for a knot in a bulrush, so that he might assiduously overthrow the tradition of the ancient Fathers by pointing out their apparent contradictions and magnifying them—failed entirely to notice either that Epiphanius differed from the other writers on a matter of such importance, or that Father Natalis Alexander had appealed improperly to Augustine’s testimony in assigning eighteen disciples to Manes.

Beausobre therefore subscribes to the more common opinion, supposing and affirming that this heretic had twelve disciples. Among them, three more celebrated heralds, who first carried out the Manichaean mission and were more wicked than all the rest, he clearly mentioned in chapter 7 of his earlier book. There, as he begins to describe what happened to Manichaeus after the death of the widow whose inheritance he had acquired, he supposes that Manes abandoned the city of Seleucia, or Ctesiphon, which the Arabs call Modain, or, as Assemani reports, the city of Citez [Note: Assemani, vol. II, part II, p. 623.], where he had first been raised and educated in the study of various sciences. He supposes that Manes eventually withdrew to Huzitis, one of the provinces of Babylonian Iraq.

He supports this conjecture by relying on the *Acts of Archelaus*, in which it is said that the heretic had been brought up in the royal city of Persia, where the school of the sciences and of magic flourished most greatly.

[Note: Beausobre, book I, chapter 7, p. 75, § 1.]

“The Greeks,” he adds, “have made scarcely any mention of Manes’s life from his twelfth year all the way to his sixtieth.”

He further observes that this latter figure is reported differently in different copies of the disputation held with Archelaus. He reserves discussion of this matter for the point at which he will speak of the time when the holy bishop met Manes at Caschara.

Therefore, so that we may not appear to wander beyond the limits of our stated purpose, from that number of twelve disciples he mentions, as we said, the three who were superior to the others: namely, Thomas, Addas, and Herma. He observes that Cyril of Jerusalem placed Buddas in the place of Addas, as may also be seen in those authors who recorded the names of each of the twelve disciples and placed Buddas second rather than Addas.

[Note: Beausobre wrongly tried to identify this Addas with Terebinthus, or Buddas, in order to maintain that what the Holy Fathers wrote about the latter’s death was false. Accordingly, he invents that Buddas was Manes’s disciple, not his leader. See what we noted earlier, especially against Beausobre, who in book I, chapter 5, p. 62, denies that Buddas was put to death by divine agency, treating as a childish tale the account given by Cyril, Epiphanius, and other Fathers. He refuses to believe that Buddas was hurled from the height of a house by an angel, and instead maintains that Buddas was still alive when Manes publicly proclaimed his heresy and was compelled to suffer the penalty of his crime.]

I shall not dwell on these matters any longer, lest this be counted a fault. And although the non-Catholic writer adds various other details concerning the mission of these three disciples, nevertheless, lest we appear to violate the rules we have set for ourselves, we shall discuss their missions and offices elsewhere. For the present, we shall speak about the killing of the son of the king of Persia by Manes.

## 42. CHAPTER VI  
### On the killing of the son of the king of Persia perpetrated by Manes. Beausobre’s fictions and conjectures are entirely rejected. Manes, thrown into prison, corrupts the guards with money, escapes, and travels to the borders of Persia and Mesopotamia.

[Col. 0824D]

After choosing the twelve disciples and sending them into the various provinces of the East to spread this foolish and sacrilegious sect, Manes himself, desirous of acquiring greater fame and displaying some extraordinary and divine power superior to that of other human beings, turned over in his mind the idea of accomplishing something beyond nature.

He thought that the undertaking would succeed and bring him good fortune when he heard from common report that the son of the king of Persia had been seized by a serious illness and was lying ill in the royal city, from which Manes was then absent. We have already seen in the preceding chapter that the kings of Persia customarily inhabited either Seleucia or Ctesiphon. Tillemont notes that both cities were situated near the river Tigris.

[Tillemont, vol. IV, *On the Heresy of the Manichaeans*, article 7.]

According to Epiphanius, therefore, although Manes was far from the royal court, he did not delay in hastening there. Trusting in the books that Terebinthus had received from Scythianus, and that Manes himself had received from the widow, the heir of Terebinthus—or Buddas—he was confident that he could find some remedy by which he might immediately relieve the royal boy’s illness, to the admiration and applause of the entire Persian kingdom.

“But when he arrived there,” says Epiphanius, “he disclosed his intention and promised certain help to the king’s son. But his hope for the future deceived him. For when he had administered certain medicines to the sick boy, he was so frustrated in his expectation that the young man finally died in his hands, thereby exposing his empty promises and lies.”

Thus far Epiphanius.

[Note: Epiphanius, heresy 66; Beausobre, book I, chapter 7, § 11, p. 76.]

### 1.

Socrates described this event somewhat differently (*History*, book I, chapter 22). He says that the Manichaean did not hasten to the court voluntarily and boldly in order to cure the sick man, but that the king of Persia himself—who was moving heaven and earth for his son’s recovery—was influenced by Manes’s reputation and, believing the man’s wonders to be genuine, summoned him as an apostle, hoping, of course, that his son would be healed through Manes’s agency.

Whether Manes had attempted, before this danger arose, to perform some feat exceeding human powers with the aid of illusions, so that the reputation of his power reached the king himself, we simply do not know. It is likewise uncertain whether the worst of magicians actually administered some medicine to the sick boy, or merely pretended to do so, or whether he used only the assistance of magical art. We consider the last possibility more probable, relying on the testimony of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, who wrote (*Catechesis* 6):

“Manes, in order to boast of the power of his goodness and virtue, promised, as though he were a pious man, that he would cure him through prayer.”

Photius likewise did not tell the story differently. Indeed, following the writings of the ancients, which he himself had collected and examined with his own eyes, he supports not only Epiphanius, Socrates, and Cyril of Jerusalem, but, after briefly describing the mission of those twelve disciples whom Manes had taken as heralds of his impious doctrine and accomplices in every crime, immediately adds:

[Note: Photius, book I *Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 12, in Johann Christoph Wolf, p. 47.]

“But that madman Manes, having become famous through crime, became known by report even to the ears of the king of Persia. Since the king had a son suffering from illness and heard that Manes had promised to rescue his son from disease by his prayers, he employed the arrogant man to treat his son. Although the physicians then present promised that the illness could easily be cured, the king dismissed them. Manes had scarcely finished his prayer when he deprived of life the one who perhaps would not have suffered this fate if he had not promised to restore his health.”

43

Thus Beausobre alone, following certain foolish and contrived rules of his own criticism, attacks Archelaus, Cyril, and Epiphanius: because they did not hesitate to relate falsehoods; because Cyril himself wished to attribute to this heretic the appearance of a trickster or madman; and because Photius absurdly described the event with excessive and exaggerated embellishment.

He complains especially that Photius said:

“But that madman Manes, having become famous through crime…”

Since Beausobre understood that these words and those that followed were directed against him, he burst out with the following:

“When have rulers ever flattered themselves that they would obtain miracles of healing through the assistance of criminals?” he says.

Finally, he adds—and here he intends especially to mock Father Natalis Alexander—that more recent writers wrongly suppose that the heretic trusted in magical arts and illusions and therefore undertook to cure the king’s son.

[Note: Natalis Alexander, century III; *Acts of the Disputation with Archelaus*.]

He invents this supposed contradiction on the ground that these writers rely on the *Acts of Archelaus*, where Archelaus, in order to prove that the heretic in question was by no means the Paraclete promised in Scripture, said:

“This man, displaying not even a single sign or wonder…”

Accordingly, the holy bishop, attacking Manes especially on this point, reasons as follows:

“The Paraclete promised by Jesus Christ ought to have glorified the Lord by an infinite multitude of miracles; but the Manichaean, throughout the entire course of his life and manifestation, produced not even the smallest wonder.”

But does it not appear that Beausobre wished to play a part upon the stage and weave a fable in place of critical history?

Since I should not undertake a lengthy disputation on this matter at present, I shall expose these fabricated fallacies by pointing out the great distinction between magical tricks and miracles, a distinction taught by the most eminent men and one that reason itself ought to make clear.

Archelaus does indeed deny—and rightly—that Manes performed any of those signs which derive from divine power and might alone. But he does not deny that the man was accustomed to practice sorcery and illusions, in which the arts of magicians consist. This is particularly clear since, according to Beausobre himself, Manes was first educated in the disciplines of magic at Seleucia or Ctesiphon.

Archelaus therefore denied that Manes could perform true miracles, because God was not with him. He denied that Manes could perform those miracles that properly belong to the Paraclete, or Holy Spirit, from whom all who habitually practice the illusions of sorcery are understood to be very far removed.

How, then, could Beausobre conclude that Natalis, Tillemont, and the more recent writers had departed from Archelaus’s testimony, to which they ought to have given credence?

[Note: Beausobre, in the passage cited above.]

He ought rather to have concluded that he either entirely failed to understand the rules of dialectic or deliberately abused them in order to deceive unwary readers—readers who, when examining his frivolous arguments without reflecting with him, would not shrink from changing the assumptions of the matter and confusing the true miracles of divine omnipotence with demonic enchantments and the illusions of magicians.

Our Catholic reader may therefore learn from this that the more recent writers did not at all contradict the statements of the ancients, but wished to adhere to them on firmer grounds. For Manes truly could perform no miracle, even though he attempted through deceptions to mock the minds, eyes, and opinions of others, among whom he had already become famous.

This is the sense in which, unless he were out of his mind, Beausobre ought to have understood the testimony of Photius, who said:

“Manes, having become famous through crime,” and so forth.

A person should be called famous through crime and wickedness when he pretends that the apostolate given by Jesus Christ has been entrusted to him for the overthrow of the truth of the Catholic religion; when he calls himself the Paraclete; when he has already sent false heralds into various parts of the world to disseminate a false religion in every direction; and when his reputation must have spread widely—not only among uneducated and common people, but also among magistrates, nobles, and rulers.

Who, then, could persuade himself that the king of Persia was unaware of Manes’s name, his crimes, his authority, and the power that he had falsely claimed for himself? The king, then, attracted by these specious claims and believing that his son might be restored to health, either wished for this reason to summon Manes to the royal court, or Manes himself decided to go there, hoping, with the assistance and protection of the demon, to apply a remedy to the royal boy lying sick in bed.

The exclamation of Beausobre, therefore, is not to be taken seriously:

“When have rulers ever hoped that criminals could help them?”

For although this is true when the most wicked people, employing no covering of piety or religion, make their evil life apparent to all, or when their character becomes known through unmistakable signs, nevertheless, if their bad conduct remains concealed and is deliberately hidden beneath the cloak of false religion and piety, even rulers can easily be deceived—and are deceived very frequently.

The words of Photius, therefore, must not be twisted so violently that we imagine Manes to have been famous for crime in the eyes of the king and his court. Rather, he was famous for crime in the sight of God and the Church, which was being overthrown by the blasphemies and errors of his heresy—especially once he had spread his perverse doctrines among the people and taken care to spread them more and more each day, in order to increase the number of his hearers and elect.

## 2.

Having thus first assailed the most ancient Fathers of the Greek and Latin Church [Col. 0827B] and the more recent writers, Beausobre says that he is annoyed to have found Gregory Abulpharagius, patriarch of the Assyrians and an Oriental writer, inclined toward the preceding opinion, which he reported as borrowed from the judgment and hearsay of others. He says, in the customary formula of historical writing, namely: “It is reported that Sapor, king of the Persians, had the skin stripped from the slain Manes, stuffed it with straw, and fixed him upon a gallows above the city walls, because, while making great claims about himself, he had been unable to cure his son of the illness that had afflicted him.” [Note: [Col. 0827D] Gregory Abulpharagius, *History of the Dynasties*, Oxford edition, 1663, pp. 80, 82.]

Beausobre therefore maintains that this Gregory, as it were, remained suspended in uncertainty about granting credence to the preceding account, and that this is indicated by the word “it is reported,” which occurs at the beginning of that passage. He further says that he is struck with astonishment that the cause of such an event, so public and memorable, should have been reported so carelessly by only one Oriental writer, since only Bar-Hebraeus—namely, Abulpharagius—remembered it; yet, because he had spoken of it as an uncertain matter, he might perhaps have been entirely ignorant of it had he not learned it from the Greek writers.

Nevertheless, he declares that he is quite willing to grant the truth of the event. But, employing all the resources of his ingenuity, he observes that the matter must be explained in another way. Manes, he says, resolved to promote the health of that prince for no other reason than that he had been overcome by the king’s entreaties, for the reputation of this man was exceedingly powerful with the king, both because of his knowledge of the sciences and because of the excellence of his character.

He says that he derives this explanation from the testimony of Socrates [Note: [Col. 0827D] Socrates, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22; Ephraem, in the *Poem against the Heretics*, in Asseman, vol. I, p. 119.], which we cited above. He adds the testimony of all the Orientals, who asserted that Manes had suddenly acquired Sapor’s confidence, by which he believed that Manes could benefit both himself and his sick son, because of his learning.

Indeed, he undertakes to demonstrate by many conjectures [Col. 0827D] that the heretical man possessed within himself everything by which he could gain royal esteem. First, because the more common opinion of men represented Manes as endowed with extraordinary and great holiness. In him they chiefly observed continence, abstinence, fasts, outward bodily devotion, and piety—all of which present the appearance of a supremely spiritual man, and by which hypocrites have usually claimed the veneration of the peoples. We need say nothing further about the austerity, sadness, and pallor with which, according to Ephraem, the devil had tinged Manes in order to deceive the unwary.

And indeed, if we consider his poverty, it is sufficiently clear that Manichaeism followed it, since he wished his elect, subject to that rule, to possess absolutely nothing. Thus experience teaches us that nothing is more effective in winning for oneself the goodwill and esteem of men than contempt for and renunciation of temporal goods; and these retain their force especially among the Orientals. For from the *Gazophylacium of the Persian Language* we know that the pagan Indians boast especially of apparent holiness when they take care to join voluntary poverty to it.

He derives a second conjecture from the fact that Manes, according to Archelaus, could be called the foremost of all the wise men of his age, especially in matters belonging to Persian sciences. Among these, medicine was held in particularly high esteem, since they considered nothing more relevant to the necessities of life, as Xenophon observed. Thus these two verses indicate that medicine was one branch of the philosophy of the Magi:

> Among the Persians he is a Magus who knows the stars,  
> who knows the powers of herbs and the worship of the gods.

[Col. 0828B]

Indulging these studies and considerations, Beausobre reasons in this way; and he has also confidently amassed many other claims entirely opposed to the tradition of the Fathers, in order to reduce the uncertain testimony of Gregory Abulpharagius, metropolitan of the Monophysites, to a definite fabulous system that would completely erase the truth of this history.

## 3.

The material he added there is therefore arranged toward this end: to persuade the reader that Manes was thoroughly versed in medical disciplines. He is led chiefly by examples that can be drawn either from Zoroaster, the Persian prophet, who in the city of Divavar ordered that a certain sick man be treated with the aid of liquid pressed from a particular plant [Note: [Col. 0828D] In Hydas, p. 300. Alexander of Lycopolis, in Combefis, *Auctuarium novissimum*, part II, p. 4.], or from Alexander of Lycopolis, who accompanied Sapor the Persian himself on campaign in the field. From this he infers that Manes had attended that king as a physician [Note: [Col. 0828D] In Asseman, vol. I, p. 143; Strabo, book XV, p. 677.].

Hence he asserts that the high honor in which physicians were held among the Persians is confirmed by Saint Ephraem, who, wishing to give his blessing to a certain Simeon before departing from the use of the light of the present world, spoke as follows:

> Like a physician in the camp, so may your name spread throughout the world.

[Col. 0828C]

Beausobre flatters himself that this manner of speaking had become among the Orientals a proverb or common saying, since, according to Strabo, the medical profession is ordered toward the preservation of human beings.

He declares that he can add to all this Scythianus, whom tradition says was Manes’ teacher and who devoted himself to medical instruction, and Hierax, one of the twelve Manichaean disciples, who applied himself to this discipline.

Finally, as though wishing to close the preceding account, he adds that many men from monastic communities, others from the profession of solitary life, and still others from the episcopal order were so diligently cultivated by the Orientals that we can easily understand how they came into the patronage and company of the Persian kings. Thus the *Miscellaneous History*, book XV, reports concerning a certain Boazane, whom Cavardes, king of the Persians, greatly loved as an excellent physician. Of this matter the most learned Asseman provides various examples in his *Oriental Library* [Col. 0828D].

Having thus laid these and similar foundations, Beausobre draws the following conclusion, which could apply to any other Persian or to anyone residing at the court of the Persian kings: namely, that Sapor summoned Manes to the court as an excellent and most distinguished physician, since popular opinion had established that he possessed the greatest experience in curing illnesses.

But where do we read, or which writer has ever asserted, that Manes claimed this reputation for himself? We have only this unfortunate experiment upon the royal child, reported even by Abulpharagius, on whom Beausobre relies [Col. 0829A]; and therefore there had previously been no reason for him to be proclaimed a most learned physician.

What then follows from that conclusion except this: that the court of the Persian kings was so furnished with a company of physicians as armies of soldiers and fleets commonly fortify a camp? But what could be less probable? Reason itself suggests that Sapor had among his household and intimate associates several men skilled in the medical art. As we have seen, he made them leave the royal palace in exile when he was informed that the impostor Manes possessed a kind of divine power in curing diseases—not because Manes was endowed with such knowledge or practiced the medical art, but because he hoped to help his sick son on account of that remarkable sanctity of life which Manes strove to counterfeit: partly for the sake of the apostleship of Jesus Christ which he falsely claimed had been given to him, and partly because of the other signs of supreme piety and religion that he cultivated with every effort.

It is more reasonable to affirm this latter point, supported especially by all the Greek and Latin writers [Col. 0829B], who, although they differ somewhat in their wording, nevertheless agree entirely with one another in their account of the event.

Beausobre further asserted that Manes was a devotee of the greatest and most extreme poverty, by which he claimed for himself a reputation for exceptional holiness. But what proof of this poverty could he produce? None is available at all. Indeed, we think it entirely obscure how a man could be called a devotee of such virtue when we do not know that he distributed the wealth he had acquired through the inheritance of the widow.

He ought therefore to have explained how, when, and for what purposes he spent his inherited wealth: whether on supporting the poor and the sick, on enriching friends and relatives, or finally on accomplishing some notable act of piety, so as to reduce himself to extreme poverty.

Beausobre did not deny in the preceding chapters that Manes had acquired immense wealth from Scythianus and from the widow whose slave he had been. Therefore, for a more accurate and careful writer, such as he boasts himself to be, it was especially fitting to reconcile these two contradictory claims according to the best rules of criticism, lest he introduce absurd accounts into a new history of the Manichaeans.

Since he neglected to do this, we shall suppose either that Manes had no poverty at all, or at least that he outwardly affected only the appearance of poverty.

## 4.

Having briefly noted all these matters, let us return to the order of the history.

Sapor, king of the Persians, deeply grieving the death of his royal son, was prepared to rage so fiercely against the author of the crime that the man would suffer the penalties due to a murderer and to a bold and most wicked impostor.

Manes was therefore seized and confined in a closely guarded prison. His disciples, whom he had brought with him, visited him there. Some of these he had previously sent, perhaps to Jerusalem or to other regions inhabited by Christians, to obtain copies of the books of the New and Old Testament. He had intended to misuse these books in order more easily to ridicule and deceive the worshipers of the Christian name.

“Having set out,” says Epiphanius [Col. 0829D] (*ibid.*, no. 5), “the disciples immediately purchased those books. Then, returning to their master, who had already been deprived of his liberty, they entered the prison and offered him the books.”

During this leisure in prison, Manes diligently began to examine the books of the divine Scriptures that he had received. Although he pretended to adopt and accept the New Testament, he nevertheless corrupted and perverted it by rash undertakings in almost innumerable places: sometimes by removing those things that exposed his false and wicked life, and sometimes by inserting various additions that would strengthen the errors, fables, and ravings of his impious sect [Note: [Col. 0829D] Epiphanius, heresy 66; Augustine, *Book on Heresies*, 46; and Saint Leo the Great, in innumerable passages, which we shall discuss below.].

### 47

Cyril of Jerusalem, addressing the catechumens, enumerates and amplifies many of the crimes, blasphemies, [Col. 0830A] obscenities, false and deceitful promises, and disgraces of this impostor. Nowhere, however, does he mention the volumes of Scripture that Manes corrupted while he was being held in prison.

He does, however, make him the object of particular ridicule because he escaped from prison. He therefore adds:

> For the man who said that he was the Paraclete and defender of the truth fled—not a successor or imitator of Christ, who came eagerly to the cross, but, by fleeing, he became his opposite.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Saint Cyril, *Catechesis* 6.]

## 5.

Such an escape or flight from prison would have been utterly impossible for the Manichaean unless the guards, bound by greed and negligence, had complied with his wishes.

That extremely cunning man certainly knew that the official in charge of the public prison could be overcome and corrupted in these two ways—namely, by entreaties and by money. Therefore, having employed both forms of assistance without delay, he easily broke his bonds.

Epiphanius relates the matter in approximately these words (*ibid.*, no. 5):

> Meanwhile, after the prison official had been won over by a great force of money and constant entreaties, he made his escape; and, leaving Persia, he entered the territory of the Romans.

The guards of the prison, says the aforementioned Cyril, experienced most cruelly the anger of the Persian king, which Manes had then escaped. For when the king discovered their disloyalty—or even their greed—he inflicted upon them the death penalty that he had determined to impose upon the Manichaean. Thus the same man who, through his arrogance, had been the cause of the royal child’s death became also, through his flight, the cause of the guards’ death.

Amid so many and such great dangers to his life—dangers brought upon him by his own wickedness and by the indignation of the most powerful king—Manes ought thereafter to have become more prudent, so that he might guard against rashly undertaking anything further that was criminal.

Yet both the most serious authorities and the surviving records of unquestionable reliability testify that the opposite occurred. For after deceitfully regaining his former freedom and withdrawing into Roman territory situated on the borders of Persia and Mesopotamia, although he sometimes appeared to devote himself to solitude, in that retreat he did not give himself over to peace and tranquility. Rather, he was plotting new crimes, in order to serve continually the spirit of pride and arrogance by which he was led.

Photius described Manes’ escape from prison somewhat differently, without expressly mentioning by what means or arts he overcame and deceived those guards. He says only:

> But since he was a slave, skilled in the arts of a slave, and knew that he would soon pay the penalty for the murder he had committed—for he had killed the king’s son by his impiety—he fled from the house and became the cause of the guards’ death. Because they had not guarded that wicked man carefully, they were all beheaded.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Photius, book I *Against the Manichaeans*, codex 12.]

What arts proper to his condition as a slave Manes may have used while he was held in chains, so that, after escaping from prison, he might avoid the punishment of death, Photius did not expressly indicate here.

But it is highly probable that the account we cited above from Epiphanius is correct: namely, that he overcame the prison official and the guards by a great force of money and constant entreaties. This is especially likely because it is well known that men of the lowly condition of slaves have never been accustomed to reject gold and wealth, and that slaves can easily be induced to sell their services.

Whether this, then, can serve as evidence of the extreme poverty into which Beausobre describes Manes as having fallen [Note: [Col. 0830D] Beausobre, chapter 7 of the earlier book, pp. 85–86. The same Beausobre, in the notes, no. 10, adding to these words—“fabricated and feigned errors”—that the words “with the name of Christ added” must also be supplied.], even before Sapor summoned him to court to aid the sick child by remedies and prayers, the reader will judge for himself. Meanwhile, before we remove our hand from the present page, we must rescue one further point, since it would completely overturn certain matters established above if we were to believe Beausobre’s conjectures possessed force and truth.

[Col. 0831A]

## 7.

Beausobre therefore persuades himself from the writings of the Orientals that the hatred of the Persian king toward the Manichaean originated not at all from the death of the royal child, but from the Christian religion that Manes professed. That king, a worshiper of idols and superstitious magic, knew that Manes had sent Thomas, Addas, Hermas, and other pseudo-apostles into various regions of the world. These men ran here and there proclaiming the name of Christ, while Manes falsely claimed, by his preaching, to be Christ’s true apostle.

Therefore, led by the firm conviction that the propagation, spread, and growth of this new sect could gradually bring idolatry and the superstitious fabrications of the Magi to ruin, he resolved to seize Manes and confine him in prison, so that he might pay the penalty for so great a crime by capital punishment.

Beausobre asserts that the cause of this royal decree is clearly reported in the *Acts of Archelaus*, where we read:

> He sends his disciples to preach fearlessly fabricated and feigned errors, and so forth. When the king of the Persians learned this, he prepared to subject him to deserved punishments.

[Col. 0831B]

It is useful to ask Beausobre the censor to what mission the quoted words from the *Acts* ought to refer. Do they refer to the earlier mission of Manes’ pseudo-apostles, which they carried out before their master was summoned by Sapor and held in prison? Or to the later mission, which they did not hesitate to undertake after they had learned that their master too was to suffer death by royal decree?

Beausobre must admit that those words cannot and ought not to refer to the first mission. For when Thomas, Addas, and Hermas returned from it to give an account of their earlier preaching, they found Manes held in prison. When they approached him, they not only reported what they had done, but also brought several copies of the books of the New Testament to be corrupted.

Guided by the testimony of Saint Epiphanius, who affirmed that Manes had already possessed Christian books before the king of the Persians [Col. 0831C] confined him in prison, Beausobre unjustifiably alleges that this preceding account of Archelaus smacks of falsehood or fable.

For he could have possessed some badly produced books of the New Testament, perhaps those that Valentinians and other heretics had corrupted, since learned men already know that Catholic Christians took great pains to preserve the canonical books intact—lest, as Eusebius relates, the pagans consign them to the flames, and lest the leaders of the heretics corrupt and pervert them. We gather that this had already happened from the book of the *Constitutions* attributed to the apostles, concerning which we shall speak more appropriately in due course.

How, then, could it have been impossible for Manes to have brought some books of the New Testament with him into prison—either complete and genuine books, which he corrupted at will, or books already perverted and corrupted according to the interpretations of Valentinus, Carpocrates, and Marcion—and to have sent his disciples into the regions of the East and Asia to obtain still others?

Or perhaps those fabulous books had not yet appeared under the name of the New Testament—books entitled the Gospels of Peter, Thomas, and Matthias? Was not the Gospel of Philip, devised by the Gnostics, already circulating? Or, finally, was there not another that the Gaianites published under the name of Judas the betrayer?

It is entirely certain that Scythianus and Manes drew their heresy from these and similar poisonous springs, concerning which Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0831D] Eusebius of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 1, and in our Rufinian edition, vol. I, p. 464; book VI of the *Constitutions*, chapter 16, concerning falsely titled books.] and the Fathers have spoken.

Those two matters, therefore, can fit together perfectly, without the slightest trace of contradiction: namely, that Manes, confined in prison, possessed some books of the New Testament, which he increasingly corrupted and perverted with fabulous inventions in defense of his sect; and that he later received others from Thomas, Addas, and Hermas when those rogues returned from their earlier mission, having purchased them among the Orientals with financial assistance.

## 8.

Who does not see that this preceding explanation is not opposed to Beausobre’s system, but rather agrees with it? For when he briefly begins to discuss the religion of Manes in the chapter mentioned, he supposes that Manes had absorbed from adolescence a form of Christianity corrupted by many errors, chiefly from the commentaries of Scythianus, which he himself perhaps later corrupted and perverted further, in order to make it agree with his own philosophy and that of the Magi.

It remains, therefore, to see whether Sapor became fiercely enraged against Manes because of that mission of the pseudo-apostles, which Beausobre himself, guided by the testimony of Archelaus, as we have seen, asserts to have been the sole cause of so great a hatred [Note: [Col. 0832D] *Acts of the Disputation*, p. 99, and Beausobre, p. 82, in the chapter cited above.]

To preserve the order of the earlier events, it can be inferred that Manes sent these disciples on two missions. The first occurred before Manes attempted to cure the royal child. When those who had been sent returned from it, they handed over several books of the New Testament to their master, who remained in chains.

We consider it more probable that the second mission followed this one. For if we wish to adhere, as we have already done, to the testimony of the *Acts of Archelaus*, then, after Manes had been visited in prison by those same disciples, he urged them to fear nothing and rose to prayer.

According to Beausobre himself, this conduct could serve as evidence both of exceptional holiness and of the greatness of spirit that a faithful disciple of Christ the Lord ought to possess. He therefore concludes that the founder of this sect could not easily have established himself unless he had possessed great qualities or prerogatives of mind.

To display this confidence of spirit more and more, Manes first pretended that he feared absolutely nothing—not the threatened punishments, not even death itself. Therefore, in order to win authority for himself and exalt his teaching, he sent his disciples out again “to preach fearlessly fabricated and feigned errors.”

No one will doubt that these last words correspond to the preceding ones [Col. 0832C]. Therefore, when Sapor became aware of such audacity and seriously reflected upon the death of his royal son, he did not permit the murderer to remain alive in prison any longer. He ordered him to undergo the death that had hitherto been postponed, since he was prepared to subject him to deserved punishments.

Before the measures that Sapor had ordered for the exemplary execution of this most impious man could be carried out, however, Manes corrupted the prison guard and the other soldiers and escaped, as we have already seen above.

We had to write and make these observations in order to refute Beausobre’s arguments, and especially to reconcile the testimonies of the ancient writers. Beausobre, insufficiently consistent with himself, turns and distorts everything upside down, and maintains that these testimonies ought to be regarded as negligible and unworthy of belief.

But now let us return to the order of the history.

# CHAPTER VII

## How and by what arts Manes attempted to overthrow the Catholic religion in Mesopotamia; the efforts of Saint Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, to frustrate these attempts; observations on Beausobre’s conjectures concerning this subject

[Col. 0832D]

## 1.

We are now about to speak of Manes’ final attempts to overthrow the Catholic faith. It is therefore necessary for our account to return to the point at which the preceding chapter came to an end.

While Manes was living in the solitude to which he had withdrawn after escaping from prison, he was informed that there was a certain outstanding man, endowed with exceptional piety, named Marcellus or Marcellinus, who lived at Caschara, a town of Mesopotamia [Col. 0833A], and that he was a thoroughly Christian man in every respect, remarkably distinguished in all the duties of justice.

Manes therefore hoped that this man might eventually become a partner in his wickedness, an avenger of his crimes, and a defender of his abominable sect, if he could entangle him in the snares of his diabolical teaching. For he imagined that he could occupy the whole province if he had first brought such a man under his control.
