Accordingly, after devising various plans, he judged it necessary to employ one or the other of only two alternatives that he was anxiously weighing in his mind.

The first was to go to him and, while conversing with him, gradually introduce harmful doctrines under the appearance of religious devotion or of seeking to secure his eternal salvation. Once Marcellus had absorbed these doctrines, the purity of the Catholic faith—which Marcellus, or Marcellinus, himself professed—would be corrupted little by little.

But Manes feared that this course of action would be less safe. For an unforeseen and sudden entry might perhaps expose him to some serious danger, resulting in his own destruction, while he was attempting to overthrow the foundations of the Catholic religion.

He therefore judged that the second plan [Col. 0833B] would be more advantageous to him: namely, to address Marcellus first by letters. If Marcellus gave them a favorable hearing, or at least did not boldly oppose them, then greater effort would be applied, so that, driven by fear or led by curiosity, Marcellus himself might demand that all the doctrines of the Manichaean sect and its empty fictions be disclosed to him.

Manes judged this final resource to be safer and more convenient. He therefore summoned Turbo, one of the disciples whom Addas had corrupted with those wicked teachings, and entrusted him with a letter to be delivered to Marcellus, ordering him to set out immediately and hasten to Caschara.

## 2.

Turbo did not delay in obeying the command. After enduring much labor and hardship during his rapid journey, he arrived, after five days on the road, at Marcellus’ hospitable house as a traveler; but he was not immediately received by the man to whom he had been sent.

For the men responsible for Marcellus’ hospitality toward travelers asked Turbo who he was, where he had come from, by whom he had been sent, and for what purpose.

He admitted that he originated in Mesopotamia, had come there from Persia, and was acting as envoy on behalf of a certain Manichaean, a teacher of the Christians, who was staying at the Arabion fortress.

But because they did not know the name of the sender, they categorically refused to receive Turbo. They drove him away from the lodging and did not even grant him access to water.

Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, describes the matter in approximately these words, adding:

> After Turbo had endured these and still worse things for several days, worn out by hardship, hunger, and distress, he would certainly not have escaped death unless at last he had told the keepers of the lodging that he was carrying letters to be delivered to Marcellus—or Marcellinus.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] Archelaus, bishop, in the *Disputation against the Manichaean*.]

## 3.

At last he handed over the letter for Marcellus to read. Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, was then present in Marcellus’ house.

When Archelaus heard the blasphemies with which the letter was filled, he began to rage against its author as though driven by zeal for religion; like a lion shut in, he gnashed his teeth and wished that Manes might be handed over to him.

Marcellus, however, was more peaceful in spirit. He promised his bishop that he would deal with the letter in such a way that Manes would nevertheless come to Caschara, as Manes himself promised, if Marcellus made the request.

How many blasphemies, and of what kind, Manes’ letter contained against God, the Mother of God, and the saints, anyone can easily learn from copies transcribed both by Epiphanius and by Archelaus [Note: [Col. 0833D] Epiphanius, heresy 66, no. 6.]. We do not think it necessary to transcribe them here at present. Nevertheless, to relieve our readers of the burden of going through them in the writers just mentioned, we shall briefly indicate here their substance or summary.

First, the copy of this letter bore a title or inscription of such a kind that it must unquestionably have driven the mind of any pious and religious person into the greatest indignation. Or, if that title or inscription had been read by someone less instructed in matters of faith or less versed in Catholic theology, it could certainly have thrown him into both amazement and anxiety.

The inscription is as follows:

> Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ, and all the saints and virgins who are with me, to Marcellus, dearest son: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; and may the right hand of the Light preserve you from this present evil age, from its ruins, and from the snares of the Evil One. Amen.

But what could that barbarous Persian devise that was bolder or more wicked, or finally more insulting to God and the saints?

Did he imagine that the name of apostle of Jesus Christ, and the gifts of which Saint Paul [Col. 0834B] chiefly boasted, could belong to him or to other men by their own choice, calling, and mission?

After cursing this first impiety against religion, he expressed other matters still more wicked in the body of the letter. In order to win Marcellus’ goodwill, he first praised his piety briefly and professed regret that Marcellus did not believe in accordance with right reason.

He further added, with great arrogance, that he had been sent for the correction of the human race and would help those who had surrendered themselves to seductions and errors. For this reason, he said, he had thought it necessary to send these writings—first, for the salvation of Marcellus’ soul, and then also for the salvation of those who were with him.

It will not be difficult to anticipate what doctrines of salvation he proposed to him, since we have already discussed them at length in chapters 3 and 4. He asserted that two Gods must necessarily be admitted, each of whom was the maker of those things corresponding to his nature. Thus he maintained that good things and light were created only by the good god, while evil things and darkness were created by the evil god.

No one could confuse and mingle these good and evil things with one another without insulting divine goodness and incurring the extreme curse of almighty God.

On the occasion of this wicked doctrine, he more boldly misused the Savior’s evangelical words:

> For a bad tree cannot produce good fruits, nor a good tree produce bad fruits.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] Matthew 7:18.]

When he attempted to draw this testimony into his own meaning through the following interpretation, he added:

> I am greatly astonished that they dare to call the Lord the maker and creator of Satan and of his evil deeds.

Bailius not only explained these fabulous opinions about the two causes of things, according to the depraved view of Manes, at considerable length in his *Historical Dictionary* [Note: [Col. 0834D] Bailius, *Historical Dictionary*, vol. II, where he composed a highly dangerous account of the doctrines and principles of the Manichaeans, which must be read with caution and is insulting to the holy Fathers.]; he also, carried away by a peculiar spirit, produced them at excessive length from the testimonies of Ovid, Zoroaster, and other pagan philosophers and poets.

Whether he did this to boast of the extent of his learning, or to lend weight to the corrupt opinion of Manes, I cannot judge. It is certain, however, that the arguments he borrowed solely from the considerations of nature appear wholly weak and frivolous, on which he claims to rely after removing divine revelation.

Did not the older Fathers and theologians, relying only upon natural arguments, prove in every age against the Marcionites, Manichaeans, and other heretics of this doctrine that there has always been only one cause of all things?

We shall explain this ourselves shortly, as we review the writings of those who opposed the Manichaeans.

But, leaving Bailius, the interpreter of his own purpose in writing, let us now examine the other errors of Manes described in his letter to Marcellus [Col. 0835A].

He next begins to philosophize about the creation of man. Distinguishing the inner man from the outer, he maintains that the two are in conflict with one another.

He then asserts that the good god is the author of the inner man, but fabricates the claim that the origin of the bodily and fleshly substance derives from the devil.

After this he attacks the Catholic mystery of the incarnation of Christ the Lord. And as though the apostles and their successors had gone astray on this greatest article of our faith, he reasons as follows:

> And would that their vanity had gone so far as not to say that Christ, the Only-Begotten One who descended from the Father’s realm, was the son of some woman named Mary, generated from blood, flesh, and the other impurities of women.

Manes therefore did not believe that the Only-Begotten Son of God the Father could have been clothed in true and corporeal flesh, or carried in a woman’s womb, or that Mary was truly the Mother of God.

Let the reader himself consider how hateful these claims must have been to upright men, Marcellus and Archelaus, learned in the sacred writings and distinguished by their supreme devotion to religion [Col. 0835B]. For we cannot address these and similar blasphemies without the greatest sorrow of heart.

### 4.

Accordingly, after reading such a letter, Marcellus decided without any delay to write back to Manes. Through this letter he would arrange matters so that, once that impostor had been summoned to Caschara, he might enter into a debate with Bishop Archelaus, in order that the truths of the Catholic religion might become increasingly clear.

Marcellus brought his letter to a close in a few words, and, to preserve the dignity of his language throughout, began with this title of majesty: “Marcellus, a man of distinction, sends greetings to Manichaeus, who has been announced to him by letter.” Then, in the body of the letter, he pretended not to understand the meaning of the letter he had received through Turbo, unless perhaps—as he said—“you explain it to us in person, word by word, just as you promised in your letter.”

When this letter of Marcellus was being handed over to Turbo for delivery, Turbo could not be persuaded by any argument to return to Manes. “Remembering,” Archelaus says, “the hardships of the journey,” he asked that someone else be sent in his place, freely declaring that he would not return to him and would have no further communion with him. But when Turbo resisted returning to Manes, Marcellus nevertheless did not abandon his decision. He summoned one of his servants, named Callistus, and ordered him to set out.

After three days had elapsed, Callistus reached the Castle of Arabion, where Manes had taken refuge. When Manes received the letter, he was partly pleased that he had been summoned to Marcellus without any delay, but partly troubled by the evil that Turbo’s absence seemed to portend. Nevertheless, the boldest of men did not postpone undertaking the journey. He took with him twelve young men who desired to cultivate virginity, so that they might attend him in an honorific retinue. Setting out for Caschara, he arrived at Marcellus’s house.

There, after vainly asking for Turbo—for after renouncing the superstitious sect of his master, revealing its secret and fabulous errors to the holy bishop, and receiving many gifts from Marcellus, Turbo had been ordered to reside in the house of Bishop Archelaus—Manes, I say, entered to greet Marcellus.

When Marcellus looked at him, he seemed to see a comical actor standing before him, much better suited to performing jokes than to discussing the affairs and doctrines of religion. Indeed, would not his gait, clothing, appearance, gestures, equipment, and ornaments have compelled any serious and sober-minded man to burst into repeated laughter?

Archelaus describes how he appeared to Marcellus’s eyes in these words:

> “For he wore a kind of footwear called quadrisole in the common language; his cloak was variegated, as though of a sky-blue hue. In his hand he held a very sturdy staff made of ebony. Under his left armpit he carried a Babylonian book. He had also covered his legs in different colors: one was reddish, while the other was, as it were, leek-green. His face had the appearance of an old Persian craftsman and commander of armies.”

[Note: Archelaus, in the *Disputation against the Manichaeans*, in Zacagnius, p. 23. He notes that prophets—that is, interpreters of sacred matters—carried staffs of ebony, as Ducange proves from Callisthenes in his *Glossary*.]

### 5.

When Marcellus first set eyes on this man, he immediately recognized all the arts of a true sycophant. Accordingly, as though disregarding him and avoiding all conversation with him, he at once sent for Archelaus.

When Archelaus realized that Manes was present, he was impelled by the greatest zeal for religion and pressed inwardly to attack him, scarcely able to restrain the hatred he had conceived against the impostor. His indignation was intensified by Manes’ very clothing, the appearance of his person, and above all by Turbo’s secret confession of all his impieties, which had been disclosed to him, and by his abhorrence of those things that had wounded the heart of that most holy Pastor all the more deeply.

But the extremely prudent Marcellus, setting aside every desire for contention, decided that both men should be heard. He summoned the principal men of the city to his house and selected four judges from among them who were Gentiles in religion: namely Manippus, a grammarian and highly skilled in the disciplines of rhetoric; Aegialeus, a most distinguished chief physician and exceptionally learned in letters; and the brothers Claudius and Cleobulus, likewise trained in the arts of rhetoric. He decreed that a full assembly should be held.

Whether the word “assembly” should be understood as referring to a synod cannot easily be determined. The principal reason is that Archelaus says that this assembly was gathered not in a church but in Marcellus’s house; moreover, he expressly describes four judges who were Gentiles in religion as having been chosen in the case of Manes.

These two facts, however, do not at all trouble those who defend the affirmative position. For other synods, or councils, were sometimes convened in the palaces of emperors and princes, as we read concerning the council held at Trullo in Constantinople. Gentile philosophers were also permitted to take part in other councils, including general councils, as is especially clear from the acts—or history—of the First Council of Nicaea.

The author of the synodical booklet likewise supports the affirmative opinion. He says that the errors of Manes were condemned at a certain synod in Mesopotamia by that great man Archelaus, Bishop of Caschara.

[Note: Photius. Commenting on his words, Christopher Wolfius wrote: “Thus he is called by many: Archelaus, Bishop of Carrhae, which is the genuine name of the city. But in other manuscripts, namely the Holsteinian ones, *Caschara* is read. Consult the final chapter of this present book.”]

This manner of speaking may indicate that the author of the aforementioned booklet interpreted the word “assembly” as “council.” But, adds Father Natalis Alexander, no ancient writer mentions such a synod.

[Note: P. Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History of the Third Century*, chapter 3, § 2.]

But how can the silence of ancient writers—namely Cyril of Jerusalem and Epiphanius, whom the learned Father Natalis cites—serve as evidence that the event was fabricated? Does Father Natalis give greater weight to the silence of two writers than to the testimony of Archelaus, who was both the author of the disputation and the convener of the assembly?

I will grant that no other bishop besides Archelaus took part in this assembly. But what of it? Shall we suppose that the presbyters and the rest of the clergy who were at least residing in the city of Caschara were absent from that gathering? I certainly will not grant that. For that Bishop Archelaus, speaking of such a gathering, calls it a “magnificent assembly,” so that Marcellus’s house, which was enormous, was filled with those who had been summoned to hear.

Yet Archelaus also testifies that, in addition to those summoned to listen, the judges chosen for the occasion were present, seated in a higher place.

### 6.

The preceding conjectures and the testimony of the synodical booklet, however, seem to totter and collapse as entirely weak if we turn our attention to the history of Photius.

[Note: Photius, book 1 *Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 13, at the beginning.]

Photius not only describes differently the events of this kind carried out by Archelaus, Bishop of Caschara, against Manes; he also indicates that that assembly and that gathering of people could by no means claim the name of a synod.

He relates how Manes, having fled and arrived in Mesopotamia, began to sow the tares of his apostasy:

> “But the Bishop of Caschara,” he says, “whose name was Archelaus, a sacred man and most skilled in divine and human affairs, having gathered a body of Greek, or Gentile, hearers, so that the truth would not seem to have triumphed through favoritism if Christians were the judges, instituted a pious disputation against the man called Manes. He so shamed and refuted the most impious man that Manes immediately fled from there.”

[Note: Photius, book 1, *History against the Manichaeans*, chapter 13, in Wolfius, p. 49.]

If, then, according to Photius, Greeks and Gentiles were permitted to take part in the disputation so that the truth would not seem to have triumphed through favoritism if Christians were the judges, in what sense, or for what reason, could that multitude and gathering of Greek, or Gentile, people be called a synod?

It was always and everywhere provided that laymen, and especially those alien to the name of Christ, should not judge matters of faith and doctrine. Catholics have defended this principle with every effort against the heterodox, from the beginnings of the Church down to our own times.

I say that, on considering these matters myself, I clearly learned that Photius’s celebrated account adds strength to the preceding conjectures rather than weakening and overturning those conjectures and the testimony of the synodical booklet. Those Gentiles ought to have attended the assembly as hearers and witnesses, so that a serious suspicion might not arise among the people and the common crowd that the Christians, in judging the case, had pursued favoritism rather than truth, to the greatest injury of justice and equity.

But what prevents this from having happened? Did not the entire multitude of believers gather for the councils at Jerusalem? Nevertheless, Catholics demonstrate with the most certain arguments—against Blondel and other mobs of heretics—that only the apostles acted as judges. We should not undertake that disputation at present, lest we seem to sing outside the choir and wander here and there, as Beausobre is accustomed to do.

When I had considered all these matters with myself, I could not at all be brought to believe that the diocesan synod in question had been entirely fabricated. Rather, we judge it more probable that, after Archelaus’s disputation had been concluded, an anathema was pronounced at least against the errors of Manes.

This would perhaps be gathered more clearly from the Acts of that disputation if the ravages of time and the negligence of translators had not corrupted or distorted them. Among others, Cyril of Jerusalem alone expressly asserts that each of the wicked doctrines of this impostor was refuted and condemned by Archelaus in debate, chiefly from the Scriptures. After citing various Scriptural testimonies, he adds the following:

[Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6.]

> “By these and many other things of the same kind the dragon was overthrown. Through such contests Archelaus overcame Manes, so that Manes fled from there again, just as he had formerly fled from the prisons.”

After being defeated and convicted, Manes decided to flee, as he had fled from the prisons, so that he might avoid not only shame and disgrace but also the fury of the people, who were seeking him for execution. He would certainly not have escaped death if Marcellus and Archelaus had not exerted all their strength to restrain the violence of the mob.

Since, therefore, in this case, or form of judgment, all the circumstances that are ordinarily found in councils against those accused of offenses against the Christian faith are present, nothing can prevent us from understanding that a council was held at Caschara under the name of an assembly.

Now, at last, let us consider the criticisms of Beausobre.

### 7.

Beausobre nevertheless devoted considerable effort to gradually undermining and overturning what has been said thus far. He then so depreciates the credibility of the Acts that he decides they must be rejected as wholly fictitious and fabulous.

[Note: Beausobre, book 1, *History of the Manichaeans*, chapter 8.]

He begins his discussion chiefly with that account which, together with Tillemont, we believe was sewn onto those Acts. In it, twelve thousand Christians are described—men, women, and children—who had left the city and withdrawn to a certain field, fasting and praying day and night, entreating the invisible God alone to send rain upon the earth and its seed at the proper seasons. It is asserted that the ancient Christians used to observe this rite there every year.

But while this people was occupied with such exercises of piety and religion, Roman soldiers who were not far from that field were gripped by a grave suspicion. They thought that the crowd had decided to remain there because it was hostile to the imperial army and intended to inflict violence upon the soldiers and their weapons if it found a suitable opportunity.

The Roman soldiers therefore did not hesitate to attack the sleeping Christians immediately. Without sparing children or women, they compelled some to perish by the sword, while others—namely, seven thousand seven hundred—after three days of travel, they led as captives to Caschara, intending to sell them into slavery for money.

When Bishop Archelaus became aware of so great a crime, he hastened without delay to Marcellus, or Marcellinus. Marcellus immediately opened all the treasures of his wealth and offered the Gentile soldiers as much gold as would be sufficient to restore that multitude of captives to their former liberty.

When the military cohorts had sufficiently marveled at such greatness of spirit and such extraordinary charity, they immediately changed their minds. Some of them abandoned their military belts and at once gave themselves to Christ by embracing his name instead of idolatrous worship. Others, accepting only the quarter of the money they needed for provisions on the journey, returned to their former posts.

### 8.

First, then, Beausobre judged that this account strongly savored of a pure and simple fable. Relying on many conjectures, he examines every detail individually and sharpens his censorial style, so that, after noting various arguments for its improbability, the reader may conclude that the Acts circulated under the name of Archelaus, together with the whole of that disputation, must be rejected as entirely spurious.

Second, he persuades himself that the aforementioned Tillemont does not at least contradict such conjectures in his notes, since Tillemont said that the preceding history bore the signs and characteristics of a little story.

This is especially so because it must be regarded as extremely difficult for twelve thousand Christians to have been found in one and the same city while idolatry was still prevailing. Beausobre also says that Tillemont’s astonishment is increased by the fact that a Christian people could have persevered for so long in a spacious field, fasting and praying, unless perhaps the Paschal fasts happened to be recurring at that time.

He finally concludes his discussion of Tillemont by saying that, although many difficulties confronted him—especially the fact that so great a multitude of people, overcome by sleep and unarmed, allowed themselves to be surprised by soldiers without having already decided, as the sun was setting, to return to the city from which they had departed—Tillemont remained suspended and hesitant amid so many knots and such serious obstacles. Rather than assert that the Acts of Archelaus had been entirely fabricated, he preferred, Beausobre says, to judge that the history under discussion was an addition by the translator, which someone had attempted to sew onto the Acts of Archelaus like a ragged appendage, though it could not deprive those Acts of their credibility and authority.

[Note: Beausobre, ibid., p. 88, at the end.]

Despite all this, after rejecting Tillemont’s opinion, Beausobre thinks that the matter can be explained in the following way, and he decides to preoccupy the reader’s mind with these precautions.

“All fables,” he says, “usually rest upon some foundation drawn from true histories.” Wishing to investigate this more carefully in the present case, he thought that the foundation could most probably be derived from an ancient testimony described by Monsieur Hyde in his work on the religion of the ancient Persians.

[Note: Thomas Hyde, *On the Religion of the Ancient Persians*, chapter 4.]

But when he subsequently consulted this testimony and examined it with his own eyes, he understood that it tottered as an inadequate foundation. Nevertheless, he did not hesitate to set it forth, lest he should at some point incur suspicion of fraud in the eyes of his readers. His reasoning is therefore as follows:

“Let us suppose, then, that the celebrated fable rests upon some foundation drawn from true history.”

### 9.

First, he says, it must be assumed that the Marcellus mentioned in the Acts was truly a famous and distinguished man, descended from a Roman family and endowed with immense wealth. He possessed great authority in Mesopotamia because he administered all affairs in the name of the emperor.

Second, we too must assume that the crowd of people whom the soldiers discovered praying and fasting in the field had been engaged in such religious exercises while observing Persian worship and rites, and not at all with reference to Christian piety or the evangelical institutions that, according to ecclesiastical tradition, are to be observed through the Lenten fasts or the fasts of the Four Seasons.

The author who discusses the religion of the ancient Persians asserts that the Persians were accustomed to gather in fields on appointed days of the year, beseeching the invisible God for the fertility of the land and the abundance of its fruits. We shall observe this ourselves shortly.

In view of the first supposition, Beausobre presents the following proposition as entirely certain: namely, that the man called Marcellus through the carelessness of copyists actually possessed the administration of all affairs in the province of Mesopotamia and presided over those peoples as their true governor under the emperor Aurelian, around the year 273 after Christ, when, after Zenobia had been defeated, he brought the Palmyrenes under Roman rule.

For Zosimus relates that a certain Marcellinus was given the administration of those provinces.

[Note: Zosimus, *History*, book 1, p. 55 of the Greek edition.]

It could therefore easily have happened that some people read “Marcellus” instead of “Marcellinus.” It is already well known that the ancients frequently fell into similar errors.

It has therefore become perfectly clear that this Marcellinus, a commander of Roman lineage, was a man of the highest and greatest integrity. This is evident from the trials and dangers in which the loyalty and constancy of certain men were repeatedly tested, and in which they could scarcely endure.

Indeed, most mortals thought that they had acquired glory and honor when, enticed by the hope of obtaining greater honor, authority, and power, they indulged their own interests and were not ashamed to scorn and violate the rights of justice and equity, turning another’s property to their own use.

The Palmyrenes, for their part, bearing with extreme difficulty the devastation of their cities and the disgrace and captivity of Queen Zenobia, were attempting to withdraw themselves from the tyranny of the emperor Aurelian. Accordingly, an offer was made to Marcellinus that he should revolt from obedience and allegiance to the emperor and, after entering into an alliance with them, claim for himself the whole kingdom both of Mesopotamia and of the East.

When Marcellinus’s spirit resisted their schemes and blandishments, he steadfastly refused to accept supreme dominion over that people. Instead, he investigated more carefully how they might put aside every impulse toward revolt and serve the Roman Empire, by which they had been conquered.

Nevertheless, he reported the matter to Aurelian, lest, as the popular uprising grew daily, they should break the yoke of servitude under which they were held.

“It could therefore have been,” Beausobre concludes, “that Marcellinus was favorably disposed toward the Christians and their religion.”

He then proceeds to the second supposition he had proposed and asserts that it is already tottering badly. For who could imagine that Roman soldiers, under the discipline of those accustomed to command armies, were so savage that they wished to destroy an unarmed multitude of children and women who were obedient to the state?

It is equally lacking in probability that they would have led away as captives free and innocent persons. If these people had been Persian by nationality, the soldiers might have suspected that they had gathered in the field as enemies in order to invade with the sword lands already subject to Roman rule.

Therefore, once the innocence of those captives had subsequently been established, the supreme administrator of that province ought to have ordered them to be restored to their former liberty without any payment of money.

As for the third supposition—namely, whether the matter concerned supplications conducted by the Persians according to superstitious worship—Beausobre initially thought that Dr. Hyde intended to indicate this.

He reached that conclusion because Hyde had described certain ceremonies of the Magi that bore some resemblance to our rites of Baptism and the Eucharist, relying on a testimony wrongly attributed to St. Chrysostom.

[Note: Beausobre, ibid., pp. 90–91.]

He included the following testimony in his notes:

> “In their sacred rites they also had Mithraic baths, as if for regeneration, in which he himself—that is, the priest—immerses certain believers and his own faithful, promising the cleansing of sins through the bath, and thus still initiates them into Mithras. This is read in Justin Martyr and Chrysostom.
>
> “These people, therefore, every year after the threshing harvest, went up a certain mountain which in their language is called the Victorious Mountain. It contained a little cave in the rock and was exceedingly beautiful, with springs and choice trees. After climbing up and bathing there, they presented themselves and prayed to God in silence for three days.”

Beausobre maintains that this structure of the account is not badly constructed. But he argues that the foundation upon which it rests is completely unstable and collapsing, since neither Justin Martyr nor Chrysostom asserted these things.

Indeed, he says, the testimony just quoted was taken from the author of the *Incomplete Work on Matthew*, a work filled with nothing but fabulous little stories. For it does not speak at all of the supplications of the Magi; rather, it discusses a certain tradition generally approved by Christians of the Eastern communion. Beausobre promises to discuss this tradition more fully when he deals with the apocryphal writings of the Manichaeans.

He therefore gradually turns his criticism even against Dr. Hyde, warning readers not to subscribe, without careful examination, to the testimonies of the ancients, even when they have been cited by learned men. Although such scholars did not intend either to lie or to sell words in their works, they nevertheless suffered from hallucination when citing and annotating similar passages.

### 10.

I have had to describe these matters at somewhat greater length, so that I might later judge whether Beausobre wished to trifle or whether, as he boasts, he pursued the truth after setting aside all partisan zeal.

First, as regards Justin, I am compelled to admit that either Beausobre read his works carelessly or at least examined them with dim eyes. The holy martyr spoke especially in three places about the rites, mysteries, and ceremonies of the Persians, and he reviewed those matters that Dr. Hyde recorded from Chrysostom concerning the ancient religion of the Persians.

His first testimony is found in the *Apology for the Christians*, commonly called the Second Apology.

[Note: Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*, and *Dialogue with Trypho* 8, in my edition, p. 296 and following. Consult also Leo the Great, sermon 6 on the Epiphany, and other passages.]

There, mentioning the sacrament of the Eucharist and proving its truth by the evangelical words of Christ, he adds:

> “This, too, the wicked demons taught those who perform the mysteries and initiations of Mithras to do by imitation.”

Thus the Persians, instructed by demons, endeavored in their supplications and solemn initiatory rites to imitate the sacred table of the Christians.

Nevertheless, Justin adds that they preserved this distinction:

> “For in their sacrifices, or sacred rite, of the person being initiated, bread and a cup of water are placed, with certain words added; you either know this or can learn it.”

We shall observe in its proper place that the Manichaeans also were accustomed to do this—namely, in chapter 9 of the second book of this history.

Justin likewise explained in his *Dialogue with Trypho* that the Persians celebrated their supplications and impious mysteries in caves and caverns, especially when the initiations of Mithras were being performed. He writes:

> “Moreover, when those who transmit the initiations of Mithras declare that he was born from a rock, and call the place where those who believe in him are said to be initiated a cavern or cave…”

Finally, speaking of the birth of the Lord Christ in Bethlehem, Justin relates how Joseph had no place where he could stay and withdrew into a certain cave near the village. While they were there, Mary gave birth to Christ and placed him in a manger, where the Magi who came from Arabia found him.

A little later he added:

> “For this reason, the devil, having incited those who instituted the mysteries of Mithras to initiate their followers in the place that they call among themselves a cavern or cave, led them to speak in such terms and to perform their secret rites.”

The Persians and Magi therefore practiced these rites and ceremonies in caves and caverns, as though guided by the purpose of serving the devil. They abused the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, by which they pretended to conform themselves to the divine institutions and mysteries of the Christians.

The foundation from which the preceding account was derived has therefore not collapsed. Rather, it ought to stand more firmly, since writers who flourished after Justin may have borrowed the rites, ceremonies, and supplications of the Persians from his statements and authority.

But who could maintain that Chrysostom made no mention whatever of these Persian rites? What of it? Could Chrysostom’s silence perhaps undermine the testimonies of Justin Martyr? Justin flourished at a time when the religion of the Persians and Magi still held the greatest sway in Mesopotamia and the other neighboring provinces, and when the name of Christ had not yet—or scarcely—been announced to their inhabitants.

[Note: Justin Martyr flourished around the year 161 after Christ, whereas Chrysostom lived in the fifth century of the Church.]

By contrast, in Chrysostom’s time, although the Christian religion had spread here and there in those regions, together with the destruction of magic and idolatry, it had not yet been entirely abolished everywhere. This was because of the ferocity of those peoples, who, following the institutions of their ancestors, were not afraid to pay the highest honors to the sun, as Chrysostom himself testifies in homily 11 *To the People of Antioch*.

Nor should Beausobre have attacked Dr. Hyde for praising the *Incomplete Work on Matthew* as a work of Chrysostom. Most of the ancients attributed it to Chrysostom, and the early editors had it printed in the second volume of Chrysostom’s works, because such homilies are commonly attributed to him in manuscript codices.

[Note: Consult William Cave, *The Age of the Arians*, in my edition, p. 215.]

Accordingly, when later scholars undertook a more careful investigation of the author of these homilies and found in them certain blemishes of Arian doctrine, and when they saw that the text had been disfigured by various interpolations, corruptions, and additions, they judged, with better discernment, that the homilies had been composed by a Latin writer and by a man whose faith was impaired, and that they were filled with the same blemishes and additions.

Yet none of these scholars dared to assert that the works contained nothing but pure fables, as Beausobre has acknowledged.

[Note: Beausobre, ibid., p. 93.]

### 10.

Beausobre now proceeds to Manes’ letter, which he arranged to send to Marcellus through Turbo. He translated it in full into French and did not hesitate to praise it as though it had been written in the style of the apostles and were everywhere filled with the phrases and modes of expression of St. Paul the Apostle.

These two claims cannot be reconciled with the character of a neophyte who had been engaged in reading the sacred Scriptures for only a few months, or with the character of a savage, barbarous, and impious man, such as the ancient writers asserted Manes to have been.

Beausobre then adds that the Manichaeans venerated St. Paul, wrongly persuading themselves that from the writings of this holy apostle they could derive foundations for proving both the existence of two principles and the natural corruption of humanity. He says this especially because Paul worked harder than the other apostles of his generation to free the Christian Church from the yoke of the Mosaic Law.

Beausobre gathered these and many other arguments of the same kind in his exposition of the Manichaean letter and his description of the heretical man’s debate with Archelaus, Bishop of Caschara. Since we are ashamed to repeat some of them, we have deemed it necessary to conceal them entirely in silence. But the remaining matters, since they concern rather Manichaean philosophy, morals, worship, and discipline, we shall attempt to explain or reject individually in their proper places, while preserving the order of the subject.

## CHAPTER VIII

Manes, having departed from Caschara and seeking hiding places, withdrew to Diodorides, a village or parish of the same city. He begins new debates with the presbyter Diodorus concerning the doctrines of the faith. After being informed, Archelaus first sent letters to Diodorus; Beausobre, discussing them, attempts through trifles to overturn ecclesiastical discipline. When Archelaus subsequently arrived, Manes tried unsuccessfully to flee.

[Col. 0842C]

### 1.

When Manes thought that he had escaped the hatred of the Persians and overcome the judgment of Caschara that we mentioned shortly before, although he had employed great fraud and deceit in every matter, he was nevertheless compelled, for the security and protection of his life, to seek a hiding place. He withdrew into a remote district, or obscure village, of the diocese of Caschara.

There, after removing far away all witnesses of his earlier wickedness and crimes, he decided to hold a disputation concerning religious doctrines with a certain presbyter, the ruler of that parish.

We cannot state with certainty whether he was alone or whether he was accompanied by those virgin disciples—namely, those who outwardly professed continence—whom he had brought with him from the Castle of Arabion when he came to Caschara.

From the celebrated Acts we learn that he immediately set out to visit a certain Diodorus, whom Epiphanius calls Tryphon, who presided over a Christian parish, in order to enter into disputations with him.

Cyril calls the location of this parish a most insignificant village.

[Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6.]

Photius agrees, writing:

> “Fleeing from there, he seized an obscure village, and there again attempted to foster and reveal his impiety.”

[Note: Photius, book 1 *Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 13, in my edition, p. 51.]

Photius makes no mention at all, however, of Diodorus, or Tryphon the presbyter, whom Manes attempted to attack and harass with new disputations.

Although this man excelled over the others present there in piety, purity of religion, and the remaining virtues, he was nevertheless so little and so inadequately versed in the sacred writings that he could easily have been deceived by Manes, who flattered himself that he would bring the presbyter over to his own opinion.

This expectation of the heresy’s author, however, deceived him. For scarcely had the presbyter heard the blasphemies into which the architect of new doctrines had burst forth when he informed Bishop Archelaus, urgently requesting instruction and assistance.

Archelaus immediately wrote a lengthy letter to his presbyter. Beausobre considered it unworthy of his history, or insufficiently suited to his purposes; he neither translated it into French nor incorporated it into his work.

[Note: Beausobre, book 1, chapter 10, p. 113.]

He nevertheless dwells on the inscription of this letter, looking for a knot in a bulrush. In that inscription he encountered two features that aroused his suspicion and, unless he was suffering from hallucination, as he says, clearly demonstrated that the letter had not been written in the time of Archelaus.

The first of these is that, according to the letter, a church had been founded there without a bishop and was governed solely by a presbyter. He therefore adds:

> “I can in no way persuade myself that, during the third century of the Church, churches were founded either in cities or in suburbs, or villages, without bishops being present. When the Church had not yet sufficiently increased in the number of the faithful, bishops had only deacons under them, who were subject to them; but these were not bishops, although they were so called and performed all the sacred functions. Only much later were such rural bishops, or chorepiscopi, stripped of every higher authority and consequently compelled to descend to the order of presbyters.”

Diodorides, therefore, was a fortress or suburb that at that time had a bishop, as Dr. Assemani appears to suggest in the *Oriental Library*.

[Note: Assemani, volume 2 of the *Oriental Library*, dissertation on the Monophysites.]

### 2.

Having presented this first difficulty, which Beausobre considers extremely serious, he immediately moves to a second, which makes Archelaus’s letter appear even more suspect.

Assuming, he says, that bishops in villages and towns had no one but ordinary presbyters to preside over the congregations, it must at least be considered beyond all doubt that those presbyters were called “brothers” by their bishops, and not “sons,” especially when the bishops addressed their writings to them.

He contrives to make the term “sons” apply exclusively to deacons, since they are properly the ministers of bishops in the performance of sacred duties. He therefore persuades himself that no example can be found in which, during the first three centuries, bishops placed the term “sons” in the heading of letters addressed to presbyters.

Thus far Beausobre.

Would he then compel his readers to believe fables? Although these may appear to have been composed with considerable ingenuity and supported by words and arguments, they can claim neither credibility nor authority except among stupid and foolish men, wholly ignorant of the Church’s hierarchy and of this ancient order and system of administration. Nor does it help him to appeal, without citing any author, to the ecclesiastical history of the first three centuries [Col. 0844A]. For, first of all, he ought to have distinguished between a particular assembly of the faithful gathered under one legitimate shepherd—namely, a bishop—and the place where those same faithful assembled for their meetings. On Sundays, that is, on the Lord’s days, they celebrated the divine mysteries under one presider, and matters of the Christian religion were discussed among them. Who is unaware that the name “Church” was suitably applied to both? Therefore, when it is asserted of the Church understood in the former sense that it could not exist without a bishop, and that each Church had its own single presiding bishop—whom the ancients, such as Justin and Tertullian, called the high priest [Note: [Col. 0843D] Tertullian, in his book *On Baptism*.]—everyone ought to understand that this refers to the episcopate according to the Church’s ancient and modern hierarchy.

But because Churches understood in this first manner were generally, and especially at that time, not confined within narrow boundaries but extended over distant regions, embracing several cities, suburbs, villages, fortified settlements, rural districts, and other places of that kind, one place of worship and one priest could not suffice for all the faithful of such a Church to celebrate the mysteries. Accordingly, within the same diocese—which they called a Church—several sacred assemblies had to be held, especially on Sundays. Priests were to preside over them, both teaching the people and celebrating the sacred synaxis, or gathering.

### 3.

Lest, in recording these matters, I seem to be telling tales to men of impaired faith, it is already known from Tertullian and Justin Martyr that such was the ecclesiastical discipline during the second century [Note: [Col. 0843D] Justin Martyr, *Second Apology*.]. In his *Apology*, published on behalf of the Christians and presented to the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, Justin clearly mentioned these sacred assemblies, celebrated on Sundays even in towns and rural districts inhabited by Christian people; he likewise described individually [Note: 61] both what was done by the presiders, what the people joyfully acclaimed, and what was finally read by the ecclesiastical readers from the memoirs of the apostles and the writings of the prophets [Col. 0844C]. All these things were followed by the prayers of the whole assembly, after the presider’s address, by which the people were instructed and encouraged to imitate such excellent things. Then they distributed to each person present the consecrated bread and the consecrated wine mixed with water. They were accustomed to send it by the deacons to those who were absent. Nor were those deprived of participation in these sacred gifts who, hindered by illness, captivity, imprisonment, or any other cause, could not attend the sacred assembly with the gathered people on Sunday. The same was done for travelers who arrived from abroad and were received as guests. For it was the duty of those same presiders to assist them, since the presider was also the caretaker of all who were in need.

Thus, from Justin’s words, which we append below, it is necessary to reason against Beausobre’s nonsense:

> In all the offerings that we make, we bless and praise the Maker of all things through his Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. And on the day called Sunday, all who live either in the towns or in the countryside assemble in the same place; and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as time permits.  
>   
> [Note: The readings from Scripture were arranged according to the variety of times, even during the second century. We discuss this practice at greater length in the notes to the letter of Saint Leo the Great to Turibius of Astorga, on the occasion of a certain fragment that scholars have hitherto sought. Justin then adds:] When the reader has ceased, the presider delivers an address in which he instructs the people and exhorts them to imitate such excellent things. After this we all rise together and offer prayers; and, when the prayers have been completed, bread is presented, together with wine and water, and the presider likewise offers prayers and thanksgivings to the best of his ability . . . . . and the distribution and sharing of the things over which thanks have been given takes place for each person present; but to those who are absent it is sent by the deacons . . . . . and what is collected in this way is deposited with the presider. He then assists the orphans and widows, those who are in need because of illness or any other cause, those who are in prison, and travelers who arrive as guests . . . . . . On Sunday we all hold our common assembly.  
>   
> Justin, *Apology*, commonly called the Second, near the end, pp. 98–99.

[Col. 0844D] In the second century of the Church, while persecutions by both Jews and pagans were still raging, the Christian population had grown so greatly that, as Eusebius says, not only in the more important cities but also in towns and rural districts, all the faithful held a common assembly on Sunday, at which the presiders or leaders of the Churches celebrated the sacred rites. Therefore, if only one bishop presided over each Church [Note: [Col. 0845D] That there was one bishop in each Church may be inferred from John’s Apocalypse, where, after mentioning the seven Churches of Asia, he assigns a single bishop to each under the name “angel.” Tertullian spoke of the succession and order of Churches, or bishops, during the latter part of the second century in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 32. See Hegesippus in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 22, and Irenaeus in the same author, book V, chapter 20. Paul says in the Epistle to Titus, chapter I, verse 5, that he left him in Crete “to appoint presbyters in every city,” whom he subsequently calls bishops. He says the same in the First Epistle to Timothy.—], as we know from John’s canonical Epistle and understand from the successions of bishops described by Hegesippus and Tertullian, it was utterly impossible for him on the same day to hurry from place to place, travel through the entire diocese, and conduct and conclude those assemblies with the expected attendance and multitude of the people of which we are now speaking.

Nor can it be supposed that the Christian people of each diocese, whenever Sunday came around, could set aside all other concerns and stream from every part of the diocese to the episcopal sees. In the first place, Justin expressly asserts that sacred assemblies were held in towns [Note: 62] and in the countryside [Col. 0845B]. Moreover, the distances between places would have prevented women, children, and the elderly from undertaking such lengthy journeys. Finally, they could easily have been seized by the imperial officials if, in groups and at fixed hours, they had been required to gather at a particular place in the presence of their own single bishop. For it is abundantly clear that bishops were then constantly sought out and arrested for execution by the imperial officials, both from the martyrdoms of Ignatius, Polycarp, Peter, and Dionysius, and from the glorious deaths of the Roman bishops who, up to Justin’s time, were deemed worthy to ascend Peter’s throne.

### 4.

If, then, in those assemblies held in towns and rural districts on Sundays, a presider and leader who performed the sacred rites commonly presided, Beausobre’s first invention collapses: namely, that during the first three centuries the terms “bishops” and “presbyters” were used to signify the same person, authority, and power [Col. 0845C]. After Aerius, Blondel, Salmasius, and the other teachers of the Puritan school repeated this refrain. Twisting the Acts and Paul’s words toward a perverse meaning [Note: [Col. 0845D] In Acts 20, when Paul was at Miletus, he is said to have summoned the presbyters from Ephesus. Then, addressing them after they had assembled together, he calls them bishops.—], they rashly dared to maintain, falsely, that the dignity and authority of presbyters and bishops were one and the same—not only in the time of the apostles but also in subsequent centuries. Refuting their nonsense cannot be the task of the present leisure, especially since among the other most distinguished men who have debated this distinction, the extremely learned Petavius has done so at greater length [Note: [Col. 0845D] Petavius, volume IV of the *Theological Dogmatics*, on the ecclesiastical hierarchy and the power of consecrating.—].

But, in order to press Beausobre still more vigorously, we have thought it better to appeal to that presbyter John whom Irenaeus mentions in Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0845D] Eusebius, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 3; and book VII, chapter 29; book VI, chapter 18.—]; or to Irenaeus himself, who exercised only the office of presbyter while Photinus, bishop of Lyons, was still alive; or to Acchillas, a presbyter of Alexandria, at the time when Theonas and Peter governed that Church. We may also appeal to Origen, who, although a presbyter, was ordained at Caesarea by the bishops of Palestine against Demetrius’s will.

Tertullian, among others, testifies that, during the latter part of the second century and the beginning of the third, presbyters did not possess equal authority and jurisdiction with their bishops in the performance of divine matters [Col. 0846A] [Note: [Col. 0846D] Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 17, p. 156 in my Venetian edition. Consult Cyprian, who during the third century established a distinction between the authority of bishops and presbyters, reserving the right to confer chrism to bishops alone, *Epistle* 73, to Jubaianus.—]. Comparing and contrasting their ministries with the rights of bishops, he says:

> The high priest, who is the bishop, has the right to administer baptism. After him come the presbyters and deacons, though not without the bishop’s authority, for the honor of the Church; when that honor is preserved, peace is preserved.

Thus Tertullian distinguished three ecclesiastical orders, assigning each its own rights. He would not have said that presbyters and deacons could not baptize without the authority of the bishops if bishop and presbyter alike had possessed a common honor and power.

The Carthaginian laws and the most ancient laws of the Catholic Church, set down in writing in the Constitutions circulated under the name of the apostles, agree with this [Col. 0846B] [Note: [Col. 0846D] Apostolic Canons 38, 31, 14. These laws are also found in the Council of Nicaea, canon 16; in Antioch, chapter 3; in book III of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 61; and in Athanasius’s *Epistle to the Orthodox*, and in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 56.—]. Most especially they agree with the provision that presbyters and deacons may not accomplish anything without the bishop’s decision, just as they may not dare to abandon the parishes assigned to them without the knowledge of their own bishop.

Therefore, if, when the ancient discipline and order of the Church are considered [Note: 63], the supreme rights of bishops were one thing and those of ordinary presbyters another, and if the latter were entirely dependent upon the bishops in carrying out their duties, I cannot understand with what disposition or on what grounds Beausobre could have maintained that Diodorus, or Tryphon, who toward the end of the third century governed a rural or suburban parish, was not, or could not have been, absent from the encounter to which Manes had so boldly challenged him, while Archelaus, his own bishop, was present.

Would he have been permitted, in the presence of his own bishop, whose commission he held in serving as rector or presider, to dispute with a heretical and cunning man? Who could have done so without injury? For, even with the bishop present, he should not have baptized—that is, administered baptism—or performed any other sacred ministry. The same Tertullian cited above [Note: [Col. 0846D] Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 17.—] warns presbyters, deacons, and all the other men of the clerical service not to assume for themselves the bishop’s appointed office, the episcopate, especially to prevent rivalry, which is the mother of schisms.

That the duty of teaching, debating and defining the dogmas of the faith, whether in councils or in other assemblies, belongs to bishops by virtue of their ordination is entirely certain. Therefore, when certain rural or suburban presbyters in the fourth and fifth centuries tried to extend the rights of their ordination, they unlawfully usurped episcopal functions through reckless acts and were deprived of and prohibited from sacred ministry both by the Apostolic See and by the bishops of the entire world, as Pope Damasus declared in his letter [Col. 0846D].

[Note: [Col. 0846D] Pope Damasus, *Epistle* 5, volume II of the Councils, p. 1025. Appealing to the statutes of his predecessors, the bishops of the Apostolic See, he seems principally to have alluded to the letters of Pope Julius and to others lost through the injury of time. As for the canons issued by the bishops of the entire world, which the pontiff praises there, we think without doubt that they were the Nicene canons. That their Arabic paraphrase contains much concerning chorepiscopi is abundantly clear from chapters 54, 55, 56, and following. Canon 14 of Neocaesarea likewise supports this, expressly mentioning the ministry of the chorepiscopi, whom it was necessary to honor as having been chosen in the likeness of the seventy-two disciples, on account of the ministry they exercised toward the poor.]

He further declared that the institution of these men [Col. 0847A] was excessively reprehensible and impious. Since they were contending for the high priesthood in episcopal sees, although they lacked all authority, their proud and superfluous exaltation was directed solely toward abolishing the sacred canons and disturbing the entire ecclesiastical hierarchy. Saint Leo the Great [Note: [Col. 0847D] Saint Leo the Great, formerly *Epistle* 85. It is now absent from Quesnel’s edition.—], adhering to the regulations of his predecessors and of the councils, defined that whatever they had done in the ministry of that supreme priesthood—the chorepiscopate—was void and empty.

Beausobre therefore invents this conclusion according to his own opinion: that during the first three centuries presbyters and bishops had the same authority and power; that the bishops did not preside over the presbyters; and that the presbyters, in governing the parishes entrusted to them and exercising other ministries among the faithful, were in no way dependent upon the bishops’ will and authority.

### 5.

When the reader has reflected upon what has been said thus far, I have no fear that he will or can judge the final objections raised by Beausobre to be any stronger. By them he attempts to prove that Archelaus’s letter to Diodorus, the subject presently under discussion, is spurious. For if, during the first three centuries, bishops did not customarily address their fellow presbyters, or suburban presbyters, as “sons,” but, treating them more honorably, instead called them “brothers” in their letters, then the divine authority of the letters of Peter and Paul would already be tottering and collapsing, since we find these expressions and marks in them.

Indeed, the apostle Peter calls Mark a bishop and addresses him as a son, writing in his First Epistle:

> The Church gathered in Babylon greets you, and Mark, my son.

Saint Paul likewise frequently employed this form of speech [Note: 64], both when he wrote in the First Epistle to Timothy [Note: [Col. 0847D] Paul, First Epistle to Timothy, chapter I, verse 2; and [Col. 0848D] the same place, verse 18; again, Second Epistle, chapter I, verse 2; and finally chapter II, verse 1.—]:

> To Timothy, my beloved son in the faith;

and again, addressing the same man, he added:

> This command I entrust to you, my son Timothy.

He used it also when he began another letter to the same man in these words:

> Paul, an apostle, etc., to Timothy, his dearest son;

or, to omit many other examples of the same kind, when he instructed Titus to appoint presbyters throughout the cities of Crete, just as he himself had arranged. In that Epistle, the words “To Titus, my beloved son according to the common faith” [Note: [Col. 0848D] The same author, Epistle to Titus, chapter I, verse 4.—] show that Titus was called Paul’s son.

What follows, then? One of two things would have to be concluded from Beausobre’s fictitious opinion: either that the cited letters of the apostles Peter and Paul bear the marks and characteristics of forgery—something wholly unheard of until now—or at least that those divine writers, in composing their familiar letters, employed a certain license entirely foreign to the courteous duties that were to be observed more strictly between co-bishops and fellow presbyters. The latter cannot be asserted without the charge of extreme audacity. For those apostles, writing under the dictation of the divine Spirit, used forms of expression more appropriate to the persons and subjects about which they intended to speak.

Thus it happened that those whom they called “sons” in one place they called “brothers” in another. For example, when Paul, held captive, wrote to Philemon [Note: [Col. 0848D] Epistle to Philemon 1: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, a brother.”—], he called Timothy a brother, an appellation he commonly applied to all who had been reborn through baptism in Christ. But when he wished to have regard to the formation of persons whom he himself had brought forth to Christ and the faith by preaching, or whom he had himself converted, baptized, and initiated into orders through the sacrament of ordination which he had conferred on them, he reasonably called them sons, as is sufficiently clear from the cited Epistles concerning Timothy, Titus, Onesimus, and others.

Since, therefore, Beausobre’s arguments are rather amusing and fabulous, there is no reason for us to reject as fictitious Archelaus’s letter to his presbyter Diodorus, or Tryphon.

### 6.

Let us now set aside Beausobre’s nonsense for a while and return to the order of our history. Relying on Epiphanius’s testimony, we maintain—or rather hold as certain—that Archelaus did not immediately set out for Diodoris, a village of his diocese, and diligently search for the wolf fleeing from Caschara without any interval of time. Rather, the matter occurred more clearly than Cyril describes it: Archelaus was initially unaware that Manes had withdrawn to that village; Manes met once and again with the presbyter who governed the parish and began a disputation concerning the doctrines of religion.

Although that presbyter, whom Epiphanius calls Tryphon, lacked eloquence and facility and abundance in speaking, he nevertheless defeated Manes. In him, in fact, that divine promise made to the apostles was fulfilled:

> Do not consider how or what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] Matthew 10:19–20.—]

Manes, however, bearing this very painfully—as though to erase the mark of disgrace—wished to attack Tryphon, or Diodorus, again with new arguments. He maintained that the two Testaments of Sacred Scripture were by no means consistent with one another, and he sought above all to demonstrate their greatest contradiction from the testimony of the Gospels.

This pure fabrication of a cunning and sacrilegious man aimed chiefly at destroying the authority of the Old Testament and thereby asserting that it had originated from some evil and eternal principle. But the presbyter Diodorus, wishing to break the audacity of so great a scoundrel, decided to report the whole matter by letter, as we have said, to Archelaus, his bishop. What those letters contained we learn both from Epiphanius [Col. 0848C] and from Archelaus.

Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0848D] Epiphanius, book III, *Against Heresies*—] asserts that Diodorus used only the following words, which he quotes:

> A certain man has come here who, like a most savage wolf, is attempting to destroy the sheepfold. But I beg you to write to me how I ought to conduct myself against him, and by what arguments I should resist his pernicious teaching. If you yourself would deign to come, you would free Christ’s sheepfold and flock from all anxiety.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] This is the letter that Beausobre foolishly claims bears the marks of forgery; its address has already been discussed.—]

But in his reply Archelaus, responding to Diodorus’s wishes and letter, makes clear that his presbyter had not merely reported these general matters to him. For, among other things, he focuses especially on demonstrating the remarkable harmony and agreement of the two Testaments, adducing various comparisons borrowed carefully from the use, condition, and substance of natural things.

Such examples include the one drawn from a single garment, which appears to be woven with warp and weft:

> This alone [he says], that we see as purple in a garment, represents the New Testament; the glory of the Lord Jesus is woven into the texture of the Old.

Or there is the other comparison drawn from a mirror:

> We are not at all accustomed to reject it when the true image of things is shown to us.

He also offers an example drawn from children being led to teachers by a pedagogue. When they have been brought to a more mature age, they ought not to dishonor the pedagogue, even though they no longer need his assistance. Finally, he proves by the example of a little child that both Testaments must be retained and venerated. A child who has been nourished on milk and is progressing to stronger food cannot, without grave injury, reject and recoil from the breasts of his nurse; rather, he venerates and honors her and acknowledges that he is her debtor for the benefit he has received.

### 7.

Archelaus suggested these and other arguments of the same kind in his very lengthy letter—which Epiphanius calls a book—to his presbyter Diodorus, in order to disclose, as we have said, the ever-wondrous and sincere harmony and complete agreement of both Testaments.

We do not, however, think that Archelaus’s entire purpose in this letter lay in asserting the complete agreement of the Testaments. Rather, we believe that the holy bishop intended to show something deeper through the arguments he introduced: namely, that human nature, already endangered amid so many and such great vices and surrounded by the darker shadows of ignorance, was not to be recalled immediately to the clear knowledge of truth or released at once from the snares of eternal death by which it was bound.

It was necessary instead that human beings—wandering like wild beasts and never thinking about divine matters—should be instructed by various heavenly steps toward eternal wisdom. First they were to be instructed through the figures and shadows of natural things, which they were to draw from the Mosaic Law as from milk; and finally through grace and the clear contemplation of divine things, which the New Testament set before them in the form of solid food: the Son himself of the eternal Father.

If Diodorus had wished to use these most weighty arguments, suggested by Archelaus, he could easily have confounded and crushed Manes. The doctrines of the Catholic faith themselves, and the divine authority of the Old Testament—which was especially being called into question—would without doubt have been confirmed.

Relying, therefore, on Archelaus’s writings, Diodorus the presbyter, although awaiting the arrival of his bishop, was compelled by Manes’s audacity to enter into the dispute again. For Manes, coming out into the middle of the village at first light, began another disputation with Diodorus [Col. 0849C]. Manes was the first to bring forward his doctrines against Diodorus. But Diodorus met every question and, according to the wisdom he had received from God, gently harried his impostor.

When at last Manes began to waver somewhat, Archelaus suddenly appeared—“unexpectedly,” says Epiphanius—like a very courageous head of a household, deeply devoted to his own people, rushing boldly upon the robber with a roar [Note: 66]. What did Manes do then? Like a crafty and shifting fox, he turned to Archelaus with feigned mildness, asking that he be allowed to debate only with the presbyter. He further asserted that it was especially unbecoming for a bishop to contend with a man inferior to him concerning matters of religion.

But the people who were present, having recognized Manes’s wickedness, attacked him so fiercely that they even tried to overwhelm him with stones. He would not have escaped this danger had he not, having fled for the third time, hurried again to the Castle of Arabion, where he had first taken refuge.

### 8.

Beausobre, however, related this new dispute between Archelaus and Manes in his *History* in a manner different from the one we have described. In order to reach the end he had already set for himself, he searches out and gathers arguments from every direction, not only to reject those *Acts* as spurious but also to denounce and rage against them as sources of many heresies.

When we discovered that the crafty and malicious mind of this acatholic man had dared to erupt into various accusations and misrepresentations wholly injurious to Bishop Archelaus and to the entire Catholic assembly, our love of truth did not permit us to pass over the matter in silence, lest he appear profound to the adherents of false criticism. Therefore it will be our task to defend the opinions of Archelaus and the arguments of that new disputation, which Beausobre twisted into various tangles [Col. 0850A], as though to contend back and forth that, during the third century, the true tradition of the Catholic and Apostolic Church concerning the principal dogmas of our faith had been corrupted, shaken, and destroyed. We shall do this in order, as far as our strength allows, to rebuke a man of such extraordinary audacity, forever dealing in trifles and inventions.

# CHAPTER IX

Archelaus’s Dispute with Manes at Diodoris Defended against Critical Objections and Beausobrian Calumnies. The Bad Faith of the Acatholic Writer in Reporting Archelaus’s Testimonies Explained. Finally, Archelaus Is Rightly Regarded as Catholic and Holy in the Church, Both from the Writings Circulated under His Name and from His Zeal for the True Religion of Christ.

### 1.

I thought that I had sufficiently discharged the duties of my office when, in the preceding chapter, I gave a brief account of what seemed to concern the disputes between Manes and Archelaus [Col. 0850B]. For it was not my intention to compose theological apologetic treatises, but to collect the history of the Manichaeans, as if in an abridgment, from certain authentic records and authors—just as distinguished men have already written separate histories of the Pelagians, Donatists, Arians, Eutychians, and other heretics who attempted to corrupt and overthrow the Catholic religion.

But while reading through Beausobre’s work [Note: [Col. 0849D] Beausobre, book I of the *History of the Manichaeans*, chapter 10.—], I encountered everywhere lies and calumnies so numerous and so great, enveloped in thick darkness, that I decided to bring them some light, so that, like mist dispersed by the sun from the East, they might be dissolved and driven away. Otherwise, if I had persisted merely in pointing out this heretical man’s bad faith, the learned men of the present age—who enjoy concerning themselves only with the surface of things [Note: 67]—might easily have concluded that Beausobre’s arguments were too weighty to be refuted by us if we touched upon them briefly or passed over them altogether.

To begin this task, we may first pass over in silence some observations of this Dutch writer [Note: [Col. 0849D] Beausobre, book I, chapter 10, pp. 113 ff.—], namely those in which he attempted to portray Bishop Archelaus as a man arrogantly boasting of the victory he had previously won: one who wished to present himself again at the village of Diodoris before his humbled and defeated enemy, binding the presbyter Diodorus, or Tryphon, to break off the contest he had begun, so that Archelaus himself might enter upon a new dispute with Manes concerning matters of faith.

I shall not conceal merely that he called the bishop’s zeal for matters of Christian religion “pride,” “swelling,” and “fury,” and that he found Manes’s manner of acting and forms of speech highly displeasing. For when the heretic implored Archelaus to allow him to bring to an end the dispute he had begun with the presbyter, fearing for that reason to contend concerning religious doctrines with a bishop superior to him in authority and dignity, Beausobre says:

> It was a grave absurdity to put these words into the mouth of a heretic.

For Manes had not merely debated publicly with Archelaus long before concerning new doctrines; he had also, in his impious arrogance, dared to call himself a disciple of Christ, an apostle of Jesus, and the Paraclete promised by the Son of God.

When Gothofredus Arnoldus recognized this most serious difficulty [Note: [Col. 0849D] Gothofredus Arnoldus, *History of the Church and of Heretics*, written in French, volume I, book III, chapter 7, § 24 ff. [Col. 0850D]—], he persuaded himself that the courteous words in question had been uttered by Manes deceitfully and ironically, as they say, so that he might guard against the humiliation he had previously been forced to endure at Caschara—especially since he had been led to hope that he could defeat a presbyter more easily than a bishop.

I therefore plainly do not see what absurdity follows from so natural an explanation, since the chief concern of heretics is that they may possess influence among the unlearned and ignorant populace through favor, authority, and reputation. Manes hoped to achieve all this if he could overcome the presbyter of the parish in debate.

Would he not, if he had defeated his opponent in the dispute he had begun, have drawn to his own opinion all the faithful who had come there from Diodoris and the neighboring places, unless they had suddenly been supported by divine assistance and enlightened by the light of truth? Beausobre therefore ought not to find it absurd that Manes, in order to avoid a new danger of shame and disgrace—which he had foreseen was certainly threatening him from the earlier experience at Caschara—refused to contend again with Archelaus concerning the doctrines of the faith.

For it is usually the prudent course of those who engage in controversy that, once overcome by their opponents, they do not again entrust themselves to a contest with the same adversaries, now stronger in resources, knowledge, and fortune, but withdraw from disputes that they know will prove fatal to them.

Since Manes had certainly learned that he had no better resources of knowledge available to him at the village of Diodoris, he ought to avoid a new kind of contest with Archelaus—especially since he knew that Archelaus was thoroughly versed in the sacred writings of both Testaments. Let us therefore not suspect those *Acts* of Archelaus of being spurious merely because Manes, publicly overcome and defeated in the controversy, refused to renew another contest, one more perilous and dangerous than the first.

## 2.

Nor can I likewise conceal the grave censure with which that same Beausobre attacks both Archelaus and the tradition of the Church and the teaching of the ancient Fathers. When he subjected this latest disputation between Manes and Archelaus to examination, he branded the holy and wise bishop with the marks of many heresies—marks which he attempted, with excessive zeal and with reckless and unjust boldness, to ferret out and bring forward from his words and opinions. [68] Therefore, lest we should seem to labor in vain, we resolved, so far as our strength allowed, to erase this stigma of infamy and to vindicate ecclesiastical tradition, by removing one by one the charges which Beausobre wrongly brought against him.

Accordingly, he proposes three principal arguments from the Manichaean disputation and appends to them an equal number of Archelaus’s replies. The first concerns the mystery of the Incarnation. Wishing to overthrow it, Manes maintained that Christ, the Son of God, had not truly been a man born of a woman, but had merely appeared as such by divine dispensation, without having united to himself a real and substantial human nature.

For this reason he abused the words of the Apostle Paul to the Philippians:

> [Note: Philippians II, 7–8: “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man.”]

By these words it was affirmed that Christ had been made in the likeness of men. But, to lend strength to his wicked doctrine, he further appealed to the words of Luke, which say:

> [Note: Luke III, 22: “And the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove.”]

The Holy Spirit, then, descended upon Christ, who had been baptized in the Jordan, in bodily form like a dove. Thus, Manes reasoned—following Beausobre—just as the Holy Spirit was not accompanied by a real and corporeal dove, but merely bore the appearance of a dove and chose to possess only an apparent likeness, so the Son of God bore only the appearance of a man, without assuming a true and real human nature.

“This crude first argument of Manes,” says Beausobre, “Bishop Archelaus refuted with the most solid reasoning; but at the same time he advanced propositions which display no less conspicuous marks of heresy.” On this matter he thought the readers ought to be warned, so that, as he says, “from such observations they may understand that faith must not be regulated according to antiquity, nor subjected to the authority of the tradition and the Fathers of the first three centuries—that golden age which they affirm was brought to ruin” (by which you are to understand the non-Catholics), “when the great Constantine held the reins of empire.”

Yet one must assert that the true faith ceased even earlier, if we suppose that the virtues of the bishops, their character, and the privilege of that age were its distinguishing features. Thus far Beausobre.

But I ask him why, abandoning his customary and familiar trifles and fables, he becomes so angry that, attacking the ancient Church, he wished to bark at and bite its most holy bishops like rabid dogs. He contends that tradition must not be admitted and that faith must not be placed in the ancient Fathers of the Church.
