But lest we should seem to be acting outside the scene, let Beausobre tell us, I beg him, by what support the Catholic doctrine of the Incarnation—on which the present disputation between Manes and Archelaus principally turned—would have been proved, if Archelaus, following merely his private spirit rather than the authority of his episcopal predecessors, had wished to interpret the testimonies of Paul and Luke just cited, which Manes twisted toward perverse meanings.

If Archelaus, abandoning the teaching and tradition of his predecessors, had wished to explain the aforementioned passages of Scripture; if, moreover, he had paid no attention to the general agreement of the other Churches, he would have added wicked novelties to new inventions. And while both men were speaking about one and the same mystery, they would have fallen from it into ever new heresies.

Yet Beausobre himself asserts that Archelaus argued and thought rightly, soundly, and wisely concerning Christ’s true flesh, his baptism, death, burial, and resurrection. Therefore he did not indulge in new and foreign doctrines; rather, he followed those which the holy leaders of the Churches who preceded him had taught.

What, then, is tradition? What is that divine rule of the Church from which the doctrines of the true faith are drawn? What are the agreement and teaching of the holy Fathers? Is it anything other than all that which Beausobre now attacks and condemns, and which he seeks to overthrow by fabulous inventions, in order to indulge his own interests and party more than the truth?

## 69. 3.

But Beausobre dares maliciously to maintain that Archelaus adhered to novelties while defending those Catholic doctrines concerning Christ’s true flesh and his true passion and death. For, he says, the bishop affirmed that Jesus had truly been fastened to the cross and that, after he himself had risen from the dead, he had been taken up to the place where Christ, the Son of God, reigns.

He therefore asserts that Archelaus explained the Lord’s descent into hell most effectively. According to this manner of speaking, the place of hell is the same as the tomb, from which Jesus, restored to life, ascended into heaven. He adds that this interpretation is reasonable and just, but contends that it is accompanied by various dreadful heresies.

He calls the interpretation reasonable and just for no other reason than that he thinks it supports Theodore Beza, Calvin, and himself, who deny that Christ’s soul descended into hell. The Fathers of both Churches have spoken everywhere about this celebrated and well-worn question, chastising those who, following the Hebrew readings, thought that “hell” should be understood more strictly as “the grave.”

> [Note: The Catholic dogma concerning the descent of Christ’s soul into hell is clearly revealed in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. Psalm XV, 8, reads: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” Referring to this prophecy of the prophet David and explaining the same words, Peter alludes to it in Acts II, 31: “Foreseeing this,” he says, “he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that he was neither abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption.” Since these testimonies express two distinct matters—one concerning the privilege of his soul, which could not be detained in the prison of the dead; the other explaining the condition of Christ’s dead flesh, which was not subject to corruption—the faithful therefore express both separately every day when they profess the solemn confession of faith, saying: “Crucified, dead, and buried, he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead.” Saint Peter the Apostle also spoke plainly of this descent into hell in his First Epistle, chapter III, 19, and chapter IV, 6. Nor does it prove anything that this descent into hell was omitted from most of the ancient Creeds of the Greek and Latin Churches, such as those of Nicaea and Constantinople, concerning which there was no controversy. For we understand that it was included in other very ancient creeds, such as the one used by the Church of Aquileia in the fourth century, which our Rufinus reports—Rufinus who was attacked with such harsh and abusive words by certain more recent slanderous writers that they caused trouble for those who defended him. Nevertheless, although this dogma was not declared in the Creeds of many Churches, it was commonly and generally received among them in faith, as is taught, among others, by Saint Justin Martyr in his Dialogue with Trypho, p. 232; Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 39; Clement of Alexandria, in the sixth book of the Stromata; Origen, book II Against Celsus, and Homily 15 on Genesis and on Exodus; Eusebius, book IV of the Demonstration of the Gospel; Tertullian, On the Soul; Lactantius, book IV, chapter 9; Julius Firmicus, On the Error of Profane Religions; Hilary, book X On the Trinity; and all the others who flourished in the Greek and Latin Church. The most learned Dionysius Petavius has set out their catalogues in book XIII of On the Incarnation, chapter 16 and following. Archelaus therefore had all these authorities on his side.]

We do not presently think it appropriate to prolong this discussion further. Learned and careful men have already published various studies rejecting the false opinions of Theodore Beza, Calvin, and Erasmus, in order to prove that the words “he descended into hell” must by no means be expunged from the Creed of faith.

But even before those learned men had accomplished this, Leo the Great, condemning the errors of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, defended the truth at issue here from many passages of Scripture. He expressed astonishment that Turibius, bishop of the Church of Astorga, had consulted the Apostolic See about this article of the Christian religion:

> [Note: Saint Leo the Great, Epistle XV, chapter XVII.]

> “I am astonished that the understanding of any Catholic should struggle as though it were uncertain whether, when Christ descended into hell, his flesh rested in the tomb; for just as it truly died and was buried, so it was truly raised on the third day.”

He then appeals to testimonies from Scripture, which we have appended in the notes, and immediately adds:

> “By these words it is plainly evident that the Lord’s flesh both truly rested in the tomb and did not undergo corruption, because, being quickly vivified by the return of the soul, it rose again. To refuse to believe this is sufficiently impious, and there is no doubt that it belongs to the teaching of Manes and Priscillian. With sacrilegious understanding they pretend to confess Christ while removing the truth of his Incarnation, death, and resurrection.”

## 4.

Since Beausobre, in the dogma under discussion, follows Manes and Priscillian, we must now take up what he finally objected against the faith of Bishop Archelaus. First, he casts suspicion upon Archelaus as one who had violated the faith because he called the divine nature “Christ,” although, he says, that term can designate only a person who has attained such status through grace, gifts, perfections, and dignity.

Such a formula of speech, he adds, had already been familiar to heretics. Although Father Petavius maintains that it was in use among Catholics—including Justin Martyr, Dionysius of Alexandria, Novatian (or the author of the book On the Trinity), and Ambrose—all of whom, except Ambrose, are regarded more and more as suspect of Arian doctrine—

> [Note: Archelaus, in the Acts, p. 93.]

For this reason, he seemed almost to think that Archelaus should be excused for using the expression. But because he bends and directs both the preceding and following parts of his discourse toward Nestorian doctrine, saying that Jesus, after the resurrection, was transferred to the place in which Christ, the Son of God, reigns, he considers him inexcusable.

For the words cited plainly suggest that Jesus and the Son of God are two separate persons, one of whom ascended to the other, as the following words show even more clearly:

> “There is one who was born from Mary, a son, who chose to undergo all this struggle—Jesus. This is the Christ of God, who descended upon him who was from Mary.”

But in order to do violence to the force of the preceding words and to increase and strengthen Beausobre’s bad faith in writing, he reasons as follows:

> [Note: Beausobre, book I, chapter 10, p. 115.]

> “The one who descended upon Jesus when he was baptized could not have been the person of Jesus himself. And since the one who descended upon Jesus is Christ, the Son of God, Jesus could not possibly have been the Son of God except after he descended upon him—that is, after Jesus had been endowed through baptism.”

He contends, appealing to Dionysius Petavius, whom he cites, that these were the heresies of Cerinthus and Carpocrates, who harassed the Church from its beginnings. He further asserts that the Ebionites taught something similar concerning Jesus. He says that the Elcesaites, Orphites, and Ophites—on the authority of Theodoret—

> [Note: Theodoret, On the Fables of Heretics, book I, 14.]

> “rashly invented that Jesus was one person and Christ another, and that Christ descended upon him.”

He concludes this first objection against Archelaus’s faith with wicked insults. Bursting, as it were, with insane fury, he devoted the holy bishop to calumnies and curses. Denying the reputation of his holiness, he imagined him branded and pierced by the same censures and anathemas, and cast outside the fellowship of Catholics, as that unhappy crowd of heretics mentioned above had been proscribed by the judgment of the Church, which was indeed more holy than that of Archelaus.

## 5.

As I reviewed these and similar matters, my spirit did not flare up against Beausobre. I merely observed his effort to twist and corrupt the preceding testimonies and opinions, so that he might utterly overthrow the authority of the Acts and completely destroy the piety of that most holy bishop.

Yet I clearly understood that Beausobre, always speaking from his own preconceived opinion, sought to tell fables, deceive, and sell nonsense to the reader by confusing the two descents of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus. Sacred Scripture most clearly testifies that one of these must be referred to his conception from the Virgin Mary and to the hypostatic union of the Son of God with human nature, while the other must be referred to the baptism of that same Christ.

Therefore, when Archelaus was discussing the mystery of the Incarnation, it could not have occurred to him that Jesus Christ was made the Son of God at the time when the Holy Spirit descended upon him after his baptism. He would thereby have departed from the question before him: whether Christ, the Son of God, had possessed a true human nature joined to him when he emerged from the virginal womb. Manes denied this, asserting that Christ possessed only a phantom humanity, while Archelaus wisely and Catholicly contradicted him.

Since the inquiry concerned only whether it was contrary to reason or unbecoming for the Son of God truly to be born from a woman and to have a true human nature joined to him in the womb, Archelaus could not have admitted that Jesus was born as one person and brought forth from the virginal womb, while, after baptism, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him, another person—the person of Christ and the Son of God—had arrived.

Otherwise, Manes’s objections would have remained standing, and Archelaus would impiously have tried to agree with the Jews and Photinus contrary to the question at hand. He would therefore rightly have been rebuked by Manes, since, constrained by the force and weight of the arguments, he would have been compelled to profess that one born and begotten from Mary was not God but a man.

Who, then, could conclude or imagine from the words Beausobre adduces that Archelaus had fallen into so dreadful a crime? For “Jesus” is the name of the true and singular man which the angel, announcing the mystery of the Incarnation, declared—by the command and authority of the Father—was to be given to his Son and proclaimed among human beings, as the Evangelists testify.

“Christ,” however, cannot be the name of a person; it is a designation of power and kingship. Archelaus proved from the sacred Scriptures and from the common agreement of his forefathers—both here and in the letter he sent to the presbyter Diodorus—that these two names belong most strictly to the one Son of God born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary, without any distinction or separation of persons.

> [Note: The Ophites maintained that Christ did not come in the substance of flesh, and held that Jesus was other than Christ: Jesus, indeed, was born of the Virgin, but Christ descended upon him from heaven. Tertullian, *On the Prescriptions*, chapter 47; Origen, book VI *Against Celsus*. They also worshipped the serpent by which Eve was deceived and called it Christ.]

He did so by refuting the ravings of those heretics who fabricated the claim that Jesus was someone other than Christ, the Son of God.

Beausobre therefore reasons falsely when he contends that the name “Jesus” in itself designates one person separate from Christ, the Son of God.

> [Note: The words of Tertullian, with which he attacks Praxeas, clearly dissolve Beausobre’s sophism by which he accuses Archelaus: “Therefore, whether only Jesus is mentioned, Christ is understood as well; or whether only Christ is mentioned, it is the same as Jesus, because Jesus is the anointed one.” One of these names is proper, having been imposed by the angel; the other is an attribute, belonging to him because of his anointing. How, then, does Beausobre derive from this that those two names signify two separate persons? Tertullian, in the cited book, chapter 28.]

For Lactantius too, speaking of these names against the Gentiles, writes:

> [Note: Lactantius, book IV, chapter 7.]

> “Although no one except him knows the name of the Son of God—which the Most High Father bestowed upon him from the beginning—he nevertheless has one designation among the angels and another among human beings. Among human beings he is called Jesus. For Christ is not a proper name, but a designation of power and kingship.”

Beausobre therefore calumniates Archelaus’s words with excessive arrogance when he observes that the holy bishop wrote:

> “There is one who was born from Mary, a Son, who chose to undergo all this struggle—Jesus.”

> [Note: Consult Ambrose on Psalm XXXIX, where he explains this struggle of Christ at great length by the example of those who wrestle.]

He alludes to the struggle which Jesus underwent on the cross in order to reign. That is, while enduring true death and burial, he appeared alive again on the third day, about to return to the Father from whom he had descended.

“This Jesus,” Archelaus adds, “is the Christ of God, who descended upon him who was from Mary.”

No one, then, unless he wishes to interpret these words maliciously and violently, will ever assert that Archelaus intended, from this diversity of names, offices, and natures, to indicate also a distinction of persons.

For the holy bishop is wholly occupied with the question of whether Christ—that is, the Son of God—assumed a true human nature from Mary. Against Manes he reasons as follows:

> “If you confess that he was born from Mary, then passion must necessarily follow; and from passion, resurrection; from resurrection, judgment; and the commandments of Scripture will remain secure.”

Therefore, as though wishing to press his adversary more forcefully, he proves from the following scriptural passages that the same and only Son of God was brought forth from Mary into the world according to a true humanity:

> “When it pleased God, he sent his Son, made from a woman.”

And again:

> “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.”

And:

> “Since God raised up the Lord, he will also raise us up by his power.”

> [Note: The Apostle, Galatians IV, 4; First Corinthians V, 7; and the same epistle, VI, 14.]

It was therefore fitting for Beausobre to compare the words he cited with the rest of the context of the disputation—

> [Note: Archelaus’s disputation, chapter 49, in Zacagnius, p. 49.]

—and with what Archelaus wrote to Diodorus, or the presbyter Trypho. There, comparing the Old and New Testaments, he proves that both are from God on account of the profound harmony of their prophecies, bringing forward many examples.

Speaking especially of Moses and Jesus, he expressly and without any obscurity calls Jesus the true Lord of Moses. He affirms that Jesus is the author of the Sabbath and the giver of blessedness. By his own power he led the people out of the bondage and captivity of sins and delivered them to eternal salvation.

All these and other similar formulas of speech clearly indicate that Jesus was the true Son of God. They likewise display and make evident the holy bishop’s sound and Catholic faith concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, without any mark of heresy.

Lest these things should appear to be our own inventions, they are amply strengthened by the opinions expressed in the letter written to the presbyter Diodorus—

> [Note: Archelaus’s letter to the presbyter Diodorus, printed from the Bobbian manuscript by the most learned Valesius at the end of the Ecclesiastical History of Socrates and Sozomen, and also in Laurentius Zacagnius, p. 71.]

—as we have said. Since diligent readers can easily examine them, we have thought it unnecessary to copy and compare the same material in this work.

## 6.

As for what Beausobre invents concerning the other descent of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus at his baptism, it is now time to explain it briefly.

From the preceding arguments, badly arranged and reasoned, by which he fabricates—at the greatest cost to truth and the deepest disgrace to holiness—that Archelaus should be associated with wicked heretics, asserting that the bishop had disputed no more piously or wisely than Manes himself concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, Beausobre advances to another argument, which he begins in these terms:

Archelaus asks his adversary Manes, and presses him to answer: if he denied Christ the Lord’s real and true birth from Mary, so that Christ appeared merely to possess the form of a man and not the reality of a body and soul, then upon whom did the Holy Spirit descend in the form of a dove? He likewise challenges him to say who, at that time, was baptized by John.

He then adds:

> “If he was perfect, if he was the Son, the Spirit could not enter into him, just as a kingdom cannot enter within a kingdom.”

After reproducing this testimony, Beausobre argues that this Latin interpretation of the Greek and Arabic texts betrays barbarism. He maintains that the Greek word rendered in Latin as “kingdom” signified rather “throne,” “dominion,” “power,” or “principality”—terms more frequently used in Scripture to designate heavenly intelligences.

> [Note: Beausobre, in the passage cited above, p. 116, note 2.]

Accordingly, our teacher of the ancient theologians criticizes Archelaus and his words, adding the following false censure: that Archelaus substituted “Christ” for “Jesus” and affirmed that Christ was born from Mary, as though Jesus could not also be called Christ according to the flesh.

[73] But this accusation of Beausobre’s ought rather to have been directed against the Evangelists. For Matthew, speaking of the generation of the Son of God born in the flesh, used both names, writing:

> “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David,”

and again adds:

> [Note: Matthew I, 1, 16: “Jesus, who is called Christ.” This twofold designation is exceedingly common in the sacred writings, as innumerable other passages show. For example, John I, 17, reads: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ”; and again, chapter XVII, 3: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” Similar examples occur in the Acts of the Apostles, chapters I, II, III, XI, XV, XXIV, and XXXI, and throughout all the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. These passages refute Beausobre’s nonsense even more abundantly.]

Since we encounter almost countless testimonies of this kind throughout Scripture, expressing the Son of God born from Mary by both names and indicating no distinction whatever of persons between Jesus and Christ, I do not see by what religious scruple or effort our critic could have imagined that, by joining those two words together, Archelaus intended to assert—or at least imply—that there were two persons.

That Beausobre fabricated this out of a desire to disparage and abuse is demonstrated most clearly by the second calumny he immediately adds. For, noticing the remaining words of the sentence cited above, he violently twists them into the opposite meaning. Imagining that he is addressing only dull and leaden minds—men who have never touched theological studies or examined the holy Fathers and the Scriptures—he again attacks the holy bishop and makes him the author of the heresy which wickedly asserted that Jesus Christ became the Son of God only after receiving baptism from John.

Otherwise, he says, one would have to maintain that there was one divine power which entered, and one Spirit who entered. For this reason, Jesus Christ would have needed to possess a true human nature so that the Holy Spirit could descend upon him.

How far the pious and Catholic mind of Archelaus was from such a way of thinking is already made perfectly clear by what has been said above. For once Manes and Archelaus agreed on this point—namely, that at the beginning of Jesus Christ’s manifestation he was truly God and the Son of God—and the controversy concerned only his true birth from Mary, his true human nature assumed in his mother’s womb and joined to the divine Word, Archelaus could not lawfully move beyond these established limits of the dispute. He could neither wander away from them nor deny Christ’s true divinity.

He had only to affirm and prove that the descent of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus at his baptism took place for the benefit of his human nature: namely, so that it might become known with certainty to the world, to angels, and to human beings that he was the helper and mediator of the human race, the true propitiator predestined from eternity and sent in time from the seat of the Father to humankind, in order to proclaim release to captives, sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution.

> [Note: Luke IV, 19 and following.]

By that descent the abundance and fullness of grace which we have all received from God through the mediator, the high priest anointed by God, was made manifest. The Holy Spirit therefore wished to indicate the ministry, power, and authority that he was afterward to exercise, on account of which he was called “the Anointed One,” just as Isaiah had long before prophesied:

> [Note: Isaiah LXI: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to heal the brokenhearted.” Cyril of Alexandria, book II Against Nestorius; Jerome, Commentary on the cited words of Isaiah. Consult Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, volume VI, *On the Incarnation*, book XI, chapter 9, §§ 10, 11 and following; Theodoret, volume IV, p. 279, book V Against Heresies; Augustine, Sermon 32 on the Words of the Apostle, chapter 2.]

Therefore, although the Fathers explained that descent of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus at his baptism in different ways, according to the Catholic sense, they all agree that it occurred so that we might learn that the first fruits of human nature had been restored, when he wished to appear as a true man capable of sanctification, as Cyril says. At the same time, it was to make known that his anointing had then been completed, because he assumed all the ministries, functions, and exercises foretold by Isaiah and belonging to the priesthood.

## 7.

From all this it follows that Archelaus was brought under suspicion of heresy with the greatest injustice because he applied both names, Jesus and Christ, to Mary’s one and only Son. He was obliged to preserve this manner of speaking in order to indicate the conjunction of the two natures, as Theodoret notes.

Indeed, according to Augustine, if someone did not know Jesus Christ as more than a man, he certainly did not know Jesus Christ. For if he is merely a man and nothing more, he is not himself Jesus Christ.

But to remove entirely any clever and deceptive interpretation imposed upon Archelaus’s words, what need have we of the manner of speech and opinions of other Catholic Fathers? That Archelaus explained himself more fully is made perfectly clear both by the arguments, sequence, and meaning of the preceding disputation and by the blasphemies of Manes and the objections which the holy bishop attempted to reject and overthrow by testimonies from Scripture.

Archelaus therefore attacked Manes with this argument:

> “For if, according to what you say, he was not born, he certainly did not suffer; for it is impossible for one who was not born to suffer. And if he did not suffer, the name of the cross is removed.”

After inserting several other arguments of this kind, he challenges Manes and adds:

> “You connect all these things while denying that he was born from Mary. For if you confess that he was born from Mary, then passion must necessarily follow; and from passion, resurrection; from resurrection, judgment; and the precepts of Scripture will remain secure for us.”

A little later he addresses him in this manner:

> “Therefore answer me concerning each point that I shall ask: How shall we reject such great and such clear words of the Apostle, which say: ‘When it pleased God among us, he sent his Son, made from a woman.’ And again: ‘Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed.’ And: ‘Since God raised up the Lord, he will also raise us up by his power’?”

> [Note: Galatians IV, 4–5; First Corinthians V, 7; the same epistle, XV, 12.]

With these and other testimonies drawn from the Apostle, Archelaus firmly insisted upon defending the sole and true birth of Jesus Christ from the Virgin Mary.

After this Archelaus proceeded to the descent of the Holy Spirit upon Jesus at his baptism, which Beausobre claims bears the marks of heresy. He again attacks the Manichaean in these words:

> “Tell me this also, O Manichaean. If you say that Christ was not born from Mary, but appeared as a man although he was not a man, this being accomplished and effected by the power that is in him, tell me: upon whom did the Holy Spirit descend like a dove? And who was baptized by John? If he was perfect, if he was the Power, the Spirit could not enter into him, just as a kingdom cannot enter within a kingdom. And to whom did the voice sent from heaven bear witness when it said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’? Come, tell me without delay: who is the one who prepares all these things and performs them all?”

> [Note: Matthew III, 16.]

## 8.

When Archelaus asked these questions, Manes dared to answer more boldly. He said that it seemed pious to him to maintain that the Son of God had needed nothing when his coming to earth was arranged: he had needed neither a dove nor baptism, neither a mother nor brothers, and perhaps not even a father—who, according to Archelaus, was Joseph. Rather, this entire descending being transformed himself into a man in whatever form he wished, in the manner in which Paul says that he was found in appearance as a man.

> [Note: Philippians II, 7.]

“Show, then,” he said, “what need there could have been for one who transformed himself into everything.”

Then, seeking to evade what Archelaus had defended in a Catholic manner, he put forward another argument, by which he imagined that he was striking at the holy bishop’s throat, saying:

> “For if you say that he was merely a man from Mary and received the Spirit at baptism, then he will appear to be the Son by advancement and not by nature.”

Finally, instituting a comparison between the Holy Spirit and Christ himself, the Son of God, he continued his reasoning:

> “If, however, I grant you the claim that he is the Son by advancement, as one made a man, do you believe him truly to be a man—that is, one who is flesh and blood? Then the Spirit too, who appeared like a dove, must necessarily be nothing other than a natural dove. For ‘like a man’ is said, and ‘like a dove’; and whatever one can suppose from the expression ‘like a man,’ conceive in the same way concerning the expression ‘like a dove.’ It is necessary to accept both equally, for this is how the things written about him are found in the Scriptures.”

> [Note: *Acts of the Disputation*, p. 92, chapter 49, pp. 91–92, in Zacagnius.]

9. Meanwhile Archelaus was turning many things over in his mind as he listened to the many and great blasphemies issuing from Manes’s mouth. Above all, he feared that, although he argued with every possible circumspection, this discussion might bring more danger than benefit to the ignorant and foolish people who were present. For he knew with certainty that understanding the Scriptures had not been granted to everyone, and therefore he could not carefully explain and resolve the question in a manner properly suited to those who were standing by and listening to them. Nevertheless, driven, as it were, by necessity because of the large crowd, he passed over some of the things Manes had raised and endeavored to snatch away and overthrow only those matters that Manes had openly proclaimed, wrapped in glaring and gross errors. Accordingly, intending to resume his encounter with him, he immediately reasoned with his opponent, as the schools put it, in these terms:

“Tell me, then: if we understand Jesus to have been naturally made a man from Mary, and understand him to have possessed flesh and blood, it is necessary also to say that the Holy Spirit was a real dove, and not the Spirit?” [Col. 0859B]

To refute this false consequence, he immediately showed that a real dove could not enter a real man and remain in him, just as flesh could not naturally enter flesh. On the contrary, we understand faithfully the manner and logic of Scripture’s speech if we profess that Jesus Christ was born from Mary as a real man with real flesh and blood, and that the Holy Spirit merely bore the form of a dove. For, according to the proper account, the Spirit dwells in a man, descends, and remains; and this is fitting, has happened, and is continually happening.

Archelaus therefore proves that the true properties of a human being ought naturally to be affirmed of Christ Jesus. But he proved most clearly that it is impious to affirm the true properties of a dove concerning the Holy Spirit, and that this is ruled out by the operation, perfections, attributes, and manner of action of the Holy Spirit. Having brought forward this very different mode of reasoning—one that neither Manes nor any other defender of impiety could contradict—he thus addressed his adversary, at once rebuking him and mocking him with humorous words.

Since Manes was claiming to be God’s Paraclete—for he had said that the Spirit had come upon him, the one whom Jesus had promised to send—and since, as Archelaus said, “from where else could he descend if not from heaven?” he confirms by these words that the Holy Spirit inhabits heaven, descends from heaven into a man, and remains in him. From this he concludes that the Spirit could descend only upon a man worthy of him, that is, one full of grace and virtue. But one should rather think that real doves had descended upon that Manichaean himself, not upon Christ:

“Let us rather regard you,” he says, “as a thief of doves, laying snares and nooses for them; for you are worthy to be mocked with ridiculous words.”

Returning immediately to the discussion from which he had digressed for a little while—namely, to that transformation by which Manes falsely imagined that God had transformed himself into a man or into the sun—Archelaus appeals to all the promises and figures expressed in Scripture concerning Christ’s birth. He appeals even to the very name of his coming, all of which would necessarily have to be erased if, while remaining in heaven, he had been able to do whatever he wished, provided that we affirm that he was Spirit alone and not a man. But he proves from the Apostle’s words to the Philippians that this was not so [Col. 0859D] [Note: Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians, chapter II, 7.].

That is:

“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

He therefore immediately adds:

“But I speak of the one who was made man from Mary.”

This manner of speaking plainly reveals the nature and person of the divine Word before his birth from the Virgin. In the same way, after the baptism, the Father’s voice wished to proclaim in the world, speaking of the Son who had been born from Mary:

“This is the Christ of God who descended upon the one who is from Mary.” [Col. 0860A]

10. I am not unaware that Beausobre does not approve sufficiently of this final phrase; indeed, he accuses it of being the source of the Nestorian heresy. But far be it from us to suppose that, even in the heat of the debate, Archelaus distinguished in Christ two persons, one human and the other divine. He had spoken only of two natures joined to one another, which the one Son of God, truly born from Mary, possessed united in himself, as he professed catholically throughout the whole discussion.

That these words of Archelaus, which Beausobre tried to interpret maliciously, mean nothing else is made perfectly clear by the following statement:

“This is the Christ of God”—that is, the Son—“who descended upon the one who is from Mary.”

A little later he asserts in unambiguous words that this Son of God was begotten from Mary. Speaking, then, of Jesus after his baptism, who had already come up from the waters of the Jordan, he says:

“For Jesus was immediately led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil. When the devil did not know him, he said to him, ‘If you are the Son of God …’ He did not know because of what he had begotten the Son of God, who was preaching the kingdom of heaven.” [Col. 0860B]

Archelaus therefore professed that the Son of God had been begotten from Mary in true humanity. He further says that this Son received the Holy Spirit at his baptism, through whom the Father’s voice bore witness, saying:

“This is my beloved Son.”

No one else could bear the Spirit except Jesus, who was born from Mary, above all the saints [Col. 0860D] [Note: Acts of Archelaus, p. 93.].

11. Since Manes had raised various objections against Archelaus that still seemed neither removed nor overthrown, the bishop wisely attempts to strike his opponent more forcefully, never departing from the boundaries of the discussion he had begun. Therefore, intending to prove that Jesus, the son of Mary, was not a man merely in outward form and apparent appearance, the bishop speaks as follows:

“If you say that he is a man only in form and appearance, how could he have been seized by the Pharisees, who were born from man and woman, and dragged before a tribunal, when a spiritual body cannot be grasped by grosser bodies?”

He then rebukes and assails the same Manes, who had said that the Son of God had transformed himself at will into every form and appearance, even into the sun. He adds:

“Go on, please, and bring me a handful of sun, or a bushelful! The sun itself, because it is a body of a more subtle kind, can cover and surround you; but you, even if you trample on it, do it no harm.”

By contrast, he concludes:

“But my Lord Jesus, if he was seized, was seized by men as a man. If he is not a man, neither was he seized. If he was not seized, neither did he suffer nor was he baptized. If he was not baptized, then none of us has been baptized. But if there is no baptism, there will be no remission of sins, and each person will die in his sins.”

12. Perceiving that these statements of Archelaus brought Manes the greatest disadvantage, Manes passed over the whole discussion and, dwelling only on its final words, introduced those two consequences. First he replied:

“Then baptism is given for the remission of sins?”

When Archelaus had answered “Amen,” Manes immediately added this other blasphemous conclusion:

“Then Christ sinned, because he was baptized?”

Archelaus recoiled from this last statement and immediately resisted it, replying, “Far be it!” Then, employing the words of the Apostle Paul, he concluded his speech in these terms:

“Rather, he was made sin for us, taking our sins upon himself. For this reason he was born from a woman, and for this reason he came to baptism: so that he might receive the sanctification of this part, and so that the body which he had assumed might be able to bear the Spirit who had descended in the form of a dove.”

Beausobre does not hesitate to contend that, in the final part of this response, Archelaus departed from the principles of Catholic truth [Col. 0860D] [Note: Beausobre, book I, chapter 10, p. 117.]. Although he had distinguished and proclaimed the supreme innocence of Jesus Christ by saying that he did not receive baptism in order to be cleansed from his own sins—a statement that would have been impious—he nevertheless added that Jesus had been baptized so that, in the aspect in which he had been born from a woman, he might receive sanctification and become capable of sustaining the Spirit who had descended upon him. For this reason, Beausobre says, he departed infinitely from the principles of the Catholic faith.

But who does not see that this contains slander and fabrication? Archelaus had already confessed throughout the entire discussion, both implicitly and explicitly, that Christ’s soul had been completely sanctified through its hypostatic union with the divine Word. There was no sin in his soul that could be removed by baptism [Col. 0861D] [Note: Acts of the Disputation of Archelaus, p. 94. Consult also the Catholic letter of Saint Leo the Great to Flavian, which is numbered 24.].

But because Christ had to undergo the harsh struggle of the cross, passion, and death, and because the Holy Spirit had descended upon him in that visible form for this reason, the weak and fleshly body that he had assumed from the Virgin also needed to be strengthened outwardly, so that it could bear all the torments of that bloody struggle.

How, then, does Beausobre infer from this statement that Archelaus departed from the Catholic faith? That body and soul, united to the person of the Word and substantially sanctified at the very instant of conception, did not need a new purification through baptism in order to become a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. Did Archelaus not confess this when he denied that Christ had his own sin, and instead said that he had been made sin for us, taking our sins upon himself?

Therefore, since he took upon himself the sins that had to be expiated, it was also necessary that he be outwardly purified through visible signs, so that by his death and passion he might nail our sins to the cross and erase them. Finally, Archelaus wished to indicate that Christ needed purification in this outward sense because he appeared in the world on our behalf as a sinner, since he himself truly took up our infirmities and bore our pains.

Did he not experience disturbances of spirit in the garden before he ascended the cross, and was he not strengthened by an angel? [Note: Beausobre, book I, chapter 10, p. 118.] Did he not, while giving up his spirit on the cross and experiencing mortal pains, pray to God the Father, saying:

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 0861C]

Catholics unanimously affirm that he had no need of assistance on account of the hypostatic union with the divine Word. But who, other than Beausobre alone, could deny that these things were necessary to reveal the true nature of a human being?

12. Finally, in order to indulge more zealously in the interests of his un-Catholic sect, Beausobre appeals to Saint Methodius, a contemporary of Archelaus, whom he attacks as a patron of Arian and Nestorian doctrine. He is guided by the desire to show that the Catholic bishops and martyrs who flourished as early as the third century of the Church were not sincere guardians of the evangelical and Catholic faith, but had weakened and corrupted it through depraved opinions.

But since our present study cannot afford to linger at length in refuting these and other similar charges, our discourse will subject to examination matters relating to the history of Manes, namely, his death. We shall thus achieve the truth more successfully than Beausobre, who testified that he had merely wished for it in words invented for the purpose—and did so only to deceive his followers ever more thoroughly and mislead unwary and superficial readers.

78

CHAPTER X

Manes, fleeing from Diodoride, is captured by Persian officials and, flayed, pays the penalty for his crimes. Beausobre wrongly makes Archelaus the author of this death, and his arguments are rejected. Finally, the Manichaeans celebrate Manes’s birthday with solemn and religious rites.

In the preceding chapters we have devoted much labor to overturning Beausobre’s calumnies against the faith and religion of the bishop Archelaus—calumnies heaped up and fabricated with malice and the greatest injustice. We were led to do so by the purpose of carefully bringing under examination, on the one hand, the things that Manichaeus, in debate, wickedly defended against Catholic truth, and, on the other, the things that the bishop Archelaus himself pronounced in order to blunt and utterly reject the heretical doctrines laid before him.

Whether Archelaus was more successful in refuting the Manichaean and defending Catholic truths than the advocate of novelties, Beausobre, judged him to be, will soon be made clear by what we say, since Beausobre accused that most holy bishop as a man who had violated the faith and as a defender of many heresies. This will be especially clear because we now intend to appeal to the judgment of those readers who are accustomed to study the writings of the holy Fathers and ancient theologians. They retain a complete and orderly memory of Christian matters and do not ordinarily seek to refresh their minds with novelties; nor are they driven by an anxious desire to acquire varied and foreign learning so that they may devote themselves more eagerly to reading un-Catholic books, through which the mind is gradually and heedlessly filled with false and prejudiced opinions, and the piety of the Christian name is weakened and corrupted.

If, however, I were to appeal to the judgment of those who, moved by love of novelties, customarily display for sale among crowds and at gatherings of superficial scholars nothing but wares borrowed from heretical books, set forth in words and fabulous assertions so that they may claim the reputation of learned men, I would already understand that my cause and Archelaus’s might be liable to collapse, although they rest solely upon Catholic truth drawn from Scripture and tradition.

1. Without departing from the purpose of our writing, and so that our manner of argument may not become too extended, we assert that Manes, utterly and disgracefully confounded, was secretly compelled to leave the parish or village of Diodoride. Beyond doubt, he would have suffered a violent death at the hands of the people’s anger and tumult if Marcellinus—an able administrator of the civil affairs of that province on behalf of the Roman Empire—and Archelaus himself, moved by gentleness, had not restrained the fury of the populace.

Thus, supported by flight as his refuge, he sought safety beyond the river Stranga and withdrew once more to the fortress of Arabion, from which he had departed some time before setting out for Mesopotamia. He perhaps flattered himself with the hope that the death sentence issued against him by the king of Persia had either been completely annulled or changed because of the political changes that may have taken place during the interval between his departure from the court and the present time.

Archelaus described the matter almost in these words in his disputation [Col. 0862D] [Note: Disputation of Archelaus, in Zacagnius, chapter 55, p. 100.], adding:

“But retracing the roads by which he had come, after crossing the river he returned to the fortress of Arabion. There he was later captured and brought before the king. The king, stirred against him by the greatest indignation and wishing to avenge two deaths upon him—one of his son and the other of the jailer—ordered him to be flayed and hung before the city gate. He also ordered his skin to be treated with medicines and inflated, while his flesh was given to the birds.” [Col. 0862D]

Nor did Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, describe Manes’s death otherwise in his instructions for catechumens [Col. 0862D] [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 6.]. He merely explained additional circumstances: namely, that Manes had been brought before the king of Persia and forced to stand in his presence, and that he had been assailed with many reproaches because of his lies and flight. The king also mocked his servile condition, accused him of the murder of his son, and ordered the guards who had been condemned because of him to be put to death.

Thus, Cyril concludes, agreeing with Archelaus’s account:

“He ordered Manes to be flayed according to Persian law, and he gave the remaining body over to be devoured by beasts. But the skin, which contained such great wickedness, he had hung before the gates like a wineskin.”

Socrates described Manes’s death in a similar manner [Col. 0863A] [Note: Socrates, History, book I, chapter 22, in the Valesian edition, p. 56.]. Wishing to report the history of ecclesiastical affairs, he had in his hands the written account of Archelaus’s disputation with Manes and had examined with his own eyes the matters we have related. He explained them in faithful narration, preserving the order of events.

To prevent what he reported there from ever being brought under suspicion of falsehood, and to free his readers’ minds from prejudice, after writing:

“But when the king of Persia discovered that the Manichaean was staying in those regions, he had him seized from there, flayed, and his skin, stuffed with straw, hung before the city gates,”

he immediately added, in order to vindicate these words as wholly trustworthy:

“We have by no means invented these things; we have excerpted them from a certain disputation of Archelaus, bishop of the city of Caschara in Mesopotamia, which we read.” [Col. 0863D]

2. This disputation of Archelaus had therefore been committed to writing, translated into Greek, and circulated. Nor did anyone from that time until the year 1740 dare to judge it false and spurious. No one, I say, asserted that it contained a fabrication of nonsense and fables. Shall we therefore suppose that this was reserved solely for Beausobre’s judgment and for a few others who attempt to flatter the aforementioned author?

We shall speak more fully about this kind of vindication in what follows. Finally, as we continue our discussion of Manes’s death, in addition to the authority of Epiphanius, who supports the preceding writers, there is also the testimony of Photius [Col. 0863D] [Note: Photius, book I Against the Manichaeans, chapter 13, in Christopher Wolf, p. 52 and following.]. Although, because of the schism he introduced into the Catholic Church, he rightly deserves to be called a man of impaired faith, no one has yet dared to deny that he applied great diligence to investigating the writings of the ancients and possessed extensive learning.

Although, then, in recounting Manes’s death and the deeds of Archelaus he does not follow the ordinary method of the preceding writers, it is nevertheless clear that he scarcely departed from their statements. For in chapter 13 he relates how Manes was forced to wander here and there in order to escape the anger and vengeance of the king of Persia. He describes the king’s agents searching for him everywhere so that they might bring him before the king, and asserts that, once brought before him, Manes was finally assailed with the gravest reproaches and underwent a death not unworthy of his horrible impieties.

He therefore concludes that chapter with these words, which we think he borrowed from Socrates and Archelaus:

“For while that unfortunate man was still alive, they removed his skin and flayed his body into a wineskin; thus they took him from life and, as it were, cut him apart. They threw the remaining body to wild beasts as prey, and hung the skin itself, filled with air like a wineskin, before the gates. Thus that apostate and most wicked man met the end of his life.” [Col. 0863C]

The same Photius, in chapter 15, again commemorates this cruel death, first mentioning the famous disputation that Archelaus held against him. He calls Archelaus a divine and holy man, bishop of Caschara in Mesopotamia [Col. 0863D] [Note: Photius, book I Against the Manichaeans, chapter 15: “And after he had gone to Mesopotamia, he was assailed with many great arguments against his impiety by the divine Archelaus, a holy man who at that time was bishop of Caschara in that region. Fleeing from there, he entered Diodoride, a village of Caschara.” In Christopher Wolf, p. 50.].

He then adds that Manes, overcome by unexpected shame in the public encounter, fled from Diodoride. He says that he was again driven to flight by the same Archelaus when the latter resumed the debate, and that Manes appeared to be a thoroughly wicked man, worthy of ridicule and detestation in all his doctrines. Finally, he says, Manes was captured by the royal officials who were searching and examining everywhere for him, and underwent those bitter punishments.

3. Although Beausobre has not dared to deny this truth, established by so many and such weighty proofs, he nevertheless attempts with great effort gradually to weaken it. In chapter 11 of the first book, when he is about to describe the death of Manes, he asserts that its author and, as it were, its agent was the bishop Archelaus [Col. 0864D] [Note: Beausobre, History of the Manichaeans, book I, chapter 11, p. 124.]. For this reason he brings forward in French the words that the bishop uttered after the disputation, namely:

“When I had learned these things, I considered it necessary to make them known to you also, because he is being sought by the king of Persia to this very day.”

I believe no one is unaware that these words refer to the crimes committed by Manes among the Persians. Archelaus seems to have been compelled to pour them forth when, after the final encounter with the Manichaean had ended, he imposed silence amid the astonishment of the people and crowds who had come there from different parts of that province to hear the two men disputing about religion, and disclosed the whole sequence of events and the crimes committed by Manes [Col. 0864D] [Note: Archelaus, in the Acts, p. 100, in Zacagnius.].

Beausobre therefore maliciously attempted to turn this conduct of Archelaus into a charge. He contends that the bishop ought not to have made known to the people those crimes of Manes for which the Persian royal officials were seeking him for execution—namely, that he had killed the king’s son. As a good shepherd, he ought merely to have spoken about the Manichaean errors concerning the faith, so that the people might guard against them.

He therefore persuades himself that he can easily discern and interpret the mind, will, and conduct of the holy bishop: namely, that Archelaus wished by his words to incite the people to fury and sedition, so that, once Manes had been captured, he might be handed over to the Persians. The Persians were living near the borders of Mesopotamia and were separated from Roman territory and military stations only by the river Stranga.

Beausobre therefore contends that the bishop’s intention was wicked and, as they call it, irregular. Once the people had understood it, he says, they rose against Manes even before the bishop had finished his speech and tried to seize him so that he might be brought in chains to the neighboring barbarians. But Manes carefully fled to the fortress of Arabion.

What wonder, then? In accordance with his own judgment, Beausobre likewise imagines that Epiphanius wished to support this malicious interpretation [Col. 0864D] [Note: Epiphanius, Heresy 66.]. He invents the claim that this holy bishop understood such conduct on Archelaus’s part to bring great disgrace upon the episcopal character. For that reason, setting aside the preceding account, Epiphanius devised an entirely different one on his own authority, writing that the people, moved by zeal for the Catholic religion, attempted to overwhelm Manes with stones, but that Archelaus restrained and prevented their fury, enabling Manes, as he fled, to find safety easily.

“Tillemont,” Beausobre adds, “persuaded himself that this brief account had been interpolated by Epiphanius, since we do not encounter it in the Acts of Archelaus.”

But even if we grant that the things Epiphanius soon related without naming an author are true, it would still follow that the bishop of Caschara desired the destruction of Manes, although he could not be reproached concerning his death. For although he opposed those who were attempting to stone this criminal, he nevertheless took care, by informing the Persian royal officials, that Manes—guilty of many crimes and being sought everywhere by public authority—should be captured and held securely, so that he might be brought before the king and suffer capital punishment.

Thus far Beausobre, attacking and harassing the bishops Archelaus and Epiphanius equally, though in different words.

[Col. 0865A] But if we examine more carefully the purpose of the account cited from the Acts of Archelaus, everything he has objected will prove unable to suppress the truth of the events; and the following observations will show that those two Fathers do not contradict one another in their descriptions of the death of Manes.

First, as regards Archelaus’s manner of acting and speaking, by which he disclosed to the people of Diodoride not only the Manichaean errors concerning the faith but also the more serious crimes committed by that wicked man, for which he was being sought for execution by public authority of the Persian king, I think that nothing at all appears in it that disgraces the episcopal character. Nor should we suppose that Archelaus spoke these things with such an intention [Note: Archelaus writes in his own disputation, § 1, in Zacagnius, p. 94: “When Archelaus had said these things, the crowds marveled at the truth of his teaching and celebrated his immense praises with shouting, so that they tried with every effort and would not allow him to return any farther to his own place; and then they departed.”].

He would have been moved by a very serious motive—one that Beausobre could easily have grasped if he had wished to examine the Acts of Archelaus carefully. We, who have chosen to read those Acts attentively and to spend a longer time on the disputation, understood very clearly that, after this final encounter had ended, a great tumult had arisen among the people who had gathered there.

Some applauded Archelaus and tried with shouting to celebrate his immense praises; others, however, burning with anger and hatred against Manes on the opposing side, were more probably driven by fury to kill him. That a tumult had arisen among the people is clearly demonstrated by the text of the Acts cited above, which we reproduce here.

It therefore appears most probable that, just as the praises of the victorious Archelaus were sung amid the crowds’ shouting, so too Manes’s heresy and disgrace, as well as his sacrilegious doctrine, were denounced and cursed with insults and reproaches.

If Beausobre should still wish to oppose me, I would ask what the word “tumult” signifies. If, according to Cicero, it means nothing other than “such great disturbance that greater fear arises from it” [Note: Cicero: “For what is a tumult except such a great disturbance that greater fear arises from it? Hence, too, the name tumult was derived.”], then we understand immediately that, since Manes’s reputation and standing had been endangered by the disputations, it is highly probable that, just as the crowds would not allow Archelaus to return to his own place, those same crowds likewise wished to detain Manes, bind him in chains, or overwhelm him with stones, lest by fleeing he escape the punishments he deserved.

Archelaus therefore may have had to restrain this tumult of the crowds by words and prayers, lest savagery arise from so great a disturbance contrary to the laws of nations and of the Church. Had not Marcellus invited Manes—in fact, by letter—to come to Caschara? The laws of nations therefore had to be observed, and it could never have been permitted, without violating the pledge that had been given, for anyone to be harmed by hostile hands, especially since Manes was subject not to the Roman Empire but to the Persians.

Accordingly, it could not have entered Archelaus’s mind, while Marcellus was present, to incite the people to sedition and demand the death of a heretic. For that reason the holy bishop, also in order to preserve ecclesiastical gentleness, urged the people not to leave the place where they had gathered, promising them that he would shortly say new things to them.

But the crowds continued to gather; these words show that neither the tumult nor the disturbance had been suppressed [Col. 0865D]. After they had assembled, Archelaus urged them to settle down and listen to what he had to say.

If the people were not in tumult against Manes, if they were not seeking his death, why did Archelaus apply new efforts and exhortations so that those who had gathered would settle down? Therefore, so that Epiphanius might describe the sequence of events more clearly, he invented nothing on his own authority. Rather, he reported things that perhaps had once been contained in those same Acts but had now been omitted through the ignorance of copyists or the unreliability of translators.

Indeed, the preceding words, which we have already transcribed at the end, indicate that a lacuna had entered the text. For after these words—

“so that they tried with every effort”—

there immediately follow other words that yield no genuine sense:

“they would not allow him farther …” [Note: Disputation of Archelaus, p. 94, as above, in Laurent Zacagnius’s Collection of Ancient Monuments of the Greek and Latin Church.]

Zacagnius, observing this lacuna in the manuscript codices, judged that at least the particle “and” should be supplied. Anyone can easily judge from the context whether this may still cause confusion and disorder in the text. I shall not strongly resist granting that nothing is missing there.

But what then? Did Epiphanius, according to his own opinion, invent that the people sought to overwhelm Manes with stones? Away with such a fiction! For the sequence of the Acts relates how a multitude of people had gathered at that parish from the whole province, with men from neighboring places also present. Once silence had been made, Archelaus began to speak about Manes in this manner.

After uttering a few words, he added the following and begged the people, laying aside all disturbance and putting away all uproar, not to refuse to hear what he had learned about Manes and what he had decided to disclose:

“But now, since I wish to say only a very few things, I beg you to listen in silence, so that you may recognize who this man is, and from where he comes, and what sort of person this newcomer is,” and so forth [Col. 0866B] [Note: Zacagnius writes in his notes that the second particle “and” is missing in the Cassinese codex, although the sequence of the speech clearly supplies it.].

Archelaus therefore had to impose silence once, twice, and finally a third time, in order to suppress the disturbance and tumult of the crowds. There was no other reason except that the people were already attempting to attack Manes. For the final words we have transcribed most clearly show that the minds of those people had been stirred against the heretic.

Since, then, Archelaus, applying sound counsel, promised to speak to the same people about the heretic’s person, condition, homeland, institutions, and crimes, he judged that by his account he could secure the attention of the assembled hearers, while meanwhile opening a clear path for Manes to flee and obtain protection for his life and safety.

And in the end it happened that, retracing the roads by which he had come, he crossed the river and reached the fortress of Arabion.

5. But let us suppose still that the people of Diodoride had not yet been stirred by anger and hatred against Manes. What follows from this? Did Archelaus, in making known Manes’s life and crimes, wish to stir up the people so that, once the heretic had been captured, he might later be led away like a victim to be slaughtered by the Persians and killed as a sacrifice? Who could judge this without being marked by rashness?

It is far more reasonable to suppose that Archelaus wished to discuss the family, birth, condition, lies, and Manichaean crimes of this scoundrel, upon whom the Persians, seeking him everywhere by public authority, had already pronounced a capital sentence, so that the simpler people and those less skilled in matters of the faith would not be seduced by belief in his false doctrine.

Did not the Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians, and, in more recent centuries, the Calvinists, Lutherans, and Socinians propagate the inventions of their heresies through preaching and disputation? This could happen to them more successfully when they relied upon the noise and power of arms; or when they became more celebrated through the authority of dignities or the teaching of the sciences; or finally when they obtained the support of some secular ruler and, casting aside every restraint of modesty and fear, were allowed to corrupt and pervert the minds, morals, and faith of others through the depravity of their opinions.

Archelaus therefore ought, while the people applauded him, to have disclosed not only that the adversary of his Catholic law possessed no true and genuine knowledge or understanding of the sacred Scriptures, but also that he overturned the chief mysteries of our faith and abolished them through his fables. He ought further to have shown that Manes had been stripped of all the goods and aids both of nature and of fortune, so that his name, evil morals, and crimes—already known to many nations—were everywhere utterly detested.

I therefore do not see at all what crime could be detected in such an account or course of action. Even if we grant that the people who had gathered at Diodoride to hear the disputation had not been stirred in the least against Manes, was it not fitting for the holy bishop to warn those people of everything he had clearly learned from the mouths of Turbon and the other disciple?

Was it not fitting for the bishop to employ every precaution and means that he judged more effective and powerful for preserving and protecting the peace of his diocese, the safety of his sheep, and the purity of Christian doctrine?

Beausobre is plainly inventing matters, attempting to turn such conduct into a charge. Especially since Archelaus did not falsely accuse Manes or flare up against him without reasonable cause by fabricating falsehoods; he merely related what, as we have said, he had learned from the mouths of Manes’s two disciples.

6. Now the preceding testimonies cited at the beginning of this chapter can fully demonstrate that the holy Fathers and writers, with the greatest unanimity, described the death of Manes. Yet Beausobre, having finished his attacks against the bishops Archelaus and Epiphanius and still seeking a knot in a rush, notices the slightly different modes of expression and phrases used by the writers mentioned above and, with a gentle hand and censorial pen, pricks them in order to show that they disagree—solely because he endeavors to undermine the credibility of the Acts of Archelaus [Note: Beausobre, chapter 11, p. 126.].

First, he says that Epiphanius, in describing the death of Manes, embellished it with new circumstances when he asserted that Manes had been flayed with the points of thorns and that his skin had been stuffed with straw [Col. 0867C]; the Syrian writer Albulpharagius seems to support him. But, he says, it is sufficiently probable that Albulpharagius learned and copied this from Epiphanius’s reading, since he was thoroughly versed in the Greek language. He adds that Photius, who examined the Greek account drawn from the Acts of Archelaus, testified that the skin of Manes had been filled with air or wind, like a bellows. He judges this last version more probable. For the skins of criminals and malefactors whom the Persians flayed were filled with air, not straw; they endeavored to preserve them in this inflated condition, as is recorded concerning the emperor Valerian, who was flayed after his death on the order of Sapor. The Persians subsequently delighted in displaying his preserved skin to ambassadors of the Roman emperors as a monument of their glorious victory.

Moreover, if the Greek readings and little narratives are to be believed, we shall have to suppose that Saint Bartholomew and the Studite monk suffered a fate equal to that of Manes [Col. 0867D]. Finally, he adds that Epiphanius was wrong to say that the Manichaeans were accustomed to lie and sleep stretched out upon straw or thorns, commemorating their patriarch, who had been flayed with the points of thorns and whose skin had been stuffed with straw or chaff. But Beausobre himself, led by Augustine’s testimony, asserts that Epiphanius invented this. Augustine relates that a schism arose among the Manichaeans at Rome when Constantius, a Roman citizen, gathered together a number of members of this sect so that they might observe the Manichaean precepts exactly; the assembly and congregation was very soon divided into two factions. Some abandoned this manner of life because of its excessive strictness, while others remained in the strict observance and practice of the aforesaid commands. Regarding this schism, described here by Beausobre, [Col. 0868A] we shall more appropriately give his own words below, especially when our account turns to the various grades of the Manichaeans.

7. In the meantime, I should like the reader to observe that all these matters which we have just described from Beausobre—namely, the different modes of expression and phrases used by the preceding writers and Fathers—by no means weaken or overturn the truth of the facts or the history of the Manichaean death. For the purpose of the writers in question was not at all to describe the minute and most delicate circumstances of this death. Some asserted more expansively, others more briefly, that Manes was stripped of his skin by the Persians, so that he might pay the penalty for his wickedness. If one of them thought fit to add something omitted by earlier writers, this may have occurred either because of a common and perhaps reliable tradition received from the Persians, or because their writings sought increasingly to adapt themselves to Persian customs, rites, and institutions.

There is, however, one point that all unanimously approved and committed to writing: Manes was stripped of his skin by royal sentence pronounced against him [Col. 0868B]. Whether he was still alive when flayed, and whether the removal of his skin was accomplished with the points of thorns or with an iron instrument, does not affect the truth of the history. Since such circumstances are of little or no importance, nor so necessary that we should accuse writers who added or omitted them of lying or of fabulously narrating events.

We must make precisely the same assertion regarding his corpse, which was by no means committed to burial, but rather left to the vicissitudes of circumstance and to become food and nourishment for beasts and birds. Beausobre, relying upon very weighty testimonies, asserts that this manner of acting did not at all carry infamy or disgrace among the Persians and other nations [Note: Beausobre, in the work cited above, pp. 126–127. Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, book IV. Strabo, book XV. Assemani, vol. III, part I, p. 409. [Col. 0868D]]. But the foundation from which the author claims to draw this conjecture not only totters as weak, but collapses altogether: namely, that the Persians abhorred disturbing the earth by digging it and making pits in it for burying the corpses of the dead [Col. 0868C], and that they were not accustomed to do so because of the great veneration they showed toward the elements.

But who does not know that the Persians possessed chambers, crypts, and caves? If, then, their religion prevented them from digging pits in the earth because they paid a certain worship and veneration to the elements, I do not see why they could not have placed the bodies of the dead in other locations where the earth itself preserves its natural hollows, pits, and caves. We therefore consider all the monuments which he collected from Porphyry, Assemani, and Hyde and appended at the end to have been improperly introduced, since they contribute absolutely nothing to our purpose—namely, that the flesh of the dead Manes was handed over and left to be devoured by beasts and birds.

8. Yet I am not unaware that so infamous and savage a death, which ought to have filled everyone with fear and terror, profoundly stirred the minds of the disciples of Manes. Indeed, they then became bolder and began to venerate it every year with the greatest signs of joy and proofs of superstitious religion [Col. 0868D]. For this reason, after abolishing the solemn feast of the Pasch of our Lord Jesus Christ—or at least having it observed by only a few with the greatest tepidity—they honored solely the day on which the Manichaean had been killed with great observances.

Augustine formerly enlarged upon the cause of this profane and sacrilegious rite [Note: Augustine, *Against the Epistle of Manes*, chapter 8; found in vol. VIII, p. 113]. He was, as it were, carried away in astonishment when he heard the teachers of the Manichaean sect. He asked them what reason there was for their not celebrating the Lord’s Pasch with any vigils, any longer fast imposed upon their hearers, or any more festive preparation, while they honored their *Bema*—that is, the day on which Manes was killed—with an exceedingly festive solemnity and the greatest devotion of mind. The *Bema* was set before the worshippers with a tribunal furnished with five steps, decorated with costly linens, and placed openly before them [Col. 0869A].

When Augustine asked this, the answer was that they ought to celebrate the day of the passion of him who had truly suffered; but Christ, who had not been born and had displayed before human eyes not real but simulated flesh, had not endured a passion but merely pretended to suffer. Observing this monstrous falsehood after his conversion, the holy Doctor groaned and cried out against such men. Although they wished to be called Christians, they denied that Christ had been born of a woman or possessed a human body, and therefore did not celebrate his passion, even though its commemoration constitutes the most festive season in the whole world. Instead, they substituted for it the sacrilegious solemnity of the *Bema* on another paschal day, which they desired to observe with exceptional devotion as most pleasing, most delightful, and worthy of the highest honor.

Whether more recent Manichaeans are still accustomed to maintain these solemn rites, I do not know at all. I could merely ask Beausobre and Bayle, who contended with every effort on behalf of the Manichaean religion, whether the practices we have reported from Augustine still remain in use. Their answers could further embellish these present investigations of ours. These, finally, are the matters concerning the life, morals, deeds, and death of Manes that emerge from the writings of the ancients. We must now return to Archelaus for a fuller knowledge of the facts: at the persuasion of Marcellus, he committed to writing the confession of Turbo and the disputations he had held with Manes.

## CHAPTER XI. The fabulous inventions of the Manichaeans’ philosophy and theology, abjured by Turbo, a disciple of Manes converted to the Catholic faith, and thereafter committed to writing by Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, at the persuasion of Marcellus, together with the disputations of Manes

Since I am undertaking to report and commit to memory the public confession and execration of crimes which Turbo, the disciple of Manes, made before Archelaus [Col. 0869C] and the others in the Mesopotamian city of Caschara, I must immediately appeal to the writings of Archelaus himself and rely especially upon them. Since he committed to writing—or ordered to be committed to writing—both what he had heard from the mouth of the penitent Turbo and what Manes himself had more boldly put forward against the Catholics in two disputations, there will scarcely be room for doubt that, in examining what is contained in the books of Archelaus, we shall attain the truth of all the facts.

Whatever Beausobre has invented on the contrary, even on this occasion, in order to overthrow confidence in these accounts, can in no way harm either us or the truth, as we shall explain more fully in its proper place. First, then, setting aside the principal and fundamental errors of this sect, which we have already noted above and which Turbo first of all abjured in his public confession, we proceed to describe the remaining impious, futile, sacrilegious, and fabulous inventions.

1. Among these fables, the principal place is occupied by those which the Manichaeans fabricate concerning the first production of human beings, their fall, and their restoration [Col. 0869D]. They assert that those two eternal, coexisting, and mutually opposed gods of light and darkness, after engaging in a great war against one another, each formed human portions. In this act of production, when the author of darkness advanced toward the light in order to obtain it, the good Father of light produced from his power a soul called the Mother of Life. Having adorned the first man with it and clothed him, as it were, with the four elements, he sent him downward to fight against the darkness.

But when the princes of darkness, as though challenged to battle, resisted the man, they inflicted enormous force upon him and consumed part of his armor, namely, the soul [Col. 0870A] [Note: Acts of Archelaus, in Valesius and Zacagnius, p. 100]. Thus, they fabulously assert that, when the first man had been placed in such great danger, he likewise suffered his first ruin, fall, and destruction. They maintained that the afflictions, sicknesses, and miseries of this first man’s soul and body had not arisen from crimes of disobedience and gluttony, but from the darkness itself, by which he was violently afflicted and oppressed.

They say that all this happened to the man before the heavens, earth, luminaries, firmament, and spheres had been created. Therefore, before the first man appeared in the world, the living chaos of darkness already inhabited it. He then entreated the Father of the lights, and was kindly, mercifully, and favorably heard. For another power, which had proceeded from the divine substance and was called the Living Spirit, was sent into him; descending, it extended its right hand to the fallen and afflicted man in order to draw him out of the darkness in which he had been endangered.

The Manichaeans did not retain this impious mystery only in their minds; they openly professed it also through external rites and ceremonies. Whenever they met one another, they gave each other their right hands [Col. 0870B], so that by this sign they might clearly indicate that they had escaped from the bosom and prisons of darkness [Note: Valesius and Zacagnius, in the disputation of Archelaus].

2. No less insane and senseless were the doctrines they devised concerning the formation of the world itself. They invent that the Living Spirit, the creator of the world, clothed with three other powers whose names they do not mention, descended in order to bring the princes of Jesus out into the firmament, which is his body and sphere. They therefore believed the firmament to be animate, as were also the luminaries which we see circling the firmament. They wished such force to reside in their vital movements that human wills, which ought to be subject to them, were compelled to act, with the injury and destruction of free will.

They added absurdities to absurdities. When reasoning about the creation, condition, and movement of the earth, they asserted that it had again been produced. They did not believe it was sustained in the middle of the world by divine power, but carried upon the shoulders of a fictitious *omophorus* (“shoulder-bearer”); and when he grows weary of carrying it, he trembles. This, they say, is the cause of an earthquake occurring outside its appointed time.

The things they invented about these earthquakes were altogether ridiculous and blasphemous. They asserted that the earthquakes were the reason why the blessed Father brought forth his Son from the wombs into the heart of the earth and its innermost parts. They also said that matter, or the earth, produced plants and shoots from itself. When certain princes had stolen these, the eternal Father summoned all the chief princes, took from them their individual powers, made this man according to the likeness of that first man, and conveyed a soul into him.

What the Manichaeans understood by the names of the chief princes is not indicated at all in Turbo’s confession. One thing alone may clearly be inferred from the preceding words: they defended the existence of two offspring of the human race. Since the former preceded the Adamite race, it may perhaps have opened that foolish and most deplorable path to those who in later times defended the pernicious and erroneous opinion of the Pre-Adamites [Col. 0870D] [Note: Archelaus, in the same disputation against the Manichaean].

3. They also attempt to derive from the latest offspring of this man another reason why the blessed Father sent his Son into the world. Not, indeed, in the manner in which Scripture testifies that the mystery of the Incarnation had been foreordained. Rather, they said that the Father was moved to send his beloved Son by the hardships and afflictions suffered in the body by the soul of this man. For this reason, and because of the *omophorus*, the Manichaeans taught that the Father sent his Son.

They fabulously asserted that this Son’s coming into the world did not occur in true and passible flesh assumed by him, but only in a simulated and apparent human form.
