Thus he appeared to the eyes of others as a man [Col. 0871A], although in reality he was not a man; and although people supposed that he had been born of a woman [Note: Consult what we said in the preceding chapter 9 of this work on the occasion of the vindications which we composed on behalf of Archelaus in order to overthrow Beausobre’s malicious interpretations and censures].

If anyone sought the purpose of this mission and coming, they denied that it had anything to do with the salvation of humanity. Nor did they believe that man had been subject to any other ruin or fall than that which arose from the bonds of flesh and body. To overturn and drive away all these evils, they asserted that a certain mechanism had been fashioned for the salvation of souls. It was formed as a wheel with twelve pitchers, by which the souls of the living were drawn up, brought into the presence of the sun, and cleansed by its rays; once purified, they were handed over to the lower luminary, namely, the moon.

But in describing the course and movement of those two luminaries, how many and how great inventions did they devise? They imagined that the sun and moon were two ships, or transporting boats, traversing the circuit of the heavens. Their arrangement was said to be such that the moon, laden first with the souls of human beings, conveyed them to the region beneath the sun [Col. 0871B]. There the souls were drawn upward and downward through certain pitchers, and the ships were loaded and unloaded, until the souls themselves could escape from the bodily afflictions by which they were oppressed [Note: Valesius, vol. II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, after the observations and notes on the History of Socrates; and Zacagnius, in the *Collection of Ancient Monuments of the Greek and Latin Church*].

They affirmed that every soul, and every moving creature, draws a portion from the substance of the good Father. They added that, when the moon had delivered the burden of souls which it carried to the ages of the Father, those creatures—namely, the living beings—remain in the pillar of glory, which is called the Perfect Man. This man, they continued, is the pillar of light, filled with purified souls; and this is the cause of the salvation of souls.

They also firmly believed that certain souls were subject to death. But how foolishly and stupidly they invented the cause of their destruction! They imagined a certain beautiful, adorned, and highly elegant virgin who furtively approached the princes dwelling in the firmament, brought forth and crucified by the Living Spirit. That they adhered in this delirious assertion to the opinion of the pagan Greeks of antiquity is clearly shown by the following words of Turbo [Col. 0871C].

They taught that this unnamed virgin [Note: The Greek myths concerning Aphrodite. Consult what we wrote in our dissertation delivered at the Pontifical Academy of Councils in 1743 and recited in the Quirinal Palace for the purpose of explaining the Canons of Gangra]—namely, Venus—appeared to males as a beautiful woman, but displayed herself to females as a handsome and desirable young man. Captivated by the beauty of her appearance and the elegance of her adornment, the princes of the firmament burned with such lustful love for her that, when they pursued her, she immediately slipped from their sight.

Then that great prince produces clouds from himself to obscure the entire world in his anger. When he has been greatly troubled, just as a man sweats after labor, so this prince sweats from his tribulation. That they intended this to refer to Jupiter, the prince of all the planets, may be conjectured from the writings of the pagans [Note: Valesius and Zacagnius, in the work cited above].

They further assert that the prince of harvests is sometimes compelled to undergo the same evil reversals. When he discovers that he has been deceived by that virgin, he is kindled and inflamed with such anger that he spreads famine over the earth and inflicts death upon human beings.

From this they taught that there are two worlds, each inhabited by human beings [Col. 0871D] 88. The lower world is this visible and perceptible one, subject to the upper world in such a way that all human beings who are below have their roots bound above. Therefore, they again fabricated a story about the same virgin, reasoning as follows:

“When, therefore, the prince of harvests has been deceived by the virgin, he will begin to cut off the roots of human beings; and when their roots have been cut off, pestilence arises, and thus they die. But if he shakes the upper parts of the root more violently [Col. 0872A], an earthquake occurs, followed by a shaking of the *omophorus*.”

They likewise believed that death derived from these evils, admitting absolutely no distinction between the sufferings and destruction of bodies and those of souls.

3. After this, Turbo himself, who had resolved to disclose and abjure all the principles of the Manichaeans’ fabulous secret philosophy, openly explained before the same bishop Archelaus, Marcellus, and the others before whom he had been ordered to appear what the Manichaeans taught, together with the school of Epicurus, concerning the transmigration of souls. He therefore added the following:

“I shall tell you how souls are also transferred into other bodies. In the present body, which the spirit now inhabits first, only a small portion of the soul is purified. It is then transferred into a dog, a camel, or the body of another animal. But if the soul enclosed in the prison of the present body has committed murder, it is then transferred into the bodies of elephants [Note: Turbo, in the disputation of Archelaus, in the work cited above]; if it has harvested a crop, into walls” [Col. 0872B].

They explained the sequence of these reversals, or transmigrations, at greater length, passing through every kind of thing. Thus, proceeding step by step from animals to plants, vegetables, shoots, and even inanimate things themselves, they professed that the human spirit could be infused into and transformed into anything whatsoever.

When we reflected upon all this, our astonishment was aroused by principles of the Manichaeans so mutually contradictory that we could scarcely believe that their falsity would not have been apparent even to an ignorant but sane person. Especially absurd were their assertions concerning the names and properties of the soul. They taught that the following attributes and properties belonged to the soul: mind, sense, prudence, understanding, and thought. Yet we know these to be more contrary and foreign to the natures of beasts, the properties of plants, and the substances of insensible things than light is distant from darkness, heaven from earth, and the stars from the elements.

Since the Manichaeans themselves maintained that there could be no agreement or bond of fellowship at all among these things of a lower order [Col. 0872C], what, I ask, were they reasoning when, uttering such inept and foolish claims, they said that thinking substances were transferred into hay, beans, barley, ears of grain, or vegetables, so that the reapers themselves might be cut down and harvested?

In a similar way they spoke about those who ate bread or killed a chicken, saying: “He who eats bread must himself also be eaten like bread. But if he kills a chicken, he himself will be a chicken.”

They also fabricated a law concerning the souls of those who abound in earthly riches: when they departed from this present bodily life, those souls were to be cast again into the bodies of the poor, compelled first to undergo every labor and hardship of begging, and thereafter handed over to eternal punishments to be tormented.

Nor did they cling only to such fictions in the question of the transmigration of souls. Since they freely granted that body and matter were the principle of all visible and sensible things, they therefore inferred that it was necessary that whoever planted a peach tree (*Persea*) must pass through many ages until that very peach tree which he had planted should fall.

They poured forth similar absurdities concerning the construction of houses and those who washed themselves in water:

“Whoever builds a house for himself is scattered through all bodies. If anyone washes himself in water, he wounds his own soul.”

This final piece of delirium proves that the Manichaeans not only abhorred every ordinary secular washing with natural water, but also that washing which the Lord Christ instituted for the regeneration of human beings. These and similar statements reveal that the members of the Manichaean sect despised and condemned every adornment and cleanliness of this mortal life. They were excessively concerned with and delighted in poverty and want, the filth and squalor of uncleanness—things which they sacrilegiously strove outwardly to simulate under the false mask of piety and religion.

For what else does that practice indicate by which they sought to be nourished by the substance of others and sustained by the sweat of others? What else do the desires reveal with which they burned most intensely, so that those called the “elect” in this sect might be fed with the finest foods, procured for them from the generosity and offerings of others?

To open a broader path for their profit and to induce others to provide for their needs and show them mercy, the Manichaeans frequently threatened them with the punishments of Gehenna and other severe—perhaps, as I think, secret—torments [Col. 0873B], saying:

“Whoever does not provide food for the elect is subjected to the punishments of Gehenna and is transformed into the bodies of catechumens until he performs many acts of mercy.”

Thus, frightened by such threats, the hearers offered the elect whatever was best among their foods. The elect, however, did not eat the food of others until they had first recited this superstitious prayer, which Bishop Archelaus recorded from Turbo’s confession in these words:

“When they wish to eat bread, they first pray, saying this to the bread: ‘I neither harvested you, nor softened you, nor threshed you, nor put you into the oven. Another made you and brought you to me. I eat you innocently.’”

After the Manichaean had uttered these words secretly and within himself, with no one hearing him, he turned to the person who had brought the food offerings and pretended to thank him with the following reply:

“I have prayed for you.”

And since he considered it wholly unlawful to perform work, the one who was eating the bread and food of others added, as a testimony to his superstitious sect:

“If anyone harvests, he will be harvested. Thus, if anyone puts grain into the mill, he too will be put into the mill. If anyone kneads, he will be kneaded. Thus, if anyone bakes bread, he will be baked.”

They therefore invoked such evils, and others like them, upon those who showed them mercy and from whom they received food or nourishment. This monstrous conduct reveals the depravity of their minds and their excessive cruelty of nature.

4. Turbo himself now continues to explain more clearly before Archelaus all the fabulous inventions concerning the essence of multiple worlds, which we touched upon briefly above:

“They also say again that there are other worlds besides this world which we see, and that the luminaries of this world rise for those worlds when they have set here.”

Inventing new forms of delirium, they neglected to understand the structure of the universe and the properties of earth and air, although they made a show of devoting themselves more than was proper to mathematics and astrology.

They held that the earth was harmed by those who walked upon it, and the air likewise by those who raised their hands upward, because they believed that the air is the soul of human beings, animals, birds, fish, and reptiles, and that it is paradise, which is called the world [Col. 0873D]. Its trees are all the desires and other seductions that corrupt the thoughts of human beings.

In defending this doctrine, they may perhaps have misused words drawn from John’s First Epistle, explaining them through such perverse allegories. They also believed that a particular tree had been planted in this paradise, from which good is known. But, following the earlier allegories, they said that Jesus and his knowledge, which is in the world, were signified there; whoever received this knowledge could distinguish good from evil.

Thus Turbo added:

“Since the world does not belong to God, but to the Father of matter, it is necessary that it and everything contained in it be destroyed. But if a soul leaves the world without having known the truth, it will be handed over to demons, so that they may tame it in the fire of Gehenna. After it has been chastised, it will be transferred into other bodies to be tamed, and thus it will be thrown into that great fire until the consummation” [Col. 0874A] 90.

5. After Turbo had narrated these and similar matters from the teaching of his master with equal execration, he began to explain what judgment or opinion the Manichaeans had formed concerning the ancient prophets. They did not believe that the prophets had ever prophesied truly. Rather, they thought that the prophets had been instructed and deceived by the spirit of impiety and falsehood and by the most wicked prince of darkness.

Therefore, they said, having been blinded in mind by the father of lies, the prophets always foretold falsehoods to the destruction of those who placed faith in their prophecies. Hence Turbo added:

“And if anyone follows their words, he will die forever, bound within the mass, because he has not learned the knowledge of the Paraclete.”

For this reason Manes himself commanded only his elect—who numbered no more than seven—that, when they had finished eating, they should pray and pour exorcised oil over their heads [Note: See what we wrote about this exorcised oil in the preceding third chapter, p. 32], invoking many names for the confirmation of faith.

What this exorcised oil was, with which they anointed their heads in that profane and superstitious rite, and what names they invoked while praying, Turbo himself entirely omitted, because he did not know them. For Manes himself and his pseudo-apostolic princes, who always boasted that they possessed profound wisdom, strove to envelop their impiety in certain secret mysteries, lest, once the disgrace of so many most wicked sacrileges had been exposed, the shamefulness of their diabolical religion should become known.

Finally, the mind recoils from transcribing what they asserted concerning Moses, the prophets, and the ancient priests. They maintained that it was none other than the prince of darkness who had addressed these prophets, and therefore that no distinction at all should be made among Jews, Christians, and pagans, since one and the same God, subject to passions and desires, was worshipped by all of them.

“This god deceives them in their desires [Col. 0874C], because he is not the God of truth. And therefore whoever hopes in that God … must be handed over with him in bonds, because they did not hope in the God of truth. For he spoke with them according to their desires.”

I am ashamed to report and transcribe such curses against the supreme and most good God, and our holy religion recoils from them. This is especially so since from that same Turbo we learn that they attacked so boldly and despised the great and honorable Lord Sabaoth, whose name the angels of heaven adore, whom the creatures of the earthly world venerate with fear, and before whom the inhabitants of the underworld tremble—whose nature is perfect goodness and whose power is omnipotence. They said that he possessed human nature and was the father of desire. Therefore, they claimed, simpler people worship desire, thinking that it is god.

This God, whom they contend to be the author of wickedness and sin, they asserted—following Scythianus, the elder and prince of this sect [Col. 0874D]—must be handed over in bonds together with the Jews, Christians, and pagans who worship him. All these notions could have been devised only by stupid and criminal men.

6. There are nevertheless two further principal inventions of the Manichaeans which must be brought forward before we proceed to describe their propagation. One concerns the fashioning of Adam and Eve; the other concerns the destruction and end of this visible world.

As to the first, the Manichaeans misused the words of Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” [Note: Genesis 1:26]. To these they added: “and according to the form which we see.” Here they introduced their prince addressing his fellow princes, as though he were saying:

“Come, give me some of the light which we have received, and let us make [man] according to our form, in which we are princes, and according to the form which we see—that is, the first man.”

Who does not understand how many and what kinds of delirium these words contain? They are profoundly injurious to the supreme God, who admits no colleague equal to himself and who can receive from no one outside himself either light, an attribute, or anything else; who has no external and visible form according to which he created creatures; and who finally created Adam himself from nothing, not according to the form of another first man, but solely in his own image and likeness.

Still, despite the opposition of the light of nature, they fabricated several equal gods possessing visible and corporeal form. These gods created man and likewise made Eve, giving her some of their own desire with which to deceive Adam. Nothing is more shameful, nor anything more criminal than these curses by which they so boldly portray the Creator of our first parents.

Could he have been the author of evil and desire whom the Manichaeans themselves asserted to have no part in the world and to be unable to rejoice over the evils occurring in it? Were they not speaking deliriously?

Scythianus, however, who was ultimately the principal founder and author of this sect, speaks as follows in his writings when discussing the end and destruction of this visible world:

“When he has made his image manifest, then the Omophorus itself leaves the earth outside itself, and thus that great fire is released which consumes the universe, in which all the souls of sinners will be eternally tormented. Then,” they added, “all these things will occur, when Jesus appears in a small ship, together with the Mother of Life and twelve helmsmen; they will also have with them the Virgin of Light and a certain third elder, whose name Turbo himself did not indicate at all. But when that great living Spirit, present in his ship, appears, there will be a wall of that great fire, a wall of wind, of air, and of the inner water. Everything, however, will dwell in the moon until the fire consumes the entire world. After this there will be a restoration of the two luminaries, and the princes will dwell in the lower regions.”

[Note: This is how it is read in Valesius’s edition, but Zacagnius, p. 22, presented the text differently.]

Thus, by these inventions they most wickedly corrupted all those prophecies that Holy Scripture teaches and proclaims concerning the destruction of the world, the final day of judgment, and the majesty of the Judge, so that, having undermined the Christian religion, people might withdraw altogether from the truth and turn instead to learning fabulous and insane fictions. Therefore Turbo concludes his faithful confession and his condemnation of this diabolical doctrine in these words:

“This is the whole doctrine that Manes handed down to his three disciples, and he ordered them to depart into the three regions of the world.”

[Note: Concerning these three disciples of Manes, sent here and there to propagate this corrupt sect, see what we wrote above in chapters 3, 4, and 5.]

7. That the principal authors and leaders of the Manichaeans therefore raved impiously as well as ineptly in their studies of philosophy and theology has, I think, been sufficiently revealed by Turbo’s confession, committed to writing by Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, or written at his command.

[Note: Whatever Beausobre brings forward against this in order to diminish the credibility of this confession, we shall remove in what follows, when we discuss the genuine Acts of Archelaus and the disputation.]

But in recounting their inventions and impieties, we have had to undertake a very considerable labor. For the disputation of Archelaus, even as it was printed through the efforts of Zacagnius, is filled with many convoluted turns of phrase and with barbarous and unusual words derived from the Persian, Syriac, and Mesopotamian languages; it also bristles with so many and such serious errors that they must have crept into it either through the carelessness of various translators or through the negligence of copyists.

Nevertheless, Turbo’s condemnation contains nothing false in itself and nothing of doubtful credibility, apart from certain harsh phrases, poorly suited to scholarly usage but contemporary with Archelaus. At that time those heresies had not yet arisen which, in later centuries, were rejected by the Church in its councils and which provided both the Fathers and theologians with a more exact and proper method of expression, one that they were also religiously bound to follow.

Augustine supports this view: throughout his works he reports here and there such nonsense and Manichaean fables, which that holy teacher not only presented to everyone as things to be avoided, but also attacked and overturned as exceedingly harmful to the truth of religion. We may therefore by no means suspect that this work of Archelaus, and the other works relating to the disputations of Diodorus or Tryphon, are not genuine, as all the ancients have testified. We reserve for a fuller demonstration of this the task of setting out a catalogue of those who have discussed Turbo’s confession.

# CHAPTER XII  
## On the Year of Manes’s Death; Various Opinions Concerning It, with Some Evidence Offered for Reconciling Them; Beausobre’s Aim in the Question under Discussion Explained

[Col. 0876B]

1. We can scarcely determine the year of Manes’s death unless we rely upon certain firm conjectures. Some of these concern the time when the heretic himself first wished to hold two encounters: one with Archelaus the bishop, and later another with Diodorus the presbyter, in which he disputed the principles and doctrines of his false sect. Other conjectures must be drawn from what we described in the second chapter of this work, where we debated with Paschasius Quesnellus the time when the Manichaean heresy became known to the world as deserving condemnation—namely, when that most wicked man began to spread his depraved doctrines throughout the world.

There, relying chiefly upon the testimony of the great pontiff Leo, who stated that Manes became known as worthy of condemnation at the time when Probus and Paulinus were holding the consulship, while the eighth persecution against Christians was already raging,

[Note: Leo the Great, Sermon 2 on Pentecost, chapter 5. Petavius, *Rationarium temporum*, and in the notes to Epiphanius. Blanchinus, in the catalogues appended to Anastasius’s *Bibliotheca*. Beausobre, book I, chapter 11, p. 128.]

we demonstrated clearly enough that these men held the consulship after the murder of the emperor Aurelian. On the basis of very weighty evidence drawn from the tables, chronicles, and catalogues of ancient and more recent writers, we proved that this must be assigned to the year of Christ 277, with the support of the authors whom we cited at the end.

But whether that was the year of Manes’s death, the Acts of Archelaus nowhere indicate. Indeed, Beausobre censures the author of these Acts as negligent, on the ground that he appears to assert that the whole Manichaean tragedy occurred under one and the same king of Persia, although this must be regarded as entirely impossible.

The distinguished Alexander Zacagnius,

[Note: Alex. Zacagnius, in the preface, §10 and following.]

who did not examine this question hastily or carelessly, reasoned differently. He first relies upon the testimony of St. Leo the Great cited above, proving that the Manichaean heresy became known to the world as deserving condemnation when Probus and Paulinus were holding the consulship. Therefore, he adds, it must necessarily be said that Archelaus’s disputation with Manes, through which Manes’s error became known to the whole world, occurred between July and December of the year of the Christian era 277.

For this reason he judged that the words of Archelaus, found in chapter 27 of the disputation, should be interpreted favorably. There, wishing to rebuke Manes before the judges who were present at the disputation, Archelaus presses him with the argument that he was not the Paraclete promised by Christ. Otherwise, Christ would long ago have left his apostles and disciples orphaned, without a rector, guide, or teacher, contrary to his divine promises, made and confirmed by his testament, passion, and death, if that Spirit of truth who was to teach all things had come nearly three hundred years later and had established himself as the heir of the Church.

We therefore believe that Archelaus did not burst into these words in order to exaggerate Manes’s stupidity, as Zacagnius wishes, but that he spoke with literal precision. Although he used the round number “three hundred years,” he nevertheless employed a certain qualification, inserting the adverb “nearly,” clearly to indicate that the third century of the Church was then tending toward its conclusion and running its course, at the time when the aforesaid disputation was held.

Archelaus himself, however, needed neither an interpreter nor an apologist in this matter. For, as his argument proceeds, in order to press Manes more and more forcefully, he appeals to those signs by which the coming of the Holy Spirit ought to have been made manifest to the whole world. Yet, whether through a copyist’s error or a translator’s carelessness, when he discusses this number of years he seems to depart from the initial method of calculation. For, invoking that promise of Christ the Lord in which it was declared that he would send the Paraclete not long afterward, to wipe away the mourning and tears of the apostles and disciples, he is found to have sent this one—who himself bears witness to himself—after more than three hundred years.

But who does not see that either an error has crept in or that Archelaus followed another method of calculation? In that passage he does not mention the Christian era, but only the years that had elapsed from the reign of Tiberius Caesar up to Probus himself. He was led by the intention of pressing and rebuking Manes more and more severely on the basis of the promises of Christ the Lord. For from the death of Tiberius to the reign of Probus, only two hundred and forty years had elapsed, as can be made perfectly clear from Petavius’s tables.

[Note: *Acts of Archelaus*, no. 23, p. 46. Dionysius Petavius, *Rationarium temporum*, vol. III, pp. 181 and 185.]

I therefore cannot at all persuade myself that Archelaus, carried away by the heat of disputation, could have fallen into so serious an error, especially since the affairs of the Roman Empire could not have been unknown to him: by that time the Romans already ruled the eastern regions and Mesopotamia, as everyone knows.

That Archelaus was speaking there not of the beginning of the Christian era, reckoned from the Savior’s Nativity, but from his death—which occurred while Tiberius was ruling the Romans and Jews—is made especially clear by the aim of his argument. What else was he trying to prove throughout that entire chapter than that Manes had falsely assumed for himself the name of the Holy Spirit and sacrilegiously pretended that the Spirit’s power, authority, and gifts belonged to him?

Accordingly, to accomplish this more effectively in his disputation, he first appeals to those definite promises of Christ the Lord in which, according to John, he had said that he would soon return to the Father in order to prepare a place for his disciples, and would ask the Father to give another Paraclete who would remain forever in the Church. He then calls this Paraclete the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him; “but you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.”

[Note: John 16.]

Finally, to confirm the truth of these statements more fully, he added: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” It can scarcely be called into question that Christ made this promise to his apostles and disciples, whom he was addressing. They were indeed to receive that Spirit not many days later, so that they might be true and sincere witnesses throughout the whole earth to his preaching, passion, death, and resurrection.

But who can be unaware that Christ made such promises while Tiberius was reigning, on the day before he suffered and after he had celebrated the Passover with his disciples, when, his final testament of will already completed, the Jews had resolved by a council to inflict a dreadful and bloody death upon him?

2. Therefore, for these promises to be fulfilled, as much time as is known to have elapsed from the reign of Tiberius to the emperor Probus could not have passed.

[Col. 0878A]

For we understand without hesitation from the tables of the Roman consuls and emperors that two hundred and forty years were consumed between the reigns of the two. When Archelaus noticed this interval, he demonstrated that the Manichaean must be rejected and expelled like a thief and robber, since he did not produce the signs and examples of the divine promises by which he could show himself to be the Paraclete prefigured by Jesus. In this connection, perhaps ignorantly, he calls Jesus a liar: Jesus, he says, had declared that he would send the Paraclete not long afterward, yet is found to have sent this one after more than three hundred years, as he himself bears witness.

Such a prolongation of time would therefore have rendered the divine promises entirely void, as Archelaus asserts. Assuming the part of those whom Christ the Lord will judge on the last day of judgment, he brings upon the stage, as it were, all who had departed this life from the reign of Tiberius to that of Probus, and addresses Manes in the following reasoning:

“What will those who have already departed this life from that time until now say to Jesus on the day of judgment? Will they not allege this: ‘Do not torture us, if we have not done your works. For why, when you promised under Tiberius Caesar that you would send the Paraclete, who would convict us concerning sin and righteousness, did you send him only under Probus? You left us orphans, although you yourself said, “I will not leave you orphans,” and although you yourself said that you would soon go and send the Paraclete’?”

[Note: Acts 1:8.]

Who, then, will deny that Archelaus himself defined the date of this disputation? For if he asserts that Probus was then holding the reins of empire, he has most clearly indicated that his encounter with Manes must be assigned to the year of Christ 277, if we accept Petavius’s calculations, or to the year 282, if we follow the testimony and arguments of the distinguished Pagius.

3. I fully understand that everything written thus far does not at all clear Archelaus of error and carelessness, even though he plainly indicated that his disputations with Manes occurred when Probus already ruled the Roman Empire. Probus reigned for six years: he received the scepter in the year mentioned above, 277, and retained it until the year 282. Pagius assigns the aforesaid disputations and Manes’s death to that year,

[Note: Pagius, *Critica historico-chronologica*, century III, p. 300.]

although Beausobre places them earlier, judging that they occurred instead in the first year of that reign. It is not possible to settle this controversy within the limits of the present discussion.

For the rest, we are convinced that the words found in the Acts of Archelaus—namely, “after more than three hundred years he sent this one”—crept into the disputation of Archelaus through a translator’s error or a copyist’s negligence, whereas the reading should rather be: “after more than two hundred years.”

For Tiberius died in the year 37, and from his death until the reign of Probus there intervened 239 years. Nevertheless, we believe that we have argued this matter sufficiently, especially since our conjecture is strengthened by those other preceding words of Archelaus in which he clearly indicated that three complete hundred years had not yet elapsed.

It would therefore be necessary either to say that Archelaus was not consistent with himself in the same chapter of the disputation—a view lacking probability—or to attribute the chronological error to the translator or the copyists. We must now proceed to other matters, so that we may pursue the remaining points that we judge to concern the destruction of Manes.

4. First, then, the sequence and catalogue of the Persian kings must be consulted, so that we may understand whether all the events concerning the Manichaean tragedy that we described above occurred under one and the same king, as Beausobre claimed Archelaus—or the author of the disputation circulated under Archelaus’s name—to have indicated, condemning him in a censorious style as negligent.

With regard, therefore, to the catalogues of the Persian kings of the middle period, it is certain that, after the line of the Parthian kings had died out and their empire had been abolished in the year of Christ 226, Artaxares—or, as Petavius notes, Artaxerxes—began to rule the Persians.

[Note: Petavius, *Rationarium temporum*, vol. III, p. 146. Agathias, book IV.]

After he had held the reins of government for fifteen years, he was succeeded by Sapor I, who, enjoying a longer reign, also inflicted enormous losses upon the Romans, as Agathias stated.

Beausobre does not contradict this account. Following the criticism of the distinguished Pagius, he extends Sapor’s reign to the year 271, or to the beginning of the following year, 272.

[Note: Pagius, under the years of Christ 271 and 272, writes: “Sapor, king of the Persians, died this year. He reigned thirty-one full years and inflicted enormous losses upon the Romans.” Agathias, book IV: “After his death, his son Hormisdas assumed the kingdom and died after one year and ten months.”]

Yet the aforementioned Beausobre, having devised a new system concerning Manichaean history, not only adheres to the Chronicle of Edessa and persuades himself that Manes was born in the year 240, but also denies, on the basis of the silence of Eastern writers, that Manes was bound to a servile condition. He supposes instead that Manes descended from the race of the Magi and had a father who was a magus and who at one time attained the episcopate, being called Manes.

In short, he imagines that Manes, the son, spent many years in writing, and that he devoted himself to the study of Greek, mathematics, music, astronomy, geography, astrology, medicine, and painting, and that he excelled especially in the art of painting, as well as in the understanding or interpretation of the Sacred Scriptures. He then asserts that Manes fell into heresy.

Consequently, after being cut off from the Church by excommunication, he obtained the favor and goodwill of the aforementioned Sapor, king of the Persians. Living among the courtiers, he was ordered to accompany the king when the latter prepared battles against the Romans, since the king believed that Manes could heal him and his soldiers.

5. Beausobre did not state in what year Sapor appointed Manes to exercise the highly esteemed office of physician. It may, however, be inferred from the period when Sapor, leading his armies, was inflicting violence and defeat upon the Romans. The records of Roman history report that this occurred especially during the reign of the emperor Valerian.

For Valerian, captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, through the treachery of the general Macrianus, and brought into Persia, was destined by divine vengeance to pay severe penalties for the innocent Christian blood that had been shed. After being held for a long time as an object of ridicule, he was finally flayed alive at the king’s command and paid the penalty for his crimes.

[Note: Orosius and Trebellius describe Valerian’s death in the *Life of Gallienus*.]

But since such battles occurred after the year 254, and Valerian, exhausted by his punishments, died in the seventh year of his reign, I do not see by what means, with what knowledge of the sciences, or with what expertise in medicine Manes could at that time have been trained, so that Sapor would have found him highly pleasing because of his cultivation of nearly all the sciences and would have employed him as an excellent and distinguished physician.

No one but a dullard and blockhead could persuade himself that this was possible. For, according to Beausobre, Manes’s birth must be assigned to the year 241.

[Note: Beausobre, book II, chapter 1, p. 161.]

But according to Baronius, Sapor began inflicting defeats upon the Romans in the year 245; Valerian’s captivity and betrayal occurred around the year 256, and his death in the year 260. Thus, when Valerian paid the penalty for his wickedness, Manes had scarcely reached his nineteenth year. When Sapor was leading his forces and army against the Romans, Manes could still have been an infant and tender youth, since Valerian’s betrayal and captivity must be assigned to the fifteenth or sixteenth year of Manes’s age.

This calculation clearly proves that Manes could not at that time have practiced the art of an excellent and distinguished physician at Sapor’s court. The same Beausobre’s accounts of Manes’s rank or priesthood, of his understanding and interpretation of all the Sacred Scriptures, and of his falling into heresy on account of that understanding, thereby losing communion with the Catholic Church and gaining admission to Sapor’s court by securing the protections of favor that the same author enumerated above, appear no less fabulous.

Equally fabulous must be judged the accounts he gives of Manes’s ministries and parish office, and of the disputations he allegedly held against Jews, magi, and gentiles in defense of the Catholic religion before he fell from the Church—things that our critic invents there without any trustworthy author.

[Note: Beausobre, *History of the Manichaeans*, book II, chapter 4.]

For what of it? When Sapor I, king of the Persians, died, Manes had scarcely reached his nineteenth or twentieth year, as we have already seen. How, then, can we suppose that he had already been ordained to the priesthood contrary to the rules of the sacred canons, had subsequently been deprived of communion because of heresy, and had been expelled from the Church before Sapor died—namely, while that king, guided by fortune and the multitude of his forces, was leading armies to inflict defeats upon the Romans?

No sane person who does not put faith in dreams could persuade himself of this. Indeed, Beausobre himself supposes that several years elapsed between Manes’s fall into heresy and Sapor’s death. He therefore ought all the more to have admitted that Manes’s ordination was premature.

Yet this careful writer on the critical art, as Beausobre boasts himself to be, paid no attention at all to this contradiction in the facts. His sole concern was to weaken and overthrow the testimonies of the ancient Greek and Latin Fathers. Therefore, preferring novelties, he transferred many paradoxes and fables into his work, praising the testimonies of Persian and Assyrian writers who flourished long after the age of Manes.

6. He then describes the character, temperament, studies, and conduct of the Persian kings, in order to display a certain breadth of learning. With a digression, he recalls the ancient religion of that people and asserts that it had long been obsolete but was revived and made to flourish through the efforts of Sapor, king of the Persians.

After praising this king’s prudence, courage, and justice, he proceeds to explain the etymology of the word “Magi,” the term by which the presbyters and philosophers of Persia were accustomed to call themselves. He also adds much concerning the philosophy, studies, theology, religion, and worship of Zoroaster.

Finally, he appended so many absurdities, inept interpretations, and jocular explanations that we judge it wholly unbecoming for a sober and religious man writing about Christian matters to report them. For this reason we have considered it necessary to pass over these and similar matters in silence.

7. We must therefore investigate under which Persian king Manes was compelled to suffer the punishment he deserved for his wickedness. We would not need to expend much effort on this task if we did not also have Beausobre as an adversary who is insufficiently consistent in his own statements.

We first recall what we described shortly before concerning the year of King Sapor’s death. When his son Hormisdas succeeded him,

[Note: Petavius, *Rationarium temporum*, part III, describing the succession of the Persian kings of the middle period, p. 146 of the Venetian edition.]

as the Persian annals prove—and as Beausobre also freely concedes—it is certain that Hormisdas spent only two years in power.

He was succeeded by Varans I, who died scarcely after completing the third year of his reign, leaving Varans II as successor and heir to that kingdom. But as to the year of Christ from which the beginning of the reign of Varans II should be reckoned,

[Note: See chapter 3 of the following book, in which the policy of the Roman pontiffs for destroying the writings of the Manichaeans is defended against Beausobre’s critical objections.]

Petavius, Pagius, and others do not agree with Beausobre. They insist that it must be dated from the year 276. Beausobre, on the other hand, relying upon various conjectures, fancifully assigns it to the following year, 277. Consequently, he flatters himself that Manes’s punishment occurred not under Varans II but under his predecessor, Varans I.

We must therefore attend to the aim of his writing and reasoning. First, as though it were certain, he assumes with Pagius that Sapor took up the reins of the Persian kingdom in the year 241 and held them until the year 272. To Hormisdas, his son and successor, he assigned not two full years but one year and ten days—or ten months—of imperial rule.

He believed that under this king Manes, after first being compelled by Sapor to go into exile from Persia, returned again to Persia and presented the new king with a certain book of Revelations adorned with various and highly accomplished paintings. Beausobre persuades himself, on the basis of a certain testimony of Photius, that this book was none other than the Gospel of Manes, which contained a false history of Jesus Christ.

He also admits that it is regrettable that copies of this work perished entirely through the hostility of time and the hatred of men, since they contained within them the offspring of a wiser man who had devoted himself in that age to the study of Oriental philosophy. Finally, he calls the religious policy of prelates and secular rulers—by which such pernicious books, suited and designed to corrupt the faith, piety, and morals of peoples, were ordered to be thrown into the flames and burned—an intolerable abuse.

He confessed that he did not know whether any remnants or fragments of this work might survive among the ancient Eastern, Arab, and Persian writers. But who does not see that here, and in many other places, Beausobre wished to attack and slander the ancient practice of the Church, which is still observed today?

We reserve the refutation of such insults and false slanders for when we discuss the decrees issued against Manichaean books by Pope Leo and the other Fathers. Nor do we need to linger over what he added in the same place when he speaks of Persian rites and ceremonies involving a certain use of a girdle. On the authority of Hyde, he asserts that this was counted among the moral precepts of Zoroaster.

From this he concludes that the Persians attribute precisely the same virtue to the girdle that Roman Catholics invent for the sign of the cross and holy water—namely, the power to drive out demons and free people from their violence. He therefore concludes that both rites, Persian as well as Muslim and Christian, are thoroughly characterized by superstition.

He further observes that Hormisdas, king of the Persians, graciously received the aforementioned Gospel of Manes and made himself a Manichaean. Since many others soon followed the example of this king, Manes easily secured a name and authority for himself among the Persians.

8. “Yet,” he adds, “the king’s protection could not do Manes much good or enable him to live more safely and securely. For when the Christians and magi understood that he was opposed to their religions, they immediately became hostile to him. To escape their fury, King Hormisdas provided him with refuge and protection in a certain impregnable fortress, so that there he might avoid the death which, beyond doubt, the fury and assault of so many enemies would have inflicted upon him.”

Hormisdas finally died, having spent scarcely two years in power, according to the common opinion of the writers, which Beausobre did not dare oppose.

[Col. 0882A]

Those who report his death assign it to the year 273 or 274 and state that his successor was Varans I, his son. Following his father’s example, Varans at the beginning of his reign provided Manes with protection and shelter. But afterward, when the persecution of the pagan magi and Jews against him intensified, and when he was defeated by them in a public disputation, he was finally killed as the author of heresies.

What kind of punishment he suffered by royal decree Beausobre does not determine with certainty. He asserts only that Manes, as a Sadducee, was killed by capital punishment, citing various opinions: Hyde’s, namely, that Manes was crucified at the city gate; and that of Abbot Renaudot, who maintains that his skin was removed while he was still alive and that the skin, stuffed with straw, was hung up as a warning to others.

To this testimony he adds the book of an unknown author who describes Persian history, or that of Abulpharagius, who says that Manes’s skin was removed after his death.

[Note: Abulpharagius, *Dynasties*. Beausobre, book II, chapter 4, p. 206.]

Beausobre judged this account more probable, led by the example of Valerian, who died a natural death and whose skin Sapor ordered to be removed, so that he might display it to the Romans and curb the arrogance of that proud nation.

To these opinions he added a third, according to which Manes was killed by being suspended and divided into two parts, one part being placed at one city gate and the other at the opposite gate. As a result, those places came to be called Upper Manes and Lower Manes. But who could persuade himself that all this occurred under Varans I?

For, in view of the testimony of the most accurate writers, it is established that Varans I had already ceased to live in the year 276. Therefore, when Aurelius Probus Augustus and Aruntius Paulinus were consuls, this heresy could not have become known as deserving condemnation; nor could Manes have disputed with Archelaus the bishop and Diodorus the presbyter—or, as Beausobre prefers, with magi, pagans, and Jews—since he was no longer alive, having suffered the death that the king’s decree had required him to undergo in the preceding year.

To avoid such labyrinths and pitfalls, therefore, and relying upon the testimonies of the Greek and Latin Fathers, we extend the death of Manes to the year 277, when Varans II ruled the Persians. We judge that scarcely, if at all, can Beausobre’s statements be accepted, since he set himself no other goal than to heap together a vain and useless apparatus of doubtful, jocular, and undigested learning, in order to deceive unwary readers by his enticements, bringing the sincere and consistent tradition of the Catholic Church to ruin through certain fabulous traditions derived from unknown and impure sources. We undertake to prove this more fully in the following chapter.

99

# CHAPTER XIII  
## Whether the Acts of Archelaus, together with the Disputations Held against Manes That Accompany Them, Are True and Genuine as They Are Circulated; Beausobre’s Opinion Examined and His Arguments Refuted as Weak

[Col. 0882D]

1. I should have seemed especially remiss if, after explaining at greater length all that relates to Manes’ origin, heresy, errors, crimes, and punishment, I had not turned my attention in due course to that disputation and those Acts which circulate under the name of Archelaus, bishop of Caschara. For this work, complete and fully edited, was entrusted to the Roman presses of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith in the year of Christ 1698; and the illustrious and highly distinguished Laurentius Alexander Zacagnius, prefect of the Vatican Library, adorned it with great learning, diligence, and labor in his collection of ancient monuments of the Greek and Latin Church.

[Note: Beausobre, book II, chapter 4, p. 201, maintains that this fabricated disputation of Manes gave the ancient Catholic writers and Fathers the occasion to compose the fabulous Acts of Archelaus. We reserve the refutation of his arguments for the following chapter.]

No one is unaware that this work was accepted by the judgment of all learned men until Beausobre’s History of the Manichaeans came to light. But when, from the year 1740 onward, Beausobre committed his work to the press at Amsterdam, even Catholic scholars began to doubt the truth of the History of Archelaus and the authenticity of the celebrated Acts. On the one hand, they reconsidered the traditions of antiquity; on the other, they weighed the arguments with which Beausobre attempted to diminish and overthrow the credibility and authority of these materials. They could therefore easily be led to believe either that the whole History was fictitious, or at least that it contained many things contrary to the truth of events, the circumstances of those times, the administration of civil affairs, and the affairs of the Church.

Having resolved either to remove all these objections or at least to reconcile them, I first encountered the silence of Eusebius of Caesarea and other writers of that age, on which Beausobre chiefly relies. From this negative argument he contends that the Acts of Archelaus and the two disputations appended to them contain invention and fables. I, however, believe that this silence of Eusebius and the other writers of that age could neither move nor ought to move the mind of any learned man. For what is the case? The affairs of the Manichaeans, the disputation, and the exile occurred toward the end of the third century of the Church, while the Acts of Archelaus and the two appended disputations were written in Persian and Syriac. It is therefore not surprising that such monuments did not reach Eusebius, who composed his Ecclesiastical History after the first celebrated Council of Nicaea, and to whom only the Manichaean heresy was known—the heresy which he described in his Chronicle under the year 277.

If the silence of the writers of that age could serve Beausobre’s purpose, he ought to have produced Syrian and Persian writers who, while describing the condition of the churches of those peoples and the affairs of the Manichaeans, denied this History of Archelaus and these disputations, or concealed them entirely in silence. But where are they? Few writers flourished in that age who could have done this. If we consult the Greeks, who knew nothing of Syrian and Persian affairs, only Anatolius of Laodicea comes to mind, who flourished under Probus; or Pierius, the Alexandrian presbyter, under Carus and Diocletian; or Methodius, who was martyred under that same Diocletian, since he wrote against Porphyry and Origen; as well as Arnobius the rhetorician and his disciple Lactantius. Who does not understand that all these men, because of the great distance between the places and because they had no intercourse with the Persians and Syrians, ought to have been ignorant of Manichaean affairs? It should therefore not seem strange that we lack writers of that age who reviewed the Acts of Archelaus and the disputations.

Yet it is beyond doubt that, not long after the first Council of Nicaea, the affairs of the Manichaeans became known to the Greeks. For in the course of the fourth century, specifically in the year 348, Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, in his sixth catechesis, not only seized the opportunity to attack the heresy of Scythianus, Terebinthus, and Manes and to expose their errors, but also mentioned Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, who met Manes as he was fleeing from prison and, convening an audience of Greeks, rebuked him even before philosophical judges, lest, if Christians had judged him, they might appear to have judged something in his favor.

Who, then, will deny that these words point to the disputations and Acts of Archelaus with Manes? But let Beausobre say, I ask, from what sources Cyril could have drawn this information, unless from a sufficiently widespread tradition—perhaps that of Macarius and Maximus, bishops of that Church, a tradition that had already acquired credibility and authority—or from some Persian or Syriac writing that he had at hand. It must in no way be supposed that Cyril dreamed this up, or deliberately wished to fabricate it, for the instruction of those who were to be enlightened by sacred baptism. Otherwise, all the Fathers who flourished in his time and after him would have accused him of error and attacked him in their writings, declaring that the disputation of Archelaus with Manes was wholly fictitious.

Meanwhile, one point must not be omitted, for it may have great force in refuting Beausobre’s various arguments. Cyril called Archelaus bishop of Mesopotamia, but nowhere indicated the city of which he had been bishop. Epiphanius, however, did not follow this same policy or caution: in heresy 66 he called Archelaus bishop of Caschara, and in the remaining matters agreed with Cyril, while composing a fuller account of these Manichaean affairs.

[Note: Book I, chapter 12, p. 130, in the notes, no. 4.]

Beausobre next contends that the autograph of this work was never written in Syriac, but first came to light through the deception of the Greeks. He therefore concludes that it gives off nothing but the odor of pure invention. He likewise reproaches Laurentius Zacagnius for having written that Epiphanius consulted Greek copies. Yet he attacks the distinguished man unjustly. Zacagnius proves the point not only by the testimony of Jerome, but also by very weighty conjectures, among them the fact that Archelaus, when discussing the length of the solar course, says in chapter 32 that the Greeks call it a “sphere.”

[Note: Jerome, On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 72.]

Thus the autograph could not have first appeared in the Greek language; rather, it must have been produced by an interpreter who translated a version of these same Acts from Syriac into Greek, so that, transferred into a more widely known language, all the faithful throughout the world might possess the fullest knowledge of them.

But the Greek version in question is demonstrably older than Epiphanius, who reports notable excerpts from it in Greek in his account of the Manichaean heresy. Nor can one say, Zacagnius adds, that Epiphanius himself translated these passages into Greek from a Syriac exemplar, since everything that Epiphanius cites from the Acts of the disputation of Archelaus with Manes is found word for word in the Latin version that we publish.

Nor does it prove anything that the first Latin writer to review such Acts was Saint Jerome, who flourished around the year 392.

[Note: Zacagnius, preface, no. 4, p. 4.]

Indeed, Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, ought rather to have mentioned these same Acts. He had composed a catalogue of heresies long before—namely, in the year 370, according to Beausobre, but more accurately, according to Cave, in the year 380.

[Note: See the preliminary discourse of Isaac Beausobre to part II of his History of the Manichaeans.]

[Note: Guilielmus Cave, The Christian Ecclesiastical History of the First Centuries, p. 172.]

Yet one may infer from Beausobre himself and from Guilielmus Cave what judgment learned men formed concerning Philastrius’ studies and writings. Almost all the works of the Greek writers had escaped Philastrius’ notice, and the work he compiled plainly displays a less accurate judgment.

2. Beausobre himself more than once accuses Philastrius of ignorance and negligence, as all who have examined his History of the Manichaeans know very well. If, then, Beausobre himself judged that no reliance should be placed on Philastrius, and for that reason attacked him, why does he later suppose that Philastrius’ silence can favor his own position? Away with such empty conjecture and reasoning.

Both Beausobre and Zacagnius speak of an interpreter, but neither gives his mind any real adherence to the same opinion. To reconcile the testimonies of Saint Jerome, Epiphanius, and Heraclianus of Chalcedon, Zacagnius appeals to the authority of Photius. In codex 87, while reporting certain excerpts from Heraclianus, Photius adds the following words, which we read in chapter 39 of these Acts and which seem to confirm that the same Acts were committed to writing by Hegemonius:

[Note: “Since Marcellus was pleased to receive and record this disputation, I could not refuse, trusting in the kindness of my readers, who will grant pardon if anything unlearned or rustic should sound in my speech. For this alone is our aim: that knowledge of what happened should be hidden from no diligent reader.” And more clearly in the same, final chapter: “After these matters had subsequently been recognized, Archelaus added them to the earlier disputation, so that they might become known to all, just as I, who wrote this account, set them forth previously.” Zacagnius, as above.]

Zacagnius therefore considers it probable that Archelaus himself later added certain things to his original disputation. He willingly adopts the view that Epiphanius and Jerome can be reconciled with Heraclianus if we say that Archelaus first published in Syriac everything he had said against Manes before the chosen judges; while Hegemonius not only arranged what Archelaus had already published in a better order, but also enriched it with a prologue, epilogue, and several other additions, so that the Acts of this celebrated disputation might be transmitted to posterity complete in every respect.

3. Beausobre will judge these arguments and conjectures of Zacagnius sufficiently plausible, but he contends that they cannot be accepted, since the formulas Archelaus used to explain the person of Christ and the mystery of the Incarnation suggest that they originated with a man who flourished and wrote after the Council of Nicaea, namely, around the year 330.

Yet it is already well established that Beausobre was not consistent with himself in composing his work, as is clear from what he previously objected against Archelaus in chapter 9.

He maintained that the disputation in question was entirely filled with expressions that openly favored the heresies of the Arians, Nestorians, and Eutychians. Accordingly, lest he cause us difficulty, in chapter 9 of this work we strove to clear Archelaus himself of such malicious accusations.

[Note: Consult what we wrote in chapters 9 and 10 of this book to clear Archelaus of every charge of heresy.]

At last the ignorant critic wrongly concludes that, since no ancient Syrian author had come before him who mentioned either Archelaus or his disputation, he was compelled to profess and conclude either that this History was spurious, or that it had been invented by Hegemonius himself, or that Hegemonius had received it from some man born in Mesopotamia—perhaps from Turbon, who had seen Manes and given his name to the sect—and then embellished it with many other circumstances invented by himself.

He concludes that he drew this judgment from a more recent learned man who believed that the work should by no means be attributed to Archelaus, but that Hegemonius had added or removed whatever he judged expedient. Beausobre confesses that he cannot depart from this opinion until clearer arguments have been presented or supplied to him.

But did you, Beausobre, truly depart from the more common view when, besides the testimonies of the writers mentioned, those of later centuries are added? When Photius, Peter of Sicily, and other men of finer critical judgment approved the celebrated Acts and disputations of Archelaus, it will not take many words to make the point clear, since we have already discussed similar negative arguments in the preceding sections, and since Beausobre himself, inventing matters solely on his own authority, proposes and resolves questions of this kind.

One such question is the one he raises: whether the disputation of Caschara really existed or should be considered fictitious. He admits that he has called it the disputation of Caschara because he cannot affirm or deny with certainty that Manes at some time disputed with an orthodox bishop about his errors or had encounters of this kind.

He says that he cannot make the readers more certain on this matter, since various examples survive in ancient writers—writers who not only invented certain spurious disputations between heretics and orthodox bishops, but also imagined that such encounters had taken place between apostles and heretics. He cites as an example the books of the Recognitions, which circulate under Clement’s name, and in which he rashly claims that the history of Saint Peter disputing with Simon Magus is fabricated.

He says that Guilielmus Cave believes this fabulous account was brought from Syria or Mesopotamia by Bardesanes, highly skilled in the Greek language. But which learned person who has examined Guilielmus Cave’s Literary History with his own eyes would accept this? Cave certainly did not assert that such a history contained a fabulous narrative.

[Note: Guilielmus Cave, Literary History, Apostolic Age, p. 18: “The presbyter Rufinus of Aquileia translated these ten books from Greek into Latin, and no one has declared that they smell of fiction.”]

He sincerely acknowledged that the work was extremely ancient and had also been praised by Origen. He did not attribute it to Clement; he listed it among Clement’s spurious works, but not in the sense that the contents of those works smelled of fables. Rather, he did so because a work that perhaps ought to have been attributed to other authors bore the name of Clement.

Beausobre therefore appealed improperly to such examples and to Cave’s testimony in order to demonstrate that the Acts and disputations of Archelaus were wholly fictitious.

Nor did Beausobre think it sufficient gradually to undermine the credibility of these Acts by such trifles. Instead, he intended to derive weightier and more evident arguments for their falsity from the very place in which the disputation is said to have occurred.

First, it is said that Manes and Archelaus disputed publicly in a city of Mesopotamia. Second, that this city had been reduced under Roman power. Third, that the city was called Caschara or Carchara. Thus the celebrated Acts themselves show that these three characteristics belong to the setting of Archelaus’ disputation.

If, then, no city can be found to which these features apply, it must necessarily be admitted that the disputation is wholly fabulous, since its author invented a scene in a place that nowhere exists.

Zacagnius, he observes, investigated this Mesopotamian city more carefully. He eventually convinced himself that the three celebrated marks or characteristics could apply to the famous city of Carrhae, which later became still more celebrated because of Crassus’ defeat, as Ammianus Marcellinus noted.

Various coins show that this city was a Roman colony, as may be seen in Spanheim, Cellarius, and others. Zacagnius’ reasoning was supported by the Latin version of certain writings, which has the name “Charra.”

Moreover, in the histories of antiquity he found no city of Mesopotamia subject to the Romans that was called Caschara or Carcar. Rather, similar names appear to have belonged to a city situated in Arabia Felix, as may be seen in the Anonymous of Ravenna, the geographical writer, or in Ammianus Marcellinus, who mentions another Carcha.

[Note: Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII: “An ancient town distinguished by the sufferings of Crassus and the Roman army. The Syrians call this city Haran, but the Greeks assert that it received the name Carrhae from the river.”]

Zacagnius replies, however, that Archelaus was bishop of neither of these cities. His disputation with Manes took place in a Mesopotamian city situated under Roman rule, whose bishopric Archelaus held, as is expressly stated by Epiphanius and in the Acts of the disputation.

The Carcha mentioned by Marcellinus lay outside Mesopotamia, beyond the Tigris, in Persian territory. Nor could Archelaus in any way have been bishop of the Arabian Carcha mentioned by the Anonymous of Ravenna, since all the ancient writers report that he was bishop not of Arabia but of Mesopotamia.

4. Beausobre says that this opinion of Zacagnius had long ago been rejected and refuted by Assemanus, the highly learned chief prefect of the Vatican Library. He adds these words of Assemanus:

“It must be said that Carrhae was written in that single passage of the Acts through the error of copyists, rather than Caschar or Carcar, both at the beginning of the Acts and in the works of the distinguished writers Epiphanius, Socrates, and Photius, who certainly would never have called Carrhae, or Harran, the most famous city of Mesopotamia, Carcara or Cascara.”

[Note: Oriens Christianus, P. le Quien, volume II, p. 1173 and following.]

Yet we find this opinion of Assemanus, otherwise a most serious man, rejected by the learned le Quien in his work entitled Oriens Christianus. In the second volume, while discussing the Chaldaean Churches, he describes the city of Caschara as situated on the borders of Mesopotamia and as very different from the other city built near Ctesiphon.

He asserts that the former city, once occupied by the worship of idols, gave its name to Christ through the preaching of Saint Thaddaeus, and that Archelaus was its bishop under Probus. The same author was unwilling in any respect to depart from Epiphanius, Jerome, or Photius; and the entire assembly of ancient writers subsequently supports him.

Even if Zacagnius’ conjecture, which Beausobre seeks to attack, should wholly fail and collapse because of a copyist’s error, it would not therefore follow that the History in question was fabulous or that the names of Archelaus or his episcopate, which are mentioned there, were fictitious.

Other conjectures proposed by Beausobre himself do, however, collapse completely. He contends that this bishop wished to examine the cause of the Catholic faith before pagan judges as well, with the people present—people who wanted to bury Manes under a shower of stones if Archelaus had given them permission.

But this is a futile conjecture. Beausobre ought first to have noticed Cyril of Jerusalem’s statement: namely, that certain pagan judges were also summoned, lest, if Christians judged, they might appear to have judged something in their favor.

Those philosophers, then, who had been called as witnesses lacked power and authority, chiefly because they were at that time subject to the Roman Empire. No one has yet denied that pagan philosophers were admitted to the Council of Nicaea to listen and even to take part in debate.

Why, then, should it be surprising if Bishop Archelaus, about to meet a heretical man who clung to the false philosophical principles of Zoroaster and the doctrines of the Magi, admitted pagan philosophers as well—men whom he believed would recoil from the fabulous and sophistical arguments of Manes?

Beausobre further adds that in these Acts Archelaus is said, moved by indignation against Manes, to have charged him with being nothing other than a priest of Mithras, that is, of the Sun, and accustomed to worship false gods.

[Note: Beausobre, book I, chapter 12, p. 134.]

He says that a pagan people and a city filled with idols could not have approved this rebuke. It would, however, have received great applause from a Christian people ruled by a Christian emperor. If matters had occurred in this way, the whole city, aroused to indignation against the bishop, would have attacked him with insults and even endangered his life.

To show that all this lacked probability, Beausobre appeals to the action or example of Julian the Apostate. During his fatal expedition against the Persians, Julian refused to proceed to the city of Edessa because a very large number of Christians lived there; instead, he turned his journey toward Carrhae in order to sacrifice to the gods.

Thus, since the people of that city were especially devoted to the worship of false gods, they buried under stones the unfortunate man who announced to them that Julian had already died.

5. This Beausobrian method of argument and this skill in disputation could easily persuade those ignorant of ecclesiastical history. But those who have learned from Eusebius of Caesarea and other trustworthy writers that the condition of the Christian communities in Mesopotamia, Persia, Egypt, Phoenicia, and Phrygia changed greatly from the year 277 to the year 293 will not give it credence. Churches that had initially been most flourishing were reduced to complete destruction when Diocletian’s persecution raged.

Who can be unaware that, before such a dreadful and severe persecution was stirred up against Christians, our people were already held in the highest honor by pagan rulers, so that the office of governing provinces was entrusted even to them? Authority to administer justice was also granted to our people. Pagan rulers allowed their wives, servants, and entire households not only to believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, but also to conduct themselves in the faith with complete confidence and freedom. They regarded such Christians as loyal and intimate associates, being certain that, for the sake of Christ’s faith, they would harbor nothing treacherous.

[Note: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book VIII, chapters 1, 2, and following.]

Petavius likewise relates, from Vopiscus, Victor, Eutropius, Hydatius in the Fasti, and Zosimus, that Christians under Marcus Aurelius Probus—elevated to the imperial power by military agreement in the year of Christ 276 or 277—enjoyed such great and happy tranquility and were honored with such offices.

[Note: Petavius, Chronological Reasoning, part I, book V, chapter 14.]

It is therefore not surprising if what Archelaus set forth in the celebrated Acts could have occurred, especially because, as we have already seen, Marcellus, or Marcellinus, who administered the affairs of the province of Mesopotamia by imperial authority, was a Catholic and desired the propagation of the truth of the faith. With military force he could have inflicted punishments and disasters upon the seditious men who rose up against Bishop Archelaus.

That Christians at that time were appointed by emperors as provincial administrators, financial officials, chamberlains, and holders of other offices of honor and authority can also be inferred from Diocletian’s decree issued at Nicomedia in the year 303, by which it was ordered that Christians should thereafter be deprived of every honor and dignity.

[Note: Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 2.]

This would plainly have been absurd unless Christians had previously been accustomed to enjoy honors and dignities. Beausobre therefore ought not to have attempted to obscure a truth brighter than daylight by turning the chronology of events upside down and persuading himself that he could deceive readers into accepting his statements.

It is therefore fabulous to claim that the Churches of the East were always harassed under pagan emperors, and that Christians endured the same condition under Marcus Aurelius Probus as they later endured under Diocletian, Sapor, and Julian the Apostate.

We could refute this invention with many other most serious arguments, if it were not already certain that Julian the Apostate’s example proves nothing. After renouncing the Catholic faith, he reopened the temples of the idols. But how could he have reopened them if they had not long before been closed for the propagation and protection of the Catholic religion?

6. After this, Beausobre turns his attention more carefully to investigating whether Carchar, or Caschar, was a city situated in Mesopotamia, Assyria, or Chaldaea, or in Persian territory not far from Seleucia, and whether it could have been subject to Roman rule during the reign of Probus.

Following his customary method of argument, he collected from various writers a variety of conjectures and arguments, appealing now to Assemanus, now to ancient and modern geographers. He brings forward such an abundance of material that he thinks he has shown that the setting of this disputation could have been neither Caschara nor Carchara, and that no fort or town of this name had been brought under Roman rule.

Since, then, he appeals to the distinguished Assemanus, it will not be inappropriate to set against him what that author described in his Oriental Library:

“Archelaus, in the year of Christ 277, restrained the heresiarch Manes in a learned disputation when he burst forth from Persian territory.”

[Note: Assemanus, volume I of the Oriental Library, final chapter, p. 555 in my edition; and volume IV of the Oriental Library. See also the Acts of the Martyrdom of the distinguished Evodius of Caschara, martyrdom under King Sapor, p. 151.]

If, then, according to the ancient monuments brought forward by Assemanus, Manes came to dispute with Archelaus after bursting forth from Persian territory, the episcopal Church was not in Persia but in another province not very far distant.

Assemanus adds:

“Saint Jerome calls him BISHOP OF MESOPOTAMIA in his Catalogue, chapter 72. Saint Epiphanius, in heresy 66, specifies the location of the bishopric; Socrates, book I of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22; and Photius, in his book Against the Manichaeans, namely: Cascar or Carchar, indeclinably, or in the plural or singular number Caschara and Carchara, a city situated on the borders of Mesopotamia. The older Syrians prefer Cascar; the more recent call it Gargar, or Carcar, or Carcha.”

I cannot conceal, however, that this highly learned man discussed this city elsewhere and, after setting out a catalogue of its bishops, placed our Archelaus after Maris. He also affirmed that the city was built in Persian territory and belonged to the province of Chaldaea.

But what if the division of the provinces was not always preserved in the same form by ancient writers and geographers, because of the fluctuations of wars and changes in the Roman Empire? The Romans, who at that time ruled the affairs of Mesopotamia, could indeed have entrusted Carchara or Caschara to the governor or proconsul of that province and subjected it to his authority. Later writers, paying more attention to the rights of the monarchy than to the geographical region, could consequently have asserted that it was situated within the borders of Mesopotamia.

The history of Roman affairs itself supplies very weighty foundations for this view. From it we gather that, from the year 235 after Christ until 276, the Persians and neighboring peoples were afflicted by the greatest disasters of war.

We read that Gordian advanced with large forces against the Persians, especially in the fifth year of his reign; that he recovered Carrhae, Nisibis, and other towns from them; and that he drove them back into their own region.

It is well known that Gordian’s successor made peace with Sapor I, king of the Persians, and returned to Rome. Yet the same peoples, invading the eastern borders with arms, plundering Antioch, and ravaging various regions subject to Roman rule, were finally vigorously suppressed by Odaenathus, a decurion of the Palmyrenes, whom Zenobia had married. He sustained the Roman state when he assumed the royal title.

After capturing Nisibis and Carrhae, recovering Mesopotamia, driving the Persian king into flight, and killing very many of his men, Odaenathus sent the satraps bound in chains and, as though he himself had conquered, did not blush to celebrate a triumph.

[Note: Petavius, Chronological Reasoning, part I, book V, chapter 12, p. 284; and Victor, Eusebius, and Zosimus.]

Trebellius records this victory under the consulship of Gallienus and Saturninus, which was the year of Christ 264. From that year, therefore, until the reign of Marcus Aurelius Probus, which, as we have seen, occurred in the year 276, the writers do not report that the affairs of the East, Persia, and Mesopotamia changed.

Since we may reasonably conclude that the Romans preserved exactly the same administrative arrangement and jurisdiction, it is not surprising if Archelaus, the author of the disputation—as Assemanus holds—or Hegemonius, who composed the entire sequence of the Acts, attributing the city to Mesopotamia and saying that it lay within its borders, followed the established order of affairs and imperial administration, even though in later divisions of the provinces it was assigned to Chaldaea.

It is sufficiently clear from ancient writers that the ancients used the term “province” to designate regions outside Italy conquered and subdued by war. Some were consular provinces, to whose administration proconsuls were sent; others were praetorian provinces, to which praetors were sent.

[Note: Cicero, On the Laws, 184. Caesar, Gallic War, book I, chapter 45.]

When this occurred, the regions were said to have been reduced to the form of a province.

Nor should anyone object to me that this may be true of Carrhae and Nisibis because we find explicit mention that these cities were conquered and subjugated to Roman rule. I say that no such objection should be made. For writers also mention other towns conquered by the right of war and subjugated to the Roman Empire after the Persians’ defeat, although their names were not recorded.

It is therefore probable that Caschara or Carcara was included in that general statement that Gordian recovered Carrhae, Nisibis, and other towns from the Persians, since it lay nearer to Persian territory.

I consider it unnecessary to linger longer over these matters, especially since the arguments Beausobre presents last are entirely negative, being drawn from the silence of Syrian writers whose purpose in writing was not to mention Archelaus and his disputation, which were known to everyone.
