They can be refuted in the fullest manner by the certain and positive testimonies of all the Greek Fathers of every age who flourished after Manes and Archelaus.

BOOK TWO. ON THE GROWTH OF THE MANICHAEAN HERESY.

107 CHAPTER I. The author’s purpose in arguing is explained.

As we undertake to describe the second part of the history of the Manichaeans, many—and indeed very serious—difficulties confront us. This is especially so because we must discuss the disciples of Manes and the genuine names of those who, after their master’s death, spread this heresy more widely in every direction; or identify the provinces and places into which it was introduced within a short time in order to undermine the Catholic religion; or finally enumerate the Fathers who attempted to destroy and refute the books, letters, and fabulous writings of those heretics.

In carrying out this task, since ancient and modern writers very often disagree among themselves, we considered it wholly difficult to establish anything certain. This was particularly true because Beausobre, indulging solely in his own interests and studies, proposed and pursued rules of criticism that do not serve the investigation of truth, but rather those very rules to which, as we have seen, he clung persistently in the preceding sections.

[Note: Beausobre, preliminary discourse to the second part, pp. 219 and following.]

We consider it unnecessary to provide a specimen of this method of proceeding at the entrance to this second book, since, in addition to the examples already presented in the previous book, countless other falsehoods, slanders, and fabulous interpretations remain to be stripped away. At their proper place and time we are prepared to note and refute them, so that we may show how fraudulently, or at least how unlearnedly, he wrote many things that we have judged either to contain nothing but an obvious error of heresy or at least to lead toward heresy.

Meanwhile, however, we cannot pass over in silence the license and freedom he employs in attacking those Fathers who either described or opposed the Manichaean heresy. He continually accuses them as though they were guilty of ignorance and inconsistency, attacking them as if they contradicted their own statements, and asserting that they did not perfectly understand the systems and mysteries of the Manichaeans—as though he alone deserved the glory and honor of having penetrated more successfully the whole philosophy, theology, and religion of that heresy.

I admit that I too have encountered much in this kind of writing that is obscure and wrapped in many shadows, and that cannot be understood without the writer’s effort and diligence. But when similar matters have confronted us, we have judged it best to report the opinions of others and sometimes to follow them, or rather to confess that we do not know what is wholly hidden, instead of wandering into fabulous and foolish narratives to which no credibility can be given.

The reader therefore has here a general, though rough, idea of what Beausobre described in his preliminary discourse to the second part of his History of the Manichaeans. Since we cannot set out every detail of those introductory remarks, we shall nevertheless not neglect, as we proceed through the rest of this work, to report at greater length whatever we judge necessary.

CHAPTER II. In what places and by what means, after the death of Manes, his heresy was propagated and increased in every direction. Beausobre’s and Cave’s errors are noted. His excessive license against Augustine is corrected. Finally, an inquiry is made into how this wicked sect weakened Armenia, Mesopotamia, and other regions of Asia.

1. After that savage death of Mani, so many and such virulent seeds of his wickedness were by no means extinguished or destroyed; rather, when scattered here and there, they quickly struck deep roots in the minds of many people through the efforts of other impious men, and extended their boundaries in hatred of the Christian religion. And first, if we give full credence to Archelaus, Turbon, and Ephraem, the deacon of Edessa [Note: In the time of St. Ephraem, the Manichaean heresy was especially ravaging Mesopotamia, as Assemanus reports, vol. I, p. 8], Manichaean doctrines were proclaimed chiefly in the East, in Syria, Mesopotamia, and Egypt. This occurred when Mani, still alive, appointed his principal pseudo-apostles over those places and provinces. Mani ordered his disciples to go forth into the three regions of the world. Of these, Addas received the portion of the East. Thomas, however, undertook the lands of the Syrians [Col. 0891C]. Hermas went to Egypt . . . . . . . for the sake of preaching this doctrine.

Nevertheless, the ancient writers differed somewhat among themselves concerning this order and division of the provinces; among others, Guilielmus Cave noted the matter [Note: *Historia litteraria*, p. 91]. For in Cyril and Epiphanius, Thomas occupies the first place, and Epiphanius affirms that he went to Judaea; yet Dionysius Petavius, in his annotations, disagrees, thinking that “India” should be read instead of “Judaea.” Theodoret likewise says that Thomas was sent to the Indians. Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 32, agrees with Theodoret. If this is so, the impostor wished to imitate Christ even in this respect, sending the apostle Thomas to India to preach his own Gospel.

2. Leaving Thomas aside, the narrative now turns to Addas, Turbon’s teacher and another leading pseudo-apostle of that same impostor Mani. Archelaus likewise asserts that Addas was sent to deceive the Syrians; but Petrus Siculus calls him Buddas [Note: Petrus Siculus, *History of the Manichaeans*, vol. XV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*; Theodoret, *Haereticarum Fabularum*, book I, chapter 26; Epiphanius, heresy 66], Cyril calls him Baddas, and Theodoret calls him Aldas. Epiphanius and Nicephorus, following the *Acts of the Disputation of Archelaus*, finally called him Addas.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the man of whom we are speaking not only followed in the footsteps of his teacher but also, by devising many other new ideas, made the Manichaean doctrines more extensive through his own efforts. For this reason he composed a book which he called the *Modion* [Col. 0892A]. The author of the Tollian formula mentions it; and, according to Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, after a succession of several years Titus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, and Diodore, bishop of Tarsus in Cilicia, directed their attacks against that volume. This demonstrates that, by the fourth century of the Church already drawing to a close, those provinces had been polluted by such a stain.

Beausobre, however, reasons differently, and with little consistency. Speaking of Titus, bishop of Bostra, he asserts that Titus rejected not Addas’s *Modion*, but a book *On the Mysteries* which circulated under Mani’s name. He says that Titus followed a different method from Epiphanius in refuting this book: it was distributed into twenty-two chapters according to the Syriac alphabet, and thereafter its errors were solidly refuted by this learned and prudent bishop, without any invective against his opponent, without calling the author a magician or an invoker of demons engaged in abominable mysteries.

He adds that Mani, the author of this book, was a philosopher who convinced himself that this world did not correspond to the idea that we possess of the divine perfections, and therefore concluded that it must have had another principle besides God himself. Beausobre says that he used the works of Titus of Bostra because Titus wrote much more accurately and moderately than Epiphanius himself [Note: Titus of Bostra, vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, part II, col. 899].

Yet what happened? After setting aside and neglecting such an apparatus of evidence, Beausobre fell into such carelessness that what he had just said soon slipped from his mind. Although he had written that Mani was not accused by Titus of Bostra of magic, the invocation of demons, and abominable mysteries, he subsequently says that this bishop took offense at, and brought under examination, what Mani had devised mystically. But while passing over in silence what Mani had invented that was more mystical—and there were many such things—he therefore says that Titus of Bostra shrank from examining what Mani had invented in a more mystical fashion. One must not think that he omitted these matters for any other reason than to avoid offending the minds of his readers, just as Saint Leo the Great refused to discuss these abominable mysteries [Note: Saint Leo the Great, sermon 4 *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*; and sermon 2 *On Pentecost*, chapter 4; likewise, sermon 2 *On Pentecost*, chapter 6. Diodore of Tarsus’s work written against the Manichaeans has been lost among the Greeks through the ravages of time].

A difficulty nevertheless remains: whether Titus of Bostra, in his work, attacked a volume of Mani’s mysteries, or rather another book, namely the *Modion* composed by Addas. Guided solely by Beausobre’s authority, I shall not decide the matter. Those who know well the care that Photius devoted to compiling his *Bibliotheca* will judge with me that Photius’s testimony ought to prevail. We shall speak below about Addas’s book.

3. With regard to Addas and his work, Guilielmus Cave once sincerely admitted that he had seriously gone astray, since he had thought that Addas was no other than Adimantus, who is so often mentioned by Augustine and whom the holy bishop refuted in a work of his own. Cave later retracted this false opinion, following the history of Petrus Siculus and the authors of the Cotelerian and Zolian formulas. Yet, in order to excuse himself at the same time, he wrongly attributes the cause of his earlier error to Augustine, whose following words he quotes:

“For that other work, which had begun to be written in the same codex, is the work of Adimantus, of that disciple of Mani who was called Addas by his proper name” [Note: Augustine, book II *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, near the end].

But what could be more careless or unfair than such an excuse? For he did not reproduce Augustine’s genuine words, but falsified them. Having removed the word *filius* (“son”) from the testimony, he introduced the pronoun *illius* (“of that man”), thereby dragging the holy Doctor’s meaning into an entirely different sense, one which Cave thought advantageous to himself. Is this perhaps an indication that he wished to rise from his earlier error and repair it, while blaming and unjustly attacking the holy Doctor? Certainly not.

Augustine’s words are in fact these:

“For that other work, which had begun to be written in the same codex, is the work of Adimantus, the son of a disciple of Mani, called Addas by his proper name, or by his *praenomen*—as the Maurist Fathers read it” [Note: In the edition of the Maurist Fathers, vol. VIII, p. 430].

Nor does Cave’s hallucination, carelessness, or bad faith consist in the word *praenomen*, which, following the authority of the manuscript codices, the Maurist Fathers recently introduced in place of the two words *proprio nomine* (“by his proper name”). Rather, it consists in the word *filius*, which he wrongly changed into the pronoun *illius*. For in no editors, nor in any manuscript copies, have we encountered the word *illius*; they consistently present the word *filius*.

Thus, from Augustine himself, it becomes clearer than daylight to us that Addas was one person and Adimantus another, although both were most impious defenders and champions of Manichaean doctrine [Col. 0893B]. Since Augustine therefore refers the name Addas not to the son but to the disciple of Mani, the conclusion follows—and this will seem especially relevant to Cave and to our subject—that Adimantus derived his natural origin from Addas as his father, or at least was called his son because of the wicked teachings which he had drawn and absorbed from him. For these reasons, the surname Addas could also have suited him: namely, to indicate Adimantus’s relationship or the school from which he had emerged.

Finally, what objection is there to the possibility that Adimantus was first called Addas by his proper name, as the word *praenomen* indicates, and later changed it, following the example of his predecessor Cubricus? Even so, this Addas would not thereby be identified with the other principal pseudo-apostle of Mani who, while his teacher was still alive, received the regions of the East as his field of travel.

4. Besides Thomas, Addas, and Hermas, Mani’s principal followers, the remaining disciples of his group of twelve also applied themselves energetically to propagating that wicked heresy [Col. 0893C]. Petrus Siculus reports that, after Mani was killed, some of his followers penetrated into Armenia as far as Samosata. There they sowed the seed of impiety and led many Armenians into deception. As this seed grew vigorously, that evil root sprouted and advanced as far as Phanaria, bringing deadly fruit to many.

Petrus Siculus, who later served for a long time as ambassador to the Armenians on behalf of the emperor Basil, briefly explained whose efforts chiefly undermined Armenia and Phanaria almost to destruction. He says that a woman named Gallinicia had twin sons, one called Paul and the other John. The viper-mother nourished these two serpents and, after instructing them in the wicked sect, sent them out from Samosata as heralds of error. When they entered the territory of Phanaria, they reached a certain village and, finding its inhabitants uncultivated and insufficiently grounded in the faith, scattered among them the poison of impiety and the dreadful tares of the hostile demon.

Dionysius Petavius asserts that this woman Gallinicia was impure and depraved [Note: Petavius, vol. VI of the *Theological Dogmas*, book XV *On the Incarnation*, chapter 7, nos. 4 and 5]. From Petrus Siculus he likewise teaches that she sent her wicked offspring into various regions of Armenia to propagate Mani’s doctrines.

Meanwhile, a serious controversy can arise concerning when such a mission occurred, and especially at what time that heresy acquired its new name from these two brothers. Since this question is enveloped in great darkness, it cannot easily be settled. For it is highly probable that Petrus Siculus intended to indicate two separate matters.

The first is that, after Mani was killed, some of that group of twelve disciples immediately entered the province of Armenia, were received there, and poured out all the poison of their evil doctrine. As it grew daily, it undermined the whole region and corrupted it with perverse teachings [Col. 0894A].

The second is that only after several centuries had elapsed since Mani’s death did that woman, Gallinicia of Samosata, send her twin sons to Phanaria as new leaders and heralds of this wicked sect, so that they might spew forth, to the destruction of ignorant peoples, the worst teachings which they had already absorbed. This could indeed have caused the ancient name of the heresy, after several centuries had passed, to change into the name of the Paulicians.

5. So that I may not appear either to be guessing in these matters or to be forced to break the thread of the whole history that we are writing, I shall bring forward the considerations on which our preceding conjectures rest. Among these, the most important must be regarded as the evidence supplied by Augustine in his book *On Heresies*.

Having been exceptionally well instructed in the mysteries and profane rites of the Manichaeans, Augustine not only describes how, after Mani was killed, one of the Elect, as though the chief of them all and the head of the entire sect, presided over twelve other Elect whom they called teachers [Col. 0894B]; he also relates how large that assembly became and how greatly it expanded. For, according to him, following the form and likeness of the Christian Catholic hierarchy, those twelve pseudo-apostles, together with their wicked and diabolical head, began to ordain seventy-two bishops. The bishops in turn ordained presbyters and chose deacons for themselves.

“For from their Elect they have twelve whom they call teachers, and a thirteenth as their chief; bishops, seventy-two, who are ordained by the teachers; and presbyters, who are ordained by the bishops. The bishops also have deacons.”

But besides those whom they ordained through profane and sacrilegious rites, and who were appointed to form the more distinguished part of that diabolical hierarchy, they also sent others from the same class of Elect here and there to deceive the more ignorant and simple people, so that they might more readily and easily either confirm their doctrines or spread them. Accordingly Augustine immediately adds:

“And now the others are merely called Elect; but even they are sent out who appear suitable for this error, either where it must be supported and increased, or where it has not yet been sown.”

Augustine also testifies in these words that this was customarily done by the Manichaeans in his own time:

“This number the Manichaeans preserve even today.”

Since Augustine, who knew the doctrines, mysteries, philosophy, ranks, ordinations, hierarchy, and expansion of the Manichaean sect extremely well, nowhere mentions these twin brothers, it may rightly be conjectured that in the year 428, when he wrote that book *On Heresies*, that offspring had not yet emerged from the infernal prisons into the world, and that the Manichaeans had then borrowed a new name from the Paulicians.

Nor may one suppose that this could have escaped Augustine because the Armenian and Asian regions in which, according to Petrus Siculus, these events occurred were extremely distant from Hippo in Africa, where Augustine composed his work. No one should suppose this. For the holy Doctor, who had fallen into the errors of the Manichaeans from childhood and had been deeply devoted to the study of their philosophy, also knew very well the names by which that sect was called. He expressly stated that it was spreading in Paphlagonia, a region of Armenia, in Gaul, in Africa, and in other regions.

Indeed, in the cited book *On Heresies*, he asserts that the Catharists were called Manichaeans, as though they were “purifiers.” From this name he takes the opportunity to attack and rebuke them more severely, because they polluted human food with appalling depravity.

Again, in *On the Nature of the Good*, he attacks certain of their obscenities. They perversely maintained that a part of God was bound through intercourse between males and females, and insultingly [spoke] against the divine Author of things; they professed that they released and purified it by eating. Augustine appeals to certain public confessions of their crimes, in which they testified in public judgment that they did this—not only in Paphlagonia but also in Gaul—as I heard from a Christian Catholic at Rome.

Augustine, therefore, who was writing these things in the year 404 [Note: Augustine, book *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 47], was firmly convinced that this heresy was spreading widely in Paphlagonia, a region of Armenia, and he reported this both from public judicial records and from the testimony of others.

He would not therefore have omitted to report and reject what the Paulicians later devised to confirm, enlarge, and strengthen this sect—things which those two criminal brothers acquired with great zeal in order to undermine the Catholic religion more shamefully and to attack and denounce Catholic ministers, the mysteries of the cross and the Eucharist, the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God, and other matters of this kind.

Since, therefore, in so many and such varied books and works written by Augustine against the Manichaeans and other heretics, the name of the Paulician brothers appears nowhere, and since he nowhere records those additions to the heresy which Petrus Siculus reports to us [Col. 0895B], I cannot in any way be persuaded to believe that, immediately after Mani’s death, those twin brothers were the defenders and founders of this heresy. For this reason, I now consider it unnecessary to discuss them at greater length. We shall need to speak of them later, when, preserving as far as possible the order and sequence of time, we describe how, in the seventh century of the Church, the offspring of this heresy spread still more widely through Syria and the regions of Asia, in contempt of the Catholic religion.

6. In the meantime, we must by no means pass over the fact that, even before Augustine’s age and at the beginning of the fourth century of the Church, Armenia and Paphlagonia had been especially undermined by such errors of Mani. This is demonstrated not only by the preaching carried on there by Mani’s pseudo-apostles, or by those deadly and poisonous writings which Thomas, Agapius, and others had disseminated everywhere during the reign of Constantius Chlorus; the surviving Acts of the Council of Gangra also provide the most certain testimony to the matter [Col. 0895C].

Only fifteen bishops, together with the great Hosius of Corduba, assembled at that synod during the time of Pope Saint Sylvester, shortly before the First General Council of Nicaea was convened. Gangra is moreover a city of Paphlagonia, situated in Asia Minor. Into this city the fifteen bishops just mentioned gathered with the great Hosius because of the Eustathian heresy, which derived its origin from various Manichaean sources and was spreading through various regions of Armenia, to the greatest detriment of the Catholic religion.

This can be understood clearly both from the Synodical Letter of the Fathers of Gangra and from the twenty-one canons issued there. In their Synodical Letter they wrote: “To the honorable fellow priests established in Armenia.” Many of the canons issued at that synod directly censure, attack, and condemn with anathema various errors of the Manichaean sect, as Severinus Binius correctly and learnedly noted long ago in his collection of the councils [Note: Vol. II of the Councils, p. 423].

Of this kind, certainly, are those canons composed in favor of marriage or married persons; those in which the lawful eating of meat is discussed; and those in which the Church’s rule concerning fasts is established. They exclude from the Catholic assembly those who rejected the Lord’s Day and the day of the Resurrection, spending it in mourning, grief, and fasting.

These and similar provisions were enacted for the condemnation of Eustathius, a monk of Armenia, who had impiously drawn his errors from no other source than the Manichaeans. In the same way he sought to overthrow and abolish entirely marriage, the procreation of children, the cultivation of virginity, sacred assemblies established by the Church, the practice of fasting, the eating of meat and animals, the possession of wealth, the celebrations of festivals and especially of the Lord’s Day, and other sacred rites approved by the Church [Col. 0896A].

There can therefore be no doubt that, by the year 324, the errors of the Manichaeans had grown so strong in Paphlagonia and the region of Armenia through the efforts of that monk Eustathius that the Fathers of Gangra had to assemble in order to restrain them and cleanse away that plague.

Finally, the Acts of this synod were approved, with the support of the apostolic see, by the First General Council of Nicaea itself, both for the hatred and destruction of the Manichaeans. This is shown not only by the embassy of Hosius of Corduba on behalf of Pope Saint Sylvester, but also by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Symmachus and Leo the Great.

Nor am I unaware that the embassy of Hosius of Corduba on behalf of the apostolic see at the Council of Gangra has been called into question—not only by Petrus de Marca [Note: Petrus de Marca, *On Ancient Collections of Canons*, dissertation, chapter 2] and Pagi, but even categorically denied altogether. The chief reason is that his name occurs in the surviving Acts not in the first but in the fourteenth place among the names of the other bishops.

In resolving such questions, however, it is not always useful to infer the prerogatives of bishops from the order in which their names are written in the codices [Col. 0896B], as we shall demonstrate in our history of the Priscillianists concerning Britto, bishop of Trier, against Tillemont and others. Sometimes, through the error of copyists, the codices may have been corrupted, or at least the genuine order of the bishops may have been disturbed.

For two reasons, however, I think that this controversy ought now to be avoided. The first is drawn from the purpose of the history that we are writing. We are not among those who, clinging to doubtful and highly obscure matters, seek to assert and defend the rights of the apostolic see. It would be exceedingly indecent or shameful, in a matter so certain and so weighty as the judicial authority and rights of the apostolic see—which shine more clearly than daylight throughout all the centuries of the Church—to indulge in personal inquiries, rely merely upon conjectures, and wander beyond the proper field, bringing into question matters which plainly do not sufficiently pertain to the case at hand.

Since, therefore, that synod was merely provincial, and since its canons received strength and approval only through the support of the apostolic see, as the compilers of the councils themselves admit, what difference can it make to us whether Hosius of Corduba served there as legate of the apostolic see?

7. The second reason is drawn from our fairness toward a most distinguished and learned man. A few years ago in Rome, in the solemn Pontifical Academy of Councils, before our most holy lord, Pope Benedict XIV, and amid the great applause of the entire learned assembly, the Reverend Father Antoninus Bremond—an eminent member of the Dominican family and distinguished theologian of the Casanatense Library, now Master General of the whole Order of Preachers, who embraces us with the greatest affection because of the exceptional kindness of his spirit—resolved and elucidated, with supreme learning, all the obscure and difficult questions which had long ago been raised concerning the date, canons, authority, and confirmation of the Council of Gangra and which may be raised in the future by students of criticism [Col. 0896D].

It is not presently permissible for us to begin a discussion of those same matters. In this investigation, as in his others, he has obtained the approval of all learned men; and it is such approval that, by the common vote of all, we promise ourselves that this work will one day be published. Since, however, in that same year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, we too delivered a theological dissertation on those same canons of Gangra in the same Pontifical Academy, we shall present it to the reader as an appendix to the Manichaean history in the final chapter of this book.

## CHAPTER III  
### On the books of the Manichaeans scattered throughout nearly the whole world in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Church

1. I believe that the preceding chapter has sufficiently and more than sufficiently established how, after Mani was killed, his disciples and followers spread this heresy here and there through various provinces, both of the East and of the West [Col. 0897A].

Yet because the defenders of such a wicked religion did not rely solely upon words and preaching to draw and lead the minds of ignorant and uneducated people toward the perversity of their doctrines, but also used the assistance of many harmful books—books whose reading ensnared unwary people, as though caught by some allure, and attached their minds to the same errors—we have therefore decided to identify these books briefly for the present.

Nor do we think that our discussion should concern only the works of Scythianus, which he left to Terebinthus at his death and which Mani himself revised and interpolated, since in the earlier chapters of the preceding book of this History we have already spoken of his four volumes, assembled from the fables of pagan philosophers and the most filthy fragments of the ancient heresiarchs.

2. So that we may not appear to wish to repeat what has already been done, our discussion now turns to the remaining writers of this sect and to a description of their works. Among these, we think that Thomas must chiefly be included—the Thomas to whom all the ancient writers attributed a certain apocryphal and spurious Gospel.

A few remarks about this work are nevertheless necessary if we examine all the older writers. They mention it as a work composed by the Manichaeans and filled with their fables. But none of them, so far as I have seen, indicated more clearly and explicitly the blasphemies contained in it.

The principal question to be investigated would be whether this Thomas composed this monstrous work of impiety in its entirety, or rather whether, having first obtained Scythianus’s Gospel, he attached his own name to it and then enlarged and exaggerated what it contained [Note: Beausobre asserted, without citing an author, that Mani had received this Gospel book, adorned with pictures, as a gift from Sapor, as we explained in the preceding book].

But who would dare to settle such a question, although the latter possibility appears more probable? For the ancient writers testified that the Manichaeans had not two Gospels but only one, and that they had attempted to circulate it improperly under the name of the apostle Thomas. Cave, however, I do not know for what reason, asserted that there was one Gospel of Scythianus and another of Thomas.

It will nevertheless be less difficult to conjecture with what fragments and blasphemies this Gospel had been filled. Since it dealt chiefly with the nativity, deeds, preaching, passion, death, and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ—and since it attacked the doctrines and mysteries of the Catholic faith concerning these matters with such audacity—it is sufficiently probable that every deadly poison was scattered there which could overturn and destroy the principal foundations of our religion.

As we have seen, they denied, according to Augustine [Note: Augustine, letter 236, chapter 2], that Christ had been born of a Virgin. They did not confess that he had true flesh, but claimed that it was fictitious and therefore false; consequently, they maintained that his passion was false and that there had been no resurrection.

Cyril of Jerusalem also indicated rather clearly that that Gospel contained wicked teachings concerning the mission and coming of the Holy Spirit, intended to reinforce another prominent error of Mani. He discussed this Gospel in a book and warned Catholics to guard themselves against reading it [Note: Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6].

We understand not only that this book of diabolical impiety was rejected among the apocryphal Scriptures by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs—namely Siricius, Innocent I, and Pope Gelasius [Note: Popes Innocent and Gelasius, and the Roman Council, *On the Canonical and Apocryphal Scriptures*, in the year 494]—but also that the most holy Pope Leo the Great decreed that it should be removed altogether and burned in the fire [Col. 0898A] [Note: Leo the Great, letter to Turibius of Astorga, chapter 15].

For Saint Leo the pontiff spoke in the following manner about these and similar writings of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, seriously warning Catholics not to allow themselves to be drawn to their reading by a certain counterfeit appearance of piety which such writings seemed to display:

“For although there are in them certain things which appear to possess an appearance of piety, they are nevertheless never free from poisons; through the allurements of fables they secretly bring this about: that those who have been seduced by marvelous stories may be entangled in the snares of whatever error.”

When the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea later took note of these decrees of the apostolic see, they spoke especially of this Gospel of Thomas [Note: Fathers of the Seventh Synod, acts 6, vol. VIII of the Councils, p. 1491]:

“Moreover”—for they are speaking of adulterine writings which once circulated under the name of Paul—“the Manichaeans introduced the Gospel according to Thomas, which the Catholic Church rightly rejects as impious.”

To all this we finally add one point: the Gospel of Thomas differs greatly from the book entitled *The Revelation of the Apostle Thomas* [Col. 0898B]. For in the same Gelasian decree, the two are discussed as distinct books, although nowhere is it indicated that the latter book—namely, *The Revelation of the Apostle Thomas*—came from the Manichaean workshop.

Nevertheless, the letter of Turibius, bishop of Astorga, to Saint Leo the Great clearly indicates that Turibius held this opinion. In chapter 5, while discussing apocryphal books, he specifically listed the *Acts of Saint Thomas* among writings composed or corrupted “by the great prince Mani and his disciples,” and similar works, from which, he says, “the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, or whatever related sect they may be, strive to confirm their entire heresy.”

3. Besides one or perhaps two volumes of Gospels, written impiously in the form and imitation of the Catholic writings, the Manichaeans also possessed another book, namely one of Epistles. The ancient writers were convinced that this work had proceeded chiefly from Mani’s workshop.

This volume, or collection of Epistles, is mentioned by Goar and Petrus Siculus, as well as by the author of the Cotelerian and Tollian formulas [Col. 0898C]. Guillelmus Cave says that the famous letter which the Manichaeans called the *Foundation*, and which Augustine so often cites in *On the Nature of the Good* and in the acts concerning Felix, certainly belonged to this collection of Epistles [Note: Guillelmus Cave, *Historia Litteraria*, p. 91] [Note: Augustine, book *On the Nature of the Good*, chapters 42 and 46].

Augustine also composed an entire book against this kind of letter. After rejecting the earlier parts of Mani’s letter, he demonstrated that, in place of the manifest and certain knowledge which Mani promised, he had offered his insane followers nothing but uncertain and absurd ravings.

The Manichaean sect, by contrast, revered this letter as the storehouse of its entire faith. Thus, according to Augustine [Note: Augustine, book *Against the Fundamental Epistle*, vol. VIII, p. 110], whenever it was read before an audience, they customarily inclined their heads and said “Amen,” as though by listening to its illumination they were giving thanks to its most wicked author.

The beginning of this letter was as follows:

“Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ, by the providence of God the Father. These are saving words from the perennial [Col. 0898D] and living fountain” [Note: Augustine, same work, chapter 5].

We have already encountered a similar beginning in the letter to Marcellus, as the Latin fragments of Archelaus cited above and Epiphanius, heresy 66, attest. But Augustine, among others, testified in book XIII, chapter 4 *Against Faustus*, that all his letters had the same beginning, addressing the Manichaeans in these words:

“For your Mani was not a prophet of the coming Christ. He calls himself his apostle, indeed, in the deceitfulness of the most shameless man.”

A little farther on he adds:

“Nevertheless, all his letters begin in this way: ‘Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ.’”

Guillelmus Cave mentions other letters of Mani on page 92.

In third place, we think that the *Book of Mysteries* should be listed. The Manichaeans themselves composed it deliberately in order to overthrow the Law and obliterate all the prophecies of the ancient prophets. Guillelmus Cave cites from Goar a fragment in which such a book is anathematized. The same author asserts that it was one of Scythianus’s books, but that Mani greatly enlarged it and interpolated it in countless places so that he might indulge his own purposes.

Accordingly, Tollius declared that it had been divided into twenty-two parts in alphabetical order and written in the Syriac and Palmyrene languages.

A fourth book followed these. Some people, on the basis of certain corrupt Greek manuscript copies, have entirely and wrongly testified that it ought to be entitled *The Business of All Things*. Guillelmus Cave, among others, observed from the writings of Timothy of Constantinople and from other more distinguished ancient copies that it had another title [Col. 0899B]. Relying on various conjectures, he therefore showed that this little book received its proper designation from the subjects it contained and was called *On the Difference of Those Who Approach the Pure Faith*.

It has already been demonstrated shortly before, from Augustine, that the Manichaeans were accustomed falsely to boast of the purity of their faith, since they called themselves Catharists, or “purifiers” [Note: Tollius, cited by Cave, p. 142].

### 4. [Cols. 0899C–0900D]

Now, however, let us come to those works which Cotelerius and Tollius published after the Goarian Formula. Another book called *Apocryphal* comes before us. In it, as Cave says, it is probable that the more hidden rites, magical practices, and execrable mysteries of the Manichaean religion were contained—rites whose doctrine was transmitted only to initiates and to those steeped in their impious orgies. We by no means reject Cave’s conjecture. For, besides those common doctrines which the school of the Manichaeans proclaimed to its hearers, it also taught and maintained other secret and more esoteric matters, known only to the leaders of this sect and its principal teachers. We have already noted in the preceding book, chapter 11, that Turbon himself clearly testified to this in his renunciation of the heresy.

It is probable that this book described all the profane rites and sacrilegious ceremonies, fasts, and prayers which the Manichaean devotees employed when they celebrated the *Bema*, their sacred and solemn festival. Accordingly, in the Cotelerian Formula books of such rites and magical practices are indicated in these words:

> [Note: Augustine, *On Heresies*, heresy 46.] Everything that they perform and celebrate in their sacred rites is to be condemned, as well as whatever is contained in the Manichaean, or magical, books.

To all these works they also added certain interpretations, called commentaries on the sayings and memorable deeds of Manes.

Among Manichaean writers, Addas—whom we also mentioned above—held no insignificant place. He therefore composed a single book called *Modion*, which was filled with numerous axioms and philosophical principles. These were recognized, even at first glance, as utterly foreign and opposed to the common principles implanted in nature. Such, certainly, were the claims by which they asserted that human beings were necessarily induced to sin by some evil author existing without beginning and opposed to God. Or such were those other propositions which they pronounced to the supreme insult of divine Providence, impiously maintaining that this visible world was in no way subject to divine rule and governance.

The author of this book had also attempted to show that the two Testaments—namely, the Old and the New—were in conflict with one another because of certain apparent contradictions, or rather allegories and mysteries. Again, in discussing the New Testament, he tried especially to demonstrate that the errors of the Manichaean sect had drawn from it their force, authority, and entire foundation. The volumes written by Titus of Bostra clearly show, I say, that these wicked and diabolical doctrines were contained in that book.

> [Note: Works of Titus of Bostra, vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 447. He flourished in the year 362.]

For that most holy bishop of Arabia, at the urging of Heracleianus, bishop of Chalcedon, as reported by Photius, directed all the strength of his scholarship toward rejecting and overthrowing the blasphemies and errors of that book.

> [Note: Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 85. Aristocritus, a Manichaean writer.]

### 5.

Nevertheless, what William Cave has recorded about Aristocritus, by no means the least of the disciples and writers of Manes, is curious. Although he did not hesitate to denounce his teacher as an evil man, he nevertheless adhered to his doctrines and published a work in which he attempted to show that the Jews, Gentiles, Christians, and Manichaeans all held one and the same doctrine. From what has already been said, it is clear that Addas likewise indicated this kind of argument in his book.

Furthermore, we learn from various records of antiquity that the earlier leaders, teachers, elect, and hearers of the Manichaean sect used not only those books. Timothy, presbyter of Constantinople, mentions a *Book of Prayers* containing formulas of prayers and magical practices. For this reason, repentant Manichaeans were also ordered to anathematize the *Book of Prayers* when renouncing their errors. The other apocryphal writings listed in the Gelasian Decree are of the same kind. Ancient writers were convinced that these had proceeded either from Manes or from his disciples, as may be seen in Cave, in the section on the Novatians, p. 92.

Cave likewise listed two other writers of this wicked sect, whose dates are uncertain but whom he asserts to have been among the more notable. The first was Agapius, “a sufficiently obscure writer,” as he says, “of whom, apart from Photius, no ancient author, so far as I know, makes mention.” Tillemont supported Cave, adhering likewise to Photius’s testimony. He makes Agapius contemporary with Eunomius and asserts that Agapius attacked and reproached him in his writings, although Agapius had already shamefully defected to the Manichaean party.

There is, however, some disagreement between them. Cave, going further back and considering what Peter of Sicily had written about Agapius, argues that Photius’s testimony can be explained differently. We have already noted, from that same Peter of Sicily, that Agapius was one of the twelve disciples of Manes and composed a book called the *Heptalogus*. How, then, could he have survived into the time of Eunomius and directed his pen against him and his errors? For more than eighty years elapsed between the time when the heresy of Manes became known as worthy of condemnation and the fall of Eunomius, the notary of Aetius. That interval of time plainly cannot be reconciled with both claims: namely, that one and the same Agapius was among the twelve principal disciples of Manes and that he lived long enough to attack Eunomius in his writings.

> [Col. 0900D]

William Cave foresaw this serious difficulty and tried with great diligence to guard against it. Yet, asserting that both circumstances might have occurred, he adduces various conjectures, drawn both from Epiphanius and from Cyril of Jerusalem, which he considers relevant to his argument, and advises the reader to weigh them. Finally, he declares that he does not wish to establish anything certain on this point. We have no leisure now to investigate more carefully the state or explanation of the matter, since those ancient records which could settle such a question have either wholly perished or at least remain entirely unknown.

> [Note: Tillemont, *Memoirs for Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 403.]

### 6.

Only a few things therefore remain to be said about Agapius’s other works, to whom the aforementioned Photius attributed two additional works. One of these was divided into twenty-two books; the other contained one hundred and two chapters. The author himself dedicated both to a certain Urania, a woman of his sect and a companion in his studies.

If we inquire more closely of Photius what sort of subjects Agapius explained in these books, it will become entirely clear that those works contained nothing but wicked and fabulous inventions—the same matters which, on the basis of Turbon’s confession and Augustine’s testimonies, we explained more fully above. We consider it unnecessary to linger over them again here.

> [Note: Consult Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 179, and William Cave, *Dissertation on Writers of Uncertain Date*, p. 165.]

William Cave also thought that a certain Alexander should be assigned to this same category of writers of uncertain date. The ancients called him Lycopolitan, from Lyco, a city of Thebaid in Egypt. At first he was a pagan in his religious practice. Later, when the Manichaeans withdrew into those regions of Egypt, he defected to their camp. Finally, after renouncing this wicked heresy, he professed the Catholic religion.

Before cleansing himself of the stain of this heresy, however, he wrote a book *On the Tenets of the Manichaeans*, which he knew thoroughly and intimately. In it, according to Cave, he accurately explains their inner meaning and solidly refutes the unsound doctrines of this sect with arguments drawn from the hidden resources of philosophy. Cave criticizes the style of this writing as somewhat harsh and not very difficult. He also did not dare to determine its date with certainty, although he suspected that Alexander was not far removed from the time of Manes, since Alexander himself states that he learned those doctrines from people who had associated familiarly with that man.

We think these words should be referred to Papus and Thomas, the disciples of Manes, since Alexander mentions only these two. William Cave finally collected and reported various details here and there concerning Alexander’s works and age. They are not entirely consistent with one another, and we pass them over lest we rely upon uncertain and doubtful matters.

> [Col. 0901C]

### 7. [Cols. 0901C–0902D]

Let us now speak of Adimantus, a celebrated disciple of the Manichaean sect, whom Cave once confused with Addas, as we have seen. Our present undertaking requires this. Augustine discussed Adimantus’s writings and deeds more than once in his works, but he engages him in such a way as to describe the man as having departed this life, and to attack and attempt to overthrow only his writings.

This is evident from the first book of the *Retractations*, chapter 13. There, reviewing the works he had composed while he was still a presbyter, Augustine says:

> [Note: That is, in the year 394 or 395, as the most recent editors of Augustine’s works have noted. Consult vol. VIII, p. 79.]

> At that time certain disputations of Adimantus came into my hands. He had been a disciple of Manes, and wrote them against the Law and the Prophets, attempting, as it were, to demonstrate that the evangelical and apostolic writings were contrary to them.

The holy Doctor therefore indicates the title and purpose of this book of Adimantus. But since he calls its author a disciple of Manes and speaks of him as a man long dead, we can scarcely doubt that Adimantus had heard Manes and, through the agency of his parent—namely Addas—had at least occupied a place among the second rank of disciples.

> [Note: Consult what we said in the preceding chapter, section 2.]

Augustine also mentions Adimantus’s works in his book *Against Faustus*. First, by placing words under Adimantus’s name, he brings Faustus, as though boasting of his own doctrine and that of Manes and Adimantus, onto the stage, so to speak. Faustus, carried away by madness, boldly asserted:

> Since errors have now been sufficiently and abundantly exposed, together with Jewish superstition and the deceitfulness of the semi-Christians, it seemed not without reason to the most beloved and, after our blessed Father Manichaeus, our sole devoted student Adimantus—

From these words of Faustus it is clear not only that the Manichaeans were accustomed to accuse the adherents of the Catholic religion of having been deceived by falsehoods and corrupt doctrines, but also that they wished to rely upon Adimantus’s writings, whom they venerated as the second leader of that profane sect after Manes.

Augustine again attacks Faustus for having fallen into more shameful error on the basis of a fictitious conflict among the Scriptures introduced by Adimantus. Faustus erred either concerning the substance of human beings, animals, and plants, about which Adimantus, following Manes, fabulously asserted that their life was of the same nature; or concerning the transmigration of souls and their migration into new bodies; or finally when he reasoned from the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments about an empty and superstitious discrimination among foods.

Augustine demonstrates more explicitly in the sixth book that Faustus had absorbed these errors chiefly from Adimantus’s volumes and had defended dreadful blasphemies on their basis.

> [Note: Augustine, book VI *Against Faustus*, chapter 6, and the book *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Manes*, chapter 12.]

Finally, the holy Doctor inveighs more harshly against Adimantus himself, refuting the error by which he taught that even rational beings—that is, human souls—could be forced into the bodies of beasts:

> What, then, will he do about such a great crime if he has beaten some sluggish beast with blows or exhausted it by driving it with the bridle, in which perhaps the soul of his father was? I say nothing of the fact that he might even have killed his parents among lice and fleas, from whose killing these people do not abstain.

Augustine also knew that some Manichaeans, pressed by arguments of this kind and similar ones, were accustomed to deny that human souls could be transmigrated even into such tiny creatures. The holy Doctor willingly granted them this escape, and used it as an opportunity to press Adimantus and the other Manichaeans still more sharply.

Proceeding, therefore, from smaller creatures to somewhat larger ones, he mocked them quite cleverly and reasoned as follows:

> What good does it do them that they sometimes deny this, and so on? They deny it lest they be held guilty of so many killings, or be compelled to spare lice, fleas, and bedbugs, and to endure such great annoyances from them without permission to kill them.

But, since they are still pressed hard, Augustine adds:

> Why could a human soul be transmigrated into a little fox, but not into a weasel, when perhaps a fox cub is even smaller than a large weasel?

Finally, to mock their claims more fully, he concludes the argument in these words:

> Then, if it can enter a weasel, why can it not enter a mouse? And if it can enter that, why can it not enter a gecko? And if it can enter that, why can it not enter a locust—or a bee, or a flea, or some other creature much smaller?

By this method of argument he demonstrates that Adimantus and the other Manichaeans become guilty of innumerable murders. For, by adhering to this superstitious and foolish belief or injunction, their consciences were burdened and seriously afflicted by these monstrous errors.

### 8. [Cols. 0902D–0903B]

In this book *Against Adimantus*, Augustine is entirely occupied with reconciling the statements of Scripture which Adimantus had gathered from the Old and New Testaments as though they were mutually contradictory. Adimantus maintained that both Testaments could not have come from one and the same author.

Augustine also mentions another book which he himself published against the same man. In it, after first setting out Adimantus’s words, the holy Father gave his own response to them. He says:

> [Note: Augustine, book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 22.]

> I completed this work in a single volume, and in it I answered certain questions not once but twice, because my first response had been lost and was found only after I had answered again. Some of those questions I resolved in popular ecclesiastical sermons; I have still not answered some others.

If anyone wishing to be more fully instructed in these matters should ask us to which ecclesiastical and popular sermons Augustine chiefly wished to refer here, we shall immediately answer that he particularly dissolved Adimantus’s slanderous objections in Sermon 12.

> [Note: Sermon 12, otherwise *On Various Matters* 16, vol. VI, pp. 50–51.]

In that sermon, wishing to deal further with the frauds and deceits of the Manichaeans, Augustine attacks Adimantus, who, deliberately corrupting and distorting the testimony of the Apostle Paul, attempted to infer that neither rulers, nor authorities, nor powers had known God. To overthrow this slander, Augustine says:

> But first I should like to ask these people where Adimantus read this in the Apostle, for he is the author of such slanders. I should like him, then, to say where he read the Apostle testifying and affirming, as he says, that neither rulers, nor authorities, nor powers knew God. Yet the Lord says that the angels of human beings who believe in him see the face of the Father every day.

> [Note: The same, chapter 11.]

Augustine brings forward these and other arguments of the same kind in order to reconcile the celebrated passage of Job, which we read in chapter 1, verse 6, with those other words of Matthew, chapter 5, verse 8, upon which Adimantus relied in order to introduce and persuade the contradiction of the two Testaments.

### 9. [Cols. 0903B–0904C]

Since nothing else worth knowing about Adimantus occurs either in Augustine’s works or in the writings of others, we must now pass over him and turn finally to Fortunatus the presbyter, also an adherent of the Manichaean sect and a defender of its doctrine.

According to Possidius, when this infamous and wicked heresy, by which he was polluted, was spreading more widely throughout the regions of Africa, it worked with excessive zeal to weaken and corrupt nearly the whole city and province of Hippo. While he was living and remaining there, the poison of this heresy quickly increased, so that very many citizens and foreigners in that city were infected by this pestilential contagion.

Meanwhile, says Possidius:

> [Note: Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 6, vol. X, p. 75, in the edition of the Fathers of Saint-Maur, and vol. VIII, p. 67.]

> The citizens of Hippo and Christian foreigners, both Catholics and Donatists, came to Augustine the presbyter and asked insistently that he see that man—namely Fortunatus, the Manichaean presbyter, whom they believed to be learned—and discuss the Law with him.

These events took place among the Africans, especially in the distinguished city of Hippo, when Arcadius Augustus and Rufinus, men of illustrious rank, were serving their second consulship; this occurred in the year of Christ 382. Accordingly, the holy presbyter Augustine, wishing to satisfy everyone’s wishes, did not refuse to undertake the task offered to him. On the contrary, he showed himself entirely ready to give an account when questioned about matters of faith.

### 10. [Cols. 0903D–0904C]

When matters had thus been arranged, the Manichaeans asked Fortunatus to face Augustine, lest the cause of their common sect be endangered. Fortunatus, however, who had once known Augustine at Carthage when Augustine himself was suffering from the same Manichaean disease, was afraid to meet him.

At last, compelled and embarrassed by the urgent pressure of his fellow believers, he promised that he would come in person and undertake the disputation. Accordingly, on the fifth day before the Kalends of the seventh month, at Hippo, in the baths of Sossius, a disputation began between Augustine and Fortunatus.

A great crowd of people had gathered to hear it, especially learned and curious men who, as usually happens, favored both sides. The notaries then opened their tablets, and Augustine began the discussion. The chief question concerned the origin of evil.

Augustine, the defender of Catholic doctrine, explained that human evil had arisen from the free choice of the will. Fortunatus, on the other hand, attempted to persuade his audience that the nature of evil was coeternal with God. But during the disputation on the final day, unable to maintain his position, he confessed that he could find nothing to say against us.

Failing in his reply, he finally said that he would consult with his elders about the matters which he had been unable to refute. He promised that, if they could not provide him with an adequate answer, he would take thought for his soul.

> [Note: Augustine, *Retractations*, book I, chapter 15; and Possidius, in the same work, chapter 6.]

Possidius recounts these events in the cited passage. We are made still more certain of them, however, by the words of Fortunatus himself, spoken publicly during the disputation on the second day. They were recorded by the notaries and faithfully committed to writing in the ecclesiastical records, as may also be seen at the end of the disputation of the second day, which appears together with the earlier disputation in volume VIII of the works of Saint Augustine.

No one should suppose, meanwhile, that Fortunatus the Manichaean, overcome by such profound shame, embarrassment, and disgrace, considered repenting of his errors or wished thereafter to join the Catholics. Any sane person who understood that the foundations of his faith were tottering and being brought to ruin would immediately have adopted such a course.

But Fortunatus, overwhelmed by such confusion, departed from the city of Hippo and never returned to it. Nevertheless, he did not become a Catholic. So far as I know, Augustine makes no further mention anywhere of this Fortunatus, the Manichaean presbyter.

> [Note: Augustine, cited book of the *Retractations*, chapter 16, and letter 79, otherwise 244.]

There survives only a certain letter of his addressed to another Manichaean presbyter, whom the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, in the most recent edition of Augustine, suspected to have been Felix. Augustine, after he had been raised to the episcopate of Hippo, addressed him in these words:

> I therefore charge you in the name of Christ: if you are ready, solve the question in which your predecessor Fortunatus failed. He departed from here and did not return, unless, after discussing the matter with his fellow believers, he found something that he could answer when disputing with the brothers.

It is therefore clear that this Manichaean presbyter, who had succeeded Fortunatus, was challenged and provoked by Augustine to solve the same question on which his predecessor had suffered a more shameful defeat. He fled from Hippo in such a way that he deliberately pretended that he wished to consult with the other leaders of the Manichaeans about the objections that had been brought against him.

### 11. [Cols. 0904C–0905D]

After this presbyter Fortunatus comes Faustus, an African by race and a citizen of Milevis, a bishop of the Manichaean sect, who flourished in the year 400. William Cave alone among others described his intellect, studies, mental gifts, and writings, saying:

> [Note: William Cave, *Literary History*, p. 218.]

> He was a man pleasant in speech, clever in intellect, more talkative than eloquent, and more superficially informed than solidly learned.

A little later he adds:

> He wrote a volume against the true Christian faith and Catholic truth.

Nevertheless, the author just mentioned did not describe the subject of this book with sufficient accuracy. Augustine, who carefully examined the work of Faustus the Manichaean, explained its contents in the second book of the *Retractations*, chapter 7, in these words:

> I wrote a substantial work against Faustus the Manichaean, who blasphemed the Law and the Prophets and their God, and who said that the Scriptures of the New Testament, by which he is convicted, had been falsified. I set out his words and gave my responses to them.

Augustine knew this man. In the sincere confession of his *Confessions*, when he was about to explain how he had fallen into the Manichaean sect, he says:

> A certain Manichaean bishop named Faustus had already come to Carthage, a great snare of the devil, and many were being entangled in him through the allurements of his sweet speech . . . For his reputation had preceded him to me: he was said to be exceedingly learned in every honorable branch of knowledge and especially well trained in the liberal disciplines.

This reputation of Faustus the Manichaean was widely spread among his followers and had long aroused in Augustine a desire to hear him teaching and disputing. For during the nine years in which the holy Father seemed, as though with a wandering mind, to have remained attached to this sect—though he had been assigned only to the class of hearers, not of the elect—he encountered difficult problems and questions which the other members of that profane religion did not know how to solve. They eagerly awaited the arrival of Faustus, whose coming and conversation, Augustine says, would have made it very easy for him to unravel these matters and any even greater questions he might raise.

> [Note: *Confessions*, book V, chapter 6.]

The other Manichaeans who disputed with Augustine about matters of faith had promised him precisely this, as though the mysteries of that wicked sect had been revealed only to Faustus the bishop.

At last, however, Augustine was deceived by the reputation of this Manichaean. “When he came,” he says, “I found a man agreeable and pleasant in speech, chattering much more sweetly about the very things they themselves usually say.” But what use to my thirst was “the most proper server of more precious cups”?

Augustine’s ears had already been sated with such things. Those doctrines did not seem better to him because they were expressed better, nor true because they were eloquent, nor the soul wise because the face was pleasing and the speech graceful.

When Augustine proceeded to examine Faustus’s particular achievements, his capacity for knowledge, and his understanding of divine and natural things, he learned through various private conversations how much ability this man—so highly esteemed by his own people—really possessed. He then delivered this final judgment concerning him. Having withdrawn from the opinion of those who thought Faustus prudent and wise because they enjoyed listening to him, Augustine writes:

> After various experiences in private conversation, I found that he was ignorant of the liberal disciplines, except for grammar, and even that only in the ordinary way. His knowledge came from having read some speeches of Cicero, a very few books of Seneca, and some works of the poets and of his own sect, if any of its volumes had been written in Latin and in a polished style. Since he had daily practice in conversation, this supplied him with a fluency that became more agreeable and more seductive through the management of his intellect and a certain natural charm.

Such gifts of mind and body, which the other Manichaeans admired in Bishop Faustus, could neither gently flatter nor seduce Augustine’s intellect. Once Faustus appeared to him sufficiently unskilled in those arts in which both reputation and Augustine himself had supposed him to excel, Augustine immediately began to despair that Faustus could open up and resolve the questions over which his mind had been deeply troubled when he considered the fabulous principles of the Manichaeans.

This happened especially when, turning his eyes to their books filled with absurdities, he desired to know and understand perfectly all that they asserted concerning the movements and properties of the heavens, the stars, the sun, and the moon. Since Faustus, who had never been trained in mathematical disciplines, was entirely unable to explain these matters—and was not ashamed to admit as much—Augustine’s entire effort to advance in that sect collapsed once he had come to know the man. He did not therefore separate himself from them completely, but, finding nothing better, remained as though he had rushed into that sect in some fashion or other.

As Augustine’s misguided desire to learn all the doctrines and mysteries of the Manichaeans gradually cooled, his mind began suddenly to waver. Although he did not immediately yield to or obey the movements of divine grace, the hands of the Lord, hidden within his providence, did not abandon his soul. Through the tears of his mother, who day and night offered sacrifice for her son from the blood of her heart, those hands worked upon him in marvelous ways.

> [Note: The same book, book V, chapter 7.]

### 12. [Cols. 0906A–0906B]

Augustine transmitted these details concerning Faustus’s deeds, manner of study, capacity for learning, knowledge of divine and human matters, and writings. We cannot linger over their examination any longer, lest we seem to wish to disclose the deeds of Augustine rather than those of this Manichaean bishop.

We think only one point should finally be added: Augustine, after being freed from the snares of the Manichaeans and raised to the episcopal order, directed his pen against Faustus and attacked him in thirty-three books.

> [Note: Augustine’s thirty-three books against Faustus the Manichaean are found in volume VIII, p. 131.]

He arranged this work with such ingenuity that he first placed Faustus’s words under his name and then appended to each chapter an equal number of Catholic responses written by himself.

As for the fate which Faustus himself suffered, Augustine recounts it in book V, chapter 8. There the holy Father is entirely occupied in reproaching the audacity of the Manichaeans, who rashly and sacrilegiously claimed that they endured persecutions and the hatred of men for the sake of justice. When the proconsuls of Africa were inflicting punishment upon this wicked sect with the full severity of the law, Faustus himself, having been convicted or having confessed that he was a Manichaean, was brought with several others before the proconsular court and banished to an island.

> [Note: Augustine, book V *Against Faustus*, chapter 8.]

We shall discuss this kind of judgment more fully and conveniently in the following chapter.

### 13. [Cols. 0906B–0907C]

It remains now to speak of another Secundinus, a defender and writer of the Manichaean sect, whom William Cave entirely incorrectly believed to have been African by birth. He further added that this man had lived after Augustine’s return to the Church and after the completion of the three books *On Free Will*. He also thought that Secundinus’s letter to Augustine and Augustine’s replies to Secundinus should be dated to the year of Christ 390.

These two claims could have been asserted only by someone who was recklessly guessing and reasoning falsely and arbitrarily about ecclesiastical writers.

First, as regards his homeland, Secundinus’s own writings indicate that he did not originate from the African people but from the Roman population. Speaking about himself, he addresses Augustine as follows:

> [Note: Letter of Secundinus to Augustine.]

> The writings of your reverend dignity have read something of my poor and whatever sort of intellect I possess as a Roman—writings in which you rage against the truth as Hortensius did against philosophy.

Secundinus therefore calls himself a Roman and refers to writings in which Augustine, already long converted to the Catholic faith, had attacked the Manichaeans.

Augustine likewise addresses this same man as a Roman, mocking the intellect of which Secundinus appeared especially proud:

> I ask you, an acute and diligent man, and, as you boast, possessed of a Roman intellect: how can the nature of good endure what it suffers, so as to consent to evil?

> [Note: Augustine, book *Against Secundinus*, chapter 19, vol. VIII, p. 383.]

William Cave’s delusion—or his negligence—in determining the time when Secundinus attacked Augustine in his writings, and when Augustine wrote a work against him rejecting all the arguments of his letter, is no less serious.

> [Note: William Cave, *Arian Age*, under the year of Christ 390, p. 184.]

If we wish to trust Prosper, Possidius, and other writers of approximately the same period, Augustine, after renouncing Manichaeism, joined the Catholic community in the year 387. If, therefore, the correspondence between this Secundinus and Augustine is to be assigned to the years after Augustine’s return to the Church, as William Cave carelessly conjectured, it would follow that it was published around the year of Christ 390.

But this conclusion would immediately collapse if Secundinus in his writings slyly taunted and attacked Augustine as one who had already attained the honor of the episcopate, and if Augustine himself, responding to his slanders, did not conceal from this crafty man that he had obtained the Catholic episcopate.

Secundinus in fact accuses Augustine of having defected from Manes, moved by fear and by a desire to attain honor. In writing, he continually used expressions of the kind that at that time were customarily addressed only to bishops, such as:

> “Your salutary and excellent holiness”;  
> “Lord, deservedly praiseworthy and deeply honored”;  
> or: “But I cannot do that to your most patient holiness.”

> [Note: The letter of Secundinus the Manichaean to Augustine is found in volume VIII, p. 370.]

He also used this expression:

> “Although it would be exceedingly absurd to say these things to your holiness,”

and other words of the same kind, with which only bishops were then honored.

What more is needed? Augustine himself, replying to Secundinus, asserts that he had already attained the honor of the episcopate:

> Therefore, although you have suspected me of evil motives, namely, that I abandoned the Manichaean heresy through bodily fear of some inconvenience that might come upon me from your fellowship, or through desire for the honor which I attained in the Catholic Church—

Why should I spend more time on this? Augustine himself has left us some account of the chronology of his books in two books of the *Retractations*. In reviewing them, he follows the order of his life and places the book under discussion among those which he composed as a bishop.

Cave would certainly have known this if he had wished to consult chapter 10 of book II of the *Retractations*, where Augustine explicitly mentions this book against Secundinus, as we shall observe below. Since Augustine, after becoming a presbyter, did not attain episcopal dignity until the year 394, it follows that this correspondence between them could not have occurred before that time.

The Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur examined this matter more carefully in the most recent edition of Augustine’s works.

> [Note: Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, in Augustine’s works; their note is found in volume VIII, *Conc.*, p. 371.]

Finally, relying on more probable conjectures, they judged that the writings both of Secundinus the Manichaean and of Augustine, the Catholic bishop, should be assigned to the year 404 or the following year, which was the tenth or eleventh year after Augustine had obtained the episcopate. They write:

> In the *Retractations* the work *On the Nature of the Good* follows immediately. That work is appended to the books written against Felix at the end of the year 404. This book, therefore—that is, the book against Secundinus—belongs approximately to the year 405.

Having now noted Cave’s errors, one concerning the homeland of Secundinus the Manichaean and the other concerning the date of the letter composed by him, we must still describe and guard against a third error, more serious than the others. For concerning this same Secundinus he wrote: “There had been a close familiarity between him and Augustine while both were involved in the Manichaean heresy.” No one who consults Augustine can fail to recognize that Cave is talking nonsense. Augustine himself sincerely confessed, without any taint of falsehood, that he had never seen this man, although both had once been entangled in the Manichaean snares at Rome. For in the cited second book of the *Retractions*, chapter 10, Augustine says the following:

> A certain Secundinus, not one of those whom the Manichaeans call the Elect, but one of those whom they call Hearers, whom I did not even know by sight, wrote to me as though to a friend, courteously reproving me because I attacked that heresy in writing, and warning me not to do so; rather, he urged me to follow it, both by defending it and by criticizing the Catholic faith.  
> [Note: Augustine, Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 10.]

Would Cave have fallen into such an opinion if he had devoted any effort to investigating from Augustine the deeds, homeland, character, and close associates of Secundinus? Or, finally, would he have asserted that there had been a close familiarity between these two men while both were involved in the Manichaean heresy, when Augustine declares that he had not even seen the man?

### 3.

Let us meanwhile pass over these matters, and turn our discourse instead to the exchange of letters that took place between Augustine and Secundinus the Manichaean, examining the contents of those letters. First, Secundinus, pretending to be Augustine’s friend, attacks, needles, and reproaches him in his letters because he had defected from the Manichaean sect. For this reason he invokes upon Augustine the anger and indignation of Manes the Persian, to be endured especially on the day of judgment.

He charges Augustine with two causes of his defection: the first arising from fear, by which he falsely imagines Augustine to dread all the bodily punishments of this world—punishments unjustly imposed upon the Manichaeans or at times inflicted by public authority; the second arising from a desire for honor, by which Augustine, supposedly afflicted with this ambition, had desired that the rank of bishop be granted to him in the Catholic Church.

Augustine therefore wished to meet these calumnies and composed a celebrated work divided into twenty-six chapters.  
[Note: Augustine, *Against Secundinus*, chapter 11.]

He chiefly endeavors to dispel two principal accusations subtly and falsely brought against him. First, he demonstrates that his defection from the Manichaean sect should be attributed to no other fear than that expressed in the Apostle’s words to Timothy, chapter 4, verse 1:

> Now the Spirit expressly says that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons—

words which all the ancients were thoroughly convinced applied to the Manichaeans.

Then, turning his discourse to the second alleged cause of his defection, he appeals to the same Apostle Paul in his letter to the Romans, employing the following words:

> Glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good,

thereby plainly and without any ambiguity confessing that these gifts derive not from the evil creator imagined by the Manichaeans, but from the supreme and immutable Good.  
[Note: The Apostle’s Letter to the Romans, chapter 2, verse 16.]

Nor does Augustine confine himself to refuting these two calumnies. As he brings forward and examines each of the institutions that Secundinus had objected to him from the school of the Manichaeans, he proceeds successfully and happily to dissolve, reject, and overthrow all the arguments of the opposing party, one by one.

Finally, while disputing against the Donatists, Augustine recorded two men bearing the same name: one he called Secundinus of Cedia, the other Secundinus of Carpis.  
[Note: In Book VI *Against the Donatists*, Augustine mentions two other Secundini.]

Since these men are entirely different from Secundinus the Manichaean, we have been obliged to note them here, lest anyone, confusing one with the other, fall into error.

After writing thus far, we ought to add the proceedings concerning Felix, formerly a Manichaean presbyter, who held at least two or three public disputations with Augustine. This would have greatly benefited the reader, since we would not force him to wander here and there in order to inspect the events involving the Manichaeans in Africa during Augustine’s lifetime; it would also enable us, under a single heading, to make clear what we promised at the beginnings of this chapter.

But because the disputation with this Manichaean seemed to us to concern not a private quarrel between individuals but the public cause of the Catholic Church; because it was held at a time when priests, secular judges, and magistrates had begun to punish the Manichaeans with various kinds of penalties; and because Felix himself, after his conferences with Augustine, having been convicted of error, first renounced his wicked heresy and then endeavored to erase every stain by joining himself to the communion of the Catholics, we shall therefore speak more suitably and as briefly as we can both about him and about the other Manichaeans convicted in Africa by public judgment.

### CHAPTER IV

The conduct of the Roman pontiffs Leo the Great, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Hormisdas in destroying and burning the books of the Manichaeans is defended against Beausobre’s critical annotations. Examples from the ancient pagans likewise show that it was always judged a grave offense to permit the people to read books from which they might, even slightly, deviate from the institutions of their ancestors in matters pertaining to religion.

[Column 0909A]

### 1.

Although I am not unaware how displeasing to some people is that policy of the Roman Church by which it has habitually destroyed and burned the books and volumes of non-Catholic persons, I must not at present pass over the matter, since an opportunity has arisen from Beausobre’s method and purpose in writing and reasoning.

Beausobre repeatedly discusses the four Roman pontiffs who prohibited the reading of Manichaean books and, with every possible diligence, ordered them to be handed over to the flames. Here and there he scatters various complaints that books of this kind, relevant to knowledge of ancient philosophy and theology, have entirely perished—books from which one might sincerely learn the doctrines and systems defended by those same heretics.  
[Note: Beausobre, Book I, chapter 12, and the preliminary discourse to the second part.]

He likewise censures, needles, and attacks this policy as unjust, but does so imprudently and foolishly. For it is utterly unbecoming in a man who boasts of such learning as his to be ignorant of practices that have prevailed in every age and among every religion.

First, then, let him observe that the ancients called that a religion which provides for the care and ritual observance of some higher nature, which they call divine. Cicero himself acknowledged that piety and holiness accompany those who preside over divine matters and administer the ordering of civil affairs. Because of the excellence of their office and the authority of their dignities, such men are necessarily responsible for prohibiting and preventing everything that can weaken or destroy the worship of the divine Power.

Accordingly, whatever was at any time devised from the opinions of the ignorant to the detriment and corruption of even a pagan religion, and whatever was gradually being introduced anew among sacred matters, every nation expelled and detested with all its strength, also restraining by various kinds of punishment those who dared, by changing the laws of their ancestors, to perform divine rites differently.

### 2.
