Although we could produce countless examples of this from Livy, the historian of Roman affairs, yet, so that we do not seem to wander beyond the prescribed limits of our controversy, we shall meanwhile bring forward only one. From it we understand that the Romans disapproved the introduction of an external and new religion and judged that it ought to be abolished as destructive to themselves, their ancestors, and their gods.

When Quintus Fabius and Titus Sempronius were serving as consuls, Hannibal spent the summer in the territory of Tarentum. As the war dragged on, religious practices too were changing among other things, especially under external influence, so that people or gods suddenly seemed to have become different. Roman rites were no longer abolished only in secret or within private walls; even in public places, in the forum and on the Capitol, crowds of women could be seen neither sacrificing nor praying to the gods according to ancestral custom.

When this evil had grown so serious and appeared more powerful than the lesser magistrates could suppress, the Senate assigned Marcus Atilius, the city praetor, the task of freeing the people from these religions. He therefore read the decree of the Senate in the assembly and issued the following edict:

> Whoever possessed books of prophecy, prayers, or a written art of sacrificing was to bring all those books and writings to him before the Kalends of April, so that no one might sacrifice in a public or sacred place according to a new or foreign rite.

### 3.

Beausobre does not deny that the Roman pontiffs and other Christian pastors and emperors employed this same zeal, inspired by a sacred and divine purpose, for the protection and defense of the Catholic religion. Yet, paying no attention at all to the policy and practice of magistrates and ancient pagan rulers, he has dared, in a censorious style, to mark and attack all the Catholic Fathers who ordered the Manichaean books to be burned and destroyed.

He not only noted this in the first part of his *History*, but explained it more explicitly in the preliminary discourse to the second part. He begins that discourse by asserting that it is very difficult, or almost impossible, in the present day to present a just and complete account of the philosophy and theology of the Manichaeans, because their written volumes no longer exist.  
[Note: Beausobre, preliminary discourse to Part II, p. 218.]

He later says that he does not know whether Leo the Great was the first among the ancients to order Manichaean books to be destroyed and burned. He does know, however, that Leo was imitated by his successor Gelasius, who ordered their books to be burned before the church of Saint Mary. Pope Symmachus followed this practice shortly afterward. For from Anastasius the Librarian we have the following account:

> He burned all the images or books of the Manichaeans together before the doors of the Constantinian basilica.

Beausobre first argues that the images of the Manichaeans could not have been burned. On the one hand, the magicians whose religion the Manichaeans followed had no idols, according to Epiphanius; on the other, the Manichaeans worshiped fire, the sun, and the moon, and images of these things could not be burned.  
[Note: Epiphanius, whom Beausobre himself cites, *Against the Heresies*.]

Finally, he concludes that Pope Hormisdas followed the example of his predecessors in dealing with these heretics.

Nothing in what has so far been described appears seriously to damage the conduct of the Roman bishops. We encounter only the weak assertion that Pope Symmachus could not have burned the images of the Manichaeans because they represented fire, the sun, and the moon—as though images of such things possessed the same power and nature as the things represented. The substance of fire, like that of the sun and moon, cannot be consumed by fire. But who will deny that their images, made of wood, clay, or metal, could be burned?

### 4.

After this, the author Beausobre gradually tries to insinuate himself into the reader’s mind. Under the pretext of a certain ignorance, he argues here and there about whether the zeal of the ancient bishops ought to be praised—the zeal by which they moved Christian emperors to decree that the books of heretics should be committed to the fire and to order the death penalty against those who dared either to read or to retain such books.

He persuades himself that the purpose and end of these laws were good, but attacks the analogous example as extremely harmful, allegedly condemned even by Christians themselves as unjust and violent. To prove or strengthen this futile and poisonous conjecture, which all the sophists of our age follow, he appeals to the second *Apology* of Justin the Martyr. There Justin bitterly laments the Roman law enacted against those who consulted the Sibylline and Hystaspes books, which Christians used to confirm their doctrines.

But who cannot understand that the complaint of Saint Justin the Martyr was entirely just? The Sibylline books were in use among the pagans. When undertaking or resolving difficult matters, the Romans themselves appealed to these books in order to draw assistance from them. Why, then, did they trust these books in affairs of state, yet, out of hatred for the Christian religion—which they at least obscurely prophesied—rage against them so violently that they destroyed them?

Justin therefore believed that these books could even provide the pagans with assistance so that they might more readily give their allegiance to Christ. They placed such confidence in them, as Livy records:

> By decree of the Senate, when no end could be found to the incurable disaster, the Sibylline books were consulted.  
> [Note: Titus Livius, Book V, chapter 13, and Book XXXVIII, chapter 45.]

Justin’s complaint, then, did not consist in the loss of sacred monuments suited and sufficient to confirm the Catholic faith, but in the fact that the pagans had deprived themselves of certain aids from which they might have drawn at least a small ray of light for our Christian faith.

Besides, who could ever have claimed that the Sibylline books were either necessary or suitable for strengthening Catholics in their faith? They were instructed by the Scriptures of both Testaments, they heard apostolic preaching, and they were enlightened by the continual experience of miracles and signs—not to mention the supreme care and solicitude of the pastors in instructing the first Christians and strengthening them in the faith. They therefore had no need to appeal to the Sibylline books.

If Justin and other ancient Fathers appealed to them in order to rebuke the pagans, we think this was done only on the basis of a certain supposition: namely, that they knew these books had been held in reverence by the pagans’ ancestors, priests, pontiffs, and magistrates.

Beausobre’s argument drawn from the complaints of Justin the Martyr therefore collapses completely. Let us consequently return to the purpose of our writing, from which we have digressed somewhat. What benefit or what assistance could Catholics have drawn from Manichaean books, so as to complain with any reason about the decrees of the Roman pontiffs?

Furthermore, in order to claim faith and authority for their books, the Manichaeans falsely bestowed upon them the most solemn and sacred names of piety: *Gospels*, *Mysteries*, *Revelations*, *Treasures*, and similar titles. Pretending that these works contained divine knowledge, they gave them the titles of sacred and canonical books under the names of the apostles. They understood very well that they could not easily deceive simple, uneducated, and unsuspecting people unless they first coated their poisonous doctrine with a kind of honey.

“As Saint Leo the Great says, they could deceive the simple more easily only if they coated their poisoned cups with some honey, so that what would prove deadly might not be perceived as wholly unpleasant.”

To prevent Catholics from imbibing corrupt and impure doctrines to the detriment and destruction of the Christian faith, it was therefore necessary that such writings be completely removed and handed over to the flames. For this reason Saint Leo the Great commands Saint Turibius, the most vigilant pastor of the Church of Astorga, not merely to prohibit the reading of copies of such writings—seedbeds of many falsehoods—but entirely to remove them and burn them.

> “Care must therefore be taken,” says Leo the Great, “and priestly diligence must above all provide that falsified books be used in no reading whatsoever. Apocryphal writings, which under the names of the apostles contain many seeds of falsehood, must not merely be prohibited but also entirely removed and burned.”  
> [Note: Saint Leo the Great, Letter 15, chapter 15.]

Who does not see that this decree of Saint Leo was equitable and just? Beausobre, with his non-Catholic allies, who affect an excessive devotion to philosophy and ancient matters, all but denies this most shamelessly. He says that, for the moment, he does not wish either to criticize or praise this practice, established by so many laws.

Second, he adds that some books are indeed worthy of burning—those, for example, that corrupt morals or completely overturn the foundations of religion and human society. But another class of books, he says, is not so harmful that it should be hidden from the people rather than entirely suppressed, since many prudent men might be able to draw benefit from them.

“If, then,” Beausobre concludes, “the books of the Manichaeans are such as they are described, I would dare to affirm that they were committed to the fire with the greatest injustice, since the Catholic faith would have gained greater advantages by preserving writings filled with ridiculous and obscene fables.”  
[Note: Beausobre, preliminary discourse to Part II, p. 219.]

This is how Beausobre reasons, adding certain fabulous sayings of the Manichaeans that we ourselves noted from the earlier *Acts of Archelaus*. He ought nevertheless to be ashamed of having written such things.

What? Do the books of the Manichaeans not overturn all the mysteries of our Catholic faith? What doctrines of our religion did they not attack, or at least attempt to overthrow? Let him run through the Apostles’ Creed and say whether they left even one article of our faith untouched.

But let us pass over these matters. It is well known and universally recognized that the Manichaeans denied the existence of one God; rejected the true incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of Christ the Lord; profaned the Eucharist and the other sacraments; and told sacrilegious fictions about the coming of the Holy Spirit.

What more need be said? Did the Manichaeans not either assert that the divinely inspired Scriptures derived from an evil author, or, if they accepted the New Testament, say that it was not to be preserved whole and perfect, but wound and corrupted it with interpolations, additions, and other false insertions?

In a word, there is nothing in the Catholic religion that the Manichaeans did not attempt to weaken and utterly overthrow. If, then, even according to Beausobre, those books must be considered worthy of burning that subvert the foundations of religion and human society, the conduct of the Roman pontiffs cannot be censured or reproached, since the Manichaean books accomplished both.

For, in addition to the crimes committed against religion, they dissolved and rejected marriages and unions, and indulged in the abominable vices of lust, which nature itself abhors. Were such things, contained in their books under the name of the apostles’ writings, to be permitted by sacred ministers? Away with such sacrilege!  
[Note: Consult what we wrote in chapter 11 of the preceding book concerning the fabulous inventions of the Manichaeans’ philosophy and theology.]

### 5.

Finally, as I reviewed these and other arguments of Beausobre’s kind, I easily came to suspect that the author had no religion, or professed one only outwardly. For if he had possessed any appearance of inward piety, he would also have recalled to mind what great and profound veneration can be gained by writings falsely circulated under the name of ancestors who already possess great authority and renown.

Nothing is more effective for dissolving religions than such books. Quintus Petillius said this to Lucius Petillius when two chests were discovered in the latter’s field, one of which contained books attributed to Numa Pompilius and written by Pythagoreans. The common opinion held that Numa had been a disciple of Pythagoras.

But when books of this kind—written in Latin and Greek, the first seven concerning pontifical law and the last seven concerning the discipline of wisdom that might have belonged to that age—were discovered, they did not decide to preserve them for the study of those subjects. After reading summaries of their contents and observing that most of the material was directed toward dissolving religion, Lucius Petillius said that he would throw the books into the fire.

Nor should Beausobre suppose that these books were thrown into the fire on private authority. The matter was first brought before the praetor, who judged that the books ought not to be read or preserved; then it was brought before the Senate, which decreed that the books should be burned at the earliest opportunity in the assembly place. Finally, the books were burned in the assembly place, in the sight of the people, in a fire made by the public executioners.  
[Note: Titus Livius, Book XL, chapter 29.]

I am entirely unaware whether anyone has ever accused or reproached Lucius Petillius the praetor, or the Senate of the Roman people, as unjust because books whose contents possessed, for the most part, merely the power to dissolve religions were handed over to the fire.

This alone is certain to me: in a public gathering of the Roman people, by the common decision of all orders, while the entire people applauded, in accordance with the laws governing the assemblies, the books in question were burned by the public executioners, who were public officials.

But I ask Beausobre: Were there not then among the Romans men who devoted themselves to pontifical law or philosophy? He must admit that there certainly were. Yet it is recorded that no man of any order existed who complained about the loss of such books. They were convinced that religion ought not to be weakened by new and foreign rites.

For, according to Cicero:

> The worship of the gods is the best, and likewise the purest, holiest, and most fully characterized by piety, when we always venerate them with a pure, whole, and undefiled mind and voice.  
> [Note: Cicero, Book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 28.]

But to what end will mind and voice preserve the purity and integrity of institutions pertaining to sacred matters if they begin to wander and take pleasure in at least some superstitious and utterly outrageous practices?

In all these matters, drawn thus far from the histories of the ancient pagans, it was necessary for our discourse to dwell somewhat more fully, lest Beausobre’s excessive indulgence in censuring the ancient customs of the Catholic Church and exercising his malicious style against the deeds of the Roman pontiffs should seem to pass without a just rebuke.

This is especially necessary because non-Catholic men of our own age, seeing their books prohibited by apostolic authority and burned by public officials in the sight of the people, loudly complain of a policy supposedly unjust and injurious, although it was adopted with the utmost holiness and religious devotion to preserve the purity and integrity of the Catholic faith.

### CHAPTER V

The severity of the imperial laws against the Manichaeans in Africa is reexamined. Terrified by this severity, and defeated by the authority and disputations of Saint Augustine, Felix at last renounced the errors of his heresy at Hippo. Finally, various questions arising in this matter are resolved.

### 1.

After the Manichaean plague had been introduced into Africa, its error began to spread so widely in a short time that in every gathering of people many men and women were found who were being shamefully polluted by it.

Since this occurred to the great insult, disgrace, and destruction of both the civil and Catholic commonwealth—for the practices and institutions of the Manichaeans first dissolved all the rights of marriage, weakened the purity of offspring through the most shameful and promiscuous indecencies, corrupted virgins devoted to a holier life and discipline while they were still of tender age, and, as though the men of this sect were subject to no divine or human laws whatsoever, poured themselves into every most wicked kind of crime, while nature itself recoiled—therefore, as soon as these long-hidden secrets and concealed way of life of the Manichaeans became known to the rulers of the world, an edict was issued against them and their sacrilegious assemblies. Various laws were enacted for this purpose, by which they were compelled to undergo many kinds of punishment.

Moreover, our mind would recoil most intensely from recounting what the Manichaean Elect were compelled to do sacrilegiously and superstitiously with every kind of food, even in consuming the venerable sacrament of the Eucharist. But the words of Augustine, which we set down below, will lessen our horror and embarrassment:

> On this account, or rather under a kind of necessity imposed by their execrable superstition, their Elect are compelled to consume what is, as it were, a Eucharist mixed with human semen, so that from it also, just as from the other foods they receive, that divine substance may be purified.  
> [Note: Augustine, *On Heresy*, 46.]

Certain other mysteries were no less impious and sacrilegious. Augustine elsewhere asserts that the Manichaeans preserved them with great abuse of our rites. For, to the great disgrace and contempt of our Catholic religion, the Hearers of this sect knelt before the Elect so that hands might be laid upon them in supplication—not only by their presbyters, bishops, or deacons, but by any of their Elect.

Behold, then, the origin of that wicked opinion which arose and prevailed: that laymen could institute and ordain the Church’s sacred ministers. This error, long since abolished, was revived after the passing of the centuries by Calvin and other most criminal authors, to the ruin of the entire ecclesiastical hierarchy.

Since the Manichaeans’ most wicked sect of the Elect had been accustomed to perform these and similar acts, the rulers of the world devoted every effort to eradicating their thoroughly corrupt practices.

Nor do we learn this merely from one or another testimony of Leo the Great, but from the Theodosian Code itself, in which several laws enacted by the emperors for the destruction of the Manichaeans are recorded, as we shall observe in a more appropriate place.

For the moment, however, we must consider the law that the two emperors Diocletian and Maximian issued at the urging of Julian, proconsul of Africa, as Tillemont also relates.

### 2.

In the year of Our Lord Christ 290, after first hearing the complaints of Julian himself, the proconsul of Africa, the two emperors learned how a new sect of men, arriving there from the borders of Persia, had stirred up great disturbances in the major cities of that kingdom, so that the affairs of the Roman Empire were being thrown into complete confusion.

Wishing to counter these evils as they increased there, they issued a law at Alexandria in March of that same year, ordering that the members of this sect, together with their wicked writings, be handed over to be burned. If any nobles were found infected with this stain, they ordered them to be deported into exile, in addition to suffering the loss of all their property. Finally, they compelled men of the lowest condition to undergo capital punishment.

Tillemont therefore more plausibly judges that such a law still remained in force in Africa during Augustine’s lifetime.  
[Note: Tillemont’s judgment, volume IV, p. 409.]

After carefully and diligently consulting the *Acts of Augustine against Felix*, he observes that this heretical man had been terrified both by episcopal authority, as he said, and by the severity of those laws that the emperors had promulgated for the destruction of this wicked sect.

The same Augustine, however, attempted to expose and thwart both of this man’s evasions. First, he showed that the authority of holy bishops, derived from God, inspires no fear in the accused when the discussion is conducted peacefully and the people attending the disputation apply no force or terror whatsoever. Second, he explained that the severity of imperial laws, arising from the right of the sword, could never harm the truth of religion or sincere confession, but had always provided an ornament, protection, and increase to the Catholic Church and its sacred doctrines.

> You also said that you are frightened by episcopal authority, although you see with what peace we act among ourselves and with what tranquility we dispute; you see how the people present apply no force to you and inspire no terror, but listen with perfect calm, as is fitting for Christians. You also said that you fear the laws of the emperors. A man whom the Holy Spirit fills would not fear this on behalf of the true faith.

For this reason he sets before him the example of the Apostle Peter, who, moved by the divine Spirit, was crucified for the Lord’s faith.

But Felix himself, driven by an excessive zeal for argument, dared to answer Augustine: “The apostles were also afraid.” Wishing to remove this new evasion of Felix the Manichaean, the holy Father immediately explained in what way the apostles had feared tyrants:

> They feared in order to take precautions, not so as to hesitate, once apprehended, to declare their faith.

A little farther on, he rebukes Felix lightly and without any ambiguity or insult in his words for not having previously feared the emperor, as Felix alleged, since he had not previously remained silent:

> For even if you had feared the emperor, you would have remained silent earlier.

And when, on the previous day, Felix had been brought under suspicion of Manichaeism, he appealed to the curator of Hippo and, after presenting a written petition, publicly shouted that he was ready to be burned, together with his books, according to Diocletian’s law, if anything evil were found in them. Augustine therefore, as though mocking him, closes his reply as follows:

> Yesterday you demanded the laws like a brave man; today, like a coward, you flee from the truth.  
> [Note: Book I of the *Acts with Felix the Manichaean*, chapter 12.]

### 3.

From these public *Acts of Augustine the Bishop with Felix the Manichaean*, then, the severity of the imperial laws under which members of this sect in Africa were punished shines forth more clearly than daylight, since professors of such a heresy were handed over to be burned together with their books.

It is also clear that the authority of the bishops extended not only to rebuking people infected with that stain so that they would renounce their errors, but also to eradicating completely from their dioceses every innovation opposed to the Catholic religion. This ecclesiastical authority of the bishop was especially evident in the case of Felix.

In the year 404, during the sixth consulship of Honorius Augustus, on the sixth day of December, Felix had rashly and openly said in the city of Hippo that he could defend the writings of Mani and assert that they contained the truth. For this reason he had rightly been accused, as we have seen, both before the city’s curator and before Bishop Augustine as guilty of execrable blasphemy. He was now being compelled to undergo a public examination.

Felix did not live in Hippo but had come there to sow Manichaean errors. Although he was one of the more learned among them, he was nevertheless uneducated in the liberal arts; yet, being more cunning than Fortunatus, he confidently hoped to spread the errors more widely.  
[Note: Augustine, Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 8; Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 16.]

Possidius adds that Felix belonged to the number whom they call the Elect and that, besides defending their wicked doctrines, they devoted themselves to the most impure indecencies and obscenities.

This meeting therefore began on the following day, that is, on the seventh of December, in the presence of the people and in the church. Augustine calls the meeting an ecclesiastical proceeding, or ecclesiastical trial, committed to writing by the notaries. During the disputation, they began from the Manichaean letter that they call “the Foundation.”

But this meeting, or episcopal proceeding, was not completed on that same day. For when Felix was pressed by the truth and especially challenged by Augustine’s arguments, he said: “I ask for a postponement, so that I may be able to answer.”

Augustine, kindly and most humanely granting his request, as was fitting for a bishop of the Catholic Church, extended the remaining proceedings of the disputation over a period of five days—that is, until the day before the Ides of December.  
[Note: Book II of the *Acts with Felix the Manichaean*, chapter 1.]

4. Although Augustine, wishing to deal more humanely with Felix, had granted him this postponement of the disputation, the holy bishop’s mind was not free from fear: he considered that Felix might take flight in order to escape the penalties imposed upon those guilty of such crimes. Accordingly, before bringing this first conference to its conclusion, he had to exercise great caution. He therefore asked Felix whether he was contemplating flight. When Felix denied this once and again, he was required to pronounce an anathema against Mani and to place himself under the custody of some person. Since Felix faithfully kept the public pledge he had given in all these matters, and since the proceedings of the first disputation had been authenticated—not only by Felix and Augustine, but also by a certain Boniface, under whose custody we believe Felix had placed himself—the earlier Acts were brought to their conclusion with great glory for Catholic truth. What happened after the lapse of five days is likewise clearly revealed by the Acts of the second day, *with Felix the Manichaean*. For when they had assembled with a considerable crowd and the notaries in the Church of Peace on the twelfth day of that same month, Augustine began the new disputation with those matters, or doctrines, at which the preceding one had ended.

“If nothing could harm God,” Augustine said, “why did he wage war against the people whom you call the people of darkness, in which war he would mingle the substance of his own nature with the nature of the demons”—that substance which, as you have already stated when questioned, is identical with himself?

Thus the holy bishop was attacking Felix. When the heretic confronted this fictitious doctrine, employing both craft and evasion, he replied that he was still unprepared and that during that period he had no book of Scripture at hand, because the books had not been returned to him, and therefore he had nothing from which to equip himself. “No one,” he continued, “enters a contest unless he has first been armed; and no litigant can plead without his documents. Likewise, I cannot answer without my book.”

By this device Felix was attempting to escape the new danger. But Augustine knew him; indeed, he knew very well the evasions of this crafty man. He therefore turned to him with a grave and authoritative speech, sharply reproaching him for trying to conceal his sacrilegious errors under this excuse. He charged him with a new offense: although he had asked for five days in which to prepare his answer, he had not even requested that the books be given to him, though they were being kept under the public seal.

Felix therefore did not obtain the desired postponement of a further two days. He was given only the books. When he had received them, the holy bishop began to press him so vigorously and to pursue him with such force and weight of argument that, once all the Manichaean’s fabulous inventions, errors, and impieties had been shaken out, Felix, finally defeated by the truth of the arguments, abjured Mani and his doctrine before so large an assembly, amid the greatest applause from the Catholics.

Meanwhile, so that everyone might know that he would sincerely and wholeheartedly pronounce an anathema against Mani and his errors, Felix asked the same Bishop Augustine to provide him with a written copy of the formula of anathematization. He especially requested that Augustine lead him, so that Felix might be more firmly confirmed: Augustine was to anathematize Mani first, as well as the spirit that had spoken through him.

At last he obtained this. For after receiving a sheet from Augustine, he cursed Mani with an anathema. Felix did the same, writing the following words in his own hand:

> I, Felix, who had believed in Mani, now anathematize him and his doctrine;

and other statements of the same kind, which everyone may conveniently read in Augustine at the end of the second book.

5. Yet those who have read the Life of Augustine, elegantly and learnedly arranged by the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, will say, we suppose, that in recounting all this we have labored in vain. For in Book V, chapter 12, they have described more fully, though in summary form, everything relating to Augustine’s present disputations with Felix.

What then? Were we not permitted to revisit the same matters, to report the law enacted by the pagan emperors against the Manichaeans, to explain how Felix appealed to it, and at the same time to show that he had feared the severity and penalties of both authorities? The very learned editors of the works of Saint Augustine may indeed have omitted all this because they thought it foreign to the purpose they had set themselves in writing: namely, to narrate only what took place between Augustine and Felix.

Since, therefore, our principal aim in composing a history of the Manichaeans was to gather into a kind of single body, while preserving as far as possible the chronological order, the crimes of that sect as reported by the most serious and trustworthy writers, we have transferred these same materials for our own use, adding everywhere the notes that others, engaged in a different task, either omitted or at least were obliged to omit.

6. Meanwhile, lest we seem to fail to mention matters relevant to our subject, we by no means conceal that three conferences, not two, were held between Augustine and Felix. Possidius intended to indicate this, at least obscurely, in the Life of Augustine. But it becomes clearer again from Augustine’s own words. In the record taken down by the notaries on the first day of the conference, he indicated an earlier meeting, addressing Felix the Manichaean as follows: “He knows that he said it yesterday.”

Again, when Felix himself was responding to Augustine’s questions, he promised to prove what he was asserting impiously and sacrilegiously if the Manichaean writings were given to him: “The five authors whom I mentioned to you,” he said, “whatever you ask me, I will prove to you.” His words must evidently refer to the books that he also requested in the final conference and that were being kept under the public seal.

[Note: Augustine, Book I, *On the Proceedings with Felix the Manichaean*, chapter 1; likewise chapter 14; and Book II, *On the Proceedings with Felix the Manichaean*, chapter 1.]

But these books had already been handed over for safekeeping under seal before the public and solemn conferences were recorded in writing by the notaries. When I consider all these matters together, I am easily led to the opinion that the holy bishop held only two conferences or disputations at the doors of the church, with the people standing by; but that these had been preceded by another before the imperial official—namely, when Felix appealed in his humble petition to the penalties of the imperial laws, and when at last he handed over the apocryphal books of Scripture to be kept under the public seal.

Thus anyone may reasonably argue who wishes to examine carefully, and not negligently, both Possidius’s testimony and the Acts of those disputations.

7. This earlier question is followed by another, which appears to concern the ecclesiastical rank of Felix the Manichaean. The occasion for this inquiry was Augustine’s Letter 79, which the holy bishop addressed to Fortunatus’s successor, a Manichaean presbyter. From it a doubt arose among the editors of Augustine’s works, leading them to suspect that this same presbyter was the Felix of whom we have been speaking.

But is this suspicion, and the evidence or conjectures on which it rests, so entirely empty and false that we must reject it? Where shall we find grounds for such a suspicion? For my part, I who am moved by no partisan interest, if I must sincerely confess what I consider, shall judge that this Manichaean presbyter, to whom Augustine addressed the letter in question, was someone other than Felix.

But lest I appear to conceal the foundations of this plausible opinion, I shall reason briefly as follows. I shall ask the most recent editors of Augustine whether Letter 79 was written after Augustine’s conferences with Felix or preceded them. It cannot at all be judged to be later than those conferences. For Felix, already converted in his heart, openly confessed the Catholic religion before the proceedings of the final conference had been brought to an end; he abjured Mani and his doctrines, and we cannot suppose, without the gravest evidence, that he relapsed into his former errors.

The editors in question, therefore, will hardly doubt that Augustine’s Letter 79 preceded the two conferences recorded in writing. We believe that they intended to indicate this when they placed the following date in the margin of their editions: “Perhaps written in the year 404.”

Even if, following certain and genuine consular dates, we assign Augustine’s public conferences with Felix the Manichaean to that year, nevertheless, since he held them toward the end of that year—on the twelfth day of December—no sane person could affirm that Letter 79 was later than them.

When I was considering these matters, I carefully compared the subject of this letter with what is described in the disputations, and I found that they do not correspond. For the Manichaean presbyter whom the editors in question suspect to have been Felix had raised a question with certain of Augustine’s brothers concerning visible death, which was not to be avoided. He maintained that death was not merely the separation of mind from body, but also the separation of good from evil.

Since this presbyter was asserting this on the basis of Manichaean doctrine, Augustine sought to rebuke him and at the same time summoned him to public disputations, so that he might resolve the question in which his predecessor Fortunatus had failed. But it is already clear from the sequence of the Acts themselves that other subjects were involved in those disputations.

Moreover, neither in the books of the *Retractations* nor in the Acts of the conferences does Augustine assert that he gave this letter to Felix; and it is plainly evident that Possidius likewise preserved the same silence in the Life of Augustine.

I therefore confess that I am entirely at a loss to know upon what conjectures I should rely if I were rashly to suspect that Augustine could have addressed the letter in question to Felix the Manichaean presbyter. Others, however, will judge this better and more easily. For the moment, in order to avoid the pitfalls into which the latest editors of Augustine’s works seem to have fallen, we shall refrain from determining anything and shall proceed instead to describe matters that are more certain.

# CHAPTER VI  
## On the Judgment Employed by the Church of Carthage in Cases Involving the Manichaeans; the Zeal of the Catholic Bishops and the Ecclesiastical Discipline Observed in Receiving Those Who Were Doing Penance

[Col. 0918B]

1. Among the many heresies ravaging Africa in the fifth century, Manichaeism held the leading place. This was either because, arising before the Arian, Priscillianist, Pelagian, and Donatist sects, it had established itself in that kingdom in the year 290, coming from Persia or Armenia, and, remaining for a long time concealed from the Catholic bishops, had put down roots now here, now there; or because, divided into two classes—namely, Hearers and Elect—it could easily attract two kinds of people: one consisting of those suffering from ignorance of the divine mysteries, and the other of those seething with the greatest ardor for the most shameful lusts.

Augustine, as we have seen, vigorously attacked and pursued both kinds of people after their conversion through conversations, disputations, and writings. But he employed still greater force in refuting and eradicating the Manichaeans when some of them had been discovered at Carthage and proceedings had been taken against them by public and ecclesiastical authority.

For it is established from Prosper’s *Chronicle* that Ursus, prefect of the imperial household of Constantius, who also possessed tribunician rank and administered civil affairs in Africa, professed the Catholic religion and defended it with all his strength. He apprehended certain of those Manichaeans whom they called Elect men and Elect women.

Accordingly, so that they might be brought before the tribunal of the Church, the tribune Rufus, the defender of our rights, ordered this to be done. There, before the bishops in whose presence the accused appeared, and with the people also present, an inquiry was instituted. First they were questioned about their crimes and doctrines; then, after the confession of all their offenses had been heard, it was decreed that action should be taken against them, as the laws prescribed.

To hear these confessions, not only were the notaries present who recorded the proceedings, but bishops were also present, sitting there as judges, so that the form and order of the entire investigation might be observed in accordance with human and ecclesiastical laws.

Except for Aurelius, who at that time presided over the Church of Carthage with the highest distinction, we know none of the bishops’ names. But it is probable that bishops had been gathered from the whole province. Augustine too was present, perhaps because the doctrines and crimes of this execrable sect were known to him better than to the others.

2. What precisely became known from these episcopal proceedings at Carthage, and how many there were in addition to those whom the tribune Rufus had arrested and ordered to be brought before the ecclesiastical judges, is very difficult to determine. Through the ravages of time, proceedings of this kind, recorded by the notaries, perished; and Augustine, as well as Prosper, merely mentioned certain women who had been violated, omitting to describe the rest of the sequence of events.

Augustine included two women in particular among their number. One was named Margarita, who disclosed that shameful practice: although she was not yet twelve years old, she said that she had been violated because of that criminal ritual.

[Note: Augustine, *On Heresies*, no. 46, and Letter 222.]

Since a certain other Manichaean woman, Eusebia, who was regarded almost as a religious woman, had likewise suffered this crime of disgraceful obscenity, Augustine scarcely compelled her to confess it. At first she falsely testified that she still retained the flower of her virginity and requested that she be examined by a midwife. When she had been examined and what she was found to be had been discovered, she likewise disclosed that most shameful bed-crime: flour was spread beneath the bed to receive and mingle the semen of the persons having intercourse—a practice which, as Margarita had indicated, she had not heard of while absent.

Thus Margarita’s confession exposed in the Church at Carthage the most shameful lusts of the Manichaeans, which they practiced among themselves, the least serious of them being the violation of virgins. But Eusebia too, compelled first to confess her own disgrace and obscenity, disclosed other abominable crimes of her sect. Among these the principal one was that, even in the abuse of women and wives, they sought only the pleasures of the flesh, while always avoiding conception and the generation of offspring, lest, as they said, the divine substance that entered into them through food should be bound by fleshly bonds in the offspring.

In this present discussion we can recount only in general terms these matters concerning the Manichaean Elect men and women examined at Carthage. It is altogether impossible to describe each detail relating to the confession of the accused and the substance of the episcopal proceedings, unless we wish to resort to conjecture.

It will be still less easy to speak of the grave horror of the Carthaginian people, which all the witnesses of this ecclesiastical inquiry must have conceived beforehand against so pestilential a sect. From it we infer not only that all the Catholics cried out for the destruction of the Manichaeans, but also that each person would have wished more readily to bind himself by an oath to disclose immediately to the ecclesiastical judges anyone who became known to him as belonging to the Manichaean sect, whenever such a person came to his notice, without any hesitation of mind or delay.

Although the Acts of the Carthaginian notaries have perished, we draw evidence of this from one or another of Augustine’s letters.

3. The first of these was written to Quodvultdeus, then a deacon of the Church of Carthage. He had asked Augustine to compose a single volume on heresies. Augustine, in reply, explained that the difficulty of the work had already been attempted by Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, and Epiphanius of Cyprus, and had been completed by them.

Afterward, giving his judgment concerning the volumes of both writers, he asserted that Epiphanius’s work ought to be preferred to Philastrius’s. But before closing the letter, he asked Quodvultdeus not to regard it as burdensome to write back and tell him how a certain Theodosius persevered in the Catholic faith, through whom several Manichaeans had been exposed. We believe that those whom he exposed were themselves corrected.

Augustine therefore plainly asserts that the Manichaeans were exposed by this Theodosius. But whether Theodosius himself had once been tainted by the Manichaean stain, although this may seem more probable and Augustine’s words obscurely suggest it, I would not dare to determine.

This letter of Augustine should be assigned to the year 428, when he addressed the book *On Heresies* to this Carthaginian deacon. At that recent time some of them had again been discovered in the same Church, as the episcopal proceedings that Quodvultdeus had sent to Augustine demonstrate. These Manichaeans likewise confessed under careful questioning—not a sacrament, but an *exsacrament*—one of them being named Viator.

On the occasion of these episcopal proceedings, the Catholic bishops also learned that a schism had arisen among the Manichaeans. For, divided into various factions, some were called Catharistae, or “purifiers”; others were called Mattarii, because they slept on mats; and still others were simply called Manichaeans.

This schism among the Manichaeans was therefore also confirmed by the proceedings reviewed at Carthage. But it is clear that Augustine had learned of it long before, from what he says in Book V, chapter 5, *Against Faustus*. We must assign it to an earlier period, as we shall explain shortly.

4. The Manichaeans therefore boasted proudly and vainly of the perfection of Christian commandments, as though they alone practiced what was commanded in the Gospel. Yet there was such a difference among them in morals and manner of life that they were by no means united in fulfilling the Manichaean laws.

Accordingly, since some among them especially vaunted Christian poverty, while others utterly despised it, Augustine, who was refuting their lies and pretenses, chiefly attacked Faustus, who taught that money should not be carried in one’s belt. He assaulted and harried him because the Manichaeans professed one thing and lived otherwise: although they carried no money in their belts, they eagerly tried to keep gold in their chests and purses.

[Note: Consult Augustine, Book V *Against Faustus*, and the book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapter 20.]

For this reason Augustine appeals to a certain Constantius, a Roman citizen once infected with the Manichaean stain, who afterward, having abjured his error, converted to the Christian Catholic religion.

He calls upon this man as a very wealthy witness. When Constantius was burning with the greatest zeal for this sect, he had invited and gathered many Manichaeans into his house at Rome in order to fulfill the precepts of Mani—precepts indeed vain and foolish, but nevertheless regarded as important by his disciples. When the weakness of the Manichaeans gave way before the severity and austerity of these laws, they dispersed, each departing on his own way.

When, therefore, each person claimed and imagined that he was free to evade the Manichaean laws, that schism arose among them of which we spoke above. “Because some sleep on mats,” the same Augustine says, they are called Mattarii; but Faustus’s feather beds and goatskin blankets were very different from their pallets. With such an abundance of luxuries, they not only despised the Mattarii but also despised the house of their father, a poor man from Milevis.

[Note: Consult the *Life of Augustine*, Book I, chapter 9.]

Here Augustine wittily mocks and taunts Faustus as he describes this schism among the Manichaeans. It was above all one of the causes that had already inspired Augustine himself with disgust for this heresy.

He recounts the matter in the book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, where he gives a fuller account of the remarkable history of Constantius, a Hearer among the Manichaeans. The story had become so widely known that the rumor of it reached even those who were absent and far away.

Augustine himself, who had first learned the entire affair accurately from his friend, the witness, later testified that he had found it entirely confirmed and established when he came to Rome around the year 383 after Christ. He relates how Constantius, deeply distressed by such a great difference in morals among the Manichaeans, tried to compel all those gathered in his house to live according to the same rule laid down in Mani’s letter.

“Many,” Augustine says, “found this intolerable and departed; nevertheless, not a few remained out of shame. They began to live as had been agreed and as so great an authority prescribed. Meanwhile, that Hearer”—namely, Constantius—“compelled them all vehemently to do everything, though he compelled no one to undertake anything that he himself had not undertaken first.

“In the meantime, quarrels arose very frequently among the Elect; accusations were brought against one another. He listened to all these things with groans and took care that they should imprudently betray themselves in their quarrelling. They disclosed unspeakable and monstrous things.”

And after a short interval Augustine adds:

> What more need be said? At last, under compulsion, they murmured that those commandments could not be maintained; then they turned to sedition.

[Note: Consult the same Augustine, *Confessions*, Book V, chapter 11, no. 21.]

5. Meanwhile, let no one think that this discussion of ours is longer than it ought to be. Nor should anyone criticize our method of writing because we have wished to mingle events that took place in Africa against the Manichaeans with those that had occurred long before at Rome.

We were led to digress for a short time from the episcopal proceedings at Carthage chiefly for two reasons. The first is that schism which became increasingly evident in the confessions recorded by the notaries of the Manichaeans. Since an earlier Roman schism corresponds closely to it, we judged it useful to our reader to mention it.

The second is the opinion of certain men formerly of great reputation, who, turning all the monuments of ecclesiastical history upside down, insist that the arrival of the Manichaeans in the city of Rome must be dated no earlier than the year 427.

If their opinion stood, not only would the reliability of the Augustinian writers be shaken, but the decrees and constitutions of several Roman pontiffs would also collapse—those from which the bishops of the African Church drew the rules of discipline by which proceedings were taken against the Manichaeans. The principal author of this opinion was Quesnellus, as we shall reserve for later chapters the task of demonstrating.

Now, returning to that law of ecclesiastical discipline from which we have digressed somewhat, another letter of the same Saint Augustine makes it abundantly clear that the law was observed with greater strictness, without any indulgence whatsoever on the part of the bishops.

For Augustine had learned that a certain Victorinus of Malliana, who held the clerical rank of subdeacon, had been polluted by the Manichaean stain. Moved therefore by zeal for the Catholic religion, he immediately wrote to Deuterius, the bishop of that same province, so that he might take precautions concerning this cleric. He feared that through negligence or carelessness the enemy, who had begun to lie in wait for the Lord’s fold, might destroy the souls of Christians purchased at so great a price.

Augustine had therefore summoned this Victorinus to judgment. Before he could be convicted by the witnesses who had accused him, he was questioned and could not deny that his faith had been compromised. Accordingly, unable to deny that he had violated his pledged faith, he confessed that he was a Hearer of the Manichaeans, not an Elect.

Augustine then submitted to Bishop Deuterius what amounted to a summary of this confession, so that, by reviewing the monstrous and sacrilegious crimes, the bishop might at least in general understand the corrupt morals and impious doctrines of this sect.

After this, Augustine wished either to suggest to him or to recall to his mind the rules of ecclesiastical discipline to be observed in receiving Manichaeans who were doing penance. When Deuterius had considered these rules and observed them carefully, Augustine, having full knowledge of Victorinus’s former manner of life, gravely suspected that Victorinus would not observe them.

Therefore, lest he appear to have been moved by a trivial suspicion, Augustine brought Victorinus’s past conduct into the open and appealed to the pretense by which Victorinus, under a simulated profession of the Catholic faith and under the guise of the sacred ecclesiastical order of subdeacon, had tried to conceal the Manichaean religion that he professed in his heart.

Moved by so grave a doubt, Augustine therefore judged that Victorinus was not to be received into the Church even after abjuring his errors as a penitent. Instead, preserving the full rigor of ecclesiastical discipline, he arranged for him to be restrained and expelled from the city and diocese of Hippo.

He nevertheless instructed his bishop Deuterius to inflict upon him another and still more severe ecclesiastical penalty: in his letters he ordered Deuterius to degrade Victorinus from the clerical rank with appropriate ecclesiastical severity, so that, deprived of every honor and communion, he might be known to all.

Finally, Augustine absolutely forbade Deuterius to grant Victorinus a place for penance unless Victorinus also exposed others whom he knew to be present there—not only in Malliana but throughout the entire province.

6. We ourselves have extracted the substance of these matters from Augustine’s Letter 236, formerly Letter 74, in order to make clear the discipline applied by the Church to the Manichaeans.

[Note: Augustine, Letter 236; it appears in volume II, page 646.]

In what year the holy teacher wrote this letter was unknown to the most recent editors of Augustine’s works, who assigned it to the fourth class of letters, namely, those whose date is less certain.

But in the preface to the two books *On the Proceedings with Felix the Manichaean*, the editors of Augustine’s works bring forward an ancient fragment of Felix’s profession, drawn both from Baronius and from the Gervasian manuscript. From it we understand that those who came from this heresy to the Church were never received unless they first exposed other men of the same sect and reported them to the bishops or pastors of their own Churches.

Nor did Manichaeans who were received as penitents disclose merely the names of other members of the sect who lived in the particular diocese into whose communion they themselves had been admitted after the sacrament of reconciliation. They were also required to expose others scattered far and wide throughout the province or in neighboring regions.

This is made perfectly clear by the confession of Felix, formerly a Manichaean, whom we mentioned above:

> I, Felix, converted from the Manichaeans, have said, under the testimony of God, that I confess everything truly. Of the Manichaeans, or Manichaean women, whom I know to be in the districts of Caesarea, I name Mary and Lampadia, the wife of Mercurius the silversmith, with whom we also prayed together with the Elect Eucharistus; Caesaria and Lucilla, her daughter; Candida, who lives at Thipasse; Victorina the Spanish woman; Simplicianus, the father of Antonius; Paul and his sister, who are at Hippo. Through Mary and Lampadia I have also learned that these are Manichaeans.

From this confession of Felix the Manichaean, returning to the Catholic faith, we learn of that ancient discipline of the Church by which it was provided that no one should ever be admitted to the sacrament of reconciliation unless, under the testimony of almighty God, he exposed all whom he knew to be tainted by that heresy.

If, finally, a penitent deceitfully failed to report someone known to him, he was thereby rendered unworthy of the reconciliation already mentioned. For this reason Felix concluded his confession with these words:

> This alone I know: if anything else should be found that I knew beyond what I have said, I confess that I myself am guilty.

7. But the system and order of that ancient discipline are not yet disclosed fully and perfectly by Felix’s preceding confession. Since most of the Manichaeans had never been regenerated by the sacred washing of baptism and had always lived almost according to the practice of the pagans, while others had fled from the Catholic community and given their allegiance to the name of Mani, the bishops could not follow exactly the same procedure in receiving both groups.

Each of those who repented was required to prepare a written confession and act of penance. In it, after first pronouncing an anathema against Mani, he had earnestly to ask that he be granted a place either among the catechumens or among the penitents.

The bishops received such writings and examined whether they conformed to the ecclesiastical rules. A letter of reconciliation was not given to them in any other way than with the date and the name of the consul, so that they would not suffer any further difficulty, either under the public laws or under ecclesiastical discipline, on account of their former conduct.

If, however, after receiving the ecclesiastical certificate and written acknowledgment, anyone still appeared to be a Manichaean on the basis of definite evidence, he was compelled to undergo the severity of justice according to the form of the civil and ecclesiastical laws. The Catholic faithful were then ordered to guard themselves entirely against such persons, in accordance with the apostolic command of Saint Paul.

Those who had received letters from the bishops were commended to devout Catholic neighbors or to their fellow residents, whether clerics or laypeople. Through the care of these persons toward them, the converts were to attend frequently to the hearing of the word of God, and through their testimony they could become known.

Thus we read in that memorandum of the Catholic Church which is commonly attributed to Augustine and which the most recent editors of Augustine’s works placed in the appendix to volume VIII.

From the same memorandum we also understand that these converted Manichaeans were not immediately admitted to baptism or to the sacrament of reconciliation. Rather, they had to remain either in the rank of catechumens or in the place of penitents until the danger of death, or at least they were compelled to remain in one or the other condition until the bishops, having examined the firmness of their faith and confirmed it by the testimony of those to whom they had been commended, judged that these penalties ought to be relaxed for them through indulgence.

8. Finally, the letter of testimony, or written acknowledgment, under which the Manichaean penitents were released was not expressed in exactly the same form. For just as the Elect were worse than the Hearers, so they were also subjected to heavier penalties.

Accordingly, the Hearers, after making their confession and pronouncing an anathema against their blasphemous, most impious, and filthy heresy, easily obtained the bishops’ letters mentioned above, for use against those who tried to reproach them for Mani’s former error.

The Elect, however, did not receive such a certificate so easily. First they were shut away with servants of God—whether clerics or laypeople—in monasteries or hospices, until, after every suspicion of their former heresy had been entirely removed, they were finally judged worthy to receive either baptism or reconciliation.

### 9

Now, however, we must pause for a while, so that we may wrest the weapons from the enemies of the apostolic see—especially those weapons which they might claim to derive from our preceding discussion. For since their endeavor is to overthrow the rights and authority of the Roman pontiffs in suppressing heresies and strengthening ecclesiastical discipline, they might now flatter themselves that the ecclesiastical laws described above originated either with Augustine or with other African bishops. For this reason, they might say, those laws acquired such force that the Roman Church, having become their follower, later adopted them for itself and wished to observe them scrupulously when judging the Manichaeans.

Thus, indeed, those people may prate who not only published that volume as though it were a genuine code of the Roman Church’s canons, although it was compiled from the statutes of other Churches and from bishops’ letters, but who also, when discussing the affairs of the Eutychians, assert that Saint Leo underwent no other struggle than those which Athanasius once underwent with the Arians, Augustine with the Pelagians, and Cyril with the Nestorians. Indeed, when treating again of the Pelagian cause, they have invented the claim that the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine received their authority only from the African councils themselves.

Against all these and similar follies and falsehoods we have wished to set the labors of our historical studies, in order to dissolve these calumnies against the apostolic see and immediately deprive them of even this objection which they might raise. For that law of ecclesiastical discipline cannot be attributed to Augustine or to any other African bishop which had already been established and defined by the apostolic see of blessed Peter before Augustine gave his name to the Catholic Church and before the African bishops confronted the Manichaeans.

Pope Siricius committed this law to writing from the apostolic tradition of the Roman see at the beginning of his pontificate, when Augustine was still involved in the errors of the Manichaeans. Indeed, at that time the African bishops had not yet begun to punish the Manichaeans with ecclesiastical penalties; for from what was stated above we understand that this first occurred at Carthage, when Augustine was already occupying the episcopal see of Hippo.

Therefore, if Augustine and the other African bishops observed, for the destruction of that sect, statutes that had long before been promulgated by the apostolic see of Saint Peter, those statutes could not have originated with Augustine or with any other African bishop according to the rule or rationale of ecclesiastical discipline.

It would now be appropriate for us to set forth the decrees of that same Pope Siricius, which afterward not only the African Fathers observed with the greatest reverence when receiving the Manichaeans, but which all the Churches throughout the world likewise guarded with extraordinary scrupulousness. But this cannot be the work of the present leisure, since in the following chapters we shall be engaging in various controversies with Paschasius Quesnel and shall reserve for that occasion the description and exposition of the deeds of several Roman pontiffs undertaken out of hatred for, and for the destruction of, the offspring of Manichaeism.

### 10

Meanwhile, however, lest we deprive the most illustrious lights of doctrine and holiness of the praise and merit due to them, we affirm that the zeal of Augustine above all, and of the African bishops, is worthy of the highest esteem. With all the powers of their souls they opposed the Manichaeans in such a way that they overthrew and destroyed that wicked sect.

Above all, every honor and praise must be paid to Augustine. From the day of his conversion, he considered nothing else than exposing the abominable and more hidden mysteries of the Manichaeans, tearing down the false doctrines of this sect, magnifying in writing their indecencies, mocking and execrating the hypocrisy of the Elect, attacking with curses the profane rites and sacraments they employed, and, moreover, challenging those more learned men whom the other Manichaeans regarded as their teachers to hold public disputations. Afterward, when the falsity of Manichaean doctrine had been discovered, he devoted himself entirely to making the holiness of the Catholic faith known to all.

These are the things which Saint Augustine the Doctor accomplished with the greatest zeal for the good, honor, and benefit of the Catholic Church. His glorious labors are celebrated not only by so many and such great learned works, especially those written against the same opponents—a catalogue of which we shall not presently enumerate, lest we depart from our purpose—but also by all the other works he wrote either against the Donatists or against the Pelagians and Arians. In them he repeatedly attempted to refute, now one and now another, of the errors of the Manichaeans.

Thus, with such an abundance of Augustine’s books enriching Africa above all, and the Catholic Church, at a time when heresies were swarming through that land like the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, the other African bishops, instructed in the rules of the apostolic Roman Church and assisted by the support of the civil laws, could now completely crush and destroy the Manichaeans.

We believe that the holy Doctor wished to indicate this in a sermon delivered to catechumens during a barbarous period, addressing them in these words:

> “The poison of the Manichaeans had crept in; it has been crushed, it has been consumed.”

[Note: Sermon to the Catechumens, *On the Time of the Barbarians*, chapter 5. It is found in volume VI, page 45.]

But it was not consumed in the sense that the Manichaeans, either having been sent into exile and departing from the African kingdom, migrated elsewhere during Augustine’s lifetime, or that, having been brought to repentance, they left that kingdom cleansed of every stain of Manichaeism. No, I say, it was not so.

For that viperous offspring, terrified by civil and ecclesiastical penalties and accustomed to seek hiding places, never entirely departed from Africa, although the Vandals later devastated that kingdom. The purpose of Augustine’s statement, therefore, was to indicate that the poison of the Manichaeans had there been crushed and consumed by anathemas and proscriptions, and that their diabolical snares had been utterly crushed and broken by the efforts and writings of Catholics, so that neither the uneducated nor the more learned could any longer be caught in such traps.

What we have described belongs to the age of Augustine. But if anything concerning the same heresy, while it was spreading through Africa, occurs to us that ought to be said, we shall indicate it more suitably in the course of this historical study, observing the sequence of the times as far as we can.

## CHAPTER VII

**The method of Saint Leo the Great in dealing with the Manichaeans is defended against the insults and curses of Beausobre. It is explained that the holy pontiff not only declaimed in sermons but also exposed their errors. It is likewise shown that Saint Augustine’s writings composed against the Manichaeans contain neither fables nor sophistries, contrary to the claims of Beausobre.**

### 1

Here we undertake to examine several questions which, once clarified, will not only shed considerable light upon our preceding statements but will also entirely remove the arguments which Beausobre directed, with excessive abuse, against Saints Leo the Great and Augustine, those vigorous opponents of the Manichaeans.

First, then, he observes how that wretched sect of the Manichaeans, after the Vandals had occupied proconsular Africa, where it had spread more widely, was compelled to go into exile. Some of its followers came to Rome, while others took care to withdraw to various places or cities. Those who came to Rome hoped to obtain comfort and assistance from their brethren, so that they might live more safely. But before long this hope deceived them.

For Saint Leo the Great, the supreme pontiff, having learned of their arrival and residence, neglected no effort or labor to cleanse his Church of this pest. Nevertheless, Beausobre says, he adopted such a method of acting against them that he drove them rather to anger and despair than stirred them to repentance and renunciation of their crimes.

Beausobre further maintains that Saint Leo convicted them of abominable ceremonies, about which he afterward warned the bishops of Italy in encyclical letters. This method of action produced two pernicious effects. The first was to arouse horror of the Manichaeans among the people and common multitude and to move the magistrates to inflict upon them the penalties already established by the laws.

The other, more pernicious effect was that it gradually inspired those same Manichaeans with the greatest horror of the Catholic Church, since they saw the bishops becoming so bitterly hostile to them while they themselves were being driven on by these accusations and most grievous persecutions. For, he says, they were not guilty of the crimes of which they were accused.

[Note: Beausobre, preliminary discourse to the second part of the *History*, page 226.]

With these curses and insults Beausobre harassed Saint Leo the pontiff, as though he ought to have been more indulgent toward the Manichaeans and to have cleared them of their abominable crimes. Shall we then patiently endure such impudence in writing or boldness in reasoning—especially when the author boasts throughout his work that he is moved by no prejudices and that, in composing his history of the Manichaeans, he has investigated nothing but the truth of events?

But the following considerations will show that in all these matters our author has splendidly lied.

First, from what source does he infer that the Manichaeans came to Rome after proconsular Africa had been devastated by the Vandals? For the members of this wicked sect had long before sought other hiding places for themselves in the city of Rome, namely during the time of Saint Pope Siricius. He ordered those who were obstinate, excessively stubbornly attached to their errors, and vehement in defending them to be sent into exile; but he admitted those who had been corrected and were penitent to the sacrament of reconciliation, provided that they completed the remainder of their lives under detention in monasteries.

[Note: See what we wrote in the preceding chapter, page 139 and following.]

Therefore, the method followed by the Roman pontiffs in dealing with the Manichaeans did not originate with Leo the Great. They were not discovered at Rome only after the Vandal devastation of proconsular Africa, as Beausobre carelessly—or, I believe, negligently—asserted. Nor was access to repentance afterward closed to them, so that they might be driven to anger and despair. Rather, with the rigor of the sacred laws placed before them on one side, and ecclesiastical peace and gentleness on the other, they could incline their minds toward the latter and be brought to amend their ways.

Saint Leo the Great’s method of dealing with the Manichaeans, therefore, should not be judged so savage that, disregarding the statutes of his predecessors, the pontiffs Siricius and Anastasius, he did not first seek the conversion of the Manichaeans and refused to receive the penitent into reconciliation.

If popular hatred was then aroused against these men because their horrible crimes had been exposed, so that even the magistrates were moved to torment them with the rigor of punishment, this must in no way be charged as a fault against Leo. On the contrary, that zeal by which he strove to cleanse the Roman Church entrusted to him from the pollution of such enormous wickedness deserves to be crowned with the highest praise.

Moreover, what if the Manichaeans conceived the greatest horror of the bishops and of the society of Catholics? It is the ordinary condition of all defendants to fear judges and to shrink from the punishments which they justly deserve.

[Note: See chapter 9 of the second book of this *History*.]

But that did not make the bishops their slanderers and persecutors, since they proclaimed in speech or writing only Manichaean crimes that had been proved in judicial proceedings through formal investigation and brought to light by the confessions of the accused.

We demonstrate more clearly that our Leo observed this procedure both in public sermons delivered to the people and when he sent his letters to all the bishops of Italy, so that they might guard themselves and their flocks against the doctrines of the Manichaeans—men who had recently been expelled from the city of Rome. We do so in our discussion of Leo’s investigation of the Manichaeans at Rome. From that dissertation the reader will find abundant grounds for refuting Beausobre’s insults and curses against Saint Leo the Great.

### 2

Nor did Beausobre think it enough, as we have seen, to criticize and assail Saint Leo the Great’s method of dealing with the Manichaeans. Proceeding to the letters and sermons of the same holy pontiff, he asserts that they contain no description whatsoever of Manichaean doctrine. Rather, he says, all Leo’s writings consist of invectives against the Priscillianists and Manichaeans, since he continually attempts to confuse these two distinct sects and subjects both to the same punishments.

He adds that Leo’s zeal deserves some praise, but that greater moderation of spirit ought to have been expected from him, since he was above all one of those chief bishops who approved the punishments of heretics as valid and just.

Finally, Beausobre concludes his discourse by saying that he had sought the cause of Leo’s great agitation and had reflected upon the character of this holy pontiff. “His character,” he says, “was that of a man carried away by ambition, thinking less about winning the spirit through gentleness and persuasion than about suppressing it by violence.”

Nor did Beausobre think it sufficient to write this. In order to vent his fury against the holy pontiff and the apostolic see more fully, he appeals in his notes to certain words of Saint Leo himself, spoken on the occasion of the killing of Priscillian and other members of his sect at Trier by the public ministers of the emperor Maximus. By these words the same pontiff seems to approve that ruler’s bloody decision. Beausobre then adds:

Quesnel’s note upon this passage deserves to be copied here:

> “But neither here—Severus Sulpicius—nor there—Jerome—nor any other of the holy Fathers who lived in the age of Priscillian approved such bloody decisions.”

That is, that Leo . . .

[Note: Consult chapter 10 of this book, in which we report in detail the Manichaean errors, doctrines, and rites from Leo’s texts.]

### 3

It will not be difficult, nor beyond our ability, to wrest all these things away from him and to turn back upon the unjust slanderers each of the insults by which Saint Leo’s reputation and holiness are assailed. Some of the charges he makes are so weak and foolish that, to refute them, it is enough merely to cast one’s eyes upon the works of Saint Leo the Great; the opponent’s lies will then be detected.

I therefore ask him where he learned that Leo did not describe the principal errors of the Manichaeans in his letters and sermons, but confined himself to declamations in the manner of rhetoricians. He certainly did not learn this from Quesnel’s notes and writings, whom, as we saw from the preceding account, he adopted as a master to be followed.

For Quesnel at least listed various errors of the Manichaeans from the holy pontiff, as is evident from chapter 10 of this book. Moreover, Leo repeatedly mentions others which Quesnel failed to record only because of his excessive carelessness.

What need would Leo have had, in sermons delivered to the people, to enumerate and set forth one by one the entire doctrine of Manichaean philosophy and theology, all their superstitious and profane rites, and all the diabolical mysteries in which that sect was involved? He had not undertaken the task of composing treatises on the doctrines of faith in order to attack those heretics. His sole desire was to warn the Roman people to guard themselves against their association and institutions.

He was accustomed to do this especially on the more solemn days of the year, while the more sacred mysteries of our faith were being celebrated in the church. It was therefore enough to point out to the people, in summary fashion, their principal errors, so that the people might abhor them. But that he followed a different method when composing letters against those same Manichaeans is made clear both by the texts themselves and by the order of the written material.

### 4

First, as regards the letter sent to the bishops of Italy, Beausobre must be judged scarcely to have glanced at it with his own eyes.

[Note: Saint Leo’s Letter 8, chapter 1.]

For if he had even cursorily touched its text, he would have understood that Leo had proposed no other purpose than to warn the bishops about what had taken place at Rome in the solemn judgment held against the Manichaeans. His concern was that, through ignorance, the seeds of vice which had been extinguished and destroyed at Rome might secretly be planted at the roots in their dioceses through new offshoots.

In a word, Leo discussed the Manichaean heresy there only in general terms and called the other bishops to share his vigilance, informing them that through his investigation he had found in the City many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety; that through his watchfulness he had brought them to light; and that through his authority and censure he had restrained them.

But since, in restraining them, he observed the solemn form and rules of judicial proceedings, he transmitted with this letter copies of everything that had been done, including the crimes recorded in public documents and established by the confessions of the accused, so that the bishops might be more fully instructed.

“As the sequence of the proceedings,” he says, “will be able to inform you, we have also sent them themselves for your instruction. When you have read them, you will be able to know everything that we discovered.”

It is indeed to be regretted that such a record of the proceedings has perished through the ravages of time. But it is even more regrettable that Beausobre neglected to examine this letter, so that he might attack the holy pontiff solely with calumnies and insults.

### 5

As for the other letter, which is Letter 15, I cannot deny that it is entirely concerned with the questions submitted to the same holy pontiff by Turribius, bishop of Astorga, when he consulted Leo concerning the Priscillianist cause.

But on this occasion Leo neither ought nor needed to compose a lengthy treatment of this heresy or of the Manichaean heresy, for he would have wandered foolishly beyond the limits of the questions proposed to him.

Nor does it matter that in the celebrated letter he discussed indiscriminately both the institutions of the Priscillianists and those of the Manichaeans. These two heresies were indeed closely related, since Priscillianism borrowed many false doctrines from Manichaeism, and both had absorbed the poison of the ancient Gnostics.

Leo, the holy pontiff, should not therefore be accused of error if he sometimes called the Priscillianists Manichaeans. For Idacius likewise relates that Manichaeans hiding in the city of Astorga, exposed by the episcopal proceedings, were brought to judgment, condemned, and publicly denounced throughout Spain.

[Note: Idacius, under Olympiad 306.]

Nevertheless, it is certain that Leo was speaking there about the Priscillianists. Jerome too did not shrink from this manner of expression, as Quesnel also noted.

[Note: Jerome, *To Ctesiphon*.]

[Note: Quesnel, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, notes on Letter 15, page 449 in my copy.]

### 6

But that he wished to attack Saint Leo even more vehemently is made perfectly clear by his final objection, in which he describes the holy pontiff as driven by ambition and fury and as approving the bloody decision of the tyrant Maximus, carried out against the Priscillianists at Trier.

If Beausobre wishes to summon Leo as a liar and impostor, let him send him to the text of Leo’s letter. From that text he will find that no more unjust insult or bolder outrage could have been devised.

Saint Leo relates, in chapter 1 of that letter, how the bishops under whose episcopates that wicked heresy broke out throughout the world had worked earnestly to drive impious fury from the whole Church.

What evil counsel was there in this? The Fathers who, after issuing an anathema against Priscillian and his associates, ordered that they be expelled either from the episcopal sees or from ecclesiastical communion and treated as heathens and publicans did nothing dishonorable to episcopal dignity or contrary to ecclesiastical gentleness.

Nor does Beausobre’s case gain support from the other kind of judgment, the bloody one, which Saint Leo immediately mentions when he writes:
