> “When even the rulers of the world so detested this sacrilegious madness that they struck down its author, together with many of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws.”

For the cause of this bloody judgment he attributes not to the bishops but to the nature and gravity of the crimes. He adds:

> “For the rulers saw that all concern for morality would be removed, every marital union dissolved, and divine and human law alike overthrown, if such men were anywhere permitted to live while professing such things.”

If the Priscillianists had opposed only the doctrines of faith, and if they had not equally subverted all laws of morality and both divine and human rights, the rulers of the world would have imposed no bloody sentence upon them. But because they broke out into such crimes as brought the whole of civil life toward destruction, the rulers therefore judged it necessary to strike down the authors of such madness with the sword of the public laws.

For this reason the same holy pontiff, lest anyone should dare to twist his preceding words into a malicious interpretation, immediately distinguishes those two kinds of judgment, explaining how ecclesiastical gentleness [lacuna], content with priestly judgment, avoids bloody punishments.

If it avoids them, it does not approve them. But he adds:

> “Nevertheless, it is assisted by the severe enactments of Christian rulers, when those who fear bodily punishment sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy.”

How, then, does Beausobre derive the claim that Leo approved bloody decisions? Perhaps because Leo said that ecclesiastical gentleness, content with priestly judgment, is assisted by the enactments of Christian rulers? But in what sense did Leo affirm this? Clearly, because those entangled in more serious crimes, seized with fear of bodily punishment, sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy by execrating their former impieties and crimes.

How vain and worthless Beausobre’s calumnies against Saint Leo the Great are is shown by this preceding method and course of argument. From these considerations the reader also has grounds for refuting Quesnel’s sly fourth annotation, although Quesnel did not devise it with quite the same audacity as Beausobre.

[Note: Quesnel, note 4, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, page 448. See the history of the Priscillianists, chapter 15.]

### 7

I had now decided to take my hand from the tablet and, leaving aside for a little while the defense of Saint Leo the Great, to proceed to plead Augustine’s cause, so that I might likewise cleanse him of Beausobre’s unjust accusations.

[Note: Beausobre, part II of the *History of the Manichaeans*, book I, chapter 2, page 256, § 3.]

But while turning over the writings of this non-Catholic author, I encountered other matters as well which seemed to injure Leo’s piety and sincere faith. I therefore judged it necessary to linger longer over their examination, lest I be judged altogether negligent by envious and critical opponents.

Once again, then, he brings the holy pontiff onto the stage, not merely so that he may play a part by discussing the doctrines of the Manichaeans, but so that he may harass him with new curses and insults.

First he fabricates the claim that Saint Leo followed the opinion of Cyril of Jerusalem, who says that Manes blasphemed by calling himself the Holy Spirit. He says:

> “At least such an accusation is more specious; and Leo would have done better to copy it out than to extend and explain it more broadly, with the unforgivable freedom of saying that the Manichaeans worshipped Manichaeus himself, the teacher of such impieties, under the name of the Holy Spirit.”

And again:

> “They believed that the Holy Spirit had appeared in their teacher Manichaeus . . . so that Manichaeus himself was nothing other than the Spirit.”

[Note: Saint Leo the Great, Sermon 4 on the Epiphany, chapter 2 and following.]

“If this had really been true,” Beausobre adds, “our heretic would have been carried by pride and blasphemy to the highest degree of wickedness.”

“But if Leo is no more faithful in his narratives than he is just in his sermons, we shall certainly be excused if we do not put faith in his statements.”

Especially, he says, since Leo, attempting briefly to refute the presumed pride of Manichaeus, broke out into the following words:

> “For he too arose from that part of the world which cannot receive the Spirit of truth.”

As though Leo were implying that the Holy Spirit is confined within narrow boundaries and that the peoples of the East are more miserable than all others.

“Indeed,” Beausobre adds, “I would never have believed that a bishop who received the surname ‘the Great’ could have uttered such an absurdity in a sermon that has been transmitted to posterity.”

Thus, he says, Leo himself forgot that the first among the Gentiles to come to worship the Messiah were the Magi, philosophers of Persia and, as it were, the forefathers of Manes. He likewise forgot that in another sermon he had said that the Magi did not recognize that Christ had been born in Judea from a celestial sign, but rather through divine inspiration acting, without doubt, in their hearts.

### 8

Here we have the whole of Beausobre’s performance, which proves the actor’s impudence and lies if we examine the Leonine context from which the three passages under dispute have been torn.

In the first of them nothing whatsoever occurs that is alien to faith or truth, and Saint Leo did not discover anything in it that the Manichaeans did not profess.

For in that fourth sermon on the Epiphany, after recalling to the people the mystery of the Incarnation and explaining at greater length what pertained to the solemnity of the day, the arrival of the Magi at Bethlehem, the gifts they offered, and that celestial sign which had brought them from the distant regions of the East, Leo attacked and harassed the Manichaeans whom he had shortly before discovered hiding in the City. In summary, he reported to the people the sacrilegious inventions and fabulous lies by which they subverted the truth of the Incarnation.

What then? So as not to detain the people with too many details, he reduced the principal points of all their errors to a brief summary: namely, that they rejected the Mosaic Scriptures, corrupted the Gospels, despised the apostolic truth of the Creed, and, denying that the living and the dead would be judged by Christ, taught that Christ should be worshipped in the sun and moon and that Manichaeus himself, the teacher of such impieties, should be worshipped under the name of the Holy Spirit.

Who does not see that these two things are very different? One is that Manichaeus called himself the Holy Spirit; the other is that his disciples worshipped Manichaeus under the name of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: We ourselves noted this in the margin of this chapter, so that the reader might understand at a single glance what Manes the teacher had taught and what the Manichaean disciples had believed in Leo’s age. Moreover, our manuscript copies have *God* in place of *holy*. Saint Leo, Sermon 2 on Pentecost, chapter 6 and following.]

Saint Leo the Great affirmed only the latter concerning the Manichaeans. He did so in precisely the same way that the sacrilegious also claimed that Christ was worshipped in the sun and moon; yet they did not babble that the sun and moon were Christ.

Nor did our Leo reason in any other way in the other sermon on Pentecost, when he undertook to refute the Manichaeans of his own age. They claimed to follow some great and sublime author and believed that the Holy Spirit had appeared in Manes, their teacher, and that the Paraclete promised by the Lord had not come before this wretched deceiver arose, in whom the Holy Spirit had dwelt in such a way that Manes himself was nothing other than the Spirit of God.

If, therefore, we attend to these words of Leo as they are presented according to the Manichaeans’ own position, we understand nothing at all that could have enabled Beausobre to call Saint Leo unfaithful and unjust. For it was established for the holy pontiff that the Manichaeans professed such perverse doctrines—not from a false rumor among men, nor from the testimony of others, but because he had proved all these things from the confessions of the Manichaeans themselves and from their execration of their crimes.

Everyone, therefore, must be convinced that the non-Catholic Beausobre was always looking for a knot in a bulrush, fabricating fraudulent interpretations.

### 9

But at least this will be true: that the holy pontiff wronged the Holy Spirit when he confined him within narrow boundaries and indicated that the peoples of the East were deprived of his assistance and protection. Away with this fiction!

Saint Leo relates how Manes appeared in the world, destined for condemnation, during the consulship of Probus and Paulinus. From this chronological indication he clearly demonstrates that, from the death of Christ until the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, the eighth persecution against Christians had already raged and innumerable martyrs had existed. According to the divine promises in Matthew 19, the Holy Spirit had been given to them:

> “Do not consider how or what you should speak,” and so forth.

Leo argues, as though following the arguments of Archelaus, that God could not have restrained the abundance of his gifts and deprived so many generations of the Church of his inspiration until the monstrous standard-bearer of vile lies was born. He immediately adds concerning Manes:

> “To him not even this can be attributed, that he received any small portion of divine inspiration, since he arose from that part of the world which cannot receive the Spirit of truth.”

These latter words, however, must not be referred either to Persia or to the whole of the East, as Beausobre interpreted them, whether through delusion or malice, but to the devil, the father of lies, whose role and functions Manes performed by teaching his doctrine.

Saint Leo immediately explained himself by adding:

> “For, filled with the spirit of the devil, he resists the Spirit of Christ; and compares this with the teaching of the Paraclete among the saints of God,” and so forth.

Since it is therefore evident—a truth also proclaimed in the divine Scriptures—that the world is divided into two parts, one ruled by God and truth, the other by the devil and lies, I do not see why the sermon of Leo mentioned above, filled with divine instruction, ought not to have been transmitted to posterity.

The Evangelist John bears witness that the Lord Christ said that the world could not receive the Spirit of truth because it neither saw nor knew him.

[Note: In John 14:16 and following we read: “And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it has neither seen him nor known him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you. ” Are not the people of this world divided into two parts and classes, one of which cannot receive the Holy Spirit?]

But who, on that account, will assert that the Holy Spirit is confined within narrow boundaries? Once this game of Beausobre’s ambiguity has been removed, all the remaining objections brought forward by the critic collapse completely. We may therefore proceed to overturn the other calumnies directed against Augustine.

Anyone who might suppose that these could be set forth by me briefly would be seriously mistaken, since there are almost innumerable malicious interpretations scattered here and there throughout Beausobre’s entire work which attack and assail the holy bishop with curses. Nor is it our intention to pursue, indicate, and refute each of them here. For our work would be extended almost without limit, and we would undertake nothing more laborious or wearisome.

148 10. Accordingly, I shall first touch briefly upon only a few of the matters contained in the preliminary discourse to the second part of his *History* [Note: [Col. 0931D] Beausobre, preliminary discourse to the second part of the *History*, p. 228. Secundinus in Augustine.].

Thus, when he is about to speak of Augustine, he begins his address with certain words of Leontius of Byzantium, who writes that no one could describe the Manichaean heresy more successfully unless he had formerly been a professed Manichaean. This statement would fit Augustine exceedingly well, since from the nineteenth to the twenty-eighth year of his life he had given his name to this sect and had vigorously defended its errors against the Catholics, successfully engaging in many controversies.

But Beausobre asserts in the same place that this must be attributed to the fervor of his eloquence and intellect. For Secundinus reproached him for not having understood the Manichaean mysteries [Col. 0931B]:

> For you seemed to me—and certainly this is so—never to have been a Manichaean, nor could you, as one who was unfamiliar with its secret mysteries, have known its hidden things and attacked Hannibal and Mithridates under the name of Manichaeus.

Beausobre ironically asserts that this paradox suffers from many contradictions. First, it was uttered by a heretic. Second, it is contradicted by the preconceived opinion of the world, namely, by those who possess greater knowledge and authority. What? Was Augustine less learned than the other Latin Fathers, less penetrating in mind, the oracle of the Western Church—and did he spend nine years among the Manichaeans without penetrating their system? Could Secundinus have uttered anything more reckless or absurd?

Therefore, he says, one of two things must be affirmed: either Augustine did not sufficiently understand their system, or Saint Augustine changed it—something which, he thinks, no one could affirm without being accused of heresy. “For my part,” he adds, “I value this Father’s excellent qualities above all others; I consider his intellect and wisdom with admiration, I honor his memory, and I esteem his long labors. But the best rules of logic and experience have taught me that one must not rely upon his statements and testimony. The ancients never claimed infallibility; it was only posterity that eventually bestowed it upon them. They were human beings, as we are.”

And shortly afterward he writes:

> I do not wish to defend the claim that Saint Augustine changed or corrupted the Manichaean system in order to win a victory; that would be to call him guilty of violating the faith. But it is certain that he made use of certain sophisms and often expressed their religion incorrectly.

These and other insults of the same kind he wrote against Augustine, which we are ashamed to report one by one. Therefore, so that he might lend credibility among his readers to what has already been said, he appends various examples and proofs.

The first of these is taken from Augustine’s words:

> For the enemy who hoped that he had crucified that same Savior, the Father of the righteous, was himself crucified; at that time one thing was done and another was displayed.

Beausobre asserts that Augustine said this according to the Manichaean opinion, and he cites both the *Epistle of the Foundation* and the *Book on Faith*, chapter 28. To these words he adds:

> The Manichaean was compelled to say that it was not Christ, but the prince of darkness with his companions, who suffered all those things.

Finally, speaking of the souls of plants—which the Manichaeans believed contained a part of divinity, whose prerogatives they said were still preserved in plants and fruits, and which alone perished and was annihilated when fruits and vegetables were taken as food; once these entered the flesh of the person eating them, they lost all understanding—and for this reason, he says, a Teacher was sent to human beings, because in them God’s part had become foolish, whereas he was not sent to melons, because they possessed a wise soul.

These three examples, then, Beausobre first brought forward as statements made by Augustine according to the Manichaean opinion, asserting that such offenses had been falsely attributed to the Manichaeans by the orthodox as doctrines of that sect.

11. I will not deny that these three matters offended me in the *Book on Faith against 149 the Manichaeans*, which had once been wrongly attributed to Augustine. But they are plainly absent from another book which Augustine certainly composed against the *Epistle of the Foundation*. I examined this work not cursorily but carefully, and found no word in it that suggested anything similar.

But who can be unaware that the *Book on Faith* was not Augustine’s work? Bellarmine, Vadingus, and others observed that it was not listed among his works, nor in the *Retractations*, nor in Possidius’s catalogue. They also noticed that its style differed from Augustine’s and that its method of argument was weaker, while its author had merely attempted to imitate Augustine—not only by expressing his ideas and occasionally using his words, but especially by drawing from the book *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*. For this reason the latest editors of Saint Augustine’s works attributed the work to Evodius and relegated it to the appendix of volume eight.

Those who have attempted to sell uncertainties as certainties and falsehoods as truths cannot marvel enough at Beausobre’s negligence—or, I should say, fraud [Note: Consult the preliminary notice of the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur concerning the *Book on Faith against the Manichaeans*, which was relegated to the appendix of volume VIII of Saint Augustine’s works, p. 25; *On the Nature of the Good*, 44; *Against Faustus*, book XX, 6; *Against Felix*, book II.].

12. Let us nevertheless grant, for the sake of argument, that Augustine wrote these things according to the Manichaean opinion, since he perhaps expressed similar ideas in *On the Nature of the Good*. What then? Did Augustine devise and fabricate similar ravings in order to arouse horror against the Manichaeans, as Beausobre subsequently suggests?

He calumniates him in other examples. For in the passages cited by Beausobre, Augustine neither relies upon false principles nor derives false conclusions from true Manichaean principles. In those passages Augustine is dealing with the disgraceful inventions and fabrications by which the Manichaeans dishonored God. Since it would be too burdensome to list them here, I pass them over, lest I appear to trouble the reader; I also consider this unnecessary, since anyone can turn to the reading of Augustine’s own text.

Nevertheless, I cannot conceal Beausobre’s license in claiming that these things were falsely derived from Manichaean principles. “For,” he says, “those unfortunate people read these things; they say this, hear this, believe this. In the seventh book of their *Treasure*—for so they call a certain Manichaean writing in which these blasphemies were recorded—it is set down in this manner: ‘Then that blessed father,’ and so forth.”

Augustine therefore added nothing from his own imagination. He appeals to the very words of the Manichaeans, copies them, and transferred them into his own work, as can be seen throughout the entire chapter cited by Beausobre.

Moreover, if Augustine had done this maliciously, does Beausobre really think that Faustus, Felix, Fortunatus, Adimantus, Secundinus, and all the others whom he attacked in his writings as offspring of Manichaeism would have remained silent instead of accusing him as a liar and impostor?

But that Secundinus did not remain silent is proved by the words cited shortly before, in which he attacks the holy bishop for not having understood the Manichaean mysteries and for attacking Hannibal and Mithridates under the name of Manichaeus.

I admit that Secundinus broke out in these words. But let Beausobre say whether Secundinus himself deserves credence, if we believe Secundinus when he criticizes Augustine because his writings shine with excessive eloquence:

> If you had wished to make this agree with the truth, it would certainly have become a great adornment for us. Do not, I beg you, act against your nature; do not be the spear of error by which the Savior’s side is pierced.

[Note: Secundinus’s letter to Saint Augustine, volume VIII of his works, p. 270; Saint Augustine’s *Against Secundinus*, in the same volume, p. 352.]

What, then, does Secundinus mock and disparage here, if not the supreme eloquence of the holy Father? Had Augustine wished to make that eloquence agree with the Manichaean principles—which the heretic claimed were holy and true, while he loudly declared the doctrines of our faith liable to falsehood—it would have become a great ornament to them.

But let us allow Secundinus to have said that Augustine was ignorant of the Manichaean mysteries. I ask, nevertheless: 150 who deserves belief? Is it the heretic, who, having a bad cause, searches everywhere for support so that he may at least make an appearance of defending it, and, lest he fall, boldly resorts to lies, exaggerations, and deceit, even lacerating the reputation and name of the holy bishop with insults? Or is it Augustine himself, who, scarcely having received the letter of this heretic, seized his pen and refuted everything alleged by his opponent?

If he had been ignorant of the Manichaean mysteries, he would have passed over the accusation in silence. But he did not remain silent. Instead, on the basis of the arguments advanced by Secundinus himself, he rejected the Manichaean sect and its doctrines even more thoroughly, with the result that the heretic, utterly and shamefully confounded, fell silent and, for as long as he lived, never again dared to attack or slander Saint Augustine.

The whole of Beausobre’s contrivance therefore collapses. Augustine understood the Manichaean system very well, and did not alter or corrupt it in the slightest respect.

12. Now, moving on to other matters, Beausobre foolishly attacks Augustine by raising the question of why the holy Doctor gave his name for nine years to the Manichaean sect, which taught such great abominations; and why he himself boldly defended those same teachings against the Catholics.

“Let him not answer,” he says, “that he belonged to the order of the Hearers, not of the Elect, and therefore was unaware of such blasphemies. For he himself asserts that they are contained in the seventh book of the Manichaeans’ *Treasure*, a book which all the sect’s followers carry in their hands.”

He then appeals to the words taken from *On the Nature of the Good* [Note: *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 44], which we ourselves cited shortly before.

Augustine, therefore, was ignorant of these blasphemies when he was a Manichaean. Or, if he was not ignorant of them, one must wonder that he remained in the sect for so long.

Beausobre heaps up these and similar arguments in order to show that the Manichaeans’ system and doctrines had been horribly altered and corrupted by false interpretations. To make this more convincing, he appeals to the two disputations which Augustine held with the presbyters Felix and Fortunatus.

He says that Felix was completely ignorant. But Fortunatus, more learned than Felix, provides some light for understanding the doctrine of that sect.

Nevertheless, it is not our present purpose to deal with these two disputations, since we have already said enough about them when reviewing all Augustine’s writings, controversies, and actions against the Manichaeans. Therefore, removing the pen from this present discussion, we have decided to investigate more carefully when the Manichaeans came to Rome.

151 **CHAPTER VIII. In what year of Christ the Manichaeans’ arrival in the City must be placed. The falsity of Paschasius Quesnellus’s judgment on this matter.**

[Col. 0933D]

1. Returning, then, to the point from which our discussion digressed, it is scarcely possible to doubt that, at the beginning of the third year of his pontificate, Saint Leo was already exercising the highest duties of the apostolate against the Manichaeans, since he publicly took action against them.

Quesnellus does not deny this. Nevertheless, according to his own manner, he describes Leo’s course of action while showing little or no concern for what had already been done against those same Manichaeans at Rome by Leo’s predecessors.

He therefore says that the Manichaeans came to Rome after their cause had been defeated in Africa and the province had been devastated by the Vandals. Now, if we trust Prosper, Victor, and Procopius, that disaster inflicted upon Africa by the Vandals occurred in the year of the Lord 427, when Geiseric crossed the sea with eighty thousand Vandals and Alans and gradually subjected the province to himself.

From this circumstance, the arrival of the Manichaeans in the City would have to be assigned only to the times of the Roman pontiffs Celestine or Sixtus. Quesnellus would consequently conclude with this further conjecture:

> This rabble of heretics remained hidden for a long time under the mask of devout people, who concealed their impiety beneath an austere appearance and way of life.

[Note: Quesnellus, volume II, dissertation on the life and deeds of Leo. See what we have already said in chapters 4, 5, and 6 above.]

But Quesnellus is forced to yield in a badly chosen cause if he observes that the Manichaeans had already long been found in the City and had been condemned to exile both by the decrees of the supreme pontiffs and by those of the emperors.

For concerning Siricius, who was elected to the pontificate in the year 384, we read:

> He found the Manichaeans and deported them into exile. He also decreed that they should not share communion with the faithful, because, with polluted mouths, they were not permitted to profane the holy body of the Lord.

Nevertheless, he did not completely deny them the salutary reconciliation of penance, provided that, sincerely returning to the bosom of the Church, they spent the remaining days of their lives confined in monasteries and devoted to fasts, prayers, and other bodily disciplines, so that, having been tested under every examination until the final day of their passing, the Church might, out of humanity, grant them the Viaticum.

2. We therefore consider it established beyond all doubt that Saint Siricius took action against this pestiferous sect in the fourth or fifth year of his pontificate.

This is clearly understood both from the novella of Theodosius the Elder, issued in the year 388, and from the rescript of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, Sabinus, Bassianus, and the other bishops of that province, sent to the same pontiff in the year 390, after they had assembled concerning the case of Jovinian.

Among other things, they assert the following:

> A Manichaean is one who denies the truth and denies the flesh of Christ; and therefore there is no remission of sins, but only the impiety of the Manichaeans, which the most merciful emperor has execrated, and which all who have encountered them have shunned as a kind of contagion.

They immediately add that the Manichaeans were expelled from Milan in Siricius’s time, with the support of the law enacted by the emperor Theodosius the Elder:

> Our brothers and fellow presbyters Crescens, Leopardus, and Alexander are witnesses—men burning with the Holy Spirit—who, after they had been condemned amid universal execration, drove them from the City like fugitives.

[Note: This rescript is found in volume II of the Councils, p. 1220.]

Siricius had sent these three presbyters, whom the Milanese Fathers call witnesses, to Milan with his letters. 152 Acting there as legates of the Apostolic See, they drove the Manichaeans from that city, as we also understand from this pontiff’s letter to the Church of Milan.

Finally, when the aforementioned Fathers of the Milanese Church conclude the same rescript, they declare that they had followed the judgment of the Roman pontiff exactly, so that they had not dared either to add anything to it or to subtract anything from it.

This clearly proves that all heresies had been condemned by the authority of the Roman pontiffs and by a certain irreversible judgment, as we ourselves demonstrated in the preceding chapters.

Accordingly, they say:

> You should know that Jovinianus, Auxentius, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Genialis, Martinianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, whom Your Holiness condemned, have also been condemned among us according to your judgment.

From this it is therefore plainly evident that the Manichaeans had already sought hiding places for themselves in Rome and in other cities of Italy at least forty years before the devastation inflicted upon Africa by the Vandals.

That pestiferous offspring was already being punished everywhere by imperial and priestly penalties in the year 390, when the Milanese Fathers issued this rescript [Note: Letter 2 of Siricius to the Church of Milan. It is found in volume II of the Councils, p. 1218.].

Gothofredus entirely supports us in his annotation on the Theodosian Code. From the words cited above, he concludes that Pope Siricius was undoubtedly the author of Theodosius’s law against the Manichaeans.

3. Nevertheless, we do not deny that this rabble of heretics, coming from Africa or other overseas regions, settled in Rome and in other Italian cities.

This can easily be inferred from the *Life of Pope Anastasius I*. After the death of Siricius, Anastasius was elevated to the pontificate and issued decrees that no foreigner from overseas should be admitted to the honor of the clergy unless he produced written recommendations from five bishops, “because at that same time Manichaeans had also been found in the city of Rome.”

But Anastasius ascended the throne of Peter in the year of Christ 398, that is, twenty-nine years before the Vandal crossed the sea with his forces.

Therefore, the migration of the Manichaeans to the City must by no means be dated from the defeat of Africa by the Vandals.

Although, in fact, we do not deny that after the devastation of Africa the Manichaeans became more numerous in the City, where people of this wicked sect had long before secured protection for themselves in hiding places.

This is what Leo’s words in sermon 15, chapter 5, signify:

> These people, therefore, utterly accursed and pestiferous, whom the upheaval of other regions has brought to us in greater numbers, reject completely from your friendship.

[Note: Saint Leo the Great, sermon 15, chapter 5.]

Because Quesnellus failed to notice this passage, he fell disgracefully.

But let us pass over Quesnellus’s error, lest we seem too eager to attack those who, both while Quesnellus was alive and now that he is dead, have subscribed so completely to his statements and opinions that they have judged him—if not in dogmatic matters, at least in historical and ancient disciplinary matters—not to have been so greatly deceived and to deserve greater esteem.

For our part, following in his footsteps only to trample them underfoot, and lest we mistake the unknown for the known and the uncertain for the certain, we wish everyone to be convinced of this one point: the arrival of the Manichaean sect in the City occurred at least forty years before Africa was occupied by the forces of the Vandals.

4. With these most solid foundations thus laid, we believe that the Manichaeans remained concealed in the regions of Italy until the pontificate of Leo.

Nor, for that reason, was the city of Rome entirely cleansed of this pollution, although civil and ecclesiastical law had already provided that such people should be sent beyond the borders of Italy under penalty of exile and that penitents should be confined in monasteries.

Those crafty men, however, after laws had been enacted against them, dared not openly profess their sacrilegious errors of superstition. Instead, they employed such complete concealment in everything that, in order to hide their infidelity more effectively, they continued to participate with Catholics in the divine mysteries, lest their superstition and condemned religion be made 153 suspect either to the ministers of the world or to those of the Church.

Moreover, they were accustomed to frequent only secluded and more secret places, especially when they celebrated their sacrilegious assemblies. Their entrances and approaches were open only to those who, first instructed in obscene and criminal rites and enticed by carnal pleasures, professed under oath that they would defend the wicked heresy.

What wonder, then, that by employing such care and exercising such diligence they were able to remain hidden for a long time?

Such is the habit of wicked people: when they wish to perpetrate the gravest crimes by more cunning means and fear the power of judges, they flatter themselves—raised up by a vain hope—that they can escape public penalties, provided they enlist hiding places as accomplices in their crimes.

Nor, finally, when that Manichaean offspring inhabited the City, had the Roman people been completely cleansed and freed from every superstition. Many remnants of the pagans and Jews still survived, engaging in public spectacles—namely, the Lupercalia, circus games, Bacchanalia, Augustalia, Saturnalia, and similar entertainments—as the letters of Pope Hormisdas and the sermons of our Leo most clearly testify.

Therefore, since the Manichaean heresy professed many errors akin to the inventions, rites, and indecencies of pagans and Jews, as we have already seen, it could easily remain hidden for a long time within the boundaries of that city, since piety, faith, and religion were not equally strong in all its citizens.

When Leo learned of this, he addressed the people publicly and did not conceal the matter. He said:

> Since the devil holds a manifold dominion over all perversities, he nevertheless built his citadel in the madness of the Manichaeans and found in them a very spacious hall in which he might display himself more exultantly; there he possessed, in general, not merely one form of depravity but a mixture of all errors and impieties at once.

Then, more directly relevant to our subject, he adds:

> For whatever is profane among the pagans, whatever is blindly carnal among the Jews, whatever is unlawful in the secret practices of magic, and whatever is sacrilegious and blasphemous in all heresies—this has flowed together into these people as into a kind of sewer, with every sort of filth coagulated in it.

[Note: Sermon 8, *On Collections and Almsgiving*, chapter 4.]

4. Therefore, so that the holy pontiff would not allow himself to be deceived by a fabricated appearance of virtue or a false shadow of piety; so that the canons of the Roman pontiffs who preceded him and the laws of the emperors would not be rendered ineffective; and finally, so that nothing should perish from the holy flock entrusted to him, he omitted nothing that might expose the institutions, corrupt life, and hidden dwellings of these heretics.

Accordingly, in order to apply a remedy to this grave evil—which spread secretly like a cancer and undermined many—and to prepare its destruction, he first began publicly to denounce that sect of the devil in the churches, when the people were gathered in greater numbers.

He showed how shameful it would be if sons whose ancestors had learned the Gospel of the cross of Christ from the very mouths of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul [Note: Saint Leo the Great, sermon 15, chapter 5, and sermon on the octave of the Apostles] allowed themselves to be corrupted by such abominable errors.

He achieved both purposes admirably. For when he continually denounced this pollution during the sacred rites and instituted a general inquiry into those heretics, some who, led astray by weakness or ignorance, had fallen into such superstitious crimes wished to cure their own guilt; with the greatest sorrow of soul and lamentation of heart, they sincerely abhorred the crimes they had committed.

Others, however, who stubbornly defended the heresy, indulging in the enticements of the flesh and other superstitions, were punished with bodily and spiritual penalties. They were not merely compelled to wander about as vagrants and fugitives, deprived of every right and honor and driven from place to place; after being proscribed by the Church and hated and expelled by all the rulers and magistrates of the state, they finally sought refuge beyond the borders of Italy.

Thus, after the cities of Catholic Italy had been cleansed, we ought to congratulate Siricius 154 and Leo—especially because in the conduct of these holy pontiffs we discover that the form of ecclesiastical inquiry against heretical depravity was established and confirmed, as will soon become clear from what follows.

**CHAPTER IX. Saint Leo the Great’s Roman inquiry into the Manichaeans. Five principal features of the form of his judgment, noted and examined both from his own writings and from the laws of the Roman emperors.**

[Col. 0936D]

1. I already foresee that what I am now about to say will prove exceedingly unwelcome, or at least scarcely agreeable, to the petty scholars—not to mention those who violate the faith.

Since they have never turned over the volumes of the ancient holy Fathers, nor drawn or tasted the history of ecclesiastical affairs from anything but corrupt and depraved sources, we shall appear to them to be trifling or inventing things.

When I once began speaking about this inquiry of Leo’s in private conversations concerning ancient literary matters, certain men who had not yet thoroughly examined the writings of the holy pontiff judged me in this way. They insisted that the rights of the Apostolic See and the structure of ecclesiastical judgments should never be derived from doubtful and uncertain conjectures.

Those who opposed my statements were really considering among themselves that the form of judgment and the name of inquiry had originated in ecclesiastical trials not from Leo but from more recent centuries.

At that time I had resolved to compose a fairly lengthy dissertation on the subject, derived from no sources other than the works of the holy pontiff. I also intended to prove in it the ancient discipline of the Church, and especially Saint Leo’s manner of acting in investigating and condemning the Manichaean heretics.

After considering the matter more carefully, however, I thought it more appropriate to postpone treating this subject to the present place. I am therefore compelled to set out the following five points.

2. First, that the term “inquiry” was already used in Leo’s time to indicate the form of judgment which the Roman Church then pursued in investigating indiscriminately Christians of every order and rank who had been infected with heretical corruption;

[Col. 0937B]

Second, that those suspected of heresy and apprehended were required to appear before the judges of the Church, so that they might answer the charge and submit to judgment;

Third, that the accused themselves, when brought before the priests, were customarily compelled both to confess their crimes and to express their detestation of them;

Fourth, that Christians of every order and condition were then also bound by a certain oath to report—or, as they say, denounce—to the presbyters of their churches or parishes anyone suspected of heresy;

Finally, that those contaminated by heresies were not merely bound by the penalties of ecclesiastical censures. If punishment had not been sufficiently exhausted, they were also handed over to the secular power, which the Church summoned to its assistance, and subjected to various other punishments.

We shall endeavor to make these five points so clear and established from Leo alone that henceforth lying lips uttering falsehood will fall silent.

[Col. 0937C]

The first point we undertake to prove here is gathered chiefly from the fifteenth sermon [Note: Saint Leo the Great, sermon 15, chapter 4], in which the holy pontiff speaks both about the fast of the tenth month and about almsgiving.

Shortly beforehand, in the presence of priests and clerics, together with the most distinguished senate of the City and other noblemen, he had taken action against certain people infected with the Manichaean taint. 155

Therefore, in order to indicate the form of judgment which his pastoral vigilance had followed, both in investigating and exposing these wicked people and in publicly denouncing and restraining them, he used no other term than “inquiry.”

In the fourth chapter, when he is about to speak of their obscene and abominable sacrifices and solemnities, he says:

> Concerning their sacred rites, however, which among them are as obscene as they are abominable, we do not remain silent about what the Lord wished to disclose to our inquiry.

He then explains how those who had been brought to judgment revealed their impious doctrines and execrable crimes. Those who were present at such a confession could scarcely hear it without the greatest horror of soul.

Since Saint Leo, endowed with divine power and forewarned by revelation, knew beforehand that only one part of the guilty people concealed in the City had been restrained and exposed in that solemn and most holy assembly, he therefore resolved not to abandon his undertaking before bringing such a homily to a close.

Indeed, he promises that he will persevere in the same inquiry until the whole City had been completely cleansed of such a contagion. His more careful vigilance in the exercise of his supreme apostolate especially demanded this:

> For this reason the merciful God disclosed to us a certain part of the guilty, so that, once the danger had been revealed, the diligence of vigilance might be aroused. What has been done must not suffice; rather, the same inquiry must continue. With God’s help, it achieves this result: not only that those who are upright may remain unharmed, but also that many who have been deceived by diabolical seduction may be recalled from error.

[Note: Leo the Great, the sermon cited above, chapter 6.]

Thus illuminated by the divine Spirit, and possessing the greatest strength of soul and firmness of mind—qualities in which our Leo excelled in conducting and governing divine and sacred matters—he rightly foresaw that nothing more useful, nothing holier or more beneficial to the Christian profession, could be desired than this method of action.

By it the integrity of faith and morals is defended and preserved, the worship and honor of God are increased, and the Church herself is kept free from the many great stains of vice by which she could be weakened through diabolical contagion.

Conversely, if people are found within the Church who are either imbued with heresies or defiled by the filth of wicked crimes, they can easily return to the right path of truth if they begin to repent. If, however, they persist in their errors with stubborn obstinacy, they are restrained by ecclesiastical censures and removed from communion with the whole Church.

Because the rulers and magistrates of the world recognized that this manner of acting was highly suited to the administration and governance of civil affairs, they eventually adopted the term to indicate the form of judgment by which those accused of treason are customarily punished.

But let us now proceed to another point.

### 3

Moreover, it is perfectly clear that what we proposed in the second place—namely, that the Manichaeans, emerging from their hiding places, were summoned to judgment at the command of Pope Leo, and that they stood before an assembly of bishops, presbyters, and other devout men as defendants accused of violating the faith, so that they might submit to the judgment of the Church. From this and other similar proceedings, including those carried out at Carthage and in other African churches, which in Augustine’s time were harassed by the Manichaeans, we understand very well that Christian offenders of whatever order and rank, condition or sex, must also be subject to the public judgments of the sacred shepherds—especially in cases in which the integrity and truth of the faith are being safeguarded.

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 46. Possidius, in the *Life of Augustine*.]

Thus their pernicious opinion is easily refuted: they wish to confine ecclesiastical jurisdiction within narrow limits and maintain that it can scarcely extend beyond those men who, through clerical orders, are devoted to the ministry of the altar. These men, they say, sacred shepherds—especially when assembled in 156 councils—may depose from their respective ranks, deprive of the benefices, titles, and prebends of their churches, and finally banish, cast, and confine within monastic enclosures or the most restrictive prisons. But laymen, they say, living outside the sacred hierarchy, ought not to be subject to such inquiries, investigations, and judgments. They have their own magistrates and judges, before whom they may be summoned to judgment; and it is chiefly the task of these authorities to investigate the lives, morals, and practices of citizens. Finally, if the prelates of the churches possess any power over laymen, it extends only to matters relating to participation in sacred communion, the administration of the sacraments, or the celebration of the divine mysteries—matters from which laymen may, for a just and reasonable cause, be deprived and excluded from sacred assemblies.

In this way, in actual fact, men ignorant of the law and corrupted in conscience could attempt to overturn the foundations of Catholic discipline. They do not possess the light of faith by which they might understand that the Church has acquired jurisdiction over all who, having first renounced every impiety of the world, have given themselves to Christ—when, that is, through more solemn rites, they swore in the chief sacrament of the Catholic religion to profess the Catholic religion throughout the whole course of their lives and to obey the Church.

What, then, are we to say? If, after violating the faith, they could in reality abuse divine and sacred things and, as it were, tear apart the body and entrails of this most holy mother—if the Church possessed no jurisdiction over laymen for restraining impiety—who would ever repair the rifts made by heresies? Who would cleanse the threshing floor? [Col. 0939A] Who, finally, could confront and heal more serious diseases, lest, as the scab of evil opinions spread, the whole community of Christians, weakened by errors, should be brought to destruction?

Could princes and the magistrates of the world perhaps do what they deny the Church is able to do? Away with such a fiction! They are occupied with the civil administration of temporal affairs. They watch lest, when the rights of nature and of governments have been violated, the commonwealths be thrown into disorder, with the greatest injury to justice, by those who, because of their crimes, do not hesitate to inflict disturbance, violence, and injury upon themselves, public affairs, and the common peace. Nevertheless, for this reason the princes of the world cannot involve themselves in ecclesiastical and spiritual matters without contempt for divine law and sacrilege, except when the priests themselves request protection and assistance for vindicating the rights of religion.

Scripture everywhere testifies to this; so do the records of the Fathers and, finally, the letters and laws of ancient kings and emperors. Our present purpose does not permit us to bring all these matters forward. We should not appear, by passing from fact to law, to wander outside the writings of Leo’s works. Yet if we wished to strengthen belief in this matter, we could appeal either to the decrees of Pope Siricius cited in the preceding chapter, or to the similar procedure maintained by the bishops of Africa in the time of Augustine and Possidius. At that time, when the tribune Ursus was in charge of the imperial household, Manichaeans discovered at Carthage were brought before the tribunal of the Church. Among them were a girl named Margarita, who, although not yet twelve years old, claimed that she had been corrupted through the ritual of their crimes, and another woman named Eusebia, regarded as a nun, who had suffered a similar corruption because of a most shameful crime.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] Concerning this African investigation of the Manichaeans, see what we wrote in chapters 5 and 6 of this book, p. 136 and following.]

These events, I say, and others of the same kind would add credibility to our assertions. But since we are dealing with the Roman investigation of the Manichaeans, the logic of our undertaking requires us to return to Saint Leo.

### 4

Leo, therefore, to establish his own credibility and to show that he had not been wholly deceived by any fraud or proceeded rashly in discovering and publishing the impieties of the Manichaeans, openly testified that he had not trusted doubtful reports or uncertain opinions. He therefore adds:

> With the bishops and presbyters seated together with me, and Christian men and nobles assembled in the same meeting, we ordered their chosen men and women to be brought forward.

They were therefore being held in chains, or at least under guard, when the holy pontiff ordered them to stand before so numerous and distinguished an assembly. For if they had not yet been apprehended and were still entirely free, who does not see that they would immediately have seized the opportunity to flee, attempting to escape the disgrace, confusion, and shame of infamy? Especially since nature itself has given to all human beings, of every order and condition, an extreme dread of the presence of a judge, the severity of a sentence, and the harshness of punishments.

When Leo himself calls the men and women brought before him “chosen,” he wished by those words to indicate that the criminals did not occupy an inferior rank within that sect but had claimed the leading position. Among them, the one who stood out most prominently had been appointed by them as a kind of bishop, so that he might preside over the others through profane rites and diabolical superstitions.

For, Leo adds:

> All the persons through whom that unspeakable crime had been perpetrated were present.

That is, the girl, who was scarcely ten years old, and the two women who had brought her up and prepared her for this crime. Also present was the adolescent who had corrupted the girl, and their bishop, the organizer of their detestable crime.

Augustine agrees with this in his *On Heresies*, writing to the Carthaginian deacon Quodvultdeus:

> Recently some of them were discovered and brought to the Church, as the episcopal records that you sent us show.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] Consult also Augustine, *On Heresies*, and his letter to Quodvultdeus. [Col. 0940D]]

Let those, therefore, who—I do not know why—are so disposed in mind and character that they dread the name and functions of sacred investigation, and who consequently venture to disparage this form of judgment, stand here with me for a little while. Let them consider whether those women or men of whom Leo speaks could once have been devoted to the ministries of the altar through clerical orders. Let them explain why that sacred assembly took action both against incontinent persons and incestuous offenders, and against pimps and corrupted women who mingled immodesty with religious matters.

If we suppose that this was done unjustly, why was no protest raised by the Senate of the Roman people, by the Roman populace, or finally by the emperor? Was it, then, by divine right that the shepherds of the Church, already in the fourth and fifth centuries, exercised indiscriminate power to punish all the baptized, so that they might restrain the audacity of those who had fallen away from devotion to the true God?

### 5

But since the matter shines forth through examples and arguments so clear and numerous, there is no reason to linger over it any longer. Those two points, which have thus far been examined through a great abundance of records and the weight of arguments, are followed by a third, radiating everywhere with the light of the most genuine truth. From it, once the order of events has first been revealed and then the public confession of crimes made by the Manichaeans has been recognized, no room for further doubt will remain concerning the ecclesiastical discipline now under discussion.

For the question was not considered merely on the basis of the indications brought forward, or even of the gravest testimonies. Rather, after a lengthy examination of the facts, the accused were brought before the assembly, questioned, and made to answer; and the notaries themselves, summoned for this purpose, recorded the proceedings. Thus, with the greatest diligence, all the doctrines, all the lies and obscenities, and finally all the unspeakable sacraments, mysteries, and solemnities of that sect were actually investigated, so that nothing remained unclear either to the less credulous or to the detractors.

I think no one can fail to see how powerful such Acts may be against the less credulous or the detractors of our own age.

The crimes of the Manichaeans were not disclosed in some secret and hidden confession, which we call sacramental confession. Rather, the entire assembly heard them in the external and solemn forum of judgment, and ecclesiastical scribes committed them to writing—as had previously been done in the Church of Carthage. Saint Leo finally ordered that these records be deposited and preserved for the memory of posterity in the archives of the Roman Church, as he himself testified not once, or twice, but at least three times in his writings.

Thus, in the sermon repeatedly cited, we read:

> All of them were alike, and there was one confession; and what was accursed was disclosed, something our ears could scarcely endure.

Lest, by speaking more openly about it, we offend chaste ears, the documentary records of the proceedings are sufficient. They teach with complete clarity that in this sect there was no modesty, no honor, and absolutely no chastity; in it the law is falsehood, the devil is religion, and sacrifice is depravity.

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Sermon 4, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month and on Almsgiving*; Sermon 2, *On Pentecost*, chapters 4 and 6.]

Here the holy pontiff reports, briefly and as though in summary, what was contained in the records of the proceedings. But in Sermon 4, *On the Epiphany*, chapter 5, after first listing many doctrines of the Manichaeans, he adds again:

> It is beneficial to the whole Church that many of them—namely, the Manichaeans—were discovered through the Lord’s mercy, and that the sacrileges in which they lived were disclosed by their own confession.

Again, in Sermon 4, *On the Nativity*, chapter 4, he writes:

> In addition to all the devilish abominations they have devised, at the very principal feast of their observance, as their recent confession has revealed, they rejoice in pollution both of soul and of body.

And in the second sermon *On Pentecost*, after explaining the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity and the sending of the Holy Spirit, he attacks in chapter 2, as we have already said, the Manichaeans who asserted that the divine Spirit had appeared in Manichaeus, their teacher, and that the Paraclete promised by the Lord had not come until this unhappy deceiver arose—one in whom the Holy Spirit had dwelt in such a way that Manichaeus himself was nothing other than the Spirit, who through the ministry of bodily voice and tongue would lead his disciples into all truth.

At that time Leo attacked and refuted only this particular error of the Manichaeans. He refrained from speaking about the rest, fearing that in so large and solemn an assembly of devout believers he might offend more sacred and purer Christian ears or prepare a stumbling block of scandal against which they might strike. He therefore concludes that chapter in these words:

> Out of modesty, these things ought not to be brought forth in our speech, since they have already been disclosed with the greatest fullness by their own confession.

The confession and abhorrence of their crimes by the Manichaeans was therefore so solemn and public that the report of the proceedings must have reached the ears of all the Romans.

[Col. 0941B] Since all these events had taken place before the eyes of the whole Church, as Prosper writes in his *Chronicle*, no sane person could fear or doubt that power and jurisdiction of the sacred prelates which the consuls, the senators, and finally the emperor himself had approved by common consent.

That no one resisted Leo’s procedure or attempted to provide assistance to the Manichaeans condemned to exile—as ordinarily happens when the legitimacy of a judge is questioned—has already been made abundantly clear in the letter to the bishops of Italy. From it we learn how, after the city had been completely purged of that heresy, he sent those bishops copies of the Acts in which the confession of the Manichaeans’ crimes and their abhorrence of them had been faithfully and sincerely recorded.

A little later, suspicion arose that the Manichaeans, by the crafty method they commonly employed, might seek new hiding places in other Italian cities and localities. Therefore, fulfilling the duties of a most watchful shepherd, he divinely provided for the safety of the other churches and for the integrity of their faith and morals. So that he might not seem to have failed either himself or his office, in the aforementioned letter he warned all the bishops of the cities of Italy about what had already taken place at Rome. He feared that, while ignorant—or at least not yet fully informed—of these matters, they might allow the seeds of vice that had been destroyed and extinguished there to be secretly planted anew through fresh shoots in their dioceses:

> We summon you, dearly beloved brothers, into partnership in our concern . . . .

And shortly afterward he adds:

> Lest the disease which, through the revelation of the Lord’s mercy, is driven away from our sheep by our care should spread through your churches while you have not yet been warned and remain unaware of what is happening; lest it should find for itself secret tunnels of concealment; lest what is extinguished by us in the City should be planted among you with hidden roots.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] Letter to the bishops of Italy, eighth in Quesnellus, elsewhere 11, chapter 1.]

### 6

The bishops of Italy could easily understand from what follows how great and manifold a debt the Roman people and the whole Church owed to him. In these subsequent words he explains with complete clarity what he had thought, what he had done, and what he had finally achieved when he discovered the followers and teachers of the Manichaean sect hiding in the City:

> Our investigation discovered very many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety in the City; vigilance exposed them; authority and censure restrained them. Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected. We compelled them publicly in the Church, by profession and by their own signatures, to condemn Manichaeus, together with his preaching and disciples; and thus, after they had confessed from the abyss of their impiety, we raised them up by granting them penance.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] See what was said in chapter 7 of the preceding chapter of this book. We have vindicated the procedure of the holy pontiff against the curses and insults of Beausobre.]

Here, then, in this one passage, is contained much concerning the authority of the Roman See and Leo’s divinely guided procedure. At the command of the Church, the teachers of the Manichaean sect and their disciples were first detained; then they were brought into an assembly so that they might be compelled to confess their crimes publicly and retract them in the same solemn profession. For the firmness of this process, the signatures of the accused and a sincere resolve to perform penance were both necessary.

Thus, through the revelation of divine mercy, our Leo employed this procedure in order to raise the rebuked and penitent Manichaeans from the abyss of their impiety. What crimes and shameful mysteries had been entered and attested in the records of the investigation was explained in full by the sequence of the proceedings.

Therefore, for the instruction of other bishops, and so that they might have a correct rule for how they ought to conduct themselves in such cases, the holy pontiff ordered various copies of those same Acts to be made and sent them, together with the present letter, to those bishops. By casting their eyes over the written volume, they could see, almost at a single glance, what had been done and what ought to be done in future cases of the same kind.

To strengthen this truth further, what else can we do but transcribe the words of the holy pontiff?

> Everything profane or shameful that they possess both in their writings and in their secret traditions, we established with certain disclosure before the eyes of the Christian people, so that our people might know what to reject or avoid. Indeed, the man who was said to be their bishop, when held by us, revealed the disgraceful things that he maintained in his mysteries, as the sequence of the proceedings can teach you. For your instruction we have also sent you the proceedings themselves; when you have read them, you will be able to know everything that was censured by us.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] In the same letter to the bishops of Italy, chapter 1. We shall present this letter, corrected against the most ancient Vatican manuscripts, with God’s help. We wish to warn the reader that we shall frequently defend their readings in these *Exercitations*, lest anyone suspect that we have departed improperly from the editions of others. [Col. 0942D]]

### 7

The fourth point that follows contains something still greater, so that nothing clearer or more illuminating for our purpose can be devised—namely, for asserting that ecclesiastical law by which all the faithful, without distinction, were commanded both to avoid the society of heretics, especially the most harmful, and to denounce those same persons to the sacred shepherds of the Church.

Leo himself, as we saw shortly before, spoke in sacred assemblies and before crowds of people about their doctrines, secret traditions, and profane and shameful mysteries for no other reason than that the people might know what to flee or avoid.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] Quesnellus deleted *quid*, despite the contrary evidence of other editions and Vatican manuscript copies, and above inserted *potestis* for *poteritis*.]

Sacred shepherds have always made it their practice to display with the greatest clarity to Catholic men the marks and signs of every false doctrine. Thus those who carried pure hearts in their breasts, abhorring the shameful appearance of superstitions, might guard against them; and weaker and more ignorant people might not, deceived by the false appearance of piety and entering into the protection and society of the wicked, be stained by a similar pollution of vice.

This was the procedure of the holy pontiff, and this was his purpose in delivering sacred homilies. Therefore, after publicly attacking Manichaeus and his disciples more than once, he did not wish their crimes and errors to be concealed under any veil of secrecy. He exposed them openly, so that they might deceive no one by their distinctions concerning food, the filthiness of their clothing, or the pallor of their faces.

Indeed, by an explicit command he wished to ensure that no Christian should have anything in common with such people:

> Let there be no society with such people, and no association.

Then, after exposing the rest of their deceptive practices, he adds, in words directly relevant to our subject:

> Thus far they have harmed the unwary; thus far they have mocked the inexperienced. After this, no one’s fall will be excusable; nor should the person henceforth be regarded as simple, but as thoroughly wicked and perverse, if he is found bound by that unspeakable error.

Similar passages are also found in other places, such as the fourth sermon *On the Nativity of the Lord* and likewise the fourth *On Lent*. In the fifth sermon *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*, which we have cited more than once here, after first generally warning all the faithful to renounce the friendship and society of the Manichaeans, he then turns specifically to women and urges them with all the strength of his soul to abstain from their acquaintance and conversations, lest, while the unwary ear delights in their fabulous stories, they fall into the devil’s snares.

Finally, to strengthen their faith and fortify their chastity, he recalls the fall of the first woman, who, deceived by diabolical suggestions, cast the entire human race forever from the happiness of paradise. Humanity would still lie in that most miserable and mournful condition unless the mercy of almighty God, breaking the snares of the demon and freeing it from the bonds of sin, had liberated it.

The devil, knowing that he had seduced the first man through a woman’s speech and cast all human beings from the happiness of paradise through feminine credulity, now also lies in wait for your sex with a more secure cunning, so that those whom he can entice through the agents of his falsehood he may strip both of faith and of modesty.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] Sermon 5, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*.]

### 8

If the fairness and justice of this command are properly considered, I can scarcely persuade myself that any sane person could criticize or disapprove of it. For it is highly consistent with all the laws of nature and of human society, by which it is forbidden for anyone, on private authority, to depart from the rites and institutions of his ancestors, to make and adopt new gods for himself, or secretly to introduce or establish another religion and sacred practices, unless all these things have been approved with the support of public authority.

Indeed, if everyone were permitted, according to his own inclination, to embrace innovations in matters concerning religion and moral institutions, to enter into society with innovators, or to join their association, what confusion and disorder would arise in sacred and human affairs? What disagreement among citizens? What, finally, diversity in rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices?

Moreover, would not the most serious quarrels, jealousies, dissensions, and perpetual wars break out among the priests and the other ministers of the altars? Therefore, to prevent these evils, the Senate, the magistrates of the commonwealths, and the colleges of priests, for the sake and advancement of public tranquillity, decreed even among the pagans that private individuals should have absolutely no permission to alter anything in the laws of their ancestors, devise new institutions, assign honors to gods, pursue the rites and customs of foreigners, enter into their protection, or attend their assemblies, lest, when serious discord arose among the citizens, the earlier institutions should be endangered.

Sacred and profane writers have discussed this matter most clearly, as may be seen in Livy and Tertullian.

Accordingly, the command of our holy pontiff was founded chiefly upon the precepts of the Old and New Laws, which require that one flee the companionship and intimate association of wicked and utterly criminal men, and renounce their society—men who, with execrable cunning, do not harm themselves through depraved morals so much as they constantly strive to harm others. For this reason above all, they are always seeking and taking as partners in crime those whom they know to be unwary, weaker, and more simple-minded.

Therefore Saint Leo, intent on providing for the tranquillity and welfare of the universal Church, first wished the Manichaeans themselves to be rejected from the society of Catholics; then he commanded each of Christ’s faithful to investigate them and denounce them to the sacred presbyters.

Nothing could be found more explicit than that apostolic command, expressed in these words:

> I also exhort and admonish you, dearly beloved, to report faithfully to our vigilance if any of you learns where they live, where they teach, whom they visit, and in whose company they rest.

He immediately makes clear that no one, even among the most upright and holy men, can be exempted from the duty of such denunciation:

> For it is of little benefit to anyone that, with the Holy Spirit protecting him, he himself is not captured by these people, if, when he understands that others are being captured, he is not moved. Against common enemies, for the sake of the common salvation, there must be one vigilance shared by all, lest other members also be corrupted by the wound of a single member.

But if there were some among them who, being little concerned with the Christian faith and ecclesiastical matters, were led by those empty pretexts which worldly honor, reputation, and a good name commonly implant in the mind, and who persuaded themselves under a flattering appearance that those weakened by heresy need not be brought before legitimate judges or accused before them, such persons certainly could neither provide for nor promote their own salvation. Rather, they would prepare a broader path for themselves toward undergoing the final vengeance.

Their silence would be exceedingly destructive: by it they would permit guilty men to remain hidden so that they would not suffer the punishments due for their crimes. Such silence is a grave offense, upon which the Lord will pass judgment on the last day, even though they had neither maintained fellowship with the heretics nor been weakened by the same errors.

The words of Saint Leo are truly golden:

> Those who think that such people ought not to be exposed will be found guilty of silence at Christ’s judgment, even if they were not defiled by consent.

[Note: [Col. 0944D] The same sermon cited above.]

### 8

But to open an even easier path and prescribe the simplest method for making such denunciations, and to prevent those who might think it burdensome, extremely difficult, and dangerous to appear before so great a judge in order to expose persons suspected of heresy, he entrusted the matter to the heads of the churches of the city of Rome. Thus each of the faithful could report the names, practices, and homes of heretics swiftly and easily, without embarrassment or shame and after casting off all fear and disgrace.

> We also exhort you to this diligence: make known to your presbyters the Manichaeans hiding anywhere. For it is a great act of piety to expose the hiding places of the impious and to defeat the devil himself whom they serve.

Shortly afterward, at the end of that chapter, he commends the greatness and excellence of this piety still further. He teaches that it is utterly wicked to leave unpunished those who remain hidden—men who reject, corrupt, or deny the mysteries of the New and Old Law, among whom nothing is holy, nothing whole, and nothing true.

He further adds:

> They must be guarded against, lest they harm anyone; they must be exposed, lest they remain in any part of our city. Before the tribunal of the Lord it will benefit you, dearly beloved, that we denounce what we denounce and ask what we ask.

Here many matters worthy of notice present themselves to us, and a broad field opens in which both the discipline of ecclesiastical investigation is vindicated and its principal method of procedure shines forth with the greatest clarity.

First, is not this precisely what nearly all heretics devote their strength and effort to overthrow? They insist that cases concerning religion and the Church must be brought before the tribunals of secular authority. Did not the Manichaean affair under discussion concern both divine and human matters? Yet it was brought neither before the Roman consuls, nor before the tribunes of the people, nor before the senators, nor finally before the emperors themselves, but before the presbyters presiding over the churches, who had been appointed by the pontiffs throughout the districts of the City and whom we now call parish priests.

Second, the holy pontiff wished to indicate that ecclesiastical jurisdiction over all the citizens and inhabitants of the city of Rome was real, not merely provisional or shadowy. He therefore used this grave and fully apostolic formula:

> They must be exposed, lest they remain in any part of our city.

No one, in a solemn assembly before a large crowd, would claim a city as his own if he had been deprived of true jurisdiction over it and merely lived there or happened to have originated there. He would surely have called it his homeland rather than his city.

Finally, leaving aside all the other points, a third matter cannot be concealed: we are clearly taught that those who, led by whatever pretext, do not obey such a command become guilty in matters of religion and depart from the law which requires that those polluted by heretical defilement, or suspected of it, be brought before an ecclesiastical tribunal.

Their transgression, since it calls down the wrath of God upon them, will not escape the penalties of vengeance—at least not on the last day, when it is shameful, indeed utterly shameful, not to have labored, insofar as we can, for the common cause of the faith and not to have wished to defeat the devil whom all heretics serve.

### 9

Yet the holy pontiff was not entirely satisfied with these proceedings. He devised another plan and announced the Manichaeans through a new sign, so that they might more easily be detected and Catholics might, as it were, be compelled to report their names.

He knew that this pestilential offspring—whether because of a feigned appearance of piety or because of the wicked doctrine they professed—habitually shrank from all wine made from grapes, whether pure or diluted with water, lest they should taste it. Perhaps they held this utterly wicked belief because they thought wine comparable to the gall of dragons and produced by a certain author of evils whom they fabricated as a god in their doctrines.

Therefore, to shake off so false and unworthy a belief, Leo, with the supreme prudence he possessed in conducting sacred affairs, imposed this rule upon all Catholics: in receiving communion of the sacraments, they were to be nourished not only by the eucharistic bread but also, bringing their mouths to the chalice, to drink the blood of redemption. By receiving communion under both kinds, they would openly display sincere testimony to both piety and faith.

Once this sign had been established, it was not difficult to reveal, even amid the sacred mysteries themselves, whether someone was practicing the impieties of the Manichaeans. Leo himself explains the matter more clearly than anyone could:

> Although they dare to attend our mysteries in order to conceal their unbelief, they conduct themselves in the communion of the sacraments in such a way that sometimes they cannot remain completely hidden: with an unworthy mouth they receive the body of Christ, but they altogether refuse to drink the blood of our redemption.

He immediately explains why he disclosed this to the faithful of Christ:

> We make this known to your holiness so that such people may be revealed to you by these signs, and so that those whose sacrilegious simulation has been detected may, once marked and exposed, be expelled from the company of the holy.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Sermon 41, elsewhere 4, *On Lent*, chapter 3.]

Quesnellus removed the two words *marked and exposed*, although they are retained in the editions of others and in the manuscript copies.

Meanwhile, let no one flatter himself that Leo’s procedure can in any way favor the Lutherans or others who harass the Roman Church, on the grounds that, according to the diversity of circumstances and times, it prohibited laymen from communion from the chalice. Laymen are not deprived of receiving the blood, even if they communicate under one kind only, as the teachers of theology demonstrate most clearly in their schools. Therefore there is no need for us to examine their arguments—or, rather, their foul inventions—since they collapse through the mere reading of Scripture.

I therefore think that what we have said thus far about the care and diligence required of all the faithful, without distinction, in denouncing heretics is more than sufficient.

### 10

We must now discuss the great piety of Catholic princes, whom the sacred shepherds customarily approached in the Church’s more serious affairs, asking them to act as defenders of those sanctions that concern the matters of faith, moral discipline, the government, rights, tranquillity, and protection of the churches.

The matter is clear and entirely straightforward, and we have reserved it for exposition here as our final point. To establish it, it would be sufficient merely to recall the imperial constitutions—what they call *divales*—which were issued only after being urgently requested by the Roman pontiffs, bishops, and general synods, and which were published throughout every region of the Catholic world, so that heretics who were more obstinate in mind might also be afflicted with the most severe temporal penalties.

It can scarcely be expressed in words how fiercely the religious zeal of the early Catholic princes burned against those who attempted to disturb, overthrow, and weaken the peace and faith of the Church. As soon as the princes gave their names to Christ, they also extended helping hands to the rulers of the churches, joining worldly power to their authority—whether so that the profane worship of idols might be abolished everywhere, or so that the decrees of earlier pagan rulers, which commanded that Christian men be treated as slaves and hunted everywhere to their deaths, might be annulled.

Moreover, they burned with such hatred against heretics that they deprived them of every honor, right, and privilege; assigned their possessions to the royal treasuries, whether those possessions were already held by them or had come to them through the inheritance of others; excluded them from all human society; and sometimes even inflicted capital punishment upon them.

[Col. 0946B] This, I say, was the religion of the great Constantine before he was deceived by the Eusebians; and thereafter all the Valentinians, Gratian, and the Theodosii, Arcadius, Honorius, Leo, and the other Catholic emperors pursued it with all the strength of their minds. Since it was clear to them that all the rights of imperial power derive from God Almighty, they were always a protection to these matters—not merely out of some liberal generosity or as a token of goodwill toward the affairs of the faith—but also because they understood that these matters concerned them more than the civil administration of affairs. They considered it a grave sacrilege if they defrauded the Church of her due and proper services or in any way failed in their duty to safeguard her security.

For what else does Saint Leo bring to the mind of the emperors when writing to Theodosius, Valentinian, and the Augusti Leo, and also to the Augusta Pulcheria, than precisely what we are discussing?
