From them he was requesting those forms of assistance which, in accordance with the dignity of their office and the power of their strength, ought to be bestowed upon the troubled and afflicted affairs of the [Col. 0946C] Church. Indeed, at times the holy pontiff demanded such assistance with so much force of spirit, as though it were owed to the Christian religion, that, while preserving the honor of the purple and the imperial diadem, he might seem excessively to press them. For he aroused and impressed upon their minds grave, terrible, and fear-inspiring thoughts: that they would incur the indignation of Almighty God, that the fortunes of the empire would be endangered, and that all temporal affairs would be thrown into confusion if the emperors themselves did not restrain heretics, or those suspected of heresy, by the power with which they were endowed, and drive them far from the society of Catholics. Therefore, in order more easily to obtain the help of divine mercy, and lest they depart from the piety and institutions of their ancestors, they devoted all the forces of the world at their disposal to the destruction and ruin of heretical men.

Nor will it be necessary here to cite, for a matter so frequent and customary, the laws of the emperors from the Theodosian Code [Note: [Col. 0945D] Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, title 5, “Concerning Heretics, Manichaeans, and Samaritans.]. We need only cast our eyes upon the novella of the Emperor Valentinian, which he himself confessed that he had composed lest he conceal the new crimes of the Manichaeans, recently discovered by Leo’s investigation and condemned by judicial sentence. We are speaking of the Manichaeans, whom the statutes of all preceding emperors judged accursed and to be driven from the whole world [Note: [Col. 0946D] Volume VI, p. 1, book XV, on the Theodosian Code, title 5, p. 115.].

Here Valentinian alludes to the statutes enacted by both Theodosii, the elder Valentinian, Arcadius, and Honorius, which may be consulted in the works of the jurist Gothofredus. But immediately after this Valentinian himself adds:

> Nor do the crimes recently discovered permit concealment. For what obscene things, disgraceful to say and to hear, were revealed in the judgment of the most blessed Pope Leo before the most distinguished senate by their own manifest confession? So much so that even the man who was said to be their bishop both betrayed it with his own voice and set forth all the secrets of his crimes.

**11.** These words of Valentinian provide new testimony from which we may learn that Saint Leo acted as a true and legitimate judge in the investigation of the Manichaeans, and also in demanding from them a confession of their crimes and their condemnation of those crimes, as we proved in the third place. Valentinian himself goes on to show that knowledge of what Leo had done in a solemn judgment could by no means have escaped him. Therefore, lest he neglect the role of defender of ecclesiastical judgments, and lest he too leave injuries against the Divinity unavenged, he added the strength of his power to ecclesiastical authority by promulgating a public law intended to last forever:

> Wherever in the world any Manichaean shall be discovered, let him receive, by the authority of public severity, the penalties which the laws have decreed against sacrilegious persons.

Here Valentinian had regard to the canonical penalties with which the Church was accustomed to punish sacrilegious persons. To prevent sacrilegious people from finding any means of evading them, he brought the whole authority of public severity to bear. And he says:

> Let it be a public crime, and let anyone who wishes have the power to accuse such persons without risk of prosecution.

Afterward, when the same most pious emperor discusses the temporal penalties by which the Manichaeans were to be punished in the future, he adds:

> Let it be lawful and safe for no one to conceal such men or to connive with them.

He further deprives them both of military rank and of residence in cities, repudiates them from the society of all human beings, forbids them to receive inheritances or to leave them, and orders all their goods and property to be gathered into the strength of the imperial treasury. By perpetual sanction he strips them of the right to enter into contracts or to bring actions for the recovery of property before judges. Finally, he imposes a fine of ten pounds of gold upon all commanders of any military branch or holders of any office if they know that anyone polluted by this superstition is serving in the army. [Col. 0947C]

For nothing excessive seems capable of being decreed against those whose incestuous perversity, in the name of religion, commits even in brothels acts unknown or shameful to mention.

With these words that energetic and great defender and champion of ecclesiastical authority closes his novella, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of Christ 445, when Valentinian himself was holding his sixth consulship with Flavius Nummus, as is sufficiently established from the ancient records of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0947D] Valentinian’s novella appears in Quesnellus, volume I of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 216.].

**165. CHAPTER X. The Roman council in the case of the Manichaeans. The judgment of Antonius Pagius and Paschasius Quesnellus concerning that question. Cardinal Baronius’s opinion finally vindicated against their critical annotations.**

**1.** Although, deprived by the injustice of time of various monuments, we are not supplied with every resource for initiating one new question after another that might increasingly illuminate that ancient form of ecclesiastical discipline by which the apostolic See of blessed Peter was accustomed to punish those contaminated by heretical defilement, nevertheless we believe that we possess an abundance of that sacred material which is considered useful—indeed necessary—for definitively settling the questions recently raised among the critics. Among this latter kind must certainly be counted the controversy which Father Antonius Pagius and Paschasius Quesnellus raised some time ago. Led by an excessive desire to argue or quarrel, they thought they could vigorously oppose Cardinal Baronius, maintaining, namely, that no council whatsoever had been convened at Rome in the case of the Manichaeans.

But since the celebrated father of the Ecclesiastical Annals [Col. 0948A] relied above all upon Leo’s letter to the bishops of Italy, and weighed all its evidence with mature judgment, we can by no means suppose that he fell so disgracefully when he openly declared that a council of bishops and presbyters had indeed been held at Rome.

As we now undertake to deal with this disagreement, we bring forward the principal arguments of the opposing party—namely, those by which Pagius and Quesnellus contend that the assembly in which action was taken against the Manichaeans at Rome was never called a council by the holy pontiff, but was merely called a gathering, a session, and a judgment. To lend strength to this conjecture, they appeal afterward to Valentinian’s novella, which, according to Quesnellus, contains the word *consessus* (“session”). Finally, they press Baronius with the following arguments:

> But a council was not necessary—for Saint Prosper does not in fact mention one—since the matter concerned neither the proscription of a new heresy nor the assertion of the faith, but the imposition of a penalty according to the canon of the Church; nor is it a council when, together with the priests, part of the senate **and part of the people** is present.

With these cold little arguments they persuade themselves that the word “council” must be completely erased. But do Quesnellus and Pagius feel no shame? With such unrestrained freedom do they dare to pick apart and criticize the statements of others, so as to imagine that Baronius can be pressed by arguments utterly foolish and deceptive? Truly, while indulging partisan interests, they anxiously seek a knot in a rush, inventing novelties. When they establish a dispute merely over words, they depart far from the truth and then attempt to struggle against its shadow.

Although, therefore, such a case does not seem in itself to belong to our principal purpose, nevertheless, lest the opinion of the distinguished man Baronius remain unvindicated, before we bring our Exercises on Saint Leo’s Works concerning the Manichaean case to an end, we shall try to overthrow each of the two critics’ little arguments.

They begin by disputing over words alone, when they deny that the gathering which the holy pontiff described at one time as a *conventus* (“gathering”), and at another as a *consessus* (“session”) and *iudicium* (“judgment”), can be called a council. Among whom are these two most serious critics arguing this point? Among beginners in the Latin language, or at least among those who have never examined the older monuments of the Church? Even writers of the golden age of Latin very frequently used *conventus* for a council, as can be seen in Livy, Cicero, and Caesar. Nor were the very ancient Christian writers far removed from this usage. When indicating sacred gatherings of Catholics for defining rules of faith or morals, they used the word *conventus*. Among them are Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0947D] Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History, book V, chapter [Col. 0948D] 28; Rufinus, in the same place.], Eusebius of Caesarea, Rufinus the presbyter of Aquileia, and many others, whose catalogue it is by no means necessary to draw up here.

What then? The word *conventus* was so commonly used to indicate a council that even today, in the general collection of synods, we encounter headings of this kind [Note: [Col. 0948D] Volume II of the Councils, p. 891, and again in the same volume, p. 1049; volume III of the Councils, p. 545.]: “The Gathering of Sirmium,” “the Gathering of Alexandria,” “the Gathering of Hippo,” and six hundred others of the same kind. These undoubtedly show that the ancients used the two words interchangeably to signify one and the same thing.

All this, however, could doubtless have been omitted, lest we be too lengthy on a matter already established. The chief reason is that Saint Leo, acting as his own interpreter, used *conventus* for a council. Let Quesnellus himself serve as a decisive witness. In arranging the works of the holy pontiff, following the authority of ancient editors and manuscripts, he printed the seventh chapter of Leo’s thirteenth letter under the following title: “On the Celebration of Provincial Councils.” In the body of this text are found the passages that appear in Distinction 18, “On Councils,” chapter 2, and in Ivo’s Decree. It is thus most firmly demonstrated that, by the two words *conventus* and *concilium*, the holy pontiff intended to indicate one and the same thing.

Lest anyone suspect me of fraud, I have no hesitation in transcribing Leo’s words as they appear in Quesnellus’s edition:

> Concerning episcopal councils, we indicate nothing other than what the holy Fathers salutarily ordained: namely, that two gatherings are to be held each year, in which judgment is to be given concerning all the complaints that customarily arise among the various orders of the Church [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Leo the Great, Letter 13, chapter 7.].

Again, in the same edition of Quesnellus, we find this heading in Letter 16, chapter 7: “On Councils to Be Celebrated Annually at Rome.” There, when the holy pontiff is discussing canon 5 of Nicaea, he adds:

> Therefore, as the first requirement for preserving the most harmonious unity, we demand this: since the holy Fathers most salutarily established that there ought to be two gatherings of bishops every year [Note: [Col. 0949D] Letter 16, chapter 7.].

The case of the two critics has therefore already deteriorated, since Leo himself, following even in the footsteps of the Nicene Fathers, wished to use the word *conventus* to indicate both provincial and general synods. This could be demonstrated more and more by many other examples drawn from the works of the holy pontiff.

Nor can their case be strengthened by the other word, *consessus*, which the ancients used to indicate a council, as is revealed by the celebrated speech of the great emperor Constantine, in which he addressed the Nicene Fathers assembled in a body. “For,” he says, “it has been very much among my wishes, dearest friends, at some time to enjoy this gathering of yours.” A little later, congratulating the same Fathers because, setting aside private interests, they were proceeding peacefully and without contention of spirit to the synodal proceedings, he adds: “And although I rejoice exceedingly when I now behold your gathering, nevertheless I judge that …”

Meanwhile, I am ashamed to be drawn into such complications and to conduct business with men who despise the elementary principles of learning. They do not reflect that among the ancients one and the same thing was often called by several words. This happened chiefly because, when words depend upon human choice, they can easily be changed while the nature and substance of things remain entirely unchanged.

Moreover, Latin speech should not be considered so impoverished that a single word must be assigned to each thing, beyond which no other word could express the things themselves or the properties, functions, and power of those things. On the contrary, according to Cicero, the Latin language is especially rich in vocabulary, so rich that its abundance surpasses even that of the Greek language:

> I hold, as I have often argued, that the Latin language is not merely not poor, as is commonly thought, but even richer than the Greek [Note: [Col. 0949D] Cicero, *De Art.*; also in Nizolius’s *Thesaurus Ciceronis*, and in Col., in the preface to book XII.].

What wonder, then, if a council—which the Greeks call a *synod*—since it signifies an assembly into which several judges customarily come together to regulate Christian affairs, naturally admits several names, all quite suitable, so that it is sometimes expressed by the ancients with the word *conventus*, and sometimes by the words *consessus* and *judgment*? Is not every council, properly speaking, a gathering, a session, and a judgment in reality?

Let the two critics reflect on these matters among themselves, and finally attribute the grave error not to Baronius but rather to themselves. It must also be supposed that, when Quesnellus wrote this annotation, he was asleep—or at least flattering himself that his readers would be so drowsy or blind that they might read *consessus* where the text says *judgment* [Note: [Col. 0949D] Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, dissertation 1, “On the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo the Great,” p. 141; Pagius, under the year 444.].

For Valentinian did not use the word *consessus* in his novella, but *judgment*; and Quesnellus himself proved that this is how it must be read. When printing Valentinian’s novella, he published the following:

> What obscene things, disgraceful to say and to hear, were revealed by their own confession in the judgment of Pope Leo before the most distinguished senate [Col. 0950A].

Nor does that word *consessus* occur anywhere from the beginning of the novella to its end.

**4.** At last it is time, leaving these words aside, to proceed to the things themselves and examine individually the remaining arguments of both critics. Unless my judgment deceives me, they are so lacking in strength that they possess neither force nor sting with which they could wound or press Baronius.

As for the first argument, nothing weaker could be devised, since it is drawn from Prosper’s silence. “He does not in fact mention a council,” says Quesnellus. What follows from that? Does Prosper expressly fail to mention the Roman council held by Saint Leo in the case of the Manichaeans? He nevertheless reported how the diligence of this holy pontiff discovered the Manichaeans hiding within the City, brought them before the eyes of the whole Church, compelled them both to condemn and to disclose all the shamefulness of that wicked doctrine, and burned their books.

Quesnellus completely concealed all these facts. But Prosper actually wrote in the public records of his Chronicle:

> During the consulship of Maximus II and Paterius—or Paternus—many Manichaeans within the City were brought to light through the diligence of Pope Leo. He drew them out of their hiding places, made them public before the eyes of the whole Church, compelled them to condemn and disclose all the shamefulness of their doctrine, and burned their books.

There can therefore be no doubt about the public and solemn condemnation of the Manichaeans. If the two critics maintain that Saint Leo carried this out without a council, they have already run upon the very obstacle which they always and everywhere strive with the utmost care to avoid. For they concede the point to us when we assert that heresies and heretics can be condemned by the authority of the Roman pontiffs alone, and that they have sometimes been condemned in this way, without any assistance whatsoever from councils [Note: [Col. 0950D] See what we said concerning this discipline of the Church in the preceding chapter 4.].

A council is necessary only when the Roman pontiffs judge that one is expedient. Ordinarily they have summoned councils when decrees of faith already defined by the apostolic See were to be solemnly accepted by the common agreement of the whole Church; when a more numerous gathering of bishops was considered very useful for restraining the boldness of heretics, so that a more solemn judgment might be rendered; or finally, when it was fitting to settle ecclesiastical affairs that had been disturbed in the Churches—whether through the wickedness of schismatics or through the power of princes and other ministers of the world—more easily and peacefully [Note: [Col. 0950D] See what we shall say in the case of the Eutychianists, when discussing the appeals of Eutyches, Flavian, Theodoret, and others to the apostolic See.].

No law, therefore, commands that councils must be held as though they were necessary to the Church. Indeed, the laws themselves provide that general councils are not to be held unless the Roman pontiff judges that they ought to be held.

If new heresies and new schisms arise in the Church, they must certainly be immediately suppressed and uprooted in accordance with the divine and apostolic commands, lest, once the seed of wickedness has been propagated or taken root to the detriment of the Catholic faith, the tares of demons be increasingly nourished and grow from day to day.

Yet the Church’s Founder did not prepare only one remedy—councils—for these evils, but several. Roman pontiffs can meet and remedy all such evils through letters filled with sacred teachings, through frequent admonitions, or finally through their legates bearing the most powerful warnings, without summoning general synods. For the solemnity of such judgments is not absolutely necessary, but only when ecclesiastical affairs have been thoroughly disturbed, or when the questions that have arisen are so doubtful, obscure, fluctuating, and entangled that, for the common peace and the salvation of many, the apostolic See judges a council expedient.

Therefore we can by no means tolerate what the two critics asserted in the case under discussion: namely, that a council was unnecessary because the matter concerned neither the proscription of a new heresy nor the assertion of the faith, but the imposition of a penalty according to the canon of the Church—as though councils had necessarily to be convened whenever either of these two circumstances occurred, or as though provincial or general synods could be summoned and held for no other reason.

Where did they draw such a doctrine from? Let them produce canons, the monuments of the Fathers, and the customs of the Churches, so that we too may learn the sources from which this singular and hitherto unheard-of secret discipline has arisen.

For our part, if we consult the Fathers, the councils, and the practice of the Church, we must defend and believe precisely the opposite. In the second century, when councils began to be held more frequently in the Church after the apostles, bishops gathered together in many places, both in Asia and in Palestine, concerning the question of celebrating Easter. The great Irenaeus, apostle of the Churches of Gaul and their most brilliant light, is witness to this; all teachers, both ancient and modern, have placed their faith in him [Note: [Col. 0951D] Irenaeus, book V of the Ecclesiastical History, chapters 23, 24, and 25.], including Eusebius of Caesarea, book V of the Ecclesiastical History, chapters 24 and 25.

Who, however, will claim that those synods dealt with the proscription of a new heresy or the assertion of the faith?

Likewise, in the third century, in Rome and Africa, in Phrygia, and at Neocaesarea in Pontus, the Fathers of the Churches held numerous gatherings, either to impose salutary penance upon those who had lapsed during times of persecution, to restore ecclesiastical discipline, or finally to rebut accusations against bishops and punish the offenders. Yet nowhere was there discussion either of a new heresy or of articles of faith, as is shown by the writings of Eusebius himself, Cyprian, Dionysius of Alexandria, and the other Fathers who flourished in that age, at least some fragments of whose writings have come down to us.

What more is needed? In the fourth, fifth, and succeeding centuries innumerable councils were held either to pronounce an anathema against heresies already condemned elsewhere; to establish various degrees of penance in the Church; to depose bishops from their sees; to restore to their own sees those who had been unjustly deposed; or finally to deal with appeals, the dedications of Churches, immunities, indulgences granted to penitent lapsed persons, and many other matters of that kind.

It is therefore falsely invented that the holy pontiff did not hold a council in the case of the Manichaeans because the matter concerned neither the condemnation of a new heresy nor the assertion of the faith. It was enough that an anathema had to be pronounced against the Manichaeans discovered in the City; it was enough that the discipline of the Roman Church required the Manichaeans to be driven far from all the borders of Italy.

Therefore, although the judgment concerning the Manichaeans dealt with the imposition of a penalty according to the canon of the Church, nevertheless, since Saint Leo made all the shamefulness of their doctrine public before the eyes of the whole Church and compelled it to be both condemned and disclosed, on the authority of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, as we have seen, nothing prevents all these things from having been carried out in a council.

This is especially so since the holy pontiff wished to establish a new arrangement of procedure both for exposing and reporting heretics and for making and receiving accusations against them. He wished the burden of these obligations to be imposed upon all Catholics under threat of the indignation of Almighty God.

What wonder, then, if, before he imposed such obligations upon both the people and the presbyters, he wished to establish a new canon to be perpetually observed in similar cases? He sought nothing else than the security of religion and of all Catholics. For that reason, after convening an assembly and conducting a judgment, he admitted part of the senate and part of the people as well, establishing a general rule of morals, to whose binding force every conscience would be subject, and from which no one could depart without the stigma of crime.

Now the two critics might applaud themselves when I fell into a more difficult knot, which they perhaps think a knot worthy of Hercules, since they have pronounced, as though from a tripod:

> Nor is it a council when, together with the priests, part of the senate and part of the people is present.

**5.** This final annotation would press Baronius if it were true, if it were sound, and finally if, contrary to the decrees of sacred synods and the rules of divine law, the case of the Manichaeans had been judged and decided with part of the senate and part of the people joining the priests and presbyters.

But first, the assertion that part of the people had been summoned and brought in when the Manichaean doctrines and crimes were being investigated is altogether doubtful. Neither Valentinian, nor Saint Leo, nor anyone else has asserted it.

In his novella Valentinian certainly testifies that their crimes had been revealed by their own confession before the most distinguished senate:

> Before the most distinguished senate, their crimes were revealed by their own confession [Col. 0952B].

Likewise Leo, describing the gathering he had convened, wrote:

> With the bishops and presbyters therefore seated with me, and Christian men and nobles gathered into the same session, we ordered their elect men and women to be brought forward [Note: [Col. 0951D] Saint Leo, Sermon previously cited, on the Epiphany, chapter 4.].

If they contend that by those two words of Leo, “Christian men,” at least part of the people was obscurely indicated, I shall not resist granting it freely. But what follows from that? Is it unusual in the Church for princes, royal ministers, the senate itself, and some members of the people to be admitted into councils as witnesses? Was that not the practice and custom of many councils?

But, to pass over the councils of the apostles, in which all the faithful and the entire multitude of believers gathered together with the apostles and the other disciples of the Lord, did not laymen highly accomplished in philosophical studies also attend the first general Council of Nicaea, apart from the bishops and the emperor Constantine? Before the whole people they held disputations with our men.

We possess the most authoritative witnesses—not only all Catholic writers [Note: [Col. 0951D] Rufinus, book X of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 3; also Eusebius, book X.], but also the heterodox themselves, namely Calvin, Illyricus, Luther, the Magdeburg Centuriators, and others, who agree with us in this thoroughly established matter. Although afterward, abusing the examples they have praised, they attempt to construct new engines against the Church, teaching altogether incorrectly that laymen are admitted into sacred synods not as witnesses but as judges, and that they can be deprived of what they call the decisive vote only through the greatest injustice.

But what have I to do with those heretics now, who corrupt everything or at least turn everything in the opposite direction? I shall return instead to Quesnellus and Pagius, and ask whether they have ever examined copies of the Acts of Chalcedon.

That synod was convened and confirmed seven years after the condemnation of the Manichaeans by the authority of the same Pope Leo, as we shall say at another time. Did only bishops, presbyters, and the other clergy and ministers of the Churches have a place there, or did the senate and some others from among the people also have a place?

If we place our trust in the authentic Acts, we read that senators and magistrates, consuls, prefects, and the other ministers of the emperors gathered at Chalcedon. Indeed, we understand that the emperor Marcian himself came to that very large assembly with a great retinue of noble and non-noble persons. Following the example of the great Constantine, he presented himself as a defender of the faith:

> We wished to attend the synod, following the example of the religious prince Constantine, in order to confirm the faith, not to exercise any power.

Thus Marcian addressed the Fathers of Chalcedon [Note: [Col. 0952D] The address of the emperor Marcian appears in volume IV of the Councils, p. 1472.].

Will that, too, not be a council in which, together with the priests, there were the emperor, the senate, the prefects of the provinces and of public affairs, and part of the people? Mere nonsense—away with such a fiction!

For the truth of councils is not at all impaired by the gathering of laymen, provided that only the bishops and their legates, or other ministers and members of religious communities, conduct ecclesiastical affairs and define matters of faith; and provided finally that only these persons, as judges, subscribe to the synodal decrees.

Nor would princes, magistrates, and the people themselves be deprived of every function in councils if they were admitted and summoned as suitable witnesses and defenders of the truth, as commonly happens.

Lest anyone suspect that this distinction between laymen and the ministers of the Churches was not observed at Leo’s gathering concerning the Manichaeans, I wish that attention be paid to the holy pontiff’s manner of speaking. He first describes the bishops and presbyters as seated with him, as though at the tribunal of a court; then he says that, with Christian men and nobles gathered, he ordered the elect men and women to be brought forward.

The noblemen, therefore, did not sit with Leo and the other bishops or presbyters. They were merely gathered when the Manichaeans’ crimes were being brought to public testimony and those crimes were being condemned, and finally when the Manichaeans whom the holy pontiff had led to penance were being received.

This is what the words of Saint Prosper mean, which we also cited above: namely, that the Manichaeans hiding in the City were made public before the eyes of the whole Church, and that all the shamefulness of their doctrine was compelled to be condemned and disclosed.

If Leo’s procedure was therefore that Manichaeans were not to be received into the Church as penitents unless the errors of their most shameful sect had first been publicly detested, why insist so vigorously that the holy pontiff’s gathering cannot be called a council because part of the senate and part of the people were present?

What is the point of all this?

For my part, setting aside every partisan interest and following only the truth, which alone ought to be sought in writing and disputation, I understand nothing whatsoever in that Roman investigation of the Manichaeans [Col. 0953C] that conflicts with the marks and characteristics of a true council—especially since we can easily overturn all the arguments advanced by Quesnellus [Note: [Col. 0953D] Quesnellus, under the year of Christ 443, in dissertation 1, “On the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo the Great,” who, in his eagerness to avoid the word “investigation,” used the word “meeting,” volume II of the Works, p. 140 [Col. 0954D] and following.] and Pagius.

Indeed, I perceive one thing that ought to be especially pleasing to all Catholics and particularly suited to preserving the purity of the faith in the Church, although I fear that it may displease many: namely, that the system of the present-day general Inquisition derived its origin from a procedure not wholly unlike Leo’s investigation of the Manichaeans.

**6.** But if learned and educated men object to us and ask whether it can be proved with sufficient consistency that this form of judgment was never changed or interrupted from Leo’s age down to our own, I wish it were sufficiently understood what our purpose has been.

We are not among those whose minds wander beyond the goal they have set themselves. Our only intention has been to correct and adorn the Works of Leo, to derive certain Exercises from his writings, and to vindicate the deeds of the holy pontiff against the criticisms of others. For that reason we have directed our care, thought, and study toward this end in such a way that, to avoid superfluity and arrogance and to escape rashness and prolixity, we should by no means mix the deeds of others with those of the holy pontiff, except when, in overturning the false opinions of others, we encountered matters from which we could not withdraw without incurring the charge of ignorance.

But if, finally, the same procedure and method was at some time interrupted in dealing with those contaminated by heresy or suspected of heretical defilement, what of it? Our Leo had not yet closed his final day when the barbarians, coming both from the North and from Africa, brought the Roman Empire to its end and so disturbed the affairs of the Catholic Church that, after forming an alliance with the powers of demons, wickedness, tyranny, and the errors of many heresies were spread far and wide. The supreme pontiffs and the other inferior clergy could scarcely devote themselves to recalling Catholics from their vices, persuading princes to abstain from massacring citizens and burning cities, and inducing heretical men—especially the Arians, of whom there was such a multitude—to renounce their errors and profess the doctrines of the true faith.

In such a great disturbance of affairs, surrounded by so many and such savage enemies, there was nothing that did not have to be feared. Therefore, with the leniency of the ecclesiastical laws somewhat tempered by severity, they fulfilled the duties of true shepherds sufficiently in uprooting the errors that were daily increasing and in driving back the vices that could corrupt and weaken the piety of the faithful.

Nevertheless, amid these straits of time, war, and changing circumstances, it cannot for that reason be said that the ancient discipline of the Roman Church was either abolished or changed, even if, for reasons of practical administration, it was not continually put into execution. It was utterly impossible that, under barbarian rulers and barbarian peoples who had been transferred into these lands and were subject to countless errors, they should maintain the form and rigor of investigation which Saint Leo had defined as to be preserved under the most pious and Catholic rulers.

Therefore, no one should be surprised if, in these times when the Christian commonwealth was so grievously afflicted, the pastors of the Churches were compelled to serve lest all Catholics, together with the sincere faith of Christ, perish under the yoke and persecutions of the barbarians.

We could explain this practical policy of the Roman pontiffs more and more by the examples of the apostles. They, while announcing the gospel of the cross to Jews and Gentiles, were compelled to accommodate themselves to circumstances in matters that did not conflict with the Christian faith, so that little by little they might win to Christ people of every rank and condition.

No one, then, should be angry with me because I have been too thorough in refuting the little arguments of Pagi and Paschasius Quesnell; [Col. 0954C] nor should anyone complain that, in vindicating Baronius, I have brought forward many things that could either have been omitted or explained more briefly. Necessity alone compelled me in both cases. For the zeal of Quesnell and others of the same kind—who, never sufficiently indulgent toward their own party, very often conceal what ought to be brought to light in the works of the holy Fathers, labor to overthrow what ought to be defended, and finally strive either entirely to diminish or at least to conceal what concerns the authority and dignity of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0954D] See Quesnell, vol. I, p. 266, and Garnerius, vol. III.]—required it.

Yet that the ancient writers followed a different method of proceeding is shown, among other documents, by the Greek letter of Theodoret to our holy pontiff Leo. In it, after sincerely enumerating the honors, prerogatives, and duties of the Apostolic See—on account of which all nations have been accustomed to hasten to this See “so that,” as he says, “we may receive from you a remedy for the wounds of the Churches; for it is fitting that you should hold the first place in all things”—he proceeds in a second section to praise certain deeds of the holy pontiff. Among these he records, as a wholly sufficient proof, that zeal against the infamous Manichaeans which, as he says, Your Holiness recently exercised, and by which you revealed how great is your love of God through your devotion to divine matters. It was by no means displeasing to us to bring the present Exercise to a close with these words.

# CHAPTER XI

After the death of Leo the Great, the Manichaeans again inhabit Rome. Pope Gelasius’s zeal in exposing them. Guillelmus Cave’s erroneous judgment concerning communion under both kinds. The same Saint Gelasius finally expels these wicked men from Rome and destroys their books, adding a sentence of anathema.

[Col. 0955A]

1. What heresy was ever more audacious and crafty than the Manichaean, or more self-confident than it? Since it was so sacrilegious in religion, so corrupted by wicked morals, and so profane in its rites, it ought at least to have guarded against inhabiting those places in which civil and ecclesiastical laws most loudly denounced it, and in which the judges of both jurisdictions had vigorously armed themselves to restrain, expel, and utterly abolish it.

To observe this audacity, it will not be necessary to withdraw far from the city of Rome itself. Although the Manichaeans had been harassed in many different ways there, had undergone sufficient punishment under the authority of Leo the Great, and had been sent into exile far from all the shores of Italy, it has nevertheless been discovered that, not long after the death of so great a pontiff, they again inhabited Rome.

When I had reflected upon this, I fell into the strong suspicion that the Manichaeans living in Rome, terrified by Leo’s general investigation already directed against them, had employed every art of the most wicked dissimulation in order to remain hidden. For this reason, lest their depravity be exposed, they had continually attended sacred assemblies and the divine mysteries sacrilegiously together with Catholic men—just as Saint Leo had complained when he denounced this most serious crime.

If this suspicion of ours is not approved by learned men, they will undoubtedly have to affirm the alternative: namely, that the Manichaeans, having already been sent beyond the borders of Italy through Leo’s action, turned their steps toward Rome after they subsequently heard of the holy pontiff’s death, seeking out their former hiding places.

Since neither of these alternatives can be established without a trustworthy witness, we shall hasten merely to describe how the Manichaeans again inhabited the city after the death of Saint Leo.

2. Saint Leo the Great therefore ended his earthly life in the year 461. Hilary succeeded him; and when Hilary was taken from the living in the sixth year of his pontificate, Simplicius became his successor. Whether the Manichaean sect inhabited Rome under these two pontiffs is not known from any sacred or secular testimony.

Therefore, so that we may not cling to uncertain monuments and facts, we shall immediately appeal to the pontificate of Pope Gelasius and to his deeds. From the *Pontifical Book* and from Anastasius, in the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, the following account is to be read:

“In the time of Gelasius, Manichaeans were discovered in the city. He ordered them to be deported into exile, and he also burned their books in a fire before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary.”

To expose these men, Gelasius adopted no other policy than that which had prevailed in the Roman Church by the decree of the great pontiff Leo. For he ordered that all who approached the sacred assembly should partake of the mysteries under both kinds, so that the Manichaeans—who, because of their excessive superstition, entirely abhorred wine and refused to receive communion from the chalice—might more easily be distinguished from the true faithful. [Col. 0955D]

Observing this Gelasian decree, Guillelmus Cave praises the holy pontiff’s method of action, by which he removed from the wicked Manichaeans the mask of Catholics under which they tried to remain concealed. He then gradually seeks to attack the Roman Church’s practice of communion under only one kind, as though it bore the mark of novelty. He further adds that Gelasius confirmed an ancient custom received in the Church from its very beginnings: that no one should communicate at sacred gatherings except under both kinds.

But this is what a man of the Reformed sect, indulgent toward his own party and wishing to follow the practice of the Greeks, had to say. Let Cave nevertheless tell us, I ask, when the Roman Church followed this custom. Let him produce the documents from which it may be learned that laypeople who did not celebrate the Eucharist were required, when gatherings were held in the Church’s earliest days, to communicate under both kinds. [Col. 0956A]

Surely, if Leo the Great and Gelasius, the Roman pontiffs, had confirmed this custom by their decrees, no Catholic before their time would have been permitted to abstain from the use of the chalice. Consequently, priests celebrating the Eucharist would have had to consecrate so great a quantity of wine at their gatherings as would have sufficed both for themselves and for the people present at the sacred mysteries.

But if this practice had existed, only the Manichaeans would then have abstained from communion from the chalice. Why, then, was it necessary to compel the faithful to communicate under both kinds? Why confirm by decree what already prevailed among all Catholic laypeople?

For if the Roman Church—which has always wished to rely upon the teaching received from the Apostles—had understood that this custom was necessarily to be followed from its origins by divine institution, it would never have deprived laypeople who did not celebrate the Eucharist of the use of the chalice, and it would never have interrupted this rite.

That the rite of offering the chalice to laypeople was not in use in Leo’s time is proved by the decree of that same holy pontiff. For reasons of policy, he bound Catholics to the use of the chalice in order to expose the Manichaeans. Once the Manichaeans had been expelled from the city, why should anyone doubt that this custom or policy was immediately discontinued?

Did not Pope Gelasius, who, according to Cave, was appointed pontiff more than thirty years after the death of Leo the Great, when he discovered the Manichaeans, compel Catholics by his decree to communicate under both kinds in order to remove from them the Catholic mask? He certainly would not have done so if that custom or rite had not been discontinued after Leo’s death.

3. I consider it unnecessary to linger longer over these trifles. For it is not only that decree of which we have hitherto spoken that reveals Gelasius to have followed Leo’s policy; it is also the zeal he displayed so that the Manichaeans discovered in the city of Rome might be compelled by judicial authority, apprehended, and deported into exile.

Yet Gelasius himself did not think that he had sufficiently safeguarded the security of the Catholic faith if, after those wicked men had been sent far from the city, books or codices containing their sacrilegious teaching still survived. Therefore, wishing in this matter also to imitate Saint Leo, he attempted utterly to destroy and abolish their volumes, which were worn by the hands of many and carried here and there to deceive many others.

For this reason, after collecting all the Manichaean books that he could find and carefully examining them so that they might not provide anyone with a stumbling block in the future, he ordered them to be burned in a fire before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary.

On this occasion it is highly probable that Gelasius also wished to hold that famous council of seventy bishops, in which, first recalling the statutes of his predecessors, he arranged a catalogue of the books of both Testaments and, identifying their authors, distinguished the authentic Scriptures from the apocrypha. [Note: [Col. 0955D] See what we wrote above in chapter 4 of this book.]

Among the latter he especially placed those books used by heretics, which the Manichaeans, Montanists, Marcionites, and others had dared falsely to introduce throughout the world under the names of the Apostles. These books, together with the other volumes that many heretics had composed either to destroy or to undermine the Catholic religion, Pope Gelasius not only rejected but also expelled from the whole Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church. With their authors and the followers of those authors, he defined, together with the entire council, that they had been condemned forever under the unbreakable bond of anathema. [Col. 0956D]

I do not think it necessary at present to report what and of what kind were the Manichaean books that Pope Gelasius proscribed by his decree as false and spurious. First, that catalogue of apocryphal books has repeatedly been brought to light and illuminated by the labors of distinguished men; and, moreover, in the preceding chapters we have already discussed such books.

# CHAPTER XII

After the death of Saint Gelasius, the Manichaeans inhabit Rome for the third time. Pope Symmachus, following the example of his predecessors, finally drives them into exile, while their images and books are burned before the doors of the Constantinian basilica. In discussing the use of these images, we explain how Symmachus, harassed in various ways by the emperor Anastasius, was wrongly accused of the Manichaean corruption.

1. After the Manichaeans had lost the houses of the city of Rome into which they had withdrawn, and had concluded that they could obtain no other more favorable place of residence, they eagerly desired, with great fervor of spirit, to return from the exile they were suffering.

But since they greatly feared the zeal of the holy supreme pontiff Gelasius, by which he had proceeded against them and their books, it does not appear entirely consistent with the truth that they returned here after exhausting their punishments while he still held the reins of the supreme pontificate.

Gelasius therefore died in the year 496, and Anastasius II succeeded him. After spending two years in the pontificate, Anastasius departed this life, without anything becoming known at that time in Rome concerning the Manichaean sect.

But the situation was certainly different in the time of Pope Symmachus. When Symmachus ascended the throne of Saint Peter in the year of Christ 498, while the very serious faction of the antipope Laurentius was pressing him, relying upon the authority and power of the emperor Anastasius, the Manichaeans—who had previously twice been sent into exile—seized the opportunity presented by that great schism to set out for Rome once again.

They perhaps thought that no other time more favorable to them could be offered than this: when both Church and empire had been split into two factions, so that neither the rigor of sacred ecclesiastical discipline nor the severity of imperial laws could easily be advanced and exercised by the ministers of either sacred or civil sovereignty.

This was indeed a most serious schism. The clergy and senate were divided into two parties: one adhered to Laurentius, a deacon of the Roman Church who had occupied the basilica of Saint Mary; the other followed Symmachus himself, who had been elected and consecrated by legitimate votes and rites in the Constantinian basilica.

With Rome shaken by these most serious disturbances, what wonder if the crafty offspring of the Manichaeans found an entrance by which to inhabit the city for the third or fourth time? Their access was made wider when Pope Symmachus and his adversary Laurentius were summoned to Ravenna by the Arian king Theodoric and compelled to appear before him, so that he, appointed as a kind of arbiter of this schism and these disturbances, might pronounce judgment upon them.

This disgraceful crime of the schism introduced into the Church a certain example of tyranny. For Symmachus, who could not be subject to the laws or decrees of lay princes in matters concerning the legitimacy of his election, was compelled, in order to prevent greater scandals and to accommodate himself to those troubled times, to submit to royal judgment and decree.

2. At that time God himself aided the equity and security of the Church in wondrous ways, lest the gates of hell should prevail against it, and brought all the disturbances of ambition and all the movements of that dreadful schism to a favorable and happy conclusion.

King Theodoric held an opinion sufficiently consonant with the sacred canons: namely, that, of the two bishops, the one who had first been ordained should occupy the Apostolic See, or that the one whose party was found to be the larger should do so.

This finally found, as I use the words of the *Pontifical Book*, “equity and knowledge of the truth” in Symmachus. “And Symmachus was made bishop.” [Note: [Col. 0957D] From the *Pontifical Book*, in the edition of the councils, vol. I.]

With matters thus arranged, Symmachus set out for Rome. There, after a synod had been assembled against the deacon Laurentius, who had attempted to invade the Roman episcopate through a fraudulent ordination, Symmachus, moved by mercy and exercising the authority of the Apostolic See, released and freed him from the canonical bonds by which he had bound himself both through his attempted schism and through his illicit ordination. He appointed him bishop in the city of Nuceria.

Meanwhile, although the factions of that dreadful schism seemed almost extinguished and abolished, the poison of hatred and envy had wounded the hearts of many clerics and patricians, including men distinguished by the consulships they had held, and had secretly corrupted them even more gravely. Consequently, Symmachus’s opponents, having grown bolder, eventually broke out into more savage seditions.

Thus, after four years had passed, when the faction of Festus and Probinus had again risen against Symmachus, they accused him as though he were a criminal before that same King Theodoric. They suborned false witnesses, secretly recalled the false pope Laurentius from the city of Nuceria so that he might proceed to Rome, and, renewing and intensifying the earlier schism, appealed to the king to grant an investigation of the Apostolic See.

As the seditions increased daily, this occurred both because of the audacity of Peter of Altinum, who, relying solely upon royal authority and power and undertaking an investigation contrary to the sacred canons, meddled in the affairs of the Roman See, and because of the fury of the former consuls Festus and Probinus, who had begun a civil war within the city itself against other senators, especially the former consul Faustus, whom they detested.

The killings and murders of that war could not be escaped even by the clergy. Some of them, and even women and virgins living in monasteries, were beaten and wounded by blows; finally, priests too, attacked out of monstrous envy either with clubs or with the sword, fell dead.

3. The records of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* make clear that these events occurred at the beginning of the sixth century, that is, in the year of Christ 502.

At that time, it may be supposed, the Manichaean offspring hiding here had never passed happier days than then, when ecclesiastical and civil affairs were thrown into such complete confusion that no one could proceed against them.

Nevertheless, it is known from Symmachus’s zeal that the joy of these men was soon turned into mourning and grief. First, after frustrating the efforts of King Theodoric and his legate Peter of Altinum, and then after driving out the invader of his See, Symmachus convened a council of one hundred and fifteen bishops at Rome. He appeared before it fearlessly and cleared himself of the accusations brought against him.

The probity of the holy pontiff’s life, the integrity of his conduct, and his other virtues—which men powerless against envy and hatred had boldly attacked with slanders—were made known throughout all the nations of the world, like gold that has been tested, with all upright men applauding.

This happy and just vindication of the holy pontiff was soon followed by another benefit: as the senators and Roman people gradually began to abstain from killings, seditions, and acts of violence, peace and tranquility dawned upon the city and the Church.

I shall not recount Symmachus’s deeds or the many different ways in which he was harassed, sometimes by the Arian King Theodoric and the Arian emperor Anastasius, and sometimes by other men of the ecclesiastical and civil establishment, lest I appear to wander beyond the subject and purpose before us.

The present discussion would become far too long if I were either to enumerate the calumnies with which Symmachus was accused or to turn to the six synods that he convened to defend the rights of his See and his own innocence, to restore and strengthen the collapsing discipline of the Roman Church, and to drive far from the fellowship of Catholics all those heretics and schismatics who, polluted by the Arian, Eutychian, or finally Acephalian corruption, infected the doctrines of true religion.

Such matters do not belong to the Manichaean history that we have undertaken to write, although many things occur in them that reveal and vindicate the supreme rights of the Apostolic See.

For the present, therefore, it is relevant to report only those matters that reveal Symmachus’s great strength of spirit in the case before us. Although he was pressed on every side by the greatest calamities, no fear of the powers of this world could induce him not to expel from the city the Manichaeans hiding in Rome and enjoying imperial patronage, to destroy their images and books, and to burn them.

“After all these things,” says the author of the *Pontifical Book* in the *Life of Symmachus*, “blessed Symmachus discovered Manichaeans in the city of Rome. He burned all their images and books in a fire before the doors of the Constantinian basilica, and sent the men themselves into exile.” [Note: [Col. 0959D] The author of the *Pontifical Book*, in the *Life of Symmachus*.]

4. In the words “all their images,” we must dwell for a moment, since they indicate some new rite or practice of the Manichaeans that we have observed nowhere else and that no one so far among those who have furnished the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* with notes has explained—a point that Beausobre dared to deny, as we saw in chapter 4 of this book.

But if we consult Augustine above all, since he described all the Manichaean practices, we might at least obscurely conjecture that the Manichaeans used profane signs and images to signify their foul and fabulous inventions and their sacrilegious theology.

This could especially be indicated by those words of Augustine in which he called the shameful religion of the Manichaeans not a sect but a “schism of the nations.” He used this expression because they agreed with the principal doctrine of the pagans, who asserted many gods, but then disagreed with the pagans in maintaining that good and evil, foul and splendid, perpetual and transitory, mutable and certain, corporeal and divine things did not have one single principle. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book XX, chapters 3 and 9.]

Faustus brought this forward against Augustine as a kind of Gordian knot or Achilles’ argument, so that he might not only reject the designation “schismatics of the nations” but also proclaim that they were far worse than the pagans.

Augustine, on the other hand, established this point by attacking Faustus and the Manichaeans: they sacrilegiously and superstitiously offered worship to the Sun and to the other signs of the heavens, to Hyle, to Earth, and to the fabricated Atlas who supported the world; they also worshiped things that did not exist and invented them for themselves.

Therefore the holy Doctor reasons from such rites and practices as follows:

“Hence we call you worse than the pagans. You are like them only in this, that you worship many gods; but you differ from them for the worse in this respect: they worship as gods things that exist but are not gods, whereas you worship things that are neither gods nor anything at all, since they do not exist in any way.”

Then the holy Doctor, bringing forward certain pagan fables invented by poets for entertainment, briefly reviews the interpretations that the pagans themselves attempted to give, with reference to the nature of things or to human conduct, concerning lame Vulcan, blind Fortune, adulterous Venus, warlike Mars, and Cupid, the boy shooting arrows and displaying an exquisite form. He concludes:

“We laugh at them for this: they worship, under an evil interpretation, things which, if they had not understood them, they would still have worshiped—though damnably, yet more excusably.”

Augustine maintained that something corresponding to all these figures could indeed be found in the nature of things, although such things are of no value for human salvation or benefit, and the interpretations drawn from them are found in the nature of things.

5. Augustine amplifies these and many other matters of the same kind in the same place, taking them from the fables of pagan poets. He sets Manichaean doctrines against these inventions in order to conclude that this pestilential offspring is worse than the sects of all nations.

Among other things, he introduces the following:

The invention by which they describe the first human being as warring together with the five elements; or the invention by which they imagined a powerful spirit making and brilliantly sustaining the world from the captive bodies of the nation of darkness—or rather from the conquered and subjected limbs of your god—and holding in his hand the remains of those same limbs of your god, while lamenting all the other things that had been captured, oppressed, and defiled; or finally the greatest Atlas, carrying beneath his shoulders the being whom they fancifully imagined and foolishly claimed to see as though drawn upon a theatrical carpet.

Augustine testified that the Manichaeans had demonstrated these and countless other things, equally foolish and insane, neither by painting or sculpting them nor by interpreting them.

But since his words appear very obscure, it will be exceedingly difficult to determine whether, in the age of the holy Doctor, the Manichaeans used statues, paintings, or images as aids by which they could more easily impress these pernicious fables upon the minds of their elect and hearers.

At the very least, it will be entirely difficult to understand from the preceding testimonies that the Manichaeans admitted this rite and practice of using pagan images. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Augustine, *Against the Letter of Manichaeus*, chapter 8, and *Against Faustus*, book VIII, chapter 5.]

6. After often reflecting upon these and similar matters, we have indicated that we must not depart far from the words of the *Pontifical Book* or from the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian, which affirm that Symmachus destroyed all the Manichaean images and all their books before the doors of the Constantinian basilica and burned them in a fire.

Indeed, we considered it a most serious offense either not to insist upon these points or to deny their credibility. For the use of images is clearly demonstrated to us, above all, by the laws of the Persians, from which the sacrilegious religion of the Manichaeans originated. It is also demonstrated by the sacred festival of the Bema, which they celebrated each year in the month of March for the cult of the death of Mani and in contempt of the Lord’s Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Anastasius the Librarian agrees with the *Pontifical Book*.]

For this reason they constructed a lofty image of a throne, decorated with a magnificent display of riches, by which they fancied that the glorious birthday of their master Mani was signified. [Note: [Col. 0959D] See what we said in chapters 4 and 5 concerning this Manichaean festival of the Bema.]

As we touch upon these matters, we do not overlook the possibility that the Manichaeans themselves wished, in honor of their master, to spread their couches upon reeds, so as to revive the memory that Mani had been flayed in Persia upon reeds, supposedly out of hatred for the truth, as Nicetas asserts. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Nicetas, *Orthodox Treasury*, book IV, chapter 33.]

Nor do we overlook those things that the Manichaeans themselves had devised as a testimony to their impious religion and as a mockery of our Catholic faith. Borrowing from us the sign of the cross, images of the Mother of God, [Note: [Col. 0960D] Peter of Sicily and Photius indicate more explicitly certain matters concerning the Manichaean images and representations—namely, the sign of the cross, the image of the Mother of God, and others of the same kind. They sacrilegiously disfigured these through certain profane rites and impure superstitions, in hatred of the Catholic faith. See book I of Photius, *Against the Manichaeans*, chapters 7, 8, 9, and 18, in Christophorus Wolfius.] and other such things, they sacrilegiously mutilated and deformed them. They then displayed these mutilated and deformed objects at one time for veneration and at another for cursing, wishing through those artificial signs to indicate the doctrines that their wicked leader had introduced throughout the world.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from believing that the great pontiff Symmachus, having clearly recognized the sacrileges and superstitions of this most wicked people, destroyed and burned in fire, in addition to all their books, all their signs and images that indicated some wicked mystery.

For the holy pontiff could not tolerate either the Manichaeans or the objects they used in contempt of our religion. The nature and duty of the supreme pontificate, which he exercised amid such great adversities, also demanded this public testimony to his sincere faith, so that everyone might know how far his mind stood from Manichaean doctrine and how intensely he abhorred that sect.

7. We believe that no one is unaware that, among the other calumnies constructed against the holy pontiff Symmachus by the envy and malice of the opposing faction, this one held no minor place: through the mouths of impious men he was paraded as though guilty of Manichaean doctrine.

His enemies proclaimed this disgrace and stain upon his faith so widely and loudly that it reached Constantinople and the ears of Anastasius, the emperor and patron of the Acacian and Severian factions.

For this reason, in order to evade the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by Symmachus and more easily to despise it, Anastasius brought this most serious crime against the holy pontiff with much reproach.

Symmachus therefore had to provide public testimonies to his faith. He did so when, after sending the Manichaeans into exile, he destroyed their books and images. [Note: [Col. 0961D] See also what we have already said in chapter 4 of this book.]

Symmachus, however, did not think that this public testimony to his faith could dissolve every calumny. When he learned that the emperor Anastasius had composed a notorious pamphlet in which he was scourged with insults and paraded before the Easterners and other peoples as though he were a Manichaean, he answered that pamphlet with an apologetic address on his own behalf. He completely purged and erased every suspicion of Manichaean corruption.

What remains to be said about this apologetic letter of Symmachus and about the emperor Anastasius, the patron of the Manichaeans, we shall explain shortly in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER XIII

On the apologetic letter of Pope Symmachus against the notorious pamphlets of the emperor Anastasius. The same emperor, defender and supporter of many heretics, also received Xenaia, the leader of the Manichaeans, into his patronage. From this we finally take occasion briefly to examine the character, way of life, and writings of Xenaia.

[Col. 0961C]

1. The enemies of Pope Symmachus had never more seriously damaged his reputation than when they dared to parade him before many peoples as an advocate of Manichaean doctrine.

This occurred especially when the emperor Anastasius composed a notorious pamphlet against the holy pontiff, filled with many insults and curses, in which the holy pontiff was publicly represented as guilty of many crimes and of violating the faith.

Placed in such grave danger, Symmachus examined the notorious pamphlets but was moved neither by hatred nor by anger. Rather, considering the obligations of his office and the honor of the Apostolic See, and never thinking of avenging the injury, he wrote with a firm pen that celebrated letter in which he answered the notorious pamphlet of the emperor Anastasius, purged each of the calumnies contained in it, and utterly destroyed them.

First, he began his defense of his Catholic faith with the example of the eight books that Ambrose had written to the emperor Gratian, since Ambrose had not begrudged praising him more gloriously and the emperor had not disdained to receive the work gratefully.

The holy pontiff then publicly reveals the strength and constancy of his spirit, since he would not fear to stand before a pagan tyrant-emperor threatening him with death. He revolved in his mind the apostolic warning of Paul and appealed to it:

“Woe is me,” he says, “if I do not preach the Gospel.” [Note: [Col. 0962D] First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter IX.]

“It is better to suffer the loss of the present life than to be punished with eternal condemnation.” [Note: [Col. 0962D] Symmachus, in the same place, quoting the words of Paul.]

2. Then, proceeding in his speech with a straightforward and measured step, and remaining steadfast in the same firmness of spirit, he approaches and addresses Anastasius as the Roman emperor and as a Catholic ruler, so that he may assume the role of one accustomed to receive graciously even the embassies of barbarian nations and to hear patiently the voice of any apostolic bishop.

As though he could be shaken by no blow of the gravest calumnies, he recalls the Lord’s promise recorded in Matthew:

“When they persecute you and say every evil against you for the sake of righteousness, rejoice.” [Note: [Col. 0962D] Matthew, chapter V.]

Unable to conceal this inward joy outwardly, he strives to return blessing for cursing, honor for insults, and charity for hatred to the emperor who was hostile to him. Yet he warns him to beware the indignation of the divine Judge, lest, the more willingly Symmachus forgave even though he had been more grievously offended, the more abundantly punishment should be exacted from the emperor who had inflicted the offense.

He adds something concerning the great scandal that had then arisen in the Church, both because of the notorious pamphlet that the emperor himself had written against the head of the Church and because of the opinions of Acacius, Severus, and the Acephali, which had been condemned by anathema and which the emperor supported.

He immediately appeals to various testimonies of Sacred Scripture, so that the emperor might derive from them the falsity of these heretical opinions.

Meanwhile, because the pontiff’s mind seeks to safeguard not his own honor but the honor and majesty of his See, he reproaches and presses the emperor on the ground that, having despised human and divine laws, he had, to the great disgrace of the imperial crown, assumed the roles of accuser and judge against the supreme pontiff of the Church.

Therefore he rebukes him, writing:

“You say that I am a Manichaean. Am I perhaps an Eutychian, or do I defend the Eutychians, whose madness especially supports the error of the Manichaeans?”

3. By this manner of speaking and figure of irony, Symmachus indicates not only that he has been unjustly accused of Manichaean corruption; he also intends to criticize Anastasius himself, who, while providing support to the Eutychians, was also patronizing the Manichaeans by receiving into his patronage Xenaia.

Xenaia was the leader of the Manichaeans and sought increasingly to cultivate the emperor’s affection toward himself by adhering to the party of the Eutychians.

Thus, in order to erase such disgraceful accusations and to show that he had never been subject to the Manichaean crime, Symmachus calls upon the city of Rome as a witness and appeals to the archives of the Apostolic See, in which the authentic acts of the sincere faith were preserved.

He challenges in these writings all who judged his religion less than reverently, or at least wished to entertain suspicions about it, so that they should not fear to enter into disputation with him and publicly produce genuine proofs of the crimes alleged against him. Otherwise, he declares, they must be regarded as infamous men and guilty of slander.

I consider it appropriate to append his words here, so that the holy pontiff’s meaning may be fully known to all:

“Rome is my witness, and the archives bear testimony whether I have in any respect deviated from the Catholic faith, which, when I came from paganism, I received at the See of blessed Peter the Apostle. Let someone come forward and convict me by some argument. Otherwise, these are insults, not proofs of crimes.”

### 4.

After this, he entrusts his case to divine judgment, whose supreme wisdom and providence he recalls having once experienced. When, namely, he had been proclaimed pope by legitimate votes and was proceeding to the Constantinian Basilica to assume the pontifical office, he escaped unharmed lest he be overwhelmed by a shower of stones. Therefore, hoping always to have God as his helper, he confidently declares that he will permit nothing that could harm himself or his see. Nor could the emperor produce any argument that God had been angry with Symmachus or with the Roman see. For this reason he addresses him with the greatest force of spirit:

> Show, then, what you think should be brought as an accusation, so that you may prove that an angry God permitted what ought not to have happened.

And, in order to cleanse or heal the ulcers that had wounded and corrupted the emperor’s mind, he adds:

> Is it because I in no way submit to the Eutychians? These things do not wound me; but they openly and plainly reveal that you have contemplated repelling the honor conferred upon me through the intervention of blessed Peter.

Thus he demonstrates, by various arguments, that God could not have been angry with him for this reason. For when he opposed the Eutychians, whom he neither admitted into communion nor whose doctrines he accepted, he was performing the duties most proper to the supreme pontiff, whose sacred power was as far removed from imperial power as divine things are distant from human affairs. Therefore, drawing a comparison between the two dignities, he addresses the emperor as follows:

> You, emperor, receive baptism from the pontiff, receive the sacraments, ask for prayer, hope for a blessing, and request penance. Finally, you administer human things, while he dispenses divine things to you.

And lest he appear to wish to claim superior honor for himself, he asserts that at least equal honor ought to be accorded to both.

Pope Symmachus brings forward these arguments and others of the same kind in defense of the glory of his pontifical dignity, as a safeguard of his innocence, and as the protection and adornment of his apostolic see—chiefly to cleanse himself of that mark of disgrace which Anastasius had unjustly branded upon him by representing him in defamatory pamphlets as a champion of the Manichaean sect.

### 5.

Since, moreover, in the aforementioned defamatory pamphlets Anastasius had declared Symmachus guilty of conspiracy against his person, alleging that he had excommunicated him while the Roman senate was conspiring with him, the pontiff, meeting this charge with remarkable and truthful arguments, easily overturned this calumny as well. First, the pontiff says that he had introduced nothing new, but had followed the policy of his predecessors:

> You say that I excommunicated you while the senate was conspiring with me. In this matter I am undoubtedly following what my predecessors did, and what they did reasonably.

Symmachus, therefore, had not been the first of all to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against the emperor Anastasius. Rather, two other Roman pontiffs—Gelasius, namely, and Anastasius II—had condemned him as a defender and patron of the Eutychian and other heresies. Symmachus would certainly have revoked that sentence if the emperor, abandoning the heretics—especially Acacius—and ending the Constantinopolitan schism that he was fostering, had wished to associate himself exclusively with Catholic and apostolic bishops. For, by withdrawing from the company of these men and no longer taking part in their assemblies, the emperor, as though now repentant of his former obstinacy, could have broken the bonds of excommunication.

Accordingly, the most merciful pontiff offers this remedy for the gravest evils by which the emperor was so greatly afflicted:

> Do not involve yourself in his excommunication—that is, Acacius’s—and you are not excommunicated by us. If you involve yourself in it, you are excommunicated not by us but by yourself. Thus, in either case—whether you withdraw or whether you do not withdraw—you are not excommunicated by us.

### 6.

After this, Symmachus attacks Anastasius at length, first because, once Symmachus had been elevated to the apostolic see of Peter, Anastasius had not written the customary imperial letters informing the pontiff of his faith and filial affection, although the care of the whole Church had been entrusted to him by the mouth of the Lord and Savior. The pontiff censures this serious omission solely lest he appear to have neglected the care of the Lord’s flock, not so that anyone might think he had wished to advance his own honor.

He then inveighs against the same emperor because, by military force, he had compelled Catholics to communicate with men polluted by schismatic and heretical defilement. He condemns this policy as a dreadful and detestable crime. For secular rulers, however great the worldly power supporting them, can neither lawfully nor properly violate those ecclesiastical rights that, from almost the beginnings of the Catholic Church, had been established and confirmed not only by divine but also by imperial laws.

Accordingly, he brings this charge against him and recalls to his mind how the Christian religion, from the apostles down to his own time, had been afflicted and assailed by its adversaries through so many and such great forms of persecution, yet could neither be crushed nor overthrown. The persecutors themselves had perished by an evil end, while orthodox truth had always and everywhere prevailed.

Meanwhile, the one matter that pressed most heavily upon the pontiff’s mind was that pagans—or men even worse than pagans—had been publicly permitted in the East, and especially at Constantinople, to profess their wicked doctrines, after the rules of apostolic tradition had been shattered by the evils of every other heresy; whereas the freedom of Catholic communion alone was thought by those who considered themselves religious to be something that had to be destroyed. Since, therefore, the pontiff’s mind felt itself tortured by these most serious evils and could not remedy them as he desired, he appealed to divine judgment—a protection which those who had attempted to attack Catholic truth with rash presumption could in no way expect for themselves.

Finally, he praises the custom of the ancient emperors, who, whether assuming the reins of empire or learning that a new prelate had been appointed to the apostolic see, immediately sent their letters to that see, thereby showing that they were its associate. Because Anastasius had failed to do this, he declared himself alienated from it; and for that reason the holy pontiff judged that he should be avoided as a rival, a guilty man, and an enemy.

The holy pontiff also briefly indicated that the emperor supported the Manichaeans, as we shall soon explain when we discuss the case of Xenaias.

### 7.

What sort of man Xenaias was, who was also called Philoxenus and whom many writers, both ancient and more recent, asserted to have been a follower of Manichaean doctrine, we shall easily understand. When he came from Persia into the territory of the Roman Empire, Peter the Fuller and the emperor Anastasius strongly supported him; and he stirred up such great disturbances and disasters against the Catholics that, when all the bonds of Christian society had been entirely dissolved, schisms or errors raged everywhere.

Pope Symmachus bore witness to this at the end of his apology against the emperor Anastasius, although he suppressed Xenaias’s name and attacked him in the following words as a champion of falsehood:

> It is no wonder that the patrons of the Manichaeans persecute Catholics, since falsehood cannot fail to persecute truth. It is no wonder that they rage against the orthodox, since those who can agree with all heresies and are friends to every error can be enemies only of those who do not err.

[Note: The apologetic letter of Pope Symmachus against the emperor Anastasius is found in volume V of the Councils, p. 430.]

Before discussing in particular the violence of this wicked man against the Catholics, however, we must speak of his homeland, origin, character, and practices. To pursue all these matters without straying far from the truth, we undertook to examine the volumes of the Oriental Library of the most distinguished Joseph Assemani, selecting whatever appeared relevant to our subject.

### 8.

Most ancient writers inform us that Xenaias was by birth a Persian, originating in the town of Tahal in the province of the Garmaeans; that he was also a slave by status and had no share in divine baptism. The same Assemanus, however, contends that these accusations can be challenged and has attempted, by adducing various arguments, to vindicate Xenaias from such a mark of disgrace. He asserts, namely, that this otherwise most wicked man had not lacked baptism and had not falsely represented himself as an ordained cleric when he came from Persia into Syria.

He advances two very weighty conjectures on this subject. The first is drawn from Xenaias’s conduct: before departing from Persia, Xenaias had vigorously opposed both Nestorian doctrines and the efforts of Ibas of Edessa and Maris the Persian in the city of the Garmaeans, together with certain others. None of this, he argues, could have suited a household slave or a man not yet baptized.

The second conjecture he attempts to derive from Xenaias’s writings. In them, Xenaias not only expresses the authentic form of baptism but also repeatedly professes that he himself was baptized and had put on Christ.

These arguments might indeed turn our mind away from the contrary opinion if we wished to follow the authority of the writer more than the force of the arguments. For he possesses such knowledge and learning in describing Syrian affairs that he surpassed both earlier and contemporary writers of his nation.
