Yet I shall ask pardon of this learned man, otherwise my very dear friend, if I assert that both conjectures on which he relied in vindicating Xenaias’s baptism are unstable.

As for the first conjecture—that Xenaias in the city of the Garmaeans, together with certain other men, opposed the Nestorian doctrine and the efforts of Ibas of Edessa and Maris the Persian—what follows? Even if these things, drawn from wholly uncertain records, were true, could a slippery man who professed the Manichaean sect have lacked the skill to conceal his impiety? The doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches directly overthrew one principal and characteristic error of the Manichaeans.

The Manichaeans denied that Christ had been a true human being, truly born, truly suffered, and truly died; they taught that he possessed nothing but a shadowy and phantom flesh. The Nestorian and Eutychian doctrines were very far removed from this error. The Nestorians taught that there were two true and distinct natures in Christ, and likewise two persons. The Eutychians, moreover, did not deny the reality of Christ’s humanity; but they maintained that, in the union, it had either been absorbed by the nature of the divine Word or been transformed into divinity.

Therefore, even if it were still certain that Xenaias had vigorously opposed both heresies, it could not be inferred from this that he had been cleansed by baptism, since he had already enrolled himself among the Manichaeans.

Furthermore, I do not know whether Xenaias could easily have opposed the efforts of Ibas of Edessa and Maris the Persian in the Persian city of the Garmaeans. We believe that it is clear to everyone that the efforts of those two bishops were undertaken only after the general Council of Ephesus, out of hatred for Cyril of Alexandria, and that hostility and hatred between them and the Alexandrian prelate intensified because of the condemnation of Nestorius and lasted until the Council of Berytus, as we understand from the tenth act of the Council of Chalcedon.

But who proves that Xenaias had by then been born, or from where can this be inferred? In the acts of the Council of Berytus, convened on account of Ibas, or in the pamphlets and writings of those who accused Ibas of Edessa both of bad faith and of various crimes, we do not encounter the name of Xenaias or Philoxenus.

[Note: Volume IV of the General Councils, p. 739, and again act 10 of the Council of Chalcedon.]

Yet we find all the names of the accusers who opposed Ibas and his efforts recorded. Finally, what if we were to grant that Xenaias had been born after the Council of Ephesus, which had condemned Nestorius? Should we perhaps suppose that he was then a man of such mature age, authority, and learning that he could have opposed the efforts of two bishops disputing about matters of faith? Certainly, the first rudiments of the faith, with which boys are ordinarily instructed, could not have sufficed for such a task. The Nestorian doctrine had presented more than two hundred bishops with an exceedingly difficult problem.

But from the rest of Xenaias’s life we learn that at that time he had either not yet seen the light of day or could scarcely have reached the years of puberty. For more than ninety years elapsed between the ecumenical Council of Ephesus and Xenaias’s death. Xenaias died, according to Assemanus as well, after the year 522, whereas the Council of Ephesus must be placed in the year 431. I therefore do not think that this standard-bearer of the Manichaeans had been born at that time.

### 9.

If it should be objected that the efforts of the Nestorians Ibas of Edessa and Maris the Persian in the city of the Garmaeans must be assigned to a later period, I shall not resist. But so much time must not be fabricated between the two events that we could reasonably conjecture that Xenaias had by then been born and had acquired such extensive resources that he could vigorously oppose the Nestorian doctrine and its champions.

Ibas did not persist in those efforts until the end of his life. After making peace with Cyril of Alexandria, he abstained from every heretical agitation before the year 445 of Christ, as we learn from the synods of Tyre and Berytus. Therefore, even if Xenaias’s birth were assigned to that year or to the following one, Assemanus’s earlier conjecture would collapse; and this monster of heresy and wickedness would have died after his seventy-seventh year—something wholly inconsistent with what Assemanus describes about this man before the end of his life.

[Note: Assemanus, volume II of the Oriental Library, chapter 2, pp. 12 ff.]

For he admits that, before his death, with the favor or command of the emperor Anastasius, Xenaias presided over several false synods; undertook various and very long journeys; was exiled from his see for four years by decree of the emperor Justin; and withdrew from place to place—at one time to Thrace, near Philippopolis, and at another to Paphlagonia, near the city of Gangra, where he died after being suffocated by smoke. Since all these events indicate and imply such a great abundance of labors and sufferings, we can scarcely be persuaded that such hardships and inconveniences could have been endured by a man living in extreme old age.

### 10.

Another conjecture advanced by Assemanus carries considerably greater weight. To prove that Xenaias had not been deprived of baptism, he first appeals to Xenaias’s own writings, in which Xenaias bears witness concerning his faith and baptism. He then attempts to show that Xenaias was baptized from the silence of the Syrian Fathers, who certainly would not have allowed Xenaias to lay hands upon them if they had known that he was neither baptized nor properly ordained.

This kind of defense, however, possesses less force if we seek testimony from the writings of others. Theodore, therefore, a lector of the Church of Constantinople who had seen Xenaias and was his contemporary, writes—not merely on the basis of rumor, as Assemanus says, but from the account of the Syrian bishops:

> A certain Persian called Xenaias, whom Calendio, during his episcopate, found adulterating ecclesiastical doctrines and raising strongholds, expelled from the region. Of this man I shall relate briefly what I investigated after hearing much from various people. Fleeing from his own master in the Persian region, he came to the Romans.  
>   
> And shortly afterward: Peter sent him in place of Cyrus as bishop of the Church of Hierapolis. Not long afterward, bishops arriving from Persia accused him as a household slave and as one deprived of divine baptism. When this was discovered, Peter, without concerning himself with what ought to have been done, said that the episcopal consecration was sufficient for him as a supplement to the divine sacrament.

[Note: Volume VIII of the Councils, p. 1019.]

If we carefully consider the force of this testimony, we shall find it difficult to contradict. Theodore the lector was not discussing a man wholly unknown to him and absent, whose principal crimes were not extremely well known both to himself and to all the inhabitants of Constantinople—especially because of the favor that Xenaias had secured for himself from the emperors Zeno and Anastasius of the East. Theodore flourished around the year 515 of Christ and therefore wrote his history not from rumor alone but from what he had seen and what he had heard from others who were his contemporaries.

Moreover, did not the Persian bishops protest when they saw Xenaias appointed to the bishopric of Hierapolis? The cries came from none other than the Persian bishops: Xenaias, consecrated bishop at Hierapolis, was a household slave and deprived of baptism.

If Assemanus thinks that no credence should be given to these men, what credence, I ask, can Xenaias deserve? He was rebuked by his fellow-countrymen among the bishops and accused as a pagan; and, to erase this mark of infamy and prevent himself from being expelled from the episcopal see, he wrote to Zeno concerning the Incarnation of the Word, in which he most craftily and excessively zealously pretended that he had been baptized.

Do not those very words on which Assemanus relies reveal Xenaias’s motive? In one and virtually the same sentence, he speaks twice, three times, indeed four times, when the opportunity is sought, about his baptism. In this respect he followed the method of all scoundrels, who attempt to clear themselves of accusations brought against them solely by their own testimony.

Here are the words of Xenaias that Assemanus quotes:

> The Only-Begotten Son is one of the Trinity, as he himself indicates when he says to his disciples: “Go, teach all peoples, and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”  
>   
> Therefore—let us note the writer’s method—I was baptized in the name of him who died; and I confess that the one in whose name I was baptized died for me; finally, I believe that I put on through baptism the one in whose name and death I was baptized.

So far, then, is this manner of writing from leading us to believe that Xenaias was baptized that it instead makes us suspect even more strongly that he had been deprived of baptism. He does not appeal to witnesses of his baptism, does not name the minister of the sacrament, and specifies neither the place nor the time when he put on Christ through baptism. He makes himself alone the witness and defender of his baptism.

### 11.

The acts of the Second General Council of Nicaea also show that Xenaias had no defender other than himself. In the fifth session, when the deacon Demetrius, keeper of the vessels, had read the words of Theodore the lector cited above, none of those three hundred and fifty Fathers rejected the testimony as fabricated or of doubtful credibility, not even out of respect for the episcopal office. Rather, all gave credence to Theodore’s account.

They gave it such credence that, when Tarasius, a most learned and holy man and bishop of Constantinople, intervened, all the other bishops pronounced an anathema against Xenaias as an unbaptized Manichaean, and against those who preached a mere appearance and denied Christ’s humanity.

I therefore do not know why, or by what reasoning, anyone could now purge Xenaias of both those stains—believing, that is, that he had neither lacked baptism nor enrolled himself among the Manichaeans—when not one of those 350 Fathers showed the slightest hesitation in accepting the testimony of Theodore just quoted.

### 12.

Lest we seem to rely solely on the testimony of Theodore the lector and the approval of the Second Council of Nicaea—which Assemanus, with the considerable care and learning he possesses, attempts to explain more mildly—I shall not hesitate to set forth the account of the Antiochene false synod convened by Peter the Fuller, as it is presented by the author of the synodical pamphlet.

After Peter the Fuller had returned from exile to the Church of Antioch, he convened this synod around the year 485 of Christ, during the reign of the emperor Zeno, who was hostile to the Catholic bishops and favored Peter. This is what Labbeus, Pagius, Stephanus Baluzius, and others have noted. At that time, driven by dreadful fury, the Fuller marked the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon with an anathema and, amid many crimes, designated Xenaias bishop of Hierapolis as a Persian by birth, deprived of baptism, a fugitive of servile condition, and a fierce leader of the heresy that denounced Christians.

[Note: The pamphlet, volume V of the Councils, p. 279, where you will also find the annotations of Labbeus, Pagius, and Baluzius.]

Theophanes spoke of these profane and illegitimate ordinations performed by Peter the Fuller, writing as follows:

> Peter the Fuller, having entered Antioch, perpetrated many unspeakable acts, such as the condemnations of synods, the deposition of bishops, the intrusion of culpable men, illegitimate ordinations, and similar deeds.

Theophanes, therefore, a writer of keen judgment, although in recounting various events of antiquity he followed Theodore the lector, was nevertheless not far removed from Xenaias’s own period. In describing the illegitimate ordinations, he wished, at least obscurely, to designate this man—an unbaptized household slave—as having been intruded into the episcopal see of Hierapolis.

For Theophanes had written a history of events among the Romans and Persians down to the year 573. The deeds of Peter the Fuller, bishop of Antioch, and the bishops illegitimately ordained by that same Peter the Fuller could not have been unknown to him.

Let no one, therefore, be angry with me or frown because, on this matter, I have not subscribed to the opinion of a most learned man who has already deserved so well of literary studies. The zeal to seek and investigate the truth, not a desire to quarrel, so affected my mind that I could not lightly depart from the testimony of Theodore the lector and the authority of the Second Council of Nicaea; and therefore I openly professed, with due reverence, what I understood in good faith.

I shall not depart from this method of proceeding when I explain Xenaias’s Manichaeism.

### 13.

The distinguished Assemanus likewise did not assert this stain against Xenaias of Mabbug, although he calls him a most wicked man.

[Note: Assemanus, volume II of the Oriental Library cited above, p. 12.]

He says:

> How far Xenaias abhorred the Manichaean heresy is clear from the many volumes to be reviewed shortly, in which he explicitly refutes the Eutychians and the Manichaeans.

But first: if Xenaias explicitly refutes the Manichaeans in his works, why does the Byzantine Theophanes write that Xenaias—also called Philoxenus—bishop of Hierapolis, who agreed with the Manichaeans, was sent into exile by Justin the Elder?

This occurred in the year 518 of Christ, as the most eminent Norisius proves in his work On the Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians. Moreover, when the same writer recounts Xenaias’s second journey to the royal city of Constantinople, why does he write:

> Anastasius summoned to Byzantium Xenaias, a follower of the Manichaeans, otherwise called Philoxenus, since he shared their opinions.

Yet the emperor Anastasius not only zealously favored the Manichaeans, as we stated above from Pope Symmachus’s apology; he also defended Manichaean doctrines because he had been born of a Manichaean mother.

Theodore the lector, an eyewitness, says:

> The Manichaeans and Arians rejoiced at the advancement of Anastasius.

And he explains:

> The Manichaeans rejoiced because his mother was an especially devoted worshiper of that sect.

[Note: Theodore the lector, Book II of the Ecclesiastical History, in Valesius, volume IV, p. 558.]

If, therefore, Xenaias and the emperor Anastasius both professed precisely the same doctrine, and if the emperor summoned that Manichaean Xenaias to Constantinople because of this doctrine; if, moreover, Anastasius’s mother was an especially devoted worshiper of the Manichaean sect—how can we despise the testimony of ancient writers, which strongly supports our position, relying instead on certain weaker conjectures?

Our forebears certainly did not act in this way. Gathering at the Second Council of Nicaea in the name of Christ, they judged that wicked Xenaias was a follower and leader of the Manichaeans, following also the testimony of another, earlier writer, John Diacrinomenus.

[Note: *Diacrinomenus* means “the separated one.” This was the name given, according to Leontius, *On the Sects*, to those who did not accept the Council of Chalcedon. Thus in Labbeus, volume VIII, p. 1019. Consult also Photius, Book I of his *History of the Manichaeans*, chapters 7 and 10. There it is read that they abhorred the figure of the venerable cross depicted in the Gospel books. In Christophorus Wolfius, p. 23: “Adding that it is impious to worship and embrace the true cross, as being wood, an instrument of malefactors, and subject to a curse.”]

John affirmed that Xenaias was accustomed to conceal in hidden places those images that represented Christ, thereby indicating, evidently, that Christ had assumed not a true human nature but only a phantom and shadowy one. We have already proved abundantly in the preceding chapters that this was the principal doctrine of the Manichaeans.

### 13.

I would now seem to be failing in my duty if I passed over in silence what Assemanus has brought forward to cleanse Xenaias of this Manichaean stain. For Xenaias wrote to certain Syrian monks a letter on the Incarnation of the Word, in which he asserted the reality of both natures in the Lord Christ, namely, the divine and the human.

Assemanus presents the substance of this letter, written in the Syriac language, divided into five chapters; under number three he adds the following words, translated into Latin:

[Note: Assemanus, *Oriental Library*, volume II, p. 29.]

> III. If he who was incarnate is God, then he who was born will also be God; and just as the one who entered into the Virgin was one spiritual being, whose spiritual nature is from the Father, so that same one came forth from the same Virgin, possessing from nature the reality of his body. Therefore the Virgin is rightly called *Dei Genitrix*—“God-bearer”—because she ineffably gave birth to the one incarnate person of God.

These and similar passages from various letters or writings of Xenaias are cited by Assemanus, and they wholly oppose the Manichaean heresy. There can be no doubt about the reliability of this writer and translator, particularly in translating documents from Syriac into Latin.

It may nevertheless be doubted whether Xenaias followed the dictate of his faith when he wrote these things. It may likewise be doubted whether the writings now circulated under Xenaias’s name actually came from his workshop, or whether they entered the books and codices of the Syrians through the contrivance and fabrication of some impostor.

These works were entirely unknown to Theodore the lector, Theophanes, Evagrius, the Persian bishops, the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea, and writers of subsequent centuries. Yet these men, moved not by empty fear but by the strongest arguments, exposed this scoundrel as a leader and chief of the Manichaeans.

It therefore seems very difficult to believe that these writings, if they truly existed, could have remained unknown to those men who described this most disgraceful man’s homeland, status, character, practices, and offices. Or, if they did exist, were they perhaps so hidden in the Syrians’ archives and enclosed in such secure custody that they could come to human knowledge only in these latest times through the study and labors of Assemani?

Certainly, Assemanus, who undertook to illustrate such works with his own observations, does not cite even a single trustworthy writer who assigns works of this kind to Xenaias. And although he sometimes appeals to one or another witness, he attacks, criticizes, and condemns these witnesses as Eutychians and Monophysites.

Furthermore, once the testimony and agreement of the earlier writers are lacking, should not corroborating responses concerning Xenaias’s letters be sought? He wrote to the emperor Zeno and to the monks living in various monasteries. Where, I ask, are the responses of all these people, so that we may examine whether they agree with one another or whether they contain any feature that betrays fabrication to the learned eye?

For, when I found myself confronted with such a serious difficulty, I was led by the greatest suspicion to believe that those works had been falsely attributed to Xenaias by some impostor. The conduct of the distinguished Assemani intensified this suspicion. When he encountered serious obstacles that he could not avoid, he asserted that either Xenaias had lied or that someone had fabricated a work under Xenaias’s name.

One such fabrication is the claim that Nestorius the heresiarch had been summoned by Pope Saint Leo to the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: Volume II of the *Oriental Library*, p. 41.]

Xenaias reports this in a letter to the monks of Senon. Assemanus, following the contents of the letter, noted that this statement must be rejected as a foul fabrication. For before Saint Leo the Great obtained the pontificate of the Catholic Church, Nestorius had already been sent to a fourth place of exile and, according to some, died in 436 with his tongue eaten away by worms; or at least, according to Socrates, lived in the Oasis until the year 439.

[Note: Socrates, Book VII, chapter 32.]

Saint Leo the Great was elevated to the pontifical throne only in the following year, 440, on 28 July. Both sacred and secular records show that he took counsel concerning the convocation of the Council of Chalcedon in the year 450 and that the council was finally celebrated in the following year.

Assemanus, I say, notes this fundamental error and, hesitating, does not know to whom to attribute it: to Xenaias, or to some Monophysite seeking a patron in Xenaias.

### 14.

The learned Assemanus therefore did not consider the cited writings sufficiently trustworthy to conclude that Xenaias had completely rejected the errors of the Manichaeans. Indeed, certain expressions of Xenaias also came to his attention that convey a heretical Manichaean meaning.

Among these, the following statement, which the Oriental writer cites from a theological book entitled *Rays*, is famous:

> Philoxenus, they say, acknowledges the sufferings of the Lord as voluntary, not natural. Moses Barcepha likewise testifies that the Lord put on Adam’s body before Adam sinned. Finally, in the history of Mar Barsuma, the body of our Lord is said not to have been like a human body.

[Note: Assemanus, ibid., pp. 4 and 2.]

Who does not know that all these expressions breathe Manichaeism and contain the fabulous inventions of the Manichaeans? Although the author of the book does not assign all of them to Xenaias or Philoxenus, our preceding investigations clearly show that each one came from the wicked workshop of Manes.

Assemanus himself asserts that this statement of Philoxenus indicates Manichaeism—namely, that the sufferings of the Lord were voluntary—and he says that it gave the writers whom we have reviewed occasion to represent Xenaias as guilty of this heresy.

The learned man nevertheless thinks either that Philoxenus fell into the error of the Incorruptibles, an error derived from Manichaean principles, or that, because of the inconstancy with which heretics are more frequently afflicted, he adhered to certain Manichaean opinions, although elsewhere in his books he consistently abominated them.

In any event, therefore, according to Assemanus himself, Xenaias cannot now be cleansed of every stain of Manichaeism; nor are the works circulated under his name and attributed to him free from spurious attributions, fragments, and interpolations. On what basis, then, once the testimony of ancient and more recent writers has been set aside, shall we judge his faith?

If we rely on the cited writings, we shall be exposed to the danger of error, since it is not certainly known whether those volumes came from Xenaias’s genuine workshop, whether he followed the dictate of his faith in composing them, or whether they were corrupted through the efforts of others to conceal or erase the mark of Manichaeism that ancient writers and the Fathers of the seventh synod had branded upon him.

I realize, however, that I have lingered longer than was proper in composing this discussion, chiefly because I can neither examine nor interpret the documents written in the Syriac language; yet these ought certainly to be available to anyone wishing to bring such a case to a conclusion.

Therefore, setting aside this line of argument, we state only that almost the whole of the East had been polluted by the Manichaean stain through the efforts of the emperor Anastasius and the Acephali. To make this clearer and more intelligible, we now compose the final chapter of the history of the Manichaeans, since what else might be said about this wicked heresy, later spread among the Armenians through the efforts of the Paulicians, has been sufficiently described by Peter of Sicily and Photius in their histories.

## CHAPTER XIV

Hormisdas the pope compels the Manichaeans still inhabiting the city of Rome, after examining them through the ordeal of scourging, to go into exile. The trifles and quibbles of Beausobre are refuted. The synod of Menna, patriarch of Constantinople, condemns Severus, Anthimus, and other leaders of the Acephali as champions of Manichaean doctrine. Finally, some observations are made concerning the Manichaeans from the historical works of Peter of Sicily and Photius.

[Col. 0971A]

1. Before undertaking to say anything about the actions of the Eastern bishops in the matter of the Manichaeans, we deem it necessary briefly to describe the policy and judgment of Pope Hormisdas concerning these same heretics. For when he discovered this viperous brood lying concealed in Rome, he devoted every resource of his mind to destroying it utterly.

Accordingly, in the year of Christ 514, while Anastasius held the reins of the empire, Pope Symmachus departed this life. The ecclesiastical records show that Hormisdas was appointed as his successor at Rome in that same year. But whether, at the beginning of this pontificate, he discovered some remnants of the Manichaean sect—survivors of Pope Symmachus’s preceding investigation and hiding there—or whether, after Symmachus’s death alone, in the third or fourth year, they had converged upon Rome from other regions of Africa, the East, or Italy, is not revealed by any record of Christian history.

Yet if we wish to follow the order of the *Pontifical Book*, in which the deeds of the Roman bishops are described, we must believe that Hormisdas discovered the Manichaeans only after several years of his pontificate had passed. For that supreme pontiff spent the first four complete years of his administration trying to bring the emperor Anastasius—who, as we have seen, was the champion and defender of many heresies—back to a better course. When he had tried unsuccessfully to achieve this once and again, both through his legates sent to Constantinople for that purpose and through 189 letters, and when the pious will of the Roman pontiff had always been frustrated, the emperor at last, struck by a thunderbolt at the divine nod, died most miserably.

When the most religious prince Justin succeeded him in the empire, Hormisdas achieved with remarkable success what he had so earnestly desired: in the year 519, legates were sent to Constantinople, among them that most holy man Germanus, bishop of Capua.

[Col. 0971B]

2. Thus peace having been restored between the Eastern churches and the Roman See, and the memory of the heretics Acacius, Euphemius, and Macedonius, as well as of the emperors Zeno and Anastasius, having been condemned, he finally compelled the offspring of the Manichaeans to leave the city in exile.

Therefore, if we suppose that the author of the *Pontifical Book*, in describing the deeds of Pope Hormisdas, followed the order of events and dates, we shall affirm that this pontiff’s judgment against the Manichaeans occurred after the year 519. But leaving aside this scarcely useful and uncertain question, let us attend to Hormisdas’s policy toward the Manichaeans.

“He found Manichaeans,” says the aforementioned writer, “and, after examining them by an investigation involving scourging, he deported them into exile.” [Note: *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Pope Hormisdas, vol. V of the Councils, p. 558.]

This is plainly a new form of ecclesiastical judgment, which the author describes as having been employed by Hormisdas against the Manichaeans. For before the time of this pontiff, we do not read that heretics were examined by ecclesiastical authority with an investigation involving scourging. And although emperors and secular judges had long decreed various kinds of punishment in order to eradicate this brood completely—either proscribing their property or depriving them of every human right and compelling them to go into exile—we do not understand that anyone had previously determined that they should be afflicted with blows and lashes. Yet we believe that this was carried out by the public authority of the age, so that the laws of leniency to which the pastors of the Church most reverently adhered would not be violated.

Moreover, after collecting all the Manichaeans’ books and writings, the supreme pontiff, following the same examples of his predecessors, burned them before the doors of the Constantinian basilica. By arousing such fear and terror in the minds of these utterly criminal men, he ensured that they did not venture to return from exile to the city.

Nevertheless, this policy of Hormisdas, Symmachus, Gelasius, Leo, and the other Roman pontiffs in burning the Manichaeans’ books was not entirely approved by non-Catholic writers. Isaac Beausobre in particular attempts to show that it was of little use and unsafe. [Note: See what we said in chapter 4.] In his books on Manichaean history, he reviewed various laws enacted by emperors and magistrates for destroying and utterly eradicating the books of heretics or Christians. He defends these laws as reasonable, on the ground that such writings contained material that corrupted religious devotion and human society; concerning this matter we ourselves have spoken at length in chapter 4 of this book. [Note: Isaac de Beausobre, in the preliminary discourse to part I of his *Manichaean History*, p. 118 and following.]

[Col. 0972B]

3. Now, rejecting Beausobre’s trivialities and fabrications, we shall proceed to examine other Manichaean customs, worship, and ecclesiastical administration from the Constantinopolitan synods. We shall show from the most certain records that one of these synods must be referred to the time of Hormisdas, while the other belongs to the age of Agapetus.

Those who have examined the Acts of these synods know that they condemned Severus, Anthimus, Zoaras, Philoxenus, and others who bore the name of Acephalites as defenders of Manichaean doctrines, with the common agreement of the Fathers. Therefore, as we reviewed those same Acts, we judged without any uncertainty that adherents of Manichaean rites had attempted to conceal themselves under the name of the Acephalites.

So that I may not seem to be telling false tales, I shall first recall what the impious emperor Anastasius did to enlarge his heresy—namely, how he brought Xenaia to Constantinople and honorably received the wicked Severus, together with two hundred monks who came with him.

“This,” says Petavius, [Note: Petavius, *Rationarium Temporum*, part I, book VII, chapter 3.] “was the beginning of that impure Severus, who in 513 forcibly seized the see of Antioch, from which Flavian had been expelled the preceding year because of his steadfast Catholic confession. He attempted to bring all the Easterners to condemn the Council of Chalcedon, and expelled from their sees the Catholic bishops who resisted.”

We consider it necessary briefly to explain who Severus was, from what people he derived his origin, and in what religion he was first instructed. Those who read through these present *Exercises* should not regard such matters as alien to our purpose in writing.

Severus was therefore born at Sozopolis, one of the cities of the province of Pisidia. When he had grown up, he was, according to Evagrius, Nicephorus, [Note: Evagrius, book III, chapter 33; Nicephorus, book XVI, chapter 29.] and the deacon Liberatus, engaged in the public life of Berytus, a city of Cilicia, while constantly devoting himself to the customs and rites of the pagans.

Later, abandoning the study of jurisprudence, he received holy baptism in the church of the admirable martyr Leontius, who is held in the highest honor in Tripoli of Phoenicia. He immediately embraced the monastic life at the place situated midway along the road between the city of Gaza and the town of Maiuma. [Note: Liberatus the deacon, chapter 19.]

Yet a pamphlet of the monks, read at the Constantinopolitan synod of Menna, reports that from his earliest age he had been discovered to practice magic and that, before his baptism, he had rendered religious worship to demons in the city of Berytus. We may therefore at least suspect that he came to receive baptism only under false pretenses, namely, to evade the punishments prescribed by the laws of the emperors for sacrilegious and magical men.

Severus’s flight increases this suspicion: he fled from Berytus in order to take refuge at Tripoli. Finally, our conjecture is strengthened still more by the fact that Severus, before the period had ended during which those recently enlightened by baptism lived in monasteries, was unable any longer to restrain the wickedness of his mind under the guise of the Catholic religion, yet could not openly return to the vomit of his former pagan belief. He therefore reached by another path the goal toward which he was striving.

[Col. 0973A]

4. Thus, driven by fear of punishment, he dreaded openly returning to the ancient rites of the pagans. Accordingly, devising new frauds, he attempted to conceal a Manichaean profession beneath the doctrines of the Acephalites, so that he might devote himself more zealously to the rites and mysteries of Manes.

It is therefore no wonder that, after Severus had renounced the Church and the one by whom he had been baptized, he immediately hastened to Constantinople to the emperor Anastasius, the patron and defender of the most wicked men. He was received by him with great rejoicing and honor, together with two hundred monks.

Supported by the protection of such power and elevated to the see of Antioch, or Theopolis, he not only ordered many bloody massacres to be carried out by military force against Catholic priests and archimandrites who vigorously opposed his unlawful ordination, made in violation of the canons; he also stained houses of God and churches, consecrated with the greatest solemn rites and mysteries, with the blood of those who had been killed. He called them lodging-houses of heresy and impiety and rejected the baptism he had received.

Now that Severus did not sincerely adhere to the Acephalites, but pretended even to profess their religion, was made clear by all that follows, as the religious monks state in the aforementioned pamphlet. [Note: The monks’ pamphlet addressed to the Constantinopolitan synod is found in vol. V of the Councils, pp. 1083 and following.]

They report, first, that he admitted no union of the two natures in Christ—what they call a “uniting” union—but only a novel one, calling it “divisive” and anathematizing it in his own writings. Although this formula of speech has an obscure meaning, it signifies that the divine Word did not assume true humanity or join it to himself.

Next, he refused to communicate with Peter Mongus, who had been intruded into the see of Alexandria because of his leadership of the Acephalites, or with those who had been seduced and instructed by that same Peter Mongus, on the ground that Peter ought to be removed from the Alexandrian Church. For this reason he wished the names of Peter Mongus and of the others who communicated with him to be erased from the diptychs of the Church of Theopolis.

Accordingly, by stirring up new disturbances every day against everyone, he attempted to overthrow and destroy not only the Catholic religion but also the religion of the Acephalites themselves and its adherents.

Then, taking as his accomplice in crimes a certain Peter—whom they call the Iberian, since he had usurped for himself the episcopal throne of Apamea—they resolved upon the final destruction of the city of Alexandria. They introduced divisions among the Alexandrians and incited the people against one another, so that civil wars might break out, many houses be burned, and the blood of many people be shed. They themselves scarcely ever escaped the punishments due for these deeds except by flight.

[Col. 0973D]

5. From this sequence of events the monks in their pamphlet wisely reasoned that Severus and Peter the Iberian, or Apamean, had nowhere been worshipers of the Christian religion, since they appeared equally hostile to Catholics and heretics. For when they had dared to anathematize the whole Church unjustly, they were deservedly anathematized by the whole Church.

And indeed, the savage and cruel manner in which they sought out the worshipers of Jesus Christ for death and destruction provided sufficient reason for their being proscribed by all under a universal anathema and for everyone to shudder at their way of life.

For after breaking and abolishing all sacred and divine laws, they delivered priests and other ministers of the Church—who inhabited the temples and served at and attended upon the altars—to violent death, strangling them with their own hands. Or, when they sought to plunder all the monasteries’ possessions, they harassed devoted monks with chains and prisons and slaughtered them with swords and weapons.

Or, while traveling along the roads, they entered the venerable monastery of Saint Simeon. After assembling a multitude of Jewish bandits, they attacked these honorable monks and, without sparing their gray hairs, carried out the work of the sword against approximately 350 of them. They scattered their limbs along the road, refusing burial to their venerable remains and sparing not even their huts.

I say that all these deeds, although they display a savage, cruel, and bloodthirsty disposition far removed from all piety and religion, would not by themselves demonstrate their Manichaean institutions unless the purpose of their actions were considered. For what else were Severus and Peter the Iberian contemplating when they perpetrated these savage massacres except to offer bloody sacrifices to the demons whom they served? It is most certain that the Manichaeans practiced this rite.

Severus and Peter also employed other superstitious and magical rites: for example, when their profane and false priests—like the diviners of the pagans—laid suffocating hands upon people and, as though over a dead person, uttered words of invocation over those who were to be ordained, speaking various things from the belly and uttering words from the earth, not from divine grace. [Note: Vol. V of the Councils, p. 1087.]

Or they did so when they attempted to overthrow and devastate the churches of God and the mystical sacraments and mysteries of our faith, establishing new conventicles and contrary baptisms, and audaciously and shamelessly stealing Christian souls for money, glory, and carnal pleasures.

For entering houses, they took captive the souls of men and women who were not firmly established, corrupting them not only in soul through perverse doctrines but also bodily.

The aforementioned assembly of archimandrites and monks from the monasteries of Saint Dalmatius, Jerusalem, the Second Syria, Mount Sinai, and the Three Palestines declares that reports of these and similar deeds had previously been sent to Hormisdas, bishop of the Roman and apostolic See, and that this supreme and greatest pontiff had issued against these heretics a sentence of deposition and anathema. Nothing else was more insistently demanded by that venerable assembly of ascetics than that these wicked men be treated and punished as Manichaeans.

[Col. 0974C]

6. That the holy pontiff Hormisdas acted against them as followers of Manichaean doctrine is made sufficiently clear by his letter to the priests, deacons, and archimandrites of the Second Syria, and to the other orthodox people living in any region of the East and remaining in communion with the apostolic See.

For Hormisdas, speaking from the apostolic throne of Peter, declares that the heresies then spreading throughout the whole East had arisen either from the impure sources of Photinus or of Manes, and that their insane doctrines had been propagated more widely through the efforts of Severus of Antioch, Xenaia of Hierapolis, Cyrus of Edessa, and Peter of Apamea. These men, continually enveloped in wicked and superstitious filth, had polluted the episcopal thrones with countless crimes.

Therefore, lest the priests, deacons, and archimandrites of the Second Syria, and the other orthodox Easterners, be deceived by profane rites, the supreme pontiff there gives a general command to reject whatever had been brought forward from certain false compositions against the rules of the Fathers:

“Let no one,” he says, “move you by incongruous precepts or novel institutions. For if they are worldly, they cannot hold churches, since it is more appropriate for them to learn than to teach.”

Finally, perhaps alluding to Manichaean offerings, he adds:

“For it is unlawful to bring foreign libations to holy altars, since God prescribed definite boundaries for religious discipline even at the very beginnings of his worship.” [Note: Letter of Pope Hormisdas to the monks of the Second Syria, vol. V of the Councils.]

[Col. 0975A]

7. Besides these records of unquestionable authority, which show that Severus, Peter of Apamea, Zoaras, and their other associates were teachers of Manichaean rites and doctrines, there survives another petition from the clergy and monks of Antioch of that period to John, bishop of Constantinople. It not only recounts the crimes described above but also many others that could belong only to worshipers of Manes.

Such, for example, were those practices Severus had borrowed from the association of the Jews. After massacres of Christians had been carried out everywhere, he threw the flesh of the holy Syrian martyr-monks to be devoured by dogs and birds. He presumed to do [something] around the fountains at Daphne and, employing magic there, worshiped demons through wicked sacrifices. He spared neither the sacred altars nor the holy vessels: he broke some and melted down others, expending money, bronze, and silver for wholly wicked and profane purposes.

Indeed, he appropriated silver chalices and golden doves suspended over the sacred baths and altars in the form of the Holy Spirit, together with other objects, saying that the Holy Spirit ought not to be named under the appearance of a dove. [Note: See what we wrote about this doctrine of Manes against Beausobre, book I, chapter 9. Consult the Acts of Archelaus in Zacagni, p. 90 and following.]

Who could deny that one of the principal doctrines of Manes lay in this accursed teaching? They stubbornly denied that God could assume bodily form. Consequently, they taught that neither the Word had assumed true human flesh nor the Holy Spirit had appeared under a visible and bodily form. Therefore, in order to overthrow these two foundations of the Christian religion, they cast down and attempted everywhere to destroy representations of Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the angels.

These, indeed, were principles of Manichaean philosophy and theology, and even the non-Catholic Beausobre could not deny this. Although, in writing the history of the Manichaeans, he indulges his own side excessively and devotes all his effort to harassing Catholics, despising and ridiculing the opinions of the Church’s most ancient holy Fathers and writers, attacking Catholics with abuse and curses, and finally attempting either to refute the principal doctrines of our faith or to pervert them more dangerously through the corrupt fabrications of Lutherans, Calvinists, and Socinians, nevertheless, in his eighth book he attributed to Manes and his followers what we have described concerning Severus, Zoaras, and the others.

Yet concerning Severus, Zoaras, and the others who in the sixth century of the Church attempted to conceal Manichaean impiety beneath the mask of the Acephalites, Beausobre said not a single word. His method and purpose of writing extend only to Manes and his earliest companions, and to their equally profane and wicked institutions. He then set aside the places in which that heresy flourished and the authors through whose assistance and efforts it was, in the course of time, propagated far and wide.

Thus, if anyone carefully considers the purpose of that author, he will understand beyond doubt—as we have already indicated above—that Beausobre did not intend to compose a sincere historical and critical work about the Manichaeans. Rather, he intended only to attack Catholics, to disparage those most holy and ancient Fathers who vigorously opposed this wicked sect, and to accuse them of ignorance and error.

[Col. 0975D]

8. But lest, in recounting Beausobre’s evil methods, we disrupt the thread and order of our history, let us add the new petitions of the orthodox Eastern bishops against Severus, Anthimus, and the other Acephalites. [Note: The pamphlet of the orthodox Eastern bishops presented to Agapetus, vol. V of the Councils, pp. 999 and following.]

From all these documents it will become especially clear that we have invented nothing in the case now under discussion and have not clung merely to conjectures; rather, we have wished both to investigate and to draw the truth of events from the most certain records.

Forty-seven orthodox bishops of the East therefore presented, either in person or through their legates, a pamphlet to Agapetus, the Roman pontiff who had been summoned to Constantinople. In it they not only testified to the criminal deeds of Severus described above but also demanded that he be condemned as a wicked defender and champion of Manichaean doctrine.

“We beseech you, most holy one … we cry out: Help us and the holy souls killed by Severus. Consider wisely that they stand before you and show you that they were handed over to death for Christ by the many-headed beast, lest once again this wicked man, through his openly displayed traffic and the error of Manes, dare in his confidence to enter the pure royal courts.”

The bishops reached this opinion, or judgment, for no other reason than that, after carefully examining Severus’s conduct and teaching, they had diligently investigated what sect’s champion and defender he ought to be called.

For when they had learned that he agreed with the pagans, pretended to hold the same opinion as Eutyches, and at times followed Nestorian practices, they rightly and truthfully called him both an instrument of the devil and a Manichaean.

Let no one therefore falsely imagine that these esteemed Eastern bishops judged rashly concerning Severus’s doctrines or errors, especially since they issued such a judgment not from uncertain popular rumor but from deeds and circumstances thoroughly observed and known.

[Col. 0976B]

9. Moreover, in accordance with the principles of Manichaean philosophy and theology, which denied the true birth of the Lord Christ from the Virgin, his true flesh, and his death, Severus himself, Peter of Apamea, Zoaras, and Isaac the Persian diligently devoted themselves to magical practices and exercises.

Beausobre himself has explained in various places that the Manichaeans were accustomed to engage in such superstitions. Concerning Zoaras, we read in the aforementioned pamphlet that he was ignorant of divine Scripture, all the sacred orders, and the Mass. Indeed, with the greatest boldness, he completely overthrew all true and sacred ecclesiastical rites through the conventicles and para-baptisms that he conducted daily.

“His synagogue,” say the aforementioned Eastern bishops to Agapetus, “is filled with little women devoted to feasting, drunkenness, luxury, and adulterous acts.” [The Latin *mulierculae* is contemptuous: “little women” or “women of low character.”]

To drive these evils far from the bosom of the Church, the other most holy Eastern bishops employed every effort. They even appeared fearlessly before the emperor and earnestly begged him not to permit bloodthirsty beasts to be joined with lambs. Otherwise, with the religion of Christ gradually polluted and weakened throughout the East, shame, justice, holiness, and the true worship of God would all eventually be brought to ruin.

10. It is established that Isaac the Persian, who had come to the East and joined himself as a companion to those other wicked men, perpetrated still graver crimes.

For when those orthodox bishops were about to speak to Agapetus about this man, they could neither restrain their tears and lamentation nor explain in words what he had not shrunk from doing with his wicked hands. They report only one crime of his, which they testify that they especially abhorred.

Namely, when he withdrew into a certain lodging where an image of the most pious and orthodox emperor Justinian had been placed, that wicked and arrogant man—“as though competing to blaspheme God according to a newer manner of speech”—did something against the image.

The preceding words plainly indicate that this Persian devised and uttered some particular kind of blasphemy against God. But what it was cannot be learned by us either from this account or from any other record, especially since the Fathers, continuing the narrative they had begun, immediately add:

“Extending the staff by which he pretended to support his dishonored old age, and at the same time displaying his feigned deceit before those who had been led astray by him, he struck without mercy the likeness of the Christ-loving emperor, calling it heretical, as though it were thus united to God, guarded by him, and preserving the truth of the preaching.”

They assert that Isaac persisted in this madness until he tore apart the garment bearing the noble image and kept one part for himself, which he also committed to the fire; but he could not destroy the whole.

At the same time, we believe that an image representing the Lord Christ had been depicted together with the emperor’s image. For in the subsequent part of their statement they add:

“For it was preserved by the better providence of the Divinity, as a manifest and known rebuke of murderous audacity.” [Note: See what we said in chapter 12 of this book.]

[Col. 0977B]

11. We judge it to be beyond all doubt that the things we have thus far either copied or explained concerning Isaac the Persian and the others expose their Manichaean customs, institutions, and wicked religion.

We are especially driven to this conviction because the sect of the Manichaeans cast down, overthrew, and rejected temples, altars, sacrifice, images, and the other mysteries pertaining to Christ’s true human nature and representing it. Instead, they gathered only with their immoral women during the night hours in certain profane meeting places, or lodging-houses, to offer certain profane oblations to God.

Beausobre, however, has discussed these institutions of theirs at greater length. [Note: Beausobre, book IX, chapter 6.] He did so with the intention of daring to argue that certain of these institutions were wholly consistent with the original religion, rites, discipline, and doctrines of the Christians—as though the Manichaeans had tried to conform themselves in everything to the apostolic men.

What is more, he maintains that the Fathers of the first three centuries thought the same as the Manichaeans. He claims that they taught only that a pure offering of prayers ought to be made to God, and he does not hesitate to appeal to Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria. He adds that the first worshipers of Christ admitted neither temples, altars, nor images, from which they abstained lest they appear to follow the religion of the pagans. [Note: Beausobre, ibid., § 3.]

But that Beausobre is trifling and plainly fabricating these claims is already clear from the very Fathers to whom he intends to appeal.

First, although Tertullian, in the book *To Scapula*—which Beausobre cites—while discussing offerings made to God, calls pure prayers of the heart “sacrifices” in a broad sense, in many places he nevertheless mentions the sacrifice of the Mass, the priesthood of the Church, and the altars and temples of Christians. This is especially so in the book *An Exhortation to Chastity*, in the books *On Monogamy* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, and elsewhere throughout his writings. In these passages he not only praises the dignity of priests but also commends and describes the rites by which the ministers of the altar are consecrated.

Beausobre likewise invents a similar deception and displays a crafty intellect when he appeals to Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*, chapter 7. Although Clement praises the offering of pure prayers, he nowhere denied either the unbloody sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood or the temples and altars of Christians. We could explain this at greater length by excerpts from his works if our purpose in writing did not prevent it.

Having noted these and other similar deceptions of Beausobre, we shall now briefly recount what specifically remains to be said concerning Anthimus.

[Col. 0977D]

12. Anthimus therefore first invaded the city of Constantinople together with his other associates. In many prominent places within the city, in its suburbs, and in his own house, he set up profane altars and alien baptisteries opposite the true altar and the holy font, and did not cease to commit wicked acts at them.

That Anthimus had done these things at Constantinople through the common efforts of Severus, Peter the Iberian, Zoaras, and Isaac the Persian was attested by the monk Marianus, together with the archimandrites of the monastery of Saint Dalmatius and the other monks and archimandrites of the monasteries of the imperial city, Constantinople, Jerusalem, Mount Sinai, and the Second Syria, in their supplicatory pamphlet presented to Justinian Augustus.

In particular, they added this concerning Anthimus: he had long since abandoned his own Church of Trapezus, in which he had been ordained bishop, contrary to divine and ecclesiastical laws, and under the false mask of continence had held conventicles with heretics, so that with their support he might seize the see of Constantinople against all ecclesiastical canons and laws.

All orthodox men abhorred this violent and unjust promotion of Anthimus to the throne of Constantinople, both because the legitimate sacraments of the Catholic Church were being overthrown and because they were forced to endure the greatest hardships.

Let us now consider what the emperor decreed amid so great a crisis in ecclesiastical affairs. For after hearing all the charges against Anthimus, he did not wish to act against him himself. Rather, the most wise prince, taking the rights of the Church and the immunity of priests into the best account, requested that canonical judgment be carried out by the Roman pontiff both against Anthimus and against his associates, persuaded that he ought not to interfere in ecclesiastical matters.

He was convinced and instructed by the commands of both Testaments that a judgment should be awaited from the universal pastor of the Church: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you”; and elsewhere: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account.” [Note: Deuteronomy 32 and the Epistle to the Hebrews 13:17.]

He also wished, as the authors of the aforementioned pamphlets had long before requested together with the Palestinian bishops and the representatives of the other Eastern prelates, that the crimes committed by Anthimus and his associates be recognized and judged by Pope Agapetus; this he ordered to be confirmed even by an imperial law.

[Col. 0978C]

13. Anthimus was condemned and deprived of all priestly honor by none other than Agapetus himself, the Roman pontiff. For when the holy pontiff had traveled to Constantinople and had examined and fully verified the impiety of Anthimus’s crimes, he expelled him from that see and declared that he was to be regarded as a heretic. He stripped him of every dignity and sacred office, and completely erased him from the register of the ministers of sacred things under the name “orthodox” and “bishop,” in which Anthimus took the greatest pride.

So that the sentence of the apostolic See might be brought to a successful conclusion, with every contradiction and obstacle removed, Agapetus himself entrusted its execution to Justinian Augustus, as the defender of the sacred canons. This was what the authors of the aforementioned pamphlet earnestly begged, saying:

“We therefore beseech your imperial authority not to disregard the just judgment of the aforesaid holy man, but to carry it out, and to free the Church of God and the whole world from the plague of Anthimus and the aforesaid heretics. For after the holy man Agapetus had been summoned from this present life, we looked after God to your piety and expected these matters to receive their conclusion from you.”

They immediately explain what role the aforementioned most pious ruler of the secular world ought to assume for the destruction of the heretics, in these words:

“Therefore, by fulfilling what he judged justly and canonically, confirming it through your general sanction, and forbidding such things to be attempted in the future, you will honor his blessed soul.”

### 14.

That the leaders of the Acephaloi were versed in this kind of Manichaean behavior and rites is clearly demonstrated by the monuments already cited from reliable sources. But while turning over the Acts of the Council of Menas of Constantinople, we have encountered other material [Col. 0979A] that not only settles the present question but also more fully refutes Beausobre’s follies noted earlier. Our purpose in writing therefore urges us to set it forth, lest we seem to have omitted it.

This material relates chiefly to Peter the Iberian, bishop of Apamea, about whom we made various observations above. The common testimony of the clergy of the holy Church of Apamea makes it known that he was a worshiper and defender of all Manichaean doctrines and rites, and that he completely overturned the sacred and divine discipline and administration of the Churches of Syria [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Letter of the Clergy of Apamea to the Bishops of the Second Syria,” vol. V of the Councils.].

Our method does not permit us to review individually everything that the aforesaid clergy of Apamea described in its letter to the most holy Fathers and bishops of the Second Syria concerning so wicked a man. Nor can we do more than indicate how, by what devices, zeal, and supports Peter obtained the see of Apamea; or speak of the crafty machinations he employed to remove entirely from the sacred diptychs [Col. 0979B] the names of the orthodox bishops of the East; or of the plunder by which he converted sacred vessels, the funds of the Churches, and their furnishings to profane use; or of the violent ordinations he frequently employed to remove from their lawful ranks humble clerics who opposed him, though they were the custodians of those goods, promoting others to higher ministries, and boldly maintaining with sacrilegious lips that even Jesus Christ crucified could not descend to rescue them from his hands.

These matters, I say, we have decided to pass over in silence, since anyone can easily examine them in the Acts of the councils. We shall set forth only those things that reveal unmistakable Manichaean behavior. Such, surely, were the actions by which he undermined holy baptism: namely, when he introduced a shameless woman, unworthy of the sacred font, and made her stand beside the holy font. “And when the divine mysteries,” says the aforesaid clergy, “are completed in the oratory of the house of the Mother of God, what disgraceful words she utters! What Christian ear could endure such impiety, spoken and done?” [Col. 0979C] [Note: [Col. 0979D] Vol. V of the Councils, p. 1194 in the Venetian edition.].

Photius testifies that all these practices came from the school of the Manichaeans. Speaking of their groups and assemblies, he says that they customarily called the places in which they met proseuchae, oratories. He adds:

“Indeed, although they reject saving baptism, they nevertheless pretend to receive it, hinting at it by uttering the words of the Gospel in the form of baptism. For, they say, the Lord declared: ‘I am living water.’”

A little later, wishing to explain how some of them, when afflicted by bodily illnesses, would sometimes ask and plead to be washed in baptism, he says that they foolishly thought the cross and baptism beneficial to the body—although they were men wholly unworthy of any advantage or assistance—yet believed that their power and efficacy had no relation either to the cleansing of the soul or to any other benefit [Note: [Col. 0979D] Photius, *Book I against the Manichaeans*, ch. 9, in Christophorus Wolfius, pp. 29–30. See also the history of Peter of Sicily. Wolfius wrote similar things about the Bogomils, a more recent offshoot of Manichaeism, in his *History*, pp. 105 ff. [Col. 0980D]].

Since, therefore, we know with certainty from the Acts of that synod that Severus, Anthimus, Zoaras, and the others hiding under the name of the Acephaloi devoted themselves to such depraved practices and institutions; that they corrupted all the sacred mysteries with profane rites and sacrileges; and that they declared war on the sacred images and the sign of the cross, breaking them and trampling them underfoot—who could deny that they were Manichaeans?

Indeed, the letters and Acts of the councils make it clear that they were condemned as Manichaeans both by Pope Hormisdas and by another Constantinopolitan synod held under Menas. Learned men can easily examine these documents [Note: [Col. 0980D] Vol. V of the *General Councils*, pp. 558 and 962.].

### 15.

Having now completed this first part of our *Exercises*, which concerns the history of the Manichaeans, we ought to report something about the sects of the Paulicians, Bogomils, Waldensians, and other heretics who absorbed the teaching of Manes and followed his institutions and practices.

Nevertheless, since Peter of Sicily, Photius, and Christophorus Wolfius have already discussed these sects—which emerged from a school of such great wickedness—in an orderly fashion, we have decided instead to describe the heresies of the Priscillianists, Pelagians, and Eutychians, which were attacked and rejected by the great pontiff Leo.

We have also grown weary of having written the two preceding books in a more expansive style. We understand clearly that, in our preceding manner of discussion, we wandered into and almost roamed through certain questions that will seem to those accustomed to judging us less mercifully and favorably not to pertain at all to the purpose and title of the work.

But who does not know that men highly trained in literary matters have sometimes scarcely been able to restrain their pens when they unexpectedly found themselves having to deal with certain people who were constantly devising new systems and attempting to overturn or abolish either the sacred religion or the apostolic form of ecclesiastical government and discipline? It was difficult to escape, in only a few words, from their objections, quibbles, and fallacies of argument.

This was especially so when we occasionally encountered questions raised by non-Catholics and schismatics, questions that could not be dissolved by the testimony of one or another holy Father alone. It is therefore not surprising that, when wishing to explain the conduct of the holy pontiff, we sometimes thought it necessary to appeal to the origin and establishment of institutions, or to bring forward the Church’s earlier practice and custom. In this way we could clearly demonstrate that St. Leo the Great had not overstepped the proper limits established by law in administering ecclesiastical affairs; that he had not labored to enlarge his own dignity by disregarding or abolishing the prerogatives of the bishops of other Churches; and finally, that he had not been moved either by ambition or by excessive severity to restrain the enemies of the Apostolic See and of the Christian religion.

We have thus far endeavored to clear him of such accusations, in opposition to Beausobre, Quesnel, and others. We hope to accomplish the same thing in the *Exercises* that follow.

Since those three theological points which, in past years, were assigned for discussion in the public pontifical academy of the most holy lord Benedict XIV are judged to belong to the history of Manichaeism, we have decided to insert in this work the *Exercise* composed by us on these matters as an appendix to the preceding ones. We did so with the advice of distinguished men, especially the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Nicolaus Antonelli, secretary of the Sacred Consistory and of the aforesaid Academy.

We therefore hope that this labor of ours, whatever its worth, will not be displeasing to readers, since it presents the ecclesiastical canons of the Council of Gangra promulgated against Manichaean doctrines. The outstanding and most learned men explained the summary, purpose, and rationale of these canons in the pontifical palace in the year of Our Lord 1743, and adorned them with the most learned observations, as we have said [Note: [Col. 0980D] See what we have already said in chapter 2 of this book, p. 113.].

[Col. 0981]

## APPENDIX TO THE HISTORY OF THE MANICHAEANS

### THEOLOGICAL DISSERTATION ON CANONS XIII AND XVII OF THE COUNCIL OF GANGRA

Delivered in the Pontifical Quirinal Palace on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1743

[Col. 0981A] 199

I am commanded to undertake a genuinely difficult question, one that, so far as I know, has not hitherto been treated in its entirety by any theologian.

The question is this: whether, from the words of the Apostle in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, verse 15—“But if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her, because her hair has been given to her as a covering”—women are forbidden to cut their hair, in accordance with canons 13 and 17 of Gangra; and, second, whether they may ever put on men’s clothing, because in Deuteronomy, chapter XXII, verse 5, we read: “A woman shall not wear a man’s clothing, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment, for whoever does these things is an abomination before God”; and, third, whether women may at least for the sake of piety cut their hair, put on men’s clothing—especially monastic clothing—and pretend to be men.

These three questions, I say, have been assigned to me for treatment today, not according to scholastic method but in the manner of an academic discourse. In explaining them I have decided to imitate the practice of Socrates. He taught that, in disputes of this kind, whose issues have not yet been sufficiently defined, speakers should introduce no judgment of their own; they should merely propose and establish what seems most probable, present the reasons, and bring forward whatever can be said on either side, adopting no authority and leaving the judgment of the hearers whole and free [Note: [Col. 0981D] Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book V.].

Following these footsteps, I shall easily avoid the hostility of those who always hold contrary opinions; and you, most learned men, will be witnesses and defenders of what I am now beginning to say in order to explain these three theological points.

There can be no doubt that, by the term “woman,” the Apostle understood the entire female sex and all its classes. This is demonstrated above all by the context of the whole Pauline passage itself; Tertullian also proves it by various arguments drawn from the texts of Scripture. Moreover, he severely censures those who rashly wished to persuade themselves that Paul had spoken only about married women, and who, with a kind of reckless audacity, maintained that unmarried women—whether with shorn heads or with curled hair—might appear without any covering at all in both sacred and civil gatherings, sometimes under the pretext of magnificently proclaiming and displaying a false virginity.

Tertullian therefore refutes their opinion as erroneous and contrary to the sacred Scriptures in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. He shows that the Holy Spirit wished, by the single term “woman,” to indicate married and unmarried women, virgins, and every class of the female sex, since the word is a general term, as is also “female.”

Once this first error has been rejected, another similar one must still be removed, into which Louis Cappel appears to have fallen, as his own treatise *On Prayer* makes sufficiently clear. This non-Catholic writer, following the commentaries of Maimonides on the *Mishnah* [200], repeatedly asserts that the Apostle’s canon under discussion must be adapted to the custom of the place in which we live.

He therefore says that one ought to pray in churches in the dress by which people customarily demonstrate their reverence and respect toward the great men and princes of this world. Later, after speaking of various rites among the pagans, Muslims, Jews, and Christians, he adds that in this canon the Apostle had regard to the civil custom then commonly observed among the Greeks and Romans to whom he was writing: all freeborn men ordinarily went out in public with their heads bare and uncovered.

Since, he concludes, civil custom is not always one and the same everywhere and at every time, but varies greatly according to the variation of times, places, and peoples, the matters belonging to ecclesiastical order (*eutaxia*, εὐταξία) likewise cannot be the same everywhere.

With a similar conviction he reasons about women’s veils and hair, maintaining that the Apostle Paul had regard only to civil custom and had therefore ordered women—“to use his words”—not to attend sacred assemblies in church unless they had veiled their faces and the rest of their heads.

But the Apostle himself contradicts Louis Cappel, Rhenanus, Münster [Note: [Col. 0981D] In the *Synopsis of Sacred Critics*.], and the other defenders of pseudo-Reformed doctrine. In the cited chapter of the Epistle to the Corinthians, Paul seemed to have said enough, from Scripture and the reasoning of nature, to persuade women of the necessity of a veil. Yet, recognizing that some people would resist such testimonies and arguments, he proposed no argument more suitable for establishing the case than the sacred custom of the Church.

He therefore said: “But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God” [Note: [Col. 0981D] First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, verse 16.].

The Apostle therefore did not appeal to local customs or civil practice in order to rebuke his opponents, but to the sacred tradition of both the Old and New Testaments. He seemed, as the most learned Melchior Cano says, to be implying:

“If anyone is so obstinate and stubborn that he is not persuaded by the arguments already given, but still maintains that a woman ought to pray with her head uncovered, I refute him in no other way than by saying that the Church of God has no such custom” [Note: [Col. 0982D] Melchior Cano, book V, proposition 6.].

Tradition has such force that Paul believed those whom neither Scripture nor the reasoning of nature had moved could be refuted by the custom and institution of the Churches.

As for the Church of the Jews, it is impious to doubt that it followed a rite other than this. Tertullian offers very clear testimony on the subject in his book *On the Crown of the Soldier* [Note: [Col. 0982D] Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 4.]. From it we learn that Jewish women were nowhere permitted to cast aside the veil of the head, the sign of subjection.

“Among the Jews,” he says, “the veil of their women’s heads is so customary that they are recognized by it.”

He confirms this institution by the example of Rebecca, who assumed a veil when she saw her bridegroom at a distance. He investigates the reason and adds: “Private modesty could not have made a law.” Finally, he concludes that the command to assume a veil derived among the Jews from sacred tradition and would at some point possess the authority of the Apostle through the interpretation supplied by reason.

Louis Cappel therefore does not reason appropriately when, in the passage cited, he says that in the time of the Apostle Paul this alone was accepted and customary: that chaste and modest women, especially those of marriageable age, scarcely ever appeared in public unless their faces were veiled. Then, turning his discussion to the Jewish people, he adds: “I do not know whether the Jewish case should perhaps be excepted.”

But, on Tertullian’s authority, it could not be excepted, since the Jewish Church did not follow civil custom—as barbarian nations did—but, instructed by the tradition of the Holy Spirit, had always followed whatever might serve the modesty and restraint of the female sex.

With these foundations laid and the opinions of non-Catholics rejected, it will not be difficult to resolve the first question if we say that the Apostle’s canon never forbade women to cut their hair, but only to cast aside the covering of the head.

Nor do we fabricate this from a recent opinion or assert it without the authority of Scripture. In the first place, the passage from which the Apostle began this canon is especially noteworthy, for he wished to teach both men and women in what dress and according to what rite they should pray in churches [Note: [Col. 0983D] Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, verse 3.].

“I want you to know,” he says, addressing the Corinthians, “that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.”

The same Apostle, consistent with himself, explains the mystical meaning of the term “head” in chapter V of the Epistle to the Ephesians, where he writes concerning women [Note: [Col. 0983D] Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter V.]: “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church.”

We therefore need not labor over the meaning of that word. It signifies government, authority, and dominion, which superiors exercise over those subject to them.

The Apostle proceeds to prescribe outward signs of subjection for men and women, so that even while praying their heads would not be dishonored. Yet he did not wish the same sign to be common to both. Rather, he prescribed different signs, especially those most suited to the sex of each and most consistent with their modesty.

Accordingly, he immediately added in the following verses: “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head.”

Paul therefore wished, through this sacred canon, to regulate the rite of those who pray [Col. 0983C], so that Christian men and women, when praying, would not at some point violate the rules of reverence, modesty, and propriety and commit something disgraceful or dishonorable.

But once the Apostle’s purpose in writing has been understood, it should by no means be inferred that in what follows he intended to forbid women to cut their hair. Neither in the cited chapter nor elsewhere do his words seem to have the force of a command. He merely praises women if they grow their hair, because long hair is becoming to the female sex.

Women are not inappropriately praised for this reason. Hair is a work of nature, and nature has customarily given women longer hair to cover the head against nakedness, to serve as an ornament against the rough and unpolished appearance of outward life, or finally as protection against the cold of winter and other harsh weather.

Perhaps moved by these considerations, the Apostle rightly wrote in verse 15: “But if a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her, because her hair has been given to her as a covering.”

As Erasmus observes, this seems to imply that women were given longer hair because they need a covering [Note: [Col. 0983D] In the notes on this Epistle, vol. VII.]. When ancient writers cited by Stobaeus noticed this truth, they called women’s hair a covering supplied by nature [Note: [Col. 0983D] *Book II of the Stromata*.]. Clement of Alexandria, writing about the creation of woman, said: “God made the female with natural hair, like a horse with a mane, so that she might glory in it.”

The Apostle’s manner of speaking, and the very words he uses, add remarkable strength to our position. Paul does not properly, but only figuratively, call hair a veil, writing: “Because the hair has been given to her as a covering.”

For if hair were properly and literally called a veil, women who had only recently begun to grow their hair would have needed no other covering in churches and public gatherings, and they would have been entirely permitted to go out in public with their heads uncovered. Not only Christian piety and religion have hitherto recoiled from such a custom, but also the dignity and modesty of every barbarian and non-Christian nation.

Again, if hair were properly called a veil, neither men who grow their hair nor those who are bald would ever appear in public or in churches with their heads uncovered. Therefore, in order to observe the Apostle’s command—which is assumed here—all men, whatever their condition or rank, would have to go about with their hair shorn in the manner of monks. I believe no one is unaware how absurd and false this would be.

Since, then, the Apostle’s statement, “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head,” must not be understood of the natural covering of hair, it follows conversely that the Apostle ordered women to wear artificial coverings in churches, so that they might more easily preserve modesty, restraint, and propriety at all times.

Finally, if hair were properly a veil, women would be permitted to go out in public with their hair loose and uncut, like maenads, without any covering placed over it. The Catholic Church has always condemned such a practice as shameful and insane, derived from the impious way of life of the pagans.

But the Apostle’s own words make our point still clearer. He does not use the expressions cited as a substitute for a veil, or in the place of a veil, or to indicate the origin of the thing. He uses them only to indicate its purpose, as is evident from the Greek manuscripts, which read:

> ἡ κόμη ἀντὶ περιβολαίου δέδοται αὐτῇ

“That hair has been given to her in place of a covering.”

From this, interpreters—namely Chrysostom, Theophylact, and the others—rightly asserted that the Apostle intended to infer from the natural covering the necessity of another covering, namely a voluntary and assumed one [Note: [Col. 0984D] Chrysostom, Theophylact, and the other Fathers on 1 Corinthians, chapter XI, verses 15 ff.].

Thus women were to learn that those things which nature intended to cover must be covered by care and art. By assuming such a covering, they would recall the original condition of woman, on account of which it was said to Eve and to all women in Genesis 3:16: “And you shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you.”

These words must not be referred merely to a subjection of love, but to their condition.
