Among the other Fathers, Augustine taught this in his *Commentary on Genesis*, book II [Note: [Col. 0984D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI.], insofar as the man must rule even over a woman who is unwilling, so that, unless this dominion is maintained, nature will be further corrupted and guilt increased.

We should therefore not be surprised that the same Apostle, referring to the woman’s veil as subjection and as its true purpose, later in verse 10 of the same chapter calls it “authority,” saying: “For this reason the woman ought to have authority over her head.”

The meaning is that the woman’s veil should be a sign of authority and an indication of subjection. This may perhaps be understood still more clearly from the Greek manuscripts, which read:

> ἑξουσίαν ἔχειν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς

“To have authority over her head.”

The Hebrew and Chaldean words *rada* and *radat* correspond especially well to this expression; they are customarily interpreted as the veil of obedience.

We can scarcely doubt, therefore, that the veil prescribed by the Apostle as an emblem of reverence, modesty, and chastity was intended to be common to all women. Thus married women who wore it would be the glory of their husbands, and virgins would possess glory in themselves.

If, on the other hand, they rejected the assumed veil, they would be false both to their own dignity and to the dignity of the Christian profession.

If we inquire more carefully what form and extent that veil ought to have, let us hear Tertullian. He says:

> “As much territory as the loosened hair can occupy, so great is the region of the veil, so that it also surrounds the neck. For the necks themselves must be subject; on their account authority must be borne over the head. The veil is their yoke” [Note: [Col. 0985D] Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*.].

Since this is the law of the assumed veil, and since this is its purpose and extent, it must not be judged that Christian women are to recoil from all these things merely because they cut their hair—provided, however, that in cutting their hair they do not obey vanity, luxury, and immodest adornment rather than Christian moderation and humility, nor set out to attain anything wicked or opposed to religion and faith, as did the women discussed in the canons of Gangra.

For the present, we shall not examine the aforesaid canons, since they have already been reconsidered in the first dissertation of this year by one of the distinguished and learned theologians of our Academy. The circumstances and the purpose of our undertaking do not permit it at this time [Note: [Col. 0985D] Deuteronomy, chapter XXI.].

I shall now bring forward two other classes of arguments by which it will become clear—more plainly than daylight itself—that women were not forbidden by any law, whether divine, ecclesiastical, or human, to cut their hair.

The first argument can be drawn from the words of Deuteronomy. There God commanded the children of Israel, when they wished to take a captive woman in marriage, not to celebrate an engagement or marriage until the hair of the woman to be married had first been cut and all her hair shaved away.

“If you go out … and see among the captives a beautiful woman, and love her, and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house; she shall shave her hair and cut her nails” [Note: [Col. 0985D] Ezekiel IX, from 2 Kings X and 1 Chronicles IX.].

Here, then, is a command of the Lord concerning the cutting, indeed even the shaving, of all a woman’s hair.

If we carefully consider and pursue the reasons for this divine command, we shall affirm that there were several. Those who have examined the writings of the ancient philosophers know this very well. From them we learn that the cutting of the hair was sometimes a sign of servile condition and captivity, as we also gather from various passages of Scripture.

Aristophanes proves that the pagans preserved this custom. Almost astonished, he once said to a certain slave who was growing his hair: “Though you are a slave, you grow your hair?”

The cutting of the hair was also the punishment for many serious crimes, as the Apostle writes in verse 6 of the cited chapter: “If a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn”—as though the woman were to be shorn and shaved as punishment for violating the law concerning the wearing of a veil.

Other crimes likewise incurred the punishment of shaving the head. This can be gathered not only from various passages of Scripture but also from the civil laws cited by Ulpian, Justinian, and Tacitus.

I believe Juvenal alluded to this custom in Satire 5, where he wrote [Note: [Col. 0985D] Isaiah III and XLVIII; Ezekiel VII; Justinian, *Novella* 63; Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*; Juvenal, Satire 5.]:

> “One day he will offer his shaven crown to be struck,
>
> and will not fear to endure
>
> the harsh lashes.”

A third reason for that divine command may have been the disfigurement of natural beauty. The Apostle also spoke of this in the same chapter: “But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.”

The holy Fathers spoke especially eloquently about this shame inflicted upon women. Among them were Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine [Note: [Col. 0986D] Jerome, on chapter VII of Ezekiel; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book VI; Augustine, letter to Possidius.]. Baronius relies on their testimonies in the *Martyrology* when describing the martyrdom of St. Fausta the virgin on 20 September.

Profane writers likewise exaggerate this disfigurement, as may be seen in Apuleius, Statius, Virgil [Col. 0986A], and others. Ovid, agreeing with them, sang:

> “A mutilated animal is shameful, a field without grass is shameful,
>
> a shrub without leaves, and a head without hair.”

A fourth reason follows from penitence, mourning, and grief [204]. Everyone should know that Jews and pagans alike were accustomed, in mourning and especially at funerals, to cut their hair.

Apart from what we read in Jeremiah 7—“Cut off your hair and cast it away, and take up a lamentation”—this is attested to us by the words of Job and Micah [Note: [Col. 0986D] Job, chapter I; Micah, chapter I.]. Herodotus, Statius, Virgil, and Seneca likewise discussed the same custom. Since it is unnecessary to quote their testimonies here, it is enough to cite these writers.

Finally, Clement of Alexandria supplies us with a reason drawn from antiquity. He asserted that in the Deuteronomic passage cited above, God commanded the captive woman who was to be taken in marriage to be shorn in order to restrain and diminish the husband’s lust. Once the woman’s head had been disfigured, the heat of carnal desire would more easily cool.

He therefore added: “For if he remains determined to marry her”—he is speaking of the Jew who takes a captive woman—“he will keep her, even if she has become ugly” [Note: [Col. 0986D] Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book II.].

That a woman makes herself less suited to excite the allurements of the flesh by cutting her hair is clear from the fact that nature placed hair on that part of the body which is more openly displayed and which women arrange with greater care.

Thus, when this natural ornament is cut away—the ornament by which they strive more and more to please and shine—they become accustomed to devote themselves to humility, penitence, chastity, and the other virtues, provided that they do not cast aside the artificial veil.

For these reasons, then, we have demonstrated thus far, in this rough discourse of ours, that women are pleasing to God and do not violate any divine or apostolic command.

It remains to present the second class of arguments, by which we shall prove beyond doubt that women were even more pleasing to God when, for the sake of religious and stricter discipline, they cut their hair.

First, there is that very famous ancient command of the Lord. Addressing Moses in the Book of Numbers, he said:

“Speak to the children of Israel: When a man or woman makes a vow, so that they may be sanctified and wish to consecrate themselves to the Lord … throughout the whole time of their separation, no razor shall pass over their head until the day is completed on which they are consecrated to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0986D] Numbers VI, 2.].

From these words it is clear that the completion of the entire sanctification, both for men and for women who professed the Nazirite state only for a time, consisted in cutting the hair and shaving the whole head.

But when the Gospel had already begun to shine, this law was not abolished. Indeed, it was especially in force when Paul wrote the Epistle to the Corinthians. For the Apostle himself shortly afterward observed the same Nazirite law.

The Epistle that we are now discussing was written before he traveled through Achaia and Macedonia and should be assigned to the fifty-seventh year of the common era, the twenty-fourth year after Christ’s death. At that time the people of Corinth sent Stephen, Fortunatus, and Achaicus from Ephesus to visit the Apostle, as is inferred from chapters IV, XI, and XVI of the same Epistle.

Yet two years later, after completing various journeys, the Apostle cut his hair at Cenchreae because of a Nazirite vow, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“After taking the four men who had a vow upon them, he ordered them first to shave their heads; and on the following day, after being purified, he entered the temple with them, announcing the completion of the days of their purification” [Note: [Col. 0987D] Acts XVI and XXI.].

That this law was common to women as well is clearly shown by the words cited above. There is therefore no reason to suppose that the Apostle’s canon—“But if a woman grows her hair,” and so forth—prohibited women from cutting their hair.

For before Paul uttered these words about women’s hair and clothing, he had already offered himself to the Corinthians as an example to imitate, saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

In our Church, men and women have indeed sought to imitate Paul—not only those who, choosing to pursue a more sacred life, resolved to live permanently in the holy houses of monasteries with shorn heads, but also all who, rejecting the allurements of the world, desired to enroll themselves in the sacred order of the clergy.

But if someone objects that in our own age women appear in churches and public gatherings with shorn heads and having cast aside the ancient veil; that they have cast off the restraints of humility and modesty together with their hair and artificial veil—what could I possibly reply?

Could I say that this should not be counted as a crime? Especially when, adopting new customs of vanity, they strive to appear everywhere as though they possessed complete freedom, with their heads, necks, throats, and shoulders entirely uncovered?

How sharply the ancient piety and modesty of Christians accuse them!

But since I have not been appointed to perform the office either of preacher or of confessor at present, I shall bring forward what Marcus Porcius Cato once said publicly in the Senate in defense of the Oppian Law:

“Our ancestors wished women to undertake no matter—not even a private one—without an adviser; they wished them to be under the authority of their parents, brothers, and husbands. We, if the gods so will, now even permit them to take part in public affairs, to mingle in the forum, in public speeches, and in the assemblies.”

A little later he added:

“Give free rein to an unrestrained nature and an untamed animal, and hope that they themselves will impose a limit on their license—unless you impose it” [Note: [Col. 0987D] Livy, book XXXIV, chapter 2.].

Thus far concerning women’s hair and head-covering. But now, lest I seem to abuse my leisure and distrust your learning, I shall pursue the remaining matters, which can occupy the final two chapters of my dissertation. For both sacred-literature interpreters and the greatest theologians have long discussed them, as may be seen in Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, or William of Paris, the Angelic Doctor, Nicholas of Osimo, and the other writers on moral theology; a catalogue of whom would contribute nothing to our purpose.

Accordingly, if we are to understand clearly whether women may ever assume male clothing, the matter necessarily requires that we examine the purpose and rationale of this Mosaic commandment: “A woman shall not wear a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment.”

Father Natalis Alexander writes first of all:

**Note:** [Col. 0987D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, dissertation 3, article 5, §3.

> The rationale of this observance is manifold. The first, and the principal, is the extermination of idolatry. For this exchange of clothing was an idolatrous rite commonly employed in the sacred ceremonies of profane peoples.

Father Calmet supports this interpretation—not to mention Grotius, Münster, Fagius, and others, whose opinions I judge not to be far removed from the mark of error. I too would have accepted this explanation, had I found it consistent with the customs of antiquity and been able, from some firm and stable principle, to infer that Moses, in establishing this law, had intended to remove the crimes and superstitions committed in certain festivals and rites of the empty gods.

Then it would readily have been possible for me to conclude that the commandment of Deuteronomy had become invalid and void, together with the other legal and ceremonial precepts, when the new evangelical law began to shine—namely, when pagan superstition began everywhere to be abolished. But that this opinion must be rejected as dangerous is demonstrated clearly not only by the Canons of Trullo but also by the decrees of the Council of Ancyra and by the consultations and statutes of Martin of Tours and Pope Zachary I.

Furthermore, it is highly uncertain that, in Moses’ time, idolaters practiced such a superstitious rite of changing clothes. For Scripture, which elsewhere records many different profane ceremonies of the gentiles, maintains profound silence concerning the matter under discussion. On the other hand, Servius, Julius Firmicus, Hesychius, Polyaenus, Plutarch, and other writers much later than Moses—whose testimonies are cited both by Father Natalis Alexander and by critics of the sacred books—report only what prevailed in their own age among the Cypriots, Assyrians, Athenians, Romans, and other peoples of the East and West. Nowhere, however, do they define the origin and antiquity of those rites.

**Note:** [Col. 0987D] Servius, on book II of the *Aeneid*; Julius Firmicus, *On the Assyrians*; [Col. 0988D] Polyaenus, book VIII of the *Stratagems*; Plutarch, *On the Priests of Hercules*.

Indeed, if it were permissible for us to wander beyond the limits of our undertaking, we could prove from the mosaics, statues, reliefs, coins, and the devices on rings of idolaters that this promiscuous confusion of garments was introduced into the world long after Moses’ time.

Perhaps the Cypriots were the first of all to devise it, when a statue representing Venus was placed in the temple of Aphrodite, at which men sacrificed in women’s clothing and women in men’s clothing, as Servius relates. At Rome, too, it was customary for the priests of the goddess Isis to dress in women’s garments, as the Capitoline relief records, most learnedly explained by the distinguished Georgius.

When the Bacchic festivals were introduced from Greece into Etruria and especially into Italy, that promiscuous use of clothing by men and women became more frequent. At Rome it first occurred in the five hundred and sixth year from the city’s foundation, 189 years before the birth of Christ, as Titus Livy records and the lists of the Roman consuls reveal.

**Note:** Titus Livy, book XXXIX, chapters 8 and 3; Petavius, *Ratio Temporum*, part III.

Some monuments of antiquity concerning this matter still survive. They display images of emperors adorned in feminine form, or women themselves dressed in masculine armor, as is shown by the relief of Marcus Antonius published by Buonarroti; or the ring bearing Venus armed, which Julius Caesar used only for sealing documents concerning matters of the greatest importance; or, finally, as is made known by the devices on other rings and coins, images of Hercules, Commodus, Martia, Nero, Ulpia Marcellina, and others, presented before our eyes clothed in garments incongruous with and contrary to their nature.

All these things indeed prove that the later pagans, who lived shortly before or shortly after Christ’s birth, practiced this profane confusion of clothing, especially when they were performing sacred rites and festivals. It is nevertheless not certain that the practice existed in Moses’ time, or that Moses prophetically had that rite in view, intending to remove the crimes and superstitions committed in the worship of certain empty gods.

But even if it were readily granted that this profane worship had prevailed in Moses’ time, what then? Should we believe that Moses established the law against confusing garments in order to place limits upon such license? The inference is wholly absurd.

For, first, the law of Deuteronomy was given to the Jews, not to the gentiles. Their women, in accordance with the Lord’s command, were perpetually excluded from sacred rites. Nor was it easy for men to fall into such a crime, because in the books of Exodus and Leviticus not only are the individual kinds of sacrifices described, but the ornaments, duties, prerogatives, and qualifications of the Levites and priests are also clearly defined. Finally, the duty of offering sacrifice had been reserved exclusively for the male descendants of Levi.

If, therefore, Moses, moved by the divine Spirit, described and defined with such care and diligence in those two celebrated books the manner, time, ornaments, rationale, and ceremonies of sacred rites and festivals, so that the Hebrews would have nothing in common with the gentiles, who could then suspect that the Deuteronomic law in question was issued primarily to exterminate idolatrous rites? For in that chapter Moses did not utter a single word about ceremonial precepts.

**Note:** Deuteronomy XXII.

The motives and reasons of this Mosaic commandment must therefore be sought at a deeper level, and from no other rule than the principles of natural reason, which Moses had in view when he committed to writing what had been established by the common law of all nations. For before Moses committed that commandment to writing, every people—even a savage and barbarous one—had used differences of clothing corresponding to persons and sex, especially so that males might be distinguished from females.

We therefore rightly believe that the Mosaic commandment must be referred to the protection of justice and truth, the destruction of error and falsehood, and, finally, the tranquillity and welfare of public affairs and private households. Since these three benefits of human life—benefits which in this world cannot be equaled by any others—direct and regulate the character and institutions of human beings, there can scarcely be doubt that the commandment is moral and that Christians are especially bound by it.

Is that not to be called moral which proceeds from nature and can be violated only in resistance to nature? Ambrose bears witness, writing:

> Why do you, a man, disguise yourself as a woman, or you, a woman, as a man? Nature has clothed each sex in its own garments. Each has a different use, color, movement, gait, and strength; a man and a woman have different voices.

**Note:** Ambrose, letter to Ireneus.

Seneca likewise bears witness, addressing Lucilius:

> Do those who exchange clothing with women not seem to you to live contrary to nature?

**Note:** Seneca, *To Lucilius*.

Diogenes Laertius also bears witness, saying:

> Law is divided into two kinds: one written, the other unwritten.

After inserting several intervening remarks, he adds:

> That law which is unwritten proceeds from nature and custom. For example, one ought not to walk naked in the forum, nor use women’s clothing.

**Note:** Diogenes Laertius, *Life of Plato*.

Our women do not understand the punishment—not, I say, of laws, which they often violate, but of the shame itself, which is most bitter—when they strip off modesty together with their garments in order to use men’s adornments. For in this promiscuous confusion of clothing there arises a kind of fictitious exchange of the sexes, called by the Greeks γενεόσεως ἐναλλαγή (*geneoseōs enallagē*, “exchange of generation or sex”), as Grotius observes, which is opposed to all the duties of nature.

Therefore, just as the authority and dignity of men are injured if they wish to perform women’s tasks, as Clement of Alexandria once observed, so a woman raises herself through an unjust claim of arrogance and boldness when she strives to imitate and counterfeit men in movement, clothing, gait, and other activities.

**Note:** Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II.

Truth, justice, and honesty oppose this manner of acting and living. If they oppose it, the rights of nature are violated, the Creator of all things is arrogantly despised, and whatever is sacred and honorable, prescribed by divine and human laws, is wholly cast aside and trampled underfoot.

It is shameful, therefore, to lie; more shameful to deceive; but most shameful to provide both oneself and others with an occasion for incontinence and lust, and to open a window to crimes. For this reason Cicero, guided solely by the light of reason, could never persuade himself that it was possible for a good man to lie for his own advantage, to accuse, or to teach deception, because all these things are contrary to nature.

**Note:** Cicero, *On Duties* III.

For this reason the ancient Romans abhorred as a supreme crime that deed perpetrated by Clodius: dressed in women’s clothing, he entered the college of the Bona Dea in order to violate a chaste matron.

And indeed, such evils—or others still more serious—can arise from that promiscuous exchange of clothing. Therefore, considering the matter according to the sounder method of reasoning, we hold that the commandment of Deuteronomy was given not primarily to exterminate idolatrous rites but to regulate human conduct.

And according to Ambrose, human behavior always becomes shameful and detestable when it is directed by the desire to conceal and disguise one’s sex:

> A lie is shameful in words, let alone in clothing.

**Note:** Ambrose; Cyprian; Augustine, *Soliloquies* II, chapter 26.

Cyprian likewise rebukes both men and women who devote themselves to these abuses as adulterers:

> They lay hands upon God, since they strive to remake what he formed.

Saint Augustine agrees with this in book II of the *Soliloquies*, chapter 16.

Let us therefore close this class of proofs with the words of Saint Thomas Aquinas, who wrote the following concerning our subject:

> That a woman should wear a man’s clothing, or conversely, is an incentive to lust and provides an occasion for sexual desire.

**Note:** Saint Thomas, question 162, article 6.

There are, however, other mystical interpretations of this Mosaic commandment that conflict with the wording of our Vulgate, which we prefer to suppress in silence rather than refute with arguments. One such interpretation is that offered by Josephus, the historian of Jewish affairs:

> The vessels or implements of a man shall not be upon a woman.

This is also the reading presented by the Chaldean texts and examined and followed by Maimonides, Münster, Fagius, Sanctes Pagninus, and others.

**Note:** Josephus, book XVI of the *Jewish Antiquities*.

Another is the interpretation of a certain jurist, Abericus, who, following an excessive desire for philosophical speculation, supposes that Moses intended by this commandment to remove from the Jews some particularly wicked crime.

It is enough for me to have pointed out these two inventions as commentaries devised by interpreters, lest I abuse your time and your kindness any further.

Meanwhile, in order to dispose very briefly of the third chapter of our dissertation, allow me to observe that we have been born under laws such that we possess principles of nature which we must obey and always follow, so that our own welfare may be the common welfare.

When, therefore, under certain circumstances, a command requires that one conceal one’s sex—for example, when one’s own life, one’s country, the preservation of virginity, or the preservation of religion is at stake—it is better to devote oneself to the common glory and welfare than to indulge one’s own inclinations. Thus, led by serious reasoning, I persuade myself that women may, when one of these circumstances presses upon them, cut their hair, assume male clothing—especially monastic clothing—and disguise themselves as men.

But to do so solely for the sake of piety can in no way be permitted unless a serious necessity of nature or some particular consideration of the good likewise urges and compels it.

And if someone should now object to me the canons of Gangra, by which women are forbidden, under penalty of anathema, to cut their hair, use masculine garments, or enter monasteries, I could easily remove that objection by considering the cause, place, and time of the council in question.

**Note:** In the codex of the Canons of the Roman Church and in the Decretals, distinction 30, chapter “If Any Woman.”

The cause was the heresy of the Manichaeans, which, under the teaching of Eustathius, execrated ecclesiastical marriages and unions. Therefore those women alone are attacked by these canons who, adhering to the doctrines of the heretics, dared to condemn marriages, unions, and the begetting of children; and who, having changed their clothing and cast off their hair—which is a token of subjection—sometimes even attempted to enter the enclosures of monks.

Who does not understand, or who could fail to know, that this did not result in the honor of nature, the protection of religion, or the common good, but in the vice of shame, the destruction of piety, and the injury of the commonwealth?

Augustine, in the *Soliloquies*, censures and rebukes as infamous those who, moved solely by private inclination, display themselves in women’s clothing.

**Note:** Augustine, *Soliloquies* II, chapter 16.

> I do not know, he says, whether it is better to call them false women or false men. Yet without hesitation we may call them true actors and true infamous persons.

But according to Augustine’s testimony in the same place, those who, moved by the desire to free their country and by zeal for securing the common good, put on women’s clothing would in no way incur that mark of infamy. Indeed, their names ought to be celebrated by all citizens with the greatest applause and honor, and the authors of such great deeds ought to receive from the commonwealth the better rewards of virtue.

Such rewards of virtue are even more due to men and women when, out of zeal for protecting virginity and religion, they assume clothing that does not correspond to their sex.

Ambrose offers two celebrated examples of this matter when discussing a Christian virgin from Antioch. During a persecution against Christians, a holy virgin was arrested, and the impious tyrant ordered her either to be taken to a brothel or to sacrifice to the gods. But while she was being held in the brothel, she had no doubt concerning her religion; she was trembling over her chastity.

**Note:** Ambrose, *On Virgins* II.

Therefore she said to herself:

> What shall we do today? Either a martyr or a virgin.

Meanwhile, turning to God in prayer, she said:

> Behold, a man of a terrifying military appearance burst in. Entering as though he were an adulterer, he suddenly changed and showed and proved himself the defender of her virginity.

To accomplish this more successfully and deceive all those who had then come to the brothel in order to violate the virgin, the soldier clothed himself in women’s garments; and the virgin, taking masculine military clothing from the soldier, escaped from the snares.

Ambrose illuminates the entire history of this event, which had occurred not long before his own time, in commentaries of the greatest learning. We refer our most learned readers to those works.

We nevertheless wished to warn our readers that Baronius, in his notes to the *Martyrology* under 28 April, was led by serious suspicion to believe that this was Theodora, a virgin of Alexandria, and that an error had entered the manuscripts of Ambrose, so that, through the ignorance of scribes, the name Antioch had been substituted for Alexandria. We have not dared to affirm anything concerning this lapse; rather, we follow the authority of the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, who compiled that *Martyrology* with the greatest zeal and labor.

We merely add that, while reading the celebrated work of Baronius, we encountered another event not unlike this one. Under 4 May he relates that Antonina, a virgin of Constantinople, assumed the masculine clothing of a certain Alexander so that she might secretly be led out of a brothel. The same cardinal therefore noted:

> Since Christian women were frequently condemned to brothels, a similar event could often have occurred.

Palladius likewise, in the *Lausiac History*, describes from Hippolytus the same thing as having happened to another virgin in the city of Corinth.

And, finally, to pass over in silence what Valerius relates about the women of Lacedaemon, the accounts that Surius, Symeon Metaphrastes, and other writers have transmitted concerning Saint Euphrosyne, a virgin of Alexandria, are not obscure. Out of a desire to preserve perpetual virginity, she left her father’s house, put on masculine clothing, and entered the enclosure of monks; there she concealed her sex and condition until her death.

Perhaps those accustomed to apply stricter rules of criticism will not so readily accept this final narrative, since it contains circumstances that appear contrary to ordinary propriety and cannot easily be reconciled with the welfare of one’s neighbors.

Yet all the dangers and evils that threaten—and that a woman with shorn hair and wearing monastic clothing might encounter—immediately disappear if that omnipotent God, who is the author of every good purpose, should deign, as he did in the case of the woman Judith, to direct, guard, and bring to completion such zeal for piety and religion.

# On the Heresy and History of the Priscillianists: A Single Book

## Chapter I. Who Priscillian was

### 1

When I considered within myself that I should commit to writing all the heresies flourishing or arising in the age of Leo, reason now demands, both with respect to the undertaking itself and to the time available, that after bringing to an end what had to be said about the Manichaean heresy, I now turn my mind and pen to reviewing the errors of Priscillian, which that same holy pontiff rejected, attacked, and proscribed.

No one until now has either accurately described or at least published what ought to be said about the author of this new heresy, about his homeland and character, about the synods convened against him and his adherents, or, finally, about the various and manifold doctrines of this wicked sect.

Therefore, when I had set my hand to composing these dissertations and had understood that the subject was full of difficulties, I judged it necessary to review the ancient and modern writers on the matter, but in such a way that, setting aside all prejudices and moved by no partisan zeal, I might present to readers only those things that either reveal the truth or at least seem to approach the truth more closely.

Accordingly, when I had first resolved to discuss Priscillian’s life and corrupt morals, I thought that no learned person would disapprove of my plan, although I might seem, at the very threshold and in the course of the dissertation, to depart somewhat from the deeds of Leo, which I intended to recount and defend.

For when, in this part of ecclesiastical history, we encountered some matters that were doubtful and obscure, others that were spurious and false, and very many that were entirely unknown, that very love of truth which alone occupies our mind compelled us to trace and set forth the whole matter from its origins.

### 2

Priscillian, then, born of noble stock and abounding in great wealth, was a man keen in intellect, restless, eloquent, learned through extensive reading, and exceedingly ready in discussion and disputation.

“Certainly a fortunate man,” says Severus Sulpicius, “if he had not corrupted his excellent talent through a perverse zeal. In him you would plainly discern many gifts of mind and body; but he was also exceedingly vain and more inflated than was proper by his knowledge of profane matters.”

**Note:** Severus Sulpicius, *History* II.

When, therefore, he had taken a certain Egyptian named Marcus into his fellowship, he drew from him and absorbed into his mind all the crimes and monstrosities that had emerged from the sects of the Gnostics and Manichaeans. Then, adding his own crimes to the doctrines of both groups, he introduced into the world a new sect in which promiscuous lusts, fornications, adulteries, the dissolution of marriages, lies, perjuries, and other things of this kind were practiced as though they were religious and lawful.

When I had reflected on all these things, I was easily brought to the conviction that no heretic had ever devised anything more harmful and shameful to natural morality, more destructive to human society, or more superstitious and sacrilegious to the ruin of religion.

For, besides the disgraces committed against themselves and their neighbors, and besides the injuries inflicted upon God, the study of astrology and the belief in a fatal necessity had such power among the Priscillianists that Priscillian devoted himself continually to magical arts.

Indeed, although he had been initiated through holy baptism and had assumed the name of the Christian faith, he nevertheless lived so deeply entangled in pagan errors that he sought to honor the stars favorable to him, as he supposed, and to appease those opposed to him, employing for that purpose profane and sacrilegious rites which the Church, from Moses down to our own time, had always avoided and abhorred.

**Note:** See Saint Leo’s letter 15, concerning which we shall speak in chapter 14 of this book.

Meanwhile, lest he appear wholly to despise every form of piety and religion, he displayed, through the excessive art of deception in which he was highly skilled, an appearance of humility in his clothing. He went barefoot, and he taught that fasts ought to be observed even on Sundays and on the Lord’s Nativity. While affecting a pretended gravity of morals, he especially captivated the minds of women, whose company he always sought.

They were easily attracted by his excessive skill in flattering; flocking to him in crowds, they were readily caught by their desire for novelty and by the license of their lusts.

No one has called into question what we have so far set forth concerning Priscillian’s morals, practices, and manner of acting. We therefore had no need either to engage in controversy or to linger longer over its explanation.

## Chapter II. The time and place from which the Priscillianist heresy chiefly began to spread; various opinions of writers are recorded

### 1

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, states that the grievous plague of Priscillianism began to spread chiefly in Spain in the year of Christ 379, during the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius. He writes:

> Gratian, after the death of his uncle, took Theodosius, the son of Theodosius, into partnership and handed over to him the empire of the East. At that time Priscillian, a bishop from Gaul, founded a heresy bearing his own name from the doctrine of the Manichaeans and Gnostics.

The consulate of Ausonius, Hermogenes, and Olybrius must be assigned to the aforementioned year 379, as the lists of the Roman consuls now plainly demonstrate.

**Note:** Prosper, in the *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius.

I know, nevertheless, that men most skilled in critical scholarship have rather believed that this heresy was propagated through Spain at a later date. William Cave, Severinus Binius, and others followed this opinion, maintaining that the heresy arose two years later and that Priscillian originated in Spain.

**Note:** William Cave, *The Arian Age*, p. 177 in my edition; Severinus Binius, notes to volume II of the *Councils*.

They assert that both points were affirmed by Severus Sulpicius. But neither will be established from his writings. For the aforementioned Severus, having undertaken to describe the evils of his own age, by which the churches had been polluted in an extraordinary manner and everything thrown into confusion, identifies their principal leaders and authors, but neither precisely fixes the date nor asserts that Priscillian arose in Spain.

Indeed, if we attend carefully to the force of Sulpicius’s words, we must believe that the sect had lain concealed for a long time before Priscillian joined it. Marcus the Egyptian, born in Memphis, first introduced the Gnostic sect into Spain with the assistance of a certain noble and very wealthy woman named Agape and of the rhetorician Elpidius. Priscillian himself later joined them, and from him the heresy took its name.

He says:

> Then for the first time that infamous Gnostic heresy was detected within Spain, a destructive superstition concealed in secret mysteries. The origin of this evil was from the East, among the Egyptians; but by what beginnings it was established there is not easy to discuss. Marcus was the first to bring it into Spain, having come from Egypt and being born in Memphis. His hearers were a certain woman named Agape, not of low birth, and the rhetorician Elpidius. Priscillian, a noble man and very rich in resources, was instructed by them, and so forth.

**Note:** Severus Sulpicius, *History* II.

Severus Sulpicius therefore distinguishes two periods in that passage: one, namely, the period in which the Gnostic sect was spreading; the other, when Priscillian, joining the Gnostics and both overcoming and enlarging their impiety, transformed the errors of Marcus, Agape, and Elpidius into the monstrous wickedness, audacity, and frenzied lust of a new and most abominable sect.

That this happened during the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, and not later, can also be established from other circumstances and from the Council of Zaragoza itself.

### 2

For, according to Sulpicius, when Priscillian recognized that the number of his followers was increasing daily, he began to summon them all together. He was accustomed to lead them into the hiding places and recesses of the mountains, where he conducted their wicked gatherings. To conceal them from the eyes and knowledge of others, he permitted his followers to pretend communion with the Catholic Church by receiving the sacred elements in their hands and carrying them away with them.

When, therefore, the bishops of Spain learned that religion, justice, and honesty were being overthrown, and that no restraint was being placed upon luxury, sacrilege, or magical incantations, they carefully established those laws and canons that they considered most necessary for restraining these grave evils.

It is therefore not plausible that what Cave and the others asserted is true—namely, that the heresy first came to light in the year of the Lord 381. How could that have happened, when in that year it had already spread widely throughout those provinces and had struck deep roots in the minds of the wicked? At that time Priscillianists held their gatherings on certain days of the year, both in the mountains and in the country estates, with great crowds of men and women attending. Finally, all the obscene and profane practices performed in their hiding places had become known to the holy pastors of the Catholic Church.

That all these things had become known is revealed by the eight canons of the Council of Zaragoza, which we shall discuss shortly.

### 3

Nor should we suppose that, as soon as the heresy became known, the holy prelates of the Church assembled in council. For when Hyginus, bishop of Córdoba and successor of Hosius the Great, first discovered the virulent corruption of Priscillian, which had also depraved and corrupted several bishops, including Instantius and Salvianus, he wished the matter to be reported to Idatius, priest of the city of Mérida.

Hyginus, however, inflamed with anger against the sectarians, attacked Instantius and his associates without restraint and beyond what was proper. “He added,” says Severus Sulpicius, “a torch to the newly kindled fire, so that he irritated the wicked rather than suppressed them.”

Once the matter had therefore been referred to Idatius, and Instantius and his associates had been attacked more severely, the matter still did not immediately proceed to a council. But after many struggles had been undertaken between the two parties, when the hope of the Catholics—that they could bring the heretics to repentance—had been completely frustrated, twelve Catholic bishops finally assembled at Zaragoza.

### 4

Having noted this earlier error of Cave, Severinus Binius, and others, we must finally guard against and remove the other error concerning Priscillian’s homeland and origin.

Lest I seem to wish to bring the nation of this or that people into disrepute, I shall touch upon the question only briefly. I shall merely point out that it is entirely wrong to attribute to Severus Sulpicius the assertion that Priscillian was born in Spain, for no such statement will be found by anyone who reads the whole of the second book of Severus’s *History*.

Indeed, if we examine the testimonies of other ancient writers, we shall still find it difficult to determine the matter. Jerome himself, who was accustomed to report the origins of others, while reviewing Priscillian’s morals, deeds, and death not once or twice but repeatedly, everywhere maintained profound silence concerning his homeland and origin.

He admits that Priscillian spread his errors throughout every gathering of men and women in Spain. He teaches that Priscillian took a Gallic woman named Galla—not a woman Gallic by nationality, but one named Galla—as an associate in wicked crimes. But from what people or place Priscillian himself derived his origin he entirely concealed or left unmentioned.

Nor is it at all certain that any one of the many ancient Fathers who wrote about this heresy supports the opinion of Cave and the other modern writers.

Augustine, in several different places, describes the errors of the Priscillianists, which, he says, “Priscillian established in Spain.”

**Note:** Augustine, *On Heresies*, heresy 70, and *Book to Orosius*, chapter 4.

Orosius, almost a contemporary of Priscillian, complained in his *Commonitory*, or consultation, addressed to Augustine, only that the heresy had spread through Spain.

Idatius mentions both Priscillian and the Priscillianists in his *Chronicle*, but nowhere indicated that Priscillian originated in Spain.

Epiphanius likewise, when discussing Priscillian in heresy 49, briefly describes his crimes and wicked deeds, but asserts nothing concerning his origin or homeland.

Finally, the author of the book *On Heresies*, which is attributed to Rufinus of Palestine in volume XXVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, has only this to say:

> Priscillian is said to have begun the seventieth heresy, that of the Priscillianists, among the Spaniards.

### 5

When I reflected on all these matters, I did so not to defend the rights of the Spanish nation or to clear them of this reproach, but rather to adhere to the truth and to take precautions against the suspicion that some might form that Priscillian was born in Gaul.

The strongest and most solid foundations for such a suspicion arose not only from the aforementioned *Chronicle* of Prosper of Aquitaine but also from many other conjectures. For both the *Chronicle* that bears only the name of Prosper of Aquitaine and the version expanded under the name of Tiro and published by Canisius explicitly read:

> Priscillian, bishop from Galatia; Priscillian, bishop from Gaul.

Moreover, they expressly indicate that the province of Aquitaine was shaken by this heresy. Among the other women, they also say that Priscillian had Euchrotia, the wife of Delphidius—or Elpidius—the rhetorician, as his associate in crimes and death.

But this Delphidius, or Elpidius, was a Gaul and taught rhetoric in the same province of Aquitaine, as has been revealed by the most ancient monuments of *Gallia Christiana*. Its compilers, when discussing the archbishopric of Bordeaux, wrote concerning Saint Delphinus under the year of Christ 380:

> Saint Delphinus, a singular ornament of the Gallican Church, participated, together with other bishops of Aquitaine, in the council held at Zaragoza in Hispania Tarraconensis in the year 380 or the following year, where Priscillian and Delphidius, an Aquitanian rhetorician, along with other adherents of wicked doctrines, were condemned.

**Note:** *Gallia Christiana*, volume II, archbishops of Bordeaux, p. 787.

Furthermore, how can we reject Prosper’s testimony, which is so open and unmistakable? Tillemont and Dionysius Petavius certainly neither rejected it nor marked it as erroneous. Although they avoid discussing Priscillian’s homeland and origin, they nevertheless, together with us, assign the beginning of that heresy to the year 379 of Christ, relying solely on Prosper’s testimony.

Prosper himself, therefore, would not have called Priscillian a Gaul—thereby bringing disgrace and reproach upon himself and upon the entire people of Aquitaine—if the matter had not been fully and sufficiently clear both to him and to everyone else.

If we were to reason in this way, contrary to the most widespread tradition and the conviction of all, we would seem to be looking for a knot in a bulrush. For we must affirm without any hesitation that Priscillian originated where his errors were first propagated.

If the words of the aforementioned *Chronicle* then appear to contradict this, since they present the word “Galatia,” we should not for that reason suppose that Priscillian was a Gaul. Learned men have most often judged that this *Chronicle* is riddled with many errors. Moreover, the ancients sometimes used that word to designate the peoples of Galatia situated within the boundaries of the Spanish provinces, as we could demonstrate with six hundred examples.

We shall principally establish this in preparing the letter of Saint Leo the Great to Turibius of Astorga. We reserve the fuller treatment of that matter for its proper place in the narrative of this history.

# CHAPTER III

Instantius and Salvianus, bishops of the Spanish provinces, following Priscillian’s practice, consecrated him bishop of Ávila. At approximately the same time, he was first condemned at the Council of Caesaraugusta and then expelled from Spain by Gratian’s edict; he proceeded to Rome to see Damasus.

[Col. 0996B]

## 1.

But now, having set aside what critical scholars have stated with insufficient accuracy, and what might lead the reader’s mind toward a false suspicion, we must return to Idacius and the other eleven bishops of Gaul and Spain who, as we have seen, after many struggles had been unable to restrain or correct either Priscillian’s boldness, his unbridled behavior, or his sacrilegious superstition, and who therefore, by the sacred authority of the Church and with unanimous agreement, issued those judgments which would best protect religion, divine worship, the mysteries of the faith, piety, moral integrity, and human society, and which would destroy and eradicate that ungodly plague.

The bishops of the sacred order who assembled at Caesaraugusta were: Fitadius, Delphinus, Eutychianus or Bastitanus, Ampelius, Augentius, Lucius, Ithacius, Splendonius, Valerius of Caesaraugusta, Symphosius, Catherius, and Idacius. All of them, as though acting upon a sacred senatorial decree, enacted eight canons, or laws; Bishop Lucius read them aloud in the assembly, so that all the bishops might proclaim an anathema against transgressors. Copies of these judgments, or laws, have been written in the second volume of the Councils, and Severinus Binius furnished them with various annotations.

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Volume II of the Councils, p. 1195.]

## 2.

Meanwhile, while these matters were being conducted at the Council of Caesaraugusta, neither Instantius and Salvianus nor Priscillian, nor anyone from his group of followers, took part in the assembly. Rather, they all refused to present themselves before those Fathers, lest they submit themselves to judgment.

Severus Sulpicius recounts the matter, adding that judgment was pronounced against those who were absent, and also against those who dared to receive the condemned into communion. “Accordingly,” he says, “after many struggles between them, struggles deserving remembrance, a synod was convened at Caesaraugusta, in which bishops from Aquitaine also took part. But the heretics did not dare submit themselves to judgment; therefore judgment was pronounced against those who were absent, and the bishops Instantius and Salvianus, and the laymen Helpidius and Priscillian, were condemned. It was also added that if anyone received the condemned into communion, he should know that the same sentence would be pronounced against him.”

When these things became known to the sectarians, they became the cause of still greater hatred toward the Church and all Catholics. For, in order to increase the disturbances and spread their more abominable errors still further, those two bishops condemned by the judgment of the Council of Caesaraugusta—namely Instantius and Salvianus—appointed the layman Priscillian, whom the same synod had marked out as the chief of all evils, bishop in the town of Labiensis, “to strengthen their power,” as the same Severus says. They evidently reasoned that, if they armed a sharp and crafty man with sacerdotal authority, they would be safer.

The impiety of so great a crime, by which the honor and authority of the priesthood were polluted with the greatest disgrace, was noted and indeed abhorred, among others, by Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon, where he describes the origin and great growth of that heresy:

“In Spain, Agape, a woman, led Elpidius, a man—a blind woman leading a blind man—into the pit; and she had as her successor Priscillian, an ardent devotee of the magus Zoroaster and, from a magus, a bishop. Galla, joined to him—not by nation but by name—made him heir of another, neighboring heresy, a sister running here and there.”

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Jerome, To Ctesiphon.]

## 3.

That the Council of Caesaraugusta was convened in the year of the Lord 381, during the pontificate of Pope Damasus, is made entirely clear by the canons published by García de Loaysa. But from what Severus Sulpicius reports, we learn that the complete Acts of that council have either perished or have not yet seen the light of day.

As we have seen, he reports that an anathema was pronounced in that sacred assembly against those who had rashly dared to receive the already condemned into communion. This judgment was directed especially against Hyginus, bishop of Córdoba. Although at first he had been eager to abolish that sect, had declared war on Priscillian and his followers, and had urged Idacius himself by letter to undertake it, he later changed his mind and did not approve the counsels of the Catholics. Having been shamefully corrupted, he abstained from the council and received the wicked heretics into communion.

The task was therefore assigned to Ithacius, bishop of Sossuba, of making the bishops’ decree known to everyone and especially of excluding Hyginus from communion. He had been the first of all to begin publicly attacking the heretics, but after being shamefully corrupted he had received them into communion.

From the sequence and account of this affair we understand perfectly that the eight surviving canons are certainly genuine and authentic, since among the bishops who signed them we find no mention whatsoever of Hyginus—or Idiginius—of Córdoba. Moreover, they attack and condemn some of the principal errors of that sect; they openly prohibit and denounce its rites, teaching, assemblies, and fasts, although they may have passed over in silence many other crimes and immoralities that perhaps had not yet been sufficiently investigated.

[Note: [Col. 0997D] In ancient authors and monuments of antiquity we encounter the name of Hyginus of Córdoba written in different forms, as may be seen in the books of Severus Sulpicius and in the surviving Acts of the Council of Caesaraugusta. We have followed their manner of writing when adducing or indicating their testimonies.

[Col. 0998D] We are not unaware, however, that the most recent writer, Francisco Girvesius, in addition to the names Iginius and Idiginius used by the ancients, adopted the other form Hyginus. See the learned dissertation of this distinguished man, printed at Rome in the year of the Lord 1750.]

## 4.

Yet the condition of those Churches was becoming more pitiable by the day. For those two Catholic bishops, especially Idacius and Ithacius, after the synodal decrees and after that disgraceful ordination of Priscillian, pressed their case more vigorously and approached the secular judges, so that by their decrees and enforcement the heretics might be expelled from the cities.

Accordingly, according to Sulpicius, “after many disgraceful proceedings, at the petition of Idacius, a rescript was obtained from Gratian, then emperor, by which all heretics were ordered to leave not only the churches but also the cities, and to be driven beyond all lands.”

Both Severus Sulpicius and the other more gentle Catholic bishops judged the course of action taken by Idacius and Ithacius to have been excessively harsh and disgraceful. For, without consulting any other bishop of Spain or Gaul, and without informing Damasus himself, the Roman pontiff, they brought the case of the sectarians before the secular tribunal. The matter concerned not lay persons but the bishops Instantius, Salvianus, and Priscillian, although they were indeed stained by heretical corruption. Nor was the question one of crimes whose investigation belonged to the emperor, but only of matters that ought to have undergone ecclesiastical judgment.

Finally, Idacius and Ithacius had approached Gratian solely on their private authority, not by decree of a council, and had sought his judgment. It was therefore rightly considered a disgrace to the Church and the greatest dishonor to the sacred order.

## 5.

Meanwhile, when Priscillian and the others who appeared to be bishops understood that they had been condemned to exile, distrusting their circumstances and not daring to contest the judgment, they voluntarily withdrew; fear scattered the multitude of laypeople. But although they were oppressed by these distressed circumstances, they did not despair of being able to find help and protection.

Therefore those three bishops, the leading figures among the other sectarians, resolved to travel to Rome, so that those who were suffering punishment for their crimes by decree of the public authority might afterward, by deceiving Damasus, the Roman pontiff, be regarded by Catholics as innocent and guiltless, once they had fraudulently obtained a kind of ecclesiastical reconciliation.

As they traveled to Rome, they journeyed from Spain through the province of Aquitaine. There they were magnificently received by the ignorant, and they scattered the seeds of their perfidy. In particular, they corrupted the people of Elusa, who at that time were genuinely good and devoted to religion, by their wicked preaching.

The city of Elusa, on the little river Gelisus, was very ancient and had formerly been the seat of the archbishops, or metropolitans, of Novempopulania, under whose jurisdiction the city of the Ausci and many others were included. From Elusa the district called Elusanus took its name; it is now part of the county of Armagnac. It is said to have been reduced to a small town because of the frequent disasters by which it was worn down by the Goths, Saracens, and Normans.

We have noted these facts from Dionysius Sammarthanus, volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, who further testified that he had recently seen a new catalogue of the bishops of Elusa.

[Note: [Col. 0998D] Dionysius Sammarthanus, volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 960.]

Priscillian and the others next went to the diocese of Bordeaux. But after being rejected by Bishop Delphinus, they stayed for some time on the estate of Euchrotia, a wicked and immodest woman, and infected several people with their errors.

From there they set out on their journey, traveling in a disgraceful and shameful company with their wives and also with other women. Among them were Euchrotia and her daughter Procla, about whom it was said in popular report that, having become pregnant by Priscillian’s adultery, she had caused herself to miscarry by means of herbs.

Whether, therefore, Procla conceived a child by Priscillian and brought about its death or abortion, or did not; whether Priscillian himself committed incest with both mother and daughter—the author, Severus, did not dare to determine any of this from anything more than the opinion of certain people.

## 6.

That Priscillian came to Rome with his associates after new, countless, and most horrifying crimes is made clear not merely by popular rumor but by the most certain records.

This course of action also supplies new examples of ecclesiastical discipline, from which we understand that those condemned in councils were accustomed to appeal and have recourse to the judgments of the Roman pontiffs, so that they, by the apostolic authority of blessed Peter, might either rescind or confirm the acts of other bishops, even when these had been determined in synods.

Although we might regard this example—taken as it is from enemies of the faith—as something of little importance, and although we do not embrace it in order to assert a supreme right belonging to the Apostolic See in establishing matters of faith, nevertheless we maintain that it must not be rejected altogether.

For the bishops of Spain did not belong to the Roman council, although Quesnellus pretends that only those bishops could have been judged by the pontiffs. Nor had Priscillian and his associates been enrolled in the register of the Roman clergy, nor did they intend to flatter the Roman See, as Launoius argues with extraordinary cleverness in similar cases. Rather, they intended to make use of a right indicated by the sacred Scriptures, proclaimed by the universal tradition of the Fathers, and finally established everywhere by the general practice of the Churches.

Such, then, was the course of action adopted by Priscillian and his associates, first after the synodal decrees and then after the sentence of the emperor Gratian: they did not appeal to a general council. Recent heretics, influenced by words and opinions of this sort, are thereby driven to confine the authority of the Roman See within narrower limits.

It is nevertheless beyond question that Priscillian tried to obtain from Damasus, the Roman pontiff, protection and support for himself and his associates. For, according to Sulpicius, when they reached Rome, they wished to clear themselves before Damasus, but were not even admitted into his presence.

This does not contradict the fact that the holy pontiff, guided by that spirit which will always endure in the successors of Peter, frustrated the unjust efforts of those men by allowing no access whatsoever for their defense. Their arrival in the City, however, in order to plead their case, is the strongest and most conclusive proof that the cases of bishops and others, already brought to a conclusion by synodal decrees, could again be reviewed and judged by the authority of the Roman pontiffs.

We have touched on these matters only briefly, lest the method of argument employed by more recent dogmatists appear unknown to us.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] See what we shall say below concerning the cases of Eutyches, Flavian, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, and Theodoret of Cyrus, who appealed to the Apostolic See in the time of Leo the Great.]

After their earlier efforts had failed, Priscillian and Instantius turned their attention to new attempts, as will become clear from what follows.

# CHAPTER IV

The emperor Gratian, having been deceived by Macedonius, orders Instantius and Priscillian to be restored to their sees. On Britto, bishop of Trier, and the honor and privileges of that see. The false conjectures of Blondel and Tillemont are rejected.

## 1.

Even after the serious rebuff they had suffered from Pope Damasus, the bishops Instantius and Priscillian did not yet believe that their affairs had been brought to complete ruin. But, in the customary obstinate cunning of heretics, and still wishing to remedy the evils and exile weighing upon them, they devised a new plan: namely, to return to Milan, perhaps led by the vain hope that Ambrose, the great bishop of that Church, would receive them into communion with the Catholics.

This conviction, however, moved only the two bishops Instantius and Priscillian. Their associate Salvianus was no longer alive; he had already died in the City.

But matters turned out very differently from what they expected. For when Ambrose learned how the Roman pontiff had acted, he likewise began to oppose them, considering it a most serious crime either to hear or to receive into communion those whom the Apostolic See of blessed Peter had rejected.

“Then,” says the same Sulpicius, “Priscillian and Instantius changed their plans, so that, since they had not deceived the two bishops whose authority was supreme at that time, they might obtain from the emperor, by bribery and solicitation, what they desired.”

## 2.

At that time Gratian himself still held supreme power over imperial affairs. Macedonius, master of the offices, having greater influence with him through dishonest methods than through authority, easily brought him to the point of issuing an order that, after the earlier decree against Priscillian and his associates had been recalled and annulled, they should be restored to the sees from which he had previously ordered them expelled.

Everyone considered this a grave and monstrous crime. For Gratian, otherwise a religious man and an exceedingly pious ruler, was deceived by the wicked master of the offices and fell into the rash undertaking not only of cancelling and destroying the earlier decrees he himself had issued with the greatest sanctity, but also of wishing to oppose the Council of Caesaraugusta, the great Ambrose, the Roman pontiff himself, and—as was more serious—himself.

Thus rejoicing at the emperor Gratian’s leniency toward them, Instantius and Priscillian did not delay long in returning to Spain. They set out at the beginning of the year 383 and took possession of their episcopal sees. Idacius was willing to resist them, but could do nothing to defend religion. He lacked the means, because the heretics had strengthened their position by corrupting Volventius, the proconsul.

Indeed, seeing themselves supported by such great secular power, they attacked the Catholic bishop Ithacius with excessive boldness and accused him before the proconsul as a disturber of the Churches. The proconsul, agreeing with their most criminal wishes and sacrilegiously violating every divine and human right, ordered Ithacius to be brought forward by a brutal enforcement.

But Ithacius fled fearlessly to Gaul and approached the prefect Gregory. When Gregory, prefect of the Gallic praetorium, had learned the entire sequence of events, he immediately ordered the instigators of the disturbance to be seized and, after informing the emperor of everything, urged him to block the heretics’ path to bribery.

“But this was useless,” adds Severus, “because there everything was for sale through the lust and power of a few.” Accordingly, by their devices and after paying Macedonius a large sum of money, the heretics obtained that jurisdiction should be taken away from the prefect by imperial authority and transferred to the vicar of Spain, Marianus—for by then they no longer had a proconsul.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] Severus Sulpicius, same work.]

Macedonius also sent military officials to Trier to drag Ithacius by force from that city and return him to Spain, where he would be subjected to the dreadful fury of the heretics. Nevertheless, the bishop of Trier resisted. Having discovered the plot, he frustrated and overturned the wicked efforts both of Macedonius, master of the imperial offices, and of the military officials, with remarkable prudence and priestly steadfastness.

## 3.

I therefore think that from what has just been said it is sufficiently clear that Britto, bishop of Trier, held no minor place among the defenders of the Catholic faith. When speaking of him, Severus Sulpicius calls him Pritanus. But we must fear either that he had two names or that an error entered the copies of Severus because of a certain similarity between the names.

For this name is entirely absent from the records of that Church. Instead, we read another name that differs little from it—Britto, or Brittonius—who subscribed to the Council of Valence in the year of the Lord 374:

“I, Britto, bishop, wish you, brothers, good health in the Lord.”

Besides the annals of that city, Bollandus indicates this on 5 May, listing Britto among the confessors of that Church. Sirmondus supports the same identification in his notes on the Council of Valence; finally, nearly all writers teach it, including Blondel and Tillemont.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] Tillemont, volume VIII, p. 556.]

## 4.

What these last two authors wrote about Bishop Britto must not be concealed, since they perhaps intended to claim for him, among Western bishops after Pope Damasus, a privilege of honor and jurisdiction.

They say that the city of Trier, because certain emperors had established their residence there, rose to such a height of honor and power that its bishops also surpassed other bishops, whether in synods or in public proceedings. For this reason, they add that the city of Trier held first place not only in Gaul but also in Spain and England. When they were in Gaul, either an imperial prefect or the emperors themselves were accustomed to reside there.

Moved by these considerations, the Eastern Fathers, in a letter written to the Roman council in the year of the Lord 382, place Britto of Trier immediately after Damasus and Ambrose, according to Theodoret, and set him before the bishops of Aquileia, Thessalonica, and Sirmium, evidently intending by this arrangement to indicate both his virtue and the extent of his authority.

What a charming and fabulous invention! It is astonishing that, because Trier was the residence of emperors, they did not assert for Britto a primatial privilege above Damasus and Ambrose.

[Col. 1001A]

Everyone can see how cold such reasoning is. The honor and privileges of episcopal sees were not derived from some civil administration of temporal affairs, from secular power, from the prefects or residences of emperors, or finally from the provincial governors—all of which, as sacred and profane records show, were subject to countless changes with changing times. Rather, those honors and privileges must be traced entirely to the origin, antiquity, and founders of the sees.

## 5.

Although metropolitan jurisdiction is found to have been attributed to certain Churches through the privileges of councils and the grants and dispensations of the Roman pontiffs, it cannot at all be demonstrated that, in Britto’s time, such jurisdiction was granted to the see of Trier above the other sees of Gaul, Spain, and Britain.

Indeed, if we are to place faith in ecclesiastical records, we must unquestionably believe that at that time the bishop of Trier did not possess primatial honor above the archbishop of Vienne, the two bishops of Narbonne, the bishop of Lyon, and certain other bishops of Gaul who assembled at the Council of Valence.

For that Britto about whom we are now disputing with Blondel and Tillemont occupies the fifteenth place in the subscription of the Acts of that synod. Let those two writers, then, who strive to sketch and fabricate a kind of new patriarch in the West over the provinces of three kingdoms at the end of the fourth century, tell us, I ask, whom we ought rather to trust: Britto himself, who is described as adorned with such privileges because of his see, or the conjectures by which some might perhaps seek to exalt the rights of the Roman See?

No sane person will ever imagine that a bishop of such honor and authority sat in fifteenth place while that council was being celebrated in Transalpine Gaul, in the city of the Allobroges, subject to the archbishopric of Vienne. Moreover, Britto himself signed those Acts after Justus, bishop of Vienne.

[Col. 1001C]

## 6.

As for the letter of the Eastern bishops cited by Theodoret, what do they say? Do they encounter Britto’s name immediately after the names of Damasus and Ambrose? But I ask: Is he the bishop of Trier? Theodoret nowhere asserts this. Indeed, Henri Valois suspected that he was the bishop of Capua.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Henri Valois, in his notes on Theodoret’s letter.]

We consider it impossible to settle the matter, since the complete Acts of that Roman synod convened by Damasus are no longer preserved in the collection of the Councils, and the subscriptions of the bishops disappeared long ago.

But let us grant that this Britto was the same as the bishop of Trier. Is such a substantial argument really drawn from that letter of the Eastern bishops that a question of such importance can be settled solely by its badly composed or transcribed heading?

Did Theodoret report it as he found it written in his autograph copy? Or did those Eastern Fathers, whether perfectly informed about the order of the Western sees or not, faithfully reproduce that order without changing anything? Who could affirm either alternative?

First of all, those Eastern bishops who had assembled at Constantinople for the council declined to attend the Roman synod of Damasus, which was then in progress. They excused themselves by saying that, after the countless and grievous hardships they had endured through the fury of the Arians, they could not undertake so long and laborious a journey in order to come to Rome.

For this reason they sent three bishops as legates to Damasus and the Roman synod—namely Cyriacus, Eusebius, and Priscillian—who brought with them the letter cited by Theodoret. Those Fathers of the East therefore had no knowledge whatsoever either of the order occupied by the Western bishops in the Roman council or of their number.

Consequently, they wrote down only the names of some of them and concluded the rest with this general formula: “And the other holy bishops convened in the renowned city of Rome.”

Finally, I shall say nothing about Theodoret’s suspect reliability in reviewing the records of antiquity, since Baronius and others justly accuse him of similar deceptions. But Sirmondus’s care indicates that such fraud is far removed from the Acts of the Council of Valence. For the learned man took pains to publish them in a more accurate form from the manuscripts of Reims, Lyon, Le Puy, Fossat, and three others belonging to the Paris College of the Society of Jesus and to the Isidorean collection. He judged those manuscripts to have been written more than nine hundred years ago. Therefore, the complete agreement of those archetypal copies removes every suspicion of fraud, as learned scholars will judge together with us.

Let us now return to Priscillian and Ithacius. When the efforts of Macedonius and his officials had been frustrated by Prittanus, or Britto, the bishop, and the way had likewise been closed to their removing Ithacius from the city of Trier and bringing him back to Spain, a serious rumor began to arise that Clemens Maximus had seized power in Britain and would soon burst into Gaul.

Ithacius therefore decided, despite the uncertainty of affairs, to await the arrival of the new emperor and to undertake nothing in the meantime. Events occurred just as rumor had reported. For, at the beginning of the year 383, Maximus, then commander of the imperial forces in Britain, seized power, was hailed as emperor by his soldiers, and, crossing with his army into Gaul, strengthened his authority through the hostility of Gratian’s legions.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Severus Sulpicius, *History*, book II.]

Baronius writes this from Victor and Zosimus in volume IV, under the year of Christ 383.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Victor, under Gratian; Zosimus, book I.]

# CHAPTER V

On the tyrant Maximus and his judgment and conduct in the case of the Priscillianists.

## 1.

While the emperor Gratian was still alive and Macedonius was managing the affairs of the empire, the Catholic bishops—and Ithacius above all—could have had no hope that the impiety and boldness of the Priscillianists would be overthrown.

But as soon as the Gallic legions hostile to Gratian, both in Britain and in other regions, proclaimed Maximus, commander of the imperial forces, emperor, the case of those same Priscillianists deteriorated and was brought to destruction.

The character of Maximus was briefly described by Gildas, surnamed “the Wise,” who said:

“Maximus, at first by cunning art rather than virtue, spreading throughout neighboring districts and provinces the nets of his perjury and deceit through his criminal kingdom against the Roman state, extending one wing toward Spain and the other toward Italy, and establishing the throne of his unjust empire at Trier, raged against his masters with such madness that he expelled two legitimate emperors, one from Rome and the other from a life of deepest piety.”

When Maximus had reached Trier and established his imperial seat there, Ithacius did not delay in informing him of everything that had so far been done by the Priscillianists, by the Catholic Fathers, and by Gratian.

Gratian was no longer alive. Abandoned by his own men—perhaps because of the excessive leniency he had shown toward the Priscillianists—he was killed at Lyon through the treachery of the general Andragathius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 383.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Marcellinus; Socrates, book V, chapter 11; Sozomen, book VII, chapter 13.]

Meanwhile, so that Maximus would not appear hostile to the affairs of the Church or allow them to become increasingly disturbed, he entrusted the judgment of the heretics to ecclesiastical pastors who were to assemble at Bordeaux.

For this reason, our Severus Sulpicius says:

“Having sent letters to the prefect of Gaul and to the vicar of Spain, he ordered that all those whom that corruption had enveloped should be brought to the Council of Bordeaux. When they assembled at the council, Instantius was the first to present himself before the judges. Ordered to plead his case, he was unable to clear himself of the charges brought against him; therefore the Fathers proceeded against him and declared him unworthy of the episcopate.”

When Priscillian noticed this and realized that his own case was worse, he immediately appealed to the emperor Maximus, in order to evade the judgment of the sacred assembly.

The same Severus describes the event in nearly these words, while also mildly reproving the Fathers of the council:

“But Priscillian, so as not to be heard by the bishops, appealed to the emperor. Our men’s inconsistency permitted this, because they ought either to have pronounced sentence against one who resisted, or, if those bishops themselves were considered suspect, to have reserved the hearing for other bishops, rather than entrust to the emperor a case involving such manifest crimes.”

Thus all those implicated in the case were brought before the ruler.

Lest we seem to act outside the subject by discussing here the violation of the rights of the Church, we deliberately pass over that matter entirely. It is enough for us merely to record the testimony of Severus Sulpicius, from which only fools or the blind could deny that the Church, from her very beginnings onward, has abhorred as sacrilegious those appeals which, as though permissible by way of abuse, one Maiemburgus defended in the past century with excessive boldness and rashness.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] He may perhaps have alluded to the Nicene canon, or to the Sardican canons, in which there is discussion of renewing judgment in cases involving bishops when the bishops who have already judged are considered suspect.]

[Note: [Col. 1004D] Eusebius of Caesarea, book VII, chapter 26. See our edition, volume I, p. 445. Rufinus, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, in the same edition of ours, volume II, p. 3.]

## 2.

Maximus, who had tyrannically overturned every right of the empire by lawful and unlawful means, did not shrink from this judicial office, after disregarding and despising the conduct both of Aurelian and of the great Constantine; rather, he immediately claimed it for himself.

The most holy bishops, including Martin of Tours, regarded this as a most serious crime and earnestly begged the emperor not to punish the heretics capitally, but, content with the priests’ judgment, to order them expelled from their episcopal sees.

At first Maximus appeared inclined to this view. Indeed, Severus Sulpicius asserts that, especially at the urging of Martin of Tours, he had already adopted it.

But while Ithacius was then acting with excessive energy as the accuser and, inflamed by intense hatred of the defendants, was pressing the emperor for their death, the matter still remained undecided. The assembly of Catholic bishops split into two factions, one refusing to communicate with the other.

The first faction maintained prudently and piously that the blood of the unfortunate must be spared. But the other, fiercer and more inhuman, desired their death, so that their crimes might be expiated through execution.

While matters thus hung in the balance, the secular tribunal postponed hearing the case for as long as Saint Martin remained at Trier. Maximus received him kindly and with great humanity and treated him with such reverence and honor that, when Martin was about to depart from Trier, he extracted from the emperor a promise that no bloody measure would be taken against the defendants.

The outcome of events, however, immediately frustrated that promise. For the emperor, corrupted by the Spanish bishops Magnus and Rufus and turned away from more lenient counsels, entrusted the case to the prefect Evodius, an energetic and severe man.

Evodius heard Priscillian in two successive proceedings, convicted him of magical practices, and found that he did not deny having devoted himself to obscene teachings, having held nocturnal meetings of depraved women, and having been accustomed to pray naked. He pronounced him guilty and remanded him to custody until he could report to the emperor.
