The ancient writers contain no mention of the sees of the bishops who had corrupted Maximus, so we cannot state the names of those sees. In the *Life of Saint Martin* we read only of a certain Bishop Rufus. Through the trickery of a certain young man who called himself and pretended to be Elijah and Christ, Rufus was so deceived that he worshiped him as the Lord. We later find that Rufus was removed from the episcopate for this reason.

## 3.

As for the badly initiated judgment begun by Evodius against the Priscillianists, there is no reason to fear that it failed to reach a bloody conclusion contrary to the promise the emperor had given to Martin.

For, once the initial investigation had been completed, the defendants’ confessions likewise heard, and the criminals themselves detained in prison, nothing remained except to summon the accusers before the defendants for the formal stages of the law, so that, once the inquiry had been strengthened and completed, the emperor could finally pronounce sentence.

“Then Ithacius,” says Severus Sulpicius, “seeing how odious it would be for him in the eyes of the bishops if he continued to be the accuser even at the final proceedings in a capital case—for the trial necessarily had to be repeated—absented himself from the investigation, his cunning crime already accomplished.”

Ithacius therefore began to shrink from the deed only because he had aroused the hatred of the Catholic bishops against himself; but he wished in vain to withdraw from the formal accusation.

For Maximus ordered Patricius, an advocate of the imperial treasury, to act in Ithacius’s place and perform the role of accuser. Through his prosecution, Priscillian was condemned to death together with Felicissimus and Armenius, who had recently defected to the side of the heretics.

Latronianus and Euchrotia, as well as Asarinus and Aurelius the deacon, were also killed by the sword.

Instantius, however, was treated more leniently. He was deported into exile to the island of Sylina, beyond Britain, where he was joined by Tiberianus, who had been deprived by judicial decree of all the property he had previously possessed.

Finally, the others—namely Tertullus, Potamius, and John—being persons of lower rank and deserving of mercy because they had betrayed themselves and their associates before the interrogation, were banished to temporary exile within Gaul.

## 4

Prosper relates that this same slaughter occurred in the year of the Lord 385, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, at which time Siricius, Damasus having already died, had assumed the helm of the Catholic Church in the preceding year. But Prosper further adds that in the following year, when Honorius and Evodius were consuls, at Bordeaux a certain female disciple of Priscillian named Urbica was killed by stoning during a popular riot because of her obstinate impiety. Yet in another Chronicle, circulated under the name of Tiro, it is related that the popular uprising against Urbica was provoked in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.

Now, once all these people had been killed or condemned to exile, the affairs of religion and the Church seemed to be driven headlong. For, first of all, the heresy that had broken out under Priscillian’s leadership was not merely suppressed; it was strengthened and spread more widely. Indeed, his followers, who had previously honored him as a saint, afterwards began to venerate him as a martyr. The bodies of those who had been killed were brought back to Spain, and their funerals were celebrated with great solemnity; indeed, it was considered the highest religious observance to swear by Priscillian.

Nor was religion undermined in Spain alone by such sacrilegious and criminal worship. In Gaul also, when a great schism had arisen, the Catholic bishops themselves divided into two factions. Some reproached Ithacius not only because, contrary to the Church’s custom and gentleness, he had persecuted those accused of violated faith, who were troubling the Church, in a capital prosecution, but also because, after being openly condemned by Bishop Theognostus, they refrained from his communion. Others, favoring Ithacius through fear of the emperor, were not at all reluctant to remain in communion with him.

# CHAPTER VI

## The tyrant Maximus gave the Roman pontiff a written confession of the Catholic faith. The emperor stirred up new disasters against the Priscillianists throughout Spain.

[Col. 1004D]

### 1

It has long been sincerely proclaimed by all learned men that emperors and secular princes, as defenders of the sacred laws and of the Catholic religion, ought to provide help and protection to the distressed affairs of the Church, lest a tyrant and the raging fury of heretics bring the divine mysteries to ruin. It is therefore not surprising that, as soon as the Roman pontiffs learned that someone had been proclaimed emperor, they demanded from him, with every insistence, a confession of the Catholic faith, without which they would have refused to maintain communion with him.

Among the most ancient examples of this procedure, Pope Saint Siricius has provided us with the following. Having been elevated to the pontificate in the year 385 [apparently an OCR error for 384], after the death of Damasus, he demanded this confession of the Catholic faith from Maximus; and Maximus, willingly, did not refuse to provide it in his letter, as has always been customary among just and Christian rulers. Thus, after first mentioning the papal letters he had received, and then extolling the greatness of the priestly office and the dignity of the most splendid city of Rome, he adds:

> As for the Catholic faith, concerning which you wished to consult our Clemency, the greater and more particular judgment of divinity I experience regarding myself, the greater care I confess that I must have—since I have ascended to imperial power directly from that saving source itself, and since God has always been present as my helper in all my endeavors and successes, and may He deign to be my protector and guardian today and, as I hope, forever, most beloved Father.

[Note: Col. 1005D; vol. II of the Councils, Venetian edition, p. 1227.]

He further promises to ensure that the priests of that same Church would handle ecclesiastical cases. At that time the matter chiefly concerned Agricius, whom the holy pontiff had recalled as having improperly attained the rank of presbyter. Accordingly, Maximus, seeking to imitate the example of legitimate emperors, says:

> What could I provide more reverently for our Catholic religion than that Catholic priests should judge what sort of man this person appears to be?

And so that the Gallic bishops and the other bishops residing within the five provinces might conveniently take part in this inquiry, he decrees that an assembly be established in whatever city they should choose, so that, while they were present and deliberating, judgment might be given as to what custom and what law required.

Finally, wishing to offer a splendid testimony to his sincere faith, he tells the pontiff how, on arriving at Trier from Britain, he found and discovered religion so polluted and stained by the crimes of many people that, unless—as he says—“our foresight and remedy, which proceeded from fear of the Most High God, had quickly brought them assistance, a great rupture and destruction would certainly have arisen, and vices would afterwards have accumulated that could scarcely be cured.”

[Col. 1005C]

But what superstition and impiety had been committed by the Priscillianists—whom Maximus calls Manichaeans there—he says was known not through arguments or uncertain suspicions, but through their own confessions brought forward in the judicial proceedings:

> It is better that Your Holiness should learn this evil from the records themselves than from our mouth, because we cannot, without shame, speak aloud of things that are not only disgraceful to do but also vile to describe.

[Note: Volume II of the Councils, p. 1227.]

It is therefore entirely certain that with this letter Maximus the Tyrant sent to Siricius the records of the entire inquiry and investigation.

### 2

What he replied to these matters, or what the holy pontiff judged from those records, cannot so far be extracted from any monument of Christian history. We understand only one thing, as absolutely certain, against certain recent dogmatists: namely, that the Roman pontiffs exercised at least an indirect authority over Catholic kings. For Pope Siricius would not have questioned the faith of the Emperor Maximus, nor demanded his profession in writing, unless, by virtue of the supreme priestly office, he possessed the authority to judge whether Maximus was ruling the empire lawfully, unlawfully, or tyrannically.

But let others discuss that matter. For the present, we observe that in this same year the bishops of the Ithacian faction assembled at Trier in council. When other bishops of more prudent judgment had also arrived, they petitioned Maximus to annul the sentence of anathema and deposition previously pronounced against Ithacius by Bishop Theognostus, and to absolve him as innocent, so that no one would be permitted to deny him communion.

Authority compelled Martin to attend the synod. After being surrounded by the imperial officials, he first promised that he had come to Trier in the peace of Christ. Then, having entered the imperial palace and been terrified by Maximus’s threats, although he both ought and wished to stand firm against the ordination of Felix, bishop of Trier, he was compelled to communicate for one hour only with the heretics who favored Ithacius. Yet no terror or threat could induce him to confirm that communion in writing.

The following day he hastened away from there. As he returned, says Severus in the Dialogues, he groaned sadly that he had been entangled even for an hour in a guilty communion:

> He sat down, turning over in his mind the cause of his grief and the deed itself, as his thoughts alternately accused and defended him. Suddenly an angel stood beside him: “You are rightly pierced with remorse, Martin,” he said, “but you could not have departed otherwise. Restore your courage; recover your steadfastness, lest you now incur not danger to your glory but danger to your salvation.”

From that time onward he took sufficient care not to mingle with the communion of the Ithacian party. He himself later experienced that, because of that guilty communion, he obtained divine help and protection for working miracles more slowly than usual, when he wished to cure certain people possessed by demons. He lived sixteen years thereafter, attended no synod, and withdrew from every assembly of bishops.

Thus Severus Sulpicius concludes that chapter in the dialogue cited above.

[Note: Severus Sulpicius, Dialogue 3, chapter 15.]

### 3

Before we speak of the year of this holy man’s death, we cannot pass over in silence the disaster that the Emperor Maximus brought upon the heretics spreading throughout Spain as a result of the decision of the Council of Trier. He resolved to send there tribunes armed with supreme authority, who would investigate those stained by heretical corruption and deprive those discovered of life and property.

But that decree, wholly opposed to ecclesiastical gentleness and overflowing with the greatest anger and hatred, tormented Martin’s spirit with inward anguish. For without any hesitation he understood that, through the extreme greed and lust of the tribunes, not only wicked and sacrilegious people would be harassed, punished, and killed, but that Catholics themselves—and even a multitude of holy persons—would be plundered, since there was scarcely any distinction between the classes of people.

For, says Severus Sulpicius, at that time people were judged solely by the eyes, so that someone was considered a heretic on the basis rather of his pallor or his clothing.

These things therefore displeased Martin greatly when he came to the council. Hence it is no wonder that after the Council of Trier he solemnly resolved that in the future he would keep away from gatherings of this kind, and refused to attend them for as long as he lived.

[Note: The same author, in the same place.]

### 4

Concerning the year of this holy man’s death, there is, says Dionysius Petavius, profound disagreement among the ancient writers. Gregory of Tours, chapter 46, relates that he died during the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, at midnight, on what was regarded as Sunday. This year, Petavius adds, is 397. Yet in that year the Sunday letter was D; consequently November 11 fell on Wednesday, not Sunday.

Sigibert, whom the Ecclesiastical Annals follow, assigns the year 402. But in that year the letter was E, and November 11 fell on Tuesday. Therefore either he died in the year 400, when the Sunday letters were A C and November 11 fell on the first day of the week, or in 401, when it fell on the second day. If we accept the former, he died on the night preceding Sunday; if the latter is preferred, on the night following Sunday.

The year 401 is supported by Severus Sulpicius, who, in the dialogue cited above, writes—as we have seen—that Martin lived sixteen years after the consulship of Evodius, which fell in the year 386; the sixteenth year from that date is A.D. 401.

Gregory of Tours, however, in Book II, chapter 43, indicates the year 400 when he writes that Clovis died 112 years after Martin’s death; Clovis died in the year of Christ 511.

The most learned Dionysius Petavius sets out the matter in this way in *The Reckoning of Time*, Part II, chapter 13; nothing has been added to his conjectures by our own investigation.

But by that time it is entirely certain that Maximus the Tyrant had perished an evil death at Aquileia. For, defeated by Theodosius and Valentinian, he was stripped, as Prosper says in the Chronicle, of his royal garments, brought before the authorities, and condemned to death.

[Col. 1007A]

His son Victor was killed in Gaul by Arbogastes in the same year, a few days later. Andragathius, Petavius adds, threw himself into the sea.

[Note: *Chronological Reckoning*, Part I, Book VI, chapter 8.]

Idatius and the aforementioned Prosper assign their deaths to the consulship of Theodosius II and Cynegius, which, according to the Church’s tables, was the year of Christ 388.

# CHAPTER VII

## On the Councils of Toledo convened on account of the Priscillianists

### 1

Pursuing the order of events, we cannot pass over in silence the way in which, as the fourth century of the Church was drawing to a close, the Priscillian plague had spread so widely that not only ordinary people but also men formerly distinguished for piety and rank were corrupted by it.

When Catholic bishops were compelled to take notice of the evils of this heresy, their minds were so troubled that they had to assemble more than once. At first, as they say, they directed against the heresy and its followers a written sentence of condemnation. But where or when they assembled is difficult to determine.

Yet the bishops of Toledo themselves, nineteen Fathers, clearly indicate in the preface to their synod that before the Council of Toledo now extant the Spanish bishops had held another council, in these words:

> All these nineteen are the men who, in other proceedings also, directed a written sentence against the followers of Priscillian and against the heresy that he had constructed.

The Fathers of Toledo may have used this old Latin formula of expression to indicate a sentence of condemnation that was not merely pronounced orally, but issued publicly in writing.

Tillemont, Sirmond, Pagi, Severinus Binius, Aguirre, and all the others who, in discussing the Spanish ecclesiastical judgments of the fourth century, failed to say even a single word about that council—which the Fathers of Toledo themselves affirm that they had held shortly beforehand—paid no attention to this procedure of the Spanish bishops in delivering judicial sentences.

Indeed, according to everyone’s judgment, this ought especially to have been accomplished by the most recent writer, Cajetan Cenni, who proposed to discuss *The Judgments of the Church of Spain during the Fourth Century*.

[Note: Volume I, dissertation on the Antiquity of the Church of Spain, p. 147 and following.]

The same might be said of Franciscus Gervesius of Urgell, a priest, who last year published here in Rome a two-part dissertation in print on the history of the Priscillianists. But both distinguished and learned men had undertaken different purposes in writing, and could not have had so much leisure as to record every detail.

For D. Cajetan Cenni, while wielding his pen against Dupin and other theologians like him, was chiefly concerned with asserting and defending the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs over the Churches of the whole world. He was so intent upon this purpose that he either paid no attention to the Acts of the First Council of Toledo or entirely neglected to examine them.

The later writer, meanwhile, wished only to indicate, in an orderly method, the origin, growth, and destruction of the Priscillianists, omitting other matters that he judged irrelevant to his subject.

[Note: Franciscus Gervesius, *On the History of the Priscillianists*, second part, p. 71.]

### 2

Patruinus, therefore, together with the other eighteen Spanish bishops, taking into account the impious doctrines of Priscillian and his followers, proscribed these doctrines, as was just, in a sentence committed to writing. Then, after a few years had passed, as is probable, they wished to assemble again in the city of Toledo, so that they might define whatever seemed necessary for ecclesiastical discipline, for removing scandals and schism, and finally for establishing complete harmony.

Accordingly, while the presbyters were seated, the deacons standing by, and the others who were present gathered in council, Bishop Patruinus said:

> Since each of us has begun to do different things in our Churches, and from this so many scandals have arisen that they have reached the point of schism, if it pleases you, let us decide by common counsel what all bishops should follow in ordaining clerics.

But when I read the Acts and canons of this Council of Toledo and compare them with the letter that Pope Siricius sent to Himerius of Tarragona and the other bishops of Spain, I find that all these matters agree with one another so closely that those Fathers decreed that nothing else should be followed except what the supreme pontiff had already commanded them to observe by apostolic authority in 385, or what had long before been established at the Council of Nicaea concerning ordinations.

This fact indicates that the bishops of Spain always consulted the Roman See when issuing ecclesiastical judgments, and never dared depart from its regulations. It rightly fills us with wonder that the earlier writers mentioned above failed to notice or record such a great agreement and correspondence among these monuments.

We do not report this in order to injure these otherwise outstanding writers, who have rendered the literary world excellent service, but to increase the force and weight of the arguments they themselves bring against innovators.

### 3

Among ecclesiastical writers there is meanwhile considerable disagreement concerning the date of this First Council of Toledo, the various questions raised there, and its genuine Acts.

Baronius asserts above all that this council was not convened until the fourth year of the pontificate of Saint Innocent, namely A.D. 405. He was led to this conclusion because he believed that Innocent himself had written to the Fathers of this synod the letter bearing the following heading:

> Innocent to the bishops of the Council of Toledo.

Although the Acts of the Council of Toledo themselves contradict Baronius’s conjectures,

[Note: Baronius, volume V, on the year of Christ 405, p. 235.]

their inscription reads:

> Council of Toledo of nineteen bishops, held in the time of Anastasius, Honorius, and Arcadius, in the consulship of Stilicho, in the Spanish era 438, in the year of the Lord 400, with Bishop Patronus presiding, on the seventh day before the Ides of September.

Nevertheless, Baronius contends that an error had entered this inscription and that the Acts should be assigned not to Stilicho’s first consulship but to his second, which fell in the aforementioned year 405.

Baronius therefore relies so firmly upon that Innocentian letter that, while disregarding the quoted title and inscription of the Council of Toledo, he did not consider it necessary to establish the name of Patruinus the presiding bishop, the Spanish era, the pontificate of Anastasius, or the Christian date of the year 400.

But all the published and manuscript copies, as well as the letter itself of Pope Saint Innocent, reveal that this learned man was mistaken. For in that letter the holy pontiff speaks of a synod in which Gregory of Mérida had been substituted for Patruinus, and he orders that Gregory’s complaints be heard.

But at the Council of Toledo of which we are speaking, Patruinus was still alive; indeed, he presided over it, as the entire sequence of the Acts will itself show the reader.

On the contrary, in the relevant chapter of that letter Innocent wrote concerning Patruinus:

> Let the complaint, if there is one, of Gregory, bishop of Mérida, who was ordained in place of Patruinus, of venerable memory, also be heard; and if he has suffered an injustice contrary to his deserts, let vengeance be taken against those who envy another’s honor, lest thereafter the spirit of faction rise up against any good man.

[Note: This letter is found among the Innocentian letters, volume III of the General Councils, p. 41.]

These words clearly convict many Spanish writers of error. Some of them believed Patronus, or Patruinus, the presiding bishop of the Council of Toledo to have been a bishop of Toledo; others thought him to have been from Braga. For from these words it is evident that they had failed to consider the fact that he was bishop of Mérida, and that Gregory succeeded him five years after his death.

### 4

Our method of discussion must therefore be entirely different, since we judge that the Innocentian letter must be assigned not to the First Council of Toledo but to a second.

Sirmond, Pagi, Petavius, Severinus Binius, Tillemont, and other writers had already pointed this out, although they were led by different arguments and conjectures. Some of them more reasonably taught that the First Council of Toledo should be placed either in the year of Christ 399 or in the following year. We omit a fuller discussion of that matter, since a more difficult and obscure question remains for us to resolve: namely, the investigation of the circumstances that gave Patronus, or Patruinus, the occasion to convene this First Council of Toledo.

The surviving monuments of that age convince us that there were many serious causes. Since ecclesiastical writers have so far neglected to enumerate them, we are compelled to review them, lest we incur the charge of negligence or excessive indulgence.

We therefore wish it to be known and understood by all that the principal reason for holding that council in the city of Toledo was a very serious schism arising from the Priscillian heresy.

Whether it was the same schism that the Ithacian faction had provoked, or rather another one, cannot be established with sufficient clarity. One thing alone is equally well known and certain: the ecclesiastical affairs of the provinces of Spain had been so disturbed and undermined by that Priscillian plague—in doctrine, morals, and discipline—that even bishops and other ministers of the clerical order, departing from the regulations of the holy Fathers, followed whatever better suited their own interests.

There was such disagreement among them and such dissimilarity in their conduct that, without any discrimination, they received penitents; they promoted to the higher sacred orders men bound by marriage, or who kept concubines and fathered children; and they admitted bigamists, men devoted to secular military service, and slaves bound to their masters to ecclesiastical ministries.

Some freely communicated with sacrilegious persons and those struck by anathema. Others, having left their own Churches from which they had departed, were not compelled to return under penalty of deposition. Others, finally, abused either their familiarity with religious young women or the sacred Eucharistic assembly; they took the surviving wives of deceased bishops and presbyters as their wives, and fell into so many other crimes of no lesser importance that not only the sanctions of the canons, through the abuse of evil practices, but also the divine and apostolic commandments themselves were brought to ruin.

The following words from the first chapter, or canon, of that earlier council clearly indicate to us that another council had shortly before been held by the Lusitanian bishops. The Fathers of Toledo say:

> It has been decided that deacons, if they are either unmarried or chaste and of a continent life, are to be appointed to the ministry, even if they have wives; provided, however, that if any of them lived incontinent lives with their wives before the prohibition established by the Lusitanian bishops, they are not to be advanced to the honor of the presbyterate.

But let us pass over the decrees, or prohibitions, of this Lusitanian council. Its Acts are lacking to learned scholars, and even Cardinal Aguirre, the most diligent collector of Spanish materials, was unable to describe anything more substantial concerning them.

### 5

Let us now address the second cause of that Council of Toledo. More celebrated writers have discussed it, among them Tillemont and Paschasius Quesnellus. They create particular difficulties for us now, when we undertake to discuss Bishop Symphosius, Dictinius, and other men of the clerical order who, returning from the Priscillian heresy, were received into communion by the Fathers of the First Council of Toledo through the efforts of Ambrose and the Roman pontiff.

Since we find the crux of the entire controversy to lie in many matters, we must first set out various points so that doubts may more easily be distinguished from certainties and falsehoods from authentic facts.

First, Symphosius, together with eleven other bishops, subscribed the Council of Zaragoza in the year of the Lord 381 and pronounced an anathema against Priscillian and his doctrines, as is clear from the Acts of that council.

Yet, in truth, if we say that only one council was convened at Zaragoza, it will have to be believed that he withdrew from communion with the other Fathers, as we shall explain in its proper place. Symphosius therefore could not at that time have been certainly corrupted by that abominable plague.

Nor had he been publicly accused of this heresy in the year of Christ 385, when Priscillian and his associates were punished, by decree of the tyrant Maximus, either with death or with exile. For Severus Sulpicius, who describes the entire matter in Book II of his *History*, listed the names of the author of the heresy and his associates, but made no mention whatsoever of Symphosius.

Although we regard this kind of argument, drawn from a writer’s silence, as weak and of little weight in other matters, it nevertheless has the greatest force here, so that we should not suppose that Severus Sulpicius ought to be charged with carelessness or negligence. Would he have concealed the name of this most celebrated bishop when he listed the names of other men of the sacred order; when he recorded the lapse of Hyginus, or Idiginus, of Córdoba after the Council of Toledo; and when, for a full knowledge of these events, he expressly named even men and women of the lowest class?

From this follows a third point: Symphosius did not break into open heresy until after Priscillian’s death, when the Ithacian schism had grown more serious, the affairs of Spain had changed, and the tyrant Maximus had been killed.

Symphosius therefore could not have been regarded as a Priscillianist before the year of Christ 389. He would not have escaped the bodily punishment that the tyranny, lust, and greed of the imperial tribunes rigorously inflicted throughout the provinces of Spain upon Priscillian’s offspring, even employing capital penalties.

Thus, lest we suppose that Symphosius escaped the investigation of the imperial tribunes by a miracle, we must unquestionably admit that he and his son Dictinius, while the tyrant Maximus was still alive, at least outwardly pretended to hold the Catholic faith.

But when they learned that Maximus had died at Aquileia, Symphosius and Dictinius cast off the fear of the death they had anticipated. They began openly, in words and writings, to teach and spread more widely those Priscillian doctrines that until then they had perhaps pursued in secret.

### 6

Among others, Augustine also discusses the works of Dictinius in his book *Against Lying, to Consentius*. There, amid his discussion of the lies devised by the Priscillianists, he describes a book of Dictinius called *The Libra*—so named because, after twelve questions had been treated, it was explained as though by twelve unciae. Dictinius, it is understood, praised it so extravagantly that he declared such a *Libra*, containing dreadful blasphemies, more precious than many thousands of pounds of gold.

[Note: Augustine, *Against Lying, to Consentius*, chapter 5, volume VI of the edition of the Fathers by the Congregation of Saint Maur, p. 330. See therefore this book of Augustine, in which he discusses not only lying, which the Priscillianists always deliberately pursued, but also matters relating to Dictinius of Astorga, as the learned Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur noted there.]

In that book, then, Dictinius taught that religious people ought to lie in order to conceal their religion. Since he attempted to derive this kind of argument from the sacred Scriptures and their examples, Augustine, in order to safeguard the holiness and authority of the divine Scriptures, applied all the strength of his lofty wisdom to refuting and destroying that book, which was especially injurious to Catholic piety.

Our Leo likewise asserts that Dictinius published other treatises in defense and protection of the Priscillian heresy, as we ourselves shall say in its proper place.

### 7

Meanwhile, so that we do not depart too far from our purpose, we are entirely convinced that the manifest lapse of Symphosius and Dictinius must be placed no earlier than the fifth or sixth year of the pontificate of Siricius.

When their impiety became known to the other bishops of Spain and Lusitania, and was more fully confirmed by the works of Dictinius, which were in everyone’s hands, Catholics began to abstain from communion with them, and, as I believe, they were condemned and proscribed by anathema in some assembly of bishops.

But concerning so obscure a matter, on which the ancient writers preserved profound silence, we entirely refrain from speaking, lest we lapse into conjecture.

Turning instead to the Chronicle of Idatius, we shall briefly explain when Symphosius and Dictinius returned to communion with the Catholics.

[Note: Consult the second part of the dissertation recently printed in Rome by D. Franciscus Gervesius of Urgell, a priest. There he attacks Quesnellus for maintaining that the Acts of the Council of Toledo were spurious.]

### 8

Idatius, therefore, the most accurate historian of Spanish affairs, asserts that a certain Council of Toledo was held during the pontificate of Anastasius, and that there Symphosius, Dictinius, and other bishops of the province of Gallaecia abjured the Priscillian heresy and condemned it by signing a profession of faith with their own hands. The Roman Church has Bishop Anastasius as its thirty-seventh bishop.

> In the province of Carthaginensis, in the city of Toledo, a synod of bishops is convened. In its proceedings it is recorded that Symphosius, Dictinius, and other bishops of the province of Gallaecia with them, followers of Priscillian, condemned his most blasphemous heresy, together with its author, by subscribing their profession.

He further adds:

> Certain matters to be observed concerning Church discipline are also established, with Bishop Ortigius participating in the same council. He had been ordained at Celenis, but, driven out by factions because of the Catholic faith, he was living in exile.

It is certainly astonishing that neither ancient nor recent writers have paid attention to so celebrated a testimony, but that some of them, concerning the causes of the council, its date, and its proceedings, have adopted one opinion and others another.

The wonder is increased by the fact that the defenders of either opinion do not rely upon the same principles. Each indulges his own studies or, as though employing divination, departs farther from the truth than is proper in a matter of no small importance.

I do not dare contend here with Baronius or the collectors of the Councils. They devoted time and labor amid such an abundance of sacred monuments and such a wealth of Christian materials, collecting, arranging, and embellishing everything, though not in such a way that they could always examine the same materials with their own eyes and bring them into conformity with the rules of the best criticism.

My discussion rather concerns and presses those who published commentaries either on Baronius or on the councils themselves. Pagi, Severinus Binius, Cardinal Aguirre, Sirmond, Baluze, and other learned writers devoted to antiquity determined the legitimate date of the Council of Toledo, but passed over in silence the other matters conducted there.

Tillemont then proceeded to examine the reasons for convening the council and invented many things about Symphosius and Dictinius when he appealed to letters 52 and 56 of Saint Ambrose, although in them he produces not a single word about the Priscillianists or about those two bishops.

Cajetan Cenni undertook to illuminate the ecclesiastical history of the first eight centuries and proposed especially to discuss the forms of ecclesiastical judgment observed in the Spanish Church. But although this learned man barely touched upon the matters relating to the date of the Council of Toledo, he passed over everything else in complete silence, leaving to us and to others a broad field opened by the case of Dictinius and Symphosius for asserting and defending the authority of the pontifical Apostolic See.

Those who read Cenni’s preface will certainly judge that in this matter he did not depart at all from the purpose he had set himself.

# CHAPTER VIII

## To refute the false opinions of certain writers, especially Paschasius Quesnellus, the case of the bishops Symphosius and Dictinius is examined more precisely from ecclesiastical records.

1. Although up to this point I have devoted much attention to examining the Acts of the Councils of Zaragoza and Toledo that concern the case and condemnation of the Priscillianists, I nevertheless believe that I have accomplished nothing unless I apply my pen more precisely to describing those matters that appear to concern the bishops Symphosius and Dictinius, once tainted by the Priscillianist corruption. For several writers, including some of more recent times, have also spoken about these two bishops; among them Paschasius Quesnellus holds the foremost place. In preparing the works of Saint Leo the Great, he indulged his own partisan inclinations excessively and, guided by no concern for truth [Col. 1012B], followed only the pleasure of argumentation. He tried to turn the sequence of ecclesiastical events upside down, and either examined the monuments of antiquity carelessly or twisted them into a perverse meaning. Finally, after abolishing the ancient discipline of the Church, he labored to devise a new system of government and administration.

In his notes and observations on Letter 15 of Saint Leo the Great [Note: [Col. 1011D] Volume II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, in the notes and observations on Letter 15, p. 449 of my edition.], he investigates at greater length the case of the Priscillianists, the councils convened against them, and the time when Symphosius and Dictinius either fell into heresy or were received into the communion of the Church. Much that we have accepted as certain would collapse headlong if Quesnellus’s conjecture possessed any force. But that writer, proceeding chiefly by tentative conjecture, places the fall of both Symphosius and Dictinius before the Council of Zaragoza of 381 [231]. He says that both were accused of this heresy in the Council of Zaragoza of the year 381 against Priscillian, and that Symphosius is said to have evaded its judgment by withdrawing from the decision of the First Council of Toledo.

I believe that this first assertion of Quesnellus is wavering. For the definitive sentence read after the Acts of the First Council of Toledo, from which he certainly drew his opinion, is by no means consistent with these statements. It is asserted there that Symphosius had kept his mind suspended in the investigation of the truth, but that he had appeared before the Council of Zaragoza for only one day; afterward, by avoiding the sentence, he had refused to hear it when present [Note: [Col. 1012D] A copy of the definitive sentence translated from the proceedings, volume I of the Councils, p. 1478.]. But how these things can be reconciled with the history of the Priscillianists is entirely unclear to me. It is absolutely certain that the bishop Symphosius subscribed to the Council of Zaragoza of the year 381. The words cited must therefore refer to another council held at Zaragoza, as many have conjectured; but its Acts do not survive.

Moreover, what follows there seems to conflict with what precedes. For they say:

> It would be difficult for us to hear the persons just mentioned; nevertheless, by the letters of Ambrose of holy memory, which he had sent to us after that council, so that, if they condemned what they had wrongly done and fulfilled the conditions that the letter contained, we might reverently receive them into peace (add: the conditions that Pope Siricius of holy memory had recommended) . . . . It is established that we showed great patience.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] The reply of the bishops Ambrose and the others to Pope Siricius, volume II of the Councils, p. 1220.]

Quesnellus transferred this entire narrative into support of his own opinion, without considering at all whether or not it agreed with the other most certain monuments of Priscillianist history. If we recall what we transcribed above from Sulpicius Severus, we find in Ambrose a somewhat different manner of acting in the same case. He did not hear or receive Priscillian, Instantius, or the other men of this sect who had refused to appear before that Council of Zaragoza in 381, even though they had gone to Milan; nor did he send any letters to the Catholic bishops of Spain on behalf of receiving them.

How, then, could the same Ambrose have heard and received Symphosius after that same Council of Zaragoza, and prescribed conditions of penance for the bishop Symphosius, his son Dictinius, and others who were weakened by the same practices and vices?

2. There is still another point in the cited narrative that cannot in any way be reconciled with the time of the Council of Zaragoza. There the decrees of the holy pope Siricius concerning the reception of repentant heretics are praised. Nor could Ambrose himself lawfully prescribe any other conditions than those decreed by the authority of the supreme pontiff. For that most holy bishop of Milan, together with the other bishops of his province already assembled in council, recognized that no one legitimately excluded from the Church could enter it again unless the supreme Doorkeeper, the successor of Saint Peter, had opened the door to him [Col. 1013B].

For this reason, when Ambrose wrote to Siricius together with the others assembled in council, he began his letter as follows:

> We have recognized in the letters of Your Holiness the vigilance of a good shepherd, who carefully guards the door entrusted to you and, with devoted solicitude, watches over Christ’s fold, etc.

Thus, in adhering to these principles, Ambrose ought to have urged the bishops of Spain to receive Symphosius and Dictinius, as penitents, into reconciliation only under those conditions that the Apostolic See had already decreed. But since decrees of this sort of Siricius did not see the light until at least four years after that Council of Zaragoza—namely, in the year 385, on the third day before the Ides of February, when Arcadius and Bauto were consuls—I can never persuade myself that the case of Symphosius and Dictinius was examined in the Council of Zaragoza of 381, or that both withdrew from the judgment of those bishops.

For if we admit the accusation invented by Quesnellus and also the alleged withdrawal from the judgment of the Fathers of Zaragoza in 381 [Col. 1013C] [232], then Symphosius and Dictinius, as contumacious persons, necessarily ought to have been summoned to the Council of Bordeaux. If they had refused to attend it, they would have suffered the same punishment as Instantius and Priscillian. What more need be said? They would certainly not have escaped the sword of the tyrant Maximus, nor finally have remained unharmed by the fury of the imperial tribunals, as we observed shortly before.

Moreover, that Council of Bordeaux was convened in the same year, 385, and under the same consuls; and the silence of Sulpicius Severus proves that nothing was said there about the accusation or contumacy of Symphosius and Dictinius.

3. We must therefore assert, in order to guard against this sort of fiction, either that through the ignorance of copyists the following words slipped into the sentence:

> After the Council of Zaragoza, in which a sentence had been pronounced against certain persons, although Symphosius had been present for only one day, he afterward, by avoiding the sentence, refused to hear it when present;

or else that the words [Col. 1013D] must be referred to a council other than the one convened in the year 381. In our opinion, this other council could have been held only after the death of Priscillian, Instantius, and the others.

Cardinal Aguirre, led by various conjectures, asserts in volume II of the Councils of Spain that, besides that first Council of Zaragoza, another was held there in the year 383. We cannot agree with him, for we maintain that it was convened later. Yet although this matter is and appears to be wrapped in much darkness, the remaining statements appended to the cited copy of the definitive sentence provide considerable light for approaching the truth more closely.

For it is stated that Symphosius, with Saint Ambrose present and hearing, accepted and imposed the following conditions: he had already withdrawn, and would withdraw forever, from the recitation of those who were called martyrs; Dictinius, having obtained ecclesiastical peace, was to retain his place in the presbyterate and was not to receive an increase of honor, as Pope Siricius had decreed in his earlier letter concerning fallen penitents.

All the conjectures of those who maintain that Symphosius and his son Dictinius fell before the slaughter of the Priscillianists therefore plainly collapse. In recounting the events of that slaughter, Sulpicius Severus says that its effect was not merely that the heresy which had broken out under Priscillian’s leadership was left unrestrained, but that it was strengthened and spread more widely. For his followers, who had previously honored him as a holy man, afterward began to venerate him as a martyr. The bodies of those who had been killed were brought back to Spain, and their funerals were celebrated with great honors. Thus, after Priscillian and his associates had been put to death, the Catholic religion began to be defiled in a more impious and superstitious manner, since those whom the secular sword had killed for more serious crimes were regarded and venerated as true martyrs.

4. Because of the novelty of this event, ecclesiastical affairs were so disturbed that many bishops of holier life, detesting that kind of judgment and punishment above all, seemed almost to defend the cause of Priscillian. They refused communion to the authors of the executions—namely Ithacius and the others—pronounced anathema against them, and stripped them of their episcopal seats; for they abhorred so grave and bloody a crime [Col. 1014B].

From that schism among the Catholics, the Priscillianists seized the opportunity to spread their sect more and more. They claimed sacred honors for the bodies of those who had been killed as martyrs and introduced among themselves and into the Churches the impious custom of reciting their names, together with the memories of other martyrs, during the divine offices [Note: [Col. 1013D] Augustine, *Book Against Lying*, chapter 5.].

Symphosius fell into such madness, deceived and ensnared by many, as the copies of the definitive sentence reveal. Of the doctrines of Priscillian, Symphosius professed only two: first, that God was unbegotten; second, that there were two principles of visible things. Yet Symphosius never used any apocryphal books or the new sciences (*scientiae*) composed by Priscillian, although Dictinius nearly fell through several letters. He condemned all of those letters in his profession [Col. 1014C] [233], asked for correction, and sought pardon at that Council of Toledo.

All these facts carry such weight with us that no consideration can induce us to adopt Quesnellus’s opinion—namely, that Symphosius was accused in that Council of Zaragoza in 381 and, as a Priscillianist, withdrew from the judgment of those Fathers. He could scarcely have earned the gift of ecclesiastical reconciliation if he had remained obstinate in his contumacy for nineteen years, the interval between that Council and this Council of Toledo.

5. Let us now proceed to other matters, which are equally obscure and filled with many difficulties because of the loss of the ancient monuments. It is now generally agreed among both ancient and recent writers that Ambrose was appealed to as mediator of peace and reconciliation by Symphosius and the others who had fallen. It is not, however, equally clear in what year Ambrose received them when they had gone to Milan and gave them letters of communion, so that under certain prescribed and accepted conditions the Catholic bishops of Spain, who had separated themselves from communion with the fallen, might admit them to peace and ecclesiastical reconciliation.

What those letters of the holy Ambrose to the bishops of Spain contained cannot be understood from every angle, since they have perished through the injury of time. From the Acts alone of this Council of Toledo, convened in the year 400, it can be established that they had been read at an earlier Council of Toledo, to which Symphosius, Dictinius, and the other fallen men had been summoned but had refused to come. It can also be established that Ambrose had acted as mediator under these conditions: Symphosius was to abstain from the office of ordination, while Dictinius, his son, was to remain permanently in the rank of presbyter, so that he and the other clergy of equal or lower rank could never ascend to higher grades in the Church [Col. 1015A].

Yet two things occurred that were entirely opposed to peace and ecclesiastical reconciliation. First, all who had approached Ambrose refused, before the synod of the bishops of Spain, to condemn what they had wrongly done, although the same bishop of Milan, relying on the statutes of the Apostolic See, had prescribed that they should do so. Then they withdrew, contrary to their pledged word, from the state and purpose of penitents.

For when the bishop of Astorga had died, Symphosius raised his son Dictinius to that see, consecrated him bishop, and Dictinius himself, together with Symphosius, ordained as bishops many others in the province of Gallaecia whose faith had not been sufficiently tested. The whole sequence of these events is contained in that copy of the definitive sentence which was issued at the Council of Toledo in the year 400.

6. It remains, therefore, to investigate the date of the Council of Toledo at which, after the letters of Ambrose had been read, those penitents were to be admitted to the peace of reconciliation, but from which Symphosius and the others withdrew.

It is more probable that this council was held before the death of Ambrose. For Paulinus, in his *Life* of Ambrose, says that Ambrose survived the most Christian emperor Theodosius by almost three years; he also writes that Ambrose ceased to live on the very day of Holy Saturday. Petavius adds: “April 4, in the year of Christ 397, with Caesarius and Atticus as consuls.” Marcellinus, however, assigns his death to the following year, 398, with Honorius and Eutychianus as consuls.

That council, therefore, could not have been convened long before the death of Saint Ambrose. All nineteen of the bishops who sent a written sentence against the contumacious absentees were still alive in the year 400; this would have been difficult if many years had elapsed between that Council of Toledo and the present one.

Paschasius Quesnellus paid no attention at all to these points or to similar ones. Instead, in accordance with his custom and disposition, he relied on conjectures and distinguished several Councils of Toledo, placing the first between the Council of Zaragoza of 381 and the Council of Toledo of the year 400, without considering at all the Council of Bordeaux, the Council of Trier, or perhaps another Council of Zaragoza, all of which certainly preceded the Councils of Toledo [234]. But let us pass over these matters, lest, by contending with Quesnellus over trifles, we seem to have gone looking for a knot in a rush.

7. Let us therefore turn our discussion to the point at which we encounter Quesnellus’s more serious errors. We consider the most conspicuous of these to be the errors with which his notes and observations on Letter 15 of Saint Leo are filled.

In the earlier edition of these works, Paschasius Quesnellus had taught, as though from a tribunal, that Dictinius had been expelled from his episcopal see because of the Priscillianist heresy and that Turribius had later succeeded him. The following words, which he claimed to quote from the Chronicle of Hydatius, gave rise to this error:

> Turribius succeeded Dictinius, bishop of Astorga, who had been expelled because of the Priscillianist heresy that he professed, together with other bishops of the same sect.

We have also discovered that the monks of the congregation of Saint Maur fell into error [Note: [Col. 1015D] Volume VI of the Works of Augustine, p. 330.]. In the edition of the Works of Saint Augustine, perhaps placing excessive confidence in Quesnellus or in some other deceitful writer, they attributed this same testimony to the Chronicle of Hydatius, despite Augustine’s contrary statements, by which he asserts that Dictinius died among the Catholic bishops of the Church.

This attribution conflicts also with Ferrarius [Note: [Col. 1015D] Ferrarius, in the general catalogue of the saints, under June 2. See also the dissertation of Francesco Gervesio, [Col. 1016D] p. 65.], who wrote that Dictinius is found enrolled in the catalogue of the holy bishops of the Church of Astorga and that it had become customary in that Church to celebrate his memory every year on June 2.

8. Meanwhile, it would be unjust to deprive Paschasius Quesnellus of his due praise. In reading through the aforementioned Chronicle of Hydatius, he admits that in the first edition he had suffered a failure of memory or a hallucination. Having become wiser through reading that Chronicle, he retracted in a second edition what he had said, but in a very crafty manner.

Who could ever cease to wonder at the character of a man who, for as long as he lived, never wished to withdraw from the statements and writings he had produced against the articles of the Catholic faith? Yet no one is unaware that such was the method of the heretics and schismatics. Whenever, in historical or similar matters that contributed little or nothing to their system, they had at times failed through ignorance, carelessness, or arrogance, they later found it easy to withdraw their errors, correct them, and cover them with certain shadows of truth, so that they might secure a reputation for truthfulness and candor among their followers, whom they wished to deceive in the rules of faith and morals.

But Quesnellus did not wholly correct that error even in his final edition. He sincerely and almost under oath confessed that those words were absent from the Chronicle of Hydatius and had not been fabricated through his own efforts. Nevertheless, he judged that the fragment, with everything built upon it, should not be erased from the final edition, hoping that it might at some time appear before learned eyes during reading and be brought to the printer for insertion into this history.

Since he persisted in this opinion, he persuades himself that the fragment is not spurious but should rather be attributed to an unknown author. Like a dreamer, he imagines many false and fictitious things that undermine the histories of the Catholic Church and the Priscillianists, render the credibility and authority of the Councils of Toledo exceedingly suspect, and—what is more serious—mutilate, corrupt, and twist the Chronicle of Hydatius, which he himself praises highly, into an opposite meaning through his perverse interpretations.

But lest I seem to be inventing this judgment of mine, I shall immediately refute each of the points that Quesnellus brings forward.

[Col. 1016C] 9. First, I ask where this writer derives the claim that Dictinius was expelled from his see of Astorga before the year 400 and that Saint Turribius was immediately substituted for him. Again, I ask where he derives the claim that Dictinius himself later occupied his first see with the approval of the Fathers of Toledo. What kind of argument is this, which invents two bishops administering the same see, contrary to the canons of the Church [235]?

Hydatius says nothing of these matters in his Chronicle, nor do the Fathers of Toledo, who did not utter a single word about the restoration of Dictinius or the ordination of Turribius. Indeed, the Chronicle and the Acts of this council agree wonderfully with one another in indicating the indulgence by which Dictinius and the other repentant bishops were kindly permitted to remain in their sees. The sole precaution was that they were to abstain from initiating bishops, priests, and deacons until they had received letters of communion from the Roman pontiff Anastasius and from Simplicianus, bishop of Milan and successor to Ambrose.

The bishops of Toledo say:

> Symphosius, a religious old man, who, as we have written above, did what he did, shall remain in his Church, destined to be more cautious concerning those whom we shall restore to him; from there he shall await communion, from where previously he had received the hope of future peace. We have decreed that this is also to be observed by Dictinius and Antherius.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] Copy of the definitive sentence of the Council of Toledo; volume II, p. 1479.]

Since the Fathers of Toledo had decreed that Symphosius, Dictinius, and Antherius ought to remain in their Churches, did Quesnellus not invent the claim that Dictinius had been expelled from his see before that council and that Turribius had been substituted for him?

The Fathers say, “Let them remain,” not “Let them recover their sees,” as our annotator imagines. Anyone who pays even slight attention can see that these expressions do not mean the same thing.

It is therefore not to be believed that Turribius was ordained in the place of Dictinius while Dictinius was still alive. Rather, Dictinius himself remained in the Church of Astorga from the day of his consecration until the day of his death.

Accordingly, two of Quesnellus’s conjectures and suspicions immediately collapse as entirely feeble: either that two bishops administered the same Church at the same time, which is forbidden by the sacred canons, or that Turribius reached an extreme old age. He would certainly have reached such an age if his ordination had to be placed before the year 400, since he was still alive and fit to undertake the most arduous journeys in the year of Christ 447, under the pontificate of Leo the Great, as may be gathered from his letter, which we shall discuss in the following chapters.

But from the surviving monuments we can establish nothing certain about the ordination of Turribius. We know only from Augustine that his predecessor Dictinius died before the year 420. For when the holy Father wrote his book *Against Lying* to Consentius in that year, he indicated that Dictinius had departed this life in these words:

> To praise deceitfully the known life or the unknown reputation of the bishop Dictinius is still more tolerable, because he is thought to have been a Catholic and to have been corrected from that error.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Augustine, *Book Against Lying to Consentius*, chapter 3.]

10. Nor can we in any way be pressed by that genuine testimony of Hydatius in which, under Olympiad 306, he wrote:

> In the city of Astorga in Gallaecia, certain Manichaeans who had been concealed for several years were exposed through episcopal proceedings. These proceedings were sent by Hydatius and Turribius, who had heard them, to Antonius, bishop of Mérida.

Quesnellus asserts, I do not know by what reasoning, that the Priscillianists are designated there by the name “Manichaeans.” Yet [Col. 1017C] [236] Hydatius never customarily confuses Priscillianists with Manichaeans in his Chronicle, although both heresies were offshoots of the Gnostics.

For under Olympiad 24, after describing the death of Priscillian and his associates, he adds:

> Thereafter the heresy of the Priscillianists invaded Gallaecia.

Again, under Olympiad 294, when speaking of Ortigius, who had been ordained at Celenis, he adds:

> But while the Priscillianists were active, he was driven into exile by factions because of the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Hydatius, *Chronicle*, Olympiad 294.]

Hydatius used this same formula of speech when discussing the letter of Saint Leo the Great to Turribius of Astorga:

> Leo is the forty-third bishop presiding over the Roman Church. His writings against the Priscillianists were carried to the bishops of Seville by Pervincus, the deacon of Bishop Turribius.

When I considered all these things carefully, I could not easily subscribe to Quesnellus’s opinion—namely, that in the first cited passage of that Olympiad Hydatius intended to designate the Priscillianists by the name “Manichaeans.” For it is clear to us and to everyone else who reads that Chronicle that he called the heretics of each sect by their proper names.

Indeed, shortly afterward, when he begins speaking of a certain Pascentius, a Manichaean from the city of Rome who had fled from Astorga, he explicitly calls him a Manichaean. Bishop Antonius of Mérida captured him and, after hearing him, had him expelled from the province of Lusitania.

Who, however, would assert that this man was a Priscillianist, since the Priscillianist plague had never been active at Rome, and especially not in the time of Leo?

But even if it were freely granted that Hydatius there called such heretics Manichaeans, what follows from this? There is no doubt that Turribius succeeded Dictinius in the episcopate after Dictinius’s death. The cooperation of Turribius with Hydatius, bishop of the city of Lemica, in exposing the Manichaeans therefore does not prevent Dictinius from having remained seated on the throne of Astorga until the day of his death. It does not prove that he had been expelled from his see, nor finally that the Church had been administered by two bishops.

For when Dictinius died, either Zosimus or Boniface held the Roman see. But when Turribius and Hydatius proceeded against the hidden Manichaeans, Saint Leo was already exercising the pontificate, as Hydatius himself states in the cited Chronicle.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Council of Toledo at which Symphosius and Dictinius were received as penitents, and on the schism of Gallaecia that arose because of them. Quesnellus’s conjectures and arguments are examined and rejected.

1. Having left Quesnellus for a while at these beginnings, we have decided to proceed to certain other matters: namely, to the Acts of the Council of Toledo; to the sequence of other events carried out in this same case; and finally to that very serious schism that arose especially in the province of Gallaecia after certain envious persons, or persons excessively devoted to preserving ecclesiastical discipline at an inopportune time, learned that Symphosius, Dictinius, and other bishops and priests once infected by the Priscillianist plague had been received and absolved by the Fathers of Toledo.

First, as regards the cited Acts, anyone who turns his eyes to them as they were published by the collectors of councils will judge that they are now preserved in a very mutilated and imperfect form—something that no one has hitherto noticed. The specimen that follows, which we present, will make this clear.

We believe that no fault has entered the heading, unless perhaps it derives from the collectors, who call this the First Council of Toledo, although Patruinus asserts in his preface that another council had already been held there by the same nineteen bishops [237], as we also observed above.

In any case, Hydatius clearly indicated in his Chronicle, under Olympiad 294, that this council was assembled during the pontificate of Anastasius, while Honorius and Arcadius were emperors, at the time when Stilicho was first appointed consul.

The heading is then followed by the titles of the chapters, which contain only a brief summary of what was decreed there for restoring ecclesiastical discipline. But an error has already entered at this point. For the cited titles, also numbered with Roman numerals, indicate that twenty-one chapters [Col. 1018C] had been confirmed; yet the last, which was “On the rules of the Catholic faith against the Priscillianists,” is entirely missing.

The titles of the chapters are followed by the preface of the council. It first lists the names of the nineteen bishops who assembled in the Church of Toledo, without mentioning the Churches over which they presided. After their names had been faithfully recorded, Patruinus, bishop of Mérida and president of the assembly, delivered a serious and concise speech. He complained that ecclesiastical discipline had fallen into ruin in the provinces of Spain and that scandals among the clergy had spread so widely that they had produced a very serious schism.

Wishing to apply a remedy to these evils, Patruinus asked the common council to determine what all bishops ought to observe in ordaining clergy. Then the president himself, first of all, gave this opinion:

> For my part, I approve that the decrees first established by the Council of Nicaea be observed perpetually, and that no departure be made from them.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Copies of the professions made at the Council of Toledo against the sect of Priscillian exist in volume II of the Councils, p. 1477 of my edition.]

All the other bishops agreed with the opinion of Patruinus, judging in addition that those who dared to do anything other than what had been established should be subjected to the penalty of anathema.

2. The preface contains nothing beyond this. It is followed, as we said, by only twenty chapters or canons, which were especially appropriate to the troubles of those times: both for cleansing the plague of evils that was daily spreading more widely and for blocking its entrance, lest it spread farther and weaken Churches and Catholics that were still unharmed.

But since the twentieth chapter, which concerns the preparation of chrism by the bishop alone, is immediately followed by the subscriptions of the bishops, it must be deeply regretted that the other part of the proceedings of Toledo has been lost—or at least torn away from its original place—so that we do not now possess the material concerning the history of Priscillian in an integral and complete form, arranged as it was by the Fathers.

This serious loss could be repaired only in part from the Acts of another council. Its Fathers, perhaps assembling near the city of Toledo after Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others who were accused of Priscillianist heresy had died, wisely considered that they should trace the history of the Priscillianists further back and learn everything that had happened in this case, lest they judge rashly or precipitately concerning the heresy and schism that had run their course.

On this occasion, therefore, they ordered the earlier definitions of the Council of Toledo to be extracted from the complete proceedings and commanded them to be read publicly so that the entire new assembly might know them.

In what year, or on what occasion, copies of these proceedings were torn from their original places and read at another, later council cannot be determined, since the surviving monuments of the Church do not reveal it. This much, however, is beyond all doubt: the excerpts were torn from the genuine Acts after Symphosius and Dictinius, the bishops, and Comasius, the presbyter, had departed this life.

The following words of the later council sufficiently indicate this:

> After the council had already been held on the Kalends of September, on the third day before the Nones of September, after various investigations had then been conducted, on the eighth day before the Ides of September the professions of the lord Symphosius and the lord Dictinius, bishops of holy memory, and of the lord Comasius, then a presbyter and of holy memory, were extracted from the complete proceedings. They had made these professions, among others, at the Council of Toledo concerning the condemnation of Priscillian or his sect.

Who, then, could persuade himself that those bishops and that presbyter would have been called “of holy memory” in the council if they were still alive? For the life or death of bishops could not have been unknown to other bishops of the same province, metropolitan bishops, or national bishops. It must therefore be believed that they had died when copies of these professions were extracted and publicly read at a much later council.

3. Quesnellus suspected that the copies of these professions bore the marks of fabrication, and we do not think that Stephen Baluzius was free from the same suspicion. Yet no one [238] has adequately indicated where the conjecture of fabrication can or should be derived from.

For Quesnellus, who in his notes on Letter 15 of Saint Leo brought forward certain supposed signs that the professions had been fabricated, departed from the proper aim of argument and invented many false and weak claims. The first of these is his objection to calling Symphosius and Dictinius “bishops of holy memory.” If such a designation might otherwise be tolerated, he says, it appears absurd in the profession by which they renounce heresy [Note: [Col. 1019D] Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, p. 450.].

Are you so scrupulous, Quesnellus, that when men once stained by heretical corruption afterward become penitents, renounce their individual errors, and, reconciled with the Church, finally fall asleep in peace, you consider it wrong to call them men of holy memory [Col. 1019D]?

Surely the entire history of Christianity, the sacred diptychs, and the ancient records of the Churches would collapse, perish, and have to be judged full of fabrications. For in antiquity, just as today, that expression was used to indicate the ecclesiastical peace and communion in which those who had departed this life had died. They were not deprived of the designation “of holy memory” because of heresy or schism into which they had fallen, provided that they died as penitents and, having been absolved before the end of life, were restored to their former communion.

Indeed, after receiving the sacrament of reconciliation, such men were held in such honor that their names were offered to God at the altar. This is clear from canon 29 of the Council of Elvira, which provided that the names of those possessed by evil spirits were not to be recited in the sacred mysteries; or from canon 19 of the Council of Mérida, which commands priests:

> On each Sunday to offer sacrifice to God and, during Mass, before the altar, to recite the names of those by whom it is established that these Churches were built, or who appear or are known to have contributed something to these holy Churches, if they are living in the body; but if they have departed, or shall depart, from this light, their names are to be recited in their proper order with the faithful departed.

The learned Albaspinaeus and Ferdinand Mendoza prove in their notes and observations on the Council of Elvira that the recitation of these names was an indication of Catholic communion [Note: [Col. 1019D] Volume I of the General Councils.].

4. But Quesnellus adds that the words “of holy memory,” even if they may be regarded as tolerable, appear absurd in the profession in which they renounce their heresy. But here, reader, I ask you to notice with us the most serious lapse of our annotator Quesnellus’s negligence, and to examine carefully the text of those professions that were issued at the Council of Toledo against the sect of Priscillian, while also considering what belongs to the later council. For the entire beginning of that text concerns the Fathers of the later council, who, moved by their zeal to investigate the truth, say that they consulted the Acts of the Toletan synod and ordered that the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius, bishops “of holy memory,” be excerpted from the full proceedings  Thus those two words are entirely outside the professions themselves; they were used only by the notaries and Fathers of the later council to indicate the ecclesiastical peace and communion in which Symphosius and Dictinius had died.

Moreover, Quesnellus should not persuade himself that the notaries of this council transferred those professions here in their entirety, just as they stood in the original document. Numerous omissions by the same men sufficiently demonstrate this, as the words show: “After some intervening matter . . . the proceedings of that same period . . . Dictinius the bishop said: ‘Hear me.’” From this it is clear that they selected from the full proceedings of the Toletan synod only those things that were said, in testimony against the crimes and in denunciation of them, by Dictinius and Symphosius, and by Comasius. Since, therefore, the profession begins with the words, “Hear me, excellent priests,” there is no reason for Quesnellus to accuse it of fabrication, since all the preceding words—among them these two, “of holy memory”—must be attributed to the notary, as will be evident to readers.

[Note: [Col. 1019D] It is indeed astonishing that Quesnellus could have fallen into such negligence, since Saint Leo the Great, when receiving into communion bishops who had fallen at the Robber Council of Ephesus, orders the names of these men to be recited at the altar. See the final part of this volume, where we discuss this matter more fully. [Col. 1020D]]

5. Let us now examine another argument for fabrication, which Quesnellus places second. “Next,” he says, “they scarcely touched upon the errors of Priscillian and his followers, speaking only of the Son’s being unbegotten, of two principles, and of the consubstantiality of the soul with the Father; and they condemn these doctrines in such a way as to seem to be practising deception and reserving for themselves the freedom to explain their professions.” To lend strength and authority to this conjecture, he appeals to Saint Leo, from whose words he intends to prove that the profession was fabricated. “For, in the third place,” he immediately adds, “it is clear from Saint Leo’s [Col. 1020D] third chapter that they said, in some sense, that the Son was capable of being born. From the fifth, it is clear that they did not expressly maintain that God and man have one nature—something that Dictinius alone reproves in that profession” [Note: Quesnellus, vol. II of the works of Saint Leo, p. 450.].

Our learned critic insists on these and similar arguments in order to lead the reader into bad faith—namely, to believe that all those professions were fabricated as a deception. Such is Quesnellus’s reasoning. But are we really to believe that all these things are true? Or should we rather fear that this clever man, while investigating the frauds and fabrications of others with excessive anxiety, may himself have invented certain fictions with excessive freedom? [Col. 1021A]

That he grievously went astray is shown by those earlier words: “They scarcely touched upon the errors of Priscillian and his followers.” Why? Were they perhaps obliged to mention and confess errors into which they had never fallen? For the text under discussion does not contain a profession of faith made at the Council of Toledo by the repentant bishops and priests; it contains only a confession and renunciation of crimes. In it they were obliged to name from the errors of Priscillian only those to which they had adhered, and then to pronounce an anathema against Priscillian, their author, and against his other blasphemies. Since, therefore, among the doctrines of Priscillian they had dared to profess that God is unbegotten, that God and man have one substance, or that there are two principles, it was necessary expressly to confess only these things and to execrate them, without making themselves guilty of crimes that they had never committed.

6. That the text contains a confession and renunciation of crimes, not a profession of faith, is made perfectly clear by the words with which Dictinius, the first of all, burst forth in repentance: “Hear me, excellent priests; correct everything, because correction has been entrusted to you. For it is written: ‘To you the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given.’ But I ask you to open for us the keys of the kingdom, not the gates of hell.” Who could deny that these are the words of a man humbly doing penance and earnestly begging pardon and absolution?

After this he disclosed his crimes one by one: “If you deem it right, I place all these things before your eyes. In myself I condemn this, that I said,” and so forth. In the same manner he retracted everything that he had written, adding: “I also accuse and condemn all my presumption concerning my writings.” After taking an oath, Dictinius declared that he rejected everything with his whole heart, and he condemned what he had written against the faith.

Thus, considered in themselves, these things show no trace of interpolation, fraud, or fabrication—especially since those penitents, appearing before the synod, recited from a written document the profession of faith accepted from them by the Fathers; and, after pronouncing an anathema against all the books and doctrines of the heretics, especially those of Priscillian, they were absolved and received into communion, as we gather from the text of the definitive sentence.

7. It is moreover entirely false that they wished to practise deception or reserve for themselves the freedom to explain their professions. From where does the annotator infer this? These and similar words addressed to the Fathers of the council indicate the opposite: “I accuse and condemn all my presumption concerning my writings.” Or these: “God is my witness.” Or these: “Whatever I have written, I reject with my whole heart; except for the name of God, I anathematize everything; everything found to be contrary to the faith I condemn together with its author.”

Those penitents of whom we speak, therefore, were not so crafty and deceitful as to have intended to practise deception or to reserve for themselves the freedom to explain away what they had uttered against the faith—as Quesnellus himself and his followers, summoned to the judgment of the Apostolic See and condemned in our own age, have very audaciously attempted to do, all justice notwithstanding.

Finally, our annotator Quesnellus made a splendid fool of himself when, appealing to the statements of Saint Leo the Great, he introduced them as though they testified to the fabrication of that profession. According to Leo, the Priscillianists absolutely asserted that God is unbegotten. “Because,” says the holy Doctor, “they do not truly honor the Word made flesh, but pretend to honor him, fasting on the same day as well as on the Lord’s Day, which is the day of Christ’s Resurrection; and they do this precisely because they do not believe that Christ the Lord was born in the true nature of man, but wish what was not true to appear to have been displayed through some kind of illusion.”

Saint Leo himself also taught, in chapter 5, that the Priscillianists expressly maintained that God and man have one substance and nature, saying: “In the fifth chapter it is reported that the human soul is of divine substance and that the nature of our condition does not differ from the nature of its Creator” [Note: From the letter to Turibius of Astorga, chap. 4; from the same letter, chap. 5.].

When I had carefully considered these two points [Col. 1022A], I was easily led to believe either that Quesnellus had indulged his own studies with excessive confidence, or that, in preparing the works of Saint Leo, he had always read through them carelessly—just as we have repeatedly made plain in these dissertations.

## CHAPTER X. On the other bishops and clerics tainted with the Priscillianist stain who were condemned or absolved at the First Synod of Toledo

1. In the preceding chapter we explained, as briefly as we could, whatever needed to be said about Symphosius and Dictinius. We shall now say a few things about certain other bishops and clerics tainted with the same Priscillianist stain, who either communicated with Symphosius and Dictinius while they were still unrepentant and had not been absolved by the Church, or allowed themselves to be promoted by them to the ministry of the sacred orders.

First, therefore, our discussion turns to those who, having been canonically summoned to the synod, did not refuse to appear before the bishops. Among these Paternus had a place, as the copies of the definitive sentence of that council, transcribed from the proceedings, make clear. Before his ordination he knew and professed the errors of Priscillian. But after obtaining the see of Braga, he renounced all the poison of that heresy through reading the books of Saint Ambrose.

2.
