Although Symphosius had ordained him contrary to the ecclesiastical laws, the Fathers, exercising a certain indulgence, allowed him to retain his see, while also promising that they—the Fathers of that First Synod of Toledo—would receive him into fuller communion when the Apostolic See had replied.

They showed the same indulgence toward Isonius, who, having recently been baptized by Symphosius, was immediately promoted to the episcopate contrary to the ecclesiastical regulations. The council judged that he should not be removed from this rank, because he replied that he adhered to what he had professed in the present council.

After the Fathers of the synod had established these matters, they proceeded to examine the case of Vegentinus [Col. 1022C], who had formerly been made a bishop before the Council of Saragossa and had likewise condemned the books of Priscillian together with their author, as the Acts testify concerning the others. But afterward he had changed his faith and wished to adhere to the Priscillianists, and so had been deprived of sacred communion.

By common agreement it was decided that he too should be shown indulgence, although he may perhaps have committed a graver offense. They received him back into his former communion, imposing and preserving this condition: that he set down in writing a sincere profession of faith.

3. We understand, however, that the matter was handled differently in the case of Bishop Herena and his clerics. For that Herena, who had preferred to follow his clerics and who, voluntarily and without being questioned, had proclaimed Priscillian a Catholic and holy martyr, and who had himself declared to the end that he was a Catholic who had suffered persecution from the bishops—this man, I say, together with all his clerics and with the various bishops, namely Donatus, Acurius, and Aemilius, who had preferred to follow the fellowship of the lost, they decreed should be removed from the priesthood.

Nor should we suppose that so important a question was settled solely by these decrees and decisions. Other matters still remained, for which provision and a remedy had to be supplied—namely, for those who had come to the council from Galicia and had always remained in communion with Symphosius while that bishop was infected with the Priscillianist stain.

For their sake, therefore, we read that this decree was made: after receiving the form sent by the council, if they subscribed it, they too should remain in the expectation of heavenly peace, awaiting, on the same precedent, what the present pope, what Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and what the other priests of the Churches might write in reply.

But if any, acting more boldly, should reject the indulgence of this council and fail to give their subscription to the form that we have sent, they were not to retain the Churches they held, nor to communicate with those who, having returned from the synod [Col. 1023A] and made their professions, had returned to their own Churches.

It was also rightly and properly enacted that no one deprived of communion might hold gatherings in women’s houses or read the apocryphal writings that had been condemned, lest those who communicated with them should be held liable to the same impiety. In this matter they especially wished Catholic bishops to be admonished not to forget their burden and office: “For whoever receives them,” they say, “must certainly be held to a still more severe sentence.”

Finally, they declared that Ortygius, the Catholic bishop of Celenis, who had been wickedly expelled from his see before this council by the factions and violence of the Priscillianists, ought to return to his own Church. Idatius also reports this in his *Chronicle* when discussing this Council of Toledo.

4. These, then, are all the measures that those Fathers of Toledo established in the year 399 or 400 for the preservation of religion, the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline, the strengthening of peace, and the establishment of an enduring concord.

But since, in framing these decrees, the revered Fathers always added the condition that they would grant a fuller remission to the penitents when the Apostolic See had replied—as we read was done in the case of Vegentinus and Paternus: “We shall also receive them into our communion when the Apostolic See has replied”; or when the question concerned the Galician bishops who had always communicated with Symphosius, to whom it was said that they should await, on the same precedent, what the present pope, what Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and what the other priests of the Churches might write in reply; or, finally, in the case of the bishops Dictinius and Anterius, concerning whom they established that this rule should be observed: they were to be kept from the ministry of sacred ordination until communion was restored to them by the pope or by Saint Simplicianus—

when, I say, we encounter such formulas of speech employed by the Spanish councils, it follows that we see, as in a mirror, that the bishops of Spain showed such and so great a reverence and obedience toward the Apostolic See [Col. 1023C] and toward the Roman supreme pontiffs that they did not at all regard judgments issued synodically by themselves in the cases of repentant bishops and clerics as firm and valid unless they had been approved by the authority of that same Apostolic See.

5. Since I know that this truth is hateful to almost all heretics and other envious men, I must immediately take away the objection they might raise. They might say that the Fathers of Spain showed equal reverence to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and to the other priests, as they decreed both in the case of the Galician bishops who had always communicated with Symphosius and in the case of the bishops Dictinius and Anterius, in which latter case judgment was likewise reserved to Saint Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and to the Roman pontiff then in office.

“But this manner of proceeding,” they say, “diminishes the authority of the Roman pontiffs by equating it with the authority of other bishops, or at least by referring these cases to a Roman council for final resolution.” Thus, indeed, they babble; and those who wish to divide ecclesiastical unity could still babble in this way, striving with excessive anxiety to make the Roman pontiffs equal to all other bishops.

But it is evident that their labor in this and similar cases is futile. To pass over other matters, about which I have either already spoken or shall speak elsewhere [Note: See what we shall say in the final part of this work when discussing the Eutychian heresy.], it is perfectly clear that the Fathers of Toledo were not led by one and the same reason to decree that they should await the letters of Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and those of the pope who was then in office.

First of all, Ambrose, the predecessor of Simplicianus, had acted as an intermediary for the Fathers of Spain, so that Symphosius and Dictinius might be received under the conditions prescribed by Pope Siricius [Note: Quesnellus wrongly contends that this letter of Pope Siricius, and other similar letters, had no place in that code of canons which he assigned to the ancient usage of the Roman Church only by inventing stories. His arguments are completely overturned both by the conduct of Ambrose and Simplicianus of Milan and by the decree of the Fathers of Toledo that we have just explained. See Quesnellus’s dissertations 12 and following, vol. II of the works of Saint Leo. We shall say something about this code of canons edited by Quesnellus in our discussion of the Pelagians.].

Those Toletan Fathers complied with the wishes of Ambrose. But because he had already departed from this life and Simplicianus had ascended his throne, while Symphosius and Dictinius had not fulfilled the prescribed conditions but, through necessity or contempt, had rendered them void in defiance of the canonical sanctions, it was necessary for that Church to be informed of this most serious crime: the violation of the faith and the injury inflicted upon the sacred canons. For this offense they had contracted the defect of irregularity and bound themselves with tighter bonds of excommunication. That Church’s pastor had undertaken the office of mediator so that those penitents might be absolved.

Therefore, since Ambrose, their intercessor, had already acted before the Catholic bishops of Spain—not so that they might be absolved from any fault whatsoever, but only under those conditions [Col. 1024B] that Siricius, the supreme and universal pastor, had prescribed for those returning from heresy—they wrote concerning Symphosius: “From there he shall await communion, from where he previously received the hope of future peace. We have decreed that this shall also be observed in the case of Dictinius and Anterius.”

Although these words must refer both to the mediator and also to the supreme judge, they do not indicate that both possessed equal authority. For in this case Ambrose exercised only the vicarious, or delegated, power of the supreme pontiff, since he himself did not prescribe the conditions under which those penitents were to be received; rather, he indicated and advised that they should be received under the conditions prescribed by Pope Siricius.

We invent nothing by our own authority. The words of the same definitive sentence mean precisely this: “By the letters of Ambrose, of holy memory, which he had sent to us after that council, so that, if they condemned the things they had wrongly done and fulfilled the conditions contained in the letters, they might reverently return to peace”—add: “the conditions that Pope Siricius, of holy memory, had advised”—[Col. 1024C] and so forth. Why would the words “which Pope Siricius, of holy memory, had advised” be inserted there if Ambrose had written to the bishops of Spain on his own authority rather than on the authority of the Apostolic See?

For it was Siricius’s, not Ambrose’s, great decree to the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Baetica, Lusitania, and Galicia, as well as to those living in the neighboring provinces. In that decree he established that pardon should be granted to penitents, to bigamists, or to husbands of widows who had improperly entered the sacred ministry, on the condition that they should regard it as a great benefit if, deprived of all hope of promotion, they remained permanently in the order in which they were found.

Since, then, the Council of Toledo was chiefly dealing with the reception of fallen penitents through a dispensation from that Sirician decree, it was necessary to have recourse to no other authority than the Apostolic See, and the definitive sentence had to be awaited entirely from it. For Pope Siricius did not grant the right of dispensing with those impeded by such an irregularity to bishops of any rank or to councils [Col. 1024D]; he reserved it to himself and his successors, as the words immediately following that decree make clear:

“After this, the chief bishops of all the provinces shall know that, if we should thereafter believe that anyone of such persons has been admitted to the sacred orders, a suitable sentence must be issued by the Apostolic See both concerning his own status and concerning the status of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and to our prohibitions” [Note: We shall deal chiefly with dispensations of this kind reserved to the Roman See in our account of the history of the Eutychians, in the final part of this work, when we reconsider the letters of Saint Leo the Great concerning the reception of those who had fallen in the Ephesian Robbery.].

[Col. 1025A] 6. Now let the defenders of the new ecclesiastical discipline, who boldly attempt to attack the rights of the Apostolic See while striving to confine them within the narrowest limits, tell me, I ask, whether so serious, so sacred, and so decisive a decree—as they call it—could have been concealed by that national council. Or could those nineteen Fathers who assembled at the council, men distinguished in piety, learning, and integrity of life, have been unaware of or disregarded that decree?

Both alternatives are utterly improbable. For this decree—or prohibition, as Siricius calls it—against promoting to the episcopate or to the sacred orders persons formerly contaminated by heretical defilement had already been known to all the Churches of Spain for fourteen years, and by it not only clerics who desired promotion but also the bishops who ordained them were bound.

Since, therefore, Symphosius, Dictinius, Anterius, Vigentinus, and all the others who, as men enrolled in the clerical service, appeared before the synod in repentance had committed such crimes [Col. 1025B] as could be fully remitted only by the indulgence of the Apostolic See, the Fathers were obliged to appeal to it, expressly mentioning the Sirician prohibition.

We have already noted above, from the lists of the Roman consuls, that the aforesaid prohibition of Pope Siricius was issued on the third day before the Ides of February in the year in which Arcadius and Bautonius, or Baudonius, held the consulship—that is, in 385.

7. Nevertheless, we are astonished that no one has yet carefully examined a matter of such importance, so well suited to illuminate ecclesiastical history, by comparing the proceedings of this council with the preceding decrees and canons of Siricius.

Nor can this letter be accused of being an interpolation or rejected among the Isidorian forgeries. Dionysius Exiguus admitted it into his collection; it was also cited both by Charlemagne in the Aachen Capitularies of 789 and by Hincmar of Reims in his *Opusculum* 10—not to mention the *Pontifical Book*, in which we read: “He issued a decree concerning the whole Church,” although the authority of that book is suspected by many critics [Note: Franciscus Gervesius attributes this suspicion to Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana*, book II, chapter 7. But it should be believed that Tillemont did not consult him, especially since he does not refute that suspicion, as was necessary. *History of Priscillian*, after p. 68.].

Indeed, our astonishment is increased above all by Tillemont’s license. Having set himself another objective besides asserting and defending the rights of the Roman See, he encountered the words of the Council of Toledo enclosed in parentheses—namely, “add: which Pope Siricius, of holy memory, had advised”—and judged that they should be sent outside the text, considering them nothing but a completely spurious addition.

But the learned man is talking nonsense here. Relying on futile conjectures, he considers it wholly contrary to reason that Saint Ambrose should on that occasion have acted, whether at Siricius’s advice or as his legate, so that Symphosius and Dictinius might be absolved by the Fathers of Toledo. Good heavens! Tillemont ought not to have reasoned in this way, lest he appear to Quesnellus or to others to wish to diminish the rights of bishops and assert the legitimate rights of the Apostolic See.

Come, then: let the learned man not adhere to the prejudices of others, nor defend them [Col. 1025D] [Note: Tillemont, vol. VIII, note 13 on the Priscillianists, p. 124.]. But let him tell me, I ask, whether those Sirician decrees [Note: The response of the bishops, Ambrose to Pope Siricius, is found in vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 1229.] could have been unknown either to Ambrose or to the bishops of Spain, or whether they could have been entirely disregarded by them. To assert or even suspect either alternative is excessively improbable.

For Ambrose’s letters to Pope Siricius manifest with extraordinary clarity how great was the reverence and submission he exercised toward the Apostolic See, and how highly he praised the Roman pontiff for the heretics who had already been condemned. Therefore, when Ambrose was dealing with the Spanish bishops concerning the reception of the penitents Symphosius and Dictinius, he could not pass over the conditions already prescribed by Pope Siricius. Nor could the Spanish bishops hear, investigate, and judge the case of the penitents except under the same conditions contained in the Sirician statutes.

Accordingly, in the decree of the definitive sentence issued by the Fathers of Toledo, it was necessary to express the following words: “Nevertheless, by the letters of Ambrose, of holy memory . . . so that, if they condemned the things they had wrongly done and fulfilled the conditions contained in the letters, they might reverently return to peace”—add: “which Pope Siricius, of holy memory, had advised”—“and so forth.”

If they had failed to do this, they could have been accused and punished not only for irreverence but also for schism and contumacy.

But lest I seem finally to be wasting my efforts either on Tillemont alone or on the enemies of the Apostolic See, let us now leave aside the Sirician decrees and the copies of the proceedings of the Council of Toledo and turn to what happened after these proceedings in those same provinces of Spain.

## CHAPTER XI. On the serious schism that arose among the Spaniards after the Toletan synod

[Col. 1026B]

1. That a serious schism was soon afterward stirred up—whether because pardon had been granted to the repentant bishops and clerics who abhorred the heresy and writings of the Priscillianists, or because indulgence had been denied to the contumacious—is made perfectly clear by the letter of Pope Saint Innocent to the Council of Toledo.

The authors of this schism were the bishops of Baetica and Carthage. They were deeply offended that the Fathers of Toledo had received Symphosius, Dictinius, and the other bishops of Galicia into communion while retaining their honors and ranks, and they separated themselves from those who had received them.

Whether envy, jealousy, and the desire to quarrel drove the minds of the Baetican and Carthaginian bishops, or whether they opposed the Toletan decrees lest the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline be relaxed too far, I do not dare to determine. This alone is certain and established: within a short time the parties of the two factions spread so widely through those provinces that, through Hilary the bishop and Elpidius the presbyter, who fled to the Apostolic See, peace was violated, the order of discipline was thrown into confusion, and, contrary to the canons, with contempt for the order of the Fathers and neglect of the regulations, many things were committed in the usurpation of the Churches. These acts, with a stubborn and rabid spirit, nearly destroyed the priestly concord on which the entire stability of our Catholic faith rests.

Meanwhile, as such evils spread more widely from day to day, Anastasius, the supreme pontiff, departed from this life. In order that Hilary and Elpidius might apply the necessary remedy, they set out for Rome, when Pope Innocent was already holding the helm of the Apostolic See.

But to which year of Christ the arrival of these men in the City should be assigned, we have been unable to infer from any record of Christian or civil affairs. The chief reason is that the letter Saint Innocent wrote to the Toletan synod to restore the extremely disturbed condition of the Churches of Spain lacks a chronological indication or consular date.

It is nevertheless more probable that several years elapsed between the aforementioned Toletan synod and the date of this letter of Innocent. During that interval the schism, first stirred up in the provinces of Baetica and Carthage, could conveniently and opportunely have spread far and wide throughout all the regions of Spain.

This is suggested to us by the death of Patruinus, bishop of Mérida, who presided over the Toletan synod, and by the appointment and ordination of his successor Gregory; also by the serious injuries Gregory suffered after obtaining the see of Mérida. Saint Innocent ordered that Gregory’s honor be vindicated, so that thereafter the spirit of faction might not rise against any good man.

Nor do the words with which Innocent begins his letter indicate that Pope Innocent confronted this grave schism at the beginning of his pontificate. He writes:

“Frequently I was kept anxious by excessive concern over the dissension and schism of the Churches, which, as rumor reports, is spreading more widely through Spain day by day and advancing at an ever faster pace. For, although I had often heard reports of such great evils, I delayed bringing them a remedy until Hilary and Elpidius, who had already come to Rome from the more distant parts of Spain, faithfully set forth, with sorrow and groaning, the ruin from which the Church was suffering in the drawing up of the acts of the presbyterial consensus.”

Innocent himself acknowledged that the time had then arrived when correction could no longer be postponed and an appropriate remedy had to be provided. Therefore he decided to write to the bishops of the Toletan synod, to chastise them gently, to rebuke and censure those who, because of the communion of the Galicians with Symphosius and Dictinius [Col. 1027B], had withdrawn from the peace of all.

But there is not sufficient agreement among writers concerning which Toletan synod Saint Innocent addressed in his letters. Baronius and others believe that the holy pontiff wrote to the previously mentioned synod, or at least to the surviving bishops who had assembled for it.

Severinus Binius, however, together with certain other writers, relying on various conjectures, thinks that these letters must be referred to a new council also convened at Toledo. Vivarius likewise supports this view, believing that five Toletan assemblies were held within a short period.

Since the resolution of this question is subject to very serious difficulties, and the necessary records for resolving or even preventing them are lacking, we shall determine nothing at all.

2. Our discussion will therefore turn instead to the point from which Saint Innocent addressed the bishops of Toledo. No one will deny that the words he used to extinguish the fire of contention completely [Col. 1027C] are full of apostolic vigor.

He attacks the authors of the schism because, with each person determined to obtain whatever he wanted, they had made “an eternal orbit of evil” and a kind of circle from such contentiousness, whereas in such matters it is better for a good man to be defeated than, by an evil custom, to obtain the perverse purpose he once embraced [Note: Pope Innocent, letter 23, chapter 2. It is found in vol. III of the *Councils*, p. 38.].

Then, to inveigh more forcefully against the authors of the dissensions, Saint Innocent compares their irregular and furious movements with the Luciferian schism. In that earlier case, obstinacy had drawn a bishop away from the concord of those who, through a prudent conversion, had condemned the Arian heresy.

He asserts that those who refused to communicate with the converted Priscillianists were moved by precisely the same spirit, even though the Church, by the authority it possesses, had already received them into her embrace after accepting their initial confession and approving their repentance and conversion.

“This useful action,” he adds, “is shown to have displeased certain people”—namely, the bishops of Baetica and Carthage. But because he knew that the bishops mentioned were bursting with envy because the Church had received Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others with their honors [Col. 1027D] and offices, he first praises their purpose of unity and concord, which led them to condemn the perverse heresy; then he expresses something like astonishment that people could be found who disliked a correction rightly carried out.

“Why,” he asks shortly afterward, “did they grieve that Symphosius, Dictinius, and the others who had condemned the detestable heresy had then been received into the Catholic faith? Did they lose any of the honors they possessed? If this wounds and irritates anyone, let him read that the Apostle Peter, after his tears, was what he had been; let him consider that Thomas, after his doubt, lost nothing of his former merits.”

3. He therefore brought forward these and similar examples drawn from the sacred writings against the authors of the schism [Col. 1028A], whether to defend the earlier decrees of the Fathers of Toledo, to remove every suspicion of heretical contamination from Symphosius and Dictinius, or finally to settle all disagreements, draw everyone into the bond of unity and concord, and cause the Churches of Spain to begin to form one unconquerable body.

He addressed all of them generally in writing as though they were individuals. He then turned to particular scandals and ordered that Rufinus the bishop be rebuked. Rufinus, having been received among the penitents at the Toletan synod, had afterward usurped the rights of his metropolitan and had dared, against the will of the people and the order of discipline, to ordain a bishop in remote places and involve the Churches in scandals.

Next he ordered that the case of the bishops of Tarragona be examined. They had likewise complained that Minucius had been ordained bishop in the Church of Gerona.

But since both Rufinus and Minucius of Gerona had everywhere claimed for themselves the right of ordination in alien Churches, to the greatest injury of the metropolitans, Innocent says that, in accordance with the Nicene canons [Col. 1028B], “a sentence must be issued concerning such usurpation.” After a full investigation of the men ordained, he decrees that they are to be deprived of the priesthood, so that, because they were improperly made, they may understand that they cannot retain for long what they acquired through a faulty beginning [Note: Innocent, in the letter cited above, chapter 2.].

4. In the third chapter he attacks the fickleness of a certain Bishop John, who, although absent from the council, had approved its proceedings at Toledo through his vicar; and although the correction of Symphosius and Dictinius, who had returned from the synod, had seemed so credible to him that he was already in communion with them, nevertheless, as time passed, he withdrew from them and joined the open schism. He therefore orders that a fuller inquiry be conducted into him and others who appeared to have withdrawn from communion, and that, once detected, they be excommunicated if they refused to return to concord.

5. Of greater, or at least equal, importance are the matters he emphasizes concerning the illicit ordinations of clerics, regarding which ecclesiastical discipline seemed either to have collapsed [Col. 1028C] or to have been entirely abolished. Therefore, although—so as to prevent greater disturbances—he does not call such ordinations into question, since they had already been performed and because of the number of those requiring correction, but leaves them to God’s judgment, he nevertheless charges them, in these words, with the defects involved in four kinds of ordination:

“For how many of those who, after receiving the grace of baptism, engaged in forensic practice and acquired a stubborn determination to win their cases have we discovered to have been admitted to the priesthood? Rufinus and Gregorius are said to have belonged to this number. How many from military service, who, while obeying the authorities, necessarily carried out severe commands? How many from the municipal curial class, who, while obeying the authorities, did what was commanded them? How many who had celebrated entertainments and public spectacles for the people have attained the honor of the highest priesthood—although not one of all these ought even to have been admitted to the fellowship of the clerical order?”

Pope Innocent could therefore have taken action against all those impeded by the defects of irregularity, or at least ordered that a full inquiry be held in a new council and reported to the apostolic see [Col. 1028D]. But the holy pontiff showed clemency, granting the offenders pardon and remission. He preferred, therefore, that the rigor of sacred discipline be preserved only for the future:

“So that, if after this they attempt to enter either the ecclesiastical order or the priesthood itself contrary to the canonical regulations, they, together with those who created them, may be deprived of the order and honor in which they are found.”

6. So that observance of the Nicene canons would not thereafter be rashly neglected, and so that he would leave no one the arbitrary freedom to interpret them otherwise, he teaches that those who, after receiving baptism, served in the army or practiced law must be barred from every ministry at the altar. Nor, he says, can anyone from the curial class enter the ecclesiastical order if, after baptism, he has either worn the crown of public office, held what is called a priesthood, or celebrated public spectacles [Col. 1029A].

He orders that those be placed over the sacred ministries who were baptized either from early childhood and joined to the service of the elect, or, having been baptized as adults—or, if they were adults, when they had received God’s grace—immediately devoted themselves to the ecclesiastical orders.

Finally, with regard to those who have married twice, he permanently excludes them from the sacred orders. Relying on the Apostle’s words, “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy, chapter 3), he refutes the error of those who argued that a wife taken before baptism ought not to be counted, since everything is remitted in baptism. He declares, however, that this must be understood only of sins:

“Only sins, certainly, are remitted in baptism; the number of wives is not abolished.”

He attacks the authors of this mistaken opinion with many arguments, the last of which is as follows:

“For if a wife taken before baptism is not counted, neither can the children begotten by her be counted among one’s children. How absurd and unacceptable this is, your prudence will judge better.” [Note: [Col. 1029D] The same Innocent, cited letter 23, no. 6.]

[Col. 1029B] 7. This, then, was the manner in which Pope Innocent acted, entirely consistent with the statutes and policy of Siricius and his other predecessors. It clearly reveals what kind and what extent of authority the apostolic See of Saint Peter continually exercised in condemning and proscribing the heretics of the Churches throughout the Catholic world; in receiving penitents and relaxing canonical penalties through clemency; and, finally, whenever necessity demanded that new statutes issued by synods should acquire force.

It also reveals that the ancient and approved canons were interpreted correctly and faithfully, and that the depraved assertions of certain persons—containing errors in matters of faith, morals, and discipline—were proscribed. Did not Pope Innocent accomplish all these things in this single letter, without anyone daring to appeal to another judgment? Did Bishop Hilary and the presbyter Elpidius travel to Rome concerning the serious cases listed above merely to consult Innocent, and not so that the same pontiff might pronounce a definitive judgment, indeed one expressed in writing [Col. 1029C]?

Those reason very foolishly, not to say stupidly, who imagine that the Roman pontiffs acted in these and similar cases as consultants and teachers rather than as judges. All Catholics who flourished even in the earliest centuries of the Church never resisted the declarations of the Roman pontiffs; rather, with the utmost reverence of spirit, they both sought out and accepted their statutes as rules of faith and morals. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Among others, Sirmond adorned this letter of Pope Innocent with many learned notes, as may be seen in volume III of the Councils, p. m. 42.]

248 Meanwhile, it is more grievous to lament that those Innocentian statutes could not easily and fully be put into effect. For although, as we have said, the exact time at which the apostolic See issued them is unknown, there is nevertheless no doubt that they were sent to the bishops of Spain when the disasters brought by the Barbarians were already threatening.

# CHAPTER XII

As the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi laid waste Gaul and the Spains ever more widely, the affairs of the Catholic religion were brought entirely to ruin.

[Col. 1029D]

1. The decrees of the Council of Toledo, the decisions of Saint Innocent, Roman pontiff, and the other enactments of the Catholic bishops could not acquire sufficient force and effectiveness for the destruction and suppression of the Priscillianist heresy, because the civil situation suddenly changed and the barbarian peoples, through their invasions, plundered the provinces of Gaul and Spain.

For in the year 409, Gaul and Spain were overwhelmed by innumerable calamities when the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi, after ravaging Gaul, crossed the Pyrenees and occupied the Spains. Idatius is the authority for this in his Chronicle. Indeed, Petavius described, for the same year of Christ, how that kingdom was divided among various provinces and consequently endured the tyranny of various Barbarians, in these words:

“The Vandals and Suebi invade Gallaecia; the Alans, Lusitania and the province of Carthaginensis; the Silingi, who were another branch of the Vandals, invade Baetica.” [Note: [Col. 1030D] Petavius, *Rationarium Temporum*, part 1, book VI, chapter 10, p. 335.]

Amid such great calamities and disturbances of that kingdom, it was utterly impossible for the Catholic bishops to assemble in one body, vindicate the rights of the metropolitans, take action against the sacrilegious, remove the badly and illicitly ordained from the sacred ministries, and faithfully fulfill the other things that Pope Innocent I had ordered to be carried out, both for abolishing the schism and for overthrowing the Priscillianist heretics.

2. That those Barbarians, beyond the plundering and destruction of cities, attempted everything to erase the Catholic religion completely; that they destroyed churches, priests, and the relics of the holy martyrs wherever they could; and that they harassed the entire clerical host even unto death—these things are revealed by the most certain records.

To begin with, let us omit the Acts of the First Council of Braga, in which learned men have detected signs of interpolation. Nevertheless, it is entirely certain that at that time the Barbarians overthrew temples, killed Christ’s servants by the sword, profaned the memorials, bones, tombs, and cemeteries of the saints, shattered the power of the empire, and that everything suffered upheaval like straw before the face of the wind.

The author who constructed those Acts relates that Pancratianus, or Pancratius, perhaps the president of that pseudo-synod and bishop of the Church of Braga, actually began his preface in this way. If there is any fabrication here, it should by no means be referred to events carried out by the Barbarians in Spain at that time, but rather to the claim made there that the See of Braga held primacy over the bishops of Gallaecia and Lusitania. The metropolitan of Braga could not have claimed that right in 411 or 415, as Antonius Pagius noted more explicitly under the year of Christ 411.

In any case, that the Spains were then afflicted by these most serious evils is shown by [Col. 1030C] Orosius, a Spaniard who was not ignorant of his native affairs [Note: [Col. 1030D] Orosius, book VII, chapter 40], as well as by Cassiodorus and Prosper in their Chronicles, under the eighth consulship of Honorius and the third of Theodosius—an office that the Roman consular lists themselves show to have fallen in the year of Christ 409.

249 Augustine, however, described the wretched condition of those Churches in his former letter 180, now letter 228 in the latest edition of the Fathers by Saint Maur, addressed to Honoratus, chapter 5, saying:

“For no one can say that ministers ought to remain where there are no longer people whom they must serve. Thus the holy bishops fled from Spain, after their flocks had been partly scattered by flight, partly slaughtered, partly consumed by siege, and partly dispersed in captivity.”

Salvian, then bishop of Massilia, asserts that the foulest lusts of the Spaniards provided the occasion for this great destruction [Note: [Col. 1030D] Salvian, *On the Government of God*, book VII]. He also described in eight books the shameful and unrestrained depravity of every kind of lust among both men and women, propagated especially among the Aquitanians and Spaniards through the efforts and doctrines of the Priscillianists. Prosper of Aquitaine likewise lamented it in a very sad and mournful poem.

Accordingly, when he recounts the duration of the disaster and the fury of the Barbarians, he declares that it lasted ten years, and that the Vandals plundered those once flourishing regions with such force that they brought even rough and difficult places to destruction.

“Alas, through a decade of slaughter,

the land is laid low by Vandal and Gothic swords.

Neither castles set upon rocks, nor towns placed

on lofty mountains, nor cities beside level-flowing rivers

could overcome the Barbarian deceits and weapons of fury:

we all suffered the utmost.” [Col. 1031A]

3. I believe the manner in which that barbarian incursion and invasion occurred is sufficiently clear to all learned persons. No one, surely, is unaware that the Barbarians, having entered into an alliance with Attalus as friends and auxiliaries, were first received in the heart of Aquitaine; but that, suddenly despising Attalus and having become instruments of divine vengeance, they turned wholly to plunder and fires, as Paulinus the former consul also relates in his poem *Eucharisticus*.

This Paulinus, born of the noble consular family of the Ausonii, explains two matters concerning himself, the latter of which I judge to be remarkably relevant to our subject. First, he admits that he had dissented from Attalus, who had appointed him count and administrator of the largesses, although he already knew that this office could not possibly continue in any meaningful way. At that time, therefore, Paulinus, rejecting the cause of the tyrant Attalus, followed the Gothic party.

The second matter was worse: he lamented with bitter repentance something wrongly done. Baronius says that it was his having turned, as a Christian, toward doctrines rejected by the Church. Yet the following verses clearly indicate that he adhered to wicked doctrines for a full fifteen-year period, after which he recalls having been restored to Catholic communion:

“But afterward, when the fifth triennium had been completed,

when Easter returned at its appointed time,

I came back duly to your sacred altars,

O Christ God, and, by your mercy, received your sacraments with joy.”

Baronius investigates by what bonds of heresy Paulinus remained bound for so long and considers it probable that he had been contaminated and entangled by the shameful errors of the Priscillianists. For, as we have already seen from the testimony of Sulpicius Severus and others, distinguished men and women in that province had been seduced by Priscillian and his followers as they traveled to Rome. Divine vengeance rightly pursued them, since neither sacred, ecclesiastical, nor civil laws had retained any force for abolishing the indecencies of that heresy.

[Col. 1031C] 4. Indeed, even the emperors of the Christian world, in order to provide the best possible protection for the affairs of the Catholic faith, enacted various laws against this Priscillianist heresy shortly before the Vandals, Goths, Alans, and other Barbarians plundered Gaul and Spain.

For Honorius Augustus issued a law against them in the West, by which he ordered the praetorian prefect Senatori to investigate the Manichaeans and the Phrygians, or Priscillianists, diligently and to restrain them by various kinds of punishment. The Emperor Augustus Theodosius likewise took measures so that they might also be destroyed in the eastern regions; for, in two rescripts addressed to the praetorian prefect Antherius, he decreed every punishment short of death against the Montanists, Priscillianists, and Eunomians.

But what happened? Perhaps because the imperial officials, through negligence, wickedness, avarice, or false religion, failed to obey those laws, the Roman Empire was, through divine vengeance, utterly destroyed in those regions, and the peoples themselves—deprived of their property, liberty, or even life—paid the deserved penalties for their heresy [Col. 1031D] and their own indecencies.

5. Since such and so many disturbances were afflicting the civil and ecclesiastical affairs of the kingdoms of Spain and Gallaecia, those Innocentian statutes could in no way be put into effect, especially because the peoples of Spain and Gallaecia were then compelled to obey not merely one prince but two rulers infected with the Arian stain.

In Spain, Athaulphus was the first of the Gothic people to reign, in the year of Christ 414. But scarcely had one year of his rule been completed when he was killed by a certain Goth. Segericus succeeded him, but after six months he too was killed. Fourteen other Arian kings of the same stock succeeded them, down to the year 568.

In Galicia and Lusitania, princes of Suevic stock ruled. Their first was Hermericus, who, dying after thirty-two years of rule, was succeeded in 440 by Rechila. After spending only seven years in power, Rechila handed the reins of the kingdom to Recciar, who had been instructed in the Catholic religion and therefore allowed the holy bishops to settle ecclesiastical affairs without great difficulty.

# CHAPTER XIII

On Turribius, bishop of Astorga; his consultations with the apostolic See; and his actions for completely extinguishing the Priscillianist heresy and restoring ecclesiastical discipline.

1. The year of Christ 446 or 447 was then in progress when Turribius, bishop of the Church of Astorga in Galicia, as a modest calm began to dawn, attempted to purge the Priscillianist plague entirely and to proscribe, destroy, or wholly consume by fire the books of Dictinius and other apocryphal writings that were either kept in private houses or read openly in the Churches [Col. 1032B].

Since he was especially intent on these things, and following the example of the other Catholic Fathers, he immediately judged that no other judge and teacher should be appealed to than Saint Leo, Roman pontiff, to whom he sent his writings. Turribius himself entrusted his deacon Pervincius with traveling to Rome and carrying such writings to Saint Leo.

Leo himself indicated at the beginning of his fifteenth letter what kinds of writings Turribius had sent to the apostolic See. He said that from the wording of the letter, the sequence of the memorandum, and the text of the little book, he had learned that the foulest mire of the Priscillianists had again grown warm in those regions.

But Turribius’s writings, from which we could more easily have understood the sorrowful condition of the Churches of Galicia and Spain, have long since perished. Some compensation for this grievous loss can be made only through the letters circulated under the name of Turribius of Astorga to the bishops Idatius and Ceponius [Col. 1032C], together with the genuine and celebrated letter that Leo wrote back to Turribius in this matter. We must therefore focus on both at present if we are to complete the history of the Priscillianists that we have undertaken to illuminate.

2. Turribius himself—or the person who assumes Turribius’s role—certainly described the deplorable condition of those Churches in that letter, when he discussed the burdensome and unpleasant journey that he had always undertaken amid twofold toil and tearful necessities [Col. 1032D].

He asserts that he had received some benefit from visiting unknown places and learning what he had not known: by this progress of mind we are enlarged, since we often come to recognize that what had seemed best among us had been rendered corrupt and utterly bad, and is restored to us according to a better understanding.

He immediately makes clear, however, in what matters Turribius became more instructed through his travels, so that he could easily recognize what had been rendered corrupt and utterly bad although it had once seemed best to him. He does this by commending above all the unity that he found in all the Churches of the provinces through which he had traveled.

There, he says, all communicated with one another in complete harmony of spirit and without any schism. After all the sects of error had been condemned, “I found that one and the same understanding of the Catholic faith was held, proceeding from the purest fountain of truth—a stream that was not split into divergent channels and scattered into many branches, so as to dissolve the level fields into muddy abysses that obstruct the straight path of faith.” [Note: [Col. 1031] Turribius of Astorga, letter to Idatius and Ceponius, chapters 1–2.]

By this account he wished to recall to the minds of those bishops nothing other than the need to promote this Catholic unity and communion. For the destructive poison of the Priscillianist heresy had long since driven out and banished this unity from the Churches of Spain and Galicia.

Therefore, to kindle in Idatius and Ceponius a zeal for religion, he sets before them the examples of the Churches he had visited. Their pastors, he says, restored those infected by the poison of corrupt doctrines through correction to the embrace of their devout mother, but expelled the obstinate from participation in the sacred inheritance as abortive offspring and illegitimate descendants [Col. 1033A].

3. After a long period of years, Turribius returned to Asturias and was cruelly tormented when he observed that traditions long before condemned by the Church, which he had believed to have been entirely abolished in those regions, still persisted with greater obstinacy.

Indeed, his anguish increased when he learned that, according to each person’s inclination and perverse will, corrupt doctrines were sprouting like multiple hydra heads. Some supplied the ancient error of the heretics with arguments drawn from their own blasphemies; others professed Priscillian’s teaching in its entirety; still others, having renounced only some of the principal doctrines that clearly opposed Catholic truth while retaining certain others, appeared to remain attached to the rest.

Turribius himself asserts that all these things had grown more freely here and there throughout Spain and Galicia, while synodal assemblies and decrees had ceased [Col. 1033B]. Finally, he lamented as the gravest and most impious crime of all that people gathered at one altar while holding different understandings of the faith.

When Turribius reviewed all these matters, he was moved solely by love for his country, not by rash presumption, from which he was entirely free. Therefore, pursuing Catholic truth with zeal, he compared the local heretics to thieves and adulterers. Having removed the truth from the sacred doctrines, they blasphemed the authority of the divine word; and, so that they might more easily corrupt it by adulteration, they rejected the canonical and evangelical Scriptures and devoted themselves exclusively to reading apocryphal books.

So that he would not become burdensome and vexatious to the bishops to whom he was writing, and would not appear to exercise a teaching authority over them, he declares that, in the service of both prudence and zeal, he offered them no exhortation based on authority at all, but only instruction in the form of a suggestion [Col. 1033C]. He considered himself guilty before God of a more serious crime if he had remained silent.

4. Such, then, was Turribius’s moderation of spirit toward his fellow bishops; such was his zeal in describing the treachery of the heretics. Whenever a Catholic reproached their doctrines and teaching with somewhat greater firmness, they immediately evaded the disputes of their encounters, denying everything and attempting to conceal treachery by treachery.

To prevent them from doing this any longer, he describes and exposes their deceitful and crafty practices: either they preferred apocryphal Scriptures to the canonical books; or they venerated hidden and secret traditions, expressed in no books, not even apocryphal ones, through which they falsely claimed that the holy Apostles had spoken; or, finally, they secretly kept certain other books among themselves, accessible, as they themselves said, only to the perfect.

5. He indicated shortly afterward which apocryphal books the Priscillianists especially used, discussing in particular the Acts circulated under the name of Saint Thomas [Col. 1033D]. He observed that one thing above all others in them deserved notice and condemnation: Thomas, he says, does not baptize with water, as the Lord’s preaching teaches, but with oil. The Manichaeans, together with their standard-bearer Mani, followed this corrupt practice.

This universally execrable offspring, condemned in every part of the world, therefore either accepted only apocryphal books or used certain other writings filled with apocryphal fables, as became known from their own confession.

But other books of the same kind were being worn out in the hands of the Priscillianists: the Acts called those of Saint Andrew; others said to be those of Saint John, which Lucius had once composed with sacrilegious mouth; and, finally, that volume, a monstrosity of every blasphemy, improperly entitled *The Memorial of the Apostles*.

In it, pseudo-apostles and pseudo-prophets falsely attributed the Lord’s teaching to themselves in order to give great authority to their perversity. The entire law of the Old Testament was overthrown, together with everything divinely revealed to Saint Moses concerning the various natures of creation and the Creator’s divinity [Col. 1034A].

6. When Turribius found Galicia and Spain especially undermined by such great hardships and such impious and sacrilegious errors, he stirred the minds of the other holy bishops to seek the remedy that was most consistent with the divine and ecclesiastical laws.

For this reason, in order to achieve it more easily, he composed a work in which he arranged the testimonies full of blasphemies found in the writings of the Priscillianists and answered them, as far as he could, according to the character of their meaning.

We think that he first arranged for this work to be circulated publicly, so that thereafter no one might say, as though unaware of the facts, that he simply possessed or read such books. Then he submitted it to the judgment, examination, and assessment of Idatius and Ceponius, so that they might weigh everything carefully and, together with the other brothers associated with them, take care to cut out and abolish whatever unmistakably appeared contrary to truth and faith [Col. 1034B].

7. A learned and educated man, Stephen Baluzius, now presents us with a difficulty, questioning the authenticity and authority of this letter of Turribius. For his observations on the Council of Astorga, held in the year of Christ 446, reveal that he detected several signs of interpolation in it.

He admitted that he drew the entire suspicion of fabrication from the words of Saint Leo. For the supreme pontiff, writing back to Turribius of Astorga, ordered:

“Let at least the bishops of Galicia assemble; our brothers Idatius and Ceponius will take charge of gathering them.”

Baluzius adds the following observation:

“There is serious reason to suspect that that letter of Leo suggested to some impostor the idea of fabricating the letter said to have been written by Turribius to Idatius and Ceponius; therefore I refrain from accepting it.”

Opposing Baluzius, however, the most learned Cardinal de Aguirre maintained that the celebrated letter must be attributed to Turribius of Astorga [Col. 1034C]. To remove the objection raised by that learned collector of the Councils, he first excuses Baluzius as one who was aware of the countless fables preserved in ancient pseudo-chronicles and who, on that account, rejected whatever was reported in them unless it rested upon or was confirmed by some certain and solid testimony.

Second, he says that the letter of Turribius under discussion was not devised and fabricated by those tricksters who distorted Hispanic history with so many inventions and absurdities, but that it is found in a manuscript codex approximately six hundred years old, and so forth.

For a long time, however, my mind remained suspended between these two contrary opinions, uncertain which one to follow. The antiquity of the codex, which Cardinal Aguirre valued so highly, does not eliminate every suspicion that the celebrated letter may have been fabricated by some ancient impostor.

Nor does it prove anything that King Philip II, in the time of Ambrosius Morales, transferred that codex from the ancient library of the famous monastery of Saint Emilianus to a newer one at Saint Laurence in the Escorial, approximately twenty years before the fabrications of Dexter, Maximus, and Julian [Col. 1034D].

What then? Were there not earlier impostors who could have fabricated it many centuries ago? All the records of the Church, as well as this letter under discussion, clearly show that, after the Apostles had died, many volumes were fabricated by impostors even under the name of sacred Scriptures.

The antiquity of that codex, therefore, would prove nothing unless we suppose that an earlier impostor, thoroughly informed about the affairs of Spain and Galicia, fabricated this single letter of Turribius sometime toward the end of the eleventh century or at the beginning of the twelfth.

8. Nevertheless, I do not readily accept Baluzius’s opinion, and I maintain that Cardinal Aguirre’s arguments are wholly weak. If I were to undertake here a discussion of the signs of fabrication found in the letter, I could admit that many things in its reading offended me—things noted neither by Stephen Baluzius, nor by the collector of Spain’s Councils himself, nor by anyone else [Col. 1035A].

One such feature is its opening, where Turribius speaks of himself as coming from a distant journey in which he had spent a long period of years. Who could suppose that this was true of a bishop supremely devoted to preserving ecclesiastical discipline?

With so many calamities pressing upon him, under the indignation of God and the Church, are we to believe that this excellent shepherd wished or was able to abandon his flock? No one will persuade me of this, especially since Saint Leo, to whom Turribius had laid bare the deplorable condition of those Churches, praises him highly for having always remained vigilant and for diligently devoting the service of pastoral duty to the Lord’s flock.

Certainly, if Turribius had undertaken his travels solely of his own choice, the holy pontiff ought rather to have criticized and reproved him for fleeing from the Lord’s flock and exposing the sheep entrusted to him to be torn apart by wolves.

He could have escaped such and similar reproaches only for two reasons: one would have been exile, if Turribius had been driven into it by the actions of Arian princes; the other would have been that he had traveled abroad for many years before being raised to the episcopate.

But neither explanation holds. If the fury of the Arian princes had blazed against him and he had suffered exile, he would have emphasized the hardships and inconveniences of exile, not of travel. Moreover, after a sentence had been pronounced against him, another intruder would already have occupied the Asturican throne, as the Arians themselves had been accustomed to do in the preceding fourth century.

What if Turribius omitted to mention this punishment of exile in his letter to the other two fellow bishops of Galicia because it was already well known to them? Would he then perhaps also have omitted to report it in his letter to Leo? Or would Leo himself, as a sign of paternal compassion, have failed to mention it in his reply?

What more need be said? Would Idatius in his Chronicle, though he described other disasters suffered by bishops, have remained silent about this one exile of Turribius? [Col. 1035C] Finally, why would all the other writers of Spain and Galicia have maintained such profound silence concerning a matter of such great importance? We must not, therefore, resort to this escape.

9. Nor could Turribius have undertaken such a long journey lasting several years before being elevated to the episcopate. For after the death of Dictinius, which occurred before the year of Christ 420, as we saw from Augustine, Turribius had already obtained the Church of Astorga [254].

At that time, however, the Catholic Church was governed not by Leo the Great but by Zosimus or Boniface. Therefore, since at the beginning of the second chapter of that letter Turribius speaks of himself as a man who had just arrived from a journey, it follows that what Baluzius and Aguirre report from the Chronicle of Idatius concerning the Council of Astorga cannot be assigned to Leo’s time, namely the year 446.

If, finally, we imagine that Turribius did not write to Idatius and [Col. 1035D] Ceponius immediately after obtaining the episcopate, nor appeal to Leo as supreme teacher and judge, but that the entire period of twenty-seven or twenty-eight years had elapsed, Turribius would immediately be open to blame for having delayed so long, while those grave evils were again increasing, to seek and bring forward a remedy, and for having wished to travel abroad after abandoning his own Church contrary to the statutes of the sacred canons.

We must therefore admit that the letter contains at least certain obscurities that cannot in any way be reconciled or made compatible with Turribius’s piety and sanctity, with ecclesiastical discipline, the sacred canons, and Christian affairs.

This is certainly what I concluded after reading the letter several times. I also encountered other features in it that at least bear the odor of a writer’s carelessness.

Such, it seemed to me, are the words found in chapter 4, “so that they may do this no longer until the end,” in which no genuine meaning can be established according to the rules of grammatical syntax; and the repetition in the following chapter 5 of the same account concerning the apocryphal Acts of Saint Thomas [Col. 1036A], along with other matters of the same kind. These certainly either demonstrate the writer’s negligence or greatly enhance the excellence of the codex in which that letter, found under Turribius’s name, was faithfully recovered.

10. Yet although many things shine forth in the letter that diverge greatly from truth, or at least from probability, I hesitate to judge that it should be rejected or regarded as spurious.

Indeed, in collecting and embellishing the works of Saint Leo the Great, just as Quesnellus incorporated it into his edition, so I consider it necessary to preserve it in another new edition that I have decided to prepare after these *Exercises*.

For this reason I have done my utmost to furnish it with various annotations drawn from highly approved writers, so that the friendly reader may guard against the equivocations and obscure meanings with which it abounds.

Meanwhile, before removing my hand from the page, I consider the material described there concerning the condition of the Churches of Galicia and Spain abundantly worthy of approval [Col. 1036B]. For it corresponds most fully with what appears in letter 15 of Saint Leo the Great, concerning whose authenticity and authority it would be a grave crime even to entertain suspicion.

Both ancient and old manuscript copies contain it as a genuine offspring of the holy pontiff; the Fathers of the Council of Braga and the Fourth General Council attributed it to Saint Leo; and all writers, without anyone dissenting, testified to this same truth. They thus opened a very broad field for editors to print it, without any remaining scruple, in all published copies.

255 # CHAPTER XIV

On letter 15 of Saint Leo the Great, written to Turribius of Astorga on the occasion of the Priscillianist heresy; and a new fragment concerning the canonical Scriptures, recovered from a codex of the Palatine Vatican Library.

1. Supported, then, by so many and such great preceding testimonies, and since we could have no serious doubt about the truth and authority of letter 15 of Saint Leo the Great, we took care only to purge it of errors, if any had crept into it [Col. 1036C].

For the successful completion of this labor, we did not lack the necessary resources. Besides various very ancient Vatican codices, which we examined with our own eyes; besides the Grimanian archetype preserved in Paris, according to whose readings Paschasius Quesnellus especially boasts of having prepared his edition, and which we ourselves, aided by friends, carefully transcribed; we also collated the same letter with the Vallicellian copy and with two Florentine exemplars, so that, with the divine Name at some point lending its aid, all the works of Leo might emerge from new presses purer, clearer, and more complete.

But now let us return to our subject.

Therefore, the praised letter of the holy pontiff to the bishop of Asturica contains sixteen chapters, because Turribius had proposed that as many matters should be discussed and defined by Leo. This is implied by these words: “Since, therefore, your Beloved, with as much faithful diligence as possible, comprised the formerly condemned opinions in sixteen chapters.” But a very ancient Vatican exemplar, together with the Grimani codex, proves that it should be read as seventeen. This is further confirmed by the division of the chapters itself, which at the end presents the following Roman numeral and title:

**Chapter XVII. Whether Christ’s flesh truly rested in the tomb.**

Those who are accustomed to commend, beyond what is reasonable, Quesnellus’s zeal, labor, and diligence in embellishing and correcting the works of the divine Leo should, I ask, take notice of the kind of negligence into which he fell. Let them see whether this provides evidence that he adopted the Grimani codex as a touchstone for establishing, with scrupulous fidelity, the readings of Leo’s text. Let them say whether he carefully examined the works of the holy pontiff who, in a poorly arranged summary, supplies only sixteen chapter titles, omitting the last, although the letter itself is divided into seventeen chapters, the final one of which [Col. 1037A] also has its own title—a title entirely absent from the preceding summary.

But this matter will be discussed more carefully in its proper place, as will the question of another very ancient Vatican Palatine exemplar of this letter, which presents us with a hitherto unpublished fragment concerning the canonical Scriptures. Whether this fragment should be attributed to Leo or not, we shall also pursue elsewhere, since it appears to concern chiefly the rite and order that the Roman Church of the holy Peter was accustomed to observe throughout the year in reading the divine and canonical Scriptures. For the present, therefore, let our discourse be permitted to range over the broad field of this Leonine letter, as it has until now appeared in all the published copies. Since the letter is everywhere filled with the most certain and abundant testimony, we shall more easily gather from it both the sources and errors of the Priscillian heresy and, at the same time, discern more clearly the authority of the apostolic see and its irrevocable judgment in refuting them.

### 2.

Saint Leo immediately taught, at the beginning of that letter, that the doctrines of Priscillian had been more wicked than the errors of all the preceding heretics and had drawn from them every poisonous contagion of impiety. He calls the sect of the Priscillianists “the foulest cesspool of all heresies.” He adds that the Priscillianists had plunged themselves so deeply into the darkness of paganism that, by employing the empty falsehoods of astrologers and the profane secrets of magical art, they placed both the faith of religion and the rule of morals under the power of demons and the influence of the stars.

Leo recounted these and other similar doctrines of that utterly detestable sect, and recalled to mind the zeal of the ancient Fathers who flourished in the preceding century and who, in councils, employed every effort to drive such impious madness from the whole Church. He then relates how the rulers of the age—namely, the tyrant Maximus—so intensely detested this sacrilegious insanity that they struck down its author, together with many of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws.

[Col. 1037C] This first kind and example of bloody judgment, by which the rulers and magistrates of the age sometimes proceeded against obstinate heretics, has hitherto been capable of greatly troubling the minds of ancient and modern writers. “I foresaw,” says Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 3, article 17, “that heretics might abuse this history, both against the office of the holy Inquisition, which delivers or leaves obstinate heretics to secular magistrates to be punished with the ultimate penalty, and against the princes and magistrates themselves, who, by their own right, inflict even capital punishment upon them.”

In the same place Father Natalis intends to defend from every censure a proposition that had slipped into an earlier edition of his work: “No Catholic has said that emperors and kings cannot proceed against a heretic even by capital punishment.” In his later edition he then explained the sense in which he had made this statement and labored to assert this power of the rulers of the age. His annotator, Constantinus Roncaglia, also wished to treat of the same authority of princes in the later Lucchese edition.

[Col. 1037D] He first shows, with the support of the canonists, that in judging cases of heresy the Church possesses authority both over matters of law and over matters of fact. He then says: “Bellarmin taught that it is not foreign to the power of princes to remove heresies, sacrileges, and the like by enacted laws and penalties,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 1038D] Constantinus Roncaglia, notes to Father Natalis Alexander’s *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, p. 72, Lucca edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1038D] See what we have already written against Beausobre in the *Exercises Relating to the History of the Manichaeans*. In chapter 7 of the second book we defended the holy pontiff against the insults and curses of that non-Catholic writer, who dared to assail him because he asserted that the bloody judgment of the tyrant Maximus had benefited ecclesiastical clemency toward the Priscillianists.]

### 3.

Indeed, if both distinguished men, and all who have discussed this and similar cases, had paid attention to our holy pontiff, they would not have labored so greatly, but would more easily and expeditiously have deprived the heterodox of whatever they can raise as an objection. Why, then, did the rulers of the age order that this bloody form of judgment be exercised against the Priscillianists? The holy pontiff Leo explains in the following words:

“For they saw”—that is, the rulers of the age—“that every concern for morality would be removed, every bond of marriage dissolved, and divine and human law alike overturned, if people of this kind were anywhere permitted to live while professing such things.”

Since, therefore, the crimes of the Priscillianists were such that they brought not merely the greatest disgrace and gravest injury upon religion, but could also drive the civil commonwealth itself to utter ruin, especially in matters that violate the laws of nature, the rulers of the age accordingly endeavored, by means of capital penalties, to destroy and abolish the profession of that sect together with its authors. Relying upon these considerations, the holy pontiff acknowledged that a similar judgment had long benefited ecclesiastical clemency. For he adds:

“This severity long benefited ecclesiastical clemency, which, although content with priestly judgment and avoiding bloody vengeance, is nevertheless assisted by the severe enactments of Christian rulers, since those who fear bodily punishment sometimes resort to a spiritual remedy.”

When the Church proceeds against obstinate heretics, therefore, it neither establishes nor inflicts capital punishments, nor seeks that they be inflicted. Always content with its own spiritual penalties, and lest it incur a defect of clemency, it avoids every kind of bloody vengeance. Nevertheless, if such penalties are established by the public decrees of secular rulers and magistrates, they greatly benefit the Church, which is especially assisted by them because offenders, terrified by the severity of bodily penalties, commonly have recourse to a spiritual remedy—that is, to renouncing their crimes and undertaking penance.

### 4.

Nor should anyone, following Leo’s similar manner of speaking, persuade himself that the obstinacy of Idacius and Ithacius, discussed above, is thereby excused—the obstinacy on account of which they were detested by the Catholic bishops, especially Martin, and Ithacius himself was openly condemned by the bishop Theognostus. No bishop can be cleared by any excuse who, indulging his own zeal, despises the judgments of his fellow bishops summoned to councils and seeks to pressure secular rulers and magistrates through his accusations, pursuing the death of the guilty.

It is entirely clear that this manner of acting is opposed to Catholic clemency. It is especially abhorrent both to the prelates of our Churches and to that holy office of inquisition against which Father Natalis Alexander foresaw that heretics might devise objections. Leo himself further confirmed that such penalties of severity had assisted the Church by observing that bodily punishments and the execution of ecclesiastical laws had been suspended for many years because of the grave vicissitudes of wars, and that even the priests of the provinces could no longer assemble frequently in one place:

“Secret perfidy found freedom, and, for the subversion of many minds, it was encouraged by the very evils by which it ought to have been corrected.”

For this reason he immediately proceeds to lament the deplorable condition of Galicia and Spain. Not only had their peoples, as Turribius had informed him, been shaken by the deadly plague of this contagious disease; more seriously, their priests too, infected by the same lethal illness, were suppressing the truth beneath many errors, preferring the teaching of Priscillian to the evangelical instructions, and finally presenting or preaching these doctrines, corrupted according to profane understandings, to the people, so that, rejecting the revelations of the Holy Spirit, they might breathe the dogmas of the devil into the minds of their hearers.

Turribius had proposed these matters to Saint Leo for the reform of the lamentable condition of those Churches. He attached seventeen chapters containing, in summary form, the formerly condemned opinions; and the holy pontiff, in keeping with the supreme dignity of his apostolate, treated them again, lest any of those blasphemies should thereafter appear tolerable or doubtful.

### 5.

Meanwhile, we think that readers will not find it unwelcome if we set down here a concise summary, as it were an epitome, of these chapters. Although several eminent theologians have long since undertaken this task in composing ecclesiastical histories, I do not know whether any of them have more successfully identified, at least in a clear outline, all the principal errors of this sect, from which the lesser ones also derived their origin.

Nor did Father Natalis Alexander fully accomplish this. When he undertook to construct a catalogue or synopsis of all the errors of the Priscillianists, I do not know by what misfortune he was misled: he recorded only fourteen and entirely omitted three others, indeed among the principal ones. Yet from this letter of Leo alone it is clearer than daylight that there were seventeen, as we shall now state.

[Col. 1039B] The holy pontiff, therefore, in order to satisfy the mind of Turribius, bishop of Asturica, reviews one by one the same chapters that the deacon Pervincus had brought from Galicia for judgment.

First, the Priscillianists held impious opinions concerning the mystery of the Trinity, proclaiming in God a single person with three names, as Sabellius and the Patripassians had taught. The holy pontiff refutes this error not only by the decrees of the Council of Nicaea but also by theological arguments whose formulas of expression seem to echo the Athanasian Creed.

Second, they invented certain virtues proceeding from God, which they asserted God had not always possessed in his essence but had begun to possess at some point, just as the Arians reasoned most perversely.

Third, they maintained that the Son of God was called “only-begotten” because he alone had been born from a Virgin. Thus, with Paul of Samosata and Photinus, they either assigned Christ a beginning from his mother, or they did not believe the Son of God to be one alone, but thought that others too had been begotten from the supreme Father, one of whom had been born from a woman. He was called “only-begotten” because none of the other sons of God had assumed this condition of birth.

Fourth, they did not believe that Christ the Lord had been born in the true nature of man. Accordingly, with Cerdo, Marcion, and Manes, they asserted that he had united to himself merely an apparent and illusory flesh. Deceived by this error, they spent the day of the Lord’s Nativity and Resurrection in sorrow and mourning, afflicting their bodies with fasts.

Fifth, they then asserted that the human soul was of divine substance and that the nature of our condition did not differ from the nature of its Creator.

Sixth, they said that the devil had never been good and that his nature had not been fashioned by God, but that he had emerged from darkness and chaos—since, clearly, he had no author of his own, but was himself the beginning and substance of all evil.

Seventh, they condemned, together with the Manichaeans, the use of weddings and marriage, specifically in order to abhor the procreation of legitimate offspring and more easily admit freedom for every kind of depravity.

Eighth was especially related to this error. They said that human bodies were fabrications of the devil, insofar as the seeds of conception were shaped in women’s wombs, and that the bodies themselves could not possibly be suited to the dignity of the soul, since they had been formed by diabolical power. Hence they denied that, once the body had been dissolved, it could and should live again through the mystery of the resurrection.

Their ninth article was no less monstrous: they proclaimed that the children of promise had been conceived not from the seed of flesh but from the Holy Spirit, and that they were entirely free from the sin and mortal contagion that, through the fault of Adam, the first parent, passes down to his descendants.

Tenth, they taught that the souls inserted into human bodies had formerly sinned in heaven, stripped of every corporeal mass; that for this reason they had fallen from higher to lower places, encountered rulers of different kinds, and, through aerial and stellar powers, had been enclosed in bodies—some harsher, others gentler—of varying fate and dissimilar condition. Thus whatever occurs variously and unequally in this life appeared, in their view, to result from preceding causes.

Their eleventh blasphemy was the belief that both the souls and bodies of human beings were bound by fatal stars. For this reason, like the pagans, they either strove to honor the stars favorable to them or to appease those that were hostile.

Twelfth, they assigned the parts of the soul to some powers and the members of the body to others. They represented the qualities of the inner rulers—namely, the virtues that they imagined governed the soul—under the names of the patriarchs, and set bodily signs opposite them, subjecting bodies to the power of those signs. They added that the parts of the human body corresponded to the twelve signs of the heavens and had been composed according to them: Aries in the head, Taurus in the neck, Gemini in the shoulders, Cancer in the chest, and so forth.

Thirteenth, they erred concerning knowledge of Scripture by understanding the body of the canonical Scriptures under the names of the patriarchs. For they imagined that the twelve virtues which effect the reformation of the inner human being were indicated by those names.

Fourteenth, they subjected human beings so entirely to the power of the stars and signs that they maintained that many things found in the holy books concerned the outward human being. Thus, in Scripture itself, there was supposedly a certain contradictory opposition between the divine and earthly natures: the rulers of the soul claimed one source, while the creators of the body claimed another.

### 6.

Fifteenth, after adulterating the true Scriptures, they introduced false ones, which they called canonical. To confront this extremely serious evil, the holy pontiff enacted that general law by which he ordered the priests of the Churches to exercise every diligence lest either corrupted books be used in public reading or apocryphal writings be kept by anyone. He wrote of these as follows:

“Apocryphal writings, which, under the names of the apostles, contain a rich seedbed of falsehoods, must not merely be forbidden but entirely removed and burned in the fire.”

[Note: [Col. 1039D] See what we said in chapter 6 of the second book of the *History of the Manichaeans*.]

Heretics and innovators, therefore, have no defense when they heap many insults upon the more recent Roman pontiffs because they proscribe their works and order them to be burned. Such discipline is exceedingly ancient in the Catholic Church. It should be traced not only to Pope Gelasius or to the council of seventy bishops held at that time, but also to Leo the Great, who impresses upon all Catholic bishops that it must be observed.

Accordingly, Leo’s manner of acting exposes and makes entirely clear how profoundly Van Espen and Beausobre, among the other non-Catholics, were deluded.

[Note: [Col. 1039D] Beausobre, part I of the *History of the Manichaeans*, book III, and elsewhere throughout. We have thoroughly rejected his absurdities concerning the ancient Manichaeans.]

For Van Espen, when in the first part of his works, entitled *The Whole of Ecclesiastical Law*, he failed entirely to take account of this decree of Leo and undertook to discuss the Church’s discipline concerning the prohibition of heretical books, relies exclusively on the Gelasian decree. He tries completely to deprive its words of force and authority, asserting, as though from the public platform, that the Church had wished to guard only against the public, not the private, reading of proscribed books.

Van Espen is spectacularly mistaken. To make this clear, there is no need for us to depart from our subject and begin discussing the Gelasian decree now.
