It has already appeared furnished with many learned notes through the study and labor of Chifletius, Holstenius, and Father Joseph Bianchini, so that it would be entirely superfluous to enrich it with new observations.

To guard against Van Espen’s error, it will suffice to consider what Saint Leo added. He prohibited Catholics not only from making public use of corrupted, apocryphal, and false books, but also from privately reading them or even keeping such copies in their homes. He placed under the charge of heresy bishops who permitted this. Accordingly, he added:

“Therefore, if any bishop has not prohibited apocryphal books from being kept in homes, or has permitted books corrupted by Priscillian’s emendation to be read in the Church under the name of canonical books, he must know that he is to be judged a heretic, since one who does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.”

After these words, a very ancient Palatine Vatican manuscript presents us with a celebrated fragment of this letter, hitherto neither noted nor published by the earlier editors of Saint Leo’s works. Although it does not seem entirely to bear the stamp of Leonine composition, the antiquity and authority of the cited codex, together with the nature of its subject—which harmonizes most perfectly with the preceding statements of the holy pontiff—lead us to the decision that we shall commit it to print, enclosed between lines, in the second volume.

As for the antiquity of the codex, those who judge ancient scripts have agreed with us that it reaches the ninth century. The subject plainly corresponds to Saint Leo’s purpose in writing. After rejecting apocryphal writings, it seemed appropriate for him to identify the canonical books and the order in which they were to be read in the Church, so that the ministers of the sacred altar might unite in complete harmony in singing the divine praises and celebrating the mysteries.

Moreover, with the addition of this fragment, the earlier and later portions are most suitably joined. In the codex we also encounter the following heading:

“Here begins the statement of Pope Leo concerning apocryphal writings.”

It begins with the words of the aforementioned fifteenth chapter of this letter to Turribius:

“Therefore care must be taken, and it must be provided for above all with priestly diligence, that corrupted books…”

and continues to the words that close this chapter in all the printed editions:

“Since one who does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.”

Immediately after these words the following is added:

“Now all the divine Scriptures of the holy canon are read in the Church of Saint Peter from the beginning of the year to its end in the following order. In the springtime, that is, from seven days before the beginning of Lent until the eighth day before Easter, the books of Moses are read together with Joshua and Judges,” and so forth.

I shall not omit to make and note just two observations here, in a brief digression. The first is that the order described in this fragment for reading all the Scriptures of the sacred canon throughout the course of the entire year does not differ from the distribution and arrangement that can still be seen today in the Roman Breviary. This proves the authority and antiquity of this sacred rite, handed down to us from our forebears, who intended to distribute and adapt the readings of Scripture according to each of the four seasons of the year—readings more suited and more consonant with the celebration of the divine mysteries in the Church—so that they might better attend to and provide for both the dignity of the mysteries and the instruction of the people.

The second observation is that the fragment cited contains all the books listed in the canon of Trent, session 4, with one or two exceptions. These two points will certainly provide a store of learned dissertations for men devoted to the study of the sacred Liturgies, who in our own times are rightly devoting great effort to this work, with considerable benefit to the study of sacred antiquity.

We do not insert the whole fragment here, lest we depart farther than appropriate from our intended purpose. Nevertheless, we shall publish it as it stands in the manuscript codex in the second volume of the complete works of Saint Leo the pontiff and furnish it with brief notes.

Returning, then, to our subject, we reason as follows. If, already in the fifth century of the Church, when the rigor of canonical discipline is considered, no one was permitted to keep in his home sacred Scriptures corrupted and falsified by heretics, how can it now be that the heterodox complain so loudly when they understand that the apostolic see has forbidden Catholics to read their books under penalty of anathema?

To linger longer over this matter, which is entirely clear, would rightly be considered a fault. We therefore proceed to the sixteenth chapter, in which the holy pontiff spoke about other books composed by the industry of heretics.

### 7.

Saint Leo the Great calls this sixteenth chapter the last, specifically in the sense that Turribius’s petition, transmitted to the apostolic see for consideration, contained sixteen chapters requiring discussion. But because the same bishop of Asturica had added something else at the end of his personal letter—namely, the question concerning Christ’s flesh, “whether it truly rested in the tomb”—we rightly judged that the old reading, “sixteen,” should be removed and that the new reading, “seventeen,” supported by the manuscripts, should be followed, as we have said.

Accordingly, in responding to the sixteenth chapter of Turribius’s petition, the holy pontiff first approves Turribius’s complaint, specifically the complaint concerning the writings and treatises of Dictinius, formerly his predecessor in the see of Asturica. That Dictinius, while infected with the Priscillianist stain, committed these books to writing has already been amply attested by the acts of the Council of Toledo, by Augustine and other contemporary writers, as we have seen, and now by Saint Leo himself.

Many people read these books with veneration, although they ought rather to have loved Dictinius’s restoration than his fall. “They are not reading Dictinius,” says the holy pontiff, “but Priscillian; and they approve what he taught while in error, not what he chose after his correction.” He therefore declares that those who used his writings were outside the ecclesiastical assembly.

The supreme pontiff certainly excepted no one. To include people of every order and condition, he pronounces from the seat of the holy apostle Peter:

“But no one should presume to do this with impunity, nor should anyone who uses writings condemned not only by the Catholic Church but also by their own author be counted among Catholics.”

After this, Saint Leo amplifies the methods of the Priscillianists and Manichaeans, which they skillfully employed to avoid the severity of imperial laws. Although the members of these sects were at heart united and professed the same sacrileges, they were known by different names. Thus, although the offspring of the Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament, which the Priscillianists pretended to accept, the intention of both, says the holy pontiff, tended toward one and the same end: “What the former attack by rejecting, the Priscillianists corrupt by accepting.”

Furthermore, I believe that the fact that the Priscillianists agreed with the Manichaeans in execrable mysteries, obscenities, and every kind of depravity has already been demonstrated by the entire course of this history. Here Leo particularly impresses this upon Turribius and refers him to the most careful investigation conducted at Rome against the Manichaeans, sending him, the bishop of Asturica, copies of the judgment and its acts.

[Note: [Col. 1041] Consult chapter 10 of book II of the *History of the Manichaeans*, where we discussed Leo’s Roman investigation of these heretics.]

### 8.

The final chapter remains, which, as we have already said, Turribius had proposed to Leo for definition at the end of his personal letter: namely, whether Christ’s flesh truly rested in the tomb. This mystery of our religion had even come into doubt for many Catholics because Christ had descended to the underworld. For the peoples of Spain could not understand how those two things—the descent into hell, namely, and the repose of Christ’s flesh in the tomb—could be joined together with genuine propriety.

The holy pontiff demonstrates by various testimonies of Scripture that these two doctrines of the Apostles’ Creed are in no way opposed to one another. There is no doubt, however, that the contrary assertion derived from the doctrines of Priscillian and Manes, who, as Leo says, “with sacrilegious understanding pretend to confess Christ in such a way that they remove the reality both of the Incarnation, of death, and of the Resurrection.”

[Note: [Col. 1043D] See what we wrote concerning this doctrine against Beausobre, in order to defend the *Acts of Archelaus* and the disputation held against Manes from the charge of forgery, in book I of the *History of the Manichaeans*.]

There is therefore no reason to doubt that, in reviewing these chapters, Saint Leo performed the role of supreme judge and teacher. Saint Leo himself makes clear that the quibbles of his opponents could have no place here. To make his own teaching and canonical judgments known to the entire body of clergy and to each of the faithful, he first ordered that encyclical letters be circulated among the bishops, designating a suitable place for the council to be held.

He then commanded the priests of the neighboring provinces to assemble there. Once the fullest severity of inquiry had been applied, he especially wished and ordered that it be investigated whether any of the bishops were infected with the contagion of the Priscillian heresy. As for those whom the council discovered to be defiled by so great a stain, he decreed that, with all the rules of these pontifical sanctions observed, they were without doubt to be separated from Catholic communion if they refused to condemn the utterly detestable sect in all its perverse doctrines.

But so that these matters relating to the rights of the apostolic see might be carried out more fully and easily, the holy pontiff was not content with this letter. Without any intervening delay, he sent other letters to his fellow bishops—namely, those of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia—in which he convoked a general council. There can be no doubt that in convoking it he exercised the supreme right of his pontificate. This is plainly revealed by these words of Leo:

“It will belong to the concern of your Beloved to see that the authority of our ordinance is conveyed to the bishops of the aforesaid provinces.”

Whether Leo wrote one encyclical letter or several in order to compel all the bishops of Spain and Galicia to come to the council, I have not dared to determine. Whatever those letters were, they have not appeared to the present day, and may perhaps have perished through the injury of time.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] That Leo sent only one encyclical letter to all the bishops of Spain and Galicia may be inferred from a similar procedure of the same holy pontiff, which he observed in the Eastern affairs later brought under examination after the Robber Synod of Ephesus, as we shall see in the final part of these *Exercises*.]

### 9.

Now, if I were permitted to question the cavillers against the rights of the Roman see, why did that great man Turribius, beset by the greatest anxieties, direct his inquiries to the one apostolic see, and not to the bishop of another see? What would Launoy, Blondel, Quesnellus, and the others among them reply?

Would they dare to contend that the entire matter had been deferred to a future council? They would certainly be deceived and would be deluding themselves. For the supreme pontiff, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, rejected each of the Priscillianists’ errors from the throne of the Vatican—not merely by theological arguments, but also by condemning them under anathema. He proscribed copies of apocryphal writings and the private as well as public reading of heretical books, ordered that they be burned, and declared those bishops who failed to obey such statutes to be outside Catholic communion.

What, then? Did he defer these matters for definition by a future council? Would the Fathers of the council even have been permitted lightly to depart from these rules and statutes? Those who invented such a claim would be speaking nonsense, since those devoted to the truth understand that only the examination of whether any of the bishops were infected with the contagion of this heresy had been referred to the Fathers of the council. Such bishops, according to the responses given to Turribius, were without doubt to be separated from communion.

“For they make use of the Catholic name in vain,” says the holy pontiff, “who do not resist these impieties.”

The council, therefore, was not to act concerning the condemnation of the heresy, which the Most Reverend Fathers and Leo himself had already condemned, but concerning the punishment of the heretics, whose case had not yet been sufficiently investigated by the apostolic see. For this reason our Leo, having already sufficiently discussed matters pertaining to law, submitted to the judgment of a general—or at least a provincial—council those matters that could concern the persons involved and the facts of the case.

### 10.

Since the entire attention of the pontiff was chiefly directed toward remedying the evils of Galicia and preventing the Catholic religion from being brought to complete ruin as those evils spread more widely through the region, he decided to adopt the following arrangement.

If anything should prevent the celebration of a general council, he ordered at least the priests of Galicia to assemble. The responsibility for convening them was entrusted to Idacius and Ceponius, distinguished by metropolitan authority; he also added Turribius’s concern to theirs, so that a provincial gathering might more quickly bring a remedy to such great wounds.

While Leo was ordering these things to be done in Galicia and Spain, and while he entrusted the letters of the pontiff to the Asturican deacon Pervincus for delivery to the bishops of both kingdoms, Calipius and Ardubare were already serving as Roman consuls. The consular lists of the Romans now make clear that this occurred in the year 447 of Christ.

If, however, students of theology and lovers of truth wish to obtain further material for refuting the errors of this utterly detestable sect, let them consult the homilies of the same holy pontiff. No sooner had Leo learned of the impiety and sacrileges of those most wicked men than he could scarcely restrain his zeal from attacking and denouncing that profane religion and its doctrines amid the celebration of the sacred mysteries.

It is enough for us to have indicated this manner of proceeding, lest our discourse become more lengthy than the subject warrants.

## CHAPTER XV. On the councils held in the kingdoms of Galicia and Spain by command of Saint Leo the Great. Paschasius Quesnellus’s false judgment concerning the ancient Codex of the Canons of the Roman Church.

### 1.

We must now write about more obscure matters, and matters much more difficult than those already discussed, especially since, through the loss of ancient records, we lack those resources [Col. 1044C] that could readily guide and assist us in discovering the truth of events. Nevertheless, we shall not withdraw our hand from the undertaking we have begun until it becomes clearer how the priests of both kingdoms obeyed the papal commands.

Since, as we have already seen, those bishops could not assemble in one general council—both because of the differing civil administrations of their territories and because of the different dynasties, dispositions, and religious commitments of their rulers—the metropolitans of each kingdom convened their own synods. For the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica, over whom, in civil affairs, Theodoric—an Arian born of the Gothic stock—ruled, held their council in that same year, 447.

I am convinced that the famous testimony supplied by the collectors of the general councils is evidence of this event. After the canons of the First Council of Toledo, one finds a certain rule of faith, bearing the following heading:

> Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillians, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, and Baetica composed and, at the command of Pope Leo of the city of Rome, sent to Balconius, bishop of Galicia; they themselves also established the twenty chapters of canons written above in the Council of Toledo. [Col. 1044D; *Tom. II Conciliorum generalium*, p. m. 1475.]

The final words indicate, therefore, that the bishops of Spain assembled at Toledo. But no one should suppose that the preceding chapters, as they are preserved today in the collection of the Councils, were published in the age of Leo. For Patruinus was the first to subscribe to them, together with the others who had assembled in the year 400 over the case of Symphosius and Dictinius. Ortigius, a bishop of Galicia, also subscribed; we have already discussed him sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, above. But that these men could still have been alive in 447, or that Ortigius could have been free to come with the bishops of Spain to this assembly, is utterly improbable. It is therefore clearer than daylight that Hardouin’s annotation should be accepted. In the edition of this council prepared by Loaysa, he wrote, the following words are found:

> The Council of Toledo ends.

These words show that the rule of faith which follows does not belong to that council at all, but must be assigned to the council convened at Leo’s command.

### 2.

Pagius certainly judged the matter in the same way. Carefully and at an earlier stage weighing what seemed relevant to ecclesiastical enactments and to the order of the records, so as to prevent confusion in the history of events, he asserted that the profession of faith under discussion was composed in Leo’s time. [Col. 1045D; Pagius, on the year of Christ 405, nos. 16–17.] Its truth is in no way undermined by the great diversity among the manuscript and printed copies that we encounter in these anathemas: some codices contain only twelve anathemas, the printed copies eighteen, while in Augustine’s works their number rises as high as twenty-six.

When Quesnellus noticed this great diversity, he thought it could serve his studies and his position. [Col. 1045D; Quesnellus, Dissertation 14, *On the Libelli contained in the codex*, no. 8.] Accordingly, at one moment he assigns the profession to Leo, conjecturing that it had been torn from the Roman codex of canons; at another, he tries to argue that it should be attributed to Augustine—as though Augustine had at some point sent it to the bishops of Spain, or as though Leo had brought it from Africa when, while still an acolyte, he carried Zosimus’s decree against the Pelagians, and so forth.

Are we to regard Quesnellus as reasoning correctly and wisely here and in what follows? Hardouin long ago noted that both claims were frivolous and groundless. Anyone who examines both the profession of faith and the eighteen anathemas appended to it will plainly understand that this Parisian editor of Leo’s works, following his usual practice, wished to invent and babble. For who would flatter himself that this rule of faith, together with the appended anathemas, had been arranged and composed long before the errors of the Priscillians, their methods, and the sources from which they flowed had become more fully known?

If we imagine that this profession of faith had been inserted into the Roman codex of canons before the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica assembled; or if we suppose that Augustine or someone else published it before Turibius consulted the apostolic see and the holy pontiff answered his questions, let Quesnellus say, I beg him: could it have remained unknown to Turibius and Leo? Such a supposition is impermissible. Both men ought to have been informed about events occurring in the Church, and the Roman pontiff above all would have known of it if he had brought this document with him to Rome from Africa and if his predecessors—or he himself—had inserted it into the Roman codex of canons.

Why, then, did the holy pontiff never appeal to this profession of faith? Why did he not set the anathemas attached to the profession against the individual articles of Priscillianism? Finally, why did Turibius himself consult the apostolic see, if the bishops of Spain had long before received from Augustine the token of faith?

My conviction, therefore, is that Quesnellus acted with complete deceit and nonsense in assigning this profession of faith to Augustine. If the bishops of Tarraconensis and the other Fathers who assembled in council had borrowed it from Augustine’s works, they would not have concealed his name; indeed, they would not have omitted indicating the canons and statutes of the Roman and apostolic see if they had taken the rule of faith from that codex. Yet in the heading we find no name other than Leo’s, for it reads:

> Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillians, which the bishops of Tarraconensis … composed and, at the command of Pope Leo of the city of Rome, sent to Balconius, bishop of Galicia. [Col. 1046A]

### 3.

Nor may one attribute this to the error or negligence of a copyist. For the Fathers of the Council of Braga, in the year of Christ 563, openly acknowledged the matter. When Lucretius, bishop and president of that sacred assembly, addressed the other bishops, he appealed to the Toledan synod held in Leo’s time and at his command. At that synod, he said, they had composed a rule of faith against the Priscillian heresy together with certain chapters, and had sent it to Balconius, then bishop of the Church of Braga. [Col. 1046D; Council of Braga, vol. VI of the *Councils*, p. 551.]

Thus, if the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica composed that profession of faith with the appended anathemas, or chapters, in the year 447, it could not have been brought to light through Augustine’s work, since the holy bishop had already ended his last day at his see of Hippo in the year 430. Finally, if those Fathers had borrowed it from Augustine’s works or from the collection of Roman canons, Lucretius would certainly not have said, “composing the rule of faith against the Priscillian heresy together with certain chapters.” Rather, he would have used the familiar expression: “The profession of faith was recited”; or, “They read the profession of faith, together with the appended chapters, from the codex”; or, “They had it copied out from the codex.”

Those who have examined the acts of councils and the histories know very well that we should not rely on such slight conjectures. But Quesnellus would also have known this, had he not, led excessively by the interests of his own position, neglected to examine or understand the acts of that same Council of Braga to which he appeals.

Did not the same Bishop Lucretius, immediately after the words quoted by us and copied out by Quesnellus himself, add the following?

> Since we have here before us, for the instruction of the ignorant, a copy of the prescribed faith together with its chapters, if it pleases your reverence, let it be recited.

Then all the bishops said:

> The reading of these chapters is exceedingly necessary. [Col. 1046C]

They give no other reason than this: that the simpler people, to whom the ancient statutes of the holy Fathers were being set forth, might recognize the inventions of the Priscillian heresy, long ago abhorred and condemned by the see of the blessed apostle Peter.

Whether these statements, I ask, cut Quesnellus down, let the reader observe. Those former statutes of the holy Fathers, by which the monstrosities of the Priscillian heresy had been condemned, are attributed to the apostolic see of the blessed Peter. Augustine, therefore, must not be called the author of that profession of faith and of those chapters. For although he was illustrious in merit, labors, and honors, when did he attain the apostolic throne of Peter?

### 4.

Nor does the great diversity in the number of anathemas, so loudly proclaimed by Quesnellus, cast darkness over this truth. In the first place, the manuscript copies from which that diversity was chiefly derived were sometimes corrupted or enlarged through the carelessness and negligence of copyists. Or, for other reasons, the Fathers themselves, appealing to the Church’s earlier statutes, brought forward only those matters that seemed relevant to newly arising questions. At times they also added other points that they judged more suitable to the matters under discussion.

What wonder is it, then, if, when we turn over the writings of the ancients, one and the same document sometimes appears interpolated and abridged, and at other times more extensive and expanded? In matters that depend on the will of those who write and use them, unless their intention is known, judgment cannot be reached without difficulty—especially when autograph copies are lacking.

### 5.

In this matter, however, I think Quesnellus should not have had to expend much effort. The same Fathers of the aforementioned Council of Braga had before them, in an authentic codex, the acts of those who had attended the Toledan synod convened in the year 447. Therefore, after reading the profession of faith with the appended chapters, they thought it necessary, 116 years later, to explain those same chapters more simply and clearly, so that the less learned might understand what, in the judgment of anathema, had formerly been condemned from the teachings of Priscillian by the apostolic see of Saint Peter.

Although, they say, the reading of these chapters has been declared necessary, nevertheless let what is execrable now be explained more clearly and simply, with the chapters set out beforehand, so that the less learned may understand, and so that the inventions of Priscillian’s error, already rejected under sentence of anathema, may likewise be condemned, and so forth.

We ought therefore to congratulate ourselves that these Fathers reconsidered the same chapters. They prepared a broad and open way by which we might more securely arrive at knowledge of how many anathemas there were, and what kind, that the Fathers of Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, and Baetica published in the year 447, at the command of Leo the Great, in order utterly to extinguish the dangerous poison of the Priscillian heresy.

If we examine these anathemas, they correspond entirely to Leo’s letter to Turibius. It is therefore impossible, on any reasonable foundation, either to assign them all to Augustine or to pretend that they were entered into the Roman codex of canons before Saint Leo.

To prevent Quesnellus’s supporters from suspecting us of invention or falsehood, we must explain why those Fathers of Braga reconsidered the very same chapters and wished to expound them more clearly. They say:

> If any cleric, monk, or layman should still be discovered to hold or defend anything of this kind—that is, anything connected with Priscillianism—let him immediately be cut off from the body of the Catholic Church as a truly rotten member, lest the hearts of those who believe rightly should regard as any reproach arising from their association with such persons either the society or the depravity of those persons.

This sentence, pronounced by Bishop Lucretius and approved by the Fathers of the entire council, contained the chapters formerly established against the Priscillian heresy, as the following words seem to indicate:

> The chapters proposed and reread against the Priscillian heresy are as follows.

But since seventeen anathemas immediately follow—anathemas that, as we have said, correspond most closely to Turibius’s questions and agree entirely with Leo’s answers, as their reading makes sufficiently clear—I regard it as beyond all doubt that the Fathers of Tarraconensis, together with the bishops of the other three provinces of Spain, wishing to obey Leo’s commands, then for the first time, namely in the year 447, published and promulgated both the rule of faith and the anathemas under discussion.

If Quesnellus denies this, he must affirm one of two things: either that Turibius’s consultations with the apostolic see had already been discussed and settled before Leo’s pontificate, or that the letter to Turibius must be attributed to a Roman pontiff other than Leo. Both alternatives plainly reek of pure invention.

### 6.

We must now anticipate and take away the escape route that Quesnellus had prepared for himself. He thought it was supplied by the heading of that profession of faith, which the collectors of the Councils presented as attached to the First Council of Toledo together with eighteen anathemas. For it reads:

> Here begins the rule of the Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillians, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, etc. [Col. 1047D; *Tom. II Conciliorum*, p. 1475.]

If, then, this profession of faith attacks and rejects all heresies, it did not first appear when those bishops of Spain assembled. It would therefore be possible to infer instead that those Spanish Fathers adapted it for their own use because they knew that it fitted the Priscillians remarkably well.

So, indeed, someone might babble who assigns this document to Augustine, or who pretends that it was borrowed from the Roman codex of canons published before Leo. But such a person would show the greatest ignorance of ecclesiastical history and, above all, of Leo’s works.

What did this holy pontiff proclaim and write about the Priscillian heresy? Did he not himself write that this heresy had derived from the sources and authors of all the preceding heresies, so that in his answers to Turibius he plainly showed that the Priscillians had accepted and defended the errors of the Gnostics, Cerdo, Photinus, Apollinaris, Sabellius, the Patripassians, Arius, Mani, and other wicked men?

Therefore, if the bishops of Spain wished to adhere to Leo’s teaching and letter, they had good reason to use the words: “against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillians.” For the holy pontiff, discussing this heresy in various places, but especially at the beginning of his letter to Turibius, writes:

> For there is no filth among the opinions of any impious people that has not flowed together into this doctrine, since they have mixed for themselves a manifold foulness from the mud of every earthly opinion, so that they alone—namely, the Priscillians—might drink in its entirety whatever others had tasted in part. [Col. 1048B]

Immediately after these words he added another statement that bears wonderfully on our subject:

> Finally, if all the heresies that arose before the time of Priscillian are carefully reconsidered, scarcely any error will be found from which that impiety did not draw the contagion.

Nor should anyone flatter himself that the holy pontiff intended merely to indicate these matters in general. When he addressed the same questions and consultations of Turibius, he specified the sources and authors from which the errors refuted in the seventeen—or eighteen—chapters of his letter had been derived.

The bishops of Spain who assembled in that council, and the Fathers of Braga who, as we have seen, subsequently reconsidered those chapters of the heresies, followed his method with the greatest exactness. Quesnellus himself honestly admitted this concerning the Fathers of Braga. Moreover, in his notes to Letter 15, he observed that the anathemas, or chapters, of this council were published according to the model of the answers that our Leo had formerly sent to Turibius.

He recognized that they had such a close relationship that he wrote:

> For there is scarcely a word that the Fathers did not borrow from Leo, and no chapter of Leo’s that they did not include among their own. The first five articles of the council correspond to the five chapters of Leo; the others correspond likewise to one another, although they agree entirely neither in order nor in number. [Col. 1047] [Quesnellus, Part II of the Works of Saint Leo, notes on Letter 15.]

But who does not see Quesnellus killing himself with his own sword? For he admits with us that the Fathers of Braga fashioned their chapters and anathemas from Leo’s judgments and words. Yet the aforementioned Fathers of Braga say that they followed chapters previously published and composed in a council of Spain by the Fathers of Tarraconensis and Carthaginensis.

Therefore, the Fathers of both councils, adhering to the instructions and definitions of the apostolic see, published and composed precisely the same chapters. There is consequently no need to attribute that profession of faith, together with its appended chapters, either to Augustine or to an unknown author of the Roman canons.

### 7.

Quesnellus and Hardouin both maintain, however, that this profession of faith is not free from every defect. They believe that it is now presented in a fuller form than it originally possessed when first brought to light by its authors, since it mentions the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. No one, they say, can doubt that these words reveal a later hand.

I could readily grant this, if I then considered individually the controversies that arose between the Roman Catholics and the Greeks because of the Photian schism, in the eighth century of the Church and afterward. But I am prevented and restrained from subscribing to the judgments of these two critics not only by the readings of Leo’s works, but also by the antiquity of the manuscripts from which we have examined copies of the works of that same holy pontiff.

When investigating this doctrine in Leo’s writings, I encounter various testimonies that resolve the question raised later. Among these, I am convinced that the principal place belongs to what he wrote against the Priscillian heresy under discussion. For, describing to Turibius and the other bishops of Galicia and Spain what must be believed concerning the mystery of the Trinity, he taught and defined, without any concealment or ambiguity of expression, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. [Col. 1049D; Leo’s letter to Turibius, chapter 1.]

In the first chapter he demonstrates how impiously those people think about the divine Trinity who assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person—as though the one God were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit, and as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeded from both were not distinct.

I believe that no one can deny that this passage not only signifies but explicitly expresses the procession of the Holy Spirit also from the Son. For when Leo affirms that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, it necessarily follows that this procession derives equally from the Father and the Son.

Theodulf reasoned in precisely this way, prompted by Leo’s testimony, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*. Instead of the past-tense word *processit* (“proceeded”), he used the present-tense *procedit* (“proceeds”).

Moreover, those words did not at all seem to the most distinguished theologians to reveal a later hand. To prove the perpetual existence of this doctrine in the Church against the Greeks, they appeal not only to Leo’s testimony but also to that profession of faith attributed by the Fathers of the First Council of Toledo.

Indeed, two other testimonies of the holy pontiff, expressed in his sermons on Pentecost, show that this doctrine of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was already widely known in the Roman Church. It is sufficient to indicate them here. We shall say something about them in the notes to those same sermons, which we shall prepare in a subsequent volume with new type. [Col. 1049C–D] [Leo the Great, Sermon 1 on Pentecost, chapter 3, and Sermon 2, chapter 2.]

## CHAPTER XVI  
Whether the profession of faith attributed to the Fathers of Toledo bears the stamp of Augustine’s style and age. It is further shown that the codex of canons published by Quesnellus was falsely attributed to the Roman Church.

### 1.

Having removed that weak annotation of both Quesnellus and Hardouin, and rejected the claims by which the aforementioned profession of faith with its appended chapters, or anathemas, was wrongly attributed to others rather than to Leo and the bishops of Spain, we must still discuss Augustine’s writings. Among them, Quesnellus alone maintains that the document under discussion has a fuller place.

He says that it is cited near the end of Book III, distinction 21, by the Master of the Sentences in these words:

> “According to this reasoning,” he says, “Augustine says: ‘If anyone says and believes that the Son of God, God, suffered, let him be anathema.’”

The same Parisian editor says:

> “The passage from Augustine marked in the margin is, I think, in a later hand: ‘Sermon on Faith, which is Sermon 3 for Thursday in Holy Week.’ In fact, Volume X of his works contains Sermon 129 *On Faith rightly held*, a sermon *de tempore*, which the doctors of Louvain did not reject into the appendix; consequently, they judged it to be Augustine’s genuine offspring.” [Col. 1049D] [Quesnellus, Dissertation 14, *On the Libelli contained in the codex*, no. 8.]

Thus far Quesnellus, who, carried away by zeal for his own position, brings forward various conjectures—very slight, mutually contradictory, and irrelevant to the subject—so that, as will become clear to readers, he seems to contend or play merely with trifles and words.

In explaining this matter, we would have to be very long-winded if we wished to note and then reject everything that he attempted to invent there. It is preferable, however, to reduce the question to several specific points, so that from them we may clearly understand how far he has departed from the truth.

### 2.

First, in the year 393, when Augustine was still a presbyter, on the occasion of the general African Council of Hippo, held in the secretarium of the Basilica of Peace, he disputed against the Manichaeans. He discussed the divine persons in such a way that he used neither a single expression resembling the wording of the aforementioned profession nor even hinted at, attacked, or refuted any one of the errors or sources of error that the profession indicates and expresses. [Col. 1050D] [From Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 17.]

Indeed, if we carefully observe what was said there about the Holy Spirit, lovers of truth will judge that the doctrine of the African Church at that time was very far from the teaching of the apostolic see. For the doctrine had not yet been discussed so fully by learned and great teachers of divine matters. Therefore, when they proclaimed the Holy Spirit to be God’s gift, they nevertheless did not describe him as begotten of the Father like the Son, nor as produced from the Son like the Father’s grandson, nor as constituting two first principles of all things, as the Manichaeans wrongly supposed. [Col. 1050D] [Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 9.]

Regarding the Holy Spirit, he says:

> The learned and great interpreters of the divine Scriptures have not yet discussed him so fully and carefully that it can easily be understood what is proper to him, by which he is made such that we cannot call him either Son or Father, but only the Holy Spirit—except that they proclaim him to be the gift of God, so that we may believe that God does not give a gift inferior to himself. They nevertheless maintain that the Holy Spirit was not begotten as a Son from the Father, for Christ is the only one. Nor do they call him the Son’s son, or grandson, of the supreme Father; yet neither do they say that he owes what he is to no one, but to the Father, from whom all things come, lest we establish two principles without a principle—which is utterly false and absurd and belongs not to the Catholic faith but to certain heretics.

Since, then, in Augustine’s time the question of the Holy Spirit’s procession was still exceedingly obscure among the Africans, the Fathers learned in the sacred Scriptures called him simply God, gift, and love—not Son and not the Father’s grandson. They never proclaimed him as proceeding from the Father and the Son as from one principle.

How, then, can these statements agree with the doctrine of the apostolic see, expressed clearly in the profession, which is filled with much clearer and more appropriate formulas and expressions? Certainly, if the expressions of the apostolic see had also been in use among the Africans, it would have been especially fitting for Augustine to use them in his exposition of the faith and the Creed. Since he did not use them, and since the learned and great interpreters of the divine Scriptures had not yet discussed the Holy Spirit so fully and carefully, this is plainly evidence that the profession of faith in question cannot bear the stamp of Augustine’s age, style, or doctrine.

### 3.

Nor do the arguments supporting Quesnellus’s opinion gain strength from the answers Augustine gave, after becoming a bishop, to Orosius’s consultation, or from what is found in his other works, especially the book *On Heresies*, composed in 428. For none of these works of Augustine contains anything from which it can be inferred that the profession of faith under discussion is his genuine offspring.

As for the book addressed to Orosius against the Priscillians and Origenists, anyone who has examined it with his own eyes will judge that it contains nothing resembling or agreeing with this profession of faith. [Col. 1050D] [*Book to Orosius against the Priscillians and Origenists*, chapter 1, volume VIII, p. 438.]

At the beginning, Augustine admits that he does not intend to address everything set out in Orosius’s memorandum:

> In certain little works of ours, he says, which you have either read or may read, many things have been said that are effective against the heresy of the Priscillians, although I did not set out to refute them. But now I understand that, while engaged in another task, I also dealt with this matter, since I have learned from you what they believe. [Col. 1051A]

Augustine, therefore, had not set out to refute the Priscillians before the year 415, since it was only in that year that he learned from Orosius, who had come from Spain, what the members of that sect believed. He nevertheless admits that, while attacking the Manichaeans, he had already written much that could apply very well against the Priscillians, who resembled the Manichaeans in many doctrines.

But no trace appears in his writings indicating that he could have composed this profession of faith. For at that time neither he nor even Orosius knew all the blasphemies or errors of the Priscillians. It would therefore be rash to say that he had taken up his pen to compose a profession of faith against a heresy whose errors were not yet known to him.

I would certainly not dare to say this were it not that Orosius’s writings to Augustine and Augustine’s book to Orosius supply the evidence. [Col. 1051D] [Orosius’s consultation, or memorandum, to Augustine concerning the error of the Priscillians and Origenists, is found in volume VIII of Augustine’s works, p. 431.]

Orosius proposes only three questions concerning the Priscillians for explanation; the others that he adds have nothing in common with Priscillian’s errors but concern the inventions of the Origenists, as both men themselves attest. Therefore, not all the Priscillian doctrines were yet known to them. [Col. 1051D] [Augustine’s book against the Priscillians and Origenists, ibid., p. 433 and following.]

We shall immediately make clear what questions Orosius proposed for Augustine to explain.

The first concerned the nature and substance of the soul. The Priscillians maintained that it was not entirely created, but fancied that it contained within itself a portion of the divine nature.

The second concerned the formation of human and bodily members. They imagined that the names of the patriarchs corresponded to these members and that the signs of the heavens had been arranged within them. They attempted to confirm this impious and superstitious monstrosity from a certain book entitled *The Memoranda of the Apostles*. Orosius himself also testifies that this book was filled with other fables and inventions.

The final question concerned the mystery of the Trinity. They proclaimed that it consisted in the word alone:

> For they assert a union without any existence or property; having removed the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they said that this one was Christ.

Since Augustine was addressing only these three errors, he could not have composed and sent to Orosius—or to any bishop of Spain—a profession of faith in which, besides the three errors just listed, fourteen or fifteen others are condemned and rejected, errors that had not yet come to Augustine’s knowledge.

### 4.

Nor should anyone object to Augustine’s letter addressed to Ceretius. [Col. 1052D] [Letter 237, formerly 253, found in volume II, p. 643.] What does it prove? Augustine’s entire purpose there is to expose the frauds by which the Priscillians corrupted the sacred Scriptures and adopted apocryphal writings for themselves, especially preferring to the canonical books a hymn that they falsely imagined had been recited by Christ the Lord in the garden before his Passion.

I do not dare to state in what year Augustine wrote such a letter. But as I carefully read through it, nothing at all appears that could support Quesnellus’s conjectures.

Nor should anyone flatter himself that support can be found in what Augustine himself wrote in 420 to Consentius against the lies and perjuries of the Priscillians, and concerning the books of Dictinius. There he attacks the nature of falsehood and refutes all the opposing arguments drawn from wrongly interpreted Scriptures. He asserts that Dictinius ended his last day in the peace of the Church as a penitent, as we have already seen. Yet throughout all these writings we see not even the slightest trace of that profession of faith.

### 5

But before we come to that sermon 129 which Quesnellus assigns to Augustine as a genuine offspring, we must say something about the book *Against All Heresies*, written by him in 428. We admit that the holy bishop of Hippo, in section 70, listed various errors of the Priscillianists at somewhat greater length [Note: [Col. 1052D] Augustine, *On Heresies*, heresy 70, vol. VIII, p. 17.]. But if we set aside the dissolution of marriages, the sexual abominations, and the contaminations in which the Priscillianists took delight and which he attacks, he adds nothing there beyond what he had already attacked either in the books addressed to Orosius and Consentius or in the letter to Ceretius. Thus, at that time, not all the secrets of that sect were yet known to Augustine or to others. For if they had become known two years before he departed this life, he certainly would not have failed to describe them, since, in composing this work, he had intended to report the errors of each heresy. Nor should this be counted against him. For at that period the affairs of both Spain and Galicia were suffering grievously; and therefore the sacred prelates of the Churches, over whom barbarian and Arian rulers held power after the Roman Empire had been divided, could neither devote themselves to convening synods, nor take action against heretics and contumacious clerics, nor finally exchange letters in response to the most serious questions that arose, nor seek from other bishops of the Catholic community those institutional aids that seemed altogether necessary.

If our reader sincerely considers these circumstances—which we have also described more fully above—he will not readily persuade himself either that we wished to bring Augustine into disrepute or that we wished to reproach him with ignorance, but only that we are reporting what is judged increasingly consonant with the truth. Nor does it help Quesnellus to appeal to the consultations of Eutropius and Paul, Spanish bishops, by arguing that they sent a certain memorandum to Augustine against the errors then spreading through the regions of Spain, and that on this occasion this little book could have been requested by the bishops of Spain and written by Augustine [Note: [Col. 1052D] Quesnellus, dissertation 14, *On Libelli*, no. 8.]. But on what basis does Quesnellus maintain this? He asserts that he derives it from Orosius’s consultation, or memorandum. Yet the words of Orosius already cause Quesnellus difficulty, for Eutropius and Paul, moved solely by concern for the salvation of all, had already issued a memorandum, Orosius says, “concerning certain heresies,” but did not indicate all of them [Note: [Col. 1052D] Orosius, in the *Memorandum to Augustine*.].

As to which heresies those two bishops consulted Augustine about, he remained entirely silent. But if they had consulted him about the Priscillianist heresy and its errors—or if Augustine, at the request of those two bishops, had written that little book and the anathemas—what need would Orosius have had to publish hastily and heap together all the trees of perdition with their roots and branches? Was not everything necessary for the destruction of that heresy contained either in that profession of faith or little book, or in the eighteen—or twenty-six—anathemas?

Furthermore, Quesnellus supposes that if those two bishops had appealed to Augustine in this matter, Augustine either satisfied them by replying to them or did not. But by either alternative he cuts his own throat. For if the first is granted, he is compelled to admit that, when Augustine was consulted again by Orosius on the same matter, Augustine did not refer him to that profession of faith and to those anathemas which he had composed at the request of Bishops Eutropius and Paul. He would certainly have referred him to them, just as he refers him to the reading of certain works published against the Manichaeans: “which you have read,” he says, “or will be able to read.” Why, then, does he admit that Augustine learned from Orosius what the Priscillianists believed, and that those most fabulous ravings had already been convicted among the Spaniards? But it has now been demonstrated, I think with the utmost clarity, that Augustine was not consulted by Eutropius and Paul about the errors of the Priscillianists, nor did he ever write anything on this matter to those bishops.

### 6

Yet, in truth, although I have written much about this little book of faith, I still seem to have accomplished nothing if, in the judgment of the most distinguished men and by the authority of manuscript copies, it were assigned exclusively to Augustine. Who, indeed, would not consider me a charming trifler, when, after examining one after another the works of Augustine in which that celebrated profession of faith neither agrees nor coheres, this single work alone remained—the one on which Quesnellus relies above all? Surely the ancient codex of the Roman canons, the *Master of the Sentences*, ancient and more recent copies, and the Louvain doctors—from all of whom Quesnellus himself borrowed the arguments for his conjectures—ought to be given credence [Col. 1053B]. But in a matter of such importance I shall not need to expend much effort if, in opposition to the judgment of the Parisian doctor, I set what the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur pronounced in the latest Paris edition of Augustine’s works.

They therefore relegated that profession of faith, together with the anathemas appended to it, which was entitled under the name of sermon 233, *On the Catholic Faith*, to the appendix of the fourth class, and judged it altogether unworthy of Augustine’s name. What judgment they passed on this sermon, we set out here. For it refutes most thoroughly each and every one of Quesnellus’s little arguments, except the one which they believe pertains to the pseudo-codex of the Roman Canons [Note: [Col. 1053] Vol. V, in the appendix of class 4, p. 272; formerly *On Time*, sermon 129, now *On Various Matters*, 233.]:

> “It is placed here in the appendix for the first time. In the Louvain edition its status is doubtful, whereas in the judgment of Verlini and Vindingi it is spurious. With the exception of the fourteen later anathemas, which were transferred here from the profession of the Catholic faith of Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch, it is nothing other than the little book of faith which is entitled as follows in the codex of the Canons of the Roman Church, chapter 40: *Augustine’s little book on the Catholic Faith against all heresies*. It is also found inserted, with some variation among the anathemas, in the Acts of the First Council of Toledo of the year 400. The Master of the Sentences cites it under Augustine’s name in book III, distinction 21, perhaps from that same Roman codex. For indeed, in the manuscripts we have nowhere seen this little book among Augustine’s sermons and minor works.
>
> “These modes of expression certainly seem less like Augustine to us: in section 1, ‘that this is the one Trinity of the divine name’; likewise, ‘not an imaginary body, or one composed of form alone’; likewise, ‘and to have experienced all the functions of the body—or, as the Roman codex reads, the *exitia*, “destructions”—’;” and in section 2, ‘that this world was not made, together with all its instruments’; finally, the word *Paraclete* is repeatedly used for the Holy Spirit. Estius, in book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 21, section 3, suspects that it was published by a writer inclined toward the Nestorians, whose error certain statements can accommodate, especially the fifth anathema.”

Thus far the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur in their edition of the said sermon [Col. 1053D].

### 7

As I go through and transcribe these matters—which contribute remarkably to our case—I am seized with great astonishment at the profound silence that the Maurist Fathers maintained, both here and elsewhere, concerning Quesnellus’s trifles. These ought by no means to have been concealed, since Quesnellus himself had hoped that those same Fathers, in the new edition of Augustine’s works on which they were then engaged, would support him and his conjectures. No learned person will fail to recognize that he indicated this plainly in the following words. After a long series of so many and such great arguments, he concludes that eighth chapter of his dissertation *On Libelli* as follows:

> “We expect more, and things worthy of so learned a man, concerning this little book from the Reverend Father Lord François Delfau [Col. 1054A], Benedictine ascetic, in the edition of Augustine’s works which he is preparing together with his colleagues of the monastery of Saint-Germain.”

Nor do I dare to maintain that those learned and studious men failed to offer fitting testimonies to their learning and sincerity of mind. But what displeases me greatly is that, in the celebrated preface to sermon 129, now 233, they seem almost to support Quesnellus by maintaining that that codex of the canons belongs to the Roman Church which they understood to be filled with monuments borrowed from various places, corrupted, and interpolated. We do not think that men renowned for piety and learning deliberately wished to lend assistance to Quesnellus in this matter. Quesnellus, always driven by the interests of his own studies, diminished the authority of the Roman Church, especially by gradually attempting to show that in its decrees and constitutions it had become the dependent follower of other particular Churches, borrowing now one monument or decree, now another, from them and adapting these materials to its own use. We consider it wrong to suspect that such men deliberately wished to follow this course.

Nevertheless, by using one or two words there, they could at least have warned the reader that the codex which Quesnellus published under the name of the Roman Church was attributed to an uncertain author and was altogether of doubtful reliability—or that this was the view of those who possessed not only a more discerning critical judgment but also some preliminary acquaintance with the basic elements and instruction of ecclesiastical history and theology.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the Asturicensian, Celenensian, and Bracarensian synods held in the kingdoms of Galicia by decree of the Apostolic See, or approved with its support

### 1

Let us now at last, setting aside the conjectures and trifles of Paschasius Quesnellus, turn our discourse to the other councils held in the kingdom of Galicia with the support or command of the holy pontiff. Since I am uncertain of the truth because of the scarcity or loss of ancient documents, I prefer to rely on the statements and observations of others rather than bring forward something new. Such, indeed, is the matter of which Idatius made notable mention in his *Chronicle*.

In the city of Asturica in Galicia, certain Manichaeans who had been in hiding for some years were exposed through episcopal proceedings; these proceedings were sent by Bishops Idatius and Turribius, who had heard them, to Antonius, bishop of Mérida. I am now uncertain whether to give my assent to Stephen Baluzius, the collectors of councils, Quesnellus, and other learned men, who judged that the word “Manichaeans” here implied and designated Priscillianists. For Idatius, the author of that *Chronicle*, certainly knew that there was a very great distinction between Priscillianists and Manichaeans, as we have explained in these dissertations.

But my uncertainty is increased by the following preceding words: “Certain Manichaeans who had been in hiding for some years.” We proved in our first two books, which we wrote on the Manichaeans under Leo the Great and from the Acts of the Roman Inquisition, that it was the Manichaeans—not the Priscillianists—who were accustomed to seek hiding places and darkness. Yet who could persuade himself that the Priscillianists, who by the very character of their conduct were utterly shameless, feared the light and were accustomed to inhabit secluded places, especially at the time when civil and ecclesiastical affairs in Galicia were being turned upside down? Moreover, when the offshoots of the Priscillianists had multiplied in those regions to such an extent that many even from the clerical and priestly orders were found to have been corrupted, how could these people ever have remained hidden?

Finally, what presses my mind into still greater uncertainty in this matter is that Idatius himself adds in his *Chronicle* that among these heretics was a certain Pascentius of the city of Rome, who had fled from Asturica as a Manichaean; Bishop Antonius of Mérida seized him and, after hearing him, also had him expelled from the province of Lusitania. Now, if we recall what we find recorded concerning the city of Rome both in the *Annals* and in the ancient sacred monuments, we shall nowhere discover that Priscillianists hid or lingered there. But that Manichaeans arriving from Africa, under Pope Siricius, sought refuges for themselves in the City, prepared hiding places, and held frequent sacrilegious gatherings of sexual depravity, to which Roman men and women used to be summoned and assemble as “the elect” and “the elect women,” is thoroughly established.

Although they remained in that city until approximately the fourth or fifth year of the pontificate of Saint Leo the Great, it nevertheless came about by divine providence that, through public proscriptions by the Church and the magistrates, they were driven into exile beyond the borders of Italy. We may at least suspect that Idatius intended to suggest this when speaking of Pascentius, the Roman Manichaean, for he wrote: “Bishop Antonius of Mérida seized him and, after hearing him, also had him expelled from the province of Lusitania.” Although the particle *etiam* (“also”) may indicate that Pascentius had undergone the punishment of exile more than once, these words can appropriately be understood of exile from the City, especially since he fled from the city of Asturica rather than being exiled from it.

### 2

The conjectures advanced thus far acquire their greatest strength both from the period to which the Council of Asturica must be assigned 274 and from the previously mentioned letter of Saint Leo the Great to Turribius. For that council was convened in the year 446, and the Manichaeans were expelled from all parts of Italy in the preceding year, 445, as is also clearly demonstrated by the novella of Valentinian. It is probable that they then withdrew to Spain and Galicia, since non-Catholic rulers governed those kingdoms.

Moreover, Leo wrote his letter to Turribius in the year 447, and the holy Leo addressed each of the questions placed before him. Do they think that the holy pontiff would have said nothing about this Council of Asturica if it had been convened against the Priscillianists? For Turribius consulted Leo not about the Manichaean errors but about the errors of the Priscillianists. Therefore, if he had transmitted the Acts of the council, together with a synodal letter, to the Apostolic See—and if Saint Leo had approved or rejected those Acts, or at least made some mention of them—especially since both in the opening and at the end of the letter he goes out of his way to praise Saint Turribius and advises him to hold either one general synod or several provincial synods, both to cleanse the stains of the Priscillianists and to restrain their wickedness and shamelessness, then, since he does not utter even a single word about the Council of Asturica already convened, who would rationally wish to flatter himself that it had acted against the Priscillianists?

Moved, therefore, by these most powerful arguments, I am more inclined to conjecture that the council praised by Idatius and convened in the year 446 attacked the Manichaeans.

### 3

Whether, however, that synod acted against the offspring of the Manichaeans or against the followers of Priscillian, it must in no way be doubted that the command of Saint Leo [Col. 1055D] cannot refer to it, but rather to another council convened in the kingdom of Galicia after Turribius had received the holy pontiff’s letter together with the resolutions of all the questions proposed.

After receiving this letter from Turribius and considering the serious obstacles that delayed the convening of a general synod, the bishops of the province of Galicia themselves deliberated about convening a particular council. In what city these bishops assembled has not yet been established with certainty. Severinus Binius persuades himself that the gathering was convened in the municipality of Celenum, near the city of Lugo, under the presidency of Balconius, bishop of the Church of Braga and metropolitan of Galicia. The preface of Lucretius to the First Council of Braga plainly supports this opinion.

But it does not agree with the words of Saint Leo, by which he entrusts Idatius and Ceponius, as distinguished by metropolitan authority, with the care and burden of assembling the bishops: “Our brothers Idatius and Ceponius shall attend to their assembly.” If, therefore, according to the holy pontiff, metropolitan dignity and honor were attributed to Idatius and Ceponius, what reason could there have been for the bishops of the four provinces of Spain to send the rule of faith which they had composed themselves to Balconius of Braga, rather than to those two men?

Certainly, if we do not wish to invent a third metropolitan in the province of Galicia, we must say that one or the other of those two bishops had died by the time that Bracarensian synod was convened, over which Balconius presided. Quesnellus reasons on grounds not without merit that Ceponius, not Idatius, had occupied this see before Balconius. But even if we grant this, the see of Idatius remains uncertain.

Sigibertus makes him bishop of the city of Lemica in his *Chronicle*. On this account, besides the metropolitan of Lugo and another metropolitan of Braga, we would be compelled to admit a third, namely the bishop of Lemica. When Quesnellus noticed this consequence, he wrote:

> “Therefore Idatius seems to have been metropolitan of Lugo, although Sigibertus makes him bishop of Lemica. But he seems to confuse two Idatii: one who lived in the time of Leo and was the author of the *Chronicle*, and another, formerly an accuser of Priscillian, who truly was bishop of Lemica.”

Seeking to explain the cause of this error, he asserts that it arose because the later Idatius declares in the preface to his *Chronicle* that he was born in the city of Lemica. But if he had obtained that bishopric, he would not have failed to mention it in that passage. Yet the same Quesnellus adds:

> “He seems to indicate his metropolitan dignity when he says in the same place that he was appointed head of the highest office.”

And at the end of the aforementioned preface he mourns, with such lamentation, the deformed state of the ecclesiastical order in the province of Galicia, as though it had particularly belonged to him, as the head of the province, to remedy and assist it in the exercise of his office:

> “To meet and assist, in the exercise of his office, the indiscriminate appointments and the almost universal decline in divine discipline.”

### 4

Relying, therefore, on these and similar conjectures in a matter enveloped in the greatest darkness, Quesnellus does not conceal his view that two synods were held in the province of Galicia for the destruction of the Priscillianists: one at Lugo and the other in the city of Braga. Ancient documents do not report whether the two provincial councils summoned by Leo’s command achieved a fortunate and successful outcome; moreover, their Acts have perished through the passage and ravages of time.

But if we are permitted to reason from the surviving records of the Church, we must believe that this heresy was not then completely extinguished and abolished in the kingdom of Galicia. For although Turribius, Idatius, Ceponius, Balconius, and other bishops restrained it through synodal proceedings, so that while they were alive and Leo the Great survived the Priscillianists did not dare to raise their head too boldly, it is nevertheless known that, after other years had passed, their revived errors again sprouted in those regions.

Before we remove our pen from the page, we shall briefly settle in the following chapter what remains to be said about the Priscillianist heresy.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### The latest Acts of the Church of Braga for abolishing certain surviving remnants of Priscillian’s error

### 1

The ancient monuments of Christianity make it sufficiently clear that the offspring of the Priscillianists, although attacked in so many and such varied ways by Roman pontiffs and other most holy bishops, as well as by synods and secular rulers, had not yet been extinguished or entirely abolished in the five hundredth year of Christ. For the poisons of this impiety and shamelessness, which here and there had corrupted the hearts, faith, and religion of many men and women in the kingdoms of Spain and Galicia, the sacred Catholic pastors were unable, within a short period, either to purge or remedy [Note: [Col. 1055] [[Col. 1055] This note appears at the foot of column 1055, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text.] Quesnellus, in his notes and observations on Epistle 15 of Saint Leo.] [Col. 1057A].

Thus, although for some time those seeds of sacrilege and blasphemy appeared to lie hidden through the efforts of the bishops, nevertheless, as the sixth century of the Church was advancing, they burst forth again into the light, especially in the kingdom of Galicia. Profuturus, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Braga, learned of this with the greatest sorrow of heart—as may be believed. After first carrying out the statutes of the Apostolic See and of the provincial synods, he again consulted that same Apostolic See by letters in the year 538, because new circumstances had arisen, which we shall soon explain.

### 2

The survivors who were then polluted by the Priscillianist stain in the kingdom of Galicia abstained from eating meat under the assumed guise of religious piety and Christian abstinence. Since Bishop Profuturus knew very well that they did this not from devotion but from a spirit of execration, he referred the matter to the Apostolic See, asking whether they were to be punished with the same anathemas by which the statutes of the holy Fathers had formerly taken action against the Manichaeans for the same crime [Col. 1057B].

At that time Pope Vigilius governed the Roman Apostolic See of Saint Peter. He immediately responded to Profuturus’s consultations and first condemned the superstition of those who believed that some food was polluted by contact with meat, because, he adds, “of all those things which the mercy of God has provided for human nourishment, nothing is judged unclean for Catholics” [Note: [Col. 1057D] Pope Vigilius, letter to Profuturus of Braga, chapter 1.].

Therefore, to provide fuller instruction to this bishop of Braga and to strengthen the decrees of the Apostolic See, he brings forward those scriptural sources by which we are taught that errors of this kind must be avoided. One such passage is what Paul wrote to Titus [Note: [Col. 1057D] Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, verse 15]: “All things are clean to the clean,” and so forth. Another is the passage in the First Epistle to Timothy [Note: [Col. 1057D] First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4, verses 1 and following]: “In the last times some shall depart from the faith,” and so forth. Finally, there is what we read in Saint Matthew the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1057D] Matthew 15:16–17]: “It is not what enters into the mouth that defiles a person, but the things that proceed from the mouth—these are what defile a person” [Col. 1057C].

Relying on these and similar testimonies of Scripture, the Fathers who preceded Vigilius judged that those in particular must be condemned who, while abstaining from eating meat, also believed that things which appeared to have been mixed with meat had to be avoided. When Vigilius wrote these words, divine providence brought it about that he used a formula of speech which would deprive malicious men and more recent sectarians of every weapon. Accordingly, he did not condemn abstinence intended to restrain the unbridled passions of our body—abstinence which the entire assembly of the holy Fathers affirms to be supremely pleasing to God.

For this reason, it is clear that the Church, both during vigils and during Lent, has reasonably prescribed a selection and discrimination of foods. But he teaches that those people must be expelled from the fellowship of Catholics because they wickedly and superstitiously recoiled from the Lord’s creatures. Therefore, he says:

> “We neither condemn abstinence that is pleasing to God, nor do we receive into our fellowship those who execrate the Lord’s creature” [Note: [Col. 1057D] Pope Vigilius, ibid., chapter 1. This remarkably agrees with the testimonies of Leo the Great in his sermons on the fast of the four seasons of the year and of Lent.] [Col. 1058D].

### 3

But the sacrilegious mind of the Priscillianists had devised another novel form of error concerning the mystery of the Trinity, although the Fathers of Toledo, Braga, and Lugo had already composed and promulgated professions of faith in the preceding councils, in order to preach and confess one substance, nature, power, and authority in the three divine persons.

Therefore, in order to overturn this doctrine, the Priscillianists and the offspring of other heretics corrupted the hymn of glorification which the Catholic Church had anciently established to be sung at the end of the Psalms, omitting one or another syllable of conjunction and saying: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, to the Holy Spirit.” The holy pontiff declares that this was a new form of error; at the same time he writes that the aim of those heretics was to teach that the Son and the Holy Spirit were only one person.

But to convict this error, it is sufficient, says Vigilius, that the Lord Jesus Christ, indicating that baptism was to be celebrated in the invocation of the Trinity, said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 1058D] Vigilius, ibid., chapter 2.]. These words show that he commanded those three persons to be named with equal distinctions [Note: [Col. 1058D] Matthew 28:19. Compare Saint Leo’s sermon on Pentecost.].

### 4

Besides these two questions, which concerned the errors of the Priscillianists, Profuturus also submitted others for discussion concerning the baptism of the Arians, the restoration and consecration of Churches, and the day fixed that year for celebrating the feasts of Easter and Pentecost [Col. 1058B].

But that consultation or question is certainly famous in which, responding in fifth place, the Roman pontiff prescribes that the ancient order of ecclesiastical discipline concerning the divine prayers to be recited in the Masses should be maintained. In this chapter we encounter many and varied statements which expose the falsifications of more recent innovators and critics concerning the canonical prayers and the festivals of God’s saints. I would willingly examine all of them if the matters imposed upon me to discuss did not interrupt the thread of this history of the Priscillianist heresy too greatly.

For the present, however, I judged that one point must by no means be omitted: namely, that bishops in the more remote parts of the world were accustomed to depend so entirely upon the commands and instructions of the Apostolic See that they referred to it not only matters concerning the determination of faith and episcopal affairs, but also matters relating to festivals, the solemn celebrations and feast days of God’s saints; with equal submission of mind they requested that these things be decided and prescribed.

When I reflected on this, I was easily led to the conviction that the rule of the canonical prayers had originally proceeded from the Apostolic See, at least in the West, and that no Church or minister of the ecclesiastical order dared to depart from it. This can be confirmed especially from that very ancient fragment of Saint Leo’s letter to Turribius which we mentioned above and which we have now decided to publish.

Finally, Pope Vigilius sent this order of the canonical prayers, received from apostolic tradition, together with this letter to Bishop Profuturus, so that he might understand what was to be followed in the festivals:

> “Therefore we have also sent below the text of the canonical prayer itself, which, by God’s favor, we have received from apostolic tradition. And so that Your Charity may know at which points you should connect anything suitable to the festivals, we have likewise appended the prayers of Easter Day.”

### 5

But to demonstrate the reverence and submission of all Churches and bishops toward the Apostolic See in every kind of matter, I think it unnecessary to dwell on this further. Vigilius himself, without any ambiguity of expression or falsification of the truth, briefly tracing the footsteps of his predecessors and the privileges of his see, proclaims, with the agreement of all believers, that the Roman Church is the foundation and pattern of all Churches.

“For,” he says, “although the election of all the apostles was equal, nevertheless it was granted to blessed Peter that he should excel all the others.” After a few intervening remarks, while discussing the principal prerogatives of the Roman Church, he asserts that it possesses primacy over all Churches in such a way [Col. 1059A] that the highest affairs, judgments, and complaints of bishops, as well as the more important questions of the Churches, must always be referred to it as to their head.

The rights established concerning the prerogative of primacy, concerning appeals from the judgments of bishops to the Apostolic See, and concerning matters reserved to that same Apostolic See as major cases, Pope Vigilius reviewed both in the passage cited and throughout the remainder of his letter. But since all these matters are well known to Catholic and highly learned men, I have decided for the present to pass them over in silence and instead to state the reasons for which anyone might be able to accuse something in that letter of fabrication.

### 6

First, what they might object on the basis of the letter’s heading must be considered devoid of force. They might say that even in ancient printed copies it bears the name of Eucherius or Eleutherius. Cardinal de Aguirre certainly did not deny this; he taught that the letter should be addressed to Profuturus, metropolitan bishop of Galicia and bishop of Braga. But what follows from this objection [Col. 1059B]? No lapse or negligence on the part of copyists could in any way harm a truth that is thoroughly established [Note: [Col. 1059D] Cardinal Aguirre, *Hispanic Councils* I, II, p. 228.].

Therefore, the learning of those who try to draw arguments for spuriousness and falsity from the corrupted title and heading of some document must be judged imprudent and utterly futile. Such copyists’ errors were exceedingly common and almost conventional, especially in transcribing the proper names of persons and places, as can be seen in manuscript copies of every period and language.

What concerns our present matter is that, in place of Eucherius or Eleutherius, the name Profuturus must be read, as the majority of manuscript codices of the finest quality have it. The catalogues of the bishops of Braga, the lists of Roman consuls, and finally the Acts of the Council of Braga held shortly afterward make this entirely unambiguous.

Indeed, several manuscript codices—the very ancient one from Lyon and two older Colbertine manuscripts, of the highest repute, from one of which the celebrated Stephen Baluzius transcribed this letter—have the name Profuturus [Col. 1059C]. That he was a bishop of Braga is testified by the first Acts of that council. Hence there is scarcely any room for doubt that he consulted the Apostolic See both about the Priscillianists and about all those other questions during the time of Pope Vigilius, and that Pope Vigilius sent him the letters in question.

“Concerning the day and year,” says the eminent Aguirre, “on which it was given, I think it useless to dispute, since the Colbertine codex establishes that it was written in the year in which John was consul after Belisarius—that is, in the year 538.”

### 7
