But if, in the second place, it should still be objected that at least the final chapter of that letter smells of spuriousness and falsity, because it discusses the primacy of the Roman Church, I would press the point already made. I could not be moved by the claim of our opponents that this chapter is absent from various codices of Gaul or that it is found only in the Pseudo-Isidorian collection [Col. 1059D].

For, first of all, this letter was written to the metropolitan of Galicia. “And therefore far greater credence must be given to all the other ancient manuscript codices of Spain, examined and collated by the most illustrious Loaysa, as well as to the printed copies, in which that chapter concerning the primacy of the Roman Church is present, than to the single Colbertine manuscript. There may be a considerable suspicion that the latter was written in Gaul at a time when the cases of bishops appealing to the Apostolic See were being debated, especially toward the end of the ninth century, under Pope Nicholas I, and later in the case of Gerbert of Rheims, near the end of the tenth century.

“For it could easily have happened that those who, in opposition to Hincmar of Laon and Rothad of Soissons, bishops appealing to the Apostolic See, were attempting to deprive the See itself of episcopal judgments, mutilated Vigilius’s letter by cutting away the chapter in which they themselves were struck down.”

Thus far Cardinal Aguirre in the passage cited above. The most recent editors of the Councils used arguments of this kind in their notes on the aforementioned letter of Vigilius, vol. V, p. 1290.

Nor would we need to say so much in refuting those two objections if we undertook to appeal to the authority of the Vatican manuscript copies. Several copies of this letter do indeed exist in that Apostolic Library, and they exhibit both the genuine name Profuturus and the chapter concerning the primacy of the Roman Church. They prove conclusively that the celebrated letter has suffered no injury whatsoever.

8. But if so many and such great supports did not assist this embattled truth, might anyone still suspect this letter of falsity and forgery? Away with such fabrication! Truth claims for itself far greater and more certain arguments from the testimony of the Bracarensian Acts and from the agreement of those Fathers whom Cardinal Aguirre, Baluze, and the editors of the Councils ought especially to have followed, and whose testimony they ought not merely to have glanced over or mentioned lightly.

Those Fathers, then, as we saw above, assembled in the year of Our Lord 563, when Pope John III already held the helm of the Apostolic See and Ariamirus, or Theodomirus, a king of Suevic stock, administered the civil affairs of Galicia and Lusitania. For a long time before they assembled, they had desired that a priestly gathering should be held among themselves, so that they might thoroughly purge the contagion of the Priscillianist heresy. Therefore they say:

“Now, then, since our most glorious and pious son, with the Lord’s favor resting upon him, has granted us by royal command the day of this gathering that we desired, let us sit down together and, if it pleases you, first investigate the statutes of the Catholic faith.”

That this gathering began on the first day of May is made clear by the following notice:

“The Second Council of Braga, held in the third year of King Ariamirus, on the Kalends of May.”

[Note: The Second Council of Braga is found in vol. VI of the Councils, p. 515.]

From what statutes of the Catholic faith that council had begun, we have already explained most fully above, when attacking Quesnellus, who was attempting with excessive confidence to wrest away the profession of faith drawn up by the Fathers of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica at the command of Pope Leo, so that he might attribute it to an entirely uncertain author. Therefore, so as not to repeat what has already been done, we undertake to examine another part of that council, in which the Fathers spoke at length both about Profuturus, bishop of the Church of Braga, and about the primacy and rights of the Roman pontiffs.

9. Accordingly, for the instruction of the entire clerical order, Lucretius ordered the earlier canons of the Church to be read aloud—those which general and provincial synods had composed as a safeguard for ecclesiastical discipline and for the dignity of sacred rites and the ministers of the Church. When all the other bishops immediately supported this proposal, they considered it necessary and very useful first to appeal to those ordinances which had once been sent from the Apostolic See of Saint Peter in response to Profuturus, his predecessor of revered memory.

The Fathers of this council therefore acknowledged that Bishop Profuturus had occupied the Bracarensian throne before Lucretius and had received from the Apostolic See of Saint Peter regulations for abolishing the surviving remnants of Priscillianist superstition. Wishing gladly to adhere to their request, Lucretius immediately replied:

“Your fraternity has rightly recalled the authority of the See.”

And, with everyone listening, he added:

“The authority of the Apostolic See once sent to Profuturus, the bishop, has been reread; because of its length it has not been inserted into these Acts.”

No one can doubt that this refers to the apostolic constitution of Vigilius. For the twenty-two chapters appended and defined there rest equally upon it, just as the preceding canons and anathemas were borrowed from the letter of Saint Leo to Turibius, which they cited.

In composing these new chapters, therefore, they set themselves this principal aim: namely, to abolish the rites, ceremonies, and every profane discipline derived from Priscillianist perversity. For those impious and sacrilegious men had not merely corrupted and undermined Catholic doctrines; they had also perverted the order of the divine offices and canonical hours. Even on the more solemn days and during vigils, they recited special readings in the celebration of Masses. They had departed from that apostolic tradition which prescribes the formula for greeting the people during the sacred mysteries. They did not observe the same order and form in completing the sacrifice and administering baptism. They publicly sang in the Church other psalms and other poetically composed writings besides those contained in the New and Old Testaments. Finally, not all the ministers of the clerical order ate meat.

Therefore, in chapter 14, they decreed:

“To cut off suspicion of the Priscillianist heresy, they must be compelled at least to taste cooked vegetables with meat; but if they refuse”—they add—“then, according to what the holy Fathers established of old concerning such persons, they must, because of suspicion of this heresy, be excommunicated from office and removed in every way.”

These things, and others of the same kind that I could add, are exceedingly clear. They reveal the primacy and prerogatives of the Apostolic See and prove the submission of mind and obedience that bishops from the most distant regions fulfilled in word and deed toward the Roman pontiffs.

280 10. The Spaniards themselves have at all times gloried in this obedience and in the sacred bond of union with the Roman Church, as, after Cardinals Baronius and Aguirre, the most distinguished and eminent cultivator of the best branches of learning, Don Ildefonsus Clemente de Arostegui—most recently one of the twelve jurist-judges of causes in the Roman forum for the kingdom of Castile in this noble city—has testified.

[Note: Cardinal Baronius, vol. VI, under the year 447. Cardinal Aguirre, vol. II of the Spanish Councils. Ildefonsus Clemente de Arostegui, in his Exhortation on Cultivating the History of the Spanish Church, p. 111 and following. See also Francisco Gervesius’s dissertation, p. 104.]

For, with the purpose of enlarging and embellishing the history of the Spanish Church, he composed at Rome, on 21 August 1747, an exhortation to the Spaniards, in order to stir them up to literary studies for the honor and benefit of their country. Among other things that he calls to the minds of the men of his nation is this: “Since from the earliest age of the Roman Church and of Spain there has been the closest union and fellowship between them, I was certain that in this city the principal records and monuments relating to our history are preserved.” A little below he adds: “Here, then, I thought that the origins and dignity of the individual Churches could easily be found; here their union, divisions, and transfer; here the Acts of councils, appeals of bishops, and decrees of the most holy pontiffs.”

When I considered these words, I was led to hope that this present work of mine, such as it is, would not prove unwelcome either to him or to any others engaged in the study of Christian affairs. For, in composing these Exercises, I have already treated various matters that most certainly disclose that very close bond, union, and fellowship with the Roman Church; and I have explained others which, as the order of matters and the method of writing itself required, can furnish not weak or doubtful arguments for understanding the ancient condition, dignities, and prerogatives of those Churches.

Since, therefore, I have at length brought to completion those matters which seemed to concern the cause and errors of the Priscillianists and the councils convened against them, and which in this affair of the greatest importance could vindicate the rights and authority of the Apostolic See from the calumnies of its detractors, I shall attempt in the following and final chapter only to remove two very slight difficulties drawn from the text and narratives of this council—difficulties which aroused in Paschasius Quesnellus and others the greatest eagerness for disputation, as we shall presently see.

# CHAPTER XIX AND LAST

Paschasius Quesnellus wrongly supposed that there were two Turibii in Leo’s time. To what year of Christ the Council of Braga discussed above should chiefly be assigned.

1. In reviewing the sequence of the Bracarensian Acts, Paschasius Quesnellus fell into the opinion that, besides that Turibius of Astorga of whom we spoke above, there was another man of this name, who performed the office of notary of the Apostolic See and carried Leo’s letters to the synod of Galicia. The words of Lucretius, speaking in the praised synod of Braga, gave occasion for this controversy: “I believe that the fraternity of your blessedness knows that, at the time when the poisons of the most wicked sect of the Priscillianists were spreading through these regions, the most blessed Pope Leo of the city of Rome, who was about the fortieth successor of the Apostle Peter, sent his writings through Turibius, notary of his See, to the synod of Galicia against the impious sect of the Priscillianist heresy.”

If these words were to be explained of Turibius of Astorga, they would contain a falsehood. For, since he was a bishop, he can neither be called a notary of the Apostolic See nor be assigned such a duty as to carry letters like a courier to the synod of Galicia. Foreseeing that this question could be raised, Baronius asserts that there was only one Turibius. Ambrosius Morales, a historian of Spain not to be despised, was the first to oppose him, maintaining that two Turibii must altogether be distinguished: one held the bishopric of Astorga, and Saint Leo the Great addressed letters to him; the other was the man through whom the holy pontiff wrote to the bishops of Spain, who was sent from Rome into Spain to deliver the praised letters. Quesnellus adopted this opinion and, indulging himself excessively, attacks the most eminent writer of the Annals and attempts to overturn his two arguments as slight and feeble, or as containing a portent of falsehood.

[Note: Quesnellus, vol. II of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 445.]

At present we cannot have leisure enough to report individually the things that Quesnellus invents by way of addition for this controversy. Such are these: “It was not always customary in letters to write the names of those by whom they were conveyed.” Leo had replied to Turibius through the same deacon Pervincius from whom he had received the inquiries. “But he ought to have sent to the synod of Galicia not a foreign cleric, but some messenger detached from his own entourage; and this office could very suitably belong to the other Turibius, not a bishop but merely a notary of the Roman See.” These assertions, I say, and others of this kind Quesnellus piles up too laboriously and magnifies grandly in order to distinguish two Turibii. Moreover, since he perceived that Baronius pressed him with the Leonine text, he tried to turn his weapons against him, maintaining that this most learned cardinal of the Roman Church and father of the Ecclesiastical Annals had forgotten “what difference there is between a bishop attending to ecclesiastical affairs with priestly concern, and a deacon or notary carrying out a bishop’s commands by order and carrying letters hither and thither like a courier.”

2. This would indeed seem a neat argument to those perhaps who, wishing to flatter Quesnellus, seek only to touch the outward surface of things. But what could be more foolish or more trifling? Does priestly concern, then, as Quesnellus says, disgrace a bishop if he conveys to the synod of his province letters received from the Apostolic See? Would he not be attending to the affairs of his Church by carrying out such pontifical commands? But let our learned critic and annotator say, pray: did Leo’s letters concern the affairs of African, Indian, or other Eastern peoples, or rather the ecclesiastical affairs of that same kingdom of Galicia, and indeed Turibius’s own diocese, already shamefully shaken on every side by the Priscillianist heresy? The matter is altogether evident. For Turibius, desiring to remedy the evils of his diocese and of Galicia, consulted and appealed to Leo, seeking from him those decrees and rules that would cleanse and destroy the Priscillianist pestilence. What wonder, then, if the holy pontiff, meeting all this bishop’s requests, entrusted to him the cases of clerics infected with that taint for presentation to the provincial synod, and charged him with circular letters concerning the convocation of the synod of Galicia?

This procedure was certainly more expedient both for restraining the Priscillianists and for extirpating abuses that had entered either into the ordinations of sacred ministers or had corrupted sacred rites and ecclesiastical discipline. For that deacon Pervincius of Astorga, who had come to Rome with Turibius’s letters and was afterwards returning home, could readily carry not only the responses to the inquiries already made but also the letters addressed to the other bishops of that province. There was no need for the supreme pontiff, to whom Turibius’s zeal for faith and religion was especially well known, to compel anyone else of the Roman clergy to undertake so long and laborious a journey. Leo’s following words plainly show that he followed this procedure: “Accordingly, we have given letters to our brethren and fellow bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia, and have appointed for them a council of a general synod.” Let Quesnellus’s adherents attend, I pray, to what follows: “It will pertain to the care of your love that the authority of our ordinance be conveyed to the bishops of the aforesaid provinces.”

3. I now ask Ambrosius Morales and Quesnellus: how could it pertain to the care of Turibius of Astorga that Leo’s ordinances or decrees should safely reach all the bishops of those provinces, unless he had delivered them, to be entrusted together with this letter to Turibius’s fidelity, to the deacon Pervincius as he returned home? Since I can see no other meaning that Leo’s words can bear, I am readily led to conclude that this same Turibius of Astorga was called by the Bracarensian Fathers notary of the Apostolic See because the written ordinances of pontifical authority had been entrusted to his fidelity. It chiefly devolved upon him to write back to Saint Leo whether it would be easy for all the bishops of those four provinces to assemble in one general council, or whether at least the bishops of Galicia, with Ceponius and Hydatius acting, would more quickly gather in a provincial assembly to apply a remedy to such great wounds.

As for Quesnellus’s addition, “The term notary is never used in ecclesiastical monuments in the sense attached to it by that author”—namely Baronius—“who endeavors to report and make known to the Roman See what is done in the provinces”: here we might appeal to the best Latin writers, who used the word notary to denote those accustomed to record the affairs of the Church in public registers. Why, then, could this duty not have been entrusted to Turibius by the Apostolic See? What violation of episcopal rights would there have been in exercising it, when the good of the Christian commonwealth was at stake, and especially of that province in which the Roman pontiff had ordered a council to be held?

4. Moreover, I still do not see why “we are compelled,” as Quesnellus says, “to recognize three entirely distinct letters of Leo, partly from Leo himself and partly from the intervention of Lucretius of Braga, but are not likewise compelled to think that they were sent at the same time.” Mere trifles. For if we imagine that those different letters of Leo were not sent at the same time, neither would the council of Galicia have to be assigned to the year 447, as Hydatius’s Chronicle records and as all ecclesiastical writers agree.

[Note: Letter to Turibius, chapter 17, near the end.]

For Leo’s first letter was written on the Kalends of August of that year, and, as we have often said, the holy pontiff gave it to the deacon Pervincius as he returned home. We should therefore have to imagine that he had wings, if we were not to judge rashly that within a short interval Pervincius reached Galicia, then other messengers returned to Rome with letters, and still others went back from the city of Rome to Galicia. Quesnellus labored excessively to establish this portent of invention, along with various other futile conjectures, gradually to insinuate into his readers his opinion about two Turibii.

5. Let us now at last pass over these things and others of the same kind, taking the final step of investigating the true date of the Bracarensian synod. In this matter it will seem sufficient, briefly recounting the opinions of others, to await the judgment of readers rather than strive to decide the matter itself. Severinus Binius, then, following the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, held that this Council of Braga was convened in the year of Christ 563; the most eminent Cardinal Aguirre, collector of the councils of Spain, agreed with him. But Garsias Loaysa dissented and affirmed that it was summoned two years earlier, namely in 561, persuading himself that the Fathers met at Braga not under Prince Ariamirus but under Theodomirus. All writers have affirmed that he was the king of the Suevi whose wonderful conversion from Arian error and impiety was especially treated by Saint Gregory of Tours.

[Note: Gregory of Tours, book V, chapters 11 and 37.]

But Cardinal Baronius has already proved from the most certain documents that both names were attributed to the same king and that no error had entered the manuscripts; Binius and the most learned Petavius, in part three of the *Rationarium Temporum*, agree with him.

[Note: Dionysius Petavius, vol. III, *Rationarium Temporum*, and others.]

Antonius Pagius, having presented both Baronius’s and Garsias’s opinions, reports that the Bollandists, under 20 March in the Life of Saint Martin of Dumio, affirm that the First Council of Braga was rightly dated by Garsias to the year of Christ 561. But, Pagius adds, this opinion has against it Gregory of Tours, a contemporary of Saint Martin of Dumio. He offers various arguments drawn here and there from Gregory of Tours’s writings which would rather show that the date of that council should be sought in the year 549, or the following year. “Nevertheless,” he says, “because Gregory is not infrequently mistaken in reporting what was done outside Gaul, I think one should not depart from Garsias, a Spanish writer.” Finally, he observes that a letter of Pope Innocent III provides grounds for saying that the council of which we speak was convened earlier still, namely in the year 560.

[Note: Baronius, under the year 560, no. 6, and under the year 563. Pagius, under the year of Christ 560, nos. 3 and 4, and under the year 563, no. 4.]

6. But amid the conflict of so many opinions, I would by no means dare to withhold belief from Baronius and Cardinal Aguirre. For all the conjectures adduced by the opposing parties bear no marks of evidence, but only of probability; and we judge it superfluous to labor further in weighing them, lest we seem at some point to indulge too much in the conjectures that we censure in others. Meanwhile, we considered it especially our business to report one thing: after that synod of Braga had been convened, no mention of the Priscillianist heresy occurs thereafter in the subsequent Acts of councils or decrees of the Roman pontiffs. But whether at that time those impious offshoots were brought to destruction by the piety of the sacred bishops and the power of the Catholic rulers who had begun to rule the Spaniards and Galicians, or whether under another feigned name—namely that of Manichaeans, Gnostics, or Montanists—they sought hiding places for themselves there, I would not dare to affirm. For it is not right to violate the rules of sound criticism. We certainly judge that those depart from them who, indulging their own pursuits too much and relying without any aid from documents upon varied and futile conjectures alone, either obscure truth itself with false colors resembling darkness or portray false appearances of things with invented outlines, so as to deceive and pervert the minds and judgments of unwary readers. That we have always recoiled from this method of proceeding will be abundantly shown both by this and by our other dissertations.

[Col. 1065]

# ON THE PELAGIAN HERESY, FLOURISHING IN THE AGE OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT: ONE BOOK

### CHAPTER ONE  
### On Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, and his efforts to spread the Pelagian heresy more widely among the people

[Col. 1065B]

1. It is already established for everyone from ecclesiastical records and the laws of the imperial decrees that Julian, bishop of Eclanum, held the leading place among the disciples of Celestius. Therefore, as long as Saint Pope Innocent I lived—through whom he had obtained the episcopal order—Julian strove by various devices of dissimulation to conceal the wicked poison of that heresy and attempted to hide his entire impiety beneath a veil of piety and charity toward the poor.

Indeed, if we trust Marius Mercator, Julian, in order to do something especially pleasing to the holy pontiff Innocent, did not refuse openly, outwardly and without any pretense or verbal concealment, to condemn Pelagius and Celestius as deserters of the Catholic faith. Celestius and Pelagius, however, do not seem to have been condemned at that time for the first time by Zosimus of holy memory, but by his predecessor Innocent of blessed remembrance, by whom Julian too had been ordained. For after their condemnation, he remained and persevered in communion with Innocent until the latter’s death, maintaining a sincere judgment and communicating with their condemner; thus, without doubt, he too condemned Pelagius and Celestius.

Would that Innocent had lived longer, or that Julian had died before Innocent’s death! The Church would not have suffered such great calamities, nor would so many once-holy bishops of Campania and Italy, under Julian’s leadership and as his standard-bearers, have stained the purity of the Catholic faith. Nor, finally, would so many writings, covered with blasphemies and filled with impiety, have been sent back and forth—something that plainly occurred through the force and fury of the bishop of Eclanum.

What he did, and what Julian attempted after Innocent’s death, we learn with certainty and in full from ecclesiastical records. For when he could no longer restrain his hatred of apostolic teaching, as though unable to control his anger, he publicly taught the people the doctrines he had already learned from Celestius. He did not hesitate to attack and disparage the holiest and otherwise most learned bishops of the Catholic Church. He invoked curses upon Augustine and the other African Fathers; and, growing worse day by day, he led many into false belief after first despising the authority, teaching, and admonitions of Saint Pope Zosimus.

Finally, rejecting the dogmatic letter of that same supreme pontiff—which they call the *Tractatoria* and which all the bishops of the Catholic communion had received with the deepest reverence as a rule of faith—Julian most shamelessly refused, together with the other bishops, to subscribe to it.

[Col. 1066B]

2. Yet he did not delay long in paying the penalty for such great crimes. First he was removed from the priestly rank; then stripped of his episcopal see; and finally, by imperial sanction, banished from every shore of Italy. He took refuge as an exile among the Eastern peoples, ultimately deprived of every hope of ever ascending either his own or anyone else’s episcopal throne.

Other bishops whom he had drawn into partnership in his wickedness, however, fearing above all the force, magnitude, and disgrace of the penalties, reflected that it would be exceedingly shameful not to obey the judgments of the Apostolic See. Therefore, abandoning Julian and condemning Pelagius and Celestius, they presented petitions as suppliants to the Apostolic See. They were mercifully received by it and restored to their own sees.

Others, who did not fear to endure the imperial and ecclesiastical penalties with stubborn hearts, were permanently deposed and deprived of office and were driven beyond all the borders of Italy.

Marius Mercator explained the whole matter in approximately these words:

“Julian and his other accomplices refused to subscribe to it”—namely, to Zosimus’s letter—“and, unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those Fathers. They were deposed and deprived of office not only by imperial laws but also by priestly decrees, and expelled from all Italy. Of these, many came to their senses, were corrected of the error mentioned above, returned as suppliants to the Apostolic See, and, having been received, recovered their Churches.”

3. When these actions of the most holy pontiff Zosimus are related from Marius Mercator, an exceedingly broad field would be opened to us for overturning all the lies and calumnies with which Paschasius Quesnellus filled his Dissertation 13 on the African Councils, written out of hatred for the Apostolic See.

For in that work, confusing everything from top to bottom and freely distorting everything, he attacks the holy pontiff Zosimus and vehemently assails him, accusing him of excessive connivance with the Pelagians. He even portrays the clergy of the Roman Church as tainted with Pelagian soot. He extends the authority of the provincial councils in Africa beyond the limits allowed by law and prescribed by the divine laws. Finally, he attempts not merely to lessen but even to overthrow the jurisdiction and dignity of the Apostolic See itself—those prerogatives which the African Fathers at that time regarded with the greatest religious devotion.

But what of these impostures? He could boldly impose them only upon his own followers, not upon us, who know perfectly well from Prosper’s *Life of Augustine* that the African Fathers, then especially dependent upon the judgment of the Apostolic See, never wished to assemble in a plenary synod until Pope Zosimus’s decree had reached them.

In consequence of that decree, 212 Fathers, wishing to support it in every respect, issued eight canons, which are wrongly attributed to the Second Council of Milevis. But, says the most learned Petavius:

“This Milevitan council established nothing against the Pelagians,”

and of those eight canons, the third, fourth, and fifth are cited by Pope Celestine under the name of the Council of Carthage.

[Note: Dionysius Petavius, *Rationale of Time*, part I, book VI, chapter 15. Pope Celestine, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, vol. III of the Councils.]

We preferred to pass over these matters in silence rather than bring them forward, since for the present we do not intend to confront and refute individually the lies and frauds of the dissertation mentioned above—especially because anyone wishing to reject them has at hand an abundant supply of material already prepared by the most eminent Cardinal Noris in his books on the History of the Pelagians.

Following his resources as well, we have chosen merely to sample those matters that seem to concern the time when this heresy arose, its authors and leaders, and finally the actions of certain Roman pontiffs. Our purpose is to prepare, by a very brief preliminary history, an easier path to what we are about to explain concerning the holy pontiff Leo.

The remaining matters touching upon the African councils and vindicating the Apostolic See from every stain we have reserved for treatment elsewhere.

### CHAPTER TWO  
### Saint Leo the Great’s efforts to overthrow Julian and the Pelagians ravaging Campania

1. To return, then, to our subject: no one should imagine that Julian and his companions in impiety endured exile and their other penalties so peacefully that they did not attempt to deceive Pope Celestine and Xystus, his successor, in order to obtain absolution.

Nor should anyone suppose that Rome, Campania, and the other regions of Italy remained entirely free from the plague of the Pelagians after Julian and the other bishops had been expelled.

Julian first, having secured the support of Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, attempted through deceit and fraud to advance his own cause and that of his associates before Saint Celestine. He repeatedly urged him to restore the episcopal sees to himself and to his expelled associates.

Meanwhile the Pelagians, scattered and multiplying here and there throughout Italy, were encouraged by the hope that their own pastors would one day be restored to them. For that reason they did not cease from complaints, disturbances, or curses.

Therefore, scarcely had Celestine died and Xystus been appointed to his see when Julian dared to test Xystus’s loyalty and apostolic vigor. He sent him petitions in which he pretended to profess the Catholic faith, so that the pontiff might restore to him his former episcopal honor and offices.

Prosper of Aquitaine relates the matter in his *Chronicle*, adding that Julian was thwarted by no one other than Saint Leo, then archdeacon of the Roman Church. Leo exerted all his strength before the holy pontiff to ensure that he and the entire Church would be protected against the feigned repentance of this heretical man:

“At that time Julian of Eclanum, the notorious advocate of the Pelagian error, whom an immoderate desire for the episcopate he had long since lost was tormenting, attempted by many forms of deceit to creep back into communion with the Church while presenting the appearance of correction. But Pope Xystus, watchfully countering these snares at the urging of the deacon Leo, permitted no access to his pestilential efforts. Thus he caused all Catholics to rejoice at the rejection of the deceitful beast as though the apostolic sword had then for the first time cut down the most arrogant heresy.”

Thus wrote the aforementioned Prosper under the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus. According to Petavius’s chronological tables, this must be assigned to the year of Our Lord 439, as the most eminent Cardinal Noris also noted.

2. Such, then, was the marvelous prudence and perceptiveness of Saint Leo, still a deacon, that he immediately recognized the deceit, bad faith, and pretenses of this standard-bearer of the Pelagians. Julian, driven only by an excessive desire for the episcopate he had lost, was demanding to be admitted into the communion of Catholics with all his honors and offices, so that he might again disturb the Church and attack it with new schemes.

After Leo, with a mind superior to every danger, had confronted these evils, he judged that the heretics—both the Nestorians and the Pelagians—should also be attacked in writing.

And as though he had foreknowledge of his own divine election to the supreme pontificate of the Church, he roused Cassian, the presbyter of Massilia, from his modest silence by repeated exhortations. By commendable zeal and the most commanding influence he overcame and, as it were, compelled Cassian’s resolve and opinion to write and publish seven books against Nestorius on the Incarnation.

In those same books he showed no consideration whatever for the Pelagians; rather, he attacked and scourged them. Thus, although Cassian had long since completed the books of his spiritual *Conferences* and had resolved to place himself in the harbor of silence, excusing by the modesty of silence the boldness of loquacity and wishing to erase the entirely false stain of being a supporter of the Semipelagians, nevertheless, from that deep retreat of his deliberately chosen silence, he came forth into public and fearful judgment at our Leo’s urging and command. He undertook a new labor even while still ashamed of his earlier works.

Cassian himself openly acknowledged this in the dedicatory letter to Leo, in which he addresses him as follows:

“For here it is now more your cause than mine that is at stake; your judgment rather than my service is in danger. Whether I am equal to your command or not, the very principle of obedience and humility excuses me to some extent . . .”

A little later he adds:

“This, therefore, is your matter, your business, the work of your honor.”

3. Not long afterward, not only did rumor—which is swifter than anything in such matters—spread everywhere, but messengers also arrived before the news that Xystus, the Roman pontiff, had departed this life.

When the Pelagians heard this, they immediately understood that new disasters threatened them if the archdeacon Leo were elevated to the pontificate. They were consequently tortured by the greatest fear and gravest dangers, and seemed to foresee that new thunderbolts were about to be hurled against them from a higher place.

And indeed, under these favorable omens, Leo began to govern the Church. For the common benefit of the Catholic faith, he immediately declared the greatest war against all heretics, especially Julian and the other Pelagians who were living in Campania.

“When we were established in Italy, throughout Campania, while Leo—venerable and to be named with apostolic honor—was overthrowing the Manichaeans, crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian . . .”

[Note: Author of *The Promises of God*, second half of the period, chapter 6.]

Yet in this matter I consider those writers entirely unworthy of being heeded who have wrongly inferred from Photius’s writings that Saint Leo sent Prosper of Aquitaine to Campania against Julian’s intrigues. For Photius asserted nothing of the kind in his *Bibliotheca*. In Codex 54 he merely wrote concerning the revival of the Pelagian [Col. 1068D] heresy [Note: [Col. 1068D] Photius, in his *Bibliotheca*, Codex 54, p. 20.]:

> “After it had not long afterward begun shamelessly to arise and spring up again, as it were from an evil root, certain men in Rome also spoke openly in favor of the heresy; but Prosper, a truly godly man, easily dispersed and extinguished them by publishing pamphlets against them for the public, while Leo, whom we have mentioned, was still governing the Roman see.”

Therefore, according to Photius, Prosper did not overthrow the Pelagians living in Campania, nor was he sent and dispatched there by Pope Leo to undertake that task, as Usserius, Cave, and others have maintained. He merely published certain pamphlets against those who spoke openly in favor of the Pelagian heresy. By these words, moreover, we believe that certain men are indicated who, neither understanding the testimonies of Scripture nor obeying the judgments of the apostolic see with the submission that was proper, aspired to an empty and ambitious appearance of learning while wishing to seem defenders of that heresy. Their practice is indeed very similar to the present-day habit of certain people, since we very often encounter loquacious and noisy teachers—or, not to call them busybodies—who are accustomed to frequent public shops selling books solely for the purpose of freely observing and criticizing the deeds and writings of others, and of describing them in slanderous verses, although—such is the extraordinary confidence of their intellects!—they have been given no ability whatsoever, either by nature, by their occupations, or by knowledge and practice of the sciences, even slightly to judge such matters.

## 4.

Saint Prosper accordingly restrained the loquacity and license of such men in four, or at least three, pamphlets. Moreover, reflecting that people are accustomed to take greater pleasure in verse than in prose, he therefore composed it metrically. Among these pamphlets the chief place [Col. 1069B] belongs to that poem *Against the Ungrateful*, in which, against the Pelagians, he not only describes the sequence of the Church’s proceedings, but also brings forward and refutes all the impious errors of that heresy. Could the people and common crowd not therefore understand, from this kind of discourse, with what and how great reverence those decrees of the apostolic see ought to be received, which were already regarded by all the bishops of the Churches as tokens of faith? Moreover, could not the title alone of this pamphlet, addressed to all who spoke openly in favor of this heresy, either awaken shame or inspire a desire to read it, since it indicated that the work contained a grave condemnation of ungrateful minds—minds whom all nations, at every time, have been accustomed to fear and to separate themselves from?

Indeed, if he must be considered ungrateful who neither returns nor possesses gratitude for benefits received, how much more so is he who even denies that he has received benefits, and who, following the practice of the ungrateful, attempts to defend their vice and its cause? [Col. 1069C] It can scarcely be doubted, therefore, that the Pelagians deservedly acquired for themselves the name of “the ungrateful,” “because no one,” says Martin Steyaert, “suffers more grievously from the vice of an ungrateful spirit than the man who impiously places human will before the divine will and mercy, as though one who is originally evil began the reception of good not from the highest good but from himself.”

## 5.

Yet the eminent Noris seems to oppose these arguments. For in Book II of his *Pelagian History* he wrote the following concerning Photius’s testimony:

> “Moreover, I think that, when Photius calls them pamphlets, he meant none of Prosper’s books against the Pelagians except those which Prosper published in Gaul against the Semipelagians; yet I have learned that they were written before Leo’s pontificate.” As for *Against the Ungrateful*, Usserius alone, without evidence, asserts on p. 380 that Prosper wrote that charming poem at Rome.”

Are these points, then, to be concealed? I do not wish to appear always to be seeking an issue with the learned man, as the Venetian writers on literature once published when our edition of Rufinus first appeared [Col. 1069D] [Note: [Col. 1069D] Venetian writers on literature, 1742.]. Must we subscribe to Noris’s conjectures in such a way that we seem to waver in our own opinion? Far be it from our thought to fall into such a course! For Photius’s testimony is not so weak that it cannot claim at least some credibility among us and among the learned. Nor do we think that we should cling to it so rigidly as to dare to attack or reject the conjectures and arguments of the most distinguished and learned man, Cardinal Noris. It would be exceedingly disgraceful even slightly to injure the reputation of so learned a man, who, after exhausting so many labors for the affairs of the Church, displayed superior examples of his studies to the Catholic world, both in composing his *Pelagian History* and in adorning the monuments of antiquity.

As I therefore reflected on these matters, and again turned my eyes to Photius’s [Col. 1070A] testimony, I came to believe that the opinions, or assertions, of both writers could easily be reconciled—especially because Photius nowhere asserts that Prosper wrote such pamphlets against the Pelagians while Leo occupied the Roman see. He says only: “Prosper, a truly godly man, easily dispersed and extinguished them by publishing pamphlets against them for the public.” This manner of speaking rather indicates that Prosper found at Rome an opportunity to publish for the common people pamphlets which he had perhaps previously composed against the Pelagians.

No one who attends to the genuine meaning of those words will deny that this is the sense conveyed by Photius, while also recalling that authors were never accustomed to distribute their own writings indiscriminately to everyone. For at that time there was not such an abundance of manuscript books that they were worn by the hands even of the common people. It would therefore be quite plausible to suppose that Prosper finally published at Rome for the public books which, perhaps—as Noris maintains—he had himself composed in Gaul, in order to disperse and extinguish the defenders of the Pelagians. [Col. 1070B]

## 6.

This final conjecture is strengthened by Jerome’s letter to Florentius, which we ourselves discussed in our edition of Eusebius. There we noted that there was a very extensive exchange of books between Jerome and Rufinus. Jerome therefore earnestly asks Florentius that, when he has received Rufinus, their common friend, as a guest, he should request from him and arrange to have sent to Jerome the commentaries of the blessed Rheticius, bishop of Autun, on the *Song of Songs*. In addition, in the name of a certain Paulus of Siena, he asks that a codex of Tertullian be returned to him from Rufinus’s homeland; likewise, an interpretation of David’s Psalms and the very lengthy book of Saint Hilary on the Councils, which Jerome himself had copied out at Trier.

From this letter we understand that codices of works composed by the Fathers were so rare in the fifth century of the Church that it was scarcely possible to obtain copies even for men of the greatest wealth, or for those who did not shrink from undertaking the burdensome labor of scribes. Although we willingly grant, then, that the pamphlets of Prosper about which Photius speaks were composed by their author in Gaul, what prevented them from afterward being published for the public as well, for the benefit of the common cause? Indeed, those who wish to interpret Photius’s words according to the strict rules of grammar will judge with us that they cannot bear any other meaning.

For does the celebrated Photius imply anything else there than this alone: that Saint Prosper brought great light and assistance to the truth by making public those pamphlets through which he easily quieted all the disturbances of the populace and fostered, strengthened, and increased both the devotion and the religion of Catholics? And indeed the common people themselves, although little versed in ecclesiastical matters and not readily obedient to the authority of a teacher, nevertheless very often, when free from necessary business and cares, do not at all refuse to listen to the speeches of slanderers. Captured by them as if by some enticement, whenever the rigor of justice is at issue they make the uprightness or integrity of judges suspect to themselves, frequently judge the crimes of the accused perversely, and, moved by a certain compassion toward the condemned—both because of the punishments they suffer and because they recoil from them—are not ashamed to attack the holiest prelates of the Church with malignant teeth.

Thus, in order to confront all these evils, and at the same time to foster and, as we have said, arouse the piety and religion of the common people, it is quite plausible that Saint Prosper wished to assail the customs and institutions of the Pelagians in mournful verses, so that the common people themselves would not allow themselves to be deceived, but would be drawn and encouraged to seek and investigate the truth. And surely we must believe that he set before their eyes the sequence and order of events, together with the impiety and errors of the Pelagians, for no other reason than that he might afterward sing the praises of divine grace, celebrate the faith and piety of the Catholic Church, and finally turn the deeds, doctrines, disasters, destruction, and disgrace of the heretics themselves into a song on people’s lips. Photius’s praised words clearly announce that Prosper achieved such a happy outcome in the celebrated poem *Against the Ungrateful* and in the other three pamphlets published for the public, whether Saint Prosper composed those pamphlets long before the pontificate of Leo the Great or during that pontificate.

## CHAPTER III. The time when Saint Prosper composed his pamphlets against the Pelagians

### 1.

Now we might seem to be straying beyond the purpose of our undertaking if we decided to investigate more carefully the date of these pamphlets. Yet I could not in any way be diverted from this task, since I saw that all previous writers had gone astray in determining that date. For the poem *Against the Ungrateful* should not be assigned to the year [Col. 1071B] 429, or to the following year; nor should those two epigrams against Augustine’s detractor be assigned to the year 417 or 418, as previous writers have asserted.

This is especially clear from Prosper himself, who begins the poem *Against the Ungrateful* in such a way as to describe all Pelagian poison as completely abolished. But to what would this language of Prosper refer if the Church’s enemy had not yet been crushed, and, still swollen with pride, had continued to raise himself up through Campania and other regions of Italy? By what reasoning could Prosper have said that the Church had won a complete victory over the Pelagians if their standard-bearer Julian could still stir up new disturbances in Constantinople, or throughout Italy and Gaul, and attempt once and again to creep back into the Catholic community?

Nor should similar expressions be referred merely to the synods of Africa or to the decrees of Pope Innocent. For, as we have understood most clearly from ecclesiastical records, Julian had not yet fallen into open heresy at that time; rather, under the mask of religion and piety, he was attempting to conceal his impious errors. Nor can Saint Prosper’s words be interpreted as referring to the constitution of Pope Zosimus or to the decrees of the Council of Ephesus, since, already under the Roman pontiffs Xystus and Leo, Julian himself and the other Pelagian prelates were stirring up new disturbances and schemes here and there, and were using every effort to have their episcopal sees, honors, and offices restored to them.

### 2.

It therefore seems to us that Prosper’s poems can fit no time better than that of Xystus or Saint Leo. Although we would not dare to assert absolutely that this poem was composed in Leo’s age, nevertheless, since it speaks in such a way as to describe the Pelagian offspring as utterly extinguished, and seems to mention a war completed, a victory won, and peace established, such a conjecture must by no means be rejected altogether, as the reader himself will be able to judge from Prosper’s poems.

> The chaste love of the race born in Christ,  
> implanted in me from above,  
> commands me to exceed my own powers  
> and to kindle pious minds with song,  
> lest, after the famous victory  
> and the war brought to an end,  
> careless peace should relax secure hearts,  
> as though, once the enemy had been crushed,  
> no fear remained,  
> nor the poisonous head of the battered serpent throbbed.

But if someone should insist that Photius’s statement—“At Rome also certain men spoke openly in favor of the heresy, whom Prosper, a truly godly man, easily dispersed and extinguished by publishing pamphlets for the public”—cannot at all be proved from the single poem *Against the Ungrateful*, I will not strongly resist. Indeed, although that work may in reality bear the name “pamphlets,” both because it was divided by its author into four equal parts, each of which has its own distinct subject—as the distinguished Antonius Salinas, a canon regular, has now demonstrated in his embellishment of Saint Prosper’s works—and also because this kind of discourse contains satirical verses composed to criticize and assail the evil customs and institutions of others, it deservedly claims the name “pamphlets” according to ordinary usage.

But lest I seem intent on opposing Noris, I pass over these minor conjectures, and my discussion turns to the other three pamphlets published by Prosper [Col. 1072A] against the Pelagians. As we have said, Prosper composed two other epigrams against the detractor of Saint Augustine, and to these he added that celebrated epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresy. But those forms of discourse would plainly have been premature if either Augustine had not yet died or if one or the other of those heresies had not yet been utterly extinguished and abolished. In fact, those two heresies were not brought to complete destruction until after Augustine had died.

Recognizing the force of this argument, Prosper’s editors asserted that the epitaph against the Nestorians and Pelagians had been composed later, assigning it to the year 432, when, after Augustine had been removed from the living, those two heresies were condemned at the plenary Council of Ephesus. Yet at least concerning the other pamphlets we are compelled by the strongest conjecture to make the same assertion. For who would suppose that, while Augustine was still alive, anyone else would have wished to assume the role of defender on behalf of his name and doctrine?

Did not the holy doctor himself, as long as he lived, always keep his pen ready against his adversaries, either touching them lightly or destroying their schemes with the gravest censures? It is therefore quite plausible that Augustine—the same Augustine who rebuked and chastised the monks of Hadrumetum for wrongly interpreting his writings; who continually attacked and assailed Pelagius and Julian; who modestly cleared his own doctrine of Jerome’s objections—did not leave these new attacks of the Pelagians unanswered, or at least that he rendered due thanks to Prosper, his defender. He would indeed have done so if he had still been alive when Prosper composed the celebrated pamphlets.

### 3.

Prosper’s two letters to Augustine then add great strength to our conjectures. But they make it clear that Cave, Usserius, John Olivarius, and the other editors of Prosper were seriously mistaken in assigning the date of the aforesaid pamphlets, if we investigate more carefully the time when such letters were written and turn our attention to their contents.

As for the date, Cave believed that they were written in the year 426. Their most recent editor, however, persuades himself that they were written toward the end of 428 or at the beginning of 429. He noted this in the margin on p. 89.

If we next weigh the contents of the letters, Prosper openly testifies in them that the remnants of the Pelagian heresy had increased in Gaul and in most other regions. He also reports that the gravest complaints had been raised against Augustine’s writings, especially against the doctrine explained in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*. Who, then, would wish to assert that Prosper had already composed the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, together with the other pamphlets praised by Photius, when he wrote these letters?

Did he not in them enumerate the gravest and most difficult questions raised by the Pelagians, which he wished Augustine to clarify for him in bright light? And, as though wavering uncertainly amid the understanding of many matters, did he not implore light from Augustine’s new writings? The first letter declares that almost all Gaul had been thrown into turmoil when Prosper wrote these things. Therefore, wishing to become better instructed by the wisdom and learning of the holy Father and to benefit many at his request, he addresses him as follows:

> “Grant us in this matter, most blessed pope, best of fathers, as much diligence of your piety as you can, with the Lord’s help, so that you may deign to disclose in the clearest explanations those matters in these questions which are more obscure and more difficult to understand.” [Col. 1073A]  
> [Note: [Col. 1073D] Prosper’s letter to Augustine, ch. 7.]

He immediately adds ten arguments concerning these most serious questions. Meanwhile, fearing to leap into the open field of debate against so many adversaries distinguished by merit and rank, and to fight against them, he restrains the ardor of his mind in silence until he obtains Augustine’s reply.

> “When all these matters have been untangled,” he begins the final chapter of his letter, “and when many further points which pertain to this question and which you are able to see with deeper insight have also been examined, we believe and hope not only that our weakness will be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but also that those whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, although distinguished by merit and rank, will receive the most purified light of grace.”

Prosper therefore could not at that time attack Augustine’s detractors in his poems, nor sing of a complete victory won over the Pelagians, if he himself, still hesitating amid one doubt after another, was asking Augustine whether Christian faith was violated by that disagreement and how much danger was exposed in the opinion of his adversaries. He also asked Augustine to explain how free will was not impeded by this prevenient and cooperating grace; whether God’s foreknowledge remained according to his purpose in such a way that the very things purposed were to be understood as foreknown; and other questions of the same kind, which anyone may examine in the eighth chapter of the same letter.

Let those who assign Prosper’s two epigrams against Augustine’s detractor to the year 417 or 418, but the poem *Against the Ungrateful* to the year 430, say, then, whether the man who is called “a truly godly man” in sacred writings could have summoned the Pelagians to war in writing when, in the year 429, he was not yet sufficiently instructed concerning the central point, foundations, and arguments of the entire controversy.

Did holy Prosper wish to engage the heretics in battle unprepared and unarmed, and, as though placing excessive confidence in himself, to fight both for the decrees of the Church and for Augustine’s doctrine when, not yet instructed in the questions mentioned above, he was wavering in mind among the various opinions and interpretations of his adversaries? Such a fabricated and fictitious story is unworthy of so great a man!

This is especially so since we understand that Augustine, shortly before his death, composed two books—*On Predestination* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—in which he untangled the questions put to him by Prosper and Hilary concerning the Massilians and the Pelagians.

Possidius relates when Augustine died in his *Life of Augustine*, writing that in the year 430, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, the holy doctor paid the debt owed by human life, at a time when the Vandals had already been besieging Hippo for three months.

### 4.

When I carefully considered all these points, I persuaded myself—contrary to almost all the opinions of previous writers—that Saint Prosper undertook to fight against the Pelagians, or their remnants, and began to attack them in writing only after Augustine had died.

Who does not know that, when the enemies of divine grace and detractors of Augustine were becoming especially prominent throughout Gaul, Prosper and Hilary traveled to Rome to Pope Celestine, so that by firm and certain testimony it might be declared how highly the doctrine of that same Saint Augustine had always been regarded by the apostolic see? Celestine’s agreement with their wishes is declared by a celebrated letter written in 430 to the bishops of Gaul, in which he writes not only the following [Note: [Col. 1073D] Letter of Pope Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 2.]:

> “We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion because of his life and merits, nor did even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever stain him. We remember that he was once a man of such learning that, even before my predecessors, he was counted among the best teachers.”

In addition to this letter, we read that the authorities of the apostolic see from earlier times concerning the grace of God and free will were appended, so that the detractors might understand what they ought to follow and profess to approve, and might understand all those things which the most sacred see of blessed Peter, the apostle, had decreed and taught against the enemies of God’s grace through the ministry of its bishops [Col. 1074A] [Note: [Col. 1073D] Preface to the authorities or chapters of the apostolic see. [Col. 1074D]].

We are not presently investigating who compiled these chapters. Their author, however, so directly contradicts more recent dogmatists that he makes it clearer than daylight that the Pelagian heresy had been proscribed and judged by the apostolic see, and that the African canons possessed only as much force as the Roman bishops bestowed upon them when they approved them.

Since these words seriously trouble Quesnel and his followers, we immediately add the following:

> “It was therefore necessary to investigate carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their times, and what they had determined should be believed concerning the grace of God against the most pernicious defenders of free will, so that we might also join to these certain judgments of the African councils, which the apostolic bishops made their own everywhere when they approved them.”

In the ninth century, when heresies are at issue, Hincmar, bishop of the Church of Rheims, openly confessed this necessity of investigating and awaiting the judgment of the apostolic see in his controversy against Gottschalk. He certainly would not have appealed to the cited words, nor transferred them in full to his own letter, if he had not accepted that judgment. The aforementioned Hincmar, together with the deacon Peter, Florus the teacher, Cresconius, Dionysius Exiguus, and Ivo, attributes these same chapters to Celestine, since they are regarded as a part and appendix of that letter.

### 5.

As these and many other matters passed through my mind, I firmly maintained—contrary to the opinion of all previous writers—that none of the celebrated pamphlets was composed by Prosper before Augustine departed this life.

The vigilance of Prosper himself seems sufficiently to warn us of this one fact: in order to prepare a defense for Augustine, who had already died, Prosper came to Rome to consult Pope Celestine about his doctrine. But if Prosper had already composed or published the celebrated pamphlets, he would have pleaded before the pontiff not Augustine’s cause but his own.

For Prosper has nothing, especially in that poem *Against the Ungrateful*, which was not drawn from Augustine, or which had not been brought into question by the Massilians or Pelagians, or which finally does not appear to have been defined in those ten chapters of the apostolic see. Nor is it probable that Saint Prosper wished, in that four-part poem *Against the Ungrateful*, either to reproduce the objections of his adversaries or to dare to clear Augustine’s doctrine of every stain of suspicion before the judgment of the apostolic see.

What, then, should be said about those ten chapters of the apostolic see? Could Saint Prosper perhaps have conceived them in his mind and set them forth in writing before he carefully investigated what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the Pelagian heresy that had arisen in their times? Away with such a fabrication!

Therefore, if an argument from similarity were valid in this kind of writing, I would certainly turn to Prosper’s book *Against the Collator*, which readers themselves recognize to have been composed after Augustine’s death. But the arguments already brought forward, and those that will shortly be brought forward, make it perfectly clear that this book must be assigned to nearly the same period as the poem *Against the Ungrateful*.

The eminent Cardinal Peronius [Note: [Col. 1074D] Cardinal Peronius, *Response to the King of England*, Book V, ch. 20, p. 13.], who was accustomed to the practice of the ancient Catholic poets and composed much in their defense, asserted that they often presented elsewhere in prose the same matters which they had expressed elsewhere in tightly compressed verse. This is clearly shown in the case of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, whom he was discussing.

We believe that this principle applies especially to Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful*, since he wrote nothing in it that he had not also set forth either in the authorities of the apostolic see or in other works of his composed in prose. The supreme authority of the apostolic see is supplied with a most powerful and certain argument by those verses in which he sings:

> First cuts off the advancing pestilence.  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> The Roman see of Peter, which, made the head of pastoral honor  
> for the world, holds by religion  
> whatever it does not possess by arms.

In his book *Against the Collator*, however, Prosper describes the sequence of events at greater length, enumerating, in chronological order, the judgments pronounced by the Roman pontiffs against the Pelagians. Beginning with Pope Innocent, he carries the account down to Celestine, and then adds the following passage for our present purpose:

> “Through this man”—namely, Celestine—“the freedom of malicious speech was taken away in Gaul from those very men who criticize the writings of blessed Augustine’s holy memory. When he accepted the action of those who consulted him and praised with approval the piety of the books displeasing to the erring, he made clear by holy eloquence what ought to be thought about their authority, plainly declaring how much the novelty of that presumption displeased him—this presumption by which certain men dared insolently to rise up against their teachers and, with undisciplined slander, obstruct the preaching of truth.”

Prosper mocks Augustine’s impious detractors in the third part of his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, refuting the objections of those Pelagians and Semipelagians who cried out that every work of free will had been removed, that punishment was due to no vices, nor rewards to merit.

Since it has been made abundantly clear that Augustine’s detractors uttered these complaints after his death, there is no need to linger over the matter any longer, especially since Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, Codex 53, and Vincent of Lérins in the final chapter of his work *Against Heresies*, support us.

## CHAPTER IV. The arguments of previous writers are refuted

### 1.

Although I noted all these matters in the preceding chapter, preserving the chronological order, it will seem that I have accomplished nothing unless I also remove the foundations of Joseph Anthelmius, Usserius, Cave, Martin Steyaert, Father Salinas, and the other writers.

They produce only one testimony of Saint Prosper, drawn from chapter 3 of the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, by which they flatter themselves that this work was composed while Augustine was still alive. Saint Prosper sings:

> Could the holy council have proceeded toward any other end,  
> a council whose leader was Aurelius  
> and whose genius was Augustine?  
> Christ’s grace, watering him with a more abundant horn,  
> gave our age a light kindled from the true light.  
> God is his food, his life, and his rest,  
> and all his delight;  
> his one love is Christ, his one honor is Christ.  
> And because he attributes no good to himself,  
> God becomes everything to him,  
> and wisdom reigns in the holy temple.

“Thus,” says Father Salinas [Note: [Col. 1075D] In the illustrated edition *Works of Saints Prosper of Aquitaine and Honoratus of Marseilles, with Notes and Observations*, Rome, 1732.], “Prosper celebrates an excellent teacher in an encomium as though he were still alive. How, indeed, would he not speak in the same place of other bishops or men who were foremost in this cause but had already died?”

### 2.

Martin Steyaert, doctor of Louvain, however, guided by precisely the same argument in embellishing and correcting this work, wrote the following note on the word “reigns”:

> “From this verb, together with the other present-tense verbs throughout the paragraph, it is inferred that this was written while the holy doctor was still alive.”

But what could be weaker than such an argument? For if we first consider the kind of praise in question—than which nothing more sublime or splendid can be said about a blessed spirit already reigning with God in heaven—it can be applied to a man still living a mortal life only with open and shameless flattery.

Moreover, in what sense or by what reasoning could Prosper, while Augustine was still alive, sing of him:

> “Christ’s grace, watering him with a more abundant horn, gave our age a light kindled from the true light”—

when afterward, after Augustine had died, that same Prosper consulted the apostolic see more carefully:

> “Whether even a rumor of sinister suspicion had stained him, or whether he had possessed such learning that he should be counted among the best teachers of the Church.” [Note: [Col. 1076D] The aforementioned Martin Steyaert, cited by the distinguished Father John Anthony Salinas, canon regular, in the Roman edition of the works of Saint Prosper.]

I plainly do not see how these statements can be reconciled, especially since Prosper, while Augustine was alive, was a layman wholly lacking ecclesiastical authority and would hardly have arrogated to himself the right to judge the writings of the holy Father before the judgment of Pope Celestine.

### 3.

Nor do the verbs in the present tense compel us, since poets always employ freer license, very often creating such images that they describe those who have already died as though they were present, and persuade themselves from their deeds and writings that the dead still live.

Prosper is in fact alluding there to Augustine’s heavenly wisdom, by which he eluded, rejected, and overturned the devices, schemes, and errors of the Pelagians and Semipelagians. For this reason, in his written works he set Augustine before himself after his death as though he were living.

Nor is it true that the entire paragraph uses verbs in the present tense. Wishing to express the thoughts of his mind poetically, Prosper turns sometimes to the present tense and sometimes to the past, and, as though taking a step upward, moves from Augustine’s mortal life to that immortal life in which he reigns with God. He describes Augustine under the name of wisdom in these words:

> “And because he attributes no good to himself, God becomes everything to him, and wisdom reigns in the holy temple.”

Do the writers whom we oppose think that these words can properly be said of some living man of great wisdom? When does God ordinarily become everything to the living, so that, while still enclosed in mortal flesh, they reign in a holy temple? Catholics are sufficiently certain that Scripture and the Fathers have asserted this truthfully only of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. But if we wish to apply such a statement to anyone else, we must necessarily come into conflict with the Catholic religion itself.

### 4.

When I seriously turned my attention to these matters, I judged the opinion exceedingly weak and insubstantial of those who thought that Prosper’s celebrated pamphlets were composed before Augustine died, or before Pope Celestine adorned Augustine’s writings with his praises, or finally before that Julian, the standard-bearer of the Pelagians, was brought with his schemes to complete destruction.

The remaining points introduced by Father Salinas collapse entirely if we attend to Prosper’s purpose in writing or to his manner of discussion. For in that poem *Against the Ungrateful* the sacred poet did not propose to honor with praises the three hundred leading men who had assembled for Pelagius’s cause; rather, he intended to attack and assail the enemies of divine grace.

There is therefore nothing surprising if, apart from Aurelius, primate of all Roman Africa, and the outstanding teacher Augustine, he concealed the names of all the others in silence—especially since, in Prosper’s time, the names of those Fathers could easily be discovered in the acts of the councils, which had not yet disappeared.

## CHAPTER V. The writings of Saint Leo the Great composed against the Pelagians
1. Now, however, the circumstances of the times and the purpose of our work require us to speak about the writings of Leo the Great. As for his writings, nothing shines forth more magnificently—especially in his homilies—than that divine teaching handed down in the sacred Scriptures concerning the power and gifts of divine grace. Therefore, after Julian had been extinguished, the Pelagians in Campania had already been wiped out, and the supporters of these heretics at Rome had finally fallen silent, what subject could he treat amid the sacred mysteries, or urge upon the assembled people, more worthy of so great a pontiff? Accordingly, on the greatest solemnities of the year and in the hearing of the Roman people, throughout his life he directed at least some part of his discourse toward attacking and overthrowing the errors of the Pelagians and other heretics. At one time, indeed, he describes the weakness and feebleness of natural powers; at another, he very frequently impresses upon his hearers the heavenly power of divine assistance, necessarily required for attaining the good of eternal blessedness. Hence, drawing upon the Apostle, the Gospel, and other testimonies of sacred Scripture, he explains that the whole offspring of Adam remained corrupted by the sin of disobedience. From this he proceeds to describe the greatest work of divine mercy: through the cross of the only-begotten Son of God and his death, once the price of our redemption had been paid, the bonds of sin were broken; and, once the yoke of hellish captivity had been shaken off, the gate of paradise was opened both to them and to all the sons of Adam. What more need be said?

2. The holy pontiff therefore continually and everywhere seeks an opportunity to attack the Pelagian doctrine, so that if any among his hearers should happen to doubt the Catholic truth or the decrees of the apostolic see, they might at last, overcome by the weight of his arguments and persuaded by the authority of apostolic speech, no longer delay condemning Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian together with their errors. For this principal reason he exhorts the people not to presume upon their own righteousness and not to distrust God’s mercy, because almighty God, in order to make his grace wondrous in him—he is speaking of himself—bestowed his gifts upon one in whom he found no support of merits [Note: [Col. 1077D] Sermon 1 on the anniversary of his accession, ch. 2]. And in the following discourse, after describing the weakness of human nature, he adds:

“Yet we do not despair, nor do we fail, because we place our confidence not in ourselves but in him who works in us” [Note: [Col. 1077D] Sermon 2, ch. 1].

But lest anyone should interpret these words as signifying the opposite position—as though he wished to assert that the powers of the human will had been so weakened by sin that the faculty of free choice had been entirely destroyed—he explained, in the following marvelous and magnificent statement, how God restores us to his image so that he may find in us the form of his goodness:

“He gives what enables us also to do what he does, kindling the lamps of our minds and setting us aflame with the fire of his love, so that we may love not only him but also whatever he loves.”

Again, elsewhere he compares human hearts to a field of earth which, if neglected through sluggish idleness and inert laziness, will produce no noble growth; covered with thorns and thistles, it will bring forth not things to be stored in barns but things to be burned by flames. Then, explaining this allegory, he broke forth in these words [Note: [Col. 1077D] Sermon 11 on the fast of the tenth month and the collections 1, ch. 1]:

“But this field, dearly beloved, is watered from above by the dew of God’s grace; it is fortified by faith, cultivated by fasts, sown with almsgiving, and made fruitful by prayers, so that among our plantings and irrigations no root of bitterness may sprout, nor may the growth of any harmful plant rise up; rather, with every seed of vice destroyed, let the flourishing harvest of virtues grow strong.”

Here the holy pontiff speaks in the person of the sacred prelates who have been appointed as laborers in the Lord’s field.

3. The holy pontiff Leo also teaches in his seventeenth sermon that the weakness and corruption of human nature—which the authors of the Pelagian doctrine stubbornly denied—are remedied by the cleansing bath of sacred baptism. Not, however, in such a way that once the original disease has been healed by the power of divine assistance, a person can thereafter subsist by his own strength, so that, while living this mortal life, he could never turn away from the grace of the righteousness he had received—even though he very often does turn away. For since our nature is mutable and mortal because of the stain of sin, although it has already been redeemed and reborn through sacred baptism, insofar as it is subject to suffering it is equally inclined toward what is worse; and it would be corrupted by carnal desire unless it were fortified by spiritual assistance:

“For,”—these words are golden—“just as he is never without a place from which he may fall, so he is always provided with a means by which he may stand.”

Nothing, then, could our most holy Leo have undertaken more gratefully and beneficially than the task of continually attacking and reproving heretical sects, while at the same time teaching the people to guard themselves against their errors. It is therefore not surprising that in almost all his sermons he rebuked the Pelagians and attacked that heresy with such weight of argument and authority from Scripture that he led very many to repentance.

4. Let the reader consult the first sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, which the Roman Church has always retained in its Breviary. Does he not, in the opening chapter, call Christ the Lord the Redeemer not only of all human beings but also of infants? For he asserts [Col. 1078B] that he is the destroyer of sin and death, who, just as he found no one free from guilt, so came to free everyone. Shortly afterward, employing those words of Job in chapter 14—“No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” [Note: [Col. 1077D] Sermon 17, ch. 1]—he overturns one of the fundamental articles of this heresy [Note: [Col. 1077D] Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord, ch. 1].

Let the reader also consult chapter 5 of the fifth sermon on the Nativity of the Lord. There, with all the force of his eloquence, he directly opposes Pelagius, who, arrogant and swollen with pride under the pretext of defending human freedom, taught that Adam’s fall harmed Adam alone, while all other human beings were born in that perfection of nature in which Adam had been created by God [Note: [Col. 1078D] Similar statements occur in Sermon 2 on the Nativity of the Lord, ch. 5, and Sermon 3, ch. 5]. In opposition to this, the holy pontiff teaches that the following is a sacrament of the Catholic faith:

“All human beings without exception perished in Adam, so that unless the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us, unless the Creator himself descended into communion with his creature, and by his birth restored the old humanity to a new beginning, death would reign from Adam to the end, and an unbreakable condemnation would remain over all human beings, since, in the condition of birth alone, there was one common cause of perishing” [Note: [Col. 1078D] He agrees with himself in Sermon 6 on the Nativity and following, chs. 3 and 6].

Finally, to pass over almost countless other passages, let the reader consult the sixth sermon on the Epiphany, chapter 4. There, after describing the frailty of the human condition, which is always slipping into transgressions, he demonstrates that one must not be quickly surrendered to deceptive pleasure, because there is no sin without delight [Note: [Col. 1078D] Sermon 6 on the Epiphany, ch. 4]. Accordingly, amid so many and such great enticements of the flesh, and with human nature surrounded by infernal enemies, a person can obtain no help or protection for himself at all unless he turns from carnal desires to spiritual assistance, and unless the mind that possesses knowledge of its God turns away from the counsels of the enemy who gives evil advice.

But whoever has already taken delight in carnal pleasures and, overcome by his enemies, is bound by the chains of sins must never feel secure about escaping punishment, because if he loses the time for repentance, he will have no place for pardon. He must utterly distrust his ability to rise by his own strength, or at least to prepare himself for justification by the motions of nature, as the Massilian and Semipelagian factions wrongly asserted; instead, he must flee to the mercy of the assisting God and ask him to break the bonds of evil habit—him who raises up all who fall and lifts up all who have been crushed. Then the prayer of the one who confesses will not be empty, because the merciful God will fulfill the desire of those who fear him and will grant what is requested, he who has given the means by which it may be requested.

Moreover, in his final sermon on the Epiphany, chapter 3, he attacks and reproves those same Semipelagians and Pelagians more openly and forcefully. There, speaking of true and heavenly virtue, he asserts that it is no virtue at all and possesses no property of divinity unless it is visited by the Spirit of its Author. For when the Lord says to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing,” he immediately adds: “There is no doubt that a person who does good receives from God both the accomplishment of the work and the beginning of the will.”
