5. Finally, in Sermon 13, which is the fifth of Lent, he prepares new weapons for the destruction of the Pelagian and Semipelagian heresy. He was proving that human hearts become, through the power of the heavenly Spirit, the temple of the living God, and he used the example and likeness of buildings constructed by human hands:

“Such buildings are maintained with praiseworthy diligence, so that if anything has been damaged either by the soaking of rains, the violence of storms, or the mere passage of time, careful attention may restore it to its former condition. In the same way,” he says, “we must continually take care that nothing disordered, nothing unclean, be found in our souls.”

Then, proceeding from human matters to divine and heavenly realities, he reasons wonderfully in support of our purpose:

“For although our building cannot stand without the assistance of its builder, nor can our structure remain sound unless the protection of its Creator is present, nevertheless, because we are rational stones and living material, the hand of our Author builds us in such a way that the one who is being restored also works together with his craftsman.”

Here Leo does not exclude the effort, cooperation, and free consent of the human will when it is supported and assisted by divine help, as Calvin, Jansenius, and Quesnellus later dared, wickedly and with excessive license, to assert. Nor did he teach that human free choice is like a stone or some other altogether lifeless thing. Rather, when it is stirred by the movements of divine grace, it must not withdraw itself from obedience to God or fall away from that good without which it cannot be good. Therefore the same holy pontiff adds the following to the words just quoted:

“Let the human will therefore not withdraw itself from obedience to God’s grace, nor fall away from that good without which it cannot be good; and if it encounters anything impossible or difficult in carrying out the commandments, let it not remain within itself, but return to the one who commands, who gives the command for this reason: to arouse desire and to provide its accomplishment” [Col. 1079C].

As I was transcribing these passages, I was meanwhile refreshed by such great pleasure that I refrained only with difficulty from reporting very many other similar ones. But I had to omit them lest I abuse the patience of my friendly reader. Nevertheless, our most holy pontiff Leo possesses very many other statements full of apostolic vigor and authority. By them not only could the Pelagians and Semipelagians—formerly enemies of divine grace—be reproved and restrained, but also very many other statements can trouble and press Calvin, Jansenius, and Quesnellus, and cut down their factions. We must now discuss the other writings of Leo the Great; we shall endeavor to do this chiefly in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER VI. On the letters written by Saint Leo the Great to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, against the supporters of the Pelagian heresy, and on Quesnellus’s method of handling these letters

[Col. 1079D]

1. Let us now turn our attention to what Saint Pope Leo decreed canonically concerning the reception into the Church of clerics who had abandoned and execrated the Pelagian heresy. In the fourth year of his pontificate, the hiss of Pelagian error could no longer be heard either at Rome or throughout Campania. If any persons tainted by this soot were still found here or there, they either, while doing penance, bitterly renounced their own errors, or, at least, struck by grave fear of punishment, pretended outwardly to profess the Catholic faith and tried to conceal their impiety beneath a kind of veil.

The latter situation, Saint Septimius, bishop of the Church of Altinum in the province of Venetia, discovered in his province. When he observed that many clerics of his diocese had merely appeared to renounce the Pelagian heresy, but afterward, once admitted into the fellowship of Catholics, secretly and as though by stealth restored the heresy they had renounced, he immediately informed the Roman pontiff of the matter by letter. Both I and all learned men have been persuaded that Septimius’s letter was lost through the ravages of time. Despite considerable effort, we have not been able to locate it. Two letters of the holy pontiff to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia and metropolitan of Septimius, nevertheless remain; from both of them we can readily recognize both the history of what occurred and the decrees of the apostolic see against the Pelagians.

2. As for the first letter, there was long uncertainty about which of the Aquileian bishops had received it. The old editors, perhaps following the testimony of certain corrupt manuscripts, read the name Nicetas instead of Januarius. Quesnellus later published the heading of that letter in mutilated form, and, retaining neither name, wrote only: “Letter to the bishop of Aquileia.” But he asserts that in this matter he followed Crabbe, Picard, Isidore, the Cologne edition of 1551, and several manuscripts.

We, however—as we shall state in the notes—on the authority of two Vatican copies, one Florentine archetype, and another Vallicellian copy of excellent quality, have restored the name Januarius. We are supported also by a manuscript Chronicle of the Bishops of Aquileia, preserved in the Vatican Library under number 5286, in which the following is read concerning our subject:

“Januarius was ordained in the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ 443. To this bishop Januarius Saint Leo writes that bishops and the rest of the clerical order who wish to return from the Pelagian and Coelestian heresy to Catholic unity are not to be restored to their sees unless they have publicly renounced their errors.”

In the same Chronicle, written by Dandulo, we likewise read the following about this Januarius:

“He was born in the city of Pola in Istria, was educated in Catholic disciplines, and, having become a bishop, preserved the people subject to him unharmed from errors through his prudence and teaching, although they were surrounded by many troubles because of the persecutions then occurring. In his praise Pope Leo says as follows: ‘Having read the letter of your Fraternity …’”

3. With these words Leo began the second letter, which was written in the year 447, as is established with complete certainty by the consular dating. But since we have decided first to discuss Leo’s canonical decrees in the case before us, we wish to begin with the letter that was especially suited to overthrowing the Pelagians and that carried the greatest weight for the authority of the apostolic see.

This letter was divided by its author, Leo, into five distinct chapters. In the first chapter, so as to remove immediately from the mind of the metropolitan of Aquileia every suspicion and scruple that the Roman see had lent an ear to false reports from certain people, he not only disclosed the name of Septimius, the bishop who had brought the accusation, but also attached to the letter copies of the accusation that had been received and sent them to Januarius. In a few words, therefore, he expressed all the evils that required the vigilance of the chief shepherd:

“From the report of our holy fellow bishop Septimius, which is contained below, we have learned that certain priests, deacons, and clerics of various orders, whom the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy had entangled, have reached Catholic communion in your province in such a way that no condemnation of their own error was required from them.”

4. After this our Leo censures the sluggish character of certain bishops who, sleeping too soundly, allowed wolves clothed in sheep’s skins to enter the Lord’s sheepfold. Contrary to the authority of the canons and decrees issued by Leo himself, they permitted erring clerics to leave their own Churches, in which they had either originally received or later regained their clerical office, carrying their instability from place to place, always loving to wander and never remaining upon the apostolic foundation.

He immediately adds what and how many evils would arise from such a violation of the canons to the detriment of the Catholic fellowship:

“For those who, without any examination having been conducted and without being bound by any prior judgment concerning their profession, seek this result above all: that, under the covering of communion, they may visit many households and, through knowledge falsely so called, corrupt the hearts of many.”

5. No one among all the learned men who have edited Leo’s writings has yet noticed or pointed out which canons or decrees issued by himself the holy pontiff intended to invoke. Yet the matter is of the greatest importance and could not have been passed over without serious negligence. For from it the supreme authority of the Roman prelate throughout the entire world in establishing ecclesiastical laws becomes clearer; and it also becomes fully apparent with what and how great honor the statutes of the apostolic see were received by all the pastors of other Churches.

Inquiring, therefore, what Saint Leo had defined in the canons to which he appeals, we were also able to understand the following from the Aquileian Chronicle cited above, together with letters 12 and 13. In the former, written to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 9, he says the following concerning these fugitive and wandering clerics [Note: [Col. 1081D] Letter 12, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, ch. 4]:

“Let no one receive or solicit another’s cleric against the will of his own bishop, unless perhaps the matter has been agreed upon through an arrangement of charity between the one who gives and the one who receives. Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own Church. But if he has withdrawn farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of your command, so that no opportunity may be left either for greed or for ambition.”

In the other, subsequent letter, addressed to the metropolitan bishops established throughout the province of Achaia, Leo discusses the manner and discipline of clerical life and the bond of priestly concord that all sacred ministers must preserve. There he not only orders that what he had written to Anastasius be religiously observed, but also wished it to be guarded that no bishop should dare to claim for himself another bishop’s cleric without the cession of the bishop to whom the cleric belongs—a cession that must nevertheless be contained in an explicit written document. For this, he says, has been defined by the authority of the canons, and the very principle of preserving unity teaches it, lest the ecclesiastical order become altogether unstable through such license.

After this he addressed the metropolitans of Achaia in these words, full of apostolic vigor:

“Let what you see to have been decreed by us through the devotion of a pious mind, therefore, descend more deeply, dearest brothers, into your hearts, so that we, who earnestly desire to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, may receive the fruit of our command and rejoice in the works of your love.”

6. Quesnellus entirely passes over what Leo asserted that he had decreed and commanded. Turning instead to the words “For this has been defined by the authority of the canons,” he seriously inquires which canons the holy pontiff had in mind there. In the end, however, he hesitates and asserts that Saint Leo seems to have been referring either to canon 16 of Nicaea, or to canons 18 and 19 of Sardica, or even to the canons of the first Council of Carthage. But he candidly admits that there is no mention in the canons of a written cession [Col. 1081D] [Note: [Col. 1081D] Volume II of the Works of Saint Leo, notes and observations on Letter 13, p. 443].

Why, then, does he not infer that this discipline was first introduced by Leo, since he does not find it expressly stated in the decrees of earlier councils and Roman pontiffs? This conclusion certainly ought not to have been concealed or omitted by a man who had undertaken to embellish Leo’s life and deeds with such devotion. But it is now useful to pass over this and similar matters. They will have to be treated by us more carefully and with equal clarity when, guided by the authority of very many Vatican archetypes, we come to discuss the titles of Pope Leo’s decrees, number 49.

7. The purpose of our work now requires us to return to the Pelagians, from whom our discourse has digressed for a little while. In the second chapter of that letter, therefore, Saint Leo ordered the metropolitan Januarius to restrain the unbridled audacity of the Pelagian clerics and bring them to detest their wicked doctrine:

“That, after a provincial synod of priests has been assembled among you, all—whether priests, deacons, or clerics of any order—who have been received from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians into Catholic communion with such thoughtlessness that they were not previously compelled to condemn their own error, may now at least, after their hypocrisy has been exposed in part, be compelled to true correction, which can benefit them without harming anyone.”

And lest any bold and crafty plan should lodge in anyone’s mind to conceal beneath the veil of hypocrisy the poison of that wicked heresy, and lest he leave an opening for individual evasions and deceit, he commanded:

“That in explicit declarations they condemn the authors of their proud error, detest everything in their teaching that the universal Church has abhorred, and declare, in full and open statements signed with their own hands, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees that the authority of the apostolic see has confirmed for the eradication of this heresy.”

8. Quesnellus sensed the force and weight of these words. Accordingly, to manufacture defenses for the bad cause he had undertaken, he noted only two of Leo’s words—“synodal decrees”—and concealed the rest, attempting to distort the holy pontiff’s entire testimony into an entirely different meaning by adding the following [Note: [Col. 1082D] Letter 6, ch. 2]:

“First, the African Churches of Milevis and Carthage, which had assembled repeatedly. Their decrees were first approved by the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine; then, by an irrevocable decree of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, together with the acts of Pope Celestine, for the condemnation of those same heretics.”

To strengthen the force of this final note, he cites the synodal letter of the Ephesian Fathers to Pope Celestine, believing, evidently, that by this means he could reinforce his preceding assertion more and more [Col. 1082C]. Clever indeed is Quesnellus, who, mixing many things together, gradually diminishes the authority of the apostolic see and elevates the rights of councils above the Roman pontiffs themselves [Note: [Col. 1082D] Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 431, col. 1].

But let him now say, I ask, whether the decrees issued by the Council of Ephesus against the Pelagians were confirmed by the apostolic see or not. Either way, he has already run upon the rocks. For if the authority of the apostolic see did not confirm them, it immediately follows from Leo’s words that the Pelagian heretics returning to the Church were by no means obliged to embrace, in their explicit declarations, what that celebrated synod had defined for the eradication of the heresy. Nor were they bound to confess, in full and open statements signed with their own hands, that they embraced and approved any other synodal decrees except those that the authority of the apostolic see had confirmed for the eradication of this heresy.

But if he says that these decrees, too, were confirmed by the apostolic see, then he is inconsistent with himself, since, when discussing the Council of Chalcedon, he denies that Roman pontiffs possess this power. Nor can that decree be called irrevocable which could have been invalid before the confirmation of the Roman pontiff.

9. How, indeed, could the Council of Ephesus have confirmed the statutes of preceding councils by an irrevocable decree, together with the acts of Pope Celestine? The annotator invents history from his own brain. For nowhere in that synod was anything done to add force to the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs whom he praises. Rather, the Ephesian Fathers themselves, moved by their zeal for truth and justice, asserted that the privilege of an irrevocable judgment belonged solely to the Roman pontiff.

They begin their synodal letter with these words:

“[lacuna] For this has become so firmly established among you that you are celebrated in all things, and that by your zeal you establish the foundations of the Churches” [Col. 1083A].

The Ephesian Fathers therefore do not arrogate to themselves the firmness of the faith. They say that it has become established that Roman pontiffs are celebrated in all things and that by their zeal they establish the foundations of the Churches.

Should we suppose that these Fathers, whom he praises, were ignorant of the rights of general councils—the rights supposedly fabricated in later centuries by certain pseudo-dogmatists? They were ignorant of them, I say, because, inspired by the divine Spirit, they depended so entirely upon the directives, admonitions, and decrees of the Roman pontiffs that they thought it not merely a serious crime but even a slight offense to depart from them. Indeed, whenever more serious cases arose, they both taught and believed that the apostolic see must perpetually be regarded as the mother and teacher of all the other Churches.

Quesnellus therefore tried in vain to prepare an escape for himself by appealing to the words with which the Ephesian Fathers close that synodal letter. They say:

“Furthermore, after the holy synod had read the records of the proceedings concerning the condemnation of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians—Coelestius, Pelagius, Julian, and Florus …—which your Piety decreed and established concerning them, we too have judged that these things ought to remain solid and firm, and we have all decreed the same with you, holding them as deposed or condemned” [Col. 1083B].

What escape can he prepare from this, when he encounters new rocks and falls into others by which he is bound more and more tightly?

10. For the records of the proceedings brought forward in the synod for the condemnation of the impious Pelagians and Coelestians were merely read and published; and those Fathers affirmed that what Pope Celestine had already decreed was firm and solid. What follows from this? Could the mere reading of those records, or the unanimous agreement of the Fathers by which they everywhere regarded as deposed and condemned those whom the Roman pontiff had condemned and deposed, possess such force as to make the decrees of the apostolic see firm and irrevocable if they were not actually so?

This is a novel invention of utter cunning. To rescue it from the greatest disgrace of its author, we must consider the purpose and intention of Pope Celestine in sending those records to the council. For the Roman pontiff did not send such acts through his legates so that they might acquire strength and firmness, but only so that they might become more widely known and be carried out more quickly. He says:

“Out of our pastoral concern we have sent our holy brothers and fellow priests, men united with us and thoroughly approved, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and our presbyter Philip, so that they may be present at what is being done and carry out what we previously established; and we do not doubt that your Holiness will grant them your assent” [Note: [Col. 1083] This is found in volume III of the Councils, p. 470, and Sirmond has furnished it with various learned notes].

There is therefore no discussion here of strengthening the statutes of the apostolic see, but only of executing them. Since this duty concerns inferiors and subjects, it must not be asserted that the acts of Pope Celestine concerning the condemnation of the Pelagians could have acquired strength and firmness from the Ephesian Fathers [Col. 1083D]. Otherwise, all the constitutions and laws of emperors, kings, and supreme magistrates would depend for their force and firmness upon those to whom the responsibility for executing them is ordinarily entrusted.

11. Our Quesnellus also invents much concerning the African canons of Milevis and Carthage. He invents much about the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface, which he asserts were confirmed by that same Council of Ephesus with an irrevocable sanction. But what does this innovator bring upon the stage?

As for the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, the wiser theologians have already understood from their synodal letter to Pope Innocent that they issued no canons whatsoever, as we also observed earlier, on the authority of Dionysius Petavius. For when those Fathers wished the apostolic see to be consulted concerning the impious disputes of the Pelagians, lest their silence itself should become a charge of negligence against them, they first reported the new inventions of the heresy without any exaggeration of language whatsoever. Then they asserted that they preferred the architects of the errors to be healed within the Church rather than, their salvation having been despaired of, to be cut off from the Church, unless necessity compelled otherwise.

They therefore detected the greatest falsehood and impiety in the words of the Pelagians, but nevertheless did not pronounce anathemas against the leaders of the heresy; instead, they judged that their case should be reserved for the apostolic see. The bishops assembled at Milevis begin their letter to Innocent in this way:

“Since the Lord has placed you upon the apostolic see as a special gift of his grace, and has given you to our times as such a man that it would count as negligence on our part if we kept silent before your Reverence about what ought to be submitted for the Church, while you could not receive it either with disdain or with negligence, we ask you to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers of Christ’s weakened members.”

At the end of the same letter they address Pope Innocent in these words:

“But we believe—by the help of the mercy of our Lord God Jesus Christ, who graciously hears you as you govern, consult, and pray—that they who hold such perverse and destructive opinions will more readily yield to the authority of your Holiness, drawn from the clear light of the Scriptures, so that we may rejoice in their correction rather than grieve over their destruction, most blessed Father.”

The Fathers of Milevis wrote these words to Saint Innocent. From them we understand clearly not only that no canons had then been issued, but also that no thought had been given to issuing any.

12. Let us nevertheless grant that Quesnellus had not read the preceding letter, but, deceived by the persuasion of others, believed the canons circulating under the name of the Council of Milevis to be genuine. Why, then, does he subsequently invent, without being moved by any authority, that these canons were first confirmed by Innocent and then, by an irrevocable decree, by the Council of Ephesus?

Quesnellus thus claims for himself great license to babble, so that he may dare to defend, as his right, whatever most strongly conflicts with pontifical authority and the government of the Church [Col. 1084C]. But let our discourse now turn to the canons issued by the Councils of Carthage against that same Pelagian heresy.

13. What new arrangement, then, is found in them? Nothing at all that harms the authority of the apostolic see. Rather, the sixty-seven bishops who assembled at Carthage in the year 419 after the Council of Diospolis declared that what they had defined a second time against the Pelagians for the preservation of the salvation of many and the correction of certain people’s perversity was altogether ineffective unless the supreme authority of the apostolic see came to add strength to it.

“This action,” say the Carthaginian Fathers to Innocent, “we have judged, brother and lord, ought to be reported to your holy charity, so that the authority of the apostolic see may also be applied to the statutes of our mediocrity, for the preservation of the salvation of many and the correction of the perversity of certain people.”

The collectors of synods have noted that the Acts of this council have been lost. Yet both among the letters of Augustine and in the collection of Councils there are preserved the replies of Pope Innocent to the Fathers of Carthage [Col. 1084D] and Milevis. Nothing more consistent or more forceful could surely be desired for asserting the rights of the Roman see.

We therefore cannot pass over what Quesnellus entirely concealed lest his cause collapse. First, Innocent praises the religious seriousness of the Carthaginian Fathers, because:

“You now establish the truth with no less reason in your consultation than you previously did when you pronounced judgment, since you approved that the matter should be referred to our judgment.”

He then adds:

“Knowing what is owed to the apostolic see, since all of us placed in this position desire to follow the Apostle himself, from whom the episcopate and the entire authority of this title have arisen; following him, we know how to condemn such evils and approve what is worthy of praise.”

He continues:

“You also rightly observe, in the priestly duty of guarding the institutions of the Fathers, that what they decreed—not by human but by divine judgment—ought not to be trampled upon: namely, that whatever might be done, even in separated and distant provinces, should not be regarded as concluded until it had reached the knowledge of this see, so that, by the full authority of this see, whatever judgment was just might be confirmed. From this source the other Churches are to receive their guidance—just as waters proceed from their native spring and flow pure and undefiled from a clear head through the various regions of the whole world—so that they may know what to command, whom to cleanse, and whom the water worthy of clean bodies should avoid, as though they had been stained by filth in uncleanable mud.”

### 14

Does Quesnellus, then, not realize that by these words he has been strangled? Let him observe, I beg, that these words contain three darts which pierce him and attack and overthrow all the contrivances of his subtlety.

The first is that the name of the episcopate, and the whole basis of its authority, proceeds from the apostolic see, to which judgment in matters of faith had always been reserved.

The second is that the holy Fathers had decreed by divine, not human, judgment that such cases—even when conducted in provinces separated and far removed—were not to be brought to an end before they had come to the knowledge of this see, so that whatever judgment was just might be confirmed by the whole authority of this see.

The third, finally, is that all the other Churches must draw Catholic doctrine from this single fountain of the apostolic see, from which, as from the pure source of Christ and the apostles, wisdom flows.

Do not these three points plainly cut away Quesnellus’s fabrications? How could all the Churches of the other regions, gathered into one through their pastors, confer firmness upon the sanctions of the apostolic see? That is impossible. For neither do the members add strength and power to the head on which they depend, nor can the waters of the streams increase the purity and sweetness of the springs from which they are drawn.

Quesnellus is therefore sowing seeds in sand when he fabricates the claim that the decrees of the Roman pontiffs issued against the Pelagian offspring were made irrevocable by the sanction of the Council of Ephesus.

### 15

But let us now pass over such complications; we shall treat the same matters more clearly again when, in refuting Quesnellus’s not dissimilar arguments, we discuss the Council of Chalcedon.

Saint Leo, then, sets forth the Catholic doctrines concerning grace in the third chapter of this same letter. Relying on the testimony of the Apostle in Ephesians 2:8, he emphasizes that such and so great is the weakness inherent in human nature, wounded by original corruption, that every gift of good works is a divine preparation, because no one is justified by virtue before being justified by grace. Grace is for each person the beginning of righteousness and the fountain and source of merits.

Moreover, in the following fourth chapter, he more carefully commends to Januarius the duties of an excellent watchman, lest through such men scandals long since extinguished should be revived, and from the doctrine once cut down some offshoot of the same evil should arise in the province of Aquileia.

Then, wishing in some measure to moderate the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline toward Pelagian penitents, he commands that those who have been perfectly corrected, after first giving signs of sincere obedience, be retained in the Church. But those who, abusing indulgence, were going to resist the commands of the Roman see, he decreed should first be removed from the clerical orders and then sent far away from the fellowship of Catholics. [Col. 1085C–D; page 305]

### 16

Finally, in the fifth chapter, he restores in full that part of ecclesiastical discipline which had formerly been established both by the holy Fathers and by himself:

> No one is to be permitted to pass from one Church to another, whether in the rank of the presbyterate, in the order of the diaconate, or in any subsequent clerical office. Whoever, moved by whatever pretext, refuses to remain where he has been ordained, so that, seeking his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, he neglects to return to his own people and his own Church, is to be regarded as a stranger both to the privilege of honor and to the bond of communion.

As he closed this letter, he sincerely confessed in weightier words that he would be deeply disturbed if what he had decreed for the preservation of the canons and the integrity of the faith were neglected:

> For the faults of those in the lower orders [Col. 1086A], he says, are to be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while they dissemble about applying the harsher medicine.

This final decree of the holy pontiff occupies the last place in that manuscript collection which is entitled in the Vatican codices *Titles of the Decrees of Pope Leo*. Under number 49 we read:

> Leo, bishop: On the preservation and discipline of the canons, so that no one may presume to approach the clerical state improperly and disorderly.

### 17

Because the letter praised above lacks a consular date, it has given almost all earlier writers an opportunity to run upon reefs. Yet we could scarcely have avoided those reefs had we read it cursorily and hastily, as is commonly done.

As for Quesnellus’s opinion, he judged that it was to be assigned to no other time than the year 444. [Note: [Col. 1085] Quesnellus, vol. II of the Works of Saint Leo, on Letter 6, p. 430, column 11.]

Dupinius, Tillemontius, and, most recently, the Reverend Father Bernard de Rubeis, an outstanding member of the Dominican order, subscribed to Quesnellus’s view in his celebrated work *On the Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*. The most eminent Cardinal Norisius, however, maintained that the letter had been written later, saying:

> “This letter was written to Januarius in the year 447, and indeed before the fourth letter addressed to that same Januarius.”

We, however, without committing ourselves to either side, shall nevertheless indicate the genuine date of this letter. For, as was observed earlier, in the first and fifth chapters of this letter the holy pontiff commands Januarius to observe canons that he had previously issued concerning the reception of heretical clerics.

Since we read such canons expressed both in the twelfth and in the thirteenth letters, it follows that the letter placed sixth in Quesnellus’s edition is later than those two letters, namely, the twelfth and the thirteenth.

Although the twelfth letter lacks a consular date, it is nevertheless most clearly shown by the following letter that it must be assigned to the year 445. That subsequent letter was written to the metropolitan bishops throughout the province of Achaia on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Symmachus—that is, in the year of Christ 446—and it mentions matters which Leo had written in the preceding letter to Anastasius. Therefore the twelfth letter must be assigned to the year 445.

Thus the opinion of Quesnellus, Tillemontius, and others, who assert that the sixth letter was written by Saint Leo in 444, not only totters but collapses entirely. For that reason we consider Norisius’s opinion more probable, since he assigned it to the year 447. [Col. 1086B–C]

### 18

Nor does it present an obstacle that another letter of Leo to Januarius was written in the same year. Why should it be impossible for the Roman pontiff, under the pressure of an extremely serious cause such as this, to send two letters within twelve months to the same bishop of Italy?

Was not the final letter written at the end of the year 447? It was dated, in fact, the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Alipius and Ardabur. The pontiff could therefore have written the earlier letter to Januarius either at the beginning or around the middle of that year, especially since the distance of the journey from Rome to Aquileia is not so great that several exchanges of letters could not have taken place between them even within five or six months.

From these considerations it is clear that these conjectures are not undermined even if the other letter to Januarius was issued on the Kalends of July, as most manuscript codices have it. I shall not linger longer over a matter so thoroughly established.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Various Opinions of Writers Concerning the Earlier Letters of Saint Leo. Our Own Position Is Established

### 1

Turning, then, from our discussion to more serious matters, we shall briefly indicate what gave more recent writers the occasion for such extensive controversy.

The reason writers diverged into different opinions was that there were two copies of one and the same letter. One was addressed to Septimius, bishop of Altinum; the other to Januarius of Aquileia. They judged the former to be wholly alien to the eloquence, doctrine, and manner of writing of the holy pontiff. On that basis they vigorously argued that one or the other copy had to be rejected as spurious and forged.

Norisius, however, in Book II of his *History of the Pelagian Controversy*, attributed both copies to Leo. He wrote:

> “When Januarius had written back to Leo—evidently after receiving that earlier letter of which we spoke above—that he would carry out all Leo’s instructions, compelling the heretics to condemn their error publicly and to confirm that condemnation by voice and writing, Leo sent two letters of the same model: one to Septimius, informing him of what he had commanded Januarius, and the other to Januarius, congratulating him on promptly carrying out what had been ordered.”

When Norisius wrote this, Quesnellus had not yet appeared upon the scene. In the final edition of the *Works of the Divine Leo*, after weighing the features and characteristics of both letters, Quesnellus abandoned the earlier view and attacked and refuted at length the conjectures of the same most eminent Norisius. He argued that the copy of this letter addressed to the bishop of Altinum displayed many signs of forgery and therefore had been falsely attributed to our pontiff. [Col. 1087A–B]

### 2

Joseph Anthelmius reasoned differently. He judged that all the evidence of forgery produced by Quesnellus against the copy addressed to the bishop of Altinum should instead be turned against the other copy, addressed to Januarius of Aquileia, and that this copy should be rejected as spurious and apocryphal.

Who does not see that we have encountered a knot which must be untied in every direction? This is especially so because later distinguished writers—Tillemontius, Dupinius, Father Bernard de Rubeis, and any others there may be—have either inclined to one side or the other or, defining nothing at all, preferred to remain suspended in uncertainty rather than rashly assert anything, hoping that in the course of time the truth, not yet sufficiently established, might be more clearly disclosed when a larger supply of documentary evidence became available.

Meanwhile, I venture to assert that Norisius did not go astray in his conjectures when he wrote that both copies of that letter proceeded from Leo: one he actually addressed to Januarius, the other to Septimius of Altinum. Perhaps Septimius was thereby to understand both that Januarius, the metropolitan, was directing all the strength of his zeal toward the destruction of the Pelagian clerics, and that Leo himself, the Roman pontiff before whom Septimius had brought the Pelagian clerics of Aquileia, had ordered what seemed necessary for the integrity of the faith.

We are persuaded that Norisius’s words quoted above can bear this meaning without any charge of foolishness or invention. Nor should this arrangement be judged unusual or alien to Leo’s customary procedure. After receiving letters from Septimius of Altinum concerning the Pelagian plague raging in the province of Aquileia, Leo sent a copy of them to Januarius, the metropolitan, so that he began his earlier letter to Januarius with these words:

> “From the report of our holy brother and fellow bishop, which is contained below, we have learned that certain presbyters and deacons …” [Note: [Col. 1087D] Letter 6, to Januarius.]

Why, then, if we adhere to this copy, should it be judged alien to Leo’s manner of acting that, after receiving Januarius’s reply, he likewise entrusted it to Septimius together with a copy of the fourteenth, or final, letter? His chief purpose would have been that Septimius too should fully understand the vigor of his metropolitan’s faith, his pastoral care, and the admonitions and sanctions of the apostolic see.

Leo certainly ought to have written back to Septimius, from whom he had received the earlier report—especially after he had read Januarius’s letter, approved the vigor of the faith that he had long known in him, and for that reason might have adopted the following arrangement: just as he had earlier entrusted Septimius’s report to Januarius, the metropolitan of the province of Aquileia, together with his first letter, so, after receiving Januarius’s reply, he might have entrusted that reply to Septimius, enclosing with it a copy of the final letter, so that Septimius might know in advance both what had been done and what was to be carried out in the future for the suppression of the Pelagians in that province.

For the rest, I consider it wrong even to suspect that this second letter, of which we are speaking, written to Januarius, is forged. The most ancient collector, Dionysius Exiguus, praises it as a genuine offspring of Leo. The Church of Aquileia always preserved it as genuine in its archives, as we ourselves have already stated from the Vatican manuscript *Chronicle*. Finally, it possesses all the marks and characteristics that sufficiently show that it was given not to some suffragan bishop but to the metropolitan of the province. [Col. 1088A]

### 3

Nevertheless, while adhering to these conjectures, I shall not deny that the other copy, entrusted to Septimius and perhaps at some time discovered in the archives of the Church of Altinum, may have suffered some corrupting fraud. It has its blemishes, from which the writers mentioned above maintain that some indications of forgery can be detected in it.

Among these are the words:

> “We have sent this written to the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia”;

and the other words that immediately follow. [Note: [Col. 1087D] Saint Leo, Letter 7, chapter 1.]

The other words immediately following are: “by which he might recognize that these matters concerned the peril of his position.” Quesnellus maintains that they do not bear the stamp either of Saint Leo’s age or of his style. [Note: [Col. 1088D] Quesnellus, vol. II, p. 432.] Yet they are not in fact of such a kind that they cannot be defended against every charge of forgery.

First, Altinum was once a flourishing city built on the coast of Venetia, as is established from Pliny, Martial, Livy, and the ancient geographical tables. Accordingly, the words “to the metropolitan … of the province of Venetia” could appropriately have been used to designate more clearly the province in which Altinum was situated, especially since in Leo’s age the metropolitan of Aquileia had under him the cities and bishops of not one but several provinces.

Furthermore, the Acts of the councils abundantly testify that Altinum had an episcopal see. At the synod of Aquileia, convened in the year of the Lord 381 under Pope Damasus, among the Italian, Gallic, and Pannonian bishops who gathered there, Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum, was also present.

Moreover, when a synod was convened at Grado in the year of the Lord 579, the bishop of Altinum attended it. For in the fifth place we read:

> “I, Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Altinum, have subscribed these acts.”

Ughellius discussed this synod in volume V of *Sacred Italy*. The Acts of the pseudo-synod of Marano also mention this Peter of Altinum, as is evident from Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 27, when, in the year 589, Severus, patriarch of Aquileia, presented a statement of his error. [Page 308]

Thus Quesnellus must be pronounced especially deluded, since he wrote so boldly:

> “The information concerning Septimius’s episcopal see remains just as obscure as if this letter had never become known. The forger who fabricated the letter assigned Septimius a see that occurred to him and seemed better suited to his fraudulent purpose. In reality, nothing concerning a bishop of Altinum of this name was discovered by Ughellius in the ancient monuments, since nothing about him is read in *Sacred Italy*.” [Note: [Col. 1088D] The same work, p. 437, column 1.]

How cleverly Quesnellus deceives us, demanding from Ughellius evidence for Septimius’s episcopal see at Altinum! For, following Dandulus, he begins his discussion only with the destruction of the city of Altinum, at which time Paul, the bishop of that city, transferred the see to Torcello.

But both Dandulus and Ughellius fell into error in this matter. They assert that this transfer was made by Bishop Paul in the year 631 and that he died in the following month. Yet in the Acts of the Roman council under Pope Agatho we read:

> “I, Paul, bishop of the holy Church of Altinum in the province of Istria, have likewise subscribed this petition, which we have unanimously composed on behalf of our apostolic faith.”

I believe no one is unaware that this council was held at Rome in the year of the Lord 680. Nor is any other bishop of this name listed in Ughellius’s catalogue.

Nor do the two words “province of Istria” present an obstacle. Earlier, when the affairs of Italy were distressed, when Aquileia—while Leo was still alive—had been captured and leveled to the ground by Attila, king of the Huns, and when in the declining fifth century it had again been shaken by the attacks of the Goths and the fury of the other barbarians, the bishops of Aquileia were finally, in the year 579, unable to endure the scourges of the impious Lombard nation. By decree and authority of the Roman pontiff Pelagius, they transferred that metropolitan see to Grado. At that time, with the suffragan bishops consenting, the fortress of Grado was made the metropolis of all Venetia and Istria. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Council of Grado, vol. VI of the Councils, p. 651.]

If the bishop of the new Aquileia was called the metropolitan of the provinces of Venetia and Istria, why could he not have been designated by the same names before old Aquileia suffered so many disasters? At that time too, the bishop of Aquileia was truly the metropolitan of the province of Venetia. [Col. 1089A–B]

### 4

Nor do those words give off any odor of forgery:

> “By which he would understand that they concerned the danger to his status.”

Those who know that Leo himself wrote in his sixth letter to Januarius will certainly not deny that they fit the age and style of Leo perfectly:

> “Let your Love have no doubt that, if—as we believe—what we decree for the preservation of the canons and the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved most deeply.” [Note: [Col. 1089D] Letter of Pelagius, vol. VI of the Councils, p. 652.]

He uses exactly the same words in the fourteenth letter, which certainly indicate threats and the future indignation of the pontiff if Januarius, the metropolitan, should hand over the decrees of the apostolic see to negligence and contempt.

Nor was the authority of the earliest Roman pontiffs in correcting and restraining the disputes and failings of lower bishops confined within narrow boundaries, so that it embraced only those who then belonged to the Roman synod, or only those who had been ordained by that Roman pontiff, as Quesnellus rashly declared. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Volume II of the *Works of Saint Leo*, p. 432, column 2, no. 3.]

It extended far and wide to the bishops of the entire world, so that the Roman pontiffs admonished and rebuked them and deprived them of communion. We could establish this with six hundred examples from Leo’s predecessors, if this dissertation did not already extend farther than is proper.

Let Quesnellus, I beg, merely run through what our Leo says in his letters to Anastasius of Thessalonica; to Flavian and Anatolius of Constantinople; to Juvenal of Jerusalem; to Turribius of Astorga; to the bishops of the province of Vienne; and to Theodoret of Cyrrhus. None of these belonged to the Roman synod, nor had they been ordained by Roman pontiffs. Yet Leo either rebukes them, admonishes them, deprives them of communion, absolves them, removes them from their sees, or restores them to those same sees. These facts are decisive evidence. [Note: [Col. 1090D] Saint Leo, Letter 12, chapter 11.]

> “The distinction concerning the form of bishops also arose, and provision was made by a great ordinance that no one should claim everything for himself, but that in each province there should be one whose judgment among the brethren would have precedence; and again, that certain men established in the greater cities should undertake a broader care, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one see of Peter, and nothing anywhere would disagree with the head.”

From these and other acts Quesnellus’s assertion falls: namely, that Leo was accustomed to use such threats against metropolitan bishops. Leo certainly did not refrain from using them when dealing with Eastern bishops; how much more, then, could he have used them when handling business with the metropolitan of Aquileia, who was immediately subject to the Roman patriarchate? [Col. 1090A]

### 5

But Quesnellus again brings himself onto the stage, arguing against Norisius that it is evidence of forgery that the two copies do not correspond exactly.

In the copy addressed to Januarius, he says, certain words that seem necessary were cut out, such as “from the fellowship of the Pelagians and Coelestians.” He then adds that in the letter to Januarius certain matters are decreed concerning clerics returning from heresy which do not appear in the other copy—namely, that they should not be promoted to a higher order but should be allowed to remain in the order they had attained.

In this matter I do not at all disagree with Quesnellus’s criticism. Nevertheless, I am not thereby led to believe that Norisius’s conjectures totter or collapse. For the objections raised by Quesnellus can mean only that one or the other copy of that letter suffered some injury or was enlarged by some addition. These matters cannot easily be recognized, especially since the oldest copies have perished, with the aid of which the letter would have come to light in a purer and more corrected form. [Col. 1090B]

## CHAPTER VIII. The Fourteenth Letter of the Divine Leo to Januarius of Aquileia Is Reexamined, and Quesnellus’s Nonsense Is Rejected

### 1

Let us not pass over anything pertaining to Leo’s actions against the Pelagians. Finally, we need only focus on the arguments of the fourteenth letter, which he wrote to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia.

First of all, there is no reason to fear that Januarius failed to obey Leo’s commands exactly. For Leo learned from his reply that Januarius had devoted even greater effort to rebuking the Pelagian clerics. Therefore, in order to increase and further arouse the vigilance of that watchful shepherd, the holy pontiff congratulates him on vigilantly exercising pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flock, lest wolves who had entered under the appearance of sheep tear the simple apart with beastly savagery—not only failing to benefit themselves from any correction but also corrupting those who were sound. [Page 310]

There can be no doubt that by such language the holy pontiff intended to mark and attack the Pelagians. For he began the first chapter of the sixth letter with a similar allegory and almost the same words, as we noted above.

He then adds that it concerns the danger of the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics and schismatics, and has in some way stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion, should, after repenting, be retained in Catholic communion without a lawful profession of satisfaction.

Wishing to remedy these evils, he prescribed for Januarius the observance of very salutary rules: namely, that Pelagian clerics, in accordance with the constitution of the canons, should lose all hope of higher promotion but should remain permanently established in the order in which they were found, provided that they had not been defiled by a second baptism.

### 2

Insisting upon these final words, Quesnellus added the following note:

> “He perhaps adds this exception with the African canons in mind, for in the twenty-seventh canon of the African collection we read: ‘Nor should it be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.’”

A witty note, worthy of its author. Are we therefore to suppose that the apostolic see wished or was able to take the African canons into account in the case of the rebaptized? How could that have happened when, after the error of the rebaptizers had been defended by the African bishops for so long, a great and dreadful schism had arisen—one that received only under the condition of a second conferral of baptism those who came from heresy into the Church or had been baptized by heretics?

But while the apostolic see labored with the utmost concern to prevent and eradicate that error, just as it refused communion to the rebaptizers, so it also did not allow the rebaptized themselves to be promoted to the sacred clerical orders. The same reasoning may readily be applied here.

For the *clinici*—that is, those who were baptized in bed—although in the same century they had not been disqualified by any sacrilege as the rebaptized were, were nevertheless barred by the ecclesiastical law enacted by Cornelius from the ministries of the sacred altar, as Eusebius says. [Note: [Col. 1091D] Eusebius, Book I of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 32.]

How much more, then, were those bound by this defect or impediment of irregularity who had been defiled by a second baptism—especially since in that century the same question of the rebaptizers, once quieted under the Roman pontiffs Cornelius and then Stephen, had again broken out among the Africans.

### 3

Let us nevertheless grant that nothing had been defined by those two pontiffs. What follows from that? Will Quesnellus perhaps conceal what the Roman synod under Pope Damasus proceeded to decree?

It is indeed regrettable that those Acts have not reached us. But the synodical letter of those Fathers survives, from which we understand that sacrilegious rebaptizers had again spread throughout Africa. Although the authority of the emperors Gratian and Valentinian had expelled them, Claudianus had nevertheless been ordained by the expelled party in the year 363 and was sent to disturb Rome as though he were a bishop. [Note: [Col. 1091D–1092D] Letter of the Roman council to Gratian and Valentinian, written in the year 378, vol. II of the Councils, p. 1187.]

Since, therefore, the Fathers of the Roman council abhorred both crimes—namely, rebaptism and the ordinations of the rebaptized—how could the laws of irregularity concerning the rebaptized have failed to operate in the Roman Church?

With this single battering ram, Quesnellus’s insidious note collapses entirely. Through it he would gradually persuade his readers that the apostolic see had sometimes become the follower of other Churches and had borrowed its laws and canons from them.

He then tries to seize an opportunity to fabricate arguments from his own imagination by which he might assign to the Roman Church the code of canons that he himself published, furnished with notes and dissertations, in the second volume of the *Works of Leo*. [Col. 1091C]

But finally let the impostor take note that the synodical letter of the Roman council was written to the emperors at a time when that African twenty-seventh canon had not yet been conceived. The letter must be assigned to the year 378, whereas the cited canon was issued at the fifth Council of Carthage, convened in the year 398.

But if Quesnellus does not wish to accept this evidence, let him at least agree with Basil, who asserts in his letter to Amphilochius, chapter 47, that the Roman Church had its own canons in the case of the rebaptized. [Page 311]

### 4

But let us now return to Leo. Before closing his letter, he first congratulates Januarius on the vigor of his faith and then suggests several other matters to be carried out, over which Quesnellus has already raised the greatest storm of controversy.

Saint Leo therefore instructed the bishop of Aquileia to join his care to the dispositions of the apostolic see and to ensure that the measures commendably proposed and ordered for the safety of the entire Church be carried out carefully and swiftly. [Col. 1091D]

Here Quesnellus brandishes his censor’s style, attacking more severely the author of the book entitled *On the Canonical Judgment of Bishops*:

> “I marvel,” he says, “at the stupidity of the writer, who abuses this expression in two places, here and in the fourth letter. ‘The canons,’ he says, ‘testify that the rules forbidding those who return from heresy to Catholic communion to be promoted to a higher clerical rank were established for the universal Church everywhere.’ These words of Leo prove it: ‘let him ensure that they be carried out carefully.’”

The author of that book had added:

> “Such canons are not numbered among the Nicene canons, nor are they found anywhere in the whole code of Justellus. Therefore, besides the Nicene decrees, there were certain other rules by which Saint Leo wished Januarius also to be bound, and which were in use throughout the universal Church in the discussion of ecclesiastical matters.”

Because the author had added this, Quesnellus, attacking him with still greater harshness, continues:

> “What sort of drowsiness is this in a man who wanted to interpret these words as referring to canons? Is it not clearer than the midday sun to anyone reading them that the matters said to have been commendably proposed are to be understood of the letters full of the vigor of faith which Januarius had written to Saint Leo, while the matters said to have been salutarily ordered refer to this very rescript of Saint Leo, in which he commands that the constitutions of the canons be observed?”

Since Quesnellus attacks the author of the cited book with these words, piling up many other matters at the same time in order to twist Leo’s words into a foreign meaning, he departs far from the purpose of the question before us.

For that author neither reviewed nor disclosed the most ancient custom of the Church or its canons concerning the reception of heretical penitents. Rather, Leo’s wording and manner of writing chiefly reveal that our Leo was dealing with a particular disposition or law enacted by him for the reception into the Church of clerics returning from the Pelagian heresy. [Col. 1092A–B]

### 5

For although many canonical sanctions had been issued on this matter in the age of the holy pontiff, none of them—if we except this letter of Leo—thereby removed from such clerics the hope of higher promotion.

We therefore rightly judge that Quesnellus made a futile attempt when he asserted that this law could be derived from the eighth canon of the first Council of Nicaea. For we find nothing in that canon which appears to concern this permanent defect of irregularity or which could settle the present controversy.

There the sole subject is the reconciliation of the heretical Cathari. The holy synod decided that leniency should be shown toward them, lest their clerics, removed from their own ranks and made to stand among the laity, be granted lay communion, as the Church was accustomed to do with the adherents of other heresies.

If, therefore, apart from that form of indulgence or leniency, these words contain and imply nothing else—

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, the pure, if at some time they return to the Catholic and Apostolic Church, it has seemed good to the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy”—

then it is certainly not one and the same thing for a person not to be removed from his own rank and for him to be unable, under any circumstances whatever, ever to be promoted to higher orders.

Saint Leo defined this latter point in the letter under discussion, wishing these clerics to be bound by a perpetual bond of irregularity as punishment for their former heresy. But the Nicene Fathers merely decreed, out of indulgence toward the Cathari, that they should remain in their orders.

Had Quesnellus reflected on the great difference between these two provisions, he would never have written so freely that Leo’s words harmonized with the eighth canon of the general Council of Nicaea.

That canon contains nothing which corresponds to these Leonine sanctions. It says nothing about permanent stability in the order already received; finally, it says nothing about removing the hope of higher promotion. All these matters were proposed and salutarily ordered by Leo’s dispositions for the safety of the entire Church. [Col. 1092B–D; page 312]

### 6

So that the dispositions of the holy pontiff may become known, we set out his words:

> “Concerning them also we command that the constitution of the canons be observed, so that they may regard it as a great benefit if, with all hope of promotion taken away from them, they remain permanently established in the order in which they are found.”

Quesnellus then reasons entirely incorrectly when he asserts that in Leo’s age only the eighth Nicene canon existed concerning the reception, in their own orders, of clerics returning from heresy to the Church, and that Saint Leo therefore had that canon in view.

Such language is wholly unbecoming to a man who boasts of possessing comprehensive knowledge of ecclesiastical discipline. For what had been decreed on this question by councils and Fathers before Leo’s pontificate, the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea in the year 787 gathered together as though into a single body.

7. For in the earlier session of this synod, when the question concerned the reception of heretics who were penitent, nothing at all was established without consulting the ancient records of the Church. Therefore John, a presbyter and monk, legate of the See of Antioch, sought to remove the controversy from their midst and proposed to the holy assembly:

“Many people have spoken of how those who return from heresy ought to be received, most holy father”—he is addressing the patriarch Tarasius in particular. “For this reason,” the same John said, “we recommend that the holy synod order the books of the holy Fathers to be brought here at once, so that we may know and consider what definite procedure ought to be observed in receiving them.”

Then an order was given for the books to be brought [Note: [Col. 1093D] Vol. VIII of the Councils, p. 1325.].

Constantine, the notary of that patriarchal see, began the reading of them not with the eighth canon of the Council of Nicaea, but with the fifty-third canon of the Apostles, whose earlier interpretation is as follows:

“If a presbyter does not receive one who turns away from sin, but rejects him, let him be deposed. For he offends Christ, who said that joy arises in heaven over the sinner who repents.”

Since this canon extended its leniency generally to all heretics who were penitent, whether they were laymen or clerics, Tarasius immediately asked: “Is there another canon on this matter?” Then Constantine the notary at once recited the eighth canon of the First Council of Nicaea.

But when Theodore, bishop of Catana in the province of Sicily, argued that this canon too could not be applied to the recently arisen heresy of the Agiomarchists, the Fathers, at the command of Tarasius, asked about other canons. Accordingly, the same notary read the third canon of the holy and ecumenical Synod of Ephesus:

“If any clerics in any city have been prohibited by Nestorius and by those who follow that doctrine, because they held an incorrect opinion, we have judged it right that they recover their own rank.”

After this the Fathers still remained uncertain whether those who returned from heresy ought to be admitted to the sacred order. Therefore the monk Stephen, holding in his hands letters of the holy Basil on this subject, had read what Basil had written about the Encratites in his first letter to Amphilochius. They then appended another letter to the Euaesians, as well as excerpts from the letter to the bishops of the West, which were more relevant to our subject, in which Basil discussed Eustathius of Sebaste.

Eustathius had repeatedly fallen into the Arian heresy. When Hermogenes, the bishop who accused him and reproved him for his perverse doctrine, confronted him, Eustathius presented a confession of the sounder faith and, having thus received the laying on of hands from him, defected again to the Arian party after Hermogenes had died. But after being expelled from Constantinople and returning to Sebaste, he offered a defense. Skillfully concealing his impious opinion and putting forward words that were not unsound but appeared to express correct doctrine, he easily obtained the episcopate.

Although many other examples of such wicked dissimulation might be found, and recounting them would burden the reader’s attention, we ask only this: how could the impediment of irregularity with which we are concerned have been defined in that eighth canon of Nicaea? Did the ordination of Eustathius not occur long after the Council of Nicaea? For it must be assigned at least to the year 376, which was fifty-one years after the Council of Nicaea. Therefore that eighth Nicene canon did not concern denying clerics who returned to the Church further promotion; rather, it sanctioned only those provisions that seemed to pertain to their reception and to the manner of reconciliation to be observed through the laying on of hands.

8. That ecclesiastical discipline is likewise echoed by the decree issued against the impious Messalians, or Euchites, at the Third Ecumenical Synod, which the deacon Stephen recited at that same Second Council of Nicaea. Its final words lend even greater strength to the arguments of our present investigation:

“It pleased all of us [Col. 1094A] ... that if anyone has rejected that very doctrine, then, if he has abjured that very doctrine, if he is a cleric, he should remain in that ordination; but if he is a layman, he should be received into communion with the Church.””

In this matter it is especially important to observe that the Fathers of the aforementioned Third Ecumenical Council wished to preserve what had been defined at the Synod of Alexandria in the year 362, when the question of receiving apostate bishops was being considered under Pope Liberius.

9. All these matters, brought together, abundantly display the canonical practice observed in the Church before the age of Leo concerning the reception of heretics. But the same Seventh Ecumenical Synod supplied us with still more abundant records, drawn partly from the works of the holy Cyril and Athanasius and partly found in the Ecclesiastical Histories of Rufinus of Aquileia and Socrates. These manifest with remarkable clarity both the point at issue and the fact that Quesnellus himself was mistaken in examining it.

Meanwhile, since from the sequence of so many and such important testimonies we have established that two questions differ greatly from one another—namely, whether heretics returning to the Church were to be received in their own orders without being stripped of office and expelled, and whether, once leniency had been granted and they had remained in the orders they had received, they were nevertheless to be bound by a perpetual impediment preventing them from ascending to higher orders—Leo’s purpose, command, and decree have now been brought to light. There is no doubt that, if Januarius had not obeyed, these matters would have stirred the holy pontiff’s mind deeply and moved him to impose some ecclesiastical penalty upon him, as the final words of that letter reveal:

“Let not Your Dilection doubt that, if—which we do not suppose—the things we decree for the preservation of the canons and the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved with still greater severity, because the faults of inferiors ought to be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great pestilence while they dissimulate and fail to apply the necessary remedy.”

10. Setting jokes aside, let the annotator Quesnellus consider this matter and ask himself whether any bishop, in matters pertaining to the safety of the entire Church, has been accustomed to address other bishops throughout the Christian world in such grave words, full of the force of authority and jurisdiction, as he himself has dared to assert with excessive freedom.

Certainly the bishops of other Churches may write, offer suggestions, discuss, and investigate all those matters that can benefit the Church’s welfare. But to define and decree something for the common good of the Christian polity itself was divinely granted, apart from general synods, only to the Roman pontiffs, as has been demonstrated in this and in our other dissertations.

11. As for Januarius’s actions, we know absolutely nothing. It is nevertheless worthwhile to suppose that all Leo’s commands and decrees were carried out by him with such care and speed that that abominable offspring of the Pelagians, which was raging especially among the clergy of that province, was almost eradicated and brought to destruction.

For, so far as we know, no further exchange of letters took place between Leo and Januarius after this. The report from Januarius to Leo was also lost through the ravages of time, and among writers of the same period such profound silence is preserved concerning the events that occurred there that no mention of those actions is found.

There nevertheless survives another letter of Saint Leo to Nicetas of Aquileia, the successor of Januarius, written in the year 458 [Note: [Col. 1094D] Letter 129 to Nicetas of Aquileia.]. From this we may reasonably and conveniently infer that at that time no remnants at all of the Pelagian offspring existed in that province.

In that letter our pontiff, by the authority of the Apostolic See, responds to seven questions submitted to him and prescribes to Nicetas of Aquileia what remedy ought especially to be applied in those grievously afflicted times, so that the wounds inflicted upon religion by the hostility of its adversaries might be healed. Since these questions have no bearing on the customs, doctrines, or history of the Pelagians, we omit them for the present, lest we seem to sing outside the scene; we shall nevertheless discuss them when we adorn the ecclesiastical discipline of that age with our observations.

12. Meanwhile, we ought rather to congratulate ourselves that the divine zeal of Saint Leo the Great in overthrowing the Pelagians and abolishing their errors achieved its desired end. To become more certain of this, we have endeavored to examine all the records of antiquity—particularly those of men who flourished in the fifth and sixth centuries of the Church—and nowhere have we encountered any mention of the Pelagian heresy as though it were then spreading.

Our conjecture is confirmed, and our congratulation at the same time strengthened, by the first letter of Pope John IV addressed to the bishops and presbyters of Scotland, which Bede also reports in Book II, chapter 19, of his *History of the English*. In it the supreme pontiff, together with the Roman clergy, discusses two questions that the clergy of Scotland had proposed to him: one concerning Easter, the other concerning the Pelagians reviving in that kingdom.

Regarding these matters Pope John IV writes:

“After the method of observing Easter had been explained, they add the following in the same letter concerning the Pelagians: ‘We have also learned that the poison of the Pelagian heresy is again reviving among you. We strongly exhort you to remove from your minds such a poisonous crime of superstition. For it ought not to be unknown to you how that detestable heresy was condemned: it was not only abolished for these two hundred years, but is also daily buried by us under a perpetual anathema.’” [Note: [Col. 1095B] It is extant in vol. VI of the Councils, p. 1509.]

If anyone wishes to dwell upon these words, he will not deny that they lend support to our conjecture. For Pope John IV held the supreme office of the Catholic society in the seventh century of the Church, namely in the year 640, after Pope Severinus had already died. If we subtract two hundred years from that date, as Pope John’s testimony indicates, the result is the year 440 of Christ, in which Saint Leo the Great was appointed pontiff of the Roman Church, as is understood from the lists of the Roman pontiffs.

It must therefore be affirmed without any hesitation that Pope John IV responded to the inquiries of the Scots in that year, 640. For although the aforementioned letter lacks a date, it nevertheless has such an opening that we may infer that, scarcely having been appointed to the Roman pontificate, John wished to comply with the wishes of the Scots, who had already sent their consultations and inquiries to his predecessor Severinus, although the bearers of those messages did not reach Rome [Col. 1096B] until after Severinus’s death.

This is plainly indicated by the words with which John began his letter:

“The writings which the bearers had brought to Pope Severinus, of holy memory—he having departed this life—reciprocal replies to the requests that had been made ...””

But now, setting aside these and similar conjectures, we decide to withdraw our hand from the present table, intending to offer much else of greater importance in what follows, since at last, as the crown of our *Exercises*, we have resolved immediately to speak about the affairs of Eutyches.

[Col. 1095]

# THE TWO BOOKS ON THE EUTYCHIAN HERESY AND ITS HISTORY

## BOOK ONE

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 1095C]

Saint Leo the Great, a vigorous champion of the Catholic faith, having already slaughtered the Priscillianists, extinguished the clandestine movements of the Manichaeans—as Quesnellus also says—and finally carried off an extraordinary triumph over Pelagianism, which was spreading through the provinces of Italy, is compelled to advance to greater struggles, to fight bravely and successfully against the Eutychians. These, like new and recent enemies emerging from the East, attacked the incarnation of Christ the Lord.

This heresy, which took its beginning and its name from a certain monk called Eutyches, archimandrite of a Constantinopolitan monastery, occupied the mind of the holy pontiff for three years in such a way that he had to devote all his effort and labor to destroying it completely. He also had to apply the most serious attention to restoring the rights of bishops and Churches, which had been violated and abolished with the greatest injustice by factious men.

I shall not recount his grave prudence in evading the arbitrary decisions and the lust for power of those who, disregarding the rules of the sacred canons and relying solely upon the authority, influence, and command of the secular age, violently expelled holy and orthodox shepherds from their sees or harassed them with various kinds of punishment.

In carrying out these duties, just as his courage, wisdom, and supreme prudence shine forth, so too that supreme and universal power divinely granted to the Roman pontiffs stands out: the power to investigate and judge all matters concerning the faith of all and the Churches.

Although it is well known that heretics and other envious men have always not merely recoiled from this special prerogative and privilege but have also endeavored to attack and destroy it—being guided by the desire to extend the rights of other bishops beyond their proper limits and, at their discretion, to enlarge the authority of synods, gradually restricting the dignity and power of the Apostolic See to narrow boundaries—we nevertheless see that their labor is in vain if, setting aside the prejudices of popular opinion, we resolve to draw the truth of all things solely from the acts of the councils and from the surviving writings of the holy pontiff.

Nor have we thought it right to refrain from discussing these matters on the grounds that Paschasius Quesnellus has described in great abundance the life and deeds of Saint Leo and admits: “I hold the pontifical dignity in greater reverence than does anyone else.”

He made that assertion deceitfully. For he omitted nothing that would introduce novelties of judgment into the Church and drive out the ancient form and structure of the sacred hierarchy praised in Scripture.

I could set before the reader nearly infinite examples of this Quesnellian method at the very threshold of my present contest, if I did not fear burdening my readers with an unwelcome task. This is especially so because, apart from the primacy of honor, he grants the same dignity nothing at all except jurisdiction over the Roman episcopate, and even makes that jurisdiction within the Roman episcopate dependent upon other bishops who were required to attend the Roman council of the Westerners.

I, therefore, who from my earliest years have been inflamed by a love of truth and have earnestly desired to draw it only from the purest sources, and to imbue with it the minds of those whose education I had been entrusted to undertake, could not observe these things without deep disgust.

I reflected that Quesnellus had adopted no other aim in similar dissertations than to draw incautious men, insufficiently versed in ecclesiastical history, over to his side and bind them with various enticements, so that little by little they might fall away from the reverence, obedience, and submission owed to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1097D] Paschasius Quesnellus, vol. II of the works of Saint Leo the Great, dissertation 1, *On the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo, Supreme Pontiff*, p. 147 according to my pagination.].

For the novelty of doctrine, which instills desire in men, has in our own age acquired such force among almost every nation that, without any genuine discernment or love of truth, people are captivated by those teachings capable of overthrowing the institutions and precepts handed down by our ancestors.

The saying of the Apostle seems to me to fit the men of our age who love to claim for themselves the name of learned men [Note: [Col. 1098D] Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4.]:

“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but will heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires, having itching ears; they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn instead to fables.”

And who could deny that Quesnellus fabricated fables in his history of Eutyches and in his account of the deeds of Leo the Great? Confusing episcopal dignity, which is common to all bishops, with jurisdiction, he openly admits that he does not wish what he venerates in one to be trampled upon in the others. He contends, on the basis of ancient custom, that neither Eutyches nor Flavian had the Roman pontiff as the legitimate and principal judge of disputes concerning the doctrines of the faith, to whom both accuser and accused voluntarily hastened to assert their rights [Note: [Col. 1098D] Baronius, under the year 449, no. 5.].

In response to these words of the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, the aforementioned Quesnellus deceitfully adds:

“We readily acknowledge the Roman pontiff as the legitimate judge of ecclesiastical disputes and, if he is compared with individual bishops, as the principal judge. But who could therefore tolerate the presentation before Leo of Flavian—whom both the prerogative of his see, his singular holiness, and his steadfastness in the faith, persevering even to martyrdom, ought to have commended so greatly—as being matched and pitted against a rebellious, ignorant, obscure, and worthless monk; an expelled presbyter against his own bishop and the bishop of the holy see; a judge against the accused; and both of them standing before Leo as though disputing over something to be divided jointly, as if they were fighting over an uncertain outcome? Let such an injury to the most sacred assembly of bishops be far removed.”

What, then? Does Quesnellus defend the supreme judicial power of the Roman pontiffs, which the testimonies of Scripture indicate and which ancient tradition and practice asserted for them?

He does not. For he calls the Roman pontiff the principal and legitimate judge of the Church’s disputes only in this sense: namely, by comparison with individual bishops residing in their own sees [Col. 1097D]. Perhaps he wishes to indicate that no judgment of the Roman pontiff should be considered firm and ratified unless it is supported and approved by the vote of other bishops convened in synods. Quesnellus himself has explained this refrain a thousand times in his writings.
