Moreover, if it were an injury to the most sacred assembly of bishops for the cases of subordinate defendants, once judged in the provinces, to be reviewed a second time by pontifical authority—as he invents—then innocent men could be harassed, oppressed, and removed from their ranks with impunity by metropolitans and the other suffragan bishops of the provinces, and there would be no judge in the ecclesiastical hierarchy able to avenge those afflicted by more serious injuries and persecutions.

Since, therefore, no one who has dared to take up arms against the mother Church can have a just cause, I could easily be led to hope that, with the divine assistance, I might likewise accomplish this task by setting my hand to writing the history of the Eutychian heresy, after noting and rejecting in the preceding books all the nonsense and inventions, especially those of Beausobre and Quesnellus.

## CHAPTER I

### Eutyches, holding an erroneous opinion about the incarnation of Christ the Lord, is accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, at the Constantinopolitan synod. Summoned a second and third time by the Fathers, he refuses to appear.

1. The case of Eutyches was investigated in a public and solemn judgment of the Church of Constantinople in the year of our Lord 448, during the consulship of Zeno and Posthumianus.

On the sixth day before the Ides of November, thirty bishops of that metropolis assembled there to settle the dispute that had arisen between Florentius, bishop of Sardes, and John and Cossinus, bishops of the same province of Lydia. At that gathering Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum in Phrygia, presented to the sacred assembly certain written accusations containing the blasphemies of Eutyches.

Eutyches presided as a presbyter and archimandrite over a Constantinopolitan monastery. Although he outwardly pretended to profess holiness and piety, he was steeped in corrupt teachings and abused both the faith and the monastic discipline. He attempted to overturn the Church’s most solid foundations by mixing together the two natures in Christ after their union and asserting, in a fable, that from the two only one had been made.

At first he taught these errors privately within the walls of his monastery, insinuating them to the monks. Then, emboldened by the favor of princes and magnates, he communicated with friends who loved innovation, until Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, discovered his wickedness. Since Eusebius had been on friendly terms with Eutyches, he repeatedly took care to correct him in a friendly manner. But when he realized that he was wasting time and effort, he accused him before Flavianus at the council [Col. 1098C], lest this deadly heresy acquire greater strength from day to day.

2. Eusebius therefore drew up written instruments of canonical accusation and presented them to the Council of Constantinople, in which he himself was also taking part, earnestly requesting that they be reread and entered into the records of the proceedings.

When the Fathers heard what the accusations contained, they asked Eusebius once and again to visit Eutyches’s monastery himself and, to prevent greater disturbances, urge the heretic to repent, sincerely repudiating the blasphemies into which he had broken out.

But the accuser did not yield to these appeals of the Fathers, and especially of Flavianus, because he had already gone to the monastery repeatedly for this reason, though without success. Therefore, so that the charge of heresy would not remain unpunished and the judgment would not proceed without hearing the other party, it was decided that John the presbyter and Andrew the deacon should be sent.

They went to the monastery, read the written accusation to Eutyches, and gave him a copy, together with the name of the accuser. They announced that he had been summoned to the council [Col. 1098D] to clear himself.

He categorically refused to appear and give satisfaction, saying that it had been decreed and determined for him from the beginning that he should never leave his fraternity’s monastery, where, in a sense, he lived as though in a tomb. He also claimed that Eusebius of Dorylaeum was suspect to him and could not properly act as a legitimate accuser: “For,” he said, “since he has long been my enemy, he composed this accusation against me out of a desire to defame and injure me.”

At length Eutyches himself admitted that he was prepared to agree to and subscribe to the exposition of the holy Fathers who had defined the faith in the Councils of Nicaea and Ephesus. He also said that he wished to search only the Scriptures, as though they were more authoritative than the expositions of the Fathers.

For this reason, he said, after the incarnation of God the Word—that is, after the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ—one nature was to be worshiped, namely that of God incarnate and made man. He was reading these propositions from a certain book.

After the Fathers had heard this account, and after it had been confirmed by Athanasius, deacon of Basil of Seleucia, who was present as a witness, Eusebius of Dorylaeum urgently requested that Eutyches be summoned a second time to the council, in accordance with the rules of law.

A summons was sent to him through the presbyters Mama and Theophilus. It ordered him to come to the council without delay:

“Lest, by evading it,” it said, “he be convicted face to face and become subject to the severity of the divine rules. For,” they added, “it is not a reasonable defense to say that you have decided not to leave the monastery” [Note: [Col. 1099D] The third session of the Constantinopolitan Council, reread at Chalcedon, is extant in vol. IV of the Councils, p. 974 according to my pagination.].

Meanwhile, as the new legates were setting out, Eusebius rose in the midst of the assembly and said that he had been reliably informed that Eutyches was turning everything upside down, sending a volume around to the monasteries, and inciting the monks to sedition. He therefore asked that Abraham the presbyter of the Constantinopolitan Martyrium, which is in the Seventh—that is, in the suburb—be summoned in order to learn with certainty about those disturbances and tumults [Col. 1099B]. [Note: “Septimum” was the name given to a suburb of Constantinople, as Labbe and Surius noted from Procopius. The passage in Procopius is in chapter 4 of *Buildings of Justinian*. “See,” say the collectors of the Councils, “what Charles du Fresne, Sieur du Cange, a man of astonishing and multifarious learning, says about Septimum, or Hebdomon, in *Constantinople Christian*, Book II, chapters 5 and 16, §44.”]

As deacons and presbyters were being sent to various monasteries to investigate the truth of these matters more fully and determine whether Eutyches had extorted from the monks subscriptions agreeing with his corrupt statements, Mama and Theophilus returned to the council. They reported that they had encountered monks at the gates of Eutyches’s monastery, who said that the archimandrite was ill and that no one could see him.

At length, when the reason for the new arrival had become known, after various disputes they brought the council’s legates to Eutyches. As soon as he saw and read the summons, he replied, under the pretext of illness and old age, that he had determined not to leave the monastery.

3. The Fathers decided that Eutyches should be summoned before the court a third time, so that the rules of the canons might be observed with the utmost care.

Therefore, after calling Memnon, keeper of the sacred vessels, and the deacons Epiphanius and Germanus, they sent a new summons to the accused Eutyches [Col. 1099C].

Fearing, however, that he might be regarded as contumacious and that the council might pronounce judgment against him in his absence, he tried to mock the Fathers by sending a certain Abraham, together with two other monks, to offer excuses on his behalf and, if permitted, to appear before the court for him and answer the charges.

Flavianus wished to receive them with great kindness, but immediately rejected their request, saying that they could not conduct Eutyches’s case there, because “it is impossible for one accused person to speak in place of another.”

The many and varied things which Abraham, the archimandrite, said to the Fathers of the council in an effort to move them to compassion toward Eutyches—and which were approved by that sacred assembly of bishops on no grounds whatsoever—are already known from the collection of the Councils [Note: [Col. 1100D] The fourth session of the Council of Constantinople, which was held on Tuesday, 16 November.].

4. It must therefore be explained how Eutyches received the third summons, delivered by Memnon and two other deacons.

After receiving and reading the document, he said that he had sent the presbyter and archimandrite Abraham to Flavianus the archbishop and to the council [Col. 1099D], so that in his name they might agree to everything that had been said by the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea and Ephesus, and to everything that had been written by the blessed Cyril.

He then resorted to his customary excuse, adding that he was being held back by illness and had therefore sent the archimandrite Abraham.

When Memnon vigorously refuted this excuse, saying, “You must come and present yourself before the holy synod and give satisfaction concerning the charges brought against you” [Col. 1100A], Eutyches, recognizing that he had been pressed hard, finally added: “I am waiting for Father Abraham; perhaps he will entreat the Lord and the holy synod.”

Memnon was consulting with him about whether he should remain in the monastery until Abraham returned. But Eutyches replied that he would prefer that the Lord Archbishop Flavianus and the holy synod be petitioned to grant him a postponement for the present week: “And on the second day of the week, God willing, I shall enter and give satisfaction to the Lord and the holy synod.”

While these matters were being discussed between Eutyches and the aforementioned legates of the synod, the Fathers were occupied in the sixth session of the council [Note: [Col. 1100D] The fifth and sixth sessions of the Council of Constantinople, vol. IV of the Councils, p. 999.]. They were hearing the reports of those whom they had sent to the various monasteries concerning what Eutyches had attempted in order to incite disturbances among the monks and lead them astray into subscribing to his corrupt statements.

Eusebius, the accuser of Eutyches, admitted that he had learned that Mama and Theophilus, who had carried the second summons to Eutyches, had heard many things from the heretic that they had not professed under the authority of the written records. Therefore, if these matters were made public, there would be certain proof that Eutyches’s faith had been violated.

Eusebius accordingly requested that they be summoned, so that they might recount under oath, over the books of the Gospels, what they had heard.

Only Theophilus was present at that time, for Mama had not yet arrived to attend the session. When questioned, Theophilus sincerely confessed that, after Eutyches had received the second summons by which he was called before the court, he had begun to debate in the presence of the presbyter Narcissus, Maximus the archimandrite, and other monks.

For he said: “In what Scripture are two natures found?” Then: “Which of the holy Fathers explained that God the Word has two natures?”

Mama answered these questions by maintaining that the expression was found not only in the Scriptures. But Eutyches replied that the term did not occur in the expositions of the holy Fathers.

Mama consistently defended the proposition that the holy Fathers proclaimed two natures, since the Son born from Mary must be called perfect God and perfect man. Mama concluded his argument with the following proposition:

“What, then, prevents us from saying that from two natures there is one Son?” [Col. 1100C]

Although Eutyches was challenged by these words, he stubbornly denied that he could agree, preferring to submit to deposition or to any other evil and disadvantage rather than confess two natures in Christ after the union.

Flavianus then asked why Mama and Theophilus had not reported these matters in the preceding session. Theophilus replied:

“Your Holiness knows that we were not sent for this reason, but only to summon the presbyter Eutyches. Since we were not questioned about it, we thought it superfluous to mention matters concerning which we had received no mandate.”

When Mama later arrived, what had been said previously was further confirmed.

5. Meanwhile, after the period of postponement that Eutyches had requested in order to appear before the court had ended, the Fathers gathered again for the seventh session on the twenty-first day of November.

After many people had searched throughout the church, at Flavianus’s command, and around the church as well, to determine whether Eutyches had arrived, and after they had found him nowhere, the presbyter John finally announced that he was surrounded by a great multitude of soldiers, monks, and apparitors of the prefecture, who refused to allow him to enter the council unless the Fathers first promised to restore his person.

The emperor also sent the Great Silentiary, who himself wished to enter the council. When permission was granted for him to enter, he immediately stated to the sacred assembly that he had received from the emperor certain written instructions that he was to communicate.

Their substance was that the emperor was concerned for the peace of the Churches and for the preservation of the faith established at the Synods of Nicaea and Ephesus. For this reason he wished Florentius, a faithful man whose orthodoxy had been confirmed by testimony, to be present at the hearing of that synod.

The emperor was then acclaimed with many years, and they gave him thanks.

Afterward Eusebius of Dorylaeum, the accuser, and Eutyches came forward, and Eutyches’s case was brought to its conclusion. The letters of Saint Cyril addressed to the Easterners were read. When the lector Aetius reached the passage stating that Jesus Christ is perfect God and perfect man, born from the Virgin Mary according to his humanity, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity, and with us according to his humanity, together with the rest that follows, Eusebius immediately said that Eutyches did not assent to these teachings.

To make the truth of this known without any appearance of ambiguity or suspicion of falsehood, they referred to what had already been recorded in the Acts. They then questioned Eutyches repeatedly. Receiving his public confession, they fully understood that he maintained and stubbornly defended a new and heretical doctrine against the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, not unlike the error and perversity of Valentinus and Apollinaris.

Therefore, weeping and groaning over his complete ruin, they deprived him of every ecclesiastical rank, the primacy of the monastery, and communion [Note: [Col. 1101D] Sentence pronounced by the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople against Eutyches: “We decree through our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed, that he is excluded from every priestly office, from our communion, and from the primacy of the monastery. Let all who afterward converse with him or come to him know this, for they too will be liable to the penalty of excommunication, since they have failed to avoid his conversations.” *Acta of the Council of Constantinople*, vol. IV of the Councils, p. 1022.].

There can be no doubt that these were the beginnings of the Eutychian heresy and that the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople observed this form of judgment with due religious care, according to the rules of the canons. We have described the matter at somewhat greater length from the surviving Acts.

In truth, this would not have been necessary for us, since the most learned and eminent Cardinal Baronius, with the great erudition in which he excelled, reviewed with greater and more exact care everything we have so far related concerning the Council of Constantinople and the beginnings of the Eutychian heresy [Note: [Col. 1101D] Baronius, vol. VI, under the year 448 of Christ.].

Let us proceed, therefore, to what follows.

## CHAPTER II

### After completing the preceding provincial synod, Bishop Flavianus sends a letter to the holy pontiff Leo the Great, together with the entire sequence of the Acts, requesting confirmation of the proceedings. Paschasius Quesnellus unjustly denies this; his arguments are presented and refuted.

[Col. 1101C]

1. Once the first Constantinopolitan synod had concluded—at which Eutyches’ errors were condemned, their author was deprived of his priestly office and of the superintendence of the archimandry, and the sentence passed against him was publicly proclaimed in various places throughout the city of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1101D] Liberatus the deacon, in the *Breviary*, chapter 11]—so that the monks and other Catholic men might be informed by a written warning that henceforth they were in no way to communicate with a heretical and contumacious man, Flavian, since the matter concerned the faith and so as not to fail in his duty, without inserting the slightest delay, sent a letter to the supreme pontiff Leo [Col. 1101D] and at the same time forwarded to him a complete account of everything that had been done.

The most faithful witness to this matter is above all Liberatus the deacon, who, after recounting the condemnation of Eutyches, immediately added: “To these proceedings the venerable Flavian joined his letter, which he sent to Pope Leo, and faithfully reported what had been done in the council” [Note: [Col. 1102D] Liberatus the deacon, in his *Breviary*, chapter 11, in Labbe, volume VI, page 436. Baronius, on the year of Christ 448, volume V of the *Annals*, page 62. Paschasius Quesnellus, as cited above]. While reviewing these words and Flavian’s own letters, Baronius rightly wrote, without any hesitation, that in doing this Flavian was following the custom of the ancients.

Quesnellus, however, repeatedly objects, especially when describing what Saint Leo the Great did in the year of Christ 449, where he says: “Saint Leo, having received no information from Flavian about any of the proceedings taking place at Constantinople, writes to Theodosius and Flavian—after receiving, that is, letters from Eutyches—lest he either condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty.” As to why Flavian did not write to Leo, he says: “It is not difficult to say whether he believed that Eutyches had been condemned by a settled judgment, or whether he thought that the case had been conducted in accordance with the canon of the Church in council and that the monk had been lawfully condemned by his own parish, so that he should not be heard again.”

Baronius believes that Flavian’s letters were either intercepted or delayed by Eutyches. Yet, on this view, it would follow that Flavian wrote nothing at all, as is clear from Flavian’s own letter, whose opening is “Piety …,” and so on. Who does not see that Quesnellus has been excessively bold, as though from an oracle, in wishing to resolve by a few—and indeed weak—conjectures a question wrapped in the gravest difficulties according to his own opinion? In fact, even if we carefully examine only those two letters of Flavian to Leo which Quesnellus himself printed in Greek and Latin, we shall not easily be able to decide to whom the first place is due. Rather, we shall be persuaded that the second should be placed first in the sequence, as we shall explain below on the basis of very weighty conjectures.

Moreover, who revealed to Quesnellus that Flavian had sent only two letters to Pope Leo? For from the Vatican manuscripts we have also brought to light a third letter written to the same Leo on the occasion of the Eutychian heresy, concerning which two clerics of the same Church of Constantinople—Gregory and John—were being accused. If, then, Flavian wrote this third letter, why could he not have written a fourth, fifth, sixth, and several others, which Eutyches might have intercepted or delayed, as Baronius reasonably suspects?

I am convinced—and every sensible man ought to be convinced—that Flavian needed to write still other letters to the holy pontiff, especially because the condemned heresy was growing more violent day by day, and because a new synod was being demanded through the agency of Dioscorus and the faction of Eutyches, with great loss to truth and faith. Flavian himself candidly acknowledged, in the two letters of his that have so far seen the light, that such a synod was by no means necessary, since “both the heresy that has arisen and the disturbances that have occurred on its account will be very easily destroyed by the sole authority of the pontiff” [Note: [Col. 1102D] Flavian’s letter placed first in Quesnellus’s edition, chapter 3, page 241; and Leo himself admits in Letter 32: “Although it plainly appears that the matter at issue in no way requires synodal deliberation”].

Tell me, I ask, does Quesnellus think that Flavian became completely silent and sent no other letters to Leo when he learned that the emperor, through the agency of the eunuch Chrysaphius and Dioscorus, was already demanding a synod in order to abolish what had already been defined at Constantinople against the rising heresy? The letters of Flavian concerning the case of those two Constantinopolitan clerics prove that this is a fabrication, as we have already indicated above [Col. 1102D]. With the Lord God’s help, we shall make them public.

2. But whatever may be the case with the other letters of Flavian—whether they perished through the ravages of time or are still preserved, now neglected, in the more secluded chests of libraries or archives [Note: [Col. 1102D] A catalogue of letters either written by Pope Saint Leo or sent to him, and of other records relating to his deeds, of which only the memory remains. [Col. 1103D] Paschasius Quesnellus, volume II of the works of Saint Leo, page 511. Nevertheless, the author of this catalogue did not mention a letter written by Flavian in the case of John, a Constantinopolitan presbyter, and his companion, whom Leo mentions in Letter 62, addressed to Anatolius, Flavian’s successor]—about which Quesnellus made not the slightest mention in the list he composed, guided by the belief that Flavian had sent Leo only those two published letters, it is therefore beyond doubt that, once that Constantinopolitan synod had ended and Eutyches had been condemned, Flavian did write to the Roman pontiff, sending him the complete record of the proceedings. Consequently, Baronius’s conjecture does not fail: he maintains that letters of this sort were intercepted or delayed through Eutyches’ efforts.

Quesnellus himself should certainly have subscribed to this conjecture if he had attended to the dates of Leo’s letters and to the time involved in their transmission. For this reason we shall not neglect to do so now, so that we may more fully overturn Quesnellus’s arguments.

We find Leo’s first letter to Bishop Flavian dated the Kalends of March, during the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes, which falls in the year 449. Flavian, writing back to Leo, indicated that Count Pansophius had carried this letter from the city of Rome to Constantinople. Yet, for the following reasons, I can never be persuaded that Flavian sent no letters to Leo before receiving the holy pontiff’s letter from Count Pansophius.

First, if we consider the time that Count Pansophius must have spent leaving the city and travelling to Constantinople; if we also take into account whatever business the nobleman may have had to transact with the emperor and the ministers of his court, as well as the journey he had to undertake in order to return to Rome, a period of three months could scarcely have sufficed. Although we must suppose that travel by sea was then easier because of the abundance of ships sailing from Rome toward Brundisium and from Brundisium onward to Constantinople, that journey was nevertheless made more difficult at the outset—that is, in March and April—when, although the sea is naturally calm, it is accustomed to become increasingly agitated and disturbed by the force of the winds during violent storms.

Let us, however, grant that Count Pansophius had a favorable voyage and that his return to Rome was delayed no more than three months, as might be inferred from another letter of Saint Leo to the same Flavian. What follows? Did Flavian delay writing to Leo about the Eutychian heresy until he received the letter after being pressed by Leo himself? No one will affirm this without being marked by rashness, especially if he attends to the subsequent letters of Saint Leo the Great.

For Saint Leo, in Letter 22, written on the Kalends of June, admits that he had received Flavian’s letters together with the synodal proceedings concerning Eutyches. He says that he took the opportunity to write from the convenient journey that the honorable man Rodanus was about to undertake toward Constantinople. At that time he wrote a very brief letter. He nevertheless promises: “But concerning this matter we shall write more fully through the one who has brought us the letter of Your Dilection, so that we may instruct Your Fraternity what ought to be determined concerning the whole case.”

3. Here I should like Quesnellus, and anyone else who indulges his views, to consider whether the honorable Count Pansophius carried Flavian’s letters together with the synodal proceedings when he brought Leo’s letters to Flavian, or whether someone else did so. It was certainly not Pansophius. The words, “Concerning this matter we shall write more fully through the one who has brought us the letter of Your Dilection,” seem to indicate some particular cleric of the Church of Constantinople—such as was then customary—sent by Flavian to deliver the letter and the synodal Acts to the supreme pontiff. Leo was supposed to send this person back with a longer letter. Who, then, will believe that an honorable man, a count of the imperial court, was to be sent back as though the office of courier had been assigned to him?

It is more reasonable, therefore, to conclude that the first letters of Flavian, together with the synodal proceedings, had a bearer other than Count Pansophius, as the two very weighty considerations that we now set forth demonstrate most clearly.

The first is that, after a few days had passed, when Leo was about to send Flavian a longer letter, as he had promised in the preceding one, he began it with these words: “Having read the letter of Your Dilection, which we marvel was so late, and having reviewed the order of the episcopal proceedings …”

Why, then, and in what sense or for what reason, would he have called Flavian’s letters “so late” if Pansophius had brought them, since Pansophius would scarcely have spent three months going from Rome to Constantinople and returning from Constantinople to Rome? If Pansophius had brought these letters together with the synodal proceedings, they would have reached the pontiff’s hands with the greatest speed, not late, as is plainly shown by the preceding calculation of time.

We must therefore infer that someone else carried these letters—someone who, whether hindered by the devices of Eutyches, by changing circumstances, or by the storms of the sea, had been detained on the journey for a long time, and whom the holy pontiff sent back to Constantinople to Flavian with another letter, namely Letter 24.

We add that the words “so late” indicate not an ordinary delay but a long lapse of time, which caused Leo’s mind to be filled with amazement, as at something outside every normal order and contrary to custom. When I considered these words carefully, again and a third time, and on the other hand learned that the provincial synod at Constantinople concerning the condemnation of Eutyches had ended in November of the preceding year, I thought it could be inferred that Flavian had written to Leo concerning the Eutychian affair immediately in the following tenth month of that same year—or at least at the beginning of January of the immediately subsequent year, 449—sending the synodal Acts and not waiting for Leo’s letters, which he says he received through the honorable Count Pansophius.

If Quesnellus should object that Flavian openly admits in that earlier letter which Quesnellus arranged to have printed in his edition that Eutyches had been accused by the most religious Bishop Eusebius, had come before the holy council, and had disclosed in his own voice to the synodical Fathers what he himself believed; and that “we deposed him as alien to the true faith, as all the Acts completed concerning him, which we have also sent with this letter, will inform Your Holiness”—as though Flavian wished to indicate that he had not written to Leo before sending the completed Acts with this letter, I shall immediately respond that the remaining context of that letter shows that Flavian had already sent this same portion of the letter to Leo long before, together with the Acts of the proceedings concerning Eutyches, and that he had been compelled to write it again when, having heard Leo’s complaints, he realized that Leo had not yet received either the letter or the completed Acts.

This seems to be indicated by the plainly expressed words: “as all the Acts completed concerning him, which we have also sent with this letter, will inform Your Holiness.” Here he seems to be speaking of a matter already carried out in the past, and of these letters as having been written previously. This should appear to sensible men from the third and subsequent part of these letters, which he added and appended at the end of the earlier one.

After recounting the disturbances that had arisen in the Church of Constantinople on this account, and proceeding in due order to discuss both the documents publicly produced by Eutyches—full, namely, of insults and lies—and the petitions presented to the emperor, filled with arrogance and insolence, he moves on to Leo’s letters, which he had recently received. “But,” he says, “after these matters had thus been completed in sequence, the letter of Your Holiness was delivered through the most admirable Count Pansophius.”

Let Quesnellus say when Leo’s letter was delivered to Flavian through Pansophius. Was it not after Flavian had sent the synodal Acts to Leo together with the preceding part of this letter—letters which, he insists, the holy pontiff received too late? If those words, considered also in light of the order of expression, admit another true meaning without distortion, learned men will be able to affirm [Note: [Col. 1105D] We followed the version of Jean-Baptiste Cotelier in transcribing the words of this letter, lest we be accused by Quesnellus’s supporters. In truth, the version of the ancient translator reveals this truth more clearly, both because of the words in chapter 2: “As all that has been done concerning him, and which we have sent with this letter of ours, will inform Your Holiness”; and because of the words with which chapter 3 begins: “But after these things had thus been done, a letter of Your Holiness was delivered to us through …”].

But now the second consideration, which we have drawn from Leo’s works, will show that no other meaning can be imposed. More than once, in two of his letters—Letters 22 and 24—the holy pontiff informed the Bishop of Constantinople himself that Flavian’s letters had been delivered to him together with the synodal Acts, but too late. One of those letters was written on the Kalends of June, the other on the Ides of that same month, when he sent Flavian’s legate back to Constantinople with fuller instructions.

It was therefore unnecessary for him to mention again these letters received with the synodal Acts, unless, when Count Pansophius was returning, Flavian had repeated the same letters together with copies of the Acts. That Flavian did repeat both is revealed by Leo’s thirty-second letter, which was issued on the Kalends of July of the same year.

Since the opening of that letter is: “I have received the letters of Your Dilection, together with the proceedings completed among you concerning the question of faith,” I was easily led to the opinion that only then was the letter, with all its parts and with a new appendix, delivered to Leo, just as it stands first in Quesnellus’s edition.

Indeed, the text of that letter indicates this to us. For when Pope Leo informs Flavian that he has received the more recent letter and synodal proceedings, he makes no further mention of Eutyches, his errors, or his appeal to the apostolic see, matters which he had sufficiently discussed in the preceding letters. Instead, he addresses only the new appendix to the repeated letter, saying: “Although it plainly appears that the matter at issue in no way requires synodal deliberation, nevertheless, dearest brother, I signify that those whom it pleased us to dispatch have followed” [Note: [Col. 1105D] In Quesnellus’s edition this Letter 32 has *subsecuturos* instead of *subsecutos*, and the editor noted in the margin: “It is clear from this letter and from Letter 34 that the legates had not yet departed.” But it can be gathered that the annotator is mistaken, both from the preceding letters and because the Ephesian synod began on the third day before the Ides of August, when the legates of the apostolic see were already present. For these reasons we rightly judged that the reading *subsecutos* should be retained, supported by the printed editions and the Vatican copies].

No one will deny that these words must refer to what Flavian had most recently written to Leo in the appendix to his letter. For Flavian had said that he received the Roman pontiff’s letters after he had sent the synodal proceedings concerning Eutyches’ condemnation together with his own letters. He then asserted that, after these matters had been completed and settled, the letters of His Holiness were delivered to him through Count Pansophius. Through them he learned that Eutyches had written documents full of every kind of deceit and trickery, claiming that he had appealed to Your Holiness at the time of the judgment, and that for this reason a rumor was circulating that a general synod was to be held. For the present, however, we shall not discuss this Eutychian appeal; we shall treat it in its proper place.

4. Meanwhile, we present other arguments by which it is clearly understood that Flavian, after Eutyches had been condemned and deposed, reasoned otherwise than Quesnellus and the innovators have imagined. He therefore not only thought of writing to Leo but actually wrote to the pontiff about the Constantinopolitan judgment. For he acknowledged that the supreme summit and authority of the priesthood had been established in Leo himself, addressing him as the legitimate guarantor of the Catholic religion, to whom it belongs [Note: [Col. 1106D] Flavian’s letter in Quesnellus, Letter 1, chapter 3] to defend the common cause and to restore harmony among the holy Churches.

Second, he asks the same pontiff to make the canonical deposition carried out against Eutyches firm and valid by his written confirmation.

Third, keeping in mind what Christ had said to Peter concerning the strengthening of the faith of the brethren, he adds: “And to confirm the faith of our most pious emperor, who loves Christ. For the matter needs only an impulse and support from you, which through your prudence will immediately bring everything to tranquility and peace.”

If, then, according to Quesnellus, the matter had been handled and concluded in the provincial synod at Constantinople; if likewise every right in this kind of judgment resided in the Bishop of Constantinople, why does Flavian appeal to Leo, saying that the matter needs the impulse and support of the apostolic see so that everything may immediately be transferred to tranquility and peace?

Unless the condemnation of that heresy had been ratified by Leo and the disturbances that had been aroused had been settled by pontifical authority, I am deceived in my opinion. Nor would the true doctrine concerning the incarnation of Christ the Lord have been made sufficiently known to Christ’s faithful, nor would the contumacious and rebellious have yielded, unless, as Flavian says, “with God cooperating, through your sacred letters.”

Finally, Flavian himself plainly asserts that only Leo’s letters could prevent the future general synod of which the rumor was spreading, saying: “And the synod that is being publicly announced as future will also be prevented, so that the Churches of the whole world may not be thrown into confusion.”

From this appendix to Flavian’s first letter, then, we clearly gather what the ancient Eastern bishops thought and judged concerning the authority of the Roman pontiffs: both in overthrowing heresies, in confirming and convening councils, and finally in receiving the appeals of those who had been condemned. Although some may oppose all this with excessive boldness, indeed almost foolishly, under the pretext of defending and vindicating episcopal dignity, Flavian’s letter, and his manner of writing and acting, most solidly prove and disclose the discipline and doctrine of the Church concerning the apostolic see, the mother and teacher of all the other Churches.

5. But let us now hasten to other matters, so that we may see more clearly how alien Quesnellus’s mind was from reverence for and submission to the apostolic see. In order to lend credibility to his preceding statements and at the same time to show that Flavian never wrote to Saint Leo except after receiving complaints from that pontiff, he appealed to various other letters of Leo written either to Flavian himself or to the emperor Theodosius.

Nevertheless, we shall say nothing here about Letter 20, which Quesnellus placed first in his edition and which was written on the Kalends of March, since he failed to attend to its date and we do not wish to repeat what has already been treated. We merely observe that Saint Leo was entitled to act as supreme judge in this case, and that Flavian could not violate the rights of the apostolic see in a matter of faith.

The holy pontiff asserts this plainly. Not only does he discuss Eutyches’ appeal, but, with reference to the cause of the condemnation, he wishes to know what Flavian had done in the Constantinopolitan synod. “But with regard to the case,” he says, “we wish to know the reason for your action.”

Nor was Flavian unjustly compelled to give an account of his actions, since the order of supreme ecclesiastical government required it, and the emperor’s will aroused the pontiff’s concern, so that, once all the dissensions that had arisen in the Church of Constantinople had been removed, the Catholic faith might be strengthened by the authority of the apostolic see.

For these reasons, in the second chapter of that Letter 20, Leo asks that Flavian inform him through a suitable person what novelty had emerged against the ancient faith and what deserved to be punished by a more severe sentence. For Saint Leo adds: “Both ecclesiastical moderation and the religious faith of our most pious prince indicate to us many causes for concern about Christian peace” [Note: [Col. 1107D] Leo the Great, Letter 20, chapter 1, volume I, in Quesnellus, page 238, and chapter 2].

If, then, these two things—the requirements of ecclesiastical government, to which Quesnellus ought to have paid attention, and the emperor’s insistence—signaled such great concern to Leo, I do not know with what brazen face Quesnellus could have maintained that Flavian did not think of writing to Leo about the matter until he learned that the pontiff, deceived by Eutyches’ wicked actions, had formed a false opinion concerning the Constantinopolitan judgment.

Saint Leo did not write to Flavian merely upon hearing of Eutyches or receiving his appeal. He did so only when he had been informed by the emperor that the Church of Constantinople had been shaken by the uproar of many disturbances and that disputes were being conducted concerning matters of faith. For Leo began that Letter 20, on which Quesnellus also insisted, with these words: “Since the most Christian and merciful emperor, solicitous in his holy and praiseworthy faith for the peace of the Catholic Church, has sent us a written report concerning the matters that have stirred up the tumult of disturbance among you.”

Quesnellus therefore ought here to have distinguished two things and omitted neither. One concerned the imperial letter; the other concerned Eutyches’ appeal. Leo says that he is surprised to have been informed of the uproar of such great disturbances only by the emperor himself, and that Flavian had not first taken care that “we should be informed by the account of your report.”

6. The unity, organization, and structure of the ecclesiastical hierarchy therefore required that the supreme pontiff be instructed by Bishop Flavian concerning the newly arisen heresy and the gravest disturbances aroused among the Constantinopolitan clergy. This manner of speaking completely overturns Quesnellus’s other fiction, namely:

“As long as this corruption confined itself within the boundaries of the Church of Constantinople, there was no need for Flavian to invoke the assistance of his colleagues. For he knew that the whole of Catholic truth had been entrusted by Christ the Lord, in its entirety and undivided, to all bishops, and that each was bound, according to his ability, to defend it and suppress the errors arising against it, as the ordinary judge in that portion of the Church which he had received. But when, warned by Leo, he learned that the arch-heresiarch had invaded the West with his letters, was spreading his poison, and that plots were being prepared against Catholic doctrine by the powers of the world, he then thought it his duty to approach the Roman pontiff. In this way the pontiff would be informed concerning the whole matter, as was owed to the head of the Church, and would diligently employ the favor that he enjoyed with the emperor, so that the schemes of the heretics might not spread far and wide and the Churches might not be disturbed by the convocation of a council, in which there was good reason to fear that wicked men would possess considerable influence by their authority” [Note: [Col. 1107D] Quesnellus, on the year 449, dissertation on the life and deeds of Saint Leo the Great, page 146].

7. What an amusing line of reasoning from Quesnellus! Yet who does not understand that it not only conflicts with ecclesiastical rules but also with the statements of Leo and Flavian, and that it completely overturns the sacred order of the hierarchy?

Thus, according to Quesnellus, if the bishop of some Church should condemn someone as a heretic, either through rash judgment or without observing the rules of law; if he should depose him from the presbyterate and his rank while the taint of that heresy remained confined within the limits of his diocese, there would be no need to invoke the assistance of his colleagues.

But whom does he understand by “colleagues”? If he means the bishops of particular Churches, whose faith can fail and has at times been shaken by heresies, I readily grant the point. But if he maintains that the term “colleague” must also extend to the Roman pontiff, guardian and judge of the Catholic faith, then he overturns and abolishes the arrangement and structure of unity and the true head, depriving him of the same power by which he has the right to extend his care and the pastoral office entrusted to him throughout the world.

Leo’s manner of acting and the force of his words plainly indicate that Saint Leo regarded himself not as a colleague but as the supreme judge of proceedings and controversies. For he compelled Flavian to bring before his knowledge the whole cause and manner of the matter, so that he might perform the office of a judge, not of a colleague. “For,” he adds, “since we wish the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, we can decide nothing concerning matters unknown to us, to the prejudice of either party, before we have truthfully heard all that has been done” [Note: [Col. 1108D] Leo the Great, cited above, Letter 20, chapter 1].

Can we suppose that these words, or those others—“We wish to know the reason for your action”—could be spoken by one colleague addressing another? All laws affirm that an equal has no authority over an equal. Yet both the entire context of that Letter 20 and the words of the subsequent letter written to the emperor Theodosius clearly show that Leo commanded Flavian by virtue of the authority he possessed.

For the emperor, considering the order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy in which Christ the Lord placed one bishop and shepherd over the other priests, did not merely invoke the assistance of the Roman pontiff to abolish those scandals that were spreading more widely among the Constantinopolitan clergy. He demanded Leo’s judgment, so that the dogma of the faith might be confirmed, the Nicene decrees preserved, and it might be determined whether Eutyches—whom ministers of the imperial court were supporting—had been justly or unjustly removed from the priestly rank and the superintendence of the monastery.

Theodosius’s letter to Leo has either perished through the ravages of time or remains neglected in the chest of some library. Leo’s letter to that same emperor, however, survives; from it the supreme rights of the pontiff can be gathered without difficulty, and it becomes entirely clear what the bishops of particular Churches must observe whenever a matter of faith is considered in that portion of the Church assigned to them.

8. In this letter Saint Leo admits that he was entirely ignorant of what had been done in so important a case. Since he had not yet received the synodal Acts together with Flavian’s letters, he says that he had written to the same Bishop of Constantinople so that he might learn that Leo was displeased that Flavian was still keeping secret what had been done, when he ought first to have made everything known to him [Note: [Col. 1108D] Letter 21, to the emperor Theodosius, chapter 2].

This was not in order to obtain assistance, but on account of the judgment of the case, which Leo asserted was owed to him for three very serious reasons: the merits of the case, the requirements of the faith, and the pious concern of the emperor. These demanded that there be no room for underhanded misrepresentation: “But first we must be informed concerning the matters for which he”—namely, Eutyches—“is judged to be liable to accusation, so that judgment may suitably be passed on matters thoroughly known.”

Finally, Leo concludes his letter to the emperor by saying that, after the admonition given to Flavian through his pontifical letters, he hoped and believed that Flavian would report everything to Leo’s knowledge, so that, once those matters that seemed hidden had been brought to light, judgment might be rendered according to what accords with evangelical and apostolic doctrine.

Let Quesnellus consider, I ask, whether Flavian rejected Leo as an incompetent judge; whether he despised the admonition; whether he at least obscurely judged that he ought not first to reveal everything to the Roman pontiff; or whether he judged that it did not belong to Leo to decide what accorded with evangelical and apostolic doctrine; whether because the corruption remained confined within the limits of the Church of Constantinople, or because the whole of Catholic truth had been entrusted by Christ the Lord not to the apostolic see but to all bishops in its entirety and undivided, so that each was bound to defend it according to his ability; and so forth—arguments of this kind, composed by Quesnellus while he was amassing the greatest absurdities, in order to fabricate the admission that, except for the honor of primacy, equal authority and jurisdiction ought to be recognized in all bishops.

[Col. 1109A] 9. We could produce here a great many passages from Leo in which, throughout his letters and sermons, he repeatedly affirmed that the prerogative of ecclesiastical primacy over the whole world belonged and was owed to himself and his successors. But lest we presently appear to sing outside the choir, we shall entirely omit them.

**CHAPTER III.** The same Paschasius Quesnellus, by newly devised doctrines, completely perverts the structure of ecclesiastical government in discussing the case of Flavian and Eutyches. Cardinal Baronius’s assertions on this matter are vindicated by the decrees of Saint Leo the Great. Saint Leo’s Letter 12, wrongly explained by Quesnellus, is expounded in its fuller form as found in a Vatican manuscript. It is shown from various other letters that, in exercising the supreme rights of the pontificate, Saint Leo the Great did not depart at all from the decrees of that letter.

1. In order to defend his corrupt doctrines more easily, and to sell the follies that he had conceived in his mind against the apostolic see of Peter, Paschasius Quesnellus repeatedly sought to stir the minds of his readers and charm them with novelties, since he was not unaware how much eagerness novelty commonly arouses in human beings [Note: [Col. 1109D] Cicero, *Ad Herennium* 23].

We and all Catholic writers must withdraw from this manner of proceeding, not merely under the pretext of preserving antiquity, but in order to take greater care to prevent those errors that suppress truth—more valuable than all other things—whether through fraud or through false opinions disseminated among the people, and bring it into hatred and contempt.

Since the author just mentioned tried above all to indulge in novelties when discussing the affairs of the Church and the form and method of its government, as we have explained in the preceding chapters, it is therefore very important, in the present leisure afforded for writing, to seek and examine that force of truth which can easily defend itself against this man’s ingenuity, cunning, and cleverness.

As we pursue the sequence of Leo’s affairs, Leo’s letters to Flavian and Flavian’s letters to Leo once again come before us. Although Quesnellus understood perfectly well that the holy pontiff assumed the role of true and supreme judge in the Eutychian case and exercised that office without anyone objecting, he nevertheless attacks Cardinal Baronius and rebukes him gently for having written:

“Following ancient practice, it is beyond dispute to confess that the Roman pontiff is the legitimate and principal judge of ecclesiastical controversies between Flavian and Eutyches, who were disputing with each other, and to whom both plaintiff and defendant freely hasten in order to pursue their rights” [Note: [Col. 1109D] Baronius, on the year 449, number 5].

2. Yet Quesnellus says, disingenuously, that he venerates the dignity of the pope [Note: [Col. 1109D] Quesnellus, *Dissertation 1 on the Life and Deeds of St. Leo the Great, Pope*, p. 147, col. 1, near the [Col. 1110D] end.]. He immediately adds:

“But since all the bishops of the Church share a common dignity with the Roman bishop—and Leo himself professes this—far be it from me to wish that what I venerate in one should be trampled upon in the others. We readily acknowledge the Roman pontiff as the legitimate judge of the Church’s controversies and, if he is compared with individual bishops, as their principal judge. But who could therefore tolerate that Flavian—whom both the prerogative of his see, his singular holiness, and his steadfastness in the faith, persevering even to martyrdom, ought to have commended so highly—should be matched and opposed to a rebellious, ignorant, obscure monk of poor character; that a deposed presbyter should be set against the bishop of his own and so distinguished a see; that the judge should be set against the accused; and that both should be brought before Leo like two men disputing over the division of 330 common property, as though they were to fight over an uncertain case? Far be such an insult from the most sacred assembly of bishops.”

These and similar arguments he invents, which he pretends can chiefly be confirmed from a letter of the same St. Leo to Anastasius of Thessalonica. He marked this letter in the margin and shamelessly flatters himself that his entire perverse interpretation of ecclesiastical judgments rests upon it and is supported by it. But I shall plainly demonstrate in what follows that no letter could be found more effective for confirming Baronius’s statements and establishing the truth.

3. First of all, then, when St. Leo speaks analogically, as they say, about the ecclesiastical body, he establishes a comparison with the Apostle Paul by likening it to a natural body. In that body, the connection of the whole produces one health and one beauty; and this connection of the whole requires unanimity, but especially demands concord among priests. To these he adds that, although their dignity is common—he did not say their jurisdiction—their order is nevertheless not general. For who has denied that the dignity received by bishops in the sacred office of ordination is common to all bishops, or has claimed that, by virtue of the sacred episcopal anointing, one bishop acquired greater or lesser dignity in shepherding his own sheep? In this office and honor of shepherding, dignity is common to all bishops; but it does not follow that their order is general, so that any one of them could judge every kind of case.

For, according to this same St. Leo, a distinction of power must be maintained even among the bishops themselves—a distinction which Quesnellus himself attempts to mix and confuse with the honor of dignity. He then adduces the example of the apostles. Although they were alike in the honor of the office they had received, a distinction among them in power, or jurisdiction, nevertheless existed; and although all had been chosen for the apostolic office, one alone stood above the others. “For,” he says, “even among the most blessed apostles, although their honor was similar, there was a certain distinction of power. And although the election of all was equal, nevertheless to one it was given to stand above the others.”

Does Quesnellus hear this? They were alike in the honor of their character and dignity, in which no difference of rank is admitted, as is perfectly clear; yet they were unequal in the prerogative of power, because one was required to preside over the others. By what reasoning, then, or guided by which words of Leo, could Quesnellus assert equality of rights among bishops? For, in exercising jurisdiction or [Col. 1110C] delivering judgments, all bishops cannot claim everything for themselves.

For, according to that same Leo, both by divine and ecclesiastical arrangement it was established that in each province there should be individual bishops whose judgment held first place among their brethren; and, again, that certain bishops established in the greater cities should undertake a wider responsibility, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one See of Peter, so that nothing anywhere would dissent from its head.

If, then, we adhere to this entire context, in what way have we contradicted the statements of Baronius? Not the ancient institution by which it was established that bishops and presbyters disputing among themselves about matters of faith should appeal to the Roman pontiff as the legitimate judge of controversies—a point we could prove from six hundred ancient examples drawn from the histories of Dionysius of Alexandria, Athanasius, Pelagius, Coelestius, Priscillian, and Dictinius [Note: [Col. 1110D] See what we said in the preceding *Exercises* concerning the heresies of the Priscillianists and Pelagians.]. We pass over these examples for the present, lest we seem to be acting outside the scene.

Nor do we contradict the final words: “to whom both plaintiff and defendant voluntarily hasten in order to pursue their rights.” For although there was the greatest distinction of rank, condition, and jurisdiction between Flavian, the bishop, and Eutyches, the presbyter, and although one was the legitimate plaintiff and ordinary judge while the other was an ignorant, rebellious, obscure, condemned monk, as Quesnellus reasonably asserts, nevertheless, since Eutyches did not accept the sentence passed against him and appealed to the one See of Peter, Leo the Great, lest he judge hastily concerning matters unknown to him, was obliged to hear Flavian as plaintiff and Eutyches as defendant, and also to question them by letter, so that they might disclose the entire sequence of events.

But what insult or affront to the prerogatives of the See of Constantinople, or to the bishop [Col. 1111A] of singular holiness who persevered in constancy of faith even to martyrdom, is involved in this? Flavian’s reputation and dignity were in no way whatsoever violated by the supreme pontiff’s procedure, through any reproach or disgrace. On the contrary, both before the facts were examined and after they had been established, Leo paid him the honor due to him and exercised every moderation and respect toward him, as all the letters addressed to Flavian himself clearly show.

If, finally, Quesnellus insists that it is injurious to the assembly of bishops for them to be brought before the apostolic see so that questions of law and fact may be resolved, then the universal care of the Church must no longer converge upon the See of Peter; everyone will be permitted to dissent from his head; and the unity of the Church will be at an end. Its structure cannot remain firm unless the bond of charity binds the bishops together in inseparable solidarity.

4. Secondly, who could rightly deny—or dare to deny—that when St. Leo dealt with cases involving bishops, he protected and upheld the honor and rights not only of his own episcopal see but also of the other episcopal sees? Indeed, even if we lacked other records, the aforementioned letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica, upon which Quesnellus relies in order to draw out and sell his novel wares, would alone suffice.

In it, discussing the various ranks of bishops—namely, metropolitans and vicars of the apostolic see—Leo commands and instructs that the legitimate rights of metropolitans be preserved perpetually, and that the right of the dignity handed down from ancient times not be violated by the Thessalonian vicars, even though they were legates of the apostolic see.

Nor did he think that the rights of metropolitans could thereby be violated if, in judging cases, bishops assembled in councils happened to disagree, whether because of the gravity of the matters or because of the difficulty of the questions. For he ordered such cases to be referred to the judgment of the apostolic see, while reserving to himself and his successors the power to establish the final sentence.

For in a very ancient synopsis, canon 7, we read: “That two provincial councils of bishops be held each year; and if a difficult matter should arise and not be settled by the judgment of the bishop of Thessalonica, let it be referred to the Roman bishop.” Nor did he therefore judge that, by this reservation, the rights of metropolitan or suffragan bishops were disturbed or diminished.

He also protected the honor and rights of the bishops with more prudent and stricter command and canon. He was concerned, namely, lest bishops suffer force or injury under the pretext of convening provincial councils. To prevent, therefore, every abuse that might inflict injury or disgrace upon bishops, he decreed in chapter 10 of the same letter that moderation be maintained by the bishop of Thessalonica when summoning provincial bishops, lest under this pretext the priestly honor be subjected to insults.

Finally, he closes his decretal letter with the last chapter to which Quesnellus appealed. Its title is so clear, both in printed editions and in the oldest manuscript copies that we ourselves examined, that we can scarcely doubt the authority of the apostolic see in reviewing cases already treated and decided in provincial synods—especially when the matter concerns the faith and disputes and scandals arise on that account, as everyone knows happened in the Eutychian case.

The title of that chapter reads: “That if a dispute should arise among them”—that is, among the bishops—“concerning a matter, everything is to be disclosed to the Roman pontiff through a report of the proceedings, so that he may arrange whatever is pleasing to God.”

Do not all these things correspond with what Baronius had written about the ancient institution of the Church? Therefore, so far are Leo’s statements in his letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica from weakening Baronius’s words, that they instead acquire greater support and strength.

5. Let us now proceed to the remaining matters. In the meantime, passing over other points that we could discuss concerning this letter—which we have not only examined and corrected against the Vatican and other manuscript copies, but have also enlarged and embellished with respect to the teaching of its eighth canon, which we found explained more fully and clearly in a Greek archetype of the same Vatican Library—we shall speak of the Greek interpretation and paraphrase of that canon in an appendix that we have appended to the same letter.

For the present, then, the sole question to be investigated is whether St. Leo issued a judgment concerning the Eutychian case and the disturbances in the East after receiving from Flavian the synodal proceedings and letters, or whether he merely offered and extended help and protection to the severely afflicted bishop of Constantinople.

Quesnellus had to assert the latter, if he was not to depart even slightly from his previous method of argument. For after he had said against Baronius that Flavian did not appear before Leo as a plaintiff but as a judge; that he had not brought Eutyches forward for condemnation but had produced one already condemned by himself; and that he had not sought a new judgment from Leo but had requested that the sentence he had issued be made known by the care of the Roman pontiff to his colleagues in the West, so that all might labor with a common faith, common concerns, common effort, and common diligence, he adds in the following chapter:

“After receiving Flavian’s letters, Leo promises his help and support against Eutyches; and through the distinguished man Rhodanus he sends a letter . . . . . which was followed by another to Theodosius, in which he professes adherence to the Nicene faith, condemns the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches, and also requests that a synod be convened within Italy.”

6. Since Quesnellus thus proposes two matters there and resolves them according to his taste in argument, it will be our task for the present to distinguish one from the other and to discuss each separately.

With respect to the first, we affirm that Flavian did indeed appear before St. Leo as a plaintiff and brought Eutyches forward as the defendant—already condemned in the provincial synod of Constantinople, but nevertheless requiring condemnation by the apostolic see itself in a more solemn, final, and peremptory judgment.

Flavian’s first letter to St. Leo plainly reveals this. Whether he wrote that letter immediately after the Constantinopolitan synod, as we proved most clearly in the preceding chapter, or only after he had learned from Leo that he was being harassed by numerous complaints, as the opponent irrationally maintains, it is always evident that Flavian hastened to the apostolic see as a plaintiff, in order to render an account of the judgment he had already approved and to obtain its confirmation.

But if, as Quesnellus contends, he neither wished nor ought to render an account of the judgment he had approved, why did he transmit the synodal proceedings? Why did he think it right to inform Leo of everything that had been done against the heresy that had recently arisen? Why, finally, did he ask that the pontiff’s mind be stirred, as was appropriate to the priestly office, so that he might declare the condemnation pronounced against Eutyches valid and make this known in his own writings?

Unless he had deeply resolved in his mind to seek this final judgment of the apostolic see, by which the risen heresy and the disturbances caused by it might most easily be destroyed, with God’s cooperation, through the pontiff’s most holy letters.

From these observations and forms of expression it is understood that Flavian did not merely request that the sentence he had issued be made known by the care of the Roman pontiff to his Western colleagues. He sought consolation and defense, by which, as he himself says, “you ought by your own agreement to bring everything to tranquility [Col. 1112D] and peace” [Note: [Col. 1112D] Flavian’s first letter, chapter 3. See what we wrote in the preceding chapter concerning this letter.].

Thus, only if Leo approved, confirmed, and strengthened in writing the judgment of Flavian and the Constantinopolitan council could either the heresy that had arisen or the disturbances that had been provoked be brought to destruction, and everything be settled in peace and tranquility. There is no mention there of the Western colleagues. There is no indication that he wished to compel them to labor with common concerns, common effort, and common diligence for the common cause of the faith. He merely closes the letter with the customary formula of greeting, saying: “I and those who are with me salute the entire brotherhood that is with you.”

Let those who are moved and influenced by no partisan zeal decide, then, whether Flavian appealed to Leo as judge and brought Eutyches forward as one already condemned, rather than as someone who still required condemnation by the Roman pontiff.

7. The other assertion that Quesnellus added likewise falters and falls, namely: “After receiving Flavian’s letters, Leo promises his help and support against Eutyches.”

We certainly encounter no word in the letter that he sent through Rhodanus which suggests such a phrase or can be interpreted in that way. On receiving the opportunity offered by the journey that the same honorable man Rhodanus was immediately undertaking toward Constantinople, Leo wrote a very brief letter. Nevertheless, he omitted none of the things appropriate to the supreme and principal judge of the Church.

For, having already been informed through Flavian’s letters and by reading the synodal Acts that Eutyches held an opinion about the faith different from what was proper . . .—though he ought not to have deviated from the Catholic tradition, but to have persisted in the same belief held by all—Leo postponed writing at greater length, but promised to write more fully about the same case: “so that,” he says, “we may instruct your Fraternity concerning what ought to be decided about the entire case.”

Nor does he claim and attribute to himself merely universal teaching authority through these words; in what follows he also promises that he will henceforth undertake the true role of judge and defender, adding:

“For we do not tolerate his”—namely, Eutyches’—“persisting in the perversity of his belief, or your Belovedness, which by its zeal for the faith resists wicked and foolish error, being disturbed by the prolonged assault of the opposing party” [Note: [Col. 1113D] Letter 22 in Quesnellus. The Grimaneus manuscript, from which Quesnellus extracted the preceding letter, reads *non patimur* (“we do not tolerate”); he himself, perhaps through the carelessness of copyists, substituted *non patiemur* (“we shall not tolerate”).].

I beg Quesnellus to consider the entire passage and sincerely admit whether these words can be understood merely of a colleague offering help to a colleague and laboring together with Western colleagues.

Although the case concerned the common faith, it was not situated in the West but in the East. Flavian himself was being harassed not by Westerners but by Easterners. If, therefore, Leo had not possessed supreme right, power, and jurisdiction over the Easterners, in what manner or with what meaning could he have promised his ministry, both to judge the Eutychian perversity and to defend Flavian’s great zeal from the prolonged assault of the opposing party?

8. Indeed, without any dispute, it may be gathered that Leo exercised in this case all three offices—of supreme judge, defender, and universal teacher—from his celebrated letter, which they call the dogmatic letter and which he wrote to the same Flavian a few days later.

I pass over the fact that at its beginning he said that he had received Flavian’s letter together with the synodal Acts very late. I likewise pass over the fact that he expounded in a divinely inspired manner the entire doctrine concerning the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ and reproached Eutyches as foolish and insane, since he did not wish to understand what would have enabled him to act rightly, though he had meditated iniquity upon his bed. These matters show that Leo claimed for himself the role of true judge and teacher.

Let me dwell only on the final chapter of that letter and use it to argue whether Quesnellus reasoned rightly or wrongly in the preceding discussion.

For Leo did not refer the examination of the Eutychian case to other Western bishops. Rather, after examining the synodal Acts himself, he found in them certain matters deserving criticism and correction, wholly inconsistent with the rules of ecclesiastical law. These matters had necessarily to be guarded against by the Easterners assembled in synod, lest the faith concerning the incarnation, namely, that two natures exist in Christ after the union, should collapse.

He says:

“When, however, Eutyches replied to the statement of the examination conducted by you, saying: ‘I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature’” [Note: [Col. 1114D] Leo’s letter to Flavian, numbered 24 in the sequence, chapter 6.].

This assertion, being wholly contrary to the dogmas of the faith, ought not to have been heard with impunity or without ecclesiastical censure when Eutyches uttered it in his reply. Rather, it should have been pierced with an anathema and execration, as something opposed to the Apostles’ Creed.

Accordingly, the holy pontiff, deeply astonished at the judges of Constantinople, rebukes them in these words:

“I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession was not reproved by any rebuke from the judges, and that a statement so foolish and so blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 1114D] Leo’s letter 24, chapter 6.].

Did St. Leo not therefore find in those Acts grounds by which he could more reasonably rebuke and denounce the judges of Constantinople for having acted less regularly, or canonically, in examining the Eutychian case and compiling the synodal Acts? Does he not judge Eutyches’ assertion to be impious and blasphemous—an assertion that Flavian, together with the entire synod, considered unworthy of any censure, or at least failed to mark with a censorial stroke?

Eutyches could reasonably have inferred from the synod’s procedure that he had spoken either correctly or tolerably, as St. Leo immediately adds, because “you have no sentence by which it was refuted.”

Wishing to remedy this evil, the holy pontiff admonishes Flavian to ensure that, if by the inspiration of God’s mercy the case should be brought to a satisfactory conclusion, the imprudence of the ignorant man might be cleansed from this plague of his understanding.

Behold, he establishes the conditions to be observed concerning the manner in which Eutyches is to be admitted to communion if he should repent. For, he says, “as the order of the proceedings made clear, he had begun well to withdraw from his belief when, compelled by your sentence, he professed that he was saying what he had not previously said and assented to the faith from which he had previously been alien.”

9. Finally, Leo commands that if Eutyches should ever repent of having said and uttered such things against the Catholic faith, and should come to the fullness of satisfaction by condemning aloud and by his present subscription everything that he had wrongly understood, he should be embraced with the greatest charity and mercy should be shown toward him once corrected.

For the successful conclusion and execution of all these matters, Leo declares that he will send four legates to the East to act as papal representatives, together with a faithful notary, “trusting,” as he says, “in the help of the Divinity, so that he who had gone astray may be saved after condemning the perversity of his understanding.”

At the conclusion of this present controversy, may I therefore ask Quesnellus, or anyone else, whether such a course of action can be understood as merely one colleague acting toward another?

First, Leo rebukes the synodal Acts of Constantinople as irregularly produced. Second, by his own authority he condemns the heretical proposition that the Constantinopolitan judges had ignored and failed to proscribe by anathema. Third, he orders that forgiveness be granted to Eutyches if he should at some point repent, and establishes the manner in which the penitent is to be received. Fourth, so that everything he had commanded might be faithfully carried out, he sends four legates from his own side to act as papal representatives. Together with the notary Dulcitius, they are to work so that the heresy may be abolished and the disturbances that had arisen may be settled.

If Quesnellus had considered this—or had not concealed it—would he, we ask, have applied so much effort to turning everything upside down? Led by envy, hatred, and an excessive desire to quarrel, would he have sought to bring the rights of the apostolic see to ruin?

Those who cultivate truth, as Quesnellus boasts that he does, are enemies of fraud. For this reason, he ought not in any way to have omitted or twisted into a perverse meaning what we have received from our forebears concerning the universal ecclesiastical government—especially since St. Leo the pontiff, always consistent with himself, explains more fully in his letter to Julian of Cos what he had said at the end of his twenty-fourth letter.

There he shows that it was necessary for Eutyches to be pressed by frequent and careful questioning from the judges so that he might give an account of his profession, and so that nothing might pass away as something empty when it was evidently an outpouring drawn from the drinking of poisonous doctrines [Note: [Col. 1115D] Letter 25, to Julian of Cos, chapter 3.].

For judgments are established either to settle controversies or to punish wrongdoing [Note: [Col. 1115D] As Cicero says in *For Quintus Roscius*.]. If judges do not press defendants—or those accused of crimes—with repeated questions, they cannot arrive sufficiently at knowledge of the truth, nor can crimes be properly and canonically proved or formally charged, as has always been judged necessary in inquiries concerning the faith.

Thus Quesnellus’s assertion also falters and falls: that nothing at all occurred in the Acts of the Council of Constantinople that had not been done properly and canonically. For we encounter at least one matter that was proscribed by the apostolic see, and we understand that the judges themselves, and Flavian himself, were rightly rebuked. A new judgment therefore had to be instituted according to the rules prescribed by St. Leo in both of the letters just cited.

Let us now begin our discussion of Eutyches’ appeal.

# CHAPTER IV  
## Eutyches’ Appeal to the Apostolic See

Quesnellus denied this with the greatest injustice. Many of his arguments are taken from the letters of Flavian and Leo and from the Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople; these arguments are here wrested away and refuted. Finally, the opinion of the distinguished Peter de Marca is reconsidered and noted as less consonant with the truth.

[Col. 1115C]

1. Up to this point we have done much to vindicate the legitimate rights of the apostolic see, first considering the conduct of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. After the sentence condemning and deposing Eutyches, Flavian sent his letters to St. Leo together with the entire sequence of the synodal proceedings, and informed him of everything that had happened.

We also understood that such a case, as one of the more serious and difficult cases, on account of which scandals and hostilities had arisen between the judges and the Eutychian faction, ought by right, according to the ancient apostolic custom, to have been reserved for the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

Finally, it was added that the Acts of the Constantinopolitan council had not been drawn up in every respect according to the rules of the canons. The judges, namely, admitted Eutyches while he was speaking—or at least concealed—a single blasphemy, the source of many heresies, which they ought to have proscribed and compelled the heretic, under ecclesiastical penalties, to condemn.

Since we established these three points in the preceding discussion to prove the judicial power of the Roman pontiffs, what remains now is to speak of appeals to the apostolic see, taking our opportunity from our opponent, who vigorously strives, by turning everything upside down, to assert these same appeals on the basis of passages found in the works of St. Leo the Great [Note: [Col. 1115D] Consult chapter 6 of letter 24 to Flavian and chapter 2 of [Col. 1116D] letter 25 to Julian of Cos.].

2. To pass over the countless places where he asserts that Eutyches never appealed to the apostolic see, I turned my attention to his seventh dissertation, entitled: “On the Case of Eutyches, Archimandrite of Constantinople, Condemned by Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, in the Synod.” Beneath this title he placed the following words as the subject of the dissertation: “Concerning the twentieth letter of St. Leo the pope to the same Flavian, and the twenty-first to Theodosius Augustus.”

I was led to hope that Quesnellus intended to examine these two letters specifically, first to confront what the holy pontiff Leo admits in them concerning Eutyches’ appeal, and then to dissolve through his replies the objections he had raised against himself.

But my expectation deceived me. He begins his dissertation by asserting that several people draw from these letters arguments intended to establish the right of appeal to the Roman see. He declares that he does not envy the rights and prerogatives of this first see, and confesses that he wishes to defend and uphold its authority and eminence as confirmed by the sacred canons.

“Yet,” he adds, “just as the true foundations on which the structure of the apostolic primacy rests remain immovable and unshaken, so those weak and deceptive arguments by which it is customarily supported through the misguided zeal of certain people must necessarily collapse of their own accord. Whoever undertakes to expose their emptiness will certainly earn no small favor from the apostolic see.”
