He closes the introduction to this dissertation by revealing the purpose he had set for himself: to leave untouched nothing among the matters in Leo that required illumination. For this reason, he says, necessity compelled him to annotate Eutyches’ fabricated appeal [Note: [Col. 1116D] Quesnellus, vol. II of the works of St. Leo the Great, dissertation 7, *On the Case of Eutyches*.].

3. After presenting such splendid and impressive verbal ornament, he draws the following conclusion:

“I therefore maintain that neither of these two letters of Leo contains anything by which it can validly be proved that the Roman pontiff was appealed to by Eutyches separately and apart from the other patriarchs and bishops of the greater dioceses.”

Nothing more solemn could have been devised by a man wholly occupied with fabricating frauds and lies, since his principal aim here is gradually to persuade his readers that appeals existed only to a future general council among the Easterners, so that the innovators, as though fighting for their altars and hearths, dared to assert this in contempt of the apostolic see.

To soften this lie with the appearance of truth, he first attempts to demonstrate from chapter 3 of Flavian’s letter that Eutyches appealed not to the apostolic see alone, but to the synods of Rome, Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica. He introduces the matter as follows:

“From this the truth of Flavian’s words shines forth, in which he replied in this way to Leo, who complained to him about Eutyches’ neglected appeal to the apostolic see.”

Here are Flavian’s words:

“Eutyches addressed to you petitions full of every kind of deception and cunning, saying that at the time of the trial he had submitted petitions of appeal, and had appealed both to us and to the holy council assembled here, to your Holiness. This was not done by him at all; in this respect also he lied, thinking that through the deception of a lie he could insinuate himself into your holy ears.”

But sane people will judge with me from the preceding words that Quesnellus’s falsehood gains no support or strength from them. Indeed, they will conclude that St. Flavian truly approved the right of appeal to the apostolic see, without any reference to the other patriarchal sees—Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Thessalonica. For the bishop of Constantinople denies only the fact that an appeal was made; he does not deny the right, which he proves to be legitimate, nor does he wish to call it into question.

Moreover, Flavian’s response had to correspond exactly to Leo’s statement. Leo had written that Eutyches had appealed to the apostolic see; Flavian replies that in this respect Eutyches had lied, saying that he had appealed to “your Holiness.”

Where, I ask, is there any mention of the other patriarchal sees and their bishops? Or, when St. Leo had named only himself and his own see, to which Eutyches had falsely claimed to have appealed at the time of the trial, why did Flavian not object to Leo that it was not customary to appeal separately and apart from the other patriarchs to the Roman pontiff, since Eutyches ought rather to have directed his petitions of appeal to all the other patriarchs?

Therefore, the preceding words of Flavian not only do not conflict with the right of appeal; they establish it and add force and strength to it. They do, however, reject and pass over in silence as something unknown the custom that certain recent pseudo-interpreters of ecclesiastical law have invented—namely, that appeals must necessarily be made to a general synod.

### 4

The matter is indeed made clearer by Leo’s own Letter 20, which Quesnellus put forward as the subject of the present dissertation and with which Flavian’s replies had to agree—and in fact do agree. What, then, follows from this Letter? That Eutyches, condemned by the Constantinopolitan synod, appealed to all the other patriarchal sees? Away with such a fabrication! [Col. 1117B]

In the first place, Saint Pope Leo complains that Flavian could have remained silent to the Roman See about the disturbances and scandals that had been stirred up, instead of ensuring that “first of all,” as he says, “your report’s disclosure should inform us.” As we have said, these words indicate how, in similar contentious cases involving articles of faith, the Roman pontiff was to be informed and consulted at the same time, so that he could not doubt the accuracy of the events that had occurred.

He then immediately added:

> For we have received the petition of the presbyter Eutyches, who complains that, although Bishop Eusebius was accusing him, he was unjustly deprived of communion, especially since he testifies that he had been present when summoned and had not denied his presence, to such an extent that he asserts that, at the very trial, he presented his petition of appeal, yet it was not received.

No one can doubt that Saint Leo is here speaking of an appeal made to himself, of the sort that those undergoing ecclesiastical judgment ordinarily used to make. But whether he had made it—or had not made it—in due time, namely when judgment was being pronounced, was unknown to Leo. He had not yet been fully informed about what had happened. [Col. 1117C] Nevertheless, it was necessary for him to believe that Eutyches had entered his appeal at the proper time. For he says:

> When Eutyches saw that his appeal had not been received, he was compelled to post contestatory petitions in the city of Constantinople.

What did he understand by the term “contestatory petitions”? Surely a public testimony committed to writing, by which he declared that the judgment pronounced against him was null and void and that he had appealed from it to the Roman pontiff.

“But,” Quesnellus will reply, “if he had entered an appeal, he would also have appealed to all the other patriarchs and to the bishops of the greater dioceses, and to their councils.” But from where did he derive this new doctrine? Let him produce those hidden monuments of antiquity from which he took it.

Relying on the testimonies of Flavian and Leo, we demonstrate that Eutyches did not appeal to the Roman council. Flavian indeed denies that an appeal was made to Your Holiness at the time of judgment; he does not deny the right. Nor does he add that Eutyches had appealed, or ought to have appealed, [Col. 1117D] to the other patriarchs and more distinguished bishops and to their councils. He merely adds:

> But in this matter he was deceived, like the father of lies, thinking that he could secretly gain access to your ears.

Thus Flavian nowhere called into question Eutyches’ right to enter an appeal to the apostolic See; he denied only that Eutyches had done so at the proper time.

Moreover, if Quesnellus’s supposition stood, then, when Eutyches appealed to the apostolic See while passing over the other patriarchs, those patriarchs would have loudly protested, recognizing that their right to hear similar contentious cases had been secretly taken from them. For nothing is more effective in provoking serious conflicts than to despise, violate, and abolish the rights of others. But where is there any evidence that they protested?

On the contrary, if Eutyches, as he prefers, [Col. 1118A] Quesnellus had appealed to all the other patriarchs and to the prelates of the most celebrated Churches, they would not have delayed giving their judgment—especially the Alexandrian, Antiochene, and Jerusalem prelates, who would scarcely, if indeed they would at all, have postponed performing the duties of their office when the matter concerned defending their right, to whose councils Eutyches had allegedly appealed.

Yet none of the bishops of the greater Churches took a hand in this matter; none wrote to Flavian; none attempted to annul the decree of the Constantinopolitan council or to confirm it, although in the meantime six or seven months had elapsed from Eutyches’ condemnation and appeal until the time when Saint Leo obtained knowledge of all the events.

I for my part believe that the prelates of the East and of the Greeks who presided over the more distinguished Churches would not have delayed so long to exercise their right. Since, therefore, they did not do so, it is evidence that Eutyches appealed neither to them nor to any established custom whereby those condemned in provincial synods appealed to the councils of [Col. 1118B] patriarchal Churches.

Finally, Eutyches’ appeal had to be understood in the way in which both Flavian and Leo the Great interpreted it. Now the manner in which both of them wrote indicates that the appeal was made to one individual bishop alone, namely the Roman bishop, who was venerated as the head and support of the whole Church, and from whom Eutyches hoped—through the deceitfulness of his lies, as Flavian seems to suggest—to obtain absolution without the facts being known.

Thus the new form of judging devised by Quesnellus totters and collapses, with no means by which it can stand. This is particularly clear since the deacon Liberatus merely asserts that Eutyches, writing to Pope Leo about his condemnation, “posted edicts at Constantinople and declared that he had suffered injury.” [Note: [Col. 1117D] Liberatus the deacon, *Breviarium*, chapter 11.]

### 5

There are nevertheless two things by which Quesnellus thought that he could make such a structure stand. The first is the testimony of the monk Constantine; the second [Col. 1118C] is Eutyches’ letter to the bishop of Alexandria.

As for the first, no one ought to be unaware who this monk Constantine was. Not only was he regarded and condemned as a heretic, but, when he wished to take Eutyches’ side at the Second Council of Constantinople, he was never consistent in his statements: under the appearance of a disturbed mind, he denied what he had affirmed and voluntarily conceded what he had previously denied. His testimony, therefore, ought to possess absolutely no weight or credibility.

Quesnellus himself readily concedes that Constantine was a heretic, while examining John David [Note: [Col. 1117D] Quesnellus, in the same place, as above. John David, [Col. 1118D] in his French work *On the Judgments of Bishops*.], who had attacked Peter de Marca by saying that the testimony of that monk—which we shall append below—was that of a heretical man, burdened with many difficulties, contradicted by Florentius himself, the Patrician, and indeed rejected by the Constantinopolitan Fathers themselves.

Here is Constantine’s statement:

[Col. 1118D]

> When the condemnation was read, Eutyches appealed to the holy council of the most holy bishop of Rome, of the bishop of Alexandria, of the bishop of Jerusalem, and of the bishop of Thessalonica; and this was not inserted in the Acts.

Upon this supposedly firmest of stones, although it was a false one, Quesnellus attempted to construct his entire new edifice concerning appeals.

Yet if he had carefully, rather than cursorily, reviewed everything that was done and said at that Second Council of Constantinople—or had not concealed it altogether—he could have recognized how much weight ought to be assigned to such testimony. Nor would he have asserted that anything true could be extracted from that man’s lie. He says:

> For a lie is excessively foul if it is not shaded with the appearance of truth. Accordingly, we learn that it was not, until those times, the custom of the Easterners to appeal to only one of the bishops, but to all those who had not participated in the judgment from which the appeal was made; [Col. 1119A] nor to the council of the Roman pontiff alone, which was that of the whole West, but also to the synod of the other patriarchs who were not suspect in the case.

> And in fact, at the very time when Eutyches wrote to Saint Leo that he had appealed to him, he also wrote to Dioscorus of Alexandria, asking him to convene an ecumenical council at which Flavian’s judgment might be examined, as Liberatus teaches us in chapter 12. Liberatus must, however, be corrected when he says that Eutyches did not think of such a council until after the Constantinopolitan gathering had concluded, at which the Acts of Flavian’s synod were reread; for below we shall show from the Acts of that gathering that the Council of Ephesus had already then been announced.

But who does not understand that to build an edifice upon a lie is the same as to deceive, and to sell a reckless fable as true history?

Quesnellus asserts that it was the custom of the Easterners not to appeal to one bishop alone, but to all those who had not participated in the judgment from which the appeal was made. But what invented examples of this alleged custom does Quesnellus possess?

And, to pass over the Africans—whom Quesnellus and Peter de Marca knew very well to have appealed to the apostolic See without any dispute whatsoever—what will he say about Athanasius? [Col. 1119B] What about John Chrysostom? They appealed to the apostolic See, under Pope Julius and under Innocent, the predecessors of Leo.

We consider it unnecessary here to examine their cases or their manner of proceeding. Quesnellus, in order to establish his position, has neither produced nor been able to produce even one example among the Easterners of anyone who appealed to all those who had not participated in the judgment from which he appealed.

### 6

Leaving aside for the moment the cases of Athanasius and John Chrysostom, about which we promise to speak later, what does he think should be said about Eutyches’ letter to Dioscorus requesting that an ecumenical council be held?

This is another new deception of Quesnellus.

Eutyches knew that enmity could easily arise between Flavian and Dioscorus, [Col. 1119C] since the defense of his case had been undertaken by Chrysaphius, Flavian’s enemy and Dioscorus’s close ally. For this reason, since Dioscorus was prelate of the city of Alexandria, he wished not only to claim for himself, after the Roman pontiff, the primacy supposedly granted him by the Nicene canons, but also insisted on exercising supreme authority over the Church of Constantinople, as the principal patriarch of the East, without regard for the third canon of the First Council of Constantinople, which had decreed that the bishop of that city should hold the second place after the Roman bishop.

The Roman Church not only did not admit this canon but abolished it, as we shall say in its proper place. Moreover, the Alexandrian bishops themselves rejected that canon as injurious to them, both when councils were to be held and when the ordinations of other bishops were under discussion.

What wonder, then, if Eutyches, under the pretext of preserving metropolitan jurisdiction, wrote to Dioscorus [Note: [Col. 1119D] Consult Letter 80 to Anatolius, in which Pope Leo is wholly occupied with firmly defending the rights of the patriarchates of [Col. 1120D] Alexandria and Antioch.], especially since he persuaded himself that he could place himself under Dioscorus’s protection through Chrysaphius’s recommendations?

Nowhere, however, will one find that he wrote to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, or to Anastasius of Thessalonica. Quesnellus ought to have proved this, if we were not to call his new form of appeal a lie and a complete absurdity, which he is trying to sell only to shallow and unlearned people.

Furthermore, it is one thing to approach someone as an intermediary and mediator; it is another to appeal to someone while observing the order prescribed by law.

I shall grant that Eutyches wrote to Dioscorus and also sent him his petition of profession. What follows from this? It is nowhere established, however, that he appealed to him.

Similarly, it does not follow that he appealed to the bishop of Ravenna, although he had written to Saint Peter Chrysologus, the prelate of that Church.

But even granting that he had also written to Anastasius of Thessalonica, could Anastasius perhaps [Col. 1120A] have heard Eutyches’ case by his own right? He was acting as the representative of the apostolic See, since he was its vicar. But for that very reason he would have acted only in the person of the Roman pontiff, not by judging; rather, he would have written to Saint Leo, as we demonstrated sufficiently and abundantly in the preceding chapter.

Let us therefore proceed to other matters.

### 7

After this Quesnellus taunts John David, as though he had forgotten his own case, because he cited in his favor the words of the bishops, who testified during the examination that they had heard no word of appeal from Eutyches—thus, as it were, cutting his own throat with his own sword.

“Since it was a council,” says Bishop Seleuchus, “and an inquiry was taking place, we knew of no such statement about an appeal having been made by the archimandrite Eutyches.”

The most reverend bishops said, “We too make the same confession.”

“Certainly,” Quesnellus adds after these words, “if he had appealed even to one Roman prelate, in the hearing of the bishops, they would have known of it—something which they deny having heard.”

Nor would the complaint of the monk Constantine have been entirely undeserving of rejection, when he protested that mention of the appeal had been omitted from the synodal [Col. 1120B] Acts. Indeed, he would have had Julian, bishop of Cos, as an advocate for his complaint, since Julian had been present both at the synod and at the later gathering.

Yet, in order to remove this new quibble of Quesnellus, although we have the testimonies of Saint Leo in his letters to Flavian, to the emperor Theodosius, and to Julian of Cos, in which this appeal to the apostolic See is indicated—and although Eutyches’ own petition supports them, together with the profession of faith that he submitted for examination by the Roman pontiff—we have nevertheless thought it appropriate to unfold more fully those Constantinopolitan Acts in which, at Eutyches’ insistence and by imperial command, the proceedings of the First Constantinopolitan Council were reread and examined.

### 8

Everyone knows, then, that the monk Constantine was acting in the person of Eutyches, with Quesnellus himself supporting this point.

First of all, the question was whether those Acts had been corrupted, falsified, and interpolated, [Col. 1120C] since it had already been decreed, at the emperor’s demand, that a general synod should be held. For Bishop Meliphthongus, after saying that the presence of the accused was necessary, especially because accusations of this kind were not made without danger, added:

> Why, then, most pious emperor . . . especially since he has ordered a universal synod to be held, and it is necessary to reserve the more important cases for that council.

Second, notwithstanding this, the examination of the documents proceeded. After Eutyches’ supplication had been read, in which he asserted:

> For yesterday I read the proceedings composed by the most reverend Flavian against me, and I found that the documents contained matters contrary to what had been done.

Third, Constantine, following the practice of heretics, openly admitted that he accepted Scripture alone, but not the teaching and writings of the Fathers, adding the following reasoning:

> Since the Fathers have spoken in different ways, I accept everything; but I do not accept it as a rule of faith.

When he recognized that murmuring and agitation [Col. 1120D] had arisen among the bishops and the others present at the gathering because of this rash and blasphemous assertion, he began to regret it, perhaps recalling to mind that the writings of the Fathers against the Arian and Nestorian heresies had been accepted at the Councils of Nicaea and Ephesus as the rule of faith.

Therefore, wishing to correct his badly spoken words, he ordered that the phrase “as a rule of faith” be erased, saying:

> I spoke without knowing, in my confusion.

All the bishops noted this man’s cunning and inconsistency. Among them was Eusebius, bishop of Ancyra, who said:

> I likewise approve that, since he assumes the person of the religious archimandrite, everything that has proceeded from his voice should remain firm for him, and that he should not wish some of what was said to be retained while rejecting other things that were said.

Such agitation consequently arose in that gathering that, while the bishops wondered [Col. 1121A] and almost quarreled with one another, they asked what should be done in this criminal case. For the man whose case was being heard was absent, and the person who ought to have taken his place was consistent neither in speech nor in his answers to the questions put to him. Hence two others, namely Andrew and Athanasius, were admitted to speak, so that the reading of the Constantinopolitan proceedings might be brought to completion.

### 9

Here, then, is the character and manner of proceeding of that monk Constantine, whose false testimony Quesnellus relied upon in order to extract the truth of the appeal with which we are concerned.

Fourth, in that gathering of the bishops mention was made of Eutyches’ petition to Saint Leo, together with his complaint and appeal; likewise mention was made of Leo’s letter to Flavian, which was read before everyone. Yet we encounter not a single word about any other letters of Eutyches, whether to Dioscorus, to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, or to Anastasius of Thessalonica.

If he had appealed to their synods, as Quesnellus invents, can we believe that mention would have been made only of Leo, [Col. 1121B] the Roman pontiff? Can we believe that, amid such a crisis over Eutychian affairs, not one of the bishops, clerics, or monks who stood in defense of Eastern rights would have failed to say that the support of at least one of the principal patriarchs or bishops of the East ought to be heard or awaited—those to whose councils Quesnellus asserts, by his invention, that Eutyches appealed according to the ancient custom?

And lest anyone suspect me of falsehood, I shall cite the words of the deacon Eleusinus, who spoke as follows about Saint Leo’s letters and Eutyches’ appeal:

> Since, however, a few days ago the letters of the most holy archbishop of the Romans, Leo, were brought to our attention, containing the statement that the most reverend archimandrite Eutyches accused [read: refused], and that at the time of the examination he appealed to your hearing by presenting a petition—and therefore, after his condemnation, they again called him archimandrite—how is it that now, while pressing his case and saying that his petition concerning the faith is before the most holy Roman [Col. 1121C] bishop, he has called his refusal an appeal in the synod?

The illustrious Stephanus Baluzius, commenting on this, aptly noted that the words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Corbie manuscript through the copyist’s error:

> For Rusticus’s annotation, he says, which is placed in the margin, cannot be referred to another passage.

It reads as follows:

> Eutyches’ manifest falsehood. And it should be noted that Pope Leo’s letters had already reached them—letters which he wrote concerning Eutyches’ absolution, though only until a fuller hearing could be held—and for that reason, after his condemnation, they again called him archimandrite.

If, then, according to Rusticus, Pope Leo’s letters had such force that they could suspend the sentence pronounced against Eutyches by the Constantinopolitan synod until a fuller hearing; and if, likewise, by the force of those letters, the Constantinopolitan Fathers, even after his condemnation, continued to give Eutyches the name and honor of archimandrite, what need is there to labor so intensely in defense of the rights of the Roman See and of the sacred and ancient custom of the Easterners, by which they either referred cases of faith to the Roman pontiffs or submitted more serious matters to them for [Col. 1121D] examination, without withdrawing from their judgment, directives, or commands?

Moreover, Eutyches himself believed that it was enough for him to have refused the sentence pronounced against him in order to be regarded as having appealed from it. Thus he testified when he said that his petition concerning the faith was before the most holy Roman bishop.

The distinguished Peter de Marca supports this view. Speaking of Flavian’s appeal, he makes the following general statement, which applies remarkably well to the question [Col. 1122A] before us:

> Since in those times refusal was also made by way of appeal, even after a definitive sentence, though not in the manner later introduced by Justinian . . .

[Note: [Col. 1121D] The distinguished Peter de Marca teaches that refusal is equivalent to an appeal and that an appeal entails refusal, when discussing Flavian’s appeal. He gently criticizes Cardinal Perronius because Perronius had written that the Constantinopolitan bishop expressed himself only in general terms and that the appeal had not been made expressly to the pope. “But,” de Marca adds, “there is no need [Col. 1122D] to go to such extremes, because, as I have said, the words taken from the legal formula signify nothing other than that Dioscorus was refused by him.” Final law *On Sentences*, laws XVI and XVIII, chapter *On Judgments*. See Cujacius, *Observations*, book IX, chapter 23.]

### 10

It should therefore be noted that Eutyches did not say here that his petition concerning his faith was before the other patriarchs or the more distinguished bishops of the East, but that it was before the Roman bishop. He therefore believed that only what he had written to the one holy Roman pontiff could support him.

Nor, finally, did Rusticus assert that the sentence of condemnation pronounced against Eutyches remained suspended because of the letters of the other Eastern bishops. He affirmed only that Leo’s letters possessed this energy and force.

All these points, if compared with one another and with what preceded, completely overturn that Quesnellian edifice. For the fabulous custom that this recent writer has so rashly defended—until now divining, inventing, and turning everything [Col. 1122B] upside down—cannot be inferred from some fabricated event.

### 11

Nevertheless, even if we granted that the monk Constantine’s lie could in no way be excused or defended, what would follow? Other considerations would already present themselves to us, proving that, after Eutyches had refused the sentence of the Constantinopolitan synod, the case had already been transferred to the supreme tribunal of the Roman pontiff.

For from those two Leonine letters we know with certainty that the holy pontiff ordered that everything be brought to his knowledge together with a report of the proceedings, so that he could judge appropriately after becoming fully acquainted with the facts [Note: [Col. 1122D] Leo the Great, Letter 20, chapter 2, and Letter 21, likewise chapter 11.].

To whoever is granted the power to investigate, decide, and judge cases, true—not arbitrary—jurisdiction must belong. This is especially so if we are dealing with matters of faith, the cognizance of which, according to the distinguished Peter de Marca as well, was reserved to the Roman and apostolic See.

Yet he himself, led I know not by what spirit, prepared the way in part for Quesnellus, as we shall shortly see, by asserting against Cardinal Perronius that Eutyches’ [Col. 1122C] appeal could not be proved from the Leonine letters; and that he had appealed elsewhere to the Roman, Alexandrian, Jerusalem, and Thessalonian synods, but secretly and in the ear of the Patrician Florentius, after the judgment had been rendered and after the synod had been dissolved. These claims, however, are consistent neither with what has been said thus far nor with the proceedings of the Second Council of Constantinople.

But let us proceed to other matters, observing that Quesnellus can find no support in what he brought forward in the course of his celebrated dissertation—namely, that Eutyches had made some mention of the Alexandrian bishop.

For this reason he thought it necessary to transcribe the words of Bishop Basil, who first, having suffered a lapse of memory, and then recalling the matter, testified:

> Now I speak truly: while the gathering was still sitting and the holy synod was proposing that this man should say that there are two inseparable and unconfused natures in one Lord, and this after the union, I know that the religious archimandrite Eutyches said: “If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I shall say this very thing.” [Col. 1122D] But he did not say this as an appellant; he said: “I did not dare to say it because of the Fathers.”

“From these and similar words,” says Quesnellus—some of which he had poured out to some people and others to others, partly on one occasion and partly on another, now publicly and now quietly, sometimes as an appellant and sometimes merely to explain his mind—“Eutyches took the opportunity to impose upon Saint Leo by letter and upon the Eastern Fathers at the Constantinopolitan gathering through Constantine; hence he falsely claimed to have appealed.”

But the present question can no longer concern whether Eutyches wished to submit himself to the judgment [Col. 1123A] of the Alexandrian bishop, since, as we have seen, he was already led by a firm hope that he could have Dioscorus favorable to him: because Dioscorus was hostile to Flavian; because he was contending with Flavian under the pretext of the prerogative of primacy; and finally because, relying on the protection of the eunuch Chrysaphius, he could easily have drawn Dioscorus over to his side [Note: [Col. 1123D] *Tomus* IV of the Councils, p. 1067 ff.].

Dioscorus’s loyalty could not have been more than sufficiently proved, as is evident from his conduct both before and afterward.

Nor does our question concern merely whether Eutyches lied to Saint Leo. For from the documents available to us we cannot confidently determine whether, at the time of judgment, while the Fathers were still sitting in council, he openly and publicly appealed.

It is nevertheless certain that he refused the sentence pronounced against him and continued in the office of archimandrite until a new investigation and a new judgment were instituted.

If, then, he refused the sentence pronounced against him; if likewise, by his petition, he called upon another judge, submitting himself to that judge’s sentence, what more ought he to have done for us to say that he truly appealed?

[Col. 1123B]

### 12

For this reason we were not easily moved by what Quesnellus wrote afterward, more to exaggerate his own learning than to attack John David, since John David opposed Peter de Marca. Quesnellus pretended to assume de Marca’s side by taking a sufficiently strange and harsh path, although the archbishop of Paris himself had not dared so confidently to deny this right to the apostolic See. We now present his words.

That same distinguished and most learned prelate of the Church of Paris asserted that the Roman pontiffs possessed the right to judge Eastern cases relating to the faith and even to the strict requirements of universal discipline. He believed that this right belonged to the apostolic See either by the force of the Sardican canons or even of the Nicene canons, in which it had been established that the ancient custom should be preserved in the conduct of judgments.

He also spoke with sufficient honor of the primacy of the Roman pontiffs throughout the universal Church. To support this position, he appealed to the testimonies of the ancient Fathers—namely Cyprian, Irenaeus, [Col. 1123C] Jerome, and Augustine—guided by the aim of preserving the principle of the center of unity and the head in the Catholic assembly.

Nor does he deny the right of appeal with which we are concerned. Indeed, he adduces various Eastern examples, namely those who, by the force of this right, appealed to the apostolic See and submitted themselves to its judgment once the parties to the dispute had been removed.

Nevertheless, when discussing Eutyches’ appeal, he says:

> I do not assign a place among appeals to the Roman bishop to the one circulated under the name of Eutyches the archimandrite, after his condemnation had been carried out by Bishop Flavian, even if it is thrust upon the public whenever controversies concerning religious matters are debated. I do not, however, wish to deny that he appealed to the Roman pontiff. Nevertheless, I maintain that he appealed not only to the Roman pontiff.

From this position he gently rebukes the most eminent Cardinal Perronius, because Perronius believed that this appeal could be proved by the authority of Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian.

He contends that the appeal to the apostolic See cannot be inferred from the same words, but only that Eutyches had presented a petition of [Col. 1123D] appeal and had been compelled to post contestatory petitions in the city of Constantinople.

But who will believe that we have encountered an insoluble difficulty? Does this most learned man say that it cannot be inferred that an appeal was made to the apostolic See? Yet Leo assumed the role of judge; Leo himself wished to be informed of everything through the communication of the synodal proceedings; and Flavian himself, who affirmed that Eutyches had lied, transmitted the synodal Acts.

Did the learned prelate recall that the ancients accepted refusal as an appeal? Did he not notice Rusticus’s annotation, in which he acknowledged that the sentence pronounced against Eutyches by the Constantinopolitan synod had been suspended by virtue of Saint Leo’s letters?

Nor does he accomplish anything by objecting that Eutyches appealed to other sees—namely, that he appealed to the Roman, Alexandrian, Jerusalem, and Thessalonian synods—but secretly and in the ear of the Patrician Florentius, after the judgment had been rendered and after the synod had been dissolved.

This conflicts with what Bishop Basil testified. Recalling what had occurred several months earlier, he testified that, while the gathering was still sitting, and perhaps when he refused the sentence pronounced against him, Eutyches entrusted himself entirely to the judgment of the Roman and Alexandrian prelates.

Certainly Basil’s testimony deserves greater weight than that of the monk Constantine, an inconsistent, heretical, and deceitful man who employed every resource of his craft in attempting to show that the Acts of that Constantinopolitan synod were corrupted and falsified.

But why Eutyches also named the Alexandrian bishop is not something we need explain, lest we repeat what has already been said.

### 13

Since the same distinguished man, Peter de Marca, adheres more firmly to the testimony of the monk Constantine in order to show that Eutyches’ appeal cannot be included among those appeals asserted to belong to the Roman See, [Col. 1124B] he established two rules, which he calls notable and which Quesnellus afterward expanded with excessive exaggeration.

The first is this:

> A case of faith, since it is common and universal, must be judged by the synods of the universal Church, especially by the Roman synod, which is first of all; then the deposition of a heretic, which follows from the decision concerning the faith, must be judged by everyone through a definitive decree, if the heresy is new and has not previously been condemned by the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Peter de Marca, book VII, chapter 6, no. 5.]

From what law—divine, ecclesiastical, or imperial—he derives this rule is entirely unknown, unless we are at least to suspect that it came from some dubious workshop. The author has not disclosed this secret.

For our part, if we attend to the conduct of the Roman pontiffs—and indeed without departing from the statements of that same author, Peter de Marca—we are convinced that Nestorius and his heresy were rightly proscribed, and that the author of the heresy was deprived of his episcopate even before a general synod was convened.

This is especially so since we know that [Col. 1124C] Cyril alone was entrusted with the task of faithfully carrying out the pontifical sentence and presenting it to the Council of Ephesus, while a delay of ten days was granted to Nestorius, during which he could consider whether he wished to abandon and renounce his perverse doctrine.

This assertion needs no explanation, since Peter de Marca himself interpreted the letter of Pope Saint Celestine to Cyril by saying:

> Celestine commands Cyril that, having assumed the authority, office, place, and pontifical power of the Roman See, he should execute this sentence and take care of that Church—namely, the Church of Constantinople.

Leo the Great had Celestine as his immediate predecessor in the pontificate.

Yet under Celestine’s rule that first rule was entirely unknown to the Fathers of the Church, although the matter concerned removing a bishop from office and a case of faith that was common and universal.

Nevertheless, Pope Celestine decrees, establishes, and judges; he grants time for repentance without awaiting the judgment or vote of the other patriarchs, but merely entrusts Cyril with the execution of the decrees he himself had issued.

Thus, even adhering to Peter de Marca’s statements, I do not see from what law, canon, or imperial constitution such a rule could be derived. It must therefore be regarded as arbitrary, arising from a system and intention of limiting pontifical authority and confining it within narrow bounds.

We would say more about this system if the purpose of our undertaking permitted it. For the present, it is useful to have seen that this rule is not excellent, as de Marca repeatedly proclaims, since we find that it is supported by neither law nor custom.

### 14

Perhaps the second rule that the same author added will secure this prerogative. Namely, appeals made to patriarchs are to be regarded as also made to their synods, as is clear from Eutyches’ formula of appeal. [Col. 1125A] But he did not appeal to the synods of the East because the patriarch of Antioch had subscribed to Flavian’s sentence, and because several metropolitans of the Asian, Pontic, and Thracian dioceses were present at the Constantinopolitan council.

Finally, so that the aforementioned prelate might secure complete credibility for these statements, he admits that he drew them from the Acts of that Constantinopolitan gathering in which the monk Constantine, acting as Eutyches’ representative, contended that the Acts published by Flavian had been corrupted and even interpolated, since Eutyches had appealed to the other synods mentioned above, although the appeal was no longer recorded in the Acts.

15. Following in the footsteps of Peter de Marca and making use of exaggerations, Quesnellus explained the preceding doctrine at greater length and with an imposing display of words; then he appended the letter of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, which he calls a synodical letter and which he copied from the works of Facundus of Hermiana. Since the conduct of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, cannot be explained adequately in a few words, it will be weighed in the controversies that follow. [Col. 1125B] For we have obtained from Vatican manuscripts substantial materials for embellishing its history. The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, copied around the seventh century, contain that celebrated Session which Quesnellus judged to be fictitious and therefore rejectable.

Meanwhile, I shall not deny that Domnus of Antioch vigorously opposed the errors of the Eutychians [Note: [Col. 1125D] In Book VIII, chapter 5, of Facundus of Hermiana, one will find the letter of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, written to the emperor Theodosius against Eutyches.]. Nevertheless, I shall argue that it may be inferred from the formula of the appeal that Eutyches did not appeal to all the patriarchs and their synods. And lest we seem to be playing with words, I think first of all that we should ask the most learned archbishop what formula he regards as the genuine one used by Eutyches.

If he calls genuine the formula which Constantine appended, then Constantine did not lie, contrary to what Quesnellus and the others affirmed; consequently, all the Fathers who, at the second Constantinopolitan assembly, opposed the statements of that procurator did an injury to the truth. For one of two things must be said: either Constantine lied [Col. 1125C] in this account of the appeal, or the Fathers of the synod lied. But who would affirm this at the cost of such an injury and disgrace to an entire episcopal assembly? Certainly not Quesnellus, who professes that in all things he wished to safeguard the honor and dignity of the bishops. Nor Peter de Marca, who affirmed that matters of faith ought to be handled by the entire body of bishops, for the common good and safety of the whole Church.

Therefore, we must not insist upon the formula supplied by the monk Constantine, lest we rashly and audaciously pass judgment upon the order of bishops and presbyters and their hierarchy. The genuine formula of the Eutychian appeal must instead be derived from elsewhere, and from no other evidence than either the words of Basil, who carefully reflected with himself upon the truth of past events, or the testimony of the deacon Eleusinus, which agrees with the statements of Saint Leo the Great.

Since the former formula also mentions Dioscorus of Alexandria, whereas the latter mentions only the supreme pontiff Leo, as we have already seen in the preceding discussion, we shall not dwell longer on examining them, lest we do again what has already been done. We have discussed both formulas sufficiently in the preceding sections.

I also think it should be added that one can scarcely understand what the same de Marca added: “He did not appeal, however,” he says, “to the synods of the East, because the patriarch of Antioch had subscribed to Flavian’s sentence, and because several metropolitans, and so forth.” But what of it? A general synod was already being contemplated, and was Eutyches arguing that the Easterners should be excluded? Did he therefore wish to be judged only by the Westerners together with the Roman pontiff? And how could the general council which de Marca asserted was necessary for the common cause of the faith have been composed solely of Western bishops? This system seemed to me to contain a profound mystery. [Col. 1126A] For that reason I have become convinced that the genuine formula of the Eutychian appeal must be drawn from other sources, as we shall clearly demonstrate in the following chapters.

# CHAPTER V

Other arguments of Quesnellus against the appeal of Eutyches are presented and more solidly examined. The letter of Eutyches written to Saint Leo the pope is brought under examination, and finally the position of Christianus Lupus is vindicated and defended.

## 1

In our preceding exercise we defended, to the best of our ability, the appeal of Eutyches to the Apostolic See, setting forth individually the considerations and arguments by which we believed we could reach the goal we had set ourselves. Nevertheless, since we were unable to fulfill all the parts of the undertaking in a single controversy—both because of what the most learned Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, wrote in his celebrated work concerning the causes and rights of the Eastern bishops, and because of the Acts of the second Constantinopolitan assembly, held on account of the Eutychian heresy, which we observed to be greatly disordered and confused—we judged that, so as not to weary readers excessively as they passed through our writings, not everything that arose for discussion in this matter should be dealt with under one and the same heading.

Since, therefore, besides what we have already explained, various other arguments of Quesnellus remain to be noted and examined—arguments which the author himself claims can be clearly deduced from the preceding letters of Flavian and Saint Leo, and which, at least in appearance, would weaken what we have said so far—we thought it appropriate to reserve them for refutation in this new dissertation.

Nor do I think it necessary, at the threshold of this controversy, to warn the reader about Quesnellus’s excessive zeal in interpreting, distorting, and mutilating the testimonies upon which he tried to rely, in order to prepare support for his cause and win the reader’s confidence. This will be sufficiently evident in his exposition of the arguments.

## 2

Let this, then, be Quesnellus’s first argument, which he proposes from the words of Flavian set against him. When he opposed the testimony of the monk Constantine, explained above, to the words of Saint Flavian, Quesnellus says:

> “In these words, besides Leo alone, no one else is named to whom Eutyches appealed.”

He then adds:

> “It is not difficult to answer. This happened for no other reason than that he was addressing Leo alone, and the heresiarch had named Leo alone when he wrote to him, thinking that by a deceitful lie he could insinuate himself into the holy ears of Leo, as Flavian writes to Saint Leo. And because Saint Leo unquestionably stood out among the patriarchs and metropolitans to whose council Eutyches was said to have appealed—and stood out by a plurality of rights—he was the one who both held primacy in the Church and was head of the entire synod to which the appeal was made [Note: [Col. 1126D] Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo, dissertation 7, no. 8.].”

Thus Quesnellus. But who does not understand that these interpretations are excessively clever, painted and disguised with the colors of honor?

Quesnellus proceeds still further, saying:

> “Although the same pontiff appears to have drawn the entire case to himself,”

since he asks to be informed about each detail and complains of Flavian’s silence:

> “Although he ought first of all to have disclosed everything to us, the reality is not so. Likewise, any other bishop to whose judgment someone might appeal by a written petition, and who requested to be informed about the matter, would also have sought information and raised complaints about silence. Leo therefore rightly, and with stronger claim, wished the account and knowledge of the entire affair to be brought before him—indeed, brought before him first, since he was the primate, who, together with the others and before the others, was to decide the matter if there was a place for an appeal.”

## 3

Let us uncover falsehoods masked by the colors and shadows of truth. In the first place, Quesnellus would assert in vain, and altogether incorrectly, that Constantine’s testimony was opposed to Flavian’s words, if the manner of speaking used by both tended toward precisely the same end.

Constantine, whom Quesnellus himself also declares to have been a heretic and a most mendacious man, testified that Eutyches had appealed to other patriarchs, to the metropolitans of the principal Churches, and to their synods. If Flavian had intended to grant what our adversary tries to make him say when he replied to Saint Leo—namely, that although he names Leo alone, this was because he was addressing Leo alone—it would follow either that Flavian did not disagree in substance with Constantine’s testimony, or that he denied any appeal made by Eutyches.

The first alternative is forbidden by Quesnellus’s convictions. For it would be impious even lightly to suspect that Flavian, a bishop of such holiness who suffered martyrdom in defense of the Catholic faith, wished to subscribe to the lying statements of the monk Constantine. The second alternative must therefore be conceded: namely, that Flavian denied an appeal made by Eutyches—not just any appeal, however, but one made at the time of the trial.

For he did not deny that, at least after the assembly had been dissolved, Eutyches appealed to the Roman pontiff Leo, since by Leo’s own letters he was already being informed about this appeal. Let Quesnellus weigh Flavian’s words, and see whether his distorted and ingenious interpretation can agree with them:

> “But after these events, letters were brought to us from Your Holiness . . . through which we learned that the same Eutyches had sent you petitions full of every kind of deceit and cunning, saying that at the time of the trial he had submitted petitions of appeal both to us and to the holy council assembled here, and had appealed to Your Holiness [Note: [Col. 1127D] Flavian’s first letter, chapter 3.].”

Let him take note especially of these words: “and had appealed to Your Holiness.” Thus Flavian wrote that Eutyches had appealed to no one other than Saint Leo. He immediately denies this by adding:

> “This he by no means did.” [Col. 1127C]

But what does Flavian deny that Eutyches had done, unless it was that the heretical archimandrite, at the time of the trial, had submitted petitions of appeal to Flavian and the council, appealing to Saint Leo?

He does not then say, “he appealed to you and to your council,” but rather, “to Your Holiness.” Furthermore, if the heresiarch, when writing to Saint Leo, named Leo alone, as Quesnellus himself asserts, and made absolutely no mention of the other patriarchs and synods, why should we say that this was done contrary to Eastern custom, inventing the claim that the patriarchs and metropolitans of the most celebrated dioceses, together with their synods, were also to be appealed to?

If such an invented custom had prevailed, Flavian, while preserving the reverence due to the head of the whole Church, would certainly have called this appeal entirely irregular and would have written back to Saint Leo that the rights of the Eastern Church had been violated and broken, since the patriarchs and metropolitans—whose judgment in similar cases was relevant—were entirely unaware of it.

Flavian’s silence on this point is confirmed by what follows, in which he addresses that same Leo as the one who alone would handle the affair and judge the heretic. He adds:

> “But in this respect also he lied, thinking that by a deceitful lie he could insinuate himself into your holy ears.”

If he had known or believed that Eutyches had also tried to insinuate himself by a deceitful lie into the ears of others through his letters, Flavian would have added to the words “your holy ears” other words, or equivalent ones, referring to the other bishops. Indeed, he ought to have added them, so that Leo might be more fully informed, as he requested.

For Leo had written:

> “And therefore, because Your Love sees that we are necessarily concerned about so serious a matter, let him hasten to indicate to us, as fully and clearly as possible, everything that happened, which he ought to have done earlier.” [Col. 1128A]  
> [Note: [Col. 1127D] Letter 21 of Leo to Flavian.]

These words are golden, indicating authority and command. For a fullest and clearest account or exposition of everything that had happened would by no means have been given if Flavian had concealed in silence either that Eutyches had appealed to the Roman See contrary to the rights of the Eastern Church, or that he had not said that Eutyches had appealed—or ought to have appealed—to the synods and the other patriarchs.

Therefore, this new form of ecclesiastical judgments of which our adversary speaks was entirely unknown to Flavian.

## 4

Perhaps Quesnellus anticipated the force of this reply. To confirm his preceding statements, he says that from Leo’s manner of writing it appears that Leo had drawn the entire case to himself, since he asks to be informed about each detail and complains about Flavian’s silence, as those words indicate:

> “Although he ought first to have disclosed everything to us.” [Note: [Col. 1127D] Leo the Great, Letter 20 to Flavian, chapters 1 [Col. 1128D] and 2. See what we said against the Quesnellian system in chapter 3 of these Exercises.]

But our adversary offers a very weak reply when he contends that this could have been done by any bishop to whose judgment an appeal was made by petition, and so forth.

Are you therefore distorting the formulas used by the Fathers, Quesnellus, by moving from one matter to another? Let us examine where the difficulty lies. First, let us ask by what right any other bishop could have received such petitions of appeal and requested to be informed about the case.

If the matter concerned an arbitrary judge appointed by mutual agreement of both parties to settle a dispute, then certainly any bishop who was chosen ought to request information, lest he pronounce judgment on matters unknown to him. But what judge is under discussion here? No other than the one established by divine and ecclesiastical laws for settling controversies of faith and for reviewing the judgments of others—namely, determining whether those judgments conformed to the rules of law and whether ordinary judges, moved by hatred, envy, or any other passion, had inflicted force and oppression upon the condemned party.

Leo the Great therefore drew the entire case to himself because Eutyches, refusing to accept the sentence delivered by his ordinary bishop and by the Constantinopolitan synod, ought to have appealed to a higher and final judge. Accordingly, in his letter the holy pontiff uses imperative expressions full of authority and dignity:

> “And therefore let Your Brotherhood indicate to us, through a person especially suitable and fully competent, by the fullest report, what novelty has arisen against the ancient faith”;  
>  
> and likewise:  
>  
> “Since we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, cannot decide anything concerning matters unknown to us, to the prejudice of either party, before we have truthfully heard everything that took place.”

## 5

These and similar words of Leo, written not in the name of the council but in his own name, possessed such force and authority that they had already moved—or at least compelled—Flavian to appear before Leo, either through suitable legates or by an authentic written report, in order to render an account of everything that had occurred.

But we have seen above that Flavian had already done this before receiving Leo’s letter. Therefore, if we bring all the evidence together, we shall have a certain argument that Leo drew the entire case to himself in such a way that no other bishop or judge would have been permitted to intervene in it except by the decision of the supreme pontiff.

Leo himself clearly indicated in the letter cited above that he had reserved the whole matter to his own authority for determination. To close off every difficulty and excuse that could be raised concerning the defiance and obstinacy of the archimandrite Eutyches, he reserves the entire matter for examination, as ecclesiastical moderation and concern for Christian peace required and as the imperial letters had also urged him:

> “So that, when dissensions have been removed, the Catholic faith may be preserved inviolate, and those who defend perverse doctrines, having been recalled from error, may be strengthened by our authority, those whose faith has been proved.” [Col. 1129A]  
> [Note: [Col. 1129D] Saint Leo, the letter cited above.]

Here Leo promises that he will accomplish three things by his own authority: remove dissensions so that the Catholic faith may be preserved inviolate; recall from error those who defended perverse doctrines; and finally provide support and protection to those whose faith had been proved.

If, therefore, Leo promises to accomplish these three things by his own authority, not that of others, there is no reason to resort to a distorted interpretation, inventing other arbiters and judges of this case and asserting that Leo, together with the other bishops and before the others, as primate, ought to decide whether there was a place for an appeal.

Quesnellus nevertheless presses the matter, objecting to these words of Saint Leo in his letter to Flavian:

> “Since we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, cannot decide anything concerning matters unknown to us, to the prejudice of either party, before we have truthfully heard everything that took place.”

From these words our adversary, happily and as though singing a triumphal song, reasons as follows:

> “These are the words of a man who does not arrogate to himself every right to render a judgment, but of a prudent, watchful, and most equitable judge, who does not wish rashly to give his vote in a case unknown to him. But why do we waste time answering such arguments drawn from Leo himself?”

The same Quesnellus says:

> “In this present case we are not asking whether Leo claimed that prerogative for himself, but whether Eutyches in fact appealed, and whether he appealed only to the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 1129D] Quesnellus, in the dissertation cited above, chapter 8, p. 297].”

What an ingenious escape! He understands that his cause is collapsing, and recognizes that those equivocal and unusual formulas—“does not arrogate to himself every right to render a judgment”—offer him no support. Such expressions imply a certain presumption, as does the other phrase, “to give his vote,” as though Leo had indicated that he wished to convene, and that it was necessary to convene, a council in order to perform the role of a watchful, prudent, and most equitable judge.

For ordinarily “to give one’s vote” signifies that a case is to be handled in an assembly, synod, or college. But Leo is profoundly silent about these matters, and nothing in what he wrote offers even the slightest indication of them.

## 6

But since Quesnellus recognized that he had a bad case and turned his reasoning to other matters, let us follow his steps gradually and attend to what he added. He says:

> “If Eutyches had appealed only to the Roman pontiff—as Saint Leo thought he had done on the basis of a crafty and lying petition—there would be no reason for us to be surprised that Eutyches, appealing to the Roman See, was readily received by the Roman pontiff, especially since the Nicene faith appeared to be at issue, to which both Eutyches himself and his accuser professed an unbroken adherence. For these are especially the duties of the Roman president, as the head of the episcopal crown: that from the first chair, as from a watchtower, he should watch over the preservation of the canons and act as guardian of the Catholic faith.”

Those who did not attend to Quesnellus’s subsequent statements might claim that no one could have written anything more honorifically in defense of the authority of the Apostolic See. Yet since, in the following paragraph—or chapter 8 of his dissertation—Quesnellus asserts that Leo should not be heeded because he is pursuing too much splendor and the rights of his own see, it is sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear that Quesnellus regarded him as speaking only craftily and hyperbolically. [Col. 1129D]

Thus he reasons:

> “But let us not put faith in Eutyches, that most cunning impostor; let us not heed Leo himself, although he was a most holy man, since he was pursuing the splendor and rights of his own see. Let us hear Flavian, bishop of New Rome and a most courageous martyr of Christ, from whom the attitude and custom of the Easterners concerning appeals, and the whole manner of Eutyches’ conduct, could not have remained hidden. Did he judge that the sentence of his council concerning Eutyches ought to be sent to Leo so that, if Leo approved it, it would stand, but, if he rejected it, it would disappear? Certainly nothing of the sort appears in either of his letters [Note: [Col. 1129D] See Quesnellus’s dissertation On the Life and Deeds of Leo the Great; and Quesnellus, dissertation On the Appeal of Eutyches, chapter 9 [Col. 1130D].].”

These and similar statements, which he set down elsewhere in the same or at least equivalent words, show that Quesnellus exaggerated beyond what his evidence could support, so that, little by little, while discussing the ancient Church’s system of government and the form and order of judgments, he could sell fables and inventions.

Who will not believe that this is an invention or an offensive fiction: that the most holy pontiff Leo, in the case of Eutyches, indulged himself excessively beyond the laws of justice and equity by claiming rights that did not belong to him?

This is that Leo, the supreme pontiff, whom the whole Church, gathered in the Council of Chalcedon, venerated as the legitimate heir and champion of all the rights of Saint Peter; who preserved unimpaired the doctrine of faith necessary for salvation; and who was appointed interpreter for all of blessed Peter’s voice. This is that great Leo by whom those Fathers, making use of the beginnings of good things for the benefit of the Church, were able to show the Church’s children the inheritance and portion of truth; and, standing together in a common crown of joy, feasting as though at imperial banquets on the spiritual delicacies which Christ had prepared through Leo’s letters for those who had been invited [Note: [Col. 1130D] Letter of the Fathers of Chalcedon to Leo the Great, in Quesnellus, volume I, p. 292. Consult Labbe, volume IV of the Councils.].

To this supreme pontiff, to whom the whole Church lent its ear, shall we refuse to lend ours, guided only by the suspicion that he was pursuing the splendor and rights of his own see—thereby wronging the see of Constantinople and despising and abolishing the rights and prerogatives of the Eastern Churches?

Only Quesnellus could reason in this way, later exaggerating unduly the prerogatives and honor of the Constantinopolitan throne. But let us inquire what and of what kind were the prerogatives and rights of this see, since Quesnellus says: “Let us hear Flavian, bishop of New Rome and a most courageous martyr.”

“New Rome” was certainly the city of Constantinople, which acquired the name through the munificence and majesty of the emperors, but not, in matters pertaining to religion, the corresponding honor and prerogatives. [Col. 1130C]

## 7

Nor was the chair of its episcopate founded either by the apostles and Saint Peter or by his disciple, as was the see of Antioch, where the prince of the apostles first sat; the see of Alexandria, where his disciple Mark was established as bishop; and the see of Rome, which Peter himself retained until his martyrdom.

These Churches are known to have been called apostolic and to have obtained the honor and prerogatives of patriarchates from the beginnings of their foundations, with the distinction of rank preserved that Saint Leo and the other Fathers handed down; this is also evident from the Nicene canons.

But the bishop of Constantinople did not enjoy the honor and prerogatives of a patriarchate at its beginnings, nor even in the age of the Council of Nicaea. He obtained the name of patriarchate only after the year 500, through the work of the emperor Justinian and with the permission of the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 1130D]

## 8

Nor does it help Quesnellus to appeal to the fifth canon of the first Council of Constantinople, convened under Theodosius the Elder, or to the twenty-eighth canon of the synod of Chalcedon, in which the honor of primacy after the Roman pontiff is asserted for the bishop of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1130D] Volume III of the Councils, and volume IV.].

For, as we saw in the preceding chapter, that canon of the Council of Constantinople acquired no force whatever, either with respect to the name of primacy or with respect to prerogatives and authority in ordaining the metropolitan bishops of the provinces of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace.

Nor does it accomplish anything that the Fathers of Chalcedon [Col. 1131A] attempted to renew and confirm that canon. First of all, the Chalcedonian Fathers were flattering themselves with the thought that the holy pontiff might willingly communicate new titles and prerogatives to the bishop of the imperial city, thereby increasing his glory if he did not disdain to grant him the privileges of ancient Rome.

They were led to this conclusion because they regarded the episcopal see of Constantinople as a kind of second part of ancient Rome and therefore thought that it ought to be raised above the other Churches of the East. Moreover, they were concerned lest the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch should suffer any injury or coercion, since they had been accustomed to regard the bishopric of Constantinople as, so to speak, a member and part of the episcopate of ancient Rome.

They further observed that the Nicene canons opposed this enactment. For that reason, the bishop of New Rome could not peacefully enjoy the privileges and prerogatives in question without an express decree of the Apostolic See and a peremptory judgment by which all disputes and conflicts—especially those concerning the Ephesians—would be permanently abolished.

Accordingly, they resolved to present that entire council, together with the whole body of the Easterners, most humbly before Leo by letter. [Col. 1131B] Nor did the Fathers of that general council, when addressing Saint Leo, use any of the phrases Quesnellus adopted to magnify the glory of New Rome and exalt the rights of that Church.

They did request confirmation of everything that had been done, especially the aforementioned fifth canon of Constantinople, and they said confidently:

> “Since the apostolic ray shines among you, you customarily extend it even to the Church of Constantinople by governing it; you spread it abroad and expand it more frequently, because without jealousy you are accustomed to enrich your household by sharing in your own goods.”

Thus, according to this formula used by the Fathers, down to those times the Roman pontiff was accustomed to extend the apostolic ray to the Church of Constantinople, governing it, just as had very often occurred in difficult matters and in cases of dissension. They therefore believed that he wished and was able to enrich his household by sharing his goods—that is, his privileges.

They then add that the papal legates had vigorously resisted this enactment and had tried to invalidate it:

> “wishing also that this good should be begun by your providence, so that, just as the result belongs to you in matters of faith, so also the effect of good order may be attributed to you.”

What, then? The Chalcedonian Fathers attribute the victory of the Catholic faith not to a Roman council and not to themselves, but to Leo. From him they likewise hoped to obtain that other arrangement of ecclesiastical government, for which they earnestly begged him.

They add, among other things:

> “We therefore ask you: honor our judgment by your decrees; and just as we have added our agreement to the head in matters of good, so let your supreme authority complete for the children what is fitting.” [Note: [Col. 1131D] Letter of the Fathers of Chalcedon, in Quesnellus, volume I, p. 294, and in Labbe’s volume IV of the Councils.]

## 9

Now, in order to determine whether Quesnellus’s cause and manner of reasoning can stand even in appearance, without collapsing utterly, allow me to reason as follows from the preceding discussion.

Could Flavian, bishop of New Rome and a most courageous martyr of Christ, have thought otherwise about the appeals of the Easterners and the judgments of the provincial synods than did the Fathers of all the Churches of the East, assembled in a general synod?

My opinion—and that of every sensible person who does not seek a knot in a reed and who, driven by an excessive desire to quarrel, does not strive to sell masked trifles as true matters—must be that Flavian could not have thought otherwise about all these matters than what those Chalcedonian Fathers, assembled in so celebrated a gathering, confessed:

namely, that the bishop of Constantinople, especially among the Easterners, was subject to the Apostolic See, and that in every sort of case he had chiefly sought, awaited, and obtained its judgment and direction.

It must therefore be held as certain that Flavian, such a great bishop, adorned with holiness and the greatest merits, without any prior prompting, disclosed the entire case of Eutyches to Leo the supreme pontiff and sent him all the synodal Acts, exercising the subjection properly due, so that the sentence passed against the heretic would stand if it were approved and would disappear if it were rejected.

We have already proved this from both of Flavian’s letters, upon which alone Quesnellus relies, in the two preceding chapters. Since we are now embarrassed to repeat what has already been said, and as though gradually to be led outside the rights of appeals into wandering elsewhere, we have decided to pass over these matters and turn our discourse to other very weighty considerations.

## 10

And, in order to discuss the rights of that Church of Constantinople in that age, we must be convinced that Flavian had no better or more sincere interpreter of his cause and conduct than Anatolius, who was appointed to the same see after Flavian’s death.

I admit that Anatolius was not endowed with equal holiness, character, and virtues, as Flavian had been. [Col. 1132B] Nevertheless, no one will deny that he labored under excessive ambition to broaden and increase the rights and prerogatives of his Church, without preserving the moderation necessary to prevent him from usurping what belonged to others through presumption and arrogance.

The subjection he maintained toward the Roman See is indicated by Anatolius himself in his letter to Leo the Great, written after the Council of Chalcedon. He first complains about Dioscorus of Alexandria, whom the synod found to be the author of so great a storm raised against the common peace.

> “It was necessary,” he adds, “to remove that wicked man, who had filled the whole world with storms and tempests.”

Dioscorus, moreover, opposed not only matters of faith but also, vigorously, the ambition of the bishops of Constantinople, claiming for himself the rights of primacy over that Church, which was regarded as second according to the Nicene statutes.

Accordingly, after Anatolius had recounted what had been established in that council concerning the Catholic faith by the common agreement of the Fathers, he began his discourse as follows concerning the confirmation and determination of the honor and prerogatives of the see of Constantinople:

> “Since it was necessary for us to dispose of other proposals as well, so that such a great synod might appear fully to provide what was required, both correction and confirmation, both in canonical matters and in other ecclesiastical matters, those who govern all things—the most magnificent and glorious princes, the illustrious and celebrated senate, the entire clergy, and the people—took care that the most holy see situated in this royal city of Constantinople should receive some increase of honor.” [Note: [Col. 1131D] We encountered this letter of Anatolius in a Greek Vatican manuscript seven hundred years old; it had nevertheless hitherto been desired by learned men, and we shall present it, furnished with various notes, in another volume.]

To make this increase of honor easier to grant, he appealed to the canon of the first Council of Constantinople under the emperor Theodosius. He also brought to the Roman pontiff’s mind the names of Nectarius the Great, Timothy of Alexandria, and others who had given their votes at that synod. Anatolius likewise declared that the matter had been handled in the council by the Fathers with the confidence that it would be approved by the Roman pontiff:

> “confident that he will approve the honor of the see of Constantinople, since it already possesses the care and concord of your apostolic throne, and in every matter has shared the common assistance it needed.”

Later, when discussing the special care that the Roman See had exercised toward the Church of Constantinople, among the many things that Bishop Anatolius himself thought should be suggested to Leo, so that Leo’s mind might be willingly moved [Col. 1132D] to confirm and ratify that canon pertaining to the honor and prerogatives of his see, he says the following. These words undoubtedly reveal clearly the doctrine of those times concerning the government of the Churches of the East and, so to speak, directly oppose the new doctrines and utterly overthrow the Quesnellian errors:

> “And whatever approval and stability we can obtain, we beseech you, most holy one, that this too may be granted by you.”

Let the reader, I beg, take note of what immediately follows:

> “For the see of Constantinople has your apostolic throne as its father, joining itself to you in a special manner, so that, because of your care for it, everyone may be convinced that you previously considered it sincerely and that even now you continuously maintain the same mind and care concerning it. It would be entirely beneficial to the ecclesiastical order if you would deign to confirm in writing what has been accomplished in the most holy and ecumenical synod. We have also taken care to send the aforesaid constitution concerning the see of Constantinople to Your Holiness, so that you may know that everything has been divinely arranged according to your wishes.”

Finally, he humbly entreats Saint Leo to respond appropriately to each proposal by sending for this purpose Lucian, bishop and legate, who would explain everything and perform his service in attendance. Lucian was a perfect man, previously dear even to the emperors, whom Leo himself had earlier sent to the synod.

> “And we beseech you to grant an appropriate response to each proposal, since the most beloved bishop of God, Lucian, will explain everything to you. He himself was present at the holy synod and, prudently presenting what he could in his zeal for our faith, was chosen by us to serve you happily in attendance. He is a perfect man, previously dear to our most august and Christian emperors, whom you, in your kindness, deigned to send to us, enjoying and rejoicing in your favor.” [Col. 1133B]

11. And so that no one may doubt that all this does not at all overturn Quesnellus’s novel doctrine and deception, let him, I ask, consider why or in what sense these things can stand together. Quesnellus denies that Flavian sent to Saint Leo the judgment of his synod against Eutyches so that it might be approved—or disappear if it were rejected. He “denies that he sent him the series of the Acts in order to discharge the obligation of a required report; he maintains that the judgment of the Council of Constantinople, [Col. 1133C] over which Flavian had presided, was definitive and that no laborious investigation was necessary. He also asserts that the slippery Eutyches would soon carry his lying complaints to other sees, especially the Roman see, and would occupy the ears of the pontiffs” [Note: [Col. 1133D] Quesnellus, as above, p. 298].

Moreover, when a rumor was spreading that the emperor was considering the convocation of a universal synod in which the whole matter would be recalled for examination, it was reasonable for Flavian to inform the primary see and the fathers of this council; and, with the Roman pontiff taking care of the matter, for the Acts of Constantinople to become known also to the other bishops of the Western region.

But if he denies such things and affirms those already mentioned, the testimony of the fathers of Chalcedon would utterly collapse: they acknowledged that the ray of the apostolic see had customarily been spread and extended as far as the Church of Constantinople in governing it, and that the Constantinopolitans were customarily enriched, as members of one household, by participation in its goods.

Second, it would no longer stand that the fathers of Chalcedon had asked the Roman pontiff to honor their judgment by his decrees [Note: [Col. 1133D] Letter of the fathers of Chalcedon to Saint Leo the Great [Col. 1134D]]. For [Col. 1133D] if, as Quesnellus wishes, the Acts of any metropolitan council do not require confirmation by the Roman pontiff, much less would the proceedings of a general synod have required such confirmation, since they had been sanctioned by the authority of the whole Church.

Third, it would smell of fiction that, in order to remove the dissensions that had previously arisen in the Church of Constantinople because of the fickleness of men’s minds and the circumstances of the times—whether because of the tumult at Ephesus, or because of the ordinations of the metropolitans of those three provinces, namely Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—the Roman pontiffs had exercised every right and authority so that the bishops of Constantinople might in a special way share in the privileges of the apostolic see. Regarding them as sons subject to their father, they embraced them with the greatest care, even in matters pertaining to the administration of ecclesiastical government [Col. 1134A].

Fourth and finally, how could Anatolius have admitted that the Church of Constantinople was not merely subject to the Roman Church under some general arrangement, but was united to it in a particular way because of the Roman pontiffs’ care for it—a care which they had exercised without interruption in former times, arranging everything useful to the ecclesiastical state?

These four points, I say, which we have not fabricated in our own minds but drawn from genuine sources—how could they be reconciled with those spurious rights and privileges whose defender Quesnellus claims Flavian to have been, lest the case of Eutyches be brought before, examined, and judged by the Roman pontiff?

12. Nor is it an objection that Flavian tried to persuade the Roman pontiff that Eutyches had already been judged according to the rules of the canons, and that the new examination and judgment which he was preparing to undertake after learning of Eutyches’s appeal would be superfluous, as Quesnellus himself asserts [Col. 1134B].

For, in the first place, Flavian nowhere indicated that Saint Leo’s examination and judgment would be superfluous. Rather, he sought it, judging only that a general council would be superfluous, lest the disagreements and contentions of the parties grow worse. He also asked that the judgment issued against Eutyches be confirmed by pontifical letters. Without that confirmation, certainly, the judgment of the Eastern bishops would have had no effect, since Eutyches was protesting and had posted public protestatory petitions in the streets of Constantinople, in which he declared that he had been deprived of communion and of the superintendence of his monastery through injustice and the malice or envy of his adversaries.

Therefore Quesnellus must not be heeded when, in order to construct some support for his ruined cause, he resorts to distorted interpretations and confidently, almost playfully, interprets Flavian’s words as follows:

“Flavian asks Leo not for judgment but for consolation; not for a sentence but for letters; for defense, not confirmation; [Col. 1134C] for personal writings, not synodal decrees. For once the anathema against Eutyches had been pronounced through episcopal judgment, the case was finished, unless a universal council should wish to draw the matter to itself or it should voluntarily be referred to the West. On this occasion the bishop of Constantinople rightly judged that this should be prevented, lest,” he says, “the most holy Churches everywhere be disturbed because of the error and malice of one restless and seditious monk.”

He must not, then, be heeded.
