For in the appendix to his letter, as that letter is circulated, Flavian asks the Roman pontiff to make the common cause of the faith his own; and at the same time he asks him to decree that the condemnation regularly pronounced against Eutyches be valid, and to dignify it with his own writings.

Could the Roman pontiff have done what Flavian asks without examining the preceding proceedings and without learning of Eutyches’s bad faith and wickedness? Could [Col. 1134D] he have decreed that Eutyches had been regularly condemned without assuming the role of judge, examining the authentic synodal Acts of the preceding judgment, and setting aside and disregarding the defenses of the condemned man?

What more need be said? Without a prior examination of all these matters, could he, in writing and not merely in words, have brought consolation to the ordinary judge by declaring that the canonical laws had been fulfilled in the investigation already conducted, and that Flavian himself had observed the strict requirements of justice—without thereby holding as ratified and secure whatever had been pronounced against Eutyches?

If these expressions do not imply that Flavian asked Leo for examination, judgment, and decree, I do not know what more precise and suitable words he could have devised to make the sentence already issued stand more firmly. Certainly subordinate judges receive great consolation and strong defense when their judgments are carried to higher tribunals and approved by the judges of those tribunals [Col. 1135A].

It is therefore not surprising that Flavian, deeply disturbed in spirit, and indeed unjustly so because of the disturbances stirred up by Eutyches, acknowledged that the judgment of the Roman pontiff would bring him consolation and defense. Nor was a synodal decree necessary, since the Roman pontiff could have provided all these things through his own letters; and for that reason Flavian asserted that these letters alone could suffice for him.

13. Quesnellus is now distressed that the translation of Flavian’s earlier letter to Saint Leo appears insufficiently accurate: “If,” he says, “it had been possible to correct it against the Greek text, which has perished through the injury of time, perhaps we would have found something clearer that supported our opinion.”

Despite this customary refrain—about ancient codices having been falsified and translations being poorly arranged, a refrain borrowed already from the earlier heretics—he confidently concludes that part of his dissertation with these words:

“From this translation, however, although perhaps made by a Western and Roman man, enough and more than enough light appears to the sincere reader who does not look for a knot in a reed, for bringing the truth to light” [Col. 1135B].

A charming piece of fiction! After employing every technique of reasoning in interpreting and distorting Flavian’s statements—which shortly before he exaggerated as clearer than daylight—he now realizes that his case may collapse before learned men and decides to procure both an escape and a defense by attacking and rebuking the ancient translator of that letter.

Yet Quesnellus would have found nothing clearer, even if the Greek text of that letter existed, that would favor his purposes. The conduct and manner of speaking of the fathers of Chalcedon and of Anatolius already reveal the doctrine of those times and the manner of administering ecclesiastical affairs that the Easterners maintained.

For the present, we have thought it necessary to inform the reader that learned men had hitherto lacked the famous letter of Anatolius. For we were the first of all, in the year of Our Lord 1738, to recover and transcribe it from Greek manuscript codices in the Vatican. Subsequently, the most distinguished Monsieur Franciscus Mariani, a scriptor of the Vatican Library and interpreter of Greek literature, rendered it into Latin with the great learning and kindness for which he is renowned [Col. 1135C]. With God’s help, we shall publish it in its entirety, in both Greek and Latin, from the public press.

14. Since Quesnellus had reflected in many ways on bringing forward everything that he thought could in some fashion support his false opinions, this resulted in his reporting—without naming him—the opinion of a man of outstanding learning who had written:

“After reading the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, everything was so approved and confirmed by Saint Leo that both Flavian and Saint Leo judged that they ought to refrain from calling a general synod.”

Because this formulation displeased Quesnellus, he added: “With due respect to this excellent man, I must say that it is very far from the truth.” Taking the opportunity, he gently portrays Saint Leo as angry with Flavian because Flavian had struck Eutyches with a harsher sentence than, as Leo supposed, was warranted, since Eutyches seemed to be adhering to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.

But, I ask, where did Quesnellus derive the origin of Leo’s anger [Note: [Col. 1135D] Letter 20 of Saint Leo to Flavian, ch. 1], unless from the fact that neither Flavian’s letter nor the synodal proceedings had yet reached the pontiff’s hands in the manner required by the order of ecclesiastical administration or moderation, as Saint Leo himself says—and as we have shown more fully? It is now superfluous to discuss this matter again.

Quesnellus nevertheless added: “As for confirmation of the proceedings he had conducted against Eutyches, Flavian was not thinking of it even in a dream.”

Really? Do those preceding words, and the phrases of Flavian that we noted above, perhaps imply that Flavian was not thinking even in a dream of the confirmation of the proceedings that he expressly requested? He made a splendid effort to deceive the reader; but truth drives out and overthrows lies.

If [Col. 1136A] we wished to continue our customary method of writing by noting step by step everything that Quesnellus wrote to abolish Eutyches’s appeal, we would now be forced to wander outside the scene. For in his dissertation he mixed in various other matters that his opponent believed favored his position, though they scarcely concern the present question.

Such, for example, is his discussion of whether a general synod should or should not be called: he pretends that its authority did not depend on the apostolic see of Saint Peter but on the emperor and the agreement of all the bishops, which, he claims, had first to be sought.

So too his discussion of the Acts of Eastern synods prepared by the metropolitans of the provinces or by diocesan bishops. He claims that these were not sent to the West for examination, but were sent there only when a particular controversy or accusation had developed into a public matter of faith; or when someone condemned in a synod appealed to the other bishops; or when heretics, abusing the emperor’s favor, caused the bishop of the primary see—who was acting with the sovereign—to be summoned, and thereby created an opportunity for him to restrain the evil schemes of obstinate heretics [Col. 1136B].

He thinks that some evidence for this has been supplied by the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Thus, in engaging Christian Lupus in controversy, he says:

“Who would believe that the Acts of the synods of Antioch and Berytus, held not long before the Constantinopolitan synod in the case of Ibas, were sent to Rome? Who would say this of another Antiochene synod, in the case of Athanasius of Perrha? Who would say that the proceedings of six hundred other synods had been brought to the Western regions up to that time? Rather, Flavian would have acted contrary to custom if he had thought of sending them before Eutyches’s obstinacy, the publication of the protestatory petitions, the letters sent to Leo, fear of imperial power, the rumor—or proclamation—of a council to be convened by Theodosius, and other circumstances of this kind had imposed upon Flavian the necessity of informing the primary see about a case that had now become a common concern.”

These are the arguments that Quesnellus arranged [Col. 1136C] in order to create a deception concerning the appeal made to the apostolic see. Since some of them concern the subsequent proclamation and convocation of a general council; others must be referred to the cases treated and decided in the ecumenical synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon; and still others concern the affair of Eutyches and Flavian, which we have thoroughly discussed and clarified, we defer speaking of them more appropriately elsewhere, lest we interrupt the thread of the historical narrative.

For the present, however, we turn specifically to the petition of appeal by Eutyches, which Quesnellus judged should be removed from the collection of Leo’s works.

## CHAPTER VI

On the letter of Eutyches and the petitions written to Saint Leo the Great. The judgment of Christian Lupus concerning these is defended against Quesnellus’s critical notes; and finally it is shown that the latter’s method of acting and writing displays nothing but deceptions and trifles.

[Col. 1136D] 1. I believe that no writer on ecclesiastical matters was as audacious as Quesnellus, nor anyone in whose mind there was a stronger desire to pervert the form and order of Christian government. Those who, without being driven by partisan zeal, have not disdained to examine our Exercises—especially the preceding chapters of this history of Eutyches—will judge that this has already been amply demonstrated.

After having written two complete chapters on Eutyches’s appeal to the apostolic see, we nevertheless thought that a third should be added. In it we would set before Quesnellus Eutyches’s letter, profession of faith, and petitions that he sent to the supreme pontiff, the great Leo, for the protection and defense of his case. Our opponent has tried in many ways to suppress all these documents and explain them away by means of a violent interpretation [Col. 1137A].

To make this easier, he persuades himself that four kinds of petitions must be distinguished—petitions which Eutyches, condemned by his bishop, either presented or falsely claimed to have presented.

“The first was the petition of appeal, of which we have spoken. The second was the protestatory petition, mentioned by Saint Leo in Letter 20 to Flavian, chapter 1: namely, after an appeal has been lodged, letters must be given by the person from whom the appeal was made to the person who will hear the appeal; these letters are called letters of dismissal or apostolic letters . . . . . . But if he does not receive it, let him protest, and so forth.”

The third petition was one of complaint. “For he sent a complaint of his sorrow to the apostolic see in petitions,” says our Leo in Letter 21 to the Emperor Theodosius Augustus.

“Moreover,” adds Quesnellus, “a petition of complaint, or of grievance, is properly and correctly said to be presented by a presbyter against a bishop, or his father. In support of this conjecture he quotes the jurists’ maxim: ‘It is just and customary for a son complaining of injuries inflicted by his father to be heard, whereas scarcely anyone tolerates him as an accuser’” [Col. 1137B].

The fourth petition, namely, a supplication, Eutyches presented against Flavian’s judgment. “Indeed, there were several of them, as may be seen in Act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon” [Note: Quesnellus, Dissertation 7, no. 15, vol. II of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 300].

2. Having prefaced his discussion with this distinction among petitions, Quesnellus reasons further as follows:

“These four kinds of petitions must first be distinguished [Col. 1137C], lest the force and effectiveness of one be attributed to another, and consequently the whole matter be obscured. The first petition, therefore, was an appeal to the council; the second was a protest to the people of Constantinople; the third was a complaint, or petition of grievance, to Saint Leo; the fourth was a supplication to the emperor.”

The first was fictitious and was not actually delivered; the other three were genuinely presented. Saint Flavian mentioned all these petitions in Letter 1 to Saint Leo.

Quesnellus concluded his dissertation with these words:

“If, then, this charming and equally ingenious distinction among the petitions, devised by our opponent, were valid, what we have written thus far about Eutyches’s appeal would already collapse in part. We would say that Eutyches made only a complaint before the apostolic see, not an appeal. But I ask our opponent where he derived this distinction, lest we conclude that it was fabricated and devised merely to create a deception.

“We have found no such distinction among four kinds of petitions in the codices or in the legal Digest, as though only one of them could possess the whole force and effectiveness. Indeed, those who, not at all deceived by the preceding apparatus of Quesnellian trifles, do not shrink from investigating the truth of the matter will affirm with us that the protestatory petition—which jurists call an evocation petition—contains an appeal, a complaint, and a supplication.”

Socrates first relates how, at the synod of Tyre, through the activity of the Meletian faction together with the Eusebians, and without observing any natural or ecclesiastical order, the great Athanasius was condemned as guilty of many crimes [Col. 1137D].

Thereupon Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops, in a protestatory petition—which today, as the distinguished Peter de Marca noted, would be called an evocation petition [Note: Peter de Marca, Book IV of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood*, ch. 2, no. 6]—ask Count Dionysius, who had been sent by Constantine to the synod to supervise the proceedings and to safeguard the preservation of fairness, not to give place to stitched-together calumnies and not to allow them to suffer injustice through the plots and false accusations of their enemies, who sat as judges in that council.

The words of the petition presented to Dionysius are these [Note: Letter of Constantine, in Baronius, year 334, § 2]:

“Since we saw a patchwork of many calumnies, and from these patchworks the plots of Eusebius, Narcissus, Flacillus, Theognis, Maris, Theodore, and Patrophilus against [Col. 1138A] us—and since at the outset it was not permitted to reject them when they objected—we necessarily proceeded to a formal protest, especially since we observed that many things were being done under our accusations for the favor of the Meletians, and many others as plots against the Catholic Church. For this reason also we necessarily present this petition to you, with many entreaties, so that, keeping the fear of God in your heart—the God who protects the rule of the most august and pious Emperor Constantine—you may reserve the examination of our cases to the emperor. For, having been sent by the emperor, it is right that you preserve this matter intact” [Note: Vol. II of the General Councils, p. 730; and in the distinguished Peter de Marca, as above].

No one can dare deny that this protestatory petition contains within itself all the force and effectiveness that Quesnellus imagines to be scattered and divided among four kinds of petitions. Do Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops not complain in it that they have been attacked by the calumnies of their enemies through falsehoods and a patchwork of accusations, through the plots of Eusebius, Narcissus, and the others? Did they not testify by solemn protest that plots against the Catholic Church had been devised in that synod under the pretext of false accusations brought against them, regarding which they pretended to conduct an investigation [Col. 1138B]? Finally, did they not ask by their entreaties that the examination of their cases be reserved to the Emperor Constantine, with the fear of God kept in mind?

The matter concerned false crimes which, had they been true, would already have affected both the civil administration of affairs and the imperial government. It is therefore not surprising that, amid such circumstances of distress, they appealed to the emperor so that new judges might be appointed who, moved neither by hatred, malice, nor wickedness, would undertake to examine their case.

It is therefore untrue that four kinds of petitions must be distinguished in similar cases, lest the force and effectiveness of one be attributed to another and the whole matter consequently be obscured. The matter of an appeal becomes perfectly clear from a single kind of petition, provided that it contains everything necessary for establishing and securing a genuine appeal.

3. The petitions and letter by which Eutyches appealed to Saint Leo are indeed of this kind, as what we are about to say will make clear [Col. 1138C].

That letter, or petition, contains three sections. One of them contains two kinds of complaint. The first is that he had been accused by Eusebius of Dorylaeum, who was hostile to him, on the charge of violating the faith; the second is that the Acts of the Constantinopolitan synod had been improperly drawn up against him.

Accordingly, after invoking the testimony of the holy pontiff concerning the meaning of his propositions and words, he adds:

“But the worst devil has bewitched this zeal and purpose of ours, against which his strength ought to have been destroyed. By feigning every manner of domestic power on his own behalf, he stirred up against me Eusebius, bishop of the town of Dorylaeum, who presented a petition to the holy bishop of the Church of Constantinople, Flavian; and, having fabricated certain other things in the same city . . . . . . , he called me a heretic, moved to accusation not by the truth.”

Afterward, in the same manner, he complains that, when he had presented his profession of faith to the fathers of Constantinople—a written petition composed and confirmed by his own subscription—Flavian neither received the petition nor ordered it to be read [Col. 1138D].

He further added that at that synod he had said and asked that the judgment of the apostolic see should be awaited:

“I asked that these matters be made known to Your Holiness and that you judge whatever seemed right to you, declaring that in every respect I would follow what you approved.”

Then, making a more serious complaint about this refusal, he immediately adds:

“But without hearing any of the things I was saying, they abruptly ended the synod and published the sentence of deposition which they had prepared against me before the examination.”

He relates that violence and deposition had also been threatened against the superiors of other monasteries so that they might subscribe to his condemnation [Note: Petition, or letter, of Eutyches, corrected in the Vatican manuscript codices, ch. 1]. These circumstances led him to satisfy the common people by publicly setting forth his confession of faith [Col. 1139A].

These, I say, are the matters belonging to Eutyches’s complaints, and they fill the entire first section of his petition.

After these complaints of distress, Eutyches proceeds to his appeal. Having rejected the prior judgment delivered at the Constantinopolitan synod, he addresses the supreme pontiff in this manner, beginning his speech with these words:

“To you, therefore, defenders of religion and those who abominate such factions, I flee for refuge.”

He more explicitly asks that the acts and decisions thus far carried out at the Constantinopolitan synod be abolished and declared void, and he begs the Roman pontiff to issue a judgment and a new sentence.

Let Quesnellus therefore attend to his following words and say whether Eutyches appealed to the Roman pontiff or not:

“And I entreat you, without allowing any prejudice to be done to me on account of what was treacherously done against me, to pronounce whatever sentence you deem right concerning the faith, and henceforth to permit no calumny by factions to proceed against me, and not to expel and remove me from the number of the orthodox, and so forth” [Col. 1139B].

4. Moreover, lest the supreme pontiff treat Eutyches’s appeal lightly, as though it were not supported by the necessary conditions prescribed by the canons, Eutyches attached both petitions to his letters.

That is, he attached the petition presented by his accuser, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, to the synod, and the petition that Eutyches himself had carried but which Flavian and the synod had not received; he also attached his profession of faith, as well as the matters decreed above by the holy fathers at the two councils [Col. 1139C].

He immediately appended this profession of faith to the aforesaid letter or petition, as we discovered from a Vatican manuscript codex written approximately six hundred years ago. After the completion of the first two sections, we find the following note: “Likewise, the words of Eutyches.”

Here we indicate only summarily what that profession of faith contains, since our controversy does not concern it. Elsewhere the distinguished Christian Lupus prepared it for publication from a Cassinese codex, although Quesnellus judged that it should be removed from his appendix.

In publishing this profession of faith, Eutyches declares that he relies entirely upon the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea and Ephesus, in which the divinity and incarnation of the Word had been discussed. He professes that he honors the doctrine and judgments of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, of both Gregories, of Atticus, of Proclus, and of all the orthodox; and he asserts that he regards them as his saints and teachers.

Finally, he pronounces an anathema against Nestorius, Apollinarius, and all heretics down to Simon, as well as against those who say that the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ descended from heaven. For he himself who is the Word of God descended from the heavens without flesh, and so forth.

5. Our opponent nevertheless judged that he should engage in controversy with the distinguished Christian Lupus [Note: Quesnellus, vol. II of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 302]. Accordingly, in another edition of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, he composed an appendix bearing this title:

“Appendix to the dissertation on Eutyches’s petition of appeal, published by Christian Lupus from the Cassinese codex: whether it is truly a petition of appeal.”

He could not establish that this letter was a petition of appeal without appearing to sing a *palinode* [Col. 1139D]. Therefore, first he censures Christian Lupus for transcribing it into his study on appeals.

Then, insisting upon the arguments already given, he denies that it can be called a petition, believing that he is strongly supported both by the heading of the document itself and by the document’s author.

“For Eutyches himself,” he says, “clearly distinguishes between petitions and this letter of his. ‘I attached to this letter of mine both petitions: the one presented to the synod by my accuser, and the one carried by me but not received.’”

Thus, according to Quesnellus, the error—or negligence—of Christian Lupus seems to consist in calling Eutyches’s letter a petition, despite the heading of the document itself [Col. 1140A].

But what follows from that? Can the designation “petition” not apply to any letter, and especially to one of this kind? I shall refrain from recalling to Quesnellus’s mind the rules of grammatical writing, and therefore omit examples that could be cited from Cicero himself. I have nevertheless not hesitated to note a few of them [Note: Cicero: “I wrote that in a certain little book, which slipped out without my knowledge and against my will,” Letter 273. “Nor have I yet abandoned hope concerning Panco, as I have observed from his little books that fell into my hands.” *Against Verres*: “Read this little book to me, then that other one of Canullus.” In these passages Nizolius attests in the *Ciceronian Thesaurus* that Cicero called letters *libelli*].

Nevertheless, I cannot deny that, even though our heading contradicts it, all the characteristics and notions of a petition apply to this letter. It contains not the account of a single matter but a narrative in which several matters are gathered together. For that reason it can properly be called a little memorandum, and those who have learned the meaning of this word from Latin authors will judge that in no respect does it differ from a petition [Col. 1140B].

It is no objection that Eutyches attached other writings to this one and called them petitions. Those writings were not sent to absent persons but were presented only in a solemn gathering of bishops. Therefore it should not be thought that Eutyches gave them both the designation of letters and that of petitions.

The first observation of our opponent is weakened not only by the matters just reviewed but also disappears entirely through his own testimony. For he admits that Saint Leo used the name “petition,” though he does not call it an appeal, but a petition of distress and complaint.

“When he mentions a petition of appeal,” he adds, “he means the one that Eutyches admitted he had presented in court, as the formal requirements of appeals demanded,” as Saint Leo says.

But he falsely claims Saint Leo as a supporter. For although I do not deny that the holy pontiff, writing to Theodosius, said: “Although the aforesaid presbyter sent to the apostolic see, by a petition, a complaint of his distress” [Note: [Col. 1139D] Saint Leo the Great, Letter 21 to Theodosius, [Col. 1140D] ch. 1, and Letter 20 to Flavian, ch. 1, See chapter 4 of these Exercises. Again, in Letter 26 to Theodosius, the holy pontiff calls Eutyches’s letter a petition, writing: “Since, in the petition which he sent to us, he reserved at least this means of obtaining pardon for himself: that he promised he would correct whatever our judgment . . . disapproved.” Almost the same words are found in Eutyches’s own petition, the one presently under discussion. Quesnellus therefore unjustly attempts to cause difficulty for Christian Lupus], nowhere in Saint Leo’s works have we found the final words that Quesnellus uses: “in court, as the formal requirements of appeals demanded” [Col. 1140C].

He fabricated these words from his own judgment in order to lend strength to his conjectures. In the letter to Flavian, in which he discusses a petition of appeal presented in court, Saint Leo says only:

“So that in the very court he asserted that he had presented his petition of appeal, yet it had not been received.”

We are compelled to note these things because of what was said earlier. For the public rejection of the sentence pronounced against Eutyches, made while the fathers of the council were still sitting, could suffice for the formal appeal; this is clear from the passages of the deacon Rusticus and of Peter de Marca himself, whom we cited, especially since Eutyches solemnly confirmed that rejection through protestatory petitions.

### 6.

Nevertheless, Quesnellus maintains that Eutyches’s letter contains nothing resembling a canonical appeal. He appeals to the passages which Christianus Lupus cited in support of his own position, saying that Eutyches intended, by the words “But I invoke your holiness as a witness to my heart and to the reasons underlying my thoughts and words,” first [Col. 1140D] to compel the reader whom he was addressing “to judge what error is contained in this sincere profession of his faith” (so Quesnellus says); and perhaps, he adds, Eutyches alludes to the Apostle’s words, 2 Corinthians 1:23: “I call God to witness against my soul.” From this Quesnellus subsequently takes occasion to criticize the translation of this letter [Col. 1141A] as rough and poorly arranged; and for that reason he divided that narrative in another way, which he thought would favor his own arguments.

But what clearer and more explicit language could be desired in this letter from which to conclude that it presents a canonical appeal? That the Roman pontiff is the legitimate judge of controversies of this kind, and especially of those arising among the clergy and in the Church of Constantinople, has been demonstrated with the most distinguished and certain testimony, both by the Fathers of Chalcedon and by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople himself, and most clearly by Flavian himself.

The point is especially strong because Eutyches not only addressed the Roman pontiff at the beginning of his letter as though he were merely a witness, but also laid out the whole sequence of events that had taken place against him. He complains not merely of the injury inflicted upon him through hatred and circumvention, but professes that he submits himself to the judgment of the apostolic see and that he will follow in every respect whatever that see should approve. Nor does it [Col. 1141B] count against this that Eutyches wrote: “I was asking that these matters be made known to your holiness, and that you judge whatever might seem right to you.” Insisting on these words, Quesnellus says: “These are the words of one making a request, not of one appealing and demanding judgment as his right.”

Eutyches is there, however, describing the manner in which he had proceeded with the Fathers of Constantinople: he had acted so as either to escape the sentence of condemnation or, at least, to have judgment in his case suspended until, after the apostolic see had been consulted, it became known what that see judged concerning the matter. At that stage Eutyches used supplications rather than an appeal, lest he appear to be proceeding through arrogance and pride, because the Fathers were still sitting in council and examining his case, and no sentence had yet been pronounced against him. He had nevertheless alleged that Eusebius—the bishop of Dorylaeum—was an accuser hostile to him and suspected of proceeding against him through a faction and by calumny. This manner of proceeding implied that, if the Fathers wished to proceed contrary to this canonical protest, he would then appeal to another tribunal.

Quesnellus therefore perhaps maliciously and deceptively tries to confuse Eutyches’s supplications to the Fathers of Constantinople, made before the sentence was issued, with the appeal lodged after the sentence had been pronounced. His entire argument consequently collapses. Wishing to explain, in his own fashion, Eutyches’s words of request, he tried to associate them with other words spoken by Bishop Basil at Flavian’s second session, namely: “If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers should command me, I say this very thing”; but Basil said this “not as one appealing,” but rather by saying: “I did not dare to say this because of the Fathers.”

We have already observed in the preceding chapter 5 that this latter action of Eutyches must be referred to what the heretic said after the sentence had been pronounced. Who, then, could believe that it can be joined together with those words of one making a request?

### 7.

Lupus therefore does not try without reason to interpret the meaning and words of this letter as an appeal, even though in another part Eutyches addresses Leo, the supreme pontiff, in the plural number, writing: “To you, therefore, defenders of religion and those who execrate factions of this sort, I flee for refuge . . . . . and I beseech you, without allowing any prejudice to be created against me from what has been done against me through intrigue, to pronounce whatever sentence concerning the faith seems right to you.”

For in that passage he asks for two things in particular and in few words: first, protection against the factious calumniators who had laid traps for him; and then judgment, or a sentence, in the matter of faith. What else do all those who customarily lodge a canonical appeal usually request except protection to overthrow the snares of their calumniators, and a sentence concerning the matters that have been disputed?

It must also be added that Eutyches rejected the sentence canonically issued against him in the council and confirmed his rejection by public instruments of protest. But that these words present a true appeal is shown more clearly by what he immediately added after the passages cited [Col. 1142A], which Quesnellus entirely omitted to note: “and henceforth not to permit any calumny by the factious to proceed against me, nor that I be cast out and removed from the number of the orthodox,” and so forth.

Does he not intend that a full and complete judgment in his case be reserved for the person to whom he writes and to whom he appeals? 362 Quesnellus therefore seems to me to be playing an inept and foolish game when, addressing Lupus as though he were bleary-eyed, he says:

> “You see, my Lupus, what you do not wish to see: that Eutyches flees for refuge to the defenders of religion, not that he appeals to judges; that he begs that no prejudice be created against him from Flavian’s sentence, rather than declaring in the language of an appeal that the judgment is void; and finally, that he asks for a sentence to be pronounced concerning the faith rather than concerning his deposition and excommunication, although, if he had appealed, the latter should have been dealt with first.”

This is plainly a childish observation—as though requesting that no prejudice be brought against him by the sentence already issued were not the same as crying out and demanding that it be annulled; or as though one who requests not to be cast out and removed from the number of the orthodox were not also requesting that a sentence be pronounced [Col. 1142B] concerning his deposition and excommunication.

Quesnellus would have seen that Eutyches requested both sentences if he had not neglected to examine that entire passage. Consequently, there can be no doubt that the mockery directed at Lupus fits its author exceedingly well, especially since from the second Council of Constantinople we learn that the sentence pronounced against Eutyches was suspended, and that his offices, honor, privileges, and title as archimandrite were granted to him by virtue of Pope Leo’s letters, which had been read to the Fathers of the council.

[Note: [Col. 1141D] See what we wrote above in chapter 4 of these Exercises, where we cited the testimony of the deacon Eleusinus in support of Eutyches’s appeal to the apostolic see. [Col. 1142D]]

Paschasius Quesnellus now flattered himself that these arguments were sufficient to refute Christianus Lupus. Nevertheless, by way of an additional legal argument, he thought it necessary to add:

> “If this entire writing was sent to Pope Leo (he says), it was not sent to him alone, nor was it prepared for him alone; rather, it is an encyclical letter to all the principal bishops of the sees, whose authority Eutyches wished to arouse against Flavian’s judgment and to render favorable to himself [Col. 1142C]. For even when those who acted on his behalf at Ephesus falsely claimed that the heresiarch had appealed, they did not name the Roman pontiff alone.”

[Note: [Col. 1142D] Quesnellus, in the appendix to Dissertation 7, at the page cited above.]

This is an equally amusing and fictitious conjecture! To confirm it, he again brings forward the testimony of Constantine the monk and heretic, as well as that other testimony of Bishop Basil, both of which have already been discussed above.

But I shall demonstrate in what follows that Quesnellus is talking nonsense. In the first place, who will affirm that a letter can be called encyclical whose superscription bears the name of one single person? An encyclical is so called because it is addressed to several persons, as can be seen from hundreds of examples drawn from ecclesiastical history and from the monuments of antiquity collected by Labbeus. But the letter under discussion displays only the name of Pope Leo.

Even if, whether through the translator’s negligence and carelessness or through estrangement of mind and malice, we do not find in it those titles of honor that occur in the writings of others, we still cannot in any way affirm that a similar copy of this letter was sent either to Dioscorus of Alexandria [Col. 1142D] or to the other bishops of the principal sees. The Cassinese and Vatican manuscript codices have no other superscription than the one that the distinguished Christianus Lupus, relying on the authority of the manuscripts, assigned to it.

Moreover, if Eutyches had sent the same letter to other bishops, would Dioscorus—a factious man whose wicked deeds were known to everyone—have omitted to read it publicly at the robber synod, or have failed to produce it against Flavian and the legates of the apostolic see, with whom he was embroiled? Certainly, lest he appear unjustly and unlawfully to be overturning everything and usurping the rights of others, especially those of the Roman pontiff, he would have displayed this letter, or libellus, and at the same time ordered it to be transcribed by the notaries into the Acts of the synod.

That alone could have cleared him of all suspicion and made it evident to everyone that he deserved the leading role in that synod and was entitled to exercise the office of president for no other reason than that, when Eutyches appealed, he had appealed from the sentence and judgment of the Council of Constantinople to Dioscorus’s see [Col. 1143A].

[Note: [Col. 1143D] See what we shall say in the following chapter concerning Dioscorus of Alexandria. He presided over the robber synod of Ephesus by imperial command, not by virtue of Eutyches’s appeal to his see. Therefore, if Eutyches had appealed to the bishop of Alexandria, Dioscorus would have displayed Eutyches’s letter, or libellus, and ordered it to be read, just as it is established that he did with the imperial letters.]

This letter, then, ought not to be called encyclical, since it displays only the name of the Roman pontiff, and since there is no trace or mention in the monuments of antiquity that it was sent to the other bishops of the principal sees. It would be superfluous to refute the other conjectures fabricated by Quesnellus in support of this position, since they collapse by their own weakness. For, apart from the fact that he himself admits that Constantine the monk and Bishop Basil—who acted on behalf of Eutyches at Ephesus—were liars, there is no reason why we should continue to lend him our ears.

### 9.

Finally, what he adds—“that it is plainly an encyclical letter, as the whole letter itself loudly proclaims, in which there is not even a syllable concerning the apostolic see or the Roman pontiff, whose prerogatives and splendor he would not have failed to praise, since at that time he was most intent upon winning over the minds of all those whose support he needed. He therefore used only words appropriate to the bishops of all the principal sees. For to which of them do these words not apply: ‘I invoke your holiness . . . . . that these matters might be made known to your holiness . . . . . To you, therefore, defenders of religion and those who execrate factions of this sort, I flee for refuge’”—[Note: [Col. 1144D] Quesnellus, in the passage cited above.]

For this reason our opponent, flattering himself excessively, concluded his appendix with these words:

> “Certainly these final words alone—‘To you, defenders of religion,’ and so forth—make it as clear as the midday sun that this writing, whatever its character, was sent not to one person but to several.”

But in my judgment Quesnellus’s conjecture could derive no greater force from these words, with which he concludes his appendix. For although, as we have said, the titles of honor are lacking in the superscription, this may perhaps be attributed to the fault of the copyist. From the words themselves, however, we have elsewhere every indication that the person addressed was Leo, pope of the city of Rome—the one person alone who, according to the rights of ecclesiastical primacy, was responsible for judging matters of faith and the deposition of presbyters.

I concede, moreover, that there is no explicit mention of the apostolic see, and that Eutyches omitted to praise its splendor and prerogatives. But what follows from that? Was this writing, whatever it may be, therefore sent to several people? Away with such a fiction! In the first place, Eutyches was not accustomed, in composing his letters and libelli, to occupy himself with praising the splendor and prerogatives of those to whom he appealed. He merely set out the account of his own affairs and difficulties, without taking time to win over the minds of those whose assistance he needed.

If our opponent—who tried to overthrow and abolish the rights of the apostolic see by weak conjectures—had not considered it burdensome to examine two of Eutyches’s writings, both addressed to the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, he would undoubtedly not have been deceived by such excessive conjecture.

### 10.

In those letters, in fact, Eutyches did not praise the prerogatives of the emperors or their supreme dominion, nor did he strive to win their favor. He set out the case brought against him by Flavian in only a few words, adding:

> “I therefore beseech your Serenity, which customarily protects the orthodox faith and the repute of my lowliness, to command the most blessed bishops,” and so forth.

Finally, when closing his supplication, he used this brief formula, which contained no praise of prerogatives:

> “Having obtained this”—namely, an examination of the proceedings [Col. 1144A] conducted under Flavian—“I may, according to custom, give thanks to the Lord, to Christ the God of all, and to your perpetual piety.”

[Note: [Col. 1144D] This letter of Eutyches exists in Greek and Latin in volume IV of the Councils, p. 1035 in my copy. Another supplication of his is read in the Council of Chalcedon, in the same volume IV, p. 1091.]

He says something similar in another letter addressed to the same emperors, as can be seen in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Eutyches therefore did not employ such an exuberant style in writing that its luxuriance would be expended in praising the honors and prerogatives of those to whom he wrote, even though he needed their assistance and protection.

Will Quesnellus perhaps deny that he needed imperial protection and patronage? Finally, according to our opponent’s own account, Eutyches addressed the person to whom he was writing as a defender of the faith and an execrator of evil factions, humbly asking that the things done against him through intrigue be allowed to create no prejudice against him, and that he not be cast out and removed from the number of the orthodox.

Who else could ever have fulfilled all these requests by right and granted the supplicant’s wishes except the supreme pontiff, when the matter already concerned a case ordinarily concluded in a provincial synod and a sentence already issued [Col. 1144B]? The Acts of such a case could be weakened, rescinded, rejected, or confirmed only by one supreme judge.

If we desire some certain testimony on this matter, it will be useful to consult Saint Peter Chrysologus. When Eutyches had appealed to him by letter, asking him to act as defender of his case, Chrysologus replied to him without circumlocution or delay:

> “In all things, however, we exhort you, honorable brother, obediently to attend to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, since blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of faith to those who seek it. For, out of our concern for peace and faith, we cannot hear cases concerning the faith apart from the consent of the bishop of the city of Rome.”

[Note: [Col. 1144D] Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches the archimandrite.]

Let Quesnellus take note! It is blessed Peter alone, who lives and presides in his own see, who grants the truth of faith to those who seek it. No other bishop, by his own right, can hear cases concerning the faith apart from the consent of the Roman bishop.

Whether what we have written thus far in these three chapters concerning Eutyches’s appeal is solid or weak, only a reader who is led by no partisan zeal will be able to judge sincerely. As a final crowning point, we thought we should add this: in defending the legitimate rights of the apostolic see and vindicating the positions of Baronius and Christianus Lupus, we have not indulged our own conjectures. We wished only to set forth what can be drawn from the monuments of antiquity, on which we have always endeavored above all to rely.

### CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Ephesian synod convened on account of the heresy of Eutyches; Saint Leo’s action with the emperor in seeking the convocation of a council in Italy; and the defense of the holy pontiff’s conduct against Quesnellus’s suspicions and critical censures. Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, presided over the Ephesian synod, unjustly arrogating this right to himself by command of the emperor Theodosius. How and when the legates of the apostolic see departed from Rome; and how Paschasius Quesnellus, in discussing them, fell into error.

[Col. 1144D]

### 1.

I would not have been permitted to treat and explain the rights of the apostolic see concerning Eutyches’s appeal solely on the authority of the monuments of antiquity, unless I had also entered into various disputes with adversaries who interpret the structure and order of ecclesiastical government differently, applying all their force and zeal to distorting either the testimony of Saint Leo the Great or the writings of others that could have led us to a complete and sincere knowledge of all the facts.

Now, however, we must undertake something more weighty. Since we do not wish to break the thread of the historical narrative, we shall proceed to describe with the greatest fidelity the events relating to the second Council of Ephesus—events that gave the heresy of Eutyches its greatest increase, with the gravest ruin of the Catholic faith, the destruction of the Eastern Churches, the disgrace of priestly dignity, the grief and groans of Saint Pope Leo [Col. 1145A].

[Note: [Col. 1145D] See Baronius, under the year of Christ 449; Paschasius Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo; Severinus Binius, in his notes on the robber synod; Labbeus; and others throughout, who have described the proceedings of this synod more fully.]

Although very many outstanding men have devoted their efforts to composing this history, the fact that they were not all guided by the same spirit of truth has caused them to reason differently concerning the rights of the apostolic see. Some have even drawn from that synod—which was transformed into a robbery through the fury and violence of Dioscorus of Alexandria and the others—arguments for ever further magnifying the authority of emperors and restricting the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs within narrow limits.

I confess that my mind is oppressed by the greatest anguish [Col. 1145B] and sorrow on account of this mournful tragedy, which filled the Church herself and almost the entire world with treacheries, killings, degradation, exiles, insults, and afflictions. I recall how ancient rivalries can corrupt the hearts of priests and private hatreds rage, when the bonds of Christian religion have been broken and ambition alone, arrogance, and presumption seek in tyrannical fashion to seize every form of domination, by right or wrong, casting aside every restraint of piety.

When such evils grow in any commonwealth, they can be exceedingly difficult to remedy, especially when the authors of scandals and rivalries enjoy the patronage of great princes, and the ministers of those same princes foster them more and more. These ministers surround the pious and merciful governors of affairs by wicked arts and, following the excesses and impulses of their own will, fill their minds with preconceived opinions, until at last, deceived by false suggestions, the rulers decree [Col. 1145C] and establish what is contrary to divine and human law.

The Eastern Church was afflicted and almost entirely crushed by these grave calamities when Chrysaphius, abusing the clemency of the most merciful emperor Theodosius, undertook to defend the base, arrogant, and heretical man Eutyches and wished the case at issue to be entrusted not to the judgment of the Roman pontiff or the examination of a universal council, but to the discretion and power of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria.

Chrysaphius, driven by his implacable hatred of Flavian, had influenced Theodosius’s will when the Council of Constantinople had been concluded, so that, under the pretext of rendering due obedience to the Roman pontiff and providing protection for ecclesiastical affairs, the emperor would write very earnestly to Saint Leo concerning peace.

Whether, in that first letter, he requested that a general council be convened is not established. Indeed, one may readily adopt the view that at that time he maintained a profound silence about holding such a council. For although Theodosius’s letters may have been lost through the ravages of time, we do not find this imperial request indicated anywhere in Saint Leo’s surviving replies to him.

This is especially so because Saint Leo says that he hoped Theodosius, after the admonition sent by letter to Flavian, would report everything to his knowledge, so that, once the matters that still seemed hidden had been brought into the light, judgment might be given in accordance with evangelical and apostolic teaching.

It is therefore probable and certain that Theodosius wrote nothing to Leo about convening a new synod [Col. 1146A]. Otherwise, he would have spoken of a matter of such importance and would not have reserved for himself the task of judging after the matters then hidden from him had been brought to light.

### 2.

Nevertheless, I cannot deny that at that time, or shortly afterward, a rumor was spread at Constantinople that a similar council was to be convened, and that this proposal had been suggested to the emperor Theodosius by the counsel of Chrysaphius and other wicked ministers and through the machinations of Dioscorus.

For, as we have seen, Flavian, compelled to write again to Saint Leo because the latter had not received his earlier letter, asked that the council rumored to be taking place be removed [Col. 1146B].

[Note: [Col. 1145D] Saint Leo, Letter 21 to Theodosius, chapter 2 at the end. As we have seen, this letter was dated on the third day before the Kalends of March.]

Although this letter lacks a date belonging to the period in question, we may conjecture that in April a rumor was spread in the East concerning the celebration of a council. Yet I am convinced that Leo still had learned nothing of this imperial deliberation by the following June.

For, writing back to the same emperor on the eighth or ninth day before the Kalends of that month, as the Vatican codices read, he addresses him with apostolic vigor [Col. 1146B], confidently urging him to be concerned for the integrity of the Catholic faith. “And this,” he says, “I ask from divine mercy with unceasing prayers: that he inspire your heart with what is true and not allow you to be deceived in any matter by the fraud of human rivalries.”

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Flavian’s letter to Saint Leo, chapter 3.]

Saint Leo had therefore understood that Theodosius’s mind had already been alienated in some way from the truth by the fraud of human rivalries and had been ensnared by the suggestions of wicked men. To frustrate these schemes, he wisely decided to ask and urge the emperor to order that an episcopal council be held within Italy, by which all the scandals that had been stirred up to disturb the entire Church might be cut away.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Saint Leo, Letter 23 in Quesnellus, addressed to the emperor Theodosius and written on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.]

Here I am compelled to admit that some theologians of our own age who are hostile to the Roman curia insist on Leo’s words, “that you order an episcopal council to be held within Italy,” in order to conclude from them that the right to convene councils belongs not to the Roman pontiff but to the emperor.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Consult our edition of Eusebius, volume II, p. 2; Leo’s letter to Flavian in Quesnellus, Letter 22, dated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.]

But since Catholic teachers commonly refute arguments of this kind, and since we have said something about the matter in another work of ours, it is not the task of the present occasion to examine this controversy [Col. 1146C]. We therefore confirm the preceding historical account with another letter of Leo addressed to Flavian.

[Note: [Col. 1146D] Nevertheless, consult what we shall say in the following chapter concerning Leo’s letter addressed to the Ephesian synod.]

In that letter he informs the holy bishop that he has received his letter together with the synodal Acts drawn up against Eutyches. He promises his concern, being unwilling in any way either for Eutyches to persist in the perversity of his belief or for Flavian himself—who resisted the wicked and foolish error out of zeal for the faith—to be disturbed by the prolonged attack of the opposing party.

In this letter, however, he does not express a single word about holding a council either within Italy or at Ephesus. Perhaps he had not yet turned the matter over in his mind; in any case, only four days later, as we have seen, he indicated to the emperor Theodosius that a council should be held.

### 3.

In commenting on Leo’s letter to Theodosius cited above, Quesnellus nevertheless suspects that the holy pontiff had already learned of the emperor’s decision [Col. 1146D] to hold a council at Ephesus. He therefore decided to append the following note at the end of the letter:

> “On the eighth day before the Kalends of June, since in Letter 27 to Pulcheria Leo expressly testifies that he received on the third day before the Ides of May the letters announcing the synod convened by Theodosius, it is strange that he makes no mention of that synod in his letter to the emperor. Perhaps the pontiff thought it best to conceal the matter, so that he could more freely ask Theodosius to convene a synod within Italy; or it must be said that in one of the two letters the number of the day or the month is corrupt.”

[Note: [Col. 1147D] Quesnellus, volume I of the Works of Saint Leo, on Letter 23; Baronius, under the year 449.]

Baronius, too, encountering this difficulty, noted that the emperor had written to the Roman pontiff after the conclusion of the second Council of Constantinople, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, concerning a council to be held at Ephesus. Saint Leo received these letters, as he himself testifies in his letter to Pulcheria, on the third day before the Ides of May. Baronius then reflects that the letters must have traveled from Constantinople to Rome within the space of a single month.

Yet the learned Cardinal Baronius offers neither illumination nor any assistance in resolving the difficulty subsequently raised by Quesnellus. Since, in the meantime, we were pressed more or less strongly by both of Quesnellus’s lines of reasoning, we prefer to admit that the number of the month or day has entered one of the letters in corrupt form rather than accuse or suspect Saint Leo of dissimulation.

Certainly, we must believe that he practiced no dissimulation with Bishop Flavian. But the letter written to him on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June contains, as we have seen, not a single word about letters received from Theodosius announcing the Ephesian council. Indeed, if the entire letter is carefully examined once and again, it becomes clear that the Roman pontiff had not even dreamed that the emperor would decide to convene such a council.

For in that letter he speaks as the supreme arbiter of all those controversies: he declares that Eutyches’s faith has been injured and that his doctrine deviates from tradition; he promises Flavian appropriate instruction, so that he may learn what ought to be decided concerning the whole case; and finally he declares that he will by no means tolerate Eutyches’s obstinacy or allow the holy bishop to be harassed by such great and serious disturbances.

If, therefore, Leo had already received from Theodosius, on the third day before the Ides of the preceding May, letters announcing the Ephesian council, none of these statements could cohere. Leo himself would not merely have been practicing dissimulation but would have been using lies by which Flavian, deceived, was awaiting the protection of the Roman pontiff—protection that Leo promised him in those letters.

[Col. 1147C]

### 4.

It remains, then, that an error entered one of the two letters, and that in the letter written to Pulcheria [Note: [Col. 1147D] Leo’s Letter 27 to Pulcheria, chapter 4.] we should read “the Ides of June” in place of “the Ides of May.”

The following words lend strength to this conjecture:

> “A greater part of the remaining time must be consumed so that the departure of the priests who are sufficient for the matter may be arranged.”

For Leo’s complaint would seem weak if almost three full months still had to elapse from the day on which he received the letters announcing the Ephesian synod, given that the council was not to begin until either the Kalends of August or the Ides of that month. Who will affirm that the remaining part of those three months would not have been sufficient for bishops to depart from Italy for Ephesus? Especially since, with the aid of ships, navigation is ordinarily calm in those months, and the entire journey can be completed within a month, as Baronius noted above.

### 5.

This consular date nevertheless does not entirely satisfy us, even if we say that perhaps “the third day before the Ides of June” should be read. For if we attend to the other letters of the holy pontiff, whether those addressed to Julian, bishop of Cos, or those directed to Theodosius and Flavian, we clearly understand that the legates of the apostolic see who were to attend the announced synod had already been designated by the Ides of that same month.

Although Leo mentions the council explicitly only in his letter to Theodosius, writing, “Since, nevertheless, your piety, which most religiously loves the Catholic truth in honor of God, has established at Ephesus a synodal tribunal” [Col. 1148A], it is difficult for me to believe that three days alone could have sufficed for Leo to dispatch from Rome three apostolic legates together with Dulcitius, the notary.

[Note: [Col. 1147D] Consult Leo’s Letters 24 to Flavian, 25 to Julian, bishop of Cos, and 26 to Theodosius. This last letter was brought to light in a more accurate form by the readings of the Vatican codices.]

Nevertheless, since the surviving monuments do not dispel all the doubts that may be raised on either side, we should not linger longer over their resolution if the sequence of events did not provide us with one further argument showing that Saint Leo could not have received Theodosius’s letters announcing the Ephesian council on the third day before the Ides of May.

Whatever may be said, then, about any error that could have entered the date of the day or month, one thing is absolutely certain: Saint Leo neither dissembled nor lied in the letters he addressed both to Flavian and to Theodosius. We believe that this is clearly established by the following calculation of the chronology.

### 6.

First, we assume that Saint Pope Leo, having been informed by the emperor about the disturbed affairs of the Church of Constantinople, sent his first letters both to Flavian and to Theodosius on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, which was the sixteenth of February.

We likewise assume that Flavian received the letters addressed to him on the twenty-fifth of April, when the second Council of Constantinople was being held. At that council, at the request of Eutyches and by order of the emperor, the Acts of the preceding council were examined and read again, under the presidency of Bishop Thalassius and the patrician Florentius.

[Note: [Col. 1148D] The Acts of the second Council of Constantinople, under the year 449, as they were reread at Chalcedon, contain the following: “In the consulship of Flavian and Protogenes, most illustrious men, and when [the matter] had been announced, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople, under sacred command, with Martial, the most magnificent count, conducting the inquiry,” and so forth. Volume IV of the Councils.]

Everyone knows that the Ides of May fell on the fifteenth day of that month. Therefore the third day before the Ides had to fall on the twelfth. Since no more than twenty-two days intervened between the twenty-fifth day of April and the twelfth day of May, it follows that Leo could not have received the letters announcing the Ephesian council from Theodosius on the third day before the Ides of May.

This is especially true because it is hardly likely that on that same twenty-fifth day of April—when Flavian’s proceedings against Eutyches were examined and read again under the presidency of Thalassius and the patrician Florentius—the emperor had already decided that a council at Ephesus should be held. First, he had to be informed of what had occurred; then sufficient time had to be granted for the machinations and counsels of Chrysaphius, Dioscorus, and the other scoundrels, as well as for the imperial decrees to be prepared.

If, then, we were to believe that all these things were completed with extraordinary speed, within two or three days, and that the prince, having been led astray, decided that the council should be held at Ephesus, what would follow? Could the letters announcing the Ephesian council have reached Leo on the twelfth day of May? This is fictitious. 369 Letters could not have been carried from Constantinople within a period of fifteen or eighteen days, as will be clear from the subsequent narrative.

Quesnellus therefore reasoned falsely when he suspected that Saint Leo had concealed the letters announcing the council under the pretext of seeking the convocation of a council within Italy.

### 7.

Let us now proceed to the imperial order by which Theodosius decreed that a general council should be convened at Ephesus. From this narrative it will become increasingly clear that what we have explained above is correct.

“After,” writes the deacon Liberatus, “nothing was proved to the notaries concerning the falsity of the proceedings, Eutyches asked Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, to investigate what had been done concerning him and to examine the case. He pleaded before the emperor that a universal synod be held, so that Flavian’s judgment might be tested. Dioscorus therefore wrote to the emperor Theodosius that another general synod ought to be held, and Eutyches persuaded him that it should be held. The emperor agreed and sent a sacred letter to Dioscorus in Alexandria.”

[Note: [Col. 1149D] The deacon Liberatus, in his *Breviarium*, chapter 12.]

If we attend to the exchange of several letters that took place among Eutyches and Dioscorus, and between Dioscorus and the emperor—a correspondence that did not begin until after the twenty-fifth of April—we must believe that the letters announcing the general Council of Ephesus were delayed until at least the final day of that month, unless we wish to affirm that they were signed only on the third day before the Ides of June, as Leo himself may perhaps have indicated when addressing Pulcheria.

In that case, through the ravages of time and the carelessness of copyists, a lacuna would have entered the text, which up to now we have not been able to restore with the assistance of the several manuscript codices.

### 8.

This conjecture gains still greater force from the words of Nicephorus. In reviewing the devices employed by Chrysaphius to circumvent the imperial mind, he describes that wicked scheming in these words:

> When they had established by their authority that those Acts and decrees were legitimate, the eunuch Chrysaphius, who shared Eutyches’ views, being unable to bear the insult, greatly increased his anger against Flavian; and he informed Dioscorus of Alexandria, that impious man, that he would gratify him in everything he desired if he defended Eutyches when he was in danger, but attacked Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum.

[Note: Nicephorus, Book XIV.]

Finally, that the chronological indication contains an error, and that Leo did not conceal the fact when he requested that a council be held within Italy, is clearly demonstrated by Theodosius’ letters serving as notices of the Council of Ephesus, whether those addressed to Dioscorus or those sent to Barsumas and the other Easterners. The emperor signed the first, addressed to Dioscorus, on the third day before the Kalends of May; the second on the Ides of May; and the third, which was sent to Barsumas, we find was written on the day before the Ides of May. It is therefore not probable that Saint Leo, residing at Rome, could have received from Constantinople the emperor’s letters announcing the Council of Ephesus on the third day before the Ides of May, if the emperor had only then scarcely begun deliberating about holding a council and on the day before those Ides had been wholly occupied with summoning to the synod the leading supporters of the Eutychian faction. It would therefore rather have to be inferred that Saint Leo received Theodosius’ letters announcing the council during the month of June—or indeed when that month was nearly over—although they had been signed on the thirteenth day before the Ides of May. This, Quesnellus insists, is what those words in the letter to Pulcheria were intended to signify.

### 9.

Chrysaphius finally achieved what he desired. For, according to Liberatus, the emperor ordered, in the sacred letter which he sent to Dioscorus, that Dioscorus himself should choose ten metropolitan bishops, whomever he wished, and should come to Ephesus; and that, once the council had been assembled, he should examine Eutyches’ case. He also ordered that Barsumas, that ruined archimandrite, should be present and act on behalf of all the monks who were accusing the Eastern bishops. But he forbade Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, to attend the council, and ordered him to remain in his own city.

For Eutyches had already, through that son of his, Chrysaphius—whom I have mentioned—banished Ibas, bishop of Edessa, into many places of exile, so that he might not attend the synod.

What this deacon Liberatus relates corresponds extremely well to what is found in the imperial rescript concerning the convocation of the Council of Ephesus, as may be seen in Baronius and in the collection of councils.

[Note: Baronius, under the year 449, and Volume IV of the Councils.]

Baronius rightly observed, however, that the chronological indication of this imperial letter had been corrupted, and that instead of “the third day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the illustrious men Zeno and Postumianus,” it should be restored to “the third day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.” We ought to note this in confirmation of what we described above.

[Col. 1150A]

Chrysaphius and Eutyches, however, did not believe that all these measures would suffice to crush the most holy men Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, together with the other men distinguished for learning and character, unless Dioscorus had been appointed by imperial mandate as the arbiter of everything that was to be done. Therefore they extorted letters from the emperor ordering that Dioscorus, as the head of all the factionaries, should preside over the council. By this means the emperor arrogated and usurped for himself a right which none of the emperors had previously dared to exercise.

To induce Theodosius to assume this right, however, his wicked ministers had impelled him under the guise of piety, so that Theodoret might not attend the council. “He presumed,” says the emperor, “to put forward propositions contrary to what the saint of blessed memory Cyril wrote concerning the faith . . . . For this reason,” he adds, “we have judged it necessary to make clear by this sacred letter addressed to Your Reverence, to Your Blessedness, and to the entire holy synod, that we, following the rules of the Fathers, grant Your Blessedness authority and primacy, not only on account of Theodoret, but on account of all the others who belong to the assembled holy synod.”

[Note: A copy of this letter is found in Baronius, under the year mentioned above, and in Volume IV of the Councils. See, however, what we shall say below, in the following chapter, on the authority of the distinguished Christian Lupus.]

Entangled in these sacrileges through his arrogation of ecclesiastical rights, Theodosius supplied protection and authority so that the Eutychians might practice all their evil deeds, deceptions, and shameful machinations with impunity. Under the pretext of Nestorian heresy, Theodoret was expelled from that assembly; Ibas was compelled to live in exile; and, conversely, those who were most devoted to Eutyches were ordered to attend and preside over the synod.

What more is there to say? To bring about the still more grievous destruction of the Catholics, Theodosius, deceived by the plotters, gave Dioscorus new letters in which he praised Barsumas as a man thoroughly approved in the faith and adorned with purity of life, and ordered him to occupy the place of all the Eastern archimandrites. On the same day, namely, on the Ides of May, he finally wrote to that same Barsumas, adorning his letter with exceptional praise of Barsumas’ labors in overthrowing the Nestorians and their heresy, and judging it just that, in the synod to be held at Ephesus, as we have said, he should occupy the place of all the Eastern archimandrites.

Thus, when matters had been arranged, the Eutychians reflected among themselves that the synod could in no way be called ecumenical if the supreme head of the Church had not been summoned to it and the Roman Pontiff did not exercise influence over it. Since, moreover, they had learned from the preceding letters that Saint Leo had condemned Eutyches and would condemn him with a more solemn judgment if he attended a general synod, they moved the emperor to give late notice of the forthcoming council. They were guided by the belief that the shortness of the time would prevent him from attending the assembly either personally or through his legates.

Since neither ecclesiastical custom, derived from the canons, nor the troubled times, because of the disasters impending through the devastation of the Huns, nor finally his love for his homeland and fellow citizens permitted him to abandon the apostolic see and leave Rome—as though he were depriving it of its father and shepherd—in order to depart for Ephesus, he judged it appropriate to excuse himself to the emperor Theodosius and to Pulcheria in these words:

> For although His Piety—that is, the emperor—believed that I too should attend the council, even if some precedent were required, this could nevertheless in no way now be fulfilled, because the condition of present affairs is too uncertain to allow me to be absent from the people of so great a city; and the agitated populace would be driven into a kind of despair if I seemed, under the pretext of an ecclesiastical case, to wish to abandon my country and the apostolic see.

[Note: Consult Saint Leo the Pontiff, Letter 26 to Theodosius, in which he censures and rebukes Eutyches as an ignorant man who held an erroneous view of the Catholic faith; he makes this clear from the sequence of the synodal Acts, by which Eutyches was exposed as ignorantly and imprudently in error. More clearly still, in Letter 24, he states: “The judgment already passed shall remain, if the impiety that has rightly been condemned persists in its perversity.” Let Quesnellus, I ask, take note of this and say whether it agrees with his preceding statements.]

[Col. 1151A]

Because the affairs of the Church in the East were especially close to the heart of the holy pontiff, and because he judged that he must look to the safety of the citizens and the welfare of the apostolic see, he did not fail to perform his part, so that the matters to be handled at the summoned Council of Ephesus might proceed according to divine and ecclesiastical law. Therefore, addressing Pulcheria, he immediately added:

> Since, then, you recognize that this belonged to the public welfare, and that—subject to your Clemency’s pardon—I could not refuse my charity and the prayers of my fellow citizens, consider me also present in these brothers of mine whom I have sent in my place, together with the others who will be present. To them I have shown clearly and fully, in accordance with the case—which is sufficiently evident to me from the sequence of the Acts and from the profession of the person under examination—what must be observed.

[Note: Saint Leo the Great, Letter 26 to Theodosius, and Letter 27 to Pulcheria, chapter 4. I do not know whether Quesnellus truly followed the authority of Griman’s manuscript in preparing the works of Saint Leo the Great, as he himself always testified. For we have discovered that this manuscript reads: “Since, then, you recognize that this belonged to the public welfare . . . my charity and the prayers,” whereas Quesnellus deletes the word “this” and introduces “me” into the text in place of “my.”]

### 10.

From this manner of proceeding the holy pontiff flattered himself that everything in that synod would be brought to a successful conclusion through his legates, provided that he first instructed them by a necessary memorandum concerning all matters to be handled and decided, making clear and fully explaining what had to be observed.

He also mentions the dispatch of these legates and their necessary instructions for everything that had to be done in the letter to the emperor, written on the same day. In that letter, likewise, he set out briefly and more precisely those three reasons, or motives, which prevented him from attending the Council of Ephesus personally. Nevertheless, he informs the emperor that from the sequence of the Acts he had learned sufficiently and beyond doubt that Eutyches had erred ignorantly and imprudently, and that he ought to abandon the opinion which he rightly rejected.

Therefore, since the emperor himself had determined that a synodal judgment should be held at Ephesus, so that the ignorant old man might come to know the truth about which he was so greatly blind, Leo wrote:

> I have sent my brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and my son Hilarus the deacon, who, according to the nature of the case, can adequately represent my presence.

He nevertheless closes this letter by indicating that he had sent Bishop Flavian letters from which it plainly appears, beyond doubt, what the Catholic Church universally believes and teaches concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Col. 1151C]

He wished to imply that neither Eutyches nor anyone else was permitted to withdraw, without the manifest charge of heresy and contumacy, from what the Chair of Saint Peter—the pillar and foundation of the true faith—proposed as binding.

### 11.

Meanwhile, the legates of the apostolic see, instructed concerning everything that had already occurred in the affair of Eutyches and having received from the supreme pontiff a written memorandum concerning each matter to be dealt with at the Council of Ephesus, promptly committed themselves to the journey.

[Col. 1151D]

It was necessary to outmaneuver all the schemes of the Eutychians. Under the pretext of the evils spreading in the East because of the new heresy, they had induced the emperor to set an extremely short period within which the bishops were to assemble at Ephesus. The legates therefore had to begin their journey with the greatest speed, in order to frustrate the wishes of Dioscorus and the others, who desired that a general council be held without the Roman pontiff, who would preside over it either directly in person or through his legates.

For this reason we cannot at all agree with Quesnellus. In his dissertation on the Life and Deeds of the Great Leo, and in his notes to Letter 32, relying on a corrupt reading borrowed from the manuscript of Grimani, he maintains that the legates of the apostolic see had not yet departed from Rome on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, although they were going to the Council of Ephesus.

The letter under discussion was written by Saint Leo to Flavian. In it he says:

> Although it is evident that the matter at issue in no way requires synodal discussion, nevertheless, dearest brother, I inform you that those whom it pleased us to send for this matter have followed.

### 12.

Quesnellus therefore expunged the word “have followed” and introduced another reading, “will follow,” into the text, following the reading of the Grimani manuscript. In the margin he added this note:

> But it is certain from this letter and from Letter 34 that the legates had not yet departed.

In fact, however, we can infer from many considerations—and especially from the preceding letter addressed to Julian, bishop of Cos—that the legates had already departed from Rome on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July and that an error had entered the Grimani manuscript. In that letter, speaking of the aforesaid legates, Leo says: “whom I have sent from my side, in my place.”

This letter was signed by the holy pontiff on the Ides of June, which was the thirteenth day of that month. If, therefore, the holy pontiff had sent his legates at that time, there is no reason why we should wish, or be able, to conjecture—disregarding the authority of all the other manuscripts and earlier editors—that they had not yet departed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, or why we should insist that this must be inferred from a single word plainly bearing and indicating the error of a copyist, when all the manuscript and printed copies offer “have followed,” not “will follow.”

Moreover, if they had delayed beginning their journey for so long, and the council was to begin on the Kalends of August, scarcely enough time would have remained for them to reach Ephesus by the appointed day. Consequently, the zeal which Saint Leo had shown in frustrating the evil schemes of the Eutychians would have been less prudent, since by such a long and considerable delay he would have exposed himself to the danger that, with the support of those who favored the Eutychian cause, the council might begin and be brought to its conclusion without awaiting the legates of the apostolic see.

Nor can that Letter 34, to which Quesnellus appeals, establish anything in his favor. He begins it with these words:

> Our men, whom we sent to you on behalf of the faith, having already departed.

That letter was signed by the same supreme pontiff on the tenth day before the Kalends of August. Nothing, I say, in this letter supports Quesnellus. For it does not specify when the pontifical legates departed from Rome; and those words can readily be reconciled with the preceding letter, in which Leo indicated that the pontifical legates had followed.

What prevents Saint Leo from having informed Flavian a second and even a third time of the legates’ departure?
