The exchange of letters was not so easy, nor so swift and secure, that he could confidently persuade himself that his letters would be carried from the city of Rome to Constantinople with the greatest speed, without any intervening obstacle delaying the course of the letters or their bearers.

Quesnellus himself readily grants this in his dissertation on the Life and Deeds of the Great Leo, asserting that the holy pontiff’s mind sometimes wavered as to whether the letters he had sent to the emperor and to the other Easterners would be faithfully delivered.

But, not to depart from the manner of proceeding that Saint Leo himself observed with Flavian, it will be useful to note here that in several letters, written at different times, he informed Flavian that he had received the synodal Acts drawn up at Constantinople against Eutyches.

[Note: “I have received the letters of Your Charity together with the Acts composed among you concerning the question of the faith.” Letter 32: “Having read the letters of Your Charity . . . and having reviewed the sequence of the episcopal Acts.”]

This is attested in Letter 32, which was written on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. Again, in Letter 24, he testifies that he had received these synodal Acts on the preceding Ides of June. Finally, in Letter 22, written on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, he admits that Flavian’s letters had already reached his hands, informing him about the case which, as he grieved, had been stirred up among them by an evil error.

For he could not have confessed that he had been more fully instructed concerning this new error, which had recently arisen, unless he had received the synodal Acts together with the letters. The zeal of the holy pontiff therefore deserves the highest praise: in matters of the greatest seriousness, he repeatedly made explicit mention of the same affair, so that if the bearers of his letters were detained by illness or were impeded by some unforeseen circumstance and forced to interrupt their journey, those to whom he had written might at least be informed, through successive letters, bearers, and messengers, of the matters then being handled through the exchange of correspondence.

If anything occurs in this chapter that has not been explained with sufficient care, it will become increasingly clear from what follows.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the various letters written by Saint Leo the Great on the occasion of the Council of Ephesus. The holy pontiff’s efforts to abolish the scandals of the Easterners and strengthen the Catholic faith. The opinion of Christian Lupus is set forth and illustrated; Dioscorus of Alexandria, however, abusing imperial power and inflicting force and oppression upon the Catholic bishops, absolves Eutyches and, turning the synod into a den of robbers, compels the legates of the apostolic see to seek protection and flee.

[Col. 1153B]

### 1.

After the legates of the apostolic see, together with the notary Dulcitius, had departed from the city of Rome, Saint Leo omitted nothing that he had considered capable of bringing the causes of the faith to a successful conclusion. At the same time, through priestly concord and peace, he sought to cut off all those scandals which, because of private rivalries and ancient hatreds, were spreading through almost the whole of the East.

Accordingly, by that supreme authority which Saint Peter had received from Christ the Lord for strengthening his brethren in the faith, Leo wished, through successive letters, to teach what all were to believe and profess concerning the Lord’s Incarnation, and what was to be established for abolishing the wicked errors that had recently arisen under the pretext of overthrowing the Nestorian heresy. If no Catholic had departed from the principles of those letters, the Catholic faith would certainly not have suffered the grave disaster about which we are now going to speak.

Therefore, on the Ides of June of that same year, he gave several letters to his legates to be carried to the East. Among them the principal place belongs to the dogmatic letter written to Saint Flavian. It was established in the Catholic Church that this letter should be held, with the complete agreement of the holy Fathers, the decrees of the councils, and the decisions of the Roman pontiffs, as the sincere rule of our faith in matters concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Attending to this letter, the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon formed the judgment that it in no respect differed from the revelation made to Saint Peter when he confessed the divinity of Christ the Lord, on account of which he was pronounced blessed. Those Fathers received it with the greatest veneration, since it agreed with that great Peter’s confession and stood as a kind of common pillar against those who held perverse opinions.

[Note: The Council of Chalcedon, action 4. Pope Gelasius, at the Roman council, concerning apocryphal writings.]

Pope Saint Gelasius also judged that it ought to be valued so highly that, when treating of apocryphal writings at the Roman council, he issued this decree:

> We approve the letter of the blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone should mark it for deletion even to a single jot, and should not receive it in every respect with veneration, let him be anathema.

### 2.

The extraordinary veneration that it obtained in the Church is also demonstrated by the custom recorded by Cardinal Baronius. He states that the Roman clergy were accustomed to read it during Advent in the divine offices. That this practice may have been observed immediately after Gelasius’ decree is indicated by the books of sacred readings used for the choir. Among these we examined with our own eyes one particularly ancient volume preserved in the Vatican Library.

The heading placed at the end of the second part of this book of readings reveals that it was written in the sixth century of the Church by the presbyter Agimundus, in Roman and uncial characters, and divided into two parts. It not only gives the name of the scribe but also indicates that the church of the Twelve Holy Apostles in the city of Rome was accustomed to use this book in celebrating the divine offices.

Reading through it in its entirety, we found nearly all the sermons and homilies of our holy pontiff, distributed according to the order of days and feasts. The writers of the Vatican Library most graciously persuaded us to append and present at the end of this work one complete specimen of that arrangement. In this way readers could gather—against certain more recent critics—that the institution of some solemnities is extremely ancient, and that the rite handed down by our ancestors and the shepherds of souls has been preserved inviolate in the Church down to our own times.

Just as this book of sacred readings will demonstrate that the ancient tradition of ecclesiastical discipline in the celebration of feasts and the performance of divine praises has by no means been changed, so heterodox writers will readily be able to argue that sacred tradition has been preserved with the greatest religious care and has remained inviolate and uncorrupted in matters pertaining to the dogmas of the faith and the administration of the sacraments. It is neither appropriate nor necessary to speak about those matters at present.

### 3.

But now, leaving this Vatican codex, let us return to the celebrated letter. In composing it, Leo the Great set himself the goal of providing protection and firmness for the faith, which was wavering and in danger in the hearts of many Easterners because of the new teaching of one ignorant old man; of condemning wicked errors; and of proposing and defining for the entire Catholic community what must be believed perpetually and inviolably.

There is no need here to review the teaching with which this letter is filled, or even to explain its individual chapters into which it is divided. We scarcely think that any theologian could be unaware of it.

We judged that only one point needed to be noted, a matter which we touched upon to some extent above: namely, that Saint Leo, without a council of the Westerners or the vote of any other bishop, condemned Eutyches’ absurd and perverse profession and rebuked with fitting severity the judges at Constantinople, who at the synod had failed to reproach an utterly foolish and blasphemous statement. They acted as though they had heard nothing offensive, although it was said with extreme impiety that the only-begotten Son of God had existed with two natures before the Incarnation, while it was asserted with equal wickedness that, after the Word had become flesh, there was in him a single nature.

[Note: Letter 24 to Flavian, chapter 6. See chapters 2 and 3 of these Exercises.]

Nevertheless, Leo commands that mercy be shown to Eutyches, provided that the following conditions are observed: that he not refuse to subscribe to this letter and that he condemn aloud the wicked doctrines he had absorbed. Finally, he asserts that he entrusted the execution of the entire matter to his legates, who were to exercise and uphold the authority of the pontiff at the council, trusting that divine assistance would be forthcoming so that the man who had erred might be saved once the perversity of his opinion had been condemned.

[Note: See Letter 29 to the Council of Ephesus.]

If anyone gives even brief attention to this manner of proceeding by the supreme pontiff, I do not know whether he could reasonably doubt that Saint Leo exercised full and absolute power and jurisdiction, whether in condemning the Eutychian heresy, in composing the rules of faith, or finally in determining the formulas and conditions under which alone Eutyches was to be received into repentance and satisfaction—if he were to renounce and reject the false doctrine which he had defended so obstinately.

This manner of proceeding is therefore very different from the one Quesnellus invents. He maintains that the affairs of the Easterners were brought not before one supreme Roman pontiff but before all the bishops and synods of the principal sees, and that those condemned by provincial or metropolitan bishops always appealed to their judgment.

Let all who tell such stories say, I ask, by whose conciliar authority this dogmatic letter to Flavian came to light, or who those bishops of the West were who cast their vote in condemning this heresy or prescribing the rule of faith. It is entirely certain that Saint Leo alone performed and had to perform all these things.

Using the fullness of the authority of his see, he indicated, defined, and prescribed what belonged to the rights of the apostolate. He then entrusted the execution of everything to his legates, whom he had ordered to act in his place at the future synod. The decrees already issued did not thereby acquire their force and validity from the votes of other bishops; they received only a more solemn promulgation. Thus those in the East whose faith was being tested, or who were under suspicion, were approved by subscribing to these letters; and whenever they refused to subscribe, they were deprived of every clerical honor and rank and expelled from the Catholic community.

### 4.

Indeed, what else do those other letters indicate which the holy pontiff gave his legates to carry to the East? A subsequent letter addressed to Julian, bishop of Cos, is consistent with this. Julian was well instructed concerning what had occurred at the two preceding councils of Constantinople, which we understand from the sequence of the Acts that he had attended. He had already sent his writings to Saint Leo through the deacon Basil. Leo says that they had pleased him greatly because of their Catholic fervor, and adds:

> We have also appended this page, which agrees with those letters.

[Note: Letter 25 of Saint Leo, chapter 1 and following.]

There can be no doubt that he is referring here to the preceding letter addressed to Bishop Flavian, since Saint Leo expressly acknowledges this at the beginning of the present letter:

> Although through our men, whom we sent from Rome on behalf of the faith, we have sent our brother Flavian the fullest letters against the error of excessive impiety . . . .

What he wished to add at that time to the aforesaid letter addressed to Flavian, so that they might resist unanimously and steadfastly those who desired to corrupt Christ’s Gospel, is clearly shown by the text that follows. In it he demonstrates that Eutyches was corrupting Christian hope and the truth of all the mysteries; that the properties of both natures remained in Christ; that Christ’s soul did not pre-exist his body, nor was his body created from nothing; and that both were of the same nature as ours.

But finally, he says, Julian had been prompted to expand his discussion by the breadth of the subject itself. Julian need not, however, labor further at speaking at length, especially since Leo had sent Flavian sufficient letters through his legates to strengthen not only the minds of priests but also those of laypeople.

Two other subsequent letters, signed on the same day, are certainly consistent with these: one addressed to Theodosius Augustus and the other likewise to Augusta Pulcheria. The same is true of the letter he sent to Faustus and Martin, archimandrites of Constantinople.

In that letter he most explicitly acknowledges that he chiefly regarded the Acts of the Council of Constantinople as authoritative. From reading them, he had learned that the Eutychian dogma had rightly been rejected; and, he adds, “we too decree that it must be detested.” He further says:

> So that, if the foolish man wishes to remain in his perversity, he may have fellowship with those whose error he has followed. For rightly he will be outside the Church of Christ who denies that Christ possesses a human nature—that is, our nature.

[Note: Letter of Saint Leo to the Council of Ephesus, chapter 2.]

[Col. 1156A]

### 5.

But let us now speak of the letter written to the Council of Ephesus. From it the holy pontiff’s efforts and manner of proceeding become better known: he sought to abolish the scandals, rivalries, and private hatreds of the Easterners and to establish the Catholic faith in everyone’s heart.

As we read through this letter, we understood that Saint Leo was entirely unaware of all the devices employed by Eutyches, Chrysaphius, and Dioscorus to pervert the pious mind of Theodosius, so that he could not even faintly suspect that the rights of the apostolic see were to be destroyed and brought to ruin at the Council of Ephesus.

Indeed, on carefully examining the text of this letter, we were rightly compelled to conjecture that the emperor Theodosius, by adhering to the divine institutions, wished—as was proper—to interpose and employ the authority of the apostolic see for convening that council. In this way, through the Roman pontiff, the successor of Saint Peter, whatever all Catholics were to hold in that controversy concerning the faith would be declared.

These considerations provided Leo with grounds for believing that the emperor had initially possessed such a disposition that he considered it wholly impious to use the protection of the council’s Fathers to violate those rights of the apostolic see which had already been confirmed and approved in previous general councils, first by divine and then by human authority.

So that I may not seem to be telling tales, I shall immediately set out the words with which the holy pontiff began his letter to the Council of Ephesus:

> The religious faith of the most merciful prince, knowing that it belongs especially to his glory if no seed of error should arise within the Catholic Church, paid this reverence to the divine institutions: it employed the authority of the apostolic see for the accomplishment of the holy disposition, as though he desired that it be declared by the most blessed Peter what had been praised in his confession.

If, therefore, Saint Leo, addressing the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus, explains why, on what occasion, and under what title the emperor employed the authority of the apostolic see, I do not see how certain writers could have asserted so confidently that the council was summoned and convened solely by the emperor’s authority.

He requested that the authority of the apostolic see be employed so that the divine institutions might be obeyed and so that the new seed of error might be uprooted completely. Moreover, if the emperor desired that the apostolic see, as though speaking through Saint Peter, should declare what had been praised by Christ the Lord in Peter’s confession, it is scarcely credible that in mind and deed he was then so opposed and hostile to the rights of the Roman pontiffs that he sought to abolish them.

We therefore firmly maintain that all the injury suffered by the apostolic see at that time must be attributed not to the emperor but to his ministers, who abused the prince’s clemency and, above all, his weakness of mind.

If we had to set out other arguments for this point, one alone would abundantly suffice in place of all the rest: the argument we gather from Theodosius’ earlier letter to Saint Leo, in which he sincerely reported all the scandals and disturbances that had arisen in the Church of Constantinople because of Eutyches’ heresy and implored Leo to apply a remedy to them.

[Note: See chapters 2 and 3 of these Exercises.]

[Col. 1156D] **6.** He made this quite clear in the present letter to the Ephesian synod 377, writing:

“But since the treatment even of such persons must not be neglected, and since the most Christian emperor wished an episcopal council to be held, so that every error might be abolished by fuller judgment, [we have sent] our brothers Julius, etc. . . . . . . and, in agreement with you, let them determine what will please the Lord.”

Here, then, the reason for holding the synod is explained with complete sufficiency. It was necessary to remedy the evils from which Eutyches suffered—for, as the same Saint Leo says, he contradicted Christ’s Gospel, demonstrating that he had never shown any zeal for learning the truth. The emperor had demanded this. Therefore, following first the dictate of the divine institutions, he employed the authority of the apostolic see for the accomplishment of this holy disposition [Col. 1157A]; he requested that an episcopal council be held [Note: [Col. 1157D] The reader himself will judge how all this coheres with what we said above in chapters 4, 5, and 6.], believing that in this way he could also safeguard and promote Eutyches’ reputation.

Since, on account of his old age and his office as archimandrite of a large and distinguished monastery, he appeared deserving of honor, as Leo himself more clearly indicated in his letter to Julian of Cos [Note: [Col. 1157D] Consult Letter 31 to Julian of Cos, in which, discussing Eutyches’ opinion before the emperor Theodosius, he writes in chapter 2: “And because the most merciful emperor, in accordance with the benevolence and piety of his disposition, wished a more careful judgment to be made concerning the condition of this man, who had previously appeared honorable, for this reason he believed that an episcopal council ought to be convened.” See also Letter 41 to Pulcheria, written after the Ephesian synod.], the emperor therefore neither despised nor rejected the authority of the apostolic see, if he wished to employ it for the holding of a synod.

There was absolutely no reason to suggest that the Roman pontiff could or should resist this desire. The principal matter at issue was the uprooting of so great and pernicious a growth of weeds, which was overturning the sacred and ecclesiastical order and administration of affairs, to the destruction of the Catholic faith. Accordingly, to silence the uproar of such great disturbances and to settle the dissensions already aroused—which on one side originated in the remnants of the Nestorians and on the other were being generated by a new error that was daily taking root and growing—it seemed fitting, indeed almost necessary, that a fuller judgment should be obtained.

[Col. 1157B] In reality, however, the matter of faith had already been sufficiently treated in the Constantinopolitan synod by Flavian, and afterward examined, approved, and confirmed by that most holy pontiff, Leo. Quesnellus must admit this, whether he wishes to or not. Nowhere did he make the distinction that was necessary between a canonical judgment and a more solemn judgment—a distinction that Saint Leo himself indicated in several places.

He indicated it especially in this very letter and in those that followed, in which he not only discussed the need for a fuller judgment or more diligent examination, but also spoke of the sentence canonically pronounced against Eutyches and approved and confirmed by the apostolic see. He further indicates that a statement had already been received from Eutyches, in which he professed, in his own words and by his subscription, that he would condemn his own opinion, promising that in all things he would follow our judgment, as the same holy Leo says.

**7.** We find similar statements in two letters likewise dated on the Ides of June, one of which [Col. 1157C] he sent to Pulcheria Augusta and the other to Julian of Cos. When Paschasius Quesnellus noticed this, he asked why Leo had sent two letters on the same day, one to Julian and the other to the Augusta Pulcheria, when a single letter to each would have sufficed—especially since neither the reason nor the subject of the new letters is apparent.

Quesnellus attempted to resolve the question by proposing various conjectures. We do not hesitate to transcribe them for the reader, so that perhaps he may infer what we ourselves have not yet fully grasped:

“Let me therefore affirm nothing certain: whether it was prompted by the arrival of a messenger who preceded the legates, or by fear that the legates might be prevented from approaching the Augusta—which certainly happened, as is sufficiently clear from Letter 41. For the other letter to Pulcheria briefly contains 378 what was written through the legates, and what we learn from the shorter letter, sent again to Flavian on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, concerning the legates’ having been detained for some time at Rome: “Since,” he says, “he must be more fully instructed by the writings which they themselves will carry.” [Col. 1157D] And again: ‘I announce that those whom it seemed appropriate to appoint for this matter will follow.’”

I frankly admit that Quesnellus’ earlier conjectures are by no means to be dismissed. The explanation he gives—that the legates were hindered from presenting themselves before the Augusta Pulcheria—may also be accepted, as appears from the whole of the aforementioned Letter 41, in which he vigorously complains that the letters he had sent to her concerning the matter of the faith through his own clerics had not reached her.

There he further makes clear, through the words of the clerics, that he intended to inform her of the legates’ mission to the Ephesian synod. He adds below:

“But since those who were sent were unable to reach your gentleness, so that scarcely one of them, our deacon Hilary, escaped and returned to us, we thought that the written communications should be repeated” [Col. 1158A].

That he wrote this letter after the Ephesian synod is evident from its entire context, about which we shall speak at a more suitable point, and also from its date. For it was dated on the third day before the Ides of October of that same year.

However the matter may have occurred—whether Leo had received a messenger who preceded the legates’ journey, or whether he feared that the legates would be prevented from approaching the Augusta—we do not know. One fact, nevertheless, is certain: Saint Leo made every effort and sought every means by which the scandals of the Eastern churches might be abolished and the Catholic faith, which had been injured there and was almost in peril, might be strengthened.

We have already rejected, in the preceding chapter, another conjecture of Quesnellus: namely, that the legates were still being detained at Rome on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. We therefore pass over it.

**8.** In the meantime, after the legates of the apostolic see had already departed, Saint Leo did not discontinue his correspondence with Saint Flavian. When he had received another letter from him through Basil the deacon, he replied on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 1158B]. In his letter he exhorted him to fight vigorously against the enemies of Christ’s birth and cross, without allowing himself to be frightened by the power and intrigues of his adversaries.

To urge this firmness of spirit upon him, he used the words of the Apostle Paul:

“In nothing be terrified by your adversaries, which is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation.”

It is permissible to infer, however, that the machinations of Dioscorus, Chrysaphius, and the other Eutychians had somehow become known to the holy pontiff. Basil, the bearer of Flavian’s letter, had recently departed from Constantinople, and the words of the Holy Father indicate that he had related much to Leo that was not contained in Flavian’s letter:

“And the aforesaid man’s conversation was suitable for a familiar inquiry; through him, now returning an exchange of greetings, we exhort your affection, by the grace of our God in whom we trust, using the apostolic words, etc.”

Nevertheless, wishing to treat the madness of the ignorant amid the conflict of such great disturbances, he instructed Flavian to apply the remedy of patience. “To treat,” he says, “the madness of the ignorant, we also wish you to apply the remedy of patience,” so that, if the Eutychians who had grown numerous should have renounced their accursed error, episcopal benevolence would not deny them mercy:

“The judgment that preceded will remain, if impiety, rightly condemned, persists in its depravity.”

Quesnellus should pay close attention to these words.

But that Saint Leo had been informed by Basil, through those familiar inquiries, about the most serious machinations that were being devised and prepared for the destruction of the faith and of Catholics is made plainly evident by another letter, dated on the third day before the Ides of August. He writes to the same Flavian, whose silence, he makes clear, was increasing the pontiff’s anxiety:

“Since, as sharers in your cares and solicitous for the defense of the faith, we have frequently sent letters to your affection on suitable occasions,” wishing to assist him with the consolations of pontifical exhortations so that he would not be moved by the goads of his adversaries, he finally exhorts him “to reply with all speed,” as he says, “to our letters, and thereafter to make us more fully informed about your actions, and those of our [Col. 1158D] legates, and about the resolution of the whole matter, so that we may lessen the anxiety which we now bear for the defense of the faith through more favorable reports” 379.

Those words show how greatly the pontiff’s spirit was then oppressed and tormented.

**9.** But what followed? He was compelled to endure even greater hardships, because the Eutychians, with Dioscorus and Chrysaphius acting recklessly, dared to mock and nullify his efforts. That Ephesian synod, convened on the Kalends of August, had a most unhappy beginning on the sixth day before the Ides of the same month, when Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria [Col. 1159A], disregarding all ecclesiastical regulations, claimed primacy for himself in it. As we have seen, he obtained for this purpose from the secular power—namely, from the emperor Theodosius—letters by which authority and primacy were granted to him.

The distinguished Christian Lupus, however, commenting on the conduct both of Dioscorus and of the emperor Theodosius, endeavors to excuse Theodosius and to interpret his letters favorably. He supposes that Theodosius had by no means intended to violate or infringe the rights of the Roman pontiff, but that Dioscorus had appointed himself president of the synod through a violent seizure of power, not through imperial delegation [Note: [Col. 1159D] Christian Lupus, *On the Ephesian Canons, Illustrated with Scholia and Notes*, chapter 5.].

He therefore advanced certain arguments not unworthy of consideration, writing:

“Far be it from us to suppose that Theodosius Augustus allowed himself to be led by the eunuch into excluding the Roman bishop from the presidency. For appended to his sacred letters to Dioscorus is the following subscription: ‘It has been written in the same terms to Juvenal, the most reverend bishop of Jerusalem.’ And Dioscorus himself said in the Council of Chalcedon to the most illustrious judges: ‘Your Clemency knows that our most holy emperor entrusted the judgment not to me alone, but also to the most blessed Juvenal and to the most holy bishop Thalassius.’”

The same Christian Lupus, wishing on the one hand to clear the emperor Theodosius of this charge and on the other to defend the rights of the apostolic see, relates how Dioscorus, attempting to usurp the presidency of the synod by force of the imperial rescript, was opposed by Julius, bishop of Puteoli [Note: [Col. 1159D] Christian Lupus incorrectly confuses Julius, bishop of Puteoli, with Julian, bishop of Cos, having been misled by the reading of the ancient editors. See what we shall say below.], one of Saint Leo’s legates. Florentius, bishop of Lydia, interpreted his words:

“‘It has been written in the same terms by the most pious and most Christian persons: our most holy pope, placed at the head of the Roman Church, has been summoned.’”

And Hilary the deacon, another of the legates sent from the side of Saint Leo, openly protested in that pseudo-synod:

“‘The most glorious and most Christian emperors, cherishing love and affection for the Catholic faith, sent venerable letters to our most blessed bishop Leo, the prelate of the apostolic see, asking him to attend this venerable and holy council.’”

From this formula of speech, the same most learned annotator concludes [Col. 1159C] that the emperor’s letters to the Roman pontiff did not contain strict commands but requests. Leo, however, wished to call them commands out of a certain reverence, in order to indicate the high regard in which he held them.

Furthermore, the following words prove that Hilary insisted that the task entrusted to him and to the other legates should not be abandoned to the dishonor and contempt of the apostolic see:

“‘The pope sent us, not doubting that he is present in us, whom he especially knows to perform everything pertaining to the sincerity of the Catholic faith and to the reverence due to the holy Apostle Peter’” [Note: [Col. 1159D] These words of the deacon Hilary accord with those that occur frequently in Leo’s letters written concerning the Ephesian synod, as may be seen in the letters to Theodosius and Pulcheria.].

**10.** The notes of Lupus seem finally to acquire greater force from what Lucentius, bishop of Ascoli, charged against Dioscorus at the Council of Chalcedon. Accusing him of a serious crime, he said:

“He must give an account of his judgment who, although he did not possess the status of a judge, presumed and dared to hold a synod”—that is, to preside over a general synod—“which, without the authority of the apostolic see, was never lawful and was never done” 380 [Col. 1159D].

These, then, are the observations that the same Christian Lupus made with a laudable display of extraordinary learning, intending to show that Theodosius could easily be cleared of the charge of schism with which, after Baronius, many—and almost all—writers have thought he might be branded on account of the violation of the rights of the apostolic see.

Nevertheless, several matters may cause difficulty for Christian Lupus and weaken his opinion. First, as regards the imperial rescript in which Dioscorus is said to have been appointed president of the synod, it is difficult to interpret it otherwise than its wording indicates. It says:

“For this reason we have deemed it necessary to use these sacred letters addressed to your Reverence, by which we make known to your Blessedness and to the entire holy synod that, following the regulations of the Fathers, we grant to your Blessedness authority and primacy, not only on account of Theodoretus but also on account of all the others who belong to the holy synod that has been assembled.”

These words, together with the whole preceding causal clause, plainly constitute and introduce an overt schism against the Roman see. Rusticus the deacon, an ancient interpreter of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, understood them in this way also. He indicated this in the following annotation, which he added to the final words:

“Openly against the Roman see.”

**11.** Nor do we think that anything can be made of the fact that in the same imperial rescript we encounter the names of Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, and Thalassius, metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia, so that we might infer that the emperor had also attributed primacy to them by virtue of that rescript. The emperor merely indicated there that he was persuaded that these two bishops would be united in mind and action with Dioscorus. But concerning the authority and power of presiding conferred upon them, he maintains a profound silence.

Let us therefore transcribe the words that follow:

“Knowing more fully that the most reverend archbishop Juvenal of Jerusalem, and the most blessed archbishop Thalassius, and every such ardent lover and champion of the orthodox faith, will be in agreement with your Holiness, radiant through the grace of God with the beauty of life and the Catholic faith.”

It is therefore evident that no authority was granted to the archbishops Juvenal and Thalassius. Otherwise anyone who had held a place in that synod and who had joined himself by consent to Dioscorus’ efforts and party could have assumed the authority of president and assigned it to him on account of the words, “and every such ardent lover . . . will be in agreement with your Holiness”—something that Christian Lupus neither does nor could do.

The remaining difficulty is whether Theodosius wrote in the same terms either to Juvenal or to Saint Leo the pope. The subscription cited by Lupus for Juvenal is uncertain. Labbeus thought that one should read “At the same time” [Note: [Col. 1160D] Consult the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of the General Councils, p. 883.], although Stephanus Baluzius judged that the earlier reading should be retained, as it appears in manuscripts written by hand. He adds:

“The Romans restored the reading: ‘It has also been written to Juvenal in the same terms,’ etc. The Royal Edition has: ‘It has also been written at the same time.’”

Baluzius therefore concludes:

“Everyone can see that the printer made an error, and I do not see why Labbeus retained it.”

In this variety among manuscript codices and printed editions, I do not see what certainty we can derive. For that reason, I do not think one should insist firmly upon this annotation, especially since it is unknown by whom or on whose authority it was added to the Acts of the councils.

Moreover, even if the reading adopted by Christian Lupus is genuine [Note: [Col. 1160D] See what we have said more fully in this chapter concerning Saint Leo’s letter to the Ephesian synod.], and no one were to call it into question, what would follow? Can those words—“It has also been written to Juvenal in the same terms”—not be explained without any violent interpretation as meaning that a letter was written to Juvenal so that he might adhere to Dioscorus with unanimous agreement?

In that case, the letter addressed to Juvenal of Jerusalem would correspond perfectly to Theodosius’ imperial rescripts sent to Dioscorus. In those rescripts, mention is made only of the fact that Juvenal and Thalassius would be in agreement in that synod with Dioscorus’ Holiness, radiant through the grace of God with the beauty of life and the Catholic faith. No consideration is given to the authority and primacy that Dioscorus alone had extorted with the greatest injustice.

The words that Dioscorus, attempting to clear himself of the crimes committed in the Ephesian synod, boldly addressed to the Fathers of Chalcedon may instead provide greater support for Lupus [Col. 1161A]:

“Your Clemency knows that our most sacred emperor entrusted the judgment not to me alone, but also gave the authority of the synod to the most blessed Juvenal and the most holy Thalassius. We therefore judged what has been judged. The entire synod agreed with us. Why, then, are these charges directed against me alone, when authority was given equally to three, and, as I have said, the entire synod agreed with what we judged?”

**12.** These final words—which Lupus omitted from his annotation—if they had not been spoken deceitfully and for the purpose of acquiring accomplices in his crimes, would provide an argument that Dioscorus had not arrogantly assumed from the emperor’s imperial rescript the authority to preside over the synod as its primate, but that this authority had been given equally to Juvenal and Thalassius.

Yet what would this imply in favor of our case? If that imperial rescript contains no mention whatsoever of Leo, the supreme pontiff, to whom, in view of all the rights and the custom of earlier councils, it belonged to preside over the synod [Col. 1161B]? I therefore do not see how Theodosius can be completely cleared of the charge that, deceived by his ministers, he willingly lent his hands to the violation of the rights of the apostolic see.

The difficulty now returns: whether Theodosius wrote to Saint Leo in the same terms. Two considerations do indeed present themselves that seem to support Lupus’ opinion. The first is what we discussed and clarified earlier in this chapter, when treating Saint Leo’s letter to the Ephesian synod. The other is the testimony of Julius of Puteoli [Note: [Col. 1161D] The distinguished Christian Lupus, following the printed editions, thought that one should read not Julius but Julian, and, following the opinion of the eminent Cardinal Baronius, persuaded himself that this was Julian, bishop of Cos. But this is false, as all the letters of Saint Leo the Great in which he speaks of his legates demonstrate most clearly. Stephanus Baluzius also noted this; with restrained criticism, he censures Labbeus for not following in his edition the reading of the ancient manuscript codices—namely, those of Paris and Dijon—which have Julius, not Julian. He further adds: “This faulty reading so misled the eminent Cardinal Baronius that, believing Julian, bishop of Cos, to be named here, he was surprised that a Greek should have spoken among Greeks through an interpreter at the synod, and he relates this to the distinction of the Roman Church.”] brought forward by Lupus himself.

As for the first point, only very serious conjectures are available. For so far the learned have not discovered Theodosius’ letters to Leo concerning the convocation of the Ephesian synod, so that we can establish with certainty that they had the same wording as the imperial rescripts sent to Dioscorus.

Only one thing is certain: Saint Leo never suspected that the prerogative of primacy and the right to preside over the synod could be assigned to him through the overbearing conduct of others [Col. 1161C]. Otherwise Theodosius would never have invoked the authority of the apostolic see, nor exposed his legates to so many labors and dangers, nor perhaps given factional men room and occasion, fully aware that circumstances cannot always be relied upon.

Such and so great was the strength possessed by the holy pontiff through his virtue that he could never be overcome by any secular power—especially when the rights and prerogatives of the apostolic see were at issue. He allowed no one even lightly to injure them, as we could demonstrate with six hundred examples drawn from his life.

Certainly, the words of Julius, bishop of Puteoli, would accomplish much. They would have authority and weight for clearing and removing the charge of schism with which the emperor Theodosius has been branded by very many writers. But the wording of Theodosius’ letters remains unknown.

Therefore those who search for a knot in a rush and who either seek to convict the emperor 382 of injured ecclesiastical jurisdiction, or endeavor to reform and utterly overthrow the authority of the Roman pontiffs in convening and holding councils, if no clearer arguments were available, would reply:

“The words ‘in the same terms’ apply only to the convocation of the council, so that Saint Leo was summoned by the emperor on equal terms with Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Thalassius. They do not at all refer to the primacy and presidency of the synod, a prerogative that was entrusted exclusively to Dioscorus, as both the aforementioned imperial rescript and the sequence of the synodal proceedings make clear.”

If this were said to me, I would nevertheless not think that Christian Lupus’ opinion should be cast aside. For it would acquire greater strength and force from the protest of the deacon Hilary, likewise a legate of the apostolic see, if that most learned man had brought it forward in its entirety, as we have deemed necessary to do. Those learned men who are attached to no party will judge the matter.

**13.** Hilary, then, a Roman deacon, with Florentius, bishop of Lydia, interpreting him, said:

“The most glorious and most Christian emperors, cherishing love and affection for the Catholic faith, sent venerable letters to the most blessed bishop Leo, the prelate of the apostolic see, asking him to attend this venerable and holy council. It might have pleased His Piety if some conformity had been maintained in this matter. For your Holiness can know better that neither at the holy Council of Nicaea, nor at the Ephesian synod, nor at any other such holy council was the pope of the most holy perpetual see present” [Note: [Col. 1162D] Volume IV of Labbe’s collection of the General Councils, p. 895.].

Hilary perhaps alludes here to what the holy pontiff wrote to the emperor Theodosius and to the Augusta Pulcheria, recounting the reasons that prevented him from traveling outside Italy to hold the council.

Hilary then added:

“For this reason, following the custom of this form, he sent us. That most holy man, not doubting that he is present here in you, whom he especially knows to perform everything pertaining to the sincerity of the Catholic faith and to the reverence due to the holy Apostle Peter, has also sent through us letters appropriate to the council of the holy Fathers. Command that they be received and read.”

This most weighty address of Hilary, and his entirely just request, grounded in the rights of the apostolic see, ought neither to have been disregarded nor rejected by Dioscorus. Hilary had testified that the holy pontiff was present at the council through his legates, and had requested that the Fathers acknowledge this [Col. 1162C] and that Leo’s dogmatic letter be received and read.

Then Dioscorus, having cast off all restraint, set himself up as the ambitious judge of everything that was to be done. Inflated by the protection of the imperial ministers and the support of an armed cohort, he boldly ordered:

“Let the writings sent to this holy and universal synod by our most holy brother and fellow bishop Leo be received.”

But he prevented them from being read aloud. In place of these letters, other imperial letters were produced, which John the presbyter and chief of the notaries held in his hands; these had been read and inserted among the records of the faith at the command of Juvenal.

These circumstances, to speak frankly, suggest that Dioscorus established himself as president of the synod by a violent seizure of power, as Christian Lupus indicated. I do not know, however, whether they entirely exclude an imperial delegation.

Rusticus, the ancient interpreter of the Acts of Chalcedon, nevertheless appears to support Lupus. Commenting on this conduct of Dioscorus, he wrote in the margin:

“The treachery of Dioscorus: the pope’s letter was to be received by the synod but not reread” [Col. 1162D].

In fairness, both to explain more fully the opinion of Christian Lupus and to resolve or illuminate certain obscure and intricate questions raised by Lupus on the occasion of his opinion, we have had to write these things at the appropriate point. We have nevertheless departed in no way from the supreme zeal of the holy pontiff Leo, who employed every stronger means [Col. 1163A] so that, in the synod he had convened, everything might be conducted according to the highest standards of justice.

383 **14.** After Dioscorus had obtained complete control of the synod, what hope of anything good remained for Leo and for the universal Catholic Church? What protection remained for Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, when they saw Elpidius present at the synod with armed troops, at the emperor’s command, having already received authority to throw into chains anyone who opposed the president’s will?

I admit that this authority was granted to Elpidius against the disturbers of peace. But how could Flavian, Eusebius, and the others who were rightly contending courageously for the Catholic faith and for the rights of the apostolic see be peaceful and even-tempered with those who, under the appearance of respectability, wished to destroy the faith of the Incarnation and oppress the defenders of Catholic doctrine?

“Bishops,” Quesnellus observes, “who had previously condemned Eutyches are forbidden to give their judgment; indeed, they are ordered to await judgment concerning their own judgment against Eutyches. Moreover, letters were sent by the Augustus to the proconsul of the province, to the magistrates, and to the army commanders, so that they might execute the decrees of the council. Finally, he addresses the synod itself, calling Flavian a turbulent man who was plotting innovations in religion, but addressing Eutyches honorably as a good man and a defender of the truth” [Note: [Col. 1163D] Quesnellus, *Dissertation on the Life and Deeds of Saint Leo*, p. 149. Baronius, under the year 449.].

These are Quesnellus’ account of the synod’s beginnings. In describing them he departs little from Baronius and others, who, using a more ordered method, describe this tragic history. We intend, however, to report it only in outline, lest we seem to repeat what others have already done.

Among the other injuries that Flavian was first compelled to suffer was this: although Domnus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Stephen of Ephesus, and others were attending that synod, Flavian was not permitted to sit after the bishop of Antioch, but was placed after Juvenal.

When one hundred and thirty bishops had assembled in the basilica of Mary the Mother of God, Dioscorus ordered the emperor’s letters addressed to himself to be read [Col. 1163C]. The legates of the apostolic see—namely, Julius, bishop of Puteoli; Renatus, presbyter of the title of Saint Clement; and Hilary, deacon—informed the synod of their legation and likewise produced the letters that Saint Leo the Great had sent both to the synod and to Flavian.

These letters were indeed received, as we saw shortly before, but they were not read. And although the pontifical legates repeatedly insisted that they be read—and although Dioscorus had promised this under oath [Note: [Col. 1163D] Council of Chalcedon, action 3.]—he preferred to become guilty of perjury, to violate the rights of the apostolic Church, and to arouse scandal throughout the whole world rather than permit them to be recited.

### 15

Instead of these letters, therefore, he preferred that the emperor’s letter should be read. When the petition was heard requesting that the matter of faith be considered, Dioscorus rejected it, saying that the emperor had decreed that the controversies which had arisen at Constantinople between Flavian and Eutyches should be examined. The notaries who were recording the Acts, acting on the mandate of that same bishop of Alexandria, added that the bishops had acquiesced in Dioscorus and had acclaimed that nothing concerning the faith should be undertaken or changed.

But this foul falsehood was exposed at the Council of Chalcedon, in its first session. Indeed, it was added that Dioscorus’s notaries had attacked the notaries of Stephen, bishop of Ephesus; that what had just been written was erased; that great violence had been used to snatch away their writing cases; and that the fingers of those who resisted had nearly been broken by the same men.

Thus, in order to carry out what Dioscorus had planned, Eutyches was ordered, at the suggestion of the count Elpidius and with the bishops’ approval, to enter and plead his case, so that he might announce what he believed concerning the faith. Using his customary cunning, he addressed the synod’s Fathers suavely, as though they were witnesses to his faith, first commending himself to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He acknowledged that he had a profession of faith in his hands, which he presented to the holy synod.

In it he asserted that from childhood he had resolved to live in silence and to spend his life into extreme old age far from every disturbance; but afterward, he maintained, he had been surrounded by the gravest dangers from those who plotted against him, because he had refused, in accordance with the definition of your former Council assembled at Ephesus, to hold any opinion beyond the faith expounded at Nicaea by the holy Fathers.

As a testimony to his sincere faith, Eutyches appended the Nicene Creed. Pretending to allude to it, he afterward said:

> Thus, having received this faith from my ancestors from the beginning, I believed; in this faith I was born, and immediately consecrated to God, and His mercy received me; and in this faith I was baptized and sealed, so that I have lived in it and desire to die in it.

He also acknowledged that he accepted what had been established by the Council of Ephesus according to the teaching of Saint Cyril, finally adding an anathema against Manichaeus, Valentinus, Apollinarius, and Nestorius, and against all heretics down to Simon Magus, as well as against those who say that the flesh of the Lord and of our God Jesus Christ descended from heaven.

[Note: The most eminent Cardinal Baronius transcribed this profession of faith by Eutyches in full in volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year 449, p. 91.]

After this he related how Eusebius of Dorylaeum, wishing to drive him from his peaceful situation, had brought a charge against him as a heretic in the synod of Constantinople under Flavian, without inserting any appearance of heresy in his written accusations. He therefore added that, at the command of the bishop of Constantinople, he had been compelled to answer the accusation.

That bishop—namely, Flavian—was, however, in many respects on intimate terms with the accuser and almost inseparable from him, thinking that I would remain in the monastery, as I usually did. He said that he had been informed of this by the eminent *Silentiarius*, whom the emperor had delegated to him, lest he expose himself to the danger of the threatened sentence of death; and that the *Silentiarius* had replied that my presence was henceforth superfluous, since, even before the investigation, I had been condemned through a conspiracy arising from private hatreds and rivalries.

[Note: Consult the same Baronius under the year 449, volume VI, p. 92, and the collectors of the councils, volume IX.]

He next related that he had come to court to answer the charge, presenting a confession of faith entirely consonant with the teaching of the Nicene Fathers, afterward confirmed by the Council of Ephesus—a confession which the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople under Flavian neither deigned to accept nor permitted to be read.

But when a disturbance arose among the secretaries and many shouts followed, by which his mind was troubled—as it was also by the judges’ statements, which he claimed to have preserved in writing—he was still being required to add something further to the decrees of Nicaea and Ephesus.

> But I, fearing to violate the definition promulgated by the holy synod gathered here by God’s will, and the decrees established by the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, asked that it be made known to your holy council, so that I might acquiesce in whatever you approved, prepared to remain in it.

We believe that the matter of the general council to which he appealed has already been demonstrated in the preceding chapters. Nor shall we linger over the rejection of this falsehood.

Yet he made this falsehood still more serious by the calumny that followed, saying that the conspiracy against him had been brought to completion because, suddenly, a sentence written long beforehand, as it seemed to him, was read out against him as a condemnation. He added that his profession of faith had afterward been altered in the series of official records; that the most reverend bishop Flavian had not said a word about his appeal to your Holiness; and that he had not been ashamed of my gray hairs, grown old in battles against heretics and in the confession of piety.

Here Eutyches especially exaggerates the merits with which he thought himself distinguished by fighting against the Nestorians, so that little by little he might obtain the judges’ favor and compassion.

But he constructed an even worse calumny against Flavian by fabricating that the holy bishop had arrogated to himself alone the right to judge matters of faith, reserving nothing of so important a judgment for your Holiness. After disclosing the wording of the sentence which the same Flavian had issued against him, and which, he said, he had caused to be read in various oratories and memorial chapels of the saints after his appeal, he continued:

> He anathematized me, and those who came to me and conversed with me, making them strangers to holy communion, without awaiting the judgment of your Holiness.

Finally, after such a long series and heap of other falsehoods, he addressed the Fathers of the Council of Ephesus in these words:

> I therefore now ask your Holiness: consider the calumny fabricated against me, the factions, and the disturbance caused throughout the holy Churches by this affair, and the scandal arising from it among many [lacuna]. For from the beginning I sought the judgment of your Blessedness, and again I call it to witness before Jesus Christ.

### 16

“Who,” writes the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, “when reading these words and not knowing that it is Eutyches who speaks, would not think that one of the holiest Fathers and chief defenders of the orthodox faith was speaking? Or who, knowing that these things are spoken by Eutyches, and knowing neither what preceded nor what followed, would not immediately associate him with the standard-bearers of the Catholic faith—Athanasius, Gregory, Basil, and Chrysostom?”

Reader, I pray, reflect on how deeply Flavian’s spirit must have been shaken when he heard himself charged as a calumniator and conspirator against another’s innocence, and when, in a full synod, he was paraded by a lying heretic as a disturber of ecclesiastical peace.

Flavian himself believed that he could remedy these sorrows of spirit; but he discovered that they became more bitter when, after Eutyches’s written profession had been read, he requested that the accuser be given an opportunity to appear and that Eusebius of Dorylaeum be ordered to enter. He was not heard, however, but rejected, and Eusebius was forbidden to be admitted into the assembly of bishops.

This new crime was later brought against Dioscorus at the Council of Chalcedon. Dioscorus shifted the disgrace of the act onto the count Elpidius, and Elpidius shifted it onto the emperor, who had given the order. They claimed that Eusebius and Flavian should be regarded neither as accusers nor as avengers of what had previously been done in the synod of Constantinople, but only as defendants, to be judged without any opportunity for defense.

Dioscorus then immediately suggested that the Acts of the Council of Constantinople against Eutyches should be read. Although Julius, the legate of the Apostolic See, opposed this and protested that he would not permit those Acts to be read unless Saint Leo’s dogmatic letter were read first—as the deacon Hilary likewise declared—the petition of the pontifical legates was rejected. Eutyches boldly came forward and maliciously proclaimed them hostile and suspect to him because they had remained with Flavian and had dined with him.

The Acts of Constantinople were therefore read. When the writings of Saint Cyril were reached, Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, suggested that, according to Cyril’s judgment, one should not speak of two natures in Christ after the incarnation, but only of one, according to Athanasius’s judgment.

The Eutychians acclaimed that the case had been won. For Bishop Eustathius did not grasp the intention of those two Fathers, who sometimes use *φύσις* (*physis*, “nature”) indiscriminately for hypostasis and person—a practice that was especially common among Greek writers before the Antiochene schism, as we have taught and demonstrated in our *Scholastic Exercises*.

Meanwhile, the other bishops, whether driven by fear of threats or corrupted by promises, did not dare openly to profess and explain the faith of the Catholic Church. But when they reached that final portion of the Acts in which Eusebius of Dorylaeum had challenged Eutyches to confess that, after the union of the Word with the flesh, two distinct natures remained in Christ, the patrons and supporters of Eutyches cried out more boldly:

> “Remove him! Burn Eusebius! Let him be burned alive! Let him be cut in two; as he divided, so let him be divided.”

### 17

Dioscorus sought to give some semblance of canonical judgment to this bandit-like method of judging. He therefore asked the synod:

> “Is this statement tolerable to you: to say that there are two natures after the union?”

The synod replied:

> “Anathema to anyone who says so.”

Baronius asserts that these words were spoken by those who were flattering Dioscorus. That most learned historian of the *Annals* derives the foundations of his account from the testimony of those Fathers who attended this synod and later reopened the entire matter at the Council of Chalcedon.

He appeals especially to Basil, bishop of Seleucia, who, through Bishop John, had asked Dioscorus to amend his statement and added:

> “For you then imposed a great necessity upon us, both from those who were outside and from your own tongue. Soldiers were rushing into the church with weapons; monks who were with Barsumas and those called Parabolani were pressing upon us, together with another great multitude.”

[Note: Baronius explains *Parabolani* as follows: “These were incorporated members of the Alexandrian Church.”]

The violence and fear tyrannically inflicted upon the Fathers by Dioscorus at that time, which we are describing, were attested at the Council of Chalcedon by the others who had attended the Council of Ephesus.

Only the legates of the Apostolic See could not be moved by fear or violence either to obey Dioscorus’s will or even slightly to depart from the instructions and written directives they had received from the holy pontiff Leo. They objected, cried out, and, as Baronius says, publicly declared that those Acts had absolutely no force, since they had been extorted solely by violence and tyranny; and that no prejudice could be inflicted upon the Catholic faith, whose formula had been sent from the See of Peter to the synod, but which the wicked Dioscorus had not allowed to be read.

Saint Leo later complained at length about the injury done especially to the authority of the Apostolic See in his letter to the emperor Theodosius.

[Note: Letter 39 to Theodosius.]

The bishops themselves, too, were compelled to suffer violence from every side. For, they say:

> “If we professed that there were two natures in Christ the Lord after the union, we were proclaimed Nestorians who ought to be killed. Condemnation was threatened against us; threats of exile were intensified; soldiers pressed upon us with clubs and swords. We feared the swords and clubs. Where there are sword and clubs, what sort of synod is it?”

Forty-two bishops were ordered to remain silent and were not permitted to utter even a single word; only fifteen, who favored Eutyches, were allowed to speak. Finally, Barsumas was portrayed as the executioner of all the orthodox. For when the Egyptians and the monks who followed Barsumas rose up, the whole crowd began to say:

> “Cut in two the one who says there are two natures; whoever says there are two natures is a Nestorian.”

### 18

The tragic end of that synod may therefore be inferred from so lamentable and deplorable an order of events, from its proceedings, and from the continuation of the Acts.

Dioscorus himself proclaimed the acquittal of Eutyches. Although Flavian objected and declared that he had not been heard, the bishops—driven by punishment, fear, and weariness, and oppressed until evening—validated Eutyches’s acquittal with their own signatures.

The condemnation of Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum followed. Dioscorus wished to proceed against them by his customary frauds, and ordered the portions of the Acts of the general Council of Ephesus pertaining to the faith to be read. When all were asked whether they assented to those decrees of faith, everyone nodded without the slightest hesitation.

Proceeding in this way, Dioscorus sought a title that would give his action a colored appearance of legitimacy, so that he would not seem to condemn the innocent. Rather, he wished to remove them from the Catholic religion as though they were guilty of violating the faith and of holding Nestorian doctrine, excluding and declaring them excluded from the episcopate and from every priestly ministry.

In the sentence he pronounced, Dioscorus expressed or indicated no other cause except this one: that Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum had violated the decrees of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, “revoking and altering almost everything, and having become a cause of scandal and disturbance to the most holy Churches and to Catholic peoples everywhere.”

He therefore concluded:

> “It is certain that these men are themselves subject to the condemnations formerly defined synodally by the holy Fathers. Accordingly, confirming what belongs to them, we judge that the aforesaid men—namely, Flavian and Eusebius—are excluded from every priestly and episcopal dignity.”

Finally, lest he appear to have constituted himself the judge of the entire case, he addressed the bishops who had assembled for the synod in these words:

> “Let each of the most religious bishops, then, acknowledge his own will, and let them make it manifest under the testimony of the records.”

[Note: Baronius, at the place cited above, p. 95.]

But why did he address the bishops in this way, when forty-two had been forbidden to speak? When men who were pious, legitimate, and most holy judges were deprived of the right to vote and to make statements, and were falsely accused and persecuted, without any opportunity being given to their protests, how could this be called a judgment?

And finally, how could they make their will known when the executioner Barsumas and the soldiers were present, compelling them, together with the others, to sign blank sheets with clubs and swords?

There exist, Baronius observes, the signatures of ninety-six bishops, later read out with great disgrace at the Council of Chalcedon. They explained that violence had been inflicted upon them: chains had been displayed and soldiers stood ready, so that anyone who resisted would be bound in chains and led into exile.

### 19

At last, distressed that the matter of faith was being brought to ruin in such a bandit council, Flavian fearlessly cried out:

> “I appeal from you.”

And Hilary, the legate of the Apostolic See, said:

> “There is opposition.”

The other legates of the same See, undeterred by fear, although they had seen the proconsul enter the place where the banditry was being conducted with soldiers, boldly resisted Dioscorus to his face, declaring that what had thus far been extorted by force and fear had no validity.

The notaries did not insert this public and solemn protest of the pontifical legates into the Acts of the synod. For the notaries composed those Acts according to Dioscorus’s will, adding some things, removing others, and finally interpreting, fabricating, and adapting still others according to their own perverse judgment.

Several of the bishops testified that no one had been able to moderate or restrain Dioscorus’s tyrannical fury and rush of malice. Among them was Basil of Seleucia, who said at the Council of Chalcedon:

> “After Flavian’s condemnation, when all of us had become sorrowful, some unwilling to raise their voices and others fleeing, Dioscorus rose and stood on high. He pointed and said: ‘See who does not wish to sign for me, or who is against me.’”

And because Eusebius, bishop of Ancyra, delayed only a little in speaking, he too was in danger of being condemned.

Some of the bishops seated there, seeing divine and ecclesiastical rights being violated and utterly destroyed so grievously, held Dioscorus by the feet, saying:

> “Since you too have presbyters, a bishop ought not to be condemned on account of a presbyter. He has done nothing worthy of condemnation. If he is worthy of reproach, let him be reproved.”

[Note: Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, session 1.]

Those bishops were Onesiphorus of Iconium, Marinianus of Synnada, and Nunechius of Laodicea.

Yet even their most humble supplications could not move the ambitious and powerful spirit of Dioscorus in the slightest. Indeed, having broken every law of Christian moderation, he became bolder. Relying especially upon imperial power and surrounded by a throng of scoundrels, he thought he had acquired such protection that it was his duty to obey himself alone, while arrogating to himself, through impious usurpation, the rights of all who were inferior, equal, and even superior to him.

Who could excuse this unrestrained desire of his, and under what pretext? Not anyone who exaggerates the excellence and dignity of the Alexandrian See, as Quesnellus habitually does, claiming that it held primacy among the Eastern sees. Nor could the merits and prerogatives of his predecessor, Saint Cyril—on account of which he presided over the general ecumenical synod held at Ephesus, as Dioscorus, excessively flattered by the imperial ministers, seemed to persuade himself, and to whom almost all the Eastern and Western Fathers showed obedience—provide such a pretext.

Nor did the cause of the Catholic faith, whether sufficiently difficult, complicated, or not yet investigated, carry him into error. Only cunning, rivalry, and fury did so.

For he knew perfectly well that the holy Chair of Peter at Rome and its bishops were to be regarded as the supreme judges and teachers of the other Churches. He had acknowledged by writings and actions that the Roman bishop was to be consulted even by the Alexandrian bishop as a father, and that the Roman bishop’s judgment was to be regarded as the firm rule of all controversies.

### 20

In the year of Christ 445, scarcely elevated to the Alexandrian See, Dioscorus himself informed the holy pontiff Leo of his ordination and election to the episcopate. Fearing that he might at some time fall short in his pastoral office, he proposed two questions for Leo to resolve.

The first concerned the ordination of bishops and presbyters—namely, when and on which days it could be performed according to apostolic tradition. The second concerned the repetition of the sacrifice on the more solemn days and recurring feasts of the year, so that the people who came in addition might be satisfied.

Saint Leo the Great responded to both matters and showed the greatest affection of charity, so that Dioscorus might recognize from this what Leo desired to establish more firmly: the beginnings of the dignity he had attained.

Beginning his letter with these words, the supreme pontiff acknowledged that he was acting toward Dioscorus as a true father and brother, so that Dioscorus might receive with gratitude and willing spirit the entire explanation and rule concerning the two questions he had raised:

> “You will be able to approve how much affection of the Lord’s charity we devote to your Beloved from this: that we desire to establish more firmly the beginnings of your office, lest anything seem lacking to your charity for its perfection, since the merits of spiritual grace, as we have proved, support you.”

[Note: Saint Leo the Great, Letter 11 to Dioscorus; in Quesnell’s edition, otherwise Letter 81.]

It is therefore entirely clear that Dioscorus was then adorned with exceptional merits, and that the blessed Leo had been informed of them. He immediately added:

> “Thus a paternal and fraternal conference ought to be most welcome to your Holiness, and you ought to receive it in such a way as to understand that it proceeds from us.”

A little farther on, in the same preface, he explains how Dioscorus ought to receive these instructions. He shows that the Roman episcopate had not only obtained primacy in the Church from the Lord but also remained firmly grounded in the institutions of blessed Peter, from which no bishop could be permitted to depart.

> “Since the blessed Peter received from the Lord the primacy of the apostolate, and the Roman Church remains in his institutions, it is wrong to believe that Saint Mark, who first governed the Alexandrian Church, established the decrees of his traditions according to other rules.”

He also testified to the necessity of the closest concord between the Roman and Alexandrian Churches by writing:

> “We therefore do not permit ourselves, while we confess that we are one body and one faith, to differ in anything, so that the institutions of the teacher may appear to be one thing and those of the disciple another.”

[Note: The same author, in the same place.]

Dioscorus therefore could neither seek nor beg for a title or pretext from the excellence of his Alexandrian Church. He had understood clearly enough that the rule of ecclesiastical government required the Roman pontiff to hold primacy throughout the universal Church, and that all bishops, even those of the principal sees, should recognize and venerate him as father and teacher.

He was therefore led into such a great rebellion by a kind of wicked fury arising from ancient rivalries and private hatreds, fully conscious that the things he had decreed against Saint Leo, his legates, and the bishops who appealed to him were invalid and entirely without force.

Nor could the example of Saint Cyril, his predecessor, furnish any title for Dioscorus’s conduct. Cyril presided over the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, not as Alexandrian bishop, but as legate of Pope Saint Celestine. He received the pontifical letters, ordered that they be read to the synod, and wished them to be regarded as the rule for everything to be done in the synod.

It remains, then, that he must have encountered some grave difficulty in the matter of faith, containing such great and indissoluble knots that he himself did not know how to untie them, so that the title of ignorance might appear capable of defending him.

But what ignorance could excuse a bishop who was otherwise well versed in the sacred canons, who presided over the principal Church of the East, and who could not have been unaware of what had been observed by his predecessors when ecclesiastical judgments were conducted?

We can clearly understand from the following words that his method of judging had no other title than the one Saint Leo assigned to it:

> “This fault proceeded for the following reason: because he [Dioscorus] and those who had assembled did not, with a pure conscience and upright judgment, according to custom, issue a decision concerning the faith and those in error. In the judgment itself, we have learned that not all who had assembled were present.”

Here is the careful selection of judges who would depend upon Dioscorus’s nod.

He then rebukes the emperor’s conduct and commands with gentle restraint, matters about which we spoke earlier when discussing Theodosius’s imperial decrees. For, he says:

> “We have learned that some were rejected and others admitted, who, according to the will of the aforesaid priest, gave their captive hands to impious signatures.”

[Note: Saint Leo, Letter 39.]

### 21

Although none of the three aforementioned titles can prepare a defense or excuse for Dioscorus, there will nevertheless be those—as there have been—who claim for emperors and princes the right to convoke synods. They may also assert and teach that the order of judicial proceedings had been prescribed for Dioscorus by Theodosius’s decree.

The emperor himself had forbidden Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, or the other bishops who had pronounced judgment against Eutyches in the Council of Constantinople, to cast their votes in the Council of Ephesus. Elpidius vigorously pressed the execution of this command, defending Theodosius’s order of procedure in these words:

> “The emperor, himself being the first to fulfill the order of the laws, of which he is the author and guardian, ordered those who had once judged to occupy the place of those to be judged.”

When Dioscorus attempted to purge himself of the charges brought against him at the Council of Chalcedon, who could now use this form of excuse to lessen, or even entirely dissolve, the mark of disgrace generally affixed to Dioscorus?

But what can be said briefly about matters that bring with them various knots and difficulties, scarcely capable of being untangled and resolved in a few words?

With the most distinguished Peter de Marca—who asserted this right for Roman princes, namely, the right at times to convoke synods and appoint judges when ecclesiastical judgments were to be held, as well as to declare councils invalid “when they exceeded the limits prescribed by the prince in the manner of proceeding, without the Fathers of the councils complaining about the prince’s incompetence, but about the subreption which they displayed to the legates sent to the First Council of Ephesus”—I would have to undertake here a long discussion and subject each point to examination, since they bear only the appearance of truth.

We think it better to reserve this for another occasion, noting only a few matters here.

[Note: Peter de Marca, *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, book IV, chapter 3, § 7; Council of Chalcedon, session 1.]

### 22

First, concerning the convocation of synods and the order of matters to be handled in them, the illustrious de Marca ought to have indicated some right that was consistent with the laws of nature and divine institutions. It is not enough to adhere to equity, concord, and the pursuit of peace, which ought to be secured between the priesthood and the empire, if many evils arise to the prejudice of one or the other.

Otherwise we shall always remain in doubt whether the general councils of earlier times were convoked solely by the authority of the emperors or also by that of the Apostolic See. And, granting for the sake of argument that the Roman pontiffs, unable to resist the emperors’ decisions, acquiesced in the convocation of synods, the question would still remain whether the princes convoked synods lawfully or unlawfully, and whether, in convoking them, they exceeded the limits of their own authority.

If we turn our attention to the First Council of Nicaea, we understand that the emperor Constantine indeed convoked it, but that he did so at the suggestion of the priests.

[Note: Rufinus of Aquileia, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 2. See our notes, volume II, pp. 4–5.]

Since such a gathering of so many bishops could neither take place nor be sustained without imperial consent, assistance, and protection, Constantine therefore sent them letters to prevent disturbances and to give the bishops freedom to leave their episcopal sees temporarily and attend the council at the appointed time. He instructed them to set out on their journey.

De Marca himself must assert that in this matter Constantine used a delegated authority, since elsewhere he sincerely admits that, according to the ancient canon of the Church, an ecumenical synod cannot be held without the judgment of the Apostolic See.

[Note: Peter de Marca, book V, chapter 6.]

If matters are thus, emperors convoked general synods not by their own authority but by that of the supreme pontiffs, exercised in delegation. This is even more clearly established by the Council of Ephesus, with which we are concerned. In his letter to that same synod, Saint Leo protested that Theodosius had employed the authority of the Apostolic See to convoke it; we cited his words earlier, and de Marca himself transcribed them in the margin beside the passage cited.

To speak frankly, considerations of equity and concord always required that, when the gravest disturbances in the Roman Empire were increasing because of scandals and rivalries among the clergy, the Roman pontiffs should not resist the petitions of princes and emperors. Otherwise, if the affairs of the Church were thrown into confusion, even the business of civil administration—which principally belonged to secular authority—would tend toward ruin.

It is therefore not surprising that, in order at times to settle disturbances that had arisen, the emperors themselves considered convoking synods and requested this power from the Apostolic See. In my opinion, this is what the distinguished Peter de Marca intended to indicate.

### 23

The matter is more difficult, however, with respect to the order of proceedings: whether Roman princes could have prescribed it. De Marca teaches this, he says, by several examples. Among them he cites the fact that Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum occupied in the synod not the place of judges but of those to be judged.

I can scarcely imagine that the justification for this Theodosian statute could have been approved by the most learned man and most illustrious prelate of the Church of Paris, de Marca, since the statute conflicts with the institutions of nature and of God.

It was established that Flavian and his synod had done nothing wrong. Why, then, would Theodosius decree such an injurious order of proceedings—one by which Flavian was deprived of the right to vote in a matter concerning the faith and Eutyches, a right entirely inseparable from the priestly dignity he exercised in the Church of Constantinople?

Moreover, what crime was charged against Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, so that they should occupy the place of defendants to be judged? Who were the legitimate accusers? What evidence and proofs were produced by which they could be judged guilty of such grave crimes?
