Eutyches asserted by word and in written petitions that he had been judged by the synod under the guise of a malicious justice, through hatred and subornation. But that prince, who claimed as his pretext the protection and preservation of Christian tranquility in Church and empire, claimed, before the case had been investigated, the right to know matters that did not belong to him, since the issue concerned a new heresy and the judgment pronounced against it. He therefore could not violate that natural law.

Elpidius calls the emperor there “the author and guardian of the laws.” But in what sense did he guard the natural and divine law, which dictates that the legitimate rights of others must not be violated and that no one may be deprived of his right without being heard, unless perhaps the fault is of such a kind as by its very nature to entail some penalty?

[Note: Chapter “Reprehensibilis,” concerning appeals, title *Contumacy*, in the *Digest*, title *On a Matter Adjudged*.]

And perhaps the punishment should not be regarded as especially severe by which both Flavian and Eusebius were deprived of the right to judge and ordered by imperial statute to occupy the place of those being judged?

Only contumacy, in relation to some present or past offense, could have permitted Theodosius either to abolish or to alter the ancient order of laws. But what of the facts? Neither Flavian nor Eusebius was warned and summoned by three edicts, or by one issued in place of three—the document commonly called peremptory—and neither had refused to appear.

They therefore could not be regarded as contumacious. Indeed, scarcely had they received the letters summoning the synod when, without delay or any invented excuse for impediment, they hurried to the assembly.

It is therefore unjustly asserted that the emperor, “himself fulfilling first the order of the laws,” ordered those who had once judged to occupy the place of those being judged, when he had observed no order, no equity, and finally no law.

I would therefore rather believe that Elpidius abused the emperor’s authority and wished to enforce that law so that, against every right, Flavian, Eusebius, and the others who were condemned though innocent and without any crime would undergo undue punishments, even when every form of defense had been excluded.

We do not, however, intend to brand the most illustrious bishop of Paris with any stain for wishing to claim such rights for secular princes. We have merely wished to explain that the principles from which he undertook to establish the order of proceedings prescribed by those princes are extremely weak and false.

24. Finally, I shall review very briefly the last part of the Ephesian proceedings, in which Dioscorus brought the robbery to its conclusion. The legates of the Roman pontiff refused to attend this synodal session; but, after receiving Flavian’s libellus of appeal, they could by no violence whatsoever be compelled to remain longer at Ephesus. They steadfastly protested, as was fitting, that the Apostolic See would in no way accept what was being decreed [Note: [Col. 1171D] Saint Leo the Great, letter to the Council of Chalcedon.].

That Dioscorus paid little heed to these protests of the pontifical legates, [Col. 1171D] or to Flavian’s appeal itself, Hilary testified in his letter to the empress Pulcheria. “After I was unable,” Hilary says, “to associate myself with the unjust will and sentence of Dioscorus, he tried to summon me by terrors and plots to another council [Note: [Col. 1171D] Hilary the deacon, letter to the empress Pulcheria. Christian Lupus, in his scholia and notes on the Ephesian council.]”—that is, as Christian Lupus explains, to another synodal session—“so that, God forbid, either by deceptions he might make me consent to the condemnation of the most holy Bishop Flavian, or, if I resisted, he might hold me back, so that I would not be able to hasten to Constantinople, to Your Piety, [Col. 1172A] or return to the Roman Church. Nevertheless, trusting in Christ’s help, so far as concerned the condemnation of that most reverend and holy man, I preserved myself innocent and blameless, although no scourges or tortures could make me consent to that sentence. Abandoning everything, I departed from there and came to Rome by unknown and impassable routes, so that I might be a suitable messenger to the most reverend pope concerning everything that had taken place at Ephesus” [Note: [Col. 1171D] Hilary was not the only one to flee; the other pontifical legates also did so. The deacon Liberatus asserts this, writing: “Moreover, the legates of the Apostolic See, fleeing from that very council, reported to Pope Leo the iniquities of Dioscorus and how Dioscorus had acted in that synod more by force than by justice.”].

Prosper in his Chronicle and Theodoret also agree with Hilary [Note: [Col. 1172D] Theodoret, Letter 115.]. Yet Dioscorus, after the flight of the pontifical legates, neither became more lenient nor feared that he would eventually have to suffer the punishment he deserved. Adding crimes to crimes, he not only absolved the monks who were contending for the Eutychian heresy and [p. 392] admitted them to communion, but also declared that many orthodox bishops ought to be expelled and driven from their sees. He transported some into exile, and, while these men were still alive, had others installed in their places.

The very first to be deposed was Theodoret of Cyrrhus: unheard, not summoned, and absent more than [Col. 1172B] fifty stations away, he was being held in exile by Theodosius’s decree. It is well known that Dioscorus had arranged the charge for his condemnation. For since Theodoret had previously attacked the chapters of Saint Cyril, he was deposed from the episcopate even after peace had been made and ecclesiastical reconciliation had been obtained. Thus deprived of his episcopal residence, he was forced to live on the donations of friends, one of whom was especially generous toward him, Bishop Uranius of Emesa.

“From there,” Christian Lupus adds, “through the patrician Anatolius he petitioned the emperor either to permit him to go to Rome to pursue his appeal, or at least to return to his monastery, in which he had formerly professed the monastic life, situated one hundred miles from the city of Cyrrhus.” But we reserve discussion of his appeal to Saint Leo for a more suitable place elsewhere.

The second whom Dioscorus determined should be expelled from his episcopal see was Ibas, metropolitan of Edessa, on account of the notorious letter, offensive to Saint Cyril of Alexandria, written to Maris the Persian. He likewise was not permitted to attend the synod and was condemned in his absence. His exclusion from the synod is discussed in the ninth session of the Council of Chalcedon and by the deacon Liberatus, chapter 12 [Note: [Col. 1172D] The deacon Liberatus, in the *Breviarium*, at the place cited above.].

Sabinian, bishop of Perrha in the province of Euphratesia, and Evagrius of Epiphania likewise suffered equal misfortune. Evagrius adds that Aquilinus of Byblus, Irenaeus of Tyre, Sophronius, bishop of Constantia and metropolitan of Cyprus, and John of Germanicia were also deposed.

The last of all to be deposed was Domnus, bishop of Antioch. Liberatus writes the following about him:

> “After all the others, Domnus of Antioch remained exempt from the deposition of the orthodox, because Dioscorus had made him a participant in the deposition of the orthodox and in the absolution of Eutyches. He was deposed through Dioscorus’s deceit as follows. After Domnus had consented to Dioscorus in everything, Dioscorus produced in their midst the letters that Domnus of Antioch had written to Dioscorus himself against Cyril’s twelve chapters, on the ground that they were obscure; and on that day he condemned Domnus, who was sick and absent” [Col. 1172D].

Finally, Dioscorus dared to appoint, elect, and ordain others in the places of the deposed bishops, usurping for himself the full authority of general councils, even contrary to the command of canon 4 of the Council of Sardica, which orders that no one be substituted in the place of a deposed bishop before the Roman pontiff has delivered judgment [Note: [Col. 1172D] Volume II of the Councils, p. 681 in my edition.].

So far from Dioscorus wishing to obey this canon—which was commended under the name of the Nicene canons—he instead, having usurped for himself control of the entire ecclesiastical administration, wished to bring everything to ruin and overthrow the condition of all the Churches, contrary to every natural, divine, and ecclesiastical right and to the faith, obeying himself alone [Col. 1173A]. But we shall discuss the elections and ordinations of these men when describing Saint Leo’s proceedings in Book II of the *History of the Eutychianists*, just as we shall discuss the Sardican canons in chapter 10 of this book.

393. CHAPTER IX. On the appeal of Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, to the Apostolic See. The false opinion of John Launoy, Paschasius Quesnel, and others—that he appealed to a new general council—is presented. Finally, their arguments, as weak and highly deceptive, are overturned and utterly refuted by certain and evident demonstrations.

1. Quesnel’s mind was so driven by a passion for novelty that, wishing to market foreign doctrines differing from more common opinions, he did not blush to reason from erroneous and false arguments, nor would he be dislodged from them when truth confronted him with a light brighter than day. Violently bound by his own prejudices, to which he always clung in disputes and debates, and departing from the paths of the most illustrious and learned men [Note: [Col. 1173D] Baronius, volume VI of the *Annals*. Bellarmine, Book II *On the Roman Pontiff*. John David, in his work written in French, *On the Canonical Judgments of Bishops*. Christian Lupus, in his notes on the Ephesian council.], he touched only the surface of matters and painted sophisms and deceptive conjectures in the colors of truth—not merely to deceive his readers, but to exercise hatred against the Apostolic See and establish a new system of government in the Church, under the pretext of pursuing and illuminating antiquity.

I am convinced that he set himself this goal in all his writings. But I understood it especially when I undertook to examine his eighth dissertation. For I supposed that, when treating there of Saint Flavian’s celebrated appeal to the Apostolic See, he had not allowed himself to be led by any spirit of hostility, but had wished to follow, in dealing with so important a subject, the footsteps of [Col. 1173C] prudent and learned writers who had long preceded him in treating this question, which we now intend to discuss: Baronius, Bellarmine, John David, Cardinal Peronius, Christian Lupus, and others.

For these men, sincerely seeking the truth, not only narrated the condition, order, and events of the Ephesian robbery without applying any false coloring, as was necessary; they also asserted that Saint Flavian’s appeal to the Apostolic See had been valid, effective, and made according to the form of ecclesiastical law.

Yet Quesnel was so far from wishing to follow this excellent path leading to a sincere study of ecclesiastical history that, abandoning the perfectly clear paths followed by those once-famous men, he instead brought them onto the stage to be attacked and branded them with ignorance because they had judged that Flavian had appealed to the Apostolic See, not to a general council. He himself, by contrast, following Launoy’s false conjectures and fabricated opinions, maintained that Flavian’s appeal had not been made to the Apostolic See or to Saint Leo, but to a general council, by which the bishop who was appealing had requested a new judgment.

As Quesnel set about beginning his dissertation, he pretends that he is composing it from what Saint Pope Leo says in Letters 39 and 40, as he wished to indicate by the following title [Col. 1174A]:

> “Eighth Dissertation on the Case of Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, Condemned and Deposed in the Ephesian Pseudosynod, with Reference to Letters 39 and 40 of Saint Leo to the Emperor Theodosius.”

2. He begins this dissertation by writing that “among the appeals said to have been brought to the Apostolic See in the earliest centuries of the Church, the most celebrated of all is that which was made by Flavian after Dioscorus had pronounced sentence against him.” In a few words he indicates the grounds of those who defend the affirmative position. He immediately adds:

> “Concerning this appeal, which constitutes the principal and almost the sole subject matter of Letters 39 and 40, the plan we have undertaken requires at least a brief discussion, although the subject does not demand a more extended treatment, since it was long ago thoroughly examined by more learned men” [Note: [Col. 1173D] Quesnel, eighth dissertation, volume II, p. 304 and following in my edition. Launoy, Part II, Letter to Jacques Boet, Letter 3, p. 22 in my edition.].

Nevertheless, so that he might gradually and more easily depart from the opinion of the learned men who had illuminated this question, he thought it necessary to note that Saint Leo had never written that Flavian had appealed to his see, but had merely said in general that an appeal had been lodged, as he puts it in chapter 3 of this letter, and that his legates had faithfully protested, and that Bishop Flavian had given them a libellus of appeal.

He believes that the Greek Acts of the Ephesian synod, reread at the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, agree with him. In them, he reports, nothing else is said by Flavian except: “I reject you,” *παραιτοῦμαί σε*; and Hilary, Leo’s legate, objects—*κοντραδίκιτουρ* (“I object”). From these statements, he says, he proceeds to reason:

> “For whether Flavian understood a true appeal, as the recent writer laboriously contends against de Marca, or a rejection, as others affirm—and as David himself finally admits—it makes no difference. This alone I assert: Flavian, whether appealing or rejecting, made no mention of Leo.”

He undertakes to defend the opinion of the illustrious Peter de Marca, which David had attacked, and vehemently assails its opponent for wishing stubbornly to uphold here the customary formulas of canonical judgments [Note: [Col. 1173D] Quesnel criticizes John David for his book entitled *On the Canonical Judgments of Bishops*, chapter VI, article 3, § 2. [Col. 1174D] Unjustly, however. For David, with a great apparatus of genuine and solid learning, explained the ancient order and practice in the conduct of ecclesiastical judgments. He showed that before the age of Justinian the two words *appeal* and *rejection* conveyed the same meaning, as is found in the law: “Both terms, both appeal and rejection, are used together.” Justinian finally abolished the confusion of the terms.], since everything Dioscorus had undertaken was known to be contrary to law and right, and the customary practices and formulas of judgments could in no way be applied to the Ephesian robbery.

> “Even if,” he says, “according to the order of law, there is no place for rejection except before sentence has been pronounced, nor for appeal except after judgment has been delivered, that is entirely proper—whether a legitimate judge has reasonably become suspect, or a judgment has been arranged by an incompetent judge.”

Finally, Quesnel concludes:

> “But you will find nothing of this kind in the Ephesian council. The synod, he says, had been legitimately assembled at the emperor’s command and with the assent of the Roman pontiff, who was also present through his legates; it therefore could not in any way be rejected or repudiated.”

Who does not see that Quesnel wished to jest here in order to deceive his readers and draw the deceived into his own opinion? He pretends to sharpen his pen against John David, Peter de Marca’s adversary, and, playing with words, flatters himself that the Ephesian synod could not be rejected or repudiated at its beginnings because it had been legitimately assembled at the emperor’s command and with the assent of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 1174D] 3. But everyone, even the purblind and the barbers, knows that the difficulty does not concern this convocation. Nevertheless, we must adhere to what was said above: Theodosius employed the authority of the Apostolic See—not merely its assent—for the holding of that synod.

Therefore, that synod could be rejected and repudiated immediately at its beginnings: namely, when Dioscorus, supported by no legitimate authority, undertook at his own discretion to constitute a synod, driving Flavian himself—the legitimate pastor of that Church—from the place in which the bishop of Constantinople ought to sit; when, having been informed of the mandates carried by the legates of Saint Leo, he gave neither them nor the other orthodox Fathers their proper place and honor [Col. 1175A] [Note: [Col. 1175D] See the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, in which Dioscorus was condemned, session 1. Consult also the deacon Liberatus, who writes in his *Breviarium*: “When those bishops were seated in the basilica of Mary, Mother of God, they did not allow the deacons of the Roman Church, who were serving as representatives of Pope Leo, to sit beside him, because precedence had not been granted to their holy see” [Col. 1176D].];

nor did he ever permit the *commonitoria* and the doctrinal letter that they presented to be read in the synod.

What more is needed? That synod could be rejected and refused when it became known to Flavian, the pontifical legates, and the other orthodox Fathers that Dioscorus was moving every stone so that those alone who adhered to the Eutychian faction might prevail in number, authority, and strength against the Catholic faith and the piety of religion.

Could not, at those beginnings, Flavian, Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, and the pontifical legates have refused to have a place in that assembly? But they were being held by imperial soldiers, who guarded the church and its doors. Yet when there are soldiers, swords, and clubs, what sort of synod is it that cannot be rejected?

Quesnel ought therefore to have considered these matters before he wrote so freely [Col. 1175B] that the synod could not be rejected at the outset. But, he adds, Dioscorus and his synod could first be rejected when Dioscorus, claiming everything for himself by force and crime and overturning every form of judgment, appeared to have changed from a bishop into a bandit and murderer, and to have transformed a legitimate synod into a robbery.

At that point, there was room not so much for an appeal—which presupposes a legitimate and competent judge—as for rejection and protest against an assembly which, as Saint Leo says, no consideration permits to be called a synod.

In my judgment, Quesnel is inconsistent with himself, or has examined the history of the Ephesian council only carelessly. Therefore, please let him say from what point this beginning of the robbery is to be taken, in which Dioscorus claimed everything for himself by crime and overturned every form of judgment.

Perhaps he supposes that Dioscorus did not begin to exercise such crime and tyranny as soon as the synod assembled? On the contrary, the crime already conceived in his mind three months earlier, which he could no longer restrain within himself, he revealed freely and almost in a frenzy at those first beginnings, and gradually increased and completed it through those tragic actions with which the entire sequence of the proceedings was filled.

If, therefore, according to Quesnel, there was room for rejection, protest, and appeal as soon as Dioscorus made himself an illegitimate and incompetent judge, it follows that Flavian could reject and repudiate that synod at its beginnings, because Dioscorus was an incompetent judge from the outset and because all the devices he had employed over the preceding three months rightly made him suspect of crimes so great.

Does Quesnel believe that Dioscorus’s devices and machinations, his ancient rivalries and private hatreds, were hidden from Flavian, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, and the pontifical legates? He is making a clever joke.

Thus, in accordance with the truth, we must conclude that this synod was legitimate only with respect to its convocation, because the emperor wished to employ the authority of the Apostolic See in convening it.

[Col. 1175D] 4. Quesnel proceeds to identify the distinction between rejection and appeal, saying that they differ in several respects. One is that rejection nullifies a sentence, as having been issued by an incompetent judge; whereas appeal merely suspends the effect of a sentence, as having proceeded unjustly from a judge who was nevertheless competent, until it is recalled for examination by a superior.

He then adds that Leo declared the Ephesian judgment unworthy of the name of a synod even before its case was reconsidered, thereby sufficiently indicating that rejection, rather than appeal, had been appropriate.

What follows from this except that the synod was illegitimate from its beginnings—something Quesnel denied shortly before? Therefore, [Col. 1176A] in order to reach another and more important goal that he had set for himself, he recited the words of Saint Leo found in several of his letters, in which Leo complains:

> “That those who assembled concerning the faith and those in error did not pronounce judgment according to custom; that the leaders of the synod spared neither those who resisted them nor those who agreed with them; that we learned that not all who had assembled were present; that some were rejected and others admitted, who, at the sole will of Dioscorus, gave their captive hands to impious subscriptions; that violence was exercised against all the Churches” [Note: [Col. 1176D] Saint Leo, Letters 39, 40, and 75. We have transcribed this passage, formed from the three letters, as it appears in Quesnel, p. 304 in my edition.].

To these words of Saint Leo Quesnel reasonably added the following:

> “Where the writings of the Apostolic See were not permitted to be published for the ears of the bishops; where its legates were not granted their proper place; where the Fathers of Chalcedon testified that extreme violence had been used.”

From all these statements, however, he believes the following conclusion may be drawn:

> “Hence you see how deservedly Flavian cried out, *παραιτοῦμαί σε*, ‘I reject you.’”

I should nevertheless like the reader to notice Quesnel’s art here: namely, how he attempts to move from rejection to appeal, and with what colors he strives to adorn that transition. For he adds:

> “Because the agreement and subscription of almost all the bishops lent some appearance of a synod to the impious assembly, and because the authority of the emperor and the civil powers intervened, Flavian thought that, when he later handed a libellus to the legates of the Apostolic See, he should use the language of appeal, so that, by the right of appeal, an opportunity might be given for a new synod.”

Does the reader see the goal toward which all Quesnel’s preceding fiction tends? From Launoy and other writers of novelties he derived this doctrine, which John David nevertheless wrested from its authors by attacking them with skill and learning, clearly demonstrating that Flavian’s formula of speech, *παραιτοῦμαί σε*, signifies a genuine appeal.

5. Indeed, after a great and useless apparatus of words, Quesnel himself was forced to concede both points: namely, that Flavian’s rejection indicated an appeal [Col. 1176C]. But he tried to interpret so maliciously every consideration that converges to demonstrate this genuine appeal that he maintained it had not been brought before the Apostolic See, because Flavian, when appealing, did not mention Leo’s name, and because Leo himself supports this view in his letters written after the Ephesian synod.

Quesnel ultimately wishes Flavian’s appeal to have been vague and directed to a new council, since Saint Pontiff nowhere asserts that his own see had been appealed to:

> “The pontiff, who was most zealous for the rights of his see, would never have omitted this if it had been so. But he asserts simply that an appeal was lodged.”

As we have said, he borrowed this doctrine from Launoy. In order to prove it against Bellarmine, Launoy transcribed the letter of the holy pontiff to Theodosius and opposed it to that eminent writer and defender of pontifical rights, writing:

> “When I examine Bellarmine’s argument and Leo’s letter, I am easily led to believe that Bellarmine did not read Leo’s letter, but was deceived by his copyist, who told him that Flavian had appealed to Leo. For the pontiff does not write this in his letter. He writes that Flavian gave a libellus of appeal, but he does not write to whom he gave it.”

From these earlier statements, therefore, he undertakes, as if divining, to reason as follows. It is credible that Flavian appealed to a council that would be freer and larger. For Leo and the Roman synod were concerned only with having the emperor order a general council to be held within Italy, one that would put an end to the disturbances and controversies that had arisen.

Finally, Launoy closes that paragraph or section of his letter with these words:

> “But even if Flavian appealed to Leo, [Col. 1177A] he did not appeal for Leo alone to judge Flavian’s case, but so that a general synod might judge together with Leo” [Note: [Col. 1177D] Launoy, Part II of the *Letters*, Letter 3.].

A charming falsehood, adopted by Quesnel, as we have said. But how can these claims be reconciled with Flavian’s purpose and manner of acting? He had previously accepted Eutyches’s appeal to the Roman pontiff as valid, expressly writing, “and he appealed to Your Holiness.” Four months earlier he had denied that his own case and that of Eutyches ought to be brought before a general council, and had entreated the holy pontiff to refrain from convening one.

Now, then, had he changed his mind and become concerned for a new general synod, lodging an appeal in order to have one convened after so many and such great disasters and calamities? What? Had Flavian perhaps foreseen that Leo would be hostile to him, although shortly before he had wished to regard Leo as the legitimate judge and had written that only the Roman pontiff’s defense, and only his assent, could benefit him and the entire Church?

Flavian, I say, according to Launoy, with Quesnel supporting him, requested a general council for his defense [Col. 1177B]. Yet he had likewise affirmed that the Churches were being disturbed everywhere because of synods, that the case under discussion required only pontifical assistance, and that he was asking to be given pontifical letters or writings.

Is this the Flavian who, having not merely considered these matters in his mind but also expressed them in writing, can plausibly be said to have appealed to a general—and indeed larger—synod after changing his judgment and plan? Away with such a fabrication!

For after the Ephesian robbery, experience had taught him that ancient rivalries and private hatreds prevailed especially in synods because of the different factions, and that the adversaries of the orthodox cause enjoyed the strongest support from the civil authorities. He therefore could not even conceive of appealing to the Roman pontiff in order to request a new synod.

Thus either Launoy wished to portray Flavian as an inconsistent or mentally deranged man, or at least he entirely failed to grasp his purpose, deliberation, and judgment. Therefore, if I were permitted to use his own formulas of speech, I would turn them against him [Col. 1177C], asserting that he had never read Saint Flavian’s letter to Saint Leo—or at least had concealed it—in order to indulge his own pursuits by selling so many and such great fictions and trifles to Jacques Boet, just as he did under the pretext of attacking Cardinal Bellarmine and overturning his doctrine.

6. Flavian’s words, which we have explained thus far without any forced interpretation, are exceedingly clear. Nor do we think we are repeating what has already been said if we set them out here. Writing to Saint Leo concerning the case of Eutyches before the Ephesian council, Flavian says:

> “For the case requires only your comfort and defense, by which, through your own assent, you ought to bring everything to tranquility and peace. For in this way, with God’s cooperation, the heresy that has arisen and the disturbances caused by it will very easily be destroyed through your most holy letters. The council that is reported to be taking place will also be removed, so that the most holy Churches may in no way be disturbed everywhere” [Note: [Col. 1177D] Flavian’s letter to Saint Leo, written before the Council of the Robbery, is found in Quesnel, volume I, p. 239; in Labbe, volume IV of the *Councils*; and in Cotelerius. [Col. 1178D] See what we wrote in chapters 3 and 4 of this *Exercitation*.].

John David opposed this testimony of Flavian to Launoy and added to it the response [Col. 1177D] in which Saint Leo the Great, answering the earlier requests of the bishop of Constantinople, said that the reason for holding a council did not arise from any necessity, but derived from the emperor’s wish to employ the authority of the Apostolic See.

And because the most merciful emperor, concerned for the peace of the Church, wished a synod to be assembled, “although it is clearly evident that the matter under discussion by no means requires synodal deliberation.”

It is therefore astonishing how Launoy and Quesnel could so confidently affirm that appeals to a general synod were necessary as a remedy for resolving the controversy that had arisen, when Flavian and Leo had taught the contrary [Col. 1178A].

Indeed, Leo himself, who had carefully examined the sequence of the Constantinopolitan proceedings, knew very well that the judgment of the Apostolic See alone was entirely sufficient for settling the disputes between Flavian and Eutyches. He could not resolve upon the plan of convening a new synod except because he was moved by the consideration that a more solemn judgment ought to be held, as he testified in his letters both to the emperor and to Julian of Cos, which we discussed above.

7. Now, leaving Launoy aside for a while, let us see how Quesnell reasons. “I read,” he says, “that the legates protested here; I read that an appeal was lodged; I also read that a written appeal was given to the legates; but to whom the appeal was made I do not read at all” [Note: [Col. 1178D] Quesnell, Dissertation 8, chapter 1, p. 309 according to my copy.]. From this he seizes the occasion to attack John David, who wrote that it was obvious that the Roman pontiff had been appealed to, since every appeal must necessarily be brought before some judge. Therefore, when Flavian gave the written appeal to the legates, he acknowledged in them jurisdiction to receive the appeal. Such a right could in no way belong to them as private persons; hence it is necessary that he handed them the written appeal as the pope’s legates, because he recognized the pontiff as a suitable judge for examining the appeal [Note: John David, in the place cited above.].

He therefore attacks David for having written this, departing from the rules of judicial jurisdiction and failing to understand what no one who has even crossed the threshold of the law courts is unaware of. Quesnell then adds that, according to the form of Roman law, the written appeal is given to the person to whom the appeal has been made, so that he may grant the litigant the *apostoli*, that is, letters of dismissal. Finally, he brings forward Paul’s example of appealing from the governor Festus to Caesar: “He directed the voice of the appellant,” he says, “to no one other than the governor himself.” Now, when Flavian appealed from Dioscorus and his ill-fated synod to another council, to whom could he have handed his written appeal except to the Roman legates, who alone, or almost alone, had not consented to Dioscorus’s wicked machinations?

Quesnell undertakes to prove by four arguments that Flavian ought to have presented the written appeal to the pontifical legates. First, because Dioscorus, acting entirely through violence and abuse of power, would have allowed no legal form to be observed; second, because all the prelates of the synod had surrendered their hands captive to Dioscorus; third, because Flavian appealed especially to the Western bishops, as did Theodoret, and consequently it was necessary that Flavian’s appeal become known to the patriarch and the primate of all; finally, because, when appealing to a universal council of the entire Church, whom should one approach with the written appeal rather than the person who is both the supreme summit of the whole Church and, in a matter of faith, its universal procurator, upon whom the principal solicitude and care of convening an ecumenical synod rests, and to whom the first sentence and the first place belong in councils?

Quesnell closes this chapter of his dissertation in these words: “These are the true reasons that moved Flavian to place the written appeal or recusal in the hands of the legates. For this purpose it was not necessary that they possess jurisdiction of their own, or jurisdiction in the pope’s name; it was sufficient that they were part of the council and suitable witnesses to the appeal that had been lodged.” Thus far Quesnell.

He employed all the resources of his craft to overthrow and abolish Flavian’s appeal to the apostolic see, bringing forward one violent interpretation after another, which he imagined both favored his own studies and assailed the teaching and arguments of the most illustrious men. Yet, just as he was prolix in his reasoning, so he appeared foolish and not at all consistent with himself in his statements. If we understood this defect from no other source, we could discern it very clearly from the note that he appended to the letters of the emperor Valentinian and of the augustae Galla Placidia and Licinia Eudoxia, addressed to the emperor Theodosius.

What does he say there? He tries to persuade his readers that the celebrated letters of Saint Leo were written at the urging of Leo and of the entire Roman synod then in session, and he adds that they were dictated by Leo himself. If, then, he thought the matter stood thus, why, when writing in this dissertation, did he say that he nowhere read to whom Flavian had appealed? For Valentinian, in his letter, affirms without any verbal circumlocution or obscurity whatsoever that Flavian appealed to Leo. “For this reason,” he says, “according to the solemnity of councils, the bishop of Constantinople also appealed to him by written petitions, because of the dispute that had arisen concerning the faith.”

Two points must here be noted, which refute Quesnell’s statements: first, that according to the testimony of the emperor Valentinian, Flavian observed the legal order by lodging his appeal “according to the solemnity of councils”; second, that Flavian appealed by written petitions to Leo, the supreme pontiff, and not to a council.

Nor does it stand in the way that the supreme pontiff discussed this appeal in the Roman synod, which he was accustomed to hold every year in the month of October [Note: See Saint Leo’s letter in Quesnell, letter 16 to the bishops of Sicily, chapter 7, where there is discussion of a council celebrated every year at Rome. To this council, the bishops of that island as well were plainly required to come, three at a time, on the third day before the Kalends of October, to be joined in fraternal council. [Col. 1180D]]. For it was entirely just that, once the deacon Hilary had arrived in the City—the most faithful narrator of all that had occurred at Ephesus—and while several bishops from other provinces who had come to the synod were still in the City, Leo should disclose to them what had been done, through the arbitrary power of Dioscorus alone, for the destruction of the Catholic faith and religion, the ruin of orthodox bishops, and the contempt of the apostolic see.

Leo ought to have reported these acts to the aforementioned gathering of bishops as null and void, condemnable and detestable, so that they might remain in communion with Flavian, refrain from Dioscorus, and defend, as was proper, the rights of the Roman see, which had been gravely injured and violated. The supreme pontiff did not need their vote, since he was already considering another way to remedy these grave evils and repair all the damage.

Saint Leo himself indicated without obscurity the reason for holding that synod every year when he wrote: “Since, with the help of God’s grace, it will more easily be provided that no scandals and no errors arise in the Churches of Christ, if it is always jointly discussed before the blessed apostle Peter that all his constitutions and canonical decrees remain inviolate among all the priests of the Lord.”

Since no more serious scandals or more pernicious heresy could have arisen in the Church than those that had nearly undermined the faith of the entire East, Leo therefore had to speak about these matters with the other bishops when the annual celebration of the Roman synod came around. He had to define that no other remedy could be applied to those grave and spreading evils than the convocation of a new general council, so that the safety of the Catholic faith might be secured, the rights of the apostolic see—shamefully violated and abolished—might be restored, and bishops who had deviated from the right path, to the great destruction of the souls subject to them, might be granted pardon through a solemn retraction freely made.

This is indicated by those other words of the emperor Valentinian, in which he recalled to Theodosius the duty of defending the faith received from his ancestors. He added that the honor of the supreme priest must likewise be defended, and that the dignity of the veneration proper to the blessed apostle Peter must be preserved undefiled in our own times, “so that the most blessed bishop of the Roman city, to whom antiquity granted the primacy of the priesthood over all, may have the place and authority to judge concerning the faith and concerning priests.”

Let Quesnell now say, I ask, how Saint Leo the Great could have safeguarded the honor of his supreme dignity, repaired the damage to his violated jurisdiction, and fully restored the authority that antiquity had conferred upon him over all, if he had not convened a synod of all the bishops of the entire world. Was not the Catholic faith, pontifical dignity, the primacy of the priesthood, and the honor of the chair of the divine Peter despised and solemnly cast down in the Ephesian synod? Therefore, in a new solemn synod, the faith had to be strengthened, and the rights of the apostolic see had to be restored. For that reason, he had to bring to the general council the appeal made to himself by Flavian, although Saint Flavian himself had appealed only to the pontiff as the legitimate judge of his case.

8. Nevertheless, so that I may not appear to depart from the ordinary path of discussion before Quesnell—or anyone else who indulges his pursuits—I shall set aside the other letters written by Galla Placidia or Licinia Eudoxia to Theodosius and turn my attention to the two letters of Saint Leo that Quesnell adopts as the foundation of his dissertation. In these letters the holy pontiff assigns three reasons that moved him to hold a new general council. The first was the wounding of the Catholic faith; the second, the grievous condition of all the Churches of the East, so greatly disturbed either because of the deposed prelates or because of those who had surrendered their hands captive through impious subscriptions, obeying Dioscorus; the third, finally, was the repeated protest of the pontifical legates when they saw that, from the beginning of the synod to its end, the rights of the apostolic see had not merely been neglected but overthrown and abolished.

Saint Leo indicated the first two reasons in these words, writing to the emperor Theodosius: “Therefore,” he says, “the council of bishops that you ordered to be held in the city of Ephesus on account of Flavian both proves harmful to the faith itself and wounds all the Churches. And we have learned these things not from an uncertain report but from the most reverend bishops themselves, who were sent by us,” and so forth.

A little farther on, wishing to express the grave wounds inflicted upon the Churches, he added: “But in that judgment we have learned that not all who had assembled were present. For we learned that some were rejected and others admitted, who, at the arbitrary will of the aforementioned priest, surrendered their hands captive through impious subscriptions. They knew that this would harm their own standing unless they did what was commanded, and that a sentence had been pronounced by him such that through it violence would be directed against all the Churches” [Note: Saint Leo, letter 39, to Theodosius.].

From there, wishing to proceed to the third reason that impelled him to hold a new council, Leo used his pontifical authority while blending the gravity of his spirit with ecclesiastical moderation. He gently reproves the emperor himself for having lent an ear to imprudent men and for not opposing their evil arts. He recalls to the emperor’s mind the dangers threatening the faith and religion, as evils of the gravest kind that must be removed from his conscience, lest human presumption do violence to Christ’s Gospel. Finally, joining supplications to his exhortations, he asks that, once all the acts of the Ephesian Robber Council have been abolished, Theodosius permit and order everything to be restored to its former condition—that is, the condition in which it had been before any judgment—until a larger number of priests from the whole world could assemble; and he asks that the emperor not allow himself to be burdened by another’s sin.

Leo himself judged that such a synod had to be held both because our men—that is, the legates of the apostolic see—faithfully protested on account of the rights of the Roman see that had been violated, and because Bishop Flavian had given them a written appeal [Note: Letter 41 to Flavian, and letter 43 to Anastasius of Thessalonica.].

It would not have been difficult for either Launoy or Quesnell to understand the purpose to which the protest of the pontifical legates was directed, if they had paid attention to the Ephesian Acts as we explained them above. For they protested against what was being done in the synod itself without the consent, authorization, and instructions of the Roman pontiff; they protested because of the injury inflicted upon the apostolic see, even before they heard that Eutyches had been absolved and Flavian condemned and deposed; they protested against the force employed to extort the votes of the prelates; finally, they protested in order to prevent the execution of the most criminal decrees made there, so that, according to the rules of law, the entire judgment would remain suspended until the prohibition of the supreme pontiff Leo, whose person they represented, could be awaited.

Who will dare deny that this protest should be called a true appeal? Or who, while searching here and there with Quesnell for every possible escape, will affirm that Flavian appealed to Theodoret merely so that the appeal might become known to the Westerners, and that he ought rather to have approached with the written appeal the person who is both the supreme summit of the whole Church and, in a matter of faith, its universal procurator?

This is a new formula of speech, a new office of the Roman pontiff, invented, so far as I know, by no one before. But, even setting aside the judgments of so many most holy Fathers who called the Roman pontiff the true and legitimate judge of controversies concerning the faith, we shall refute this fiction before removing our hand from the present page [Col. 1181B].

9. Indeed, if the pontifical legates had received Flavian’s written appeal in order to bring it to Leo as the procurator of this case, Saint Leo certainly would not, before the ecumenical synod that he was preparing to convene, have issued any decree or prohibition; he would not have solemnly declared in his various letters that the Acts of Ephesus were null and void; he would never have removed from the midst, as unjust, the sentence pronounced against Flavian by Dioscorus and that synod; and, in letters written to the augusta Pulcheria, he would not have said on his own authority: “Bishop Flavian remains in communion with us and with all.”

As procurator, he could indeed have communicated, according to the rules of law, with Flavian, who had been excommunicated by the synod. But by what authority could he induce all the other priests of the Roman synod to communicate with him? What more is needed? Before the new ecumenical council that he was striving to assemble, he condemns Dioscorus himself as guilty of a great crime: “A great crime,” he says in his letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica, “has been committed, with the bishop of Alexandria as its author or executor.”

Moreover, it was not only Leo and the Roman synod who wished to communicate with Flavian. He also wrote to the clergy, the honored officials, and the people of Constantinople, so that, deterred by no threats or driven by fear, they might separate themselves from their legitimate bishop. He added this declaration of the highest authority: “Whoever, while your bishop Flavian is alive and unharmed, dares to invade his priesthood will never be regarded as being in communion with us, nor will he be able to be counted among the bishops” [Note: Saint Leo, letter 45, to the clergy, honored officials, and people of the city of Constantinople.].

Who, then, can turn his mind without the taint of envy to Saint Leo’s entire course of action and persuade himself that, by virtue of that appeal, the Roman pontiff acted in the role of a procurator? Where have we ever known procurators and advocates of cases to pronounce judgments, issue decrees, declare the sentences of preceding judges null and void, absolve the condemned, and ask, demand, and command that everything be restored to the condition in which it was before the cases were investigated?

I, who have not even crossed the threshold of a court or law forum, certainly do not see how all these things can cohere. For I have always heard that procurators may only press for the settlement of cases before legitimate judges, bringing forward in writing or speech those reasons and laws capable of leading the judge’s mind to the knowledge and pursuit of truth.

But let Quesnell say, I ask, before which judge he believed Leo had pressed, or ought to have pressed, the advocacy of Flavian’s case as an appellant. Before the emperor, perhaps, whom Leo urgently begged to order that a new council be assembled within Italy? Yet Leo was pressing and urging the emperor to ensure the free and solemn execution of his decrees, so that the truth of the Catholic faith, assailed by so many and such great dangers, might be made manifest to the whole world; so that the scandals already raging throughout the East might be abolished, the strength of the sound might be increased, and medicine might be provided for the diseased, if they were willing to be healed.

That Saint Leo was moved by these considerations to request that a new council be held is attested by his letters written to the emperor and to the augusta Pulcheria, to the clergy and honored officials of Constantinople, to Julian of Cos, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, and to Paschasinus and the emperor Marcian. We consider it unnecessary here to set out in detail the significant points of those letters.

10. Nevertheless, despite the force of such grave arguments—which have explained and demonstrated that Saint Leo, both because of the protests of the pontifical legates and because of the appeal lodged by Flavian, performed the true and legitimate functions and office of a judge—Quesnell flatters himself that he has won the case. He loudly celebrates the fact that letter 40 of Leo supplies him with an exceedingly strong argument in favor of his opinion, by which it is established that Flavian appealed to the synod and then to Leo as the head of the synod.

Let us therefore examine the adversary’s artful reasoning. “Since,” he says, “he derives from that bishop’s appeal the necessity of convening an ecumenical synod, it is clearer than daylight that the synod was appealed to, and that the authority of no other person was challenged by the written appeal, so that a judgment might be pronounced concerning the sentence of the Ephesian Robber Council.”

He immediately adds Leo’s words, from which he imagines that the preceding argument can be drawn. That this should necessarily be required after an appeal had been lodged, he says, is testified by the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea.

“For if,” Quesnell adds, “an appeal was made to one of the Western bishops together with a provincial or diocesan synod, why would he not alone, with his fellow provincials, arrange the judgment? Why are the priests of all the Churches removed from their sees, if the case can be ended by the judgment of one? Why is an ecumenical synod necessarily demanded when an ecumenical synod was not appealed to? If the primary see has been named in the written appeal, let the pontiff bring the litigants before his own see, investigate the matter, seek the judgment of the bishops, pronounce the decision, and the case is finished” [Note: Quesnell, in the same place, p. 305, no. 4.].

Quesnell added these and other arguments of the same kind according to his taste for reasoning, in order to force the testimony of the holy pontiff into a violent meaning. What must be observed above all is that he pretends that the deacon Liberatus favors his position, although Liberatus expressly writes: “Moreover, those occupying the place of Pope Leo contradicted everything that was done; but Flavian, against the sentence pronounced against him, appealed by a written petition through his legates to the apostolic see” [Note: The deacon Liberatus, in his *Brief Account*, chapter 12. The author of the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* also speaks of the protest of the pontifical legates, as may be seen in volume V of the Councils. Finally, it is established from the first act of Chalcedon that Flavian appealed not to the council but to the apostolic see. Consult Saint Leo’s letter 42 to Flavian.].

Nevertheless, since Quesnell insists chiefly upon the necessity of convening a new ecumenical synod, a necessity so emphatically urged by Leo with tears and groans when he wrote his fortieth letter to the emperor Theodosius, I do not see that Quesnell has improved his case by failing to refute what we brought forward above.

11. First of all, it is useful to ask the adversary who judged that an ecumenical synod was necessary amid the clash of such great events and disturbances: Flavian, or the supreme pontiff Saint Leo? Certainly not Flavian, whom we have seen to have appealed only to the apostolic see and whom, in all likelihood—and with the greatest certainty, indeed—we know not even to have thought of a general synod.

This is clear not only because four months earlier he vigorously opposed the rumor that a synod was to be convened on behalf of his own case and that of Eutyches, but also because from Leo’s letters we clearly infer that he placed his written appeal in the hands of the pontifical legates in such a way that he wished and requested to have Saint Leo alone as judge of his case.

This is sufficiently indicated by Saint Leo’s words found in letter 42. For, having received through the deacon Hilary the written appeal of the holy bishop, Leo wrote to him as the sole and supreme arbiter of that case, assuring him that he was neglecting nothing required for their common cause, so that first we might deserve to reach those matters that could affect the whole body of the faithful.

He then says that he is writing a very brief letter. But he adds that, in such a great and grievous condition of mourning and sadness, Flavian could receive some consolation from the bearer of that letter, who would be able to explain in words everything toward which, with the Lord’s help, Leo was directing his efforts in devotion to the faith and charity.

I ought not to have brought these words to Quesnell’s attention, since he has undertaken to illuminate and adorn the writings of Saint Leo and cannot be unaware of them. But let him observe, I ask, that when Leo says he is neglecting nothing for their common cause, he means to indicate that he is applying every concern so as to provide for his own cause, Flavian’s cause, and the cause of the entire body of the faithful.

He says not one word about a synodal judgment to which the case ought by right to be referred. Nor does he assert that a synod had to be held because the rules of the canons prescribed it whenever someone appealed from a preceding synod. For if it had been an established, ordinary, customary, and accepted practice that appeals presented to the apostolic see were thereafter to be referred to another general synod, Saint Leo would have adopted a different wording in his letter and would never have told Flavian that the bearer of the letter would be able to explain everything toward which, with the Lord’s help, Leo was directing his efforts in devotion to the faith and charity.

Who, then, believes that Leo needed to devote effort to determining the most effective means and remedy by which to uproot and abolish completely the evils then raging in the Church, if the canons had already established and determined that cases of appeal were to be settled in ecumenical councils? Do not the words “everything toward which, with the Lord’s help, we are directing our efforts” imply that the Roman pontiff possessed full authority to define, deliberate, prescribe the method and order, and determine the remedy itself by which he might provide for the failing faith and the charity ruptured among the priests of the East?

12. Quesnell would have perfectly understood that the holy pontiff Leo was moved by those two causes—faith and charity—to decide that an ecumenical synod should be employed as a necessary remedy, if he had not torn the words to which he appeals and upon which he insists from their setting, neglecting the other words with which the holy pontiff addressed the emperor Theodosius.

Leo therefore explains the most wretched condition of all affairs, indicating that the judgment and Acts of the Ephesian Robber Council had devolved upon the tribunal of the apostolic see, both because of the protest of his legates and because of Bishop Flavian’s appeal: “Because our men faithfully protested, and Bishop Flavian gave them the written appeal.”

From this premise he immediately adds the following, as necessarily connected with the rights of the apostolic see: “Order a general synod to be held within Italy, which may either remove or mitigate all offenses in such a way that nothing further may remain doubtful in the faith or divided in charity” [Note: Saint Leo the Great, letter 40, chapter 3.].

So that this decree of his might not appear unjust or unreasonable to the emperor Theodosius, Leo recalls to his mind the supreme necessity and miserable condition of the Churches of the East. Some of their bishops had shamefully fallen in the Ephesian synod, some had been deposed, and others had been overcome by threats and subjected to injuries. For all these circumstances he prescribes an ecumenical council as the one necessary remedy.

He affirms that by this remedy alone everything can be restored to the former path of truth. Thus those who, driven either by fear or deceived by ignorance, had deviated from the ordinances of faith and charity—and even those who had maliciously stained themselves with crimes—would neither fall away from nor be separated from the unity of the Church, whenever, having changed their minds, they were brought back to repentance through a proper and solemn retraction.

Quesnell therefore ought to have considered the meaning of the following words before congratulating himself on having won the case against John David and the other writers of better judgment and learning. “When the bishops of the provinces of the East assemble,” Saint Leo says, “let those who, overcome by threats and injuries, have deviated from the path of truth be restored through salutary remedies; and let those whose case is more difficult not fall from the unity of the Church, if they yield to better counsels.”

That this should necessarily be required after an appeal had been lodged, the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify . . . .—those decrees established by the priests of the whole world and appended below.

13. It is therefore clear what disposition the most holy pontiff Leo intended happily to bring about. Neither the emperor nor anyone else could have rejected it as unjust or unsuitable to the evils then raging, for two most serious motives expressed in the law, upon which the supreme pontiff relied in determining that a council should be held: one motive was drawn from the genuine Nicene canons established by the priests of the whole world; the other arose both from the solemn protest of the pontifical legates and from Flavian’s appeal.

Since these two matters had not previously been distinguished by the writers, they were thereafter free to reason according to their own preference and to adopt different judgments and opinions, as will be evident to those who have examined the writings of Launoy, Peter de Marca, Quesnell, John David, and others. Nevertheless, we consider it unnecessary at present to set out here the various interpretations of these writers, who disagree with one another.

None of them grasped the method of reasoning employed by the holy pontiff in writing. Although they attended exclusively to the Sardican canons and used various conjectures, we shall refrain for the present from discussing them, so that we may devote our attention, as far as possible and step by step, to examining Quesnell’s statements.

“It was not therefore,” he says, “to one of the Western bishops together with a provincial or diocesan synod that the appeal was made.”

But who has ever affirmed, or will ever affirm with truth, what Quesnell imagines? What person so dull and leaden could adopt this view? We do not say that the Roman pontiff was appealed to together with a provincial or diocesan synod because, when Hilary, the legate of Saint Leo to the Ephesian synod, came to Rome while the annual council was being held, he laid the entire matter before the Fathers assembled in the City in order to confer with them about it.

It is entirely clear that the Fathers made no decision at all concerning that deeply troubled condition of the Churches of the East. What is established is only that they joined their bitter lamentations, tears, and groans to those of the supreme pontiff, in order to move the mind of the emperor Theodosius to grant free permission for the holding of a new ecumenical synod, just as the supreme pontiff himself had decided immediately upon receiving Flavian’s appeal.

But Quesnell adds: “Why is an ecumenical synod necessarily demanded when an ecumenical synod was not appealed to?” He further contends that, in so great a crisis of affairs, “if Flavian had appealed to Leo alone, as the one and only bishop, he could have summoned the litigants before him, investigated the matter, sought the judgment of his fellow bishops, and pronounced the decision.”

I am truly astonished to hear a man whom those who revised and approved these studies of his on the works of Saint Leo judged to be endowed with great learning and thoroughly versed in ecclesiastical affairs inventing such arguments, with no regard whatsoever for the laws of equity, prudence, and justice that always guided Saint Leo in his counsels and deliberations.

The judgment of the holy pontiff had to be pure, correct, and subject to no exception. Its force ought to depend not only upon authority and power, but also upon those solemnities required to restore to their former condition the rights of his see that had been overthrown. He could never have fully obtained that restoration without the solemnity of the entire universal Church.

Moreover, what kind of remedy would he have applied by summoning the litigants before him, investigating the matter, and pronouncing judgment? If the dispute had existed only between Flavian and Eutyches, Saint Leo might perhaps have done this, because he possessed plenary authority and would not have been compelled by the various other grave circumstances and calamities of the situation to determine that an ecumenical synod was necessary.

But let Quesnell say, I ask, how Saint Leo could have compelled Dioscorus and the entire Eutychian faction to appear before the apostolic see; how he could have brought ninety-two bishops who had offered their hands captive through impious subscriptions at the Ephesian synod to a public and solemn retraction; and finally, how he could have broken the intolerable audacity of the monks of Constantinople and Egypt, so that they might not, after abandoning all arrogance and impiety, fall from the unity of the Church as penitents.

The supreme pontiff certainly owed it to Flavian’s justice and holiness to provide the necessary protection, but at the same time he had to prescribe the kind of remedy that would benefit everyone else. Otherwise, together with the authors of so many crimes and their associates, the entire body of Catholics in the East would have perished.

Quesnell could therefore have foreseen [Note: Quesnell, in the same dissertation, p. 306, no. 4.] that the following passage, which he himself transcribed concerning the case of Saint John Chrysostom—unjustly deposed—from Sozomen, would be especially relevant to our subject [Note: Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 16]. He writes of Pope Innocent I:

“He endeavored to convene an ecumenical synod, and, writing to the clergy of Constantinople, he asked in these words what remedy should be applied: ‘But what remedy shall we presently bring to these circumstances? A synodal inquiry will be necessary, which we have already said should have been convened long before now. For it alone can blunt the force of storms of this kind. Until we obtain it, it is expedient to entrust the healing of this calamity more to the will of God and of his Christ, our Lord.’”

Later, concerning the same synod that he had decreed and wished to be put into effect, Innocent says that he deliberated greatly, adding: “We indeed deliberate at length about how an ecumenical synod might be convened, through which, by the will of God, these turbulent disturbances might be quieted.”

Who, then, does not understand that Quesnell is killing himself with his own sword by appealing to Pope Innocent? For the holy pontiff had decided that an ecumenical synod had to be held for no other reason than that Chrysostom had appealed to him.

### 14

Notwithstanding these considerations, our adversary flatters himself that he possesses profound insight, and insists that two conclusions of the greatest importance can be drawn from what precedes. The first, he says—and this is what we rejected above—is that Flavian’s appeal devolved not upon some single pontiff, but upon all, or at least all the bishops of the West. The second is that the legates of the Apostolic See attended the Second Synod of Ephesus not merely in the name of the Roman pontiff alone, nor did they customarily attend the ecumenical councils convened in the East in any other capacity, but rather as deputies of all the bishops of the West, whose representation they undertook when those bishops could not attend in person.

“This,” he adds, “was customary for the Roman bishop: whenever a universal synod was first announced, he would notify all the bishops of his patriarchate of the matter and himself convene a synod at Rome, to which the Westerners who had been invited would assemble” [Col. 1186A].

These are indeed matters of great importance, which he attempts to sell to men entirely unacquainted with the history and affairs of the Roman pontiffs. Let us examine the two claims briefly according to the rules of law and truth, so that we may determine from what source they have been drawn and on what grounds appeals made to the one supreme pontiff are held to have devolved upon all, or at least all the bishops of the West.

Either, then, he must believe that such cases devolved upon a synod by the will and intention of those who lodged the appeals, or by the decree and disposition of that single bishop to whom the appeal was made. If the former, then the appellant ought not to address his petition to one bishop alone; or, if he directs his petition to one alone but wishes to be judged by other bishops of the West as well, he must necessarily state this explicitly.

But from where does he infer that Flavian mentioned any Western bishop [Col. 1186B] in his petition? From what we and other writers have so far noted, it is certain that he appealed only to the Apostolic See and to the one pontiff, Saint Leo. Hence John David’s argument would here carry considerable—indeed, very considerable—weight: he demonstrates that Flavian delivered his appeal not to the bishop of Milan, Aquileia, Ravenna, Arles, or Lyons, but solely to the Roman bishop, while that bishop’s legates protested.

It remains, therefore, that Flavian’s case could have devolved upon a Western council only by the will and decree of Saint Leo. But what derogation from the supreme authority of the Roman pontiffs would result if they themselves decided to discuss, examine, and settle affairs in this or that order, manner, or formality? Can they not call some or many bishops of the West into partnership in their pastoral care, disclose and explain to them the entire sequence of matters to be handled, and also seek their votes, so that nothing might appear to be lacking from the solemnity of the judgments which Saint Leo wished to indicate by the following manner of writing: “Leo, and the holy synod which has assembled at Rome” [Col. 1186C]?

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Leo the Great, Letter to Theodosius 26, to the Synod of Ephesus 32, and elsewhere passim.]

### 15

Still more serious, however, is that other fallacy which Quesnell introduced and employed solely to exalt the authority of the Roman pontiffs while confining it within the narrowest limits. We must therefore ask him where he learned that Saint Leo’s legates had been appointed to this office by the mandate and delegation of the entire Western synod.

That Saint Leo sent them from his own side, without consulting any other bishop, is made clear to us by those formulas of writing: “Those whom I have sent from my side”; “that they may attend the holy assembly of your fraternity in my place”; “that they may adequately supply the place of my presence”; and other expressions of this kind, which we frequently encounter in letters written both before and after the Council of Ephesus.

Either, then, Quesnell must grant that the authority of the entire Western synod resided in the Roman bishop alone, or [Col. 1186D] that those legates represented the person of the Roman pontiff alone. If the first is true, then the Roman pontiff alone possesses the authority of the entire synod: he alone can establish, define, judge, and decree, and his decrees will have as much force and authority as they would have if they had been issued by the entire Western synod. The same follows if the legates represented the Roman pontiff alone. Thus, whichever way he turns, Quesnell cuts his own throat by proposing this new fallacy. For whichever alternative he grants, he will be forced to admit that those legates represented Saint Leo alone.

But it is clear that the legates of whom we are speaking ought not to have received a mandate from a Western synod of bishops. For we have seen above that Saint Leo the Great could not compel a synod of the Western bishops, even if he had wished to do so. At the end of May he received Theodosius’s letters concerning the convocation of the Synod of Ephesus, and he immediately sent delegates to it, as is evident from his letters to Flavian, Theodosius, Julian of Cos, the Empress Pulcheria, and to the Synod of Ephesus itself, written on the Ides of June.

Could he, then, within the course of a few days, have announced, held, and completed a council of the Western bishops, so that its authority might equip the legates and send them from Rome toward the East? Let Quesnell say, I beg him, whether he foresaw this argument while arranging and preparing the writings of the holy pontiff; and, if he foresaw it, how he intended to evade it.

### 16

Those two fabrications which he introduced to mislead his readers cannot in fact rescue him. He maintains repeatedly that the same thing was done by the Roman pontiffs either when the ecumenical council was to be held under Pope Celestine, or when the Western legates were required to proceed to the Sixth Synod.

First, then, he observed that Saint Cyril, repeating the judgment of the legates of the Apostolic See at the Council of Ephesus, speaks as follows:

“For they deposed them, supplying the place of the Apostolic See and of the entire synod of the most holy and most beloved Western bishops.”

And in the report sent to the emperor:

“The most pious archbishop of your great Rome, and the entire Western synod, through the most holy bishops whom it itself sent to us,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 1187D] Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, Part II, Act 3.]

He adds:

“It is manifest from the Acts of the Sixth Council, where the bishops of Portus, Paternus, and Rhegium are said to occupy the place of the council of ancient Rome, at which one hundred and twenty bishops had assembled. Hence, very frequently, when our pontiff sends legates from a synod, he writes not only in his own name but also in the name of the council, in this form: ‘Leo, and the holy synod which has assembled at Rome,’ and so forth.”

Thus far Quesnellus, who either wished to deceive the reader under the guise of truth, or showed that he was entirely ignorant of the histories to which he appealed. To explain both points [Col. 1187C], we do not at all deny that the Roman pontiffs, when the opportunity arose—when many bishops came to Rome for the annual synod, or when they themselves approached the thresholds of the holy apostles to seek counsel from the Apostolic See concerning the affairs and business of their dioceses—sometimes held assemblies, or that, in the customary synods recurring each year, they regularly proposed matters which had been brought to them from the East.

This happened especially when the matter concerned the condemnation of new heresies and precautions against their authors: namely, lest some error should gradually be introduced that might corrupt the hearts of the simple, or lest the faithful should communicate with men whose faith had been violated. In both cases, therefore, questions of law as well as of fact were discussed in the synods held at Rome, and the Roman pontiff sent their resolutions to the Eastern synods or bishops as the firmest rules to be followed by all.

That this occurred in the case of the Nestorian doctrine, before the ecumenical Council of Ephesus was convened, is demonstrated most clearly by the letters of Pope Saint Celestine to Saint Cyril of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1187D] Celestine’s letter is found in Volume III of the Councils, Part I of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus. Baronius, year 430, no. 1 and following.]. In them he commands that, unless Nestorius within ten days should recant by a retractation both in preaching to the people and in writing, he should be struck with anathema and another bishop appointed to the See of Constantinople.

Our adversary cannot call this into doubt, since the synod held in that year did not deal with sending legates to the East for the purpose of convening the ecumenical Council of Ephesus. The legates of the Apostolic See, therefore, of whom Quesnellus speaks, were appointed at another Roman synod, likewise held in the following year in the case of Nestorius.

When I first turned my eyes to that passage of the Council of Ephesus on which our adversary insists, I was led by a grave suspicion to think that the matter had been presented differently from the way it actually stood. I discovered, however, that I had not been deceived by this suspicion. For when I examined the Acts of the Roman synod convened by Celestine in the year 431, I understood very clearly not merely that Quesnellus’s structure was tottering, but that it had entirely collapsed.

In the Acts of that council, then, as the most learned Stephen Baluzius also wisely observed, we encounter two classes, or, so to speak, two orders of legates. Some were appointed by the Roman synod for the execution of the sentence issued against Nestorius; others were chosen by Pope Celestine himself to occupy his place and exercise his authority at the ecumenical synod.

One of Saint Celestine’s legates was Cyril, archbishop, or patriarch, of Alexandria; the other was Philip, a Roman presbyter. The pontiff sent Philip from his own side. To Saint Cyril, who never came to Rome for the synod, he entrusted, after a lengthy exchange of letters, the exercise of his own legation and that of the Apostolic See at the ecumenical synod.

And because the decree of the Roman synod had determined that a legation should be sent to the Synod of Ephesus, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus were selected for this task, so that they might set forth the judgment of the entire holy Western synod.

Quesnellus could therefore have seen that the legates of Pope Celestine and those of the Western synod were not the same. He could also have understood that the former legates had been charged with representing the supreme pontiff and occupying his place, whereas the latter had been sent to present the judgment of the entire holy Western synod to the ecumenical council.

This difference, then, between the persons and the legations completely overturns Quesnellus’s fiction, by which he maintained that the legates of the Apostolic See had attended the synod in the name of all the Westerners and represented them all.

### 17

We likewise infer this distinction from the Acts of the general Council of Ephesus, nor are we compelled by the words of Saint Cyril quoted by Quesnellus. For although Saint Cyril does not there make a distinct mention of each of the individual legates, he indicates, without expressing their names, first those who occupied the place of the Apostolic See and then those whom the Western synod convened under Celestine had appointed. Hence he said:

“For they deposed them, supplying the place of the Apostolic See and of the entire synod of the most holy and most beloved Western bishops” [Note: [Col. 1188D] Volume III of the Councils, p. 559 in my copy, from Baluzius’s new collection.]

That both groups of legates were required to act impartially on behalf of the rights of the Apostolic See is evident from the instruction which Saint Celestine himself had given them. He commanded that, when they arrived at Ephesus, they should refer all counsel to “Saint Cyril, our holy brother and fellow bishop,” and do whatever they saw to be his judgment [Note: [Col. 1188D] This instruction of Saint Celestine is found in Volume III of the General Councils, p. 560 in my copy.]

He then added:

“And we command you to preserve the authority of the Apostolic See.”

Finally, he indicated in the following words how they ought to conduct themselves in that synod: “If perhaps the matter should come to debate, you are to judge their opinions, not enter into the contest.”

By this instruction Celestine wished to safeguard the honor and authority of his own see and of the entire Western synod, and to act in the persons of these men as the supreme judge of ecclesiastical affairs and matters of faith—he who had already settled the case of Nestorius at Rome, and from whom nothing further was desired except the execution of the sentence issued against Nestorius.

It is therefore not surprising that, from the heading of the aforesaid instruction, we understand that the bishops and presbyters going to the East were equally charged with carrying out the sentence of the Roman pontiff and of the Western synod. For all of them, together with Cyril, were to labor so that the wishes of the Roman pontiff might be fulfilled.

[Col. 1189A]

### 18

I would nevertheless gladly grant that Quesnellus could not have gathered the great diversity between the aforementioned legates from the preceding material, either because he examined the Acts of the Council of Ephesus too hastily, without carefully considering whether the sequence of events supported his interpretations, or because, led by his zeal for defending a new opinion and indulging the assertions of his amanuensis, he flattered himself that, apart from the legates of the Western synod, no others had been sent to the ecumenical Council of Ephesus to represent Pope Celestine and occupy his place.

But I can scarcely regard him as deserving of excuse for failing to notice what is made entirely clear in the same action, in the preceding action, and in those that follow. For these proceedings repeatedly speak of Philip, the Roman presbyter, who occupied Celestine’s place and exercised the legation of the Apostolic See.

They then speak of the two bishops, Arcadius and Projectus, who are designated as legates of the Roman Church. In these proceedings as well, the first to rise to speak was Philip, to whom the first place was given. By virtue of the legation which he held, he occupied Celestine’s place; hence in the Acts we read: “Philip, presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See, said.”

Arcadius and Projectus, although they held the higher clerical rank, spoke after Philip. To indicate their delegation, the notary of the council used the following words:

“Arcadius, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, said.”

And again:

“Projectus, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, said.”

When I noticed this difference in the formulas of speaking and writing, I understood perfectly that Quesnellus’s entire preceding structure had been destroyed and reduced to nothing—especially when we consider that Philip himself, speaking second, requested that the letters of Pope Saint Celestine be read in the synod. After they had been read, he gave thanks to the ecumenical council and briefly proclaimed the rights, prerogatives, and primacy throughout the whole Church of the Roman pontiffs [Col. 1189C].

[Note: [Col. 1189D] Philip the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See said: “We give thanks to the holy and venerable synod because, when the letters of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you, you, holy members, have joined yourselves by your holy voices to the holy head, and by your holy acclamations as well . . . . . . For your Blessedness is not unaware that the blessed apostle Peter is the head of the whole faith, indeed even of the apostles.
