Therefore, since our humble person, tossed about and afflicted by many storms, has arrived late, we ask that you order us to be informed of what was done in this holy synod before our arrival, so that, in accordance with the judgment of our blessed pope and of this present holy assembly, we too may confirm it, in conformity with their deposition.” Act 2 of the Council of Ephesus, Volume III, pp. 1150 and following.]

Furthermore, because he had been tossed about and afflicted by many storms and could not reach Ephesus by the appointed day, before the general synod had begun, and because the first session had already been concluded while Bishops Arcadius and Projectus were still absent, he asked that the proceedings be explained to him, so that, by the authority given him by the Roman pontiff, he might confirm them.

In the second session as well he proclaimed similar things in praise of the Roman pontiff, the successor of blessed Peter, adding:

“He sent us to the holy synod to supply his presence” [Note: [Col. 1190D] See also the deposition of the same Philip the presbyter, conducted in the third session, p. 1154.]

### 19

Let us now inquire whether the Acts of the Sixth Council can support Quesnellus’s opinion. Here too, however, the Roman synod convened by Agatho in the case of the Monothelites reveals that Quesnellus stood opposed to manifest truth by means of a falsehood.

For although the three legates—John of Portus, Abundantius of Paternus, and John of Rhegium, or Regitanus—had been chosen at this synod, the supreme pontiff wished to safeguard his own rights and added his own legation to that public delegation.

For this task he selected Bishop Theodosius, the presbyter George, the deacon John, and the subdeacon Constantine. To these men, as Anastasius the Librarian says, he gave, in his own name alone, a certain letter addressed to the emperor [Col. 1190A].

Thus a twofold legation must also be admitted for the Sixth General Synod. Lest the testimony of Anastasius the Librarian be considered spurious or wrongly interpreted, it will be useful to bring forward the Acts of the Sixth Council itself. Although they were interpolated and corrupted by the Greeks out of hatred for Honorius and the Apostolic See, they nevertheless provide the material from which we can demonstrate most clearly the truth at issue.

The first of all who subscribed the Acts of the general synod were Agatho’s legates. For we read:

“Theodore, humble bishop of the holy Roman Church, acting in the place of Agatho, thrice-blessed and universal pope of the city of Rome, have subscribed and signed.”

The other two legates of Agatho used a substantially similar formula of subscription, although they were not of episcopal rank. Immediately after Theodore, before any other bishops or episcopal legates, they subscribed as follows:

“George, humble presbyter of the holy Roman Church, and acting in the place of Agatho, thrice-blessed and universal pope of the city of Rome, have subscribed and signed.”

Finally, in third place, John the deacon, likewise Agatho’s legate, subscribed with them.

If, however, we examine the subscription of the legates of the Roman synod, we shall find that it was very different. In ninth place appears the name of John, bishop of Portus, with the following formula:

“John, unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Portus, legate of the entire council of the holy Apostolic See of the city of Rome, have subscribed and signed in defining.”

Finally, in twelfth and thirteenth place, the subscriptions of two other legates of that same Roman synod were entered under the preceding formula.

Where, then, does Quesnellus get the idea that the legates of the Roman pontiffs represented and customarily represented the persons of the entire Western council in the ecumenical synods? Where does he infer that the legates of the Apostolic See attended the ecumenical councils convened in the East not merely in the name of the Roman pontiff alone, but in place of all the bishops of the West, whose representation they carried when those bishops could not attend in person?

Those two examples invented by him plainly prove the exact opposite. It will therefore be permissible to conclude that Quesnellus’s mind was not seeking truth by adhering to the facts of ecclesiastical history, but rather wandered here and there and clung to the nonsense of dreamers, who, while asleep, are accustomed to imagine that they have already found whatever, while awake, they most earnestly desired [Col. 1190C].

[Note: [Col. 1190D] Anastasius the Librarian, in the Life of Agatho. See also the recent edition of the most illustrious Father Joseph Blanchini, Volume III. See likewise Volume VII of the Councils, p. 1063.]

### 20

Yet Quesnellus still flattered himself that the preceding nonsense could possess force and authority. Accordingly, without abandoning his plan, he appeals to Letter 77 of Saint Leo, written to the bishops of Gaul.

But, failing to keep before his eyes the purpose, time, and circumstances that moved the pontiff to compose this letter, he turns his attack upon John David, criticizing him because he had written:

“Since it was said that the petition of appeal had been handed over to the legates, he asserted that Flavian had appealed to Leo alone. He immediately adds: ‘For it is evident from the foregoing that the legates did not represent the person of the pontiff alone, but that of all the Westerners; consequently, the appeal was brought before all those in whose name they attended the synod.’”

Behold a new dream of Quesnellus [Note: [Col. 1190D] Quesnellus, in the aforementioned Dissertation 8, no. 5, p. 307]. He now imagines that he has defeated his adversary David and sings victory because he has supposedly proved that appeals to the one Roman pontiff are contrary to ecclesiastical custom and the rights of synods—when he ought rather to have mourned the disaster threatening him on account of the gravest fabrications, perhaps artfully assembled to exalt and diminish the authority of the Roman pontiffs.

For the moment, however, our method of writing does not permit us to discuss what must be said about the letter of the holy pontiff to the bishops of Gaul. We shall treat it in another volume of the Works of Saint Leo, when we review his actions after the Council of Chalcedon, lest we seem to confuse the chronology.

For now we merely note that the letter contains no mention of Flavian’s appeal, around which our controversy turns. Leo merely informs the bishops of Gaul that he has received their confession of faith, formally presented, by which they subscribed to the dogmatic letter on the incarnation of the Word, which he had long before written to Flavian as a certain rule of faith to be followed by all.

He gives thanks to God that they had chosen to adhere, with complete unanimity and without the tumult of disputes, to the evangelical and apostolic tradition [Col. 1191B]. We find not a single word that could now support Quesnellus’s cause, which has been utterly ruined.

### 21

It will therefore be necessary to proceed to other matters that meet us in number six of the same dissertation, where he begins his discussion with the Nicene canons praised by Saint Leo in the aforementioned Letter 40.

First, in the margin, he notes:

“David argues badly from the Sardican canons praised by Leo.”

And then, in the body of the same chapter, alluding to the same David, he says:

“But that writer,” he says, “maintains that Saint Leo cites the authority of the Nicene canons—or, in this passage, of the Sardican canons—in order to assert the justice of his request following Flavian’s appeal. Yet the Sardican canons mention no appeal except one that concerns the Roman bishop alone. Therefore, either Saint Leo misuses the decrees of the synod and applies them improperly to this case, he says, or he understood Flavian’s appeal to have devolved upon himself.”

Quesnellus, our adversary, denies that David’s cause can be supported by these weak props in comparison with the contrary arguments he himself has proposed. And since no mention of appeals occurs in the Nicene canons, he almost mocks David for wishing, together with other writers, to rely on conjecture.

He nevertheless concedes, not unwillingly, that the Sardican canons, here wearing another name, were cited by Leo to demonstrate the necessity of an ecumenical council. But if this method of argument stands, he says, no one could regard it as worthy of Leo.

He then brings forward an argument which in the schools is called a syllogism, in order to attack David. And, as those boys commonly do who practice themselves in the first lessons of dialectic, he says:

“You see, my David, how absurd is that major premise upon which your argument must rest?”

He then contends that the syllogism, arranged and explained according to David’s method, must instead be set out in another way, so that it may yield the conclusion that, by the decree of the Sardican canons, a council had to be convened in which the appeal could be examined [Col. 1191D].

Following the scholastic method, he proceeds to posit “one thing,” which he considers foreign to David’s mind and regards as of the greatest importance. Namely:

“The pontiff was persuaded that, when the Sardican synod granted bishops the power to appeal to the Apostolic See, or to the Roman bishop, it intended the appeal to be brought not to the bishop taken in isolation, but to him surrounded by the bishops of his dioceses; nor did it consider the case to be judged otherwise than by all the Western bishops assembled under the patriarch.”

Thus he strains in vain every resource of his learning to defend the system he has adopted.

He then introduces those words of Saint Leo urging the emperor Theodosius:

“Whenever the bishops of the provinces of the East assemble,”

and adds:

“Then the pontiff’s reasoning, by which he urges Augustus, will not be defective, but will rather agree in every respect with the rules of dialectic.”

To demonstrate this, Saint Leo’s enthymeme must be resolved into a syllogism; and from that resolution everyone should see more clearly than in the light of midday what he had in mind and what must necessarily be supplied.

### 22

It is indeed a beautiful structure, painted only with the color of truth; but because it has been badly built, it must appear utterly ruinous to those who do not merely contemplate the outward appearance of things, but strive to investigate and examine them as they are truly constructed.

For the present, then, I shall set aside the subsequent syllogism which Quesnellus constructed in order to attack David. In constructing it, Quesnellus labored under a false supposition—as the schools say. Accordingly, it does not merely totter; it collapses entirely [Col. 1192B].

Nor should David be brought against me on the ground that, under the name of the Nicene canons, he understood the Sardican canons and appealed to them. Quesnellus concealed the reason why David introduced these Sardican canons.

David was arguing against Launoy and the other supporters of this opinion [Note: [Col. 1191D] Launoy, Letters, Part II, Letter 3, p. 3 in my copy. There, in opposition to Bellarmine, whom he attacks in a letter written to Boethius of Saint Victor, he transcribes three Sardican canons—namely, the third, fourth, and seventh—by which he asserts that Pope Gelasius insisted in his letter to the bishops of Dardania [Col. 1192D].]

Therefore, wishing to criticize these men, David first had to proceed from the same principles; and, in refuting their opinions, he was at least bound to prove that, by force of ecclesiastical law, Flavian’s appeal devolved upon the sole and unique Roman pontiff, not upon a Western synod.

I do not see, then, how David can be charged with wrongdoing. Rather, his adversaries—and Quesnellus above all—must bear the mark of blame, since they have failed entirely to grasp the holy pontiff’s manner of speaking and his method of conducting affairs.

To understand the mind of the holy pontiff, two things must be distinguished. Neither of them should be referred to the Sardican canons: one belongs to divine law, the other to the fifth [Col. 1192C] and sixth Nicene canons, to which, in my judgment, Saint Leo principally appealed.

For the right to receive appeals and, above all, to hear the cases of appealing bishops, the Roman pontiffs received not merely from the decrees of the canons but from divine institution. Consequently, after receiving the petitions of appellants, it belonged to them alone to determine and establish the type of judicial process which they judged most suitable and necessary to the circumstances of the case, the changes of the times—for at times they were compelled to accommodate themselves to irregular movements of secular powers—and the usefulness of the Churches and the peace of the priests.

We should therefore not be surprised that, although after receiving appeals it remained within their power to choose and establish one or another kind of remedy, they should determine upon that which was more consonant with the sacred canons and which would provide for and benefit the whole body of the faithful, not merely the interests of a few.

Since, then, the condition of the Churches of the East was such as the Robber Council of Ephesus demonstrates it to have been, our most holy pontiff, keeping both rights before his eyes—namely, divine and ecclesiastical law—wished, by virtue of the appeal he had received, to decree and establish that the cases of all the Easterners should be solemnly treated and concluded in a new general council.

For the holding of that synod he prescribed rules of such a kind that they would repair the rights of his see, violated by Dioscorus’s arrogance, and which he judged capable of benefiting the universal Church.

This is plainly indicated by the words of Leo that we explained above. Quesnellus had shortly before objected only to their first part, imagining that it could support his ruined cause.

[Col. 1193A]

### 23

“Whenever the bishops of the provinces of the East assemble, so that if any of them, overcome by threats and injuries, have departed from the path of truth, they may be restored by salutary remedies; and so that those whose case is more difficult, if they yield to better counsels, may not fall away from the unity of the Church.”

That this should necessarily be required after an appeal had been lodged is attested by the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world and are appended below [Note: [Col. 1193D] Letters 39 and 40 of Saint Leo.]

Quesnellus adds:

“For those decrees enacted at Nicaea and praised by Saint Leo are so obscure to most people that nothing could be more obscure. Nothing of the kind is found among the Nicene canons; and David is compelled to take refuge among the Sardican canons, which he conjectures Leo cited under the name of the Nicene canons, as many before him conjectured. Yet we willingly concede that the Sardican canons, here wearing another name, were cited by Leo to demonstrate the necessity of an ecumenical council.”

Thus far Quesnellus. Arbitrarily attacking David without distinction, he then appends two syllogisms: one which David had constructed from his own principles, and another which Quesnellus himself fabricated from his own brain in order utterly to weaken and overthrow the opinion of David and other sensible men.

Finally, he busies himself only with determining Saint Leo’s intention from the Sardican canons. He transcribes three Sardican canons—namely, the third, fourth, and seventh—and maintains that the preceding words of Saint Leo must be referred to them.

But all who are unwilling to cling merely to the final words of the holy pontiff and who do not refuse to attend carefully to the structure of the entire context, the order of the words, and their meaning, will judge with me, without the slightest hesitation, that Quesnellus has wasted both time and effort.

When all these things are compared with the Nicene canons, the conjectures of the many will finally cease—conjectures into which most of them have fallen because, under Quesnellus’s influence, those decrees were considered so obscure that nothing more obscure could be desired or found [Col. 1193C].

### 24

Let us therefore set forth the fifth Nicene canon:

“Concerning those who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, let the regular sentence of the bishops in each province prevail, so that those who are rejected may not be received by others. Let inquiry also be made lest the bishops appear to have excluded them from the assembly through faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault.

Therefore, so that inquiry may be conducted more appropriately, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops of the province assembled together, such questions may be examined; and thus those who have sinned against their bishop may clearly and reasonably be regarded as excommunicated by all, until it please the assembly of the bishops” [Note: [Col. 1193D] This fifth Nicene canon, according to the interpretation of Dionysius Exiguus [Col. 1194D], is found in Volume II of the Councils, p. 44 in my copy.]

The collectors of the councils placed the following in the margin:

“Either by the common judgment, or by the bishop’s judgment, it may please him to give a more merciful sentence in such cases,” and so forth.

25. [Col. 1193D] Let Quesnellus now compare whether the words of the holy pontiff urging the emperor bear any resemblance to the decree of this canon—while preserving, nevertheless, that mode of reasoning which the schools call “from the lesser to the greater.” For what is there in Leo’s words that does not correspond to this canon? Here the matter concerns a layman or cleric cut off and expelled from his rank through oppression, violence, and the tyranny of a judge. Leo, however, deals with bishops who, overcome by threats and injuries, have solemnly strayed from the path of truth. The council, discussing certain evils spreading through a single province—laymen or clerics irregularly excommunicated, and finally bishops exercising violence and tyranny—prescribes as a remedy that a provincial synod be convened, at which the matter may be investigated more appropriately and such questions discussed. [Col. 1194A] The holy pontiff, however, was not approached by a petition of appeal to investigate questions belonging to one province, but was appealed to in order to abolish the scandals of the entire East, defend the faith of Catholics, and rescue from unjust oppression the most holy bishops who had been excommunicated and deposed through violence, fury, and wanton abuse of power. He therefore requests that a general synod be held, and prescribes it as a remedy that must necessarily be applied, so that, as he says, they may be restored to wholeness by salutary remedies.

The Council of Nicaea finally decrees that no indulgence be shown to those whom the synod shall reasonably judge to have been excommunicated by the bishop, until it has pleased the agreement of the entire synod or the bishop’s will to pronounce a more lenient sentence in their case. In the same way, when Saint Leo speaks of those bishops who, maliciously, at the Ephesian Robber Synod, impelled by hatred or ancient rivalries, acted treacherously—men whose case was more difficult if they wished, through repentance, to submit to better counsels—[Col. 1194B] he prescribed that they were not to be cut off from the unity of the Church. Let Quesnellus, I beg, say whether this decree of Leo corresponds most closely to the Nicene canons. Let him point out the difference.

26. But some will answer that Launoy and Quesnellus have already pointed out the difference, saying that the words of Saint Leo the Great in no way correspond to the Nicene decrees, since none of the latter makes mention of appeals. For since this opinion concerning appeals can be gathered only obscurely from those three canons of Sardica, it supposedly follows, with good reason, that the holy pontiff had in mind these canons, disguised under the name of the Nicene canons.

But what does this answer accomplish? Those who are accustomed to examining the writings of the holy pontiff ought to know that Leo’s words bear another meaning. For he did not claim that, by force of the canons, he possessed the right to receive, examine, and decide the cases of bishops who appealed to him. Rather, he prescribed that kind of remedy which alone could assist and benefit the distressed affairs of the East, the endangered faith, [Col. 1194C] and its oppressed defenders. This is what was necessarily demanded after an appeal had been lodged, as the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea testify.

He therefore assumes that the right of appeals was owed to him for another reason, and that he could and should receive appeals not because of the decrees of the canons, but because that right derived from divine institution, by which his administration of ecclesiastical affairs extended throughout the whole world. He speaks of this divinely entrusted care in many letters. But when writing to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, whom he had taken into partnership in his solicitude by delegating to him a share in his governance, he assigns no other reason than this: “That we may exercise the care which, by divine institution, we principally owe to all the Churches.” And in the final chapter of the same letter, distinguishing various ranks of bishops—some established in the lesser cities, others in the greater cities of the provinces, and consequently assuming either lesser or greater responsibility—he says: “Through whom [Col. 1194D] the care of the universal Church would flow together toward the one See of Peter, and nothing anywhere would be at variance with its head.”

We encounter a similar manner of expression in the letter to the monks of Palestine, which he began with these words: “It has been made known to my solicitude, which I owe to the universal Church and to all its sons, through the reports of many.” Later, when he more seriously considered the extremely heavy burden imposed upon him by God on the anniversary of his elevation, he declared that the administration of all and each of the bishops formed a portion of his labor, saying:

> “While people from the whole world gather at the See of blessed Peter the Apostle, and that love for the universal Church which the Lord entrusted to him is also demanded from our administration, we must feel the burden pressing upon us all the more, inasmuch as we owe more to everyone.”

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Epistle 12, chapters 1 and final; Epistle 47, chapter 1; Sermon 4, On the Anniversary of His Elevation, chapter 2; and elsewhere throughout.]

That Leo exercised this universal care in Eastern affairs at times, indeed very frequently, independently of any synod—or reserved the exercise of it to himself—is clearly evident from a certain letter written to Anatolius. In it, speaking of those who had sinned more gravely in the case of Eutyches and therefore claimed a superior place for themselves in that unfortunate synod—that is, the Ephesian synod—in order to burden the simplicity of their humbler brethren with the prejudices of their own arrogance, Leo writes that if they should repent and, ceasing to defend their conduct, turn instead to condemning their own error, then, if their satisfaction were such as not to appear unacceptable, it should be reserved for the more mature deliberations of the Apostolic See, “so that, after all matters have been examined and weighed, it may be determined what ought to be decreed concerning their actions.”

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Epistle 65, chapters 2 and 3.]

[Col. 1195B] Saint Leo wished this reservation of judgment to himself to carry such weight that neither Anatolius nor the presbyters of the Constantinopolitan Church were permitted to recite the names of the fallen at the altar before the pontiff had determined, in light of the course of events, that the satisfaction of these penitents ought to be admitted. He immediately added:

> “Nor, before the course of events shows what ought to be determined concerning them, is the name of any such person to be recited at the altar in the Church over which the Lord wished you to preside, as we have already written.”

Finally, he closes the letter by saying that he had instructed his legates, whom he had sent as his representatives, concerning everything that was to be done and carried out at the new synod of Chalcedon. But if anything should arise for deliberation beyond what he had set out in his memorandum, he requests that everything be reported to him, so that he might carefully determine what was to be observed. “And if,” he says, “anything concerning certain matters requires further deliberation, let a report be quickly sent to us, so that, after the nature of the cases has been considered, our solicitude may determine what ought to be observed.”

27. [Col. 1195C] From what has been said, it is therefore evident that Quesnellus and his other supporters are pressed much more severely. For why did Leo need to claim for himself the right of appeals made by Eastern bishops by virtue of the Sardican decrees, when he himself, consistently throughout all his writings and judgments, says that the authority by which he could care for all the Churches, judge questions of faith, define and settle contentious cases, and relax canonical penalties arose from the divine dispensation?

Why was it necessary for him to insist upon canons composed in the fourth century for the defense of the prerogatives and privileges of his see, when he affirmed that he was obliged to exercise solicitude for the universal Church and all its children, and that this care had been entrusted to him by the Lord because of the administration of his office—a burden he regarded as exceedingly heavy because he owed more to all the faithful?

And finally, was the referral of cases to the Apostolic See begun merely by virtue of the privilege of the Sardican canons, when, by divine institution, the care of the universal Church was to flow together toward the one See of Peter? Nonsense—mere nonsense. Saint Leo reasoned otherwise, so that the members might adhere to their head without the slightest disagreement.

[Col. 1195D] It is therefore not surprising that, under the title of the ecclesiastical primacy granted to him, even independently of any synod, he prescribed rules for matters to be conducted at synods, including ecumenical synods, which were to be observed inviolably; that he confined their authority in issuing judgments within narrow limits; and that he finally reserved to himself the task of examining and weighing whether the satisfaction and repentance of certain persons who had fallen into graver crimes deserved pardon and reconciliation.

There remains something still more serious with which Quesnellus, and the others mentioned above along with him, must be confronted. Namely, Saint Leo is shown to have taken precautions that even the bishops assembled at the celebrated Council of Chalcedon should not grant indulgence to certain persons already deprived of communion. [Col. 1196A] He forbade Anatolius and the other presbyters or bishops of the Constantinopolitan Church to dare recite their names at the altar before the Apostolic See itself had determined what was to be done. “So that,” he says, “after the nature of the cases has been considered, our solicitude may determine what ought to be observed.”

28. These are the matters that we have considered it necessary to write in order to expose Quesnellus’s absurdities and deceptions, and to wrest away and overturn the false arguments of that writer and others concerning the appeal of Saint Flavian to the Apostolic See and to the one supreme pontiff, Saint Leo.

We have not, however, been able to adduce all the points scattered throughout the works of the holy pontiff in which he asserts that the care of his pontificate extends throughout the whole world by divine institution, lest this present exercise should grow, as it were, without limit. Wishing therefore to bring it to an end, we have judged that one further point should be added: namely, that when Saint Leo wrote his letters to Theodosius, he had regard not only to the genuine fifth [Col. 1196B] Nicene canon but also to the sixth.

Nor is the latter to be understood in the manner in which the commonly circulated codices present it, but in the form in which it was recited at the Council of Chalcedon: namely, “that the Roman Church has always held the primacy.” The bishops of the whole world, approving this reading, plainly testified above all that the primacy of the Roman pontiff depends upon divine institution.

Leo therefore had no need to appeal to other canons besides the Nicene ones, or to bring forward the Sardican canons, disguised under the name of the Nicene canons, in support of his rights. Finally, because Quesnellus, wishing to make trouble for the Roman pontiffs, devoted much effort to interpreting the Sardican canons according to his own will, we reserve our discussion of them for the following exercise, to which we now turn our pen as an appendix to this one.

# CHAPTER X

## The Three Sardican Canons Are Discussed Especially, to Which Launoy, Quesnellus, and Others Appeal

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Launoy, part II, epistle 3.]

Launoy, Quesnellus, and others contend that Saint Flavian, moved solely by the force and authority of these canons, appealed to Saint Leo the Great so that his case might be brought to a new examination in a more numerous synod.

Their arguments are brought forward and overturned as altogether weak or false from the letters of the holy pontiffs Julius, Leo, and Gelasius.

[Col. 1196C]

1. Those who have examined the works of John Launoy, Paschasius Quesnellus, and other writers of this school will perhaps think that I have not yet said enough in the preceding discussion about the appeal of Saint Flavian to the one and only supreme pontiff, Saint Leo. In examining these works, they know very well that appeals of bishops to the Roman pontiffs, when acting together with a council of Western bishops, are assigned no other right than an ecclesiastical one, derived, moreover, from the Sardican canons.

[Col. 1196D] When I first examined the opinion of these writers, I was uncertain whether it was necessary to compose a new exercise, distinct from the preceding one and serving as its appendix, in which I might investigate more carefully the purpose and intention that moved the aforementioned Fathers to enact those three oft-mentioned canons. I reflected that they could hardly have been unaware of, or wished to conceal, the divine right by which Roman pontiffs have been granted the authority to judge all and every kind of ecclesiastical case.

On the other hand, however, when, in reading either Launoy’s letters, I encountered the one addressed to James Boetius, or when I carefully considered the final part of Paschasius Quesnellus’s eighth dissertation, I decided to discuss the Sardican canons separately, lest what had been set forth in the preceding work should appear uncertain, weak, and entirely without force.

To establish the truth of what has been said ever more firmly, [Col. 1197A] I thought that the conduct of those supreme pontiffs who preceded the Council of Sardica could be of the greatest value. Without anyone objecting, they received the appeals of others and issued definitive sentences and judgments. I persuaded myself that the celebrated case of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria belonged to this category.

The Sardican canons had not yet been enacted. For only five, or at most seven, years later did those Fathers assemble for that synod, when Athanasius, accused falsely of various crimes by the factions of the Eusebians and Arians, had been both condemned by the judgment of the Eastern synods and deprived of his episcopate. He was therefore compelled to come to Rome, so that he might plead his case before Julius, the Roman pontiff, recount the most serious persecutions he was suffering because of hatred of the faith, and at the same time request a new examination of his case, lest the decisions of Tyre and Mareotis should pass into res judicata.

[Col. 1197B] I think that no one can call into question the fact that Athanasius appealed from the judgment of the Easterners and demanded the judgment of the tribunal to which he fled and before which he wished to appear. But what rights supported Athanasius, so that he could appeal to one and only one among so many Western episcopal sees, whose judgment his adversaries themselves could neither refuse nor reject? I do not see, unless we have recourse to divine and apostolic authority.

The Sardican canons, which had not yet been enacted, certainly did not support Athanasius. Nor, according to Quesnellus, Launoy, and the others, did any other canons exist in which the right of receiving appeals was assigned to the Roman pontiffs.

2. Nor ought we especially to lend an ear to Quesnellus, who repeatedly says in his writings, in order to evade or diminish the authority of the Roman pontiffs, that a certain right common to all Catholic bishops exists, by which they are obliged to devote their efforts [Col. 1197C] to matters concerning the faith and the Church.

For at that time, in Athanasius’s case and in other similar cases, the matter was not merely one of undertaking labor for the common stability and preservation of the faith, or of serving the Church’s welfare. It concerned the issuing of what is called a peremptory judgment, the abolition of the synodal decrees of the Easterners, and the restraint of the rash acts of many factional bishops who had violently driven Athanasius from his see and, by every lawful and unlawful means, assigned his episcopate to a heretical intruder.

Furthermore, if every bishop is obliged to devote his efforts to similar cases, why did Athanasius appeal to one and only one person, Julius the Roman pontiff? Why did Julius himself, wishing by a solemn judgment to investigate Athanasius’s innocence more carefully and make it known to all Catholics, compel the accusers, at least through their legates, to come to Rome and give an account of the fact that they had assembled at Tyre without the consent of the Apostolic See in order to bring false charges against the most holy man?

Why, finally, when the Arians and Eusebians were summoned by Julius himself [Col. 1197D] to plead their case before him, did they not protest that the judge was incompetent? That they employed one evasion after another in order to forestall the public disgrace they knew was impending is established by the most certain records. We also know that they wore out Athanasius, who waited fifteen months for their arrival in the City, as they had promised.

But who ever could or can assert that they denied that the case at issue could be brought before the tribunal of the Apostolic See, to which Athanasius had appealed?

3. It is plainly evident that the Eusebian and Arian bishops did not dare deny the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, by which they understood themselves to have been compelled to come to Rome, from the repeated disturbances they later stirred up against Athanasius after the emperor Constantine’s death.

[Col. 1198A] They therefore bore with difficulty the restoration of this holy bishop to his see after fifteen months. When the Eusebians had been summoned by the emperor Constantius to the dedication of the Antiochene basilica begun by Constantine, they took the occasion to hold a council. Equipped with new schemes and relying upon the favor and authority of the prince, they drove out Athanasius and installed Gregory in the Alexandrian see. Gregory, surrounded by five thousand armed men, drove out the holy bishop and seized the Church by violence and arson.

Saint Julius, the pontiff, therefore again assumed the defense of Athanasius, and he did so alone. Athanasius, together with Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, and others whom the Eusebian faction had arranged to send into exile, had requested that a new judgment be instituted, so that the case of him and his associates might be brought back for examination from the beginning.

No one is unaware of the outcome of this case. Athanasius, Paul the bishop of Constantinople, Lucius of Adrianople, Marcellus of Ancyra, Asclepas of Gaza, and many others were solemnly acquitted [Col. 1198B] by Julius and the Roman synod and declared innocent. They were therefore judged worthy to return to their sees without any canonical impediment whatsoever.

In order that this judgment might be regarded by all as irreformable, Pope Julius fortified it with all the conditions expressed in the law. Namely, by canonical summons he compelled the leaders of the Eusebian faction to come to Rome and give an account of the unjust judgments held at the synods of Tyre and Antioch. In this matter, Theodoret says, he followed the canon of the Church, which provided that judgments were not to be held when one of the litigating parties had not been heard, nor was a sentence ever to fall upon the absent.

The Eusebians, however, distrustful of their case and knowing that the forces of Roman soldiers and the record-keepers could not support them, offered various useless and deceitful excuses. They alleged the shortness of the time allotted to them, the emperor’s war against the Persians as an obstacle to travelers, and other such arguments which they thought would favor concealment and [Col. 1198C] evasion.

4. Nevertheless, when they heard that their judgments had been rescinded and abolished by Julius and the Roman synod, they paid no attention either to what Sozomen says—that the whole burden of care belongs to the Roman pontiff—or to what Socrates writes—that the Roman Church possesses a privilege above the others. The Eusebians, deeply agitated, assembled again at Antioch and wrote to Julius a letter ornamented with elegant language, yet full of irony and not free from the gravest insults.

Sozomenus recounts this agitation of the Eusebians. But we understand the truth of the matter more clearly from the genuine letter of Pope Julius, in which, answering their objections one by one, he overturns their false arguments and vigorously defends the rights of the Roman See as deriving by custom from the apostles.

[Col. 1198D]

Severinus Binius extracted a sufficiently careful summary of their complaints from the letter of Julius and listed them in the following order.

[Note: Severinus Binius, volume II of the Councils, p. 558.]

[Col. 1199B] First, they had resented, with indignation, having been summoned to Rome. Second, the time fixed for holding the council had been excessively short. Third, because they were displeased that the proceedings of the assembly at Tyre had been examined again by Julius, they wrote that it was improper for one synod to reopen what had already been settled in another, and for Julius to weaken what they themselves had judged.

Fourth, in order to evade the judgment of the Roman Church—which was a characteristic mark of all heretics—they insisted that the dignity of bishops was by no means to be measured according to the size of cities.

Fifth, they complained against Julius because, although he wrote to them, he had not addressed letters to all of them individually; the superscription of his letter had been: “To Eusebius and his associates.”

Sixth and finally, in their letter to Julius they complained that Athanasius, Marcellus, and other bishops whom they had previously condemned had been received into Catholic communion.

[Col. 1199A] Sozomenus adds that in their letter they declared that they would never make peace and concord with Julius unless he approved what they had established.

5. Who would not marvel at such audacity on the part of the heretics? But why? Because they were contending in words with Julius, the supreme pontiff, and denying that he possessed those rights which antiquity teaches were derived from the apostles?

What should we conclude in the meantime? That they had a better understanding of the rights and prerogatives of the Roman pontiffs than they had judged concerning the divinity of Christ the Lord and the consubstantiality of the divine Word with the Father? It is well known that they were by no means afraid to deny these things concerning Christ the Lord.

Therefore, if the Eusebians were guided by no law other than their own will, it is not surprising that they refused to obey any ecclesiastical precept. In order to defend their stubborn obstinacy with some specious color, they fabricated canons providing that the judgments of one synod could not be dissolved by the examination and decrees of another synod.

But what sort of image were they constructing? First, they themselves had convoked several synods to abolish the Nicene decrees. Then, when they were summoned to Rome by the supreme pontiff Julius to plead their case, they did not allege that the judge was incompetent. They did not challenge the summons or citation. They merely delayed, resorting to various evasions.

Since the pontiff could no longer continue waiting for their arrival, and since their legates secretly fled—imprudently leaving the records of the synods of Tyre and Mareotis in the pontifical hands—the truth of the entire matter was clearly ascertained, and a decree of acquittal was issued in favor of Athanasius and his companions. All the proceedings composed in the East through fraud and calumny, violence and tyranny, were declared void.

Then, realizing that all the devices of their wickedness had been completely exposed and that the Roman See had issued a true judgment, they began to contend against its authority and attack it boldly. They would have preferred the Roman pontiff to accommodate himself to their perverse opinions by confirming and ratifying the wicked decrees they had enacted.

[Col. 1199C]

Saint Julius the pope, however, most effectively refutes this new zeal and perverse ambition as contrary to the sanctions of the Apostle Paul and the teaching of the Fathers. He attacks the authors of these innovations in words that apply remarkably well to those who invent for themselves the claim that appeals can and ought to be made only from one council to councils of greater size.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] The complete letter of Pope Julius exists in Greek and Latin in volume II of the Councils, in Labbe, p. 515.]

> “Are you unaware that it is the custom that we should first be written to, so that what is just may be determined from this place? Therefore, if such a suspicion had arisen there against a bishop, it ought still to have been referred to our Church. But now, without informing us at all, after they have already done what they pleased, they want us to be supporters of their condemnation, although we were not present. The ordinances of Paul do not say this; the Fathers did not teach this. Rather, this is arrogance and a new undertaking.”

Finally, the supreme pontiff, using an appeal, urges the obstinate Eusebians to listen:

> “What we have received from blessed Peter the Apostle, I make known to you. Otherwise I would not write what I think you already know, unless the facts themselves had disturbed us.”

And, enumerating all the evils occurring in the Church through their zeal and schemes, so that they might refrain from similar conduct in the future and oppose those who dared such things, he earnestly entreats them, with the greatest moderation of spirit, not to become objects of ridicule among the pagans.

6. If I wished to discuss at greater length this letter of Julius to the Eusebians, I could show more clearly that the authority of the Apostolic See mentioned by the pontiff is founded upon divine law and apostolic canon, as the distinguished Christian Lupus has learnedly demonstrated.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Christianus Lupus, On the Sardican Canons, p. 141.]

He adduces various examples drawn from ecclesiastical [Col. 1200A] history, especially those which that learned man believes can be taken either from the History of Eusebius of Caesarea or from the writings of others. He also adds the well-known testimony of Tertullian, in Against Praxeas, concerning Montanus’s case, in which an appeal was made to Zephyrinus, and the decree of the Council of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, which acquired force only after confirmation by Dionysius of Rome, as we have elsewhere described in preparing the Latin Rufinian edition of Eusebius of Caesarea.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Volume I of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, book VII, chapter 26, p. 442 and following.]

We now pass over these and similar examples, to which outstanding men have appealed in explaining the divine and apostolic right granted to the Roman pontiffs for receiving every kind of appeal, lest we wander outside our field or seem to repeat work already done by others.

We adhere only to the testimony of the aforementioned Pope Julius, which the Eusebians did not dare oppose. For who will believe that that most cunning faction of heretics, driven by hatred and fury against Athanasius, would have remained silent if Julius had falsely adduced, in defense of his rights, the customs of the Churches, [Col. 1200B] the ordinances of the apostles, and the teaching of the Fathers—especially since he had attacked them for being afflicted by excessive ambition and devoted to innovations?

7. But this custom and exercise of divine law, which the Eusebians did not attack, Quesnellus and Launoy at least denied.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Quesnellus, volume II, dissertation 8, p. 308 and following.]

Although they concede that Julius wished in the year 341 to examine the case of Athanasius and the others, even in the presence of the legates whom the Arians had sent to him, they conceal the fact that these men were acquitted and restored to their sees. They merely assert that the Roman council was summoned and celebrated as the result of a compromise between the two parties.

They therefore suppose that the Roman pontiff possessed no authority other than that which he received from the litigants. Launoy, using a similar fallacy, further contends that Julius was appointed arbitrator by the Eusebians themselves to judge Athanasius’s case, in such a way that he could judge [Col. 1200C] only if they requested it—just as people sometimes act when, in settling certain disputes, they abandon the ordinary judges established by law and, by making a compromise, choose new arbitrators for themselves.

To deceive his friend John Bono and sell him this argument, Launoy appends the following words of Athanasius:

> “These things the Egyptians wrote to everyone and to the Roman bishop Julius. For the Eusebians also sent letters to Julius, and, in order to frighten us, ordered a synod to be convened; and they offered the arbitration of the case to Julius himself, if he wished.”

The fabrications both of Quesnellus and of Launoy immediately collapse, however, when one considers the words of Pope Julius quoted above. Returning to the legitimate rights of a judge at greater length, he invokes the ancient custom, the ordinances of the apostles, and the teaching of the Fathers.

Launoy ought therefore rather to have objected to them that the Eusebian faction had already made a compromise, and he ought to have publicized it, so that everyone might know that Julius had intervened in the affairs of the Eastern synods for no other reason than that the litigants, having mutually agreed, had entrusted him with the power of judging them.

[Col. 1200D] On the contrary, Julius treats them as adversaries, almost accusing them of ignorance and reproving them by saying:

> “Are you unaware that it is the custom that we should first be written to, so that what is just may be determined from this place?”

It was therefore not within the power of the Eusebians to appoint Julius as arbitrator and make a compromise by which he would decide the litigants’ case according to the laws of justice and equity. He had received from God the authority to judge matters concerning the Church and bishops, and from the time of the apostles the Roman pontiff had remained in possession of such rights.

Launoy was also exceedingly inept in adducing Athanasius’s words in order to investigate the intention and purpose of the Eusebians [Col. 1201A] when they appealed to Julius. For what else can be gathered from those words except that the Eusebians, in order to boast that they had a good case and to frighten the holy bishop Athanasius, had already given an undertaking that they would regard as valid either the judgment of the Roman synod or that of Julius himself, as the ordinances and custom of the apostles required?

For *arbitrium* does not mean, nor does it imply, a compromise, as both adversaries contend. Among Latins of that period it indicates judgment, or command—things which ordinarily derive only from those who possess legitimate authority, as we could prove from Horace and Cicero.

### 8.

But we have not yet perfectly grasped the force of Athanasius’ words unless we consider that no one can be deterred by the sentence of an arbitrator, issued by force of a *compromissum*—an agreement that cannot exist unless the litigants, mutually concurring, promise that they are willing to abide peacefully by the judgment that will follow.

Since, therefore, the Eusebians, when they sent letters to Pope Julius so that, if he wished, he himself might judge Athanasius with the entire synod set aside, intended to deter him, they were already preparing to appeal to that tribunal beyond which they could no longer seek evasions or lodge appeals, because a final and ultimate judgment was to be pronounced. Once that judgment had been rendered—as the Eusebians themselves desired—Athanasius would no longer have been permitted to return to his Alexandrian Church. For the condition of a final and ultimate judgment is that, once a person has been condemned, every hope of further dispute is removed; and consequently only this kind of judgment can inspire fear.

Moreover, the Eusebians were compelled to send their legates to Rome not under the law of a *compromissum*, but by way of a genuine appeal. They nowhere said a word about holding a council, except when, seeing themselves convicted and thoroughly defeated by Athanasius’ legates, they sensed that their cause was collapsing. They therefore did not initially refuse to have Julius as the legitimate judge of the entire dispute. [Col. 1201B]

Only then did they begin to refuse him, when they had been shamefully convicted and utterly defeated by their adversaries’ legates. Pope Julius himself, attacking the Eusebians over this conduct, reproached them in these words:

> Since your legates—the presbyter Macarius, and the deacons Hesychius and Martyrius—were in no way equal, when they came here, to the presbyters sent by Athanasius, and were continually convicted and refuted by them, they then asked us to convene a council and to send letters both to the Eusebians and to Athanasius at Alexandria, summoning them, so that everyone’s case might be investigated by a just judgment. For then, they said, they would prove against Athanasius what they could no longer prove.

Nor may it be suspected that Julius’ words are to be understood as referring to some private disputation held between the legates of the two parties. For the holy pontiff immediately added these words, indicating the solemnity of the judgment and inquiry:

> For Martyrius and Hesychius were publicly refuted in our presence, while Athanasius’ presbyters resisted them confidently and vigorously. Martyrius and his companions were everywhere routed—if the truth must be spoken—and therefore he requested a general council.

Thus they did not initially request that a general synod be held; they did so only when they realized that the case they were conducting had been lost. Then, following the tactics of heretics and schismatics, they decided to withdraw from the judgment of the supreme pontiff and, attempting to deceive the holy pontiff by the evasions of rebels, requested that a council be convened. [Col. 1201C]

Meanwhile, it is clear that this petition had no force whatsoever. For the pontiff, exercising the authority he had received from God and following the rules of law, declared Marcellus and Athanasius innocent of all the charges and received them into communion. He declared invalid and entirely without force the records of the proceedings drawn up at the synods of Tyre and Mareotis. Consequently, Athanasius’ and the other Catholics’ accusers, driven to despair lest they suffer the penalties of false accusers according to the decrees of the canons, left the city of Rome by night and took flight.

Nevertheless, when Pope Julius himself noticed the irregular flight of these legates, he attempted, with the utmost gentleness, to bring the grave disputes of the Easterners to an end. Therefore, having admitted the appeal of those same legates, although no necessity compelled him to convene a council, he ordered Eusebius and his associates by letter to come to Rome for the holding of a council. [Col. 1201D]

But when that schismatic faction once again frustrated the pontiff’s hope through evasions and prolonged delay, the council again declared Athanasius and his associates guilty of no crime and decreed that they deserved to be restored to the sees from which they had been expelled through violence.

Accordingly, as though wishing to give an account of what he himself had done, Julius addressed them in these words:

> You ought, therefore, beloved brothers, to have come here and by no means to have evaded the matter, so that the case might be brought to an end. For reason requires this . . . . [Col. 1202A] They would have come, as I said, if they had had good hopes concerning their cause. For the Eusebians never denied to the Roman pontiff the right to summon the bishops of the Eastern Churches, nor did they claim to be exempt from that duty of obedience by which the Churches of the entire Christian world are bound to obey the holy apostolic Roman See.

### 9.

Launoius, however, realizing that he was constrained by the sequence of these events, devised the following escape, saying:

> Athanasius was restored to his see neither by the decree of Pope Julius nor by the sentence of the Roman synod, but by the judgment of the Sardicenses. That synod, far more numerous than the Roman synod, confirmed whatever had been done by the Roman synod.

This is a deplorable argument, constructed contrary to every rule of law and dialectic reasoning. For Launoius tries to confuse the right to judge with the execution of a decree already issued, so that he may wrongly infer that the judgments of the Roman pontiffs are to be considered of little or no importance unless they have been confirmed by general synods and treated as ratified.

But let him say whether the judgment and sentence of Julius and of the Roman council were delayed lawfully or unlawfully. Not lawfully, certainly, since both the Eusebians and Athanasius with his associates did not refuse to recognize the Roman pontiff as judge, as is evident from what has preceded. The Arian faction therefore unlawfully opposed the statutes of Julius and of the Roman synod. Since the authority and violence of the emperor Constantius supported that faction, measures were taken to prevent Athanasius and the others from being restored to their sees.

But Launoius and Quesnellus ought to have noticed that the Sardicenses added no force and no confirmation to Julius’ judgment or to the sentence of the Roman synod, since they used the following solemn declaration:

> From this the equity of the judgment of our brother and fellow bishop Julius will most clearly appear. He did not pronounce sentence with rash counsel, but after mature deliberation, so that no doubt whatever remains concerning the communion of our brother Athanasius.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] Acts of the Council of Sardica, vol. II of the Councils in Labbe.]

Another escape also collapses: the claim concerning the supposedly much more numerous synod, on which both our adversaries insist. For the authority of synods is not to be derived from the greater or lesser number of pontiffs; rather, it derives from the person who possesses the power to convene them and from observance of the canonical and apostolic rules governing the form and order of judgments. Saint Leo the Great clearly indicated this in Letter 80 to Anatolius of Constantinople; we shall discuss it in chapter 10 of the following book. [Col. 1202B]

Therefore, if the argument of our adversaries were valid, the Council of Sardica itself could not have heard the case of Athanasius and his associates, since the matter had already been decided several times:

> First, in our own province, when almost one hundred bishops had assembled for this purpose; and secondly, at Rome, when we appeared there together with the other adversaries of Eusebius.

There were, however, more than fifty bishops in that assembly.

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Athanasius, at the beginning of the *Second Apology*.]

If, then, the weight and authority of a judgment were derived from the number of bishops, the decrees of the Alexandrian and Roman synods ought rather to have stood than those of Tyre and Mareotis. Both the Alexandrian and the Roman synods were more numerous than the latter, and in both Athanasius was acquitted and restored to his see.

Speaking also of the latter synod, Athanasius says in his *Second Apology*:

> The presbyter Vitus brought more than fifty bishops to the council, where our defense was accepted and we were judged worthy of communion and the love-feast (*agape*).

But besides the Roman pontiff and the bishops brought to the council by the presbyter Vitus, others may perhaps also have attended the assembly. We cannot affirm this with certainty, owing to the lack of records.

In truth, Saint Leo the Great long ago overturned this escape of our adversaries when he rebuked Anatolius, who thought that the more numerous Council of Chalcedon could support him in setting aside the Nicene canon concerning the rights and privileges of the Churches. [Col. 1203A]

### 10.

The Eusebians had attempted in many different ways to make contentious this ancient possession of so many rights by the apostolic see. At last, however, Ursacius and Valens were led to repentance and testified under oath that in the future they would regard those rights as ratified and firm, in these words:

> Indeed, we also promise this: if at any time the Easterners, and even Eusebius himself, should maliciously wish to summon him to judgment, we shall not go there without your sentence.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The penitential statement of Ursacius and Valens is found in vol. II of the Councils and in the new edition of the works of Saint Hilary.]

Or, as we read more accurately in fragments of Saint Hilary:

> We shall not appear without your knowledge.

We therefore cannot doubt, from the sequence of these events, that even before the Council of Sardica the apostolic custom had prevailed whereby the Roman pontiffs received appeals from bishops, judged their cases either in synods or outside synods, and allowed no one to pronounce judgments in episcopal cases without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff.

Thus the entire structure which our adversaries Launoius and Quesnellus attempted to construct solely from the Sardicene canons collapses. They sought to maintain that the Roman pontiff could receive and judge appeals from bishops condemned in the provincial synods of the East by no other right than an ecclesiastical right derived from the Council of Sardica. [Col. 1203B]

Nor may Launoius, especially when attacking Bellarmine, appeal to the testimony of Pope Gelasius, who wrote in a letter to the bishops of Dardania:

> We do not conceal what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the See of blessed Peter the Apostle possesses the right to release those whom the sentences of any pontiffs have bound, since it is permitted to judge concerning the whole Church; nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment. For if the canons should wish appeals to be made to it from any part of the world, no one is permitted to appeal from it.

[Note: [Col. 1204D] It is found in vol. V of the Councils, in Labbe, p. 324.]

Because Bellarmine suppressed the words “if the canons should wish appeals to be made,” Launoius maintains that the Roman pontiff can receive appeals solely by canonical or ecclesiastical right, and that this right must be derived only from the councils of the Church, which, he says, decreed that this should be done for the common benefit of all. Thus Launoius reasons, unjustly attacking Bellarmine.

For Pope Gelasius in his letter did not depart at all from the judgments of his predecessors, who, as we have seen, affirmed that the bishops of the Roman See could by divine right judge the cases of all the Churches, without anyone being permitted to judge its judgment. Nor can our arguments, or Bellarmine’s, be weakened by the words “if the canons should wish appeals to be made.” For in that passage Gelasius did not use the word *canons* to mean the decrees of councils, as the adversary wrongly attempts to explain it. Rather, the pontiff used the term to indicate that rule established by divine disposition and confirmed by usage, by which the See of blessed Peter was given the right to release the judgments of all the Churches, and no one was permitted to judge its judgment.

And lest I seem to be selling words through empty talk, I shall ask Launoius in particular whether he has ever examined the letter of Gelasius under discussion. He must be believed to have examined it, since he accuses Bellarmine of fraud for suppressing the words “if the canons should wish appeals to be made.” [Col. 1204A]

He ought therefore to have recognized that the aforesaid letter bears this title:

> Gelasius shows that Acacius was lawfully condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see alone.

He could not have failed to understand how, in the body of the letter, the pontiff explained that, when he was treating the condemnation of Sabellius, the defeat of the Arian heresy at the Council of Nicaea, and the various synods held on various occasions, no Christian could be unaware that, once the decision of a particular synod had received the assent of the universal Church, no other see ought to carry it out more fully than the first See, which confirms every synod by its authority and safeguards it through continuous governance—on account, of course, of its primacy, which blessed Peter the Apostle received by the command of the Lord’s voice, with the Church following thereafter, and which he has always held and continues to hold.

Thus Gelasius relates how the apostolic see obtained that primacy by the Lord’s command and always retains it; by its authority it is to confirm every synod and safeguard it through continuous governance. Surely, if it confirms every synod, why does Launoius contend that this is not true of general synods?

Moreover, to prove that the apostolic see had acted by divine right in condemning Acacius, Gelasius himself never appeals to the canons of synods, but to his pontifical predecessors, who had judged similar cases, with absolutely no reference to the sanctions of the Sardicene pontiffs.

Accordingly, in the same place he adduces the following as another argument for his supreme authority:

> Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see has frequently possessed, as has been said, according to the custom of our ancestors, even without any preceding synod, the power both of absolving those whom a synod had unjustly condemned and of condemning, when no synod existed, those whom it was right to condemn.

He then adds examples which wonderfully support the question now before us: namely, Athanasius of Alexandria, condemned by Eastern synods but absolved by the apostolic see; John of Constantinople, whom a synod of Catholic bishops had condemned, but whom the apostolic see, even by itself, absolved because it did not consent; and likewise Flavian of holy memory, condemned by an assembly of Greek pontiffs, whom the apostolic see absolved in the same manner, because the apostolic see alone did not consent . . . . . . . . . and, by refusing consent, removed the impious synod—that is, the robber council of Ephesus—and decreed by itself that the Council of Chalcedon should be held for the sake of the truth.

It is entirely clear that, in adducing these examples, Gelasius had no regard for the Sardicene canons. For, as we have seen, he asserts that these rights were assigned to the apostolic see by the Lord’s command and that the Roman Church always remained in possession of these privileges, although heretics and schismatics, driven by envy and hatred, attempted with great contentiousness to raise questions concerning this legitimate possession.

Furthermore, as we have seen above, even seven years before the Council of Sardica was convened, the Roman Church exercised such rights by absolving Athanasius of holy memory. [Col. 1204B]

### 11.

But let us grant that Launoius ought to have concealed all these facts so that he might attack the learned man Bellarmine with impunity and merely out of a contentious spirit. Could Quesnellus perhaps have done the same, although, in preparing the works of Saint Leo, he had to examine this Letter 89, addressed to the bishops of the province of Vienne, among others, more than once?

Saint Leo himself, when discussing the right of appeals, supports the testimony of Saint Pope Julius and most fully affirmed that appeals derive from no other source than divine institution. Without making any reference to the Sardicene canons, he writes that, because of its reverence, the apostolic see had been consulted by the priests of all the provinces through innumerable reports, and that, through appeals in various cases, as ancient custom required, judgments had either been reconsidered or confirmed.

Quesnellus commented on this testimony. But, abandoning the preceding expression concerning the authority of judgments accepted through the litigants’ *compromissum*, he nevertheless attempted to diminish the force of these words, writing in the margin of his edition:

> He claims the right of appeals for himself only on the basis of ancient custom.

I do not at all see how this annotation can benefit Quesnellus’ cause. Indeed, I understand that Quesnellus can be convicted either of negligence or of excessive dishonesty. For in the same passage the holy pontiff intends to explain the ancient custom through the innumerable consultations and appeals made to the apostolic see, since in the preceding chapter of the same letter he had already discussed the form of ecclesiastical government, arranged by Christ the Lord in such an order that He placed it principally in blessed Peter, supreme among all the apostles, wishing His gifts to flow from Peter, as from a kind of head, into the whole body, so that anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness (*Petri soliditas*) would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery.

Saint Leo therefore affirmed in that passage that consultations and appeals were brought to the apostolic see by the priests of all the Churches on two grounds: first, by divine title, because of the form of ecclesiastical government instituted by Christ the Lord; and second, by the title of fact, which he intended to establish from ancient custom, namely, through appeals in various cases, by which the judgments of other bishops and synods had either been confirmed or reconsidered.

Nor should Quesnellus dare to claim that this form of government, the order of ecclesiastical judgments, the dignity of bishops, or the authority of the Churches could be harmed by it. For the holy pontiff himself magnificently asserts that these things cohere with one another through divine disposition, adding:

> Since our solicitude, seeking not its own interests but those of Christ, did not abolish the dignity divinely granted either to the Churches or to the priests of the Churches.

[Col. 1205A]

No right of dignity or of another’s authority can be harmed within the episcopal order, provided that all, seeking the things that belong to Jesus Christ, do not dare to overturn His arrangements and adhere in matters of faith and in the affairs of the Churches to the supreme head, through whom the heavenly gifts must flow into the whole body. For, he adds:

> Nor can those who dare to depart from Peter’s firmness be participants in the divine mysteries.

[Col. 1205B]

### 12.

In the preceding sections we have explained that Athanasius adhered to this firmness of Peter, while the Arians and Eusebians departed from it. But whether Quesnellus has chosen to stand for Athanasius or for the Eusebians in judging this case, I do not see clearly enough.

I understand only this: our adversary has strained every sinew of his intellect in order to assign the right of appeals to the Roman pontiffs solely on the basis of the Sardicene canons, and to claim that these canons were enacted for Athanasius’ benefit and, in accordance with his own intention, established as though by way of a precedent created by his journey to Rome.

But who, devoted to the sincere investigation of truth, could read the following without indignation?

> A bishop who has been unjustly deprived of communion and of his episcopal see, and wickedly sent into exile, if he appeals to the firm See of Peter, creates a precedent against himself and infringes the rights of others, if he adheres to the head through whom divine gifts flow into the members, while seeking at the same time the things that belong to Jesus Christ and pertain to His Church.

He certainly created a precedent against himself in the judgment both of the Arians and of Quesnellus, but by no means in the sound opinion of the orthodox. Since obedience to the divine commands is dear to them, and they never dare to overturn the arrangements and divinely established order of Christ the Lord, they have taught that appeal must always be made to that tribunal which received its firmness from the very founder of the Church. We could prove this, if useful, by innumerable examples borrowed from the writings of others. [Col. 1205C]

### 13.

Quesnellus proceeds to reason as follows. Having now inserted those three Sardicene canons in his eighth dissertation, he inquires what the pontiffs (*PP.*) presupposed when they issued those rules and begins to explain it.

> First, they presuppose that a bishop has received a sentence from the council of his own province; but, thinking that he has been wronged, he asks that the council be renewed.

In order gradually to draw the reader into his belief in a new right granted to the Roman pontiff by the council, he depicts Hosius of Córdoba, worn out by the schemes of the heretics, as thinking it best that, if someone were granted by a council the power to determine whether and when there should be room for an appeal, ecclesiastical judgments would not be more exposed to the tricks of certain rogues than secular judgments.

> For, he says, you have the relevant title in book seven, title 65, and so forth. Whom, he continues, could the synod have more appropriately honored with this office than the Roman pontiff, father of all, in whom the memory of Saint Peter the Apostle was to be honored? A provincial synod was suspect to the condemned man, while it was not in the interest of the Church to assemble the bishops of neighboring provinces for that reason. This burden was therefore assigned to the Roman pontiff, who did not need laborious investigation or a careful examination of the entire matter for this task, but only to learn and decide summarily, or from the letters of the earlier judges, which appeals the laws of civil jurisprudence permitted to be received—just as it is easy for a secular judge immediately to determine which appeals the laws of civil law permit him to accept.

But who does not see that this supposition of Quesnellus is false and fictitious? He supposes that the Sardicene pontiffs granted a new right to the Roman pontiff, so that the whole Church might venerate him as the father of all and as the one in whom the memory of Saint Peter was to be honored.

According to Quesnellus’ opinion, then, before these canons were enacted, was it unlawful for the Roman pontiff to judge either provincial synods, to undertake a laborious investigation for restoring to their sees bishops expelled through hatred and rivalry, or, finally, to declare invalid and void the ordinations of those who had been intruded into the sees of deposed bishops? [Col. 1206A]

Indeed, if the conclusions drawn from Quesnellus’ system were valid, the ancient right that Pope Julius asserted against the Arians and claimed for himself would have been entirely chimerical. We would also have to say that the judgment he pronounced in the case of Athanasius and his associates at least five or seven years earlier was invalid and imposed by violence, since it had been pronounced by one who did not yet possess the requisite authority.

That Julius judged the case of Athanasius and the orthodox cannot be doubted. For, besides the preceding letter of Julius and the apologies of Athanasius cited above, there exists another letter of the same pontiff, written to the presbyters, deacons, and people of Alexandria. In it he urges them to welcome Athanasius, returning to his see, with great joy: he is restored to them pure and innocent from such great dangers and evils, and has been judged such not merely by our judgment, but by that of the universal synod.

[Note: [Col. 1205] It is found in vol. II of the Councils, p. 539. See our *Exercise on the Appeal of Eutyches*.]

I do not know, however, how Quesnellus can remain consistent with himself in the other matters described above. For he himself boldly denied that Eutyches appealed to the apostolic see, maintaining instead that he appealed to the bishops of the principal Churches and to their synods. He further maintained that this was the custom of Easterners who appealed.

Here, however, he says that the matter concerns this new right granted to the Roman pontiffs by the Sardicene canons, and that this burden was imposed upon them: they were to determine summarily and from the letters of the earlier judges which appeals the laws of civil jurisprudence allowed them to receive.

But what is this except the power to judge the decrees of synods, to determine that a sentence pronounced against a condemned person was lawful or unlawful, and to suspend or annul that sentence until the pontiffs, either by themselves or together with others, conducted a fuller inquiry into the earlier judgments? Quesnellus does not assert that a council was necessary for carrying out all these things; nor should it truly be called necessary, if the pontiffs could determine all these matters summarily and from the letters of the earlier judges. [Col. 1206B]

### 14.

Nevertheless, remaining consistent in his assertions, Quesnellus expressly contends that this right of appeals was then newly assigned to the Roman pontiffs and to Julius himself.

But by what means did he prove this? Perhaps by inventing the claim that the Sardicene canons contain certain apparent contradictions, which, among others, the distinguished Christian Lupus long ago removed through learned explanations.

[Note: [Col. 1207D] Christian Lupus, *Canons of Sardica Illustrated with Notes and Scholia*, p. 135.]

Or perhaps by asserting that the Sardicene pontiffs, through later deliberations, derogated from their earlier decisions, so that the interpretation of the earlier decrees must be derived from the later ones and that, in that seventh canon, the authority of the Roman pontiff was confined within narrow limits—although in the third and fourth canons they had assigned him the broadest authority?

Quesnellus is entirely mistaken. [Col. 1207B] Those canons in no way conflict with one another. The supreme right which the third and fourth canons confirm as belonging to the Roman pontiff in receiving appeals is confirmed more and more in the fifth, or seventh, canon: it is in his power either to judge personally, to delegate the judgment of the case to others, to summon the litigating parties to himself, or to convene a new synod in which the entire matter under dispute may be solemnly recalled for a new examination.

Therefore, lest we seem to be telling stories, let us attend to the canons.

That third canon first of all restrained the Eusebian faction, which was disregarding the Nicene canons. For, with reckless boldness, that faction was expelling orthodox bishops and clerics from Churches that did not belong to it and intruding other condemned and heretical persons into their cathedrals and places.

To conceal, or at least disguise, the reckless conduct of this Eusebian faction, Quesnellus did not transcribe the canon in full as it is found in the manuscripts of Dionysius Exiguus. Instead, perhaps through negligence, he omitted the following first four lines:

> Bishop Hosius said: This too must necessarily be added: that bishops must not pass from their own province into another province in which there are bishops, unless they have perhaps been invited by their brothers, lest we seem to close the door to charity.

He appended only the remainder, which follows:

> Namely, if some province, etc.

As we said, the distinguished Lupus illustrated this canon with learned scholia and notes, and observed that it consists of four parts. In the second, condemned foreign judgments are found—judgments especially accustomed to being issued by the Eusebians. The third treats of the judges of provincial synods, whose duty it is to write to the Roman pontiff so that the episcopal judgment may be referred to the apostolic see, as Pope Innocent I explained in his letter to Victricius of Rouen.

[Note: [Col. 1208D] Letter of Pope Innocent to Victricius, vol. III of the Councils; Saint Leo the Great, Letter 12 to Quesnellus, chapter 1.]

Finally, the fourth part of that canon concerns the right of the apostolic see which Quesnellus has hitherto called new. [Col. 1207C]

But it cannot be called new, since it proceeds from divine institution. That it proceeds from divine institution rather than from canonical law, insofar as this concerns the care which the Roman pontiffs exercise over all the Churches, is evident from what has already been written. Saint Leo the Great teaches it clearly in his letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, and Pope Julius himself in the aforementioned letter to the Eusebians.

Since, then, the entire controversy between Julius and the Eusebians concerned the exercise and use of this care and authority, which the factious Eusebians called into question, the Sardicene pontiffs declared that the tribunal of Saint Peter was to be honored, so that in the future neither provincial synods nor any other bishop of the Catholic Church would dare to despise or violate the decrees and judgments of the apostolic see:

> Let those who have judged write to Julius, bishop of Rome; and, if necessary, let the judgment be renewed by the bishops of the neighboring province, and let him provide judges.
