But if he cannot establish that the case is of such a kind that it ought to be judged again, let the matters once judged not be weakened.

If these words of the canon are accepted in their genuine sense, without violent interpretation, they must certainly be referred to the audacity of the Eusebians, who contended that the memory of Saint Peter the Apostle need not be honored, but that the judgments of provincial synods must be held firm and ratified, so that no one could rescind or abolish them.

The Sardicene pontiffs, therefore, wishing to break such audacity, merely declared that the memory of blessed Peter was to be honored: “Let those who have judged write,” and so forth.

They followed the same procedure in composing the fourth canon, which concerns bishops deposed by synodal judgment. They did not want anyone else to be placed in the see of such a bishop before the Roman pontiff, having examined the case, had pronounced sentence. [Col. 1208A]

Here they decided that the judgment of the synod should be submitted anew to the judgment of the Roman pontiff. In this way they ratified and declared as corresponding to divine right what Pope Julius had written at least five years earlier belonged to him, when he learned that Gregory of Cappadocia had been intruded into the Alexandrian see without his knowledge.

Therefore, nothing was assigned to the Roman pontiff in those two canons that he did not already possess by right of possession, as they say. It was only men of impaired faith who attempted, though unsuccessfully, to deny or disturb this peaceful possession. Just as they sought completely to overturn and abolish the rules of the Nicene doctrines, so they also attempted to attack the authority of the supreme judge and guardian of the canons.

Thus, so that in the future provincial councils might not attempt to injure or violate this peaceful possession of the Roman pontiffs, the Sardicene assembly wished to enact the two aforementioned canons as an appendix to the Nicene canons. For at the preceding Council of Nicaea it had been established that the privileges and prerogatives of the Churches were to be preserved, and the pontiffs had said:

> The Roman Church has always held the primacy.

This was read at the Council of Chalcedon, as we observed above.

Now let Quesnellus tell us what is found in the seventh canon that would lead us to understand that it derogated from the earlier canons. [Col. 1208B]

For in that canon the authority of the Roman pontiff in receiving and judging the cases of those who appeal is explained so clearly that the disputes of the Eusebians and of all schismatics are completely settled. They denied that the judges of provincial synods should be summoned to give an account of their previous judgments. Yet this was necessary to restrain the judges’ impotence, hatred, and fury toward those whom they had condemned. Pope Julius proved this against those same schismatics from the Nicene canons, writing:

> Those who hold a sound opinion concerning what they have done, and concerning matters in which they themselves were judges, are not accustomed to resent it if what they have judged is examined by others. They are secure, since what they themselves have judged just can never become unjust.

> Therefore the bishops assembled in the great synod at Nicaea, not without God’s counsel, permitted the acts of an earlier synod to be examined in another synod, so that those who had been judges, keeping before their eyes the judgment that was to follow concerning the matter, might weigh the case with complete diligence; and so that those who had received the sentence might know for certain that they had been condemned not through the animosity of the earlier judges, but lawfully and deservedly.

Quesnellus should attend, I ask, to the following words, so that he may understand that this rule had already prevailed by apostolic custom and was merely renewed and explained at the Council of Nicaea.

> But if, Saint Julius adds, such a custom once existed, and its memory has been preserved and committed to writing in the great synod, and you do not allow it to prevail among you, you are certainly acting disgracefully.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Letter of Pope Julius to the Eusebians, cited above, p. 659. We have followed the interpretation of Gentianus Hervetus.]

Let us now set forth that fifth Sardican canon, which the codices of Dionysius Exiguus present outside its natural position, and which Quesnellus cited mutilated and truncated by the omission of two words, contrary to the versions of all interpreters.

Bishop Hosius said:

“It has seemed good that, if any bishop has been accused and the bishops of the same region, having assembled, have removed him from his rank, and if, as though appealing, he has taken refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church and wishes him to hear the case, and if he has judged it just that the examination of the matter be renewed, he shall deign to write to the co-bishops who are near the province, so that they themselves may diligently and carefully investigate each point and, in fidelity to the truth, deliver a judgment concerning the matter.

“But if anyone should request that his case be heard again, and if, at his supplication, the Roman bishop should deem it appropriate to judge the matter by sending presbyters from his own side, it shall be in his power to do whatever he determines to be right. And if he should decide that men ought to be sent who will judge together with the bishops, possessing the authority of him by whom they were sent, this too shall be permitted. But if he should think that the examination of the matter and the bishop’s judgment are sufficient, he shall do whatever, according to his most prudent counsel, appears to be right.”

The bishops answered: “The things that have been said are approved.”

[Note: Sardican canon 5, or 7, is found in volume II of the General Councils.]

Christianus Lupus observed that this canon wonderfully agrees with the two preceding ones. Indeed, the words which indicate that the Roman pontiff may send presbyters as legates from his own side—who may examine and conclude the case either alone or together with bishops of another neighboring province—already prove that it was issued in order to explain more fully the authority of the Roman pontiff, so that appeals might not be prolonged indefinitely. Nevertheless, it by no means permits the bishops of the neighboring province to judge alone, without the assistance of Roman presbyters.

I admit that, on the occasion of this canon, interpreters have raised various questions among ancient and more recent writers, as may be seen in the work of the most distinguished Christianus Lupus.

[Note: Christianus Lupus, in his scholia and notes on the Sardican canons, p. 147 and following.]

Yet no one has tried to interpret it with such zeal and violence as our adversary Quesnellus. For, having arbitrarily supplied a new structure for the canon and removed those words which indicate the full authority of the Roman pontiff in receiving and resolving the cases of appellants, he argues that “the renewal of the judgment” and “the renewal of the council” must be understood as one and the same thing.

He further adds:

“And indeed, if ‘judgment’ were taken to mean a sentence, it should not have been said *in judicio* (‘in the judgment’) but merely *judicio* (‘by judgment’). It is therefore clear that the council of the Roman bishop is meant here. But what sort of council? This remains for us to investigate.

“He asserts that many kinds of councils are subject to the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, after introducing the familiar distinction among the degrees of ecclesiastical administration belonging to the Roman pontiff—namely, bishop of the City, metropolitan of the Roman province, primate of the suburban dioceses, patriarch of the Western region, and head and summit of the whole Church—he concedes that the pontiff may arrange different synods according to the nature of the cases. But he does so with this qualification: that he himself may never judge alone, although proper consideration must be given to the cases which he ought to examine.

“Thus, when an appeal is made to him within his parish, or his own diocese, from the sentence of an inferior judge, the appellant’s case must be judged by a parish synod, or by the supreme pontiff himself, enclosed within the counsel of his clergy; when the case comes from a province, it belongs to the provincial synod; when from the suburban dioceses, to the diocesan synod; when from the Western region, to the Western synod; and when from other parts of the Church, to an ecumenical and universal synod—unless the free choice and written petition of the appellants indicate otherwise.

“Accordingly, if I am not mistaken, the meaning of the Sardican canon must be derived according to this rule, and the same principle must be applied in judging the appeal of Flavian.”

This is an amusing, but highly ingenious, interpretation of pontifical law—if only it could stand. Yet, although Quesnellus employs various supports to sustain it, the words of the canon itself first cause it to collapse. Next, it is undermined by the most ancient interpreters who explained the canon; and finally by the conduct of Pope Leo and other Roman pontiffs, who, after taking up the cases of appellants, either immediately pronounced a definitive judgment themselves, as they say, or merely decreed that a general council should be convened when they judged the public solemnity of a judicial process necessary for removing the gravest dissensions and schisms. These had been wickedly disturbing, to the ruin and scandal of Catholics, the condition of the most holy Churches through the various factions of depraved men; such councils were also necessary for breaking the obstinacy of those who had strayed from the rules of faith and ecclesiastical discipline, reconciling repentant offenders who had renounced the crimes they had committed after making a solemn confession of the Catholic faith, and finally carrying out each and every statute of the apostolic see that appeared necessary in accordance with the circumstances of the times and the character of the affairs.

Four things, therefore, must be distinguished.

First, the protest of the deposed bishop who objects and appeals from the sentence or judgment of the provincial synod.

Second, the tribunal of the apostolic see, to which the appeal is made.

Third, the judgment of the apostolic see itself—or of the Roman pontiff pronounced in a parish synod or in a consistory—concerning the appellant’s case and rights, as well as concerning the prior sentence of the provincial synod.

Fourth, the execution of the judgment of the apostolic see. Since the apostolic see often cannot undertake this itself, or cannot do so without the convocation of a new patriarchal or general synod, the Roman pontiffs send legates from their own side, so that each matter defined by them may faithfully be put into execution.

It is therefore not true that “the renewal of the judgment” and “the renewal of the council” must be taken as one and the same thing, as Quesnellus imagines. For once an appeal has been made, the renewal of the judgment certainly is required—a point which the adversary must admit, whether he wishes to or not—but not another convocation of a council.

For in the final canon that we have just transcribed we read expressly:

“But if anyone should request that his case be heard again, and if, at his supplication, the Roman bishop should deem it appropriate to judge the matter by sending presbyters from his own side, it shall be in his power to do whatever he determines to be right.”

But what free power would the Roman pontiffs possess to do whatever they determined to be right if they could not, by right, judge the case themselves or send presbyters from their own side to hear the matter for which the appellant had appealed?

Indeed, if the Fathers had not assigned full authority to the Roman pontiffs, but had wished to restrict pontifical rights merely to one new council, they ought to have used a different form of expression. For, among the many means suitable for a renewed examination of the matter, they gave the pontiffs the free power to choose whatever course their most prudent judgment should determine to be more appropriate and suitable. The final words of that canon, which we have just reviewed, expressly imply this.

Meanwhile Quesnellus tries, by flattering himself excessively, to enjoy the satisfaction of having been able to prove that the case of Flavian was brought before a general synod by virtue of an appeal resting exclusively upon the Sardican canons. Moreover, after employing various twisted interpretations—which we clearly proved in the preceding Exercise to be wholly deceptive—he once again turns his censorious style against John David and attacks him as a player and deceiver because he wrote that Flavian had appealed to one and only one Roman pontiff.

But who would not thoroughly understand the man’s confidence if he wished to compare our arguments—not devised by mere imagination, but drawn from truthful records—with the many and great inanities, quibbles, false conjectures, and interpretations that Quesnellus has laboriously heaped up and displayed to his readers with excessive zeal in order to establish and strengthen his new system?

## CHAPTER XI

After abolishing the Acts of the Ephesian Robber Synod, Saint Leo wrote various letters to the Easterners. Saint Flavian died a martyr’s death, and Anatolius was substituted in his place. The Roman pontiff does not consent to Anatolius’s ordination until he makes a solemn profession of faith according to the formula prescribed by the pontiff. To receive this profession, he sends four legates from his own side, who are to travel to Constantinople.

### 1

As soon as the great Leo learned, from the deacon Hilary, the legate of the apostolic see returning to Rome, everything that had occurred at the Ephesian Robber Synod, although he was oppressed by profound sadness and grief on account of the collapse of the Catholic doctrine of faith and the universal overthrow of all the Churches of the East, he nevertheless did not refrain from delivering judgment. Without any hesitation, fearlessly, he employed that vigilance and those principles of administration which most befitted his supreme pastoral office over the entire Church. By his authority and favor he immediately wished to confront the many and great evils that had arisen through the schemes of Chrysaphius, the blasphemies of Eutyches, and the impiety of Dioscorus, so that he might at once remedy them and abolish them completely.

First, therefore, he abolished all the Acts of that predatory synod, as null and invalid—something which Pope Gelasius also indicated quite clearly when he wrote to the bishops of Dardania.

[Note: See what we said in chapter 9 of the preceding Exercises.]

In the same manner he absolved Flavian, the pontiff of holy memory—understand, the Greek pontiff—who had been condemned by the assembly, since the apostolic see alone had not consented. Rather, he condemned Dioscorus, the ruler of the second see, who had been received there; by withholding his consent he removed the impious synod; and, for the sake of the truth, he alone decreed that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

Nor should anyone object to me, on the basis of Launoy’s opinion, that Gelasius, the supreme pontiff, had referred to ecclesiastical canons, and that the words cited seem to indicate that the Great Leo had merely employed their authority and privileges. For Saint Gelasius himself explained how and by what rules the apostolic see, adhering to them, customarily rejects what has been badly conducted in synods, or approves and confirms what agrees with truth and justice.

He adds:

“Here it is also consequently shown that a synod badly conducted—that is, against the Scriptures, against the teaching of the Fathers, and against the ecclesiastical rules—which the whole Church rightly did not receive and which especially the apostolic see did not approve, could and should be changed by a properly conducted synod—that is, one held according to the Scriptures, according to the tradition of the Fathers, and according to the ecclesiastical rules, and promulgated for the Catholic faith and communion—which the whole Church received and which the apostolic see most especially approved. But a properly conducted synod, according to the method described above, is in no way to be changed by a new synod.”

[Note: Pope Gelasius’s letter to the bishops of Dardania, letter 13, is found in volume V of the General Councils, p. 326 and following. The testimony of the ancient editors and manuscript codices also supports this reading.]

That Gelasius was there speaking of judgments made by the apostolic see alone, without the assembly of any councils, is clear from the context of the entire letter. The pontiff gathered the records of those judgments from the authentic archives of the apostolic see, or retained them in memory as an eyewitness of everything that had occurred in the case of Flavian and the Eutychians. For he was elevated to the pontificate in the year 492, while Saint Leo had departed this life in 461.

We can scarcely doubt, therefore, that the apostolic see—faithful interpreter and guardian of the sacred Scriptures and the teaching of the Fathers, according to whose standard it directs its judgments—could invalidate any synod that did not conform to those rules, and thereafter disclose its own decrees to other bishops, lest they dare to approve what the apostolic see had rejected.

That Saint Leo followed this course of action is clear from what will shortly be described. When autumn returned, the season in which the anniversary synod was solemnly celebrated at Rome, he informed the bishops and the other ministers of the Churches who had assembled there that the Ephesian predatory synod had been badly conducted, so that no one would thereafter dare to communicate with Dioscorus and the Eutychian faction, but that all should adhere to Saint Flavian.

Moreover, taking pity on the unhappy condition of all the Churches of the East, he judged that a general council ought to be convened. Since the entire matter had devolved upon him by every divine and ecclesiastical right—both because of the protest of his legates and because of the appeals of Flavian and others—he therefore had to choose remedies better suited to the situation: remedies that would strengthen the collapsing faith, raise up fallen bishops, condemn the contumacious and obstinate, and grant freedom to those who, driven by fear of threats, had offered captive hands to impious subscriptions, so that they might solemnly retract.

For this reason Saint Leo, dealing gently and graciously with the Emperor Theodosius, tried through various letters to suggest to him that, after removing every obstacle, he should order everything to be restored to the condition in which it had been before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world could be assembled.

To these appeals he likewise added the prayers of the Western bishops, writing:

“All the Churches of our regions, all the priests, with groans and tears, entreat your gentleness.”

[Note: Letter 40 to Theodosius.]

They were moved to make these supplications for no other reason than that he might more easily and speedily remedy the gravest evils by which the Churches of the East were distressed.

### 2

Meanwhile, to provide some consolation for Flavian’s distress, he wrote a letter to him, expressing profound sympathy for the grievous evils with which he was afflicted. He testified that he grieved over the ruin brought about by those through whom the truth was attacked and the very foundations of the entire Church were shaken. He also informed him that he was laboring for the common cause, so that “we may first deserve to reach those things which benefit the whole body of the faithful.”

[Note: Letter 42 to Flavian.]

This letter indicates to us that the holy pontiff Leo had not yet learned of Flavian’s death. Accordingly, the learned Cardinal Baronius, supported also by Quesnellus, noted that various reports concerning the death of this holy bishop had circulated because writers differed in their accounts.

[Note: Baronius, volume VI, under the year 449 of Christ, p. 97.]

Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, says that Saint Flavian passed to Christ in a glorious end while in the hands of those who were leading him into exile. Nicephorus asserts that he died three days later. In Count Marcellinus and in the Greek *Menologion* we read that he was banished to Epypa in Lydia, and there, worn down and exhausted by disgust, grief, and torments, he died.

The Eutychianists’ brief account gives a similar report:

“Flavian is led into exile and, at Epypa, which is a city of Lydia, died—whether death came upon him or was inflicted upon him.”

The *Synodical Book*, chapter 85, says that he was killed by kicks. The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon accuse the monk Barsumas of being the author of the murder. Evagrius, in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, attributing the account to Eusebius of Dorylaeum, assigns his death to Dioscorus; he says that Flavian was attacked by him, expelled from the church, and killed.

“Certainly,” says Quesnellus, “no one doubts that by his impulse he was treated most cruelly.”

Finally, many at the Council of Chalcedon called Dioscorus the striker and murderer of Flavian and another Cain.

Amid such great diversity among the writers, one fact is absolutely clear: Flavian died after being beaten and exhausted by the greatest sufferings. Although the time of his death cannot be determined with certainty, we may conjecture that it occurred only in the following year, 450, probably in winter, as can easily be inferred from the ordination of his successor.

The Greeks therefore celebrate his triumph every year on February 18, the day on which his translation took place at Constantinople under Marcian. Hence Baronius reports this proclamation from the Greek *Menologion*:

“Commemoration of our holy father Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, who, expelled by the impious Dioscorus and the heretics who conspired with him and sent into exile, was harassed by various pressures and hardships and died.”

The Western Church sings a similar hymn on the same day.

Finally, I consider it by no means permissible to omit that Cardinal Baronius himself, from all the opinions cited above, judged the following account the more credible: Flavian proceeded into exile; indeed, after being battered by blows from soldiers and led away bound in chains, he there enlarged his victorious soul with the crown of martyrdom, adorned with triumphal glory, and departed to God.

That the Roman Church held Flavian’s virtues in the highest honor, as well as his glorious struggles in defense of the Catholic faith, is shown by those paintings executed in mosaic in the distinguished Oratory of the Holy Cross. Hilary, the legate of Saint Leo, built it to the right of Constantine’s baptistery; he later succeeded Saint Leo in the Roman pontifical see.

Although the entire oratory was leveled to the ground under Sixtus because of the wars then raging in Italy, its memory, Baronius says, was at least restored in written records.

[Note: Theodoret celebrated the victories of Saint Flavian in a letter addressed to him with joyful words and outstanding praises, which Baronius reproduced in full in the volume cited above. See also the Roman Martyrology under February 18.]

### 3

Meanwhile the Church of Constantinople, deprived of its holy shepherd, was afflicted with mourning and grief—and all the more when it saw Anatolius substituted in the place of the deceased.

Since Anatolius had formerly been the *apocrisarius* of Dioscorus of Alexandria and had been protected by the patronage of the emperors, Saint Leo reasonably feared that, even in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, he might have been excessively inclined toward Eutyches and his faction.

Nevertheless, it can be demonstrated by several arguments that, after obtaining the see of Constantinople, Anatolius did not adhere to Dioscorus.

First, when Dioscorus learned that Saint Leo, together with the Roman council, had solemnly abolished and declared invalid all the Acts of the Robber Synod, he, unable to restrain his anger, returned to Alexandria and held an assembly of bishops in which he pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the supreme pontiff. He committed a crime that none of the most depraved men would have imagined. He was able to induce only ten bishops to this gravest of offenses, and even they did so weeping and unwillingly. From this it is completely certain that Anatolius did not at all support his party.

Second, Anatolius himself, as though anticipating that his election as bishop of Constantinople would be less pleasing and acceptable to the supreme pontiff Leo—or rather, that for many reasons it would be highly suspect to him, since Leo, moved by weightier considerations drawn from the Nicene canons, might refuse to regard Anatolius as legitimately elected and to communicate with him—humbly requested, in letters written by himself and by the emperor, perhaps toward the end of May, that he might thereafter be received into communion with the apostolic see.

It is probable that Anatolius’s letter was either lost through the ravages of time or is still preserved in more secret archives. Only a fragment survives, in Greek and Latin, in Quesnellus’s edition. He says that it was extracted from a manuscript of the Royal Library; it sheds some light on the history we are describing.

From it we learn that, after Flavian’s death, the Emperor Theodosius took care that the Constantinopolitan clergy should inquire who might govern that Church. At first, he says, the emperor instructed the most religious clergy of that city to select those best suited to its administration, reserving to himself the election of the foremost among them.

Yet the emperor’s command could not easily restrain the corrupt ambitions of certain persons. For when excessive disagreement arose among the electors and, as a result, they were divided in their preferences toward many candidates, the emperor again ordered that clerics in the imperial city should be sought out, including some who were residing there from other cities on various affairs—as commonly happens—so that the most distinguished among them might be promoted to the episcopal dignity without any partiality.

By these words Anatolius evidently wished to clear himself of the charge of ambition, which could justly have been brought against him because of the close association he had previously maintained with Dioscorus.

Finally, he says that he was elected chief bishop by the votes of all, “not because of my own justice,” he says, “but so that Christ Jesus might show in me all his patience,” according to the Apostle.

The election was followed by ordination. For, he adds, the synod of bishops residing at Constantinople proceeded without delay to ordain him.

These are the only details concerning Anatolius’s election and ordination indicated by the cited fragment of the letter. It is therefore especially regrettable that the remainder is missing, since from it we would understand that Anatolius not only requested the customary communion from Saint Leo, but also asked him especially to approve and graciously confirm his election as bishop of Constantinople. We have made various observations on this matter earlier, when discussing the appeal of Eutyches, and we shall explain it again when we discuss the letter that Anatolius wrote to Saint Leo after the Council of Chalcedon.

It is even more regrettable that the letter written by Theodosius to the same supreme pontiff in Anatolius’s favor has entirely disappeared. We can gather something of its meaning, however, from the reply of the same holy pontiff to the emperor.

Commenting on this, Baronius says:

“Although, unhappy man, he had been deceived and driven astray by Eutyches and Dioscorus and had approved Flavian’s condemnation, he was nevertheless not sunk so deeply into impiety as to consider the authority of the Roman Church wholly contemptible. Rather, understanding that see to be the head of all, he did not think that Anatolius, whom Dioscorus had substituted in Flavian’s place, should be received until he had been approved by the assent of the Roman pontiff. He therefore wrote to Saint Leo about these matters, seeking to ascertain his will and imploring his assistance.”

Baronius adds that this is proved exactly by the letter of the holy pontiff, of which we shall speak shortly.

A serious question nevertheless arises if we compare this letter of the holy pontiff with the fragment of Anatolius’s preceding letter. For Saint Leo’s words seem to indicate quite clearly that Anatolius had not yet been initiated by sacred episcopal ordination: the pontiff suspended his consent to Anatolius’s ordination and demanded a profession of faith. We read the same thing in the first chapter of the synopsis of this letter.

The point is made still clearer by Leo’s own words:

“But lest I should appear to have acted to the prejudice of the defense of the Catholic faith, I thought that nothing should yet be rashly written in either direction concerning the ordination of him who had begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople—not denying affection, but awaiting the manifestation of Catholic truth.”

[Note: I do not know what reason led Quesnellus to remove the word *temere* (“rashly”) from Leo’s text. It is found not only in the other printed editions but also in all the Vatican codices. We have learned from the manuscript copy transmitted to us that the Grimanian manuscript, so highly praised by Quesnellus, likewise contains it. The remaining words of the passage show that it is necessary to indicate Saint Leo’s cautious manner of acting.]

These words could certainly be explained, without any forced interpretation, as meaning that Anatolius had not yet been ordained but had merely been elected bishop, and that he was then awaiting the consent of the Roman pontiff in order to receive the gift of sacred ordination.

But this explanation does not at all agree with Anatolius’s words, in which he admitted that the synod of bishops residing at Constantinople had proceeded without delay to ordain him.

Therefore, in order to reconcile the meaning of the two letters, I believe the following must be affirmed: the emperor wrote to Saint Leo immediately after Anatolius’s election as bishop and before he was ordained by the bishops, confidently flattering himself that the Roman pontiff would by no means reject Anatolius’s ordination; and, moved by the same spirit that had led him to procure Anatolius’s election, he shortly afterward acted to have the synod ordain him.

From this observation the other conclusion necessarily follows: that the fragment of Anatolius’s letter has been placed outside its proper position in Quesnellus’s edition and should therefore have followed Theodosius’s letter.

### 4

Whatever may be said about this highly ambiguous question, I do not think it belongs to the purpose of our present undertaking. Above all, the rights of the apostolic see remained completely safe and intact through Leo’s manner of administration. He remained suspended in granting his consent to Anatolius’s ordination until he had obtained certain and solemn testimonies both concerning the new bishop’s character and the sincerity of his faith, and also concerning those with whom he maintained communion.

Accordingly, while treating the emperor with reverence and simultaneously maintaining and exercising the majesty and authority of pontifical dignity, he asked that the emperor himself not take offense at the pontiff’s hesitation, saying:

“I beg your Clemency to bear this patiently, so that, when he has shown himself to be toward the Catholic faith such as we desire, we may rejoice more fully and securely in his sincerity.”

Thus, in order to remove every unfavorable suspicion, he sought to eliminate the occasion of the entire difficulty—not by demanding anything burdensome, but by inviting Anatolius to do something that no Catholic could reject.

Specifically, he asked that Anatolius recall to mind the teaching of the Greek and Latin Fathers concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, through which the Nestorian heresy had already been condemned. He should also reread what had been preached by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in the exposition of the Nicene faith, which the archives of the apostolic see had received from Cyril.

He should also, Leo says, review the Acts of the Ephesian synod, in which Cyril of holy memory had inserted and cited, against the impiety of Nestorius, the Catholic testimonies of priests concerning the Incarnation of the Lord.

[Note: Leo’s Letter 53 to Theodosius, chapter 1, in Quesnellus, p. 272 of the first volume.]

Leo added that Anatolius should not disdain to reread his own letter—namely, Letter 24 to Flavian—which he would find in complete agreement with the piety of the Fathers.

When Anatolius recognized that this was being sought and desired from him for his own benefit, he should consent wholeheartedly to the judgments of the Catholics, so that he might declare, by a fully explicit subscription, before all the clergy and the entire people, a sincere profession of the common faith, to be published to the apostolic see and to all priests and Churches.

### 5

Because all these things could have been supplied by Anatolius—whose faith was rightly suspect to the apostolic see—only deceitfully and outwardly, while the Roman pontiff, because of the great distance between the places, could not ascertain the truth of what had been done with certainty, he took every precaution against being deceived.

He therefore suggested to the emperor that he deal with Anatolius so that, as soon as possible, writings from the bishop of Constantinople should reach the pontiff—writings such as a tested and Catholic priest ought to produce—openly and clearly declaring that, if anyone believed or asserted anything concerning the Incarnation of the Word of God other than what the profession of all Catholics and of Leo himself declared, Anatolius should separate that person from his communion, so that the pontiff might rightly extend fraternal charity in Christ to Anatolius.

[Note: Leo’s Letter 53 to Theodosius, chapter 1, in Quesnellus, p. 272 of the first volume.]

Saint Leo required this of Anatolius, and expressly added that Anatolius should pronounce an anathema against Dioscorus, Eutyches, and all their followers.

[Note: Baronius, volume VI, p. 115.]

Anatolius’s faith therefore had to be examined in such a way that every ambiguous or contrary suspicion would be removed from the pontiff’s mind. For this reason, without delay, Leo decided to send four legates of proven character from his own side to Constantinople. They were to receive Anatolius’s profession, entirely consonant with the pontifical instructions, so that it might then be determined whether the new bishop ought to be regarded as worthy of communion with the apostolic see.

In the same letter he notified the Emperor Theodosius of this solemn legation in the following words:

“But so that, with the Lord’s help, a swifter and fuller effect may be produced through the faith of your Clemency for these salutary concerns, I have sent to your Piety my brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as Basil and Senator, presbyters whose devotion has been tested by me. Through them, by means of the instructions we have sent, you may graciously recognize what our rule of faith is. If the bishop of Constantinople consents to the same confession with all his heart, let us rejoice in the peace of the Church, secure—as is fitting—and let nothing appear to remain ambiguous, lest we labor over perhaps needless suspicions.”

Leo therefore did not demand just any profession of faith from Anatolius, but one that corresponded exactly to the instructions of the legates, to the formula written by Leo himself and presented to the new bishop. Anatolius was thereafter also required to bind himself under oath, solemnly, before the entire clergy and the people of Constantinople, to preserve and profess it perpetually.

There is therefore no need to review here what the rights of the supreme pontiff were in the Eastern Churches, since this manner of acting, which clearly indicates supreme and greatest authority, makes them fully known to everyone.

### 6

The following words of Leo’s letter show that he directed the mission of these legates toward another objective as well:

“But if some dissent from the purity of our faith and from the authority of the Fathers, may your Clemency grant that a universal council be held within Italy, as the synod that assembled at Rome for this reason asks together with me, so that, when all who have fallen through ignorance or fear have come together, provision may be made for them through remedies of correction.”

Anyone who carefully considers this statement will readily understand that Leo was led to prescribe a general synod for no other reason than that, when all who had fallen had assembled together, remedies of correction might be supplied to them through priestly authority.

The general synod was therefore not demanded by Flavian’s appeal, nor by his expulsion from ecclesiastical affairs, as Galla Placidia says.

[Note: Galla Placidia’s letter to the Augusta Pulcheria is found in volume IV of Labbe’s General Councils.]

Nor could the Roman pontiff’s mind have been moved to request it by those causes, since in the meantime Flavian had already departed from this life and a new bishop had been substituted on the throne of Constantinople.

We therefore gather new arguments to strengthen the preceding Exercises, written in the earlier chapters.

To the preceding letter the same supreme pontiff wrote another, not dissimilar, to the Augusta Pulcheria, whose synopsis contains the substance of the entire text. It is as follows: he was awaiting Anatolius’s profession of faith; he had sent legates to the East; and the scandals had to be removed through a general council.

If this letter is compared with the preceding one written to Theodosius, it will be evident that the two differ from one another only in wording. At the end of the letter, Leo appeals to the Augusta’s clemency so that, through her support, an order might be issued for a universal council of priests to be held within Italy. There, with every deceptive device removed, it might finally become clear, upon fuller deliberation, what ought either to be restrained or to be healed.

[Note: See what we wrote in chapters 6, 8, 9, and 10 concerning the appeals of Eutyches and Flavian.]

7. In the meantime, we think it necessary to inquire more diligently why St. Leo, the supreme pontiff, remained hesitant in granting his assent to Anatolius, who had already been appointed to the episcopate of Constantinople, and delayed writing to him—not denying him affection, but awaiting a manifestation of the Catholic truth. Above, we indicated that this hesitation of the pontiff’s mind arose from several causes. Yet St. Leo himself expressly disclosed two of them among the rest in another letter written to the archimandrites of the monasteries of Constantinople, which is letter 53 in Quesnellus, but formerly 34.

In this letter, he declares that he is troubled by an anxiety that compels him to fear that Eutychian wickedness, which ought to have been cut off at its roots, might with the passage of time become more obstinate and more widespread. His apprehension was increased by the conduct of the new bishop of Constantinople and of those who had consecrated him:

[Col. 1217B]

> Apart from what concerned the ordination of the new bishop, they gave us no information about the errors that had been suppressed or renounced, as though no scandal or offense had existed in that Church, or as though the merit of the one ordained ought not chiefly to be demonstrated by this: that he had taught that doctrines contrary to Catholic convictions were alien to him.

Thus St. Leo had merely been informed of Anatolius’s ordination. Neither the emperor nor the bishops who had assembled to ordain Anatolius had given the Apostolic See a sincere report concerning the condition of the Church of Constantinople, or offered a trustworthy testimony regarding the faith, merits, and qualifications of the newly elected bishop. Yet Anatolius not only intended to communicate with the Roman pontiff; he further requested that his election and ordination as bishop be regarded as canonical.

Therefore, lest—as St. Leo says—what commonly occurs between distant regions should cause the examination of the truth to be prolonged by excessive delays, and lest he should act rashly to no purpose or approve anything that might harm the cause of the faith and the rights of the Roman See, [Col. 1217C] he resolved upon that solemn legation, giving those most trustworthy men sufficient instruction in the authority of their fathers. He adds:

> We desire, dearest brothers, that in all things you assist them with your diligence and concern.

Finally, confident in the faith and doctrine of the distinguished archimandrites, whom he knew to love the truth above all, he exhorts them in these honorable words to undertake labors on behalf of the faith, commending the mystery of the Catholic faith and the authority of the Roman See:

> Therefore, since you are justified by faith because you love the Catholic truth, and have been taught by the Holy Spirit concerning the unique mystery of human salvation, labor together with us and strive with all the devotion of which you are capable, so that, falsehood having been destroyed and the solidity of the faith defended, we may enjoy God’s peace securely throughout the whole world.

8. Yet although Leo ardently desired the firmness of the Catholic faith and the tranquility of the Eastern Churches, it seemed to him that he had not yet employed every precaution and necessary means if, apart from the letters written to Theodosius, 437, Pulcheria, and the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, he did not continue laboring until the happy conclusion of this affair. Therefore, while the four legates [Col. 1217D] he had sent were already traveling anxiously toward Constantinople, the holy pontiff himself wrote still other letters.

One was addressed to Martin the presbyter and the other members of his company. From the context itself, Quesnellus rightly noted in the margin that Leo praises them for the sufferings they had endured in the defense of the truth, [Col. 1218A] whose unity is not divided by distances between places. Finally, he declares that he has sent his legates to strengthen the courage of holy minds, and urges them to join care and counsel to their pious work.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] This letter, number 55 in Quesnellus and formerly 36, was written on the Ides of September in the year 450, when Abundius of Como and Asterius, together with two other pontifical legates, had already set out for Constantinople. In the Grimani manuscript, this letter is filled with various false readings, [Col. 1218D] as we shall more suitably show elsewhere.]

Another letter, likewise, he wrote not long afterward to two presbyters, Faustus and Martin. Whether the Martin to whom this new letter is addressed is the same Martin to whom the preceding letter was given, I shall not decide.

[Note: It should certainly not be omitted that some manuscript copies and editions read *Martianus* instead of *Martinus*.]

It is nevertheless highly probable that there was one and the same presbyter of that name. The supreme pontiff therefore wished these presbyters to be partners in the labors he was undertaking for the care of the universal Church. And, convinced that he had already received from the legates then staying in Constantinople a complete briefing on everything that needed to be done, he says:

> Even now, through our son Count Maximinus, we continue to encourage you by conversation, so that, since the freedom of the Catholics has greatly increased by the favor of the Lord, you may take spiritual courage against the precursors of Antichrist.

St. Leo himself immediately explained in the following chapter that by these final words he wished to attack [Col. 1218B] and denounce Nestorius and Eutyches. Yet he did not indicate how the freedom of the Catholics had increased, from which the distinguished presbyters were to derive spiritual courage against the precursors of Antichrist. We have therefore had to seek this information in other records, in order to make clear to our readers what Quesnellus entirely neglected to note.

We understand, then, that the freedom of the Catholics had increased for two reasons. The first was that, while the gravest schism continued in the East—with the Egyptian, Thracian, and Palestinian bishops following Dioscorus, while the Eastern, Pontic, and Asian bishops supported the party of Flavian and the Catholics, as the deacon Liberatus says in his *Breviary*, chapter 12—the emperor would not have seen that schism abolished after Flavian’s death unless he had begun seriously to reflect upon the evils that had befallen the Eastern Churches.

Although Theodosius had long before been formed by Pulcheria’s excellent instruction, he was afterward [Col. 1218C] corrupted in character, to the ruin of the Church, by the eunuch Chrysaphius and his wife Eudocia. By favoring and protecting heretics, schismatics, and plunderers up to that time, he had provided the occasion for so many and such great evils to spread in the East. Nevertheless, enlightened by divine light, he realized that he had been deceived by the eunuch’s cunning and by the schemes of his wife Eudocia.

He therefore resolved, in the future, to expiate the crime he had committed, acting upon new and most holy admonitions from Pulcheria. Since he could not undo the murder of St. Flavian, he poured out all his fury upon Chrysaphius. First stripping him of his rank, and then of all his property, he banished him to an island, as Nicephorus reports; Nicephorus relates that he was swallowed by the waves while sailing. Cedrenus, however, also speaking of him, insists that he was killed by Jordanes. Marcellinus Comes seems partly to support this account, for he says:

> Pulcheria handed over that most unjust eunuch Chrysaphius to Jordanes, the son of John, whom Chrysaphius had treacherously killed; and [Col. 1218D] Jordanes repaid him in kind.

[Note: Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 49; Cedrenus, page 334; Baronius, volume VI, page 117 in my edition.]

The same Theodosius had already offered other signs of repentance. 438 He assailed his wife Eudocia, as though she were another source of all the evils of the East, with severe reproaches, sent her to Jerusalem to do penance, and performed many other acts described by Nicephorus. Yet Baronius rightly warns his readers that Nicephorus was mistaken when he wrote that Theodosius ordered the sacred body of Flavian [Col. 1219A] to be transferred with solemn pomp to the city of Constantinople.

[Note: Baronius, volume VI, page 117 in my edition.]

For it is certain that this translation took place by order of Marcian.

9. There is no need at present to investigate how these events occurred. Since nothing else now presents itself to us concerning Leo’s conduct as pontiff, we therefore withdraw our hand from this Exercise. Only one very brief letter remains, written to the presbyter Faustus, in which St. Leo praises his faith and urges him to vigilance. Whether this letter should be joined to the preceding ones is not indicated by its text, in which no mention is made of matters to be handled by the legates at Constantinople; nor can it be inferred from the consular notice, which is lacking.

We shall therefore reserve for the following chapter our discussion of the synod of Constantinople, in which Anatolius made a solemn profession of faith, and of the other actions undertaken by St. Leo the Great before the Council of Chalcedon.

# CHAPTER XII

Theodosius Augustus dies in repentance. Through the efforts of Pulcheria Augusta and by decree of the Senate, Marcian is proclaimed emperor. He immediately orders the Eutychians to undergo punishment. He writes to St. Leo concerning the holding of a new general synod. He honorably receives Abundius and Leo’s other legates. The council of Constantinople is held concerning Anatolius and those who had fallen away. Marcian and Pulcheria again ask St. Leo that a general council be held. Letters of the bishops Theodoret, Ibas, and Aquilinus to Abundius, the legate of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 1219B]

1. The freedom of the Catholics, increased by the repentance of the emperor Theodosius, received still greater growth when Chrysaphius died and Eudocia was sent far away from the imperial court. The most holy Pulcheria, whom the emperor loved above his other sisters and had named Augusta, was gradually able to revive in her brother’s mind those instructions in sincere piety with which she had imbued him from childhood. For his most devout [Col. 1219C] elder sister had raised her younger brother almost from infancy until at least his twentieth year.

Thus Theodosius, intending to give still greater signs of repentance, built a magnificent church dedicated to the Mother of God. As his death drew near, he went to Ephesus to venerate St. John the Evangelist. Entering the church, he devoted himself to prayer, and in that prayer asked God to reveal to him who would succeed him in the Roman Empire. When God had shown this to him in a vision, he returned to Constantinople. His death followed shortly afterward.

For, while leading an army against Attila, he had gone out of the city and, falling from his horse while riding, dislocated a vertebra of his spine. He was therefore carried back to the palace in a litter. When he realized that he was dying, he secretly summoned his sister Pulcheria and spoke with her about Marcian the tribune as his successor in the empire, saying that it was pleasing and acceptable to God that Marcian should administer the Roman dominion after him.

Baronius copied this account almost word for word from Nicephorus. [Col. 1219D]

[Note: Socrates, book VII, chapter 22; Sozomen, book IX, chapter 1; Nicephorus, book XIV, chapter 17.]

Baronius observes that the cause of Theodosius’s death is described differently by Theodore in his *Collections*. Theodore says:

> The younger Theodosius went out hunting, was swept away into the River Albus, and died the following night. He was buried in the tomb of his father Arcadius. The empress Eudocia departed for Jerusalem and did not return thereafter.

Among the other matters relevant to the purpose of our Exercises, we do not think that the date of this death should be neglected, since from it we may determine whether the Constantinopolitan synod held by order of St. Leo in the affair of Anatolius took place while Theodosius was still alive, or after Marcian had taken up the reins of empire.

Baronius asserts that Theodosius died [Col. 1220A] on the fourth day before the Kalends of August in the year 450, in the fiftieth year of his age. Shortly afterward, by the will of St. Pulcheria, the empire was conferred upon Marcian by decree of the Senate. Writers especially praised the judgment of this holy woman because she wished to raise to the imperial office, under the title of marriage, a man mature in age, serious in counsel, approved for self-restraint, and distinguished on every side for military virtue—so that, through this election and prudence, the affairs of both the empire and religion might be more easily safeguarded.

Indeed, scarcely had Marcian put on the imperial purple when he displayed every evidence of piety toward religion. First he issued a law against the Eutychians, decreeing that they should be punished by the same penalties established by earlier laws against heretics:

> We order that they be detained and expelled beyond the soil itself of the Roman Empire, just as the enactments of the earlier laws decreed concerning the Manichaeans. Given on the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian VII and Avienus.

Then, turning his eyes toward the Roman pontiff and resolving to do everything according to his direction, he sent a letter to St. Leo. [Col. 1220B] He informed him of his election as emperor and finally declared that, for the abolition of every impious error and the establishment of the affairs of the Christians in complete peace, he most willingly consented to the holding of a synod under Leo’s authority. For he says:

> So that, every error having been removed through the holding of a synod under your authority, the greatest peace may be established among all the bishops of the Catholic faith, remaining pure and undefiled from every crime.

[Note: This letter of Marcian exists in Greek and Latin in volume IV of Labbe’s *General Councils*. Paschasius Quesnellus also included it in his edition, volume I, page 176.]

That this letter was written in the year 450 is known from the consular notice. It is certain, however, that it was not delivered to Leo until the following year, when Adelphius was consul.

2. During this interval Abundius and Asterius, together with two other legates, who had been sent to Constantinople in the affair of Anatolius, arrived there. They presented to Marcian, the successor of Theodosius, the pontifical letters that had been addressed to Theodosius, who was already dead.

After receiving them and treating the legates with the greatest honor, Marcian ordered that all St. Leo’s requests be fulfilled. Without delay, a provincial [Col. 1220C] synod was convened at Constantinople, at which both Anatolius’s faith and the restoration of those who wished to come to repentance after their fall were discussed.

It is deeply regrettable that the Acts of this synod, along with many other records relating to the matter, have been lost through the injury of time. [Col. 1220D] Nevertheless, from a certain fragment of them [Note: Baronius, volume VI, page 119 and following in my edition.] and from the letters of the emperor Marcian, Augusta Pulcheria, and Anatolius himself, the bishop of Constantinople, the eminent Baronius has described almost the complete sequence of events. On certain other matters later treated in that Constantinopolitan synod, however, he remained uncertain and hesitant, believing that they could eventually be gathered with probability from the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon.

We therefore need not linger over the examination of these matters. We shall indicate only briefly what took place.

[Note: That fragment of the Acts of the aforesaid synod appears in volume IV of the Councils, with notes by Severinus Binius, page 751.]

After hearing the petitions of the legates, Marcian therefore ordered by his pragmatic sanction that all the bishops who, while contending for the Catholic faith, had adhered to the party of Flavian in the Ephesian Robber Council should be recalled from exile and immediately return freely to their own sees.

Then, wishing above all to obey the commands of the Roman pontiff, he granted the legates unrestricted authority to summon from neighboring places even bishops who had fallen away, so that they might be admitted into communion with the Catholic Church, provided that the pontifical instructions were observed.

Accordingly, when that synod of Constantinople had been convened, Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople of New Rome, received St. Pope Leo’s letter concerning the confirmation of the Catholic faith against the madness of the heretics and read it publicly before everyone.

[Note: Formerly letter 10; in Quesnellus’s edition, letter 24.]

Blessed Abundius had likewise presented the letter to him publicly. [Col. 1221A] Anatolius therefore subscribed with full devotion to this letter of St. Leo, which contained the truth of the Catholic faith and agreed with the testimonies of the Fathers contained in the decrees of that Apostolic See. He pronounced an anathema against Eutyches and Nestorius, against their doctrine, and against their followers.

All the bishops, presbyters, archimandrites, and deacons present did the same. The hearts not only of the imperial Augusti but also of the holy men Abundius and Asterius, the bishops, and Basil and Senator, the presbyters, were filled with the greatest joy. For they said:

> Thanks be to Almighty God, because we have learned that the professions of the revered bishops, presbyters, archimandrites, and the entire clergy confess the true faith handed down by the Fathers.

Their subscription, inserted into the official record, makes this clear.

The legates also added that they had been sent from Rome by Leo to make the Catholic faith known to all. Therefore they too pronounced an anathema against Eutyches and against anyone who followed his unbelief, and against those who said that there were two natures in the Lord Christ before the incarnation and [Col. 1221B] only one nature after the incarnation.

Those who were absent were instructed to carry out the same act through the legates.

The legates of the Apostolic See then sent to each of the metropolitans of the East the celebrated letter of St. Leo to Flavian, so that all might subscribe to it, as may be gathered from Action 4 of the Council of Chalcedon.

Finally, this synod decreed that bishops who had fallen away in the Ephesian Robber Council and wished to return to communion with the Church should receive communion only on behalf of themselves, not on behalf of the entire Church. It was also decreed that the names of Dioscorus of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Eustathius of Berytus should not be recited at the altar, since they were regarded as impenitent and as leaders of the schismatics.

Here we think it necessary to observe that [Col. 1221C] Hardouin fell into error. In his notes on this council, he wrongly suspected that the anathema was then pronounced against Photius of Tyre, when he wrote:

> This was perhaps the same synod of bishops at which Photius, bishop of Tyre, was excommunicated by Anatolius of Constantinople, as is reported in Action 4 of the Council of Chalcedon.

But who could ever believe that a matter so contrary to the canons of Nicaea and so injurious to the religion and innocence of Photius could have been treated in a synod convened by the most holy men—the legates of the Roman pontiff—against the commands of the Apostolic See?

Therefore, the excommunication of Photius of Tyre, and the violation of his metropolitan rights undertaken by Eustathius of Berytus and reinforced by Theodosius’s pragmatic decree, must be referred not to this synod but entirely to another synod of the preceding year, at which Anatolius was raised to the throne of Constantinople.

We have written a complete dissertation on this matter under the auspices of our Most Holy Lord Benedict XIV and read it at the Academy of Councils. We shall publish it in a subsequent volume, in which we discuss the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1221D]

[Note: I cannot agree with Paschasius Quesnellus, who reasons differently in volume II, dissertation 1, *On the Life and Deeds of St. Leo the Great*, page 154. He maintains that the council in the affair of Anatolius was not convened by the authority of Abundius and the other legates of the Roman pontiff, but that Anatolius himself summoned a gathering of the bishops present in the city. He unjustly attacks Baronius for assigning that right to the Roman legates.

Away, I say, with this erroneous opinion, which injures pontifical rights and contradicts the truth of the events! What? While Anatolius’s election and ordination—carried out by Dioscorus, a heretic and schismatic who had usurped the authority of the patriarchate of Antioch—were still under judgment, and while the legitimate delegated judges were present, could Anatolius himself have convened an assembly, gathering, or synod? Who could assert this without deliberately provoking controversy, especially since the arguments that Quesnellus adduces from Action 4 of Chalcedon [Col. 1222D] must be referred not to this synod of Abundius but to the preceding synod of the year 449, as we shall demonstrate with complete clarity in our dissertation on the action concerning Photius of Tyre mentioned above?

Moreover, the erroneous judgment of our adversaries is refuted by Theodoret’s letter to Abundius of Coena. Theodoret did not attribute the council and its proceedings to Anatolius’s authority but to the supreme power of the pontifical legates, as will become clear from what follows.]

441 3. With the affairs of the Church of Constantinople thus settled in peace, the emperor Marcian meanwhile resolved seriously to remove all the evils of the East and abolish the schisms.

First he ordered that the body of St. Flavian be carried [Col. 1222A] to Constantinople with solemn ceremony and pomp and buried in the basilica of the Apostles, where the remains of his episcopal predecessors had been placed.

Then he wrote new letters to the supreme pontiff Leo. In them, having testified to Anatolius’s faith, he reverently invited Leo to come to the East and celebrate a synod, so as to satisfy the wishes of Marcian and his Augusta wife and determine what would benefit the sacred religion.

He adds:

> If it is burdensome for you to come to these regions, let your Holiness make this known to us by letter, so that our sacred letters may be sent throughout the entire East, and into Thrace and Illyricum themselves, wherever it pleases us that all the most holy bishops should assemble, and that they should declare, according to the ecclesiastical rules and as your Holiness shall have defined, what is beneficial to the Christian religion and the Catholic faith.

Thus far Marcian in another letter written to St. Leo.

[Note: On this matter, consult St. Leo’s letter to Anatolius, formerly 40, in Quesnellus 60, chapter 3.]

A similar letter was also written on the same occasion by his wife Pulcheria. [Col. 1222B] We reasonably believe that these letters were carried to the Roman pontiff by the clergy of Anatolius, who had been sent to Rome with the profession of faith, as we shall say in its proper place.

4. Meanwhile Theodoret rejoiced with great joy because, through Marcian’s pragmatic decree and the efforts of the pontifical legates, he and the others who had contended against Eutyches were to be recalled from exile, so that they could recover their episcopal offices and their own Churches.

He therefore did not delay in writing to Abundius, the legate of the Roman pontiff. First he testified that the true and apostolic faith was preserved with devout mind in the Roman Church of the West, and confessed that he had therefore given thanks to Almighty God—especially because the religion that had been endangered in the East had been renewed and brought into the light through Your Holiness.

He compared this Roman faith to Noah’s ark, inasmuch as the Western Church had been preserved from the flood of the Eutychian heresy, so that the Eastern Churches as well might preserve the true religion which the sacrilegious new heresy had already attempted to devastate and utterly consume.

He added that he had learned the full truth of the faith from the letters of the most holy and religious archbishop, Lord Leo, whom he called the great advocate and defender of the truth. He affirmed that he had assented to those letters and subscribed to them together with Ibas of Edessa and Aquilinus of Byblus, bishops, against whom the inventors of the new heresy had armed the power of the emperors.

He concluded his letter with the following words:

[Note: This letter appears in Baronius, volume VI, page 125, and in the collection of Theodoret’s works prepared by the learned Jesuit Garnier.]

> It remains for you, together with the holy men, to bring aid to the holy Church and remove the impious wars that were impending. Therefore suppress the sacrilegious sect that has risen against piety, and restore the former peace to the Churches, so that you may receive from the Lord the fruits of your apostolic labors, since He has promised that He will repay those fruits.

We could add here many other proofs of Theodoret’s submission and reverence toward the Apostolic See, which would make perfectly clear the doctrine of the Eastern bishops of that age concerning the governance of ecclesiastical affairs. They also indicate that only heretics and schismatics had dared to deny the Roman pontiffs those supreme rights that concern judging matters of faith, receiving appeals from every part of the world, convening general synods, and either confirming, revising, or abolishing their judgments.

Yet, lest I appear to depart from the task of recounting St. Leo’s deeds, I shall omit these matters for the present, since much must later be said in another Exercise about the appeal of that bishop of Cyrus to the Apostolic See—an appeal which Quesnellus attempted to attack and overturn.

# CHAPTER XIII

The affairs of the East are changed for the better; they prepare destruction for the Eutychians, protection for the Catholics, and turn the grief of the great pontiff Leo into joy. He gave testimony to this joy in various letters written to Marcian, Pulcheria, Anatolius, and Julian of Cos. Julian’s homeland is investigated. The opinions of Baronius, Henricus Valesius, and the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius are noted. Finally, the holy pontiff devoted every effort to securing the holding of a general synod.

[Col. 1223B]

1. I have often and at length reflected within myself on whether the affairs of the Eastern Church brought more grief or more joy to the mind of Leo the Great: first, because they had been so greatly disturbed by the Eutychian heresy and its supporters and had almost been brought to ruin; and afterward, because they had been happily settled in complete tranquility, with the triumph and glory of the Catholic faith, through pontifical labor and care, so that the virgin Church, bride of the one husband, Christ, might seem not to have been corrupted in any way by the frauds of the wicked.

Yet I have not dared to decide the question.

[Note: Leo’s letter, formerly 38, is number 53 in Quesnellus. It appears in volume I of St. Leo’s works, page 276, and in volume IV of the Councils.]

Therefore, lest my labor be spent on uncertain investigations, I shall affirm only that Leo’s mind was filled with great joy when he learned that his previous labors and sorrows had already contributed greatly to ecclesiastical freedom and to the administration of divine affairs.

Among other things, those letters provide us with evidence of this pontifical joy which St. Leo wrote to Marcian, Pulcheria, and Anatolius of Constantinople, [Col. 1223C] after receiving the fullest report of the Constantinopolitan council, which Abundius and the other legates had sent to Rome.

Accordingly, after considering the greatest benefits bestowed upon the Catholic Church by divine generosity, he immediately wrote to Marcian, without any delay, to express the pleasure of his mind that the integrity of the faith had been defended more securely from the snares of its enemies by imperial protection. He confessed that he owed Marcian many thanks, which he could have conveyed not in words but through the benefits he had conferred upon the Church.

He added that he had not been able to write a longer letter because the clergy whom Anatolius had sent with his profession of faith were about to depart from the city. He continues:

> We have sent through our legates fuller writings concerning everything that pertains to my care for the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the Lord’s priests.

That he had sent new legates to Constantinople is made clear by these final words.

443 Nevertheless, since the reason for this new delegation is not stated in this letter, we must seek it in the letters that follow.

At first I thought—since the writings mentioned there are missing—that Leo had decreed [Col. 1223D] a solemn legation to Marcian in order to congratulate him on having attained the Roman Empire and to secure greater protection for himself and for the affairs of the Church. But that the legates mentioned there had been sent for another purpose is made clear by Leo’s writings to the emperor and by the letters written on the same day to Pulcheria, Anatolius, and Julian, bishop of Coena.

In the first place, when St. Leo wrote to Pulcheria on that same day, he praised her piety, by which, supported by the assistance of divine mercy, she had endured labors so that the two heresies—Nestorian and Eutychian—would neither remain hidden nor gradually weaken the hearts of Catholics.

That he intended to indicate this in the following words is certain:

> And those who had chosen for themselves the separate parts of the twofold impiety fell together before the one truth of the Catholic faith.

This is especially clear because, after reviewing Pulcheria’s efforts to break the obstinacy of the Nestorians, he immediately added that she was owed a second crown of triumph and palm for the destruction of Eutyches’ error.

Therefore, in the following section of his letter, he continues to congratulate her and the emperor in the name of the Church for the works and assistance they had provided to the legates of the Apostolic See:

[Col. 1224A]

> You have brought back to their Churches the Catholic priests who had once been unjustly expelled from them by the sentence of Dioscorus; and you have caused the relics of the blessed Flavian, of holy memory, [lacuna] to be restored with due honor to the Church which he had rightly governed.

He added other matters that concerned either the bishops who had fallen away, who were to be received into communion if, retracting their own evil deeds against the faith, they subscribed to the faith, or the Church of Dorylaeum, whose legitimate pastor, Eusebius, a participant in communion with the Roman pontiff, was then staying in Rome while the aforesaid [Col. 1224B] Church was being ravaged by an intruding plunderer.

He therefore rightly took the opportunity to commend the Church of Dorylaeum to imperial protection, as well as Julian, bishop of Coena, and the Constantinopolitan clergy, who had already adhered to Flavian with faithful service.

This is the substance of the letter to Augusta Pulcheria. We believe that the letter which Leo confessed he had sent to Marcian through his legates was similar, since we know that Leo consistently gave the same response concerning matters to be handled, especially when he was compelled on the same day to send letters to the East about one and the same affair.

2. Something more distinctive deserves attention in the two other letters that follow, likewise dated on the same day, one of which he sent to Anatolius and the other to Julian of Cos. Yet the entire difference between the letters arose from no other cause than the difference between the offices they held in the Church.

After congratulating Anatolius [Col. 1224C] on the profession of faith that he had made according to the rules prescribed by Leo himself and had signed in his own hand, Leo says that he was sending back to the East three clerics of the Constantinopolitan Church who had delivered the letters just mentioned. After explaining the names and ranks of these legates, he writes:

> Therefore, so that your affection might be strengthened by mutual expressions with ours, we have sent back, after the venerable day of the Easter feast, our sons Casterius—or Castorius—the presbyter, and Patricius and Asclepiades, the deacons, who brought us your letters.

Then, as bishop of the Church of Constantinople, he commands Anatolius to take care that, in the conduct of divine affairs, none of the presbyters or bishops should dare to recite at the sacred altar the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, or Eustathius, since our men—that is, the legates—who had been established there had said that this should be done.

[Note: Formerly letter 40; now in Quesnellus’s edition, letter 60, chapters 1 and 3.]

Furthermore, if Quesnellus had attended to these words, I do not know whether he could have maintained that the synod, or assembly of bishops, had been convened by Anatolius rather than by the pontifical legates. On this matter, see what we have already noted in the preceding chapter.

[Col. 1224D]

Finally, the remaining matters that he writes in chapter 3 of that letter correspond exactly to those that we have just reviewed from the letter to Pulcheria.

3. As for Julian, bishop of Cos, nothing occurs to us that needs saying beyond what we understand can be gathered from these same letters. It is well known that Julian gave the Roman pontiff letter after letter on the occasion of the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies. But since all his letters have been lost—as Paschasius Quesnellus also recorded in his catalogue of documents relating to St. Leo—we can speak of them only on the basis of conjecture.

Meanwhile, what Julian wrote to St. Leo, and on what occasion, in the closing months of [Col. 1225A] 450 or at the beginning of 451, is indicated to us by Letter formerly 41, now 61 in Quesnellus, which the Roman Pontiff began in these words:

“I have received the letter of your fraternity through our sons, the Constantinopolitan clerics, messengers of your salvation, in which you indicate that you have been burdened with great tribulations.”

For many reasons Julian, bishop of Cos, was hated by the Eutychian faction. He exercised vicarious authority among the Easterners on behalf of the Apostolic See. At the Ephesian Robber Council he resisted Dioscorus to the utmost, never departing from the directives of the pontifical legates, as can be gathered from another earlier letter of St. Leo written to the same man on the Ides of October 449.

Another reason why he was detested by the Eastern heretics and schismatics may have arisen from his homeland. Since he was an Italian, the Easterners did not willingly hear his name, bearing with the greatest difficulty the fact that a man of a foreign nation exercised authority over them. He also devoted himself with the utmost vigilance to ensuring that ecclesiastical regulations were not neglected, diligently working so that [Col. 1225B] the mandates of the Apostolic See would be carried out and its rights not violated.

Accordingly, compelled to endure the gravest labors among insolent adversaries of the Catholic faith, and as his spirit—firmly attached to the truth—was worn down by excessive strain, he was driven by necessity to desire to present himself to Leo and to his homeland. “This,” says St. Leo, “I had truly hoped would happen, so that through your mouth I might learn more openly the evasions of all the heretics. Nevertheless, protected by divine assistance, when he had escaped unharmed from the hands of his impious enemies, so that he might be able to benefit the affairs of the Church, it was granted to him to remain among those whose probable agreement has become known to us, as the writings of our brother Anatolius attest and the acts conducted in his presence before our representatives demonstrate.”

After this, Leo returns Julian’s greeting and exhorts him to persevere prudently in applying diligent care against the cunning of falsehood, “since for this purpose both your own spirit and our authority support you.”

To some, however, [Col. 1225C] our statement that Julian of Cos was by nationality an Italian may appear less secure, since we have followed chiefly the opinion of the most illustrious Stephen Baluzius [Note: [Col. 1225D] See Baluzius’s new collection of Councils, p. 955.]. In his new collection of Councils, while discussing this Julian, bishop of Cos and legate of the Apostolic See, Baluzius maintains that he was a Greek. He also notes the error of Baronius and Henri Valois, who, occasionally misled by corrupt readings in manuscript codices, confused this man with Julius of Puteoli, the bishop whom St. Leo had sent, together with others, to the Robber Council.

Baluzius therefore asserts that Julian, bishop of Cos, was a Greek, and that Leo first charged him with rendering into Greek the letter written to Flavian [Note: [Col. 1225D] St. Leo the Great, Letter 102, in Quesnellus]. He says that this was not difficult in a short and modest composition, since Flavian undoubtedly had some knowledge of the Latin language. Later, after the Council of Chalcedon, Leo likewise commissioned Julian to translate into Latin the acts of Chalcedon, written in Greek. “It was,” he says, “a greater undertaking to translate those extensive acts from Greek into Latin—especially for a Greek, who, although he was a legate of the Apostolic See among the Greeks, [Col. 1225D] nevertheless could not have possessed a complete knowledge of the Latin language.” Yet pardon must be granted to this most diligent man, who failed to notice the letter of Leo explained above.

4. In the meantime, the emperor Marcian, seriously reflecting that the prosperity he had attained through the whole empire depended chiefly upon religious affairs, and seeing that the affairs of the Eastern Churches could [Col. 1226A] soon be brought to ruin by their various factions and the hatred of the bishops unless a general synod were convened, as St. Leo had already decided, wrote letters to the holy pontiff asking him to deign to visit the East, hold a council there, and decree everything believed beneficial to religion. If this should seem burdensome to him, he added, His Holiness should make this known by letter, so that imperial letters might be sent throughout the East, and into Thrace and Illyricum themselves, ordering all the most holy bishops to assemble at a place to be determined and, as His Holiness had defined according to ecclesiastical regulations, to declare by their own decision whatever would benefit the Christian religion and the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1225D] This letter of Marcian exists in Greek and Latin in vol. I of St. Leo’s works in Quesnellus, p. 279, and in vol. IV of the General Councils.].

The prefect of the city of Rome, Titianus, delivered this letter to Leo, as we gather from the reply Leo himself sent to the emperor. In it, after praising Marcian’s zeal, he congratulates him on striving to restore both the affairs of the faith and those of the empire, so that, once God had been propitiated by a single confession, both heretical falsehood and barbarian hostility might be destroyed.

Since the pontiff [Col. 1226B] judged that conducting the business of a new synod through letters sent back and forth would be very difficult, he first informed the emperor that the matter must concern only those who had gone astray, and not the faith or the Scriptures, which he considered it impious to interpret otherwise than the holy Fathers had done. He therefore responded to the emperor’s concern by announcing a legation “which, God willing, will immediately reach Your Clemency, and through which whatever I judge relevant to the usefulness of the case will be presented more fully and appropriately” [Note: [Col. 1226D] Letter formerly 42, now 62 in Quesnellus.
