The pontiff wrote it on the ninth day before the Kalends of May 451, or, as two Vatican codices and Grimanius have it, on the eighth day before the Kalends of that month.].

The pontiff himself did not delay long in sending a new letter to the emperor, perhaps because within an interval of forty-seven days he had received another letter from the emperor. For on the seventh day before the Ides of June he says that he took up the confidence to reply both from the emperor’s letters and from the report made to him by Abundius and the other legates returning from the East. They demonstrated, he says, not merely by assertions in words but also by the actual results of their deeds, that “divine protection is active in you for the defense of the Catholic faith” [Note: [Col. 1226D] Letter formerly 44, now 63, chapter 1.].

Among other matters that he adds there, he relates that he had already sent Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius, [Col. 1226C] “who may fulfill the duties of my concern,” as he had promised earlier. He dispatched them to reconcile the fallen bishops, so that the wishes of those who had repented would not be wearied by prolonged delay, and so that harmful leniency would not receive them rashly and without discrimination.

He admits that he had requested a general synod, as the emperor had suggested. But the necessity of that time in no way allowed the priests of all the provinces to assemble, because of the impending wars, which prevented certain bishops—especially those who were to be summoned—from leaving their Churches. He therefore judged that the convocation of the bishops should be reserved for another time.

On the same day he wrote a similar letter to the Augusta Pulcheria, commending the aforementioned legates to her, condemning the Eutychian blasphemy, and finally asking the Augusta that Eutyches himself be transferred to a more distant place and that a Catholic abbot be placed over his monastery, one who could both free that congregation of servants of God from its corrupt doctrine and instruct it in the institutions of truth [Note: [Col. 1226D] Letter formerly 45, now 64, chapter 3.].

[Col. 1226D] 446

5. Having taken these measures with the emperor Marcian and the Augusta Pulcheria, the holy pontiff did not abandon the work he had begun. On the same day he also wrote to Anatolius, whom he had formerly received into communion, approving and confirming his election as bishop of Constantinople. Explaining the necessity that had moved him to send new legates into the East—Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius—he instructed Anatolius to receive the penitent fallen bishops back into reconciliation through satisfaction [Col. 1227A] and an unequivocal profession of faith, while observing such moderation that neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice would be neglected, and that the divine judgment would be considered in everything without respect of persons.

But in another chapter of the same letter, speaking of those who had sinned more grievously at the Robber Council by claiming for themselves a higher place in that unhappy synod, he says:

“If such satisfaction is offered by them as does not appear open to rejection, their case is to be reserved for the more mature counsels of the Apostolic See, so that, after everything has been examined and weighed, it may be determined what ought to be decided concerning their actions.”

He also forbids their names to be recited at the altar until the course of events should show what ought to be decided concerning them.

The authority of the Roman See in judging the cases of the Easterners outside the council is made perfectly clear not only by this reservation concerning the admission of the leaders of the heretics to reconciliation, but also by what he wrote in another chapter of the letter, where he orders that, if it should happen that certain other cases required further deliberation, a report should quickly be sent to us, “so that, after the character of the cases has been considered, our concern may determine what ought to be observed” [Col. 1227B].

6. Here, then, unless my opinion deceives me, two matters must be noted, both of which present clear and decisive evidence of the supreme moderation exercised by the Roman pontiffs in the affairs of the Eastern Churches.

The first concerns those penitents who had fallen through fear. For receiving these people, Leo himself prescribed rules that did not conflict with justice and did not favor indulgence at the expense of justice. To reconcile them he sent the two aforementioned legates, Lucentius and Basilius. Since he had given them the necessary instructions and admonitions, no one—not even Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople—could lawfully depart from their directives, even slightly.

Thus, all the fallen who were to be restored from this category to their former ecclesiastical offices, dignities, and ranks could be absolved only by the authority of the Apostolic See and permitted to enjoy their ancient honors. As for the others, [Col. 1227C] who were regarded as authors of the schism and whose case was harsher and more serious, Leo’s decree established that they could be either admitted or excluded from honors and ranks, communion and reconciliation, on the basis of any sign or testimony of satisfaction; for the supreme pontiff had reserved to himself a more mature judgment concerning them and concerning other cases that might arise.

Quesnellus must be judged to have deliberately concealed these two points. He was guided by the consideration that otherwise he would have been forced to admit what he consistently denies in preparing the works of the holy pontiff—namely, the authority of the Roman pontiffs in judging the affairs of the Easterners. He relied upon so many violent interpretations that he considered them sufficient to abolish that authority.

That he deliberately concealed the arguments of this letter is revealed by the annotations he placed at the end of the second volume of the Leonine letters. For among the other letters he completely passed over this one, as though it were unworthy of his notes and observations.

But what of this? Leo himself, who needs no interpreter, [Col. 1228A] left posterity still clearer evidence of this supreme authority in issuing judgments concerning Eastern affairs in Letter 67. While Flavian was still alive, two presbyters of the Church of Constantinople—Basilius and John—had been accused either of the Eutychian or of the Nestorian heresy and came to Rome to remove this stigma of infamy.

After both had cleared themselves before the Apostolic See, and were later about to return to the East, the holy pontiff wrote to Anatolius, bearing witness that, after undertaking the labor of a distant journey, they had disclosed at the Apostolic See the convictions of their hearts, condemning, he says, both heresies mentioned above.

Thus, closing this very brief letter, the holy pontiff addresses Anatolius:

“Therefore, dearest brother, through these men, returning [Col. 1228B] to their own country with our testimony, we have sent our letter to Your Charity, confidently requesting that those who are honored by the grace of the Apostolic See may also rejoice in being assisted by your favor in every respect” [Note: [Col. 1227C] Letter formerly 48, now 67 in Quesnellus.].

I am not unaware that those who look for a knot in a rush may argue that this letter is less suitable for proving our thesis, because of the harsh words “confidently requesting,” which seem unworthy of the authority of a judge. But the dispute is settled either by the variety of the readings or by a certain fragment of Flavian’s letter, recovered from the Vatican Library and not yet published, which we shall present in the following volume.

For most codices, and Grimanius himself, as Quesnellus wrote in the margin of his edition, read “confidently urging.” Moreover, the affair of the two presbyters must be assigned to the year 449. Although the entire, complete series of the Leonine letters is lacking, that single fragment of Flavian’s letter written concerning their case makes it clear that St. Leo truly acted in the capacity of a judge: that the two presbyters [Col. 1228C] came to Rome to give an account of their faith; and finally that Leo received them into communion and declared them innocent, not out of some indulgence, but after investigating and approving the case.

For the fragment we mentioned contains nothing other than Flavian’s report to St. Leo concerning the faith and conduct of the presbyters Basilius and John, as we shall explain more fully.

The holy pontiff wrote this letter on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, shortly before he appointed legates to the new general council and sent them from the City to the East.

Since what follows constitutes, as it were, the preliminaries of the Council of Chalcedon, in convening and canonically ordering which the zeal of the holy pontiff Leo was diligently engaged, we reserve discussion of these matters for the chapters of the following book.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1227]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1227D] 448

Among the principal reasons why so many people, out of hatred for sincere truth, abuse the Acts of Chalcedon and the writings of Leo in order to abolish or at least diminish the rights of the Apostolic See, one must certainly be judged to be either a certain malicious interpretation of the monuments of antiquity or insufficient care in reading, examining, and comparing them.

For if [Col. 1228D] both theologians and writers on ancient affairs had set aside the partisan spirit of every side and wished to debate the questions we have undertaken to discuss and to give judgment—as the circumstances of the age required—they would have brought great light to certain obscure facts. We and other writers would not then have had to labor so greatly to expose and refute the fabrications they devised to conceal and suppress the truth, filling and corrupting the minds of others with prejudices and false opinions.

Thus, since in the preceding Exercises I have attempted to bring out of darkness many matters relating to the author of the Eutychian heresy and to its defenders and champions; and since I also dealt at length with the ecclesiastical judgments concerning the condemnation of Eutyches and others’ appeals, explaining clearly the supreme rights of the Apostolic See and its practice in judging and reconsidering even the cases of the Easterners, along with many other matters of this kind, I now understand that I must [Col. 1229A] examine and review what was finally done against the same Eutychian faction at the Council of Chalcedon in accordance with Leo’s judgment, as well as what the same holy pontiff faithfully accomplished during the remainder of his life for the good of the Christian commonwealth.

I admit that in composing the preceding Exercises I sometimes used a lengthy manner of exposition, from which the men of our age commonly shrink, being accustomed to take pleasure in the lighter surface of things rather than to exercise themselves in the sincere investigation of those same truths. But many reasons compelled me at times to adopt a more extended discourse.

One arose from the use of the educational methods that I had been accustomed to explain in schools of theology over many years. In treating these matters, a brief and compressed style cannot be used without leaving the hearers insufficiently instructed. For that reason I have found it very difficult to overcome this habit, acquired through long practice.

The other reason must be attributed to our adversaries. After they had raised certain obscure questions surrounded by many sophistries, which I had [Col. 1229B] to address for the purposes of the present work, it would have been entirely impossible to seize and refute their arguments in a few words. I repeatedly had to appeal to genuine sources and their interpreters in order to demonstrate the poorly assembled and constructed buildings and systems they had erected.

Nevertheless, in the final part of these Exercises I shall strive throughout to pursue brevity. Some matters I shall indicate or supplement with the help of notes; others I shall reduce to an outline, with scarcely any direct confrontation with the adversaries; and still others, which the breadth and difficulty of the questions would require me to discuss, but which have already been illuminated by certain men of excellent faith and learning, I have decided to leave virtually untouched, referring our readers to the writers who preceded us.

## CHAPTER I

The emperor Marcian finally permitted the long-desired general synod of Leo the Great to be held in the East. Although the holy pontiff, moved by weightier considerations, could have opposed the emperor’s decision, he was prevented from attending the synod and therefore sent four legates to the East to preside over it in his name, in his place, and with his authority. Accordingly, he arranged everything that was to be done, sending for this purpose successive letters to Paschasinus, Marcian, Anatolius, the Augusta Pulcheria, and Julian, bishop of Cos.

[Col. 1229C]

1. Once a new mission of legates had been undertaken in the East for the sake of certain people wishing to come to repentance and be received back, both the supreme pontiff and the Augustus Marcian finally deliberated about holding a general synod.

That Leo had desired this is shown immediately by the letters he wrote to Theodosius in the same year, 449, in the month of October, as soon as he heard of the disastrous outcome of the Ephesian Robber Council; we discussed these letters in the Exercises of the preceding book.

But since the Augustus Theodosius, inclined toward Eutyches, had been surrounded by factious men whose guidance he followed, the pontiff’s wishes were then rendered entirely ineffective, until Marcian was raised to the imperial throne and the affairs of the East, already nearly ruined, were restored.

The emperor therefore came over to Leo’s view, but they did not agree about the place and time. Leo preferred that the synod be convened in Italy, considering how he might prevent all the evils by which the memory of the Ephesian Robber Council was gravely afflicted, and also desiring to be present at the council.

But the emperor, seeing heresy [Col. 1230A] spreading throughout the East, believed that it had to be cut down there. Accordingly, after letters had been sent back and forth, Marcian—moved by the necessity of the situation and urged by the Eastern bishops—judged that the assembly of the synod should no longer be postponed.

Since neither custom nor love of his homeland nor the foreign enemy, the Huns under Attila, allowed Leo to leave Italy, he chose Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to fulfill his duties. Few equaled him in learning, holiness, and reputation.

The great strength and steadfastness of this bishop’s spirit had already been tested by the harsh and prolonged captivity he endured among the barbarians. His knowledge is also especially well known from the correction of the Paschal cycle, concerning which St. Leo had consulted him.

Moreover, St. Leo valued him so highly that two years earlier he had entrusted him with the task of restoring the ancient discipline and reforming the morals of the Sicilian Church, as can be gathered from Letter formerly 4, now 16 in Quesnellus. He concluded its final chapter in these words:

“Those matters which, with the Lord inspiring us, we have judged ought to be communicated to you, we wish to reach your knowledge through our brothers and fellow bishops Baccillus and Paschasinus. Through their report, may we learn with what reverence the institutions of the Apostolic See are observed by you.”

He therefore wished to send him new letters, [Col. 1230B] as a kind of anticipation of the office he was shortly afterward considering entrusting to him. To prepare his spirit with the necessary instruction, he sent him the celebrated letter to Flavian, which, he says, “the universal Church embraces,” and which he had sent to him for careful review and understanding.

He discusses at length the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies. In order to cleanse the Church of Constantinople from their stain, he relates that he had already sent pontifical legates there. They proclaimed concerning the mystery of the Incarnation what the holy Fathers had taught and what the whole body of the Churches had long held, and they successfully obtained the restoration of the entire Church of Constantinople, together with all its monasteries and many bishops, to sound doctrine.

These men gave their agreement and, by their signatures, [Col. 1230C] anathematized Nestorius and Eutyches together with their doctrines. So that Paschasinus might learn these matters clearly, Leo says, “I have sent certain written materials to Your Charity.”

He then adds:

“You should also know that recently I received a letter from the bishop of Constantinople reporting that the bishop of Antioch—namely Maximus—[Note: [Col. 1229D] Letter 68, chapter 1], having sent doctrinal letters throughout his provinces, obtained the agreement of all the bishops with my letter and condemned Nestorius and Eutyches with a common subscription.”

In this matter we cannot at all lend our ears or credence to Quesnellus, who ascribed all these actions to Anatolius, supposedly as president of that assembly [Note: [Col. 1229D] See how foolishly Paschasius Quesnellus fabricated his account in the case of Domnus, the predecessor of Maximus of Antioch, flattering himself that no reason could be found why St. Leo could have approved this election and the deposition of Domnus. These two considerations chiefly led him to that absurd opinion, so that he rejected the Chalcedonian action concerning Domnus as spurious and false. Did he not, even before the Council of Chalcedon, cleanse the patriarchate of Antioch from the Nestorian and Eutychian stain with which Domnus had infected it? See what we have already written concerning that action, following in the footsteps of the illustrious Stephen Baluzius.].

For St. Leo, wishing to instruct Paschasinus about many matters, sent him the sequence of everything that had been done by his legates at Constantinople. He certainly did not credit Anatolius with the purification of the Church of Constantinople or with the condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches. He mentions Anatolius only insofar as he had already received from him a report concerning what Maximus had religiously carried out in the provinces of [Col. 1230D] Antioch for the defense and protection of the faith.

Indeed, could Anatolius, whose faith had been suspect, have presided over an assembly at Constantinople in the presence of the pontifical legates? It is a fiction, and we refute it in our dissertation on Photius of Tyre, to which we refer our readers.

2. Finally, in the last part of his letter, the holy pontiff asks Paschasinus about the rule to be followed for the Paschal feast in the year 455, because in a note of Theophilus he had found that the Alexandrian [Col. 1231A] bishop of blessed memory had determined that Easter should be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May—something which, he says, we find entirely alien to ecclesiastical rule.

“For,” he adds, “in our Paschal cycles, as you are pleased to know well, it is written that Easter is to be celebrated in that same year on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

Therefore, wishing to prevent every error and remove every ambiguity, he orders Paschasinus to investigate and examine more carefully, together with knowledgeable men, the new reckoning of times and the rule and course of the heavenly bodies. But concerning this Paschal cycle, which St. Leo the Great desired to have corrected, we shall speak in due order when discussing the events that followed the Council of Chalcedon.

It is nevertheless remarkable that in this letter nothing was indicated to Paschasinus about undertaking the journey toward Nicaea, so that he might exercise the pontifical office at the synod which Marcian had demanded should be held without delay.

For since Leo wrote the aforementioned letter on the eighth day before the [Col. 1231B] Kalends of July, and we find that only two days later he wrote three other letters—one to the Augustus Marcian, another to Anatolius, and finally a third to Julian, bishop of Cos—in which he mentions that legates had already been appointed for the new synod, it is reasonable to argue that on the seventh day before the Kalends of that same month he received imperial letters demanding that the synod no longer be postponed.

In commenting on these letters, Quesnellus completely concealed everything that reveals the rights of the supreme pontiffs. He merely turned his attention to exaggerating how reluctantly Leo endured the synod’s neither being postponed nor being held in Italy, and how the wishes of Anatolius and the Easterners prevailed over his own.

The supreme pontiff, however, did not intend to abandon plans for peace by delaying them. I fear that our interpreter did not grasp the purpose of the pontifical will through these conjectures.

Leo could have resisted the wishes of the emperor Marcian, as he sincerely [Col. 1231C] admitted in the letter written to him on this occasion. He delayed opposing the emperor’s will for no other reason than that he did not wish to appear to resist the devotion of the prince.

Let Quesnellus—and all who habitually jest with him—please attend to these words. Leo begins the letter as follows:

“We believed that Your Clemency could grant this desire of ours: that, in view of the present necessity, you would order the priestly synod to be postponed to a more suitable time.”

The foundation of this pontifical confidence was the following:

“So that, once priests had been summoned from every province, the council might truly be universal.”

3. For who does not know that the external circumstances of those distressed times could have prevented the bishops of many provinces from leaving their dioceses, lest they abandon the peoples entrusted to them like orphans to the fury of the barbarians and expose themselves to the dangers ordinarily suffered from enemy forces?

Leo therefore did not take the postponement of the synod badly because he was being pressed by an imperial order which he could not resist, but because that time seemed less suitable for the safety of the priests and [Col. 1231D] clergy, which he wished to protect. Moreover, the city of Nicaea, to which the bishops were to assemble, frustrated the pontiff’s desire to be present personally at the general synod.

When he understood that the imperial order arose from love of the Catholic faith and that the rights of the Apostolic See were not being lightly injured, he did not wish to oppose it. He explained this clearly in the words that follow:

“But because you have wished the assembly to take place now out of love for the Catholic faith, so that I might not appear to oppose your devoted decision, I have sent my brother and fellow bishop Paschasinus …”

Furthermore, if the wishes of Anatolius and the Easterners had any influence in this matter, it must be attributed to pontifical indulgence: Leo did not wish to resist the devoted decision of Marcian.

But who could suppose that he was prevented by some law or necessity from opposing it, [Col. 1232A] when he mentions only the imperial decision? He possessed a courageous spirit in defending the prerogatives and rights of his see, and merely permitted great princes, out of indulgence, to do what could redound to the common benefit of the Church and, on the other hand, would neither injure his authority nor inflict a wound or disgrace upon pontifical dignity.

4. He then added the presbyter Boniface from the city of Rome to Paschasinus and sent them to the same synod. He also ordered that the two legates already sent to Constantinople—namely Lucentius and Basilius—be associated with them. They had been sent to hold a synodal assembly for receiving the fallen who were doing penance.

Finally, he appointed Paschasinus president of the general synod—not for the reason Quesnellus attempted to assign, namely, that Catholic steadfastness might resist a storm of falsehoods, as though Paschasinus were a man who had undertaken the labor without hatred or favor solely for the destruction of heretical impiety, but because he had to assume and discharge the office of the supreme pontiff.

We have therefore judged that Quesnellus’s [Col. 1232B] marginal note should be deleted, since it conveys an ambiguous meaning. He wrote it in the margin of his edition:

“Note the reason why Leo wishes his legate to preside over the universal synod.”

But the following words of the pontiff indicate that this office was owed to his legate:

“It is fitting that the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop of mine preside over the synod in my place.”

St. Leo therefore did not merely desire this; he clearly indicated that it was fitting and required—especially for restoring those rights of the Apostolic See that had been ruined and abolished through the unrestrained power of a single man, Dioscorus, at the Ephesian Robber Council, as is established by the definition of the Council of Chalcedon.

The holy pontiff is consistent with himself in the following letter to Anatolius, in which he states more clearly that he did not wish to oppose the arrangement of the most merciful prince, especially because Marcian himself had demanded a general council with great eagerness.

But since it would have been very difficult for those four men from Sicily and Italy, traveling to the East for so grave a matter, to execute Leo’s commands precisely [Col. 1232C] unless they were assisted by a man of proven faith who thoroughly understood all the procedures, interests, devices, cunning, and evasions of the Easterners, Leo—rightly and prudently fearing that Paschasinus and the other legates might be deceived in carrying out their duties—charged Bishop Julian of Cos to offer them whatever warnings and advice he judged could help abolish and overturn scandals and meet emerging needs.

We are inventing nothing according to our own judgment. This is indicated by the words of the most holy pontiff Leo addressed to the same bishop of Cos:

“So that the uproar of all scandals may be removed, we necessarily enjoin upon your fraternity what may benefit the entire Church: that you join your care and action with our brothers and fellow bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius … whom we command to go in our place to the aforementioned assembly, using in everything the authority of our command.”

The following words deserve attention:

“Since we know that you have a greater knowledge than our representatives of everything that has been done [Col. 1232D] there, so that, when you associate your care and counsel with theirs, they may not be deceived in any respect” [Note: [Col. 1231] Letter 71. This letter, together with the two preceding ones, was given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July in the year 451.].

5. It did not yet seem to Leo that he had sufficiently consulted the common good of the Churches unless he sent to the synod, which was first convened at Nicaea and then at Chalcedon, rules that necessarily had to be followed. Therefore, on the same day, the fifth day before the Kalends of July, he wrote a letter to all the Fathers of this general synod, containing three principal sections in which the entire procedure for conducting its business was set out. For who could fully and perfectly explain the force, weight, and energy with which the text of this whole letter is filled? It plainly reveals the majesty of his dignity, the authority of the supreme head, and the jurisdiction possessed by the Roman pontiff over the whole Church, even when assembled in councils, without any bishop—whether from the foremost or the lesser sees—daring to oppose him. He began the letter in these words, full of authority and majesty:

“I had indeed hoped, beloved, out of our charity toward our college, that all the priests of the Lord would persist in one devotion to the Catholic faith, and that no one, through favor or fear of secular powers, . . . [lacuna] so as to depart from the way of truth.”

Here he gently reproves those who, in the preceding predatory synod, overcome by friendship with wicked men or deterred by fear, had fallen—through the machinations of Dioscorus and Chrysaphius—into those appalling and grievous crimes. He asserts that their punishment had therefore been delayed until then, so that God’s mercy might be granted to those who repented.

He adds that he had been invited by the emperor to preside over the synod, while the right and honor of the blessed apostle Peter were preserved. Neither the necessity of those troubled times nor any established custom allowed him to refuse the emperor’s request. Nevertheless, he acknowledges that he would be present at and preside over the synod in two ways: first, through those four legates who acted as his representatives; and second, through the preaching of the divine word, fully set forth in the celebrated letter to Flavian. From that letter, he says, they could not be ignorant of what “we believe according to the ancient tradition,” and therefore “you cannot doubt what we desire” [Col. 1233B].

In the second section he asserts that it had already been made completely and most clearly evident to everyone what all ought piously and sincerely to confess concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, through the letter that he had sent to Flavian, of blessed memory. Finally, observing the wicked rivalries of factional men—Catholic bishops having been unjustly expelled from their sees and transported into exile, while others had been substituted in the place of those who survived—he orders that the remedy of justice be applied first, so that no one might be deprived of his own possessions or make use of another’s.

From this command of Leo the Great, the pontiff, we understand that Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Theodoret of Cyrus, and the other Catholic bishops who had suffered violence were to be restored to their own sees. But Domnus of Antioch, who had supported the wishes of Dioscorus and Eutyches, could no longer have had any right to be restored to the former honor and dignity of which he had been deprived [Col. 1233C]. Indeed, if Quesnellus had taken account of this Leonine prescription, he would scarcely have raised one of so many questions by asking why, once Leo had annulled the acts of the Ephesian robbery, Domnus had not been permitted to return to the see of Antioch, for which Maximus had been ordained; nor would he have labored so fruitlessly to argue that the proceeding concerning Domnus of Antioch was spurious.

6. But wishing to return once more to our subject, Leo the Great did not abandon the purpose with which he had begun. For when the presbyter Boniface was about to depart from the city of Rome to serve at the synod as the pontiff’s vicar or legate, Leo entrusted him with a new letter to be delivered to the emperor Marcian Augustus. The letter was divided into only two sections. In the first, he renewed to the emperor the earlier request that the synod be postponed until calmer times, far removed from the fear of hostile invasion.

He nevertheless praised the emperor’s pious zeal, by which he placed divine matters before human concerns, asking whether there might be disagreement of opinion among the priests [Col. 1233D] or any discord in the preaching of the Gospel. These two considerations moved the pontiff’s mind and prevented him from resisting the arrangements for holding the synod outside Italy and at such a time. He desired, he says, that the Catholic faith—which cannot be anything other than one—might be strengthened in the hearts of all.

After this he discusses both councils of Ephesus. He asserts that the first had rightly and justly condemned Nestorius, his doctrine, and its adherents. The second, however, which had been held on account of Eutyches, could not be called a council, since it was plainly conducted for the overthrow of the faith and had subsequently been annulled, chiefly by ecclesiastical authority and then by the imperial authority of Marcian himself.

7. The holy pontiff relates that he had prescribed the framework for the future judgment to be held at the synod to all the Fathers through the four legates sent to Chalcedon—in this letter, in the following one, and finally in one letter to the empress Pulcheria Augusta—prohibiting the institution of any inquiry concerning the faith. For it would have been exceedingly injurious and wholly offensive [the reading *obsonum* is uncertain] to reconsider as doubtful the faith that the blessed Fathers had preached as handed down to them by the apostles.

Finally, he promises that he would be present at the council in the persons of his legates, saying:

“Nor should you believe that I, too, as your Clemency wished, am absent from that council, since in these brethren whom I have sent—namely, the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, the presbyters Boniface and Basil—and also in my brother Julian, whom I wished to share in their mission, my own presence too is to be reckoned there.””

The holy pontiff wrote this letter on the sixth day before the Kalends of July in the year 451. But fifteen days later, when he had been informed that Paschasinus had sailed from Sicily toward the East to carry out the mandates of the apostolic see, he decided to give a new letter to the emperor Marcian, in which he commended his legates to him and again requested that no disputation concerning the faith be initiated there [Col. 1234B].

He did the same with the empress Pulcheria, to whom he sent a letter through Theoctistus the *Magistrianus*. In this letter, after first speaking of his legates sent to the council, he again explains how he had desired that a synod be convened in Italy. He then commands that complete moderation be observed in ecclesiastical causes—a moderation entirely absent from the Ephesian robbery, where the leaders of the synod spared neither the brethren who resisted them nor those who consented to them. Therefore, wishing to apply medicine to the greater wounds, he decreed that pardon should not be denied to those who had been corrected.

Finally, desiring to secure the extinction of heresy, he determined that the heresiarchs themselves, if they asked for indulgence, should neither be rejected nor rashly received. Although after the unjust judgment they were no longer honorable to the Catholic brotherhood as they had been, nevertheless, since they still possessed their own sees and enjoyed the honor of their episcopate, he ordered that ecclesiastical peace not be denied them if they came to their senses after making a true and necessary satisfaction [Col. 1234C].

8. Thus, in this and the preceding letters, as well as in the memorandum given to his legates, St. Leo proposed, prescribed, and definitively established the rules for all the matters to be conducted at the synod. No one could have been permitted to depart from them, lest the synodal Acts be rendered invalid and void, as we shall see at the appropriate place when discussing the primacy of the see of Constantinople after the Roman pontiff—a primacy which those Fathers, excessively favoring Anatolius’s ambition, were attempting to establish.

Since, however, in the letters mentioned above the holy pontiff chiefly discusses the unanimous assertion of the dogma of faith according to the celebrated letter he had written to Flavian, and since he also orders ecclesiastical peace to be granted to those who had fallen away from the Catholic communion through the Ephesian robbery—making themselves unworthy of the ecclesiastical honors, ranks, and prerogatives they had possessed—he commands that those who had fallen, if they desired to come to sincere repentance, be received once they had first made the required satisfaction. He also orders that this safeguard be maintained: even the principal heresiarchs who ask for indulgence should neither be rejected nor rashly received.

Accordingly, with every punishment remitted to those who repented, he permits them to return to their former episcopal sees or to retain them, provided that other Catholic bishops had not already been substituted in the place of those who had fallen, and that the fallen men still enjoyed the honor of their episcopate. We believe that this is precisely what he intended to indicate, without any forced interpretation, when he said that complete indulgence was to be granted to those who requested it, provided that they still possessed their sees and enjoyed the honor of their episcopate [Note: [Col. 1233D] I believe that the Fathers at the tenth session of Chalcedon intended to allude to this command of St. Leo when they said that the acts of the Ephesian synod had no force, except for what concerned the most holy Maximus, bishop of the great city of Antioch; [Col. 1234D] “because the most holy Leo, archbishop of Rome, receiving him into communion, ordered him to preside over the Church of Antioch.”].

Since Quesnellus had by no means understood this Leonine policy and method of writing, he raised many questions by reopening the case of Domnus, formerly bishop of Antioch. That learned man, compelled to wander in his mind here and there, asks why Thalassius of Caesarea, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Eustathius of Berytus—who had likewise played leading roles in the Ephesian robbery together with Dioscorus and the Eutychian faction—were able to retain their sees with the support of the Council of Chalcedon, whereas Domnus, whose case was equal to theirs, was not permitted to return to his see of Antioch.

Indeed, if he had considered Leo’s preceding decree and reflected that Domnus at that time no longer possessed a see or enjoyed the honor of his episcopate—because, once the Ephesian robbery had been completed, Maximus, a Catholic bishop, had been substituted in his place—he would not have labored so greatly to persuade his readers that Domnus was no longer alive at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, nor would he have rejected as false and fabricated the proceeding of the Council of Chalcedon that was written concerning him [Col. 1235B].

But the illustrious Stephanus Baluzius [455] proved, with the most serious and evident arguments and with the supreme learning in which he excelled, that this synodal proceeding is genuine and authentic. Although he did not bring Leo’s celebrated passage against Quesnellus, that testimony was highly suitable for refuting several of his adversary’s more important arguments, as we shall note below when discussing the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon.

## CHAPTER II

Why the general synod summoned at Ephesus was transferred to Chalcedon. Concerning St. Leo’s letter to Ravennius. The bishops of Gaul meet in two synods and send to the apostolic see their synodal letters, adorned with great wisdom and sacred learning. Finally, the synod of Eusebius of Milan is discussed, together with its synodal letters sent to St. Leo.

1. Once the edict had been published for a new general synod to be held in the East [Col. 1235C], the emperor Marcian saw the old disturbances of the Eutychians being renewed here and there, partisan zeal being stirred up everywhere, and riots being provoked. For those who had once adhered to Eutyches, says Baronius, persisted in their opinion lest they be accused of fickleness; with every effort they defended the unjust cause they had once undertaken, if in no other way, at least by acclamations in Eutyches’ name.

The emperor’s edict to suppress and abolish these disturbances makes clear that they were first aroused in Constantinople amid great sedition. Since they were nourished by the most serious hatreds and rivalries, the city was in danger lest the Constantinopolitans kill one another in mutual slaughter. Therefore, with God favoring the emperor’s edict, issued on the third day before the Ides of July, the disturbances were calmed, when the factious men of both parties understood that they would be punished with the ultimate penalty if they persisted in sedition.

It must therefore be supposed that Marcian’s mind was somewhat disturbed by these events. It is also plausible that he regretted not having allowed the synod to be held in Italy [Col. 1235D], as Leo had desired with all his wishes, precisely to prevent those seditious disturbances and grave upheavals that the two opposing factions had already provoked. The emperor also feared that these disturbances might be transferred to Nicaea in Bithynia, where the synod was to be held.

For this reason the empress Pulcheria wrote to Strategius, the provincial governor, instructing him—in her desire to safeguard the common peace and to ensure that the Catholic faith be preserved undisturbed and unshaken against every kind of person—not to allow anyone to approach that city without the consent of the bishops summoned to the general synod. Indeed, he was to expel from the city and from the surrounding places all monks and laymen whom no legitimate reason called to the synod:

“So that, when the holy synod has settled into complete discipline [Col. 1236A], all may jointly confirm, without any disturbance or contention, what has been revealed by the Lord Christ.”

2. While these things were taking place, the emperor was informed that Illyricum was being especially disturbed because of fear of a barbarian invasion. Reflecting, therefore, that it was not very safe to move far from Constantinople, he summoned the Fathers of the council by renewed letters to Chalcedon, which was near Constantinople, so that he might more easily and securely provide for the safety of the holy bishops and the welfare of the empire.

Meanwhile Baronius here describes the severe defeat inflicted on the Roman Empire by Attila, king of the Huns [Note: [Col. 1235D] Baronius, for the year 451, *Annales*, book VI, p. 101], concerning which Sidonius Apollinaris, Gregory of Tours, Salvianus, bishop of Marseilles, and other writers have spoken. We mention the matter here only so that everyone may understand how wisely St. Leo the pope had desired that the general synod be postponed until safer and more peaceful times.

Leaving these matters aside, then, before beginning a brief account of the proceedings of Chalcedon, we hasten to speak of certain acts of St. Leo [Col. 1236B], of the two synods of Gaul, and of the other synod of the Milanese bishops.

3. First we encounter the very brief letter of the holy pontiff to Ravennius of Arles, which the most learned Sirmond made publicly available and which Paschasius Quesnellus later transferred into his new edition. In it the holy pontiff discusses the celebration of Easter in the following year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, 453. The letter’s summary makes clear that the announcement of the celebration of that day belonged to the Roman pontiff. “Thus,” he says, “those whose confession is one in the faith may also have one devotion in this festival.”

Around the same time the bishops of Gaul also wrote two letters to our holy pontiff. In them they display such obedience, zeal, and devotion toward the apostolic see that they considered it sacrilegious to depart either from its decrees or from the Catholic truth set forth in the letter to Flavian. Since the Gallican prelates always strove with every effort to hold and preserve this observance, they kept that Church undefiled by every stain of heresy, adhering to the Roman Church by the strictest bond of obedience, just as they had received it from their ancestors.

No one can deny that this may be inferred from the letter bearing the names of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius. Although learned men have regarded the episcopal sees of these prelates as uncertain and very obscure, and have consequently reasoned from one conjecture after another, they nevertheless judged by common agreement, without hesitation or suspicion of fraud, that the bishops of Gaul were the authors of the letter in question.

Accordingly, after receiving a copy of the letter to Flavian, rich in the abundance of divine teaching, they first returned thanks, recognizing the paternal care and solicitude of the Roman pontiff, because he had wished to offer them the benefits of remedies through anticipatory treatment before they experienced the evils. In it, they profess, they recognized his particular affection for their Churches, by which he took care of their safety while, stationed upon the watchtower of the apostolic see, he cried out in care and concern lest an unforeseen enemy arrive when they were unsuspecting, or lest “careless security,” as they say, “give an opportunity to the wound.”

They also congratulate the Roman pontiff because the celebrated letter was so widely celebrated in the assemblies of all the Churches that the opinion of everyone truly declared that the primacy of the apostolic see had rightly been established there, from which the oracles of the apostolic spirit were still being disclosed.

4. After these praises had been lavishly bestowed upon Leo’s doctrinal letter, they address the holy pontiff as follows:

“We earnestly beg that your Holiness deign to read through this work, useful both for the present and for future times, which we have taken care to commit to writing on sheets for the purpose of preserving it; and, if anything is lacking through the copyist’s error, deign to correct it. Or, if by some exertion of your own you have added any argument to this salutary page for all who will read it [Col. 1237A], command with solicitous devotion that the same be added to this little book. Thus not only may many of our holy brother bishops throughout Gaul, but also many of your sons among the laity, who greatly desire this letter for the manifestation of the truth, deserve to have it transcribed, read, and preserved after it has been sent back to us and corrected by your holy hand.”

Many other matters worthy of notice occur in this letter, which either Baronius, Quesnellus, or perhaps others have already indicated; there is no need to linger over them. I shall add only two points.

First, those three bishops addressed the holy pontiff twice, and a third and fourth time, with the words “most blessed pope,” although Quesnellus denies that such expressions were in use at the time of the Council of Chalcedon and uses this to infer that the proceeding concerning Domnus of Antioch is false and spurious.

Nevertheless, [457] that editor of Leo’s works was mistaken, as is proved both by this letter and by the following synodal letter of Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul, whose heading contains these words:

“To the truly holy Lord, deservedly most blessed in Christ, and venerable for apostolic honor, Pope Leo: Ravennius.”

Although, employing a certain forced interpretation in his notes on this subsequent letter, he argues that those expressions, as well as the other titles “your apostolate” and “the apostolic see,” were spoken of all bishops whatsoever and of their sees, as we shall see below.

In noting these matters, we do not at all intend to deprive Quesnellus of the praise due to him. He investigated with great diligence the episcopal sees of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius, but labored in vain because of the loss of the ancient records. Accordingly, following the statements of Baronius, Sirmond, and other earlier writers, he asserts that Salonius and Veranius were sons of St. Eucherius of Lyon; he judges that Ceretius and Salonius took part in the Council of Orange; and finally he notes that Veranius survived into the time of Hilary and served as a legate of the apostolic see in Gaul, defending the rights of the Church of Vienne and the decree of St. Leo against the bishop of Arles, as may be seen in volume V of the Councils.

5. The synodal letter of Ravennius of Arles and the other bishops reveals that the entire assembly of the bishops of Gaul, gathered in synod, displayed toward the apostolic see a similar obedience and no lesser reverence and devotion.

At the outset the bishops ask that they be pardoned for the delay by which they had been held back from assembling promptly, and they assert that two things had prevented them from holding the synod more quickly: the distance between places and the unseasonable weather, which that year afflicted the bodies of living creatures in Gaul with illnesses.

Therefore, lest they appear sluggish or less obedient in carrying out the commands of the apostolic see, they immediately add:

“Let your Apostolate therefore pardon our delay, which arose not from leisure but from certain necessity; and although it deprived us of the favor of speed, it could not take away from us the occasion for rejoicing.”

They openly testify that they experienced the greatest joy when they received and read through that doctrinal letter, which was especially suitable for instructing all who lived within Gaul. They likewise say:

“We grieve together with you for those who, having abandoned the light of the Catholic faith, have fallen into the darkness of errors.”

Thus they confess that they received the letter as a rule and a symbol of faith. Through this service, they understand and judge that not Gaul alone but the whole world has been adorned with most gracious jewels, and they assert that no one could offer worthy thanks for it.

Accordingly, they explain in the following words how Leo’s doctrine greatly benefited both the faithful and the unbelieving:

“Every believer owes it to your teaching, after God, that he may steadfastly hold what he believed. The unbeliever owes it the same, so that, having recognized the truth, he may depart from his perfidy and, suffused with the light of apostolic instruction, abandon the darkness of his error,” and so forth [Col. 1238A].

They then add that they had at one time wished to send a letter to the emperor Marcian, the most faithful ruler, in which they would congratulate him, inform him, and make known to him the solicitude with which they followed the pontifical teaching in Christ. But when a messenger arrived among them from the regions of the East, they judged that this was no longer necessary.

Therefore, attributing the triumph of the faith to Leo’s vigilance, zeal, and ministry, they humbly pray God to preserve “your Apostolate” and the Church herself, spread throughout the whole world. Keeping this always before their eyes, they promise to offer God unceasing thanks and prayers:

“Rejoicing that, through the favor of Christ, he has given an overseer of such holiness, such faith, and such apostolic teaching to the apostolic see, from which the fountain and origin of our religion has flowed”; and they also ask that he preserve the gift granted and bestowed upon them by the pontiff’s office through an exceedingly long life, for the building up of their Churches.

6. This eulogy of Leo and his Roman see, publicly recited in that Gallican synod of forty-four bishops [Col. 1238B] and committed to writing for the perpetual memory of posterity, offers firm and weighty testimony to the greatest devotion and obedience with which they then gloried in being bound to the apostolic see.

The Gallican Church never departed from the institutions and footsteps of those bishops, whether because of changes in the times or because of the superstitions of false opinions. For its prelates had always been ready, with the Lord strengthening them, to lay down their lives together with the Roman pontiff for the truth and to dedicate their life to the author of salvation and giver of eternity.

The forty-four bishops conclude their letter with these words, and each of them subscribes it, using formulas by which the supreme governance of the Church is commonly shown to belong to the Roman pontiffs.

Paschasius Quesnellus, in volume II of the works of St. Leo, reviewed individually the episcopal sees of these Gallican prelates from various records, as may be seen on page 478, to which we refer the reader [Col. 1238C], lest we wander too far beyond our proposed subject.

After the holy pontiff Leo had received this synodal letter of the Gallican bishops, he did not delay long in writing back to them. Maintaining the grandeur of his office, he began his letter with these weighty words:

“We had indeed wished to receive your fraternity’s letter at the time when you had promised it, so that the profession of your judgment might also be joined to that of our brethren departing for the East, whom we sent in our place to the holy synod for the defense of the Catholic faith” [Note: [Col. 1237D] Letter of Leo 37, chapter 1].

He nevertheless says that he excuses their delay because of unforeseen obstacles that prevented them from assembling sooner. He then asserts that he reviewed their letter with great joy and approved it, because he had recognized in it, flourishing through the instruction of the Holy Spirit, the doctrine that the craft of the devil had tried to trouble in the Eastern Churches through its followers, so that, by the operation of divine grace, it might ultimately become stronger and clearer.

Finally, he says that he rejoices with great exultation because, “as the cause required, you have faithfully and obediently increased in the Lord the confidence that we have in you” [Col. 1238D].

Would that Quesnellus had paid attention to these last words! He would not have stirred up such disturbances in the past century, nor provided an occasion for such grave disorders, if, following the example of the Gallican bishops, he had not frustrated the confidence that the Roman pontiffs initially placed in him and had not refused faithfully and obediently to profess the definitions of the apostolic see.

7. In the second section of his letter he relates how, through the zeal and devotion of the pontifical legates, it had fully and clearly appeared in the Council of Chalcedon, consisting of six hundred Fathers, to the priests of Christ, to Christian princes and authorities, and to all the clergy, peoples, and orders, that the doctrine communicated in that doctrinal letter was in harmony with the evangelical and apostolic tradition concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1239A]. For this reason Nestorius and Eutyches had been condemned.

He reviewed and attacked their errors in the following third section, so that it might become increasingly clear how greatly they were to be rejected. In the subsequent fourth section he then relates how the holy Council of Chalcedon, in religious unanimity, had agreed with his doctrinal letter, strengthened by the authority of “my most blessed Lord, the apostle Peter,” and by its merit, cutting away the reproach from the Church of God and condemning Dioscorus of Alexandria in his impiety:

“Lest that Church which, at the very beginnings of the Gospel, had as its founder the blessed Mark, the disciple of the most blessed apostle Peter, entirely consonant in all things with the teaching of his master, should remain shaken.”

When I saw these words enclosed by lines in the Grimanic codex, I judged that either an ancient copyist or some learned man had wished to indicate the profound bond that had been maintained from the beginning between the Roman and Alexandrian Churches—not only because of the universal teaching of St. Peter [459], but also because of that origin from which the Alexandrian Church itself had derived its beginning [Col. 1239B].

Hence the holy pontiff brings forward the examples of Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril, whom he calls most approved prelates. Since this manner of speaking displeased Quesnellus—for some reason unknown to me—he thought it necessary to note:

“Anyone will be surprised that Leo counts Theophilus among the most approved prelates and considers him worthy to be proposed to Dioscorus as an example” [Note: [Col. 1239D] Quesnellus, volume II, p. 481, in the notes and observations on this letter].

Then, wishing to forestall the answer that might be offered, he immediately adds:

“Lest this be restricted merely to sincerity of faith, the obstacle is that he is called ‘of holy memory’ by the same man in Letter 94 to the emperor Marcian and in Letter 68 to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum; and his writings are cited with praise for his holiness both in Letter 134 to Leo Augustus and in the excerpts of the Holy Fathers read again at Chalcedon.”

He further adds:

“Nor could St. Leo have been unaware how wickedly and with what open violence Theophilus persecuted and finally [Col. 1239C] overthrew St. John Chrysostom.”

Whether he repented before his death of so many crimes, Quesnellus does not explain. Instead, he refers his readers to the work written in French by Godefroid Hermant on the Life of St. John Chrysostom, and finally concludes:

“I would conclude from these expressions concerning the holiness of bishops that no judgment should be made, since we see the most depraved men adorned with the same titles even in ecumenical councils, and since this custom prevailed in those times, namely, that any bishops who had in no way departed from the Catholic faith and had died in communion with the Church were entered in the sacred diptychs and called men of holy memory.”

8. But who does not understand that this criticism of Theophilus is excessively severe and malicious? It not only exaggerates his disputes with Chrysostom but also suggests that the judgment of St. Leo and the proceedings of Chalcedon should be treated lightly, as though Theophilus had neither been a most approved prelate nor reasonably been called a man of holy memory [Col. 1239D].

Quesnellus argues that the deeds he performed against Chrysostom stand in the way. But if we consider these matters, they are by no means of such a kind that they should wear away Theophilus’s reputation or make him comparable to the most depraved men.

Those disputes had no other origin than his zeal by which he sought everywhere to attack the pagans and heretical anthropomorphites, while also endeavoring to turn Catholic men away from reading the books of Origen, because of the manifest errors found in Origen’s writings. Therefore, when Theophilus himself had ordered that they be condemned by all, and when the Long brothers and their followers refused to obey, he expelled them from Egypt and, after convening a synod at Alexandria, condemned Origen himself together with his books. He also acted so that Origen and his books would be condemned in another synod in Cyprus, over which Epiphanius presided.

Up to this point Theophilus had not been hostile to Chrysostom. But when he heard that the monks he had expelled had been kindly received by Chrysostom at Constantinople, he was moved by his zeal to uphold ecclesiastical discipline and, as though wishing to defend the rights of the Alexandrian see, began to attack John. Perhaps he had not yet sufficiently investigated John’s manner of acting; nevertheless, he went to Constantinople and, after convening a synod, deposed John as a violator of the canons, even though the people protested.

I grant that Theophilus did not then maintain the moderation of spirit that befitted a bishop, and that he investigated this matter with precipitate judgment, driven by excessive zeal. But do these things prevent him from being called a most approved prelate and a man of holy memory? Let Quesnellus, I ask, consider the reasons that guided him and recall the remarkable and outstanding virtues with which he was endowed.

For, in addition to his knowledge of sacred matters, in which he especially excelled, he abhorred every heresy for as long as he lived, devoted all his strength to the conversion of the Jews, sought to lead the pagans to the worship of the true religion, and neglected nothing that could contribute to the protection, defense, and advancement of the Catholic faith [460].

But I am now weary of dwelling longer on these matters, especially since in another work, while treating the Rufinian vindication, I have described how Theophilus attacked Origen and the Origenists [Note: [Col. 1239D] Volume II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 98, 108, and passim elsewhere, under “Theophilus.”].

I shall add only that the opinion of Quesnellus or of any other recent writer could never acquire enough force to weaken or overthrow the testimony and judgment of Leo the Great and the Fathers of Chalcedon. No one is unaware that the most serious disputes once raised among the holiest men could in no way harm their holiness or renown, even if they suffered some human weakness by clinging too vehemently to their own studies and opinions—as we ourselves could prove by six hundred examples.

9. Finally, we must speak of the synod of Milan [Col. 1240C], which St. Leo ordered to be held for no other reason than that, with the common agreement and public subscriptions of the bishops of that province, his doctrinal letter to Flavian might be received. This, says Baronius, was carried out diligently [Note: [Col. 1240D] Baronius, volume VI of the *Annales*].

At that time Abundius of Como and the other pontifical legates had returned from the East to Rome, intending to give an account in words of everything that had occurred at the Council of Chalcedon. Therefore, so that it might be known by certain documents that all the bishops of the West accepted the rule of faith written and defined by Leo himself, the holy pontiff instructed Bishop Abundius and his colleague Senator, presbyter of Milan, as Abundius returned to his homeland and bishopric, to meet with Eusebius so that a synod might be summoned.

Eusebius presided over this synod, which was attended by eighteen other bishops, either in person or through their legate-presbyters. Many of them were especially renowned for holiness and learning: namely, Maximus, bishop of Turin; Abundius of Como himself; Crispinus of Pavia; and others whose names have been entered with great praise in the records of the Church, as may be seen in Baronius under the year cited above.

From this we can easily conclude that those writers who said that Maximus of Turin died during the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius departed far from the truth. For how could this have happened, if he not only took part in this synod of Milan but also subscribed to the Acts of the Roman council under Pope Hilary?

Whatever others may have said about these and similar questions, let us not investigate them during the present leisure. We shall merely review the substance of this synodal letter in a few words.

All the manuscript codices and editors have presented it as divided into three sections. In the first, Eusebius declares, together with his colleagues, that they rejoice because the legates of the Apostolic See sent to Chalcedon had achieved the happy and favorable outcome of the mission entrusted to them. They assert that this had occurred to the praise of God and the preservation of the Christian faith, through the protection of the divine Majesty: “When,” they say, “He placed you, worthy defenders of His worship, as bishop in the seat of His apostle.”

In the second section of the letter, they praise the doctrine contained in the letter to Flavian as wholly consonant with the assertions of the prophets, the authority of the Gospels, and the testimonies of the Apostles. They say that it shines with a certain brilliance, with the splendor of light and truth, and agrees with all the points that blessed Ambrose, moved by the Holy Spirit, inserted in his books concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

Finally, in the third section, Eusebius and his colleagues profess that they have pronounced an anathema against the Eutychians. “Following,” they say, “the form of your letter, we have shown by the letters sent through our brother and fellow bishop Cyriac that we have observed the procedure prescribed by you.”

These words clearly imply that the form and order prescribed by the holy pontiff for handling all the matters had been observed by them without opposition, thereby manifesting the due obedience that the bishops of the whole world, even when assembled in synods, have always rendered to the Roman pontiffs.

461. One further point in this synodal letter has aroused our attention: despite the agreement of the commonly circulated and manuscript copies, it is presented differently in the Quesnellian edition. Eusebius, wishing to bring his address to a close, invokes divine assistance and attributes to the zeal of Pope Leo the destruction of the Eutychian heresy, the triumph of the faith, and the crown of the completed struggle, to be retained in perpetual peace. He then adds:

“Leave this as something memorable for future ages: so that the insolence of the impious sect, extinguished in the present time, may be seen to lie eternally prostrate and succumb to you, defenders [of the Catholic faith].”

Surius, the collectors of the councils, and others, using the commonly circulated copies, agree with this reading; and some manuscript exemplars also support it. We are persuaded that their authority should be followed. Quesnellus, however, substituted *exstitisse* for *exstincta* and perhaps, through the carelessness of his copyist, admitted *pugnatoribus* in place of *propugnatoribus*.

Nevertheless, in his notes on this letter he admits that the passage cited required correction. After collating it with the manuscripts of Trecop. and Thuan., he emended it as follows, in accordance with the common text:

“May you, with the Lord’s favor, retain it perpetually, and leave this as something memorable for future ages: so that, from the present time, the insolence of the impious sect, extinguished, might be seen to lie prostrate forever, overthrown by new purifications.”

No one will deny that this reading is false and corrupt if he considers it carefully and then compares it with the preceding context of the letter, in which, as we have said, the destruction of the heresy, the triumph of the faith, and the crown of the completed struggle are all attributed to the supreme pontiff Leo. New purifications, therefore, were not to be applied so that the extinguished heresy might lie prostrate forever.

For this reason, the most recent edition of the Venetian printer Augustine Savioli caused me the greatest astonishment by introducing this corrupt reading into the text of the letter and expunging the reading that Surius, the collectors of the councils, and Quesnellus himself judged should be retained. My astonishment was increased by the fact that the editor himself professed to have followed the testimony and authority of the best manuscript codices, although, from this and similar lapses, I may reasonably infer that he consulted no codices at all. I shall reserve further discussion of this matter for another volume of the Leonine Works.

# CHAPTER III. On the Date, Number of Fathers, and Sessions of the Council of Chalcedon

Everything that St. Leo desired was successfully carried out. The Catholic faith was established. The fallen bishops were received into penance. Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned; and finally, the rights of the Apostolic See, abolished in the Ephesian synod, were restored and confirmed with the greatest unanimity.

## 1

The emperor Marcian, for the reasons reviewed above, ordered that the bishops summoned to the general council should assemble at Chalcedon and meet in the basilica of St. Euphemia the Martyr, in the suburbs outside the city. It began on the eighth day before the Ides of October in the year 451 and was concluded on the Kalends of November.

Writers, as Cardinal Baronius observed among others, do not agree in determining either the number of the Fathers or the number of the sessions. Marcellinus, in his *Chronicle*, says that six hundred and thirty bishops were present; Liberatus the deacon and Photius support him. Nicephorus prefers to say that the number was twice that of those who had attended the ecumenical Council of Nicaea, namely, six hundred and thirty-six.

St. Leo, however, who had recently been informed by his legates arriving from the East and by copies of the Acts, wrote to the bishops of Gaul: “A synod of almost six hundred of our brother bishops and fellow bishops was assembled.”

[Note: Marcellinus, *Chronicle*. Liberatus the deacon, *Breviary*, chapter 3. Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 2. Photius, *On the Seven Councils*, chapter 4. St. Leo, formerly letter 52, now 77 in Quesnellus’s edition. Baronius, volume VI of the *Annals*, pages 139 and following.]

Considering all this, Baronius believes that nearly half the bishops were omitted from the surviving copies of the Acts, since in the first session of the same council only three hundred and forty bishops are found subscribed. We shall speak of this difficulty in the session concerning Domnus of Antioch, approving the observations of Stephen Baluzius.

The number of sessions likewise appears uncertain, and writers offer differing opinions about it. Baronius believes that the number of sessions should be inferred from the number of days during which that holy assembly lasted. Since twelve days intervened between the eighth day before the Ides of October and the Kalends of November, and since it is reasonable to suppose that the Fathers met on each day, he concludes that twelve sessions, or secretariats, must have been held.

Liberatus, in the passage cited, counts fifteen sessions; but the Greek and Latin copies contain sixteen, although many things appear in the Latin copies that are absent from the Greek, and conversely. If, however, we carefully attend to all the matters discussed in that council, we are compelled to admit that several proceedings took place within the same session, as will become clear when we discuss the cases of Photius of Tyre and Domnus of Antioch.

## 2

The writers of ecclesiastical history who preceded us have reviewed with the greatest diligence each of the matters contained in those Acts. We omit that task at present, lest we repeat what others completed long ago. This is especially true because the authors whom we have repeatedly praised—namely, Baronius, Christian Lupus, Father Natalis Alexander, Stephen Baluzius, and John David—each described the same Acts according to the purpose he had adopted in writing and treated various incidental questions, some of which we have omitted because we judged them unrelated to our subject.

Since, as we said above, there are three matters that concern the wishes of the great pontiff and that were ultimately entrusted to faithful execution in that council, I shall indicate each of them.

The first concerned the case of the faith, which began to be treated at the opening of the council. Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, obeying Leo’s instructions, requested that Dioscorus withdraw from the council, since he should be admitted only among the accused, not among the judges. Although this request seemed severe, the judges, in order to restrain certain movements of dissension that had arisen among the Easterners and to prevent the delays that normally result from canonical summonses, ordered that Dioscorus sit in the midst of the assembly as one who was to be judged.

Then, after Eusebius of Dorylaeum had been given permission to accuse Dioscorus, he charged him both with violating the faith and with sacrilegious homicide because of the death inflicted upon Flavian. When the written accusation presented to the emperor Marcian had been read, Dioscorus attempted to refute the charges by saying that Flavian had been lawfully condemned in a synod assembled by the authority of the emperor Theodosius.

The judges then asked what the Acts of the Robber Council contained, and the reading of those Acts began. When they came to the constitution of Theodosius, which had provided that Theodoret should not participate in the preceding Ephesian Robber Council, the judges requested that Theodoret be brought into the council. We omit discussion of his case here, since later we shall have to refute Quesnellus’s dissertation.

Meanwhile, the bishops who had fought on the side of Dioscorus and Eutyches confessed that fear of the soldiers had compelled them to depose orthodox bishops. Moved by the goadings of conscience, they cried out: “We have all sinned; we all ask pardon.”

As the reading of the Acts of the pseudo-synod continued, Dioscorus was accused of having forbidden the dogmatic letter of St. Leo—sent to the synod as the rule of faith—to be read. To make the violence inflicted upon St. Flavian and the orthodox bishops more fully known, all the Acts of the Council of Constantinople in which the condemnation of Eutyches had been conducted were read in full.

From this reading, the legates of the Apostolic See established that Flavian was truly Catholic, whereas Eutyches was an impious heretic. But Dioscorus, no longer able to restrain the wickedness of his bad faith, dared to assert by way of an intervention that Flavian had rightly been condemned because he had said that after the union there were two natures in Christ. He dared to defend this contrary opinion obstinately before the Fathers.

Many other matters were subsequently read, which Baronius discusses in summary fashion; we too shall indicate them on the occasion of the following Exercises. Finally, the definition of the faith was postponed until the next session, which was held on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

## 3

In that session the Nicene Creed was recited, and all the Fathers testified that the writings of Cyril of Alexandria and the letter of Leo, the Roman pontiff, agreed with it. Praising Leo’s letter with extraordinary commendations, they acclaimed:

“This is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the Apostles. We all believe thus; we orthodox believe thus. Anathema to anyone who does not believe thus.”

“Peter has spoken through Leo in this way.”

“The Apostles taught thus.”

“Leo taught piously and truly.”

“Cyril taught thus.”

“Leo and Cyril taught alike.”

Who does not understand that, by these solemn and universal acclamations of the Fathers, honor was rightly and carefully bestowed upon the Apostolic See and upon St. Leo, whose rights and prerogatives Dioscorus had trampled underfoot and abolished in the preceding synod?

With one voice they venerated Leo as Peter’s successor, as a sincere guardian of the Catholic faith, and as the supreme interpreter of the sacred Scriptures, clearly in order to erase that disgraceful stain which, to the supreme dishonor of the Apostolic See, Leo himself and his legates had suffered and borne in the Ephesian Robber Council.

Because Dioscorus had to undergo the appropriate punishment for this crime, his condemnation was pronounced in the following, third session. Only the bishops, without the secular magistrates, attended this session. Dioscorus was also absent from the council, being held under military guard.

Although his crimes had become sufficiently known to everyone in the first session, the written accusation of Eusebius of Dorylaeum was nevertheless read again, in order to preserve the form and order of canonical law. And lest sentence be pronounced against one who was absent, they summoned him to come to the council by canonical citations once, twice, and three times.

Dioscorus offered various kinds of excuses: either that he was detained by illness or that it had been provided that he should appear before the synod only in the presence of the secular judges. Cecropius, bishop of Sebaste, who had been sent to summon him, entirely invalidated this latter excuse, saying:

“When certain matters regulated by the canons—that is, ecclesiastical affairs—are being examined, neither other judges nor laymen ought to be present.”

[Note: See our following dissertation on the case of Photius of Tyre, which the distinguished Mr. Nicolaus Antonelli, secretary of the Pontifical Benedictine Academy of Councils, assigned to us for examination and explanation.]

While these things were taking place and the Fathers of the council were awaiting Dioscorus’s responses within the prescribed periods, four petitions were read: those of Theodore, Ischirion, the Alexandrian deacons, Athanasius the presbyter, and Sophronius of Alexandria, a Christian man. They bear this heading or inscription:

“To the most holy and blessed universal patriarch of great Rome, Leo, and to the holy universal Council of Chalcedon.”

Quesnellus did not place these petitions, which were addressed to Pope Leo, among the Leonine Works; nor, in his synopsis of the Acts of Chalcedon, did he indicate that they at least bore the name of Leo, although he had undertaken to prepare his edition with all the monuments written by the holy supreme pontiff himself and by others to him.

[Note: See volume II of the Works of St. Leo, page 511.]

Such petitions exist in Greek and Latin in volume IV. We have corrected them according to the reading of the Vatican codices and shall take care that they appear in the following volume among the Works of St. Leo the Great.

## 4

These petitions contained descriptions and attestations of Dioscorus’s most serious crimes. We consider it unnecessary to indicate their substance here, since they are known to learned men and may be examined by anyone.

When Dioscorus, summoned to the council for the third time, refused to obey, John, bishop of Germanicia, was unable to move him. He said:

“The offenses of priests are a common disgrace. Therefore, if Your Holiness knows that you are suffering calumny from certain persons, the holy synod is not far away. Do not trouble yourself; prove the falsehood.”

Since nothing remained for Dioscorus’s defense, the papal legates, acting in the person of Leo, pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him. We omit reproducing it here, lest our Exercises grow excessively long contrary to their intended purpose.

Those who wish to know whether all the rights of the Apostolic See remained restored in that judgment, as St. Leo had desired after the Ephesian Robber Council, may easily examine the entire sequence, order, and decrees of this session in the collectors of the councils, volume IV, third session.

The other Fathers unanimously ratified the sentence of deposition and degradation pronounced against Dioscorus by the papal legates. They later wrote synodal letters to the emperors Valentinian and Marcian and to the empress Pulcheria concerning what had recently been established. The decree of this condemnation was also publicly posted and was communicated to Dioscorus himself and to the Alexandrian clergy.

## 5

In the following session, which was the fourth, the case of the bishops who had played the leading roles with Dioscorus in the Ephesian Robber Council was brought forward for examination again. Dioscorus himself testified that, by order of the emperor Theodosius, they had likewise presided in that synod. He claimed to have a common case with Domnus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eustathius of Berytus, Eusebius of Ancyra, and Basil of Seleucia.
