But because St. Leo had ordered that they be received into communion and that their canonical penalties be remitted if they showed themselves repentant, provided that other Catholic bishops had not already been appointed in their sees—as we have already seen from the preceding letters and from the instruction given to the legates—they were ordered to enter the council after they had approved the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds, the decrees of Ephesus, and the letter of St. Leo the pontiff, pronouncing anathema upon those who held contrary opinions. They had been excluded from the council, but, once ecclesiastical peace had been obtained, they were admitted to Catholic fellowship.

We shall explain in a separate dissertation why Domnus of Antioch was not present.

The Egyptian bishops were also admitted. The papal legates ordered them to pronounce an anathema against Eutyches and to subscribe to St. Leo’s letter. At first they refused to do either, awaiting the election of a new Alexandrian bishop, whom they promised to follow in subscribing. But when the synod pressed them to condemn Eutyches, they finally consented.

When they were still pressed to subscribe to St. Leo’s letter, however, they refused absolutely. Prostrating themselves, they requested that the holy synod first permit an Alexandrian bishop to be elected. The synod granted their supplications, but imposed the condition that they not leave Chalcedon and that they await the election of the new bishop.

[Note: On this supplication of the Egyptians, consult Christian Lupus, in the appendix to the ninth session of the Council of Chalcedon.]

The eminent Cardinal Baronius and the distinguished Stephen Baluzius observed that the Greek copies of the Acts of Chalcedon contain the sessions just mentioned in a different distribution. In the dissertation we composed on Domnus of Antioch, we maintain that this should be attributed to the bishops’ notaries.

## 6

In the fifth session, an inquiry began concerning the definition of the faith, which all were to hold as a firm rule. Carosus, Dorotheus, and other Eutychian archimandrites had given the emperor Marcian a petition requesting permission to dispute matters of faith with the Catholics.

When they entered the council and presented their petition to the Fathers, they were recognized as having petitions in support of Dioscorus. In it they professed that they embraced only the Nicene faith and admitted no exposition of it. They added that they would rather live separately from the communion of others than allow anything new to be introduced into the faith.

“Thus,” says Baronius, “those hypocrites, after the manner of Eutyches and Dioscorus, were fostering a new heresy beneath the false cloak of the Nicene faith.”

Another petition, presented by Catholic archimandrites, was brought before the synod in opposition to theirs. Meanwhile, the heretics were given a period of three days in which to come to their senses and subscribe to the Catholic faith against Eutyches. Among them was an archimandrite named Maximus, who was said to have been Eutyches’ teacher.

The deceitful conduct of the heretical archimandrites wearied the synod and provoked disturbances among the Fathers. Paschasinus and the other papal legates wanted St. Leo’s letter to be accepted by everyone as the standard of faith, for the destruction and condemnation of the Eutychian heresy. Anatolius of Constantinople, however, who until then had secretly supported Dioscorus and the Eutychian faction in part, opposed this in many ways.

First, he presented to the Fathers for approval a certain definition of faith recited by Asclepiades, a Constantinopolitan deacon. The vicars of the Apostolic See, together with certain Eastern bishops, rejected it as favoring the disturbances of the heretics and did not permit it to be inserted into the synodal Acts.

Second, Anatolius maintained that nothing new should be added to the ancient sanctions of the faith. Thus, apart from the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds and the decrees established at Ephesus against Nestorius and his followers, he would admit no definition for proscribing the Eutychian doctrine.

Third, he asserted that Dioscorus had not been condemned and removed from the episcopate because he had violated the faith, but because he had excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo and, having been summoned a third time, had therefore been condemned.

The deceitful conduct of Anatolius was thoroughly understood by Paschasinus and the other papal vicars. Therefore, lest any avenue remain for the Eutychians to interpret the Creed of the faith differently, they added to the preceding Nicene, Constantinopolitan, and Ephesian decrees:

“The letter of the most blessed and most holy archbishop Leo, bishop of the great and elder city of Rome, written to the archbishop Flavian of holy memory to destroy the false understanding of Eutyches, as agreeing with the confession of that great Peter and existing as a common pillar against those who think perversely, was suitably adapted for the confirmation of correct doctrines,” and so forth.

After the definition of the faith had been read in full, they judged that it should be communicated to the emperor Marcian according to the decision of the judges, as reported by Facundus of Hermiana and Liberatus the deacon, so that the bishops might subscribe to it unanimously in the following session.

[Note: Whoever wishes to learn more about this and the following session should consult the highly learned annotations of the distinguished Stephen Baluzius in the new collection of the councils.]

## 7

The sixth session was therefore held on the eighth day before the Kalends of November. As is clear from copies of the Acts, all the bishops subscribed to the synodal definition.

At that point the emperor Marcian arrived, together with the empress Pulcheria and other noble ministers of the imperial court. Marcian himself addressed the Fathers of the council in a few words.

[Note: This address of the emperor exists in Greek and Latin in volume IV of the Councils, page 1421 in my pagination. See the annotations of Stephen Baluzius in the passage cited above.]

When the address had been concluded, Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, recited what had been done up to that point, together with the subscriptions of all the bishops.

The emperor then asked the council whether the definition just reread had been issued according to the exposition of all the holy bishops. They all cried out:

“We all believe thus; one faith, one will,” and so forth.

The Fathers then turned to the emperor and said:

“Marcian, new Constantine; new Paul; new David.”

“Many years to David the emperor!”

They likewise wished the empress many years. Addressing both of them, they added:

“Guard the luminaries of the world, Lord.”

They adorned both with many other true and deserved praises.

With the matters of faith thus arranged and firmly established, the emperor proposed to the synod certain chapters to be determined as canonical statutes, for the honor of the clerical militia and the monastic life:

“Since we judge it proper that these matters should be formed by you in due canonical fashion through a synod, rather than sanctioned by our law.”

[Note: You will find three such chapters set out in volume IX of the Councils, page 1510.]

The bishops, exhausted by their excessive labors, repeatedly and earnestly begged the emperor to dismiss them. Marcian, however, turned to the synod and said:

“You are indeed greatly wearied by the journey and by enduring hardship. Nevertheless, endure for another three or four days. In the presence of our most distinguished judges, raise whatever matters you wish, and you will obtain appropriate relief.”

Finally he added:

“Let none of you depart before the holy council has pronounced all the definitive judgments on every matter.”

Thus far, with whatever brevity I could, I have summarized the first six sessions of the Council of Chalcedon. From them it cannot be doubted that the wishes of St. Leo the Great were successfully fulfilled, and that the rights of the Apostolic See, which Dioscorus and the Eutychian faction had previously violated and abolished most disgracefully in the Ephesian synod, were restored by the solemn and universal judgment of the whole Church.

We shall explain the remaining matters, since they concern the particular cases of certain bishops, in the following Exercises.

# CHAPTER IV. Dissertation on the Fourth Session of the Council of Chalcedon, Delivered at the Pontifical Academy of Councils in the Year of Our Lord 1747

## 1

I am now ordered to examine the case of Photius of Tyre, which the Fathers of Chalcedon considered in the fourth session of this council. I shall speak only of the three matters prescribed for discussion by the members of this Academy this year, which, under the eighth heading, are expressed in the following order and terms.

First, whether the ancient custom alleged by Anatolius in the fourth session, in the case of Photius, bishop of Tyre—namely, that bishops residing in Constantinople, together with the patriarch, determined the cases of all who appealed to them—was legitimate; and, if this is granted, why the judgment in the case of Photius was revoked.

Second, whether ecclesiastical cases were to be judged according to the canons or also according to the pragmatic sanction; this was discussed in the fourth session in the same case of Photius.

Third and finally, whether a bishop, if unworthy of the episcopate, could be placed in a lower order—a proposition which the papal legates appear to deny in the fourth session.

To investigate all these matters would require a lengthy discourse if I were free to traverse the extremely broad field of such a subject. But since I must not abuse the kindness of a most exalted, most merciful, and most wise prince, I shall not be able to review everything that might be said. I shall explain at greater length certain matters that have not yet been sufficiently examined; I shall merely touch upon what is better known; and I shall not conceal those arguments which, having been entangled by many sophistries of more recent royalists, are brought forward in similar cases to weaken or entirely overthrow ecclesiastical government and, above all, the rights of the Apostolic See. Following the footsteps of the Fathers of Chalcedon, I shall attempt briefly to refute them.

## 2

Before we undertake to resolve the questions of the present controversy, we must investigate what sort of case it was, and what caused so many and such great disagreements to arise between Photius of Tyre and Eustathius of Berytus.

It has been established from the ecclesiastical records that the city of Tyre was originally the metropolis of all Phoenicia Prima, and that twelve other cities and bishops had been subject to it from the beginnings of the Church down to the year 450. The bishop of Berytus was one of these.

The first man who attempted to violate the rights of this kind of metropolitan was Eustathius. Setting aside the regulations of the Nicene Fathers and driven by an intense desire to enlarge his own see, he obtained from the emperor Theodosius a *pragmaticum*—that is, an imperial decree or rescript—by which, after the province of Phoenicia Prima had been divided into two parts and the metropolitan rank and honor had been conferred upon the Church of Berytus, he brought under his own authority the administration and ordinations of the Churches of Tripolis, Byblos, Botrys, Orthosias, Arca, and Antaradus, which had been subject to Photius, the lawful metropolitan of Tyre.

Eustathius did not shrink from so grave a crime, since he was accustomed to turn all the affairs of the Church upside down and had been the author of many schisms and disputes. Unable to restrain his anger and hatred, he had not feared, in the Ephesian Robber Council, to assume the leading role against St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople and predecessor of Anatolius, and against Eusebius of Dorylaeum, on behalf of the faction of Dioscorus and Eutyches, so that the Catholic faith might be brought to complete destruction.

For this reason, we read the name of Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, in the sacred records only with the greatest disgrace. When the Fathers of Chalcedon, in the first session, began to rescind and abolish the Acts of the preceding Robber Council, they decreed that all the authors of its disturbances and crimes should be punished with precisely the same penalty that those men had inflicted with the utmost injustice upon the aforementioned bishops, namely Flavian and Eusebius.

## 3

Although Eustathius, together with five other bishops who were the authors of the entire schism, had possessed power and authority in that predatory synod; although he had also secured the favor of Dioscorus of Alexandria, as well as of Chrysaphius and the other imperial ministers who supported Eutyches, he nevertheless dared to attempt nothing against either Photius of Tyre or his Church. He considered it sufficient, for the time being, to have obtained such powerful support, through which, at a more favorable opportunity, he might easily indulge his ambitions and his desires for honor and authority.

Therefore, when in the year 449, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, the Robber Council had ended, and Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, after being subjected to blows, beatings, and insults, had been driven from his see and forced into exile, Eustathius nevertheless persuaded himself that he could obtain the honor he desired more easily if he maintained peace and friendship with the new bishop eventually appointed in Flavian’s place, so that his own business might be brought to a more successful conclusion.

It must not, therefore, be said that, while the affairs of the East were in such great danger, the Fathers of the pseudo-synod committed that other most serious crime—namely, that while Flavian was still alive they appointed Anatolius in his place and ordained him bishop of Constantinople.

For although this contrary opinion had sometimes been approved by many writers, both Catholic and heterodox, it has been clearly shown by the letters of Theodosius and by those of Anatolius himself to St. Leo to be nothing but a sheer fabrication. Flavian did not depart this life as a martyr until the following year.

After his death, the emperor Theodosius instructed the clergy of Constantinople to determine and approve those most suitable for carrying out that office, reserving to himself the election of the foremost candidate.

[Note: Christian Lupus, in his scholia on the Council of Chalcedon. Petavius, *Rationarium temporum*, part I, book VI, chapter 19, page 369. William Cave, *Ecclesiastical History of Writers*, under “Anatolius C. P.”]

But as the gravest disputes were daily increasing among the Constantinopolitan clergy, chiefly through the activity of the faction of Dioscorus and the emperor’s ministers, Theodosius ordered that clerics be sought out in the royal city—and, as Anatolius puts it, also from other cities, where they were staying on various kinds of business—so that the most distinguished among them might be promoted to the episcopal dignity, as we have already observed in the preceding book.

## 4

Many true and noteworthy matters would now present themselves for discussion if considerations of time and the present purpose of our discourse did not stand in the way. I shall touch only lightly upon the one point that seems relevant to our subject.

The elevation of Anatolius to the Constantinopolitan throne greatly favored the designs of Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, but proved exceedingly destructive to Photius, bishop of Tyre. For there had been a very close relationship between Eustathius and Anatolius. Since Anatolius had been a presbyter of the Alexandrian Church and the *apocrisiarius* of the bishop Dioscorus, and had been elevated to the episcopate of Constantinople through the efforts of that schismatic faction, his mind was already prepared to indulge the wishes and petitions of those who had fought against the most holy Flavian on behalf of the Eutychian doctrine.

## 5

Meanwhile, various assemblies of bishops were held at Constantinople. In one of them, by order of the emperor Theodosius and without awaiting the letters or judgment of the Roman pontiff, the bishops consecrated Anatolius. Anatolius mentions this council in his letter to St. Leo:

“Therefore it became the responsibility of the holy synod of the bishops residing at Constantinople to proceed without delay to ordain me.”

[Note: See what we said about the ordination of Anatolius in chapter 4 of the preceding book.]

The same holy pontiff then ordered another council to be held. Toward the end of July in the year 450, after receiving letters from both Anatolius and the emperor Theodosius concerning Flavian’s death and the election of a new bishop, and reflecting upon the dreadful schism that had torn apart the Catholic fellowship in the East, he remained suspended in uncertainty and did not wish to declare either the acts of the election and consecration valid or invalid.

Instead, he delayed communion with Anatolius until four legates of the Apostolic See, sent from the papal side, had traveled to Constantinople and received from the new bishop, before all the clergy and people, a sincere profession of faith, signed in his own hand and precisely corresponding to the wishes and commands of the pontiff.

Several letters of the holy pontiff still survive: to Theodosius, to the empress Pulcheria, to the clergy of Constantinople, to the archimandrites of that city, and finally to the presbyter Martin. From them we understand not only the sequence of events with the greatest clarity, but also the pontiff’s manner of acting, his zeal for religion, his strength of mind, and his supreme administration over all parts of the world, all shining forth more clearly than the light of day.

[Note: The letter of Anatolius to St. Leo, page 272, volume I, in Quesnellus.]

6. But that nothing was done concerning the case of Photius of Tyre at this last synod of Anatolius—which must be assigned at least to the ninth or tenth month of that same year—is clearly apparent from the most weighty considerations. In the first place, Theodosius the Younger, from whom Eustathius had obtained the imperial pragmatic rescript, had died on 18 July, at which time his letter had scarcely yet reached St. Leo; and the papal legates, who were to convene this council, had either not yet begun their journey or, if they had begun it, were still staying in the suburbs of Rome. For Leo’s letter of 469 suggests as much, since it was dated at Rome on 17 July, three days before Theodosius died at Constantinople. The papal legates must then be believed to have arrived in that city no earlier than the eighth or ninth month, in view of the hardships of the journey and the distance of the place. Moreover, since they wished to discharge their office faithfully, they would certainly not have allowed Anatolius—who had been brought under suspicion of impaired faith—to assume the leading role in a synod which they themselves were convening at the command of the Roman pontiff, to arrange everything according to his own pleasure, and to abolish ecclesiastical laws. Rather, he ought to have appeared before those legates and the other bishops as an accused man suspected of bad faith.

[Col. 1249C] 7. The case of Photius, therefore, must be referred entirely to an earlier synod, which preceded the death of Theodosius. When Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, produced the surreptitious imperial rescript that he had received, all the bishops who had assembled at Constantinople—either out of favor toward Anatolius or deterred by threats of punishment—gave their assent, even contrary to the prohibition of the ecclesiastical rules. At that time, therefore, through the agency of Chrysaphius and the other imperial ministers, who strongly favored Eustathius, not only was the Theodosian rescript confirmed; they also took care that Maximus, patriarch of Antioch, who was absent from that synod although he was staying at Constantinople, should regard as ratified and firm the measures more recently enacted to enlarge the dignity, honor, and prerogatives of the Church of Berytus. For the province of Phoenicia Prima, with its metropolitan of Tyre and its other bishops, was subject to the administration and ordination of the patriarch of Antioch.

How these events occurred is related by that same Maximus when he was later questioned by the Fathers of Chalcedon:

“I was at Constantinople. But when a council was being held concerning this matter, I was not present; a document was brought to me, and I signed it.”

[Note: [Col. 1250D] Act 4 of the Council of Chalcedon.]

What more is needed? In this council of Anatolius, since everything was being done out of hatred for the most holy bishop Photius of Tyre and in contempt of the ecclesiastical laws, threats and terrors shook the spirit of Photius, the metropolitan, with especial severity, and the penalty of deposition was held over him unless he signed the synodical decree. Photius says in a petition presented to the emperor Marcian, successor of the emperor Augustus Theodosius:

“When I had signed it—not intentionally, but out of fear of the threats directed against me—I indicated by my signature the necessity imposed upon me. For I wrote that I had signed under compulsion, knowing that this could cause me no prejudice, since the sacred and divine laws declare that acts performed not intentionally but under necessity have no force.”

8. Whoever carefully examines the acts of this council of Anatolius, which we encounter scattered here and there among various ancient writers, will readily admit that it was scarcely unlike the Robber Council of Ephesus, or that it may rightly be called an appendage of that council. Accordingly, when the Fathers of Chalcedon had been entrusted with judging matters of faith and violations of the rights of bishops, and with restoring and repairing everything that had been turned upside down, as St. Leo had instructed the legates of the apostolic see, they brought three principal charges against Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, when they were about to judge the case of Photius. The imperial judges in civil cases briefly indicated these three points, addressing the general Council of Chalcedon as follows:

“Let the holy synod declare whether it was lawful for the most holy archbishop Anatolius, while the most reverend bishop Photius was absent, to send him a sentence of excommunication and order that certain Churches in the province be taken away from him; and whether an assembly of bishops staying in the royal city ought to be called a synod.”

As to this last question, Tryphon, bishop of Chios, seriously maintained that an assembly of bishops staying in the city could be called a synod. Perhaps wishing to flatter both Anatolius and the imperial ministers, he first pointed to the dignity and grandeur of the royal city and then recounted the frequent arrival of the bishops of the East, who, while dealing with civil affairs and suffering some oppression in the defense of their rights, were required to assemble at Constantinople. He openly declared:

“It is called a synod; they assemble, and those suffering some oppression obtain their rights.”

Neither the holy general council nor any other bishop supported Tryphon’s response, lest the rights of the other patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—should be violated. For it is clear from the ecclesiastical records that the jurisdiction of the bishop of Constantinople was then very narrowly confined. Apart from that part of Asia which extended toward the regions of Pontus, he could initially administer only the dioceses of Thrace; their rights were later extended as far as Illyricum by a rescript of Theodosius the Younger. The dioceses of Phoenicia Prima, by contrast, belonged to the patriarchate of Antioch, as we have said. Therefore, to prevent all the disturbances that might arise, the entire synod decided that Tryphon’s opinion and judgment should be regarded as neither ratified nor annulled.

9. But the matter did not proceed in this way when the other question—concerning the excommunication imposed by Anatolius’s synod upon Photius of Tyre in his absence—was submitted for examination. The entire Council of Chalcedon condemned this act as a monstrous crime contrary to divine and human laws. In that session we read that Atticus, bishop of Zelum, declared that no one should condemn a person in his absence. All the most reverend bishops acclaimed:

“No one condemns a person in his absence.”

Thus, by this unanimous acclamation of the Fathers of Chalcedon, the synodical decrees of Anatolius were completely abolished. When Anatolius’s spirit, incapable of tolerating any diminution of his honor and ambition, bore this indignantly, he appealed to the custom that we are now discussing, in order to purge himself of every accusation of injustice and to safeguard the grandeur of his see. But who could fail to see that this custom was wholly illegitimate and that Anatolius appealed to it only as a deliberate evasion? A custom cannot be considered legitimate when it conflicts with divine and human laws. Accordingly, both Eusebius of Nicomedia and Photius of Tyre, together with the entire synod, steadfastly rejected all of Anatolius’s excuses as contrivances of unjust ambition, by which he sought to conceal the truth of the matter, lest they should enter into a dispute over a custom that might have acquired the force of abuse.

[Col. 1251A] Eunomius of Nicomedia, addressing the judges, spoke to them confidently as follows:

“Your Magnificence has asked us whether it is permissible to condemn a person in his absence. I answer in the Roman manner, and, using the words of the apostle Paul in Acts 25:16, I say: ‘It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man before the accused has his accusers present and has been given an opportunity to refute the charges.’”

Photius subsequently agreed with him and earnestly begged the synod and the imperial judges that, after every unjust custom had been set aside and abolished, only the canonical laws should be enforced. Photius said:

“I ask and implore nothing else from your just judgment except that you ensure that the rules remain in force; that those who were lawfully ordained by me but were later expelled and reduced to the rank of presbyters be restored; and that I receive back my Churches.”

At last the entire synod, without any delay, acclaimed:

“This is a just request. Let the rules prevail. The request of Photius, the most reverend bishop, is just.”

[Col. 1251B] The spirit of Anatolius, yearning for the grandeur of honor and power, was grievously tormented by the words of this decree. He wished the dignity and authority of the see of Constantinople to be made equal in every respect to the prerogatives of the apostolic see of the divine Peter. Yet he was not tormented in such a way that he sought to have the case of Photius and Eustathius reserved for another judgment; rather, he understood that, once the judgment of his synod had been annulled, the bishops of Constantinople were now deprived of the power which, through an injury to the canons and at the expense of other rights, they had gradually attempted to usurp for themselves.

The grandeur of the imperial city, the authority of the royal power, and the favor and protection of the imperial ministers had aroused such exaltation in the minds of the Constantinopolitans that they maintained that the ecclesiastical power of bishops ought to be measured by their administration of civil affairs. Moreover, since the emperors themselves wished to call Constantinople “New Rome,” and adorned it, after the model of ancient Rome, with the most splendid sacred and secular buildings, and since Constantine the Great and his sons, Arcadius and both Theodosiuses, enriched it with immense resources, wealth, honors, and privileges, the bishops, clinging to these injurious customs, attempted, in manifest contempt of the sacred canons, to draw to themselves jurisdiction over all the ecclesiastical cases of the East.

Finally, the ambition and arrogance of those bishops were increased by the third canon of the First Council of Constantinople. In it, 150 Fathers of the East under the elder Theodosius decreed:

“The bishop of Constantinople shall have the prerogative of honor after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome.”

But what follows from that canon? It could establish no legitimate custom, both because the apostolic see never approved it and because it seriously injured the rights of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch. Yet even if we were to grant that this canon had remained in force from the year 381, when it was issued, until the time of Anatolius, what would follow? Could the bishops of Constantinople thereby have been made equal to the Roman pontiffs, and have jurisdiction over all the affairs of the East and answer consultations from everyone? Away with such a fiction! What was granted to them, for the sake of the emperor Theodosius, was merely the honorary dignity of a patriarchate, not an enlargement of their power.

For in the preceding second canon, those same Fathers, adhering to the Nicene laws, asserted and confirmed the rights first of Alexandria and then of Antioch, listing for that purpose the individual regions and dioceses that were to depend upon their administrations and synods. We understand that they did this precisely so that the patriarch of Constantinople, content with honor alone, would not dare to interfere with the administration of all the Churches of the East.

11. In the course of time, however, the patriarchs of Constantinople threw everything into confusion. Wishing to add power to honor and to an empty title, they wrongfully usurped the ordination of many bishops in Pontus, Asia, and Thrace, evidently in order to make themselves equal to the patriarch of ancient Rome. For this reason Anatolius himself made many attempts at the general Council of Chalcedon to preserve these unjustly usurped rights and to have privileges equal to the prerogatives of the Roman pontiffs decreed for himself and his see.

To accomplish this affair more successfully and without opposition, throughout the council he sought to flatter the legates of the apostolic see by courtesies, gifts, and other means. He affected the greatest reverence toward the apostolic see, pretending that all honor and all the privileges of the bishops of Constantinople redounded to the glory, protection, and adornment of the Roman see. Finally, he asserted that the new canon which he swore was to be issued for strengthening the rights of his see would injure no one, being led by the empty pretext that the long prescription of sixty years supported his desires.

Although Anatolius presented all these arguments in words and writings, with flattering language and much pleading, they could not move the mind of the Roman pontiff or of his legates. I could demonstrate this more fully from the most certain records, without any partisan bias, if time permitted, or if the instructions of others did not prohibit me from wandering beyond the proposed questions. I shall add only this: it is perfectly clear that the custom alleged by Anatolius must be referred both to the third canon of the Second General Council of Constantinople and, finally, to the gravest abuses that had crept in over time in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs and in the ordination of metropolitans and bishops. This is most evidently established by the letters of St. Leo to the emperor Marcian, to the empress Pulcheria, to Anatolius himself, and likewise to Julian, bishop of Cos.

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Letters 78, 79, 80, and 81 of Leo the Great.]

12. It remains now to speak of the pragmatic sanction which Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, had obtained by stealth from the most pious emperor Theodosius as the reward for his earlier crimes. First of all, the term “pragmatic sanction” signifies a case debated in the emperor’s consistory before the nobles of the sacred palace. Thus Gratian, who described it in these words, also added:

“An imperial constitution issued after the examination of a case is called a pragmatic sanction.”

[Note: [Col. 1251D] Gratian’s Decree, distinction 2, “The Two Metropolitans.”]

Jacobus Gutherius, however, although he does not contradict Gratian, described the idea of a pragmatic sanction more clearly, saying:

“A pragmatic command, or sanction, is not issued in response to the petitions of individuals concerning private matters, but only in response to the petitions of some body, college, city, or province.”

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Gutherius, *On the Offices of the Imperial Household*, book I, chapter 32.]

It is well established among jurists that such pragmatic commands are to be numbered among general laws. Yet the aforementioned Gutherius distinguishes in some degree between pragmatic commands and pragmatic sanctions, adding:

“Pragmatic commands are those which order something.”

Whether, then, we ought to classify the pragmatic rescript concerning the metropolitan rights of the Church of Berytus among imperial commands or sanctions, or whether it was issued in response to the petitions of some body or city, need not be determined. But if we were required to discuss this latter point, we could at least suspect that it arose from the petitions of the eunuch Chrysaphius and the entire faction of Dioscorus, since Eustathius repeatedly appealed before the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon to the emperor as witness that he himself had not petitioned concerning this matter.

The truth of this testimony seems to be revealed by the very Theodosian law inserted into Justinian’s Code:

“For many just reasons, we decree that the city of Berytus—already crowned with its own virtues—be adorned with the name and dignity of a metropolis.”

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Justinian’s Code, book II, title 21.]

The emperor makes no mention there either of Eustathius’s petitions or of his personal merits. He praises the city of Berytus alone as crowned with many virtues.

We encounter other matters in that rescript which expose the impotence of Anatolius and his Constantinopolitan synod, as well as Eustathius’s extreme ambition. The emperor did not command that the rights of the Church of Tyre be diminished and divided between two equal metropolitans of the same province; rather, he decreed that Tyre should remain in its ancient right. He was moved by the consideration that he should neither invalidate the decrees of his ancestors nor abolish the sacred canons by means of the pragmatic rescript. He says:

“Let nothing be taken away from Tyre’s right. Let it be the mother of the province, by the benefit of our ancestors; let this city enjoy its dignity by our favor, and let both enjoy equal dignity.”

If we examine the words of the Theodosian law for a moment with the learned Christian Lupus, we shall understand that the emperor decreed for Berytus nothing more than the name and honor of a metropolitan city. Moreover, he neither assigned suffragan bishops to this new metropolitan nor wished to enlarge his power in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs by injuring the metropolitan of Tyre and altering its status.

13. Why, then, the synod of Anatolius interpreted the Theodosian law differently; why, without hearing Photius, the former metropolitan, six suffragan Churches were torn away from his jurisdiction; and why, finally, a sentence of excommunication was issued against Photius in his absence, from which he was absolved only after 122 days, has already been explained sufficiently and at length above.

To rescue the Church of Tyre from all these evils and at the same time heal its wounds, the Council of Chalcedon ordered that everything be restored to its original condition. And although that pragmatic command of Theodosius, issued in the preceding year, had already become *res judicata*—both through the decrees of the synod of Anatolius and through the consent of Maximus, patriarch of Antioch—it was nevertheless decreed that ecclesiastical cases must be settled not according to the sacred pragmatics of emperors and kings, but according to the standard of the sacred canons.

The mind of the emperor Marcian could hardly have been opposed to this course of action. Photius appealed to him in his petition—not, as the royalists claim, so that Marcian himself might judge either the law of the deceased emperor, which injured and destroyed the rights of the Church of Tyre, or so that he might remove the pragmatic sanction and take action against Eustathius and his ambition. Such a power is not granted to secular rulers in ecclesiastical affairs, lest the administration of civil matters, which belongs to them alone, be mixed with spiritual concerns.

Rather, Photius addressed his petition to the emperor Marcian so that he might show himself the defender of the sacred canons and provide the necessary protection, lest Photius be overwhelmed by fabricated charges brought by envious and uncontrollably ambitious men. For, Photius says:

“It is established by nature that the rights of priests are never diminished by the vanity of prefects.”

At that time this statement was also on everyone’s lips: neither royal ministers nor the emperors themselves, to whom the administration of temporal affairs had been entrusted, could diminish, pervert, or alter the rights of priests by their laws.

The judges of the emperor Marcian themselves sincerely affirmed this without any contradiction, saying:

“It has pleased the most holy lord of the City that the affairs of the most holy bishops should proceed not according to sacred or pragmatic rescripts, but according to the rules laid down by the holy Fathers.”

And lest anyone, clinging too zealously to royal power and majesty, should call the intention of the emperor Marcian into doubt, the imperial judges immediately pronounced unequivocally:

“Therefore, with every definition drawn from sacred pragmatics set aside, let the canons issued concerning this matter be read.”

It was as though the judges wished to indicate that pragmatic sanctions could neither possess any force against the canons of the Church nor inflict any injury upon them.

14. It is therefore no surprise that, after the fifth canon of the Council of Nicaea had been read, the entire synod declared that there should be only one metropolitan in each province:

“We wish there to be one metropolitan, according to the rules of the holy Fathers. We ask that the rules of the holy Fathers remain in force.”

From this form of discussion and judgment we are clearly taught above all that ecclesiastical cases must be handled according to the canons. The laws of princes, however, are not to be despised; they must be taken into account when they have been given for the execution, support, protection, and defense of the canons, and when they neither injure nor overwhelm and abolish the force of the sacred canons. In such circumstances, the rights of the hierarchical order are not violated; rather, those laws work together to protect the powers of the priesthood and the empire. I could explain this by hundreds of examples drawn from the laws of Constantine, Theodosius the Elder, the Valentinians, and others, if time did not prevent me.

The reasoning must be different when pragmatic laws conflict with the canons, when they overwhelm and subvert them. To insist upon pragmatic laws then, and to derive from them the forms and principles of judgment, is entirely foreign to the practice, privileges, and rights of the Church; and if we followed them, we would lead the ecclesiastical order to destruction.

Atticus, bishop of Nicopolis in Epirus, was well aware of this. After the decree of the Council of Chalcedon had been ratified—in which Photius was restored, with the overwhelming agreement of all, to the honor and administration of his original metropolitan see, while Eustathius was forbidden to claim anything further for himself from the pragmatic rescript—Atticus earnestly begged the imperial judges, in the name of the entire assembly, to prevent all abuses that might at any time creep in. He addressed them in these words:

“We beseech you to ensure even now that the force of the rules prevail in all things and in all the provinces, with all pragmatic measures set aside—those which arise from lobbying and ambition and overturn what the holy Fathers have established spiritually and according to God.”

We have copied out and recited these words in order to refute the opinions of those royalists who say that the Theodosian pragmatic law was abrogated and abolished not by the decree of the Council of Chalcedon but by the sanction of Marcian and the imperial judges. They maintain that this rule of the council applies only to the particular case proposed—namely, to matters concerning the organization of Churches. If anyone wishes to extend it to other cases, they say, it should be extended only to those in which the discipline of the canons is purely ecclesiastical.

But the authors of these opinions plainly invent such claims. For it was expressly declared, in general and without any exception, that pragmatic sanctions issued against the truth and piety of the canons are entirely devoid of authority and force. The constitution of the emperors Valentinian and Marcian, issued in the year 454, states in these words:

“We decree that all pragmatic sanctions which, through the intervention of favor and ambition, have been elicited against the ecclesiastical canons shall cease, deprived of their force and validity.”

15. The celebrated synod of Chalcedon judged the bishops ordained by Photius in the same manner. After they had attained the episcopal order and see, Eustathius and Anatolius, with the greatest injustice, ordered that they should be merely presbyters. But who does not know that it is altogether sacrilegious to reduce a bishop to the place of a presbyter? For if they removed those men from the exercise of the episcopate for a just reason, they ought not to have retained the place of presbyters either.

Thus, once these matters had been settled, the case of Photius of Tyre—including that of those bishops who had been unjustly reduced to the place and rank of presbyters—was prudently, justly, and most holily brought to a successful conclusion, while the legates of the apostolic see were acting in that council.

Since this final judgment concerning bishops who had descended to a lower rank was regarded as valid and firm, without distinction, both by Anatolius and by Maximus himself, the patriarch of Antioch, there is no reason for us to linger longer over this controversy. The agreement and practice of the universal Church, the decrees of councils, and the constitutions of the apostolic see teach us that those removed from the episcopal order for a just reason cannot continue in the rank and place of presbyters. I could demonstrate this most clearly from the beginnings of ecclesiastical affairs down to our own times.

But it was not the intention of the mercy of that supreme and most wise father and prince—to whom all ecclesiastical affairs owe greater splendor, the commonwealth of letters its advancement, the happiness of all its protection, and this illustrious institution its origin—to abuse that mercy further by detaining the most distinguished scholars.

475 **CHAPTER V.** It is shown that Theodoret, deposed by Dioscorus at the Robber Council of Ephesus, appealed to the apostolic see, and was judged by St. Leo and restored to his see. The arguments of Launoius and Paschasius Quesnellus are refuted. The opinions of the illustrious Peter de Marca and Christian Lupus concerning this case are set forth. Finally, both from the eighth session of Chalcedon and from Letter 93 of St. Leo, it is proved that the judgments of the apostolic see are supreme and irrevocable.

1. Paschasius Quesnellus, wishing to bring the case of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, to examination, began his dissertation with these words from Letter 93 of St. Leo, written to that same Theodoret:

“Blessed is our God, whose invincible truth has shown you, according to the judgment of the apostolic see, to be cleansed from every stain of heresy. You will render Him worthy thanks for so many labors if you preserve yourself, as we have proved you to be, for the defense of the universal Church.”

From such an opening I promised myself that Quesnellus would at last assert for the apostolic see and for the Roman pontiffs themselves those rights which, on the occasion of his preceding dissertations, he had until then attempted either to deny, diminish, or finally abolish altogether. But my expectation deceived me.

For, immediately pretending to inquire what that judgment of the apostolic see had been, he says that many have hitherto asked the question and that various opinions have been advanced. First, therefore, he reports the opinion of certain people who maintain that St. Leo issued a decree, either in a synod or outside a synod, for Theodoret’s restoration, after Theodoret had brought his case to him by a letter of appeal. Yet when he realized that this opinion was inconvenient to him, he rejected it with the following negative argument:

“Since not even the slightest trace of such a decree appears either in the Acts of Chalcedon or in other records of the events of that period, it is refuted as easily as it is proposed.”

He then presents the opinion of others who say that “Theodoret was restored by the same synodical and judicial sentence by which the pseudo-synod of Ephesus was annulled.” Once again he appeals to the synod to which Valentinian and the empress wrote to Theodosius concerning the rescission of the acts of that assembly.

Finally, Quesnellus asserts that he is certain that no sentence at all was issued in the case of Theodoret, whether by Leo alone or by a synod. He says that Leo mentions only the judgment contained in the letters of communion. For since the pontiff willingly received Theodoret’s complaints and granted him his communion, it followed that he had judged him cleansed from every stain of heresy.

Quesnellus wrote these and other similar arguments at the beginning of his tenth dissertation, with the intention of placing the entire matter briefly before the reader’s eyes.

2. I cannot pass over what has just been described without first asking whether this new opinion of the learned doctor, and the conclusion he draws from his earlier arguments, can be reconciled with the ordinary form of judgments, Leo’s method of action, and the other records in which mention is made of Theodoret’s case.

In the first place, the form of judgment completely overturns Quesnellus’s system. Since Theodoret was suspected of bad faith, accused by his adversaries, and already condemned by a synodical decree, St. Leo would never have granted him communion and declared him cleansed from every stain of heresy unless he had examined the case.

For what of Leo himself? Shortly before, after receiving the appeal and complaints of Eutyches, together with the letters of Theodosius Augustus in which the emperor supported Eutyches, Leo had acted with such circumspection that he refused to decide anything without a full examination of the entire case. He immediately wrote to Flavian:

“We who wish the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature can define nothing to the prejudice of either party while the facts remain unknown, before we have truthfully heard what has taken place.”

If, then, the supreme pontiff prescribes a form of judgment to other bishops and acted with such caution lest he judge hastily or rashly, could he, without knowing the case, without fully weighing the complaints of the accusers, or without examining the records of the inquiry, have shown Bishop Theodoret to be cleansed from every stain of heresy according to the judgment of his see?

But what sort of judgment would that have been, when later, merely because he suspected that Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, was either a man of impaired faith or excessively lenient toward heretics, Leo could not be induced by any of Anatolius’s petitions or by the offices of the emperor Theodosius to communicate with him until it had first been firmly established that, by a public profession of faith made before the legates of the apostolic see—sent from the West to Constantinople for this very purpose—in the presence of the entire clergy and the people of Constantinople, Anatolius was not tainted by any stain of heresy?

We gather this method of action of St. Leo from other letters that we cite in the notes below, and about which we have spoken at greater length in the preceding Exercises.

[Note: [Col. 1255D] Leo’s letters to Theodosius, to Pulcheria, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, to the archimandrites of Constantinople, and to Julian, bishop of Cos; these are discussed in the preceding chapters, etc.]

We therefore cannot accept Quesnellus’s claim that Theodoret was shown to be cleansed from every stain of heresy by the judgment of the apostolic see merely because Leo communicated with him.

3. To demonstrate still more clearly the falsity of this Quesnellian opinion, it will be useful to ask Quesnellus himself whether, after the Robber Council of Ephesus, the supreme pontiff communicated with Theodoret by right or merely out of indulgence when he received Theodoret’s letter of appeal.

Not by right, certainly, since the adversary maintains that Leo issued no decree, either in a synod or outside a synod, after receiving Theodoret’s appeal. Nor did Leo, out of some indulgence, permit Theodoret to be restored to the see of Cyrus, since Theodoret himself had never adhered to the faction of Eutyches. Moreover, a person who has been shown by a legitimate judge to be cleansed from every stain of heresy has no need of indulgence.

But both Quesnellus and others have thought that the higher judgment in Theodoret’s case must be traced to Dioscorus himself. Dioscorus had earlier been Theodoret’s enemy because of Theodoret’s exceptional learning and holiness of life, by which Dioscorus—a man excessively eager for praise—believed that his own reputation was obscured, and because Theodoret had once opposed the anathemas of St. Cyril, Dioscorus’s predecessor.

For this reason the Alexandrian patriarch had already begun to brand Theodoret as a heretic, to pursue him, to assail him with every kind of slander, and to harass him by every means. Quesnellus then describes everything Dioscorus did against Theodoret before the emperor and at the Robber Council of Ephesus, which we have reviewed above and need not describe again.

Finally, Quesnellus concludes that the emperor had taken precautions to prevent Theodoret from attending the synod being prepared, because Dioscorus feared that Theodoret, the most vigorous opponent of heretics, would oppose Eutyches with all his strength. Thus, after everything in that synod had been thrown into confusion, he cast Theodoret down from the episcopal order, directing against him the sentence of deposition just as he had done against the other bishops who defended the Catholic faith.

### 4

Theodoret, therefore, having learned these things, grieving over his plight and unable to obtain assistance from the Eastern bishops—almost all of whom were either raging or oppressed—turned to the Westerners and solicited their support, as Quesnellus likewise asserts. Accordingly, he wrote letters to the patriarch of the West,[Col. 1257B] the head of all bishops and father of the communion of the entire Church, imploring his assistance and that of all the bishops of the West alike.

“Liberatus,” he says, “says nothing about an appeal. In chapter 12 he writes only this: ‘Theodoret, the bishop, informed the pope how many evils he had suffered through the plots of Dioscorus, asking that such a cause be speedily aided through another assembly of bishops.’”

Quesnellus then proceeds gradually and with much ingenuity to explain his system, which he had taken from Launoius.[Note: [Col. 1257D] Launoius, part II, letter 2. Joannes David, *On the Canonical Judgments of Bishops*, article 4, p. 313.] He attempts to establish a certain distinction between refuge and appeal, and asserts that Theodoret sought refuge, but did not appeal to Saint Leo. Among other writers, Joannes David rejected and refuted this manner of speaking in his work *On the Canonical Judgments of Bishops*, written in French, as entirely novel and opposed to the decrees of the councils and to the other records of the Church.

But, lest we seem at present to wander here and there, it is useful first to transcribe Theodoret’s own words,[Col. 1257C] from which Cardinals Baronius and Peronius judged that his appeal ought to be inferred:

> “I await the judgment of your apostolic see,” he says, “and I beg and beseech your holiness that your just judgment assist me as an appellant, and command me to hasten to you and demonstrate that my teaching follows the apostolic footsteps.”

Baronius himself was the first to assert that this was the genuine reading of the preceding text of Theodoret. Having discovered the Greek manuscript of Theodoret’s letters in the Vatican Library, he arranged for them to be rendered into Latin by Fredericus Metius, highly skilled in both languages.[Note: [Col. 1257D] Baronius, under the year 449, vol. VI, p. m. 101. Sirmond’s and Garnerius’s edition of Theodoret’s works, Greek and Latin, vol. III, p. 986. Quesnellus, dissertation 10, vol. II, p. 323, and vol. I, p. 268, chapter 5 of Theodoret’s letter.] If we adhere to this reading, we must acknowledge that nothing more solemn could be offered for establishing Theodoret’s appeal. For, having been deposed and expelled from the episcopate, he asks and begs that assistance be granted him on the basis of the sentence and judgment of the apostolic see; and, following the procedure of an appeal, he declared himself ready to come to Rome in order to prove that he was free from every stain of heresy.

Nevertheless, since this original interpretation did not please Launoius or Quesnellus, they introduced new words into the text. Following instead another interpretation by Gentianus Hervetius,[Note: [Col. 1257D] This interpretation of Gentianus Hervetius differs, unjustly, from the other interpretation prepared by Fredericus [Col. 1258D] Metius at the command of Cardinal Baronius. For ἐπικαλέομαι, when used actively, means, among other things, “I appeal,” or “I appeal to a higher authority”: Plutarch, ἐπικαλεῖται τοὺς δημάρχους, “he appeals to the leaders of the people,” that is, to the tribunes of the plebs. Likewise, in Acts 25:11: Καίσαρα ἐπικαλοῦμαι, “I appeal to Caesar.” We could produce countless examples of this matter, but we think that the passage in Acts is sufficient for all of them.] both removed the word “appellant” and substituted another word, namely “one invoking,” so that they might more easily trouble Baronius and Peronius.

Moreover, Quesnellus and Launoius do not agree with each other in the remaining details. Launoius substitutes “tribunal” for “judgment.” Quesnellus, indeed, disagrees even with himself: in the dissertation under discussion he uses the word “judgment,” while in the earlier volume, where he presents Theodoret’s entire letter in Greek and Latin types, he retains “tribunal.” The diligent Joannes David did not notice this diversity of readings, perhaps because he was wholly preoccupied with refuting the trifles and sophistries of his opponent. Consequently, accepting without question the reading on which Launoius insisted, he undertook a more careful investigation of the distinction between refuge and appeal.

Thus, lest he play with words, as did the adversary whom he was attacking, he appealed to the words of the Council of Sardica in order to close off that escape. “When a bishop,” the fourth canon reads, “has been deposed by the judgment of bishops residing in neighboring places, and has declared that his case ought to be conducted in the city of Rome”—the seventh canon, David says, reads: “If the man who has been expelled appeals and flees for refuge to the bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard.”

Here, then, are the statutes of the Sardican canons concerning those who appeal from the sentence of their judges.[Col. 1258B] Theodoret followed them with the greatest scrupulousness. He recounted the unjust condemnation inflicted upon him by Dioscorus, and for that reason said that he awaited the judgment of the apostolic see. He asked Saint Leo to undertake the examination of his case, so that he might experience both the effect of his authority and that of his protection. Finally, he expressly requested a mandate from the apostolic see enabling him to appear before it and render an account of the apostolic teaching which alone he pursued.

No one can deny that Theodoret fulfilled these conditions, defined by the councils for appeals. But that he proceeded still further is indicated by his subsequent words, in which he asks to be informed whether he ought, or ought not, unjustly to acquiesce in his deposition. He asserts that he awaits the definition of this question, so that, once he has heard the pontifical mandate, he will not thereafter seek any other judgment from any human beings, but will await the righteous judgment of God the Savior:

> “Above all,” he says, “I beg to be taught by you whether I ought to acquiesce in this unjust deposition or not. For I await your judgment; but if you command me to remain in what has been judged, I shall remain, and henceforth I shall trouble no human being, but shall await the righteous judgment of God our Savior.”

### 5

Let us nevertheless consider Quesnellus’s amusing interpretation. He advances these same words as a defense of his collapsing case. He has therefore tried with great diligence to prove that they are the words of a man seeking advice and requesting assistance—just as though awaiting a judgment and an order concerning whether he ought to remain in what had been judged were the words of a most prudent prelate, such as he declares Theodoret to have been, merely awaiting counsel and wishing to be informed whether, for the sake of the Church’s peace, he ought to abide by Dioscorus’s judgment. Had he reflected that he was appealing to another tribunal for a new judgment, he might have become an occasion for new disturbances.

To strengthen these feeble conjectures of his interpretation, he adduces other words of Theodoret from his letter[Col. 1258D] to Renatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church:

> “For this reason, therefore, I beg your holiness to persuade the most holy and most blessed archbishop to use his apostolic authority and command me to hasten to your council.”

Theodoret was therefore asking Saint Leo to grant him assistance so that he might be judged by a new council of Westerners. The adversaries contend that this is even more clearly demonstrated by other words of the same bishop of Cyrus,[Col. 1259A] in a letter to Anatolius the Patrician:

> “I beg your Magnificence to obtain this favor from the victorious emperor: that I may go to the West and be judged by those most beloved of God and most holy bishops; and if I am found to have transgressed even in the slightest against the rule of faith, let me be thrown into the depths of the sea.”

Quesnellus flatters himself excessively that he has grasped the genuine meaning of Theodoret’s words, by which he sought assistance and protection from Leo, and consequently that he has won his case. But this is false.

In the first place, I could reply that the words addressed to Renatus, in which a council is mentioned, are not at all to be understood as referring necessarily to an assembly of bishops convened for the purpose of this appeal, but to the tribunal of the apostolic see, to which Theodoret desired to hasten in order to be judged. That Theodoret used the three words “tribunal,” “judgment,” and “council” interchangeably is evident from the three letters cited above. But neither Launoius nor Quesnellus, nor anyone else, can truthfully affirm that he intended merely to submit his appeal for examination by a council and to restrict Leo’s pontifical authority[Col. 1259B] to this type of judgment.

Furthermore, if the testimony of the deacon Liberatus, upon which the adversaries insist, is presented in full rather than truncated—as Quesnellus perhaps deliberately did—it will show that no council was necessarily required and that Theodoret had demanded one through an appeal. For Liberatus recounts there how the orthodox bishops opposed the Ephesian robbery. Theodoret, following them, informed the pope how many evils he had suffered through the plots of Dioscorus, asking that such a cause be more swiftly aided through another assembly of bishops, lest the heretical doctrines of Eutyches remain confirmed by Dioscorus.[Note: [Col. 1259D] Liberatus the deacon, *Brief Account of the Heresy of the Eutychianists*, chapter 12, vol. VI of the Councils, p. 429.]

Theodoret therefore informed Leo of the necessity of holding a new council in order to eradicate entirely the Eutychian doctrines which Dioscorus and his faction had sacrilegiously confirmed. He was by no means asking or desiring that it be held as a defense of his own case, since he had already sincerely confessed in his letter that he wished to obey the pontifical directives in every respect.

Nor do Theodoret’s words in the letters to the presbyter Renatus or to the Patrician Anatolius prove anything, since no one is unaware that cases solemnly heard and handled in the tribunal of the apostolic see are brought to conciliar examination, whether in consistories or in assemblies of bishops—assemblies which have long since acquired the name “congregations.”

If, therefore, Theodoret, as a suppliant, prayed that he might hasten to a Roman council or tribunal; if likewise he desired to be judged by the Western bishops, his appeal had not thereby been transferred to a council. He had appealed solely to Leo, intending wholly to adhere to his disposition, to the procedure of judgment, and to whatever form and character Leo should prescribe.

### 6

The distinguished Petrus de Marca, however, reasoned differently about this case. Carefully observing what Leo had done, he readily concedes, without verbal dispute or ambiguity, that the oppressed Theodoret appealed to Pope Leo, by whom he was received into communion and thereby received his bishopric.[Col. 1259D]

Nevertheless, the most learned Parisian archbishop believed that Leo’s decree had not been absolute, but was subject to the conditions that Theodoret attend the council as Dioscorus’s accuser and finally receive from the council itself a decree of restoration. He therefore adds:

> “He was subsequently admitted to the Council of Chalcedon, and this became the occasion of a serious controversy. To settle it, the judges said that he had come only as an accuser. Theodoret’s restoration, therefore, was not absolute.”[Note: [Col. 1260D] Petrus de Marca, *Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, book VII, chapter 8, p. 1025 and following, according to my pagination.]

As soon as I turned my eyes to these assertions of Petrus de Marca, I understood that he differed greatly from the preceding writers, though I did not entirely grasp his meaning. For he either believed that Leo had issued a conditional decree restoring Theodoret to the episcopate under the force of some coercive law,[Col. 1260A] or that Leo had used the authority at his disposal to defer the outcome of this case to the determination of the Council of Chalcedon.

Neither of these alternatives is established by the ecclesiastical records. Indeed, if we examine the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon in Theodoret’s own case, we can affirm with certainty that nothing whatsoever is recorded concerning such a conditional absolution and restoration.

In the first place, we learn that when the Acts of the Ephesian robbery were being read at the Council of Chalcedon, and Constantine had produced the imperial document of the younger Theodosius ordering Theodoret to be content with communion in his own Church and not to attend the Ephesian synod, the judges said:

> “Let the most reverend bishop Theodoret enter, so that he may take part in the council, because the most holy archbishop Leo restored his episcopate to him, and the most pious emperor”—namely Marcian—“decreed that he attend the holy council.”

The words transcribed here make no mention of conditional restoration, nor do they employ any formula such as “if it pleases” or “if it seems good to the council.”[Col. 1260B]

Moreover, even if certain men who condemned Theodoret’s earlier conduct, wishing to flatter Dioscorus, shouted, “Throw him out! Throw out Nestorius’s teacher!” no one nevertheless dared to deny that Leo could have possessed this right. It must also be added that the cries and complaints of the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops, raised in order to have Theodoret expelled, would have been pointless if his case had ultimately been destined to be examined by the council.

The first matter to be dealt with would rather have been his faith: it would have been necessary to investigate rigorously whether he was free from every mark of heresy, compel him to clear himself of the accusations directed against him, and hear the arguments of both sides, so that his restoration could be finalized. Since none of this was done, I do not see on what basis Leo’s restoration of him should not be called absolute.

The Eastern bishops—those of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—restrained the cries and complaints of the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops in a definite manner. Wishing to protect Theodoret’s innocence and to excuse themselves as men oppressed and deceived by Dioscorus’s schemes and violence, they openly complained and replied:

> “We signed Theodoret’s condemnation at the Ephesian robbery on a blank sheet of paper. We were beaten, and so we signed.”

When Dioscorus heard them speaking in this way, as though he wished to give an account of the decree he himself had issued against Theodoret, he interjected:

> “Why is Cyril being expelled, since he was anathematized by this man?”

He wished to recall to the minds of the judges the former hostilities that had existed between Cyril and Theodoret. He made no mention of the peace that had subsequently been established between them, and thought that he might thereby obtain some support or excuse for himself.

Nevertheless, all the Easterners who were already favoring Theodoret shouted:

> “Throw out Dioscorus the murderer! Who does not know Dioscorus’s deeds?”

After some dispute, the judges themselves, without showing regard for either side, declared:

> “The most reverend bishop Theodoret, receiving his proper place from the most holy bishop of the city of Rome, has entered in the place of an accuser.”

I do not conceal that, in order to restrain the cries already raised by the faction of Dioscorus and Eutyches, those same judges employed a certain procedural expedient. They immediately replied:

> “Allow what has been begun to be brought to an end, so that no confusion may arise in the assembly.”

They added:

> “For no prejudice will arise from the person of the most reverend bishop Theodoret, since every accusation is reserved for later—for you, for him, and for whatever you may wish to bring against one another—because he holds the right faith, especially since, even without written documents, the most reverend bishop of Antioch, the great city, bears witness to him as a believer in the catholic faith.”[Col. 1261A]

Although, I repeat, I must not pass over these matters, I can scarcely grant that Theodoret was declared free of error by the apostolic see in the sense that the decree of the Roman pontiff was to be subjected to the judgment of the council.

Rather, I am compelled, with the distinguished Christianus Lupus, to acknowledge that the entire controversy raised by the Eutychian faction against Theodoret must have concerned only the adversaries’ contention that his restoration was surreptitious—as though the pontiff’s mind had been deceived by certain false representations, so that Theodoret might regain his former rank and honor in the council.

For the sixth canon of Constantinople had decreed that a degraded bishop should lack the right to accuse another bishop.[Note: [Col. 1261D] Christianus Lupus, in the appendix to the Council of Chalcedon, p. 894 and following.] Consequently, although the case required extensive examination, the judges, faithfully adhering to Saint Leo’s decree, freely granted Theodoret the right to accuse for the time being, reserving to themselves the careful examination, in another session, of the charges brought against him.

By adopting this prudent procedure, they neither did violence to Leo’s decree, which ordered that Theodoret take part in the council because he had been restored to the episcopate, nor did they close access to Theodoret’s adversaries, who wished to investigate whether he had been restored by surreptitious means or whether he was infected with Nestorian corruption. The Egyptians shouted:

> “Do not call him a bishop! He is not a bishop! Throw out the enemy of God! Throw out the Jew! Theodoret accused Cyril. We expel Cyril if we accept Theodoret. The canons expel this man. God is against him.”

These, then, were the crimes the Egyptians brought against Theodoret. He had previously condemned Cyril’s Chapters, and for this reason they had condemned him as a heretic, wholly disregarding the fact that, after all ambiguities had been removed and the decrees of the general ecumenical council obeyed, he had thereafter maintained complete concord with Cyril.

What wonder, then, if the judges, observing these clandestine machinations of Dioscorus and seeing that the synod had been split into two opposing factions—the Easterners proclaiming Theodoret orthodox and saying, “Let the orthodox remain in the council; throw out the seditious; throw out the murderers”—feared still graver dangers and declared with indignation:

> “These popular acclamations befit neither bishops nor the parties. Allow the reading of all the proceedings.”

What wonder, I say, if the Egyptians still refused to desist from the shouting with which they had begun, and the judges, acting seriously and with the authority at their command, ordered silence for all and commanded Constantine to read the entire Acts of the Ephesian robbery?[Col. 1261C]

In these circumstances, who does not see that the judges would have acted less cautiously and more precipitately than prudently if they had decided to give Bishop Theodoret a place among the judges? First, from the complete reading of the Acts, it was necessary to inquire whether Dioscorus had even the semblance of a title authorizing him to depose or degrade Theodoret along with the other orthodox bishops.[Col. 1261D] In this matter he certainly could not act as a judge according to all the laws, but only as an accuser.

If, therefore, Theodoret entered the council as a true bishop, even by the judgment of the judges, I do not see how it can be said that Leo’s decree restoring him to his see and episcopal honor was not absolute—especially since he was later admitted to the synodal vote and to the full communion of all the most holy bishops.

### 7

The difficulties thus far clarified, derived from the opinions of other writers, would contribute little to the present case unless our discussion again turned to Quesnellus. He not only denies Theodoret’s appeal[Col. 1262A] but also denies the judgment of the apostolic see itself. Accordingly, in constructing a new history of the events, he has mixed everything together and brought forward a great many matters that merely wear the appearance of truth.

I shall therefore endeavor, as briefly as I can, to collect the many points he has introduced.

First, he readily concedes that no council was convened by Saint Leo in Theodoret’s case. His letters to the supreme pontiff are known; what the Roman pontiff wrote is not known.

Second, he asserts that Leo held no judgment for examining Theodoret’s case, but remained joined to him without an interruption of communion. This, he says, may be inferred from Leo’s fortieth letter, in which he speaks of the necessity of summoning a general council; or from his forty-seventh letter, from which it may be gathered that he regarded all the proceedings of the Ephesian robbery as null and void and asked the emperor Theodosius to order that everything remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment, until a larger number of priests from the whole world could be assembled.

Third, he says that Theodoret was permitted to remain in his see because Dioscorus’s sentence against him was treated as null, and because the pontiff had still received testimony from the East through Anatolius, recently ordained, that Theodoret had already subscribed the encyclical letter to Flavian and had condemned not only the Nestorian and Eutychian doctrines but had also pronounced anathema against Nestorius and Eutyches themselves.

For this reason Quesnellus cites the testimony of Saint Leo from letter 68 to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, chapter 5, which he himself says, “We now publish for the first time.” He therefore concludes that, both from the report he had received and from Theodoret’s own letter, the Roman pontiff understood and judged him to be free from every stain of heresy, so that nothing prevented him from granting him communion in the usual manner and Theodoret from retaining his own Church in ecclesiastical peace.[Col. 1262B]

“This,” he adds, “is the judgment of the apostolic see mentioned in the letter we are discussing. It does not demonstrate that his see was restored by a judicial sentence of the pontiff, but only that a certain suspicion of error was removed.”[Col. 1262C]

Fourth, under number 5 he asserts that neither Anatolius of Constantinople, nor Maximus of Antioch, Theodoret’s metropolitan, nor any other Eastern bishops ever broke the bond of communion with him. He therefore continues that he cannot assert that the whole matter was ended by Leo’s action, “since it is known to anyone who reads the Acts of this council that it was again brought to the anvil by the Fathers of Chalcedon.”

Here he repeats many things he had said earlier and, in order to impress his system upon his readers, celebrates with considerable exaggeration the outcries “not of a few,” he says, “but of very many Palestinian, Egyptian, and Illyrian bishops, who insisted that Theodoret ought to be expelled from the council. These bishops, as though by indulgence and dispensation, acquiesced in the testimony of Maximus of Antioch.”[Col. 1262D]

Fifth, he describes what took place in the eighth session of the Council of Chalcedon in Theodoret’s case. After narrating the events according to his own wishes, he made every effort to suppress whatever he judged contrary to himself and his system. Finally, he concluded that Theodoret was restored to his see for no other reason than that he anathematized both Nestorius and Eutyches, not only in writing but also orally, in his own voice, in the presence of the entire assembly.

### 8

From the five points we have just noted, as well as from those previously advanced, Quesnellus flattered himself that complete and unquestionable credibility ought to be granted to his opinion. Perhaps he trusted that, after him, no one would wish to revisit Theodoret’s case or submit his writings to examination.

He therefore turned his style against certain unnamed persons who, he claims, diminish and ridicule the sacred authority of bishops assembled in an ecumenical council—much more so outside a council—and maintain that, by virtue of their office, they are entitled merely to execute pontifical commands, both in this case under discussion and in all others.[Note: [Col. 1262D] Quesnellus, vol. II, dissertation 10, chapter 4, p. 324.]

Yet, he says, it is rather a signal distinction of the apostolic see that it is the executor of ecumenical councils—a prerogative of which Pope Gelasius boasted in letter 13.

If all these arguments which the Parisian writer brings forward in defense of his system agreed with the truth, everything we have so far noted in this case would completely collapse. But since they contain fallacies, the argument of our *Exercitation* is thereby strengthened more and more.

To begin with, what inference could there be—and it cannot be drawn either from Leo’s writings or from any other records—that a council had been held by the Roman see in Theodoret’s case? “Therefore Leo held no judgment for examining Theodoret’s case.” What kind of conclusion is this, entirely opposed to the words of the holy pontiff from which the adversary began his dissertation?

> “Blessed be our God, whose invincible truth has demonstrated, according to the judgment of the apostolic see, that you are free from every stain of heresy.”[Col. 1263A]

Are we to suppose that Leo was lying?

Nor can the adversary find support in the letters of Leo that he himself cites, written to Theodosius after the Ephesian robbery. In them Leo asks that everything be kept in the condition in which it had been before any judgment, and therefore, Quesnellus claims, that the bond of communion with Theodoret had nowhere been broken.

For a restoration of matters to their former condition, pending the assembly of a larger number of priests from the entire world, is not the same as issuing a definitive decree; it means reserving the cases for future examination until a more careful inquiry can be made. Theodoret’s faith and innocence were therefore not judged in that manner merely because the pontiff abolished the acts of the robbery, since at the same time he decreed that judgment concerning all the matters should be reserved for another time and another assembly.

Consequently, even if Theodoret and the other bishops who had been degraded were permitted to return to their sees after the abolition of those Acts,[Col. 1263C] it was nevertheless not established whether they had been deposed justly or unjustly, nor whether they were permitted to retain their sees by right or through dispensation and indulgence. This had to be investigated by a new inquiry and demonstrated by a new decree; in the meantime, their case remained, as they say, in reserve until a definitive sentence.

The argument introduced in third place is extremely unstable if we attend to what we described in the preceding chapters. For Anatolius’s testimony could not have supported Theodoret’s case before Leo, since Anatolius’s faith, ordination, and close association with Dioscorus and the Eutychian faction had aroused such suspicions in the pontiff’s mind that Leo, disregarding the pleas of the emperor Theodosius and the empress Pulcheria, was unwilling to communicate with Anatolius or with those who had ordained him.

Only after Abundius of Como had been sent, together with three other apostolic legates, and a public assembly had been held, was Anatolius ordered solemnly in that assembly to make a profession of faith,[Col. 1263D] pronounce anathema against Nestorius and Eutyches, and subscribe the letter to Flavian.
