Unless Anatolius had faithfully obeyed these commands, Leo and the orthodox would never have regarded him as a legitimate bishop.

But, I ask, from what record did Quesnellus learn that Anatolius had given—or could have given—testimony concerning Theodoret’s faith?

What we know is that Leo received good testimony concerning Theodoret’s faith and purity, and concerning his readiness of mind, by which he gladly subscribed the pontifical letter to Flavian for the destruction of the heresies. But Leo learned all these things from Abundius’s report while Abundius was still in Constantinople—for, as we have seen, he was informed that Theodoret himself and the bishops Ibas and Aquilinus had sincerely offered proofs of their faith.[Col. 1264A]

Furthermore, Saint Leo was thoroughly informed concerning the faith, conduct, and policies of Theodoret and the other Easterners through the continuous exchange of letters he maintained with the Constantinopolitan clerics and archimandrites who adhered to Flavian, with Julian of Cos, with the empress Pulcheria, with other orthodox men who came to Rome from various parts of the East or traveled to the East, and finally with Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, who had come to Rome after the Ephesian disaster to defend before Leo the cause of himself and the other Catholics.

The judgment of the apostolic see in the case under discussion was therefore not merely that Leo had never interrupted communion with Theodoret, or that he had received testimony concerning Theodoret’s faith from Anatolius, recently ordained. Such considerations could have contributed little or nothing to Theodoret’s cause, so that the holy pontiff could truthfully affirm that the bishop of Cyrus had been demonstrated, by decree of the apostolic see, to be free from every stain of heresy.[Col. 1264B]

I shall not assert that Anatolius broke the bond of communion with Theodoret. I do not know, however, how Theodoret could have continued in communion with Anatolius—or how Anatolius could not have broken that bond—since Anatolius had been elevated to the throne of Constantinople after Flavian’s death solely because of the services he had rendered to Dioscorus, Chrysaphius, Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, and the other members of the Eutychian faction.

Could he have supported the interests and desires of heretics and promoted their causes, as is evident from the proceedings against Photius of Tyre,[Note: [Col. 1263D] We discussed the words of this letter of Theodoret to Abundius in chapter 12 above. Concerning the case of Photius of Tyre, see what we said in the academic dissertation on the Councils delivered before our most holy lord Benedict XIV, which we published in the preceding chapter; from it Anatolius’s devotion to the Eutychian faction is abundantly clear.[Col. 1264D]] and yet not break communion with Theodoret of Cyrus, who was laboring for the faith and was so greatly hated by that company of factional men?

Indeed, was Theodoret not persecuted by them all the more vehemently the more closely he adhered to Flavian, to the apostolic see, and to its legates? Unless Quesnellus produces new records that describe the entire sequence of events differently, wise readers will never place faith in him.

### 9

Indeed, no credibility can be granted him on the basis of what he recounted from the eighth session of the Council of Chalcedon.[Col. 1264C] What does that session show? The outcries of many bishops against Theodoret, whom they unjustly suspected of being stained with Nestorian soot; he was compelled in the full council to pronounce anathema against Nestorius; he was required to accept the definition of faith issued by that same Council of Chalcedon.

After he declared that he had already subscribed both the definition of faith and Saint Leo’s letter, and after every doubt that he had obtained a surreptitious decree from the apostolic see had been removed, a solemn sentence was finally pronounced:

> “The most glorious judges said: ‘All doubt concerning Theodoret has now been removed [lacuna]. It therefore remains for your Reverence to pronounce the sentence, so that he may receive his Church, just as the most holy archbishop Leo judged.’”

Accordingly, the adversaries immediately ceased their disturbances and cries. Indeed, all the bishops of that great council shouted:

> “Theodoret is worthy of the see of the Church [lacuna]. Let the Church receive its shepherd. Let the Church receive its orthodox teacher [lacuna]. Many years to Archbishop Leo! After God—or, with God—Leo has judged.”

These, then, are the things which anyone can faithfully gather from the sequence of that eighth session, without any deception whatsoever.

They plainly correspond to the decree pronounced by Paschasinus and Lucentius, bishops; Boniface, a presbyter; and Julian, bishop of Cos—the legates and representatives of the apostolic see. We have decided to transcribe it faithfully here, so that what Quesnellus suppressed—whether deliberately or through negligence, I do not know—may become known:

> “The most holy and venerable bishop Theodoret was long ago received into communion by the most holy and most blessed bishop of the universal Church, Leo of the city of Rome”—notice the following words—“as the letters from him to our humility testify.”

They added these further words:

> “Therefore, if he declares the catholic faith as he promises, and, in accordance with the aforesaid blessed bishop, pronounces in his own written statement that he has subscribed to it, and if, moreover, in another statement given to our humility, he has shown that he has anathematized both Nestorius and Eutyches, not only in writing but also orally, in his own voice, in the presence of the entire assembly, then by this judgment the most holy and most venerable synod, and in addition our humility, has decreed that his own Church be restored to him.”

### 10

Who, then, does not see that the whole controversy turned on whether Theodoret had obtained from the Apostolic See, by stealth and subterfuge, a decree restoring him and recognizing the integrity of his faith? For they did not call into question the judgment and authority of the Roman pontiff, nor did they add weight to his decision; they merely wished to be assured, by Theodoret’s solemn confession pronounced aloud, that he sincerely anathematized Nestorius, just as he had already attested in his written declaration addressed to the Roman pontiff.

This procedure, just as it did not injure the authority of the Roman See—which had long before received Theodoret into communion and judged him worthy to recover his own see, as the Fathers of Chalcedon themselves declared—so neither can it be considered injurious to the dignity of bishops assembled in councils, provided that, both in councils and outside them, they adhere to their head when delivering their judgments. Therefore Quesnellus’s complaint seemed to me exceedingly misplaced, when he assumes that the authority of bishops is diminished if they are ordered to carry out the commands of the Apostolic See.

For what diminution of episcopal rank can there be if the individual pastors of all the Churches, scattered throughout the world, adhere with the supreme pontiff, the head of the entire body of the faithful, to those matters that pertain to faith, morals, and discipline [485]? The bond of ecclesiastical society consists in this: that all bishops, with irrevocable assent, venerate the judgments of the Apostolic See and submit themselves to them with that subjection which we recognize as maintained between the members and the head, and which Christ, with extraordinary graciousness, ordained for the perfect unity of the mystical body, so that through the head alone he might more easily diffuse the gifts of his goodness to all the members.

Therefore the holy pontiff, in his letter to that same Theodoret, established a distinction between the role of the Roman See and the authority of the bishops assembled in ecumenical synods. He wrote as follows, to suit our purpose [Note: [Col. 1265D] Psalm 123, verse 8]:

> Hence we glory in the Lord, singing with the prophet: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth,” who did not permit us to suffer any loss among our brethren. But what he had previously defined in the exercise of our own ministry, he confirmed with the irrevocable assent of the entire brotherhood, so that he might show that what had first been formulated by the first of all sees and had then been received by the judgment of the whole Christian world had truly proceeded from him, so that in this also the members might agree with the head.

Who, moreover, does not see that Leo asserted one mode of action for himself and another for the bishops assembled in synod [Col. 1265D]? He claims for himself the ministry of defining, but assigns to the bishops the right—or rather the duty—of giving assent.

Furthermore, does not Saint Leo, in the same passage, distinguish between the judgment formulated by the first of all sees and that judgment which is said to have been received by the entire Christian world [Note: [Col. 1266D] The letter to Theodoret cited above, chapter 1]? This cannot be denied.

Therefore, if the divine institution and order is such that, in more serious matters pertaining to faith and morals, the Church makes use of the ministry of the Roman See in definitions and judgments, so that a judgment first formulated by the first of all sees is solemnly received by the entire Christian world with irrevocable and firm assent, it follows that the execution of the decrees of the Apostolic See has been entrusted to bishops assembled in an ecumenical synod. This is made clear by the Acts of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon [Col. 1266A], and will become even clearer in what follows, where we shall show that Dioscorus was judged guilty of the gravest crime because, when he refused to carry out Saint Leo’s commands in the second synod convened at Ephesus, he transformed the synod into a robber council. But Leo himself became his own interpreter in this matter.

Indeed, speaking in the same chapter of this letter about the consent of the bishops expressed in the Acts of the councils, he asserts that it was obtained from the Apostolic See neither by flattery nor by subterfuge. To remove such suspicions, and even if some persons had been found who, incited by the author of the dissension, doubted the judgments of the Apostolic See, nevertheless, for the greater confirmation of the truth, this was permitted by God’s will so that a greater good might be attained. For he says:

> Lest the consent of the other sees toward the one which the Lord established to preside over all the others should seem to be mere flattery, or lest any other contrary suspicion should creep in, those who first doubted our judgments were found. And while some, incited by the author of the dissension, rushed into the battles of contradiction [Col. 1266B], through the dispensation of the author of all goodness the evil was turned toward a greater good.

I am not unaware that Quesnellus removed from the text of this letter some readings found in the older editions, introducing new ones, as he himself says, with the assistance of his manuscripts, or that he composed various annotations at the end of the second volume according to his own judgment, evidently so that he might persuade readers of what he most desired.

Would that those who labor to introduce a new form of judgment into the Church, in order to cast down the authority of the Apostolic See, would turn their eyes to this chapter of the letter and, laying aside every violent interpretation, understand the distinction that Saint Leo indicated between canonical judgment and consent, between the rights that belong to the first see and those that are attributed to bishops assembled in synod [486]. They would not have raised so many grave and erroneous questions, akin to schism, in which they try to extend the authority of bishops beyond its proper limits, so as to confine the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs within excessively narrow boundaries.

Nevertheless, the efforts of our opponents benefit the truth of the matter more than they can harm it, since, as Leo himself says:

> The truth itself shines forth more clearly and resists more strongly when later examination confirms what the faith had previously taught.

Finally, the authority of the episcopal order is not diminished but shines more brightly when the authority of the supreme pontiffs is preserved in such a way that the freedom of those below is thought to be diminished in no respect. The outcome of the examination advances the greater glory of God when it takes on the confidence to overcome opposition, lest what is shown in itself to be reprobate should, through the prejudice of silence, appear to have been suppressed.

From these forms of expression we clearly understand how the rights both of the Roman pontiffs and of the bishops are preserved in synods, with each exercising the authority and jurisdiction proper to him. The Roman pontiffs compare matters of faith with the rules of the apostolic creed and pronounce their judgments under the special inspiration of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1266D], in order to overthrow heresies.

But when the zeal of factious men is directed toward overthrowing the sincere doctrine of Christ, and when they seek to attack and utterly abolish those genuine doctrines derived from the apostles, the Roman pontiffs therefore present their definitions with the greatest care to bishops assembled in synod, so that the bishops may give the necessary assent. They must not offer that assent without examination, especially since they have to deal with men who have violated the faith, who cling obstinately to pernicious errors and altogether resist submitting to decrees that, besides the sentence of anathema, carry with them other penalties as well—namely, deposition, degradation, and exile.

Let Quesnellus therefore say, I ask, in what sense and for what reason he thinks the authority of the bishops diminished [Col. 1267A], when, according to Leo, the bishops themselves are granted the power to confirm the truth of the faith by their examination and assent. They also act so that the dignity of their priestly office may shine forth, since, while preserving the authority of the supreme pontificate to which they adhere, their freedom is not diminished by unanimity and harmony of spirit but is increased.

Thus, for the greater glory of God, the examination undertaken with confidence in overcoming opposition is beneficial, lest what is shown in itself to be reprobate should, through the prejudice of silence, appear to have been suppressed.

### 11

It therefore seems to me that Quesnellus labored in vain in his dissertation on Theodoret, proposing one question after another that had little relevance to the goal he had set himself, since anyone could have resolved them very easily from Leo’s own statements and from the manner in which he acted.

This is especially true because he also appealed irrationally to the testimony of Pope Gelasius, which he ought at least to have presented in its entirety, so that the reader might understand, without further investigation, the sense in which the pontiff spoke.

Gelasius, then, affirmed nothing at all [Col. 1267B] that conflicts with what we have said above. Indeed, if we weigh his words, Quesnellus’s system will be utterly destroyed.

In the preceding exercises we saw that, in writing to the bishops of Dardania, the pontiff wished to demonstrate that Acacius had rightly been condemned by the judgment of the Apostolic See alone. Therefore, at the beginning of his letter, he attacks those who thought Acacius had been condemned unjustly because he did not appear to have been deposed by a special synod.

He then cites examples of heretics showing that certain persons tainted by heretical corruption had been condemned in synods, but not in such a way that the Roman See could not also have condemned or absolved them without synods.

Since it belongs to the Roman See to give synods strength and authority, the same pontiff therefore declares that no one who considers what has been handed down from the ancient tradition of the Fathers can be ignorant that, of the constitution of any synod approved by the assent of the universal Church, no see ought to carry it out more than the first see, which confirms each synod by its authority and preserves it through continuous governance, in accordance with its primacy—which the blessed Apostle Peter received from the voice of the Lord, and which, with the Church following, he has always held and continues to hold [Col. 1267C] [Note: [Col. 1267] Pope Gelasius, Letter 13. It is found in volume V of the General Councils, p. 324 ff.].

Quesnellus sought to suppress, or at least conceal, the final words of this text, which he enclosed in brackets. But if these words are compared with what precedes, it will be evident that nothing can be extracted from this testimony that conflicts with our earlier statements.

For what did Gelasius say belongs to bishops assembled in synod, or to Roman pontiffs who confirm or invalidate the constitutions of councils? The bishops approve by their assent and submit themselves to those statutes and rules that are proposed in synods and committed to writing. These acquire force and authority insofar as the Apostolic See confirms each synod by its authority and judgment and preserves it through continuous governance.

Moreover, it belongs especially to this see [Col. 1267D] to enforce those statutes once confirmed and preserved, by ordering and commanding that they not remain neglected or violated in the conduct of ecclesiastical affairs.

Gelasius asserts most clearly that this duty belongs to the Roman See by virtue of its primacy, which the blessed Apostle Peter received from the voice of the Lord and which, with the Church following, he has always held and continues to hold. This is understood not only from the words cited by Quesnellus but also from the context of the entire letter. We shall discuss this matter ourselves when treating the canons of Sardica.

### 12

Quesnellus has still amassed much material under some pretext—I do not know what one—for attacking his opponents. These matters ought rather to be referred to the entire history of the Council of Chalcedon, and we shall make our observations on them while following the order of events.

But since one point remains among them that concerns Theodoret himself—namely, whether Leo himself, after the Synod of Chalcedon, confirmed both Theodoret’s restoration, which had been admitted with the assent of the Fathers, and the other judgments of that synod concerning the private cases of bishops, a claim that certain writers, following Quesnellus, have denied—it should also be observed here that the same Parisian scholar, in order not to attribute Theodoret’s restoration fully to Leo but rather to the synod, wrote:

> Furthermore, the Roman pontiff later gave his assent to the decision of the synod, whose judgment he had anticipated, both in other letters and especially in the one that he sent to Theodoret himself some time after the synod had ended.

Quesnellus therefore attributed Theodoret’s restoration entirely to the synod, concluding that “Leo had merely anticipated it.” To make this easier to fabricate, he appeals to the testimony of Saint Leo cited above, with which he began his dissertation, and, in his customary manner, entirely omitted whatever he thought opposed his own purposes.

But the holy pontiff’s following words expose his evil deception. After congratulating Theodoret on having preserved himself as the man whom he had proved and continues to prove himself to be, in defense of the universal Church, he immediately adds:

> For inasmuch as God has frustrated the deceits of all slanderers, we recognize the greatest care of the blessed Peter for us all. After he had confirmed the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith, he did not permit anything blameworthy to appear concerning any of you who labored with us for the Catholic faith; for, with the Holy Spirit judging, none of those whose faith had already conquered could fail to emerge victorious.

Let Quesnellus therefore attend to these words, understand their force and weight, and from them infer whether Theodoret’s restoration should be attributed to the synod or to the pontiff.

He attributes the definition of the Catholic faith to the care of the blessed Apostle Peter, who confirmed the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith and did not permit anything blameworthy to appear concerning those persons who had labored with the same supreme pontiff for the Catholic faith [Col. 1268C].

Leo therefore attributes to the Apostolic See a twofold right in dispelling the deceits of slanderers [488]. One is judgment and definition in matters of faith; the other is the freedom of orthodox bishops who had been rescued from the preceding oppression of factious men.

If only I were now granted enough time to go through, annotate, and, if necessary, refute the other matters that Quesnellus has assembled there in his discussion. But since, as we have already said, those matters belong more properly to the history of Chalcedon than to the case of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, we shall not abuse the patience of our friendly reader. We shall therefore proceed to examine the case of Domnus of Antioch.

## CHAPTER VI

The Chalcedonian action concerning Domnus of Antioch is not spurious. Rusticus the deacon translated it from Greek into Latin together with the remaining Acts. Quesnellus denied this with the greatest injustice, although the learned and distinguished Stephen Baluzius has already rejected his arguments as false and entirely weak and has resolved them with great and remarkable erudition. In describing this exercise, we have accordingly had to follow his footsteps frequently.

[Col. 1268D]

### 1

Among Quesnellus’s dissertations we encounter one placed ninth, in which the author undertook to examine the case of Domnus, formerly bishop of Antioch. In discussing Domnus’s condemnation, the ordination of Maximus as his successor, and various letters of Saint Leo and the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, he proposes to illustrate these materials and finally flatters himself that he can demonstrate—or has demonstrated—that the action concerning Domnus inserted among these Acts may be fictitious.

Indeed, the author promised himself this in the title, or heading, of the same dissertation, but unjustly. For all the points that he gathered here and there in support of his case either collapse of themselves as weak or are shown by the sequence of events to be entirely irrelevant to the question under discussion.

He therefore begins the dissertation by asking why the ordination of Maximus was confirmed while the deposition of Domnus was not revoked. He adds:

> Nearly all Catholic writers who deal with this question advance the following explanation: although Maximus had been elected by suspicious men, consecrated by the bishop of Constantinople contrary to canonical rule, and installed over Domnus while Domnus was still alive, he was nevertheless received by the synod because he had been confirmed in the episcopate by Saint Leo.

He notes that the deposition of Domnus and of the other bishops at the Ephesian Robber Council had been carried out with the greatest impiety, yet Domnus alone, while the others were restored, was not returned to his see. This procedure, he says, gives rise to a more difficult problem.

He adds that the Acts of the Ephesian Robber Council had been declared null by the Westerners before the Council of Chalcedon, and that Pope Leo had insisted that everything should be restored to the condition in which it had been before the ill-fated synod, until all matters could be reformed by an ecumenical council [Col. 1269B] [Note: [Col. 1269D] Quesnellus, volume II of the Works of Saint Leo, p. 312].

It followed that the deposition of Domnus and the ordination of Maximus ought to have been null, and that Domnus should have recovered his position.

He presents the view of Baronius, who affirmed that Saint Leo, after examining the case, understood that Domnus had been justly condemned [Note: [Col. 1270D] Baronius, year 451, no. 128].

After this he reports the conjecture of those who claimed that Domnus had voluntarily submitted to his own deposition, enticed by the delights of the solitary life in which he had formerly been nurtured by the abbot Euthymius. When, contrary to the holy Father’s advice, he was planning to abandon these delights in order to help his uncle John, who had turned away from the Catholic faith, he heard from Euthymius these words, which foretold the future:

> If, disregarding these things and content with endurance, you attempt to leave the Laura, you will indeed obtain the administration that your uncle now possesses, but evil men and deceivers will again take it away from you after you have first been led astray by them through ignorance.

He reports these and similar matters from Cyril the monk’s account of the deeds of Euthymius.

### 2

In the third place Quesnellus concludes:

> Those who think that Leo’s authority caused Maximus, installed in the see of Antioch under such evil auspices, to remain there and compelled Domnus to surrender his place, say that this is clearly established by the Acts of Chalcedon. For in the action entitled “Concerning Domnus of Antioch,” it is expressly stated that Maximus had been confirmed by Leo’s authority.

Quesnellus finally transferred the entire action into his dissertation, in order that the reader might more easily form a judgment about it with the text before his eyes while investigating the truth of ecclesiastical history.

After prefacing the matter with such a great apparatus of questions and words, Quesnellus admitted that the action concerning Domnus of Antioch, reported among the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, was not at all fictitious, and professed to desire with all his heart that it should be genuine:

> For if this were so, he says, we would have before us a testimony of the highest authority concerning the power of the Roman pontiff both over synods and over Eastern bishops—over bishops, I mean, of the major and first sees. For how great a power would it be if the consecration, or at least the confirmation, of the bishop of Antioch, and consequently of the bishop of Alexandria and other bishops, belonged to the Roman bishop, as Cardinal Bellarmine and his apologist Jacobus Gretser argue from this passage? What a prerogative it would be if, when several bishops had been deposed by force and crime by an ill-fated synod, their condemnation and deposition were ordered to remain valid because the Roman pontiff judged that they should remain valid, while the substitution of another bishop in the place of only one of them could take effect only if that same pontiff had confirmed it! How clearly, finally, would this demonstrate his supreme power over synods, whose Acts would possess force in that part to which he had added force, while those Acts would be void and null that he had wished to be null!

> Yet just as it is characteristic of a learned and wise theologian to defend the true and genuine primary privileges of the first see with all his heart and on the basis of solid and authentic proofs, so it is a sign of a scarcely sincere and liberal spirit either to enlarge those privileges beyond their prescribed limits or to support them with uncertain, transient, and false aids and props.

He concludes:

> For truth does not need a lie; rather, through association with a lie, even the most thoroughly established truth is accustomed to be called into suspicion of falsehood.

Who, however, could persuade himself that Quesnellus made this protest sincerely and with all his strength? If he had genuinely desired that the action concerning Domnus of Antioch should be not fictitious but authentic, he would have recanted and repudiated his ninth dissertation, written for this cause, and would have consigned it to flames and fire.

For while Quesnellus was still alive, the distinguished Stephen Baluzius, applying the greatest zeal and undertaking the most laborious and expensive efforts, obtained new information from various scholars devoted to ancient literary studies. Thus Quesnellus himself could finally have judged, without any hesitation, that he had been deceived and had gone astray in his own investigations, and that the action in question could not be called fictitious [Col. 1270B].

Therefore Baluzius, both for the usefulness of literary scholarship and for the advancement and benefit of ecclesiastical history, answered and resolved each and every one of Quesnellus’s arguments in preparing a new collection of the Councils, and dispelled from the minds of readers the suspicions of falsehood that they might have absorbed.

### 3

Quesnellus therefore gathers his first argument from the Greek manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon, in which this action is absent.

> This, he says, is certainly no slight indication that it was fabricated by some Latin impostor. For if it had really taken place in the council, it would of course have been in Greek and would be found inserted with the other actions in the Greek Acts of this synod. For what reason this one alone should have been separated from the body of the other Greek actions is entirely unclear.

Who, however, will not judge this first conjecture of Quesnellus to be exceedingly deceptive? Quesnellus may suspect that the action was fabricated by a Latin impostor because it does not appear in the surviving Greek manuscripts; why should he not rather suspect that the Greeks sought to suppress it and attempted to separate it from the body of the other actions, so that they might more easily contend with the Roman bishop over primacy?

Did not the Easterners, in the fifth, sixth, seventh, and following centuries, claim for themselves the honors and prerogatives of primacy on the grounds that the Church of Antioch had first been founded by Saint Peter? Did not the Acephali and Eutychians, immediately after the Council of Chalcedon, move every stone in an attempt to abolish that council?

When they could never achieve this, they at least wished to erase the memory of the fact that the Eastern bishops—the bishops of Antioch and Alexandria—were regarded as canonically elected only with the consent or confirmation of the Roman pontiff [Col. 1270D].

Quesnellus ought certainly to have considered this, especially since, after Maximus and Basil, the Catholic bishops who occupied the see of Antioch, many bishops belonging to heretical, schismatic, and utterly criminal sects sat there. We could list them from the Acts of subsequent councils if we were dealing with a man entirely unacquainted with ecclesiastical history.

For the moment, however, setting aside what might be said about Peter the Fuller, Severus, Macarius the Monothelite, and other men belonging to condemned sects who may have labored to remove this action altogether from ancient Greek copies, lest there remain a certain and indisputable monument of the full power of the Roman pontiff, at least in confirming the elections and consecrations of Eastern patriarchs [Col. 1271A], let us consider whether the preceding argument totters or collapses.

Certainly, if our opponent wished to weaken it merely through Quesnellus’s suspicions, he ought to have produced for us some Greek original manuscript of the same Acts of Chalcedon and obtained support for his conjectures from it. Since neither he nor anyone else among the Greeks has so far been able to do this, we now proceed to examine another of Quesnellus’s arguments.

### 4

In the second place he argues that this action came from a single manuscript, which no authority or antiquity commended, since it was merely on paper and was said to have been obtained from two unknown German scholars.

Those devoted to ancient literature owe much to the distinguished Stephen Baluzius. In order to refute this difficulty raised by our opponent, he judged it more prudent and sensible to investigate the matter so that he would not introduce fables into his collection of the Councils.

Suspending judgment while hesitating to accept Quesnellus’s word, he first began examining with his own eyes the Latin versions of the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1271B]. He then asked his friends whether manuscript copies were preserved in other libraries outside France in which the action concerning Domnus had been written.

Among those who responded to his wishes was the distinguished and most eminent Jerome Cardinal Casanata, an expert in ancient matters. His memory will never perish, on account of the exceptional benefits and advances that he bestowed upon the republic of letters.

When consulted by Baluzius, Casanata ordered the most learned men to examine many manuscripts in the Vatican Library, of which he was in charge. When the action in question was found there, he not only freed those imaginary German scholars, whom Quesnellus suspected, from the charge of imposture and ignorance, but also demonstrated through numerous arguments that Quesnellus himself had seriously gone astray.

In the first place, the action in question was contained in Greek in the manuscript of Patricia Julia, which Rusticus mentions, although it was absent from other manuscripts that he had revised [Col. 1271C]. For Rusticus himself, after the sixth action of the Council of Chalcedon, added the following note, which the Bohier manuscript exhibits:

> Here ends action 6. Here begins action 7, concerning Domnus of Antioch, formerly patriarch, translated from Greek into Latin.

In the course of time this further note was added to Rusticus’s annotation:

> Other manuscripts, however, present it at the end of action 10 [Note: [Col. 1271D] Volume IV of the General Councils, p. 1514].

### 5

Quesnellus ought therefore to have noticed two things. First, the manuscripts that mention this action as translated from Greek into Latin were not on paper but made of parchment; they were not recent but of the greatest antiquity. Consequently, he was not entitled to assert that the Greek collection of the Acts of Chalcedon could never have been separated from the rest, since the ancient interpreters of that synod stated that they had encountered the action placed seventh.

Second, the action did not come from a single manuscript commended by no authority or antiquity merely because it was on paper and was said to have been obtained from two unknown German scholars.

For what prevents a paper copy of an ancient monument from having been transcribed from older archetypes? There are countless manuscript copies, even those written in more recent scripts, that were copied from the most ancient parchments—as plain as day to anyone with eyes.

Therefore, before defining the matter as though from a tripod, he ought to have investigated more carefully whether older copies of this action, written on parchment, could be found in libraries and archives.

At the very least, he ought to have placed some trust in the eminent Baronius, who wrote:

> This same action is placed under the ninth action, on the same day—namely, the sixth day before the Kalends of the same month of November—in an ancient Latin Vatican manuscript said to have belonged to Proculus and Albinus.

Baronius made such use of this manuscript that, when he wished to refute the argument drawn from the constitution of the emperor Justinian addressed to John the supreme pontiff, in which we read:

> The holy Council of Chalcedon condemned Domnus, who had been made bishop of Antioch after death, and who dared to write that one ought only to remain silent concerning Cyril’s Twelve Chapters,

Baronius, wishing to remove this argument, adds that the Emperor Justinian was unaware of this action [Note: [Col. 1271D] Baronius, volume VI, year 451, p. 155].

Baronius’s statement gives considerable support to the conjectures we have advanced, namely, that the Eastern Acephali and Eutychians applied all the strength of their efforts to destroy the Greek action under discussion.

But divine providence, which has always watched over the government of the Church, willed that the action should at least be preserved in the oldest Latin copies.

The aforementioned Cardinal Casanata communicated to the distinguished Baluzius three manuscripts of exceptional importance from the Vatican Library alone, noting the various readings found in them through the careful work of highly skilled scholars.

> Among them, he says, there is one of the greatest antiquity, since in the judgment of experts it was written at least a thousand years ago.

So that Baluzius might not be deprived of the praise due to him, the same Cardinal Casanata committed the words of his letter to print:

> The oldest Vatican manuscript, no. 1322, presents the action concerning Domnus of Antioch. It is written in the large script of the second age and appears to have been copied at least a thousand years ago. Its beginning is damaged and mutilated, though it has been supplemented by a hand more than eight hundred years old. The various readings annotated in the margin were taken from two other manuscripts of the same Vatican Library, nos. 1321 and 1323.

No one can doubt that these manuscripts are not on paper but written on parchment.

Besides these three manuscripts, however, Casanata also affirms that other, more recent copies were found in the Vatican archives, writing:

> Two other Vatican manuscripts, numbers 5405 and 4166 [492], are very recent and contain nothing worthy of note.

Nor ought Quesnellus to have been unaware of the other manuscripts used by the earlier editors—namely, the Corbie and Dijon manuscripts. Although they do not agree with one another in the order of the actions, the action concerning Domnus is absent from neither of them. He therefore ought not to have relied solely upon the authority of a single paper manuscript bearing no mark of antiquity.

For in the Bohier manuscript this action is placed at the beginning of the seventh action, as we have said.

In Crabbe’s edition it is appended to the same seventh action, preceded by the following notice to the reader:

> This was found in the parchment manuscript of the Fathers of Julia, transcribed from an ancient paper manuscript, and is said to have belonged to Proculus and Albinus, German scholars.

Nevertheless, the difference in order provides no basis for rejecting it as spurious. For in his edition Crabbe appended the following words to the tenth action of that council:

> At Constantinople, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction, on Friday.

These words must be attributed to Rusticus, deacon of the Holy Roman Church; with the help of the Bohier manuscript, Crabbe vindicated them for the same translator. Since they had long caused readers considerable difficulty, Roman and other editors thought that they ought to be removed [Note: [Col. 1272D] Volume IV of the Councils, p. 1598].

### 6

Let us now inquire, following Baluzius, why in some manuscript copies we find the action concerning Domnus of Antioch placed immediately after the sixth action and at the beginning of the seventh, before the assembly of Juvenal of Jerusalem and Maximus, the successor of Domnus; while in others it is postponed and placed in the ninth action, or in the tenth, as it now stands in Labbe’s collection of the Councils.

The cause of such great differences must be attributed to the discretion and carelessness of the notaries.

But lest the learned man appear to be relying on conjecture, he wisely observed that when bishops traveled to synods, they were accustomed to take their notaries with them, who recorded the synodal proceedings in writing. When the synod had ended, each bishop would take the copy of the Acts back to his homeland.

He first proves this custom from the observations of Henri Valois on Evagrius.

We can confirm it even more strongly from the letters of Saint Leo the Great. When he was about to send legates to the Second Synod of Ephesus, he joined the notary Dulcitius, whose fidelity he had sufficiently tested, to his legates—namely, Julius, Renatus, and Hilary. He testified to this both in Letter 24 to Flavian and in Letter 29 to that same Synod of Ephesus.

Baluzius, however, omitted this observation and reported another drawn from the Council of Chalcedon itself, which he supported with learned notes.

He says:

> In the first action, when part of the proceedings of the Ephesian Robber Council had been read aloud and certain bishops cried out that they were false, Theodosius, bishop of Claudiopolis, said concerning Dioscorus: “Let him produce his notaries.” But after dismissing everyone else’s notaries, Dioscorus had his own write.

> When the judges and the senate asked by whose hand the records of the proceedings had been written, Dioscorus said: “Each person wrote through his own notaries: my notaries wrote my material; the most reverend bishop Juvenal’s wrote his; the most reverend bishop Thalassius’s wrote his. There were also many notaries of other most reverend bishops recording the proceedings. If this is not the handwriting of my notaries, it is because each person has his own.”

From this Baluzius concludes that, when the scribes produced the books of the records in written pages, each arranged them according to his own understanding and preference. Thus it happened that some placed the beginning of a case—for example, that of Ibas—in the sixth action, others in the seventh, others again in the ninth, and still others in the tenth, and likewise with the remaining actions.

### 7.

In explaining these matters, however, we have departed somewhat from the order followed by Quesnellus, who sought entirely and unsuccessfully to demonstrate that this Action of Domnus was spurious. For although he was well aware that it was found either in the Bohierian codex praised above or had been judged [493] to stand after the sixth action, as having been translated from Greek into Latin [Col. 1273C], he nevertheless preferred to accuse the deacon Rusticus of bad faith, as a schismatic struck with anathema by Vigilius, rather than to persuade himself that it was a genuine offspring of the Fathers of Chalcedon.

What? He falsely believed that the translation of this Action could be attributed to Rusticus, although Rusticus appended his name only to the first Action, in the following manner, according to the Bohierian manuscript codex:

> The first inquiry of the Council of Chalcedon ends here . . . . Having corrected and compared the manuscripts from the day before the thirteenth day before the Kalends [that is, Wednesday in December, indiction 13, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April; the transmitted dating is internally inconsistent], Rusticus, by the grace of God deacon of the Holy Roman Church, compared, annotated, [Col. 1273D] and punctuated it. Thanks be to God.

He further adds what is found in the edition of Petrus Crabbe, of the Order of Friars Minor, namely:

> End of the first inquiry of the Council of Chalcedon, which was completed and corrected in the year of our Lord 417 [in the margin corrected either to 454 or 457; Labbe says that the date is extremely corrupt throughout], on Wednesday, indiction 13, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. Rusticus, by the grace of God deacon of the Holy Roman Church, compared, annotated, and punctuated it. Thanks be to God.

> The same thing is found, finally, in the Roman edition, with a few variations.

“Therefore,” Quesnellus concludes, “nothing certain can be established from annotations of this kind,” since they do not agree among themselves; and consequently, he says, the mention in the Bohierian codex must not belong to one Rusticus but to several annotators. From this and that point he gathers various considerations, in order finally to persuade his readers that Rusticus reread the Council of Chalcedon against the Acaemetian codex, which earlier correctors themselves had already compared and corrected; and that he likewise added his own attestation, just as they had added theirs. Those men, he says, reviewed the remaining Actions, whereas Rusticus does not seem to have proceeded beyond the first.

He adds that the years indicated by the earlier annotation cannot belong to the age of Rusticus, and that the earlier annotation is rendered suspect by the following handwritten word. The word “before” [*ante*] was entirely superfluous [Col. 1274A] before God had bestowed upon mankind the art of printing books. He continues:

> And even if we grant that all the Actions of Chalcedon were reread and corrected by Rusticus, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, it is clear that the Action under discussion was not discovered by him.

### 8.

Quesnellus therefore exaggerated these and similar conjectures in the fifth and sixth sections of his dissertation, with the zeal customary to him, but entirely without success. For, as Stephanus Baluzius himself observed, Paschasius Quesnellus not only failed to ascertain the date of the edition made by Rusticus, but, suffering elsewhere from the vice of inconsistency, denied what he ought to have affirmed both in his notes on Letter 24 of Saint Leo and in his discussion of the case of Theodoret.

As for the date of the edition, Baluzius notes that Rusticus came to Constantinople in the year of our Lord 547 with his uncle, the Roman pontiff. Later, at the beginning of 549, he deserted him and in the following year was deprived of the rank and office he held. Before [Col. 1274B] his deposition, however, he undertook the correction of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon on the tenth day before the Kalends of March in the year 519, and completed it the following year, on the third day before the Kalends of April, having devoted a full year and somewhat more to this work.

It is uncertain, however, whether he did this at Constantinople or at Chalcedon. The reasons that lead me to favor Chalcedon are the extremely corrupt notes appended to the end of the first Action, from which I seem to have detected the ancient and true reading, as I explain there. Yet, Baluzius adds, this conjecture appears to be opposed by the mention of the Acaemetian codex, which everyone knows was located at Constantinople.

This, however, must be explained by saying that Rusticus is not speaking of the Constantinopolitan Acaemetes, but of those who were under the bishop of Chalcedon. Their archimandrite John subscribed the petition of the monks submitted to Menas, the patriarch, and to the entire synod, in the fifth session of the Council of Constantinople under Menas. So that no one could [Col. 1274C] doubt the truth of this, we gladly resolved to consult the passage cited by Baluzius [494], and we encountered the name of the archimandrite John written as follows, which we add in the note placed at the foot of the page:

> [Note: [Col. 1273D] In Volume V of the Councils, p. 1103, one reads: “John, by the mercy of God priest and venerable archimandrite of the great monastery of the Acaemetes, under Photinus, most holy bishop of Chalcedon, have subscribed.” [Col. 1274D]]

### 9.

The remaining difficulty, then, is whether the deacon Rusticus corrected the other Chalcedonian Actions in addition to that first one. Quesnellus’s arguments are that nowhere in the Acts is there any mention of a correction made by Rusticus except in the first Action. Later he adds that he does not wish these points to be accepted as certain.

“Quite rightly,” writes Baluzius. For he himself, above—namely, in his discussion of Letter 24 of Saint Leo, which was written to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, and which was reread in the second Action of the Council of Chalcedon—seems to acknowledge that this Action too was corrected by the deacon Rusticus. In his dissertation on the case of Theodoret, he likewise acknowledges that Rusticus carefully checked the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon against the codices of the Acaemetian monastery.

I add that the words placed at the foot of the fifth Action [Col. 1274D] in the codices of Rusticus—“the same man compared it”—must necessarily refer to the person who compared the preceding Actions with the ancient codices, namely Rusticus, whose name alone is mentioned in the codices corrected in antiquity.

For the conjecture of that most distinguished man—that the Acaemetian codex which Rusticus had begun to examine was first corrected in the East by men older than Rusticus, who had added their own attestations to it, and was later brought to the West and copied by several people, so that the corrections placed in the margins belonged not to one Rusticus but to several different annotators—is, if I may say so with due respect, mere conjecture unsupported by reason.

For in the remaining Actions we expressly encounter notes indicating that there was one and the same annotator and translator. Nor is it an obstacle that the Action under discussion [Col. 1275A] is lacking in Greek. Many writings of the ancient Greeks now survive only in Latin, and are not for that reason considered less authentic, as is clear from the numerous examples brought forward by the same most distinguished Stephanus Baluzius. He collected them from the Acts of the Council of Ephesus and from the Council of Chalcedon itself, in which the Action concerning Domnus was also held.

Finally, Rusticus testifies that this Action was translated from Greek, and it is at least obscurely indicated that a Greek copy still existed in his own age. Baluzius also gently reproaches Quesnellus, as though for carelessness, for having misunderstood the annotation of Rusticus, who wrote:

> Action concerning Domnus of Antioch, which I found transcribed in a new parchment codex of Patricia Julia from an ancient paper codex, which she herself said had belonged to Proculus and Albinus, scholastic brothers.

Everyone therefore understands that this Action was not transcribed from a new codex but from one that was already ancient in the age of Rusticus, and that had belonged to Proculus and Albinus, most eloquent brothers. That it did not derive from a single paper codex [Col. 1275B] is proved by the copies used by Crabbe, Baronius, and Hieronymus Casanata; the codices of Corbie and Dijon also indicate this.

Since, then, the antiquity and agreement of the codices bear witness to it, it is scarcely possible to understand why Quesnellus tried so strenuously to diminish and entirely destroy the authority of this Action. He further maintains that the same Action was not known even to Facundus of Hermiana in Africa, a bishop who composed his work in defense of the Three Chapters.

Indeed, when Facundus speaks of Domnus, he numbers him among the holy Fathers and venerable teachers of the Church, together with John Chrysostom and Gregory of Nazianzus, as may be seen in Book II, chapter 1.

What displeases Baluzius even more is that Quesnellus called the good faith of Rusticus into suspicion of falsification. The whole Church, after all, owes Rusticus a very great debt [Col. 1275C] for the excellent work he devoted to the Latin translation of the Acts of Chalcedon.

It is unjust to suspect that Rusticus fabricated this Action in order to show that Domnus had not been condemned after his death. For some people in the age of Rusticus had been falsely persuaded of this, as Baluzius explained when he immediately began refuting Quesnellus’s other arguments [495].

One of these arguments is the one that we also cited above from Baronius, concerning the emperor Justinian and the bishops of the Fifth Council. Baluzius asserts, however, that this argument totters and collapses entirely in view of the historical errors found throughout the Constitutions of the emperor Justinian and of the other manifestly untrue matters inserted into the Acts of the Fifth Council.

Although none of this ought to have escaped Quesnellus himself, Baluzius did not wish to waste time proving it, especially since nothing concerning the death or condemnation of Domnus appears in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Anyone wishing to rely upon the testimonies of Justinian and the Fifth Council would have had to investigate that matter carefully.

### 10.

Quesnellus now argues that Domnus had departed this life [Col. 1275D] by the time the Council of Chalcedon was held, relying upon the testimony of the deacon Liberatus and upon other statements of the ancients, although he interprets them forcibly.

First, the deacon Liberatus relates how Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, in the Ephesian Robber Council deposed the orthodox bishops Ibas of Edessa, Theodoret of Cyrus, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, Flavian of Constantinople, and others, with the consent of Domnus of Antioch, whose authority Dioscorus was abusing. After all the others, he continues:

> And Domnus of Antioch, who remained from the deposition of the orthodox, because he had become a participant with Dioscorus in the deposition of the orthodox and in the absolution of Eutyches. He was deposed by the deceit of Dioscorus in this way. After he had agreed with Dioscorus in everything, when his letters were brought forward—the letters that Domnus of Antioch had written to Dioscorus against the twelve chapters of Cyril—he condemned the sick man, who was absent on that day.

> [Note: [Col. 1275D] Liberatus, chapter 12 of the *Breviary*.]

Nicephorus, however, reported another reason for the deposition of Domnus [Col. 1276A], writing:

> Together with these, Domnus, the successor of John in Antioch, confirmed these things by his own annotation. But when he had been restored to his authority, he retracted what he had conceded to them, resisting Dioscorus and the prominent men from the imperial court, and crying out against the decrees, since they had been made contrary to the ecclesiastical sanctions; he called the synod impious and finally demanded that his subscription be returned to him. For this reason the synod also deprived this priest of his dignity.

> [Note: [Col. 1275D] Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 47.]

Quesnellus adds:

> These two authors can easily be reconciled if you say that Nicephorus gave the true reason why Dioscorus considered deposing Domnus. But the text of Liberatus has been corrupted through the carelessness and confusion of scribes or printers, and the words contain a tautology. They should therefore be corrected according to Augustine’s meaning, so that instead of *remaining* [*remanentem*] from the deposition of the orthodox, we should read *recoiling* [*resilientem*], or rather *returning* [*remeantem*].

He therefore cites a similar passage from Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book II [Col. 1276B]:

> Whom we desire to return to the peace and unity of the holy Church;

and another from Letter 172 to Crispinus:

> Unless they had returned to your communion.

Baluzius, however, does not approve this paraphrase by Quesnellus. Instead, he explains the much-disputed passage with all his strength, judging that the true and genuine meaning of Liberatus’s words is as follows: Dioscorus, in the Ephesian Robber Council, deposed the orthodox bishops; but he did not depose Domnus, although Domnus himself was orthodox, because Domnus had already agreed with Dioscorus in the deposition of the orthodox and in the absolution of Eutyches.

But he later condemned Domnus, who remained without condemnation, after all the others had been condemned, because Domnus had written a letter to Dioscorus against Cyril’s twelve chapters. Thus he was not deposed by the synod, because he publicly regretted having given his consent against the orthodox.

### 11.

Nor does the aforementioned Baluzius approve another conjecture of Quesnellus, which Quesnellus claims may be inferred from the testimony of Liberatus: namely, that Domnus was condemned while sick and absent, and therefore did not long survive his deposition or live until the Council of Chalcedon.

Baluzius adds [496]:

> This conjecture could have been supported by the testimony of Eutychius, who writes in his *Annals* that Domnus died in the year following that Ephesian synod. But he refrained from doing so, as I think, because that author is full of historical and chronological errors and can provide nothing certain concerning the life and death of Domnus.

But Baluzius opposes Liberatus to Liberatus himself. Shortly afterward, Liberatus described the death of Flavian and related how Anatolius had been ordained in his place. In the same manner he says that Maximus was ordained in the place of Domnus, but he does not add that Domnus was dead.

Indeed, what follows demonstrates that Liberatus spoke as though Domnus were alive. After recounting the death of Flavian and the ordination of Anatolius, he goes on to mention the ordination of Maximus in the place of Domnus, of Nonnus in the place of Ibas, and of Athanasius in the place of Sabinianus, without mentioning the death of any of them.

Just as, therefore, Ibas and Sabinianus had not died before the Council of Chalcedon, since they took part in that synod, so it should not be inferred that Domnus had died before this council because he was sick at the time of the Ephesian Council.

An equally negative argument, drawn from the silence of Liberatus—who, while reviewing the individual Actions of the Council of Chalcedon, makes no mention of the case of Domnus [Col. 1276C], although he would undoubtedly have done so if the events related in this Action had truly occurred—is easily refuted. So too is another conjecture drawn from the words of Evagrius Scholasticus, who, writing that Domnus had been deposed at the Ephesian synod, says that he could not discover what later happened to him, and, when reviewing the Acts of Chalcedon, is completely silent about Domnus.

> [Note: [Col. 1276D] Evagrius Scholasticus, Book X, chapter 10.]

But what do the silence of both writers—or Evagrius’s ignorance itself—prove in favor of Quesnellus’s system? Both writers used codices in which the Action concerning Domnus was absent. As Baluzius says, it is still absent from the codex that we call the Parisian codex [Col. 1277A].

Yet it is not for that reason false. For just as, if the art of printing had not yet been invented and someone using that codex omitted this Action, his omission would seem to prejudice nothing against the authority of the codices in which the Action is found, so the silence of the deacons Liberatus and Evagrius cannot prejudice the codices that are known to have contained the said Action in their age.

### 12.

Baluzius entirely resolves and explains this and similar arguments with the utmost erudition of which he was capable, clearly demonstrating the origin of such great diversity among the Greek codices. We consider it necessary to reproduce his words, so that we may completely remove every suspicion of fabrication.

The learned man observes, then, that the Council of Chalcedon in fact ends with the sixth Action, so that the canons are included in it as well [Col. 1277B]. Although the Actions that follow were conducted at the council, they did not concern the matter of faith but private affairs. For that reason many bishops, after the decree of faith had been written, set out on their journey and returned to their own sees.

He gathers this from the *Life of Saint Euthymius the Abbot* and from the letter of Pelagius to the bishops of Istria. In the *Life of Euthymius* one reads that Stephen, bishop of Famnia, and John, bishop of the Saracens, who were present at the Council of Chalcedon, brought the decree of faith to Euthymius after it had been issued, departing very quickly because they thought that the synod had already been completed. Hence their names appear nowhere in the Actions that follow the sixth.

Pope Pelagius teaches this even more clearly:

> The fact that most of the older Greek codices contain the synod only in six Actions, with the canons appended, demonstrates that they altogether lack the remaining matters that had been undertaken for private purposes.

And shortly above [Col. 1277C]:

> Therefore, with vigilant care, observe that in the sixth Action of that council the profession of the holy faith is completed; immediately afterward, in the seventh, the rule of the canons is established for the instruction of those who are already believers; but in the subsequent Actions nothing concerning the matter of faith is treated, only private affairs.

If any credence may be given to the deacon Paul, Saint Gregory writes something consistent with this to his predecessor—or rather to himself—in a letter to Secundinus:

> The holy Council of Chalcedon dealt with general matters up to the definition of the faith and the promulgation of the canons. For after the promulgation of the canons, it sought to settle the particular disputes of the bishops.

What wonder, then, if most Greek codices, and especially the older ones, once did not contain the Actions that follow the sixth? Later, therefore, when they added them and inserted them into the Acts, they did so in various ways, without preserving the order of events at all: each person inserted or omitted one Action or another according to the inclination that guided him.

Baluzius concludes:

> The ancient collector omitted the Action concerning Domnus, but an ancient exemplar contained it, from which the codex of Julia Patricia was copied.

### 13.

Moreover, in order to strike his opponent Quesnellus more forcefully, Baluzius adduces the example of a Chalcedonian Action [Col. 1277D] in which the case between Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius of Berytus was heard and decided. The ancient collations of the Council of Chalcedon did not contain this Action.

It emerged, however, from a Greek Vatican codex through the efforts of Cardinal Baronius, who found it placed at the end of the fourth Action. Balsamon, in his scholia on canon 29 of Chalcedon, nevertheless testifies that it was placed at the end of the Acts in the codex he used.

We discussed this matter more fully in the dissertation of the Pontifical Academy of Councils in the year 1746, which we have already reproduced in the preceding chapter. Therefore, leaving it aside for the present, we turn our discussion to the silence of Evagrius, who was a citizen and advocate of Antioch, as the distinguished Henricus Valesius explicitly proves.

It certainly seems difficult to suppose that Evagrius was ignorant [Col. 1278A] of what had happened to Domnus, if Domnus really survived his deposition and if an allowance had been assigned to him at the Council of Chalcedon from the resources of the Church of Antioch for the support of his life.

Baluzius admits that this creates a serious difficulty, but he asserts that it in no way supports Quesnellus’s opinion. For the words of Evagrius seem to be confirmed by the author who wrote the *Life of Euthymius*. That author says that Euthymius had foretold Domnus’s unhappy life in the episcopate and that he would later undergo deposition through the efforts and devices of evil men and impostors. Domnus, moved to repentance because he had not obeyed the abbot’s salutary counsels, returned to the same Euthymius in Palestine.

“From this,” says Baluzius, “it happened that the man who spent his life far from Antioch and in obscurity fell into oblivion among the Antiochenes.” Thus it is true that after his deposition Domnus withdrew into the desert; and Theophanes the chronicler, as well as Anastasius the Librarian, who received the account from him, committed this to literary memory, although they give a different reason for his withdrawal from that supplied by the author of the *Life of Saint Euthymius*.

### 14.

If someone should contend that greater credence ought to be given to Evagrius, who wrote his history toward the end of the sixth century, than to Theophanes and Anastasius, who lived much later than the time at which these events are said to have occurred, I would not object.

But Quesnellus ought to have considered the words of Evagrius, which cannot indicate that Domnus, condemned by Dioscorus while absent and sick, did not long survive, but rather that he died. For how could his death have remained hidden if his illness had not remained hidden?

It must therefore be said that Domnus fully recovered from that illness. But, worn down by the weariness of his troubles and supported by shame—for he had obeyed the impious devices and commands of Dioscorus—he wished to withdraw from the company of men. He therefore withdrew far from the Antiochene patriarchate into a secluded desert of Palestine, in order to complete the remainder of his life.

Baluzius also rightly observed that the testimony of Evagrius does not conflict with the writings of Theophanes [Col. 1278C] and Anastasius, although they wrote differently. The words of Theophanes and Anastasius show that Domnus wished to remain so concealed that, unless Cyril of Scythopolis—who was an inhabitant of the same desert inhabited by Domnus—had revealed that secret, even now, together with Evagrius, we would undoubtedly be ignorant of what had happened to him.

### 15.

[498] The arguments that Quesnellus adduces to confirm his opinion concerning the death of Domnus are less substantial. He argues that Domnus’s condition was worse than that of Juvenal of Jerusalem and the others to whom the synod granted indulgence in its fourth Action, and whose names Anatolius mentioned in writing to Saint Leo for recitation at the altar.

But where is it established that Domnus sought indulgence after displaying genuine signs of repentance?

Saint Leo ordered that some of those who had fallen in Dioscorus’s Ephesian synod be received, but under the conditions that he himself prescribed in Letter 64, discussed above. He sent two embassies to the Easterners: one consisting of Abundius and his companions, and the other of Lucentius and Basilius, for the reception of certain fallen persons who had repented and made the required [Col. 1278D] satisfaction.

He nevertheless reserved judgment concerning the more serious cases, as is clear from the memorandum given to Lucentius and Basilius, the final legates sent from Rome to Constantinople for the reception of the repentant fallen.

But who does not understand that Domnus belonged among those whose case appeared more serious? Therefore, the judgment and examination of this case had been reserved exclusively to the great Leo. The distinguished Baluzius entirely failed to observe this, and the case of Domnus was not among those about which either the papal legates, Anatolius, or anyone else could pass judgment.

> [Note: [Col. 1277] See what we said concerning Leo’s actions before the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 15.]

Another argument brought forward by Baluzius nevertheless remains valid: after his deposition, Domnus withdrew to Palestine to Abbot Euthymius and ceased to be counted among the bishops. Consequently, no question could arise concerning the inclusion of his name with the other names of the bishops in the recitation at the altar [Col. 1279A].

Quesnellus is also strongly pressed by another argument that Baluzius adds. He says that if Domnus must be considered dead because Anatolius makes no mention of him in his letters to Saint Leo the Great, then Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea, Eusebius of Ancyra, and Basilius of Seleucia must also have been dead.

For when Leo replied to Anatolius, he made no explicit mention of those men who had shared in the Ephesian Robber Council with Dioscorus, Juvenal, and also Bishop Eustathius.

### 16.

Nor should many other arguments be considered more compelling. Quesnellus gathered them with excessive industry, ranging here and there in defense of his case, in order to show that the Action under discussion was spurious.

If we weigh them carefully, as the aforementioned Baluzius has already done, we shall understand that they contain nothing but words, deceptive arguments, and violent interpretations.

An argument of this kind is the one that Quesnellus thought he could borrow from the letter of Gelasius to the bishops of Dardania [Col. 1279B]. In that letter the pontiff, adducing numerous examples of judgments in order to explain the authority of his see, lists bishops condemned by a synod whom the Apostolic See absolved. He says that he granted pardon to those who had fallen in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, while annulling that synod, but makes no mention of Domnus of Antioch.

Therefore, Quesnellus concludes, Domnus had died before the ordination of Maximus, his successor.

But what should be said about Ibas of Edessa and Sabinianus of Perrha, in whose places Nonnus and Athanasius had been ordained? They too had fallen in the Ephesian Robber Council, yet Gelasius makes no mention of them in his letter.

Were they therefore also dead before the Council of Chalcedon? Both ancient histories and the Acts of Chalcedon plainly show that this inference is entirely false.

Nor does another conjecture carry greater weight. Quesnellus draws it from Leo’s course of action. After annulling the Acts of the Ephesian Robber Council, Leo did not think of excepting the deposition of Domnus; instead, he asked the emperor Theodosius to order that everything remain in the condition in which it had been before any judgment.

Quesnellus therefore persuades himself that the sentence pronounced against Domnus could have had no effect if Domnus had been alive.

This is a new fallacy. The deposition of Domnus would indeed have had no effect if he had consented to the deposition of the orthodox and the absolution of Eutyches out of fear of punishment, or through ignorance and deception. But because he had played the leading role in that Ephesian synod together with Dioscorus and was regarded as the leader of the Eutychian faction, his case was, as we have said, among the more serious.

Therefore, as a punishment for his former wickedness, while he was still alive Saint Leo rightly confirmed both the ordination of Maximus and Domnus’s own deposition. Indeed, we believe that the Fathers of Chalcedon were so horrified by Domnus’s earlier conduct—by which he had surrendered himself, defeated, into the hands and will of Dioscorus—that they too pronounced a sentence of deposition against him, just as they had done against Dioscorus.

We gather this from the words of Maximus, by which he entreated the judges and the universal synod. Maximus, the most reverend bishop of Antioch, said:

> I beseech your most magnificent and glorious Excellencies, and this holy and universal synod, to deign to exercise humanity toward Domnus, who was bishop of Antioch, and to assign him a fixed allowance from the Church that is under me.

Anyone who is not deceived by carelessness and does not wish to interpret Maximus’s words violently will now fully understand that Domnus had incurred such canonical prejudices that Leo the Great and the Council of Chalcedon should by no means have annulled his deposition. Because of that deposition, he had been entirely deprived both of the episcopate and of its revenues.

Accordingly, Maximus, Domnus’s successor, wishing in part to show mercy to him, earnestly appealed to the council to deal with him more mildly and humanely and to permit him to receive a portion of the ecclesiastical revenues for as long as he remained alive.

The council therefore assented to Maximus’s request, and the legates—or vicars—of the Apostolic See, through Paschasinus, inserted the following decree:

> The holy and most blessed pope, who confirmed the episcopate of the holy and venerable Maximus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, appears by a sufficiently just judgment to have approved his merit. [lacuna] Maximus, at his own discretion, wished provision to be made for Domnus, let him grant him an allowance from his own Church, out of consideration for mercy, in whatever amount he judges appropriate, so that Domnus may remain content with his maintenance in the future.

Maximus was therefore moved solely by mercy to grant Domnus this portion of the ecclesiastical revenues while Domnus was still alive, although Domnus could in no way by right be restored to his episcopal see.

Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, likewise praised this indulgence and mercy of Maximus, saying:

> I too praise the compassion [elsewhere: sympathy] of the most blessed Maximus, bishop of Antioch, who of his own free will offered such prayers that he might provide an allowance to Domnus, who had been bishop of the holy Church that is under him, without this aforesaid man requesting anything beyond this.

[Source ends here.]

17. As for the fact that St. Leo the Great ought not to have annulled this deposition, besides what we have brought forward above and sufficiently explained in expounding the holy pontiff’s Epistle 64, Quesnellus and Baluzius could still have understood it from the letter he wrote to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem—especially since, under no. 45, he affirmed that the matter was difficult to investigate. Juvenal had indeed consented with Dioscorus in the Ephesian Robber Council, but he was neither deposed nor did he persist in his obstinacy. Nevertheless, he would subsequently have been deposed by St. Leo and by the Council of Chalcedon, because he had created grounds for his own deposition: grounds by which he had made himself not merely hateful to all the orthodox, but also thereafter unworthy of the episcopate. For these reasons he had to remain for some time far from his see, until, by the proper satisfaction of penance, he chose repentance during the time of clemency.

In the fourth session of Chalcedon, the case of the bishops who had presided with Dioscorus over the Ephesian Robber Council was brought forward, and inquiry was made whether they ought to undergo the same censure of condemnation as Dioscorus and be deprived of their churches. All the judges and bishops were in suspense. Since the question seemed sufficiently difficult to them, they asked that a postponement of five days be granted, so that they might deliver a more mature judgment, in accordance with the rules of the Nicene canons. Meanwhile, Juvenal, Thalassius, Eusebius of Cappadocia, Eustathius of Berytus, and Basil of Seleucia were denied a place in the council; they had to wait as persons doing penance. “Let the hearing,” we read, “be deferred for five days, so that in the meantime your holiness may assemble with the most holy archbishop Anatolius and deliberate together about the faith.”

Again, in the same session, after all had cried out that Dioscorus had rightly been deposed and condemned by Christ, a short time having passed, the imperial judges, awaiting the emperor’s command, said: “The most pious emperor, learning of your requests, has permitted you to deliberate concerning Juvenal, Thalassius, Eusebius, Basil, and Eustathius, the most reverend bishops, as you have desired.” Anatolius said: “We ask that they enter”; and the other bishops shouted: “We ask that they enter.” [Note: Tom. IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, p. 1359; Baronius, vol. VI of the Annals, p. 146, in the same section.]

They obtained a place in the council in no other way than after their faith had first been examined. They had approved the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds, accepted the decrees of the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, subscribed, together with the other bishops, the letter of St. Leo to Flavian, and condemned those who held contrary opinions. Domnus was certainly not among them: partly because he had withdrawn into the desert of Palestine, and partly because he had not given signs of repentance at the appropriate time—namely, when St. Leo was not unwilling, through the clemency of the apostolic see, to grant indulgence to those who had fallen.

St. Leo’s letter to Juvenal agrees entirely with this. Rebuking him for his former excesses, he says:

“I grieved that you yourself had become the cause of your own adversities and had lost the steadfastness with which you resisted heretics, because they think that you are not free to rebuke those whom you have professed to have pleased you in their error.”

He then assigns the reason why, after such a grave fall, Juvenal was permitted to return to the see of his episcopate, adding:

“Therefore, since during the time of indulgence you chose repentance rather than obstinacy, I rejoice that you sought heavenly medicine, so that at last you may be a defender of the faith attacked by heretics.” [Note: Epistle, from chapter 1.]

Who does not see, meanwhile, how seriously Quesnellus was mistaken when he maintained that, by the decree which annulled the acts of the Ephesian Robber Council, Leo had granted indulgence to all who had fallen, and had not thought of excepting Domnus’s deposition? What? Perhaps, by rescinding the acts of the Robber Council, he intended indulgence to be granted to the leaders of that synod even if they had not repented, even if they had not humbly asked that pardon be granted them, after fulfilling all the conditions that the holy pontiff prescribed for Anatolius, Juvenal, Thalassius, and the others who had communicated with Dioscorus and Eutyches and had conspired against Flavian, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, and the other orthodox?

It was therefore unnecessary for him to except Domnus’s deposition when the acts of the Robber Council were annulled, since Domnus and the other leaders of the Eutychian faction had no further right to persist in the episcopate. They could have retained it thereafter only through St. Leo’s indulgence, had they done penance. Here especially, I think, Quesnellus’s deception must be noted. Discussing the acts of the Robber Council and the letter written by St. Leo to the emperor Theodosius Augustus, in which he asked him to order that everything be restored to the condition in which it had been before that unfortunate synod, Quesnellus flatters himself with the belief that the holy pontiff thought indulgence should be shown to those who had fallen in such a way that the guilt of those who, by right and wrong alike and to the destruction of the faith, had filled all the Churches of the East with scandals, killings, enmities, and hatred would remain wholly unpunished.

Leo did not possess such an attitude at all, as his subsequent words demonstrate. For he reserves to himself the full judgment of all these matters and of their authors until the greater part of the priests from the whole world could assemble—so that, when the bishops had gathered for a synod in Italy, the faith and crimes of those who had fallen might be solemnly judged according to the rigor of the canons. Therefore it could not have been lawful for the bishops who had fallen after the Ephesian Robber Council, the authors of schisms and bound by ecclesiastical censures, to retain their sees; nor were the canonical penalties they had incurred relaxed for them by Leo through the abolition of the acts of the Robber Council. Perhaps Domnus, carefully considering this, preferred, driven by shame and embarrassment, to spend the private life of a penitent far from the crowds of men and of his fellow citizens rather than appear in public assemblies and synods, where he would have had to furnish the due proofs of his faith, penance, and satisfaction.
