18. The arguments that Quesnellus brings from the imperial constitution of Theodosius to prove Domnus’s death are plainly judged childish. In that constitution the acts of the pseudo-synod are confirmed, and Domnus is described as “the man who was bishop of Antioch.” He adds that, in the fourteenth session of Chalcedon, Athanasius, bishop of Perrha and ordained in place of Sabinianus, is said to have stated—giving the reason why he had avoided Domnus’s judgment—“He himself, who judged, was my enemy, the bishop of Antioch.” [Note: Tom. IV of the Councils, session 14 of Chalcedon, p. 1679.] From this he argues that Domnus must already have been dead.

First, if the argument stood, it would already prove that Domnus had died scarcely after that Robber Council had ended, since the constitution of Theodosius was issued and promulgated immediately, at the instigation of Chrysaphius and Dioscorus. Consequently, his death could have been hidden from no one, and Evagrius could not truthfully have written that he was completely ignorant of what had happened to Domnus. Nor does Athanasius of Perrha speak there of Domnus as dead, but of the man who at that time was conducting the council of Antioch. Therefore, says Baluzius, these are indeed expressions of the past tense, but of the imperfect past, as grammarians call it; and it is embarrassing to spend more time explaining them.

In truth, however, Quesnellus eventually learned both that Domnus was not dead when the Council of Chalcedon was being held and that St. Leo had annulled all the acts of the Robber Council except Domnus’s deposition and Maximus’s ordination. While examining the tenth session of Chalcedon, he encountered the statement of Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, who maintained that everything done against the canons by the predatory synod had been abolished, except what had been done against Domnus, because:

“the ordination of Maximus, the God-loving bishop, performed in his place canonically in the metropolitan Church of Antioch by the most holy archbishop Leo, and accepted in the presence of this holy and universal council, had been received.”

Understanding the weight of these words, Quesnellus perceived that the edifice he had falsely constructed might collapse entirely. Seeking supports here and there, he consoled himself with the thought that it ought not immediately to fall, writing that the statement should not be valued highly because it was unique and came from a man whom, in the following session, we read to have been deposed for crimes by which he had secured his advancement to the see of Ephesus. Thus, he said, it was plausible that Stephen had wished, out of hatred for Domnus, to have his condemnation ratified.

But how does Quesnellus think that such an escape can help him? I will grant that those guilty of very serious crimes are not admitted as witnesses. Yet the crimes charged against Stephen had not then been proved; since his case had not yet been heard, he had not been convicted of the alleged crimes. What, then, can they prove? Nothing. Otherwise the Fathers of Chalcedon would have admitted among the bishops and judges of the principal sees a man whom the canons declared wholly deposed.

Indeed, the following events show that Stephen of Ephesus performed the true role of a judge at the Council of Chalcedon. In the third session he condemned Dioscorus with the other bishops. In the fourth he praised and accepted Leo’s letter to Flavian. In the sixth he subscribed, before the emperor, to the definition of the faith. In the seventh he confirmed the agreement between Juvenal and Maximus. From where, then, does Quesnellus conclude that Stephen was moved by hatred to confirm Domnus’s deposition, except by mere conjecture?

It would rather be reasonable to suppose that Stephen ought to have favored Domnus, whom Dioscorus had deposed by deceit. Hence the most distinguished Baluzius, reflecting on Stephen of Ephesus’s conduct, judged that he had not spoken as he did from hatred or ill will, but because he knew that Domnus, having been deposed, had returned to a monastery in order to devote himself to quiet and solitude and had perhaps submitted, as was customary in those times, a written defense, so that Maximus’s canonical ordination might take effect.

[Col. 1282D] 19. But with this celebrated support, Quesnellus’s entire edifice still collapses. For Stephen’s testimony is neither unique, nor did any of the Fathers oppose it. In particular, when, in the tenth session, the question was raised whether all the acts of the Robber Council ought to be reread, so that nothing might be lacking—“for those who must judge justly,” as the deacon Theophilus said—all the representatives of the apostolic see immediately declared through Paschasinus:

“That cannot be called a synod in which those wicked crimes were reread.”

A little later he insists that those acts had been declared vain and invalid by St. Leo, adding that it was therefore clear “that the most holy bishop of the city of Antioch is outside these matters”—Rusticus added the following note: “Concerning Maximus, ordained at Ephesus”—“whom afterward the most blessed bishop received into his own communion.” To these final words Rusticus added the following annotation: “The acts that followed confirm what Leo confirmed.”

If Quesnellus had paid attention to this—he who boasts that he labored over the examination of both manuscript and printed copies in preparing the Works of the divine Leo—I do not know whether he would have freely pronounced Stephen’s testimony to be unique, with none of those Fathers supporting it.

But let him also attend to what Anatolius pronounced after the papal representatives. After the synod’s definition, he said, none of the things done at the Ephesian synod had any force, except what concerned “the most holy bishop of the great city of Antioch,” because “the most holy Leo, archbishop of Rome, having received him into communion, judged him worthy to preside over the Church of the Antiochenes.” [Note: Session 10 of the Council of Chalcedon, vol. IV of the General Councils, pp. 1583 ff.]

Finally, is it not clear from those acts that these three statements were supported by all the other Fathers, with absolutely no one dissenting? Let readers go through them, and they will clearly understand that Maximus’s ordination and Domnus’s deposition were judged ratified for no other reason than that Pope Leo had confirmed them.

[Col. 1283B] 20. Quesnellus sensed that he was seriously pressed by those three testimonies, which he did not overlook. [Note: Quesnellus, in the dissertation cited above, vol. II, p. 219, no. 29 ff.] Therefore, believing that he had sufficiently weakened Stephen’s statement by his own arguments, he turned his pen against the other two statements of Paschasinus and Anatolius, which we have already brought forward. The same Stephen Baluzius, thoroughly aware of his serious contention, says under no. 52:

“It remains for us now to reconsider Paschasinus’s statement, which we described a little earlier, both to defend the truth of the proceedings and to show that what the highly learned and excellent man Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, said is true. He treated the case of Maximus of Antioch in Book III of *On Concord*, in order by this example also to teach that the authority of the Roman see, in moderating the execution of the canons and granting dispensations, extended to the Churches of the East as well. Maximus had been ordained by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in place of Domnus, who had been condemned by Dioscorus. This ordination had two grave defects: first, that Domnus had been condemned by an impious synod; second, that the ordination had been carried out by Anatolius contrary to the canons.”

“What,” Leo wrote to the emperor Marcian, “we have not ceased to reconsider out of love for restoring the faith and from zeal for peace.” Leo could therefore, as de Marca says, have reconsidered Maximus’s ordination, had he not treated him kindly. This is also confirmed by the fact that Maximus was received by the Council of Chalcedon for the sole reason that the most holy Father Leo had approved his ordination and communion.

To demonstrate that this is true, Baluzius transcribes the words of Paschasinus cited above and notes that the following words—“whom afterward the most blessed bishop received into his own communion”—are absent from the Greek text, but that they were nevertheless retained by the ancient translator in accordance with the testimony of the ancient codices.

Quesnellus, who does not wish these words to have been spoken by Paschasinus, twists himself in extraordinary ways in order to establish a satisfactory meaning for that passage without them, adding certain things on his own authority, removing some, and changing others. To confirm his opinion, he says that there is no need for the words of the legates of the apostolic see to be strengthened by Anatolius’s statement, which de Marca had therefore immediately cited, since those words are sufficient in themselves to be understood:

“Whether their judgment,” he says, “differs from Anatolius’s support or agrees with it, it nevertheless does not prove that the legates said what they are alleged to have said, since all the copies of the original Acts indicate that it was not said.”

Thus this distinguished man makes two claims: first, that the meaning is complete without Paschasinus’s words; second, that those words are absent from all copies of the original Acts.

As to the first, I appeal to the judgment of the public: is it not manifest that the meaning is incomplete without those words? For after Paschasinus had said that Leo the Father had annulled the Ephesian synod, he added that it was clear that Maximus’s ordination was not included in those general words because Leo had received him into his communion. Unless Paschasinus had supplied this reason, the sense would not have been complete, and the bishops would afterward have expected him to say something further. Moreover, the following words have no connection with the matter unless the words ‘for it is necessary’ are added; these too are plainly absent from the Greek text.

But are they absent from all the Greek copies, which the same distinguished man calls “original”? First, one must ask whether Greek copies can truly be called original when the Roman pontiff’s legates were speaking Latin. Certainly, Rusticus is not found to have noted in this passage that this statement of the pope’s legates was written in Latin in the ancient codices. Yet since elsewhere he himself says that they spoke Latin and that their statements were written in Latin in the ancient Greek copies, and since the compiler of the proceedings does not say here that they spoke through an interpreter, it is reasonable to judge that Paschasinus spoke Latin. Accordingly, if an error was committed here, it does not seem attributable to the Latin interpreter but to the Greek interpreter—or rather to the copyist, who through error omitted what is absent from the Greek text. For we have already demonstrated above that the ancient Greek codices of the Council of Chalcedon are not sound; there too we noted that the most distinguished Cardinal Baronius believed that they ought to be corrected on the basis of the Latin witnesses. This is how Baluzius reasoned.

21. Quesnellus also brings forward certain indications of falsity in the session under discussion, arguing that it was not the custom of that age for the Roman pontiff to be designated by the single word *papa*, without any addition; nor does any passage occur in the Acts of Chalcedon in which that word is not accompanied by a reference either to the city of Rome, the apostolic see, or something similar.

The aforementioned Baluzius removed the force of this argument with a twofold response. First, he says, it was not necessary that, in Domnus’s age, the word *papa* should be used alone when the Roman bishop was meant; it is sufficient that such a usage had become customary in the interpreter’s time. In one statement by Boniface, a Roman presbyter, which appears after the bishops’ subscriptions in the sixteenth session, the Greek word *ἐπίσκοπος* corresponds to the word *papa*. Second, the solitary word *papa* is found in Domnus’s age used of the Roman pontiff—indeed, in the very proceedings of Chalcedon, in Hilary’s letter to the empress Pulcheria, and in the brief history of the Eutychianists.

“I shall begin,” says Baluzius, “with the proceedings of the council. In session 1, among the acts of the Second Synod of Ephesus, Julius, the bishop and vicar of Pope Leo, says: ‘Let the pope’s letter be read first.’ This is found not only in the Latin text but also in the Greek, which reads: ‘Let the letter sent by the pope be read first’ [the supplied Greek is corrupt]. Again, in session 2, the most reverend bishops shouted: ‘Pope Leo has interpreted it thus,’ which agrees with the Greek, where it reads: ‘Pope Leo interpreted it thus.’ Indeed, Evagrius, when recounting this, did not include the word ‘Leo’ in this passage, but simply said: ‘The pope interpreted it thus.’ And that is so in all the Greek editions of Evagrius.

“As for the Latins, Hilary the deacon’s letter to the empress Pulcheria, written after the Ephesian Robber Council and cited by the same distinguished man among the letters of St. Leo, provides sufficiently strong evidence that Roman pontiffs were then accustomed to be called simply popes. For he says: ‘Manifest necessity compelled me to present to your Clemency the letters addressed to you by the blessed pope.’ [Note: Vol. I of the Works of St. Leo, in Quesnellus.]

“I shall not use the authority of Galla Placidia’s letter to the same empress Pulcheria, in which it is written: ‘Leo the pope, surrounded by a multitude of priests,’ since it could be argued that the word *papa* here has an accompanying qualification. The *Brief History of the Eutychianists* says: ‘When Uranius, the assistant, arrived and brought the emperor’s sacred letter against John, who was already bishop, the pope was suspended from confirming that episcopate.’”

These examples, I think, are sufficient to weaken the force of the argument that Paschasius Quesnellus brought against this passage.

22. Since our opponent had gathered a mass of material into his dissertation in order, by undermining the session concerning Domnus of Antioch, to abolish altogether the authority of the Roman pontiffs in confirming the ordinations of bishops and rescinding the decrees of councils, we had to proceed gradually through the individual points that he collected in that dissertation.

Nevertheless, since our labor has been greatly lightened by the study and diligence of the distinguished Stephen Baluzius, we preferred to transfer to our defense what he had most carefully noted, adding certain points from our own industry that responded especially well to what we had said in our preceding *Exercises*, rather than compose an entirely new *Exercise* from the beginning.

Since, finally, Paschasius Quesnellus brought forward many errors—indeed grammatical ones—that had crept into the session under discussion, and noted that the names of the bishops who took part in that session had not been recorded there, thereby increasing suspicions of interpolation, since Maximus there presented his petitions to lay judges in an ecclesiastical matter while setting aside the leading bishops of the synod, we have decided, lest we appear negligent, to meet these Quesnellian scruples as well, together with Baluzius. [Note: Baluzius, in the *New Collection of Councils*.]

As for the grammatical errors, if Quesnellus’s suspicion were valid, all the Acts of Chalcedon and all the proceedings of the other general councils would have to be called interpolated, especially those translated from Greek into Latin. Does Quesnellus perhaps not know how much later translators labored so that we might at least have the ancient version as Rusticus corrected it?

What, then, of the bishops’ names? It was not necessary for them to be recited after Domnus’s session. Those names had been recorded sufficiently in other sessions and were entered in the register at the end of the proceedings.

Finally, says Baluzius, the case under discussion was not merely ecclesiastical but also civil. In this respect we do not agree with him, since the matter concerned a pension to be given to Domnus from ecclesiastical revenues—a payment voluntarily proposed by Maximus himself as evidence of the compassion to be shown toward Domnus. Just as Domnus had been deprived by canon law of the title and benefice of the Church, so he could not receive revenues from the Church of which he had been deprived. Therefore, so that ecclesiastical rights might not be violated, a decree of the synod had to be interposed, which the lay judges eventually approved as witnesses.

The conduct of the emperor Marcian makes this clear. After leaving the synod following the definition of the faith, he ordered the bishops to remain for three or four days and instructed each one to present whatever he wished before the great judges. Nor does it matter that the judges and the most illustrious Senate were named first. They were not sitting as arbiters of ecclesiastical affairs, but merely served as witnesses and provided protection, so that all cases might be brought to a conclusion without quarrels and disputes. We proved this in the *Exercise* delivered on the fourth session of Chalcedon, concerning the case of Photius of Tyre, which was judged there not according to the civil enactments of the age but according to the canonical laws.

23. Finally, Quesnellus argues that it was highly indecent and ridiculous for Domnus to have been presented there as a beggar, anxious to obtain subsistence. Domnus, he says, was bishop of so great a see as Antioch; and, having succeeded to the place of his uncle, he ought to have been powerful in wealth, friends, and authority. He therefore could not have fallen into such an abyss of calamity that he entirely lacked food, unless provision had been made for him at the discretion of his successor.

But where does Quesnellus derive all these things, which he now invents? Domnus did not come to the synod; he did not ask that those expenses be granted to him; no one else asked it on his behalf; Maximus did it of his own accord.

Indeed, if we compare what we described above with the words of Evagrius, cited shortly before, it may be suspected that Domnus never received any such assessed pension. Content with his lot, he spent the rest of his life concealed in a monastery, having nothing further in common with the Antiochenes.

The other points Quesnellus added to prove the session interpolated—that it had been separated from the rest of the Greek body of the Council of Chalcedon, that it had so far found no fixed place, and that it had been inserted long after the Acts had been compiled—totally waver and collapse.

What? If the arguments he brings had force, it would follow that the session concerning Photius and Eustathius, which in the time of Rusticus, Liberatus, and Evagrius had been separated from the body of the other Greek sessions of the Council of Chalcedon, was false and interpolated. Was it not inserted long after those Acts had been collected? Yet when Balsamon found it in an ancient copy that he used, and it was subsequently seen in various other codices, no learned man has therefore judged it interpolated, because it corresponds exceptionally well to what happened at the Ephesian Robber Council and at the two Constantinopolitan synods, in which the election of Anatolius and his ordination as bishop of Constantinople were treated.

Have we not clearly proved from the Acts of Chalcedon that Domnus’s session has similar characteristics and marks? The session concerning Photius of Tyre was likewise tossed among uncertain locations. In Balsamon’s codex it was read at the end of the proceedings; now, however, in the common editions it is placed at the end of the fourth session.

The words of Facundus of Hermiane, which Quesnellus brings against us, provide no support whatsoever for his fallen case. They do not pertain to the question at issue, since all that can be elicited from Facundus of Hermiane’s silence is that Domnus of Antioch was not condemned at the Council of Chalcedon—a point that we ourselves have already freely granted.

24. Would that Quesnellus had not been so indulgent toward his own studies: now inventing fictions, now weaving deceptions, and now striving to drag the testimonies of the ancient Fathers toward distorted and violent interpretations, in order to defend his chimerical system concerning the authority of the Roman pontiffs. He repeatedly employed those poisonous supports of conjecture that overturn ancient ecclesiastical history, abolish the sacred order of governance, and introduce a new discipline contrary to the canons.

Who, however, will say that he intended, and expended his labor, to prepare the writings of St. Leo the Great? Surely anyone who is not blind must admit with us that he disfigured, mutilated, and distorted the Works of Leo, supplying the enemies of the Catholic Church with weapons that, as a priest of the clerical order, he ought to have snatched from their hands.

Finally, I must lament that some have hitherto been found who, adhering to Quesnellus’s principles, have dared publicly to defend the claim that this session is spurious.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the remaining sessions of the Council of Chalcedon, and especially the final one, in which, contrary to the ecclesiastical canons, canon 28 was drawn up concerning the new honor and prerogatives of the see of Constantinople, against the rights of the bishop of Alexandria and also of the bishop of Antioch

1. Once the cases of Photius of Tyre, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Domnus of Antioch had been reconsidered and settled, as the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of St. Leo inform us, scarcely anything serious would have remained for us to treat, if, in the final session, Anatolius had not sought to acquire primacy over the other principal Churches of the East at the expense of the rights of those Churches, desiring to make his see almost equal to the apostolic see of Rome.

Anatolius restrained this ambition by many acts of dissimulation until the council’s conclusion. But when permission was finally granted for particular questions to be raised in the synod, in order to prevent or remove certain abuses that had occurred in ecclesiastical administration, he reserved for himself the task of increasing his own rights, diminishing the honor of others, and, under the pretext of the imperial city called New Rome, obtaining immediately after the apostolic see of Rome the primacy over the others.

Accordingly, after the definition of the faith had been made, the Fathers of the synod examined, besides the cases of those three bishops, the case of Ibas of Edessa. For, through the agency of Dioscorus, he had been deprived of the priesthood in the Ephesian Robber Council while absent and unheard. Therefore he had presented a petition to the emperor in defense of his case, and the emperor referred the matter to the synod.

After examining the synodal Acts of Tyre and Berytus and hearing the testimony of the Edessene clergy, the Fathers found him, according to the papal legates, to be of approved faith and blameless life; he was therefore restored to the priesthood and to his see.

Some matter concerning Nonnus, who had received the see of Ibas while the synod was still deliberating, was nevertheless referred for judgment to Maximus of Antioch. Maximus decided that Nonnus should not be deprived of the episcopal honor until he could deliberate otherwise with the bishops of his diocese.

Quesnellus further adds that a decree was issued abolishing the memory of the Ephesian pseudo-synod and striking it from the number of synods, and that the emperor was to be asked to forbid by decree that it be called a synod or that its acts be accepted.

“Maximus’s ordination,” he adds, “had already been ratified by the holy synod, since he had been legitimately consecrated by the bishops of the province and admitted into communion with the most holy patriarch Leo. For this reason the exception mentioned by a few was superfluous, since the legates of the apostolic see also declared that it ought not to be counted among the Ephesian Acts. The session concerning Domnus is fictitious, as we prove elsewhere.”

Thus far Quesnellus, with whom we do not now intend to begin a new contest. But for a fuller statement of the truth he ought to have added two things.

First, the acts of the Robber Council had already long before been proscribed and abolished by St. Leo, because the Ephesian synod had been conducted contrary to the canons and its acts were judged illegitimate and improperly executed. Thus we read in the ancient synopsis of Epistle 39 to the emperor Theodosius Augustus, found in the Vatican manuscripts and in the Florentine codex; the ancient editors, the collectors of the Library of the Fathers and of the councils, preserved it. Although Quesnellus removed it while preparing the Works of St. Leo and introduced an entirely different passage into his edition without manuscript authority, as we shall observe in the notes.

From this follows the second point: namely, that Paschasinus, Leo’s legate, fully aware of the pontifical decree previously issued, wished by a solemn declaration made in the synod for the said Acts to be proscribed as invalid and void; and, in order to deprive the Eutychian faction of every means of escape, he sought to have this sanction strengthened by imperial law. In other words, he wanted the former public law of Theodosius abolished—the law by which Theodosius had ordered and established that no one might reject or infringe those synodal Acts of Ephesus of which Dioscorus had been the author.

Paschasinus’s cited words clearly indicate this:

“If,” he says, “everything done there has been regarded as void by the most blessed and apostolic bishop of the city of Rome, it is clear that the most holy bishop of the city of Antioch is outside these matters, whom afterward the most blessed bishop received into his own communion. For it is necessary that we again approach that most tranquil and Christian ruler, so that by a sacred and pious law he may order that that council not even be named.” [Note: Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, vol. IV, p. 1587.]

From this it is rather clear that, as early as the year 449, the Acts of that synod had been declared void and abolished by the decree of the most holy supreme pontiff Leo the Great. Nothing new, therefore, was defined by the Fathers of Chalcedon themselves.

2. The controversy between Bassianus and Stephen occupied the two following sessions, 11 and 12: the former was deposed from the see of Ephesus, and the latter substituted in his place.

Stephen, who had been substituted in his see, testified that Bassianus had been removed from the episcopate of Ephesus, which he had obtained by usurpation, at the command of the holy pontiff Leo the Great. [Note: Session 11 of Chalcedon, vol. IV of the Councils, p. 1614.] Since Stephen himself had acquired the episcopate through a conspiracy, it was justly judged that another should be elected—one who both knew the faith completely and was known to be adorned with a life suitable for a bishop.

In the two sessions that followed, 13 and 14, the dispute between Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, and Anastasius of Nicaea was heard. Accusations were brought forward by both sides, concerning the extent to which Anastasius had usurped the metropolitan right for himself by withdrawing from the subordination of the bishop of Nicomedia. After canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea had been read, by which it had been established that a bishop should be ordained by all the provincial bishops, together with Valentinian’s law enacted for the people of Nicomedia, it was finally judged that Nicaea, being subject to Nicomedia, had been granted honor but not metropolitan jurisdiction by Valentinian’s edict; and that, according to the Council of Nicaea, there was only one metropolis in each province.

3. In the fourteenth session a dispute arose concerning the episcopate of Perrha. Athanasius, having been accused by his own people and repeatedly summoned to judgment by Panolbius, then by his successor, and finally by Domnus, patriarch of Antioch, who was conducting the council, refused to appear. He was therefore deposed, and Sabinianus was ordained in his place after Dioscorus had driven him from the see.

The case was consequently discussed in the synod and referred to Maximus of Antioch and the council that was with him, with the stipulation that the investigation be conducted within eight months, counted from the present day. If Athanasius were found guilty, he was to be deprived of his see; if innocent, he was to be restored. Sabinianus, however, was to retain the honor, but not the jurisdiction, of a bishop, and was to be fed—so they say—as the most reverend bishop Maximus of Antioch should determine from the resources of the most holy Church of Perrha.

### 4

With complete peace and without the disturbance of any contention, all the cases brought before the synod were reviewed and settled. But when the Constantinopolitan clerics, at the prompting of Bishop Anatolius, were being led by ambition to increase the honor of their Church, the Fathers asked that they deign to establish something. The judges advised them to refrain from delivering a judgment and declared that the matter belonged to the synod; then they withdrew without any delay, and the legates of the Apostolic See followed them.

Nevertheless, the Fathers who remained and were then present issued various canons: thirty, according to the Greek manuscripts translated by Gentianus Hervetus, as appears on p. 508 of Labbe’s collection; [Col. 1288D] the Latins, however, have twenty-eight, the last of which concerns the see of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1288D] Actio 14 exstat tom. IV Concil., p. m. 1679.], in which what had been established under Theodosius the Elder, in the time of Nectarius, at the ecumenical council concerning its patriarchate was renewed and confirmed.

When the papal legates learned of this, they wished on the following day—that is, on the Kalends of November—to invalidate Anatolius’s unjust attempts. Therefore, as the deacon Liberatus reports [Note: [Col. 1288D] Liberatus diaconus, in *Breviario*, cap. 13.], they asked that they again assemble with the judges for the council. When the judges asked the council what had been decreed on the previous day, the acts were read and they learned what had occurred. It was therefore ordered that the decree enacted on the preceding day be read. After it had been read, the appended subscription of the bishops was recited, and Anatolius was placed first.

The legates of the Apostolic See rightly protested; and Lucentius addressed the judges in particular as follows: [Col. 1289A]

“First, let Your Glory consider by what deception the holy bishops were treated, so that they were compelled to subscribe to canons that had not been written down, although mention had been made of them.”

Then, in order to render wholly invalid the attempts of Anatolius and the Constantinopolitan clerics, who, setting aside the Nicene decrees, were striving to prevail upon the Constantinopolitan canon established by the one hundred and fifty Fathers nearly eighty years earlier, he added:

“If, then, they made use of this benefit in those times, what do they seek now? If they never made use of it, why do they seek it?”

After this, the legates were asked to produce the mandate they had received from Saint Leo. Boniface read it:

“You must not permit the constitution of the holy Fathers, once promulgated, to be violated or diminished through any rashness; rather, preserve in every way the dignity of our person in you, whom we have sent in our place. And if any persons, perhaps relying on the splendor of their cities, should attempt to usurp something for themselves, repel it with all the firmness that the matter requires.”

Who would not understand that Saint Leo the Great had already perceived from afar the enormous ambition of Anatolius and even of the Constantinopolitan clerics? [Col. 1289B]

### 5

Meanwhile, both sides appealed to the canons; and Paschasinus read the fifth Nicene canon concerning the distinction of dioceses, which begins:

“The Roman Church has always held the primacy.”

But when another manuscript of the Nicene canons was produced, Aetius, the deacon of the Constantinopolitan see, mutilated it; after deleting that opening, he introduced the sixth canon, written in different words and a different order, and immediately appended the canon of the Council of Constantinople under Nectarius.

When, however, despite the subornation of the judges and their deceptions, the matter had again inclined toward Anatolius’s position, Lucentius entered the following protest:

“The Apostolic See, which commands us to be present, must not be humbled. Therefore, concerning everything done yesterday, in our absence, to the prejudice of the canons or rules, we ask Your Sublimity to order that it be annulled. Otherwise, let our opposition remain attached to these acts, so that we may know what we ought to report to the apostolic man, the pope of the universal Church, in order that he himself may pronounce judgment either concerning the injury done to his see or concerning the overthrow of the canons.” [Col. 1289C]

Baronius described this history at greater length and in a fuller style. Readers may consult him in order to refute what Paschasius Quesnellus has fabricated concerning the privileges of the Roman Church, arguing:

“These privileges were derived from the Fathers because of the Roman Empire: the one hundred and fifty Fathers assembled at Constantinople under Nectarius granted Constantinople equal privileges, because the New Rome was adorned with an empire and senate just as the old Rome was.” [Note: [Col. 1289D] Quesnellus, tom. II, pag. 161, colum. 1, ad actionem 15 Chalcedonensis synodi.]

Nevertheless, lest we pass over without due criticism this Quesnellian assertion—which was devised gradually to weaken and overturn the foundation of the Catholic hierarchy and society—we consider it necessary to compare it with the preceding protest made by Bishop Lucentius.

Lucentius’s protest contains two points. The first is that, by that twenty-eighth canon, the Apostolic See was humbled and injury was inflicted upon it; [Col. 1289D] the second is that the canons were overthrown. Concerning these matters, the apostolic man, the pope of the universal Church, was to pronounce judgment.

Some who do not carefully investigate the force and purpose of this canon might think that it could neither humble nor injure the Roman Church, but that both effects rather redounded to the detriment of the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, one of whom had held second place and the other third place among the patriarchs by peaceful and long-established possession.

Since, therefore, the ancient privileges of the Roman pontiffs were preserved and assigned to them intact, without any trace whatsoever of injury, it might not be apparent why the legates of the Apostolic See should have been so vehemently disturbed and should have resisted so strongly a decree that concerned only the Eastern patriarchs in agreement among themselves. [Col. 1290A]

Those reasoning in this way could do so only if they were wholly ignorant of the rights of the Apostolic See and failed to grasp the force, order, and rationale of the decree in question.

First, the force of that decree lay in deriving the honor, dignity, and privileges of episcopal sees from the splendor and magnificence of cities and from the glory of princes and magistrates, with absolutely no regard either for divine institution or for the apostles who founded those Churches. The papal legates could not concede this without injury to the Apostolic See.

For the primacy of this see over all bishops, and its governance over the universal Church, did not derive from some ecclesiastical arrangement or from the sanction of canons. Rather, it came from the Lord himself, who established Peter as his vicar and as the head of the entire ecclesiastical assembly. By legitimate right of succession, the prerogatives of that authority remain and will remain perpetually in the Roman Church.

In that canon they deliberately and with great care suppressed this divine and apostolic right, as though it were something to be regarded as insignificant. Although in the first, third, and sixth [Col. 1290B] sessions, and repeatedly elsewhere, they had asserted it to the Roman bishop Leo, as well as in the synodical letter, as we shall note shortly.

Lucentius therefore understood perfectly that the Roman pontiff had been deprived of his legitimate rights and that the order of ecclesiastical hierarchy derived from Christ the Lord was being abolished, with no arrangement preserved except that which arose from the civil administration of the Roman Empire, to which they claimed that the Church’s canons had looked. He therefore rightly protested, saying that the Apostolic See must not be humbled and could not endure so grave an injury.

### 6

If we then consider the order and rationale of that canon, who does not see that it inflicted violence and injury upon the Roman pontiff and the other patriarchs?

For the Fathers of the council were not permitted to define anything that in any respect disagreed with the Nicene canons. “Whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution will never obtain the consent of the Apostolic See.” [Note: [Col. 1290D] Saint Leo the Great, in his letter to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 5.]

Thus, in this respect also, a grave wound was inflicted upon pontifical authority, since the Nicene canons were overthrown. The Roman pontiffs necessarily had to safeguard their observance with all the strength of their spirit. Just as they never permitted the rights of their own see to be violated, so they could not permit the rights of others to be stolen by ambitious men.

If the Fathers of synods could not, as we have seen, without consulting the Roman bishop grant indulgence and relaxation of penalties to the lapsed under the rules of the canons, how much more ought such caution to have been observed when the matter concerned abolishing the sixth Nicene canon and overthrowing the rights of the Alexandrian and Antiochene patriarchates?

### 7

As for the Alexandrian patriarchate, let us consider the excessively fraudulent conduct of the Constantinopolitan clerics and of Anatolius himself.

After Bishop Dioscorus had been deposed—he who had always fought most fiercely to defend the privileges of his see, even against the rules of law, as we saw in chapters 6, 7, and 8 of the preceding book—there was no one present at the final session [Col. 1290D] who could restrain the ambition of the Constantinopolitans or oppose their attempts. That Church was still deprived of its legitimate pastor.

Although, in the sixth session, the Egyptian bishops had been ordered not to leave Chalcedon but to await the election of a new bishop, this election was ultimately postponed until the council had been completed, so that no one would be present to declare himself aggrieved by the usurpation of rights.

No one is unaware how gravely the rights of the Alexandrian see were subsequently wounded in matters concerning the ordination of bishops for the provinces of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace. Anatolius, using as a pretext the need to prevent schism in the future, sought to claim for himself and his see the honor of conducting these ordinations, [Col. 1291A] although the Thracians resisted and not a few men from the other provinces, who could not be deceived, protested that the rules handed down from antiquity and their order ought not to be changed.

The most learned Christian Lupus described and elucidated this entire controversy more fully and with the erudition in which he excelled, in the appendix to the Council of Chalcedon, p. 1011 in my edition. We refer readers to that work.

For the moment, we add only that the words of the praised canon 28 can be examined by everyone in the collections of the councils; meanwhile, we shall proceed in a more orderly fashion to the measures undertaken by Saint Leo to abolish that canon.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The measures undertaken after the Synod of Chalcedon in favor of Anatolius. The letters of the Fathers of the general synod and of the emperors Marcian and Pulcheria to Saint Leo for confirming and ratifying the praised twenty-eighth canon. The conduct of the holy pontiff in annulling and cancelling that canon. The interpretations of Paschasius Quesnellus examined. Finally, we reject Launoy’s criticism of the most learned Cardinal Bellarmine as false and unjust.

[Col. 1291B]

### 1

After a most grievous wound had been inflicted upon the Acts of Chalcedon by the ambition of Anatolius alone, the Easterners themselves did everything in their power to remedy it. They did so both in the synodical letter written to Saint Leo after the synod and by seeking and obtaining the support of the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria. Through this support they earnestly worked to ensure that the same holy pontiff would not abolish the twenty-eighth canon concerning the privileges of the Church of Constantinople, but would confirm it with the other decrees and approve it as ratified.

Moreover, Anatolius reflected upon the efforts and honor with which he had assiduously treated Saint Leo and the papal legates up to that day. He flattered himself that the pontiff’s mind might be softened by his letters if, recalling what Anatolius had hitherto done in testimony to the Catholic faith and in honor [Col. 1291C] and service of the Apostolic See, the pontiff should wish to repay him with some worthy reward for so many labors.

He also believed that Bishop Julian of Cos, who among the Easterners performed the office of apostolic vicar, could assist his desires. Therefore he did not delay enlisting Julian’s services, so that, having taken on the role of intermediary, Julian too might act before the same holy pontiff to increase the rights and privileges of the Constantinopolitan episcopate.

When I carefully considered the conduct of all these men, I became firmly convinced that the bishops of the entire East, especially when gathered in general synods, and the emperors themselves, firmly believed that no conciliar decrees could possess authority in the Church or retain the force of a canon unless they had been approved by the Roman pontiff; indeed, that they would collapse with all their force whenever they were expressly rejected by him. We explained this clearly in the preceding book, especially in chapters 4, 5, and 6, and most recently indicated it from what has just been said concerning session 11 of this Council of Chalcedon. [Col. 1291D]

### 2

To discuss the matter truly and solidly, we may first note what they wrote to the holy pontiff in their synodical letter concerning that twenty-eighth canon.

On this occasion, let us also observe that they called Leo the legitimate interpreter of the voice of blessed Peter and, in a sincere confession, assigned to him the primacy of the supreme head, against whom the Alexandrian bishop Dioscorus had vented his madness by plotting excommunication.

After achieving a glorious victory following so many and such great disasters, by which the Church of the East had remained especially afflicted for three years, they rejoiced because the holy pontiff had hastened successfully to unite the body of the Church.

They then added:

“These are the things that we have accomplished together with you, who were present in spirit and deliberated as though among brothers, and who, through the wisdom of your vicars, seemed almost to be among us.”

Thus, just as they praise the triumph of the faith, achieved with supreme felicity through the support, wisdom, and influence of Saint Leo, so they strive to persuade him that they had been led by a desire for peace and tranquility to define certain statutes intended to safeguard the welfare of the Churches:

“For we know,” they say, “that Your Holiness will accept, approve, and confirm these same provisions.”

To make it easier to obtain confirmation of these statutes, they appeal to a custom already established for a long time, namely, that the holy Church of God at Constantinople had exercised authority to ordain the metropolitans of the provinces of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace; and that they had now confirmed this by synodal decree—not so much granting something to the see of Constantinople as providing suitable tranquility for the metropolitan cities, since, when bishops frequently die, many disturbances arise, with clerics and peoples in those cities left without a ruler and the ecclesiastical order thrown into confusion. [Col. 1292B]

### 3

By means of this requested pretext of ecclesiastical tranquility, through which they claimed to promise themselves many benefits, they attempted to shield from every censure the audacious acts by which the ancient custom of discipline was being overthrown.

Therefore, lest the holy pontiff take offense that the judicial order he had established had not been observed at all in the council, and that they had proceeded to enact the statutes in question contrary to the instructions, commands, and protests of the legates, they recalled to his mind the former dissensions, rivalries, and quarrels of the Church of Ephesus, from which certain persons had repeatedly caused trouble for him.

They then described how they had confirmed the Constantinopolitan canon, decreeing that, after the most holy and apostolic see of Saint Leo, Constantinople should have the place of honor—“being ranked second.”

For this reason they earnestly begged Saint Leo to deign to honor by his pontifical decrees the judgment already rendered by them. Since we have already discussed this petition in the preceding book, chapter 6, there is no reason to treat it again here.

When I occasionally considered this synodical letter of the Fathers of Chalcedon silently within myself, I was deeply moved against those who had dared to assign complete force and authority to the canons even of general councils while removing every approval and confirmation of the Apostolic See.

I was moved still more when I turned my eyes to another letter written by the emperor Marcian. Although accustomed to devote himself to the administration of civil affairs, and although he was laboring with excessive zeal to increase the honor and prerogatives of the imperial city, he nevertheless believed that this increase of honor could depend neither on himself nor on the decree of the synod unless it were ratified and made firm by the Roman supreme pontiff himself.

### 4

Accordingly, after the emperor had thought it proper to congratulate Leo and himself because, “after every contention and disagreement that the envy hostile to the faith had thrown in the way” had been cast out [Col. 1292D], he related how he too had hastened to attend the holy synod, although, as he said, “expeditions and public necessities were keeping us in other places.”

He then briefly proceeded to describe how everything in the synod had unfolded with the triumph of truth and the glory of the faith:

“When all had assented to the exposition according to the demands of truth, in accordance with the letters of Your Holiness.”

Finally, coming to the decree of the Council of Constantinople, renewed or confirmed in this synod, he appealed to the pontiff to deign also to give this part his personal consent, although “the most reverend bishops who had come to the holy synod as representatives of your religion had opposed it.” [Note: [Col. 1291D] In describing this letter of Marcian, we have followed the version of Lucas Holstenius, although Paschasius Quesnellus, in the second edition of the works of Saint Leo, 1700, with the Greek text added, offers another version made by Andreas Arnoldus of Nuremberg, which readers may easily consult, although in reality it differs little from the preceding version of Holstenius.]

Saint Leo himself also makes clear, from the letter he wrote in reply to her, that the empress Pulcheria had undertaken the role of intermediary for this reason. Although the letter of Pulcheria on this subject has so far been unavailable to scholars, it is nevertheless evident from Leo’s reply that Anatolius and the Constantinopolitan clerics placed great confidence in the services of a woman who devoted her efforts to so great a cause with such virtue and authority.

Bishop Julian of Cos also showed no less concern for this matter. Although his letter has not yet seen the light of day and may perhaps have been lost through the ravages of time, a letter of the holy pontiff survives in which Leo reproves him for having loved Anatolius and for wishing to favor him in an unlawful cause against the order of the universal Church. It is therefore now perfectly clear that Julian too had undertaken the role of intermediary.

### 5

Finally, Anatolius himself, by no means doubting that he could move the pontifical mind to grant what he desired, driven by the greatest ambition, sent the supreme pontiff a sufficiently lengthy letter [Col. 1293B]. He devoted all his efforts to insinuating himself into Leo’s patronage and to persuading him that the new honor of the Constantinopolitan see would increase the prerogatives of the Roman episcopate, on the principle that the honor of sons wholly redounds to the glory of their parents.

We noted this letter of Anatolius, which had been absent from earlier editions, in chapter 5 of the preceding book of the history of the Eutychians, p. 562 and following. As we said, we transcribed it from a Greek manuscript in the Vatican in the year 1738, and the distinguished Sir Franciscus Mariani, a writer and translator of Greek in the Vatican Library, rendered it into Latin.

### 6

As Saint Leo reviewed these letters, his mind could not even slightly have been moved to indulge the ambition of Anatolius after the Nicene decrees had been set aside, or to bend before the petitions of the secular authorities and the entire synod.

Therefore, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June in the year 452 [Col. 1293C], he took up his pen and replied to the letters mentioned above, employing that firmness and courage of spirit which most befitted the supreme pastor of the universal Church.

First, we shall speak of the letters to Marcian and Pulcheria, which also occupy the first place in Quesnellus’s edition.

In beginning to address the emperor in his letter, Saint Leo declares that one must rejoice in the victory of the faith, which, through the great gift of divine mercy, had overflowed upon the whole Church. After adding certain passages borrowed from the testimonies of Scripture, which manifest the existence of two natures in Christ the Lord after their union, he immediately attacks, in the second chapter of the letter, the unjust ambition of Anatolius. Rather, Anatolius ought to have been advised to abandon the error of those who had ordained him and to pass, through a salutary correction, into agreement with the Catholic faith.

Saint Leo always had reasonable doubts that Anatolius had at some time been stained by Eutychian soot, since Anatolius had been the representative of Dioscorus and had been elevated to the Constantinopolitan see by the Eutychian faction and by the machinations of the eunuch Chrysaphius after the death of Flavian. Saint Leo, the supreme pontiff, would never have admitted him to communion or approved his election and ordination unless Marcian and Pulcheria had overcome the pontifical mind by their petitions, and unless Anatolius had made a public confession of the faith before the entire clergy and people of Constantinople in the hands of the papal legates. For this reason Leo had sent them especially to Constantinople, as we saw in the preceding book, chapter 12.

Saint Leo therefore recalls all these matters to the emperor’s mind, saying:

“He ought nevertheless to have taken care that what he is known to have obtained through your benefit”—many manuscripts, as Baronius and Quesnellus note, have *our* instead of *your* in the margin—“should not be disturbed by any depravity of desire.”

Because the emperor and the empress Pulcheria had vouched for Anatolius’s faith so that he might be received into communion with the Apostolic See, Leo adds:

“Having regard to the intervention of your faith, when the beginnings of his consecration wavered according to the authors of that consecration, we wished to be more merciful toward him than strict.”

Leo intended to indicate that Anatolius’s ordination, having been performed by heretics and schismatics, was entirely unlawful, and that Anatolius could have been deposed from the episcopal ministry, since he was bound by canonical penalties on account of which he ought to have remained perpetually prevented and suspended from the exercise of his sacred office.

Therefore, as evidence of the mercy shown toward Anatolius and in order to remove all the disturbances that had been stirred up through the activity of the devil, Leo says that he had employed remedies of leniency which ought to have made Anatolius more moderate rather than immoderate.

Because Leo was arguing with a most Christian, religious, and truly orthodox ruler, whom he knew to care about the defense of the faith and ecclesiastical discipline, he assigned even stronger foundations for the rejection he had given.

Even if Anatolius had been touched by no stain whatsoever, but had been lawfully and solemnly ordained on the basis of outstanding merits and the best judgment, he nevertheless could not have been supported by any votes against the reverence due to the paternal canons, against the institutions of the Holy Spirit, and against the examples of antiquity.

After he had asserted that he neither wished to ratify nor could consent to the canon under discussion, Leo protested that the glory of the city of Constantinople could not be diminished even if its bishop did not rise to a higher rank and order.

“Yet,” he says, “the order of secular matters is one thing, and that of divine matters another. Nor, apart from that rock which the Lord wondrously placed in the foundations, was that structure stable; rather, he loses what is his own who covets what does not belong to him.”

By distinguishing between the imperial city and the Apostolic See, he indicated the source from which the privileges of the Churches derive, adding:

“For the privileges of the Churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea, cannot be shaken by any wickedness or violated by any novelty.” [Col. 1294C]

In carrying out this work faithfully with Christ’s help—the reader should not overlook the weight of the following words—it is necessary that I show myself persistent in service:

“Because the stewardship entrusted to me tends toward my accountability, if, with me—God forbid—conniving, the rules of the paternal sanctions established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God should be violated, and if the will of one brother should have greater weight with me than the common welfare of the whole household of God.”

### 7

If I were not pressed too tightly by the desire for brevity in composing this work, a very broad field would open before me for overturning the system of those who claim that the Roman pontiffs are subject to the sanctions of councils. Quesnellus likewise wished to judge this matter when he slyly wrote in the margin of that passage:

“The Roman pontiff is bound by the canons and must serve them in dispensations.”

For neither is the universal authority of the Roman pontiffs limited, nor are the Roman pontiffs said to be subject to councils if, in matters concerning the universal governance of the Church, they wish to preserve the rules of the sanctions established under the instruction of the Spirit of God and strive to have them faithfully carried out.

Roman pontiffs can, however, do in the Church what general councils have taken care to establish. Indeed, they can abolish, annul, reform, and declare as void the statutes of synods that conflict with ecclesiastical rules and that have been devised to subvert the order and administration of discipline. Such acts certainly provide no argument that they are subject to general councils; rather, they show that councils themselves obtain their force and authority from the Roman pontiffs alone.

Moreover, since the dispensation of the canons has, according to Leo himself, been entrusted to the Roman pontiff alone, and since it tends toward his accountability if, after neglecting the welfare of the universal Church, the will of one brother, ambition, and the desire to dominate others should prevail with him, the question is no longer whether the Roman pontiff possesses authority over councils, but under what circumstances and in what cases he ought to exercise it, lest dispensations tend toward his accountability.

In other matters concerning ecclesiastical governance, he is subject only to the most just judgment of the Lord God; he could not violate and overturn without guilt the rules inspired by the Holy Spirit.

### 8

Let us nevertheless pass over these matters, which can be explained at greater length by those accustomed to treat such arguments in the schools.

We add only one other point concerning the custody and observance of the canons. After Anatolius had departed from them by disregarding the commands of the Fathers, he produced fresh evidence of his ambition in the ordination of Maximus, bishop of Antioch, which he had usurped for himself without any precedent.

Saint Leo wished to conceal this new offense as contrary to peace and priestly concord. He asserts that he did not retract that ordination out of love for restoring the faith and from a desire for peace, although Anatolius had in no way been permitted to ordain a bishop for the Church of Antioch, without precedent, contrary to the institutions of the canons.

He states that he could easily have declared this ordination invalid and legally null. He refrained from doing so solely out of concern for the faith and peace.

Moved, therefore, by these and other most serious considerations, he reverently begged the emperor Marcian not to take this rejection amiss. He appealed to him to suppress by a salutary intervention the wicked attempts contrary to Christian unity and peace, refusing them, as he says, “the assent of Your Piety,” and to restrain beneficially the harmful desire of his brother Anatolius if he should persist.

Finally, he testifies that Bishop Lucian and the deacon Basil, who had delivered the imperial writings to him, had fulfilled the obligations of their legation.

“For one must not be judged to have failed in the business whom rather the cause itself abandoned.”

With these words he closed his letter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the year 452, as we have said.

Quesnellus adorned this letter with notes and observations in the second volume of his edition. [Note: [Col. 1295D] Quesnellus, vol. II of the works of Saint Leo the Great, p. 85, col. 1.]

After first listing the various readings found in the printed editions and manuscript copies of others, he raises a question concerning the words in chapter 3:

“Let him not disdain the imperial city, which he cannot make an apostolic see.”

“Apostolic sees, or Churches,” he says, “are so called for more than one reason.”

He then states that ancient writers customarily applied this designation to Churches for six principal reasons, as he asserts on the basis of Tertullian, Theodoret, and Augustine, but he does not indicate the principal reason for which the Roman Church is repeatedly called the Apostolic See by Saint Leo.

He therefore says:

“The Roman see is called apostolic antonomastically [*ἀντονομαστικῶς*], because it was founded by the princes of the apostles and consecrated by the blood of both.”

He adds that this designation also applies, for various other reasons, to the Churches of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Ephesus, and to certain others, according to the Fathers’ different formulas of expression, which he describes in the same place.

What he wished to suggest to readers by such an incongruous display of erudition, I entirely fail to understand. Indeed, if I were permitted to speculate, I would conclude that he wished by this means to diminish the prerogatives of the Roman pontiffs, since he suppresses the principal reason why the Roman see is called apostolic.

Granting, then, that the Churches of others were called apostolic by the ancients for various other meanings and as a mark of honor, nevertheless no Church was called so in a more principal sense and with complete propriety except the Roman see alone. Saint Leo himself has acknowledged in innumerable passages that the authority of blessed Peter lives in that see and will endure perpetually. The Roman pontiffs, Peter’s successors by hereditary right, extend that authority throughout the entire body of the Church, so that nothing at all can exist in the other members that does not flow from this head.

Neither the Alexandrian nor the Antiochene Church, nor any other Church to which the apostolic name has been given in various senses, could ever possess this special prerogative. This can be seen in Leo himself—in his sermons delivered on the anniversary of his accession to the pontificate, in his letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica, in his letter to the emperor Theodosius, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, and in his letter to the empress Pulcheria, in the case with which we are concerned, as we shall see shortly. [Note: [Col. 1296D] Consult chapter 9 of the preceding book, concerning the appeal of Saint Flavian to the Apostolic See, p. 393.]

### 9

The Roman Church, therefore, was not called the apostolic see merely because it was founded and consecrated by the blood of the apostles, but because the authority of the holy apostle Peter and his primacy in the universal Church still live and endure in the Roman pontiffs, as Saint Leo himself also asserts in Letter 79 to Pulcheria. For in matters pertaining to ecclesiastical governance, the Roman pontiffs do nothing without the authority of the holy apostle Peter; and certainly this privilege was granted to no other bishop, since to them alone it was given by hereditary succession to preside over the other bishops. [Col. 1296B]

Hence Saint Leo, remarkably consistent with himself throughout his writings, wished to employ this authority of the holy Peter when he completely set aside and annulled that canon concerning the primacy of the bishop of Constantinople, which Anatolius had unjustly usurped for himself. For after saying that the canon—already issued sixty years earlier, in the time of the elder Theodosius, and repeatedly invoked by Anatolius with much boasting—could in no way support the see of Constantinople, he proceeds to restrain the spirit of arrogance that dominated Anatolius:

> “For nearly sixty years,” he says, “they boast of this connivance, by which the aforesaid bishop thinks himself supported, vainly desiring that what no one could obtain, even if someone dared to wish for it, should benefit him.”

Accordingly, he proposes Flavian’s modesty and humility for Anatolius to imitate:

> “If he wishes,” he says, “to shine with his virtues, he will be praiseworthy and will gain the greatest affection everywhere—not by seeking human things, but by earning divine ones. In this observance I also promise to join my own disposition to his, and the affection of the apostolic see, which we have always shown to the Church of Constantinople, shall not be violated by any change.” [Col. 1296C]

Finally, when he comes to that canon, issued with the consent of the bishops despite the protests of the pontifical legates, he completely nullifies it:

> “By the authority,” he says, “of the blessed apostle Peter, we utterly annul it by a general definition, obeying in all ecclesiastical matters those laws which the Holy Spirit established for the peaceful observance of all priests through the three hundred and eighteen bishops.”

Quesnellus foresaw that these words would cause him serious difficulty. He therefore devoted considerable effort to reducing and avoiding their force. Completely concealing and neglecting those earlier words—“by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, we utterly annul it by a general definition”—in which the entire weight of this most important judgment lies, and which unmistakably reveal the extent and character of the authority exercised by the Roman pontiffs in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, he thought attention should be directed solely to the expression “we annul,” saying:

> “He uses this same word in the following letter, as well as in Letter 73, chapter 1, and Letter 99; but the meaning of the word is not always the same. For usually it means ‘to make void’; sometimes, however, ‘to be annulled’ means ‘to be void and deprived of all authority’; and sometimes, likewise, ‘to annul’ means ‘to declare void,’ ‘to declare annulled,’ or ‘to pronounce annulled.’ This seems to me to be its meaning here in Saint Leo.”

But the whole context of the statement proves that this assertion of Quesnellus is frivolous and fabricated. For it is plainly evident that Leo used the expression “we annul” in the first sense indicated by Quesnellus from the manner and procedure of the holy pontiff himself. Leo says that he acts in the person of blessed Peter and employs Peter’s authority in utterly condemning and abolishing that canon, already issued by the council and presented to the apostolic holy see for confirmation and ratification. [Col. 1297A]

Who does not see that Leo was then truly acting in the role of supreme judge? When the rights of the Churches were at issue, it was necessary for him to weaken, abolish, and deprive entirely of force the solemn agreement concluded at the council by the mutual consent of the parties. By that agreement the bishop of Constantinople claimed for himself the prerogatives that the bishop of Antioch had voluntarily ceded to him, as well as those belonging to the Church of Alexandria, which at that time had no bishop and for which none of the Eastern bishops seemed willing to offer support—either because they desired the glory, greatness, and power of the imperial city, or because they persuaded themselves that, once the ordinations of the Pontic, Asian, and Thracian provinces had been assigned to the bishop of Constantinople, the tranquility and peace of those Churches would be better secured.

None of the Fathers opposed that solemn agreement, apart from the pontifical legates. [Col. 1297B] Indeed, one of them, Julian, bishop of Cos and vicar of the apostolic see among the Easterners, joined the opinion of the others and assigned the primacy after Rome to the bishop of Constantinople. Thus the Fathers of the council were not merely solemn witnesses to the transaction concerning those rights: they were also its judges. They ordered it to be entered in the public records of the councils, and subscribed to it freely, without coercion or fear.

We therefore do not think that the canon should be called merely devoid of force and authority in the sense adopted by Quesnellus, who, doing violence to Leo’s words, adds:

> “What is entirely devoid of authority, what is immediately and without hesitation annulled as presumptuous, what is already void from its beginning and has long since collapsed, does not need to be made void and annulled by any sentence or authority; it need only be declared and announced to be void and annulled. This is what Leo does as guardian and executor of the canons, with the piety of imperial faith joined to him.” [Col. 1297C]

But what follows from this weak and purely fictitious argument? He ought first to have noticed—or at least not concealed—the formula used by the holy pontiff, who asserts that he employs the aforesaid authority of Peter when he declares: “We utterly annul it by a general definition.”

These words, it is said, were employed by judges, according to the jurists, to indicate a definitive sentence, one delivered as final and bringing the entire matter to an end; this is found in the Code, under *On Sentences*. Accordingly, no one could any longer institute a new trial or interpret the pontifical definition in another way. Since it was general, it applied to every person, individually and collectively, of whatever order, rank, or condition; and under penalty of schism all were bound to obey it.

### 10

Nor can it rightly be objected to me that the cited canon was contrary to the Nicene decrees, and that Saint Leo, as guardian and executor of the canons, could not permit it to be wounded. For I shall ask Quesnellus whether the Fathers of Chalcedon were ignorant of this. [Col. 1297D] It is perfectly clear that they were not. For the Nicene canons—and specifically the sixth, read at the insistence of Paschasinus, and then read again in the synod—were heard by everyone.

Accordingly, those Fathers either indicated that the sixth Nicene canon could no longer support the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch because of the various circumstances of the times and affairs, or they judged that they possessed the authority to render old canons obsolete and to establish new ones better suited to the administration and tranquility of the Churches, in matters relating to discipline and ecclesiastical management. [517]

Whatever their judgment may have been, Leo abolished, annulled, and nullified it. Since he did this not as a particular but as a universal bishop, reforming, annulling, and abolishing the judgment of a general synod, he thereby made it completely evident that he himself was subject neither to the decrees of synods nor to any force or validity of synodal decrees without his assent and confirmation. [Col. 1298A]

### 11

It is now necessary to examine Launoy’s frivolous interpretations, as I long ago made it my practice to do in the schools of the Urban College of Propaganda Fide when treating arguments of this kind. Taking up for examination the question concerning the pontifical confirmation of universal synods, Launoy severely attacks Cardinal Bellarmine because, in Book II *On Councils*, chapter 17, he wrote that the Roman pontiff is simply and absolutely above the universal Church and a general council, so that he recognizes no judgment above himself.

Among the other arguments brought forward by Bellarmine in support of this position is the argument drawn from this letter of Leo to Pulcheria. But Launoy denies that the assumption can be proved. Indeed, he accuses Bellarmine of fraud because he mutilated the testimony of the holy pontiff, removing the words “with the piety of your faith joined to us,” which pertain to Pulcheria; and then, after withdrawing from the middle of the sentence the words that follow—“we utterly annul it by a general definition”—he completely suppressed them. [Col. 1298B]

> “Continuing his reasoning,” Launoy says, “Bellarmine removed the preceding words so that what belonged to Leo had been common with Pulcheria, and so that Pulcheria would not be thought to have participated in the abrogation of the canon by which the prerogative of the Church of Constantinople was sanctioned; and, with these matters thus arranged, he could more easily conclude that the pope is above the council.”

Further on, Launoy explains why the holy pontiff wished to have Pulcheria’s piety of faith joined with him in abrogating that canon, adding:

> “But the pontiff added those words because he knew that princes are charged with the care of safeguarding the canons. For he writes this in Letter 74 to the emperor Leo.”

Finally, investigating why Bellarmine cut away the later words, our critic concludes:

> “He did so lest he should present the pontiff as obedient to ecclesiastical laws, and lest it should become clear to his reader that the pontiff was doing what he did by the authority of the Nicene synod. Thus that author mutilated Leo—not appropriately with regard to the truth of the matter, but with regard to the aim of his work.” [Col. 1298C]

At the end, as though wishing to evade the matter while excusing Bellarmine, Launoy says that Bellarmine wrote this at Rome, where he would incur no slight censure—not from the apostolic see itself, but from the Curia—and be placed on the Index.

Thus far Launoy, in his letter to Jacobus Bevilaqua, to which he adds several other matters that may be seen in Part II, Letter 4, page 53 of my edition.

### 12

Everyone understands that this is a serious criticism of Bellarmine; yet I do not know whether everyone would condemn it as unjust. We shall easily establish the latter, however, by observing that Bellarmine’s purpose was not to transcribe Saint Leo’s entire and complete letter and adapt it to his own use, but merely to cite those words that bore upon the question he had undertaken and set before himself—especially those that indicated ecclesiastical authority and jurisdiction. [Col. 1298D]

Who, then, among theologians, even of the lowest standing, has ever fabricated the claim that women of any condition or rank, however endowed with supreme secular power, possessed jurisdiction in the Church and lawfully exercised it? Not even the heterodox—for the moment excluding the Montanists and Cataphrygians—ever dreamed that women could employ the authority of the apostle Peter in preserving, establishing, or abolishing ecclesiastical laws. [518]

By the piety of faith they may indeed obey and observe the laws of the Church; they may devote their efforts to having those laws executed, restrain the wicked attempts of rebels by punishments, and provide ecclesiastical judges with the assistance ordered toward preserving the canons. But who could ever dream, or even think, that any woman could exercise even the slightest authority and jurisdiction by judging ecclesiastical prerogatives, rights, canons, ordinances, and other matters of that kind, which were then under discussion?

Certainly all this would follow if, as Launoy foolishly argues, “what belonged to Leo had been common with Pulcheria, and Pulcheria were thought to have participated in the abrogation of the canon by which the rights of the Church of Constantinople were sanctioned.” [Col. 1299A]

Therefore, if women must be entirely deprived of such rights by divine law, no opportunity could have remained for Bellarmine, that learned and Catholic man, to make that authority and jurisdiction common to Leo and the empress Pulcheria, on account of which the supreme pontiff writes:

> “With the piety of your faith joined to us, we set it aside, and by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter we utterly annul it by a general definition.”

Let Launoy, then, be ashamed that he wished to reason in this way. Let him attend to the fact that Saint Leo asked Pulcheria to participate in the abrogation of the canon for two reasons only, neither of which supports Launoy’s system.

The first was the piety of the empress’s faith, by which she had always, in many ways and by many means, labored to fulfill Leo’s wishes—both in matters concerning the cause of Flavian and of all the orthodox, and in the other matters directed toward the destruction and condemnation of the Eutychians.

The second was the preservation of ecclesiastical peace and tranquility, which would certainly have been entirely wounded and disrupted if the sixth Nicene canon, enacted for the pacification of all priests, had ultimately remained unjustly abolished.

Desiring to indicate this, the holy pontiff immediately added:

> “Obeying in all ecclesiastical laws which the Holy Spirit established for the pacification of all priests through the three hundred and eighteen bishops.” [Col. 1299B]

Leo therefore appeals to Pulcheria to abandon Anatolius’s side, whose cause she had begun to support with great zeal, and—while preserving the customary piety of faith by which she was joined to the apostolic see—not to resent his setting aside the consent of the Chalcedonian bishops when it opposed the rules of the holy canons established at Nicaea, and his annulling it by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter through a wholly general definition.

### 13

No one will deny that this is the genuine meaning of Leo’s words who observes that Pulcheria and Marcian had become arbiters and mediators between Anatolius and the Roman pontiff, so that canon 28 might be ratified and confirmed. [Col. 1299C]

Leo himself had learned very well from their letters that Marcian and Pulcheria had been predisposed in Anatolius’s favor. Yet, relying especially on Pulcheria’s piety of faith, by which she was united to the apostolic see, he did not hesitate most courteously to deny what she requested. Indeed, he sought to suppress and frustrate Anatolius’s excessive ambition completely by withdrawing the support through which Anatolius had sought to secure their patronage.

That Saint Leo had placed the greatest confidence in the piety of the empress Pulcheria is evident from the fact that he entrusted her with restraining and suppressing Anatolius’s ambition, closing his letter with these words:

> “And since it is your custom to labor for the peace and unity of the Church, restrain my brother Anatolius the bishop, whom your recommendation has made dear to me, in those matters that will benefit him; so that, just as the glory of your clemency is magnified by the restoration of faith, so it may also be proclaimed for the suppression of ambition.” [Col. 1299D]

We pass over in silence the other conclusions that might be drawn from these words to overthrow Launoy’s system still further, since each of our readers can understand with complete clarity how and in what matters Pulcheria was always united to the apostolic see by the piety of faith.

[519]

## CHAPTER IX

Saint Leo the Great restrained Anatolius’s ambition in many ways. Questions of theologians resolved from the writings of the holy pontiff. Paschasius Quesnellus’s evasions described, and the decree concerning the preservation of the privileges of provincial primacies explained. The case of Aetius and Andrew of Constantinople presented. Julian, bishop of Cos, appointed vicar of the apostolic see, whose duties and prerogatives Paschasius Quesnellus unjustly attempted to diminish.

### 1

We have already explained at sufficient length in the preceding sections that the efforts of Anatolius of Constantinople were entirely frustrated, although he flattered himself that he had obtained from the secular powers the most effective support for his ambition. [Col. 1300A]

He became aware of this not only through the reports of the emperor Marcian, the empress Pulcheria, and Julian, bishop of Cos, but also through the letters of the holy pontiff himself, who wrote back to him in a forceful style in order to restrain and suppress his ambition.

Anatolius ought then to have recognized above all the strength and firmness of Saint Leo’s character.
