Leo was moved by no consideration to violate or abolish those ecclesiastical laws that were most consistent with justice and equity, and that the Fathers, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, had wisely established at Nicaea for the good of the entire Church.

First, therefore, the holy pontiff recalls to Anatolius’s mind that admonition of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 28:

> “Do not pursue your desires, and turn away from your will,”

words that clearly convey a grave form of reproof.

Then he approaches him gradually and gently. On the one hand, he reproaches him with the earlier crimes into which he had fallen; on the other, he recalls the leniency and indulgence shown toward him, by which Leo had tolerated the defects of his ordination and the fault he had incurred by unjustly claiming for himself the ordination of the bishop of Antioch.

He says that he had tolerated these faults out of zeal for restoring the faith and out of love for concord. Nevertheless, he asserts that he could not patiently endure a new fault by which Anatolius attempted to violate the most sacred enactments of the Nicene canons, taking advantage of the favorable moment when the see of Alexandria had lost the privilege of second rank and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third dignity:

> “so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor.” [Col. 1300B]

Thus he reproaches Anatolius as guilty of a new schism. Anatolius had waited for an opportune moment, when the see of Alexandria was vacant because of Dioscorus’s deposition and when he had the bishop of Antioch allied with him because of the sacred ordination recently conferred upon him. He had then attempted something wholly unheard-of and unprecedented, turning a synod convened solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith into an opportunity for ambition. [Col. 1300C]

To forestall the excuses he offered—particularly his claim that the Council of Chalcedon had been twice as large as the Council of Nicaea—Leo asserts that Chalcedon could neither be compared with nor preferred to Nicaea, since the Nicene synod had been consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments were held by fewer or by more bishops, everything contrary to its constitutions was entirely devoid of authority.

He also does not conceal the way in which Anatolius had obtained that multitude of the Chalcedonian Fathers through a certain connivance, flatteries, and services, and had driven them to his opinion—circumstances that demonstrated that the Fathers had been seduced by Anatolius’s schemes into approving his excessively perverse and wicked efforts.

Hence the holy pontiff says:

> “This proud elevation tends toward the disturbance of the whole Church. It wished to abuse the synodal council in such a way that, having summoned the brethren only for the matter of the faith and completed the definition of the case that required attention, it might either lead them, by corrupting them, into consenting to him or compel them by frightening them.” [Col. 1300D]

Meanwhile, by making these accusations against Anatolius and condemning that canon as entirely devoid of force—since it had proceeded from men who lacked authority and from men who, either seduced by evil devices or deterred by threats, had by no means possessed complete freedom—Leo wished to indicate that even bishops assembled in general synods could undertake and define no cases other than those that the apostolic see of Peter had proposed for examination.

For this reason the pontifical legates used protests and objections to protect themselves from the drafting of a canon that wholly contradicted the instructions and directives of the apostolic see.

When Anatolius himself wished to complain about their protests in a letter to the holy pontiff, Leo rejected the complaint by replying:

> “In this matter, by writing these things to me, you commend them greatly. But you accuse yourself because you refused to obey them while contriving unlawful things, foolishly desiring what cannot be granted and is harmfully contrary to you—things that will never obtain the consent of any of us.” [Col. 1301A]

### 2

I must now dwell on these matters briefly, so that we may grasp the ancient doctrine of those times and understand whether the pontifical legates were granted merely the first place of honor in general synods, or also jurisdiction; whether synods had the legal power to establish anything when the legates of the Roman pontiffs protested and objected; and finally, whether a general synod itself possessed authority over the Roman pontiff.

Who does not see that these three questions—which, because of certain new doctrines spread improperly among the people, have sometimes tormented the minds of theologians—were clearly resolved here by Saint Leo?

For the pontifical legates were not merely placed ahead of the other bishops in honorific title; the other bishops were bound to obey them. We are not bound to obey anyone deprived of jurisdiction, nor can anything be legally valid and ratified to which the pontifical legates themselves oppose their protests and objections.

Indeed, the authority of the Roman pontiffs over general councils is explained all the more evidently by the fact that, when both Anatolius and the Fathers of Chalcedon insisted on adhering to the decree of another general synod drawn up sixty years earlier, Leo nevertheless rejected it. The Easterners themselves had supported that earlier decree, during the reign of the elder emperor Theodosius and in honor of the great Nectarius, in order to increase the honor, privileges, and prerogatives of the see of Constantinople. [Col. 1301B]

The holy pontiff asserts that this canon also lacked all effect because Leo’s predecessors had not approved it and because the Fathers of Constantinople had not sent it to the apostolic see to obtain confirmation. Saint Leo writes:

> “Your persuasion is in no way supported by the written decision of certain bishops made sixty years ago, as you boast, never transmitted by your predecessors to the knowledge of the apostolic see. From its very beginning you have wished to prop up with late and useless supports something that was already precarious and long since collapsed, eliciting from the brethren an appearance of consent which, wearied by shame, they might offer to their own injury.” [Col. 1301C]

All writers who have investigated why this canon, written sixty years earlier at the Council of Constantinople, had remained without effect have labored over the question and arrived at differing opinions, reasoning in various ways—especially since our holy pontiff asserts:

> “Never transmitted by your predecessors to the knowledge of the apostolic see,”

while it is known from another source that the First Council of Constantinople had been received by the apostolic see.

Among those who raised this question was Paschasius Quesnellus, but he could have resolved it with little difficulty if he had attended to the holy pontiff’s manner of speaking. [Note: Quesnellus, in the notes and observations on this letter, vol. II, p. 484.] [521]

He says that the canon had fallen from the beginning and had long since collapsed, intending thereby to indicate that the principal bishops of the East, whose rights were being violated, had been unwilling to support this decree or enactment.

Indeed, we might perhaps suppose that they had protested by objections and had continued to oppose it, never at any time giving their assent—an assent which, worn down at last by Anatolius’s long and grievous pressures, they gave at the Council of Chalcedon, to the injury of their own sees. [Col. 1301D]

### 3

I consider this, and no other, to be the genuine interpretation of Saint Leo’s words; it can easily untie all the knots into which earlier writers fell.

For it cannot be asserted that the Roman pontiffs had no knowledge of the First General Council of Constantinople, since the synodal letter of its one hundred and fifty Fathers still survives. It was written to Pope Damasus, Ambrose of Milan, Britton of Trier, and other Western bishops. In it they mention only the heresies condemned at that synod; they do not contain a single word about the third canon that they had composed in favor of and in honor of the archbishops of Constantinople. [Col. 1302A]

Who, then, will believe that they wished or were able to conceal the decree of this canon from the apostolic see and from the other Western bishops to whom that synodal letter was addressed, if they had composed it with unanimous consent and without the tumult of protests and objections?

Therefore, if, according to Leo, they regarded that canon from its beginning as precarious and collapsed, it was also entirely without effect among the Easterners. The Alexandrians and Antiochenes did not allow the rights of their Churches to be infringed and violated, nor did they at that time give even the appearance of consent.

This interpretation of ours completely overturns Quesnellus’s contrary opinion. He preferred to imagine that the synodal letter mentioned not a word about the canon concerning the rights and privileges of the see of Constantinople, which they knew would be wholly displeasing to the Westerners:

> “Either they were persuaded that, when the Eastern bishops decreed something concerning the administration of the Eastern Churches, the consent of the Westerners was by no means necessary; or else,” he adds, “it was sufficient if they arranged for whatever concerned the symbol of faith against the heretics to come to the Westerners’ attention. For since the cause of faith is common not only to all bishops but also to the Catholic laity, and is the proper subject matter of an ecumenical council, it is necessary that everything relating to it become known to all, and especially to the head of all the bishops, whose principal duty it is, from the watchtower of the apostolic see, to oversee the preservation and purity of the faith.” [Col. 1302B]

But everyone can understand how full of errors and deceptions this reasoning of Quesnellus is. We consider it unnecessary to refute them one by one at present, since throughout these writings of ours we have repeatedly proved that the decrees even of general synods are entirely without force unless they are approved and confirmed by the consent of the apostolic see; that the apostolic see alone can dispense from ancient canons established by the Church; and, finally, that the same apostolic see has a special care and diligence for all the Churches of the East even in matters concerning discipline and ecclesiastical governance. This is made perfectly clear by the six hundred examples set forth in these *Exercises*, as well as by others to be presented below. [Col. 1302C]

### 4

Saint Leo observed that, beyond usurping for himself the second place to the injury of the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, Anatolius had also wished to tear down the rights of provincial primacies and deprive metropolitan bishops of privileges established in antiquity, thereby disturbing the universal Church. Leo therefore ordered this part of ecclesiastical discipline and governance to be restored and preserved in its entirety, commanding:

> “Let the rights of the provincial primacies not be overthrown, nor let metropolitan bishops be deprived of privileges established in antiquity. Let none of the dignity that the see of Alexandria earned through Saint Mark the evangelist, the disciple of blessed Peter, perish; and, while Dioscorus falls because of his obstinate impiety, let the splendor of so great a Church not be obscured by alien darkness.” [Col. 1302D]

Then, immediately discussing the rights of the see of Antioch, he commands:

> “Let the Church of Antioch also, in which, when blessed Peter the apostle preached, the Christian name first arose, remain in the order established by the fathers; and, placed in the third rank, let it never make itself inferior.”

Let the reader now compare these passages that we have cited from Leo with what Quesnellus fabricated, and judge whether the synodal decrees of the Easterners concerning the discipline and governance of those Churches were subject to the approval, annulment, and judgment of the Roman pontiffs.

Let him consider what credence should be given to Quesnellus’s stories, especially since, suffering from inconsistency, he was forced to admit that the rights of the provincial primacies had remained entirely abolished. [Col. 1303A]

> “Unless Saint Leo had firmly opposed the measures already begun, by which he at least achieved that the unrestrained ambition of that bishop should proceed no further.” [Note: Quesnellus, vol. II of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, in the notes and observations on Letter 80.] [Col. 1303D]

### 5

We have now been supplied with other most evident arguments concerning the authority of the Roman pontiffs over the discipline and administration of the Churches of the East, drawn from the letters of our holy pontiff Leo, written in the following year in the case of Aetius and Andrew, deacons of the Church of Constantinople.

Anatolius was excessively devoted to innovations—not only usurping the rights of others for himself, but also removing thoroughly orthodox men from their offices. He degraded Aetius, archdeacon of the Church of Constantinople, under the pretext of conferring honor, and transferred the administration of all ecclesiastical business and care to Andrew the Eutychian.

Saint Leo himself testified in his letter to Marcian and Pulcheria that Aetius had been one of those Constantinopolitan clerics who had constantly fought against the Nestorians and Eutychians and had always adhered to Saint Flavian. [Col. 1303B]

Moreover, Aetius’s piety in matters of faith and his diligence in carrying out affairs had long been known throughout the world, from the offices he had held—not only that of archdeacon but also that of chief of the notaries of the city of Constantinople—as the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon attest.

Anatolius therefore ordained him a presbyter under the appearance of granting him honor. But, as Saint Leo says, finding nothing in his faith to accuse and nothing in his morals to censure, he assigned him to celebrate the sacred mysteries in a cemetery far from the city, so that he might undergo a kind of punishment of exile.

Saint Leo commended him to the imperial piety, so that he might no longer be burdened by harmful intrigues:

> “The Lord,” he says, “has placed him, as I have learned, under your protection.”

Nor could anyone deny that Andrew’s ordination was wholly irregular—not only because of the Eutychian heresy to which he had adhered, but also because of the false accusations he had fabricated against Saint Flavian. It was therefore unlawful for Anatolius to promote him to higher orders and place him above the other Catholic clerics. [Col. 1303C]

Accordingly, the holy pontiff begged the emperor Marcian to rebuke Anatolius, who was out of harmony with his own profession and, as Leo says, had become excessively forgetful of the emperor’s testimony and favor:

> “Let him cease,” Leo adds, “to persecute Catholics; let him cease to crush those who were pleasing to Flavian of holy memory, and to choose the company of those whom Flavian condemned” (that is, the Eutychians). [Note: Saint Leo, Letter 84, chapter 2.] [Col. 1304D]

Finally, lest he appear to be abandoning responsibility for the affairs of the East in matters that might arise over time—as though it were not his duty to remain vigilant both in matters of faith and in other matters relating to the tranquility and discipline of the Churches—he appointed Julian, bishop of Cos, as vicar of the apostolic see. He wished Julian to be held in the favor of the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria:

> “Through his services, an image of my presence may be rendered to you. For, trusting in the sincerity of his faith, I have delegated to him my place against the heretics of our time; and, for the preservation of the Churches and of peace, I have required that he not be absent from your court.” [523]

The holy pontiff is entirely consistent with himself in the two following letters, written on the same day, one of which he sent to the empress Pulcheria and the other to Julian of Cos.

In the latter he added only two matters that he had not mentioned in the preceding letters. One concerned the Egyptian and Palestinian monks who were in turmoil; he did not know whether they were serving Eutychian impiety or whether they were lamenting without reconciliation that their bishop had been led into the impiety in which they knew he had departed from the truth of the Lord’s incarnation:

> “In a matter of such importance,” he says, “I wish to be more fully informed, so that suitable attention may also be devoted to correcting such people.”

He also added that he wished to learn what true reports were being conveyed to Julian concerning the peace of the Church of Alexandria. He wanted Julian to know, by sending copies, what letters he had directed to Proterius, the recently ordained bishop of that Church, and to those who had ordained him—that is, to the clergy. [Col. 1304A]

The other matter he considered necessary to add to this letter to Julian concerned the letter on the Lord’s incarnation, written to Flavian four years earlier, and the synodal acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

For the holy pontiff suspected that the celebrated letter he had sent through the deacon Basil had not been delivered to Julian. Moreover, since he had found the synodal acts insufficiently clear because of the difference of language, he therefore instructed him:

> “Have everything gathered together into a single book, translated into the Latin language in a most complete rendering, so that we may not be left in doubt about any part of the proceedings, and so that nothing may in any way remain ambiguous that your diligent effort has brought to full understanding.”

6. Quesnellus, in the second volume of the Works of Saint Leo, aptly noted that the origin and custom of papal envoys derived from this office then entrusted to Bishop Julian of Cos—something that some might perhaps readily concede. But when he adds that, following the learned men who had dealt with the matter reasonably well, he compares these envoys with the apocrisarii of the Eastern patriarchs, while preserving various distinctions between the two groups, we cannot wholly agree with him.

First, he says, apocrisarii were sent by the patriarchs to the court of the Eastern emperor when the seat of the empire had been transferred to Byzantium, whereas vicars were instituted somewhat before or somewhat after the Council of Chalcedon. Second, the patriarchs’ apocrisarii remained at court not on matters of faith but for the particular affairs of the Church or diocese, while the Roman envoys were ordered to reside there for the care of matters of faith. Third, the former were generally chosen from the ranks of deacons or priests for this office, whereas the latter were sometimes even chosen from among bishops, on account of the dignity of the Apostolic See, as is evident in Julian’s case.

The same Quesnellus further adds:

> “In instituting this vicar, therefore, Leo imitated the custom of the Eastern patriarchs, yet in many respects distinguished himself from them by virtue of his prerogative, completing and adorning this office with definite additions and enhancements. I believe that it will not be useless, nor foreign to the present subject, to examine this carefully.”

### 7

Although this Quesnellian doctrine may seem to bear some appearance of truth, it falters in many respects. It neither indicates the actual course of action of Saint Leo nor explains, as it should, the offices entrusted to Julian of Cos.

It falters first—and indeed collapses entirely—with regard to the origin of the apostolic envoys. For if we confuse the vicars of the Apostolic See with apostolic envoys, the letters of the Roman pontiffs—namely, of Pope Damasus, Siricius, Innocent I, Zosimus, and Celestine—show that the origin of both must be traced further back.

The distinguished D. Franciscus Antonius de Simeonibus treated this question of the vicars of the Apostolic See, their ancient institution and authority, with a great apparatus of learning. Following Holstenius’s Roman collection, he proves that Acholius had already exercised this office of vicar among the Illyrians before Pope Damasus, and that Anysius succeeded him, on the basis of Pope Innocent I’s letter to Rufus. But from where does Quesnellus derive the claim that the name and office of apocrisarius had already been indicated by the ancients?

The preceding doctrine also falters if we compare apostolic vicars with apocrisarii. For what could the word *apocrisarius* have signified among medieval writers except any legate, or minister sent by the pope or by bishops, as is found in the *Constitutiones*, Novel 123? By contrast, the name and office of apostolic vicar, since it implies acting in the place of another person, involved the responsibility of those to whom this office had been entrusted by the Roman pontiffs: they were to preside over the Churches of regions far removed from the city of Rome and immediately to confront all the evils that arose.

We gather this conception of pontifical vicars from many ecclesiastical records, which we consider it unnecessary to cite individually. But lest we seem to dwell only on Leo’s course of action—about which Quesnellus wrongly asserted that our holy pontiff imitated the institutions of the Eastern patriarchs—we gladly set forth the words of Pope Innocent I to Rufus, his vicar in Illyricum:

> “Therefore, since this grace proceeds divinely, and since the Churches separated from me by such long distances require care, I judge that the care and the causes, if any should arise among the Churches of Achaia, Thessaly [lacuna], should, with the assent of Christ the Lord, be entrusted to your prudence and gravity. Indeed, by his most sacred admonitions, we most earnestly impose this solicitude upon the foresight and strength of your sincere character.”

Nor is it true that apostolic vicars were instituted by the Roman pontiffs only for matters of faith. They were also appointed to deal with certain serious offenses which, as Pope Celestine says, “because we are farther away, do not reach us as they occurred, owing to the intervening passage of time. We wish all of these to be cut off through the intercession of our brother and fellow bishop Rufus, whose tested experience in all cases and actions of life is clearly evident.”

[Note: Saint Celestine I, in his letter to the bishops established throughout Illyricum.]

No sane person will deny that these words show that true and legitimate authority to act on behalf of the pontiff had been delegated to such vicars. That apocrisarii possessed this authority cannot be demonstrated by any certain testimony.

What offices, then, the holy pontiff Leo the Great had entrusted to Julian, bishop of Cos, we already indicated in the earlier book of this history, chapter 13, page 444; and we shall demonstrate them more fully from what we are about to say in the following chapter.

### 525. CHAPTER X

The ambition and course of action of Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, favoring the Eutychians, provokes new disturbances in the East. Saint Leo, admonished by the emperors Marcian and Leo, asserts that he has already confirmed the synod in matters of faith. Paschasius Quesnellus denies this, but his arguments are overturned. Finally, Saint Leo makes his will clear to everyone in new letters confirming the synod, and also attacks the deceitful practices of Anatolius.

[Col. 1305C]

### 1

The ambition of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and his deceitful course of action would have revived the sacrilegious audacity of the Eutychians—already suppressed at the Council of Chalcedon and by the sanctions of the holy pontiff—if the emperor Marcian and Julian, bishop of Cos and legate of the Apostolic See, had not disclosed to the holy pontiff Leo, with great concern, the new disturbances and schemes that had again arisen in the East.

The cause of these disturbances and upheavals, however, was not one but several. One arose from the protest of the pontifical legates, who vigorously opposed Anatolius’s attempts to usurp for himself the privileges of the other sees of the East. Another was the rumor spread throughout the East that the Council of Chalcedon had not been accepted by Saint Leo, since it had already become known that its twenty-eighth canon had been declared null and devoid of force and that the metropolitan primates of the provinces had been restored to their ancient rights.

From the abolition of this canon, therefore, many suspected and maintained that all the synodal acts had likewise been invalidated, so that they had no force even in matters pertaining to the decrees of faith.

The third cause was Anatolius’s conduct. He had been deeply displeased by the holy pontiff’s rebukes and severe rejection, through which Leo both reproached him for his crimes and restrained his ambition. Driven by anger and moved by shame, Anatolius sought to prevent public disgrace by concealing those letters of Saint Leo in which the pontiff declared that he embraced wholeheartedly the synodal acts celebrated at Chalcedon for the confirmation of the faith.

[Note: Saint Leo, Letter 80 to the Council of Chalcedon, chapters 1 and 2.]

At the same time, Leo wholly rejected whatever that wicked ambition had sought against the Nicene canons, with the diminution of the rights of the principal Churches.

Nevertheless, these rebukes and rejections by the holy pontiff did not shake Anatolius’s hope of obtaining the honor he desired. Indeed, when writing to Julian of Cos, the holy pontiff says:

> “We also wish you to know that, after our correction, Bishop Anatolius persists so recklessly in the audacity of his presumption that he summoned the Illyrian bishops in order that they might subscribe to him.”

[Note: Letter 88, chapter 5.]

This new attempt so disturbed the holy pontiff that he had already decided not to send his letters to Anatolius in the future, although, he says, Julian himself requested that this be done, “because we have seen that he does not wish to be corrected.”

### 2

I believe that Saint Leo suffered an even greater disturbance of mind when, after receiving new letters from the emperor Marcian, he learned that the entire East was in turmoil and astonished because the pontifical rescripts concerning the acts of Chalcedon had not reached it. For lack of these documents, all hearts remained wavering, wondering whether the acts of that council had been confirmed by the Apostolic See.

The emperor says:

> “We are greatly astonished that, after the synod celebrated at Chalcedon and the letters of the venerable bishops sent to Your Piety, in which they set forth the entire sequence of events conducted at the synod, no letters have by any means been issued by Your Holiness, although, once read in the holy Churches, they ought to have reached the knowledge of all.”

Marcian Augustus thus clearly indicated that an ancient custom was then in force: letters of the Apostolic See supplied definite evidence that synods had been celebrated and confirmed and were to be held as matters of unquestionable faith, without anyone calling them into doubt. He also wished to make clear that the synodal decrees possessed, and could possess, coercive force only after such letters confirming the synods had been read in the holy Churches and had reached the knowledge of all.

For it was an established rule of those times, received by all Catholics and heretics alike through usage and common consent, that ecumenical councils had to be decreed and confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiffs.

Hence Marcian adds:

> “Accordingly, a great scruple has been introduced into the minds of some who still adhere to the false opinion and depravity of Eutyches: whether Your Blessedness, who decreed the synod, has confirmed it.”

It must be believed that Quesnellus either failed to understand the force and meaning of these words or deliberately concealed them. Throughout his preparation of the Works of Saint Leo, he repeatedly attributes to the emperors the power to summon councils and maintains that synodal decrees possess force and authority of themselves, apart from any confirmation by the Apostolic See, as we shall say shortly.

Who does not see, then, that the emperor Marcian reasoned otherwise? He considered this confirmation by the Apostolic See so necessary that, without it, he believed the synodal acts themselves to be weak and devoid of force. For this reason he immediately adds a solemn and authoritative testimony of the pontifical will and judgment:

> “Therefore may Your Piety deign to issue letters by which all Churches and peoples may know that the acts of the synod have been approved by Your Blessedness.”

The emperor Marcian likewise asserted for the Roman pontiff the right to abolish and annul the canons and decrees of general councils. For after he had learned from the preceding letters received from Saint Leo that the pontiff wholly rejected those acts of Chalcedon that supported Anatolius’s ambition and endangered the rights of the other Churches, he abandoned the plan which he had earlier pursued with the empress Pulcheria and Julian of Cos, acting as mediator before the Apostolic See in order to increase the honor and prerogatives of the see of Constantinople.

He now addresses Saint Leo in this manner, and praises his steadfastness of mind in the highest terms because he had not permitted the ancient customs and order of the Churches to be abolished by any innovation. He says:

> “Your Holiness has admirably performed what befits the bishop of the Apostolic See: you have preserved the ecclesiastical canons and have allowed nothing to be abolished by any innovation of the ancient custom and order once established and steadfastly observed down to this day.”

At the end of this letter Marcian insists even more strongly that Saint Leo should make known everywhere, as soon as possible, through his letters that—as he says—he clearly regarded the Council of Chalcedon as approved, so that no suspicion might remain for those eager for disagreement and dissension concerning the judgment of Your Holiness.

### 3

Paschasius Quesnellus translated this letter, which we have just summarized section by section, from the Greek and Latin of the Bodleian Oxford manuscript into his second edition, and was the first of all to publish it. Nevertheless, I may reasonably suspect either that he did not examine it carefully or that he deliberately omitted from his annotations what it contains.

As to the first point, who could ever believe that he examined this letter when he wrote:

> “The approval of this synod arose only from the occasion of a calumny: namely, lest some person’s deceitful pretense should claim to possess its judgment, and lest, through malicious interpreters, it should seem doubtful whether he approved what had been established concerning the faith at the Council of Chalcedon.”

He then adds:

> “He therefore did not write this letter of approval so that the sacred decrees might not lack force, but so that he himself might not be branded through contempt for the venerable synod; so that those who opposed the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon might not glory under his leadership; and finally, so that he might not seem to contradict the imperial will, which he openly professes must be obeyed in every way.”

Thus Quesnellus writes in his notes on Letter 87, addressed to the bishops who attended the Council of Chalcedon.

He finally summons John Launoy to the defense of his position, in Part II of his letter to the distinguished man Jacob Bevilaqua, where Launoy dealt with this confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon.

[Note: Quesnellus, volume II, notes and observations on Letter 87, page 496.]

That Quesnellus deliberately omitted from his annotations the contents of Marcian’s preceding letter is absolutely certain, since he adorned it with no notes or observations, lest he be forced to retract what he had written against the authority of the Apostolic See in decreeing and confirming synods.

Who, however, can conceal what Quesnellus falsely fashioned and wrote against manifest truth? He asserts that the confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon arose only from the occasion of a calumny, whereas Marcian writes:

> “We are greatly astonished that, after the synod celebrated at Chalcedon and the letters of the venerable bishops sent to Your Piety . . . no letters were by any means issued by Your Holiness, although, once read in the holy Churches, they ought to have reached the knowledge of all.”

Marcian’s astonishment, therefore, could certainly not have arisen from an unusual matter, omitted because the practice had not yet been adopted. It arose from a violated custom by which the Roman pontiffs, after receiving the synodal acts, sent to the fathers of the synod encyclical letters confirming the decrees or canons. These letters were publicly read in the Churches so that the coercive force of the decrees might reach the knowledge of all.

That this confirmation was considered necessary is clearly indicated by the final words: “they ought to have reached the knowledge of all.”

Moreover, what calumny could have moved Leo to undertake an unusual action and Marcian to request it? Was it perhaps because, since the matter concerned only the decrees of faith, Leo was being suspected of Eutychianism or Nestorianism, so that he had to give public testimony to his faith?

Away with such a fabrication—one not even invented by fools! Had he not, over the course of many years, endured grievous and strenuous labors to extinguish both heresies? All his letters, sent in every direction and especially to the Easterners, bore witness to this. Marcian and the empress Pulcheria also bore witness to it, so that there could never have been any room for calumny.

### 4

One must next wonder that Quesnellus asserts that Leo did not write that letter to the Council of Chalcedon in order to give force to the council’s sacred decrees, “but so that he himself might not be branded through contempt for the venerable synod; so that those who opposed the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon might not glory under his leadership; and finally, so that he might not seem to contradict the imperial will.”

Only someone who had never examined the Works of Saint Leo or ever cast his eyes upon the acts of Chalcedon could have dreamed up such things.

What? Did not all the fathers of the Council of Chalcedon earnestly ask Leo to honor their judgment with his decrees? They say:

> “We therefore ask you: honor our judgment with your decrees; and just as we have added our agreement to the Head in what is good, so may Your Eminence complete for the sons what is fitting.”

What? Did not Anatolius himself, hoping that the acts of Chalcedon would receive approval and stability through Leo’s decrees, believe that they ought to obtain complete and consummate force from the Apostolic See? The synod, he says, furnished such an example in relation to Your Holiness, so that we might obtain whatever approval and stability we can; and we pray, most holy one, that this may be granted by you.

Marcian’s similar words to the same supreme pontiff, written scarcely after the general council had concluded, make the point equally clear:

> “And we ask that Your Reverence also command that what the holy synod has established be observed perpetually.”

What else can this mean? Those statutes, which require another’s command in order to bind perpetually and possess coercive force, obtain strength and stability from the one who commands their observance.

Quesnellus therefore acted very badly in the service and protection of his lost cause when he wrote that the confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon arose only from the occasion of a calumny, so that Saint Leo the Great might not be branded, and that it could not have given force and authority to the synod’s statutes.

### 5

Shall we finally believe that Saint Leo wrote letters confirming the synod so that he might not seem to contradict the imperial will, which he openly professes must be obeyed in every way? Or shall we at least accept as certain and infallible Launoy’s doctrine, to whom Quesnellus appealed as his forerunner and teacher of great authority?

Nonsense—mere nonsense!

Saint Leo always paid due honor to the powers of this world and did not resist complying with their wishes in matters that did not conflict with divine and ecclesiastical rights. But whenever the matter concerned the violation of canons, the endurance of some injury in matters pertaining to the universal and supreme administration of the Church, or anything that might redound to the disgrace of his office and the Apostolic See, he never wished to obey the wishes of the emperors.

Quesnellus would have understood this clearly and distinctly if he had not concealed the steadfastness and courage with which Saint Leo opposed the petitions of Marcian and Pulcheria, who repeatedly begged and implored that the splendor of the imperial city be increased.

So far was he from complying with their wishes that he abolished and annulled the canon concerning the privileges of the Church of Constantinople, removing from Anatolius the rights of ordination that he had usurped.

Marcian and Pulcheria, instructed by Christian piety that they had been appointed to rule only over human and civil affairs, were not in the least moved by the severe rejection they received from Leo. That rejection certainly redounded to the disgrace of the two august rulers, since they desired just as strongly as Anatolius to increase the honor and splendor of the royal city.

Moreover, in what sense can Quesnellus’s general assertion be true—that “Saint Leo did not wish to contradict the imperial will, which he openly professes must be obeyed in every way”—if Leo had already fulfilled the duties of his office and confirmed the Council of Chalcedon in matters pertaining to the decrees of faith?

### 6

Regarding this confirmation of the synod, already made by Saint Leo, there is no need to consult Launoy, a subverter of pontifical rights, to whom Quesnellus referred his readers. Let us instead run through the letters of the holy pontiff.

First, in Letter 88 to Julian, bishop of Cos, Leo admits that he had already fulfilled what the emperor Marcian had suggested to him:

> “That I should send writings to all the brethren who attended the Council of Chalcedon, by which I might demonstrate that I approved what our holy brethren had confirmed concerning the rule of faith.”

This was done, he explains, on account of those who wished to make the council’s statutes appear weak or doubtful as an opportunity for concealing their perfidy, because they had not been strengthened by the judgment of his consent.

What else could Leo have done? If, under some false appearance and a new pretext not sanctioned by any custom, Nestorians or Eutychians had wished to seize an opportunity to conceal their perfidy, arguing that the council’s statutes appeared weak or doubtful because they had not been strengthened by the judgment of pontifical consent, would Leo not have rejected this argument as deriving from a false premise? Would he not have declared such arrogance unjust?

Certainly he would have done so. But the holy pontiff answered differently, saying that long before, after the return of the brethren whom he had sent in his place, he had already given letters to the bishop of Constantinople:

> “So that, if he had wished to publish them, it could abundantly have been recognized from them how greatly I approved what they had decreed concerning the faith.”

This letter, in which he asserts that he had approved the synodal decrees of faith, must be dated, together with the return to Rome of the pontifical legates, to May of the preceding year, during the consulship of the distinguished man Herculanus.

[Note: Letters of Leo 78, 79, 80, and 81.]

That calumny, however, which arose from malicious interpreters and raised doubts about whether Leo approved what had been established concerning the faith at the Council of Chalcedon, was heard and spread among the people in the following year, in the month of February, when Opilio was already serving as consul.

[Note: Letter of Marcian Augustus to Saint Leo, volume I, in Quesnellus, page 307; Leo’s Letter 88 to Julian of Cos, Letter 89 to Marcian, and Letter 90 to Pulcheria.]

From where, then, does Quesnellus conclude that the letter of approval was written by Leo “so that he himself might not be branded through contempt for the venerable synod, and so that those who opposed the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon might not glory under his leadership”?

### 7

I am now ashamed to have lingered so long in refuting Quesnellian nonsense. For Leo himself, in the letters noted at the foot of the page, attributes the origin of all the disturbances, suspicions, and false rumors to Anatolius’s evil practices.

When the letters of the year 452 mentioned above, confirming the synod and addressed to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, contained a reply restraining his ambition, Anatolius, Leo says, wished it to remain unknown “what I thought concerning the fraternal constitutions, so that it might not at the same time become known what I had written in response in defense of the inviolable authority of the Nicene canons.”

He used almost identical wording when writing to the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria. In those letters he admits that, when Bishop Lucian returned to Constantinople—he had already come to Rome with letters from Anatolius—he had sent writings to the bishop of Constantinople that clearly showed that he approved what had been defined concerning the Catholic faith at the aforementioned synod.

But, because in those same letters he had rebuked what had been wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod, Anatolius preferred to keep Leo’s congratulation silent rather than make his own ambition public.

Finally, he says to Pulcheria:

> “What I had written could have reached the knowledge of all through the bishop of Constantinople, to whom I had generously disclosed my joy, unless he had preferred to keep my joy silent rather than have the rejection of his ambition made public.”

Thus, after attacking Anatolius, Leo composed encyclical letters confirming the synod. In order that they might reach the knowledge of all priests and Churches, he invoked the command and authority of Marcian himself, hoping that, once every opportunity for dissent had been removed, the peace and truth of apostolic teaching would reign everywhere.

## 530. CHAPTER XI

Saint Leo devotes every effort to extinguishing the remnants of the Eutychians. He instructs Maximus of Antioch to preserve the rights of his Church. A serious controversy arises concerning the Paschal cycle. The emperor Marcian dies, and Leo, a tribune, is raised to the imperial office. The sedition of the Eutychians against Proterius of Alexandria and against all Catholics, and their efforts to abolish the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1310B]

### 1

Much would still remain for me to write if I wished, following an ordered and strict method and preserving the sequence of Saint Leo’s letters, to report individually everything he accomplished during the remaining years of his pontificate for the government, welfare, and security of the universal Church.

But since various matters arise that seem far removed from our present purpose, and since the adversaries with whom we have dealt in the preceding sections provide no serious motives for undertaking new controversies, we shall narrate in a running account what the same holy pontiff necessarily established and commanded for extinguishing the remnants of the Eutychian heresy.

In the first place, many monks and archimandrites of monasteries had been displeased by the condemnation of Eutyches and were attempting to stir seditions and riots among the people. Therefore the holy pontiff applied himself through his recommendations to having their ignorant madness restrained by an edict of the emperor Marcian, and to having the superiors of the monasteries rebuked by the empress Pulcheria.

[Note: Letter 88 to Julian of Cos, chapter 2, and Letter 89 to Marcian, chapter 2.]

Since such seditions were chiefly stirred up by monks while they delivered sacrilegious sermons against the faith, Leo also appealed to the imperial authority so that in the future they might be prohibited from the office of preaching, lest—as he says—they dare to claim for themselves what belongs to priests.

Finally, he hoped to kindle the emperor’s zeal against the Alexandrian parricides, so that he might do what he understood would benefit ecclesiastical peace.

[Note: Letter 91 to Julian of Cos, chapter 2, and the following Letter 92 to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 6.]

### 2

He also judged that provision should be made for the affairs and rights of the Church of Antioch. Although he was not unaware of the purity and greatness of Maximus’s faith, he nevertheless recalled to his mind the prerogatives of that see and how the Christian faith, announced to the whole world through the special teaching of Saint Peter, had been entrusted to the Churches of Antioch and Rome.

The holy pontiff therefore trusted that Maximus would firmly adhere to the institutions of Saint Peter, the founder. He not only encouraged Maximus to repel every Nestorian and Eutychian madness, but also commended to him all the Churches of the East subject to him, so that they might not be shaken or corrupted by wicked and unjust errors:

> “Since it is fitting that you resist these things with priestly authority, and that you frequently inform us through reports concerning the progress of the Churches and what is taking place.”

In the same way, he urged Maximus to become a participant in the Apostolic See, carefully preserving the privileges of the third see, which must never be diminished by any ambition. A little later he adds:

> “For although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees remain. Although rivals may perhaps bring some disturbance against them, they cannot diminish their dignity.”

That Leo wished here to criticize Anatolius’s wicked ambition and persuade Maximus to oppose with all his strength whatever could infringe or diminish the privileges of the Church of Antioch is also made clear by the following words:

> “Therefore, whenever Your Belovedness believes that something must be done for the privileges of the Church of Antioch, take care to explain it in your own letters, so that we may be able to respond fully and appropriately to your consultation.”

But it is my opinion that Saint Leo may also have wished gently to rebuke Maximus, bishop of Antioch, and make him more cautious in the future in securing observance of the Nicene statutes.

In the year 450, Maximus had been too ready to indulge the efforts and ambition of Eustathius of Berytus, to the destruction of the Church of Tyre and its metropolitan, Photius. For this matter he was accused at the Council of Chalcedon in its fourth session, as we saw in chapter 4 of this book, page 468.

For Saint Leo, in the subsequent chapter of his letter, setting forth a general rule, says:

> “If anything has been attempted by anyone against the statutes of the Nicene canons in any synod, or appears for a time to have been extorted, it can cause no prejudice to inviolable decrees. It will be easier to dissolve agreements of whatever disagreements than to corrupt the rules of the aforementioned canons in any respect.”

In reviewing this rule, therefore, as we have said, it is highly probable that Saint Leo wished to criticize the excessive readiness or indulgence of Maximus of Antioch, by which he allowed Eustathius to withdraw himself from the metropolitan jurisdiction of the Church of Tyre, to which the Church of Berytus had been subject from its earliest foundation.

Our conjecture is strengthened by the words of both Eustathius and Photius recorded in the fourth session, which we have already discussed above.

### 3

In that same year a serious controversy arose concerning the celebration of Easter. To settle it, Leo says that, mindful of the stewardship entrusted to him, he sought the assistance of the emperor Marcian’s efforts, so that in an observance that is always subject to variation according to precise calculation, no error might be incurred.

[Note: Letter 94 to Marcian Augustus.]

He asserts that responsibility for the Paschal cycle had formerly been entrusted to the bishop of Alexandria. But he adds:

> “The blessed Theophilus, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, after having collected into a numerical sequence one hundred years of this observance, determined that the Paschal feast of the seventy-sixth year should be kept in a manner quite different from what the others had decreed.”

He reviews the causes of this entire great controversy. Then, so that the changing lunar cycle might not provide an occasion for error, he addresses the emperor in these words:

> “I beseech Your Clemency to deign to offer your assistance, so that the Egyptians, or any others who appear to possess definite knowledge of this calculation, may resolve the scruple of this concern, and so that the general observance may be directed to that day which neither abandons the rule of the ancestral constitutions nor wanders beyond the prescribed limits.”

He also asks Julian, bishop of Cos and vicar of the Apostolic See, to investigate this same question carefully and to write back as soon as possible.

[Note: Letter 91.]

The great concern of our holy pontiff in defining those rites pertaining to the solemnity of the Paschal feast, so that all the faithful might conform to the same observance, is disclosed not only by the two preceding letters. It is also indicated by the Paschal canon carefully composed for this purpose by Victor of Aquitaine.

At the command of the same holy pontiff, Hilary, archdeacon of the Roman Church, commissioned Victor to put the Paschal cycle into tables and, after explaining the causes of the disagreement that arose from different methods of calculation, finally to make clear what was more consistent with the truth.

Victor of Aquitaine—or, as others prefer, Victorinus—was a man endowed with the highest piety and highly practiced in mathematical calculations. He undertook and perfectly completed the work assigned to him by Hilary.

The distinguished Aegidius Bucherius, S.J., was the first to publish it, adorned with highly learned commentaries; and we have once again corrected it against the readings of the Vatican manuscripts, so that it may occupy its proper place among the Works of Leo.

I do not think that this decision of ours can be disapproved by those who at some point examine the aforementioned canon. For, besides the fact that Victor composed it out of a desire to obey the pontifical commands, he also resolved the very serious question concerning Easter, marked in the ancient cycles by a double designation, by writing:

> “This is not determined by my judgment, but has been preserved for the peace of the Churches by the choice of the Apostolic Pontiff. Thus I would not omit what belonged to my office, while the matter would be placed within the judgment of him who presides over the universal Church: namely, which days should chiefly be assigned to the solemnity under such circumstances.”

[Col. 1312B]

Proterius of Alexandria, recently appointed to govern that Church, also devoted his labor to resolving this very serious question at the command of the emperor Marcian. Writing to our holy pontiff, he asserts that Theophilus’s hundred-year calendar had been corrupted by the fault of a copyist or defective manuscript. Therefore, he says, one must never depart from the hundred-year cycle of that same most blessed father and our bishop Theophilus, which agrees entirely with the pages of the ancients.

[Note: Letter of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Saint Leo, chapter 1.]

### 4.

I now understand that, mentally diverted from the purpose I had established, I have wandered beyond the boundaries of the Eutychian heresy and, as though heedlessly following the order and numbering of Leo’s letters, have fallen into that most serious question which long and greatly troubled the pontiff’s mind, and which contains within itself exceedingly difficult knots, not easily untied even by those diligently practiced in mathematical calculations and computations.

That this question gravely agitated the pontiff’s mind may be inferred from various other letters of the same man [Note: St. Leo mentions this controversy concerning the Paschal feast in Letters 100 and 102 to Julian, bishop of Cos. He mentions it again in Letter 105 to the Emperor Marcian, and in Letter 109 to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.].

As for the affairs of Anatolius, the surviving remnants of the Eutychians, and their wicked machinations, it remains finally for us to describe them. Anatolius, after being severely rebuked by the Emperor Marcian, was brought back to a better disposition. St. Leo promises that he will receive him again into his favor, provided that he satisfy the canons and not overturn the rights of priests.

Once he had been assured of this promise, Anatolius did not delay writing his letters to the holy pontiff. In them he most humbly complained about the interruption of their correspondence, which had brought him a considerable increase of anxiety and grief, since he had desired to enjoy the pontiff’s utterances more frequently. He declared himself ready, through obedience, to fulfill whatever appeared pleasing to Your Holiness’s altogether perfect judgment.

As further evidence of this, he first stated that Aetius, having been removed from the ministry of archdeacon, had now been restored to his former position and ecclesiastical honor [Col. 1312D]; but that Andrew, who had been honored with the dignity of archdeacon, had now been separated from the Church and deprived of his rank because he had fought on Eutyches’ side against St. Flavian—although, through the many excuses and personal subscriptions that had been appended to Your Holiness’s letter, they had previously appeared to have made satisfaction.

In this letter he also offered two other proofs of his repentance. The first concerned the peace and complete union that he desired henceforth to have with the Roman pontiff Leo and to preserve by an inviolable bond. The second concerned his previous guilt in seeking advancement [Col. 1313A], which he removed from himself and transferred to the zeal of his clergy and of the Eastern bishops.

He added one point that utterly overturns the theories of Quesnell and Launoy: he affirmed that the entire force and confirmation of the acts of Chalcedon had been reserved to the authority of the Apostolic See. “And since likewise”—so that I may not seem foolishly to invent Anatolius’s words, I quote them—“since likewise the entire force and confirmation of the acts has been reserved to the authority of Your Blessedness” [Note: Anatolius’s letter to St. Leo is found in volume I of Quesnell’s edition, p. 325.].

### 5.

After receiving this letter, St. Leo did not delay replying to Anatolius. Without diminishing anything of the pontifical majesty, he recalled to his mind the firm and unchangeable purpose by which he ought to devote himself to the common care of grace, so that he would cause himself no anxiety.

He added that he had wished to have as a partner in ecclesiastical affairs a man such as many of Anatolius’s predecessors had shown themselves to be toward the Apostolic See. Among these he expressly named John Chrysostom, Atticus, Proclus, and Flavian.

He further praised Anatolius for correcting certain abuses in the duties of clerics [Col. 1313B], for restoring the presbyter Aetius to favor and affection, and for removing Andrew from the office of archdeacon.

Nevertheless, wishing to show some indulgence toward those who had once been infected with the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies and had fought against Flavian, he instructed Anatolius to grant pardon to them if they condemned the execrable doctrines and produced evidence of correction. For he said:

> “As for Andrew, who was reasonably deprived of the office of archdeacon, and Euphratas, who, as I have learned, proved himself a wicked accuser of Flavian of holy memory, if, in fully written professions, they condemn not only the Eutychian but also the execrable Nestorian doctrine, you shall ordain as presbyters those whose pardon ought to be granted once they have been corrected.”

A little farther on, speaking of others stained by the same error, he added:

> “If they ask for pardon with a similar profession and with satisfaction, they should be restored to their own orders, admitting to the highest offices only those who are shown to have been free from every error” [Note: Letter 106, chapters 1 and 2.].

### 6.

While preserving the majesty of pontifical authority, he then proceeded to discuss the interruption of their correspondence, which had been caused by the attempt at advancement, when he had utterly annulled and abolished the notorious Canon 28 by the authority of St. Peter.

Desiring greater sincerity from Anatolius in acknowledging his fault, and greater effectiveness in detesting it, he openly admitted that the fault in question could not be transferred solely to the counsels of the clergy of Constantinople. “This,” he said, “could not have been attempted without your consent. For just as one sins through evil persuasion, so one also sins through an evil confession.”

He then added that it was not unwelcome to him that what could no longer be pleasing was displeasing to Anatolius. Following this conviction, Leo promised him the restoration of his former favor, especially with the testimony of the Christian prince supporting it.

The holy pontiff agreed with himself on this point in another letter written on the same day to the Emperor Marcian, expressly affirming that he had received Anatolius back into his favor “because in every respect it pleases me to obey Your Clemency.” He further added:

> “Let him show himself affectionate and faithful, and let him henceforth never separate himself by any change from that charity which I promise him, joining to himself in sincere affection those whom we have approved as defenders of the Catholic faith” [Note: St. Leo, Letter 107, chapter 3.].

Meanwhile, looking to the greater good and tranquility of the Church of Constantinople, he asked the emperor to ensure that the monk Carosus—exceedingly ignorant and exceedingly perverse—would no longer, “as I have learned,” exercise his poisons through the benefit of Your Piety. Carosus was seeking, with excessive boldness, to revive the extinguished efforts of the heretics by defending the Eutychian perfidy and violating synodal authority.

St. Leo’s petition was neither useless nor without the desired effect [Col. 1314A]. For in the following year, 456, on the third day before the Ides of February, he returned due thanks to the same Emperor Marcian because he had expelled Carosus and his associate Dorotheus from their ancient monasteries. They had supported, to the destruction of many, errors condemned for their heretical perversity. The emperor had ordered them to live among people whom they could not harm—“which, I hope, will be a remedy for many whom you have freed from perverse teachers.”

Finally, St. Leo believed that Carosus had expelled the poison of heresy through a sincere confession of faith, according to the report he had received from Julian of Cos [Note: St. Leo, Letter 113, chapter 1.].

534 Nevertheless, the same letter informs us that Carosus was still deprived of ecclesiastical communion because of certain disagreements with Anatolius. I do not think that it belongs to the purpose of our undertaking either to investigate or to report the origin of these disagreements, since we intend only to bring to completion those Exercises on the Works of the Lord Leo that we have recognized as pertaining to the Eutychian heresy and its history.

### 7.

I would suffer the greatest injustice if those who attend to my present method of writing were to blame me for entirely omitting the narration of that most grievous calamity inflicted upon the Roman Western Empire, by which the city itself was captured, burned, and plundered by the Vandals [Col. 1314B].

This disaster affected the holy pontiff’s mind with such sadness and grief that at that time he could not devote himself at all to Eastern affairs. Indeed, as Quesnell himself testifies, after all correspondence had been interrupted, Leo devoted himself entirely to repairing the devastation of the city and its churches, and was obliged to spend nearly a full year assisting the needs of his afflicted homeland.

Yet in his letters St. Leo makes no mention of this calamity inflicted upon the city by the Vandals. He described it only briefly in the addresses he delivered to the Roman people.

We have nevertheless already observed, from his letters to the Emperor Marcian and to the Empress Pulcheria when he was being urged to attend the Council of Chalcedon, that he feared this event and had foretold it, in a certain prophetic spirit, five years earlier.

Nor did this barbarian sack of the city alone torment the pontiff’s mind. His grief was greatly increased by the death of the Emperor Marcian, an excellent ruler who, as long as he lived, depended entirely upon the holy pontiff’s intimations, admonitions, and suggestions, never once departing from his wishes.

Marcian therefore departed this life after having spent six years, as well as six months and two or three days, in the empire. Leo, the tribune, succeeded him in the imperial office by the common agreement of the Senate.

Marcian’s death, however, gave the Eutychians who were hiding in Egypt and in other Eastern provinces an opportunity to attack the Catholic bishops. They most audaciously insisted that the acts of Chalcedon should be reconsidered and that a new council should be held to debate the matter of the faith.

The Alexandrians became more audacious than the others. They had always remained attached even to Dioscorus, although he was dead, and they especially hated the holy bishop Proterius, a Catholic adorned with every kind of virtue [Col. 1314D].

They did not shrink from attacking him and sacrilegiously murdering him. Having stirred up the greatest disturbances throughout Egypt and also in the Church of Constantinople, they flattered themselves that they could achieve their intended goal if they obtained some support from the new emperor and his ministers.

But they were deceived in their wicked hope. When Leo learned that the tribune Leo had been appointed to rule the Eastern Empire, he congratulated him by letter and added his supplications that he provide protection for the interests of the Catholic faith, lest the Church of Alexandria, harassed and attacked by the fury of the heretics, be brought to complete destruction.

“This work,” he said, “which is suited to Your Virtues and Glory, will quickly receive from God the favorable outcome it deserves, if you permit the holy Council of Chalcedon, confirmed concerning the incarnation of the Lord Christ, to be disturbed by no reconsideration” [Col. 1315A].

Nor were all the efforts of the Eutychians unknown to the Emperor Leo. After Marcian’s death they had attempted, through many and varied schemes, to surround the new emperor and bring him to the opinion that the Council of Chalcedon should be abolished. But the emperor’s great prudence and religious zeal had rendered their wicked attempts completely futile even before the holy pontiff made his supplication.

St. Leo had learned of this from the reports of many people. He therefore now begged Leo not to be moved from such steadfastness of mind, but to persist in it more firmly, adding:

> “Therefore, what you have willingly seen must be denied to them: it is glorious for you, at my supplication, to grant to the universal Church, and to preserve immutably and perpetually, that those things which according to the Gospel of Christ and the truth of apostolic preaching have been strengthened throughout all past ages by one faith and one understanding may no longer be overturned by any proceeding.”

He finally concluded the letter by urging the emperor to provide for the restoration of peace in the Church of Alexandria and “to order that, through Catholic priests, such a bishop be appointed that nothing blameworthy can be found either in the integrity of his conduct or in his profession of faith” [Note: St. Leo the Great, Letter 115 to the Emperor Leo, chapters 1 and 2.].

### 8.

St. Leo clearly indicates that the preceding letter to the new emperor had been written at the persuasion of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, by replying to Anatolius himself.

From him Leo had received a full account of what had occurred at Alexandria to the disgrace of the Christian religion, and of what the wicked Eutychians were attempting in order to abolish the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon—but also that their plots had been vigorously repulsed by the emperor himself.

Leo therefore praised Anatolius for the care he had devoted to the good of the Churches, in urging that imperial assistance be sought through pontifical prayers, so that the remedies necessary both for healing the wounds and for breaking the audacity of the heretics might be applied [Col. 1315C].

He also reminded him of the letters already written to the emperor for this purpose. Finally, he added:

> “It remains for Your Fraternity, taking advantage of the presence of the most faithful emperor, to strive with greater earnestness to entreat him that the statutes of the Council of Chalcedon be preserved without any reconsideration.”

### 9.

We must now report the cause and authors of such great disturbances, so that we may understand what follows concerning the history of the Eutychians and explain the matters in which the apostolic solicitude of St. Leo was engaged.

The deacon Liberatus narrated the whole sequence of events. He said that after the Council of Chalcedon Dioscorus had been compelled to live in exile in the city of Gangra, and that the bishops and clergy of Alexandria had been ordered, by the authority of the Council of Chalcedon and by the imperial command of Marcian, to elect a new bishop, as we ourselves have also noted from the Acts of Chalcedon.

“Therefore,” said Liberatus, “the nobles assembled in order to elect one who was worthy of the episcopate in life and speech . . . . When considerable doubt had arisen about this matter, and the citizens wished to ordain no one at all lest they appear adulterers”—since Dioscorus was still alive—“the judgment of all finally turned to Proterius. Dioscorus himself had commended the Church to him and had made him archpresbyter” [Note: Liberatus the deacon, chapter 19 of his *Breviary*.].

The election and subsequent ordination of Proterius as bishop of Alexandria therefore became the cause of a very great schism. Its authors tried to conceal their secret machinations by pretenses for as long as Marcian remained alive and emperor.

After Marcian’s death, however, the Egyptians believed that the faith could easily be overthrown, and they stirred up the rebellion that they had long harbored in their minds. For Timothy Aelurus and the deacon Peter Mongus, both ordained by Dioscorus, ran throughout the city and began winning over the populace, which was eager for novelty.

After gathering crowds of heretics who followed Dioscorus, and taking along two bishops who had already been deprived of the priesthood for their open heresy, Timothy Aelurus, the leader of the sedition, was ordained bishop and invaded Proterius’s see, expelling the legitimate shepherd.

Proterius, wishing to escape the fury of the Eutychians, withdrew into the baptistery. But Timothy’s attendants did not shrink from invading the place. They killed Proterius himself, dragged his body through the streets with a hook, tore it apart, threw it out, and burned his remains, scattering his ashes to the winds.

The deacon Liberatus narrates the whole matter in chapter 15, adding: “From this Timothy onward, there began to be two bishops in Alexandria.” Consequently, the people and clergy were divided into two opposing factions: some defended the Council of Chalcedon, while others pressed the Emperor Leo more vehemently for the abolition of the Council of Chalcedon.

But Liberatus adds that the emperor, reading the petitions of both parties and considering it excessively burdensome to force priests to undertake such a long journey—the Eutychians were requesting a new council—when age, illness, or poverty prevented many of them from bearing this burden, judged that they could not be assembled.

He therefore wrote to the bishops of the individual cities concerning both matters: the ordination of Timothy Aelurus and the petitions made to him for the abolition of the Council of Chalcedon.

By divine providence, all the bishops who had assembled at the Council of Chalcedon immediately replied without the slightest hesitation: the Council of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it held no other faith than that established by the Council of Nicaea; and Timothy was not only not to be counted among the bishops, but was also to be deprived of the Christian name.

I do not know, however, why Liberatus, while faithfully describing this preceding sequence of events, completely omitted to report what St. Leo had done for the inviolable observance of the decrees of Chalcedon, for removing Timothy Aelurus from the Alexandrian see [Col. 1316C], and for abolishing that dreadful schism which afflicted that Church and was bringing the Catholic faith to destruction. For the acts of our pontiff could not have been unknown to Liberatus.

### 10.

Meanwhile, while the Church of Alexandria was tossed upon the high waves of the storms of heretics and seditions, St. Leo the pontiff sought to encourage the steadfastness of the Catholics. For this purpose he issued new letters, either to Julian, bishop of Cos, or to Basil, recently appointed bishop of Antioch, or to Euxitheus of Thessalonica, or to Juvenal of Jerusalem, or to all the metropolitans of the Eastern Churches.

He exhorted each and every one of them to oppose the crimes of the wicked with holy and vigorous constancy, so that “in none of us may the common faith be found either fearful or lukewarm” [Note: Letter 118 to Basil of Antioch, and Letter 119 to Euxitheus of Thessalonica and Juvenal of Jerusalem.].

He was firmly persuaded that if episcopal constancy did not depart from the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon, “the most merciful and most Christian ruler will gladly defend his own decision, and what he has already granted of his own accord he will accomplish much more readily when asked, so that what has been well concluded and settled may not be violated by any novelty” [Note: Letter 120 to Julian, bishop of Cos.].

The pontiff’s zeal for defending the Catholic faith and completely extinguishing the evils oppressing the Church of Alexandria did not merely stir him to write encyclical letters and to ask the emperor not to lend his ears to the wicked petitions of the Eutychians. He also urged Julian of Cos and the presbyter Aetius to ensure that the pontifical writings reached each of the metropolitan bishops as quickly as possible, so that they might resist the novelties with all their strength.

He then expressed his astonishment at the audacity of certain slanderers who, looking for a knot in a reed, accused the pontifical letter written to Flavian—which had been accepted by everyone as a rule of faith—as obscure in meaning or ambiguous in expression, as though the assertions of that letter had not been derived from evangelical and apostolic doctrine.

“I am truly astonished,” he said, “that anything in my letter, which has pleased the whole world, should still appear obscure to the vanity of its slanderers, so that they think it ought to be more suitably explained; for its assertion of that preaching is so full and solid that it admits no novelty either in meaning or in expression. Whatever we wrote then is demonstrably taken from evangelical and apostolic doctrine” [Note: Letter 120 to Julian of Cos.].

Wishing to refute this vanity of the slanderers and to prove most clearly that there could be no place for new explanations of the kind the Eutychians were requesting—at least in order to wound the authority of the Council of Chalcedon—he sent his vicar Aetius copies of the letters that the Gauls and Italians had written to him, to show that all the bishops of the West likewise professed the same doctrine with complete agreement.

“We have also sent copies of the letters that the Gallic and Italian bishops sent to us with concordant faith, so that it may not remain unknown how their faith is also one with ours” [Note: Letter 121 to Aetius, chapter 2.].

These matters certainly deserved at least a brief indication by the deacon Liberatus when he was writing the history of the Eutychianists. Just as he could not conceal what St. Leo had done to abolish the Ephesian Robber Synod, to restrain and condemn the impiety of Dioscorus and Eutyches, and finally to explain the zeal he had employed in strengthening the Catholic faith at the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, so he ought also briefly to have described how much and what kind of work our holy pontiff had undertaken both to uphold the decrees of that council and to repair the grievous evils which, after Marcian’s death, through the wicked machinations of the Eutychians, were violently afflicting Alexandria, Egypt, and even the Church of Constantinople, to the destruction of the Catholic faith.

But let us grant pardon to Liberatus, the Carthaginian deacon. Although, as he himself asserts in the preface to this little work, he had before him the acts of the councils and the letters of the holy Fathers while composing his *Breviary* on the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, he nevertheless did not preserve complete diligence. In the matter before us, he was concerned more with reporting the very serious Alexandrian schism than with indicating the zeal and strenuous efforts of the Apostolic Roman See to suppress and repair it.

### 11.

Moreover, what St. Leo had done before and after the death of Proterius to frustrate the wicked schemes of the Alexandrians and to lead their Church back to complete tranquility and peace could not have been unknown to Liberatus.

After receiving letters from Proterius announcing his ordination, Leo did not delay replying to him. Beginning with expressions of congratulation, he said:

> “The letters of your affection have made me glad, letters which our brother and fellow bishop Nestorius”—Bede reads *Nectarius*—“adopted with pious affection. For it was fitting that such writings should be sent from the bishop of the Church of Alexandria to the Apostolic See, writings showing that, through the teaching of the blessed Apostle Peter, he had learned from the beginning through the blessed Mark, his disciple, this truth: that the Egyptians believed what it is established that the Romans believed” [Note: Leo’s Letter 103 to Proterius, chapters 1 and 2.].

In the same letter he then defended at length the doctrine contained in his letter to Flavian against the calumnies of the heretics. He wished it to be read in a frequent assembly, so that the Alexandrians might become acquainted with his doctrine.

Finally, he ordered Proterius to compare publicly the testimonies of the Fathers with his own letter, so that it might become clear that Proterius condemned Nestorius just as he condemned Eutyches.

We have already observed throughout the course of these Exercises, by various arguments, that the Roman pontiff always exercised special care for the Church of Alexandria. This care increased all the more as the necessities pressing upon that Church became greater and the Roman pontiff had to provide for them.

### CHAPTER XII AND LAST

The supreme zeal that St. Leo displayed until the end of his life in strengthening the decrees of Chalcedon, repairing the calamity of the Church of Alexandria, and extinguishing the Eutychian heretics.

### 1.

We could not adequately express in words St. Leo’s zeal in repairing the calamity of the Church of Alexandria unless his method of action after Proterius’s death made it plainly evident.

But in addition to the evidence already brought forward above to establish this truth, further evidence remains from which we clearly recognize that St. Leo spent the remaining days of his mortal life frustrating, restraining, and crushing every effort and scheme of the Eutychians; defending the Council of Chalcedon; supporting the Catholic faith; and freeing orthodox bishops who had been oppressed and forced into exile by the faction of the seditious from the hardships they were suffering.

We gather this especially from the third letter he wrote to the Emperor Leo. First, he congratulated him on his willingness to preserve the Council of Chalcedon. Then, turning to the obstinate and treacherous disputes of the heretics, he asked him, for the safety and welfare of the Christian commonwealth and the empire, to use his royal power to restrain and curb them.

“Their obstinate and treacherous contention,” he said, “will immediately fall silent if it is curbed by imperial power” [Note: Letter 122].

That St. Leo wished to advise the emperor to drive the Alexandrian heretics into exile and punish them with other penalties is indicated by the words of the following letter, written to the Catholic bishops of Egypt. After the ordination of Timothy Aelurus, these bishops had abandoned their sees and come to Constantinople seeking consolation and protection.

The pontiff consoled them as exiles for the faith and urged them patiently to endure adversity for the mystery of the Incarnation, trusting that:

> “Through your patience,” he said, “the devotion of many may be strengthened, and, with the glory of the revered prince, the Church of Alexandria, once the heretics have been driven away, may recover her ancient dignity” [Note: Letter 123].

The pontiff’s will, however, did not fully achieve its effect, whether because of the emperor’s excessive clemency or Anatolius’s negligence. As a result, even among the clergy of Constantinople there were some who adhered to the Alexandrian robbers and had absorbed the Eutychian doctrines, showing the greatest contempt for and inflicting the greatest injury upon the decrees of Chalcedon.

When the holy pontiff learned this, he took up his pen and first wrote to Anatolius of Constantinople. He aroused his vigilance against the efforts of the heretics and rebuked him because, “as it is said, there are certain persons among Your Affection who connive at the perversity of the adversaries, and the vessels of wrath are mingled with the vessels of mercy.”
