He then pressed Anatolius to restrain and investigate the heretics with appropriate severity, so that, where correction could not help, amputation would not be spared [Col. 1318D].

Finally, he recalled to his mind the Gospel’s command: if an eye, a foot, or a right hand scandalizes us, it must be removed from the body’s structure, because it is better to lack these members’ services in the Church than to go with them into eternal punishment.

He sought to press Anatolius still more strongly and to arouse his vigilance in another letter written to him somewhat later. We cannot determine its exact date, since it lacks a consular notation. It is Letter 126 among Leo’s letters.

### 2.

The holy pontiff had recently received a letter from Anatolius describing the tearful condition of the Church of Alexandria, although the letter could not set forth the atrocities committed there in full [539]. Leo declares that he learned of them with the greatest grief.

But since the great distance between the places and the assaults of the Eutychians did not allow Leo to break their unbridled obstinacy, and since they feared neither ecclesiastical laws nor penalties, he urged Anatolius not to cease entreating the emperor and, through frequent appeals, to ask that the Church of Alexandria be freed as soon as possible from its usurpers.

He further declared that he had received consolation from the report that, among the entire number of bishops presiding over the Egyptian dioceses, only four of those long ago condemned could be found who were joined to Timothy both in the impiety of heresy and in the criminality of his brigandage. Such men could in no way be admitted to request a council, even if they were accused only of heretical error.

He also testified that he had commended to the emperor the Catholic bishops who had fled Egypt and assembled at Constantinople, so that they might obtain assistance.

Finally, he turned his pen against Anatolius himself and vehemently rebuked him for failing to restrain the obstinacy of Atticus, a presbyter of Constantinople, who had advanced to such insolence that he had dared to dispute in church against the Catholic faith and the Council of Chalcedon.

“I am compelled,” he said, “to complain more vehemently about your dissimulation.” He threatened that he would act by his own authority if Anatolius refused to cut off from communion Atticus and Andrew, his associate in impiety.

“We would prefer,” he said, “if possible, that he be corrected rather than perish.”

What evidence of correction Leo prescribed is understood from what follows. He wished Atticus to become openly a preacher of the faith in the very place where he had argued at length against the Catholic faith, and to condemn, in the hearing of the Christian people, every element of Eutychian doctrine without omitting anything, by a public declaration of his own profession [Note: Leo’s Letter 126.].

It is evident from Anatolius’s complaints that he was seriously displeased by this kind of rebuke, as though he himself did not care for the affairs of his Church and was concealing what was happening in the Church of Constantinople to the destruction of the Catholic faith.

Leo nevertheless received Anatolius’s complaints moderately. He told him that he had delegated an inquiry into whether the things rumor had spread about Atticus were true.

“Nor have I injured your honor in any respect,” he added. “I entrusted to you the examination of what had been reported to me.”

Finally, to remove every suspicion by which Atticus was being denounced in everyone’s mouth as a man who had injured the faith, Leo warned and commanded that Atticus condemn the Eutychian error not only orally but also by his own subscription, in a public statement to be recited in church in the presence of the Christian people. He was also to profess that he adhered to the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, which had been confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See.

### 3.

This controversy concerning the presbyter Atticus, however, was not new. St. Leo had already written to the emperor that clerics of ambiguous faith were present in the Church of Constantinople. He asked that they be expelled and rebuked Anatolius for negligently tolerating people who thought and spoke perversely about the faith.

Accordingly, he addressed the emperor, stirring him to the justice of punishment so that the purity of the Church of Constantinople would not be obscured:

> “In that Church there are found certain clerics who agree with the thinking of the heretics, thus assisting heretics by their assertions within the very entrails of the Catholic body. If my brother Anatolius is found sluggish in removing them because he spares them with excessive kindness…” [Note: Letter 126.]

The pontiff therefore asked the emperor to provide this remedy for the Church, for the sake of his faith, so that such men would be expelled not only from the clerical order but also from residence in the city, “lest the holy people of God thereafter be polluted by the contagion of perverse men.”

The emperor granted Leo’s request and compelled Atticus to write to the Roman pontiff concerning his faith, making a considered profession in order to remove every suspicion about his doctrine.

Atticus outwardly did what the emperor had ordered. He composed a confession of faith and sent it to Rome, but it was exceedingly obscure and entangled in verbal ambiguity.

When St. Leo had examined this profession of faith and carefully attended to the force and meaning of its words [Col. 1320A], he judged it so uncertain that it had confirmed rather than dispelled everything that rumor had brought to him about Atticus.

For, he said, if Atticus had wished to prove his conscience sincere, he ought to have confessed not merely that Eutyches was hateful to him, but that he rejected and condemned Eutyches’ perfidy [Note: Letter 128.].

This, then, was Atticus’s deceitful course of action: he professed that Eutyches was hateful to him and did not refuse to pronounce an anathema against him, but he did not reject his wicked doctrines.

Therefore, wishing to elude his cunning, St. Leo demanded from him such a profession of faith that no one could ever doubt it. Otherwise, he ordered that Atticus and Andrew, his associate in the same crime, be removed from the clerical order and deprived of every clerical honor.

“Atticus and Andrew,” he wrote to the presbyters, deacons, and clerics of the Church of Constantinople, “whose names I indicated in a previous letter sent to my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, and whom I have learned to dissent from your praiseworthy faith and most openly to connive at the perfidy of the Eutychians—unless they first condemn the hostile doctrines with their own voice and subscription, and profess in church, in the presence of the Christian people, that they will follow the faith strengthened by the Council of Chalcedon—must be deprived of the honor of their order” [Col. 1320B].

What outcome the case of Atticus and Andrew finally obtained, we have been unable to determine either from St. Leo or from any other record of Christian affairs.

It is nevertheless beyond doubt that either, after all the conditions specified had been observed, they abandoned their perfidy, or else they were torn away from the fellowship of the Catholics and deprived of their clerical honor, since the most holy pontiff never withdrew from his decisions.

4. It remains finally to see what happened to the Eutychians who had seized the Alexandrian Church, after the holy pontiff had repeatedly sought the emperor’s assistance through his letters, asking that Timothy the Cat, the robber and usurper of that see, be expelled and that another bishop be appointed who would profess the Catholic faith. There can be no doubt that the emperor Leo employed his aid and authority so that matters might be brought to a favorable [Col. 1320C] conclusion. Yet he could not easily guard against all the intrigues of the Eutychians, who pretended that a new synod was necessary for settling the affairs of the Church and the empire. The holy pontiff had frustrated their hope by repeated letters; once that proposal had been cut off, they at least requested a public conference with those whom Saint Leo might choose.

This final request of the Eutychians certainly appeared equitable to those who did not understand their deceitful maneuvers, especially since the request was accompanied by rumors that they sincerely wished to be instructed in the truth of the faith and were not so obstinately attached to their opinions that they would refuse to correct them if they were shown to be false. The Eutychians therefore approached the emperor through court officials, to persuade him to grant this conference. Having been surrounded by the counsels of others, he wrote to Saint Leo, asserting that a synod was being requested without purpose, since the controversy had been settled by the Council of Chalcedon: perfection admits no increase, and fullness no addition. Saint Leo transferred these words into his own letter, praising the emperor’s judgment.

[Col. 1320D] Accordingly, with the humanity and readiness of spirit that were customary to him, Saint Leo immediately replied to the imperial letters and, expressing his joy of heart, congratulated the emperor: “I recognize,” he said, “that the outstanding faith of Your Clemency is increasing …” [Note: [Col. 1320D] Letter 132, chapter 1 and following.] He proclaimed that the solidity of the faith had been built upon the firmest rock, from which every variation of opinion must be kept far away, lest we be found ungrateful for the gifts of divine mercy and, as though we had attained nothing, instead expect contrary things. For, he adds, “to seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been perfected, and to overturn what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what has been received and to extend the wicked desires of deadly covetousness toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

He further denies that he wishes to have communion [Col. 1321A] with heretics who boast of the cleverness of their arguments in order to contradict Christ’s Gospel. Yet, confident in every respect in the emperor’s piety, he promises to send certain legates, not to dispute with the Eutychians but to instruct them, since “with regard to matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as God willed, we dare enter upon no discussion.” [Note: [Col. 1321D] Letter 131 of Leo.] At the end of the letter he commends the failing Alexandrian Church to the emperor, asking him, after expelling the parricides from the city, finally to restore it to liberty.

The preceding celebrated letter of Saint Leo was written toward the end of March, while Leo and Majorian were serving as consuls, which falls in the year 458. He did not, however, immediately send the legates whom he had promised to send. For from a subsequent letter, written on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September of the same year, we learn that he had only then decided to dispatch the bishops Domitian and Geminianus. Acting on behalf of the pontiff, they were to seek peace for the Church without allowing matters already rightly defined to be brought back for a new discussion.

[Col. 1321B] He adds that all disputes must be entirely avoided whenever matters of faith are being treated, and he adduces the example of Christ, who entrusted the doctrine of the Gospel, to be announced to all nations, not to orators and philosophers but to fishermen and humble men. The Eutychians opposed this example, insisting on bringing into dispute a doctrine defined by the synod.

At last Leo pressed the emperor to lend a kindly ear to the petitions of the legates whom he had sent—not to debate with the condemned, but only to plead with you for the firmness of the Catholic faith—and not to allow human remission to be granted to the Alexandrian parricides, who were unworthy of every indulgence, since only he should be entreated who can worthily punish such acts, and only he can release from them through ineffable mercy. Regarding the Eutychians who adhered to the party of Timothy the Cat, he orders that different ecclesiastical measures be observed: namely, that penitence not be denied to those who corrected themselves, while he wished the obstinate to remain under the synodal [Col. 1321C] sentence. [Note: [Col. 1321D] Letter 133, chapters 2, 3, and 4.]

5. On the occasion of this legation he wrote another letter to the same emperor. In Quesnellus it is numbered 134, but in the older editions it is numbered 97. As Quesnellus also observed, this letter contains a longer and more careful treatment of the mystery of the Incarnation. It includes very numerous and extensive testimonies of the holy Fathers, by which it is shown that the error of Eutyches had long since been condemned.

At the end of this letter, however, he recalls to the emperor’s mind that nothing is more consistent with imperial authority than for him, by his own decree, to provide for the peace of the Lord’s Churches and to defend God’s gifts among all his subjects, refusing in any way to allow, through the devil’s envy, the devil’s ministers to rage to anyone’s destruction.

What Leo had long desired he finally obtained. For the emperor, after hearing the petitions of the pontifical legates and reflecting upon what the holy pontiff had written to him in various letters, wisely decided that he could no [Col. 1321D] longer tolerate the grievous division of the Alexandrians or allow the impious Timothy to retain the see that he had invaded. He joined his own authority to that of the bishops, ordering Timothy, who had already been condemned, to withdraw from the episcopate.

How precisely these events occurred does not clearly appear from the surviving records. Quesnellus, who never departed from his own system, imagines that an assembly of bishops was held at Constantinople, perhaps on the occasion of Anatolius’s death and the election of a new bishop of Constantinople. In the presence of the pontifical legates, the bishops Domitian and Geminianus, all the letters of the metropolitans, together with the bishops’ subscriptions, which had been sent to the emperor, were supposedly read; Saint Leo’s Letter 134 to the same emperor, with the testimonies of the holy Fathers appended to it, was also read; and, with the consent of those present and absent, [Col. 1322A] Timothy himself was condemned. 542

Quesnellus says that this sentence against Timothy is referred to in Saint Leo’s letter to Gennadius, the successor of Anatolius: “Constrained by the sentences of all the Lord’s priests.” And again, when the holy pontiff wished to explain the joy of the universal Church at the expulsion of the wicked Timothy from the Alexandrian see, he wrote to the emperor: “Let Your Clemency know that all the Churches of God rejoice together and exult with praise of you, because the wicked parricide has been driven from the yoke of the Alexandrian Church.” [Note: [Col. 1322D] Letter 139 of Leo.]

I certainly admit that all the bishops rejected Timothy the Cat’s intrusion into the Alexandrian episcopate, abhorred him as a parricide and heretic, and expressed their grief and the calamity of the Alexandrian Church in so many and such extensive letters recorded in the collection of encyclicals, which we have already mentioned. But what follows from this? Is it a conjecture that an assembly was held at Constantinople in conciliar form so that a canonical sentence might be issued? Had not this canonical sentence already been [Col. 1322B] pronounced by Saint Leo the Great, who repeatedly, even before he sent the legates, had asked the emperor to carry out the expulsion of Timothy the usurper and to have a new Catholic bishop elected by the Alexandrians?

It should not therefore be said that, because all the bishops—both those absent and those residing at Constantinople—desired and applauded the deposition of Timothy the Cat, he was condemned and expelled by their legal sentence. The cited words indicate only this: “Constrained by the sentences of all the Lord’s priests.” But, considering the gravity of his crimes, all the bishops with the greatest unanimity pressed for the sentence of deposition pronounced against Timothy the Cat by Saint Leo to be carried out without delay.

6. Timothy, although expelled from the Alexandrian throne, did not abandon every hope. He flattered himself that he could regain it, and, employing his customary devices, obtained pardon from the emperor and came to [Col. 1322C] Constantinople, where he communicated with the Catholics as though he were innocent.

Saint Leo was informed of this by Gennadius, the new bishop of Constantinople, and, as he says, after hearing the report of his brother and fellow bishops Domitian and Geminianus, who had come from the East to Rome, he wrote back to the same Gennadius. He strongly complained that Timothy was communicating with the Catholics and proved by many arguments that Timothy was not merely unworthy of the episcopate but must also be avoided because of the parricide and sacrileges he had committed.

He therefore ordered Gennadius to exclude him not only from the Church’s public assembly but also from the fellowship of the faithful:

“Thus your beloved self must strive and labor with the vigilance for which you are distinguished, so that no conversation, whether private or public, may be held with so wicked a man; nor, under the pretext of correction, may an opportunity be offered for his participation in any gathering, lest he obtain complete freedom to return—he concerning whom the most Christian ruler has already passed judgment in his edicts.”

At last two months had passed when, behold, two legates from the Alexandrian Church arrived: namely, the presbyter Daniel and the [Col. 1322D] deacon Timothy, bearing letters from the new bishop of Alexandria, who had been duly consecrated. For the people and clergy of Alexandria, by common agreement and vote, had duly and solemnly proclaimed Timothy, surnamed Solophaciolus, bishop, and had then ordained him.

Saint Leo rejoiced with the greatest joy at this event and immediately wrote three letters on the same day. The first was addressed to the new bishop, elected and consecrated. He congratulated him and urged him “to obtain earnestly, through the prayers of the Church, the reconciliation to God of those who in some measure resisted the truth.”

He wrote the second letter to the presbyters and deacons of the same Alexandrian Church. He likewise congratulated them on the most devout affection by which, united among themselves, they had preserved the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, having removed from themselves that beast of discord which, as the prophetic [Col. 1323A] psalm sings, was laying waste with singular savagery the vineyard of the Lord’s planting.

He also urged them to procure the repentance of Christians of every rank, so that, especially after rejecting Eutychian impiety, they might more easily reach the remedies of satisfaction. 543 [Note: [Col. 1323B] Letter 140.]

Finally, he wrote a third letter to ten bishops of Egypt. It differs from the preceding letter in only a few words. With these bishops he shared his joy that the man had been ordained bishop whom no ambition had drawn, no sedition driven, and no wickedness incited; rather, with the holiness of his merits set openly before them, the whole body did not hesitate to place above all others the man whom it desired to preside over it. [Note: [Col. 1323B] Letter 141. All these letters were written on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 460.]

These events, as described thus far, correspond remarkably with what Liberatus the deacon reports in his *Breviarium*. In explaining how peace was restored to the Alexandrian Church, he relates that the emperor Leo wrote to Stilas, the commander at Alexandria, instructing him by every means to remove Timothy from the episcopate but to enthrone another bishop, chosen by popular decree, who would vindicate the synod [Col. 1323B]—that is, the Council of Chalcedon.

Then, speaking of the new bishop elected for Alexandria, Timothy surnamed Solophaciolus, or Asbus, he says:

“He lived quietly in the Alexandrian Church, without sedition, throughout the entire reign of Leo and throughout the entire reign of Zeno, until Basiliscus seized the tyranny and Zeno fled into Isauria.”

The Catholics could expect no assistance from Basiliscus, who had secretly, at least, long supported Timothy the Cat and the Eutychians. It is therefore not surprising that, after obtaining imperial power by tyranny, he sent throughout the world an edict of his own, which he called an encyclical against the Council of Chalcedon, and restored Timothy the Cat to his episcopate, so that the Catholic Timothy hid in the fortress of Canopus and in a monastery. [Note: [Col. 1324B] Liberatus the deacon, *Breviarium*, chapters 13 and 16.]

Saint Leo, pope, did not see this new destruction of the Catholic religion, since he had already departed [Col. 1324A] this life many years earlier. For, according to the tables of the most learned Dionysius Petavius, Basiliscus [Col. 1324B] tyrannically obtained supreme imperial power in the year 476, when Pope Simplicius had already begun to hold the helm of the Church, and Saint Leo had ceased to live in the year 461.

7. What and how great labors Saint Leo endured for the Church and Christ, and what fierce battles he undertook against the enemies of the faith, conquering heresies by word and writing and defeating them with the triumph of victory, is clearly evident from what has been set forth in these historical Exercises of ours.

It is easy to understand, or to grasp mentally, with what prudence he governed the Church and with what constancy he defended the rights of his apostolic see, always preserving and maintaining the majesty of his office. Nothing could make him retreat or deviate from it—not the disturbances of divided Churches, the efforts of the Eastern bishops, or the machinations of heretics.

For he stood fearlessly against the petitions of rulers whenever they opposed the canons of Nicaea and the laws of justice. Whenever synods and their decrees were inconsistent with divine and apostolic institutions, he abolished and revoked them. He enacted highly salutary laws to restore and protect the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline. He prohibited the granting of indulgence to the fallen whenever they had not sincerely renounced their former obstinacy through saving repentance. Finally, he did not wish canonical penalties to be relaxed for them unless some circumstance of public benefit and complete harmony required it.

Certainly he proved himself magnificent, glorious, and truly admirable in the administration of the Church’s affairs. Most especially, after he had attained the supreme pontificate, the Church was being defiled by those four dreadful heresies; the entire East was disturbed for twelve years, with the pillars of the Church thrown down or tottering; yet he did not depart this life until peace had been secured everywhere and the throngs of heretics had been silenced on every side.

**END OF THE SECOND PART.**

# APPENDIX TO THE FIRST PART OF THE VOLUME

[Col. 1325]

[Note: [Col. 1325D] See the note enclosed in parentheses in the text above, col. 760, C. EDIT.]

## LETTER 88. On the privilege of chorepiscopi, or presbyters

[Col. 1325A] Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and of the apostolic see, sends greetings to all the bishops of the regions of Germany and Gaul.

When, in the name of God, we had held in the Roman Church an assembly of bishops, or of the other fellow priests and faithful of Christ, [Note: [Col. 1325D] The Vulgate, with certain manuscripts, reads *coadunatum* (“assembled”). We have emended the text from the manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, marked no. 237.] and had diligently dealt with illicit ordinations, about which reports from those regions who frequently traveled to us had reached us, as well as with other necessary ecclesiastical matters, carefully rereading the sacred canons, [Note: [Col. 1325D] The same manuscript of the Holy Cross reads *a quibusdam* (“by certain persons”).] many people reported to us with tearful faces that certain bishops of the cities of Germany and Gaul frequently sent chorepiscopi—who, according to the canons of Neocaesarea, or according to the decrees of other Fathers, are the same as presbyters—or presbyters to erect altars in the bishop’s absence and consecrate basilicas.

It is not surprising that men ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline should have ordered what is contrary to the canonical rule, having been transferred and promoted immediately from secular military service to the priestly ministry. Therefore, so that such license may no longer be usurped by you, it was necessary to establish by common decision that you know this: just as the consecration of an altar is illicit for a chorepiscopus or presbyter, so also is its establishment.

For in the divine Scriptures, at the Lord’s command, Moses alone erected an altar in God’s tabernacle, and he alone anointed it. He was, of course, the high priest of God, as it is written of him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.”

Therefore, what was commanded only to the chief priests, whose type was represented by Moses and Aaron, has been entirely decreed not to be undertaken by chorepiscopi or presbyters, who bear the figure of the sons of Aaron. For although they share with bishops the administration of very many ministries, they must recognize that certain functions are prohibited to them by the authority of the old law and certain others by the ecclesiastical regulations of the new law, such as the consecration of presbyters and deacons or of virgins, and the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar. [Note: [Col. 1325D] Another reading in two manuscripts: *Caesarienses* (“Caesarean”).]

Thus they are permitted neither to erect altars nor to consecrate churches or altars, [Note: [Col. 1326D] The manuscript of the Holy Cross reads: “as is the consecration of presbyters and deacons and virgins.”] nor, through the laying on of hands, to impart the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, to the faithful being baptized or to converts from heresy; nor to prepare the chrism; nor to mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism; nor even publicly in the Mass to reconcile any penitent; nor to send canonical letters to anyone. [Col. 1325D–1327A]

All these things are illicit for chorepiscopi, who are known to exist after the example and pattern of the seventy disciples, or for presbyters, who bear the same figure. [Note: [Col. 1327B] The printed editions read *formam* (“form”). We have preferred the reading of two of our copies of the collection, 11 and 20.] For although they possess consecration, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. The canons prescribe that all these functions belong exclusively to the highest pontiffs, so that both the distinction of ranks and the summit of the supreme pontiff’s dignity may thereby be demonstrated.

Nor is it permitted for presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of the bishop, or to baptize or sign a child while the bishop is present, or to reconcile a penitent without the bishop’s instruction, or, unless he orders it, to celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in his presence; nor, while he is present, to teach, bless, or greet the people; nor, of course, to exhort the congregation.

[Col. 1326]

## 1270. CANON VII OF THE SECOND COUNCIL OF SEVILLE

Held in the time of King Sisebutus in the year of Christ 619,

From the edition of García de Loaysa.

[Col. 1326A] At the seventh inquiry it was reported to us that the once most revered Agapius, bishop of the city of Córdoba, had frequently sent presbyters to erect altars in the bishop’s absence and to consecrate basilicas. It is not surprising that a man ignorant of ecclesiastical disciplines should have ordered this, having been transferred immediately from secular military service and appointed to the priestly ministry.

Therefore, so that such license might no longer be usurped by us, it was necessary to establish by common decision—knowing that, just as the consecration of an altar is illicit for a presbyter, [Note: [Col. 1326D] The same manuscript reads: “we permit him to consecrate.”] so also is its establishment—that in the divine Scriptures, at the Lord’s command, Moses alone erected an altar in God’s tabernacle, and he alone anointed it, because he was indeed God’s high priest, as it is written: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.”

Therefore, what was commanded only to the chief priests, whose type Moses and Aaron represented, presbyters, who bear the figure of the sons of Aaron, must not presume to undertake. For although they share with bishops the administration of very many ministries, they must recognize that certain things have been prohibited to them by the imperial Novels and by ecclesiastical regulations, such as the consecration of presbyters and deacons and virgins, and the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar. [Note: [Col. 1326D] Another edition adds: “to the chorepiscopus.”]

Indeed, they are not permitted to consecrate churches or altars, or through the laying on of hands to impart the Paraclete, the Spirit, to the faithful who have been baptized or to converts from heresy; nor to prepare chrism; nor to mark the forehead of the baptized with chrism; nor publicly in the Mass to reconcile any of the penitents; nor to send canonical letters to anyone. All these things are illicit for presbyters, [Note: [Col. 1326D] Another edition adds: “certain things nevertheless by the authority of the old law.”] because they do not possess the summit of the episcopate; and the canons prescribe that they belong solely to bishops, [Note: [Col. 1326D] Another edition adds: “or chorepiscopi.”] so that both the distinction of ranks and the summit of the supreme pontiff’s dignity may thereby be demonstrated.

Nor is it permitted for presbyters to enter the baptistery in the presence of the bishop, or to baptize or sign an infant while the bishop is present, or to reconcile penitents without the command of their bishop, or to celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in his presence, or, while he is present, to teach, bless, or greet the people, or to exhort the congregation. [Note: [Col. 1328B] Another edition adds: “All these things are known to have been prohibited to them by the apostolic see.”]

Remedies of life granted to the dead, 134. Hosts and offerings are beneficial to them, ibid. Masses for the dead, ibid. and following. The sacrifice makes satisfaction for the dead, 135. It is offered so that they may rejoice in the glorious heavenly seat, 137; so that eternal light may possess their souls, 136; and so that they may rejoice in the fellowship of the saints, 138. The nobility and praises of the virgin Demetrias, to whom the letter on humility was written, 260. She was commended by holy men, 261 note. When she returned from Africa to Rome, 749. Desire for the good comes from God, 175.

God is supreme reason, 126. He beholds all things simultaneously, 247. He is wholly present everywhere, 294. In God all things are eternal and unchangeable, 245. In him greater and lesser are excluded, 290. In God’s mind all created things existed before creation, 108. Everything that lives belongs to God, 102. God is the origin and perfection of all virtues, 119. Glorious in the saints, 4. Victorious in the martyrs, 2, 5, 7. Wonderful in the saints, he sought everlasting blessedness for them and prepared aids suited to our frailty, 14.

God must continually be praised, 11, 62, 125. He works wonders through the least things, 155. Creator and ordainer of all things, 188. With God there is a twofold order, 214. He orders the whole human race by heavenly law, 120. He governs the Church with a special dispensation, ibid.

God provides more than we ask or deserve, 108. He anticipates the prayers of those who ask, ibid. We must ask God for what pleases him, 204. Things worthy of God are to be requested, 121. If God hears, it is the grace of mercy; if he does not hear, it is the judgment of truth, 214.

God’s providence, and the fact that it must not be complained of, 107. His counsels are hidden, 188. By his hidden judgment the differences among human beings have been ordered, ibid. God tolerates the wicked for the sake of the good, 223. He scourges bodily so that we may progress in mind, 125. By chastising he heals, and by restoring he teaches benevolently, 58. He makes good use of evil, 1535 note.

God’s gifts were given not to be worshipped but to be used, 172. In God alone we must glory, 271. Why gifts are offered to God, 68. He who needs no gifts, 67.

God wills the salvation of all, 185, 212. This statement of the Apostle must be understood fully, ibid., 212, 213. God extends the bowels of his mercy toward the salvation of all nations, 194. He wills that prayer be made for all, 186. Why he has mercy on some and not on others, 190. He chose without works, 192. Why at the very end of life he converts some criminals while abandoning others who are less wicked is inscrutable, 191, 192. God is more inscrutable when choosing than when punishing, 210. His judgment is inscrutable in the discrimination among little children, 190.

God’s goodness was not lacking toward the ungodly before the flood, 223. He repays our evils with good, 93. It is proper to God to have mercy, 22. His ways are mercy and truth, 59. By showing mercy he always anticipates our evil merits, 22. While bestowing aids upon the unworthy, he exhorts them to become worthy to receive better things, 77. Amid troubles he provides necessary help, 62. He does not cease to assist his people with saving aids, 9. By purifying minds he justifies them, and by justifying makes them capable of immortality, 58.

God is not known except by God’s gift, 267. God gives right understanding and willing, 180. He makes us know what ought rightly to be done and grants the ability to carry it out, 65. As he gives, so each person progresses, 217. We always need God’s help, 266. See Grace.

The devil, see Demon.

The ordination of deacons, 112. Chastity prescribed for them, see Chastity.

Dictinius, a Priscillianist bishop in Spain, abjures the heresy, 1373. His genuine profession is defended, ibid. note.

The universal flood, 392.

Two dioceses in Gaul established by Constantine under two vicars: one of the Five Provinces, the other of the Gauls, 1011. Dioscorus of Alexandria is elected, 435. Favoring Eutyches, he requests a synod, 460. His primacy at the Ephesian pseudo-council is censured, ibid. note. When Leo believed that he could dispense from observance of the canons, and when he believed that he could not, 527 note.

Divisions of the provinces, see Division of the provinces. Of the dioceses, see Dioceses.

Good rich people are not lacking, 265. They are protectors of the poor and stewards of the Churches, ibid.

Sunday was assigned for ordinations, 1306. Whether Sundays after the Ember fast lacked an office, 1308 note. Whether Mass was celebrated at Rome only on Sundays, 1310 note. Sunday called the day of the resurrection, 1074.

Domnus, bishop of Antioch, was the first to expose Eutyches’ impiety, 448 note. His synodical letter to the emperor, 1103. When it was written, 448 note. His case, 1183. Deposited at the Ephesian Robber Council, 465. Concerning his withdrawal from the episcopate, 1184. The Chalcedonian session concerning him examined, 1185. Dorotheus the monk, and his case brought before the Council of Chalcedon, 510. He was expelled from the monastery, 562.

The bishop of Ebredunum, formerly metropolitan of the Maritime Alps, 1049. Later made subject to Arles, ibid.

The verses of the poet Edesius, 328, 335.

It does not remove the duty of prayer, 249.

Almsgiving is refreshment for the dead, 363.

A passage of Ennodius emended, 1471.

The acts of the Ephesian Robber Council, 464. From it Bishop Flavian of Constantinople and Bishop Theodoret of Cyrrhus appealed; see Flavian and Theodoret. Leo annulled its acts, 1159.

The anniversary of consecration was celebrated, 114, 120. To what extent bishops ordained without legitimate procedure were not regarded as bishops, 1587 note.

It is the duty of bishops to do what is right and preach what is true, 119. How bishops ought to conduct themselves, 120. Episcopal cases, see Major Cases, Appeals. Punishment for bishops who transfer to another see out of greed, ibid. Bishops who could enjoy communion only with their own Churches, and with whom they were forbidden to communicate, 1462.

Peace letters, or letters of ecclesiastical communion, 1507.

The Eucharist called the heavenly mystery, 5. It contains Christ’s body and blood, 56, 64, 67. It makes us sharers in the divine nature, 64. What it provides for us, 103, 104, 134. St. Eugenia, 148.

Eusebius, bishop of Milan, 1471.

God’s grace is not given on the basis of merits, 191. The election of grace cannot be attributed to the merits of the wills, 189. Rather, the entire basis of receiving grace is God’s will, 193. The late conversion of the wicked proves grace to be gratuitous, 191. Why one person rather than another receives the grace of conversion is inscrutable, 212, 213.

Prevenient grace, 22, 62, 257, 321. It is not preceded by the human will, 273, nor by our merits, 257. The necessity of grace, 22. Without its help we can do nothing good, 8, 68, 76, 139, 168, 176. Unless we are aided by grace, we cannot avoid the devil’s snares, 253, 337. The necessity of internal grace, 267.

The manner in which grace acts, 238. It does not remove the freedom to turn toward vices, 220, 257. There is power to dissent even from efficacious grace, 240. Freedom exists under grace, 222. The will is the servant of grace, and its consent, 239. Cooperation with grace is a gift of God, 247. Internal grace can be resisted, and many resist it, 682. The wickedness of the impious resists God’s grace, 209. Grace is entirely rejected unless it is entirely received, 266.

The gift of grace, 7. It enables willing, acting, and completion, 68, 69, 76. Grace gives the good will and the ability to do good, 125. It perfects virtue in weakness, 119. It heals nature, 174. It is the principle of every merit, 193. Grace makes it possible for God to be loved and for us to love ourselves truly and freely, 124. It acts so that we may act, 201. It also grows, 221.

The efficacy of the commandments comes from God’s grace, 60. Through grace we make good use of free will, 254. Every holy thought and movement of a devout will comes from grace, 255. Sufficient grace is given to some as a remedy, and to all as a testimony, 226. Its efficacy in subjecting rebels to God, 227. Its dominion and victories, 230. Grace is more manifest the more hardened are those whom it subjects to itself, 227. The efficacy of grace in St. Hilary, 361.

By general grace God wills all to be saved, 237, 242. The author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations* admits that general internal grace was also bestowed upon all, 675, but not grace that actually saves all, 678. Grace has not been entirely withdrawn from anyone, 196. It has been withdrawn from no age, 216. The difference of grace according to different periods, 215. Special grace in addition to general grace, 236. Particular grace was not given to all, 237, 243. The measure of grace, 204. The first seeds of grace are sometimes perfect, 221. Grace was also bestowed upon Cain, 678. Grace called perpetual redemption, 7.

All the Church’s prayers resound with grace, 256. Grace must be requested from God, so that we may be good and carry out the good, 61. A commandment is therefore given so that the help of the one who commands may be sought, 279. The grace of supplication is from God, 74. In matters concerning grace, what is clear must not be obscured by what is obscure, 178.

Thanksgiving must always be rendered to God, 60, 77. Gratitude makes progress, 107, 110.

Gratus, bishop of Carthage, praises the Sardican canons at the council, 1350, 1351 note.

St. Gregory the martyr, 15, 145. St. Gregory the martyr of Sipontum, and his annual feast, 15 note.

The minor works of St. Hilary of Arles, 328, 343 and following.

The Saturday fast before Pentecost, 22, 24, 25 n., 1092. Its ancient origin, 1094 n. Seats were prepared in the church for those fasting, so that they could hear the word of God, 327 n.

When John Cassian wrote his books on the Incarnation, 403, 408, 409 n. He dedicated them to Leo, 403 n., 410. Whether he was a Gaul or a Scythian, 409. When he came to know Leo, 403 n.

The praises of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, 153, 154. The praises of Saint John the Baptist, 29–32. He first perceived the beginnings of grace before those of nature, 221. A fast before his feast, 29. His office, ibid. The feast and praises of Saints John and Paul, 33. Saint Jovianus the martyr, 148.

The obstinacy of the Jews at Christ’s coming, 226. Saint Leo entrusted Julian of Cos with his powers, 537. Why, ibid. n. He was not a legate to the Synod of Ephesus, 1413 n. Nor did he attend it, 1413 n. An error noted in the commonly circulated Acts of Chalcedon, where Julianus is read instead of Julius, ibid. He was appointed as a kind of apostolic nuncio before the emperor, 1508 n. Julian, bishop of Caballicum, 1478. Julian the Pelagian, his efforts and journeys, 439. Julian Pomerius the true author of the books *On the Contemplative Life*, 165.

Julius, bishop of Pozzuoli, sent by Saint Leo to the Synod of Ephesus, 1411. It is proved that he also attended that synod, 1413 n.

Ecclesiastical jurisdiction established from three sources, explained, 919 ff. Metropolitan jurisdiction, when removed by a personal penalty, revives in the successors, 1059, 1061. Justice must be pursued, 19. Divine justice concerning human sufferings, 235. The patronage of the righteous is greatly beneficial, 95.

Juvenal of Jerusalem sought primacy in Palestine, 405. His case with Maximus of Antioch settled at the Council of Chalcedon, 512. The proceedings concerning this settlement presented from three versions, of which the oldest and most exact is given, 1222, 1223, 1231. Tumults raised against him by heretics after the Council of Chalcedon, 540. He fled to Constantinople, ibid. Restored to his see, he convened a synod, 556.

## L

The blessing of milk and honey, 24. The commemoration of Saint Lawrence the martyr, 9. His martyrdom and praises, 87–91. His vigil, 91 n. An octave celebrated, 92. He is shown to have been a Roman, 92 n.

Legates *a latere*, 1438. Saint Leo’s legates at the Council of Chalcedon were not legates of the Roman synod but of the pontiff, 1465 n. Legates of the apostolic see at the general synods of the East did not act as legates of all Westerners, 1175. Why a double legation was sent to the Sixth Council, one from the pope and the other from the Roman synod, 1181.

The homeland and birth of Saint Leo, 399 n. In what year he was born, 400. His baptism, ibid. His clerical service in the Lateran basilica, 402 n. He was sent to Africa as an acolyte, 401. When he became a deacon, 403. Cassian’s books against Nestorius were dedicated to him as deacon, 403 n. Leo was responsible for having them written, 408. Administrator of Pope Celestine, 405. Cyril wrote to him, ibid. He defended Pope Sixtus III, 409. He exposed the schemes of the Pelagian Julian, 411. He reconciled the commanders of the Roman army, 412.

Leo was elected pontiff while absent, 413. On what day he was elected, 412 n. A legation was sent to him in his absence, 413. With what disposition he undertook the burden, ibid. His fear and confidence at once, 414. What the condition of the Church then was, and how difficult the circumstances, 416. He associated learned men with himself, among them Saint Prosper, ibid. How firmly he adhered to the canons, 423. When he exercised dispensations, ibid.

Leo attacked the Manichaeans, 425. He held a Roman assembly against them, either correcting them or expelling them from the city, ibid. At the same time he crushed the Pelagians, 429 n. His two actions against them must be distinguished, 432 n. He restored relaxed discipline, 430. The controversy concerning Easter in the year 444, 429. He appointed Anastasius of Thessalonica as vicar, 433. The letters to him must be distinguished, and the matter of Atticus, 437 n.

Leo’s conflict with Hilary of Arles, 435. His judgment concerning Celidonius defended, 915 ff., 1063, 1066. Likewise his judgment against Hilary, ibid., 993, 1053, 1063. Hilary himself acquiesced in this judgment, 1057. And the Gallicans carried it out, 1059. Whether Leo’s tenth letter, in Hilary’s case, was inserted among the canons, 766. It was inserted in Gallican collections, 910. Passages of this letter explained, 913, 1001. The same letter was sent to bishops of several provinces, 911. How much weight should be given to Leo in what he reports concerning Hilary’s proceedings at Rome, 902, 917. Imperial law confirmed Leo’s judgment, 798, 991.

Leo received letters from Flavian of Constantinople against Eutyches, 154. He sent the famous letter against the heresy of Eutyches to the East, 457. It was subscribed by all, 482. It was praised at the Council of Chalcedon, 506. It was read publicly at Alexandria, 549. It was explained craftily, and whether it was falsified, 550 n. Under Leo and under Anastasius II, an opinion prevailed that its interpretation had been corrupted in a different sense, ibid. The Gallicans asked Leo for a copy of this letter, 492.

The appeal of Eutyches from Flavian’s sentence to Leo. See *Eutyches*. Legation I sent by Leo to the East, 462. Legation II, 481. Legation III, 495. Legation IV, 496. Legation V, 577.

Leo convoked a Roman council against the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, 466. He sent many letters to the East for this reason, 467. They were inscribed in his name and that of the Roman synod, 468. Why, 1157. He declared all the proceedings of the pseudo-synod invalid, 1159, 1208 n. He asked Theodosius for a council in Italy, 462 n., 470 n., 494 n. Why he considered this synod necessary, 1163. After Theodosius’s death he no longer considered it necessary, 494 n. At last, in order to satisfy Marcian and Pulcheria, he agreed to the convocation of a synod, 497.

The appeals of Flavian and Theodoret to Leo; see *Flavian* and *Theodoret*. Leo was asked by the bishops attached to the see of Arles to confirm the privileges of that see, 491. Theodore of Forum Julii consulted him about penitential discipline, 529. Leo’s legation to Attila, who withdrew after promising peace, ibid., 530. Concerning the date of this legation, 534 n. Concerning his dealings with Anatolius, 533, 536 n. See *Anatolius*. Because of the disturbances of the Palestinian monks, he wrote to Julian, 542 n. And to Eudocia, 542. See *Palestinians*.

Concerning Easter in the year 455, he consulted Paschasinus, 559. He foretold the destruction of the city, 564. He went out to meet the Vandal and obtained from him a promise to abstain from fire and slaughter, ibid. He turned to restoring the city and its churches, 566. Legates from Africa to Leo, 565. Leo granted their requests, 566. He consoled the Egyptian bishops exiled for the faith, 571. Leo was invited by the emperor Leo to Constantinople, 571. He excused himself, 572. Atticus gave Leo an account of his faith, 574. He wrote to Nicetas of Aquileia, 579; to Neon of Ravenna, 580; to the bishops of Campania, 579; and to Timothy Salophaciolus, appointed bishop of Alexandria, 584.

Leo died, 583. On what day, 586 n. Basilicas built by him, 584. The feasts of Leo I and Leo II confused, 590. Ancient martyrologies that commemorate him, 591 ff. Days consecrated to Leo I, of his deposition and translation, 587 n., 597, 598, 600. His relics carried to various places, 602. Three translations of Saint Leo, 604–606. Three others indicated: two, 602 n.; the third, 606 n. Whether a coin was struck in memory of Saint Leo, 608 n. The latest decree of Benedict XIV concerning the title of Doctor and the cult to be accorded to Saint Leo, 609.

Leo is defended against the charge of seeking to enlarge his jurisdiction, 1345 n. How sound his doctrine was, 683. He is not the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, 667. Nor of the *Chapters on Grace*, 722. Nor of the letter to Demetrias, 743. Nor of the letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, 1266. Yet this letter was not fabricated by Isidore, ibid. n. The piece appended to Sermon IV on Lent is shown to be spurious, 1086, 1088 n. His letter to the Moors was not in the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, 1337 n.

Leo is not the author of the *Sacramentary* reprinted in this volume, Preface. Nevertheless, certain prayers and prefaces in it bear the imprint of Leo’s style, Preface, 11 n., 20 n., 23 n., 25 n., 26 n., 27 n., 28 n., 35 n., 39 n., 45 n., 56 n., 64 n., 80 n., 98 n., 129 n., 132 n. On what day Saint Leo II died, 590. A passage of Leo III explained, 1275. Whether he was the author of the letter concerning chorepiscopi, 1276 n.

Leo the emperor was elected after Marcian’s death, 567. He invited Pope Leo to Constantinople, 571. He wished bishops to be sent from the West, 576. He wrote to all the metropolitans, especially to the Roman pontiff, requesting an answer concerning the faith, 570 n. Pope Leo’s reply to him, 572, 578.

Leontius, bishop of Forum Julii, friend of Saint Honoratus, 355. The consent of the elder Leontius, bishop, was sought by Leo in order to convene synods from the various provinces of Gaul after this right had been taken from Hilary of Arles, 1047. This Leontius was different from the bishop of Forum Julii, 897 n., 1325 n. Pope Hilary granted Leontius, bishop of Arles, a certain monarchical authority and the right to summon all metropolitans to synods, 1047.

The monastery of Lérins, 355. Its distinguished institution, 357. Praised by the priest Salvianus, 358. The confession of faith of Leporius, 1559. The cooperation of free will, 174. Freedom under grace, 222. See *The mode of grace’s operation*. The price at which Christian liberty must be purchased, 264.

The diversity of languages, which dissolves the construction of the proud tower, became useful through the apostles for the building up of the Church, 26. Thirty-two languages arising from the confusion of languages, 225. Notable features of the ancient Roman liturgy, Preface.

Lucentius, Saint Leo’s legate for granting communion, 487. Likewise at the Council of Chalcedon, 488. Concerning his true name, 1219 n.

## M

The praises of the Holy Maccabean Martyrs, 374. The Manichaeans do not receive communion under the appearance of wine, 426. A certain superstition of theirs passed over to Christians, 427. See *Leo*.

The case of Marcian, bishop of Arles, according to Quesnel’s interpretation, 825. This is refuted, 930, 935. The emperor Marcian was elected, 480, 481. His first actions, 472 n. His address to the Council of Chalcedon, 511. The council’s address to him, 517. He suppressed the disturbance of the Palestinian monks, 540 n., 541. He asked Leo to write to Eudocia, 542. Leo asked Marcian to send a messenger to Alexandria to establish the date of Easter in the year 455, 560. Marcian suppressed the disturbance of the Egyptian monks, 552 n. He died, 565.

Saint Mary gave birth to God and man, 153. The Virgin gave birth, ibid. Her childbirth was brought about without human concupiscence, 149. Marinus, bishop of Arles: why he is named first in the inscription of the Council of Arles of 314, 1033.

Countless martyrs, 13. Rome’s surrounding area is crowned especially with the countless palms of the martyrs, 84. An encomium of the martyrs, 41. The martyrs confirm the truth of the faith, 12. Their blood was poured out as testimony to the truth, 17. What they confer upon us, 13, 83. Their patronage, 7. Their intercession, 86.

Death is glorious to the Church, 96. Called a *natalitium*, 7. We celebrate the triumph of the martyrs so that we may imitate their steadfastness, 8. When the feast of all the martyrs was instituted, and on what day it was celebrated, 2 n. The martyrs were granted the ability to suffer through Christ’s power, 4. Why their sufferings proceeded from Christ’s cross, 35. God granted them both endurance in persecution and victory in suffering, 13. God’s power shines forth in the martyrs, 138. The Eucharist conferred splendor upon them in persecution, 82. Their blessedness is everlasting, 14. Eternal happiness awaits them, ibid. Their venerable confession won heavenly reward for them, ibid. Concerning the martyrdom of holy women, 97, 140, 141.

Maximus, bishop of Antioch, ordained in Domnus’s place contrary to the canonical regulations, 1183, 1203, 1211 n., 1215. In what sense Stephen of Ephesus called his ordination canonical, 1205 n. It was confirmed by Leo, 1226. Why, 511 n. Whether he was ordained at Antioch, 512 n. Leo wrote to him, 546. Maximus, bishop of Avignon, 1476.

The synod of Milan praises Leo’s letter to Flavian, 493. The blessing of honey and milk, 24. All merit is a gift of God, 202. Without merit, each person is given that by which he may strive toward merit, 218. That the election of the saved is not based on merits is clear in the case of infants, 197.

Ecclesiastical metropolises were instituted late in Gaul, 999, 1031, 1035 ff. In Spain, 1033. At first they were not adapted to the civil arrangement, 1037. Metropolitans were ordained by their comprovincial bishops, 1471. Some, however, must be excepted, ibid. n. Why and from what source the jurisdiction of metropolitans and other principal sees was established, 978. Nothing arising from this can prejudice the right of the Roman pontiff, 979. Metropolitans were first to be consulted by their comprovincials before a letter was sent to the chief see, 529.

The praises of Saint Michael, 99, 100. The dedication of his basilica, 99 n. The *Miscellaneous History* examined, 531. God’s mercy throughout all the ages both nourished bodies and aided minds, 220. It was greater toward the Gentiles after Christ’s coming, and less toward the Jews, 219.

The frequently offered sacrifice of the Mass benefits us, 124. It appeases God, 75. It also provides both the remission of sin and sanctification, 72. In celebrating Mass, the work of our redemption is carried out, 11. Formerly Mass was celebrated in cemeteries in memory of the martyrs buried there, 3 n., 93 n. The origin of the three Masses celebrated on the Nativity of the Lord, 1311 n.

The Roman Missal contains several prayers that derive from the *Book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church*, printed in this volume and the oldest of all, Preface and nearly all the notes from col. 3 to 159.

Man is everywhere subject to death, 235. The beginning of the creation of the world, 388. How the waters were separated from the waters in it, 389. Other matters noted concerning the creation of the world, ibid., 390.

## N

At the time of the First Council of Arles, Narbonensis was divided into two provinces, Viennensis and Narbonensis, 1021. The various divisions of Narbonensis; see *The civil division of the provinces in Gaul*. Narbonensis Prima, 854, 998 n. From what Narbonensis Secunda was divided, 1021. To which metropolitan it was subject, 854 n., 1042. When it passed into the jurisdiction of the bishop of Arles, 1043. This jurisdiction lasted only briefly, ibid. Whether it was assigned to the bishop of Aix, 1045.

The bishop of Narbonne was metropolitan before Pope Zosimus, 997. He obtained an apostolic privilege, ibid., 1040. Leo’s testimony concerning his ancient metropolitan right is defended, 1001. Boniface’s decree for restoring the same right is affirmed, ibid. Quesnel’s objections answered, 1003. He did not usurp the right of Arles, 1040. The church at Narbonne built for Bishop Rusticus, 1577.

The Nativity of Jesus Christ and many matters concerning it, 148 ff. Three Masses celebrated on that day, and why, 1311 n. Human nature corrupted by the wound of sin, 102. Because of Adam’s sin, its condition became subject to misery and condemnation, 141. What it is like without grace, 194.

Nectarius, bishop of Digne, 1475. Sent to Leo by Hilary of Arles, 334. Neo, bishop of Ravenna, to whom Leo wrote, 580.

The excellence of the Council of Nicaea, 526. The Nicene canon concerning the Cathari explained, 1596 n. A passage of the synodical letter of the same council concerning the Meletians explained, 1598 n. The Nicene canon concerning a metropolitan in each province, recited by Boniface I, is not found among the Nicene canons, 1043.

Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, questioned Leo about several doubts, 579. Concerning his name, and other Nicetas who must be distinguished, 1552. Noah’s ark was a figure of the Church, 224.

The *Notitia Dignitatum*: where and when it was written, 1013. It is less accurate concerning Western matters, ibid. It was corrected, 1011. The vicar of Gaul must be supplied in it, 1013. The *Notitia Galliarum*, 802 n. It is not an ecclesiastical but a civil register, 1025. Nor was it composed for the benefit of the bishop of Vienne, 1027. When it was written, 1025. Its antiquity defended, 1027. The register of the provinces published by M. Scipione Maffei from the manuscript of the chapter of Verona, 1011, 1013. Written under Theodosius I, 1015. Another register, called the *Booklet of the Provinces*, ancient but written after the preceding one, 1015. Novempopulana counted among the five provinces, 1011 ff. The kinds and origin of apostolic nuncios, 1508 n.

Marriage instituted by God, 131. From two it makes one, ibid. It requires a suitable age, 130. What is sought in a wife, 131. The Mass at weddings and the nuptial veiling, 129. Concerning this rite of veiling, ibid. n.

## O

The offerings of virgins at the sacred altar, 35. They were made so that, with God’s help, they might preserve their resolve of chastity, ibid. The names of those making the offerings were recited, ibid.

Octodurum: to which ecclesiastical province it belonged in Leo’s time, 1049. The stewards of the Church of Constantinople, 553. The effect and sufficiency of works, 24. No holy action is without reward, 5.

The disposition of prayer comes from God, 73. Why God delays hearing those who pray, 64. While granting what is asked, he causes the hoped-for things to be sought with greater confidence, 77. If we are to obtain what we ask, we must always ask for what is pleasing to God, 78. Adam sinned when, trusting in his own integrity, he did not seek divine assistance, 141. God wills that prayer be offered for everyone, 186. The Church prays for everyone, especially on Good Friday, 185. Why some do not pray, 179. See *Prayers*.

Whether ordinations were performed on Easter Day, 1073. A notable exception, 1306 n. When they were performed, ibid. To whom the ordinations of bishops belonged, 1491. The right of the Roman pontiff defended, ibid. n. The ordinations of metropolitans; see *Metropolitans*. The repetition of ordination in the case of Cathari or Meletians returning to the Church is wrongly understood and excluded by the canon and synodical letter of the Council of Nicaea, 1595 n., 1598 n. When the right of ordination was introduced in Gaul, 1035. It did not always belong to the bishop of Arles, 1039. Concerning the ordination of the bishop of Vaison by Ravennius, see *Ravennius*.

The name “East” taken broadly, so as to distinguish it from the West, 1528 n. Who the *originarii* were, and how they were removed from the clergy, 1292.

## P

The disturbance of the Palestinians against the Council of Chalcedon, 539. When it became known at Rome, and what Leo did to suppress it, ibid. n. What the emperor Marcian did, 540. The same disturbances quieted, 556.

The title “pope” given to other bishops, 1480 n. Infants who died before baptism excluded from blessedness, 233. Their eternal misery, 190, 235. What the premature death of infants teaches, 334.

Easter. The controversy concerning Easter in the year 444, 429 n. Another concerning Easter in the year 455, 557. Responsibility for the Alexandrian computation of Easter delegated to the bishop of Alexandria, 558. The antiquity of the Easter letters, 1019. Easter prayers, 12.

Saint Pastor the martyr, 148. Shepherds ought to love their flock, 121. The title of patriarch bestowed upon ordinary bishops under certain barbarian rulers, 903.

Patroclus of Arles deceived Zosimus concerning the prerogatives of the see of Arles, 539, 997, 1043 n. The question he raised against Proculus of Marseille; see *Proculus*.

Saint Paul; see *Saints Peter and Paul*. Poverty is good, 106. Peace provides everything, 56. In peace it is easier to serve God, ibid.

Original sin, 174. How many evils the sin of the first man produced, 392. We readily fall into sin, 121. Sins stir up wars, 56. They cause enemies to dominate, 57. Concealment of sins accumulates God’s vengeance, 101. No sinner’s conversion is to be despaired of, 10, 250. Sinful Christians called false confessors, 10 n. Prayer for the conversion of sinners, 9.

The Pelagians at Rome under Leo, and what was done against them, 665. The Pelagian doctrine, 237. The Pelagian interpretation of a Pauline passage, 206. The errors of the Pelagians, not of the Semi-Pelagians, noted in the letter to Demetrias, 746.

Pentecost, 22, 23. Prayers at Pentecost for those ascending from the font, 23. Persecution did not destroy the martyrs, 34. What perseverance requires, 222. It is a gift of God, 241, 253. To persevere is not to be overcome by temptation, 206.

The three divine persons have one substance, 298. Their divinity and equality, ibid. The unity of their operation in the unity of their nature, 303.

Petronianus, an itinerant who passed himself off in Gaul as a deacon of the Roman Church, 469 n. Petronius, legate of the bishops of Gaul to Saint Leo, 798.

Saint Peter Chrysologus. Why Eutyches wrote to him after his condemnation, 1129. What he replied, 1130. Two editions of this letter of Saint Peter must be distinguished, 1403 n.

The Apostles Peter and Paul died on the same day but at different times, Preface, 47. Gelasius attributes this to the heretics, ibid. The encomium of Peter and Paul, 33, 37, 47. Through them the Church took the beginning of its religion, 35.

Saint Peter the Apostle, the foremost disciple, 241. With what eyes Christ looked upon him, ibid. The chief confessor of the faith, 47. His dignity, 15. His power magnified in every place, ibid. Raised to the summit of apostolic dignity, 36. The power of binding and loosing was given to him not so much on behalf of the other apostles as above the other apostles, 1321 n.

The see of Saint Peter became the government of the whole Church, 44. In it lies the center and origin of unity, 830 n. “Let the Church accept what this see has judged, since God willed it to hold the primacy,” 43. “What this see has preached must be preserved,” 44. The gates of hell do not prevail against the apostolic confession, 116. The right of apostolic primacy is established at Rome, 37. The chains of Saint Peter, given by Eudocia, 478 n. Concerning the basilica of Saint Peter, see *Basilica*.

A passage of Philaster explained, 1010. The controversy of Photius, bishop of Tyre, at the Council of Chalcedon, 510. A passage of Photius of Constantinople concerning Saint Prosper’s attack on the Pelagians at Rome explained, 666.

The form of penitence expressed as supplication, 329. The archdeacon’s address to the bishop concerning the reconciliation of penitents, 161. Public penance was by no means imposed upon clerics being restored to their rank, 1593 n. Those subjected to public penance had been excluded from the clergy, 1595 n. The canon and synodical letter of the Council of Nicaea explained, 1596 n., 1598 n. Secret penance imposed in confessions, 329 n.

Saint Pontianus the martyr, 93. The primacy of the Roman pontiff, 230. The primacy of apostolic jurisdiction established in the Roman citadel, 37, 39. Unity of faith with the faith of Peter and the Roman pontiffs is necessary, 1319 n. “Only those are sons of the truth who do not depart from the principal tradition,” 39. See *The See of Peter* and *The Faith of the Roman Church*.

The Roman pontiffs have always fulfilled the office of herald in the Church, 413, 418, 419. They make their own the judgments they approve, 252. They are called equal to bishops according to the rule of humility, but not in jurisdiction, 537 n. Their right in major cases; see *Major cases*. It is not their custom to attend councils outside Italy, 462. See *Roman pontiff*.

All the commandments are contained in love of God and neighbor, 10. Their violation expelled mankind from paradise; their observance restores it to blessedness, 23. Predestination neither removes freedom nor diligence in prayer, 249. See *Election*.

How the office of preaching was chiefly entrusted to Peter and his successors, 1315 n. The practice of preaching by Roman pontiffs defended against Sozomen, 1417 n. During preaching, seats were prepared for hearers on fast days, 325 n.

Foreknowledge is not the cause of sins, 224. Prayers obtain all just things, 75. How they should be made, ibid. See *Prayer*. Daily prayers, 52, 72. Morning prayers, or prayers at evening, 71. At the nuptial veiling, 130. On account of drought, 132. Against enemies of the Catholic confession, 26. After illness, 40, 42.

The ordination of priests, 117. The order of seniority must be observed among priests, 445. The primacy of the Roman pontiff; see *The Primacy of the Roman Pontiff*.

The sect of the Priscillianists revived in Spain, 440. The case of Proculus of Marseille examined at the Synod of Turin, 1035, 1040. It was brought before Pope Zosimus, 835 n., 1043. Quesnel’s criticism rejected, 983. What Zosimus decreed concerning him, 1043.

The letter of Projectus, a Gallican bishop, to Leo concerning the bishop placed over him, 842. Leo’s account wrongly called into suspicion, 843. It is defended, 993. In which province Projectus was bishop, 844. Quesnel’s opinion refuted, and it is proved that he was bishop in a province outside Hilary of Arles’s jurisdiction, 993, 997.

It is not necessary for the promulgation of decrees that they be inserted into the book of canons, 1296 n. The mysteries preached by the prophets were not unknown to them, 230.

Prosper of Aquitaine is not the author of the book *On the Promises*, 433. Nor of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, 622, 662. Nor of the books *On the Contemplative Life*, 165. Nor of the letter to Demetrias, 743, 751. Whether the *Chapters on Grace* appended to Celestine’s letter to the Gallicans should be attributed to this Prosper, 694, 722. On what occasion they were written, 723. The booklets offered by Prosper himself against the Pelagians at Rome, 666. He wrote a book against the Vincentian objections before coming to Rome and obtaining Celestine’s celebrated letter, 723. Prosper’s cycle, 561.

Prosper of Orléans is not the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, 621. But another unknown Prosper is, 165. Earthly prosperity ought not to impede heavenly joys, 59. The only true prosperity is not to have departed from God, 57.

Saint Proterius placed at the head of the Alexandrian Church, 545. His letters to Pope Leo, 548. Leo’s reply, 549. He was killed, 567.

God’s providence in all things, 103, 107. Toward all nations, 172. Nor does it abandon the unjust and wicked, 107. Providence is subordinate to God’s more hidden counsels, 215.

The civil division of the provinces in Gaul varied, 848. What it was under Augustus, 1005. Under Diocletian, ibid. Under Constantine, 1007. The division of the province of Narbonensis belongs to an uncertain period, 849. Four divisions of the provinces in Narbonensis in the fourth century, 1021. Narbonensis as a whole was first divided into two provinces, ibid. Its other divisions, ibid. Quesnel believes that it was divided into four parts before the middle of the fourth century, 852. He also thinks that it was subsequently divided into five provinces toward the end of the same century, as do most others, 1007. The basis of this view, ibid. It is refuted at length, ibid. ff. The establishment and division of the five provinces, 1009. Apparently by Constantine, 1011. Not all of Narbonensis as a whole was included within the five provinces, ibid. What the five provinces were, ibid. Aquitania counted among the five provinces, 1009. Likewise Novempopulana, ibid. Around the year 369, the five provinces became six, ibid., 1013. Then seven provinces were established, 1014. These seven provinces were formed from the division of the five provinces, without any addition, 1015. The designation “five provinces” continued for some time even after the division into seven provinces had been introduced, and why, ibid. The division into seven provinces is earlier than the fifth century, ibid. It was in force under Theodosius I, 1017. Narbonensis Secunda was cut off rather from Viennensis than from Narbonensis, 1021. Why it was called Narbonensis if it was cut off from Viennensis, 1023. Which nine provinces are noted in a certain inscription, 1015 n. See *Dioceses*.

The neighbor must be loved, 59. How, 55. Pulcheria associates Marcian with the imperial throne, 480. She attended the Council of Chalcedon in its sixth session, 511 n.

## Q

The Lenten fast; see *Fasting*. Quesnel refuted, elucidated, or supplemented, in nearly all the notes from col. 410 through 1588.

## R

Human reason is insufficient for faith, 175. Ravennius ordained bishop of Arles, 469 n. Which bishops attended his ordination, 794 n. His ordination was not contrary to Leo’s decree, which concerned only Hilary personally, 993 n., 1059. The source of the primatial prerogative left to Ravennius by Leo, 795 n., 1059. The controversy concerning the ordination of the bishop of Vaison performed by Ravennius was brought before Leo, 797. It was rightly brought before him, 982 n.

Rebaptism; see *Baptism*. God safeguards kingdoms, 102. Their rights are in God’s hand, ibid. Gifts of relics given, 906. A passage of Saint Gregory concerning relics explained, ibid. Relics called *sanctuaria*, that is, linens, veils, and other objects that had touched the bodies of the saints, ibid.
