# TABLE OF THE CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

Preface to the book of the Sacraments of the Roman Church, 9.

**THE BOOK OF THE SACRAMENTS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH**, the most ancient of all, attributed in the commonly printed editions to Pope St. Leo, 21.

**ADDRESS OF THE ARCHDEACON TO THE BISHOP concerning the reconciliation of penitents**, together with an admonition concerning it, 157.

[Col. 1364] Admonition concerning the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, ibid.

**THE TWO BOOKS ON THE CALLING OF ALL NATIONS**, wrongly attributed by Quesnell to Leo the Great, but seemingly to be assigned to an otherwise unknown Prosper, 159.

**AUTHORITIES OF THE BISHOPS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE WHO LIVED BEFORE**, concerning the grace of God, which Quesnell believed had been collected by St. Leo, then a deacon of the Roman Church, ibid.

**LETTER OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR TO THE HOLY VIRGIN DEMETRIAS**, or a treatise on humility, which Quesnell attributed to Leo the Great, 161.

Admonition concerning the *Breviary against the Arians*, 179.

**BREVIARY AGAINST THE ARIANS**, inscribed to Pope Leo in certain manuscripts, but incorporated into his works in others; its author is unknown, though nearly contemporary with that pontiff, 181.

**Life and Minor Works of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles**, more extensive in this edition than in Quesnell’s, and corrected against outstanding manuscript codices, 183.

**DISSERTATIONS OF PASCHASIUS QUESNELL ON THE WORKS OF ST. LEO THE GREAT**, with annotations and observations on them, 183.

Admonition concerning Quesnell’s first dissertation, ibid.

**FIRST DISSERTATION.**—On the life and deeds of St. Leo the Great, in which, preserving the order of the years, both the distinguished things accomplished by him and each of his writings are reviewed, ibid.

Appendix, in which a document is presented by which it is established that St. Leo the Great is to be honored by Benedict XIV with the title and cult of a Doctor, 335.

**DISSERTATION II.**—On the author of the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, commonly attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine: in which they are both taken away from Prosper and vindicated for Leo the Great, 339.

The editors’ observations on Quesnell’s second dissertation, 371.

**DISSERTATION III.**—The chapters, or authorities of the bishops of the Apostolic See who lived before, concerning the grace of God and the free exercise of the will, which are commonly attributed to Pope Celestine, are vindicated for Leo the Great; and the celebrated exception concerning the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise is reconsidered, 387.

Part One, ibid.

Part Two, 399.

The editors’ observations on Quesnell’s third dissertation, 409.

**DISSERTATION IV.**—On the author of the little book or letter to the virgin Demetrias, hitherto attributed to Prosper: in which, on the basis of conjectures, it is maintained that it belongs neither to Prosper nor to anyone other than Pope Leo I, 413.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation, 423.

**DISSERTATION V.**—An apology for St. Hilary of Arles and the ancient rights of the Church of Arles, divided into three parts, 429.

Preface, ibid.

First part of the dissertation, concerning the case of Celidonius, 432.

**CHAPTER I.**—The origin and status of the entire controversy, ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—In which province Celidonius obtained the episcopate: whether in Maxima Sequanorum; the passage in the *Life of St. Romanus the Abbot* is examined, 435.

**CHAPTER III.**—It is proved by other arguments that Celidonius was neither bishop of Vesontio nor bishop of any metropolitan see, 440.

**CHAPTER IV.**—St. Hilary of Arles was the legitimate judge of Celidonius, because metropolitan authority over the province of Vienne belonged to the bishop of Arles. Traces of this authority from the time of St. Trophimus to the Council of Turin, 443.

**CHAPTER V.**—What the Council of Turin conferred upon the bishop of Arles in respect of primacy or metropolitan authority, 446.

**CHAPTER VI.**—The decrees of Pope Zosimus, by which metropolitan authority is asserted for the bishop of Arles, are examined and defended against suspicions of forgery, 449.

**CHAPTER VII.**—Honorius Augustus; the Roman pontiffs Boniface, Celestine, and Leo himself; and likewise Valentinian III Augustus regarded Hilary as metropolitan, 454.

**CHAPTER VIII.**—From what was done after Hilary’s return to Gaul until his death, and at the ordination of Ravennius, the metropolitan dignity of the Church of Arles is confirmed, 457.

**CHAPTER IX.**—The same is established from the ordination of the bishop of Vaison, the division of the province that followed it, and Leo’s letter sent concerning the matter, 460.

**CHAPTER X.**—An objection drawn from the list of the provinces and cities of Gaul against the antiquity of metropolitan dignity in the Church of Arles is resolved; and the date of that list is fixed here for the first time, 464.

**CHAPTER XI.**—Other objections are dissolved, by which metropolitan dignity seems to be asserted for the bishop of Vienne, 466.

**CHAPTER XII.**—The state of the Church of Vienne in the time of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, when the martyrs of Lyons completed their contest, 469.

**CHAPTER XIII.**—It is probable that there was only one bishop in Gaul at the time when Irenaeus was placed over the Church of Lyons, [Col. 1366] 475.

**CHAPTER XIV.**—What should be thought concerning Celidonius’s appeal to the Apostolic See; and whether Hilary of Arles, by opposing it, disturbed the order preserved by his predecessors; here, first, the case of Marcian, bishop of Arles, 480.

**CHAPTER XV.**—The case of Marcian of Arles is illuminated from the discipline of the same period, as settled in a synod, 485.

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Other cases of bishops that arose in Gaul before Hilary, after the Councils of Nicaea and Sardica, are examined, 488.

Second part of the dissertation, concerning the case of Projectus, 493.

**CHAPTER I.**—The state of the question is disclosed, and an inquiry is made into the province of which Projectus was bishop, ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The bishop of Arles, formerly metropolitan of the undivided province of Narbonensis, rightly and lawfully claimed its principal parts for himself after the division; here that division is examined, and an inquiry is made into the subscriptions of the First Council of Arles, 496.

**CHAPTER III.**—It is established from the letters of Pope Zosimus that both Narbonese provinces were formerly subject to the bishop of Arles, 501.

**CHAPTER IV.**—Boniface’s decree is examined and compared with Zosimus’s letters, and the latter are defended against interpolation, 504.

**CHAPTER V.**—Whether Boniface’s constitution took effect in Gaul; and what happened after him concerning this matter in both Narbonese provinces, 507.

**CHAPTER VI.**—Concerning the right of the bishop of Arles over the province of the Maritime Alps, 511.

**CHAPTER VII.**—Concerning the province of the Graian Alps. What right did the bishop of Arles possess over it? 514.

Third part of the dissertation on behalf of St. Hilary, 516.

**CHAPTER I.**—Whether, and in what sense, Hilary of Arles claimed, or could have claimed, the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul for himself, 517.

**CHAPTER II.**—Whether in this conduct, which the pontiff rebukes in Hilary, any pride, presumption, or arrogance appeared, 520.

**CHAPTER III.**—What he could answer to that part of the letter in which Hilary had no reasonable point to present before the holy council of priests; and what is to be thought concerning the witnesses produced by Celidonius, 523.

**CHAPTER IV.**—The remaining points of the accusations are examined, especially those by which Hilary is accused of harshness and inhumanity, 525.

**CHAPTER V.**—Hilary’s piety toward the poor is examined, and several testimonies of distinguished men concerning him are reported, 527.

**CHAPTER VI.**—Whether St. Leo was moved against Hilary because the Semipelagian taint had infected him; whether he persisted in it until death; ancient testimonies on behalf of Hilary are presented, 529.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation of Quesnell, 533.

Preface, ibid.

Observations on the First Part, concerning the case of Celidonius: here the right of episcopal appeals to the Apostolic See is discussed more fully, 534.

**CHAPTER I.**—The documents available in this case and their authority are established, ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—Celidonius is established as bishop of Vesontio, 538.

**CHAPTER III.**—The deposition of Celidonius by Hilary and his restoration by Leo are examined, 542.

**CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning Leo’s right in the case of Celidonius, judged in Gaul by Hilary of Arles; or, concerning the right of appeals to the Apostolic See. Several principles are set forth beforehand, from which the whole matter must be decided. Omissions in Quesnell’s discussion. How badly Quesnell constructed Hilary’s Apology. In a question of fact, which he had proposed to address alone, he entangles a question of law, and audaciously portrays Hilary as failing to recognize the Apostolic right in episcopal appeals and as resisting it justly, 544.

**CHAPTER V.**—The title of custom asserted by Leo concerning episcopal appeals to the Roman See is vindicated; and Quesnell’s efforts to take it away from him are defeated, 548.

**CHAPTER VI.**—Concerning appeals to the Roman See by ecclesiastical law. The fourth canon of Antioch is examined, which seems to exclude every appeal. The Sardican canons are explained. Quesnell’s fictions concerning them are scattered. How they were received even in Gaul. What of the Africans? Concerning pontifical constitutions regarding appeals. An observation on the canon of the First Council of Constantinople, 557.

**CHAPTER VII.**—Concerning appeals to the Roman See by divine law, and the extent to which the right of appeal has its root in the primacy, [Col. 1367] 576.

**CHAPTER VIII.**—The two objections raised against Leo in the case of Celidonius are refuted, 584.

Observations on the Second Part, concerning the case of Projectus: here the ecclesiastical provinces and metropolitan sees of Gaul are discussed, 585.

**CHAPTER I.**—It is shown that Quesnell wrongly established two heads of accusation against St. Hilary of Arles in the case of Projectus, ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—It is demonstrated that Hilary carried out an ordination in another province. The First Narbonese province is shown to have always been subject to the metropolitan of Narbonensis, and is taken away from the metropolitan of Arles. Zosimus was deceived by Patroclus concerning the mission of St. Trophimus, 587.

**CHAPTER III.**—Concerning the civil arrangement of the provinces of Gaul, especially with regard to undivided Narbonensis. The five provinces were not cut out of Narbonensis alone but included Aquitania and Novempopulana. Another division of six provinces under Theodosius I. The division into seven provinces in the fourth century is demonstrated. The division of all Gaul into two dioceses, which were subject to two vicars under the prefect of the Gauls. Concerning the list of the provinces published from the Veronese manuscript, which is shown to be older than the *Book of the Provinces* and the *Notitia Dignitatum* of both Empires. The catalogue of the bishops of the First Council of Arles is vindicated; and another, earlier division of undivided Narbonensis is conjectured, 592.

**CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning the prerogatives of Arles and Vienne in the civil arrangement. The origins of both metropolitan sees are established. The *Notitia of Gaul* presents a civil, not an ecclesiastical, arrangement. Its antiquity is defended against Quesnell’s censures, 602.

**CHAPTER V.**—Concerning the ancient establishment and arrangement of the provinces and ecclesiastical metropolitan sees in Gaul, especially in the provinces divided from undivided Narbonensis. It is demonstrated that their beginnings were late and not altogether modeled on the civil arrangement, 607.

**CHAPTER VI.**—Concerning metropolitan right in the Churches of the provinces of Second Narbonensis, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps, 613.

Observations on the Third Part, 618.

**CHAPTER I.**—Two censures of Leo against St. Hilary are wrongly softened by Quesnell. A fairer defense of St. Hilary is proposed, ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—It is proved against Quesnell that neither Hilary nor the Gallican bishops resisted Leo’s decree, 620.

**CHAPTER III.**—Leo’s words are vindicated, in which he stated that Hilary had brought forward nothing reasonable. Concerning the witnesses produced by Celidonius. St. Leo’s judgment is defended. What should be thought concerning several accusations against Hilary inserted in Leo’s letter, 624.

**DISSERTATION VI.**—On the observance of the Saturday fast in the Roman Church in Letter I of Pope St. Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, chapter 1: “With the Saturday fast continued, and with this conclusion of the sermons on the fasts of the seventh and tenth months and of Pentecost: Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us likewise keep vigil at the blessed Apostle Peter.” It is shown that these words are to be rejected from Sermon IV on Lent, where they have hitherto been wrongly read as inserted, and the origin of the interpolation is demonstrated, 627.

**DISSERTATION VII.**—On the case of Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople, condemned by Bishop Flavian of Constantinople in a synod; concerning the twentieth letter of Pope St. Leo, 645.

Appendix to this dissertation. Concerning Eutyches’s petition of appeal, published by Christian Lupus from a Cassinese manuscript: whether it really is a petition of appeal, 661.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation of Quesnell concerning the case of Eutyches, 663.

**DISSERTATION VIII.**—On the case of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and deposed in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, 669.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation of Quesnell concerning the case of St. Flavian, 685.

**DISSERTATION IX.**—On the case of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, and his condemnation; and on the ordination of his successor Maximus: in which the letters of St. Leo and the acts of the Council of Chalcedon are illuminated, and the action concerning Domnus inserted in those acts is demonstrated to be fabricated, 701.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation, 725.

**DISSERTATION X.**—On the case of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, deposed by the judgment of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, restored by Pope St. Leo, and cleared at the Council of Chalcedon, 739.

The editors’ observations on this dissertation, 753.

**DISSERTATION XI.**—On the spurious composition of the letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi, or presbyters, fabricated under the name of Pope Leo I, which appears as Letter LXXXVIII in earlier editions, 757.

# TWO BOOKS ON THE MANICHAEAN HERESY AND ITS HISTORY.

Source/review notes: The draft introduced an unsupported main title and column reference at its opening.; It mistranslated S. C. in the account of Marcian’s proclamation as “the holy Council”; it denotes a decree of the Senate.

**BOOK ONE** 783

**CHAPTER ONE.**—On the principal founders of the Manichaean sect. 784

**CHAPTER II.**—At what time Mani in particular began to spread his doctrines throughout the world. The testimony of St. Leo the Great is elucidated, and Paschasius Quesnellus is convicted of excessive negligence. 788

**CHAPTER III.**—The false arguments of Isaac de Beausobre, contrary to the preceding two chapters, are refuted. 793

**CHAPTER IV.**—On Mani and his principal doctrines. Further Beausobrian fabrications are exposed and overturned. 812

**CHAPTER V.**—The number of Mani’s pseudo-apostles established from the holy Fathers. The opinion of Natalis Alexander is reported and rejected. 822

**CHAPTER VI.**—On the killing of the son of the King of Persia perpetrated by Mani. Beausobrian fabrications and conjectures are wholly rejected. Mani, thrust into prison, corrupts the guards with money and, having effected his escape, departs from Persia toward Mesopotamia. 824

**CHAPTER VII.**—How and by what arts Mani attempted to subvert the Catholic religion in Mesopotamia. The zeal of St. Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, in thwarting these attempts. Beausobre’s conjectures on this subject are noted. 832

**CHAPTER VIII.**—After departing from Caschara, Mani, seeking hiding places, withdraws to the quarter, or parish, of Diodoris in the same city. There, having found Diodorus the priest, he undertakes new controversies concerning the doctrines of the faith. Archelaus, having been warned, first sent letters to Diodorus; in discussing them, Beausobre attempts by his absurdities to overturn ecclesiastical discipline. Then, when Archelaus arrived, Mani attempted in vain to flee. 842

**CHAPTER IX.**—Archelaus’s disputation with Mani at Diodoris is defended against critical observations and Beausobrian calumnies. The bad faith of the non-Catholic writer in reporting Archelaus’s testimony is exposed. Finally, it is demonstrated from the writings that circulate under his name and from his zeal for the true religion of Christ that Archelaus deservedly is regarded in the Church as Catholic and holy. 850

**CHAPTER X.**—As Mani fled from Diodoris, he was apprehended by Persian officials and, stripped of his skin, paid the penalty for his crimes. Beausobre wrongly makes Archelaus the author of this killing; his arguments are rejected. At length the Manichaeans celebrate Mani’s birthday with a solemn and religious rite. 861

**CHAPTER XI.**—The fabulous inventions of Manichaean philosophy and theology, execrated by Turbo, Mani’s disciple converted to the Catholic faith, and committed to writing by Archelaus, bishop of Caschara, at the persuasion of Marcellus, together with the disputations with Mani. 871

**CHAPTER XII.**—On the year of Mani’s death. Various opinions concerning it, with some considerations offered for reconciling them. Beausobre’s aim in the question under discussion is explained. 876

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Whether the Acts of Archelaus, together with the disputations held against Mani that accompany them, are true and genuine as they circulate. Beausobre’s opinion is subjected to examination, and his arguments are refuted as weak. 882

**BOOK TWO.—ON THE GROWTH OF THE MANICHAEAN HERESY** 889

**CHAPTER ONE.**—The purpose of the author’s discussion is explained. *Ibid.*

**CHAPTER II.**—In what places and by what means, after Mani’s death, his heresy was propagated and enlarged here and there. The errors of Beausobre and Cave are noted. The latter’s excessive license regarding Augustine is corrected. Finally, it is investigated how this impious sect weakened Armenia, Mesopotamia, and other regions of Asia. 891

**CHAPTER III.**—On the books and writers of the Manichaeans, dispersed through nearly the whole world in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Church. 896

**CHAPTER IV.**—The conduct of St. Leo the Great, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Hormisdas, Roman Pontiffs, in destroying and burning the Manichaeans’ books is defended against Beausobrian critical observations. It is also shown, from examples of the ancient pagans, that it was always judged a most serious offense to permit the people to read books from which, in matters pertaining to religion, they might even slightly deviate from the institutions of their ancestors. 909

**CHAPTER V.**—The severity of the imperial laws against the Manichaeans of Africa is reconsidered. Frightened by it, and overcome both by the authority of St. Augustine and by disputations, Felix finally renounced the errors of his heresy at Hippo. The various questions arising in this matter are then resolved. 913

**CHAPTER VI.**—On the judgment applied by the Church of Carthage in cases involving Manichaeans. The zeal of the Catholic bishops [Col. 1369] and the method of ecclesiastical discipline in receiving those same persons when doing penance. 918

**CHAPTER VII.**—St. Leo the Great’s conduct toward the Manichaeans is defended against Beausobrian reproaches and insults. It is explained that the holy Pontiff not only declaimed in sermons but also exposed their errors. It is likewise shown, against Beausobre, that St. Augustine’s writings composed against the Manichaeans contain neither fables nor sophistries. 925

**CHAPTER VIII.**—From what year of Christ the arrival of the Manichaeans in the City is to be dated. Paschasius Quesnellus’s false judgment on the matter. 933

**CHAPTER IX.**—The Roman inquisition of St. Leo the Great against the Manichaeans. Five principal features of its form of judgment are noted and examined, drawn both from the writings of the same holy Pontiff and from the laws of the Roman emperors. 936

**CHAPTER X.**—The Roman council concerning the Manichaean case. The erroneous judgment of Antonius Pagi and Paschasius Quesnellus on that question. Cardinal Baronius’s opinion is finally defended against the critical annotations of these writers. 947

**CHAPTER XI.**—After the death of Leo the Great, the Manichaeans again inhabit the City. The zeal of Pope Gelasius in detecting them. William Cave’s erroneous judgment concerning communion under both kinds. The same St. Gelasius finally expels these impious men from the City and destroys their books, adding a sentence of anathema. 954

**CHAPTER XII.**—After St. Gelasius had died, the Manichaeans for a third time inhabit the City; Pope Symmachus, following the example of his predecessors, finally drives them into exile, while their images and books are burned before the doors of the Constantinian Basilica. In discussing the use of these images, we explain how Symmachus, harassed in various ways by the emperor Anastasius, was wrongly accused of Manichaean contamination. 957

**CHAPTER XIII.**—On Pope Symmachus’s apologetic letter against the notorious pamphlets of the emperor Anastasius. The same emperor, a champion and supporter of many heretics, also received Xenaias, the leader of the Manichaeans, into his patronage. From this we finally take occasion briefly to examine the character, institution, and writings of Xenaias himself. 961

**CHAPTER XIV.**—While the Manichaeans still inhabit the City of Rome, Pope Hormisdas, having examined them by means of scourging, compels them to go into exile. Beausobre’s absurdities and quibbles are refuted. The synod of Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, condemns Severus, Anthimus, and other leaders of the Acephali as though they were defenders of Manichaean doctrine. Finally, some points are noted concerning the Manichaeans from the historical works of Peter the Sicilian and Photius. 970

**Appendix to the history of the Manichaeans.** A theological dissertation on Canons XIII and XVII of the Council of Gangra. 981

**ON THE PRISCILLIANIST HERESY AND HISTORY: ONE BOOK** 991

**CHAPTER ONE.**—Who Priscillian was. *Ibid.*

**CHAPTER II.**—At what time and from what source the Priscillianist heresy principally began to spread. 993

**CHAPTER III.**—Instantius and Salvianus, bishops of Spain, following Priscillian’s ways, consecrated him bishop of Ávila. At approximately the same time he was first condemned in the Synod of Zaragoza, then expelled from Spain by Gratian’s edict, and proceeded to Rome to Damasus. 996

**CHAPTER IV.**—The emperor Gratian, having been deceived by Macedonius, orders Instantius and Priscillian to be restored to their sees. On Britto, bishop of Trier, and the honor and prerogatives of that see. The false conjectures of Blondel and Tillemont against the rights of the Apostolic See are overturned. 999

**CHAPTER V.**—On Maximus the Tyrant and his judgment and conduct toward the Priscillianists. 1002

**CHAPTER VI.**—Maximus the Tyrant submitted to the Roman Pontiff a written confession of the Catholic faith. The emperor stirred up new disasters against the Priscillianists throughout Spain. 1006

**CHAPTER VII.**—On the councils convened concerning the case of the Priscillianists at Toledo. 1007

**CHAPTER VIII.**—To refute the false opinions of certain writers, and especially those of Paschasius Quesnellus, the case of the bishops Symphosius and Dictinius is more precisely reconsidered from ecclesiastical records. 1012

**CHAPTER IX.**—On the Council of Toledo in which Symphosius and Dictinius were received as penitents, and on the schism of Galicia that arose on their account. 1018

**CHAPTER X.**—On the other bishops and clerics polluted by the Priscillianist stain who were condemned or acquitted at the First Council of Toledo. 1022

**CHAPTER XI.**—On the grave schism that arose in Spain after the Council of Toledo. 1026

**CHAPTER XII.**—As the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi ravaged Gaul and [Col. 1370] the Spains more widely, the affairs of the Catholic religion were brought wholly to ruin. 1029

**CHAPTER XIII.**—On Turribius, bishop of Astorga; his consultations with the Apostolic See; and the measures undertaken by him to extinguish the Priscillianist heresy completely and restore ecclesiastical discipline. 1032

**CHAPTER XIV.**—On St. Leo the Great’s fifteenth letter, written to Turribius of Astorga on the occasion of the Priscillianist heresy. A new fragment concerning the canonical Scriptures, recovered from Codex Palatinus of the Vatican Library. 1036

**CHAPTER XV.**—On the councils held in the kingdoms of Galicia and Spain by order of St. Leo the Great. Paschasius Quesnellus’s false judgment concerning the ancient Codex of the canons of the Roman Church. 1044

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Whether that profession of faith attributed to the Fathers of Toledo bears the style and age of Augustine. It is further shown that the codex of canons edited by Quesnellus was falsely attributed to the Roman Church. 1049

**CHAPTER XVII.**—On the councils of Astorga, Celenum, and Braga, held in the kingdoms of Galicia by decree of the Apostolic See or approved with its support. 1054

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—The latest acts of the Church of Braga for abolishing certain surviving remnants of Priscillian’s error. 1056

**CHAPTER XIX.**—Paschasius Quesnellus wrongly imagines that two Turribii existed in the time of Leo. To what year of Christ the Council of Braga discussed above is principally to be assigned. 1062

**ON THE PELAGIAN HERESY: ONE BOOK** 1065

**CHAPTER ONE.**—On the Pelagian heresy, which grew daily stronger in the age of Leo the Great. On Julian, bishop of Eclanum, and his conduct in spreading the Pelagian heresy more widely among the people. *Ibid.*

**CHAPTER II.**—The zeal of St. Leo the Great in overthrowing Julian and the Pelagians who were ravaging Campania. 1067

**CHAPTER III.**—On the time when St. Prosper composed his treatises against the Pelagians. 1071

**CHAPTER IV.**—The arguments of the preceding writers are refuted. 1075

**CHAPTER V.**—On the writings of St. Leo the Great composed against the Pelagians. 1076

**CHAPTER VI.**—On St. Leo the Great’s letters written to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, against the supporters of the Pelagian heresy. Quesnellus’s procedure in preparing these letters. 1079

**CHAPTER VII.**—On the various opinions of writers concerning the preceding letters of St. Leo the Great. Our own position is then established. 1086

**CHAPTER VIII.**—The fourteenth letter of the Divine Leo, to Januarius of Aquileia, is reconsidered, and Quesnellus’s absurdities are rejected. 1090

# ON THE EUTYCHIAN HERESY AND HISTORY: TWO BOOKS

## BOOK ONE 1095

**CHAPTER ONE.**—Eutyches, holding erroneous views concerning the Incarnation of Christ the Lord, is accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, in the Synod of Constantinople. Summoned a second and a third time by the Fathers, he refuses to appear. 1098

**CHAPTER II.**—After the preceding provincial synod had been completed, Bishop Flavian sent a letter to the holy Pontiff Leo the Great, together with the complete record of the proceedings, requesting confirmation of what had been done. Paschasius Quesnellus unjustly denies this; his arguments are presented and simultaneously overturned. 1101

**CHAPTER III.**—In discussing the case of Flavian and Eutyches, the same Paschasius Quesnellus wholly perverts the form of ecclesiastical government through newly devised doctrines. Cardinal Baronius’s assertions on this matter are defended by the decrees of St. Leo the Great. The twelfth letter of the same holy Pontiff, wrongly explained by Quesnellus, is expounded in its fuller form as found in a Vatican manuscript. From various other letters it is explained that St. Leo the Great did not depart from the decrees of that letter when exercising the supreme rights of the pontificate. 1109

**CHAPTER IV.**—On Eutyches’s appeal to the Apostolic See. Quesnellus denied it with the greatest injustice; many of his arguments, drawn both from the letters of Flavian and Leo and from the Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople, are demolished and refuted. Finally, the opinion of the distinguished Peter de Marca is reconsidered and noted as less consonant with the truth. 1115

**CHAPTER V.**—Other arguments of Quesnellus against Eutyches’s appeal are presented and examined more solidly. Eutyches’s letter written to St. Pope Leo is subjected to examination, and finally the judgment of Christian Lupus is defended and maintained. 1126

**CHAPTER VI.**—On Eutyches’s letter and petitions written to St. Leo [Col. 1371] the Great: Christian Lupus’s opinion concerning them is defended against Quesnellus’s critical observations; and finally it is shown that Quesnellus’s method of acting and writing displays nothing but fallacies and absurdities. 1136

**CHAPTER VII.**—On the Council of Ephesus convened on account of the Eutychian heresy. St. Leo’s conduct before the emperor in favor of convening a council in Italy. The zeal of the same holy Pontiff is defended against Quesnellus’s suspicions and critical observations. Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, presided over the Council of Ephesus by order of the emperor Theodosius, who unjustly arrogated this right to himself. How and when the legates of the Apostolic See departed from the City; in discussing them, Quesnellus fell into error. 1144

**CHAPTER VIII.**—On various other letters of St. Leo the Great written on the occasion of the Council of Ephesus. Christian Lupus’s opinion concerning the holy Pontiff’s zeal to abolish the scandals of the Easterners and strengthen the Catholic faith is presented and elucidated. Dioscorus of Alexandria, however, abusing imperial power and inflicting force and oppression upon the Catholic bishops, absolved Eutyches and, turning the synod into a robbery, compelled the legates of the Apostolic See to seek protection and take flight. 1153

**CHAPTER IX.**—On the appeal of St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, to the Apostolic See. The false opinion of Launoy, Paschasius Quesnellus, and others—that he appealed to a new general council—is presented. Their arguments, as weak and highly deceptive, are then overturned and wholly dismantled by certain and evident demonstrations. 1173

**CHAPTER X.**—Three Sardican canons in particular are discussed. Referring to them, Launoy, Quesnellus, and others contend that St. Flavian appealed to St. Leo the Great solely by their force and authority, so that his case might be reconsidered in a new and larger synod. Their arguments are brought forward and overturned as wholly weak or false from the letters of the holy Roman Pontiffs Julius, Leo, and Gelasius. 1196

**CHAPTER XI.**—After the acts of the Ephesian robbery had been abolished, St. Leo wrote letters to the Easterners. St. Flavian died a martyr, and Anatolius was appointed in his place. The Roman Pontiff did not consent to his ordination until Anatolius had made a solemn profession of faith according to the form prescribed by Leo. To receive this profession he sent four legates from his own entourage to Constantinople. 1211

**CHAPTER XII.**—The emperor Theodosius Augustus died in penitence. Through the efforts of the empress Pulcheria and by decree of the Senate, Marcian was proclaimed emperor. He immediately ordered the Eutychians to pay the penalties. He wrote to Leo concerning the convocation of a new general council. He received Abundius and Leo’s other legates honorably. The Council of Constantinople was celebrated concerning Anatolius and the fallen. Marcian and Pulcheria again requested St. Leo to convene a general council. The letters of the bishops Theodore, Ibas, and Aquilinus to Abundius, the Roman Pontiff’s legate. 1219

**CHAPTER XIII.**—The improved condition of affairs in the East brought destruction upon the Eutychians, protection to the Catholics, and changed the sorrow of the great Pontiff Leo into joy. He gave testimony to this joy in various letters written to Marcian, Pulcheria, Anatolius, and Julian of Cos. The latter’s homeland is investigated. The opinions of Baronius, Henri Valois, and the distinguished Étienne Baluze are noted. Finally, the holy Pontiff devoted every effort to holding a general synod. 1223

## BOOK TWO

**CHAPTER I.**—The emperor Marcian finally permitted the long-desired general synod of Leo the Great to be held in the East. Although the holy Pontiff, moved by weightier considerations, could have resisted the emperor’s arrangement, he nevertheless, prevented from attending the synod, sent four legates to the East to preside over it in his name, place, and stead. He therefore arranged everything that had to be done, sending various letters for this purpose to Paschasinus, Marcian, Anatolius, the empress Pulcheria, and Julian of Cos. 1229

**CHAPTER II.**—Why the general synod announced for Ephesus [Col. 1372] was transferred to Chalcedon. On St. Leo’s letter to Ravennius. The bishops of Gaul met in two synods and sent to the Apostolic See their synodal letters, adorned with much wisdom and learning. Finally, the Synod of Eusebius of Milan is discussed, together with the synodal letter sent from it to St. Leo. 1235

**CHAPTER III.**—On the date, number of Fathers, and sessions of the Council of Chalcedon. Everything that St. Leo desired was successfully carried out. The Catholic faith was established; fallen bishops were received into penance; Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned; and finally the rights of the Apostolic See, abolished at the Ephesian synod, were restored and established with the greatest unanimity. 1241

**CHAPTER IV.**—A dissertation on the fourth session of the Council of Chalcedon, delivered at the Pontifical Academy of Councils in the year of the Lord 1747. 1246

**CHAPTER V.**—It is shown that Theodoret of Cyrrhus, deposed by Dioscorus in the Ephesian robbery, appealed to the Apostolic See, was judged by St. Leo, and restored to his see. The arguments of Launoy and Paschasius Quesnellus are refuted. The opinions of the distinguished Peter de Marca and Christian Lupus concerning this case are presented. Finally, both from the eighth session of Chalcedon and from St. Leo’s ninety-third letter, it is proved that the judgments of the Apostolic See are supreme and irrevocable. 1255

**CHAPTER VI.**—The Chalcedonian session concerning Domnus of Antioch is not spurious. Rusticus the deacon translated it from Greek into Latin together with the rest of the proceedings. Quesnellus denied this with the greatest injustice, but the distinguished Étienne Baluze has already rejected and, with the highest learning, resolved his arguments as false and wholly weak. In describing this exercise, we have finally had to follow Baluze’s footsteps throughout. 1268

**CHAPTER VII.**—On the remaining sessions of the Council of Chalcedon, and especially on the last, in which, contrary to the ecclesiastical canons, Canon XXVIII was composed concerning the new honor and prerogatives of the See of Constantinople, against the rights of the bishop of Alexandria and the bishop of Antioch. 1286

**CHAPTER VIII.**—On what was done in favor of Anatolius after the Council of Chalcedon. The letters of the Fathers of the general synod and of the emperors Marcian and Pulcheria to St. Leo, requesting that Canon XXVIII of the council be confirmed and ratified. The holy Pontiff’s conduct in annulling and canceling that canon. Paschasius Quesnellus’s interpretations are reviewed. Finally, we reject as false and unjust Launoy’s censure of the most learned Cardinal Bellarmine. 1291

**CHAPTER IX.**—St. Leo the Great restrained Anatolius’s ambition in many ways. The theologians’ questions are settled from the writings of the holy Pontiff. Paschasius Quesnellus’s evasions are described, and the decree concerning the preservation of the privileges of provincial primacies is explained. The case of Aetius and Andrew, clerics of Constantinople, is presented. Julian, bishop of Cos, is appointed vicar of the Apostolic See; Paschasius Quesnellus attempted unjustly to diminish his duties and prerogatives. 1299

**CHAPTER X.**—Anatolius’s ambition and conduct, favorable to the Eutychians, stirred up new disturbances in the East. When admonished by the emperors Marcian and Leo, St. Leo asserted that he had already confirmed the synod in matters of faith. Paschasius Quesnellus denies this; his arguments are overturned. Finally, in new letters confirming the synod, the holy Pontiff made his will known to all and also assailed Anatolius’s deceitful arts. 1305

**CHAPTER XI.**—St. Leo devoted every effort to extinguishing the remnants of the Eutychians. He ordered Maximus of Antioch to preserve the rights of his Church. A serious controversy arose concerning the Paschal Cycle. The emperor Marcian died, and Leo Tribunitius was elevated to the imperial office. The revolt of the Eutychians against Proterius of Alexandria and against all Catholics, and their attempts to abolish the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. 1310

**CHAPTER XII.**—Finally, St. Leo exerted the utmost zeal until the end of his life in strengthening the decrees of Chalcedon, repairing the disaster of the Church of Alexandria, and extinguishing the Eutychian heretics. 1318

**END OF VOLUME FIFTY-FIVE.**
